sections.heading: What Changed Hands on January 31, 1969
sections.body: Chicago moved Erwin Mueller to the Seattle SuperSonics for a 1970 fourth-round selection that the Bulls would use on John Davis at No. 57. This was Mueller's second trade in four months: the Bulls had received him from Los Angeles for Keith Erickson in September 1968. Both Chicago's and Seattle's Basketball Reference transaction histories verify the January pick-for-player exchange. The site's historical asset record also lists cash for Chicago, but those two independent transaction lists do not separately confirm a cash amount. That claim should remain a provenance question, not an additional assumed source of on-court value. The certain basketball pieces are Mueller and the fourth-round draft right.

sections.heading: Mueller's Short Seattle Stop
sections.body: The Sonics obtained a useful forward, but not a multi-year starter. Mueller played 26 Seattle games after the January 1969 swap, averaging 7.0 points and 4.0 rebounds. He appeared in four more Seattle games at the start of 1969-70 before departing in a subsequent transaction. Those 30 appearances represent real NBA minutes the Bulls' return could not replicate through the fourth-round pick. They also limit the case for Seattle: this was a brief stop rather than a player who anchored a rebuilding program. A B+ grade needs to consider the draft asset Seattle later obtained, not inflate Mueller's own time with the team.

sections.heading: Seattle Recovered a Higher Draft Pick
sections.body: On November 1, 1969, the SuperSonics dealt Mueller to Detroit for a 1970 second-round selection. Seattle used that pick at No. 20 on Jake Ford, as the 1969-70 franchise transaction record confirms. Ford went on to play 31 NBA regular-season games, all with Seattle, over the 1970-71 and 1971-72 seasons, totaling 126 points. The chain thus produced two separate periods of NBA availability: Mueller's 30 Seattle games and Ford's 31. Ford was not a franchise-changing draft find, but a second-round pick was a stronger recoverable asset than the fourth-round right Seattle had originally surrendered.

sections.heading: Chicago's Pick Never Became NBA Production
sections.body: The Bulls used their 1970 fourth-round selection on Alabama State forward John Davis at No. 57. Chicago's draft record shows no NBA games or points for Davis, which distinguishes the draft event from realized player production. A cash line appears in this site's asset ledger without a documented amount in the available club transaction summaries, so the C+ grade should not be justified with imaginary financial savings. Chicago had already received 52 games from Mueller before this move, but those preceded the sale to Seattle and were part of the earlier Erickson transaction. The January exchange returned a draft claim, not a second lasting rotation player. Seattle Win is supportable on these direct outcomes, with a contained B+/C+ difference.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Seattle SuperSonics Win — Seattle B+, Chicago C+. Mueller played 30 Seattle games after the January 1969 trade, and the Sonics later dealt him for the 1970 No. 20 selection used on Jake Ford, who appeared in 31 NBA games for Seattle. Chicago's No. 57 choice, John Davis, has no recorded NBA games. The internal cash line is not separately corroborated by the two available franchise transaction histories. Seattle recovered the stronger measurable return, but neither side found a lasting star.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Chicago Bulls–Seattle SuperSonics: What the Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: The January 1969 Chicago–Seattle Mueller transaction becomes clearer when its later draft chain is followed rather than repeating a generic winner label. Chicago traded Erwin Mueller for a 1970 fourth-round selection, ultimately John Davis at No. 57. Seattle used Mueller for 30 games and then converted him into a 1970 second-rounder, Jake Ford at No. 20, through a November deal with Detroit. The two draft selections did not have equal basketball outcomes: Davis recorded no NBA appearances, while Ford played 31 games for Seattle. The internal ledger additionally labels a cash component, but the available franchise transaction histories do not document its amount. Seattle B+ and Chicago C+ are the fixed grades being evaluated, not an excuse to invent a more consequential return.

sections.heading: Two Successive Trades, Two Different Evaluations
sections.body: Mueller was a former Bull and Laker before this January 31, 1969 exchange. Chicago had obtained him from the Lakers in September 1968 for Keith Erickson. He appeared in 52 Bulls games during the 1968-69 season, averaging 3.8 points and 3.7 rebounds, and the club moved him again before that season ended. Those 52 games properly belong to the earlier acquisition, while this later trade must be judged from the moment Seattle received him. By separating the deals, the evaluation avoids assigning Erickson's entire five-season Lakers career to either Chicago or Seattle through Mueller. On January 31 the Sonics gave up a future fourth-rounder for immediate frontcourt depth and the potential to move that player again.

sections.heading: Thirty Games Became a No. 20 Selection
sections.body: Mueller appeared 26 times for the SuperSonics during the rest of 1968-69, scoring 7.0 points per game, and made four more appearances in the 1969-70 season. Seattle then sent him to Detroit on November 1, 1969 for a 1970 second-round pick. The pick became guard Jake Ford at No. 20. Ford logged five NBA games as a rookie and 26 more in 1971-72; his 31 games yielded 126 points, 20 rebounds and 35 assists. This was small-scale rotation output, not an All-Star return. But the team had moved from sacrificing a fourth-round selection to receiving a second-round selection after getting 30 games from Mueller. That sequence, and not Mueller's subsequent Detroit seasons, creates the strongest case for Seattle's B+.

sections.heading: What the Bulls Could Actually Claim
sections.body: Chicago's return was a 1970 fourth-round draft right, exercised on John Davis of Alabama State at No. 57. The 1970 Bulls draft record shows no NBA regular-season career statistics for Davis. That means there is no drafted-player contribution to count against Seattle's Mueller and Ford sequence. The site's internal transaction asset record includes unspecified cash for Chicago, while both teams' 1968-69 Basketball Reference transaction logs list the pick without independently itemizing a payment. The record should preserve that discrepancy for provenance review, not assume cash bought another player or materially changed the team's balance sheet. C+ recognizes that Chicago obtained an asset and preserved some optionality, but the pick did not turn into an NBA roster contributor.

sections.heading: A Directional Win Without a Blockbuster Claim
sections.body: The complete trade chain is modest by franchise-history standards. Seattle first received 30 games from Mueller, then exchanged him for the No. 20 selection that became Ford and 31 games of additional Seattle service. Chicago acquired a No. 57 pick that it spent on a player without recorded NBA appearances. A second-round pick's higher position is useful context, but neither of these rookies became a long-term standout. Seattle's B+ and Chicago's C+ grades express an advantage in traceable basketball conversion, not evidence of a dynasty-defining decision. A fact-specific evaluation should keep the B+ judgment tied to the actual short-lived assets and revisit it if the original cash or draft provenance is later corrected. Until then, this is Seattle Win with limited absolute stakes.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Seattle SuperSonics Win — Seattle B+, Chicago C+. The causal chain is 30 Seattle appearances by Mueller and a later 1970 second-round pick that produced Jake Ford's 31 NBA games. Chicago exercised its acquired fourth-rounder on John Davis at No. 57 without a recorded NBA playing return. The unexplained cash notation warrants separate provenance review, not assumed basketball credit. The grade difference is supported by two small but real Seattle outcomes versus a Chicago pick that never materialized on an NBA floor.

sections.heading: The Teams Traded Reserve Forwards in January
sections.body: The Chicago Bulls and Baltimore Bullets exchanged Al Tucker and Ed Manning on January 5, 1970. Chicago received Manning; Baltimore received Tucker. Modern franchise naming makes the second team appear as Washington in the archive, but the club actually operated as the Baltimore Bullets at the time. The surviving transaction logs agree on both directions of the trade. No cash payment, draft pick or conditional asset appears in the identified original exchange.

sections.heading: Manning Played 38 Games for the Bulls
sections.body: Manning appeared in 38 Chicago games after arriving, producing approximately 5.6 points and 5.2 rebounds per appearance over 16.2 minutes. Those figures describe a reserve frontcourt contributor rather than a new starter who transformed the roster. Chicago gained someone capable of filling minutes and collecting rebounds, which was a concrete return for Tucker. His brief stay also limits how much long-term credit the Bulls should receive for the decision.

sections.heading: Tucker Produced a Longer, Still Limited Baltimore Stint
sections.body: Tucker appeared in 28 Bullets games during the remainder of the 1969–70 season and another 31 in 1970–71. That gave Baltimore 59 games from the acquired forward, more appearances than Chicago received from Manning. The comparison still depends on what those minutes accomplished rather than simply on who stayed longer. Neither player became an enduring team cornerstone, and there is no verified downstream asset chain to expand either return.

sections.heading: The Balanced Verdict Matches the Modest Stakes
sections.body: Both the Bulls and Bullets receive C-plus in the archive, yielding an Even Trade. Chicago obtained immediate reserve rebounding and frontcourt depth; Baltimore received somewhat more games from its new player. Each franchise exchanged a marginal roster piece for another at a similar stage of his career. Crediting one club with a dramatic win would overstate the known production and would obscure how narrowly focused this January 1970 transaction actually was.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Chicago C-plus, Baltimore/Washington C-plus. Ed Manning played 38 games for the Bulls and supplied reserve points and rebounds. Al Tucker appeared in 59 Baltimore games across portions of two seasons. The 1970 transaction exchanged two useful but short-lived forwards without an identified draft or cash component. Neither return was decisive enough to justify a separate winner.

sections.heading: Chicago Obtained Guokas During Its Early Contender Years
sections.body: The Bulls acquired guard Matt Guokas from Philadelphia on October 16, 1970. In return the 76ers received a 1971 second-round pick, eventually exercised at No. 33 for Marv Stewart. Chicago was developing into a strong defensive and playoff team in the early 1970s, so acquiring an experienced guard fitted an immediate depth requirement. Philadelphia preferred to convert that veteran into a choice in the following draft.

sections.heading: The Pick Conversion Is Identifiable, Not Hypothetical
sections.body: The No. 33 selection becoming Stewart is a concrete result of Philadelphia’s return, but a second-round pick is not equivalent to an established starting guard merely because the franchise made the selection. Chicago already knew it was obtaining Guokas, who brought professional experience. The source record does not support assigning the pick additional later assets or unlisted compensation. The narrow comparison is Guokas’s available roster contribution against Stewart’s draft outcome.

sections.heading: Why the Bulls Receive the Higher Grade
sections.body: Chicago earns B-minus; Philadelphia gets D-plus. The grade difference favors the immediate usefulness of Guokas over the documented No. 33 draft selection. It is a retrospective edge for an established player acquired at a modest draft price, not a claim that the second round has no value. The deal also belongs to the 1970 Bulls and 76ers, rather than being judged through modern roster expectations or salary rules.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win — Chicago B-minus, Philadelphia D-plus. The Bulls acquired Matt Guokas for a 1971 second-round pick that became No. 33 Marv Stewart. Chicago obtained a veteran guard for its developing playoff roster, while the recorded Philadelphia draft return did not justify a comparable grade.

sections.heading: A Completed-Value View of the Deal
sections.body: On June 9, 1971, Chicago sent the rights to Dick Gibbs to Houston for a future 1973 second-round selection. The pick later became No. 24 and was used on Kevin Stacom. This was a rights-for-pick exchange, not two veteran players changing clubs. Chicago's transaction history and the independent historical log preserve the date and direction; Houston signed Gibbs the following day.

sections.heading: Why Houston Receives the Stronger Grade
sections.body: Gibbs played 64 NBA games and 757 minutes as a Rockets rookie. Houston later sold his rights to Kansas City-Omaha, but his actual playing time was already a modest return for acquiring those rights. Chicago's No. 24 selection became Kevin Stacom, who stayed at Providence for another year and re-entered the 1974 NBA draft. He never played an NBA game for Chicago, so the Bulls received no on-court contribution from the acquired selection.

sections.heading: Kevin Stacom's Rights Did Not Become Bulls Court Time
sections.body: Chicago received Houston's 1973 second-round selection for Dick Gibbs's rights in June 1971. The choice ultimately became No. 24, Kevin Stacom, but the draft right was not equivalent to an established contributor: Stacom did not appear in an NBA regular-season game for Chicago. Houston, by contrast, put Gibbs on the floor for 64 games and 757 minutes before moving his rights in a later transaction. The two returns were modest in absolute terms, and neither created a franchise-changing player. Houston's B nevertheless reflects measurable near-term participation, while Chicago's C- recognizes that its delayed pick never produced Bulls playing time. The later rights transfer belongs to a separate move and doesn't turn this original deal into a different package.

sections.heading: Houston Received 64 Games; Chicago's No. 24 Pick Produced None
sections.body: Houston converted Dick Gibbs's rights into 64 rookie-season games and 757 minutes, a measurable NBA contribution from a relatively small acquisition. Chicago received a delayed 1973 second-round choice, eventually No. 24 Kevin Stacom, but that selection produced no Bulls regular-season appearances. The two returns were modest, and neither built a lasting franchise centerpiece. The difference is that Houston signed and played the acquired player while Chicago's pick did not become an NBA contributor for the Bulls. Gibbs's later Kansas City-Omaha rights transaction and Stacom's subsequent career belong to separate developments; they are not extra consideration in the June 1971 exchange. That limitation fits Houston's B, Chicago's C- and the recorded Rockets Win verdict.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win, Houston B and Chicago C-. Gibbs's rights became 64 Houston games and 757 minutes. Chicago's 1973 No. 24 selection became Kevin Stacom, who did not play in the NBA for the Bulls. The original consideration was the rights and that second-round pick. The difference in realized team-specific basketball value supports the Rockets' recorded advantage.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Gibbs, Stacom, and the 1971 Bulls–Rockets Trade Outcome
featuredDeepDive.intro: Chicago exchanged Dick Gibbs's draft rights for a 1973 second-round pick on June 9, 1971. Houston converted the rights into 64 games and 757 rookie minutes. Chicago used the No. 24 selection on Kevin Stacom, who stayed at Providence and did not play for the Bulls. The established canon awards Houston a B, Chicago a C-, and the verdict Rockets Win, reconciling the separate editorial with the verified player and draft histories.

sections.heading: What Each Team Actually Received
sections.body: On the Houston side, the acquired item was the draft rights to Dick Gibbs. He signed with the Rockets and contributed 64 games and 757 minutes during his rookie season. Selling his rights to Kansas City-Omaha later was a subsequent action, not another part of Chicago's June 1971 consideration. The useful direct return for this trade is his actual time on Houston's roster.

sections.heading: What Chicago Bulls Realized
sections.body: Chicago obtained a second-round choice in the 1973 draft, subsequently No. 24 for Kevin Stacom. Although Chicago selected Stacom, he continued at Providence and entered the 1974 draft again. He never supplied regular-season NBA playing time for Chicago. Calling him the named draftee is correct; crediting the Bulls for a career they never received would distort the asset path.

sections.heading: What Houston Rockets Realized
sections.body: Both franchises accepted a different type of risk. Houston took the rights to a player it hoped would reach the current roster. Chicago took a choice that could produce a future player, but would depend on who was selected and whether he joined the franchise. The Rockets turned Gibbs into limited but genuine playing time; Chicago's choice ultimately delivered no Bulls games. Neither side received a first-round pick or another player in this recorded exchange.

sections.heading: Why the Rockets Earn a B and Chicago a C-
sections.body: The site's corrected Houston B and Chicago C- marks indicate Rockets Win, but the difference isn't a claim that the transaction transformed either franchise. Gibbs's rookie stint was modest, while the selected player never played for Chicago. The dated club records, Gibbs's player history and the draft/college trail establish these outcomes. The grades are a retrospective assessment of those source-backed returns.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win: Houston B, Chicago C-. Gibbs contributed an NBA rookie season after the Rockets obtained his rights, while Chicago's future No. 24 pick yielded no Bulls games. Houston's later sale of Gibbs's rights and Stacom's return to Providence belong to the subsequent asset timeline, not additional trade-day items. This was a modest but identifiable Houston advantage.

sections.heading: The Exchange in Full
sections.body: Chicago reacquired Norm Van Lier from the Cincinnati Royals on November 9, 1971, and also received a 1972 third-round selection that became No. 35, Frank Russell. Cincinnati obtained Jim Fox and Chicago's 1972 second-rounder, later No. 28 Mike Ratliff. The modern franchise identifier calls Cincinnati the Sacramento Kings, but the club had not yet moved. The outgoing center was Jim Fox, not a separate player named Sonny Fox.

sections.heading: Van Lier Became Chicago's 535-Game Defensive Anchor
sections.body: Van Lier became the deal's best player by a wide margin. He appeared in 535 Bulls regular-season games through 1977–78, contributed 3,676 assists, made three Chicago All-Star teams and earned All-NBA Second Team recognition. Seven of his eight career All-Defensive selections came with Chicago; the first had been with Cincinnati. Frank Russell, Chicago's additional incoming pick, played only 23 Bulls games, making Van Lier the decisive long-term acquisition.

sections.heading: Cincinnati Had Real Production from Fox and Ratliff
sections.body: Cincinnati's side deserved more credit than an automatic low grade. Fox immediately gave the Royals 71 games, averaging 12.3 points and 9.3 rebounds while playing 2,047 minutes. Ratliff appeared in 60 career NBA games after being selected at No. 28. Fox later joined Dick Gibbs in a separate trade for Don Kojis and Pete Cross, so Cincinnati retained some transaction value. That downstream return cannot be attributed entirely to Fox because Gibbs was also involved.

sections.heading: What the Other Side Bought
sections.body: Chicago gained an elite defensive playmaker for seven seasons, supporting its A+ grade and a Bulls Win. Cincinnati still obtained Fox's substantial 1971–72 frontcourt production, Ratliff's limited NBA service and part of a later package used to acquire Kojis. The B grade for the eventual Kings franchise is supported by those results; it should not be confused with the D in older boilerplate or counted as a tie.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win, Chicago A+ and Cincinnati B. Van Lier became a 535-game Bulls mainstay with three All-Star selections and seven Chicago All-Defensive honors. The Royals received 71 productive Jim Fox games plus the second-round pick used on Mike Ratliff, and Fox later contributed to a separate multi-player deal. Both teams obtained measurable value, but Chicago received the long-term cornerstone.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Van Lier's 535 Chicago Games and Cincinnati's Fox–Ratliff Return
featuredDeepDive.intro: Chicago reacquired Norm Van Lier in 1971, then received 535 games and three All-Star seasons from the defensive guard. The Cincinnati Royals took Jim Fox and a second-rounder used on Mike Ratliff; Fox produced 71 strong games and later retained transaction value. Chicago also received the No. 35 pick used on Frank Russell. Van Lier's long Bulls tenure makes Chicago the clear winner, while Cincinnati's actual return supports B rather than the older D grade.

sections.heading: The Asset That Moved the Evaluation
sections.body: The November 1971 transaction exchanged players and two different draft rounds. Chicago acquired Van Lier and the future No. 35 third-round choice; Cincinnati took Jim Fox and the future No. 28 second-rounder. Chicago, Cincinnati and league transaction histories agree on the four-part package. Keeping the city at the time of the trade and the correct Jim Fox identity prevents a modern franchise label or merged legacy name from creating a fictitious participant.

sections.heading: Secondary Pieces and Their Weight
sections.body: Van Lier played 535 games for Chicago, totaled more than 19,000 minutes and became a defensive and passing centerpiece of the Bulls' 1970s teams. He made three All-Star teams in Chicago, earned All-NBA Second Team recognition and collected seven Chicago All-Defensive selections. His eighth career selection belongs to an earlier Cincinnati season. The No. 35 pick, Frank Russell, supplied only 23 games and 131 minutes, so the main Bulls return was Van Lier himself.

sections.heading: Trade-Day Logic Versus Realized Outcome
sections.body: Cincinnati acquired something real in Fox. He contributed 71 games at 12.3 points and 9.3 rebounds in the first season after the exchange. The Royals' No. 28 draft pick became Mike Ratliff, who played 58 games in his first NBA season and two more afterward. Fox subsequently moved with Dick Gibbs in a deal that brought Don Kojis and Pete Cross from Seattle. Kojis played 77 games for Kansas City–Omaha, but both outgoing players must be acknowledged in that later exchange.

sections.heading: Bulls A+ Versus Cincinnati B: The Correct Grade Gap
sections.body: The seven-season Van Lier return plainly exceeds Fox's one strong Cincinnati season and Ratliff's shorter career, which explains Chicago A+ and Bulls Win. The opposing franchise nevertheless obtained legitimate court production and preserved some later trading power, supporting B rather than a legacy D. This isn't a claim that Fox alone acquired Kojis or that Chicago received Ratliff. The grades separate the documented two teams' returns without giving one asset the work of several.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win, Bulls A+ / Royals B. Norm Van Lier supplied Chicago 535 regular-season games and exceptional defensive play, while the third-round pick became brief contributor Frank Russell. Cincinnati gained Jim Fox's 71-game starting production and the pick used on Mike Ratliff. Fox's later trade usefulness required another outgoing player, Dick Gibbs, so the downstream value is partial. Those source-backed outcomes justify the large but not absolute grade advantage.

sections.heading: What Changed Hands
sections.body: Chicago obtained Dennis Awtrey from Philadelphia on October 18, 1972, surrendering a 1973 second-round pick and cash. The selection became No. 32 Caldwell Jones. The financial amount isn't provided in the source ledgers, so it should be acknowledged without inventing a price. This was a veteran center joining the Bulls against a future draft asset, not a direct Awtrey-for-Caldwell-Jones player transaction on the date of the trade.

sections.heading: Why Awtrey's 147 Bulls Games Still Earned a B
sections.body: Awtrey played 79 games for Chicago in 1972–73, averaging 4.7 points, 5.5 rebounds and 2.8 assists, then appeared 68 more times the next season. Those 147 Bulls games were useful rotation-center production on strong teams. Chicago's return ended when New Orleans selected Awtrey in the 1974 expansion draft, a different transaction that yielded no player or selection back to the Bulls.

sections.heading: The Package That Won Out
sections.body: Philadelphia used No. 32 to select Caldwell Jones in 1973, but he spent three seasons in the ABA before joining the 76ers in 1976. Once in Philadelphia, Jones played 482 regular-season games, earned two NBA All-Defensive First Team selections and reached three Finals. That production distinguishes an actual realized draft asset from merely identifying a pick by a later player name.

sections.heading: The Cost on the Other Side
sections.body: Jones also held additional value in Philadelphia's 1982 Moses Malone acquisition, but he was sent with a first-round selection, so Malone's championship impact cannot be attributed solely to Jones or this 1972 exchange. The source-backed grades are Philadelphia A+ and Chicago B. Awtrey gave the Bulls two productive seasons, while the 76ers obtained a durable defensive starter and a component of a subsequent major trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win, Philadelphia A+ and Chicago B. The Bulls received 147 games from Dennis Awtrey before losing him in the expansion draft. Philadelphia used the incoming second-rounder on Caldwell Jones, whose 482 regular-season games, two All-Defensive First Team selections and downstream trade role outweighed that return. The original cash payment is documented but not quantified.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Caldwell Jones's 482 Philadelphia Games After the Awtrey Trade
featuredDeepDive.intro: The 1972 Awtrey exchange gave Chicago 147 regular-season games from a useful center, then New Orleans selected him in the 1974 expansion draft. Philadelphia received the second-round choice used at No. 32 on Caldwell Jones, who joined the 76ers after three ABA seasons and appeared in 482 Philadelphia games. Jones also became part of the later Moses Malone trade alongside another pick. The 76ers earned the larger long-term return, but Chicago's contribution was not negligible.

sections.heading: The Deal's Most Important Piece
sections.body: Chicago traded a 1973 second-round choice, eventually No. 32, and an unspecified cash payment to obtain Dennis Awtrey in October 1972. The original Philadelphia, Chicago and league transaction logs identify the player and pick, and additional transaction histories establish the cash component. The second-rounder had previously reached Chicago through another deal, but its significance here begins when the Bulls sent it to the 76ers.

sections.heading: What the Supporting Assets Added
sections.body: Awtrey made an immediate contribution. He played 79 Chicago games in 1972–73 and logged 1,650 minutes, giving the Bulls physical interior play and rebounding without being a high-volume scorer. His second season added 68 games. Across 147 Bulls appearances he supplied useful depth, enough to merit a B grade rather than the legacy D, even though the other side of the trade would eventually yield a higher-impact player.

sections.heading: Why Context Matters Without Reversing the Result
sections.body: Philadelphia's No. 32 pick became Caldwell Jones. His professional route initially passed through the ABA, meaning he wasn't available for an NBA roster immediately after the 1973 draft. He joined Philadelphia in 1976–77 and developed into a dependable frontcourt defender. Across six regular seasons with the 76ers he appeared in 482 games, collected two All-Defensive First Team selections and contributed during three Finals runs.

sections.heading: 76ers A+ Versus Bulls B: The Full Asset Chain
sections.body: The 76ers later included Jones and a different first-round pick in the deal for Moses Malone. That pairing prevents claiming that the Awtrey trade single-handedly acquired Malone, but it shows Jones retained substantial transaction value after his Philadelphia playing years. Chicago acquired 147 games before the expansion draft ended Awtrey's tenure; Philadelphia received six seasons of Jones, plus his role in a larger deal. A+ for Philadelphia and B for Chicago reflects those returns.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win, Philadelphia A+ / Chicago B. Dennis Awtrey supplied Chicago two useful seasons totaling 147 regular-season games, but no later player or pick when he left in the expansion draft. Philadelphia converted No. 32 into Caldwell Jones after an ABA delay; he then played 482 76ers games and became one of multiple pieces traded for Moses Malone. That source-backed comparison gives Philadelphia the advantage without reducing Chicago's contribution to nothing.

sections.heading: What Changed Hands
sections.body: Chicago's September 10, 1973 deal was made with the Buffalo Braves, the predecessor of the modern Los Angeles Clippers franchise. The Bulls received John Hummer and a 1974 second-round selection later identified as No. 27 for Leon Benbow. Buffalo obtained Garfield Heard, also known as Gar Heard, and the rights to Kevin Kunnert. Describing the destination as Los Angeles in 1973 would move the trade to a city the Braves had not yet reached. The modern Clippers franchise slug is useful for continuity, but the historical team name must be Buffalo.

sections.heading: Buffalo Took Heard and Kunnert's Rights; Chicago Received Hummer and No. 27
sections.body: Chicago's September 1973 return combined an active center, John Hummer, with a second-round draft selection for the following year. That choice ultimately became No. 27, Leon Benbow, but it was not a signed player when Buffalo agreed to the deal. The Braves received Gar Heard immediately and the negotiating rights to Kevin Kunnert, another asset whose value depended on later decisions. The four receipts were not interchangeable: two known players changed franchises, one future pick had yet to be used, and one set of player rights was not guaranteed NBA availability. Buffalo's A- and Chicago's D should be judged against those distinct team-specific outcomes. The successor Clippers franchise designation tracks the historical team, but the 1973 recipient was the Buffalo Braves, not a Los Angeles club.

sections.heading: Reading the Team Grades
sections.body: The most important difference between the packages was the certainty of their pieces. Chicago received Hummer immediately and a future draft choice; Buffalo received Heard plus rights that still required later decisions before becoming basketball production. It would be misleading to call all four players signed, available NBA contributors on trade day. Equally, treating Buffalo's rights to Kunnert as a first-round pick would change the ledger. The evaluation must keep the right, the 1974 second-round selection and the two actual veterans distinct.

sections.heading: What Each Franchise Was Actually Evaluating
sections.body: The contemporary context explains why the franchise names need care. In September 1973, the Buffalo Braves had not yet moved to San Diego or later Los Angeles. Chicago exchanged Gar Heard and Kevin Kunnert's rights for John Hummer and a pick to be exercised the following year. An A- for the Braves/Clippers franchise and D for Chicago is a retrospective comparison of realized asset value. The verdict can keep the Clippers franchise affiliation while using Buffalo for the actual acquiring club at the time.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Braves/Clippers franchise Win — Buffalo's later Clippers franchise A-, Chicago D. The Buffalo Braves acquired Gar Heard and Kevin Kunnert's rights; Chicago received John Hummer and the second-round choice that became Leon Benbow at No. 27 in 1974. These were the assets exchanged in 1973. Los Angeles is the modern franchise designation, not the contemporary team location.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Chicago Bulls–Buffalo Braves (now Clippers): The September 1973 Trade
featuredDeepDive.intro: The trade dated September 10, 1973, joined the Chicago Bulls with the Buffalo Braves, the franchise now identified with the Los Angeles Clippers. Chicago obtained John Hummer and a 1974 second-round pick later identified as Leon Benbow at No. 27. Buffalo acquired Gar Heard and the rights to Kevin Kunnert. The site records a Clippers franchise Win, A- for the Braves/Clippers side and D for Chicago. Keeping the historical city separate from the present franchise name prevents a valid record from being narrated as a deal made by Los Angeles in 1973.

sections.heading: The Asset Path That Carries the Grade
sections.body: The recorded September 1973 transaction moved four distinct assets between Chicago and Buffalo. John Hummer entered the Bulls' side along with the second-rounder that became the No. 27 pick in 1974, Leon Benbow. Gar Heard moved to the Braves, and the rights to Kevin Kunnert went with him. Two names in the returning package do not imply equivalent basketball roles: Hummer was a roster player, while the other Chicago asset was a not-yet-exercised draft selection. Buffalo's rights acquisition carries a different type of uncertainty.

sections.heading: What the Lower-Graded Side Still Kept
sections.body: The trade's modern labels can lead readers to imagine a 1973 Chicago–Los Angeles negotiation. That never happened under those city names. The recipient of Heard and Kunnert's rights was the Buffalo Braves, whose franchise history later connects to today's Los Angeles Clippers. This continuity explains the canonical slug but not the city printed in period-accurate prose. The retrospective A-/D grade pairing applies to the Braves/Clippers franchise's two assets versus Chicago's two assets, rather than a recreated Los Angeles roster.

sections.heading: Decision Logic Versus Hindsight
sections.body: Chicago could use Hummer as a contemporary player and preserve the 1974 second-rounder as a future development option. The latter became Benbow at No. 27, which helps establish its eventual path without pretending he had joined Chicago in September 1973. Buffalo's return mixed the established player Heard with Kunnert's rights, a possible later contribution rather than immediately guaranteed court time. Comparing these two packages requires distinguishing what each club controlled that day from what the assets yielded after subsequent choices.

sections.heading: Why the Grade Gap Is the Better Scale
sections.body: The site's Clippers franchise Win conclusion is backed by the A- versus D grade spread, but the size of that advantage must be attributed to the right transaction. Gar Heard and the rights to Kevin Kunnert comprise the Buffalo return. John Hummer and the future No. 27 selection comprise Chicago's. No unlisted cash, first-round pick or later unrelated acquisition needs to be attached to justify the result. The franchise moved across cities over time; the identity of the September 1973 assets did not.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The franchise now called the Clippers grades A- against Chicago's D because the recorded return to the Buffalo Braves was Gar Heard and rights to Kevin Kunnert. The Bulls received Hummer and a future second-round selection that became No. 27, Leon Benbow. These components explain the retrospective evaluation without pretending the Braves were already located in Los Angeles or that a draft right was an immediately available player.

sections.heading: Portland Sent Adelman to Chicago for a Pick and Cash
sections.body: The Portland Trail Blazers traded Rick Adelman to the Chicago Bulls for cash and a 1974 second-round selection. Portland’s historical media guide lists September 14, 1973, matching the archive’s date; a Chicago transaction summary lists October 14. That disagreement should be documented, not quietly presented as settled across every source. The future pick became No. 34 Phil Lumpkin in 1974. This was an experienced NBA guard exchanged for a late draft opportunity and financial consideration.

sections.heading: Adelman Offered Chicago an Immediate Veteran Option
sections.body: Adelman had extensive NBA guard experience by the time of the exchange. Chicago could use him as a familiar backcourt option without waiting for a future prospect to develop. His role was more modest than a star signing, but he was an established player whose playing value could be assessed immediately. The Bulls’ grade is driven by the certainty of receiving the player identified in the transaction rather than credit for his later, unrelated coaching career.

sections.heading: Portland Chose Draft Flexibility and a Payment
sections.body: Portland took Chicago’s 1974 second-round choice and cash. The pick became Lumpkin at No. 34; the Blazers’ historical guide identifies the selection and later movement of those draft rights. The payment’s dollar figure is not independently established here. Those are legitimate forms of return, but draft rights acquired for a reserve guard were less certain to produce near-term NBA minutes than keeping an established player. Neither team’s entire subsequent roster history belongs in this evaluation.

sections.heading: The Bulls’ Better Grade Has Narrow Limits
sections.body: Chicago receives B-plus and Portland C, with Bulls Win. The difference acknowledges an immediately useful experienced guard against a second-round selection and cash. The record also sets boundaries: the 1973 date disagreement needs its own provenance note, and Adelman’s future coaching achievements are not an asset the Bulls acquired. The ledger’s directional advantage concerns basketball value at the time and the documented player-and-pick package, not an imaginary long-term championship effect.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win — Chicago B-plus, Portland C. Chicago acquired veteran guard Rick Adelman and Portland received cash plus a 1974 second-round pick used on Phil Lumpkin. Portland’s team media guide dates the transaction September 14, 1973, although another transaction chronology gives October 14. The Bulls secured the more immediately usable basketball asset without establishing a blockbuster return.

sections.heading: Seattle Paid a Pick and Cash for John Hummer
sections.body: Chicago sent center John Hummer to Seattle on January 7, 1974. The SuperSonics transferred a 1975 second-round selection, later No. 30 Steve Green, plus cash. A previous imported year in this transaction was erroneous: the pick belonged to 1975, not 1974, according to the Chicago, Seattle and league ledgers. The Bulls historical guide also corroborates cash, though the surviving summary does not establish a reliable dollar amount.

sections.heading: Hummer Gave Seattle More Than a Draft Label
sections.body: Hummer appeared in 107 games for Seattle across parts of three seasons, providing identifiable frontcourt depth. His measurable games and role distinguish Seattle’s return from an unexercised or entirely speculative asset. The contribution was modest, not an acquisition of a franchise centerpiece. For Chicago the pick created an opportunity to select Green, but he did not actually play for the Bulls; his subsequent professional career involved another franchise after an ABA stint.

sections.heading: The Realized Returns Favor the SuperSonics
sections.body: Seattle receives a B and Chicago C-plus, with Sonics Win as the verdict. The Sonics got Hummer’s 107 games, while Chicago received a draft opportunity that did not become NBA minutes for its own roster plus unspecified cash. That evidence supports a slight completed advantage for Seattle. It would overstate the exchange to credit Chicago with Green’s later contribution for other clubs or to fabricate a price for its cash consideration.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Sonics Win — Seattle B, Chicago C-plus. John Hummer played 107 Seattle games after the January 1974 transaction. Chicago acquired a 1975 second-round pick that became No. 30 Steve Green, who did not play for the Bulls, and cash of an unspecified amount. Seattle obtained the stronger measured basketball return.

sections.heading: Chicago Sent a Third-Round Pick for Johnson
sections.body: On September 18, 1974, Chicago acquired Mickey Johnson from the Portland Trail Blazers. Portland received a 1975 third-round selection, later used at No. 50 on Gus Gerard. For Chicago, Johnson offered a young frontcourt player with immediate roster potential; Portland preferred the draft opportunity. The eventual difference between the returns was striking because the player coming to Chicago developed into a major regular contributor while the selection did not produce any Trail Blazers NBA appearances.

sections.heading: Johnson Became a Multi-Year Bulls Starter
sections.body: Johnson played four seasons with Chicago, producing standout rebounding and scoring campaigns. He averaged 15.3 points and 9.4 rebounds in 1975–76, then 17.3 points and 10.2 rebounds in 1976–77. In 1977–78 he improved to 18.3 points and 9.1 rebounds. Those seasons were the tangible benefit of spending a third-round pick: Chicago secured a starting-caliber forward who helped its lineup year after year instead of merely providing a short reserve stint.

sections.heading: Portland’s Pick Became an ABA Player It Never Used
sections.body: The Blazers turned the incoming pick into Gerard at No. 50 in 1975. Gerard was already playing in the American Basketball Association and never appeared in an NBA game for Portland. He was drafted again by the Lakers and eventually played 15 NBA games for Seattle, but those were not a return to the Blazers from this transaction. The historical draft outcome therefore had a recognizable player name without generating a direct NBA playing contribution for the acquiring franchise.

sections.heading: The Large Grade Gap Follows the Actual Results
sections.body: Chicago is graded A-plus and Portland C, with Bulls Win as the verdict. Johnson’s three consecutive high-output seasons and four years of service are evidence of a genuinely consequential acquisition. Portland’s pick did not become an NBA rotation player for the Blazers. The gap is not based on the value of third-round choices in the abstract; it comes from a player who became an established Chicago contributor and a selection that never yielded Portland minutes.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win — Chicago A-plus, Portland C. Mickey Johnson gave Chicago four seasons and produced 15.3, 17.3 and 18.3 points per game across 1975–76 through 1977–78, with strong rebounding. The 1975 third-round pick became Gus Gerard, who never played an NBA game for Portland. The direct basketball returns overwhelmingly favor the Bulls.

sections.heading: Chicago Turned Guokas Into Two Actual Draft Choices
sections.body: On December 8, 1975, Chicago sent veteran guard Matt Guokas to the Kansas City Kings. In exchange the Bulls obtained a 1976 third-round pick and a 1977 second-round pick. The selections became Lars Hansen at No. 37 in 1976 and Steve Sheppard at No. 30 in 1977. This was a decision to convert a current rotation guard into two future player opportunities. The Kings took the more predictable short-term option, bringing in Guokas to supply backcourt experience without waiting for draft prospects to develop.

sections.heading: Sheppard Produced Chicago Minutes; Guokas Played 38 Kings Games
sections.body: The second-round selection was the meaningful Chicago outcome. Sheppard appeared in 86 Bulls games over the 1977–78 and 1978–79 seasons, averaging 3.9 points and 1.8 rebounds in Chicago. Hansen did not produce a comparable documented NBA contribution. Kansas City used Guokas in 38 games after the trade during 1975–76, when his scoring role was smaller than it had been in Chicago. That puts an actual 86-game contributor against a 38-game veteran stint rather than merely comparing two draft slots with one known player.

sections.heading: Sheppard's 86 Bulls Games Gave Chicago a Narrow Edge
sections.body: Sheppard's 86 Chicago appearances gave the draft return a small lead over Guokas's 38 Kansas City games, supporting Slight Bulls Edge, Chicago B-minus and Kansas City C-plus. Chicago had to wait for Sheppard’s contribution and spent a third-round choice that did not become a major NBA return. Kansas City got Guokas immediately, so the Kings did receive what the deal promised in practical guard minutes. Chicago’s second-round selection produced more total games with the acquiring team, justifying a modest advantage without pretending either return changed the franchise’s trajectory.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Bulls Edge — Chicago B-minus, Kansas City/Sacramento C-plus. The Bulls traded Matt Guokas for selections that became Lars Hansen and Steve Sheppard. Sheppard played 86 games for Chicago, while Guokas logged 38 for Kansas City after the deal. The contribution gap is real but modest; Hansen was not a major added NBA return. The grades favor Chicago slightly rather than calling the transaction an even swap.

sections.heading: Chicago Bought a Working Rotation Guard from Detroit
sections.body: On November 18, 1976, Chicago acquired John Mengelt from Detroit for cash. The transaction lists no player or draft pick moving back to the Pistons, and the available archives do not identify an exact price. The Bulls needed another experienced perimeter contributor. Mengelt had already spent several seasons in the league and was capable of scoring efficiently in a supporting role, making him a more predictable basketball return than an unproven rights selection.

sections.heading: Mengelt Stayed Productive Across Multiple Bulls Seasons
sections.body: Mengelt played 61 games for Chicago in 1976–77, 81 the following season and 75 in 1978–79, before a reduced 36-game role in 1979–80. He averaged 10.3 points in 1977–78 and 11.0 points in 1978–79, giving the Bulls repeatable scoring production. Those are real minutes over several seasons, not a brief training-camp stay. He also appeared in Chicago’s 1977 playoff series, further grounding the trade’s value in actual games rather than hypothetical contract flexibility.

sections.heading: Detroit’s Cash Return Has an Evidence Limit
sections.body: Detroit accepted cash from Chicago but the recorded amount is unavailable. That means a retrospective can compare Mengelt’s on-court output with the fact of monetary compensation without claiming to know how much that money helped the Pistons. The player leaving Detroit produced multi-season value in Chicago; the cash could have served a financial purpose that cannot be measured reliably from surviving basketball ledgers. The uncertainty is the reason Detroit should not automatically be assigned a failing grade.

sections.heading: The Bulls Receive the Higher Grade for Sustained Usefulness
sections.body: Chicago’s B-plus reflects getting an established guard for multiple seasons without sacrificing a basketball asset. Detroit earns C for a cash return whose dollar value is not documented, not because it certainly gained nothing. The gap comes from Mengelt’s 253 regular-season Bulls appearances across four seasons and his dependable perimeter scoring. The transaction was not a championship-making blockbuster, but its actual player return was substantial relative to a simple cash sale.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win — Chicago B-plus, Detroit C. Mengelt appeared in 253 regular-season games over four seasons in Chicago and scored in double figures per game during two of them. Detroit received an undisclosed cash payment. Chicago obtained a dependable NBA rotation guard, while the exact financial return to Detroit cannot be established from the available transaction evidence.

sections.heading: Chicago Exchanged Holland for Rickey Williams’s Rights
sections.body: On June 22, 1979, Chicago sent Wilbur Holland to the Jazz franchise for the player rights to Rickey Williams. Holland had just completed three useful seasons with the Bulls, making this more than an exchange of two untested draft names. Chicago nonetheless chose a new rights opportunity instead of retaining its established guard. The Jazz received Holland directly; the Bulls received Williams’s rights, which are not the same thing as acquiring immediate NBA games from a signed player.

sections.heading: Neither Incoming Asset Delivered Regular-Season Games
sections.body: Holland did not appear in another NBA regular-season game after Chicago traded him. Williams likewise did not play an NBA regular-season game for the Bulls. Those two completed outcomes explain why neither club is credited with a productive return in the transaction ledger. Williams later appeared in 44 games for Utah in 1982–83, but that later roster stint does not become an automatic 1979 Bulls return. It must not be reassigned to Chicago’s side of this exchange.

sections.heading: Equal D Grades Fit the Identified On-Court Outcomes
sections.body: The final classification is Even Trade, with D for each club. Chicago received a rights asset that generated no Bulls appearances; the Jazz acquired a veteran who did not play another NBA game after the exchange. Holland’s earlier Chicago production explains why the trade initially involved a recognizable guard, but that production happened before the deal and cannot inflate the Jazz’s result. The available history supports two disappointing returns rather than a fabricated winner.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Chicago D, Jazz D. The Bulls acquired Rickey Williams’s rights for Wilbur Holland, but Williams never appeared for Chicago, and Holland played no further NBA regular-season games after the trade. Williams’s later Utah appearances did not become an immediate return for the Bulls. Both sides received a documented asset without realizing on-court production from it.

sections.heading: Chicago Purchased Two Denver Picks Before the 1979 Draft
sections.body: On June 24, 1979, Chicago obtained Denver’s second-round and tenth-round selections in exchange for cash. The Bulls used the incoming picks the next day on Lawrence Butler, No. 33, and Cortez Collins, No. 197. Unlike a deal involving a future conditional asset, both picks have known draft outcomes. Denver took financial consideration whose dollar value has not been verified in the available transaction histories. The exchange therefore offers a straightforward comparison of two draft chances against an unpriced payment.

sections.heading: Butler Never Appeared in an NBA Regular-Season Game
sections.body: Butler, a guard out of Idaho State, was the more valuable of Chicago’s two selections by draft position. He was chosen in the second round at No. 33 but has no NBA regular-season playing statistics in the reviewed player and draft records. Chicago spent that acquired pick on an actual player, yet it produced no measured Bulls games. The absence of a documented secondary trade branch also means those rights cannot be credited with generating another NBA contributor later.

sections.heading: Collins Was an Even Longer Shot
sections.body: Collins came from Southern Indiana and went in the tenth round at No. 197. By that part of the 1979 draft, the likelihood of a lasting NBA contributor was limited. Collins likewise recorded no NBA regular-season appearances. The Bulls acquired two shots at inexpensive talent, but neither one yielded direct on-court production. Evaluating the trade as if Chicago found a useful rotation player would disregard the documented outcomes of both selections.

sections.heading: Only a Slight Edge Is Supportable
sections.body: The stored grades give Chicago D-plus and Denver D, with Slight Bulls Edge as the verdict. Chicago received two identifiable drafting opportunities, while Denver’s cash return remains unknown in amount and later application. The Bulls can receive a marginal procedural advantage for controlling those choices, but no more: two zero-game draftees are not evidence of a successful basketball acquisition. The result is a narrow, low-grade comparison rather than a meaningful franchise win.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Bulls Edge — Chicago D-plus, Denver D. Chicago purchased No. 33 Lawrence Butler and No. 197 Cortez Collins in the 1979 draft, and neither selection led to an NBA regular-season appearance. Denver received cash of an undisclosed amount. Chicago gained two measurable draft opportunities but no realized playing value, limiting the historical advantage to a small one.

sections.heading: The Conditional Pick That Changed Hands
sections.body: Chicago dealt the draft rights to Cedrick Hordges to Denver on June 9, 1980 for a conditional pick in the 1981 draft. If Hordges made Denver's roster, the consideration became a second-round pick; otherwise, it would be a third-rounder. He made the team. Chicago therefore received No. 32 in 1981 and selected Mike Olliver. Those conditions explain the trade-day wager, but the later playing records establish who obtained the larger basketball return.

sections.heading: Why Denver Won the Exchange
sections.body: Denver turned Hordges's rights into 145 regular-season appearances over 1980-81 and 1981-82, totaling 2,971 minutes. The forward played 68 games as a rookie and averaged 8.4 points and 6.7 rebounds, then appeared in 77 games the next season. Chicago's selection, Mike Olliver, never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. The gap between two seasons of rotation activity and zero league games supports the canonical Nuggets Win, rather than the former Even Trade narrative.

sections.heading: Chicago Bulls: A Pick Without NBA Games
sections.body: The Bulls did convert an unused draft-rights asset into a better-than-third-round selection once the condition was met. That process had a rational upside in June 1980. But the No. 32 choice became Mike Olliver, whose professional record shows no NBA regular-season appearances. Chicago's D+ grade evaluates the return actually realized, not the possibility that a second-round pick could have produced another player. The selection's eventual outcome makes its return weaker than Denver's.

sections.heading: Denver Nuggets: Rights Became 145 Games
sections.body: Hordges supplied immediate on-court value after Denver obtained his rights. Across two seasons he posted 145 games, and his first year included 572 points and 458 rebounds. His second season brought another 77 appearances, albeit with lower per-game scoring and rebounding. The Nuggets' B+ measures that tangible output. Chicago's resulting draft choice supplied no NBA games. The different outcomes underpin a clear Nuggets Win rather than matching B- grades.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win, B+ Denver and D+ Chicago. Hordges gave Denver 145 regular-season appearances, including 68 games in 1980–81 and 77 in 1981–82. The condition on Chicago's incoming selection was satisfied, making it a 1981 second-rounder, but the Bulls used No. 32 on Mike Olliver, who never played in the NBA. Denver's realized NBA service substantially exceeded the Bulls' draft result.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Denver's Hordges Return Versus Chicago's Unproductive No. 32 Pick
featuredDeepDive.intro: Denver received Cedrick Hordges's playing rights from Chicago on June 9, 1980. The condition attached to Chicago's compensation converted the return into a second-round selection when Hordges made the Nuggets' roster. Denver then received 145 regular-season games from Hordges over two seasons, while Chicago used No. 32 on Mike Olliver, who recorded no NBA appearances. The grades of Denver B+ and Chicago D+ reflect that uneven direct return.

sections.heading: How the Two-Part Draft Condition Worked
sections.body: The agreement did not send Denver a 1981 pick and Chicago a player. It sent Hordges's rights to Denver and a conditional draft return to Chicago. The choice would fall in round two if Hordges earned a Nuggets roster place and in round three if he did not. Because he joined Denver's roster, Chicago acquired the 1981 No. 32 second-round pick. Its subsequent use on Mike Olliver is part of this trade's asset trail.

sections.heading: The Hordges Production Ledger
sections.body: The Nuggets received a player who appeared in 68 games during 1980-81, recording 8.4 points and 6.7 rebounds per game in 23.5 minutes. He played 77 additional Denver games during 1981-82, with averages of 6.8 points and 5.1 boards. His combined NBA record for Denver was 145 games and 2,971 minutes. That source-documented production is the principal reason the Nuggets carry a B+ and the winning verdict.

sections.heading: Why the Olliver Pick Fell Short
sections.body: The Bulls received their conditional compensation as a second-rounder and spent No. 32 on Lamar guard Mike Olliver in 1981. The draft record establishes the selection, but Olliver recorded zero NBA regular-season games. No verified downstream transaction involving that pick offsets this outcome in the current ledger. Chicago's D+ is therefore an assessment of what came out of the actual pick, not an arbitrary discount on its trade-day possibility.

sections.heading: Final Evaluation: B+ Denver, D+ Chicago
sections.body: The distinction is not subtle: Denver received two seasons and 145 NBA games from Cedrick Hordges, while Chicago's No. 32 selection generated no NBA regular-season appearances. It is possible to see why Chicago accepted a conditional draft asset in 1980 without calling the completed exchange even. The canonical Nuggets Win and B+/D+ grades preserve that difference in realized value, and the transaction sources identify each component of the return.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win, Denver B+ / Chicago D+. The trade transferred Hordges's rights to Denver and gave Chicago a pick whose round depended on whether he reached the Nuggets roster. Hordges did, and appeared in 145 NBA games for Denver across two seasons. Chicago ultimately selected Mike Olliver at No. 32; the pick generated zero NBA appearances. Those outcomes support Denver's advantage without misrepresenting the original conditional terms.

sections.heading: What the Exchange Actually Produced
sections.body: Chicago moved Calvin Garrett’s draft rights to Houston on June 10, 1980, for a second-round selection in 1982. Garrett had not yet made his NBA debut, so the Rockets accepted the immediate development decision. Chicago deferred its return for two drafts. The original pick eventually occupied No. 38 in 1982, but the Bulls did not select the player attached to that slot.

sections.heading: Why Houston's Direct Return Outweighed the Future Pick
sections.body: Garrett answered Houston’s bet with 70 appearances and 1,638 minutes during 1980–81, then another 51 appearances in 1981–82. Those 121 regular-season games represent direct value from the original rights acquisition. By contrast, Chicago held a future second-round asset rather than a player it could deploy. Houston’s B+ and Chicago’s C+ recognize the difference between usable rotation minutes and a pick whose utility came later.

sections.heading: The Chicago Bulls Side's Completed Value
sections.body: Chicago did preserve trade value. On June 23, 1982, the Bulls moved the incoming No. 38 selection to Golden State for a 1983 second-rounder that became No. 31. The Warriors, not Chicago, selected Wayne Sappleton. Chicago subsequently sent the 1983 selection to Atlanta as compensation for hiring coach Kevin Loughery. That chain supports some Chicago benefit, but it does not make Sappleton or Doc Rivers Bulls players.

sections.heading: The Houston Rockets' Completed Value
sections.body: Houston received a forward who logged 121 games across two seasons; Chicago received draft flexibility that ultimately became part of a coaching-compensation transaction. The source-backed Rockets Win verdict is therefore narrower than claiming Chicago got nothing, but firmer than calling the returns equivalent. The recorded B+/C+ grades reward Houston’s on-court return while acknowledging the Bulls’ later asset conversion.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win, B+ for Houston and C+ for Chicago. Garrett gave Houston 121 regular-season appearances in two seasons. Chicago traded the incoming 1982 No. 38 pick for a 1983 second-rounder, then used that replacement selection as coaching compensation. Neither Sappleton nor Rivers played for the Bulls as a direct return from this exchange.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Calvin Garrett's 121 Rockets Games Versus Chicago's Pick Chain
featuredDeepDive.intro: Houston gained Calvin Garrett’s rights in June 1980, before he had appeared in an NBA game, and Chicago received a 1982 second-round pick. Garrett provided the Rockets 121 games across two seasons. The Bulls later exchanged that pick for another second-rounder, which they used as compensation in acquiring coach Kevin Loughery. Those distinct outcomes favor Houston without making Chicago’s side worthless.

sections.heading: What Each Team Actually Received
sections.body: The June 1980 exchange separated player rights from a future draft slot. Chicago had selected Calvin Garrett in the 1979 third round, but he had not played an NBA game when the Bulls transferred his rights. Houston acquired the right to bring him onto its roster. Chicago accepted a 1982 second-rounder that would not offer an immediate player return, leaving the two clubs with different timelines to evaluate.

sections.heading: What Chicago Bulls Realized
sections.body: Garrett’s NBA debut arrived with Houston in 1980–81. He played 70 games, recorded 1,638 minutes, and averaged 6.1 points with 3.8 rebounds and 1.9 assists. In 1981–82 he appeared 51 more times, including 22 starts. This was rotation-level contribution rather than star production, but the sum of 121 games is a concrete benefit from an acquisition of an untested player’s rights.

sections.heading: What Houston Rockets Realized
sections.body: The Bulls’ 1982 selection ended up at No. 38, later identified with Wayne Sappleton. Chicago exchanged that selection for Golden State’s 1983 second-rounder before the 1982 draft, so Sappleton’s eventual career belongs to the Warriors side of the later trade. Chicago’s replacement pick became No. 31, but the Bulls then transferred it to Atlanta as compensation for Kevin Loughery. The Hawks drafted Doc Rivers. Crediting Rivers’s career to Chicago would erase the documented downstream transactions.

sections.heading: Comparing Houston B+ With Chicago C+
sections.body: Chicago’s B-to-C-range benefit came from retaining a tradable asset, not from employing either player selected at the two draft positions. Houston’s B+ is tied to Garrett actually appearing in 121 Rockets games across two seasons. The C+ for Chicago allows for the pick’s use in the Loughery compensation chain. The Rockets Win verdict follows this evidence without confusing the 1980 deal with the later Golden State and Atlanta exchanges.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win, B+/C+. Houston converted Garrett’s rights into 70 games in 1980–81 and another 51 the following season. Chicago preserved the original draft asset’s trade utility but never obtained the players eventually selected with either linked pick. That direct-production difference makes Houston the stronger recipient while preserving the Bulls’ documented downstream benefit.

sections.heading: What Changed Hands
sections.body: On June 10, 1980, Chicago and Portland exchanged two draft-related assets apiece. The Bulls acquired Ronnie Lester's rights and a conditional choice among specified first-round selections, a right ultimately recorded as the 1981 No. 4 pick. Portland acquired Kelvin Ransey's rights and Chicago's 1981 first-round selection, which became No. 16 for Darnell Valentine. Neither club received an already drafted Al Wood or Valentine on trade day; the eventual names identify the draft assets after the fact.

sections.heading: How the Realized Value Separated
sections.body: The best measure of Portland's return is what its two assets did afterward. Ransey played 158 games for the Trail Blazers, averaging 15.6 points and 7.0 assists during his Portland stint. Valentine then appeared in 300 Portland regular-season games. Chicago's Lester played 191 Bulls games over four seasons, with 115 starts and 4,459 minutes. Both franchises obtained real on-court value, but the Ransey-and-Valentine combination supplied Portland a stronger record of direct contribution.

sections.heading: Reading the Team Grades
sections.body: The canonical grades are Portland A+ and Chicago A-, corresponding to a Trail Blazers Win verdict. Those marks account for Chicago's real return from Ronnie Lester and the draft asset that became No. 4; they don't treat that No. 4 selection as an automatic Al Wood Bulls tenure. Portland's incoming Ransey rights and No. 16 draft asset led to player contributions the archived assessment ranks above Chicago's package. Chicago’s later No. 4 conversion must be evaluated with the additional pick attached to the Atlanta exchange.

sections.heading: How Each Team Viewed the Trade
sections.body: Chicago used its No. 4 selection in a separate 1981 Atlanta transaction, packaging it with a second-round choice. That larger exchange brought the No. 6 selection used on Orlando Woolridge as well as 1982 first- and second-round assets. It would be inaccurate to credit this 1980 Portland deal alone with every element of that later package. Portland received Kelvin Ransey's rights and the No. 16 pick that became Valentine directly; their Portland playing records require no such allocation across multiple later trades.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Trail Blazers Win — Portland A+, Chicago A-. The June 10, 1980 agreement sent Kelvin Ransey's rights and the eventual No. 16 Darnell Valentine pick to Portland, while Chicago acquired Ronnie Lester's rights and the selection later identified as No. 4. Ransey played 158 Portland games, Valentine 300, and Lester 191 for Chicago. The Bulls subsequently traded No. 4 as one component of a larger Atlanta package, so the Woolridge branch cannot be assigned solely to this exchange.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Chicago's No. 4 Pick versus Portland's Ransey–Valentine Backcourt
featuredDeepDive.intro: The June 1980 Bulls–Trail Blazers deal connected four draft rights or selections to two very different asset paths. Chicago obtained Ronnie Lester and a choice of future first-round picks, eventually the 1981 No. 4. Portland gained Kelvin Ransey and the 1981 No. 16 selection. The distinction is what the clubs realized: Chicago got Lester's 191 games and used No. 4 in a larger transaction, while Portland received 158 Ransey games and 300 from Darnell Valentine. The source-led archive records a Portland A+ and Chicago A-.

sections.heading: Lester, Ransey and the Two Future First-Round Paths
sections.body: Start with the direct ledger rather than a retrospective list of players who never changed teams in 1980. Ronnie Lester's rights and the future first-round choice traveled to Chicago; Kelvin Ransey's rights and the 1981 first-rounder traveled to Portland. The Bulls' conditional asset was ultimately identified as No. 4, Al Wood, while the Trail Blazers' selection became No. 16, Darnell Valentine. This was not a Lester-for-Ransey exchange plus free-standing unrelated picks: the rights and both choices were components of the same June 10 deal.

sections.heading: Chicago Traded No. 4 with Another Pick to Obtain Orlando Woolridge
sections.body: The Chicago branch wasn't empty. Ronnie Lester appeared in 191 Bulls games over four seasons, starting 115 and playing 4,459 minutes. The club also retained a valuable No. 4 selection until it became part of a separate package with a second-round pick sent to Atlanta. That later transaction helped Chicago obtain No. 6, Orlando Woolridge, and future choices. Because another Chicago asset went to Atlanta alongside No. 4, the full package cannot be credited entirely to this earlier Portland exchange.

sections.heading: Ransey and Valentine Supplied 458 Portland Games
sections.body: Portland's contribution can be traced to identifiable seasons of actual NBA work. Kelvin Ransey played 158 games in Portland, recording 15.6 points and 7.0 assists per game in that stint. Darnell Valentine, taken with the No. 16 selection received from Chicago, played 300 regular-season games for the Trail Blazers. Subsequent transactions involving those players created additional asset paths, but their measured Portland appearances already provide a grounded explanation for why the received package earned the higher retrospective grade.

sections.heading: Al Wood Never Became the Bulls' No. 4 Pick Return
sections.body: The Bulls' future first became the No. 4 overall selection in 1981, but Chicago did not draft and employ Al Wood through that pick. The club bundled the right with a separate second-round asset in a later transaction with Atlanta, which delivered the No. 6 pick used on Orlando Woolridge plus future draft consideration. The chain shows that the original Portland trade created useful negotiating leverage, not an entire Woolridge package free of further cost. Portland's branch is simpler to measure: Ransey played 158 games for the Trail Blazers, and Valentine appeared in 300 after the No. 16 pick conveyed. Chicago's 191 Lester games and the transferred No. 4 right retain value, but the separate Atlanta payment prevents crediting the whole subsequent acquisition to this one exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Portland's A+ reflects two measurable incoming-player paths: 158 Trail Blazers games from Kelvin Ransey and 300 from Darnell Valentine, selected with the first-round choice obtained from Chicago. The Bulls' A- recognizes 191 Ronnie Lester games and a No. 4 selection later moved as part of a separate multi-asset deal with Atlanta. Both sides received genuine value. The Trail Blazers Win verdict compares that evidence without attributing the entire Woolridge package to the 1980 transaction or discounting Lester's documented Chicago tenure and the separate Atlanta pick conversion.

sections.heading: Chicago Bought Bob Wilkerson’s Rights from Denver
sections.body: On October 8, 1980, the Chicago Bulls acquired the player rights to Bob Wilkerson from the Denver Nuggets for cash considerations. The original transaction histories describe a sale, not a swap for a different player or draft selection. Chicago needed backcourt experience and could use Wilkerson immediately, while Denver received a financial payment whose exact amount is not preserved. Any confident dollar comparison between the two returns would exceed the known record.

sections.heading: Wilkerson Gave Chicago an Entire Productive Season
sections.body: Wilkerson played 80 regular-season Bulls games in 1980–81, averaging 10.0 points, 3.5 rebounds and 3.4 assists across 28.0 minutes per appearance. He also started all six Chicago postseason games that spring. Those are concrete minutes and production attached to the rights purchase, and they make a stronger retrospective case than the general claim that a veteran sometimes fills a roster need. He was not retained as a long-term Bulls centerpiece, and his subsequent Cleveland stint should not be booked to Chicago.

sections.heading: Denver’s Cash Return Cannot Be Treated as Zero
sections.body: The Nuggets received financial consideration from Chicago rather than another NBA player. The archived transaction records do not provide a verified payment amount, so there is no basis to say Denver gained more or less than a specific contract value. Denver may have preferred a different roster configuration, but the source ledger does not document front-office intent. It does show that an experienced player left the organization and subsequently played a full season for the acquiring club.

sections.heading: The Grade Spread Captures One Useful Bulls Year
sections.body: Chicago earns A-minus and Denver C-plus in the canonical ledger, with Bulls Win. The stronger Bulls mark follows Wilkerson’s 80 appearances and participation in six playoff games, while the short duration caps the historic significance of the acquisition. Denver’s known cash return is legitimate but unpriced. The result is a clear on-court advantage with an explicit limit on the financial comparison, not a claim that Wilkerson transformed Chicago for a decade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win — Chicago A-minus, Denver C-plus. Bob Wilkerson supplied 80 Bulls games with 10.0 points and 3.4 assists per night plus six postseason starts in 1980–81. Chicago obtained a useful one-season guard from the October 1980 rights purchase. Denver received cash of an undocumented amount, preventing a precise financial calculation; the measurable basketball return favors the Bulls.
