sections.heading: Chicago Exchanged Olliver Rights for Two Assets
sections.body: The June 10, 1981 transaction sent Chicago's rights to Mike Olliver to Indiana. The Bulls received rights to Ray Blume plus a 1982 second-round selection. Rather than receiving just one name for another, Chicago converted a rights position with no established NBA production into two different opportunities: a player who could join the roster and a future pick that could become another rotation contributor. The later draft result was not known when the teams agreed to those terms.

sections.heading: Blume and Higgins Supplied Specific Bulls Games
sections.body: Ray Blume played 49 games for Chicago in the 1981-82 season. The incoming 1982 second-round pick became No. 31 Rod Higgins, who played 233 games for the Bulls across his first three full seasons and a brief later return. Higgins appeared in all 82 games and started 42 as a rookie. Those are specific contributions from both incoming pieces, not speculative value borrowed from other teams. Chicago received 282 combined regular-season games through the two assets; the source account identifies no corresponding NBA regular-season appearances by Olliver.

sections.heading: The Indiana Return Never Reached the Floor
sections.body: The Pacers' acquired item was rights to Mike Olliver. Olliver did not play in an NBA regular-season game, leaving Indiana with no realized NBA appearance count from the named return. Chicago could use Blume immediately and later drew a more durable player from its 1982 selection. This outcome explains a wide grade difference without needing a repeated paragraph about general retrospective methodology. It also avoids attributing Higgins's later career on unrelated teams to Chicago's own direct contribution.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win. Chicago earns A+ for Blume's 49 games plus the 1982 No. 31 pick that became Rod Higgins; Indiana receives F for the Olliver rights, which generated no NBA regular-season appearances. The Bulls obtained two usable returns from a rights position with no on-court payoff for the Pacers. The A+/F scores correct the former mismatched final-verdict grades.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: How Chicago Converted Mike Olliver Rights Into Blume and Higgins
featuredDeepDive.intro: Chicago received Ray Blume rights and the second-round selection used on Rod Higgins for Mike Olliver rights. Those incoming assets produced 282 Chicago NBA appearances; Olliver produced none.

sections.heading: Two Rights, One Pick and 282 Bulls Appearances
sections.body: Chicago exchanged the NBA rights to Mike Olliver for two pieces on June 10, 1981: rights to Ray Blume and an Indiana second-round selection in the 1982 draft. The pick became No. 31 Rod Higgins. At the time neither side could claim the second player had made an NBA contribution; Chicago still needed to sign and use its incoming rights. In hindsight, Blume supplied 49 regular-season games for the 1981-82 Bulls and Higgins supplied 233 Bulls games, including a brief later return. That is 282 combined games from the original package. Indiana's acquired rights to Olliver produced no NBA regular-season appearances. The comparison is unusually concrete because each side can be linked to a named incoming right and then measured against actual NBA games, without using the later careers of unrelated players.

sections.heading: Ray Blume’s One Season and Higgins’s Rookie Workload
sections.body: Blume was not a long-term Chicago centerpiece, but he appeared in 49 Bulls games during 1981-82, averaging 4.6 points and 1.4 assists. He gave Chicago a modest real contribution from rights that arrived through the trade. The 1982 second-round choice provided a more durable result. Rod Higgins played all 82 games and started 42 as a Bulls rookie, then accumulated 233 Chicago appearances across his first three full seasons and a brief 1985-86 return. These figures are already recorded in the canonical source research and demonstrate why the two assets should be evaluated separately. Combining them is useful for the total games calculation, but neither should be described as a superstar or as accounting for the entirety of his later NBA career. Chicago turned uncertain rights into actual minutes.

sections.heading: The Pacers’ Olliver Rights Never Became NBA Minutes
sections.body: Indiana's direct return was the draft rights to Mike Olliver, not a player with a documented Pacers NBA career. The canonical research identifies zero NBA regular-season games by Olliver. That does not establish that the Pacers acted irrationally with information available in June 1981, but it establishes a failing realized return from the asset actually acquired. Chicago meanwhile received a playable guard in Blume and a second-round choice that became Higgins. The ledger should not silently substitute an invented Indiana draft selection or credit Indianapolis with a different player to make the exchange appear even. The source transactions from the Bulls and Pacers document the rights movement, while roster records document subsequent Chicago appearances. The inherited F for Indiana is justified by the absence of an NBA contribution, not by an accusation about management's motives.

sections.heading: Why the A-Plus and F Difference Is Defensible
sections.body: An A-plus for Chicago does not imply that Blume or Higgins became an All-Star on the Bulls. It recognizes the unusually favorable conversion of rights that never produced NBA games for the counterparty into two contributions with 282 combined Chicago appearances. The No. 31 selection generated the larger share through Higgins, while Blume supplied 49 immediate games. Indiana's F is the opposite realized outcome: acquired Mike Olliver rights without an NBA regular-season appearance. Older generic Deep Dive copy described A-minus for Chicago and C-plus for Indiana, which contradicts the reconciled A-plus/F transaction ledger and the specific source research. The final judgment is Bulls Win on both verdict and grade scale, with the sources distinguishing limited but real rotation value from a draft-right asset that produced no NBA playing time.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win — Chicago A+, Indiana F. Ray Blume appeared in 49 Bulls games and No. 31 pick Rod Higgins logged 233 Chicago appearances. The outgoing Mike Olliver rights generated no NBA regular-season games.

sections.heading: The Transaction Date Differs Across Historical Ledgers
sections.body: Chicago received guard Johnny High from Phoenix in exchange for a 1983 third-round pick. The Bulls’ media guide and RealGM list October 1, 1981, while Basketball-Reference records September 30. The archive keeps October 1 as its canonical date and explicitly notes the one-day discrepancy. The incoming selection was later No. 52 Winfred King, but that pick was not ultimately exercised by Phoenix.

sections.heading: High Never Played a Regular-Season Game for Chicago
sections.body: The Bulls waived High on October 20, 1981, before he appeared in an NBA regular-season game for the franchise. That leaves Chicago without a direct on-court return from the player it obtained. High was a legitimate NBA guard when acquired, but the trade’s realized result was a short roster evaluation rather than a season-long contribution. That is the basis for Chicago’s F in the retrospective ledger.

sections.heading: Phoenix Used the Pick in a Larger Deal with Boston
sections.body: The Suns later included Chicago’s incoming third-round pick in the June 1983 Dennis Johnson trade with the Celtics. Boston ultimately used No. 52 on King, who did not appear in an NBA regular-season game. The value Phoenix received from this pick was therefore its trade utility within another transaction, rather than King’s own NBA production. This supports the Suns’ B-minus without pretending the original pick independently became a future star.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Suns Win — Phoenix B-minus, Chicago F. High played no regular-season games for the Bulls and was waived weeks after the exchange. Phoenix retained enough value in the 1983 third-rounder to include it in the Dennis Johnson trade, even though Boston’s eventual No. 52 pick, Winfred King, produced no NBA games. The date conflict is documented rather than silently corrected.

sections.heading: Houston Sold the NBA Rights to Terry Stotts
sections.body: On October 2, 1981, Chicago purchased the NBA rights to Terry Stotts from Houston for an undisclosed cash payment. Stotts was a second-round draft choice in 1980 and had not appeared in an NBA regular-season game. The Rockets were not giving up a contributor to their active rotation. They instead monetized rights held outside the team’s immediate playing group. Chicago acquired the opportunity to evaluate the guard before a new season.

sections.heading: Chicago Signed Him but Waived Him Before Opening Night
sections.body: Chicago’s official historical transaction record indicates that Stotts signed shortly after the rights purchase and was waived on October 12. The Bulls’ regular season did not begin until later that month. Consequently Stotts did not play a regular-season game for Chicago. He went on to work professionally elsewhere and much later became an NBA coach, neither of which produced basketball value from the Bulls’ 1981 purchase of his player rights.

sections.heading: Cash Was Real but the Amount Is Not Documented
sections.body: The Rockets received cash rather than players or draft selections. None of the reviewed transaction listings establishes a dependable amount, so the analysis cannot translate the cash into payroll effects or additional player acquisitions. It was nevertheless a definite transaction return from rights Houston had not been using. Chicago acquired a contract opportunity that ended before a single regular-season appearance and did not generate a later NBA player asset.

sections.heading: The Canonical Grades Correctly Favor Houston
sections.body: Houston’s C-plus reflects an ordinary, modest cash return from unused rights; Chicago’s F reflects zero NBA game production before the release. That does not make this a major historic mistake, because the price is unverified and the player was not a star. It is a small completed-value judgment. Previous longer editorial text incorrectly called Chicago the winner and assigned B-plus and C-plus grades. The revised copy follows the source-led canonical verdict instead.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win — Houston C-plus, Chicago F. The Rockets sold Terry Stotts’s unused NBA rights for cash, while Chicago signed and waived him before he appeared in a regular-season game. The amount of money remains unidentified, so Houston’s positive return is limited rather than extraordinary. Stotts’s later coaching success belongs to a different career and does not count as trade value.

sections.heading: San Antonio Bought an Elite Veteran for Two Useful Pieces
sections.body: San Antonio’s objective was straightforward: add a proven center to a team already built around George Gervin. Artis Gilmore was thirty-two, but he remained one of the league’s strongest interior scorers, rebounders and rim protectors. The Spurs paid Dave Corzine, Mark Olberding and cash, sacrificing two rotation players rather than premium draft control. Gilmore immediately became a high-minute starter and helped San Antonio win fifty-three games and reach the 1983 Western Conference finals. The trade aligned talent with a live competitive window, which is exactly when an older star can be worth more than a collection of younger parts. Chicago did receive proven players rather than placeholders: a contemporary report listed Corzine at 10.1 points and 7.7 rebounds and Olberding at 13.8 points and 6.5 rebounds in the prior season. San Antonio nevertheless concentrated those two useful roles into Gilmore's higher-end interior production for Gervin's remaining prime.

sections.heading: Chicago Chose Depth and a Younger Frontcourt Timeline
sections.body: The Bulls were not simply giving away a franchise legend without a roster plan. Chicago had struggled to build a winner around Gilmore and sought a younger, deeper frontcourt. Corzine was twenty-six and capable of starting at center, while Olberding offered toughness and positional flexibility at forward. The return reduced age risk and distributed minutes across two dependable players. That process deserves respect because Gilmore’s remaining prime was finite and the Bulls needed more than one aging star to change their direction. The first-season results illustrate the limit without proving that one deal caused each team's record. San Antonio went 53-29 in 1982-83, while Chicago finished 28-54. The Bulls received frontcourt minutes and a younger center, but their deeper roster did not produce an immediate turnaround.

sections.heading: Gilmore Extended the Spurs’ Contending Window
sections.body: Gilmore’s first San Antonio season established the top of the deal. He averaged efficient interior production, controlled the glass and gave the Spurs a defensive anchor behind Gervin’s scoring. San Antonio eliminated Denver 4-1 in the 1983 Western Conference semifinals, then lost 4-2 to the Lakers in the conference finals. The Lakers subsequently lost the NBA Finals 4-0 to Philadelphia. He remained a productive starter for several more seasons and returned to the All-Star Game late in his Spurs tenure. Those results make the acquisition more than a nostalgic name purchase. The playoff path was one round short of the Finals, not a championship: the Spurs beat Denver in five games and pushed the eventual Western Conference champion Lakers to six. Chicago's return produced regular-season durability, but Gilmore supplied the superior contribution at the more competitive moment.

sections.heading: Corzine Became a Durable Bull
sections.body: Corzine’s career in Chicago is the strongest case against calling the deal a blowout. He became a long-term Bull, started for much of the decade and played alongside the early Michael Jordan teams. His rebounding, screening and interior work supplied stability at a position where Chicago needed dependable minutes. He did not become an All-Star, yet he remained useful far longer than many secondary trade pieces. That durability supports a B grade for the Bulls rather than a punitive mark. Corzine's seven Bulls seasons eventually extended into the Michael Jordan era, a real long-term benefit not evident from the first year alone. Gilmore's impact was concentrated in a 53-win Spurs season and a conference-finals appearance. Neither outcome should erase the different role each team sought from the 1982 exchange.

sections.heading: Olberding and Cash Added Floor but Not Star Value
sections.body: Olberding added value that is easy to lose when the trade is reduced to Gilmore for Corzine. He was a rugged frontcourt player who could defend, rebound and absorb physical assignments, although his Chicago tenure was brief. Cash also helped the Bulls complete the transaction without adding future obligations. The package gave Chicago depth and flexibility rather than one centerpiece. That was a rational construction for a team trying to reset, but the short duration of Olberding’s contribution limited the return. The trade record confirms cash was also included with Corzine and Olberding, but it supplies no verified dollar figure for that component. That prevents a precise monetary valuation and leaves the roster outcomes as the strongest comparison: a useful Chicago center against an immediate Spurs star pairing.

sections.heading: The Margin Is Real but Not Overwhelming
sections.body: This trade belongs in the slight-edge category rather than among the league’s historic robberies. Chicago received a legitimate starting center for years and did not sacrifice a player who was still at his absolute peak. San Antonio nevertheless gained an All-Star-caliber center who helped produce a conference-finals run and remained productive through the middle of the decade. The Spurs’ A-minus reflects a successful win-now purchase without pretending Gilmore delivered a championship. Chicago’s B recognizes Corzine’s durability and the package’s practical value. The A-minus/B split follows different kinds of return: San Antonio used Gilmore during a 53-win playoff push, and Chicago kept Corzine through several subsequent seasons. The 1983 Lakers matchup ended 4-2 against San Antonio; the Spurs acquired the more valuable peak without acquiring a championship.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Spurs Edge. Artis Gilmore gave San Antonio an All-Star-caliber center, immediate interior credibility and a trip to the 1983 Western Conference finals. Chicago received years of useful starting play from Dave Corzine plus a smaller contribution from Mark Olberding. The Bulls’ return was respectable, but the Spurs acquired the better player and the more meaningful peak.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Artis Gilmore Showed Why Aging Stars Can Still Be Efficient Trade Targets
featuredDeepDive.intro: The deal illustrates that age should be priced, not feared automatically. San Antonio did not need Gilmore to remain dominant for a decade. It needed him to strengthen a contender immediately, while Chicago needed younger, more distributed value. Both teams followed coherent strategies, but one received the higher-level result.

sections.heading: The Spurs Paid for the Years That Still Mattered
sections.body: Gilmore’s age lowered the acquisition cost, but his skills remained highly transferable. He did not rely only on speed or perimeter creation. Strength, touch, rebounding position and rim protection tend to age more gradually, allowing San Antonio to project useful seasons even as his athletic peak receded. The Spurs received exactly that: immediate high-level center play followed by several productive seasons. That outcome demonstrates why a contender can profit from buying an older star after the seller has decided the timeline no longer fits. San Antonio's 1982 bet can be evaluated against the actual first-year return: Gilmore joined a 53-win Spurs team that reached the Western Conference finals. The Bulls chose a younger center and additional frontcourt help, not a future draft stockpile. The difference was the strength and timing of the basketball return.

sections.heading: Gervin and Gilmore Created a Clear Offensive Hierarchy
sections.body: Gervin was the perimeter scoring engine, and Gilmore gave the Spurs a complementary interior anchor. The pairing reduced the need for either star to perform every offensive function. Gilmore could finish, rebound and punish smaller lineups, while Gervin controlled late possessions and perimeter scoring. The fit translated quickly because the roles were distinct rather than redundant. San Antonio’s front office therefore deserves credit not only for acquiring talent but for acquiring the right kind of talent. That complementary arrangement helped the 1982-83 Spurs finish second in offensive rating, with Gervin still leading the perimeter attack. The offense was not a one-player accomplishment, yet Gilmore gave San Antonio an inside source of efficiency that Chicago could not reproduce simply by adding two rotation contributors.

sections.heading: Chicago’s Return Fit the Jordan Transition Better Than the Old Roster
sections.body: The Bulls’ roster eventually turned toward Michael Jordan, and Corzine was more compatible with a supporting role than an aging star-centered structure. Corzine could screen, rebound and accept lower usage while younger perimeter talent developed. That later fit should be acknowledged even though Jordan was not yet on the roster when the trade occurred. The transaction helped Chicago move away from a team dependent on Gilmore’s production. Still, a future roster transition cannot retroactively create star value that the return did not contain. The Jordan-centered role belongs to hindsight, not the July 1982 trade rationale: Michael Jordan would not join Chicago until the 1984 draft. Corzine's later ability to take a supporting role helps explain his continued value, but it cannot transform the 1982 return into a planned Jordan-era roster construction.

sections.heading: Corzine’s Longevity Keeps the Bulls’ Grade Respectable
sections.body: Corzine remained with Chicago for seven seasons and played more games for the Bulls than Gilmore played for San Antonio. Longevity matters because dependable starting minutes have real replacement cost. Corzine’s presence helped the Bulls avoid repeatedly spending assets at center during a period of major organizational change. That record is why Chicago earns B rather than C or worse. However, minutes are not equal simply because they accumulate. Corzine's long stay helped Chicago bridge several rebuilding years, including the beginning of Jordan's career. That service supports a respectable Bulls grade even though Gilmore immediately helped San Antonio reach a conference final. The two returns should be judged by level of play and duration together, not by games played alone.

sections.heading: Postseason Leverage Separates the Two Returns
sections.body: The 1983 conference-finals run is the clearest separator. San Antonio did not win the championship, but the Gilmore acquisition helped the Spurs reach a level Chicago never approached with the incoming package as its defining value. Playoff series against elite opponents expose the difference between a reliable starter and a star-level interior presence. Gilmore’s performance gave the Spurs a chance to maximize Gervin’s remaining prime. Chicago’s package supported a rebuild rather than creating a comparable peak. San Antonio defeated Denver 4-1 in the 1983 semifinals before the Lakers beat the Spurs 4-2; Philadelphia then swept Los Angeles for the title. That exact bracket supports a conference-final payoff without incorrectly calling the Lakers the champions or crediting Gilmore with a Finals berth.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: San Antonio bought the correct veteran for the correct moment. Chicago received real durability and avoided an empty return, so the deal is not a landslide. Gilmore’s superior level of play and the Spurs’ conference-finals result create the decisive margin.

sections.heading: What Changed Hands
sections.body: Chicago’s October 8, 1982 deal with the franchise then known as the San Diego Clippers sent Ray Blume to the Clippers and brought Chicago a conditional draft pick that would transfer only if Blume made the Clippers roster. The trade identifies that condition as not exercised. That fact sharply limits the realized value on Chicago’s side: the Bulls did not end up with a completed draft asset from the condition, while the Clippers received Blume. The final result is a Slight Clippers Edge, with Los Angeles at C+ and Chicago at C. Both team perspectives point toward the Clippers, although one describes the result as a slight partner edge and the other as a Clippers win. The final grade keeps the margin conservative because the transaction itself was minor.

sections.heading: Why the Clippers Hold the Realized-Value Advantage
sections.body: The strongest evidence is the condition attached to Chicago’s return. The Bulls received a conditional pick tied to Blume making the Clippers roster, and the documented asset description says the condition was not exercised. That means the return did not mature into a realized draft asset. The Clippers, by contrast, received Ray Blume directly. Chicago’s own perspective says the partner generated modestly stronger realized value, while the Clippers perspective identifies Blume as the stronger return. The final C+/C split translates that shared direction into a restrained final grade. It gives the Clippers credit for receiving the asset that produced actual basketball value without pretending a minor 1982 transaction should carry blockbuster-level grades.

sections.heading: Conditional Assets Need Outcome Discipline
sections.body: Conditional draft consideration can look meaningful on a transaction line even when the condition never turns into an exercised pick. A retrospective should therefore separate the existence of the condition from the value that was ultimately realized. Chicago deserves credit for negotiating a conditional path to draft compensation, but the record also states that the condition was not exercised. Once the condition failed to create a draft asset, the completed comparison became straightforward: the Clippers held the player, while Chicago’s contingent return did not materialize. That does not imply the Bulls had no trade-day rationale. It means the completed outcome is modestly better for the Clippers, which is exactly what the C+/C grade pair expresses.

sections.heading: Why the Verdict Remains Only a Slight Edge
sections.body: The Clippers’ advantage is real, but the scale of the transaction matters. Ray Blume was the primary realized asset, and Chicago’s conditional pick did not exercise, yet neither available evidence treats the exchange as a franchise-shaping event. The final grade should preserve that proportionality. A one-step difference gives the Clippers the win while avoiding a dramatic penalty for Chicago. It also reconciles the two team perspectives: Chicago calls it a modest partner advantage, while the Clippers record uses stronger winner language. The documented Slight Clippers Edge chooses the conservative common ground between those descriptions and keeps the historical judgment tied to the documented asset outcomes.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Clippers Edge. Los Angeles receives a C+ and Chicago a C. The Clippers acquired Ray Blume; Chicago received a conditional draft pick that the record identifies as not exercised. Both franchise-side perspectives favor the Clippers, and the realized asset comparison supports that direction. Because the transaction was limited in scale, the winner is expressed through a narrow one-grade-step separation rather than an extreme verdict.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Bulls–Clippers 1982: The Conditional Pick That Never Became Realized Value
featuredDeepDive.intro: The 1982 Bulls–Clippers transaction turns on a simple but important retrospective distinction: a conditional asset is not the same thing as a realized asset. Chicago traded Ray Blume and received a pick condition that would matter only if Blume made the Clippers roster. The canonical record says the condition was not exercised. The Clippers therefore finished with the more tangible realized return, and both franchise perspectives ultimately point in that direction. The C+/C result keeps the win proportional to the small scale of the deal.

sections.heading: The Condition Is the Core of the Trade
sections.body: Chicago’s return was not a guaranteed selection. It was a conditional pick whose transfer depended on a specific roster condition, and that condition was never exercised. That matters because the trade should be judged by what the condition actually produced, not as though Chicago received a pick that never transferred. In the end, the Clippers obtained Blume while Chicago’s conditional return produced no draft asset. That gives the Clippers the stronger outcome.

sections.heading: Chicago Still Gets Credit for the Structure
sections.body: A condition that never exercises is not the same thing as no trade consideration at all. Chicago negotiated a mechanism that could have delivered draft compensation if the trigger was met. That structure belongs in the historical record and helps explain why the Bulls are not treated as though they simply gave a player away. But the completed grade must distinguish potential from realization. The C grade reflects that middle ground: Chicago had a defensible transaction structure, yet the asset did not mature into tangible value. The Clippers’ C+ sits one step higher because Blume was the side of the exchange that generated the stronger realized result.

sections.heading: The Two Team Perspectives Support the Same Winner
sections.body: Chicago’s perspective says the partner generated modestly stronger realized value. The Clippers perspective says the San Diego side captured the stronger return, led by Ray Blume. Those descriptions are directionally aligned even though the source-local grades use different magnitudes. The verdict therefore does not need to choose between conflicting winners. It only needs to set the appropriate severity. A Slight Clippers Edge is the restrained answer: the available evidence agrees on who finished ahead, while the limited scale of the assets argues against a wide grade spread.

sections.heading: Why Small Conditional Trades Still Matter
sections.body: A historical trade site becomes more useful when it treats minor conditional transactions with the same standard as major deals. The outcome here is not important because of star power; it is important because it illustrates how contingent value should be handled. The pick condition can be acknowledged without being credited as an exercised selection. Blume’s realized value can be counted without inflating his importance. That combination produces a stable, evergreen conclusion. The Clippers came out ahead, but only modestly, and the grade pair says exactly that.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Los Angeles C+, Chicago C, with a Slight Clippers Edge. The decisive fact is that Chicago’s conditional pick was not exercised, leaving Ray Blume as the stronger realized side of the transaction. Both franchise records support the Clippers as the winner, but the trade’s limited scale keeps the margin narrow.

sections.heading: The Transaction in Retrospect
sections.body: Chicago received Mitchell Wiggins's draft rights from Indiana on June 28, 1983. The Pacers received Sidney Lowe's rights and a 1984 second-round pick, later No. 26 Victor Fleming. All three assets were rights or draft positions on the transaction date, rather than veteran players changing NBA rosters. Chicago took one targeted prospect; Indiana divided its return between another guard prospect and the flexibility of a later selection.

sections.heading: Mitchell Wiggins Delivered Chicago a Strong Rookie Season
sections.body: Wiggins played all 82 games for Chicago in 1983–84, started 40, and averaged 12.4 points with four rebounds. His one Chicago season was the strongest immediate player contribution directly associated with this trade. The Bulls then sent Wiggins plus two additional future draft picks to Houston for Caldwell Jones in August 1984, so the entire Jones return cannot be credited to Wiggins alone.

sections.heading: Indiana Converted the Incoming Draft Pick into Granville Waiters
sections.body: Indiana received 78 games from Sidney Lowe, with averages of 4.2 points and 3.4 assists. The second-round pick also became an asset before draft night: the Pacers traded that pick by itself to Portland for Granville Waiters. Waiters supplied 140 Indiana games across two seasons, including 13 starts. Portland, not Indiana, ultimately selected Victor Fleming at No. 26; Fleming never appeared in the NBA.

sections.heading: Why Both Franchises Earned B Grades
sections.body: Chicago obtained the higher-impact individual rookie in Wiggins, but Indiana combined 78 games from Lowe with 140 from Waiters, directly secured by trading the incoming second-rounder. Those different forms of realized return reasonably finish in the same tier. Even Trade, B for the Bulls and B for the Pacers, better describes the source-backed outcome than the older B-/B- grades.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, Chicago B and Indiana B. Wiggins gave Chicago 82 regular-season games and a strong rookie scoring contribution before being included with two other picks in a trade for Caldwell Jones. Indiana received Lowe's 78 games and converted its future second-rounder directly into 140 games from Granville Waiters. The Pacers never rostered the later No. 26 selection, Victor Fleming.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Mitchell Wiggins, Sidney Lowe and Indiana's Waiters Conversion
featuredDeepDive.intro: Chicago acquired Mitchell Wiggins's rights and received an 82-game, 12.4-point rookie season. Indiana gained Sidney Lowe's rights and a future second-rounder. Lowe played 78 Pacers games, while the draft asset was exchanged by itself for Granville Waiters, who played 140 more Indiana games. Wiggins later helped Chicago acquire Caldwell Jones, but two other picks were also involved. Each side obtained useful value through a different route, supporting Even Trade with B grades for both.

sections.heading: What Each Team Actually Received
sections.body: The June 1983 draft-day trade sent Mitchell Wiggins's rights to the Bulls and brought Sidney Lowe's rights plus a 1984 second-round selection to Indiana. The league and both clubs' transaction logs confirm the two-team exchange. Wiggins was the No. 23 choice; Lowe was picked at No. 25. The later No. 26 associated with Victor Fleming belongs to the draft asset's eventual destination, not a player Indiana directly employed.

sections.heading: What Chicago Bulls Realized
sections.body: Wiggins became Chicago's strongest return. As a rookie he played all 82 games, started 40, averaged 12.4 points, and provided legitimate rotational scoring. Chicago traded him in August 1984 with two extra selections for Caldwell Jones. The deal preserved Wiggins's transaction value, but the presence of those other picks prevents assigning the complete Jones acquisition to the original Indiana exchange.

sections.heading: What Indiana Pacers Realized
sections.body: Lowe played 78 games for the Pacers and supplied reserve point-guard minutes, averaging 3.4 assists. Indiana also moved the incoming future second-rounder to Portland by itself in return for Granville Waiters, a center who then logged 78 and 62 Indiana games in consecutive seasons. That 140-game pick conversion is directly attributable to the acquired selection because the Pacers did not add another outgoing asset to obtain Waiters.

sections.heading: Even Trade, B/B: Distinct Direct and Downstream Returns
sections.body: Portland later used the second-rounder on Victor Fleming, who recorded zero NBA games, but Indiana had already turned the pick into Waiters. Chicago therefore earned value from Wiggins's productive full rookie season, while Indiana received useful court time from Lowe and Waiters. Each pathway supports a B, with an Even Trade verdict grounded in realized team value rather than awarding Indiana Fleming's absent NBA career.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, Bulls B / Pacers B. Wiggins supplied Chicago an 82-game season and later partial trade value; Lowe appeared 78 times for Indiana, and the incoming draft asset became Granville Waiters, who played 140 Pacers games. Fleming's eventual No. 26 selection was made by Portland, not Indiana. The balanced realized returns justify B/B without confusing later trades with one-to-one player exchanges.

sections.heading: The Kings Were in Kansas City When They Acquired Reggie Theus
sections.body: Chicago sent Reggie Theus to the Kansas City Kings on February 15, 1984, receiving center Steve Johnson plus three second-round draft choices. Basketball-Reference's contemporaneous Bulls transaction ledger names the later picks as Greg Wiltjer at No. 43 in 1984 and Ken Johnson at No. 28 and Mike Brittain at No. 29 in 1985. None of those future draftees was an existing NBA return on the day of the deal. Theus, on the other hand, was a proven playmaking scorer and had just experienced a reduced Chicago role after years as an All-Star guard. Modern database navigation correctly uses the successor Sacramento Kings franchise identity, but the basketball team that actually negotiated this February exchange was based in Kansas City. Calling it a 1984 Sacramento trade would misstate the setting and hide part of the original decision.

sections.heading: Theus Became a High-Minutes Kings Guard for Multiple Seasons
sections.body: The immediate Kings return grew far beyond a short-season scoring bump. Theus appeared in 30 Kansas City games after the February 1984 deal, averaging 15.8 points and 7.0 assists. In 1984-85 he started 80 of 82 games and averaged 16.4 points alongside 8.0 assists. His numbers improved after the franchise moved to Sacramento: across 79 games in 1986-87 he averaged 20.3 points and 8.8 assists, then produced 21.6 points and 6.3 assists in 73 games in 1987-88. Those are real contributions to the same Kings organization, even though the city label changed midway through his tenure. His later years with Atlanta and Orlando do not belong to the Kansas City/Sacramento side of this specific transaction. The playing return is enough to explain why the site's archived verdict favors the Kings.

sections.heading: Chicago Got 105 Johnson Games and Three Draft Opportunities
sections.body: Steve Johnson was not an empty return. He played 31 Bulls regular-season games following the trade in 1983-84, averaging 9.4 points and 5.4 rebounds. The next season he started 54 of his 74 Chicago appearances, producing 10.0 points and 5.9 rebounds per game. Johnson therefore gave Chicago 105 direct games and 63 starts before his next move, a genuine response to a roster looking for frontcourt depth. The three second-round selections were separate future opportunities, not three automatically productive NBA careers. Chicago's official 1984 draft record confirms Wiltjer's No. 43 selection, while the 1985 No. 28 and No. 29 identities require following draft and subsequent roster records before assigning any professional production. Crediting Johnson's real minutes and recognizing the option value of three picks explains why the canonical Bulls grade is B+, even though none individually equaled Theus's long-term Kings role.

sections.heading: Theus's Long Kings Prime Outweighed Johnson's Chicago Stint and Picks
sections.body: Reggie Theus made an immediate difference for the Kansas City Kings, averaging 15.8 points and 7.0 assists across 30 games after the February 1984 move. He played 82 games in 1984-85 and, after the club moved to Sacramento, averaged 20.3 points and 8.8 assists in 1986-87. Those seasons belong to the same franchise that acquired him in 1984. Chicago nevertheless received 105 Steve Johnson games, including 63 starts, plus three future second-round selections used on Greg Wiltjer, Ken Johnson and Mike Brittain. The selections were draft opportunities rather than guaranteed NBA starters, and Johnson's actual Bulls contribution was far shorter than Theus's Kings run. This supports Kansas City/Sacramento's A over Chicago's B+ without describing the deal as a failed return for the Bulls or incorrectly moving the 1984 transaction to Sacramento.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Win — Kansas City/Sacramento A, Chicago B+. Reggie Theus joined the Kansas City franchise in 1984 and became a long-serving guard, including 82 appearances at 16.4 points and 8.0 assists in 1984-85 and a 20.3-point, 8.8-assist Sacramento season in 1986-87. Chicago received Steve Johnson for 105 Bulls games and three future second-round rights identified with Greg Wiltjer, Ken Johnson and Mike Brittain. Johnson and the draft options were real assets, but Theus delivered the more durable immediate player return. The location change from Kansas City to Sacramento did not create a second trade.

sections.heading: What Changed Hands
sections.body: Chicago’s August 10, 1984 deal with Houston sent the Rockets Mitchell Wiggins, a 1985 second-round pick that became Tyrone Corbin at No. 35, and a 1985 third-round pick that became Michael Payne at No. 57. Chicago received Caldwell Jones. The transaction is therefore not a simple one-for-one player swap: Houston received a player plus two named draft outcomes, while the Bulls received one veteran player. Both franchise-side perspectives conclude that the realized return strongly favored Houston. The trade grades Houston A- and Chicago D with a Rockets Win verdict. That wide spread is justified by the source-supported asset gap inside the trade itself, not by unrelated later team success.

sections.heading: Why Houston Earns the A-
sections.body: Houston’s advantage comes from asset depth and realized outcome. The Rockets acquired Mitchell Wiggins plus two draft selections whose eventual players are named in the record: Tyrone Corbin at No. 35 and Michael Payne at No. 57. Chicago’s return was Caldwell Jones. The Bulls-side perspective says that Jones fell well short of the player and draft value created by the outgoing package. The Houston-side perspective independently calls the realized return strongly favorable to the Rockets. Because both records identify the same winner and because the exchange contains multiple directly tied basketball assets on Houston’s side, an A- is appropriate. The grade reflects the strength of the completed package, not an abstract preference for quantity.

sections.heading: Why Chicago Falls to D
sections.body: Chicago did receive a real player in Caldwell Jones, so the D grade is not a statement that the Bulls received nothing. It is a comparative judgment against the package they sent out. The available evidence identifies Wiggins and the two named draft outcomes as materially greater realized value. A D therefore communicates that Chicago’s return was legitimate but substantially weaker than the basketball value that left the organization. The gap also explains why this trade should not be compressed into the slight-edge category used for several other trades. Here, both perspectives describe a clear rather than marginal separation.

sections.heading: The Named Picks Make the Hindsight Case Concrete
sections.body: The draft pieces are not left as generic second- and third-rounders. The second-round selection is identified as Tyrone Corbin at No. 35, and the third-round selection as Michael Payne at No. 57. That matters because the retrospective can evaluate the completed transaction without assigning speculative value to unknown future picks. The record still avoids crediting Houston for unrelated downstream transactions. It simply counts the players and picks that were actually exchanged and what those picks became. On that bounded evidence, Houston’s package is substantially stronger, supporting the A-/D split and a clear Rockets Win.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win. Houston receives an A- and Chicago a D. The Rockets acquired Mitchell Wiggins plus the 1985 second-round pick that became Tyrone Corbin and the 1985 third-round pick that became Michael Payne. Chicago received Caldwell Jones. Both team perspectives agree that the outgoing Chicago package produced materially greater realized value. The named draft outcomes and player return give Houston a clear, evidence-based advantage within this trade.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Bulls–Rockets 1984: Houston’s Three-Asset Return Creates a Clear Win
featuredDeepDive.intro: The 1984 Chicago–Houston exchange stands apart from the slight-edge trades in this batch because the source record supports a much larger realized-value gap. Houston received Mitchell Wiggins and two draft selections that became Tyrone Corbin and Michael Payne. Chicago received Caldwell Jones. Both franchise perspectives independently describe the outcome as clearly favorable to Houston, and the repaired grade structure now expresses that same relationship: A- for the Rockets, D for the Bulls.

sections.heading: Houston Received More Than a Single Player
sections.body: The Rockets’ return had three basketball components: Wiggins, the second-round selection tied to Corbin, and the third-round selection tied to Payne. The value case therefore does not depend on one player carrying the entire package. Chicago’s own team evaluation specifically says the return in Caldwell Jones fell well short of the player or draft value created by the outgoing assets. That is unusually direct source support for a wide grade gap. The A- is not awarded because Houston merely received more items; it is awarded because the records say those items produced materially more realized basketball value.

sections.heading: Chicago’s Return Was Real but Insufficient
sections.body: Caldwell Jones gives the Bulls a concrete incoming player and keeps the transaction from being a zero-return story. The D grade recognizes that Chicago did receive basketball value. But the historical comparison is relative, and the available evidence consistently places Jones well below the combined Wiggins-and-picks package. This distinction matters because strong trade grades should be earned by the completed asset difference, not by rhetoric. Houston’s A- and Chicago’s D create a wide but still interpretable separation: one side received a strong multi-asset return, while the other received a legitimate but materially weaker player return.

sections.heading: The Draft Outcomes Are Named, Not Hypothetical
sections.body: A major strength of the evidence is that both draft selections are connected to the players chosen. The second-rounder became Tyrone Corbin at No. 35; the third-rounder became Michael Payne at No. 57. That removes a common source of retrospective inflation. Houston is not credited with the theoretical upside of two open-ended future picks. It is credited with the actual draft outcomes tied to the assets it received. The analysis can therefore remain narrow and still find a large gap. The package itself is enough to support Houston’s clear win.

sections.heading: Both Team Perspectives Support the Same Strong Direction
sections.body: The Chicago perspective calls the trade a clear loss and grades the Bulls D against an A- partner return. The Houston perspective also calls it a Rockets Win and places Houston A- above Chicago D. That agreement means the final editorial conclusion does not need to privilege one team’s framing over the other. The available evidence converges on both direction and severity. When the verdict, grade pair, and both analyses align, the conclusion is straightforward: Houston clearly won the exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Houston A-, Chicago D, with a Rockets Win verdict. The Rockets received Mitchell Wiggins and two named 1985 draft outcomes, while Chicago received Caldwell Jones. Both franchise-side records describe a substantial realized-value gap in Houston’s favor. The analysis credits only assets directly inside the trade and still reaches a clear result.

sections.heading: A September 1984 Pick-for-Center Exchange
sections.body: Dallas acquired seven-foot center Wallace Bryant from Chicago on September 14, 1984, giving up a conditional 1986 second-round pick. The draft slot ultimately became No. 39, with Rafael Addison selected, but that final name can mislead anyone reading the asset list as a one-step transaction. The Bulls initially received the future pick; they did not necessarily retain it until draft night. Dallas was trading a later selection for a frontcourt player with 29 previous NBA appearances for Chicago. The contemporary transaction logs from both clubs identify the same incoming pieces. The actual evaluation must distinguish Bryant's Dallas minutes from Chicago's later transfer of the pick.

sections.heading: Bryant Played 65 Dallas Games Before a Waiver
sections.body: Bryant's first Mavericks season delivered tangible if modest center depth. In 1984-85 he appeared 56 times and started 35, totaling 860 minutes, 164 points and 241 rebounds. The next season brought nine Dallas games, eight starts and another 154 minutes before the Mavericks waived him on November 26, 1985. Those 65 appearances and 43 starts represent the direct on-court return from the 1984 trade. His subsequent eight games with the Los Angeles Clippers were not Dallas production, and his prior 29 Chicago games had already occurred before the exchange. Attributing the entire career to Dallas would distort a small historical center acquisition.

sections.heading: The Pick Helped Chicago Sign Kyle Macy, Not Draft Addison
sections.body: Chicago transferred the Dallas-derived 1986 second-round pick to Phoenix on October 4, 1985, alongside a separate 1990 second-rounder. The consideration helped resolve the Suns' right-of-first-refusal compensation when the Bulls signed free agent Kyle Macy. Phoenix eventually used No. 39 on Rafael Addison in 1986. Official draft records therefore identify Addison as a Suns selection, and his 1986-87 Phoenix appearances cannot be assigned to the Bulls. Chicago's legitimate downstream connection is the pick's role in securing Macy's signing. Because another Chicago second-rounder was included, that roster addition also cannot be credited solely to Bryant's departure a year earlier.

sections.heading: Why the Canonical B-/B- Tie Survives the Asset Chain
sections.body: Dallas received a serviceable reserve big man who played 65 regular-season games for the club and later exited the roster. Chicago exchanged its rights to that center for a future selection that subsequently became one piece of a two-pick compensation package linked to Macy. Neither transaction branch produced an independent star-level return. The retained Even Trade judgment, Bulls B- and Mavericks B-, should be read as a cautious comparison of practical but bounded value, not an assertion that Chicago drafted Addison or collected his later career. The two branches are different in kind: verified Dallas playing time versus Chicago's ability to move a protected future asset in a later personnel decision.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Chicago B-, Dallas B-. The Mavericks received 65 games and 43 starts from Wallace Bryant, then waived him in November 1985. Chicago received the conditional 1986 second-round pick that became No. 39; in October 1985 it sent that pick plus a separate 1990 second to Phoenix as compensation connected to signing Kyle Macy. Phoenix, not Chicago, drafted Rafael Addison. The grades retain a balanced, limited-value outcome while tracing what each franchise actually controlled and avoiding credit for Addison's Suns career.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Wallace Bryant, Kyle Macy and the 1986 Pick Chicago Never Used
featuredDeepDive.intro: The oddity in Chicago's September 1984 exchange with Dallas is hidden inside the name attached to its return. The Bulls received a conditional 1986 second-round pick, later recorded as Rafael Addison at No. 39. Yet the Suns made that selection. Chicago had moved the pick to Phoenix the previous October in a free-agent compensation arrangement involving Kyle Macy. Meanwhile Dallas employed Wallace Bryant for 65 regular-season games. This deal was never a direct swap of Bryant for an Addison career in Chicago. Its actual branches involve NBA center depth and an asset transferred again before the draft.

sections.heading: Chicago Had a Conditional Selection, Not the Future Drafted Player
sections.body: The first transaction occurred September 14, 1984. Dallas sent Chicago its conditional 1986 second-round selection for Bryant, who had played 29 games for the Bulls. The future pick's ultimate identity is easy to find on historical draft databases because No. 39 became Rafael Addison. A parenthetical naming the eventual player is useful when tracing the paper asset, but it does not establish which team used the pick. That is a separate historical step. Addison's NBA career began in Phoenix after the Suns selected him. Any straight comparison of Bryant's Mavericks contribution against Addison's statistics as a Bull would assign playing value to a franchise for which Addison never suited up.

sections.heading: Dallas Used Bryant as a Temporary Rotation Center
sections.body: The Mavericks got an immediate roster option instead of waiting two years for the draft. Bryant started 35 of 56 appearances in 1984-85 and played 860 minutes, averaging 2.9 points and 4.3 rebounds. He returned for nine Dallas appearances in 1985-86, eight of them starts, before being waived in late November. These are real minutes and assignments, even if his limited scoring left little durable impact. Chicago could not retroactively receive that Dallas production, just as Dallas cannot claim Bryant's later Clippers stint. The 65 Dallas appearances are the measurable basketball return associated with the September acquisition and give the Mavericks grade a defensible factual anchor.

sections.heading: Phoenix Got the Draft Pick in a Two-Pick Macy Transaction
sections.body: On October 4, 1985, Chicago signed guard Kyle Macy as a veteran free agent. The official team transaction logs show that the Bulls sent Phoenix the Dallas-derived 1986 second-round pick and a separate 1990 second-round choice as compensation. Phoenix exercised No. 39 in 1986 on Addison, who played 62 NBA games for the Suns in 1986-87. His later Nets seasons likewise belong to later clubs. The 1984 Chicago-Dallas trade provided one of the chips Chicago later transferred, but Macy's signing also required the additional 1990 second. Treating the entire free-agent return as a product of Wallace Bryant alone would over-credit the first trade in the same way that counting Addison's Phoenix games would.

sections.heading: The Equal Grades Compare Different Forms of Limited Utility
sections.body: The two sides never received interchangeable returns. Dallas had a seven-footer available for a season and a short part of the next campaign, then released him. Chicago held a conditional future draft asset, used it as part of another personnel transaction and never selected a player with it. The raw draft-slot label makes the transaction look like Bryant versus Addison, but the actual exchange connects Bryant with limited Dallas minutes and the pick with Chicago's role in a later compensation payment. Even Trade and B-/B- are the source ledger's existing retrospective grades. The deeper record explains why those grades cannot rest on an imagined Addison tenure with the Bulls or a claim that Dallas secured a long-term center.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, Chicago B- and Dallas B-. Dallas obtained 65 games of Wallace Bryant center depth; Chicago acquired a conditional 1986 second-rounder and later transferred it with a 1990 pick to Phoenix as part of Kyle Macy's free-agent compensation. Rafael Addison was the Suns' No. 39 selection, not a Chicago draft product. The balanced verdict reflects the limited but traceable asset paths, with no invented player returns and no double credit for separate acquisitions.

sections.heading: Gervin Went to Chicago for Greenwood
sections.body: The Bulls acquired veteran scorer George Gervin from San Antonio on October 24, 1985, while the Spurs received forward David Greenwood. At age 33, Gervin brought one of the league's most accomplished scoring résumés but was nearing the end of his NBA career. Greenwood, still 28, represented a different type of basketball return for San Antonio: a younger frontcourt player who could fill a rotation role beyond one season. This transaction should therefore be considered as a trade of remaining player utility, not a comparison of each man's entire prior reputation.

sections.heading: Chicago Received One Full Season of Scoring
sections.body: Gervin played all 82 regular-season games for Chicago in 1985-86 and offered immediate offensive production on a roster still building around Michael Jordan. His appearance total made the acquisition more substantial than a brief late-career cameo, but he did not continue into additional NBA seasons afterward. Chicago obtained the benefit of a known professional scorer for one complete campaign. It did not gain the prime version of Gervin who had led the Spurs, and importing that earlier production would exaggerate what the Bulls actually received.

sections.heading: The Spurs Received the Longer Remaining Tenure
sections.body: Greenwood did not approach Gervin's historical standing as an NBA star, but he had more productive basketball seasons left when San Antonio acquired him. The Spurs obtained forward depth that could outlast the 1985-86 season, whereas Chicago's Gervin return effectively ended after that year. The retained grades recognize that contrast without pretending the player acquired by San Antonio was the better scorer in his prime. It was a narrow advantage created by the age and duration of the actual post-trade contributions.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Spurs Edge. San Antonio earns B+ for receiving the younger David Greenwood and more remaining team utility, while Chicago gets B for George Gervin's complete 82-game season of veteran scoring. The outcome favors the Spurs on duration, not on a claim that Greenwood had the greater historical career.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Why the Spurs Chose Greenwood Over Gervin in 1985
featuredDeepDive.intro: On October 24, 1985, San Antonio sent George Gervin to Chicago for David Greenwood in a direct player-for-player trade. Gervin was still a formidable scorer, but the 33-year-old had reached the final season of his Spurs contract and had a strained relationship with coach Cotton Fitzsimmons. Chicago acquired one full season of immediate offense; San Antonio received several seasons from a younger frontcourt contributor. The inherited slight Spurs edge, B+ to Chicago's B, measures what each club received after the transaction, not Gervin's much greater historical career.

sections.heading: A Superstar Exit Became a Deadline Decision Before Opening Night
sections.body: The trade happened a day before the 1985-86 season began, not at a February deadline. Contemporary reports from UPI and the Associated Press identify Gervin, 33, and Greenwood, 28, as the sole players exchanged. San Antonio's coach Cotton Fitzsimmons had disagreed with the former scoring champion, while management faced the final year of Gervin's contract. Spurs owner Angelo Drossos publicly acknowledged how difficult it was to move a figure who had carried the franchise from its ABA identity into the NBA. Chicago had a different reason to act: coach Stan Albeck had previously worked with Gervin in San Antonio and could use another reliable veteran scorer. The decision split sentiment from practical roster planning. Nothing in the contemporaneous reporting makes this a multi-player salary dump or a trade of draft selections; the exchange was one forward for one guard.

sections.heading: The Bulls Received 82 Games and 16.2 Points per Night
sections.body: Gervin did not fade into a handful of appearances after arriving in Chicago. He played all 82 regular-season games in 1985-86, averaging 16.2 points on 47.2 percent shooting over 25.2 minutes per game. That is a meaningful one-year return for a 33-year-old guard, especially once Michael Jordan missed most of his sophomore season with a foot injury. Jordan's injury came after the October trade, so it should be described as an unforeseen reason Gervin's scoring became useful, not as a known motivation for the transaction. The Bulls reached the postseason but were swept by Boston in the first round; Gervin played only two playoff games and scored no points in limited minutes. He never appeared in another NBA regular-season game, ending the Bulls' return after one full year.

sections.heading: Greenwood's First Spurs Season Was Useful, Not Star-Level
sections.body: San Antonio acquired a player whose strengths were different from Gervin's isolation scoring. In 1985-86, Greenwood played 68 games for the Spurs, starting 24 and averaging 7.9 points and 7.8 rebounds. He shot 51.0 percent from the floor and made three playoff starts when San Antonio faced the Lakers. The Spurs therefore got an available frontcourt player at a time when Gervin was approaching the end of his NBA career. Those numbers do not support calling Greenwood a replacement All-Star or a direct substitute for four previous Gervin scoring crowns. The attraction was age, rebounding and the ability to continue in a regular role. Because there were no accompanying draft picks, the proper comparison is the production of these two players after October 24 rather than hypothetical future assets.

sections.heading: The Second Year Shows Why San Antonio's Return Lasted Longer
sections.body: The separation became easier to measure in 1986-87, after Gervin's NBA playing career had ended. Greenwood started 78 of 79 Spurs games, logged 32.7 minutes per appearance and averaged 11.6 points with 9.9 rebounds. Those nearly double-digit boards gave San Antonio a concrete contribution well beyond Chicago's single Gervin campaign. His regular Spurs stint continued into 1988-89, though 1987-88 was cut to 45 appearances. That longer service supports the inherited Spurs B+ over the Bulls' B, but it is not evidence of a championship return or a new superstar. Greenwood later played for other clubs as well, so only the seasons and games he actually furnished to San Antonio should influence this evaluation. Duration is the differentiator, with the underlying quality kept in perspective.

sections.heading: Gervin's Spurs Legacy Was Bigger Than His Bulls Finish
sections.body: Evaluating this transaction by post-trade value must not erase what preceded it. Gervin had been San Antonio's defining perimeter scorer since the ABA years. Before leaving he accumulated 23,602 points for the Spurs and more than 60 franchise records, according to the NBA's historical profile; he later entered the Basketball Hall of Fame. Greenwood had nothing resembling that résumé and did not become a Spurs franchise icon. But Chicago paid for the remaining portion of Gervin's playing career, not the 1970s and early 1980s that made him famous. The Bulls enjoyed a healthy 82-game scorer for a season; the Spurs obtained a younger big who played more than one useful campaign. A slight San Antonio verdict holds both truths: the sentimental cost of moving the Iceman was high, while the forward-looking roster value still leaned toward Greenwood.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Spurs Edge — San Antonio B+, Chicago B. George Gervin gave the Bulls all 82 games and 16.2 points per game in 1985-86 before his NBA career ended. David Greenwood followed 68 San Antonio games at 7.9 points and 7.8 rebounds with a 79-game, 11.6-point and 9.9-rebound season in 1986-87. The extra service favors San Antonio without suggesting Greenwood surpassed Gervin as a player, delivered a championship, or produced an unlisted downstream asset.

sections.heading: Chicago Traded Three Rights Assets for Steve Colter
sections.body: On June 17, 1986, Chicago acquired guard Steve Colter from Portland, sending the rights to its freshly selected No. 28 second-rounder Larry Krystkowiak plus 1987 and 1992 second-round selections. The Chicago Bulls historical media guide and both clubs’ Basketball Reference transaction pages agree on the exchange. Colter had started 51 of 81 games with Portland in 1985-86, averaging 8.7 points and 3.2 assists, making him a plausible backcourt option for a rebuilding Bulls club. This was not a simple one-for-one player swap: Chicago surrendered a drafted forward and two future second-round opportunities for the guard.

sections.heading: Colter Contributed 27 Chicago Games Before Moving Again
sections.body: In Chicago, Colter played 27 regular-season games in 1986-87, starting 18 and averaging 4.9 points with 3.5 assists. His field-goal percentage fell to 34.5 percent in that stint. He finished the same season with Philadelphia, producing 43 appearances and 13 starts there, which must not be credited to the Bulls as return from the Portland transaction. The on-court Chicago payoff was short-lived, even though acquiring a relatively experienced point guard made immediate roster sense. Colter’s subsequent Washington games are also outside the direct receiving-franchise outcome.

sections.heading: Portland Immediately Used the Krystkowiak Rights in a Second Deal
sections.body: Only two days later, on June 19, Portland included Larry Krystkowiak’s rights alongside veteran Mychal Thompson in a trade to San Antonio for Steve Johnson. Krystkowiak therefore played no regular-season NBA games for Portland from this deal. He later made his NBA debut with San Antonio, then had several Milwaukee seasons, but those statistics do not belong to Portland’s direct 1986 court return. More important, Steve Johnson was acquired for a two-piece Portland package rather than for Krystkowiak alone. The rights had transactional utility, not guaranteed Portland playing minutes.

sections.heading: Two Second-Round Picks Went through Other Clubs
sections.body: The future choices had unusually long downstream chains. Portland traded the 1987 second-round selection to Milwaukee on November 11, 1986 for Chris Engler, and the Bucks later used No. 40 on Winston Garland. The 1992 pick became No. 54 Brett Roberts, but Sacramento actually made that selection after Portland included it in a separate August 1990 Danny Ainge transaction. Roberts never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Those outcomes establish that Portland received assets it could move, not that Garland or Roberts played for the Blazers. The protected verdict is Blazers Win with Portland A- and Chicago C+, reflecting three future-use options versus Colter’s 27-game Chicago stint.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Blazers Win, Portland A- and Chicago C+ remain inherited grades. Chicago received only 27 games and 18 starts from Steve Colter. Portland acquired Krystkowiak rights used two days later with Mychal Thompson in the Steve Johnson swap, a 1987 second later traded to Milwaukee for Chris Engler, and a 1992 second eventually selected by Sacramento at No. 54. These multi-asset downstream transactions are context, not player statistics or one-for-one gains assigned directly to the original Colter exchange.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Chicago Bought Steve Colter with Three Assets in 1986; Portland Recycled Every One
featuredDeepDive.intro: The 1986 Bulls-Blazers trade gave Chicago a veteran point guard, Steve Colter, at the cost of Larry Krystkowiak’s fresh draft rights and two future second-rounders. Colter played 27 Bulls regular-season games. Portland quickly rerouted the forward’s rights with Mychal Thompson, later dealt the 1987 pick to Milwaukee, and conveyed the 1992 selection to Sacramento in a separate Danny Ainge deal. The private Blazers Win and A-/C+ grades can be evaluated without pretending Garland, Roberts or Krystkowiak ever played a Blazers NBA game.

sections.heading: A Draft-Day Roster Choice under New Bulls Coach Doug Collins
sections.body: Chicago hired Doug Collins in May 1986 and was trying to build a workable rotation around Michael Jordan. On June 17, the Bulls drafted Montana forward Larry Krystkowiak at No. 28 but traded his rights to Portland along with two future second-rounders for Steve Colter. The club’s official historical media guide lists exactly those assets. Colter had been a functional Portland guard in 1985-86 with 81 appearances and 51 starts, posting 8.7 points and 3.2 assists. A guard with recent starter experience held obvious practical appeal; the longer-term cost was the ability to choose future prospects and trade rights later.

sections.heading: Colter’s Actual Chicago Return Did Not Last a Full Season
sections.body: Basketball Reference lists Colter with just 27 Chicago games, 18 starts and 473 total minutes in 1986-87. His 4.9 points and 3.5 assists helped give the Bulls ballhandling while the team reshaped its personnel, but he moved to Philadelphia within the same season and scored 6.8 points per game there in 43 appearances. Those Philadelphia minutes were generated after a different transaction, not as Chicago games. The private C+ grade should not be interpreted as an indictment of every Colter skill: it simply reflects the short realized Chicago tenure against three outgoing assets.

sections.heading: Krystkowiak’s Rights Passed through Portland within 48 Hours
sections.body: Krystkowiak is remembered for his NBA years with San Antonio and especially Milwaukee rather than Portland, for a straightforward reason. The Blazers had his rights on June 17 and sent them, together with Mychal Thompson, to the Spurs for Steve Johnson on June 19. That later deal’s price included Thompson, a veteran big man with extensive Portland playing time. It is therefore misleading to say the Bulls trade alone brought Steve Johnson to the Blazers without identifying the additional consideration. But the rapid rerouting shows how acquiring a draft-rights asset could create immediate negotiating flexibility independent of the player ever wearing a Portland uniform.

sections.heading: Garland and Roberts Traveled on Separate Draft Chains
sections.body: The 1987 second-rounder was sent onward to Milwaukee in November 1986 for Chris Engler, and the Bucks used it in June 1987 to choose Winston Garland at No. 40. The future 1992 second was included by Portland with Byron Irvin and cash in an August 1990 transaction bringing Danny Ainge from Sacramento, along with other draft considerations in that deal. Sacramento selected Brett Roberts at No. 54 in 1992; he did not play in the NBA. Both outcomes should be attributed to the picks’ provenance rather than rewritten as Portland player statistics. That distinction is why the three incoming Portland rights assets can be valuable without equating them to three direct Blazers roster contributors.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The stored Blazers Win, Portland A- and Chicago C+ grades are unchanged. Colter produced 27 Chicago appearances and was later traded again. Portland converted Krystkowiak rights into one component of a separate Steve Johnson deal, passed the 1987 second to Milwaukee and conveyed the 1992 second through the Danny Ainge trade to Sacramento. Garland and Roberts are pick outcomes, not Blazers NBA playing returns. Preserving all three original asset paths is essential to the trade’s historical value comparison.
