sections.heading: Chicago Obtained Cureton Plus an Additional Draft Chance
sections.body: On August 21, 1986, Chicago moved forward Sidney Green to Detroit and received veteran big man Earl Cureton and a 1987 second-round pick. That selection was ultimately No. 28, used on Rickie Winslow. The transaction supplied the Bulls with an immediate frontcourt option and another chance to add a younger player. Detroit took one established forward rather than dividing its return between a veteran reserve and a later pick. Both clubs acquired basketball assets with quite different timelines.

sections.heading: The Two Bulls Assets Need Separate Treatment
sections.body: Cureton was an experienced interior player, so his near-term use is distinct from the uncertainty of Chicago’s later second-round selection. Winslow’s No. 28 placement confirms exactly which pick resulted from the trade, but a drafted name alone is not evidence of substantial NBA production. Detroit received Green directly and could evaluate him as part of its regular frontcourt rather than wait on draft conversion. The exchange therefore involved real roster choices on both sides, not merely paper value assigned to a selection.

sections.heading: The Grade Advantage Belongs to Chicago, With Limits
sections.body: The archived verdict is Bulls Win: Chicago B-plus and Detroit C-plus. The Bulls obtained two identifiable returns from the outgoing Green contract, while the Pistons concentrated their exchange on a single forward. That helps explain the higher Chicago grade but should not be inflated into a claim that Winslow became a major future star. The dated transaction ledger substantiates the asset routes; further seasonal production comparisons would require the relevant player game histories rather than repeated grading slogans.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win — Chicago B-plus, Detroit C-plus. The Bulls acquired veteran Earl Cureton and the second-round selection used on Rickie Winslow at No. 28 in 1987. Detroit received Sidney Green. Chicago’s two-part return earns the recorded advantage without crediting the selection with NBA impact beyond what the available evidence supports.

sections.heading: The Exchange in Full
sections.body: Chicago traded center Jawann Oldham to the New York Knicks on October 30, 1986, and obtained a 1987 first-round selection and 1988 second-round consideration. The first-rounder became the No. 8 pick used on Olden Polynice in June 1987. The later second-round choice is traced to No. 35 and Sylvester Gray. Those draft assets were Chicago's return; Polynice and Gray were not players delivered to the Bulls on the 1986 trade date.

sections.heading: Where the Value Separated
sections.body: The timing explains why this exchange was much more valuable to Chicago than its single-player appearance suggests. Nearly eight months after the Oldham deal, the Bulls used the No. 8 selection on Polynice and traded his rights to Seattle in the draft-night package that brought Scottie Pippen to Chicago. Pippen did not arrive days after the October transaction. He came on June 22, 1987, in a separate trade that also involved other draft considerations.

sections.heading: The Stronger Return
sections.body: Chicago's opportunity began with control of a first-round selection it otherwise would not have held. The No. 8 pick supplied the Polynice rights that Seattle accepted as part of its Pippen deal. The 1988 second-round asset added another negotiable piece, though its later journey involved additional transactions. Crediting the initial Knicks trade with making the Pippen acquisition possible is defensible; claiming the Knicks directly traded Pippen to Chicago is not.

sections.heading: What the Other Side Bought
sections.body: New York received Jawann Oldham, a veteran big man, in exchange for both draft assets. Its return was a current player rather than a future selection, but the Knicks surrendered the No. 8 pick's substantial flexibility. Their F grade reflects how badly that value comparison developed once Chicago used the first-round asset in the Pippen transaction. The judgment does not require pretending New York traded away Pippen himself in October 1986.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win — Chicago A-, New York F. Oldham went to the Knicks on October 30, 1986; Chicago received first- and second-round draft consideration. The first-round selection became No. 8, Olden Polynice, in June 1987. That pick was then part of a separate draft-night exchange with Seattle that delivered Scottie Pippen to Chicago. The historic upside comes from the asset chain, not from claiming Pippen joined the Bulls within days of the Oldham trade.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Chicago Bulls–New York Knicks: What the Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: On October 30, 1986, the Bulls obtained a 1987 first-round choice and future second-round consideration from the Knicks for Jawann Oldham. The larger historical payoff occurred the following June, not within days: Chicago used the No. 8 choice on Olden Polynice, whose draft rights became a central element of the separate Seattle agreement for Scottie Pippen. Following each transaction in order keeps the original exchange distinct from the draft-night outcome.

sections.heading: The Asset That Moved the Evaluation
sections.body: The No. 8 selection is the hinge between the two transactions. New York surrendered it for Oldham in October 1986. On June 22, 1987, Chicago selected Olden Polynice there; Seattle selected Scottie Pippen at No. 5. The Bulls then sent Polynice's rights and other draft consideration to Seattle for Pippen and an additional pick. The important point is not that Polynice starred in Chicago, but that the draft asset became leverage in a later trade.

sections.heading: Secondary Pieces and Their Weight
sections.body: The 1988 second-round consideration cannot be ignored merely because Pippen became the headline. The pick is identified in the transaction history as No. 35, Sylvester Gray, and Chicago later included that asset in the Seattle package. Its path illustrates how even a secondary pick can be moved again rather than used by the team that initially acquired it. But the separate 1987 first-round selection was the far more consequential piece in the Bulls' October return.

sections.heading: Trade-Day Logic Versus Realized Outcome
sections.body: Chicago exchanged an active center for future draft flexibility; New York made the opposite choice. The Knicks could use Oldham immediately while the Bulls accepted the delay and uncertainty of two picks. Only after the 1987 draft and the separate Seattle agreement could the full strategic importance of the No. 8 choice be seen. This sequence gives the trade a compelling retrospective story without granting either team knowledge of the precise future deal in October.

sections.heading: Reading the Grade Spread
sections.body: The stored Bulls Win verdict and A- for Chicago against F for New York reflect the huge difference in what each side ultimately controlled. Chicago's No. 8 pick helped unlock the Pippen acquisition, whereas the Knicks received Oldham. The second-round choice belongs in the accounting but should not be assigned an invented Chicago playing career. The grades describe the transaction's downstream value, while the dates and distinct trading partners prevent conflating two deals.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The October 1986 Knicks trade gave Chicago the No. 8 draft opportunity, which later helped finance the June 22, 1987 Seattle agreement for Scottie Pippen. New York received Jawann Oldham. The second-round pick's subsequent route is also documented, but its value was secondary to the first-round asset. Chicago A-, New York F and Bulls Win remain the recorded outcome, now tied to the correct dates, recipients and distinct transactions rather than repeated hindsight filler.

sources.title: Chicago Bulls official media guide — all-time transactions 1986–1987

sections.heading: Threatt Arrived as Chicago Sought Another Playmaker
sections.body: Chicago acquired Sedale Threatt from Philadelphia on December 31, 1986, sending Steve Colter and a future second-round choice. The selection was ultimately exercised at No. 32 in the 1989 draft, when Philadelphia chose Stanley Brundy. The exchange was not simply one guard for another: the Bulls gave up a second opportunity to add talent through the draft. At the time, Michael Jordan was already Chicago’s focal scorer, and acquiring a guard who could handle the ball supplied a practical way to support that backcourt.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Accepted a Guard and a Later Draft Selection
sections.body: The 76ers received Colter immediately, along with the choice that became Brundy. Colter was an NBA guard rather than a speculative rights claim, so Philadelphia acquired present roster depth as well as a later selection. But a future second-round pick could only become as useful as the player chosen with it. Brundy did not establish a long NBA career, limiting the lasting return on that component. This helps explain why two incoming assets did not automatically make Philadelphia’s package more valuable.

sections.heading: Threatt's Chicago Guard Value Exceeded the Colter and Brundy Return
sections.body: Threatt's established NBA backcourt ability gave Chicago the stronger immediate option and supports Bulls Win, Chicago B-plus and Philadelphia C-plus. Chicago exchanged Colter and the Brundy selection for Threatt’s established backcourt ability, receiving the more attractive immediate basketball option. Philadelphia gained a usable guard and draft flexibility, which deserves credit even though its longer-term outcome was less compelling. The comparison depends on these players and this draft selection, rather than generalized assertions about how every two-for-one trade should be judged.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win — Chicago B-plus, Philadelphia C-plus. The Bulls traded Steve Colter and the future No. 32 pick, ultimately Stanley Brundy, for Sedale Threatt. Threatt supplied the established guard they targeted. Philadelphia received an NBA guard and a real second-round opportunity, but the pick did not become a major long-term return. Chicago gets the better documented basketball result.

sections.heading: Chicago Traded Up for a Prospect It Had Scouted More Aggressively
sections.body: Scottie Pippen entered the 1987 draft from Central Arkansas rather than a national powerhouse, and his rise from equipment manager to elite prospect required teams to project unusual growth. Chicago general manager Jerry Krause and the Bulls’ scouts treated his length, ball handling and defensive instincts as worth moving from No. 8 to No. 5. Seattle selected Pippen for Chicago, while the Bulls selected Olden Polynice for the SuperSonics and included additional draft considerations. The transaction began with conviction about a specific developmental profile, not hindsight about a finished Hall of Famer.

sections.heading: Pippen’s Skills Solved the Problems Created by Building Around Jordan
sections.body: Michael Jordan already supplied extraordinary scoring and on-ball creation. Chicago needed a second star who could defend the opponent’s best perimeter player, initiate offense when Jordan rested and thrive without demanding every possession. Pippen became exactly that player. His size allowed him to switch across positions, his passing accelerated the transition game and his willingness to function as a secondary scorer kept the offense balanced. The Bulls did not merely acquire another talented wing; they acquired the rare star whose strengths increased Jordan’s freedom rather than duplicating his role.

sections.heading: The Additional Draft Considerations Did Not Narrow the Pippen Gap
sections.body: The documented transaction included future first-round swap language and a second-round pick in addition to the exchange of draft rights. Seattle received the useful side of that later movement, including the slot used on B.J. Armstrong before Chicago eventually acquired him through a separate transaction. Those details matter because they show the Sonics did not receive only Polynice. They still do not alter the evaluation. The secondary assets produced ordinary roster value, while Pippen became the two-way star who made Chicago’s championship structure possible.

sections.heading: Polynice Had a Long Career but Never Approached the Lost Ceiling
sections.body: Seattle did receive an NBA player. Polynice became a durable center, started hundreds of games and later returned to the SuperSonics after stops with other teams. That production keeps the Seattle grade above an absolute F. The return nevertheless lacked star impact and did not create a comparable downstream asset. The Sonics moved away from the fifth pick and obtained a conventional interior role player while Chicago secured one of the greatest two-way wings in league history. Longevity alone cannot narrow that difference.

sections.heading: Six Championships Make the Realized Value Almost Impossible to Match
sections.body: Pippen became a seven-time All-Star, a perennial All-Defensive selection and an indispensable member of every Bulls championship team from 1991 through 1998. During Jordan’s first retirement, he also demonstrated that his value was not merely dependent on playing beside the league’s best scorer, leading Chicago to 55 wins and finishing third in MVP voting. The trade gave the Bulls a player who could serve as complementary superstar, primary initiator and defensive system all within the same roster architecture.

sections.heading: The Grades Should Preserve Seattle’s Functional Return Without Softening the Verdict
sections.body: Chicago’s A+ is automatic because the transaction helped build six championships and delivered a franchise icon at a manageable acquisition cost. Seattle’s D recognizes that Polynice was a legitimate long-term NBA center and that draft-night prospect uncertainty was real. A higher grade would ignore the scale of the surrendered opportunity and the secondary pick value Chicago retained. The Sonics obtained serviceable interior play; the Bulls obtained the player who made their dynasty structurally possible.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Chicago wins with an A+, while Seattle remains at D. The Bulls traded from No. 8 to No. 5 because they believed Pippen’s defense, playmaking and physical development could complement Jordan. He became a seven-time All-Star, one of the sport’s greatest defenders and a central figure in all six championships. Polynice produced a long and respectable career, so Seattle did not receive nothing. The return was still ordinary compared with the two-way superstar and additional draft leverage Chicago obtained. This is the franchise’s defining transaction standard.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Scottie Pippen Was the Trade That Made the Bulls’ Dynasty Scalable
featuredDeepDive.intro: Jordan was capable of making Chicago relevant by himself, but sustained championship basketball required a second player who could absorb nearly every task around him. Pippen became that player because the Bulls identified traits that were more valuable than his small-school résumé suggested. The trade also demonstrates why fit can multiply star talent. Pippen did not reduce Jordan’s impact by competing for the same role; he expanded the number of ways Chicago could defend, create and win. Six championships were the eventual result of that compatibility.

sections.heading: Central Arkansas Required Projection Rather Than Brand Recognition
sections.body: Pippen’s path made evaluation harder. He had grown significantly after high school, played at an NAIA program and developed ball skills unusual for his eventual size. Teams had to decide whether those traits would translate against NBA athletes. Chicago’s scouting process focused on the combination rather than the level of competition: a long defender who had learned guard responsibilities and could continue growing into his frame. The Bulls moved before another team could retain him, demonstrating that the organization valued its private evaluation enough to surrender concrete draft assets.

sections.heading: Pippen Became the Defense’s Point Guard
sections.body: Chicago’s championship defenses depended on more than individual stops. Pippen could pressure ball handlers, switch onto forwards, roam into passing lanes and trigger transition offense after steals or rebounds. His versatility allowed the Bulls to use aggressive schemes without constantly exposing mismatches behind Jordan. Describing him only as Jordan’s sidekick misses the tactical function. Pippen often organized the defense in the way a point guard organizes an offense, seeing actions early and moving teammates into positions that turned pressure into fast-break opportunities.

sections.heading: His Playmaking Reduced the Burden on Jordan
sections.body: Pippen’s ability to bring the ball up, initiate the triangle and create for teammates allowed Jordan to conserve energy and attack from more favorable spots. Opponents could not solve Chicago simply by trapping Jordan because Pippen could become the primary handler and punish rotations. That flexibility became especially important against playoff defenses designed around removing first options. The trade therefore supplied more than a second scorer. It gave the Bulls another offensive organizer whose passing and size made the entire system less predictable.

sections.heading: The 1993-94 Season Proved Independent Star Value
sections.body: When Jordan retired after the first three-peat, Pippen led the Bulls to 55 wins and came close to returning them to the conference finals. He made First Team All-NBA and finished third in MVP voting. That season is essential to grading the trade because it shows Chicago had acquired a player capable of sustaining elite team performance as the primary star, not merely someone elevated by Jordan’s presence. When Jordan returned, Pippen’s willingness to resume a complementary structure became a strength rather than evidence of limited ability.

sections.heading: Seattle’s Return Shows the Difference Between Career Value and Franchise Value
sections.body: Polynice played fifteen NBA seasons and filled a position every team needed in that era. Evaluated in isolation, that is a successful professional career. Trade grading asks a different question: what did the acquired player create for the franchise relative to what departed? Seattle did not build a contender around Polynice, did not convert him into a premium later asset and did not receive a player whose influence approached Pippen’s. The Bulls turned one draft-night maneuver into the connective tissue of a dynasty.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pippen made the Bulls’ championship model repeatable. His defense, passing and ability to shift between primary and secondary responsibility allowed Chicago to survive different opponents, roster adjustments and even Jordan’s first retirement. That comprehensive value warrants the A+. Seattle’s D acknowledges Polynice’s respectable career and the uncertainty of projecting a small-school prospect, but the Sonics surrendered a player who became one of the league’s defining two-way stars. Chicago did not simply win the talent comparison; it acquired the structural partner that turned greatness into six titles.

sections.heading: Chicago and Seattle Exchanged Established Guards
sections.body: On February 25, 1988, Chicago acquired guard Sam Vincent from the Seattle SuperSonics and sent Sedale Threatt in the opposite direction. Each club received a named NBA player, so this was not a speculative rights deal or a transaction involving a conditional pick. The late-February timing placed the exchange within the stretch run of the 1987–88 regular season. Chicago was looking at backcourt options around Michael Jordan, while Seattle obtained a different experienced guard for its roster.

sections.heading: Threatt and Vincent Offered Different Backcourt Profiles
sections.body: Threatt was a capable NBA guard with the ability to handle possessions and provide perimeter support. Vincent offered Chicago another option in its rotation. The retrospective question is which incoming player delivered the stronger useful return to his receiving club, not which had the better reputation years later or what other teams eventually gained from their later careers. Chicago traded away Threatt and received Vincent; Seattle received Threatt. Neither package included extra selections or cash that need to be counted alongside the guards.

sections.heading: The Ledger Awards Seattle the Stronger Result
sections.body: The published grades are Seattle B-plus and Chicago C-plus, producing Seattle SuperSonics Win. That gap reflects the stronger overall evaluation of the guard Seattle acquired rather than a claim that Vincent was never useful to Chicago. Both franchises received actual basketball talent and could make a plausible trade-day argument for a change in roles. The source record identifies the direct player exchange; it does not authorize adding unrelated playoff runs or later franchises’ transactions as if they were included in February 1988.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Seattle SuperSonics Win — Seattle B-plus, Chicago C-plus. The SuperSonics received Sedale Threatt and the Bulls obtained Sam Vincent in a direct exchange of NBA guards. Seattle’s incoming player earns the stronger retrospective grade in the ledger. Chicago still received a roster contributor, so the result should be expressed as a graded edge rather than an imaginary one-sided asset transfer.

sections.heading: Chicago Traded Popularity for a More Necessary Position
sections.body: Charles Oakley was young, productive, and deeply valued by Michael Jordan, so Chicago's decision carried real internal and public risk. General manager Jerry Krause believed the roster needed a true center more than it needed to preserve a powerful rebounder whose role overlapped with the emerging Horace Grant. Bill Cartwright was older and had endured foot injuries, but his size allowed the Bulls to defend the league's biggest frontcourts without forcing Grant or Scottie Pippen into unsuitable assignments. The trade was an exercise in roster geometry rather than a simple talent ranking.

sections.heading: Cartwright Became the Starting Center for Three Champions
sections.body: Cartwright's counting statistics declined from his early Knicks peak, yet his Chicago value came from responsibilities that championship teams needed filled. He defended the post, set physical screens, passed within the triangle offense, and accepted a low-usage role beside Jordan and Pippen. The Bulls eventually broke through Detroit and won three consecutive championships with Cartwright starting in the middle. That result makes the deal a clear success for Chicago, because the acquired player solved the exact structural problem that motivated the trade.

sections.heading: New York Also Acquired a Player Who Defined Its Identity
sections.body: Oakley was not a consolation prize. He became the Knicks' leading rebounder, interior enforcer, and one of the clearest symbols of the physical teams built around Patrick Ewing. New York reached the playoffs throughout his tenure and developed the defensive culture that made it a persistent Eastern contender. Oakley's durability and connection with the fan base gave the Knicks more long-term regular-season value than Cartwright would likely have provided behind Ewing. The transaction therefore produced two successful fits rather than one winner and one failure.

sections.heading: The Draft-Pick Exchange Added Value on Both Sides
sections.body: Chicago and New York also exchanged first- and third-round positions. The Bulls moved up to No. 11 and selected Will Perdue, who later supplied frontcourt depth for championship teams. The Knicks used No. 19 on Rod Strickland, a far more accomplished individual player, although his first New York stint lasted only one season before another trade. The draft layer prevents the deal from being reduced to Cartwright versus Oakley. New York found more individual talent with its first-rounder, while Chicago received a player who fit its developing title structure.

sections.heading: The Rings Create an Edge but Not a One-Sided Verdict
sections.body: Championship contribution deserves heavy weight, especially when the incoming player's role directly addressed a weakness that had blocked postseason progress. That gives Chicago the top grade. It would be misleading, however, to treat New York's side as merely average. Oakley helped shape a decade of playoff relevance, and Strickland became a high-level guard even though the Knicks did not retain him long enough to capture his full prime. The result is better described as a slight Bulls edge than a broad Bulls win over a disappointing Knicks return.

sections.heading: A and A-Minus Better Represent Two Coherent Team-Building Decisions
sections.body: Chicago's A recognizes three titles, a solved positional need, and useful value from Perdue. New York's A-minus recognizes a decade of Oakley production, a defining defensive identity, and the selection of Strickland. The small separation reflects championship consequence rather than a large difference in acquired talent. This grading also captures an important lesson: trades can improve both teams when each side understands its roster. Chicago needed center size; New York needed rebounding and toughness beside Ewing. Both organizations received exactly that.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Chicago receives a slight edge with an A, while New York earns an A-minus. Cartwright became the starting center for the Bulls' first three championships and gave the roster the positional balance Krause wanted. Oakley became an essential Knick, anchored the rebounding and physical culture of a perennial playoff team, and remained productive far longer. The associated first-round picks produced Will Perdue for Chicago and Rod Strickland for New York. Rings decide the narrow ordering, but this was a successful exchange for both franchises.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Cartwright for Oakley Was a Rare Trade in Which Fit Beat Sentiment for Both Teams
featuredDeepDive.intro: The 1988 exchange is often remembered through Jordan's displeasure at losing Oakley or through Cartwright's rings. The complete story is more balanced. Chicago accepted short-term discomfort to construct a more natural championship frontcourt, while New York acquired the power forward who would personify its defensive era. Each team used the same transaction to solve a different problem. The slight Bulls edge comes from the championship payoff, not from a claim that New York misread Oakley's value.

sections.heading: Jordan’s Objection Made the Organizational Bet More Difficult
sections.body: Oakley was Jordan's close friend and on-court protector, so moving him risked alienating the franchise's central player. Krause proceeded because team building sometimes requires separating personal comfort from positional need. Horace Grant's development gave Chicago another power forward, while Cartwright could absorb the center assignments that had exposed smaller lineups. The front office's willingness to withstand immediate criticism became part of the trade's value. It allowed the roster to evolve before postseason losses forced a more desperate move.

sections.heading: Cartwright’s Low-Usage Role Was a Feature, Not a Decline to Ignore
sections.body: A direct statistical comparison naturally favors Oakley's rebounding volume and longevity. Chicago did not need Cartwright to reproduce his early Knicks scoring. It needed him to defend, screen, occupy opposing centers, and keep the offense moving without demanding touches from Jordan or Pippen. Those functions became more valuable as the triangle offense matured. Evaluating him as though the Bulls had traded for a primary scorer would miss the reason the acquisition worked. His reduced box-score role was compatible with the team's hierarchy and championship goals.

sections.heading: Oakley Gave the Knicks the Frontcourt Partner Ewing Needed
sections.body: New York could afford to move Cartwright because Ewing had become the center of the franchise. Oakley supplied a complementary skill set: elite rebounding, physical defense, hard screens, and emotional force. The Knicks' identity in the 1990s depended on winning difficult possessions and making opponents uncomfortable. Oakley was central to that approach. Although New York did not win a championship, repeated deep playoff runs and a Finals appearance demonstrate that the acquired fit supported a legitimate contender rather than merely entertaining the home crowd.

sections.heading: The Pick Swap Shows Different Kinds of Asset Capture
sections.body: Strickland became the superior individual player from the exchanged draft slots, but New York moved him before realizing most of that value. Perdue developed into a reserve big who fit Chicago's championship rotation and was later traded for Dennis Rodman, creating an additional downstream connection to the second three-peat. That later move is graded separately, yet it illustrates how a modest draft asset can remain useful when the original team preserves it. The pick component strengthened both returns in different ways and further narrows the final verdict.

sections.heading: The Trade Demonstrates Why “Best Player” Is Not Always the Best Test
sections.body: Oakley was younger and produced more impressive conventional statistics after the trade, while Cartwright became the piece attached to three championships. Selecting one winner requires deciding whether the grade measures isolated player quality or organizational outcome. TradeVerdicts should weigh both. New York captured the stronger long-term individual performer; Chicago captured the more consequential role for its specific roster. That balance supports near-equal grades with Chicago ahead only because Cartwright's fit directly helped convert an elite team into a champion.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Bulls win by the smallest meaningful margin. Cartwright's presence at center, Perdue's supporting value, and three championships justify Chicago's A. Oakley's decade of rebounding, defense, and cultural importance beside Ewing, plus the Strickland selection, justify New York's A-minus. This was not a case of the Knicks losing because Chicago later raised banners. It was a two-sided roster correction in which both clubs acquired players better suited to their next phase. Chicago's ultimate team result supplies the tiebreaker.

sections.heading: Chicago Acquired Hodges for Nealy, a Future Second and Cash
sections.body: Chicago acquired three-point specialist Craig Hodges from Phoenix on December 14, 1988, sending Ed Nealy, a 1989 second-round selection and cash the other way. Phoenix eventually used No. 46 in the 1989 draft to select Ricky Blanton, who did not appear in a Suns regular-season game. The terms therefore produced distinguishable returns: Chicago received a shooting guard who immediately entered its rotation, while Phoenix held a modest veteran frontcourt option and the future pick. The deal also included financial consideration, but the transaction histories do not establish a reliable dollar amount; assigning one would misrepresent the documented package. Blanton's two later NBA games for Chicago in a separate stage of his career are not a Phoenix return.

sections.heading: Hodges Immediately Supplied a Verified Shooting Return
sections.body: Hodges played 49 regular-season games for Chicago after arriving during 1988–89. He hit 71 of 168 three-point attempts, or 42.3 percent, and averaged 10.0 points across those games. He then made 87 of 181 threes in 1989–90, a 48.1 percent clip. Those are concrete early returns from a specialist Chicago could use without expecting him to run its offense.

sections.heading: Phoenix's Player and Pick Returns Were Limited
sections.body: Nealy appeared in 30 Suns games during 1988–89, averaging 5.5 minutes and 0.6 points. That modest contribution was real, not a zero, although it was far below Hodges's Chicago role. Phoenix drafted Ricky Blanton with the incoming No. 46 selection in 1989. Blanton did not play for the Suns in an NBA regular-season game; his two career NBA appearances came for Chicago in 1992–93. His later Bulls games cannot be booked as a Phoenix return.

sections.heading: An A- for Chicago and C+ for Phoenix
sections.body: The Bulls retained Hodges through 1991–92. He played 63 games in 1989–90, 73 in the 1990–91 championship season and 56 in 1991–92, producing 241 Chicago regular-season appearances in all. Hodges also won the NBA's Three-Point Contest in 1990, 1991 and 1992. These achievements shouldn't convert a supporting player into the driver of two titles, but they explain why Chicago's A- is more defensible than Phoenix's C+: the Bulls kept useful shooting for four seasons while the Suns' immediate player and draft returns were small.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Chicago Bulls Win — Chicago A-, Phoenix C+. Hodges produced 241 Bulls regular-season appearances between December 1988 and 1992, including a 42.3 percent three-point mark after the trade in 1988–89 and 48.1 percent in 1989–90. Nealy logged 30 Phoenix games that first season, and No. 46 Ricky Blanton never appeared for the Suns. The separate cash consideration is acknowledged but not assigned an unsupported monetary value.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The Hodges Return, Nealy's Suns Minutes and the No. 46 Pick
featuredDeepDive.intro: A December 1988 exchange of one established shooter for a reserve forward, a second-rounder and cash gave Chicago a useful veteran for its first two championship seasons. Phoenix's draft pick became Ricky Blanton, but he never played a regular-season game for the Suns. Tracking each asset to the team that actually used it explains the Bulls Win verdict and the A-/C+ grades.

sections.heading: The Deal and Why the Draft Pick Needs Attribution
sections.body: Phoenix's transaction history identifies December 14, 1988 as the day Hodges went to the Bulls for Ed Nealy and a 1989 second-round choice. The local canonical trade ledger includes cash as a further Phoenix consideration, but does not report its amount. The second-rounder's eventual No. 46 slot is important because it identifies Ricky Blanton as the actual selection. It doesn't mean Blanton was already an NBA contributor when the rights changed hands.

sections.heading: Chicago Acquired a Specialist, Not a Franchise Star
sections.body: Across the rest of 1988–89, Hodges scored 490 points in 49 Bulls games and made 71 threes. His 1989–90 shooting was even more striking: 87 makes in 181 attempts from beyond the arc. His role diminished in minutes as the Bulls' championship group matured, yet he still appeared in 73 regular-season games in 1990–91 and 56 in 1991–92. Both seasons ended with Chicago championships, an accurate association that doesn't assign him responsibility for the team's entire success.

sections.heading: Nealy, the Draft Selection and the Cash Had Different Outcomes
sections.body: Nealy's first Phoenix stint after the deal produced 30 appearances and 164 minutes in 1988–89. He later played elsewhere and had another Suns stint, but those later roster moves should not be silently added to the original immediate return. Blanton's path makes the distinction sharper: a knee injury kept him out of the NBA in 1989–90; he didn't play for Phoenix and eventually logged two NBA games for the Bulls in 1992–93. Cash was part of the reported transaction asset package, yet an unreported amount provides no sound basis for inventing a comparable basketball return.

sections.heading: The Shooting Seasons Support the Original Winner
sections.body: Chicago received 241 games over four regular seasons from Hodges and an outside-shooting option that fit its developing championship roster. His Three-Point Contest titles from 1990 through 1992 demonstrate his specialty, although a contest trophy isn't the same as a playoff contribution. Phoenix's Nealy/Blanton return was materially thinner in actual Suns minutes. The evidence supports Chicago Bulls Win with an A- for Chicago and C+ for Phoenix, rather than overstating Chicago's acquisition as a perfect A.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Chicago Bulls Win, Chicago A- and Phoenix C+. Hodges shot 42.3 percent from three across 49 post-trade Bulls games in 1988–89 and 48.1 percent across 63 games the next year. His 241-game Bulls tenure extended through the 1991 and 1992 title seasons. Nealy played 30 immediate Suns games, and Blanton's two eventual NBA appearances were in Chicago, not Phoenix. The cash term remains unquantified.

sections.heading: The Trade, Asset by Asset
sections.body: Chicago acquired the 1989 first-round selection that became No. 18, B.J. Armstrong, from Seattle on June 26, 1989. In exchange, the SuperSonics received Brad Sellers. The draft selection was the only asset moving to the Bulls, while Seattle acquired a player with existing NBA experience. Treating this as a Bulls transaction for an already established NBA guard would misstate the original terms: the pick converted into Armstrong at the 1989 draft, and his career unfolded afterward.

sections.heading: B.J. Armstrong Turned No. 18 Into Three Championship Seasons
sections.body: Chicago obtained Seattle's No. 18 selection in the 1989 NBA draft and used it on B.J. Armstrong. He became a dependable guard beside Michael Jordan and Scottie Pippen, contributed to all three Bulls championships from 1991 through 1993 and later made the 1994 All-Star team. That is sustained Chicago-specific production from the precise draft right acquired for Brad Sellers. Seattle received a player with NBA experience, but Sellers did not produce an equivalent long-term SuperSonics contribution. The disparity supports the Bulls' A+ and Seattle's B without treating Armstrong's eventual awards as information either front office could have known in June 1989. The original agreement exchanged one player for one draft right; no second player, cash amount or other pick belongs to this transaction.

sections.heading: The No. 18 Pick Became a Three-Time Bulls Champion and 1994 All-Star
sections.body: Chicago surrendered Brad Sellers, a player already on an NBA roster, to acquire Seattle's No. 18 selection in the 1989 draft. The Bulls exercised that right on B.J. Armstrong, who supplied guard minutes throughout the 1991, 1992 and 1993 championship runs and made the All-Star team in 1994. The difference did not exist as a known certainty on trade day: a future first-round choice requires a successful selection and subsequent development. It became Chicago's much larger realized asset once Armstrong established himself. Sellers was a valid immediate veteran acquisition for Seattle but did not deliver an equivalent long-term SuperSonics role. The Bulls' A+ and Seattle's B recognize the original player-for-pick exchange without silently adding later trade consideration.

sections.heading: The Return That Fell Short
sections.body: Chicago preferred the opportunity to use No. 18 in the 1989 draft to retaining Brad Sellers. Seattle instead acquired Sellers, a player already known to NBA front offices. The timing created different uncertainties for the clubs: the Bulls had to choose and develop a rookie, while the SuperSonics could make an immediate player evaluation. Hindsight favors Chicago because Armstrong proved valuable, but that later success wasn't guaranteed when Seattle agreed to the trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win. The grades are Chicago Bulls A+ and Seattle SuperSonics B. The trade itself was: Chicago Bulls received 1989 first round pick (#18-B.J. Armstrong), while Seattle SuperSonics received Brad Sellers. The realized-value outcome is a clear Chicago win. Armstrong became an All-Star and starting guard on three championship teams. Sellers did not provide comparable long-term value. That evidence is enough to preserve the verdict without rewriting the trade around hindsight that is unrelated to the assets actually exchanged. The grade evaluates the completed transaction, not whether every front-office motive was unreasonable on the day of the deal. On that basis, Chicago Bulls produced the stronger realized return, and the A+/B grade relationship captures how clearly that side finished ahead.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Chicago Bulls–Seattle SuperSonics: What the Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: The deeper story of the June 26, 1989 Chicago Bulls–Seattle SuperSonics trade is the difference between the transaction's surface simplicity and the value that emerged from its component parts. The four locked transaction sources document the exchange from both franchise histories, while the canonical record supplies the Bulls Win judgment and the explicit A+/B grades. The deal moved 1989 first round pick (#18-B.J. Armstrong) and Brad Sellers. Following those pieces keeps the review disciplined: the analysis can recognize trade-day context, but the historical verdict stays anchored to what Chicago Bulls and Seattle SuperSonics actually received from this specific exchange.

sections.heading: The Center of the Winning Package
sections.body: The dated 1989 transaction involved Brad Sellers moving to Seattle and a first-round pick moving to Chicago. That Bulls pick was used at No. 18 on B.J. Armstrong. The original consideration should not be expanded into a package of future first-round choices or salary payments; the ledger documents only these two assets. The later identity of the pick provides a direct way to evaluate what Chicago actually received.

sections.heading: How the Rest of the Exchange Registers
sections.body: Armstrong's Bulls career, including roles on three title teams and eventual All-Star recognition, supplies a specific realized outcome for the pick Chicago acquired. His contributions were connected to the No. 18 selection rather than an unrelated free-agent signing. That explains why the archive awards the Bulls an A+ and a favorable verdict, even though the front office's original decision involved draft uncertainty rather than guaranteed veteran production.

sections.heading: Why a Defensible Plan Can Still Lose
sections.body: Seattle gained Brad Sellers as a veteran instead of keeping the selection that became Armstrong. Sellers had a separate professional history and shouldn't be reduced to his trade-date reputation alone, but his contribution to the SuperSonics didn't match the long-term value Chicago obtained. The retained Seattle B grade is a site assessment rather than proof that the team had no justification for preferring an available player over a draft opportunity.

sections.heading: The Historical Meaning of the Grades
sections.body: The Bulls Win verdict is grounded in the contrast between Armstrong's eventual contributions and the return from Sellers. Chicago's A+ and Seattle's B describe the site's existing retrospective grade pair without inventing additional players or later draft mechanisms. Separating the original 1989 exchange from Armstrong's later development produces a more defensible explanation of why a one-for-one pick-and-player trade favored Chicago.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win — Chicago A+, Seattle B. The turning point wasn't the trade-day reputation of either asset. It was what Chicago's No. 18 selection produced after the Bulls drafted B.J. Armstrong: a long-serving guard who contributed to three championship teams and earned an All-Star selection. Seattle received Brad Sellers, an established professional, but the SuperSonics didn't realize a comparable multi-season return. Seattle's B recognizes that the club acquired a usable NBA player rather than nothing. Chicago's A+ captures a stronger result from a single draft opportunity, without inventing extra cash or selections in the original agreement.

sections.heading: Chicago Moved a Veteran Center to Orlando for Two Future Seconds
sections.body: On June 27, 1989, Chicago sent center Dave Corzine to the expansion Orlando Magic for second-round selections in 1990 and 1992. Corzine had been a long-serving Bulls reserve and occasional starter during the Michael Jordan era, but he was 32 and nearing the end of his NBA career. Orlando wanted NBA experience for its first season, while Chicago valued future drafting opportunities. The immediate price was not a first-round pick or an already signed European forward. In 1990 the Bulls used the earlier selection at No. 29 to choose Croatian star Toni Kukoc, who remained abroad for three seasons before joining the team. The later 1992 second, also No. 29, changed hands in a separate transaction well before that draft. The two rights followed very different NBA paths.

sections.heading: Kukoc Joined in 1993 and Helped Win Three Chicago Championships
sections.body: Kukoc stayed with European clubs after Chicago chose him No. 29 in 1990, so the trade produced no Bulls regular-season minutes from him until 1993-94. Once he arrived, he played 75 games in his rookie NBA season and 81 in both 1994-95 and 1995-96. He won the 1995-96 Sixth Man of the Year award and contributed to Chicago's 1996, 1997 and 1998 NBA titles. His versatility and passing made him an important complement to Jordan and Scottie Pippen, especially when the team needed second-unit scoring or another forward playmaker. The long wait for an international draftee turned into exceptional value from a second-round selection. His accomplishments were directly tied to the rights acquired from Orlando, unlike another player's NBA career merely associated with the 1992 pick.

sections.heading: Orlando Received Six Corzine Games, Not Twenty-Eight
sections.body: Corzine played only six Orlando regular-season games in 1989-90, starting three and averaging 3.7 points with 3.0 rebounds in 13.2 minutes. The Magic did not obtain a dependable full-season center from this transaction. A recurring mistake in older copy credits him with 28 Orlando games, but the 28 games were played for Seattle in 1990-91, a different franchise during the following season. His seven productive earlier Chicago seasons also cannot be counted as Orlando contribution. The Magic were an expansion team with a plausible reason to seek a veteran, and six appearances are still real minutes. The inherited Orlando D grade makes sense in light of the very short stay and the first outgoing second becoming Kukoc, rather than on an incorrect claim that Corzine supplied a sustained reserve season in Florida.

sections.heading: The 1992 Pick Was Traded to New Jersey for Dennis Hopson
sections.body: The second Orlando pick never became a Bulls draftee. On June 26, 1990, Chicago packaged the future 1992 second with its 1990 first and a 1991 second to acquire Dennis Hopson from New Jersey. The Nets later exercised the 1992 No. 29 choice on P.J. Brown. His career ultimately included long stretches as a capable forward for other franchises, but none of his NBA production was directly Chicago playing value from the Corzine transaction. Chicago did retain a useful tradable draft right and spent it on another roster negotiation, although Hopson was acquired only by adding two other selections. It would be misleading to describe Brown as a player the Bulls developed or to credit the entirety of the Hopson acquisition to the 1989 second-round right. The distinction keeps the asset trail accurate.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win — Chicago A+, Orlando D. The Magic played Dave Corzine in only SIX 1989-90 regular-season games, not 28 (that was a later Seattle season). The 1990 No.29 second became Toni Kukoc, a 1996 Sixth Man of the Year and three-time Bulls champion. Chicago separately sent the 1992 second to New Jersey with two other picks for Dennis Hopson; the Nets drafted P.J. Brown, not the Bulls.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Dave Corzine to Orlando in 1989: Toni Kukoc Rights and P.J. Brown Pick Path
featuredDeepDive.intro: Orlando surrendered 1990 and 1992 second-round rights for Dave Corzine, who played six Magic games. Chicago selected Kukoc at No29 in 1990 and traded the other right to New Jersey before Brown was drafted.

sections.heading: The Expansion Magic Paid Two Second-Round Chances for Experience
sections.body: Orlando's first NBA season called for veterans capable of helping a new team through an unfamiliar schedule. Corzine had been a steady Chicago frontcourt presence, playing 81 games for the Bulls in 1988-89, so acquiring his contract was understandable. But he appeared in only six games for the Magic in 1989-90 and did not fill a long-term rotation role. The franchise had surrendered second-round choices in two separate future drafts, creating opportunity cost well beyond the short contract. One of those picks would be used by Chicago on Kukoc, whose international playing obligations delayed his American arrival until 1993. The Magic could not have known his later NBA awards in 1989, but the realized difference was large. A historical assessment should record the expansion-year rationale without assigning Corzine Seattle's subsequent 28 games or his earlier Chicago statistics.

sections.heading: The Waiting Period Did Not Make the Kukoc Pick Worthless
sections.body: The Bulls selected Kukoc in 1990 but had to wait until 1993 before he signed to play in Chicago. He was a leading European player in the intervening years, and there was no guarantee an international prospect would join a particular NBA team in that era. Once he arrived, Chicago had a skilled multiposition forward who could facilitate offense and score from the bench. He averaged 13.1 points per game in 1995-96 and earned Sixth Man of the Year honors while the Bulls completed a historic title season. He then helped the club win championships again in 1997 and 1998. Those achievements belong to Chicago because the Bulls owned and exercised the acquired Orlando pick. The three-year delay was part of the risk the team accepted for an eventual payoff, not proof the selection remained unused.

sections.heading: The Brown Association Belongs in a Pick Chain, Not Bulls Games
sections.body: Chicago acquired a second future Orlando selection for 1992, but its first use was as compensation in another trade. In June 1990 the Bulls sent the pick, a 1990 first and a 1991 second to New Jersey for Dennis Hopson. The Nets eventually chose P.J. Brown at No. 29 in 1992. Brown would play a lengthy NBA career, but he was not a Chicago draft pick or a Bulls player through these rights. The original 1989 transaction did grant Chicago control over an asset it could move in 1990, which has financial and roster-negotiation value. However, Hopson's acquisition required significant additional draft capital and was not simply a direct conversion of the Corzine pick into a veteran starter. Accounting for the whole package avoids double-counting another franchise's successes.

sections.heading: The Bulls A-Plus Follows Kukoc and a Six-Game Orlando Return
sections.body: The site grades Chicago A-plus, Orlando D and records Bulls Win. The verdict rests on the first 1990 second becoming Kukoc, a Sixth Man of the Year winner and a contributor to three Chicago championship teams, while Orlando received only six regular-season games from Corzine. The second incoming right was also transferable, although Chicago sent the future 1992 No. 29 selection to New Jersey in a separate deal for Dennis Hopson alongside two additional picks. P.J. Brown's later career therefore does not belong in the Bulls playing ledger. The result was an exceptional 1990 draft conversion against a disappointing veteran expansion acquisition. It can be explained without describing Corzine as a 28-game Magic contributor, claiming Kukoc played in Chicago immediately in 1990 or treating Brown as another Bulls-developed player.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Chicago A-plus, Orlando D in the preserved Bulls Win. Kukoc joined the NBA in 1993, contributed to three Bulls titles and won Sixth Man in 1996; Corzine provided six Magic appearances. Chicago traded the later 1992 pick in its separate Dennis Hopson deal, so P.J. Brown was selected and developed outside Chicago.

sections.heading: Chicago Turned Hopson Into Hansen and a Draft Pick
sections.body: On November 4, 1991, Chicago dealt Dennis Hopson to Sacramento for veteran guard Bobby Hansen and a 1992 second-round selection. That pick became Corey Williams at No. 33. The two assets served different purposes: Hansen could join the Bulls’ current rotation, while the selection gave the franchise another chance to add depth in the next draft. Sacramento accepted Hopson as the immediate player return. Chicago was the defending champion, so a reliable supporting guard had practical short-term value.

sections.heading: Hansen Contributed During Another Championship Season
sections.body: Hansen became part of Chicago’s 1991–92 roster, which repeated as NBA champion. He wasn’t the offensive centerpiece of a club built around Michael Jordan and Scottie Pippen, but a veteran reserve role still mattered to its depth. Chicago released Hansen in June 1992. Williams, selected later that month with the acquired No. 33 choice, was a separate result of the deal; his draft position should not be confused with Hansen’s championship-season contribution.

sections.heading: The Kings Return Had a Shorter Useful Window
sections.body: Sacramento received Hopson, a former high draft pick whose Chicago tenure had not developed as hoped. Bringing him in offered the Kings a chance to reassess a player with scoring ability in a different setting. The canonical result nevertheless favors the Bulls, B-plus to C-plus. Chicago obtained a reserve who actually played on the 1992 title team plus a second-round choice, whereas Hopson did not become an equivalent Sacramento building block. The grade difference is tied to the identified incoming assets, not the Bulls’ reputation as champions.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win — Chicago B-plus, Sacramento C-plus. Hansen served as a supporting guard on Chicago’s 1992 championship team, and the accompanying second-rounder became Corey Williams at No. 33. The Kings received Dennis Hopson without an equivalent lasting return. Chicago got the more useful near-term player and retained a draft chance; the outcome is favorable without turning a bench trade into a franchise-defining transaction.

sections.heading: Chicago Exchanged Green’s Rights for a Future Selection
sections.body: The Bulls sent Orlando the draft rights to Litterial Green on July 7, 1992. In return Chicago took a 1993 second-round pick, later No. 41 Anthony Reed. Green had been an incoming 1992 draft prospect, so the Magic could pursue his development immediately. The Bulls instead retained an additional selection for the next draft. This was a choice between two development opportunities, not a transaction involving an established NBA starter.

sections.heading: The Identified Players Define the Completed Return
sections.body: Green and Reed should be compared as the actual players involved through the rights and pick rather than as anonymous second-round abstractions. Orlando acquired Green’s rights, while Chicago’s choice became Reed. A later player’s career elsewhere cannot be automatically credited to the franchise that once controlled that draft asset. The source-backed transaction does not identify an extended chain yielding premium compensation for either side.

sections.heading: The Bulls and Magic Receive Equal Midlevel Grades
sections.body: Chicago and Orlando are both graded C-plus, and the archive records Even Trade. The dated rights-to-pick exchange created legitimate opportunities but no clear long-term asset outcome that decisively favored one club. Calling one side a winner solely because a future second-round pick was involved would ignore Green’s identifiable rights value. Likewise, no verified postseason or franchise transformation can be attributed to acquiring Green from Chicago.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Chicago C-plus, Orlando C-plus. The Magic obtained Litterial Green’s draft rights, while the Bulls acquired the 1993 second-round selection that became No. 41 Anthony Reed. Both sides took developmental opportunities, with no documented downstream return that separates the two grades.

sections.heading: February 1994: Stacey King for Luc Longley and a Future Second
sections.body: On February 23, 1994, Chicago transferred Stacey King to Minnesota for Luc Longley and a future draft consideration later identified as a 1995 second-round selection. Minnesota's 1993-94 transaction log explicitly ties that selection to No. 31 Dragan Tarlać in 1995. On the 1994 trade date, it was not a named rookie joining the Bulls. Longley was a young center who had spent two seasons with the Timberwolves and could help Chicago add size after Michael Jordan's first retirement. Minnesota acquired an established reserve big who had already played on Bulls championship teams. The exchange thus included a ready-to-play center and a future pick for Chicago, not simply a one-for-one veteran swap. The asset identity and timeline underpin the original grade comparison.

sections.heading: Longley Started at Center in Three Chicago Championship Seasons
sections.body: Longley made 27 Chicago regular-season appearances in 1993-94, then 55 in 1994-95, before starting 62, 59 and 58 games in 1995-96, 1996-97 and 1997-98. Those season totals sum to 261 Bulls regular-season games after the acquisition. He became the starting center in Chicago's 1996, 1997 and 1998 NBA championship teams, contributing passing within the triangle offense, interior screens and defensive size around the stars. The three titles were the result of a much larger roster, so the Longley trade should not be credited with every championship win. It did give the franchise a usable, reasonably durable starting center before the second three-peat group was complete. His later 1999 Suns appearances belong to an entirely separate transaction.

sections.heading: The No. 31 Pick Became Tarlać, Who Later Played Forty-Three Games
sections.body: The second-round selection from Minnesota resolved at No. 31 in the 1995 draft and Chicago selected Dragan Tarlać. He stayed in European professional basketball for several years, then arrived in the NBA for the 2000-01 season. Tarlać made 43 Bulls regular-season appearances, 12 starts, and averaged 2.4 points and 2.8 rebounds. That modest later outcome is still actual Chicago playing contribution from the acquired pick, rather than a permanent unused right. It was much smaller than the starting-center return from Longley, and it occurred after the Bulls' late-1990s title run. The two branches of the original package should be credited separately to avoid pretending the 1995 pick became a championship-era contributor.

sections.heading: Stacey King Supplied Minnesota Sixty-Eight Regular-Season Games
sections.body: Minnesota received Stacey King, who appeared in 18 Timberwolves games after the February 1994 trade and 50 more during 1994-95. In those first 18 Minnesota appearances, he averaged 11.8 points and 6.1 rebounds, giving the club real short-term center production. Those 68 games were not an empty return, and King's previous Bulls title years cannot be assigned to Minnesota as new team success. Chicago nonetheless gained 261 Longley regular-season appearances and a starter on three championship teams, plus 43 Tarlać games much later. The inherited Bulls Win, Chicago A and Minnesota D-plus capture a large realized-value gap without claiming that King never played for the Timberwolves. The comparison is about years, role and actual club-specific production after February 1994.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win — Chicago A, Minnesota D-plus. Longley gave Chicago 261 regular-season appearances and started at center on the three 1996-98 title teams. The incoming 1995 second became No. 31 Tarlać, who played 43 Bulls games in 2000-01. Minnesota acquired Stacey King, who appeared in 68 Timberwolves games across two seasons with useful immediate scoring but no comparable multi-year championship-center role.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Chicago Bulls–Minnesota Timberwolves: What the Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: On February 23, 1994, Minnesota sent Luc Longley and a future 1995 second-round pick to Chicago for Stacey King. Longley later played 261 Bulls regular-season games and started at center for the 1996-98 championship teams; the second became No. 31 Dragan Tarlać, who joined Chicago for 43 games in 2000-01. King supplied 68 Timberwolves regular-season appearances. These distinct returns explain the inherited Chicago A/Minnesota D-plus result.

sections.heading: The 1994 Agreement Included a Future Second, Not Tarlać by Name
sections.body: The Bulls acquired Luc Longley and a future consideration from Minnesota for Stacey King on February 23, 1994. The later documented selection was Chicago's 1995 No. 31 pick used on Dragan Tarlać, but the draft had not yet occurred when the transaction was completed. The Basketball-Reference team transactions, the executive Jerry Krause record and the historical transaction archive all confirm the pick chain. Longley was a former first-round center who could join Chicago immediately. King had just helped its earlier championship teams, giving Minnesota a player with established NBA experience. The terms gave Chicago two different potential horizons: a frontcourt player for the current roster and a second-round development avenue a year later. Both must remain in the trade-day asset ledger.

sections.heading: The Direct Return: 261 Longley Bulls Games and Three Title Runs
sections.body: Longley played 27 games with Chicago during the remainder of 1993-94 and 55 the following season. He then appeared in 62, 59 and 58 regular-season games in Chicago's three consecutive championship years from 1995-96 through 1997-98. During the title seasons he started every regular-season game in which he appeared, anchoring a frontcourt role alongside Michael Jordan and Scottie Pippen. His contribution was valuable because the Bulls needed a center who could pass from the high post and screen within their offense without demanding superstar scoring volume. The acquisition preceded Jordan's return and therefore cannot be portrayed as a player added after the second dynasty was assembled. Longley gave Chicago 261 direct post-trade regular-season games before the separate Phoenix move.

sections.heading: Tarlać Took Six Years to Reach Chicago but Contributed NBA Minutes
sections.body: The 1995 second-round pick became No. 31 Dragan Tarlać. He remained with European clubs through the rest of the 1990s and signed to play for Chicago during 2000-01, making 43 NBA regular-season appearances with 12 starts. He averaged 2.4 points and 2.8 rebounds in that season. This was a small but identifiable return of future draft consideration that had belonged to Minnesota in February 1994. It did not help Chicago win the 1996-98 championships because Tarlać had not yet joined its roster. Minnesota's return of King was similarly limited in duration: 18 regular-season appearances in 1993-94 and another 50 in 1994-95, with respectable immediate frontcourt scoring. The original two-piece Chicago package provided larger playing value but both sides received basketball contributors.

sections.heading: The A and D-Plus Pairing Reflects Actual Team-Specific Results
sections.body: The recorded Bulls Win grades Chicago A and Minnesota D-plus, a gap centered on Luc Longley's role in three Bulls title teams. Chicago additionally realized 43 Tarlać regular-season games years after acquiring the future second. Minnesota had 68 Stacey King appearances and short-term offensive production, but did not replace Longley with a starting center for its own championship contention. No later Phoenix Longley games or previous Bulls King titles should be reassigned to the acquiring teams in 1994. The second-rounder was real and not a phantom future asset, but its eventual 2000-01 NBA minutes were far less important than Longley's earlier contributions. These facts support a strong Chicago retrospective without attributing Jordan's career achievements or the Bulls' entire second three-peat to a single midseason trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Chicago A and Minnesota D-plus preserve the existing Bulls Win grade result. Chicago got Longley before the second three-peat and used him as a starting center in three Finals-winning seasons, plus a future second later used on Tarlać. King contributed 18+50 Minnesota regular-season games; the opposing return was real, not zero. Tarlać's 43 Bulls appearances came years after the championships, and Longley's later Suns tenure was separate from this original trade.

sections.heading: Chicago Took $100,000 and Further Cash for Blount
sections.body: On June 30, 1995, Chicago transferred Corie Blount to the Los Angeles Lakers. The Bulls received $100,000 and additional future cash considerations. The recorded initial dollar amount distinguishes this transaction from cash sales whose prices have been lost to history. It does not, however, provide a verified total for the later consideration. Los Angeles acquired a frontcourt player who could occupy roster minutes, while Chicago prioritized the financial payment instead of retaining Blount.

sections.heading: Blount Supplied a Player Option the Lakers Could Use
sections.body: The Lakers obtained an established NBA big man, not merely the draft rights to someone who had never entered the league. Blount offered size and frontcourt depth as Los Angeles reworked its roster during the mid-1990s. Chicago’s incoming consideration was money rather than a replacement player, so there is no direct Bulls player performance to count from this exchange. The future cash qualifier remains important: the full cash amount cannot be asserted from the surviving transaction record.

sections.heading: A Modest Lakers Advantage Fits the Archive
sections.body: The ledger records Lakers Win with Los Angeles B and Chicago C-plus. The grade difference credits the Lakers for obtaining an NBA roster contributor, while also recognizing that Chicago secured a documented $100,000 and further money. The result should not be inflated into a major draft coup or assigned to later Lakers championships that depended on many unrelated transactions. This was a specific player-for-cash deal with a bounded, useful playing return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win — Los Angeles B, Chicago C-plus. The Lakers acquired Corie Blount as an NBA frontcourt option, and the Bulls took $100,000 plus later cash consideration of an unspecified total. A player return helps Los Angeles earn the better grade, while the documented money prevents describing Chicago’s side as empty.

sections.heading: A Dynasty Breakup Led to a Sign-and-Trade
sections.body: Chicago traded Scottie Pippen to Houston for Roy Rogers and a future second-round selection. The Bulls had just lost Michael Jordan to retirement and were unwinding the roster that had won six championships. Houston wanted another experienced defender and distributor alongside Hakeem Olajuwon and Charles Barkley. The team histories identify the completed deal as January 22, 1999; the existing TradeVerdicts route retains January 21 in its historical identifier, a discrepancy separately flagged for canonical-date review.

sections.heading: Houston Received an Actual Playoff Starter
sections.body: Pippen played all 50 regular-season games during the lockout-shortened 1998–99 season. The Rockets finished 31–19 but lost to the Lakers in the first round, so the acquisition did not bring the championship run their veteran core wanted. Pippen nevertheless supplied real two-way minutes rather than an empty name on a roster. That immediate contribution explains the difference between Houston’s outgoing reserve-and-pick package and the player it acquired. His fit with Barkley was not frictionless, which limits how triumphantly the season should be remembered.

sections.heading: Chicago’s Second-Round Pick Became Jake Voskuhl
sections.body: The incoming future pick became the No. 33 selection in the 2000 draft, used on Jake Voskuhl. Roy Rogers had a very short Bulls stay and was waived in February 1999. Chicago had less bargaining leverage because Pippen was departing, but the actual package produced very little basketball value relative to his immediate Rockets contribution. The source-backed outcome is an unfavorable return for the Bulls, not proof that a front office could have demanded a modern superstar haul in those circumstances.

sections.heading: The Rockets Still Held a Tradable Asset Months Later
sections.body: Houston dealt Pippen to Portland in October 1999 for Stacey Augmon, Kelvin Cato, Ed Gray, Carlos Rogers, Brian Shaw and Walt Williams. That six-player follow-on package did not turn every incoming name into a long-term contributor; Cato and Williams were among its more useful rotation pieces. It does, however, show Houston retained leverage after one difficult season rather than simply losing Pippen for nothing. The original trade’s Rockets A-plus and Bulls F grades reflect the immediate player, the minimal Bulls return and that identifiable subsequent transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win — Houston A-plus, Chicago F. Pippen gave Houston a complete 50-game regular season of elite-level experience before producing a six-player return in the later Portland trade. Chicago received Roy Rogers and a second-rounder that became Jake Voskuhl. The sign-and-trade context explains Chicago’s reduced leverage without making the basketball outcomes equivalent.

sections.heading: Chicago Received a Center During the Lockout Season
sections.body: The Bulls acquired Andrew Lang from Milwaukee in January 1999, sending a conditional future second-round selection to the Bucks. The pick eventually became No. 51 Andre Hutson in 2001. Chicago wanted a veteran frontcourt option for an unusually compressed, lockout-delayed season. Milwaukee took the longer draft route instead. This was not a trade of an All-Star or major first-round selection, and the conditional timing distinguishes it from a guaranteed immediate pick.

sections.heading: The Incoming Pick Became a Real Selection for Milwaukee
sections.body: Milwaukee ultimately controlled the second-round choice used on Hutson, while Chicago gained Lang directly. The pick number and player identity belong in the asset comparison, but do not by themselves establish NBA rotation success. Chicago’s immediate benefit was access to a playable center; Milwaukee’s was the chance to add a future player. Both franchises were making roster decisions with different timing and limited overall expected impact.

sections.heading: A Midlevel Tie Is the Supported Verdict
sections.body: The source-backed grades are B-minus for the Bulls and B-minus for the Bucks, recorded as Even Trade. The archives identify Lang and the eventual No. 51 Hutson selection but do not establish a dramatic later asset branch from either side. An even judgment therefore follows the completed, modest basketball returns. The result should not be converted into a Chicago win merely because Lang was experienced or a Milwaukee win simply because it received a draft asset.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Chicago B-minus, Milwaukee B-minus. The Bulls acquired Andrew Lang during the 1999 lockout-shortened season, while Milwaukee received a conditional second-rounder that became No. 51 Andre Hutson in 2001. Both gained a limited roster opportunity without a decisive documented long-term advantage.

sections.heading: Longley Traded to Phoenix for Three Veterans and a First
sections.body: Chicago sent center Luc Longley to Phoenix on January 23, 1999, obtaining Mark Bryant, Martin Müürsepp, Bubba Wells and a conditional first-round selection. The Suns had acquired a player who started at center on the Bulls' 1996, 1997 and 1998 championship teams. Chicago was beginning a post-championship rebuild and received several veteran options plus a future pick. The original terms allowed the less favorable of specified 1999 firsts or a 2001 alternative, according to the historical transaction ledger. That contingent right was not Ron Artest on the day of the trade: Chicago selected him at No. 16 during the 1999 draft. The distinction between the original four-asset package and later selection prevents anachronistic claims about what the teams knew in January.

sections.heading: Phoenix Got 111 Games From Longley Over Two Seasons
sections.body: Longley was not completely unavailable in Phoenix after leaving Chicago. He started all 39 Suns regular-season games in the shortened 1998-99 campaign and appeared in another 72 games during 1999-2000, starting 68. That is 111 Phoenix appearances and 107 starts, a verifiable center return across two seasons. The statistics do not recreate his three Bulls title seasons, which belong to Chicago before the trade. Health, declining role and a shorter Phoenix tenure limited the result compared with the value of an eventual first-round selection. The inherited Suns D can acknowledge those genuine minutes without asserting that Phoenix acquired an unusable player. When comparing this trade, the correct question is how much Longley produced for Phoenix, not how impressive his Chicago championship résumé had been.

sections.heading: Chicago Turned the Pick Into No. 16 Ron Artest
sections.body: The 1999 conditional first conveyed at No. 16, which Chicago used on Ron Artest, later known as Metta World Peace. He appeared in 72 Bulls games as a rookie in 1999-2000, starting 63, and averaged 12.0 points with 1.7 steals. He then played 76 more games for Chicago in 2000-01, providing measurable defensive development before a separate later trade. His Defensive Player of the Year award and NBA championship came while playing for other organizations, so they are evidence of his eventual ability rather than Chicago team achievements. The Bulls nevertheless made a productive first-round selection with an asset received from Phoenix. That is the most important enduring part of the January 1999 package, beyond the three veterans also acquired.

sections.heading: The Veterans and Artest's Later Exit Require Separate Ledgers
sections.body: Mark Bryant, Martin Müürsepp and Bubba Wells were actual Chicago incoming names but provided very different returns. The Bulls waived Müürsepp and Wells on January 27, only four days after the Longley deal, so neither became a multi-year Bulls contributor through it. Bryant was a veteran center whose own usage must not be inflated into the value of the incoming first. Chicago later sent Artest with Ron Mercer, Brad Miller and Kevin Ollie to Indiana on February 19, 2002 for a package headed by Jalen Rose. That was a separate multi-player trade; Chicago cannot assign its entire Jalen Rose return solely to the old 1999 first. The original Bulls Win grade A versus Phoenix D primarily reflects obtaining and developing the No. 16 prospect against Longley's finite Suns stint.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win — Chicago A, Phoenix D. Phoenix got 111 regular-season appearances and 107 starts from Longley over two seasons, not zero playing return. Chicago received three veterans and a conditional 1999 first used on No. 16 Ron Artest, who produced immediate Bulls defense and was later included in a separate four-player 2002 trade. Artest's later Pacers awards and Lakers championship cannot be credited as Chicago team achievements.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Chicago Bulls–Phoenix Suns: What the Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: Chicago sent Luc Longley to Phoenix on January 23, 1999 for Mark Bryant, Martin Müürsepp, Bubba Wells and a conditional first-round selection.
