Artest played substantial Bulls minutes before a separate 2002 multi-player deal with Indiana; his later Defensive Player of the Year honor and 2010 championship belonged to different NBA clubs.

sections.heading: A Conditional First Alongside Three Immediate Veterans
sections.body: The Phoenix-Chicago trade was completed January 23, 1999. The Suns received Luc Longley, while the Bulls obtained Mark Bryant, Martin Müürsepp, Bubba Wells and a conditional first-round choice. The conditional language allowed a particular less favorable 1999 selection or a 2001 alternative; the recorded right ultimately became No. 16 in the 1999 NBA draft. Chicago was not handed an already selected future Defensive Player of the Year, because Artest had not yet been drafted. The Bulls were evaluating the upside of a future choice and short-term roster cover; Phoenix was acquiring an experienced championship center immediately. Both sides had defensible motivations, but the eventual club-specific playing production and pick value must be separated from those expectations.

sections.heading: Longley Played Real Center Minutes After the Bulls Dynasty
sections.body: Longley started 39 Suns games in the lockout-shortened 1998-99 season and made 72 Phoenix appearances in 1999-2000, 68 starts. That 111-game total is the direct playing return from acquiring a former Bulls championship starter. It corrects any suggestion that the Phoenix acquisition produced only injuries and no actual NBA service. His previous Chicago Finals starts cannot be reassigned to Phoenix, nor can his final brief New York tenure. Phoenix did not acquire the long-term draft value later attached to No. 16, and that difference informs its inherited D grade. Still, the Suns received a player who participated in regular-season and postseason rotations, not a draft right or an empty roster claim. A credible retrospective should place those verified games beside Chicago's young-player outcome.

sections.heading: No. 16 Became Artest, With Most Later Honors Elsewhere
sections.body: Chicago exercised the conditional 1999 first on Ron Artest at No. 16. Artest averaged 12.0 points and 1.7 steals in 72 Bulls games as a rookie, then appeared in 76 more Chicago games in the following season. He developed the perimeter defense that would later define his career. His All-Star recognition, 2004 Defensive Player of the Year award and 2010 championship were earned with teams other than Chicago; they do not become Bulls wins simply because Chicago drafted him. The Bulls also sent Artest away in the February 2002 four-player transaction with Indiana, obtaining Jalen Rose and other assets. That follow-on could be traced, but a defensible grade cannot attribute the entire package return to this one former 1999 selection.

sections.heading: Chicago A and Phoenix D Follow Distinct Realized Returns
sections.body: The stored Bulls Win verdict and Chicago A versus Phoenix D grades recognize an unusually successful draft pick produced by trading a veteran center. Phoenix received 111 Longley regular-season appearances, while Chicago received three veteran contracts and the 1999 No. 16 right that became Artest. The Bulls waived Müürsepp and Wells within days, so the first was the durable source of upside. Artest himself played substantial Chicago minutes and later moved to Indiana in a separate four-player trade, with his highest NBA honors won elsewhere. This analysis credits Chicago for choosing a strong young defender, Phoenix for legitimate Longley minutes and neither side for games or championships before the January 1999 exchange. The outcome depends on a real asset chain, not just the reputation of two famous players.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Bulls Win conclusion and Chicago A versus Phoenix D grades are retained. Chicago turned Longley into the No. 16 Ron Artest pick, along with three veteran pieces; Müürsepp and Wells were waived within days. Longley nevertheless supplied 111 Suns regular-season games and real starts. Chicago's best return was young Artest playing time and subsequent trade value, rather than his later accomplishments for Indiana or Los Angeles, and the 2002 multi-player trade is judged separately.

sections.heading: What Changed Hands
sections.body: Chicago traded Brent Barry to Seattle on August 12, 1999, receiving guards Hersey Hawkins and James Cotton. Both clubs' transaction logs list the same three players and no draft pick. Barry had arrived in Chicago only months earlier on a six-year contract, making his departure unusually quick for someone initially presented as part of the rebuilding effort. The Bulls shifted from the younger Barry to a package consisting of an established veteran and another guard. Seattle consolidated its return in Barry instead of retaining Hawkins and Cotton.

sections.heading: Why the Record Supports a Slight Chicago Bulls Edge
sections.body: The contemporary explanation is more specific than a retrospective letter grade. Bulls executive Jerry Krause publicly identified Hawkins' veteran presence as a reason for acquiring him, particularly around Chicago's younger players. Barry had averaged 11.1 points, 3.9 rebounds, and 3.1 assists over 37 games in the shortened 1998–99 season. Hawkins brought extensive NBA experience, while Cotton had played only ten games for Seattle the previous season because of injury. The decision traded a known younger contributor for a different mix of experience and uncertain depth.

sections.heading: Hawkins' Veteran Role Was the Bulls' Immediate Return; Cotton Was a Risk
sections.body: Hersey Hawkins came to the Bulls as an established guard whose experience Jerry Krause publicly valued around a young rebuilding team. James Cotton was a second incoming guard, but his recent Seattle season had been limited to ten games because of injury. Seattle acquired one player, Brent Barry, who had averaged 11.1 points, 3.9 rebounds and 3.1 assists across 37 Chicago games during the lockout-shortened 1998-99 season. The trade therefore exchanged an already productive younger guard for a veteran role and a less certain depth option. Chicago's B+ against Seattle's C+ represents a retrospective editorial assessment, not a rule that two incoming players automatically beat one. Each club's actual receiving-team career, rather than its trade-day roster count, must determine the eventual comparison.

sections.heading: Trade-Day Logic and Completed Hindsight
sections.body: Chicago sought a different backcourt composition in the post-championship transition, placing particular emphasis on Hawkins' experience. Seattle considered Barry worth moving two guards to acquire. That gives each club an understandable roster argument even before later results are considered. The trade should be evaluated using Hawkins and Cotton for the Bulls versus Barry for the SuperSonics, without importing the Sonics' simultaneous free-agent signings or later Bulls personnel decisions as if they were consideration in the August 12 exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The site's Slight Bulls Edge verdict assigns Chicago B+ and Seattle C+. The Bulls received Hawkins and Cotton to gain an established veteran presence and another backcourt option; the SuperSonics took Barry. Both teams' transaction records confirm that three-player exchange, and contemporary reporting explains Chicago's priority. The grade is a retrospective editorial judgment, not proof that two incoming players must outweigh one.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Chicago Bulls–Seattle SuperSonics: What the 1999-08-12 Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: The August 1999 Bulls–SuperSonics deal swapped one younger Chicago guard for two players coming from Seattle. Chicago received veteran Hersey Hawkins and James Cotton; Seattle acquired Brent Barry. Contemporary reporting identifies the Bulls' desire for Hawkins' experience and the unusual timing of moving Barry shortly after signing him to a long contract. The archived grades favor Chicago, but the transaction itself is most intelligible as two very different backcourt plans.

sections.heading: The Asset Path Behind the Edge
sections.body: The transaction is documented in Chicago's and Seattle's 1999–2000 team transaction lists: Chicago acquired Hersey Hawkins and James Cotton, while Seattle acquired Brent Barry. No picks, draft rights, or cash are identified. The trade followed a brief Chicago stint for Barry, who had signed a long-term contract in January 1999 and then changed teams in August. That sequence makes the deal more than an ordinary two-for-one player count: the Bulls were revising a recent roster commitment rather than moving a long-held veteran.

sections.heading: Why the Other Side Still Matters
sections.body: The contemporary personnel contrast explains what each side believed it was buying. Hawkins entered the deal as an experienced guard who could help a young Chicago roster; Cotton's limited prior-year availability made him a less certain second component. Barry was younger and had already played an important role for Chicago during the lockout-shortened season. Seattle preferred to concentrate its backcourt investment in Barry. The three-player ledger is complete without attributing the SuperSonics' separate free-agent activity to the Bulls transaction.

sections.heading: What the Grade Gap Adds
sections.body: Chicago's B+ and Seattle's C+ are the archive's assigned grades. They should not be presented as if a three-step grade spread mechanically establishes actual NBA value. The Bulls' argument rests on veteran leadership and depth from Hawkins and Cotton; Seattle's rests on the player it acquired in Barry. Contemporary reports also show why the Bulls were making that choice: their management specifically emphasized Hawkins' role with younger teammates. Distinguishing that rationale from later career outcomes keeps the verdict appropriately conditional.

sections.heading: Trade-Day Logic Versus the Completed Result
sections.body: The most revealing context comes from the summer of 1999 itself. Chicago was rebuilding after the dynasty, and moving Barry only months after signing him made Hawkins' experience an unusually visible priority. Seattle had a different personnel need and valued Barry highly enough to surrender Hawkins and Cotton. The archived Slight Bulls Edge verdict is one retrospective interpretation, but the defensible historical explanation begins with the precise asset directions and the clubs' stated motivations. Neither team received an unlisted draft asset that could change the calculus.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Chicago B+, Seattle C+ — the archive's Slight Bulls Edge. Chicago traded Brent Barry months after signing him and acquired Hersey Hawkins plus James Cotton, explicitly valuing Hawkins' veteran presence. Seattle preferred Barry to the two players it surrendered. The documented deal includes no pick or cash, so the evaluation should stay anchored to those three guards, the roster motivations stated at the time, and their actual on-court opportunities.

sections.heading: Chicago Bought a Season of Center Depth With Its 2000 Second
sections.body: The Bulls sent a 2000 second-round pick to Dallas on September 29, 1999, acquiring Australian center Chris Anstey. Chicago was rebuilding after the championship era, so the possibility of giving a young big man regular minutes had immediate utility. Anstey had appeared in 82 Mavericks games over two prior seasons, mostly as a backup; the incoming player was not a speculative draft right. The future pick became No. 31 overall in June 2000, later marked with Dan Langhi's name. Unlike Dallas, Chicago could evaluate the player in regular games that season. Unlike Chicago, Dallas held a draft asset it could redirect rather than just a player whose role was already becoming limited.

sections.heading: Anstey Contributed 73 Chicago Games, Then Was Released
sections.body: The Bulls played Anstey in 73 regular-season games in 1999-00 and started him 11 times. His 1,007 minutes yielded 439 points and 280 rebounds, averages of 6.0 points and 3.8 rebounds per appearance. The rebuilding club went 17-65 and lacked frontcourt continuity, making those minutes useful even though Anstey was not a long-term solution. Chicago released him on September 20, 2000, and he did not play another NBA season. The trade's direct return was therefore a single year of backup center service. It should not be measured by his Dallas totals before the exchange or by unrelated international accomplishments afterward.

sections.heading: Dallas Drafted Langhi and Immediately Exchanged His Rights
sections.body: Dallas used the former Chicago pick at No. 31 in the 2000 draft and selected Vanderbilt forward Dan Langhi. But Langhi never provided Mavericks playing value. On the same June 28 draft night, Dallas traded his rights to Houston for Oklahoma forward Eduardo Nájera's rights and an additional 2001 second-round choice, eventually used on Kyle Hill. Contemporary reporting and the Mavericks' own draft guide confirm the direct Langhi-for-Nájera-and-pick exchange. Nájera became a much more useful piece in the Mavericks' early-2000s rotation than the Langhi label alone suggests. Dallas's legitimate result is a draft-rights conversion, not Langhi's later playing career with Houston.

sections.heading: An Even Grade Can Cover Immediate Minutes and a Draft Conversion
sections.body: Chicago received 73 NBA appearances and more than a thousand minutes from Anstey, then released him before the following season. Dallas converted the conditional future second into a different draft-night package involving Nájera and a later pick. These are dissimilar forms of return, and the existing Even Trade with B-/B- grades is a cautious retrospective rather than a claim the player and pick had identical market value. The asset chain is also where any grading uncertainty lies: Nájera arrived through the direct Langhi rights transfer, while his entire later career could not have been known in September 1999. The story is stronger when grounded in one year's center production and a separately documented draft-night conversion.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Chicago B-, Dallas B-. The Bulls received one season from Chris Anstey: 73 games, 11 starts, 439 points and 280 rebounds in 1999-00 before releasing him. Dallas obtained Chicago's 2000 No. 31 second-round pick, drafted Dan Langhi and immediately sent his rights to Houston for Eduardo Nájera's rights plus a future second-rounder. Langhi's Houston minutes were not Mavericks value. The matching grades preserve the canonical even assessment while explaining the radically different playing-time and asset-conversion paths.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The Chris Anstey Swap Behind Dallas's Eduardo Nájera Draft-Night Deal
featuredDeepDive.intro: On paper, the September 1999 trade appears to be Chris Anstey for Dan Langhi. That is only half the history. Chicago got one actual NBA season from the Australian center, while Dallas used the acquired second-round pick at No. 31 in 2000 and moved Langhi's rights immediately for Eduardo Nájera and another draft pick. Anstey's 73 Bulls games give the first side a clear statistical return; Dallas's second transaction explains why a player Dallas never fielded still represented useful draft capital. The correct comparison traces both branches beyond the final name printed next to the pick.

sections.heading: The Bulls Were Buying Immediate Frontcourt Availability
sections.body: By the fall of 1999 Chicago was rebuilding with Tim Floyd on the bench and Elton Brand arriving as the new first overall pick. Anstey had spent two years with Dallas, making him a known backup option rather than a fresh prospect. Chicago could use his size and experience on a team still experimenting with lineups. He appeared 73 times that season, started 11 and recorded 1,007 minutes. His 439 points and 280 rebounds were modest in the context of a 17-win season, but these numbers came directly after the trade and directly for the acquiring team. That limits the verdict to a real one-year return instead of either dismissing the pickup entirely or treating Anstey as a long-term center anchor.

sections.heading: One Release Closed Chicago's Direct Asset Trail
sections.body: Anstey did not continue playing for the Bulls after 1999-00. Chicago released him in September 2000, leaving the September 1999 acquisition with a clearly defined one-season window. His pre-trade Dallas appearances belong to the Mavericks; any later overseas play was a separate step. The Bulls used the roster spot for the season they had chosen to obtain and then moved on. That is a more precise outcome than the generic statement that two pieces were comparable because neither became a franchise star. Basketball value can be limited yet directly visible. Chicago got minutes, rebounds and occasional starts even if it did not get continuity.

sections.heading: Dallas's No. 31 Pick Turned Into Nájera and Kyle Hill Rights
sections.body: The pick originally belonged to Chicago, moved to Dallas in exchange for Anstey and came due in 2000. Dallas selected Dan Langhi 31st overall, then moved his rights on June 28 to Houston. The Rockets supplied Eduardo Nájera's draft rights and a 2001 second-round selection later used on Kyle Hill. The Mavericks' official media guide lists that exchange directly, and contemporary draft-night reporting corroborates it. Nájera joined Dallas as a defensively useful forward, making this a documented path from Chicago's 1999 second-round asset to new Dallas rotation personnel. The Nájera deal is a distinct second transaction, so it should be identified rather than collapsing all transactions into an implausible direct Anstey-for-Nájera swap.

sections.heading: Why Langhi's Box Scores Are the Wrong Dallas Measurement
sections.body: Dan Langhi was selected with the pick Dallas received, but his professional NBA appearances occurred with teams including Houston, not Dallas. Counting those statistics as Mavericks production misreads what draft-rights ledgers mean. Dallas converted the right to select him into Nájera's rights and another future choice; those became the useful downstream branches. Chicago's direct value came from Anstey playing 73 games, not from any rights exercised in 2000. The existing B-/B- Even Trade label therefore sits atop a real contrast: one club used a center for a season, while the other parlayed the departing center into draft resources. Any fuller comparative grade would have to isolate the additional trade considerations and the subsequent contracts rather than assume either team received Langhi's career.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, Chicago B- and Dallas B-. Chris Anstey played 73 games for Chicago in 1999-00 and was released the next September. The 2000 No. 31 pick Dallas acquired became Dan Langhi's rights, which the Mavericks traded to Houston for Eduardo Nájera's rights and a future second-rounder that yielded Kyle Hill. That identifiable downstream return deserves discussion; Langhi's Houston performances do not count as Dallas games. The canonical tie is retained while replacing a generic comparison with the documented player and draft-rights chains.

sections.heading: The Clippers Acquired a Proven 20-and-10 Forward at Age 22
sections.body: Elton Brand had already shared Rookie of the Year honors and averaged roughly 20 points and 10 rebounds in each of his first two seasons when Chicago traded him to the Clippers for Brian Skinner and the rights to Tyson Chandler. Los Angeles was not buying an aging star or a player nearing free agency. It acquired a young, productive power forward with a demonstrated NBA floor and room to improve. The Clippers had spent years cycling through prospects and short-term veterans, so Brand offered unusual certainty. He immediately became the team’s primary interior scorer, rebounder and defensive presence. The transaction gave Los Angeles the best established player in the deal without sacrificing an existing star, and Brand’s age aligned with the rest of the young roster.

sections.heading: Brand Delivered the Clippers’ Best Season in Decades
sections.body: Brand spent seven seasons with the Clippers, made two All-Star teams and reached his peak in 2005-06. That team won 47 games, defeated Denver in the first round and pushed Phoenix to seven games in the conference semifinals. Brand averaged elite scoring, rebounding and shot-blocking numbers and finished near the top of the MVP ballot. The run was the franchise’s first playoff series victory since the Buffalo Braves era, giving the acquisition historical weight beyond box scores. Injuries later reduced his availability, and he left for Philadelphia in 2008 without a trade return. Those limitations keep the grade below A-plus, but the Clippers received a long prime, star recognition and a postseason breakthrough for a prospect-based package.

sections.heading: Chicago’s Twin-Towers Plan Was Understandable but Poorly Timed
sections.body: The Bulls wanted to build around two teenage centers, Chandler and Eddy Curry, believing their size and upside could become the foundation of the post-Jordan era. Chandler eventually developed into an elite defender, rebounder and champion, proving that the scouting premise was not absurd. The problem was timing and fit. Chicago traded a proven 22-year-old star for a high-school prospect who needed several seasons to mature, then struggled to develop Chandler alongside Curry in an unstable environment. By the time Chandler’s defense became reliable, the organization had changed direction and signed Ben Wallace. The Bulls accepted more uncertainty than necessary and never received Chandler’s eventual peak while he was under their control.

sections.heading: Chandler Produced Real Chicago Value Before the Bulls Moved Him
sections.body: The existing D grade is too harsh because Chandler was not a complete failure in Chicago. He became a strong rebounder and defender, contributed to playoff teams and retained enough value to be traded for P.J. Brown and J.R. Smith in 2006. His offense remained limited and injuries interrupted development, but he supplied several seasons of rotation value. Chicago then failed to maximize the next branch, moving Smith quickly and receiving only a short veteran contribution from Brown. The original Brand trade should account for what the Bulls actually realized: useful Chandler years and a later package, but not the Defensive Player of the Year or championship seasons he achieved elsewhere. A C better balances that legitimate value against the star-level return Los Angeles enjoyed.

sections.heading: Brand’s Free-Agent Departure Limits Downstream Credit but Not the Core Win
sections.body: Los Angeles did not convert Brand into a major outgoing package. After an Achilles injury, he entered free agency and signed with Philadelphia. That ending matters because the Clippers lost control of the asset without replenishing the roster. It prevents the transaction from being treated like an A-plus value chain. Still, seven seasons of a young All-Star and a landmark playoff run are sufficient for an A. Teams acquire players to win games and build meaningful eras, not only to preserve resale value forever. The Clippers received the best player’s prime and a level of postseason success rare in franchise history. Chicago received development years from Chandler but moved him before his greatest seasons.

sections.heading: Brand's Seven Clippers Seasons Beat Chandler's Chicago Development Years
sections.body: Los Angeles acquired Elton Brand at 22, already a 20-point, 10-rebound producer, in exchange for Brian Skinner and the draft rights to Tyson Chandler. Brand gave the Clippers seven seasons, two All-Star appearances and an All-NBA-level peak, helping the 2005-06 team win its first playoff series since the Buffalo era. That is an A return even though an Achilles injury preceded his eventual free-agent departure without a trade package. Chandler supplied Chicago with genuine rebounding, defense and several seasons of development, then brought back P.J. Brown and J.R. Smith in a separate 2006 deal. The Bulls' C recognizes that tangible value rather than treating Chandler as a failed prospect. But his best defensive seasons and later championship were earned after he left Chicago; they cannot erase the earlier loss of Brand's Clippers prime.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win — Los Angeles A, Chicago C. Brand gave the Clippers seven seasons, two All-Star appearances and their first playoff series victory in three decades. Chandler developed into a useful defender and rebounder in Chicago, but his greatest seasons came after the Bulls traded him, and the later Brown/Smith return was not maximized. Chicago obtained real value; Los Angeles obtained the established star’s prime and the transaction’s defining team success.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Elton Brand, Tyson Chandler and the Risk of Replacing Certainty With Projection
featuredDeepDive.intro: The 2001 trade placed two different forms of value against each other. Brand was young but already proven: a 20-and-10 forward with a stable role and star-level production. Chandler was even younger, physically gifted and capable of becoming a defensive anchor, but his development path was uncertain. Chicago chose the prospect and attempted to synchronize him with Eddy Curry. Los Angeles chose certainty and immediately gained a franchise centerpiece. Chandler eventually fulfilled much of his promise, which makes the trade more nuanced than a simple bust story. The Bulls’ failure was not scouting him incorrectly; it was giving up Brand, developing Chandler through difficult seasons and then moving him before the peak. The Clippers won because they captured the highest realized value during the years they controlled the asset.

sections.heading: Brand Gave the Clippers a Reliable Half-Court Foundation
sections.body: Young Clippers rosters often had athleticism without a stable offensive center. Brand changed that. He could score on the block, finish pick-and-rolls, rebound on both ends and protect the rim without needing a complex system. His consistency allowed guards and wings to operate around a dependable interior option. In 2005-06, that foundation supported Sam Cassell, Cuttino Mobley, Corey Maggette and a deep frontcourt, producing a balanced team rather than a collection of prospects. Brand’s value was especially important in the playoffs, where transition opportunities shrink and reliable half-court scoring becomes necessary. The Clippers acquired a player who solved immediate structural problems while still being young enough to grow with the roster.

sections.heading: Chandler’s Slow Development Was Predictable but Costly for Chicago
sections.body: High-school centers often require years to add strength, learn defensive positioning and develop confidence. Chicago accepted that curve while simultaneously trying to rebuild an entire franchise. Chandler showed flashes, but injuries and inconsistent offense made it difficult to establish a stable role. The Bulls’ environment changed coaches, teammates and strategic priorities before he reached his mature form. The trade therefore exposed the team to a development risk that Brand had already passed. Chandler’s later success proves the talent was real, but it also highlights the cost of choosing a long runway without the patience or infrastructure to see it through. A prospect can be correctly identified and still become the wrong asset for a particular organization.

sections.heading: The 2006 Playoff Run Is the Strongest Direct Evidence for Los Angeles
sections.body: Brand’s individual averages were excellent across several seasons, but the 2006 postseason converts those numbers into team value. The Clippers beat Denver and came within one game of the conference finals. Brand was the central scorer and defender, and the team’s success changed how the franchise was viewed. That achievement does not equal a championship, yet it represents a concrete return that Chicago never received from Chandler. Historical context matters: for a club with decades of limited success, a second-round run led by the acquired star carries more value than the same result might for an established contender. It is the clearest reason Los Angeles deserves an A rather than B-plus.

sections.heading: Chicago’s Later Chandler Trade Prevented the Original Asset From Maturing
sections.body: By 2006, the Bulls had signed Ben Wallace and decided Chandler no longer fit the frontcourt. They sent him to New Orleans for Brown and Smith. Brown helped a playoff team for one season, but Smith was quickly rerouted before his scoring talent became useful. This later decision is separate, yet it determines how much value Chicago ultimately extracted from the original Brand return. The Bulls controlled Chandler and chose to move him; they therefore receive only the value they realized before and through that conversion. His championship and Defensive Player of the Year seasons with other clubs demonstrate his ceiling but cannot be counted as Chicago production. This keeps the Bulls at C despite the player’s excellent eventual career.

sections.heading: The Trade Was Not Even Merely Because Both Main Players Became Good
sections.body: A common shortcut is to call the deal balanced because Brand became an All-Star and Chandler later became a champion and elite defender. That comparison ignores team control and timing. Los Angeles received Brand’s star seasons directly. Chicago received Chandler’s developmental years and traded him before his peak. The Bulls cannot claim full credit for achievements produced after they surrendered the player. Trade evaluation follows the value each franchise actually retained, not the total career quality of every name involved. Once that principle is applied, the Clippers’ advantage is clear. Chicago’s return was meaningful enough for C, but it did not equal Brand’s prime or the 2006 postseason breakthrough.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win. Los Angeles received the proven young star and kept him through the best seasons of his career, including a landmark playoff run. Chicago acquired a legitimate future defensive anchor but endured the development years and moved him before the peak, then failed to maximize the next package. Chandler’s later greatness improves the process context, not the Bulls’ realized return. A for the Clippers and C for Chicago is the correct separation.

sections.heading: Chicago Exchanged Sean Lampley’s Rights for a Future Pick
sections.body: On October 1, 2001, Chicago traded the draft rights to Sean Lampley to Miami for a 2003 second-round pick. The Bulls had selected Lampley No. 44 earlier that year; Miami preferred a prospect it could evaluate rather than keep the future selection. That second-round pick eventually became No. 53 Tommy Smith. The transaction was a specific two-asset rights exchange, with neither side sending an established starter or an identified first-round selection.

sections.heading: Miami Took an Immediate Look at Lampley
sections.body: Lampley signed with Miami in October 2001, but the Heat waived him later that month. His rights gave the club a chance to test a recent draft choice, not an established productive NBA player. Chicago instead retained a future opportunity that would be decided two draft cycles after the deal. The early waiver is a concrete limit on Miami’s first expected return; the Bulls’ future pick should also be judged on what the identified selection actually produced, not a hypothetical best-case second-round player.

sections.heading: The Outcome Supports an Even Midlevel Grade
sections.body: Both Chicago and Miami carry C-plus grades with Even Trade as the recorded verdict. Chicago acquired the No. 53 2003 draft outcome and Miami obtained Lampley’s initial player opportunity. Neither side can claim a documented long-term success sufficient to overwhelm the other’s return. The distinction between draft rights and signed player minutes should remain visible: the Bulls received a selection; the Heat received the rights to evaluate Lampley directly after the 2001 draft.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Chicago C-plus, Miami C-plus. The Bulls received a 2003 second-rounder that became No. 53 Tommy Smith, while Miami acquired Sean Lampley’s draft rights after Chicago selected him No. 44 in 2001. The Heat’s early look at Lampley ended quickly. Neither side has a documented enduring return that warrants a higher grade.

sections.heading: Indiana Rebalanced Around Defense, Size and a Younger Core
sections.body: Indiana’s 2002 trade was not a simple salary move or a surrender of a leading scorer. The Pacers sent Jalen Rose, Travis Best, Norm Richardson and a second-round pick to Chicago for Ron Artest, Brad Miller, Ron Mercer and Kevin Ollie. Rose had been central to Indiana’s 2000 Finals run, but the roster was shifting toward Jermaine O’Neal and a younger defensive identity. Artest and Miller gave the Pacers size, toughness and years of team control, while Mercer supplied immediate scoring depth. The return addressed multiple structural needs rather than replacing Rose point for point. Chicago obtained an established offensive creator while Indiana bet on a new frontcourt. Pacers president Donnie Walsh described the move at the time as an effort to address roster weaknesses, and the four incoming players offered more than a direct replacement for Rose's points. The final assessment has to weigh that stated purpose against what each player eventually supplied.

sections.heading: Chicago Acquired the Proven Scorer It Wanted
sections.body: The Bulls’ objective was understandable after years of rebuilding frustration. Rose was a versatile wing creator, Chicago native and proven playoff scorer who could handle the ball and carry a large offensive role. Best added veteran guard depth, and the second-round pick became Lonny Baxter, whom Chicago selected at No. 44 in the 2002 draft; that asset later joined Rose in the Bulls' December 2003 deal with Toronto. Rose immediately produced strong scoring numbers for a team that badly needed a credible primary option. The acquisition gave Chicago a marketable veteran and reduced reliance on inexperienced guards and forwards. The problem was that individual scoring did not deliver a lasting team turnaround. Chicago's own December 2003 announcement lists 128 Bulls appearances and 21.4 points per game for Rose. Chicago subsequently sent him, Donyell Marshall and Baxter to Toronto for Antonio Davis, Jerome Williams and Chris Jefferies, preserving some movable value without recreating Indiana's competitive trajectory.

sections.heading: Artest Became the Deal’s Highest-Impact Player
sections.body: Artest developed into one of the league’s most disruptive defenders in Indiana. He could guard stars across several positions, force turnovers and add enough shooting and post strength to remain valuable offensively. By 2003-04 he was an All-Star and Defensive Player of the Year on a Pacers team that won sixty-one games. That peak was the most consequential contribution generated by the trade. Indiana acquired him before his full value emerged and placed him beside O’Neal in a system that magnified his physical defense. Chicago surrendered the defender who would win the NBA's 2003-04 Defensive Player of the Year award. The Pacers finished 61-21 that season and reached the Eastern Conference finals before losing 4-2 to Detroit. That was an elite contention window, though not a championship, and Artest's defensive contribution was more distinctive than a simple points comparison with Rose would show.

sections.heading: Brad Miller Added All-Star Value Before His Departure
sections.body: Miller’s contribution made the deal more than an Artest gamble. He became an All-Star center, spaced the floor with passing and shooting, and gave Indiana another skilled frontcourt option. Although his Pacers tenure after the trade was relatively short, his value remained high enough to support a sign-and-trade departure to Sacramento. The Pacers therefore received direct performance and retained a route to another usable asset. Chicago lost a player who had already shown promise but had not been fully prioritized in its rebuild. Miller became a 2003 All-Star before Indiana moved him to Sacramento in a separate July 24, 2003 three-team transaction. That deal also sent Ron Mercer to San Antonio, with Scot Pollard and Danny Ferry arriving in Indiana. The additional return was not part of the original 2002 package, but it demonstrates how Indiana used its acquired players in later roster decisions.

sections.heading: Rose Produced in Chicago Without Changing the Team’s Direction
sections.body:
Jalen Rose was a genuine Bulls scorer, not a 41-game veteran or an empty return. Chicago official December 1, 2003 trade announcement lists 128 Bulls regular-season appearances with 126 starts and averages of 21.4 points, 4.8 assists and 4.2 rebounds. His Chicago debut after the February 2002 deadline produced 30 games, and he played all 82 games in 2002-03 before making 16 more Bulls appearances the following fall. The second-round selection in the 2002 trade became No. 44 Lonny Baxter, who added 69 Bulls games before both players were sent to Toronto. Those are direct assets and performance from the February 2002 transaction.

Chicago then moved Rose, Donyell Marshall and Baxter to Toronto for Antonio Davis, Jerome Williams and Chris Jefferies. The entire 2003 package does not become unearned original February 2002 consideration, but Rose was clearly still marketable. Artest Defensive Player of the Year honor and Indiana 61-win season, along with Miller 2003 All-Star performance, gave the Pacers more elite value. Chicago C and Indiana A reflect that unequal real return. The old imported Chicago source F rating ignored the strong documented Bulls production.

sections.heading: The Pacers Won Despite the Later Artest Breakdown
sections.body: The Malice at the Palace and Artest’s later trade complicate the grade but do not reverse it. His suspension damaged Indiana’s best championship opportunity, and the relationship eventually became untenable. The Pacers later moved him for Peja Stojaković, limiting the duration of the original return. Those consequences keep Indiana below an unquestioned A-plus. Even after the breakdown, the Pacers received a Defensive Player of the Year, an All-Star center and a sixty-one-win season from the incoming package. The Pacers' 61-win 2003-04 campaign ended in the Eastern Conference finals against Detroit rather than a title, and the subsequent suspension is a real limitation in evaluating the longer-term return. Nonetheless, Indiana developed Artest into a Defensive Player of the Year and extracted both an All-Star season from Miller and further value in the 2003 Sacramento-San Antonio transaction. Chicago did not get an equivalent multiyear team result from Rose.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pacers Win — Indiana A, Chicago C. Artest became the 2003-04 Defensive Player of the Year on Indiana 61-win conference finalist and Brad Miller played 101 Pacers games after the trade, earning a 2003 All-Star selection. Chicago nevertheless obtained 128 Jalen Rose regular-season games at 21.4 points and 4.8 assists, plus 69 NBA appearances from acquired second-rounder Lonny Baxter, all before a separate 2003 Toronto exchange. A Chicago F erases meaningful return; C is the supported grade, while Indiana assembled the higher-value contender.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Indiana Won by Trading One Established Creator for Two Emerging Two-Way Pillars
featuredDeepDive.intro: The exchange demonstrates how a team can improve by moving the most famous current player in the deal. Rose was the proven scorer, yet Artest and Miller offered defensive impact, frontcourt skill and age alignment that better suited Indiana’s next roster. Chicago bought certainty; Indiana bought development and fit.

sections.heading: Rose’s 2000 Finals Role Gave Chicago a Credible Bet
sections.body: Chicago was not chasing an empty reputation. Rose had played a major role for the Pacers team that reached the 2000 Finals and had developed into a versatile scorer and facilitator. He could operate from multiple positions, create late in the clock and absorb high usage immediately. For a young Bulls roster lacking structure, that skill set had legitimate appeal. The trade failed to create a winner, but the player evaluation was not absurd. Rose was already a high-usage, postseason-tested creator when Chicago made the deal. The Bulls were also acquiring a second-round pick that would become Lonny Baxter in 2002, so the wager was not solely on Rose. The mistake in hindsight was surrendering both Artest's future defensive peak and Miller's skilled frontcourt role at the same time.

sections.heading: Artest’s Defense Changed the Pacers’ Competitive Identity
sections.body: Artest allowed Indiana to build a defense around pressure rather than protection alone. He attacked passing lanes, denied primary scorers and brought a level of physicality that changed how opponents initiated offense. Combined with O’Neal’s rim protection, his perimeter defense gave the Pacers a championship-caliber backbone. The 2004 Defensive Player of the Year award captured only part of that influence. Chicago had not yet created an environment where Artest’s strengths outweighed his volatility. In 2003-04, Indiana allowed only 85.6 points per game, the NBA's third-lowest mark, and finished 61-21. Artest's individual award is evidence of his contribution, but O'Neal and the rest of the Pacers' personnel also deserve credit for that team defense. The Eastern Conference finals loss to Detroit was the ceiling of this particular season.

sections.heading: Miller’s Passing and Size Expanded Indiana’s Options
sections.body: Miller’s skill set made him especially valuable beside O’Neal. He could pass from the high post, shoot from outside the paint and defend center minutes, allowing O’Neal to remain at power forward. That fit helped Indiana diversify its offense without sacrificing size. Even after Miller left, the Pacers had benefited from an All-Star season and retained value through the transaction that sent him to Sacramento. The Bulls lost more than a defensive wing; they also lost a skilled big man entering his prime. The value had a second stage in July 2003. Miller was sent to Sacramento and Mercer to San Antonio in a three-team transaction that brought Scot Pollard from Sacramento and Danny Ferry from San Antonio to Indiana. Those assets came from the later deal, not directly from Chicago in 2002, a distinction necessary for credible trade-chain analysis.

sections.heading: The 2004 Collapse Was a Cost of the Return, Not Proof the Trade Failed
sections.body: The 2004 brawl and Artest’s suspension inflicted enormous damage on Indiana. A complete grade must acknowledge that the player acquired in the trade became central to the event that destroyed a championship season. The Pacers lost continuity, incurred reputational cost and eventually had to move him. Yet those consequences occurred after Artest had already delivered elite value and helped create the contender that made the loss so painful. The trade acquired both his brilliance and his volatility. The chronology limits both exaggerations: the Pacers reached the 2004 Eastern Conference finals before Artest's November 2004 suspension, then later moved him to Sacramento for Peja Stojaković. The harm was profound for the 2004-05 season, but it does not make the already-achieved 61-win campaign disappear. Indiana's grade reflects a top defensive peak with a shortened useful tenure.

sections.heading: Chicago’s Grade Improves Because Rose Retained Market Value
sections.body:
Chicago’s return can be independently counted without attributing every later Chicago result to Rose. From the February 2002 exchange to the December 1, 2003 transaction with Toronto, Rose played 128 Bulls games, starting 126 and averaging 21.4 points, 4.8 assists and 4.2 rebounds, according to the Bulls official release. He played 30 games in 2001-02, 82 in 2002-03 and 16 more before departing in 2003-04. Lonny Baxter, drafted with the acquired 2002 No. 44 second-round right, played 69 Chicago NBA games before being included in the same Toronto trade. That return has more value than the prior incoming F grade allows.

Indiana still obtained the larger competitive peak: Artest became 2004 Defensive Player of the Year and Brad Miller earned a 2003 All-Star selection during his 101 Indiana games, with his later Sacramento seasons belonging to a separate team and transaction. Chicago 2003 trade to Toronto returned Antonio Davis, Jerome Williams and Chris Jefferies for a larger package that also included Donyell Marshall; those were not February 2002 direct assets. Retaining a C for Chicago and A for Indiana respects both the direct scoring and the asymmetry of the two franchises competitive achievements.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Indiana accepted more volatility and received far more competitive upside. Chicago acquired a productive scorer and later recycled him, so its side was not empty. The Pacers win because Artest and Miller became central pieces of a genuine contender, even after accounting for the painful way the Artest era ended.

sections.heading: Chicago and Toronto Swapped Three-Player Packages
sections.body: On December 1, 2003, Chicago traded Jalen Rose, Donyell Marshall and Lonny Baxter to Toronto. The Bulls received Antonio Davis, Jerome Williams and Chris Jefferies. The deal exchanged six existing player assets rather than future picks or a cash-only package. Chicago sought a veteran frontcourt presence as it changed direction around a younger team, while Toronto acquired a prominent scoring wing and additional help. Both clubs accepted multiple contracts and the challenge of fitting their new players into a different roster.

sections.heading: The Raptors Acquired the Main Scoring Return
sections.body: Rose offered Toronto experienced perimeter scoring and playmaking; Marshall added an outside-shooting forward option. Baxter occupied a smaller supporting place in the package. Chicago acquired Davis for veteran big-man minutes, with Williams contributing physical frontcourt play and Jefferies representing a lesser developmental chance. Those incoming players were not worthless. The distinction is that Toronto received the more impactful combined offensive assets from this particular six-player transaction.

sections.heading: Rose and Marshall Delivered Toronto's Stronger Scoring Return
sections.body: Rose and Marshall supplied the stronger scoring and creation, supporting Raptors Win with Toronto at B-plus and Chicago at D. The large spread should be explained by what Rose and Marshall offered compared with the Chicago trio, not by claiming Chicago’s frontcourt veterans never played. The record establishes no additional lottery selection or unrelated future franchise success from this trade. Separating the stars of the transaction from the supporting pieces is enough to show why Toronto’s return earns the stronger mark.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Raptors Win — Toronto B-plus, Chicago D. Toronto acquired Jalen Rose, Donyell Marshall and Lonny Baxter, adding the more important scoring talent. Chicago obtained Antonio Davis, Jerome Williams and Chris Jefferies as a veteran-heavy frontcourt return. The multi-player packages were real on both sides, but the identifiable basketball value favored Toronto.

sections.heading: A Second December Exchange Between Chicago and Toronto
sections.body: Chicago sent Roger Mason Jr. to Toronto for Rick Brunson in mid-December 2003. A contemporary UPI report dated December 15 described the trade, while season transaction databases list its processing on December 16. The archive retains its December 15 identifier and should acknowledge that reporting-versus-transaction date distinction rather than silently implying the sources agree on one timestamp. This was a straight guard swap between clubs that had already completed a larger trade earlier in the month.

sections.heading: Brunson Was a Veteran Depth Option for the Bulls
sections.body: Brunson brought experience at point guard and could cover minutes without demanding a central offensive role. The contemporary report noted that he had averaged 2.5 points and 1.8 assists over 193 NBA games before the exchange. He had appeared in only three Toronto games that season when Chicago acquired him. His return was therefore an immediately available reserve rather than a player with a long record of high-volume scoring.

sections.heading: Toronto Took a Younger Guard in Mason
sections.body: Mason offered Toronto a younger backcourt prospect to evaluate. Acquiring him did not guarantee the Raptors a new starting guard, and his later work for other clubs should not automatically be credited to this particular Toronto transaction. The source record names only Mason moving north and Brunson moving to Chicago. That prevents the December 1 exchange involving Jalen Rose and Antonio Davis from being folded into the grade for this separate deal.

sections.heading: The Even Result Reflects Two Narrow Returns
sections.body: Chicago and Toronto each receive C-plus in the ledger. Brunson answered a reserve need; Mason gave the Raptors a younger guard under consideration for a role. Neither side obtained established premium talent or a traceable extra draft pick through this swap. The equal assessment comes from the comparable, limited usefulness of the incoming guards, not an assumption that every trade involving two backcourt players must be even.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Chicago C-plus, Toronto C-plus. The Bulls acquired veteran reserve Rick Brunson and the Raptors received younger guard Roger Mason Jr. A report announced the deal December 15, 2003, while transaction ledgers record December 16. Both teams obtained a plausible backcourt option without a documented major long-term advantage. The grade concerns this guard swap alone.

sections.heading: The Suns Sold No. 7; Chicago Acquired Deng
sections.body: On June 24, 2004, Phoenix selected Duke wing Luol Deng seventh overall and immediately sent his draft rights to the Chicago Bulls. Phoenix's original announcement confirms the exchange: the Suns received the rights to No. 31 pick Jackson Vroman, a future first-round pick protected through No. 3 in 2005 and No. 1 in 2006, and cash. The Bulls' future pick eventually landed at No. 21 in 2005 and was used on Nate Robinson. The site's canonical ledger calls the cash $3 million, while the contemporary Suns announcement describes an undisclosed amount; the exact figure is not independently corroborated by that announcement. For Chicago, the tangible new asset was one potential franchise wing. Phoenix instead chose two draft-related claims and a financial payment, leaving future conversion rather than an immediate seventh-pick player as the test of its return.

sections.heading: Deng Became a Ten-Season Chicago Fixture
sections.body: Deng supplied value Chicago could repeatedly put on the floor. The Bulls' own retrospective identifies ten seasons with the club, 637 regular-season appearances, 10,286 points and 4,078 rebounds. He became a two-time All-Star in 2012 and 2013, earned 2011-12 All-Defensive Second Team honors, and led the league in minutes per game in both All-Star years. During 2010-11 Chicago won 62 regular-season games, with Deng starting all 82 and supplying a vital scoring-and-defense role alongside Derrick Rose. The acquisition also brought eight Bulls playoff appearances, although that team success can't fairly be assigned to one player. The A+ grade is built around Deng's decade of direct service and difficult wing assignments, not his later seasons elsewhere or an invented championship.

sections.heading: Vroman and the Pick Did Produce a Later Phoenix Branch
sections.body: Vroman appeared only ten times for Phoenix in 2004-05, averaging 1.6 points and 1.3 rebounds. The Suns moved him to New Orleans on January 21, 2005 in a multi-player deal that brought Jim Jackson and a separate second-round pick to Phoenix. The bigger delayed asset from the Deng exchange was the protected Chicago first-round selection. Phoenix took Nate Robinson at No. 21 in 2005 and then traded his draft rights alongside Quentin Richardson to New York for Kurt Thomas and the rights to Dijon Thompson. Thomas played 120 regular-season Suns games over 2005-07, starting 63. That is a real traceable return through the initial pick, though the Knicks trade also cost the Suns Richardson, so all of Thomas' production cannot be credited solely to the Bulls' pick.

sections.heading: A Bulls Win With a More Nuanced Phoenix Return
sections.body: The Chicago and Phoenix returns were unequal, but Phoenix did not receive nothing. Chicago obtained one seventh-overall wing who grew into a ten-season starter and two-time All-Star. Phoenix obtained Vroman's brief roster contribution, later used him in its Jim Jackson transaction, and converted the future first-rounder into a No. 21 draft right that helped acquire Kurt Thomas. The 2005 New York transaction included Quentin Richardson as additional outgoing compensation, so its later value must be apportioned carefully. Phoenix's own 2004 release does not independently establish the precise $3 million cash figure preserved in this site's ledger; that remains a separate source-verification issue. Bulls A+ and Suns D are the existing canonical grades. The main directional result is secure, while the downstream Thomas and Jim Jackson branches deserve explicit consideration in any eventual regrading.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win — Chicago A+, Phoenix D in the existing ledger. Deng played 637 Bulls games across ten seasons, won two All-Star selections and an All-Defensive Second Team honor. Phoenix's draft rights became Vroman, who played ten Suns games and later figured in the Jim Jackson deal, and a No. 21 pick later used with Quentin Richardson to acquire Kurt Thomas. The outcome favors Chicago, but those indirect returns are meaningful and deserve consideration when evaluating Phoenix's existing grade.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Chicago Bulls–Phoenix Suns: What the Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: Chicago's 2004 draft-night trade for Luol Deng is remembered as a seventh-pick acquisition, but the Suns' later asset chain makes it more interesting than a simple player-versus-cash score. Phoenix received Jackson Vroman's draft rights and a protected future first, which became the 2005 No. 21 selection of Nate Robinson. Both assets moved again: Vroman became part of a deal for Jim Jackson, while the Robinson rights went with Quentin Richardson to New York for Kurt Thomas and another draft right. The Suns received usable basketball value downstream, even if the biggest individual career belonged to Deng. A source-led deep dive should account for those distinct asset chains without awarding Phoenix full credit for players acquired with additional outgoing assets.

sections.heading: A Seventh Pick for a Protected First and a Second-Rounder
sections.body: The Suns' June 24, 2004 press release provides the decisive trade-day record. Phoenix selected Luol Deng at No. 7, transferred his rights to Chicago, and received the rights to No. 31 Jackson Vroman, a conditional future first and cash. The first was protected through the top three spots in 2005, the top one spot in 2006 and would have become unconditional in 2007 if necessary. Phoenix actually received it the next year at No. 21. This was not an unconditional choice with instant equal value to Deng's seventh slot, and Vroman was a second-round prospect rather than an established veteran. The release confirms that cash changed hands but calls the amount undisclosed. The site's $3 million cash notation should be retained as a research lead rather than presented as if this official release independently supplied the figure.

sections.heading: Chicago Turned the Rights Into a Reliable Two-Way Forward
sections.body: Chicago's reward was unusually durable. Deng played ten seasons for the Bulls, appearing in 637 regular-season games, scoring 10,286 points and recording 4,078 rebounds. He was selected to the 2012 and 2013 All-Star teams and made the 2011-12 All-Defensive Second Team. Deng also helped Chicago reach the postseason eight times. During the franchise's 62-win 2010-11 campaign, he played every regular-season game and was a major defensive wing and secondary scoring option; the Bulls' broader turnaround depended on more than him alone. The strong A+ grade follows that sustained receiving-team contribution, which no other basketball asset in the direct June 2004 package approached. It does not count Deng's later Cleveland, Miami or Los Angeles seasons as production for Chicago.

sections.heading: The Phoenix Return Has Two Traceable Next Trades
sections.body: The Suns played Jackson Vroman in ten 2004-05 games, using him primarily as a reserve, then included him with Casey Jacobsen and Maciej Lampe in the January 2005 Jim Jackson acquisition from New Orleans. Because two other Phoenix players were sent, the entire incoming Jackson value is not solely Vroman's. The following June, Phoenix exercised the conditional Chicago pick at No. 21 on Nate Robinson. Rather than retain Robinson, the club sent his rights and Quentin Richardson to the New York Knicks for Kurt Thomas and Dijon Thompson's rights. Thomas eventually supplied 120 Suns games with 63 starts and averaged 6.4 points and 6.6 rebounds. This is concrete return that a simplistic account of 'Vroman played ten games' misses. But Phoenix had to include Richardson in that later exchange, and Thomas himself was later traded with two future firsts in a separate salary move.

sections.heading: Why the Initial Deal Still Favors Chicago
sections.body: The Suns obtained usable assets from the Deng transaction, yet the route to that value was less direct and required additional deals. Chicago kept the actual seventh-overall player, turning his draft rights into years of reliable two-way wing play, two All-Star selections and postseason continuity. Phoenix converted its No. 31 right through a package for Jim Jackson, and its protected first through another package for Kurt Thomas. Those later contributors had real Suns roles but were not one-to-one replacements for Deng. Bulls A+ and Phoenix D are the canonical grades carried through this retrospective. The direction is strongly supported, but the losing team's grade deserves later independent review now that the sources establish Thomas' 120 Suns games and the Vroman-to-Jackson chain. Such a review would need to distinguish value derived from the two original assets from Richardson, Jacobsen and Lampe, which Phoenix also surrendered.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win — Chicago A+, Phoenix D are the unchanged canonical grades. The 2004 No. 7 Deng rights became a ten-season Chicago starter and two-time All-Star. Phoenix received Vroman and a conditional first, later using the first on Nate Robinson and including his rights with Quentin Richardson in the Kurt Thomas trade. The Suns had downstream value, but it took added assets to realize. Phoenix's precise cash amount and whether D adequately captures the indirect return warrant separate research rather than speculative edits.

sections.heading: Six Players Moved Between Chicago and New York in August 2004
sections.body: Chicago sent guard Jamal Crawford and forward Jerome Williams to New York on August 5, 2004. In return the Bulls acquired Dikembe Mutombo, Othella Harrington, Frank Williams and Cezary Trybanski. Chicago's own 2006 retrospective confirms the exact four-player incoming package and explains that the larger goal was financial flexibility, not a bet that those four would reproduce Crawford's scoring. The Knicks took on two contracts, including Williams' longer-running salary commitment. That makes the original transaction a player exchange with a salary-planning motive, rather than a disguised future draft-pick deal or a player-for-cash swap. The archived direction of all six names is retained without adding conditional choices.

sections.heading: The Bulls Prioritized Expiring Contracts Over Crawford's Production
sections.body: Bulls executive John Paxson later described the trade as a way out of Jerome Williams' multiyear contract burden. In the team's 2006 account, all four incoming players were on one-year commitments that would expire, enabling Chicago to pursue later roster changes. This rationale is concrete, even though it doesn't prove every later signing was caused by the Crawford deal alone. A basketball-only comparison makes Chicago's return look poor because none of the four incoming veterans developed into a long-tenure cornerstone from this exchange. A payroll analysis explains the risk Chicago intentionally accepted. The team was choosing future spending freedom over retaining a young scorer whose long NBA career later made the lost talent easy to criticize.

sections.heading: Crawford Became a High-Usage Knicks Guard
sections.body: Crawford arrived in New York at age 24 and immediately played a major offensive role. The NBA's career statistics record 70 games and a 17.7-point average with the Knicks in 2004–05. In 2007–08, he averaged 20.6 points and five assists across 80 appearances for New York. Those numbers describe the player the Knicks actually received and used, not later production in Golden State, Atlanta or Los Angeles. The scoring case is especially strong because New York acquired him at a relatively early career stage; his later longevity gives the trade additional hindsight weight but cannot be counted as Knicks playing time after he left. The four-for-two agreement also gave New York Jerome Williams, whose contribution should be evaluated independently.

sections.heading: Crawford's Knicks Scoring Was Immediate; Chicago Bought Salary Flexibility
sections.body: New York received Jamal Crawford and Jerome Williams for Dikembe Mutombo, Othella Harrington, Frank Williams and Cezary Trybanski. Crawford averaged 17.7 points in his first Knicks season and reached 20.6 points per game in 2007-08, producing several seasons of offense the Bulls could no longer use. Chicago had another objective: John Paxson's own retrospective says the four incoming players held short commitments and that moving Williams' longer contract enabled future roster flexibility. That was a deliberate salary strategy, not a comparable return in immediate court production. Chicago subsequently moved Mutombo again, and later free-agent additions required decisions beyond this one trade. The Knicks' A rewards the direct long-running scorer they acquired; Chicago's D recognizes that the salary reset didn't create equal player value within the original deal.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win — New York A, Chicago D. Jamal Crawford gave the Knicks multiple scoring seasons, including 17.7 points per game in 2004-05 and 20.6 in 2007-08, while Jerome Williams added a separate veteran role. Chicago received Mutombo, Harrington, Frank Williams and Trybanski, four shorter-term contracts that front office executive John Paxson identified as a way to gain salary flexibility. The Bulls realized that financial objective, but the acquired players did not provide a lasting on-court equivalent to Crawford. New York captured the better direct basketball return; later Bulls signings should not be attributed entirely to this single exchange.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Crawford, Jerome Williams and the Bulls' 2004 Salary Decision
featuredDeepDive.intro: The August 2004 Chicago–New York trade gave the Knicks a young scoring guard and gave the Bulls four short-term contracts in exchange for Crawford and Jerome Williams. New York enjoyed multiple seasons of Crawford's offense; Chicago wanted flexibility to reshape its roster. The Bulls' own retrospective establishes what management was buying with the move, and NBA statistics show exactly what the Knicks received. The archive's Knicks Win and A/D grades are left intact while the two sides' different calculations are examined separately.

sections.heading: The Four-for-Two Ledger and Contract Intent
sections.body: The original transaction had six player contracts and no direct incoming draft picks for either team. New York took Jamal Crawford and Jerome Williams. Chicago received Dikembe Mutombo, Othella Harrington, Frank Williams and Cezary Trybanski. A Chicago Bulls feature written in 2006 lays out that direction and says the four contracts coming back were scheduled to expire after one season. Paxson linked the exchange to the club's desire to remove Williams' longer obligation. That contemporary management account is unusually important because this kind of transaction can appear one-sided when reduced to later points per game. The Bulls did not acquire four similarly productive long-term replacements for Crawford; they acquired expiring commitments as a separate kind of roster value.

sections.heading: New York's Direct Basketball Return Was Crawford's Scoring
sections.body: Crawford became a productive Knicks guard almost immediately. Official NBA career numbers show 70 games, 67 starts and 17.7 points per game in 2004–05, followed by 14.3 points in 2005–06, 17.6 in 2006–07 and 20.6 in 2007–08. He also averaged five assists in that final full Knicks season, making him more than a narrow off-ball shooter. New York's broader team results were not equally successful, so scoring output alone cannot establish a championship-building trade. Nonetheless, those repeated seasons of real Knicks minutes represent a more tangible player return than the Bulls' short contracts. The guard's later play elsewhere belongs to subsequent transactions and isn't silently included in New York's 2004 acquisition.

sections.heading: What Chicago Could Do With Expiring Obligations
sections.body: Chicago's rationale was more complicated than choosing four veterans over a younger guard on pure talent. Paxson later called the Crawford move a follow-up to the earlier Jalen Rose and Donyell Marshall salary restructuring and emphasized that Jerome Williams' contract had become a constraint. The four players acquired from New York were short-term obligations, helping management plan for future spending. The Bulls signed Ben Wallace in 2006, but it would be too simple to say the August 2004 deal alone financed that signing: other choices, cap rules and contracts were involved. In a grade review, the proper benefit is flexibility at the time, not full credit for every good team decision made over the next two years. That prevents the argument from becoming an untestable counterfactual.

sections.heading: The Archived Grades Favor the Acquired Guard
sections.body: The stored Knicks Win verdict assigns New York A and Chicago D. Crawford's Knicks scoring in 2004–05 and 2007–08 is a documented on-court return supporting the higher grade. The Bulls' incoming quartet, by contrast, existed largely to satisfy contract and payroll objectives, as the team's own management account acknowledges. Such flexibility can be valuable even when it doesn't create a long-lasting player return from the trade itself. The lower Chicago mark can be discussed without claiming that its front office had no plan. A rigorous reassessment would weigh the money freed, later roster choices and opportunity cost consistently across all similar transactions; this editorial replacement neither assumes that those downstream moves were guaranteed nor quietly revises the published grades.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: New York acquired Crawford and Jerome Williams and received several seasons of Crawford's scoring, while Chicago accepted four expiring contracts to regain financial flexibility. The official Chicago retrospective and NBA career figures establish both rationales without treating later Bulls signings as direct 2004 trade consideration. The archive keeps Knicks Win, New York A and Chicago D. Any alternative grade would need a separate methodical evaluation of the salary benefit versus the scorer surrendered.
