sections.heading: Houston Acquired Mutombo for Three Supporting Players
sections.body: On September 8, 2004, Houston acquired veteran center Dikembe Mutombo from Chicago for Eric Piatkowski, Adrian Griffin and Mike Wilks. Mutombo had arrived in Chicago during an earlier multiteam roster change and was not part of the Bulls’ intended young frontcourt. Houston had Yao Ming as its starting center and sought an experienced backup who could anchor defensive possessions, rebound and protect the rim. The Rockets acquired a known specialist instead of several different rotation candidates.

sections.heading: Mutombo Provided Multiple Seasons of Defensive Insurance
sections.body: Mutombo became a valuable backup for Yao across five Houston seasons. In 2004–05 he supplied about 5.3 rebounds and 1.3 blocks in limited minutes, and later played a larger role when Yao was injured. His defensive positioning, rebounding and shot-blocking allowed Houston to maintain a credible interior presence. This was more than a one-season rental: Mutombo’s usefulness persisted long after the individual Chicago acquisitions had become minor depth players or left the roster.

sections.heading: Chicago Did Receive Some Real Guard-and-Wing Minutes
sections.body: Piatkowski played 68 games for Chicago in 2004–05, averaging 4.8 points in about twelve minutes a night while spacing the floor. Griffin appeared in 69 games and supplied defensive wing depth. Wilks was waived before the season began. Those were legitimate modest contributions to a Bulls team that made the playoffs, but the three-player total does not automatically equal the multi-season value Houston received at center. Chicago’s return was useful but not the stronger package.

sections.heading: Mutombo's Five Houston Seasons Outweighed Chicago's Depth
sections.body: Houston acquired a durable reserve center in Mutombo, whereas Chicago's return was concentrated in shorter-term guard and wing depth. Three short-term Chicago acquisitions did not equal Mutombo's multi-season impact. Rockets Win, Houston A-minus and Chicago C-plus reflect those observed contributions. Houston acquired a lasting defensive insurance policy while Chicago received smaller, largely short-lived role-player contributions. Mutombo's long-term role, rather than the count of players in each package, explains the stronger Houston grade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win — Houston A-minus, Chicago C-plus. Mutombo provided five seasons of defensive help behind Yao, including important minutes when the starting center was unavailable. Chicago obtained usable 2004–05 minutes from Piatkowski and Griffin, but waived Wilks before opening night. The Rockets’ longer and more consequential return outweighs Chicago’s depth, reversing the old template-based Bulls verdict.

sections.heading: On 2006 Draft Night, Chicago Paid for the No. 13 Rights
sections.body: Philadelphia selected Swiss wing Thabo Sefolosha at No. 13 in the 2006 NBA draft, then transferred his rights to Chicago. The 76ers received the rights to No. 16 Rodney Carney, a 2007 second-round pick and $1 million in cash. The pick would ultimately become No. 38 Kyrylo Fesenko, whose identity was not known on the 2006 transaction date. The league and Philadelphia transaction histories confirm all pieces, so the deal must not be described as a straight Sefolosha-for-Carney player exchange. Chicago accepted the cost of a future second and immediate cash to obtain a wing prospect it valued more highly. Philadelphia preferred Carney plus two kinds of additional consideration. Both choices occurred while the players were still draft rights rather than established NBA contributors.

sections.heading: Sefolosha Contributed 183 Bulls Games Before a 2009 Trade
sections.body: Sefolosha played 71 regular-season Bulls games as a rookie in 2006-07, another 69 in 2007-08 and 43 before being traded in 2008-09. That is 183 Bulls appearances and 40 starts, according to the club's February 2009 trade announcement. He averaged 5.0 points and 2.9 rebounds across his Chicago tenure, and his main contribution was perimeter defense rather than high-volume scoring. The Bulls did not retain him through the Oklahoma City contender years that later made him better known. On February 19, 2009 they sent Sefolosha and cash to the Thunder for a first-round pick in an entirely new transaction. Those 183 games and the traceable asset conversion are Chicago's direct returns from acquiring his rights three years earlier.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Received Carney, a Pick and Cash
sections.body: Rodney Carney played 67 Philadelphia regular-season games in his 2006-07 rookie year and 70 in 2007-08, providing 137 appearances during his first stint with the 76ers. He later played for Minnesota and returned to Philadelphia in a separate transaction, which should not be counted as one uninterrupted rookie-contract stay. The 2007 second-round selection received from Chicago became No. 38 Kyrylo Fesenko. Philadelphia drafted Fesenko and subsequently sent his rights to Utah for Herbert Hill during a separate draft-night trade. That move is an actual way the 76ers reused their second-round consideration, not evidence that Fesenko played NBA games in Philadelphia. The club also obtained the documented $1 million payment. These three different pieces support an assessment of Philadelphia's return beyond Carney alone, even with a low inherited grade.

sections.heading: The Sefolosha Follow-On Produced the Taj Gibson Pick
sections.body: Chicago later dealt Sefolosha and cash to Oklahoma City on February 19, 2009 for a 2009 first-round pick. The first was the less favorable of rights associated with Denver and San Antonio, as the Thunder's official release explained. It eventually became No. 26 Taj Gibson in the 2009 draft. That pick was not part of the 2006 Philadelphia-Chicago exchange, and Chicago paid cash as well as sending Sefolosha in the later move. The genuine chain makes Chicago's original acquisition useful beyond his 183 games, but the later first-round outcome should not be attributed solely to Sefolosha with cash ignored. Chicago's stronger outcome rests on 183 Sefolosha games, plus the later separate deal that turned him and cash into the first-round pick used on Taj Gibson. Philadelphia still obtained 137 Carney games in his first two seasons, draft rights later exchanged for Herbert Hill and $1 million, so its actual return should not be treated as zero.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win — Chicago B-plus, Philadelphia D. Chicago obtained 183 Sefolosha games before later moving him and cash to Oklahoma City for the first-round choice that became Taj Gibson. Philadelphia received Carney's rights, 2007 second No. 38 eventually used on Fesenko before his rights were sent to Utah, and $1 million cash. Carney played 137 regular-season Sixers games over his original two seasons, a return that cannot be reduced to zero despite the unfavorable inherited grade.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Chicago Bulls–Philadelphia 76ers: What the 2006-06-28 Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: On June 28, 2006, Chicago acquired Thabo Sefolosha's No. 13 draft rights for Rodney Carney's No. 16 rights, a future 2007 second and $1 million. Sefolosha played 183 Bulls games before a separate 2009 trade plus Chicago cash produced a first that became Taj Gibson. Philadelphia got 137 Carney games during his initial stay and moved No. 38 Kyrylo Fesenko's rights to Utah for Herbert Hill on draft night 2007.

sections.heading: The 2006 Package Was Rights, a Future Second and One Million Dollars
sections.body: The Philadelphia 76ers chose Thabo Sefolosha at No. 13, then accepted Rodney Carney's No. 16 draft rights from Chicago with a future 2007 second-rounder and a $1 million cash payment. This was a rights exchange agreed on the June 28, 2006 draft, not a midseason trade involving two established NBA starters. The selected No. 38 Kyrylo Fesenko label was attached to the future pick only when the 2007 draft took place. The original Philadelphia decision gave up a higher-selected European wing in return for another first-round prospect plus immediate money and a second-round opportunity. Chicago focused its package on one incoming defender who could join the roster after the draft.

sections.heading: Sefolosha Provided Defense and a Later Traded Asset
sections.body: Sefolosha appeared in 183 Chicago regular-season games, including 40 starts, from 2006 through the February 2009 deal. He contributed 5.0 points and 2.9 rebounds per game on average, while the organization valued his perimeter defense. Later playing seasons with Oklahoma City and other clubs are not direct Chicago on-court production. The Bulls did control a player who could be traded again. On February 19, 2009 they sent him and cash to the Thunder for a 2009 first-round selection that ultimately became Taj Gibson at No. 26. That provides a real linked asset outcome without changing the fact that the later move was a separate transaction with additional Chicago consideration. The original June 2006 acquisition thus produced both usable role-player minutes and a later tradeable asset.

sections.heading: The 76ers Converted the Second-Round Right Again
sections.body: Philadelphia received Carney's draft rights, a future second and $1 million in cash. Carney appeared in 137 regular-season games for the 76ers during the 2006-07 and 2007-08 seasons, followed by a separate later Philadelphia return after playing for Minnesota. The 2007 second became No. 38, and Philadelphia selected Kyrylo Fesenko before sending his rights to Utah for Herbert Hill in another 2007 draft-day exchange. A retrospective cannot assign Utah's Fesenko appearances to the 76ers or pretend that the original pick had no downstream use. Cash was valuable consideration but did not itself create an NBA scoring line. These distinct outputs are what the stored Philadelphia D needs to be considered against, rather than an account limited solely to Carney's draft-night name.

sections.heading: Bulls Win Relies on Direct Minutes and a Separate 2009 First
sections.body: The grade pairing is Bulls Win, Chicago B-plus and Philadelphia D. Chicago obtained a defensive wing with 183 Bulls regular-season appearances and later moved his contract, with an additional cash component, for the first-round choice that became Taj Gibson. Philadelphia received a real rookie-contract Carney return, money and the future No. 38 selection, which it converted into Herbert Hill rights. Neither club received a championship solely through the 2006 draft trade, and Sefolosha's later Thunder tenure belongs to Oklahoma City. The Chicago asset chain is therefore favorable but cannot be judged by crediting all of Gibson's eventual playing seasons solely to the 2006 acquisition. These conditional connections explain a stronger Bulls retrospective while keeping the true draft-night package and subsequent transactions separate.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Chicago B-plus versus Philadelphia D gives the stored Bulls Win verdict. Chicago acquired Sefolosha's defensive contributions across 183 regular-season games and later obtained a first-round pick for him plus a separate cash payment, resulting in No. 26 Taj Gibson. Philadelphia secured Carney, a 2007 No. 38 selection later traded for Herbert Hill rights, and $1 million. Neither Sefolosha's Thunder career nor Fesenko's Utah games belongs to the original receiving clubs.

sections.heading: Portland Used the Fourth Pick to Acquire the Player It Preferred at No. 2
sections.body: The Trail Blazers selected Tyrus Thomas fourth in the 2006 draft, then sent his rights and Viktor Khryapa to Chicago for the rights to second pick LaMarcus Aldridge and a future second-rounder. Portland’s maneuver was purposeful rather than passive. The club valued Aldridge’s size, scoring touch and polished half-court game, while Chicago prioritized Thomas’s explosive athleticism and defensive upside after his NCAA tournament run. Portland converted the lower selection into its preferred prospect and added another asset rather than paying a premium to move upward.

sections.heading: Aldridge Became the Stable Frontcourt Piece of a Volatile Era
sections.body: Portland’s young core initially appeared to include Aldridge, Brandon Roy and Greg Oden. Injuries ended Roy’s prime and prevented Oden from becoming the expected franchise center, leaving Aldridge as the durable star who carried the roster between eras. He developed into a four-time All-Star with the Blazers, became one of the league’s best mid-post scorers and helped Portland return to the playoffs repeatedly. The trade’s value increased because Aldridge remained productive when the original rebuilding plan around him collapsed.

sections.heading: The Lillard Partnership Extended the Return Into a Second Competitive Cycle
sections.body: Aldridge did not only support the Roy-era playoff teams. After Portland drafted Damian Lillard, he became the established interior scorer beside a new perimeter star. Their partnership produced consecutive playoff appearances and the 2014 first-round victory over Houston, Portland’s first series win in fourteen years. That second life matters to the grade. The acquired player adapted from young prospect to franchise centerpiece to veteran co-star, giving the Blazers useful value across several different roster constructions.

sections.heading: Chicago’s Bet on Thomas Was Understandable but Never Stabilized
sections.body: Thomas entered the league after a spectacular NCAA tournament run in which his length, speed and shot blocking suggested a rare defensive ceiling. The Bulls already had a competitive team and believed his athleticism could raise its upside. He flashed that ability but never developed the offensive skill, decision-making or consistent role required to justify the trade. Chicago moved him to Charlotte during his fourth season for Flip Murray and Acie Law, ending the experiment without recovering a premium asset. Khryapa also provided little lasting value.

sections.heading: Aldridge’s Departure in Free Agency Does Not Erase Nine Productive Seasons
sections.body: Aldridge left Portland for San Antonio in 2015 without generating a trade return, which prevents the outcome from being perfect in every respect. Trade grading still must account for the nine seasons before his departure: multiple All-Star selections, franchise statistical milestones and repeated playoff relevance. A front office can win an acquisition even if later contract management fails to preserve downstream value. Chicago received far less production and then moved Thomas for a modest return, so the later Aldridge exit does not meaningfully narrow the original exchange.

sections.heading: Chicago’s Grade Should Rise Slightly Above F Without Changing the Winner
sections.body: An F implies there was no defensible evaluation or useful production. Thomas did become a rotation player, helped an athletic Bulls team and had a prospect case supported by his college performance. A D- better captures the result: understandable upside, sporadic flashes and no sustained payoff. Portland retains an A+ and the decisive verdict because Aldridge became the best player in the transaction by an enormous margin and served as a star through two separate roster cycles. The second-round pick only widens an already clear advantage.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Portland wins with an A+, while Chicago moves from F to D-. Aldridge gave the Trail Blazers nine seasons, four All-Star selections and frontcourt stability through the collapse of the Roy-Oden plan and the rise of Lillard. Thomas had a coherent athletic upside case and produced some useful minutes, but he never became a dependable core player and was traded during his fourth season for a modest return. The Blazers moved from No. 4 to their preferred No. 2 prospect and added a second-round asset, making this one of the strongest draft-night executions in franchise history.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: LaMarcus Aldridge Kept Portland Competitive Through Two Different Rebuilds
featuredDeepDive.intro: The Aldridge trade was valuable not only because Portland selected the better player. It gave the franchise continuity when almost every other part of its original plan changed. Roy’s knees ended a brilliant career early. Oden’s injuries removed the expected defensive anchor. Lillard then arrived and created a new competitive identity. Aldridge remained productive through each transition, supplying scoring and credibility while the organization rebuilt around him more than once. Chicago’s athletic gamble never developed comparable stability.

sections.heading: Thomas’s Tournament Run Shaped Chicago’s Upside Bet
sections.body: Thomas had overwhelmed college opponents with quickness, rebounding and rim protection during LSU’s Final Four run. His defensive plays against Texas, including Aldridge, strengthened the argument that he possessed the draft’s highest physical ceiling. Chicago wanted more length and athleticism for a young playoff roster, so the attraction was understandable. The weakness in the evaluation was assuming those tools would translate into a reliable offensive role and consistent professional decision-making. Portland preferred the player whose scoring foundation and size offered a clearer developmental path.

sections.heading: Aldridge’s Mid-Post Game Became Portland’s Offensive Floor
sections.body: Aldridge developed a dependable turnaround jumper, face-up game and pick-and-pop range that allowed Portland to create offense even when guard play changed around him. He could punish smaller defenders without requiring constant double teams and space the floor far enough to open lanes for Roy or Lillard. That style was not always spectacular, but it gave the team a repeatable half-court option across regular seasons and playoff series. His reliability became especially important after injuries removed the more dynamic pieces of the original young core.

sections.heading: The Roy and Oden Injuries Increased the Trade’s Importance
sections.body: Portland’s 2006-07 rebuilding sequence is often remembered for the promise of three young stars. When Roy and Oden could no longer remain healthy, the franchise could easily have fallen into another complete reset. Aldridge prevented that collapse. He became the first option, made All-Star teams and kept Portland respectable until Lillard arrived. The trade therefore provided insurance no one could have anticipated on draft night. The acquired player was durable and versatile enough to preserve organizational relevance after the surrounding plan failed.

sections.heading: The Lillard Era Showed Aldridge Could Share a New Hierarchy
sections.body: Lillard immediately assumed major ball-handling responsibility, but Aldridge did not become obsolete. His interior scoring gave the young guard a proven partner, and their contrasting strengths forced defenses to cover multiple areas of the floor. Portland won 54 games in 2013-14 and advanced after Lillard’s iconic shot against Houston. Aldridge had scored 46 and 43 points in the first two games of that series, demonstrating that the veteran remained central to the breakthrough. The trade’s return was still producing elite playoff value eight years later.

sections.heading: The Bulls Never Found a Role That Converted Thomas’s Tools
sections.body: Thomas could block shots, run the floor and create occasional bursts of energy, but Chicago struggled to define whether he was a power forward, small-ball center or developmental project requiring a larger offensive opportunity. His minutes and responsibilities fluctuated, and the hoped-for skill growth never matched the physical promise. By 2010, the Bulls preferred Murray and Law for immediate depth. That return did not continue the asset chain. Portland’s side became a multi-era star; Chicago’s side ended as a short experiment and two temporary rotation players.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The A+ belongs to Portland because Aldridge became the franchise’s stabilizer, not merely its leading scorer. He supported the Roy teams, carried the roster through injury-driven transition and then formed a new playoff partnership with Lillard. Chicago’s D- recognizes that Thomas was a legitimate high-upside prospect whose athleticism produced moments of value, but the Bulls never converted those tools into a lasting role or downstream asset. Portland acquired the clearly superior player, received nine seasons of star production and navigated two competitive cycles with the same draft-night return.

sections.heading: What the Trade Actually Moved
sections.body: The Bulls' decision on J.R. Smith was part of a rapid summer reshuffle, not a long evaluation of his play in Chicago. Chicago had acquired Smith only six days earlier in the Tyson Chandler deal with New Orleans/Oklahoma City, then sent him to Denver on July 20. The Bulls took back veteran guard Howard Eisley and two 2007 second-round selections, subsequently used on Aaron Gray at No. 49 and JamesOn Curry at No. 51. Eisley was waived the following day, leaving the draft choices as the practical return. Denver obtained a 20-year-old scorer for a player it did not keep and two second-round picks, an unusually modest acquisition cost for a guard who would spend five seasons in its rotation.

sections.heading: Why the Verdict Lands Here
sections.body: The verdict is Nuggets Win, with Denver Nuggets graded A and Chicago Bulls graded D-. The strongest evidence for Denver's A is the production Smith supplied while actually wearing a Nuggets uniform. He averaged 13.0 points across 63 games in 2006-07, then 15.2 points in 81 games during Denver's 2008-09 trip to the Western Conference finals. His role as an attacking reserve gave the team a scoring option beyond its starters. The 2012-13 Sixth Man of the Year award came with the Knicks, so it confirms his later career development but isn't production Denver can claim. Chicago's D- reflects how little comparable return its two picks and waived guard provided.

sections.heading: The Winning Side: Denver Nuggets
sections.body: Denver Nuggets' side of the trade centered on J.R. Smith. Smith gave Denver a long-term perimeter scorer at the cost of a veteran it could spare and two second-round selections. His 2008-09 season — 81 appearances, 15.2 points per game, and regular work alongside Carmelo Anthony and Chauncey Billups — demonstrates the direct basketball return. He stayed through 2010-11. Denver did not receive the championship rings he later won elsewhere or his Knicks Sixth Man award; it received five seasons of athletic shooting and bench offense, with flaws in shot selection that help explain why his grade isn't a claim of perfection. The unusually low price makes the A defensible.

sections.heading: What Chicago Bulls Still Received
sections.body: Chicago's return had one tangible rotation contributor. Howard Eisley was waived on July 21, 2006, so he never provided the Bulls with games from this transaction. The 2007 No. 49 choice became center Aaron Gray, who appeared in 61 games as a rookie and 56 more during 2008-09. The No. 51 selection became JamesOn Curry, who never played a regular-season game for Chicago and later made a single NBA appearance with the Clippers. Gray's modest interior minutes deserve credit; the other two assets added little on-court value. That narrow return doesn't approach five Denver seasons from Smith and supports Chicago's D-.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win — Denver A, Chicago D-. On July 20, 2006, Denver gave up Howard Eisley and two future second-round picks for J.R. Smith. The Nuggets received five seasons of perimeter scoring, including 15.2 points per game during their 2008-09 conference-finals run. Chicago waived Eisley the next day. Pick No. 49 became reserve center Aaron Gray, while No. 51 became JamesOn Curry, who did not play in a Bulls regular-season game. Gray had real utility, but Denver obtained much more NBA production at a modest price.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Chicago Bulls–Denver Nuggets: What the Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: Chicago never used Smith in a game. Six days after receiving him alongside P.J. Brown in the Tyson Chandler trade, the Bulls sent him to Denver for Howard Eisley and two second-round selections. The timing makes this a study in how quickly a franchise can convert a young player's upside into draft capital. Eisley was waived almost immediately, Aaron Gray eventually supplied reserve-center minutes, and JamesOn Curry never appeared for Chicago. Smith, meanwhile, became a regular Nuggets scorer for five seasons. The long-term comparison is narrower and more revealing than the number of assets on either side.

sections.heading: The Asset That Defined the Trade
sections.body: Denver's return can be measured without borrowing Smith's later Knicks or Cavaliers achievements. The Nuggets' own franchise history lists 63 games and 13.0 points per game in his first Denver season, followed by 74 games at 12.3 points and an 81-game 2008-09 campaign at 15.2. That third season coincided with a run to the Western Conference finals, and his bench scoring made the club harder to defend when the starters sat. There were uneven outings and defensive limitations, but the five-year contribution was far larger than the acquisition price would suggest.

sections.heading: What the Secondary Pieces Added
sections.body: Aaron Gray is the strongest argument against treating Chicago's return as literally empty. Selected 49th in 2007, the seven-foot center played 61 Bulls games as a rookie and 56 more in 2008-09, sometimes starting while providing rebounding and size in short shifts. That is genuine use from a second-round pick. The other selection, No. 51, became JamesOn Curry, who never logged a Bulls regular-season appearance. Eisley was released the day after the trade. Denver's two picks therefore produced one low-minute center and one non-contributor for Chicago; Smith supplied a more durable role at the other end.

sections.heading: Why Context Does Not Erase Outcome
sections.body: The transaction was not Chicago's initial decision to move Tyson Chandler. The Bulls had already dealt Chandler to New Orleans/Oklahoma City for P.J. Brown and Smith on July 14; the Smith-to-Denver exchange on July 20 was a separate step. Conflating those two trades would distort the price Denver paid, just as attributing Smith's later New York Sixth Man award to Denver would inflate its return. The record supports judging this deal on Eisley, the two Chicago-controlled 2007 picks and Smith's actual Denver career. Draft flexibility may have appealed to the Bulls, but the documented result favors the team that retained the young guard.

sections.heading: How the Grades Fit the Record
sections.body: An A for Denver recognizes an unusually inexpensive five-year scoring contributor, not an assumption that Smith became a franchise star. A D- for Chicago still permits credit for Gray's minutes. The key distinction is conversion: one franchise used a spare veteran and two later second-round choices to obtain a rotation guard, while the other waived the veteran and saw only one pick grow into sustained NBA minutes on its own roster. This is a decisive winner even though the losing return was not absolutely worthless. The grade gap describes actual team-specific use rather than a retrospective ranking of the players' complete NBA careers.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win — Denver A, Chicago D-. Smith produced five Nuggets seasons, including 15.2 points per game on their 2008-09 conference-finals team. Chicago waived Eisley immediately, obtained useful but limited bench-center minutes from Gray, and received no Bulls games from Curry. The extra perspective clarifies the asymmetry without counting Smith's later award or championships for Denver.

sections.heading: The Trade, Asset by Asset
sections.body: Chicago brought Brad Miller and John Salmons from Sacramento at the February 18, 2009 deadline. The Kings received Andres Nocioni, Drew Gooden, Cedric Simmons and Michael Ruffin. This was a two-player incoming package against four outgoing player names, not a pick-centered exchange. Chicago traded several contracts for a center who could pass and a perimeter scorer who could handle a larger offensive role. Sacramento accepted the broader return and the different roster commitments attached to it.

sections.heading: The Outcome Behind the Verdict
sections.body: The Bulls were adding two players who fit specific immediate needs. Miller supplied passing and veteran frontcourt play, while Salmons offered scoring from the wing as Chicago fought for the 2009 postseason. Unlike a speculative draft trade, the basketball effects could be judged that spring. The archive's A- Chicago versus D Sacramento grades favor what the Bulls actually received; the judgment shouldn't rely on claims that the Kings received a draft choice, because none appears in this exchange.

sections.heading: The Side That Captured More Value
sections.body: Salmons gave Chicago another way to create shots without waiting for a prospect to develop. Miller brought a different contribution: frontcourt experience, rebounding and facilitation. Their roles complemented one another, so the two-person return shouldn't be collapsed into a generic count of veterans. The Bulls' 2009 playoff run offers relevant near-term context, but it does not turn every subsequent move involving either player into a result of this Sacramento transaction.

sections.heading: The Return That Fell Short
sections.body: Sacramento acquired Nocioni, Gooden, Simmons and Ruffin. Each represented a distinct incoming player, but that quantity was not a guarantee of comparable production. The Kings had to decide what to do with multiple veterans and roster slots rather than the two more clearly defined Chicago arrivals. Their D grade in the recorded verdict reflects the less effective return, not a claim that none of the four ever provided useful basketball elsewhere.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win — Chicago A-, Sacramento D. Chicago secured Brad Miller and John Salmons, two different active contributors for its 2009 push. Sacramento received Andres Nocioni, Drew Gooden, Cedric Simmons and Michael Ruffin. The judgment is driven by the practical contribution of the Bulls' two-man return, not by a simplistic two-versus-four count or an undocumented draft selection.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Chicago Bulls–Sacramento Kings: What the Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: This February 2009 trade is easier to judge by what each front office was trying to accomplish than by counting names. Chicago wanted usable center play and perimeter scoring; Sacramento took four players instead of two. Brad Miller and John Salmons went to the Bulls, while Andres Nocioni, Drew Gooden, Cedric Simmons and Michael Ruffin went to the Kings. Those are the transaction's boundaries, and they supply the evidence behind the recorded Bulls Win result.

sections.heading: The Center of the Winning Package
sections.body: John Salmons is the clearest reason Chicago's acquisition can be described as more than a salary rearrangement. The Bulls obtained an active wing scorer at the trade deadline and could use him in consequential late-season games. That immediate access contrasts with the Kings' need to make something useful out of four different incoming contracts. Brad Miller was separately valuable as an experienced passing center, rather than a redundant second name included only to make the exchange look larger.

sections.heading: How the Rest of the Exchange Registers
sections.body: The Kings received four individuals with different roles: Nocioni and Gooden were familiar NBA frontcourt options, Simmons carried another roster decision, and Ruffin was a veteran defensive specialist. None was a future pick. Their presence explains why Sacramento's side should be evaluated as its own roster package, but they should not be portrayed as collectively equal to Miller and Salmons merely because four exceeds two. Chicago's pair had a more legible immediate purpose.

sections.heading: Why a Defensible Plan Can Still Lose
sections.body: Timing is central to the February 18 decision. Chicago was able to fold Miller and Salmons into a season already underway and test the return against late regular-season and playoff opposition. Sacramento's package required more separate judgments about minutes, contracts and future personnel choices. A retrospective A-/D split can consider those outcomes without assuming that either team knew the precise playoff story ahead of time. The clubs made different bets on current roster utility.

sections.heading: The Historical Meaning of the Grades
sections.body: The Bulls Win result, Chicago A- and Sacramento D, fits the distinct incoming returns: Miller plus Salmons offered two complementary rotation functions, while the Kings acquired Nocioni, Gooden, Simmons and Ruffin. The difference is not a claim that every Chicago possession was better or that the four Sacramento players lacked careers. It is the archive's retrospective assessment of the value attached to the specific February 2009 trade, with no invented picks or cash.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The central advantage was Chicago's ability to use Salmons on the wing and Miller in the frontcourt during the same season. Sacramento took four named players, but the archive grades its realized package lower. Preserving the full list is important: Nocioni, Gooden, Simmons and Ruffin all headed to the Kings. With the exchange correctly confined to those six player assets, Bulls Win and the A-/D marks are supported without manufactured side agreements.

sections.heading: Salmons and a Protected Pick Swap Went to Milwaukee
sections.body: On February 18, 2010, Milwaukee acquired John Salmons from Chicago, along with the right to swap 2010 first-round picks if the Bulls selection fell outside the protected top ten. The Bucks also received Chicago’s 2011 and 2012 second-round selections. In exchange, the Bulls received Hakim Warrick, Joe Alexander and Milwaukee’s first-round position in the draft swap. The option was exercised: Milwaukee selected Larry Sanders at No. 15, and Chicago received the No. 17 selection that became Kevin Séraphin.

sections.heading: Salmons Immediately Strengthened Milwaukee’s Playoff Run
sections.body: Milwaukee had lost key backcourt scoring after Michael Redd’s injury and needed a veteran able to create his own shots. Salmons arrived in the middle of a playoff push and provided the secondary offensive option the Bucks lacked. Milwaukee earned a postseason berth and pushed Atlanta to seven games. His role was direct and immediate; the trade did not require years of development to produce value. That on-court contribution is the first reason the Bucks earned an A in the ledger.

sections.heading: The Pick Swap Added Sanders Rather Than Just Another Selection
sections.body: The Bucks moved up two spots and selected Larry Sanders, who developed into a valuable defensive center before his career took an unusual turn. Chicago’s No. 17 position became Séraphin, but that pick did not supply an equivalent long-term Bulls contributor. The second-round selections were real assets, yet Milwaukee later moved some of those draft rights in other transactions. Isaiah Thomas’s later production should not be credited to Milwaukee as though he played for the Bucks simply because one acquired pick ultimately became No. 60 in 2011.

sections.heading: Chicago’s Short-Term Returns Were Modest
sections.body: The Bulls moved Salmons’ future salary obligations while receiving Warrick and Alexander. Warrick provided immediate frontcourt minutes, then left through a separate sign-and-trade with Phoenix that returned a 2011 second-round selection. Alexander did not become a core player. Creating salary room for Chicago’s 2010 offseason was a rational strategic motive, but it should not be confused with acquiring a ready-made long-term scorer or automatically credited for every unrelated subsequent roster decision.

sections.heading: A Bucks Win That Still Recognizes Chicago’s Salary Objective
sections.body: Milwaukee gets A for Salmons’ 2010 production and the No. 15 pick that became Sanders. Chicago receives C because the players and No. 17 position it gained did not produce matching basketball output, even though its contract flexibility had value. The grade difference follows two identifiable advantages: Salmons during a successful playoff push and Sanders as a developed defensive big. It does not require assigning imaginary gains from all future second-round picks.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win — Milwaukee A, Chicago C. Salmons immediately helped Milwaukee reach the playoffs, and the pick swap yielded Larry Sanders at No. 15. Chicago received Warrick, Alexander and No. 17 while gaining salary flexibility, but those returns did not match the Bucks’ player value. Later picks that moved again must be evaluated as assets traded onward, not NBA production automatically retained by Milwaukee.

sections.heading: Chicago Sent Hinrich and the No. 17 Pick to Washington
sections.body: The July 8, 2010 transaction sent Kirk Hinrich, cash and the draft rights to No. 17 pick Kevin Seraphin from Chicago to Washington. The Bulls received the rights to Vladimir Veremeenko and a traded-player exception. Washington confirmed Hinrich, Seraphin and the cash consideration in a February 2011 follow-up release; contemporary Chicago and Washington coverage identifies Veremeenko's rights moving the opposite way. An agreement had been reached around the June draft, but the formal transaction was completed in July once the new league-year rules allowed it. None of the elements was a future unrestricted first-round selection: Seraphin had already been chosen in the 2010 draft, and Veremeenko had been selected in 2006.

sections.heading: The Bulls Used the Trade to Clear Hinrich's Salary
sections.body: Chicago was creating salary space amid the 2010 free-agency market. Hinrich was owed about $9 million, and the Bulls moved that contract rather than demand an established NBA starter back. The timing was explicit: Chicago confirmed the trade as its front office announced the signing of free-agent forward Carlos Boozer, who arrived through a separate agreement with Utah. Boozer must not be added to the direct Washington exchange. Veremeenko represented a draft-rights entry rather than an immediate rotation forward, while the traded-player exception had financial utility rather than ordinary scoring or rebounding. That distinction explains the business purpose of a move that looks unfavorable in a straight asset-for-asset comparison. The 2010 summer cap maneuver and the 2010-11 Bulls team success are not a single trade receipt.

sections.heading: Washington Gained a Veteran Guard for John Wall's First Season
sections.body: The Wizards had just used the 2010 No. 1 pick on John Wall. Bringing in Hinrich added an established guard who could play either backcourt spot and help a young roster, not merely an expiring contract to hold. In Washington's 2010-11 regular season, Hinrich played 48 games and averaged 11.1 points and 4.4 assists according to the Wizards' official February 2011 transaction release. He started 29 of those games, recording useful perimeter shooting and playmaking minutes while Wall began his career. Washington later traded Hinrich to Atlanta in February, receiving Mike Bibby, Maurice Evans, Jordan Crawford and a first-round pick in a separate deal. Those later Hawks assets were not automatically part of the original 2010 Bulls package.

sections.heading: Seraphin Provided Five Washington Seasons; Veremeenko Did Not
sections.body: Seraphin was a 2010 No. 17 selection whose rights arrived in Washington with Hinrich and cash. The French center played five seasons for the Wizards, totaling 326 games and averaging 6.4 points with 3.7 rebounds. He became a real bench and occasional starting big man rather than a rights entry that expired without NBA minutes. Chicago's received rights to Veremeenko did not create an equivalent Bulls playing tenure; they were an asset the franchise could hold but not a direct basketball return. These different outcomes explain why the stored evaluation treats Washington's package more highly. Chicago's original objective was cap maneuvering, so a useful audit must separate that objective from whether the received rights later yielded production.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The retained Wizards Win verdict assigns Washington A and Chicago D. On July 8, 2010, Washington received Hinrich, Seraphin's No. 17 draft rights and cash; Chicago received Veremeenko's rights and a trade exception. Hinrich played 48 Washington games at 11.1 points and 4.4 assists, and Seraphin supplied five seasons and 326 games. Chicago cleared roughly $9 million in Hinrich salary to support wider free-agency plans, with Boozer arriving through a separate Utah transaction. The team's later 62-win season is not an asset directly obtained from Washington.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Hinrich and Seraphin: Washington's Gain, Chicago's 2010 Cap Gamble
featuredDeepDive.intro: The Bulls and Wizards completed a draft-night-negotiated agreement July 8, 2010: Hinrich, the No. 17 Kevin Seraphin rights and cash to Washington for the Vladimir Veremeenko rights and a trade exception. Chicago wanted room for free agents; Washington obtained actual backcourt minutes and a young center who played five seasons. The preserved A/D grade gap measures on-court returns, not the full value of Chicago's separate free-agent strategy.

sections.heading: The Draft-Night Agreement and July Finalization Are Different Dates
sections.body: Chicago and Washington reached their arrangement during the June 2010 draft period, but the completed transaction is dated July 8, 2010 in the canonical ledger. Chicago had selected Seraphin at No. 17 and then transferred his rights alongside veteran guard Kirk Hinrich and cash. Washington sent Veremeenko's earlier draft rights and created a traded-player exception for Chicago. The Washington Post's July 9 account describes the transaction as a deal reached three weeks earlier, which explains apparent discrepancies between stories dated June and July. A historical archive should use the completed July date without claiming the teams first discussed the trade that morning. Treating agreement and completion as separate steps avoids duplicate trade records.

sections.heading: Hinrich's 48 Wizards Games Were an Actual Short-Term Return
sections.body: Hinrich spent less than one full season in Washington, but his stint provided recognizable on-court value. The veteran averaged 11.1 points and 4.4 assists over 48 Wizards games, making 29 starts, and supplied shooting and point-of-attack experience around rookie John Wall. The Wizards' February 23, 2011 official release provides those exact averages when announcing his move to Atlanta. That departure generated another independently negotiated package involving Mike Bibby, Maurice Evans, Jordan Crawford and a first-round pick. The latter trade can be discussed as a subsequent asset chain but should not be counted as four additional players magically acquired in July 2010. Hinrich's own minutes and the separate Hawks transaction belong to different dates.

sections.heading: Seraphin Was More Than a Draft-Rights Footnote
sections.body: At age 20 Seraphin arrived with a 2010 No. 17 pedigree and a French professional background, but his Washington history can be measured rather than assumed. Across five Wizards seasons he appeared in 326 regular-season games, started 31 and averaged 6.4 points, 3.7 rebounds and 0.8 blocks. His 2014-15 final Washington season included 79 appearances and 6.6 points per game. He was a rotation big man rather than an All-Star, so his contribution should not be exaggerated. Yet it was vastly more on-court service than Chicago received from Veremeenko's unused NBA draft rights. This durable playing value is separate from the 2010 cash considerations Washington also obtained.

sections.heading: Chicago's Salary Strategy Explains the Asymmetric Grades
sections.body: The Bulls gave away an established backcourt contributor and first-round prospect to make room in a historically expensive free-agent market. Carlos Boozer's Chicago arrival on July 8 was a separate free-agent or Utah sign-and-trade operation, while the Hinrich deal supplied space for broader roster construction. Chicago subsequently won 62 games in 2010-11 behind Derrick Rose and a deep supporting roster, which shows the team succeeded broadly without proving the Veremeenko rights themselves delivered that success. Washington's return included Hinrich's useful opening-season production and five years of Seraphin. The canonical verdict remains Wizards Win, Washington A and Chicago D. Those are inherited editorial letter grades, not a claim that salary-cap flexibility had no real strategic purpose.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wizards Win, Washington A and Chicago D remain the canonical labels. Washington acquired Hinrich, the already-selected No. 17 Kevin Seraphin rights and cash. Hinrich played 48 Wizards games at 11.1 points and 4.4 assists before a separate February 2011 Atlanta transaction; Seraphin delivered 326 Washington appearances over five seasons. Chicago received Veremeenko's draft rights, which produced no Bulls NBA playing tenure, and a trade exception while shedding Hinrich's approximately $9 million salary. That salary clearing helped the Bulls pursue their 2010 free-agent program, including the separate Carlos Boozer agreement with Utah. Later playoff runs and a 62-win Bulls season cannot be counted as directly sent by Washington in the Hinrich exchange. The editorial grades are preserved without erasing the strategic cap reasoning or silently rewriting the transaction assets.

sections.heading: A Sign-and-Trade Moved Warrick to Phoenix
sections.body: Chicago signed and traded Hakim Warrick to the Phoenix Suns in July 2010 for Phoenix’s own 2011 second-round pick. The Bulls had acquired Warrick from Milwaukee in February; their official announcement said he had averaged 8.7 points and 3.6 rebounds in 28 Chicago games. Phoenix was acquiring a veteran forward it wanted to sign, while the Bulls turned an outgoing free agent into a future draft asset. The exchange was not an unrestricted purchase of a young prospect.

sections.heading: Chicago Quickly Converted the Pick Into C.J. Watson
sections.body: The second-rounder eventually became the No. 44 selection in 2011, used on Charles Jenkins, but Chicago did not make that pick itself. The Bulls sent the acquired selection to Golden State on July 22, 2010 as part of their deal for guard C.J. Watson. That identified follow-on transaction is central to Chicago’s return: the actual value to the Bulls was a usable rotation guard, not years of development from Jenkins in a Bulls uniform.

sections.heading: Phoenix Received a Frontcourt Contributor
sections.body: Warrick gave Phoenix an athletic forward option following an offseason when the Suns were changing their frontcourt. They received the player named in the transaction, not a speculative right to negotiate with him later. The downside was the commitment attached to a new veteran contract and a departed future selection. Warrick’s value should be evaluated on his Phoenix contribution rather than crediting him for his earlier Chicago numbers or assuming the Suns retained that draft choice.

sections.heading: Why the Equal Grades Are Defensible
sections.body: The Even Trade verdict assigns C-plus to Chicago and Phoenix for two returns that worked in different ways. Phoenix acquired Hakim Warrick through the sign-and-trade, gaining an established forward for its changing frontcourt. Chicago obtained the Suns’ 2011 second-round pick rather than a player. The Bulls then used that selection in a separate July 22, 2010 transaction to bring in C.J. Watson from Golden State. When the pick eventually became No. 44 in 2011, Charles Jenkins was selected by Golden State; he was not a player who joined Chicago because of the Warrick exchange. Phoenix received direct frontcourt depth, while Chicago redirected a future draft right into a rotation guard. Neither chain establishes a decisive long-term franchise win, which supports the two matching C-plus assessments without double counting the same second-round pick.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Chicago C-plus, Phoenix C-plus. The Suns obtained Hakim Warrick through a sign-and-trade. Chicago received Phoenix’s 2011 second-round pick, later No. 44, and sent that asset to Golden State in the C.J. Watson transaction. Chicago gained a new rotation guard from its asset chain, while Phoenix filled a frontcourt role. Both returns were useful without establishing a decisive winner.

sections.heading: Chicago Moved James Johnson for Miami’s 2011 First-Rounder
sections.body: On February 22, 2011, the Chicago Bulls sent James Johnson to Toronto for the Miami Heat’s 2011 first-round selection, which Toronto held from the prior Chris Bosh agreement. Chicago’s official announcement confirms the players, pick origin and date. Johnson had struggled for minutes behind Chicago’s crowded wing rotation, appearing in only 13 Bulls games during 2010-11 before the move. The first-round choice was lottery-protected in 2011 and ultimately became No. 28. The Raptors took a 23-year-old forward who could enter the lineup right away, while Chicago converted a reserve prospect into a future draft asset rather than gaining an immediately playing NBA veteran.

sections.heading: Johnson Played 87 Toronto Games and Started 65
sections.body: Johnson joined Toronto for 25 regular-season games in the rest of 2010-11 and started all 25, supplying energetic wing defense and secondary offense. During the lockout-shortened 2011-12 season, he appeared in 62 further Raptors games and started 40, producing a receiving-team total of 87 appearances and 65 starts. He averaged approximately 9.2 points and 4.7 rebounds in the first portion, then 9.1 points and 4.7 rebounds the following season. His later 2012-13 Sacramento games and his return to Toronto in 2014 were separate transactions, not a single uninterrupted tenure funded by this February 2011 deal.

sections.heading: The Bulls Used Pick 28 to Help Obtain Nikola Mirotić
sections.body: Chicago’s acquired 2011 first-rounder became the No. 28 selection Norris Cole, but the Bulls did not retain Cole to play for them. On June 23, 2011, Chicago sent Cole’s rights, Malcolm Lee’s rights and cash to Minnesota for the rights to No. 23 Nikola Mirotić. The Bulls themselves and their historical transaction ledger confirm all components. Mirotić later played hundreds of Chicago NBA games, but he was obtained only after Chicago contributed two drafted rights and cash in an additional draft-night agreement. Therefore the 2011 James Johnson trade gave Chicago a valuable part of the Mirotić package, not Mirotić outright for Johnson or any direct Norris Cole NBA appearances.

sections.heading: The Original Bulls Win Grade Needs the Two-Step Asset Chain
sections.body: The preserved verdict is Bulls Win, Chicago B+ and Toronto C-. Toronto got 87 immediate Johnson appearances and 65 starts, a tangible but limited two-season tenure. Chicago received a protected future first-rounder, later resolved to No. 28, and then spent that right with No. 43 Malcolm Lee and cash to obtain Mirotić’s rights in a separate deal. Johnson contributed legitimate Raptors minutes, which makes dismissing Toronto’s return as nothing inaccurate. But the Bulls retained more tradable flexibility and later converted their pick as part of a player-rights acquisition. The grade should describe those steps explicitly rather than crediting another franchise’s Norris Cole minutes or overstating that Chicago acquired Mirotić directly.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win with Chicago B+ and Toronto C- remains the archived evaluation. Johnson logged 87 Raptors games and 65 starts across 2010-12. Chicago acquired Miami’s protected 2011 first-rounder, which became No. 28 Norris Cole; the Bulls then sent his rights plus Malcolm Lee and cash to Minnesota for Mirotić’s rights in a distinct June 2011 deal. Johnson’s Toronto role and the multi-asset draft chain should both be acknowledged.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The 2011 James Johnson Deal: Toronto’s 87 Games and Chicago’s Draft Chain
featuredDeepDive.intro: The Bulls traded James Johnson to Toronto in February 2011 for Miami’s lottery-protected first-rounder held by the Raptors. Johnson played 87 Toronto games and started 65 in his first two Raptors seasons. The acquired pick became No. 28 Norris Cole, whose rights were later moved with Malcolm Lee and cash to Minnesota for Nikola Mirotić’s rights. The saved Bulls Win, Chicago B+ and Toronto C- is evaluated against both that immediate player output and the additional assets needed for Chicago’s subsequent draft-night result.

sections.heading: The Toronto Pick Origin Was Miami, Not a Raptors Selection
sections.body: Toronto had acquired Miami’s 2011 first-round pick through the Chris Bosh sign-and-trade arrangement of July 2010. Chicago’s official February 22, 2011 announcement specifies that this was the choice received for James Johnson. The pick was protected if it landed in the 2011 lottery, otherwise resolving at a late first-round position. Miami’s strong season caused it to convey at No. 28. The Bulls did not receive Toronto’s own top-five 2011 selection used on Jonas Valančiūnas, and that distinction prevents a much larger pick-value claim from entering this editorial.

sections.heading: The Raptors Put Johnson into the Starting Lineup
sections.body: Johnson had made zero Bulls starts in his 13 pretrade appearances in 2010-11. In Toronto he started all 25 games after the trade, then played 62 times with 40 starts in 2011-12. The combination was 87 Raptors NBA appearances and 65 starts across two segments. His athletic defense and rebounding were useful to a rebuilding club and reflected a larger role than he had occupied in Chicago. When he moved to Sacramento in 2012, that began a different roster chapter. His later second Toronto tenure did not flow directly from the first acquisition in February 2011 and is excluded from the receiving-team subtotal.

sections.heading: Cole and Lee Were Additional Payment for Mirotić Rights
sections.body: The Bulls selected Norris Cole at No. 28 with the Miami pick and Malcolm Lee at No. 43 in the same 2011 draft. Chicago then sent both sets of rights and cash to Minnesota for Mirotić, who was selected No. 23. A later official Bulls release itemizes those rights and monetary components and confirms Mirotić eventually played extensive NBA seasons for Chicago. This was a worthwhile secondary asset conversion, but it was not a free swap of one Chicago player for Mirotić. Cole’s playing career with Miami and other teams is also outside Bulls on-court production, even though Chicago briefly held his draft rights.

sections.heading: Why the Archive’s Bulls Edge Is Defensible but Conditional
sections.body: Toronto obtained a usable wing who played 87 games and started 65 in his first stay, so an argument based on no Raptors return would misstate the record. Chicago received the future No. 28 choice and then combined that right with another pick and cash to seek a larger development project. The archive’s B+ Chicago and C- Toronto can be viewed as a judgment about longer-term flexibility, though the later Bulls Mirotić contribution required independent consideration. This boundary is more credible than counting all of Mirotić’s eventual NBA statistics as a one-for-one payoff from Johnson alone or treating Miami’s No. 28 as Toronto’s No. 5.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Chicago B+, Toronto C- and Bulls Win stay unchanged. Johnson gave Toronto 87 NBA games and 65 starts. Chicago acquired a lottery-protected Miami first-rounder that conveyed at No. 28, then traded Cole and Lee rights with cash for Mirotić rights in June 2011. That two-step chronology protects the value of the pick without inventing a straight Johnson-for-Mirotić exchange.

sections.heading: The Trade, Asset by Asset
sections.body: Chicago came away from its June 23, 2011 draft-night transaction with the rights to Nikola Mirotic. Minnesota received the rights to Norris Cole and Malcolm Lee, plus cash considerations. No established NBA veteran was directly exchanged as an active player. The clubs were allocating future roster opportunities, with Chicago concentrating on one prospect and the Timberwolves accepting two separate sets of draft rights and a financial component. Any assessment must keep those rights distinct from the later teams on which the players actually appeared.

sections.heading: The Outcome Behind the Verdict
sections.body: Mirotic eventually supplied Chicago with NBA scoring and a useful trade asset. The Chicago source perspective also records a subsequent return involving first-round value. That later contribution is the strongest evidence supporting the Bulls Win verdict and Chicago's A grade. It isn't necessary to suggest the Bulls gained the career accomplishments of every player associated with the transaction. They gained Mirotic's rights; the value they eventually realized from him is the relevant outcome. Minnesota's incoming Cole and Lee rights must be evaluated on their own terms rather than erased from the history.

sections.heading: The Side That Captured More Value
sections.body: Chicago accepted a concentrated outcome. Instead of taking multiple draft rights and money, it secured the ability to bring Nikola Mirotic into its own system. That distinction is especially useful in hindsight because the eventual contribution can be traced to one asset without assigning other franchises' roster decisions to the Bulls. Mirotic became a productive scorer for Chicago and later generated value through a subsequent move. The A grade recognizes both stages, not merely the familiar player name on the original paperwork.

sections.heading: The Return That Fell Short
sections.body: Minnesota's documented return contained Norris Cole's rights, Malcolm Lee's rights and unspecified cash considerations. Cole later had a useful NBA career, but possession of his rights on this particular night doesn't prove the Timberwolves retained him for that career. Lee's rights similarly require a distinction between a recorded acquisition and any realized minutes. Minnesota's D+ grade is the historical evaluation of the package as credited to the club, not a claim that two names plus cash amounted to nothing the moment the trade happened.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win — Chicago A, Minnesota D+. The Bulls received Nikola Mirotic's draft rights, later converted into NBA scoring and additional trade value. Minnesota received the rights to Norris Cole and Malcolm Lee and cash. Cole's career should not be automatically attributed to Minnesota, and the unspecified cash should not be treated like playing production.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Chicago Bulls–Minnesota Timberwolves: What the Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: On June 23, 2011, Chicago acquired the rights to Nikola Mirotic while Minnesota took the rights to Norris Cole and Malcolm Lee plus cash. The difference between acquiring draft rights and obtaining later NBA production is the key to the recorded A/D+ grade gap.

sections.heading: The Center of the Winning Package
sections.body: The comparison begins with a draft-rights transaction, not a veteran-for-veteran trade. Chicago received Mirotic's rights and Minnesota accepted Cole's rights, Lee's rights and cash. Those asset labels are crucial. Draft rights are an opportunity to secure a player, not an immediate record of NBA games for the acquiring franchise. Chicago's later return from Mirotic is a realized outcome; the other players' later careers need separate ownership histories before they can be counted for Minnesota.

sections.heading: How the Rest of the Exchange Registers
sections.body: Mirotic is the asset that carries Chicago's strong retrospective grade. He became a scoring option for the Bulls, then supplied additional value when Chicago later moved him. The archived Chicago perspective specifically connects his contribution and later first-round return to the evaluation. That's a more defensible explanation than claiming every draft choice Chicago held in 2011 became valuable. This trade gave the Bulls one set of rights, and the player associated with those rights produced a traceable basketball and future-asset benefit.

sections.heading: Why a Defensible Plan Can Still Lose
sections.body: The Timberwolves received two different sets of rights rather than a guaranteed pair of rotation players. Norris Cole's later NBA success is relevant background, but it shouldn't be presented as production he necessarily delivered in Minnesota. Malcolm Lee also was a distinct prospect, while the cash portion had financial rather than on-court value. Reconstructing those pieces helps avoid the false impression that Chicago won solely because Minnesota accepted an empty return. The outcome favored Chicago because its particular rights acquisition translated into greater realized value.

sections.heading: The Historical Meaning of the Grades
sections.body: Chicago A and Minnesota D+ are grades for the eventual value tied to the documented transaction. They don't establish that Minnesota should have known how Mirotic's later Bulls career or subsequent trade would develop. They also don't turn Minnesota's cash consideration into an NBA player. The Bulls Win judgment rests on Mirotic's recorded production and later asset return compared with the less valuable Minnesota package. Treating rights, cash and NBA performance as different kinds of consideration makes that disparity intelligible.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mirotic's eventual scoring for Chicago and later first-round asset return underwrite the Bulls' A. Minnesota's incoming Cole and Lee rights and cash remained separate components whose realized benefit didn't match the Bulls' outcome. This was a draft-rights allocation; evaluating it without inventing direct player tenure or an unsupported cash amount explains the D+ on Minnesota's side.

sections.heading: Denver Exchanged McDermott for Two First-Round Prospects
sections.body: On draft night June 26, 2014, Denver sent Chicago the rights to No. 11 selection Doug McDermott and forward Anthony Randolph. The Bulls sent back the rights to No. 16 Jusuf Nurkić and No. 19 Gary Harris, plus a 2015 second-round choice that eventually became No. 53 Sir'Dominic Pointer. Chicago was buying a polished college scorer and outside shooter. Denver preferred two young prospects with defensive potential and a later draft asset. The Nuggets had selected McDermott first, but the trade transferred his rights before he suited up. The historical verdict must evaluate what the receiving teams ultimately got, not simply the original draft-night announcement.

sections.heading: Harris Became Denver's Long-Term Starting Guard
sections.body: Harris needed a rookie season to adjust before he earned 76 starts in 2015-16. His scoring, perimeter defense and shotmaking developed alongside Denver's rising core. In 2017-18 he averaged roughly 17.5 points per game, appearing in 67 games with 65 starts. Those contributions extended far beyond the speculative promise of a 19th pick. Denver still controlled Harris for years, and he eventually figured in a separate 2021 trade to Orlando for Aaron Gordon. Gordon's entire subsequent value cannot be assigned to Harris alone because Denver surrendered additional assets in that trade. The more direct value was a real multiyear Nuggets starter.

sections.heading: Nurkic Contributed and Later Became Part of Another Trade
sections.body: Nurkic entered the league as a physical young center and logged NBA minutes for Denver across three partial seasons. He was not merely a speculative draft-rights name. With Nikola Jokić emerging as the club's longer-term center, Denver traded Nurkic in February 2017 along with a lottery-protected 2017 first-round selection to Portland for Mason Plumlee. That later arrangement gave Nurkic a different career chapter, and all of his Portland production belongs to Portland. Denver received real center development and then a contribution to another deal, but Plumlee's full return cannot be treated as a direct consequence of this June 2014 exchange alone.

sections.heading: Chicago's Return Was Not Empty, but It Fell Far Behind
sections.body: McDermott developed into a usable NBA shooter. For Chicago he scored 9.4 points per game on 42.5 percent three-point shooting in 2015-16, and produced 10.2 points per game before his February 2017 trade to Oklahoma City. His long professional career after leaving the Bulls is not part of Chicago's direct realized return. Randolph provided little lasting Bulls rotation value. The difference between one modest scoring wing and Denver's years of Harris plus the Nurkic development window supports the canonical Nuggets Win, Denver A+ and Chicago F. The 2015 second-round pick added depth to Denver's asset package, even though its eventual recipient Pointer did not become a meaningful Nuggets player.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win — Denver A+, Chicago F. Denver traded McDermott's No. 11 rights and Anthony Randolph for No. 16 Jusuf Nurkić, No. 19 Gary Harris and a 2015 second-rounder that became No. 53 Sir'Dominic Pointer. Harris became a multiyear starting guard and Nurkic gave Denver real center minutes before a separate Portland trade. McDermott provided Chicago shooting, but far less sustained team value. The outcome favors Denver without attributing Aaron Gordon's later career or Nurkic's Portland years wholesale to this one draft-night exchange.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Harris and Nurkić for McDermott: Denver's 2014 Draft Bet
featuredDeepDive.intro: Denver's June 2014 draft-night swap with Chicago ultimately changed the shape of the Nuggets' developing roster. The Bulls consolidated rights to two first-rounders into Doug McDermott, a proven college scorer selected No. 11, and received Anthony Randolph. The Nuggets went the other direction, taking No. 16 Jusuf Nurkić, No. 19 Gary Harris and a future second-round pick. The lasting difference was not simply picking two players instead of one. Harris grew into an NBA starter and Nurkić became a playable big man and later trade asset, while Chicago moved McDermott after less than three seasons.

sections.heading: The 2014 Draft Values Were Not Obvious on Selection Night
sections.body: Chicago's motivation was credible: McDermott had led the country in scoring at Creighton and was an established high-volume shooter. Denver's front office, under Tim Connelly, was emphasizing young two-way potential and deeper draft coverage. The Nuggets' own release listed the exchange as rights to Harris and Nurkić and a 2015 second-round choice for rights to McDermott plus Randolph. Harris had already built a strong collegiate defensive reputation at Michigan State, while Nurkić was coming from European competition. The difference between an immediately recognizable offensive college star and two younger development bets made their eventual career trajectories uncertain in June 2014.

sections.heading: Gary Harris's Starter Years Drove Most of Denver's Edge
sections.body: The decisive asset was Harris. After a 55-game rookie year, he started all 76 games he played in 2015-16. He made another 56 starts in 2016-17 and 65 of 67 games in 2017-18, when his scoring reached 17.5 per game. The draft-night No. 19 selection turned into years of reliable perimeter play and contributed to Denver's eventual playoff rise. He later participated in a multicomponent trade to acquire Aaron Gordon in 2021, but that deal also sent Denver's R.J. Hampton and a future first-rounder to Orlando. Harris' valuable Nuggets seasons are directly attributable to this trade; Gordon's entire subsequent production is not.

sections.heading: Nurkic Was Another NBA Rotation Player, Not Just a Pick
sections.body: Nurkic's Denver tenure featured injuries and a growing roster-role conflict once Jokić established himself. Still, the big man taken at No. 16 appeared in regular-season games for multiple seasons and became an asset Denver could move. In February 2017 the Nuggets sent Nurkić plus a protected first to Portland and received Mason Plumlee. This follow-on transaction again prevents assigning a later player one-for-one to a single draft right. The Portland return had an extra pick attached to it, and Nurkić's largest later NBA seasons came outside Denver. His Denver center minutes and trade value remain an independent contribution beyond Harris.

sections.heading: McDermott's Chicago Shooting Had a Clear Ceiling
sections.body: Chicago obtained a shooter who improved during his second professional season, when he hit 42.5 percent of his three-point attempts and averaged 9.4 points over 81 games. He continued scoring in 2016-17 and was part of the February 2017 Bulls transaction that sent Taj Gibson and a second-round pick to Oklahoma City for multiple players. The McDermott portion cannot be credited with every incoming asset from that later deal because Gibson and the pick were also sent out. McDermott subsequently stayed in the NBA with other franchises, but those later seasons do not represent Bulls production. Against Denver's two multiyear contributors, the single Chicago scorer did not deliver equivalent completed value.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Denver A+, Chicago F: Nuggets Win. In the original June 26, 2014 exchange, the Nuggets obtained Gary Harris, Jusuf Nurkić and the 2015 second-round pick that became Sir'Dominic Pointer for Doug McDermott's rights and Anthony Randolph. Harris supplied years of starting perimeter production; Nurkić provided center minutes and later trade leverage. McDermott gave Chicago useful shooting but was traded after fewer than three seasons. Neither Aaron Gordon's later full career nor Portland's subsequent Nurkić seasons should be counted as a direct standalone return from this transaction.

sections.heading: Chicago Moved Greg Smith Three Months After Signing Him
sections.body: The Bulls signed Greg Smith on April 14, 2014, after Houston waived the forward-center during an injury-disrupted season. He never played an NBA game for Chicago. On July 14, the Bulls traded him to Dallas for the draft rights to Tadija Dragicevic, an overseas forward who had been selected 53rd in the 2008 draft. Chicago's own announcement confirms both the date and the direction of the swap. For the Bulls, the transaction was primarily a payroll and roster decision rather than a search for an immediate substitute at center. Dallas received the player, while Chicago held foreign draft rights it was not about to turn into NBA rotation minutes.

sections.heading: The Bulls Were Clearing Room for a Different Frontcourt
sections.body: Smith was earning slightly under $950,000, a modest salary in absolute terms but relevant to Chicago's July 2014 free-agency planning. On the same day, the Bulls also traded Anthony Randolph, draft picks and cash to Orlando for Milovan Rakovic's rights. Those were separate transactions, both connected to making room for the arrivals of Pau Gasol and Nikola Mirotic. Dragicevic's rights gave Chicago formal consideration for Smith without requiring a new salary for an active NBA player. The eventual Gasol and Mirotic signings should not be credited wholly to this single small exchange: the team made several moves to create the necessary room.

sections.heading: Greg Smith Actually Played 42 Games for Dallas
sections.body: The Mavericks' official media guide records Smith at 42 appearances and two starts in 2014-15. He averaged 8.6 minutes, 1.9 points and 1.9 rebounds, making 30 of 49 field-goal attempts. His playoff contribution was one appearance lasting a single minute. Those numbers are limited, but they establish an important difference between the two sides: Dallas acquired a player who appeared in real games, whereas the Bulls retained draft rights to someone who never entered the league. Dallas wanted low-cost frontcourt depth after pursuing Chandler Parsons and reacquiring Tyson Chandler. Smith's actual role was a bench contingency, not a central piece of the playoff rotation.

sections.heading: Why the 2014 Greg Smith Deal Was an Even Trade
sections.body: The Even Trade verdict grades both Chicago and Dallas B-minus, reflecting two modest but different returns. Dallas acquired Greg Smith, who appeared in 42 games during 2014-15, made two starts and averaged 1.9 points in 8.6 minutes. Chicago took the rights to Tadija Dragicevic, who never played an NBA game, while moving Smith's salary out of its plans. The Bulls were also dealing Anthony Randolph, draft picks and cash to Orlando that same day, a separate transaction identified in Chicago's official historical ledger. Both moves preceded the Gasol and Mirotic signings, but neither the full value of those signings nor the other trade's assets belong to this particular Smith-for-rights swap. Dallas received some immediate bench minutes; Chicago gained roster flexibility without surrendering a starter. Neither team emerged with an enduring rotation piece, supporting the limited, even assessment.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Chicago B-, Dallas B-. The Bulls traded Greg Smith for Tadija Dragicevic's rights as part of a broader effort to free payroll and frontcourt room in July 2014. Dragicevic never played in the NBA. Smith supplied 42 Dallas games, averaging 1.9 points in 8.6 minutes, and appeared for one playoff minute. Neither return grew into a long-term rotation building block. The trade provided narrow, different kinds of utility without warranting a new winner or a change to the established grades.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Greg Smith for Tadija Dragicevic: A 2014 Bulls Salary Decision
featuredDeepDive.intro: The July 14, 2014 Bulls-Mavericks transaction transferred Greg Smith to Dallas and Tadija Dragicevic's draft rights to Chicago. Smith had never played for the Bulls after signing in April. Chicago was creating room for a different frontcourt while Dallas bought an inexpensive chance at additional depth. The eventual on-court return was 42 regular-season games from Smith for the Mavericks and none from Dragicevic for the Bulls.

sections.heading: Smith Was a Recent Chicago Signing, Not a Lost Starter
sections.body: Chicago signed Smith after the Rockets cut him near the end of the previous season. Knee trouble and an already crowded Houston frontcourt had limited him to 11 appearances in 2013-14. The Bulls did not see him suit up before trading him in July, which puts their decision in perspective. The club was relinquishing the prospect of a cheap reserve big, not moving a player responsible for its previous playoff production. Dallas could accept that risk because the acquisition cost only overseas draft rights. Chicago could accept the return because a player who was not projected to join the NBA would not take the same payroll slot.

sections.heading: The 2008 Draft Rights Were Legitimate Consideration
sections.body: Dragicevic was taken 53rd overall by Utah in 2008, then his rights moved through later transactions to Dallas before the 2014 swap. Those rights were a recognized trade asset even though Dragicevic had never signed an NBA contract. Chicago did not receive his existing NBA services, and he did not later become a Bulls player. This makes it inaccurate to describe the exchange as two comparable NBA forwards exchanging teams. One team gained the right to sign a player if circumstances changed; the other acquired an active NBA contract. Their financial and roster functions differed from the outset.

sections.heading: The Mavericks Got Depth, but Not a Breakout
sections.body: A Dallas media guide records 42 games and two starts for Smith during 2014-15. His averages of 1.9 points, 1.9 rebounds and 8.6 minutes reflect a limited role behind a more established frontcourt. There was one playoff appearance of one minute. The small contribution was nevertheless real, and it should not be erased simply because Dragicevic never played in the NBA. At the same time, Smith's 42 outings cannot be stretched into an explanation for Dallas's broader season, the Tyson Chandler return or Chandler Parsons's arrival. Those were independent roster decisions with far larger effects.

sections.heading: No Single Salary Dump Signed Pau Gasol
sections.body: The July 14 deal sits beside Chicago's separate Randolph-to-Orlando transaction and other free-agent arrangements before signing Pau Gasol and Nikola Mirotic. Contemporary reporting identified Smith's sub-million-dollar salary as one piece of the larger plan. Treating Gasol's subsequent All-Star production as an exclusive consequence of receiving Dragicevic's rights would exaggerate causality. The more defensible evaluation gives Chicago credit for reducing committed salary and maintaining flexibility, and Dallas credit for the actual modest minutes Smith provided. These limited outcomes explain the inherited B-/B- grade pairing more accurately than an invented long-term winner.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Chicago B-, Dallas B-; Even Trade. Chicago removed Smith's contract while adding an unexercised overseas draft-rights asset, and Dallas received 42 games of deep-frontcourt availability. Neither side acquired a future building block. Chicago's Gasol/Mirotic signings involved additional transactions and cannot be counted entirely as the return for Smith. The grades and verdict are preserved, with the documented transaction and actual Dallas usage replacing generic value language.
