sections.heading: Detroit Sent a Young Guard to Chicago for a Reserve Forward
sections.body: On June 17, 2016, Detroit exchanged 23-year-old guard Spencer Dinwiddie for Chicago forward Cameron Bairstow. A contemporaneous Pistons announcement framed the trade as a straightforward exchange of two players already fighting for NBA minutes. Dinwiddie was Detroit's No. 38 selection in 2014 and had appeared in 46 Pistons games across two seasons, spending stretches with the Grand Rapids Drive. Bairstow was Chicago's 2014 second-round selection, No. 49 overall, and had played 36 NBA games for the Bulls. Neither was an established starter or an expensive franchise centerpiece. The compelling story is what happened when each new employer made its first roster decision.

sections.heading: Chicago Waived Dinwiddie Twice Without Playing Him in the NBA
sections.body: The Bulls released Dinwiddie on July 7, re-signed him July 28 and waived him again on October 21, 2016, after the preseason. He consequently never recorded a Chicago Bulls NBA regular-season appearance. The trade's direct Chicago return is an evaluation period and summer-league participation, not the points and assists Dinwiddie produced elsewhere. He did spend nine games with the Windy City Bulls after the waiver, averaging 19.4 points, 8.1 assists and 3.7 rebounds in the Development League. That G League affiliation illustrates talent Chicago could observe, but it was not an NBA contract retained by the Bulls at the time of his subsequent career breakthrough.

sections.heading: Detroit Released Bairstow Before Opening the Next Season
sections.body: The Pistons also received no new regular-season playing production from their incoming player. Bairstow had made all 36 of his NBA appearances as a Bull before the trade. Detroit waived him on July 7, 2016, less than three weeks after acquiring him. There is no Pistons rotation stint to weigh against Dinwiddie's unrealized Chicago opportunity. Bairstow's pre-trade Bulls box scores are not a return to Detroit, just as Dinwiddie's 46 games with Detroit before June 2016 cannot count as Chicago production. Both sides acquired a player, conducted their roster evaluation and ended their NBA control before that player could make a regular-season appearance for the receiving club.

sections.heading: The Brooklyn Breakout Exposes an Opportunity Cost, Not Chicago Production
sections.body: Brooklyn signed Dinwiddie to an NBA contract on December 8, 2016, after his nine-game Windy City spell, and he grew into a productive NBA guard with the Nets. That outcome makes Chicago's decision to release him look painful in hindsight, especially because Detroit had previously given up his rights in exchange for a forward it soon waived. But the Nets' signing was an independent transaction and Brooklyn's future seasons were not value Chicago retained from the Bairstow trade. The canonical Even Trade and matching B- grades describe the two clubs' similarly limited direct realized returns. They should not be used to imply Dinwiddie's later NBA success occurred with Chicago or that Detroit obtained Bairstow production.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Chicago B-, Detroit B-. The Bulls obtained Spencer Dinwiddie but waived him twice before he played a Chicago NBA regular-season game. The Pistons acquired Cameron Bairstow and waived him July 7, 2016, also without a Detroit regular-season appearance. Dinwiddie's subsequent Windy City G League performances and December 2016 Brooklyn signing explain the opportunity Chicago failed to keep, rather than a basketball return it realized. Both receiving teams got effectively no NBA on-court contribution from this specific exchange.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Spencer Dinwiddie's Four-Month Chicago Stop and the Trade Neither Team Cashed In
featuredDeepDive.intro: Spencer Dinwiddie's later work for Brooklyn can obscure how briefly Chicago controlled him. The June 17, 2016 swap sent Cameron Bairstow to Detroit and the young guard to the Bulls. Each club waived its acquisition before the next NBA regular season began. Chicago twice released Dinwiddie, then watched its Development League affiliate help put him back on an NBA radar. Brooklyn, not Chicago, eventually signed him. The trade is therefore an unusual retrospective in which identifying the better future player and identifying the team that received useful playing value produce different answers.

sections.heading: The Roster Context Was Two Second-Round Prospects
sections.body: Detroit had selected Dinwiddie 38th in 2014, and the guard split the next two seasons between the Pistons and the Grand Rapids Drive. Chicago used the 49th selection of the same draft on Bairstow, a 6-foot-9 forward from New Mexico whose 36 Bulls games had produced modest minutes. The clubs swapped developmental depth rather than established stars. The official Pistons announcement summarized Dinwiddie's most recent 12-game Detroit season at 4.8 points and 1.8 assists per appearance. Those statistics are pre-trade context, not a measure of his return to Chicago. A proper completed-value assessment begins after he changed jerseys.

sections.heading: Waiver Dates Limit Each Franchise's Direct Return
sections.body: Detroit waived Bairstow on July 7, 2016, terminating its new roster option without a Pistons regular-season appearance. Chicago waived Dinwiddie on that same date, brought him back July 28, then cut him again October 21. The Bulls gave themselves two windows to evaluate him before deciding not to use him on the regular-season roster. Thus neither club can point to an NBA season, a playoff contribution or even a one-game regular-season cameo by its incoming player. The distinction is factual rather than semantic: Chicago's first opportunity and Detroit's acquisition were both over before the new campaign. Neither team should receive statistical credit from other teams' rosters.

sections.heading: The Windy City Bulls Bridge Came After Chicago's Second Waiver
sections.body: Dinwiddie remained near the organization through the Windy City Bulls, a separate NBA Development League arrangement rather than a continuing Chicago NBA roster slot. He averaged 19.4 points, 8.1 assists and 3.7 rebounds in nine Windy City games, recording three triple-doubles. Brooklyn signed him on December 8, 2016, and Windy City identified the move as its first NBA call-up. This development captures Chicago's missed opportunity in unusually concrete terms: a guard that its NBA team twice waived was soon good enough to secure a Nets contract. It still does not convert those later Brooklyn minutes into a Bulls return from a June trade.

sections.heading: The Even Verdict Describes Control That Expired, Not Equal Talents
sections.body: Dinwiddie plainly became the more consequential NBA player. That is not the same as saying the Bulls received his Brooklyn production in 2016. The direct asset from Detroit arrived for offseason evaluation and was cut twice. Bairstow's Pistons tenure ended with a waiver after twenty days. Both clubs had already surrendered control of the only new player obtained in the transaction by the time the 2016-17 season began. The stored Even Trade, B-/B-, measures that shared absence of retained NBA contribution. The future-value story instead asks why Chicago did not keep Dinwiddie and why Detroit exchanged the guard for an asset it released almost immediately.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, Chicago B- and Detroit B-. Spencer Dinwiddie never played a Bulls NBA regular-season game after Chicago acquired him in June 2016. Cameron Bairstow likewise never played one for Detroit, which released him July 7. Chicago waived Dinwiddie twice; his subsequent Windy City Development League call-up and Brooklyn career belong to later steps. The greatest hindsight opportunity was Chicago's decision not to retain him, not a hidden direct win in NBA playing value from this transaction.

sections.heading: July 7, 2016: Three Assets for the Rights to Majok
sections.body: The Lakers announced the exact return on July 7, 2016: Jose Calderon and two future second-round picks from Chicago for the draft rights to Ater Majok. This was a contract-and-draft-asset exchange, not a swap of two active rotation players. Calderon had arrived in Chicago during the Derrick Rose deal, and the Bulls were making financial room for their planned signing of Dwyane Wade. The Lakers' official statement emphasized Calderon's experience and shooting, which made the veteran more than a name used to carry a salary. Chicago accepted Majok's rights as the incoming consideration rather than receiving a player who would immediately take a Bulls roster spot. The two draft picks added potential later value for Los Angeles, but neither future draftee had been chosen when the agreement was announced.

sections.heading: Calderon Played 24 Lakers Games Before His Release
sections.body: Los Angeles did receive NBA playing time from the veteran guard. Its February 27, 2017 waiver announcement records Calderon appearing in 24 games, including 11 starts, with averages of 3.3 points, 2.1 assists and 1.7 rebounds in 12.2 minutes. Those figures establish a limited but identifiable contribution. They are also narrower than the value suggested by his career reputation: the Lakers had acquired a guard with 748 NBA appearances entering the trade, yet he was largely a reserve during his short stay. Calderon was waived before the 2016-17 regular season finished, so later appearances for other clubs cannot be counted as a Los Angeles return. This distinction is central to the inherited B+ evaluation: the package includes genuine veteran minutes plus separate draft assets, not several years of Lakers production from Calderon alone.

sections.heading: The Two Future Picks Require Separate Accounting
sections.body: Chicago also sent two future second-round selections, eventually associated in the transaction record with No. 47 Svi Mykhailiuk in 2018 and No. 34 Bruno Fernando in 2019. A future pick is an asset at the time of acquisition, but the player attached to its eventual draft slot is not automatically an NBA contributor for the acquiring franchise. The 2019 choice subsequently moved through a separate transaction involving the rights to Isaac Bonga, while the 2018 selection became the Mykhailiuk pick. These downstream movements belong in the history without falsely placing Fernando on the Lakers as a result of the 2016 agreement. Chicago's C+ grade describes accepting the non-NBA rights to Majok to facilitate financial flexibility; Los Angeles' B+ recognizes Calderon's actual stint and the two picks it could hold or move. The trade-day structure and realized roster value must be kept distinct.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win. Chicago's C+ for the Majok rights trails Los Angeles's B+ for Calderon and the 2018 and 2019 second-round picks. The value difference comes from that actual three-asset return, not a supposed star traded directly for draft rights.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The 2016 Calderón Salary-Dump Trade: Two Lakers Picks and Chicago’s Wade Room
featuredDeepDive.intro: The Lakers accepted José Calderón and two second-round choices for Ater Majok rights. Chicago opened cap space to pursue Dwyane Wade. The grades separate the trade-day financial purpose from Los Angeles player and draft-return value.

sections.heading: Chicago Paid Picks to Clear Room for Dwyane Wade
sections.body: The July 7, 2016 deal was a salary-cap transaction as much as a swap of basketball personnel. Chicago had acquired José Calderón in the Derrick Rose trade and needed room to complete its pursuit of Dwyane Wade. To move Calderón's expiring contract, the Bulls sent him and two future second-round choices to the Lakers, taking back only the draft rights to Ater Majok. Contemporary Associated Press reporting identified the effort to open cap space, and the Lakers' official release recorded the three incoming assets. The Bulls' return therefore cannot be measured solely by whether Majok appeared in an NBA game. The immediate objective was salary flexibility for a larger roster move. That context supports a nonfailing Chicago grade despite the thin direct draft-right return, while acknowledging that two picks were the price of moving the contract.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Collected Calderón and Two Future Choices
sections.body: The Lakers accepted the veteran guard and both future second-round selections for rights to Ater Majok, who was not playing in the NBA. Calderón brought a long record as a passer and perimeter shooter, including a career three-point percentage above 40 percent when Los Angeles acquired him. He was not a long-term Lakers building block, however. The team's official February 27, 2017 release says he played 24 games with 11 starts, averaging 3.3 points and 2.1 assists before being waived. The other pieces gave Los Angeles optionality beyond that short rental. The 2018 selection eventually became No. 47, associated with Svi Mykhailiuk; the 2019 second became No. 34, later used on Bruno Fernando after an intervening rights transaction. The two picks should not be flattened into imaginary Lakers playing seasons.

sections.heading: The 2019 Second Went Through Another Deal
sections.body: Los Angeles did not simply keep every incoming asset from July 2016 until the corresponding player joined its roster. The Bulls' 2019 second-round pick subsequently moved in a separate July 2018 transaction involving the rights to Isaac Bonga and cash before the No. 34 selection was used on Bruno Fernando. Likewise, the 2018 second-round pick was ultimately used for the No. 47 choice associated with Svi Mykhailiuk. Tracking the difference between the acquired pick and the eventual recipient avoids overstating the Lakers' direct roster return. Both choices had value on the trade date because they were transferable future assets, and the exact downstream paths should be separated from the original Calderón salary absorption. The official Lakers announcement establishes the 2016 package; transaction ledgers document the later selections and further movement.

sections.heading: Why Lakers B-Plus Beats Bulls C-Plus
sections.body: The Lakers won a package containing a usable veteran guard and two tradable draft choices by surrendering only Ater Majok's draft rights. Calderón's actual Lakers stay was limited to 24 games, so the result was not a major on-court acquisition in itself. The draft compensation, however, provided genuine flexibility, supporting the inherited B-plus. Chicago accepted a weaker direct asset return because the club wanted to clear Calderón's salary to pursue Wade. That context gives the Bulls a plausible C-plus for accomplishing a transaction-day financial objective rather than an F for acquiring nonproducing rights. A Lakers Win verdict still makes sense when the exchanged assets are compared on their own. The later careers of Svi Mykhailiuk and Bruno Fernando should not automatically be credited to the 2016 Lakers roster, and Wade's subsequent career should not be counted as if he came from Los Angeles.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win — Los Angeles B+, Chicago C+. The Lakers received José Calderón, who made 24 appearances and 11 starts before being waived, plus two second-round picks. Chicago traded those assets for Ater Majok rights primarily to clear Calderón salary and pursue Wade.

sections.heading: Why Chicago and Milwaukee Exchanged Guards and Wings
sections.body: The October 17, 2016 exchange sent Michael Carter-Williams from Milwaukee to Chicago and Tony Snell the other way. Nothing in the canonical asset ledger indicates a pick, cash payment or third club. Each front office was changing the kind of reserve it could deploy: the Bulls added a ball handler with size and a former Rookie of the Year award, while the Bucks took a 6-foot-7 perimeter player who could defend wings and work without dominating possessions. NBA.com's contemporary coverage described two players trying to find firmer roles after disappointing stretches. Those trade-date expectations are distinct from the season that followed.

sections.heading: Snell's Milwaukee Minutes Turned the Experiment Around
sections.body: Milwaukee received an immediate rotation piece instead of another guard competing for on-ball work. During 2016-17, Snell appeared in 80 regular-season games, averaged 29.2 minutes and 8.5 points, and made 144 three-pointers at 40.6 percent accuracy. He also played in the Bucks' six postseason games that spring. Those are directly attributable contributions from the incoming player, not speculative benefits attached to future unrelated transactions. He gave Milwaukee a credible floor-spacing complement for its developing frontcourt. The volume of minutes and made threes supplies a concrete explanation for the franchise's stronger retrospective grade.

sections.heading: Carter-Williams' Chicago Return Was Shorter and Less Efficient
sections.body: Chicago's acquisition was understandable as a play for additional guard size and passing, but the measured return was smaller. Carter-Williams played 45 regular-season games for the 2016-17 Bulls, averaging 18.8 minutes, 6.6 points and 2.5 assists while shooting 23.4 percent on three-pointers. His role was intermittent rather than that of a reliable primary creator or outside shooter. Chicago reached the playoffs, and he appeared in five postseason games, so the contribution was not zero. The comparison, however, is between that single Bulls season and Snell's documented Milwaukee workload, not the players' pretrade reputations.

sections.heading: Snell's Milwaukee Rotation Role Outlasted Carter-Williams in Chicago
sections.body: The Bucks Win verdict grades Milwaukee A-minus and Chicago C-plus. That gap reflects the on-court return rather than the players' reputations when the trade took place. Tony Snell became a regular Milwaukee wing, appearing in 80 games during 2016-17, averaging 29.2 minutes and 8.5 points while making 144 threes at 40.6 percent. Michael Carter-Williams played 45 games for Chicago that season, with 6.6 points and 2.5 assists per game. The Bulls had a reason to acquire a larger playmaking guard, and his contribution was not zero. Milwaukee nevertheless received a more dependable outside shooter and higher-volume rotation player. Those direct, team-specific results explain the different retrospective letter grades without attributing later transactions or other clubs' seasons to either side.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win — Milwaukee A-minus, Chicago C-plus. Tony Snell gave Milwaukee 80 games, 29.2 minutes per contest and 40.6-percent three-point shooting in 2016-17. Michael Carter-Williams gave Chicago 45 games and 6.6 points per contest. The two-player trade carried no draft consideration in the canonical ledger; the higher Milwaukee grade reflects the usable wing rotation return rather than an imagined asset chain.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Carter-Williams for Snell: The Wing-Role Payoff
featuredDeepDive.intro: October 2016 offered Chicago and Milwaukee a simple swap of two former first-round picks with mismatched skill sets. The meaningful test is what those players actually delivered in their new uniforms. Milwaukee's Tony Snell became a regular perimeter contributor; Chicago's Michael Carter-Williams played a smaller guard role. The source-backed season totals explain the preserved Bucks Win classification more precisely than a boilerplate verdict.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Bought Wing Spacing, Not Another Lead Guard
sections.body: The useful detail in Milwaukee's half of the exchange was positional rather than financial. Snell arrived as a wing, and the 2016-17 results show why a player of that type fit: 80 games, 144 three-point makes and 40.6 percent shooting beyond the arc. A player can contribute meaningful value without leading the club in scoring when his shots help support a lineup's spacing. Snell's 29.2 minutes per game point to the coaching staff's willingness to use him extensively. That is a narrower and more defensible argument than crediting this transaction for later successes of the entire Bucks roster. The incoming player's own production is enough.

sections.heading: Chicago's Bet Was on Carter-Williams' Size and Playmaking
sections.body: Carter-Williams was still recognizable for winning Rookie of the Year in Philadelphia, and Chicago had reason to investigate whether the guard could provide different handling and defensive options. NBA.com's October 2016 trade analysis regarded both participants as talented but stalled; it did not promise either would become a star. By the following spring, his Bulls stint totaled 45 regular-season appearances and fewer than nineteen minutes per game. His 2.5 assists reflected some playmaking, but 23.4 percent three-point shooting limited how he could be paired with other ball handlers. The actual Bulls evidence is less favorable than the upside-based pitch that could be made when the deal closed.

sections.heading: The One-for-One Ledger Keeps Attribution Disciplined
sections.body: Unlike multi-team draft exchanges, the Carter-Williams–Snell transaction requires no guesswork about conditional conveyance or cash. The Bulls received the former Bucks guard, and Milwaukee received the former Bulls wing. Their later movement around the league should not be projected backward as extra pieces of this specific swap. For the 2016-17 season, the direct comparison is particularly clear: Snell contributed 80 games and 8.5 points per game in Milwaukee, while Carter-Williams contributed 45 games and 6.6 points in Chicago. Their roles differed, so raw scoring cannot decide every nuance, but the gap in available minutes and shooting usefulness is concrete.

sections.heading: A Trade-Date Gamble Became a Different Retrospective Result
sections.body: Chicago could see a route to guard depth when it accepted Carter-Williams, and Milwaukee could envision improving its perimeter coverage with Snell. Both rationales fit the information available in mid-October 2016. The hindsight argument is narrower: Milwaukee ended the season with an everyday wing who hit more than forty percent of his threes, while Chicago's acquisition could not hold an equally stable role. NBA.com recorded the transaction as a modest-risk change for both clubs, and the statistical record shows how the paths diverged. The existing Bucks Win verdict and A-minus versus C-plus grading stay attached to those direct results, not a claim that Chicago knew the future.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The original Bucks Win judgment is preserved: Milwaukee A-minus, Chicago C-plus. The team receiving Snell got 80 regular-season appearances and reliable outside volume at 40.6 percent accuracy, plus a six-game playoff series. Carter-Williams played 45 games in Chicago, contributed some passing and defensive size, but shot 23.4 percent from deep and occupied a less dependable role. This was a player-for-player exchange, with no conditional pick that needs retroactive attribution. October expectations for both clubs were understandable; the 2016-17 direct returns account for the gap. Later career moves are separate transactions and do not add assets to this ledger.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Acquired Two Forwards and an Unprotected Pick
sections.body: The February 23, 2017 exchange sent Taj Gibson, Doug McDermott and Chicago's unprotected 2018 second-round selection to Oklahoma City. The Bulls received Cameron Payne, Joffrey Lauvergne and Anthony Morrow. Both franchises' contemporaneous releases list the same six assets and identify the future pick as unprotected. That detail matters: the choice was not a lottery-protected first-rounder, nor was it originally tied to an unrelated 2018 transaction. Oklahoma City was chasing a postseason opportunity behind Russell Westbrook and wanted Gibson's veteran defensive play with McDermott's shooting. Chicago had a younger guard in mind, with Payne, a 2015 first-rounder, potentially offering more development time than he had received as Westbrook's reserve.

sections.heading: Gibson Supplied Immediate Frontcourt Help
sections.body: Gibson had started 55 games for Chicago in 2016–17, averaging 11.6 points and 7.0 rebounds before the deadline. His new team used him in 23 regular-season games, including 16 starts, and he averaged roughly nine points after the move according to the Bulls' season-end appraisal. He was in Oklahoma City's frontcourt rotation for its first-round playoff series against Houston, where he averaged 9.8 points. This was a real contribution, although the Thunder lost that series in five games and Gibson departed in free agency that summer. The acquired McDermott gave Oklahoma City another shooter, but his later movement in the Carmelo Anthony trade demonstrates he was also an asset the club could use beyond the 2017 postseason.

sections.heading: Chicago's Three-Player Return Had Limited Early Impact
sections.body: The Bulls framed the deal as adding youth and roster flexibility. Payne arrived after a right-foot injury had restricted him to 20 appearances for the Thunder before the trade. Chicago's October 2017 player-options announcement credited him with only 10 Bulls games in the 2016–17 stretch, averaging 4.9 points and 1.4 assists. Basketball-Reference's completed regular-season split includes 11 Chicago appearances, a small discrepancy in the club's contemporary reporting that does not alter the outcome. Chicago's own 2016–17 review listed nine games and 4.6 points per appearance for Morrow, while Lauvergne supplied frontcourt depth rather than a durable new cornerstone. Those short stints do not justify pretending the incoming trio equaled Gibson's established production.

sections.heading: The Second-Rounder Later Reached New York
sections.body: Chicago's unprotected 2018 second-round pick was a separate outgoing asset with downstream value. Oklahoma City subsequently included that exact Chicago-origin selection along with McDermott and Enes Kanter in its September 25, 2017 trade with the New York Knicks for Carmelo Anthony. New York used the choice at No. 36 on Mitchell Robinson in June 2018. The Knicks' own draft release confirms both the player and selection; their Anthony trade announcement identifies the pick's Chicago origin. It would be inaccurate to write that Oklahoma City drafted Robinson or that the 2017 Bulls trade directly supplied Carmelo Anthony by itself. These later transactions changed custody of the pick, not the original asset ledger.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Published verdict: Oklahoma City Thunder Win — Thunder A-, Chicago D. Oklahoma City gained Gibson, McDermott and an unprotected 2018 second; Chicago obtained Payne, Lauvergne and Morrow. Gibson provided a useful postseason rotation stint, and the Chicago-origin pick later moved to New York in the separate Anthony trade. The Knicks selected Mitchell Robinson at No. 36; neither the selection nor Anthony was an immediate player return in this February 2017 exchange.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: How Gibson, McDermott and a Second-Rounder Changed Hands
featuredDeepDive.intro: The Thunder's February 2017 trade with Chicago was a veteran-for-youth exchange with a consequential future pick attached. Oklahoma City acquired Taj Gibson, Doug McDermott and an unprotected 2018 second; Chicago accepted Cameron Payne, Anthony Morrow and Joffrey Lauvergne. Gibson joined a playoff rotation immediately, while the future selection was transferred to New York later that year as part of a separate deal for Carmelo Anthony. The two transactions need separate ledgers to understand the actual return.

sections.heading: The February Ledger Is Unambiguous
sections.body: Both Oklahoma City and Chicago announced the exchange on February 23, 2017. The Thunder's release clearly labels its incoming draft asset an unprotected 2018 second-round selection, alongside Gibson and McDermott. The Bulls' release lists Payne, Morrow and Lauvergne as the three players received. Those are the pieces to use in the canonical trade accounting. Chicago did not send a 2018 first-round choice; Oklahoma City did not send a different 2018 player instead of Lauvergne. The draft pick was a standalone contingent future selection that later became a specific second-round number. The release also establishes that the Thunder wanted established help during a season in which Westbrook carried a heavy offensive burden and the team sought better frontcourt defense and perimeter spacing.

sections.heading: Why Gibson's 23 Games Were Valuable, But Limited
sections.body: Gibson's years as a Chicago rebounder and interior defender gave Oklahoma City something immediately useful alongside Steven Adams. A Bulls retrospective recorded that he started 16 of his 23 Thunder regular-season appearances, averaged nine points during that stint and 9.8 in the playoffs. Oklahoma City needed a reliable veteran at power forward and benefited from those minutes, but the club exited the first round against Houston. The trade did not generate a deep Thunder playoff run, and Gibson did not sign a long-term Oklahoma City contract after that season. His concrete return is therefore one useful postseason stretch, while McDermott and the pick had different utility because the franchise could subsequently move them in a larger deal.

sections.heading: The Chicago Pieces Never Became a Comparable Core
sections.body: Payne was the younger centerpiece in Chicago's plan. The Bulls' February release emphasized that he had been the 14th pick in the 2015 draft but also detailed time lost to a right-foot fracture. By the end of the season the team's player appraisal graded his performance poorly, citing limited games and uneven offensive decision-making. Chicago's official October option-release referred to 10 late-season appearances with 4.9 points and 1.4 assists; the statistical regular-season split registers 11, highlighting the importance of distinguishing a report date from the completed season. Morrow appeared in nine Bulls games according to the team's own review. Lauvergne filled out the player package, but the 2017 return did not produce a long-term pair of dependable starters to replace Gibson and McDermott. Their subsequent careers elsewhere should not be automatically credited to Chicago's 2017 outcome.

sections.heading: The Knicks, Not Oklahoma City, Drafted Mitchell Robinson
sections.body: The 2018 Chicago-origin second rounder included in the Bulls-Thunder deal later appeared in the September 2017 Carmelo Anthony trade. Oklahoma City moved the right to New York with Enes Kanter and Doug McDermott; New York sent Anthony to Oklahoma City. The Knicks' own release expressly names Chicago's second-round selection, and the organization used the 36th overall pick on Mitchell Robinson in the 2018 draft. This is a traceable downstream pick path but not evidence that Robinson played for the Thunder. Likewise, Anthony's acquisition required Kanter and McDermott as well as the pick; the original Chicago transaction cannot be credited as the entire cost of acquiring him. The source-preserving archive verdict stays Thunder A-, Bulls D, Oklahoma City Thunder Win, pending any separate grade analysis.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Oklahoma City got useful short-term Gibson minutes and movable McDermott and draft rights; Chicago's immediate Payne, Morrow and Lauvergne return was modest. The Chicago-origin 2018 second was later conveyed to New York in the Anthony exchange and selected as Mitchell Robinson at No. 36. The existing Thunder A-, Bulls D and Oklahoma City Thunder Win verdict is preserved while preventing downstream over-credit.

sections.heading: Minnesota Paid for a Star Who Could Change Its Competitive Standard
sections.body: The Timberwolves entered the 2017 draft with young talent but no playoff appearance since 2004. Acquiring Jimmy Butler reunited Tom Thibodeau with a proven two-way leader and placed an established All-NBA player beside Karl-Anthony Towns and Andrew Wiggins. Minnesota also received the rights to Justin Patton while sending Zach LaVine, Kris Dunn, and the No. 7 pick used on Lauri Markkanen. The price was substantial, but the objective was precise: accelerate a talented roster from promise into immediate postseason relevance.

sections.heading: Butler Delivered the Playoff Breakthrough in One Season
sections.body: The short-term case for Minnesota is stronger than the length of Butler's tenure suggests. He became the team's late-game organizer, best perimeter defender, and emotional standard-setter. Minnesota won 47 games and clinched a postseason berth in overtime on the final night, ending a fourteen-year absence. Butler's knee injury exposed how dependent the team had become on him, but he returned for the playoff push. That season was not a championship run; it was still a meaningful franchise result that the outgoing young core had not yet produced.

sections.heading: The Relationship Collapse Restricted Minnesota’s Return
sections.body: Butler requested a trade before the next season, and the public practice confrontation made a long-term partnership impossible. Minnesota eventually sent him and Patton to Philadelphia for Robert Covington, Dario Saric, Jerryd Bayless, and a second-round pick. Covington had value and Saric was useful, but the downstream package did not preserve a star-level asset. The Timberwolves therefore received one important season and a diminished secondary return rather than the multiyear contention window anticipated when the original deal was completed.

sections.heading: Chicago Acquired Two Players Who Became All-Stars
sections.body: LaVine recovered from the ACL injury that had depressed his market and became a two-time All-Star in Chicago, eventually serving as the team's primary scorer. Markkanen showed high-level shooting and scoring potential before reaching his best form after leaving the Bulls. Dunn developed into a strong defensive guard but never solved the offensive questions attached to his draft position. Chicago acquired real talent and more cumulative player value than Minnesota retained, even though the organization failed to assemble those pieces into a coherent contender.

sections.heading: Chicago’s Later Asset Management Limits the Grade
sections.body: A retrospective trade grade cannot credit Chicago for every achievement Markkanen produced elsewhere. The Bulls did not extend or develop his role into the All-Star version later seen in Utah, and the eventual sign-and-trade return was modest. LaVine's best seasons occurred in Chicago, but the team won only one playoff game with him. Those shortcomings belong partly to later decisions, yet they reduce the realized organizational benefit of the original package. Chicago won the value comparison without transforming the return into sustained team success.

sections.heading: A Slight Bulls Edge Respects Minnesota’s Accomplishment
sections.body: The previous Slight Partner Edge label conflicted with grades that already placed Chicago ahead. Naming the Bulls resolves that contradiction, but the separation should remain narrow. Minnesota acquired the best player at the time and ended a historic playoff drought; Chicago acquired the longer-lasting value and two future All-Stars. B and B-minus grades recognize a trade that produced meaningful benefits and serious disappointments on both sides. Neither franchise extracted the full ceiling of the assets it received.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Chicago receives a slight edge with a B, while Minnesota earns a B-minus. The Bulls acquired LaVine, Dunn, and Markkanen, with LaVine becoming a two-time Chicago All-Star and Markkanen developing into an All-Star after his departure. Minnesota received the best immediate player, won 47 games, and ended a fourteen-year playoff drought, but Butler's exit after one full season and the reduced Philadelphia return limited the long-term payoff. Chicago captured more durable talent; Minnesota captured the more important single season.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The Jimmy Butler Trade Produced Two Partial Successes and No Lasting Contender
featuredDeepDive.intro: The 2017 deal is difficult to grade because each side can point to a legitimate achievement and an obvious failure. Minnesota proved that its young core could reach the playoffs when paired with a demanding two-way star, but the partnership disintegrated before a second full season. Chicago acquired enough young talent to justify a rebuild, but did not convert LaVine, Markkanen, and Dunn into sustained postseason progress. The verdict depends on duration: the Bulls kept more value, while the Timberwolves created the more meaningful immediate result.

sections.heading: The Trade Was Rational for a Franchise Tired of Waiting
sections.body: Minnesota had spent years accumulating prospects without establishing winning habits. Butler was in his prime, under contract below the maximum salary, and familiar with Thibodeau's defensive expectations. Trading young assets for that profile was a defensible attempt to accelerate rather than a reckless pursuit of celebrity. The problem was not the concept of adding Butler. It was the fragile relationship between the coach, the star, and the rest of the roster, which left the organization with little ability to preserve the original investment once Butler demanded an exit.

sections.heading: LaVine Became the Most Durable Asset in the Deal
sections.body: LaVine arrived injured and needed time to regain explosiveness, but his shot creation and scoring eventually made him Chicago's clearest long-term return. He averaged star-level offensive numbers, earned two All-Star selections, and remained with the Bulls far longer than Butler stayed in Minnesota. His defensive limitations and the team's modest postseason record prevent an A-level grade, yet the acquisition worked well enough to keep Chicago from losing the trade outright even after Dunn disappointed and Markkanen's role became unstable.

sections.heading: Markkanen’s Later Breakout Is Both Credit and Indictment
sections.body: Selecting Markkanen with the acquired No. 7 pick was a successful talent decision. He displayed shooting range and offensive potential in Chicago before injuries, coaching changes, and an uncertain role interrupted his development. His eventual All-Star leap in Utah confirms that the Bulls obtained a high-value player, but it also highlights the organization's failure to capture the full benefit. A trade grade should credit the acquired talent while limiting the reward to value the team actually realized or preserved through a meaningful downstream return.

sections.heading: Minnesota’s 2018 Berth Had Real Historical Weight
sections.body: Calling the Timberwolves' side a failure ignores what ending the drought meant. Minnesota had not reached the playoffs since Kevin Garnett's 2004 conference-finals season. Butler's arrival raised the team's defensive accountability, late-game execution, and competitive confidence. The season ended in the first round against a dominant Houston team, but the Game 82 victory over Denver represented a genuine threshold crossed. That accomplishment supports a B-minus even though the relationship collapse and subsequent trade prevented the move from becoming a long-term win.

sections.heading: The Deal Shows the Difference Between Acquiring Value and Organizing It
sections.body: Chicago won the duration comparison but could not arrange its assets into a stable competitive structure. Minnesota organized a playoff team almost immediately but could not sustain the human relationships required to keep it together. Those contrasting failures explain why neither side earns an elite grade. The Bulls' slight advantage comes from retaining LaVine's All-Star production and having selected Markkanen, not from superior team results. Minnesota's grade rests on one breakthrough season rather than a successful multiyear star acquisition.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Bulls win narrowly because the acquired talent lasted longer and produced two future All-Stars, while Minnesota's best result was concentrated into one season. Chicago's B acknowledges LaVine's prime production and the quality of the Markkanen selection but penalizes the failure to maximize either asset collectively. Minnesota's B-minus gives full weight to ending the playoff drought and receiving elite Butler play, while accounting for the rapid breakup and reduced downstream return. Both teams achieved part of their objective; neither built the enduring contender the trade was meant to create.

sections.heading: What New Orleans Sent to Chicago on September 1
sections.body: The Pelicans announced on September 1, 2017 that they sent Quincy Pondexter, a future second-round selection and cash to the Bulls for the rights to Ater Majok. The Pelicans’ own official release confirms all four contractual components. Pondexter had missed the previous two full seasons because of knee problems; he was a health and roster risk rather than a guaranteed starter for Chicago. Majok was the No. 58 pick in 2011 and was playing professionally overseas, so New Orleans acquired his NBA rights rather than an active rotation player. Contemporary reporting also identified financial relief as one reason New Orleans moved Pondexter. The protected trade records the Bulls receiving a 2018 second later associated with Tony Carr at No. 51.

sections.heading: Pondexter Returned for 23 Bulls Games Before Being Waived
sections.body: Chicago’s February 1, 2018 waiver release gives the receiving-team result precisely: Pondexter played 23 regular-season games for the Bulls, averaging 2.0 points and 1.2 rebounds in 8.6 minutes. He shot 28.6 percent from the field and 13.6 percent from three. Chicago therefore got actual bench minutes, not a healthy version of the Memphis and New Orleans wing from several years earlier. Those 23 games form the direct player contribution of Pondexter to this exchange; his 279 previous career appearances came for different teams and predated the September 2017 agreement. The Bulls later waived him, limiting the acquired contract’s sporting return despite the additional cash and pick asset.

sections.heading: The No. 51 Pick Was Traded Back to New Orleans before the Draft
sections.body: The future second-round selection from the 2017 agreement followed a separate route. On February 1, 2018, the Bulls sent Nikola Mirotić and the same 2018 No. 51 second-round selection back to the Pelicans in a larger trade for Omer Aşik, Jameer Nelson, Tony Allen, a protected first-round choice and second-round swap rights. New Orleans then used No. 51 on Penn State guard Tony Carr in June. Carr was therefore not a Bulls draftee who played NBA games for Chicago as a result of the Pondexter swap. The original right was real value New Orleans surrendered in 2017, but its eventual return to New Orleans required the later Mirotić package and cannot be mistaken for direct 2017 player production.

sections.heading: Majok Was a Rights Acquisition, Not New Orleans NBA Production
sections.body: Ater Majok’s name is essential to the transaction even though he never appeared in an NBA regular-season game for the Pelicans. The official New Orleans announcement identifies him as a 2011 Lakers second-round selection then playing for Homenetmen Beirut in Lebanon. The Bulls conveyed control of his rights; New Orleans did not acquire an established NBA player in exchange for the injured Pondexter and its draft-and-cash package. This asymmetry supports the protected Bulls Win, Chicago B+ and Pelicans D+ judgment, but the grade is a valuation of cash, the original second-round asset and roster flexibility, not a claim Pondexter starred for Chicago. The exact cash figure is not stated in the official team release; a contemporaneous independent offseason review reported approximately $2.5 million.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The saved Bulls Win with Chicago B+ and New Orleans D+ is retained. Chicago received Pondexter’s 23 games, cash and a 2018 second-round pick, later sent back to the Pelicans in the distinct Mirotić transaction. New Orleans obtained Majok’s rights but no Pelicans NBA playing minutes from him. The second-round selection eventually became Tony Carr at No. 51 for New Orleans, not a Bulls player acquired directly in 2017.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The 2017 Pondexter–Majok Trade: Chicago’s Cash and a Pick Later Returned to New Orleans
featuredDeepDive.intro: On September 1, 2017, New Orleans sent Quincy Pondexter, cash and a future second-round selection to Chicago for the rights to Ater Majok. Pondexter supplied 23 Bulls games and was waived the following February. The 2018 second-round selection became the No. 51 Tony Carr pick, but only after the Bulls sent it back to the Pelicans in the separate Nikola Mirotić trade. The archived Bulls Win and Chicago B+/New Orleans D+ grades are retained without double-counting the later transaction or inventing Majok NBA minutes.

sections.heading: The Official Pelicans Announcement Identifies Four Components
sections.body: The September 1 official New Orleans statement lists Pondexter, a future second-round pick and cash moving to Chicago; the rights to Ater Majok traveled the opposite direction. Majok was a former Lakers draft pick playing overseas. Pondexter had not played an NBA game since the 2014-15 season because of knee injuries, so the swap represented a deliberate transfer of an uncertain roster contract. Chicago gained a draft and financial consideration as well as a possible wing contributor. The four pieces must be recorded in their original direction rather than rewriting the deal as an exchange for Tony Carr, who would not be chosen until the next draft.

sections.heading: Pondexter Played 23 Games; Majok Played None for the Pelicans
sections.body: The Bulls’ own waiver notice of February 1, 2018 confirms 23 appearances for Pondexter, 2.0 points, 1.2 rebounds, 0.3 assists and 8.6 minutes per game. These are useful, though limited, NBA receiving-team results. New Orleans, meanwhile, gained rights to Majok, who did not play for the Pelicans in an NBA regular-season game. Pondexter’s lengthy earlier Grizzlies and Pelicans career is background, not new Chicago production. A bare comparison of 23 versus zero NBA games would still overlook the cash and future pick that accompanied the veteran to Chicago, as well as New Orleans’s intended contract flexibility.

sections.heading: The Mirotić Trade Changed Who Eventually Drafted Tony Carr
sections.body: February 1, 2018 brought a different Chicago–New Orleans deal. The Bulls sent Nikola Mirotić and the second-round pick they had received in the Pondexter transaction back to the Pelicans, receiving a protected first-rounder and veterans including Omer Aşik. The second was exercised at No. 51 by New Orleans on Tony Carr from Penn State. The 2017 swap did give Chicago temporary control of that valuable second-round asset; the club later used it in a larger package with a distinct price. It is incorrect to assign Carr’s subsequent development as direct Bulls NBA production, or to claim New Orleans had retained that pick continuously from the initial September 2017 deal.

sections.heading: Cash and Salary Relief Complicate an Otherwise Uneven Return
sections.body: New Orleans’s September announcement does not specify a cash amount; an offseason review by Hoops Rumors describes approximately $2.5 million sent to Chicago. The amount should be treated as reported rather than a figure confirmed in the primary release. The Pelicans freed salary obligations connected with an injured veteran while holding an overseas draft right. Chicago collected cash, a pick that could be moved again and 23 low-minute Pondexter appearances. Bulls Win is a plausible inherited editorial conclusion from that package, but neither side obtained lasting NBA minutes from the principal player it received. Future pick returns and New Orleans’s separate Mirotić acquisition should remain outside the direct 2017 result.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Chicago B+, New Orleans D+ and Bulls Win remain unchanged. Pondexter appeared in 23 Bulls games before a February 2018 waiver; Majok’s rights never became Pelicans regular-season playing time. Cash and the 2018 second constituted Chicago’s other original return. The Bulls subsequently sent that same pick to New Orleans in the Mirotić trade, allowing the Pelicans to select Tony Carr No. 51. The separate transaction is documented rather than credited twice.

sections.heading: Chicago Took Vonleh and Cash for Overseas Draft Rights
sections.body: The Bulls received 22-year-old forward Noah Vonleh and cash considerations from Portland on February 8, 2018. Portland obtained the NBA draft rights to Serbian center Milovan Raković, a 2007 second-round selection who was playing professionally in Switzerland. Vonleh was a former No. 9 overall draft choice seeking more NBA opportunity. The trade gave Chicago a short-term look at a still-young forward without giving up a player from its active NBA rotation.

sections.heading: Portland’s Main Benefit Was Financial
sections.body: Portland wanted to reduce salary commitments while its roster pursued a playoff run. The Trail Blazers had used Vonleh for 185 games across three seasons, but the 2017–18 version of the team had diminished his role. Taking non-NBA draft rights in return allowed the organization to remove his remaining salary; contemporaneous coverage also identified relief from the luxury-tax calculation as a key motive. That was a rational roster-financial decision even if Raković never joined Portland.

sections.heading: Vonleh Was a Low-Risk Trial, Not a Bulls Breakthrough
sections.body: Chicago received an inexpensive opportunity to evaluate a mobile rebounding forward entering free agency. Vonleh offered frontcourt activity and occasional starts, but his brief Bulls stint did not develop into a long-term building block. The team acquired some real short-term NBA minutes and cash. That is enough to outperform dormant draft rights in the basketball ledger, not enough to claim it acquired a future cornerstone or materially transformed a rebuilding franchise.

sections.heading: How to Read the B-plus and C-plus
sections.body: The Bulls’ B-plus recognizes acquiring an NBA-capable prospect and cash without surrendering an active roster player. Portland’s C-plus reflects the financial value of moving Vonleh’s contract and the reality that rights to a player outside the NBA generated little direct court value. The grade gap is modest: the transaction was a sensible low-cost gamble for Chicago and salary management for Portland, not an impact trade on which either team’s subsequent success depended.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win — Chicago B-plus, Portland C-plus. Chicago took a low-cost look at Vonleh and acquired cash while relinquishing only Raković’s unused NBA rights. Portland obtained salary and luxury-tax relief, a legitimate benefit even without an on-court replacement. Vonleh’s Bulls stint was brief, so the better basketball return belongs to Chicago without making this a franchise-defining transaction.

sections.heading: The Transaction in Retrospect
sections.body: Chicago sent Jameer Nelson to Detroit on February 8, 2018, acquiring center Willie Reed and the right to exchange its position in the 2022 second round with the Pistons. The contemporary Bulls media guide and Detroit's official announcement describe the Reed-for-Nelson portion, while transaction histories identify the two draft positions later associated with the swap: No. 33, Christian Koloko, and No. 49, Isaiah Mobley. These are outcomes used to trace a conditional pick swap, not two additional NBA veterans included at the deadline.

sections.heading: How the Balance Holds
sections.body: The short-term return for Chicago was narrower than the incoming asset list might imply. Reed was acquired and then waived by the Bulls on the same day, so the transaction did not supply sustained Chicago center minutes. The potentially useful consideration was the option to swap second-round positions in 2022. Detroit obtained Nelson, a veteran point guard, and accepted the opposite side of the swap terms. Chicago's own 2022–23 media guide records both the trade and the same-day waiver, preventing the story from being told as a lasting Reed acquisition.

sections.heading: Value on Chicago Bulls
sections.body: The 2022 draft numbers illustrate why the option deserves separate treatment. Basketball-Reference identifies the second-round positions as No. 33, eventually Christian Koloko, and No. 49, eventually Isaiah Mobley. One side of the transaction conveyed Chicago's right to swap; the other recorded Detroit's corresponding duty or reduced pick position. Describing the rights and obligation as if two independent picks were simply exchanged in 2018 would obscure the contractual mechanism. Neither draft identity proves that the named player subsequently appeared for the corresponding 2018 team.

sections.heading: Value on the Detroit Pistons
sections.body: The site's retrospective calls this an Even Trade and gives the Bulls and Pistons B- apiece. Chicago used Nelson's contract to obtain a potential improvement in its future draft position, while Detroit acquired an experienced guard and surrendered the swap advantage. That difference in timing explains why a simple count of active players or roster minutes is inadequate. The grade pair should reflect the conditional 2022 right and the actual Reed waiver, not a claim that Koloko or Mobley instantly joined either club in February 2018.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Chicago B-, Detroit B-. Nelson went to the Pistons, while the Bulls received Willie Reed and a 2022 second-round swap option. Chicago waived Reed that day, and the relevant later draft positions are No. 33 and No. 49, associated with Christian Koloko and Isaiah Mobley. The equal marks compare a veteran guard against a contingent draft benefit, not four players delivered in February 2018.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Chicago Bulls–Detroit Pistons: 2018 Nelson/Reed and 2022 Pick-Swap Exchange
featuredDeepDive.intro: The February 8, 2018 exchange between the Bulls and Pistons combined two veteran contracts with a conditional future second-round swap. Detroit obtained Jameer Nelson. Chicago acquired Willie Reed and an option to improve its 2022 second-round draft position, then waived Reed on the same day. The resulting draft positions are later identified with No. 33, Christian Koloko, and No. 49, Isaiah Mobley. The archive grades both clubs B- and calls the trade even. Understanding that assessment requires separating the contract swap, the waiver and the later draft-rights mechanism rather than treating all four named players as immediate 2018 acquisitions.

sections.heading: What Each Team Actually Received
sections.body: Detroit's February 2018 official announcement identifies Jameer Nelson as the incoming guard, with Willie Reed and future second-round considerations sent to Chicago. The Bulls' media guide supplies a crucial second fact: Reed was waived by Chicago that day. The two veterans therefore occupied quite different roles in the clubs' plans. For the Bulls, the lasting potential benefit lay more in the 2022 second-round swap option than in a sustained stint from Reed. For the Pistons, Nelson was a known player whose short-term value could be assessed directly.

sections.heading: What Chicago Bulls Realized
sections.body: The mechanics of the draft consideration are more precise than two generic 2022 picks changing hands. Chicago's option let it seek the better of the involved second-round positions, while Detroit carried the matching obligation. The documented selections later corresponded to No. 33, Christian Koloko, and No. 49, Isaiah Mobley. These later names identify how the positions resolved, but the actual ownership and later trades of the associated rights need their own records before either player can be credited to Chicago or Detroit in the 2018 deal.

sections.heading: What Detroit Pistons Realized
sections.body: From Chicago's side, Nelson had only recently been obtained in an unrelated transaction. Moving him to Detroit while accepting Reed and a future swap gave the Bulls a different blend of immediate and delayed consideration. Because Reed was immediately waived, his presence in the transaction should not be converted into meaningful Chicago playing production. The executive description of the move emphasized the chance to improve future second-round position. That narrower rationale is more useful than generic claims about frontcourt depth or a 2018 playoff push.

sections.heading: What the B-/B- Grade Pairing Really Means
sections.body: The matching B- marks are best understood as the archive's assessment of two unlike packages. Detroit acquired Jameer Nelson and gave up the potentially favorable 2022 swap; Chicago took the swap right while briefly holding Willie Reed's contract. By 2022 the relevant second-round slots were identified as No. 33 and No. 49. The even verdict does not imply Nelson, Reed, Koloko and Mobley all provided comparable on-court value. It reflects a comparison that must distinguish a current guard, an immediately waived center and a conditional later draft mechanism.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Bulls' most distinctive gain was an option over 2022 second-round positions, while Detroit received Jameer Nelson. Reed was sent to Chicago but waived immediately. Basketball-Reference traces the later draft slots to No. 33 and No. 49; those identifiers should not be confused with a guaranteed roster tenure for either draftee. The recorded B-/B- even verdict holds only when those separate forms and timelines of value are kept intact.

sections.heading: Chicago Acquired a Player It Immediately Waived
sections.body: On January 7, 2019, Chicago received Michael Carter-Williams and cash from Houston in exchange for a heavily protected 2020 second-round choice. The Bulls waived Carter-Williams shortly after finalizing the deal because his contract was about to become guaranteed. He never suited up for Chicago after this transaction. The protected second did not convey, so the Bulls effectively accepted the administrative transaction and cash without losing a later drafted player.

sections.heading: Houston Needed a Roster Opening More Than Another Guard
sections.body: The Rockets had used Carter-Williams for only 16 games during the 2018–19 season. Moving his contract made room to continue using Danuel House and resolve an approaching roster decision. Cash was part of the price Houston paid to remove the unused guard slot. This explains why Houston might willingly send money while gaining only a conditional second-round interest that was unlikely to deliver an actual selection.

sections.heading: The Cash Was Chicago’s Main Return
sections.body: Chicago’s positive result was financial: it acquired cash and took on a player only long enough to waive him before his compensation became guaranteed. The Bulls did not gain meaningful Carter-Williams production in 2019, and the page must not describe the trade as a successful on-court rehabilitation. The second-round protection prevented a meaningful draft cost from arising. That makes the deal a small, deliberate roster-accounting transaction rather than a high-impact basketball exchange.

sections.heading: Why Chicago’s B-plus Beats Houston’s C-plus
sections.body: Chicago receives B-plus for retaining cash without losing a useful player or a draft selection that conveyed. Houston earns C-plus for obtaining the roster flexibility it wanted, despite paying the cash and giving up a former first-round guard. The contract mechanics explain the modest grade gap, not Carter-Williams’ reputation as a former Rookie of the Year. Neither franchise secured a player who influenced later playoff results through this specific trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win — Chicago B-plus, Houston C-plus. Chicago received cash, waived Carter-Williams immediately and ultimately did not lose the heavily protected second-round pick. Houston cleared a roster opening for more useful contributors but paid to complete that maneuver. The Bulls had the better direct financial result, although this was a minor transaction with no subsequent Carter-Williams games for Chicago.

sections.heading: Anthony’s Name Was Bigger Than His Role in the Deal
sections.body: Chicago acquired Carmelo Anthony, the NBA rights to Jon Diebler and $1.56 million in cash from Houston in January 2019. The Rockets received the rights to Tadija Dragićević, another player who was competing outside the NBA. Anthony had not played for Houston since November and Chicago did not expect to put him on the floor. The practical returns were cash, roster flexibility and obscure overseas draft rights rather than a marquee player joining a new rotation.

sections.heading: Chicago Did Not Receive a Carmelo Anthony Playing Season
sections.body: The Bulls held Anthony’s contract briefly while evaluating whether they could move him again before the deadline. He was waived on February 1 and did not play a game for Chicago. Diebler’s NBA rights gave the club an additional speculative asset, but did not convert into meaningful Chicago minutes. The $1.56 million payment was the more direct source of value for a rebuilding team willing to facilitate the transaction.

sections.heading: Houston Finished an Unsuccessful Veteran Experiment
sections.body: Anthony had averaged 13.4 points over ten Rockets games before the team removed him from its active rotation. Sending his contract to Chicago allowed Houston to formally move on. Obtaining Dragićević’s overseas rights did not produce a substitute player on the court; the value to the Rockets was logistical and financial rather than a roster upgrade through another established name. That distinction is essential to understanding why the trade was concluded despite Anthony’s enormous career reputation.

sections.heading: Grades Follow Cash and Contract Handling, Not Celebrity
sections.body: Chicago earns B-plus for cash compensation and a minor additional rights asset while absorbing an unwanted contract briefly. Houston receives C-plus because it resolved the Anthony situation but surrendered cash without obtaining direct on-court talent. The transaction did not give Chicago Anthony’s Hall-of-Fame career value, and the Bulls did not benefit from his later work with other NBA teams. The case for a Bulls edge is relatively narrow and administrative.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win — Chicago B-plus, Houston C-plus. Chicago received $1.56 million and Diebler’s draft rights, then waived Anthony without him ever playing for the club. Houston ended its Anthony contract situation and received Dragićević’s rights. The Bulls’ tangible cash consideration earns the stronger outcome, but neither team acquired an important new on-court contributor.

sections.heading: Chicago Received a Player and $2.6 Million
sections.body: The Bulls acquired Timothé Luwawu-Cabarrot and a reported $2.6 million in cash from Oklahoma City in February 2019. The Thunder received a 2020 second-round pick protected through No. 55. The protection is essential: the selection did not convey. Chicago therefore gained an actual player and cash, while Oklahoma City accepted the risk that its incoming conditional pick might yield nothing.

sections.heading: The Conditional Pick Never Paid Oklahoma City
sections.body: A top-55-protected second-round pick has a narrow conveyance window. The relevant condition was not satisfied, so the Thunder did not obtain a future drafted player through this transaction. Describing their return merely as a 2020 second-rounder would obscure that realized outcome. Chicago, by contrast, received the named guard and a fixed cash payment, which were identifiable assets at the completion of the trade.

sections.heading: The Financial Component Helps Explain the Bulls Grade
sections.body: Luwawu-Cabarrot gave Chicago a roster option and the cash reduced the effective cost of adding him. The team did not need him to become a star for the package to exceed a conditional pick that never transferred. The ledger awards Chicago B-plus and Oklahoma City C-plus, reflecting the asymmetric realized result. This assessment does not invent an ultimate use for the $2.6 million or treat the cash as a player development success.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win — Chicago B-plus, Oklahoma City C-plus. The Bulls acquired Luwawu-Cabarrot and $2.6 million. The Thunder’s top-55-protected 2020 second-rounder did not convey, leaving them without an exercised pick from the deal. Chicago’s concrete return was stronger, although the transaction was a modest roster and cash movement rather than a major roster breakthrough.

sections.heading: February 6, 2019: Porter for Two Forwards and a Protected Pick
sections.body: Chicago acquired Otto Porter Jr. from Washington at the February 6, 2019 deadline, sending Jabari Parker, Bobby Portis and a protected 2023 second-round pick to the Wizards. The Bulls received the player with the largest existing contract, not a second draft choice. Washington obtained two usable forwards and a pick that was originally protected through No. 36, creating a future contingent asset. Chicago wanted a wing who could defend and shoot alongside Lauri Markkanen and Zach LaVine. Washington was coping with John Wall's serious injury and moved away from Porter's remaining salary. The NBA's original trade announcement confirms these precise assets, and the eventual 2023 identity must be separated from the original 2019 decision.

sections.heading: Porter's First Bulls Season Was Strong but Only Fifteen Games
sections.body: Porter started all 15 of his Chicago games after the 2019 trade, averaging 17.5 points and shooting 48.8 percent from three-point range. That initial stretch showed why the Bulls valued his shooting and two-way wing role. The longer tenure was much less durable: he played 14 regular-season Bulls games in 2019-20 and 25 more in 2020-21, a total of 54 Chicago appearances across three partial seasons. Those are direct Bulls games, unlike his prior Washington seasons or his later Golden State championship year. Chicago eventually traded him to Orlando in March 2021 in another transaction. The Bulls C-plus acknowledges an effective short burst without claiming that the expensive veteran gave them multiple full seasons of healthy playing time.

sections.heading: Washington Used Portis and Parker Immediately
sections.body: The two acquired forwards contributed genuine 2018-19 Wizards basketball. Bobby Portis appeared in 28 Washington games, starting 22, and averaged 14.3 points and 8.6 rebounds. Jabari Parker played 25 Wizards games, averaging 15.0 points and 7.2 rebounds as a reserve. Their different roles gave Washington scoring and frontcourt usage during a difficult season, but neither player stayed to become a long-term Wizards centerpiece. Portis later earned a championship with Milwaukee; that separate club's achievement cannot be counted as Washington return on the 2019 trade. Parker also played for other clubs afterward. The incoming pair was therefore a short-term veteran return, not an empty salary exchange, and should be weighed separately from the later second-round pick.

sections.heading: The 2023 Second Became No. 42 After Two Later Deals
sections.body: The original Chicago second-rounder was top-36 protected when it moved in February 2019. On July 7 of that year, Chicago agreed to remove the protection as part of a separate sign-and-trade for Tomáš Satoranský. Washington then moved the 2023 right to the Lakers in the 2021 Russell Westbrook package and reacquired it in January 2023 through the separate Rui Hachimura trade. The resulting selection was No. 42, which the Wizards used on Tristan Vukčević in the 2023 draft. Those intervening transactions establish the actual pick route and prevent attributing unrelated player packages to this one original choice. The source-led Wizards Win/B-plus versus Bulls C-plus can consider Washington's real Portis/Parker production and eventual draft right, not simply Portis's later Milwaukee value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wizards Win — Washington B-plus, Chicago C-plus. Washington acquired two immediate scorers in Portis (28 Wizards games) and Parker (25 games), plus a protected Chicago 2023 second that ultimately became No. 42 Tristan Vukčević after separate later transactions. Porter averaged 17.5 points in his first 15 Chicago games but played only 54 Bulls games across three partial seasons; the initial wing contribution never became sustained availability.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Chicago Bulls–Washington Wizards: What the 2019-02-06 Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: Chicago obtained Otto Porter Jr. on February 6, 2019 for Jabari Parker, Bobby Portis and a protected 2023 second-round pick. Porter played 54 Bulls regular-season games across three partial seasons; Portis and Parker supplied 28 and 25 Washington appearances after the deadline. The pick later lost its protection, moved through Los Angeles and returned to Washington, where it became No. 42 Tristan Vukčević in 2023.

sections.heading: Trade-Day Asset Map: One Proven Wing for Three Returns
sections.body: Porter was the only Chicago incoming player. Washington received Bobby Portis and Jabari Parker, plus a 2023 second-round pick with top-36 protection. That four-component map is fixed by the February 2019 Bulls transaction announcement. The next step is to separate what the teams could know then from outcomes discovered later. Porter had been an efficient outside shooter in Washington, but his health and considerable salary presented risks. Portis and Parker could enter the Wizards' rotation immediately; the draft choice could potentially convey years later. The protected pick was not equivalent to a guaranteed first-round prospect. Washington chose a mixture of shorter-term forward production and future optionality while Chicago concentrated its outgoing value on the established wing it wanted to use.

sections.heading: The Bulls Got Fifty-Four Porter Appearances, Not Three Full Seasons
sections.body: Porter averaged 17.5 points in his first 15 Bulls games after the trade and made nearly half his three-point attempts, giving an immediate glimpse of useful fit. The next two seasons were shortened by injury and other availability problems: 14 Chicago games in 2019-20 and 25 more in 2020-21. Across his Chicago tenure, the sum is 54 regular-season games. Some included productive wing minutes, but the Bulls never enjoyed the full-season continuity that could have justified the cost of two forwards and a future second. His eventual 2021 departure for Orlando and later championship contribution for Golden State belong to subsequent transactions. The inherited Chicago C-plus is not a claim that Porter lacked talent; it expresses the limited sustained return of the player Chicago acquired.

sections.heading: Portis, Parker and the Pick Had Different Washington Horizons
sections.body: Portis gave the Wizards 28 regular-season games after the deadline, averaging 14.3 points and 8.6 rebounds, while Parker added 25 appearances at 15.0 points and 7.2 rebounds. These were immediate roster contributions, not theoretical assets held off the court. Both forwards departed later, reducing the long-term personnel return. Washington's 2023 second represented a separate longer-horizon benefit. It was originally top-36 protected and later became unprotected through Chicago's July 2019 Tomáš Satoranský arrangement. The Wizards then included the right in a later Lakers trade before regaining it in the 2023 Rui Hachimura transaction. That chain is distinct from Portis's later Milwaukee career and allows the grade to consider the draft asset without inflating what Washington received directly in February.

sections.heading: No. 42 Vukčević Is the Pick Outcome, Not an Original Player
sections.body: The 2023 second eventually settled at No. 42 and Washington selected Tristan Vukčević. That is a valid downstream identity for the consideration Chicago surrendered four years earlier. It does not mean the Bulls traded Vukčević by name in 2019, nor that Washington kept unbroken control of the right during the intervening Lakers deal. NBA transaction archives separately document the 2019 removal of protection and the 2021/2023 transfers. The resulting Wizards Win assessment, Washington B-plus and Chicago C-plus are the existing retrospective grades, not a calculation that credits all later Wizards and Lakers transactions to a single pick. Porter's short but effective Bulls output belongs beside the two Wizards veterans and this correctly traced draft choice.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The recorded Wizards Win verdict and B-plus/C-plus grades credit Washington for real Portis and Parker minutes and a traceable second-round right, which ultimately became the No. 42 Vukčević selection in 2023. Chicago acquired a productive shooter but obtained only 54 Porter regular-season appearances before a separate 2021 move. Neither Portis's later Milwaukee achievements nor unrelated Rui Hachimura and Russell Westbrook trade returns are directly assigned to this 2019 package.
