sections.heading: The December Trade Sent Cleveland’s Leading Scorer to San Antonio
sections.body: On December 23, 1981, the Cavaliers sent Mike Mitchell and Roger Phegley to the Spurs for Ron Brewer, Reggie Johnson and cash. The historical Cleveland and San Antonio transaction logs independently list all five players and the direction of the money. Mitchell had averaged 24.5 points and 6.1 rebounds for Cleveland in 1980-81, earning an All-Star selection. Trading him was a substantial decision rather than the routine exchange of bench contracts. San Antonio paired Mitchell with George Gervin for the rest of a competitive 1981-82 season. Cleveland chose two younger rotation pieces and cash, with the cash amount not specified in the archival transaction records.

sections.heading: Mitchell Scored 21.0 Points in His First 57 Spurs Games
sections.body: The forward played 27 Cleveland games in 1981-82 before the move, averaging 19.6 points. His first 57 San Antonio appearances that same season brought 21.0 points and 7.9 rebounds per game; he started all 57 and shot 53.9 percent from the field. Those are team-specific numbers, not his combined 84-game line. Mitchell followed with 80 games at 19.9 points in 1982-83, then 79 at 23.3 in 1983-84. The Spurs had acquired a proven scorer who adapted immediately alongside Gervin, rather than waiting on a prospect to develop into a rotation player.

sections.heading: Cleveland Received 68 Brewer Games and 23 Johnson Games
sections.body: Brewer appeared in 47 Cavaliers games after the 1981 trade, starting 41 and averaging 19.4 points. He stayed for another 21 Cleveland games in 1982-83, adding 18 starts before moving to Golden State. Johnson played 23 Cleveland games, starting 22, at 9.7 points and 5.4 rebounds. On February 16, 1982, the Cavaliers sent Johnson to the Kansas City Kings for Cliff Robinson. These two incoming players were legitimate Cleveland contributors, but neither stayed as long as Mitchell did with San Antonio. The separate Robinson acquisition should be recorded as a later asset conversion, not another piece received directly from the Spurs.

sections.heading: Phegley Supplied Guard Depth Rather than a Second Spurs Star
sections.body: Roger Phegley played 54 San Antonio games and one start in 1981-82 after leaving Cleveland, producing 5.7 points in 11.4 minutes a night. He appeared in 62 more Spurs games in 1982-83, largely as a reserve, and three in 1983-84 before finishing that season in Dallas. His direct San Antonio total from the trade was 119 regular-season games. Phegley mattered as an actual roster arrival but did not account for the exchange’s largest value. That distinction helps avoid reducing the deal either to a Mitchell-only one-for-two swap or to an inflated four-year contribution from Phegley.

sections.heading: Mitchell’s Seven Spurs Seasons Reached 488 Appearances
sections.body: Across his Spurs regular-season stints from 1981-82 through 1987-88, Mitchell played 57, 80, 79, 82, 82, 40 and 68 games. That totals 488 San Antonio appearances, with his strongest sustained seasons producing 23.3 points in 1983-84, 22.2 in 1984-85 and 23.4 in 1985-86. He later shifted into a smaller role as he aged, playing 40 games in 1986-87 and 68 in 1987-88. The 1981 trade did not guarantee a championship; it supplied a high-volume scorer for seven Spurs seasons. Cleveland’s 1981-82 team finished 15-67, showing the difficult rebuilding situation surrounding its decision to move an established All-Star.

sections.heading: Spurs Win Accounts for Both the Production and Cash Uncertainty
sections.body: The archived grading is Spurs Win, San Antonio A+ and Cleveland B. That outcome follows directly from Mitchell’s 488 Spurs games and Phegley’s reserve depth compared with the 68 Brewer and 23 Johnson games Cleveland received. However, Cleveland acquired cash along with two players, and the public historical ledgers used here do not reliably name the cash amount. Any firm conclusion about its full economic value would need contemporary financial evidence. The subsequent Johnson-for-Cliff Robinson deal can be discussed as an independent Cleveland decision, but Robinson’s games cannot be credited as a direct incoming Spurs asset on December 23.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The original Spurs Win verdict and San Antonio A+/Cleveland B grades are preserved. Mitchell delivered 488 Spurs games over seven seasons, including multiple 22-plus-point campaigns; Phegley added 119 reserve appearances. Cleveland received 68 Brewer games, 23 Johnson games and unspecified cash, then separately moved Johnson for Cliff Robinson. The receiving-team production favors San Antonio without fabricating a cash amount or folding future trades into the initial exchange.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Mitchell to the Spurs in 1981: 488 Games for Brewer, Johnson and Cash
featuredDeepDive.intro: Cleveland moved All-Star forward Mike Mitchell and reserve guard Roger Phegley to San Antonio on December 23, 1981 for Ron Brewer, Reggie Johnson and cash. Mitchell went on to play 488 Spurs games across seven regular-season segments. Cleveland got meaningful short-term guard minutes from Brewer and briefly employed Johnson before trading him again. The inherited Spurs Win, A+ for San Antonio and B for Cleveland are examined against those receiving-team totals, with the unspecified cash value explicitly unresolved.

sections.heading: San Antonio Added an Established All-Star Scorer Beside Gervin
sections.body: Mitchell arrived from a Cleveland franchise that had relied on his scoring for multiple seasons. He averaged 22.2 points in 1979-80 and a career-high 24.5 the following year, earning his All-Star selection in 1981. The Spurs already had George Gervin, so acquiring another reliable forward scorer strengthened rather than replaced their main offensive star. Mitchell started all 57 remaining Spurs games in 1981-82, putting up 21.0 points and 7.9 rebounds while hitting 53.9 percent of his shots. Roger Phegley also came over, but his 54 San Antonio games in that half-season were mostly off the bench. The December package therefore joined immediate elite offensive production with modest depth.

sections.heading: The Spurs’ Return Lasted Through 1987-88
sections.body: The Mitchell team splits tell the strongest story: 57 games with San Antonio in 1981-82, followed by 80, 79, 82, 82, 40 and 68. The sum is 488 regular-season Spurs appearances. He averaged 19.9 points in 1982-83 and then 23.3, 22.2 and 23.4 across the next three seasons, before a late-career reduction in 1986-87 and 1987-88. These numbers exclude 27 Cleveland appearances before the trade and do not conflate his postseason games with regular-season totals. Mitchell provided a player whose peak and duration exceeded what either of the returned Cavaliers contributors eventually achieved for Cleveland.

sections.heading: Brewer and Johnson Made Cleveland’s Return More than Nothing
sections.body: Ron Brewer scored 19.4 points over 47 Cleveland games in 1981-82, starting 41, and appeared 21 more times the next season. Reggie Johnson brought 23 Cavaliers appearances and 22 starts at 9.7 points and 5.4 rebounds in 1981-82. Cleveland exchanged Johnson for Cliff Robinson in February 1982 and eventually sent Brewer to Golden State. Short contracts and follow-on trades explain why these players generated fewer Cavaliers games, not a complete lack of talent. The cash accompanying them was a legitimate contractual asset, but its unverified dollar figure must not be inferred from Mitchell’s future scoring or Cleveland’s overall performance.

sections.heading: The Cleveland Transaction Chain Changed Again in February
sections.body: Historical team transaction logs make an important chronology distinction. The Spurs sent Brewer, Johnson and cash on December 23; on February 16 the Cavaliers traded Johnson to the Kansas City Kings for Cliff Robinson. Cleveland also completed a major separate move involving Bill Laimbeer and Kenny Carr that February. Those later personnel decisions affected the club’s 15-67 season, but are not all consequences of moving Mitchell. Assessing this particular deal should identify its initial two-player-and-cash package, then discuss asset conversions as separate steps. San Antonio did not send Robinson, and Cleveland did not acquire him until a later negotiation.

sections.heading: The Verdict Favors Proven Duration over Unpriced Cash
sections.body: The archived A+ Spurs/B Cavaliers spread makes sense through the seven-year Mitchell tenure. Phegley supplied 119 Spurs games, but Mitchell was the scorer who allowed the franchise to keep a second major offensive option during much of the 1980s. Cleveland obtained useful near-term offense from Brewer and a brief starting forward in Johnson before moving both assets onward. It is possible that an independently documented cash payment would alter some financial interpretation; absent that record, there is no basis to invent a number. The comparison also stops short of claiming a title directly resulted from the trade, since roster context and other acquisitions shaped both franchises afterward.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: San Antonio A+, Cleveland B and Spurs Win are retained. Mitchell played 488 Spurs regular-season games through 1987-88, and Phegley logged 119. Brewer appeared in 68 Cleveland games, while Johnson played 23 before the February 1982 deal for Cliff Robinson. The cash amount is unverified and left unresolved rather than assigned a speculative value. The long Spurs scoring tenure supports the protected decision without treating subsequent Cavaliers swaps as direct December returns.

sections.heading: The February 16 Package Sent Laimbeer to Detroit
sections.body: Cleveland sent Bill Laimbeer and Kenny Carr to Detroit on February 16, 1982. The Pistons returned Phil Hubbard, Paul Mokeski, their 1982 first-round selection and a second-round selection that had previously come from Kansas City. The Cavaliers used those choices on John Bagley at No. 12 and Dave Magley at No. 28. These six identified assets define the deal more clearly than an abstract description of buying roster flexibility. Laimbeer had not yet built his Detroit reputation, and neither incoming Cleveland rookie had played in the league. Each club could evaluate the players and draft positions it held, but neither knew Laimbeer would spend another thirteen seasons in Detroit or lead its championship frontcourt.

sections.heading: Laimbeer Became a Long-Term Pistons Center
sections.body: Detroit received 937 regular-season appearances and 857 starts from Laimbeer after acquiring him. His tenure lasted through the 1992-93 season, a stretch during which he became a four-time All-Star and played center for the Pistons teams that won the 1989 and 1990 championships. He was not merely present on the title rosters: Detroit used his rebounding, durable minutes and outside shooting within a physical defense led by Chuck Daly. Basketball-Reference documents his team seasons, while the Pistons historical account places the transaction among the defining moves before the Bad Boys era. The club obtained more than an average veteran; it acquired a center who stayed through the championship build and nearly all of its competitive peak.

sections.heading: Cleveland Received Four Distinct NBA Contributors
sections.body: The Cavaliers got real output from every named incoming branch, though none rivaled Laimbeer as a franchise centerpiece. Phil Hubbard appeared in 469 Cleveland regular-season games. No. 12 pick John Bagley made another 375 appearances, including 231 starts. Paul Mokeski provided 51 Cleveland games and 19 starts, while No. 28 Dave Magley appeared 14 times without starting. Together those returns equal 909 regular-season games for Cleveland. That is why a B for the Cavaliers is more defensible than grading the package as completely wasted. The problem was not that Cleveland acquired nobody useful; it was that Detroit acquired the substantially more influential individual player.

sections.heading: The Teams Were Years Away From Detroit's Titles
sections.body: The transaction took place in Isiah Thomas' rookie season. Detroit had not yet drafted Joe Dumars or assembled the championship group surrounding Thomas, Laimbeer and Dennis Rodman. Looking backward from 1989 can conceal how early the Pistons committed to this particular center. The Cavaliers, meanwhile, chose immediate forward and reserve help plus two picks for a frontcourt player they were willing to surrender. Hubbard and Bagley later held real roles for Cleveland, so the original decision cannot be reduced to giving away Laimbeer for nothing. The contrast is instead organizational: Detroit kept a valuable big man as its roster matured, while Cleveland spread the return among several players who did not become a comparable perennial All-Star.

sections.heading: Carr Also Had a Verifiable Second Transaction
sections.body: Kenny Carr was the less famous Detroit incoming player, but his value did not end with an initial short stay. On June 23, 1982, Detroit sent Carr to Portland in a separate one-for-one transaction for the No. 18 draft selection. The Pistons chose Ricky Pierce with that pick; he played 39 regular-season games for Detroit before continuing his much longer career elsewhere. This is a traceable downstream use of Carr because he was the sole outgoing asset in that later exchange. It does not transform Pierce's subsequent seasons for other clubs into Detroit playing production. The extra pick also should not be attributed to Laimbeer or inserted into the original February trade package.

sections.heading: The Winning Margin Comes From Who Detroit Kept
sections.body: The grades are Pistons A+ and Cavaliers B, with Detroit the winner. Cleveland's Hubbard, Bagley, Mokeski and Magley gave the team 909 regular-season appearances and several productive roles, an outcome far better than an empty draft haul. Detroit, however, controlled 937 Laimbeer appearances and a center who started on back-to-back championship teams. Its separate Carr conversion into the Ricky Pierce pick added a smaller branch of value. Comparing total games without identifying playing quality would miss the distinction between four Cleveland contributors and one established Detroit championship anchor. Detroit's win therefore rests on documented performance and roster impact, not on a claim that Cleveland received no basketball value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Detroit A+, Cleveland B. Detroit received 937 games and 857 starts from Bill Laimbeer, a four-time All-Star and center on the 1989 and 1990 champions, then separately turned Kenny Carr into the No. 18 Ricky Pierce pick. Cleveland obtained 909 total games from Hubbard, Bagley, Mokeski and Magley, including 231 Bagley starts. Those were real returns, but none matched Laimbeer's long-term Detroit value.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Detroit Kept Laimbeer Through 1993; Cleveland Took Players and Picks
featuredDeepDive.intro: On February 16, 1982, Cleveland dealt Bill Laimbeer and Kenny Carr to Detroit for Phil Hubbard, Paul Mokeski and two 1982 draft choices. Cleveland selected John Bagley at No. 12 and Dave Magley at No. 28 with those picks. This deeper account isolates the Laimbeer years and championship role, the Cavaliers' 909 combined player appearances, and Detroit's separate Carr-for-Ricky Pierce conversion. Each result is credited to the receiving club and to the correct subsequent transaction.

sections.heading: Roster Ledger: Two Assets Versus Four
sections.body: The February 1982 trade is easiest to audit with each player and selection on the correct side. Detroit received Bill Laimbeer and Kenny Carr. Cleveland received Phil Hubbard and Paul Mokeski plus a first-rounder from Detroit and a second-rounder originally obtained from Kansas City. The Cavaliers later selected John Bagley at No. 12 and Dave Magley at No. 28. Those draft names are downstream identities, not players included as already drafted rookies at the February trade deadline. Basketball-Reference and the Pistons team account document the exchange date and major participants. The second pick's origin is especially worth retaining because its route through another club does not make that other club a participant in this specific trade.

sections.heading: Detroit Obtained a Center It Could Keep Through 1993
sections.body: Laimbeer made his first Detroit appearances in 1981-82 and stayed with the franchise through 1992-93. The team ledger totals 937 regular-season games and 857 starts over that period. He was a four-time All-Star, supplied defensive rebounding and spacing from the center position, and started in the 1989 and 1990 NBA Finals championship seasons. A Detroit grade of A+ is unusually well documented because it does not depend on a speculative unexercised draft right or an invented future player. The benefit accrued on Detroit's own roster over more than a decade. No Cleveland branch matched the combination of Laimbeer's longevity, peak recognition and direct title-era playing role.

sections.heading: Bagley and Hubbard Help Explain Cleveland's B
sections.body: Bagley played 375 Cavaliers regular-season games after being selected with the incoming No. 12 choice; he started 231 of those. Hubbard supplied 469 additional Cleveland games as a forward and scorer. Those two returns account for 844 of the 909 Cleveland appearances eventually tied to the original exchange. The remaining 65 came from Mokeski and Magley. Bagley and Hubbard did not become Detroit-style title-center equivalents, but both provided sustained roster minutes rather than vanishing after draft night. The Cavaliers' B grade reflects that usage without requiring every asset to become a cornerstone. This is a case in which losing a trade does not automatically mean every incoming piece failed.

sections.heading: The Carr-to-Pierce Trail Should Not Be Inflated
sections.body: Detroit converted Kenny Carr into a separate first-round selection only four months after acquiring him. The June 23, 1982 Portland exchange sent Carr out and brought the No. 18 selection that became Ricky Pierce. Pierce appeared 39 times for the Pistons during his rookie season, with one start, before his later career developed in other cities. Crediting the No. 18 right as Carr's traceable return is reasonable because the follow-up was one-for-one. Crediting all of Pierce's later NBA production to Detroit would be different and unjustified. This branch gives the original trade an additional asset result but does not supply the main reason for the Pistons' A+; that is Laimbeer's Detroit career.

sections.heading: Why the Same February Package Produced Different Results
sections.body: Both teams received useful possibilities in February 1982, but their subsequent outcomes diverged. Cleveland translated two picks and two veterans into 909 total regular-season games, with Bagley and Hubbard accounting for most. Detroit developed Laimbeer into a four-time All-Star and a central piece of two championship teams, while separately trading Carr for a 1982 first-round pick. The deal should not absorb Isiah Thomas' rookie production, future Dumars draft choices or Cleveland players acquired in unrelated trades. Those other parts of roster history help explain the circumstances but are not components of the exchange itself. By isolating the actual returns, the Pistons Win result and A+/B grade pairing are supported without reducing the Cavaliers' respectable haul to zero.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Detroit receives A+ for a thirteen-season Laimbeer career, championship-center production and a separate Carr-for-Pierce draft-right conversion. Cleveland earns B because Hubbard (469 games), Bagley (375), Mokeski (51) and Magley (14) supplied a combined 909 team appearances. The difference was one franchise-changing Detroit player versus a broader but lower-ceiling Cleveland package; Pistons Win preserves both sides of that comparison.

sources.title: NBA trades: The best trade made in the history of every team

sections.heading: Cleveland Exchanged Johnson for a 21-Year-Old Starter
sections.body: The Cavaliers obtained 21-year-old Cliff Robinson from the Kansas City Kings on February 16, 1982, sending Reggie Johnson the other way. Robinson was young enough for Cleveland to evaluate as a long-term frontcourt player rather than a short-term veteran rental. The clubs entered this deal at different stages: Cleveland sought a player who could occupy major minutes immediately, while Kansas City accepted another forward and the possibility that a change of team might improve his contribution.

sections.heading: Robinson Started 174 Games for the Cavaliers
sections.body: Robinson became an immediate Cleveland starter. Across parts of three seasons he played 180 regular-season games, starting 174, and averaged roughly 17 to 18 points per game. Johnson appeared in 81 Kansas City games with nine starts over parts of two seasons, before the Kings sold his rights to Philadelphia for cash in February 1983. Those different roles establish a strong direct on-court return for Cleveland without relying on either player’s accomplishments with other teams.

sections.heading: A Later Three-Piece Deal Needs Careful Attribution
sections.body: Cleveland subsequently included Robinson and the rights to Tim McCormick, the club’s 1984 first-round selection, in a trade for the rights to Melvin Turpin. That later exchange cannot be credited entirely to Robinson because McCormick was an additional asset. It does show that Robinson had value as part of a subsequent package. Cleveland receives A-minus while Kansas City/Sacramento receives C-plus. The difference rests chiefly on Robinson’s 180 games and 174 starts compared with Johnson’s 81 games and nine starts.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win — Cleveland A-minus, Kansas City/Sacramento C-plus. Robinson delivered 180 Cavaliers games, starting 174, while Johnson played 81 games with nine starts for the Kings before his rights were sold. Cleveland also later traded Robinson as part of a package that included Tim McCormick’s rights. The substantial direct playing return explains the grade gap without misattributing the entire later deal.

sections.heading: Cleveland Traded a 1986 Second-Rounder for Reserve Center Steve Hayes
sections.body: On October 7, 1982, Cleveland acquired center Steve Hayes from Detroit for its 1986 second-round pick. Both franchises' historical transaction pages record that date and the conditional-looking future asset as a straight second-round selection. At the time, the deal was a routine exchange of a distant draft pick for immediate frontcourt depth; the Cavaliers were not knowingly offering a future Hall of Famer. Detroit had used Hayes for 26 games during 1981-82 after acquiring him from San Antonio and did not lose a proven starter. Cleveland, meanwhile, was assembling its rotation before a difficult 1982-83 season. The distance between the transaction's modest contemporary stakes and its final draft outcome makes it unusually consequential in hindsight.

sections.heading: Hayes Supplied 65 Cleveland Games but Did Not Stay
sections.body: Hayes appeared in 65 Cavaliers regular-season games during 1982-83, starting three and averaging 3.6 points and 3.6 rebounds in 16.3 minutes. He gave Cleveland genuine reserve-center minutes; the return was not literally zero. But he played no further NBA season for the Cavaliers, moving on to Seattle and other clubs in later years. Cleveland finished 23-59 in 1982-83, which further limits any claim that the temporary frontcourt addition transformed its competitive results. Hayes's 65-game stint is the correct measurement of what Cleveland received directly from the October deal. All of his later playing appearances with other franchises must stay outside the Cavaliers' trade value.

sections.heading: Detroit Used That Pick on No. 27 Dennis Rodman in 1986
sections.body: The future Cleveland-origin second-rounder became the 27th overall selection in the 1986 NBA draft, and Detroit used it to select Dennis Rodman from Southeastern Oklahoma State. Rodman played 549 regular-season games for the Pistons between 1986 and 1993, developing from a reserve forward into an elite rebounder and defender. He won NBA Defensive Player of the Year in both 1989-90 and 1990-91, collected top rebounding totals, and helped Detroit win consecutive league championships in 1989 and 1990. This was not merely a pick that yielded a modest role player. It became a central part of the Pistons' best period of the era, with Rodman's Detroit career far exceeding what Hayes supplied Cleveland in one season.

sections.heading: The Grade Gap Reflects a Rare Four-Year Draft Conversion
sections.body: The final A+ for Detroit and F for Cleveland is the inherited score pair, and the direct source chain explains its breadth: a reserve center and a future second became 65 Cavaliers games versus the draft rights to a long-term championship cornerstone. That result deserves a clear Pistons Win label. Still, a historical verdict must distinguish realized outcome from prediction. No front office in October 1982 could know exactly which player the No. 27 pick would become four drafts later; Rodman's individual development and the Pistons' coaching environment helped create the enormous payoff. Nor were the 1989 and 1990 titles produced by one draft selection alone. The precise claim is that this specific trade delivered the selection Detroit used to draft Rodman and Cleveland received a short-term reserve in return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win (Detroit A+, Cleveland F on the inherited retrospective scale). Cleveland received 65 reserve-center games from Steve Hayes in 1982-83, averaging 3.6 points and 3.6 rebounds. Detroit received Cleveland's 1986 second-round pick, drafted Dennis Rodman at No. 27, and got 549 Pistons games and two Defensive Player of the Year seasons from that selection. The trade supplied the pick, not a guarantee of Rodman's later development or a claim that a single player caused both Detroit championships.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: 65 Steve Hayes Games for Cleveland Versus the Dennis Rodman No. 27 Pick
featuredDeepDive.intro: Cleveland traded a 1986 second-round pick to Detroit for reserve center Steve Hayes on October 7, 1982. Hayes played 65 Cavaliers games, started three and averaged 3.6 points and 3.6 rebounds in 1982-83. Four years after the exchange, the Cavaliers-origin pick became No. 27 in the 1986 draft; Detroit selected Dennis Rodman, who supplied 549 Pistons games, two Defensive Player of the Year seasons and contributions to the 1989 and 1990 championships. Cleveland's inherited F grade acknowledges a real but brief center contribution against Detroit's extraordinary A-plus outcome. The 1982 trade conveyed a future draft pick, not a fully formed Rodman or a guarantee of future championships. Both franchises' official historical ledgers and the league register independently document the asset chain.

sections.heading: The Trade Details Before the Narrative
sections.body: On October 7, 1982, Cleveland exchanged its 1986 second-round pick for reserve center Steve Hayes from Detroit. Hayes was not a frontline starter leaving the Pistons: after arriving from San Antonio the preceding season, he'd played 26 games for Detroit in 1981-82. Cleveland wanted immediate size; Detroit accepted a draft selection four years in the future. Hayes eventually delivered 65 Cavaliers appearances in 1982-83, averaging 3.6 points and 3.6 rebounds, while the original Cleveland pick became No. 27 in the 1986 draft. Detroit used that selection on Dennis Rodman. This is the exact historical link between the teams, not a hypothetical trade package or a claim that Rodman was available as a known commodity in October 1982.

sections.heading: The Deal's Most Important Outcome: Detroit Pistons
sections.body: Four years after acquiring Cleveland's distant second-rounder, Detroit selected Dennis Rodman at No. 27 out of Southeastern Oklahoma State. Across seven Pistons seasons from 1986-87 through 1992-93, he played 549 regular-season games and grew into a relentless rebounder, versatile defender and crucial member of the championship rotation. Detroit won the NBA Finals in 1989 and 1990; Rodman earned Defensive Player of the Year in 1989-90 and again in 1990-91. No trade executive knew those honors were attached to a future second-round selection in 1982. The A+ retrospective grade credits the *actual selection Detroit exercised* and its extraordinary on-court return while recognizing that Rodman's development also required scouting, coaching and a title-winning team around him.

sections.heading: Comparing Realized Value, Not Reputation: Cleveland Cavaliers
sections.body: Cleveland did receive NBA minutes for the pick. Steve Hayes appeared 65 times in the 1982-83 season, made three starts, and supplied 3.6 points and 3.6 rebounds in 16.3 minutes a game. His center depth was real, but the Cavaliers finished 23-59 and he never played another season for Cleveland. Meanwhile the selection sent to Detroit became Rodman's No. 27 draft slot in 1986. The Cavaliers' inherited F grade reflects that enormous difference in *realized return*, not an assertion that Hayes had zero value or that Cleveland's staff could have predicted Rodman's future career. Cleveland paid with an asset whose ultimate use proved historic; its return was a one-season reserve role.

sections.heading: How Far the Evidence Really Goes
sections.body: This is a trade whose 1982 price and 1986 outcome must be kept on separate calendars. Detroit received one second-round pick from Cleveland, held or retained its value for four drafts, then used the No. 27 selection on Rodman. Those draft rights were connected directly to the Hayes exchange, so Rodman's 549 Pistons games, two Defensive Player of the Year awards and contributions to the 1989 and 1990 championships are legitimate hindsight evidence. But his personal growth, the roster around him and the coaching that helped Detroit win titles cannot be treated as guarantees created by a routine 1982 reserve-center deal. The Pistons Win label and A+/F grade gap describe the disparity in the returns each side ultimately received.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win, Detroit A-plus and Cleveland F are retained. Detroit's future 1986 second-round draft pick from the October 1982 Steve Hayes deal became No. 27 Dennis Rodman. Rodman delivered 549 Pistons games, two Defensive Player of the Year honors and key minutes across two championship seasons; Hayes provided 65 Cavaliers appearances and three starts in one season. The extraordinary grade difference belongs to the eventual realized return, not a claim that Cleveland knew Rodman's future or that the pick alone guaranteed the Pistons' championships.

sections.heading: Cleveland Traded Brewer for a Proven Scorer
sections.body: On December 15, 1982, Cleveland acquired World B. Free from Golden State in exchange for Ron Brewer. The transaction was a straight guard-for-guard trade. A contemporary UPI report described Golden State’s reasoning: the Warriors wanted Brewer’s off-ball fit beside their existing players, while Cleveland wanted Free’s ability to attack the basket and reach the free-throw line. Neither side acquired draft compensation or future rights through this particular exchange.

sections.heading: Free Became a Four-Season Cleveland Scoring Anchor
sections.body: Free delivered exactly the higher-volume offense the Cavaliers sought. He averaged 24.2 points across 54 Cleveland games in the remainder of 1982–83, then more than 22 points per game in each of the next three seasons. His Cleveland totals reached 275 games and 247 starts with a 23.0-point scoring average. That volume was sustained, not a brief run of hot shooting, and it helped make the club competitive enough to reach the 1985 postseason.

sections.heading: Brewer’s Golden State Tenure Was Much Shorter
sections.body: Brewer was a real NBA guard with established scoring ability. Golden State used him for 53 games in 1982–83 and another 13 in 1983–84, or 66 in total. He started 37 of them and averaged 11.3 points in his first Warriors season. That supplied backcourt help but never approached Free’s 275-game Cleveland return or his importance to the offense. Later Brewer appearances for other franchises cannot be credited as Warriors value from the trade.

sections.heading: The Grades Reflect a Large, Verified Gap
sections.body: Cleveland receives A-plus and Golden State C, producing a Cavaliers Win. The Cavaliers got a principal scorer for parts of four seasons, including a return to the playoffs; Golden State acquired a useful guard whose stint lasted only parts of two seasons. The distinction is measurable in games, starts and offensive responsibility. Giving both sides equal marks would disregard the long and productive period Free spent in Cleveland.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win — Cleveland A-plus, Golden State C. World B. Free delivered 275 Cavaliers games, 247 starts and a 23.0-point average, including the club’s 1985 playoff return. Ron Brewer appeared in 66 Warriors games and produced a more limited short-term return. The straight 1982 guard swap decisively favored Cleveland on realized NBA playing value.

sections.heading: Cleveland Bought Larry Kenon’s NBA Services
sections.body: On January 8, 1983, the Cavaliers acquired veteran forward Larry Kenon from Golden State for cash. No player or draft selection went to the Warriors in the canonical asset ledger. Kenon had previously been an accomplished scorer and rebounder, so Cleveland was acquiring a recognizable NBA talent rather than the rights to an unknown prospect. The importance of the deal depends on what Kenon could contribute at that stage of his career.

sections.heading: Golden State Received Money of Unspecified Value
sections.body: The Warriors took a cash payment. The surviving transaction citations identify the type of consideration but do not establish a dependable dollar amount. That prevents any precise basketball-versus-financial valuation. Cleveland gained a player whose roster contribution could be measured in NBA minutes, while Golden State accepted direct compensation without adding a replacement player. It would be misleading to invent a later pick or assign a financial return calculated from an unverified sum.

sections.heading: Both Clubs Received the Same B-minus
sections.body: Cleveland and Golden State each receive B-minus under the recorded verdict. Cleveland obtained an established veteran for no draft capital, and Golden State received consideration for moving his rights. The available evidence supports the nature of both returns but cannot prove that the undisclosed cash was either trivial or exceptionally valuable. The equal grade acknowledges that limitation rather than creating a false winner from incomplete financial information.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Cleveland B-minus, Golden State B-minus. The Cavaliers obtained veteran forward Larry Kenon for cash, while the Warriors received no player or pick. Kenon’s basketball value can be assessed from his career; the undisclosed cash amount cannot be reliably priced. The ledger therefore keeps the outcome even.

sections.heading: What Cleveland and Phoenix Exchanged
sections.body: Cleveland sent center James Edwards and the 1983 first-round pick that became No. 21 Greg Kite to Phoenix. The Cavaliers received Jeff Cook, Phoenix’s 1983 first-rounder that became No. 20 Roy Hinson, a 1983 third-round pick that became Derrick Hord and cash. Phoenix’s own historical account describes the first-round component as a swap that would occur if the Suns’ pick were the better selection, which it ultimately was by one slot. The transaction therefore was not simply Edwards for Hinson. Cleveland moved an established center and a first while receiving another center, a slightly better first, an additional third and cash. The direct draft result looked modest on paper—one place in the first round—but the identity and later trade value of Hinson changed the historical ceiling of Cleveland’s return.

sections.heading: Roy Hinson Became the Decisive Cleveland Asset
sections.body: The Cavaliers selected Hinson 20th overall in 1983, and his value grew substantially during three seasons in Cleveland. By 1985-86 he had developed into a high-scoring starting forward. Cleveland then converted that directly tied asset in June 1986, sending Hinson and cash to Philadelphia for the No. 1 overall pick. The Cavaliers used that pick on Brad Daugherty, who became a five-time All-Star and one of the central players of the franchise’s late-1980s and early-1990s rise. That later transaction should not be treated as if the 1983 Suns trade single-handedly acquired Daugherty; Cleveland had to add cash and make a separate decision three years later. But Hinson was the named player Philadelphia accepted for the top pick, so his preserved trade value is legitimate downstream credit. That asset chain is the strongest reason Cleveland reaches A-.

sections.heading: Phoenix Solved a Real Basketball Problem
sections.body: Phoenix’s C+ should not be confused with a claim that Edwards failed. The Suns were seeking more size at center alongside Alvan Adams, and their own historical account identifies that need as the reason for the February move. Edwards provided exactly the kind of interior option Phoenix wanted and remained with the Suns for several seasons. By 1987-88 he was still productive enough to average roughly 16 points and eight rebounds before Phoenix traded him to Detroit for Ron Moore and a second-round pick. The Suns therefore received meaningful direct production and retained some later transaction value. Their problem in the retrospective grade is opportunity cost. The one-slot first-round exchange produced Hinson for Cleveland, and Hinson eventually carried premium trade value. Phoenix’s return was useful, but it did not create a comparable franchise-level asset chain.

sections.heading: The Smaller Pieces Matter Without Driving the Verdict
sections.body: Cook, Hord, cash and the exchanged first-round positions round out the trade details. Cook was not the centerpiece of Cleveland’s long-term result, and Hord did not become a major NBA contributor. Those pieces still matter because they show Cleveland received more than a simple one-for-one player exchange, but the A- grade does not depend on inflating their impact. On the Phoenix side, the No. 21 pick became Kite and was later involved in the Suns’ Dennis Johnson trade with Boston, which makes its connection to later value complicated; it should not be treated as an isolated star asset created by this deal. A focused comparison keeps the verdict focused on what can be traced cleanly: Edwards gave Phoenix real center production, while Hinson gave Cleveland both on-court development and unusually strong later trade utility.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win. Cleveland receives A- because the deal produced Roy Hinson at No. 20, and Hinson later became the central player Cleveland sent to Philadelphia for the No. 1 pick used on Brad Daugherty. Jeff Cook, Derrick Hord and cash add secondary value but are not the basis of the grade. Phoenix receives C+ because James Edwards was a useful, productive center for the Suns and later returned another player plus a second-round pick; the Suns had a legitimate roster reason for making the move. The separation comes from the long-term value of Hinson’s asset chain. Cleveland’s result became materially more consequential than Phoenix’s, even after accounting for the fact that the Cavaliers had to add cash in the later 1986 trade. This is a strong hindsight win for Cleveland without rewriting Phoenix’s original need for size as an irrational decision.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Deep Dive: How a One-Pick Swap Helped Lead Cleveland to Brad Daugherty
featuredDeepDive.intro: The February 1983 Cleveland-Phoenix trade is a good example of why historical grading cannot stop at the transaction date. Phoenix received an established center it wanted, while Cleveland moved down the experience curve and collected several pieces. The first-round picks were only one slot apart. Yet Cleveland used the higher pick on Roy Hinson, developed him for three seasons, and then traded Hinson for the first selection in the 1986 draft. That does not make every later Cleveland success part of the 1983 ledger, but it gives the original return a traceable second life that Phoenix’s package never matched.

sections.heading: Phoenix Was Trading for Size, Not Making a Draft-Day Bet
sections.body: The Suns’ own history places the move in a clear roster context. Phoenix had Alvan Adams but wanted another true center after earlier frontcourt changes, and James Edwards offered established size. The deal sent Jeff Cook, cash and a third-round pick to Cleveland and included the conditional exchange of 1983 first-round positions if Phoenix held the better pick. When the draft order settled, Cleveland moved from No. 21 to No. 20. That one-place jump sounds trivial when viewed without player names. It became important only because Cleveland chose Hinson at 20 and Phoenix’s outgoing first became the asset that generated him. The transaction was therefore reasonable for a Suns team addressing an immediate positional need, while Cleveland accepted uncertainty and multiple assets because its competitive timeline was very different.

sections.heading: Hinson’s Development Changed the Asset Math
sections.body: Hinson was not an instant franchise player. His importance to this grade comes from how his value developed. Cleveland selected him 20th, gave him room to grow, and by his third season he had become a productive starting forward with enough league value to interest Philadelphia. In June 1986, the Cavaliers sent Hinson and cash to the 76ers for the No. 1 overall pick. Cleveland then selected Daugherty. Official Cavaliers retrospectives explicitly connect Hinson to that draft-day reset. Because Hinson himself was the player moved in the later transaction, partial downstream credit is warranted. The analysis stops there: Daugherty’s entire career is not assigned backward as if Phoenix traded him directly. Instead, the 1983 return gets credit for producing an asset valuable enough to become the principal basketball piece in Cleveland’s acquisition of the top pick.

sections.heading: Edwards Gave Phoenix More Value Than the C+ Might Suggest at First Glance
sections.body: A losing grade can still contain a successful player acquisition. Edwards filled the size need Phoenix identified, stayed with the club for years and remained productive into the 1987-88 season. When the Suns eventually moved him to Detroit, he was averaging about 16 points and eight rebounds and returned Ron Moore plus a second-round pick. That is meaningful realized value. The C+ is therefore not based on a bust narrative. It reflects the comparative opportunity cost of what Phoenix surrendered. The pick swap and additional pieces gave Cleveland Hinson, and Hinson’s later trade utility dwarfed the secondary value Phoenix eventually received for Edwards. In a completed-value framework, a solid veteran return can still lose decisively when the other side develops and preserves a premium asset.

sections.heading: Why the Daugherty Chain Counts—but Only Partly
sections.body: Connection to later value is where historical trade grades can become exaggerated. Cleveland did not receive Brad Daugherty from Phoenix in 1983. It received the pick used on Hinson. Three years of development, a separate negotiation with Philadelphia and additional cash were required before Hinson became the No. 1 pick. The correct approach is to recognize the chain without collapsing those separate decisions into one event. Hinson’s presence in the 1986 deal proves that the asset retained substantial value; that is stronger evidence than a hypothetical claim about what Cleveland could have done. At the same time, the later cash contribution and Philadelphia’s independent decision reduce how much of Daugherty’s eventual value should be assigned to the original Suns trade. That calibrated credit is enough for an A- rather than an automatic A+.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win, Cleveland A- and Phoenix C+. Phoenix acquired the established center it wanted and received several seasons of useful James Edwards production, so this was not a one-sided transaction on the floor. Cleveland’s return simply had a more powerful second life. The No. 20 pick became Roy Hinson; Hinson developed into a valuable forward; and Cleveland later used Hinson plus cash to acquire the No. 1 pick that became Brad Daugherty. That chain is direct enough to matter but separate enough that the grade stops short of treating Daugherty as an original 1983 asset. Cook, Hord, the cash component and Phoenix’s later Edwards return remain part of the accounting, but Hinson’s preserved value is the decisive difference. The final result is a clear Cleveland win produced by patient asset development rather than an obvious robbery on the day of the trade.

sections.heading: Cleveland Exchanged Tillis for a Future Draft Asset
sections.body: In August 1983, the Cavaliers dealt Darren Tillis to Golden State in return for a 1986 second-round selection. Cleveland eventually used that pick at No. 29 on Johnny Newman. Golden State obtained a player it could bring into its frontcourt immediately, while Cleveland traded current roster depth for a future development opportunity. The recorded deal contains one player on the Warriors side and one pick on the Cavaliers side, with no verified additional cash or selections.

sections.heading: The No. 29 Pick Eventually Became Johnny Newman
sections.body: Newman went on to have a substantial NBA career, showing what could be found in the early second round. His later overall career should not be confused with the length of his Cavaliers tenure or credited to separate franchises that later employed him. The verifiable transaction chain is that Cleveland possessed the selection and made the No. 29 choice. Golden State’s side was Tillis, a different kind of asset that had to produce immediate roster usefulness.

sections.heading: An Equal C-plus Assessment Is the Official Grade
sections.body: Cleveland and Golden State each receive C-plus, and the current verdict is Even Trade. Some older generic analysis described a Cavaliers win with B versus C-minus; that conflicts with the canonical grades. This revised account retains the stronger eventual name recognition of Newman without pretending that such recognition automatically proves the Cavaliers gained a much better completed return from the specific 1983 exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Cleveland C-plus, Golden State C-plus. Cleveland obtained the 1986 No. 29 second-round pick later used on Johnny Newman; Golden State received Darren Tillis. Newman’s NBA career was noteworthy, but the canonical assessment gives both sides the same grade and does not support the previous, contradictory Cavaliers-win narrative.

sections.heading: Russell Rejoined Cleveland Under a Roster Condition
sections.body: The Cavaliers acquired Campy Russell from the New York Knicks on September 29, 1984. New York’s potential return was a conditional second-round pick in the 1985 draft, payable only if Russell was still on the Cleveland roster on December 1, 1984. The transaction ledger indicates that the condition was not met and the pick was not exercised. This is essential: the Knicks did not receive an actual selected player who can be credited with an NBA career.

sections.heading: The Pick’s Condition Limits What New York Received
sections.body: Cleveland obtained an established veteran and the option to use him in its early-season rotation. New York accepted a contingent draft opportunity rather than immediate incoming player production. Because the specified roster condition did not result in the pick being transferred, the Knicks’ possible future asset did not become the realized return a guaranteed selection would have been. Russell’s previous career with Cleveland establishes familiarity with the franchise, but his earlier points and games cannot be counted as value newly generated by this 1984 deal.

sections.heading: The Grade Difference Is Real but Bounded
sections.body: Cleveland receives B-plus and New York B-minus, with Cavaliers Win recorded. That gap follows the difference between securing Russell’s services and holding a conditional selection that did not convey. It does not require claiming Russell immediately became an All-Star or inventing another Knicks compensation package. The Dec. 1 trigger and the unexercised status explain why this small transaction ultimately favors the Cavaliers even though New York had a rational contractual condition in place.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win — Cleveland B-plus, New York B-minus. Cleveland acquired Campy Russell, while the Knicks held a conditional 1985 second-round pick dependent on Russell’s Dec. 1 roster status. The condition was not satisfied and the pick did not convey. Cleveland obtained the real player option; New York never realized its contingent draft return.

sections.heading: Indiana Acquired Ron Anderson for a Distant Draft Chance
sections.body: The Pacers obtained Ron Anderson from Cleveland on December 10, 1985. Cleveland took a 1987 fourth-round pick in return, a future selection with considerably less certainty than an existing player. The pick was ultimately No. 80, used on Carven Holcomb. This deal is best understood through that specific contrast: Indiana added an NBA-capable forward, and Cleveland accepted a draft opportunity two years down the road. There is no verified cash element or additional player in the exchange.

sections.heading: The Fourth-Round Pick Produced a Limited Documented Return
sections.body: A selection near No. 80 offered Cleveland a low-cost route to acquiring a prospect, but it did not confer the immediate roster assurance of Anderson. The stored record identifies Holcomb as the eventual choice and provides no evidence of a substantial Cavaliers playing return attached to that pick. Anderson’s later NBA career also should not be automatically credited to Indiana when it occurred with other clubs. What matters here is the Pacers’ receipt of an established player versus Cleveland’s later draft consideration.

sections.heading: The Pacers Grade Above Cleveland Without a Blockbuster Claim
sections.body: Indiana receives B and Cleveland C-plus, with Pacers Win as the recorded verdict. The difference reflects the more tangible short-term player asset Indiana acquired and the relatively small recorded result of the fourth-round selection. That is a defensible preference without pretending Anderson became a franchise star in Indiana or that Holcomb’s pick had been assigned his name in 1985. The exact two-year delay and the fourth-round status explain why Cleveland’s return carried more uncertainty.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pacers Win — Indiana B, Cleveland C-plus. Indiana acquired Ron Anderson, while Cleveland received the 1987 fourth-round pick later used at No. 80 for Carven Holcomb. The Pacers received an established NBA player; Cleveland’s speculative future selection did not deliver a comparable documented return. The grades recognize that difference without assigning unrelated later achievements to Indiana.

sections.heading: Cleveland Obtained the No. 1 Pick for Roy Hinson
sections.body: Cleveland acquired the top selection in the 1986 NBA draft from Philadelphia on June 16, one day before the draft. The Cavaliers sent Roy Hinson, a productive veteran forward, and the surviving trade ledger also lists cash consideration without a confirmed amount. The formal Cleveland and Philadelphia transaction histories identify Hinson as the player exchanged for that pick. Cleveland exercised the No. 1 choice on North Carolina center Brad Daugherty on June 17. This was not an acquisition of an existing 76ers NBA player; the franchise secured control over the first draft slot and made the selection itself. Other Cleveland moves that summer, including the acquisition of Mark Price through a separate Dallas transaction, should remain distinct from this deal.

sections.heading: Daugherty Became an Eight-Season Cleveland Anchor
sections.body: Daugherty played his entire NBA career for Cleveland, appearing in 548 regular-season games. He averaged 19.0 points, 9.5 rebounds and 3.7 assists, a productive blend of scoring, rebounding and passing for a starting center. The club's official history credits him with five All-Star selections and a major role in the Cavaliers' late-1980s rise. His 10,389 points and 5,227 rebounds were among the franchise's leading totals when his No. 43 jersey was retired in 1997. Those are returns directly attributable to exercising the acquired No. 1 pick. Injuries eventually shortened his career, but they do not diminish the long stretch of legitimate franchise-center output. A historical A-plus for Cleveland is supported by the player who actually took the floor.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Received a Real Veteran, Not Empty Rights
sections.body: Hinson was coming off a 1985-86 Cleveland season in which he averaged 19.6 points and 7.8 rebounds while starting all 82 games. Philadelphia's decision to obtain him had a concrete basketball rationale rather than the goal of acquiring a long-term speculative right. In 1986-87 he played 76 games for the 76ers, started 58 and averaged 13.9 points with 6.4 rebounds. That is meaningful immediate production. He appeared in another 29 Philadelphia games in 1987-88 before the club moved him to New Jersey. The team therefore received a usable forward but only a limited period of service. His subsequent Nets performances should not be credited back to Philadelphia, and the incoming cash has no independently established amount in the source ledger.

sections.heading: The Grade Gap Follows Career Value and Team Longevity
sections.body: Philadelphia gave up the No. 1 choice that became a five-time All-Star Cleveland center and received a veteran whose 76ers career was much shorter. Daugherty played 548 NBA games exclusively for Cleveland, averaging 19.0 points and 9.5 rebounds; the team eventually retired his jersey. Hinson averaged 13.9 points during his first 76ers season and was still capable of helping an NBA rotation, but he did not deliver comparable sustained Philadelphia value. Cleveland's A-plus recognizes both the peak and the duration of a franchise cornerstone. Philadelphia's D recognizes the poor relative return rather than dismissing Hinson as worthless. The 1986 pick was the decisive traded asset, not some unrelated later rookie or a hypothetical draft choice. Cavaliers Win fits the documented history.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win — Cleveland A+, Philadelphia D. Cleveland exercised the No. 1 pick on Brad Daugherty, who made five All-Star teams and played 548 Cavaliers games. Roy Hinson provided Philadelphia a useful 76-game first season but a much shorter team tenure; no cash figure is independently established in the preserved asset ledger.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Brad Daugherty and the 1986 No. 1 Draft Pick: The Hinson Deal
featuredDeepDive.intro: Cleveland obtained the 1986 top pick for Roy Hinson and associated cash, then drafted Brad Daugherty. The center became an eight-season Cavaliers cornerstone while Hinson made a smaller Philadelphia contribution.

sections.heading: The 1986 Draft Rights Were the Entire Turning Point
sections.body: Philadelphia controlled the first selection in the 1986 NBA draft and sent it to Cleveland for Roy Hinson in a June 16 agreement. The Cavaliers' existing draft strategy could then center on Brad Daugherty, a 7-foot North Carolina center, rather than the veteran forward they surrendered. Daugherty was chosen one day later. The official transaction pages do not establish a specific cash figure, even though the preserved source asset inventory includes cash with Hinson; adding a dollar amount would be unjustified. Cleveland's subsequent acquisition of Mark Price and the selection of Ron Harper were other, separate 1986 transactions. The impact of the top pick alone is compelling enough to explain the deal. A precise account does not need to attach every piece of the franchise's rebuild to the single Hinson trade.

sections.heading: Ten Thousand Points in One Cavaliers Uniform
sections.body: Daugherty retired having scored 10,389 NBA points and collected 5,227 rebounds, all in a Cleveland uniform. He also averaged 3.7 assists over his career, giving the Cavaliers a center who could participate in the team's passing game rather than simply finish possessions. The franchise retired his No. 43 in March 1997 and identified him as a foundational player in its post-1986 resurgence. He made five All-Star teams, beginning in 1988, and earned an All-NBA selection in 1991-92. Those outcomes were realized after Cleveland exercised the pick it received for Hinson. Injuries ended his playing career earlier than his peak performance might have suggested, but the accumulated value was exceptional for the original transaction cost. This is sustained team contribution, not borrowed prestige from a later franchise.

sections.heading: Hinson's First Philadelphia Season Explains the Trade-Day Appeal
sections.body: Roy Hinson entered the 1986 offseason as an established scorer and rebounder, not an unknown prospect. He had averaged 19.6 points for Cleveland in 1985-86 and arrived in Philadelphia at 25 years old. The 76ers got 76 regular-season games in his first year, with averages of 13.9 points and 6.4 rebounds, before his local tenure ended after another 29 games the following season. It is reasonable to see why the team wanted a ready veteran rather than waiting for a rookie center. Hindsight judges the choice differently because Daugherty became a durable All-Star and Hinson's Philadelphia period was relatively brief. This contrast gives the D grade its proper meaning: the decision produced NBA minutes but surrendered far greater long-term upside and realized output.

sections.heading: The Final A-Plus and D Must Follow the Original Packages
sections.body: The completed record offers a clear comparison: Cleveland exercised the incoming No. 1 pick on Daugherty and received eight NBA seasons, 548 games and five All-Star appearances. Philadelphia obtained Hinson, who had a productive first 76ers season but did not spend comparable years with the club. Cash was included in the local asset ledger without a defensible published amount, and its presence does not close that gap. A-plus for the Cavaliers rewards the long-term starting center, not hypothetical success from every member of the team's roster. D for Philadelphia reflects a short-lived useful forward against the cost of losing a franchise player. Cleveland's championship attempts and Daugherty's individual recognition belong to his career, but the trade result is established simply by the two assets' team-specific outcomes.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cleveland A-plus, Philadelphia D: the incoming No. 1 choice became a franchise center with 10,389 Cavaliers points and five All-Star selections. Hinson was a legitimate 76ers contributor, not an equal eight-year return. Cash was recorded but its specific amount is not established.

sections.heading: Dallas Drafted Price at No. 25 and Sent His Rights to Cleveland
sections.body: On June 17, 1986, Dallas used the No. 25 selection on Georgia Tech point guard Mark Price but immediately traded his draft rights to Cleveland. The Mavericks received the Cavaliers' 1989 second-round choice, ultimately used at No. 53 to select Jeff Hodge. Cleveland's transaction record and Dallas's matching draft ledger establish the date, teams and specific pick; a Pro Sports Transactions draft chain also lists cash or future considerations without supplying a confirmed dollar figure. Price had not played an NBA game when Cleveland acquired him, so this was a bet on a newly drafted guard rather than the purchase of established veteran production. Cleveland was also adding Brad Daugherty and Ron Harper during the same 1986 draft, a wider roster reset that should not be incorrectly counted as part of the Price trade itself.

sections.heading: Price Played 582 Cavaliers Games and Scored 9,543 Points
sections.body: The original draft-rights acquisition produced nine Cleveland seasons, 582 regular-season appearances and 495 starts. Price scored 9,543 points and recorded 4,206 assists for the Cavaliers, shooting 47.9% from the field, 40.9% from three and 90.6% at the free-throw line during his Cleveland tenure. In 1988-89 he averaged 18.9 points and 8.4 assists, and in 1989-90 he posted 19.6 points and 9.1 assists. Those are actual Cavaliers contributions traceable to the rights Dallas surrendered, not statistics borrowed from a future team. Price's 722 NBA career games include later spells with Washington, Golden State and Orlando; crediting all 722 to Cleveland would overstate the direct return. Four All-Star selections and four All-NBA selections further distinguish this second-round pick from an ordinary short-term rotational success.

sections.heading: Dallas's 1989 No. 53 Selection Had a Much Smaller Return
sections.body: Dallas's identifiable basketball consideration was the future 1989 second-rounder, a three-year wait that became pick No. 53 and Jeff Hodge. The Mavericks also listed unspecified cash or future considerations in one surviving draft chain, but neither a verified additional player nor an exact payment is established by the present primary transaction records. Dallas's own 1988-89 team ledger shows it drafted Hodge at No. 53. The comparison therefore is not a same-day exchange of two known NBA guards: Dallas chose draft flexibility and a later lottery-free selection, whereas Cleveland retained the player who evolved into its offensive organizer. Attribution should stop with the 1989 selection unless a sourced later pick trade supplies a separate legitimate chain. That constraint prevents both inventing Dallas NBA games for Hodge and overstating the unspecified financial portion of the original deal.

sections.heading: A+ for Cleveland, F for Dallas Reflect an Unusually Uneven Outcome
sections.body: The historical verdict is Cavaliers Win, Cleveland A+ to Dallas F, and the results explain the wide difference without relying solely on Price's reputation. Cleveland got a nine-year starting-level guard, 9,543 points, 4,206 assists and an efficient shooting profile before he moved elsewhere. Dallas took a distant No. 53 pick and undefined other considerations, neither equivalent to what Price eventually gave the Cavaliers. Cleveland reached the postseason seven times during Price's years, although the franchise's broader wins cannot all be assigned to one transaction. The four All-Star and four All-NBA honors provide a player-specific impact measure that makes the grade persuasive. One caveat concerns the extra 'cash / future considerations' in the imported asset ledger: the sources do not establish a dollar amount, and the favorable Cleveland verdict does not justify fabricating one. The two canonical team grades and private/archive eligibility are preserved.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win — Cleveland A+, Dallas F. On June 17, 1986, Cleveland acquired the draft rights to Mark Price for its 1989 second-round choice, later No. 53 Jeff Hodge, with other considerations incompletely documented. Price delivered 582 Cavaliers games, 9,543 points and 4,206 assists over nine seasons, plus four All-Star selections. Dallas received the later pick but nothing documented that approached Price's direct production. The 722-game figure is his entire NBA career, not his Cavaliers total, and no unsupported cash figure has been added.
