sections.heading: The Lakers-Origin 2019 Second Changed Hands in July 2015
sections.body: Cleveland moved the NBA draft rights to Rakeem Christmas to Indiana on July 23, 2015 and received the Lakers' own 2019 second-round selection. The Cavaliers' official release identified both the former rights holder and the four-year draft horizon; Christmas was the No. 36 selection from that June and had not yet played an NBA regular-season game. Indiana had obtained that Lakers second in a separate Roy Hibbert transaction earlier in July. Cleveland therefore traded one newly acquired prospect right for a pick that could be held or exchanged later. The deal did not deliver a current NBA player to the Cavaliers. It also was not the separate 2019 Minnesota second Cleveland acquired through the Tyus Jones-Cedi Osman arrangement in June 2015. Distinguishing the two 2019 rights is essential to tracing the selection correctly.

sections.heading: Indiana Signed Christmas, Who Played Thirty NBA Games
sections.body: Indiana converted Christmas's incoming rights into a real but brief NBA opportunity. He signed with the Pacers four days after the trade and appeared in one game during 2015-16 and 29 more in 2016-17. The official Pacers media guide and his NBA statistical record identify 30 regular-season appearances, no starts and 225 total minutes. Those 30 games are direct Indiana roster production; Cleveland cannot claim them as its own return after trading the rights. His developmental-league assignments were a different level of basketball and cannot add NBA regular-season minutes to the transaction grade. Christmas was waived in July 2017. The Pacers' inherited D grade therefore reflects the limited duration of the player they received, without inaccurately saying their draft-rights purchase produced zero NBA appearances.

sections.heading: The No. 41 Pick Later Moved Cleveland to Atlanta to Golden State
sections.body: The Lakers-origin 2019 pick did eventually become No. 41 Eric Paschall, but not in a Cavaliers uniform. In October 2017 Cleveland sent the less favorable of its Lakers- and Minnesota-origin 2019 seconds to Atlanta as part of a separate Richard Jefferson and Kay Felder trade. An NBA.com report then records Atlanta sending the No. 41 choice to Golden State at the June 20, 2019 draft in exchange for cash and a future second. The Warriors selected Paschall, as the NBA draft record confirms. That is a genuine asset trail, not proof Cleveland received Paschall's subsequent Warriors minutes. The original Cavaliers B+ versus Pacers D can credit Cleveland for obtaining tradeable draft capital while Indiana received 30 Christmas games, but later Golden State player development belongs to Golden State.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win. Cleveland carries B+ for the 2019 second-round pick that became No. 41 Eric Paschall; Indiana carries D for the Rakeem Christmas draft rights. The greater identified value arose from the pick's conversion rather than an immediate 2015 player-for-player exchange.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: 2015 Rakeem Christmas Rights and Cleveland’s Lakers Second-Round Pick
featuredDeepDive.intro: Cleveland moved Rakeem Christmas draft rights for a 2019 Lakers second-round choice. Christmas played 30 Pacers games; the pick eventually became No. 41 Eric Paschall, drafted by Golden State rather than Cleveland.

sections.heading: Cleveland Received the Lakers’ Future Second
sections.body: Cleveland moved the draft rights to Rakeem Christmas to Indiana on July 23, 2015. The official Cavaliers announcement identified the return as the Los Angeles Lakers' 2019 second-round pick, which had been held by the Pacers. This was not a trade of an established NBA rotation player for another active player. Christmas had just been selected No. 36 in the draft, while the incoming pick would not be exercised for four seasons. For Cleveland, the immediate value was flexibility: a second-round right could be retained or used in a later transaction. The 2019 selection eventually became No. 41 and was used on Eric Paschall, but the club responsible for Paschall's NBA playing career must be distinguished from the Cavaliers who originally acquired the pick. The chronology should not invent Paschall minutes for Cleveland.

sections.heading: Christmas Became a Pacers Player, Not a Lost Right
sections.body: Indiana did turn its incoming draft rights into an NBA player. Rakeem Christmas signed with the Pacers shortly after the July 2015 transaction and eventually appeared in 30 regular-season games across 2015-16 and 2016-17. The club's own historical roster records list one game in his first season and 29 in the second, totaling 225 minutes and 63 points. He never started a Pacers game and was waived in July 2017. That is a small but real return, not zero appearances. The D grade reflects how little NBA value the club ultimately obtained for surrendering a future second-round pick with its own trade possibilities. His developmental-league assignments and college accomplishments explain the original scouting idea without inflating what he did for Indiana in NBA regular-season games.

sections.heading: The Lakers-Origin Pick Passed From Cleveland to Atlanta and Golden State
sections.body: The Cavaliers received the Lakers' own 2019 second from Indiana in July 2015. They did not exercise it themselves. In October 2017, Cleveland moved the less favorable of that Lakers second and a separate Minnesota second to Atlanta alongside Richard Jefferson and Kay Felder, acquiring different overseas rights in another transaction. That 2019 right ultimately became No. 41. NBA.com documents Atlanta transferring No. 41 to Golden State on June 20, 2019 for $1.3 million and a 2024 second-round selection. The Warriors drafted Eric Paschall and later developed him as a rotation player; none of those Warriors appearances are Cavaliers production. This two-step chain explains the draft name attached to the original 2015 asset, while preserving which team made each decision. The 2015 trade is still Christmas rights to Indiana for a future Lakers pick, not a direct Cleveland-for-Paschall player trade.

sections.heading: The Limited Indiana Return Explains the Direction
sections.body: The Cavaliers Win verdict preserves the judgment that Cleveland acquired the more flexible asset in 2015. Indiana took Christmas's draft rights and turned them into 30 appearances and no NBA starts before waiving him in 2017. Meanwhile, Cleveland acquired a 2019 Lakers second-round selection that ultimately corresponded to No. 41, later used by another club on Paschall. A B-plus for Cleveland and D for Indiana should be read as an asset-value comparison rather than a claim of direct superstar production. The Pacers did have a reasonable prospect-development rationale, supported by Christmas's Syracuse career and summer-league performance, but the two-season NBA result was modest. Keeping the original July 23 deal distinct from the pick's eventual draft outcome produces a more accurate story than generic grade language or borrowed Warriors statistics.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win — Cleveland B+, Indiana D. Cleveland obtained the Lakers 2019 second-round right, eventually associated with No. 41 Eric Paschall. Christmas played 30 NBA regular-season games for Indiana before being waived. Paschall never played for Cleveland, so his Warriors production is not counted as Cavaliers value.

sections.heading: Dellavedova’s Move Was Structured as a Sign-and-Trade
sections.body: Milwaukee acquired guard Matthew Dellavedova from Cleveland in July 2016 after he agreed to a new contract. The Cavaliers received the draft rights to Albert Miralles. The central context is that Cleveland was dealing with a departing free agent, not bargaining over an established player under a long guaranteed contract. Moving the transaction through a sign-and-trade allowed Cleveland to receive an asset instead of letting the guard leave with no trade compensation.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Obtained an Experienced NBA Guard
sections.body: Dellavedova had played meaningful minutes for a championship-level Cleveland team. Milwaukee acquired him for defense, ball-handling and veteran backcourt experience as it built around a younger roster. His Bucks tenure gave the club legitimate NBA rotation production. He later moved back to Cleveland in another transaction, which underscores that his contract remained a movable veteran piece rather than vanishing immediately after signing.

sections.heading: Cleveland’s Rights Did Not Become Comparable Production
sections.body: Miralles was a draft-rights asset, not a ready-made Cavaliers contributor. Those rights did not become meaningful NBA minutes for Cleveland. A return with no realized on-court value is less useful in hindsight, but it was still a rational form of compensation for a free agent already choosing another team. The Cavaliers’ decision should be understood as salvaging an asset, not voluntarily exchanging a controlled productive guard for a non-NBA player.

sections.heading: The Bucks Win Without Implying Cleveland Blundered
sections.body: Milwaukee receives an A because Dellavedova supplied multiple seasons of usable guard play. Cleveland receives a C because Miralles’s rights produced no comparable roster result. The trade winner is therefore clear on completed on-court output; the grades also preserve the contractual circumstances. Cleveland’s negotiating position was inherently narrower than Milwaukee’s ability to offer the new role and contract.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win — Milwaukee A, Cleveland C. Dellavedova provided real NBA backcourt minutes after joining the Bucks, while the draft rights to Miralles brought Cleveland no comparable production. The Cavaliers still recovered something from an outgoing free agent. The completed returns favor Milwaukee without implying Cleveland rejected an equivalent offer of established NBA talent.

sections.heading: The trade details
sections.body: On January 6, 2017, Cleveland traded a 2017 first-round selection to Portland for a 2018 first-round asset. The outgoing pick later became No. 26, Caleb Swanigan; the incoming 2018 selection later became No. 25, associated with Moritz 'Moe' Wagner. Those names identify the eventual draft outcomes, not players switching teams on the January 2017 trade date. This was a swap of rights tied to different drafts, with a year's timing difference and no active NBA player transferred.

sections.heading: How the Returns Diverged
sections.body: The Cavaliers preferred the later first-round choice, postponing their draft opportunity while taking the risk of where that selection would land. Portland obtained access to a 2017 pick sooner. The final positions were adjacent — No. 25 in 2018 and No. 26 in 2017 — but neighboring draft numbers don't automatically mean equal realized value. The recorded Cavaliers Win verdict reflects the archive's assessment of the eventual assets, not a direct Wagner-for-Swanigan playing-career transaction.

sections.heading: The Stronger Package
sections.body: Cleveland's incoming consideration was a single 2018 first-round asset. The future pick would later be identified with Moe Wagner at No. 25, although any intervening changes in pick ownership need their own transaction history. It would be inaccurate to say Cleveland acquired Wagner as a player in January 2017 merely because the canonical draft label names him. The value of a draft right is its flexibility and future selection opportunity, which can be used or traded again.

sections.heading: The Cost on the Other Side
sections.body: Portland received the earlier 2017 first-round pick, subsequently No. 26 for Caleb Swanigan. The Blazers could act on that selection sooner than Cleveland could act on the 2018 asset, so they chose certainty of timing over the later pick. Their recorded D grade compared with Cleveland's B+ is a retrospective result, not proof the Blazers were already choosing between Swanigan and Wagner at the moment of the trade. The transaction moved selections, not two signed players.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win — Cleveland B+, Portland D. The exchange moved a 2017 first-round asset to Portland and a 2018 first-round asset to Cleveland. Their eventual No. 26 Caleb Swanigan and No. 25 Moe Wagner labels identify the picks, but aren't proof that the named players changed teams in January 2017. The recorded grade gap evaluates those two draft opportunities rather than a fictional player swap.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Cleveland Cavaliers–Portland Trail Blazers: What the 2017-01-06 Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: The Cleveland–Portland deal on January 6, 2017 exchanged one future first-round asset for another in a different draft year. The Cavaliers received the 2018 selection later labeled No. 25, Moe Wagner. The Trail Blazers received the 2017 choice later labeled No. 26, Caleb Swanigan. Keeping the draft dates and eventual names apart from the actual trade date prevents a common analytical error: attributing a player's later roster career to the club that once held the associated pick.

sections.heading: The Core Hindsight Asset
sections.body: The trade's unusual feature was its one-year offset. Portland gained access to a first-round selection in 2017, while Cleveland accepted the longer wait for the 2018 choice. The positions ultimately became No. 26 and No. 25 respectively. That is useful evidence for comparing asset outcomes, but the numerical closeness alone says nothing about which team retained the draft rights through every later transaction or how much NBA production each selected player supplied.

sections.heading: What the Supporting Assets Added
sections.body: The two names in the ledger play different documentary roles from team names. Caleb Swanigan is the eventual player associated with Portland's incoming 2017 pick; Moe Wagner identifies the 2018 pick that Cleveland acquired. Neither was an active trade participant in January 2017. An asset-by-asset review must avoid describing the deal as Cleveland trading Swanigan the player for Wagner the player. The obligations and draft rights moved first; the selections came later.

sections.heading: The Difference Between Intent and Result
sections.body: Cleveland's decision can be understood as exchanging nearer-term draft access for an additional year of uncertainty. Portland chose the earlier opportunity instead. When the 2017 and 2018 drafts eventually arrived, the resulting selections supplied the facts used in the archive's grade assessment. But a grade written with hindsight should not imply either front office knew the precise later draft slots at the time of the trade. The timing choice is what each organization actually controlled.

sections.heading: The Scale of the Final Margin
sections.body: The archive assigns B+ to Cleveland and D to Portland, producing Cavaliers Win. Those grades concern the value associated with the later No. 25 pick relative to the earlier No. 26 choice. They should be interpreted alongside the transaction's limitations: no active player, cash transfer or second pick appears in the stored exchange. An accurate evaluation follows the two distinct selections and avoids inventing Cleveland playing time for Wagner or Portland assets that were never listed.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cleveland accepted the 2018 draft-right timetable; Portland chose the 2017 one. Once the selections could be identified, the archive awarded the Cavaliers the better retrospective result. The Cavaliers Win judgment and B+/D scores can stand without claiming a 2017 trade of Wagner and Swanigan as signed NBA players. Chronology and pick ownership must be traced independently before drawing conclusions about later roster contributions.

sections.heading: Cleveland Acquired Dekker and Two Additional Assets
sections.body: The Cavaliers received Sam Dekker, the draft rights to Renaldas Seibutis and cash from the Clippers in August 2018. Los Angeles received the draft rights to Vladimir Veremeenko. The exchange was built around one current NBA player and older international draft rights. Cleveland obtained the only player on the incoming lists who could immediately occupy an NBA roster spot; the cash and Seibutis rights supplied additional considerations.

sections.heading: Dekker Supplied the Immediate Basketball Possibility
sections.body: Dekker was an established NBA forward option at the time, although not a franchise cornerstone. That made him different from the rights to Seibutis or Veremeenko, which represented control of a potential future acquisition rather than guaranteed NBA playing time. The direct player acquisition is central to Cleveland’s grade. The rights and cash should still appear in the asset list, but the source records do not support promising substantial NBA minutes from either unsigned rights holder.

sections.heading: The Clippers Chose a Rights Asset Instead
sections.body: Los Angeles received Veremeenko’s rights instead of an immediate rotation forward. This gave the Clippers a distinct, more speculative asset without a documented comparable on-court contribution from the transaction. The ledger grades Cleveland B and the Clippers C-minus, and calls the result a Cavaliers win. The difference arises from Dekker’s roster utility and Cleveland’s supplementary assets, not from inventing an overseas success that became NBA value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win — Cleveland B, Los Angeles Clippers C-minus. Cleveland secured Dekker, Seibutis’s rights and cash; the Clippers took Veremeenko’s rights. Dekker supplied an identifiable near-term NBA roster option that the opposite package could not match through established league production. The rights remain genuine considerations, but do not reverse the documented result.

sections.heading: Cleveland Turned an Aging Specialist into a Multi-Asset Package
sections.body: Cleveland moved Kyle Korver to Utah for Alec Burks and two future second-round picks. The timing mattered. The Cavaliers had fallen out of contention after LeBron James' departure, while Korver was 37 and more valuable to a playoff team that needed shooting than to a rebuilding roster. Cleveland converted that mismatch of timelines into a younger rotation player and two draft assets. Burks was on an expiring contract, which gave the Cavaliers additional flexibility, and the picks extended the return beyond one season. The move therefore accomplished exactly what a rebuilding team should seek when selling a veteran specialist: immediate salary flexibility, a usable player and future draft currency rather than a one-for-one lateral swap.

sections.heading: Burks Became More Than a Temporary Throw-In
sections.body: Burks played only part of the season in Cleveland, but his value did not disappear when he left. In February 2019 the Cavaliers sent him to Sacramento in a three-team trade and received a larger package from Houston that included Brandon Knight, Marquese Chriss, a 2019 first-round pick and a 2022 second-round pick, while Cleveland also sent other assets in that separate transaction. The original Korver trade should not receive full credit for the entire later package. It should receive proportional credit for the fact that Burks remained a movable NBA asset. Cleveland extracted useful transactional value from him after already acquiring two seconds from Utah.

sections.heading: Utah Got the Shooter It Wanted, but Paid a Heavy Price
sections.body: The Jazz had a clear basketball problem. NBA.com's trade tracker noted that Utah was shooting 31.9 percent from three at the time, near the bottom of the league, and Korver was one of the best shooters in NBA history. He immediately addressed spacing around Donovan Mitchell and Rudy Gobert. That fit prevents Utah's side from being treated as purposeless. The D+ comes from price and duration. Utah surrendered Burks plus two second-round picks for an older specialist who could improve a contender but was unlikely to create long-term value. Cleveland's ability to keep extracting assets from the package makes the Jazz's outgoing cost look increasingly expensive in retrospect.

sections.heading: The Second-Round Picks Added Real Optionality
sections.body: Cleveland received Utah's 2020 second-round pick and a 2021 second originally from Washington. The selections were later associated with Justinian Jessup at No. 51 and Greg Brown III at No. 43. Neither outcome by itself would justify an A-range grade, and Cleveland should not be credited with every later career move involving those players or picks. Their importance is cumulative. The Cavaliers received two draft opportunities on top of Burks and then used Burks as part of another asset-generating trade. That layered return is why Cleveland rises to A-. Utah received useful shooting, but the Cavaliers built a much broader and more flexible package from a veteran who no longer fit their competitive window.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win. Cleveland earns A- because it converted a 37-year-old specialist into Alec Burks plus two second-round picks, then retained enough value in Burks to use him in another multi-team transaction. The two seconds became additional draft opportunities, giving the Cavaliers multiple independent branches of value from one veteran sale. Utah receives D+ because Kyle Korver addressed a genuine need for shooting and spacing, but the Jazz paid a younger rotation player and two picks for a short-horizon upgrade. The documented Cavaliers Win verdict follows the completed asset chain: Utah received useful present value, while Cleveland received present flexibility, future draft capital and a player who remained marketable enough to create another return.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Deep Dive: Cleveland Sold Kyle Korver at the Right Point in the Rebuild
featuredDeepDive.intro: The Korver trade is a timing story. Utah was trying to improve a playoff roster and needed shooting. Cleveland was beginning a rebuild and had little reason to hold an aging specialist whose value was highest to a contender. The Cavaliers used that difference in team timelines to collect three assets and then kept the chain moving through Burks.

sections.heading: Korver's Utah Fit Was Obvious
sections.body: Utah did not need to guess about Korver's skill set. He had already played for the Jazz earlier in his career, and his shooting profile directly attacked a weakness on the 2018-19 roster. NBA.com noted Utah's poor three-point percentage at the time of the deal, while the Jazz's own release highlighted Korver's career 43.2 percent shooting from deep. That context matters because the D+ should not imply Utah received a bad player. Korver was still a dangerous floor spacer and made sense around Mitchell. The issue is that role-player fit has a price ceiling. Burks plus two seconds gave Cleveland more long-term value than Korver could realistically return in a limited competitive window.

sections.heading: Cleveland Monetized Age and Timeline
sections.body: The Cavaliers were 4-16 around the time of the trade and had already shifted away from the assumption that the post-LeBron roster would remain a playoff team. Korver's value to Cleveland was therefore declining even if his shooting ability remained intact. Selling him for a 27-year-old expiring guard and two picks was a textbook timeline conversion. Rebuilding teams often lose value by holding veterans until contenders no longer need them. Cleveland did the opposite. The front office moved Korver while his specialist skill still had a clear market. That decision produced a package with both immediate flexibility and future options, which is the foundation of the A- rather than any single player outcome.

sections.heading: Burks Extended the Trade's Asset Life
sections.body: Burks' Cleveland tenure lasted only months, but short tenure does not mean low value. He was a functional rotation player on an expiring deal and remained desirable enough to be sent to Sacramento in the February 2019 three-team transaction. Cleveland's return in that later trade included a first-round pick among other assets, though the Cavaliers also contributed additional pieces, so the Korver deal cannot claim the entire return. The relevant point is narrower: Burks was liquid. Cleveland did not merely receive salary filler that expired unused. The Cavaliers preserved optionality and turned one component of the Korver return into another transaction before losing control of the asset.

sections.heading: Two Picks Made the Value Gap Durable
sections.body: Even if Burks had simply expired in Cleveland, the two seconds would have given the Cavaliers a plausible positive result. Utah's 2020 second and Washington's 2021 second ultimately became selections in the 40s and 50s. Those are lower-probability assets, but they matter because they can be drafted, traded or combined. Cleveland received both in addition to Burks. Utah's return, by contrast, was concentrated almost entirely in Korver's immediate shooting. The structure therefore favored the rebuilding team over time. A contender can reasonably make that trade, but hindsight still asks whether the improvement justified the surrendered options. In this case, Cleveland's layered return proved stronger.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win, Cleveland A- and Utah D+. The Jazz acquired exactly the kind of shooter they wanted, and Korver's fit on a playoff roster was real. Cleveland nevertheless captured the superior asset structure. Burks was younger, expiring and still marketable; the Cavaliers later used him in another transaction rather than losing his value for nothing. Two second-round picks came with him, creating additional draft flexibility. Cleveland therefore transformed one aging specialist into three separate assets while rebuilding. Utah concentrated its value in a short-term veteran upgrade and surrendered more future optionality than that upgrade ultimately justified. The result is a clear Cleveland win without denying the logic behind Utah's original move.

sections.heading: Reading the Team Grades

The wider draft ledger later shows exactly which three Detroit incoming selections could be identified. The Pistons obtained 2020, 2021 and 2023 second-round opportunities, conditional 2024 consideration that ultimately did not convey, and cash. Their recorded B+ against Cleveland's C+ reflects the archive's retrospective preference for that combined package. The gap should not be explained by pretending the unexercised fourth pick was a realized draftee or by assigning unspecified cash an invented dollar amount.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Detroit B+, Cleveland C+. The Cavaliers acquired Kevin Porter Jr.'s rights; the Pistons received 2020, 2021 and 2023 second-round rights later associated with Jessup, Boston and Phillips, another conditional 2024 right that wasn't exercised, and cash. Detroit's multi-asset return earned the higher stored grade, with the important caveat that an unexercised selection isn't an additional player.

sections.heading: The Asset Path That Carries the Grade
sections.body: Detroit exchanged Kevin Porter Jr.'s newly drafted rights for Cleveland's future package. For the Cavaliers, the immediate decision was concentrated: one prospect and the development risk associated with him. The Pistons received several second-round paths and cash consideration, offering multiple later opportunities rather than one player ready to contribute in June 2019. The recorded picks eventually corresponded to No. 51 in 2020, No. 51 in 2021 and No. 35 in 2023; each has a different draft-year identity. Calling all three instant Detroit roster contributors would confuse an asset's historical selection result with its ownership and usage in later transactions. sections.heading: What the Lower-Graded Side Still Kept
sections.body: Cleveland's consideration involved future second-round selections subsequently recorded as Justinian Jessup at No. 51 in 2020, Brandon Boston Jr. at No. 51 in 2021 and Julian Phillips at No. 35 in 2023. There was also a 2024 second-round right protected through No. 55, and that protection is recorded as not exercised. The three actual later selections and the expired protected item have different accounting: an unexercised choice cannot be added as a fourth drafted player. sections.heading: Decision Logic Versus Hindsight
sections.body: Neither organization could know the final 2020, 2021 and 2023 draft positions when the Porter Jr. rights moved in June 2019. Detroit was taking on the uncertainty of distant draft slots, a protected additional 2024 chance and cash, while Cleveland secured a particular player to evaluate and develop. The different timing is central to the trade. Even after the picks acquired their later selection labels, identifying Justinian Jessup, Brandon Boston Jr. and Julian Phillips does not establish that Detroit personally drafted or retained each athlete. Those distinctions keep the transaction's original rights separate from intervening trades. A retrospective win-loss evaluation may use the eventual asset paths, but not an invented guarantee of four Detroit players.

sections.heading: Why the Grade Gap Is the Better Scale
sections.body: The saved result awards Detroit B+ and Cleveland C+, a Pistons Win in the archive's retrospective grading. That preference considers the multiple second-round rights and cash taken for one player's rights, while acknowledging that the 2024 protected second was never exercised. Porter Jr. was the Cavaliers' direct acquisition; the final draft numbers were not known on trade day. Equating the later picks with confirmed Pistons NBA games would inflate the Detroit return, just as disregarding the completed selections would erase real traded assets. The gap is an editorial comparison of what each team secured from the deal, not proof that every future right became an impact contributor for the same franchise.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Detroit traded the rights to a specific 2019 prospect for a broader set of later draft assets and money. Three future picks can now be identified, but another protected pick never conveyed. Cleveland's Porter Jr. return was a different kind of basketball opportunity. The recorded Pistons Win result and B+/C+ marks reflect those contrasting packages without inventing roster tenure, extra compensation or an exercised 2024 selection.

sections.heading: Cleveland Bought Drummond at a Low Player Cost
sections.body: The February 6, 2020 exchange brought Andre Drummond from Detroit to Cleveland for Brandon Knight, John Henson and a future second-round selection. Drummond was the clearly established center in the trade rather than an unproven draft-rights acquisition. Detroit received two veterans whose contracts created a different type of flexibility, plus a pick with protections attached to the exact selection it would ultimately convey. The Cavaliers did not surrender a first-rounder or one of their leading young pieces. That is why the incoming center carried greater immediate basketball value than the number of assets heading to the Pistons might suggest.

sections.heading: The 2023 Second Eventually Became Isaiah Wong
sections.body: The second-round selection was specified as the less favorable of Cleveland's and Golden State's 2023 choices and ultimately appears in the trade record as No. 55, Isaiah Wong. Naming that selection is useful for asset tracing, but it does not automatically credit Detroit with the whole later career of every person connected to the pick. Detroit also took Knight and Henson, with contract and roster considerations influencing the original decision. Those were separate pieces of compensation, not a hidden additional first. Cleveland's side was Drummond alone, making the central comparison one established starting center against a smaller set of veteran and lower-round assets.

sections.heading: A Modest Cleveland Edge, Not a Franchise Turnaround
sections.body: Drummond gave Cleveland a known rebounding and interior presence after the deadline. His arrival did not by itself complete a contender, and an analysis of the acquisition shouldn't borrow championships or long-term results from other clubs. Detroit's package had financial utility even if the immediate on-court return lacked the same ceiling. Because the deal was a short-horizon center acquisition rather than a major lottery exchange, the value gap was more limited than some star-player trades. The correct conclusion is that Cleveland acquired the most productive direct piece while Detroit retained enough compensation to avoid an extreme losing grade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win. Cleveland receives B+ for acquiring Andre Drummond at a cost of Knight, Henson and one future second. Detroit receives B- for those veterans, cap flexibility and the 2023 selection later identified as No. 55 Isaiah Wong. The edge comes from the center's direct value, not an invented future pick or a championship attributed to this deal.

sections.heading: Official Trade Terms: Drummond for Two Veterans and a Lesser Second
sections.body: On February 6, 2020, Cleveland acquired Andre Drummond from Detroit for Brandon Knight, John Henson and the less favorable of the Cavaliers' and Golden State's 2023 second-round picks. The Cavaliers' official release explicitly describes the conditional choice, so neither a guaranteed first-round pick nor an unrestricted 2023 second belongs in this account. Drummond was 26 and had already earned two All-Star selections with Detroit, but his prior Pistons playing years would not become Cleveland production. Knight and Henson were recognizable NBA veterans whose outgoing contracts created a different rebuilding route for Detroit. The transaction offered Cleveland a high-volume rebounder without surrendering a leading young Cavaliers player, while Detroit received future draft consideration and roster flexibility. Those are documented terms, not an estimate of unreported cash or exceptions.

sections.heading: Drummond Played Thirty-Three Cleveland Games, Then Was Waived
sections.body: Cleveland used Drummond in eight regular-season games after the February 2020 trade, starting all eight. He returned for 25 more games in the 2020-21 season, again starting each one. His Cleveland total was therefore 33 appearances over two disrupted seasons, not the 591 Detroit games cited when the deal was announced. The Cavaliers subsequently kept him out of the rotation and waived him on March 26, 2021, after which he joined the Lakers. Cleveland did gain genuine rebounding and center minutes during those 33 games, but the relationship ended without a long-term playoff core built around Drummond. The source-locked Cavaliers B-plus should be read against that bounded service rather than his earlier Detroit awards or later games for other teams.

sections.heading: The 2023 Second Changed Owners Before No. 55 Isaiah Wong
sections.body: Detroit gained a real conditional 2023 second-round right, not the rights to a player who could join the Pistons in 2020. The original pick did not turn Wong into a Pistons roster contributor. Historical transaction records trace the choice through other organizations before Indiana made the selection, with the wider later packages requiring their own accounting. Similarly, Cleveland did not select Wong and cannot claim his subsequent Indiana appearances. The future asset created optionality for Detroit even though the direct result of the 2020 Drummond exchange was mostly short-term veterans and the pick right. Each later club deserves its actual player contributions only.

Cleveland acquired a proven center for two veteran contracts and a conditional future second, then received 33 Drummond regular-season games before waiving him in March 2021. Detroit received Knight, Henson and the pick right, but could not book Drummond's Cleveland minutes or Isaiah Wong's eventual Indiana service as its own team production. The transaction helped move Detroit away from a long-standing center-centered roster without yielding an immediate first-round replacement. This is a modest inherited grade preference, not proof of a Cavaliers championship return or of a Pistons No. 55 draft choice in 2023. finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict

sections.heading: A 2020 Exchange of an NBA Center and a Future Right
sections.body: Cleveland acquired JaVale McGee and the Lakers' own 2026 second-round draft pick on November 23, 2020. The Lakers obtained Alfonzo McKinnie and Jordan Bell, as the Cavaliers confirmed in their contemporaneous team announcement. The asset difference was visible immediately: McGee had just played 68 games for the 2019-20 champion Lakers, while the draft selection was still six years from use. That second-rounder was a right Cleveland could retain or convey, not a player who appeared for the Cavaliers in 2020. It is also distinct from the separate 2025 Milwaukee second-round pick Cleveland acquired days earlier in a different transaction. Keeping those picks separate prevents the 2020 Lakers exchange from absorbing unrelated assets or later results.

sections.heading: McGee and McKinnie Produced Measurable, Limited Returns
sections.body: McGee played 33 games for Cleveland in 2020-21, averaging 8.0 points, 5.2 rebounds and 1.2 blocks in 15.2 minutes. In March 2021 the Cavaliers separately moved him to Denver for Isaiah Hartenstein and two future second-round choices; that later package was not compensation directly sent by the Lakers in November. Los Angeles received 39 regular-season games from McKinnie that season, with averages of 3.1 points and 1.4 rebounds. Bell, the other incoming forward, was waived on November 25, 2020, before playing a Lakers regular-season game. The immediate comparison therefore is 33 Cleveland games from an established center plus a future pick, against one limited Lakers wing stint and a waived player. Each figure belongs only to the receiving club and period in which it occurred.

sections.heading: The 2026 Lakers-Origin Pick Became No. 54, Not a Cleveland Draft Choice
sections.body: The deferred second-round selection is no longer an unresolved draft outcome. NBA Communications listed the 2026 No. 54 choice as originating with the Lakers and reaching Golden State through Cleveland, Miami and Toronto. Golden State's February 5, 2026 announcement explains its final acquisition: the Warriors received the Lakers-origin second-rounder from Toronto in exchange for Trayce Jackson-Davis. At the June 2026 draft, Golden State selected Florida State wing Lajae Jones at No. 54. This establishes the pick's eventual identity without pretending the Cavaliers drafted Jones or obtained his later NBA playing time. Cleveland received the tradeable right in 2020, then it continued through other clubs before the Warriors used it. The inherited A-/C- result can now describe a resolved draft asset while keeping its subsequent transfers separate.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win — Cleveland A-, Los Angeles C-. McGee supplied 33 Cavaliers regular-season games, while McKinnie played 39 for the Lakers and Bell was waived before an appearance. The Lakers-origin 2026 second-round pick later became No. 54 Lajae Jones, selected by Golden State after subsequent transfers; Jones is NOT a Cleveland on-court return.

sections.heading: Cleveland Received a Contingent Pick, Not a Played Rookie
sections.body: The Cavaliers traded Kevin Porter Jr. to Houston on January 22, 2021, for a 2024 second-round selection carrying top-55 protection. Cleveland's own announcement called the return a future second, while the full protection detail appears in transaction trackers. The pick was tied to Golden State and ultimately landed in the protected range, so it did not convey to Cleveland. No 2024 drafted player should be credited as the Cavaliers' return from this transaction. What the franchise actually obtained was the conditional right and the ability to move on from a player it no longer planned to keep. That distinction is essential: contractual compensation existed when the teams agreed to the trade, but it did not become a usable selection years later. The official Cavaliers statement framed the decision around the organization's direction and environment rather than immediate roster improvement.

sections.heading: Porter Produced Three Real Houston Seasons
sections.body: Houston obtained a 20-year-old guard who had averaged 10.0 points in 50 Cleveland games the previous season. In Texas, Porter developed into a high-usage scorer and secondary playmaker. He averaged 15.6 points and 6.2 assists in 61 games in 2021-22, followed by 19.2 points and 5.0 assists in 59 appearances during 2022-23, according to his NBA player biography. Those are genuine Rockets contributions and far greater playing value than the protected pick Cleveland received. Houston invested minutes in him during a rebuilding stretch and also made a separate long-term contract decision in 2022. The on-court evidence cannot be removed merely because his Houston tenure later ended. It provides the clearest basketball case that the Rockets made an inexpensive acquisition with significant short-term production.

sections.heading: The October 2023 Departure Came at Another Cost
sections.body: Porter's Rockets tenure ended after serious off-court allegations and a September 2023 arrest. The Associated Press reported that Houston barred him from the team, and on October 17 the Rockets traded Porter plus two future second-round selections to Oklahoma City for Victor Oladipo and Jeremiah Robinson-Earl. The Thunder announced that Porter would be waived immediately. That 2023 transaction is not part of Cleveland's original January 2021 compensation, but it is relevant to judging the full Houston outcome. The Rockets gained useful scoring seasons at very little acquisition cost, then paid additional draft capital to move the contract and end the roster relationship. The B-minus grade can acknowledge both the basketball production and the costly, shortened ending without making unsupported findings about allegations or future legal proceedings.

sections.heading: Why an Even Verdict Needs More Than Identical Grades
sections.body: The preserved ledger assigns B-minus to both clubs and records an Even Trade, but the returns were not symmetrical. Cleveland's heavily protected second did not convey, so its direct draft value was zero. The Cavaliers' side must instead be described as a roster and organizational decision with a very limited asset recovery, not a useful 2024 draft selection. Houston got a player who averaged 19.2 points in his final Rockets season, then surrendered two later second-round picks when trading him away. Those years of production are real, and the 2023 exit changed the retrospective balance. An even verdict is a qualitative assessment of an imperfect outcome on each side; it should not imply Cleveland received a productive player or that Houston never got meaningful minutes. The acquired asset and the separate exit transaction require separate accounting.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Cleveland B-, Houston B-. The protected 2024 second never conveyed to Cleveland, while Porter delivered multiple productive Houston seasons. The Rockets separately sent two future seconds to Oklahoma City to move Porter in October 2023. Matching grades describe a complicated complete outcome, not comparable incoming playing production.

sections.heading: The Protection Clause Determined Cleveland's Final Pick Return
sections.body: The 2021 Cavaliers-Rockets agreement sent Porter to Houston for a future Warriors second-round right with protection covering selections in the top 55. The value could have been different if the pick had fallen outside that range, but it ultimately did not reach Cleveland. This is not the same as the Cavaliers selecting a 2024 prospect and then losing that player in a later deal. There was no completed draft selection generated for Cleveland by this trade. The January 22 official team release is the starting record; Hoops Rumors' contemporary in-season trade tracker provides the originating pick and protection terms. Once the right expired without conveying, the asset ledger should record the outcome as unexercised. Cleveland's front office still had reasons for deciding to end Porter's tenure, but those reasons are separate from the pick's realized basketball value.

sections.heading: Houston's Scoring and Playmaking Evidence
sections.body: Porter's Houston role went well beyond a short-term audition. The guard averaged 15.6 points and 6.2 assists across 61 games in 2021-22, then improved his scoring average to 19.2 in 59 starts the following season. The official NBA player profile also credits 5.0 assists per game in 2022-23. Those results show why the Rockets continued to give him responsibility after acquiring him for a conditional second that never conveyed. His production occurred on rebuilding rosters rather than in a deep playoff run, which limits the team-achievement argument but not the existence of his statistical contribution. The grades should not inflate the period into a star-led championship push, nor should they suppress actual Houston games to make the ledger's even conclusion seem effortless. Houston acquired a talented, productive young guard at little direct cost.

sections.heading: The Thunder Deal Was Separate From the Cavaliers Exchange
sections.body: October 2023 created a second, materially different asset flow. Houston transferred Porter, a 2027 second-round pick and a 2028 second-round pick to Oklahoma City; the Rockets received Victor Oladipo and Jeremiah Robinson-Earl. NBA.com and Basketball-Reference record the deal, and Oklahoma City announced its plan to waive Porter immediately. The incoming Oladipo and Robinson-Earl were not originally supplied by Cleveland in 2021, nor were the two 2023 outbound draft choices additional compensation promised to the Cavaliers. The second negotiation took place after Porter's Rockets playing years and amid serious off-court issues. Tracking it separately allows the 2021 acquisition to be credited for actual scoring while acknowledging the subsequent financial and roster consequences. It also avoids converting the Thunder's waiver into a fictional Cleveland return.

sections.heading: A Source-Based B-Minus Pairing With Different Risks
sections.body: The Cavaliers' side is judged by a difficult player-retention decision and a conditional pick that never became an actual selection. The Rockets' side is judged by several years of on-court production followed by an exit that required additional future draft capital. These are qualitatively different kinds of results, so matching B-minus grades cannot be explained by saying both teams received comparable playing production. One club obtained no direct player return; the other played Porter extensively. The preserved Even Trade verdict can be retained as an editorial judgment that neither complete organizational outcome proved unambiguously favorable once the costs and circumstances were considered. Any stronger claim that the expired pick gave Cleveland tangible draft production would conflict with the protection terms. Any claim that Houston acquired nothing would contradict Porter's NBA seasons. The historical record needs both realities.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cleveland B-, Houston B- in the preserved Even Trade verdict. Cleveland made an organizational decision but received no exercised 2024 pick. Houston received Porter scoring years, then traded him with two additional future picks in 2023 before Oklahoma City waived him. The asset chains and playing-time returns are materially different.

Neither can responsibly be given a future star value merely because a second-round pick could someday produce one. Hartenstein was the tangible younger player Cleveland acquired. McGee's Denver return was an immediate veteran presence with different competitive purposes. The analytical advantage for Cleveland therefore should come from the identified player and genuine optionality, not a claim that two later picks delivered major returns.

sections.heading: Hartenstein Had a Longer Development Path
sections.body: Hartenstein became a more valuable NBA rotation center as his career progressed, although much of his eventual production occurred after leaving Cleveland. Those later seasons can't all be counted as direct Cavaliers minutes. The narrower historical conclusion is that Cleveland obtained a young player with meaningful market and development value while Denver received a short-term veteran role from McGee. That is enough to support a Cleveland edge without inventing playoff appearances or future draft results. The transaction also demonstrates why a player acquired as part of a deadline deal may provide a different value than a departing older center, even when each fits its own team's immediate objectives.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win. Cleveland receives A- for acquiring Isaiah Hartenstein and the two separately tracked second-round obligations; Denver earns C+ for McGee's veteran backup role. The 2023 pick was forfeited and 2027 remains pending. The grade doesn't presume either selection became a real player or credit all of Hartenstein's later career to Cleveland.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Deep Dive: What Decided Cavaliers Win on 2021-03-25
featuredDeepDive.intro: Cleveland sent veteran JaVale McGee to Denver on March 25, 2021 for Isaiah Hartenstein and 2023 and 2027 second-round rights. Hartenstein appeared in 16 Cavaliers games, averaging 8.3 points and 6.0 rebounds; McGee contributed 13 Nuggets games at 5.5 points and 5.3 rebounds. The 2023 right was subsequently forfeited without a draftee, while the 2027 outcome is unresolved in the 2026 source record. Those club-specific, dated returns define the grade comparison.

sections.heading: March 25 Deadline: Cleveland Collected a Center and Two Seconds
sections.body: Cleveland traded JaVale McGee to Denver on March 25, 2021 for Isaiah Hartenstein and two future second-round selections. The Nuggets' official announcement and NBA transaction tracker identify the same three pieces moving to the Cavaliers, including one protected second. The more detailed Denver and Cleveland transaction ledgers trace the picks to 2023 and 2027. McGee had played 33 Cleveland regular-season games before the deadline, averaging 8.0 points and 5.2 rebounds. Those games are the sending team's prior service, not fresh Denver value. Hartenstein had appeared in 30 Nuggets games before this swap and represented a younger center Cleveland could evaluate, while Denver was reacquiring a veteran with playoff experience. The draft-right tail must be evaluated separately from the players who actually changed teams.

sections.heading: Hartenstein Produced Sixteen Actual Cavaliers Games
sections.body: After joining Cleveland, Hartenstein played 16 Cavaliers regular-season games, starting twice while averaging 8.3 points, 6.0 rebounds and 2.5 assists. His 17.9 minutes per game were substantially more than his earlier 9.1-minute Denver role. Those figures are tangible Cavaliers production and a promising evaluation window, not an established long-term Cleveland starting job. He subsequently joined the Los Angeles Clippers for 2021-22 and later developed into a strong player with New York and Oklahoma City. Those later clubs received the relevant future on-court value, which cannot all be awarded to Cleveland as direct 2021 trade production. The inherited Cavaliers Win grade reflects the modest acquisition price, an informative young-center trial and future draft options; it must not claim that Hartenstein played his successful later seasons for the Cavaliers.

sections.heading: McGee Had Thirteen Denver Games Before a Playoff Appearance
sections.body: Denver used McGee in 13 regular-season games after the trade, starting once with averages of 5.5 points, 5.3 rebounds and 1.1 blocks. That is smaller direct regular-season output than his 33 pre-trade Cleveland games, which count for the sending franchise instead. The Nuggets wanted a veteran backup behind Nikola Jokic, and the club reached the 2021 Western Conference semifinals after winning its first series against Portland. McGee's team-specific minutes should not be confused with that broader team achievement or with his earlier championship runs elsewhere. Denver acquired short-term experienced reserve coverage, not another season of full-time starter performance. Hartenstein's 16 Cleveland appearances and the draft rights supplied a different sort of return to the Cavaliers, combining an immediate development look with unresolved later asset value.

sections.heading: The 2023 Pick Was Forfeited; the 2027 Right Is Not Completed
sections.body: The future seconds are not interchangeable completed selections. Basketball-Reference's dated team transaction ledgers identify the 2023 second as forfeited and never exercised, so neither franchise can legitimately name a 2023 draftee supplied by that right. The other second was Denver's own 2027 selection, a future right rather than a named NBA player as of the current 2026 audit. The archives do not support inventing its ultimate draft position or future traded player production. Cleveland received Hartenstein for 16 regular-season appearances and two draft rights with different later states; Denver received McGee for 13 games. The inherited Cleveland A-minus and Denver C-plus grades and Cavaliers Win verdict are retained, but the analysis clearly distinguishes a real young-center trial and incomplete draft upside from years of performance Hartenstein delivered to subsequent teams.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win — inherited Cleveland A-minus versus Denver C-plus. Hartenstein made 16 Cleveland NBA appearances before continuing his career with other franchises, and Denver got 13 regular-season McGee games. The Cleveland-acquired 2023 second was forfeited without a player, while the 2027 second remained a future right rather than a completed draft result at the 2026 audit. The archived edge rests on young-center optionality and a future selection, not on assigning Hartenstein's later success elsewhere to Cleveland.

sections.heading: Dallas and Denver Exchanged Vandeweghe's Rights for Two Firsts
sections.body: Dallas sent Kiki Vandeweghe's draft rights and its 1986 first-round pick to Denver, receiving the Nuggets' 1981 and 1985 first-rounders. The historical transaction date is disputed: Dallas's and the league's retrospective transaction lists use December 3, 1980, while Denver's official media guide and a separate draft-trade ledger specify December 10. The canonical record presently uses December 3 even though its legacy URL contains December 10. The disagreement doesn't change the four identified assets or justify creating a second transaction.

sections.heading: Rolando Blackman Became the Mavericks' Long-Term Payoff
sections.body: The incoming 1981 first became No. 9 Rolando Blackman, who played 865 Dallas regular-season games and scored 16,643 points over eleven Mavericks seasons. He made four All-Star teams as a Dallas player and helped the club reach the postseason six times. That is the strongest single return from this trade. Dallas also received the future selection eventually made at No. 20 on Sam Vincent in 1985, but traded it to Boston beforehand for another first-round pick and a 1988 second. Vincent's games for Boston are not Dallas production.

sections.heading: Kiki Vandeweghe Delivered Denver Its Own All-Star Forward
sections.body: Denver was far from an empty-handed loser. Vandeweghe played 293 Nuggets regular-season games across four seasons and scored 6,829 points. He made All-Star teams in 1983 and 1984, averaging 26.7 and 29.4 points during those campaigns. In June 1984, Denver traded him to Portland for a multilateral player-and-pick return including Lafayette Lever, Calvin Natt and Wayne Cooper. The club also used Dallas's original 1986 first at No. 16 on Maurice Martin, who appeared in 69 Nuggets games. The later Portland package is evidence of Vandeweghe's retained trade value but was not part of the 1980 transaction.

sections.heading: The Difference Is Blackman's Eleven Years Against Denver's Four
sections.body: Dallas received an eleven-season cornerstone and managed the second future first as an asset before it was exercised. Denver acquired four high-scoring Vandeweghe years, two Nuggets All-Star appearances, a later trade return and a smaller draft contribution from Martin. Both earned A-range grades. Blackman's 865 games and 16,643 Dallas points make the Mavericks' advantage larger in longevity than Denver's direct player return, supporting the canonical Slight Mavericks Edge, Dallas A+ and Denver A. The difference is not a claim that Vandeweghe underperformed.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Mavericks Edge — Dallas A+, Denver A. Blackman supplied 865 Dallas games, 16,643 points and four All-Star selections; Vandeweghe gave Denver 293 games, 6,829 points, two All-Star seasons and later multi-asset trade value. Dallas redirected its 1985 first before Boston picked Sam Vincent, while Denver used the 1986 No. 16 first on Maurice Martin. The December 3/10 date disagreement is documented without duplicating the trade.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Blackman's Dallas Career, Vandeweghe's Denver Peak and a Disputed December Date
featuredDeepDive.intro: Dallas acquired the first-round pick that became Rolando Blackman; Denver secured Kiki Vandeweghe's rights and another future first. Each franchise found an All-Star. Blackman stayed eleven Dallas seasons, while Vandeweghe played four Denver campaigns before producing a further substantial return in a Portland trade. The original record also contains a December 3 versus December 10 date conflict, so the asset history should be clearer than the archival slug.

sections.heading: The Source Dates Differ, but the Transaction Package Agrees
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's 1980–81 Dallas and Denver logs place the transaction on December 3. The Nuggets' official historical media guide instead records December 10, as does Pro Sports Transactions' draft-trade ledger. All list the same major components: Vandeweghe's rights and Dallas's 1986 first going to Denver, with 1981 and 1985 Denver firsts going to Dallas. Rather than inferring which database date is unquestionably correct, the article preserves the canonical December 3 value and the older December 10 slug as a documented source conflict.

sections.heading: Blackman's 1981 Draft Pick Became Dallas's Lasting Foundation
sections.body: Dallas used Denver's 1981 first at No. 9 on Rolando Blackman. He remained with the Mavericks through 1991–92, accumulating 865 regular-season appearances, 16,643 points and four All-Star selections. The team reached six playoffs during those years. No hypothetical scoring or later franchise accomplishment is required to show his importance. The second Denver first eventually became the No. 20 choice in 1985, but Dallas transferred it to Boston before the draft for another 1985 first and a 1988 second. Boston selected Sam Vincent, so he was not a Maverick from this original pick.

sections.heading: Denver Had High-End Production and Another Trade Branch
sections.body: Vandeweghe's Nuggets totals were 293 appearances, 6,829 points and two All-Star selections, with an especially strong final Denver season at 29.4 points per game. His value also survived a second transaction: Denver dealt him to Portland in 1984 for several assets including Lafayette Lever, Calvin Natt and Wayne Cooper. The 1986 Dallas first from the original swap was exercised on Maurice Martin at No. 16; Martin supplied 69 Denver games. These outcomes make Denver's A a genuine high mark, even if it falls slightly short of Dallas's eleven-year Blackman result.

sections.heading: The A+/A Distinction Measures Duration, Not an All-Star Monopoly
sections.body: Each team obtained an All-Star player, so a one-sided A+/D verdict would misread the transaction. Dallas had Blackman's eleven seasons and 16,643 points, plus the subsequent handling of the 1985 first. Denver had Vandeweghe's four effective seasons, later trade value and Martin's smaller roster contribution. The difference is accumulated franchise-specific production and Blackman's longevity. A Slight Mavericks Edge conclusion with Dallas A+ and Denver A matches the canonical assessment and avoids assigning Sam Vincent's Celtics games to the Mavericks.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Mavericks Edge, Dallas A+ and Denver A. Blackman became an 865-game Mavericks cornerstone with four Dallas All-Star appearances, while Vandeweghe's 293 Nuggets games included two All-Star seasons and led to further player-and-pick returns. Dallas traded the 1985 pick to Boston before Sam Vincent was drafted; Denver's No. 16 Maurice Martin selection added 69 games. The December 3 versus December 10 source conflict remains disclosed as a provenance issue.

sections.heading: The Two-for-One Dallas Deal Had No Hidden Pick or Cash
sections.body: On August 20, 1981, the second-year Mavericks sent Bill Robinzine to Utah for Allan Bristow and Wayne Cooper. Dallas, Utah and league transaction histories all identify the same three players, without a draft selection or financial consideration. The basketball comparison therefore begins with what these players actually contributed to their new clubs, not a conjectured rights exchange. Two incoming players weren't automatically worth more than one; the evidence comes from their Dallas roles and Utah's single outgoing return.

sections.heading: Bristow Gave Dallas 119 Games and Immediate Playmaking
sections.body: Bristow played all 82 Dallas games in 1981–82, starting 54, and averaged 10.1 points, 6.0 rebounds and 7.9 assists. A forward distributing nearly eight assists per game gave a young roster an identifiable offensive role. He made 37 more Mavericks appearances in 1982–83, for 119 total games across the two seasons. Those 54 starts and his first-year passing production are more precise measures of his value than generic claims that the Mavericks gained a veteran rotation player.

sections.heading: Cooper Added a Starting Center and a Later Asset
sections.body: Cooper contributed 76 Dallas games and 38 starts in 1981–82, averaging 13.5 points, 10.9 rebounds and 2.1 blocks. He provided the frontcourt production Utah no longer retained, distinct from Bristow's passing. Dallas later included Cooper and a separate 1985 first-rounder in a transaction for Kelvin Ransey. Cooper's original season and additional roster flexibility are relevant, but Ransey's full value cannot be attributed solely to the veteran center when another first also changed hands.

sections.heading: Robinzine's Utah Season Was Shorter and Less Productive
sections.body: Utah's incoming player, Robinzine, appeared in 56 Jazz games in 1981–82, starting nine, and did not play another NBA season. Bristow and Cooper together supplied Dallas with 195 regular-season appearances and 92 starts; Utah received 56 appearances and nine starts. The Mavericks' 1981–82 record was still poor, so those totals do not imply an immediate team turnaround. The direct contrast does support Mavericks Win with Dallas A- and Utah D, rather than the earlier editorial's Dallas B grade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win — Dallas A-, Utah D. Bristow logged 119 Dallas games with 54 starts; Cooper added 76 games with 38 starts, averaging 13.5 points and 10.9 rebounds in his Mavericks season. The Jazz received 56 Robinzine games with nine starts in his final NBA campaign. These verified franchise-specific outcomes support the Dallas advantage without adding nonexistent picks or crediting an entire later multi-asset trade to Cooper.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Bristow's Assists, Cooper's Interior Work and Robinzine's Last Season
featuredDeepDive.intro: Dallas moved one veteran forward to Utah in 1981 and received two players who filled different needs. Allan Bristow became a forward playmaker, while Wayne Cooper started 38 games at center. Bill Robinzine played 56 Jazz games and then left the NBA. The specific playing records justify the Mavericks' higher grade; counting two players against one without examining roles would not.

sections.heading: Both Clubs' Transaction Logs Establish a Straight Player Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Dallas and Utah transaction records and the Jazz's own historical guide agree on the August 20, 1981 deal: Bill Robinzine for Bristow and Cooper. No incoming 1981 pick, retained rights or unreported cash is required to reconstruct the exchange. It was an immediate personnel trade, not a speculative future-draft transaction. That limits the responsible grade analysis to identifiable playing returns, with later transactions traced only when their additional outgoing assets are made clear.

sections.heading: Bristow Was a Forward Who Functioned as a Primary Distributor
sections.body: The usual label of rotation forward obscures Bristow's actual Dallas responsibilities in 1981–82. He played 82 games, made 54 starts, and averaged 7.9 assists alongside 10.1 points and six rebounds. His 82-game first season represented more than a short rental. After 37 further appearances in 1982–83, his Mavericks total reached 119 regular-season games. Those are substantive point-forward contributions, even if the franchise was still developing and did not win many games immediately.

sections.heading: Cooper's Production and Separate Trade Branch Need Attribution
sections.body: Cooper played 76 Dallas games at 13.5 points, 10.9 rebounds and 2.1 blocks per game, starting half his appearances. His size and interior production complemented Bristow's ball distribution. Dallas subsequently traded Cooper alongside a 1985 first-round selection for Kelvin Ransey, creating another asset branch after the original Utah exchange. That move shows Cooper was still tradable, but a fair historical ledger must acknowledge the additional first-rounder; Ransey did not simply arrive as a one-for-one return for Cooper.

sections.heading: Dallas's 195 Appearances Outpaced Utah's 56
sections.body: Robinzine played 56 Jazz games with nine starts in 1981–82, his final NBA season. Dallas's two acquisitions appeared a combined 195 times, starting 92 of those games, with distinct roles: Bristow's passing and Cooper's scoring and rebounding. A larger package does not automatically prove better value, but this one generated more direct playing opportunity and useful production than the lone Jazz return. The canonical Mavericks Win and Dallas A-/Utah D grades follow the actual evidence, not a claim that Dallas became a contender because of one transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win, Dallas A- and Utah D. Bristow supplied 119 regular-season Mavericks appearances and 54 starts, including a 7.9-assist average in 1981–82. Cooper added 76 games, 38 starts and 10.9 rebounds per game. Utah's Robinzine played 56 games with nine starts before his NBA career ended. The later Cooper-for-Ransey branch included a separate first-rounder and isn't credited entirely to this trade.
