sections.heading: Portland Moved the No. 18 Rights and Cash for No. 15
sections.body: On draft night June 25, 1997, Dallas selected center Kelvin Cato with the fifteenth overall pick and sent his draft rights to Portland. In return, the Mavericks received the rights to Australian center Chris Anstey, whom the Trail Blazers had selected eighteenth, plus cash. Both organizations were trading first-round selection rights, not players already under NBA contracts. Dallas' own media guide confirms the exact arrangement and identifies the money as additional compensation. A reliable dollar amount is not given in that record, so an evaluation cannot invent one. The actual difference between the two rights became clearer only after both centers joined their new clubs.

sections.heading: Anstey Played 82 Dallas Games Without a Long-Term Role
sections.body: Anstey reached Dallas after finishing his Australian club obligations and made 41 appearances in the 1997-98 NBA season. He started eight games, scored 240 points and pulled down 157 rebounds. The shortened 1998-99 season brought another 41 games, four starts, 134 points and 97 rebounds. Across two Mavericks seasons that was 82 appearances, 374 points and 254 rebounds. The club got NBA service rather than an entirely unused draft asset, but the playing time and efficiency declined in year two. He was no longer with Dallas when he played 73 games for Chicago in 1999-2000; those later Bulls games do not belong to this trade's direct Mavericks return.

sections.heading: Cato Provided Immediate Portland Defensive Minutes
sections.body: Cato was a real rotation option from his rookie season with Portland. In 1997-98 he appeared in 74 games, played 1,007 minutes and blocked 94 shots, scoring 282 points while collecting 252 rebounds. During the lockout-shortened 1998-99 season he added 43 games, 151 points, 150 rebounds and 56 blocks. The two-year Portland totals reached 117 appearances and 150 blocked shots. Those results reflect a useful defensive reserve, not an automatic star. He played more games in Portland than Anstey did in Dallas, with rim protection standing out as the strongest observable difference. He would later produce a longer NBA career, largely away from Portland.

sections.heading: Cato Also Helped Fund a Much Larger 1999 Trade
sections.body: On October 2, 1999, Portland sent Cato with Stacey Augmon, Ed Gray, Carlos Rogers, Brian Shaw and Walt Williams to Houston for Scottie Pippen. The later trade was materially important for Portland, but the Blazers paid six players, not only Cato. His presence demonstrates continuing transactional value after the original rights exchange, while the multi-player price prevents crediting all of Pippen's future Portland tenure to this draft-night choice. Dallas received Anstey's limited two-season output and unquantified cash. Portland received a defensive center who appeared in 117 games and was subsequently included in a major acquisition. Those direct, documented differences support the canonical Blazers Win, Portland A and Dallas D.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Blazers Win — Portland A, Dallas D. The Trail Blazers exchanged Chris Anstey's No. 18 rights and cash for Kelvin Cato's No. 15 rights in June 1997. Cato appeared in 117 Portland games and blocked 150 shots across two seasons before becoming one of six players moved for Scottie Pippen. Anstey played 82 Dallas games, with declining minutes in his second season. The cash amount is undocumented, and Pippen's whole value cannot be attributed to Cato alone.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Kelvin Cato for Chris Anstey: The Defensive Center and the Six-Player Trade Chain
featuredDeepDive.intro: Dallas and Portland swapped the rights to two centers selected three spots apart in the 1997 NBA draft. The Mavericks had picked Kelvin Cato fifteenth; the Trail Blazers had taken Australian Chris Anstey eighteenth. Portland sent Anstey's rights and cash to Dallas for Cato's rights. The completed value was not equal. Cato gave Portland 117 games of reserve defense and later became part of the larger Scottie Pippen package, while Anstey played 82 Dallas games without establishing a durable role. Both performances deserve to be separated from the later transactions involving those players.

sections.heading: The Transaction Was a Swap of Negotiating Rights
sections.body: Neither Cato nor Anstey was an established NBA veteran at the time. The June 25 draft selections gave Dallas the rights to No. 15 Cato and Portland the rights to No. 18 Anstey. The Blazers then agreed to take Cato, while Dallas accepted Anstey's rights and cash compensation. The Dallas club media guide explicitly records the rights-and-money exchange. Because the cash value is not confirmed, it would be speculative to assign an exact price or claim it offset any later basketball deficiency. The comparison begins with what each team actually acquired and who later contributed minutes in the receiving team's uniform.

sections.heading: A Slow Start for Anstey Still Produced Real Dallas Games
sections.body: Anstey was completing his commitments to the South East Melbourne Magic before joining the Mavericks in 1997. His rookie NBA line was 41 games and 240 points, including eight starts and 157 rebounds. The following season was truncated league-wide by the lockout, but his personal role also contracted. Across another 41 games, he scored 134 points and grabbed 97 rebounds. Two Dallas seasons therefore amounted to 374 points and 254 rebounds over 82 games. This was not zero realized value; it was a brief bench-center opportunity. His subsequent season with Chicago should not inflate Dallas' return.

sections.heading: The Blazers Got Shot Blocking Before Losing Cato's Contract
sections.body: Cato's strongest Portland contribution was protecting the basket. He recorded 94 blocked shots in 1997-98 and 56 more in 1998-99, totaling 150 over 117 regular-season games. His scoring was modest at 433 combined points, but that does not make a center's defensive minutes meaningless. He played 74 games his rookie year and 43 during the league's shorter 1998-99 schedule. Portland then moved him to Houston in October 1999. Any later Cato points or rebounds for the Rockets and other clubs are outside the period of direct Portland playing value, even though his overall NBA career lasted considerably longer than Anstey's.

sections.heading: A Valuable Piece of the Pippen Deal Is Not the Entire Price
sections.body: Portland received Scottie Pippen from Houston in October 1999, sending Cato and five other players in return. The historical significance of the move is clear, and Cato's contract and playing history were part of the Blazers' outgoing consideration. Still, the exchange also included Augmon, Ed Gray, Carlos Rogers, Brian Shaw and Walt Williams. Any assessment that describes Cato alone as the price of Pippen erases five other real assets. The responsible retrospective credits Portland for getting two years of useful defensive minutes and retaining a tradeable center; it credits Anstey's own Dallas games and the cash Dallas received without pretending either party acquired a star outright in the original 1997 transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Blazers Win, Portland A and Dallas D. Draft-rights No. 15 Kelvin Cato delivered 117 Blazers appearances, 150 blocked shots and a place among six players later exchanged for Scottie Pippen. Dallas got No. 18 Chris Anstey's rights and cash, followed by 82 Mavericks games across 1997-98 and 1998-99. The unreported cash figure and other five players in the Pippen package limit exact valuation, but Portland's defensive and transactional return was stronger.

sections.heading: Dallas Used the Sixth Pick to Control the Draft Board
sections.body: Dallas did not simply wait for Dirk Nowitzki to fall to No. 9. The Mavericks selected Robert Traylor at No. 6 because Milwaukee wanted the powerful Michigan center and was willing to send the ninth pick plus Pat Garrity to secure him. That arrangement let Dallas obtain its preferred prospect while extracting another first-round asset. The maneuver required conviction that Nowitzki would remain available and that his unusual combination of size, touch and perimeter skill would translate from Germany. It was a scouting win, but it was also an execution win: Dallas converted knowledge of another team’s preference into additional value without losing the player it wanted.

sections.heading: Nowitzki Rewrote the Competitive History of the Mavericks
sections.body: Nowitzki became the organizing force of the franchise for 21 seasons. He won the 2007 MVP award, carried Dallas to the 2006 Finals, returned with a more complete team to win the 2011 championship and earned Finals MVP during one of the defining postseason runs of the era. His scoring gravity allowed the Mavericks to build many different styles around him, from the Nash-Finley offenses to the defense-and-depth champion. The trade therefore cannot be judged as a favorable prospect swap alone. It produced the player who turned Dallas from a chronically unstable club into a perennial playoff organization with a durable basketball identity.

sections.heading: Pat Garrity Added a Second Branch to the Draft-Night Return
sections.body: Garrity never played a regular-season game for Dallas, but his inclusion was not decorative. The Mavericks used his rights in the separate draft-night transaction that brought Steve Nash back from Phoenix. Nash developed into an All-Star in Dallas and helped create the high-powered teams that established Nowitzki as a contender before returning to the Suns. The later Nash outcome does not belong entirely to the Traylor trade because Dallas also surrendered other pieces, yet Garrity supplied a necessary component. That secondary branch illustrates why the transaction was so damaging for Milwaukee: Dallas received both the generational centerpiece and an asset that helped acquire another foundational guard.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Chose Immediate Physical Certainty Over Rare Upside
sections.body: Traylor was a celebrated college player with strength, rebounding ability and a body that appeared ready for NBA contact. Milwaukee’s preference was understandable within a late-1990s environment that still prized interior bulk and treated international prospects as unusually uncertain. The error was not merely that Traylor failed to become a star. The Bucks paid an extra first-round asset to move toward the safer archetype while passing on a skill package the league was about to value more every year. Traylor became a reserve whose conditioning and mobility limited his ceiling. Milwaukee’s process favored familiarity over the possibility of a player who could change offensive geometry.

sections.heading: The Grade Reflects a Franchise Outcome, Not Hindsight Mockery
sections.body: An F for Milwaukee can sound cruel because draft evaluation is probabilistic and few observers predicted the full scale of Nowitzki’s career. The grade is nevertheless appropriate for realized trade value. Milwaukee surrendered the rights to a future MVP and champion, added Garrity to complete the exchange and received only four seasons of reserve production from Traylor. Dallas deserves an A+ because no plausible additional return was needed: the player acquired became the greatest Maverick, stayed for his entire career and delivered the franchise’s first title. The gap is not based on one statistical peak but on two decades of organizational consequence.

sections.heading: The Transaction Validated International Scouting Before It Became Fashionable
sections.body: Dallas trusted Donnie Nelson’s extensive work on Nowitzki at a time when European prospects were often discussed as projects rather than potential franchise leaders. That trust mattered beyond one selection. The Mavericks built a reputation for identifying talent outside conventional American pipelines and for designing development around individual skill rather than forcing players into older positional templates. Nowitzki’s success helped normalize the idea that a seven-footer could function as a primary perimeter scorer and championship offensive hub. The trade’s historical importance therefore extends beyond Dallas and Milwaukee: it became evidence that global scouting and stylistic imagination could create an advantage over teams anchored to familiar prototypes.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win, with Dallas at A+ and Milwaukee at F. Dallas used Robert Traylor’s draft rights to secure Dirk Nowitzki and Pat Garrity, then turned Garrity into part of the Steve Nash acquisition. Nowitzki became an MVP, a Finals MVP, the centerpiece of the 2011 champion and the defining player in franchise history. Milwaukee’s preference for Traylor was defensible as a draft opinion, but the trade result was catastrophic: the Bucks paid extra to move away from a transformational prospect and received limited reserve value. Few transactions have produced a wider or more durable separation.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The Dirk Trade Was a Scouting Bet That Became an Organizational Blueprint
featuredDeepDive.intro: The 1998 exchange is often reduced to a punch line about Robert Traylor and Dirk Nowitzki, but its deeper significance lies in how Dallas created and then supported the advantage. The Mavericks recognized a rare player, manipulated the draft order to obtain him with an extra asset and remained committed through a difficult rookie season and several painful playoff failures. Milwaukee’s loss came from both evaluation and transaction structure: it preferred the conventional prospect and paid to make that preference actionable. The resulting careers make the verdict obvious, yet the process explains why this was more than luck.

sections.heading: Nelson’s Information Edge Turned a Preference Into Leverage
sections.body: Donnie Nelson had watched Nowitzki closely in Germany and saw a primary scorer where many teams saw a tall developmental gamble. That conviction allowed Dallas to negotiate from a position of informational strength. The Mavericks knew Milwaukee wanted Traylor and believed Nowitzki would survive until the ninth pick, so they selected the Bucks’ target first. The extra Garrity rights were the price for access. Every draft contains uncertainty, but teams can still create leverage through preparation. Dallas did not know Nowitzki would become a champion; it knew more clearly than its counterpart what kind of player it was pursuing and used that clarity to improve the package.

sections.heading: A Difficult Rookie Year Could Have Broken the Plan
sections.body: Nowitzki arrived during the lockout-shortened 1998-99 season, struggled with physicality and publicly wondered whether he belonged in the league. Dallas could have treated those early difficulties as confirmation of the skepticism surrounding international players. Instead, the organization allowed his strength, confidence and positional freedom to develop. That patience is inseparable from the trade’s success. Acquiring an unusual prospect is only the first step; the team must resist evaluating him exclusively through the habits of the old system. Nowitzki’s later rise rewarded Dallas for maintaining belief when the immediate evidence was mixed and the franchise still lacked stability.

sections.heading: The Nash Connection Magnified an Already Historic Return
sections.body: Garrity’s movement to Phoenix helped Dallas reacquire Nash, who had been blocked behind established guards with the Suns. Nash and Nowitzki became elite offensive partners, and Michael Finley gave the Mavericks a third high-level creator. Dallas did not win a title with that exact trio, but the group ended a decade of irrelevance and established the habits of contention. Garrity should not be credited for Nash’s entire career or for the later 2011 championship. His role is narrower and still meaningful: the extra asset obtained in the Traylor exchange helped Dallas add another future MVP-caliber talent at the beginning of its transformation.

sections.heading: Milwaukee’s Return Never Produced a Comparable Second Chance
sections.body: Traylor played useful minutes as a reserve and later moved through Cleveland, Charlotte and New Orleans, but Milwaukee never recovered a major asset branch from the deal. There was no later trade that converted his contract or rights into a compensating star, and no extended period in which his play altered the Bucks’ ceiling. That absence matters because some apparent draft-night losses soften when the acquired player becomes part of another valuable transaction. Here the value chain remained one-sided. Dallas received a franchise icon and a useful trade chip; Milwaukee received a player whose most important historical role was being the mechanism through which Nowitzki left.

sections.heading: The 2011 Championship Completed the Argument
sections.body: Nowitzki’s regular-season résumé already made the trade lopsided, but the 2011 title transformed it into a complete franchise victory. Dallas defeated Portland, the defending champion Lakers, Oklahoma City and Miami without another current All-Star. Nowitzki’s scoring and late-game control were the constant across that run, while the roster around him reflected years of adaptation. The championship answered the lingering criticism created by the 2006 Finals loss and the 2007 first-round upset. It also gave the trade the highest possible realized outcome: the acquired player did not merely produce awards and revenue; he led the organization to the championship it had never won.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The full available evidence supports the strongest possible Dallas verdict. The Mavericks identified Nowitzki before the league understood his archetype, controlled the draft-night sequence, gained Garrity as additional value and then developed their new centerpiece with unusual patience. Milwaukee received the player it preferred, but Traylor never approached star impact and did not create a later value created by those assets that narrowed the gap. Nowitzki’s 21 seasons, MVP, Finals MVP and 2011 championship would alone justify A+. The Nash-related value of Garrity makes the return even richer. Milwaukee’s F reflects the complete absence of a comparable benefit after paying to move away from a generational player.

sections.heading: Dallas Bought a Point Guard Before His Prime
sections.body: Steve Nash was coming off two quiet seasons in Phoenix when Dallas traded for him on draft night in 1998. The Mavericks were betting on skill development and fit rather than established stardom. Nash joined fellow young cornerstone Dirk Nowitzki and scorer Michael Finley, giving Dallas a three-player offensive foundation that would pull the franchise out of a decade of losing.

sections.heading: Phoenix's First-Round Pick Became Shawn Marion
sections.body: The deal was not Nash for spare parts. The future first-round pick landed at No. 9 in 1999 and became Shawn Marion, a four-time All-Star and elite two-way forward for the Suns. Marion's rebounding, defense, transition scoring, and positional versatility made him a central part of Phoenix's next contender. That outcome is the reason Phoenix earns a solid grade despite trading a future Hall of Fame point guard.

sections.heading: Nash Helped Transform Dallas Before His MVP Years
sections.body: Nash did not win his MVP awards until he returned to Phoenix as a free agent in 2004, but his Dallas tenure was still highly valuable. He became an All-Star, helped the Mavericks establish one of the league's best offenses, and reached the 2003 Western Conference finals. The trade should be judged by those six Dallas seasons, not dismissed because his absolute peak came later.

sections.heading: The Secondary Players Did Not Decide the Deal
sections.body: Phoenix also received Bubba Wells, Martin Müürsepp, and the draft rights to Pat Garrity. None became a lasting Suns cornerstone. Garrity was quickly used in the separate trade that brought Orlando's draft rights to Phoenix, while Wells and Müürsepp had limited NBA impact. The lasting comparison is Nash's Dallas run against the Marion pick.

sections.heading: Nash's 2004 Return Is a Separate Front-Office Decision
sections.body: Phoenix deserves credit for signing Nash in free agency and building a revolutionary offense around him, but that later decision does not retroactively turn the 1998 trade into a Suns win. Dallas acquired and developed Nash, received six productive seasons, then chose not to match Phoenix's contract. The free-agent loss is a Mavericks mistake separate from the value of the original acquisition.

sections.heading: Why Dallas Wins a Strong Two-Sided Trade
sections.body: The grades—Dallas A-minus and Phoenix B-minus—recognize that both teams found a star. Dallas receives the higher mark because it acquired the deal's best player and used him to transform the franchise from lottery regular to contender. Phoenix's pick became an excellent cornerstone, but the secondary package did not close the gap completely. The correct verdict is Mavericks Win, narrowly.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Dallas won the 1998 trade by acquiring a future Hall of Fame point guard before his prime and turning him into an All-Star centerpiece of a conference-finals team. Phoenix received outstanding value when the first-round pick became Shawn Marion, making this a strong trade for both franchises rather than a robbery. Dallas remains A-minus, Phoenix remains B-minus, and the verdict changes to Mavericks Win.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The Trade That Gave Both Teams a Future Star
featuredDeepDive.intro: Few transactions produce a player as important as Nash for one side and a player as important as Marion for the other. That balance makes the deal historically unusual, but balanced value does not require an Even verdict when one team still acquired the better and more franchise-changing player.

sections.heading: Dallas Was Building a Core in One Draft Week
sections.body: The Nash acquisition came as Dallas was also securing Nowitzki's draft rights. Neither player was yet a finished star. Together with Finley, they gave the Mavericks shooting, passing, and offensive intelligence that changed the franchise's identity. The trade's value is inseparable from that developmental environment: Dallas acquired a player whose skills amplified the young core around him.

sections.heading: Nash's Dallas Peak Was Already All-Star Caliber
sections.body: By the early 2000s, Nash had become one of the league's most efficient and creative point guards. Dallas won 53, 57, and 60 games in his final three seasons, including the 2003 conference-finals run. His later MVP seasons in Phoenix were greater, but the Mavericks had already received elite regular-season production and meaningful playoff success from the trade.

sections.heading: Marion Made Phoenix's Return Substantial
sections.body: Marion was not merely a good pick attached to a bad package. He became a rare defender who could guard across positions, rebound like a power forward, run the floor, and score without dominating the ball. He was central to the Suns teams that later paired him with Nash. Phoenix's B-minus reflects a genuine franchise cornerstone, not consolation value.

sections.heading: The Irony of Nash and Marion Reuniting Elsewhere
sections.body: Nash later returned to Phoenix, while Marion eventually joined Dallas and helped the Mavericks win the 2011 championship. Those later crossings make the trade feel circular, but they should not blur the original accounting. In 1998, Dallas received Nash's six-year rise; Phoenix received the pick that became Marion. Later free-agent and trade decisions belong to later evaluations.

sections.heading: A Near Win-Win Still Has a Direction
sections.body: Both franchises improved their futures, which is why neither deserves a poor grade. The directional edge comes from scarcity. A lead creator who organizes elite offense is harder to acquire than even an outstanding two-way forward. Dallas obtained that creator for six seasons and reached the conference finals with him, giving the Mavericks the narrow win.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: This was one of the better two-sided trades in league history, but Dallas still finished ahead. Nash became the lead guard of the franchise's revival, while Marion made Phoenix's return highly credible. Mavericks Win by a modest margin: Dallas A-minus, Phoenix B-minus.

sections.heading: Draft Night: Dallas Paid a Second and Giriček Rights for No. 29
sections.body: The June 30, 1999 agreement delivered San Antonio’s first-round No. 29 pick Leon Smith to the Mavericks. In return, Dallas sent the draft rights to Croatian guard Gordan Giriček, selected at No. 40, along with a second-round selection in the 2000 draft. The Dallas Mavericks media guide and the NBA transaction ledger list the same three assets and directions. The Spurs subsequently used that future selection at No. 41 on Duke forward Chris Carrawell. This was an exchange of rights and an unsigned future selection, not an immediate swap of established NBA starters.

sections.heading: Smith Never Appeared in a Mavericks NBA Game
sections.body: Smith was a first-round prospect whose Mavericks rights did not become regular-season production. He never played an NBA game for Dallas. The eventual league debut came for Atlanta in January 2002, when he logged 14 Hawks games; he later appeared once for Seattle. His full 15-game NBA career therefore occurred with two different teams, not with the Mavericks. That fact provides a concrete rationale for the inherited Dallas D grade. It would be misleading to credit Dallas with either his later CBA development or his NBA games after the franchise moved on.

sections.heading: The Second-Round Selection Became Chris Carrawell
sections.body: San Antonio used the 2000 second-round selection received from Dallas on Chris Carrawell, No. 41 overall. Duke’s June 2000 draft coverage explicitly identifies the pick as coming from the Mavericks. Carrawell had been ACC Player of the Year, but Duke’s later career profile confirms that he was cut before his rookie NBA season and never appeared in an NBA game. The Spurs did obtain a usable draft selection and exercised it; they did not receive on-court NBA minutes from the selected player. That difference between holding a pick and realizing its playing value must be clear in the trade ledger.

sections.heading: Giriček Became a Future Second Instead of a Spurs Rotation Guard
sections.body: Giriček continued playing in Europe after the rights were transferred, and San Antonio never used him in a regular-season NBA game. In June 2002, the Spurs traded his rights to Memphis for a 2004 second-round selection later used on Romain Sato. Giriček reached the league with Memphis in 2002-03, playing 49 games before a separate move to Orlando. Those minutes belong to other franchises. The archive records Spurs Win with San Antonio A and Dallas D, which is best understood as superior rights management despite zero direct Spurs playing games from Giriček or Carrawell.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The saved Spurs Win, San Antonio A and Dallas D verdict stays unchanged. Smith’s rights resulted in zero Mavericks regular-season games. San Antonio received Giriček’s rights and a 2000 second used on Carrawell; neither played for the Spurs. The rights to Giriček were exchanged again in 2002 for the later Romain Sato selection. This was an advantage in retaining transferable draft assets, not a source of immediate Spurs player minutes.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The 1999 Leon Smith Draft Trade: No Mavericks Games and Two Spurs Assets
featuredDeepDive.intro: Dallas acquired Leon Smith’s No. 29 draft rights from San Antonio for Gordan Giriček’s rights and a 2000 second-round pick on June 30, 1999. Smith never played a Mavericks regular-season game. San Antonio used the pick at No. 41 on Chris Carrawell and later exchanged Giriček’s rights for another future second, though neither incoming player ever appeared for the Spurs. The stored Spurs Win and A-to-D grade gap concerns rights and future options, not direct NBA court output.

sections.heading: The Full Draft-Night Package Was Three Assets
sections.body: The official Dallas media guide identifies Giriček’s draft rights, selected No. 40 by the Mavericks, and a second-round selection the following summer as the price for Smith, whom San Antonio had chosen No. 29. The Spurs’ transactions confirm those directions. Manu Ginóbili was also drafted by San Antonio in 1999, but at No. 57 as an entirely separate Spurs selection. Neither he nor any of his later championships was acquired from Dallas in the Smith agreement. Separating contemporaneous selections prevents a memorable San Antonio draft class from inflating this trade.

sections.heading: Dallas Acquired Rights but Never Got Smith onto the Court
sections.body: Smith never played a Mavericks NBA regular-season game. He later appeared 14 times for Atlanta in 2001-02 and once for Seattle in 2003-04, fifteen career NBA appearances spread across other clubs. That delayed and limited debut cannot be counted as Dallas receiving-player production. In particular, Smith’s 1999 draft slot does not convert automatically into guaranteed minutes, starts or points for the Mavericks. The inherited D assessment is most directly supported by that absence of player contributions, whatever promise the front office had seen in acquiring the first-round rights.

sections.heading: Carrawell Was Drafted with the Dallas Selection, Then Cut
sections.body: The Duke University draft report from June 28, 2000 explicitly says San Antonio chose Carrawell No. 41 with a selection acquired from Dallas. He had won ACC Player of the Year, creating reasonable hopes of a rotation opportunity. Duke’s later profile, however, says he never played an NBA game and was released before the season. This makes the Carrawell piece an exercised draft option with no realized NBA playing return. Its presence nonetheless distinguishes this three-asset exchange from a straightforward one-for-one player swap.

sections.heading: The Giriček Rights Produced a Separate 2004 Pick
sections.body: After keeping Giriček’s rights while he played abroad, San Antonio sent them to Memphis in June 2002 for a different second-round selection. That choice was later used on Romain Sato in 2004. Giriček logged 49 NBA games with Memphis in 2002-03 and another 27 with Orlando following a separate trade; neither team’s court results belong to the Spurs. The later draft choice was acquired through a new negotiation, not supplied directly by Dallas in 1999. The original advantage is therefore an asset-conversion argument, not a claim of Spurs minutes from Giriček.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Spurs Win with an A for San Antonio and D for Dallas stays protected. Smith made zero Mavericks NBA appearances, and neither Giriček nor Carrawell logged a Spurs NBA game. Carrawell was the eventual No. 41 choice from the Dallas second-rounder; the Giriček rights were later converted into a different future second. That chronology supports the Spurs retaining multiple opportunities while avoiding fabricated on-court credit.

sections.heading: From Trade Line to Completed Outcome
sections.body: On September 1, 1999, Dallas sent veteran A.C. Green to the Lakers for center Sean Rooks and a 2000 second-round pick. Los Angeles wanted experienced frontcourt support after bringing Phil Jackson in to coach Shaquille O'Neal and Kobe Bryant, while Dallas added a younger reserve center and another chance to draft. The Lakers' selection eventually became the No. 58 pick, Pete Mickeal, on June 28, 2000. This was a two-for-one package of identifiable assets, not a swap for cash or an undefined future option. The year that followed provides the actual test: Green started all 82 games for the champions, while Dallas used Rooks for 71 games and converted its new draft pick on draft night.

sections.heading: Why One Side Finished Ahead
sections.body: Green's return to Los Angeles was not a headline star acquisition, but it gave the 1999-00 title team a dependable power forward. At age 36, he played and started all 82 games, averaging 5.0 points, 5.9 rebounds and 23.5 minutes. He also appeared in all 23 postseason games as the Lakers defeated Indiana for their first championship since 1988. Dallas got real use from Rooks, who appeared in 71 regular-season games with 13 starts, plus the No. 58 selection. But neither became a comparable title-season starter for Dallas. Lakers Win with B+ versus C+ acknowledges that both clubs got playable value while Los Angeles converted its veteran acquisition into an immediate championship role.

sections.heading: How the Better Package Paid Off: Los Angeles Lakers
sections.body: A.C. Green had played for the Lakers from 1985 to 1993, so the September 1999 transaction brought back a familiar part of the organization's previous championship period. His second Los Angeles stint was compact but productive. Green started 82 of 82 games during the 67-15 regular season, contributing 5.0 points and 5.9 rebounds in 23.5 minutes. In the playoffs he played 23 games, with his role dropping to 18.7 minutes per night as Jackson adjusted the postseason rotation. The Lakers won their fourth title of Green's NBA career and the franchise's first of the O'Neal-Bryant era. That actual, defined one-season use is the foundation of the Lakers' B+ rather than a claim that Green alone created the championship.

sections.heading: Where the Other Package Fell Short: Dallas Mavericks
sections.body: Dallas received Sean Rooks, who played 71 games and started 13 for the 1999-00 Mavericks, alongside the future second-rounder that became No. 58 Pete Mickeal. Neither piece was a dead asset. On June 28, 2000, Dallas traded Rooks to the Clippers for Eric Murdock, while the club moved Mickeal and Erick Strickland to New York for Donnell Harvey and John Wallace. Those separate transactions are important: the two original Lakers assets provided the Mavericks with further opportunities after their first season. Yet their value was spread across a reserve-center stint and later role-player exchanges, not a championship starting job like Green's in Los Angeles. Dallas's C+ reflects the real but narrower return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win. Dallas Mavericks receive C+, while Los Angeles Lakers receive B+. The verdict follows the realized value of the trade: Los Angeles Lakers' side, led by A.C. Green, finished ahead of Dallas Mavericks' side, led by Sean Rooks and 2000 second-round pick (#58-Pete Mickeal). The result is not based on package length or hindsight name recognition alone. It is based on the production, draft conversion, role, timing, and asset consequences described in the underlying trade details. That evidence supports the explicit grade split and leaves enough completed-value separation to preserve Lakers Win.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: A.C. Green's 82 Championship Starts Against Dallas's Rooks-and-Pick Return
featuredDeepDive.intro: The Lakers brought A.C. Green back in September 1999, then started him in all 82 regular-season games and used him throughout their 23-game 2000 championship playoff run. Dallas received 71 Sean Rooks appearances and the 2000 second-round choice later used on Pete Mickeal at No. 58. Both were real assets, and the Mavericks redeployed them in separate transactions, but Green provided immediate starting minutes beside Shaquille O'Neal rather than speculative draft value. That direct champion-season service explains the Lakers' B-plus over Dallas's C-plus without crediting the whole title to one veteran.

sections.heading: The Trade Details Before the Narrative
sections.body: September 1, 1999 produced a straightforward but revealing swap: Los Angeles sent Sean Rooks and its 2000 second-round pick to Dallas; Dallas sent A.C. Green back to his original NBA club. The teams were in different places. The Lakers had hired Phil Jackson and needed veterans who could support Shaquille O'Neal and Kobe Bryant immediately. Dallas was assembling the roster that would soon grow around Dirk Nowitzki, and Rooks offered center depth while the pick offered a separate draft opportunity. One asset became Green's full-season starting role on the 2000 champions; the other two became 71 Dallas games from Rooks and the No. 58 selection of Pete Mickeal. Tracking both sides by their actual roster use, rather than their pick count, explains the B+/C+ grade gap.

sections.heading: The Deal's Most Important Outcome: Los Angeles Lakers
sections.body: A.C. Green started all 82 games for the 1999-00 Lakers at age 36, a strikingly durable return for the center and late second the team surrendered. His nightly work was specific: 23.5 minutes, 5.0 points and 5.9 rebounds beside Shaquille O'Neal in a 67-win regular season. Los Angeles used him for all 23 playoff games as it beat Sacramento, Phoenix, Portland and Indiana to win the title. Green was not the offensive centerpiece and his postseason minutes dropped to 18.7, so credit for a championship cannot be assigned to him alone. Still, he answered a real lineup need that season and rejoined a franchise where he'd previously won titles in the 1980s. Los Angeles received a useful, trusted starter without paying a future first or moving a core player. That is the concrete foundation for the inherited B+.

sections.heading: Comparing Realized Value, Not Reputation: Dallas Mavericks
sections.body: The Mavericks did more with the two incoming components than simply let them expire. Sean Rooks gave Dallas 71 regular-season appearances in 1999-00, including 13 starts. The Lakers' second-round selection became Pete Mickeal at No. 58 in June 2000. Dallas then turned Rooks into Eric Murdock through a Clippers trade, and paired Mickeal's rights with Erick Strickland in a Knicks exchange for Donnell Harvey and John Wallace. Neither later move should be represented as part of the September 1999 Lakers trade: each required its own compensation and decision. Those conversions show that Dallas received assets with genuine trade value. But the first-year outcome still favors Los Angeles, where Green started every game for a champion. Dallas's C+ recognizes the reserve minutes and asset flexibility without equating them to that immediate role.

sections.heading: How Far the Evidence Really Goes
sections.body: A.C. Green's 2000 championship role is attributable to the September 1999 acquisition, but it is not the only explanation for a 67-win Lakers team. The franchise also had O'Neal, Bryant and a new coaching staff led by Phil Jackson. Dallas's No. 58 selection is similarly attributable to the Lakers trade, but the players eventually obtained for Pete Mickeal and Erick Strickland cannot be credited as if Mickeal alone bought them. Sean Rooks' 71 Dallas games are direct; his June 2000 move to the Clippers for Eric Murdock is a later, separate use of his value. Keeping those stages distinct leaves a modest but identifiable Los Angeles advantage: an every-game starter for a championship roster versus a useful center, a late pick and further transactions requiring new decisions.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win remains the deep-dive conclusion. Dallas Mavericks are graded C+; Los Angeles Lakers are graded B+. The stronger completed return was A.C. Green, while the other side's case rests on Sean Rooks and 2000 second-round pick (#58-Pete Mickeal). Both sides receive credit for value that actually materialized, but the evidence-based comparison leaves Los Angeles Lakers with the better historical outcome. The practical gap is Green's every-game starting role on the 2000 champions versus Rooks's 71 Dallas games and a late pick moved in a later trade, with neither asset treated as worthless.

sections.heading: Orlando Sold No. 13 Rights for Future Draft Consideration
sections.body: On June 28, 2000, the Orlando Magic sent Dallas the draft rights to Courtney Alexander, the thirteenth overall selection. The Mavericks supplied a 2000 second-round pick, a lottery-protected 2001 first-round pick and $3 million in cash. Orlando was not exchanging a current rotation player; it was monetizing a fresh selection for cash and two future or lower draft assets. The No. 31 second-round selection is associated with Dan Langhi, while the future Dallas first eventually conveyed at No. 23 in 2001 and is associated with Brandon Armstrong. These labels track the destination of individual draft picks, not proof that both named players became Orlando contributors.

sections.heading: Alexander Played Only 38 Dallas Games Before a Package Trade
sections.body: Alexander reached the Mavericks as a rookie but did not secure a durable backcourt role. He played 38 regular-season games for Dallas in 2000-01, making six starts and scoring 160 points in 472 minutes. On February 22, 2001, the Mavericks sent him with Hubert Davis, Christian Laettner, Etan Thomas, Loy Vaught and cash to Washington for Juwan Howard, Calvin Booth and Obinna Ekezie. Alexander found a larger offensive role after arriving with the Wizards, but those later Washington points were not scored for Dallas. The Mavericks did use his contract in a consequential multi-asset trade; the other outgoing players and cash still have to be counted before giving Alexander credit for the entire Howard package.

sections.heading: The Magic Had Two Separately Tradable Draft Assets
sections.body: The No. 31 selection in 2000 passed through several deals during draft night, eventually resulting in Langhi's NBA rights being traded onward. The protected 2001 first-rounder was a different sort of asset: it conveyed at No. 23, the selection ultimately associated with Brandon Armstrong. Orlando later moved that first-round position into a separate transaction with Houston during the 2001 draft period. A complete evaluation follows the pick chain rather than implying the Magic rostered Langhi and Armstrong for the full term of either player's career. The actual bargain granted Orlando $3 million plus the ability to redeploy two draft choices while Dallas used Alexander in a limited rookie role.

sections.heading: The Cash and Pick Flexibility Carry the Magic's Advantage
sections.body: Neither side can be graded solely by a player's later points with an unrelated franchise. Alexander gave Dallas 38 games and short-term trade-package utility; Orlando obtained a reported $3 million payment plus two picks that changed hands in subsequent movements. The Magic's final return did not become a star directly traceable to this one agreement, yet it included additional draft flexibility and a stated cash amount that the Mavericks surrendered. The canonical Magic Win, Orlando B and Dallas C+, records that broader asset advantage without treating the Wizards' later use of Alexander as Dallas production or the Magic's numbered picks as if they were automatically NBA rotation players.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Magic Win — Orlando B, Dallas C+. Dallas obtained Courtney Alexander's draft rights, got 38 NBA games and 160 points from him, then included him with five other assets in a later Washington deal. Orlando received the No. 31 pick in 2000, a lottery-protected first that conveyed at No. 23 in 2001 and $3 million cash. Each draft slot later moved through separate transactions. The cash and two tradable picks support Orlando's edge without crediting it for other clubs' eventual player careers.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Courtney Alexander's Draft-Night Price: Two Picks and $3 Million
featuredDeepDive.intro: The June 2000 Dallas–Orlando deal concerned one first-round rookie's draft rights, but the price was not merely a future selection. The Mavericks acquired Courtney Alexander at No. 13 and transferred a 2000 second-round pick, a lottery-protected first in 2001, and $3 million to Orlando. Alexander never became a lasting Dallas player, though he subsequently entered a large trade for Juwan Howard. Orlando could use or exchange both picks, and its future first converted into the No. 23 choice. The distinction between the first transaction and what happened in later packages is what makes this a legitimate source-specific retrospective rather than a list of draft names.

sections.heading: Dallas Bought the Rookie It Wanted With Three Assets
sections.body: Alexander was a first-round guard prospect when Orlando selected him thirteenth on draft night. Dallas wanted his rights and paid with No. 31 in 2000, its lottery-protected 2001 first-round selection and an expressly recorded $3 million cash payment. Each piece had a different opportunity cost. Cash was immediate spending, the second-round pick represented a prospect or later tradable right, and the next year's first could still yield a valuable position depending on Dallas' finish. Orlando's incoming assets should not be reduced to one future player name. Dallas bought a specific rookie's development opportunity and gave the Magic substantial optionality in return.

sections.heading: Thirty-Eight Games Were the Direct Dallas Player Return
sections.body: Alexander's initial NBA season in Dallas lasted 38 games, with six starts, 160 points and 472 minutes. The limited playing sample cannot be expanded by adding the 27 Wizards games he played after leaving Dallas in February. He did move to Washington in a package that helped Dallas acquire Juwan Howard and other players, which makes his tradeability relevant. But the Dallas outgoing package included Christian Laettner, Hubert Davis, Etan Thomas and Loy Vaught, as well as cash. It would be unsound to describe the resulting return as something Alexander alone delivered. His direct playing production and his role as one component of that group are separable.

sections.heading: The Two Orlando Picks Followed Different Paths
sections.body: The No. 31 second-round choice in 2000 eventually was used on Dan Langhi, after a chain of transactions involving other clubs. Orlando did not simply retain a long-term Langhi season because it temporarily obtained that selection from Dallas. The second pick was lottery protected and conveyed in 2001 at No. 23, identified with Brandon Armstrong's selection. That position also became part of a Houston transaction, rather than remaining a permanent Orlando draft-rights holding. These movements illustrate why draft picks are often valuable as trade currency before any associated player contributes to the NBA team that first received them.

sections.heading: A Stronger Return Without Inventing a Star
sections.body: Orlando had a defined $3 million cash component and control of two draft positions. Dallas received Alexander and later used his contract inside a six-piece outgoing Washington package, but its direct Alexander minutes remained limited. The Magic did not land an All-Star merely by holding pick No. 23, and Dallas did not acquire Howard simply by giving up one rookie. The canonical B for Orlando and C+ for Dallas puts a modest advantage on the broader draft-and-cash return while recognizing the real, if short, Dallas usage. This is a case in which a three-asset draft-night payment mattered more than the raw box-score total of the named newcomer.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Magic Win, Orlando B and Dallas C+. Courtney Alexander played 38 Dallas games before going to Washington as one of multiple players and cash moved for Juwan Howard's trade package. Orlando took a 2000 No. 31 selection, a lottery-protected 2001 first that became No. 23, and $3 million. The pick rights subsequently changed hands again, so their full later careers cannot be attributed to Orlando. Two tradable draft assets plus cash support the Magic advantage over a short Mavericks rookie stint.

sections.heading: The June 2000 Draft Exchange
sections.body: Dallas selected Dan Langhi at No. 31 in the 2000 NBA draft, then sent his rights to Houston on draft night. In exchange the Mavericks acquired Eduardo Najera, whom Houston had selected at No. 38, plus the Rockets' future second-round selection. Contemporary UPI reporting and Dallas' own media guide both describe the same two-for-one transfer of rights. When that additional pick came due in 2001, Dallas used it on Kyle Hill at No. 44. This is a draft-night rights transaction rather than a deal for two established NBA players. Its eventual imbalance came from what the rookies contributed after the selections were exchanged, not from a difference in their draft slots. The future pick was a real contractual asset, but its value must also be tested against Hill's subsequent playing record.

sections.heading: Najera Became the Return That Houston Did Not
sections.body: Dallas receives the B+ grade because Najera turned a second-round gamble into several seasons of regular NBA work. Basketball-Reference records 40 Dallas appearances in 2000-01, followed by 62 in 2001-02, 48 in 2002-03 and 58 in 2003-04. The 2001-02 season alone brought 1,357 regular-season minutes, a useful indicator of how the Mavericks deployed him beyond the ceremonial presence of a draft choice. Houston's Langhi appeared in 33 games as a rookie and 34 in 2001-02, totaling 675 minutes over those two years. Dallas also received the 2001 pick that became Kyle Hill, but that selection did not produce a comparable NBA stint. The B+/C split therefore rests principally on Najera's actual roster contribution against Langhi's limited Houston opportunity rather than on the number of assets written on the transaction sheet.

sections.heading: Dallas Built Depth From a Lower Draft Slot
sections.body: Najera came to Dallas through the rights to the 38th selection, seven slots after the Mavericks had initially picked Langhi. He was not a top-of-the-lottery star, but four Dallas regular seasons supplied a useful combination of rebounding, physical play and lineup coverage. In 2001-02 he appeared in 62 games, starting 11, and collected 342 rebounds. The following season brought 48 appearances and another 223 boards. Those are modest figures beside Dallas' leading scorers, yet they are tangible production obtained without surrendering an existing rotation player. The additional 2001 second-rounder was used on Kyle Hill at No. 44; the draft record lists the selection but not an NBA playing contribution by Hill. Crediting Dallas for Najera's minutes while declining to inflate the pick's on-court return is the distinction behind its B+ grade.

sections.heading: Houston Received a Prospect, Not Comparable Minutes
sections.body: Houston used the rights to Dan Langhi, the No. 31 selection, instead of retaining the rights to Eduardo Najera and the future second-round pick. Langhi received two seasons with the Rockets: 33 games and 241 minutes in 2000-01, then 34 games and 434 minutes in 2001-02. His later NBA appearances elsewhere do not turn into Houston roster value after he left the franchise. That does not mean the draft-night idea lacked logic: Langhi was a different positional prospect and no second-round pick carried a guarantee of useful minutes. The retrospective C grade, however, reflects what Houston actually obtained from this particular rights exchange. Najera supplied Dallas with a longer-lived contributor, and the extra draft choice gave Dallas another selection, even if Kyle Hill did not become a rotation player.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win. Dallas Mavericks receive B+, while Houston Rockets receive C. The verdict follows the realized value of the trade: Dallas Mavericks' side, led by draft rights to Eduardo Najera and 2001 second-round pick (#44-Kyle Hill), finished ahead of Houston Rockets' side, led by draft rights to Dan Langhi. Najera supplied 208 Dallas regular-season appearances from 2000-01 through 2003-04 after the rights exchange. Houston instead obtained 67 Langhi regular-season games over two seasons; the No. 44 Kyle Hill selection never produced a Mavericks NBA rotation player. That evidence supports the explicit grade split and leaves enough completed-value separation to preserve Mavericks Win.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Eduardo Najera's 208 Mavericks Games and the 2001 No. 44 Pick
featuredDeepDive.intro: Dallas traded the No. 31 rights to Dan Langhi in June 2000 for No. 38 Eduardo Najera and a future second-rounder. Najera logged 208 Mavericks games across four seasons, while Langhi's first two Houston campaigns totaled 67 appearances. The extra pick became No. 44 Kyle Hill in 2001, but Hill never appeared in an NBA game. Dallas's B-plus grade is anchored to Najera's real rotation service, not an imagined second productive draftee; Houston's C recognizes the actual Langhi opportunity without overstating his stay.

sections.heading: The Original Rights and the Deferred Selection
sections.body: The June 28, 2000 transaction can be read without guessing at cash or unrecorded compensation. Dallas' drafted Langhi at No. 31 moved to Houston; Houston's No. 38 choice Najera moved to Dallas together with one future second-rounder. UPI listed the exchange immediately after the draft, while ESPN's 2000 draft record and a later Dallas Mavericks media guide independently match the components. The latter also shows that the deferred selection became Kyle Hill in the 2001 draft, No. 44 overall. A key distinction is timing: Hill was not already an NBA player transferred in June 2000. Dallas first received a right to a later selection, and the player identity was determined the following year. Treating Hill's draft slot as known on trade day would be hindsight disguised as a transaction fact.

sections.heading: Four Dallas Seasons Give the Grade Its Evidence
sections.body: Najera's regular-season Dallas line is useful because it identifies how much actual playing opportunity the traded rights yielded. Across 2000-01 through 2003-04 he appeared in 208 games for the Mavericks. His 62 games and 1,357 minutes in 2001-02 were followed by 48 games and 1,103 minutes in 2002-03. Dallas had turned the 38th pick into a genuine working member of the rotation, not merely a name attached to a pick. That contribution is different from crediting the organization with all team wins during those seasons, which cannot be attributed to this exchange. The record supports a narrower conclusion: Najera had a sustained role for Dallas that substantially exceeded the return Houston drew from Langhi. Kyle Hill's later draft selection adds proper transactional context, but not fabricated NBA output.

sections.heading: Why the Houston Side Stopped Short
sections.body: Langhi's draft profile was not interchangeable with Najera's, so a fair review has to distinguish the decision made in 2000 from the career evidence that followed. Houston acquired the No. 31 draft rights and offered Langhi 33 regular-season games in his rookie year. His field-goal percentage that season was .374, according to Basketball-Reference, and he played only 241 minutes. He saw 34 more Houston appearances in 2001-02 before continuing his brief NBA career elsewhere. Those actual opportunities justify a restrained C rather than pretending Houston received no NBA player at all. They also make the side-by-side result difficult to call even. Najera lasted through four regular Dallas seasons while the Rockets parted with both his rights and the pick that ultimately became Hill. The grade compares benefits realized by each receiving club, not theoretical draft-day optimism.

sections.heading: Separating the Second Pick From the Main Return
sections.body: The 2001 second-round pick was part of the original consideration and deserves its own accounting. Dallas' media guide and the published 2001 draft list identify Kyle Hill as the player chosen with the selection, No. 44 overall. The later draft record shows no NBA playing totals for him. Hill therefore cannot be treated as another Najera-level acquisition just because his name appears beside the traded pick. That distinction actually strengthens the precision of the verdict: Dallas' B+ grade principally rewards one durable contributor, while the future selection is additional but limited realized value. Houston's C corresponds to Langhi's brief rotation experience there. The 2000 draft order also clarifies the scale of the gamble: Dallas ultimately did better with the rights to the No. 38 player than Houston did with the rights to No. 31, even though the higher selection could have looked more attractive at the time.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win remains the deep-dive conclusion. Dallas Mavericks are graded B+; Houston Rockets are graded C. The stronger completed return was draft rights to Eduardo Najera and 2001 second-round pick (#44-Kyle Hill), while the other side's case rests on draft rights to Dan Langhi. Both sides receive credit for value that actually materialized, but the evidence-based comparison leaves Dallas Mavericks with the better historical outcome. The Dallas advantage is Najera's 208 Mavericks appearances and the additional No. 44 Hill draft right against Houston's 67 Langhi games, without assigning unrelated later NBA returns to either organization.

sections.heading: What Changed Hands
sections.body: The June 28, 2000 Dallas-New York deal combined an NBA player exchange with two sets of draft rights. The Mavericks obtained John Wallace and the rights to Donnell Harvey. The Knicks took Erick Strickland and the rights to Pete Mickeal. Each side therefore received one established player plus one drafted prospect, but the players and rights have to be judged independently: Harvey did not become an automatic Dallas rotation piece merely because his rights changed hands.

sections.heading: Wallace Never Played in Dallas, While Strickland Played 28 Knicks Games
sections.body:
The June 28, 2000 exchange has four distinct assets. Dallas got John Wallace and Donnell Harvey, whom the Knicks had just drafted No. 22. New York got Erick Strickland and Pete Mickeal, whom Dallas selected No. 58. John Wallace was a roster asset, not a realized Dallas player. On August 29 the Mavericks bundled him with Cedric Ceballos and Eric Murdock for Detroit’s Christian Laettner and Terry Mills, meaning Wallace recorded zero Dallas regular-season games. Harvey did reach Dallas, appearing in 18 games in 2000-01 and another 18 in 2001-02, but played relatively few minutes.

Strickland came off 67 starts in 68 Dallas games in 1999-00, then played only 28 Knicks games in 2000-01 as a bench guard. He averaged 4.3 points and 1.9 assists for New York before another January trade. Mickeal never played in the NBA, although his rights were real draft-night consideration. The Knicks B versus Dallas B- is a modest comparison, not evidence that Wallace gave the Mavericks a full season of on-court production.

sections.heading: The Two Downstream Deals Had Other Players and Picks
sections.body:
The Mavericks August 29, 2000 Detroit deal included Wallace AND Cedric Ceballos and Eric Murdock plus cash for Laettner and Mills; the entire Laettner return cannot be treated as an isolated payoff for Wallace. Dallas subsequently included Donnell Harvey with Tim Hardaway, Juwan Howard and a 2002 first-rounder in February 2002 to get a four-player Denver package including Nick Van Exel and Raef LaFrentz. Harvey’s presence in that deal proves his rights had retained some transferable value, but other Mavericks assets carried independent value.

On January 30, 2001, the Knicks sent Strickland AND two 2001 draft choices (a first that became Jamaal Tinsley and a second that became Antonis Fotsis) to Vancouver for Othella Harrington. The Knicks did not trade Pete Mickeal to get Harrington, nor did Strickland alone purchase the power forward. New York used the guard obtained in June as a component of its subsequent frontcourt deal; Dallas used Wallace similarly in a different contract exchange.

sections.heading: The Narrow Grade Margin Is About Transferable Value, Not Star Production
sections.body:
This is a useful example of a draft-night exchange whose principal value came through later transactions rather than a player starring on the first receiving team. Wallace never played for Dallas and Harvey made 36 Mavericks appearances. Strickland played 28 for the Knicks before moving again, while Mickeal did not enter the NBA. That does not make both returns zero: player contracts and unsigned draft rights can be retained, renegotiated, or routed onward to create options for a front office.

The site’s current B for New York and B- for Dallas, with Slight Knicks Edge, rates the Knicks slightly higher for briefly using Strickland and converting him in a later multi-asset move. A different evaluator could favor Dallas for the Wallace and Harvey paths; the source facts do not mathematically establish a winner. The important correction is distinguishing the actual post-trade player appearances from the longer chains instead of claiming Wallace logged limited Dallas NBA minutes.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Knicks Edge — Knicks B, Mavericks B-. Dallas received Wallace and Harvey rights but Wallace played no Dallas NBA games before moving with two other Mavericks players to Detroit; Harvey played 36 Dallas games over two seasons. New York received Strickland for 28 games plus Pete Mickeal rights, then used Strickland with two separately owned picks in its Othella Harrington transaction. The mild Knicks advantage is a bounded editorial judgment about movable assets, not a claim that any full subsequent trade package belongs to this deal alone.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: John Wallace Never Played in Dallas: The 2000 Mavericks–Knicks Draft-Night Asset Chain
featuredDeepDive.intro: On June 28, 2000, Dallas moved Erick Strickland and the draft rights to Pete Mickeal to New York for John Wallace and No. 22 Donnell Harvey rights. The names suggest a straightforward player-for-player exchange, but the minutes and transaction records tell another story. Wallace never appeared for Dallas before being included in a larger Detroit trade on August 29. Strickland lasted 28 Knicks games before New York used him alongside two picks in a January 2001 deal with Vancouver. Harvey supplied 36 Dallas appearances and later moved with more substantial Mavericks assets to Denver. Mickeal never reached the NBA. The narrow Knicks B to Dallas B- grade difference should be read through those asset paths rather than an imagined season of Wallace Dallas play.

sections.heading: The Draft-Night Rights Belonged to Two Different Picks
sections.body:
The Knicks drafted Donnell Harvey at No. 22 in the first round of the June 2000 draft; the Mavericks selected Pete Mickeal at No. 58. Their rights moved in opposite directions as part of the same four-piece deal that sent John Wallace to Dallas and Erick Strickland to New York. That is important because a draft-rights transfer is not the same thing as a player already joining an NBA rotation. Harvey eventually signed with Dallas, while Mickeal never appeared in an NBA regular-season game.

The transaction is directly recorded in both teams’ 1999-00 Basketball Reference histories and in the Dallas Mavericks official historical media guide. Mickeal went on to have an accomplished overseas career, but his later non-NBA performances should not be assigned to the Knicks as NBA trade production. The actual immediate return was Strickland rostered for the following season and two rights/contracts capable of further transfers.

sections.heading: Wallace Was Converted Into a Piece of the August 2000 Laettner Deal
sections.body:
Wallace’s most easily overlooked role came two months after the draft. On August 29 the Mavericks sent him with Cedric Ceballos, Eric Murdock and cash to Detroit for Christian Laettner and Terry Mills. Contemporary August 30 coverage from the Washington Post, LA Times and ABC specifically notes that Wallace never played a Dallas NBA game. The official Mavericks transaction list records the same exchange, including the additional outgoing contracts.

It is reasonable to say Dallas used the asset it bought from New York in a subsequent attempt to strengthen its frontcourt. It is not reasonable to give the original four-asset Knicks deal all of Laettner’s subsequent impact; Dallas contributed two other players and cash to that Detroit package. The absence of Wallace Dallas box-score minutes is a source-supported fact, not an indication that the draft-night trade had literally no value for Dallas.

sections.heading: Harvey Played 36 Mavericks Games Before the Denver Blockbuster
sections.body:
Donnell Harvey played 18 regular-season games for Dallas in 2000-01, averaging 1.2 points and 1.1 rebounds over 3.6 minutes per appearance. He played 18 more Mavericks games the following season, for a Dallas total of 36 regular-season appearances. NBA and Mavericks historical records then place him in the February 21, 2002 package to Denver alongside Juwan Howard, Tim Hardaway and a 2002 first-round pick.

The 2002 Mavericks return included Nick Van Exel, Raef LaFrentz, Avery Johnson and Tariq Abdul-Wahad. That trade cannot be reduced to Harvey-for-Van-Exel; the more experienced outgoing players and first-round selection were essential separate considerations. Harvey’s role illustrates that a little-used young forward could still travel as one item in a later deal, not that he delivered a large block of Dallas playing time in his first two years.

sections.heading: Strickland Played in New York Before Becoming Part of the Harrington Package
sections.body:
Erick Strickland had started 67 of 68 Dallas games in 1999-00, then entered a much deeper New York backcourt where he was behind Allan Houston, Latrell Sprewell, Charlie Ward and Chris Childs. His Knicks tenure covered 28 games at approximately 4.3 points and 1.9 assists per game. On January 30, 2001, New York traded him to Vancouver along with a conditional 2001 first-rounder and a 2001 second-rounder for Othella Harrington.

Those two picks later became associated with Jamaal Tinsley and Antonis Fotsis. Contemporary ESPN/AP reporting specifically names Strickland and both picks in the exchange, confirming that Harrington cannot be presented as the sole direct return on Strickland’s 2000 acquisition. The Knicks were using an acquired veteran as one of three moving parts to address a frontcourt need; his NBA playing contribution was modest, but the ability to trade him was consequential.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Knicks Edge, Knicks B versus Mavericks B-. New York used Erick Strickland for 28 games and later included him with two picks in the Harrington trade; Pete Mickeal never appeared in the NBA. Dallas received Donnell Harvey for 36 appearances and John Wallace’s contract as a component of the later Detroit-Laettner exchange, with zero Wallace Dallas games. Neither franchise received a star directly from the June 2000 swap. The grade edge is modest, and the later full-package returns belong to separate transactions.

sections.heading: A Five-Player Deal After the Ewing Megatrade Fell Apart
sections.body: Dallas and Detroit settled on a smaller transaction on August 29, 2000, after an elaborate proposed trade involving Patrick Ewing and several teams collapsed. The Mavericks took in Christian Laettner and Terry Mills. Detroit received Cedric Ceballos, John Wallace and Eric Murdock, plus reported cash. Contemporary coverage framed Laettner as an intended frontcourt addition for Don Nelson rather than a long-term franchise centerpiece. Wallace and Murdock were especially unusual outgoing pieces: Dallas had acquired both during the June draft period, and neither had played a game for the Mavericks. The move swapped Dallas roster inventory for a veteran big man while giving the Pistons a new wing option and financial consideration.

sections.heading: Why Dallas Wanted Laettner
sections.body: Nelson publicly emphasized the need for another big player alongside a roster that featured Shawn Bradley. Laettner could work at center or forward, giving Dallas a more versatile frontcourt option after the failed larger deal. There was an immediate limit to the package, however. Dallas waived Mills on October 2, barely a month after the exchange, so treating the two incoming veterans as equal long-term contributors would distort what followed. Laettner was the usable part of the return and the reason Dallas made the swap. His value to the Mavericks was not measured solely by how long he stayed, because he later became part of another substantive transaction.

sections.heading: Laettner Became a Piece of the Juwan Howard Deal
sections.body: On February 22, 2001, Dallas sent Laettner to Washington as one of six outgoing players or cash components in the deal that brought Juwan Howard, Calvin Booth and Obinna Ekezie to the Mavericks. That is an identifiable continuation of Laettner as an asset, but the entire Howard return cannot fairly be credited to the August deal. Five other Dallas assets went to the Wizards in that later exchange. Dallas received a temporary rotation option and subsequently used that player in a larger package. The narrow value of the Laettner component supports the existing B- grade without turning the 2000 deal into an indirect claim that Dallas obtained Howard for Ceballos, Wallace and Murdock alone.

sections.heading: Detroit Got Cash and a Short-Lived Player Return
sections.body: The Pistons added Ceballos while reshaping their roster after Grant Hill left for Orlando. Contemporary reports also put the cash component at approximately $3 million. The player return did not become a lasting core. Detroit waived Murdock in September; Ceballos appeared in 13 games for the Pistons before a November 26 transaction sent him to Miami with draft considerations. Wallace logged 40 Detroit appearances during the 2000-01 season, offering a more concrete on-court return than Murdock. Detroit gained several pieces and financial flexibility, but neither the short tenure of Ceballos nor the reserve use of Wallace establishes a decisive win. The inherited verdict is Even Trade, with B- grades for each club.

sections.heading: Cash and the Listed Exception Need Separate Accounting
sections.body: The source histories distinguish the roughly $3 million cash payment from a separate $4 million traded-player exemption listed in the imported asset ledger. Contemporary Associated Press reporting supports cash accompanying the player exchange, but the news accounts do not independently establish how the exception was later used. These entries cannot be added together as though Detroit received $7 million in cash. Nor can an exception be converted into invented playing minutes or a player acquisition. The August 29 five-player exchange stands apart from the proposed Patrick Ewing deal and from the later February 2001 Juwan Howard transaction. Laettner was only one outgoing component in the latter package, which had other Dallas consideration. This distinction supports the inherited Even Trade assessment, with B- for each club: Dallas obtained temporary frontcourt depth and a subsequently tradable veteran, while Detroit received cash and short-lived player returns. The exact cap treatment remains a documented source-provenance hold.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Dallas B-, Detroit B-. Dallas obtained Laettner as a frontcourt option, waived Mills and eventually packaged Laettner in a broader move for Juwan Howard. Detroit received Ceballos, Wallace, Murdock and reported cash; the player returns proved short-lived or limited. Neither side acquired a durable centerpiece through this exchange. The tied inherited grades are retained, and the later Howard trade is not assigned wholly to Laettner.
