sections.heading: October 17, 2000: Two Dallas Guards for Loy Vaught
sections.body: Dallas acquired veteran forward Loy Vaught from Detroit on October 17, 2000 for Dana Barros and Ansu Sesay. The Mavericks' season transaction archive identifies all three players and the exact date. Vaught had once been a reliable Clippers starter, but injuries reduced his availability and effectiveness before this exchange. Barros was an experienced guard coming from a different role, while Sesay was a younger forward whose Dallas tenure had not produced regular-season NBA games. The deal contained no recorded first-round pick or other contingent draft consideration. Dallas wanted size in its frontcourt as Dirk Nowitzki's club improved; Detroit wanted guard service from Barros and a possible development piece in Sesay. The source history must credit only the games these players later supplied to their receiving clubs.

sections.heading: Vaught Logged Thirty-Seven Mavericks Games Before Washington Deal
sections.body: Vaught appeared in 37 Dallas regular-season games during 2000-01, starting once, averaging 3.1 points and 3.3 rebounds in 10.6 minutes per game. Those limited numbers were sharply below his healthy peak years with the Clippers. On February 22, 2001 the Mavericks included him in a separate multi-player transaction with Washington involving Juwan Howard, Calvin Booth and other players. Vaught then played 14 Washington games, which are not Dallas return from the October Detroit trade. The receiving Mavericks club obtained half a season of reserve size, not a dependable starting power forward. His earlier Detroit and Clippers statistics belong to those teams before the acquisition. The short timeline gives a measurable basis for Dallas's preserved C-plus grade rather than simply repeating a narrative about injury risk.

sections.heading: Barros Brought Detroit Eighty-Nine Regular-Season Games
sections.body: Detroit received substantially more NBA playing time from Barros than Dallas obtained from Vaught. Barros appeared in 60 Pistons games in 2000-01, averaging 8.0 points in 18.0 minutes. The following season he made another 29 Detroit appearances, starting 20 and averaging 6.7 points with 2.7 assists. That is 89 Pistons NBA regular-season games across the two seasons, all after the Dallas transaction. His three-point shooting helped provide a veteran outside threat even as his role changed. The 72 Boston games he played in 1999-00 preceded the trade and cannot be counted as Detroit service. Barros provided rotation value without being a franchise star, an outcome appropriately distinguished from Vaught's brief Dallas tenure.

sections.heading: Sesay Had No Pistons NBA Games, Despite Later Sonics Service
sections.body: The second Detroit acquisition, Ansu Sesay, did not play in an NBA regular-season game for the Pistons. He spent the 2000-01 season outside the league after previous injury and CBA work. Sesay later appeared in NBA games with Seattle and Golden State, beginning with the SuperSonics in 2001-02; none of those belong to his receiving Pistons club. That absence does not erase Barros's 89 Detroit games, but it prevents inflating the deal into two established Pistons rotation pieces. The archived Pistons Win verdict and Detroit B versus Dallas C-plus grades reflect one productive veteran guard return against 37 Vaught Mavericks appearances. There was no source-verified Detroit starting forward value supplied by Sesay at the time.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Detroit B and Dallas C-plus preserved. Detroit gained 89 regular-season NBA appearances from Barros over two years; Sesay played zero NBA games for the Pistons. Dallas obtained 37 Vaught games before a separate February 2001 Washington transaction. No pick or later unrelated player should be credited as part of the October 2000 exchange, and the preserved grades describe a modest veteran-playing-time edge.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Dallas Mavericks–Detroit Pistons: What the 2000-10-17 Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: On October 17, 2000, Dallas traded Dana Barros and Ansu Sesay to Detroit for Loy Vaught. Vaught supplied 37 Mavericks games before being moved to Washington in February 2001. Barros played 60 Pistons games in 2000-01 and 29 more in 2001-02, while Sesay never appeared for Detroit in an NBA game. The stored Pistons B versus Dallas C-plus outcome is a narrow return-on-court comparison, not an assertion that Sesay's later Seattle or Golden State years were Detroit production.

sections.heading: Vaught Was a Former Clippers Starter, Not a Present Star
sections.body: Detroit was trading away a name with a stronger past than present. Vaught had started all 82 Clippers games during 1996-97, but injuries drastically shortened his subsequent seasons. He made 37 appearances for Detroit in 1998-99 and 43 in 1999-00 before joining Dallas in the October 2000 swap. The Mavericks could hope his rebounding and size would rebound in a new situation, yet his 2000-01 Dallas record shows just 37 games and one start. His old peak of double-digit rebounds is historical context for Dallas's gamble, not NBA production acquired for 2000-01. Accounting for the player's actual later minutes explains why the stored C-plus score is modest without rewriting the initial team rationale as an obviously impossible decision made with perfect future knowledge.

sections.heading: Dallas Moved Vaught Again During February 2001
sections.body: Vaught's Dallas tenure lasted only a portion of one NBA season. The Mavericks acquired him October 17 and sent him to Washington on February 22, 2001 in a separate multi-asset transaction that brought Juwan Howard and Calvin Booth into the Dallas organization. Basketball-Reference's team transaction log confirms both events and does not identify the earlier Barros-Sesay package as a direct part of the Washington deal. The distinction is important: Juwan Howard was not received from Detroit for Barros in October. Vaught's subsequent 14 Wizards games likewise belong to Washington. The first exchange produced a 37-game Mavericks reserve, followed later by a different roster reshaping. Combining the two deals into one imaginary return would inflate both the transaction asset list and the original on-court value.

sections.heading: Barros Was the Only Incoming Detroit Player With NBA Games
sections.body: Barros suited up in 60 Detroit regular-season games in 2000-01 and another 29 in 2001-02. He averaged 8.0 points the first season, then 6.7 with 2.7 assists in his second, and made 20 starts in that latter year. His veteran scoring and shooting gave the Pistons 89 games of actual service. Sesay, the second name Detroit acquired, produced no Pistons NBA appearances. His later 111 regular-season games with Seattle and 16 with Golden State arose through later arrangements and cannot be attributed to Detroit's team production. That leaves one productive rotation player against Dallas's brief Vaught return, explaining the limited but measurable gap in the saved team grades. Neither player should be described as a new Pistons franchise centerpiece.

sections.heading: The Pistons Grade Rewards Useful Service, Not Later Accomplishments
sections.body: The retained result is Pistons Win, Detroit B and Dallas C-plus. Barros played 89 Detroit games over two seasons, while Vaught played 37 for the Mavericks before being dealt again in February 2001. Sesay played none for the Pistons, and Detroit did not obtain a draft choice that later became a named star. These are modest outcomes compared with trades that moved future Hall of Fame talent. Yet they support a narrow Detroit edge: a veteran guard supplied significantly more receiving-team court time than the injured forward Dallas acquired. The later Washington Vaught stint and Seattle Sesay career are relevant to tracking the players, not to assigning Dallas or Detroit extra basketball value. The grade gap is contextual and bounded to these named returns.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Detroit B and Dallas C-plus keep the historical Pistons Win judgment. Barros gave Detroit 60 games and 8.0 points per game in 2000-01, followed by 29 games and 6.7 points in 2001-02. Sesay had no Pistons NBA appearances. Dallas received only 37 Vaught appearances and traded him to Washington four months later, after which the Wizards received his NBA service. Those source-traced returns support a narrow grade edge without borrowing other teams' games or inventing draft consideration.

sections.heading: A Three-Team Deal Centered on Glen Rice and Shandon Anderson
sections.body: The August 10, 2001 agreement connected Dallas, New York and Houston. Houston signed and traded Shandon Anderson to the Knicks, and acquired Glen Rice from New York plus the rights to Dallas second-rounder Kyle Hill. The Knicks added Howard Eisley from Dallas and Anderson from Houston while sending Rice and Muggsy Bogues out. Dallas received Bogues and a $3.2 million trade exception associated with Houston, rather than an incoming player who would contribute that season. The contemporaneous UPI and Washington Post reports identify the five named NBA veterans and one draft-rights asset. The private Dallas-sourced record is a view of this shared three-team package, not a stand-alone Bogues-for-Eisley trade.

sections.heading: Dallas Created a $3.2 Million Exception, Not Bogues Minutes
sections.body: The historical Dallas transaction ledger records a $3.2 million trade exception and Bogues as incoming. Bogues did not play an NBA game for the Mavericks, a fact corroborated by his own career biography and final NBA statistics. The exception was salary-cap flexibility, not a player or a guaranteed later signing. Dallas sent Eisley to the Knicks after his 82-game, 40-start 2000-01 season for the Mavericks and moved Hill rights to Houston. That explains how Dallas could prefer the salary mechanics even though the incoming veteran provided no court production. Bogues was not an interchangeable replacement for the player whose contract left.

sections.heading: Houston Had the One-Year Delay and a New Shooting Option
sections.body: The agreement was announced August 10 but the Rockets did not finalize it until August 17. The Houston Chronicle reported that final approval followed additional unspecified future consideration from both Dallas and New York. The original report identified those considerations as cash according to unnamed sources but did not state a reliable dollar amount. Houston gained Glen Rice, who averaged 9.9 points in 20 regular-season games in 2001-02 and returned for 62 games the following season. The rights to Kyle Hill were a separate prospect asset, not a second established NBA player in the deal. Both the late completion and conditional consideration should stay distinct from what was already identified in the August 10 package.

sections.heading: New York Took On Two Guards with Different Outcomes
sections.body: The Knicks acquired Shandon Anderson through Houston’s sign-and-trade and Howard Eisley from Dallas. A contemporaneous Washington Post account described Scott Layden’s crowded guard rotation immediately after the deal, rather than claiming either arrival solved the backcourt. Eisley played 39 Knicks games in 2001-02 at 4.4 points and 2.6 assists, then 82 games the next season. New York relinquished Rice, a proven shooter, and Bogues, who had never appeared for the Knicks. The private verdict assigns a Slight Rockets Edge, with Houston B-, New York B- and Dallas C+. Those inherited grades should be read against concrete roles and contract obligations, not against imagined long-term Bogues production.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Rockets Edge is preserved alongside Houston B-, New York B- and Dallas C+. Houston obtained Glen Rice and Kyle Hill rights while moving Shandon Anderson through a sign-and-trade. New York gained Anderson and Eisley for Rice and Bogues. Dallas obtained a $3.2 million trade exception but no Bogues NBA games, sending Eisley and Hill rights away. The August 17 additional considerations have uncertain amounts, so the protected future-consideration row is not assigned a manufactured value.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The 2001 Rice-Anderson-Eisley Three-Team Trade: Dallas’s $3.2 Million Exception
featuredDeepDive.intro: The August 2001 agreement sent Glen Rice to Houston, Shandon Anderson and Howard Eisley to New York, and Muggsy Bogues plus a $3.2 million exception to Dallas. The deal was announced August 10 and finalized a week later after further consideration was arranged. Dallas also transferred rights to Kyle Hill to the Rockets. The inherited Slight Rockets Edge and B-/B-/C+ grades stay intact, but a fair assessment must separate an unused Dallas player, actual Knicks guard minutes and Houston’s veteran shooter from uncertain late-added cash.

sections.heading: The Announcement Listed Five Veterans and a Draft Right
sections.body: August 10 reports from United Press International and the Washington Post describe a three-team effort to reorganize backcourts and contracts. New York sent Glen Rice to Houston and Muggsy Bogues to Dallas, receiving Shandon Anderson and Howard Eisley. Dallas moved its rights to Kyle Hill to Houston. The Houston sign-and-trade enabled Anderson to land in New York after his prior Rockets service. The $3.2 million exception received by Dallas is verified by Basketball Reference and the contemporaneous Houston Roundball Review. This framework prevents a Dallas-centric import from omitting Houston’s most recognizable incoming player or New York’s two arrivals.

sections.heading: Why August 17 Belongs on the Transaction Timeline
sections.body: The August 10 announcement did not complete immediately. Houston Chronicle reporting dated August 18 says the Rockets finalized the acquisition of Rice on August 17 after Dallas and New York supplied additional future considerations. The report described the consideration as cash according to sources, without identifying an exact amount. The source transaction ledger preserves an August 17 amendment, but its precise future-consideration mapping is not fully resolved. The archived record therefore holds the future-consideration field for provenance review rather than silently rewriting it as a specified check or assuming that the $3.2 million exception was simply that payment. Salary matching and supplemental consideration were related parts of closing the deal, not identical accounting items.

sections.heading: Actual Player Production Diverged across the Three Clubs
sections.body: Muggsy Bogues finished his NBA career without appearing for Dallas. His personal site explicitly says he did not play for either the Knicks or Mavericks, making the trade exception the more useful documented Dallas arrival. Howard Eisley played 39 New York games in 2001-02, and later started 76 of 82 Knicks games in 2002-03, so his return cannot be dismissed as zero. Glen Rice played 20 Rockets games in 2001-02, then 62 in 2002-03. Those seasons belong to Rice’s Houston stint, not to Kyle Hill’s draft-rights line. The records show distinct timelines of usable veteran minutes, a dormant incoming name and potential cap flexibility.

sections.heading: The Archived C+/B-/B- Verdict Needs a Defined Scope
sections.body: A Slight Rockets Edge is a defensible historical ledger verdict without requiring Houston to have landed a star in his prime. The Rockets acquired a veteran shooter and a draft-rights option while moving Anderson, then secured the necessary late closing considerations. The Knicks turned Rice and an inactive Bogues contract into two guards who would occupy real rotation slots. Dallas obtained roster and salary flexibility but gave up Eisley and the Hill option for a player who never took the floor. The private record’s individual grades are preserved, and no inference about downstream franchise wins is counted as a direct return.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Houston B-, New York B-, Dallas C+ and Slight Rockets Edge stay unchanged. The three-team package delivered Rice and Hill rights to Houston, Anderson and Eisley to New York, Bogues and a $3.2 million exception to Dallas. Bogues logged no Mavericks NBA appearances. August 17 future consideration supported completion but lacks a reliably published dollar amount; it is retained as an open provenance question rather than fabricated asset value.

sections.heading: Dallas Exchanged Howard and a First for Veteran Help
sections.body: Dallas acquired Nick Van Exel, Raef LaFrentz, Avery Johnson and Olivier Saint-Jean from Denver at the February 21, 2002 deadline. The Nuggets received Juwan Howard, Donnell Harvey, Tim Hardaway, a 2002 first-round pick and $1 million cash. The selection became No. 25, associated with Frank Williams. Those details make this a substantial multi-player agreement, not a simple Van Exel-for-Howard swap. Dallas was buying proven rotation options during a playoff-contender period, while Denver took an established forward and future draft and financial assets. Neither side's valuation can be reduced to the number of recognizable veteran names alone.

sections.heading: Van Exel and LaFrentz Helped a Deep Dallas Run
sections.body: Van Exel supplied off-bench scoring and playmaking while LaFrentz provided interior minutes and shooting. Avery Johnson offered additional veteran guard depth. The acquired group was part of the Dallas competitive window that reached the Western Conference finals in 2003. That is direct basketball production for the Mavericks and the strongest case for the positive grade. But LaFrentz's substantial contract also affected the team's future flexibility, meaning Dallas did not receive unrestricted value without a cost. The same players who improved one playoff run could also impose longer financial obligations. Those outcomes both belong in a complete evaluation of the original deadline decision.

sections.heading: Denver Kept a First and Reworked Its Payroll
sections.body: Juwan Howard gave Denver an established forward as the organization changed its roster, while Harvey, Hardaway and the named No. 25 selection formed separate parts of the return. The $1 million cash item was financial consideration, not a hidden additional player. Denver's ability to reset contracts and use its draft option mattered even if those benefits did not equal Dallas's more immediate competitive success. Since the Mavericks also accepted LaFrentz's contract burden, a dramatic A-plus versus failing-grade narrative would ignore real tradeoffs. A modest Dallas victory better represents the playoff payoff alongside the future roster costs that neither team could fully avoid.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win. Dallas receives B+ for the Van Exel, LaFrentz and Johnson impact during its 2003 conference-finals run, with Saint-Jean also included. Denver earns B- for Howard, Harvey, Hardaway, the No. 25 pick and cash. The margin recognizes the Mavericks' playoff benefit while accounting for the long LaFrentz obligation and Denver's flexibility.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Deep Dive: What Decided Mavericks Win on 2002-02-21
featuredDeepDive.intro: Dallas acquired Nick Van Exel, Raef LaFrentz, Avery Johnson and Tariq Abdul-Wahad (formerly Olivier Saint-Jean) from Denver on February 21, 2002 for Juwan Howard, Donnell Harvey, Tim Hardaway, its 2002 first and cash. Van Exel and LaFrentz played all 20 Dallas playoff games in 2003; Denver exercised the first at No. 25 on Frank Williams but traded his rights with other pieces to New York that June. This review distinguishes that separate draft conversion from the immediate Mavericks playoff value.

sections.heading: Tariq Abdul-Wahad and Olivier Saint-Jean Are the Same Player
sections.body: The February 21, 2002 deal was a four-player package to Dallas: Nick Van Exel, Raef LaFrentz, Avery Johnson and Tariq Abdul-Wahad. The last player is labeled Olivier Saint-Jean in the inherited TradeVerdicts asset ledger; Basketball-Reference and Denver's official media guide confirm that Saint-Jean was Abdul-Wahad's former name, not a fifth incoming player. Denver received Juwan Howard, Donnell Harvey, Tim Hardaway, Dallas's 2002 first and financial consideration. This was a salary-heavy exchange for different roster directions during a Mavericks contention window. Neither club gained a new draft slot for every incoming veteran, and the four named Dallas arrivals must not be overcounted because of a historic name alias. The official Denver transaction register independently uses Abdul-Wahad on the same date.

sections.heading: Van Exel and LaFrentz Both Played in the 2003 West Finals Run
sections.body: Nick Van Exel supplied high-value Dallas bench scoring in the 2003 postseason, averaging 19.5 points across 20 playoff appearances. His standout series came against Sacramento in the Western semifinals: 25.3 points per game over seven contests, helping the Mavericks win the series and advance. Van Exel then averaged 17.5 against San Antonio in the six-game Western final. Raef LaFrentz played all 20 postseason games for Dallas that year, with 16 starts and an average of 8.0 points and 4.4 rebounds. The Dallas frontcourt could use his outside shooting and shot blocking around Dirk Nowitzki. Those games are direct receiving-club value from the February 2002 trade; future Spurs, Denver or Portland roster decisions are not part of this trade's production.

sections.heading: Denver Used the No. 25 Frank Williams Pick in Another Trade
sections.body: The future first received by Denver became the No. 25 pick in the June 26, 2002 draft, used on Illinois guard Frank Williams. The Nuggets did not retain his NBA playing career: Denver sent Williams' rights, Antonio McDyess and a 2003 second to New York for Marcus Camby, Mark Jackson and Nenê's rights in a separate draft-night exchange. Basketball-Reference's Denver and Knicks season transaction histories identify the pick and both later packages. That is genuine downstream optionality attributable in part to Dallas's outgoing first, but the complete McDyess transaction cannot be credited to the No. 25 selection alone. The original Mavericks swap also gave Denver three veterans and cash; those components have their own value independent of what eventually happened to Frank Williams after Denver dealt him onward.

sections.heading: Dallas Secured the 2003 Playoff Return; Denver Kept a Rebuild Option
sections.body: Nick Van Exel scored 19.5 points per game across all 20 of Dallas's 2003 playoff games, while Raef LaFrentz appeared in those same 20 contests and averaged 8.0 points and 4.4 rebounds. That is a measurable Mavericks contribution to the conference-finals run, not a hypothetical future payoff. Denver received Juwan Howard, Donnell Harvey, Tim Hardaway, cash and the No. 25 first-round pick used on Frank Williams. The Nuggets subsequently included Williams, Antonio McDyess and a 2003 second in a separate draft-night exchange for Marcus Camby, Mark Jackson and Nenê's rights. Treating every piece of that later package as value created by the No. 25 pick would inflate the 2002 Mavericks trade. Dallas's B+ acknowledges its immediate postseason benefit alongside LaFrentz's long salary commitment; Denver's B- recognizes a genuine draft and roster reset without equating it with Dallas's 2003 on-court peak.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win is the source-locked verdict, Dallas B-plus versus Denver B-minus. Van Exel averaged 19.5 Dallas points across the 2003 postseason and LaFrentz contributed in 20 playoff games as the Mavericks reached the West finals. Denver used the No. 25 Frank Williams rights as one part of a separate June 2002 trade for Marcus Camby, Nenê rights and Mark Jackson; the entire later return does not belong to that one pick. Tariq Abdul-Wahad and Olivier Saint-Jean are the same player, and Dallas also accepted a substantial LaFrentz contract cost.

sections.heading: Dallas Drafted Xue Yuyang and Immediately Moved His Rights
sections.body: The Mavericks selected Chinese center Xue Yuyang with the 57th pick in the 2003 NBA draft, then dealt his rights to Denver in exchange for a 2004 second-round selection. Dallas did not trade an established rotation player or a pick that had already delivered on-court results; it traded the rights to a player who would not appear in an NBA game. The deal appears in the Mavericks’ official team history under June 26, 2003. Basketball-Reference’s transaction logs label the arrangement June 23, a historical date discrepancy best handled by identifying the 2003 draft-day exchange instead of implying there were two different Xue trades. Both franchise transaction histories agree on the player and future-pick direction.

sections.heading: The Future Pick Became No. 50 in 2004
sections.body: Denver’s outgoing second-round selection became the 50th overall pick in the 2004 draft. Dallas used it on Greek guard Vassilis Spanoulis, so the connection between Xue and Spanoulis is a documented pick conversion, not a retrospective comparison between two unrelated prospects. The official Mavericks media guide lists Xue as the 57th selection in 2003, the rights transfer to Denver, and Spanoulis at No. 50 the following year. Xue never reached the NBA. Spanoulis also never played for Dallas, but that does not make the acquired pick valueless: the Mavericks kept a transferable draft asset through the next draft.

sections.heading: Dallas Exchanged Spanoulis for Luis Flores
sections.body: On June 24, 2004, the Mavericks moved the rights to Spanoulis to Houston and acquired the rights to Luis Flores, the 55th pick, in return. The Rockets’ official media guide confirms that exact rights-for-rights swap. This is the traceable downstream use of Denver’s 2004 pick; saying only that Spanoulis never played for Dallas misses the intermediate asset conversion. Flores was the actual Dallas return at the end of the known rights chain. Any later Flores deal must be evaluated on its own terms rather than credited wholesale to the initial Xue transaction.

sections.heading: Why the Existing B-Minus Tie Is Retained
sections.body: Denver received a draft-rights gamble on Xue, while Dallas converted a future second-rounder into Spanoulis and then Flores. Neither original asset delivered a sustained NBA role for the team that acquired it in 2003. That supports the inherited Even Trade verdict and matching B- grades as a limited retrospective rather than a claim that Denver acquired a proven center or Dallas secured an NBA contributor. The grade should not treat Spanoulis’s later international career as production for Dallas, and it should not assign every Houston transaction to this exchange. What is demonstrable is a one-year pick conversion and a further draft-rights swap, with no enduring direct rotation return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Dallas B-, Denver B-. The 2003 draft-night deal sent Xue Yuyang’s rights to Denver for the future second-rounder Dallas used at No. 50 in 2004. The Mavericks then traded Spanoulis’s rights for Luis Flores at No. 55. The trackable conversion gives Dallas an additional step in the transaction chain, but neither side extracted a durable NBA rotation player from the original assets. The inherited tied grades and verdict are preserved.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Xue Yuyang, the Denver Pick, and Dallas’s 2004 Draft-Rights Chain
featuredDeepDive.intro: The 2003 Mavericks-Nuggets swap is more specific than an exchange of two marginal names. Dallas drafted Xue Yuyang 57th overall and sent his rights to Denver for a future second-rounder. That selection became Vassilis Spanoulis at No. 50 in 2004; Dallas then dealt his rights to Houston for Luis Flores at No. 55. The inherited verdict is Even Trade with B- grades on both sides, and each link needs separate attribution.

sections.heading: The Pick Was Future Consideration, Not Spanoulis Yet
sections.body: At the time of the 2003 transaction, Dallas received a 2004 second-round pick, not an agreement to acquire a particular player. Only after that draft did the asset have the identity Vassilis Spanoulis. The Mavericks’ official history and the historical pick-conversion table connect Denver’s outgoing selection to No. 50. This distinction keeps the analysis from reading later scouting information backward into the original exchange. Denver could evaluate Xue immediately as a draft-rights prospect; Dallas accepted the uncertainty of an unselected player a year away. Neither club knew the final name attached to the future pick when the trade was executed.

sections.heading: Why Xue Was a Draft-Rights Prospect
sections.body: Xue was listed at center and drafted 57th in 2003, then his rights were sent west to Denver. The Nuggets took on the possibility that an overseas prospect could develop into an NBA option without using their own 2004 selection. Xue never appeared in an NBA regular-season game, so his potential never became verified production for Denver. The absence of NBA games is a proper part of the completed-value grade, but it is not evidence that the club could not reasonably have valued international development or contract flexibility on draft night. The historical record supports a rights acquisition, not a veteran-player contribution.

sections.heading: Dallas Turned the Selection into a Second Rights Deal
sections.body: The 2004 draft gave Dallas the 50th pick through this earlier agreement, and the team selected Spanoulis. Houston wanted his draft rights and offered the rights to Luis Flores, selected five spots later. The Rockets’ team history and Dallas’s media guide independently document the exchange. Spanoulis eventually played in the NBA for Houston, not Dallas. For the Mavericks, the directly traceable result was the Flores rights, not Houston’s later use of Spanoulis. This is the critical editorial difference between saying that a draft pick produced no Dallas games and saying that it had no transactional value.

sections.heading: The Even Result Has a Narrow, Verifiable Basis
sections.body: Neither Xue for Denver nor the rights retained from the original future pick for Dallas produced a long-term NBA contributor from the 2003 swap itself. Dallas did make another exchange with the selection; Denver retained the unfulfilled hope attached to Xue’s rights. Those are distinct paths, yet their eventual team-level consequences do not clearly prove a decisive winner. The site’s established B-/B- grades and Even Trade verdict are preserved, rather than manufacturing a new score from international accomplishments or a downstream deal containing unrelated assets. The key historical claim is the precise chain of selections and rights, corroborated by franchise histories.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, B- for Dallas and B- for Denver. Xue’s rights went to the Nuggets, and the future second-rounder went to the Mavericks. The pick became No. 50 Vassilis Spanoulis, whose rights Dallas traded to Houston for No. 55 Luis Flores in 2004. The future-selection conversion is real, but neither side’s original return generated a lasting NBA player contribution for the acquiring team. No unrelated later asset value is added to the grades.

sections.heading: Dallas Acquired Jamison in a Nine-Player Exchange
sections.body: Dallas received Antawn Jamison, Danny Fortson, Chris Mills and Jiří Welsch from Golden State in August 2003. The Warriors took Nick Van Exel, Avery Johnson, Ronald "Popeye" Jones, Antoine Rigaudeau and Evan Eschmeyer. The number of players gives the deal a complicated appearance, but Jamison was the dominant basketball piece on the Mavericks' side. Golden State's return offered multiple established veterans and roster options instead of one comparable new centerpiece. Dallas was seeking another scorer for a team that already had major offensive talent. This was a direct player-package exchange, not a transaction in which a hidden first-round pick explains the verdict.

sections.heading: Jamison Produced and Then Helped Finance Another Deal
sections.body: Jamison played the 2003-04 season for Dallas and won NBA Sixth Man of the Year. That direct contribution makes the trade useful even without considering the next step in his asset path. The following summer Dallas included Jamison in its arrangement with Washington that brought back Devin Harris and Jerry Stackhouse through draft rights and player routing. The later exchange was a separate transaction, so not every accomplishment of those incoming players can be assigned to the original Golden State move. It does show that the Mavericks were able to use Jamison again as valuable consideration after already receiving a productive season.

sections.heading: Golden State Received Veterans Without the Same Return
sections.body: Van Exel was the best-known immediate Golden State acquisition, with Johnson, Jones, Rigaudeau and Eschmeyer filling out the package. Those names were genuine roster assets rather than empty compensation, which keeps the Warriors' grade from the bottom of the scale. But the combination didn't give Golden State the same direct high-level season and valuable downstream trade piece that Jamison supplied Dallas. The grade difference should stay restrained because Jamison's own Mavericks tenure was short. Treating the deal as if he spent his entire All-Star career in Dallas would overstate the return, just as assigning no value to the Warriors' veterans would undervalue their side.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win. Dallas receives B for Jamison's Sixth Man of the Year season and the later trade value attached to him, with Fortson, Mills and Welsch also incoming. Golden State receives C+ for Van Exel, Johnson, Jones, Rigaudeau and Eschmeyer. The Mavericks gained the most consequential player, but the limited length of his direct tenure keeps the edge modest.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Deep Dive: What Decided Mavericks Win on 2003-08-18
featuredDeepDive.intro: On August 18, 2003, Dallas moved Nick Van Exel, Avery Johnson, Popeye (Ronald) Jones, Antoine Rigaudeau and Evan Eschmeyer for Antawn Jamison, Danny Fortson, Chris Mills and Jiří Welsch. Jamison played 82 Mavericks games, won Sixth Man of the Year and was later included in a separate Washington trade returning Stackhouse, Laettner and the No. 5 Devin Harris right. Van Exel played 39 Golden State games, Avery Johnson 46, Popeye five, and Rigaudeau was waived before playing.

sections.heading: August 18, 2003 Was a Nine-Player Trade, Not Two Separate Deals
sections.body: Dallas sent Nick Van Exel, Avery Johnson, Popeye Jones, Antoine Rigaudeau and Evan Eschmeyer to Golden State for Antawn Jamison, Danny Fortson, Chris Mills and Jiří Welsch on August 18, 2003. The official Warriors transaction register and contemporaneous UPI news describe a nine-player completed exchange. The older TradeVerdicts asset ledger calls the forward Ronald Jones, his legal name; that is Popeye Jones, not a tenth player. Likewise Danny Forston in the inherited asset display refers to Danny Fortson, as contemporary reporting confirms. Golden State chose five contracts and experienced guard options rather than one high-volume scorer. Dallas placed more of its incoming value in Jamison's scoring and a shift toward a larger roster. The two clubs did not exchange draft picks in this original August package.

sections.heading: Jamison Played Every Dallas Game and Won Sixth Man in 2004
sections.body: Jamison joined the Mavericks and appeared in all 82 regular-season games during 2003-04, starting only two and averaging 14.8 points and 6.3 rebounds in 29 minutes a night. He earned NBA Sixth Man of the Year for that one Dallas season, a tangible contribution that did not require him to remain with the club for years. Golden State had used him as a much higher-volume starter at 22.2 points a game the previous season. He adjusted to Dallas's existing Dirk Nowitzki, Steve Nash and Michael Finley core rather than replacing any one of them. Jamison then played five Dallas playoff games in spring 2004 before a different offseason trade. His later Washington All-Star seasons belong to Washington, not this particular Dallas NBA box-score return.

sections.heading: Golden State Received Thirty-Nine Van Exel Games and Short Stints
sections.body: Nick Van Exel was the leading Warriors scorer among the acquired group for the following season: he played 39 regular-season games in 2003-04 with 29 starts, averaging 12.6 points and 5.3 assists. Avery Johnson provided 46 appearances as a reserve and occasional starter. Popeye Jones, listed as Ronald Jones in the legacy data, played only five Golden State games and scored no points. Golden State waived Antoine Rigaudeau in early September 2003 before he played an NBA game for the club. These are genuine veteran assets, but not one full-season equivalent to the high-volume Jamison sixth-man role. Their prior Dallas service and later seasons with other teams must not be counted as Golden State receiving-team production from the August trade.

sections.heading: Jamison Later Became Part of the Wizards–Mavericks Harris Exchange
sections.body: Dallas converted Jamison into additional trade value on June 24, 2004, sending him to Washington in a separate deal for Jerry Stackhouse, Christian Laettner and the Wizards' No. 5 draft selection. Washington used that choice on Devin Harris on Dallas's behalf; he joined the Mavericks. The contemporary Washington Post account records the full package, so this was not a direct one-for-one Jamison-for-Harris swap. Jamison had already supplied his 82-game award-winning Dallas season, giving the original Golden State exchange both direct player and separate downstream asset value. However, the complete 2004 Washington return depended on additional considerations, and not every later Harris, Stackhouse or Laettner season is attributable solely to the nine-player 2003 deal. The inherited Mavericks Win, Dallas B versus Golden State C-plus recognizes a modest franchise-specific advantage.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win, Dallas B and Golden State C-plus preserve the earlier narrow value judgment. Jamison played all 82 Dallas games at 14.8 points and won the 2003-04 Sixth Man award, then became one part of a separate trade for Stackhouse, Laettner and No. 5 Devin Harris. Golden State used Van Exel for 39 games and Avery Johnson for 46; Popeye/Ronald Jones played five and Antoine Rigaudeau was waived without a Warriors NBA game. The original nine-player deal delivered measurable service on both sides but the Dallas high-end and downstream return was stronger.

sections.heading: The Rights Swap on Draft Night
sections.body: On June 24, 2004, Utah selected Pavel Podkolzine at No. 21 and sent his draft rights to Dallas for a future Mavericks first-rounder. Contemporary Deseret News reporting identified the pick as protected and explained that Utah did not want to bring three rookies into an already young roster. The first eventually landed at No. 27 in 2005. Its importance is not that Utah drafted and developed Linas Kleiza: the Jazz moved this asset again before that selection was made.

sections.heading: How Utah Used the Acquired First
sections.body: On June 28, 2005, Utah combined the incoming Dallas No. 27 pick with the No. 6 selection and a protected 2006 first in a trade with Portland. In return, the Jazz obtained the No. 3 pick and selected Deron Williams. The Dallas pick was one part of a three-first package, so Utah cannot credit this single 2004 transaction with every point or assist Williams later recorded. It did, however, turn speculative rights to Podkolzine into an asset that materially helped the Jazz reach the top three of the 2005 draft.

sections.heading: Dallas Received a Very Short NBA Tenure
sections.body: Podkolzine did not deliver the center development Dallas sought. Across the 2004-05 and 2005-06 seasons he appeared in six Mavericks regular-season games, totaling 28 minutes. The Mavericks relinquished an eventual first-round pick for those draft rights. That realized playing return supports a poor Dallas grade even without guessing what a No. 27 selection might have achieved had the club retained it.

sections.heading: Why the Kleiza Career Belongs Elsewhere
sections.body: Portland received the No. 27 pick from Utah and selected Linas Kleiza, then traded Kleiza and Ricky Sanchez to Denver for Jarrett Jack. Kleiza became a useful Nuggets rotation scorer, not a Jazz player. Utah should be credited for deploying the Dallas pick inside its Deron Williams package; Portland and Denver made the separate Kleiza moves. With those chains distinguished, Utah deserves its A- for upgrading a speculative right into valuable draft capital, while Dallas gets D for six total Podkolzine games.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Jazz Win. Utah exchanged the rights to Pavel Podkolzine for a 2005 first that became No. 27, then packaged that selection with two other firsts to acquire the No. 3 pick used on Deron Williams. Dallas got only six NBA games from Podkolzine. Linas Kleiza was subsequently selected by Portland and acquired by Denver, so his production cannot be assigned to Utah. The Jazz A- and Mavericks D reflect the traceable pick value and limited Dallas return, without attributing the entire Williams career to this single trade.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Six Podkolzine Games Versus Utah's Deron Williams Draft Pick Chain
featuredDeepDive.intro: Dallas committed a protected 2005 first-rounder for Pavel Podkolzine's rights in June 2004, then received just six NBA games and 28 minutes from the center. Utah turned the eventual No. 27 choice into part of a three-first-round-pick package that obtained No. 3 Deron Williams the following summer. Portland, not Utah, eventually drafted Linas Kleiza at No. 27. Tracking which team controlled each pick separates the Jazz's actual A-minus asset return from Dallas's D, without implying one late first-rounder alone bought Williams.

sections.heading: The No. 21 Podkolzine Rights Traded for a 2005 First
sections.body:
Utah faced a genuine draft-night roster decision, not a simple hindsight trade of No. 21 for the player later taken at No. 27. The Jazz had already selected Kris Humphries at No. 14 and Kirk Snyder at No. 16. In contemporaneous reporting, executive Kevin O'Connor said he had planned to move the third selection rather than put three rookies on a young team. The Jazz drafted 7-foot-5 Pavel Podkolzine and immediately sent his rights to Dallas for a protected future first, preserving a chance to add or trade talent later instead of investing a third roster slot that summer.

The contract on the pick also carried specific uncertainty. The original Deseret News report said Dallas would retain a top-three choice in 2005, deferring the obligation to 2006 or potentially later; the pick was not guaranteed to convey the following year. Dallas ultimately finished outside that protected range, and the Jazz received No. 27 in 2005. Only then could Utah include the actual selection in the separate Deron Williams draft-up package. This is a different question from rating Podkolzine's six Mavericks games: the 2004 choice was between present roster space and a conditional future asset, before anyone knew its draft position.

sections.heading: Utah Traded the Dallas Pick Again to Reach No. 3
sections.body: Utah did not sign or develop Linas Kleiza from the acquired No. 27 selection. On June 28, 2005 the Jazz packaged the Dallas-origin No. 27 with their No. 6 choice and a protected 2006 first-rounder to Portland. Utah received the No. 3 selection and chose point guard Deron Williams, as the 2005 transactions ledger documents. The Dallas pick was one piece of a three-first package; no single component alone should be credited with all of Williams' later NBA statistics. The original return still had real value to Utah because it helped assemble the compensation needed to move into the top three. This asset trail is the principal basis of the Jazz A-minus, not imaginary Kleiza playing time for Utah.

sections.heading: Podkolzine Produced Just Six Mavericks NBA Games
sections.body: Dallas obtained the draft rights to Podkolzine and later used an NBA roster spot on him, but the realized playing return was very small. The Mavericks recorded six regular-season appearances across the 2004-05 and 2005-06 seasons, totaling 28 minutes. That is the complete NBA contribution credited to Dallas from the player acquired in this rights trade. His size had made him a distinctive draft prospect, yet he did not develop into an NBA rotation center during his brief Dallas tenure. The Mavericks had surrendered an eventual first-round selection to acquire that chance. A D grade reflects the mismatch between that surrendered draft capital and six games of on-court return; it does not depend on forecasting what Dallas hypothetically would have done with No. 27 had it kept the choice.

sections.heading: Kleiza Played Elsewhere and the Two Grade Paths Stay Separate
sections.body: Portland used the No. 27 choice to draft Linas Kleiza, then sent Kleiza and Ricky Sanchez to Denver in a separate transaction for Jarrett Jack. Kleiza became a useful NBA scorer for the Nuggets, but never for Utah as a result of this trade. The Jazz should therefore be credited with turning the Dallas first into part of the Deron Williams draft-up package, not with Portland's draft decision or Denver's subsequent player production. Dallas should be credited with Podkolzine's actual six NBA appearances and 28 minutes, not with an invented later trade return. The canonical Jazz Win, Utah A-minus and Mavericks D reflect two traceable asset chains: Utah exchanged the original rights for useful leverage, while the prospect delivered little playing value to Dallas.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Jazz Win — Utah A-minus, Dallas D. The protected first Utah received for Podkolzine's 2004 draft rights became No. 27 in 2005 and helped the Jazz package up to No. 3 for Deron Williams. Dallas got six NBA appearances and 28 minutes from Podkolzine. Portland later drafted Kleiza and Denver subsequently acquired him, so Kleiza's playing career is not credited as direct Utah production.

sections.heading: Two Second-Round Choices Changed Hands on Draft Night
sections.body: Dallas used the No. 50 selection in 2004 on Vassilis Spanoulis, a guard playing professionally in Greece, and sent his draft rights to Houston. The Mavericks received the rights to No. 55 selection Luis Flores plus cash. No NBA players changed teams that night; both franchises dealt the ability to negotiate with a newly drafted prospect. The historical transaction ledgers show the rights moving in opposite directions and identify the additional cash as Dallas consideration. They do not establish a dependable public dollar amount, so the money cannot be assigned an invented basketball-equivalent value. That distinction is essential for a modest draft-night exchange whose participants were still prospects.

sections.heading: Houston Waited Two Years and Got 31 NBA Games
sections.body: Spanoulis stayed overseas for the first two seasons after Houston acquired his rights. He joined the Rockets for 2006-07 but played just 31 regular-season games, all off the bench, recording 85 points and 28 assists in 272 minutes. That season was his entire NBA regular-season career. He later returned to European basketball, where he enjoyed a far more decorated run. Houston's decision to buy the rights was defensible as a low-cost search for an international guard, but the resulting NBA contribution was narrow. His achievements in Greece are real; they do not convert retroactively into Rockets playing time.

sections.heading: Dallas Passed Flores Along in a Much Larger Deal
sections.body: Flores also never logged a Mavericks regular-season appearance. On August 24, 2004, Dallas sent his rights to Golden State as one piece of the multi-asset Erick Dampier trade. That later exchange involved other Dallas players and draft assets, making it inaccurate to say acquiring Flores alone produced Dampier. Flores eventually played 16 NBA games for Golden State and Denver in 2004-05, scoring 35 points, but none for Dallas. The Mavericks did receive an undisclosed cash payment in the original June deal. Its precise value and any economic benefit are separate from documented on-court return.

sections.heading: Even Grades Fit Two Limited, Different Returns
sections.body: The canonical Even Trade rating, B- for Dallas and B- for Houston, compares two minor draft-rights opportunities rather than a pair of durable NBA contributors. Houston held the rights to a prospect who later appeared in 31 Rockets games. Dallas took a different prospect's rights, moved them in an August package and kept unquantified cash from Houston. Neither team obtained a stand-alone player who reshaped its NBA rotation through this deal. The rights were valid assets with optionality, but the completed record supports balance rather than a dramatic winner. Later multiclub deals should be mentioned to trace the asset chain, not credited in full to this isolated swap.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Dallas B-, Houston B-. The Mavericks traded Vassilis Spanoulis' draft rights for Luis Flores' rights plus cash in June 2004. Houston eventually received 31 NBA games from Spanoulis, while Dallas moved Flores' rights to Golden State in a larger August trade without using him in a Mavericks game. The cash amount is not reliably documented. These modest, distinct outcomes warrant matching grades, not a claimed win based on Spanoulis' later European career or the entire Erick Dampier package.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The Spanoulis–Flores Rights Swap Wasn’t a Star-for-Star Trade
featuredDeepDive.intro: The names in Dallas and Houston's June 24, 2004, exchange suggest a conventional player trade, but the paperwork concerned second-round draft rights. Dallas had selected Vassilis Spanoulis at No. 50; Houston acquired those rights and sent the Mavericks Luis Flores' No. 55 rights and an unspecified amount of cash. The difference between controlling a player's draft rights and receiving actual NBA production defines the retrospective. Neither player became a meaningful rotation contributor for the club that held his rights immediately after this transaction, and both asset chains changed direction later.

sections.heading: Draft-Rights Control Is an Opportunity, Not a Contract
sections.body: Spanoulis was already playing in Greece when Dallas selected him, so Houston was purchasing the exclusive NBA negotiation position associated with his draft slot, not an active Rockets roster spot. Flores had a different development path, but Dallas likewise acquired a right rather than an immediately signed guard. The exchanged slots were Nos. 50 and 55, both in the second round. The difference in selection number cannot explain an outsized retrospective grade when the realized league careers were so short. The cash to Dallas supplied extra compensation, yet the contemporaneous source record available here does not establish its amount.

sections.heading: Houston Finally Signed Spanoulis for One NBA Season
sections.body: The Rockets waited through the 2004-05 and 2005-06 NBA schedules while Spanoulis continued in European competition. He came over in 2006-07, totaled 31 Houston appearances without a start and played 272 minutes. His 85 regular-season points and 28 assists are measurable but not an extended NBA return. Spanoulis later became an international and EuroLeague standout. The remarkable European career is part of his biography, but it did not unfold inside Houston's NBA rotation. Treating his later continental achievements as full Rockets transaction value would substitute reputation for the actual result.

sections.heading: Flores Was Quickly Rolled Into Golden State Negotiations
sections.body: Dallas sent Flores' rights to Golden State about two months after draft night, as part of an August 24 package that landed Erick Dampier and other pieces with the Mavericks. Flores was only one element among Dallas outgoing players and picks. The rights did not result in Flores wearing a Dallas jersey in an NBA regular-season game. His 16 appearances in the 2004-05 season were divided between Golden State and Denver. That chronology makes the Dallas return neither an immediate on-court gain nor worthless paper: it was a transferrable asset inside a transaction whose other costs must stay visible.

sections.heading: The Same Grade Need Not Mean the Same Asset Type
sections.body: Houston kept the Spanoulis rights long enough to sign him and evaluate him in NBA games. Dallas took Flores' rights, passed them into a broader roster trade, and received cash whose total is not independently confirmed. Comparing 31 Rockets appearances to zero Dallas Flores appearances alone misses the fact that Dallas disposed of Flores as trade consideration. Conversely, declaring Dallas the winner because the subsequent August package included Dampier would assign every other outgoing asset no price. The disciplined Even Trade, B-/B- conclusion acknowledges different but similarly constrained forms of completed value from a small draft-night trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, B-/B-. Houston acquired Spanoulis' 2004 draft rights and eventually received 31 NBA regular-season appearances. Dallas received Flores' rights and cash, never rostered Flores for an NBA game and later included his rights in a multi-asset move to Golden State. Cash value is unverified; no evidence justifies giving Dallas exclusive credit for Dampier or Houston credit for Spanoulis' European honors. The best documented comparison is a limited two-sided return.

sections.heading: Seattle Traded Calvin Booth for Danny Fortson in July 2004
sections.body: Dallas and Seattle exchanged forwards on July 26, 2004: Danny Fortson moved to the SuperSonics and Calvin Booth returned to the Mavericks. Seattle's contemporary Post-Intelligencer report describes a straight player-for-player deal with no additional cash or draft picks. Seattle had finished the previous season last in team rebounding and was seeking a more physical presence in the paint; Fortson had built his career around collecting boards despite being undersized for the position. Dallas acquired the taller Booth as reserve center depth. The transaction needs to be judged by the actual roles each man filled at his new destination, not by assuming other acquisitions or an unlisted pick belonged in the package.

sections.heading: Fortson Gave Seattle 62 Games in Its 52-Win Season
sections.body: Fortson gave Seattle 62 appearances during 2004-05, averaging 7.5 points and 5.6 rebounds in only 16.9 minutes. He added 11 playoff games as the SuperSonics won 52 regular-season games and reached the Western Conference semifinals. His playing time and effectiveness fell afterward: 23 games in 2005-06 and 14 in 2006-07, for 99 Seattle regular-season appearances altogether. Booth's Dallas stint was much shorter, totaling 34 games, one start, 82 points and 58 rebounds during 2004-05 before he played elsewhere. This makes Seattle's B+ the stronger return, particularly for its timely rebounding depth. Dallas C+ recognizes that Booth was a real reserve rather than a nonexistent asset.

sections.heading: Dallas Received 34 Games of Calvin Booth Center Depth
sections.body: Dallas received a player who had averaged 4.9 points, 3.9 rebounds and 1.4 blocks in 71 Seattle games the previous season, including 35 starts. The Mavericks did not use Booth nearly as heavily. Back in Dallas in 2004-05, he averaged 7.7 minutes and 2.4 points, appeared 34 times and started once. His limited 262 regular-season minutes gave the club occasional center coverage, but not a lasting rotation answer. Booth later played 17 games for Milwaukee that same season, so his subsequent statistics cannot all be credited to this Dallas exchange. The Mavericks' 58-24 campaign was a team-wide performance and does not establish that Booth provided an important individual return.

sections.heading: Fortson's Seattle Role Declined After 2004-05
sections.body: Fortson answered Seattle's initial rebounding need with a concentrated and useful first season. In 2004-05 he produced 348 rebounds, 463 points and 1,047 minutes in 62 regular-season appearances. The SuperSonics finished 52-30 and advanced through the first playoff round, with Fortson appearing in 11 postseason games. The limitations are also part of the grade: he never started a Seattle regular-season game, drew frequent fouls and appeared only 37 times combined in the next two seasons. His overall Seattle stint of 99 games was not a long-term franchise solution. Still, it supplied substantially more interior work than Booth's 34-game Dallas stint, making the B+/C+ edge credible rather than an automatic award for the better-known player.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Seattle SuperSonics Win — Seattle B+, Dallas C+. Fortson supplied 62 Seattle games at 7.5 points and 5.6 rebounds in 2004-05, plus 11 playoff appearances, before his role declined. Booth played 34 Dallas games, averaging 2.4 points and 1.7 rebounds. Seattle acquired useful rebound production at a position of need; Dallas received limited reserve center minutes. The gap was real but neither player became a long-term cornerstone.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Dallas Mavericks–Seattle SuperSonics: What the 2004-07-26 Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: Seattle's front office wanted rebounding when it acquired Danny Fortson from Dallas in July 2004, while Dallas added a conventional reserve center in Calvin Booth. The following season offers the clearest test. Fortson played 62 times, rebounded at 5.6 per game and contributed to a 52-win Seattle team that advanced to the conference semifinals. Booth played 34 times and averaged 2.4 points for Dallas before appearing later in the season for Milwaukee. That result does not require counting Seattle's entire playoff success as Fortson's achievement. It requires recognizing a direct fit between the Sonics' stated need and the work their new forward supplied.

sections.heading: The SuperSonics Needed Rebounding After a Last-Place Season
sections.body: Seattle's July 26, 2004 reporting establishes why this was more than a surname exchange. The team had been the league's poorest rebounder the previous season and believed Fortson's physicality could address that weakness. His career had already included an 11.7-rebound season with Golden State. Booth was 6-foot-11 and brought shot-blocking ability, but his preceding Seattle year yielded just 3.9 rebounds per game despite 35 starts. Dallas was seeking a different reserve skill set and could see value in that height. There was no reported pick or cash balancing the deal. The proper evaluation is the usefulness of the two incoming players in the roles their receiving clubs actually gave them.

sections.heading: Fortson's 348 Rebounds Marked a Useful First Year
sections.body: Fortson's best Seattle season came immediately in 2004-05: 62 regular-season games, 463 points and 348 rebounds. In 16.9 minutes he averaged 7.5 points and 5.6 boards, a useful rebounding rate for a bench big man. The SuperSonics went 52-30 and won a playoff series, and he appeared in 11 postseason games. Those contributions were particularly timely given Seattle's stated need when it traded for him. Yet he averaged only 3.3 points and 2.4 rebounds in those postseason appearances, and his regular-season role was already defined as reserve work. Seattle benefited from the transaction without having acquired a star or a long-term starter.

sections.heading: Booth's Dallas Stint Ended After 34 Appearances
sections.body: Booth's Dallas production was more modest. He played 34 Mavericks regular-season games, logging 262 minutes with 82 points, 58 rebounds and 16 blocks. The 2.4-point, 1.7-rebound averages provide limited evidence of impact compared with the larger role he had held in Seattle. He moved to Milwaukee later in the 2004-05 season and appeared 17 times there; that is a separate employment path, not additional Dallas basketball value. The Mavericks finished 58-24 and won a playoff series, but the trade did not require Booth to carry the frontcourt. Dallas C+ is a fair grade for temporary depth, provided it is not confused with a contribution on the scale of Fortson's first Seattle season.

sections.heading: Why Seattle B-Plus Outweighs Dallas C-Plus
sections.body: Fortson's Seattle tenure became less useful after the initial year. He appeared in 23 regular-season games during 2005-06 and only 14 in 2006-07, totaling 99 Sonics games across all three seasons. That decline prevents assigning a perfect grade. Booth's own Dallas period lasted only 34 appearances and one start, making the duration and workload comparison straightforward. Seattle B+ versus Dallas C+ reflects a timely defensive-rebounding role with some later decline, not proof that Fortson caused Seattle's 52 wins. The original one-for-one swap produced a stronger destination-team return for Seattle despite neither player becoming a major offensive option.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Seattle SuperSonics Win — Seattle B+, Dallas C+. Fortson provided 348 rebounds and 463 points across 62 Seattle games in 2004-05, while Booth logged 82 points and 58 rebounds in 34 Dallas appearances. Fortson's later availability declined sharply, making this a useful short-term acquisition rather than a durable star return. Dallas' 58-win season and Seattle's playoff progress were broader team outcomes, not automatic trade credits.

sections.heading: Dickau Was One Piece of the Eight-Player Dampier Deal
sections.body: Dallas received Dan Dickau on August 24, 2004, but the guard did not travel in an independent one-for-one trade for a Golden State exception. Contemporary UPI coverage identifies the larger Dallas-Golden State package: Erick Dampier, Dickau, Evan Eschmeyer and the rights to Steve Logan went to the Mavericks. Golden State received Christian Laettner, Eduardo Nájera, Luis Flores rights, Mladen Sekularac rights, two future first-round selections and cash. Dampier was the centerpiece, signing with Golden State in order to complete a sign-and-trade to Dallas after a 12-point, 12-rebound Warriors season. The private canonical Dickau-for-exception row is only one accounting slice of that broader deal. Treating the row as the complete 2004 transaction would conceal most of the value changing hands.

sections.heading: Golden State Obtained Transaction Flexibility, Not Armstrong
sections.body: The Warriors received a trade exception in the August 2004 arrangement, while Dallas received Dickau among its incoming contracts. An exception is a salary-cap accounting mechanism for eligible later transactions, not a player capable of producing minutes or scoring. Contemporary transaction ledgers record the trade exception but also list the additional contracts, cash and draft rights that traveled in the Dampier package. This means Golden State’s C+ in this archived subrecord should not be taken as a comprehensive grade for the full Dampier exchange. The assertion in older copy that Dallas rerouting Dickau somehow gave Golden State’s exception a return was a false link between two unrelated assets. The team that later traded Dickau was Dallas, not Golden State.

sections.heading: Dallas Rerouted Dickau and a Second for Darrell Armstrong
sections.body: Dickau stayed with the Mavericks only until December 3, 2004, when Dallas traded him to the New Orleans Hornets for veteran guard Darrell Armstrong. The Dallas season transaction log also lists a 2005 second-round selection going to New Orleans in that swap; the pick was eventually No. 57 Marcin Gortat. Accordingly, Armstrong cannot be treated as a pure one-for-one return from Dickau. A December 25 contemporary newspaper feature traced Dickau’s repeated moves across several clubs and confirmed his August trip through Golden State and December departure from Dallas. This downstream path is relevant to the limited Dickau component, but it does not reroute Dampier or quantify the Golden State trade exception.

sections.heading: Keep the Archived B and C+ Separate from the Full Deal
sections.body: The private subrecord carries Mavericks B, Warriors C+ and Mavericks Win. Those inherited marks are retained without modifying the canonical asset list, yet they require a clear boundary: Dallas received the rights to Erick Dampier and other players as part of the same 2004 multilateral asset package, and Golden State obtained two draft picks, players, rights, cash and an exception. The basketball-record and RealGM ledgers independently list those broader pieces, including what became the 2007 Petteri Koponen selection. The grade cannot credibly be used as a verdict on that entire deal when this one indexed row contains only Dickau and an exception. The defensible use is a narrow archival comparison, flagged for transaction-provenance reconciliation.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The inherited row reads Mavericks Win, Dallas B, Golden State C+, and remains private. In August 2004 Dallas acquired Dan Dickau as one of four incoming pieces in the broader Erick Dampier sign-and-trade. Golden State received an exception alongside other players, draft rights, picks and cash. Dallas later traded Dickau plus a separate second-round pick to New Orleans for Darrell Armstrong. The subrecord is not a complete grade of the Dampier deal, and the Golden State exception did not become Armstrong. Canonical boundaries and grade interpretation are held for independent provenance review.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Dickau and the 2004 Dampier Sign-and-Trade: Why the Exception Was Only a Slice
featuredDeepDive.intro: August 24, 2004 did not produce a stand-alone Dan Dickau-for-trade-exception basketball trade in the ordinary sense. Dickau moved from Golden State to Dallas inside the larger Erick Dampier sign-and-trade, which carried eight players or draft-rights names, two future firsts and cash. The archived Dallas B/Golden State C+ row captures Dickau and a salary-cap exception rather than the complete deal. Tracing Dickau’s subsequent December trade and keeping the exception on the Warriors side corrects the most misleading part of the old editorial without changing the protected trade ledger.

sections.heading: The Actual August 24 Package Put Dampier First
sections.body: Dallas president Donnie Nelson and the Mavericks had pursued size, and Erick Dampier was the principal acquisition. He had averaged 12.3 points and 12 rebounds in 74 games for the Warriors in 2003-04, a strong performance entering free agency. Golden State completed a sign-and-trade and also sent Dan Dickau, Evan Eschmeyer and Steve Logan’s rights. Dallas shipped Christian Laettner, Eduardo Nájera, Luis Flores and Mladen Sekularac rights, two future first-round selections and cash. UPI’s same-day account and the Washington Post’s August 25 recap agree on the broad flow. Dickau’s secondary role explains why his asset line exists, but it does not justify replacing the broader transaction with a fictional stand-alone deal.

sections.heading: A Golden State Trade Exception Was Not a Draft Pick
sections.body: Golden State’s trade exception was a mechanism for possible salary-matching flexibility. It was not an extra player, and it was not the reason Dallas later received Armstrong. Basketball Reference and RealGM preserve the larger deal with conditional pick descriptions. One of the outgoing 2007 first-round assets eventually connected to No. 30 Petteri Koponen; another protected first did not convey, with a cash payment noted by secondary transaction compilers. The Warriors’ full package therefore had its own complicated outcomes. None of those results can be folded into a two-field archived row without explicitly expanding its historical scope and reconciling its grade.

sections.heading: From Portland to Golden State to Dallas to New Orleans
sections.body: Dickau had arrived in Golden State on July 20, 2004 from Portland alongside Dale Davis for Nick Van Exel. He went to Dallas on August 24 and to New Orleans on December 3. A contemporary Spokesman-Review feature followed his unusually active early-career transaction history and confirms the August and December legs. The December Mavericks-Hornets ledger adds a 2005 second-rounder, later No. 57 Marcin Gortat, to the outgoing Dallas side, with Darrell Armstrong coming back. If the reader is tracing realized returns, that additional pick must accompany the Armstrong link rather than awarding Armstrong solely to Dickau. It is a separate downstream transaction, not a return to the Warriors.

sections.heading: How Much Can the B/C+ Archived Grade Really Say?
sections.body: The stored Mavericks Win verdict and Dallas B versus Golden State C+ marks are unchanged. They are not a valid complete assessment of trading Dampier after his breakout year, nor of the two 2007 first-round picks and other rights. Within the Dickau slice, Dallas obtained a movable guard who was part of a later two-asset exchange, while Golden State acquired a trade exception that offered potential transaction flexibility. The archive is intentionally nonindex and should stay that way until its parent trade and allocation policy are reviewed. The correction here is editorial: explain the historical scope, avoid double-counting later value, and identify exactly where independent provenance is still unresolved.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Dallas B, Golden State C+ and Mavericks Win are preserved as inherited scores for the narrow private Dickau-versus-exception row, not asserted as a fresh grade for the entire Dampier sign-and-trade. Dickau went to Dallas in the August 24 package, then went to New Orleans with a second-round pick for Darrell Armstrong. The Golden State trade exception stayed a Warriors asset. A separate provenance review is required before either club’s full 2004 package can be graded from this fragment.
