sections.heading: What Changed Hands
sections.body: On December 3, 2004, Dallas acquired veteran guard Darrell Armstrong from the New Orleans Hornets. The Hornets received Dan Dickau and a 2005 second-round draft choice that later became No. 57, Marcin Gortat. This was not an equal player swap: New Orleans received both a current guard and a later draft asset, while Dallas obtained one established veteran. The Hornets' franchise is now represented under the Pelicans name in the trade ledger.

sections.heading: How the Realized Value Separated
sections.body: Armstrong could help Dallas immediately with backcourt experience and depth during the mid-2000s. That near-term usefulness was one reason to surrender draft flexibility. New Orleans accepted a different timeline: Dickau was a current player, but the No. 57 selection wouldn't be made until the following summer. Both incoming Hornets items must be included before considering why the recorded verdict favors New Orleans.

sections.heading: Reading the Team Grades
sections.body: The second-round choice is the distinctive piece of the exchange. Its later No. 57 identity, Marcin Gortat, gives the pick an unusually recognizable name. That isn't proof Gortat joined the Hornets as an active player or supplied his later NBA production for New Orleans; draft rights can move again. The historical value of the pick should be traced through any subsequent ownership transaction rather than attributed mechanically to the initial recipient.

sections.heading: How Each Team Viewed the Trade
sections.body: Dallas received Darrell Armstrong and no draft choice in this December transaction. The Mavericks' C grade acknowledges that a veteran could supply useful roster support, even when the other side's package earned a better later assessment. The Hornets' recorded B+ gives weight to Dickau plus the future second-rounder. The comparison doesn't require claiming Armstrong contributed nothing, nor that a recognizable eventual draftee played for the Hornets.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans Win — New Orleans B+, Dallas C. Darrell Armstrong moved to the Mavericks, and the Hornets received Dan Dickau plus the 2005 second-round choice later labeled No. 57, Marcin Gortat. The pick added future value to the New Orleans package, although its eventual draftee's NBA career cannot automatically be assigned to the Hornets. The archived team grades are preserved with that distinction.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Dallas Mavericks–New Orleans Pelicans: What the 2004-12-03 Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: Dallas and the New Orleans Hornets exchanged two different timetables in December 2004. Armstrong moved to Dallas as immediate veteran guard depth; New Orleans took Dan Dickau and a later second-round draft opportunity. The eventual No. 57 label attached to Marcin Gortat is important, but player identity and actual pick ownership are not the same thing. This distinction helps preserve the Pelicans Win verdict without overstating the Hornets' direct benefit from Gortat's career.

sections.heading: Darrell Armstrong Went to Dallas for Dickau and a Future 2nd-Rounder
sections.body: Darrell Armstrong provided the Mavericks with a known backcourt option. He didn't have to wait for the 2005 draft to become available, which gave Dallas a real basketball reason to make the move. New Orleans' return began with Dan Dickau, another active player, but extended beyond him to a second-round selection. This additional item differentiates the exchange from a simple guard-for-guard transaction and explains why both sides deserve their own analysis.

sections.heading: What the Other Side Still Received
sections.body: The 2005 pick later became the No. 57 selection associated with Marcin Gortat. His long NBA career makes the asset interesting in hindsight, but readers shouldn't assume the Hornets received those playing years. The identity label establishes the selection's lineage, not necessarily the team on which the draftee first appeared. Following that right into any subsequent trade is necessary before giving a particular franchise the full benefit of Gortat's NBA production.

sections.heading: Decision Logic Versus Hindsight
sections.body: New Orleans was willing to part with Armstrong for a younger guard and an additional draft opportunity; Dallas chose a more immediate veteran option. The actual 2004 decision involved a player who could play now against one player and a selection that might or might not produce later value. The archived result grades Dallas C and the future Pelicans franchise B+, a judgment made with subsequent outcomes in view. It does not erase the immediate reason Dallas sought Armstrong.

sections.heading: Why the Grade Gap Matters
sections.body: Pelicans Win with New Orleans B+ and Dallas C is the stored outcome. The Hornets received Dickau and a future pick, while Dallas received Armstrong. The grade gap is defensible only if the pick's later value is handled with correct provenance; crediting the Hornets for every game of Gortat's career without checking where his rights went would distort that comparison. The trade's two components on the Hornets' side should remain visible even with that caveat.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Dallas bought near-term guard experience through Armstrong. New Orleans collected a different guard and a second-round selection that later gained a familiar identity. The Hornets' B+ exceeds Dallas's C in the canonical editorial, yet the longer-term draft-right chain must be verified before concluding which franchise realized Gortat's contributions. Pelicans Win can be presented without confusing a future pick label with immediate NBA roster service.

sections.heading: Dallas Moved J.R. Pinnock Rights for a Future Lakers Pick
sections.body: The June 28, 2006 draft-night exchange involved only future-oriented rights. Dallas had selected George Washington guard J.R. Pinnock (also listed as Danilo Pinnock) at No. 58, then sent his rights to Los Angeles. The Lakers returned a 2007 second-round pick, which they had previously received from Miami. The Dallas Mavericks' franchise media guide identifies the 2006 No. 58 selection as traded to the Lakers for a future second, while the Lakers' 2005-06 transaction ledger identifies Renaldas Seibutis as the player selected with the transferred right one year later. Neither club traded a contracted NBA starter, and neither owed the other another veteran player. This was a draft-rights valuation decision, with one team preferring the guard available in 2006 and the other waiting for another selection.

sections.heading: The Dallas Pick Became Renaldas Seibutis at No. 50
sections.body: Dallas exercised the Lakers-origin second-round right in the 2007 draft with the 50th overall selection, choosing Lithuanian guard Renaldas Seibutis. His name appears in the Mavericks' official draft history, and contemporary coverage described him as a 21-year-old player based with Maroussi in Greece. He had professional experience abroad and remained an international stash rather than joining Dallas for its 2007-08 NBA schedule. The draft selection represented real scouting optionality, but the club did not obtain regular-season games from him during the Dallas period. His later European basketball career cannot be treated as NBA playing production for the Mavericks. The transaction's only realized draft conversion was the No. 50 right becoming his NBA rights. It did not produce an NBA roster contributor, so the grade requires that explicit limitation.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Got Pinnock, Not Another Mavericks Player
sections.body: The Lakers acquired the rights to Pinnock, a 6-foot-5 guard from George Washington who had been selected late in the 2006 second round. The Lakers did not receive Maurice Ager, Dallas's first-round selection, or a cash payment from this particular exchange. Pinnock did not establish an NBA regular-season career with Los Angeles. A draft right can have utility through summer-league evaluation and a possible contract negotiation, but neither opportunity should be conflated with confirmed NBA games. The important Lakers result is therefore the failure of the incoming prospect rights to develop into a lasting team contributor. The club had the ability to consider Pinnock, rather than the certainty of receiving 2006-07 rotation depth. In hindsight, giving up the 2007 No. 50 opportunity did not cost an eventual NBA star.

sections.heading: The Even Verdict Is About Two Unused NBA Opportunities
sections.body: Dallas finished with Seibutis's draft rights and no NBA regular-season production from the guard. Los Angeles finished with Pinnock's rights and no Lakers regular-season production from him. That is a balanced completed on-court result for this particular 2006 deal, though the prospects followed different overseas and domestic development paths. The original canonical ledger grades both B-minus and calls the exchange Even Trade. Those inherited letters should not be interpreted as evidence of substantial NBA playing value for either franchise. Both organizations obtained a legitimate draft evaluation option without a successful NBA roster conversion. That distinction is more meaningful than a generic assertion that each side won or that valuable second-round picks always turn into players. The known asset history supports an even outcome with a modest rather than exceptional practical return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Dallas B-, Los Angeles B-. The Mavericks moved J.R. Pinnock rights to the Lakers for a 2007 second used on No. 50 Renaldas Seibutis. Neither Pinnock nor Seibutis played NBA regular-season games for the acquiring club. The matching grades are inherited; this was a balanced, unconverted prospect-rights exchange.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: J.R. Pinnock Rights for the 2007 No. 50 Pick: Seibutis and the Lakers
featuredDeepDive.intro: The 2006 draft-night transaction sent Pinnock rights from Dallas to Los Angeles for a future second. Dallas used the 2007 pick on Seibutis at No. 50. Both rights remained unconverted into NBA regular-season games for their acquiring clubs.

sections.heading: Dallas's Draft-Night Choice Deferred Its Opportunity by a Year
sections.body: By drafting Pinnock at No. 58 and immediately sending his rights to Los Angeles, Dallas turned a current rookie prospect into a future selection. The return was a 2007 second-round choice that originally had belonged to Miami and later came through the Lakers. In 2007 Dallas selected Seibutis with that No. 50 pick. The draft position improved numerically by eight places, but the rights changed draft classes, so it would be simplistic to call the trade an automatic eight-place talent upgrade. Every draft cohort offers different players and different team needs. Dallas obtained a choice it could use after a further year of scouting and selected a Lithuanian professional who remained outside the NBA. That outcome should be reported as a converted selection and retained rights rather than Mavericks regular-season scoring, assists or starts.

sections.heading: Seibutis's International Career Did Not Become Mavericks Games
sections.body: Contemporary Mavs Moneyball coverage described Seibutis as a young Lithuanian guard playing for Maroussi Athens, with an attacking style and draft evaluation focused on his professional European production. Dallas used the No. 50 choice on him in 2007, a factual draft result supported by NBA and Basketball-Reference records. He did not suit up in an NBA regular-season game for Dallas. International basketball can be a meaningful career, and the NBA draft is not the only measure of player quality, but the ledger here evaluates the NBA returns of the specific trading franchises. Seibutis's rights continued to have theoretical negotiation value without producing Mavericks playing minutes. His status differs from a drafted NBA guard who later came off the bench for a season; there were no Dallas appearances to credit.

sections.heading: J.R. Pinnock Was a Legitimate Guard Prospect, Not a Lakers Veteran
sections.body: Pinnock was one of Dallas's two choices in 2006, picked 58th after the Mavericks selected Maurice Ager in the first round. The Lakers obtained Pinnock's rights directly in this deal. His George Washington playing record gave Los Angeles an opportunity to evaluate an athletic college guard without using its own 2006 draft pick on him. Yet the available NBA transaction and draft ledgers show no Lakers regular-season output from Pinnock. It would be wrong to import a later international contract, a summer appearance, or a collegiate scoring average into the Lakers' NBA box score. The outcome represents an unconverted prospect right, which is particularly relevant when comparing it with Dallas's later international selection. Both teams spent draft-rights capital on players who did not enter their regular-season rotations.

sections.heading: B-Minus on Both Sides Does Not Mean Both Found Stars
sections.body: The preserved grades are Dallas B-minus, Lakers B-minus, and the recorded verdict is Even Trade. The best historical explanation is not that both teams received substantial NBA production, but that neither team's right turned into an NBA regular-season contributor. Dallas used the incoming 2007 second on Seibutis; Los Angeles received Pinnock from the 2006 No. 58 selection. Both prospects offered some chance of future value when the teams made the trade, and both opportunities remained unrealized on NBA game nights. This is a low-stakes exchange, distinct from pick swaps involving future All-Stars. The unchanged B-minus marks are inherited editorial grades; the accompanying explanation should state their limits instead of using identical generic paragraphs as proof of value. Neither front office secured a decisive completed competitive edge.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Dallas B-minus, Lakers B-minus in the preserved Even Trade verdict. Dallas used the future No. 50 right on Seibutis after sending Pinnock to Los Angeles. Neither incoming right became regular-season NBA production for the recipient. The historical result is even, but not a story of two productive rotation additions.

sections.heading: What Changed Hands
sections.body: Dallas sent Marquis Daniels to Indiana for Austin Croshere on July 12, 2006, a one-for-one player exchange without additional cash or draft consideration recorded in the two franchise transaction ledgers. Daniels was 25 and had started 29 games in Dallas' 2005-06 Finals season. Croshere was 31 and had spent the previous eight seasons with Indiana, averaging 8.2 points and 5.3 rebounds the year before the trade. Dallas was acquiring experienced frontcourt depth; Indiana was acquiring a younger wing who could play more minutes in the next phase of its roster. The original return needs to be measured by those destination roles, not by the Mavericks' overall win total.

sections.heading: How the Realized Value Separated
sections.body: Indiana B versus Dallas C+ reflects a clear difference in the roles the acquired players ultimately filled. Daniels played 173 Pacers games over three seasons, averaging 9.6 points and starting 48 times. His 2008-09 season included 43 starts in 54 games and 13.6 points per game. Croshere contributed to 61 Mavericks games in one season, starting twice and averaging 3.7 points in 11.9 minutes. Both offered utility, but the Indiana return was longer and more productive. Daniels' injuries and uneven outside shooting kept him from becoming an elite wing, which makes a B more proportionate than an A. The grade pairing describes an ordinary trade with a real Pacers edge.

sections.heading: Reading the Team Grades
sections.body: Croshere's contribution was not zero, but it was substantially smaller than his Indiana role. For Dallas in 2006-07, he appeared 61 times, produced 227 points and 186 rebounds, and shot 35.1 percent from the field. He had been a 23-minute-per-game player for Indiana in 2005-06; under Avery Johnson he averaged fewer than twelve minutes. Dallas won 67 games and finished first in the Western Conference during his season there, but those team results cannot be credited primarily to a reserve who started twice. The Mavericks then lost to Golden State in six games in the first round. Croshere provided one year of depth, an acceptable C+ return rather than a durable trade win.

sections.heading: What Each Franchise Was Actually Evaluating
sections.body: Daniels supplied Indiana with a more sustained perimeter option. He played 45 games with four starts during 2006-07, followed by 74 games with one start in 2007-08. His role expanded in 2008-09 to 54 games, 43 starts and 1,700 minutes, delivering 733 points and 4.6 rebounds per game. His Pacers tenure totaled 1,659 points across 173 games. Indiana did not make the playoffs in any of those three seasons, and Daniels was not a star; those limits prevent an inflated result. However, his final-season workload and three years of rotation appearances gave Indiana significantly more direct basketball value than Dallas received from Croshere's single reserve season.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pacers Win — Indiana B, Dallas C+. Daniels played 173 Pacers games over three seasons, totaling 1,659 points and starting 43 times in 2008-09 alone. Croshere played 61 games for Dallas in one season, scoring 227 points. Indiana acquired longer-lived wing production; Dallas acquired short-term veteran depth. Neither player became an All-Star for his new club or directly delivered a championship through this trade.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Marquis Daniels' 173 Pacers Games versus Austin Croshere's Dallas Season
featuredDeepDive.intro: This 2006 trade is a comparison of actual destination-team workloads, not the overall success of either club. The Mavericks used Croshere for 61 games in 2006-07 and moved on. Indiana employed Daniels for three seasons, eventually relying on him for 43 starts in 2008-09. Indiana's historical media guide identifies the July 12 exchange and provides his complete Pacers statistics. With no extra pick or cash asset to dilute the comparison, the core conclusion is straightforward: Daniels grew into a more useful rotation role than Croshere found in Dallas. The Pacers' B and Mavericks' C+ need only reflect that measured advantage.

sections.heading: Indiana Pursued a Younger Wing; Dallas Took a Veteran Forward
sections.body: Croshere had just played 50 Pacers games at 23.0 minutes per night in 2005-06, with 8.2 points and 5.3 rebounds. Daniels, then 25, had appeared in 62 Mavericks games with 29 starts, posting 10.2 points and 2.8 assists per game. Indiana was receiving a player younger and potentially more adaptable on the wing; Dallas was receiving an established veteran forward. Neither club received a contingent pick, trade exception or recorded cash line in this exchange. Croshere's earlier playoff experience and Daniels' place on a Finals roster could influence front-office expectations, but the retrospective grade comes from minutes and production after they changed teams.

sections.heading: Croshere Scored 227 Points as a Dallas Reserve
sections.body: Croshere played 727 regular-season minutes for the 2006-07 Mavericks, averaging 11.9 per game. His two starts and 227 total points illustrate that Dallas treated him primarily as a reserve. The team was excellent, going 67-15, yet the top seed's first-round exit against Golden State illustrated how little the regular-season win total says about this specific one-for-one trade. Croshere also appeared in three postseason games for Dallas, so his Mavericks contribution must not be erased. The C+ grade credits what he actually produced for one season, while recognizing that Dallas moved on rather than building a longer role around him.

sections.heading: Daniels Grew from a Reserve into a 43-Start Pacers Season
sections.body: Daniels' Indiana career developed in stages. In 2006-07 he played 45 games and scored 320 points. In 2007-08 he played 74 games and reached 606 points, functioning mainly as a reserve. In 2008-09 he started 43 of his 54 appearances and scored 733 points, the best season of this three-year Pacers stretch. The official Indiana roster ledger documents 173 games, 48 starts, 4,046 minutes and 1,659 points overall. Those figures support a meaningful multi-season contribution, but not an All-Star comparison. His three seasons did not include a Pacers playoff run, and accomplishments earned with subsequent franchises do not belong to this deal.

sections.heading: A 112-Game and 46-Start Edge Defines the Measured Return
sections.body: The directly observed roles justify a contained Pacers edge. Daniels played 173 Indiana games, 48 starts and 4,046 minutes across three years, totaling 1,659 points. Croshere gave Dallas 61 games, two starts, 727 minutes and 227 points in one season. Indiana therefore received 112 more appearances, 46 more starts and a much larger total scoring contribution from the player it acquired. That is a larger workload without a claim that Daniels became an All-Star or carried the Pacers into the playoffs. Dallas's 67-win 2006-07 team was powered by far more than Croshere; the 67 wins cannot be assigned to his trade return. The original Indiana B and Dallas C+ ratings fit this limited but real difference.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pacers Win — Indiana B, Dallas C+. Daniels provided three seasons, 173 appearances and 48 starts with Indiana, highlighted by 13.6 points per game in 2008-09. Croshere played 61 Mavericks games and averaged 3.7 points in 2006-07. Those destination-specific outcomes substantiate a modest Indiana edge without attributing the Mavericks' 67 wins or unrelated future successes to this player-for-player transaction.

sections.heading: Dallas Paid Three Players for an Immediate Backup Guard
sections.body: The Mavericks acquired Anthony Johnson from Indiana on July 24, 2006. The Pacers received Darrell Armstrong, Josh Powell and Rawle Marshall, a three-player package with sharply different career stages. Johnson was an experienced point guard brought in to supplement a Dallas rotation preparing to contend again after reaching the 2006 NBA Finals. Indiana exchanged one established backcourt option for veteran leadership and two less established roster candidates. The documented trade contains those four players, not a draft pick or cash payment.

sections.heading: Johnson Was Not a Long-Term Dallas Piece
sections.body: Johnson gave Dallas another point guard during the first part of the 2006–07 season, but the arrangement did not last through the campaign. On February 22, 2007, the Mavericks sent him to Atlanta for a second-round selection that became No. 34 Nick Fazekas. That is a traceable downstream return from the incoming guard. It does not retroactively make Johnson an All-Star, but it means Dallas recovered another tradable asset instead of receiving only a few months of backcourt depth.

sections.heading: Indiana Acquired Three Different Kinds of Roster Value
sections.body: Armstrong arrived as a veteran organizer, Powell as a younger frontcourt prospect and Marshall as an additional wing option. Their incoming value should not be described as three equal starters; each offered a separate, more limited role. Indiana received immediate experienced guard depth and prospects it could evaluate. Those were real personnel returns even if no one player was guaranteed to replace Johnson’s playmaking. The package gave the Pacers several paths to useful roster contribution rather than tying the entire deal to one veteran guard.

sections.heading: A Small Pacers Edge, Not a Major Dallas Failure
sections.body: The canonical scores are Pacers B and Mavericks C-plus, with Pacers Win. Indiana’s additional player options explain the narrow preference, while Johnson’s short Dallas stint and later second-round compensation deserve credit on the other side. The grade gap is modest because both clubs received plausible basketball value and neither established a centerpiece through this exchange. The March or April results of unrelated Mavericks transactions cannot be assigned to this deal.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pacers Win — Indiana B, Dallas C-plus. The Pacers received Armstrong, Powell and Marshall as multiple roster options; Dallas got experienced guard Anthony Johnson, then moved him to Atlanta in February 2007 for the pick used on Nick Fazekas. That downstream asset limits the Mavericks’ downside. The recorded grade gap favors Indiana, but neither package produced a franchise-defining return.

sections.heading: Dallas Bought a Different Draft Prospect
sections.body: Dallas acquired the draft rights to Reyshawn Terry from Orlando on June 28, 2007. The Mavericks sent the draft rights to Milovan Rakovic and cash. Both rights were distinct prospects selected during the 2007 draft, and neither club was moving a long-established rotation player. The transaction gave Dallas the specific wing it preferred while Orlando took a different prospect and immediate financial consideration. The recorded cash leg should not be assigned an invented dollar figure.

sections.heading: The Rights Created Opportunities, Not Certain NBA Production
sections.body: Terry was a developmental wing prospect, and Rakovic was a frontcourt prospect whose future NBA availability was uncertain. The value of either selection depended on signing and future performance, not simply being listed as draft property. Dallas was not receiving a guaranteed starting wing, just as Orlando was not necessarily obtaining a future regular center. The exchange is better understood as a modest rearrangement of individual draft evaluations than as a major completed roster transformation.

sections.heading: Equal Grades Reflect the Documented Outcome
sections.body: Both Dallas and Orlando carry C-plus and the archive returns Even Trade. The Mavericks obtained Terry’s rights; the Magic obtained Rakovic’s rights and cash. No source-supported later rotation breakthrough or additional asset chain overturns the even assessment. The cash is real consideration, but the amount is not verified in the available transaction references and cannot be converted into a fabricated basketball return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Dallas C-plus, Orlando C-plus. Dallas received Reyshawn Terry’s draft rights, while Orlando acquired Milovan Rakovic’s rights and cash. The clubs exchanged development possibilities rather than established performers. Neither recorded rights outcome provides enough identified NBA production to establish a decisive winner.

sections.heading: Dallas and Minnesota Swapped Veteran Wings
sections.body: The Mavericks acquired Trenton Hassell from the Timberwolves on September 28, 2007, sending Greg Buckner in return. Both were experienced perimeter players valued in part for defense and complementary lineups. Dallas was seeking another versatile wing alongside its established scoring core; Minnesota was adjusting its roster after a transformative summer. No draft pick or cash is recorded as additional consideration in this two-player exchange.

sections.heading: Hassell and Buckner Offered Similar Types of Work
sections.body: Hassell brought a reputation for taking difficult perimeter assignments and playing without a high-volume scoring role. Buckner was also valued for defense and veteran reliability. Minnesota and Dallas therefore did not exchange dramatically different positions or upside profiles. Each franchise obtained a known NBA role player and gave up another. The useful question is how the incoming wing fit the team, not whether a nominal salary move counts as a basketball victory.

sections.heading: The Equal B-minus Verdict Fits the Close Comparison
sections.body: The archive assigns Dallas B-minus and Minnesota B-minus. Neither club received an emerging franchise star or an extra first-round pick, and the recorded returns were of comparable role-player caliber. The 2007 timing is useful: Dallas wanted to supplement a contender, while Minnesota was rebuilding. The same trade can be understandable for two clubs in different competitive positions without producing a pronounced winner.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Dallas B-minus, Minnesota B-minus. Hassell went to the Mavericks; Buckner went to the Timberwolves. Both teams exchanged established defensive-minded wings with similar role profiles, making the balanced grades more defensible than awarding a decisive win for a minor veteran adjustment.

sections.heading: One Dallas Wing for Two Future Picks, a Veteran and Cash
sections.body: On October 10, 2008, Dallas acquired Shawne Williams from Indiana. The Pacers received the veteran Eddie Jones, approximately $1.8 million in cash, the Mavericks' 2009 second-round selection and another conditional Dallas second-round selection for 2010 or 2011. The 2009 pick became No. 52 A.J. Price; the later draft right is recorded at 2010 No. 57 Ryan Reid. The option language represents one contingent second-rounder, not a pair of additional picks. Dallas hoped an athletic young forward could find a useful role beside an established veteran core. Indiana chose draft flexibility and cash instead of continuing to develop Williams. It is important to distinguish an asset sent in a draft-pick slot from any player's later work for clubs that never acquired the player in this specific exchange.

sections.heading: Williams Played Just 15 Mavericks Games
sections.body: The direct Dallas outcome was exceptionally small. Williams appeared in 15 regular-season Mavericks games in 2008-09, never started and averaged 2.8 points across 11.3 minutes. His shooting percentage was 28.6%, and he spent 2009-10 without an NBA appearance even though his contract stayed on Dallas' books until a later transaction. Those are the minutes attributable to this trade. His subsequent appearances for New York and New Jersey should not be retroactively credited to Dallas. The inherited Dallas D captures a limited player return relative to a package containing cash and multiple draft opportunities. The 15-game figure is a better measure of the Dallas result than Williams' earlier first-round draft status in 2006.

sections.heading: A.J. Price Produced Indiana Minutes; Ryan Reid Was a Separate Asset
sections.body: Indiana used the 2009 No. 52 selection on guard A.J. Price, who played 56 Pacers games as a rookie and another 50 the following season. Price eventually logged 150 regular-season appearances for Indiana through 2011-12, a measurable reserve-guard return that exceeds Williams' brief Dallas usage in its own right. The second-rights chain identifies No. 57 Ryan Reid in 2010, but Reid was subsequently transferred onward rather than becoming a long-term Indiana NBA player. Price and Reid therefore cannot be counted as identical on-court contributors. Eddie Jones was a veteran contract, not a player who supplied years of additional Pacers production from this transaction. The roughly $1.8 million payment provided financial value, but cash has no directly comparable points-per-game statistic.

sections.heading: Indiana Received More Direct NBA Value Than Dallas
sections.body: The direct return supports a Pacers Win. Dallas received just 15 regular-season appearances from Shawne Williams, with no starts and 2.8 points per game. Indiana obtained Eddie Jones, approximately $1.8 million in cash and two second-round opportunities. No. 52 A.J. Price supplied 150 regular-season Pacers games, while the right that became No. 57 Ryan Reid did not yield a comparable Indiana playing stint. The Pacers' C-plus and Mavericks' D grades recognize a modest but measurable Indiana return without treating every future draft right as an NBA contributor.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pacers Win — Indiana C+, Dallas D. Williams played just 15 Mavericks regular-season games at 2.8 points per appearance, while Indiana received Eddie Jones, about $1.8 million in cash and two second-round opportunities. One became A.J. Price, who logged 150 Pacers games; the other was tied to No. 57 Ryan Reid and should not be credited with additional Pacers NBA minutes. Indiana secured the more useful return, but its draft choices and cash should be evaluated separately rather than credited with unearned production.

sections.heading: What Changed Hands
sections.body: Dallas took the draft rights to Nick Calathes from Minnesota on June 25, 2009. The Timberwolves received cash and a 2010 second-round selection described as the less favorable of Portland's and Chicago's picks, later recorded at No. 51 for Magnum Rolle. Because the pick carried a comparative condition, its identity should not be rewritten as a simple Mavericks-owned selection with no restrictions. Neither side traded an established NBA rotation player on this draft night.

sections.heading: The Two Teams Obtained Rights, Not an Immediate NBA Player
sections.body:
In the 2009 draft Minnesota chose Nick Calathes at No. 45 and sold his NBA rights to Dallas. The Mavericks compensated Minnesota with an unspecified cash payment and a previously acquired 2010 second-rounder defined as the less favorable of Portland and Chicago selections. Pro Sports Transactions traces that right to No. 51 Magnum Rolle. None of the compensation required Calathes to report to Dallas, and he remained in Europe for four more seasons.

Minnesota did not turn this pick directly into a Timberwolves rookie. It forwarded that selection, together with another 2010 second-rounder and Etan Thomas, to Oklahoma City on July 27, 2009 in return for Chucky Atkins and Damien Wilkins. Dallas held the Calathes rights until 2013, when they became a negotiable asset in a separate Memphis agreement. The grades are B for each team and the canonical decision is an even trade, reflecting two forms of transferable value rather than equal numbers of NBA games.

sections.heading: The No. 51 Pick Left Minnesota Before the 2010 Draft
sections.body:
The full chain matters because the name Magnum Rolle can make it appear that Minnesota drafted or developed him. The future selection Dallas sent to Minnesota was the less favorable of external 2010 second-round positions. The Timberwolves passed it along to the Thunder the next month in a larger deal involving Etan Thomas, Chucky Atkins and Damien Wilkins, so the later rights to Rolle were in Oklahoma City control when the 2010 draft arrived. Oklahoma City then sent Rolle rights to Indiana in a draft-night exchange for Ryan Reid rights and cash.

The Pacers, not the Timberwolves, subsequently held Rolle rights. Minnesota obtained a cash payment in the original Calathes exchange and used its pick as one component of a later roster transaction. Crediting the team with Rolle professional career or the full Atkins-Wilkins package would overstate what one pick generated. The outgoing pick is real and traceable, but the later NBA results belong to separate transactions.

sections.heading: Dallas Waited Four Years Before Moving the Calathes Rights
sections.body:
Dallas never brought Calathes into a Mavericks regular-season game. The guard signed in Europe and subsequently played for Panathinaikos and Lokomotiv Kuban while Dallas retained his NBA rights. In July 2013 Memphis acquired those rights. Contemporary reporting explains the return in a less obvious way than another simple second-round choice: Dallas already held Memphis 2016 second-round selection from an earlier trade, and the Grizzlies removed its remaining top-55 protection as consideration for Calathes rights.

The removal of restrictions made an existing Dallas draft-right claim more useful, but it was not a brand-new 2016 second-rounder handed over as part of the original 2009 deal. Memphis rostered Calathes for his NBA career, so his 129 NBA games and 4.6 points per game are not Dallas on-court production. This history supports describing the Mavericks benefit as retained optionality later exchanged for a clearer conditional pick claim.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Dallas B, Minnesota B. The Mavericks received No. 45 Nick Calathes rights in June 2009 and held them until Memphis agreed in 2013 to remove protection from an existing 2016 second-round obligation. Calathes never played for Dallas. Minnesota received cash plus a 2010 selection that became No. 51 Magnum Rolle, but it conveyed that pick onward to Oklahoma City before the draft. The shared grade reflects distinct, tradeable assets and later flexibility rather than pretending Rolle or Calathes played for the original receiving teams.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Nick Calathes Never Played for Dallas: How Minnesota 2009 Pick Became a Memphis 2013 Deal
featuredDeepDive.intro: When Dallas bought Nick Calathes rights from Minnesota on 2009 NBA draft night, the incoming asset was a second-round NBA claim on a player who already had an overseas career in view. Minnesota accepted cash and a 2010 second-rounder that had passed through Portland-related conditions. The two rights moved in different directions: the Timberwolves dealt the future pick to Oklahoma City in weeks, while Dallas kept Calathes four years before dealing with Memphis. Neither team acquired immediate basketball production from the specific player named in the original exchange. Their later negotiating use of those assets is the central reason the inherited even-trade verdict can be discussed without pretending the B/B grades measure identical returns.

sections.heading: Why Calathes Could Be Drafted Yet Not Join Dallas
sections.body:
Minnesota selected Calathes at No. 45 in the 2009 draft and conveyed the rights to Dallas the same night. Calathes chose European basketball instead of an immediate NBA role, and the Mavericks did not compel him to join the roster. He played for Panathinaikos and Lokomotiv Kuban while the club retained the NBA claim. That decision deprived Dallas of a ready reserve guard but did not make the draft rights worthless: a team can hold an unsigned international prospect and later assign his rights as consideration in another transaction.

By July 2013 the guard had established a meaningful European record. Memphis acquired his NBA rights that summer and he subsequently appeared in 129 NBA games, all with the Grizzlies. The correct Dallas outcome is not 129 Calathes games or the rookie contribution he gave Memphis. Dallas owned and eventually traded the rights. That distinction is why the deal must be graded around asset control and the precise later exchange.

sections.heading: The Timberwolves Pick Became No. 51 But Not a Minnesota Draft Selection
sections.body:
The outbound Dallas consideration was the less favorable 2010 second-round pick under conditions tied to Portland and Chicago, ultimately identified as No. 51 Magnum Rolle. Dallas had obtained that conditional second from Portland as part of a separate June 24, 2009 draft-night negotiation. Minnesota received it from Dallas the following day with an unspecified cash payment, then moved the pick to Oklahoma City on July 27 in a package that also included Etan Thomas and another 2010 second.

The Thunder used the No. 51 choice on Rolle and immediately exchanged his rights with Indiana for Ryan Reid rights and cash. Oklahoma City and Indiana, not Minnesota, are the teams directly connected to the player at the 2010 draft. The Timberwolves obtained value from conveying the pick in their earlier Atkins-Wilkins transaction, but assigning the whole value of the larger multi-asset move to Calathes rights would distort the original exchange. The traceable benefit is cash plus a usable pick that Minnesota was able to include in a later deal.

sections.heading: Memphis Removed Protection Rather Than Simply Handing Dallas a New Pick
sections.body:
The 2013 Memphis transaction is easy to misstate. Contemporary FOX Sports and NBC reporting says the Mavericks already held the Grizzlies 2016 second-round pick through an older transaction involving Corey Brewer and Rudy Fernandez. Memphis removed the protection on that existing obligation to acquire Calathes rights. Basketball Reference labels the transaction a second-round pick-for-rights exchange; the reporting supplies the important contractual context. Dallas received improved certainty on an asset it already had, not a fresh unrelated Memphis draft choice created in 2009.

That distinction also prevents an exaggerated claim about the future No. 45 Demetrius Jackson selection. The 2016 pick can have downstream routes, and the NBA games of later rights holders are not Dallas return. Dallas did gain negotiating leverage from an unsigned guard after four years of patient rights ownership. Whether such optionality deserves a B is editorial judgment; no source establishes that Dallas gained a new rotation player from the original trade.

sections.heading: B/B Is a Limited-Scale Verdict, Not Proof the Player Returns Matched
sections.body:
Dallas retained one clear draft-right claim and then improved the terms of an existing future pick obligation. Minnesota received a small cash payment of undisclosed size and a conditioned second-rounder that became part of another roster transaction before the 2010 draft. Neither was acquiring a star or exchanging a protected first-rounder. As a result, a shared B in this historical archive should be read as a positive result relative to modest cost and limited opportunity, not as a declaration that each team realized equal on-court production.

Calathes later Grizzlies appearances and Rolle draft selection are useful identity evidence, but assigning those players NBA totals to the original receiving teams would create a false comparison. This trade is best used to explain how teams acquire, hold and spend rights that may never bring a prospect into their own uniform. The even verdict is defensible only with that narrower asset-value framing.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, Dallas B and Minnesota B. The Mavericks acquired Calathes rights, kept them while he played abroad and ultimately exchanged them in 2013 for Memphis removing protection from a previously held second-round obligation. The Timberwolves received cash and a conditional second that became No. 51 but had already been conveyed to Oklahoma City before Rolle was selected. Dallas did not roster Calathes; Minnesota did not draft Rolle for its own team. Both obtained movable rights, not immediate NBA production.

sections.heading: Dallas Exchanged Jawai and Cash for a Protected Future Pick
sections.body: The Mavericks sent Nathan Jawai and cash considerations to Minnesota on October 20, 2009. Dallas received a 2012 second-round pick protected through the first 55 selections. The ledger says that pick was not exercised. This is an important detail: the Mavericks did not ultimately gain a named 2012 draft prospect from this transaction. Minnesota took an actual player plus money, while Dallas held a conditional possibility that would only convey under narrow circumstances.

sections.heading: Minnesota Received a Center It Could Evaluate Immediately
sections.body: Jawai was an identifiable NBA big man, not a distant draft-rights claim. The Timberwolves could use him for frontcourt depth and decide whether his development justified further roster time. The accompanying cash provided another tangible part of the incoming package, although the amount is not available in the stored transaction sources. Jawai was not a franchise centerpiece, but Minnesota at least received the ability to assess a current player rather than wait for the outcome of a protection clause.

sections.heading: The Top-55 Protection Defines the Dallas Outcome
sections.body: A second-round choice protected through No. 55 would only transfer if it fell among the last five selections of the draft. The record lists this 2012 right as not exercised, so crediting Dallas with an eventual drafted player would create an asset that never arrived. Conditional draft choices have trade-day value as possibilities, but an outcome-based verdict must separate that speculative value from a pick that actually conveys. The unrealized condition limits the Mavericks’ completed return.

sections.heading: Why Minnesota Receives the Higher Grade
sections.body: The source ledger awards Minnesota B-plus and Dallas B-minus, with Wolves Win as the verdict. Minnesota acquired Jawai and cash; Dallas did not obtain a realized second-round selection. This is a relative comparison between two modest packages rather than a claim that Jawai became an elite NBA center. The protected-pick mechanics and cash qualifier explain the historical result without attributing later unrelated Timberwolves or Mavericks transactions to this exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wolves Win — Minnesota B-plus, Dallas B-minus. The Timberwolves acquired Nathan Jawai and cash considerations in 2009. Dallas received a top-55-protected 2012 second-round pick that was not exercised, so no player arrived from the conditional selection. Minnesota obtained the more tangible package even though this remained a small roster transaction.

sections.heading: Dallas Acquired Three Rotation Names for the Playoff Push
sections.body: Dallas obtained Caron Butler, Brendan Haywood, DeShawn Stevenson and cash from Washington on February 13, 2010. The outgoing package included Josh Howard, Drew Gooden, James Singleton and Quinton Ross. This was a deadline trade with a specific team-building purpose: the Mavericks wanted additional established players around their contender rather than a collection of untested future draft assets. Butler provided scoring on the wing, Haywood strengthened the interior rotation, and Stevenson offered a defensive perimeter role. The fact that Dallas received three contributors with different jobs helps explain why the deal's value extended beyond the initial comparison of Butler and Howard.

sections.heading: Haywood and Stevenson Reached the 2011 Title
sections.body: The acquired players didn't all have identical post-trade careers or postseason roles. Butler helped Dallas after arrival but was injured for the 2011 championship run, so the title should not be credited to him as an active Finals contributor. Haywood and Stevenson, by contrast, participated in the championship roster and gave the Mavericks additional lineup options when the postseason demanded them. That distinction supports the grade without inflating any one player's direct minutes. The most persuasive return is a multi-player roster improvement with contributions continuing into a championship season, not a claim that the whole 2011 run came from a single February trade.

sections.heading: The Washington Veterans Could Not Match the Return
sections.body: Washington accepted Josh Howard, Drew Gooden, James Singleton and Quinton Ross in the same exchange, obtaining recognizable veterans but no comparable sustained championship-window impact. Howard was the biggest known name in that group, yet the relative timing and later production favored Dallas. The packages should be traced as they existed in the deal: no first-round picks were the foundation of the original comparison. Washington's return had immediate roster value and a different contractual purpose, but those facts didn't reverse the large gap in achieved results between the clubs.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win. Dallas earns A- for the Butler, Haywood and Stevenson package and its contribution to the club's title window. Washington receives F for Howard, Gooden, Singleton and Ross, whose realized team impact was much smaller. Butler's injury during the 2011 title postseason is part of the history; Haywood and Stevenson were the acquired contributors on that winning roster.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Deep Dive: What Decided Mavericks Win on 2010-02-13
featuredDeepDive.intro: On February 13, 2010 Dallas traded Josh Howard, Drew Gooden, James Singleton and Quinton Ross to Washington for Caron Butler, Brendan Haywood, DeShawn Stevenson and cash. Butler appeared in 56 Dallas regular-season games across 2009-10 and 2010-11 but missed the 2011 championship playoffs after injury. Haywood and Stevenson each made 72 regular-season appearances during the title year; Howard made only 22 Wizards games over two seasons. This separates actual team contributions from broader championship credit.

sections.heading: February 13 Dallas Package Added Three Players Plus Cash
sections.body: Dallas acquired Caron Butler, Brendan Haywood, DeShawn Stevenson and cash in the February 13, 2010 deal with Washington. The Wizards received Josh Howard, Drew Gooden, James Singleton and Quinton Ross. The Washington transaction log records the seven players and date, and the contemporaneous ESPN report separately confirms cash to Dallas, so neither an additional draft pick nor a fourth Mavericks player belongs in this trade. Washington was starting a financial and roster reset, while Dallas wanted veteran depth beside Dirk Nowitzki for its playoff window. Butler was the established scorer, Haywood the interior reserve and Stevenson the defensive wing; all three were distinct incoming Mavericks assets. Washington obtained a formerly productive Dallas forward but also absorbed contracts with differing remaining value. The exchange preceded, but did not itself guarantee, the next season's championship.

sections.heading: Butler Produced Fifty-Six Dallas Games but Missed Title Playoffs
sections.body: Butler appeared in 27 Dallas regular-season games after the trade during 2009-10, starting all of them and averaging 15.2 points. He then played 29 games in 2010-11 with 15.0 points per appearance before a knee injury ended his season. His direct Dallas output across those two years was 56 regular-season games, with no on-court participation in the Mavericks' 2011 championship playoffs. The title therefore cannot be described as a playoff run in which Butler personally scored for Dallas. He helped stabilize the roster before the injury, whereas other incoming players continued to contribute during the postseason. Later Clippers seasons were Butler's work for another franchise and do not increase Dallas basketball production from the 2010 Washington transaction. The archived Mavericks edge survives this necessary player-specific distinction.

sections.heading: Haywood and Stevenson Were Actual Members of the Title Rotation
sections.body: The deal produced durable playoff-era contributions from two players beyond Butler. Haywood appeared in 28 Dallas games during 2009-10 and 72 more in the 2010-11 regular season, working as a backup center on the team that won the Finals. Stevenson made 24 Mavericks appearances after the 2010 deadline and another 72 in 2010-11, with 54 starts during the latter season. He supplied perimeter defensive minutes and timely outside shooting during the championship campaign. Those are direct Dallas appearances rather than later work for different employers. The transaction helped Dallas address more than one roster role at once, which is why a retrospective should not assign its entire success to Butler. The later championship involved Nowitzki and numerous other Mavericks too; Haywood and Stevenson were meaningful members, not exclusive causes.

sections.heading: Washington Howard Played Twenty-Two Games Across Two Seasons
sections.body: Washington received a recognizable former All-Star in Josh Howard, but his post-trade Wizards NBA tenure was limited by injuries. He played four Washington games in 2009-10, then 18 more in 2010-11, totaling 22 receiving-team appearances before moving elsewhere. Drew Gooden was subsequently rerouted in the Wizards' separate February 17, 2010 multi-team trade, so that later transaction cannot be blended into this original Dallas package. Quinton Ross and James Singleton were additional direct Washington acquisitions whose values should be evaluated without claiming Dallas playoff output for them. The source results favor Dallas A-minus over Washington F because the Mavericks gained multiple contributing players and a later title-team role, while the Wizards received a shorter Howard tenure and financial flexibility. The inherited Mavericks Win conclusion stays bounded to these actual asset paths.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win — Dallas A-minus and Washington F preserved from the archive. Butler gave Dallas 56 regular-season games but missed the 2011 championship postseason. Haywood and Stevenson provided legitimate title-season rotation minutes, each appearing in 72 Mavericks regular-season games during 2010-11. Howard played 22 Wizards games across two years, and Gooden moved on in a separate later deal. The grade compares those received assets, not a title accomplished by Butler on the 2011 playoff court.

sections.heading: Toronto Reacquired Its Own 2013 Second in January 2011
sections.body: On January 24, 2011 Dallas sent center Alexis Ajinça, cash considerations and a conditional 2013 second-round selection to Toronto for the NBA draft rights to Greek forward Giorgos Printezis. The pick had originally belonged to Toronto and had been sent to Dallas in the June 2010 Solomon Alabi rights exchange. Returning that future choice was therefore a tangible part of the new package, not an extra first-rounder or an invented player. The Canadian Press report of the January transaction confirms the pick return and the roster move, which accompanied Dallas's signing of Peja Stojaković. Toronto received a young center it could try immediately and regained future draft flexibility. Dallas instead held international rights that did not themselves add an NBA roster contributor.

sections.heading: Ajinça Provided a Brief Raptors Stint, Not His Later Pelicans Career
sections.body: Ajinça had appeared in ten Dallas games earlier during 2010-11 before this transaction; those games cannot be credited as Toronto production. He joined the Raptors after the trade, but the team did not retain him beyond that season. His later NBA comeback and several New Orleans seasons followed a separate free-agent signing years afterward and do not belong in the 2011 Toronto return. The receiving club did obtain a real center and a short evaluation period, not merely an abstract contract. The existing Toronto B-plus grade is strongest when that limited player use is combined with the regained second-round draft asset and later trade flexibility. It should not be defended with any unverified claim that Ajinça became a long-term Raptors starting center or delivered his later Pelicans statistics in Toronto.

sections.heading: Printezis Rights Never Became Dallas NBA Minutes
sections.body: Dallas received the draft rights to Giorgos Printezis, a player selected in the 2007 second round who continued his professional career overseas. Possessing his NBA rights created a potential roster avenue without an immediate player appearance. He did not join the Mavericks for a regular-season game. The rights were later included in a separate multi-team transaction around Dallas's December 2011 Tyson Chandler departure, but the value of that complicated exchange cannot be assigned solely to Printezis. This is why the return can be evaluated without pretending Dallas received no consideration whatsoever or claiming a direct contribution from an overseas player who never suited up. The inherited Mavericks C-plus is a judgment about optionality and subsequent asset control, not NBA points recorded by Printezis for Dallas.

sections.heading: The No. 41 Pick Later Helped a Separate Rudy Gay Deal
sections.body: The second-round selection reacquired by Toronto ultimately became the No. 41 pick in the 2013 NBA draft. Toronto did not use that selection on Jamaal Franklin itself. On January 30, 2013, the Raptors included the choice in a separate three-team trade involving Memphis and Detroit that brought Rudy Gay and Hamed Haddadi to Toronto. Memphis later selected Franklin with the pick. This downstream transaction establishes that the future second had real exchange value to Toronto, but the pick was only one item in the larger 2013 package. Crediting every Rudy Gay point to the original Ajinça-for-Printezis exchange would be misleading. The January 2011 verdict Raptors Win with Toronto B-plus and Dallas C-plus rests on short-term player control plus traceable draft leverage versus unused Mavericks NBA rights.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Raptors Win — Toronto B-plus, Dallas C-plus. Toronto acquired Ajinça, cash of unspecified value and its own 2013 second-round pick back from Dallas. The pick later moved to Memphis in the larger 2013 Rudy Gay transaction and became No. 41 Jamaal Franklin, who was not a Raptors draftee. Dallas obtained Printezis rights, not direct NBA player minutes, and moved those rights through another multi-team deal later in 2011.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Dallas Mavericks–Toronto Raptors: What the 2011-01-24 Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: Dallas sent Alexis Ajinça, cash and Toronto's previously traded 2013 second-round pick back to the Raptors on January 24, 2011 for the rights to Giorgos Printezis. Ajinça had a brief Toronto stay, while the reacquired future choice later entered the 2013 Rudy Gay three-team package and became No. 41 Jamaal Franklin in Memphis. Dallas held Printezis rights but no Mavericks NBA appearances. This review separates that original January exchange from both later multi-asset moves.

sections.heading: Dallas Traded a Center, Cash and a Future Second for Rights
sections.body: The original ledger records three pieces going to Toronto: Alexis Ajinça, unspecified cash considerations and a 2013 second-round selection. Dallas acquired only the draft rights to Giorgos Printezis, who had been selected by San Antonio in 2007 and whose rights Toronto subsequently obtained. The January 2011 deal was not a direct exchange of already-active NBA players; the Mavericks chose optionality rather than a new rotation player. Toronto had already sent the same 2013 second to Dallas the previous June for Solomon Alabi rights, so the pick came back to its original club. The timing matters: the transaction happened while Dallas was arranging a roster spot for Peja Stojaković. The cash amount remains unspecified and should not be assigned an invented figure when comparing the two sides.

sections.heading: Toronto Got a Temporary Center and a Reusable Draft Asset
sections.body: Ajinça was a first-round pick from 2008 whose size gave Toronto an immediate player it could evaluate. His stint with the Raptors was brief and he eventually continued his professional career elsewhere, including a later return to New Orleans. The better downstream asset was the club's own 2013 second-round pick, reacquired in January 2011. In January 2013 Toronto sent the choice to Memphis as part of the separate three-team Rudy Gay transaction, and it became No. 41 Jamaal Franklin. Reusing the selection in a real transaction was not hypothetical value, though the other pieces of that multi-asset deal also contributed to Toronto's return. The source ledger is therefore more informative than judging this exchange solely from the short Ajinça tenure or Franklin's later NBA career.

sections.heading: The Mavericks Held Printezis Rights Rather Than Player Service
sections.body: Printezis was an experienced international forward, but Dallas never received a Mavericks regular-season appearance from him after obtaining his rights. International draft rights can be held, transferred or used if a player eventually joins an NBA team, so they were a legitimate form of consideration on January 24. Later in 2011 those rights moved through another multi-team deal connected with Tyson Chandler, demonstrating that Dallas could transact with the asset rather than simply discard it. The full later package contained multiple players and other rights, which prevents crediting the entire transaction to Printezis alone. Dallas's C-plus therefore recognizes its contingent asset position without fabricating on-court playing time, and the Raptors' B-plus can recognize the future second without claiming Toronto drafted the eventual No. 41 prospect for its own rotation.

sections.heading: A Narrow Raptors Win From the Reacquired Pick and Its Use
sections.body: The retained Raptors Win verdict gives Toronto B-plus and Dallas C-plus, a close retrospective rather than a sweeping condemnation of acquiring draft rights. The Raptors took on Ajinça, whose direct tenure was short, and regained the future second-round pick that helped build a separate January 2013 trade package for Rudy Gay. Dallas took only Printezis' rights, did not roster him for an NBA game and later used those rights within another transaction. Toronto also received unspecified cash, which is real consideration but cannot be priced without a source. Neither team should be credited with Jamaal Franklin's later Memphis games or with the entire result of a multi-asset trade that followed. The advantage is the documented future pick control and its subsequent use rather than a fictional dominant 2011 NBA player.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Toronto B-plus and Dallas C-plus yield a Raptors Win for the restored second-round pick and its subsequent use as one piece of a 2013 trade package. Ajinça's direct Toronto contribution was short, and Printezis never played an NBA game for Dallas. The pick was ultimately exercised by Memphis on Jamaal Franklin, and the later Rudy Gay package involved other assets. The inherited grades are preserved without counting those unrelated downstream NBA careers as a direct 2011 acquisition.

sections.heading: Dallas Sent Two Wings to Denver for One Protected Future Second
sections.body: On December 13, 2011, Dallas shipped Rudy Fernández and Corey Brewer to Denver in exchange for a 2016 second-round selection originally belonging to Memphis. Denver's official December 15 feature confirmed both players and the future pick. The draft choice was protected in the top 55 when the teams struck the agreement, not an unconditional No. 45 asset known five years in advance. Dallas had just won the 2011 championship and was reorganizing a crowded wing rotation ahead of the lockout-delayed season. Denver obtained two playable veterans without surrendering an existing rotation player, while the Mavericks exchanged them for a distant asset whose chance to convey depended on its protections.

sections.heading: Brewer Played Fifty-Nine Games While Fernández Played Thirty-One
sections.body: Denver received immediate basketball minutes from both newcomers. Brewer appeared in 59 of the Nuggets' 66 regular-season games in 2011-12, started 17 and averaged 8.9 points in 21.8 minutes. Fernández appeared 31 times, started once and averaged 8.6 points with 2.4 assists in 22.9 minutes. Those totals show distinct roles: Brewer offered athletic perimeter depth across almost the entire shortened schedule, while Fernández provided another shooter and passer before his season ended early. Neither was an established All-Star leading Denver's offense, yet the pair provided actual wing minutes that Dallas could no longer use. The Nuggets went 38-28, though their record reflected the rest of George Karl's roster too.

sections.heading: Dallas Received a Pick Whose Protection Was Subsequently Changed
sections.body: The second-round right deserves its exact chronology. Basketball-Reference records it as a 2016 second originally protected in picks one through 55; later arrangements removed that protection. The right ultimately corresponded to No. 45 in the 2016 draft, the choice associated with Demetrius Jackson. An independent draft-rights transaction chronology traces the later movement and mentions a July 2013 transaction involving the rights to Nick Calathes, as well as a later Mavericks-Celtics transaction. Those are separate links in the chain rather than additional players Denver sent in 2011. Counting Jackson as an instant Dallas NBA contributor would be particularly misleading; the Mavericks acquired a distant contractual right, not an established young guard.

sections.heading: Nuggets B and Dallas C-Plus Reflect Different Time Horizons
sections.body: The inherited result says Nuggets Win, Denver B and Dallas C-plus. Denver made the better immediate use of its resources by adding Brewer's 59 appearances and Fernández's 31 while giving up one heavily protected future second. Dallas received a right that acquired more certainty through later changes and eventually related to a No. 45 draft selection, but that did not replace two wings during the 2011-12 campaign. Denver's advantage should not be inflated into a franchise-defining steal because neither acquired player became a lasting All-NBA-level centerpiece. Equally, the Mavericks' return should not be assessed as though the pick never existed. The stated grades remain original editorial judgments, with full pick conditions and player roles documented.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win, Denver B and Dallas C-plus are preserved. Denver acquired Brewer, who played 59 games in 2011-12, and Fernández, who played 31. Dallas received a Memphis-origin 2016 second originally protected in the top 55; later moves changed the condition, and the eventual No. 45 right related to Demetrius Jackson. Later Calathes and Celtics asset transactions are not additional pieces exchanged in December 2011. The short-term playing minutes favor Denver, but the original grades are retained without overstating either side's upside.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Rudy Fernández and Corey Brewer for a Protected 2016 Second: Denver's December 2011 Trade
featuredDeepDive.intro: Denver acquired two former Dallas wings in December 2011 for a Memphis-origin 2016 second-round right initially protected in the top 55. Brewer played 59 Nuggets games and Fernández 31 during the lockout-shortened 2011-12 season. Dallas held a future asset whose protections and ownership changed later, eventually tied to the No. 45 Demetrius Jackson selection. The original Denver B, Dallas C-plus, Nuggets Win result is evaluated against these actual dates and participant records.

sections.heading: A Lockout-Compressed December Created Denver's Opportunity
sections.body: The 2011 NBA lockout compressed training camps, signings and roster changes into a short December period. Dallas had recently acquired Fernández through a different transaction after his Portland tenure, while Brewer was coming off limited Dallas appearances and a championship as a depth player. Denver needed wings and benefited from obtaining both without losing a current player. ESPN's same-day report confirms the December 13 date, the two incoming Nuggets and the Memphis-origin 2016 second. The earlier Fernández trade that also affected Andre Miller and Raymond Felton is not part of this one, and it would be inaccurate to credit Dallas or Denver with that prior package twice. This is a narrow two-players-for-one-future-rights move.

sections.heading: Brewer's Season-Long Workload Was the Main Direct Return
sections.body: The 66-game 2011-12 season gives a clear way to weigh Denver's immediate acquisition. Corey Brewer made 59 appearances and 17 starts, averaging 8.9 points in 21.8 minutes. Rudy Fernández played 31 games, scored 8.6 per game and made 32.8 percent of his threes. Fernández's shorter tenure and Brewer's steadier availability are not equivalent, and neither should be described through vague promises of future star power. They added guard-forward rotation options to a 38-28 playoff club that also relied on Ty Lawson, Danilo Gallinari and others. The direct price was a future second-round right. Those concrete season counts explain why Denver received a favorable B grade without requiring that the players produce championship-level scoring.

sections.heading: The No. Forty-Five Conversion Came Through Multiple Later Moves
sections.body: Dallas acquired a protected future second, with original top-55 language that potentially could have prevented the pick's conveyance. Later agreements changed that condition; the final 2016 No. 45 selection is associated with Demetrius Jackson. A draft transaction ledger connects the rights to a later deal involving Nick Calathes and a subsequent Mavericks-Celtics trade in December 2014. None of those subsequent trades changes what the Nuggets gave up on December 13, 2011. Denver surrendered the underlying draft interest once, while Dallas managed or moved the resulting right as its front office made later decisions. It is important not to confuse a pick's eventual selected name with someone who ever played NBA games for the original acquiring club.

sections.heading: What the Original B and C-Plus Grades Can Justify
sections.body: Denver B and Dallas C-plus are preserved alongside Nuggets Win. The immediate comparison is favorable for Denver: Brewer's 59 games and Fernández's 31 gave it two useful rotation options in a shortened playoff season for the price of one uncertain far-off second. Dallas's side was not a direct player contributor but an asset that eventually appeared at No. 45 after protections were amended and rights moved. The difference in chronology cautions against automatically awarding the entire subsequent Demetrius Jackson draft outcome to Dallas or making later Calathes and Celtics transactions part of Denver's initial return. This is a moderate advantage grounded in actual roster use, not proof that both Dallas's veteran wings were stars or that its draft right lacked value.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Denver B and Dallas C-plus grades, and Nuggets Win verdict, stay in place. Corey Brewer contributed 59 games and 17 starts to the 2011-12 Nuggets while Rudy Fernández appeared 31 times. In exchange, Dallas acquired a protected Memphis-origin 2016 second whose top-55 restriction was later changed; the right eventually tied to 2016 No. 45 Demetrius Jackson through additional asset-chain moves. The Nuggets received useful immediate wing depth. Dallas gained a contingent pick, not another established player or a certain 2016 starter. Tracing subsequent Calathes and Celtics dealings is useful for provenance but must not silently rewrite the December 13, 2011 transaction.

sections.heading: Chandler Returned to Dallas with Raymond Felton
sections.body: Dallas reacquired Tyson Chandler from New York in June 2014, adding Raymond Felton in the same deal. The Mavericks sent Jose Calderon, Shane Larkin, Wayne Ellington, Samuel Dalembert and two 2014 second-round picks. The agreement was broader than a veteran-center swap, but Chandler was the player Dallas most wanted: a proven rim protector who had already helped the franchise win the 2011 championship during his earlier Mavericks tenure. His return gave the team another season with a starting center capable of anchoring its defense. That direct post-trade value must be assessed separately from the championship that occurred three years before this transaction.

sections.heading: New York Took Four Players and Two Picks
sections.body: New York received Calderon, Larkin, Ellington and Dalembert plus the No. 34 pick used on Cleanthony Early and No. 51 used on Thanasis Antetokounmpo. Calderon provided an established playmaking option, Larkin was a younger guard and the draft choices offered two chances to improve the roster. Each named item matters for identifying the package; it would be inaccurate to say the Knicks acquired only one veteran in exchange for Chandler. The selection names should also be distinguished from any later careers after players' rights changed hands. The trade yielded quantity, but not an equivalent replacement for Chandler's immediate interior contribution to Dallas.

sections.heading: The Mavericks Won through the Most Valuable Player
sections.body: Felton supplied another guard option while Chandler became the clear headliner of Dallas's return. The Mavericks' 2014-15 season benefited from his rebounding and defense, though the team did not repeat its earlier title run. New York's package included NBA veterans and draft rights, so its return deserves more than an automatic failing grade. The difference is that Dallas received a starting center who immediately raised the standard of its lineup, whereas the Knicks spread their compensation across several smaller roster and development possibilities. Hindsight should compare those actual team tenures, not assume every future achievement by a drafted player belonged to New York.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win. Dallas earns B+ for Tyson Chandler's return and Raymond Felton. New York receives B- for Calderon, Larkin, Ellington, Dalembert and two second-round picks later used on Early and Antetokounmpo. The Mavericks gained the strongest immediate contributor, but the Knicks' six-part return had meaningful roster and draft utility.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Deep Dive: What Decided Mavericks Win on 2014-06-25
featuredDeepDive.intro: Dallas reacquired Tyson Chandler with Raymond Felton from New York on June 25, 2014, surrendering Jose Calderon, Shane Larkin, Wayne Ellington, Samuel Dalembert and second-round picks Nos. 34 and 51. Chandler started 75 Mavericks games in 2014-15, averaging 10.3 points and 11.5 rebounds, while Felton played 109 Mavericks games over the next two seasons. New York got 114 Calderon starts, 56 Cleanthony Early appearances at No. 34 and two Thanasis Antetokounmpo appearances at No. 51, in addition to the other acquired players.

sections.heading: June 25, 2014: Dallas Reacquired Tyson Chandler Plus Felton
sections.body: The Knicks sent Tyson Chandler and Raymond Felton to Dallas on June 25, 2014 for Jose Calderon, Shane Larkin, Wayne Ellington, Samuel Dalembert and two 2014 second-round picks, Nos. 34 and 51. New York's contemporaneous official release lists the full player-and-draft-rights exchange, not simply a one-for-one Chandler-Calderon move. Dallas wanted its 2011 championship center back beside Dirk Nowitzki, and also accepted an experienced reserve point guard. Phil Jackson's Knicks sought more bodies and contract flexibility while changing the roster. The draft choices were not yet named prospects on June 25; one subsequently became Cleanthony Early and the other Thanasis Antetokounmpo. The trade offered Dallas immediate interior talent and a second guard option, whereas New York distributed its return among four veterans and two draft opportunities.

sections.heading: Chandler Played Seventy-Five Dallas Games Before Leaving Again
sections.body: Chandler started each of the 75 regular-season games he played for Dallas in 2014-15. His averages of 10.3 points and 11.5 rebounds supplied the Mavericks reliable interior efficiency and rim protection during that campaign. His 2011 title with Dallas was a previous Mavericks stint and should explain organizational familiarity, not be counted as championship hardware won through a 2014 acquisition. Chandler left for Phoenix in 2015 free agency, so his subsequent Suns appearances and later NBA service belong to other transactions. Felton, the second Dallas piece, played 29 games in 2014-15 and 80 in 2015-16, 109 regular-season Dallas appearances over two seasons. The combination yielded a one-season starting center and continuing backcourt coverage, not another multi-year Chandler tenure that should be assumed from his prior career.

sections.heading: Calderon Had 114 Knicks Games and Two-Year Starter Service
sections.body: New York did not get only speculative second-round choices. Calderon played 42 Knicks regular-season games in 2014-15 and another 72 in 2015-16, starting each of those 114 appearances. He averaged 9.1 points and 4.7 assists in the first season, then 7.6 points and 4.1 assists in the second. That is substantial if modest point-guard service. Larkin, Ellington and Dalembert were separate incoming assets, and the 2014 deal was explicitly broader than Calderon versus Chandler. Their playing time, however, cannot be conflated with the Knicks' draft selections, and their later movement through other teams requires separate transactions. The archived New York B-minus grade therefore accounts for actual guard starts as well as asset optionality, even though Dallas received the better immediate center return.

sections.heading: Early and Thanasis Picks Became Real but Limited NBA Returns
sections.body: The first incoming second-round right became No. 34 Cleanthony Early in the June 2014 draft. Early appeared in 39 Knicks games in 2014-15 and 17 in 2015-16, totaling 56 regular-season New York appearances. The other selection became No. 51 Thanasis Antetokounmpo, who appeared for the Knicks in two NBA games during 2015-16. His later lengthy Milwaukee tenure is not Knicks on-court value attributable to the original June trade. The actual Knicks outcomes therefore include 114 Calderon starts, 56 Early games and two Thanasis appearances, alongside the other three players in the incoming package. Dallas got 75 Chandler games and 109 Felton appearances over their respective stays. The preserved Mavericks Win, Dallas B-plus versus New York B-minus, is a measured retrospective favoring the center acquisition without erasing New York's real player and pick returns.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win, Dallas B-plus versus Knicks B-minus as archived. Chandler's return gave Dallas 75 starts and 11.5 rebounds per game in 2014-15 before he left for Phoenix; Felton supplied 109 Mavericks regular-season games over two seasons. New York obtained 114 Calderon starts, two second-round players who logged 56 Early and two Thanasis Knicks appearances, plus Larkin, Ellington and Dalembert. The 2011 Dallas championship and Thanasis's later Bucks service are distinct team histories, not direct 2014 trade NBA output.
