sections.heading: What Changed Hands—and What Lasted
sections.body: Dallas acquired veteran center Zaza Pachulia from Milwaukee on July 9, 2015 for a conditional 2018 second-round pick protected through No. 55. The Mavericks' announcement confirms the exchange, while Milwaukee's transaction history establishes that the selection never conveyed. A pick with that protection could transfer only if Dallas' original second-round position landed in the final five slots of the round; it wasn't an unconditional draft choice. Pachulia arrived after a 73-game Bucks season in which he had averaged 8.3 points, 6.8 rebounds and 2.4 assists. Dallas needed a capable center immediately, but its future compensation to Milwaukee was unusually limited. The difference between acquiring a known contributor and surrendering only a contingent pick defined the deal from the outset.

sections.heading: How the Margin Became Clear
sections.body: The 2015-16 results made the exchange lopsided. Pachulia started 69 of his 76 regular-season games for Dallas, averaging 8.6 points, 9.4 rebounds and 1.7 assists across 26.4 minutes. He also collected 249 offensive rebounds and helped fill the center spot on a 42-win playoff team. Milwaukee did not receive a player from this exchange, and its 2018 conditional second-round selection expired without transferring. The Bucks' actual basketball return was therefore zero, even though freeing a veteran's place on the roster could have been a trade-day objective. Dallas B+ and Milwaukee D+ describe one useful season acquired at negligible realized draft cost; they do not imply Pachulia's later Golden State championships happened in a Mavericks uniform.

sections.heading: The Return That Carried the Deal: Dallas Mavericks
sections.body: Pachulia became Dallas' most-used center in his lone Mavericks season. He logged 2,004 regular-season minutes, more than Salah Mejri, JaVale McGee and the other reserve centers, while grabbing 718 total rebounds. The 9.4 per-game rebounding average was his highest across a full NBA season to that point. He supplied interior rebounding and screening alongside Dirk Nowitzki as Rick Carlisle's club went 42-40 and earned the West's No. 6 seed. The playoff run ended in five games against Oklahoma City, so the trade did not deliver a deep postseason payoff or a multi-season Dallas starter. It did provide dependable center minutes without consuming an eventually conveyed second-round asset. A B+ captures that narrow but highly efficient return.

sections.heading: The Return That Could Not Match It: Milwaukee Bucks
sections.body: Milwaukee exchanged a center who had just played 73 games and started 45 for a highly conditional 2018 draft claim. With protection through No. 55, the pick could transfer only if Dallas landed in one of the round's last five positions. That didn't happen: the Mavericks held the No. 33 selection in 2018, and the Bucks' conditional return was not exercised. A pick that never conveys does not create drafted-player or future-trade value for its intended recipient. Milwaukee may have valued roster space and flexibility when it moved Pachulia, but this transaction did not deliver an NBA player, cash payment or realized draft choice to the Bucks. The D+ recognizes how thin the completed basketball return was while leaving room for a separate evaluation of roster-management intent.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win — Dallas B+, Milwaukee D+. Pachulia played 76 games and started 69 in his lone Mavericks season, averaging 8.6 points and 9.4 rebounds. The only consideration due to Milwaukee was a top-55-protected 2018 second-round pick, which never conveyed. Dallas received productive center minutes for no realized draft cost. The grade belongs to that Dallas season, not to Pachulia's later Warriors championships or Brunson's later career.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Deep Dive: Why Mavericks Win Fits Dallas Mavericks and Milwaukee Bucks
featuredDeepDive.intro: The 2015 Pachulia transaction illustrates how protection language can make a seemingly ordinary player-for-pick swap unusually favorable to one side. Dallas received a veteran center with immediate starting utility. Milwaukee received the possibility of a 2018 second-round selection, but only if Dallas' pick landed after No. 55. The Bucks never collected it. Rather than counting a hypothetical draft prospect or mistaking Pachulia's later Warriors years for Dallas value, the proper retrospective tracks 76 Mavericks games, a playoff appearance and a contingent pick that expired. The difference explains the B+/D+ grades while keeping the scope of the trade deliberately small.

sections.heading: The Transaction's Value Map
sections.body: Milwaukee's only incoming asset was not a standard future second-rounder. A 2018 Dallas second-round pick protected through selection No. 55 would go to Milwaukee only if it fell between Nos. 56 and 60. Dallas' own second-round position ended at No. 33 in the 2018 draft, comfortably inside the protected range. The Bucks therefore obtained no selection and no player they could trace to this transaction. Dallas' return was not conditional in the same way: Pachulia joined the team in July 2015 and played for it that autumn. Separating guaranteed present production from a contingent, ultimately extinguished right is more informative than treating the two package lines as equivalent.

sections.heading: The Asset That Moved the Balance: Dallas Mavericks
sections.body: Pachulia's 2015-16 box-score record is concrete: 76 appearances, 69 starts, 650 points, 718 rebounds and 128 assists in 2,004 minutes. For a club that needed a center behind its perimeter attack and Nowitzki's frontcourt offense, that workload was valuable. Dallas finished 42-40 and returned to the playoffs, where Oklahoma City eliminated it in five games. The deal did not make Pachulia a long-term Mavericks cornerstone; he left for Golden State the next offseason. That limit matters when assigning B+ instead of assuming all 16 years of his NBA career are attributable to Dallas. The franchise bought one useful season and gave up no realized second-round selection.

sections.heading: Context Without Rewriting the Trade: Milwaukee Bucks
sections.body: Milwaukee's position was different from Dallas'. The Bucks had used Pachulia in 73 regular-season games during 2014-15 and could reasonably prefer to open minutes for other players. Their consideration from Dallas, however, was protected so heavily that the club had very little chance to collect it unless Dallas emerged as one of the league's top regular-season teams by 2017-18. The selection never conveyed. Without a pick to draft or trade, Milwaukee cannot claim the 2018 No. 33 selection or the player Dallas took with it. The record supports a small basketball return, not a fictional second-round prospect. Distinguishing the front office's possible roster priorities from the assets it actually gained keeps the grade grounded.

sections.heading: Why the Final Grades Hold
sections.body: Dallas went on to use its retained 2018 No. 33 pick on Jalen Brunson, as the Mavericks' own draft announcement confirms. But the Pachulia trade did not send Brunson from Milwaukee to Dallas, and crediting Brunson's later career as a direct Pachulia acquisition would be misleading. The narrower, supportable conclusion is that Dallas protected its 2018 second-round flexibility while securing a productive veteran center in 2015-16. Milwaukee agreed to a conditional right that ultimately produced nothing. The B+ grade is for an inexpensive season of starting-caliber center play; the D+ is for a return that never materialized into a drafted player or game on Milwaukee's roster.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win — Dallas B+, Milwaukee D+. The Mavericks got a 76-game, 69-start center whose rebounding aided a 42-win playoff team. Milwaukee received no NBA production or conveyed selection because the conditional No. 56-60-only draft right expired. Dallas later used its own 2018 No. 33 pick on Jalen Brunson, but Brunson's career is not counted as a player acquired in the 2015 Pachulia transaction.

sections.heading: Dallas Received Bogut and the Future No. 31 Pick
sections.body: On July 7, 2016, Dallas acquired Andrew Bogut and a future Golden State second-round draft pick. The Warriors received a Dallas second-round selection that was protected through No. 55 for 2019; it never conveyed. Both franchises issued same-day statements describing the center and future draft considerations. This was a two-team salary-and-picks arrangement, not a straight Bogut-for-Durant player trade. Golden State also generated a traded-player exception in the accounting ledger, and the Dallas archive records that exception separately from the unexercised conditional pick. The incoming Golden State selection eventually became No. 31 in 2020, allowing Dallas to draft Tyrell Terry. Those realized details make the 2016 receipt testable rather than a vague set of future choices.

sections.heading: The Warriors Were Clearing a Roster and Salary Slot
sections.body: Golden State's decision coincided with Kevin Durant's July 2016 free-agent arrival, but Durant was not a player sent by Dallas. Bogut had helped the Warriors win the 2015 championship and appeared in 70 games during the historic 73-win 2015-16 regular season, starting 66 and averaging 5.4 points, 7.0 rebounds and 1.6 blocks. Warriors executive Bob Myers publicly credited Bogut's value after the exchange. Moving that existing veteran contract gave the front office space to reorganize its center position around a much more expensive free-agent acquisition. The team subsequently signed Zaza Pachulia to play in the frontcourt. A retrospective can explain this consequential salary decision without listing Durant or Pachulia as received assets in the July 7 deal.

sections.heading: Bogut's Dallas Season Was Short but Produced Real Minutes
sections.body: Bogut's direct Mavericks return was more limited than the pre-trade résumé suggested. He played 26 regular-season games for Dallas in 2016-17, started 21 and averaged 3.0 points, 8.3 rebounds and 1.0 blocks in about 22.4 minutes. His defensive rebounding and screening gave Rick Carlisle a familiar veteran interior option, but health and roster direction restricted the experiment. Dallas later sent Bogut with Justin Anderson and a protected 2017 first-rounder to Philadelphia on February 23, 2017, receiving Nerlens Noel. That was a new transaction with new compensation, not a continuation of the exact July 2016 asset bundle. The 26-game Mavericks stat line keeps the immediate player return in perspective, even if the initial front-office reasoning was understandable.

sections.heading: The Golden State Pick Became Tyrell Terry in 2020
sections.body: The less visible Dallas return did not expire in 2017 with Bogut's departure. Golden State's 2020 second-round pick transferred through the July 2016 agreement and landed at No. 31 overall. Dallas selected Stanford guard Tyrell Terry at that slot in November 2020. The NBA's official draft ledger lists the Mavericks as choosing Terry, while the 2020 pick-trade history identifies the original Golden State-to-Dallas route through Bogut. Terry eventually appeared in only 13 NBA games for Dallas, so the pick's actual basketball outcome was modest even though its draft position was strong for the second round. Separating a relatively favorable draft slot from the modest realized player's career helps distinguish opportunity from results.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win (Dallas B, Golden State C-plus) is the preserved editorial verdict, not a newly recalculated grade. Dallas acquired Bogut for 26 games and a 2020 Golden State second used at No. 31 on Tyrell Terry. The Dallas top-55-protected 2019 second never conveyed; Golden State also recorded a traded-player exception. Clearing Bogut's contract helped reorganize the Warriors' 2016 offseason, but Durant joined as a free agent, not as a direct Dallas trade asset. The basketball impact and cap benefits are distinct.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Bogut, the Durant Summer, and the Dallas Pick That Became Tyrell Terry
featuredDeepDive.intro: Golden State traded Andrew Bogut and a 2020 second-round selection to Dallas on July 7, 2016. The return included a top-55-protected 2019 second that never conveyed and a trade exception. Bogut supplied 26 Dallas appearances before a separate Noel trade; the Golden State selection became No. 31 Tyrell Terry in 2020. The transaction facilitated, but did not itself transfer, the Warriors' prized free-agent signing.

sections.heading: Two 2016 Team Releases Anchor the Exact Transaction
sections.body: The Dallas July 7 announcement names Bogut and Golden State's future second-round selection as the assets coming to the Mavericks. The Warriors' version describes Bogut leaving and draft considerations traveling in both directions. Both are contemporary, team-issued records rather than retrospective guesses. The more detailed transaction ledger identifies the Dallas 2019 second as top-55 protected and not exercised, alongside a traded-player exception for Golden State. The Dallas side received the pick eventually used on Tyrell Terry. None of these original statements say Dallas traded for Kevin Durant, even though the Warriors had to make broader roster and cap decisions to sign him as a free agent. Precise legal trade terms should come before a shorthand narrative about the Durant-era Warriors.

sections.heading: Bogut's Previous Defensive Role Explains Both Teams' Incentives
sections.body: The 31-year-old center had offered rim protection, passing from the high post and screening for Stephen Curry and Klay Thompson during the Warriors' rise. Golden State credited his championship contribution and its 73-win season when announcing his departure. Dallas could reasonably expect an experienced defender next to Dirk Nowitzki without giving up an unprotected selection in return. The gamble was whether Bogut's health and remaining mobility would allow that profile to translate into sustained Mavericks availability. His actual Dallas tenure lasted 26 appearances, with 21 starts and useful rebounding but little scoring. Golden State's evaluation differed: the freedom to support its high-profile free-agency roster outweighed retaining a respected prior starter.

sections.heading: The 2017 Noel Transaction Was a New Dallas Decision
sections.body: On February 23, 2017, Dallas moved Bogut again, packaging him with Justin Anderson and a protected first-round choice for Philadelphia big man Nerlens Noel. NBA.com's 2016-17 transaction tracker confirms that separate group of assets and the date. Because Noel arrived through a later, larger deal, it would be inaccurate to say Golden State sent Noel directly in July 2016. Nor can the eventual 2017 draft protection be folded into the 2019 second-round conditions in the original Warriors swap. This is an important chain-of-custody distinction for trade archives: one transaction can establish control of a player, but the subsequent trade has different negotiating parties and costs. Bogut's limited Dallas minutes remain the direct statistical return from his first move.

sections.heading: The Conditional Pick Was Worth More Than Its Final NBA Minutes
sections.body: Dallas' protected 2019 second-rounder did not convey to Golden State, while the Mavericks actually received a 2020 Golden State second. That pick became No. 31 overall following the Warriors' difficult 2019-20 season, and Dallas drafted Tyrell Terry. A high second-round pick can offer contract and development optionality, but Terry's brief 13-game Mavericks career limits the realized on-court payoff. Golden State, meanwhile, acquired cap flexibility in a championship-oriented summer; the team subsequently won the 2017 and 2018 titles, though attributing those solely to the Bogut transaction would be misleading. The original canonical grade pair is Mavericks B and Warriors C-plus, with Mavericks Win as the verdict. Those stored values are preserved while the analysis distinguishes the assets actually conveyed from salary strategy and later roster achievements.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The recorded verdict is Mavericks Win, with Dallas B and Golden State C-plus, unchanged. The July 2016 Mavericks receipt consisted of Andrew Bogut and Golden State's eventual 2020 second-rounder, which Dallas used on No. 31 Tyrell Terry. Bogut's Mavericks tenure was limited to 26 games, 21 starts and 8.3 rebounds per contest before the distinct February 2017 Philadelphia deal. Dallas' own 2019 top-55-protected second never conveyed, while Golden State recorded a traded-player exception. The Warriors moved a respected former starter in the same offseason as Kevin Durant's free-agent arrival and subsequently won further titles. Those later championships explain the financial stakes but should not be misidentified as assets Dallas directly traded away. Terry's brief career also limits the pick's ultimate realized value. Preserving these boundaries is more useful than reversing inherited grades without an authorized independent provenance decision.

sections.heading: Dallas Sold a Waiver Pickup for Cash
sections.body: The Mavericks traded DeAndre Liggins to Houston on June 28, 2017, in exchange for cash considerations. He had arrived in Dallas only in April, when the club claimed him off waivers from Cleveland, and appeared in the Mavericks' final game of the season. That single Dallas appearance yielded eight points and seven rebounds in 25 minutes. It provided a glimpse of a defensive-minded reserve rather than a long-established Maverick. An official Dallas announcement confirms the cash return but does not disclose how much Houston paid. Dallas' completed gain from this particular exchange was financial, and there is no basis for manufacturing a dollar figure or a subsequent draft pick.

sections.heading: Houston Used Liggins in the Chris Paul Package the Same Day
sections.body: Houston acquired Liggins from Dallas during a burst of June 28 transactions. The Rockets' official Chris Paul announcement then listed him among the outgoing assets sent to the Los Angeles Clippers in the much larger Paul acquisition. That transaction also required Patrick Beverley, Sam Dekker, Montrezl Harrell, Lou Williams and other players, a first-round pick and cash. Liggins was therefore an actual part of a major trade package, but his individual value cannot be separated from all that other consideration. He never played a Rockets regular-season game between the Dallas transaction and the Clippers deal; his traceable role was as a transferable contract inside an assembled package.

sections.heading: The Asset Kept Moving After the Paul Deal
sections.body: The Clippers received Liggins in the Paul exchange, but that was not the end of his summer transaction history. In September 2017, Los Angeles sent him and cash to Atlanta for a conditional second-round pick that ultimately did not convey. The Hawks later waived him. Those movements demonstrate that Liggins had transactional utility even without becoming a durable Los Angeles rotation player. They also limit hindsight scoring: Atlanta's short-term contract decision and the failed pick condition occurred in subsequent deals with their own consideration. Dallas cannot claim those assets, and Houston cannot claim every benefit from obtaining Paul simply because Liggins appeared on the paperwork.

sections.heading: Even Grades Distinguish Facilitation From Superstar Value
sections.body: The canonical verdict is Even Trade, B- for Dallas and B- for Houston. Dallas cashed out a short-tenure defensive guard; Houston acquired a movable player contract that became one input in the separate, multi-asset Chris Paul deal. Neither side received a directly measurable, enduring on-court return from this standalone Dallas-Houston exchange. Houston's downstream trade purpose was clearer than a routine bench tryout, yet the price of that blockbuster included far more than Liggins. A retrospective that awards Houston the whole Paul acquisition for a single cash-for-player step would be just as misleading as treating Dallas' unknown cash payment as a major win.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Dallas B-, Houston B-. The Mavericks received undisclosed cash for DeAndre Liggins on June 28, 2017. Houston immediately included the guard among numerous players, a first-round pick and cash sent to the Clippers for Chris Paul, without Liggins playing a Rockets regular-season game. The exchange supplied one useful contract to a larger operation but cannot bear the value of Paul by itself. Dallas' financial return also lacks a verified public amount.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Why the Mavericks’ Liggins Cash Trade Appears in the Chris Paul Timeline
featuredDeepDive.intro: The Dallas-Houston exchange of DeAndre Liggins looks routine until its date is compared with the Chris Paul trade. The Mavericks received cash for the guard on June 28, 2017; Houston then transferred him to the Clippers that same day as one of many pieces in the blockbuster. This is a real instance of a small transaction supplying an asset for a bigger move. It is not evidence that Dallas delivered Chris Paul to Houston or that Liggins was the decisive consideration. A careful retrospective follows both transactions without collapsing their different costs into one story.

sections.heading: Dallas' Connection Was Brief and Measurable
sections.body: The Mavericks claimed Liggins from waivers in April 2017 after Cleveland had released him. Dallas used him in one NBA game, when he recorded eight points and seven rebounds, and then chose to monetize the contract before the June offseason roster changes. The team was not surrendering years of its own player development. It received cash, but its announcement did not attach a price to that consideration. This makes the Dallas side easy to identify and difficult to quantify in basketball terms. A cash return is still a real asset; the historical record simply cannot establish whether Dallas could have negotiated more.

sections.heading: Houston Bought a Contract It Could Immediately Send Out
sections.body: The Rockets' June 28 Chris Paul announcement separately identified their earlier acquisition of Liggins from Dallas. A few hours later the complete Clippers package included him alongside multiple rotation players and a protected first-round selection. It would be too reductive to describe this as a Liggins-for-Paul trade. Houston used a basket of assets to acquire a star, and Liggins constituted only one contract among them. His presence in the package is evidence of a useful intermediate transaction, not a reason to assign Paul's scoring, passing, or future playoff impact exclusively to the smaller cash deal.

sections.heading: A Subsequent Clippers Trade Reinforces the Boundaries
sections.body: Liggins was not a Rockets roster contributor and did not stay with the Clippers for the next regular season. The Clippers sent him to Atlanta that September together with cash for a conditional second-round pick, and the condition was not satisfied. Atlanta eventually released him. That sequence reinforces the difference between using a player contract in roster transactions and receiving minutes from the player. The Clippers and Hawks made their own choices after receiving him. The value of those later choices belongs in those transaction ledgers, not in a claim that Dallas or Houston secretly obtained a productive NBA player in June.

sections.heading: The Verdict Prices a Minor Step, Not the Entire Offseason
sections.body: Houston achieved a transformational acquisition that summer, but the documented Chris Paul trade sent many players and other assets to Los Angeles. Dallas executed a much smaller transaction and obtained cash without a disclosed figure. When the original cash-for-Liggins deal is evaluated in isolation, it produces no direct Rockets games and no identifiable Dallas basketball acquisition. Houston used the movable contract; Dallas obtained a financial payment. The matching B- grades do not say each input had identical monetary value. They say the information supports an even, modest outcome rather than attributing the entire blockbuster to one fringe-player transfer.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, B-/B-. Dallas turned its short-lived DeAndre Liggins roster interest into cash, while Houston transferred Liggins into the larger June 28, 2017 Chris Paul deal without using him in an NBA game. The Clippers later moved the contract again. The source record supports Houston's contract-facilitation benefit, but not an assertion that Liggins alone acquired Paul or that Dallas received a known cash windfall. The balanced grade reflects that limited direct return.

sections.heading: Dallas Turned a Late-Season Prospect Into Cash
sections.body: The Mavericks sent Jarrod Uthoff to Houston on June 29, 2017, receiving cash considerations. The transaction followed a brief period of roster evaluation in Dallas: Uthoff had joined on two 10-day contracts in March and signed a longer agreement on March 29. He appeared in nine regular-season games for the Mavericks before the season ended. Dallas had a young forward worth looking at, but this was not the departure of an established starter. By moving his contract at the start of the offseason, the Mavericks converted a fringe-roster player into cash. The available transaction records confirm the payment but do not establish an amount.

sections.heading: The Nine Dallas Games Were Already in the Books
sections.body: Uthoff's Dallas sample totaled 115 minutes, 40 points and 22 rebounds in the 2016-17 season. His strongest opportunities came in April as the Mavericks assessed their roster after playoff hopes had faded. Those minutes demonstrate why he drew a look from other teams, but they happened before the June trade and cannot be counted as Houston's return. He was an undrafted prospect whose contracts had changed several times in only a few months. Dallas was selling the chance to evaluate him going forward, not transferring an asset with a multi-year NBA production record.

sections.heading: Houston Paid for an Opportunity and Waived Him
sections.body: Houston acquired Uthoff at the end of June, then waived him on July 30, before the 2017-18 NBA regular season. He recorded no NBA appearances for the Rockets. That short window is decisive for a retrospective based on realized basketball contribution. The Rockets obtained the right to assess and retain a player, but the opportunity did not result in meaningful playing time for the acquiring team. Uthoff eventually returned to the league in 2019-20 with Memphis and Washington; those later appearances followed separate contracts and belong to neither the June 2017 Houston deal nor the Mavericks' cash receipt.

sections.heading: An Equal Grade Doesn't Mean Equal Kinds of Value
sections.body: The canonical ledger rates the trade Even, with B- grades for Dallas and Houston. One return was cash of an undisclosed amount, while the other was short-lived rights to a reserve forward who never played a Rockets regular-season game. Dallas realized a financial asset but no linked player or draft choice. Houston received a player-evaluation option, then ended it within a month. Neither side has a documented major basketball windfall directly traceable to this transaction. Treating the entire career of Uthoff as a Rockets gain would be inaccurate, as would inventing a price for Dallas' payment to assign a dramatic victory.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Dallas B-, Houston B-. Dallas received undisclosed cash for Jarrod Uthoff in June 2017 after he had played nine Mavericks games. Houston kept him briefly, then waived him July 30 without a Rockets regular-season appearance. The payment's amount isn't reliably established, and Uthoff's later NBA appearances came with other clubs. The documented record is an exchange of limited, different forms of value rather than a clear basketball winner.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Uthoff for Cash: Why Neither Team Got a Lasting NBA Return
featuredDeepDive.intro: A June 2017 cash transaction involving Jarrod Uthoff can look more substantial than it was when every appearance in his career is treated as relevant. The key dates narrow it considerably. Dallas signed the forward during March, watched him play nine NBA games, and traded him to Houston on June 29. Houston waived him on July 30 before he could suit up in a Rockets regular-season game. Dallas got a payment that its public transaction log does not quantify. The trade is best judged as a small offseason roster-and-cash move rather than a failed attempt to acquire a future starting forward.

sections.heading: The Mavericks Had Already Completed Their Trial
sections.body: Uthoff came through Dallas on two March 2017 10-day agreements before receiving a multi-year contract late that month. Nine regular-season appearances, 115 minutes and 40 points gave the front office a limited professional sample. Those numbers belong to Dallas' evaluation period, not the consideration acquired by Houston. Trading him for cash at the end of June ended an inexpensive roster experiment with a documented financial return. The absence of a reliable dollar figure means the retrospective cannot claim that Dallas gained a specific salary saving or received more money than any disclosed alternative.

sections.heading: Houston's Roster Decision Came One Month Later
sections.body: The Rockets' June 29 transaction list records cash going to Dallas for Uthoff. By July 30, Houston had waived him. There were no Rockets regular-season box scores to assess, no development trajectory inside that team's rotation, and no asset subsequently exchanged for him in a documented Houston deal. The club effectively bought and declined a short evaluation opportunity. That is a narrower result than calling the entire NBA career of an acquired player a Rockets return. Later movement through other clubs does not revive the original Houston asset once its contract has been terminated.

sections.heading: Later Appearances Cannot Be Borrowed Backward
sections.body: Uthoff appeared again in the NBA in 2019-20, playing for Memphis and Washington. The gap between those games and his July 2017 Houston waiver included different organizations and fresh contractual decisions. Even his nine Dallas appearances predated the Rockets' acquisition. Using either period to measure Houston's realized on-court value would incorrectly shift performances across transactions. That discipline also prevents Dallas from claiming a return tied to anything Uthoff subsequently did with another team. The exchange itself produced cash for one party and a short-lived roster right for the other.

sections.heading: The Even Label Reflects Thin, Unequal Evidence
sections.body: Both clubs could justify the decision from their immediate positions. Dallas was ready to convert an undrafted, short-tenure player into cash; Houston had roster space or an offseason reason to inspect another forward. But the public ledger does not show the cash amount, and Uthoff never reached the Rockets' regular-season roster. The B-/B- assessment therefore acknowledges the limited documented benefits and avoids reading large victory margins into a minor deal. Cash can have real organizational value even when it cannot be translated into basketball points or minutes. A non-producing trial can have a reason at the time without becoming a strong realized player return.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, B-/B-. Dallas converted a forward with nine prior Mavericks NBA appearances into an undisclosed cash payment. Houston acquired Jarrod Uthoff and waived him a month later without a Rockets regular-season appearance. His later Memphis and Washington games resulted from unrelated agreements, while the dollar value of Dallas' payment isn't public in the reviewed ledger. Neither club has a demonstrated, lasting basketball return from this exchange.

sections.heading: Miami Sent McRoberts, Its 2023 Second and Cash for Hammons
sections.body: On July 7, 2017, the Heat confirmed they traded Josh McRoberts, a 2023 second-round draft selection and cash considerations to Dallas for young center A.J. Hammons. The contemporary Miami release records all four assets, while the Mavericks historical media guide confirms the same package. Basketball Reference itemizes the cash as $5.1 million, whereas the Heat’s own announcement did not specify the amount. This was principally a salary-clearing transaction: Miami sought financial room to formalize deals for James Johnson, Dion Waiters and Kelly Olynyk. Dallas accepted McRoberts’s expiring contract and received future draft and cash assets.

sections.heading: McRoberts Made Only Two Mavericks Appearances Before His Waiver
sections.body: Dallas’s February 2018 official release says McRoberts played two NBA games for the Mavericks and spent the opening 37 games of 2017-18 on the inactive list while rehabbing a left foot injury. The team requested waivers on him February 10. His two Mavericks games were a minimal court return and did not amount to receiving a veteran rotation contributor. The trade still supplied Dallas a future draft choice and cash, so evaluating only McRoberts’s on-court performance would omit much of the organization’s incoming value. His earlier Miami games do not belong to the Dallas receiving-team tally.

sections.heading: Hammons Never Played a Miami Regular-Season Game
sections.body: Hammons had made 22 Dallas appearances in 2016-17 before the exchange, averaging 2.2 points in 7.4 minutes. He did not play an NBA regular-season game for the Heat after joining Miami. The Heat assigned him to the Sioux Falls Skyforce of the G League in October 2017, recalled him in February 2018 and waived him on February 8. G League assignments are valid development history but cannot be entered as NBA Miami appearances. Miami’s return was therefore short-lived prospect rights and financial room, rather than immediate center production. Dallas’s 2016-17 Hammons statistics are pretrade context.

sections.heading: The 2023 Second Became No. 50 Keyontae Johnson
sections.body: The second-round pick sent from Miami to Dallas ultimately became the 2023 No. 50 selection, used on Keyontae Johnson. That is the original asset’s final pick identity; it does not establish that Johnson played his NBA games for Dallas. Draft-right movements and roster destinations after the 2017 transaction require separate provenance checks. Dallas acquired the option of a distant second selection plus cash in exchange for taking McRoberts, while Miami gained contract flexibility during its summer signings. The protected Mavericks Win verdict and Dallas B+/Miami B- acknowledge those different strategic values without inventing receiving-team production.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win, Dallas B+ and Miami B- are retained. McRoberts played two Dallas NBA games and was waived in February 2018; Hammons played none for Miami and was waived the same month. Dallas also took a 2023 second that later became No. 50 Keyontae Johnson and cash described as $5.1 million in transaction records. Miami achieved a salary-clearing objective, not a new long-term NBA center.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The 2017 McRoberts Salary Trade: Dallas Bought a Future Second and Cash
featuredDeepDive.intro: The July 7, 2017 agreement moved Josh McRoberts, a 2023 second-round pick and cash from Miami to Dallas for A.J. Hammons. McRoberts logged only two Mavericks appearances and Hammons never played for the Heat. Dallas’s future selection eventually became No. 50 Keyontae Johnson, while Miami was clearing room for multiple free-agent agreements. The inherited Mavericks Win, B+ Dallas and B- Miami is assessed as a financial and asset transaction, not a contest between two productive receiving-team players.

sections.heading: Two Teams Confirmed the July 2017 Contract and Pick Package
sections.body: Miami’s original release identifies a veteran McRoberts, a 2023 second and cash for center A.J. Hammons. Dallas’s official team media guide repeats the transaction. The Heat wanted cap room while arranging contracts for James Johnson, Dion Waiters and Kelly Olynyk, a motive explained in contemporary Hoops Rumors reporting. The NBA release does not provide a dollar amount for the cash; Basketball Reference’s transaction ledger later records $5.1 million. Using both records makes the cash distinction transparent rather than inventing an original press-release quote or omitting a real asset.

sections.heading: McRoberts Was Injured and Played Two Games for Dallas
sections.body: The Mavericks announced in February 2018 that McRoberts had remained inactive for 37 games because of a left foot injury and had appeared just twice since his arrival. The club requested waivers February 10. Consequently, Dallas did not receive the healthy frontcourt depth a reader might infer from McRoberts’s prior reputation. However, the team also got money and a future second-rounder for accepting the player contract. His 81-game Miami career stint and earlier seasons elsewhere are unrelated receiving-team NBA output and do not turn the two-game Mavericks tenure into a longer one.

sections.heading: Miami Acquired Hammons but Used Him Only in the G League
sections.body: Hammons was originally the No. 46 pick by Dallas in 2016 and played 22 Mavericks NBA games during 2016-17, scoring 2.2 points a night. Miami acquired him the following summer, sent him to the Sioux Falls Skyforce on October 22, 2017 and eventually waived him February 8, 2018. He never appeared in a Heat NBA regular-season game. The assignment shows the club did use a developmental roster slot, but it would be misleading to portray his Skyforce minutes as production for Miami. This transaction produced cap relief and a short-lived prospect, not a lasting rotation big man.

sections.heading: The Long-Dated Draft Pick Is Distinct from Later Player Returns
sections.body: The pick Miami surrendered eventually became 2023 No. 50 Keyontae Johnson, as listed in the historical transaction entries. That final selection identifies the path of the draft asset, not the full NBA playing destination or guaranteed payoff to Dallas. Evaluators should not assign any games Johnson played elsewhere to the Mavericks based solely on the old conditional pick. The directly documented 2017 benefit was receiving a future draft choice and cash while accepting an injured veteran salary. The Heat’s concurrent free-agent signings required additional cap planning and should not all be treated as one-for-one direct compensation sent through this deal.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Dallas B+, Miami B- and Mavericks Win remain unchanged. Dallas received McRoberts for two NBA appearances plus cash and a future second-round choice; Miami received Hammons but no Heat NBA regular-season games. The 2023 pick later resolved to No. 50 Keyontae Johnson. The protected verdict is principally an asset-and-cap judgment, without attaching future players, unrelated acquisitions or G League minutes to the wrong receiving franchise.

sections.heading: Dallas Split No. 54 Into Two Later Second-Round Rights
sections.body: The June 21, 2018 trade sent Dallas's draft rights to No. 54 Shake Milton to Philadelphia. Dallas received two other selections from the same draft: No. 56 Ray Spalding and No. 60 Kostas Antetokounmpo. The Mavericks' official announcement and the NBA's 2018 draft trade tracker independently confirm the direction of all three rights. These were draft-night rights, not existing contracts held by the acquiring clubs. Philadelphia could build a developmental guard around Milton; Dallas chose two frontcourt prospects for the price of one late second. The deal did not send a future first-round pick or veteran to either side. All later NBA contracts and assignments were subsequent decisions, not hidden assets of this June exchange.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Converted the No. 54 Right Into a Rotation Guard
sections.body: Shake Milton signed a two-way agreement in July 2018 and later earned a standard NBA contract in July 2019, according to Philadelphia's official media guide. The same guide lists 254 Philadelphia appearances and career averages of 9.3 points, 2.4 rebounds and 2.7 assists through the 2022–23 season. He appeared in 76 games during 2022–23, which is much more sustained rotation use than one would automatically expect from the 54th pick. The franchise's 2021 draft retrospective recorded his growth from a 4.4-point rookie to 13.0 points across 63 appearances in 2020–21. Those figures are Philadelphia production, rather than later performances with teams Milton joined after his Sixers tenure.

sections.heading: The Two Dallas Prospects Had Limited Mavericks NBA Minutes
sections.body: Spalding and Antetokounmpo were legitimate second-round prospects when Dallas acquired their rights. The official Mavericks release cited Spalding's rebounding and interior scoring at Louisville and Antetokounmpo's developmental potential at Dayton. But the 2019 Dallas announcement of a separate Kristaps Porzingis trade states Spalding had appeared in only one Mavericks game, and an official Dallas May 2019 report says Antetokounmpo played two NBA games while spending most of the year with the Texas Legends. Those direct Dallas figures are much more appropriate measures of the immediate return than future championship rings, family connections or NBA appearances for other teams. The initial trade offered two chances; neither produced a substantial Mavericks rotation stint.

sections.heading: Why Philadelphia Got More Value From the 2018 Draft-Rights Swap
sections.body: The 76ers Win verdict grades Philadelphia A-minus and Dallas D, reflecting the difference between Shake Milton's extended Sixers tenure and Dallas's brief looks at Ray Spalding and Kostas Antetokounmpo. Philadelphia's own media guide records 254 Milton appearances through 2022-23. Spalding appeared in one Mavericks game, while Antetokounmpo played two for Dallas, according to the franchise's later accounts. The Mavericks had a reasonable draft-night argument for exchanging one late second-round right for two developmental prospects, and neither team knew those eventual NBA totals on June 21, 2018. The grades assess what the clubs actually received over time: one useful Philadelphia rotation guard versus two Dallas prospects who didn't establish comparable roles. Those are direct receiving-team results, not a transfer of later clubs' seasons or unrelated draft assets into the original package.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Recorded 76ers Win — Philadelphia A-, Dallas D. No. 54 Shake Milton went to Philadelphia for Dallas's rights to No. 56 Ray Spalding and No. 60 Kostas Antetokounmpo. Milton became a 254-game Sixers contributor through 2022–23; Dallas's own releases identify only one early Mavericks game for Spalding and two for Antetokounmpo. Philadelphia's on-court return was far more substantial. The archived assets, letter grades and verdict are preserved.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Why the 2018 Shake Milton Rights Trade Favored Philadelphia
featuredDeepDive.intro: Dallas exchanged the draft rights to 54th choice Shake Milton for the 56th and 60th picks on June 21, 2018. The Mavericks took Ray Spalding and Kostas Antetokounmpo, while the Sixers obtained a guard who would eventually earn a full NBA contract. By 2023, Philadelphia's media guide credited Milton with 254 Sixers appearances. Dallas's own later reporting documented very limited Mavericks NBA minutes for its two draftees. The archived 76ers Win and A-/D grades stay unchanged; the source review distinguishes draft-night promises from the actual years that followed.

sections.heading: Three Draft Rights, Two Teams, One Specific Exchange
sections.body: The original Dallas release states that Philadelphia transferred No. 56 Ray Spalding and No. 60 Kostas Antetokounmpo to the Mavericks in exchange for No. 54 Shake Milton. The NBA's draft-night transaction tracker repeats that three-right map. None of the incoming rights represented a veteran contract, and there was no additional first-round selection included as part of this trade. The original archive correctly labels all three as draft rights; converting them to direct established-player transfers would confuse the draft-day agreement with July contract signings. Dallas opted for two young frontcourt possibilities instead of one guard. Philadelphia chose to consolidate the two later picks into the guard's rights, betting that Milton's scoring and ballhandling would earn a meaningful role.

sections.heading: Milton's Philadelphia Development Has Official Statistical Support
sections.body: Philadelphia's 2021 draft review describes Milton's first three NBA seasons as an improving progression: 20 games at 4.4 points per outing as a rookie, 40 games at 9.4 points in year two, then 63 games at 13.0 points in 2020–21. Its 2023 media guide later reports 254 career Sixers games with a 9.3-point scoring average and 2.7 assists through that postseason. The guide also traces the July 2018 two-way contract and the July 2019 NBA deal. These are concrete results of the acquired player right under Philadelphia's development program. They do not require claiming Milton was a star or treating subsequent performances for another franchise as Philadelphia's own return.

sections.heading: Dallas's Actual Use of Spalding and Antetokounmpo
sections.body: Dallas had a reasonable reason to split one draft slot into two: Spalding brought an athletic rebounding profile from Louisville, while Antetokounmpo offered physical tools and G League development time. The team's June 2018 release described each prospect's college production. A later Dallas report says Spalding had played one NBA game for the Mavericks by the time of their January 2019 Kristaps Porzingis transaction. A separate official May 2019 feature says Antetokounmpo played two Mavericks games while spending most of the season with Texas Legends. Those small NBA samples make it difficult to claim Dallas found a lasting first-team answer from either 2018 right. Their later career stops are separate from the return generated for Dallas on its own roster.

sections.heading: A Grade Comparison Without Borrowing Other Teams' Results
sections.body: Philadelphia's recorded A-minus corresponds with a useful second-round guard whose meaningful NBA minutes continued through the 2022–23 season. Dallas's D is consistent with the much shorter NBA roster impact of the two young rights it chose instead. That does not imply the Mavericks' decision was irrational on draft night, nor should Antetokounmpo's basketball accomplishments with later teams become retrospectively counted as Mavericks production. The trade's outcome is unusually measurable because both clubs have published contemporaneous asset announcements and later player-usage records. An independent grading audit can still discuss development opportunity cost and second-round uncertainty, but changing the 76ers Win verdict or current letters would require a consistent cross-archive standard rather than a single anecdote.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Dallas obtained Spalding's No. 56 rights and Antetokounmpo's No. 60 rights for No. 54 Shake Milton. Milton produced 254 Sixers appearances through 2022–23; Dallas officially documented one early game for Spalding and two for Antetokounmpo. That evidence supports the stored 76ers Win, Philadelphia A- and Dallas D. No future pick or later franchise's player production is inserted into the original ledger.

sections.heading: August 2018: Dallas Received Onuaku, Cash and a Swap Option
sections.body: On August 2, 2018 Dallas acquired Chinanu Onuaku and cash from Houston for the draft rights to Maarty Leunen. The Mavericks also gained the right to swap a Golden State-origin 2020 second-round pick with the Rockets' 2020 second. That optional swap was never exercised, so it should not appear as an outright selection transferred to Dallas. The Associated Press report and the Mavericks' official history identify the transaction terms. Onuaku was a young center who had played six NBA games with Houston, while Leunen was an overseas forward rather than a current NBA rotation player. The cash component had a real immediate value, but the potential draft improvement was contingent. Both teams exchanged different forms of roster flexibility, not established starters.

sections.heading: Dallas Waived Onuaku Four Days After Acquiring Him
sections.body: The transaction did not give Dallas even a full month to evaluate Onuaku. The Mavericks' dated transactions show that they acquired him August 2 and waived him August 6, 2018. He never appeared in a regular-season game for the club. His six earlier NBA games were with Houston, so assigning those to Dallas would fabricate production from this deal. The team did receive cash and the choice whether to use the 2020 second-round swap, but the swap was not exercised. Dallas could use the center's acquisition as a short offseason evaluation rather than a long-term roster commitment. Its B-minus grade is an inherited appraisal of small direct and contractual benefits, not a claim that Onuaku developed into a starting Mavericks center.

sections.heading: Houston Reacquired Leunen Rights Without NBA Court Time
sections.body: Houston originally chose Maarty Leunen in the second round of the 2008 draft, but his professional playing career continued abroad. By July 2018 Dallas had acquired those rights from the Los Angeles Clippers through a separate Johnathan Motley-related transaction. The Mavericks then transferred Leunen's rights to Houston on August 2, bringing them back to the club that originally drafted him. That circuit explains the rights ownership but should not be confused with Leunen physically joining the Rockets roster. His later overseas production cannot be credited as Houston NBA regular-season minutes. The Rockets also sent cash and agreed to the optional draft swap, neither of which ultimately conveyed an NBA player to the other club through a selection. Houston received rights control rather than present playing production.

sections.heading: The Unused 2020 Option Limits Both Sides' Grade Claims
sections.body: The Even Trade verdict gives Dallas and Houston B-minus apiece. As the NBA's original transaction report explains, Dallas sent the draft rights to Maarty Leunen to Houston and received Chinanu Onuaku, cash, and an option to exchange a Golden State 2020 second-round pick it held for Houston's 2020 second. Onuaku never appeared in a Mavericks regular-season game: Dallas waived him on August 6, four days after the transaction. The future swap was never exercised, so it did not yield a new selection for either club, and Leunen's rights brought Houston no regular-season playing time. The swap is listed in both team asset records because it was one conditional exchange right, not two extra picks. Neither club acquired durable on-court production directly, and the preserved equal grades reflect similarly limited immediate returns rather than an invented draft outcome.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Dallas B-minus, Houston B-minus. Dallas received Onuaku, cash and an optional 2020 pick swap but waived Onuaku four days later without a Mavericks regular-season appearance; the swap was not exercised. Houston reacquired Leunen's draft rights, with no resulting NBA regular-season games. The conditional swap is one unexercised mechanism, not a traded 2020 second-round selection that produced an identifiable NBA player.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Deep Dive: Why Dallas Mavericks and Houston Rockets Finish Even
featuredDeepDive.intro: On August 2, 2018 the Mavericks obtained Chinanu Onuaku, cash and a conditional option to swap a 2020 Golden State-origin second-round pick with Houston. The Rockets received Maarty Leunen's draft rights. Dallas waived Onuaku four days later, Leunen never appeared in Houston regular-season games and the 2020 swap was not exercised. The inherited B-minus/B-minus grade comparison concerns those limited assets, not two productive on-court contributors.

sections.heading: The Official Dallas Transaction Line Confirms the Swap Terms
sections.body: The Mavericks' media guide and NBA.com's contemporaneous August 2018 account agree: Dallas acquired Chinanu Onuaku from Houston for Maarty Leunen's draft rights, while also receiving cash and the option to exchange the Warriors-origin 2020 second with Houston. Leunen had arrived in Dallas from the Clippers less than two weeks earlier. The swap option differed from the right to own Houston's pick outright. It could only improve Dallas's eventual second-round position if exercised under its contractual terms, and it was never exercised. Reading that record correctly prevents two opposite mistakes: treating the conditional mechanism as nothing that existed in 2018, or crediting either club with a 2020 player the swap did not convey.

sections.heading: The Mavericks Never Played Onuaku in a Regular-Season Game
sections.body: Onuaku had totaled six NBA appearances in Houston before moving to Dallas, so the acquiring team had some professional scouting material. Yet the Mavericks placed him on waivers on August 6, just four days after the transaction, and he never appeared for them in a regular-season game. Dallas did not receive the center career that a generic prospect narrative might imply. The cash supplied by Houston was an immediate financial benefit, and the swap right remained a separate contingent consideration even without being exercised. Those items can justify modest value without inventing a successful NBA development story. The Mavericks' inherited B-minus grade should be read as a low-stakes roster and asset-management result rather than proof that the young center produced NBA statistics in Dallas.

sections.heading: Houston Held Leunen Draft Rights, Not an Incoming Veteran
sections.body: The Rockets drafted Leunen out of Oregon in 2008 and, a decade later, reacquired his NBA rights from the Mavericks. He had played professionally in several European leagues while the rights moved through NBA organizations. Dallas obtained them from the Clippers on July 23, 2018 in the Johnathan Motley and Renaldas Seibutis exchange before forwarding them back to Houston August 2. Those were two distinct transactions involving different teams. Houston did not acquire Leunen as an active NBA center who played Rockets games during 2018-19; instead it held a possible future contractual avenue for a player competing abroad. That is real but limited optionality and explains why a B-minus rather than a superstar-level outcome is attached to this side of the ledger.

sections.heading: An Even Grade Pairing Does Not Imply Identical Returns
sections.body: Dallas and Houston received unlike assets despite the matching B-minus grades. The Mavericks briefly held Onuaku, received a cash payment and could have considered a second-round pick swap in 2020; the center was waived and the swap went unused. The Rockets held Leunen's NBA rights but did not convert them into regular-season playing time through this deal. Both clubs could achieve a small contractual purpose without either obtaining a lasting NBA contributor. Counting Onuaku's earlier six Houston games as Dallas value or Leunen's overseas seasons as Rockets NBA production would reverse that careful attribution. An Even Trade verdict acknowledges two minor outcomes and the absence of realized roster impact, not a guaranteed equality of cash amounts or player development.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Both clubs receive B-minus in the preserved Even Trade verdict. Onuaku never played an NBA game for Dallas after arriving on August 2, 2018; the Mavericks received cash and an unused 2020 second-round option. Houston held Leunen's rights but obtained no direct NBA player production from them. The two organizations realized different limited contractual benefits and neither gained a long-term roster contributor through this narrow rights exchange.

sections.heading: Sacramento Took Harrison Barnes for Jackson and Randolph
sections.body: On February 6, 2019, Sacramento announced it had acquired wing Harrison Barnes from Dallas for Justin Jackson and Zach Randolph. The Kings release was dated late on February 6, while the Mavericks’ formal completed-deal release and the protected transaction ledger use February 7. These refer to the same two-for-one player trade. Dallas gave up a forward who had started 49 games and averaged 17.8 points for the Mavericks that season. Sacramento received an established rotation starter who could play either forward spot alongside its developing guards. Dallas received a younger wing prospect and the salary of veteran Randolph, whom it did not intend to feature in its on-court plans.

sections.heading: Barnes Played 399 Kings Games through 2023-24
sections.body: Barnes immediately started all 28 Sacramento games following the February 2019 trade. He then started 72 games in 2019-20, 58 in 2020-21, 77 in 2021-22 and all 82 in both 2022-23 and 2023-24. These six receiving-team segments total 399 Kings regular-season appearances and 399 starts. His scoring was 14.5 points in 2019-20, 16.1 in 2020-21 and 16.4 in 2021-22, while he provided steadier lower-usage minutes in subsequent seasons. Barnes started every game of the Kings’ 2022-23 return to the playoffs, helping a team that had missed the postseason since 2006. His later Spurs appearances after 2024 do not belong to this Sacramento return.

sections.heading: Justin Jackson Gave Dallas 94 Games, Randolph Zero
sections.body: The Mavericks received Justin Jackson, a second-year forward who had appeared in 52 Kings games earlier in 2018-19. After the transaction he played 29 Dallas games with 11 starts, contributing 8.2 points a night; in 2019-20 he appeared 65 times with three starts, averaging 5.5 points. That makes 94 direct Dallas regular-season appearances across two seasons. Randolph was a legitimate second incoming contract, but Dallas waived him on February 8, 2019, before he appeared in a single Mavericks regular-season game. The NBA transaction chronology records the next-day waiver, preventing any mistaken claim that Randolph’s career scoring or earlier Sacramento service continued with Dallas.

sections.heading: Barnes Gave Sacramento 399 Starts; Dallas Received 94 Jackson Games
sections.body: Harrison Barnes started all 28 Kings games after his February 2019 arrival and then 72, 58, 77, 82 and 82 in the next five seasons through 2023-24: 399 Sacramento games, all starts. He was a useful forward during the club's return to the playoffs in 2023, although the postseason berth was a collective achievement rather than a one-player result. Dallas received Justin Jackson and Zach Randolph in the original two-for-one exchange. Jackson contributed 94 Mavericks regular-season appearances; Randolph was waived the following day without appearing for Dallas. That large gap in directly controlled player service supports the Kings' A against the Mavericks' C-. Dallas's separate Kristaps Porzingis acquisition explains its wider roster strategy, but it was not compensation received from Sacramento; Barnes's later San Antonio games are likewise outside this deal.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The saved Kings Win, Sacramento A and Dallas C- stand. Barnes logged 399 Kings games and starts across six receiving-team segments and appeared on the 2022-23 playoff roster. Jackson played 94 Dallas games, while Randolph was waived the day after the completed transaction and played none. The separate Porzingis roster construction in Dallas and Barnes’s later Spurs career are not part of the assets exchanged in February 2019.

sections.heading: Two Official Announcements Show One February Trade
sections.body: The Kings announced the Barnes acquisition late February 6. The Mavericks published a completed-transaction notice the following morning, February 7, identifying the same three players. Sacramento sent Justin Jackson and Zach Randolph to Dallas, and Barnes came back to the Kings. The announcement timing explains the two dates without changing the protected 2019-02-07 ledger. Barnes had produced 17.8 points over 49 earlier Mavericks games that season and arrived as a credible veteran starter. The Kings were using a young wing and an inactive veteran contract to secure experience and forward depth, not receiving an extra draft pick that appears nowhere in either official release.

sections.heading: The Six Sacramento Segments Sum to 399 Starts
sections.body: Barnes started all 28 of his first Kings games in the remainder of 2018-19. He followed with 72, 58, 77, 82 and 82 starts during 2019-20 through 2023-24. The resulting 399 starts show unusual continuity for a player acquired near the trade deadline. His scoring ranged from 16.4 a night in 2021-22 down to 12.2 during 2023-24 as other Kings scorers took on larger roles. His contributions also included 82 starts in 2022-23, when Sacramento returned to the postseason. Barnes moved to San Antonio in the 2024 offseason, so the Spurs’ later games are not counted as ongoing Kings production from the original Dallas exchange.

sections.heading: Dallas Got Two Assets but Only One Played
sections.body: Justin Jackson’s Mavericks debut occurred after 52 Sacramento games in the first part of 2018-19. He played 29 Dallas games and started 11 over the remaining schedule, then appeared in 65 more games, starting three, in 2019-20. He offered reserve forward minutes but never occupied the long-term starting role Barnes held in Sacramento. Zach Randolph’s situation was different: Dallas took on the veteran forward’s contract, then waived him February 8, before he played for the Mavericks. His 17-year NBA playing history cannot be transferred into the Dallas side of the deal. Both assets should be included in the formal archive, but their court production is 94 and zero games respectively.

sections.heading: A Team-Building Verdict without False Championship Credit
sections.body: The Mavericks were restructuring around Luka Doncic and had also acquired Kristaps Porzingis near the end of January. The Barnes trade can be considered part of the wider roster reshaping, but the Kings did not send Porzingis or any other Knicks assets to Dallas. Sacramento got a reliable starting wing for six partial or complete seasons, a tenure that extended into the franchise’s 2023 postseason return. Whether the Kings would have reached those results without Barnes is unknowable. What the receiving-team records actually establish is 399 Barnes starts, 94 Jackson games and no Randolph Mavericks appearance. That difference is the most defensible basketball foundation for the inherited A versus C- assessment.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Sacramento A, Dallas C- and Kings Win are preserved. Barnes played and started 399 Kings games through 2023-24; Jackson appeared 94 times with Dallas, and Randolph was waived without a Mavericks game. The Kings’ late-February-6 press release and Mavericks’ February-7 transaction date are consistent with one exchange. The 2023 Sacramento postseason and Dallas’s broader roster overhaul supply context, not unearned additional trade assets.

sections.heading: Dallas Traded Sirvydis for Roby and Two Future Second-Round Picks
sections.body: The 2019 draft-night transaction began with Deividas Sirvydis at No. 37 and Isaiah Roby at No. 45. Detroit obtained Sirvydis’s rights from Dallas. In return, the Mavericks received Roby’s rights plus a 2020 Utah-origin second-round pick and a 2021 Portland-origin second-round pick. Detroit’s official June 27 announcement names those future selections explicitly. At the time, neither future pick had a player name attached. The original imported transaction mistakenly presented Brandon Boston Jr. as a player acquired by Dallas in 2019; he was instead selected with the 2021 Portland pick two years later, after Dallas had already traded that selection away. The corrected canonical asset ledger stores a 2021 draft pick, not a player, and keeps the original team directions intact.

sections.heading: Dallas Used the 2021 Pick in the Delon Wright Deal
sections.body: Just 12 days after draft night, Dallas sent Memphis two future second-round selections and the draft rights to Satnam Singh in the July 8, 2019 sign-and-trade for guard Delon Wright. Memphis’s official release verifies the two-pick structure. The Portland 2021 second that Dallas acquired from Detroit was one of those selections, and it ultimately became No. 51 Brandon Boston Jr. in 2021. That makes the 2021 pick a useful piece of Dallas’s Wright package, not a player who suited up for the Mavericks in 2019. The 2023 second-rounder in the Memphis transaction had a separate origin and should not be counted as an extra piece in the Detroit trade. This sequence supplies a real downstream outcome without inventing a player transfer across draft years.

sections.heading: The 2020 Utah Pick Helped Bring Cauley-Stein to Dallas
sections.body: The other future selection from Detroit was Utah’s 2020 second-round pick, ultimately No. 51 Justinian Jessup. Dallas had already traded that pick to Golden State in January 2020 for center Willie Cauley-Stein, who was brought in after Dwight Powell’s Achilles injury. The Mavericks’ official announcement explicitly traces the Utah pick to the previous summer’s Detroit exchange. Jessup therefore was never directly drafted by Dallas through this swap. The pick’s value to Dallas was the ability to obtain immediate center help in 2020; the selection’s later player name is an identifying outcome, not proof that Jessup was a Mavericks roster asset. Distinguishing asset conversion from who eventually made the draft choice is essential to an accurate assessment.

sections.heading: Roby Was Also Reused in a Separate 2020 Transaction
sections.body: Dallas signed Roby in August 2019 but did not put him into an NBA regular-season game for the Mavericks. In January 2020, the club sent him to Oklahoma City for Justin Patton and cash, then waived Patton while opening a roster spot for Cauley-Stein. Roby later developed into an NBA contributor elsewhere; crediting all of his later Oklahoma City production as Dallas on-court output would be misleading. The inherited Mavericks Win verdict (Dallas B, Detroit C+) is preserved, but its factual basis is narrower and more specific: Dallas turned the 2021 pick into part of the Wright acquisition and the Utah 2020 pick into Cauley-Stein, while using Roby in an additional roster-management trade. Detroit received Sirvydis’s rights. Those separately documented paths support a directional judgment without assigning Dallas another club’s player statistics.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win — the inherited grades are Dallas B, Detroit C+. The draft-night return to Dallas was Isaiah Roby’s rights plus a 2020 Utah second-rounder and 2021 Portland second-rounder, not Brandon Boston Jr. as a 2019 player. Dallas subsequently used the 2021 pick in the Delon Wright transaction, the Utah pick for Willie Cauley-Stein, and Roby in a separate Oklahoma City deal. Detroit acquired Sirvydis’s rights. These source-backed asset chains justify reviewing Dallas’s transactional return while preserving the stored grades and the privacy policy.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Isaiah Roby, Two Picks, and the 2019 Dallas–Detroit Draft-Night Deal
featuredDeepDive.intro: Detroit traded Isaiah Roby’s draft rights and the future Utah 2020 and Portland 2021 second-round picks to Dallas for Deividas Sirvydis’s rights on draft night in 2019. The original ledger imported Brandon Boston Jr. as if he were an existing 2019 player, but his identity belongs to the 2021 pick. Dallas then used those two selections in the Willie Cauley-Stein and Delon Wright transactions before either selection was made. The inherited Mavericks Win, Dallas B/Detroit C+, is retained.

sections.heading: Why Two Future Selections Matter More Than Two Future Players
sections.body: The original June 2019 NBA and Detroit press announcements identify two unnamed future second-round selections: Utah’s 2020 second and Portland’s 2021 second. The 2020 selection eventually became No. 51 Justinian Jessup, and the 2021 selection became No. 51 Brandon Boston Jr. Neither future player was traded directly by the Pistons to the Mavericks in June 2019. That legal and chronological distinction changes the transaction model: the franchise received picks it could move or exercise, not the rights to players who had yet to be drafted. Sirvydis and Roby were the actual two drafted players whose rights exchanged sides during the night. Keeping the exact draft years and originating teams avoids accidentally creating an impossible 2019 NBA appearance or player acquisition.

sections.heading: The Portland Pick Went to Memphis After Twelve Days
sections.body: Dallas used Portland’s future 2021 second-rounder as part of its July 8, 2019 agreement with Memphis. The Grizzlies sent Delon Wright in a sign-and-trade and received a package that included that selection, another future second-rounder and the rights to Satnam Singh. The separate pick ultimately became Brandon Boston Jr. at No. 51 in the 2021 draft. The Dallas value to discuss here is the future pick’s participation in a real guard acquisition, not Boston’s subsequent career. The second future selection in the Wright trade was separate from the Detroit draft-night package, and its draft identity cannot be used to inflate the original deal.

sections.heading: The Utah Pick Helped Address an Injury at Center
sections.body: Dallas converted Utah’s future 2020 second into the January 2020 Willie Cauley-Stein transaction with Golden State. The Mavericks’ contemporaneous announcement says the team acquired the center because Dwight Powell’s Achilles injury had left a frontcourt need, and confirms the outgoing selection came from the Detroit draft-night exchange. The pick later produced Justinian Jessup at No. 51 for the franchise that ultimately exercised it. That is a distinct type of value from a Dallas-drafted player: the outgoing pick obtained a veteran center for a short-term positional need. The trade should be credited for the pick’s traceable usefulness without also adding Jessup’s later history as another Dallas contributor.

sections.heading: Roby’s Dallas Tenure and the Kept Grade
sections.body: Roby was the third piece Dallas received by acquiring his draft rights at No. 45. The Mavericks signed him, developed him in the G League and then traded him to Oklahoma City with no Mavericks NBA game appearances. Dallas received Justin Patton and cash in the January 2020 transaction and waived Patton shortly afterward. Roby’s later NBA production belongs to his subsequent franchises; it does not show that Dallas kept a long-term rotation player. The inherited B/C+ relative grades and Mavericks Win headline have been left intact pending independent grading review. Unlike the old boilerplate, the revised analysis grounds the value case in the separately sourced conversions of the two future picks and Roby, rather than in fictional 2019 ownership of Brandon Boston Jr.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Dallas holds the inherited B grade and Mavericks Win verdict, Detroit C+. The deal transferred Isaiah Roby’s rights and two future second-round picks to Dallas for Sirvydis’s rights. Those picks later identified as Jessup (2020) and Boston Jr. (2021), but Dallas exchanged them for Willie Cauley-Stein and in the Delon Wright package before the selections. Roby later moved to Oklahoma City. All asset identities are tied to draft timelines; no player from the 2021 draft is represented as an actual player acquired in 2019.
