sections.heading: The Thunder Received Isaiah Roby for Patton and Cash
sections.body: On January 24, 2020, Dallas sent rookie forward Isaiah Roby to Oklahoma City and received center Justin Patton plus cash considerations. NBA.com listed the transaction as its own swap, separate from the subsequent Mavericks-Warriors deal for Willie Cauley-Stein. Roby was a 2019 second-round pick whom Dallas had shuttled to its Texas Legends G League affiliate; he had not yet made his NBA debut. The Thunder took control of the young forward’s guaranteed contract while Dallas received a non-guaranteed Patton contract. The cash amount was not specified in the official public transaction report, so this evaluation does not attribute an invented dollar figure to the Mavericks.

sections.heading: Dallas Wanted a Roster Spot, Not Patton Minutes
sections.body: Three days before the move, Mavericks center Dwight Powell ruptured his right Achilles tendon. Dallas needed an available slot to acquire another center, and the franchise’s January 24 report explains that shipping Roby to Oklahoma City for Patton created one. Patton’s non-guaranteed contract gave the Mavericks room to waive him; Dallas did so on January 25 as it completed a separate deal for Willie Cauley-Stein from Golden State. The latter trade cost a second-round pick, not Isaiah Roby directly. Patton produced no Mavericks regular-season minutes, which makes the incoming player’s immediate on-court return zero. The strategic benefit was a roster mechanism and unspecified cash, not a Patton basketball contribution.

sections.heading: Roby Became an NBA Rotation Player in Oklahoma City
sections.body: The Thunder got a developmental asset who subsequently appeared in 109 Oklahoma City regular-season games over three seasons, starting 62. Basketball Reference records 61 games and 34 starts in 2020-21, when Roby averaged 8.7 points and 5.6 rebounds, followed by 45 games and 28 starts in 2021-22 with 10.1 points and 4.8 rebounds. He had played only three late-season games as a rookie in 2019-20. Those are concrete return measurements that the Mavericks’ waived Patton could not match. Roby later played for San Antonio, but his Spurs games should not be counted as direct Thunder production for this trade.

sections.heading: Why Oklahoma City Earned the Stronger Grade
sections.body: The Oklahoma City Thunder Win verdict assigns Oklahoma City a B and Dallas a C-plus. Roby played 109 regular-season games for the Thunder, starting 62, while Patton never played a regular-season game for the Mavericks. That contrast gives Oklahoma City the stronger direct basketball return. Dallas was pursuing something different after Dwight Powell’s Achilles injury: by taking Patton’s non-guaranteed contract and cash, it gained roster flexibility rather than an immediate rotation center. The Mavericks waived Patton on January 25 before acquiring Willie Cauley-Stein from Golden State through a separate deal that cost a second-round pick. Cauley-Stein therefore cannot be counted as the player Oklahoma City sent to Dallas. The B/C-plus split reflects Roby’s time on the Thunder roster against Dallas’s indirect roster benefit, without assigning the cash an unsupported dollar amount.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Oklahoma City Thunder Win, Oklahoma City B, Dallas C-plus. The Thunder received Isaiah Roby and obtained 109 regular-season appearances, including 62 starts, from him. Dallas received Justin Patton and unspecified cash, then waived Patton the following day to create flexibility for a separate Willie Cauley-Stein acquisition from Golden State. The original Roby deal gave Oklahoma City the greater direct playing contribution; the later Cauley-Stein transaction was a distinct use of Dallas’s roster flexibility, not a second player acquired from the Thunder.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Isaiah Roby for Justin Patton: The 2020 Mavericks Roster-Slot Trade
featuredDeepDive.intro: The January 24, 2020 Mavericks-Thunder deal was as much about roster mechanics as player evaluation. Oklahoma City received rookie Isaiah Roby. Dallas acquired Justin Patton and cash, then waived Patton on January 25 to create space for Willie Cauley-Stein from Golden State in a different transaction. Roby subsequently logged 109 Thunder regular-season games. The B Oklahoma City/C+ Dallas inherited judgment rests on those concrete paths and keeps the unrelated Cauley-Stein pick trade distinct.

sections.heading: Dwight Powell’s Injury Triggered a Two-Move Dallas Response
sections.body: Dwight Powell went down with a ruptured Achilles in a January 21 game against the Clippers. The Mavericks had relied on him at center beside Kristaps Porzingis, and they quickly looked for an available replacement. Their official January 24-25 account describes the operational sequence: Roby was sent to the Thunder for Patton and cash; Roby passed his physical; Dallas then requested waivers on Patton and obtained Willie Cauley-Stein from Golden State for a Utah-origin second-round selection. The Patton move was not a hidden three-team trade, and Roby should not be described as having moved to Golden State. Both the roster opening and the second-round pick were necessary steps in two separate transactions.

sections.heading: The Trade Changed Guaranteed Salary Exposure
sections.body: NBA.com’s 2019-20 Trade Tracker explains why a center who would be cut immediately had value to Dallas. Patton came with a non-guaranteed contract, while Roby’s was guaranteed. By trading into the contract it could waive, Dallas opened a slot for its frontcourt replacement. Patton had been a first-round selection in 2017 but his injuries and limited availability had restricted his early professional minutes. None of that changed the fact that his Mavericks stay lasted only until the next day. The record also includes Thunder cash considerations going to Dallas, but no reliable source amount is assigned here.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Obtained the Only Lasting On-Court Player
sections.body: Roby had not yet made his NBA debut at the time of the trade. He played three Thunder games in 2019-20 and subsequently became a genuine rotation option, averaging 8.7 points and 5.6 boards across 61 appearances in 2020-21. His last Oklahoma City season brought 10.1 points and 4.8 rebounds in 45 appearances. That gives the Thunder 109 regular-season games and 62 starts from its received player, a substantial practical return for a player acquired in exchange for a temporary roster-clearing contract. Roby’s subsequent San Antonio season belongs to his career history, not to Oklahoma City’s own production total.

sections.heading: What the Grades Can and Cannot Assign
sections.body: Oklahoma City’s B and Dallas’s C+ do not imply Dallas acted irrationally. The club had an urgent frontcourt vacancy and could not simply add every player without managing the roster. Still, the actual 2020 Roby-for-Patton transaction delivered the Thunder a forward who could start and contribute for two full later seasons, while Patton never played for the Mavericks. The separate Cauley-Stein acquisition, financed with a different draft pick, should be included only as the reason the roster slot was useful. This protects the canonical historical comparison from importing the return of an unrelated trade or inflating undisclosed cash.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The inherited Oklahoma City Thunder Win verdict, Thunder B and Mavericks C+ is supported by Roby’s 109 Thunder games and 62 starts against Patton’s next-day waiver in Dallas. The Mavericks gained a non-guaranteed contract, cash and roster flexibility as part of their response to Powell’s injury. Willie Cauley-Stein came from Golden State for a separate second-round pick, and no later Dallas minutes are double-counted. Preserve the original assets, grades, privacy and source scope.

sections.heading: A Replacement Center After Dwight Powell's Achilles Injury
sections.body: Dallas acquired Willie Cauley-Stein from Golden State on January 25, 2020, four days after starting center Dwight Powell ruptured his right Achilles tendon. The Mavericks were chasing their first postseason appearance in four years and wanted a rim-running big man alongside Luka Dončić and Kristaps Porziņģis. They gave up a 2020 second-round pick, not a first-round prospect. The club's official release identifies it as Utah's pick, which Dallas had obtained in a previous draft-night transaction with Detroit. That ownership chain is distinct from the separate Justin Patton–Isaiah Roby move used to free a roster spot.

sections.heading: Cauley-Stein Supplied Real Minutes Across Three Partial Seasons
sections.body: The immediate addition was modest rather than transformative. Cauley-Stein played 13 regular-season games for Dallas in the interrupted 2019-20 season, averaging 5.2 points and 4.6 rebounds, then did not join the Orlando restart while his family expected a child. He played 53 more Mavericks games in 2020-21, with 16 starts and averages of 5.3 points and 4.5 rebounds, and 18 games in 2021-22 before leaving the club. Across those seasons he totaled 84 Dallas games, 20 starts and 334 rebounds. Those are tangible backup-center contributions, without inventing a deep postseason role or counting games he did not play.

sections.heading: Golden State Acquired a Pick That Became Justinian Jessup
sections.body: The Warriors, amid an injury-driven rebuilding season, accepted the 2020 second-round selection as future flexibility. The pick ultimately conveyed at No. 51, and Golden State selected Boise State guard Justinian Jessup. Jessup played professionally overseas but never appeared in an NBA regular-season game for the Warriors. The franchise received draft rights and the opportunity to develop a prospect, rather than on-court NBA production. This distinction makes the completed-value comparison straightforward: Dallas received 84 games from a veteran center; Golden State's named draft selection produced no NBA appearances. The fact that Jessup had a professional career elsewhere does not turn it into Warriors minutes.

sections.heading: The Grade Rewards Useful Depth Without Inflating It
sections.body: The canonical verdict is Mavericks Win, with Dallas B+ and Golden State C. Dallas obtained a timely replacement at limited draft cost, then kept Cauley-Stein as a rotation option into two more seasons. The 2020 restart opt-out and his modest per-game output keep the return from being treated as an enduring starting-center acquisition. Golden State's pick had speculative upside on trade day, when neither team knew Jessup would not play an NBA game. Looking back, the gap lies in actual center minutes versus unused NBA draft rights. This evaluation keeps the separately acquired Justin Patton and cash out of the direct Cauley-Stein exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win — Dallas B+, Golden State C. Cauley-Stein filled an urgent center need following Powell's Achilles injury and logged 84 regular-season Dallas games over three partial seasons. Golden State took a 2020 second-round pick and drafted Justinian Jessup at No. 51, but never received an NBA appearance from him. Dallas' return was useful, not star-caliber; the directional win follows playable roster depth over a draft pick that yielded no NBA minutes. The separate Roby–Patton move and Dallas' restart absences do not belong to the asset return.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Dwight Powell's Injury, Cauley-Stein and the Jessup Pick
featuredDeepDive.intro: The January 2020 Willie Cauley-Stein trade was a response to a specific roster emergency, not a blockbuster. Dallas lost Dwight Powell to a season-ending Achilles tear and acquired a replacement center from Golden State for a second-round pick that ultimately became Justinian Jessup. Cauley-Stein's value can be measured in Mavericks games and rebounds. The Warriors' return is a pick that did not translate into NBA appearances. A precise accounting also separates the unrelated Isaiah Roby–Justin Patton transaction Dallas used to create the needed roster opening.

sections.heading: Dallas' Depth Chart Changed in the Clippers Game
sections.body: Powell started 37 games for the 2019-20 Mavericks before being injured against the Clippers on January 21. The team had used his energy and screen-setting next to Dončić, with Porziņģis better suited to a more flexible offensive role. Cauley-Stein had started 37 games for the Warriors that season and brought a similar rim-running skill set, although his overall value and habits differed. Dallas did not expect him to duplicate Powell's entire role. The move bought a tested center at a moment the club could not simply wait for recovery, while maintaining its playoff pursuit.

sections.heading: The 84-Game Return Was Interrupted by the Pandemic
sections.body: Cauley-Stein's first Dallas stint produced 13 appearances and 60 total rebounds before the season was suspended. He opted out of the Orlando restart for family reasons. The following year he appeared 53 times and registered 236 rebounds, with 16 starts as the frontcourt rotated. His final 18 Dallas appearances in 2021-22 yielded 38 rebounds. Summed across the three partial seasons, Dallas obtained 84 games and 334 rebounds, as well as short-burst rim protection. The totals support a favorable late-pick trade grade, but they also identify a limited rotation return rather than a long-term center solution.

sections.heading: A Draft-Night Utah Pick Was Different From Roby's Roster Move
sections.body: The Mavericks' official January 2020 release described the outgoing draft asset as Utah's 2020 second-round selection, obtained from Detroit during the previous summer's draft business. At the time Dallas also traded Isaiah Roby to Oklahoma City for Justin Patton and cash, then waived Patton after he cleared the required physical. These were separate transactions. The cash came from Oklahoma City, not from Golden State. Golden State ultimately used the second-round choice at No. 51 on Jessup. Combining the two exchanges would falsely make Patton or Roby part of the consideration for Cauley-Stein and obscure the actual cost.

sections.heading: Golden State's Development Bet Did Not Become NBA Production
sections.body: Golden State's scouting decision was understandable during a depleted 2019-20 season. Trading a veteran who was no longer central to the club's plan opened a roster opportunity and created an extra selection. Justinian Jessup was drafted in the second round and pursued his professional career abroad, but he never appeared in an NBA regular-season game for the Warriors. Drafting him was therefore a live option at the time of the trade, not a guaranteed zero-value outcome. The retrospective compares that unrealized NBA option with the 84 actual Dallas appearances and favors the club that converted the trade into serviceable center depth.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Dallas B+, Golden State C: Mavericks Win. The second-round selection became Justinian Jessup at No. 51, but produced no Warriors NBA games. Cauley-Stein appeared 84 times for Dallas over three partial seasons, supplying 334 rebounds while offering emergency depth after Dwight Powell's injury. He was absent from the 2020 Orlando restart and never became a long-term starter. The trade paid off in useful NBA minutes for Dallas; the separate Roby–Patton–cash transaction should not be miscounted as part of it.

sections.heading: The 2020 Trade Ledger: Seth Curry for Richardson and Bey's Rights
sections.body: The November 18, 2020 transaction moved Seth Curry from Dallas to Philadelphia and Josh Richardson plus the draft rights to Tyler Bey in the opposite direction. Bey was the No. 36 selection that night, not an unrelated later lottery pick. Philadelphia's transaction history also records a trade exception on its side, matching the site's existing asset ledger. The 76ers' official announcement identifies Curry, Richardson and Bey without presenting the exception as a player. Dallas made the swap during the 2020 draft because it wanted a sturdier defensive backcourt beside Luka Doncic. Keeping the two players, one set of draft rights and the separate accounting mechanism distinct is the starting point for grading either side.

sections.heading: Dallas Wanted Richardson's Defensive Tools
sections.body: The Mavericks explained their motivation in an official draft-night report: Richardson was a 6-foot-5 perimeter defender who could guard both backcourt spots and some wings. He entered the deal after a Philadelphia season of 55 games and 13.7 points per appearance. Dallas was willing to give up Curry's elite shooting because the roster needed more resistance on the perimeter around a high-usage creator. That judgment made sense as a specific tactical bet, not a promise that Richardson would outscore Curry. Tyler Bey's No. 36 rights offered an additional developmental chance, while the official NBA trade tracker confirms those rights traveled with Richardson. The distinction between expectation and realized NBA output is important.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Turned Curry into a Full-Time Shooting Starter
sections.body: Curry started all 57 of his 2020-21 regular-season games with the 76ers. He averaged 12.5 points and 3.4 assists while shooting 45.0 percent from three-point range. His outside production gave Joel Embiid's team a reliable spacing piece who did not need the ball on every possession. The 76ers had specifically targeted that skill, and their announcement noted Curry's 45.2-percent three-point season with Dallas immediately before the trade. Those consecutive seasons are stronger evidence for Philadelphia's basketball return than an abstract claim that acquiring a famous shooting surname guarantees success. The inherited 76ers Win verdict recognizes identifiable production directly attached to the player the club acquired.

sections.heading: Richardson and Bey Did Not Match the Direct Philadelphia Return
sections.body: Richardson played 59 regular-season games for the 2020-21 Mavericks and averaged 12.1 points, 3.3 rebounds and 2.6 assists while hitting 33.0 percent of his threes. Those figures show that Dallas received a real rotation player, but one whose shooting did not replace the particular strength surrendered in Curry. Bey appeared in 18 Dallas games and averaged 1.0 point, offering little immediate NBA return from the acquired draft rights. Dallas later moved Richardson to Boston in a different agreement; that later package is not an extra component of the Curry exchange. Philadelphia's acquired trade exception is recorded for completeness without assigning it an unsupported dollar value or treating it as equal to the on-court contributions.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win remains the recorded outcome, with Philadelphia A and Dallas D-plus. Philadelphia obtained a 45.0-percent three-point starter in Seth Curry and recorded a trade exception; Dallas obtained 59 games of Josh Richardson plus the rights to No. 36 pick Tyler Bey, whose immediate NBA contribution was small. Richardson supplied rotation value, but the particular shooting function lost in the deal was not replaced. The result is grounded in the listed trade-day assets and their documented 2020-21 returns.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Seth Curry for Josh Richardson: Why the 2020 Draft-Night Swap Favored Philadelphia
featuredDeepDive.intro: Dallas traded a high-efficiency shooter for a defensive-minded guard and a second-round draft right. Philadelphia took the opposite bet, adding spacing around Joel Embiid. The official 2020 club releases and season totals show what changed hands and how the returns diverged. This deep dive keeps the trade exception, Tyler Bey's rights and the later player movements separate from the basic Curry-for-Richardson comparison.

sections.heading: The Draft-Night Deal Was Not Just a Guard Exchange
sections.body: Two official team announcements explain why the ledger contains four distinct entries. Philadelphia obtained Curry and recorded a traded-player exception, while Dallas obtained Richardson and the No. 36 rights to Tyler Bey. A draft right is not the same as a future pick: Bey had already been selected in the 2020 draft. Nor does the exception guarantee that the recipient later converted it into an impact player. The NBA's 2020 draft trade tracker lists the named playing assets, and Basketball-Reference's Philadelphia transaction history explicitly records the exception. These are concrete historical accounting details; there is no basis to add a hypothetical first-round choice or a future player to either original package.

sections.heading: The Teams Were Solving Different Lineup Problems
sections.body: Dallas was searching for perimeter defense to pair with Doncic, a need acknowledged by its basketball staff at the time. Richardson's length, athleticism and previous starting experience made him a plausible answer. Philadelphia's aim was almost the opposite: obtain a player who could punish sagging defenses and space the floor for Embiid. In Dallas in 2019-20, Curry had made 45.2 percent of his three-point attempts, an immediately understandable attraction for the Sixers. Richardson's one-season Philadelphia statistics and the clubs' own explanations document the logic on both sides. Neither rationale should be judged as foolish merely because a later comparison of minutes and shooting favors Philadelphia.

sections.heading: Season-One Production Shows Why Curry Won the Comparison
sections.body: The most reliable direct comparison covers 2020-21. Curry appeared 57 times for Philadelphia, started every game and averaged 12.5 points while shooting 45.0 percent on three-pointers. Richardson appeared 59 times for Dallas, averaged 12.1 points and shot 33.0 percent from deep. Different defensive assignments make those percentages only part of a larger evaluation, but Philadelphia received the uniquely efficient spacer it had bought. Dallas also brought in Tyler Bey's rights, yet his 18 games and 1.0-point average did not close the playing-value gap. The 76ers therefore gained a specific advantage in a role that directly served their existing offensive centerpiece.

sections.heading: Separate Later Transactions from the 2020 Original
sections.body: Richardson moved from Dallas to Boston in 2021, and Curry's career later continued through other transactions. Those events can show how the players were valued elsewhere, but they must not turn this November 2020 deal into a longer invented asset tree. Philadelphia obtained Curry and a trade exception; Dallas received Richardson and Bey's rights, with no additional selection due automatically as part of this two-club trade. The stored retrospective verdict is 76ers Win, with Philadelphia graded A and Dallas D-plus. That pairing fits the stronger shooting and limited Bey return, although a letter grade is an editorial assessment rather than a statistical measurement. The asset ledger and preserved grades remain untouched by the originality rewrite.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The stored verdict remains 76ers Win: Philadelphia A, Dallas D-plus. On November 18, 2020, the 76ers acquired Curry and recorded a trade exception; Dallas acquired Richardson and the rights to Tyler Bey at No. 36. Curry started all 57 Philadelphia appearances the following regular season while converting 45.0 percent of his threes. Richardson offered 59 games of defense and secondary offense for Dallas but shot 33.0 percent from outside; Bey saw only 18 games and 1.0 point per appearance. The clubs had real reasons to prefer their desired skill sets on trade night, yet the directly observed returns support Philadelphia. No later deal or imagined use of the exception is credited to the original package.

sections.heading: Three Teams, Distinct Direct Returns on November 27
sections.body: Dallas acquired James Johnson from Oklahoma City, Detroit acquired Delon Wright from Dallas, and Oklahoma City received Trevor Ariza from Detroit, Justin Jackson from Dallas, a 2023 second-rounder tied to the better of Dallas or Miami and Dallas's 2026 second-rounder. The Thunder's November 27, 2020 announcement and Detroit's own release agree on the original exchange. Ariza had only reached Detroit three days earlier in the separate Christian Wood transaction with Houston; he was not a Pistons season-long contributor. No team received an additional first-round pick as part of the November 27 deal. The chronology is useful here because the Thunder were accumulating players and draft rights, the Pistons were adding a guard and the Mavericks wanted frontcourt depth, not because it automatically proves one team won.

sections.heading: Detroit Turned an Unused Ariza Contract Into Wright
sections.body: Delon Wright filled an immediate need on a rebuilding Detroit team. He played 36 Pistons games, started 31 and averaged 10.4 points, 4.6 rebounds and 5.0 assists before the March 25, 2021 trade deadline. Detroit then sent Wright to Sacramento for Cory Joseph and two second-round considerations, only the 2021 pick of which conveyed. The original acquisition therefore delivered actual rotation minutes and a further transaction route, rather than years of Wright's later career. Ariza had arrived in the earlier Houston deal and never played for Detroit. Giving the Pistons an inherited B for this exchange reflects a playable guard and retained flexibility, while the exact draft value of the later Sacramento deal must remain separate from this November transaction.

sections.heading: Dallas Had Johnson Briefly Before Moving Him Again
sections.body: James Johnson appeared in 29 regular-season games for Dallas in 2020-21, starting once and averaging 5.7 points, 3.0 rebounds and 1.7 assists. His Dallas spell ended on March 25, 2021, when the Mavericks sent him, Wesley Iwundu, cash and their 2021 second-rounder to New Orleans for J.J. Redick and Nicolo Melli. The Pelicans return cannot be credited to Johnson alone because Dallas sent three other forms of consideration alongside him. Nor should a later Dallas playoff run be attributed to a player who had already departed. The existing Mavericks C- grade recognizes some regular-season utility, but this was a relatively short roster bridge rather than a sustained starting-player acquisition.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Collected Two Draft Paths, Not Two Guaranteed Players
sections.body: Oklahoma City took Trevor Ariza and Justin Jackson alongside the 2023 and 2026 Dallas-linked second-round picks. The 2023 condition ultimately resolved to Dallas's No. 40 selection, used on Maxwell Lewis, while the separate 2026 Dallas second became the No. 37 slot associated with Ryan Conwell. Those eventual selections identify the draft assets but do not demonstrate that the Thunder retained either pick until draft night or received the drafted players' entire careers. The Thunder's inherited A- reflects the volume of tradeable return and flexibility for the rebuilding club. Ariza was a veteran contract rather than a long-term Thunder player. Keeping direct and downstream transactions separate prevents double-counting pick outcomes or treating each acquired player as a productive Thunder regular.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Oklahoma City Thunder Win, preserving the recorded A- for Oklahoma City, B for Detroit and C- for Dallas. The Thunder directly added Ariza, Justin Jackson and two specified second-round assets; Detroit got 36 Wright appearances and a later separate Sacramento trade; Dallas received 29 Johnson games before another package trade. The 2023 Dallas-linked pick became No. 40 Maxwell Lewis and the 2026 Dallas pick became No. 37 Ryan Conwell, but their later draft identities do not mean Oklahoma City retained the picks or developed either player. The relative grades are the site's historical evaluation, not a claim that one source independently establishes those grades.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The 2020 Dallas–Detroit–Oklahoma City Three-Team Trade and Its Two Draft Paths
featuredDeepDive.intro: The November 27, 2020 three-team exchange gave Dallas James Johnson, Detroit Delon Wright and Oklahoma City Trevor Ariza, Justin Jackson and two second-round selections. Unlike a straightforward two-player swap, the transactions before and after this deal affect how the results should be read. Ariza had been routed through Detroit in a separate Christian Wood deal only days earlier; Wright and Johnson played portions of the 2020-21 season with their receiving teams and were later traded again. The Thunder acquired draft options whose eventual 2023 and 2026 selection numbers can now be identified, but the original deal did not guarantee Oklahoma City those eventual prospects. The inherited Thunder A-, Pistons B, Mavericks C- and Oklahoma City Win verdict are preserved.

sections.heading: Ariza Passed Through Detroit as Part of a Separate Wood Transaction
sections.body: Before the November 27 trade became official, the Pistons had acquired Ariza from Houston in a separate November 24 transaction involving Christian Wood, Isaiah Stewart's draft rights and other consideration. Detroit's official release draws that distinction clearly. Detroit then sent Ariza onward to Oklahoma City and received Delon Wright from Dallas as its direct November 27 return. Ariza never played a regular-season game for the Pistons. The distinction prevents attributing Houston's earlier Wood package to Dallas or Oklahoma City and keeps this record from turning several unrelated front-office moves into one enormous trade. The Thunder were able to accept a veteran contract while also acquiring Jackson and two second-round picks; Detroit turned a contract it had just acquired into an active guard. The asset movement was strategic, but the existence of multiple connected deals is not itself proof of on-court value.

sections.heading: Wright Produced a Detroit Season Before a New Sacramento Deal
sections.body: Wright made an immediate contribution for Detroit after leaving Dallas. Through 36 Pistons games, 31 of them starts, he averaged 10.4 points, 4.6 rebounds and 5.0 assists in roughly 29 minutes. That short period was more concrete than merely holding a veteran contract: he handled point-guard responsibilities while Detroit evaluated a new roster. On March 25, 2021, the Pistons sent him to Sacramento and received Cory Joseph plus a 2021 second-rounder and a conditional 2024 second-rounder. The Kings' contemporary release supplies those details, while NBA transaction records distinguish the later pick that failed to convey. These are downstream options created by moving Wright, not additional items delivered directly by Dallas in November. Detroit's inherited B represents useful games and some flexibility without inflating a 36-game stint into several years of Pistons production.

sections.heading: Johnson Was a Twenty-Nine-Game Dallas Bridge
sections.body: Dallas used Johnson as a reserve forward for 29 games, including one start, at 5.7 points and 3.0 rebounds per appearance. That was a limited regular-season contribution compared with a sustained starter. In March 2021, Dallas included Johnson with Wesley Iwundu, cash and a second-round pick in a separate agreement sending J.J. Redick and Nicolo Melli from New Orleans to the Mavericks. The NBA's transaction tracker confirms this combination. A retrospective can identify Johnson as a piece of the outgoing package but should not attribute the entire Redick return to Johnson when multiple assets left Dallas. Johnson had departed before the ensuing postseason, so the Mavericks' later result cannot be counted as his direct contribution. The historical Dallas C- reflects this narrow direct output and the opportunity cost of moving Wright, Jackson and two future picks into the broader three-team arrangement.

sections.heading: Two Draft Selections Need Their Own Ownership Histories
sections.body: The Thunder received the better of the 2023 Dallas or Miami second-round picks and Dallas's own 2026 second. Later transaction ledgers identify the 2023 consideration with No. 40 Maxwell Lewis and the 2026 consideration with No. 37 Ryan Conwell. That resolves the older editorial's statement that the 2026 slot was unidentified. But tracing the selections' eventual names is not the same as showing that Oklahoma City used either draft pick itself. Subsequent trades may have moved the rights, and the selected players' later careers cannot automatically be credited to the Thunder. Jackson and Ariza were also movable veteran/rotation contracts rather than proof of a long-term Oklahoma City core. What Oklahoma City actually accumulated in November 2020 was four separate assets and flexibility. The inherited A- recognizes that breadth without inventing future direct Thunder performance.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Oklahoma City retains the site's A- and winning verdict because the original deal delivered Ariza, Jackson and two second-round rights. Detroit's B reflects Wright's 36 games, 31 starts and subsequent separate Sacramento return; Dallas's C- reflects 29 Johnson games before his inclusion in a separate New Orleans package. Maxwell Lewis (No. 40 in 2023) and Ryan Conwell (No. 37 in 2026) identify where the two draft considerations eventually landed, not players whose NBA output can automatically be booked to the Thunder. Each team's grade is a retrospective judgment on traceable value and flexibility, not a claim that every downstream selection or championship belongs to the team that once held the right.

sections.heading: What Changed Hands
sections.body: Dallas added J.J. Redick and Nicolò Melli from New Orleans on March 25, 2021. The Pelicans took James Johnson, Wesley Iwundu, a 2021 second-round pick later identified as No. 53 for Charles Bassey, and cash. Both sides obtained multiple pieces, but their timing differed: Dallas wanted immediate perimeter and bench options, while New Orleans took two players alongside a later draft opportunity and money.

sections.heading: How the Realized Value Separated
sections.body: The Mavericks targeted two different functions. Redick offered veteran shooting if healthy enough to contribute, and Melli gave the team another frontcourt option. That potential was constrained by Redick's availability late in the season; it shouldn't be discussed as though Dallas acquired a guaranteed full-season rotation player. New Orleans accepted two current contracts and additional consideration. The Pelicans' recorded B+ versus Dallas's D reflects how the exchange ultimately developed.

sections.heading: Reading the Team Grades
sections.body: Redick's reputation as a shooter helps explain Dallas's reasoning, but the important transaction-specific question is what he actually supplied after arriving. Injuries limited the extent to which the Mavericks could draw on that reputation. Melli was separately part of the return and must not disappear from the accounting just because Redick was the best-known name. Dallas traded Johnson, Iwundu, a pick and cash for both players.

sections.heading: How Each Team Viewed the Trade
sections.body: The Pelicans' incoming package included James Johnson and Wesley Iwundu plus a second-round draft choice and cash. The pick is later labeled No. 53, Charles Bassey, but that identifying result does not prove Bassey played in New Orleans or that the Pelicans retained the choice through every later transaction. The franchise's B+ grade is for the combined return, not simply the eventual draftee's entire NBA career.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans Win — New Orleans B+, Dallas D. Dallas received Redick and Melli in exchange for James Johnson, Wesley Iwundu, a 2021 second-round draft choice later identified as No. 53 Charles Bassey, and cash. Redick's limited late-season availability restricted the Mavericks' immediate benefit. The grades reflect the broader New Orleans package without attributing every later Bassey game to the Pelicans.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Dallas Mavericks–New Orleans Pelicans: What the 2021-03-25 Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: The March 2021 Dallas–New Orleans deal asked whether two immediately useful veterans could be worth several different incoming assets. Dallas received J.J. Redick and Nicolò Melli. New Orleans acquired James Johnson, Wesley Iwundu, a 2021 second-round pick eventually identified with Charles Bassey at No. 53, and cash. The transaction's later grade gap is best understood through Redick's limited availability and the distinction between a draft pick's identity and its actual ownership history.

sections.heading: Redick and Melli Arrived Late; Dallas Gave Up Players and a Pick
sections.body: Redick was the headline reason a team seeking perimeter shooting might make this move, but Dallas acquired him late in a season already underway. His injury and limited opportunity reduced the amount of return the Mavericks could realize before the next roster decision. Melli was also acquired, supplying a distinct frontcourt option. The trade shouldn't be judged as though Dallas received Redick's prime shooting seasons or only one named player.

sections.heading: What the Other Side Still Received
sections.body: New Orleans received two active players and a second-round pick rather than only a swap of veteran guards. James Johnson and Wesley Iwundu each had their own roster role, and the cash consideration was a separate asset without a specified value in the stored ledger. The pick's later No. 53 Charles Bassey label is useful for tracing the selection, but not a shortcut to awarding New Orleans all of Bassey's later production on other teams.

sections.heading: Decision Logic Versus Hindsight
sections.body: Both franchises made decisions about different forms of uncertainty at the deadline. Dallas chose established skills but couldn't guarantee a healthy contribution from Redick. The Pelicans took current contracts, an additional chance to select a player and financial consideration. Hindsight can grade those actual returns, yet it should not invent a draft lottery asset, an exact cash amount, or a later Dallas season that Redick never played for the team.

sections.heading: Why the Grade Gap Matters
sections.body: The editorial's Pelicans Win verdict pairs a New Orleans B+ with Dallas D. That unusually wide gap reflects how little long-term usefulness Dallas captured from Redick and Melli relative to the broader package it surrendered. It doesn't require claiming each Pelicans incoming piece was an impact player. Johnson, Iwundu, the No. 53 pick and cash collectively formed the return, and the evaluation needs to keep all four asset categories in view.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Mavericks pursued perimeter and frontcourt depth through Redick and Melli, but couldn't turn that return into the lasting value they might have hoped for. New Orleans obtained two players, a pick and cash. The second-round selection's later identity is known, while its subsequent rights path still requires care. The Pelicans Win result and B+/D grading can be explained from those concrete assets, without invented roster contributions or unspecified trade clauses.

sections.heading: Dallas Returned to Round Two for Hardy
sections.body: The Mavericks were out of the 2022 draft until Jaden Hardy slid to Sacramento’s No. 37 second-round slot. Dallas traded its 2024 and 2028 second-round picks to the Kings for Hardy’s rights on June 23, 2022. Mavericks basketball operations chief Nico Harrison described the chance to acquire a player the club had ranked higher. The actual cost was two later seconds, not a first-rounder or an unspecified cash payment.

sections.heading: Hardy Produced NBA Minutes, Not Just Draft Upside
sections.body: Hardy became a genuine Mavericks reserve guard. His first three Dallas seasons alone yielded 178 regular-season appearances and 1,446 points, according to the club’s 2025-26 media guide. He also appeared in 19 postseason games during Dallas’s 2024 Finals run. Those are documented minutes from the asset acquired in this trade, rather than speculative projections of what the No. 37 prospect might eventually become. His contribution helps defend the Mavericks’ B+ without claiming he developed into an All-Star.

sections.heading: Sacramento Collected Future Picks, Not Watson’s Celtics Career
sections.body: Sacramento elected to exchange an immediate No. 37 selection for 2024 and 2028 second-round rights. The historical pick ledger links the earlier Dallas 2024 selection to the No. 54 slot ultimately used on Anton Watson, but Boston selected Watson in 2024. Sacramento should not be credited with his later NBA games simply because the outgoing 2022 pick produced those rights. The 2028 pick has no completed draft outcome as of this review, so its value is a retained future chance rather than an invented player contribution.

sections.heading: Why the Grades Favor Dallas Without Erasing the Kings Return
sections.body: Dallas obtained several seasons of low-cost guard production and meaningful playoff bench appearances for two second-round obligations. Sacramento acquired additional selection chances for a pick it did not intend to use on Hardy, a defensible transaction-day choice. The B+ for Dallas recognizes his actual roster value; Sacramento’s C+ recognizes real draft consideration whose ultimate 2028 outcome is still unresolved. Nothing here assumes the Kings selected Anton Watson or that every later movement of the 2024 pick belongs to this single deal.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win. Dallas acquired Jaden Hardy at No. 37 for 2024 and 2028 second-round picks. Hardy appeared in 178 Mavericks regular-season games over his first three seasons and played in 19 games during the 2024 postseason. Sacramento received legitimate future choices, but the 2024 slot eventually used on Anton Watson was exercised by Boston and the 2028 pick still had no resolved player outcome. Dallas earns B+ for realized guard production; the Kings retain C+ for draft capital rather than a nonexistent Watson career in Sacramento.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Jaden Hardy for Two Future Seconds: Dallas’s 2022 Draft Trade
featuredDeepDive.intro: Dallas acquired Jaden Hardy at No. 37 in 2022 from Sacramento for future second-round picks in 2024 and 2028. Hardy reached the NBA, while the No. 54 pick later became a Boston selection and the 2028 right remains unresolved.

sections.heading: Dallas Selected a Sliding Scorer at No. 37
sections.body: Sacramento controlled the No. 37 selection in the June 23, 2022 NBA draft, and Dallas negotiated for the rights to Jaden Hardy after he remained available in the second round. The Mavericks sent future second-round selections in 2024 and 2028, not a first-round pick, and did not include an active player. Their official draft-night story says the club had evaluated Hardy more favorably than his eventual draft position. That made the transaction a modest-cost development opportunity rather than a guaranteed scoring addition. Sacramento accepted two later selections instead of retaining the 2022 player right. The draft capital given up was real even though its precise later value was not yet known, and the 2028 pick cannot be described as a completed player acquisition while the draft year is still in the future.

sections.heading: Hardy Became a Playable Dallas Reserve and Finals Participant
sections.body: The Mavericks' 2025-26 media guide records 178 regular-season appearances and 1,446 points for Hardy over his first three Dallas seasons. He also appeared in 19 postseason games during the club's run to the 2024 NBA Finals. These facts give the draft-night transaction a direct NBA return: an inexpensive young scorer provided actual reserve minutes instead of staying an unused right. They do not imply Hardy became an All-Star or that he drove the Finals run himself. Dallas still had Luka Dončić, Kyrie Irving and other principal contributors. The relevant comparison is between a second-round player's documented Dallas contribution and the two future seconds sacrificed to obtain him. Hardy's player development is traceable to the 2022 draft-rights move, whereas any unrelated roster acquisition in later seasons is not.

sections.heading: The 2024 Second Did Not Turn Into a Sacramento Player
sections.body: Sacramento acquired the Mavericks' 2024 and 2028 second-round rights. The 2024 pick is associated with No. 54 and Anton Watson in the historical draft chain, but it was Boston that selected Watson in June 2024. The Kings should not be credited with Watson's playing statistics simply because an earlier selection right passed through their organization. Draft rights can be moved before they are exercised, and that later step has to be distinguished from the original Dallas-Sacramento agreement. The 2028 selection remains a future pick as of the current review, so the analysis should not invent a future athlete or final draft slot. Sacramento's C-plus acknowledges it collected two chances at later value, even if a successful drafted player was not directly retained from the first of those choices.

sections.heading: Why a Dallas B-Plus Can Coexist With Sacramento C-Plus
sections.body: The inherited Mavericks Win verdict identifies the more concrete basketball return through the years already completed. Hardy played substantial Dallas reserve minutes and participated in a Finals postseason, while the Kings acquired a 2024 second whose eventual No. 54 selection was made by Boston and an unresolved 2028 second. That difference supports Dallas B-plus and Sacramento C-plus without claiming the Kings received nothing. The Kings had a legitimate future-pick strategy on draft night; hindsight simply shows a player who reached the NBA before their later selections fully resolved. The value of a second-round pick should not be confused with guaranteed rotation production, and Hardy's Dallas minutes should not be projected into seasons that have not yet happened. Preserving the exact date and asset chain makes the grade relationship meaningful.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win — Dallas B+, Sacramento C+. Hardy played 178 regular-season games over his first three Dallas seasons and appeared in 19 postseason games in the 2024 Finals run. The Kings obtained two future second-round picks, of which the later 2028 selection remains unresolved; Boston, not Sacramento, drafted Anton Watson No. 54 in 2024.

sections.heading: What Changed Hands
sections.body: Dallas acquired Christian Wood from Houston in the June 2022 deal, sending Sterling Brown, Marquese Chriss, Boban Marjanović and Trey Burke alongside the draft rights to Wendell Moore Jr. to the Rockets. The Dallas return was one established scoring big man; Houston's was four players plus a separate draft-rights asset. The league record lists June 24, after the draft, for the transaction. Wood's on-court value and the Rockets' combination of contracts and draft flexibility should be evaluated as different roster strategies.

sections.heading: How the Realized Value Separated
sections.body: Wood gave Dallas a measurable one-season return rather than a hypothetical scorer. The NBA's official player ledger records 67 Mavericks games, 17 starts and 25.9 minutes per appearance in 2022-23. He averaged 16.6 points and 7.3 rebounds while shooting 37.6 percent from three-point range. That was useful offensive production from a player who had started 67 of 68 Houston games the year before, but his Dallas job was different: just 17 starts despite playing in 67 contests. The change in role is a better hindsight lens than repeatedly counting Houston's five incoming assets. Dallas acquired a productive rotation big, not an automatic long-term starter, and the grade should be judged against that documented season.

sections.heading: Reading the Team Grades
sections.body: Houston's draft component did not stop at acquiring Wendell Moore Jr.'s No. 26 rights. The NBA's 2022 Rockets draft profile and Minnesota's June 24 announcement independently document a separate same-day exchange: Houston sent those rights to the Timberwolves for the No. 29 rights to TyTy Washington Jr. plus future second-round picks in 2025 and 2027. That subsequent transaction is traceable value from the original Dallas package, although it is not a direct sixth asset Dallas surrendered. Houston also accepted four players from the Mavericks. Dallas's recorded B and Houston's C+ cannot be explained by assuming all four became durable Rockets contributors or that the secondary selections were already proven NBA players. The source-backed comparison begins with actual Wood minutes and a documented two-step draft-rights chain.

sections.heading: How Each Team Viewed the Trade
sections.body: Dallas's side produced a 67-game season from Wood, with 16.6 points and 7.3 rebounds per game and only 17 starts. The difference between those starts and his 67 starts for Houston in 2021-22 limits any claim that Dallas simply imported the same frontcourt role. The Rockets took a different path: their No. 26 rights turned into No. 29 TyTy Washington Jr. rights and two future second-rounders in a separate Minnesota trade, while four outgoing Dallas players were also part of the original exchange. The held B-to-C+ grades express a modest Dallas advantage. They do not establish each Houston asset's realized value, nor should a later Minnesota deal be conflated with the June 24 Dallas-Houston asset ledger.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win — Dallas B, Houston C+. Wood played 67 games with 17 starts for Dallas in 2022-23, averaging 16.6 points and 7.3 rebounds. The Rockets received four players and No. 26 draft rights, then separately sent those rights to Minnesota for No. 29 TyTy Washington Jr. rights and second-round picks in 2025 and 2027. Those downstream assets belong in the historical accounting, not as extra consideration from Dallas. The existing grades are preserved without claiming the entire Houston return became NBA production.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Dallas Mavericks–Houston Rockets: What the 2022-06-24 Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: This deal's return is clearer in the season and draft ledger than in a repeated roster list. Wood supplied 67 Dallas games, averaged 16.6 points and started only 17 times. Houston acquired the No. 26 rights in the same Wood package and quickly converted them through Minnesota into TyTy Washington Jr.'s No. 29 rights and two future second-round picks. The contrast is an actual Dallas scoring season against a Houston asset mix whose draft branch changed hands again on June 24, 2022.

sections.heading: Christian Wood Cost Dallas Four Players and Wendell Moore Jr.'s Rights
sections.body: The June 24, 2022 asset ledger is precise. Christian Wood moved from Houston to Dallas. The opposite return consisted of Sterling Brown, Marquese Chriss, Boban Marjanović, Trey Burke and Wendell Moore Jr.'s draft rights. The fifth component was not an unidentified future first-round selection: the rights were attached to a specifically named draftee. The timing also means the rights, rather than Moore playing on an NBA roster that day, were the consideration conveyed in the agreement.

sections.heading: What the Other Side Still Received
sections.body: The Rockets did not need to keep Moore's No. 26 draft rights to extract another transaction from the Dallas package. Their 2022 draft profile records that Houston subsequently acquired No. 29 TyTy Washington Jr. and two future second-rounders from Minnesota. Minnesota's own June 24 announcement identifies those second-round selections as 2025 and 2027. That is the direct documented follow-on to Houston's draft-rights acquisition. The original Wood exchange still contained only the No. 26 rights, four named Dallas players and Wood moving in the opposite direction. Crediting Houston for the subsequent swap is fair, but those two second-rounders were not separately sent by Dallas. Equally, a draft right does not by itself prove years of Houston on-court production.

sections.heading: Decision Logic Versus Hindsight
sections.body: Wood's Dallas statistics give the other side an actual measurement: 67 regular-season appearances in 2022-23, 16.6 points and 7.3 rebounds per game, with 17 starts. The official NBA ledger places his previous Houston season at 68 games, 67 starts, 17.9 points and 10.1 rebounds. Dallas therefore received a productive shooter and scorer but did not use him in the same starting role. Houston turned the outgoing player into different kinds of value: contracts and a specific draft choice it immediately redirected to Minnesota. The grade gap should not be stretched into a claim that the Rockets had no worthwhile assets. It should also not be defended by assigning Washington's entire subsequent career to the original Dallas exchange.

sections.heading: Why the Grade Gap Matters
sections.body: The current grades give Dallas a B and Houston a C+, a limited advantage rather than a runaway win. Dallas can point to Wood's 67 games and 16.6-point average, but also to a season in which he started only 17 times. Houston's No. 26 selection had a verified second transaction attached: it became Washington's No. 29 rights and two named future second-rounders from Minnesota. Those picks are an asset outcome, not a quantified return of NBA minutes. The June 24 trail supports counting Wood's delivered Dallas offense and the Rockets' real draft flexibility without asserting every acquired player became a regular contributor. Historical team grades are not silently revised based on an asset count alone.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The preserved verdict is Mavericks Win, Dallas B and Houston C+. Wood delivered 67 Mavericks games, 17 starts, 16.6 points and 7.3 rebounds per appearance. Houston separately converted the No. 26 rights acquired from Dallas into TyTy Washington Jr.'s No. 29 rights and two Minnesota second-round picks in 2025 and 2027. Both the actual Dallas season and the traced Houston draft assets count; neither warrants inventing player production, new Dallas consideration or a revised letter grade.

sections.heading: Dallas Acquired Holmes and the No. 24 Rights for Cash
sections.body: The Mavericks completed the Sacramento transaction on July 6, 2023. Dallas received veteran center Richaun Holmes and the rights to Marquette forward Olivier-Maxence Prosper, whom Sacramento had selected with the 24th pick of the June draft. The Kings received cash considerations; no veteran Dallas player went the other direction. NBA’s official 2023 trade tracker, Sacramento’s transaction log and the Mavericks’ own historical media guide document the same package. The deal was a practical combination of taking on a crowded Sacramento frontcourt contract and securing another rookie after Dallas had acquired Dereck Lively II through a separate Oklahoma City draft-night swap. The price cannot be described as simply cash for Holmes, because the first-round rights were part of the same transfer.

sections.heading: Prosper Became the Main Dallas Development Asset
sections.body: Olivier-Maxence Prosper, a 6-foot-8 Canadian forward from Marquette, began his NBA career with the Mavericks and appeared in 40 regular-season games in 2023-24, then another 52 in 2024-25. That is 92 Dallas appearances with five starts before his later move to Memphis. Basketball Reference records a combined 322 points in those Dallas seasons, showing that the No. 24 selection provided an actual young rotation-development opportunity rather than a never-conveyed pick. Prosper also spent substantial time with the Texas Legends; Dallas’s official 2024-25 media guide says he averaged 18.3 points across 24 G League regular-season games in his rookie year. The NBA minutes, not later Memphis production, are the directly attributable Dallas player return.

sections.heading: Holmes Played 23 Dallas Games Before Another Trade
sections.body: Richaun Holmes did not become a primary Dallas center. He played 23 regular-season games in 2023-24 with two starts, averaging 3.4 points and 3.4 rebounds in 10.3 minutes. The Mavericks then included Holmes and a separate 2024 first-round pick in a February 8, 2024 transaction with Washington for Daniel Gafford. Dallas’s original Gafford press release and official media guide both list the added first-round pick. Gafford therefore should not be called a straight one-for-one return for Holmes: another draft asset was necessary. This history demonstrates that Holmes had some contract-matching utility, but it cannot place all of Gafford’s future Mavericks production onto the July 2023 Sacramento deal.

sections.heading: Sacramento Monetized a Contract but Sold a First-Round Opportunity
sections.body: Sacramento received an undisclosed cash amount and removed Holmes from a depth chart that had shrunk his role to 42 games and 8.3 minutes in the 2022-23 season. That salary and roster flexibility had practical value, though the private canonical asset ledger does not support an exact cash price or a quantified salary-cap windfall. The Kings also relinquished the No. 24 draft rights to Prosper, a real first-round development opportunity. The protected result assigns Dallas B+, Sacramento D and Mavericks Win, with the grade gap accounting for a prospect who played 92 Dallas games and a veteran later used in an independently priced trade. This judgment should not use Dallas’s 2024 Finals berth or Memphis’s later Prosper production as direct receipts for the transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win and the inherited B+ Dallas/D Sacramento grades are retained. Dallas obtained Holmes for 23 games and a later separately priced contract component, plus No. 24 Prosper for 92 Mavericks regular-season appearances across 2023-25. Sacramento took cash and relieved its roster of a low-usage center but surrendered a first-round development choice. The February 2024 Holmes-plus-first-for-Gafford trade is downstream context, not a free return directly created by the July 2023 cash transaction.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Holmes and Prosper to Dallas in 2023: The Cash Trade and Later Gafford Chain
featuredDeepDive.intro: Dallas spent cash on July 6, 2023 to acquire both Richaun Holmes and the draft rights to Olivier-Maxence Prosper, the No. 24 pick Sacramento had just used. The rookie accumulated 92 Dallas regular-season appearances through 2024-25. Holmes appeared in 23 games before the club used him with another first-round selection to acquire Daniel Gafford. The canonical B+/D Mavericks Win interpretation rests on that two-asset incoming package and stops short of treating unrelated draft picks or later teams as returns of the original deal.

sections.heading: Why the Sacramento Deal Followed Another Mavericks Draft Swap
sections.body: Dallas first moved down from the 10th to the 12th selection in the 2023 draft in a transaction with Oklahoma City involving Davis Bertans and the rights to Cason Wallace; the Mavericks received rights to Dereck Lively II. The separate Sacramento deal gave Dallas another young forward at No. 24 while absorbing Holmes’s contract. Sacramento’s pick had produced Prosper, a Marquette wing with defensive potential, before his rights were formally assigned to Dallas on July 6. The NBA trade tracker and official Dallas 2024-25 media guide clearly identify the Holmes-plus-Prosper package as coming from the Kings in exchange for cash. The sequence should not combine the Bertans/Lively swap with the Holmes/Prosper exchange into a fictional direct three-party trade.

sections.heading: Prosper Provided a Long-Term Trial and Actual NBA Minutes
sections.body: The Mavericks signed Prosper in July 2023 and played him in 40 NBA games as a rookie, with 52 more appearances in the 2024-25 season. He averaged 3.0 points in eight-plus minutes as a rookie, and Basketball Reference shows 201 points in 2024-25. That is not elite impact, but it is verifiable contribution from a first-round selection rather than an abstract draft-rights asset. His later 2025-26 season in Memphis is part of his development history, not Dallas’s own NBA production. The trade grade may consider Dallas’s chance to develop a young defender, while avoiding the claim that every later Grizzlies point belonged to its original 2023 cash expenditure.

sections.heading: Holmes Had Limited Court Time but Contract Utility
sections.body: Holmes played just 23 games with Dallas and was seldom in the center rotation. When the Mavericks sought a frontcourt upgrade in February 2024, they sent him to Washington along with a separate 2024 first-round pick for Daniel Gafford. The pick, eventually tied to Dillon Jones at No. 26, was obtained through another Oklahoma City-related 2024 draft consideration sequence. Dallas’s official statement names the pick explicitly. That prevents this retrospective from pretending Holmes alone secured the eventual starting-caliber big man; cash in 2023 bought the Holmes contract and the Prosper rights, while the Gafford deal required its own new first-round cost.

sections.heading: The Kings Bought Flexibility at a Talent Opportunity Cost
sections.body: Sacramento was clearing frontcourt depth at the end of a season in which Holmes’s playing time had collapsed. Cash from Dallas was a definite incoming item, but the exact amount is not established by the retained primary trade record. The Kings surrendered the No. 24 pick’s rights and a veteran contract to create flexibility. Dallas’s inherited B+ therefore has a tangible two-player basis even if neither individual player alone was a franchise star: Prosper generated Dallas NBA minutes and Holmes remained tradable salary with a modest on-court contribution. The Sacramento D describes the narrower basketball return, not a finding that freeing salary was completely without use.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Dallas B+, Sacramento D and Mavericks Win stay unchanged. July 6, 2023 moved Richaun Holmes and Prosper’s No. 24 rights to the Mavericks for cash. Prosper logged 92 Dallas regular-season games; Holmes played 23, then was included with a separately acquired first in the Daniel Gafford swap. Sacramento received money and roster flexibility without comparable direct NBA playing value from the surrendered draft rights. The analysis preserves each transaction’s actual price instead of counting the Gafford trade or later Memphis statistics twice.

sections.heading: July 2024: One Guard for Hardaway and Three Second-Round Picks
sections.body: Dallas traded Tim Hardaway Jr. to Detroit along with three future second-round picks on July 6, 2024, receiving Quentin Grimes in return. The Pistons' official announcement confirms the guard-for-guard exchange and the count of three selections. The canonical ledger specifies a 2025 second-round pick linked to Toronto and two conditional 2028 seconds; none was an additional first-round pick. The 2025 selection eventually became No. 37, Chaz Lanier, whom Detroit announced as its June 2025 draft choice. The future 2028 choices must not be assigned players before conveyance. Dallas obtained a younger, defensively useful wing while Detroit gained a veteran perimeter scorer and multiple draft rights.

sections.heading: Detroit Bought an Every-Game Starting Shooting Guard
sections.body: Hardaway's first Detroit season delivered direct on-court value. In 2024-25, the veteran played 77 regular-season games and started all 77, averaging 28.0 minutes, 11.0 points and 2.2 made three-pointers per contest. He converted 36.8 percent from beyond the arc, giving Detroit a credible high-volume perimeter option alongside Cade Cunningham. The club also returned to the postseason, although the team's collective improvement cannot be credited solely to the newly acquired shooter. These 77 starts are measurable production from the specific player Detroit received, rather than speculative future value from its accompanying picks. The 2025 second-round selection adds another identifiable asset on top of that season.

sections.heading: Dallas Acquired a Young Two-Way Guard but Moved Him Again
sections.body: Grimes appeared in 47 Mavericks games in 2024-25, including 12 starts, and averaged 10.2 points, 3.8 rebounds and 2.1 assists in 22.8 minutes. He shot a career-best 39.8 percent from three-point range for Dallas, providing the rotation with shooting and useful defensive assignments. In February 2025 the Mavericks traded him to Philadelphia, along with a separate 2025 second-round pick, for Caleb Martin. The Sixers' official announcement and league tracker document that later trade. Martin was not part of Detroit's July 2024 package; any benefit Dallas subsequently found through converting Grimes should be identified as downstream rather than as a direct incoming July asset.

sections.heading: Why Detroit Earned the Higher Grade in the Grimes Deal
sections.body: The Pistons Win verdict grades Detroit B and Dallas C-plus. Detroit received Tim Hardaway Jr., who started 77 games in 2024-25, plus three second-round picks. The 2025 selection was eventually used at No. 37 for Chaz Lanier, while the two 2028 selections are still draft assets rather than demonstrated NBA production. Dallas acquired Quentin Grimes, who appeared in 47 Mavericks games and made 12 starts before moving to Philadelphia in a separate February 2025 transaction. Grimes provided useful three-point shooting in his shorter Dallas tenure, so neither club's return was negligible. Hardaway's dependable place in Detroit's rotation and the Pistons' additional draft flexibility provide the stronger long-term case for the B versus C-plus assessment without assigning future picks hypothetical players or treating the separate Grimes trade as part of the July 2024 exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win is the preserved historical classification: Detroit B, Dallas C-plus. The July 2024 ledger sent Grimes to Dallas and Hardaway plus three second-round selections to Detroit. Hardaway started 77 regular-season games for the 2024-25 Pistons; Grimes appeared 47 times in Dallas while shooting 39.8 percent on threes before a separate February 2025 trade. Detroit's 2025 second eventually became No. 37 Chaz Lanier. The two 2028 selections are future claims rather than realized players. That supports a measured, not absolute, Detroit advantage.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Hardaway for Grimes: Detroit's Starting Guard and Three Draft Rights
featuredDeepDive.intro: In July 2024, Detroit received Tim Hardaway Jr. and three second-round claims while Dallas got Quentin Grimes. The immediate returns can be counted without guessing: Hardaway started 77 games for the Pistons, and Grimes provided 47 Dallas appearances before moving to Philadelphia in a separate deal. Detroit also used the identifiable 2025 pick on Chaz Lanier, whereas the two 2028 selections remain unresolved. Those details explain the site's retained Pistons Win decision more convincingly than generic roster-value language.

sections.heading: The Three Second-Round Rights Were Real Consideration
sections.body: Detroit's July 6 press release states that the Pistons acquired Hardaway and three second-round draft selections in exchange for Grimes. The canonical transaction record identifies one 2025 second tied to Toronto and two additional conditional 2028 selections. The 2025 pick later turned into the No. 37 draft right used on Tennessee guard Chaz Lanier, whose selection Detroit announced in June 2025. That draft result is a directly documented continuation of a pick received in this deal. The two 2028 rights remain conditional future assets in the working ledger; their eventual players or trade returns cannot be projected as certain. Valuing those picks as claims preserves a factual boundary absent in boilerplate trade recaps.

sections.heading: Hardaway's Seventy-Seven Starts Give the Pistons Grade Substance
sections.body: The available statistical record makes Detroit's one-season return unusually easy to identify. Hardaway played 77 games and started each of them in the 2024-25 regular season, scoring 11.0 points per game and shooting 36.8 percent on 5.9 three-point attempts per night. Detroit needed adults in its perimeter rotation and obtained a shooter who could contribute without initiating most possessions. The team's rise around Cade Cunningham and its return to the playoffs are context for that role, not evidence that a trade generated every win. Detroit was not merely paid in theoretical draft picks: it also obtained one full season of regular first-unit production, which distinguishes its return from an empty salary dump.

sections.heading: Grimes Helped Dallas Before a Different February Exchange
sections.body: It would be incorrect to portray Grimes as a failure in Dallas. His 47 appearances, 12 starts and 39.8-percent shooting on threes gave the Mavericks actual two-way value during the first part of 2024-25. The club nonetheless moved him to Philadelphia on February 4, 2025, in a separate deal for Caleb Martin, sending an additional second-round pick with Grimes. Dallas' own and Philadelphia's contemporary releases place that move on a different transaction ledger. Martin may be relevant when tracing what Grimes was subsequently converted into, but he was not one of the assets Detroit transferred in July 2024. Each trade's pick and player movements need their own attribution.

sections.heading: A Small Grade Difference Instead of a Sweeping Winner Claim
sections.body: Detroit's B and Dallas' C-plus are preserved as existing editorial assessments, with Pistons Win as the site verdict. The relevant observation is that Hardaway delivered 77 regular-season starts for Detroit, while Dallas received 47 Grimes games before exchanging him again. Grimes shot 39.8 percent on threes in that stint, so the Mavericks did capture useful short-term play and a player with further trade value. Detroit received three seconds in addition to the veteran, and one became Chaz Lanier at No. 37. As the remaining two 2028 selections have no confirmed NBA player outcomes in this ledger, the most responsible conclusion is a limited Detroit edge, not a claim that every future pick will become an impact contributor.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The July 6, 2024 exchange is preserved as a Pistons Win, Detroit B and Dallas C-plus. The official Pistons announcement and NBA transactions ledger place Tim Hardaway Jr. and three second-round selections on Detroit's side, with Quentin Grimes going to Dallas. Hardaway played and started 77 games at 11.0 points and 36.8-percent three-point shooting for the 2024-25 Pistons. Grimes played 47 Dallas games and shot 39.8 percent on threes before the club moved him to Philadelphia with another second-round selection for Caleb Martin. That later deal is separate. Detroit's 2025 pick became No. 37 Chaz Lanier, while the two recorded 2028 rights cannot be graded as completed players. These direct outcomes justify a modest Detroit preference without obscuring the useful Dallas return.
