sections.heading: George Johnson Was the Basketball Return
sections.body: Milwaukee acquired George Johnson from Denver in May 1980. Denver received cash rather than a player or draft selection, making this a different kind of decision for each club. The Bucks obtained the rights to a known NBA big man, while the Nuggets converted his value into financial consideration. The source ledger does not establish the cash amount. There is no basis for adding an unrecorded draft choice or describing the sale as a direct exchange of two players.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Had a Player to Use, Denver Had Money
sections.body: Johnson gave Milwaukee an identifiable basketball asset that could fill frontcourt minutes. His eventual usefulness is measurable in a way the Nuggets’ return is not: games and roles can be examined, while an undisclosed payment cannot be accurately converted into on-court wins. Denver still received consideration with real financial potential. It would be misleading to say the Nuggets received nothing simply because the package did not feature a named player.

sections.heading: Why the Original Article’s Letter Grades Needed Correction
sections.body: The current canonical ledger gives Milwaukee a B and Denver a C-plus, with the official classification Slight Bucks Edge. Earlier editorial copy incorrectly described a B-plus against D and called the transaction a decisive win. Those numbers overstated the recorded grade gap. A small Bucks advantage is more appropriate to the known exchange: Milwaukee acquired a player, but the cash payment prevents a complete financial assessment of Denver’s result.

sections.heading: The Missing Cash Figure Is an Actual Limitation
sections.body: A retrospective assessment can favor the acquired player without inventing how much cash changed hands or what Denver later did with it. Johnson’s known identity and immediate roster potential support Milwaukee’s higher mark; the unquantified payment leaves open how helpful the sale was to Denver’s finances. That uncertainty is why the conclusion stays limited to the existing B versus C-plus relationship. It is a modest comparison of two different returns, not an assertion that cash can never be useful.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Bucks Edge — Milwaukee B, Denver C-plus. Milwaukee obtained George Johnson, a recognizable NBA frontcourt contributor, while Denver received an undisclosed cash payment. The basketball return can be evaluated more directly than the payment’s financial effect. The archival grades support a mild Milwaukee advantage, not the wider discrepancy incorrectly stated in the earlier editorial.

sections.heading: A 1980 Guard-for-Future-Picks Decision Took Three Years to Resolve
sections.body: Denver acquired defensive wing T.R. Dunn and Portland's 1983 first-round choice on August 15, 1980. The Nuggets surrendered their own 1983 first-rounder and a 1984 second-round selection. Those picks would not become players for several seasons, making the draft consequences easy to overlook if the trade is viewed only as an immediate 1980 roster move. Dunn was already an NBA rotation player with the Trail Blazers, while the Nuggets wanted defensive work and rebounding from their backcourt. Portland took the longer view and held Denver's future draft capital. The eventual picks were not vague rights: Portland's 1983 first became No. 14 Clyde Drexler, its 1984 second became No. 33 Steve Colter, and Denver's incoming 1983 first became No. 15 Howard Carter. The actual positions established the long-run grade difference.

sections.heading: Dunn Was a Useful Nugget, Not a Failed Acquisition
sections.body: T.R. Dunn gave Denver considerable real basketball value. He became one of the team's principal perimeter defenders through much of the 1980s, earned three NBA All-Defensive selections across his career and added rebounding at shooting guard. His role on Doug Moe's high-paced Nuggets was not built around scoring, yet his ability to guard opposing wings was important to the lineup. Dunn later returned to Denver after a short stint with Phoenix, extending his association with the franchise. That contribution justifies Denver receiving a B instead of being described as the team that obtained nothing. The loss was an opportunity cost in the draft selections it surrendered, not a complete failure of Dunn as a player. His performance should be evaluated with its defensive context rather than compared with Drexler only through points per game.

sections.heading: The Difference Between Howard Carter's 55 and 66 Games
sections.body: Denver used the No. 15 choice it received in the 1983 draft on LSU guard Howard Carter. His NBA career totaled 66 regular-season games, but only 55 of those were played for Denver in 1983-84. The other 11 came with Dallas the following season. The distinction is important when allocating value to each trade partner: the Nuggets cannot be credited with Carter's full league total as their direct playing return. He averaged 6.2 points in 12.5 minutes for Denver before moving on. The incoming first-round choice therefore produced a brief rookie contributor rather than a star or multi-year starter. That limited selection outcome sits alongside Dunn's lengthy defensive tenure on Denver's side of the original transaction. It also corrects older generic copy that cited 64 Carter games for the Nuggets, a number unsupported by his season-by-team ledger.

sections.heading: Portland Obtained Drexler and Another Playing Guard
sections.body: The Trail Blazers used Denver's 1983 No. 14 selection on Clyde Drexler, who went on to play 867 regular-season games and score 18,040 points for Portland. Drexler's ten All-Star selections were earned across his entire NBA career, while his franchise record with the Blazers is the direct return relevant here. Portland also converted Denver's 1984 second-round pick into Steve Colter at No. 33. Colter played 78 games as a rookie and 81 in his second Blazers season, totaling 159 Portland appearances before playing elsewhere. Together these returns make the Portland side far stronger than the trade's 1980 appearance suggested. Drexler became a franchise-defining wing, and Colter provided additional short-term NBA depth. The grade does not require attributing Drexler's later Houston championship or Colter's later stops to Portland.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Trail Blazers Win — Portland A+, Denver B. Denver received defensive specialist T.R. Dunn and the No. 15 pick that became Howard Carter (55 Nuggets games). Portland used the No. 14 choice on Clyde Drexler (867 Portland games) and No. 33 on Steve Colter (159 Portland games). Dunn was valuable, but the draft exchange favored the Blazers.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: T.R. Dunn for the Drexler Pick: The 1980 Denver-Portland Draft Exchange
featuredDeepDive.intro: The 1980 trade moved defensive specialist T.R. Dunn to Denver and eventually gave Portland the 1983 No. 14 Clyde Drexler pick plus the 1984 No. 33 Steve Colter pick. Denver obtained No. 15 Howard Carter.

sections.heading: Why Dunn's Defense Still Belongs in the Verdict
sections.body: Denver's side cannot be described accurately without T.R. Dunn. Although he averaged modest scoring totals, Dunn became a respected defensive specialist and earned All-Defensive recognition during his Nuggets career. His rebounding from a guard position helped a club whose playing style emphasized pace. The direct playing value was sustained across many seasons, whereas the future first-round choice acquired alongside him yielded 55 Denver games from Howard Carter. It is reasonable that an editor would give the Nuggets a respectable B on the strength of Dunn's role. What makes Portland the winner is not that Dunn lacked NBA ability, but that the franchise surrendered the pick that became Clyde Drexler. The value of an eventual Hall of Fame wing dwarfed the defensive return, without negating the contributions of the player who came to Denver.

sections.heading: The Three-Year Delay Is Central to Portland's A-Plus
sections.body: From the viewpoint of August 1980, Portland traded away a 25-year-old perimeter defender and its future 1983 first while acquiring Denver's future 1983 first and a 1984 second. The teams did not know their exact positions three years in advance. When the 1983 draft arrived, Denver's transferred first sat at No. 14 and Portland chose Drexler; the Nuggets used No. 15 on Carter. Those adjacent numbers make the retrospective gap especially striking. Drexler became a perennial All-Star and accumulated 18,040 points for the Blazers, while Carter played 55 games for Denver. The 1984 selection gave Portland another actual contributor in Colter. The final grading properly credits the realized draft positions and player outcomes without pretending the front offices knew the exact 1983 draft order when they agreed to the 1980 exchange.

sections.heading: A Two-Pick Return With Two Different Portland Outcomes
sections.body: Drexler and Colter were not equivalent contributors, but both originated in the Denver selections acquired by Portland. The No. 14 first-round choice in 1983 produced the franchise's long-term shooting guard and future Hall of Famer. The 1984 No. 33 second-round pick yielded Colter, who supplied 159 Blazers appearances across his first two NBA seasons. The second return is useful because it shows Portland obtained more than a single successful draft position; however, the much larger share of historical value came from Drexler's extended Portland career. Colter's later NBA appearances for other organizations belong to those teams. The draft paths also prevent an error common in trade summaries: Howard Carter's full 66-game NBA career was not the Denver return, just his 55 games for the Nuggets. Team-specific totals keep the comparison on an accurate footing.

sections.heading: The Trail Blazers Win Does Not Erase Denver's B
sections.body: Portland's A-plus reflects an extraordinary return from two future draft choices, led overwhelmingly by Drexler's 867 games and 18,040 points in a Trail Blazers uniform. Denver's B reflects its long-tenured defensive specialist T.R. Dunn, plus the limited production of No. 15 Howard Carter. Dunn's defensive awards and contribution through the 1980s are concrete reasons not to label the Nuggets' side a complete loss. The transaction still favored Portland decisively because it delivered a historically important player at No. 14 and another useful NBA guard the next year. In this ledger the winner and each team's letter grade answer different questions: Portland assembled the better total return; Denver did receive legitimate basketball value. Nothing in the analysis requires inventing a later transaction, changing the original picks or counting either drafted player's games with another franchise as part of the acquiring team's result.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Portland A-plus and Denver B. Drexler scored 18,040 Portland points in 867 games, with Colter adding 159 appearances. Dunn supplied Denver years of defensive work and three career All-Defensive selections, while Carter played 55 Nuggets games. The winner is Portland without denying the Denver contribution.

sections.heading: Denver Acquired Billy McKinney for Carl Nicks
sections.body: The Nuggets exchanged rookie guard Carl Nicks for veteran Billy McKinney on December 22, 1980. The Jazz and Denver transaction lists agree on the one-for-one deal. Utah wanted Nicks, an early-career guard who had worked into Denver's rotation, while the Nuggets obtained McKinney's established professional scoring and ball-handling. There were no draft picks in this particular swap, so the retrospective should follow each player's actual games with the receiving team and only later trades directly tied to that same player.

sections.heading: McKinney Gave Denver 198 Games and Starting Minutes
sections.body: McKinney played 49 Nuggets games after the exchange in 1980–81, averaging 10.7 points and 4.1 assists. In 1981–82 he appeared 81 times with 27 starts, averaging 10.8 points and 4.2 assists. Another 68 games and 38 starts followed in 1982–83 at 9.8 points and 4.2 assists. His 198 total Denver appearances over parts of three seasons were a dependable backcourt return, not a handful of reserve minutes. Across two of those seasons he also took on substantial starting responsibilities.

sections.heading: Nicks Produced Two Useful Jazz Seasons
sections.body: Utah did receive a real rotation guard. Nicks played 40 Jazz games in 1980–81 after the trade, averaging 6.3 points in 15.4 minutes. He then appeared in 80 games during 1981–82 and averaged 7.4 points and 2.0 rebounds. That made 120 Utah regular-season games across parts of two seasons. His later nine appearances in Cleveland belong to another franchise and cannot be added to Utah's return. The Jazz's B grade reflects this useful, if shorter, tenure rather than labeling the deal a complete failure.

sections.heading: Richard Anderson Added a Traceable Denver Return
sections.body: On October 4, 1983, Denver sent McKinney straight to San Diego for Richard Anderson. There was no second Nuggets player or separate draft asset bundled into that exchange, so Anderson's 78 Denver appearances in 1983–84 can reasonably be tracked as McKinney's downstream value. Anderson started 17 games and averaged 8.5 points, 5.2 rebounds and 2.5 assists. The Nuggets thus received 198 McKinney games and an additional direct trade return. That supports Nuggets Win with Denver A- against Utah B, not the old even C-/C- copy.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win — Denver A-, Utah B. McKinney played 198 Denver games across parts of three seasons and was later exchanged directly for Richard Anderson, who added 78 Nuggets games. Nicks provided 120 Jazz games across two seasons. Both sides gained rotation players, but Denver's longer immediate tenure and one-player downstream conversion produced the stronger club-specific return.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Billy McKinney's 198 Denver Games and the Straight-Across Anderson Trade
featuredDeepDive.intro: The December 1980 Denver–Utah guard exchange delivered basketball value to both clubs. Nicks appeared 120 times for the Jazz, while McKinney played 198 games for the Nuggets and later turned directly into Richard Anderson, a 78-game Denver contributor. The later transaction is especially important because McKinney was sent alone, making the player-for-player downstream branch traceable without splitting an unrelated multi-asset package.

sections.heading: A Simple 1980 Trade That Didn't Involve Draft Picks
sections.body: The team transaction logs and Denver franchise chronology identify a December 22, 1980 exchange: Carl Nicks to Utah, Billy McKinney to Denver. The package contained one guard each way. It is easy to overcomplicate historical trade reviews with theoretical cap or draft-option narratives, but neither is documented as part of this particular consideration. The two players' performance with the new franchises, followed by an attributable McKinney trade, offers a more precise basis for the verdict than an abstract notion that both sides got a useful name.

sections.heading: Denver Kept McKinney in Its Rotation for Three Partial Seasons
sections.body: The 49-game 1980–81 McKinney stint gave the Nuggets 10.7 points and 4.1 assists per game shortly after the deal. He appeared in nearly a full 1981–82 season, with 27 starts and averages of 10.8 points and 4.2 assists, then started 38 of his 68 appearances in 1982–83. The combined 198 regular-season games and repeated starting use reflect a sustained NBA role. It's more defensible to give Denver credit for that documented workload than to elevate a two-team narrative solely because a later transaction appears in the ledger.

sections.heading: Utah's Return Was Productive, Not Illusory
sections.body: Nicks played 40 Utah games during the balance of 1980–81, scoring 6.3 per appearance, and returned for all 80 games of his next Jazz season at 7.4 points and 2.0 rebounds. Those 120 appearances gave the Jazz a rotation option over parts of two seasons. A B grade fits that actual benefit; it would be inaccurate to call Nicks an unused asset or a first-month waiver. The difference from Denver arises in the longer McKinney tenure and later direct conversion, not in a claim that Utah received no value at all.

sections.heading: Anderson's 78 Nuggets Games Are Directly Attributable
sections.body: The final Denver branch occurred October 4, 1983, when the Nuggets traded McKinney to San Diego for Richard Anderson in a straight player-for-player deal. Anderson then logged 78 Denver games and 17 starts during 1983–84, averaging 8.5 points, 5.2 rebounds and 2.5 assists. Unlike a trade involving several outgoing Nuggets, this exchange makes the downstream return attributable to McKinney alone. The first trade therefore produced substantial McKinney use plus another full season of Anderson minutes; Denver A- and Utah B capture that wider verified return without claiming either player became a franchise cornerstone.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win, Denver A- and Utah B. McKinney furnished 198 Denver regular-season games and a later direct one-for-one trade return in Anderson, who played 78 more games for the Nuggets. Utah received 120 appearances from Nicks. Both clubs got tangible playing value, but the Nuggets' longer two-player chain justifies the higher grade and directional verdict.

sections.heading: Denver Acquired Dennard for a Third-Round Selection
sections.body: On September 26, 1983, Denver obtained Kenny Dennard from the Kansas City Kings. The Kings received a 1985 third-round pick, eventually No. 66, used on Michael Adams. These were different roster timelines: the Nuggets took a player they could try out immediately, while the Kings accumulated a future late draft choice. The transaction must be described using Kansas City, since the franchise had not yet relocated to Sacramento.

sections.heading: The Draft Pick Had a Named, Traceable Result
sections.body: No. 66 became Michael Adams, a guard who later developed into a productive NBA player. That subsequent career demonstrates the potential upside of a third-round pick but does not establish that every later Adams season belonged to Kansas City. The central question is what the Kings realized or transferred from their acquired rights. Denver acquired Dennard directly and accepted the more immediate player risk; the Kings had to wait until the 1985 draft before converting the selection.

sections.heading: Dennard's Denver Opportunity Outweighed a Distant Third-Round Right
sections.body: Denver brought in Kenny Dennard from Kansas City for an immediate chance to evaluate a prospect in its rotation. The Kings accepted a future 1985 third-round selection, eventually No. 66 Michael Adams, but that pick's later identity could not have been guaranteed in September 1983. Adams went on to an NBA career, though that does not establish years of Kansas City Kings on-court contribution from this particular right; his notable subsequent Denver production arrived through other transactions. The Nuggets' C and Kings' C- describe only a narrow advantage, consistent with a low-cost player-versus-distant-draft-rights swap. The difference should not be exaggerated into a lopsided franchise-building decision, and neither club's later unrelated acquisitions are included as trade receipts.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Nuggets Edge — Denver C, Kansas City/Sacramento C-minus. Denver received Kenny Dennard; the Kings took a 1985 third-round pick that became No. 66 Michael Adams. The pick conversion is traceable, but the stored verdict recognizes only a narrow Denver advantage rather than the contradictory Kings-win claim in older boilerplate.

sections.heading: The Nuggets Dealt With the San Diego Clippers
sections.body: Denver acquired forward Richard Anderson on October 4, 1983, sending Billy McKinney to the Clippers. Although today’s team taxonomy labels the other party Los Angeles, the franchise was still playing in San Diego at the time. That distinction belongs in any historical account of this exchange. The Nuggets chose Anderson for an immediate frontcourt role while the Clippers acquired a guard with existing professional experience.

sections.heading: Anderson and McKinney Met Different Rotation Needs
sections.body: Anderson’s size gave Denver another forward option. McKinney, an experienced guard, was the corresponding backcourt addition for San Diego. The trade did not include draft selections or a financial component in the verified asset ledger. That directness narrows the assessment: no unconnected later pick or team success can be credited to either franchise. The Nuggets’ advantage depends on the specific contribution they gained by changing the positions represented on their bench.

sections.heading: A Modest Denver Edge Fits the Stored Result
sections.body: Denver receives B-minus and the Clippers C, with Nuggets Win. The difference reflects a slightly more favorable outcome for the Anderson acquisition rather than a blockbuster talent reversal. Both players were useful enough to attract an NBA trade but neither was the sort of centerpiece that could independently redirect a franchise. The San Diego context and one-for-one roster exchange explain what the teams actually sought to accomplish.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win — Denver B-minus, San Diego Clippers C. Denver added forward Richard Anderson and sent guard Billy McKinney to the then-San Diego franchise. The recorded grade favors Denver’s roster return by a narrow margin; no picks, cash or large downstream asset chain belongs in this comparison.

sections.heading: Kiki Vandeweghe Went to Portland for Five Denver Assets
sections.body: On June 7, 1984, Denver sent established scorer Kiki Vandeweghe to Portland for guards Fat Lever and Calvin Natt, center Wayne Cooper, a 1984 second-rounder and a 1985 first-rounder. The choices became No. 42 Willie White and No. 15 Blair Rasmussen. Portland was buying an All-Star scorer who had just averaged 29.4 points with the Nuggets. Denver was exchanging one headline player for several immediate starters plus future draft depth, a different form of roster construction whose actual returns can be measured separately.

sections.heading: Fat Lever and Calvin Natt Delivered All-Star Production
sections.body: Lever became Denver's starting guard, appearing in 474 regular-season games across six seasons and earning two All-Star selections. His 1986–87 campaign brought averages of 18.9 points, 8.9 rebounds and 8.0 assists along with All-NBA recognition. Natt was immediately valuable too: he averaged 23.3 points and 7.8 rebounds in 78 Nuggets games during 1984–85 and earned an All-Star selection. Natt's stay ultimately totaled 148 Denver games. Their combined work changed the club's backcourt and scoring options almost immediately after Vandeweghe left.

sections.heading: Cooper and Two Picks Added Years of Nuggets Depth
sections.body: Cooper started 78 of his 80 Denver games in 1984–85, contributing 12.1 points, 7.9 rebounds and 2.5 blocks per outing. The acquired 1984 second-rounder became Willie White, who appeared in 82 Nuggets games over two seasons. The following year's first-rounder became Blair Rasmussen at No. 15, and he played 429 Denver regular-season games through 1990–91. These weren't merely abstract extra assets: they were documented rotation minutes and starting-center production beyond Lever and Natt, making the five-piece package unusually effective.

sections.heading: Portland's Kiki Vandeweghe Return Still Deserves an A-
sections.body: Vandeweghe scored 6,698 points across 285 Trail Blazers regular-season games and averaged 26.9 points at his Portland peak in 1986–87. He provided several years of the high-efficiency scoring Portland sought, not a failed acquisition. The Nuggets nonetheless secured a two-time All-Star in Lever, an All-Star season from Natt, reliable center play and productive draft choices. Those club-specific returns support the Nuggets Win verdict and the canonical Denver A+/Portland A- grades. Reducing Portland to the prior C- unfairly erased the considerable scoring production it actually acquired.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win — Denver A+, Portland A-. Denver received Lever, Natt, Cooper and the picks that became Willie White and Blair Rasmussen, producing multiple starting roles and years of depth. Lever made two Nuggets All-Star teams; Natt was a 1985 All-Star; Rasmussen logged 429 Denver games. Portland still obtained 285 games and 6,698 points from Vandeweghe. Denver gained more total value without making Portland's elite scorer a bad acquisition.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Five Nuggets Returns Versus Vandeweghe's 6,698 Portland Points
featuredDeepDive.intro: The 1984 Vandeweghe exchange became one of Denver's most productive multi-asset deals. Lever grew into an All-NBA guard, Natt became a Nuggets All-Star, Cooper started at center and two draft picks yielded useful players. Portland didn't walk away empty: Vandeweghe scored 6,698 points for the Trail Blazers. The comparison supports Denver A+ and Portland A- rather than the older portrayal of a good Denver trade that supposedly devastated Portland.

sections.heading: The Exchange Was One Elite Scorer for Three Players and Two Picks
sections.body: Denver moved Vandeweghe on June 7, 1984, receiving Lever, Natt, Cooper, Portland's 1984 second-round choice and its 1985 first-round choice. The draft selections subsequently became Willie White at No. 42 and Blair Rasmussen at No. 15. Vandeweghe was an established 29.4-point scorer, so the Trail Blazers were paying for immediate offensive certainty. Denver accepted a more diversified package: new lead-guard responsibility, an established scoring forward, a defensive center and two opportunities to reinforce its roster in successive drafts.

sections.heading: Lever and Natt Turned the Nuggets Return Into an All-Star Core
sections.body: Lever started all 82 games in his first Denver season, with 12.8 points, 7.5 assists, five rebounds and 2.5 steals per game. His game grew further: he earned All-NBA recognition for 1986–87 and made two All-Star teams during his 474 Nuggets appearances. Natt averaged 23.3 points in the initial 1984–85 season and also reached the All-Star Game. Injuries later shortened Natt's Denver tenure, but his first-year performance and Lever's six-season run alone gave the Nuggets high-end return from two of the three incoming veterans.

sections.heading: Cooper and the Draft Rights Continued Paying Off
sections.body: Cooper's 80 appearances and 78 starts in 1984–85 gave Denver a genuine defensive anchor with 2.5 blocks and 7.9 rebounds per game. The 1984 second-rounder yielded White and 82 Nuggets games. The 1985 first-rounder, used at No. 15 on Rasmussen, was much more productive, supplying 429 regular-season appearances and developing into a frequent starting center. Those results all trace to assets in the Vandeweghe package. Counting them individually avoids the mistake of crediting Denver only for Lever's later celebrity.

sections.heading: Portland Received the High-Volume Scorer It Expected
sections.body: Vandeweghe averaged 22.4 points after arriving in Portland and later reached 26.9 points per game in 1986–87. Across 285 Blazers appearances, he scored 6,698 points. The league statistical record makes it untenable to label that a C- quality acquisition simply because Denver's return was even stronger. The Trail Blazers paid considerable roster depth for a scorer who performed at a high level for several seasons. A- recognizes that return; Denver's A+ accounts for the broader set of starters, two All-Star contributors and draft choices that survived into the early 1990s.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win, Denver A+ and Portland A-. Lever's 474 Nuggets games and two All-Star appearances, Natt's 1985 All-Star season, Cooper's immediate starting-center role and draft returns White (82 games) and Rasmussen (429 games) outweigh Vandeweghe's 285 Trail Blazers games. Portland's 6,698 points from Vandeweghe still justify a high grade. The outcome is a Denver win between two productive receiving teams, not a one-sided failure.

sections.heading: The 1986 Arrangement Was Free-Agent Compensation, Not a Player Swap
sections.body: On October 9, 1986, Denver agreed not to exercise its right of first refusal over free-agent forward Richard Anderson. Houston compensated the Nuggets with its 1988 third-round draft selection, which became No. 66 Dwight Boyd. The Rockets signed Anderson as a veteran free agent on October 11, according to the 1986-87 transaction ledger. This is not a conventional trade sending an active Denver player directly to the Rockets; Denver relinquished an existing matching right, and Houston gained the ability to sign the forward. The dates describe different aspects of the same player-movement sequence and should not be silently collapsed into a phantom Anderson-for-Boyd direct player swap. The third-round pick was a future opportunity whose NBA return could be evaluated only after the 1988 draft.

sections.heading: Anderson Actually Played Sixty-Three Houston Games
sections.body: Houston did convert its rights decision into NBA playing time. Anderson appeared in 51 Rockets games in 1986-87, averaging 2.8 points and 1.5 rebounds in 6.1 minutes per game. He also played 12 games for Houston in 1987-88 before moving to Portland for another 62 appearances that season. Those 63 combined Rockets games represent the direct team-specific playing return attributable to the free-agent signing. His Portland games should not be credited to Houston, just as his earlier NBA experience elsewhere does not become an acquisition result. The small role explains the inherited D-plus without suggesting the Rockets received nothing. The club obtained an available veteran forward, but it did not develop him into a dependable starter or a long-running contributor.

sections.heading: Denver Used the Incoming Third-Rounder on Dwight Boyd
sections.body: The draft compensation became concrete on June 28, 1988, when Denver selected Memphis State guard Dwight Boyd at No. 66. The Nuggets' official media guide lists the choice in its 1988 draft history, and a pick-tracking ledger connects that slot to the 1986 Houston agreement. Boyd never appeared in an NBA regular-season game for Denver. The selection therefore had value as a draft opportunity and a scouting decision, but it produced no Nuggets playing minutes. That difference between a valid acquired right and an on-court return should be stated plainly. A third-round pick in the late 1980s carried much greater risk of never producing an NBA rotation player than an early first-rounder. Denver took that risk by accepting the pick as compensation for releasing its right to match Anderson's free-agent offer.

sections.heading: Matching D-Plus Grades Reflect Limited Rather Than Identical Returns
sections.body: The inherited Even Trade verdict and D-plus grades do not mean the two teams obtained identical assets or playing records. Houston received the ability to sign Anderson and got 63 Rockets games from him over parts of two seasons. Denver received a 1988 third-round choice, selected Boyd at No. 66 and got no NBA regular-season games from him. The Rockets produced some brief playing value; the Nuggets exercised a draft option without a completed roster return. Those are different forms of limited value, both well below a major franchise acquisition. An even editorial judgment can reflect modest total impact while recognizing that Houston received actual court time. The result should not be inflated by Anderson's later 62 Portland appearances, nor by Boyd's college accomplishments with Memphis State.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Denver D+, Houston D+. The Rockets obtained the right to sign Richard Anderson and played him in 63 games across two seasons. Denver received a 1988 third-round selection, which became No. 66 Dwight Boyd but produced no Nuggets NBA regular-season appearances. Matching grades reflect limited impact, not equal court time.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Richard Anderson’s 1986 Matching Rights and Denver’s No. 66 Boyd Pick
featuredDeepDive.intro: Denver declined its right of first refusal over Richard Anderson in return for a Houston 1988 third-round pick. The Rockets received 63 Anderson games; the Nuggets drafted Dwight Boyd at No. 66 without an NBA roster return.

sections.heading: Denver's Right of First Refusal Was the Actual Bargaining Tool
sections.body: Anderson had spent previous years with Denver, and the club retained matching-right leverage as Houston pursued him in 1986. The October agreement records Denver's decision not to exercise its right of first refusal in return for a third-round selection. In free agency, a team can obtain compensation by declining a contractual option without transferring a player under an ordinary signed contract. That distinction explains why Houston's incoming side should be described as the ability to sign Anderson rather than a standard player-for-pick swap. The Rockets completed the signing on October 11, while some trade trackers date the compensation arrangement October 9. The preserved asset line uses the earlier date. Both dates can be included without declaring either a nonexistent transaction. The opportunity cost for Denver was giving up a chance to retain a veteran forward, not surrendering new draft capital.

sections.heading: A Sixty-Three-Game Houston Return, Not a Full Career
sections.body: Anderson's NBA stat history shows a limited Houston role: 51 regular-season games in 1986-87 and 12 more in 1987-88. He averaged 2.8 points in his first Rockets campaign and 2.7 in his brief second. Later that second season he appeared in 62 Portland games, averaging 6.7 points there, but the Trail Blazers performance was not a direct Houston return. The right-to-sign agreement should therefore be evaluated through 63 Rockets appearances and the club's ability to use the roster spot, not through Anderson's entire career total. He was an experienced forward with a legitimate professional background and could help as a reserve, but the agreement did not produce a high-minute starter or durable multi-year Houston success. That modest use is consistent with the recorded low grade.

sections.heading: The Third Round Was a Long-Shot Compensation Asset
sections.body: Denver exercised Houston's 1988 third-round choice at No. 66 on Dwight Boyd. The franchise's official media guide and the independent historical draft-pick trade ledger align on the selection and the origin of the pick. That gave Denver a real right to evaluate a player at a defined draft position. It did not yield an NBA career for Boyd with the Nuggets. The third round in 1988 had more distant professional prospects than the first two rounds, and a team could reasonably accept a low-cost chance while releasing a limited veteran matching right. In hindsight, the NBA game ledger is straightforward: Denver's draft conversion supplied zero appearances. Neither international or minor-league development nor a college basketball résumé should be counted as Nuggets regular-season production. The grade should separate opportunity from return.

sections.heading: An Even Historical Verdict With a Small Houston Edge in Minutes
sections.body: The canonical ledger records Even Trade, Denver D-plus and Houston D-plus. On the narrow NBA playing-time measure, Houston has an advantage: Anderson gave the team 63 regular-season appearances, while Boyd never joined Denver's NBA roster. The grades can remain as inherited because the exchange involved a low-order draft right and a modest reserve forward rather than major competitive assets, but the source narrative must admit the difference in actual output. Denver received a genuine third-round selection and made a valid drafting decision, even though no NBA minutes resulted. Houston obtained the freedom to sign a player it used for parts of two seasons. Neither outcome transformed the club, and neither requires a dramatic winner label. A careful account keeps both the 1986 matching-right compensation and the 1988 draft outcome visible.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Denver D-plus and Houston D-plus in the inherited Even Trade verdict. Houston compensated Denver for not matching Richard Anderson, then used him in 51 plus 12 games. Denver exercised the compensation choice on Boyd at No. 66 in 1988, with zero direct NBA playing return. The original 1986 agreement was about free-agent rights, not two contracted players.

sections.heading: Denver Sent Pete Williams to Milwaukee for a Seventh-Round Choice
sections.body: On October 24, 1986, Denver transferred forward Pete Williams to Milwaukee for a 1987 seventh-round selection. Team transaction histories record the exchange as one player for one future draft choice, not a package involving a first-round pick, cash, or an established Bucks rotation player. Denver wanted a later opportunity to select a prospect while Milwaukee acquired the rights to a forward with NBA experience. Williams had appeared for Denver during 1985-86, but those earlier games could not be newly created Bucks production. The acquired pick was still a future right on trade day and would ultimately be used by Denver at No. 156. The original exchange was small, and the surviving evidence gives no basis for describing a franchise-altering impact or an immediate playing-time payoff for either club.

sections.heading: Williams Had NBA Experience but No Recorded Bucks Games
sections.body: Williams's documented NBA playing record belongs to Denver, not Milwaukee. He appeared in 53 Denver regular-season games in 1985-86, with 11 starts and 151 points, before the October 1986 exchange. His player ledger also lists five Denver appearances in 1986-87, but no regular-season season line for the Bucks. This means a retrospective cannot credit Milwaukee with the earlier 53 Denver games or invent a Bucks role that the career record does not show. Milwaukee may have been interested in evaluating an inexpensive forward or controlling his rights, but a claim that he became a Bucks contributor needs separate evidence. The surviving statistics demonstrate that the incoming player did not generate verified Milwaukee NBA box-score production from this transaction. That narrower outcome is the reliable starting point for a grade explanation.

sections.heading: Denver Used the 1987 No. 156 Choice on Curtis Hunter
sections.body: The future draft right conveyed as the 156th overall selection in the seventh round of the 1987 NBA draft. Denver chose Curtis Hunter, a prospect who did not record NBA regular-season playing time. The draft register establishes that the pick was used, which is different from a protected right expiring without a selection. It does not establish that Hunter joined Denver's rotation, started games, or scored for the Nuggets. By acquiring the seventh-round choice, Denver purchased another scouting opportunity instead of retaining Williams. Under the seven-round draft system then in force, a late selection offered a modest possible return but little guarantee of an NBA contract. Hunter's name belongs in the draft chain as the eventual pick, not as evidence that Denver received a productive on-court player.

sections.heading: The Inherited Bucks Win Is Not Established by Player Minutes
sections.body: The existing editorial ledger grades Milwaukee B-plus and Denver D-plus, with Bucks Win. Those values must be distinguished from verifiable receiving-team basketball output. Williams has no recorded Milwaukee NBA regular-season games, and Hunter supplied no Nuggets NBA appearances after Denver selected him in 1987. There may have been rights, personnel or financial reasons behind the inherited preference, but the presently reviewed records do not demonstrate a material Milwaukee playing return. The grade spread therefore requires a provenance review rather than a fabricated success story about Williams in a Bucks uniform. This article retains the established grades as archival editorial metadata while spelling out the evidence limit. An absence of NBA games is not the same as proof that either team made an irrational trade-day decision.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Recorded result: Bucks Win, Milwaukee B+, Denver D+. Denver traded Pete Williams for a 1987 seventh-round selection used on No.156 Curtis Hunter. Williams had no recorded Bucks regular-season appearances, and Hunter never produced Denver NBA games. The inherited grade gap is not established by team-specific NBA output; hold its reasoning for historical provenance review, rather than inventing Milwaukee rotation success.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: 1986 Pete Williams Trade: Milwaukee Rights, Denver Seventh Round and Grade Review
featuredDeepDive.intro: Denver received the 1987 seventh-round selection used on No.156 Curtis Hunter for Pete Williams. Neither asset became verified NBA playing production with its new club, complicating the inherited B+/D+ grading.

sections.heading: A Player-for-Future-Rights Exchange Was Small by Design
sections.body: The October 1986 transaction moved one named player and one future seventh-round pick. Milwaukee received Pete Williams, a forward who had appeared in 53 Denver games the previous season, while Denver received a chance to make another selection in the 1987 draft. Neither club gave up a contemporary starter with a proven multi-year tenure. The draft right carried uncertainty because Denver could not know which player would be available at its eventual position. The player carried a different uncertainty: Williams had professional NBA appearances but lacked an established high-minute offensive role. Comparing these two types of value requires accounting for both the original opportunity and the final outcome. It does not justify multiplying the trade into additional draft assets or importing Williams's prior Nuggets production into Milwaukee's team totals.

sections.heading: The Bucks' Acquired Forward Has No Verified NBA Season There
sections.body: The career ledger for Williams lists Nuggets appearances, including 53 games during 1985-86, but no Bucks regular-season games. That matters because Milwaukee's B-plus grade might otherwise be mistaken for an evaluation of documented rotation minutes. The acquisition of a player's contract or rights can have a purpose even if he never plays an official NBA game for that franchise; training-camp evaluations and roster alternatives have some potential utility. Those possible explanations should not be asserted as completed events without contemporary coverage. The defensible conclusion is narrower: no recorded Milwaukee NBA box-score contribution can be attached to Williams after the October exchange. Denver's later five-game 1986-87 entry also deserves separate chronological source scrutiny, not an unsupported story about a documented return transaction that the current reviewed ledger does not establish.

sections.heading: Hunter Was an Actual Denver Pick, Not an NBA Rotation Return
sections.body: The seventh-round pick acquired from Milwaukee was used at No. 156 in 1987 on Curtis Hunter. The draft record preserves the selection and team identity, so the original return was real as draft capital. There is no resulting NBA regular-season stat line for Hunter, which limits the basketball output Denver received. These two observations should appear together: Denver exercised an available pick, but the selected prospect did not become a measurable Nuggets contributor. The rights were not comparable to an earlier-round guaranteed contract, particularly in the seven-round draft structure of the era. Without independent evidence of a later trade of Hunter's rights, the record should stop at the selection itself. An acquired seventh is a legitimate scouting opportunity, not the equivalent of an established player simply because a name is attached to it.

sections.heading: The B-Plus and D-Plus Pairing Needs an Evidence Qualification
sections.body: The site's recorded verdict is Bucks Win, with Milwaukee B-plus and Denver D-plus. Those grades are preserved as part of the historical editorial ledger, not independently validated by the current player and draft statistics. Milwaukee received Williams but did not obtain a recorded NBA season from him; Denver selected Hunter at No. 156 but did not obtain recorded NBA regular-season games from the pick. That is a nearly symmetric on-court result for a small transaction. A stronger Milwaukee grade could conceivably reflect other contract rights or contemporaneous strategic value, yet supporting evidence is absent from the reviewed sources. The proper editorial result is to flag the grading rationale as unresolved rather than claim the Bucks obtained durable player production. Future primary-source documentation can be added without rewriting the factual asset chain.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Inherited Bucks Win and B+/D+ grades preserved, with source caution: the documented Williams NBA games belonged to Denver, not Milwaukee; Denver exercised No.156 in 1987 on Curtis Hunter but gained no NBA games from that selection. Neither club received verified NBA playing production from its incoming asset. Grade provenance remains unresolved pending a better contemporaneous source.

sections.heading: Denver Sold Smith’s Rights for Cash in December 1987
sections.body: Denver had selected Otis Smith in the 2nd round of the 1986 draft and used him sparingly during his first two NBA seasons. The Nuggets’ 1987-88 log lists 15 early games for Smith at 6.3 points a game before the franchise sent him to Golden State in exchange for cash. Both Basketball-Reference’s NBA transaction register and the Warriors’ own history place the rights transfer on December 22, 1987. A Denver media-guide chronology instead prints December 2, a date discrepancy that does not alter the exchange participants or asset direction. The traded consideration was a real player’s rights, not an unused future draft pick. The amount of cash Denver received is not specified in the cited public transaction logs.

sections.heading: The Warriors Immediately Got a Scoring Guard
sections.body: Golden State acquired more than a distant roster option. Smith appeared in 57 games for the Warriors during the rest of 1987-88, started 12 of them and averaged 13.1 points, 3.8 rebounds and 2.5 assists in 23.8 minutes. He shot 50.6% from the field. Those numbers come from the Warriors’ 1987-88 season totals and his Basketball-Reference career ledger, not from an estimate of how he might develop. Denver had received money but gave up a guard who became a useful regular-season contributor almost immediately. The cost was especially tangible because Smith had already spent time on Denver’s NBA roster; this was not a speculative international rights swap.

sections.heading: One Additional Full Season of Golden State Value
sections.body: Smith stayed with the Warriors for 1988-89 and appeared in 80 games, averaging 10.0 points and 4.1 rebounds. Golden State did not acquire an All-Star, and the subsequent Orlando years belong to a different franchise, but the December 1987 purchase produced 137 Warriors regular-season appearances across two seasons. That is a concrete return against an undisclosed cash outlay, not merely transactional flexibility. It also explains why a cash-for-rights label can understate this particular exchange: the incoming asset quickly became a rotation player. Golden State's 57 appearances in the first season and 80 more the following year provide the strongest direct evidence of value without presuming an undisclosed cash price.

sections.heading: Why Otis Smith's Warriors Tenure Beat an Undisclosed Cash Return
sections.body: The Warriors Win verdict grades Golden State C-minus and Denver D. In the 57 games Smith played for the Warriors after their December 1987 acquisition, he averaged 13.1 points, 3.8 rebounds and 2.5 assists. He followed with 80 appearances and 10.0 points per game in 1988-89. That 137-game direct receiving-team return gave Golden State a legitimate rotation guard rather than a speculative draft right. Denver received cash, but no publicly verified amount in the cited transaction records, so a dollar-for-dollar efficiency calculation would invent precision. The modest grades acknowledge that Smith was useful without treating him as an All-Star, while the result favors Golden State's documented on-court contribution. Denver's media-guide December 2 date conflicts with the December 22 transaction log; the discrepancy does not create a second trade or change the assets.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win — the inherited record assigns Golden State C- and Denver D. The Warriors acquired Otis Smith from Denver for cash in December 1987. Smith played 57 Golden State games at 13.1 points a game that season and another 80 the next year at 10.0 points. Denver’s financial return has no reliably documented figure in the cited logs. The positive on-court return supports the directional verdict; grade calibration and the competing December 2/22 date references require separate provenance review.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Otis Smith for Cash: The 1987 Golden State Return
featuredDeepDive.intro: Golden State bought Otis Smith’s rights from Denver for cash in December 1987. Rather than waiting on an untested draftee, it acquired a guard already on an NBA roster who soon supplied 57 games of double-digit scoring and another full Warriors season. NBA transaction records date the move December 22, while one Nuggets historical guide prints December 2. The inherited result is Warriors Win, Golden State C- to Denver D, with grade calibration held for additional review.

sections.heading: A Cash Sale, Not a Future Draft Pick
sections.body: Smith was selected by Denver in 1986 and appeared in 28 games in 1986-87 plus 15 early games in 1987-88. The Nuggets therefore held rights to a player who had already reached the NBA. Golden State paid cash to take those rights in December 1987. Both franchise and league transaction records describe a direct Nuggets-to-Warriors move, and the Warriors’ official transaction history explicitly names cash as the outgoing consideration. The original trade ledger properly retains money received by Denver and Smith’s rights received by Golden State. A later claim that this was simply an unexercised pick or an uncertain prospect would be inaccurate. The sale gave the Warriors a player available to contribute immediately.

sections.heading: The First Fifty-Seven Games Made the Difference
sections.body: Smith played 57 games for Golden State after the sale, averaging 23.8 minutes and 13.1 points. He also produced 3.8 rebounds and 2.5 assists a night, hitting 50.6% of his field goals. Across the entire 1987-88 season, he recorded 72 appearances split between Denver and Golden State, so using his 72-game total as a Warriors-only result would overstate the transaction’s direct impact. The 57-game split is the correct attribution. That is why the season totals are more informative than merely comparing a listed cash line with a name. The Warriors obtained an actual rotation contributor rather than a theoretical ability to sign someone later.

sections.heading: What the Second Warriors Season Adds
sections.body: In 1988-89 Smith returned for 80 Warriors games, producing 10.0 points and 4.1 rebounds per appearance. His NBA career continued with Orlando after the Warriors tenure, but those later Magic seasons do not automatically count toward the Warriors’ realized-value result. Golden State’s direct return from this swap is clear: 57 games in 1987-88 and 80 more in 1988-89. The two-season NBA evidence should inform any future regrading review, alongside contract context and the unknown cash amount. The existing C- mark is a locked inherited judgment, not a measurement produced by these box-score totals.

sections.heading: Date and Grade Provenance Stay Visible
sections.body: Basketball-Reference’s team and league histories and the Warriors’ media guide report December 22, 1987. A Nuggets media-guide summary prints December 2. This ten-digit day discrepancy needs historical source reconciliation, not a speculative new trade row. The financial side of the exchange is also incomplete because published logs do not give the cash figure. Consequently, the source review locks the original date, direction and grades while marking those uncertainties for follow-up. The editorial case for Warriors Win is grounded in actual Golden State production, but neither the unknown price nor the inherited D/C- scale should be promoted as something these transaction lists independently prove.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The inherited decision is Warriors Win (Golden State C-, Denver D). For undisclosed cash, Golden State obtained a guard who played 137 games across two Warriors seasons, averaging 13.1 points over 57 appearances in 1987-88 and 10.0 across 80 games the next year. Denver’s own historical day-of-month disagrees with the Warriors’ and NBA transaction logs; no asset, date or grade change is made without reconciliation.

sections.heading: March 1988: Clippers Released Their Claim to Michael Brooks
sections.body: Denver's March 4, 1988 transaction was a transfer of free-agent negotiating control, not a player-for-player trade. The Clippers agreed not to exercise their right of first refusal on Michael Brooks, and Denver surrendered a 1988 third-round choice identified with pick No. 73. A contemporary Los Angeles Times game report published March 5 confirms that Los Angeles had dealt Brooks's rights to the Nuggets for a third-rounder. Denver then signed Brooks to help replace injured forward Calvin Natt. Brooks had been the San Diego Clippers' first-round pick in 1980 and suffered a serious knee injury in 1984, which helps explain why neither side was exchanging an established current rotation performer. The pick was future consideration for the Clippers' waiver of control; it was not a veteran player moving to Denver from Los Angeles.

sections.heading: Brooks Produced 16 Denver Regular-Season Games
sections.body: The immediate basketball return was modest. Brooks played 16 regular-season games for Denver in 1987-88, totaling 133 minutes, 43 points and 44 rebounds without starting. That is an average of 2.7 points and 2.8 rebounds in roughly eight minutes, far less than the production he had delivered before his long knee rehabilitation. The Nuggets were a 54-28 division winner that season, but the team record belongs to its wider core rather than to Brooks's brief arrival. On June 23, Charlotte selected him from Denver in the 1988 expansion draft. Consequently the Nuggets did not keep him through the next NBA season as an active rotation contributor. Some sites combine regular-season and playoff games in a 20-game total; the 16-game Basketball-Reference season line is the appropriate measure of the acquired asset's regular-season Denver contribution.

sections.heading: No. 73 Was Ultimately Drafted by Indiana, Not the Clippers
sections.body: The draft-pick history is more complicated than the original agreement's two-party wording suggests. Pro Sports Transactions traces the 1988 No. 73 third-round choice from the Clippers' waiver of Brooks's rights, but also documents an older Clippers–Indiana obligation concerning that same slot. Basketball-Reference's Denver transaction log simplifies the compensation as a third-rounder sent to Indiana, while the Los Angeles Times account on March 5 describes the contemporaneous Clippers rights deal. Indiana's 1988 team transaction ledger and official Pacers draft history show that the Pacers ultimately used No. 73 to select Michael Anderson. Those records are not evidence that Anderson played for or was drafted by the Clippers. The safe interpretation distinguishes who surrendered negotiating rights from who exercised the draft choice. Any missing intermediate paperwork must be held as provenance, rather than assigning Anderson's later value to Los Angeles.

sections.heading: The Archived Clippers Edge Has a Provenance Qualification
sections.body: The current canonical verdict is Clippers Win, graded Los Angeles C and Denver D+. Denver obtained a veteran who played 16 regular-season games before departing in expansion, whereas Los Angeles converted an unused right into draft consideration. That direction is plausible, but the exact economic benefit Los Angeles retained is less obvious because pick No. 73 ended up in the Pacers' draft ledger. A C versus D+ gap is already narrow; the original record should not describe Michael Anderson as a Clippers contributor or imply that Denver received a long-term player. The source histories of Indiana compensation and the Clippers' older draft obligation should be reconciled before any change to grade or asset-routing fields. The article can describe the rights arrangement faithfully while preserving the existing private archive and canonical verdict pending that research.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win is the inherited archival classification, Los Angeles C and Denver D+. The Clippers surrendered their refusal rights to Michael Brooks for third-round consideration, and Brooks supplied 16 Denver regular-season appearances before Charlotte selected him in the 1988 expansion draft. Contemporary Los Angeles reporting confirms the Clippers–Nuggets rights agreement, but Indiana's records show that the Pacers ultimately drafted Michael Anderson with the No. 73 choice. That downstream pick-path uncertainty limits how much numerical draft value can safely be credited to Los Angeles until the historical ledger is reconciled.

sections.heading: Denver Turned Two 1990 Firsts Into the No. 3 Selection
sections.body: On June 22, 1990, Denver sent Miami the No. 9 and No. 15 selections in that month's NBA draft for the third overall pick. The exchange was agreed before anyone had been chosen, so the asset at stake was draft position, not yet the particular NBA career of Mahmoud Abdul-Rauf. Denver had acquired the ninth selection from Dallas only a day earlier by trading guard Fat Lever; No. 15 was Denver's own pick. That earlier Mavericks transaction made the Miami deal possible, but Fat Lever was not sent directly to the Heat in this swap. Miami's expansion-era front office valued two chances to address multiple needs.

sections.heading: Abdul-Rauf Made the Higher Selection Valuable
sections.body: Denver used No. 3 on Chris Jackson of LSU, who later changed his name to Mahmoud Abdul-Rauf. He needed time to become the club's primary guard, then started all 81 games he played in 1992-93, averaging 19.2 points and 4.2 assists while winning Most Improved Player. In 1993-94 he averaged 18.0 points and helped Denver become the first No. 8 seed to beat a No. 1 seed in the playoffs; in 1995-96 he again averaged 19.2 points, now with 6.8 assists. Six Denver regular seasons turned a one-step move up the draft into productive shot creation and sustained starting value.

sections.heading: Burton Produced Early; Miami Then Rerouted No. 15
sections.body: Miami used No. 9 on Minnesota forward Willie Burton. He was a genuine contributor, averaging 12.0 points in 76 rookie games and 11.2 in 68 games in 1991-92. The other pick requires a different account. The Heat selected Dave Jamerson at No. 15, then traded his rights together with No. 30 pick Carl Herrera to Houston for No. 12 selection Alec Kessler. Jamerson's later 90-game NBA career was not a direct Miami playing return because the Heat immediately transferred him. Kessler's Miami minutes resulted from a subsequent two-for-one draft-day transaction, not from the No. 15 pick acting alone.

sections.heading: The A- and C+ Grades Follow Different Types of Return
sections.body: The trade left Denver with a gifted scorer and Miami with two first-round chances. Burton's early production was tangible and Miami also used the other slot as a negotiating piece for Kessler, so its return was not empty. Denver's gain, though, required no follow-up two-asset deal to become a productive starter: Abdul-Rauf was the direct No. 3 selection and a multi-season fixture. The canonical Nuggets Win, Denver A- and Miami C+, recognizes the stronger realized basketball value without implying the Heat wasted every asset. It also keeps the Fat Lever and Herrera exchanges separate rather than counting their full outcomes inside the June 22 swap.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win — Denver A-, Miami C+. Denver consolidated No. 9, obtained from Dallas for Fat Lever a day earlier, and its own No. 15 to acquire No. 3, which it used on Mahmoud Abdul-Rauf. He became Most Improved Player in 1992-93 and a productive starting scorer. Miami drafted Willie Burton at No. 9, gaining two useful early seasons, and moved No. 15 Dave Jamerson with Carl Herrera to Houston for Alec Kessler in a separate trade. The outcome favors Denver without erasing Miami's direct Burton return or overstating the Kessler attribution.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The 1990 Three-for-Two Draft Trail Behind Mahmoud Abdul-Rauf
featuredDeepDive.intro: A modern transaction record names Mahmoud Abdul-Rauf, Willie Burton and Dave Jamerson, but on June 22, 1990, Denver and Miami were exchanging draft positions before any of the three had been selected. The Nuggets packaged Nos. 9 and 15 for the Heat's No. 3. No. 9 had reached Denver only through a separate Fat Lever trade with Dallas the preceding day. Miami later traded its No. 15 selection with another pick on draft night. Following the chronology shows why Abdul-Rauf supplies Denver's strongest value and why Miami's return must be split into Burton's actual minutes and a subsequent asset conversion.

sections.heading: Fat Lever's Departure Created the No. 9 Bargaining Chip
sections.body: Denver and Dallas had agreed to a separate deal on June 21: Fat Lever went to the Mavericks, and the Nuggets acquired the No. 9 pick plus a 1991 first-round selection. On June 22 Denver used only the 1990 No. 9, along with its original No. 15, to obtain Miami's third selection. News coverage at the time explicitly described Miami's acceptance as a bet on depth in a draft where it saw relatively little difference between the available prospects. That was a rational trade-day view even if the finished careers favored Denver. The 1991 first Denver got from Dallas did not enter this Heat transaction.

sections.heading: A Breakout at Guard After Two Development Seasons
sections.body: Jackson arrived from LSU as a prolific college scorer but did not become a full-time NBA starting point guard immediately. He averaged 14.1 points as a Denver rookie and 10.3 in his second season. In 1992-93, now a regular starter, he averaged 19.2 points and 4.2 assists, earning the Most Improved Player award. His 1993-94 18.0 points per game and 95.6 percent free-throw shooting supplied a major part of the Nuggets' offense in their famous first-round upset of Seattle. By 1995-96 he added 6.8 assists per game to another 19.2-point scoring season. That sustained six-season Denver record is the most persuasive measurable result of the draft-position swap.

sections.heading: The Heat's Ninth Pick Was a Player, Not Merely a Miss
sections.body: Willie Burton joined a franchise still only two seasons old and was named to the All-Rookie team after playing 76 games in 1990-91. His 12.0 points a night gave Miami dependable wing scoring, followed by 11.2 the next year. Burton's role diminished in later Miami seasons, and most of his higher-scoring post-Heat work cannot be credited to this trade as if it happened in South Florida. Nevertheless, the No. 9 selection generated real NBA value for Miami. The C+ grade should reflect those first two seasons instead of treating the return as two wholly unsuccessful draft picks.

sections.heading: Miami Turned Jamerson Into Part of the Kessler Price
sections.body: The other incoming selection, No. 15, carried a complicated path. Miami drafted Dave Jamerson but never developed him on its own roster. On June 27 the Heat sent Jamerson's rights and Carl Herrera's rights, taken at No. 30, to Houston for draft rights to Alec Kessler. Kessler played for Miami, which gives the No. 15 asset an indirect connection to later team production. But Herrera was the other asset Miami surrendered in that second deal. Treating all of Kessler's playing value as the direct result of the June 22 Denver trade would omit Herrera's cost. The same rule keeps any future Denver moves involving Abdul-Rauf separate from the value he generated while the Nuggets controlled him.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Denver A-, Miami C+: Nuggets Win. The June 22, 1990 draft-position exchange gave the Nuggets the No. 3 pick used on Mahmoud Abdul-Rauf, a 1992-93 Most Improved Player and multiyear starting scorer. Miami obtained No. 9 Willie Burton, who offered solid early scoring, and No. 15 Dave Jamerson, whose rights were combined with Carl Herrera in a subsequent deal for Alec Kessler. That indirect pick path keeps Miami's return from being reduced to Jamerson's NBA minutes, while the direct Abdul-Rauf value makes Denver's advantage durable.

sections.heading: The September 1990 Trade Was for Cook, but Pick Histories Disagree
sections.body: Denver and Detroit agree on the named player and the date: the Nuggets acquired Anthony Cook from the Pistons on September 28, 1990. The return draft consideration is disputed between historical ledgers. Basketball-Reference lists a conditional **1992 second-round pick** and explicitly says that condition never conveyed. Pro Sports Transactions instead identifies a **1995 second-round pick that became No. 44 Anthony Pelle**. Both accounts cannot be collapsed into one certain pick outcome without reconciling the original protection terms. The source record should preserve what is established while marking the draft chain uncertain; treating Pelle as an undisputed Pistons selection, or assuming the 1992 conditional pick conveyed, would exceed the evidence.

sections.heading: Cook Supplied Eighty Denver Games, Including Twenty-Five Starts
sections.body: Cook joined the Nuggets after declining to report to Detroit following the 1989 draft. In 1990-91 he played 58 games for Denver with 25 starts, averaging 5.3 points, 5.6 rebounds and 1.2 blocks in 19.3 minutes. He returned for only 22 more Nuggets appearances in 1991-92, with no starts, averaging 1.5 points and 1.5 rebounds. The receiving club therefore obtained exactly 80 regular-season games and 25 starts across two years, rather than a long-term starter or an empty roster slot. His later injuries and subsequent Orlando, Milwaukee and Portland appearances are not additional Denver returns from the September 1990 transaction. This direct player value is documented independently of the disputed conditional draft choice.

sections.heading: The 1995 No. 44 Selection Appears Again in a Separate 1993 Exchange
sections.body: Pro Sports Transactions traces the 1995 second that became No. 44 Anthony Pelle from Denver to Detroit in the 1990 Cook exchange, then back to Denver in the November 19, 1993 trade involving Alvin Robertson, Marcus Liberty and Mark Macon. Contemporary UPI reporting confirms Denver received Robertson, a 1995 second-round pick and future considerations for Liberty and Macon. Basketball-Reference confirms Denver ultimately drafted Pelle at No. 44 in 1995. The identification of that 1993 incoming second with the 1990 Cook exchange is a plausible secondary-ledger chain, not a sufficiently reconciled fact: the Basketball-Reference September 1990 record instead calls the outgoing pick a conditional 1992 second that did not convey. Pelle never appeared in an NBA regular-season game, and the 1993 compensation also involved other players.

sections.heading: An Even C-Minus Grade Is Inherited, Not a Proven Pick-Outcome Calculation
sections.body: The saved Even Trade with Denver C-minus and Detroit C-minus was assembled before the conflicting 1992-versus-1995 pick descriptions were reconciled. Denver clearly received limited but genuine rotation play from Cook: 80 games and 25 starts. Whether Detroit ever obtained the stated pick, or instead held 1995 rights that were returned in 1993, cannot be decided by a generic claim that both sides finished equally. Matching grades may be retained as inherited archive metadata while the route stays private, but a verified verdict requires the actual original pick instrument and subsequent chain. The source conflict should be resolved against contemporary team transactions or other primary records before changing the canonical asset label, grade or route eligibility.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict — Provenance Review Hold
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, Denver C-minus and Detroit C-minus are the inherited archive labels, not a source-verified equal-return result. Anthony Cook appeared in 80 Nuggets games and started 25 after the September 1990 trade. Basketball-Reference identifies a conditional 1992 second that never conveyed; Pro Sports Transactions instead traces a 1995 No. 44 Anthony Pelle selection back through a separate 1993 Nuggets-Pistons exchange. Until those competing pick records are reconciled, the draft consideration and balance of return should stay on a private research hold.

sections.heading: Denver Obtained Avery Johnson for a Conditional Pick
sections.body: On October 24, 1990, Denver acquired point guard Avery Johnson from the Seattle SuperSonics. Seattle’s consideration was a conditional second-round pick dated to 1997. The source ledger does not conclusively establish that this later pick was exercised, so it would be misleading to name a selected player or award Seattle certain draft production. The transaction was a present-day guard for possible distant draft compensation, made by two Western Conference franchises in different roster situations.

sections.heading: A Guard Could Help Immediately; the Pick Might Not Materialize
sections.body: Johnson was an established professional ballhandler, giving Denver someone who could organize possessions and fill point-guard minutes without waiting years for a prospect. His later career accomplishments elsewhere are not a return Denver automatically owned. The Nuggets’ relevant gain is the guard acquired at that point in his career. By contrast, Seattle retained a conditional right rather than a guaranteed player or a clearly exercised high pick. That makes the documented value of the packages uneven even if Denver’s acquisition was not a blockbuster.

sections.heading: The Protection Uncertainty Must Stay in the Verdict
sections.body: Denver holds B-plus in the current archive, compared with Seattle C-plus. The source record supports a Nuggets edge because it confirms a playable guard coming in, while the specified second-round asset has an uncertain exercise outcome. It does not establish an exact dollar equivalent for Johnson or a definitive fate for the conditional pick. Those gaps limit the claim to the identified assets and avoid assigning later unrelated Johnson success to his relatively brief Denver tenure.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win — Denver B-plus, Seattle C-plus. The Nuggets received point guard Avery Johnson in October 1990. Seattle took a conditional 1997 second-round pick whose exercise is not confirmed by this ledger. The immediate player contribution was more definite than the conditional draft possibility; the grade advantage does not rely on Johnson’s separate later career accomplishments.

sections.heading: Denver Received Kevin Brooks and a Future Pick, But the Date Needs a Note
sections.body: The historical Denver record lists an exchange dated June 26, 1991 in which the Nuggets acquired Milwaukee draft choice Kevin Brooks, a 1994 second-round pick and unspecified additional consideration for the rights to Anthony Avent. Denver’s official franchise guide instead dates the completed three-team rights sequence July 1: the Nuggets first acquired Avent from Atlanta in the Blair Rasmussen deal, then moved Avent rights to Milwaukee for Brooks rights and the second. The Bucks transaction ledger agrees with that July 1 chronology. The original June 26 slug is preserved as an inherited archive identifier, not promoted as a resolved league execution date. There is no verified dollar amount or separate player identity for the additional consideration.

sections.heading: Brooks Delivered 126 Low-Minute Nuggets Games Over Three Seasons
sections.body: Brooks played all 126 of his NBA regular-season games with Denver in 1991-92, 1992-93 and 1993-94, but started only two. His 37, 55 and 34 appearances generated 1,031 total minutes and 417 points, a career average of 3.3 points in 8.2 minutes. Those numbers show an actual reserve contributor rather than zero return, but they cannot sustain the earlier claim that Brooks was the dominant asset of this exchange. His one-time first-round No. 18 draft selection is not itself evidence of NBA playing value. Denver also controlled the future second-round choice, whose history must be considered separately from Brooks’s actual minutes.

sections.heading: Avent Started 98 Bucks Games and Was Traded Again
sections.body: Avent spent 1991-92 playing professionally in Italy before joining Milwaukee’s NBA roster. In 1992-93 he started 78 of 82 games, averaging 9.8 points and 6.2 rebounds. The following season he played another 33 Bucks games with 20 starts, producing 7.4 points and 4.7 rebounds per game before Milwaukee sent him to Orlando on January 15, 1994. That was 115 Milwaukee appearances and 98 starts across the two seasons, compared with only two Denver starts by Brooks. Milwaukee subsequently received Anthony Cook and separate draft considerations from Orlando, but that later exchange should not be counted as if its whole return arrived directly from Denver in 1991. Avent’s own Milwaukee production already supplies a substantial reason for reviewing the prior Denver-favored grade.

sections.heading: The 1994 Pick Became Rodney Dent and Helped Denver Acquire Dele
sections.body: The official Denver media guide resolves the otherwise unidentified future second-round selection: Denver later sent the pick to Washington, Washington sent it to Orlando, and the Magic selected Rodney Dent at No. 31 overall in 1994. The Nuggets traded Anthony Cook, Todd Lichti and that 1994 second to Orlando on August 19, 1993 for Brian Williams, later called Bison Dele. This gives the second a documented downstream role even though Dent never played for Denver. It would be misleading to award Denver all 143 of Dele’s later Nuggets appearances as the pure return on one second-round pick, since two other players formed part of the 1993 package. The asset was useful; its share of the combined deal cannot be precisely priced from the records.

sections.heading: A Bucks Win Is Better Supported Than the Inherited Nuggets Grade
sections.body: The prior Nuggets Win verdict and Denver B versus Milwaukee D+ pair treated Brooks and uncertain future considerations as stronger than the Bucks’ proven starter. Available records show the opposite direct outcome: 115 Milwaukee Avent appearances with 98 starts, versus 126 Denver Brooks games with two starts. Denver did obtain an additional moveable 1994 second, which helped assemble the later Dele transaction; Milwaukee also turned Avent into a separate 1994 package. On those documented team-specific returns, Milwaukee B+ and Denver B- better capture the balance, giving Milwaukee a win without claiming a one-sided disaster for Denver. The archive date and unitemized consideration still require provenance review, but those gaps do not justify invented draft assets or old boilerplate evaluations.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win — Milwaukee B+, Denver B-. Milwaukee received Anthony Avent, who made 115 Bucks appearances and 98 starts before being traded to Orlando in 1994. Denver received Kevin Brooks, who played 126 Nuggets games with two starts, plus a second that became 1994 No. 31 Rodney Dent and contributed to the separate Bison Dele trade package. The official Denver media guide dates the rights exchange July 1, 1991, rather than the legacy June 26 route; date and unspecified consideration remain flagged rather than silently rewritten.
