sections.heading: Denver Paid a Future Second for Garland
sections.body: On June 26, 1991, Denver acquired guard Winston Garland from the Los Angeles Clippers. Los Angeles received a future second-round draft choice, which eventually became the No. 39 selection in 1996 used on Russ Millard. There was no major first-round compensation or multiteam structure. Denver wanted an experienced ballhandler in the immediate lineup, while the Clippers accepted deferred draft rights rather than retaining a guard they were no longer using.

sections.heading: Garland Started Most of the Nuggets’ 1991–92 Games
sections.body: Garland played in 78 games for Denver in 1991–92 and started 67, averaging 10.8 points and 5.3 assists. That was a genuine one-season starting-guard return from an acquisition that cost only a future second. Denver was not a playoff contender that season, so the trade should not be credited for postseason success it did not produce. Its value was simpler: Garland handled meaningful minutes and organized possessions for a club that needed reliable backcourt play.

sections.heading: The Clippers Received a Long-Delayed Pick
sections.body: The acquired second-round selection did not convey until 1996, five years after the trade, when Russ Millard was selected at No. 39. Millard did not provide an NBA career comparable to Garland’s immediate Denver workload. Los Angeles had a reason to prefer draft optionality over a player who might not fit its next season, but the eventual draft outcome was not a substantial win. The gap in time also matters when comparing an immediate starter to a late future pick.

sections.heading: The Return Justifies an Uneven Pair of Grades
sections.body: Denver’s B is supported by 67 starts and over ten points per game in Garland’s lone Nuggets season. The Clippers’ D-plus reflects the much smaller realized NBA impact of their eventual second-round return. That does not mean the exchange transformed Denver’s franchise: Garland moved on after a year and the club still struggled. It means the Nuggets got the only substantial contribution directly traceable to these assets.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win — Denver B, Los Angeles D-plus. Garland started 67 games and averaged 10.8 points and 5.3 assists for Denver in 1991–92. The Clippers obtained a delayed second-round choice that eventually became Russ Millard at No. 39 in 1996, without a comparable NBA contribution. Denver received more direct value, even though its improvement was short term.

sections.heading: Detroit Received the Established Scorer Orlando Woolridge
sections.body: On August 13, 1991 the Detroit Pistons traded reserve big man Scott Hastings and a 1992 second-round pick to Denver for Orlando Woolridge. Woolridge was coming off an unusually high-volume season in Denver: 25.1 points across 53 games, 50 of them starts, during the Nuggets’ fast-paced 1990-91 campaign. The Pistons were moving beyond their Bad Boys championship seasons and saw an experienced forward who could add offense alongside Isiah Thomas, Joe Dumars and Dennis Rodman. Detroit’s acquisition was not a rights-only investment; it added an NBA player with a verifiable scoring history. The historical NBA transaction ledgers record the August date and identify both pieces going back to Denver.

sections.heading: Woolridge Became a Full-Time Detroit Rotation Player
sections.body: The veteran appeared in all 82 Pistons regular-season games in 1991-92, starting 61 while averaging 14.0 points and 3.2 rebounds. He logged 2,113 minutes for a team that finished 48-34 and reached the playoffs, where he also played five games. In 1992-93 Woolridge added 50 Detroit games and 47 starts at 13.1 points before finishing the season with Milwaukee. That gives Detroit 132 regular-season appearances and 108 starts as direct player production across the two seasons following the deal. It was less scoring than his unusual Denver year, yet much greater playing value than the outgoing reserve and pick ultimately delivered back to the Nuggets.

sections.heading: Denver Received Hastings and No. 46 Rob Werdann
sections.body: Scott Hastings, a depth forward and center, played 40 games with Denver in 1991-92, making four starts and averaging 1.5 points and 2.5 rebounds in 10.5 minutes. He returned for 76 appearances in 1992-93 but without becoming a regular starter. The 1992 second-round pick conveyed by Detroit was No. 46, with Denver selecting Rob Werdann. Werdann appeared in 28 Nuggets NBA games in 1992-93, averaging 1.9 points. Neither player matched the offense or high-volume minutes Woolridge gave Detroit during his 82-game first Pistons season. The pick outcome is a later consequence of the 1991 asset, not a named prospect Detroit promised in August.

sections.heading: The Archived A-Minus Versus B-Plus Has Context
sections.body: The protected retrospective calls the outcome a Slight Pistons Edge with Detroit A- and Denver B+. Those marks do not require the Nuggets to have received an equivalent scoring forward. Denver gained two playable depth assets and flexibility while moving a veteran who had occupied a very large share of its offense in the prior season. Detroit acquired a proven wing who started 108 games over two seasons and helped fill the mid-1990s transition away from its championship backcourt. Denver’s Werdann pick did yield real NBA appearances, so it cannot be described as never producing an NBA player. The comparison is best grounded in those measured roles without counting every later team win as trade-specific value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Pistons Edge is preserved, with Detroit A- and Denver B+. Woolridge played 132 Detroit games, with 108 starts across 1991-93, including 14.0 points per game in his first season. Denver received Scott Hastings for 116 regular-season appearances over two seasons and pick No. 46, which became Rob Werdann and yielded 28 Nuggets games. The Pistons obtained the more productive established scorer; the Nuggets retained real depth and draft value, albeit less on-court impact.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: 1991 Woolridge to Detroit: 132 Pistons Games Against Hastings and Pick No. 46
featuredDeepDive.intro: Detroit acquired Orlando Woolridge from Denver on August 13, 1991, sending Scott Hastings and a 1992 second-round draft selection in return. Woolridge started 108 of 132 Detroit regular-season appearances over two seasons. The Denver pick became Rob Werdann at No. 46, while Hastings served as a depth big. The preserved Slight Pistons Edge verdict and Detroit A-/Denver B+ grades are evaluated through those genuine player and draft returns, without introducing later teams or unrelated draft transactions.

sections.heading: What Each Team Was Purchasing in August 1991
sections.body: The Nuggets had run a pace-heavy offense under Paul Westhead, and Orlando Woolridge had scored 25.1 points per game in 53 appearances during 1990-91. Detroit, a franchise that had won the title in 1989 and 1990, was no longer relying only on its familiar title contributors. Acquiring Woolridge offered immediate wing and forward scoring, whereas Denver was willing to replace some of that high-volume offense with a reserve frontcourt player and a future pick. Basketball Reference’s 1991-92 transaction lists for both clubs show the same straightforward two-team exchange, and neither a third team nor a hidden first-round pick should be invented.

sections.heading: Woolridge Still Produced After Leaving Westhead’s System
sections.body: Scoring rates can shift when an athlete changes systems. Woolridge went from 25.1 points per game in Denver to 14.0 in Detroit in 1991-92, but he played all 82 games with 61 starts. The NBA historical statistics also show 3.2 rebounds and an average of 25.8 minutes, useful rotation contributions rather than an unused salary asset. His subsequent 1992-93 stint covered 50 Pistons games and 47 starts at 13.1 points before he went to Milwaukee. Those Detroit figures span exactly 132 regular-season games and demonstrate that the value of this trade was a serviceable scorer, not a promise of replicating 1990-91’s unusually large Denver shooting load.

sections.heading: Two Denver Returns Were Real but Limited
sections.body: Scott Hastings supplied frontcourt coverage over 40 games in the immediate 1991-92 season and 76 in 1992-93. His first season produced just 58 total points and four starts, with his value located in depth rather than offense. In the following June draft Denver selected Rob Werdann with the Detroit-origin second-rounder at No. 46. Werdann appeared in 28 Nuggets NBA games and scored 53 points over the 1992-93 season. The pick therefore did turn into a real professional contributor, however briefly. His later New Jersey appearances in the mid-1990s should not be added to Denver’s direct return from the original 1991 trade.

sections.heading: Why the Pistons Receive the Slight Historical Edge
sections.body: Detroit got one of the few players who could produce double-digit points every night while remaining available. The 82-game 1991-92 season and another 50 Detroit games make the direct acquisition much easier to evaluate than an abstract hypothetical second-round outcome. Denver kept two actual roster options in Hastings and Werdann, but both were largely reserves. That supports the protected A- Pistons and B+ Nuggets split and a Slight Pistons Edge rather than a sweep. It does not assert Woolridge carried Detroit to a championship, nor that Hastings and Werdann were without practical use; the differential is the minutes and scoring generated by the exchanged assets.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The protected A- Detroit, B+ Denver and Slight Pistons Edge remain intact. Woolridge supplied 132 Pistons games with 108 starts, while Denver obtained 116 Hastings appearances and 28 Werdann games from the 1992 No. 46 selection. Both teams obtained actual NBA players, but Detroit secured the stronger immediate scorer without the risk of waiting for a later draft. No career statistics outside the receiving team are double-counted.

sections.heading: Pack Went to Denver for a Second-Round Choice
sections.body: On October 23, 1992, Denver acquired Robert Pack from Portland. The Trail Blazers received a 1993 second-round pick that ultimately became No. 48 Kevin Thompson. Pack had entered the NBA undrafted and supplied quickness and aggressive guard play, attributes Denver valued as it rebuilt around a young core. Portland received the chance to add another player at a late draft position instead of keeping a reserve guard whose future role was uncertain.

sections.heading: Pack Became an Important Reserve on a Historic Playoff Team
sections.body: Denver’s own historical retrospective credits Pack with 259 games across two Nuggets stints and averages of 9.4 points and 4.9 assists. He was a key reserve on the 1993–94 club that upset top-seeded Seattle in the first round. In the series-clinching Game 5, Pack led Denver with 23 points; that is a specific, memorable postseason return from the guard acquired for a second-rounder. The upset was a team achievement, but Pack’s contribution was direct rather than incidental.

sections.heading: The Denver Tenure Also Had an Injury Limit
sections.body: Pack’s best regular-season scoring campaign with Denver came in 1994–95, when he averaged 12.1 points and 6.9 assists but appeared in only 42 games because of injury. He was not a perennial All-Star or an uninterrupted starting point guard, and that keeps the retrospective result short of an A grade. Still, his shot creation off the bench and multiple NBA seasons with Denver provided much more realized value than a late second-round selection could reasonably guarantee.

sections.heading: Portland’s Draft Return Did Not Match Pack’s Output
sections.body: The 1993 No. 48 pick became Kevin Thompson, whose NBA contribution did not approach Pack’s Denver years. Portland might have valued its own backcourt depth and the flexibility of a draft selection, but the comparison of completed returns is straightforward. Denver receives B for multiple seasons of useful point-guard play and a defining playoff performance. Portland receives D-plus because the selection brought no similarly important on-court result.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win — Denver B, Portland D-plus. Pack provided valuable guard minutes over multiple seasons and scored 23 in the deciding game of Denver’s historic 1994 upset of Seattle. Portland received the 1993 No. 48 pick that became Kevin Thompson without a comparable impact. The grade gap follows the actual guard production, not the draft slot’s hypothetical potential.

sections.heading: Denver Sent No. 43 Grant and a 1994 Second for Mee Rights
sections.body: On June 30, 1993, Denver sent newly drafted Josh Grant at No. 43 and a future 1994 second-round pick to Golden State for the draft rights to Darnell Mee, selected No. 34 by the Warriors. The Golden State Warriors official media guide records the same draft-night structure, including the future pick that later became No. 39 Anthony Miller. Both players were second-round choices from the 1993 draft; no first-rounder or cash was involved in this particular exchange. Denver consolidated an incoming guard prospect into one roster option while Golden State accepted a forward prospect and another selection the following summer. This trade occurred alongside larger draft-night events but must be evaluated on its own rather than borrowing value from Golden State's unrelated Chris Webber deal.

sections.heading: Darnell Mee Played Forty Regular-Season Games for Denver
sections.body: Mee joined Denver for the 1993-94 campaign and played in 38 NBA regular-season games, none as a starter, averaging 1.9 points over 7.5 minutes per appearance. He made another two Nuggets regular-season appearances in 1994-95. Together the 40 games and 76 points represented a modest but tangible basketball return from the No. 34 draft right. Mee also appeared in three Denver playoff games during the 1994 run, a separate postseason contribution. His long professional playing career abroad did not occur in a Nuggets uniform and must not be added to this two-season Denver tally. Denver's C-plus is an inherited grade that recognizes a usable reserve opportunity but does not imply the trade produced a starting NBA guard or a star scorer.

sections.heading: Josh Grant Played Fifty-Three Warriors Games in 1993-94
sections.body: Golden State acquired Josh Grant's No. 43 draft rights and used him in 53 regular-season games during 1993-94. He averaged 3.0 points, 1.7 rebounds and 7.2 minutes per game, with no starts. The Warriors thus received more immediate NBA appearances than Denver obtained from Mee across his entire two-season Nuggets stay, although minutes and quality are not measured only by game counts. Grant played one NBA season and did not develop into a multi-year Golden State starter. His eventual international basketball history is not equivalent to more Warriors NBA games. This 53-game contribution is the first piece behind the archive's one-step Warriors edge; the accompanying 1994 second-round pick supplies the distinct second part of the return.

sections.heading: The 1994 No. 39 Pick Became Anthony Miller and Then Another Second
sections.body: The future second-round choice from Denver eventually became No. 39 overall in the 1994 NBA draft. Golden State selected Anthony Miller, sometimes called Pig Miller, rather than retaining an undefined generic 1994 pick. On July 1, 1994 the Warriors transferred Miller to the Los Angeles Lakers for a 1995 second-round selection that was later used on Dwayne Whitfield. That was a separate transaction and did not deliver all of Miller's later career to Golden State. The underlying two-step pick exchange is traceable through Warriors official archives and the Don Nelson transaction register. The stored Slight Warriors Edge, Golden State B-minus and Denver C-plus should reflect Grant's 53 regular-season games and the converted 1994 draft asset against Mee's 40 Denver games, without exaggerating their careers.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Warriors Edge — Golden State B-minus, Denver C-plus. The Warriors gained 53 games from Josh Grant and a future second used at No. 39 on Anthony Miller, whom they later traded for another second-round pick. Denver obtained Mee's rights, resulting in 40 regular-season Nuggets appearances and three 1994 playoff games. The dated 1994 Miller-for-pick deal was separate from this June 1993 exchange.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Denver Nuggets–Golden State Warriors: What the 1993-06-30 Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: On June 30, 1993, Denver sent Josh Grant's No. 43 rights and a 1994 second to Golden State for the rights to No. 34 Darnell Mee. Mee played 40 Nuggets regular-season games; Grant played 53 Warriors games. The later second became No. 39 Anthony Miller, whom Golden State sent to the Lakers in a separate 1994 move for another future second. This is a small draft-asset transaction, not part of the simultaneous Warriors-Magic blockbuster.

sections.heading: The 1993 Swap Was Two Draft Rights Plus a Future Pick
sections.body: Darnell Mee went to Denver on June 30, 1993, shortly after Golden State selected him at No. 34 in the NBA draft. Denver had chosen Josh Grant at No. 43, and his rights traveled to the Warriors with a 1994 second-round selection. Golden State's official transactions ledger independently identifies that future pick as No. 39 Anthony Miller. The two draft positions establish what each franchise surrendered that night, but the future selection was not a player already identified in 1993. Denver traded quantity and a later option for a particular guard prospect; Golden State accepted a different player position and another round-two opportunity. The remaining basketball outcomes can be examined separately from Golden State's high-profile simultaneous Anfernee Hardaway and Chris Webber swap.

sections.heading: Mee Offered Denver Reserve Guard Minutes, Not a Star Turn
sections.body: Mee appeared in 38 Nuggets regular-season games in 1993-94 and two the following year, totaling 40 appearances and 293 minutes in Denver. He scored 73 points in the first season and three in the second, according to Basketball-Reference player statistics. He also took the floor in three Denver playoff games in 1994, but those contests were not the foundation of the club's breakthrough against Seattle. Mee never started a Nuggets regular-season game and did not become a long-term NBA rotation piece, although he later built a professional basketball career elsewhere. The record therefore supports giving Denver credit for actual reserve depth without awarding it value from later non-NBA seasons or from other picks and players acquired in unrelated Nuggets transactions.

sections.heading: Grant Supplied Immediate Games and the Extra Pick Added Depth
sections.body: The Warriors used Grant in 53 games during 1993-94, no starts, for 157 points and 89 rebounds. Those are direct Golden State returns from the newly acquired No. 43 draft rights, rather than figures recorded for Denver, the club that originally selected him. Golden State also kept the distinct future second-round asset until the 1994 draft. That pair gave the organization more optionality and slightly more immediate NBA service than Denver received from Mee. Still, Grant's 7.2 minutes a game were limited, and the second was a late selection, not a promised lottery player. The preexisting Golden State B-minus should not be read as evidence of championship impact or of a future All-Star acquired through this modest rights trade.

sections.heading: Miller to Whitfield Is a Later Chain, Not Part of June 1993
sections.body: Golden State used the eventual No. 39 selection on Anthony Miller in June 1994, then traded Miller to the Lakers on July 1 for a 1995 second that became Dwayne Whitfield. Those source-dated transactions provide a real path for the acquired second, but the later Lakers trade was not agreed upon on June 30, 1993 and had its own club-specific return. Grant's 53 Warriors games and the future second together support a Slight Warriors Edge over Mee's 40 Denver regular-season appearances. The letter grades of Golden State B-minus and Denver C-plus are retained from the archive. They are a modest relative judgment: neither club acquired an instant star, and Golden State cannot claim Miller's Lakers statistics as direct Warriors scoring.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Golden State B-minus versus Denver C-plus produces a narrow Slight Warriors Edge, not an overwhelming victory. Grant played 53 Warriors NBA games and the additional 1994 second became No. 39 Anthony Miller before a different July 1994 Lakers transaction; Mee played 40 Denver NBA regular-season games and three postseason appearances. Each club obtained a useful but limited right and associated minutes. The record does not borrow contributions from the Warriors' separate Hardaway-Webber trade.

sections.heading: August 1993: Orlando Sent Brian Williams to Denver
sections.body: On August 19, 1993, the Orlando Magic sent center Brian Williams, later known as Bison Dele, to Denver for Todd Lichti, Anthony Cook and a 1994 second-round selection. Orlando's official historical media guide uses the name Brian Williams, while modern NBA transaction databases identify the same player as Bison Dele. Those names refer to one person, not two incoming Denver assets. The future second was an actual pick right rather than another 1993 rookie. Denver had obtained the right in an earlier 1991 three-team exchange; it would become No. 31 Rodney Dent in June 1994. This transaction was a two-team exchange in 1993, distinct from the earlier Atlanta-Milwaukee-Denver movement of that pick.

sections.heading: Dele Played 143 Denver Regular-Season Games
sections.body: Dele gave Denver 80 regular-season appearances during 1993-94, averaging 8.0 points and 5.6 rebounds while largely coming off the bench. The next season he played 63 more Nuggets games, including ten starts, with averages of 7.9 points and 4.7 rebounds. The total direct Denver return was therefore 143 regular-season games across two seasons, far more than a theoretical draft prospect. He also played 12 postseason games in Denver's 1994 playoff run, averaging 9.3 points and 7.4 rebounds, then three postseason games in 1995. Denver's upset of Seattle in 1994 involved multiple Nuggets contributors, so it would be misleading to credit the entire playoff result to this trade. Dele was a real rotation big during that period.

sections.heading: Lichti Played Four Orlando Games; Cook Played Two
sections.body: The Magic received two named veterans, but neither became a lasting NBA rotation player in Orlando. Todd Lichti appeared in four Magic regular-season games during 1993-94 before the club waived him on February 24, 1994. His other nine games that season came with Golden State and Boston, not Orlando. Anthony Cook missed most of the period while recovering from knee surgery and appeared in only two Magic games after being activated in late December. Orlando traded Cook to Milwaukee on January 15, 1994 with other assets to acquire Anthony Avent; that later package must be evaluated on its own. These verified club-specific numbers explain why the direct Lichti/Cook contribution was limited without pretending the incoming players never existed.

sections.heading: Orlando Selected Rodney Dent With the Received No. 31
sections.body: The 1994 second-round pick that Orlando obtained from Denver became No. 31 Rodney Dent. Basketball-Reference's 1994 draft and Orlando transaction ledger record the Magic as the selecting club, while contemporary draft reporting traces the choice through Washington, Milwaukee and Denver before Orlando received it in this deal. Dent did not play an NBA regular-season game for the Magic, so that selection provided identifiable draft rights but no immediate NBA production. The pick had entered Denver through the separate July 1, 1991 three-team trade, which must not be merged into the August 1993 exchange. The stored Nuggets Win grade A-minus versus Orlando D follows Dele's two productive Denver seasons against four Lichti games, two Cook games and an unused NBA pick outcome.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win — Denver A-minus, Orlando D. Brian Williams/Bison Dele played 80 Nuggets regular-season games in 1993-94 and 63 in 1994-95, plus 12 Denver playoff games in 1994. Orlando got four Todd Lichti and two Anthony Cook regular-season appearances before both left in separate moves, while the acquired 1994 second became No. 31 Rodney Dent without Magic NBA games. That direct difference supports the existing Denver-grade advantage.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Denver Nuggets–Orlando Magic: What the 1993-08-19 Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: On August 19, 1993, Denver acquired Brian Williams, later Bison Dele, from Orlando for Todd Lichti, Anthony Cook and a future second. Dele played 143 Nuggets regular-season games and 12 Denver playoff games in 1994; the two players sent to Orlando combined for six Magic appearances. The second became No. 31 Rodney Dent in 1994, with no Orlando NBA playing contribution. The earlier 1991 origin of that selection was a separate three-team transaction.

sections.heading: A 1993 Center-for-Two-Players-and-Second Deal
sections.body: The trade-day asset map was straightforward: Denver received Brian Williams/Bison Dele, and Orlando obtained Todd Lichti, Anthony Cook and a future second. The dated August 19, 1993 transaction appears identically in Denver and Orlando season logs and in the Magic's official historical transaction register. The second was later used on Rodney Dent at No. 31, not on a first-round lottery player. The fact that the draft selection had reached Denver through a separate 1991 Bucks-Hawks-Nuggets exchange explains its provenance without changing the August 1993 package. Orlando was exchanging an underused young center for multiple options; Denver consolidated three assets into a rotation frontcourt contributor. The record can evaluate that strategy using actual team production rather than generic pick-value claims.

sections.heading: Denver Received Two Full Seasons and 1994 Playoff Minutes
sections.body: Dele appeared in 80 regular-season Denver games in 1993-94 and another 63 in 1994-95. He averaged 8.0 points and 5.6 rebounds during the first campaign and 7.9 points and 4.7 rebounds in the second. He supplied frontcourt depth alongside Dikembe Mutombo and played all 12 Nuggets postseason games in 1994, scoring 9.3 points with 7.4 rebounds per game in the playoffs. That was a meaningful contribution to a roster that upset the top-seeded SuperSonics, although his presence alone did not create the entire postseason upset. His later Clippers, Bulls and Pistons seasons happened after subsequent separate transactions and signings. Counting those later accomplishments as Nuggets performance would inflate this original return.

sections.heading: The Magic Got Six Combined Games From Lichti and Cook
sections.body: Orlando's two veteran arrivals combined for only six Magic regular-season appearances in 1993-94: four from Todd Lichti and two from Anthony Cook. Lichti was waived in February and finished that season with Golden State and Boston. Cook had undergone knee surgery before being acquired and was traded again to Milwaukee on January 15, 1994 with a conditional first and future second for Anthony Avent. Contemporary reporting from January identifies his two Orlando appearances and the recovering-knee context. That later move gave Orlando another roster asset, but it involved other draft compensation and cannot be assigned entirely to Cook from the Denver trade. The original pair therefore supplied very little direct on-court service, while the center Orlando relinquished played 143 Denver regular-season games.

sections.heading: The 1994 No. 31 Pick Did Not Make Orlando's Roster
sections.body: Orlando used the future second-round choice on Rodney Dent at No. 31 in the 1994 draft. The selection had passed from Milwaukee to Denver through a three-team deal in July 1991 before Denver traded it to the Magic in August 1993. Draft archives confirm the club and draft slot; they do not record any NBA regular-season games from Dent, so his later rights cannot be counted as played Magic minutes. The Nuggets A-minus and Magic D verdict was an inherited judgment that ranks Dele's 143 regular-season appearances plus 1994 playoff minutes above Orlando's six combined veteran games and an unproductive NBA draft right. Neither the 1991 trade that originated this pick path nor Orlando's 1994 Cook-for-Avent exchange is an extra incoming item in the original 1993 Dele transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Denver A-minus versus Orlando D supports Nuggets Win from the documented team-specific return: 143 Dele regular-season appearances and 1994 postseason depth for Denver against six combined Lichti and Cook Magic appearances plus No. 31 Rodney Dent rights without NBA games. Orlando subsequently moved Cook as one part of a larger Bucks exchange. Denver had obtained the draft pick in a different 1991 three-team transaction. Neither later deal should be collapsed into the August 1993 player trade.

sections.heading: What Changed Hands
sections.body: On November 19, 1993, Denver sent Marcus Liberty and Mark Macon to Detroit for Alvin Robertson, a conditional 1995 second-round draft right and unspecified future consideration. A contemporaneous Washington Post transaction report identifies the 1995 right as a Denver selection the Nuggets had previously traded to Detroit for Anthony Cook. The original UPI wire account also confirms a 1995 second and future considerations, without assigning a dollar amount. There is a consequential later-source conflict: Basketball-Reference's Denver and Detroit season transaction ledgers say the conditional 1995 pick did not convey, whereas the Pro Sports Transactions draft ledger maps Denver's No.44 Anthony Pelle selection to the exchange. Denver did select Pelle in 1995, but the precise path and whether this clause was exercised cannot be treated as independently settled.

sections.heading: How the Realized Value Separated
sections.body: Robertson was the central named NBA veteran going to Denver, with a conditional second-round selection as a possible future asset and undefined consideration. Detroit obtained Liberty and Macon immediately. The February 1995 draft record and Denver's selection of Anthony Pelle do not alone prove that the particular 1993 conditional asset became the No.44 pick; the contemporaneous description of a returned Denver-owned right and the later did-not-convey notation pull in different directions. Consequently, credit for Pelle cannot be automatically assigned to this trade when comparing realised results, and the unknown future clause is not a cash figure or another identifiable player.

sections.heading: Reading the Team Grades
sections.body: The archive assigns Denver A+ and Detroit A-, alongside Nuggets Win, but those are inherited editorial grades, not proof that the conditional pick conveyed or that Robertson produced an exceptional new Denver career. The short relative grade gap should not disguise a material source disagreement about a future asset. Detroit's incoming value was the immediate roster rights of Liberty and Macon. A retrospective explanation can preserve the published grade labels while documenting the evidentiary limitation: neither the disputed pick return nor the undefined future clause can be valued with confidence until the chain is reconciled.

sections.heading: What Each Franchise Was Actually Evaluating
sections.body: Denver accepted the veteran Robertson and the conditional prospect of a 1995 second, while Detroit acquired two players it could evaluate at once. The November 1993 UPI and Washington Post reporting establish the teams and the conditional draft element; the Denver and Detroit transaction tables agree about the named players but say the conditional second did not convey. Pro Sports Transactions assigns the later No.44 pick to this history. Those records should be read together, not silently combined into a certain Pelle return. Neither a speculative pick conveyance nor invented consideration terms should be used to justify the winner or grade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win remains the site's inherited verdict, with Denver A+ and Detroit A- recorded as editorial grades, not independently calculated impact figures. Denver received Alvin Robertson and a conditional 1995 second-round right plus unspecified future considerations in return for Marcus Liberty and Mark Macon. The two 1993 contemporary reports confirm the package; a later pick-chain dispute affects the value assessment. Detroit and Denver transaction ledgers say the conditional 1995 second did not convey, while another draft ledger links the exchange to Denver's eventual No.44 Anthony Pelle choice. That 1995 selection is real, but attributing it to this agreement without resolving the conditional clause risks counting an unrelated outcome. No supported value exists for the future-considerations term.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Denver Nuggets–Detroit Pistons: What the 1993-11-19 Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: Denver's November 19, 1993 exchange with Detroit is a test of source provenance before historical trade grading. Contemporary accounts agree that Alvin Robertson, a conditional 1995 second-round right and unspecified future considerations went to Denver for Marcus Liberty and Mark Macon. One report describes the future pick as Denver's own selection returning from the Pistons. The complication comes later: Basketball-Reference's two team ledgers say the conditional pick never conveyed, but a draft-rights ledger attributes Denver's actual No.44 Anthony Pelle selection to that earlier trade. A Deep Dive must keep the two claims separate rather than invent a certain asset chain or a value for the unknown clause.

sections.heading: The Asset Path That Carries the Grade
sections.body: The trade's documented immediate result was Robertson going to Denver and Liberty and Macon to Detroit. There was also a conditional 1995 second-round right and further consideration left undefined in contemporary reporting. Washington Post described the pick as Denver's own right returning from Detroit after the earlier Anthony Cook deal. A later draft-transaction chain names Anthony Pelle at No.44, while both 1993-94 team transaction registers say that conditional 1995 pick did not convey. Identifying Denver as the club that actually drafted Pelle establishes the NBA draft fact, not an undisputed link to the conditional trade term.

sections.heading: What the Lower-Graded Side Still Kept
sections.body: Robertson's arrival gave Denver a recognizable veteran rather than a guaranteed multi-season acquisition. The Nuggets' conditional pick and undefined future consideration require separate treatment from the players Detroit obtained immediately. The inherited A+/A- grades are retrospective editorial opinions, and neither that rating nor the No.44 draft listing establishes a financial value or a verified conveyed pick for this specific November 1993 agreement. The safest reading credits neither club with speculative future assets until a reconciled pick-chain source explains the conflict.

sections.heading: Decision Logic Versus Hindsight
sections.body: Detroit acquired Marcus Liberty and Mark Macon, giving the Pistons two players rather than waiting for a draft selection. The archive awards Detroit A-, not a failing grade, so its written analysis should preserve the substance of that incoming package even while describing a Nuggets Win verdict. No credible evaluation can turn the absence of a listed draft pick on Detroit's side into proof that both players had zero value. Their specific future productivity needs separate player evidence.

sections.heading: Why the Grade Gap Is the Better Scale
sections.body: A+ for Denver versus A- for Detroit signals the archive's slight preference, but the available evidence cannot demonstrate a comparable measurable return. Liberty and Macon were Detroit's confirmed incoming players, Robertson was Denver's confirmed veteran, and the additional conditional and future elements lack an agreed realized chain. UPI and the Washington Post confirm the original agreement; Basketball-Reference labels the pick unexercised, while Pro Sports Transactions identifies the No.44 draft choice as linked. This is an unresolved provenance limitation, not support for turning a draft name into certain extra Denver games.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Denver A+ and Detroit A- grades and Nuggets Win label are preserved as the archive's historical judgment, not independently verified numerical returns. The certain named exchange was Alvin Robertson to Denver and Marcus Liberty and Mark Macon to Detroit. The 1993 reports also mention a conditional Denver second-round right for 1995 and further unspecified consideration. Washington Post says that future right was Denver's own previously traded pick, but Basketball-Reference records it as not conveyed; a competing draft ledger connects the package to Denver's later No.44 Anthony Pelle selection. Until that chain is reconciled, the Pelle outcome must not be assigned as an indisputable benefit from this agreement. The resulting case for a strong Nuggets edge is less secure than the inherited marks imply.

sections.heading: The Package in Full
sections.body: Denver's June 28, 1995 draft-night exchange with the Los Angeles Clippers sent Rodney Rogers and the rights to Brent Barry to Los Angeles. The Nuggets acquired Randy Woods and the rights to Antonio McDyess. The distinction between a player and unsigned draft rights is fundamental: both teams were exchanging an NBA roster asset plus control of another player through the draft. The subsequent careers of Barry and McDyess can explain outcomes, but neither right was identical to signing its player to a long-term contract at the moment the trade was recorded.

sections.heading: How the Value Separated
sections.body: McDyess became Denver's most important return. The forward developed into an All-Star and earned All-NBA recognition while playing for the Nuggets, giving the team a clearly traceable high-value outcome from the draft rights acquired in 1995. Randy Woods was a separate incoming asset, not an extra first-round selection. The Clippers obtained Rodney Rogers and Barry's rights. The archive grades Denver A and Los Angeles C+, producing a Nuggets Win based on the difference in their realized packages rather than merely counting two names on each side.

sections.heading: Why Denver Nuggets Grades Higher
sections.body: Los Angeles did receive substantial basketball opportunities. Rogers was a current NBA forward, and the rights to Brent Barry offered a route to add another player in the draft. Barry later enjoyed a long NBA career, but assigning his entire professional production to the Clippers would overstate what this transaction yielded for Los Angeles. On Denver's side, the noteworthy result is McDyess's actual impact as a Nuggets forward. This asymmetry explains why a two-for-two asset count alone cannot settle the archived grade comparison.

sections.heading: The Case for Los Angeles Clippers' Return
sections.body: The asset trail begins at the 1995 draft, not at a future deadline with anonymous picks. Denver acquired rights to Antonio McDyess together with Randy Woods. The Clippers received Rodney Rogers and rights to Brent Barry. A named draft-rights claim should not be confused with another pick that might be selected several years later, and neither package includes cash in the documented ledger. The A/C+ grade gap should follow these specific players and rights through the value each acquiring club realized.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win — Denver A, Los Angeles C+. Denver acquired Randy Woods and the rights to Antonio McDyess; the Clippers obtained Rodney Rogers and the rights to Brent Barry. McDyess's successful NBA development in Denver is a documented club-specific reason for the favorable grade, while Barry's later career should not all be attributed to the Clippers. Four assets moved, none of them cash or an unlisted future selection.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Denver Nuggets–Los Angeles Clippers: June 1995 McDyess–Barry Draft-Rights Trade
featuredDeepDive.intro: On June 28, 1995, Denver traded Rodney Rogers and rights to Brent Barry to the Los Angeles Clippers in exchange for Randy Woods and rights to Antonio McDyess. Each team received a named player and a drafted player's rights. McDyess went on to become an All-Star and an All-NBA forward with Denver, supporting the archived Nuggets Win verdict and A for Denver against the Clippers' C+. The source-specific retrospective should follow those actual acquiring-club contributions and avoid converting the entire later careers of the prospects into automatically realized trade value.

sections.heading: The Most Important Piece
sections.body: This trade joined two established player movements with two draft-rights movements during the same 1995 draft. The Nuggets obtained Randy Woods and McDyess's rights; the Clippers acquired Rogers and Barry's rights. The four components have distinct histories, so a Deep Dive needs to separate the players already available in the league from each team's new claim to a drafted prospect. The archival Nuggets Win judgment rests on the useful basketball value those four assets created after their respective transfers.

sections.heading: Depth, Picks, and Supporting Value
sections.body: Antonio McDyess is the clearest Denver-side success attached to the trade. His All-Star and All-NBA seasons with the Nuggets provide a concrete reason the team's incoming package rates an A in the archive. Randy Woods remains part of Denver's return even if McDyess drives most of the assessment. The two shouldn't be collapsed into one asset or supplemented with another draft selection that wasn't conveyed. Denver's benefit can be explained through McDyess's actual seasons rather than unrelated later success for the franchise.

sections.heading: Intent Versus Realized Value
sections.body: Rodney Rogers and the rights to Brent Barry were meaningful considerations for Los Angeles. Rogers could contribute as a player while the Barry rights represented a pathway to add a prospect. Barry's longer NBA career is relevant historical context but requires attribution to the clubs where he actually played; its entirety was not a guaranteed Clippers benefit arising from one draft-night trade. The C+ grade for Los Angeles evaluates the franchise's own return without pretending that receiving two assets was worthless.

sections.heading: What the Historical Record Shows
sections.body: The critical comparison is Denver's McDyess development against the Clippers' different combination of Rogers and Barry rights. A grade of A for the Nuggets versus C+ for Los Angeles reflects the stronger actual Denver return and the direct club-specific evidence behind it. Both clubs also obtained secondary assets, Woods for Denver and Rogers for the Clippers, which must be kept in the ledger. This transaction does not require a third team, later anonymous selection or undisclosed cash payment to explain the verdict.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The strongest piece of Denver's 1995 return was Antonio McDyess's rights, which developed into All-Star and All-NBA production for the Nuggets. Randy Woods also moved to Denver; Rodney Rogers and Brent Barry's rights went to the Clippers. The archive's A/C+ grade comparison and Nuggets Win verdict concern those four returns, not a different later trade or the entire careers of players with other teams.

sections.heading: The September Agreement Was Brian Williams for Elmore Spencer
sections.body: The Clippers and Nuggets completed a one-for-one exchange on September 19, 1995: Los Angeles sent center Elmore Spencer to Denver and acquired Brian Williams, the player later known as Bison Dele. The contemporaneous Los Angeles Times and UPI stories use the name Williams, while retrospective basketball databases identify the same player as Dele. Those are not two incoming Clippers. The transaction had been planned around the June draft but was delayed by the NBA lockout and salary-cap maneuvering. It also was separate from the clubs’ earlier draft exchange involving Antonio McDyess, Rodney Rogers and Brent Barry, none of whom belongs in this Spencer-for-Williams asset ledger.

sections.heading: Dele Started All 65 Clippers Games He Played in 1995-96
sections.body: The Clippers received a real starting center. Williams, later Dele, appeared in 65 games for Los Angeles in 1995-96 and started every one, averaging 33.2 minutes, 15.8 points and 7.6 rebounds. He scored 1,029 regular-season points, pulled down 492 rebounds and shot 54.3 percent from the field. Those figures came after a 1994-95 Denver campaign of 63 appearances, only ten starts and 7.9 points per game. The change illustrates how his opportunity expanded after the trade. The Clippers nevertheless finished 29-53; Dele’s statistical leap did not transform a weak club into a playoff contender or guarantee that Los Angeles would retain him long term.

sections.heading: Spencer Played Six Nuggets Games and Never Scored for Denver
sections.body: Denver’s actual receiving-team return was far smaller. Spencer appeared in only six games for the Nuggets during 1995-96, starting none and playing 21 total minutes. He missed his only field-goal attempt and recorded zero points, four rebounds and no blocked shots in that Denver sample. The club waived him on December 21, 1995. Spencer subsequently played 11 games for Portland later that season, with 14 total points, and one game for Seattle in 1996-97. Those later appearances belong to those teams, not to the Nuggets. His pretrade 139 Clippers appearances are also historical context, not production Denver gained after September 19.

sections.heading: Why the Clippers Gained a Starting Center While Denver Got Little
sections.body: The Clippers Win verdict grades Los Angeles A-minus and Denver C-plus. The Sept. 19, 1995 exchange sent Elmore Spencer to Denver and Brian Williams, later known as Bison Dele, to Los Angeles. Dele started all 65 Clippers games he played in 1995-96, averaging 15.8 points and 7.6 rebounds. Spencer's direct Nuggets return was six appearances, 21 total minutes and no points before he was waived in December. Denver's own historical media guide independently confirms Dele's September 19 departure to the Clippers, while the NBA's player record identifies the 65-start Los Angeles season. Williams filled an immediate center need while Stanley Roberts recovered from Achilles problems, as contemporary Los Angeles reporting explains. Neither Dele's later 1997 Bulls championship nor his Detroit years were Clippers production; the grade gap instead follows the two players' sharply different first-season results for their actual receiving teams.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The protected Clippers Win, Los Angeles A- and Denver C+ are retained. Brian Williams, later Bison Dele, started all 65 Clippers games in 1995-96 and produced 15.8 points and 7.6 rebounds a night. Elmore Spencer played six Denver games, scoring zero points, before the Nuggets waived him December 21. Separate draft-night transactions and the players’ later teams are not part of the direct September return.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Brian Williams for Elmore Spencer in 1995: Sixty-Five Clippers Starts, Six Denver Games
featuredDeepDive.intro: Los Angeles traded Elmore Spencer to Denver for Brian Williams on September 19, 1995. Williams later adopted the name Bison Dele, explaining why modern transaction ledgers identify him differently from contemporary reports. The Clippers received 65 starts, 1,029 points and 492 rebounds in his 1995-96 season. Spencer logged six Nuggets games and zero points before being waived in December. This unusual contrast supports the preserved Clippers Win and Los Angeles A-/Denver C+ grades without confusing the transaction with an earlier Denver–Clippers draft swap.

sections.heading: The Post-Lockout Transaction Was Not the McDyess Draft Deal
sections.body: Both teams were involved in more than one notable 1995 exchange. An earlier draft-day move sent Rodney Rogers and Brent Barry’s draft rights to the Clippers and Antonio McDyess’s rights to Denver. The September transaction was different: Los Angeles sent Spencer for Williams. A September 20 Los Angeles Times report says that the deal was held up by a lockout and completed only after the Clippers renounced the rights to Harold Ellis and Michael Smith to create room. Those renunciations were accompanying salary-cap actions, not additional player assets acquired by Denver. The contemporary name Brian Williams refers to the same individual that historical NBA career pages list as Bison Dele.

sections.heading: Dele Replaced Reserve Minutes with a Full-Time Starting Role
sections.body: The receiving-team split is unusually striking. In 1994-95 Williams was a 20-minute Denver player with 63 games and ten starts, scoring 7.9 points while collecting 4.7 rebounds. The Clippers started him in every one of his 65 appearances in 1995-96, raising his workload to 33.2 minutes and his averages to 15.8 points, 7.6 rebounds and 1.9 assists. That produced 1,029 points and 492 rebounds for Los Angeles. UPI’s September 19 account described the club’s interest in his size and frontcourt versatility. None of his later Bulls or Pistons performances was earned while wearing a Clippers uniform, even if those seasons help establish his overall ability.

sections.heading: Denver Received Only Twenty-One Spencer Minutes
sections.body: Spencer’s 1995-96 NBA year was split between Denver and Portland, but the clubs’ totals must stay distinct. He logged six games, zero starts, 21 minutes, zero points and four rebounds with the Nuggets. Denver waived him December 21. Portland later used him for eleven games and he scored fourteen points there; he subsequently appeared for Seattle once in 1996-97. These were brief NBA opportunities elsewhere, not delayed Denver returns. Spencer’s prior role with the Clippers had been much larger, including 76 appearances and 63 starts in 1993-94, but those minutes occurred before he joined the Nuggets and cannot improve the 1995 Denver-side assessment.

sections.heading: The Basketball Comparison Is Stronger than the Clubs’ Records
sections.body: The Clippers finished 29-53 in 1995-96, while Denver went 35-47. Those records do not independently establish which team won a two-center trade because each roster contained many other players and both franchises made additional transactions. A better test is the specific production received after September 19. Los Angeles obtained an established starter for 65 games; Denver got six reserve appearances and then released the incoming center. The protected A- Clippers grade and C+ Denver grade are therefore supported by the asset-specific evidence. The subsequent disappearance of Williams from the Clippers roster and Spencer’s later minor stints do not alter the initial 1995-96 receiving-team difference.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win with A- Los Angeles and C+ Denver stays unchanged. Brian Williams/Bison Dele gave Los Angeles 65 starts, 15.8 points and 7.6 rebounds per game; Elmore Spencer gave Denver 21 minutes over six games and no points before being waived. The earlier McDyess–Rogers–Barry exchange, later Portland appearances and Dele’s championship-season work elsewhere are separate histories, not additional assets from the September swap.

sections.heading: Jackson and Rose Changed Teams Alongside a Pick Swap
sections.body: Indiana sent Mark Jackson, Ricky Pierce and its No. 23 selection in the 1996 draft to Denver on June 13. The Nuggets sent Jalen Rose, Reggie Williams and the No. 10 pick the other way. That meant Indiana moved up thirteen draft positions as well as acquiring a 23-year-old guard-forward with room to develop. Denver obtained Jackson’s established playmaking, Pierce’s veteran shooting and the later selection that became Efthimios Rentzias.

sections.heading: Indiana Was Trying to Get Younger Without Abandoning Reggie Miller
sections.body: Pacers president Donnie Walsh described youth and improved draft position as central motives when the trade was announced. Jackson had organized a veteran Pacers offense, but the front office believed Travis Best could assume more point-guard responsibility. Rose offered a different type of lineup versatility alongside Reggie Miller, while Williams provided a short-term veteran option. It was a calculated reallocation of established guard value rather than a random exchange of contracts.

sections.heading: Rose Became the Long-Term Indiana Return
sections.body: Rose developed into a featured scorer and creator for Indiana, winning the NBA Most Improved Player award in 2000 and playing a major role on the Pacers team that reached that year’s NBA Finals. Indiana also selected Erick Dampier at No. 10; that pick was real draft capital even though Dampier’s own Pacers career did not become the principal return. The combined developmental upside ultimately exceeded the value Indiana surrendered in 1996.

sections.heading: Denver’s Jackson Acquisition Was Useful but Brief
sections.body: Jackson supplied reliable playmaking to Denver, which had been searching for a steadier offensive structure. Yet his first Nuggets stint lasted less than a season. In February 1997, Indiana reacquired Jackson and LaSalle Thompson for Vincent Askew, Eddie Johnson and two second-round selections. Rentzias did not become a substantial Denver NBA contributor. Denver therefore received a capable guard temporarily without keeping a comparable young centerpiece from its side of the original trade.

sections.heading: Why the A-plus and D Grades Are So Far Apart
sections.body: The Pacers’ A-plus credits Rose’s rise during their strongest late-1990s and early-2000s run, the move up to No. 10 and even the eventual return of Jackson in a separate deal. Denver’s D reflects a short veteran stint and a later pick that did not develop into equal value. The subsequent reacquisition cost Indiana additional assets and should not be portrayed as free; it nevertheless left the franchise with both Rose and Jackson during its 2000 Finals run.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pacers Win — Indiana A-plus, Denver D. The Pacers exchanged Jackson, Pierce and No. 23 for Rose, Williams and No. 10, then later reacquired Jackson in another transaction. Rose became a leading player on a Finals team, while Denver retained its veteran point guard for only part of a season. The grade gap reflects those specific career outcomes and the difference between the two draft positions.

sections.heading: What Changed Hands
sections.body: Denver moved Mahmoud Abdul-Rauf to Sacramento on June 13, 1996, receiving Sarunas Marciulionis and a second-round choice in that month's draft. The selection later became No. 37, Jeff McInnis. Those were distinct Denver assets: one established guard and one pick that still had to be exercised. Sacramento obtained Abdul-Rauf as an immediately recognizable player. Treating the exchange as an ordinary guard-for-guard move would omit the draft position that the Nuggets also acquired.

sections.heading: How the Realized Value Separated
sections.body: The two teams faced different roster questions. Sacramento could use Abdul-Rauf's skills as a scorer and ball handler rather than wait for a prospect to develop. Denver chose Marciulionis, another established guard, and retained a second route to possible value through the No. 37 choice. The archive records a Nuggets Win, with Denver graded A and Sacramento D+, but that gap should be traced to the specific returns rather than presumed additional roster moves or general impressions of the two franchises.

sections.heading: Reading the Team Grades
sections.body: The draft asset belongs to June 1996, not to a future protected selection whose destination could not yet be known for years. The incoming Denver second-round pick is identified as No. 37, Jeff McInnis. That provides a concrete way to examine part of Denver's return without asserting that the picked player was an experienced NBA contributor when the deal was made. Sacramento received no corresponding choice in the transaction ledger. It obtained Abdul-Rauf, making the return a single-player basketball decision.

sections.heading: What Each Franchise Was Actually Evaluating
sections.body: The source histories identify Denver's receipt of Sarunas Marciulionis and the second-rounder in exchange for Mahmoud Abdul-Rauf. The relevant grade pairing is A for Denver and D+ for Sacramento, a considerably wider margin than an even trade. The evaluation still needs to distinguish trade-day possibilities from completed results: Marciulionis was a known player, the draft pick an opportunity, and Abdul-Rauf a current guard. No cash or additional team is listed as consideration.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win — Denver A, Sacramento D+. Denver obtained Sarunas Marciulionis and the 1996 second-rounder later used at No. 37 on Jeff McInnis. Sacramento acquired Mahmoud Abdul-Rauf. The pick and the veteran belong in separate parts of the valuation, because McInnis was a draft outcome rather than an established player delivered on June 13. No other incoming asset is recorded for the Kings.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Denver Nuggets–Sacramento Kings: June 1996 Abdul-Rauf Exchange
featuredDeepDive.intro: On June 13, 1996, Denver acquired Sarunas Marciulionis and a second-round draft selection that became No. 37, Jeff McInnis, while Sacramento took Mahmoud Abdul-Rauf. The Nuggets' package mixed a current NBA guard with a draft opportunity, whereas the Kings received one immediately established player. The site's historical verdict favors Denver, A to Sacramento's D+. A defensible Deep Dive follows both the player exchange and the same-year draft selection without counting the pick as an additional veteran or borrowing value from later unrelated trades.

sections.heading: The Asset Path That Carries the Grade
sections.body: Denver's return can be divided cleanly between immediate player rights and an additional draft opportunity. Sarunas Marciulionis was the player received from Sacramento; the No. 37 second-round pick in 1996 later became Jeff McInnis. Sacramento received Mahmoud Abdul-Rauf. That pairing is the core of the archived Nuggets Win verdict. It does not depend on Denver receiving an unlisted first-rounder or on treating McInnis as a seasoned NBA player before the draft happened.

sections.heading: What the Lower-Graded Side Still Kept
sections.body: The Nuggets were exchanging an established scorer for another established guard plus the chance to select or use the rights to a second-round prospect. Marciulionis supplied an immediately named player return, while the McInnis pick created another future path. The A grade for Denver is the site's evaluation of that total package, not merely the numerical fact that Denver obtained two assets. Either piece needs to be judged by what it actually yielded, with the date and selection number kept distinct.

sections.heading: Decision Logic Versus Hindsight
sections.body: Sacramento's side was different and easier to state: the Kings received Abdul-Rauf. The club did not acquire the 1996 No. 37 selection from Denver or any other future pick under this trade record. That absence is important when comparing the D+ for Sacramento with Denver's A. The Kings chose the ability of a known guard instead of the particular mix of Marciulionis and a draft chance, and the retrospective grades show how the archive judges those alternatives after the fact.

sections.heading: Why the Grade Gap Is the Better Scale
sections.body: The 1996 trade is also a useful example of why a later draft player's name should not substitute for the terms of a transaction. Denver acquired a second-round selection, and its later identity is McInnis at No. 37. That fact alone does not describe all subsequent contracts, player moves or years of production. The archived A-versus-D+ outcome should be explained through the acquired guard and pick versus Abdul-Rauf, with any later personal achievements assigned only to teams supported by separate transaction histories.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The archive favors Denver's mix of Sarunas Marciulionis and a 1996 second-round choice over Sacramento's acquisition of Mahmoud Abdul-Rauf, grading the clubs A and D+. The choice became No. 37, Jeff McInnis, but it should not be described as an additional June 1996 veteran. These exact rights and player transfers, not unrelated subsequent roster moves, support the Nuggets Win verdict.

sections.heading: Indiana Reacquired Mark Jackson Within a Season
sections.body: The Pacers brought Mark Jackson and LaSalle Thompson back from Denver in February 1997. The Nuggets received Vincent Askew, Eddie Johnson and two second-round selections that became Jason Lawson at No. 41 in 1997 and Tremaine Fowlkes at No. 54 in 1998. Jackson had been sent to Denver only months earlier in a deal involving Jalen Rose. Bringing him back was an unusually direct admission that Indiana still needed his veteran playmaking.

sections.heading: Jackson Helped Organize a Successful Pacers Era
sections.body: Indiana restored an experienced point guard beside Reggie Miller and a roster that soon made several deep Eastern Conference playoff runs. Jackson’s ability to organize possessions was particularly useful to a veteran club built on clear roles and disciplined execution. He was part of the Indiana team that reached the 2000 NBA Finals. Thompson contributed a lesser part of the package; Jackson was the principal reason the returning assets became important.

sections.heading: Denver Received Depth but No Equivalent Foundation
sections.body: Askew and Johnson offered immediate veteran experience, and the two selections gave Denver developmental opportunities. Neither pick turned into a performer matching Jackson’s sustained role in Indiana. Denver therefore obtained an assortment of useful possibilities without a comparable defining player. This does not mean the second-round picks were worthless when acquired; the completed history simply shows that the Pacers converted their side into considerably more valuable basketball results.

sections.heading: Why Indiana’s A-plus Is Justified
sections.body: The Pacers receive A-plus for reacquiring their floor general before a run of conference finals appearances and an NBA Finals berth. Denver receives C for its veteran depth and two late picks. Reversing the earlier Jackson move cost Indiana additional assets, but the immediate correction strengthened its best competitive years. The verdict is grounded in that specific roster outcome, not in assuming every point guard always outranks every draft package.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pacers Win — Indiana A-plus, Denver C. Reacquiring Jackson restored the organizing guard for a series of deep playoff teams, including the 2000 NBA Finals squad. Denver received Askew, Eddie Johnson and two second-round selections without matching that sustained impact. Indiana paid to reverse a recent decision but ultimately secured the far better on-court return.

sections.heading: Denver Received Three Assets for Ervin Johnson in 1997
sections.body: The June 25, 1997 transaction sent center Ervin Johnson from Denver to Milwaukee. The Nuggets received veteran wings Johnny Newman and Joe Wolf along with the draft rights to Danny Fortson, whom the Bucks selected No. 10 in the 1997 NBA draft. The trade was not an exchange of Fortson as an established NBA contributor. Denver was taking on a recent college forward while adding two veteran contracts; Milwaukee preferred a proven starting center and rim protector. The four components were split three to Denver and one to Milwaukee, but an item count says little about long-term value. The actual playing records for both teams show productive contributions, and any retrospective verdict needs to consider Milwaukee's multi-season defensive-center return.

sections.heading: Newman Was an Immediate High-Usage Denver Wing
sections.body: Newman was not just salary filler. In 1997-98 he appeared in 74 Nuggets regular-season games, started 15 and averaged 14.7 points in 29.4 minutes. His scoring made him one of Denver's substantial perimeter contributors during a difficult season for the team. The Nuggets finished 11-71, which cautions against describing his production as proof that the transaction made Denver competitive. Nevertheless, a veteran wing offering that scoring workload has direct basketball value and belongs in the asset return. Wolf's role was smaller: he appeared in 57 games, averaging 10.9 minutes and 1.5 points while contributing reserve frontcourt minutes. Neither should be treated as a draft asset or mislabeled as an outgoing piece.

sections.heading: Fortson Supplied a Strong Rebounding Season Before Leaving Denver
sections.body: Fortson played 80 games in his first Denver season, starting 23 and averaging 10.2 points and 5.6 rebounds. In the shortened 1998-99 campaign he started 38 of 50 games, raising his rebounds to 11.6 per contest with 11.0 points. His ability to secure offensive rebounds made him a genuine development success from the No. 10 draft right. Denver traded Fortson in August 1999 to Boston as part of a larger subsequent transaction that also involved other players and a future pick. That later deal should be tracked separately rather than credited as an extra 1997 Milwaukee asset. The two initial seasons are enough to establish meaningful return from the rights Denver obtained.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Got Far More Than a One-Year Backup Center
sections.body: Johnson became a regular Milwaukee center for six NBA seasons rather than a quick roster stop. In 1997-98 he started all 81 appearances, averaged 8.0 points, 8.5 rebounds and 2.0 blocks, and played about 28 minutes per night. He continued to provide rebounding and interior defense in subsequent years, appearing in 80 games during 1999-00 and all 82 in 2000-01 as the Bucks reached the Eastern Conference Finals. Those franchise-level results cannot be solely attributed to him, but his long tenure and specialized defensive contribution are directly relevant. That record makes a claim that Milwaukee simply received a lower-value, fleeting asset untenable.

sections.heading: The Different Time Horizons Are the Heart of the Comparison
sections.body: Denver received an immediate 14.7-point wing in Newman and a draft-rights player in Fortson who averaged double-digit points over his first two seasons, including 11.6 rebounds in 1998-99. Milwaukee received one center with established defensive value who played through the 2002-03 campaign. Neither package can be evaluated solely from the 1997-98 team standings or from the number of ledger entries. Fortson's later move to Boston limits how much of his extended NBA career can be attached to Denver; Johnson's Milwaukee seasons belong directly to the Bucks' side. Wolf was a minor but genuine depth contributor. A factual review of these distinct returns is more defensible than recycling a generic winner description.

sections.heading: Why Denver Has an A-Plus and Milwaukee a C-Plus
sections.body: The Nuggets Win verdict grades Denver A-plus and Milwaukee C-plus, but the gap is not simply a reward for receiving three assets in exchange for one. Johnny Newman averaged 14.7 points for Denver in 1997-98, and Danny Fortson reached 11.6 rebounds per game in 1998-99. Those were concrete returns, even while the Nuggets struggled in the standings. Milwaukee's side also deserves attention: Ervin Johnson started all 81 games he played in 1997-98, averaging 8.5 rebounds and 2.0 blocks, and continued as a Bucks center through 2002-03. The two packages served different purposes. Denver acquired scoring, depth and a young rebounder; Milwaukee acquired durable interior defense. The A-plus/C-plus spread is a retrospective judgment of those different returns, not a mathematical formula. Readers who place greater weight on Johnson's six-season Milwaukee tenure could reasonably see a closer outcome.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The stored outcome remains Nuggets Win, Denver A-plus and Milwaukee C-plus, pending a separate grade-provenance review. Denver acquired Newman (74 games, 14.7 points in 1997-98), Wolf (57 reserve appearances) and the rights to Fortson (11.0 points, 11.6 rebounds in 1998-99). Milwaukee received Johnson, who played six Bucks seasons and averaged 8.0 points, 8.5 rebounds and two blocks in his first. That durable defensive return does not fit a claim of negligible Bucks value. The historical letter gap should be treated as inherited rather than automatically proved.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Fortson's Rebounding, Newman's Scoring and Johnson's Six Bucks Seasons
featuredDeepDive.intro: Denver swapped veteran center Ervin Johnson in June 1997 for Johnny Newman, Joe Wolf and Milwaukee's draft rights to No. 10 pick Danny Fortson. The Nuggets got a strong scoring season from Newman and two productive seasons from Fortson. The Bucks gained Johnson's interior defense for six years. That is a more nuanced record than the original repeated template, which treated Denver's A-plus versus Milwaukee's C-plus as self-evident. The canonical grades stay unchanged while the divergent playing returns are documented and the grading magnitude is flagged for a future source-based review.

sections.heading: The Bucks Drafted Fortson Before His Rights Went to Denver
sections.body: Fortson was selected by Milwaukee with the 10th overall choice of the 1997 draft, then sent to Denver as part of the Ervin Johnson transaction. That distinguishes the rights he carried from the direct transfer of Newman and Wolf, both NBA veterans. The trade did not include another separate first-round pick on top of Fortson's rights. Its immediate composition is therefore three Denver incoming assets, including one unsigned rookie, against a Bucks incoming starting center. Treating those pieces as comparable from the first night would ignore timing: the Nuggets were paying for upside and veteran wing points, while Milwaukee was buying an established rim protector.

sections.heading: Newman and Wolf Supplied Different Pieces of the Denver Return
sections.body: Newman gave the 1997-98 Nuggets 74 appearances and 14.7 points a night, with substantial playing time despite a team record of 11-71. That production was much more than a minimum-minute salary slot. Wolf, meanwhile, played 57 regular-season games at 1.5 points and 2.2 rebounds across roughly eleven minutes per contest. The difference illustrates why a three-item package should not be graded by counting entries alone. Newman supplied immediate wing offense; Wolf supplied limited depth; the rights to Fortson offered a possible longer-term starting rebounder. Each has its own measured outcome and cannot be collapsed into a blanket assertion that every Denver acquisition was equally valuable.

sections.heading: Fortson Had an Outstanding Rebounding Peak in 1998-99
sections.body: Denver obtained 80 rookie games from Fortson at 10.2 points and 5.6 rebounds, then 50 lockout-shortened 1998-99 games at 11.0 points and 11.6 rebounds, with 38 starts. The second year in particular demonstrates the upside Milwaukee relinquished as part of the trade. However, Fortson departed in August 1999 in the Boston transaction involving Ron Mercer and other assets, so his later career with the Celtics and Warriors cannot simply be booked as continuous Nuggets production. Evaluating the downstream asset chain requires consulting that distinct 1999 transaction. His direct Denver work is solid without crediting the Nuggets for years he spent elsewhere.

sections.heading: Johnson's Milwaukee Longevity Challenges an Easy A-Plus Versus C-Plus Story
sections.body: Johnson played 81 Bucks games with 81 starts during 1997-98, averaging 8.0 points, 8.5 rebounds and two blocks per game. He also appeared in 50 games in 1998-99, 80 in 1999-00 and 82 in 2000-01, then stayed for two more seasons. The role was primarily rim protection and rebounding, not offensive creation. Milwaukee's trip to the 2001 Eastern Conference Finals involved Ray Allen, Glenn Robinson, Sam Cassell and other critical players; it should not be attributed wholly to Johnson. But six seasons of a credible interior defender complicates any simplistic statement that the Bucks surrendered more durable value just because Denver received three named assets. A transparent grading explanation has to confront that tenure.

sections.heading: Keep the Verdict and the Provenance Question Separate
sections.body: The database retains Nuggets Win, Denver A-plus and Milwaukee C-plus. Neither the newly researched game totals nor the trade-day ledger, by themselves, settle whether such a wide letter spread is justified. Denver acquired Newman's productive wing season and Fortson's two active rebounding seasons; Milwaukee acquired a six-season defensive center, and Wolf was a comparatively small Denver contributor. The correct editorial action is to present each factual return and flag grading magnitude for later source review without inventing an authoritative newer verdict. Any eventual regrade should be a separate, documented decision based on an agreed methodology that accounts for years played, role, and subsequent asset conversion. This repair only replaces repetitive copy with evidence-based direct outcomes.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win, Denver A-plus and Milwaukee C-plus are preserved historical site judgments, not independently regraded conclusions. Newman gave Denver 74 games and 14.7 points per night in 1997-98; Joe Wolf contributed 57 reserve appearances. Fortson was a serious rebounder, averaging 11.6 boards with 11.0 points in the 50-game 1998-99 campaign before moving to Boston the next summer. Milwaukee received Ervin Johnson, who started all 81 games in his first Bucks season, averaged 8.5 rebounds and two blocks, and continued through 2002-03. Those results give both franchises meaningful value. The original letter gap may require adjudication; the correct current step is to replace generic winner prose with verifiable figures, preserve every asset and prevent a silent grade change.
