sections.heading: Denver and Seattle Exchanged Draft Rights
sections.body: Denver obtained the rights to Bobby Jackson in the June 1997 exchange. Seattle received James Cotton and a 1998 second-round pick. One year later, that second-round selection became No. 32 Rashard Lewis. The draft rights are the foundation of the retrospective comparison; this was not a trade of an established Lewis for Jackson in 1997. At the time, the SuperSonics were receiving a future chance to select someone, and the later name gives that chance its historical value.

sections.heading: Rashard Lewis Became the Most Durable Return
sections.body: Lewis developed into a long-tenured NBA scorer and later an All-Star after Seattle selected him. Finding that caliber of player in the second round was an unusually productive result. This is why Seattle’s side earns an A-plus, rather than because the original draft slot was obviously worth more than Denver’s incoming rights. The selection’s identity and subsequent performance are part of the same asset chain, and that chain is the decisive reason the two packages do not grade evenly.

sections.heading: Denver Still Acquired a Legitimate Player in Jackson
sections.body: Jackson was more than a nominal right or an unidentified future pick. He became an NBA guard who could handle and create offense, giving Denver a substantial basketball return from the trade. That is reflected in the Nuggets’ A-minus, a strong grade in its own right. The Jazz or any other franchise’s separate transactions do not affect the comparison. It is possible for both sides to do well, especially when each acquired the rights to a player who would develop into a real NBA contributor.

sections.heading: A-plus Versus A-minus Is the Appropriate Difference
sections.body: The verdict is Seattle SuperSonics Win, with Seattle A-plus and Denver A-minus. Lewis’s extended high-end NBA impact distinguishes the Seattle return, while Jackson’s career prevents Denver from being treated as a losing package in the ordinary sense. James Cotton belongs in the exchange ledger but is not the source of the greatest difference. The right retrospective question is which selection eventually produced more attributable value, not whether either club understood every later career development in June 1997.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Seattle SuperSonics Win — Seattle A-plus, Denver A-minus. Seattle’s 1998 second-round selection became Rashard Lewis, the standout long-term contributor from the exchange. Denver received Bobby Jackson’s rights and obtained a legitimate NBA guard. Both teams secured meaningful value, but Lewis gives the SuperSonics the stronger historical return.

sections.heading: Dale Ellis / Greg Graham, Steve Scheffler and second-round picks: What Actually Changed Hands
sections.body: Denver acquired Greg Graham, Steve Scheffler and two second-round picks that became Ryan Bowen and Francisco Elson. Seattle reacquired veteran scorer Dale Ellis. The deal produced useful value on both sides rather than the lopsided result implied by the old grade split. Seattle acquired Dale Ellis, the scorer it knew, while Denver accepted Greg Graham, Steve Scheffler and a pair of second-round selections. Those picks eventually became Ryan Bowen and Francisco Elson, so Denver did not rely on a single veteran to justify its return.

sections.heading: Dale Ellis / Greg Graham, Steve Scheffler and second-round picks: Where the Stronger Value Emerged
sections.body: Denver’s edge comes from asset depth. Bowen and Elson became NBA players, and Graham was quickly used in another trade that brought Sherman Douglas and an additional second-round pick. Multiple pieces therefore remained useful beyond the initial transaction. Denver accumulated several chances for useful basketball value: Graham became part of a later deal that brought Sherman Douglas and a second, and the Bowen and Elson selections both produced NBA players. None needed to become an All-Star for the return to exceed the cost of giving up Ellis.

sections.heading: Dale Ellis / Greg Graham, Steve Scheffler and second-round picks: What the Other Side Still Received
sections.body: Seattle still got what it wanted: Ellis returned as an experienced perimeter scorer and contributed for two seasons. He was later included in the 1999 trade with Orlando that brought Horace Grant, so his value did not simply expire at the end of his second Seattle stint. Seattle obtained actual scoring rather than merely a name from its past. Ellis spent two more seasons with the Sonics, then figured in the Orlando transaction involving Horace Grant. The Sonics therefore turned their reacquisition into both immediate minutes and later trade utility.

sections.heading: Dale Ellis / Greg Graham, Steve Scheffler and second-round picks: The Asset Chain After the Trade
sections.body: Denver can trace value through the drafted players and Graham’s follow-on trade, while Seattle can trace Ellis into the later Horace Grant package. With meaningful chains on both sides, the appropriate conclusion is a narrow Denver edge rather than a decisive win. Graham’s subsequent exchange and the two named second-round draftees supply Denver with identifiable follow-on assets. Seattle’s Ellis-to-Grant route is also documented, limiting Denver’s advantage: there were tangible chains in both directions, not a winner and a team left without value.

sections.heading: Dale Ellis / Greg Graham, Steve Scheffler and second-round picks: Timeline, Contract and Role Context
sections.body: The Nuggets were rebuilding and benefited from accumulating several chances to create future value. Seattle was a contender that could prefer a proven scorer over distant second-round outcomes. The different windows make both strategies defensible. The October 1997 timing put Denver in a position to collect multiple lower-cost chances while Seattle could reasonably prioritize a veteran perimeter shooter. Ellis’s experience fit a competitive club; Bowen, Elson and the Graham follow-on package better suited a club working through a roster reset.

sections.heading: Dale Ellis / Greg Graham, Steve Scheffler and second-round picks: grading scale
sections.body: Denver B+, Seattle B. Denver gets the slight edge for producing several usable assets from one veteran, including named second-round players and a follow-on trade. Seattle’s direct Ellis production and later trade utility warrant a solid B rather than the old low aggregate. Denver earns B+ for the combination of Graham’s subsequent trade value and two second-round selections that became NBA players. Seattle gets B because Ellis contributed during his second Sonics stint and could be included in the Horace Grant deal. The difference is modest, not a historic mismatch.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Nuggets Edge — Denver B+, Seattle B. Denver turned Dale Ellis into several distinct assets: Greg Graham was used in a follow-on deal, while draft opportunities led to Ryan Bowen and Francisco Elson. Seattle obtained two seasons of Ellis's perimeter scoring and later included him in a trade for Horace Grant, so the SuperSonics did not come away empty. Denver's wider and more durable asset chain earns the narrow advantage over an established veteran whose Seattle value was real but shorter-lived.

sections.heading: Denver Acquired an All-Star Guard on 1998 Draft Night
sections.body: On June 24, 1998, the Nuggets acquired Nick Van Exel from the Lakers for Tony Battie and the rights to newly drafted guard Tyronn Lue. The NBA historical transaction ledger and contemporaneous reporting identify this complete one-for-two exchange. Van Exel had been a 1998 All-Star, providing Los Angeles with 13.8 points and 6.9 assists per game across 64 appearances in 1997-98. Lakers executive Jerry West publicly characterized the move as a fresh start after tensions between the point guard and coach Del Harris. Denver, which had finished the prior season with the NBA’s worst record, wanted immediate backcourt production from a veteran rather than waiting for the development of two prospects.

sections.heading: Van Exel Provided 245 Denver Games through February 2002
sections.body: The point guard started all 50 Nuggets games during the lockout-shortened 1998-99 season, averaging 16.5 points and 7.4 assists. He followed with 79 starts and 16.1 points in 1999-2000, then 71 appearances and 17.7 points in 2000-01. He played another 45 Denver games in 2001-02 before being traded to Dallas, scoring 21.4 points and adding 8.1 assists per game during that Denver portion. These receiving-team segments total 245 regular-season appearances, 243 starts. His 27 Dallas games after the 2002 trade and prior Lakers All-Star season cannot be counted as games produced for Denver by the 1998 transaction.

sections.heading: Tyronn Lue Was a 61-Game Lakers Reserve
sections.body: The Lakers received Tyronn Lue’s draft rights in the exchange and used him sparingly. Lue appeared in 15 Lakers regular-season games in 1998-99, eight in 1999-2000 and 38 in 2000-01, giving him 61 appearances and one start before leaving. His receiving-team points per game in those seasons were 5.0, 6.0 and 3.4. That was real bench depth and championship-era roster membership, but not comparable to the Denver starter’s 245 games. Lue subsequently played much larger roles in Washington and Orlando; those seasons were not played for the Lakers and do not increase the direct 1998 return.

sections.heading: Tony Battie Was Rerouted before the Lockout Season Began
sections.body: The other incoming Laker was Tony Battie, a forward and center from Denver. However, the 1998-99 NBA lockout delayed the season’s first games until February 5, 1999. On January 21, the Lakers traded Battie to Boston for Travis Knight, meaning Battie appeared in zero regular-season Lakers games after the June 1998 exchange. The Battie-to-Knight deal is genuine downstream asset conversion, but Knight was acquired at the additional price of giving up Battie and was not a direct player Denver sent to Los Angeles. Ignoring the unusual lockout timeline could make Battie appear to have spent half a season on the Lakers court when he never played for them.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Chose Flexibility While Rebuilding Its Guard Rotation
sections.body: Van Exel’s exit removed an experienced scorer and playmaker but also cleared a contentious relationship in Los Angeles. The 1997-98 Lakers had won 61 games, yet their postseason ended against Utah. Contemporary reports describe West seeking a different group dynamic alongside Kobe Bryant and Shaquille O’Neal. Battie and Lue were therefore options rather than proven like-for-like replacements. Lue stayed as a reserve through the 2001 championship season; Battie was converted into another reserve before the lockout ended. The subsequent Lakers titles cannot be attributed solely to this trade, just as Denver’s losing seasons do not erase the individual production Van Exel supplied.

sections.heading: The Protected Nuggets Win Is Based on On-Court Return
sections.body: The archived grades are Nuggets Win with Denver A and Los Angeles B-. Van Exel’s 245 receiving-team starts and appearances made Denver the clear beneficiary of direct player contribution. Los Angeles acquired Lue’s rights and moved Battie for Knight, a practical though narrower return. A review that credits Knight’s future games directly to the Nuggets exchange would skip a separate January 1999 trade; one that credits Van Exel’s entire later Dallas career to Denver would be equally wrong. The historical conclusion can favor Denver while acknowledging that Los Angeles deliberately prioritized guard and locker-room changes.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win, Denver A and Lakers B- are preserved. Van Exel produced 245 Denver regular-season appearances with 243 starts across four season segments. Lue provided 61 Lakers games and one start, while Battie was sent to Boston before the 1998-99 lockout season started and played no Lakers regular-season games. The separate Battie-for-Travis Knight move and later team results do not alter the original draft-night asset list.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Van Exel for Battie and Lue in 1998: 245 Denver Games against Lakers Depth
featuredDeepDive.intro: On June 24, 1998, Denver sent Tony Battie and the rights to Tyronn Lue to the Lakers for All-Star point guard Nick Van Exel. The veteran played 245 Nuggets regular-season games, starting 243, before moving to Dallas. Lue saw 61 Lakers games across three seasons, and Battie left for Boston in January 1999 before playing a regular-season game in Los Angeles. The preserved Nuggets Win and Denver A/Lakers B- verdict follows those direct receiving-team outcomes and distinguishes the later Battie-for-Travis Knight exchange from the original 1998 agreement.

sections.heading: The 1998 All-Star and the Draft-Night Rights Package
sections.body: Van Exel had joined the Lakers as a 1993 second-round pick and developed into an All-Star guard by the 1997-98 season, averaging 13.8 points and 6.9 assists on a 61-win Lakers team. Yet his public frustration with coach Del Harris created pressure for change. Denver had struggled throughout 1997-98 and saw a veteran floor leader as a needed immediate upgrade. In exchange, Los Angeles took young forward Tony Battie and the rights to 1998 No. 23 pick Tyronn Lue. Contemporary June 24 coverage and the two teams’ transaction ledgers agree on these assets; no additional first-round pick or unreported cash payment is introduced.

sections.heading: Denver Used the Guard for 50, 79, 71 and 45 Games
sections.body: The posttrade Denver seasons show a reliable high-minute player. Van Exel started all 50 games in 1998-99, when the lockout shortened the league season, averaging 16.5 points and 7.4 assists. In 1999-2000 he started 79 games and added 9.0 assists a night. The next year brought 71 games and 8.5 assists. In 2001-02 he played 45 final Denver games at 21.4 points and 8.1 assists before moving to Dallas. Added together, he registered 245 Nuggets appearances and 243 starts. Neither the remaining 2001-02 Dallas stint nor his later seasons elsewhere belonged to Denver’s realized trade return.

sections.heading: The Lockout Makes Battie’s Lakers Timeline Unusual
sections.body: Los Angeles held the contract of Battie after the June 1998 agreement, but regular-season basketball did not resume until February 5, 1999 because of the league lockout. The Lakers traded Battie to Boston for Travis Knight on January 21, several weeks before their first game. Battie therefore had no NBA regular-season appearances with the Lakers despite being an incoming named asset in the source trade. Knight was a later exchanged player, not a direct Nuggets contribution. The original evaluation should record both that the Lakers used Battie as tradable value and that the on-court payoff for his Lakers tenure was zero.

sections.heading: Lue Was a Lakers Guard, Not Denver’s Retained Pick
sections.body: Tyronn Lue was selected at No. 23 by Denver and his rights were transferred to Los Angeles on draft night. He appeared in 15 Lakers games as a rookie, eight in the 1999-2000 title season and 38 in 2000-01, totaling 61 games and one start. Los Angeles ultimately obtained some reserve depth, and Lue’s subsequent NBA career made him more than an abandoned prospect. But his 71 Washington games in 2001-02 and later Orlando production happened under different teams and contracts. They should not be presented as a retrospective Lakers return while comparing directly with Van Exel’s Denver court time.

sections.heading: The Lakers Could Benefit Organizationally without Winning the Player Ledger
sections.body: Jerry West’s decision was partly about team fit, not just an arithmetic comparison of points. Reports at the time describe strained communication and frustration between Van Exel and the Los Angeles coaching staff. Removing that friction may have had value as the Shaquille O’Neal and Kobe Bryant core evolved, but quantifying championships as a direct result of one draft-night trade is unsupportable. Denver paid with an unproven young big and a draft right for four seasons of a starting playmaker. Los Angeles received useful flexibility, yet realized only 61 direct Lakers games from the transferred Lue and none from Battie. That distinction supports the protected A Denver and B- Los Angeles split.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The stored Nuggets Win, Denver A and Lakers B- verdicts stay intact. Van Exel logged 245 Denver games and 243 starts, while Lue played 61 Lakers games and Battie was rerouted for Travis Knight before the 1998-99 season tipped off. A later organizational benefit for Los Angeles and the separate Knight transaction do not equal Denver’s direct starting-point-guard output. The comparison excludes Dallas Van Exel minutes and Lue appearances after leaving the Lakers.

sections.heading: Denver Sent Mercer and Billups in a February Exchange
sections.body: Denver traded Ron Mercer, Chauncey Billups and Johnny Taylor to Orlando on February 1, 2000. The Nuggets acquired Tariq Abdul-Wahad, Chris Gatling, $3 million cash and a lottery-protected first-round obligation. The record also identifies a later modification of that pick branch to the rights to Omar Cook on June 27, 2001. This was not a straightforward unconditional draft pick swap. Denver was pursuing current frontcourt players and financial consideration, while Orlando assembled a package of talented guards and other roster options. The protected and subsequently altered asset needs to remain visible rather than being treated as a fresh lottery selection Denver received.

sections.heading: Orlando Did Not Realize Billups’ Later Star Career
sections.body: The eventual reputation of Chauncey Billups can distort this transaction. Billups did not play for the Magic because of injury, so Orlando cannot receive direct credit for his later peak as an NBA champion with Detroit. Ron Mercer supplied the clearer immediate Orlando scoring return, while Johnny Taylor formed another piece of the inbound group. That gives Orlando a legitimate realized benefit without inventing years of Billups production in an Orlando uniform. The distinction matters when comparing teams rather than player careers. A trade can transfer rights to a future star while producing little direct value from that particular player for the receiving franchise.

sections.heading: Cash and Modified Draft Compensation Limited Denver’s Downside
sections.body: Denver received Abdul-Wahad and Gatling as usable NBA bodies plus documented cash and a draft obligation eventually described through Omar Cook's rights. Those components show why the deal had a short-term logic, although they did not give the Nuggets a durable answer equal to the talent sent out. A later modification to the pick branch should not be silently converted into a separate extra first-round asset. Orlando's stronger completed outcome came from Mercer's scoring and roster flexibility, not from claiming that the Magic built Billups into the player he later became elsewhere. That narrower comparison supports the retained grades more accurately than a career-total comparison alone.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Magic Win. Orlando receives B+ for Mercer and its incoming roster options, while Denver receives D for Abdul-Wahad, Gatling, the $3 million cash and modified protected-pick branch. Billups' later career is not counted as direct Orlando basketball production, and the draft terms remain attached to their actual later modification.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Deep Dive: What Decided Magic Win on 2000-02-01
featuredDeepDive.intro: The 2000-02-01 transaction between Denver Nuggets and Orlando Magic is best understood by following the assets through their completed outcomes rather than judging the package by size alone. The canonical grades are Denver Nuggets D and Orlando Magic B+, with the record resolving to Magic Win.

sections.heading: The Asset That Most Changes the Evaluation
sections.body: Billups is the most famous name in retrospect, but the available evidence warns against treating his entire later career as Orlando value. He never played for the Magic, which limits how far that fact can drive the grade. Orlando obtained Billups's contract in 2000 but none of his later Detroit championship-era NBA games, so this return must be valued separately from his eventual Pistons career.

sections.heading: The Secondary Value Still Matters
sections.body: Ron Mercer matters because he supplied actual immediate scoring for Orlando. That direct production helps support the Magic win even after discounting the Billups hindsight effect. Mercer was the receiving Magic player with immediate scoring use; the protected first and later Omar Cook rights instead belonged to Denver's outgoing Billups-Mercer side of the ledger.

sections.heading: Immediate Value Versus the Longer Tail
sections.body: The protected first eventually became rights to Omar Cook, so Denver's future asset did not become a counterweight to the outgoing talent. The cash and contract relief also did not erase the gap. The modified first-round consideration eventually traced to Omar Cook rights, while Denver's known immediate package was Abdul-Wahad, Gatling and $3 million cash.

sections.heading: Where the Retrospective Grade Must Stop
sections.body: This is a case where hindsight must be controlled. Denver should be penalized for what it surrendered and what it received, but Orlando should not be credited as though it developed Billups into his eventual peak. The Magic B-plus assessment relies on Mercer and roster flexibility, not imaginary Orlando NBA appearances by Billups, while the Denver D describes the actual player, cash and amended draft asset return.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Magic Win. The strongest completed-value evidence is the combination of the trade details and the two team perspectives: Orlando received the stronger realized side even though Chauncey Billups never played for the Magic because of injury. Ron Mercer supplied immediate scoring, and Orlando reduced exposure to longer-term contracts. Denver did receive players, cash and a protected first-round obligation. Those assets gave the Nuggets a defensible short-term rationale even though the later result was poor. That balance supports the documented Magic Win result without changing either explicit team grade.

sections.heading: Denver Traded a 2001 First for the 2000 No. 26 Pick
sections.body: On June 23, 2000, Denver acquired Utah's No. 26 choice in that summer's draft in exchange for a first-round pick in 2001. The Nuggets used No. 26 on Mamadou N'Diaye; the surrendered 2001 claim eventually became No. 21 Joseph Forte. Both franchises' historical transaction accounts identify the year, draft slot and direction, so the exchange shouldn't be treated as a direct player-for-player trade. At the moment of the deal, Forte had not yet been drafted, and Utah was receiving a future contractual right rather than his NBA services. Denver sought a current first-round selection, accepting the cost of a deferred pick in order to make a choice immediately.

sections.heading: N'Diaye Signed, Then Left Denver Without a Long NBA Tenure
sections.body: The Nuggets' historical media guide records a July 17, 2000 signing of N'Diaye after the draft-night acquisition. That confirms Denver had obtained a usable player contract rather than merely an abstract pick entry. The center did not, however, grow into a long-term Nuggets contributor: the club traded him to Toronto on January 12, 2001 with Keon Clark and Tracy Murray in a separate exchange for Kevin Willis, Aleksandar Radojevic, Garth Joseph and a second-round right. The later Toronto deal has its own ledger and must not be counted as compensation sent by Utah in June 2000. The immediate Denver return was the ability to draft N'Diaye; the later trade is a distinct use of that player asset.

sections.heading: Utah's 2001 First Went to Boston Before the Draft
sections.body: Utah's 2016–17 historical media guide states that the club acquired Denver's 2001 first in the June 23, 2000 exchange and sent the same right to Boston in a later trade. Boston's transaction log places that multi-team deal on August 16, 2000. It involved the Celtics, Jazz, Mavericks and Warriors and transferred Utah's 2001 first to Boston along with a number of separate players and considerations. Boston later used the 21st overall selection on Joseph Forte. Thus Forte is a useful identifier for the pick's eventual position, but he never became the Jazz's draft selection or a Utah return on the floor. Treating him as a Utah roster acquisition would distort the record.

sections.heading: An Even Result Does Not Mean the Pick Paths Were Identical
sections.body: Denver chose immediately at No. 26, signed N'Diaye, and then included him in another transaction less than seven months later. Utah converted the 2001 right into part of an August 2000 multiteam package that also carried Howard Eisley, Adam Keefe and other clubs' contracts. Neither side's original choice became an obvious long-tenure star directly on its roster. The archive records an Even Trade with C for Denver and C for Utah. Those grades remain unchanged in this audit, but the supporting case is the traceable sequence of draft rights and later separate deals, not a vague assertion that both players produced equal statistics. The fair comparison is control of the assets each club obtained, followed by an honest account of their subsequent use.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Recorded verdict: Even Trade — Denver C, Utah C. Denver obtained the 2000 No. 26 pick, drafted and signed Mamadou N'Diaye, then traded him separately in January 2001. Utah acquired a 2001 first that became No. 21 and passed it to Boston in August 2000; the Celtics, not the Jazz, selected Joseph Forte. Both teams received real draft assets, but neither immediately retained the eventual named player as a long-term core contributor. The existing grades stay unchanged.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The 2000 Denver–Utah First-Round Pick Exchange and Its Later Routes
featuredDeepDive.intro: Denver's June 23, 2000 deal with Utah swapped the timing of first-round draft rights: a current No. 26 pick moved to the Nuggets, and a future 2001 first went to the Jazz. That later choice became No. 21, but it was Boston that selected Joseph Forte. Denver drafted Mamadou N'Diaye and subsequently moved him to Toronto. The historical record therefore requires separating the original two-right agreement from two later multiteam trades. The archive's Even Trade and C/C marks are preserved rather than revised by inference.

sections.heading: Official Club Transaction Logs Establish the Original Two Assets
sections.body: The Denver Nuggets' historical media guide lists a June 23 acquisition of the 26th choice in the 2000 draft from Utah in exchange for a 2001 first-rounder. The Utah Jazz's own media guide independently reports the same deal from the other direction, identifying the later No. 21 Joseph Forte outcome of the transferred 2001 right. On June 23, though, Forte was not a named NBA draft asset: the right concerned the 2001 choice that would be exercised later. Denver's first-round pick was immediately available and became Mamadou N'Diaye at No. 26. The original ledger therefore contains one first-round selection in each direction, from different draft years, with no cash, veterans or secondary pick quietly appended.

sections.heading: Denver's Immediate Draft Choice and January 2001 Exit
sections.body: Denver could draft N'Diaye in June and formally signed him in July, according to the franchise's season transaction history. That is tangible use of an asset the Nuggets would not otherwise have possessed in the same form. Yet the decision did not establish a lengthy Denver playing career. On January 12, 2001, Denver sent N'Diaye, Keon Clark and Tracy Murray to the Toronto Raptors in a larger agreement, receiving Kevin Willis, Aleksandar Radojevic, Garth Joseph and a second-round right. Those Toronto pieces were compensation for a separate January trade, not a hidden return from Utah. Any later Toronto appearances by N'Diaye are similarly outside his realized Nuggets playing contribution. This sequencing distinguishes a drafted player who was subsequently traded from someone who delivered seasons of NBA production for the drafting club.

sections.heading: How the Utah Pick Became a Boston Selection
sections.body: Utah didn't wait for the 2001 draft to use the future right. The Jazz's official all-time transactions identify its transfer of that first-round claim to Boston during August 2000. Boston's historical transaction ledger identifies a four-club deal with Utah, Dallas and Golden State on August 16, with several moving player contracts and Utah's 2001 first going to the Celtics. Boston eventually chose North Carolina guard Joseph Forte with the 21st overall selection. An NBA player profile corroborates that Forte was drafted in 2001 at No. 21, but the profile doesn't turn him into a Utah acquisition. The Jazz's realized benefit must be studied through the separate August exchange rather than crediting the club with Forte's later games in Boston and Seattle.

sections.heading: Assessing the Original C/C Without Importing Later Trades
sections.body: The stored result is Even Trade and C for both teams. That is an assessment of a June 2000 draft-right swap, not a claim that N'Diaye and Forte compiled identical statistics. Denver chose an immediate prospect who was soon included in the Toronto deal. Utah took a future first and redeployed it inside a Boston-led four-team agreement before it came due. Both choices had value as trade currency even if the eventual named draftees weren't retained on their originating teams. A grade revision would require valuing Denver's rights in January 2001 and Utah's separate August 2000 package using consistent criteria across the archive, rather than assigning all of those downstream assets to the June 23 trade. Until that independent comparison is sourced, the original Even/C/C evaluation stays intact.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The June 23, 2000 exchange was Denver's 2001 first for Utah's current No. 26 choice. Denver drafted N'Diaye and moved him again in January 2001. Utah transferred the future first in August 2000; Boston selected Forte at No. 21 the following summer. Their player outcomes were not direct one-for-one returns for Utah and Denver. The archive retains Even Trade, Denver C and Utah C, with downstream multiteam packages accounted for separately.

sections.heading: Denver Sent Gatling and the Eddie House Pick to Miami
sections.body: On June 27, 2000, Denver sent Chris Gatling and a 2000 second-round draft choice to Miami for Voshon Lenard and Mark Strickland. The Heat selected guard Eddie House from Arizona State at No. 37 with that choice the next day. Miami's own official team media guide confirms the players, the pick and both dates. Denver obtained two veterans who could contribute immediately, and Miami exchanged two forwards or guards from its rotation for a veteran frontcourt piece and an incoming draft opportunity. Although the exchange contains two listed assets on each side, the draft selection was not already a contracted NBA player. The trade must also be kept separate from Denver's February 2000 acquisition of Gatling from Orlando, which was a different transaction.

sections.heading: Lenard Delivered Immediate Denver Production and Later Left
sections.body: Lenard provided the clearest direct Nuggets return. He appeared in 80 Denver games with 58 starts in 2000-01, scoring 12.2 points per night and hitting 38.5% of his three-point attempts. He added 71 appearances in 2001-02 with 19 starts and an 11.5-point average. That is 151 games across the two seasons immediately following the exchange. These documented minutes help explain why the inherited Denver A outpaces the Miami B+ in the source record, but they do not prove that every later stop with the Nuggets came from this June 2000 trade. Strickland supplied additional depth in the deal, although his relative impact should not be inflated above the directly measurable Lenard contribution.

sections.heading: Miami's No. 37 Pick Became a Genuine NBA Contributor
sections.body: The Heat used the choice on Eddie House, whose first three NBA seasons were actually played in Miami: 50 appearances in 2000-01, 64 in 2001-02 and 55 in 2002-03. He averaged 5.0, 8.0 and 7.5 points over those seasons, a real developmental and rotation return rather than an unused pick. His later role on Boston's 2008 championship team cannot be counted as direct Heat value. Miami also took Gatling, but a separate August 2000 transaction later moved him in a larger package. Any major acquisition attached to that later, multi-piece deal cannot be awarded entirely to this one June swap. Miami earned an actual player from its second-round draft opportunity, which helps explain its solid B+ rather than treating it as a failed deal.

sections.heading: The Narrow Grade Gap Is More Informative Than a Dominant Winner
sections.body: The current canonical verdict is Nuggets Win, Denver A and Miami B+. Lenard's 151 Denver games in two seasons and immediate starting role provide direct support for a Denver edge. House's 169 Miami games over his first three years are an equally concrete counterweight and explain why Miami does not receive a low letter grade. The top-level partnerAggregate remains A- and imported perspectives disagree about the two franchise grade values, which requires a separate historical reconciliation before any broader grade correction. For this original account the defensible conclusion is that Denver received experienced perimeter production while Miami turned a draft pick into a useful reserve. Neither club's unrelated later franchise results are assigned to this trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win — the current canonical grades are Denver A and Miami B+. Lenard supplied 80 Denver games and 58 starts in 2000-01, then another 71 appearances the next year. Miami acquired Gatling and used No. 37 on Eddie House, whose first three Heat seasons totaled 169 games, preserving a meaningful counter-return. The June 27 exchange is confirmed in Miami's official media guide. Imported perspective-grade differences are a separate provenance hold; the original date, assets, eligibility and published source ledger were not reclassified.

sections.heading: The September 2000 Exchange Was a Shooter for Rebounding and a Pick
sections.body: Denver traded Popeye Jones and a future second-round draft choice to Washington for veteran forward Tracy Murray on September 25, 2000. The Nuggets' official media guide records the deal, while a Washington Post report published the following day explains the Wizards wanted Jones's rebounding and physical presence. Murray had been a productive perimeter scorer for Washington, averaging 10.2 points in 80 games during 1999-2000, with his strongest years earlier in the decade. The deal offered Denver a shooter and Washington a frontcourt reserve plus draft flexibility. The pick's eventual association with Rod Grizzard belongs to the 2002 draft and was not known on trade day. Neither club acquired a guaranteed All-Star, and the two-year wait on the selection complicates any comparison based solely on the number of assets received.

sections.heading: Murray's Denver Stay Lasted Only Thirteen Games
sections.body: The immediate Denver return was smaller than Murray's Washington career might suggest. He played 13 regular-season games for the Nuggets in 2000-01, averaging 3.8 points in 10.4 minutes, before moving again in January. On January 12, 2001, Denver included Murray, Keon Clark and Mamadou N'Diaye in a separate deal with Toronto. That later transaction brought Kevin Willis, two other players and a second-round selection back to the Nuggets. It is useful to know Murray remained tradable, but those Toronto assets were negotiated for multiple outgoing players, not for Murray alone. The original September exchange supplied limited Denver on-court production and a contract that could be combined with other roster pieces. This modest result supports assessing the incoming veteran by his actual Nuggets games rather than his earlier career scoring peak.

sections.heading: Jones Became a Forty-Start Wizards Contributor
sections.body: Washington received more direct playing time from Popeye Jones than Denver received from Murray. Jones appeared in 45 Wizards games in 2000-01, averaging 3.6 points and 4.9 rebounds. In 2001-02 he played 79 games, started 40 and averaged 7.0 points with 7.3 rebounds. That gives him 124 Washington games across the two seasons, including a genuinely useful second-year rotation role. The Washington Post's original reporting described a need for hustle and physical rebounding after several frontcourt departures. Jones was not an offensive centerpiece, and prior back injuries made his acquisition risky. Nevertheless, the realized 2001-02 rebounding contribution was far more durable than Murray's 13-game Denver stint. This is the strongest direct basketball basis for the inherited slight Washington advantage.

sections.heading: The Second-Round Right Became Rod Grizzard's Selection
sections.body: The additional draft asset moved from Denver to Washington in 2000 and was later exercised in the 2002 draft on Alabama wing Rod Grizzard. The preserved transaction ledger calls it No. 38; historical draft lists that include the forfeited Minnesota first-round slot number Grizzard No. 39. Both descriptions concern the same Washington-controlled second-round choice, so they should not be treated as two different picks. The Wizards waived Grizzard before the regular season, and he never played an NBA regular-season game for the team. The pick therefore produced a real draft opportunity without a direct Wizards playing return. It was nonetheless extra consideration received alongside Jones for the same outgoing Murray contract. Washington's grade rests more strongly on the established forward's 124 games than on Grizzard's prospective NBA career.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Wizards Edge — Washington B+, Denver B. Popeye Jones gave Washington 124 games across two seasons, including a 79-game year with 7.3 rebounds per game. Tracy Murray played 13 Denver games before a separate Toronto trade. Washington also received the 2002 second used on Rod Grizzard, who did not play a Wizards regular-season game.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Popeye Jones, Tracy Murray and the 2002 Rod Grizzard Second-Round Pick
featuredDeepDive.intro: In September 2000 Denver exchanged Popeye Jones and a future second for Tracy Murray. The Wizards got 124 Jones games and a draft pick later spent on Grizzard; Murray played only 13 games in Denver.

sections.heading: Denver's Rationale Was Perimeter Scoring
sections.body: When the Nuggets acquired Murray, they were hoping a known shooter could help a roster in transition. Murray had averaged 15.1 points for Washington in 1997-98 and 10.2 in 1999-2000, with a productive history from beyond the arc. Denver was not acquiring a raw draft prospect; it was trading away a veteran big and a future second for a player whose shooting résumé was established. The problem became his availability and usage with the new team. He appeared in just 13 Denver games before the January 2001 Toronto transaction. The historical assessment should not compare Murray's best Wizards season with Jones's subsequent Washington minutes as though those performances occurred simultaneously after the swap. The trade acquired potential fit, while the completed Nuggets return was a short stretch of bench playing time and later transferable salary.

sections.heading: Washington Had a Concrete Need for Popeye Jones
sections.body: The September 26 Washington Post account identified rebounding and physical play as reasons the Wizards sought Jones. Several frontcourt departures had left the team needing help around the basket, and the former Dallas rebounder could provide it if healthy. His injury history had limited his previous years, including only 40 Denver appearances in 1999-2000. In Washington he played 45 games in the first season after the move, then delivered 79 games and 40 starts in 2001-02. He averaged 7.3 rebounds in that second campaign, giving the team a meaningful role player despite its overall struggles. The direct comparison does not require pretending Jones was a star or that the Wizards became contenders. It demonstrates that the practical reason behind the transaction produced more playing time than the shooter Denver acquired.

sections.heading: The 2002 Draft Pick Did Not Become a Wizards NBA Player
sections.body: The second-round selection was important because Washington received it in addition to Jones. Transaction records associate the choice with Rod Grizzard in 2002; the NBA's official draft conventions and some compiled draft tables show him 39th overall, while older trade tracking tables use 38th because of the forfeited first-round slot. Washington did choose Grizzard, but it waived him before the 2002-03 regular season. As a result, the draft right did not create a Wizards regular-season contributor. It would overstate the trade to add Grizzard's later professional experiences as Washington NBA minutes. The pick still gave management an opportunity to select a player while it was rebuilding. The realized advantage, however, rested on Jones's two seasons rather than a successful draft conversion.

sections.heading: A Narrow Wizards Edge, Not a Franchise-Defining Deal
sections.body: The canonical verdict grades Washington B-plus and Denver B, with a Slight Wizards Edge. The team-specific results explain the direction, even though the letters are generous for a relatively minor exchange. Murray supplied 13 Denver games before becoming part of a separate multiplayer trade. Jones appeared in 124 Washington games, including 79 and 40 starts in his second year. The Wizards also secured a second-round selection later used on Grizzard, who supplied no regular-season minutes. This is a modest advantage built primarily on frontcourt availability and rebounding, not a claim that Washington found a future All-Star in the draft. Denver had a defensible shooting rationale and was able to trade Murray again, but the actual basketball contribution from the original acquisition was brief. A source-specific account supports the preserved verdict without inflating either outcome.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Washington B-plus, Denver B in the preserved slight Wizards advantage. Jones supplied 124 Wizards appearances and useful 2001-02 rebounding. Murray gave the Nuggets a short 13-game stint and later trade flexibility. Grizzard provided a draft selection but no Washington NBA games; the traded pick has differing 38/39 numbering conventions.

sections.heading: Denver Acquired a Protected First and Veteran Don Reid
sections.body: On August 1, 2002, Denver sent Orlando a 2004 second-round pick and received forward-center Don Reid plus a protected first-round selection. The first was protected through several drafts and ultimately became the No. 22 selection in 2006, used on Marcus Williams. Orlando’s second became No. 49 in 2004, used on Sergei Lishchuk. The package consisted of a modest veteran and potentially valuable higher-round draft control, rather than a simple exchange of two comparable prospects.

sections.heading: Why Denver Preferred a Protected First
sections.body: The Nuggets were early in a rebuilding period and had room to take a chance on conditional first-round value. A protected pick could convey later if Orlando kept its higher selections, which is why the actual arrival year changed. Reid provided a veteran frontcourt option, but his brief contribution was not the basis for treating the trade as a strong Nuggets outcome. Moving a second-round choice for a first-round interest was the important value proposition, with both protection risk and eventual draft position relevant.

sections.heading: Orlando Moved the Incoming Second Before It Was Used
sections.body: Orlando did not build a long-term roster around the No. 49 player. Basketball-Reference records that the Magic sent the 2004 second-round pick onward with Mike Miller, Ryan Humphrey and a first-round selection in a February 2003 deal with Memphis for Drew Gooden and Gordan Giriček. The second later became the rights to Lishchuk. That makes its 2004 result an identifiable downstream pick outcome, not proof that Lishchuk contributed NBA minutes to Orlando. The Magic used the asset within a separate larger trade.

sections.heading: A Better Asset Tier, Not an Instant Star
sections.body: Denver’s B-minus reflects gaining a protected first-round opportunity for the price of a second and taking Reid’s contract and limited frontcourt help. Orlando’s D reflects giving up the higher-round asset while gaining only a second-round opportunity in return, although it subsequently used that selection as part of a useful separate deal. The 2006 No. 22 name must be understood as the eventual selection attached to the pick lineage; later moves of draft rights are distinct transactions.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win — Denver B-minus, Orlando D. Denver traded a 2004 second for Reid and the first-round choice that ultimately conveyed at No. 22 in 2006. Orlando moved its incoming second onward before it was selected at No. 49. The recorded asset tiers support Denver’s advantage, but the transaction did not immediately produce a star for either club.

sections.heading: Denver Acquired a Former Lottery Forward for Three Assets
sections.body: On October 1, 2002, Denver traded Don Reid, Mengke Bateer and a protected 2004 first-round selection to Detroit for Rodney White. The Nuggets were taking a chance on the ninth overall choice from the 2001 draft, who had played only 16 games during his Pistons rookie season. Detroit preferred a reserve frontcourt package and future draft leverage. The acquired first ultimately conveyed at No. 17 in 2004, but the Pistons did not use the pick themselves. The Hawks selected Josh Smith after receiving that right in a different deal. Evaluating the original swap therefore requires separating White's Denver appearances, the short Pistons service of Reid and Bateer, and the first-round asset's later use in the Rasheed Wallace transaction.

sections.heading: Rodney White Played 186 Denver Regular-Season Games
sections.body: White was not a failed acquisition who never appeared for the Nuggets. He played 72 games and started 19 in 2002-03, averaging 9.0 points and 3.0 rebounds. His second Denver season comprised another 72 games, all as a reserve, at 7.5 points and 2.3 rebounds. He appeared in 42 more Nuggets games in 2004-05 before finishing that season with Golden State, bringing his Denver total to 186 regular-season appearances. The acquisition yielded several seasons of wing scoring, although not the star production once expected from a top-ten draft choice. His 16 earlier games with Detroit and 16 subsequent appearances for the Warriors do not belong in Denver's direct return. The franchise could justify exploring his upside without claiming the 2004 first cost nothing.

sections.heading: Reid Played Once and Bateer Was Moved Two Days Later
sections.body: Detroit's initial player return did not sustain its frontcourt. Don Reid, who had previously played for the Pistons earlier in his career, appeared in just one 2002-03 Detroit game after the exchange, scoring one point in ten minutes. The team traded Mengke Bateer to San Antonio on October 3, only two days after acquiring him, for a 2003 second-round selection. The Spurs deal was a separate transaction, and the resulting choice became No. 58 Andreas Glyniadakis in 2003. Those moves explain why the first-round asset, rather than sustained Reid or Bateer playing time, carried the larger Detroit value. Neither Bateer's Spurs minutes nor Glyniadakis's later non-Detroit career can be described as on-court contributions delivered directly by this original October 1 agreement.

sections.heading: Detroit Used Denver's 2004 First in the Rasheed Wallace Transaction
sections.body: Denver's protected first-round selection in the October 2002 Rodney White trade eventually conveyed as No. 17 in the 2004 NBA draft, but Detroit did not use the pick on Josh Smith. The Pistons sent the right to Atlanta in the February 2004 three-team transaction that brought Rasheed Wallace to Detroit. The Hawks exercised the selection on Smith; his long Atlanta career is therefore not Pistons court production. Detroit's value came through an actual transaction chain: part of the package acquired for White helped purchase a veteran who became a frontcourt contributor on the 2004 championship team. That result should not be presented as if the Denver first alone acquired Wallace, who moved with several other players and picks. Denver received 186 White regular-season games, and Detroit's other direct returns were brief—Don Reid played once, while Mengke Bateer was rerouted after two days.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Detroit B+, Denver C on the inherited ledger. Denver obtained 186 Rodney White games, while Reid returned for just one Detroit game and Bateer was traded onward to San Antonio for a 2003 second. The 2004 first conveyed at No.17; Detroit had previously transferred the right to Atlanta in the separate Rasheed Wallace three-team transaction. The Hawks selected Josh Smith; his later games were never Pistons return.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Rodney White for a 2004 First: Denver Minutes and Detroit Rasheed Pick Chain
featuredDeepDive.intro: Denver acquired a former No. 9 draft forward. The future first it sent Detroit eventually helped the Pistons acquire Rasheed Wallace; Atlanta used the pick on Josh Smith after another trade.

sections.heading: White's Original Draft Position Made Denver's Gamble Plausible
sections.body: Detroit had chosen White ninth overall in 2001, but he played only 16 Pistons games during his rookie year. Denver saw a recent lottery pick whose offensive skills might become more valuable with extended playing time. The Nuggets committed a reserve forward, another center and a future first to acquire his contract. In the following season White appeared in 72 games, scored 650 points and made 19 starts. He had a further 72-game campaign and 42 games in a third partial season before Denver moved on. Those numbers demonstrate that the move produced genuine NBA utility, rather than an entirely theoretical prospect. Yet they also fall well short of the returns Denver could have hoped to receive when surrendering a draft right that became a mid-first-round selection two years later.

sections.heading: Detroit's Immediate Frontcourt Return Lasted Only Days
sections.body: Detroit received Reid and Bateer with the 2004 first. Reid had already played for the Pistons before joining other franchises, and his post-trade return consisted of one game in 2002-03. Bateer was gone by October 3, exchanged with San Antonio for a 2003 second later used on Andreas Glyniadakis. That rapid follow-up is important: the Pistons did not acquire Bateer to occupy years of starting-center minutes, and Reid was no substitute for the departed White's regular-season offense. Detroit's 2002-03 roster was instead strengthening around Chauncey Billups, Richard Hamilton and Ben Wallace. The first-round draft right supplied a longer-term option, while the new second gave the franchise another prospect opportunity. Both later uses need attribution to their separate transactions rather than automatic credit for this one.

sections.heading: The Draft Right Moved to Atlanta Before Josh Smith Was Picked
sections.body: The original Denver first was lottery protected and eventually conveyed in 2004 at No. 17. Detroit did not draft Josh Smith with that pick. In February 2004 the Pistons used the future selection in a three-team transaction with Atlanta and Boston to acquire Rasheed Wallace. Atlanta then exercised the choice on Smith during the June draft. Smith became a productive Hawks forward, but his games and achievements are Atlanta outcomes, not Pistons return from the Rodney White deal. The pick's value to Detroit was its negotiating role in obtaining Wallace. Other players and financial considerations also participated in that later arrangement, so crediting the entire championship center rotation to one Denver pick would be an overstatement. A proper rights ledger distinguishes the recipient of a draft right from the eventual drafting franchise.

sections.heading: A Pistons B-Plus and Nuggets C Need a Qualified Verdict
sections.body: The inherited site verdict is Pistons Win, Detroit B-plus and Denver C. White's 186 Nuggets games show he supplied playable scoring and was not a total bust, whereas the two immediate Detroit players barely contributed after October 1. The decisive difference is the first-round right: it conveyed as No. 17 and helped Detroit acquire Rasheed Wallace in a separate multi-team trade that preceded the 2004 title. Atlanta selected Josh Smith from the resulting draft position. Detroit therefore realized value from the pick as a trade component, not from Smith's later NBA performance. Denver got three partial seasons from a former lottery forward, but had surrendered more draft leverage than that production ultimately justified. The grades can retain their historical direction while making the attribution and limits explicit.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Detroit B-plus, Denver C, Pistons Win retained. Denver obtained 186 White appearances over three partial seasons; Detroit received a lottery-protected first and two short-term players. Detroit moved the first to Atlanta in the Rasheed Wallace package. Atlanta, not Detroit, selected Josh Smith at No.17. Detroit also traded Bateer to San Antonio for a separate 2003 second.

sections.heading: Orlando Used a Future Pick to Solve a Present Point-Guard Need
sections.body: The Magic entered the 2004 draft with the first overall pick and a chance to reset the franchise around Dwight Howard, but they also needed a guard who could organize the new era. Jameer Nelson had just completed a decorated college career at Saint Joseph’s and slipped to the twentieth selection. Denver drafted him, then sent his rights to Orlando for a protected future first. The Magic accepted the delayed cost because Nelson’s style fit the roster they were building: he could shoot, run pick-and-rolls, compete defensively and grow on the same timeline as Howard. The trade did not require Orlando to surrender a current rotation player, so the club could add a ready prospect without weakening the young core. Future picks are valuable, but they are most useful when converted into players who match a clear organizational plan. Orlando identified that match and acted before another team could turn Nelson’s slide into its own advantage.

sections.heading: Denver Converted the No. 20 Pick Into a Later First With Protection
sections.body: Denver’s side was not irrational. The Nuggets already had Andre Miller at point guard and were building around Carmelo Anthony, so Nelson did not fill the most urgent immediate need. By moving his rights, Denver obtained a future first whose protections created a chance at a comparable or better selection. The asset conveyed in 2005 at No. 20, the same numerical slot used on Nelson, and Denver selected Julius Hodge. In process terms, the Nuggets rolled a pick forward one year while preserving first-round value. The failure came in player evaluation and development rather than a complete absence of logic. Hodge never became a stable NBA contributor, while Nelson grew into a long-term starter. Because the picks landed in the same range, the outcome offers an unusually clean comparison: Orlando selected the right guard for its timeline, and Denver exchanged that player for another prospect who delivered almost no equivalent return.

sections.heading: Nelson Became a Ten-Year Piece of the Magic’s Identity
sections.body: Nelson spent a decade in Orlando, far exceeding the ordinary return from the twentieth pick. He developed from a reserve into a reliable starter, earned an All-Star selection in 2009 and became one of the primary organizers of a team built around Howard’s interior dominance and a spread floor. His shooting forced defenders to respect the point of attack, while his pick-and-roll chemistry helped Orlando create efficient possessions without relying on isolation basketball. Nelson’s tenure included multiple playoff runs and the 2009 trip to the NBA Finals. A shoulder injury interrupted his All-Star season and complicated the postseason rotation, but it did not erase the larger value of the acquisition. The Magic received years of cost-controlled development followed by veteran continuity at the league’s most important decision-making position. That durability is why Orlando’s side earns an A-plus rather than merely credit for one strong season.

sections.heading: Julius Hodge Could Not Preserve Denver’s Asset Value
sections.body: Hodge was a respected college player with size and versatility, but his NBA career never took hold. He appeared in only a small number of games for Denver, struggled to establish a role and was later moved. A serious off-court shooting incident also disrupted his development, adding circumstances beyond ordinary basketball evaluation. Even with that context, the Nuggets’ return from the trade remained minimal. The future first had done exactly what Denver reasonably hoped in one respect: it conveyed as a first-round pick at the same slot. The organization simply failed to transform it into a player comparable to Nelson. That distinction matters because the trade was not lost through unfavorable lottery luck or oppressive protections. Denver had a fresh opportunity one year later and chose a prospect who did not become a rotation fixture. Orlando’s scouting decision and Denver’s miss widened a transaction that initially looked close in abstract pick value.

sections.heading: The 2009 Finals Run Demonstrated the Strategic Fit
sections.body: Nelson’s value was not limited to counting statistics. Orlando’s best teams required a point guard who could punish defenses for crowding Howard, keep the ball moving to shooters and attack gaps when opponents overplayed the perimeter. Nelson provided that blend. During the 2008-09 season he played at an All-Star level before injury, and his return during the Finals became a major storyline because the team had reached the championship round without him. Although the comeback did not produce the desired result, his importance to the system was already established. Orlando had acquired a player whose skills aligned with the roster’s central strategy and remained useful as the team added Hedo Türkoğlu, Rashard Lewis and other veterans. Denver’s later pick never affected a comparable competitive stage. The difference between a useful prospect and a strategically essential starter is the heart of the grade gap.

sections.heading: The Same Draft Slot Removes Most Excuses From the Comparison
sections.body: Trades involving future picks often require complicated adjustments for protections, lottery movement and changing draft strength. This one is unusually direct. Denver used No. 20 on Nelson in 2004 and received a pick that became No. 20 in 2005. The Nuggets were not punished by a disastrous slide in draft position. Orlando simply ended up with the far better NBA player. Denver receives a C because the club retained a first-round asset, addressed its roster logic and had a legitimate chance to recover value the next year. It does not deserve a failing process grade. Orlando earns A-plus because Nelson became an All-Star, a decade-long contributor and a central player on a Finals team for the cost of one later first. The Magic’s victory reflects decisive scouting and fit rather than an accidental lottery windfall.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Magic Win. Orlando traded a future first for Jameer Nelson and received ten seasons, an All-Star selection and a starting point guard for a Finals core. Denver’s replacement asset conveyed at the same No. 20 slot but became Julius Hodge, whose NBA impact was brief. Orlando earns A-plus; Denver receives C for defensible asset logic that failed in execution.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Why the Jameer Nelson Deal Was a Triumph of Fit Over Abstract Pick Value
featuredDeepDive.intro: On the trade details, Denver traded one twentieth pick for another twentieth pick a year later. The enormous difference came after the exchange. Orlando selected a player whose strengths matched a new franchise center, while Denver’s replacement selection never entered the regular rotation. The deal shows that identical draft slots can carry radically different organizational value.

sections.heading: Nelson’s College Résumé Reduced the Usual Late-First Uncertainty
sections.body: Nelson arrived with more evidence than most players drafted in the twenties. He had led Saint Joseph’s through an elite season, won major national player-of-the-year honors and demonstrated command of an offense over several college campaigns. His size created questions, which helped push him down the board, but his shooting, leadership and decision-making were comparatively mature. Orlando was not merely buying an unknown athletic profile. It was acquiring a guard with a long record of controlling games and a skill set that could translate beside Howard. That maturity mattered to a franchise undergoing a major reset. The Magic needed young players, but they also needed someone capable of giving structure to the transition. Nelson could develop without requiring the team to tolerate total point-guard chaos. The trade therefore reduced both talent risk and functional roster risk.

sections.heading: Howard and Nelson Created a Shared Development Timeline
sections.body: The most valuable young cores often emerge when key players learn together. Howard and Nelson entered Orlando in the same draft and spent years developing the timing of their pick-and-roll actions, defensive communication and late-game responsibilities. Nelson did not need to be the franchise’s best player; he needed to make the franchise player easier to deploy. His pull-up shooting and willingness to attack created space around Howard’s dives, while his competitiveness helped establish continuity in the backcourt. Because both players were on rookie-scale contracts, Orlando could add veteran shooting and size around them. A future first might eventually have produced another young contributor, but it would have arrived a year later without the same immediate bond to Howard’s development. The Magic chose synchronization over waiting, and that synchronization became part of the 2009 Finals foundation.

sections.heading: Denver’s Roster Logic Was Better Than Its Prospect Result
sections.body: The Nuggets already employed Andre Miller, a durable floor general who fit a young Carmelo Anthony. Keeping Nelson could have created redundancy and limited minutes for a small rookie guard. Rolling the asset into a future first therefore had strategic merit. The mistake was not recognizing that every future first is only an opportunity, not guaranteed value. When the pick conveyed, Denver selected Hodge, whose strengths did not translate into a lasting role. The Nuggets could not turn the asset into another trade or a useful second contract. This is why Denver’s grade is C rather than D or F: the front office maintained draft capital and avoided forcing a poor positional fit, but the eventual conversion failed. Process credit cannot fully offset a decade of Nelson production on the other side.

sections.heading: Nelson’s Injury Does Not Undermine the Trade’s Competitive Impact
sections.body: Nelson’s shoulder injury during his 2009 All-Star season is sometimes treated as evidence that Orlando’s success belonged entirely to other players. The opposite interpretation is more accurate. His absence was so important that his unexpected Finals return created a difficult rotation decision after Rafer Alston had helped the team advance. That controversy reflected Nelson’s established status. He had been central to the regular-season offense and remained part of the organization’s long-term plan after the Finals loss. Injuries affect every retrospective evaluation, but one interrupted postseason does not outweigh ten years of contribution. The Magic reached elite status with a player acquired for a future pick, and Nelson continued to provide leadership and production after the championship window narrowed.

sections.heading: A Late Pick Can Be Worth A-plus When It Produces Continuity
sections.body: A-plus grades are sometimes reserved for transactions that deliver an MVP or multiple championships. Nelson’s deal demonstrates another route. Orlando paid a limited, clearly defined cost and received far more years and competitive importance than the average twentieth pick supplies. He became an All-Star, helped organize a Finals offense, remained through several roster versions and gave the franchise a recognizable leader. Denver’s pick produced almost none of those benefits. The surplus value was enormous relative to cost even though Nelson was never a top-five NBA player. Trade grades should measure what a team purchased for what it surrendered, not only whether the incoming player became a universal superstar. By that standard, Orlando’s conversion of one future first into a decade-long point guard is an A-plus outcome.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Orlando won because it knew what kind of guard its new core required and acted when Nelson was available. Denver preserved the shape of a first-round asset but not its substance. The identical No. 20 slots make the result especially revealing: one team found a decade of stability, while the other received only a brief prospect evaluation.

sections.heading: Denver Added Nájera and a Protected Future First
sections.body: On February 24, 2005, Denver acquired Eduardo Nájera, Luis Flores and a top-seven-protected 2007 first-round pick from Golden State. The Warriors received Nikoloz Tskitishvili and Rodney White. The package differed in two respects: Denver gained an experienced frontcourt role player and a later first-round chance, while Golden State received two young forwards it could evaluate. The protection on the pick belongs in the record because the selection was not an unconditional high-lottery asset.

sections.heading: Nájera Supplied the Useful Immediate Return
sections.body: Nájera was a defensively minded forward whose rebounding, physicality and willingness to fill lower-usage roles suited a Denver rotation built around more prominent scorers. That is where the Nuggets received their clearest on-court return. Flores was an additional guard prospect but did not contribute comparable sustained production. The trade did not depend on Flores becoming a star; Denver had obtained a functional veteran plus future draft value for players it was prepared to move.

sections.heading: The 2007 Selection Became No. 30
sections.body: The protected first eventually conveyed as the final selection of the 2007 first round, when No. 30 was used on Petteri Koponen. That particular outcome should be stated as a late first-round draft asset, not as a top-seven selection. The precise subsequent handling of Koponen’s NBA rights requires separate documentation and should not be credited to Denver beyond the traced pick without independent support. The first-round component still made the incoming package broader than Nájera alone.

sections.heading: Golden State’s Incoming Forwards Did Not Match the Package
sections.body: Golden State received Tskitishvili and White, both young forwards with paths to playing time but uncertain development. Neither yielded a sustained Warriors impact comparable to Nájera’s role in Denver. The ledger therefore assigns Nuggets A-plus, Warriors B-minus and Nuggets Win. That difference reflects the veteran’s documented usefulness plus draft flexibility against two speculative roster returns; it does not imply the protected No. 30 pick developed into a future NBA superstar.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win — Denver A-plus, Golden State B-minus. The Nuggets acquired Nájera, Flores and a protected first that ultimately became No. 30 in 2007, while the Warriors received Tskitishvili and White. Nájera furnished the strongest practical frontcourt contribution. The draft selection provided additional value, but its later rights pathway should not be overstated without supporting transactions.

sections.heading: The January 2007 Exchange: Blake for Boykins, Hodge and Cash
sections.body: Denver and Milwaukee finalized a four-component transaction on January 11, 2007. The Nuggets received point guard Steve Blake, while the Bucks obtained Earl Boykins, Julius Hodge and cash considerations. Denver's official media guide lists precisely those pieces, as does Milwaukee's historical transaction ledger. A contemporary report identified the cash as $700,000, matching the existing canonical amount, even though the team guide only states 'cash considerations.' There was no draft pick, conditional selection or additional franchise involved. The exchange happened after Denver had acquired Allen Iverson and traded away Andre Miller, creating a specific need for a conventional distributor while Milwaukee dealt with injuries across its guard rotation.

sections.heading: Steve Blake Became a Forty-Start Distributor in Denver
sections.body: Blake arrived with a different point-guard profile from the smaller, scoring-oriented Boykins. In 49 regular-season Denver appearances during 2006-07, Blake started 40 games and averaged 8.3 points, 6.6 assists and 33.5 minutes. His passing and ability to organize possessions gave the Nuggets a dependable complement for an offense with Iverson and Carmelo Anthony. Those totals are directly attributable to the acquired player and cannot be ignored because Milwaukee's return had more components. Denver reached the 2007 playoffs, but the team's postseason performance was not created by this transaction alone. Blake's contribution was a substantial half-season of starting playmaking, not a long-term star acquisition.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Received a Scoring Guard Amid Injuries
sections.body: The Bucks had been playing without several starters when they made the deal, and their general manager stressed the need to compete through an injury-heavy stretch. Boykins brought immediate shot creation after averaging 15.2 points in 31 pretrade Denver games that season. Once in Milwaukee, he played 35 games, started 19 and averaged 14.0 points with 4.5 assists and 41.9-percent shooting on threes. That is a meaningful on-court return rather than a purely contractual benefit. Milwaukee also received Hodge, although its own transaction guide records that the club waived him on February 7, 2007. The $700,000 cash payment further distinguishes the deal from a direct one-for-one guard swap.

sections.heading: The Narrow Bucks Edge Keeps Both Returns in View
sections.body: The Slight Bucks Edge verdict grades Milwaukee B-plus and Denver B. Both teams received immediate help at point guard but in different forms. Boykins played 35 games for Milwaukee, averaging 14.0 points and 4.5 assists while injuries affected the Bucks, and Milwaukee also received Julius Hodge and the documented cash consideration. Denver acquired Blake, who made 40 starts across 49 games and averaged 6.6 assists, providing the steadier distribution its reshuffled backcourt needed. Hodge was waived in February, limiting his direct Bucks value, and neither acquired guard became a long-term centerpiece. The narrow grade difference reflects Boykins' short scoring contribution and the additional cash asset versus Blake's consistent starting playmaking. The 2007 transaction does not justify crediting either side with a future draft pick or treating the clubs' very different roster needs as identical.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The historical verdict stays Slight Bucks Edge, Milwaukee B-plus and Denver B. Boykins provided 35 Bucks games at 14.0 points and 4.5 assists after the January 11, 2007 deal; Hodge was waived in February and a separately reported $700,000 traveled with the two players. Blake supplied 49 Denver games, 40 starts and 6.6 assists per contest. Both guards addressed specific roster needs for the balance of that season. Neither return justifies treating the trade as a blowout or attaching unrelated players or picks.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Steve Blake for Earl Boykins: Different Needs in January 2007
featuredDeepDive.intro: After adding Allen Iverson, Denver sought a more traditional passer and exchanged its quick-scoring guard Earl Boykins and Julius Hodge, with cash, for Steve Blake. Milwaukee needed offense while injuries depleted its rotation. Blake started forty Denver games after the swap; Boykins scored fourteen points per game for Milwaukee. Those identifiable roles supply the basis for the inherited one-step grade spread while the short Hodge tenure and payment are accounted for separately.

sections.heading: Denver Needed a True Pass-First Guard After Its Iverson Deal
sections.body: The Nuggets had rearranged their backcourt weeks earlier by adding Allen Iverson and sending Andre Miller to Philadelphia, so acquiring another guard who could direct the offense had a practical purpose. Blake filled it: 40 starts in 49 games, 33.5 minutes and 6.6 assists per outing for Denver in 2006-07. Boykins, the outgoing player, had been productive as a compact scoring point guard and averaged 15.2 points in his 31 Denver appearances that season. This was a deliberate skill-set exchange rather than a salary-only giveaway. Contemporary reporting noted the pressure created by several roster interruptions, while the Denver season record establishes that Blake became a normal starting option.

sections.heading: The Injury-Hit Bucks Obtained Immediate Offense
sections.body: Milwaukee's context was unusual. Michael Redd and several other starters were dealing with injuries in January 2007, and general manager Larry Harris publicly challenged his team to keep competing. Boykins answered that short-term need with 35 Bucks games, including 19 starts and averages of 14.0 points and 4.5 assists. His 41.9-percent three-point percentage for Milwaukee was valuable for a scorer asked to generate offense without a fully healthy supporting rotation. The Bucks also accepted Julius Hodge, but a February 7 waiver in the franchise media guide limits the playing value attributable to that acquisition. The trade was thus driven overwhelmingly by Boykins' remaining-season offense and the separate cash consideration.

sections.heading: The Cash Amount Is Supported Differently From the Player Ledger
sections.body: The team's official transaction chronologies agree on Boykins, Hodge, Blake and cash, but neither short ledger entry independently specifies the exact payment. Contemporary reporting identified $700,000 going to Milwaukee, which is the amount in the canonical record. The evidence should be described at its correct level: the club guide confirms cash considerations, while the dated account supplies the number. There is no reason to invent draft compensation or treat salary relief as an additional player transferred from Denver. The Bucks waived Hodge less than a month after receiving him, leaving little direct court return beyond Boykins. This kind of asset-specific check prevents a generic three-piece package summary from overstating the value of every item.

sections.heading: Two Temporary but Meaningful Basketball Outcomes
sections.body: Denver obtained a passing guard who started forty times and helped manage possessions in a suddenly different lineup. Milwaukee obtained a creator who scored fourteen points per game after the trade and had room to play because of injuries. The Nuggets' side produced more starts from Blake; Milwaukee's side produced more points from Boykins and collected cash. Neither team controlled its principal acquisition for a prolonged stretch. The inherited B for Denver and B-plus for Milwaukee signal only a slight historical preference, not a declaration that Blake was ineffective or that Hodge developed into a significant Bucks contributor. Evaluating these actual 2006-07 roles is more useful than exaggerating unrelated later roster movements.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The transaction delivered immediate but temporary returns to both clubs. Denver acquired Steve Blake, who averaged 8.3 points and 6.6 assists in 49 appearances with 40 starts during the 2006-07 season. Milwaukee gained Boykins, who played 35 games at 14.0 points per contest, plus Julius Hodge and cash considerations. The Bucks' own record shows Hodge was waived February 7; contemporary reports identify the payment as $700,000. The historical grades, Denver B and Milwaukee B-plus, and Slight Bucks Edge verdict remain intact. A narrow edge can recognize Milwaukee's scoring and money without dismissing Blake's value as a starter or inventing draft rights and future player returns that never changed hands.
