sections.heading: What Changed Hands
sections.body: Denver and Philadelphia exchanged different kinds of roster consideration on September 10, 2007. The Nuggets received Steven Hunter and Bobby Jones, two named players who could be evaluated as part of an NBA roster. The 76ers acquired Reggie Evans and the rights to Ricky Sanchez. Sanchez's rights were not a second incoming active player; they gave Philadelphia control of a potential later opportunity. Describing this as Hunter and Jones for Evans alone would omit a contractually distinct part of the trade.

sections.heading: How the Realized Value Separated
sections.body: The Nuggets focused on adding Hunter and Jones, giving the club two separate players rather than a draft choice to be used years later. Philadelphia took Evans, a known frontcourt player, and an asset with uncertainty: the rights to Ricky Sanchez. The site's Nuggets Win label grades Denver A+ and Philadelphia C+. Those marks reflect its retrospective judgment, but the asset types deserve a more precise explanation than a general statement that the team receiving more names got the better deal.

sections.heading: Reading the Team Grades
sections.body: The delayed potential in Philadelphia's return is what distinguishes this transaction from a conventional two-for-one veteran swap. Reggie Evans could contribute to an NBA lineup; Sanchez's rights required later player and contract decisions before producing anything on the court. Denver did not obtain Sanchez or a future second-round pick under the recorded terms. It received Hunter and Jones, so its return was entirely named roster personnel at the trade date. The difference in certainty should be retained when explaining the grade gap.

sections.heading: What Each Franchise Was Actually Evaluating
sections.body: The transaction histories establish the September 2007 date and the four considerations that moved. Denver obtained Steven Hunter and Bobby Jones, while Philadelphia acquired Reggie Evans and rights to Ricky Sanchez. The rights were not equivalent to having Sanchez under an NBA contract, and the deal does not list cash or an additional first-round selection. The archive's A+/C+ difference is sizable, but later unrelated moves involving these players should not be imported into the evaluation without a separate documented asset path.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win — Denver A+, Philadelphia C+ in the archive. Denver received Steven Hunter and Bobby Jones, while the 76ers took Reggie Evans plus Ricky Sanchez's rights. The latter did not guarantee Philadelphia a second active roster player in September 2007. The recorded grade gap applies to these four defined considerations and must not be bolstered with an undocumented first-rounder or unrelated later trade.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Denver Nuggets–Philadelphia 76ers: September 2007 Hunter/Jones for Evans/Rights
featuredDeepDive.intro: On September 10, 2007, Denver acquired Steven Hunter and Bobby Jones from Philadelphia. The 76ers received Reggie Evans and the rights to Ricky Sanchez. The distinction between those assets is important: Hunter, Jones and Evans were identifiable NBA players, while Sanchez's rights were a separate possible future benefit. The archived verdict favors Denver, A+ to Philadelphia's C+. A source-led analysis needs to distinguish actual roster access from rights ownership before judging whether the final difference justified that grade spread.

sections.heading: The Asset Path That Carries the Grade
sections.body: Philadelphia's side of the deal combined one immediate player acquisition with a rights claim. Evans was a current NBA forward who could enter the 76ers' personnel plans. The rights to Ricky Sanchez were a separate, conditional asset whose value depended on whether and how those rights were subsequently used. Denver received two different active players, Hunter and Jones. That difference between present availability and future optionality is more informative than calling the trade a generic exchange of four basketball names.

sections.heading: What the Lower-Graded Side Still Kept
sections.body: Denver's return can be assessed individually. Steven Hunter provided one player at center, while Bobby Jones supplied another roster option. Neither asset should be confused with the Sanchez rights that went in the other direction. The recorded A+ for Denver is the site's retrospective assessment of its incoming package, not evidence that both players necessarily produced long and equally valuable stints with the Nuggets. The precise roster contribution of each requires results beyond the mere asset list.

sections.heading: Decision Logic Versus Hindsight
sections.body: The 76ers accepted the prospect that an established contributor in Reggie Evans and a future rights claim might outperform the two players they surrendered. Those were different ways to obtain value, not interchangeable player slots. Sanchez's eventual career path or a later trade involving his rights belongs to its own dated transaction if it is to be credited. The C+ recorded for Philadelphia acknowledges a lesser assessed outcome without proving its incoming package contained no usable basketball value.

sections.heading: Why the Grade Gap Is the Better Scale
sections.body: The Nuggets Win verdict comes with an A+ grade for Denver and C+ for Philadelphia, a wide distinction in the archived scale. The supported 2007 transaction is nevertheless straightforward: Hunter and Jones to Denver, Evans and Sanchez's rights to Philadelphia. The only defensible way to explain the magnitude is to compare the realized contributions of those assets after they changed hands. Adding an unlisted draft pick, an unspecified cash payment or an unrelated later player movement would undermine that comparison rather than strengthen it.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Nuggets' recorded A+ is based on incoming players Steven Hunter and Bobby Jones; Philadelphia's C+ covers Reggie Evans and the rights to Ricky Sanchez. The rights were an option, not an immediately available NBA forward. Any deeper hindsight claim requires tracing what those exact assets yielded, without counting later moves as though they were terms of the original September 10, 2007 deal.

sections.heading: Reading the Transaction Through Realized Value
sections.body: On July 15, 2008, Denver sent Marcus Camby to the Los Angeles Clippers in return for the right to swap second-round picks in the 2010 NBA Draft. The documented swap positions later became No. 38, associated with Andy Rautins, and No. 54, associated with Willie Warren. Those are two sides of one swap arrangement, not two additional players transferred to either roster in 2008. Denver's own announcement also identified a $10 million trade exception created by the transaction, a salary-cap consequence rather than a separate player or draft pick in the recorded consideration.

sections.heading: Where the Separation Emerged
sections.body: The Clippers obtained a veteran center with an established defensive record. Denver's 2008 announcement said Camby had led the NBA in blocked shots for three consecutive seasons and had won Defensive Player of the Year in 2006–07. Los Angeles acquired that immediate basketball contribution, while the Nuggets took a conditional future second-round improvement and the ability to use a $10 million exception. The archive's Clippers Win verdict, Los Angeles A- and Denver D, reflects a clear basketball advantage for the club receiving Camby, even though Denver also gained financial flexibility.

sections.heading: The Winning Return in Context: Los Angeles Clippers
sections.body: The future-pick history adds an important limitation to simple hindsight accounts. The No. 38 selection, eventually Andy Rautins, can be traced to the swap structure, but Denver traded that 2010 second-round asset to New York on July 28, 2008, in a separate deal involving Taurean Green, Bobby Jones, Renaldo Balkman and cash. Rautins therefore cannot be credited as if he played for the Nuggets merely because his name appears in the July 15 ledger. The later No. 54 identification with Willie Warren likewise names a draft outcome, not a 2008 player acquisition.

sections.heading: The Losing Return in Context: Denver Nuggets
sections.body: The transaction's two motivations should be kept separate. The Clippers had a direct interest in Camby's rebounding and rim protection, while Denver sought spending flexibility and a possible second-round draft advantage. The $10 million exception is documented by the Nuggets and helps explain the trade-day decision; it should not be treated as ordinary cash paid by Los Angeles. With no first-round selection moving in the original deal, the A-/D grade comparison rests on the veteran Camby against the more limited draft and salary-cap benefits attached to moving him.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win — Los Angeles A-, Denver D. The Clippers acquired Marcus Camby, while the Nuggets received a conditional 2010 second-round swap right and gained a $10 million trade exception under the salary-cap rules. The later No. 38 Andy Rautins and No. 54 Willie Warren pick identifiers don't make those players incoming 2008 assets. Denver also moved the No. 38 right in a separate July 28 trade, which requires its own ledger treatment.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Denver Nuggets–Los Angeles Clippers: 2008 Camby and the 2010 Second-Round Swap
featuredDeepDive.intro: Marcus Camby's July 15, 2008 move from Denver to the Los Angeles Clippers was a rare trade of an accomplished defensive center for a conditional second-round draft swap. The Nuggets' official announcement identified both the right to swap 2010 second-round selections and a $10 million trade exception created by the deal. The picks later corresponded to No. 38, Andy Rautins, and No. 54, Willie Warren, but that draft identification isn't evidence either player joined a club in 2008. The archive gives Los Angeles A- and Denver D; a useful assessment separates basketball production, the option over later draft position, and salary-cap flexibility.

sections.heading: Start With the Actual Package
sections.body: Denver's official announcement described the exchange as Camby for the right to swap 2010 second-round picks. The conditional nature of the pick arrangement is crucial: it gave the Nuggets an option over draft position rather than an already identified future NBA player. The pick histories later associate the involved second-round slots with No. 38, Andy Rautins, and No. 54, Willie Warren. Those names trace the asset, but using them to assign production to the Nuggets or Clippers without following subsequent ownership would manufacture an outcome.

sections.heading: Where the Best Value Landed: Los Angeles Clippers
sections.body: The Clippers were acquiring a decorated defensive center, not a speculative rookie. Camby's previous seasons in Denver included Defensive Player of the Year honors and several seasons of league-leading blocked-shot totals, facts Denver itself cited in its release. That direct veteran value supports the archive's Los Angeles A- compared with Denver D. It remains important, however, to distinguish the scale of the on-court advantage from the separate financial benefit Denver said it received through the $10 million trade exception.

sections.heading: Why Secondary Pieces Still Matter: Denver Nuggets
sections.body: The draft opportunity moved again within two weeks. On July 28, 2008, Denver sent the future 2010 second-round selection that became No. 38 to New York in a distinct trade with other personnel and cash. That subsequent deal can be studied as part of an asset trail, but it is not part of the consideration exchanged with the Clippers on July 15. Neither Andy Rautins nor Willie Warren was available to either 2008 roster merely because the 2010 draft later supplied names for those positions.

sections.heading: What the Grade Gap Is Measuring
sections.body: The Clippers' return was concentrated in Camby's immediate defense and interior presence. Denver's return was more indirect: a conditional chance to improve a 2010 second-round pick and a salary-cap trade exception generated by moving Camby's contract. Both have legitimate transaction value, but neither guarantees production comparable with the center Los Angeles acquired. The archived Clippers Win, A- versus D, should be explained through those exact differences rather than by describing the trade as a swap of three veteran players or an undocumented cash payment.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Los Angeles obtained a proven defender in Camby and earned the archive's A- versus Denver's D. Denver's documented consideration was the right to exchange 2010 second-round positions, with a $10 million exception arising from the transaction. No. 38 was later identified as Andy Rautins, but Denver transferred the future pick in another July 2008 deal. The original Clippers trade should not take credit for Rautins as a Nuggets player or confuse the exception with cash paid by Los Angeles.

sections.heading: Denver Received a Point Guard, Not Three Long-Term Players
sections.body: The November 3, 2008 transaction sent Allen Iverson from Denver to Detroit for Chauncey Billups, Antonio McDyess and Cheikh Samb. Detroit's own announcement identifies all four players. Although three names entered Denver's incoming ledger, Billups was the lasting centerpiece. McDyess was waived on November 10 and later returned to Detroit under the waiting rule then in effect. Samb was not a comparable rotation acquisition. The difference between the three names formally traded and the one guard who actually anchored Denver's next playoff run is central to assessing the deal. An accurate history lists all three original incoming assets without depicting McDyess as a season-long Nugget.

sections.heading: Billups Became the Engine of Denver's 2009 Run
sections.body: The 2008–09 Nuggets finished 54–28, won the Northwest Division, defeated New Orleans and Dallas in five games apiece and reached the Western Conference finals. Billups averaged 17.9 points and 6.4 assists during the regular season according to the NBA's conference-finals history. Denver lost the final series to the Lakers in six games, so the acquisition did not produce a championship. Nevertheless, Billups supplied the primary-playmaker role alongside Carmelo Anthony that the roster needed. That on-court fit is a stronger basis for the Nuggets' A+ recorded grade than merely counting how many player names arrived in the transaction. It was real playoff production, not a hypothetical future asset.

sections.heading: Iverson Produced Points, but Detroit's Season Went Backward
sections.body: Detroit acquired a former NBA MVP and an established elite scorer in Iverson. He played 54 games for the Pistons during 2008–09, averaging 17.4 points, 4.9 assists and 3.1 rebounds, per his NBA player statistics. Those totals are substantial enough that the return should not be characterized as zero production. The Pistons nevertheless finished 39–43 and lost their first-round playoff series to Cleveland in four games. The team-wide result had multiple causes and cannot all be assigned to the trade. Still, replacing Billups with a short-term Iverson stint plainly failed to reproduce Detroit's earlier postseason standard. The existing F grade is grounded in that unfavorable comparative result.

sections.heading: Why the Other Two Detroit Outgoings Still Count
sections.body: The original November 3, 2008 exchange sent Chauncey Billups, Antonio McDyess and Cheikh Samb from Detroit to Denver for Allen Iverson. Denver waived McDyess on November 10, and he returned to the Pistons in December after the waiting period; that later signing was a separate roster decision, not a revision of the trade package. Samb supplied little sustained Denver rotation value. Billups provided the lasting return, leading the Nuggets as their point guard during a 54-win season and a Western Conference finals run in 2009. Iverson still averaged 17.4 points in 54 Pistons games, but Detroit finished 39-43 and exited in the first round. Those receiving-team outcomes support the Nuggets Win verdict and the different retrospective grades, Denver A-plus and Detroit F, without treating every original player sent to Denver as a full-season contributor.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Published result: Nuggets Win — Denver A+, Detroit F. Billups averaged 17.9 points and 6.4 assists for a 54-win conference-finalist; Iverson averaged 17.4 points across 54 Detroit games before a 39–43 finish and first-round sweep. McDyess was traded and then separately waived and re-signed with Detroit. The four original player transfers and existing grades are preserved.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The 2008 Billups–Iverson Trade: Why the Fit Outweighed the Names
featuredDeepDive.intro: The headline on November 3, 2008 was Allen Iverson moving to Detroit, but Denver's acquisition of Chauncey Billups ultimately defined the exchange. Detroit sent Billups, Antonio McDyess and Cheikh Samb, receiving Iverson. McDyess quickly came back to Detroit after a Denver waiver, while Billups became the point guard for a 54-win Nuggets club that reached the 2009 Western Conference finals. The transaction requires two timelines: what each team received on trade day and what those players actually did afterward.

sections.heading: The Official Announcement and Its Four-Player Ledger
sections.body: The Pistons' contemporaneous release listed Iverson as the lone player acquired from Denver, with Billups, McDyess and Samb going the other direction. Joe Dumars described adding a historically accomplished guard, and the release catalogued Iverson's MVP, scoring and All-Star credentials. It also recalled Billups' role in Detroit's 2004 title and McDyess' contributions to a conference contender. The contractual ledger therefore cannot be shortened to Iverson for Billups simply because those were the biggest names. Nor should it credit Denver with a full year of McDyess, who was waived on November 10. Preserving both the formal package and the later waiver yields a clearer outcome narrative.

sections.heading: How Denver Used Billups in a Deep Playoff Run
sections.body: Denver entered the season with Carmelo Anthony as its principal offensive star, but acquiring Billups supplied an experienced lead guard. The 2008–09 club won 54 games, the NBA's season history records 17.9 points and 6.4 assists for Billups, and he finished sixth in MVP voting. The Nuggets eliminated the Hornets 4–1 and Mavericks 4–1 before losing the Western Conference finals to the Lakers 4–2. Billups averaged 18.2 points and 6.0 assists during those six conference-final games. These outcomes can be connected directly to the point guard Denver received, without assuming the trade alone caused every improvement by a roster that also featured Anthony and several established contributors.

sections.heading: Detroit's Iverson Year Was a Real, Short-Term Return
sections.body: Iverson was not absent or unproductive for Detroit: the NBA credits him with 54 appearances, 17.4 points and 4.9 assists per game in 2008–09. Yet the Pistons finished 39–43, below .500, and Cleveland swept them in the first round. That contrasts sharply with the Billups-led Detroit teams that had repeatedly reached the Eastern Conference finals. It is tempting to attribute Detroit's entire decline to one deal, but changes in coaching, the surrounding roster and the injury picture also belong in any broader account. The more defensible conclusion is narrower: Detroit traded a foundational guard for a famous scorer whose one-season return did not deliver comparable team results.

sections.heading: McDyess's Return and the Limits of Asset Counting
sections.body: The Denver transaction history lists McDyess as acquired on November 3 and waived on November 10. Detroit later re-signed him after the required waiting period, a sequence confirmed by a Pistons retrospective discussing why the league later revised that rule. The re-signing was not part of the original contract exchange; it is a separate roster transaction that changed where McDyess ultimately played. Samb, the other smaller incoming piece for Denver, never provided the same sustained value as Billups. For grading, this means the Nuggets' demonstrated advantage came overwhelmingly from one player, while the Pistons received meaningful short-term Iverson scoring but little comparable postseason payoff. Keep the Denver A+, Detroit F and Nuggets Win verdict pending any independent grade-policy reassessment.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The sourced November 2008 ledger was Iverson for Billups, McDyess and Samb. Billups became the lead guard on Denver's 54–28 Western Conference finalist, whereas Iverson's 54 Detroit games preceded a 39–43 season and a sweep. McDyess's separate waiver and return must not distort the original transfer. The published Nuggets Win verdict, Denver A+ and Detroit F survive the source audit.

sections.heading: The Clippers Took Samb and Cash for a Distant Second
sections.body: Denver sent 7-foot center Cheikh Samb and cash to the Los Angeles Clippers on January 5, 2009, in exchange for a conditional 2015 second-round draft pick. A contemporaneous Los Angeles Times account quoted Clippers coach and general manager Mike Dunleavy explaining that the team wanted to take a look at Samb amid injuries and roster changes. The cash helped defray the remainder of Samb's 2008-09 salary, making this a small roster-evaluation transaction rather than a bid for an established starting center. Samb had appeared in only six Nuggets games that season, and Denver had assigned him to the Colorado 14ers. The trade freed Denver to use that roster place elsewhere while retaining a future draft asset.

sections.heading: Samb Supplied Ten Clippers Games Before Being Waived
sections.body: The Clippers evaluated Samb for roughly six weeks. He made ten appearances, all off the bench, totaling 51 minutes and averaging 1.1 points and 1.3 rebounds. Los Angeles waived him February 16, 2009. The exchange therefore produced a small amount of NBA playing time but not a durable rotation piece. Dunleavy's January explanation confirms the acquisition was framed as an opportunity to assess size and potential during an injury-heavy season. Counting Samb as a long-term Clippers asset would ignore the February exit; counting his earlier Nuggets or later Knicks games as a Clippers return would make the same attribution error. Cash was a component of Los Angeles's actual compensation, not proof that Samb improved team results.

sections.heading: Denver Held the Pick Until It Became No. 57 in 2015
sections.body: The future selection came with top-55 protection, an important limitation for a draft asset acquired six seasons before it would be exercised. It eventually conveyed as the No. 57 overall pick in 2015, used on Serbian guard Nikola Radičević. Basketball-Reference's team transaction histories and the independent 2015 draft-pick chain trace that result to the Clippers' January 2009 exchange. Radičević did not produce NBA games for Denver; the value was a late draft right rather than realized scoring or a starting role. A 57th selection is a long shot, but it is an identifiable return for a player Denver was not using. The fact that this particular conditional pick did convey is more informative than an abstract claim about the value of second-rounders.

sections.heading: The Inherited Grades Are Stronger Than the Basketball Gap
sections.body: The preexisting retrospective gives Los Angeles C+ and Denver C-, describing a Clippers Win. The actual difference is much smaller in immediate playing value: Samb appeared in ten Clippers games before a waiver, while Denver secured the eventual No. 57 selection and opened a roster spot. The trade records also list a trade-exception mechanism for Denver, but that accounting item should not be turned into a separate cash receipt without reliable documentation. The cash paid by Denver and its six-year protected pick return further complicate a winner label based only on a player's name. The C+/C- spread is an inherited editorial choice, not evidence that Samb became a meaningful NBA center or the drafted guard joined Denver's roster. Both sides' realized returns were limited.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win under the inherited grades (Los Angeles C+, Denver C-), with a narrow evidence-based qualification. Cheikh Samb played ten Clippers games, averaging 1.1 points, before his February 2009 waiver; cash from Denver also formed part of the return. The Nuggets received a protected 2015 second-round pick that conveyed at No. 57 Nikola Radičević, but it produced no Denver NBA playing time. Both outcomes were minor, so the original grading edge should not be read as a major basketball windfall.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Deep Dive: Why Clippers Win Fits Denver Nuggets and Los Angeles Clippers
featuredDeepDive.intro: On January 5, 2009 Denver sent Cheikh Samb and the cash needed to cover his remaining salary to the Clippers for a top-55-protected 2015 second-round selection. Samb played ten Clippers games before a February waiver; the conditional pick eventually became No. 57 Nikola Radičević but yielded no Nuggets NBA minutes. This review keeps the salary aid, roster decision and future pick chain distinct instead of implying a major player-for-player exchange.

sections.heading: January 2009: A Center Evaluation for a Protected Second
sections.body: Denver moved center Cheikh Samb and cash to the Los Angeles Clippers on January 5, 2009, receiving a future second-round choice protected through the first 55 selections. The cash was meant to cover the remainder of Samb's 2008-09 salary, according to contemporary coverage. Clippers coach and general manager Mike Dunleavy described the acquisition as an opportunity to evaluate a very tall prospect while the club dealt with injuries. Denver had used Samb sparingly and had assigned him to the Colorado 14ers. No established starter or first-round pick moved in this transaction. The timing and compensation make it a modest roster-management exchange rather than a major competitive investment. Both the conditional protection and the wage contribution belong in the record because the pick was years away and the Clippers' immediate exposure was reduced.

sections.heading: Samb's Los Angeles Audition Ended After Ten Games
sections.body: Samb appeared in ten Clippers regular-season games after the trade, playing 51 total minutes and averaging 1.1 points and 1.3 rebounds. He never developed into the size-based rotation solution Los Angeles might have hoped to find. The Clippers waived him on February 16, 2009, about six weeks after taking him and Denver's cash compensation. Those are the direct basketball results behind the inherited Clippers C-plus grade: a few NBA appearances and the subsidized opportunity to assess a prospect, not a season-long contribution. The club's decision to examine his potential was understandable amid roster injuries, but the eventual team-specific benefit was limited. His earlier Denver assignments or subsequent appearances with another franchise cannot be reassigned to the Clippers for the purpose of grading the January deal.

sections.heading: Denver's Conditional Right Became the No. 57 Selection
sections.body: The Nuggets acquired a 2015 second-round pick with top-55 protection, which is a materially different asset from an unprotected future selection. Six years later it did convey, resolving as the No. 57 choice in the 2015 draft, used on Serbian guard Nikola Radičević. The draft-pick chain and transaction registers document that result. Radičević did not become a Denver NBA regular-season contributor, so the Nuggets' return is the value of possessing and using a late draft right rather than minutes earned by the named player. Acquiring an eventual No. 57 pick for an end-of-bench center was not meaningless, especially when the franchise could open a roster slot. Still, the conditional right supplied much less certainty than an earlier or more favorable selection.

sections.heading: A C- Versus C+ Comparison With Modest Direct Returns
sections.body: The source grade remains Clippers Win, Los Angeles C-plus and Denver C-minus, but the margin cannot be inflated into a blockbuster result. The Clippers received cash and ten games of Samb while Denver received a protected draft right that eventually became No. 57, without subsequent Nuggets NBA minutes from Radičević. Denver also had a roster-opening incentive, while Los Angeles had a short injury-period evaluation need. The later trade-exception accounting attributed to the Nuggets must not be confused with extra cash sent by the Clippers, and the documented cash moved toward Los Angeles. Those details explain the different types of value, not a large disparity in on-court results. The letter grades are an inherited comparative judgment; the direct evidence supports calling this a small transaction with limited realized basketball returns for either side.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win — Los Angeles C-plus, Denver C-minus. The Clippers acquired cash and a ten-game Samb audition, ending in a February 2009 waiver; Denver acquired the conditional 2015 second that became No. 57 Nikola Radičević but no direct NBA player minutes from that selection. Both clubs obtained modest forms of value, and the inherited grade edge is narrow rather than evidence of a major roster gain.

sections.heading: What Changed Hands
sections.body: The June 25, 2009 Denver–Houston transaction was a rights-for-cash exchange. Houston received the rights to Sergio Llull, while Denver received cash considerations. For basketball value, the Llull rights are the meaningful asset while the cash remains part of the documented transaction. The overall verdict is Rockets Win, with Houston graded B- and Denver D. Denver's evaluation has long graded its side D and Houston B-. Houston's own analysis also favored the Rockets, but the displayed counterpart grades had incorrectly shown B-/B-. Correcting those grades restored Denver's D as the counterpart grade without changing the underlying prose or trade facts. That leaves a consistent comparison in which Houston is the higher-graded side.

sections.heading: Why Houston’s Rights Asset Drives the Result
sections.body: Houston’s return is the rights to Sergio Llull, an identifiable basketball asset that the Rockets acquired directly from Denver. Denver’s return is cash considerations. The grade structure therefore reflects more than the number of trade details entries; it distinguishes a substantive player-rights asset from non-substantive cash consideration. The available evidence places Houston in the B- band and Denver in the D band, and both perspectives now agree on that relationship. This analysis does not need to invent later NBA production for Llull or attach unrelated organizational moves to the trade. The rights themselves are the directly tied asset that the available evidence values above Denver’s cash return. By keeping the analysis focused on those assets, the Rockets Win verdict can remain meaningful without claiming value that is not documented in the transaction history.

sections.heading: Rights Value Is Not the Same as NBA Box-Score Value
sections.body: A draft-rights asset can still carry value even when the player never logs NBA minutes for the acquiring team. It can provide control, optionality, negotiation value, or strategic flexibility, but those benefits should not be overstated without evidence of a later payoff. Here, Houston acquired the Llull rights and Denver received cash. The grades are B- for Houston and D for Denver. Houston's return was the rights themselves; there is no need to invent a later conversion or NBA production that never occurred. That keeps the analysis focused on what actually changed hands and what can reasonably be credited to this trade.

sections.heading: Why the Grades Differ
sections.body: Houston's analysis strongly favors Houston and carries a Rockets Win verdict. Houston's B- reflects the stronger return, while a B-/B- tie would not fit the analysis. Denver's D better reflects the weaker side of the deal. Together, the two evaluations support a B-/D relationship in Houston's favor, with a clear but not elite margin.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win. Houston receives a B- and Denver a D. Houston acquired the rights to Sergio Llull; Denver received cash considerations. The Llull rights are the trade's meaningful basketball asset, while the cash remains part of the documented transaction. Both analyses now point in the same direction. The verdict, stated winner, prose, sources, and underlying trade facts did not change. The final analysis therefore reflects the existing judgment rather than introducing a new one. Within the terms of the trade, Houston's B- sits clearly above Denver's D and supports the Rockets Win classification.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Denver Nuggets–Houston Rockets: Why a Rights-for-Cash Trade Still Needs a Clear Accounting
featuredDeepDive.intro: The Denver–Houston exchange on June 25, 2009 looks small compared with blockbuster NBA trades, yet it illustrates a difficult archival question: how should a database grade a player-rights asset against cash? Houston acquired the rights to Sergio Llull and Denver received cash considerations. The reconciled record grades Houston B- and Denver D. The important editorial task is not to inflate the significance of the transaction; it is to explain why the rights qualify as substantive basketball consideration, why cash does not, and why the source perspectives can support a directional result without inventing later value that is not traceable to the exchange.

sections.heading: Player Value Versus Other Consideration
sections.body: Both sides of the trade are documented, but a player or draft-rights asset carries different basketball value from cash. That distinction matters here because a cash-only return is not the same kind of basketball value as a player, pick, or draft-rights asset. Houston received the rights to Sergio Llull, while Denver received cash. That does not mean cash had no organizational value; it means the basketball comparison centers on Llull's rights. Those rights give the retrospective a concrete basketball asset to evaluate.

sections.heading: Avoiding an Unsupported Realized-Production Story
sections.body: The strongest version of this analysis is also the most disciplined. It would be easy to treat every draft-rights asset as though it necessarily became NBA production or downstream trade value, but that would overstate what the available evidence shows. The transaction history proves that Houston acquired Llull’s rights. The two analyses grade that acquisition above Denver’s cash return. Those facts are sufficient for the trade's evidence-based judgment. The analysis therefore does not assign hypothetical NBA statistics, invent a later conversion, or borrow value from unrelated Houston transactions. By avoiding those shortcuts, the B-/D comparison remains tied to the exact exchange confirmed by four public sources and what changed hands.

sections.heading: Why the Two Perspectives Can Now Be Read Together
sections.body: Denver's evaluation gives Denver D and Houston B-, saying Houston received the superior realized return. Houston's evaluation also favors Houston and supports a B- result. A B- for Houston and D for Denver captures the same direction across both analyses. The agreement is evidence-based: Houston's return was stronger, while Denver's side fell well short.

sections.heading: A Directional Verdict Without Overclaiming Significance
sections.body: Rockets Win does not mean this transaction should be treated as a franchise-defining event. The grades themselves communicate scale and quality: Houston B-, Denver D. The result is directional because the available evidence values the substantive rights asset above the cash return, not because the trade produced a superstar outcome. This distinction matters when comparing hundreds of historical trades. Smaller transactions deserve the same standard as major trades, but their prose should remain proportional to the evidence. Here, the correct conclusion is clear, bounded, and modest: Houston obtained the better recorded basketball asset, Denver’s return was cash, both analyses agree, and the page now has enough structured context to explain that result responsibly.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Houston B-, Denver D, Rockets Win. The exchange was the rights to Sergio Llull for cash considerations. The available sources confirm the deal, and the exchange itself shows the Llull rights as the meaningful basketball component. Houston's grade matches the Rockets Win verdict and stated winner. Denver's evaluation independently carries the same B-/D relationship. The analysis does not invent NBA production or unrelated downstream value for the Llull rights. It stays within the assets actually exchanged and supports the same conclusion: Houston received the stronger basketball asset and deserves the higher grade.

sections.heading: Denver Bought a Starting Wing for One Future Second
sections.body: On July 13, 2009, Detroit traded Arron Afflalo and Walter Sharpe to Denver for a 2011 second-round selection. Both clubs’ transaction ledgers additionally show cash going from Detroit to Denver, contrary to the protected imported cash-direction entry. Afflalo had started only eight games in 2008-09 with the Pistons while averaging 4.9 points, but the Nuggets saw a player who could defend perimeter scorers beside Carmelo Anthony and Chauncey Billups. Denver was seeking a response to Dahntay Jones leaving in free agency. The actual return was more than a bench flyer: Afflalo quickly became the starting shooting guard, turning a conditional late draft asset into several seasons of real production.

sections.heading: The 2011 Pick Eventually Became Vernon Macklin
sections.body: The outgoing Nuggets selection was the less favorable of their own or Portland’s 2011 second-round pick under the original terms. Detroit eventually selected Vernon Macklin at No. 52. He played 23 Pistons regular-season games in 2011-12, with no starts, at 2.0 points and 1.5 rebounds per appearance. That was the direct NBA return from the future pick, not an established 2009 veteran Detroit could immediately use. The inherited Detroit C grade recognizes that cap and cash considerations may have influenced the summer transaction, but Macklin’s short NBA stint did not equal the starter Denver developed from Afflalo.

sections.heading: Afflalo Played 213 Consecutive-Cohort Nuggets Games
sections.body: In his first Denver season Afflalo played all 82 games, starting 75, averaging 8.8 points while hitting 43.4 percent of his three-pointers. The next season he started all 69 appearances and raised his scoring to 12.6 points, shooting 42.3 percent from long range. In the lockout-shortened 2011-12 campaign he played 62 games, starting every one and scoring 15.2 points per contest. That totals 213 regular-season Denver games in the three seasons after this deal, with 206 starts. Denver’s December 2011 official re-signing announcement corroborates his growth into a key two-way starter, rather than attributing his later Orlando or Portland statistics to this transaction.

sections.heading: Sharpe Was Rerouted and Cash Must Be Reconciled
sections.body: Walter Sharpe never contributed NBA regular-season games to Denver. On July 31, only 18 days after arriving, the Nuggets sent him, Sonny Weems and cash to Milwaukee for Malik Allen. That later deal is a separate multi-asset swap and does not mean Sharpe alone was traded for Allen. A more serious archive issue concerns the first deal’s cash: Basketball Reference’s Denver and Detroit transaction pages say the Pistons sent cash to Denver with Afflalo and Sharpe, while this private source-imported record assigns cash to Detroit. The exact amount and origin of the discrepancy are unresolved; the canonical asset is left unchanged and marked for high-priority independent reconciliation, not silently flipped.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win, Denver A and Detroit C are preserved. Afflalo supplied 213 Denver regular-season games over 2009-12, with 206 starts and increased his scoring every year. Detroit used the future second to select Vernon Macklin at No. 52, getting 23 NBA games. Sharpe was later moved in a separately priced deal. Multiple transaction ledgers list cash moving to Denver, the opposite of the protected private import; the inconsistency is explicitly held for source review and no amount is invented.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The Afflalo Trade in 2009: Denver’s 213-Game Starter for Pick No. 52
featuredDeepDive.intro: Denver acquired Arron Afflalo and Walter Sharpe from Detroit on July 13, 2009 for a future second-round pick. That selection eventually became Vernon Macklin, No. 52 in 2011. Afflalo played 213 Denver regular-season games, starting 206 and becoming an important two-way guard. The private canonical record carries Denver A, Detroit C and Nuggets Win, but its cash direction conflicts with the two teams’ public transaction histories. The editorial corrects the explanation, preserves the protected ledger and opens a provenance hold rather than changing financial assets without approval.

sections.heading: Why Joe Dumars Moved Two Young Wings
sections.body: Detroit signed Ben Gordon and Charlie Villanueva in the 2009 offseason and was juggling salary and perimeter minutes after its veteran contender era. Contemporary Detroit reporting described the departure of Arron Afflalo and Walter Sharpe as clearing roughly $1.8 million in additional cap room. Afflalo had delivered limited rotation production in his first two seasons after being drafted at No. 27 in 2007. Denver, which had reached the 2009 Western Conference Finals, needed defense at shooting guard after Dahntay Jones joined Indiana. A single future second-round pick offered a lower-cost way to meet that need than acquiring a more expensive established starter.

sections.heading: Afflalo’s Three-Season NBA Return Was Concrete
sections.body: The guard became a starter almost immediately. He logged 82 games and 75 starts in 2009-10, posting 8.8 points and 43.4 percent three-point accuracy. In 2010-11 his averages grew to 12.6 points, 3.6 rebounds and 2.4 assists; Denver’s official 2011 signing release highlighted his 49.8 percent field-goal accuracy and 42.3 percent outside shooting. He added 15.2 points across 62 starts during the 2011-12 lockout season. These 213 games and 206 starts are directly attributable to his first tenure in Denver. Later years after other trades or his eventual Nuggets return should not be folded into the 2009 three-season outcome.

sections.heading: Detroit’s No. 52 Became a Brief Reserve
sections.body: The 2011 second-rounder conveyed as the 52nd pick, and Detroit drafted Vernon Macklin out of Florida. Basketball Reference lists a single 2011-12 NBA season for him: 23 Pistons games, zero starts, 135 total minutes and 46 points. That is measurable contribution but a small fraction of the court time Afflalo provided Denver. Detroit gained future optionality and flexibility in 2009 rather than an immediate established wing. Walter Sharpe’s subsequent July 31 transfer alongside Sonny Weems and cash to Milwaukee brought Malik Allen to Denver in a distinct transaction; its additional asset costs prohibit crediting Allen as a straight Sharpe return.

sections.heading: A First-Party Cash-Direction Disagreement Needs Its Own Hold
sections.body: Both Basketball Reference team ledgers and the contemporaneous 2009-10 NBA transaction database explicitly put cash with Afflalo and Sharpe as outgoing Detroit assets received by Denver. A protected TradeVerdicts private source-import row instead lists cash received by Detroit. The discrepancy may originate from an old secondary transaction digest: one archived Pro Sports Transactions row also places cash on the Denver-outgoing side. That evidence cannot be reconciled simply by selecting whichever version supports a grade. This audit leaves the asset row and Denver A, Detroit C untouched, records the disagreement with the relevant historical URLs and excludes an unsupported dollar value from the verdict.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win, Denver A and Detroit C remain inherited grades. Afflalo provided three seasons of productive starter minutes, while the 2011 No. 52 pick became Vernon Macklin’s 23-game Detroit stint. Sharpe left Denver after 18 days in a separate exchange with Milwaukee. The protected cash asset conflicts with independent public ledgers indicating Detroit paid Denver, so the financial direction stays under a formal high-priority source hold rather than being treated as verified.

sections.heading: July 2009 Sent Malik Allen to Denver and Three Pieces to Milwaukee
sections.body: Denver acquired Malik Allen from Milwaukee on July 31, 2009, sending Walter Sharpe, Sonny Weems and cash considerations to the Bucks. The teams' transaction chronologies and a contemporary report agree on the named players; the current ledger also records cash but does not assign an independently verified dollar amount. Sharpe had come to Denver just eighteen days earlier in a separate transaction with Detroit that included Arron Afflalo. These linked summer moves should not be conflated: Afflalo was not part of the July 31 Allen trade. Denver sought veteran frontcourt depth, while Milwaukee accepted a pair of younger wings and a financial contribution. Any subsequent movement of Weems belongs to a distinct second transaction.

sections.heading: Allen Played Fifty-One Reserve Games for the Nuggets
sections.body: Allen supplied Denver with measurable but modest depth. He appeared in 51 games during the 2009-10 regular season, started three, averaged 2.1 points and 1.6 rebounds, and logged a total of 456 minutes. That works out to fewer than nine minutes per appearance, far from the load of a frontcourt cornerstone. The Nuggets went 53-29 that season and lost to Utah in the first playoff round, but their broader performance cannot be attributed to a player with such a small role. His direct return was the presence of an experienced reserve whom Denver could deploy behind its larger contributors. The trade did not add another star or a future draft selection to the Nuggets' ledger.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Moved Weems Again Before the Season
sections.body: The Bucks did not use Sonny Weems as a regular 2009-10 rotation piece. On August 18, just eighteen days after acquiring him, they sent Weems and Amir Johnson to Toronto for Carlos Delfino and Roko Ukić. Toronto's official press release identifies all four athletes in that later agreement. Weems was a real incoming asset for Milwaukee, and his subsequent use in a multi-player exchange is relevant to an asset chain. But the July 31 Denver transaction did not directly bring Delfino and Ukić to the Bucks, and Weems was not the only player Milwaukee surrendered for them. Sharpe did not become a Bucks rotation contributor either; Milwaukee's October 26 transaction entry records his waiver.

sections.heading: The Inherited Bucks Grade Needs a Proportional Reading
sections.body: The preserved historical result calls this Bucks Win, Milwaukee B-plus and Denver B-minus. Those marks are reproduced without amendment, though they should not be defended by crediting Milwaukee with an entire later Toronto trade package that also required Amir Johnson. Denver got 51 limited Malik Allen appearances. Milwaukee obtained cash, briefly held Sharpe before waiving him, and used Weems alongside another asset in its August acquisition of Delfino and Ukić. This is a narrow chain of actual movements, not an instant two-player upgrade bought solely with Allen. Milwaukee's immediate options and cash support some value; the provenance of the relatively high B-plus rating should be separately reviewed if the site wants to make a stronger claim.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The canonical verdict remains Bucks Win, with Milwaukee B-plus and Denver B-minus. Denver obtained 51 games and 456 reserve minutes from Malik Allen. Milwaukee received Sharpe, Weems and cash; it waived Sharpe on October 26 and included Weems with Amir Johnson in a separate August 18 deal for Carlos Delfino and Roko Ukić. This original swap contained no draft pick, and the later return cannot be allocated entirely to Weems. Preserving the inherited grades does not remove the need for a separate provenance review of their magnitude.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Malik Allen for Weems, Sharpe and Cash: A Short Asset Chain
featuredDeepDive.intro: The July 2009 Nuggets-Bucks exchange is easiest to judge by separating the initial trade from the next transaction eighteen days later. Denver received veteran reserve Malik Allen. Milwaukee acquired Sonny Weems, Walter Sharpe and cash, then combined Weems with Amir Johnson in a separate trade with Toronto. Allen's 51 Denver appearances, Sharpe's waiver and the documented later Weems move replace generic package-size claims with a traceable chronology. The site's historical grades remain in place pending a separate provenance review.

sections.heading: Denver's Summer Asset Chain Had Two Separate Dates
sections.body: Denver first acquired Walter Sharpe and Arron Afflalo in a July 13, 2009 agreement with Detroit. On July 31 it sent Sharpe and Sonny Weems, with cash, to Milwaukee for Malik Allen. The distinction is visible in the Nuggets' 2009-10 transaction history and prevents the review from assigning Afflalo to the wrong opponent or transaction. Denver was not swapping a starting forward for a proven impact center; it was consolidating fringe player holdings into a veteran reserve. Allen then supplied 456 minutes in 51 games. His small but concrete contribution should be counted on its own, while Afflalo's later Nuggets production must stay attached to the earlier Detroit trade, not the Allen deal.

sections.heading: Milwaukee's Weems Holding Period Lasted Eighteen Days
sections.body: Sonny Weems became Bucks property on July 31 and was transferred to Toronto on August 18. The Raptors' public announcement makes clear that Weems traveled with Amir Johnson and that the Bucks received Carlos Delfino and Roko Ukić in that later exchange. Milwaukee therefore had a usable transaction piece in Weems rather than an NBA player who produced a full season for the Bucks. It is reasonable to trace the asset into the subsequent trade, but it would be false to say Weems alone fetched both Toronto players. Any grade comparing Milwaukee's return with Denver's must acknowledge Johnson's separate contribution to that second transaction and the cash from the first.

sections.heading: Walter Sharpe and the Cash Do Not Equal a Hidden Draft Haul
sections.body: The July 31 Bucks ledger contains Walter Sharpe, Sonny Weems and cash, with no future pick named. Sharpe had appeared in only eight Detroit games as a rookie before Denver acquired him earlier in July. Milwaukee eventually waived him October 26, before he delivered a sustained contribution in its regular-season rotation. A contemporary July 31 report described Allen as a veteran who had averaged 3.2 points for Milwaukee in 2008-09, explaining why a team might prefer younger contracts and cash. But no audited primary source in this packet assigns a definite dollar amount to the payment, and it would be inappropriate to invent one. The future trade possibilities of younger assets were the real alternative to retaining Allen.

sections.heading: What the Letter Grades Can and Cannot Show
sections.body: Milwaukee's preserved B-plus and Denver's B-minus are original editorial judgments, not automatic outputs from a box-score formula. The direct Nuggets side consists of 51 Malik Allen games and a small reserve workload. Milwaukee received two young players and cash; one player was soon waived, and the other served as part of a later package that also included Amir Johnson. These specifics distinguish the deal from an even one-for-one swap without proving that Milwaukee independently obtained all of Delfino and Ukić for Allen. The Bucks Win direction is retained, but its magnitude is a separate grading-provenance question best addressed through source-linked asset attribution rather than repetitive assurances that every outgoing piece creates significant downstream value.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win, Milwaukee B-plus and Denver B-minus, remain the stored classifications. The July 31, 2009 ledger sent Allen to Denver for Sharpe, Weems and cash. Denver used Allen for 51 games and only 456 minutes, while Milwaukee never had a prolonged on-court contribution from Sharpe. Weems had further transaction value, but Milwaukee's August 18 acquisition of Delfino and Ukić from Toronto also cost Amir Johnson; it cannot be credited entirely to Weems or backdated as a July 31 incoming asset. Cash is real but its exact amount is unverified in the referenced team histories. Those records explain the deal's limited direct returns and document why a standalone source-based grade review should accompany rather than be hidden inside the originality repair.

sections.heading: James White Went to Denver for the Rights to Axel Hervelle
sections.body: On September 22, 2009, Denver received guard James White from Houston and surrendered the NBA draft rights to Belgian forward Axel Hervelle. The Rockets had used White in only four games during the closing weeks of 2008-09, totaling 11 minutes, according to the contemporaneous Houston Chronicle report. Hervelle was not an NBA player changing uniforms: Denver had selected him 52nd in the 2005 draft, and he was still playing for Real Madrid. Houston was acquiring the option to negotiate with an overseas prospect, not adding a frontcourt contributor to its 2009-10 rotation. That distinction is the starting point for evaluating a small trade that produced little direct NBA playing time.

sections.heading: Houston Preferred an Overseas Right to Its Last Guard Spot
sections.body: Reporting on the day of the trade described White as facing long odds of making Houston's roster. The Rockets were also bringing guards Garrett Temple and Will Conroy into camp, making the White transaction part of an active competition for limited guard places. Hervelle, then 26, had a longer professional record abroad: Jonathan Feigen reported 8.1 points and 4.5 rebounds per game for Real Madrid in the previous domestic season, with 6.4 points and 5.1 rebounds in EuroLeague play. The international numbers explain why Houston might retain interest in the draft rights, but they are not Rockets NBA production. His subsequent European career cannot simply be counted as games won by the Houston franchise.

sections.heading: Denver Released White Before the Season Started
sections.body: White's time with the Nuggets did not become a regular-season role. RealGM's Denver transaction history lists him as acquired September 22 and waived October 21, 2009; his contract subsequently cleared. The acquisition therefore gave Denver a brief opportunity to evaluate a perimeter player in camp, not rotation minutes across the Nuggets' 53-win 2009-10 season. The costs were equally limited on the basketball side: Denver had controlled Hervelle's rights for four years without bringing him to the NBA. Houston's official transaction listings document the rights-for-player exchange, while RealGM also notes a trade-exception mechanism in its accounting. That ledger detail should not be inflated into an unverified cash payment or a separate established player.

sections.heading: Neither Incoming Asset Became an NBA Contributor for Its Buyer
sections.body: Both clubs ended up holding a different type of uncertainty. Denver briefly obtained an available guard but waived him before opening night; Houston retained negotiating rights to a successful European forward who never suited up for the Rockets. Those are more precise outcomes than describing White as a Denver contributor or Hervelle as a Houston center. The existing C for Denver and C- for Houston imply only a slight Nuggets advantage. With no regular-season Nuggets games from White and no Rockets appearances by Hervelle, those inherited grades are a narrow editorial judgment about short-term roster flexibility, not evidence of an appreciable performance gap. The trade's actual return is modest on either side.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Nuggets Edge (inherited grades: Denver C, Houston C-), but with little realized NBA value for either franchise. Denver evaluated James White briefly before waiving him October 21, 2009. Houston exchanged its fringe guard for the rights to 2005 No. 52 pick Axel Hervelle, who continued his career abroad and never played for the Rockets. The one-grade-step result is not a claim that White helped Denver win games; both acquisitions were ultimately non-contributors at the NBA level.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: James White for Hervelle Rights in 2009: Why Neither Played for the New Team
featuredDeepDive.intro: Denver received James White for Houston rights to Belgian forward Axel Hervelle, and waived White before the next regular season. Hervelle never appeared in an NBA game for the Rockets.

sections.heading: White Was an Evaluation Contract, Not Nuggets Rotation Production
sections.body: Denver acquired James White from Houston on September 22, 2009, while parting with rights to Belgian forward Axel Hervelle. White had played only four Rockets games in 2008-09, totaling eleven minutes, according to a contemporary Houston Chronicle transaction report. The Nuggets were evaluating a guard with NBA experience rather than filling a guaranteed rotation role. That experiment ended before the regular season: Denver's transaction history records White's October 21 waiver. His Denver NBA regular-season contribution was therefore zero, despite the potential usefulness of assessing him in training camp. It would be inaccurate to assign him the 53 wins achieved by Denver's full 2009-10 roster. Those came from players who actually appeared in its schedule, not from a contract released before opening night.

sections.heading: The Forward's European Success Was Not Rockets NBA Output
sections.body: Hervelle had been Denver's No. 52 selection in 2005 and was still playing in Spain when the September 2009 rights exchange occurred. Houston's interest lay in controlling his possible future NBA contract rather than adding an active forward to its next game roster. Contemporary coverage listed his preceding Real Madrid domestic production at 8.1 points and 4.5 rebounds, with different EuroLeague averages, showing that the club was evaluating a legitimate international professional. Those Spanish and continental statistics are not Houston NBA minutes. Hervelle never played an NBA regular-season game for the Rockets. A future negotiation opportunity existed, but the outcome did not become a new rotation member. The source ledger's C-minus Houston grade should be understood against that absence of direct NBA appearances.

sections.heading: September Trade and October Waiver Close Denver's Direct Chain
sections.body: The sequence is unusually short and clear. Houston sent White to Denver for Hervelle rights on September 22. Denver waived White on October 21 before the 2009-10 NBA regular season began. Those two dated transaction entries establish both the acquisition and the endpoint of the Nuggets' control. No later Denver trade return involving White is established in the reviewed source file, so it would be improper to credit the team with compensation it never documented. Houston retained an overseas draft-rights asset but similarly received no NBA production from Hervelle. The clubs traded distinct types of opportunity, one immediate player evaluation and one possible future negotiation. Neither converted to receiving-team games. This is the relevant outcome, not a generalized discussion about hypothetical draft pick values or franchise success.

sections.heading: An Inherited One-Step Denver Edge Lacks an On-Court Margin
sections.body: The published archive gives Denver C and Houston C-minus with Slight Nuggets Edge. Those letter grades may be retained as historical editorial metadata, but the reviewed NBA outcomes are effectively even in direct player-games: White never appeared for Denver and Hervelle never appeared for Houston. The grade difference could reflect the relative liquidity of an available guard contract or the residual potential of overseas rights, yet the current evidence does not quantify those opportunities. There is no support for claiming either acquired player delivered meaningful NBA scoring after the transaction. The accurate summary is a short training-camp evaluation against an unexercised NBA draft right, with both outcomes clearly bounded. That distinguishes a small, inconclusive deal from template language asserting a decisive realized advantage without documented production.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Inherited Slight Nuggets Edge: Denver C, Houston C-minus. White was acquired September 22 and waived October 21 before any Nuggets regular-season games. Hervelle rights never yielded Rockets games. The grade difference is an editorial opinion not confirmed by receiving-team NBA appearances. The original asset label spells Alex Hervelle while independent research spells Axel; leave canonical player ID unchanged pending alias resolution.

sections.heading: Denver Converted a Forced Exit Into a Competitive Roster
sections.body: Carmelo Anthony had made clear that he wanted a move, and Denver faced the usual danger of losing leverage as the deadline approached. Instead of settling for one prospect, the Nuggets collected Danilo Gallinari, Wilson Chandler, Raymond Felton, Timofey Mozgov, Kosta Koufos, draft assets, cash, and future swap control. The veterans were not decorative pieces. They allowed Denver to remain a playoff team immediately rather than treating Anthony's departure as permission for a long collapse.

sections.heading: New York Received the Star and the Contract Extension It Wanted
sections.body: The Knicks did not trade for an uncertain rental. Anthony signed an extension as part of the transaction, giving New York a hometown superstar to pair with Amar'e Stoudemire. He became the center of the offense, won the 2013 scoring title, and powered the franchise to a 54-win season and its first playoff-series victory in more than a decade. Those results keep the Knicks side above average even though the price stripped away depth and future control.

sections.heading: The Immediate Denver Return Had Real Basketball Value
sections.body: Gallinari became a primary scorer, Chandler supplied two-way wing minutes, Felton stabilized the point before being redirected, and Mozgov and Koufos strengthened the frontcourt. Denver won 50 games in the first full season after the deal and reached 57 wins in 2012-13. That matters because the Nuggets did not have to choose between preserving competitiveness and building for later. The package gave them enough playable talent to do both for several seasons.

sections.heading: The 2016 Pick Swap Extended the Trade Into a Championship Era
sections.body: The most important delayed asset was Denver's right to swap 2016 first-round picks with New York. The Knicks finished with the No. 7 selection, Denver held No. 9, and the swap placed the Nuggets in position to draft Jamal Murray. Murray eventually became Nikola Jokic's championship backcourt partner. A transaction that began as the end of the Anthony era therefore retained influence all the way into the roster that won Denver's first NBA title.

sections.heading: Minnesota Was a Facilitator Rather Than the Center of the Verdict
sections.body: The Timberwolves helped complete the three-team structure, moving Corey Brewer and Kosta Koufos while receiving Anthony Randolph, Eddy Curry, and draft consideration. Their role did not carry the franchise-altering stakes attached to Denver and New York, but it was not value-free. A middle grade fits a team that used the transaction to reshuffle salary and assets without producing a defining long-term gain or accepting the central risk of the blockbuster.

sections.heading: Denver Won Without Pretending New York Received Nothing
sections.body: The trade should not be reduced to the later Murray connection alone. New York acquired a genuine star, regained national relevance, and enjoyed its best modern regular season. Denver still deserves the top grade because it navigated a pressured negotiation, remained competitive, and preserved draft rights that became part of a championship foundation. The difference is the breadth and duration of the Nuggets' return, not a claim that Anthony failed in New York.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Denver wins the transaction with an A, while New York and Minnesota receive B grades. The Knicks obtained the best established player and secured several meaningful seasons, including a 54-win campaign, but the Nuggets received useful rotation players, immediate competitive continuity, and the 2016 swap that became Jamal Murray. That combination carried value across two distinct eras. New York paid a substantial premium for certainty; Denver turned a forced departure into the deeper and more durable result.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The Carmelo Trade Kept Paying Denver Long After the Original Players Left
featuredDeepDive.intro: The unusual strength of Denver's return was its layered timetable. Some assets played immediately, some were moved again, and the most consequential draft right did not mature for five years. New York received the star it had pursued, but Denver built a package capable of surviving roster turnover and organizational change. That is why the deal still belongs in the story of the Nuggets' championship construction rather than only in the history of Anthony's arrival at Madison Square Garden.

sections.heading: Anthony Gave New York a Real, Measurable Peak
sections.body: Anthony's Knicks tenure should not be rewritten as empty celebrity. He became one of the league's premier scorers, led the 2012-13 team to the East's second seed, and helped New York defeat Boston in the first round. The cost of the trade limited the supporting cast, but the acquired player delivered the exact star-level production the Knicks expected. Their B grade recognizes that the basketball return was substantial even though it did not create a lasting contender.

sections.heading: Denver Avoided the Standard Superstar-Exit Crash
sections.body: Many teams trading a dissatisfied franchise player accept a temporary talent vacuum. Denver instead received enough shooting, size, and lineup flexibility to keep winning. Gallinari and Chandler could occupy major offensive roles, while the centers provided practical depth in a demanding conference. The Nuggets were able to evaluate and redirect pieces from a position of competence. That immediate stability made the future picks more valuable because the organization was not forced to spend them repairing every part of the roster at once.

sections.heading: The Murray Connection Was a Right, Not a Lucky Footnote
sections.body: Denver negotiated the swap before anyone knew where the 2016 selections would land or which prospects would be available. The outcome required both foresight and later execution: the Nuggets had to preserve the right, receive the favorable position, and select Murray. Chance always exists in draft transactions, but the opportunity itself came directly from the leverage Denver retained in 2011. The championship payoff therefore belongs in the trade's asset chain rather than being dismissed as unrelated hindsight.

sections.heading: New York Chose Immediate Certainty Over Waiting for Free Agency
sections.body: The Knicks could have gambled that Anthony would arrive later, but waiting carried its own risks. Another team might have acquired and retained him, the roster might have stalled, or the market might have changed. New York paid heavily to eliminate that uncertainty and secure an extension. The mistake was not wanting Anthony; it was surrendering so much depth and draft flexibility that subsequent roster errors became harder to survive. The deal raised the ceiling while narrowing the margin for error.

sections.heading: Three-Team Complexity Should Not Blur the Main Exchange
sections.body: The complete transaction involved thirteen players and multiple draft mechanisms, but the central comparison remains clear. New York received Anthony and Billups; Denver received a broad package designed to compete now and later; Minnesota enabled the structure. Evaluating every participant separately prevents the common shortcut of treating the deal as a simple Anthony-for-Murray swap. Denver still finishes first, but the grades reflect the real benefits New York received and the more limited role Minnesota played.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Nuggets earn the win because the return functioned in stages. It produced immediate starters, protected Denver from a post-star collapse, and ultimately delivered the draft position used on Jamal Murray. New York received a productive, extended superstar and its strongest season in years, which is why a B is more accurate than a failure grade. Minnesota receives a B for competent facilitation. Denver's A reflects the rare achievement of turning a public trade demand into both short-term relevance and championship-era value.

sections.heading: Denver Acquired Maduabum’s Draft Rights
sections.body: Denver acquired the rights to Chukwudiebere “Chu Chu” Maduabum from the Lakers during the 2011 draft period. Los Angeles received a future second-round pick, initially protected in the top 40 for 2013 and otherwise due in 2014. The pick was ultimately exercised in 2013 at No. 57 on Alex Oriakhi. Each franchise traded a speculative draft asset, not an established NBA player with a known rotation role.

sections.heading: The Protections Defined What Los Angeles Could Receive
sections.body: The Lakers’ incoming selection was not simply an unconditional pick at the moment of the trade. The top-40 protection in 2013 and the later unprotected provision were part of the bargain. The pick eventually conveyed as the No. 57 choice, a late second-round opportunity. Oriakhi was the outcome of that specific draft right, so Los Angeles’s return can be described precisely without claiming a higher selection was guaranteed.

sections.heading: Denver Accepted Prospect Risk in Exchange for Pick Risk
sections.body: Maduabum’s rights gave Denver control of one identified prospect’s NBA opportunity. Los Angeles exchanged those rights for a different future opportunity. Neither side emerged with a documented major NBA return from the direct exchange. Matching C-plus grades are therefore more defensible than elevating one club for a hypothetical development that was not realized in this transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Denver C-plus, Los Angeles Lakers C-plus. Denver obtained Maduabum’s rights, while the Lakers eventually received the 2013 No. 57 second-round selection used on Oriakhi. The conditional timing is part of the trade, and neither documented draft asset developed into a decisive NBA return. A modest, evenly graded result fits the two speculative rights packages.

sections.heading: The Four-Team Structure Was Bigger Than Dwight Howard
sections.body: The headline sent Dwight Howard to the Lakers, but Orlando's return came from several directions. The Magic received Nikola Vucevic and Maurice Harkless from Philadelphia, Arron Afflalo and Al Harrington from Denver, Josh McRoberts and Christian Eyenga from Los Angeles, and a package of first- and second-round picks. Denver received Andre Iguodala, Philadelphia received Andrew Bynum and Jason Richardson, and Los Angeles built a short-lived superteam around Howard.

sections.heading: Why Orlando Chose Volume and Flexibility
sections.body: Howard's relationship with Orlando had reached the point where a trade was unavoidable. Instead of demanding one replacement star, the Magic prioritized young players, draft capital, a large trade exception, and contracts that could be moved again. That approach looked underwhelming on announcement day, but it reduced the risk of tying the rebuild to one expensive veteran. The return gave Orlando several independent chances to recover value.

sections.heading: Nikola Vucevic Became the Lasting Centerpiece
sections.body: Vucevic developed from a lightly established second-year center into a two-time All-Star in Orlando. He became the team's offensive hub and, nearly nine years later, produced another major return when the Magic traded him to Chicago for Wendell Carter Jr., Otto Porter Jr., and two first-round picks. One of those selections became Franz Wagner. That downstream chain is the strongest reason Orlando earns the highest grade in the deal.

sections.heading: Denver's Iguodala Season Was Good but Brief
sections.body: Iguodala fit Denver's fast, deep roster and helped the Nuggets win 57 games in 2012-13, the best regular season in the franchise's NBA history at the time. He defended, handled the ball, and connected lineups exactly as expected. The limitation is duration: after one season and a first-round loss, he left for Golden State in a sign-and-trade. Denver received a strong season, not a long-term cornerstone.

sections.heading: Los Angeles and Philadelphia Absorbed the Worst Risk
sections.body: Howard played one turbulent season with the Lakers before leaving in free agency, and the team was swept in the first round. Philadelphia's result was far worse: Bynum never appeared in a regular-season game for the 76ers because of knee problems. The Sixers surrendered Iguodala, Vucevic, Harkless, and draft value for a center who never played. Those outcomes justify the C-minus for Los Angeles and the F for Philadelphia.

sections.heading: Why Orlando, Not 'Even,' Is the Verdict
sections.body: The grade order already tells the story: Orlando B-plus, Denver B, Los Angeles C-minus, Philadelphia F. Orlando did not replace Howard with another superstar immediately, but it acquired the deal's longest-lasting star, additional rotation players, and a pick-and-player chain that extended into the next rebuild. Denver had a productive one-year result. The other two teams lost substantially more value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Orlando won the four-team trade. Vucevic became a two-time All-Star and later generated another premium package, while Harkless, Afflalo, and the draft assets gave the Magic additional value and flexibility. Denver's one season of Iguodala earns a solid B, but Los Angeles received only one disappointing Howard season and Philadelphia received no Bynum games at all. The verdict changes from Even Trade to Magic Win.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The Dwight Howard Trade Looked Worse for Orlando Before It Looked Better
featuredDeepDive.intro: The 2012 blockbuster was judged initially by what Orlando failed to receive: a ready-made star. Over time, the more important question became what each franchise actually retained. The answer turned a mocked rebuild package into the best side of a four-team transaction.

sections.heading: The Announcement-Day Optics Favored Los Angeles
sections.body: Howard was the dominant name, and the Lakers paired him with Kobe Bryant, Pau Gasol, and Steve Nash. Orlando's collection of prospects and picks did not offer the same immediate spectacle. That imbalance shaped the early narrative. But trade value is not awarded for the press conference; it is awarded for games played, development, contract control, and what the assets later become.

sections.heading: Vucevic Outlasted Every Other Headline Piece
sections.body: Howard, Bynum, and Iguodala were the established stars involved, yet Vucevic became the player who spent the longest productive stretch with an acquiring team. Orlando developed him into a reliable scorer, rebounder, passer, and two-time All-Star. His eventual Chicago return then extended the transaction's value into Carter and two first-round selections, making the original deal a multi-generation asset chain.

sections.heading: Denver Captured a Peak Season but Could Not Keep It
sections.body: The Nuggets' 57-win season demonstrates that Iguodala was not a failed acquisition. He gave Denver an elite defensive wing and secondary creator for a roster built around pace and depth. The problem was control. His departure after one season prevented the Nuggets from compounding that success, and the first-round loss kept the short window from producing a deep playoff payoff.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Took the Most Concentrated Gamble
sections.body: The 76ers exchanged several useful young assets and an All-Star wing for Bynum's elite upside. When his knees prevented him from playing, there was no secondary path to value. Orlando's return was diversified; Philadelphia's was concentrated almost entirely in one player's health. The contrast explains why the same trade can merit a B-plus for one team and an F for another.

sections.heading: The Rebuild Value Continued After Vucevic Left
sections.body: Orlando eventually moved Vucevic rather than allowing the original trade's value to end with him. Carter became a starting center, and the first-round return included the selection used on Wagner, a central piece of the next competitive core. That later move is not a separate excuse for the 2012 trade; it is the realized value of the controllable asset Orlando acquired in 2012.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Orlando accepted an unpopular package and ultimately produced the deal's most durable value. Denver received one excellent regular season, while the Lakers and 76ers paid star-level prices for outcomes that disappeared almost immediately. Orlando B-plus, Denver B, Los Angeles C-minus, Philadelphia F, Magic Win.
