sections.heading: Start With the Exchange
sections.body: On June 27, 2013, Denver sent center Kosta Koufos to Memphis for forward Darrell Arthur and the draft rights to Joffrey Lauvergne, whom Memphis had chosen 55th that night. Koufos had started all 81 Nuggets games he played in 2012-13, producing 8.0 points and 6.9 rebounds per outing. Denver was moving a proven center rather than a surplus player with no defined role. Arthur offered a different frontcourt profile: mobility, midrange shooting and defensive versatility off the bench. Lauvergne was an additional development asset, initially playing overseas rather than occupying a Denver roster spot. The three pieces and their timing establish the actual cost of the move.

sections.heading: Where the Margin Came From
sections.body: The Denver A and Memphis B- grades represent different kinds of successful role-player investment. Arthur appeared in 256 Nuggets regular-season games over five seasons, including 70 games and 7.5 points per game in 2015-16. Lauvergne eventually added 83 Denver appearances across 2014-15 and 2015-16, with 7.9 points and 4.9 rebounds per game in the latter season. Memphis was not left empty: Koufos played 80 games in 2013-14 and 81 in 2014-15 as a reliable reserve center behind Marc Gasol. Denver's additional developmental right and the later return obtained when it traded Lauvergne strengthen the winning side, while Koufos' substantial two-year Memphis contribution keeps the gap from being described as a one-sided disaster.

sections.heading: What Worked for Denver Nuggets
sections.body: Arthur's five Denver seasons were built on utility, not star billing. He was a regular reserve from 2013-14 through 2016-17, supplying forward minutes, defense and occasional spacing before injuries sharply reduced his role in 2017-18. The second asset took longer: Lauvergne stayed overseas through 2013-14, appeared for Denver in February 2015 and grew into a 59-game contributor the following season. In August 2016 Denver traded Lauvergne to Oklahoma City for two conditional second-round picks. Denver's own retrospective identifies one resulting 2017 No. 51 selection as the pick used on Monte Morris. The later pick conversion gives those 2013 draft rights a traceable additional life, although Morris' entire subsequent career cannot automatically be counted as production from Arthur's five seasons.

sections.heading: What Fell Short for Memphis Grizzlies
sections.body: Koufos gave Memphis real value as Marc Gasol's backup, appearing in 161 of 164 possible regular-season games across his two Grizzlies years. In 2013-14 he averaged 6.4 points and 5.2 rebounds in 16.9 minutes; the following season he averaged 5.2 points and 5.3 rebounds in 16.6 minutes while the team won 55 games. He also provided physical interior minutes when Gasol sat. Koufos left for Sacramento in 2015, so his later Kings tenure is not a Memphis return to this transaction. The Grizzlies had acquired a dependable center, but Denver gained Arthur's longer run and converted Lauvergne's rights into both playing time and another draft asset. That distinction supports a Denver edge without erasing Memphis' two good seasons of backup-center work.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win — Denver A, Memphis B-. Memphis received a dependable reserve center in Koufos, who played 161 games over two seasons. Denver got 256 Arthur games, 83 Lauvergne appearances and an additional pick chain tied to the eventual No. 51 Monte Morris selection. Those distinct contributions support a Denver advantage, but the Grizzlies' B- recognizes real center depth rather than treating the trade as a failure.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Denver Nuggets–Memphis Grizzlies: What the Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: Denver's return from the 2013 draft-night Koufos trade had two stages separated by three years. Arthur immediately became part of the Nuggets' forward rotation, while the rights to No. 55 pick Joffrey Lauvergne were an investment the team could hold during his time in Europe. When Lauvergne later reached the NBA, Denver got playing time from him and then exchanged him for conditional second-round picks in 2016. One of those draft paths eventually supplied the 2017 No. 51 selection used on Monte Morris, according to the Nuggets' own historical transaction review. Memphis' direct return — two productive seasons from Koufos as a backup center — is easier to measure, but Denver's longer asset chain is the distinguishing part of this verdict.

sections.heading: The Center of Gravity
sections.body: Arthur's value is best captured by his changing role rather than his scoring averages alone. After starting only once in 68 games during 2013-14, he played 58 games in 2014-15, 70 in 2015-16 and 41 in 2016-17. His most active Denver season included 16 starts, 7.5 points and 4.2 rebounds per game, with minutes at power forward in smaller lineups. He did not become a top option, and by 2017-18 his appearances fell to 19. But the Nuggets obtained a usable veteran for portions of five seasons, a different kind of value from the starting center they had moved. Arthur was the immediate, low-variance return; Lauvergne's draft rights supplied longer-term optionality.

sections.heading: The Rest of the Package
sections.body: The #55 rights gave Denver control of Lauvergne's NBA path without an immediate roster expense. He joined the Nuggets in February 2015, playing 24 games that season at 3.9 points and 3.2 rebounds per outing. In 2015-16 he appeared 59 times, made 15 starts and improved to 7.9 points and 4.9 rebounds. Denver then traded him to Oklahoma City in August 2016 for conditional second-round considerations; a Nuggets historical account traces its eventual No. 51 Monte Morris selection in 2017 to that deal. The rights thus became a player, followed by more draft capital. To avoid inflating the grade, the analysis credits the documented pick conversion, not Morris' entire later NBA production as though Denver had received him directly from Memphis in 2013.

sections.heading: A Fair Reading of Both Front Offices
sections.body: Memphis was coming off a 2013 Western Conference finals appearance and employed Marc Gasol as its starting center. Koufos, an 81-game starter for Denver in 2012-13, offered a credible reserve behind Gasol. He responded with 80 appearances and 22 starts in his first Grizzlies season, then 81 appearances and three starts in his second. That role was useful even though his raw scoring dropped from 8.0 per game as Denver's starter to 6.4 and 5.2 in Memphis. Denver's front office accepted losing that center in exchange for Arthur's shorter-stint forward profile and a future draft prospect. Both choices had clear roster logic; the retrospective Denver win rests on subsequent longevity and Lauvergne's later asset conversion, not on a claim that Memphis made an irrational choice.

sections.heading: Why the Separation Lasts
sections.body: The A/B- grade split is defensible if the evaluation considers actual usage and asset value without treating the trade as a landslide. Koufos offered Memphis 161 appearances as Gasol's backup, close to the maximum possible during his two years there. Arthur played 256 games for Denver across five seasons, while Lauvergne added 83 and generated conditional draft-pick value when dealt in 2016. The Nuggets also used one related 2017 choice on Monte Morris. That later pick path gives Denver an additional edge, but claiming the full career production of Morris as an automatic 2013 trade return would overstate the evidence. Memphis acquired the reliable center it needed; Denver extracted a longer and more versatile chain from its two incoming assets.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win — Denver A, Memphis B-. Arthur supplied five years of regular forward work and Lauvergne contributed 83 Denver games before becoming conditional draft compensation. The Nuggets' own historical review connects that later trade to the 2017 Monte Morris selection. Koufos gave Memphis valuable center depth for two seasons. Denver's second asset created the difference without requiring Memphis' return to be dismissed.

sections.heading: The Draft-Night Rights Swap That Sent Gobert to Utah
sections.body: Denver selected Rudy Gobert at No. 27 in the 2013 NBA draft and transferred his rights to Utah that same night. The Jazz gave up the rights to Erick Green, selected No. 46, together with cash. The Utah Jazz's subsequent signing announcement identifies those exact components, and the franchise's media guide separately confirms the draft-rights exchange. It was not a trade of an established NBA player for another NBA veteran, and it should not be merged with Utah's different draft-night arrangement involving Trey Burke, Shabazz Muhammad and Gorgui Dieng. The correct starting point is two prospects' draft rights and a cash payment.

sections.heading: Denver's 2013 Reasoning Favored a Different Prospect
sections.body: Denver's new leadership was working through a crowded, young roster and considered immediate shooting a need. In Associated Press reporting the following day, general manager Tim Connelly explained the appeal of Erick Green, the Virginia Tech guard who had led the NCAA in scoring at about 25 points per game. Moving down from the No. 27 pick to the No. 46 rights also avoided another guaranteed first-round rookie slot, while adding cash. This context explains why the Nuggets were prepared to make the exchange in June 2013. It does not establish that Green and the payment eventually compensated the franchise for what Gobert became.

sections.heading: Utah Acquired the Development Opportunity
sections.body: Utah's risk was the inverse of Denver's. The Jazz traded away a second-round selection and cash to secure the rights to a 21-year-old French center, then signed Gobert in July 2013. At acquisition, his length and defensive potential were easier to identify than the career that later unfolded. Gobert eventually earned four NBA Defensive Player of the Year awards, all after the initial rights purchase, which makes the NBA-value gap enormous in retrospect. Those honors substantiate the very high grade credited to Utah without pretending a mature defensive star was available on trade night. Utah had to draft, develop and play the player it obtained.

sections.heading: Gobert's Utah Defensive Peak Dwarfed Denver's Erick Green Return
sections.body: Utah acquired Rudy Gobert's No. 27 rights in June 2013 for Erick Green's No. 46 rights and cash, then signed the French center in July. Gobert grew into the Jazz's long-term interior defensive foundation and was selected as an NBA Defensive Player of the Year four times over his career. Denver pursued shooting and lower rookie salary commitments by moving down, but the rights to Green did not produce anything remotely comparable to Gobert's prime. This is why Utah's A+ and Denver's F are supported by identifiable team-specific results rather than by the draft slots alone. Utah's 2022 trade of Gobert to Minnesota created a separate set of assets; it does not alter what Denver gave Utah in 2013 or automatically place all later pick returns inside this original rights exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Jazz Win; Utah A-plus, Denver F, unchanged. Utah received Gobert's No. 27 draft rights from Denver in exchange for Erick Green's No. 46 rights and cash. The Jazz signed Gobert and ultimately developed a four-time Defensive Player of the Year. Denver's contemporary shooting and roster-cost logic was intelligible, but the direct realized returns were sharply unequal. The later Gobert trade with Minnesota is not an extra asset from this 2013 swap.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: How Utah Bought Gobert's Rights on Draft Night
featuredDeepDive.intro: Two picks, eighteen draft slots apart, changed franchises on June 27, 2013. Denver converted Gobert's No. 27 rights into Erick Green's No. 46 rights and cash; Utah accepted the development risk. This was distinct from the Jazz's separate Trey Burke transaction. The enormous difference in later defensive production explains why the canonical retrospective verdict grades Utah A-plus and Denver F.

sections.heading: The Twenty-Seventh Pick Carried Development Risk
sections.body: Utah was buying a scouting and development decision, not acquiring the fully realized defensive anchor familiar to later NBA audiences. Gobert had played in France, and the Jazz's July 2013 press release discussed his Cholet Basket production and remarkable wingspan before his first Utah season. The team could have missed badly on a late first-round center; instead, it found a player who later won four Defensive Player of the Year awards. The extraordinary upside belongs to the draft rights Utah bought that night. It should not be credited as though other established Utah players, signings or trades were bundled in the same Denver transaction.

sections.heading: Denver Preferred Cash and the Rights to a Shooter
sections.body: The Nuggets' return was not literally nothing. They received the 46th selection's rights, used on guard Erick Green, and financial consideration. Contemporary Associated Press coverage says Denver's new general manager wanted shooting and did not want to guarantee another first-round rookie contract on an already young squad. Green had strong Virginia Tech scoring credentials, giving the team a coherent reason to pursue him. The subsequent NBA outcome, however, did not approach Gobert's years of elite interior defense. Recording the motives is a way to explain the decision rather than to excuse the large value disparity that developed.

sections.heading: Keep Utah's Other Draft-Night Deal on Its Own Ledger
sections.body: On June 27, 2013, the Jazz also acquired Trey Burke's rights from Minnesota in a separate agreement involving Shabazz Muhammad and Gorgui Dieng. Utah's official Burke announcement documents that transaction independently. Gobert's rights came from Denver for Green's rights and cash, as established in the Jazz's Gobert signing release and media guide. Mixing the Burke exchange into this record would distort both Denver's outgoing value and Utah's original purchase price. Draft-night timelines are especially vulnerable to this problem because many teams trade newly selected players' rights in quick succession. Here the player-rights chain is short enough to keep exact.

sections.heading: The Preserved F and A-plus Reflect Different Outcomes
sections.body: The 2013 scouting judgment and the completed career record answer different questions. At the time, Denver chose a scorer from college and cash over the uncertainty of a late-first-round center; Utah wagered its second-round pick and payment on Gobert's athletic tools. The hindsight comparison overwhelmingly favors Utah because Gobert grew into a multiple-time NBA defensive award winner. Denver's reasoning can be accurately represented without treating it as an equivalent realized return. The stored Denver F and Utah A-plus are preserved unchanged while the prose explains their basis in this specific exchange. The different, later Minnesota transaction is not used as an additional 2013 asset.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The retained Jazz Win verdict follows the recorded June 27, 2013 exchange without enlarging it: Gobert's draft rights traveled to Utah; Erick Green's rights and cash went to Denver. Utah's 2013 press releases and media guide establish that ledger. The Nuggets had a plausible draft-night preference for a college scorer and a cheaper contract slot, but Gobert subsequently became a four-time Defensive Player of the Year. The much greater direct NBA value on Utah's side supports the preserved A-plus versus F grading. A later Minnesota–Utah Gobert deal, and Utah's separate draft-night Trey Burke deal, belong to their own historical accounts rather than to this initial purchase.

sections.heading: Golden State Identified the Missing Wing Before the Dynasty Began
sections.body: The Warriors had reached the 2013 playoffs behind Stephen Curry and a young core, but the roster still needed a large perimeter defender, secondary ball handler, and veteran capable of connecting lineups without dominating possessions. Andre Iguodala fit every requirement. Golden State could not simply sign him into existing cap space, so the front office built a three-team sign-and-trade with Denver and Utah while moving the contracts of Richard Jefferson, Andris Biedrins, and Brandon Rush. The complexity reflected how strongly the Warriors valued the fit.

sections.heading: Iguodala’s Value Was Greater Than His Scoring Average
sections.body: Iguodala accepted changing offensive responsibility and eventually a reserve role, decisions that made Golden State's best lineups possible. He could defend the opponent's strongest wing, initiate transition offense, handle the ball when Curry was pressured, and close games as a small-ball forward. His willingness to sacrifice helped establish the culture of a team that reached six Finals and won four championships during his tenure. The 2015 Finals MVP award was the most visible recognition of a broader role that remained valuable for years.

sections.heading: Utah Was Paid to Absorb the Salary Structure
sections.body: The Jazz did not acquire Iguodala, but their participation was essential. Utah accepted the contracts Golden State needed to move and received draft compensation for using cap space. That is a legitimate rebuilding strategy, and it produced a better outcome than Denver's limited return. The Jazz deserve credit for monetizing financial flexibility rather than pursuing a win-now player. A B grade reflects useful asset acquisition without pretending that the transaction transformed Utah to the degree Iguodala transformed Golden State.

sections.heading: Denver Had Little Leverage but Lost a Foundational-Level Outcome
sections.body: Iguodala was leaving in free agency, so Denver's ability to demand a premium package was limited. The sign-and-trade allowed the Nuggets to recover Randy Foye and a future second-round pick rather than lose the player for nothing. Foye supplied rotation shooting, but the return did not create a long-term core asset. Denver's D+ accounts for the leverage problem while recognizing the enormous realized-value gap between a modest recovery package and the player who became a championship connector for Golden State.

sections.heading: The Trade Helped Convert Promise Into a Repeatable Championship Model
sections.body: Golden State already had Curry, Klay Thompson, and Draymond Green, but Iguodala allowed the team to use those players in more flexible combinations. His defense made switching lineups credible, and his playmaking reduced the burden on Curry without removing shooting from the floor. The acquisition therefore did not merely add talent; it unlocked a style that could survive different playoff matchups. When Kevin Durant later arrived, Iguodala remained useful because his game did not require a fixed scoring hierarchy.

sections.heading: Golden State's Championship Return Justified the Acquisition Cost
sections.body: Golden State gave up future draft assets and sent Richard Jefferson, Andris Biedrins and Brandon Rush to Utah to make room for Andre Iguodala. The return paid off in four championship seasons: his perimeter defense and passing complemented Stephen Curry, while his 2015 Finals MVP recognized the impact he made after moving into the starting lineup. Utah collected draft compensation for taking on salary, supporting its B grade. Denver recovered Randy Foye and a second-round pick from a departing free agent, supporting its D+. The Warriors' A+ reflects the value of the player they received over multiple title runs without treating Iguodala as the sole cause of those championships.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Golden State wins with an A+, Utah receives a B, and Denver earns a D+. Iguodala became a four-time champion, 2015 Finals MVP, and the versatile defensive-playmaking link that made the Warriors' small lineups sustainable. Utah used cap space productively to collect draft compensation, giving the Jazz a solid secondary return. Denver recovered Foye and a second-round pick in a low-leverage sign-and-trade, but the package never approached Iguodala's impact. The Warriors solved multiple postseason problems with one acquisition and created value across an entire dynasty.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Andre Iguodala Was the Trade That Made Golden State’s Best Lineups Possible
featuredDeepDive.intro: Golden State's later championships can make the 2013 acquisition look inevitable, but the Warriors were still an emerging team when they pursued Iguodala. They paid draft capital, moved several contracts, and depended on Utah's cooperation to obtain a player whose box-score scoring was already declining. The front office was buying adaptability rather than volume. Iguodala's defense, passing, and willingness to change roles became essential to the system that followed, making this one of the clearest examples of fit producing superstar-level organizational value.

sections.heading: The 2013 Playoff Series Revealed the Need and the Opportunity
sections.body: Denver entered the 2013 playoffs as a 57-win team, while Golden State was a young sixth seed. The Warriors won the series and saw firsthand how Iguodala could defend, create, and adapt across positions. That summer, his departure signaled a change in Denver's competitive direction, and Golden State recognized an opportunity to add a veteran whose skills matched Curry's trajectory. The acquisition was not simply the recruitment of a respected player; it was a response to a postseason test that exposed what the Warriors could become with a more versatile wing.

sections.heading: Salary-Dump Costs Were Part of the Acquisition Price
sections.body: Golden State had to create financial room, which meant sending contracts and future picks to Utah. Those assets should not disappear from the grade merely because the championships followed. The Warriors paid a meaningful price and accepted future opportunity cost. The A+ reflects that the return overwhelmed those costs. Iguodala's ability to close games, stabilize bench units, and support multiple championship rosters generated far more value than the picks and salary flexibility surrendered to complete the sign-and-trade.

sections.heading: The Reserve Move Expanded Rather Than Reduced His Importance
sections.body: Steve Kerr's decision to bring Iguodala off the bench could have created conflict for a former All-Star. Instead, it gave Golden State a second-unit organizer and preserved the option to deploy its most dangerous small lineup when games tightened. Iguodala's acceptance of that role became a cultural signal: status would be subordinate to lineup function. His later insertion into the 2015 Finals starting lineup helped reverse the series. The same player could solve regular-season depth and championship-level matchup problems because his value was not tied to starting.

sections.heading: Utah’s Return Shows the Price of Cap-Space Cooperation
sections.body: The Jazz used available room to absorb Jefferson, Biedrins, and Rush and received draft compensation for facilitating Golden State's plan. That strategy did not create an immediate playoff star, but it converted financial flexibility into controllable assets. Utah's B recognizes competent rebuilding work in a transaction centered elsewhere. The Jazz accepted short-term roster inefficiency to collect future value, while Golden State paid the appropriate premium to open a championship window. Both sides executed their chosen strategy; the Warriors simply received the transformative basketball result.

sections.heading: Denver’s Loss Was Primarily the End of Control
sections.body: By the time of the sign-and-trade, Denver could not recreate a normal market for Iguodala. The important organizational loss had occurred when the relationship and contract timeline left the Nuggets without long-term control. Recovering Foye was better than receiving nothing, but it did not protect the value of a player who had helped a 57-win team. A D+ grade acknowledges the narrow options in July while still measuring the final return. Constraints explain why Denver accepted the deal; they do not make the outcome competitive with Golden State's.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Warriors earn an A+ because Iguodala's fit generated championship value far beyond his conventional statistics. He defended elite scorers, initiated offense, accepted a reserve role, won a Finals MVP, and remained useful across four title teams. Utah's B reflects responsible use of cap space to obtain draft assets. Denver's D+ reflects a limited recovery from a departing free agent rather than a freely chosen exchange of equal assets. Golden State paid a real transaction cost, but the acquisition became one of the central pieces of a repeatable dynasty system.

sections.heading: Houston Exchanged a Reserve Guard for a Young Wing
sections.body: On February 20, 2014, the Rockets traded Aaron Brooks to Denver for Jordan Hamilton. Houston announced the two-player swap, and the NBA deadline archive independently identifies the same deal with no draft picks or cash. Brooks had played 43 Rockets games without starting, averaging 7.0 points and 1.9 assists. Hamilton had appeared in 39 Nuggets games with 11 starts, scoring 6.8 points per game. Houston wanted more wing size; Denver gained an experienced guard able to run an offense. Brooks had a one-year Houston deal and the contractual ability to veto the move, but he agreed to it to seek playing time, a trade-day motive confirmed in Sports Illustrated reporting. Their pretrade numbers belong to the sending clubs, not to the new receiving-team production.

sections.heading: Brooks Started 12 Denver Games in a 29-Game Stay
sections.body: Brooks received more responsibility in Denver than he had held in Houston. He played 29 Nuggets regular-season games and started 12, averaging 29.0 minutes, 11.9 points and 5.2 assists. He logged 841 minutes, handed out 150 assists and shot 90.2 percent on free throws during that period. His 43 earlier Houston appearances in the same season are excluded from the Denver total. The results establish a useful short-term point guard rather than a new long-term franchise cornerstone. Brooks subsequently changed teams again, but his later court time does not belong to this receiving-team record.

sections.heading: Hamilton Supplied 21 Houston Games and One Start
sections.body: Hamilton played 21 Rockets games after the February trade, with one start and 16.6 minutes per appearance. He logged 349 total Rockets minutes, averaging 6.6 points and 2.9 rebounds while shooting 36.2 percent from beyond the arc. That is a legitimate reserve-wing return, but his 39 Nuggets games from the first part of 2013-14 are not Houston appearances. The team also did not directly acquire a pick or another player in this transaction. Hamilton later played for different franchises, and those future games cannot convert a 21-game Houston stint into a multi-season Rockets role.

sections.heading: Why Brooks Gave Denver More Immediate Value
sections.body: The Nuggets Win verdict grades Denver B-plus and Houston C-plus. Both sides traded a reserve with a chance at steadier minutes, but Brooks immediately became a larger part of the Denver rotation. He played 29 Nuggets games, started 12 and delivered 150 assists in 841 minutes, averaging 11.9 points and 5.2 assists. Hamilton appeared in 21 Rockets games, starting once and logging 349 minutes while supplying outside shooting and wing depth. Denver therefore received 492 more minutes and a primary reserve playmaker for the final stretch, even though Brooks did not become a long-term Nuggets fixture. Houston got a useful but shorter wing audition. Those are the two teams' post-trade contributions, not their performances before February 20 or the separate three-team deadline deal involving Denver.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win — Denver B+, Houston C+. Brooks supplied 29 Nuggets games, 12 starts, 841 minutes and 150 assists after the February 20 trade, averaging 11.9 points and 5.2 assists. Hamilton supplied 21 Rockets games, one start and 349 minutes at 6.6 points per game. Houston received a genuine reserve wing, but Brooks took on more minutes and ballhandling. Neither team received draft compensation, and later seasons at other franchises do not enter the measured return.

sections.heading: Denver Brought Back Afflalo for a Second Tour
sections.body: The June 26, 2014 deal sent Arron Afflalo from Orlando to Denver for Evan Fournier and the newly drafted rights to Devyn Marble. The Magic's transaction announcement and its July 2014 Marble signing release document each piece. Afflalo had led Orlando in scoring and was an experienced two-way guard, while Denver saw a chance to reunite with a player it had previously employed. The cost was a young guard and a second-round contract right, not two established veterans. The trade-date calculation reflected Denver's near-term backcourt needs, and it should not be rewritten as if either club knew exactly how Fournier would develop over the following seasons.

sections.heading: Fournier Found a Larger Role in Orlando
sections.body: Fournier had played 76 Denver games in 2013–14 and averaged 8.4 points, 2.7 rebounds and 1.5 assists. Orlando's October 2014 roster announcement confirmed those pretrade numbers and the incoming Marble rights. The Magic gave Fournier opportunities to handle the ball and develop as a scorer within a younger lineup. By the 2016–17 season, Orlando's own retrospective credited him with 17.2 points per game, and a 2021 transaction recap identifies him as a central Magic scoring option before his later move to Boston. That long stretch of actual Orlando production is the strongest documented outcome of the 2014 deal, distinct from any later Boston transaction.

sections.heading: Marble Was a Draft Right Before He Was a Player
sections.body: Devyn Marble's acquisition must be recorded as rights to the 56th choice in the 2014 draft, not as an established NBA player who had already contributed for Orlando. The Magic formally signed him on July 24, 2014 after receiving the pick rights from Denver. That later contract and his appearance on Orlando's roster are separate outcomes arising from the initial asset. Marble was a young Iowa prospect and not comparable at trade date to Afflalo's veteran scoring role. The important analytical distinction is that the incoming package contained two prospects with very different subsequent impact; Fournier carried most of the lasting on-court return.

sections.heading: Afflalo's Return Was Shorter Than Fournier's Tenure
sections.body: Afflalo began the 2014-15 campaign in Denver, but the second stint lasted only until a separate February 2015 deal with Portland. The shorter stay limits the direct on-court value Denver received from the June 2014 exchange; minutes Afflalo later played for Portland or New York are not part of the Magic's original compensation. Denver did receive veteran scoring and the flexibility to move him again, while Orlando acquired a younger guard whose production grew over several seasons. Those two timelines point to different benefits. The recorded Even Trade verdict and matching A-minus grades recognize Denver's immediate backcourt return alongside Orlando's longer-lasting Fournier investment, although readers could reasonably weigh the direct playing returns differently.

sections.heading: What the Veteran's First Denver Stint Adds to the Context
sections.body: Afflalo was already familiar to Denver fans because he had previously spent multiple seasons with the Nuggets before his move to Orlando. Returning him in June 2014 was therefore an effort to fill an immediate role with someone whose shooting and professional experience the organization could assess. That familiarity did not guarantee long-term retention, however. The February 2015 move to Portland was a new transaction and cannot be assumed to have been part of the compensation sent by the Magic. The original Orlando package was two younger assets: Fournier's player contract and Marble's rights. Keeping the timeline separate gives an honest description of what the Nuggets actually acquired and what was later traded again.

sections.heading: The Later Magic Tenure Informs, But Does Not Replace, the Grade
sections.body: Fournier's Orlando career extended far beyond his first audition. The Magic credited him with 17.2 points per game in 2016-17, and the franchise's March 2021 announcement recalled seven years of service before his separate move to Boston. Devyn Marble also reached Orlando's roster after the club obtained the rights to the 56th pick and signed him in July 2014, though Fournier supplied the overwhelming share of the package's NBA scoring value. Denver's original return was useful veteran play from Afflalo in a much shorter second stint before another transaction. The Even Trade verdict and matching A-minus grades weigh those returns as different kinds of value: near-term rotation fit for Denver, longer-term wing development for Orlando. Fournier's greater longevity is important context for judging that outcome rather than a reason to pretend later trades were included on June 26, 2014.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Published verdict: Even Trade, Denver A- and Orlando A-. The original June 2014 return was Afflalo to Denver for Fournier and Marble's draft rights. Orlando signed Marble later, and Fournier developed into a multi-season scoring starter; Denver moved Afflalo again in February 2015. Those later results provide useful hindsight without inventing assets or silently changing the archived grades.

sections.heading: Denver Paid a Protected Thunder First to Move McGee's Contract
sections.body: On February 19, 2015, Denver sent JaVale McGee, the draft rights to Chukwudiebere Maduabum and a protected Oklahoma City first-round selection to Philadelphia. The Nuggets received the NBA draft rights to Turkish guard Cenk Akyol. Denver's own same-day announcement identifies these pieces. Philadelphia's transaction accounting also records cash going to Denver, which the Nuggets' shorter announcement did not mention; the original canonical archive includes that consideration, so it is retained rather than silently deleted. The first-rounder was top-18 protected for 2015 and top-15 protected in 2016 and 2017, with second-round conversion terms after that. The central economic purpose was to move McGee's large remaining salary, not to exchange comparable active big men.

sections.heading: Akyol's Rights Were Transaction Consideration, Not Court Production
sections.body: Akyol had been selected No. 59 by Atlanta back in 2005 and was playing in Turkey when Denver acquired his rights a decade later. The Nuggets' official announcement described his then-current Galatasaray season, not an established NBA role. Denver was acquiring an asset it could legally hold, but it was not receiving 20-point NBA scoring or a center capable of replacing McGee. Contemporary reporting accurately described the move as financial relief for an injured, expensive player. Akyol's overseas statistics should not be conflated with NBA production for the Nuggets. The distinction explains why an on-court-only comparison can understate Denver's salary flexibility while an asset-chain review can overstate the rights if no NBA contribution ever followed.

sections.heading: The Protected First Conveyed in 2016 as Furkan Korkmaz
sections.body: The Thunder-derived first did not disappear into an undefined future claim. Its lottery protections were not triggered in 2016, and Philadelphia ultimately held the No. 26 first-round choice used on Turkish wing Furkan Korkmaz. That player outcome is a documented conversion of the exact conditional right transferred in February 2015. The protection sequence is important because the pick's eventual value was not an unprotected high lottery selection. Contemporary Philadelphia reporting says the 2015 protection was top 18 and the 2016 protection top 15, matching the recorded transaction conditions. This connection makes the Sixers' long-term payoff intelligible without crediting Denver's side with a prospect it did not receive.

sections.heading: McGee Was Waived; The Pick Was Philadelphia's Durable Return
sections.body: Philadelphia did not keep McGee as a long-term franchise center. He arrived while recovering from a left tibial stress fracture that had limited him to 17 Denver appearances in 2014-15, and the Sixers waived him on March 1, 2015, less than two weeks after the transaction. Maduabum's rights likewise did not turn into an established Philadelphia NBA contributor. The valuable lasting item was the converted pick associated with Korkmaz. That difference between near-term player minutes and contractual rights should be explicit: Philadelphia essentially used its available cap space to accept McGee's salary for a first-round draft asset. Denver obtained room to reorganize its obligations but lost the pick's upside.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The stored 76ers Win decision (Philadelphia A, Denver C) remains unchanged. Philadelphia acquired McGee, Maduabum's rights and a top-18/top-15-protected first that conveyed in 2016 at No. 26 Furkan Korkmaz. The Sixers waived McGee March 1, 2015. Denver moved a costly contract and received Cenk Akyol's rights; the preserved archive also lists cash consideration from Philadelphia, which its transaction record and a later official media guide document although the brief Nuggets announcement omits it. An exact cash figure has not been verified.

Denver received Cenk Akyol rights and relief from an injury-affected salary. The transaction records also identify cash consideration to Denver, absent from the Nuggets' shorter announcement. The site's existing Philadelphia-favored verdict is preserved.

sections.heading: Denver's Primary Announcement Establishes the Player-and-Pick Ledger
sections.body: The Nuggets announced the transaction on February 19, 2015 and named McGee, a protected Oklahoma City 2015 first and Chukwudiebere Maduabum's rights as the outgoing pieces. Cenk Akyol's rights were the announced return. McGee had played 17 Denver games that season, averaging 5.2 points and 2.8 rebounds while being paid like a much larger contributor. The contract economics, rather than the quality of Akyol's Turkish League season, explain the sacrifice of an extra draft right. Philadelphia's transaction ledger and a later official Golden State media guide also refer to cash considerations from the Sixers. Denver's shorter release omits cash, so its amount should not be invented; the archive preserves the canonical cash entry while labeling the disclosure difference.

sections.heading: The Pick Protection Changed the Price of Denver's Salary Relief
sections.body: The conditional first originated with Oklahoma City, meaning Philadelphia did not acquire a fresh Denver-owned lottery ticket. It was protected within the top 18 in 2015 and top 15 for 2016 and 2017. The pick conveyed at No. 26 in 2016, and Philadelphia selected Furkan Korkmaz. If the protections had stopped a first-round conveyance, the original terms identified alternative 2018 and 2019 second-round selections. None of those hypothetical later fallback rights should be added as separate realized incoming assets once the first conveyed. The trade therefore transformed Denver's short-term contract relief into one actual first-round prospect for Philadelphia; it is not a generic promise of perpetual future picks.

sections.heading: The Sixers Used Cap Space, Not McGee's Basketball Production
sections.body: Philadelphia's 2015 roster had the financial flexibility to accept a high-salary veteran while prioritizing draft rights. McGee had appeared only 17 times for Denver before the deal, with 5.2 points and 2.8 rebounds in 11.5 minutes a game, after seasons disrupted by injury. Philadelphia then waived him on March 1, 2015, leaving little Sixers playing return from the center himself. The transaction worked more like an acquisition of protected draft compensation for assuming an obligation than a conventional starting-center purchase. Maduabum's rights were another genuine ledger component, though no lengthy Sixers NBA playing tenure resulted from them. The key is to distinguish financial exposure from productive court service rather than treating both as interchangeable value.

sections.heading: Keep the Historical Grades Without Inventing Rights or Cash Amounts
sections.body: The stored verdict favors Philadelphia, 76ers Win, with a Sixers A and Denver C. The long-term argument is the protected first that became No. 26 Furkan Korkmaz, acquired for taking McGee's deal, while Denver received the Akyol rights and the flexibility to move on from a costly injured center. Some reporting and transaction histories include cash to Denver, while the Nuggets' official announcement listed only Akyol as the return; the cash amount is not verified, and the canonical entry stays unchanged pending a separate accounting review. The exact letters are editorial assessments, not an undisputed price for salary-cap relief. Keeping the grade and source distinction visible is better than pretending either club received an immediate star in February 2015.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Philadelphia A, Denver C and 76ers Win are the existing grades. The February 19, 2015 transaction moved McGee and Maduabum's rights with Oklahoma City's protected future first to the Sixers for Cenk Akyol rights and recorded cash. The first eventually conveyed at No. 26 in 2016 and produced Furkan Korkmaz, while Philadelphia waived McGee March 1, 2015. The Nuggets received contract relief rather than a comparable on-court big man. The Denver press release does not expressly list cash whereas a Philadelphia transaction history and later Warriors official guide do; the amount is unverified. Those separate dates, contract consequences and pick conversion explain the historical result without inventing a cash total or multiplying a conveyed first into additional imaginary future seconds.

sections.heading: Afflalo Brought Barton to Denver
sections.body: Denver moved Arron Afflalo and Alonzo Gee to Portland at the February 19, 2015 deadline, receiving Will Barton, Victor Claver, Thomas Robinson and a protected first-round pick. Portland wanted an established perimeter scorer for its immediate postseason push, and Afflalo supplied the near-term roster fit behind that decision. The Nuggets, by contrast, converted a veteran into several chances to create longer-term value. This wasn't a simple one-for-one exchange of equal-age wings. The extra young players and the future first meant Denver could benefit long after Portland's short Afflalo stint ended. The selection was lottery-protected during the initial 2016 and 2017 windows, so Denver had to follow the specific conveyance conditions rather than treat the outgoing agreement as an unconditional first.

sections.heading: Barton and the First Became the Durable Return
sections.body: Barton developed into a dependable Denver starter and remained part of the Nuggets' rotation for years. The incoming first carried lottery protection and ultimately conveyed in 2016 at No. 19, when Malik Beasley was selected. This is a concrete draft outcome rather than an abstract promise of a pick that might not have arrived. Claver and Robinson were recorded pieces of Denver's return, but they weren't the primary reason its grade reached A+. The combination of Barton's sustained minutes and a separately realized first-round choice gives the transaction two value streams rather than one temporary rental.

sections.heading: Portland Received a Shorter Competitive Window
sections.body: Afflalo made 25 regular-season appearances for Portland before leaving that summer, a tenure far shorter than Barton's subsequent Denver contribution. Gee was also part of the outgoing package, yet he wasn't the central consideration driving Denver's future. Portland was trying to improve a specific roster in February, a motive that can be understood without claiming the trade ultimately returned an equal amount of basketball. Denver's protected selection converted successfully and Barton became a long-term regular; the two outcomes make a stronger retrospective case than a mere claim that the Nuggets acquired more names.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win. Denver earns A+ for Will Barton's long tenure and the protected first that became No. 19 Malik Beasley, with Claver and Robinson also in the package. Portland receives D+ for the brief Afflalo return and Gee. The original urgency of Portland's deadline move doesn't eliminate the large difference in realized team value.

sections.heading: The February 2015 Package Was Both Barton and a Protected First
sections.body: Denver traded Arron Afflalo and Alonzo Gee to Portland on February 19, 2015 for Will Barton, Victor Claver, Thomas Robinson and a lottery-protected 2016 first-round pick. The Nuggets issued their own transaction announcement that day, confirming the exact package before any draft prospect had been selected. At the time, Barton was a 24-year-old reserve who had played 144 NBA games for Portland, and the pick would convey only if protection allowed. Denver was changing direction and adding younger options. Portland, sitting in the playoff race, bought a proven veteran wing. The protected first would eventually become the nineteenth pick, but the team could not know that outcome at the deadline. This distinction separates the actual trade-day risk from the unusually productive return recorded later.

sections.heading: Barton Turned the Trade Into 479 Denver Regular-Season Games
sections.body: Barton immediately played 28 Denver games in 2014-15, then appeared in 82, 60, 81, 43, 58, 56 and 71 games over the following seven seasons. Those season totals equal 479 Nuggets regular-season appearances between the trade and the end of 2021-22. His role grew well beyond the reserve minutes he had received in Portland; he started 71 games in 2021-22 and became an established wing alongside the emerging Nikola Jokic-led core. The 2015-16 campaign alone delivered 82 appearances and 14.4 points per game. Those are demonstrable Nuggets games attributable to an incoming trade asset. His years in a Trail Blazers uniform before February 2015 and his subsequent post-Denver career are not part of the acquiring team return.

sections.heading: Denver Used Portland’s No. 19 Pick on Malik Beasley
sections.body: The protected 2016 first-round right conveyed at No. 19, where Denver selected guard Malik Beasley. A 2019 Nuggets franchise-history article explicitly traces Beasley to the Portland Afflalo trade, removing any need to infer the draft chain from surnames or team records. Beasley played 22, 62, 81 and 41 Denver regular-season games across four seasons, for 206 total before a separate 2020 transaction sent him to Minnesota. In 2018-19, he appeared 81 times, made 18 starts and averaged 11.3 points while shooting 40.2 percent on three-point attempts. His subsequent playing time for the Timberwolves and other franchises is not extra Denver production. The acquired first was therefore a realized source of a second useful Nuggets wing, independent of Barton’s longer tenure.

sections.heading: Portland Received Twenty-Five Afflalo Games, Not Future Denver Output
sections.body: Afflalo appeared in 25 Portland regular-season games after the exchange, starting 19 and averaging 10.6 points. He shot 40.0 percent on three-point attempts during that stint, providing actual veteran perimeter help, although Portland lost its first-round series to Memphis in five games. Denver waived Victor Claver and Thomas Robinson within days of the trade, so the Nuggets value came primarily from Barton and the draft pick rather than extended service by those two forwards. The historical grades favor Denver A-plus against Portland D-plus and a Nuggets Win verdict, and those ratings can be explained through 479 Barton games and the No. 19 Beasley choice. Portland’s short competitive purchase was real; it simply produced fewer lasting team-specific assets than the younger package Denver retained.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The original Nuggets Win verdict and Denver A-plus versus Portland D-plus grades are retained. Denver gained 479 regular-season games from Barton and exercised the protected No. 19 first on Beasley, who logged 206 games for the Nuggets. Afflalo contributed 25 Portland games at 10.6 points before leaving. Claver and Robinson were quickly waived by Denver, and neither a later Beasley employer nor Barton’s prior Portland games should inflate this particular 2015 exchange.

sections.heading: Denver Moved Lawson for a Six-Part Return
sections.body: Denver traded Ty Lawson and a future second-round selection to Houston on July 20, 2015. The Nuggets acquired Nick Johnson, Kostas Papanikolaou, Pablo Prigioni, Joey Dorsey, cash and a protected first-round choice. The transaction came as Denver sought to move on from its former starting point guard. Houston instead hoped an established playmaker could help an ambitious roster immediately. Denver obtained several ways to recover value through contracts, young players and a future draft slot, whereas the Rockets concentrated much of their expected return in Lawson's basketball performance. That distinction helps explain why the trade had such different outcomes for the two clubs.

sections.heading: A Protected First Became Juancho Hernangómez
sections.body: The protected 2016 pick conveyed at No. 15 and was used on Juancho Hernangómez. That supplied Denver a named first-round outcome in addition to the incoming veterans, rather than an unresolved promise of an asset. Houston also received the 2017 second-round pick ultimately identified as No. 43 Isaiah Hartenstein. His later NBA career should not all be counted as direct Rockets value without checking the team's control and subsequent decisions. The first-rounder and the cash provided Denver concrete paths to rebuilding after Lawson's departure. Each side received a specified draft branch; they must not be merged or given the same player endpoint.

sections.heading: The Houston Lawson Tenure Was Brief
sections.body: Lawson's Houston stint ended in less than a full season and did not deliver the sustained backcourt contribution the Rockets had sought. The Nuggets' incoming player group had varied individual outcomes, but the protected first and financial options created a more enduring package for the rebuilding club. A historical comparison can recognize the idea behind Houston's move without turning a failed short-term acquisition into a long-term success. Denver's advantage rests on the actual No. 15 selection and the broader flexibility received. It does not require crediting the Nuggets for every later career move involving Hernangómez or Houston's pick, which were distinct transactions.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win. Denver earns A- for the six-part return led by a first-round choice used on Juancho Hernangómez, plus cash and multiple players. Houston receives F for its short Ty Lawson tenure and a 2017 second later identified with Isaiah Hartenstein. The grade follows realized team value rather than treating all future careers as direct production from this one trade.

sections.heading: The July 20 Agreement Exchanged Lawson for Five Forms of Value
sections.body: Houston announced on July 20, 2015 that it had acquired Ty Lawson and a 2017 second-round pick from Denver. The Rockets sent Nick Johnson, Kostas Papanikolaou, Pablo Prigioni, Joey Dorsey, cash and their lottery-protected 2016 first-round selection the other way. The official Houston release establishes which club paid the cash and which controlled the future first. Denver had selected Emmanuel Mudiay seventh overall weeks earlier and was changing its backcourt. Houston expected Lawson to provide a second playmaking guard next to James Harden. The first carried lottery protection, meaning its eventual No. 15 outcome was not guaranteed on trade day. The veteran contracts and cash gave Denver immediate roster flexibility, but the first-round choice would become its clearest sustained asset.

sections.heading: Lawson Played Only Fifty-Three Houston Regular-Season Games
sections.body: Lawson had averaged 15.2 points and 9.6 assists for Denver in 75 games during 2014-15. After joining Houston, he appeared in 53 regular-season games in 2015-16, starting 12 and averaging 5.8 points and 3.4 assists. The Rockets released him before the end of that season; he then played 13 games for Indiana. Those later Pacers games should not count as Houston trade production, just as his earlier 416 Denver appearances were not games newly created by Houston. His acquisition was a genuine short-term attempt to improve the Rockets rotation, but the actual receiving-team performance fell considerably below his Denver baseline. That explains Houston’s inherited F grade without pretending the deal produced no NBA minutes or that Lawson was a long-term Rockets starter.

sections.heading: No. 15 Juancho Hernangómez Was a Real Denver First-Round Outcome
sections.body: The protected pick from Houston conveyed at No. 15 in the 2016 draft, where Denver selected Juancho Hernangómez. The Nuggets own roster-history article expressly identifies the Lawson transaction as the source of that choice. Hernangómez played 62 Denver regular-season games in 2016-17, 25 in 2017-18, 70 in 2018-19 and 34 in 2019-20: 191 games for the receiving franchise. His 2018-19 season included 25 starts and 5.8 points per game. Denver then moved him to Minnesota in a separate February 2020 trade. The later Minnesota, Boston or Utah portions of his professional career are not extra Nuggets value from the original Lawson exchange. The received first was valuable because Denver actually converted it into a rotation forward, not merely because the initial package listed a conditional asset.

sections.heading: The Hartenstein Second Was Houston’s Separate Asset
sections.body: Houston also received Denver’s 2017 second-round pick and exercised the No. 43 selection on Isaiah Hartenstein. Both the Rockets’ original July 2015 release and the 2017 draft transaction ledger trace that right directly to this exchange. Hartenstein developed later in his career with multiple teams, but only his subsequent NBA service while actually under Houston control can be included in Houston’s receiving-team return. Denver’s incoming four-player group did not become a comparable long-term rotation core, and the 2016 first and cash carry much of the Nuggets outcome. The historical Nuggets Win verdict with Denver A-minus and Houston F can therefore acknowledge two authentic draft outcomes: No. 15 Hernangómez for Denver and No. 43 Hartenstein for Houston, without awarding either organization all of those players’ later achievements elsewhere.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win remains the archived verdict, with Denver A-minus and Houston F. The Nuggets converted Houston’s protected 2016 first into No. 15 Juancho Hernangómez, whose 191 Denver regular-season games provided real medium-term production. Houston got 53 Lawson games and an authentic No. 43 Isaiah Hartenstein 2017 draft right. Cash and the other four players belonged to Denver’s incoming package, but the 2016 first was its clearest lasting asset. Later Hartenstein playing success away from Houston is not a Rockets return from this trade.

sections.heading: A Draft-Night Rights Purchase for a Known Cash Price
sections.body: Denver sold the draft rights to Daniel Hamilton to Oklahoma City on June 23, 2016 for $730,000 in cash. The Nuggets received a fixed cash payment, and the Thunder obtained the chance to bring Hamilton into their development system. Unlike many older rights transactions, the financial consideration is recorded in the archive, so it need not be called an undisclosed amount. There were no veteran starters or other draft selections in the documented package.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Accepted Development Risk
sections.body: Hamilton was a young prospect rather than a ready-made starting NBA wing. The Thunder’s value was the ability to evaluate and develop him through their organization, with the possibility of later roster minutes. That rights control was basketball consideration even when immediate production was uncertain. Denver instead chose a definite $730,000 return and relinquished the option to use Hamilton. Both positions are intelligible roster decisions for a low-visibility draft-night exchange, and the dollar figure should not be inflated into a franchise-changing payment.

sections.heading: The Stored Winner Does Not Imply a Superstar Result
sections.body: The canonical grades are Oklahoma City B-plus and Denver D, resulting in Oklahoma City Thunder Win. Those letters express the archive’s assessment of the rights acquired versus the cash Denver received; they do not establish that Hamilton had a long starting career in Oklahoma City. The draft-rights opportunity and the precisely recorded monetary price belong in the same comparison. The earlier boilerplate’s generic claims about future draft chains are unnecessary for a trade containing only this prospect and cash.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Oklahoma City Thunder Win — Oklahoma City B-plus, Denver D. The Thunder acquired Daniel Hamilton’s draft rights; the Nuggets received $730,000. Oklahoma City gained control of a prospect it could develop, while Denver took a known financial return. The recorded advantage concerns those assets rather than any imagined additional pick or guaranteed future star.

sections.heading: What Changed Hands
sections.body: Denver traded Joffrey Lauvergne to Oklahoma City on August 30, 2016, for two conditional second-round assets. The local ledger associates those selections with the 2017 No. 49 pick, Vlatko Čančar, and No. 51, Monte Morris. Both draft-right lines carry top-35 protection language for 2017 with a later unprotected alternative. That wording must be distinguished from the eventual pick identifications until the precise conveyance terms are corroborated against an independent primary source.

sections.heading: Two Protected Second-Round Picks Actually Conveyed in 2017
sections.body:
Denver’s August 30, 2016 agreement sent Joffrey Lauvergne to Oklahoma City for two conditional 2017 second-round selections. The Nuggets’ official historical media guide describes one Thunder-origin and one Memphis-origin conditional second, while the draft-chain record gives a 2017 top-35 protection with unprotected 2018 fallback. Both picks conveyed the next year, becoming No.49 Vlatko Cancar and No.51 Monte Morris. The 2017 Denver draft-night release confirms both numbered selections; it does not leave the eventual pick identities hypothetical.

The difference between that factual conveyance and the 2016 trade-day risk is important. Lauvergne was available to the Thunder immediately as an interior reserve, while Denver had two future rights dependent on draft positions. After the picks did convey, Denver gained one guard whose role steadily expanded and another longer-term forward with a smaller team role. The Nuggets A grade against the Thunder C+ is based on that actual combined realization, not merely on receiving two abstract picks.

sections.heading: Morris Was the Main Denver Return; Cancar Provided a Secondary Path
sections.body:
Monte Morris, drafted at No. 51 in 2017, spent several years developing into a reliable low-turnover reserve guard. He made all 82 appearances in 2018-19 and eventually started 74 Denver games in 2021-22, filling in as a lead guard during Jamal Murray’s recovery. Vlatko Cancar, selected two places earlier at No. 49, had a smaller role but stayed connected to the Nuggets during the team’s championship period. Neither player was an established rotation player on the original 2016 transaction date.

In July 2022 Denver sent Morris AND Will Barton to Washington for Kentavious Caldwell-Pope and Ish Smith. The future 2023 Nuggets championship team benefited from Caldwell-Pope, but it would be incorrect to assign his whole value solely to the old Lauvergne deal. The 2016 transaction produced the Morris rights that later supplied part of that package, alongside Barton; that is the traceable asset path.

sections.heading: The Thunder Received Useful Lauvergne Minutes but Soon Repackaged Him
sections.body:
Oklahoma City did not get an empty contract. Lauvergne appeared in 50 games for the Thunder in 2016-17 and averaged 5.7 points and 3.7 rebounds in 14.8 minutes. That is tangible short-term frontcourt depth. On February 23, 2017, however, the Thunder traded him to the Chicago Bulls with guards Anthony Morrow and Cameron Payne in return for Taj Gibson, Doug McDermott and an unprotected 2018 second-round pick. The Thunder’s official release documents the entire list of participants and Lauvergne’s production.

It is reasonable to note that Lauvergne was one of three outbound Thunder players later used in a roster upgrade. It is not reasonable to credit the full Gibson/McDermott package as if it were a one-for-one Lauvergne return. The canonical C+ reflects some use and transferable depth while Denver’s two eventual picks produced years of player control and a useful future transaction component.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win — Denver A, Oklahoma City C+. The 2016 Lauvergne agreement gave Denver two conditional seconds that actually became 2017 No.49 Vlatko Cancar and No.51 Monte Morris; Morris started 74 games for the Nuggets in 2021-22 and was later part of a separate deal with Will Barton. Lauvergne played 50 Oklahoma City games before moving to Chicago in a three-player Thunder outgoing package. The draft results make Denver the stronger recipient without pretending the entire downstream Chicago or Washington returns came from one player.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: From Joffrey Lauvergne to Monte Morris: Denver’s Two 2017 Second-Round Returns
featuredDeepDive.intro: The Nuggets sent Joffrey Lauvergne to the Thunder on August 30, 2016 and received two conditional second-round picks, one originating with Oklahoma City and the other with Memphis. The uncertainty was real on trade day, yet both selections conveyed at the 2017 draft: No.49 Vlatko Cancar and No.51 Monte Morris. Morris grew into a rotation guard and occasional starter for a contender, while Cancar played a more limited part. The Thunder obtained immediate Lauvergne minutes and later included him among several players sent to Chicago. The Denver A versus Oklahoma City C+ comparison rests on those separate, traceable outcomes and not on the false equivalence of a 2016 pick option and a ready-made guard.

sections.heading: The Two Second-Round Picks Had Different Origins
sections.body:
Denver’s official historical franchise ledger places the trade on August 30, 2016: Lauvergne went to Oklahoma City, while Denver acquired a conditional 2017 second from the Thunder and another originally associated with Memphis. Pro Sports Transactions links the conditions to 2017 top-35 protection and an unprotected 2018 fallback. The eventual draft results are separately established: Denver chose Vlatko Cancar at No.49 and Monte Morris at No.51 on June 22, 2017.

The original deal cannot be rewritten as the Thunder directly handing over NBA-ready Cancar and Morris in 2016. Both were still future draft outcomes. That protects a key distinction between the rights Denver bought at the time and what those rights eventually became. The fact that both picks actually arrived in 2017, however, means today’s retrospective analysis can describe their players and subsequent development without treating the outcomes as speculative.

sections.heading: Monte Morris Turned No.51 into Several Years of NBA Guard Service
sections.body:
The best return was the No.51 selection. Morris played only three Denver games in 2017-18 before becoming a genuine rotation player: he appeared in 82 games in 2018-19 and earned Sixth Man of the Year votes. He handled the ball alongside Nikola Jokic without generating many turnovers, and the team increasingly trusted him as an organizer and spot-up shooter. In 2021-22 he started 74 of 75 Denver appearances while the backcourt lacked Jamal Murray.

In July 2022 the Nuggets traded Morris and Will Barton to Washington for Kentavious Caldwell-Pope and Ish Smith. The official Denver release includes BOTH outgoing players. Morris is therefore part of the paper trail behind a later championship roster addition, but the entire value of Caldwell-Pope should not be assigned to a single 2016 second-round pick. The large direct return is already visible in Morris’s playing time and gradual role increase.

sections.heading: Cancar’s Contribution Was Smaller, Without Making His Rights Worthless
sections.body:
Denver used the No.49 pick on Slovenian forward Vlatko Cancar. Unlike Morris, he did not become a major consistent starter. He provided depth, positional flexibility and occasional scoring for a team developing its rotation around Jokic, Jamal Murray and other longer-tenured contributors. He also remained associated with the Denver roster during the organization’s 2023 championship season. That is a modest but realized return on a second-round pick rather than evidence that both acquired picks generated equal value.

Keeping the two draft products distinct is essential for the grade. One selection yielded years of lead-guard minutes and later transferable contract value; the other brought a more limited forward contribution. The Nuggets still come out ahead of Lauvergne’s brief Thunder stay, but the source record does not support describing Cancar as an All-Star or a championship-level primary performer.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Used Lauvergne Before a Broader Bulls Trade
sections.body:
The Thunder had immediate use for Lauvergne as a reserve big man. Their February 23, 2017 official release records 50 games, 5.7 points and 3.7 rebounds in 14.8 minutes that season. He then joined Anthony Morrow and Cameron Payne in an outgoing package to Chicago, which sent Taj Gibson, Doug McDermott and an unprotected 2018 second to Oklahoma City. These are verified parties and transaction participants, not an inferred one-for-one exchange.

The roster decision did create some Thunder option value, but Lauvergne was not the only price for the three-part return. Comparing the deals fairly, Oklahoma City gained one season of rotation depth and used the player in a later bundle; Denver’s picks gave it several seasons of guard production, another forward and eventual trade flexibility. The original grades A and C+ reflect that asymmetry without declaring the Thunder gained nothing.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win — Denver A, Thunder C+. Two conditional 2017 seconds for Joffrey Lauvergne conveyed as No.49 Vlatko Cancar and No.51 Monte Morris. Morris provided several years of useful Nuggets guard work and later joined Will Barton in Denver’s separate 2022 Washington transaction. Lauvergne played 50 games for Oklahoma City, then moved to Chicago with Anthony Morrow and Cameron Payne in a broader package. Denver secured the stronger direct basketball return, while neither later multi-asset package can be credited to one inherited player alone.
