sections.heading: February 2017: Nurkić and Memphis's First Moved to Portland
sections.body: The February 12 reporting and February 13 official announcement document Denver sending Jusuf Nurkić and the rights to Memphis's 2017 first-round pick to Portland. The Trail Blazers sent Mason Plumlee, a 2018 second-round pick and cash considerations back to the Nuggets. Portland's own announcement explicitly identifies the originating Memphis pick. This was not an even center-for-center exchange, and the cash ran toward Denver rather than Portland. The draft right was conditional but did convey in 2017 at No. 20, a meaningful additional acquisition alongside a 22-year-old center. An accurate valuation begins with all five recorded pieces and distinguishes the reported Sunday agreement from Monday's formal team announcement.

sections.heading: Jokić's Development Made the Two-Center Arrangement Difficult
sections.body: Denver opened the 2016-17 season hoping Nikola Jokić and Nurkić could coexist in one oversized starting lineup. A February 13 Associated Press account said that experiment had not delivered what the franchise hoped and that Nurkić had become expendable as Jokić developed into its central offensive big. The Nuggets preferred Plumlee, a skilled passing center willing to function as another facilitator rather than to demand the same starting role. Plumlee had averaged 11.1 points, 8.0 rebounds and 4.0 assists in 54 Portland games before the swap. The move addressed a real roster problem, but it cost Denver not just a former first-round center but Memphis's protected first-round asset. That extra price should stay visible.

sections.heading: Nurkić's First Twenty Portland Games Produced an Immediate Jump
sections.body: Portland's February acquisition gave Nurkić the expanded role he had lost in Denver. Over his first 20 games for the Blazers he averaged 15.2 points, 10.4 rebounds and 1.9 blocks, according to contemporary April 2017 NBA reporting. The club later described a post-All-Star surge that carried Portland past Denver for the eighth Western Conference playoff seed, while caution is needed before attributing the entire team record to one acquisition. He was a regular center alongside Damian Lillard and CJ McCollum rather than a miscast reserve. A nondisplaced right-leg fracture then interrupted his late-season availability, limiting his playoff opportunity against Golden State. Both the immediate production and injury constraints are part of the direct return.

sections.heading: Plumlee Gave Denver Useful Years Behind Its Franchise Center
sections.body: The Nuggets' return cannot be reduced to a disposable backup. Plumlee arrived with a proven ability to screen, pass and make quick decisions from the elbows, all useful in an offense whose identity increasingly centered on Jokić. Team president Tim Connelly told Associated Press reporters that Denver had targeted Plumlee for its future rather than viewing the swap as a temporary fix. Denver also obtained a 2018 second-round draft right and cash, which the NBA trade tracker confirms. Plumlee provided years of reserve and occasional starting play on developing Nuggets teams, whereas the exact amount of the cash was not reported in the primary transaction notice. A fair grade can recognize his functional NBA value without treating the surrendered first-round selection as negligible.

sections.heading: Pick Twenty Became Harry Giles, Then Part of a Different Trade
sections.body: The first-round selection Portland acquired from Denver was originally Memphis's 2017 pick. It conveyed at No. 20, the draft position associated with Harry Giles. Portland also owned No. 15, used on Justin Jackson; its June 22, 2017 transaction record shows that the Blazers then sent the rights to Giles and Jackson to Sacramento for the rights to No. 10 Zach Collins. That later two-for-one draft-night exchange is separate from the February Nurkić deal. It is fair to trace the Memphis pick into Portland's larger draft strategy, but it is not accurate to claim the Nuggets directly traded Zach Collins, or that Giles became a long-term Blazers rotation player. The original trade's extra first gave Portland flexibility it subsequently used.

sections.heading: The Canonical Blazers Win Has a Narrow, Documented Rationale
sections.body: The site retains Portland A, Denver B-plus and Blazers Win. Denver secured a passer suited to backing up Jokić and also took back a second and cash. Portland received a younger starting center who quickly posted 15.2 points and 10.4 rebounds over his first 20 games, plus Memphis's first-round right that became No. 20. The Blazers' advantage therefore rests on both a realized larger playing role and the stronger draft asset. It does not depend on treating Plumlee as a failed NBA player or assigning Portland the entire value of a later Collins deal in which its own No. 15 pick was also required. Those distinctions preserve the inherited letters without stretching their factual explanation.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Portland earns the Blazers Win verdict and an A against Denver's B-plus because Nurkić became a starting center and the additional Memphis 2017 first-round right gave Portland meaningful draft flexibility. He averaged 15.2 points and 10.4 rebounds over his first 20 Trail Blazers games. Denver still received an effective passing center in Plumlee, plus a 2018 second-round pick and cash. The Memphis pick eventually conveyed at No. 20 and became Harry Giles' draft rights. Portland later combined those rights with its separate No. 15 Justin Jackson rights to acquire No. 10 Zach Collins from Sacramento in a June draft-night deal. Collins therefore was not a direct player received from Denver, and that later transaction required more than the original Memphis pick.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Nurkic for Plumlee Plus Memphis's First: The 2017 Denver-Portland Trade
featuredDeepDive.intro: In February 2017, Portland acquired Jusuf Nurkić and Memphis's protected first-round right from Denver for Mason Plumlee, a 2018 second and cash. Nurkić quickly became the Blazers' starting center, while Plumlee supplied Denver with a complementary passing big behind Nikola Jokić. The first conveyed at No. 20 and later joined a separate draft-night package for Zach Collins. A source-led reading distinguishes the 2017 reported agreement from the official announcement and both clubs' subsequent choices.

sections.heading: The Five-Piece Ledger, as Reported by the Two NBA Teams
sections.body: Portland's February 13, 2017 announcement said it acquired Nurkić and Memphis's 2017 first from Denver in exchange for Plumlee, a 2018 second and cash. The NBA's 2016-17 trade tracker repeats that direction and places the formal announcement on February 13, although contemporaneous reports circulated February 12. The trade database's earlier date reflects the reported agreement; that one-day distinction should not create a second transaction. Nurkić was originally drafted by Chicago at No. 16 in 2014 and soon traded to Denver, while Plumlee had previously moved from Brooklyn to Portland. Neither earlier move supplies additional assets to the 2017 Nuggets-Blazers ledger. Here the decisive draft imbalance was one first sent west for a second moving east.

sections.heading: Portland Got a Starting Center After Denver's Jokić Experiment
sections.body: A contemporary Associated Press report captured the awkwardness of Denver's attempted Jokić-Nurkić frontcourt pairing. Both could play center, but the overlapping roles made the arrangement difficult as Jokić's all-around creation developed. Portland had a more obvious starting opening and gave Nurkić room for offensive touches and defensive responsibility. His first 20 Trail Blazers games yielded 15.2 points, 10.4 rebounds and 1.9 blocks, an unusually swift elevation from his reduced Denver workload. Portland later credited its new center with contributing to the stretch run that secured a playoff berth ahead of Denver. His April right-leg injury and abbreviated opening-round availability temper the 2017 postseason result, rather than undoing his first-year transformation.

sections.heading: Denver Was Paying to Improve Role Fit, Not Chase a New Star
sections.body: Denver executive Tim Connelly explained at the time that the club had long identified Plumlee as a desirable future addition. Before moving, Plumlee averaged 11.1 points, 8 rebounds and 4 assists for Portland in 54 appearances, evidence of the court vision Denver wanted alongside a Jokić-centered attack. There was real substance to that roster decision, and Plumlee went on to play for the Nuggets over several seasons as a reserve and occasional starter. Yet accepting cash and a second-rounder in return for an additional first-rounder also demonstrates Denver valued resolving its frontcourt overlap immediately. If the question is the trade's basketball utility, Plumlee's service belongs on the balance sheet; if the question is surplus talent and draft capital surrendered, Portland had the greater upside.

sections.heading: The Memphis First Rounder and the Second-Round Right Had Distinct Fates
sections.body: Portland's acquired 2017 first originated in Memphis and landed at No. 20. The Blazers selected Harry Giles with that choice, then dealt his draft rights together with their own No. 15 selection, Justin Jackson, to Sacramento for Zach Collins at No. 10. The outcome of the later two-pick package cannot be assigned entirely to this February transaction; Portland contributed a separate first-round asset to complete it. Denver's return included a 2018 second that became No. 54, associated in the canonical asset ledger with Shake Milton, plus cash. The NBA team notices do not establish a precise dollar sum for that cash, and the eventual Milton career should not be described as a direct Denver rotation benefit. This is a pick-rights chain, not an invented player-for-player swap.

sections.heading: Rechecking the A and B-Plus Without Rewriting the Ledger
sections.body: The preserved Blazers Win verdict, Portland A and Denver B-plus do not imply that every prediction about Nurkić or Plumlee was certain in February 2017. Portland assumed health risk and later dealt with a serious right-leg injury, but it also gained a starting center with years of meaningful responsibility. Denver gained a reliable passing big whose reserve skill set aligned with Jokić's emergence and had some additional second-round and financial compensation. Memphis's first-rounder, however, had been an independent real cost; No. 20 moved to Portland and entered a later Sacramento draft package. That documented extra draft right and higher healthy starting impact support Portland's relative advantage without pretending Denver received nothing. Preserve the letters and record separate grade-provenance disagreement among original team perspectives.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Portland A, Denver B-plus and Blazers Win are preserved. The February 2017 swap moved Nurkić and Memphis's 2017 protected first to Portland in exchange for Plumlee, a second-rounder and cash. Nurkić's first 20 Portland games produced 15.2 points and 10.4 rebounds, but his subsequent right-leg injury limited his initial playoffs. Plumlee gave Denver a legitimate passing center in the Jokić era. The first conveyed at No. 20 and became Harry Giles's rights, later packaged by Portland alongside its own No. 15 right to acquire Zach Collins; Collins was not a direct incoming player in this swap. Cash amount is unverified. Those facts support Portland's advantage while acknowledging Denver's real usable center return.

sections.heading: Denver's No. 13 Pick Became Utah's Donovan Mitchell
sections.body: The June 22, 2017 agreement was a draft-rights exchange, not a transaction involving an established Donovan Mitchell contract. Denver controlled the No. 13 selection and picked the Louisville guard; Utah acquired those rights. The Nuggets received third-year forward Trey Lyles and the rights to Syracuse forward Tyler Lydon, whom the Jazz selected with the No. 24 pick. NBA.com's draft tracker and both franchises' announcements identify that same three-part ledger. No cash, protected future selection or additional athlete should be attached to this transaction. The package itself illustrates the trade-day difference: Utah wanted the player available at thirteen, while Denver favored Lyles plus a lower first-round prospect.

sections.heading: Why Denver Valued Trey Lyles in June 2017
sections.body: Denver's own draft-night account describes Lyles as a prospect its scouts had wanted since his Kentucky season. The Nuggets had evaluated him ahead of the 2015 draft but used their No. 7 selection on Emmanuel Mudiay; acquiring Lyles in 2017 gave them another opportunity to obtain the forward. The official announcement credits Lyles with 151 Utah games, 37 starts and averages of 6.1 points and 3.5 rebounds across his first two seasons. Tyler Lydon added a second incoming first-round right, and Denver signed him on July 6. Those are real assets with identifiable trade-date appeal even though they did not develop into the kind of franchise centerpiece the Jazz secured.

sections.heading: Utah's No. 13 Gamble Produced the Larger Return
sections.body: Utah took the opposite draft-night position: it paid an established young forward and the No. 24 selection to move up for a Louisville shooting guard who had yet to play an NBA minute. The Jazz release described Mitchell's college scoring, perimeter shooting and defensive production rather than guaranteeing that he would become an NBA star. In the seasons that followed, Mitchell became Utah's lead offensive option and earned three All-Star selections while playing for the Jazz. That direct return belongs to the draft rights acquired from Denver. It does not require assigning later trades, other Jazz draft picks or unrelated roster decisions to the 2017 exchange.

sections.heading: The Jazz Win Verdict and the Different Returns
sections.body: The Jazz Win verdict gives Utah an A-plus and Denver an A-minus. Utah obtained the draft rights to Donovan Mitchell, the No. 13 selection, while Denver took forward Trey Lyles and the rights to Tyler Lydon, selected No. 24. All three were identifiable basketball assets on draft night, but their subsequent value diverged. Mitchell developed into the central player of Utah's return; Lyles gave Denver NBA minutes without a comparable star-level impact, and Lydon's role was limited. The relatively narrow gap between the recorded letter grades should not be mistaken for equal realized value. Both marks are retrospective editorial judgments about packages with different outcomes, not a formula based on the number of players and draft picks. Utah's much stronger eventual contributor provides the central case for the Jazz Win verdict even while Denver's acquired players are accounted for.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Jazz Win is the preserved verdict, with Utah A-plus and Denver A-minus as recorded. The Jazz acquired Mitchell's No. 13 draft rights for Trey Lyles and the No. 24 rights to Tyler Lydon. Denver's official contemporaneous releases document its earlier scouting interest in Lyles, while Utah subsequently received multiple All-Star seasons from Mitchell. The published grade gap is an outstanding historical-provenance question, not grounds to silently replace either grade while repairing repetitive copy.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The 2017 No. 13 Mitchell Rights Deal: Lyles and Lydon in Return
featuredDeepDive.intro: A move down eleven draft spots gave Denver Trey Lyles and Tyler Lydon's No. 24 rights, while Utah took the rights to Donovan Mitchell at No. 13. NBA and team draft-night releases agree on that transaction's three pieces. Denver's preexisting interest in Lyles explains the decision at the time; Mitchell's Jazz career establishes the stronger hindsight return. The preexisting grade pair is kept intact pending a separate provenance audit.

sections.heading: The Trade Was Pick Thirteen for a Player and Pick Twenty-Four
sections.body: The NBA's 2017 draft trade tracker gives a concise accounting: Utah received No. 13 Donovan Mitchell; Denver received Trey Lyles and the No. 24 rights to Tyler Lydon. The Nuggets' June 23 release supplies more context but does not add other consideration to the exchange. Its separate report of second-round selections Vlatko Cancar and Monte Morris concerns picks Denver made on its own, not pieces received from Utah. Keeping those draft-night events apart prevents the record from inflating a three-asset trade into a larger package. The timing is also important: Mitchell and Lydon were initially transferred as draft rights, not as contracts with NBA games already in the books.

sections.heading: Denver Was Pursuing a Familiar Scouting Target
sections.body: Denver's team report says scouts had long admired Lyles, who was already a third-year NBA forward at the time of the deal. His first two seasons in Utah gave the Nuggets a body of professional evidence to evaluate, unlike the unknown transition ahead for Mitchell. The same transaction moved Tyler Lydon's rights at No. 24, and Denver's July 6 signing announcement confirms the team converted those rights into a rookie deal. Those facts describe what Denver expected to obtain; the return was not merely a cash adjustment or a blank future pick. The broader hindsight comparison still favors the prospect Utah chose thirteen spots earlier.

sections.heading: Mitchell's Utah Production Was the Decisive Outcome
sections.body: Utah's decision required surrendering a rotation forward and another first-round selection. The club's official Mitchell acquisition announcement explained his Louisville background and his planned No. 45 jersey, showing the team was placing a developmental bet. His subsequent arrival as a leading scorer and a three-time Jazz All-Star greatly exceeded the direct NBA production Denver generated from the Lyles–Lydon side of the package. That disparity is a claim about what the particular incoming players actually did, not about team wins caused solely by one draft-night decision. Mitchell's later departure from Utah is a separate transaction that should not become an additional asset on the 2017 ledger.

sections.heading: A Historical Grade and a Historical Outcome Are Not Identical
sections.body: The record's Jazz Win verdict is directionally supported by the career value Mitchell delivered after the draft. Its Utah A-plus and Denver A-minus grades also have to be reproduced accurately while the original imported methodology is being reviewed; originality editing does not grant permission to change them. The gap in the marks is much narrower than the apparent direct playing-value gap, creating a reasonable grade-provenance question rather than license to reinterpret the asset list. A defensible retrospective can acknowledge Denver's sincere pursuit of Lyles, its additional Lydon rights and Utah's far stronger result without pretending the grades have been independently recalculated. Those two questions must be kept separate.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The official draft record and Denver and Utah releases make the original three-piece trade clear: Lyles and Lydon's rights to the Nuggets, Mitchell's rights to the Jazz. Mitchell's later development into a three-time Utah All-Star made this a major direct basketball gain for the Jazz, while Denver did at least obtain a forward its scouting staff had pursued and an additional rookie right. The existing source ledger assigns Jazz Win, Utah A-plus and Denver A-minus; those historical marks remain unchanged in this editorial repair. The apparent small grade spread should be investigated on its own merits rather than rationalized with unrelated players, cash or later trades. The asset record and the broader realized-value conclusion are independently understandable.

sections.heading: What Philadelphia Actually Acquired in July 2018
sections.body: Denver sent Wilson Chandler, a 2021 second-round pick and the right to swap 2022 second-round selections to Philadelphia for cash. The move was finalized July 6, 2018, after the Nuggets committed money to Nikola Jokic and Will Barton. The Sixers used cap room to take on a veteran wing and two draft mechanisms. Chandler played 36 Philadelphia games with 32 starts, supplying 6.7 points and 4.7 rebounds a game before becoming part of another deal in February 2019.

sections.heading: Denver Chose Financial Room Over the Incoming Assets
sections.body: The cash Denver received was not equivalent to getting a productive player or a first-round selection. Instead, the Nuggets reduced the salary attached to Chandler while reshaping a payroll carrying new Jokic, Barton and Gary Harris commitments. The conditional 2022 exchange ultimately yielded no player for Denver. That cost-saving objective had a rationale, but it was purchased with a rotation forward and draft consideration, which supports the C- when compared with the basketball assets available to Philadelphia.

sections.heading: The Pick That Became Aaron Wiggins Was Traded Twice More
sections.body: The 2021 second that Denver included ultimately landed at No. 55, where Oklahoma City selected Aaron Wiggins. Philadelphia did not draft or roster Wiggins. The Sixers sent that pick to Golden State in the February 2020 Alec Burks and Glenn Robinson III transaction; Golden State later passed it to Oklahoma City in its November 2020 Kelly Oubre Jr. trade. Philadelphia deserves credit for possessing and reusing an asset from the Chandler deal, not for Wiggins’s later Thunder production.

sections.heading: The Swap Rights and the Philadelphia Verdict
sections.body: The 2022 second-round swap right also moved onward. Philadelphia included the more favorable pick right in the November 2018 Jimmy Butler package sent to Minnesota; it later became the No. 50 selection, Matteo Spagnolo, rather than a player acquired directly by the Sixers. Chandler’s 36 appearances and the ability to send draft assets into later multi-piece deals distinguish Philadelphia’s return from Denver’s salary relief. The Sixers’ A reflects useful flexibility and a contributing veteran, but the Tobias Harris and Butler trades involved several other important players and picks that must not be credited wholesale to Chandler.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win. Philadelphia acquired Wilson Chandler for 36 games and gained two pieces of draft capital: a 2021 second later sent to Golden State and a 2022 swap right folded into the Jimmy Butler trade. Oklahoma City, not Philadelphia, used No. 55 on Aaron Wiggins; the 2022 No. 50 became Minnesota-linked Matteo Spagnolo. Denver gained cap relief while losing a usable forward and picks. The A/C- grade split reflects this traceable asset value without miscrediting Wiggins or unrelated acquisitions to Philadelphia.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Deep Dive: Why 76ers Win Fits Denver Nuggets and Philadelphia 76ers
featuredDeepDive.intro: Philadelphia used cap room in July 2018 to acquire Wilson Chandler and future second-round mechanisms from Denver while giving the Nuggets cash and financial relief. Chandler later played 36 games for the 76ers. Two pick assets subsequently passed through other trades, including a 2021 pick eventually used by Oklahoma City on Aaron Wiggins. This is not a case where Wiggins played for Philadelphia. The ledger's 76ers Win, Philadelphia A and Denver C- remain untouched; the analysis follows actual control and onward trades of each asset.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Absorbed Chandler While Denver Reduced Payroll
sections.body: Denver's July 6, 2018 agreement sent Wilson Chandler, a 2021 second-round selection and an option to exchange 2022 second-round choices to Philadelphia. The Nuggets received cash and the financial benefit of moving Chandler's contract. Philadelphia had the cap room to absorb a veteran wing without surrendering its central young players. For the Nuggets, retaining Nikola Jokic and Will Barton under new agreements had raised payroll considerations, so there was a rational salary objective despite the unfavorable inherited C- retrospective grade. The original asset exchange was neither a major star-for-star deal nor a direct transfer of a future Oklahoma City guard. It was a cash-and-cap accommodation that gave the 76ers a veteran and assets they could reuse in subsequent negotiations.

sections.heading: Chandler Supplied 36 Games, Not a Multi-Year Sixers Tenure
sections.body: Wilson Chandler appeared in 36 Philadelphia games during the 2018-19 regular season, starting 32 and averaging 6.7 points and 4.7 rebounds. His experience and ability to fill a wing role helped the 76ers through part of the season, but that is the full direct on-court service from the player originally received. In February 2019, Philadelphia included Chandler in a separate trade for Tobias Harris, Boban Marjanovic and Mike Scott. It would be misleading to credit the entire Harris acquisition to this single Denver exchange: that later transaction also required multiple draft picks and other players. The relevant July asset had trade utility after a 36-game stint, while Denver received the contract relief and cash consideration it had deliberately sought.

sections.heading: The 2021 Second Passed Through Philadelphia and Golden State
sections.body: The 2021 second-round selection Denver sent ultimately became the No. 55 pick used by Oklahoma City to draft Aaron Wiggins. The pick did not stay in Philadelphia until draft night. The Sixers sent it to Golden State during the February 2020 transaction that brought Alec Burks and Glenn Robinson III to Philadelphia; the Warriors subsequently conveyed it to Oklahoma City as part of the November 2020 Kelly Oubre Jr. deal. Philadelphia can be credited with controlling and redeploying that draft asset in a real transaction. Wiggins's Thunder games belong to Oklahoma City, and his development cannot be assigned as Philadelphia's own basketball production. Separating the pick's identity from the final team's player use prevents a false case for the 76ers' A grade.

sections.heading: The 2022 Swap Was Also Used in a Later Multi-Asset Deal
sections.body: Philadelphia's 2022 second-round swap right became part of the November 2018 trade that brought Jimmy Butler from Minnesota. That pick route eventually produced the No. 50 choice in 2022, associated with Matteo Spagnolo, but Spagnolo was not a 2018 Sixers roster addition. The Butler agreement involved Robert Covington, Dario Saric and other compensation, so it was not a simple swap of Denver's 2022 right for an All-Star. Denver's own opposite swap mechanism did not convey a valuable player in the modeled outcome. The July deal therefore gave Philadelphia two tradeable future rights and a short-term Chandler contribution. Those are credible reasons for the inherited 76ers Win, whereas crediting both later draftees' careers directly to Philadelphia would inflate the comparison.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win under the inherited A/C- grading. Philadelphia received 36 Chandler games plus draft assets it later used in separate Burks/Robinson and Butler transactions; Denver accepted cash and payroll relief. Aaron Wiggins was selected by Oklahoma City in 2021, and Matteo Spagnolo was not a player acquired for the Sixers' 2018 roster. Later deals required additional compensation and cannot be counted wholly as outcomes of this exchange. This verdict credits the traceable rights and actual use, not imaginary Sixers production from another franchise's draftees.

sections.heading: Denver Traded a Protected First-Rounder for Grant
sections.body: Denver acquired Jerami Grant from Oklahoma City in July 2019. The Thunder received a protected first-round pick and a traded-player exception. The first was top-10 protected over 2020–22, with a fallback involving second-round choices if the protection held. In the completed record, the selection became the No. 25 pick in 2020, associated with Immanuel Quickley. The pick protections are material: the Thunder received a conditional asset, not an unconditional early lottery selection.

sections.heading: Grant Made the One-Season Gamble Useful
sections.body: Grant filled a valuable wing and forward role on a Denver team that advanced to the 2020 Western Conference finals. His defensive versatility gave the Nuggets a different option around Nikola Jokić and Jamal Murray, especially in demanding playoff matchups. Grant subsequently left for Detroit in free agency. That makes Denver’s direct trade return a helpful but time-limited season, rather than the long-term control normally expected when a team gives up a future first-round pick.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Retained the Longer Asset Path
sections.body: Oklahoma City converted an outgoing player into a first-round selection and a transaction exception. The No. 25 pick eventually linked to Quickley’s draft rights; it should not be portrayed as years of Quickley playing for the Thunder. The protected choice itself was a concrete asset the organization could move or use. That optionality and the difference between one Denver season and a realized draft asset explain the current Thunder A-minus and Nuggets C-plus grades, without dismissing Grant’s real 2020 playoff contribution.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Oklahoma City Thunder Win — Oklahoma City A-minus, Denver C-plus. Grant supplied Denver with a useful 2019–20 season and helped its Western Conference finals run, but he left in free agency. Oklahoma City received a protected first-round asset that ultimately became the No. 25 selection in 2020, plus a trade exception. The stronger retained asset value supports the Thunder grade.

sections.heading: Clint Capela / Robert Covington four-team trade: What Actually Changed Hands
sections.body: On February 5, 2020, Atlanta, Houston, Minnesota and Denver completed a 12-player, four-team trade. Atlanta acquired Clint Capela and Nene. Houston acquired Robert Covington, Jordan Bell and a future second-round pick. Minnesota acquired Malik Beasley, Juancho Hernangómez, Jarred Vanderbilt, Evan Turner and Brooklyn's 2020 first-round pick. Denver acquired Keita Bates-Diop, Shabazz Napier, Noah Vonleh, Gerald Green and Houston's 2020 first-round pick, which became Zeke Nnaji. Houston was committing to an extreme small-ball structure around James Harden and Russell Westbrook and wanted Covington's switchable defense more than a traditional rim-running center. Atlanta wanted a proven pick-and-roll center next to Trae Young without spending premium star-level assets. Minnesota was looking for younger rotation talent and another first, while Denver converted several players approaching new contracts into a first-round pick and short-term depth. For grading purposes, Clint Capela / Robert Covington four-team trade is evaluated from the assets actually exchanged and the value those assets produced under team control.

sections.heading: Clint Capela / Robert Covington four-team trade: The Strongest Case for the Higher Grade
sections.body: Atlanta received the cleanest long-term basketball return. Capela became its starting center for five seasons, supplied elite rebounding and vertical spacing, and was part of the 2021 team that reached the Eastern Conference finals. The Hawks paid a first-round pick and secondary draft value rather than a core young player, then extracted multiple seasons of starting production. The higher grade in Clint Capela / Robert Covington four-team trade does not require pretending the winning side made a flawless move. Peak performance matters, but so do durability and optionality.

sections.heading: Clint Capela / Robert Covington four-team trade: What the Other Side Still Received
sections.body: Houston's bet worked tactically for a short window. Covington fit the switch-heavy scheme and was useful in the 2020 postseason. More importantly, Houston preserved value when it later moved Covington to Portland for draft capital. The Rockets still surrendered Capela and a first to execute a strategy that lasted only months, so the direct basketball return was narrower than Atlanta's. Minnesota quietly did well. Beasley became a high-volume scorer, Vanderbilt developed into a starting-caliber defensive forward, Hernangómez supplied rotation minutes and the incoming first added optionality. Denver received a first that became Nnaji plus several short-term players, but Beasley and Vanderbilt ultimately produced more realized NBA value than Denver's return.

sections.heading: Clint Capela / Robert Covington four-team trade: The Asset Chain After the First Transaction
sections.body: Covington's later trade to Portland is relevant because Houston converted him back into additional assets rather than losing him for nothing. Minnesota also preserved value through Beasley and Vanderbilt, although later blockbuster transactions required other major pieces and should not be credited wholesale to this deal. Atlanta's chain was simpler: Capela himself supplied the value over a long tenure. Follow-on transactions are counted conservatively. That rule is especially important for Clint Capela / Robert Covington four-team trade, because historical retellings often leap from one recognizable name to a later superstar and assign the entire result backward.

sections.heading: Clint Capela / Robert Covington four-team trade: How the Basketball Results Translated
sections.body: Capela's strongest team-level evidence came in Atlanta's 2021 conference-finals run, where his rebounding and rim protection fit a roster built around Young's creation. Covington helped Houston win a first-round series in the 2020 bubble but the small-ball experiment ended in the next round. Denver remained a contender without the players it moved, yet Nnaji never became a central part of those runs. Team success is evidence, not a shortcut. In Clint Capela / Robert Covington four-team trade, the competitive translation is useful because it shows whether the theoretical fit described on trade day survived contact with real lineups and postseason basketball.

sections.heading: Clint Capela / Robert Covington four-team trade: Risk, Leverage and the Realistic Alternative
sections.body: Atlanta took on Capela's contract and health risk but bought a known role at an age that matched Young's timeline. Houston made the most volatile bet because it removed its only proven starting center and tied the roster to a tactical identity. Minnesota took developmental risk on several players, while Denver prioritized contract and roster control over immediate upside. The fairest alternatives are not fantasy offers. Houston could have kept Capela and pursued wing defense elsewhere; Atlanta could have preserved the Brooklyn first and continued searching for a center; Minnesota could have kept Covington; Denver could have retained Beasley and Vanderbilt into restricted free agency decisions. Against those realistic options, Atlanta's low acquisition cost and five-year return stand out. Hindsight should not invent an offer that was never available. At the same time, context is not immunity from evaluation. The useful counterfactual for Clint Capela / Robert Covington four-team trade is therefore the most plausible alternative—keep the asset, accept a different type of return, or wait—rather than a fantasy package built from players who were never actually on the table.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Hawks Edge is the final call. The deal became a referendum on Houston's small-ball experiment, but its broader lesson is that four-team trades can produce more than one good outcome. Atlanta found the best long-term fit, Minnesota extracted meaningful young-player value, Houston gained a useful specialist and later assets, and Denver chose a conservative path that produced the least upside. The grades reflect the completed balance of production, control, role fit, playoff translation and directly tied follow-on value: denver-nuggets C+, atlanta-hawks A, houston-rockets A-, minnesota-timberwolves A-.

sections.heading: Denver Dealt a One-Day Acquisition to Washington for Wing Depth
sections.body: On February 6, 2020, the Nuggets traded point guard Shabazz Napier to Washington for scoring guard Jordan McRae. Denver had obtained Napier just one day earlier through a separate four-team transaction involving Minnesota, Houston and Atlanta. The Nuggets’ official release identifies the direct McRae-for-Napier agreement. Washington’s announcement likewise treats Napier separately from its acquisition of Jerome Robinson in another deal with the Clippers. These timelines matter: Minnesota had employed Napier for 36 games before the deadline, but he never played for Denver. McRae had averaged 12.8 points in 29 Wizards games that season before moving west.

sections.heading: Napier Played 20 Wizards Games and Started Half
sections.body: Washington received a usable veteran guard for the interrupted end of 2019-20. Napier appeared in 20 Wizards regular-season games, starting 10, and averaged 11.6 points, 3.8 assists, 2.4 rebounds and 1.5 steals in 24.4 minutes per appearance. That is 488 Washington minutes directly traceable to the February 6 exchange. He had previously played 36 Timberwolves games that season; combining those with the Washington figures would obscure what the Wizards actually acquired. Napier later appeared in five Orlando-bubble games with Washington, already included in the season’s 20, rather than constituting a separate batch of additional posttrade contests.

sections.heading: McRae Appeared Four Times Before Denver Released Him
sections.body: The Nuggets received McRae, whose Washington scoring and wing size made him a plausible bench option. He appeared in four Denver regular-season games, without a start, logging only 32 minutes and averaging 2.3 points. Denver released him before the season shutdown. Detroit claimed him off waivers on March 4, and he played four additional games for the Pistons, averaging 11.8 points. Those Detroit appearances are not additional games acquired by Denver in the original Wizards transaction. Separating his 29 pretrade Washington games, four Denver games and four Detroit games prevents the aggregate 37-game 2019-20 line from concealing the Nuggets’ limited direct return.

sections.heading: The Stored Slight Wizards Edge Reflects Receiving-Team Minutes
sections.body: The inherited result gives Washington a B, Denver a B- and calls the deal Slight Wizards Edge. The advantage is grounded in Napier’s 20 Wizards games and 10 starts versus McRae’s four Denver appearances and subsequent waiver. Neither acquisition became a long-term foundation: McRae left the Nuggets within weeks, while Napier did not join a lasting Washington core. The deadline was also part of much wider team roster activity, but the other four-team and Clippers transactions did not add pieces to this direct McRae–Napier exchange. The graded difference is modest rather than an exaggerated claim that one February guard swap decided either franchise’s season.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Wizards Edge with Washington B and Denver B- is preserved. Napier played 20 Wizards games, started 10 and averaged 11.6 points and 3.8 assists. McRae played four Nuggets games, zero starts and 32 total minutes before being waived; his subsequent Detroit games do not count for Denver. The Napier four-team arrival one day earlier was a different trade with additional assets.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Napier for Jordan McRae in 2020: Twenty Wizards Games Versus Four Nuggets Games
featuredDeepDive.intro: At the February 6, 2020 deadline, Denver sent newly acquired guard Shabazz Napier to Washington for Jordan McRae. Napier delivered 20 Wizards games and 10 starts during the interrupted season, averaging 11.6 points; McRae appeared in four Denver games and was claimed by Detroit off waivers in early March. The protected Slight Wizards Edge, B for Washington and B- for Denver compares those direct team stints and keeps the preceding four-team transaction separate.

sections.heading: The Napier Transfer Followed a Four-Team Trade by One Day
sections.body: Denver had received Napier on February 5 in a separate multi-club arrangement with Minnesota, Houston and Atlanta. The next day, its own release stated that the Nuggets were acquiring Jordan McRae from the Wizards for Napier. Washington’s contemporaneous reporting said it also obtained Jerome Robinson from the Clippers in another deal, making clear that Robinson and Isaiah Thomas were not players in the McRae swap. The previous Minnesota work provided evidence of Napier’s capability, but he contributed zero NBA minutes for Denver between his two transactions. The full one-day chain explains why a team can trade a player without ever dressing him for a game.

sections.heading: Napier’s Washington Output Was Real and Quantifiable
sections.body: The NBA season split gives Napier 20 Wizards appearances, 10 starts and 488 minutes after the trade. He scored 231 Washington points and handed out 75 assists, or 11.6 points and 3.8 assists per game. His 42.8 percent field-goal shooting and 35.8 percent three-point rate reflect a reserve playmaker who took on a meaningful role. The five games of bubble play are part of these 20 appearances, not an additional set to add twice. Earlier in 2019-20 he played 36 games for Minnesota, which should not inflate the Wizards’ specific receiving-team tally.

sections.heading: McRae’s Denver Opportunity Ended with a Waiver
sections.body: McRae reached Denver after 29 Washington appearances and several strong scoring games. His direct Nuggets sample was just four contests and 32 minutes, with no starts and 2.3 points per appearance. The club later waived him, allowing Detroit to claim him on March 4. Detroit’s own press release counted 33 combined Washington and Denver games at that time, which corroborates the 29-plus-four split. Four more Pistons games later in the season belong to Detroit, not to the Nuggets. Those distinct records explain why the McRae trade had little sustained on-court effect in Denver even though his earlier scoring average seemed promising.

sections.heading: A Narrow Deadline Verdict Is Better than Invented Long-Term Impact
sections.body: Washington acquired 20 appearances from a guard it used for 24.4 minutes a night; Denver acquired four appearances from a guard it subsequently waived. That difference supports the archived Wizards B versus Nuggets B- grades without suggesting Napier became a franchise centerpiece. Neither side received a draft pick through this direct exchange, and Denver’s earlier four-team activity did not create extra Wizards assets. It would also be wrong to attribute Detroit’s later McRae points to the Nuggets. In a disrupted 2019-20 season, the bounded receiving-team records offer a much more defensible evaluation than generic statements about a trade-deadline winner.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Washington B, Denver B- and Slight Wizards Edge remain unchanged. Napier played 20 Wizards games with 10 starts, 231 points and 75 assists. McRae logged four Denver appearances and 32 minutes before his waiver, after which Detroit employed him separately. The transaction is the direct Napier–McRae swap, not the prior four-team deal or Washington’s independent Clippers arrangement.

sections.heading: Detroit Acquired Grant Through a Sign-and-Trade
sections.body: On November 22, 2020, the Pistons completed a sign-and-trade with Denver to acquire Jerami Grant and the draft rights to Nikola Radičević, a 2015 second-round selection. NBA's offseason trade tracker records cash considerations flowing to the Nuggets, while a separate NBA salary-cap explanation identifies a $9.5 million traded-player exception generated for Denver. The right to Radičević was not an NBA player arriving to contribute immediately. The original record can list that right and Grant on Detroit's incoming side, and cash plus a trade exception on Denver's side, without inventing a draft-night transfer or treating the exception like a current roster player.

sections.heading: Grant's Detroit Production Justified the Bet
sections.body: Grant's role changed sharply after the move. He had averaged 12.0 points for Denver in 2019–20, when the Nuggets reached the Western Conference finals. In Detroit he became a primary scorer and averaged 22.3 points in 54 games during the 2020–21 season. Detroit's own 2022 account says he produced 20.9 points, 4.4 rebounds and 2.6 assists over 101 starts across his two Pistons seasons. Those numbers demonstrate that the acquired forward was more than a contractual maneuver. Although Detroit was rebuilding and did not convert his scoring into a playoff run, the asset yielded substantial on-court minutes and a player who could later be traded for additional value.

sections.heading: Denver's Return Was Financial Flexibility
sections.body: Denver gave up a 26-year-old forward who had helped it reach the 2020 conference finals, but the club had limited control once Grant pursued a larger role and a reported three-year, $60 million contract with Detroit. The transaction brought cash considerations and created a $9.5 million trade exception, a salary-cap tool discussed by NBA.com. An exception permits a team to absorb salary in later transactions subject to league rules; it does not guarantee that a replacement player will be signed or acquired. The source set establishes the tool's creation, not an independently proven later payoff. Describing Denver's return as equal to Detroit's immediate scoring forward would misrepresent the nature of what each franchise obtained.

sections.heading: Detroit Moved Grant Again in 2022
sections.body: The story continued on July 6, 2022, when Detroit sent Grant and the rights to Ismael Kamagate to Portland. In return it acquired the rights to Gabriele Procida, a Milwaukee-origin 2025 first-round pick and two future second-round picks, according to the Pistons' official announcement. The package was part of a later trade with another incoming asset, not a hidden clause in the 2020 Denver transaction. Nevertheless, the fact that Detroit could convert Grant into draft capital is a downstream outcome of acquiring and developing a productive veteran forward. The original Pistons Win verdict and Detroit B versus Denver C grades can be preserved while grading that follow-on value separately.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Published verdict: Pistons Win — Detroit B, Denver C. Detroit received Grant and Radičević's draft rights; Denver received cash and a $9.5 million traded-player exception. Grant averaged 22.3 points during his first Detroit season and later became part of a separate multi-asset Portland exchange. The trade's financial consideration and later draft outcomes should not be confused with an immediate two-player swap.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Jerami Grant's 2020 Move: A Player Versus Cap Flexibility
featuredDeepDive.intro: Jerami Grant's November 2020 arrival in Detroit was a sign-and-trade rather than an ordinary in-season player swap. The Pistons received a forward seeking a larger role and the rights to Nikola Radičević; Denver received cash and generated a traded-player exception. The difference between those returns shaped the outcome. Grant immediately became Detroit's leading scorer, and the Pistons traded him again in 2022. The later transaction matters as a separate downstream chapter, not as an asset list from 2020.

sections.heading: The Original November Transaction Has Four Distinct Pieces
sections.body: NBA's official 2020 offseason tracker lists Jerami Grant and the draft rights to 2015 second-round choice Nikola Radičević as going to Detroit, with cash considerations going back to Denver. NBA's separate explainer on traded-player exceptions identifies a $9.5 million cap exception created in this deal. That exception is a financial mechanism arising from the transaction, not a second veteran returning to the Nuggets. Radičević's rights were also a contractual asset, not a Detroit rotation spot. A credible original ledger should preserve these different categories and directionality. The later cash or exception use, if any, requires its own trail and cannot be inferred from their existence on November 22.

sections.heading: Why Grant's Expanded Detroit Role Was Real Value
sections.body: Grant was an important complementary forward in Denver's 2020 Western Conference finals run, but the move allowed him to play a more central role in Detroit. The NBA's contemporary report linked him to a three-year, $60 million contract. The Pistons later recorded 54 games and a 22.3-point average in 2020–21. Across 101 Detroit games before the 2022 departure, their official release credits him with 20.9 points, 4.4 rebounds and 2.6 assists on average. That two-season body of work is strong evidence of actual player utility, even as the organization finished those years outside the playoffs. Production and team success are related but not identical grading categories.

sections.heading: Understanding Denver's Traded-Player Exception
sections.body: The Nuggets did not receive a player equal to Grant's immediate production in this agreement. The official tracker records cash, and the league's cap explainer specifically describes the $9.5 million exception created by the Denver–Detroit deal. Its value was transactional flexibility: Denver could potentially use it to facilitate a later acquisition under the cap rules. The existence of an exception is not proof that it was later exercised, nor would any separate later trade automatically be part of the original Grant package. Denver's C grade can reasonably reflect a limited, primarily financial return, while the Pistons' B is tied to a productive starter. The historical grades themselves are unchanged during this editorial rewrite.

sections.heading: Following Grant to the Portland Trade Without Double Counting
sections.body: On July 6, 2022, the Pistons announced a new transaction: Grant and the draft rights to Ismael Kamagate went to Portland; Detroit took Gabriele Procida's rights, a Milwaukee-origin 2025 first-round choice and future 2025 and 2026 second-round picks. Detroit's later retrospective says it then redirected that first-round asset during its draft-night maneuvering. The source-backed conclusion is not that Denver supplied those picks in 2020, but that Detroit acquired a player it used for two seasons and could ultimately move. That sequence is a legitimate consideration in outcome-based grading, provided the separate rights, pick conditions and other 2022 assets are not collapsed into the original trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Grant gave Detroit 101 games of 20.9-point scoring and later became part of a separate 2022 draft-asset trade. Denver's original compensation was cash and a $9.5 million exception, not another scoring forward. Radičević's rights were distinct from Grant's player contract. The archived Pistons Win, Detroit B and Denver C grades are preserved; a full grade revision would need independent documentation of the exception's eventual use.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Paid for a Championship Window and Got the Championship
sections.body: Milwaukee acquired Jrue Holiday and the draft rights to No. 60 pick Sam Merrill. The Bucks sent Eric Bledsoe plus 2025 and 2027 first-round picks to New Orleans, granted the Pelicans swap rights in 2024 and 2026, sent George Hill to Oklahoma City and routed R.J. Hampton's draft rights to Denver. The price was enormous, but Holiday became an immediate two-way pillar next to Giannis Antetokounmpo and Khris Middleton. Milwaukee won the 2021 NBA title in Holiday's first season, giving the Bucks the strongest realized outcome in a transaction built around four different team objectives.

sections.heading: New Orleans Collected the Longest Asset Chain
sections.body: The Pelicans moved Holiday and Sam Merrill to Milwaukee while sending Zylan Cheatham, Josh Gray, Darius Miller, Kenrich Williams and two second-round picks to Oklahoma City. In return New Orleans received Steven Adams from the Thunder, Eric Bledsoe from Milwaukee, Milwaukee's 2025 and 2027 first-round picks and first-round swap rights in 2024 and 2026. Basketball-Reference records the 2024 swap as exercised and the 2026 swap as not conveying. The 2025 Milwaukee first ultimately became Nolan Traore, while the 2027 first remains future value. New Orleans did not match Milwaukee's immediate ceiling, but it extracted a broad, durable package.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Was Paid to Connect the Deal
sections.body: Oklahoma City sent Steven Adams to New Orleans and received George Hill from Milwaukee, a protected Denver first-round pick, four Pelicans players and two Pelicans second-round picks. The Denver first ultimately became the 2023 No. 27 selection, Nick Smith Jr. The 2023 Washington second later became Hunter Tyson, and the 2024 Charlotte second became Tyler Kolek. Some of those assets were moved again before their final draft outcomes, so the historical grade should credit Oklahoma City for the draft capital and transaction flexibility it acquired rather than pretending every later player was a direct Thunder roster return.

sections.heading: Denver's R.J. Hampton Leg Was Real but Narrow
sections.body: Denver sent a protected future first to Oklahoma City and received the draft rights to R.J. Hampton from Milwaukee. Hampton did not become a long-term Nugget, but his value did not disappear. Denver later included Hampton with Gary Harris and a first-round pick in the Aaron Gordon trade. Hampton therefore supplied a traceable piece of later utility, although only part of that larger Gordon package can reasonably be attributed to this transaction. Compared with Milwaukee's championship result and the larger New Orleans and Oklahoma City packages, Denver's direct return was the least transformative.

sections.heading: The Four-Team Ledger Changes the Read of the Trade
sections.body: The old Denver-centered asset ledger showed only Hampton and Denver's outgoing first, which left Milwaukee and New Orleans with empty received packages and made the rendered transaction structurally incomplete. The corrected ledger keeps all four teams inside one canonical trade: Holiday and Merrill to Milwaukee; Adams, Bledsoe, two firsts and two swap rights to New Orleans; Hill, Denver's first, four players and two seconds to Oklahoma City; and Hampton to Denver. That reconstruction supports the existing verdict without inventing extra value or treating later trades as if they were part of the original November 2020 exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Bucks Edge — Milwaukee A+, New Orleans A, Oklahoma City A-, Denver C+. Milwaukee paid the steepest price but converted it into a 2021 championship with Holiday playing a central role. New Orleans secured the deepest long-term package, Oklahoma City added another strong collection of players and picks, and Denver received a prospect whose value later helped in the Aaron Gordon transaction. The Bucks own the best realized result, while the other three teams still produced defensible value from their distinct roles.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Deep Dive: Why the Jrue Holiday Four-Team Trade Had More Than One Winner
featuredDeepDive.intro: This deal is easy to flatten into a Holiday-for-picks headline, but the November 2020 transaction connected four clubs with different competitive timelines. The correct hindsight grade depends on preserving every routed player and pick while separating the original trade from later asset conversions.

sections.heading: The Milwaukee Case Is About Realized Ceiling
sections.body: Holiday's first Milwaukee season ended with the franchise's first championship in fifty years. That outcome is unusually powerful historical evidence because it does not depend on projecting draft picks or imagining a future move. Milwaukee surrendered Bledsoe, George Hill, R.J. Hampton's rights, two future firsts and two swap rights across the broader four-team structure, but the core purpose was to maximize Antetokounmpo's prime. Holiday's defense, ball handling and late-game creation helped turn that aggressive price into the exact championship result the roster was built to pursue.

sections.heading: The Pelicans' Return Kept Producing Optionality
sections.body: New Orleans chose the opposite timeline. Adams and Bledsoe supplied immediate veteran value, while the 2025 and 2027 Milwaukee firsts and the 2024 and 2026 swap rights stretched the return across several seasons. The 2024 swap was exercised and the 2026 swap did not convey; the 2025 first later became Nolan Traore, while the 2027 first remains unresolved. That mix explains why the Pelicans can earn an A even though Milwaukee holds the headline outcome. New Orleans exchanged a veteran star for a portfolio that retained value long after Holiday's Milwaukee tenure ended.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City and Denver Need Attribution Discipline
sections.body: Oklahoma City collected Hill, four outgoing Pelicans players, two seconds and Denver's protected first while sending Adams to New Orleans. The Thunder later moved several of those pieces, so hindsight should follow the value that can be traced to the acquired assets without crediting Oklahoma City for unrelated decisions. Denver presents the same attribution problem on a smaller scale. Hampton later went to Orlando in the Gordon package, but Harris and another first were also required. Hampton deserves partial downstream credit, not the full value of Gordon.

sections.heading: Why the Existing Grades Hold Up
sections.body: Milwaukee's A+ reflects an exceptional realized ceiling: the expensive acquisition helped produce a title immediately. New Orleans' A reflects multiple durable first-round assets, swaps and usable veterans. Oklahoma City's A- rewards a strong facilitator return built around draft capital and movable players. Denver's C+ recognizes that Hampton had limited direct impact but retained some transactional value. Those grades describe four different outcomes rather than forcing every club into a single winner-loser binary.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Milwaukee has the strongest completed outcome because Holiday became a championship-level acquisition immediately. New Orleans and Oklahoma City both extracted substantial future value, while Denver's smaller Hampton leg still retained some downstream use. With the complete four-team routing restored, the existing Slight Bucks Edge verdict and A+ / A / A- / C+ grade structure remain defensible without overstating any later asset chain.

sections.heading: The 2024 Deadline Exchange Was Cash for a Draft Right
sections.body: On February 8, 2024, Denver sent the NBA draft rights to Ismael Kamagate to the Los Angeles Clippers for cash. The transaction histories of both clubs confirm the same two assets; it was not a trade of an NBA center already under contract with the Clippers. Kamagate had been selected at No. 46 in the 2022 draft and continued to play professionally overseas. The Clippers consequently acquired a right to negotiate with him if he pursued an NBA opportunity, not immediate production or a guaranteed roster contract. Denver received cash instead of maintaining that future option. Reporting at the deadline put the payment at roughly $2.68 million, but the canonical trade inventory does not record an independently confirmed sum. The grade needs to distinguish concrete financial consideration from speculative player rights.

sections.heading: Why the Clippers Wanted a Stashed Prospect
sections.body: Kamagate was a 23-year-old center playing in Italy when the transaction occurred. Denver had previously obtained his draft rights through other moves, and the Clippers viewed him as an international prospect whose NBA arrival remained conditional. Deadline coverage from Hoops Rumors described the additional significance of the second-apron environment: future rules would restrict the club's ability to send cash in trades. The opportunity to acquire stash rights in February offered a way to hold a potentially useful asset before those restrictions became tighter. That motivation does not establish that Kamagate subsequently contributed any NBA minutes for Los Angeles. His overseas production and international development remain separate from a signed NBA player return. The Clippers' side was primarily an option, and Denver's side was a definite payment.

sections.heading: Denver Took Money Rather Than Retaining Kamagate Rights
sections.body: For the Nuggets, the February deadline produced a cash payment in exchange for rights to a player who had not joined their NBA rotation. Denver did not surrender a current starting center or a future first-round draft selection. Reports estimated the cash at $2.68 million, although that amount is sourced to contemporary reporting rather than specified in the original transaction ledger. A D for Denver is a retrospective asset-value judgment, not a claim that receiving money was inherently irrational. Cash can have organizational value, but it does not itself supply regular-season minutes or direct draft capital. The club chose certainty over holding a speculative overseas asset. The review should not invent a hidden player movement or count Kamagate's European games as Denver NBA production, because neither is supported by this trade.

sections.heading: The Narrow C-Minus vs. D Gap Reflects Uncertainty
sections.body: The preserved Clippers Win verdict grades Los Angeles C-minus and Denver D. That spread is modest, which fits the unusually limited basketball returns. Los Angeles received a prospect's draft rights, with no established Clippers NBA playing contribution arising from the February 2024 deal. Denver received cash whose exact amount is not listed in the canonical inventory, although contemporary reports estimated a specific figure. Neither asset should be treated as an NBA All-Star, an automatic pick conversion or a successful draft selection for the acquiring team. The Clippers won the ledger comparison through the potential value of controlling a player right; the Nuggets gained a definite financial return. Those are fundamentally different assets, and the grade should reflect uncertainty rather than force a sweeping verdict.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win — Los Angeles C-, Denver D. The Clippers obtained Ismael Kamagate draft rights, not an active NBA player. Denver took cash, estimated at roughly $2.68 million in contemporary reporting; its exact amount is not supplied in the preserved transaction ledger.

sections.heading: Kamagate Was a 2022 Second-Round Selection, Not a 2024 NBA Player
sections.body: The Clippers bought the rights to Ismael Kamagate, a former No. 46 selection in the 2022 NBA draft. He had been playing in Europe instead of joining Denver's NBA roster, and the February 2024 trade did not require the Clippers to sign him immediately. That distinction frames what the new team actually acquired: a restricted future option to pursue the 6-foot-11 center's NBA services. The NBA transaction ledger confirms that Denver sent only the rights, and CBS Sports' contemporary report notes that he remained overseas. It would inflate the deal to treat those rights as a ready-made NBA reserve or give the Clippers credit for European minutes. The benefit was the possibility of later conversion, not present on-court production. Denver relinquished that possibility in exchange for cash.

sections.heading: The Second-Apron Rules Help Explain the Timing
sections.body: Hoops Rumors' February 8, 2024 deadline report identified the Clippers' second-apron position as important context. The club faced future restrictions on including cash in trades, creating an incentive to use this transaction channel before it became less available. Kamagate had once been drafted by Detroit and had already passed through other teams' rights inventories before reaching Denver. Buying those rights therefore fit an asset-management strategy, even without certainty the center would sign in the NBA. The transaction does not require imagining a secret multi-team roster exchange or an immediate Clippers player slot. Denver received cash, and Los Angeles held the right to negotiate with an overseas prospect. Understanding the deadline timing makes the move more interesting than generic descriptions of which team 'won' a trade.

sections.heading: A Reported Payment Has Different Value From a Draft Right
sections.body: Contemporary reporting attributed an approximately $2.68 million payment to the transaction. That figure helps explain why Denver was willing to surrender its position in the prospect, but it is a report rather than an amount spelled out in the preserved canonical asset line. The Nuggets acquired financial resources they could use under league rules, not a future draft pick or another NBA player. The Clippers acquired the prospect rights and accepted the risk that Kamagate might never join their NBA roster. Neither return should be converted into a fictional box score. A retrospective C-minus for Los Angeles and D for Denver expresses a cautious preference for the speculative player right over cash, not proof that the international prospect developed into a Clippers starter. The reported price and the formal asset definition belong in separate sentences.

sections.heading: A Clippers Win With Modest, Not Transformative, Stakes
sections.body: The final accounting is smaller than the grades might suggest at first glance. New York was not involved, no first-round selection moved, and the Clippers did not receive an active Denver center. Los Angeles bought international draft rights to Kamagate; Denver received cash. The rights offered optionality in a future roster decision, while the money supplied immediate financial consideration. The canonical Clippers Win verdict with a C-minus and D spread is a narrow outcome based on those different forms of value. It should not be embellished with invented NBA appearances or unrelated later transactions. This deal belongs in the NBA asset-history record because the parties and mechanisms are documented, not because it produced a franchise-defining basketball moment. The limited scale is precisely why a source-specific analysis serves readers better than repeated generic grade formulas.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win — Los Angeles C-, Denver D. Los Angeles acquired a contingent overseas draft right; Denver received cash. No NBA player appeared for the Clippers as a direct result at the time, and the reported cash value should not be confused with an independently documented canonical amount.
