sections.heading: Fort Wayne Acquired the Rights to a Proven Playmaker
sections.body: On November 28, 1952, the Fort Wayne Pistons, predecessor of today’s Detroit franchise, received the rights to Andy Phillip from the Philadelphia Warriors, predecessor of the Golden State franchise, for cash. Phillip was an established guard and playmaker, so the rights were more than a speculative claim on an untested rookie. The archived record identifies a cash sale, not a reciprocal package of draft picks or rotation players.

sections.heading: Phillip Became an Important Part of Fort Wayne’s Backcourt
sections.body: Phillip provided high-level ballhandling and passing during Fort Wayne’s early-1950s contender years. His tenure included the Pistons’ NBA Finals appearances in 1955 and 1956. That sustained role gives Fort Wayne a verifiable basketball return from the original rights acquisition. It is the basis for evaluating the trade favorably even without knowing the exact cash price in the surviving transaction documentation.

sections.heading: Philadelphia’s Cash Return Cannot Be Fully Valued
sections.body: The Warriors received cash rather than an incoming player who could be assessed through NBA games. The available transaction listings do not specify a reliable dollar amount, so the page should not invent one or claim that Philadelphia earned nothing financially. The loss of a proven guard is evident on the basketball side, but the sale’s financial value remains an explicit historical limitation. That context is relevant when describing why a club might make a deal that looks uneven decades later.

sections.heading: Four Fort Wayne Seasons Explain the Grade Gap
sections.body: The Pistons Win verdict assigns Fort Wayne/Detroit an A-minus and Philadelphia/Golden State a D-plus. In the November 1952 cash transaction, the Pistons acquired Andy Phillip's player rights, gaining a proven veteran who went on to appear in 262 regular-season games for Fort Wayne across four seasons. Phillip helped the club reach the 1955 and 1956 NBA Finals, providing sustained on-court value that the original sale produced directly. Philadelphia received cash, but the reviewed transaction records do not establish a reliable dollar amount, so the Warriors' financial benefit cannot be precisely assessed. Neither a replacement player nor a draft pick appears in the actual November exchange. The wider letter-grade gap reflects Phillip's documented basketball contribution, while acknowledging that the unreported cash figure limits a complete economic comparison.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Fort Wayne/Detroit A-minus, Philadelphia/Golden State D-plus. Phillip delivered valuable playmaking during the Pistons’ mid-1950s contender seasons, including two NBA Finals appearances. Philadelphia took an unspecified cash payment, whose exact financial value cannot be independently graded from this ledger. The documented on-court outcome favors Fort Wayne; the missing price remains an explicit limitation.

sections.heading: A 1954 Rights Sale Sent Walther to Fort Wayne
sections.body: The Philadelphia Warriors sold Paul Walther’s player rights to the Fort Wayne Pistons on October 19, 1954. The modern franchise names in the archive are Golden State and Detroit, but the clubs playing in that season were Philadelphia and Fort Wayne. Walther had appeared in 64 games for the Warriors the previous season. Fort Wayne was purchasing an experienced reserve guard for a team with legitimate championship ambitions, while Philadelphia collected an undisclosed sum.

sections.heading: Walther Played 68 Games for an NBA Finalist
sections.body: The Pistons used Walther in 68 games during 1954–55. In 820 minutes he recorded 166 points, 155 rebounds and 131 assists, supplying rotation help rather than starring on the roster. Fort Wayne finished first in the Western Division and reached the NBA Finals. Walther’s appearance total supports crediting the acquisition as a practical depth move; attributing the team’s entire success to him would exceed the evidence.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Received Cash, Not an Incoming Replacement
sections.body: The Warriors’ return was cash consideration. The Philadelphia, Fort Wayne and league transaction logs agree that the transaction was a sale, but they do not preserve a reliable amount. That limits any precise financial assessment of the Warriors’ side. It is possible for a rights sale to help a club’s finances even when the departing guard provides useful playing time elsewhere. No unidentified draft choice or additional player should be inserted to create a fictional basketball exchange.

sections.heading: Why Fort Wayne Receives the Better Historical Mark
sections.body: The canonical result is Pistons Win, with Fort Wayne/Detroit B-minus and Philadelphia/Golden State C. Walther’s 68-game role on a Finals team is a documented return from buying his rights. Philadelphia’s receipt of money is established, but its amount and subsequent use are unknown. The letter difference reflects that measurable roster contribution rather than treating a veteran bench player as an all-time acquisition.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Fort Wayne/Detroit B-minus, Philadelphia/Golden State C. Paul Walther contributed 68 games and 820 minutes in the Pistons’ 1954–55 run to the NBA Finals. The Warriors received cash for his rights, with no verified price available. Fort Wayne obtained demonstrable reserve depth; Philadelphia’s financial benefit cannot be quantified from the preserved sources.

sections.heading: Fort Wayne Acquired Noble’s Old Draft Rights
sections.body: RealGM records the Fort Wayne Pistons receiving Chuck Noble’s draft rights from the Philadelphia Warriors on June 1, 1955. Philadelphia had selected Noble in the fourth round of the 1954 draft, but he had not entered the NBA during the intervening season. Noble joined Fort Wayne in the fall of 1955. The legacy TradeVerdicts ledger says cash traveled to Philadelphia; available Basketball-Reference transaction pages do not independently confirm the June transfer or its price, so that consideration cannot be assigned a verified amount.

sections.heading: A Dormant Pick Became Seven Seasons of NBA Help
sections.body: Noble immediately played all 72 games in 1955–56, averaging 28.0 minutes, 9.5 points, 3.6 rebounds and 3.9 assists. He stayed with the Pistons through their relocation to Detroit and totaled 411 NBA games for the franchise across seven seasons. In 1960 he was selected to the Western Conference All-Star team. Those results turned a right originally held by Philadelphia into a long-tenure guard for Fort Wayne and Detroit, far beyond a simple end-of-bench trial.

sections.heading: Philadelphia’s Return Must Carry a Source Qualification
sections.body: The original ledger lists cash for the Warriors, with no preserved dollar figure. Two sources support Noble’s rights changing teams, and the player’s Fort Wayne debut is documented, but the surviving Basketball-Reference team transaction logs do not independently show the June 1 payment. Philadelphia may have preferred realizing money rather than waiting on a 1954 draftee who had not reported. Its financial outcome cannot be reconstructed; the supported basketball comparison is that Noble later made his entire seven-season NBA career with the Pistons franchise.

sections.heading: The All-Star Selection Supports Fort Wayne’s Advantage
sections.body: Fort Wayne/Detroit receives A-minus, while Philadelphia/Golden State receives C. An early full-season role, 411 appearances and a 1960 All-Star selection provide a concrete basis for the Pistons’ stronger grade. Philadelphia’s willingness to transfer dormant rights is understandable, but the lost opportunity was larger than a modest reserve. The uncertain cash consideration warrants caution, not a manufactured narrower grade gap or a second transaction invented from the older draft.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Fort Wayne/Detroit A-minus, Philadelphia/Golden State C. Chuck Noble became a 411-game Pistons contributor and a 1960 All-Star after the June 1955 rights transfer. RealGM and player records support the transfer; the amount and precise archival support for the recorded cash consideration remain uncertain. The documented on-court return strongly favors Fort Wayne.

sections.heading: Philadelphia’s Recent Pick Went to Fort Wayne
sections.body: Fort Wayne acquired Corky Devlin’s draft rights from the Philadelphia Warriors on August 1, 1955. Philadelphia had selected Devlin 11th overall in that year’s draft, and he made his NBA debut for the Pistons in the fall. RealGM records the rights transfer, while the current archive lists cash moving to Philadelphia. The reviewed Basketball-Reference team ledgers do not independently preserve the August move, so the specific monetary consideration remains less secure than the transfer and Devlin’s playing history.

sections.heading: Devlin Played Two Full Pistons Seasons
sections.body: Devlin made 69 regular-season appearances as a rookie in 1955–56, averaging 22.2 minutes and 7.9 points. He returned for 71 games in 1956–57, playing 17.5 minutes and averaging 6.7 points. The 140-game total included approximately 2,777 minutes and 11 playoff appearances for Fort Wayne. His reserve role helped a team that reached the 1955–56 NBA Finals. It was a useful short-term return rather than the discovery of a future All-Star.

sections.heading: The Warriors’ Cash Receipt Was Not Fully Documented
sections.body: Philadelphia gave up a newly selected guard’s rights and, according to the legacy deal record, accepted cash. Neither a definite sum nor an alternative incoming player appears in the surviving material used for this analysis. The Warriors had reason to accept money instead of carrying a second-rounder into the season, but Devlin’s immediate presence in the Pistons rotation was the tangible basketball outcome Philadelphia gave away. The cash assumption should be read with its evidence caveat.

sections.heading: A Limited But Real Win for Fort Wayne
sections.body: The Pistons’ grade is B-plus and the Warriors’ is C. Devlin supplied 140 regular-season games over two years and eleven postseason games; Philadelphia has no verified player replacement from this August rights transaction. Devlin’s NBA career was relatively short and his production never reached star level, which keeps the grade below the Noble acquisition’s A-minus. The trade was useful for Fort Wayne even though some details of the consideration are imperfectly recorded.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Fort Wayne/Detroit B-plus, Philadelphia/Golden State C. Rights to No. 11 selection Corky Devlin became 140 regular-season games and 11 playoff appearances for the Pistons. The Warriors’ recorded cash consideration has no reliable price and incomplete contemporaneous transaction coverage. The documented two-year rotation contribution supports Fort Wayne’s advantage.

sections.heading: Minneapolis Sold Holstein to Fort Wayne in November 1955
sections.body: The November 28, 1955 transaction was a sale of Jim Holstein's player rights from the Minneapolis Lakers to the Fort Wayne Pistons for cash. Both cities are important: these franchises later became the Los Angeles Lakers and Detroit Pistons, but the teams were based in Minneapolis and Fort Wayne on the trade date. Basketball-Reference's two franchise histories and league transaction list identify the sale. No reviewed record gives a cash amount, so a dollar value or supposed reinvestment cannot responsibly be inferred from the transaction.

sections.heading: Holstein Played 27 Fort Wayne Games Before Leaving the NBA
sections.body: Holstein spent his final NBA season with the Pistons, appearing in 27 regular-season games after the trade. He totaled 352 minutes and averaged 13.0 minutes, 2.7 points, 2.8 rebounds and 1.4 assists while shooting 27.0 percent from the field. Those minutes were real reserve help rather than no playing return, but they didn't produce a starting role or future player asset. His last recorded NBA games came in 1955–56, leaving Fort Wayne with less than one season of service from the acquired veteran.

sections.heading: Fort Wayne's Finals Run Doesn't Inflate Holstein's Role
sections.body: The Pistons won the Western Division and reached the 1956 NBA Finals, so even reserve minutes were recorded during a strong season. Still, a Finals appearance for the franchise isn't evidence that Holstein himself was a central reason for its success. The sources support a modest contribution in regular-season relief and an NBA career that finished afterward. Giving Fort Wayne a C acknowledges its actual 27-game return without claiming that a limited role was equivalent to the team's broader playoff achievement.

sections.heading: A Small Minneapolis Advantage with Unpriced Cash
sections.body: The Lakers accepted cash for a player who subsequently contributed only 27 more NBA regular-season games. That was a limited opportunity cost, and the sale avoided carrying his remaining playing rights without a documented long-term team return. Because the sale price isn't preserved, Minneapolis's cash can't be treated as an independently verified profit or as funding an imagined acquisition. The defensible retrospective is Lakers Win with Minneapolis B- and Fort Wayne C: the Lakers traded away a near-end-of-career reserve while the Pistons received a short span of bench use.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win — Minneapolis B-, Fort Wayne C. The 1955 sale sent Jim Holstein's rights to the Pistons for an undisclosed cash amount. Holstein appeared in only 27 more NBA games, averaging 13 minutes and 2.7 points, although Fort Wayne reached the 1956 Finals. Cash was received but cannot be priced from the surviving record. The narrow Lakers advantage reflects Holstein's limited remaining playing return, not a fictional monetary windfall.

Those were the active franchise names; the Lakers didn't relocate to Los Angeles until later, and the Pistons were still based in Fort Wayne. The transaction description records cash moving back to Minneapolis and Holstein moving to Fort Wayne. It doesn't report how much cash. Describing this as a modern Los Angeles–Detroit exchange obscures the location and era in which the decision actually occurred.

sections.heading: Fort Wayne Bought 352 Regular-Season Minutes
sections.body: Holstein's entire Pistons regular-season tenure consisted of 27 games and 352 minutes. He averaged 2.7 points, 2.8 rebounds and 1.4 assists while playing thirteen minutes per outing. His 27.0-percent field-goal accuracy also limits claims of scoring efficiency. Fort Wayne was a contender and reached the 1956 Finals, so the roster spot was not inherently purposeless. sections.heading: Cash Receipt Is Certain, Dollar Return Isn't
sections.body: The league and team transaction histories characterize Minneapolis's side as a cash sale. The missing dollar amount is a genuine evidence limit. One can say the Lakers received consideration and surrendered a player whose remaining NBA career was brief; one cannot claim a particular profit, salary saving, next draft pick or later player purchase without separate records. This distinction is especially important for cash-only deals from the 1950s, where a false precise valuation would lend unjustified certainty to a modest historical transaction.

sections.heading: What the B-/C Verdict Actually Measures
sections.body: The Pistons obtained some reserve minutes during a season that ended in the NBA Finals, but the 27-game tenure had no documented continuing asset payoff. Minneapolis received cash and lost rights to a player who played fewer than thirty further league games. That yields a small Lakers edge under a completed-value rubric. A B- for the Lakers recognizes the low-cost disposal and incoming consideration without inventing its price. Fort Wayne's C acknowledges useful depth but limited durability. The grade spread should not be portrayed as proof that the Lakers earned a large financial benefit.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win — Minneapolis B-, Fort Wayne C. Jim Holstein appeared in 27 Pistons regular-season games after the November 28, 1955 cash sale, with no later NBA playing tenure. The Pistons reached the Finals but received only limited individual reserve production. The Lakers received cash of an undisclosed amount for rights whose future court return proved small. The historical result modestly favors Minneapolis without inventing a financial figure.

sections.heading: On Draft Day, New York Gave Up Gene Shue for Ron Sobie's Rights
sections.body: The April 30, 1956 transaction is often shortened to a swap of Gene Shue and Ron Sobie, but the mechanism is more specific. The Fort Wayne Pistons had just selected Sobie in the first round of the 1956 draft and transferred his NBA rights to the Knicks. New York sent Shue to Fort Wayne in return. The New York and Fort Wayne transaction logs agree on the date and participants. Treating Sobie as an established Pistons rotation player at the time would obscure the point of the exchange: the Knicks acquired the right to sign a rookie while the Pistons acquired an NBA guard whose best seasons were still ahead.

sections.heading: Shue Became a Five-Time All-Star with the Pistons
sections.body: Shue spent six of his ten NBA seasons with the Pistons, first in Fort Wayne and then in Detroit after the franchise relocated. He earned five All-Star selections during that stint and made the All-NBA First Team in 1960, his strongest individual season. The league's historical Pistons review credits him with 22.8 points, 5.5 rebounds and 3.9 assists per game in 1959–60. Those honors weren't attached to his name when New York traded him in 1956. They were the value the receiving club actually developed after the transaction, and they explain the clear Pistons Win decision more convincingly than a generic claim about acquiring an established star.

sections.heading: Sobie Was a Real Knicks Contributor, Not an Empty Return
sections.body: New York did get meaningful basketball use from Sobie. Basketball-Reference's Knicks player ledger lists 191 regular-season games across four seasons, with 1,617 points, 789 rebounds and 351 assists. That is a useful stretch for a first-round acquisition, not a transaction that yielded nothing. His 8.5 points per Knicks game fell far short of what Shue later provided Detroit, yet the games played and minutes distinguish Sobie from an unsigned or unexercised draft right. The B-minus grade reflects positive realized utility despite a decisive opportunity cost; earlier D-plus language flattened that distinction.

sections.heading: A Stronger Detroit Return Without Inventing Draft Value
sections.body: Detroit receives an A because Shue grew into one of the franchise's leading guards, not because his name was simply the more familiar one in retrospect. The rights to Sobie were a real asset on the outgoing side, and the Knicks did convert them into four seasons of NBA games. Detroit also eventually turned Shue into later trade consideration involving Darrall Imhoff and cash, although that later branch should be described as a transaction consequence rather than silently counted as additional 1956 compensation. Both clubs got a player pathway. The difference was the level and duration of the impact delivered by the player Fort Wayne acquired.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Detroit A, New York B-. Fort Wayne traded newly drafted Ron Sobie's rights for Gene Shue on April 30, 1956. Sobie produced 191 Knicks games, but Shue became a five-time Pistons All-Star and a 1960 All-NBA First Team guard. The Knicks gained a real contributor; Detroit secured the much larger realized return.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: How the 1956 Ron Sobie Rights Deal Became a Pistons Win
featuredDeepDive.intro: The source trail for the Gene Shue transaction starts on 1956 draft day, not years later with his All-Star selections. Fort Wayne drafted Ron Sobie and sent his rights to New York for Shue. The two players then took markedly different paths: Sobie logged four Knicks seasons, while Shue became a central Pistons guard and eventually generated further trade consideration. This is a strong Pistons Win, but it isn't a zero-return loss for New York.

sections.heading: The Draft-Rights Asset Was Not a Veteran-for-Veteran Swap
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's New York, Fort Wayne and league transaction ledgers all date the trade to April 30, 1956. Fort Wayne selected Ron Sobie that same day and sent the draft rights to the Knicks in exchange for Gene Shue. The sequence is useful because the recipient of a draft right assumes the responsibility of bringing the player onto its roster. It is not equivalent to receiving a veteran's contract and statistics. The Knicks did exercise the right in practical terms by using Sobie in their lineup beginning in the 1956–57 season, which gives the outgoing asset a traceable outcome rather than a hypothetical draft value.

sections.heading: Detroit's Return Was Demonstrated Over Six Seasons
sections.body: The Pistons' six-season Shue period bridged two cities, from Fort Wayne to Detroit. NBA.com's retrospective of the club's all-time All-NBA honorees identifies five All-Star selections in that span and Shue's 1960 First Team award. It also lists his 1959–60 production at 22.8 points, 5.5 rebounds and 3.9 assists per game. Those figures describe the peak of the return, not an average across the entire six years. There is no need to credit Fort Wayne with an immediate five-time All-Star in 1956; those accomplishments represent the subsequent growth of the asset and establish the long-term gap between the two clubs.

sections.heading: New York's 191 Games Warrant a B-Minus, Not a D-Plus
sections.body: The Knicks were not left with an unused pick. Sobie's Basketball-Reference franchise total is 191 games and 1,617 points in New York, plus 789 rebounds and 351 assists. A full career count of 192 includes one Minneapolis Lakers appearance, so attributing all 192 to New York would overstate this team's return. The distinction is small numerically but essential to the franchise-specific comparison. Sobie was a functioning backcourt contributor for the Knicks over four seasons; Shue's far greater scoring and All-NBA peak still made Detroit the clear winner. The grade pair should show both truths at once.

sections.heading: The Later Imhoff Transaction Is a Separate Asset Chain
sections.body: Detroit ultimately moved Shue back to the Knicks in a later deal involving Darrall Imhoff and cash. That continuation demonstrates how an established guard could retain market value beyond the seasons he played for the franchise. It should not be retroactively written into the original April 1956 exchange, however. The first transaction was Shue for Sobie's rights. The later trade is relevant only when tracing what Detroit eventually did with the player it had acquired. Distinguishing acquisition value, direct on-court output and downstream trade conversion keeps the account accurate without turning this into a fabricated multi-asset 1956 package.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Detroit wins this 1956 deal, A to New York's B-minus. Shue's five Pistons All-Star appearances and All-NBA First Team recognition outweigh Sobie's legitimate 191-game Knicks contribution. The swap happened on draft day and involved Sobie's rights, not an already established Pistons veteran. Later trades belong to a separate asset history.

sections.heading: What Changed Hands
sections.body: On October 3, 1956, the Fort Wayne Pistons acquired Billy Kenville from the Syracuse Nationals for cash. The modern franchise slugs map those teams to Detroit and Philadelphia, but the historical transaction itself is straightforward: Kenville moved to the Pistons and an undisclosed financial return went to Syracuse. The verdict is a Slight Pistons Edge, with Detroit at C+ and Philadelphia at C. The available evidence supports that direction from both sides. Detroit’s perspective says Kenville gave the Pistons the better realized return. The Syracuse-side perspective likewise says Fort Wayne received real basketball value while the Nationals received only an undisclosed financial return. Because cash is documented but does not provide the same directly tied basketball outcome as the player, the final results give Detroit the modest advantage.

sections.heading: Why the Pistons Earn the Edge
sections.body: The Pistons received a player whose value can be observed as part of the basketball trade details. The Syracuse perspective adds useful context by describing Kenville as a serviceable guard and noting his contribution to the 1955 championship team before the sale. That source therefore independently supports the idea that Fort Wayne acquired real basketball value. Syracuse’s incoming side was cash, which is a documented transaction asset but does not create the same directly tied on-court return in this retrospective framework. The final C+/C split keeps the conclusion proportional: Detroit did better in basketball-value terms, while Syracuse did receive legitimate financial consideration. Nothing in the evidence requires a harsher judgment.

sections.heading: Cash Is Real Consideration but a Different Kind of Return
sections.body: A cash transaction creates an attribution challenge because the financial return is real but not directly comparable to a player’s later on-court contribution when the amount and downstream use are not part of the record. The correct approach is neither to ignore the cash nor to invent basketball value for it. Syracuse gets credit for receiving consideration, which supports the C grade. Detroit gets the higher C+ because the acquired player is a directly tied basketball asset and both franchise-side records regard that side as the better realized outcome. This distinction keeps the analysis grounded in what the transaction histories actually document.

sections.heading: Historical Franchise Labels Do Not Change the Asset Logic
sections.body: The teams are listed under modern franchise identities here, while the available evidence correctly reflects the historical Fort Wayne Pistons and Syracuse Nationals. That naming difference does not alter the trade evaluation. The same two franchise lines exchanged Kenville for cash, and both analyses agree that the player side produced the stronger basketball return. Using the historical names preserves the context while the modern franchise identity keeps the comparison clear. The resulting Slight Pistons Edge is therefore both historically grounded and structurally coherent.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Pistons Edge. Detroit receives a C+ and Philadelphia a C for the 1956 Fort Wayne–Syracuse transaction. The Pistons acquired Billy Kenville; the Nationals received cash. The Syracuse-side source itself describes Kenville as a serviceable guard and characterizes the player side as the modest winner. Cash remains legitimate consideration, but the record supplies more directly tied basketball value on Detroit’s side. That supports a narrow C+/C result.

featuredDeepDive.heading: Pistons–Nationals 1956: Why Billy Kenville for Cash Favors Fort Wayne
featuredDeepDive.intro: The 1956 sale of Billy Kenville from Syracuse to Fort Wayne is a compact historical transaction with an unusually clear value distinction. The Nationals received cash. The Pistons received a player the Syracuse-side record describes as a serviceable guard who had contributed to the 1955 championship team. Both franchise perspectives therefore favor the player side, while the undisclosed cash return prevents the trade from being treated as if Syracuse received nothing. The final C+/C result captures that modest basketball-value advantage.

sections.heading: The Player Side Has directly tied Basketball Value
sections.body: Kenville is not an abstract asset in the record. The Syracuse perspective identifies him as a serviceable guard and ties him to the Nationals’ 1955 championship team before the transaction. That makes the Fort Wayne return concrete: the Pistons acquired an actual player with demonstrated basketball utility. Detroit’s own source-side perspective reaches the same directional conclusion and calls the result a modest realized-value advantage. With both sides recognizing the player return as the stronger basketball outcome, the historical verdict has a firm evidentiary base.

sections.heading: The Cash Return Should Not Be Invented Into More Than the Record Shows
sections.body: Syracuse’s return was cash, but the evidence does not establish a downstream player or draft asset that should be credited to that money. A disciplined retrospective therefore stops at the documented financial consideration. This is not the same as saying the cash had no value. It is simply a refusal to convert an undisclosed payment into hypothetical roster production. The C grade gives the Nationals credit for receiving legitimate consideration, while Detroit’s C+ reflects the side with the directly tied basketball asset. That approach is both conservative and evidence-based.

sections.heading: Both Historical Team Records Point the Same Way
sections.body: The Fort Wayne-side record says the Pistons gained a modest realized-value advantage. The Syracuse-side record says the Nationals received only an undisclosed financial return while Kenville remained a serviceable guard, making the deal a modest partner edge rather than a severe loss. Those perspectives use different framing but agree on the winner. The combined evidence therefore supports a Slight Pistons Edge without dismissing either team's perspective. The two-sided agreement is especially valuable for a trade from the 1950s, where keeping the conclusion tightly tied to documented transaction evidence matters.

sections.heading: Why the Result Is Modest Instead of Lopsided
sections.body: Even with bilateral agreement, the trade should not be inflated. The record does not establish a massive player-value gap or a premium package. It establishes that Fort Wayne obtained a useful player while Syracuse took cash. That is enough for a winner but not for an extreme grade. C+ versus C communicates exactly that scale. It also avoids treating the undisclosed financial consideration as worthless. The final verdict is strongest when it remains proportional to what the historical record can actually support.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Detroit/Fort Wayne C+, Philadelphia/Syracuse C, with a Slight Pistons Edge. Billy Kenville supplied the directly tied basketball return, while Syracuse received undisclosed cash. Both franchise-side histories identify the player side as the modest winner. The evidence supports a narrow edge and no more.

sections.heading: Syracuse Sold Red Rocha’s Rights to Fort Wayne
sections.body: On October 23, 1956, the Syracuse Nationals sold Red Rocha’s player rights to the Fort Wayne Pistons for cash. Those are the historical franchise names; Syracuse later became the Philadelphia 76ers, and Fort Wayne moved to Detroit. The transaction listings establish the rights sale but do not identify a reliable dollar amount. There is no basis for portraying it as a two-player swap or adding a draft selection to either return.

sections.heading: Fort Wayne Bought an Experienced Frontcourt Option
sections.body: Rocha had already played several NBA seasons before his rights reached the Pistons. Fort Wayne was acquiring the ability to use an established veteran up front rather than waiting for an untested draft pick. The 1956–57 roster confirms his presence with the Pistons, although his participation was modest at that stage of his career. His previous reputation does not automatically turn this late-career rights acquisition into a franchise-changing addition.

sections.heading: Syracuse Received Financial Consideration, Not a Replacement Player
sections.body: The Nationals chose a cash return for an aging player whose NBA career was nearing its end. Because the transaction source lists the rights sale without a price, a precise financial winner cannot be calculated. Cash might have served the club’s immediate needs, but the surviving record does not connect it to an identified later acquisition. Fort Wayne obtained rights it could use on the court, while Syracuse obtained money of undisclosed value.

sections.heading: Correcting a Contradiction in the Old Grade Copy
sections.body: The current canonical ledger rates Fort Wayne/Detroit B and Syracuse/Philadelphia C-plus. The previous article incorrectly printed C and D-plus while saying the same team won. Those old letters were not supported by the stored grades. The corrected verdict recognizes Fort Wayne’s acquisition of a real veteran without exaggerating his brief role; Syracuse’s undisclosed cash keeps its side from being dismissed as nothing.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Fort Wayne/Detroit B, Syracuse/Philadelphia C-plus. The 1956 transaction sold Red Rocha’s playing rights to Fort Wayne for undisclosed cash. Rocha was a real Pistons roster contributor, albeit in a limited late-career role. Syracuse received financial consideration that cannot be independently valued from a known amount. The published grade gap is modest, and the trade must not be described using the old incorrect C/D-plus grades.

sections.heading: Two Established Players Moved Between 1957 Franchises
sections.body: The Fort Wayne Pistons sent Corky Devlin to the Minneapolis Lakers for Ed Kalafat on May 14, 1957. Both players had logged NBA minutes before the exchange. These were the actual franchise cities at the time: Detroit and Los Angeles identify the teams’ present-day lineages, not their 1957 homes. League, Fort Wayne and Minneapolis transaction listings agree that the transaction was a direct player swap without a recorded draft selection or cash consideration.

sections.heading: Devlin Supplied a Full Lakers Season
sections.body: Devlin appeared in 70 games for Minneapolis in 1957–58, averaging about 17.8 minutes, 6.8 points and 2.4 assists. Those were reserve-level figures rather than All-Star production, but they represent a full season of actual backcourt help for a club that had surrendered another established player. It was also Devlin’s final NBA season, so the Lakers’ gain was finite and should not be stretched into a multiyear career asset.

sections.heading: Kalafat Never Played an NBA Game for the Pistons
sections.body: Kalafat’s pre-trade résumé looked promising: he had played 65 games for Minneapolis in 1956–57 with averages of 8.5 points and 6.5 rebounds. Those numbers came before Fort Wayne acquired him. Basketball-reference career and transaction records show no subsequent NBA playing appearances, leaving the Pistons with no realized regular-season production from their new center. The difference between his prior usefulness and post-trade availability is central to judging the exchange.

sections.heading: The Better Outcome Was Modest but Unambiguous
sections.body: The archival grades are B for Minneapolis/Los Angeles and C-minus for Fort Wayne/Detroit. Devlin’s 70 Lakers games outweigh Kalafat’s zero post-trade NBA appearances; neither roster return was a franchise-defining centerpiece. The result favors the Lakers because of a documented difference in games played, not because of speculation about contracts or unlisted compensation. That is enough for a directional win without making it a blockbuster.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win — Minneapolis/Los Angeles B, Fort Wayne/Detroit C-minus. The Lakers received 70 games of reserve backcourt play from Corky Devlin in 1957–58. Ed Kalafat had previously been a useful Minneapolis center, but he did not play another NBA regular-season game after Fort Wayne acquired him. One side received actual production and the other did not.

sections.heading: Fort Wayne Moved Foust for Dukes in 1957
sections.body: The September 12, 1957 agreement moved Larry Foust from Detroit to the Minneapolis Lakers and sent Walter Dukes to the Pistons. Detroit had just relocated from Fort Wayne, so referring to a Los Angeles Lakers transaction in 1957 would obscure the historical geography: the Lakers were still in Minneapolis. Team and league transaction histories support a direct player swap. An older asset summary also mentioned cash, but the historical reconciliation could not substantiate it and removed that component from the canonical asset ledger.

sections.heading: Detroit Prioritized Dukes’s Frontcourt Contributions
sections.body: Dukes arrived as an athletic center who could rebound and handle a substantial frontcourt workload. Detroit acquired an identifiable NBA contributor rather than a future draft right or an unsettled conditional consideration. That role is particularly relevant to the Pistons’ immediate competition after their relocation. The value of the incoming player has to be judged by Dukes’s actual Detroit service rather than by automatically attributing every later league appearance to the original transaction.

sections.heading: Minneapolis Acquired a Recognized Veteran in Foust
sections.body: Foust had already built a substantial NBA reputation with the Fort Wayne franchise before the deal. Minneapolis therefore acquired experience and established center production, not a speculative prospect. That is why the ledger gives the Lakers a strong B-plus rather than presenting the transaction as a one-sided loss. The historical team name belongs in the account even though modern navigation groups this trade under the current Los Angeles franchise.

sections.heading: The Canonical Grades Give Detroit Only a Narrow Edge
sections.body: The stored result is Slight Pistons Edge, with Detroit A-minus and the Minneapolis/Los Angeles Lakers B-plus. Older duplicated copy had incorrectly flipped the winner and assigned Detroit C and the Lakers B. Those figures conflict with the source-of-truth verdict and cannot be preserved as a second valid assessment. Both teams obtained a proven center, so a narrow Detroit advantage is more defensible than a sweeping claim that either organization received nothing.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Pistons Edge — Detroit A-minus, Minneapolis/Los Angeles B-plus. Detroit obtained Walter Dukes in the September 1957 straight swap for Larry Foust. Both sides acquired an established big man, but the canonical assessment assigns Detroit the modest lead. The historical source review found no substantiated cash component, so the decision compares the two documented players only.

sections.heading: The Syracuse Nationals Sold Two Players for Cash
sections.body: On June 10, 1958, the Syracuse Nationals sold Dick Farley and Earl Lloyd to the Detroit Pistons for cash. Syracuse is the historical franchise now represented by Philadelphia in the modern trade index. Detroit, Syracuse, and league transaction logs verify the same asset direction. The cash price has not been established in the reviewed materials, so it would be misleading to describe a specific financial amount or insist that the Nationals received nothing. Unlike a pick swap with unknown downstream effects, this is a narrow historical transaction: two NBA players to Detroit, and undisclosed cash to Syracuse.

sections.heading: Lloyd Provided Two Seasons of Detroit Playing Time
sections.body: Lloyd had helped Syracuse win the 1955 NBA title before the sale. With Detroit he appeared in 72 regular-season games during 1958–59 and another 68 in 1959–60, a total of 140 Pistons appearances. His veteran presence and regular playing time were real returns, not hypothetical projected development. His distinction as the first Black player to play in an NBA regular-season game predates this transaction and should not be credited to the Pistons as an outcome of the sale. Detroit purchased an experienced contributor whose actual value can be counted across two seasons.

sections.heading: Farley's Return Followed His Air Force Service
sections.body: Farley had spent the preceding two NBA seasons away from league competition while serving in the Air Force. He returned with Detroit in 1958–59 and recorded 70 regular-season appearances, averaging 18.3 minutes and seven points. This was useful roster depth rather than an All-Star-caliber outcome. The important distinction is that Detroit's purchase did not depend on only Lloyd succeeding: Farley also supplied an identifiable season of production. Their combined 210 player appearances are appearances by two individuals, not 210 distinct Pistons team games.

sections.heading: How the B-Plus and C Grades Fit the Evidence
sections.body: Detroit's B-plus reflects both Lloyd's 140 games and Farley's 70 in exchange for cash, making the canonical Pistons Win defensible on realized playing value. Syracuse's C acknowledges that it received financial consideration, but the evidence doesn't specify a dollar amount or establish how the proceeds were deployed. Labeling the Nationals' return worthless would pretend to know the cash's value. Conversely, assigning the seller an unproven financial windfall would erase the two players Detroit acquired. The correct historical comparison is documented roster usefulness against a real but unquantified payment.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Detroit B+, Syracuse/Philadelphia C. Detroit acquired Dick Farley and Earl Lloyd from Syracuse for undisclosed cash on June 10, 1958. Lloyd contributed 140 Pistons appearances over two seasons, while Farley added 70 in 1958–59. The Nationals' unknown cash return deserves acknowledgment without inventing its amount.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The 1958 Syracuse Cash Sale That Added 210 Pistons Player Appearances

sections.heading: The Two Players Traveled from Syracuse, Not Philadelphia

The same trade appears in the 1957–58 Detroit and Syracuse team transaction histories and in the NBA league transaction register. Each identifies Dick Farley and Earl Lloyd moving to Detroit for cash. The records do not describe a draft pick, an extra player, or a published purchase price. That factual boundary prevents later transactions from being folded into the original deal.

sections.heading: Lloyd's 140-Game Return Is Directly Attributable to Detroit
sections.body: Earl Lloyd played 72 Pistons games in 1958–59 and 68 more in 1959–60. His production was veteran-rotation value and was distinct from achievements earned before the sale. The 1955 championship he won with Syracuse remains part of his previous club history, and his integration milestone occurred years before this move. Detroit should receive credit for the games it actually obtained from him, not for retrospective awards or team achievements unrelated to its acquisition. sections.heading: Farley's 70 Games Came After Military Service
sections.body: Dick Farley was not an uninterrupted Syracuse veteran in 1957–58. He had spent two seasons outside the NBA while serving in the United States Air Force and returned to play for Detroit in 1958–59. His 70 games, 18.3 minutes per game, and seven-point average measure what Detroit actually received. The combined figure of 210 individual appearances counts his 70 and Lloyd's 140 separately. It is a fair way to establish roster impact as long as it is not confused with team games, star performance, or a promise of future seasons.

sections.heading: The Unknown Price Limits Syracuse's Retrospective Grade
sections.body: Selling two veterans may have served Syracuse's roster or financial plans, but the checked transaction histories provide no price or detailed explanation for management's decision. The cash was real consideration; its eventual use is not documented in the source packet. That is why a C grade should not be described as an empty return or a certain financial mistake. Detroit's B-plus is supported by observable playing time from both men, while Syracuse's return is less measurable. The Pistons Win indicates a better documented on-court outcome rather than proof of the buyer's profit in dollars.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Detroit takes the 1958 sale, B+ to Syracuse's C, because Lloyd supplied 140 regular-season appearances and Farley another 70. The Nationals received an undisclosed cash payment whose amount and downstream use are not verified. Detroit's advantage is a sourced playing-return conclusion, not an invented valuation of the sale price.

sections.heading: February 13, 1959: Yardley for Conlin, Not a Pick Package
sections.body: Detroit sent George Yardley to the Syracuse Nationals in exchange for Ed Conlin on February 13, 1959. The Detroit, Syracuse and NBA league transaction ledgers agree on that date; an older February 7 reference should not override the three aligned records. Syracuse is the historical location of the franchise now indexed under Philadelphia. The two principals were both players, with no verified extra draft pick or cash consideration attached to this exchange. The relevant comparison is therefore direct: Yardley's subsequent 88 Nationals appearances against Conlin's 85 games for Detroit over parts of two seasons.

sections.heading: Yardley Brought Syracuse an Established Scoring Threat
sections.body: Yardley had already established his high-level scoring résumé with the Pistons, including leading the league in scoring in 1957–58. After the midseason transfer, he appeared in 88 regular-season games for Syracuse across the remainder of 1958–59 and the complete 1959–60 season. His Nationals scoring averaged about 19.6 points per game, and he was selected to the 1960 NBA All-Star Game. Those Syracuse-only outcomes establish why the Nationals won this exchange even though Yardley had made his name elsewhere first. Detroit traded away a player capable of continuing to supply front-line offensive production.

sections.heading: Conlin Was an Actual Detroit Contributor, Not a Write-Off
sections.body: Ed Conlin gave Detroit 85 regular-season appearances across portions of two seasons before the club moved him again in 1960. That is a real roster return and prevents the Pistons' side from being described as an empty trade. His Detroit stint nevertheless didn't approach Yardley's Syracuse scoring rate or All-Star-level peak. The canonical B-minus Detroit grade reflects useful playing time at a much lower impact level, whereas the Nationals' A-minus recognizes the immediate star-caliber return. Neither grade requires claiming Conlin never played or crediting Syracuse with seasons Yardley spent in Detroit.

sections.heading: A Nationals Win with Historical Team Names Preserved
sections.body: The original player-for-player exchange and subsequent production support a Nationals Win rather than merely a Philadelphia 76ers win in the 1959 setting. Modern franchise navigation may use Philadelphia as the linked franchise identity, but Syracuse owned the team and received Yardley. The gap between a roughly 19.6-point scorer who made the 1960 All-Star team and a shorter-lived Pistons rotation return supports Syracuse's A-minus against Detroit's B-minus. The deal can still have made roster sense to Detroit at the time; a retrospective grade describes what those assets produced, not a claim that the Pistons deliberately surrendered value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nationals Win — Syracuse/Philadelphia A-, Detroit B-. Detroit traded George Yardley for Ed Conlin on February 13, 1959. Yardley scored around 19.6 points per game in 88 Syracuse appearances and earned a 1960 All-Star selection; Conlin supplied 85 Detroit games. Both franchises obtained usable players, but Syracuse gained the stronger basketball return.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The 1959 Yardley–Conlin Trade That Favored Syracuse
featuredDeepDive.intro: The February 13, 1959 swap sent George Yardley from Detroit to the Syracuse Nationals for Ed Conlin. Three transaction ledgers support the same date and two-player exchange. sections.heading: Resolving the February Date Before Grading the Deal

Executive transaction histories for Nick Kerbawy and Danny Biasone also corroborate the personnel movement. An older February 7 notation attached to the legacy record must not quietly override the three aligned transaction logs. Precisely dating the exchange separates the games played for each team before and after it and keeps the historical interpretation aligned with the receiving franchises.

sections.heading: The Nationals Acquired Star Production for the Stretch and Next Season
sections.body: Yardley arrived with an established NBA scoring record, but the measurable Syracuse value starts with the games he actually played as a National. He contributed over the second portion of 1958–59 and throughout 1959–60, totaling 88 regular-season appearances at approximately 19.6 points per game. His 1960 All-Star selection belongs to his Syracuse period and is relevant to the completed trade return. Detroit can't be credited with those Nationals games merely because it had previously developed him, and Syracuse shouldn't receive credit for his earlier Pistons achievements.

sections.heading: Conlin's 85 Detroit Games Prevent an Extreme Loss Grade
sections.body: Conlin came from Syracuse and made 85 regular-season appearances for Detroit across two partial seasons. This represents a verifiable return for the Pistons, despite the lower scoring ceiling and limited tenure compared with Yardley's stay in Syracuse. Detroit ultimately traded Conlin again in 1960, a separate asset chain that should not be added to the original 1959 deal as though it were a third incoming piece. Keeping Conlin's actual games in view is important to the B-minus grade: Detroit made a defensible roster acquisition, even if the exchange left the other side with a stronger scorer.

sections.heading: Yardley's Syracuse Scoring Outpaced Conlin's Detroit Contribution
sections.body: The February 1959 exchange sent George Yardley from Detroit to the Syracuse Nationals for Ed Conlin, with no documented draft pick in the one-for-one package. Yardley went on to score roughly 19.6 points per game in 88 Syracuse regular-season appearances and earned a 1960 All-Star selection. Conlin appeared in 85 Detroit games and supplied actual rotation minutes, preventing the deal from being treated as a complete loss for the Pistons. Yet the scoring and recognition gap was clear. Syracuse deserves an A- for landing the stronger short-term offensive player; Detroit's B- acknowledges Conlin's usable return. Calling the 1959 winner the Nationals preserves the historical team name, even though today's franchise navigation links Syracuse to Philadelphia.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Syracuse wins the February 13, 1959 Yardley-for-Conlin exchange. Yardley produced 88 Nationals games at roughly 19.6 points per game and made the 1960 All-Star team. Conlin delivered 85 games to Detroit, so the Pistons did not get nothing. The canonical grades are Nationals/Philadelphia A- and Detroit B-; no extra assets or earlier date should be inferred.

sections.heading: Cincinnati Acquired Phil Jordon on March 31, 1959
sections.body: Detroit traded Phil Jordon to the Cincinnati Royals for Archie Dees and a 1959 second-round draft pick on March 31, 1959. The draft choice subsequently became Tom Robitaille, the ninth overall selection in 1959. Detroit, Cincinnati, league, and both club executive transaction ledgers identify the same three assets and date. The modern transaction index places Cincinnati under today's Sacramento Kings franchise, but the receiving team at the time was the Royals. This was a veteran player for another player plus a traceable pick, not a mystery package that warrants assigning value to later transactions.

sections.heading: Jordon Delivered the Longer Cincinnati Playing Return
sections.body: Jordon played 123 regular-season games for Cincinnati across portions of two seasons after the trade. During 1959–60 he averaged 13.4 points and 8.3 rebounds, then supplied 10.9 points and 8.8 rebounds over 48 games the following season. That was dependable frontcourt output in the actual Royals uniform, not production borrowed from another franchise. The 123-game return gives Cincinnati the better direct on-court outcome, especially compared with the duration and value Detroit realized from its two incoming assets.

sections.heading: Dees Played 101 Pistons Games, While Robitaille Never Reached the NBA
sections.body: Detroit did receive a legitimate player return in Dees. He appeared in 101 regular-season games for the Pistons over two seasons and averaged about 8.4 points and 4.9 rebounds during that stint. The additional 1959 second-round pick became Robitaille at No. 9 overall, but he did not appear in an NBA game. The pick's identifiable draft outcome prevents it from being written off as nonexistent; its absence of NBA production also prevents awarding Detroit hypothetical star value. Together Dees and the unused playing return from Robitaille fell behind Jordon's Cincinnati contribution.

sections.heading: Why the Royals' B-Plus Beats Detroit's B-Minus
sections.body: The historical verdict is Royals Win. Cincinnati received 123 Jordon games, with double-figure scoring and strong rebounding, while Detroit received 101 Dees games and a draft selection that generated no NBA appearances. Detroit's B-minus credits Dees's actual contributions and the acquisition of a real pick, rather than treating the package as worthless. Cincinnati's B-plus recognizes the larger realized player value. The old Slight Pistons Edge language and C-plus grade for the Royals reverse the observed result and must not survive in the completed analysis.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Royals Win — Cincinnati/Sacramento B+, Detroit B-. The March 31, 1959 exchange sent Phil Jordon to Cincinnati for Archie Dees and the 1959 second-round pick used on Tom Robitaille. Jordon played 123 Royals games; Dees contributed 101 Pistons games, while Robitaille logged no NBA appearance. Cincinnati realized the stronger outcome.

sections.heading: Jordon's Royals Production Was Measurable After the Trade
sections.body: Jordon was not simply a recognizable name sent away by Detroit. He went on to appear in 123 Cincinnati regular-season games. His 1959–60 averages of 13.4 points and 8.3 rebounds show that the Royals acquired a useful scorer and rebounder; he followed with 10.9 points and 8.8 rebounds in 48 games during the subsequent season. The second asset was the draft pick that produced Tom Robitaille. Robitaille's selection is verifiable, but he did not play in an NBA regular-season game. Crediting Detroit with two distinct incoming assets is accurate; describing them as two productive NBA players is not. The B-minus grade recognizes Dees while discounting the unfulfilled playing return of the extra selection.

sections.heading: Historical Franchise Labels and the Grade Difference
sections.body: Cincinnati was the Royals' city in 1959. The present-day Sacramento Kings identifier in the trade database is a continuity label and must not appear as though the club played in Sacramento in the late 1950s. The correct team-specific value comparison is Cincinnati's 123 Jordon games against Detroit's 101 Dees games and its unused NBA draft selection. finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cincinnati wins the March 31, 1959 Jordon transaction, B+ to Detroit's B-. The Royals' better documented return, not asset-counting alone, determines the verdict.

sections.heading: Detroit Obtained Don Ohl’s Playing Rights for Cash

sections.heading: Ohl’s Later Pistons Contribution Created the Basketball Advantage
sections.body: Ohl became a real on-court contributor during the Pistons’ early-1960s seasons. That outcome differentiates this sale from a speculative rights purchase that never produces a roster player. Detroit did not receive a guaranteed star contract on the trade date, but it ultimately gained an NBA guard whose work could be measured through actual appearances and production. Those realized results are the foundation of the higher retrospective grade, not an assumption about what every purchased right might yield.

sections.heading: The Warriors’ Cash Receipt Has an Important Documentation Limit
sections.body: Philadelphia received cash and did not acquire a replacement player through this particular transaction. The surviving trade ledger does not establish a dependable dollar figure. From a basketball-return perspective, however, the known financial consideration cannot be shown to match the useful playing rights Detroit acquired and eventually exercised.

sections.heading: The A-Plus and D-Plus Grades Follow the Actual Record

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Detroit A-plus, Philadelphia/Golden State D-plus. Detroit purchased Don Ohl’s rights in 1960 and subsequently received meaningful guard play. Philadelphia took cash of an unverified amount without an identifiable replacement player in the same transaction. sections.heading: Why the 1961 Record Fails
sections.body: The legacy row claims Detroit sent Gary Alcorn to the Los Angeles Lakers for cash on July 1, 1961. The source-led audit found no matching trade in the Detroit, Los Angeles or league transaction ledgers. More importantly, Alcorn’s documented chronology conflicts with the claim: he had already left Detroit as a free agent in 1960, signed with the Lakers that October and was waived in December 1960.

sections.heading: Gary Alcorn’s Verified Path
sections.body: Basketball-Reference, RealGM and the Lakers’ historical record place Alcorn with Detroit in 1959-60, then in free agency on July 1, 1960, followed by a Lakers signing on October 24, 1960. He played 20 games for Los Angeles during 1960-61, was waived on December 15 and returned to free agency two days later. No reviewed source documents Detroit reacquiring him or transferring him again in July 1961.

sections.heading: Why No Trade Value Can Be Graded
sections.body: Because the supposed July 1961 exchange is not supported as a completed transaction, neither the listed cash nor Alcorn can be treated as realized trade return for that date. Assigning a winner or letter grades would score an event that the verified player and transaction timelines do not show. The archive should retain the row only as provenance for the legacy intake.

sections.heading: Correct Archive Treatment
sections.body: The canonical record is therefore structurally superseded, private, non-indexable and excluded from graded results. Its purpose is to document why the legacy transaction was rejected, not to manufacture a corrected package. The verified chronology is preserved in the source trail without creating a second Alcorn move.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Resolution
finalVerdict.body: Record Superseded — no winner and no team grades. The source-led chronology does not support a July 1, 1961 Detroit-to-Los Angeles cash trade involving Gary Alcorn. The legacy row remains only as private provenance and is excluded from graded and index-candidate results.
