sections.heading: The Knicks Reacquired Shue for a Center and Cash
sections.body: On August 29, 1962, Detroit sent Gene Shue back to the Knicks in exchange for Darrall Imhoff and cash. New York had originally traded Shue to the Fort Wayne Pistons in 1956, making this a return rather than an entirely new relationship between player and franchise. The Detroit, New York, and NBA transaction histories agree on the direction of the exchange. They do not state the amount paid in cash, so the payment cannot be priced retrospectively. No draft pick was included. Detroit gained a center and financial consideration, while New York gained a veteran guard.

sections.heading: Shue Played 78 Games in His Return to New York
sections.body: Shue appeared in 78 Knicks regular-season games in 1962–63, averaging 11.7 points and 3.3 assists over 29.3 minutes per game. That was a substantial rotation role, even though his five earlier All-Star appearances belonged to the Pistons and cannot be counted as achievements earned by New York. The Knicks later traded Shue alongside Paul Hogue to acquire Bill McGill. That later move shows Shue retained value as a transaction asset, but Hogue was also part of the package. The Knicks should not receive sole credit for every game McGill subsequently played.

sections.heading: Detroit Used Imhoff for 103 Games
sections.body: Detroit received 103 regular-season appearances from Darrall Imhoff over two seasons and also collected the original cash payment. Imhoff's tenure was useful, not an empty asset, and the Pistons later sold his rights to the Lakers in April 1964. That separate sale belongs to the follow-on asset history rather than being inserted into the 1962 exchange. The cash amount remains undisclosed in the checked sources. Detroit's B grade recognizes Imhoff's actual playing contribution and the financial asset without inventing a transaction price or future draft compensation.

sections.heading: A Knicks Win Without Pretending Detroit Received Nothing
sections.body: New York received a guard it could play for 78 games and later combine with Hogue in an additional transaction. Detroit obtained 103 center appearances from Imhoff plus money of unverified amount. Those outcomes support the canonical Knicks Win, with New York at A-minus and Detroit at B, rather than the old A and C-plus editorial grades. The margin is meaningful but limited by the fact that both teams got tangible return. Downstream McGill production must be attributed to the separate Shue-and-Hogue package, not solely to this first deal.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win — New York A-, Detroit B. Shue returned to New York on August 29, 1962 for Darrall Imhoff and undisclosed cash. Shue played 78 Knicks games; Imhoff supplied 103 Pistons appearances. Shue was later traded with Paul Hogue, so the next acquisition cannot be credited to Shue alone.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Gene Shue Returns to the Knicks in the 1962 Imhoff Deal
featuredDeepDive.intro: Shue's 1962 transfer back to New York followed six seasons with the Pistons organization. Detroit received Darrall Imhoff and cash; the Knicks acquired a guard who played 78 games for them and later joined another outgoing package. The receiving franchises both got measurable value, while later transactions must be separated from what changed hands on August 29.

sections.heading: A Return Trade Rather Than a New Draft-Rights Transaction
sections.body: The 1962–63 Knicks, Pistons, and NBA transaction ledgers give August 29, 1962 as the date and list Gene Shue moving to New York, with Darrall Imhoff and cash moving to Detroit. Six years earlier New York had sent Shue to the Fort Wayne version of the Pistons in a separate rights transaction. The prior trade makes this a notable return, but it does not change the 1962 compensation. There is no identified draft selection, and the source logs do not quantify the payment. The correct original package is one veteran guard against one veteran center and cash.

sections.heading: Shue's Knicks Return Was a Rotation Season
sections.body: Shue played 78 games for New York during 1962–63 and averaged 11.7 points, 3.3 assists, and 29.3 minutes. His earlier five All-Star appearances had taken place while with the Pistons, so those honors are part of his incoming reputation rather than proof of post-trade Knicks production. When New York later traded Shue and Paul Hogue together to acquire Bill McGill, it demonstrated a continuing asset chain. McGill would average 16.0 points in 68 Knicks games in 1963–64, but attributing that entire result to Shue alone would ignore Hogue's explicit contribution to the second transaction.

sections.heading: Imhoff Provided Real Detroit Games and Retained a Sale Path
sections.body: Imhoff logged 103 regular-season Pistons games over portions of two seasons. Detroit then sold his rights to the Los Angeles Lakers in April 1964, creating a follow-on transaction branch rather than an additional incoming asset from New York in August 1962. The original cash payment from New York is another real piece of the initial package but has no reliably identified sum in the source ledger. Those distinctions explain why Detroit's canonical grade is B: it acquired usable basketball minutes and unquantified financial consideration, not a player whose value automatically vanished.

sections.heading: Comparing the Grades With Downstream Credit Limited
sections.body: New York's A-minus reflects a veteran guard who filled a substantial one-season role and retained trade utility. Detroit's B reflects a center who played 103 games and cash, followed by a later rights sale. Neither return should be dismissed, yet the Knicks won on the canonical retrospective assessment of the exchange. Avoid counting all of Bill McGill's 1963–64 output as Shue's direct 1962 contribution, since New York supplied Hogue too. The correct evaluation credits the identified playing time to each receiving club and marks subsequent asset moves separately.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win, New York A- and Detroit B. Shue played 78 Knicks games after the August 1962 deal and later moved in a separate two-player package. Imhoff contributed 103 Detroit appearances plus the original undisclosed cash consideration. Later asset paths explain residual value without rewriting the compensation.

sections.heading: San Francisco Bought a Veteran, Not a Draft Asset
sections.body: Detroit sold George Lee’s player rights to the San Francisco Warriors on September 19, 1962. The Warriors paid cash, with no reliable public figure for the transaction price. Lee had already spent three seasons with Detroit after being selected in the 1959 draft, so the acquired asset was an experienced forward who could join a rotation. San Francisco’s first season after the franchise moved west provided the setting for this purchase.

sections.heading: Lee Played 148 Games for the Warriors
sections.body: Lee appeared in 64 games in 1962–63, averaging 7.0 points and 3.4 rebounds in 18.6 minutes. His role became smaller: 54 appearances followed in 1963–64 and 19 in 1964–65. He spent 1965–66 on the coaching staff before returning for one game in 1966–67 and ten in 1967–68. Across those five playing seasons following the transaction, the Warriors received 148 regular-season appearances, though most were reserve minutes.

sections.heading: Detroit Received Money, Not a Traceable Player Replacement
sections.body: The Pistons’ return was cash, and the surviving transaction records do not establish its amount. Selling rights to a player they had already used for three years may have suited Detroit’s roster decisions, but assigning the payment an invented dollar value would distort the exchange. No player or draft selection is documented as part of this September sale. The franchise’s inability to trace the money to a later basketball asset is an evidence limitation, not proof the cash had no value.

sections.heading: A Useful Reserve Gives San Francisco a Narrower Victory
sections.body: The current grades are Warriors B and Pistons C-plus. Lee’s 148 games, including 64 in his first Warriors season, deliver a concrete return that supports the Warriors winning. His shrinking minutes and intermittent playing history keep the acquisition well below a major star-level result. Detroit’s undisclosed cash is a legitimate counterweight but cannot match the documented on-court record with the evidence available.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win — San Francisco/Golden State B, Detroit C-plus. Buying George Lee’s rights produced 148 Warriors appearances across five playing seasons, beginning with 64 games at 7.0 points per game in 1962–63. Detroit received cash of an unknown amount, so the identifiable basketball return favors San Francisco without proving the money was valueless.

sections.heading: Imhoff Was Sold to the Lakers for Cash
sections.body: Detroit transferred Darrall Imhoff to Los Angeles on April 16, 1964 in return for cash considerations. This was not a two-player swap: the Pistons received money and the Lakers received a recognized NBA center. League, Detroit and Lakers transaction logs corroborate the rights sale. Because the surviving source packet does not document the amount, the financial side cannot be assigned a reliable per-game or player-equivalent monetary value.

sections.heading: Imhoff Supplied Several Seasons of Lakers Center Play
sections.body: Imhoff subsequently appeared in 316 regular-season games for Los Angeles. That was an identifiable long-term playing return from a cash acquisition, substantially more than a brief look at a reserve big man. His role was not equivalent to that of the Lakers’ leading scorers, but having a durable center available across multiple seasons made the transaction meaningful. The grade can recognize that demonstrated contribution without inventing advanced statistical impacts or making him the sole reason for team success.

sections.heading: He Also Appeared in the Chamberlain Trade Package
sections.body: Imhoff later became one of the Lakers players moved to Philadelphia in the 1968 transaction that brought Wilt Chamberlain to Los Angeles. This is a real connected asset movement, although the Chamberlain acquisition involved other players and cannot be credited wholly to the 1964 cash sale. The traced connection gives the Lakers an additional identifiable downstream role for the center they originally purchased. It should be described as participation in a larger package, not as an even exchange of cash for Chamberlain.

sections.heading: The Cash Amount Limits Detroit’s Retrospective Grade
sections.body: Los Angeles earns A-minus while Detroit receives D-plus. The gap reflects 316 Lakers games and the player’s inclusion in a consequential later package, against an undisclosed cash payment to Detroit. The Pistons may have valued that payment for financial reasons, but the documented record cannot show what it purchased or how it was used. Older repeated editorial text incorrectly assigned the Lakers C-plus. That contradiction should not override the canonical A-minus grade or the actual asset history.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win — Los Angeles A-minus, Detroit D-plus. The Lakers received Darrall Imhoff for undisclosed cash, used him in 316 regular-season games, and subsequently included him in the 1968 Wilt Chamberlain package. Detroit’s financial return is documented only as cash of an unknown amount. The on-court and later linked transaction value favor Los Angeles without assuming that Imhoff alone produced the Chamberlain deal.

sections.heading: Baltimore Received the Deeper Package
sections.body: The 1964 deal sent Terry Dischinger, Don Kojis and Rod Thorn to Detroit for Bob Ferry, Bailey Howell, Don Ohl and the rights to Les Hunter and Wali Jones. Archival public sources disagree on whether the transaction should be dated June 9 or June 18, but the player package is consistent. The Bullets received five assets, including an established star in Howell, a productive guard in Ohl and two recent draft rights. Detroit received the youngest headline scorer in Dischinger, who remained excellent immediately. The difference is depth. Baltimore did not need every incoming player to hit because the package supplied multiple productive contributors at once, while Detroit's side became much more dependent on Dischinger.

sections.heading: Detroit Did Get an All-Star Season from Dischinger
sections.body: Detroit's B grade matters because this was not a one-sided disaster in which the Pistons received nothing. Dischinger played all 80 games in 1964-65, averaged 18.2 points and 6.0 rebounds, and made the All-Star team. He was only 24 and had already been Rookie of the Year earlier in his career. That is substantial value. The complication is what followed: Dischinger missed the next two seasons while serving in the military, interrupting the continuity Detroit expected from the centerpiece. Kojis and Thorn did not supply enough additional production to match the combined package Baltimore received. Detroit's return was good; Baltimore's was simply broader and more durable.

sections.heading: Howell and Ohl Gave Baltimore Immediate High-End Production
sections.body: Baltimore's incoming veterans immediately changed the quality of the roster. Howell averaged 20.8 points and 10.5 rebounds in 1964-65 and remained an All-Star-level forward. Ohl provided major backcourt scoring, while Ferry added frontcourt depth. The Bullets finished 37-43 but reached the Western Division Finals after winning a playoff series, a meaningful step for the franchise. The trade should not be credited with every team accomplishment, yet the incoming players were central enough to demonstrate immediate realized value. Baltimore did not have to wait for the draft rights to justify the move; Howell and Ohl alone supplied a formidable veteran return.

sections.heading: Wali Jones Added Another Productive Branch
sections.body: The rights to Wali Jones gave Baltimore another young guard who played 77 games as a rookie and made the All-Rookie team. He later had a long professional career. Les Hunter was less impactful in the NBA, but the pair of draft rights increased the number of ways Baltimore could win the transaction. That breadth is what pushes the Bullets' grade to A+. Howell and Ohl were established contributors, Ferry had value, and Jones became another useful player. Detroit's best asset, Dischinger, was excellent enough to keep the Pistons at B, but one star-level season plus secondary pieces could not match the total volume of quality Baltimore received.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wizards Win. The Baltimore franchise, represented here by the modern Wizards lineage, earns A+ because it acquired Bailey Howell, Don Ohl, Bob Ferry and the rights to Wali Jones and Les Hunter in one transaction. Howell and Ohl delivered immediate high-level production, Jones became a useful rookie and long-term professional, and the package had unusual depth. Detroit receives B because Terry Dischinger was genuinely excellent, making the All-Star team in his first Pistons season, and the Pistons also received Don Kojis and Rod Thorn. Dischinger's two-season military absence then interrupted the expected value of the centerpiece. The documented Wizards Win verdict reflects aggregate realized value, not a claim that Detroit received a poor player.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Deep Dive: The 1964 Blockbuster Was Bigger Than Terry Dischinger versus Bailey Howell
featuredDeepDive.intro: This eight-player exchange was enormous by the standards of its era. It is also easy to oversimplify into a comparison between Dischinger and Howell. The deeper ledger matters more. Baltimore acquired several players who contributed immediately, while Detroit concentrated much of its upside in one young All-Star whose career was soon interrupted by military service.

sections.heading: The Date Is Less Certain Than the Package
sections.body: Historical transaction public sources do not perfectly agree on the date. RealGM records the deal on June 9, while Basketball-Reference places it on June 18. The disagreement is worth acknowledging because it illustrates the limits of archival precision for early NBA history. The asset exchange itself is consistent across the sources: Detroit received Dischinger, Kojis and Thorn; Baltimore received Ferry, Howell, Ohl and the rights to Hunter and Jones. The grade therefore does not depend on resolving a nine-day archival discrepancy. It depends on the players and rights that actually changed hands and the value those assets subsequently created for the two franchises.

sections.heading: Dischinger Was a Legitimate Centerpiece
sections.body: A harsh Detroit grade would ignore how good Dischinger was. He had already won Rookie of the Year and made All-Star teams before the trade, then averaged 18.2 points in 80 games in his first Pistons season and was an All-Star again. Detroit had acquired a 24-year-old scorer with a clear star résumé. That is why the Pistons remain at B despite losing the overall trade. The problem was concentration risk. Dischinger then missed two full NBA seasons because of military service, and the supporting return from Kojis and Thorn did not compensate for the depth Baltimore had received. A strong centerpiece can still lose a trade when the other side acquires several quality pieces.

sections.heading: Baltimore Added Proven Scoring and Rebounding
sections.body: Howell arrived as a multi-time All-Star and immediately averaged 20.8 points and 10.5 rebounds for Baltimore. Ohl also brought major scoring from the backcourt. Those were not speculative assets whose value depended on development; they were proven NBA players capable of helping immediately. Baltimore's 1964-65 club reached the division finals after winning a playoff series, and the incoming veterans were part of that competitive leap. The analysis does not assign the entire playoff run to the trade, but the direct production is difficult to miss. Baltimore received enough established talent that the deal was already strong before the rookie rights to Jones and Hunter are considered.

sections.heading: The Draft Rights Turned Depth into Overwhelming Depth
sections.body: Wali Jones gave Baltimore yet another useful outcome. He played 77 games as a rookie, made the All-Rookie team and became a long-term professional guard. Hunter's NBA impact was smaller, but the rights still represented another development opportunity. When those players are added to Howell, Ohl and Ferry, Baltimore's package becomes unusually broad. Detroit had the single best young scorer in the transaction, but Baltimore had several assets capable of producing value simultaneously. That is the difference between A+ and B. The grade does not require every Bullet to become a star. It reflects the sheer number of productive branches created by the outgoing Detroit package.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wizards Win, Baltimore/Washington A+ and Detroit B. The Bullets acquired a deep package led by Bailey Howell and Don Ohl, received immediate playoff-caliber production, and added Wali Jones as another useful young player. Detroit's return deserves respect because Terry Dischinger remained an All-Star and averaged 18.2 points in his first Pistons season. His subsequent two-year military absence reduced the continuity of that value, while Kojis and Thorn did not close the broader gap. Archival sources disagree on whether the trade should be dated June 9 or June 18, but they agree on the players involved. On that stable list of assets, Baltimore clearly accumulated more total realized value.

sections.heading: Detroit Sold Warlick’s Rights to the San Francisco Warriors
sections.body: On September 1, 1966, Detroit sold Bob Warlick’s player rights to the San Francisco Warriors for cash. The modern TradeVerdicts entry attributes San Francisco to the Golden State Warriors franchise. No draft selection or returning player is listed for Detroit; the package was a player-rights sale. Warlick was an NBA-capable guard, so San Francisco obtained a basketball opportunity rather than an indefinite future asset whose eventual identity was unknown.

sections.heading: Warlick Supplied Two Seasons of Warriors Minutes
sections.body: Warlick appeared in 81 games for the Warriors across the next two seasons. His larger run came in 1967–68, when he played 69 games and averaged 8.9 points, 3.8 rebounds and 2.3 assists. Those numbers show a practical reserve or rotation return rather than a short-lived rights claim that never reached the court. San Francisco could use him, while Detroit gave up that potential on-court contribution in exchange for money whose amount is not established in the cited record.

sections.heading: The Measurable Playing Time Drives the Slight Warriors Edge
sections.body: The canonical grades are San Francisco/Golden State B-minus and Detroit C-plus. The Warriors obtained a player who subsequently made 81 appearances, while the Pistons’ cash consideration remains unquantified. It is inappropriate to assume that Detroit received no financial value, just as it would be inaccurate to award the Warriors later accomplishments unrelated to Warlick. The outcome is a slight on-court advantage grounded in the exact rights sold and the appearances that followed.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Warriors Edge — San Francisco/Golden State B-minus, Detroit C-plus. Warlick played 81 games for the Warriors over two seasons, including 69 games in 1967–68 at 8.9 points per game. Detroit took undisclosed cash for his rights. The Warriors’ measurable guard contribution supports the narrow result without attaching invented value to the undocumented sale price.

sections.heading: Baltimore Sold Hightower's NBA Rights, Not a Season of Production
sections.body: On January 29, 1967, the Baltimore Bullets sold the NBA player rights to Wayne Hightower to the Detroit Pistons for cash. The Baltimore, Detroit and league transaction records agree on the date and structure. The present-day Washington Wizards franchise identifier refers back to Baltimore, not to the city where the Bullets played in 1967. The cash consideration has no verified dollar figure in the record, so it cannot be priced or dismissed as trivial. Detroit purchased a possible future NBA contributor; Baltimore received the only immediately identifiable realized consideration.

sections.heading: Hightower Never Played a Pistons NBA Game
sections.body: Detroit's prospective value depended on Hightower eventually appearing for the club, but that did not happen. His player history instead records a May 16, 1967 signing with the Denver Rockets of the American Basketball Association, less than four months after Detroit's NBA rights acquisition. The ABA signing is a separate career move, not a transfer of NBA playing time to the Pistons. The reviewed trade record supplies no ensuing Detroit NBA appearance or additional basketball asset obtained for his rights. A player with an established career elsewhere does not become a productive Detroit acquisition merely because the club briefly held his NBA rights.

sections.heading: Baltimore Had a Cash Return, Though the Price Is Unspecified
sections.body: The Bullets' return from selling Hightower's NBA rights was cash. Transaction ledgers do not identify the amount, so it would be a mistake to present the sale as a verified financial windfall. But cash is still an asset received, unlike Detroit's rights purchase, which generated no NBA games before Hightower signed in the ABA. The canonical C-plus for Baltimore reflects that modest, documented outcome. It does not prove the seller earned an exceptional amount or that its executives knew where Hightower would sign in the spring.

sections.heading: Why the Grades Favor the Bullets Rather Than Detroit
sections.body: The appropriate retrospective verdict is Slight Bullets Edge: Baltimore/Washington C-plus and Detroit D-plus. The distinction rests on an actual payment to Baltimore versus rights that gave the Pistons no observed NBA production or trade conversion. Detroit may have made an understandable low-cost bet on a former NBA player, but the records do not establish the acquisition price or a resulting Detroit playing contribution. The previous Slight Pistons Edge and C/C-minus framing credited speculative rights more heavily than a tangible realized return. A modest Bullets advantage is the defensible sourced conclusion.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Bullets Edge — Baltimore/Washington C+, Detroit D+. The Bullets sold Wayne Hightower's NBA rights to Detroit for unspecified cash on January 29, 1967. Hightower never appeared in an NBA game for Detroit and signed with the ABA's Denver Rockets on May 16. Baltimore received the only documented realized return.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The 1967 Hightower Rights Sale: Baltimore's Small Advantage
featuredDeepDive.intro: Baltimore's January 1967 cash sale of Wayne Hightower's NBA rights to Detroit was a wager on whether those rights would become playing value. They did not. Within four months Hightower signed in the ABA, and the Pistons never received an NBA appearance or traceable subsequent basketball consideration from him. Baltimore's money cannot be priced, but it can be distinguished from an unrealized rights acquisition.

sections.heading: The Transaction Ledgers Record a Rights Sale on January 29
sections.body: The NBA, Baltimore Bullets and Detroit Pistons transaction ledgers list a January 29, 1967 sale of Wayne Hightower's rights to Detroit for cash. Although modern franchise navigation links the Bullets to the Washington Wizards, the 1967 seller was Baltimore. The player-rights mechanism is important because an NBA club could purchase rights without thereby guaranteeing that the player would sign or suit up. No published cash amount accompanies the record, and no player, draft pick or future compensation is identified alongside the rights. That limits the original package to Hightower's NBA rights against money.

sections.heading: The May ABA Signing Explains the Missing Pistons Outcome
sections.body: Hightower's historical player transaction record shows he signed with the Denver Rockets of the ABA on May 16, 1967. This subsequent signing did not turn into Detroit NBA production: Hightower recorded no regular-season appearances for the Pistons. His ABA career therefore should not be added to Detroit's return, nor should his earlier NBA experience be treated as games supplied by the new rights holder. The evidence supports a failed basketball realization of the acquired rights, while leaving unanswered whether Detroit had any informal expectations for his availability when purchasing them.

sections.heading: What the Bullets Actually Received Cannot Be Numerically Priced
sections.body: Baltimore obtained a cash payment and gave up a right that did not produce a Pistons NBA game. The money itself is unquantified in the cited transaction histories, making it impossible to calculate the precise profit or infer how the organization used the proceeds. This uncertainty should moderate the grade, not reverse the direction of the result. The team that sold the rights obtained an identifiable financial asset; the buyer had no documented on-court payoff. The C-plus Baltimore/Washington grade reflects that limited but realized consideration rather than treating the money as a known major transaction.

sections.heading: A Small Bullets Edge Instead of a Retrospective Pistons Win
sections.body: Detroit's D-plus is an outcome grade on the acquired NBA rights: the club had an opportunity to sign Hightower but received zero Pistons NBA games and no supported downstream basketball asset. Baltimore's C-plus recognizes a real cash consideration of unknown magnitude. The size of the grade gap is deliberately modest, because the source record does not prove what the clubs thought Hightower's rights were worth or establish a transfer price. The stronger retrospective side was the one that received something traceable. That is why Slight Bullets Edge is more precise than the older editorial's contrary Pistons win.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Baltimore receives C+ and a Slight Bullets Edge for the 1967 cash sale of Hightower's NBA rights. Detroit receives D+ because the rights did not produce any NBA games or identified later basketball value. The cash amount is unknown, so the advantage is modest and source-limited, not an invented financial windfall.

sections.heading: LaRusso’s Rights Changed Hands Again in August 1967
sections.body: Detroit sold Rudy LaRusso’s player rights to the San Francisco Warriors for cash on August 31, 1967. These were the rights to an established veteran, not the rights to a rookie draft choice. LaRusso had reached Detroit through a January three-team transaction but had not reported to the Pistons. The first-round compensation connected to that earlier transaction belongs to January and was not an extra asset in the August sale.

sections.heading: The Warriors Got Two All-Star Seasons
sections.body: San Francisco received an immediate starting-caliber contributor. In 1967–68 LaRusso played 79 games and averaged 21.8 points and 9.4 rebounds, earning an All-Star selection. In 1968–69 he appeared in 75 games at 20.7 points and 8.3 rebounds, again making the All-Star team and earning All-Defensive Second Team honors. Those 154 regular-season appearances are the clearest outcome of the August rights purchase.

sections.heading: Detroit Monetized Rights It Was Not Using
sections.body: The Pistons received cash, but the preserved transaction ledgers do not disclose a dollar amount. After LaRusso declined to report, obtaining money for his rights gave Detroit some return from a situation it could not turn directly into playing time. The club’s earlier first-round compensation cannot be counted twice. Detroit therefore receives credit for a practical recovery rather than being portrayed as if it had freely surrendered a productive Pistons starter.

sections.heading: The Performance Difference Explains the Grades
sections.body: The current ledger gives the Warriors A and Detroit C-plus. That grade gap is supported by two LaRusso All-Star selections, his All-Defensive recognition and back-to-back scoring seasons above 20 points per game. The Warriors received a lead offensive player; Detroit received an undisclosed payment for rights to someone who had not joined its roster. The sale was understandable for Detroit, but the known results overwhelmingly favor San Francisco.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win — San Francisco/Golden State A, Detroit C-plus. The August 1967 rights sale brought the Warriors 154 Rudy LaRusso games, two All-Star seasons and an All-Defensive honor. Detroit collected undisclosed cash for a player who had not reported. The earlier compensatory draft pick belongs to a different January deal and is excluded from this verdict.

sections.heading: Fort Wayne’s Successor Franchise Traded a Pick for Chappell
sections.body: Detroit acquired Len Chappell from the Cincinnati Royals on November 27, 1967. The price was a 1968 third-round selection that Cincinnati used on Fred Foster, No. 28 overall. Detroit was seeking an experienced frontcourt contributor while Cincinnati accepted an additional route into the next draft. A legacy import listed cash alongside the pick; the verified Detroit, Cincinnati and league transaction ledgers did not substantiate that payment, so the cash entry has been excluded from the corrected asset package.

sections.heading: Chappell Played Well but Departed Quickly
sections.body: Chappell gave Detroit 57 games, averaging approximately 10.0 points and 6.1 rebounds. He filled a real NBA rotation need, but Detroit did not keep that contribution for several seasons. Milwaukee selected Chappell in the 1968 expansion draft, cutting off his Pistons return. That short stay is the central limitation of Detroit’s otherwise useful acquisition and keeps the club below an A-level outcome.

sections.heading: The Pick Became a Productive Royals Player
sections.body: Cincinnati used the pick on Foster, who played 131 regular-season games for the Royals. He averaged 14.8 points per game in 1969–70 and later entered a package with Connie Dierking that brought Darrall Imhoff and a future draft choice to Cincinnati. The subsequent exchange is meaningful because it extended the value of the specific player the Royals obtained with Detroit’s pick. Foster’s documented stint and later transfer distinguish this from a third-round gamble that yielded nothing.

sections.heading: The Different Timelines Explain the Grade Gap
sections.body: The current grades favor Cincinnati/Sacramento A-minus over Detroit B-minus. Detroit received immediate forward minutes but lost Chappell through expansion. Cincinnati received a selected player who contributed and then formed part of another trade return. The franchise names in the modern archive refer to the present-day Kings and Pistons; the 1967 participants were the Cincinnati Royals and Detroit Pistons. No unverified cash payment should influence the ranking.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Royals Win — Cincinnati/Sacramento A-minus, Detroit B-minus. Chappell contributed 57 Pistons games but moved on in the 1968 expansion draft. The No. 28 pick became Fred Foster, who played 131 games for Cincinnati and later featured in another transaction. The reliable historical sources do not establish the legacy cash component, so the comparison uses the verified player-for-pick exchange.

sections.heading: New York Traded Star Production for a Better Structural Fit
sections.body: The Knicks sent Walt Bellamy and Howard Komives to Detroit for Dave DeBusschere in December 1968. Bellamy was a former No. 1 pick and established scoring center, so New York did not acquire DeBusschere at a discount built from unwanted contracts. The Knicks paid with recognizable talent because their frontcourt had become awkward: Bellamy and Willis Reed both occupied central interior roles, while the roster needed defense, rebounding and mobility at forward. DeBusschere allowed Reed to settle at center and gave the lineup a more coherent distribution of responsibilities.

sections.heading: DeBusschere Changed the Knicks’ Defensive Identity Immediately
sections.body: DeBusschere could guard powerful forwards, switch onto smaller players and rebound without requiring the offense to revolve around him. His arrival allowed New York to play a connected team defense around Reed, Walt Frazier, Bill Bradley and Dick Barnett. The Knicks became more physical and versatile while retaining enough scoring from their existing stars. He was not simply an additional famous name. His willingness to defend, pass and take fewer shots made every other member of the core easier to deploy in an efficient role.

sections.heading: The Trade Produced the Only Two Championships in Franchise History
sections.body: New York won the 1970 championship and returned to win again in 1973. DeBusschere was an All-Star in each of his five full Knicks seasons and earned repeated All-Defensive honors. His contributions included guarding elite opposing forwards, finishing possessions with rebounds and making timely perimeter shots. Championship credit belongs to the entire roster, especially Reed and Frazier, but the timing is impossible to ignore. The Knicks acquired DeBusschere in the middle of 1968-69 and became the complete team that defined the franchise’s greatest era.

sections.heading: Detroit Received an Established Center but Did Not Build Around the Return
sections.body: Bellamy remained a productive scorer and rebounder after the trade, making Detroit’s return more substantial than the existing F grade suggests. He did not remain long enough to anchor a new Pistons contender and was later moved to Atlanta. Komives provided guard minutes but did not become a franchise-level piece or a premium later asset. Detroit obtained credible immediate talent, which supports a C rather than a failing grade. The problem was the loss of a hometown star whose all-around impact proved more valuable than the statistics coming back.

sections.heading: DeBusschere’s Player-Coach Past Made the Acquisition Unusual
sections.body: Before the trade, DeBusschere had served as Detroit’s player-coach while still in his twenties, an extraordinary burden that reflected both his basketball intelligence and the instability around him. Returning to a full-time playing role in New York allowed him to focus on the skills that made him elite. The Knicks already had strong coaching and a defined system, so his understanding of spacing, defensive communication and team responsibility translated immediately. New York acquired a player whose experience exceeded his age and whose temperament fit a veteran contender.

sections.heading: The Grades Should Separate Detroit’s Real Return From New York’s Historic Payoff
sections.body: New York deserves an A+ because the trade supplied the final frontcourt balance for two championship teams and delivered a Hall of Famer at his peak. Detroit’s original F was too absolute because Bellamy was still a high-level player and Komives had legitimate NBA value. A C recognizes that immediate return while accounting for its limited duration and lack of postseason consequence. The Knicks’ advantage remains enormous. They converted overlapping talent into perfect fit; Detroit converted perfect fit into respectable but temporary production.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: New York wins with an A+, while Detroit moves to C. DeBusschere became the defensive and emotional connector of championship teams in 1970 and 1973, earned All-Star and All-Defensive recognition and allowed Reed to occupy his best position. Bellamy was a genuine star and Komives was a useful guard, so Detroit did not receive an empty return. Their value was shorter and did not create a contender. The Knicks exchanged more individual scoring for the exact player who completed their structure, producing the most important trade in franchise history.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Dave DeBusschere Was the Final Piece Because He Needed the Fewest Possessions
featuredDeepDive.intro: Great teams do not always need another primary scorer. The late-1960s Knicks already had offensive talent and strong individual reputations, but their frontcourt roles overlapped. DeBusschere changed the team because he could influence every possession without controlling the ball. His defense, rebounding, passing and physical temperament connected the roster’s existing strengths. Detroit received a statistically accomplished center, yet New York received the player whose style converted good pieces into the only championship teams the franchise has produced.

sections.heading: Bellamy and Reed Created a Positional Redundancy
sections.body: Bellamy was a powerful interior scorer, and Reed was capable of playing forward or center. Using them together could produce points and rebounds, but it also made the frontcourt slower and left fewer touches for other creators. DeBusschere’s arrival allowed Reed to become the full-time center around whom New York’s defense and half-court offense could be organized. The trade was therefore not a simple talent upgrade. It was a reallocation of positional responsibility that made the entire starting five more balanced.

sections.heading: Defense Was an Active Source of Offense for the Knicks
sections.body: DeBusschere’s stops and rebounds did more than suppress opponents. They enabled Frazier and the Knicks’ guards to run, created early scoring opportunities and prevented New York from beginning every possession against a set defense. His ability to guard star forwards reduced the help required from teammates, keeping the floor organized when the Knicks regained the ball. The championship teams are remembered for unselfish offense, but that style depended on a defense capable of ending possessions cleanly and turning collective effort into transition chances.

sections.heading: His Shooting Pulled Power Forwards Away From Reed
sections.body: DeBusschere was not a modern high-volume three-point shooter, yet his willingness to make outside shots mattered in an era of crowded paint. Defenders could not completely abandon him to double Reed or clog Frazier’s drives. That spacing created room without demanding plays be called specifically for DeBusschere. He could score when the defense conceded an opportunity and then return to the less visible work of screening, rebounding and defending. The Knicks gained offensive balance precisely because the new star did not require star-level possession volume.

sections.heading: The 1970 and 1973 Titles Confirmed Repeatable Value
sections.body: One championship can emerge from a favorable matchup or exceptional short-term health. Winning again three years later showed that DeBusschere’s fit survived roster aging, tactical adjustments and a different playoff path. He remained part of the core when New York returned to the Finals in 1972 and won in 1973. His contribution was durable because it was based on transferable skills rather than a temporary scoring spike. The trade gave the Knicks a player whose value remained high even as teammates’ roles and production changed.

sections.heading: Detroit’s Side Was Better Than F but Far Below Championship Value
sections.body: Bellamy’s résumé and immediate production require respect. He remained a formidable rebounder and scorer, and Komives offered backcourt competence. Detroit did not receive prospects who failed to make the league. The return still did not solve the franchise’s larger problems, and Bellamy’s stay was brief. DeBusschere became a Hall of Fame centerpiece elsewhere while the Pistons continued searching for direction. A C accurately distinguishes a credible basketball return from an outcome that could not approach New York’s titles and long-term identity.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Knicks’ A+ reflects more than two rings. DeBusschere gave the team positional clarity, elite defense and a star who strengthened teammates without competing for their touches. His five full seasons in New York produced five All-Star selections and the franchise’s only championships. Detroit’s C acknowledges that Bellamy and Komives were real players and that the trade returned immediate production. The Pistons nevertheless surrendered the player whose fit became historic. New York understood that the missing piece was not another scorer; it was the defender and connector who made the roster complete.

sections.heading: Detroit and Baltimore Exchanged Players and Draft Positions
sections.body: The Pistons acquired Bob Quick and Baltimore’s 1970 second-round selection on February 1, 1970. In return the Bullets received Eddie Miles and Detroit’s fourth-round pick. The future draft selections became No. 32 Ken Warzynski for Detroit and No. 54 Bill Stricker for Baltimore. This was a balanced attempt to alter existing player depth while creating two additional later draft outcomes. The Bullets are represented by the present-day Washington franchise in the archive, but Baltimore was the team name at the time.

sections.heading: Quick and Miles Both Became NBA Contributors
sections.body: Quick appeared in 93 Detroit games over parts of three seasons, including a 56-game 1970–71 stretch averaging 8.0 points and 4.1 rebounds. Miles played 66 games for Baltimore over parts of two seasons, with 63 appearances and 9.9 points per game during the club’s 1971 Finals season. Those are measurable returns for both partners. The documented records do not support treating one veteran as completely useless just because the other had a respectable season.

sections.heading: Neither Draft Selection Broke the Tie
sections.body: Warzynski, taken with Detroit’s acquired second-rounder, never played in the NBA. Baltimore’s fourth-rounder became Stricker, whose one NBA appearance came with Portland rather than the Bullets. The two selections therefore failed to generate valuable sustained roster contributions for the clubs acquiring them. With both Quick and Miles providing some immediate production, the archived grades are Detroit B-minus and Baltimore/Washington B-minus. The Even Trade result is supported by those comparatively close player outcomes, not a repeated formula about the nominal rank of second versus fourth rounds.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Detroit B-minus, Baltimore/Washington B-minus. The Pistons received Bob Quick and the pick used on Ken Warzynski; Baltimore obtained Eddie Miles and the pick used on Bill Stricker. Both veterans supplied identifiable NBA minutes, while neither draft pick generated sustained value for the receiving club. The archive therefore leaves the teams level.

sections.heading: The Trade Bought Detroit an Established Big Man
sections.body: Detroit received veteran forward Jim Davis from the Houston Rockets in December 1971. The Pistons sent Houston their 1972 first-round draft choice in return. Team transaction histories list the exchange on December 10, one day after the date encoded in this archive record. The underlying player-for-pick exchange is not in dispute. Detroit elected to use an available selection to acquire an experienced frontcourt player instead of waiting for its next first-round rookie.

sections.heading: The No. 4 Pick Did Not Stay in Houston
sections.body: Houston held the first-rounder through the winter, then traded it to Phoenix on April 7, 1972, acquiring center Otto Moore. Phoenix used the fourth overall pick on Corky Calhoun. Calhoun was not sent directly from Detroit to Houston, and the Rockets did not select him with this pick. Tracking the actual sequence is necessary to evaluate what Houston received: draft flexibility that yielded Moore, rather than retroactively crediting Houston with a player another franchise drafted.

sections.heading: Davis Provided Real Detroit Minutes
sections.body: Davis played a substantial stretch for the Pistons following the trade, making this more than a failed attempt to buy veteran depth. Detroit received an immediate NBA contributor and did not simply give up its selection for nothing. Its return still needs to be weighed against Houston turning the first-round asset into another established player. The comparison is between the Davis stint and a pick that produced a later player acquisition, not between Davis and Calhoun’s career with Phoenix.

sections.heading: The Recorded Grades Call It a Narrow Rockets Win
sections.body: The canonical ledger grades Houston B-plus and Detroit B, with Rockets Win as the final result. Houston extracted an additional maneuver from the selection by turning it into Moore; Detroit secured Davis for its own roster. The small grade difference fits the documented paths without portraying either side as an overwhelming loser. This historical note also preserves the date discrepancy for separate archive-identity review rather than quietly rewriting a published slug.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win — Houston B-plus, Detroit B. Houston obtained Detroit’s 1972 first-round pick in exchange for Jim Davis, then sent that pick to Phoenix for Otto Moore. Phoenix drafted Corky Calhoun at No. 4; he was not an incoming Rockets player. Detroit received a genuine veteran contribution from Davis, leaving Houston with only a modest documented advantage through the pick’s next transaction.

sections.heading: Houston and Detroit Swapped Guards on August 1, 1972
sections.body: Detroit traded Jimmy Walker to the Houston Rockets for Stu Lantz on August 1, 1972. The two clubs and league transaction records agree on the exchange; there was no attached pick or cash payment listed in the original package. The Detroit and Houston sides were both guard acquisitions, making actual playing time, scoring and later asset paths useful ways to measure the result. The canonical record favors Houston slightly instead of calling the swap an Even Trade. It recognizes real value on each side but finds that Walker carried the larger workload for Houston and remained tradable afterward.

sections.heading: Walker's Rockets Tenure Included a Full 81-Game Season
sections.body: Walker appeared in 81 Houston regular-season games in 1972–73, logging 3,079 minutes and averaging 18.0 points. That season is the clearest on-court benefit the Rockets received from the exchange. He made three more Houston appearances before the club later sent him to Kansas City–Omaha in a separate deal for Matt Guokas. Those three additional games and the Guokas branch are part of the post-trade asset record, but they should not be silently rolled into Walker's 81-game scoring line or credited to Detroit. Houston obtained an established offensive contributor capable of playing heavy minutes.

sections.heading: Lantz Contributed 101 Pistons Games and Playoff Minutes
sections.body: Detroit obtained a useful player in Lantz, who appeared in 101 Pistons regular-season games over two seasons with per-season scoring averages of 9.6 and 8.9 points. He also played seven postseason games during the Pistons' 52-win 1973–74 campaign. New Orleans subsequently selected him in the 1974 expansion draft, ending the Pistons' direct playing return. Those contributions justify the canonical Detroit B grade: he was not a failed acquisition, although his Detroit scoring and usage did not match Walker's first Houston season.

sections.heading: Houston's B-Plus Reflects the Larger Immediate Return
sections.body: Houston's B-plus reflects Walker's 81-game, 18.0-point season, three further appearances and the fact the Rockets later moved him for Matt Guokas. Detroit's B reflects Lantz's 101 games and seven playoff appearances before an expansion-draft loss. The margin is moderate rather than overwhelming: each club used its incoming guard, and Detroit participated in a successful 52-win season while Lantz was on the roster. But Walker's stronger direct workload and additional asset continuity support Slight Rockets Edge. The previous Even Trade and C/C grades understated both acquisitions and erased the difference.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Rockets Edge — Houston B+, Detroit B. The August 1, 1972 Jimmy Walker–Stu Lantz exchange gave Houston an 81-game, 18.0-point Walker season plus three later appearances; he was subsequently traded for Matt Guokas. Detroit received 101 Lantz regular-season games and seven playoff appearances before the 1974 expansion draft.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Why the 1972 Walker–Lantz Swap Slightly Favored Houston
featuredDeepDive.intro: A guard-for-guard exchange on August 1, 1972 sent Jimmy Walker from Detroit to Houston and Stu Lantz the other way. Both franchises gained genuine NBA playing time. Walker's 81 games and heavy scoring workload in 1972–73, followed by later asset continuity, put the Rockets narrowly ahead of the Pistons' 101-game Lantz return and seven playoff outings. The canonical grades are Houston B-plus and Detroit B, not the outdated Even Trade and C/C shorthand.

sections.heading: The Original Trade Was One Guard for Another
sections.body: The 1972–73 Detroit, Houston and NBA transaction ledgers identify the August 1, 1972 trade of Jimmy Walker for Stu Lantz. Executive histories for Detroit's Edwin Coil and Houston's Ray Patterson reinforce that direct player exchange. The original compensation does not include a draft pick, cash, or Matt Guokas. Guokas entered the story in a later Rockets deal after Houston had already used Walker, while New Orleans acquired Lantz in an expansion draft much later. Distinguishing the original player swap from subsequent franchise transactions is essential before weighing the teams' outcomes.

sections.heading: Walker Was a Primary Houston Scorer Before the Guokas Move
sections.body: During 1972–73 Walker appeared 81 times for Houston, producing 3,079 minutes and 18.0 points per game. He logged three more appearances the following season before Houston traded him to Kansas City–Omaha for Matt Guokas. His Rockets tenure thus amounted to 84 regular-season appearances, with the workload highly concentrated in his first season. The later Guokas exchange shows that Houston converted the departing guard into another roster asset; the records do not justify adding all of Guokas's later career production to Walker as if that had already been promised in August 1972.

sections.heading: Lantz Was a Useful Piston and a Seven-Game Playoff Contributor
sections.body: Lantz appeared in 101 regular-season games for Detroit across the next two seasons, averaging 9.6 points in one and 8.9 in the other. He played seven postseason games when the Pistons reached 52 wins in 1973–74. His contribution is not negligible simply because Houston received the higher retrospective grade. The Pistons later lost him when the New Orleans Jazz selected him in the 1974 NBA expansion draft. That explains why Detroit's direct value had an endpoint and why further Lantz seasons with other franchises do not belong to the original Pistons return.

sections.heading: A Modest Rockets Edge, Not an Imaginary Blowout
sections.body: Walker provided Houston a full heavy-minutes scoring season, three further games and enough remaining value to enter a separate Guokas deal. Lantz supplied Detroit 101 games and postseason use before the expansion draft. Both sides realized production, so the grade difference is deliberately narrow: Rockets B-plus, Pistons B. Calling the swap an Even Trade ignores the disparity between Walker's 18.0-point offensive season and Lantz's lower Detroit scoring, while grading Detroit C erases a useful rotation contribution to a strong Pistons club. The historically defensible result is Slight Rockets Edge.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Houston earns a slight edge, B+ to Detroit's B. Walker logged 81 Rockets games and 18.0 points per game in 1972–73, then three more games before the Guokas trade; Lantz appeared 101 times for Detroit, including seven postseason games. Both produced, but the Rockets' first-season scoring return was stronger.

sections.heading: Detroit Sold Howie Komives for a 1973 Second-Round Choice
sections.body: On September 29, 1972, the Detroit Pistons sent Howie Komives to the Buffalo Braves for Buffalo's 1973 second-round draft pick. The pick eventually became No. 20 overall and was used on Mike D'Antoni, but Detroit never selected D'Antoni itself. The trade ledgers show the Pistons sent the choice onward on November 9, 1972, to the Kansas City–Omaha Kings in return for John Mengelt. The modern Clippers franchise identifier refers to the former Buffalo team, not a Los Angeles club in 1972. That additional pick conversion makes the direct trade much more than a routine draft-rights exchange.

sections.heading: Mengelt Was Detroit's Real Return from the Draft Pick
sections.body: The acquired draft pick lasted in Detroit only until November 9, when the Pistons exchanged it with Kansas City–Omaha for John Mengelt. Mengelt appeared in 291 regular-season games across four Pistons seasons, averaging 10.3 points per game. That is the basketball value actually traced through the pick, rather than hypothetical production by its eventual No. 20 selection, Mike D'Antoni. D'Antoni's subsequent career should not be credited to the Pistons when they had already traded away the pick. Detroit turned an outgoing veteran into several years of playable roster production through a documented second transaction.

sections.heading: Buffalo Received One Season from Howie Komives
sections.body: Komives played 67 regular-season games for Buffalo after the swap, averaging 6.1 points and 3.6 assists. Those numbers represent real on-court value, and the Braves' return should not be marked as zero merely because Detroit's downstream outcome was larger. But 67 games of modest scoring and passing are a narrower contribution than the 291 Pistons games that flowed from the exchanged selection. The fact that Buffalo eventually became the Clippers franchise is relevant to modern navigation, not to an evaluation of its 1972 player roster.

sections.heading: A-Minus for Detroit, B-Minus for Buffalo Fits the Asset Chain
sections.body: The canonical verdict is Pistons Win, with Detroit at A-minus and Buffalo at B-minus. Detroit received a second-round selection and promptly converted it into Mengelt, who supplied 291 games across four seasons; Buffalo received 67 Komives games. The source record validates both the September deal and the later November pick transfer, distinguishing Detroit's realized value from any imaginary D'Antoni stint in a Pistons uniform. The older B-plus/C grades understated the strength of Detroit's outcome and diminished Buffalo's actual short-term player contribution.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Detroit A-, Buffalo/Clippers B-. Detroit traded Howie Komives to Buffalo for a 1973 second-rounder on September 29, 1972. Detroit sent that pick to Kansas City–Omaha for John Mengelt, who logged 291 Pistons games; Komives provided Buffalo 67 games. Mike D'Antoni was the eventual No. 20 pick, not a Detroit draftee.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: How Detroit Turned Komives into 291 Games from John Mengelt
featuredDeepDive.intro: The September 29, 1972 Komives deal looks minor until its draft-pick path is followed correctly. Detroit obtained a 1973 second-round choice from Buffalo, then traded it to Kansas City–Omaha for John Mengelt before the draft occurred. Mengelt gave Detroit 291 games over four seasons. Buffalo received 67 games from Komives. The eventual No. 20 draft selection of Mike D'Antoni does not make D'Antoni a Pistons contributor, because the franchise had already moved the pick.

sections.heading: The September Exchange and November Conversion Are Distinct Deals
sections.body: Detroit transferred Howie Komives to Buffalo on September 29, 1972, receiving a 1973 second-round choice. Detroit and Buffalo transaction histories and the league register support that initial exchange. The Pistons then sent the choice to Kansas City–Omaha on November 9 to acquire John Mengelt. This second deal belongs in the asset chain, but it is not a player Buffalo originally handed to Detroit. The subsequent draft record identifies the same pick as No. 20 and its eventual selection as Mike D'Antoni. Correcting the chain avoids making Detroit the team that drafted D'Antoni.

sections.heading: Mengelt's Detroit Production Is Traceable through the Pick
sections.body: Mengelt played in 291 Pistons regular-season games across four seasons and averaged 10.3 points during that time. The return came from Detroit's decision to exchange its newly acquired draft asset for a player who could contribute immediately and across several years. No speculative draft development path is needed to support the value. This is also not the same as saying Detroit received both Mengelt and D'Antoni. The pick could produce one downstream chain, and Detroit's verified path ended in Mengelt's roster production rather than the eventual draftee's later career.

sections.heading: Komives Provided Buffalo a Modest but Recorded Return
sections.body: Komives appeared 67 times for the Buffalo Braves, averaging 6.1 points and 3.6 assists. That playing return justifies the B-minus grade rather than treating Buffalo's side as nonexistent. However, it was limited to a short stint, and the Pistons' eventual 291-game payoff was longer and more productive over time. Using Buffalo as the historical name also prevents the misleading image of a Los Angeles-based Clippers club making the trade in 1972. The franchise continuity is real, but the roster and city belong to the early Braves years.

sections.heading: Detroit's A-Minus Reflects Actual Player Value, Not Draft Fame
sections.body: The old editorial focused on Mike D'Antoni as if Detroit drafted and used him. The reliable record instead shows that Detroit sent the 1973 second-rounder away in November 1972 and received Mengelt, who remained productive with the Pistons. The resulting 291 regular-season games clearly exceed Komives's 67-game Buffalo stint on a longevity measure, while Komives's assists still record useful play. Pistons Win with Detroit A-minus and Buffalo B-minus captures the realized disparity without inflating the pick through a player who never joined Detroit from that selection.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Detroit wins the 1972 Komives transaction, A- to Buffalo's B-. The 1973 second-rounder Detroit received was later exchanged for John Mengelt, whose 291 Pistons games were the genuine downstream return. Komives played 67 games for Buffalo. Mike D'Antoni was the eventual No. 20 selection by another team, not a Pistons contributor.

sections.heading: Detroit Exchanged a Draft Pick for Mengelt
sections.body: On November 9, 1972, the Pistons acquired guard John Mengelt from the Kansas City–Omaha Kings. The Kings received a 1973 second-round selection, eventually No. 20, that became Mike D’Antoni. These teams were solving different immediate needs: Detroit wanted an experienced guard it could use in its rotation, while Kansas City–Omaha preferred the chance to select a player in the next draft. The recorded swap involved one player and one pick, not an additional cash component.

sections.heading: The D’Antoni Selection Was a Real Kings Return
sections.body: D’Antoni later became far better known as a coach, but his future coaching achievements cannot be assigned to a 1972 draft pick as NBA playing value. What the Kings acquired was the selection they converted at No. 20. Detroit, on the other hand, acquired Mengelt directly and could obtain playing time from him before that draft occurred. The outcome should compare those two roster assets rather than later notoriety unrelated to the player’s contribution on the receiving team.

sections.heading: The Pistons Win in the Current Canonical Record
sections.body: Detroit receives A-minus and Kansas City–Omaha/Sacramento B-minus, with Pistons Win. Older templated paragraphs mistakenly asserted that the Kings won with different grades. That is a grade-to-verdict error, not a legitimate second evaluation that can coexist on one page. The corrected assessment follows the official ledger: both clubs obtained an identifiable player or selection, but Detroit’s side is judged more valuable in this specific trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Detroit A-minus, Kansas City–Omaha/Sacramento B-minus. Detroit received John Mengelt and sent the 1973 second-round choice that became No. 20 Mike D’Antoni. The official grade favors the immediate Detroit player return, not the contradictory Kings-win grades inherited in the older narrative. Mengelt’s role with the Pistons is the specific basketball outcome the higher grade evaluates.

sections.heading: Detroit Exchanged Its First-Rounder for Howard Porter
sections.body: On December 24, 1974, the Pistons traded a 1975 first-round pick to the Knicks for forward Howard Porter. New York obtained the selection that was eventually used at No. 10 on Bill Robinzine, although the Knicks themselves traded the pick onward before the draft. Detroit was seeking a proven forward to improve its rotation rather than waiting for a prospective rookie. Contemporary team transaction summaries list December 24; a different draft-pick chain source shows December 26, so the precise reporting-date conflict should not change the established roster exchange.

sections.heading: Porter Provided Several Seasons of Real Detroit Production
sections.body: Porter had been used sparingly in New York, averaging 1.9 points over 17 appearances early in 1974–75. In Detroit he averaged 10.6 points and 5.3 rebounds across 41 games that season. He returned for 75 games in 1975–76 and 78 more in 1976–77, giving the Pistons considerably more than a brief stopgap. Those appearances and the expanded scoring role make Detroit’s incoming package a dependable, realized basketball return.

sections.heading: New York Used the Pick Before Robinzine Was Selected
sections.body: The Knicks did not directly turn their acquired No. 10 rights into Robinzine’s minutes. In February 1975 they included the first-round pick with Henry Bibby in a trade to the New Orleans Jazz for Jim Barnett and Neal Walk. The selection later traveled to another franchise before Robinzine was drafted. That distinction prevents the retrospective from crediting New York with the entire career of a player it did not actually select or roster through this pick. The Knicks did use the draft asset to obtain immediate players, so the pick was not worthless.

sections.heading: Why Detroit Gained More From Howard Porter Than New York Did From the Pick
sections.body: The Slight Pistons Edge verdict gives Detroit A and New York B-plus. Howard Porter played 41 Detroit games after the December 1974 trade, then 75 in 1975-76, 78 in 1976-77 and eight more in 1977-78: 202 direct Pistons appearances in all. New York received a 1975 first-round selection with real trade value, but sent the pick with Henry Bibby to New Orleans in February 1975 for Jim Barnett and Neal Walk. The Jazz later moved the selection to Kansas City, which ultimately drafted Bill Robinzine at No. 10. New York should receive credit for converting the pick into Barnett and Walk, not Robinzine's later NBA production. Porter's longer Detroit contribution gives the Pistons the stronger direct player return, while the Knicks' downstream trade provides a narrower but genuine benefit. Contemporary transaction registers place the Porter swap December 24, although other draft-lineage accounts use December 26; the historical record keeps that difference visible instead of inventing two deals.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Pistons Edge — Detroit A, New York B-plus. Porter became a useful forward for several Pistons seasons, including 10.6 points a game after the 1974–75 acquisition. The Knicks received a first-round selection and traded it onward as part of a package for Jim Barnett and Neal Walk. The later No. 10 pick became Bill Robinzine, but his career was not a direct Knicks return.

sections.heading: The May 28 Transaction Was Cancelled
sections.body: The surviving Detroit and Phoenix transaction ledgers resolve the central issue: the reported May 28, 1975 Earl Williams-for-Willie Norwood exchange did not become a completed NBA trade. Basketball-Reference's 1975-76 Detroit page says Williams was originally traded for Norwood on May 28 but that the trade was cancelled, and the Phoenix page records the same cancellation. The proposed conditional 1976 pick therefore belongs to the cancelled package, not to a completed transaction.

sections.heading: Neither Player Changed Teams Through This Record
sections.body: Because the May deal was cancelled, Earl Williams did not become a Piston through this transaction and Willie Norwood did not become a Sun through it. Norwood remained under Detroit control and was waived in October. Any retrospective that assigns Williams' later Detroit games or Norwood's later career to the May proposal creates a false value chain. This record is useful as transaction provenance, but it cannot support a winner or team grades.

sections.heading: Detroit Acquired Williams in a Separate September Trade
sections.body: Detroit eventually did acquire Earl Williams, but on September 30, 1975 in a different completed deal. The Pistons sent Phoenix a 1976 second-round pick that became Earl Tatum. Both team transaction pages and the league-wide 1975-76 ledger distinguish that September trade from the cancelled May proposal. Williams' later Detroit production belongs to the September transaction and must not be backfilled into this record.

sections.heading: The Correct Archive Treatment Is Supersession
sections.body: The legacy May entry is retained only so the source history is not erased. Its listed player and conditional-pick terms describe a proposal that was later voided, while the completed September exchange has different consideration. Treating the May record as an ordinary graded trade would duplicate Williams' move and award value to assets that never legally changed teams. The defensible treatment is structural supersession: private, noindex, no ads, no winner and no grades.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Resolution
finalVerdict.body: Record Superseded — cancelled transaction, no winner and no team grades. Detroit and Phoenix did not complete the May 28, 1975 Earl Williams-for-Willie Norwood proposal. Williams reached Detroit only through the separate September 30 trade for a 1976 second-round pick that became Earl Tatum. The May record remains in the archive for provenance, but it is excluded from graded and index-candidate results.

sections.heading: Buffalo Sent Two Forwards and a Future First to Detroit
sections.body: The trade completed on November 23, 1977, when the Buffalo Braves sent John Shumate, Gus Gerard and a future first-round choice to the Detroit Pistons. Buffalo received Marvin Barnes and two Detroit draft selections: a 1978 second-rounder and a 1978 fourth-rounder. The Detroit and Buffalo transaction ledgers agree on the five pieces and the date. Although the modern archive links Buffalo to the Clippers franchise, the 1977 team was still playing in Buffalo, not Los Angeles. The first-round pick was ultimately exercised by Detroit at No. 10 in 1979, with Roy Hamilton selected. The two outgoing Detroit picks became No. 38 Lew Massey and No. 73 Larry Harris in the 1978 draft, but their later destinations cannot be inferred from those names alone. Buffalo's transfer was an actual three-asset package, not a direct exchange of Shumate for Barnes.

sections.heading: Shumate and Gerard Combined for 109 Pistons Games in 1977-78
sections.body: Detroit acquired immediate frontcourt production from the veteran pair. In 1977-78 John Shumate appeared in 62 games for the Pistons, averaging 15.5 points, 8.9 rebounds and 2.0 assists while playing 35 minutes per game. Gus Gerard added 47 appearances, averaging 7.9 points and 3.1 rebounds in a little over 17 minutes. That is 109 combined regular-season appearances during the season of the trade, distinct from games either man played for another club. Shumate's Detroit output was an especially tangible return: 62 games of near-starter playing time after Buffalo had used him in only 18 games earlier that season. Gerard's tenure with Detroit continued briefly into 1978-79 before he moved to Kansas City, so his later Kings production should not be credited here. The historical Detroit advantage is grounded in actual Pistons minutes, not only the future pick's theoretical value.

sections.heading: Barnes Played 48 Buffalo Games; Massey's Pick Was Traded to the Lakers
sections.body: Buffalo also received a genuine NBA contributor. Marvin Barnes played 48 games for the Braves after arriving from Detroit, averaging 11.8 points, 7.3 rebounds and 2.4 assists in 28.7 minutes. That was real rotation value, even though Buffalo finished 27-55 and Barnes moved on to Boston for 1978-79 rather than becoming a lasting Braves or Clippers fixture. The draft return took another route. On June 7, 1978, Buffalo sent the second-round selection that became No. 38 Lew Massey to the Lakers for Tom Abernethy, according to both teams' transaction logs. It is therefore inaccurate to treat Massey's subsequent playing career as automatically belonging to Buffalo. The fourth-round choice ultimately identified with Larry Harris was a separate, later No. 73 selection. Those picks had option value, but they did not turn the Barnes transaction into three long-serving Buffalo players.

sections.heading: Roy Hamilton Was the First-Round Return, but Shumate Supplied More Production
sections.body: Detroit turned the first-round right received in the November 1977 Marvin Barnes trade into the No. 10 pick of the 1979 draft, selecting UCLA guard Roy Hamilton. The Pistons' own draft retrospective traces that choice to the deal with Buffalo. Hamilton played 72 Detroit games as a rookie, averaging 4.6 points in 15.5 minutes; the pick became a real NBA player, though not a high-impact one. The stronger Detroit return came immediately from John Shumate, with 62 appearances and 15.5 points per game in 1977-78, and Gus Gerard, with 47 appearances that season. Buffalo received 48 games of Marvin Barnes and two Detroit draft selections, one second-round choice later transferred to the Lakers for Tom Abernethy. Detroit's combined frontcourt return and realized first-round option justify its A- against Buffalo's B, but Barnes' production and the Braves' retained draft value keep the retrospective verdict at Pistons Edge rather than a one-sided victory.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Edge — Detroit A-, Buffalo Braves/Clippers B. Detroit acquired John Shumate (62 Pistons games in 1977-78), Gus Gerard (47 that season) and the first-round right later used at No. 10 in 1979 on Roy Hamilton, who played 72 Detroit games. Buffalo received Marvin Barnes for 48 games along with a 1978 second-round pick later dealt to the Lakers for Tom Abernethy and a fourth-round pick associated with Larry Harris. Detroit converted more of the package into direct roster production and a tangible first-round selection, but Barnes was not an empty return for the Braves. The narrower edge reflects both teams' realized outcomes without borrowing later performances at other franchises.
