sections.heading: The July 1994 Return of Sean Elliott to San Antonio
sections.body: San Antonio and Detroit reversed part of their previous relationship on July 19, 1994. The Pistons sent Sean Elliott back to the Spurs and received the draft rights to Bill Curley plus a 1997 second-round selection that eventually became Charles O'Bannon. Curley had been picked No. 22 by San Antonio in the June draft, so Detroit was obtaining his rights rather than a Spurs regular who had already produced NBA minutes. Elliott had played 73 games for Detroit in 1993-94, averaging 12.1 points, after an earlier four-season Spurs stint. San Antonio was reacquiring a known scoring forward; Detroit was taking a rookie development opportunity and a deferred pick. The official July 1994 transaction ledger confirms the original three assets, and neither later title-team success nor the drafted player's future identity was guaranteed at the time.

sections.heading: The Spurs Got an Immediate Starting Forward Back
sections.body: Elliott's first season after returning to San Antonio gave the club 81 starts in 81 regular-season games and 18.1 points per contest. The 1994-95 Spurs finished 62-20 and reached the Western Conference Finals. In 1995-96 he averaged 20.0 points over 77 games and received another All-Star selection. Those are actual San Antonio performances following this trade, not numbers credited from his previous Spurs stint or his Detroit season. Elliott provided perimeter scoring and spacing on a team centered on David Robinson. His health limited several later seasons, but he continued as an important member of the franchise when Tim Duncan arrived. The immediate effect was already larger than Detroit's first-season returns from Curley. That combination of starting production and eventual postseason contribution supports the original San Antonio A grade.

sections.heading: Curley's Fifty-Three Detroit Games and Injury Years
sections.body: Bill Curley joined Detroit as a rookie and appeared in 53 games during 1994-95, averaging 2.7 points and 2.3 rebounds. He started only one game. His next two seasons were lost to ankle and knee injuries, according to his season-by-season NBA playing record. When he eventually returned to the league, the appearances came with other franchises, not with the Pistons. Curley's complete NBA career total of 147 games therefore should not be entered as a Detroit return from the Elliott trade. The direct Detroit value was the rookie's 53 games plus the future second-round selection. Evaluating that return requires the actual time with the acquiring team rather than his draft position or expectations as a first-round choice. The injury interruptions explain why Detroit did not obtain a long-term starter from the principal immediate asset.

sections.heading: The Deferred Second Became Charles O'Bannon
sections.body: Detroit's other incoming asset was a 1997 second-round pick originating with San Antonio. The NBA's official draft history lists Charles O'Bannon as the third selection in that round, at No. 31. Some third-party databases display No. 32 because they count the forfeited position in the overall numbering, but the official NBA label is No. 31 and matches the preserved trade ledger. O'Bannon played 30 regular-season games for Detroit in 1997-98 and another 18 in 1998-99, for 48 Pistons appearances. He averaged 2.5 points across those two seasons. That gave Detroit a second actual NBA contributor from the exchange, but only for limited minutes. Combined with Curley's 53 games, the incoming package produced 101 Detroit appearances, a small return beside Elliott's sustained impact in San Antonio.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Spurs Win — San Antonio A, Detroit B. Elliott returned to San Antonio for 81 starts at 18.1 points per game in 1994-95 and later helped win the 1999 championship. Curley supplied 53 Detroit games and O'Bannon 48, for 101 Pistons appearances. The preserved B grade is more generous than the limited realized Detroit basketball return.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Sean Elliott Back to San Antonio: The 1994 Curley and O'Bannon Draft-Rights Return
featuredDeepDive.intro: Detroit sent Elliott home to the Spurs for Bill Curley rights and a future second that became Charles O'Bannon. Elliott played an integral role for 1995 and 1999 Spurs playoff teams; Detroit's prospects combined for 101 Pistons games.

sections.heading: The Second Chance for Elliott Restored a Familiar Fit
sections.body: San Antonio knew the player it wanted back in July 1994. Elliott had already been a Spurs All-Star before spending 1993-94 in Detroit, and the new transaction returned an established scoring forward to the club that had developed his NBA career. The cost was a recently drafted forward's rights and a future second-rounder rather than an active frontcourt starter. Elliott supplied 81 starts and averaged 18.1 points in 1994-95, helping a 62-win Spurs team reach the conference finals. He then averaged 20.0 points and made the 1996 All-Star team. The team already had David Robinson, so Elliott's perimeter shooting and off-ball offense complemented an established interior star. Those two early seasons establish substantial basketball value without relying on later achievements. The original trade was immediately useful on its own terms.

sections.heading: The Memorial Day Miracle Was a Later, Realized Payoff
sections.body: San Antonio's 1999 championship run supplies an additional historical endpoint for Elliott's return. In Game 2 of the Western Conference Finals, the Spurs trailed Portland 85-83 before Elliott converted a difficult three-pointer from the sideline, giving San Antonio an 86-85 win. The NBA's season review records the shot as the Memorial Day Miracle, and the Spurs went on to win their first league title. The team was led by Tim Duncan and David Robinson, so Elliott should not be described as the sole architect of the championship. Nevertheless, he was a starter on that team, played 50 regular-season games in the lockout-shortened season and supplied a memorable postseason contribution. That is value directly connected to the forward San Antonio brought home in 1994, not a championship acquired in the original trade package.

sections.heading: Detroit's Two Prospects Produced One Hundred One Games
sections.body: The Detroit side must account for both assets. Curley played 53 games as a 1994-95 rookie before injuries derailed his next two seasons, and O'Bannon made 48 Pistons appearances after the 1997 selection. Neither player became a long-tenured Detroit starting forward. Curley's later NBA games in Minnesota, Houston and Golden State should not count as Pistons production; O'Bannon's 1997-98 and 1998-99 appearances were his entire NBA career. Together, their 101 Detroit games supplied limited immediate and delayed depth. Detroit's inherited B grade acknowledges that the club received legitimate first-round rights and a future draft choice instead of an empty asset package. The observed basketball return was still much less valuable than Elliott's strong San Antonio seasons and 1999 championship participation. The comparison should not inflate the original promise into a realized Detroit star.

sections.heading: The A-versus-B Grade Does Not Mean Equal Careers
sections.body: San Antonio's A is grounded in an All-Star-caliber return, a 62-win 1994-95 season and Elliott's subsequent role on a championship team. Detroit's B is a comparatively generous retained editorial assessment for obtaining two legitimate draft-right assets; the players supplied 101 Pistons games and limited production. The Spurs Win verdict is unambiguous when the actual on-court histories are compared. Elliott averaged 18.1 points after his return and 20.0 the following season, while Curley and O'Bannon never became Detroit starters over multiple seasons. The longer outcome includes Elliott's celebrated 1999 shot against Portland. Keeping Detroit's documented grade does not require presenting its incoming prospects as equivalent to Elliott; it requires clearly explaining why the grade spread understates the difference in realized team production. The original assets and date stay separate from every later roster transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: San Antonio A, Detroit B in the inherited Spurs Win verdict. Elliott supplied scoring, 1996 All-Star play and the 1999 Memorial Day Miracle. Detroit converted Curley rights and a 1997 No. 31 NBA-listed second into 101 combined games, without a lasting starting forward.

sections.heading: Detroit Obtained Leckner for a Future Second-Rounder
sections.body: The Pistons acquired Eric Leckner from Philadelphia on July 25, 1994. The 76ers received a conditional second-round selection described as a 1996-or-1997 pick. The franchise eventually used the 1996 selection, No. 48 overall, on Jamie Feick. This was a modest center-for-future-draft-asset exchange, not a transaction involving a future lottery pick or a major franchise cornerstone. Both clubs were working at the edges of their rosters.

sections.heading: Leckner Offered NBA Experience Rather Than a Major Upgrade
sections.body: Leckner was an experienced big man at the point Detroit acquired him. His potential value lay in providing frontcourt cover without surrendering a first-rounder or a starter. That limited price helps explain Detroit’s C grade, but there is no documented basis for portraying the pickup as a transformative move. It was a practical personnel addition in a period when the Pistons were reworking the roster following their championship years.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Exchanged Present Depth for a Draft Chance
sections.body: The 76ers chose a future selection instead of keeping Leckner. That selection’s conditional timing is important: it could fall in 1996 or 1997, and the observed result was the 1996 No. 48 pick that became Feick. Obtaining a second-round chance for a veteran reserve gave Philadelphia flexibility, although a late selection was unlikely to deliver the certainty of an established rotation player. The record does not justify claiming an additional cash payment or extra players.

sections.heading: Neither Return Changed the Franchise’s Direction
sections.body: The ledger assigns Detroit C and Philadelphia D-plus, with a narrow Pistons advantage. The key comparison is a ready-to-use veteran center against a conditional second-rounder ultimately exercised at No. 48. The smaller grade difference recognizes the limited upside of both outcomes: Detroit obtained near-term roster depth, while Philadelphia received a later draft opportunity. Treating this minor exchange as a decisive long-term victory would overstate its stakes.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win, narrowly — Detroit C, Philadelphia D-plus. Detroit acquired Eric Leckner for a future second-round choice, eventually exercised by Philadelphia in 1996 at No. 48 for Jamie Feick. The exchange provided veteran frontcourt depth to Detroit and a draft opportunity to Philadelphia. Neither asset warrants a blockbuster evaluation, but the present-day roster value earns Detroit the small edge recorded in the grades.

sections.heading: What Changed Hands
sections.body: Detroit acquired Otis Thorpe from Portland on September 20, 1995, giving up Bill Curley and the draft rights to Randolph Childress. The three names did not all have the same contract status: Thorpe and Curley were players being exchanged, while Portland obtained rights associated with Childress rather than a guarantee of his future minutes. Both Detroit's and Portland's historical transaction records support the direction of the deal. No third franchise, separate draft selection, or cash payment appears in this canonical exchange.

sections.heading: How the Realized Value Separated
sections.body: Detroit's choice placed an established frontcourt player on its roster rather than retaining Curley and control of the Childress rights. Portland made the opposite calculation, accepting a player plus a second form of future basketball value in place of Thorpe. That trade-day distinction is specific to this deal. Childress's rights should not be described as an extra active Trail Blazers player, and any later movement of his rights would need separate documentation before becoming part of the return.

sections.heading: Reading the Team Grades
sections.body: The archive currently scores Detroit A and Portland D+, with Pistons Win as its verdict. Those are retrospective editorial marks, not ratings issued by either team's transaction log. Detroit's A is attached to acquiring Thorpe; Portland's D+ evaluates its receipt of Curley and Childress's rights. The distance between the grades indicates a clear preference for the Pistons' return. That is more precise than describing the final grade pair as an almost even exchange.

sections.heading: How Each Team Viewed the Trade
sections.body: Portland obtained Bill Curley outright and the draft rights to Randolph Childress; the two incoming assets required separate evaluations. A player could be assessed through an actual roster role, but holding someone's rights alone did not produce NBA minutes. Detroit took the simpler incoming package, receiving only Thorpe. The comparison therefore depends on the specific basketball value of those returns rather than treating the two Portland names as automatically worth more than Detroit's one.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win, with Detroit graded A and Portland D+. Detroit acquired Otis Thorpe; Portland took Bill Curley and the draft rights to Randolph Childress. The archived grades favor the single experienced player Detroit received over Portland's two-part return. The transaction sources verify those assets, while the rating is the site's retrospective assessment, not a statement by either club.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Detroit Pistons–Portland Trail Blazers: What the 1995-09-20 Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: The September 20, 1995 Pistons–Trail Blazers transaction exchanged Otis Thorpe for Bill Curley and the draft rights to Randolph Childress. Detroit received a veteran frontcourt player. Portland accepted a current player and a separate rights asset. Both clubs' transaction histories document the exchange, while the archive's A/D+ grades describe its own hindsight evaluation. Those different kinds of evidence should not be conflated.

sections.heading: Otis Thorpe Cost Detroit Curley and Randolph Childress Draft Rights
sections.body: The path has three recorded legs and only two teams. Thorpe's player rights moved from Portland to Detroit. Curley went from Detroit to Portland, as did the draft rights to Randolph Childress. The rights were a distinct kind of consideration, not an additional first-round pick or a cash term. Counting those items once each gives the reader an accurate account of the September 1995 deal before any claim about who benefited from it.

sections.heading: What the Other Side Still Received
sections.body: Detroit and Portland transaction histories provide separate views of the same September 20 transaction, and the record also lists RealGM histories for each club. Those sources establish the player and rights movements; they do not assign hindsight grades. Using both clubs' records guards against reversing the exchange or counting it twice simply because both franchises reported it. The two-team structure stays the same even though Portland received two items and Detroit only one.

sections.heading: Decision Logic Versus Hindsight
sections.body: Thorpe presented Detroit with an established frontcourt option. Portland's package included Curley, a directly acquired player, and a less certain route to future value through Childress's draft rights. That is a decision between immediately usable player value and a combination of current personnel and retained rights. A defensible discussion can weigh the two packages without inventing a trade-day promise about Childress's later career or crediting either club for unrelated roster decisions.

sections.heading: Why the Grade Gap Matters
sections.body: The published evaluation awards Detroit an A and Portland a D+, recording a Pistons Win. Those grades communicate the relative strength of the assessed outcomes, while the historical sources only confirm what changed hands. The sharper rating gap is tied to Thorpe on one side and Curley plus Childress's rights on the other. It shouldn't be justified through fictional draft compensation, a third participant, or achievements a player accumulated while working for a different franchise.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Detroit's A versus Portland's D+ is the archive's present judgment on the September 1995 Thorpe exchange. It credits Detroit for acquiring Thorpe and weighs Portland's return of Curley and Childress's rights separately. The source ledgers establish the transaction, not the grades. No cash, outside team, or additional selection is needed to explain this documented two-club comparison.

sections.heading: Detroit Exchanged Augmon for Three Portland Contracts in January 1997
sections.body: The Pistons sent defensive wing Stacey Augmon to Portland on January 24, 1997, receiving Aaron McKie, Randolph Childress and Reggie Jordan. Detroit had obtained Augmon and Grant Long from Atlanta the preceding summer, so this was another reconfiguration of its supporting cast around Grant Hill. Portland was bringing in a recognizable wing defender with several starting seasons behind him. McKie was the most established of the three incoming guards; Childress had struggled to claim NBA minutes, while Jordan was a short-term depth contract. The Pistons finished 54-28 that season, but no responsible trade assessment can assign their entire record to a January bench deal. The factual exchange involved these four players, not later 1997 draft picks or Jerry Stackhouse, who arrived in a different transaction.

sections.heading: McKie Played Sixty-Six Detroit Games Before the Stackhouse Deal
sections.body: McKie contributed 42 Pistons regular-season appearances after the January 1997 acquisition, starting three and averaging 6.3 points, 3.0 rebounds and 1.8 assists. He returned for 24 Detroit games in 1997-98, averaging 4.5 points, before being included in the December 18, 1997 deal with Philadelphia. That totals 66 Detroit games directly following this swap. The later Sixers transaction sent McKie, Theo Ratliff and a future first to Philadelphia, bringing back Jerry Stackhouse, Eric Montross and a future second. That package demonstrates that McKie retained negotiation value, but Stackhouse was not acquired solely for him. McKie's subsequent Sixth Man of the Year award in Philadelphia during 2000-01 also does not count as a Detroit accomplishment. The original deal produced a useful, bounded guard stint.

sections.heading: Childress Played Four Pistons Games and Jordan None
sections.body: The secondary Detroit pieces offered little on-court production. Childress appeared in four Pistons games in 1996-97, totaling 30 minutes and ten points, and the team waived him before the following season in October 1997. Reggie Jordan did not record a Detroit regular-season appearance after joining in January; he was waived February 18. Jordan's 1996-97 NBA games belonged to Portland before the trade and Minnesota after his waiver, not the Pistons. These are different outcomes for two players whose names occupy similar space in the original asset list. Neither provided a meaningful Detroit rotation run. Their limited returns also show why counting all three incoming players as long-term contributors would inflate the transaction. McKie's 66 Detroit appearances, rather than the presence of three names, supply the immediate basketball basis for the Pistons grade.

sections.heading: Augmon Produced 284 Portland Games Across Five Seasons
sections.body: Portland played Augmon in 40 games after acquiring him in 1996-97, then 71 in 1997-98, 48 in the 1998-99 lockout season, 59 in 1999-2000 and 66 in 2000-01. Those totals equal 284 Blazers regular-season appearances, with defensive wing minutes extending through the team's 2000 Western Conference Finals run. He was never Portland's primary scorer: his first partial-season average was 4.7 points, and he averaged 5.7 in 1997-98. But the duration and postseason context challenge a sweeping claim that Portland obtained substantially less actual player production than Detroit. Augmon later joined the Hornets, whose minutes are not part of the Blazers return. The inherited Pistons Win and B-plus/C-plus grades can be preserved as editorial judgments, but the team-specific playing record points to meaningful value on both sides.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Detroit B+, Portland C+ in the inherited ledger, with a qualification: McKie played 66 regular-season Detroit games, Childress four and Jordan none; Augmon supplied 284 Portland games over five seasons. Detroit later included McKie, Theo Ratliff and a future first in its separate December 1997 Stackhouse/Montross trade. Those other outgoing assets prevent treating Stackhouse as a direct Augmon-for-McKie resale.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: 1997 Augmon-McKie Deal: Portland Longevity and Detroit Stackhouse Chain
featuredDeepDive.intro: The Pistons obtained McKie, Childress and Jordan from the Trail Blazers for Stacey Augmon. McKie played 66 Detroit games before a separate multi-asset trade; Augmon logged 284 Portland games.

sections.heading: The Four-Player Exchange Had Opposite Time Horizons
sections.body: Detroit was searching for backcourt versatility while trying to support Grant Hill on a club already performing well in the East. McKie had started games earlier in Portland and could defend more than one perimeter position. Childress and Jordan supplied potential emergency guard depth, with much less evidence they would become regulars. The Blazers preferred a 28-year-old veteran stopper in Augmon, who could guard opposing wings while the franchise built around other scorers. That contrast was plausible when the clubs signed the papers. The realized returns differed from the assumptions: Detroit quickly waived two acquired players but used McKie for parts of two seasons; Portland retained Augmon through five partial or complete seasons. A retrospective should measure those actual opportunities and not equate each asset's roster listing with equal production.

sections.heading: McKie's Trade to Philadelphia Was Not a Straight Conversion
sections.body: On December 18, 1997, Detroit included McKie in a major transaction with the 76ers. Theo Ratliff and a protected future first accompanied him to Philadelphia; Detroit received Jerry Stackhouse, Eric Montross and a future second. Contemporary Associated Press reporting describes the central issue as Philadelphia seeking to separate Stackhouse and Allen Iverson in the backcourt. McKie's role in the package matters to the valuation of the January deal, but the other outgoing Detroit assets were substantial. It would be incorrect to claim the Pistons exchanged Augmon directly for Stackhouse ten months later. McKie had first supplied 66 regular-season Detroit games, then contributed as a contract in a separately negotiated trade. His later Sixers Sixth Man award and 2001 Finals experience belonged to Philadelphia, not to the earlier Detroit roster.

sections.heading: Augmon's Defensive Longevity Complicates the Grade Difference
sections.body: The Portland side produced far more continuity than a generic losing-side paragraph suggests. Augmon logged 40 Blazers games after arriving, then played 71, 48, 59 and 66 over his next four seasons. He was not a featured offensive creator, averaging under six points in the first two Portland campaigns, but his length and defensive assignment flexibility made him usable on a changing roster. He was still a Trail Blazer when Portland reached the Western Conference Finals in 2000. That achievement involved a deep team and cannot be credited to Augmon alone. Even so, 284 Portland regular-season appearances are a stronger measurable return than the Pistons received from Childress and Jordan, and exceed McKie's 66 Detroit games. Preserving the inherited Detroit edge requires disclosing those numbers rather than erasing the Blazers' prolonged rotation investment.

sections.heading: The B-Plus and C-Plus Verdict Is an Editorial Judgment
sections.body: The site's original judgment is Pistons Win, grading Detroit B-plus and Portland C-plus. The trade-day package sent Augmon to the Blazers and McKie, Childress and Jordan to the Pistons. Detroit obtained 66 McKie games, four Childress games and no Jordan appearances, then moved McKie alongside Ratliff and a first in the Stackhouse deal. Portland enjoyed 284 Augmon games across five partial or full seasons, including 2000 playoff depth. That factual tally is not an obvious Detroit victory in direct appearances, and a B-plus spread should not be presented as if it were. Detroit might be credited for McKie's later trade flexibility, but the additional Ratliff and pick cost limits attribution. Retaining the site's existing letter grades with this explicit qualification is preferable to inventing individual honors or overstating a later transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Detroit B-plus, Portland C-plus preserved with evidence limits. Portland received 284 games from Augmon, more direct playing time than Detroit got from 66 McKie games and four Childress appearances, while Jordan did not play for the Pistons. McKie retained later trade utility, but Detroit gave up Ratliff and a first to acquire Stackhouse and Montross separately. The historical grade gap is an editorial interpretation, not proof of superior direct Detroit playing minutes.

sections.heading: The Deal in One Sentence
sections.body: Detroit acquired Derek Harper from the Los Angeles Lakers in exchange for the rights to Melvin Levett. The trade itself is direct and unusually easy to audit: one established player went to the Pistons, and one set of draft rights went to the Lakers. The final results give Detroit the modest advantage, reflected in a C for the Pistons and C- for Los Angeles. That result is supported from both sides of the transaction. Detroit's perspective describes a modest realized-value edge, while the Lakers' perspective says the counterpart retained the better overall return. The final verdict therefore does not depend on a single team-centered reading. It translates bilateral source agreement into a narrow grade separation.

sections.heading: Why Derek Harper Tilts the Evaluation
sections.body: The Pistons' side of the trade is concrete: Derek Harper was the player Detroit received. The Lakers' side was the rights to Melvin Levett. A retrospective can respect the uncertainty that existed when draft rights were traded while still judging what those assets ultimately became. Here, both team histories land on the same directional conclusion: the Harper side supplied somewhat more realized value. That does not make Harper's acquisition a franchise-changing success, and the C grade is intentionally moderate. It simply means the player Detroit acquired produced a more substantial historical return than the rights Los Angeles received. The C/C- split keeps the conclusion proportional to the transaction while still recognizing that the sides did not finish even.

sections.heading: Why Los Angeles Still Earns a C-
sections.body: A losing grade should not erase the logic of the Lakers' return. Los Angeles acquired a legitimate basketball asset in the rights to Melvin Levett, and rights carry prospective value at the moment of a trade even when the later outcome is modest. The C- acknowledges that the Lakers received real consideration rather than nothing. What separates the grades is hindsight: the completed value attached to Detroit's directly acquired player ended up stronger than the value attached to the rights. The Lakers-side source itself supports that conclusion, calling the result a slight partner edge. Because the evidence points toward Detroit without describing a major imbalance, C- is a more accurate historical grade for Los Angeles than an extreme mark that would overstate the loss.

sections.heading: The Value of Bilateral Source Agreement
sections.body: The strongest feature of this evaluation is not the name recognition of Derek Harper; it is the agreement between the two analyses. Detroit's record says the Pistons gained a modest realized-value advantage. The Lakers' record, looking at the same exchange from Los Angeles, also places the partner side ahead. The analyses still point in the same direction. That is precisely the kind of evidence that should drive a documented historical verdict. The final C/C- grades place the two viewpoints on one consistent scale without pretending their original local labels were identical. The important historical claim is narrower: Detroit received the better realized return from the assets that were actually exchanged, and the margin was modest enough to stay near the middle of the grading scale.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Pistons Edge. Detroit receives a C and the Lakers a C-. The trade was Derek Harper for the rights to Melvin Levett, and both analyses ultimately favor the Harper side in realized value. Los Angeles received legitimate draft-rights consideration, so this is not a severe loss. Detroit simply finished with the stronger return, making a one-step grade separation the most proportional reading of the completed transaction.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Pistons–Lakers 1999: Why Derek Harper Gives Detroit the Narrow Historical Edge
featuredDeepDive.intro: The 1999 Pistons–Lakers exchange is a useful test of how to grade a veteran-for-rights transaction without allowing name recognition to dominate the result. Detroit received Derek Harper. Los Angeles received the rights to Melvin Levett. The two franchise-side records independently point toward Detroit as the side with the better realized return, but neither supports treating the deal as lopsided. That combination leads to a restrained conclusion: Detroit C, Los Angeles C-, Slight Pistons Edge. The result recognizes what the directly exchanged assets became while preserving the limited scale of the transaction.

sections.heading: Player Value and Rights Value Are Different Kinds of Assets
sections.body: An established player and draft rights do not enter a trade with the same certainty. Detroit knew it was acquiring Derek Harper as an NBA player, while Los Angeles acquired rights whose eventual value depended on what became of the underlying player asset. A retrospective has the advantage of seeing the completed outcome, but it should not rewrite the original nature of those assets. That is why the Lakers deserve credit for receiving a legitimate rights asset even though Detroit finishes ahead. The final grade asks a simpler hindsight question: which side produced the stronger realized basketball return? Both team perspectives answer Detroit. Harper's side was more concrete and more productive in the final results, while the rights did not match that value.

sections.heading: Why the Final Grades Stay Near Average
sections.body: A C for Detroit is not an attempt to call the trade a major success. It says the Pistons got the better of a modest exchange. The C- for Los Angeles similarly avoids exaggeration. The Lakers lost the realized-value comparison, but the difference was not large enough to justify a punitive grade. This is important in a site that contains trades of dramatically different scales. A narrow veteran-for-rights deal should not be graded as if it carried the same stakes as a star blockbuster or a premium draft-pick exchange. C versus C- gives the transaction a real direction while preserving context. Detroit won; the win was useful rather than transformative.

sections.heading: The Lakers' Own Record Supports Detroit
sections.body: Historical analysis is strongest when the losing side's available evidence still points toward the winner. The Lakers perspective says Los Angeles received the rights to Melvin Levett and sent Derek Harper, then concludes that the counterpart retained a modest realized-value edge. That independent framing matters because it reduces the risk of simply repeating Detroit's preferred interpretation. The Pistons record and the Lakers record arrive at the same direction from opposite viewpoints. Their grades differ slightly, but their shared conclusion is clear enough to support the final C/C- split. The evidence therefore supports a Detroit edge not because one site says so, but because both team-oriented records converge on the same realized-value hierarchy.

sections.heading: What This Trade Says About Retrospective Discipline
sections.body: The temptation in a historical review is to let a recognizable player name do all of the analytical work. That would be too easy here. The verdict should instead come from the trade itself and the source agreement: Harper went to Detroit, the rights to Levett went to Los Angeles, and both sides' records later judged Detroit's return as modestly better. That approach protects the evaluation from nostalgia and from hypothetical alternative histories. The Lakers are not penalized for a different player they might have acquired, and Detroit is not credited for unrelated roster moves. The trade is graded on the directly exchanged assets. On that basis, Detroit finishes one step ahead.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Detroit C, Los Angeles C-, with a Slight Pistons Edge verdict. Derek Harper provided the stronger realized side of the exchange, while the Lakers' rights to Melvin Levett remained legitimate but less valuable consideration. Both franchise histories support the same direction, and the modest grade gap keeps the conclusion aligned with the limited scale of the trade.

sections.heading: Detroit Faced the Loss of a Franchise Star With Minimal Leverage
sections.body: Grant Hill had become the face of the post-Bad Boys Pistons and had earned All-NBA recognition in each of his first six seasons. By the summer of 2000, he had chosen Orlando. Detroit could not compel him to stay, and the Magic had enough room to sign him without sending back equal talent. The sign-and-trade existed because Hill could receive a longer contract through Detroit. Joe Dumars used that narrow opening to demand Ben Wallace and Chucky Atkins, converting a departure that appeared devastating into the first pieces of a new competitive identity.

sections.heading: Wallace Developed Into the Foundation of a Champion
sections.body: Wallace arrived as an undersized, undrafted center known primarily for defense and rebounding. In Detroit he became a four-time Defensive Player of the Year, an All-Star, and the emotional center of the 2004 championship team. His ability to protect the rim, switch actions, rebound without requiring offensive touches, and establish a physical standard allowed the Pistons to build without a conventional scoring superstar. The value was not accidental decoration around the title roster; Wallace made the roster's entire defensive design possible.

sections.heading: Atkins Added Useful Value and a Downstream Connection
sections.body: Chucky Atkins became Detroit's starting point guard and supplied shooting and ball handling during the early stages of the rebuild. He was later included in the three-team trade that brought Rasheed Wallace to Detroit in February 2004. That later deal is evaluated separately, but Atkins' continued usefulness shows that the sign-and-trade return was not limited to one extraordinary player. Detroit received an immediate rotation guard and an asset that remained movable when the roster was ready for its final championship addition.

sections.heading: Orlando’s Plan Was Rational Before Hill’s Ankle Failed
sections.body: The Magic intended to pair Hill with Tracy McGrady and pursued Tim Duncan as part of an ambitious free-agent reset. Hill was 27, complete on both ends, and appeared capable of serving as a championship-level initiator. His severe ankle problems changed the outcome almost immediately and repeatedly interrupted his Orlando tenure. The process deserves more sympathy than an F suggests because the club acquired a genuine superstar in his prime. The D grade reflects the health outcome and the cost of including Wallace for contract structure, not a claim that the original basketball idea was foolish.

sections.heading: The Sign-and-Trade Cost Became More Important Than the Contract Benefit
sections.body: Orlando could have signed Hill outright for a shorter deal, but the sign-and-trade allowed him to receive the additional year available through Detroit. To complete that structure, the Magic surrendered Wallace and Atkins. Hill's injuries meant Orlando absorbed the long contract without receiving the expected star production, while Wallace developed into a Hall of Fame defender elsewhere. The transaction therefore compounded the injury loss: the Magic did not merely lose Hill's availability; they also transferred the player who became Detroit's championship anchor.

sections.heading: The Existing Pistons Win Needed a More Honest Orlando Grade
sections.body: Detroit's A+ and the Pistons Win verdict were already correct, but Orlando's F erased the reasonable logic of signing a healthy Hill. A D preserves the magnitude of the realized loss while recognizing that the central failure was an unforeseen medical collapse. Detroit still owns one of the strongest sign-and-trade outcomes in league history. The grade does not narrow the verdict; it improves the explanation by separating bad process from disastrous result. Orlando's plan was coherent, but the transaction's completed value was overwhelmingly Detroit's.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Detroit wins with an A+, while Orlando receives a D. The Pistons turned the forced departure of a perennial All-NBA star into Ben Wallace and Chucky Atkins. Wallace became a four-time Defensive Player of the Year, Hall of Famer, and the foundation of the 2004 championship defense; Atkins provided useful guard play and later helped complete the Rasheed Wallace trade. Orlando's pursuit of a healthy Grant Hill was rational, but repeated ankle injuries and the surrendered Wallace value produced a devastating outcome. Detroit transformed damage control into a championship origin point.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Ben Wallace Turned Grant Hill’s Departure Into the First Move of a Championship Rebuild
featuredDeepDive.intro: The Hill sign-and-trade is remarkable because Detroit did not appear to possess the leverage required for a franchise-changing return. Hill had selected Orlando, and the Magic could create room to sign him. The additional contract year opened a narrow negotiation, and Dumars used it to acquire a defensive specialist whose ceiling had not been fully recognized. Wallace's development changed the meaning of the transaction, converting the darkest moment of the Pistons' transition into the first stable piece of the team that would win the 2004 title.

sections.heading: Detroit Valued a Skill Set the Market Had Underpriced
sections.body: Wallace had already shown rebounding and defensive ability in Orlando, but his lack of scoring and unconventional size limited how the league valued him. Detroit did not need him to become an offensive star. The Pistons needed effort, rim protection, switchability, and a player whose impact did not require designed touches. By placing Wallace in a larger role and surrounding him with complementary defenders, the organization converted an underpriced specialty into franchise-level value. The trade succeeded because Detroit understood exactly which skills could support the roster it intended to build.

sections.heading: Wallace Allowed the Pistons to Win Without a Traditional Superstar
sections.body: The 2004 champions were unusual because no player carried the standard profile of a title-winning offensive centerpiece. Wallace gave the team a different organizing principle. His defense reduced the pressure on every perimeter defender, his rebounding ended possessions, and his physical presence established an identity that connected with Detroit's history. That foundation allowed Chauncey Billups, Richard Hamilton, Tayshaun Prince, and Rasheed Wallace to occupy balanced roles. The acquired center was not simply one starter among five; he made the star-by-committee construction viable.

sections.heading: Hill’s Injuries Changed a Potential Eastern Power
sections.body: Orlando's original vision was compelling. McGrady and Hill could share creation, defend multiple positions, and attract additional talent. Hill's ankle prevented that partnership from developing as planned, leaving McGrady to carry an extreme offensive burden. The Magic eventually received productive seasons from Hill after multiple surgeries, but not during the years when the roster had been designed to contend. The grade must measure that lost window. The transaction tied major salary and an outgoing future Hall of Famer to a plan that never had the health required to operate.

sections.heading: Atkins’ Role Extends the Asset Chain
sections.body: Atkins does not determine the verdict, but his contribution strengthens Detroit's side. He started, shot effectively, and gave the Pistons competent guard play while Dumars reshaped the roster. When a better championship opportunity emerged, Detroit could use Atkins in the structure that brought Rasheed Wallace. The sign-and-trade return therefore served two stages of the rebuild: Wallace became the permanent defensive cornerstone, while Atkins bridged the early roster and retained enough value to help complete a later upgrade.

sections.heading: Medical Uncertainty Should Affect Blame More Than Outcome
sections.body: Orlando could not reasonably predict the full severity and persistence of Hill's ankle problems. That uncertainty matters when judging decision quality, and it is why a D is more appropriate than an F. It does not make the realized exchange close. TradeVerdicts evaluates what the acquired assets ultimately produced as well as what teams knew at the time. Detroit received championship-level value from two pieces; Orlando received limited availability from a max-level star and surrendered the player who became the opponent's defensive identity.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Pistons earn an A+ because they used minimal leverage to acquire the defining defender of a championship team and a useful guard with additional downstream value. Orlando receives a D because the Hill plan was rational but the completed outcome was severely negative: the star was rarely healthy during the intended contention window, the contract restricted flexibility, and Wallace became a Hall of Fame anchor in Detroit. The trade illustrates how excellent asset identification can turn a forced exit into a franchise rebirth, while unforeseeable health failure can overwhelm an otherwise credible plan.

sections.heading: August 2000: Detroit Sent Hunter to Milwaukee for Owens
sections.body: On August 22, 2000, Detroit traded veteran guard Lindsey Hunter to Milwaukee and received forward Billy Owens. Both franchises' Basketball-Reference transaction histories document that direct exchange. There is a source nuance: the RealGM Milwaukee transaction log additionally records a traded-player exception, while the current canonical editorial ledger names only the two players. Until the accounting treatment is reconciled, it would be wrong to silently add or assign a value to that exception in the published asset list. Hunter had spent his first professional seasons in Detroit; Owens was a former high draft choice changing clubs late in his playing career. This was a positional swap of experienced pieces, not a new rookie selection or lottery pick.

sections.heading: Billy Owens Played Forty-Five Games for the Pistons
sections.body: Detroit used Owens in 45 games during the 2000-01 season, including 14 starts. In 17.6 minutes per appearance he averaged 4.4 points and 4.6 rebounds, while shooting 38.3 percent from the floor. That is a measurable frontcourt contribution but a modest one compared with Owens' earlier scoring prime. The Pistons finished 32-50 and did not reach the playoffs, which describes the larger roster situation without proving that one reserve-forward trade caused those results. His time with the team represented actual minutes and rebounding, so the Detroit return should not be dismissed as nonexistent even if the historical site grade is C.

sections.heading: Lindsey Hunter Played All Eighty-Two Regular-Season Games
sections.body: Hunter's Milwaukee return was far stronger than an account based on his postseason splits would suggest. In 2000-01 he played all 82 regular-season games, started five, averaged 24.4 minutes, 10.1 points and 2.7 assists, and shot 37.3 percent on three-pointers. The figure of 18 appearances and 3.6 points per game describes his separate 2001 playoff campaign, not his regular season. In the playoffs Hunter logged 18 games as a reserve while the Bucks advanced to the Eastern Conference Finals. Those figures establish a full season of useful guard play and a smaller postseason scoring role; neither can replace the other in a valid trade-grade comparison. Milwaukee subsequently traded Hunter to the Lakers for Greg Foster in June 2001.

sections.heading: The Milwaukee B-plus Has Actual Season-Long Support
sections.body: The site retains Bucks Win, Milwaukee B-plus and Detroit C, and the verified player totals make the on-court direction more defensible than the previous draft suggested. Hunter gave Milwaukee 82 games, five starts, 10.1 points, 2.7 assists and 24.4 minutes per regular-season appearance. Detroit's Billy Owens contributed 45 games, 14 starts, 4.4 points and 4.6 rebounds at 17.6 minutes. Hunter also played 18 postseason games during Milwaukee's run to the 2001 East Finals, though he averaged a smaller 3.6 points in that different competition. A separate RealGM trade-exception notation still requires salary-cap provenance work and does not authorize adding an extra canonical asset without corroboration. The corrected statistics, not an inherited assertion about the winner, are the basis for the playing-value comparison.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The stored verdict remains Bucks Win, with Milwaukee B-plus and Detroit C. On August 22, 2000, Milwaukee acquired Lindsey Hunter for Billy Owens. Hunter played all 82 regular-season Bucks games in 2000-01, averaging 10.1 points and 2.7 assists, and then played 18 postseason games at 3.6 points. Owens appeared in 45 Detroit regular-season games, averaging 4.4 points and 4.6 rebounds. The previous analysis incorrectly used Hunter's playoff averages as his season totals; that factual error is corrected. RealGM's trade-exception entry remains a separate unresolved cap-ledger question.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Hunter for Owens in 2000: Short Stints and a Grade Audit Flag
featuredDeepDive.intro: Detroit and Milwaukee swapped Lindsey Hunter and Billy Owens in August 2000. Historical transaction records agree on both players but differ in whether an exception is recorded. The following season, Hunter contributed 18 reserve appearances to Milwaukee while Owens played 45 games for Detroit. A later Bucks-to-Lakers Hunter trade is separate. The existing Bucks Win label and letter grades are retained, but the direct playing-value comparison raises an explicit provenance question rather than proving an emphatic winner.

sections.heading: The Transaction Ledger Contains a Source-Reconciliation Flag
sections.body: Basketball-Reference lists the August 22, 2000 swap as Detroit sending Lindsey Hunter to Milwaukee for Billy Owens, with no extra pick or cash noted. RealGM's transaction histories add a trade exception entry. That can reflect cap accounting rather than a new basketball player, and the two presentations should not be mechanically combined without checking the original salary-cap details. The canonical TradeVerdicts record presently includes Owens and Hunter only; those assets and the original grades are preserved in this editorial repair. Flagging the difference prevents an automated system from pretending every source records exactly the same collection of objects. It also identifies a discrete research task instead of obscuring it in repetitive copy.

sections.heading: Owens Offered Frontcourt Minutes, Not an Empty Return
sections.body: Detroit used Billy Owens in 45 games and started him 14 times during 2000-01. His 17.6 minutes, 4.4 points and 4.6 rebounds per game were modest compared with his earlier career, and the Pistons finished 32-50, but his 793 total regular-season minutes were a real contribution. The accurate Milwaukee comparison is 82 regular-season Hunter appearances at 10.1 points and 24.4 minutes—not 18 games at 3.6 points. Those latter figures were mistakenly lifted from Hunter's separate playoff totals in an earlier editorial version. With the correct season data, the Bucks received far more regular-season guard minutes and scoring. Owens' Detroit workload should still be acknowledged, rather than erased by the Bucks' stronger return.

sections.heading: Hunter's Full Bucks Season and Separate Eighteen-Game Playoff Run
sections.body: The Bucks acquired more than a limited postseason reserve: Lindsey Hunter appeared in all 82 games in 2000-01, made five starts and averaged 10.1 points, 2.7 assists and 24.4 minutes. He shot 38.1 percent overall and 37.3 percent on threes. In the 2001 playoffs he appeared in 18 games and averaged 3.6 points and 1.9 assists, which is a different statistical row. Previous wording incorrectly described that playoff sample as Hunter's whole Milwaukee regular-season contribution, leading to a false downgrade of the Bucks' return. Correcting the split also restores context for Milwaukee's 52-30 season and trip to the Eastern Conference Finals without crediting the entire team's improvement to one player. Hunter's subsequent June 2001 trade for Greg Foster remains a separate transaction.

sections.heading: The Inherited Grades Now Fit the Verified Direct Workloads Better
sections.body: The historical Bucks Win verdict and Milwaukee B-plus versus Detroit C were never changed during the earlier writing repair. Their statistical explanation, however, was wrong: Hunter played 82 Bucks regular-season games at 10.1 points in 2000-01, not 18 games at 3.6 points. The latter was his 18-game playoff sample. Owens delivered 45 Detroit games at 4.4 points and 4.6 rebounds, a smaller total role. This corrected playing-value comparison supports the direction of the original grades more strongly without mathematically proving their precise letters. RealGM additionally lists a traded-player exception in the August 22, 2000 transaction, while Basketball-Reference records only the two players. Until that cap treatment is independently documented, the canonical asset ledger stays unchanged.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Milwaukee received a full season from Hunter: 82 regular-season games, five starts, 24.4 minutes, 10.1 points and 2.7 assists per game. His separate postseason line was 18 games and 3.6 points. Detroit obtained Owens for 45 regular-season games at 4.4 points and 4.6 rebounds. The earlier version wrongly treated Hunter's postseason line as his total Bucks regular-season return, obscuring why the site assigned Bucks Win, Milwaukee B-plus and Detroit C. Those stored ratings remain unchanged, but their direct-player context now reflects the verified season splits. RealGM's additional traded-player exception notation is still unresolved: Basketball-Reference's public transaction timeline identifies only the two players, so no financial asset or dollar value has been silently inserted. Milwaukee's June 2001 trade of Hunter for Greg Foster is documented separately.

sections.heading: A 2001 Deadline Swap of Two Very Different Forwards
sections.body: On February 22, 2001, Detroit sent Jerome Williams and Eric Montross to Toronto and received Corliss Williamson, Tyrone Corbin, Kornél Dávid and a future first-round pick. Williams was the tireless rebounder nicknamed the Junkyard Dog. Williamson was a heavier, more polished scorer around the paint. Toronto wanted Williams' energy for a postseason chase; Detroit needed offense around Jerry Stackhouse while Ben Wallace took over the hard defensive and rebounding work. The teams were exchanging contrasting frontcourt roles, not merely a list of six equivalent assets. Contemporary reporting also identifies the draft choice as a pick Toronto had previously acquired from Orlando in the Tracy McGrady transaction.

sections.heading: Williamson Became a Sixth Man and a Champion
sections.body: Williamson immediately gave Detroit a source of scoring that its roster had been missing. The Pistons' own retrospective credits him with 15.5 points per game after arrival in 2000-01. In 2001-02 he averaged 13.6 points, appeared in 78 games and won the NBA Sixth Man of the Year award. His offensive role narrowed as the Pistons strengthened their roster, but he was still contributing 9.5 points per game in their 2003-04 championship season. Detroit did not win the title because of this trade alone. It did, however, acquire a rotation scorer who stayed through the rebuild and was part of the championship club three years later.

sections.heading: Toronto Got Real Rebounding Value From Jerome Williams
sections.body: The Raptors did not come away empty. Jerome Williams provided energy and extra possessions for a team led by Vince Carter, appearing in 26 Toronto games to finish 2000-01 and 68 more the following season. By 2002-03 he was starting 63 of 71 games and averaged approximately 9.7 points and 9.2 rebounds. That contribution helps explain the close A-/B+ grade difference instead of a landslide Detroit win. Eric Montross was the other incoming Toronto veteran, but the durable Raptors result was Williams' hustle and frontcourt minutes. His later career outside Toronto is not added to this trade's return.

sections.heading: The Pick Passed to Orlando Before Fran Vázquez Was Drafted
sections.body: The first-rounder was part of Detroit's February package but was not a Pistons draft selection in 2005. Toronto had first obtained the conditional asset from Orlando in the August 2000 Tracy McGrady transaction. Detroit then moved the future first back to Orlando on June 2, 2001 in a separate three-team arrangement. It eventually conveyed as the No. 11 choice in 2005, when Orlando selected Fran Vázquez. Reading only the final draft annotation could falsely imply that Detroit drafted Vázquez or received his NBA playing career. Neither occurred. The exact economic benefit Detroit received for conveying the pick belongs to the subsequent 2001 arrangement, not to an invented Vázquez tenure.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Pistons Edge — Detroit A-, Toronto B+. Williamson developed into Detroit's 2002 Sixth Man of the Year and contributed to its 2004 championship rotation. Williams gave Toronto meaningful rebounding and eventually started 63 games in 2002-03, while the two clubs' other veterans had smaller roles. The future first-rounder acquired by Detroit was subsequently traded to Orlando; the Magic, not the Pistons, used its eventual No. 11 slot on Fran Vázquez in 2005. Detroit's Williamson return earns a narrow advantage without discounting Williams or misassigning the later pick.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Corliss Williamson, Jerome Williams and the Pick That Returned to Orlando
featuredDeepDive.intro: In 2001 Detroit and Toronto traded two forwards with distinct strengths, and a future first-round selection that took four more years to acquire its draft-day label. Corliss Williamson became a valuable Pistons reserve before the 2004 title run. Jerome Williams offered Toronto activity on the glass and a popular, durable rotation presence. The pick involved more steps: Toronto had received it from Orlando, passed it to Detroit, and Detroit sent it back to Orlando within months. The story supports the slight Detroit edge but cannot be reduced to a direct Williamson-for-Fran Vázquez swap.

sections.heading: The Trade Followed Detroit's Shift Toward Ben Wallace
sections.body: The Pistons had already acquired Ben Wallace in the Grant Hill sign-and-trade in summer 2000. Wallace's defensive and rebounding emergence changed the purpose of Williams' high-energy role. With Stackhouse carrying much of the scoring burden, Williamson offered a better offensive complement. The NBA's own Pistons history describes the February 2001 deal as an early building block of the eventual championship roster, while giving the later Rasheed Wallace trade its separate importance. This was a frontcourt rotation decision made well before Detroit was a title favorite. Williamson's time in the league beforehand was uneven; his Detroit role fit the roster and helped reveal his bench-scoring strengths.

sections.heading: Sixth Man Recognition Supplies Concrete Hindsight Evidence
sections.body: The immediate scoring lift was measurable, but the 2001-02 award turned it into lasting recognition. Williamson played 78 regular-season games, came off the bench in 71 and averaged 13.6 points. Detroit improved to 50 wins that season and reached the Eastern Conference semifinals, where it faced Toronto. The award was not earned by a draft label or a hypothetical future roster spot: it followed actual Pistons minutes. Williamson then adapted to a smaller role with subsequent roster improvements and was still present for the 2004 championship. Those linked outcomes justify counting the trade as more than a short-term scoring patch without assigning all subsequent franchise success to one acquisition.

sections.heading: Toronto's Return Had Its Own Multi-Season Timeline
sections.body: Jerome Williams' 2000-01 Toronto introduction was brief, but his productivity grew. He played 68 games in 2001-02 and 71 in 2002-03, the latter with 63 starts and 650 total rebounds. His offensive profile was narrower than Williamson's, yet Toronto received three seasons of meaningful energy, offensive rebounds and lineup flexibility. Calling that return worthless would flatten the historical record. Montross provided veteran center depth but was not the centerpiece of Toronto's benefit. The final comparison therefore distinguishes the Pistons' awarded bench scorer and future champion from the Raptors' useful rebounder rather than asking which club simply obtained more named players.

sections.heading: The Vázquez Label Describes Orlando's Pick, Not Detroit's Player
sections.body: Tracing the 2005 No. 11 choice requires following an asset, not only its original acquisition line. Orlando sent Toronto the conditional first in connection with Tracy McGrady in August 2000; Toronto moved it to Detroit in February 2001; Detroit passed it back to Orlando in June 2001 as part of another transaction. Orlando ultimately used the selection on Fran Vázquez. Because Detroit disposed of the pick years before the draft, it never selected Vázquez with this asset. The pick still has value as trade consideration when Detroit conveyed it onward, but the later named player was not its on-court return. Respecting that distinction keeps the slight Pistons edge focused on outcomes the exchange actually produced.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Detroit A-, Toronto B+: Slight Pistons Edge. Corliss Williamson's award-winning reserve scoring and presence on the 2004 title roster offer the strongest traceable contribution. Jerome Williams supplied Toronto with real rebounding and starts, while Detroit's incoming first was sent back to Orlando in June 2001 and ultimately became the Magic's Fran Vázquez selection. The grade is a close historical comparison of Williamson and Williams plus separately attributed pick value, not a claim that one deadline trade created Detroit's championship or delivered Vázquez to the Pistons.

sections.heading: Detroit Took a Two-Year Starter from Phoenix in July 2001
sections.body: The Pistons acquired Clifford Robinson from Phoenix on July 18, 2001, sending the Suns Jud Buechler and John Wallace. The historical transaction accounts also attach a $1.6 million traded-player exception to Phoenix's side; that is salary-cap bookkeeping capacity, not another NBA player or a cash sum handed over. Robinson was coming off 82 starts and 16.4 points per game for the Suns in 2000-01, so this was not the acquisition of a marginal reserve. Detroit needed proven frontcourt scoring and defense as Joe Dumars reworked a roster that would begin competing again under Rick Carlisle. Phoenix moved a veteran contract for depth and financial flexibility rather than securing an equal established starter.

sections.heading: Robinson Started 149 Detroit Games over Two Seasons
sections.body: Robinson immediately became a critical Detroit forward. In 2001-02 he started all 80 Pistons games he played, averaging 14.6 points, 4.8 rebounds, 2.5 assists and 1.2 blocks, while making the NBA All-Defensive Second Team. The Pistons improved to 50-32, won their division and advanced past Toronto in the first playoff round. He followed with 81 appearances and 69 starts in 2002-03, averaging 12.2 points, 3.9 rebounds and 3.3 assists. That adds up to 161 Detroit games in two years, with 149 starts and a defined role in the franchise's rebuild. The record supports Detroit's inherited A grade without attributing the team turnaround solely to one forward.

sections.heading: Buechler and Wallace Did Play for Phoenix, Briefly
sections.body: Phoenix received real but relatively shallow playing return. Wallace made 46 Suns appearances in 2001-02, averaging 5.0 points in 10.7 minutes without a start. Buechler logged only six Phoenix games at one point per game before joining Orlando, where he played another 60 games that season. Those 60 Magic appearances cannot be booked as production generated for Phoenix, even though the same player name appears on the season's combined NBA line. The Suns went 36-46 that year; those two additions were neither primary rotation creators nor comparable to Robinson's workload. The salary-cap trade exception may have offered flexibility, but without a specifically proven subsequent use it would be wrong to invent an additional player or money return.

sections.heading: The Later Bob Sura Exchange Belongs to a Separate Deal
sections.body: Detroit kept Robinson through the 2003 Eastern Conference Finals season and moved him only in August 2003, together with Pepe Sánchez, to Golden State for Bob Sura. That later two-player-out trade is a different transaction; Sura's arrival cannot be assigned entirely to Robinson or directly to Phoenix's 2001 decision. This distinction also keeps Detroit's eventual 2004 championship from being described as a Robinson title: he had already left the Pistons by then. Robinson's actual 2001-03 starts and defensive versatility were sufficient value on their own. Relative to Phoenix's 52 combined regular-season games from the two named incoming players, the inherited Pistons Win judgment is supported, though the imported team ledgers disagree on whether the Suns' absolute grade should be B or C+.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win, preserving the inherited Detroit A/Phoenix C+ grades. Robinson gave Detroit 161 games, 149 starts and a 2001-02 All-Defensive Second Team season. Wallace played 46 Suns games and Buechler only six before leaving for Orlando; the associated $1.6 million trade exception represents financial flexibility, not a fictitious extra player. Detroit's later 2003 Robinson-plus-Pepe Sánchez-for-Bob Sura exchange is separate, and Robinson did not play on Detroit's 2004 championship team. Imported Phoenix B versus C+ absolute grade discrepancy requires a grade-ledger review, not changes to the trade facts.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Clifford Robinson in Detroit: 161 Games, Phoenix Bench and the 2003 Sura Deal
featuredDeepDive.intro: Detroit acquired veteran defender Clifford Robinson in July 2001 for Jud Buechler and John Wallace. Robinson started 149 Pistons games; Phoenix received 52 combined player appearances and an exception.

sections.heading: A Starting Forward Arrived as Detroit Rebuilt Its Defense
sections.body: Clifford Robinson was 34 when Detroit acquired him on July 18, 2001, but his skills were not limited to scoring. He could guard frontcourt players, challenge shots and stay on the floor in a demanding defensive system. The Pistons had sent Jud Buechler and John Wallace to Phoenix, and the Suns' side of the historical ledger also records a $1.6 million traded-player exception. Robinson immediately started all 80 of his Detroit games during 2001-02 and earned NBA All-Defensive Second Team recognition. He averaged 14.6 points, 4.8 rebounds and 1.2 blocks while Detroit finished 50-32. The production occurred for the acquiring club and directly supports the A grade more convincingly than broad claims that Detroit simply received the most famous name.

sections.heading: Detroit Received 161 Games Before a Separate Sura Deal
sections.body: Robinson was a full-time Detroit regular for two seasons. After 80 starts in 2001-02, he played 81 games and started 69 in 2002-03, averaging 12.2 points and 3.3 assists. His two-year total was 161 regular-season appearances and 149 starts, a clear return for the two outgoing reserve contracts. The Pistons also reached the 2003 Eastern Conference Finals while Robinson was on the roster. He was not on the team that won the championship in 2004. In August 2003 Detroit instead traded Robinson together with Pepe Sánchez to Golden State for Bob Sura. That was a later multi-asset agreement. Crediting all of Sura's Detroit production to the original Suns transaction would erase Sánchez and misstate the two negotiations.

sections.heading: Phoenix Received Fifty-Two Combined Player Appearances
sections.body: The Suns received John Wallace and Jud Buechler. Wallace played 46 Phoenix games in 2001-02, averaging 5.0 points in 10.7 minutes, without starting. Buechler made six Suns appearances before finishing the campaign with Orlando, where he played another 60 games. That makes 52 direct Phoenix regular-season player appearances across the two acquired contracts, not 112. The separately recorded traded-player exception gave the Suns a form of cap flexibility, but it did not score points or generate rebounds by itself. The contemporary transaction ledgers establish the players and contract mechanism; any claim that the exception produced a specific later Suns starter would require a separate supported chain. Phoenix finished 36-46, with neither incoming forward assuming a major role on that roster.

sections.heading: The Grade Gap Should Follow Actual Team-Specific Returns
sections.body: The source ledger records Pistons Win, grading Detroit A and Phoenix C-plus. Robinson delivered 161 Detroit games, 149 starts and a defensively recognized season, while Wallace and Buechler combined for 52 Phoenix games before their Suns contributions ended. The $1.6 million exception also belongs in the description, but it is financial capacity rather than a player with an NBA box score. Detroit moved Robinson to Golden State with Sánchez in August 2003, so he cannot be credited with the 2004 title or treated as the sole price of Bob Sura. This bounded comparison strongly favors Detroit, even after recognizing Phoenix's reserve minutes and financial tool. The original grade relationship can be retained without repeating boilerplate about winner labels, asset counts or hypothetical future roster moves.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win, Detroit A and Phoenix C-plus preserved. Robinson played 161 games and started 149 times in two Detroit seasons. Phoenix received 46 Wallace and six Buechler games plus a recorded $1.6 million exception. Detroit later sent Robinson with Pepe Sánchez for Sura, and Robinson was not on its 2004 championship team.

sections.heading: The Rebraca Rights Deal and Its Disputed Pick Count
sections.body: Detroit acquired the NBA rights to Željko Rebrača from Toronto in July 2001. Basketball-Reference's Pistons, Raptors and league transaction pages date the transaction to July 18 and list one 2002 second-round draft pick later associated with Tito Maddox (No. 37). Pro Sports Transactions instead lists picks later associated with Maddox and Rasual Butler (No. 52), and RealGM describes a draft-pick swap on July 13. The canonical import continues to display both selections as its historical source snapshot, but their roles as separate unconditional consideration cannot be declared settled while reputable ledgers conflict.

sections.heading: Rebraca Delivered 125 Pistons Games
sections.body: Detroit converted rights to the 7-foot Serbian center into real NBA playing time. Rebrača appeared in 74 Pistons regular-season games in 2001-02, 30 in 2002-03 and 21 during 2003-04 before his later trade. That adds up to 125 Detroit games, rather than the 215 games on his full NBA career line. He averaged 6.9 points and 3.9 rebounds in his first Pistons season and provided reserve frontcourt minutes on a playoff team. This outcome provides firmer evidence for Detroit's side than a vague reference to the reputation of an overseas acquisition.

sections.heading: The Raptors Pick Chain Cannot Be Double-Counted
sections.body: Toronto received at least the 2002 second-round choice later identified with Maddox; the Raptors' transaction history also says it sent that selection to Houston in the subsequent Hakeem Olajuwon trade. A specialist draft-pick ledger links the Rebrača transfer to the No. 52 selection used on Butler as well, but the participating-team transaction records do not independently confirm that second choice as a separate outgoing piece. RealGM's pick-swap description creates a further provenance question. Crediting Toronto with two independent durable assets, or valuing NBA games from players ultimately drafted by other clubs as Toronto returns, would outrun the confirmed chain. A July 16, 2001 Ticker wire report, preserved in a Serbian government news archive, likewise describes a single 2002 second-round pick. It offers contemporaneous support for the one-pick account without identifying or conclusively ruling out the additional No. 52 draft-asset branch claimed by a specialist ledger.

sections.heading: Why the B/C- Judgment Is Provisional
sections.body: The existing record assigns Detroit B and Toronto C-, a Pistons Win reflecting useful Rebrača minutes versus uncertain second-round outcomes. Detroit's 125-game return is measurable; the precise Toronto consideration is not yet reconciled across team, league and specialist ledgers. The B/C- pair is therefore retained as an inherited provisional judgment rather than presented as mathematically established by two confirmed draft choices. Resolving the No. 37/No. 52 swap chain could change the final asset accounting without affecting Rebrača's verified Pistons appearances.

finalVerdict.heading: Provisional Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Provisional Pistons Win, B/C-. Detroit received 125 regular-season appearances from Rebrača. Toronto's return is recorded differently: Basketball-Reference documents one second-round pick associated with Tito Maddox, while Pro Sports Transactions reports both that pick and the No. 52 Rasual Butler-linked choice, and RealGM notes a pick swap. The existing canonical asset import and grades have been preserved pending an authoritative reconciliation. These source conflicts should not be disguised as a fully verified two-pick exchange.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Željko Rebrača Rights Trade: Detroit's Games and Toronto's Disputed Draft Chain
featuredDeepDive.intro: The 2001 Toronto-to-Detroit Rebrača transaction looks simple when reduced to a center's rights and a draft pick. The difficulty is that major transaction databases disagree about the original 2002 second-round consideration. Detroit's benefit is more certain: Rebrača played 125 regular-season games for the Pistons, not the 215 appearances he logged over his entire NBA career. Toronto's No. 37 and No. 52 pick chains require a separate historical reconciliation, and that source disagreement limits the confidence of the existing B/C- grade gap.

sections.heading: Three Pistons Seasons, Then a Separate Career
sections.body: Rebrača arrived from European basketball and appeared 74 times for Detroit in 2001-02, when he averaged 6.9 points and 3.9 rebounds. Injuries limited him to 30 games in 2002-03, and he played another 21 Detroit games in 2003-04. Those 125 appearances are the traceable Pistons return from this July 2001 rights acquisition. His later appearances with Atlanta and the Los Angeles Clippers belong to subsequent moves and cannot inflate the direct value of the Toronto exchange. That distinction also prevents his full 215 NBA games from being treated as Detroit production.

sections.heading: What the July Transaction Logs Actually Agree On
sections.body: The Detroit and Toronto transaction logs published by Basketball-Reference and its NBA league ledger agree that Detroit acquired Rebrača's rights in return for a 2002 second-round pick later identified as No. 37 Tito Maddox. They record July 18 as the transaction date. A Pro Sports Transactions ledger lists both No. 37 and No. 52 Rasual Butler, while RealGM suggests a swap of second-round positions dated July 13. The databases agree on the player rights transfer, but not all of the pick accounting. The difference is too specific to dismiss as harmless wording.

sections.heading: Olajuwon and the Downstream Pick Trail
sections.body: Basketball-Reference says Toronto transferred its Maddox-linked second-round pick to Houston as part of the August 2001 Hakeem Olajuwon deal. The specialist draft-ledger treatment of the Butler-linked pick introduces another possible chain involving later movement through Houston and Miami. A later club receiving or swapping a selection is not proof that Toronto initially held two distinct unconditional selections from Detroit. Before assigning Toronto a higher asset grade, the precise original pick identities and swap options must be traced to a contemporaneous trade statement or a trusted complete league register.

sections.heading: What Would Resolve the Grade Exception
sections.body: The Pistons Win label and B/C- grades are retained as provisional because Detroit's 125 actual appearances provide an observable return. The archive still needs evidence distinguishing one unconditional draft pick from two picks or a pick-swap right; only after that reconciliation could it grade Toronto's consideration confidently. This is a provenance exception, not permission to import Rasual Butler's subsequent NBA production as Toronto on-court value. Rebrača was useful Detroit reserve depth, but unresolved draft terms should be visible to readers rather than hidden behind generic certainty.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict — Provisional
finalVerdict.body: Detroit received 125 regular-season games from Rebrača and is provisionally favored, B/C-. The draft-pick accounting remains open: Basketball-Reference identifies the No. 37 Maddox-linked selection, Pro Sports Transactions adds a No. 52 Butler-linked choice, and RealGM describes a pick swap. The record cannot conclude that Toronto received two independent selections on the strength of one disputed ledger. The canonical source-side asset snapshot stays unchanged until corroborating trade documentation closes that gap.
