sections.heading: Milwaukee Turned a Restricted Free-Agent Exit Into a Championship Core Piece
sections.body: The Bucks were prepared to move on from Brandon Jennings rather than commit to his preferred long-term role and price. Instead of losing leverage, Milwaukee used a sign-and-trade to acquire Brandon Knight, Khris Middleton and Viacheslav Kravtsov. Knight was the established young guard and therefore the visible return. Middleton had played sparingly as a rookie and entered the deal as a secondary prospect. The transaction became exceptional because Milwaukee preserved value at the point of Jennings’ departure and then discovered that the least celebrated player in the package possessed the shooting, size and decision-making required to become a long-term partner for Giannis Antetokounmpo.

sections.heading: Middleton’s Development Created the Separation
sections.body: Middleton immediately earned a larger role in Milwaukee, starting 64 games in his first season with the Bucks and gradually expanding from floor spacer to secondary creator. He became a three-time All-Star, a dependable late-clock scorer and one of the franchise’s most important playoff performers. His value was not limited to regular-season production. During the 2021 championship run he repeatedly carried offensive possessions when Antetokounmpo was pressured or unavailable, including a 40-point Finals performance. Detroit’s F and Milwaukee’s A+ are rooted in that realized evolution: the Pistons surrendered a title-level wing before understanding what they had.

sections.heading: Knight Gave the Bucks Additional Short-Term Value
sections.body: Even without Middleton’s breakout, Milwaukee did not receive an empty placeholder. Knight averaged close to 18 points in his second Bucks season and became valuable enough to headline the 2015 three-team trade that brought Michael Carter-Williams, Tyler Ennis and Miles Plumlee. That later decision did not maximize Knight’s value, but his presence demonstrates the strength of the original return. The Bucks received a productive young guard plus the eventual championship wing for a player they were prepared to let leave. Kravtsov contributed little, yet the package had two meaningful branches and did not require Milwaukee to surrender draft capital.

sections.heading: Jennings Gave Detroit a Brief Spark Before the Achilles Injury
sections.body: Detroit’s side should not be reduced to immediate incompetence. Jennings brought speed, passing and shot creation to a roster that needed guard play, and during the 2014-15 season he helped drive a dramatic midyear improvement before rupturing his Achilles tendon. That injury altered his career and makes the outcome partly tragic rather than purely evaluative. The Pistons could not predict the exact event. They can still be criticized for surrendering Middleton before fully exploring his upside and for prioritizing a more visible lead guard over a two-way wing archetype that would soon become scarce. Jennings’ peak in Detroit was real but too brief to offset the outgoing value.

sections.heading: The Trade Became a Lesson in Evaluating Low-Usage Young Players
sections.body: Middleton’s rookie numbers did not advertise future stardom because Detroit gave him limited minutes and offensive responsibility. His later career shows why teams must separate role from capability. He already possessed size, shooting touch and defensive potential, but those traits needed repetition and developmental trust. Milwaukee created the environment in which they could compound. The deal is often described as a hidden steal, yet the more important point is that the Bucks were willing to treat a lightly used second-round prospect as a legitimate asset. Detroit valued the player it had already seen produce in Jennings more than the one whose future required projection.

sections.heading: The Secondary Prospect Outlasted the Headline Guard
sections.body: Jennings gave Detroit real scoring and playmaking before an Achilles rupture disrupted his Pistons tenure; that injury was not a predictable trade outcome. Milwaukee's advantage unfolded on a different timeline. Knight supplied immediate starting minutes and later became useful in another transaction, while Middleton progressed from a lightly used rookie into a reliable late-game scorer on the 2021 championship team. The Bucks' A-plus does not depend on blaming Detroit for medical bad luck. Milwaukee acquired two assets with separate paths to value for a guard it did not plan to retain on his preferred terms. Detroit obtained a capable lead guard whose peak there was brief and relinquished a future cornerstone. The F reflects the realized exchange rather than certainty that Jennings would get hurt.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win, with Milwaukee at A+ and Detroit at F. The Bucks transformed Jennings’ restricted free agency into Brandon Knight and Khris Middleton, receiving a productive guard and the future secondary star of the 2021 champion. Middleton’s three All-Star selections, playoff shot creation and long partnership with Antetokounmpo created franchise-defining value. Jennings provided Detroit with exciting stretches before an Achilles injury changed his career, but the Pistons surrendered Middleton after barely evaluating him. The injury explains part of the loss; it does not erase the enormous value gap.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The Middleton Trade Shows How Championship Players Can Hide in Secondary Roles
featuredDeepDive.intro: The 2013 sign-and-trade did not look like a franchise-changing event when it occurred. Jennings was the recognizable scorer, Knight was the prominent young return and Middleton was a former second-rounder with 27 NBA games. Milwaukee’s advantage emerged because the organization identified, developed and retained the player whose skill set fit the league’s next decade. Middleton became the rare wing who could defend, shoot, create difficult half-court offense and accept a complementary role beside a superstar. The trade is therefore a study in both acquisition and stewardship: finding undervalued talent mattered, but turning that talent into a champion required years of role expansion and trust.

sections.heading: Jennings’ Contract Situation Gave Milwaukee a Decision Point
sections.body: Restricted free agency can pressure a team into matching a contract it does not fully believe in or losing the player for little return. Milwaukee used Detroit’s interest to create a third option. The Bucks accepted Knight’s rookie-scale value, Middleton’s developmental upside and Kravtsov as additional depth rather than committing to Jennings as the long-term lead guard. That choice was not guaranteed to work; Knight and Jennings were both promising young players with different strengths. The advantage came from widening the number of possible outcomes. Milwaukee acquired multiple controlled assets, while Detroit concentrated its bet in the player whose role and salary expectations were already clear.

sections.heading: Middleton Became the Ideal Counterweight to Antetokounmpo
sections.body: As Antetokounmpo grew from prospect to MVP, Milwaukee needed perimeter shooting and a reliable scorer who could operate when the defense formed a wall. Middleton’s patient footwork, pull-up jumper and ability to attack smaller defenders made him that counterweight. He did not require the same transition lanes or rim pressure, so the partnership created tactical diversity. Defensively, his size allowed the Bucks to switch and preserve lineup flexibility. The trade’s value cannot be separated from this fit. Middleton was not merely an All-Star acquired cheaply; he was an All-Star whose game solved the precise postseason problems created by the franchise player’s strengths and limitations.

sections.heading: The 2021 Run Converted Long Development Into the Highest Outcome
sections.body: Milwaukee’s years with Middleton included painful playoff losses, coaching changes and questions about whether the core could win at the highest level. The 2021 postseason supplied the definitive answer. Middleton delivered major late-game shots throughout the run, scored 38 points in a conference-finals win and posted 40 in Game 4 of the Finals. Antetokounmpo was the dominant force and Finals MVP, but the championship required Middleton’s ability to manufacture difficult offense. That title turns the transaction from an excellent talent-development story into a complete franchise victory. The acquired player became indispensable at the moment the organization achieved its central goal.

sections.heading: Detroit’s Evaluation Error Was Larger Than the Injury Misfortune
sections.body: It is tempting to attribute the entire loss to Jennings’ Achilles rupture, because he had been playing the best basketball of his Pistons tenure. Yet even a healthy Jennings would have faced a difficult comparison with Middleton’s eventual career. Detroit included a 21-year-old wing after one season in which he received fewer than 500 minutes, suggesting that the front office did not value his developmental profile. The trade therefore combined bad luck with an avoidable assessment error. Injuries can change any transaction, but teams still control which young players they expose before understanding their strengths. Detroit surrendered the archetype that became more valuable as the league emphasized shooting and switchable size.

sections.heading: Retention Completed Milwaukee’s Work
sections.body: The Bucks did not treat Middleton as a temporary bargain. They extended him, expanded his responsibility and kept him through the franchise’s rise, allowing continuity with Antetokounmpo to become a competitive advantage. Long-term contracts always carry risk, especially after injuries, but Milwaukee repeatedly chose to preserve a proven playoff partnership. That patience matters when assigning trade credit. Some organizations acquire a useful player and lose the value before it peaks; the Bucks captured Middleton’s development, prime and championship contributions. The original trade opened the opportunity, while a decade of roster decisions ensured that the opportunity became durable franchise value rather than a brief surplus.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The deep-dive evidence confirms Bucks Win and the A+/F split. Milwaukee received two young assets for Jennings, developed Middleton into an All-Star and championship closer, and retained him long enough for the partnership with Antetokounmpo to deliver a title. Detroit received a talented guard whose best stretch ended with a devastating injury, but it also made the avoidable decision to give away a lightly used wing before his skills had been properly tested. Middleton’s later résumé is not a speculative trade tree; it is direct value produced by the player Milwaukee acquired. That makes this one of the clearest modern examples of a secondary prospect becoming the central prize.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Sent Its Stretch Forward to Detroit for Unguaranteed Contracts
sections.body: On June 11, 2015, the Bucks traded Ersan Ilyasova to Detroit for Caron Butler and Shawne Williams. Milwaukee’s official announcement and the Pistons’ contemporaneous reporting list those three players. The unusual feature was contractual: Butler and Williams had nonguaranteed following-season salaries, while Ilyasova had a guaranteed 2015-16 year worth roughly $7.9 million. Detroit used cap room to bring in a starting-caliber stretch power forward; Milwaukee wanted the option to waive the incoming contracts and open payroll space. This was not a basketball evaluation where both clubs necessarily expected to use the arriving players on the court.

sections.heading: Ilyasova Made 52 Detroit Starts before the Harris Deal
sections.body: The Pistons started Ilyasova in all 52 regular-season games he played for them during 2015-16, receiving 11.3 points, 5.4 rebounds and 1.5 three-pointers per game. He played 1,434 Detroit minutes and shot 36.3 percent beyond the arc, useful floor spacing beside Andre Drummond and Reggie Jackson. Detroit then traded him with Brandon Jennings to Orlando on February 16, 2016 for Tobias Harris. The team’s own announcement explicitly lists both departing players, so Harris was not a direct one-for-one return for Ilyasova’s June 2015 arrival. Ilyasova’s 22 subsequent Orlando games likewise cannot be counted as extra Detroit output.

sections.heading: The Bucks Waived Both Incoming Players before the Season
sections.body: Milwaukee acquired Butler and Williams on June 11 but waived them on June 30. As a result, each logged zero NBA regular-season games for the Bucks from this particular trade. Butler subsequently signed with Sacramento and played 17 games there in 2015-16; those were not Milwaukee contributions. Milwaukee’s payoff was instead escaping guaranteed Ilyasova salary and gaining flexibility for a summer that included its Khris Middleton contract decisions and other roster additions. Contemporary reporting estimated approximately $5.8 million in non-guaranteed Butler and Williams salaries could be cleared, but that amount describes contract options, not money the Pistons sent to Milwaukee.

sections.heading: The Saved Bucks Win Grade Depends on a Cap-Room Interpretation
sections.body: The archive gives Milwaukee an A-, Detroit a C and records Bucks Win. Looking only at games, that ranking would be counterintuitive: Ilyasova provided 52 starts for Detroit while Butler and Williams never appeared for Milwaukee. The original Bucks verdict can instead be explained as a salary-management judgment, because Milwaukee intentionally acquired contracts that could be waived without assuming Ilyasova’s guaranteed salary. Detroit also benefited from a legitimate starter and later used Ilyasova with Jennings in a separate Harris exchange. Preserving the inherited assessment does not require falsely claiming the Bucks received on-court minutes, nor does it justify awarding all of Harris’s later Detroit production to this June trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win, Milwaukee A- and Detroit C are retained as the original cap-flexibility judgment. Milwaukee waived Butler and Williams on June 30 before either played a Bucks game. Detroit received 52 Ilyasova games and starts at 11.3 points and 5.4 rebounds, then moved him with Brandon Jennings in a separate February 2016 trade for Tobias Harris. The Bucks return was contract flexibility, not scored baskets.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The 2015 Ilyasova Salary Trade: Detroit Got 52 Starts, Bucks Got Cap Room
featuredDeepDive.intro: Milwaukee traded Ersan Ilyasova to Detroit for Caron Butler and Shawne Williams on June 11, 2015. The Pistons obtained 52 starts and productive stretch-four play before later packaging Ilyasova with Brandon Jennings to acquire Tobias Harris. The Bucks waived both incoming players before the 2015-16 season, deliberately using their nonguaranteed contracts to create financial flexibility. That contrast is central to understanding the archived Bucks Win, A- Milwaukee/C Detroit, which is an economic evaluation rather than a straightforward comparison of receiving-team games.

sections.heading: The Deal Occurred before the 2015 Free Agency Window
sections.body: Detroit’s June 11 team analysis described acquiring Ilyasova as an early, low-risk solution at power forward for Stan Van Gundy. The player had spent his entire previous NBA tenure in Milwaukee and offered a perimeter-shooting fit beside Andre Drummond. The Pistons surrendered Butler and Williams, whose 2015-16 contract amounts were nonguaranteed, and Milwaukee acquired those deals primarily for their release flexibility. Ilyasova’s approximately $7.9 million guaranteed year would instead have occupied Bucks cap space. Contemporary independent reporting treated the move as a salary dump as much as a player trade, helping explain why a transaction can favor the outgoing-player club financially even when it receives no future player minutes.

sections.heading: Fifty-Two Ilyasova Starts Were Meaningful Detroit Production
sections.body: The 2015-16 Pistons roster gives Ilyasova 52 games and 52 starts, with 11.3 points, 5.4 rebounds and 27.6 minutes per game. He attempted 4.1 threes nightly and hit 36.3 percent, providing spacing for the Pistons’ guards and center. On February 16, 2016, Detroit and Orlando completed a separate transaction in which the Pistons sent Ilyasova and Brandon Jennings for Tobias Harris. Detroit’s official release confirms the three players. It would be inaccurate to say Harris was received directly from Milwaukee in June 2015, or that Jennings contributed nothing to the Orlando transaction. The original Ilyasova pickup was useful as both a starter and later movable salary.

sections.heading: Butler and Williams Generated No Milwaukee Court Return
sections.body: Milwaukee waived both incoming contracts on June 30, 2015, well before the next regular-season schedule. Neither Caron Butler nor Shawne Williams played a 2015-16 NBA game for the Bucks as a result of this exchange. TheScore and contemporary NBC coverage identify the nonguaranteed contract structure and the expected cap-space effect. Butler subsequently joined the Sacramento Kings; later games outside Milwaukee do not increase its receiving-team playing total. The economic benefit was the ability to clear salaries that otherwise could have tied up approximately $5.8 million of next-season commitments. That does not mean Detroit sent Milwaukee $5.8 million cash or that the Bucks acquired replacement veteran scoring.

sections.heading: The Grade Is a Financial View, Not a Head-to-Head Player Victory
sections.body: A purely on-court 2015-16 comparison would award more direct player performance to Detroit, because Ilyasova started 52 games and the two incoming Bucks players produced zero games. Milwaukee’s preserved A- and Bucks Win can be explained only by the club’s freedom from Ilyasova’s guaranteed 2015-16 salary and its subsequent roster-building opportunities. Detroit’s stored C should not be misreported as proof Ilyasova failed; he met a starting need and later helped fund another trade. The downstream Tobias Harris acquisition involved Brandon Jennings as an additional asset. Explicitly describing those separate mechanics makes the inherited judgment reviewable rather than concealing the financial assumption behind generic trade-grade language.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The archive’s Bucks Win, Milwaukee A- and Detroit C remain unchanged, interpreted as an inherited cap-space grade. Butler and Williams never played for the Bucks and were waived June 30. Ilyasova provided Detroit 52 starts, 11.3 points and 5.4 rebounds before an additional February 2016 trade bundled him with Brandon Jennings to acquire Tobias Harris. No salary saving is falsely presented as cash from Detroit.

sections.heading: Phoenix Sent Three Players to Detroit for a 2020 Second-Rounder
sections.body: On July 9, 2015, Detroit acquired Marcus Morris, Reggie Bullock and Danny Granger from Phoenix for its 2020 second-round draft pick. Both franchises announced the exchange at the time. The three incoming names were not three comparable contributors: Morris had just averaged 10.4 points in 81 Suns games, Bullock was a former first-round pick with little NBA court time, and Granger was recovering from injuries. Phoenix's decision was tied to its pursuit of salary-cap room during the LaMarcus Aldridge free-agency chase. For Detroit, absorbing those contracts bought access to an established forward and another young shooting prospect at the price of a distant second-rounder.

sections.heading: Morris Became an Everyday Detroit Starter
sections.body: Morris supplied the largest immediate return. He started all 80 Pistons games he played in 2015-16 and averaged 14.1 points, 5.1 rebounds and 2.5 assists as Detroit made the playoffs. He followed with 79 games and 14.0 points per game the next season. Detroit then traded him to Boston in July 2017 for Avery Bradley and a second-round pick, a separate transaction that demonstrated his value as a movable starter. Bradley and the extra pick came in exchange for Morris, but should not be credited to the 2015 Suns trade as though they were handed over by Phoenix. Detroit received two seasons of useful production before making that later move.

sections.heading: Bullock Developed; Granger Never Played for Detroit
sections.body: Bullock took longer to contribute. He made 37 Pistons appearances during 2015-16, then became a starter, opening 52 of his 62 games in 2017-18 and hitting 44.5 percent of his three-pointers. His development gave Detroit a second piece of realized on-court value from the same 2015 package. In February 2019, the Pistons dealt him to the Lakers for Svi Mykhailiuk and a future second-round pick; those later assets belong to a distinct two-sided trade rather than being free bonuses from Phoenix. Granger, meanwhile, was waived October 26, 2015, without playing a Pistons regular-season game. He was part of the financial cost of the original deal, not a third success story.

sections.heading: Phoenix's Pick Became No. 35, Not a Suns Player
sections.body: Phoenix received Detroit's 2020 second-round selection, a real future asset but no immediate rotation help. The pick ultimately landed at No. 35 and was used for Xavier Tillman, who entered the NBA with Memphis after the Sacramento Kings traded his rights to the Grizzlies on draft night. It would be inaccurate to count Tillman's Memphis games as Phoenix Suns production. The exact subsequent consideration Phoenix obtained when moving the pick warrants its own asset-chain attribution, separate from this July 2015 exchange. Phoenix freed room for its short-term plans but relinquished two players who later helped Detroit. That documented imbalance supports a Pistons Win verdict, with the inherited A-/D editorial grade spread treated as a strong retrospective judgment rather than proof that every member of the incoming trio delivered.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win. Detroit's inherited A- is supported primarily by Morris's 159 regular-season appearances as a Pistons starter over two seasons and Bullock's later emergence as a shooter and starter. Granger never played for Detroit. Phoenix's inherited D reflects the opportunity cost of accepting one future second-rounder while clearing salary; the pick eventually became No. 35 Xavier Tillman, but he was drafted via Sacramento and began his NBA career in Memphis, not Phoenix. The source perspectives contain a conflicting Phoenix C rating that still requires grade-ledger reconciliation; the original trade package and the Pistons' clear basketball advantage are independently documented.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Deep Dive: Why Detroit Pistons Finished Ahead of Phoenix Suns
featuredDeepDive.intro: The July 9, 2015 transaction is a useful example of why trade evaluation has to move beyond the first line of the ledger. Detroit Pistons and Phoenix Suns exchanged different kinds of value, and some of that value only became clear after the players, picks or financial pieces were actually used. The deeper review asks where the durable return landed, how much credit the losing side still deserves, and whether the explicit A-/D grade split is supported by the completed record.

sections.heading: What Each Team Actually Received
sections.body: The list of assets sets the boundaries of the review. Detroit Pistons received Marcus Morris, Reggie Bullock, and Danny Granger; Phoenix Suns received 2020 second round pick (#35 – Xavier Tillman). Looking at the entire transaction as Marcus Morris, Reggie Bullock, Danny Granger, and 2020 second round pick (#35 – Xavier Tillman) prevents the analysis from overfocusing on a single recognizable name while ignoring picks, rights, cash, exceptions or secondary pieces that were part of the same exchange. At the same time, those components are not treated as equal merely because they appear on the trade details. The evaluation weights what each piece actually produced for the franchise that received it.

sections.heading: How Detroit Pistons Created the Better Return
sections.body: The winner-side evidence is strongest when read as a completed-value chain rather than a trade-day forecast. Detroit won the deal, acquiring Marcus Morris, Reggie Bullock, Danny Granger for 2020 second round pick (#35 – Xavier Tillman). Detroit clearly won the trade. Detroit's return centered on Marcus Morris, Reggie Bullock, Danny Granger, while the outgoing package centered on 2020 second round pick (#35 – Xavier Tillman). The incoming side produced the transaction's clearly superior long-term value. That documented sequence is what moves Detroit Pistons to an A-. It credits production and asset outcomes that actually materialized, while avoiding credit for hypothetical branches that never became franchise value. The result is a narrower and more defensible claim: within this transaction, the return controlled by Detroit Pistons proved more consequential than the package sent away.

sections.heading: The Case for Phoenix Suns—and Its Limit
sections.body: The losing-side perspective still matters because it tests whether the verdict is overstated. On July 9, 2015, the Phoenix Suns acquired 2020 second-round pick (#35-Xavier Tillman) from the Detroit Pistons in exchange for Marcus Morris; Reggie Bullock; Danny Granger. Phoenix traded Marcus Morris, Reggie Bullock and Danny Granger for a second-round pick that became Xavier Tillman. Morris and Bullock became productive rotation players in Detroit, while Phoenix’s return was limited to one future second. The transaction sacrificed substantially more realized player value than it recovered. In other words, Phoenix Suns had something concrete to show for the deal, and the D grade should be read as a measure of that return rather than a dismissal of it. The problem is comparative. Once the two sides are placed next to each other, the best documented value on Phoenix Suns' side does not erase the stronger production, pick outcome or strategic benefit that accumulated for Detroit Pistons.

sections.heading: Keeping Hindsight Inside the Transaction
sections.body: Hindsight should stay focused on value tied directly to the trade. This evaluation credits later player production or draft outcomes when the trade connects them to the assets exchanged, but it does not assume every future move was foreseeable or back-credit unrelated transactions. That distinction matters for a deal involving Marcus Morris, Reggie Bullock, Danny Granger, and 2020 second round pick (#35 – Xavier Tillman). It keeps the analysis focused on what this exchange actually created. On that basis, the A- for Detroit Pistons and D for Phoenix Suns describe both the quality of each return and the meaningful distance between them.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win remains the deep-dive conclusion. Detroit Pistons earn A-; Phoenix Suns earn D. The available evidence supports the result from both directions: the winner-side evidence identifies the transaction's stronger realized value, while the losing-side evidence shows why the other franchise still deserves credit for 2020 second round pick (#35 – Xavier Tillman). The final separation comes from what the assets became, not from retrospective name recognition alone. With Marcus Morris, Reggie Bullock, and Danny Granger on the winning side and 2020 second round pick (#35 – Xavier Tillman) on the other, the production, draft conversion and strategic value are sufficient to preserve the winner without inflating the case beyond the evidence.

sections.heading: February 2016: Detroit Chose Harris Over Two Expiring Roles
sections.body: On February 16, 2016, the Pistons acquired Tobias Harris from Orlando for Brandon Jennings and Ersan Ilyasova, with no draft picks listed in the original two-team exchange. Harris was 23 and could score at either forward position. Jennings was returning from an Achilles injury and had lost his former starting role to Reggie Jackson; Ilyasova had given Detroit floor-spacing minutes but was not a fixture in its long-term plans. Orlando was seeking flexibility and different veterans in a changing rotation. Detroit's official announcement records the exchange, the age of Harris and the immediate role that the Pistons hoped he could fill. That context is more useful than treating the trade as a generic exchange of famous names.

sections.heading: Harris Supplied 157 Detroit Games in His First Stint
sections.body: Harris played 27 regular-season games for Detroit after the deadline in 2015-16, averaging 16.6 points and 6.2 rebounds while starting 25 times. He then appeared in all 82 games in 2016-17, scoring 16.1 points per game, before playing 48 more Pistons games in 2017-18 at 18.1 points per game. That is 157 Detroit appearances in the continuous run directly following this trade, a meaningful multi-season return. He also offered forward versatility and improving outside shooting as the team reshaped the roster around Andre Drummond. Those are direct contributions, not speculative credit based on an unrelated later career elsewhere.

sections.heading: Orlando Got a Brief Pair of Veterans, Not Equivalent Control
sections.body: Jennings played 25 games for Orlando in the remainder of 2015-16, averaging seven points, and Ilyasova appeared in 22 Magic games at 8.1 points per game. Both contracts helped the Magic adjust their roster and near-term options, but neither established a durable productive role with Orlando. Jennings moved to the Knicks the following season. The acquired forwards and guards were real professional contributors and the exchange was a defensible attempt to change the roster mix; their Magic tenure was far shorter than Harris's Detroit stay. The historical imbalance is rooted in those distinct team-specific appearances, not a judgment of each player's entire career.

sections.heading: The 2018 Griffin Package Is a Second Transaction
sections.body: Detroit later sent Harris to the Clippers on January 29, 2018 as part of a much larger trade for Blake Griffin. The outgoing package also included Avery Bradley, Boban Marjanovic and future first- and second-round draft picks. Harris had genuine value as one ingredient of that deal, but Griffin cannot be counted as if Harris alone bought him. That attribution limit still leaves a clear result: 157 Pistons appearances from a productive young scorer followed by inclusion in a high-value multi-asset exchange. Orlando's 47 combined games from its two incoming veterans in 2015-16 did not provide comparable long-term team value. The canonical Pistons Win, Detroit A- and Orlando F reflects that gap.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Detroit A-, Orlando F. The Pistons exchanged Brandon Jennings and Ersan Ilyasova for 23-year-old Tobias Harris and received 157 regular-season appearances in his first Detroit stint: 27 in 2015-16, 82 in 2016-17 and 48 before the January 2018 Clippers deal. Orlando obtained 25 games from Jennings and 22 from Ilyasova, with no sustained team return. Harris later joined a bigger Detroit package for Blake Griffin, which included Bradley, Marjanovic and picks; Griffin's total value must not be credited solely to the 2016 trade. Harris's on-court Detroit production supports the substantial grade advantage.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Tobias Harris in Detroit: A 2016 Deadline Decision That Paid Off
featuredDeepDive.intro: The decisive part of Detroit's February 2016 deal was not simply getting a younger player. It was acquiring a forward who immediately joined the rotation, became a dependable scorer over two further partial or complete seasons, and still carried trade value when the franchise pursued Blake Griffin in 2018. Orlando's incoming package, Brandon Jennings and Ersan Ilyasova, had recognizable veterans but no comparable continuity with the Magic. Following the player appearances rather than jumping straight from the trade to Griffin produces a clearer evaluation of the original transaction and shows why the canonical grade spread is wide.

sections.heading: Why Harris Was Available at Age 23
sections.body: Harris had signed a substantial four-year deal with Orlando in the summer of 2015, but the Magic's offensive and positional mix changed. Scott Skiles had coached him earlier in Milwaukee and did not treat him as untouchable. Detroit general manager Jeff Bower publicly emphasized Harris's ability to handle the ball, score and play both forward spots. The exchange cost Detroit two players who had filled useful roles but did not solve its long-term scoring problem. This was a bet on a specific young scorer rather than a package of picks or a contract dump, with upside obvious enough for Orlando to have demanded a much larger return in hindsight.

sections.heading: Harris Made the Basketball Return Visible Immediately
sections.body: After 49 starts for Orlando in 2015-16, Harris joined Detroit for its final 27 regular-season games and started 25 of them. His 16.6-point, 6.2-rebound averages stabilized the forward positions during a playoff push. The next season he played all 82 games, averaged 16.1 points, and alternated between starting and high-minute reserve roles. In 2017-18 he raised that figure to 18.1 points in 48 games before leaving. Across the complete continuous Pistons stint, he played 157 games, enough to evaluate his actual production without borrowing accomplishments from later teams. He provided both present scoring and flexibility for future decisions.

sections.heading: What Jennings and Ilyasova Actually Brought to Orlando
sections.body: The Magic received guard Brandon Jennings and forward Ersan Ilyasova for the final part of 2015-16. Jennings made 25 appearances with six starts after having endured a major Achilles injury the previous season. Ilyasova played 22 games and started four, posting 8.1 points per game in that stretch. These outputs establish that Orlando acquired actual NBA minutes rather than an entirely empty exchange. But the two veterans did not become part of the next multi-year Magic core. Comparing the team-specific records against Harris's lengthy first stint in Detroit is the concrete basis for the lopsided retrospective.

sections.heading: The Griffin Trade Demonstrates Value Without Erasing Its Other Assets
sections.body: In January 2018 Detroit packaged Harris with Avery Bradley, Boban Marjanovic and two future draft selections to bring in Blake Griffin, Willie Reed and Brice Johnson. The Pistons could make that later offer in part because Harris was a valuable productive forward at the time. It would still be false to state that Harris was directly traded one-for-one for Griffin. The Clippers received additional players and protected picks, each with independent cost. The 2016 trade generated immediate production and later flexibility, but the only fully attributable guaranteed basketball return is what Harris himself supplied while Detroit controlled his contract. Even on that narrower accounting, the Pistons obtained far more than Orlando did.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win, Detroit A- / Orlando F. Harris produced 157 Detroit regular-season games from his February 2016 arrival through January 2018, with scoring averages of 16.6, 16.1 and 18.1 in those respective team-year splits. Jennings and Ilyasova combined for 47 Orlando games during the remainder of 2015-16, with no multi-year Magic role. Harris later contributed to the larger Griffin package, but Bradley, Marjanovic and draft picks also made that deal possible. The documented Pistons scoring return and Orlando's short tenure, not a fictional one-for-one Griffin conversion, support the original grade difference.

sections.heading: Houston Took Hilliard in a Cash Transaction
sections.body: Detroit sent guard Darrun Hilliard to Houston on June 28, 2017 and received cash considerations. Hilliard was not an entrenched Pistons starter, so the acquisition offered Houston a limited player and roster-management option rather than a new leading scorer. Detroit converted a marginal roster asset into money. No draft picks or unidentified extra players appear as consideration in this specific transaction record, and the reported sources do not establish a dependable amount of cash.

sections.heading: The Rockets Acquired a Tradable Player, Not a Guaranteed Star
sections.body: Hilliard’s value to Houston lay in having his contract and rights available during a period of roster changes. His potential usefulness should be separated from later multi-player transactions; when a player forms part of a broader package, that package’s full return cannot be credited to him alone. Detroit’s side is even narrower: a cash payment rather than a replacement NBA contributor. Neither return establishes a lasting centerpiece from a minor June roster exchange.

sections.heading: A One-Notch Grade Advantage Matches the Scope
sections.body: The archive gives Houston C and Detroit D-plus, recording a Rockets Win. That is a modest edge for obtaining a player asset instead of an undocumented dollar amount. The result does not require claiming Hilliard starred in Houston or that Detroit received no compensation. It simply preserves the identified guard-for-cash exchange and the small retrospective difference between an asset a club can use in roster decisions and an unpriced monetary payment.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win — Houston C, Detroit D-plus. Houston acquired Darrun Hilliard as a player and contract asset, while Detroit received unspecified cash considerations. The documented transaction was small; it neither guaranteed Houston a productive NBA starter nor established a known large cash return for Detroit. Houston’s one-grade-step advantage is limited to the recorded assets.

sections.heading: Detroit Bought Star Power Without a Stable Contending Base
sections.body: The Pistons acquired Blake Griffin because the roster had stalled and the franchise needed a recognizable centerpiece to energize a new arena era. Griffin was still capable of carrying an offense, but Detroit was not adding him to a deep, young or flexible contender. The team surrendered Tobias Harris, Avery Bradley, Boban Marjanović and two draft picks while assuming the balance of a five-year maximum contract. That price made sense only if Griffin could remain healthy and elevate the roster for several seasons. Detroit received one excellent year, but the surrounding structure never became strong enough to turn his individual brilliance into a sustainable competitive window.

sections.heading: Griffin’s 2018-19 Season Was a Real Return, Not an Illusion
sections.body: A fair review must credit Detroit for Griffin’s peak. He expanded his playmaking, shot more threes, averaged career-best scoring and earned All-NBA recognition while leading the Pistons to the playoffs. For a franchise that had reached the postseason only once in the previous eight seasons, that mattered. The trade was not an immediate collapse or a case in which the star stopped contributing upon arrival. Griffin gave Detroit a legitimate offensive engine and played through physical pain to finish the season. That performance supports a B- rather than an F, because the Pistons did receive meaningful short-term value and a memorable individual campaign.

sections.heading: The Contract and Injury Curve Quickly Consumed the Upside
sections.body: The risk embedded in the deal became decisive after Griffin’s knee problems intensified. He appeared in only 18 games in 2019-20, struggled to regain explosion and eventually reached a buyout with Detroit in 2021. The Pistons were left paying for a star-level contract without receiving star-level availability or a tradeable asset. Because the team had already surrendered Harris and draft capital, it could not easily pivot. This is the central reason the transaction grades below average for Detroit: the organization concentrated too much value in a player whose physical history required a stronger supporting roster and a shorter path to contention than the Pistons possessed.

sections.heading: The Clippers Converted the Return Into Flexibility and More Assets
sections.body: Los Angeles received Harris, Bradley, Marjanović, a protected first-round pick and a second-round pick. Harris became the best immediate player in the return and later helped the Clippers remain competitive without Griffin. The front office then moved Harris, Marjanović and Mike Scott to Philadelphia for Landry Shamet, Wilson Chandler, Mike Muscala and additional first-round value. That sequence helped preserve cap flexibility and draft capital before the 2019 acquisition of Kawhi Leonard and Paul George. The Griffin trade did not directly produce every piece of the later contender, but it removed a long contract and created optionality at the exact moment the organization wanted to reset its timeline.

sections.heading: The Emotional Cost Was High, Yet the Strategic Choice Was Correct
sections.body: Griffin had transformed the Clippers from a punch line into a relevant franchise and had recently been presented as a lifelong cornerstone during free agency. Trading him months after that presentation damaged trust and made the organization appear cold. Sentiment, however, cannot erase the basketball logic. Los Angeles recognized that the Lob City core had reached its ceiling and that Griffin’s contract could prevent a broader rebuild. The Clippers accepted reputational discomfort to avoid being trapped by nostalgia. An A grade acknowledges the strong return and the flexibility created, while stopping short of A+ because the later championship goal was not achieved and some of the asset chain depended on separate decisions.

sections.heading: The Verdict Should Name the Clippers Instead of Hiding Behind Partner Win
sections.body: The original Partner Win label avoided identifying the team that held the A grade, even though the record itself made the direction clear. Clippers Win is the accurate verdict. Los Angeles received useful players, draft capital and financial flexibility, then used those resources during a successful transition. Detroit received Griffin’s outstanding 2018-19 season but absorbed the injury decline and ultimately bought out the remaining contract. The revised label does not erase Griffin’s value or claim that Detroit received nothing. It states that the total exchange favored the organization that exited the long-term risk while retaining multiple paths forward.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win, with Los Angeles at A and Detroit at B-. Griffin delivered an All-NBA season and ended Detroit’s playoff drought, so the Pistons deserve credit for real short-term value. The larger transaction still favored Los Angeles. The Clippers escaped a long, injury-sensitive contract, received Tobias Harris and draft capital, and converted parts of the return into additional flexibility before building the Leonard-George roster. Detroit’s gamble required a healthier star and a stronger supporting cast than the franchise could provide. The result was one peak season followed by injuries, limited mobility and a buyout.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The Blake Griffin Trade Was a Test of Whether a Franchise Could Let Go of Its Own Revival
featuredDeepDive.intro: Blake Griffin was not simply another Clippers star. He was the player who made the franchise entertaining, credible and commercially relevant after decades of dysfunction. That history made the 2018 trade emotionally jarring, especially because Los Angeles had just re-signed him and celebrated him as a permanent figure. The decision nevertheless became a model of separating gratitude from roster planning. Detroit saw the same player as a shortcut to relevance; Los Angeles saw the contract and aging curve as obstacles to its next phase. Both evaluations contained truth, but only one matched the organization’s actual timeline.

sections.heading: Detroit’s Need for an Identity Increased Its Willingness to Overpay
sections.body: The Pistons were moving into Little Caesars Arena and lacked a clear star around whom fans and the roster could organize. Griffin supplied immediate visibility and a player capable of creating offense from the frontcourt. That need made Detroit more tolerant of the contract and injury risk than a more patient organization might have been. The problem was that acquiring an identity is not the same as acquiring a championship foundation. Andre Drummond, Reggie Jackson and Griffin could produce enough offense to chase a lower playoff seed, but the roster lacked the two-way depth and young upside necessary to justify sacrificing Harris and picks. The trade addressed perception faster than structure.

sections.heading: Griffin Reinvented His Game Before His Body Failed Him
sections.body: Detroit’s best season from Griffin showed how intelligently he adapted. He handled more playmaking responsibility, increased his three-point volume and operated as a point forward rather than relying entirely on the explosive finishing that defined his early Clippers years. That evolution made his All-NBA campaign especially impressive and explains why the trade briefly appeared defensible. The cruel part of the outcome is that skill development could not fully compensate for accumulated knee damage. Griffin’s decline was not caused by a lack of effort or basketball growth. It demonstrated that even a star who expands his game can become a poor long-term investment when physical reliability is the foundation of the price.

sections.heading: Harris Gave Los Angeles a Bridge Instead of a Bottom-Out
sections.body: The Clippers did not have to become intentionally uncompetitive after trading Griffin. Harris fit beside Lou Williams, Patrick Beverley and a resilient veteran group that reached the 2019 playoffs and pushed Golden State in the first round. His production preserved credibility while the front office prepared for a larger move. When Philadelphia offered another package, Los Angeles converted Harris into additional assets without sacrificing the season’s competitive culture. That bridge value is easy to overlook because Harris was not on the later conference-finals roster. His role was to keep the team functional and marketable while the organization changed its cap sheet and accumulated the flexibility needed for the next star pursuit.

sections.heading: The First-Round Pick Added Value Even Though the Draft Outcome Was Complicated
sections.body: Detroit’s protected first-rounder conveyed in 2018 and became the pick used on Miles Bridges, whose rights were then moved in a draft-night transaction involving Shai Gilgeous-Alexander. The Clippers’ later handling of that selection should be evaluated separately from the decision to acquire it. What matters for the Griffin trade is that Los Angeles received a premium controlled asset in addition to Harris and useful veterans. Draft capital gave the front office options that a long guaranteed contract would not. Even when a pick’s ultimate chain is complex, its presence can increase negotiating power, facilitate later moves and reduce the need to force a single immediate outcome.

sections.heading: Detroit’s Buyout Closed the Case on the Competitive Gamble
sections.body: By the time Griffin and the Pistons agreed to part ways, Detroit had shifted into a rebuild and could not find a trade that returned meaningful value for his contract. The buyout allowed Griffin to join Brooklyn, but it confirmed that the asset acquired in 2018 had become a sunk cost before the deal expired. The Pistons had already moved Harris and the picks, so there was no remaining branch capable of reversing the result. That ending distinguishes the trade from a merely disappointing star acquisition. Detroit did not retain a young player, a useful contract or draft compensation after the peak; it retained the financial consequences of a window that lasted one postseason appearance.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The evidence-based record supports Clippers Win. Detroit’s case rests on a genuine All-NBA season, a playoff berth and the value of briefly having a high-level offensive creator. Los Angeles’ case is broader and more durable: Harris supplied immediate production, the draft picks preserved asset value, the later Harris trade added another layer of flexibility and the Griffin contract no longer constrained the roster. The Clippers’ presentation of Griffin as a lifelong star makes the move ethically uncomfortable, but the basketball outcome is clear. An A for Los Angeles and B- for Detroit recognize both the real peak and the decisive long-term separation.

sections.heading: Memphis Sent Ennis to Detroit for a Future Pick and a Young Forward
sections.body: The Pistons acquired James Ennis III from Memphis on February 8, 2018. The Grizzlies received Brice Johnson and a 2022 second-round selection identified as the less favorable of the Chicago and Detroit picks. The draft asset eventually became the No. 49 selection in 2022, used on Isaiah Mobley. This was a trade of an available veteran wing for a prospect and a delayed draft opportunity, not a swap of two established starters.

sections.heading: Ennis Was an Immediate Rotation Option for Detroit
sections.body: Ennis brought perimeter size and experience to a Pistons club seeking useful wing minutes after its Blake Griffin acquisition. His 2017–18 Pistons stint consisted of 27 games, offering a short-term contribution rather than several seasons of guaranteed team control. Detroit could fairly prefer help available that spring, but the brevity of the return limits the retrospective grade. The analysis cannot credit Detroit with Ennis’s previous Memphis work or subsequent production for other franchises.

sections.heading: The Grizzlies Received Two Distinct Chances to Build Value
sections.body: Memphis accepted Johnson, a former first-round selection who had not established himself, and the protected future second. Johnson was a developmental flyer rather than a guaranteed replacement for Ennis. The 2022 second became an identified No. 49 draft asset, a meaningful second route to value even if its later movements were separate transactions. The Kings, Cavaliers or another later holder of a selection should not be confused with the club that initially acquired the pick.

sections.heading: How the Ennis Deal Became a Later Memphis Draft Opportunity
sections.body: The Grizzlies Win verdict grades Memphis B-plus and Detroit C. Detroit acquired James Ennis III and received 27 games from him after the February 2018 deal; Memphis instead received Brice Johnson and a 2022 second-round pick. That pick had a traceable later use: Memphis included a 2022 second along with Robert Woodard II's draft rights in its separate November 2020 exchange for Xavier Tillman Sr. The selection subsequently reached Cleveland, which drafted Isaiah Mobley at No. 49 in 2022. Tillman was not part of the original Ennis trade, and Mobley was not selected by Memphis. The grade gap reflects the Grizzlies' additional roster and draft options compared with Detroit's short-term wing minutes, not an invented immediate payoff or a claim that Johnson became a starting forward.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Grizzlies Win — Memphis B-plus, Detroit C. Memphis exchanged James Ennis III for Brice Johnson and the protected 2022 second-round selection whose eventual slot was No. 49, used on Isaiah Mobley. Detroit obtained 27 games from Ennis during its 2017–18 playoff pursuit. That near-term help was real, but the Grizzlies retained two separate opportunities beyond the season, supporting the recorded grade advantage.

sections.heading: Detroit Bought Khyri Thomas at Pick No. 38
sections.body: The Pistons acquired the rights to Khyri Thomas on June 21, 2018, after Philadelphia selected the Creighton guard 38th. Detroit sent two future second-round selections, rather than a current roster player, to secure a defensive prospect. The club’s own June 22 announcement emphasized Thomas’s two Big East Defensive Player of the Year honors and his junior-season average of 15.1 points, along with 41 percent three-point shooting. The Pistons also selected Bruce Brown at No. 42, but Brown was their separate draft pick, not part of this exchange. This was a wager on Thomas’s defensive translation, not a trade for an established starting guard.

sections.heading: Two Future Seconds Ultimately Became Nos. 32 and 31
sections.body: The picks surrendered by Detroit eventually landed at No. 32 in the 2021 draft and No. 31 in 2023. The final player identities in the transaction ledger are Jeremiah Robinson-Earl and James Nnaji. Those names are hindsight identifiers, not players Philadelphia knew it would acquire in 2018. The 2021 draft itself demonstrates why that distinction is important: Robinson-Earl was chosen at No. 32 by New York and immediately traded to Oklahoma City for the rights to No. 34 Rokas Jokubaitis and No. 36 Miles McBride. Philadelphia did not directly retain an NBA tenure from Robinson-Earl. The 2023 No. 31 selection also moved through later exchanges before Nnaji ended up routed toward Charlotte.

sections.heading: Thomas Played Only 34 Pistons Games
sections.body: Thomas appeared in 26 Detroit games in 2018-19 and eight in 2019-20, with no starts across 34 regular-season appearances. His 2.3 points per game in both seasons came in roughly seven and a half minutes per appearance, not in a sustained rotation role. In November 2020, Detroit moved Thomas and Tony Snell to Atlanta for Dewayne Dedmon; the Hawks waived Thomas. The later trade involved two outgoing players, so assigning Dedmon’s entire value to Thomas would overstate the direct return on the 2018 draft-rights investment. Detroit had paid two future selection opportunities for limited on-court production and a subsequent ancillary trade piece.

sections.heading: The Philadelphia Grade Rewards Flexibility, Not Two Stars
sections.body: The original verdict favors Philadelphia, 76ers Win, with the Sixers graded B and Detroit C-. That is a credible retrospective about retaining transferable future draft capital rather than acquiring a star from the Thomas trade. The two original picks were later traded onward, and their eventual draft-slot labels should not be interpreted as direct Philadelphia player development successes. Detroit’s evaluation is more direct: Thomas had a reputable college defensive profile but played only 34 Pistons games. The pick numbers, names and later routings identify what Philadelphia once controlled; the grades capture what Detroit actually obtained versus the optionality it spent.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win — Philadelphia B, Detroit C-. Detroit used two future second-rounders to obtain No. 38 Khyri Thomas in 2018. Thomas played 34 Pistons games and was included with Tony Snell in a separate 2020 trade. The picks became No. 32 in 2021 (Jeremiah Robinson-Earl) and No. 31 in 2023 (James Nnaji), but neither was directly developed by Philadelphia from this transaction. The verdict reflects the value of two transferable picks relative to Thomas’s narrow Detroit role.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Khyri Thomas in 2018: Two Future Seconds for a Creighton Defender
featuredDeepDive.intro: On draft night 2018, Philadelphia selected Khyri Thomas 38th and sent his rights to Detroit for future second-round picks in 2021 and 2023. The Sixers’ two picks ultimately corresponded to draft slots later occupied by Jeremiah Robinson-Earl and James Nnaji, after several subsequent trades. Thomas made just 34 regular-season Pistons appearances. The inherited 76ers Win verdict and B/C- grades can be explained through that direct exchange without crediting Philadelphia with every player subsequently selected through the moving picks.

sections.heading: A Clear Prospect Rationale at the Time
sections.body: Detroit had reason to like Thomas. He was a 6-foot-3 guard who averaged 15.1 points as a Creighton junior while shooting 41 percent from beyond the arc, and his repeated Big East defensive honors were prominent in the club’s June 2018 announcement. No. 38 is not a lottery expenditure, but giving up two future second-round choices still creates a real opportunity cost. Bruce Brown, taken separately by Detroit at No. 42, does not belong on the asset side of this transaction. Detroit’s case for the trade was that the specific defender available at No. 38 offered more immediate promise than uncertain future picks.

sections.heading: The Actual Pistons Tenure Was Small
sections.body: Thomas entered the NBA with defensive credibility but never secured a lasting Detroit rotation role. Basketball Reference records 26 appearances during 2018-19 and eight during 2019-20, averaging 2.3 points in about 7.5 minutes over his combined 34 games. Detroit then sent him with Tony Snell to Atlanta in the November 2020 Dewayne Dedmon deal, after which Atlanta waived him. A later five-game Houston stint in 2020-21 was a different organization and did not retroactively improve Detroit’s draft investment. The 2018 grade must be anchored to his Pistons opportunity and the picks sacrificed to take it.

sections.heading: What the First Future Selection Became
sections.body: The 2021 selection tied to the original agreement eventually became pick No. 32, associated with Jeremiah Robinson-Earl. NBA.com’s draft ledger lists New York as the drafting team, followed by the rights transfer to Oklahoma City. The Thunder’s official transaction announcement records sending the rights to Nos. 34 and 36 in exchange. This distinction is central to honest pick accounting: Robinson-Earl’s development and appearances for Oklahoma City are not Philadelphia accomplishments from a pick the Sixers surrendered onward. What the 2018 trade purchased for Philadelphia was the ability to use future selections as assets, not guaranteed long-term rights to the eventual players.

sections.heading: The Second Pick Moved Before James Nnaji Was Selected
sections.body: The other outgoing Detroit pick became No. 31 in the 2023 draft, used on James Nnaji. NBA.com lists the Pistons as the drafting team and identifies the eventual move to Charlotte via Boston. A contemporaneous pick-routing ledger traces the original Detroit-origin choice through Philadelphia and several later transactions before its 2023 draft destination. Those transfers are not one giant 2018 three-team deal; they are separate events over five years. The stored 76ers Win verdict, Philadelphia B and Detroit C-, reflects two assets preserved and redeployed versus 34 Pistons games from Thomas, with no invented direct Sixers claim over Nnaji.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Philadelphia’s B and Detroit’s C- are retained with 76ers Win. Thomas supplied 34 Detroit appearances after being acquired for two second-rounders. The 2021 No. 32 and 2023 No. 31 picks eventually produced Robinson-Earl and Nnaji for other organizations through later draft transactions, not straightforward Philadelphia player returns. The retrospective edge is asset flexibility against a short Detroit tenure, not the fiction that the Sixers selected and developed either eventual player.

sections.heading: Detroit Took Snell and the Last Pick in Round One
sections.body: On June 20, 2019, Detroit agreed to acquire Tony Snell and the rights associated with Milwaukee's No. 30 selection, which the Bucks used to draft Kevin Porter Jr. In exchange Milwaukee received Jon Leuer, a veteran forward whose contract was approaching expiration. The transaction combined a usable wing with a late first-round opportunity, but the rookie's subsequent NBA career did not unfold in Detroit. That crucial distinction keeps the ledger accurate. The team was receiving Snell's contract and control of an unsigned draft asset, not immediate possession of Porter as a Pistons rotation player. Milwaukee was primarily changing salary obligations rather than improving its center rotation.

sections.heading: Snell Started 57 Games and Shot 40.2 Percent From Three
sections.body: Snell delivered a measurable return in Detroit during 2019-20. Across 59 regular-season appearances, including 57 starts, he scored 474 points, made 102 of 254 three-point attempts and recorded a 40.2 percent long-range rate. His 1,641 minutes and 127 assists made him a meaningful short-term piece of the team's perimeter lineup, despite limited rebounding and secondary shot creation. Those are Pistons statistics, not numbers from his earlier Milwaukee years or later seasons in Atlanta. Detroit ultimately moved Snell to Atlanta in November 2020, as a separate trade involving draft considerations and other pieces. The 2019 arrival nevertheless gave Detroit a full season of starting wing minutes.

sections.heading: Porter Became Four Seconds and Cash in a Separate Cleveland Deal
sections.body: Detroit did not retain Kevin Porter Jr.'s draft rights. Six days after the June 20 agreement, the Pistons sent the No. 30 rights to Cleveland for cash and four future second-round selections. The Pistons' June 27 official release identifies the incoming Utah 2020 second, Portland 2021 and 2023 seconds, and Miami 2024 protected second. The Miami selection ultimately did not convey. Three other draft rights supplied potential downstream value and were later routed in different transactions. Porter's later scoring career belongs to the clubs that acquired or signed him, not to Detroit. The proper Pistons return is Snell's direct season and the specific pick-and-cash package received from Cleveland.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Was Buying Payroll Room, Not Leuer Minutes
sections.body: The Bucks' side requires a different frame. Leuer never played for Milwaukee after the transaction and was waived in July 2019. Reporting before the draft explained that moving Snell's multiyear commitment for Leuer's expiring contract would create more flexibility for a summer that included decisions on Khris Middleton and Brook Lopez. The Bucks did retain considerable roster success after that summer, but none of it can be attributed in full to one salary-management trade. Giving up the No. 30 pick was an actual opportunity cost alongside Snell's 2019-20 Detroit production. That combination supports the canonical Pistons Win, Detroit B+ and Milwaukee D+, while recognizing that Milwaukee's objective was not simply immediate points from Leuer.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Detroit B+, Milwaukee D+. Detroit acquired Tony Snell and the No. 30 rights later used on Kevin Porter Jr., receiving 59 games and 57 starts from Snell in 2019-20. Detroit separately sent Porter's rights to Cleveland for cash and four future seconds, one of which was protected and did not convey. Milwaukee received Jon Leuer, waived him without a Bucks appearance and used the transaction to improve salary flexibility. Detroit's directly documented playing and asset returns support the edge without crediting it for Porter's career.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The Tony Snell Deal Also Put Kevin Porter Jr. Into Detroit's Draft Assets
featuredDeepDive.intro: Milwaukee's June 20, 2019, exchange with Detroit was reported as a salary move: the Bucks would send Tony Snell and the last first-round draft slot to the Pistons for Jon Leuer. The package had two very different post-trade outcomes. Snell played almost all his next NBA games that season in a Detroit starting role. The No. 30 pick became the rights to Kevin Porter Jr., but Detroit traded those rights to Cleveland in exchange for four second-round selections and cash. Milwaukee later waived Leuer. The result is a lesson in following both on-court production and the separate chain of future draft choices.

sections.heading: A Salary Decision Made a Late First Available
sections.body: Milwaukee had reached the Eastern Conference Finals in 2019 and faced an offseason involving expensive core contracts. Snell was a useful floor-spacing wing, but the remaining guaranteed money and player option on his deal restricted flexibility. Leuer's contract was shorter, allowing the Bucks to shift future salary exposure even though Leuer had missed time with injuries and was not positioned for a major playing role. Detroit could absorb Snell as a potential starter and receive a first-round selection as compensation. That was a real opportunity cost for Milwaukee, but it also had an identifiable cap rationale. A hindsight analysis should neither ignore the salary motive nor mistake it for direct player production.

sections.heading: The Pistons Actually Used Snell
sections.body: Snell's Detroit year supplied 59 appearances and 57 starts, with 474 points and 127 assists in 1,641 minutes. He shot 40.2 percent from three-point range on 254 attempts, evidence of a defined floor-spacing role rather than star-level offensive creation. His 2019-20 work is easy to credit because it happened immediately after the original trade and on the acquiring club. Detroit later changed directions and sent him to Atlanta, which requires a separate asset ledger. The initial exchange had already produced a substantial run of starter minutes, something Milwaukee never received from Leuer in its own uniform.

sections.heading: Cleveland Bought Porter Rights for a Four-Pick Package
sections.body: Porter was selected thirtieth on draft night by Milwaukee on Detroit's behalf. The Pistons did not wait to see him develop as a player. They transferred his draft rights to Cleveland in a June 26 deal announced officially June 27, receiving cash plus second-round picks originating with Utah in 2020, Portland in 2021 and 2023, and Miami in 2024. The Miami pick was protected and did not convey. This record is more specific than saying Detroit traded Porter away for unnamed compensation, but it also establishes a firm limit: Porter never produced an NBA Pistons season. Any later Cavaliers or Rockets statistics occurred after the rights had left Detroit.

sections.heading: An Expiring Contract Still Had a Strategic Price
sections.body: Milwaukee waived Leuer in July without using him in a Bucks regular-season game. A player-only grading would therefore see Detroit with a useful wing and the Bucks with no on-court return. The financial rationale complicates that framing: Milwaukee was clearing multiyear salary exposure before retaining major contributors. Yet success from Middleton, Lopez or later Milwaukee rosters followed many other front-office decisions and should not all be attributed to this one trade. The canonical B+ for Detroit and D+ for Milwaukee puts more weight on the delivered Snell minutes and first-round-derived assets. It is a strong Detroit edge in directly realized basketball terms, not a claim that the Bucks had no reason to pursue the deal.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win, Detroit B+ and Milwaukee D+. Tony Snell provided Detroit 59 games, 57 starts and 102 three-pointers in 2019-20. The No. 30 pick became Kevin Porter Jr.'s draft rights, then four future second-round selections and cash in a separate Cleveland exchange. Milwaukee got Leuer's expiring contract and salary flexibility, waived him in July and received no direct Bucks playing time. Porter's later NBA career and Milwaukee's subsequent team success cannot be credited wholly to either side of the June draft transaction.

sections.heading: Detroit Bought No. 38 Rights and a Center for Cash
sections.body: During the November 2020 draft transaction period, Detroit acquired the rights to Saben Lee, selected 38th overall, and center Tony Bradley from the Utah Jazz. The Utah franchise received cash considerations, with a traded-player exception recorded in the transaction ledger. No named outgoing Pistons player was part of this specific exchange. Utah had acquired the Lee selection in a separate draft-night move, and Detroit wanted another young guard to evaluate while reconstructing its roster. The Jazz's own November 22 announcement names both Bradley and Lee, so there is no need to infer the asset package from later outcomes. The cash amount was not disclosed in the sources consulted and should not be assigned a fictional player-value equivalent.

sections.heading: Lee Played 85 Pistons Games Over Two Seasons
sections.body: Detroit signed Lee to a two-way contract after acquiring his draft rights. He appeared in 48 games with seven starts in 2020-21, totaling 267 points and 174 assists. The following season he played 37 games, adding 208 points and 107 assists. In all, Detroit received 85 regular-season games and 475 points from the second-round guard. These were reserve contributions, not star-level production, but they were concrete NBA minutes from an inexpensive developmental asset. The primary return in this transaction was therefore the right to sign and evaluate Lee, and the resulting two-season Pistons record is directly attributable to that acquired draft slot.

sections.heading: Bradley Turned Into Zhaire Smith Within a Day
sections.body: Bradley never played a regular-season game for Detroit. On November 23, the Pistons sent the center to Philadelphia in a separate exchange for guard Zhaire Smith, as the franchise's own announcement confirms. Detroit waived Smith on November 30 before he appeared in a Pistons regular-season game. This brief chain is important because it makes Bradley a piece of immediate roster maneuvering rather than a second durable playing return. The November Utah transaction gave Detroit both Lee's rights and Bradley's contract, but that center's short stop produced no Pistons court statistics. Smith's prior games for Philadelphia cannot be credited to this chain.

sections.heading: The Retrospective Edge Is Useful but Modest
sections.body: Detroit received 85 games from Lee and used Bradley to acquire a separate player whose Detroit tenure ended before the season. Utah received cash and transaction-exception flexibility without a direct on-court player arriving in the trade. Cash and a salary mechanism can have legitimate financial or team-building value even if no downstream transaction is clearly attributable; their unknown magnitude limits the certainty of a basketball-centered grade. The canonical Pistons Win with Detroit B- and Utah C- accordingly identifies a modest realized player contribution, not a lopsided star-for-nothing result. It would be inaccurate to count Tony Bradley's later 76ers games or Utah's use of any unrelated cap space as direct results of this transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Detroit B-, Utah C-. Detroit acquired Tony Bradley and 2020 No. 38 draft rights to Saben Lee for cash considerations and an exception mechanism recorded in the transaction history. Lee played 85 Pistons games across 2020-21 and 2021-22, totaling 475 points and 281 assists. Bradley was traded to Philadelphia for Zhaire Smith on November 23, and Smith was waived before playing for Detroit. Utah received financial flexibility, but the available records do not price its cash benefit or establish a later on-court return. The measurable Pistons guard minutes justify an edge without exaggerating the size of the gain.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: What Detroit Really Received in the Saben Lee and Tony Bradley Trade
featuredDeepDive.intro: Utah's decision to sell the rights to a second-round guard and send out a reserve center became a small but useful developmental win for Detroit. The Pistons received Saben Lee, the No. 38 pick in 2020, and Tony Bradley in exchange for cash. The two pieces took very different paths: Lee signed a two-way agreement and played 85 Pistons games, while Bradley was redirected to Philadelphia almost immediately. A source-specific hindsight grade should treat the Lee minutes as the measurable return and recognize that cash and exception flexibility have value that cannot be quantified from the public ledger. The deal was more than a roster placeholder, but far less than a franchise-altering acquisition.

sections.heading: The Jazz Sold Rights They Had Acquired in Another Draft Move
sections.body: Utah's official announcement identifies Lee's rights as the 38th selection of the 2020 draft and names Bradley as the accompanying outgoing center. The Jazz had obtained the Lee pick through an earlier draft-night transaction with New York, but Detroit's incoming rights were part of this later exchange with Utah. The sequence means the Pistons were not receiving an already-established professional with a known NBA role. They were buying the opportunity to sign a young guard out of Vanderbilt who had yet to play in the league. Cash went the other way, and the amount was not publicly specified. The trade's age and draft setting explain why its potential value rested primarily in Detroit's player development rather than immediate rotation certainty.

sections.heading: Lee Supplied Real Backup Guard Time
sections.body: Lee immediately entered Detroit's development program on a two-way contract. During his rookie season he played 48 regular-season games with seven starts, scoring 267 points and recording 174 assists over 781 minutes. He returned for 37 games in 2021-22, with 208 points and 107 assists. Those 85 appearances and 281 assists show actual Pistons value from the acquired rights. He was not an established starting guard, and the two-season total should not be spun into long-term franchise control. It nevertheless exceeded what a purely symbolic cash-for-rights exchange might have produced, giving Detroit a real opportunity to evaluate a second-round player at NBA speed.

sections.heading: Bradley Produced No Pistons Box Scores
sections.body: Detroit held Bradley only briefly. On November 23, 2020, one day after the Jazz's public announcement, the Pistons transferred him to Philadelphia for Zhaire Smith. Detroit then waived Smith on November 30, before a Pistons regular-season appearance. Neither subsequent player produced an NBA box score for Detroit as a result of that chain. Bradley's earlier Jazz statistics belong to Utah's prior ownership, just as his future Philadelphia minutes belong to Philadelphia. Keeping those timelines separate is essential: this was not a deal in which Detroit added two contributors who each played the 2020-21 season for the Pistons. Lee alone supplied the direct post-transaction basketball production.

sections.heading: Utah's Return Cannot Be Reduced to Zero Without Pricing It
sections.body: The Jazz received cash and transaction-exception flexibility, not an incoming named player. The primary team announcement does not specify the cash price, and the available ledger does not establish a directly attributable Utah acquisition made with that particular financial benefit. It is tempting to call such a return worthless because it cannot be shown in a scoring table. That would confuse missing public valuation with zero financial value. The practical comparison is more limited: Detroit obtained 85 games of developmental guard production and a short-lived contract movement, while Utah monetized assets it chose not to retain. This justifies the modest B- to C- directional advantage but not an invented dollar-for-points conversion.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win, Detroit B- / Utah C-. Lee's No. 38 rights generated 85 Detroit games, 475 points and 281 assists over two seasons. Bradley was moved to Philadelphia almost immediately, and the Zhaire Smith return was waived without a Pistons regular-season appearance. Utah took undisclosed cash and exception flexibility; no confirmed public valuation permits its consideration to be scored as zero dollars or as a player. The modest Detroit edge follows Lee's identifiable NBA contribution and respects the unknown financial side of the trade.
