sections.heading: May 7, 1971: Lucas Went East While Russell Went West
sections.body: On May 7, 1971, the Warriors traded veteran Jerry Lucas to New York for former Knicks forward Cazzie Russell. The NBA's Jerry Lucas historical profile confirms both the exact date and that the exchange was one-for-one. The league's description is important because neither club sent a hidden future pick or salary exception as part of this particular transaction. Lucas had just averaged 19.2 points and 15.8 rebounds in the Warriors' 1970-71 season and was a 1971 All-Star, while Russell had fallen into a smaller role with the Knicks after being a major scorer earlier in his career. Both incoming players offered actual NBA ability rather than a draft-rights placeholder.

sections.heading: The Knicks Needed Lucas Behind an Injured Willis Reed
sections.body: New York already had championship experience, but its frontcourt was increasingly dependent on Willis Reed's health. The NBA's retrospective explains that Lucas was initially acquired to support the forwards and spell Reed, not to replace a healthy center by design. Early in the 1971-72 schedule, Reed suffered a season-ending injury and Lucas moved into extensive center duty. That unexpected responsibility changed how much the acquisition helped: Lucas played 77 regular-season games, started 68, averaged 16.7 points and 13.1 rebounds, and gave the Knicks the interior continuity that an unplanned absence otherwise threatened. Team success was shared with Walt Frazier and the rest of New York's roster.

sections.heading: A Finals Run in 1972 Led to the 1973 Title
sections.body: With Lucas taking over substantial pivot responsibilities, New York returned to the NBA Finals in 1972 but lost to the Los Angeles Lakers. The next season, the Knicks defeated those Lakers to win the 1973 championship. By 1972-73 Lucas's regular-season role had changed again: he appeared in 71 games, started 38 and averaged 9.9 points and 7.2 rebounds. In the championship postseason, he played all 17 Knicks games, but his 7.5-point average came with a smaller offensive burden than in the prior year. Those distinctions keep the 1973 title in its proper context. Lucas was a valuable member of the winning rotation, not a one-man explanation for a well-balanced team.

sections.heading: Golden State Received an All-Star Season From Russell
sections.body: The Warriors' side of the exchange cannot be reduced to a footnote about New York's ring. Russell joined Golden State for 1971-72 and immediately produced the most prolific season of his career: 79 games, 36.7 minutes, 21.4 points and 5.4 rebounds per appearance. He received an NBA All-Star selection that year, while the team also relied heavily on Nate Thurmond and Jeff Mullins. Russell supplied 15.7 points in 1972-73 and another 20.5 in 1973-74, playing at least 79 games in each of his first three Warriors seasons. Those are tangible multi-year scoring returns. The team reached the playoffs, but a comparison must distinguish Russell's work from results achieved by the entire roster.

sections.heading: The 1975 Warriors Championship Was Not Russell's Trade Return
sections.body: The Warriors eventually captured the 1975 NBA championship, but Russell was no longer with the franchise that season after moving to the Lakers in a separate transaction. His Golden State seasons from 1971-72 through 1973-74 are the relevant direct return on the Lucas swap. Similarly, Lucas's years with other teams before 1971 do not count as Knicks production. The ledger should credit Golden State with a scorer who had one All-Star season and two more productive campaigns, while New York received frontcourt durability during a major Reed absence and participation in a title-winning group. The dates prevent later career events from becoming imaginary assets or points in a trade grade.

sections.heading: Why the Knicks Edge Still Gives Russell His Due
sections.body: The Knicks Win verdict grades New York A and the Warriors B-plus. Jerry Lucas filled a crucial frontcourt role after Willis Reed's injury and helped New York reach the 1972 NBA Finals before contributing to the 1973 championship. That result supports the Knicks' stronger grade without crediting Lucas alone for a team achievement. Cazzie Russell provided Golden State with a substantial return of its own: 241 games across three seasons, including an All-Star 1971-72 campaign averaging 21.4 points and two more productive scoring seasons. The Warriors traded Lucas when the franchise still played in San Francisco, and Russell's later time with the Lakers should not count toward this exchange. New York gained the right veteran for two deep playoff runs; Golden State received a three-season scorer. The narrow grade difference fits those distinct contributions better than dismissing the Warriors' side.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The original decision stays Knicks Win, New York A and Golden State B-plus. On May 7, 1971, New York acquired Jerry Lucas for Cazzie Russell. Lucas averaged 16.7 points and 13.1 rebounds when Reed missed most of 1971-72, reached the Finals and helped the 1973 champions in a smaller role. Russell's first Golden State year delivered 21.4 points and an All-Star honor, followed by productive 1972-73 and 1973-74 seasons. The championship strengthens New York's case without making the Warriors' return unsuccessful.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Jerry Lucas for Cazzie Russell: Two Strong 1971 Returns, One Knicks Title
featuredDeepDive.intro: In the May 7, 1971 one-for-one trade, the Warriors sent Jerry Lucas to New York for Cazzie Russell. Lucas became indispensable when Willis Reed got hurt and later contributed to a 1973 Knicks championship. Russell immediately averaged 21.4 points per game for Golden State and made the 1972 All-Star team. Those different returns explain the unchanged Knicks Win, New York A and Warriors B-plus grades more accurately than a simplistic championship-versus-no-value story.

sections.heading: The Original One-for-One Trade and the Two Franchise Timelines
sections.body: NBA's historical profile identifies the exact May 7, 1971 transaction: the Warriors sent Jerry Lucas to the Knicks and received Cazzie Russell. Neither player was a rookie or an unexercised draft selection. Lucas had just completed an All-Star campaign in the San Francisco Warriors era, averaging 19.2 points and 15.8 rebounds in 1970-71. Russell had started his career as a prominent Knicks scorer but had slipped in their rotation as New York's established title core evolved. The transaction should not be expanded into an unverified multi-team package because of later career moves involving either player. Golden State's current franchise name and the historic San Francisco designation refer to the same Warriors organization at different dates.

sections.heading: Reed's Injury Converted Lucas From Insurance to a Starter
sections.body: The Knicks did not acquire Lucas as a full-time replacement for Willis Reed in an ordinary healthy year. The NBA's retrospective says he was expected to back up the frontcourt, but Reed's injury in the eleventh game of 1971-72 forced Lucas into the pivot. He made 68 starts in 77 games, played 38 minutes per game and averaged 16.7 points with 13.1 rebounds. His perimeter-friendly shooting for a big man also helped New York's spacing relative to traditional post centers. That production is the clearest direct basketball return from the exchange, regardless of whether the 1972 Finals appearance is credited across the whole Knicks roster. Lucas helped solve a very specific roster problem in a high-pressure season.

sections.heading: New York's Ring Came With a Smaller Lucas Workload
sections.body: The historical shorthand that Lucas won a Knicks championship is true, but it hides a change in his playing burden. The 1971-72 Finals run required much heavier Lucas minutes because Reed was injured, whereas the 1972-73 championship roster was deeper in the frontcourt. Lucas averaged 9.9 points, 7.2 rebounds and 28.2 minutes in the title-winning regular season, making 38 starts in 71 appearances. In the championship playoffs, he appeared in 17 games and averaged 7.5 points in 21.6 minutes. Those numbers affirm real roster service while avoiding the exaggeration that he was the sole driver of New York's second championship. That distinction strengthens the grade explanation because the actual workload remains impressive.

sections.heading: Russell Produced Three Strong Golden State Seasons
sections.body: Cazzie Russell's first Golden State season in 1971-72 was a direct answer to anyone who would call this trade a salary dump. Over 79 games, he averaged 21.4 points, 5.4 rebounds and 3.1 assists while playing 36.7 minutes, earning an All-Star selection. He added 15.7 points over 80 games in 1972-73 and 20.5 points over 82 games in 1973-74. That is 241 regular-season appearances in three consecutive seasons with no need to infer later selections or conditional assets. Golden State also had Nate Thurmond and Jeff Mullins taking major offensive and defensive responsibility. Russell's production therefore has to be counted in its own right, not credited for everything good or bad about the team.

sections.heading: Direct Outcomes Support the Stored Narrow New York Advantage
sections.body: The canonical Knicks Win verdict is paired with a New York A and Golden State B-plus, not an invented A-plus versus F blowout. Lucas gave the Knicks immediate frontcourt insurance, answered the loss of Reed with 16.7 points and 13.1 rebounds in 1971-72 and joined the 1973 title rotation. Russell gave the Warriors an All-Star 21.4-point first season and two more seasons averaging 15.7 and 20.5 points. Russell's later Lakers seasons and Lucas's earlier Cincinnati service are separate histories. A direct-return assessment can prefer the championship-connected Knicks outcome without minimizing the considerable productive scoring acquired by Golden State. Exact letter values are inherited editorial judgments and have not been silently updated.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win, New York A and Golden State B-plus remain the unaltered canonical marks. Lucas played 77 Knicks games at 16.7 points and 13.1 rebounds in 1971-72 after Reed's injury, then contributed 71 regular-season and 17 postseason appearances to the 1973 title team in a smaller role. Russell gave the Warriors three substantial scoring seasons: 21.4, 15.7 and 20.5 points per game, with 1972 All-Star honors. Both were real, valuable NBA players, and the original transaction involved just their exchange. The Knicks' championship-connected return tips the retrospective toward New York without inventing a pick, denying Golden State's All-Star or crediting Russell with a 1975 Warriors championship after he had left the club.

sections.heading: Golden State Moved Chamberlain’s Rights to Phoenix
sections.body: On January 24, 1974, Golden State sent Bill Chamberlain to the Phoenix Suns for a 1975 third-round draft selection. The Warriors later used that choice at No. 40 on Otis Johnson. These were two specific assets, not interchangeable draft or player placeholders: Phoenix obtained an available reserve, while Golden State deferred its return until the following draft. The original deal did not include a documented conditional first-rounder, and no downstream premium pick should be attributed to it.

sections.heading: Chamberlain Provided Real Suns Games
sections.body: Chamberlain made his Phoenix debut three days after the trade and appeared in 28 games, averaging about 5.5 points and 2.9 rebounds. That production did not turn the Suns into a new contender, but it gave them an identifiable half-season contribution. The rights transaction succeeded at the narrow task of supplying a reserve who could immediately enter games. It is reasonable to describe that value as limited while still distinguishing it from a player who never appeared.

sections.heading: The Pick Did Not Become a Warriors Contributor
sections.body: Golden State selected Otis Johnson with the acquired No. 40 pick in 1975, but Johnson never appeared in an NBA game. The trade’s measurable on-court return therefore rested with Phoenix. The correct retrospective grades are Suns B-minus and Warriors D-plus, with Suns Win as the verdict. Older body copy called it an even C-minus/C-minus result; that wording contradicted the canonical transaction analysis and the known Chamberlain game record. There is no documented later asset chain that reverses the basic comparison.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Suns Win — Phoenix B-minus, Golden State D-plus. Bill Chamberlain played 28 games after arriving from the Warriors in January 1974. Golden State’s 1975 third-rounder became No. 40 Otis Johnson, who never appeared in the NBA. Phoenix’s brief but tangible reserve contribution gave it the better completed return.

sections.heading: This Is a Duplicate Import, Not a Second Trade
sections.body: This Golden State row is the opposite-team import of the same September 3, 1974 Nate Thurmond transaction already preserved in the Chicago canonical record. Both rows describe the same date, teams and asset movement: Thurmond to Chicago, with Clifford Ray, Chicago’s 1975 first-round pick and cash going to Golden State. The source-led audit found no second same-day transaction.

sections.heading: The One Verified September 3 Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference’s Warriors, Bulls and league transaction pages all describe one September 3 exchange. Chicago acquired Thurmond. Golden State acquired Ray and the 1975 first that became No. 14 Joe Bryant, while Chicago historical material supports cash as part of the consideration. Those sources corroborate the surviving Chicago canonical record rather than establishing a separate Warriors-side trade.

sections.heading: Why a Second Grade Would Double-Count Value
sections.body: Leaving both imports as independently graded transactions would count Thurmond, Ray, the same first-round pick and the same cash twice. It would also distort player relationship pages, team-pair histories and aggregate trade counts. The Golden State import adds source provenance, but it cannot receive a separate winner or grades without scoring one economic event two times.

sections.heading: Correct Archive Treatment
sections.body: The surviving canonical transaction is nba-trade-chi-1974-0039. This Golden State row is retained privately to preserve the independent source intake and audit trail. Its status is structural supersession, not a negative evaluation of either team’s real 1974 trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Resolution
finalVerdict.body: Record Superseded — duplicate canonical import, no separate winner and no team grades. The September 3, 1974 Nate Thurmond exchange is already represented by nba-trade-chi-1974-0039. Grading this Golden State import independently would double-count the same transaction.

sections.heading: The Warriors Sold Joe Bryant’s Rights Before the 1975–76 Season
sections.body: Golden State sold Joe Bryant’s player rights to Philadelphia in September 1975. Basketball Reference dates the completed transaction September 12, although the historical archive slug uses September 11. The 76ers obtained a young forward they could bring to their roster; Golden State received cash with no established price in the league transaction listing. This was a rights sale, not a swap involving another named NBA player or an identifiable draft choice.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Received Four Seasons of NBA Contribution
sections.body: Bryant went on to play 75 regular-season games for the 76ers in 1975–76, followed by 61, 81 and 70 games in the next three seasons. That is 287 Philadelphia appearances across four years after the rights acquisition. His role varied, and he was never the team’s principal star, but the length and continuity of that return give Philadelphia a concrete roster asset. He was also part of the 76ers’ 1977 NBA Finals season.

sections.heading: Golden State’s Cash Cannot Be Graded as a Dollar Figure
sections.body: The Warriors converted a young player’s rights into financial consideration. The verified transaction histories do not state an amount, making it inappropriate to invent a purchase price or estimate a profit. Golden State was coming off a championship season and could make a different roster calculation from Philadelphia. That context explains why teams might choose distinct returns, but it does not erase the NBA minutes the 76ers later received from Bryant.

sections.heading: The Canonical Grades Correct a Clear Old Editorial Error
sections.body: Philadelphia holds an A and Golden State C-minus in the canonical ledger, with 76ers Win. The old analysis incorrectly assigned Philadelphia B and Golden State F. The more defensible retrospective case is that a modest cash receipt, whose amount is unknown, did not match four seasons of identified NBA service. That does not imply Philadelphia bought a superstar or won another championship solely because it acquired Bryant’s rights.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win — Philadelphia A, Golden State C-minus. The September 1975 rights sale gave Philadelphia Joe Bryant for four seasons and 287 regular-season games, while the Warriors received cash of an undocumented amount. The known roster return favors the 76ers; the financial valuation remains uncertain. The former article’s B/F grades were incorrect and have been reconciled to the canonical A/C-minus marks.

sections.heading: Golden State Bought Bernard King Before His Reputation Recovered
sections.body: Golden State acquired Bernard King at a moment when his talent was obvious but his league-wide value had fallen. King had already shown that he could score at a high level, yet his brief Utah tenure was shaped by inconsistency and off-court concerns. The Warriors sent Wayne Cooper and a second-round pick, a modest price for a former top-ten selection with star-level offensive ability. King responded with two productive seasons and an All-Star appearance, restoring both his performance and his trade market. The Warriors accepted reputational risk without sacrificing a premium asset. King rewarded Golden State with 160 regular-season appearances over the next two years and improved from 21.9 to 23.2 points per game. He earned 1982 All-Star and All-NBA Second Team honors. Those are direct Golden State returns; his later New York peak belongs in career context, not the Warriors' own scoring ledger.

sections.heading: Utah Chose a Safer Interior Package
sections.body: The Jazz’s decision had a coherent roster-building logic. Cooper was a young seven-footer who could rebound, defend the interior and occupy center minutes, while the second-round pick added another controllable asset. Utah was a young franchise operating with limited resources and could value dependable size over a volatile scorer. The package offered floor rather than ceiling. That approach deserves more than an automatic failing grade because Cooper became a long NBA player even though most of his best seasons came elsewhere. Cooper actually appeared in 71 Jazz games before his later years with Denver and Portland. The future pick was a 1981 second-rounder, with Ken Green ultimately selected after the right passed through another transaction to Denver. Utah's return included a usable center, but the club did not retain him long enough to gain his later-career value.

sections.heading: King Reestablished Himself as an Elite Scorer
sections.body: King’s Golden State seasons established the decisive value gap. He averaged more than twenty points, attacked efficiently from the wing and became one of the league’s most difficult one-on-one scorers. The Warriors did not become a contender, but King’s production rehabilitated a player whose market had become depressed. That performance created direct on-court value and a new trade asset. The acquisition shows how a rebuilding team can profit by buying talent before reputation and circumstance realign with ability. Golden State obtained two 20-point seasons, plus an unusually valuable second year recognized by All-NBA voters. King gave the Warriors wing scoring that the small Cooper-plus-pick outgoing package could not replace. A transaction grade should distinguish this two-season Warriors performance from his 1984-85 scoring title with the Knicks.

sections.heading: Wayne Cooper Gave the Jazz Limited Return
sections.body: Cooper’s inclusion prevents the Jazz side from being entirely empty. He was a legitimate NBA center, later becoming a productive starter and rebounder for Denver and Portland. In Utah, however, his contribution was brief and did not establish the long-term frontcourt foundation the franchise needed. The difference between career value and value delivered to the acquiring team is important. Utah can receive some credit for identifying a durable player, but it cannot claim the seasons Cooper produced after leaving. Cooper's subsequent NBA longevity is genuine evidence that the Jazz did not acquire a nonplayer. Yet his direct Utah contribution was 71 appearances, and the franchise moved on while King earned an All-Star berth for Golden State. Comparing direct team value rather than career totals is necessary for a defensible C-plus Utah assessment.

sections.heading: The Second-Round Pick Did Not Change the Balance
sections.body: The second-round pick became Ken Green and added little NBA value. Second-round selections are inherently uncertain, so the pick should not be criticized merely because it failed. It did, however, represent the only future upside in Utah’s package beyond Cooper. When that selection did not become a rotation player, the Jazz were left without a meaningful secondary return. The outcome magnified the importance of King’s revival in Golden State. The 1981 second-round claim followed Utah to Denver, where Ken Green became the selection. Green should not be counted as a Jazz player simply because the originating draft pick appeared in this exchange. The Warriors gave up a future selection; the draft record shows that Utah did not turn it into a long-term player on its own roster.

sections.heading: Golden State Turned Two Seasons Into More Asset Value
sections.body: Golden State later traded King to New York in a package centered on Micheal Ray Richardson and a draft pick. That follow-up did not produce another star equal to King’s Knicks peak, but it demonstrates that the Warriors preserved asset value after receiving two productive seasons. King’s performance made him tradable again. The Warriors therefore benefited on the court and retained the ability to reshape the roster. Utah’s return did not produce a comparable continuation. The inherited Warriors A-plus/Jazz C-plus grades fit the realized production and subsequent asset chain better than calling Cooper worthless. Golden State matched a Knicks offer sheet and sent King to New York in October 1982 for Micheal Ray Richardson plus a 1984 fifth-round pick. It then traded Richardson to New Jersey in February 1983 for Sleepy Floyd and Mickey Johnson, further extending the value of the initial acquisition.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win — Golden State A+, Utah C+. Bernard King supplied 160 Warriors games over two seasons, averaged 21.9 and 23.2 points and earned an All-Star selection plus All-NBA Second Team honors in 1982. The Warriors later converted him into Micheal Ray Richardson, and the ensuing Richardson deal brought Sleepy Floyd and Mickey Johnson. Utah got 71 games of Wayne Cooper and a second-round selection that ultimately became Ken Green in Denver. Cooper was a useful center, but his Utah stint did not approach the star production or directly traceable asset chain Golden State received. The A+ rewards both King's impact and the unusually strong follow-up return; the C+ gives the Jazz credit for Cooper's real, if short-lived, contribution.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Bernard King’s Revival Made the Trade a Lesson in Buying Distressed Talent
featuredDeepDive.intro: The transaction shows how reputation, environment and timing can create a temporary gap between a player’s ability and his market price. Golden State did not need to prove that King was risk-free. It needed the upside to exceed the modest cost, and his immediate resurgence did exactly that.

sections.heading: King’s Skill Set Was Too Rare for the Price
sections.body: King’s scoring package was already unusually advanced. He could attack from the mid-post, finish through contact and create efficient offense without relying on a traditional point guard to manufacture every touch. Players with that level of shot creation rarely become available for a center and a second-round pick. Golden State correctly recognized that the discount was larger than the uncertainty. The Warriors did not need King to become a perfect franchise savior for the trade to work. The Warriors' original risk was bounded: one center and a 1981 second-round choice, not another star or an unprotected first. King produced 21.9 points per game in his first Golden State year before an All-Star season at 23.2. Those two years make the success visible without needing to borrow the later 1984-85 Knicks scoring title.

sections.heading: Golden State Provided a Cleaner Offensive Role
sections.body: The Warriors gave King a prominent role and a clearer path to rebuild his standing. Rather than treating him as a secondary option within a confused rotation, Golden State allowed him to function as a primary scorer. That responsibility matched his strengths and produced immediate statistical and market recovery. Environment does not excuse every prior problem, but it can determine whether talent is used coherently. The Warriors created conditions in which King’s value could become visible again. Golden State converted that role into both points and future negotiating leverage. In October 1982 the team matched a Knicks offer sheet, then executed a sign-and-trade for Micheal Ray Richardson and a fifth-round pick. The two years of King production were direct value, while the Richardson trade was a distinct secondary return.

sections.heading: Utah’s Risk Reduction Came With a Severe Ceiling Loss
sections.body: The Jazz reduced volatility, which can be sensible for a young organization. Cooper offered size and the pick offered another low-cost chance, but the return lacked a plausible route to replacing King’s top-end ability. Diversification only works when the components collectively carry enough expected value. In this case, the pieces produced too little for Utah. The decision protected the team from one category of risk while creating another: the risk of selling rare talent at its lowest point. Utah had only 71 Cooper appearances in this particular tenure before his later NBA career unfolded elsewhere. Its 1981 second-round draft right was later exercised by Denver on Ken Green, which limits how much of that asset can be credited as Jazz on-court production. The original trade cannot be evaluated by treating later Nuggets and Knicks games as if they occurred for Utah or Golden State.

sections.heading: King’s Later Knicks Peak Confirms the Talent Was Real
sections.body: King’s later scoring explosion with the Knicks is not direct Warriors value, but it helps explain the original evaluation. His New York peak, including a scoring title and historic playoff performances, demonstrated that the Golden State revival was not a temporary statistical accident. The underlying offensive talent remained elite. The Warriors did not retain him long enough to receive that later peak, so their grade stops at A rather than becoming even higher. Utah cannot be charged with every point King scored elsewhere. King's All-NBA Second Team selection in 1982 predates his departure from the Warriors, while his 1984-85 scoring title happened with New York. That distinction gives Golden State a documented peak of its own without importing his subsequent best scoring year. Utah's error was disposing of his 1980-era talent for a short-term Cooper stint and a future pick.

sections.heading: The Deal Rewarded a Team Willing to Separate Risk From Ability
sections.body: Successful distressed-asset trades require a team to identify which concerns are temporary and which are permanent. Golden State accepted uncertainty but limited the cost, which is the ideal structure for such a bet. If King had failed, the Warriors would have lost a serviceable center and a second-round chance. When he succeeded, the upside was star production. Utah’s return did not contain a similar asymmetry. The trade rewarded the team willing to make a measured wager rather than the team seeking the safest immediate package. There was a verifiable second payoff after the scoring revival. The Warriors' 1982 King-for-Richardson transaction also brought a 1984 fifth-round choice, and the separate February 1983 Richardson-for-Sleepy Floyd/Mickey Johnson deal added two more NBA players. This chain is not equivalent to receiving Floyd directly from Utah, but it demonstrates retained value from King's recovered trade market.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The 1980 deal grades Golden State A+ and Utah C+. King's 160 games and 1982 All-Star/All-NBA season already create a wide gap over Cooper's single Utah season. Golden State then preserved value by exchanging King for Micheal Ray Richardson and later acquiring Sleepy Floyd and Mickey Johnson through that same asset chain. Utah's second-round pick did not turn into a lasting Jazz contributor, although Cooper's 71 appearances deserve credit. The verdict is Warriors Win because both immediate production and attributable later transactions favor Golden State, not because King's subsequent Knicks success can be credited to his former team.

sections.heading: Golden State Received a Starting Guard for One Season
sections.body: On June 8, 1981, Golden State acquired Mike Gale from Portland for second-round picks in 1982 and 1985. Gale was no end-of-bench salary filler: he started 70 of his 75 Warriors games in 1981-82 and averaged 5.6 points, 3.5 assists and 1.6 steals in almost 24 minutes. He supplied a full regular season of experienced guard play. His NBA career ended after that season, however, and Golden State had no second-year benefit or subsequent trade branch to offset the pair of picks it surrendered.

sections.heading: Audie Norris Extended Portland's Return Across Three Seasons
sections.body: Portland used the first incoming pick, No. 37 in 1982, on Audie Norris. Norris played 187 regular-season games for the Trail Blazers over three seasons. He was not a high-volume scorer, and a second-round pick should never be judged as though it promised an All-Star. Nevertheless, three seasons of dependable frontcourt depth were a tangible result from one half of the consideration that Portland received for Gale. Norris alone lasted far longer in Portland than Gale remained in Golden State.

sections.heading: The 1985 Pick Produced a Different Kind of Asset Chain
sections.body: The later second-round pick became No. 25 overall in 1985, used on Mike Smrek. Smrek never suited up for Portland. The team instead moved his rights to Chicago for Ben Coleman and Ken Johnson. Coleman did not appear for the Trail Blazers, but Johnson logged 64 Portland games in 1985-86, averaging 4.1 points and 3.8 rebounds. The Smrek branch thus produced usable NBA minutes without the selected player ever entering Portland's rotation. That is legitimate realized value from the 1981 trade.

sections.heading: Why the Blazers Win Without Treating Gale as a Failure
sections.body: Gale earned a B- for Golden State's one-season starter role, not a failing grade. Portland receives A- for converting two outgoing second-round picks into 187 Norris games and another 64 Johnson games. Those minutes were spread over multiple seasons and two separate asset paths. The difference is material but not the gulf between a franchise cornerstone and a worthless return. This was a productive veteran rental for Golden State and an even better long-term use of picks for Portland.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Blazers Win — Portland A-, Golden State B-. The Warriors obtained 75 games and 70 starts from Mike Gale, a legitimate single-season return. Portland's 1982 second-rounder became Audie Norris, who played 187 games for the Blazers; the 1985 pick became Mike Smrek, whose rights were immediately converted into Ben Coleman and Ken Johnson. Johnson contributed another 64 Portland games. Portland extracted more seasons and two useful branches from the draft consideration, while Gale's NBA career ended after his lone Warriors season.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Audie Norris's 187 Blazers Games and Ken Johnson's 64 From the Mike Gale Picks
featuredDeepDive.intro: Golden State bought a one-season veteran guard in June 1981, giving Portland two future second-round selections for Mike Gale. Gale started 70 of 75 Warriors games in 1981-82, a useful return that ended with his NBA career. Portland's 1982 No. 37 choice yielded Audie Norris for 187 Blazers games, while the 1985 No. 25 Mike Smrek rights were exchanged to Chicago in a separate deal that ultimately yielded 64 Ken Johnson games. Those distinct follow-on paths explain Portland's A-minus against Golden State's B-minus without pretending Gale contributed nothing or that Smrek himself played for Portland.

sections.heading: The Risk Golden State Accepted
sections.body: Golden State did not trade a first-rounder or a star for Gale; it gave up second-round selections in 1982 and 1985. That made the deal reasonable on trade day. A veteran with ABA and NBA experience filled a guard need immediately, started 70 games and helped provide defensive pressure. The risk was duration. The 1981-82 season became Gale's last in the league, and Golden State possessed neither his rights as a future trade chip nor the picks that could have supplied replacements.

sections.heading: Why Norris Is the Core of Portland's Case
sections.body: Audie Norris was drafted at No. 37 in 1982 using the earlier pick. His 187 Portland games across three seasons are the strongest direct result. He was a rotation forward rather than a transformed franchise centerpiece, so his value should be described as continuity and frontcourt depth. Counting those appearances gives Portland more durable realized production than the one-year Gale rental without inventing any star-level impact that Norris never had.

sections.heading: How the Smrek Selection Became Ken Johnson
sections.body: The 1985 pick came later and was used on Mike Smrek at No. 25. Portland immediately traded Smrek's draft rights to Chicago for Ben Coleman and Ken Johnson. Coleman did not appear for Portland, but Johnson played 64 games in 1985-86. Evaluating this trade only by Smrek's zero Blazers appearances would erase the consequence of trading his rights. Conversely, attributing unrelated later successes to the branch would overstate it. Johnson's identifiable tenure is the defensible downstream credit.

sections.heading: The Grades Respect Both Timelines
sections.body: Golden State's B- recognizes a real 75-game, 70-start season from Gale. Portland's A- reflects the longer useful reach of two picks: 187 games from Norris and 64 from Johnson. The gap is moderate rather than absolute. The Blazers received two assets that generated more regular-season service, while Golden State knowingly prioritized immediate veteran minutes. Looking at the full traceable return, Portland's package wins.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Blazers Win, Portland A- and Golden State B-. Gale delivered the steady starting season the Warriors sought but no lasting return. Portland transformed the 1982 and 1985 second-rounders into 187 games of Audie Norris plus a 64-game Ken Johnson branch through the Mike Smrek rights exchange. The judgment rewards attributable outcomes without treating second-round draft picks as guaranteed stars or dismissing Gale's useful season.

sections.heading: New York Acquired Bernard King Before His Best Seasons
sections.body: The Knicks obtained Bernard King from Golden State in October 1982 for Micheal Ray Richardson and a 1984 fifth-round pick. King had already been an All-Star and an explosive scorer, but his greatest NBA seasons were still ahead. New York was not paying for a completed peak. It acquired a 25-year-old forward whose power, touch and transition scoring could become the center of the offense. That age-and-upside combination distinguishes the deal from veteran name recognition and explains why the return grew so quickly.

sections.heading: King Became a Playoff Offense by Himself
sections.body: King averaged 21.9 points in his first Knicks season, 26.3 in his second and a league-leading 32.9 in 1984-85 before injury. His 1984 playoff run produced back-to-back 40-point games against Detroit and pushed Boston to seven games. Opponents knew where the ball was going and still struggled to stop his post seals, baseline drives and quick release. The trade gave New York more than an All-Star scorer; it gave the franchise a player capable of carrying an entire postseason attack against elite competition.

sections.heading: The Christmas Day Performances Became Part of the Franchise Memory
sections.body: King scored 60 points against New Jersey on Christmas Day 1984, then an NBA holiday record. One year earlier, he had scored 50 on Christmas against the same opponent. Those games matter because they capture the scale of his New York peak and the cultural resonance of acquiring him. The Knicks did not win a championship during his tenure, but the trade produced some of the most enduring individual performances in Madison Square Garden history. Franchise value includes those era-defining peaks when they are supported by elite team impact.

sections.heading: The Knee Injury Ended the Peak Without Invalidating the Acquisition
sections.body: King suffered a devastating knee injury in March 1985 after averaging nearly 33 points. He missed all of the next season and most of the following one before continuing his career elsewhere. Hindsight grading should not treat an injury as proof that the original transaction was poor when the team had already received multiple elite seasons and historic playoff production. The injury limited duration and championship opportunity, but it did not transfer value back to Golden State. New York had already captured the trade's decisive return.

sections.heading: Richardson Was Talented but Did Not Stabilize Golden State
sections.body: Micheal Ray Richardson had been an All-Star, led the league in assists and steals and possessed rare two-way guard talent. That background means Golden State's return was not valueless on trade day. His Warriors tenure lasted only one season before he was traded to New Jersey, and substance-abuse problems later ended his NBA career. The fifth-round pick became Scott McCollum and produced no meaningful NBA value. D is more accurate than F because Richardson was a real asset; the short tenure and absent downstream return keep the grade low.

sections.heading: The Verdict Should Explicitly Name the Knicks
sections.body: King's Knicks peak included two All-Star selections, a scoring title pace, unforgettable playoff series and a 60-point Garden performance. Golden State received one Richardson season and no meaningful value from the draft pick. The existing A+ for New York remains correct, while the Warriors should rise modestly from F to D to acknowledge Richardson's established ability. Partner Win should become Knicks Win so the record aligns directly with the grades and realized outcome.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: New York wins with an A+, while Golden State rises to D. King delivered the best seasons of his career, carried the Knicks through a memorable 1984 postseason and produced some of the most iconic scoring performances in franchise history before his knee injury. Richardson was a high-level talent and prevents the return from being described as nothing, but he lasted one Warriors season and the fifth-round pick added no significant value. The outcome is decisively Knicks Win.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Bernard King Gave the Knicks an Offensive Identity at the Exact Moment They Needed One
featuredDeepDive.intro: The Knicks of the early 1980s were searching for a star who could make difficult offense reliable. King arrived with elite scoring traits but without the full reputation he would build in New York. The trade worked because his physical style translated perfectly to Madison Square Garden and playoff basketball. He could establish position before the defense loaded, finish through contact and score quickly from the baseline. For a short, brilliant peak, the Knicks possessed one of the league's least solvable players.

sections.heading: Golden State Matched the Offer and Chose a Sign-and-Trade Exit
sections.body: King had signed an offer with New York, and the Warriors exercised their right of first refusal before trading him. That sequence gave Golden State leverage to recover an established guard rather than lose King outright. Richardson's résumé made the decision understandable. He had led the league in assists and steals and had been an All-Star. The mistake was not taking an obviously worthless player; it was accepting a volatile asset and a negligible pick without creating protection against the possibility that King was entering a higher tier.

sections.heading: King’s Scoring Was Built for the Possessions Playoffs Create
sections.body: He did not depend on open transition lanes or a high volume of three-pointers. King sprinted into early post position, attacked from the mid-post and elevated before double-teams could settle. Those skills became more valuable as playoff games slowed. In 1984 he averaged more than 34 points across twelve postseason games, overcoming finger injuries and heavy defensive attention. That run is one of the strongest pieces of realized trade value because it demonstrated that his regular-season scoring could become even more forceful under postseason pressure.

sections.heading: The Boston Series Elevated a Good Knicks Team Into a Threat
sections.body: New York pushed the eventual champion Celtics to seven games in the 1984 Eastern Conference semifinals. Boston possessed Bird, McHale, Parish and a deep championship roster, yet King's scoring repeatedly kept the Knicks alive. The series did not end with a title, but it established a credible ceiling around the acquired star. Trade grading should reward the ability to make a team dangerous against a historically great opponent, especially when the incoming package cost no future first-rounder or young cornerstone.

sections.heading: The Injury Creates a Duration Debate, Not a Winner Debate
sections.body: King's major knee injury shortened what might have been a longer Knicks prime. That limitation separates the trade from acquisitions that produced a decade of contention. It does not make the sides comparable. Golden State never received an equivalent peak from Richardson or the pick, and King's elite years were already delivered before the injury. A+ can still be justified because the acquisition price was modest and the ceiling extraordinary. The grade reflects value per asset surrendered, not only the number of healthy seasons.

sections.heading: Richardson’s Later Story Shows Why Risk Must Be Priced
sections.body: Richardson was traded from Golden State to New Jersey after one season and later banned by the NBA for repeated drug-policy violations. Those later events were not fully predictable, and the Warriors should not be graded as though they knowingly acquired no value. They are relevant to realized outcome. The organization accepted substantial personal and availability risk without securing a premium pick alongside him. New York received the healthier, younger scoring star and captured his best years. The D acknowledges the initial talent while recognizing the result.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Knicks Win verdict rests on elite peak value at a low acquisition cost. King became a devastating playoff scorer, produced a 60-point Christmas performance and gave New York a genuine offensive centerpiece. The knee injury reduced the tenure but did not undo what had already been realized. Golden State's return included a talented former All-Star, which supports D rather than F, yet Richardson's one-season stay and the empty fifth-round pick left the Warriors without a durable counterweight.

sections.heading: Houston Chose Availability Over the Last Image of the Twin Towers
sections.body: The Rockets were only eighteen months removed from an NBA Finals appearance built around Hakeem Olajuwon and Ralph Sampson, so moving Sampson required separating his reputation from his condition in December 1987. He was a former No. 1 pick, Rookie of the Year, four-time All-Star and the author of the shot that eliminated the Lakers in the 1986 Western Conference finals. He was also dealing with knee trouble, diminished mobility and a deteriorating relationship with coach Bill Fitch. Houston therefore treated the trade as a health-and-function decision rather than a referendum on Sampson’s peak. Joe Barry Carroll gave the Rockets a center who could absorb regular-season minutes beside Olajuwon, while Sleepy Floyd supplied another experienced ballhandler and scorer. The incoming names lacked Sampson’s theoretical ceiling, but they were more likely to be available and useful immediately. Houston surrendered the most famous player in the deal while protecting the competitive years it still had with Olajuwon.

sections.heading: Golden State Bought the Ceiling That Houston No Longer Trusted
sections.body: Golden State’s logic was understandable because distressed stars are rarely available without an obvious defect. The Warriors had already experienced the limitations of building around Carroll and Floyd, and Sampson offered the possibility of changing the franchise’s status in a single move. At seven-foot-four with guard-like coordination, he could score, pass and run in ways that fit Don Nelson’s preference for unconventional lineups. Steve Harris added a young guard to the return, but the transaction was fundamentally a wager that Sampson’s body would stabilize outside Houston. The Warriors were not giving away empty contracts: Floyd had been an All-Star and one of the league’s most explosive scoring guards, while Carroll remained a productive starting center. Golden State accepted a large reduction in dependable depth because healthy Sampson represented a rarer archetype than either outgoing player. The gamble failed not because the upside was imaginary, but because the medical downside controlled nearly everything that followed.

sections.heading: The Immediate Rotation Math Favored the Rockets
sections.body: Houston replaced one compromised star with two established rotation players and cash. Floyd became a long-term backcourt contributor, capable of initiating offense or attacking as a secondary scorer, and he remained with the Rockets into the 1990s. Carroll’s Houston stay was shorter, yet he provided useful scoring and size during a period when the club needed to keep Olajuwon from carrying every interior responsibility. The Rockets did not recreate the 1986 Finals formula, but they preserved playoff-level competence and avoided tying their near future to Sampson’s rehabilitation. Golden State, meanwhile, lost the combined shot creation and minutes supplied by Carroll and Floyd. Sampson could not replace that volume consistently because injuries limited both his availability and his effectiveness. A two-for-one trade can work when the incoming star consolidates production at a higher level; here, the supposed star side delivered fewer dependable possessions. The practical nightly value moved toward Houston even before the long-term verdict became obvious.

sections.heading: Sampson’s Injuries Turned the Upside Bet Into Dead Weight
sections.body: The decisive fact is that Golden State never received a sustained healthy version of Sampson. His knees had already altered his game before the trade, and the Warriors could not reverse that trajectory. He appeared in only a limited portion of the remaining 1987-88 schedule, never regained his Houston mobility and was no longer an All-Star-level force. The next season provided more games but not a return to dominance, and Golden State eventually moved him again. The organization had paid with two proven starters for a rehabilitation project whose contract, reputation and positional needs demanded patience. Because Sampson’s decline was medically visible at the time, hindsight does not create the entire criticism; it magnifies a risk Houston had already decided was unacceptable. Golden State deserves some credit for pursuing a ceiling unavailable through normal roster building, but the cost required a far stronger probability of recovery. Once the health bet failed, there was no secondary asset in the package capable of preserving value.

sections.heading: Floyd Supplied the Most Durable Post-Trade Value
sections.body: Sleepy Floyd was not the centerpiece in public discussion, yet he became the transaction’s most durable contributor. Houston gained a veteran guard who could create offense, play beside different backcourt partners and remain useful as the roster evolved around Olajuwon. His presence did not produce a championship, and the Rockets eventually moved toward a different supporting cast, but several seasons of credible guard play mattered more than Sampson’s abbreviated Golden State tenure. Carroll also prevented the return from being a one-player bet. Even if his fit and reputation were imperfect, Houston received a known scorer rather than a distant pick or speculative prospect. That distinction separates the trade from a pure salary dump: the Rockets converted uncertain star equity into actual NBA minutes. Golden State received the most celebrated name but the least reliable stream of production. When a trade is graded by realized value, the useful years accumulated by Floyd are central rather than incidental.

sections.heading: The Grades Reflect Risk Allocation, Not a Rewrite of Sampson’s Greatness
sections.body: A Rockets win does not mean Sampson lacked historic talent or that Golden State was irrational to investigate the opportunity. It means Houston correctly identified which side should carry the medical risk. The Rockets earn an A-minus because they obtained two established players, improved lineup reliability and moved on before Sampson’s injuries erased most of his remaining value. The grade stops short of A-plus because neither Carroll nor Floyd became the missing piece of another Finals run, and Houston did not convert the trade into a title. Golden State receives a D because the club surrendered two productive players and cash for a star whose physical decline was already a major part of the evaluation. The Warriors’ ceiling case was real enough to avoid an F, but the realized return was brief, diminished and difficult to build around. The trade’s lesson is not to avoid injured stars; it is to price the probability of recovery with much greater discipline.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win. Houston moved Ralph Sampson before his health decline consumed the remaining value of his contract and received usable seasons from Sleepy Floyd plus short-term help from Joe Barry Carroll. Golden State bought a spectacular theoretical ceiling but paid with two proven starters and never saw a healthy version of the player it acquired. The grades are Houston A-minus and Golden State D.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: How the Sampson Trade Ended One Houston Era and Exposed Golden State’s Desperation
featuredDeepDive.intro: The deal is often reduced to a simple injury story, but it also captured two franchises making opposite organizational decisions. Houston chose to narrow its identity around Olajuwon and dependable supporting pieces. Golden State chose volatility because ordinary roster maintenance had not created a contender. The contrast explains why the same transaction could feel bold on one side and necessary on the other.

sections.heading: The Twin Towers Had Already Reached a Height Few Experiments Ever Touch
sections.body: Sampson and Olajuwon were not a failed concept from the beginning. Together they helped Houston upset the defending conference champion Lakers and reach the 1986 Finals, proving that two elite big men could share the floor at the highest level. Sampson’s perimeter skill and passing allowed Olajuwon to occupy the interior without reducing the offense to static post-ups. That success made the eventual breakup emotionally difficult and encouraged Golden State to believe the original version of Sampson might still be recoverable. Yet the Rockets were evaluating the player in front of them, not the memory of the 1986 run. Knee injuries had changed his movement, and tension with Fitch added organizational strain. The previous peak made Sampson famous enough to command a meaningful return, but it also risked disguising how much the situation had changed. Houston’s advantage came from recognizing the gap between the established résumé and the likely future.

sections.heading: Golden State Needed a Transformational Story After Years of Instability
sections.body: The Warriors had not developed a stable contender around Carroll and Floyd. Both players produced, but the team remained outside the league’s upper tier, and the organization had repeatedly searched for a defining star. Sampson offered more than basketball value; he offered a new narrative. A healthy former No. 1 pick could sell hope, alter matchups and make Golden State relevant in a way that incremental additions could not. That context helps explain why the Warriors accepted an uneven availability profile. Franchises trapped in mediocrity often pay for the possibility of escape because another forty-win projection has little appeal. The problem is that desperation can turn a medical discount into an illusion. Golden State was not acquiring Sampson at a low cost merely because his market had fallen. It was still giving up two starters whose combined production created a substantial floor. The Warriors purchased the story of a comeback without enough protection against the much more probable outcome.

sections.heading: Houston’s Return Was Better as a Portfolio Than as a Headline
sections.body: Neither Floyd nor Carroll carried Sampson’s celebrity, but together they spread the risk across positions and roles. Floyd could handle the ball, score in bursts and reduce the pressure on Houston’s other guards. Carroll could play center minutes, score from the frontcourt and allow Olajuwon to move between matchups. Cash added a small financial benefit. A portfolio return is especially valuable when the outgoing asset has a binary health profile: one setback can erase the star’s contribution, while two established players are less likely to fail simultaneously. Houston did not maximize future draft control or obtain another cornerstone, so the return was not flawless. It was, however, constructed for continuity. The Rockets could keep competing while adjusting the roster later. That flexibility contrasts with Golden State’s dependence on Sampson becoming something close to his previous self. One side diversified; the other concentrated nearly all of the transaction’s value in a damaged body.

sections.heading: The Trade Foreshadowed Houston’s Full Commitment to Olajuwon
sections.body: Moving Sampson clarified the hierarchy of the franchise. Olajuwon became the unquestioned interior centerpiece, and future decisions could be judged by how well they supported his defense, post scoring and durability. That clarity did not immediately produce a second Finals appearance, but it reduced the structural ambiguity of the roster. Houston no longer needed to preserve a two-center identity or allocate major resources around the possibility that Sampson might recover. Floyd’s guard play was useful precisely because it complemented rather than competed with Olajuwon’s role. Over time, the Rockets would continue reshaping the supporting cast until championship-level combinations emerged in the mid-1990s. The 1987 trade should not receive direct credit for those later titles, but it belongs in the sequence of decisions that established whose timeline mattered. Houston chose its healthier superstar and converted the other into pieces that could function around him.

sections.heading: Realized Value Makes the Verdict Clearer Than the Original Debate
sections.body: At the moment of the trade, observers could reasonably disagree about whether Golden State had stolen a superstar or Houston had escaped a worsening problem. Years later, the uncertainty disappeared. Sampson’s Warriors tenure was short and injury-limited. Floyd supplied Houston with several useful seasons, and Carroll offered immediate production before moving on. The Rockets did not need either incoming player to equal Sampson’s peak; they only needed the pair to exceed the diminished future Golden State actually received. They did. This is why retrospective grading must distinguish between peak reputation and post-trade contribution. Sampson remains the greatest talent in the transaction, but the Rockets owned his best years before the exchange. Golden State acquired the name after the value curve had already turned. The D and A-minus grades capture that timing difference without pretending the original decision was free of uncertainty.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Houston won by transferring the injury risk at the moment it became more important than Sampson’s résumé. Floyd and Carroll gave the Rockets a usable floor; Sampson gave Golden State only a brief and diminished glimpse of the ceiling it imagined. The transaction ended the Twin Towers era, but it also preserved Houston’s ability to keep building around the healthier tower.

sections.heading: Golden State Bought a Center with a First
sections.body: Golden State acquired Alton Lister from the Seattle SuperSonics on August 7, 1989. The consideration was the Warriors' 1990 first-round draft pick, so the club took a known center in exchange for a selection whose precise position would not be determined until the following year's lottery. The deal was far riskier in hindsight than a generic late first-rounder-for-reserve swap: the pick ultimately landed at No. 2, an exceptionally valuable opportunity for Seattle. That actual draft position is critical to assessing the package rather than guessing which player Golden State would have chosen.

sections.heading: Seattle Used No. 2 on Gary Payton
sections.body: The pick became the second overall selection in the 1990 NBA draft. Seattle chose Gary Payton, who went on to spend thirteen seasons with the SuperSonics and became the team's defining perimeter defender and star point guard. Payton's tenure was direct Seattle production from the acquired selection, not value earned by a different franchise many years later. Lister supplied Golden State with a playable veteran big man, but the gap between his tenure and the star Seattle obtained from that exact pick is unusually wide.

sections.heading: The Lottery Result Changed the Scale
sections.body: The trade should be judged using the realized No. 2 selection while acknowledging that the Warriors did not know the final draft position in August 1989. That uncertainty explains the original risk but doesn't erase the outcome. Seattle converted the future asset into an enduring franchise player, while Golden State obtained a veteran center who could not match that return. This is an example of a seemingly serviceable immediate acquisition becoming extremely costly once the transferred pick reaches the top of the draft.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: SuperSonics Win. Seattle's A+ reflects the No. 2 pick that became Gary Payton and his thirteen seasons with the franchise. Golden State's F reflects surrendering that premium result for Alton Lister. The lottery position was uncertain when the deal was signed, but the completed exchange produced an overwhelming realized Seattle advantage.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: How the Alton Lister Trade Delivered Gary Payton to Seattle
featuredDeepDive.intro: Golden State returned Seattle's 1990 first-round pick to the SuperSonics on August 7, 1989 for center Alton Lister. The Warriors had first obtained that Seattle-origin right six weeks earlier by exchanging the 1989 pick Seattle used on Dana Barros. Lister produced 126 Golden State regular-season appearances over four seasons, while Seattle used the restored 1990 first at No. 2 on Gary Payton. Payton played 13 seasons as a SuperSonic, led a 64-win 1996 Finals team and earned the 1995-96 Defensive Player of the Year award.

sections.heading: June 1989 Pick Swap Explains Seattle Getting Its Own First Back
sections.body: The first-round selection Golden State surrendered in August had already changed hands once. On June 27, 1989 the Warriors sent the first-round choice that Seattle used at No. 16 on Dana Barros to the SuperSonics for Seattle's 1990 first. Six weeks later, on August 7, Golden State returned that 1990 first to Seattle to acquire veteran center Alton Lister. Thus the 1990 draft right moved Seattle-to-Golden State-to-Seattle across two separate trades, not an original Warriors first that happened to become the second overall pick. The league and both team transaction ledgers document those dates. Golden State was buying known immediate interior depth, while Seattle regained control of its own upcoming first and preserved future lottery upside.

sections.heading: Golden State Actually Received 126 Lister Regular-Season Games
sections.body: Lister was not an empty trade asset, even though his Warriors stay began with injury-related limitations. He appeared in three Golden State regular-season games during 1989-90. His healthiest Warriors season came in 1990-91: 77 appearances, 65 starts and averages of 6.4 points, 6.3 rebounds and 1.2 blocks. He added 26 appearances in 1991-92 and 20 in 1992-93, producing 126 regular-season Warriors games over four seasons in the club's record. Those figures represent the center value Golden State bought with a future pick. They do not make him the franchise player that the reacquired selection produced for Seattle. Lister's earlier SuperSonics years and later Milwaukee appearances belong to those other receiving clubs, not to this Golden State return.

sections.heading: Seattle Used No. 2 in 1990 to Select Gary Payton
sections.body: The lottery gave Seattle the second overall selection in 1990, and the SuperSonics took Oregon State guard Gary Payton. That result was not known in August 1989 when Golden State traded away the future right. Payton played 13 seasons in Seattle, became a nine-time All-Star, earned the 1995-96 Defensive Player of the Year award and helped the Sonics reach the NBA Finals in that same season. The 1996 club won 64 regular-season games before losing the Finals to Michael Jordan's Chicago Bulls. Those are Seattle achievements tied directly to the draft choice received for Lister. Payton later played for Milwaukee, the Lakers, Boston and Miami, but his 2006 Heat championship and other post-Seattle NBA seasons are separate accomplishments, not additional Sonics playing time from this deal.

sections.heading: A Healthy 1990-91 Lister Season Cannot Offset 13 Payton Years
sections.body: The two teams received returns on very different horizons. Golden State got a veteran big whose first season yielded just three appearances, followed by 77 games and 65 starts during 1990-91. Payton immediately played all 82 Seattle games as a rookie in 1990-91 and grew into the club's defensive identity, playmaking engine and 1990s contender. One season of dependable Lister rebounding and rim protection was real value, but it was not comparable with 13 seasons of high-level Payton service. The relative outcome explains the recorded Seattle A-plus and Golden State F without claiming that the Warriors expected a No. 2 pick on the day they made the trade. Evaluating only the pick's anticipated summer 1989 value would miss the immense documented payoff.

sections.heading: The Finals Run Was Seattle's, Not an Oklahoma City Achievement
sections.body: Payton and Shawn Kemp formed the SuperSonics core that reached the 1996 NBA Finals after 64 regular-season victories. Payton's nine All-Star selections, defensive award and long Seattle tenure became symbols of the club's identity well before its eventual relocation to Oklahoma City. The archive uses the successor Oklahoma City Thunder franchise key for historical Sonics transactions, but the games, standings and title opportunities in this trade belong to Seattle. Golden State got 126 Lister regular-season appearances and a temporary center role; Seattle obtained Payton at No. 2 with the reacquired future selection. Both original dates also matter: the June Barros pick swap was a separate transaction, while the August Lister exchange is the trade being graded. The legacy SuperSonics Win conclusion rests on those actual asset paths and club-specific results.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: SuperSonics Win — Seattle A-plus versus Golden State F as archived. The Warriors received 126 Lister regular-season games, including 77 appearances and 65 starts in 1990-91. Seattle converted its own reacquired 1990 first into No. 2 Gary Payton, a thirteen-season Sonics cornerstone and leader of the 1996 Finals team. The earlier June 1989 first-round choice swap was a separate deal; Payton's later Miami title and Oklahoma City years are not Seattle achievements.

sections.heading: Golden State Exchanged Shot Blocking for the 1991 First-Round Pick
sections.body: On August 1, 1990, Golden State sent 7-foot-7 center Manute Bol to Philadelphia for the 76ers' 1991 first-round selection. Coach Don Nelson described the move at the time as a way to accumulate draft choices and address the Warriors' need for an all-around center. The Warriors had a second future first-rounder to work with, rather than a guaranteed replacement player immediately. Philadelphia's front office valued Bol's rim protection, which had produced 238 blocked shots across 75 Golden State appearances in 1989-90. Contemporary UPI and Associated Press coverage establish the trade's actual rationale and direction. The agreement did not move Chris Gatling as a contracted player: the pick acquired in August 1990 was not used until June 1991, when Golden State selected him at No. 16.

sections.heading: Gatling Played 311 Golden State Games Before Moving On
sections.body: The 1991 first-round choice became Chris Gatling, a productive reserve forward and center in Golden State. He appeared in 54 Warriors games during 1991-92, 70 in 1992-93, 82 in 1993-94 and 58 in 1994-95. Those first four seasons totaled 264 games; he added 47 Golden State appearances in 1995-96 before being moved during that season, bringing his direct Warriors total to 311. His production climbed to 13.7 points and 7.6 rebounds in 1994-95, following averages of 5.7, 9.3 and 8.2 points in the preceding three years. That is real value from the draft right Golden State acquired. Gatling's subsequent NBA All-Star selection and production with other franchises cannot all be credited to the Warriors' 1990 trade.

sections.heading: Bol Provided Philadelphia with Three Seasons of Rim Protection
sections.body: Bol was hardly an unused asset for Philadelphia. He played all 82 games in 1990-91 and blocked 247 shots, then appeared in 71 games with 199 blocks the following season. In 1992-93 he played another 58 regular-season games with 121 blocks, giving the Sixers 211 appearances and 567 blocks over his first three Philadelphia seasons. His value was specialized defense rather than high scoring, which helps explain why a simple comparison of points per game would be misleading. The 76ers gained an established veteran immediately, while the Warriors accepted a one-season wait followed by uncertainty about a rookie's development. Bol's brief later return to Philadelphia in 1993-94 is separate from the first uninterrupted stay and should not be double-counted as a new trade acquisition.

sections.heading: Why the Recorded B Versus C+ Is a Narrow Warriors Advantage
sections.body: The archived Warriors Win verdict and B/C+ grades are plausible when limited to actual franchise outcomes: Gatling supplied 311 Golden State appearances and eventually developed into a strong scoring and rebounding reserve, while Bol contributed 211 games and a substantial shot-blocking total in three Philadelphia seasons. Both sides received something tangible. The draft pick was a long-term roster resource for Golden State, and Philadelphia's defensive need was immediate. Neither Bol's earlier Warriors seasons nor Gatling's later All-Star career after Golden State should inflate one side's return. The narrow half-step grade advantage does not imply Philadelphia was left with nothing, nor does it require assigning any unrelated pick or player to the exchange. The original 1991 No. 16 selection is the entire incoming Golden State draft asset.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win — Golden State B, Philadelphia C+. The Warriors converted the 1991 first-rounder acquired for Manute Bol into Chris Gatling at No. 16; he played 311 actual Golden State games and averaged 13.7 points in 1994-95. Philadelphia received 211 Bol appearances and 567 blocks in his first three 76ers seasons. Both franchises benefited in different ways, but Gatling's longer productive Warriors run supports the narrow archived grade edge without borrowing his later All-Star seasons elsewhere.

sections.heading: A No. 43 Draft Right Became Two Future Second-Round Picks
sections.body: On the night of the 1991 NBA draft, Golden State traded the rights to No. 43 pick Lamont Strothers to Portland for the Blazers' second-round selections in 1995 and 1999. The Warriors' official historical media guide confirms the exchange, and both clubs' transaction histories identify its later picks: No. 47 Tyus Edney in 1995 and No. 56 Tim Young in 1999. That notation describes where the draft assets ultimately landed, not a promise that Golden State later employed both players. The original transaction was a deliberate move from a single immediate late-round prospect to two distant chances. Portland preferred a guard it could try immediately, while Golden State accepted the uncertainty and possible resale value of future draft capital.

sections.heading: Golden State Moved the Edney-Origin Pick to Sacramento in November
sections.body: The first of those distant seconds became part of a separate, much larger trade only four months later. On November 1, 1991, the Warriors sent Sacramento the Portland-origin 1995 pick together with Mitch Richmond and Les Jepsen for the draft rights to Billy Owens. Sacramento retained that second-round pick and eventually selected UCLA guard Tyus Edney at No. 47 in 1995. Edney's NBA minutes were Kings minutes, not a Warriors return from Strothers. The 1991 Portland transaction created an asset Golden State could spend, but Owens cannot be credited wholly to the pick because Richmond and Jepsen were also substantial outgoing considerations. The Warriors' own archival media guide explicitly lists the November Billy Owens package and the provenance of Portland's second.

sections.heading: The 1999 Second Finally Produced Tim Young’s 25 Warriors Games
sections.body: The second selection stayed on the Golden State draft path through 1999. The Warriors selected Stanford center Tim Young at No. 56, and he appeared in 25 NBA regular-season games for Golden State in 1999-2000. He averaged 2.2 points and 1.4 rebounds in 5.5 minutes, a modest reserve contribution rather than a long-term frontcourt solution. Those 25 games are the directly realized player minutes attributable to one of the two incoming 1991 draft choices. His later career should not be inflated into a durable rotation role, and Edney's separate Sacramento career cannot be added to Young's totals. Even so, two transferable second-round picks provided more flexibility than the original single draft-rights contract would have given the Warriors if they had kept Strothers.

sections.heading: Portland Received Only Four NBA Games from Strothers
sections.body: Strothers signed with Portland and played four NBA games in 1991-92, averaging 2.5 points in 4.3 minutes, then appeared for Dallas the following season. His Dallas appearances were not a Trail Blazers benefit. Portland had surrendered two future seconds for a local look at one late draft pick, and that chance did not develop into a dependable Blazers player. Golden State turned the 1995 selection into part of the Owens trade and made a 1999 pick that yielded a short stint, so there is a supportable Warriors Win in asset flexibility even with a modest direct player return. The inherited B Warriors/C+ Portland spread is less severe than the Golden State source's D- assessment of Portland; that grading discrepancy should be reconciled as editorial judgment without rewriting the verified transaction chain.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win on the inherited Golden State B/Portland C+ scale, with an important attribution limit. Golden State received two future seconds: the 1995 No. 47 pick became part of the multi-asset 1991 Billy Owens deal and was eventually used by Sacramento on Tyus Edney; the 1999 No. 56 pick became Tim Young, who played 25 Warriors games. Portland received four games from Lamont Strothers. Golden State's source-side grade ledger instead gives Portland D-, a discrepancy to reconcile separately. Edney was not a Warrior, and Owens was not purchased by the second-round pick alone.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Deep Dive: Why Golden State Warriors Finished Ahead of Portland Trail Blazers
featuredDeepDive.intro: The June 26, 1991 Warriors-Blazers deal exchanged No. 43 Lamont Strothers' rights for Portland's 1995 and 1999 seconds. Strothers played four Portland NBA games. Golden State sent the eventual No. 47 Tyus Edney right to Sacramento as one part of a separate November 1991 Billy Owens trade, while the No. 56 Tim Young right produced 25 Warriors games in 1999-2000. The difference is future asset flexibility, not imaginary Edney games for Golden State.

sections.heading: Golden State Exchanged a Fresh No. 43 Draft Right for Two Future Seconds
sections.body: On June 26, 1991 Golden State selected Lamont Strothers with the No. 43 pick, then transferred his rights to Portland for the Trail Blazers' second-round selections in 1995 and 1999. The Warriors official media guide confirms the future-year picks, and transaction archives identify their ultimate draft positions as No. 47 Tyus Edney and No. 56 Tim Young. Neither draftee existed as a selected NBA asset in 1991. Portland gained the rights to a college scorer while Golden State deferred its potential return across four and eight years. The original transaction involved only these draft rights and selections, not the November Billy Owens blockbuster that later used one of the Warriors' acquired picks.

sections.heading: No. 47 Became Sacramento's Pick Through a Different Owens Trade
sections.body: Golden State did not ultimately select Tyus Edney. On November 1, 1991, the Warriors sent the Portland-origin 1995 second plus Mitch Richmond and Les Jepsen to Sacramento in return for Billy Owens' draft rights. Sacramento held the transferred selection and used No. 47 on Edney in 1995. His later NBA games were not Golden State games. This is a meaningful conversion of a 1991 Strothers asset into a component of a larger Warriors transaction, but it is not sound to assign Owens' entire Golden State career to that one future second. Sacramento also received an established high-scoring guard in Richmond and another player. The original Golden State-versus-Portland comparison therefore includes pick flexibility but no Edney player production for the Warriors.

sections.heading: No. 56 Gave the Warriors Only Twenty-Five Tim Young Games
sections.body: The other acquired second stayed in the Golden State draft chain until 1999. The Warriors used the No. 56 pick on Stanford center Tim Young, who played 25 regular-season games for them in 1999-2000, never started and averaged 2.2 points with 1.4 rebounds in 5.5 minutes. That modest NBA tenure was the direct Warriors on-court return from one of the two future seconds. The 1995 choice supplied trade consideration rather than Golden State playing time, making it incorrect to add Tyus Edney's Sacramento games to Tim Young's Warriors total. Golden State's original trade cost was the rights to No. 43 Strothers, so this case evaluates a late prospect against two future draft opportunities and their actual destination-specific outcomes.

sections.heading: Strothers Played Four Portland Games, Not a Full Blazers Season
sections.body: Portland signed Lamont Strothers after acquiring his No. 43 rights, but he made only four Blazers regular-season appearances during 1991-92, averaging 2.5 points in 4.3 minutes. He subsequently played for Dallas in a different season; those Mavericks games are not Portland return. Golden State made the stronger asset choice in hindsight because its two seconds eventually became the Owens-deal consideration and a 25-game Warriors center, although that is not equivalent to acquiring Edney or Owens directly through this June transaction. The archived Warriors Win, Golden State B versus Portland C-plus is preserved as an asset-option judgment; the separate source-side Portland D-minus is a grade-ledger contradiction to resolve on its own, not grounds for silent regrading.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The inherited Warriors Win, Golden State B and Portland C-plus are retained. Portland got four games from Strothers. Golden State later bundled the Portland-origin 1995 No. 47 selection with Mitch Richmond and Les Jepsen for Billy Owens' rights, and drafted Tim Young with the remaining 1999 No. 56 choice for 25 Warriors games. The source-perspective archive separately rates Portland D-minus, which requires an explicit independent grade reconciliation. No Tyus Edney Sacramento production or all of Owens' later Warriors service belongs solely to the 1991 pick rights.
