sections.heading: Golden State Chose Stephen Curry’s Future Over Monta Ellis’s Present
sections.body: The 2012 trade is often described as the Andrew Bogut deal, but its first strategic effect was clarifying the Warriors’ backcourt. Monta Ellis was an established high-volume scorer and the most recognizable player on the roster. Stephen Curry was younger, more efficient and more fragile because of recurring ankle injuries. Keeping both had produced defensive and size problems without a clear offensive hierarchy. By moving Ellis, Golden State committed to Curry’s development and created room for Klay Thompson. That decision looked risky enough that fans booed ownership shortly after the trade, yet it became one of the foundational choices of the coming dynasty.

sections.heading: Bogut Supplied the Defensive Position Golden State Could Not Develop Internally
sections.body: Milwaukee sent Bogut while he was recovering from an ankle injury, so the Warriors did not receive immediate production. They received a former No. 1 pick with elite passing instincts, size and rim protection if healthy. Once available, Bogut became the defensive center who could cover mistakes, direct traffic and initiate offense from the high post. His screens created separation for Curry and Thompson, while his passing punished traps and movement defenses. The box score never captured his full influence. Golden State was buying a structural fit, not a conventional scoring star, and that fit became central to the 2015 championship.

sections.heading: Stephen Jackson Was Converted Into Another Championship Piece
sections.body: Jackson did not remain with Golden State after the transaction. The Warriors quickly sent him to San Antonio in a deal that brought Richard Jefferson and a first-round pick, which became Festus Ezeli. Jefferson’s contract was not an obvious prize, but Ezeli developed into a rotation center on the 2015 title team and provided depth when Bogut was unavailable. This secondary conversion strengthened the original return. It did not create a superstar, but it showed that the package contained multiple usable pathways. Milwaukee’s side, by contrast, centered on Ellis’s scoring and Udoh’s defense without producing an equivalent postseason asset chain.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Received Talent but Not a New Competitive Direction
sections.body: Ellis could create shots, attack the rim and carry offensive volume, while Udoh offered defensive energy and Kwame Brown’s expiring contract created financial flexibility. The Bucks were not giving Bogut away. They were moving an injured center for a proven scorer and a recent lottery big. Ellis helped Milwaukee reach the 2013 playoffs, but the team was swept, and he left after the season. Udoh became a useful reserve rather than a core player. The return therefore produced some functional value, which supports a C+, but it did not change the franchise’s ceiling or yield a premium later asset.

sections.heading: The 2015 Championship Validated Both the Player and the Strategic Choice
sections.body: Bogut started at center for a 67-win champion and gave the Warriors a defensive identity that balanced their revolutionary shooting. He did not finish every Finals game because Golden State shifted to smaller lineups, yet that tactical adjustment should not erase his season-long role. The team needed his rim protection, screening and passing to reach the point where versatility became possible. More broadly, Curry’s rise after Ellis departed confirmed that the organization had chosen the correct guard to empower. The trade’s championship value came from both sides of that decision: the center Golden State acquired and the backcourt hierarchy it created.

sections.heading: Warriors Win Remains the Correct documented Ruling
sections.body: The existing A+ for Golden State and C+ for Milwaukee already fit the realized outcomes. Golden State gained a title-starting center, a pick that became another championship rotation player and the roster clarity that allowed Curry and Thompson to become the permanent backcourt. Milwaukee gained a talented scorer and useful pieces but no sustained contender or long-term cornerstone. The deal should not be rewritten as though Ellis lacked ability or Bogut was healthy from day one. Its power lies in organizational fit. Golden State accepted short-term uncertainty to build the structure its best young players needed.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win, with Golden State at A+ and Milwaukee at C+. Bogut became the defensive, screening and passing center of the 2015 champion, while Jackson’s quick rerouting helped produce the pick used on Festus Ezeli. Trading Ellis also ended the backcourt ambiguity and committed the organization to Curry and Thompson. Milwaukee received real scoring and defensive depth, but Ellis’s stay was short and the package did not create comparable long-term value. The championship payoff and strategic clarity make the verdict decisive.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The Bogut Trade Was the Moment Golden State Chose Its Championship Architecture
featuredDeepDive.intro: Golden State’s dynasty is usually explained through draft success, but the roster also required a trade that connected its shooting core to a credible defense. The 2012 exchange accomplished that while forcing the organization to choose Curry over Ellis. Bogut’s injury delayed gratification and made the move deeply unpopular at first. The later result shows why transaction grading must account for role, fit and organizational direction rather than simply comparing scoring averages at the moment of the deal.

sections.heading: The Public Backlash Reflected How Uncertain the Decision Looked
sections.body: Ellis had been loyal, productive and available during difficult Warriors seasons, while Bogut was injured and unable to help immediately. Fans saw a recognizable scorer leave for a center in rehabilitation, and ownership heard that anger during Chris Mullin’s jersey-retirement ceremony. That reaction is part of the trade’s history because it demonstrates that the outcome was not obvious. Golden State’s front office had to trust Curry’s ankles, Thompson’s development and Bogut’s recovery simultaneously. The transaction became a triumph of long-term roster logic over the safer short-term popularity of keeping the established star.

sections.heading: Bogut’s Passing Made the Shooting System Harder to Defend
sections.body: A traditional rim protector could have improved Golden State’s defense, but Bogut offered more. From the elbow and top of the floor, he could find cutters, reverse the ball and free shooters with physical screens. Those skills fit the motion principles that later flourished under Steve Kerr. Opponents could not simply ignore the center when he moved away from the basket because his decisions created layups and open threes. The trade therefore acquired a player whose offensive value was expressed through teammates rather than personal scoring, an ideal complement to a backcourt that already possessed elite shot creation.

sections.heading: The Ellis-Curry Choice Changed the Franchise’s Resource Allocation
sections.body: Once Ellis was gone, Curry had greater control of the offense and the organization could build around his strengths rather than compromise between two small scoring guards. Thompson’s size and defense made him the more natural partner. The Warriors also gained the confidence to invest in wings and versatile forwards instead of continually trying to patch the same backcourt problem. This structural effect cannot be measured as a direct incoming asset, but it belongs in the analysis because the trade was the mechanism that forced the choice. Golden State selected the player and style that eventually transformed the league.

sections.heading: Milwaukee’s Side Was a Floor-Raising Move Without Ceiling Value
sections.body: The Bucks added offense to a team that needed shot creation, and Ellis was capable of winning regular-season games. Pairing him with Brandon Jennings produced speed and volume, but the small backcourt faced many of the same defensive and efficiency concerns Golden State had experienced. The 2013 playoff berth was an outcome, yet the sweep and Ellis’s departure showed the limited durability of the plan. Udoh defended well but did not become a high-end starter. Milwaukee’s C+ recognizes that the return was useful, not catastrophic; it simply lacked the championship leverage created on the other side.

sections.heading: The Trade’s Legacy Is a Lesson in Complementary Value
sections.body: The Warriors did not win because Bogut was better than Ellis at every basketball skill. They won because Bogut’s strengths were scarcer and more complementary to Curry, Thompson and Draymond Green. Trade value is contextual. A lower-scoring player can be more important when he unlocks a system, covers defensive weaknesses and accepts a role that preserves touches for stars. Golden State identified that relationship before its core had proven itself. The A+ grade rewards the front office for acquiring the right kind of value rather than the most obvious individual production.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The evidence-based history reinforces Warriors Win. Golden State received the center who organized its defense, enabled its motion offense and started for the 2015 champion. The secondary Jackson transaction added Ezeli, and Ellis’s departure cleared the path for Curry and Thompson. Milwaukee’s package produced respectable short-term offense but no equivalent core asset or postseason result. The trade became one of the decisions that transformed a losing franchise into a dynasty, which is why the existing A+ and C+ grades should remain.

sections.heading: The Thunder Moved from No. 29 to No. 26 for Roberson
sections.body: On June 27, 2013, Oklahoma City traded draft rights to No. 29 pick Archie Goodwin plus cash considerations to Golden State for No. 26 pick Andre Roberson’s rights. The Thunder’s official draft-night release names every element of that transaction. Golden State had acquired the No. 26 selection earlier in the evening from Minnesota; that preceding arrangement is a different exchange and not part of the Thunder package. Oklahoma City wanted a defensive wing prospect from Colorado with strong rebounding credentials. The Warriors accepted a slightly lower first-round right and financial consideration. The amount of cash is not specified in the primary official release and should not be invented.

sections.heading: Roberson Contributed 302 Thunder Games and 269 Starts
sections.body: Roberson played his first NBA regular-season games for the Thunder in 2013-14 and went on to record 302 appearances and 269 starts with Oklahoma City. His season-by-season Thunder games were 40, 67, 70, 79, 39 and seven. The largest role came in 2016-17, when he started all 79 appearances, averaged 30.1 minutes, 5.1 rebounds and 1.2 steals, and earned NBA All-Defensive Second Team recognition. His major knee injury in January 2018 interrupted that run and cost him the entire 2018-19 season. The defensive contribution was genuine long-term Oklahoma City value even though his scoring average was modest. Five subsequent Brooklyn games were for another franchise and are excluded.

sections.heading: Goodwin’s Warriors Return Was a Right, Not NBA Playing Time
sections.body: Golden State received Archie Goodwin’s draft rights at No. 29 rather than a player already under contract. The club did not field Goodwin in an NBA regular-season game. His NBA career subsequently began with Phoenix, not Golden State, and his later performances with the Suns, Nets or New Orleans do not constitute Warriors receiving-team minutes from this agreement. The Warriors also received the reported cash considerations, a real financial component whose amount cannot be confirmed from Oklahoma City’s draft release. A draft right can still be useful as an asset to reroute, but the original Golden State return should not be inflated into multiple seasons of Goodwin NBA scoring.

sections.heading: The Protected Thunder Win Reflects Defensive Starter Value
sections.body: The ledger’s verdict is Oklahoma City Thunder Win with a B+ for Oklahoma City and D+ for Golden State. Roberson provided 302 Thunder games, 269 starts and an All-Defensive Team season. Golden State acquired a lower draft slot in Goodwin’s rights plus unspecified cash, with zero direct NBA games from Goodwin for the Warriors. The Thunder’s later playoff outcomes depended on many teammates and decisions, not this trade alone. Roberson’s long defensive tenure is nevertheless a much larger demonstrated direct basketball return than Golden State’s acquired player rights produced on its roster. Keeping cash unpriced and preceding draft rights transactions separate supports the inherited assessment without converting a draft-right swap into a false player-for-player career comparison.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The saved Oklahoma City Thunder Win, Thunder B+ and Warriors D+ remain unchanged. Roberson played 302 Thunder regular-season games with 269 starts and made the 2017 All-Defensive Second Team. Golden State received Goodwin’s No. 29 draft rights and unspecified cash, but Goodwin never played a Warriors NBA game. His later other-team career and the Warriors’ separate acquisition of pick 26 are not part of Oklahoma City’s direct playing return.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: 2013 Roberson for Goodwin and Cash: 302 Thunder Games from Pick 26
featuredDeepDive.intro: Oklahoma City moved from the No. 29 to No. 26 draft right on June 27, 2013, acquiring Andre Roberson for Archie Goodwin’s rights and cash. Roberson started 269 of his 302 Thunder regular-season appearances and earned a 2017 All-Defensive Second Team nod. Goodwin never played for Golden State, making this an exchange best assessed through the rights and cash actually received rather than his later Phoenix playing career. The original Thunder Win, Oklahoma City B+ and Warriors D+ are preserved.

sections.heading: The Official Thunder Release Lists Two Rights and Cash
sections.body: Oklahoma City’s 2013 draft release records that it acquired Roberson’s No. 26 rights from Golden State and gave up No. 29 Goodwin rights plus cash considerations. A draft blog explains that the Warriors had obtained No. 26 earlier from Minnesota, after which Oklahoma City moved up three positions. The selection of Steven Adams at No. 12 and Alex Abrines at No. 32 were other Thunder draft decisions, not assets transferred by Golden State under the Roberson agreement. The specified cash had value but the primary release omits a dollar amount, so the editorial treats it as unpriced rather than asserting a round number or a cash balance for either franchise.

sections.heading: A Defensive Starter Emerged by the 2016-17 Season
sections.body: Roberson initially played 40 NBA games with 16 starts in 2013-14. His role expanded to 67 games and 65 starts in 2014-15, 70 starts in 2015-16 and all 79 games started in 2016-17. In that last healthy season he contributed 5.1 rebounds, 1.2 steals and one block per game while defending important opposing scorers. Basketball Reference lists his 2017 All-Defensive Second Team honor and the fifth-place Defensive Player of the Year vote result. The six Thunder playing segments total 302 regular-season appearances, including his seven-game 2019-20 return after injury. His five Brooklyn games in 2020-21 fall outside the Thunder total.

sections.heading: The January 2018 Knee Injury Reduced the Last Two Seasons
sections.body: Roberson’s defensive effectiveness was not matched by uninterrupted availability. He played 39 Oklahoma City games in 2017-18 before a major left patellar tendon injury in January 2018. He missed the entire 2018-19 season, then returned for seven NBA regular-season games in 2019-20. The team had already received more than four full years of development and major starting-lineup defense before that injury, so treating the acquired No. 26 right as worthless due to the ending would disregard 269 documented Thunder starts. His limited later appearances are part of a clear injury chronology, not evidence that the original draft selection generated 2019-20 starter minutes it did not supply.

sections.heading: The Golden State Right Never Became Goodwin Warriors Minutes
sections.body: Goodwin was selected at No. 29 by Oklahoma City and immediately sent to Golden State as part of the Roberson swap. The Warriors did not use Goodwin in any regular-season NBA game; he debuted later for Phoenix after his rights moved elsewhere. That later receiving team’s scoring cannot be attributed to the Warriors merely because Golden State temporarily held the draft right. The cash consideration is an independent financial asset, but without an official amount, an exact dollars-per-game comparison would be invented. The historical Thunder B+ versus Warriors D+ distinguishes actual Oklahoma City defense and starts from a Golden State rights position that yielded no Goodwin Warriors games.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Thunder B+, Warriors D+ and Oklahoma City Thunder Win remain unchanged. The No. 26 Roberson right resulted in 302 Thunder appearances, 269 starts and All-Defensive recognition. The No. 29 Goodwin right supplied no Goodwin Warriors NBA appearances, although Golden State received cash consideration with an unspecified amount. The Warriors’ earlier draft pick source and Goodwin’s eventual Phoenix career are distinct rights movements that do not alter this original June 2013 agreement.

sections.heading: Golden State Reached Nedovic Through Three Separate Draft-Night Trades
sections.body: Golden State's path to the 30th pick was longer than the two-team transaction suggests. On June 27, 2013, the Warriors first obtained No. 26 Andre Roberson's draft rights and guard Malcolm Lee from Minnesota for a future second-rounder and cash. They then sent Roberson's rights to Oklahoma City for No. 29 Archie Goodwin's rights and cash. Only in the last step did Golden State trade Goodwin's rights and Lee to Phoenix for No. 30 Nemanja Nedovic's rights. The Warriors' own media-guide transaction log lays out those three moves separately. For this page, the direct Phoenix return is Goodwin plus Lee, not the pick and cash from Minnesota or the exchange with Oklahoma City. The chain explains why Golden State was willing to consolidate two assets into one target, but it cannot expand the direct Phoenix deal's asset ledger.

sections.heading: Phoenix Received 150 NBA Games from Goodwin, but None from Lee
sections.body: The clearest Phoenix return was Goodwin. Drafted 29th, he appeared in 52 Suns games in 2013-14, 41 in 2014-15 and 57 in 2015-16. Those 150 appearances produced 6.2 points per game over three years. His strongest Suns season was the last, when he averaged 8.9 points before the club waived him in October 2016. Lee, the other acquired player, never appeared in a Suns NBA game. Phoenix included Lee with Marcin Gortat, Shannon Brown and Kendall Marshall in an October 2013 trade to Washington for Emeka Okafor and a protected 2014 first-round pick. That larger package creates an indirect asset connection, not proof that Lee alone generated a first-rounder. Phoenix's tangible outcome from the June rights exchange rests mainly on Goodwin's rotation minutes.

sections.heading: Nedovic's Short NBA Stint Supports the Original Suns Advantage
sections.body: Nedovic joined Golden State as a 2013 first-round prospect, but his NBA role never developed into the return the Warriors hoped for. He played 24 regular-season games in 2013-14, averaging 1.1 points and 0.5 assists in 5.9 minutes, and did not become a contributor to their 2015 title run. That is a much smaller NBA return than Goodwin's 150 Suns appearances, even though neither prospect became a long-term starter. The original Suns Win verdict with Phoenix B and Golden State D+ follows that difference in traceable playing time. Phoenix did not acquire a proven star, and Lee supplied no Suns minutes, so the B should describe a useful but limited draft-night advantage rather than an enormous franchise-altering steal.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Suns Win — Phoenix B, Golden State D+. The Wizards were not part of this June 27 exchange: the Warriors sent Archie Goodwin's rights and Malcolm Lee directly to Phoenix for Nemanja Nedovic's rights. Goodwin played 150 games for the Suns, averaging 6.2 points, while Nedovic's Warriors tenure lasted 24 NBA appearances at 1.1 points. Lee played none for Phoenix, though he was included in a separate October package sent to Washington. Those outcomes favor the Suns without treating that later multi-player trade as a return produced solely by Lee.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Golden State–Phoenix 2013 Draft: Goodwin, Nedovic and the Separate Rights Chain
featuredDeepDive.intro: The 2013 Golden State–Phoenix draft-night swap was not a pick-for-cash shortcut. Golden State traded the rights to No. 29 pick Archie Goodwin and guard Malcolm Lee to Phoenix for the rights to No. 30 pick Nemanja Nedovic. The Warriors had obtained Goodwin's rights from Oklahoma City only after a separate transaction involving Andre Roberson's rights; Lee had arrived in an earlier Minnesota deal. The completed NBA outcomes gave Phoenix 150 games from Goodwin and Golden State 24 from Nedovic. Lee supplied no Phoenix game appearances before his inclusion in a later Washington trade. The Suns Win result and inherited Phoenix B/Golden State D+ ratings are preserved, with the distinction between direct and downstream assets intact.

sections.heading: Golden State Built the No. 30 Rights Chain Across Three Clubs
sections.body: The transaction began outside Phoenix. Golden State obtained Andre Roberson's No. 26 rights and Malcolm Lee from Minnesota, sending a future second-round pick and cash. Then the Warriors converted Roberson's rights into Archie Goodwin's No. 29 rights plus cash from Oklahoma City. The third deal moved Goodwin's rights and Lee to the Suns in exchange for No. 30 Nemanja Nedovic's rights. Golden State's 2016-17 official media guide identifies each date and consideration. Separating the moves prevents an appealing but false claim that the Suns directly received the additional cash Golden State acquired from Oklahoma City. The direct two-team question is whether Goodwin and Lee ultimately delivered more NBA value to Phoenix than Nedovic did to the Warriors. That is different from ranking every move the Golden State front office made on draft night.

sections.heading: Goodwin Earned a Three-Season Suns Role
sections.body: Goodwin became a real Phoenix rotation option, even if his peak was short. As a 19-year-old rookie, he made 52 appearances in 2013-14. He played 41 more games in 2014-15, then took on a larger workload with 57 games, 13 starts and 8.9 points per game in 2015-16. Across his Suns tenure, that adds up to 150 regular-season games and a 6.2-point scoring average. Phoenix's own October 24, 2016 waiver announcement verifies both numbers and his departure after three seasons. It is fair to describe the No. 29 right as a measurable return from the June 2013 exchange, but not to suggest that Goodwin developed into a Suns franchise cornerstone. The B grade captures the advantage over the other side, not a claim that the selection produced a star.

sections.heading: Lee Never Played for Phoenix and Later Traveled in a Larger Trade
sections.body: Malcolm Lee was an actual second asset in the Phoenix package, but not a second source of Suns playing time. Basketball-Reference shows his previous NBA seasons with Minnesota and a subsequent 2014-15 appearance for Philadelphia, with none for Phoenix. On October 25, 2013, the Suns included Lee, Marcin Gortat, Shannon Brown and Kendall Marshall in a Washington transaction that returned Emeka Okafor and a protected 2014 first-rounder. That later pick was part of the compensation for a four-player package. It would be misleading to count it as if Lee alone, acquired in the Nedovic trade, yielded a first-round selection. The more careful ledger credits Phoenix with control of Lee's contract and his presence in that separate package, while acknowledging that the identifiable basketball production came from Goodwin.

sections.heading: Nedovic's 24 Warriors Games Make the Outcome Uneven
sections.body: Golden State's targeted prospect received only a brief NBA opportunity. Nedovic made 24 Warriors regular-season appearances in 2013-14 and averaged 5.9 minutes and 1.1 points. He was not a member of the Warriors' later 2014-15 championship rotation, so that title cannot be attached to the 2013 rights exchange. The club was chasing one prospect it preferred to two incoming Phoenix assets, a defensible developmental idea on draft night. Hindsight is less flattering because Goodwin furnished a three-season NBA contribution for the Suns. Nor was Goodwin's career long enough to justify treating the deal as a decisive franchise turning point. The Suns' B and Warriors' D+ preserve the inherited relative judgment while keeping each team's realized role and the boundaries of the trade documented.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Phoenix won this narrowly scoped June 2013 rights exchange on actual NBA output. Goodwin's 150 Suns appearances and 6.2 points per game outweighed Nedovic's 24 Warriors games and 1.1 points, while Lee logged no Suns minutes. Golden State had first acquired the outgoing pieces through separate Minnesota and Oklahoma City moves; Phoenix later included Lee in a multi-player Washington transaction. Neither surrounding deal adds a second direct Phoenix return to this ledger. The published grades stay Phoenix B and Golden State D+, with the Suns Win verdict tied to these verified outcomes rather than generic draft-night hindsight.

sections.heading: Golden State Refused to Let Durant Leave for Nothing
sections.body: Kevin Durant had chosen Brooklyn, and Golden State’s championship partnership with him was ending. The Warriors could have lost an unrestricted free agent without receiving a replacement asset. Instead, they negotiated a sign-and-trade that brought D’Angelo Russell, Shabazz Napier, Treveon Graham and a trade exception, while sending Durant and a conditional 2020 first-rounder to the Nets. The protected first did not convey, and Brooklyn instead received the 2025 second-round pick ultimately used at No. 48 on Javon Small. Russell was an imperfect fit beside Stephen Curry and the injured Klay Thompson, but he preserved a maximum-salary asset slot that the capped-out Warriors could not recreate in ordinary free agency. The move was less about replacing Durant’s talent directly than maintaining transactional flexibility. Brooklyn obtained the superstar it wanted, while Golden State transformed a departure into a new branch of value. Brooklyn's own transaction announcement identified Russell, Napier and Graham as the outgoing assets. Wiggins and Kuminga entered Golden State's ledger only through the later Minnesota trade, not through this July 2019 agreement.

sections.heading: Brooklyn Used Russell’s Rights to Land a Generational Star
sections.body: Brooklyn’s side began with the most valuable player in the transaction. Durant was recovering from a ruptured Achilles, but his scoring, shooting and playoff résumé made the medical wait acceptable for a franchise trying to become a championship destination. The Nets surrendered Russell, whose restricted rights no longer fit after the arrivals of Durant and Kyrie Irving, plus two smaller contracts. Brooklyn also received a protected first from Golden State, reflecting Durant’s leverage in approving the structure. The Nets acquired a player capable of becoming the best performer in any playoff series. The risk was enormous, yet the cost in outgoing basketball value was manageable because Russell was already being displaced. Brooklyn's protected 2020 first-round return did not convey, leaving the conditional 2025 second-rounder eventually used on Javon Small. The pick's outcome should not be mistaken for a first-round prospect acquired alongside Durant.

sections.heading: Russell Became the Bridge to Wiggins and Kuminga
sections.body: Golden State’s Russell tenure lasted only part of one season, but the next conversion defined the return. The Warriors traded Russell, Jacob Evans and Omari Spellman to Minnesota for Andrew Wiggins, a protected first and a second. The first conveyed at No. 7 in 2021 and became Jonathan Kuminga. Wiggins developed into an All-Star starter and one of Golden State’s most important players during the 2022 championship run, defending elite wings and delivering major Finals rebounds and scoring. Kuminga added a young, controllable lottery asset. The sign-and-trade therefore became a direct bridge from Durant’s departure to a title contributor and a premium prospect. NBA.com's 2022 Finals roster history identifies Wiggins as the February 2020 acquisition and Kuminga as the No. 7 choice from Minnesota's top-three-protected 2021 first. The Warriors' championship return required that additional trade rather than emerging immediately from Brooklyn's 2019 package.

sections.heading: Durant’s Nets Tenure Was Brilliant but Interrupted
sections.body: Durant’s Brooklyn career contained extraordinary basketball and persistent disruption. He missed the entire first season while rehabilitating, then returned as one of the league’s most efficient scorers. In the 2021 playoffs, his near-series-winning performance against Milwaukee showed the exact ceiling Brooklyn purchased. Injuries, Irving’s availability and James Harden’s later departure prevented the group from becoming a stable contender, and the Nets won only one playoff series with Durant. That limited direct team success matters, but it does not erase the elite play Brooklyn received. The Nets also retained Durant’s market value when the partnership ended rather than allowing another superstar exit without compensation. Their February 2023 four-team trade with Phoenix brought Bridges, Johnson, four specified future firsts and a 2028 pick swap. Those were realized assets from Durant's later exit, not promises made in the 2019 sign-and-trade.

sections.heading: Both Franchises Extended the Chain Far Beyond the First Players
sections.body: Brooklyn’s 2023 trade of Durant to Phoenix produced Mikal Bridges, Cameron Johnson, four first-round picks and a swap. The Nets later traded Bridges to the Knicks for five first-round picks, a swap and additional pieces, greatly expanding the original asset chain. Golden State’s chain produced Wiggins, Kuminga and a 2022 championship before later roster changes continued. These downstream results are unusually direct and should be included because both franchises intentionally preserved value through the initial sign-and-trade. Neither side merely rented a player and watched the asset disappear. The transaction became a branching exchange that continued shaping both organizations for years. The 2024 Knicks package for Bridges contained four unprotected firsts, one protected Milwaukee first, a 2028 swap and veteran contracts. Brooklyn's return deserves to be traced in stages: Russell helped acquire Durant in 2019, Durant became the Phoenix assets in 2023, and Bridges generated the New York haul in 2024.

sections.heading: An Even Verdict Can Still Carry Two A-Plus Grades
sections.body: Even trades are not limited to modest swaps in which both sides receive B-level outcomes. Brooklyn acquired Durant, experienced a real championship window and later converted him into one of the league’s largest collections of players and draft capital. Golden State converted Russell into Wiggins and Kuminga, with Wiggins playing a central role on a championship team. Both sides achieved outcomes worthy of A-plus when measured against what would have happened without the sign-and-trade. The Nets could have lost Russell’s rights for little, and the Warriors could have lost Durant for nothing. The shared structure created exceptional value on both sides, making Even Trade the correct verdict. Golden State's more immediate team outcome was Wiggins contributing to the 2022 title; Brooklyn's return was elite Durant scoring followed by a larger pool of draft capital. Neither later outcome was locked in on July 7, 2019, and both depended on separate front-office decisions.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Brooklyn acquired Kevin Durant, received elite play and later converted him into Mikal Bridges, Cameron Johnson and major draft capital that expanded again through the Bridges trade. Golden State turned D’Angelo Russell into Andrew Wiggins and Jonathan Kuminga, with Wiggins helping win the 2022 championship. Both franchises created A-plus value from assets that otherwise might have departed.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The Durant–Russell Sign-and-Trade Became Two Separate Asset Engines
featuredDeepDive.intro: The first transaction looked like a superstar choosing a new team and a champion salvaging an All-Star guard. Its true importance emerged through later conversions. Brooklyn and Golden State each used the incoming asset as a bridge to a much larger return, making this one of the strongest examples of mutual value preservation in modern roster building.

sections.heading: Golden State’s Salary Structure Made Russell More Valuable Than His Fit
sections.body: The Warriors were operating above the cap and could not simply replace Durant with another maximum player. Acquiring Russell allowed Golden State to keep a large salary slot alive, even though a Curry-Russell backcourt raised defensive and stylistic questions. In that context, Russell’s contract was itself a strategic asset attached to a talented player. The Warriors used the slot within months rather than treating fit concerns as a reason to accept nothing. That cap mechanics advantage is central to the grade because the alternative was not signing an equivalent free agent. Brooklyn cooperated because the structure also delivered Durant and resolved Russell’s restricted free agency. Golden State separately moved Andre Iguodala and a protected future first to Memphis in July 2019 as part of its roster and salary reworking. That cost belongs to the Warriors' wider offseason, not to the Nets' direct return for Durant.

sections.heading: Wiggins Turned an Accounting Move Into Championship Production
sections.body: Wiggins supplied the exact two-way wing role Golden State eventually needed. His Minnesota contract had been viewed as burdensome, but the Warriors placed him in a lower-usage environment where defense, cutting and secondary scoring mattered more than primary creation. During the 2022 playoffs he guarded top opponents, rebounded at a high level and produced critical Finals performances. The championship makes the chain’s value concrete. Kuminga’s selection with Minnesota’s first added another significant outcome. Golden State’s A-plus comes from converting an awkward interim fit into both present and future value. Wiggins became a 2022 All-Star starter before helping win the championship, while the top-three-protected Minnesota first conveyed at No. 7 to become Kuminga. Those separate outcomes offer a more specific measure of return than Russell's half-season fit alone.

sections.heading: Brooklyn Received Durant’s Peak Skill Without Durant’s Full Availability
sections.body: Durant remained devastating when available for Brooklyn. His shooting and size allowed him to carry lineups in ways few players could, and the 2021 Milwaukee series came down to the narrowest possible margin. Yet his first season was lost to rehabilitation, later seasons included injuries, and the surrounding superteam never developed continuity. The Nets therefore did not receive the volume of contention they expected. They did receive proof that the talent assessment was correct and enough retained market value to command a historic return. That combination keeps Brooklyn’s grade elite despite the absence of a Finals appearance. Durant missed all of 2019-20 and played 35 regular-season games in 2020-21. Brooklyn's 2021 loss to Milwaukee came despite his brilliant series, illustrating both the individual ceiling the Nets acquired and the narrower postseason payoff they actually realized.

sections.heading: The Phoenix and Knicks Trades Extended Brooklyn’s Return
sections.body: The Phoenix package gave Brooklyn Bridges, Johnson and four firsts plus a swap. Bridges then became the centerpiece of a separate trade with New York that returned five firsts and another swap. Those transactions cannot be credited entirely as guaranteed outcomes of the 2019 deal, but the chain is direct: Durant’s contract and performance created the market that produced the assets. Brooklyn’s front office repeatedly chose to preserve and multiply that value. The original sign-and-trade therefore remained productive long after Durant left. Golden State’s chain was more immediately championship-oriented; Brooklyn’s became heavily future-oriented. The Nets' February 2023 return included 2023, 2025, 2027 and 2029 first-round picks and a 2028 swap. The separate 2024 Bridges deal added four unprotected future firsts, one protected Milwaukee first and another swap, rather than transferring that entire later package in 2019.

sections.heading: The Deal Shows Why Downstream Value Must Be Traced Carefully
sections.body: Asset-chain analysis can become misleading when every distant move is attributed to an original trade. This case is unusually strong because the links are clear and major. Russell directly became the central matching salary in the Wiggins trade, and the included first directly became Kuminga. Durant directly became the Phoenix package, and Bridges directly generated the Knicks haul. Each step required a new decision, so later front offices deserve separate credit. The original transaction still created the assets that made those decisions possible. Tracing the chain clarifies why both teams earned A-plus rather than forcing a winner based only on the first season. Russell's February 2020 departure also included Jacob Evans and Omari Spellman on Golden State's side; Brooklyn's later Bridges return involved contracts and protected as well as unprotected draft selections. Those accompanying pieces must stay attached to their own transaction dates so the original Durant trade isn't credited with assets it never directly contained.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Brooklyn obtained the superstar and later a vast rebuilding portfolio. Golden State obtained the mechanism that produced a championship wing and a lottery prospect. Because both sides converted departing free agents into extraordinary long-term value, the transaction remains an even trade at the highest grade level.

sections.heading: Golden State Turned a Temporary Durant Bridge Into a Championship Wing
sections.body: D’Angelo Russell arrived through the sign-and-trade that allowed Kevin Durant to leave for Brooklyn without the Warriors losing all salary-slot value. Russell was talented but an awkward long-term fit beside Stephen Curry and Klay Thompson. In February 2020, Golden State converted that bridge asset into Andrew Wiggins, a protected first-round pick and a second-round pick. Wiggins carried a negative contract reputation after inconsistent Minnesota seasons, yet his size, durability and defensive tools matched needs the Warriors would have when healthy. The front office used one temporary star slot to acquire a two-way wing who later became indispensable to another championship.

sections.heading: Minnesota Paid to Unite Russell With Karl-Anthony Towns
sections.body: The Timberwolves wanted a lead guard who could run pick-and-rolls, shoot off the dribble and share a close relationship with Karl-Anthony Towns. Wiggins’s contract and fit had become burdens, so the team accepted the cost of a lightly protected first-round pick to exchange one former No. 1 selection for another. Russell gave Minnesota scoring and helped the club reach the 2022 playoffs, which prevents the return from being dismissed as valueless. The trade nevertheless asked the Wolves to surrender both a player who would improve elsewhere and a premium pick that landed seventh. The immediate chemistry goal did not produce a lasting contender.

sections.heading: Wiggins Became the Exact Defender Golden State’s Core Needed
sections.body: The Warriors reduced Wiggins’s offensive burden and demanded consistent point-of-attack defense, rebounding and selective scoring. By 2022 he had become an All-Star starter and, during the championship run, took primary assignments against elite wings while creating second-chance possessions. In the Finals he defended Jayson Tatum, attacked the glass and supplied reliable scoring when Boston loaded toward Curry. Calling him merely a reclaimed contract understates the result. Golden State acquired a player whose role was more valuable in its ecosystem than his larger statistical role had been in Minnesota.

sections.heading: The First-Round Pick Added Another Premium Asset
sections.body: Minnesota’s 2021 first-round selection was protected only in the top three and conveyed at No. 7, where Golden State selected Jonathan Kuminga. Kuminga’s development has been uneven, and the trade’s verdict does not require treating him as a finished star. The pick still represented significant surplus value on top of Wiggins. Golden State had acquired a championship starter and retained a lottery asset that could contribute, be extended or support another trade. The second-round pick became the selection used on Miles McBride before later movement. The key point is that Minnesota paid meaningful future capital rather than completing a simple distressed-contract swap.

sections.heading: Russell’s Later Conversion Gives Minnesota More Credit Than a D-Plus
sections.body: Russell’s Minnesota tenure ended in a 2023 three-team trade that brought Mike Conley, Nickeil Alexander-Walker and draft compensation. Conley and Alexander-Walker became important pieces of a stronger defensive team and helped Minnesota reach the 2024 Western Conference finals. That downstream return does not erase the original cost, but it improves the Wolves’ side of the trade details. A D+ treats Russell as though he produced no useful basketball or later value. C+ is more accurate: Minnesota lost the trade clearly, yet it received a starting guard, reached the playoffs and eventually converted him into players who fit the next version of the roster better.

sections.heading: Warriors Win Still Reflects a Major Asset-Management Success
sections.body: Golden State’s A+ remains secure. The organization preserved value after Durant’s departure, recognized that Russell was not the final fit, bought low on Wiggins and extracted a lightly protected first. The result was a 2022 championship with Wiggins as one of the team’s most important postseason players. Minnesota’s revised C+ acknowledges the 2022 playoff berth and the later Conley-Alexander-Walker chain without pretending those gains matched a title starter plus a lottery pick. The verdict is not close, but evidence-based grading should distinguish a losing return from a total failure.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win, with Golden State at A+ and Minnesota revised to C+. Wiggins became an All-Star starter and a two-way pillar of the 2022 championship, while the first-round pick conveyed at No. 7 and became Kuminga. Russell helped Minnesota reach the 2022 playoffs and was later converted into Conley, Alexander-Walker and draft value, so the Wolves’ outcome was better than the previous D+ implied. Golden State still captured the superior player fit, the premium pick and the championship payoff.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The Wiggins-Russell Trade Extended Golden State’s Dynasty Through Asset Preservation
featuredDeepDive.intro: The Warriors’ 2020 move was the middle link of a broader strategy. Durant’s departure could have ended a maximum-salary asset slot, but the sign-and-trade for Russell preserved it. Russell could then be exchanged for a wing whose size and defensive potential better matched Curry’s eventual return, along with a valuable pick. Minnesota pursued a different goal: remove a difficult contract and install Towns’s preferred guard. The outcome shows why preserving optionality matters. Golden State was able to change the identity of the asset twice until it found a championship fit.

sections.heading: The Trade Was Negotiated During Golden State’s Lost Season
sections.body: Curry and Thompson were unavailable for most or all of 2019-20, leaving the Warriors at the bottom of the standings and making immediate fit less important than long-term design. Russell could post large scoring numbers without revealing how he would function next to the championship backcourt. Golden State used the deadline to act before that fit question became a public problem. Minnesota, meanwhile, had pursued Russell in free agency and remained motivated to pair him with Towns. The mismatch in urgency allowed the Warriors to demand a protected first-round pick in addition to Wiggins.

sections.heading: Wiggins’s Contract Became an Advantage Once His Role Shrunk
sections.body: In Minnesota, Wiggins had been paid like a primary creator and judged against that responsibility. Golden State did not need him to initiate every possession. The Warriors needed a durable wing who could defend the opponent’s best scorer, cut when Curry drew attention and attack mismatches without controlling the offense. The same contract looked less damaging when attached to a player performing a scarce championship role. This is a powerful trade lesson: negative value can be situational. A player may be overpaid for one assignment and appropriately compensated for another that better uses his skills.

sections.heading: The 2022 Playoffs Supplied the Strongest Possible Validation
sections.body: Wiggins’s rebounding and defense became increasingly important as the Warriors advanced. Against Dallas and Boston, he accepted difficult wing assignments while maintaining efficient enough offense to punish neglect. His 26-point, 13-rebound performance in Game 5 of the Finals came when Curry did not make a three-pointer, demonstrating the secondary scoring value Golden State had hoped to unlock. The championship does not mean every later Wiggins season was equally successful. It means the trade produced elite value at the moment the franchise needed it most, which is the core of the A+ grade.

sections.heading: Minnesota’s Later Success Came After Moving Beyond the Russell Fit
sections.body: Russell’s playmaking and shooting helped the Wolves return to the playoffs, but defensive limitations and contract questions made the partnership with Towns and Anthony Edwards difficult to sustain. The 2023 trade for Conley and Alexander-Walker improved lineup balance and connected Minnesota to a more mature version of its roster. That downstream conversion deserves credit because trade assets can retain value after the original player leaves. It also highlights why Golden State won: the Warriors obtained the better immediate fit and a premium pick, while Minnesota needed another transaction to reach the structure it ultimately preferred.

sections.heading: Revising the Wolves to C-Plus Improves the Verdict’s Precision
sections.body: Grades should change when later asset chains reveal more value than an earlier snapshot captured. Minnesota’s original D+ was too punitive once Russell contributed to a playoff berth and became the outgoing salary in a trade that delivered two important rotation players. C+ does not create false equivalence. The Wolves still surrendered Wiggins at the point he was about to thrive in a lower-usage role and gave up the pick used on Kuminga. The revision simply separates a clear loss from a barren return, maintaining confidence in the Warriors Win label while improving the accuracy of the partner grade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The full outcome confirms Warriors Win. Golden State transformed a temporary Russell asset into Wiggins, a lottery pick and a second-rounder, then received championship-level defense, rebounding and secondary scoring from Wiggins in 2022. Minnesota achieved some of its goals, reached the playoffs and later converted Russell into a better-fitting veteran package, which supports raising the Wolves to C+. The championship and draft-value gap remain decisive. This is one of the clearest examples of a contender preserving a departing superstar’s asset slot until it became another title piece.

sections.heading: Portland Held Post’s Rights Briefly Before Selling Them for Cash
sections.body: Golden State acquired the draft rights to 7-foot center Quinten Post from Portland in a July 6, 2024 transaction, paying cash considerations rather than surrendering a player or another draft pick. The Trail Blazers' own announcement details the immediately preceding rights chain: Portland first obtained the 52nd overall selection, Post, and cash from Oklahoma City for the rights to No. 40 Osasere Ighodaro. Portland then transferred Post's rights to the Warriors for cash. Those are two separate transactions, and Ighodaro was consideration in Portland's deal with Oklahoma City, not in the later Golden State-Portland sale. Golden State's original draft-night interest in Post became a concrete roster opportunity when it secured the rights back. The precise cash amount in the final exchange was not disclosed in the official release.

sections.heading: Post Produced Real Golden State Minutes as a Rookie
sections.body: Post did not stay an unsigned draft-rights placeholder. He made his NBA debut in December 2024 and played 42 regular-season games for Golden State in 2024-25, starting 14 and averaging 8.1 points and 3.5 rebounds in 16.3 minutes. His 40.8 percent three-point shooting gave the Warriors a genuine floor-spacing option at center. Those minutes are a specific, verifiable payoff for the July 2024 cash expense. They also show why comparing the franchises' returns solely by the number of trade components would miss the result: the Warriors received the right to bring a usable player into their system, while Portland knowingly took a cash payment. The later NBA games were earned in Golden State's rotation, not with Portland.

sections.heading: A Second Season Established More Than an Early Flash
sections.body: Post followed the rookie season by appearing in 67 Warriors games in 2025-26, making 35 starts and averaging 7.7 points, 4.0 rebounds and 1.4 assists in 17.3 minutes. His three-point accuracy slipped to 33.6 percent, so the second year was not a simple upward trend in every category. Still, 109 total games over two seasons provided a verifiable return from the rights deal. A center who can pass and take outside shots has utility even without a major scoring role, and his contribution explains why the Warriors' B rating is supported by basketball evidence rather than an abstract claim that developmental players always have upside. Those results should be compared with the cash Portland obtained, whose precise amount is not publicly established in this transaction.

sections.heading: Portland’s Cash Has Value but Cannot Be Priced from Thin Air
sections.body: The Blazers did receive consideration: cash from Golden State after the separate Oklahoma City swap. Portland's official announcement does not assign a dollar amount, so the return cannot be converted into a fabricated salary or spending figure. The former Post draft right eventually became 109 Warriors regular-season games, while Portland recorded no direct player or draft-pick asset in the second exchange. The inherited Warriors Win label with Golden State B and Portland D+ follows that realized disparity. Portland's alternative source-side assessment assigns Golden State A-, a conflict over the precise winning grade rather than over the trade identity. The sensible interpretation is a favorable low-cost Golden State acquisition, without treating cash as worthless or assuming Portland could have forecast Post's actual future playing time on July 6.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win, preserving the inherited Golden State B/Portland D+ pairing. Golden State paid undisclosed cash for Post's rights, then received 42 rookie games at 8.1 points and 40.8 percent from three, followed by 67 games at 7.7 points in 2025-26. Portland acquired cash, not a later NBA player or pick. The same official Trail Blazers release distinguishes its earlier OKC/Ighodaro exchange from this Golden State cash transaction. The imported Portland perspective uses an A- winning grade that still needs ledger reconciliation.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Quinten Post from Portland: Draft Rights, Two Warriors Seasons and the Cash Price
featuredDeepDive.intro: The Warriors acquired the rights to Quinten Post from Portland for cash after the separate earlier Oklahoma City draft swap. His first two NBA seasons brought 109 Golden State appearances, including outside shooting from a 7-foot center.

sections.heading: Portland's Two Draft-Day Deals Were Distinct
sections.body: Portland first acquired Quinten Post's No. 52 rights from Oklahoma City on 2024 draft night in a separate exchange involving No. 40 Osasere Ighodaro and cash. The Trail Blazers then sent Post's rights to Golden State for cash in the July 6 transaction recorded here. These are two deals with different counterparties, so the Ighodaro component should not appear in the Warriors-Portland asset ledger. Golden State gave up financial consideration rather than a named active player or draft pick and received the right to sign Post. Portland took payment instead of preserving the roster option. The franchise's official release gives the sequence clearly, making it possible to judge the real trade rather than conflating it with the preceding Thunder transaction. The cash amount is not established in the cited announcement.

sections.heading: Post's First Golden State Season Produced Rotation Value
sections.body: The Warriors brought Post into the NBA during the 2024-25 season. In 42 regular-season appearances, including 14 starts, he averaged 8.1 points and 3.5 rebounds in 16.3 minutes per game. He also hit 40.8 percent of his three-point attempts, an unusual dimension for a 7-foot center used to create spacing. Those are direct Golden State statistics from a player whose rights the team acquired for cash, rather than speculative projections attached to a draft pick. His contribution did not make the transaction a franchise-altering blockbuster, but it established playable value in the first season. Portland's compensation was the cash received in July 2024; the Trail Blazers did not receive some downstream Golden State player once Post began logging those NBA games. The timeline supports the inherited Warriors Win direction.

sections.heading: Another Sixty-Seven Games Reinforced the Development Case
sections.body: Post added 67 regular-season appearances in 2025-26 and started 35, averaging 7.7 points, 4.0 rebounds and 1.4 assists. His three-point percentage dropped to 33.6, so the second season showed progress in playing time and rebounding without identical shooting efficiency. The combined 109 Golden State games across two years were the actual outcome of acquiring his rights, not 109 projected appearances assumed at the 2024 trade date. Keeping the numbers by season helps avoid manufacturing an uninterrupted upward trend. Portland could rationally accept cash for a second-round international-style developmental opportunity, but hindsight compares a cash receipt against an NBA center who reached the rotation. The asset chain ends with Golden State's own games, not with later hypothetical transactions that are not in the research record.

sections.heading: Golden State B and Portland D-Plus Reflect Real, Unequal Returns
sections.body: The canonical grades are B for Golden State and D-plus for Portland. The Warriors received a low-cost center with 109 appearances across 2024-25 and 2025-26, including contributions as a floor-spacing reserve and 49 combined starts. The Trail Blazers received cash and did not retain the player's NBA rights in this particular transaction. Their earlier Oklahoma City draft swap was separate, while the amount of Golden State's cash payment remains undisclosed in the official Portland announcement. A different imported source-side grade assigned Golden State A-minus; that unresolved perspective difference should not silently overwrite the reconciled canonical B. The Warriors Win conclusion is grounded in Post's actual playing time and shooting profile, but the scale should not overstate the importance of a reserve center or describe Portland's cash return as nonexistent.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win — Golden State B, Portland D+. Post produced 42 Warriors games in 2024-25 and 67 more in 2025-26 after the July 2024 cash acquisition. Portland received cash without a documented dollar amount; the earlier Ighodaro rights swap involved Oklahoma City separately.

sections.heading: An Expansion-Era Swap with Older Team Names
sections.body: The franchise now called the Houston Rockets was still based in San Diego when it sent Jim Barnett to the expansion Portland Trail Blazers on May 11, 1970. Larry Siegfried went to the Rockets in return. That geography is not cosmetic: applying modern franchise cities to every vintage transaction can obscure who actually negotiated it. The trade belongs to the period when Portland was building its inaugural NBA roster and San Diego was making veteran personnel decisions before the franchise later moved to Texas.

sections.heading: Barnett Was Portland's Incoming Player
sections.body: Portland acquired Barnett directly, not a draft slot or unspecified future consideration. For a new team assembling usable NBA veterans, a player with established professional experience offered immediate value that could be evaluated on the court. That is the basis of the B+ Portland grade. The deal should not be confused with the expansion draft, even though the timing is close to the franchise's first season. This was a distinct player-for-player exchange with an identifiable outgoing piece.

sections.heading: Siegfried's Role on the Other Side
sections.body: San Diego obtained Larry Siegfried, an experienced guard, in exchange for Barnett. Siegfried had NBA credentials, so the Rockets' C+ is not equivalent to receiving nothing. The smaller evaluation reflects how the completed return compares with Portland's rather than a judgment about either man's earlier career. Neither the transaction ledger nor the preserved supporting references justify attributing later unrelated player movements to this May agreement. The record is a two-player comparison and should stay one.

sections.heading: Reading the Historical Verdict
sections.body: The Trail Blazers Win conclusion awards Portland B+ against the Rockets' C+. What separates the clubs is the realized usefulness of Barnett's Portland acquisition against Siegfried's San Diego stint, not an invented chain of draft assets. The deal's greatest historical interest lies in its timing: one expansion franchise acquiring an NBA veteran from an established team in another city before the established club changed its own location. An accurate retrospective can tell that story without pretending this modest exchange determined either team's future.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Trail Blazers Win, Portland B+ and the Rockets C+. Barnett gave the expansion club the stronger completed return. Siegfried was a real acquisition by San Diego, and the margin should be assessed between those two players rather than expanded into unsourced later transactions.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Houston Rockets–Portland Trail Blazers: What the 1970-05-11 Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: San Diego's Rockets traded Jim Barnett to the expansion Trail Blazers in May 1970 for Larry Siegfried. The modern Houston slug points to the same franchise, but the actual transaction predates its move. Two experienced players, not a hidden pick package, anchor the comparison.

sections.heading: What the 1970 Date Explains
sections.body: Portland acquired Jim Barnett for its inaugural 1970-71 season, and the NBA's own player ledger shows why his arrival was useful: 78 games, 18.5 points, 4.8 rebounds and 4.1 assists per game in 30.4 minutes. Larry Siegfried gave the San Diego Rockets a different sort of contribution, averaging 8.0 points and 6.5 assists in 53 games that season. The veteran guard was a legitimate return, but Barnett's scoring and availability favor the expansion club's B+ over San Diego's C+. The geographic distinction is essential: Houston did not acquire Siegfried in Texas, and the deal was an ordinary two-player trade during Portland's roster construction, not a selection in the expansion draft.

sections.heading: No Downstream Picks to Manufacture
sections.body: Unlike several early-1970s deals with later converted draft rights, this recorded exchange supplies a player on each side and no documented contingent selection. A source-led verdict therefore compares Barnett and Siegfried on their own terms. Portland's B+ and San Diego's C+ reflect a genuine edge, but the material does not support a detailed second or third transaction that never appears in the asset record.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Portland received Barnett and the San Diego Rockets received Siegfried before the latter franchise moved to Houston. The B+ to C+ verdict belongs to those players, not to a fabricated downstream draft tree.

sections.heading: What Changed Hands
sections.body: On April 7, 1972, Houston sent a first-round choice to Phoenix for Otto Moore. The pick was not Corky Calhoun's player contract: Phoenix subsequently used that selection at No. 4 on Calhoun. Houston had previously obtained the choice from Detroit in a separate Jim Davis transaction. The Rockets' direct incoming asset was Moore, while the Suns' incoming asset was a selection that had yet to be exercised. This distinction makes the original exchange easier to trace without merging three transactions.

sections.heading: How the Realized Value Separated
sections.body: Moore immediately gave the Rockets a strong 1972-73 season: 82 starts, 11.7 points and 10.6 rebounds per game, while playing 33.1 minutes. After another 13 Houston appearances the following season, he went to Kansas City-Omaha for Ron Riley in November 1973. Riley subsequently appeared in 178 more regular-season Rockets games and eight playoff games. That two-stage return explains why Houston's side earned a solid B rather than being evaluated solely on Moore's short direct tenure.

sections.heading: Reading the Team Grades
sections.body: Phoenix used the No. 4 selection on Corky Calhoun, who appeared in 172 Suns games before the team sent him to Los Angeles for two future picks. The 1976 second-rounder was traded to Portland for Phil Lumpkin, who played 34 regular-season games and 17 playoff games for the 1976 Finals Suns. The 1977 third-rounder became Mike Bratz at No. 66; Bratz contributed 239 Phoenix regular-season games and 25 postseason appearances. Those later steps are separate transactions, but both arose from the asset Phoenix received here.

sections.heading: What Each Franchise Was Actually Evaluating
sections.body: The current source-led grades are Phoenix B+ and Houston B, and the verdict is Slight Suns Edge. Houston gained the more productive single-season center and later retained value through Riley. Phoenix's less spectacular individual players accumulated depth across a longer chain: Calhoun, then Lumpkin and Bratz. Calling this a large Suns win would ignore Moore's 82-game double-double season; calling it a Rockets win would omit the two later selections and their realized Phoenix roles.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Suns Edge — Phoenix B+, Houston B. Houston acquired Otto Moore for the 1972 first-round choice that Phoenix spent on Corky Calhoun at No. 4. Moore produced an 82-game, 11.7-point and 10.6-rebound season, then became Ron Riley, who supplied 178 more Houston games. Calhoun appeared 172 times for the Suns and later became two picks, converted into Phil Lumpkin and Mike Bratz. Houston had the best immediate individual season; the broader documented downstream return favored Phoenix slightly.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Houston Rockets–Phoenix Suns: What the 1972-04-07 Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: The Rockets acquired Otto Moore on April 7, 1972, and the Suns acquired a draft selection later used at No. 4 on Corky Calhoun. Moore started 82 Houston games that first season; the Rockets later exchanged him for Ron Riley. Phoenix got 172 Calhoun appearances and converted his contract into two picks, which yielded Phil Lumpkin and Mike Bratz through additional transactions. Those downstream branches account for the updated slight Suns advantage: Phoenix B+ and Houston B, because Calhoun’s later conversion gave Phoenix additional players and postseason opportunities.

sections.heading: The Asset Path That Carries the Grade
sections.body: The source transaction history places a 1972 first-round choice, not a drafted Calhoun, on the Phoenix side of the April 7 exchange. Houston sent that choice and received Otto Moore. Phoenix then exercised No. 4 for Corky Calhoun three days later. Houston's earlier acquisition of the pick from Detroit is a separate ledger entry and cannot be treated as if Detroit participated in this specific Suns–Rockets trade. Once the starting assets are established, each later player or selection can be followed without mixing trade dates or adding an invented third club.

sections.heading: What the Lower-Graded Side Still Kept
sections.body: Houston's immediate return was unusually productive. Moore played all 82 Rockets games in 1972-73, started every one and averaged 11.7 points alongside 10.6 rebounds. His next Houston season lasted just 13 games before the November 1973 exchange for Ron Riley. Riley's 36, 77 and 65 regular-season appearances across three Rockets seasons totaled 178, with eight postseason games in 1975. That is meaningful value across two players; it supports Houston's B even though the club did not keep Moore beyond 1973.

sections.heading: Decision Logic Versus Hindsight
sections.body: Phoenix's first step was Calhoun, who played 82 games as a rookie, 77 in 1973-74 and 13 more in 1974-75: 172 in total. The November 1974 Lakers trade produced two later selections. Phoenix converted the 1976 second-round pick into Phil Lumpkin, who appeared 34 times in the regular season and 17 times during the Suns' Finals run. The third-round choice became Mike Bratz in 1977. Bratz played 239 Phoenix regular-season games and 25 playoff games. Their contributions are credited through a documented asset chain, not by placing them in the original trade.

sections.heading: Why the Grade Gap Is the Better Scale
sections.body: The comparison isn't Moore against Calhoun alone. A correct hindsight account includes Riley's 178 Rockets games after Moore was moved, but also Calhoun's later conversion into two Phoenix selections. Houston received the strongest single immediate season; Phoenix secured more separate roles and playoff appearances across time. Lumpkin and Bratz contributed 42 combined Suns playoff appearances after their assets originated from Calhoun's trade. That supports Phoenix B+ against Houston B and a narrow Suns advantage, not the older claim of a Rockets edge.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The source-led verdict gives Phoenix B+ and Houston B. Moore delivered Houston a full 1972-73 season and Riley added 178 Rockets games; that return deserves real credit. Phoenix's No. 4 pick became Corky Calhoun, and his later trade produced choices converted into Lumpkin's 1976 Finals role and 239 regular-season games from Bratz. The 42 combined postseason appearances of Lumpkin and Bratz help explain the Suns' greater asset depth. Every later transfer is a separate dated transaction; none makes those players part of the April 1972 exchange.

sections.heading: The Confirmed Deal Was Hayes for Marin
sections.body: Houston sent Elvin Hayes to the Baltimore Bullets on June 23, 1972 and received Jack Marin. The team and league transaction logs identify those two players as the confirmed exchange. A separate Houston legacy source also mentions future considerations with a question mark, but does not provide a verifiable player, draft choice or cash amount. That entry is preserved as uncertain provenance rather than counted as additional realized value for Houston. Marin was already an All-Star, so this was a meaningful player acquisition even though its eventual return would be dwarfed by Hayes' longer run with the Bullets franchise.

sections.heading: Marin Gave Houston Production and Another Trade
sections.body: Marin appeared in 128 regular-season games for Houston and scored 1,998 points, including an All-Star season in 1972-73. The Rockets later included Marin and Matt Guokas in the February 1974 exchange with Buffalo for Kevin Kunnert and Dave Wohl. That additional transaction yielded identifiable players, but credit cannot be assigned entirely to Marin because Guokas was also outgoing consideration. Houston's original return was therefore more than a short bench stint, yet it did not approach the sustained production the opposing franchise received from its incoming star.

sections.heading: Hayes Anchored a Bullets Championship Era
sections.body: Elvin Hayes stayed with the Baltimore, Capital and Washington Bullets franchise for nine seasons, reached repeated All-Star and All-NBA levels and was part of the 1978 NBA championship team alongside Wes Unseld. His first season after the trade included averages of 21.2 points and 14.5 rebounds. That is direct multi-season franchise value, not an accomplishment borrowed from an unrelated team. Marin's useful Houston stint and later asset conversion deserve recognition, but Hayes supplied a much longer and higher-level return to the franchise receiving him in 1972.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bullets Win. Washington/Baltimore receives A+ for nine seasons of Elvin Hayes and the 1978 championship run. Houston earns B for Jack Marin's 128 games, All-Star contribution and subsequent trade utility. Unconfirmed future considerations are excluded from the outcome, preserving the player-for-player deal supported by the league transaction logs.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Elvin Hayes for Jack Marin in 1972: Nine Bullets Seasons and Houston’s Two-Year Return
featuredDeepDive.intro: On June 23, 1972, Houston sent Elvin Hayes to Baltimore and acquired All-Star forward Jack Marin. Contemporary transaction records establish those two players; one later legacy summary alludes to unspecified future considerations, but no additional asset with a verifiable outcome has been identified. Hayes became a foundational Bullets scorer and rebounder through their 1975 and 1978 Finals appearances, helping win the 1978 championship alongside Wes Unseld. Marin furnished 128 Houston games before a separate February 1974 trade. The inherited Bullets Win verdict and Washington/Baltimore A+ against Houston B are preserved, with the original deal and subsequent moves kept apart.

sections.heading: Baltimore Received a 27-Year-Old Franchise Scorer
sections.body: Hayes was already one of the NBA's leading big men when Houston traded him in June 1972. During 1971-72 he played all 82 Rockets games and averaged 25.2 points and 14.6 rebounds. Baltimore obtained that established production, not a prospect who needed multiple years to establish a rotation role. Marin arrived in Houston after his own 1971-72 All-Star season with the Bullets, so the transaction did deliver a respected NBA player in exchange. Still, the competing long-term value was different from day one. Hayes could score in volume, dominate the glass and anchor the frontcourt next to Wes Unseld. Some historical summaries list ambiguous future considerations alongside Marin, but there is no securely identified draft pick, cash amount or extra player to score. The confirmed comparison is between Hayes's eventual Baltimore/Capital/Washington output and Marin's Rockets seasons.

sections.heading: The First Baltimore Season Proved Hayes Still Had His Peak
sections.body: Hayes immediately carried his production to his new team. For Baltimore in 1972-73, he played 81 games at 21.2 points and 14.5 rebounds, earned All-Star honors and a second-team All-NBA selection. The franchise became the Capital Bullets for 1973-74 and then the Washington Bullets, but those changes in name did not mean he was playing for a different franchise. He averaged 21.4 points and 13.7 rebounds in 1973-74 before rising to 23.0 points and 12.2 rebounds in 1974-75. Washington went 60-22 that year and reached the NBA Finals, losing in a surprising four-game sweep against Golden State. That setback is part of the accurate record: Hayes's first three Bullets seasons brought star-level output and a Finals berth, but the championship did not arrive until 1978.

sections.heading: Marin Produced 128 Houston Games and an All-Star Selection
sections.body: Houston's return should not be dismissed as nothing. Marin started his Rockets career with 81 appearances in 1972-73 and totaled 1,496 points, a per-game scoring average of 18.5, alongside an All-Star selection. He added 47 Houston games and 502 points in 1973-74 before leaving on February 1, 1974. Across the two partial-to-full seasons that totals 128 games and 1,998 points for the Rockets. At 28 on arrival, Marin was a real wing scorer, but the accumulated Houston service was much shorter than Hayes's nine seasons with the Bullets organization. The distinction matters because one could casually compare their entire Hall-of-Fame-level versus All-Star careers, but the trade should be graded by the value each acquiring team actually got afterward. Marin's Houston output deserves recognition; it just cannot match the longevity of Hayes.

sections.heading: Houston Exchanged Marin Again With Matt Guokas in February 1974
sections.body: Marin's asset trail has a second stage separate from the Hayes exchange. On February 1, 1974, the Rockets traded Jack Marin and Matt Guokas to the Buffalo Braves for Kevin Kunnert and Dave Wohl. Both Houston's and Buffalo's transaction histories record four named players in that deal. That provides a genuine downstream link from the 1972 acquisition, not a reason to add Kunnert and Wohl directly to Baltimore's original return. There is also no basis for treating the whole Kunnert-Wohl package as value generated solely by Marin: Guokas was also sent to Buffalo. Future value must be attributed with that additional outgoing player in view. Houston did recover two roster pieces through a later transaction, but the original Hayes trade remains a confirmed Hayes-for-Marin player exchange absent reliable evidence specifying the supposed future considerations.

sections.heading: The 1978 Championship Is a Direct Bullets Payoff
sections.body: Hayes's Washington-era impact was not confined to regular-season scoring. The Bullets returned to the Finals in 1978 and defeated the Seattle SuperSonics in seven games. In that championship season Hayes averaged 19.7 points and 13.3 rebounds over 81 regular-season games, leading the club in scoring while Wes Unseld supplied rebounding, screens, passing and veteran leadership. The NBA's 1977-78 season review identifies Hayes as a central part of the organization's lone championship, while Unseld earned Finals MVP honors. Baltimore, Capital and Washington were all names of the same franchise, so the title is directly attributable to the team that obtained Hayes in June 1972. This is where the relative grades diverge most: Marin's All-Star Rockets campaign made Houston's B defensible, but Hayes contributed to multiple Finals trips and a championship, justifying the inherited A+ on the receiving side without inventing auxiliary draft returns.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bullets Win — Washington/Baltimore A+, Houston B. Hayes brought nine seasons of elite frontcourt output to the Bullets franchise, including the 1975 Finals and the seven-game 1978 title victory over Seattle. Marin gave Houston 128 appearances and 1,998 points, plus a place in the later trade in which he and Matt Guokas brought back Kevin Kunnert and Dave Wohl. That second deal is not the June 1972 Hayes transaction and cannot be attributed solely to Marin. No unsupported future consideration is counted as an extra asset. Hayes's championship and long tenure make the advantage clear while preserving Marin's substantial short-term production.
