sections.heading: What Houston and New York Exchanged
sections.body: Houston received Moochie Norris, Vin Baker and a 2006 second-round pick that became Steve Novak; New York received Maurice Taylor. Those four assets give this 2005 trade more substance than its modest grades might suggest. Both teams' analyses point in the same direction: Houston finished with the stronger realized return. The final grades are C for the Rockets and D for the Knicks, which intentionally distinguish the sides without turning a useful asset win into a blockbuster result. Houston's advantage comes from the depth of the package it received and the identifiable outcome of the second-round pick, not from speculative credit for moves outside this transaction.

sections.heading: Why the Pick Matters to the Rockets' Side
sections.body: The 2006 second-round pick is especially important because the trade details identify its realized outcome as Steve Novak. That allows the pick to be evaluated as a named asset rather than as an abstract future selection. Houston also received Moochie Norris and Vin Baker, giving the Rockets multiple directly tied pieces in exchange for Maurice Taylor. The analysis describes the realized return as strongly favoring Houston, while the final C/D grades keep the scale conservative. This is a useful distinction: a team can win the asset comparison clearly without the deal becoming historically transformative. The pick outcome adds concrete value and depth to Houston's side, but the retrospective still measures only what emerged from this trade rather than attaching unrelated later team success.

sections.heading: What New York Received and Why It Trails
sections.body: The Knicks acquired Maurice Taylor, a legitimate established-player return. That matters because the D grade should not be read as if New York received no basketball value. The problem in hindsight is comparative: New York sent three pieces, including a second-round pick with an identifiable player outcome, while Houston's package ultimately provided the broader realized return. The Knicks-side perspective itself acknowledges that the partner finished with the better overall result. That bilateral agreement is what makes a directional verdict appropriate. New York gets credit for the player it acquired, but the completed list of assets leaves the Knicks behind Houston once Norris, Baker and the Novak pick are considered together.

sections.heading: Why C Versus D Fits Better Than an Extreme Split
sections.body: The source language can sound stronger than the final letter grades, so grading scale matters. Houston's side says the realized return strongly favored the Rockets, and New York's side says the partner finished with the better overall return. Even so, the assets involved were not premium first-round picks or franchise-level stars. A C for Houston says the Rockets clearly came out ahead in this specific exchange without treating the deal as a foundational win. A D for New York reflects the weaker realized package while acknowledging that Maurice Taylor was real consideration. The final gap therefore separates direction from magnitude: Houston won the trade comparison, but the historical scale of the transaction still belongs in the middle-to-lower portion of the grading range.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Rockets Edge. Houston receives a C and New York a D. The Rockets acquired Moochie Norris, Vin Baker and the 2006 second-round pick that became Steve Novak; the Knicks acquired Maurice Taylor. Both franchise-side perspectives ultimately favor Houston, and the directly traced asset outcomes support that direction. The grades remain moderate because this was not a premium-asset blockbuster, but Houston's deeper package produced the better completed return.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Rockets–Knicks 2005: How Package Depth and the Steve Novak Pick Tilted the Trade
featuredDeepDive.intro: The February 24, 2005 Houston-New York transaction involved two different kinds of return. New York received veteran forward Maurice Taylor; Houston took Moochie Norris, Vin Baker and a future second-round pick. The draft right later became the 2006 No. 32 selection of Steve Novak. That final piece deserves careful wording: Novak was not a player sent across in 2005, but a later draft outcome attached to the acquired pick. In hindsight the Rockets' three-piece package earns C against the Knicks' D, a favorable comparison for Houston without turning a modest exchange into a franchise-defining one.

sections.heading: Three Incoming Pieces Give Houston More Paths to Value
sections.body: New York concentrated its return in Maurice Taylor while Houston divided its consideration between two named players and a 2006 second-round selection. Norris and Baker were immediate roster assets; the selection created an additional future possibility. Listing the pieces accurately is more useful than arguing that three assets automatically beat one. A pick can fail to produce a meaningful return, and veteran players can provide only limited value. Here the source ledger records a concrete future result at No. 32, Steve Novak. That named conversion lets Houston's return be assessed without guessing at other draft choices or crediting the original trade with unrelated later acquisitions.

sections.heading: The Novak Outcome Is Evidence, Not a Hypothetical
sections.body: The 2006 second-rounder became the No. 32 pick used on Steve Novak, which gives the 2005 trade a specific follow-through. It is important not to reverse the timeline by writing that New York traded Novak directly to Houston; the player was drafted a year after Taylor changed teams. Nor should the pick's value be multiplied by imaginary alternative selections. The retrospective has a clear chain: Taylor went to the Knicks, Norris and Baker went to the Rockets, and Houston also gained the draft asset subsequently identified with Novak. That is the evidence behind the pick's contribution to the Rockets' stronger total package.

sections.heading: Both Team Perspectives Converge on Houston
sections.body: The franchise perspectives can both be accounted for without claiming the Knicks received nothing. New York obtained Taylor and accepted an immediate single-player return. Houston received Norris and Baker plus an additional draft chance that ultimately had a named outcome. The final grades, Rockets C and Knicks D, put Houston ahead because the completed pieces favor its side; they do not require describing every Houston acquisition as a long-term success. With multiple smaller assets involved, the verdict is a comparison of what the transaction returned, not a claim that a single player on either side carried the entire historical judgment.

sections.heading: Why the Knicks' Maurice Taylor Return Still Counts
sections.body: Taylor was the Knicks' acquisition, and that direct player return must not disappear behind discussion of the Novak pick. The question is whether it offset all three pieces New York sent away. In the recorded retrospective the answer is no: Houston's combination of Norris, Baker and the 2006 No. 32 selection is preferred, producing a Slight Rockets Edge. The C/D scores still acknowledge a limited-scale transaction rather than a transformative one. The safest historical account credits Houston for the draft right that became Novak, credits New York for Taylor, and stops short of attaching unrelated future team accomplishments to the 2005 exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Houston C, New York D, with a Slight Rockets Edge verdict. The Rockets' return combined Moochie Norris, Vin Baker and the second-round pick that became Steve Novak, while the Knicks received Maurice Taylor. Both analyses point toward Houston, and the named pick outcome adds concrete depth to the Rockets' side. The result is a defensible Houston win whose grades remain proportional to the transaction's modest overall scale.

sections.heading: Houston Paid for Certainty Around Yao and McGrady
sections.body: The Rockets entered the 2006 offseason with a clear objective: maximize the healthy overlap of Yao Ming and Tracy McGrady. Rudy Gay’s draft rights represented youth, athleticism and a higher individual scoring ceiling, but Houston did not need another developmental wing to command possessions. It needed a defender, floor spacer and low-maintenance connector who could improve two established stars immediately. Shane Battier fit that description almost perfectly. He could guard elite wings, make the extra pass, hit open threes and absorb difficult assignments without demanding a large offensive role. Stromile Swift’s return to Memphis also removed a disappointing Houston contract from the rotation. The Rockets chose role certainty over star upside, a decision that looked conservative on draft night but made sense within a narrow contention window. The trade should be judged against that objective rather than as a simple comparison of career scoring averages.

sections.heading: Memphis Acquired the Best Long-Term Individual Asset
sections.body: The Grizzlies were moving away from an older core and needed a player with the potential to become a primary scorer. Gay, the eighth pick, offered size, athletic finishing and shot-creation ability that Battier was never going to provide. Memphis also reacquired Swift, though his second stint delivered limited value. Gay became the durable centerpiece of the return. He averaged significant scoring totals, signed a long-term contract and remained with the franchise through the early development of the group that would become known for grit, defense and physicality. His presence gave Memphis a marketable young star during a rebuilding period. The later tension was that the best Grizzlies playoff breakthrough came while Gay was injured, and the front office eventually moved him to rebalance the roster. Even so, Memphis controlled a valuable young scorer for more than six seasons and later converted him into additional players. That longevity gives the Grizzlies the slight edge.

sections.heading: Battier Was More Valuable to Houston Than His Box Score Suggested
sections.body: Battier’s Houston impact was built on assignments and decisions that ordinary scoring totals miss. He routinely defended the opponent’s best wing, helped structure the team’s rotations and spaced the floor for Yao’s post game and McGrady’s creation. The Rockets won fifty-two games in his first season, fifty-five in his second and produced the celebrated twenty-two-game winning streak in 2007-08. Injuries to the stars repeatedly limited the team’s postseason ceiling, but Battier was part of a defense-first identity that kept Houston competitive through instability. In 2009 the Rockets finally advanced beyond the first round and pushed the eventual champion Lakers to seven games despite losing Yao during the series. Battier did not solve the franchise’s health problems, yet he performed the role Houston purchased. The club received several seasons of high-level complementary play rather than an empty win-now rental.

sections.heading: Gay’s Scoring Did Not Automatically Create More Team Success
sections.body: Gay became the more productive individual scorer, but Memphis’s results complicate a runaway verdict. The Grizzlies missed the playoffs during his first four seasons. When they earned the franchise’s first series victory in 2011, Gay was sidelined by a shoulder injury, and the lineup’s identity increasingly centered on Zach Randolph, Marc Gasol, Mike Conley and Tony Allen. Gay remained talented, but his shot profile, salary and overlap with the team’s preferred style led Memphis to trade him in 2013. That later deal brought Tayshaun Prince, Ed Davis, Austin Daye and a second-round pick through a three-team structure. The return helped maintain depth but did not become another star. Memphis deserves strong credit for acquiring and developing Gay, yet his presence did not independently transform the franchise. This is why the margin over Houston is slight rather than decisive.

sections.heading: The Deal Was a Genuine Timeline Exchange
sections.body: Many draft-night trades are described as win-now versus rebuild even when both sides are simply guessing. This one embodied the distinction. Houston exchanged a young, high-variance scorer for a veteran whose value was clearest beside existing stars. Memphis exchanged a proven complementary player for a prospect who could grow into a larger offensive role. Each team largely received what it sought. The disagreement comes from how to weigh the years and control attached to Gay against Battier’s fit and playoff utility. Memphis gained more long-term individual value, but Houston did not make a reckless error. The Rockets were trying to contend before injuries and age closed the Yao-McGrady window, and Battier improved that effort immediately. A slight Grizzlies edge recognizes that Gay’s extended production and later trade value exceeded Battier’s return without pretending Houston’s side lacked strategic success.

sections.heading: The Grades Reward Both Outcomes but Separate Their Scale
sections.body: Memphis earns an A-minus because Gay became a high-level scorer, stayed through multiple phases of the roster and retained enough value to support a later trade. The grade stops short of A or A-plus because Swift contributed little, Gay was not central to the first great playoff run and the eventual return did not create another foundational asset. Houston earns a B-plus because Battier was an excellent fit, improved the defense, supported several fifty-win teams and helped the Rockets win a playoff series. The Rockets do not receive an A because they surrendered the rights to a younger player with far greater individual upside and did not reach the conference finals during Battier’s tenure. The transaction is a strong example of both sides making coherent decisions while one side still captures more cumulative value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Grizzlies Edge. Memphis acquired six-plus seasons of Rudy Gay’s scoring and retained later trade value, while Houston received exactly the elite complementary defender and spacer it wanted around Yao Ming and Tracy McGrady. Battier made the Rockets better, so this is not a lopsided loss. Memphis earns A-minus; Houston receives B-plus.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Why the Battier–Gay Trade Still Resists a Simple Winner
featuredDeepDive.intro: The transaction became a long-running argument about how teams should value fit, upside and timing. Gay was the better individual scorer and the younger asset. Battier was the better immediate role player for Houston’s stars. Both descriptions are true, which is why the verdict depends on separating team objectives from total realized value.

sections.heading: Battier Was a Scarce Type of Win-Now Player
sections.body: Veterans are often labeled win-now acquisitions merely because they are older. Battier’s value was more specific. He could guard multiple forward types, understand complex help responsibilities, make quick decisions and space the floor without disrupting star usage. Those traits are difficult to find in one player and become especially valuable on a roster already committed to two high-usage creators. Houston did not need Gay to become a twenty-point scorer several years later if the championship window closed first. It needed someone who could improve playoff matchups immediately. Battier’s influence on shot quality, communication and lineup balance made him a premium role player rather than ordinary depth. The Rockets’ decision therefore represented a deliberate purchase of scarce fit. The price was high, but the target was not replaceable by any low-usage wing.

sections.heading: Gay Gave Memphis a Developmental Centerpiece During a Transition
sections.body: The Grizzlies had reached the playoffs with veterans but had not won a series, and the roster needed another long-term direction. Gay supplied a player fans could watch develop through mistakes and expanded responsibility. His athleticism created transition offense, his size allowed him to shoot over defenders and his scoring improved as he gained experience. Memphis could market a young wing while rebuilding around future pieces. Even though the later grit-and-grind identity did not depend on Gay as its sole engine, his acquisition helped the franchise bridge from the Pau Gasol era to the next core. Young players with demonstrated twenty-point scoring ability retain market value, and Memphis eventually used Gay in another roster-balancing deal. The Grizzlies’ edge begins with that extended control.

sections.heading: Houston’s Missing Playoff Breakthrough Was Mostly About Star Health
sections.body: It would be misleading to blame Battier for Houston’s limited postseason results. McGrady and Yao repeatedly suffered injuries that disrupted the intended roster. The 2009 team finally won a first-round series, then lost McGrady before the playoffs and Yao during the second round. Battier defended Kobe Bryant and contributed within a group that pushed Los Angeles to Game 7. A role player cannot compensate fully for the absence of franchise stars. The Rockets acquired Battier to complement health, not replace it. This context supports the B-plus grade. Houston paid a significant opportunity cost, but it also received a player who performed his job in high-leverage games. The deal’s failure to produce a title was not evidence that the fit thesis was wrong.

sections.heading: Memphis Eventually Decided Gay’s Salary and Role Did Not Fit Its Best Team
sections.body: By 2013 the Grizzlies had found a different formula. Conley organized the offense, Randolph and Gasol controlled the interior, and Allen defined the perimeter defense. Gay’s scoring remained useful, but his contract and shot volume complicated the team’s financial and tactical balance. Memphis traded him in a three-team deal and continued reaching the playoffs. That decision does not erase the value of acquiring Gay in 2006. It does show why the grade should not become A-plus simply because he scored more than Battier. The Grizzlies eventually concluded that the roster could function better with depth and flexibility. Gay was a valuable asset, but not an irreplaceable franchise engine. The slight-edge verdict captures that limitation.

sections.heading: The Best Evaluation Separates Decision Quality From Outcome Quantity
sections.body: Houston made a defensible decision and received a successful role player. Memphis received the greater quantity of long-term individual production. Those conclusions can coexist. A trade grade should not force every coherent win-now move into a loss simply because the prospect became a scorer, nor should it ignore the extra seasons and control attached to the prospect. The Rockets’ B-plus measures how well Battier served the intended window. Memphis’s A-minus measures the larger cumulative value of Gay and his later convertibility. The narrow spread respects both strategy and result. It also explains why the debate lasted: each side can point to a different form of success without inventing facts or relying on hypothetical championships.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Memphis wins by a small margin because Gay delivered the longer and more valuable asset life. Houston still deserves substantial credit for identifying a near-perfect complementary piece and receiving meaningful playoff utility. This was a good trade by the Rockets and a slightly better one by the Grizzlies.

sections.heading: Houston Received Scola Rights and Jackie Butler for Two Assets
sections.body: On July 12, 2007, Houston received the NBA rights to Argentine power forward Luis Scola and center Jackie Butler from San Antonio. The Spurs acquired Vassilis Spanoulis and Houston's 2009 second-round selection, eventually the No. 53 choice used on Nando De Colo. The original transaction has those four specific assets, according to the teams' transaction histories. The trade was not an exchange of two already established NBA starters, nor does it need an invented extra consideration. Houston could bring the seasoned overseas star Scola into the league while absorbing Butler's contract; the Spurs obtained a contract and another second-round opportunity.

sections.heading: Scola Logged 386 Rockets Games and 343 Starts
sections.body: Scola became the source of Houston's on-court return. From 2007-08 through 2011-12 he played 386 regular-season games, starting 343, and averaged 14.5 points and 7.7 rebounds. He earned All-Rookie honors, then started all 82 Rockets games in 2008-09 at 12.7 points and 8.8 boards; in the 13-game 2009 postseason he contributed 14.4 points and 8.4 rebounds per game. The five-year Houston stint ended when the Rockets used the 2012 amnesty provision to waive him and Phoenix claimed him. That wasn't a later trade asset Houston received. Jackie Butler played no Houston NBA games; he was waived October 29, 2007.

sections.heading: Spanoulis Was Waived but the Pick Yielded De Colo
sections.body: San Antonio waived Spanoulis on August 13, 2007, so he contributed no regular-season games for the Spurs after this transaction. The second-rounder did convert into No. 53 Nando De Colo in 2009. After three seasons in Spain, he joined San Antonio for 2012-13 and played 72 NBA games at 3.8 points per game; he added 26 Spurs appearances in 2013-14 before a separate February 2014 trade sent him to Toronto for Austin Daye. The Spurs therefore obtained 98 De Colo games plus his eventual trade value, not literally zero basketball return. That small delayed benefit and the contract consequences do not approach five Scola seasons, supporting the preserved Houston A+ against San Antonio D.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win — Houston A+, San Antonio D. Houston converted Scola's rights into 386 NBA games, 343 starts and five years of 14.5-point, 7.7-rebound production; Butler was waived without a Rockets regular-season appearance. San Antonio waived Spanoulis before opening night but used No. 53 on De Colo, who played 98 Spurs games before a separate 2014 trade. The graded basketball edge favors Houston without inventing extra consideration, erasing De Colo's legitimate playing time or counting Scola's Phoenix years as Houston output.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Luis Scola to the Rockets: Five Houston Years for Spanoulis and the De Colo Pick
featuredDeepDive.intro: The July 12, 2007 Rockets–Spurs exchange paired rights with contract considerations rather than two equivalent current NBA players. Houston received the NBA rights to Luis Scola and Jackie Butler; San Antonio received Vassilis Spanoulis and Houston's 2009 second-round pick. The pick turned into Nando De Colo at No. 53 and eventually delivered 98 regular-season Spurs appearances. Scola produced 386 Rockets games and a five-season average of 14.5 points and 7.7 rebounds. Neither Butler nor Spanoulis played a regular-season game for the acquiring club after the deal. The original Rockets Win and Houston A+/San Antonio D grades stay intact, with Houston's later 2012 amnesty decision and San Antonio's 2014 De Colo trade treated as separate acts.

sections.heading: The NBA Rights Structure Made Scola Accessible to Houston
sections.body: Scola had played professionally overseas while San Antonio controlled his NBA rights. The 2007 transaction transferred those rights, not a player already established as a Spurs NBA rotation contributor. Houston simultaneously acquired Jackie Butler, who had played for the Spurs, and sent San Antonio former Rockets guard Vassilis Spanoulis and a future second-round pick. The July 12, 2007 league transaction log names those four pieces without a separately identifiable extra first-rounder or player. Acquiring rights mattered because Houston still needed to bring Scola into the NBA after his international career. The Rockets achieved that aim and signed a productive forward alongside Yao Ming and Tracy McGrady. San Antonio's motives included player control and contract management, but those considerations do not transform the rights to Scola into any San Antonio on-court contribution after the deal.

sections.heading: The Five Rockets Seasons Add Up to 386 Games
sections.body: Houston's return was unusually reliable for an overseas-rights conversion. In the 2007-08 rookie NBA season, Scola appeared in all 82 games and made 39 starts while averaging 10.3 points and 6.4 rebounds, earning All-Rookie First Team recognition. He started all 82 games in 2008-09, scoring 12.7 points with 8.8 rebounds per game. Scola then averaged 16.2 points and 8.6 rebounds in 2009-10, followed by further productive campaigns in 2010-11 and 2011-12. The official Phoenix Suns release when the Suns claimed him through amnesty in July 2012 records 386 Houston games, 343 starts and 14.5 points with 7.7 rebounds over five seasons. Those figures belong directly to Houston, not to hypothetical future team achievements. His Rockets tenure ended through an amnesty waiver, not a trade that returned a new draft pick to Houston.

sections.heading: The 2009 Playoffs Showed Why His Starting Role Was Valuable
sections.body: Scola's contribution translated into postseason possessions. During Houston's 2009 playoff run he started all 13 games and averaged 14.4 points with 8.4 rebounds, helping the Rockets reach a seven-game Western Conference semifinal series against the Lakers. That is a specific, documentable contribution from the 2007 trade rather than a vague claim that he helped the club contend. It also has limits. Houston did not win a championship with Scola, and his later time with Phoenix, Indiana and Toronto cannot be counted as Rockets production. Houston's A+ is rooted in the player it was able to field over five NBA seasons and the rebounding and scoring he supplied alongside the team's stars. The trade's usefulness survived changes in the surrounding Rockets roster because Scola continued to provide an inside scoring option after McGrady's and Yao's availability fluctuated.

sections.heading: The Spurs Waived Spanoulis but Their Pick Yielded De Colo
sections.body: The other side of the transaction was not literally without value. San Antonio waived Spanoulis on August 13, 2007, meaning the former Rockets guard never appeared in a Spurs NBA game. But the acquired 2009 second-round choice became the 53rd overall selection, French guard Nando De Colo. After developing overseas, De Colo signed with San Antonio in July 2012 and played 72 games in 2012-13, followed by 26 Spurs games in 2013-14. He averaged 3.8 points in his first Spurs season and 4.3 in his second. On February 20, 2014, San Antonio traded De Colo to Toronto for Austin Daye, another transaction that was not part of the original Scola package. The 98 NBA games and later tradeability of a No. 53 selection deserve recognition, though they are much smaller than Houston's 386-game starting forward return.

sections.heading: Neither Acquired Secondary Player Played for the New Club
sections.body: The Butler and Spanoulis pieces illustrate why counting incoming names is not enough. Butler arrived at Houston with a contract and previous NBA minutes, but the Rockets waived him on October 29, 2007, before he logged a regular-season game for the franchise. Spanoulis had appeared in 31 games for Houston the previous season, but San Antonio waived him in August 2007 before its new campaign began. Neither player's earlier experience should be moved into the receiving team's results. The Spurs' real late basketball value came from De Colo via the second-round pick, not from Spanoulis; Houston's direct value came from Scola, not Butler. In July 2012, the Rockets used amnesty to waive Scola and Phoenix claimed him, another distinct step that did not create a new Rockets trade return. That bounded reading supports Houston's decisive advantage without erasing or manufacturing any source asset.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win — Houston A+, San Antonio D. Scola produced 386 Houston appearances, 343 starts and five useful NBA seasons at 14.5 points and 7.7 rebounds per game. The Spurs' incoming Spanoulis contract ended with an August 2007 waiver, but the 2009 second-rounder became No. 53 Nando De Colo, who later played 98 Spurs games before the 2014 Toronto transaction. Jackie Butler played no Houston regular-season game. Financial context helps explain San Antonio's original decision, while the documented playing return justifies the much stronger Houston grade.

sections.heading: A Late-Summer Exchange of Two Young Guards
sections.body: Houston traded Sean Singletary to Phoenix for D.J. Strawberry on August 25, 2008. Both were guards whose value centered on whether they could earn a place in a rotation rather than established starting-level contributions. Houston received Strawberry directly and Phoenix received Singletary directly; this was a simple player-for-player exchange with no verified cash payment or conditional pick. The timing put each club in position to reassess a backcourt option before the coming season.

sections.heading: Neither Player Turned the Transaction Into a Major Return
sections.body: The transaction swapped one low-cost guard prospect for another. Each team gained a new player to evaluate but surrendered a similarly uncertain option. The surviving transaction histories identify who changed teams; they do not support inventing a major subsequent asset chain or turning either young player into a proven star. The useful conclusion is the limited scale of what both clubs exchanged, not a generic formula about all roster moves in the offseason.

sections.heading: The Matching Ds Fit a Marginal Personnel Swap
sections.body: Houston and Phoenix each receive a D, with an Even Trade verdict. That conclusion reflects two comparable, low-impact roster opportunities and the absence of a documented breakout attributable to either acquisition. Houston’s calculation favored Strawberry over Singletary; Phoenix made the opposite exchange. Nothing in the cited ledger establishes a return that merits calling one franchise the durable winner.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Houston D, Phoenix D. The Rockets obtained D.J. Strawberry and the Suns acquired Sean Singletary in a direct swap of young guards. The sourced record does not show a decisive downstream gain for either club. Both received a limited roster option, supporting equal low grades rather than a manufactured winner.

sections.heading: Houston Purchased Jermaine Taylor’s Draft Rights
sections.body: On June 25, 2009, Houston obtained the rights to Jermaine Taylor from Washington. The Wizards received cash considerations, not an incoming player or another draft choice. The rights transaction gave Houston the opportunity to bring an identified prospect into its system while allowing Washington to collect money for the asset. Keeping the outgoing return labeled as cash is important because the source records do not supply a price that could support a monetary profit calculation.

sections.heading: A Cash-for-Rights Swap Carries Different Risks for Each Club
sections.body: Washington converted Taylor’s rights into a known type of financial consideration, while Houston accepted the uncertainty attached to an incoming player prospect. The trade record supports that contrast without proving why each front office preferred its route. Houston could evaluate Taylor’s roster fit and potential development; Washington no longer carried that player’s rights. No extra player movement should be attributed to the Wizards or Rockets because it is absent from the documented exchange.

sections.heading: Why Neither Side Receives More Than a D
sections.body: The canonical ledger assigns each club D and records an Even Trade. Taylor’s rights were identifiable basketball property, but the exchange itself does not establish a standout eventual return for Houston. Washington’s cash figure is unavailable, so a higher valuation would require unsupported financial assumptions. The equal low grades communicate the limits of the documented upside on both sides rather than treating the deal as a zero-value transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Houston D, Washington D. The Rockets received Jermaine Taylor’s draft rights; the Wizards received cash considerations of an unverified amount. Houston acquired a player-development opportunity, while Washington chose a financial return. Neither documented outcome justifies a clear higher grade, and no additional assets belong in the transaction.

sections.heading: The Knicks Reacquired Marcus Camby for a Five-Part Houston Return
sections.body: In July 2012, New York brought veteran center Marcus Camby back from Houston in a sign-and-trade. The Rockets received guards Toney Douglas, Jerome Jordan and Josh Harrellson, plus second-round selections in 2014 and 2015. The eventual selections were Nick Johnson at No. 42 in 2014 and Montrezl Harrell at No. 32 in 2015. Houston collected more than a temporary salary filler: the draft choices were two distinct future roster opportunities.

sections.heading: Camby’s Second Knicks Stint Was Short and Limited
sections.body: Camby had been a productive rebounder and defender for many years, including part of the prior season in Houston. New York acquired him at age 38 to provide familiar frontcourt support. His 2012–13 return amounted to only 24 regular-season games, with four starts and 10.4 minutes per appearance. That restricted availability is the clearest reason the Knicks’ F grade is so much lower than a review based on Camby’s earlier reputation might suggest.

sections.heading: Houston’s Picks Created Longer-Term Value Options
sections.body: Douglas, Jordan and Harrellson did not form a new Rockets core, but the package did not depend solely on their individual scoring. The 2014 second-round selection produced Nick Johnson, and the 2015 choice produced Montrezl Harrell. Harrell later became a useful NBA frontcourt player, even though not all of his later performance belongs directly to Houston’s roster. His selection remains attributable to the draft capital the Rockets acquired in this deal; it should not be confused with an unrelated pick.

sections.heading: The C Versus F Result Follows the Identified Return
sections.body: Houston has a C in the canonical ledger, compared with F for New York. Those grades express a clear Rockets win without treating every incoming prospect as a long-term success. Houston obtained five named assets and two later selections, while the Knicks’ immediate intended benefit produced just 24 Camby games. The trade shows the cost of paying multiple younger assets and picks for a veteran whose health and age restricted the actual playing return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win — Houston C, New York F. Houston received Toney Douglas, Jerome Jordan, Josh Harrellson and the 2014 and 2015 second-round picks that became Nick Johnson and Montrezl Harrell. The Knicks received only 24 regular-season games from 38-year-old Marcus Camby in his return. The documented difference in usable assets supports the strong retrospective grade gap without crediting unrelated later moves.

sections.heading: Houston Paid for the Player Harden Could Become
sections.body: The Rockets sent Kevin Martin, Jeremy Lamb, two first-round picks, and a second-round pick to Oklahoma City for James Harden, Cole Aldrich, Daequan Cook, and Lazar Hayward. Harden had already won Sixth Man of the Year and displayed elite efficiency, but he had never controlled an NBA offense. Houston evaluated his creation skills rather than his bench label and immediately committed to making him the franchise centerpiece.

sections.heading: The Role Change Revealed an MVP
sections.body: Harden's transition from third option to primary engine was immediate. He became one of the league's highest-volume scorers and playmakers, eventually winning the 2018 MVP while leading Houston to a franchise-record 65 victories. Across eight full seasons, the Rockets built multiple contenders around his isolation scoring, pick-and-roll command, foul pressure, and passing. The trade did not merely add a star; it established an entire organizational identity.

sections.heading: Houston Reached the Edge of the Finals
sections.body: The Rockets reached the Western Conference finals in 2015 and again in 2018. The second run produced a 3-2 lead over the defending champion Warriors before Chris Paul's hamstring injury and Houston's Game 7 shooting collapse. A championship never arrived, but sustained contention against a dynasty carries major value. Harden gave the franchise repeated legitimate title chances that the outgoing package could not approach.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Received Useful Pieces, Not a Replacement
sections.body: Kevin Martin supplied efficient scoring for one season, Lamb developed into an NBA rotation wing, and the draft return produced Steven Adams, Mitch McGary, and Alex Abrines. Adams became a long-term starting center and an important part of several playoff teams. That value prevents the trade from being literally empty, but none of the pieces replaced Harden's creation or preserved the historic ceiling of the Durant-Westbrook-Harden core.

sections.heading: Financial Pressure Does Not Reduce the Outcome Cost
sections.body: Oklahoma City's decision was tied to contract negotiations, tax concerns, and the belief that the roster could remain elite without paying Harden as a maximum-level star. Those constraints explain the process but do not change the result. The Thunder moved a 23-year-old future MVP before testing him in a larger role, and the return never recreated his offensive value. The D grade reflects the magnitude of that lost upside.

sections.heading: Why the Verdict Is Overwhelming
sections.body: Houston surrendered real assets and deserves credit for recognizing a market inefficiency. Harden's production, MVP, scoring titles, playoff runs, and eventual trade value overwhelmed the cost. Oklahoma City found a quality center and several contributors, yet the franchise broke apart one of the greatest young cores ever assembled. The A-plus versus D split is not hindsight exaggeration; it matches the difference between a franchise era and a supporting package.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Houston won decisively. The Rockets identified a future primary creator before the league had fully priced him, handed Harden the offense, and received an MVP plus eight seasons of contention. Oklahoma City's return included Steven Adams and useful rotation value, but it did not replace Harden or preserve the ceiling of the Durant-Westbrook core. The grades remain Houston A-plus and Oklahoma City D, with Rockets Win.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The Trade That Turned a Sixth Man Into a Franchise
featuredDeepDive.intro: The central insight behind Houston's 2012 gamble was role projection. Harden's Oklahoma City résumé already showed efficiency, passing feel, and late-game skill, but the Thunder's hierarchy concealed how much offense he could carry. The Rockets paid a substantial prospect-and-pick package before his next contract was resolved, then designed the team around the exact abilities that had been compressed in a sixth-man role.

sections.heading: The Timing Made Houston's Evaluation More Valuable
sections.body: Harden was traded days before the season, leaving Houston little time to integrate a new centerpiece. That urgency could have magnified the risk, but it also allowed the Rockets to acquire him before another year of expanded production raised the price. The deal rewarded a front office willing to make its largest decision from underlying skills rather than waiting for conventional superstar credentials.

sections.heading: Harden Gave Houston a Repeatable Offensive Advantage
sections.body: His ability to create threes, rim attempts, free throws, and passes from the same action made Houston difficult to scheme against. Different supporting casts came and went, yet the Rockets could remain competitive because Harden generated efficient offense at extraordinary volume. The transaction's value therefore extended beyond his individual awards; it gave the organization a stable framework for roster construction.

sections.heading: The 2018 Team Shows the Difference Between Failure and No Title
sections.body: Houston's best Harden team won 65 games and pushed Golden State to seven games. The Rockets did not finish the championship run, but a trade is not worthless unless it produces a ring. Creating one of the few teams capable of threatening a dynasty is meaningful realized value. Harden's presence made that level possible, and it kept Houston relevant across seasons in which many contenders rose and disappeared.

sections.heading: Steven Adams Was a Good Outcome Inside a Bad Exchange
sections.body: The pick that became Adams gave Oklahoma City a physical, durable center who started for years and fit beside Westbrook and Durant. Acknowledging that success improves the analysis because it shows the Thunder did not receive nothing. The problem is scale. A strong starting center, a one-year scorer in Martin, and additional prospects are not an adequate replacement for a player who became an MVP-level offensive system.

sections.heading: The Trade Changed Both Franchises' Historical Narratives
sections.body: Houston's modern identity is inseparable from Harden's scoring, playmaking, and postseason runs. Oklahoma City's history is equally marked by the question of what the Durant-Westbrook-Harden core might have achieved if preserved. That asymmetry is the deepest evidence of the verdict. One side acquired the defining player of an era; the other side is still asked why it allowed that player to leave.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Rockets made one of the most consequential trades in modern NBA history. Harden became an MVP, a perennial scoring leader, and the engine of multiple conference-finals teams, while the Thunder's respectable return never approached his value. Steven Adams gives Oklahoma City a meaningful asset to credit, but the trade still separated the franchises dramatically. Houston A-plus, Oklahoma City D, Rockets Win.

sections.heading: Houston Traded Veterans for an Unproven Lottery Forward
sections.body: On February 20, 2013, Houston acquired Thomas Robinson, Francisco García and Tyler Honeycutt from Sacramento. The Kings received Patrick Patterson, Cole Aldrich, Toney Douglas and cash considerations. Robinson had been selected fifth overall in the previous draft but had not developed quickly in Sacramento. The Rockets hoped a change of setting would unlock a high-upside big man while García offered veteran perimeter play. Sacramento obtained older NBA contributors it could use immediately.

sections.heading: Patterson Gave Sacramento a Real NBA Rotation Player
sections.body: Patrick Patterson was an established, versatile frontcourt option after his Houston seasons. Sacramento received immediate shooting and defensive usefulness, though he later moved to Toronto in a separate Rudy Gay transaction. Douglas brought guard depth and Aldrich offered a reserve-center option, neither of whom became a franchise centerpiece. The undisclosed cash payment was additional consideration that should be recorded without inventing its dollar amount or attributing unrelated later Kings transactions to this exchange.

sections.heading: Robinson’s Rockets Stay Was Short but Had a Follow-On Return
sections.body: Thomas Robinson played only nineteen regular-season games for Houston in 2012–13 before the Rockets moved him to Portland that July. That later trade returned two players’ rights and two second-round selections, eventually associated with Richaun Holmes and Dillon Brooks, although their full careers belong to subsequent transaction paths rather than automatically to Houston. García provided Houston with some useful wing minutes. Honeycutt made no meaningful long-term impact. The short Robinson tenure did not vindicate the original prospect gamble on its own.

sections.heading: The Grades Distinguish Sacramento’s Immediate Players from Houston’s Upside Bet
sections.body: Sacramento receives B-plus because Patterson provided a verified contributor and the return included Douglas, Aldrich and cash. Houston earns C-minus because the intended high-pick reclamation player was moved again within months and the other additions were mostly limited role players. The team got follow-on draft rights from moving Robinson, which prevents describing the first trade as entirely wasted. It did not realize a sustained breakout from Robinson himself.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Win — Sacramento B-plus, Houston C-minus. The Kings converted Robinson, García and Honeycutt into Patterson, Douglas, Aldrich and cash. Patterson was a dependable frontcourt contributor while Houston moved Robinson again after nineteen games. The Rockets recovered later assets through a separate Portland trade, but their original lottery-forward investment did not become lasting production. Sacramento obtained more direct basketball usefulness.

sections.heading: Houston Sent Marcus Morris to Phoenix for One 2013 Second
sections.body: On February 21, 2013, Houston traded Marcus Morris to Phoenix for the Suns' 2013 second-round pick. The Rockets' own trade-deadline recap confirms the exact direction and distinguishes this deal from Houston's separate acquisition of Thomas Robinson from Sacramento. Morris was a young forward already playing NBA minutes; the Rockets received a future draft choice rather than an immediate veteran. That Suns-origin selection became No. 34 in the June 2013 draft, when Houston chose guard Isaiah Canaan of Murray State. Treating Canaan as if he had been an existing Phoenix player in February would distort the original transaction. The two clubs made different bets: one obtained a forward who could contribute immediately, and the other accepted a later chance to draft a guard.

sections.heading: Morris Became a Regular Phoenix Forward Alongside His Twin
sections.body: Phoenix's official records establish that Morris arrived in February 2013 and later played 186 Suns games across parts of three seasons before moving to Detroit in July 2015. The split is 23 Phoenix appearances after the first trade, followed by 82 in 2013–14 and 81 in 2014–15. In his final Suns season he averaged 10.4 points, 4.8 rebounds and 1.6 assists, showing that Phoenix received more than a brief trial from the acquired forward. Joining his twin brother Markieff was part of the team's initial story, but their family relationship is not an extra trade asset. Phoenix eventually sent Morris to Detroit in a different three-player package, a separate transaction that should not inflate or erase the return on the 2013 trade.

sections.heading: Canaan Produced Real Houston Minutes Before His Own Trade
sections.body: Houston used the No. 34 pick on Isaiah Canaan and later brought him into its guard rotation. The NBA's player record lists 22 Rockets games in 2013–14 at 4.6 points per contest, followed by 25 games at 6.2 points in 2014–15. That was legitimate, limited NBA production from a second-round choice, not a total failed draft right. In February 2015, the Rockets sent Canaan and another 2015 second-round pick to Philadelphia for K.J. McDaniels, according to Houston's official announcement. The extra choice attached in 2015 must not be retroactively counted as part of the price Phoenix paid for Morris two years earlier. Canaan's later 76ers minutes also belong to his new team rather than Houston's direct 2013 return.

sections.heading: Why Phoenix Has the Higher Grade
sections.body: The Suns Win verdict assigns Phoenix B-minus and Houston D-minus. Marcus Morris played 186 regular-season games for Phoenix after the trade, including 81 appearances and 10.4 points per game in 2014-15. Houston's return became the No. 34 selection in the 2013 draft, Isaiah Canaan, who logged 47 games for the Rockets across two seasons. The difference in direct on-court use was considerable, although a second-round pick was always a developmental asset rather than a guarantee. Phoenix's advantage is credited to Morris's Suns tenure, not the seasons he later played for Detroit or other clubs. Likewise, Canaan's NBA production after leaving Houston belongs to his later teams, not to the Rockets' direct 2013 return. Those team-specific outcomes explain the higher Phoenix grade without presenting letter grades as a precise statistical formula.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Published Suns Win — Phoenix B-, Houston D-. On February 21, 2013, Phoenix acquired Marcus Morris for its 2013 second-round pick, which Houston used at No. 34 on Isaiah Canaan. Morris played 186 Suns games across parts of three seasons; Canaan appeared in 47 Rockets games before a separate 2015 trade involving another pick. The original transaction transferred a forward for one draft choice, not later Detroit or Philadelphia assets. The archived grades stay intact.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Marcus Morris for the Pick That Became Isaiah Canaan
featuredDeepDive.intro: The Rockets moved forward Marcus Morris to Phoenix at the 2013 deadline for a second-round selection later used on Isaiah Canaan. The Suns got three partial or full seasons of useful rotation minutes; Houston obtained a developing guard who played 47 games for the club before another deal. Both the original trade and the June draft selection are documented by Houston, while Phoenix's later release records 186 Morris appearances. A precise retrospective separates those direct returns from the later Morris-to-Detroit and Canaan-to-Philadelphia transactions and preserves the site's stored Suns Win verdict and B-/D- grades.

sections.heading: The Correct February 2013 Ledger and June Draft Conversion
sections.body: Houston's February 21, 2013 deadline recap identifies the outgoing player as Marcus Morris and the consideration from Phoenix as the Suns' 2013 second-round pick. That is a single future draft right, not a package of multiple selections or the rights to an already-drafted player. Four months later Houston selected Isaiah Canaan at No. 34. The Rockets' draft-night article identifies the Murray State guard and explains the team's interest in his perimeter shooting. The time separation is necessary to read the transaction correctly: Morris moved into the Suns' existing roster immediately, while the Rockets held a draft claim that could be exercised in June. The record should not confuse Houston's separate deadline trade involving Patrick Patterson and Thomas Robinson with this simpler player-for-pick exchange.

sections.heading: Why Morris Had Tangible Value During His Suns Tenure
sections.body: Phoenix reunited Morris with his twin Markieff, but the best performance evidence is ordinary NBA participation. The Suns announced in July 2015 that Morris had played 186 games for the club after arriving in February 2013. His Phoenix seasons included 82 games at 9.7 points in 2013–14 and 81 at 10.4 points in 2014–15. That gave the team repeatable forward depth over a period when it was experimenting with its roster and offensive spacing. In the 2014–15 campaign he also collected 4.8 rebounds and 1.6 assists per contest. Morris' eventual trade to Detroit in July 2015 involved Danny Granger and Reggie Bullock as well, so the future second-round compensation in that later agreement cannot be assigned solely to the original Houston transaction.

sections.heading: The Rockets' Pick Had Value but a Short First-Team Run
sections.body: Canaan's NBA record for Houston shows 22 appearances in his rookie season and 25 during 2014–15 before his transfer. He averaged 4.6 then 6.2 points while with the Rockets, working primarily as a developing perimeter guard. That is a return from a late second-round choice, even though it fell short of Morris' direct Phoenix game total and minutes. Houston's February 2015 announcement reveals that Canaan was later traded with an additional second-round pick to Philadelphia to acquire K.J. McDaniels. The 2015 pick was not supplied by Phoenix in February 2013 and must be tracked separately. Canaan then contributed to Philadelphia, but those 76ers starts cannot be counted as Rockets games. The grade should reflect Houston's own realized use and separate follow-up decisions.

sections.heading: How to Audit the B-Minus and D-Minus Without Borrowing Outcomes
sections.body: The current archive gives Phoenix a B-minus, Houston a D-minus, and records Suns Win. Phoenix received an active forward who appeared 186 times and took a regular role in two full Suns seasons. Houston turned the pick into a young guard with 47 regular-season appearances before moving him again. Those numbers are grounded in official team and player records, not assumptions about what a generic second-rounder should yield. Houston still had legitimate reasons to draft for shooting, and Canaan was not without NBA utility; both points temper a purely retrospective judgment. Changing the D-minus or B-minus would require comparing this deal with other archive cases using the same weighting of draft uncertainty, immediate production and downstream trade utility. The editorial repair leaves the stored result alone rather than automatically regrading.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Phoenix acquired Marcus Morris, who played 186 Suns games, and Houston acquired the 2013 second-round selection it used on No. 34 Isaiah Canaan, who played 47 Rockets games. The original exchange involved those two assets only. The later Morris/Granger/Bullock trade to Detroit and Houston's separate Canaan-plus-pick trade to Philadelphia are distinct. Suns Win, Phoenix B- and Houston D- are preserved pending consistent independent grading review.

sections.heading: The July 2013 Deal Cleared Robinson's Salary for Houston
sections.body: Houston sent 2012 No. 5 pick Thomas Robinson to Portland on July 10, 2013. In return the Rockets received the NBA rights to European forwards Kostas Papanikolaou and Marko Todorović, plus second-round choices for 2015 and 2017. The 2015 right was the less favorable of Denver's and Minnesota's selections; the 2017 choice later became No. 45. Houston had just made a major free-agent commitment to Dwight Howard, making flexibility on the roster and salary ledger valuable. This was not a direct trade of Robinson for a future All-Star or for two immediate rotation players. The Rockets obtained two uncertain international options, two transferable second-round assets and financial room. Portland acquired a recent lottery prospect who had struggled to establish himself in Sacramento and Houston.

sections.heading: Papanikolaou Produced Forty-Three Houston Games
sections.body: The first incoming player right to become NBA production for Houston was Papanikolaou. He came from Europe for the 2014-15 season and played 43 regular-season games, averaging 4.2 points, 2.7 rebounds and 2.0 assists in 18.5 minutes. Those modest statistics are an actual Rockets return and should not be replaced with his European achievements. The other acquired international right, Todorović, did not produce NBA regular-season games in Houston. A C grade for the Rockets must therefore account for one short supporting stint alongside the flexibility provided by the draft rights. The deal's greater value was that Houston kept the option to negotiate future moves involving both selections. Those later transfers require separate asset accounting, because Richaun Holmes and Dillon Brooks did not play for Houston as a direct result of the July agreement.

sections.heading: The 2015 No. 37 Right Was Used in a Philadelphia Deal
sections.body: Houston held the 2015 second-round selection ultimately associated with No. 37 Richaun Holmes, but did not draft the forward for its own roster. On February 19, 2015, the Rockets sent that pick and guard Isaiah Canaan to Philadelphia in a separate trade, acquiring K.J. McDaniels. The 76ers exercised the No. 37 choice on Holmes in June. That makes Holmes's later NBA production a Philadelphia-related draft result, not a Rockets box-score return. The selection still had real value to Houston because it helped complete the McDaniels transaction. Its trace runs from Denver and Minnesota draft conditions through Portland and Houston before reaching the 76ers. The Rockets' grade should credit negotiable pick value without pretending Holmes ever played for the franchise.

sections.heading: The 2017 No. 45 Pick Became a Memphis Rookie
sections.body: The other future choice became No. 45 Dillon Brooks in the 2017 draft. Houston made the selection and immediately transferred the rights to Memphis for a future second-round pick. The NBA's draft trade tracker and the Grizzlies' official announcement both identify this exchange. Brooks then began his NBA playing career with Memphis, not Houston. The future second Houston received in that 2017 agreement was a separate asset from the original 2013 Portland transaction. This is why saying Houston 'got Dillon Brooks' in 2013 can be misleading: the Rockets controlled a selection that ultimately bore his name but chose to exchange the draft right. Brooks's later Memphis defensive and scoring contributions do not become Houston team production. The real Houston benefit was the opportunity to transact again.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win — Houston C, Portland D. Houston cleared Thomas Robinson salary and acquired Papanikolaou rights (43 subsequent Rockets games), Todorovic rights and future 2015/2017 seconds. Houston later moved the No. 37 right to Philadelphia, which drafted Holmes, and the No. 45 Brooks right to Memphis. Portland received 102 Robinson games, not zero return.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Thomas Robinson to Portland in 2013: Houston’s Four-Asset Pick Chain
featuredDeepDive.intro: Portland took Robinson in July 2013, while Houston gained European rights and two future seconds. Later trades sent the picks associated with Richaun Holmes and Dillon Brooks to Philadelphia and Memphis; neither NBA career was Houston production.

sections.heading: Robinson's Portland Audition Was More Than Zero Minutes
sections.body: Portland actually played Thomas Robinson after acquiring him. The power forward appeared in 70 Blazers regular-season games in 2013-14, then 32 in 2014-15 before he moved to another team. His scoring never matched the expectations of a fifth overall draft selection, but he supplied interior rebounding and reserve minutes. Treating the move as if Portland received an injured player who never reached its roster would exaggerate the loss. The franchise was taking a low-cost opportunity on a former top-five prospect during a period when LaMarcus Aldridge and Damian Lillard were central to its roster. The experiment lasted 102 combined regular-season appearances without developing into a long-term Portland starting role. That is a modest direct return from the original exchange, distinct from the four incoming Houston rights and picks.

sections.heading: The European Rights Had Different Outcomes
sections.body: Houston received the draft rights to Papanikolaou and Todorović from Portland, but their eventual NBA histories were not identical. Papanikolaou joined the Rockets in 2014-15 and played 43 regular-season games with an identifiable passing and shooting role. Todorović remained outside the NBA, so his international career should not be counted as Rockets playing production. Both rights had value on trade day because Houston could negotiate with the players or move those rights as components of later agreements. The fact that only one became an actual Houston contributor explains why the retained C grade is more restrained than the mere count of four incoming assets might imply. The other two assets were future draft choices, which delivered their clearest value when Houston later used them in separate Philadelphia and Memphis transactions.

sections.heading: The Holmes and Brooks Names Are Asset-Chain Labels
sections.body: Holmes and Brooks appear in the canonical ledger because the 2015 and 2017 seconds acquired from Portland were ultimately used at No. 37 and No. 45. Neither player belonged to Houston's regular-season lineup through those picks. Houston exchanged the No. 37 right with Isaiah Canaan to Philadelphia in the February 2015 K.J. McDaniels deal, and the 76ers selected Holmes. Houston then selected Brooks at No. 45 in 2017 but transferred his rights to Memphis for another future second. These steps are useful proof that the 2013 compensation remained tradable over time. They are not proof that Houston developed either NBA contributor. A retrospective grade must distinguish a pick's eventual name from the NBA franchise that exercised and retained the player. Otherwise a fair account of salary-clearing flexibility becomes an invented Rockets player history.

sections.heading: A Rockets Win Based on Flexibility and a Smaller Direct Return
sections.body: The original ledger preserves Rockets Win, Houston C and Portland D. Houston obtained two international rights plus future second-round choices; it received 43 actual Papanikolaou games and later used the picks in separate trades for other assets. Portland obtained 102 Robinson regular-season appearances across parts of two campaigns before abandoning the long-term prospect experiment. The Rockets also gained flexibility by moving Robinson's contract at an important point in their Dwight Howard offseason. None of this implies that Houston directly received the later NBA careers of Holmes or Brooks, or that Portland received no basketball minutes. The grade spread is modest and appropriately limited: Houston achieved a payroll and optionality objective, while Portland made a speculative player bet that never produced a sustained starting forward. The historical winner should follow those actual asset paths.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Houston C and Portland D in the preserved Rockets Win verdict. The Rockets gained salary flexibility and tradable rights, with Papanikolaou contributing 43 games. The 2015 No. 37 Holmes pick went to Philadelphia in a separate trade, and 2017 No. 45 Brooks rights went to Memphis. Portland received 102 Robinson games without a long-term starter.

sections.heading: Houston Acquired McDaniels at the Deadline
sections.body: Houston took K.J. McDaniels from Philadelphia on February 19, 2015. The Rockets sent Isaiah Canaan and a 2015 second-round pick, described as the less favorable of the Denver and Minnesota selections. That additional draft consideration is vital to the comparison. Philadelphia wasn't exchanging McDaniels for Canaan alone, and Houston didn't merely acquire a prospect without giving the 76ers a later selection. The two organizations chose different combinations of immediate guard depth and future draft value.

sections.heading: The Second Became Richaun Holmes
sections.body: The selection sent to Philadelphia became No. 37 in 2015 and was used on Richaun Holmes. The Sixers therefore received both Canaan and a specific prospect outcome. Houston's incoming side was limited to McDaniels in the recorded package. The identity of the Holmes choice explains why a second-round pick was more than an abstraction in this trade, though any value generated after that asset left Philadelphia must be traced rather than simply credited for his entire career elsewhere.

sections.heading: Two Philadelphia Returns Outweighed One Rocket
sections.body: The Rockets chose McDaniels as an immediate acquisition, but the 76ers' combination of Canaan and Holmes's draft position provided more evaluated value. The retained team grades heavily favor Philadelphia. This is not a claim that Houston knew in advance exactly what No. 37 would become. It is a review of how the incoming assets ultimately developed compared with the single McDaniels return. The source package remains straightforward: one player sent by Philadelphia, one veteran and one pick sent by Houston.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win. Philadelphia receives A for Isaiah Canaan and the 2015 No. 37 selection used on Richaun Holmes, while Houston receives F for K.J. McDaniels. The pick conversion and two-part compensation supported the stronger Sixers outcome in this specific deadline transaction.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: 2015 McDaniels Trade: Isaiah Canaan and the Pick That Became Richaun Holmes
featuredDeepDive.intro: On February 19, 2015, Houston acquired K.J. McDaniels from Philadelphia in exchange for Isaiah Canaan and the less favorable of the Denver and Minnesota 2015 second-round draft picks. The Rockets' official transaction announcement documents both pieces of outgoing compensation. That pick became No. 37, which Philadelphia used on Richaun Holmes. McDaniels never established a substantial Houston role; Canaan played in 99 games for Philadelphia and Holmes made 156 appearances over three 76ers seasons before a separate 2018 sale of his contract to Phoenix for cash. The original 76ers Win, Philadelphia A/Houston F grades are retained, with the pick's direct Philadelphia value separated from Holmes's later production with other NBA teams.

sections.heading: Houston Paid a Player and a Conditional Second for McDaniels
sections.body: The Rockets' February 19, 2015 announcement identifies the price precisely: Isaiah Canaan plus the less favorable of the Denver Nuggets and Minnesota Timberwolves 2015 second-round picks. Philadelphia sent K.J. McDaniels, a rookie defender who had already appeared in 52 games for the Sixers with 9.2 points, 3.8 rebounds and 1.3 blocks per game. Houston saw upside in a young wing's defense while challenging for Western Conference playoff position. The trade was not Canaan for McDaniels alone. Nor should it be collapsed into Houston's entirely separate deadline acquisition of Pablo Prigioni from the New York Knicks, which cost Alexey Shved and different second-round assets. The original pick's unusual protection was important because it determined the later selection Philadelphia owned, while the subsequent Prigioni package belonged to a different transaction.

sections.heading: The No. 37 Pick Became a Three-Year 76ers Center
sections.body: The second-round selection Houston conveyed landed at No. 37 on June 25, 2015. Philadelphia selected Bowling Green center-forward Richaun Holmes, a direct and named conversion of the acquired draft asset. Holmes played 51 games for the Sixers as a rookie at 5.6 points and 2.6 rebounds, then 57 games in 2016-17 at 9.8 points and 5.5 rebounds. A final 48-game Philadelphia season in 2017-18 completed 156 appearances in three years, averaging 7.4 points and 4.2 boards. Philadelphia's own July 2018 release confirms those totals and explains the endpoint: the team sent Holmes's contract to Phoenix for cash considerations. His subsequent Phoenix, Sacramento and other NBA output is real career history, but it must not be credited as on-court Philadelphia value after the 2018 departure. The 2015 pick nevertheless became an unusually useful late second-round choice.

sections.heading: Isaiah Canaan Played 99 76ers Games After the Deadline
sections.body: Canaan supplied the additional direct return that made the trade more than a single pick conversion. Following the February 2015 move, he played 22 Philadelphia games, started 12 and averaged 12.6 points and 3.1 assists, shooting 36.4 percent from deep. He then logged 77 games in 2015-16, starting 39 with an 11.0-point average and 2.3 made 3-pointers per game. Across those two partial/full Philadelphia seasons he appeared in 99 games. Canaan was not the center of a successful team rebuild, but he furnished actual guard minutes during a period when the Sixers were developing and testing younger players. By comparison McDaniels made just ten Houston regular-season appearances after the 2015 deadline and averaged 1.1 points before totaling 37 Houston games in 2015-16 and 29 more before departing in 2016-17. The contrast is between a 99-game guard return, Holmes's three Sixers seasons and a limited Rockets wing role.

sections.heading: Why the Outcome Is Strong for Philadelphia Without Inflating the Return
sections.body: The original Philadelphia A against Houston F grades reflect an unusual imbalance for a trade of modestly known players. The Rockets acquired McDaniels with hope of defensive development, but he never became a consistent rotation player for the club. The Sixers received Canaan, used the pick on Holmes, and later obtained cash in a separate 2018 contract sale. That later sale is a documented downstream step, not a second draft pick or a major return for the original McDaniels trade. Holmes's best NBA years in Sacramento and elsewhere similarly cannot be imported into Philadelphia's total. The original acquisition still looks lopsided on results: the Sixers got 99 Canaan regular-season games plus 156 Holmes games before the cash transaction, whereas McDaniels produced 76 total Rockets games in three partial seasons with limited minutes. Hindsight supports a clear Philadelphia win without claiming that the 2015 trade single-handedly built a future contender.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win — Philadelphia A, Houston F. Houston traded Isaiah Canaan and a protected-by-comparison 2015 second-round selection to obtain K.J. McDaniels. Philadelphia got 99 games from Canaan and selected Richaun Holmes 37th overall; Holmes added 156 76ers appearances before a separate 2018 trade to Phoenix for cash. McDaniels played 76 total Rockets regular-season games, generally in a limited reserve role. The separate Prigioni deadline trade and Holmes's post-Philadelphia career are excluded from this transaction's direct player-return calculation.
