sections.heading: The Buffalo Braves Sent Smith to Los Angeles for McMillian
sections.body: The original team sending Elmore Smith was the Buffalo Braves, the earlier franchise lineage now indexed as the Clippers. The Lakers sent Jim McMillian to Buffalo for the 7-foot center in September 1973. Two primary historical ledgers disagree on the precise calendar day: the Lakers' 2025-26 official media guide prints September 17, while Basketball-Reference's Buffalo transaction record uses September 12. The site's preserved canonical date follows the Lakers guide. No additional cash or draft pick is documented in the direct 1973 exchange. After Wilt Chamberlain's departure, Los Angeles wanted size and rim protection; Buffalo, built around Bob McAdoo, needed a productive scoring forward. These were different roster needs, not proof that Buffalo surrendered a star for nothing.

sections.heading: Smith’s First Lakers Season Brought a Defensive NBA Record
sections.body: Smith played 81 Lakers games in 1973-74 and averaged 12.5 points, 11.2 rebounds and 4.9 blocks per game. The most memorable performance came October 28, 1973 against Portland: 17 blocks, 12 points and 16 rebounds in a 111-98 Lakers victory. NBA.com's official account identifies those 17 rejections as the single-game record, dating to the first season the league officially tracked blocks. Smith was not just a name later included in a major trade; he supplied a full season of substantial interior defense right after arriving. The Lakers lost their championship-contender stability after Chamberlain retired, but the center they acquired gave the team a measurable skill it badly needed. Those blocks and rebounds are the immediate value of the original exchange.

sections.heading: Buffalo Received an 82-Game, 18.6-Point Starter
sections.body: McMillian's first Braves season was productive from beginning to end. In 1973-74 he played all 82 games, averaged 18.6 points and 7.4 rebounds with 3.1 assists, and provided perimeter scoring alongside league scoring champion Bob McAdoo. Buffalo finished 42-40 and made the playoffs after missing out the year before. That was genuine direct return from the Lakers, not the consolation prize of an unused draft right. His role complemented McAdoo rather than duplicating a second center, giving the Braves lineup balance as Ernie DiGregorio developed at point guard. A Buffalo A- grade fits a team acquiring a full-season offensive contributor. The later Kareem trade changes the Lakers' long-run advantage, but it should not erase what McMillian did in Western New York.

sections.heading: The Following Seasons Separate Availability From Star Power
sections.body: Smith played another 74 Lakers regular-season games in 1974-75, producing 10.9 points, 10.9 rebounds and 2.9 blocks per game. His block rate fell from the extraordinary 4.9 of his debut Lakers season but remained useful. McMillian, meanwhile, had 62 Buffalo appearances in 1974-75 at 14.3 points and 6.2 rebounds, then 74 more in 1975-76 at 15.8 points and 5.3 rebounds. These totals demonstrate that both receiving teams collected several seasons of basketball value from the 1973 move. They also show why the historical grades must account for different kinds of value. Buffalo got continued scoring and forward minutes; Los Angeles got a physically imposing center who later served as a pivotal component in a much larger negotiation.

sections.heading: The 1975 Kareem Trade Included Four Lakers Players
sections.body: On June 16, 1975, the Lakers sent Smith, Brian Winters, Dave Meyers and Junior Bridgeman to Milwaukee and received Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and Walt Wesley. Both the Lakers' own transaction guide and the NBA's 1975-76 historical review identify the complete four-player outgoing package. Because Smith arrived from Buffalo in 1973 and was personally part of that 1975 agreement, the path from the Braves deal to the Abdul-Jabbar acquisition is real and traceable. But Smith was one of four assets, not the single player exchanged for Kareem. Winters, Meyers and Bridgeman were significant considerations that cannot be erased to exaggerate the 1973 deal. This two-step chain gives Los Angeles a powerful later use for its acquired center, separate from Smith's two regular seasons in a Lakers uniform.

sections.heading: Lakers A+ and Braves A- Give Credit to Both Routes
sections.body: The inherited verdict favors Los Angeles but does not treat Buffalo's return as a failure. McMillian played 82 games at 18.6 points for the 1973-74 Braves and remained a useful forward in the following seasons. Smith recorded the 17-block record and averaged 4.9 blocks during his first Lakers season, then became one of four players sent away in the distinct Kareem Abdul-Jabbar agreement in 1975. The latter transaction helped define the Lakers' future, but no championship was directly delivered by Smith in 1973-74. The original trade's normalized Clippers franchise ID refers to the historical Buffalo Braves, not a Los Angeles Clippers team playing in 1973. With both roster contributions and the defensible downstream Smith asset path properly weighted, the recorded Lakers A+/Braves A- grades and Lakers Win verdict are retained.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win, Los Angeles A+ and Buffalo Braves (later Clippers lineage) A-. The Lakers received two useful Smith seasons, including an NBA-record 17 blocks against Portland on October 28, 1973, then sent Smith as ONE of four players in the separate 1975 package for Abdul-Jabbar and Walt Wesley. Buffalo received McMillian's 82-game, 18.6-point season and two additional useful forward seasons. Basketball-Reference dates the original swap September 12 while the Lakers' media guide lists September 17; the existing canonical September 17 has been preserved pending a definitive reconciliation.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Elmore Smith’s 17 Blocks, Buffalo’s McMillian and the Later Kareem Package
featuredDeepDive.intro: The September 1973 trade of Elmore Smith for Jim McMillian between the Buffalo Braves and Lakers gave both teams real playing value. Buffalo benefited immediately from an 82-game scoring forward, while Los Angeles acquired a 7-footer who led the NBA in blocks and later became part of the blockbuster Kareem Abdul-Jabbar package. The record warrants a narrow distinction: Smith's participation makes the later acquisition a legitimate downstream link, but four Lakers players went to Milwaukee, not Smith alone. The primary sources also disagree on the initial date, September 12 in Basketball-Reference versus September 17 in the Lakers' own guide. The original grades stay Lakers A+ and Braves A-.

sections.heading: A 1973 Date Disagreement, One Identifiable Buffalo-Lakers Deal
sections.body: The transaction's original franchise was the Buffalo Braves, the team later represented by the Clippers lineage in this database. Elmore Smith, a former third overall selection with two Buffalo seasons, went to the Lakers for Jim McMillian, a forward who had helped Los Angeles win its 1972 championship. The Buffalo Basketball-Reference transaction log dates the move September 12, 1973; the Lakers' official 2025-26 media guide prints September 17 and accidentally labels the acquired player 'Elmore Spencer.' Both point to the same McMillian-for-Smith exchange. The site's existing September 17 date is retained rather than silently changed in response to a conflict among primary historical records. Most important for the basketball evaluation, this was a direct two-player swap, with no attached draft choice, cash consideration or conditional rights stated by the original logs.

sections.heading: Smith’s 1973-74 Season Was About Protecting the Basket
sections.body: The Lakers had just lost Wilt Chamberlain from their active center rotation, which created a direct opportunity for Elmore Smith. In 81 games in 1973-74 he posted 12.5 points, 11.2 rebounds and a remarkable 4.9 blocks per game. NBA.com recounts the October 28 victory against Portland in which he played all 48 minutes and recorded 17 blocks, 12 points and 16 rebounds. That 17-block mark still tops the league's official single-game list. Those were on-court results received because Los Angeles acquired him in September. They show immediate defensive usefulness independent of later events and rebut any evaluation that treats Smith only as a placeholder in a future Kareem trade. Smith played 74 more Lakers games in 1974-75, adding 10.9 rebounds and 2.9 blocks per night before his next transaction.

sections.heading: McMillian Helped a Young Braves Team Reach the Postseason
sections.body: Jim McMillian arrived in Buffalo after averaging 18.9 points for the 1972-73 Lakers. His first Braves campaign produced 18.6 points, 7.4 rebounds and 3.1 assists across all 82 games. Alongside Bob McAdoo and rookie playmaker Ernie DiGregorio, that veteran scoring helped Buffalo finish 42-40 and qualify for its first NBA playoff series. Buffalo's subsequent McMillian seasons were less uniform but still valuable: 62 games at 14.3 points in 1974-75 and 74 at 15.8 points in 1975-76. That output is the direct source-backed Buffalo side of the ledger. McMillian did not win another championship with the Braves, but he contributed to a franchise emerging from poor early seasons. A Braves A- is thus grounded in actual points, minutes and playoff qualification, rather than reputation inherited from his time with the Lakers.

sections.heading: June 1975 Connected Smith to Abdul-Jabbar but Not Alone
sections.body: The clearest later link is the June 16, 1975 agreement with Milwaukee. The Lakers' own all-time transaction ledger lists Elmore Smith, Brian Winters, Dave Meyers and Junior Bridgeman as outgoing, with Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and Walt Wesley arriving from the Bucks. That exact package appears in the NBA's historical 1975-76 season review as well. Smith was therefore a real piece received from Buffalo in 1973 and later deployed for one of the sport's defining centers. However, the other three Lakers players were not marginal footnotes and the transaction also included Wesley on the incoming side. The 1973 exchange must not be summarized as Buffalo's Jim McMillian single-handedly turning into Abdul-Jabbar, nor should Smith be credited with all of Kareem's eventual Lakers titles. The durable value was a traceable key outgoing piece in a later multi-asset negotiation.

sections.heading: Both Grades Reflect Real Production and Different Timelines
sections.body: The historical verdict stays Los Angeles A+ versus Buffalo A-, a high score for each team with the Lakers slightly ahead. Buffalo obtained useful scoring from McMillian during three Braves seasons and the team reached the 1974 playoffs. Los Angeles got two solid Smith center seasons, an extraordinary single-game block record and a center with enough value to feature in the Abdul-Jabbar trade. It would be unfair to treat Buffalo as a loser without a return or to count every subsequent Lakers championship as caused by one September 1973 move. The exact timing dispute between September 12 and September 17 belongs in the source ledger, not in an invented explanation of changed players. The real reason for the Los Angeles edge is that Smith had both immediate defensive utility and documented later asset value when the franchise secured Abdul-Jabbar through a separate agreement.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Los Angeles Lakers A+, Buffalo Braves/Clippers lineage A-, Lakers Win. McMillian contributed 82 games at 18.6 points in 1973-74 and continued for two more Buffalo seasons; Smith delivered 81 Lakers games at 4.9 blocks per game and later took part with three other players in the 1975 Abdul-Jabbar and Walt Wesley acquisition. Both halves of the 1973 deal produced meaningful team-specific value. The dates differ in Basketball-Reference and the official Lakers guide, so September 17 is preserved as the existing canonical entry while the conflict is disclosed.

sections.heading: Phoenix Acquired a Veteran From the Buffalo Braves
sections.body: On August 25, 1976, Phoenix acquired Tom Van Arsdale from the Buffalo Braves, the predecessor of today’s Clippers, for a 1977 second-round draft selection. Pro Sports Transactions also lists cash, while Basketball-Reference’s transaction ledgers omit that component. This qualification should remain visible rather than silently treating an uncorroborated payment as primary-source fact. The pick was No. 27 Glen Williams and subsequently belonged to Milwaukee through another Braves transaction.

sections.heading: Van Arsdale Contributed for Phoenix
sections.body: Van Arsdale appeared in 77 Suns games during 1976–77 and averaged 5.8 points, 2.4 rebounds and 0.9 assists. Phoenix received one season of measurable guard/forward rotation depth from the acquired veteran. It was not a star-level addition or a long future asset chain. Still, 77 actual appearances represent useful realized value compared with a draft selection that failed to produce a player for the original receiving franchise.

sections.heading: The Draft Route Explains a Slight Suns Advantage
sections.body: Buffalo’s incoming draft selection later connected to Milwaukee as part of the August 1976 Bird Averitt dispersal-pick transaction. Milwaukee used No. 27 on Williams, who never played an NBA regular-season game. That downstream ownership is important: the Braves did not themselves receive NBA production from Williams. Phoenix is graded B and the Buffalo/Clippers lineage B-minus, consistent with a Slight Suns Edge. The secondary-source cash claim does not justify inventing a stronger Buffalo basketball return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Suns Edge — Phoenix B, Buffalo/Clippers B-minus. Van Arsdale supplied Phoenix 77 games in 1976–77. The second-round pick that began with Buffalo reached Milwaukee, which selected Glen Williams at No. 27; he played no NBA games. An additional cash claim appears in one transaction source but not the principal league/team ledgers.

sections.heading: Buffalo Sold a Former MVP to New York for Gianelli and Cash
sections.body: The transaction took place on December 9, 1976, between the New York Knicks and Buffalo Braves, the team whose franchise lineage later became the Los Angeles Clippers. New York acquired former league MVP Bob McAdoo and forward Tom McMillen. Buffalo received veteran center John Gianelli and a major cash payment, reported in contemporary Associated Press coverage as $2.5 million. The large financial component should not be described as an NBA player or converted into invented points and wins. The Braves were facing financial pressure in the difficult post-merger period, which helps explain why management accepted a package with a much smaller immediate basketball return. The Knicks, meanwhile, were buying elite offensive production from a player in his twenties. Both economic considerations and the actual roster transaction are necessary to understand the deal.

sections.heading: McAdoo's First Fifty-Two Knicks Games Justified the Basketball Gamble
sections.body: McAdoo did not arrive as a former star whose scoring days had already ended. In 52 New York regular-season appearances during 1976-77 after the trade, he averaged 26.7 points and 12.7 rebounds, immediately giving the Knicks a high-volume inside-outside offensive threat. He followed with a 26.5-point average during 1977-78 and finished his Knicks tenure with 171 regular-season appearances. McMillen offered an additional but smaller on-court return: 56 games and averages of 9.4 points and 5.7 rebounds in 1976-77. New York never captured a championship with McAdoo, so the direct return is best measured through his production rather than borrowing title success he later experienced elsewhere. When the Knicks eventually dealt McAdoo to Boston, they obtained Tom Barker and three first-round selections, an additional asset conversion achieved in a separate transaction.

sections.heading: Gianelli Played Fifty-Seven Buffalo Games Before Another Trade
sections.body: Gianelli was a real professional center, not a fictional throw-in used to disguise a purely cash-based transaction. He appeared in 57 regular-season games for Buffalo after the December 1976 swap, giving the Braves a brief, identifiable frontcourt return. In September 1977 the team moved him to Milwaukee for a 1979 first-round selection, which later became associated with the No. 10 choice used on Roy Hamilton through subsequent draft-rights history. That later first was received in a second negotiation, so neither Hamilton's entire career nor the whole value of the pick can be described as someone Buffalo obtained directly from New York in 1976. The cash payment was substantial in the period's financial context, although it did not replace McAdoo's star scoring. Buffalo had measurable assets to show for the transaction, but not comparable immediate basketball production.

sections.heading: The Knicks A-Plus and Buffalo C-Plus Depend on Different Outcomes
sections.body: The canonical result is Knicks Win, with New York A-plus and the Clippers franchise lineage C-plus. Those letters make the most sense when the 1976 team is called Buffalo, rather than pretending the modern Los Angeles Clippers completed the exchange. New York acquired a former MVP who promptly averaged 26.7 points and 12.7 rebounds and later brought additional first-round rights through another trade. Buffalo received 57 Gianelli games, a separately tradable center contract and a reported $2.5 million payment, then converted Gianelli into a future first in 1977. That is a meaningful return in financial and roster-management terms, even if it could not match McAdoo's on-court productivity. Preserving both sides avoids either overcrediting later pick outcomes or treating the Braves' original consideration as worthless because it contained cash.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win — New York A-plus, Buffalo/Clippers lineage C-plus. McAdoo delivered elite scoring in 171 Knicks games and later yielded three first-round picks and Tom Barker. Buffalo received Gianelli, a subsequent first-round return and a reported $2.5 million, which made the decision financially understandable without matching the Knicks’ basketball gains.

sources.title: Ranking biggest trades in Knicks history

sections.heading: Philadelphia Traded a Young Scorer for a Very Distant Claim
sections.body: In October 1978 the 76ers sent World B. Free to the San Diego Clippers for a 1984 first-round pick. The unusual distance between the trade and the draft made the transaction difficult to evaluate in real time. Free was only twenty-four and already an explosive scorer, while the pick would not convey for six seasons. Philadelphia was a contender with Julius Erving and other established options, so it could afford to move an offense-first guard whose role might remain constrained. The Clippers needed exactly the opposite: a featured scorer who could energize a struggling franchise immediately. Both teams had coherent reasons. The extraordinary outcome came from the absence of protection and the Clippers’ eventual record. The pick landed fifth in a historic draft, allowing Philadelphia to select Charles Barkley. A transaction that began as a long-horizon asset play became one of the most valuable delayed returns in league history.

sections.heading: The Clippers Received Real Star Production Before Paying the Final Cost
sections.body: San Diego did not get nothing. Free became one of the league’s leading scorers, made the 1980 All-Star team and gave the Clippers a compelling offensive identity for two seasons. He was a legitimate attraction and produced at a level that would normally justify a first-round price. This matters because the trade should not be described as Philadelphia surrendering a marginal player for Barkley. The Clippers acquired a young star and enjoyed immediate value. Their problem was duration. Free was traded to Golden State in 1980, while the future first remained owed for another four years. San Diego had converted a six-year asset into a short burst of scoring without securing playoff success or a comparable downstream return. By the time the pick conveyed, the player was long gone and the franchise had no protection against its own poor record.

sections.heading: The Sixers Waited Through an Entire Competitive Cycle
sections.body: Philadelphia had to carry the pick through coaching changes, roster adjustments and a championship run before it became usable. The 76ers reached the Finals multiple times and won the 1983 title during the waiting period. That success makes the eventual reward even more remarkable: a reigning champion-level organization added the fifth pick one year later without having to bottom out. Barkley joined a veteran team and immediately provided rebounding, efficiency and force. The original trade therefore extended the competitive life of a franchise that had already reached the summit. Distant picks are often discounted because front offices and fans may not survive long enough to use them, but Philadelphia preserved the asset and maintained enough organizational stability to make the selection. Patience became a competitive weapon.

sections.heading: Barkley’s Career Turned a Good Asset Bet Into an A-plus Result
sections.body: Barkley became an eleven-time All-Star, league MVP and one of the greatest power forwards in basketball history. In Philadelphia he produced eight seasons of elite rebounding and scoring, led playoff teams and became the face of the franchise as the 1983 championship core aged. The Sixers later traded him to Phoenix for additional players, extending his asset life beyond the original selection. The pick’s fifth slot mattered, but the organization still had to identify Barkley in a draft that contained several famous prospects. His size raised questions, and he was not chosen until after Hakeem Olajuwon, Sam Bowie, Michael Jordan and Sam Perkins. Philadelphia’s scouting and willingness to embrace an unconventional forward completed the transaction. The trade earns A-plus because the distant first became a generational player and because the Sixers received both years of direct production and later trade value.

sections.heading: Free’s Value Keeps the Clippers at B Rather Than a Failing Grade
sections.body: A B grade acknowledges that Free was excellent in San Diego. He scored at an elite level, earned an All-Star selection and gave the franchise immediate relevance. The Clippers did not make an irrational move for a declining player. They acquired a young star and paid with a future asset whose final position was unknowable. The grade cannot rise higher because the team failed to translate Free’s production into the playoffs, moved him after two seasons and remained responsible for the unprotected first. The ultimate cost became Barkley, but even without using his name, surrendering a six-year-out first without protection was a dangerous structural choice for an unstable franchise. San Diego received a successful player outcome and a poor asset outcome. Both must appear in the grade.

sections.heading: Philadelphia’s Victory Came From Protection Discipline and Patience
sections.body: The central lesson is not that every contender should trade young scorers for distant picks. It is that Philadelphia obtained an unprotected claim from a franchise with significant long-term uncertainty and then refused to dilute it. The Sixers could have traded the pick during the early 1980s for immediate help, especially while chasing Boston and Los Angeles. Instead, they retained it, won a championship through other moves and used the selection when it matured. That sequence created value independent of luck. The Clippers’ poor finish determined the slot, and Barkley’s development exceeded ordinary expectations, but Philadelphia had positioned itself to benefit from both outcomes. The 76ers earn A-plus; the Clippers receive B. The grade gap is large because short-term star production cannot equal eight seasons of Barkley plus the later asset return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win. San Diego received two high-scoring seasons and an All-Star appearance from World B. Free, so the Clippers’ side was not empty. Philadelphia waited six years for an unprotected first that became Charles Barkley, then received eight elite seasons and later trade value. The Sixers earn A-plus; the Clippers receive B.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: How a Six-Year Wait Produced Charles Barkley for a Championship Contender
featuredDeepDive.intro: The most striking feature of the deal is time. Philadelphia traded a productive young guard in 1978, won a championship in 1983 and then used the Clippers’ pick on Barkley in 1984. The asset survived long enough to connect two competitive eras, proving that distant draft control can outlive the roster assumptions present when a trade is signed.

sections.heading: Unprotected Distance Created Enormous Variance
sections.body: The farther a pick sits in the future, the less confidence either team can have about the sender’s record. Ownership decisions, injuries, relocations and roster cycles can change completely. San Diego accepted that variance without protection. The Clippers may have believed Free’s presence would stabilize the franchise and keep the eventual selection away from the top of the draft. Instead, he left after two seasons and the team remained vulnerable. Philadelphia owned the upside of every future failure without sharing the downside. If the Clippers had improved, the Sixers still would have received a first. If they struggled, the value could rise dramatically. The fifth pick was therefore not a random gift; it was the high end of a range Philadelphia had deliberately acquired.

sections.heading: The Sixers Did Not Need the Pick to Save Them
sections.body: Many celebrated draft picks arrive because a rebuilding team is desperate for talent. Philadelphia’s situation was different. The Sixers were already a perennial contender and added Moses Malone in 1982, winning the championship the next spring. The Clippers pick functioned as surplus future value rather than the only hope for recovery. That allowed the front office to wait and select for talent instead of immediate desperation. Barkley entered a veteran environment with Erving, Malone, Maurice Cheeks and a standard of playoff expectation. He could learn while contributing immediately. The trade demonstrates how strong teams can use external draft capital to avoid the normal aging curve. Philadelphia did not have to dismantle the roster to obtain a top-five pick; another franchise’s earlier decision supplied the renewal mechanism.

sections.heading: Free’s San Diego Success Makes the Trade More Instructive
sections.body: If Free had failed immediately, the lesson would be simple: never trade a distant first for an unproven scorer. He did not fail. He became an All-Star and one of the league’s most productive guards. The Clippers still lost the transaction because a successful player acquisition can be undermined by weak asset structure and insufficient duration. Free’s two seasons could not compensate for six years of unprotected exposure, especially after the team traded him away. This distinction matters for modern evaluations. Teams often defend expensive deals by pointing to the incoming player’s statistics. Production is only one side of the equation. Contract control, downstream return and the assets surrendered determine whether the production creates surplus value. San Diego got the player right and the price wrong.

sections.heading: Barkley Extended the 1983 Core Without Replicating It
sections.body: Barkley did not simply replace one aging veteran. His rebounding, transition power and interior efficiency created a different style for Philadelphia. As the championship roster declined, he grew into the primary star and kept the Sixers relevant through the late 1980s and early 1990s. That transition is a major part of the trade’s value. The pick allowed Philadelphia to change identities without first enduring a full rebuild. Barkley’s personality and production also gave the franchise a new public face after Erving retired. A single delayed asset therefore affected basketball strategy, roster continuity and organizational relevance. Few first-round picks produce that breadth of value.

sections.heading: The Later Barkley Trade Added Another Layer to the Return
sections.body: Philadelphia eventually sent Barkley to Phoenix in 1992 for Jeff Hornacek, Tim Perry and Andrew Lang. The Sixers did not maximize that later return, and the franchise entered a difficult period, but the ability to trade Barkley at all was part of the original asset chain. He had delivered eight seasons and still possessed substantial market value. The Clippers had no comparable continuing branch from Free by 1984. Downstream value should not be overstated when later management is poor, but it reinforces the difference in control. Philadelphia owned an elite player long enough to use him, build around him and move him. San Diego’s benefit was finished years before the pick even conveyed.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Philadelphia’s patience converted a distant, uncertain claim into a generational player without interrupting a championship pursuit. San Diego received a real star, but for too short a period and at too dangerous a price. The Barkley outcome makes the victory historic; the unprotected structure explains why the Sixers were positioned to receive it.

sections.heading: From Trade Line to Completed Outcome
sections.body: On October 27, 1982, the San Diego Clippers received veteran guard Lionel Hollins from Philadelphia. The 76ers took back two future draft selections: a 1983 fourth-rounder later identified as No. 74 for Kalpatrick Wells, and a 1984 second-rounder later identified as No. 29 for Stuart Gray. The Clippers would not move to Los Angeles until 1984, so their modern franchise slug shouldn't turn this into a 1982 Los Angeles trade. San Diego acquired an immediately recognizable NBA player; Philadelphia accepted draft opportunities in two separate years.

sections.heading: Why One Side Finished Ahead
sections.body: The exchange put a known guard against two choices with uncertain future basketball value. Hollins could be evaluated for San Diego directly after the deal, whereas Philadelphia had to wait for the 1983 and 1984 drafts to determine who would be selected. A fourth-round selection, especially, should not be recast as the equivalent of a first-round opportunity. The archive favors the Clippers franchise, B+ versus the 76ers' D+, and that assessment should be attached to Hollins and those precisely identified picks rather than to later personnel moves.

sections.heading: How the Better Package Paid Off: Los Angeles Clippers
sections.body: Philadelphia's incoming assets were not two NBA players already serving on the 76ers roster in October 1982. They were future selections that subsequently received the names Kalpatrick Wells at No. 74 and Stuart Gray at No. 29. Those identities help complete the asset history without establishing lasting NBA production merely by appearing in the draft record. San Diego received Hollins alone and no additional cash payment or pick in the documented exchange. This one-player-for-two-picks structure is the right starting point for interpreting the verdict.

sections.heading: Where the Other Package Fell Short: Philadelphia 76ers
sections.body: The franchise geography creates a separate accuracy requirement. On the date of the transaction, the Clippers were based in San Diego, not Los Angeles. The archived Clippers Win verdict can remain attached to the modern franchise, but the original decision was made by the San Diego organization and the Philadelphia 76ers. Its comparison of B+ for the Clippers and D+ for Philadelphia refers to realized return from the specific veteran and selections, not a later California relocation or unrelated draft history.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers franchise Win — San Diego B+, Philadelphia D+. San Diego obtained Lionel Hollins, while the 76ers gained a 1983 fourth-rounder later used at No. 74 on Kalpatrick Wells and a 1984 second-rounder later used at No. 29 on Stuart Gray. The city was San Diego in 1982, and neither draftee was an incoming NBA player at the moment of the trade.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: San Diego Clippers–Philadelphia 76ers: October 1982 Hollins for Draft Picks
featuredDeepDive.intro: The October 27, 1982 Philadelphia–San Diego Clippers trade exchanged an established NBA guard for two later draft selections. San Diego received Lionel Hollins, while Philadelphia took a 1983 fourth-round choice later No. 74 Kalpatrick Wells and a 1984 second-round choice later No. 29 Stuart Gray. The franchise now uses the Los Angeles Clippers identifier, but this was a San Diego transaction. The archive's B+ Clippers to D+ Philadelphia grades compare a known player against two future opportunities whose value depended on draft results.

sections.heading: The Trade Details Before the Narrative
sections.body: The Clippers' return was immediate: Lionel Hollins joined the San Diego franchise as the veteran guard obtained from Philadelphia. In exchange, the 76ers acquired a 1983 fourth-round selection and a 1984 second-round selection. The eventual numbers were No. 74, Kalpatrick Wells, and No. 29, Stuart Gray. Their staggered dates are important because the two picks did not represent available players at the October 1982 deadline. This was a clear preference for veteran certainty on one side and future selection flexibility on the other.

sections.heading: The Deal's Most Important Outcome: Los Angeles Clippers
sections.body: Philadelphia acquired two draft opportunities across consecutive years, but their value couldn't be established by merely counting two assets versus one. The 1983 fourth-rounder was a comparatively late choice, and the 1984 second-rounder was still future consideration when Hollins moved. The names Wells and Gray give the selections eventual identities, not automatic NBA career returns. The archive's D+ for Philadelphia reflects an unfavorable retrospective, even though the team did receive tangible draft considerations rather than nothing.

sections.heading: Comparing Realized Value, Not Reputation: Philadelphia 76ers
sections.body: San Diego's acquisition of Hollins offered a different type of return. A current NBA guard could join personnel planning without a draft lottery or later contract negotiation determining the identity of the player. That distinction supports why the archive values the Clippers' side more favorably at B+. It does not mean every minute Hollins ever played elsewhere can be credited to this transaction. The relevant question is the actual contribution and value stemming from the 1982 acquisition rather than unrelated portions of his career.

sections.heading: How Far the Evidence Really Goes
sections.body: The historical franchise name needs to be preserved alongside the modern Clippers canonical route. The original recipient was the San Diego Clippers; Los Angeles became the home only later. Philadelphia's outgoing player was Lionel Hollins and its incoming package comprised the two numbered draft opportunities. An evaluation that changes the city, upgrades the fourth-rounder to a premium pick or counts Wells and Gray as veteran players on the trade date would undermine the documented result. Within the proper scope, the recorded Clippers Win, B+ versus D+, is an understandable hindsight judgment.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The archived B+/D+ grade spread favors the then-San Diego Clippers' acquisition of Lionel Hollins. Philadelphia received two selections, later identified as No. 74 Kalpatrick Wells in 1983 and No. 29 Stuart Gray in 1984. Keeping the years, pick rounds and original city intact explains the exchange without manufacturing a Los Angeles 1982 roster or treating future selections as immediately acquired veterans.

sections.heading: September 1984 Moved a Franchise Scorer for Three Young Bucks
sections.body: Milwaukee sent Marques Johnson, Junior Bridgeman, Harvey Catchings and cash to the newly relocated Los Angeles Clippers on September 29, 1984. The Bucks received Terry Cummings, Ricky Pierce and Craig Hodges. Each club’s 1984-85 transaction ledger confirms the three-for-three player exchange and cash direction. Johnson was a four-time All-Star Milwaukee forward; Cummings was only 23 and had won Rookie of the Year with the San Diego Clippers in 1983. The organizations were trading different timelines, not simply equivalent scoring wings. Los Angeles pursued the established Johnson and veteran depth, while Milwaukee obtained an emerging frontcourt scorer and two younger perimeter players. The cash amount is not reliably itemized in the consulted archives.

sections.heading: Terry Cummings Supplied 319 Bucks Games in His First Four Seasons
sections.body: Cummings immediately justified a large part of Milwaukee’s gamble. In 1984-85 he played 79 Bucks regular-season games, started 78 and averaged 23.6 points with 9.1 rebounds. He followed with 82 games at 19.8 points in 1985-86, 82 at 20.8 in 1986-87, and 76 at 21.3 in 1987-88. Those four seasons alone total 319 Milwaukee games; they are not his entire Bucks tenure, which extended beyond this early window. Cummings made the 1985 All-Star team and All-NBA Second Team in his first Milwaukee campaign. His combination of immediate production and continued availability was more durable than the Clippers’ short peak from Johnson before the severe neck injury.

sections.heading: Johnson Was a Real Clippers Star before His Neck Injury
sections.body: The return to Los Angeles was not simply a failed trade from day one. Johnson played 72 Clippers games in 1984-85, scoring 16.4 points per game, then 75 in 1985-86 at 20.3 points and earned another All-Star appearance. In 1986-87 he played only ten games before a serious neck injury interrupted his career. His direct Clippers tenure totaled 157 regular-season appearances, 153 starts and included a meaningful second-year scoring peak. The injury then kept him out of the NBA during 1987-88 and 1988-89. That later development strongly affected how the clubs’ exchanged assets compared over time, but it was not a guaranteed outcome when the Clippers acquired him in 1984.

sections.heading: Hodges Added Guard Shooting and Pierce Became a Major Reserve
sections.body: Hodges supplied all 82 Bucks games in 1984-85, starting 63 and averaging 10.6 points with 4.3 assists. The next year he scored 10.8 a game and converted 45.1 percent of his three-point attempts over 66 games. Milwaukee also acquired Pierce, whose scoring role expanded over the following seasons, including the 1987 NBA Sixth Man of the Year award. The combination gave the Bucks depth around Cummings rather than requiring the new forward to carry their entire offense. Hodges later won NBA championships with Chicago after leaving Milwaukee, but those Bulls titles are not direct Bucks games from the 1984 trade. Pierce’s eventual recognition needs its own timeline instead of being collapsed into an immediate 1984 contribution.

sections.heading: Bridgeman and Catchings Offered Depth, While Cash Stayed Unpriced
sections.body: Junior Bridgeman had been a productive and trusted reserve in Milwaukee, playing substantial minutes throughout his first decade in the league. Los Angeles received his veteran guard-forward experience alongside defensive center Harvey Catchings. Neither arrival was the same type of long-term franchise scorer as Cummings, and neither should be omitted merely because Johnson and Cummings headline the exchange. The protected original transaction also included cash sent from Milwaukee to the Clippers. Without a supported cash figure it would be inaccurate to manufacture a payment or treat the asset as meaningless. The more defensible retrospective distinguishes roster usefulness, cash consideration and the large gap in sustained on-court output between Cummings and the veteran Los Angeles package.

sections.heading: Why Terry Cummings and Milwaukee’s Supporting Guards Outlasted the Clippers Return
sections.body: The Bucks Win verdict grades Milwaukee A-plus and Los Angeles C-plus. The September 29, 1984 exchange delivered Terry Cummings, Craig Hodges and Ricky Pierce to Milwaukee, while Los Angeles acquired Marques Johnson, Junior Bridgeman, Harvey Catchings and cash. Cummings contributed 319 Bucks appearances in the first four seasons alone, averaging 23.6 points as an All-NBA forward in 1984-85; he played for Milwaukee well beyond that four-year sample. Hodges gave the Bucks 82 games in his first season and Pierce eventually earned Sixth Man of the Year recognition in 1987. Johnson was no empty return for the Clippers: he scored 20.3 per game in 1985-86 and earned an All-Star appearance, but a severe neck injury disrupted his subsequent career. Bridgeman and Catchings supplied veteran depth, and the original unpriced cash should not be invented or discarded. Milwaukee's multi-season combination of frontcourt scoring and backcourt contributions gives the Bucks a convincing retrospective edge, without treating Johnson's later injury as something the clubs could know in September 1984.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win with Milwaukee A+ and Los Angeles C+ remains unchanged. Cummings delivered 319 games across his first four Bucks seasons alone, including 1985 All-NBA recognition; Hodges offered immediate guard minutes and Pierce developed into an elite reserve. Johnson supplied 157 Clippers appearances and a 1986 All-Star season before a serious neck injury. Bridgeman, Catchings and the unpriced cash were legitimate Clippers assets, but the Milwaukee package produced the more durable basketball return.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The 1984 Cummings–Marques Johnson Trade: Milwaukee Bought Years of Star Production
featuredDeepDive.intro: The Bucks acquired Terry Cummings, Craig Hodges and Ricky Pierce on September 29, 1984 in exchange for Marques Johnson, Junior Bridgeman, Harvey Catchings and cash. Cummings became a major Milwaukee scorer and an immediate 1985 All-NBA Second Team selection; Hodges played 82 games in his first Bucks season, while Pierce later won a Sixth Man award. Johnson was still productive in Los Angeles but logged just 157 Clippers games before a serious neck injury. The archived Bucks Win, A+ Milwaukee/C+ Clippers grades stay intact, with the injury and unspecified cash treated carefully rather than as preordained facts.

sections.heading: A Young Former Rookie of the Year Replaced a Four-Time All-Star
sections.body: The trade followed the Clippers’ move from San Diego to Los Angeles and a Bucks era built around Marques Johnson, Sidney Moncrief and a deep rotation. Johnson had four Milwaukee All-Star appearances before he was dealt, while Terry Cummings had scored 23.7 points per game during his 1983 Rookie of the Year season in San Diego. Neither organization exchanged only one headliner: Milwaukee also brought in Ricky Pierce and Craig Hodges, and Los Angeles added Bridgeman, Catchings and cash. The 1984-85 transaction pages identify each asset and September 29 date. Milwaukee accepted the risk of moving a beloved established player because Cummings offered younger star-level production and the two incoming guards could fill rotation needs.

sections.heading: Cummings’ 1984-88 Milwaukee Numbers Did Not Require Projection
sections.body: In his first Bucks season Cummings scored 1,861 points in 79 regular-season appearances at 23.6 per game and pulled down 9.1 rebounds. He started 78 times, was selected to the 1985 All-Star Game and made the All-NBA Second Team. He followed with 82 games in both 1985-86 and 1986-87, then 76 in 1987-88, totaling 319 in the four-year sample alone. The associated 19.8, 20.8 and 21.3 points-per-game averages show that the success was not confined to a single season. His longer Milwaukee tenure gave the Bucks additional value, but the four-segment sample is already sufficient to distinguish the direct output from the Clippers’ injury-shortened Johnson tenure.

sections.heading: Johnson’s Clippers All-Star Year Deserves Independent Credit
sections.body: The former Bucks star averaged 16.4 points and 6.3 rebounds over 72 Clippers games in 1984-85. He played 75 games and started every one the following season, scoring 20.3 points and earning the 1986 All-Star nod. Los Angeles had obtained a legitimate lead scorer and the move was not instantly disastrous on the court. In 1986-87, however, Johnson appeared ten times and suffered the neck injury that kept him from NBA games over the next two seasons. Those 72, 75 and ten Clippers appearances sum to 157. His brief 1989-90 return with Golden State must not be folded into the Los Angeles return, just as his previous Milwaukee prime should not count as new Clippers production.

sections.heading: Hodges and Pierce Turned the Trade into More than Two Stars
sections.body: Hodges was an active starting-caliber Milwaukee guard at the outset, playing 82 games and starting 63 in 1984-85. His 10.6 points and 4.3 assists supplied real value beside Cummings; his 45.1 percent three-point shooting during the next season further increased his usefulness. Pierce evolved into a valuable bench scoring weapon and won Sixth Man of the Year in 1987. His later 1990 award and continuing NBA career are relevant to longer-term development but do not become fabricated first-year achievements. Milwaukee therefore received two distinct kinds of guard value in addition to its new star forward. Los Angeles brought in veteran frontcourt and wing depth, yet those arrivals lacked the same combination of youth, minutes and lasting award-level production.

sections.heading: Cash, Injury and the Causation Boundary
sections.body: The official league-history transaction logs say Milwaukee sent cash to Los Angeles in addition to Johnson, Bridgeman and Catchings. They do not identify a trustworthy amount in the sources reviewed, so the archive’s cash row stays in place without an invented dollar value. A C+ Clippers grade is partly a consequence of Johnson’s later injury, not proof that Los Angeles knowingly acquired damaged goods. Milwaukee’s A+ reflects demonstrated Cummings, Hodges and Pierce outcomes, not hypothetical championship credit or a retroactive change of who the Clippers sent. The Bucks continued to make other roster decisions, and those downstream moves should be evaluated separately from this September 1984 exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Milwaukee A+, Los Angeles C+ and Bucks Win are preserved. In the first four Bucks seasons alone Cummings logged 319 games and earned All-NBA and All-Star recognition, with Hodges contributing immediate backcourt play and Pierce later becoming a decorated reserve. Johnson supplied 157 Clippers regular-season games and made the 1986 All-Star team before injury. Bridgeman, Catchings and unquantified cash were genuine incoming Clippers assets, but Milwaukee secured the longer and deeper basketball return without the retrospective benefit of assuming an injury in advance.

sections.heading: January 1986: Valentine and Two Second-Round Rights Changed Direction
sections.body: The Los Angeles Clippers acquired point guard Darnell Valentine from Portland on January 14, 1986, giving up a 1986 first-round selection and agreeing to exchange 1988 second-round choices. That 1986 pick was actually Boston-origin draft capital the Clippers had obtained in September 1985 when they sent Bill Walton to the Celtics. The Blazers later exercised it at No. 24 on Arvydas Sabonis. The future second-round rights developed into No. 26 Rolando Ferreira for Portland and No. 45 Tom Garrick for Los Angeles. Contemporary Los Angeles Times and UPI reports describe the original deal as the first-round transfer and the planned second-round swap, not an exchange of four named draft-night players in January 1986.

sections.heading: Valentine Supplied 178 Clippers Games After Leaving Portland
sections.body: Valentine was an established NBA guard at the time, having played his first four seasons in Portland and started regularly before losing standing under coach Jack Ramsay. The Clippers gave him a new opportunity and used him in 178 regular-season games after the exchange, according to Basketball-Reference's teams-as-trade-partners ledger. He averaged 8.4 points and 5.3 assists as a Clipper, useful immediate backcourt service. Those games did not represent the player's prior 300 Portland appearances or later professional career and should not be transferred between franchises. Los Angeles therefore received more than an empty veteran contract. The retrospective difference comes from the much longer eventual Portland Sabonis tenure, not from the claim that Valentine contributed nothing in the first seasons after this trade.

sections.heading: Portland Had to Wait Nine Years to Get Sabonis on an NBA Court
sections.body: The first-round choice conveyed to Portland became No. 24 Arvydas Sabonis at the June 1986 NBA draft. Sabonis was an established international center but did not join Portland for the 1986-87 season. Soviet-era transfer barriers and subsequent commitments delayed his NBA arrival until 1995-96, nine years after the selection. When he finally played, he supplied 470 Trail Blazers regular-season appearances over seven NBA seasons, averaging 12.0 points and 7.3 rebounds. Those statistics belong to the Portland team that ultimately signed its draft-rights player, not to the Clippers who traded the original selection. The late arrival also means one should not attribute the Blazers' late-1980s or early-1990s Finals appearances to immediate on-court Sabonis production.

sections.heading: The 1988 Pick Swap Delivered Garrick and Ferreira
sections.body: The future second-round swap matured in the 1988 NBA draft. Portland received the No. 26 selection and used it on Rolando Ferreira, who appeared in 12 Trail Blazers NBA regular-season games. Los Angeles held the No. 45 choice and selected Tom Garrick, who contributed 211 Clippers appearances, averaging 5.8 points and 3.6 assists. These are separate named outcomes of the two draft rights, not players who were already on either roster at the 1986 transaction date. The Clippers return was thus Valentine's 178 games plus Garrick's 211, with differing levels of contribution; Portland received Sabonis's eventual 470 games and Ferreira's 12. The historical Blazers Win and A-plus Portland versus A-minus Clippers grades recognize very different long-term value despite real utility on both sides.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Blazers Win — Portland A-plus, Los Angeles Clippers A-minus, inherited grades unchanged. Portland obtained the No. 24 draft right to Arvydas Sabonis, who joined its NBA roster nine years after selection and eventually played 470 games. The Clippers received 178 regular-season games from Valentine plus the No. 45 Garrick pick, whose player supplied 211 more Clippers games. Portland also used the acquired 1988 No. 26 pick on Ferreira, a 12-game Blazer. The timing and long-term upside explain Portland's edge without denying Los Angeles its real guard return.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Los Angeles Clippers–Portland Trail Blazers: What the 1986-01-14 Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: In January 1986 the Clippers traded a Boston-origin first and one of their 1988 second-round rights to Portland for Darnell Valentine and another 1988 second. The first became No. 24 Arvydas Sabonis, whose Portland NBA debut came in 1995 and whose Blazers tenure totaled 470 games. Valentine played 178 Clippers games, and the two 1988 choices became No. 26 Rolando Ferreira for Portland and No. 45 Tom Garrick for Los Angeles. Both clubs received actual player service on different timelines.

sections.heading: The First Moved From Boston to LA Before Reaching Portland
sections.body: Los Angeles did not trade its own original 1986 first-round choice in the Valentine transaction. Its outgoing No. 24 pick had come from Boston as part of the September 6, 1985 Bill Walton-for-Cedric Maxwell arrangement. The subsequent January 14, 1986 Portland deal transferred that right to the Trail Blazers. A contemporaneous Los Angeles Times report explicitly identified the Boston origin of the traded first and the future 1988 second-round swap. The Portland and Clippers team season transaction ledgers corroborate the same draft paths. Keeping these separate dated stages prevents treating Boston as a third participant in the January Clippers-Blazers deal. The Clippers controlled a Celtics-origin future first by January and chose an established point guard over the option to exercise the pick that June.

sections.heading: Valentine Was an Immediate Guard Return Despite Modest Hindsight Grade
sections.body: Valentine had already played 300 regular-season games with Portland before the Clippers obtained him. After the January deal, he appeared in 178 Los Angeles games with averages of 8.4 points and 5.3 assists, accounting for real immediate playmaking. The contemporary UPI story describes Portland moving a once-regular starting guard after his role deteriorated under Jack Ramsay. Los Angeles was seeking guard stability rather than waiting for a draft prospect. A 178-game return has basketball value even if later selection No. 24 developed into a much stronger long-term player for Portland. The archived A-minus Clippers grade must not imply the team received Sabonis, and Portland's later NBA seasons cannot be treated as if the future center had played for the Blazers in 1986.

sections.heading: Sabonis Became a Great Blazer but Did Not Play There Until 1995
sections.body: Portland selected Sabonis 24th in the 1986 draft using the Clippers-origin right. His overseas career and the geopolitical limitations on joining the NBA meant the Blazers did not record NBA appearances from him until the 1995-96 season. He went on to play 470 Portland regular-season games, averaging 12.0 points and 7.3 rebounds, a remarkable long-term outcome for the 24th pick. That player value is directly traceable to the January 1986 trade, but the timing differs from Valentine's immediate Los Angeles minutes. Portland's 1990 and 1992 Finals teams should not be credited with court production from Sabonis before his NBA arrival. This dated distinction is essential when comparing both the original front-office trade logic and the later realized team return.

sections.heading: Both 1988 Seconds Produced NBA Games for Their Drafting Clubs
sections.body: The associated 1988 second-round rights were real assets on both sides. Portland got the No. 26 pick, which became Rolando Ferreira and 12 Trail Blazers regular-season appearances. Los Angeles used No. 45 on Tom Garrick, who played 211 Clippers games and provided useful reserve guard minutes. Together with Valentine's 178 games, Garrick gave the Clippers a meaningful two-player basketball return rather than a lopsided zero-production trade. Portland's main payoff was Sabonis's much later seven-year, 470-game tenure; Ferreira made only a brief contribution. The stored Blazers Win and Portland A-plus versus Clippers A-minus grading favors that long-term star-level return while acknowledging the practical player minutes delivered to Los Angeles. The original archive also records future considerations without verified terms, so their value is not invented.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The archived Blazers Win, Portland A-plus and Clippers A-minus is a long-range draft-outcome judgment. Sabonis became a 470-game Blazer after a long delay from the 1986 No. 24 selection. Valentine gave Los Angeles 178 games in the meantime and the received 1988 No. 45 pick became 211-game Clippers guard Tom Garrick. Ferreira added 12 Portland appearances from the No. 26 second. These source-dated chains credit the correct franchises and keep the prior Walton-Boston first-pick trade and unidentified future considerations separate.

sections.heading: Derek Smith package / Larry Drew, Mike Woodson and picks: What Actually Changed Hands
sections.body: The Clippers acquired Larry Drew, Mike Woodson, a 1988 first-round pick that became No. 6 Hersey Hawkins, a 1989 second-round pick that became Jay Edwards, and cash. Sacramento acquired Derek Smith, Franklin Edwards and Junior Bridgeman. The Clippers received Larry Drew, Mike Woodson, cash and two selections: the 1988 first that landed at No. 6 and the 1989 second that became Jay Edwards. Sacramento took Derek Smith, Franklin Edwards and Junior Bridgeman. The disparity comes from the draft capital attached to the veteran exchange, not just the names swapped in August 1986.

sections.heading: Derek Smith package / Larry Drew, Mike Woodson and picks: Where the Stronger Value Emerged
sections.body: Los Angeles received both immediate veteran depth and premium draft capital. The first-round pick landing at No. 6 gave the Clippers a particularly valuable asset, and the breadth of the return comfortably exceeds what Sacramento obtained from the outgoing veteran package. Los Angeles acquired ready-made guard depth in Drew and Woodson while also obtaining a first-round opportunity that became the Hersey Hawkins selection at No. 6. A team seldom gets that combination of immediate contributors and a premium future slot for a group of veterans. The second-round pick added another chance without carrying the main grade.

sections.heading: Derek Smith package / Larry Drew, Mike Woodson and picks: What the Other Side Still Received
sections.body: Sacramento did receive established players rather than empty contracts, and Derek Smith was the most important of the incoming names. That prevents an absolute zero grade, but injuries, age and limited tenure kept the Kings’ realized value well below the package they surrendered. Sacramento acquired recognizable veterans, with Derek Smith the principal talent in the incoming package. But injuries and short tenures reduced what the Kings actually received on court. The deal should not be described as receiving nothing, even though the sacrificed first-round value became hard to ignore.

sections.heading: Derek Smith package / Larry Drew, Mike Woodson and picks: The Asset Chain After the Trade
sections.body: The strongest directly tied component is the 1988 first-round pick that became Hersey Hawkins. Even though later decisions involving Hawkins are separate transactions, the conversion of the pick into a high draft selection is direct evidence of the value embedded in the Clippers’ return. The first-round pick’s eventual position at No. 6 is the directly attributable outcome. The Clippers’ later handling of Hawkins is a separate decision and need not be credited to this acquisition. Los Angeles also obtained the Edwards second-round pick, giving it more than one identifiable draft return.

sections.heading: Derek Smith package / Larry Drew, Mike Woodson and picks: Timeline, Contract and Role Context
sections.body: This trade took place before modern pick-protection conventions became as standardized, making the unprotected or lightly constrained draft value especially important. Sacramento paid a large future opportunity cost for veteran help, while Los Angeles diversified across players, picks and cash. Sacramento chose an established-player package in 1986 while the Clippers accepted a mix of veterans, cash and future selections. The 1988 first became the swing factor because the draft opportunity arrived after the immediate veteran value on Sacramento’s side had faded. The time lag made the trade look increasingly unequal.

sections.heading: Derek Smith package / Larry Drew, Mike Woodson and picks: grading scale
sections.body: Clippers A+, Kings D. Los Angeles earns an elite grade for receiving useful veterans plus a top-six first-round outcome and another draft pick. Sacramento receives some credit for established players but not enough to offset the surrendered asset depth. Los Angeles earns A+ for acquiring two established guards and a top-six first-round selection, plus the later second. Sacramento earns D rather than F because it received actual veterans, including Smith, but their realized contributions did not come close to replacing the surrendered draft upside.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win — Los Angeles A+, Sacramento D. The Clippers collected usable veteran depth alongside draft capital that included a first-round choice ultimately reaching No. 6 in 1988. Sacramento received established talent led by Derek Smith, but limited tenure and injury concerns reduced the realized return. Giving the Kings credit for acquiring NBA players does not offset the depth and high-value pick surrendered. The top-six selection is the central difference between an outstanding Los Angeles return and a disappointing Sacramento one.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Swapped the No. Three Rights for Hawkins and a First
sections.body: On June 28, 1988, the 76ers selected Pittsburgh forward Charles Smith at No. 3 and sent his rights to the Clippers. Philadelphia received the No. 6 rights to Bradley shooting guard Hersey Hawkins plus a 1989 first-round selection that later became No. 19 Kenny Payne. The Los Angeles Times and same-day draft history describe the move as part of a wider deal involving Seattle rather than a spontaneous stand-alone Clippers-Sixers negotiation. Chicago and future NBA championship rosters were not parties. This site's two-team record covers only Smith for Hawkins plus the first; Seattle's role explains where that pick originated without creating a third incoming NBA player for Philadelphia.

sections.heading: Hawkins Filled Philadelphia's Perimeter Scoring Need
sections.body: Hersey Hawkins supplied immediate offense beside Charles Barkley. In 1988-89 he started all 79 games he played, averaged 15.1 points and shot 42.8 percent from beyond the arc. By 1990-91 his scoring had risen to 22.1 points over 80 starts, earning an All-Star selection that season. Those regular-season numbers establish more than an appealing collegiate draft profile; the Sixers acquired a durable NBA scoring guard who could defend and stretch the floor. Their decision to accept No. 6 instead of keeping Smith at No. 3 was therefore an actual positional choice with substantial payoff. The separate 1989 pick broadened that return, although its later No. 19 selection should be graded on its actual contribution rather than its draft label alone.

sections.heading: Charles Smith Produced Genuine Clippers Frontcourt Value
sections.body: The Clippers did not exchange Hawkins for a failed third pick. Charles Daniel Smith played 71 games and started 56 in 1988-89, averaging 16.3 points and 6.5 rebounds. In 1989-90 he averaged 21.1 points and 6.7 rebounds over 78 games, providing the sort of interior scoring Los Angeles hoped to pair with No. 1 pick Danny Manning. These totals make the Clippers' B-plus plausible as an inherited evaluation of the player acquired, even though the franchise did not suddenly become a playoff contender. Smith was a legitimate young forward with useful production, and comparing him to Hawkins must acknowledge different positions. Philadelphia's extra future first-round asset remains an important differentiator beyond the players' first seasons.

sections.heading: The Seattle Pick and Gary Grant Came From a Connected, Distinct Leg
sections.body: Contemporary reports describe the larger June 1988 draft-night arrangement. The Clippers separately sent NBA rebounding leader Michael Cage to Seattle, receiving the rights to No. 15 Gary Grant and a future Seattle first. That 1989 first then went to Philadelphia with Hawkins for Smith. It is accurate to trace the origin of the No. 19 right to the SuperSonics and the Cage exchange, but incorrect to say Philadelphia directly gave up Michael Cage or that Gary Grant arrived with Smith from the Sixers. The current ledger lists only the Clippers-Philadelphia leg, including Hawkins and the future first moving east. Separating interconnected draft rights from direct personnel outcomes prevents double credit across transaction pages.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The canonical 76ers Win verdict, Philadelphia A-plus and Clippers B-plus are preserved. Philadelphia swapped Charles Smith's No. 3 draft rights for Hersey Hawkins's No. 6 rights and a future Seattle-origin 1989 first that became No. 19 Kenny Payne. Hawkins developed into a 22.1-point All-Star; Smith delivered 21.1 points for the Clippers in 1989-90. This two-team ledger forms one leg of a larger Clippers-Seattle-Philadelphia draft arrangement, so Michael Cage and Gary Grant must not be counted twice as direct exchanged players.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The 1988 Three-Team Draft Deal Behind Hawkins, Charles Smith and Pick Nineteen
featuredDeepDive.intro: The 76ers accepted No. 6 Hersey Hawkins and a Seattle-origin 1989 first in exchange for No. 3 Charles Smith's draft rights. The Clippers acquired a productive young forward, but Philadelphia secured years of Hawkins backcourt scoring plus another first-round pick that became No. 19 Kenny Payne. The arrangement involved a separate Michael Cage-to-Seattle leg and Gary Grant rights to Los Angeles. The original 76ers Win grades remain in place without folding the entire three-team move into a single direct two-team asset list.

sections.heading: A Three-Team Draft-Night Mechanism, But a Two-Team Grade Ledger
sections.body: The historical June 28, 1988 maneuver linked Philadelphia, Los Angeles and Seattle around draft slots No. 3, No. 6 and No. 15. Los Angeles selected Danny Manning at No. 1 independently; Philadelphia selected Charles Smith at No. 3 and sent his rights to Los Angeles. The Clippers' No. 6 rights to Hawkins and a Seattle-supplied 1989 first went to Philadelphia. In another leg, Los Angeles sent Michael Cage to Seattle for No. 15 Gary Grant rights and the first used in the swap. This explains how Philadelphia acquired a first for dropping three positions in the draft. It does not authorize importing Manning, Grant or Cage as direct players in the Smith-Hawkins two-team archive record.

sections.heading: Hawkins Had a Higher Philadelphia Scoring Peak Than His Rookie Year
sections.body: The No. 6 guard was a strong long-range contributor rather than a one-season novelty. In 1988-89 Hawkins averaged 15.1 points in 79 starts and made more than 42 percent of his threes. He started all 82 games in 1989-90 with 18.5 points, then averaged 22.1 in 80 appearances in 1990-91 and made the All-Star team. Those figures help explain why Philadelphia favored a college scoring star who fit beside Barkley and who could remain central to its backcourt. The separate 1989 first added draft flexibility. His sustained NBA service, not a claim that No. 6 should always outproduce No. 3, is the meaningful realized player value for this particular team.

sections.heading: Smith's Early Clippers Numbers Explain the Counterargument
sections.body: Smith immediately gave Los Angeles a credible frontcourt scorer. His rookie 16.3 points and 6.5 rebounds in 71 games increased to 21.1 and 6.7 in his second season. Those are not the totals of an injured nonparticipant or an automatically lost first-round gamble. Contemporary draft-night coverage also identified the Clippers' frontcourt plans around Manning, Smith and Benoit Benjamin, making the organizational rationale concrete even if the roster took time to develop. Philadelphia received the more successful perimeter scorer for its needs plus a first-round right, but the Clippers captured several productive forward seasons. The site retains B-plus for Los Angeles rather than portraying its acquired player as worthless.

sections.heading: The 1989 No. Nineteen Was Compensation Beyond Hawkins
sections.body: Philadelphia's additional asset became the 1989 first-round No. 19 selection associated with Kenny Payne. Draft-rights registries trace the pick from Seattle to the Clippers as part of the Michael Cage exchange and then onward to the Sixers for Smith's rights. That chain is the distinguishing component of the June 28 trade: Philadelphia gained both the player it wanted at No. 6 and an additional future first. The eventual selected player should not be assigned the career production of a hypothetical better selection, nor should the pick be described as an unprotected top lottery choice. The stored result, 76ers Win with Philadelphia A-plus and Los Angeles B-plus, recognizes the actual additional selection and Hawkins's career without erasing Smith's Clippers success.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Philadelphia A-plus, Los Angeles B-plus and 76ers Win are the stored grades and verdict. Philadelphia sent No. 3 Charles Smith to the Clippers for No. 6 Hawkins and a Seattle-origin 1989 first later used at No. 19 for Kenny Payne. Hawkins immediately averaged 15.1 points and developed into a 1991 All-Star at 22.1, while Smith delivered a genuine 21.1-point Clippers season in 1989-90. Seattle acquired Michael Cage and sent Gary Grant rights and the future first to Los Angeles in a linked leg; neither Cage nor Grant is a direct asset on Philadelphia's Smith-for-Hawkins exchange. The player and draft-rights timeline explains the grading advantage without imagining a third NBA participant in the canonical two-team record.
