sections.heading: Corey Maggette, Keyon Dooling and Derek Strong for a Protected First: The Draft-Night Price
sections.body: On draft night in 2000, Orlando sent Corey Maggette, Derek Strong, the rights to tenth pick Keyon Dooling, a second-round pick and cash to the Clippers for a future first-round pick protected across several seasons. The Magic were clearing salary and roster space for an ambitious free-agent summer built around Tracy McGrady, Grant Hill and Tim Duncan. The Clippers were collecting young talent and could afford to absorb contracts. The future first did not convey until 2006, when Orlando used the twenty-second pick on Marcus Williams and traded his rights. By then Maggette had developed into a high-volume scorer and long-term starter in Los Angeles, while Dooling contributed as a rotation guard. The exchange is one of the clearest examples of a team paying too much real player value for flexibility and a delayed, heavily protected draft asset.

sections.heading: Maggette Alone Justified the Clippers' Side
sections.body: Maggette spent eight seasons with the Clippers, grew from an athletic reserve into a starter and regularly created free throws through aggressive drives. He averaged more than twenty points per game in three seasons and provided a reliable offensive option during a period when the franchise struggled to retain talent. His defense and decision-making were imperfect, and injuries interrupted several campaigns, but his production far exceeded the value of the eventual pick Orlando received. The Clippers also benefited from his contract control through his prime and later allowed him to leave in free agency only after extracting years of scoring. A single player delivering that amount of direct value would be enough to win the deal. The additional assets widen the margin.

sections.heading: Dooling and Strong Added Depth to an Already Excellent Return
sections.body: Dooling did not become a star, but he played four seasons with the Clippers and developed into a useful guard whose speed and defense allowed him to handle reserve minutes. Strong supplied veteran frontcourt depth, and the second-round pick and cash added smaller value. None of those pieces changes the historical verdict by itself. Together they show how much Orlando included to complete the cap-clearing objective. Los Angeles did not have to choose between one prospect and another; it received a young scorer, a lottery guard, a veteran and secondary consideration for one protected future pick. That asymmetry supports an A-plus even though the Clippers did not build a contender around the return.

sections.heading: Orlando's Free-Agent Ambition Explains the Risk
sections.body: The Magic were trying to create enough room to sign multiple stars, and the plan was not irrational. McGrady became a superstar, while Hill's injuries prevented the intended pairing from reaching its ceiling. Duncan remained in San Antonio. The Maggette transaction should therefore be evaluated within a broader strategy that produced one major success and two disappointments. Salary space can be as valuable as a player when it creates access to elite free agents. The problem is that Orlando surrendered several controlled assets and received only a distant protected first directly in this trade. The broader free-agent summer does not assign all of McGrady's value to this specific move, especially because other cap-clearing decisions contributed. A D credits the strategic purpose and the eventual first-round pick while recognizing the enormous direct value gap.

sections.heading: The Protection Schedule Delayed Orlando's Payoff
sections.body: The pick was protected heavily enough that the Clippers retained it through several drafts. Delay reduces draft value because the receiving team cannot use the asset when the trade is made and faces uncertainty about where it will land. When the selection finally conveyed at No. 22 in 2006, Orlando chose Marcus Williams and later moved his rights. The downstream path did not approach Maggette's eight seasons. The long wait also meant the pick did nothing to support the McGrady era that motivated the cap strategy. Orlando accepted both outcome risk and time risk, while the Clippers put young players on the floor immediately.

sections.heading: Why the Magic Avoid an F
sections.body: An F would imply that Orlando received no plausible benefit or pursued an incoherent objective. The Magic created real cap space, signed McGrady and obtained a first-round pick that eventually conveyed. The 2000 offseason was one of the franchise's boldest attempts to build a contender, and clearing Maggette's contract helped make the larger plan possible. Those facts matter. The grade remains low because the transaction's direct return was dramatically weaker than the assets surrendered and because the delayed pick did not restore the lost value. A D distinguishes a failed exchange from a senseless one. The Clippers' A-plus reflects exceptional acquisition efficiency; Orlando's D reflects a defensible strategy executed at an excessive price. The timing of the comparison also favors Los Angeles. Maggette began producing before Orlando's pick could convey and remained useful through the entire delay. Every protected season represented another year in which the Clippers controlled the better asset while the Magic waited. By the time the obligation became Marcus Williams, the original free-agent plan had already run its course and McGrady had left Orlando. The delayed return arrived too late to support the strategy that justified the sacrifice.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Clippers won because Maggette became a long-term twenty-point scorer, Dooling supplied useful rotation seasons and the rest of the package added depth, all for one heavily protected future first. Orlando's cap-clearing plan had a legitimate purpose and helped create the 2000 free-agent opportunity, but the eventual No. 22 pick did not come close to replacing the direct player value surrendered.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The Protected Pick That Could Not Keep Up With Eight Seasons of Production
featuredDeepDive.intro: Orlando's return looked flexible and potentially valuable because the final draft slot was unknown. Los Angeles' return looked messy because it contained several young and veteran pieces. Over time the uncertainty disappeared. Maggette became a reliable scorer, Dooling became a rotation guard and the protected pick remained delayed until late in the first round. The comparison shows how protection and time can quietly erode the value of a future asset.

sections.heading: Maggette Developed in the Exact Role Orlando Could Not Offer
sections.body: Orlando was preparing to give major wing responsibility to McGrady and Hill, making Maggette less central to the immediate plan. Los Angeles had minutes, touches and patience available. That environment allowed him to develop through mistakes and expand his offensive game. His ability to attack the rim and draw fouls became the foundation of his value. The Magic's roster logic explains why he was movable, but it also illustrates the danger of treating a blocked young player as expendable. A crowded depth chart can reduce internal opportunity without reducing market value. The Clippers recognized that distinction.

sections.heading: The 2000 Free-Agent Plan Was Bold Enough to Merit Context
sections.body: Orlando entered the summer with a credible chance to sign Duncan and ultimately landed McGrady and Hill. Few teams create that level of access, and clearing money was essential. If Hill had remained healthy or Duncan had joined, the Maggette cost might be remembered as an acceptable sacrifice within a championship build. Trade grading still must isolate what this transaction produced. McGrady's signing was influenced by the full cap plan, not only this deal, and the Magic surrendered more talent than the protected pick returned. Context prevents an overly punitive grade; it does not erase the imbalance.

sections.heading: Protection Transferred Most of the Draft Risk to Orlando
sections.body: Because the pick could not convey in the protected range, the Clippers kept the most valuable early outcomes. Orlando waited until Los Angeles improved enough for the obligation to become a late first. That structure protected the team sending the pick and limited the upside for the receiver. It is a useful lesson in why the words 'future first-round pick' can overstate value without the protection schedule. The Magic received a nominal first but little chance at a premium selection, while the Clippers received players whose upside was immediate and visible.

sections.heading: The Clippers Still Failed to Maximize the Broader Roster
sections.body: An A-plus trade does not imply that Los Angeles built an excellent team around it. The Clippers missed the playoffs throughout most of Maggette's tenure and often struggled with injuries, continuity and management. The 2005-06 team reached the second round, and Maggette was part of that competitive period, but the franchise did not turn the asset haul into sustained contention. The grade belongs to the transaction itself: acquiring substantial talent at minimal cost. Later organizational shortcomings do not reduce the value received on draft night.

sections.heading: A Better Orlando Structure Would Have Included More Certainty
sections.body: The Magic could have sought a less protected pick, an additional young player, multiple selections or a later transaction after the primary free agents committed. Any of those approaches might have preserved more value. The urgency of opening maximum cap space weakened leverage, and the Clippers used that urgency effectively. Orlando's mistake was not believing in a star-driven plan; it was concentrating too much cost in one cap-clearing trade while accepting a return whose upside was heavily restricted. That pricing error is the heart of the verdict.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Los Angeles converted one protected future first into a young scorer who stayed eight seasons, another lottery prospect, a veteran and secondary assets. Orlando's larger free-agent strategy explains the willingness to sacrifice talent, but the protection schedule and delayed No. 22 pick left the direct return far behind. The Clippers receive an A-plus for acquisition efficiency; the Magic receive a D for paying a coherent strategic cost at an unreasonable level.

sections.heading: Alvin Gentry Opened the Clippers Wing Rotation
sections.body: Los Angeles sent Tyrone Nesby to Washington on November 28, 2000, getting Cherokee Parks and Obinna Ekezie. The immediate issue was not that Nesby had no place in the NBA; the Clippers were trying to divide perimeter minutes among Lamar Odom, Darius Miles, Quentin Richardson, Corey Maggette and Eric Piatkowski. Coach Alvin Gentry told the Los Angeles Times that the crowded wing group needed relief so the young players could progress. Nesby was 24 and averaging 7.7 points through 14 games. The Clippers accepted two frontcourt contracts because the trade exchanged a redundant role for positional depth rather than because either incoming player was projected as a franchise piece.

sections.heading: Michael Jordan Wanted a Wing; Washington Paid Two Big Men
sections.body: The Wizards approached the move differently. Basketball operations president Michael Jordan said Nesby filled a need at small forward without dismantling Washington’s existing rotation. Parks and Ekezie had only arrived from Vancouver in the August 2000 Isaac Austin transaction, and both were in the last year of their contracts. The November exchange is therefore a clear two-for-one, not a hidden pick swap or a stand-in for the larger 2001 Juwan Howard deal. Washington sought a 6-foot-6 wing who could play that season, while Los Angeles wanted playing time and a taller body for the frontcourt. Those contemporary team explanations are useful checks against generic hindsight about which team supposedly acquired more talent.

sections.heading: Ekezie Returned to Washington Almost Immediately
sections.body: The most revealing aftermath involved Obinna Ekezie. Los Angeles waived him on November 29, one day after acquiring him; Washington claimed him on December 1. That sequence makes the exchange a very short actual Clippers tenure for one of the two incoming players, not two full-season contributions. Ekezie later appeared in Washington’s February 22, 2001 multi-player trade with Dallas alongside Calvin Booth and Juwan Howard. That later deal had numerous other assets and must not be credited in full to the November Clippers trade. What the Clippers actually retained from the immediate bargain was Parks, a needed large player, plus extra opportunity for its young wings.

sections.heading: Parks Supplied More Frontcourt Time Than Ekezie
sections.body: Cherokee Parks appeared in 52 Clippers games during 2000-01, starting 31. Washington received 48 regular-season games from Nesby in its uniform, with 22 starts and 8.4 points per game. Those are useful, bounded returns, not evidence that either player became a star. Los Angeles finished 31-51 and Washington 19-63, but neither club’s entire record can be attributed to a November exchange. The original retrospective grades are Clippers B, Wizards C-, and the verdict Clippers Win. They can be defended on the Clippers’ positional adjustment and Parks’s tangible appearances while recognizing Washington gained a real, if modest, scoring wing.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win — Los Angeles B, Washington C-. Nesby played 48 Washington games after the deal; Parks appeared in 52 Clippers games and started 31. Ekezie was waived by Los Angeles the following day and reclaimed by Washington on December 1. Gentry gained room for a crowded young wing rotation, and Parks provided actual frontcourt minutes. The assessment does not conflate Ekezie’s later inclusion in the Dallas deal with this three-player swap.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: 2000 Clippers-Wizards: A Wing Logjam, Two Bigs and a Two-Day Return
featuredDeepDive.intro: On November 28, 2000, the Clippers acquired Cherokee Parks and Obinna Ekezie from Washington for Tyrone Nesby. Contemporary reporting made each club’s reason explicit: Los Angeles had too many young wings competing for minutes, while Michael Jordan’s Washington front office wanted a small forward. Ekezie was waived the following day and reclaimed by the Wizards on December 1. The stored Clippers Win verdict (B against Washington C-) needs that unusual sequence, not an invented lasting two-player return.

sections.heading: Why a Third-Year Wing Was Expendable
sections.body: Nesby was an active Clippers contributor, not an unattached contract or an unused draft right. In his first 14 games of 2000-01 he had averaged 7.7 points, yet the organization wanted more opportunities for rookies Darius Miles and Quentin Richardson alongside Corey Maggette and Lamar Odom. In the Los Angeles Times report, Alvin Gentry described an overloaded collection of perimeter players and his desire to create a more practical rotation. That is specific roster context rather than a generic claim that one franchise prioritized depth and the other future value. Los Angeles was trading away a position where it had several developmental options and adding size where it believed it had fewer.

sections.heading: The Washington Decision Was Immediate, Not a Future-Pick Bet
sections.body: Washington had just received Parks and Ekezie from Vancouver in an August 22 transaction built around Isaac Austin. Both frontcourt players were heading toward expiring contracts. Michael Jordan, then president of basketball operations, viewed Nesby as a young player who addressed an immediate wing shortage. The Wizards were not adding a draft pick or unloading a distant protected obligation; they gave up two big men to secure one player who could contribute at small forward. Nesby’s eventual 48 games, 22 starts and 8.4-point scoring average in Washington substantiate limited near-term use without turning the trade into a decisive breakthrough.

sections.heading: The Waiver and Reclaim Complicate the Asset Count
sections.body: Los Angeles waived Ekezie on November 29. Washington claimed him on December 1, three days after surrendering him in the November 28 trade. Under the ordinary transaction ledger, this is a genuine incoming player who nonetheless did not provide sustained Clippers minutes. In February 2001 Washington moved Ekezie, Calvin Booth and Juwan Howard to Dallas in a much broader deal that brought back Courtney Alexander, Hubert Davis, Christian Laettner, Etan Thomas, Loy Vaught and cash. That package should not be counted as the direct return for Nesby. It underscores that Ekezie reentered the Wizards’ transaction inventory through a separate waiver claim.

sections.heading: Why the B Versus C-Minus Outcome Is Narrow
sections.body: Parks made 52 Clippers appearances, including 31 starts, while Nesby played 48 Washington games and started 22. The comparison shows both teams received playing-time value, although Washington did not keep two players and the Clippers did not actually retain Ekezie. The season records, 31-51 for Los Angeles and 19-63 for Washington, reflect whole-team circumstances and should not be used as a stand-alone causal verdict. Clippers B against Wizards C- and Clippers Win is the inherited grade outcome. It reflects useful size plus relief for the Los Angeles wing rotation rather than a claim that either acquired a long-term star.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Clippers’ B and Wizards’ C- remain attached to a documented three-player swap: Nesby for Parks and Ekezie on November 28, 2000. Nesby supplied 48 Washington games, Parks supplied 52 Los Angeles games, and Ekezie was back with Washington through a December 1 waiver claim. The original Clippers Win verdict is best understood as a short-term rotation decision with a peculiar asset return, not as a championship-defining deal.

sections.heading: What Changed Hands
sections.body: The October 29, 2001 exchange between the Los Angeles Clippers and Portland Trail Blazers was narrow and easy to define: Los Angeles received Will Perdue, while Portland received the rights to Doron Sheffer. That clear picture of what changed hands matters because the retrospective does not need to borrow value from unrelated roster moves or later transactions. The Clippers received a veteran player; the Blazers received draft rights. The final results give Los Angeles the modest advantage because Perdue supplied the more practical realized return. The final grades settle at C+ for the Clippers and C for Portland, which is deliberately a small separation. Both analyses point toward Los Angeles, and the final grade gap reflects that modest edge. The useful conclusion is therefore not that Portland made a disastrous move. It is that the directly exchanged assets produced slightly more directly tied basketball value on the Clippers side.

sections.heading: Why Los Angeles Holds the Edge
sections.body: The case for Los Angeles starts with the simplest fact in the record: the Clippers turned their outgoing rights to Doron Sheffer into Will Perdue. The Los Angeles perspective describes Perdue as the better overall return, and the Portland perspective independently says the outgoing Perdue side supplied more practical value than the rights Portland acquired. That bilateral agreement is more important than the exact letter grade attached inside either available evidence. The final C+/C split preserves the modest nature of the advantage while making the directional judgment explicit. Nothing in the evidence supports a dramatic blowout. Portland did receive a legitimate asset in Sheffer’s rights, and the transaction was a direct exchange rather than a giveaway. But when the evaluation is limited to the value that actually came from the assets that moved, the evidence consistently leaves Los Angeles a step ahead.

sections.heading: How to Read the C+ and C Grades
sections.body: A C+ for the Clippers and C for Portland signals a successful but limited edge. This was not a franchise-changing transaction, and the analysis should not pretend that it was. The grade difference reflects relative realized value, not the fame of the names involved or the later fortunes of either organization. Los Angeles received a player who provided the more practical return; Portland’s draft-rights asset did not match that realized contribution. The one-step separation is useful because it avoids the common retrospective mistake of turning every identifiable winner into an extreme grade. A slight edge can still be historically meaningful when both sides of the trade details point the same way. Here, the source evidence is strong enough to choose a winner but not strong enough to justify a wide gulf. That is exactly what C+ versus C is meant to communicate.

sections.heading: What Portland Still Received
sections.body: Portland’s side should not be erased simply because Los Angeles finished ahead. The Blazers acquired the rights to Doron Sheffer, which were a real basketball asset at the time of the exchange. A rights-based return carries uncertainty by definition, and hindsight can evaluate what that asset became without pretending the outcome was knowable in advance. The Portland-side perspective is especially helpful because it does not describe the deal as a total loss; it says the outgoing Perdue side supplied more practical value while Portland’s package kept the margin narrow. That framing fits the final grade well. Portland gets credit for receiving legitimate consideration, but the completed asset comparison still favors Los Angeles. The final verdict therefore respects both sides of the historical record: the Blazers had an asset-based rationale, while the Clippers ultimately received the better realized return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Clippers Edge. Los Angeles receives a C+ and Portland a C. The transaction was Will Perdue for the rights to Doron Sheffer, and both franchise-side records identify the Perdue side as the better realized return. The margin remains narrow because Portland did receive a legitimate draft-rights asset and because the available evidence supports a modest advantage rather than a dominant one. The verdict counts only value directly tied to the two assets that actually changed hands. On that disciplined basis, the Clippers finished one step ahead.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Clippers–Trail Blazers 2001: Why a Small Asset Swap Still Produces a Real Winner
featuredDeepDive.intro: Small transactions are often harder to grade well than blockbuster trades because the temptation is either to ignore them or to exaggerate the winner. The 2001 Clippers–Trail Blazers exchange rewards a narrower approach. Los Angeles received Will Perdue. Portland received the rights to Doron Sheffer. Both team-side transaction records agree that the Perdue side produced the better practical return, but neither record supports treating the deal as lopsided. That makes the trade a useful example of how an evergreen retrospective can identify a winner while keeping the magnitude proportional to the evidence.

sections.heading: A Clear Exchange Makes the Evaluation Stronger
sections.body: There is very little ambiguity about what belongs inside this trade. The Clippers’ return was Will Perdue; Portland’s return was the rights to Doron Sheffer. Because the exchange is so compact, the analysis does not need to rely on speculative chains or distant downstream events. The rights can be judged by what they produced, and Perdue can be judged as the directly acquired player. That narrow focus improves confidence in the conclusion. Los Angeles does not receive credit for unrelated roster construction, and Portland is not penalized for unrelated decisions. The only question is which side of this specific swap produced more realized basketball value. Both analyses answer that question in favor of the Clippers.

sections.heading: Why the Winner Does Not Need an Extreme Grade
sections.body: The fact that Los Angeles won does not automatically make the trade a major success. The final C+ grade says the Clippers came out ahead without turning a modest transaction into something larger than it was. Portland’s C makes the same point from the other side: the Blazers received legitimate consideration, but the asset did not produce the same practical return as Perdue. This kind of proportional grading is important in a historical site. If every clear winner becomes an A and every losing side becomes an F, the grades stop distinguishing a useful marginal win from a transformational one. C+ versus C keeps the evaluation tied to the scale and certainty of the evidence.

sections.heading: The Two analyses Converge on the Same Story
sections.body: The Los Angeles record calls the result a slight Clippers edge and identifies Will Perdue as the better overall return. The Portland record describes the transaction from the opposite side and still says the outgoing Perdue side supplied more practical value, producing a slight partner edge. Those records are independent in framing but aligned in direction. That convergence matters because it reduces the chance that the final verdict is simply a home-team interpretation. The exact internal grade labels differ, but the historical point does not: the directly acquired Clippers asset delivered the stronger realized value. The documented C+/C result translates that shared directional judgment into one consistent final grade pair.

sections.heading: What the Trade Teaches About Rights Versus Realized Value
sections.body: Draft rights are valuable because they preserve the possibility of future player value, but a retrospective eventually has to distinguish possibility from realized outcome. Portland’s acquisition was not meaningless simply because Los Angeles later received the better practical return. The rights to Doron Sheffer were still consideration and deserve to remain inside the evaluation. At the same time, hindsight is precisely what allows the final results to say that Perdue produced more usable value. The trade therefore illustrates a balanced retrospective principle: respect the asset as it existed at the time, then use the completed outcome to separate the grades. That produces a modest but defensible Clippers win.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Los Angeles C+, Portland C, with a Slight Clippers Edge verdict. The exchange was compact, the available sources agree on what changed hands, and both team perspectives favor the Perdue side. Portland’s draft-rights return was real, so the margin stays small. But the completed value attached to the directly exchanged assets leaves the Clippers with the better historical result.

sections.heading: The Clippers Acquired the Adult Their Young Core Needed
sections.body: Los Angeles entered the 2005 offseason with Elton Brand, Corey Maggette and emerging size, but the roster lacked a proven point guard capable of organizing close games. Sam Cassell supplied that missing authority. He was thirty-five and coming off an injury-disrupted season in Minnesota, yet his résumé included championships, an All-Star appearance and a history of controlling late possessions. The Clippers did not merely swap Marko Jarić for an older guard. They also received a protected first-round pick, shifting future value toward Los Angeles while solving an immediate leadership problem. Cassell’s confidence, pull-up shooting and command of tempo gave the team a reliable offensive structure. For a franchise that had rarely sustained success, the psychological component mattered as much as the tactical fit. The trade told the roster that the organization expected to win now, and Cassell had enough game left to make that expectation credible.

sections.heading: Minnesota Committed Long-Term Money and a Pick to the Wrong Guard
sections.body: The Timberwolves viewed Jarić as a younger, taller playmaker who could defend multiple positions and grow beside Kevin Garnett. Because Jarić was a restricted free agent, the transaction was completed through a sign-and-trade tied to a six-year contract. Minnesota therefore assumed two forms of risk: long-term salary and a first-round pick that could eventually become unprotected. The appeal was understandable after Cassell’s difficult final season with the Wolves, when injuries and contract tension clouded his future. Jarić, however, never became the stable lead guard Minnesota needed. His shooting and decision-making fluctuated, the team missed the playoffs, and the contract became difficult to move. Lionel Chalmers added little. The Wolves exchanged an older player whose value appeared to be declining for youth, but they paid as though youth alone guaranteed improvement. The attached pick made the miscalculation far more expensive.

sections.heading: Cassell Immediately Changed the Clippers’ Competitive Ceiling
sections.body: The 2005-06 Clippers won forty-seven games, captured their first playoff series since the franchise’s 1970s Buffalo era and pushed Phoenix to seven games in the second round. Cassell was central to that breakthrough. He scored, created for Brand, managed pace and provided a late-game option who was not intimidated by the franchise’s history. His value was concentrated into a short period, but concentration is exactly what a win-now trade seeks. Los Angeles did not need six average seasons; it needed one or two seasons capable of turning a promising roster into a credible postseason team. Cassell delivered that transformation immediately. The Clippers later declined as injuries and roster issues accumulated, yet the absence of a conference-finals appearance does not erase the significance of the 2006 run. For a franchise with so little prior success, one veteran guard helped establish a new competitive high.

sections.heading: The Protected First Became Part of the Chris Paul Acquisition
sections.body: The draft pick attached by Minnesota extended the trade’s value well beyond Cassell’s playing tenure. Its protections delayed conveyance until 2012, when it became the No. 10 selection. Before the draft, Los Angeles had included the asset in the package used to acquire Chris Paul from New Orleans. The pick ultimately became Austin Rivers, but the Clippers’ realized benefit was its use as a central piece in landing a franchise-changing point guard. This downstream conversion is unusually powerful: the Cassell trade first produced the veteran who led the club’s 2006 breakthrough, then supplied draft value that helped bring the next great point guard era. The later Paul transaction required additional assets and should not be credited entirely to this deal, but the Minnesota first was a material component. A trade that creates both immediate playoff success and future star-acquisition leverage deserves an elite grade.

sections.heading: Jarić’s Minnesota Tenure Never Justified the Contract or Opportunity Cost
sections.body: Jarić had useful skills. At six-foot-seven, he could handle the ball, see over defenses and guard more than one perimeter position. Minnesota’s error was projecting those tools into a stable lead-guard role and paying a long-term price before the fit had been proven. He struggled to provide efficient scoring or consistent creation, and the Wolves remained outside the playoffs during his tenure. The contract later became part of another large trade, but Minnesota never recovered value comparable to Cassell’s Clippers impact plus the outgoing first. The problem was compounded by Garnett’s timeline. The Wolves needed immediate competence around an MVP-level star, not another multi-year experiment at point guard. By choosing Jarić and attaching the pick, Minnesota reduced both current performance and future flexibility. That is why the grade falls to D despite the reasonable desire to get younger.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Earns an A Because Both Timelines Paid Off
sections.body: The Clippers receive an A rather than A-plus because Cassell’s prime contribution lasted only a short window and the team did not advance beyond the second round. Still, the transaction succeeded on every core objective. Cassell fixed the point-guard position, helped produce a historic season, elevated Brand’s effectiveness and established veteran standards. The first-round pick retained value through years of protections and later helped acquire Paul. Minnesota receives a D because Jarić did not become the anticipated long-term starter, Chalmers added little, the team absorbed a burdensome contract and the pick eventually escaped the protection structure. This was not simply a case of an old player outperforming a young one for one season. Los Angeles received the better player for the relevant window and the better future asset. The structure was favorable at signing and became even stronger with time.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win. Sam Cassell immediately led Los Angeles into its first playoff-series victory in three decades, while the protected first-round pick later helped the franchise acquire Chris Paul. Minnesota received a younger guard, but Jarić’s long contract and uneven play did not solve the point-guard problem. The Clippers earn A; the Timberwolves receive D.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: One Sam Cassell Trade Connected Two Landmark Clippers Eras
featuredDeepDive.intro: The deal’s unusual power comes from its double life. Cassell drove the franchise’s 2006 breakthrough, and the first-round pick attached to him remained protected long enough to become useful in the Chris Paul trade. Los Angeles did not merely win a veteran swap. It created a bridge between the best Clippers team in decades and the Lob City era.

sections.heading: Cassell’s Leadership Had Tactical Substance
sections.body: Calling Cassell a leader can obscure the basketball mechanisms behind his influence. He could run pick-and-rolls with Brand, punish defenders from the elbows, back down smaller guards and control the final possessions of close games. The Clippers previously had talent but often lacked an organizer who could decide which matchup to attack. Cassell gave coach Mike Dunleavy a veteran extension on the floor. His willingness to take difficult shots also reduced pressure on younger teammates who had not experienced playoff basketball. Leadership was therefore visible in shot selection, pace and communication, not merely speeches. That tactical authority helped Los Angeles convert a talented roster into a forty-seven-win team. The trade succeeded because the veteran’s specific skills matched the weaknesses of the roster rather than because experience is automatically valuable.

sections.heading: The 2006 Run Changed the Franchise’s Baseline
sections.body: For many organizations, a second-round loss would be a disappointment. For the Clippers, reaching Game 7 of the conference semifinals represented a historic break from decades of instability. The team had not won a playoff series since the franchise was known as the Buffalo Braves. Cassell helped make postseason success tangible for players and fans who had mostly known potential without results. That change in baseline matters in trade evaluation. A transaction can create value by altering what an organization believes is possible, especially when the incoming player performs at the center of the breakthrough. The Clippers did not sustain the momentum immediately, but the 2005-06 season became a reference point for later teams. Cassell’s impact was short, yet it was not shallow.

sections.heading: The Pick Protection Delayed the Cost Until It Hurt Minnesota Most
sections.body: Minnesota protected the first for years, which limited the immediate danger but did not eliminate it. As the Wolves struggled, the asset remained unresolved and continued occupying future flexibility. Eventually the protection expired, and the pick became a lottery selection. Long protection schedules can create a false sense of safety because the sending team retains the pick during its worst seasons while still owing a valuable asset later. The obligation can also complicate other trades. Los Angeles benefited from patience: the Clippers did not need the pick to convey quickly because Cassell had already delivered the immediate return. When the selection finally became available, it was valuable enough to help support a superstar acquisition. The same delay that softened Minnesota’s initial risk increased the duration of the burden.

sections.heading: The Chris Paul Connection Is Real but Must Be Credited Carefully
sections.body: The Clippers did not obtain Paul for the Minnesota pick alone. The trade also included Eric Gordon, Al-Farouq Aminu and another first-round asset. It would be inaccurate to claim that Cassell directly turned into Paul. The proper conclusion is that the pick preserved and increased the value of the original 2005 transaction. It gave Los Angeles one more meaningful asset when a rare superstar became available. Because the pick was unprotected by 2012, New Orleans could value it as a legitimate lottery opportunity, and it became Austin Rivers at No. 10. Downstream analysis should acknowledge the entire later package while still recognizing the material role of the inherited first. The Cassell deal created leverage that the Clippers used correctly seven years later.

sections.heading: Minnesota’s Decision Reflected a Recurring Failure Around Garnett
sections.body: The Wolves repeatedly struggled to balance Garnett’s immediate championship window with attempts to find younger, cheaper support. In this trade they moved away from an aging, frustrated Cassell, but the replacement did not improve the team and required a long commitment. Jarić’s versatility looked attractive in theory, yet Minnesota needed high-level creation and shooting more than positional novelty. The first-round pick further reduced the resources available to repair the roster. Garnett remained elite while the supporting cast deteriorated, and the franchise eventually had to enter a larger reset. The Cassell transaction did not cause every problem, but it illustrates how one misjudged fit can consume salary, draft capital and precious seasons of a superstar’s prime.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Los Angeles won twice: first when Cassell gave the Clippers a historic playoff run, and again when Minnesota’s protected first became leverage in the Paul trade. The Wolves’ youth bet never produced a comparable basketball or asset return. Few transactions connect two distinct franchise peaks as clearly as this one.

sections.heading: The Jazz and Clippers Swapped Veteran Backup Guards
sections.body: Utah traded Jason Hart to the Los Angeles Clippers on July 23, 2008, receiving Brevin Knight in a straight, one-for-one exchange. The Deseret News and Salt Lake Tribune covered the transaction that day, and the Clippers' subsequent team transaction record independently confirms the direction. Knight had started 39 of 74 games for Los Angeles in 2007–08, while Hart appeared in 57 for Utah, all off the bench. Neither club received a draft choice or cash in the deal. The point was to change the reserve point guard behind each team's preferred starter, not to obtain a future superstar. Confusing these players' original 2007–08 clubs with the clubs that acquired them in 2008 would reverse the deal.

sections.heading: Hart Returned to the Clippers but Played Sparingly
sections.body: Hart's arrival was a reunion with the Clippers, for whom he had played 23 games in 2006–07 before signing with Utah. At the Jazz, he lost reserve minutes to Ronnie Price during 2007–08, which explains Utah's willingness to move him. In 2008–09 he appeared in just 28 games for the Clippers, starting twice and averaging about 11 minutes. Basketball-Reference lists 65 points in that Los Angeles stint, modest production for a player the club was acquiring primarily for experience and backup coverage. The Clippers waived him in February 2009. His subsequent 11 Denver appearances belong to a separate contract, not to Los Angeles's realized return on the July 2008 trade.

sections.heading: Knight Became a Steady Utah Reserve for One Season
sections.body: Knight had been a starting-caliber playmaker earlier in his career, but Utah acquired him at age 32 to support Deron Williams rather than to replace him. The Jazz used Knight in 74 games in 2008–09, with no starts. Basketball-Reference credits him with 2.4 points and 2.6 assists per game, alongside 12.7 minutes. He was a low-scoring reserve but provided considerably more regular-season availability for Utah than Hart gave the Clippers in that same campaign. The clubs did not trade identical statistical profiles: Knight emphasized passing and experience, while Hart offered a familiar guard who had already spent time with Los Angeles. The direct tenure of each veteran lasted one season or less.

sections.heading: How the Short-Term Guard Returns Compare
sections.body: The July 23, 2008 exchange is graded an Even Trade, with a C for both Utah and Los Angeles. Brevin Knight appeared in 74 regular-season games for the Jazz in 2008-09, averaging 2.4 points and 2.6 assists as a reserve behind Deron Williams. Jason Hart made only 28 appearances for the Clippers before being waived, so the new clubs did not receive identical immediate availability. Neither guard became a long-term fixture for his acquiring team, however, and the swap included no draft choices or additional future assets. Those limited returns help explain the comparable overall grades without equating their box-score production. Utah obtained more one-season reserve minutes, while Los Angeles received a familiar veteran but used him less. Any reader weighing those differences should count only each guard's actual time with his new club, not later contracts or unrelated transactions.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Published Even Trade — Clippers C, Jazz C. Los Angeles received Jason Hart, who made 28 Clippers appearances in 2008–09; Utah acquired Brevin Knight, who played 74 games as a reserve. The 2008 exchange was a straight guard-for-guard swap, not a draft-rights deal. Utah obtained more immediate appearances, but neither return was long-lasting. Grades stay preserved pending a broader comparable-trade review.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The 2008 Hart–Knight Backup-Guard Swap: Who Played Where?
featuredDeepDive.intro: On July 23, 2008, the Clippers acquired Jason Hart from Utah and sent Brevin Knight to the Jazz. Both veterans were seeking reserve minutes rather than new roles as franchise stars. Knight played 74 games for Utah in 2008–09, while Hart appeared only 28 times for Los Angeles before being waived. The underlying asset direction is supported by contemporaneous Utah reporting and Clippers transactions, and the games are documented in season player records. The site's Even Trade verdict and C/C grades are preserved.

sections.heading: Getting the Direction Right on July 23
sections.body: The Salt Lake Tribune reported that the Jazz sent Jason Hart to the Clippers for Brevin Knight, and the Deseret News described the transaction as a direct one-for-one agreement on the same date. Los Angeles's own season transaction history lists the acquisition of Hart for Knight. Those records eliminate any possibility of a third club or separate future draft choice being hidden in the package. They also help avoid confusion because Hart had previously worn a Clippers uniform and Knight had joined Los Angeles only in 2007. At the time of the exchange Hart was a Utah reserve and Knight was a Clippers guard. The archive correctly lists Hart coming to Los Angeles and Knight coming to Utah; no canonical player direction needs adjustment.

sections.heading: What Los Angeles Actually Got From Hart
sections.body: Hart had lost playing time in Utah to Ronnie Price, despite appearing in 57 Jazz games in 2007–08. The July trade sent him back to a Clippers backcourt with other needs and opportunities, but his second stint did not create a durable rotation role. His 2008–09 player record shows 28 games, two starts and 312 minutes for Los Angeles, translating to just over 11 minutes per game. He scored 65 points with the Clippers and was waived in late February 2009. The later Denver appearance line comes after a separate agreement and should not be imported into Los Angeles's return. Judging this transaction as a long-term Clippers point guard solution would ignore the actual brevity of his stay.

sections.heading: What Utah Received From Knight
sections.body: Knight had supplied veteran ballhandling and spot starts for the Clippers during 2007–08, appearing in 74 games and starting 39. Utah needed a reserve behind Deron Williams after Hart's role diminished. In 2008–09 Knight again appeared in 74 games, this time with zero starts and an average of 12.7 minutes. He added 2.6 assists against 2.4 points per contest, a profile consistent with a pass-first reserve. Utah obtained one dependable season of backup availability, not a new starting point guard or a player who would become a building block for years. The 74-to-28 games comparison is the clearest direct outcome difference between the acquired veterans.

sections.heading: The C/C Assessment and the Limits of a One-Season Swap
sections.body: The site's grades are Los Angeles C and Utah C with an Even Trade verdict. Since the two players were veteran backups, a low or middle-tier grade for each can be explained by limited long-term return rather than dramatic draft consequences. The immediate evidence is not wholly balanced: Knight played far more games for the Jazz that season than Hart did for the Clippers. That distinction should be presented directly instead of smoothed away by generic even-trade prose. A future sitewide grade audit might revisit whether the Utah side deserves an edge, but it would need consistent weights for minutes, contract terms, opportunity cost and comparable low-impact exchanges. The original grades and published outcome are deliberately unchanged during this source-quality audit.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Utah received Knight for Hart on July 23, 2008. Knight played 74 Jazz games in 2008–09 as a reserve; Hart played 28 Clippers games before a February waiver. The stored Even Trade, Clippers C and Jazz C remain as archived. Utah clearly received more direct appearances, but neither team obtained lasting high-impact value. An independent grading review can weigh the usage gap without changing the original asset ledger.

sections.heading: Two-for-Two Agreement Announced November 21
sections.body: The Clippers announced on November 21, 2008 that they would receive Zach Randolph and Mardy Collins from the Knicks for Tim Thomas and Cuttino Mobley. Los Angeles wanted another frontcourt scorer after Elton Brand had departed, while New York was trying to create greater salary flexibility under its new management. The official Clippers release identifies exactly these four players, with no draft pick in the exchange. The announcement date is the preserved archive date, but the trade was finalized on November 25 after New York reviewed medical findings concerning Mobley. Those separate announcement and finalization dates should not become two trade records. Randolph came in as the established scorer; Collins was a younger guard prospect, and both names deserve an independent accounting.

sections.heading: Randolph Scored 20.9 a Night but Played Only 39 Clippers Games
sections.body: Randolph averaged 20.9 points and 9.4 rebounds in 39 Los Angeles regular-season games during 2008-09, starting 34 and shooting 48.7 percent from the field. That was legitimate high-volume production for a club searching for another scorer. His Clippers stay nevertheless ended after that one partial season. In July 2009, Los Angeles traded him to Memphis for Quentin Richardson in a separate transaction. Randolph eventually became a cornerstone of the Grizzlies, but his 551 Memphis games are not additional Clippers performances from the Knicks exchange. The original acquisition brought immediate points and rebounds, not a lasting Los Angeles star tenure. The A-plus Clippers grade is inherited; it should be evaluated against this accurately bounded output instead of a claim of years of team control.

sections.heading: Collins Also Played 82 Clippers Games Across Two Seasons
sections.body: Collins was more than an unexamined second name in the package. He played 39 regular-season games with Los Angeles in 2008-09, making 14 starts and averaging 5.9 points and 2.6 assists. In 2009-10 he added 43 Clippers appearances without a start, scoring 2.6 points and assisting on 1.0 basket per game. Across the two seasons, his Clippers contribution totaled 82 NBA appearances. Collins had appeared in nine early 2008-09 Knicks games before the deal, and those belong to New York, not to the receiving franchise. His short rotation run was less consequential than Randolph's scoring, but the first two seasons of player-specific records show actual depth from both Los Angeles acquisitions.

sections.heading: Thomas Played 36 Knicks Games; Mobley Played None
sections.body: New York received 36 regular-season appearances from Thomas during 2008-09, with one start and averages of 9.6 points and 3.1 rebounds. The other incoming name did not take the court for the Knicks. Mobley underwent further testing after his trade physical raised concerns about his heart, then announced his retirement on December 11, 2008 because of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. That medical issue delayed the trade finalization and ended his playing career, but it should not be framed as a performance decision made by New York or a prediction of what he might have produced. The Knicks gained Thomas's modest rotation minutes and financial-contract flexibility, while the Clippers received Randolph's 39 games and Collins's two-year 82-game stint.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win — Los Angeles A-plus, New York B-minus in the existing archive. The Clippers got Randolph's 39 games of 20.9-point, 9.4-rebound basketball and 82 Collins games over two seasons. The Knicks got 36 Thomas appearances and no Mobley games after his December 2008 retirement following medical testing. New York also pursued financial flexibility, while Randolph's later Memphis production is not Los Angeles team value.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Randolph's 20.9-Point Clippers Burst and Mobley's Medical Halt
featuredDeepDive.intro: The November 2008 Clippers-Knicks swap was announced on the 21st and finalized four days later after medical review of Cuttino Mobley. Los Angeles received Zach Randolph, who averaged 20.9 points and 9.4 rebounds in 39 Clippers games, plus Mardy Collins, who supplied 82 appearances across two seasons. New York received Tim Thomas for 36 games and Mobley, who retired without playing a Knicks regular-season game. The Clippers' A-plus over the Knicks' B-minus reflects bounded on-court returns while recognizing New York's financial motivation and the medical delay, not an invented additional pick or later Knicks production.

sections.heading: The Deal Was Delayed Four Days by Mobley's Medical Review
sections.body: Although announced on November 21, the trade was not completed until November 25. New York examined concerns revealed in Mobley's medical review, while Randolph and Collins had to wait to play for their new club. A contemporaneous Los Angeles Times report documents the approval delay and eventual completion without adding another player or a draft choice. Mobley retired on December 11 after subsequent testing found a serious heart condition. None of those developments changes the four-player asset ledger, but they explain why the Knicks did not get game production from one of the two veterans. Reporting the health circumstances factually avoids suggesting that Mobley simply refused to join New York. The original Clippers announcement date stays in the canonical record; the approved completion is a distinct procedural milestone.

sections.heading: Randolph Provided a Twenty-Point Scorer, Then Was Moved Again
sections.body: During his 39 Clippers regular-season appearances, Randolph averaged 20.9 points and 9.4 rebounds, giving Los Angeles high-volume post scoring after Elton Brand left. He started 34 games and remained a productive NBA forward despite the club's poor results. That output is directly attributable to the November Knicks trade. Los Angeles then moved Randolph to Memphis in a separate July 2009 deal for Quentin Richardson. The later Grizzlies years, All-Star selections and postseason successes belong to Memphis, not to the Clippers team that briefly held him. This is a short but substantial direct return followed by another identifiable roster decision. The separate Memphis transaction also stops the original Knicks-Clippers trade from being inaccurately credited with every achievement of the eventual Memphis core.

sections.heading: Collins and Thomas Had Smaller, Measurable Team-Specific Roles
sections.body: Collins logged 39 Los Angeles games after the exchange in 2008-09 and another 43 in 2009-10. His initial Clippers stint included 14 starts, while the following season consisted entirely of reserve appearances. Thomas, meanwhile, played 36 Knicks games in 2008-09 with just one start, averaging 9.6 points while hitting 42.1 percent of his three-point attempts for New York. Those totals give three of the four traded players identifiable receiving-team service. Collins's earlier Knicks appearances and Thomas's preceding Clippers seasons must stay with the sending clubs, not be presented as new production. The practical difference was Randolph's higher scoring contribution, while the other two delivered less prominent bench or spot-start duty on their receiving teams.

sections.heading: The Grade Requires the Knicks' Financial Purpose in View
sections.body: The stored verdict calls this Clippers Win with Los Angeles A-plus and New York B-minus. The Clippers landed Randolph for a 39-game scoring burst and Collins for 82 games over two seasons. New York received Thomas for 36 appearances and Mobley for none after the medical issue forced his retirement. The Knicks' organizational motivation included contract flexibility while preparing for a future free-agency period, which cannot be reduced to the 2008-09 box score alone. The archived grade comparison is a discretionary assessment, not a claim that the Clippers kept Randolph for his later Memphis successes. Naming the deal's health complication, finite playing time and financial context makes the conclusion traceable to the original four assets rather than repetitive commentary about hypothetical returns.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The retained A-plus Clippers and B-minus Knicks grades are a retrospective preference for immediate Randolph scoring over the modest New York playing return. The four-player trade cleared medical review November 25, 2008, and Mobley retired December 11 without a Knicks game. Thomas appeared 36 times for New York, while Randolph gave Los Angeles 39 games and Collins 82 games across two seasons. The later Memphis Randolph years and earlier Knicks or Clippers player seasons are excluded from receiving-team NBA production.

sections.heading: Memphis Bought Low on Production the League Had Learned to Distrust
sections.body: Zach Randolph arrived in Memphis with established scoring and rebounding numbers but a reputation that had lowered his trade market. He had moved from Portland to New York and then to the Clippers, with questions following him about defense, conditioning, decision-making and whether his production translated into winning. Memphis saw an opportunity rather than a disqualifier. The Grizzlies surrendered Quentin Richardson, a veteran wing they had acquired only weeks earlier, and obtained a 27-year-old power forward who had just averaged roughly 20 points and 10 rebounds. The talent gap was obvious; the risk was cultural.

sections.heading: The Clippers Prioritized a Reset Around Blake Griffin
sections.body: Los Angeles had drafted Blake Griffin first overall and needed frontcourt minutes, financial flexibility and a cleaner developmental hierarchy. Randolph's contract and ball-dominant style did not fit that plan. Acquiring Richardson was less about securing a comparable player than moving a veteran salary and opening Griffin's path. Richardson was then traded again within days, eventually reaching Miami after a chain of transactions. The Clippers therefore achieved an organizational objective, but they did not capture meaningful basketball value from Randolph himself. A rebuild can make a sale rational without making the return strong.

sections.heading: Randolph Became an All-Star as Soon as Memphis Gave Him Stability
sections.body: In his first Grizzlies season, Randolph averaged 20.8 points and 11.7 rebounds and earned his first All-Star selection. The immediate response mattered because it disproved the idea that Memphis needed a long rehabilitation project before receiving value. Randolph's low-post footwork, offensive rebounding and ability to create a reliable shot late in possessions gave the young roster a physical offensive identity. He later earned a second All-Star selection and remained with the franchise for eight seasons, turning a one-year gamble into one of the longest and most productive partnerships in team history.

sections.heading: The 2011 Upset Converted Good Statistics Into Franchise History
sections.body: Memphis entered the 2011 playoffs as the eighth seed and defeated top-seeded San Antonio for the first series win in franchise history. Randolph was the central offensive force, including a 31-point performance in the clinching Game 6. That postseason changed how the trade should be viewed. The Grizzlies had not merely found an efficient scorer at a discount; they had acquired the player who could impose their style against an elite opponent. The upset created the foundation for seven consecutive playoff appearances and turned Grit and Grind from a slogan into a repeatable competitive identity.

sections.heading: The Core Four Fit Made Randolph More Valuable Than His Raw Numbers
sections.body: Randolph's Memphis value cannot be separated from Marc Gasol, Mike Conley and Tony Allen. Gasol covered space defensively and passed from the high post. Conley organized the offense and defended point guards. Allen set the perimeter tone. Randolph supplied the bruising half-court scoring and rebounding none of the others replicated. Memphis did not transform him by asking him to abandon his strengths. It built a roster that absorbed his weaknesses and magnified what he did best. That contextual success belongs to the Grizzlies' front office and makes the acquisition more impressive than a simple box-score comparison.

sections.heading: The Grade Gap Should Name Memphis as the Winner
sections.body: Memphis holds an A+ because Randolph became a two-time All-Star, the franchise's playoff scoring and rebounding standard-bearer and the emotional center of its most successful era. The Clippers remain at C because clearing the frontcourt for Griffin had strategic logic and the transaction was part of a broader reset. Yet Richardson did not stay, and the downstream return never approached Randolph's eight-year impact. Calling this Partner Win obscures the result. The verdict should identify the Grizzlies directly.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Memphis wins the trade with an A+, while the Clippers remain at C. Randolph immediately became an All-Star, powered the franchise's first playoff-series victory and spent eight seasons defining the Grit-and-Grind era. Los Angeles had a defensible reason to clear salary and touches for Blake Griffin, but that roster-management benefit did not produce comparable incoming value. Memphis converted a distressed asset into a retired-number franchise icon for the price of a player who never appeared for the Grizzlies and was quickly rerouted by the Clippers.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Zach Randolph Found the Team That Turned His Reputation Into an Identity
featuredDeepDive.intro: The Randolph trade is one of the strongest examples of organizational context changing how a player's value is realized. His scoring and rebounding were never hidden, but previous teams had treated the rest of the package as too difficult to build around. Memphis made a different calculation. It accepted the limitations, placed him beside complementary defenders and decision-makers, and gave him the stability to become a civic and competitive symbol. The price was minimal because the market focused on his reputation; the return was enormous because the Grizzlies understood his fit.

sections.heading: The Market Discount Was the Entire Opportunity
sections.body: Randolph had already demonstrated that he could produce 20-and-10 seasons, yet his trade path kept reducing the price attached to that production. By July 2009, Memphis did not need to win a bidding war. It needed to decide whether the negative external evaluation was more important than the skill set. The front office effectively wagered that a defined role and a stable environment would matter more than previous stops. That is a classic buy-low trade: the receiving team does not discover talent the league has never seen; it values known talent differently because it believes it can create a better setting.

sections.heading: His Post Game Gave Memphis a Playoff Offense That Traveled
sections.body: Grit and Grind is often remembered primarily as defense, but Randolph supplied the half-court scoring that made the style sustainable. He could establish deep position, score with either hand, use angles against longer defenders and create second chances on the offensive glass. Those possessions mattered most in the playoffs, when transition opportunities declined and every team understood the first action. Memphis could enter the ball to Randolph and force a defense to commit. That reliability helped the Grizzlies upset San Antonio and later reach the 2013 Western Conference finals.

sections.heading: Marc Gasol Was the Ideal Frontcourt Counterweight
sections.body: Randolph and Gasol were not redundant big men. Randolph operated as the physical scorer and rebounder, while Gasol supplied rim protection, passing vision and defensive organization. Their contrasting games allowed Memphis to play through two bigs without losing all spacing or decision-making. Gasol's presence also reduced the defensive burden on Randolph, letting him conserve energy for the glass and the post. The trade succeeded partly because the Grizzlies already possessed the rare partner who could make Randolph's style more valuable rather than less playable.

sections.heading: The Relationship With Memphis Outgrew the Transaction
sections.body: Randolph became associated with the city's toughness and embraced community work that deepened the connection beyond basketball. Memphis later retired his No. 50, making him the first player in franchise history to receive that honor. Retired numbers do not automatically prove a trade win, but this one reflects the full return: production, playoff breakthroughs, identity and civic attachment. The Clippers were trying to create space for a new era. Memphis acquired the person who came to represent its own era more completely than anyone expected on trade day.

sections.heading: The Clippers Logic Deserves Context but Not an Inflated Grade
sections.body: Griffin's arrival changed the Clippers' priorities, and moving Randolph reduced a potential positional conflict. The franchise eventually built Lob City around Griffin and Chris Paul, so the reset itself was not a failure. The trade grade must still measure what was exchanged. Los Angeles did not receive a draft asset that became part of Lob City, nor a young player who developed with Griffin. Richardson was another movable contract. The Clippers achieved subtraction; the Grizzlies acquired creation. That difference is why C versus A+ remains the right separation.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Grizzlies Win verdict captures both the talent result and the organizational achievement. Memphis did not merely receive better statistics; it created the environment in which Randolph became an All-Star, a playoff centerpiece and a retired-number icon. The Clippers' decision to clear the frontcourt for Griffin was understandable and prevents an F, but the incoming package generated no enduring asset. Few trades show more clearly how one franchise's unwanted contract can become another franchise's culture.

sections.heading: Portland Bought Rebounding and Rim Protection from Los Angeles
sections.body: The February 16, 2010 trade sent Marcus Camby from the Clippers to Portland for guard Steve Blake and forward Travis Outlaw. Portland needed frontcourt support after injuries reduced its available center rotation. Camby had 51 Clippers appearances that season, every one as a starter, and was still a high-level rebounder at age 35. Portland was not purchasing a young long-term centerpiece. It was acquiring immediate defensive production from a veteran who had been NBA Defensive Player of the Year in 2007. That differed from Los Angeles’s incentive to convert an expiring big-man contract into two players and more flexibility along the perimeter.

sections.heading: Camby Delivered 122 Blazers Games across Three Seasons
sections.body: Camby appeared in 23 Portland regular-season games after arriving in 2009-10 and started all of them, pulling down 11.1 rebounds and blocking 2.0 shots per game. He returned in 2010-11 for 59 games and 51 starts, averaging 10.3 rebounds and 1.6 blocks. During 2011-12 he played 40 more Blazers games, all starts, before Portland traded him to Houston in a separate deal. Those three Portland stints total 122 regular-season games and 114 starts received from the 2010 acquisition. Any subsequent Rockets or Knicks appearances fall outside the direct Portland basketball return and cannot inflate this trade’s score.

sections.heading: The Clippers Received Two Real Roster Contributors
sections.body: Steve Blake played 29 Clippers games after the exchange, starting 10, and averaged 6.8 points and 6.1 assists over 26.3 minutes. His three-point accuracy during that stretch reached 43.7 percent, a useful addition to the backcourt. Travis Outlaw appeared in 23 Clippers games and started six, scoring 8.7 points in 21.7 minutes on average. Outlaw had been limited by injury in Portland earlier that season, so Los Angeles took on some availability uncertainty. Both players left after that shortened 2009-10 stint, meaning their combined 52 receiving-team games should not be presented as multi-season Clippers control.

sections.heading: The Preserved B Versus B-Plus Grades Recognize Different Timelines
sections.body: The historical verdict reads Slight Blazers Edge, Portland B+ and Los Angeles B. Portland secured three stretches of center minutes during an injury-affected period, while Los Angeles added two usable players for the remaining weeks of 2009-10. The Clippers finished 29-53, and Blake and Outlaw did not become long-term building blocks there. This does not mean the veteran Camby was without value to the Clippers before the trade, nor that his whole career or Portland’s later team record resulted from one February move. The advantage comes from the longer realized defensive and rebounding return Camby generated after he changed teams.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Blazers Edge is preserved with Portland B+ and Los Angeles B. Camby recorded 122 Portland regular-season games and 114 starts through 2011-12. Blake played 29 Clippers games and Outlaw 23, totaling 52 receiving-team appearances in 2009-10 without a follow-on season in Los Angeles. That contrast supports the inherited narrow Portland advantage, while avoiding credit for Camby’s later Houston or New York seasons.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Marcus Camby to Portland in 2010: Three Seasons of Defense for Two Clippers Rentals
featuredDeepDive.intro: Portland traded Steve Blake and Travis Outlaw to the Clippers for Marcus Camby on February 16, 2010. Camby then logged 122 Portland regular-season games across the remainder of 2009-10, 2010-11 and part of 2011-12, with 114 starts. The Clippers received 29 games from Blake and 23 from Outlaw before both departed. The stored Slight Blazers Edge, Portland B+ and Los Angeles B grades are measured through those direct receiving-team contributions, not through veteran reputations or later stops elsewhere.

sections.heading: Portland Needed an Actual Center after Frontcourt Injuries
sections.body: The Trail Blazers had dealt with major injuries to Greg Oden and Joel Przybilla, making a defensive rebounding presence an urgent roster need. The veteran Camby had already started all 51 of his Clippers games that season before being traded. His value was clearest around the rim and on the glass, not from a high scoring average. The Blazers surrendered two players who had been part of their guard and wing rotation, Steve Blake and Travis Outlaw. The timing makes sense only with that injury context: Portland paid with backcourt depth to get an available center capable of starting immediately.

sections.heading: Three Distinct Portland Stints Set the Return at 122 Games
sections.body: Basketball Reference separates Camby’s 2009-10 Clippers and Portland lines: 51 games before the trade and 23 after. The 23 Portland games included 11.1 rebounds and 2.0 blocked shots per outing. In 2010-11 he returned for 59 games with 51 starts, averaging 10.3 rebounds; in the shortened 2011-12 campaign he logged 40 Blazers games and 40 starts before leaving for Houston. Added together, those Portland receiving-team segments give 122 regular-season appearances and 114 starts. Counting all of his 74 combined-team games in 2009-10 as Portland production would improperly add the 51 Clippers starts from before the exchange.

sections.heading: Blake and Outlaw Filled Roles without Lasting in Los Angeles
sections.body: Blake supplied 177 assists in 29 Clippers appearances after joining in February, shooting 43.7 percent from three. He had started 28 games in Portland earlier in the season, but only his 29 Los Angeles games count as the Clippers return here. Outlaw played 23 games in his new uniform after a difficult injury-interrupted Portland season, scoring 8.7 points per game with six starts. Both left after the year. Their contributions were real, so the Clippers should not be treated as having received nothing; they simply did not provide the long-duration frontcourt service Camby gave Portland.

sections.heading: Separate Later Moves Cannot Be Backdated into This Deal
sections.body: Camby was still a Trail Blazer during most of 2011-12 but was subsequently sent to Houston. Steve Blake continued his NBA career elsewhere, including a later Lakers stint, while Outlaw also played for another franchise. None of those later team minutes belongs to Los Angeles or Portland’s direct February 2010 received-player record. The B+ versus B split remains narrow because the Clippers gained immediately useful backcourt depth while Portland acquired someone who could start 114 games and address a specific injury-driven defensive need. That is stronger evidence than treating total later franchise wins as the outcome of a single transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The stored Slight Blazers Edge with Portland B+ and Los Angeles B remains intact. Portland got Camby for 122 regular-season games and 114 starts; Los Angeles used Blake for 29 games and Outlaw for 23, a combined 52 in their immediate Clippers stints. Camby’s later Rockets games, Blake’s post-Clippers seasons and Outlaw’s later career are excluded. The source-specific comparison favors Portland’s sustained center help over two shorter return pieces.
