sections.heading: The Clippers Acquired a Player Who Could Define Every Possession
sections.body: Los Angeles sent Eric Gordon, Chris Kaman, Al-Farouq Aminu, and Minnesota's unprotected 2012 first-round pick to New Orleans for Chris Paul and two future second-round picks. The cost included a promising scorer, a starting center, a recent lottery wing, and a valuable pick. The Clippers accepted that price because elite point guards in their prime rarely become available, and Paul could immediately organize a young roster built around Blake Griffin and DeAndre Jordan.

sections.heading: Paul Changed the Franchise Before the First Playoff Series
sections.body: The Clippers had long been defined by losing seasons, instability, and limited relevance in Los Angeles. Paul's arrival changed expectations immediately. He controlled tempo, created efficient shots, improved late-game execution, and made the team nationally visible through the Lob City partnership with Griffin and Jordan. The franchise produced six winning seasons during his first stint and reached the playoffs every year he was there.

sections.heading: The Competitive Results Were Historically Significant
sections.body: The Paul-era Clippers won their first two Pacific Division titles and three playoff series. They never reached the conference finals, which prevents the trade from being graded as a completed championship success, but the sustained floor was unprecedented for the organization. Paul became the franchise's all-time assists leader and repeatedly earned All-NBA and All-Defensive recognition while establishing Los Angeles as a credible destination.

sections.heading: New Orleans Received Quantity Without a Cornerstone
sections.body: Gordon had the highest upside in the return, but injuries and an unhappy tenure prevented him from becoming the replacement star New Orleans needed. Kaman stayed only briefly, Aminu developed into a useful defender but reached his best role elsewhere, and the first-round pick became Austin Rivers. Each asset had legitimate value, yet the package never produced a player or chain capable of replacing Paul's influence.

sections.heading: The Rejected Lakers Deal Shaped the Pressure
sections.body: The league-owned Hornets had already agreed to a three-team trade that would have sent Paul to the Lakers before the transaction was rejected. New Orleans then had to reopen the market while Paul's departure remained inevitable. The Clippers package emphasized youth and draft value, which was sensible for a franchise awaiting stable ownership. That context explains the return but does not improve how its pieces ultimately performed.

sections.heading: Why the Grades Are Far Apart
sections.body: Los Angeles received six seasons of elite point-guard play and a complete change in organizational identity. New Orleans received several credible assets, but no durable cornerstone and no comparable competitive era. The Clippers' A-plus rewards both production and transformation. The Pelicans' D-plus recognizes that the return was not empty, while acknowledging that the franchise failed to convert its best outgoing player into lasting star value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Clippers won the trade by a wide margin. Chris Paul created the most successful sustained era in franchise history to that point, led six straight winning seasons and playoff appearances, and made the organization relevant to players and fans. New Orleans received legitimate prospects, a veteran center, and the pick used on Austin Rivers, but none became a comparable cornerstone. The grades remain Los Angeles A-plus and New Orleans D-plus, with Clippers Win.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: How Chris Paul Made the Clippers Matter
featuredDeepDive.intro: The Paul trade was bigger than the highlight lobs that gave the era its name. Los Angeles acquired a player capable of controlling the game, holding teammates accountable, and establishing professional expectations inside an organization with little history of sustained success. New Orleans assembled a package that looked credible on transaction day, but the absence of a lasting centerpiece allowed the gap to widen every season Paul remained elite.

sections.heading: The Price Reflected Paul's Scarcity
sections.body: Gordon was coming off a promising start to his career, Aminu had been a recent lottery pick, Kaman had All-Star experience, and the Minnesota pick was unprotected. Los Angeles was not exploiting a giveaway. It was choosing to consolidate several uncertain assets into one known elite organizer. That is often the correct decision when the acquired player can raise the value of every remaining young piece on the roster.

sections.heading: Lob City Was a Basketball System Before It Was a Brand
sections.body: The spectacular finishes mattered because Paul consistently created them through pace, spacing, and precise reads. Griffin became more dangerous as a screener and short-roll creator, while Jordan received high-efficiency rim opportunities. Paul also supplied mid-range scoring and turnover control when the transition game disappeared. The entertainment value grew from a repeatable offensive structure, not only from athleticism.

sections.heading: The Ceiling Was Lower Than the Talent Suggested
sections.body: The Clippers' inability to reach the conference finals remains the strongest limitation on the grade. Injuries, blown series leads, and a difficult Western Conference prevented the core from converting regular-season excellence into a title run. Even so, trade evaluation should compare the outcome with the cost and the franchise's prior baseline. Paul delivered years of contention and relevance that the outgoing assets never matched.

sections.heading: New Orleans Needed One Asset to Become the Next Foundation
sections.body: The package offered several possible paths, but none developed into the star bridge the franchise required. Gordon's injuries reduced his availability, Rivers struggled before finding a later role elsewhere, and Aminu became more valuable after leaving. The Hornets gained flexibility and respectable talent, but the absence of a retained centerpiece made the rebuild dependent on future draft luck rather than this return.

sections.heading: The Trade Altered Future Recruitment
sections.body: Paul's tenure helped the Clippers become a place where star players could imagine winning. That reputation outlasted Lob City and formed part of the organization's later pursuit of Leonard and George. Not every future decision can be credited directly to one trade, but franchise credibility compounds. Paul helped replace the expectation of dysfunction with the expectation that Los Angeles would operate as a serious playoff team.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Clippers made the clearly superior trade. Paul became the engine of six straight winning seasons, the franchise's all-time assists leader, and the defining player of an era that permanently raised expectations. New Orleans's package was defensible in structure but disappointing in realized value, with no asset developing into a comparable cornerstone. Los Angeles A-plus, New Orleans D-plus, Clippers Win.

sections.heading: The Clippers Moved Mullens and a Future Second
sections.body: On February 20, 2014, Los Angeles announced that it sent Byron 'B.J.' Mullens and a conditional second-round draft selection to Philadelphia for a separate future conditional second. NBA's historical trade ledger identifies the Clippers' outgoing selection as a 2018 second-round pick, while the Sixers' outgoing conditional selection was due in 2014. Those were separate draft rights, not an exchange of players. The Clippers were preparing for the postseason and used Mullens sparingly: their official announcement lists 27 appearances, 2.5 points and 1.2 rebounds in just 6.2 minutes per game. Philadelphia was rebuilding and could absorb a marginal veteran while acquiring potential future draft capital. The direction of both picks is central to grading the transaction.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Got Eighteen Real Games From Mullens
sections.body: Mullens' short Philadelphia tenure can be measured precisely. He appeared in 18 games, started none and averaged 6.8 points with 3.3 rebounds in 13.7 minutes, according to NBA and Basketball-Reference season statistics. Those totals were greater than the 2.5 points and 6.2 minutes he had averaged for the Clippers, but not the production of a long-term cornerstone. His field-goal percentage rose to 46.5 percent in the Philadelphia sample, while he played fewer than 250 total minutes for the Sixers. The extra roster opportunity was real and modest. Hindsight should not convert that eighteen-game stretch into a sustained starting career or disregard it simply because Philadelphia valued future picks more than a short-term win total.

sections.heading: The 2014 Return to Los Angeles Never Conveyed
sections.body: The conditional 2014 second-round pick that Philadelphia offered to the Clippers did not convey, as both clubs' archived season transaction records indicate. The original agreement's protection meant that Los Angeles could receive a selection only within the agreed draft range. That result left the Clippers without a realized incoming pick from this February exchange, although they had created a roster opening and moved on from a little-used contract. The Clippers signed other veterans after the deadline, but those subsequent transactions require their own ledgers and cannot be described as players traded for Mullens. A grade has to consider both the failed conditional pick and the team's roster flexibility rather than assigning a fictional 2014 draftee to Los Angeles.

sections.heading: The 2018 Second Passed Through New York and Denver
sections.body: The Clippers-origin 2018 second-rights asset carried identifiable value after Philadelphia received it. The selection later passed to the New York Knicks, and the Knicks sent the relevant second-round choice to Denver in the February 2018 three-team Emmanuel Mudiay exchange. Denver held the No. 43 selection at the 2018 draft and selected Maryland forward Justin Jackson; Orlando then acquired Jackson's rights in a separate draft-night deal for Jarred Vanderbilt and another future second. NBA's 2018 draft transaction tracker confirms the Denver-to-Orlando rights transfer. Philadelphia did not select Jackson, and neither Mullens nor the old 2014 Clippers return automatically bought Orlando a player. The published 76ers Win, B+ Philadelphia and F Clippers grades are retained while the exact intermediate pick conditions undergo provenance review.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Stored result: 76ers Win — Philadelphia B+, Clippers F. Philadelphia obtained Mullens, who played 18 games, plus a 2018 Clippers-origin second that ultimately became No. 43 Justin Jackson after passing through other teams. Los Angeles received a conditional 2014 second that did not convey. Jackson was selected by Denver and acquired by Orlando, not drafted by Philadelphia. Grades stay unchanged pending exact cash and pick-chain verification.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Byron Mullens and the Second-Round Pick That Reached No. 43
featuredDeepDive.intro: Philadelphia's February 2014 acquisition of Byron Mullens looked like a small deadline transaction, but a separate 2018 second-round pick gave it a longer documentary trail. The Clippers exchanged the lightly used center and future second-round consideration for a conditional 2014 pick that did not convey. Mullens played 18 games for the 76ers. The Clippers-origin future selection later moved through New York and Denver before the Justin Jackson selection at No. 43, then to Orlando. Distinguishing ownership of the draft right from the eventual player is the key to reading the deal accurately.

sections.heading: The Clippers' Announcement Distinguishes Both Trades
sections.body: Los Angeles made two unrelated February 20 announcements in the same team press release. One dealt Antawn Jamison to Atlanta for Cenk Akyol's rights; the other sent Mullens and a conditional second to Philadelphia for a future second-round selection. Those trades should not be collapsed just because they shared a date and press release. NBA's all-time deadline record describes the Philadelphia outgoing 2018 second and an additional cash component not separately itemized in the original Mullens paragraph. The current archival ledger records Mullens and the pick, but does not list that cash for the Sixers. The cash reporting difference is flagged for source-specific adjudication rather than automatically editing the canonical asset list. The core player and pick directions are supported by the team's own account.

sections.heading: Eighteen Philadelphia Games, Not a Turnaround
sections.body: Mullens had spent most of his 2013–14 Clippers tenure on the bench. His Los Angeles averages were 2.5 points and 1.2 rebounds in 27 games, with 6.2 minutes per appearance. After the move to Philadelphia he played 18 times with no starts, averaging 6.8 points, 3.3 rebounds and 13.7 minutes. NBA's official player profile and Philadelphia's season roster corroborate those numbers. This is a useful contrast: Philadelphia got more immediate use from Mullens than Los Angeles had recently obtained, but the absolute contribution still came from a reserve on a rebuilding team. It is also a different return from the future pick. Evaluating them separately prevents a brief scoring spike from being inflated into a long-term roster benefit.

sections.heading: The Two Conditional Picks Had Different Final Outcomes
sections.body: The protected 2014 second Philadelphia gave Los Angeles was not exercised, according to the Clippers and Sixers' transaction histories. The 2018 second the Clippers supplied was a different asset with a longer route. Secondary pick-chain records show the Clippers-origin right transferring out of Philadelphia to New York in October 2014; the Knicks later moved a corresponding 2018 second to Denver during the February 2018 Mudiay multi-team exchange. Denver's own season transactions list Justin Jackson, selected 43rd overall in 2018. NBA's draft-night tracker subsequently records Denver trading those rights to Orlando for No. 41 Jarred Vanderbilt and another second. The evidence supports the final path but a legal description of the intermediate swap rights should be checked before assigning each protection clause as a certainty.

sections.heading: Why No One Can Credit the 76ers With Jackson's Career
sections.body: Justin Jackson was not an immediate Philadelphia acquisition on February 20, 2014. The club received future draft rights, not a player under contract. Four years later the Clippers-origin asset stood at No. 43, but Denver selected Jackson and Orlando took his rights through its separate trade. The later 2018 moves involved Emmanuel Mudiay, Devin Harris, Doug McDermott, Jarred Vanderbilt and additional picks, none of whom were directly exchanged for Mullens in 2014. Los Angeles meanwhile never got its conditional 2014 selection. Those differences help explain why the stored archive favors Philadelphia, but the B+/F gap is still an editorial judgment requiring measured discussion of Philadelphia's early asset value and Los Angeles' roster flexibility. The official ledger also leaves a cash-reporting question open, so no grade change should occur on assumption alone.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Clippers moved Mullens and future 2018 second consideration to Philadelphia for a protected 2014 second that did not convey. Mullens produced 18 Sixers appearances; the later No. 43 Justin Jackson pick passed through New York and Denver, then went to Orlando. The source-based B+/F and 76ers Win verdict is preserved, with cash and intermediate pick-swap terminology held for independent review.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Got Jared Dudley and the Better Draft Asset
sections.body: Milwaukee acquired Jared Dudley and a protected 2017 first-round pick while sending Carlos Delfino, Miroslav Raduljica and a protected 2015 second-round pick to Los Angeles. Dudley immediately became useful on a Bucks team that jumped into the playoffs, appearing in 72 games and supplying veteran wing minutes, shooting and defense. The first-rounder gave Milwaukee another valuable asset beyond Dudley's season.

sections.heading: The Clippers Barely Got Basketball Value Back
sections.body: Los Angeles made the move partly to clear Dudley after a disappointing, injury-affected season and to create financial flexibility. The basketball return was extremely thin. Delfino never played for the Clippers while recovering from foot injuries, Raduljica was waived before the regular season and the protected second-round pick did not approach the value of the first-rounder Los Angeles surrendered. Cap relief was useful, but the price was high.

sections.heading: The First-Round Pick Matters Without Borrowing OG Anunoby's Career
sections.body:
Milwaukee later traded the incoming first-round asset to Toronto in the Greivis Vasquez deal. That proves the pick retained real market value, but it does not mean the Bucks should receive credit for OG Anunoby, whom Toronto eventually selected with the pick. The Bucks deserve credit for owning and monetizing a first-round asset. Even with that conservative treatment, Dudley plus the pick comfortably exceeded the Clippers' return.

The draft timing is the clearest way to avoid overstating Milwaukee's win. The Bucks acquired a protected first-round right that ultimately became the 2017 No. 23 selection, but they moved that right to Toronto before the draft as part of their Greivis Vasquez transaction. OG Anunoby subsequently became the named draft outcome under Toronto's control. Milwaukee should be credited for receiving and then using a tradeable first-round asset, not for Anunoby's NBA development in another city. Los Angeles instead got a protected second-round asset, along with a salary-management benefit and very little player production. Those are unequal returns without inventing a Bucks Anunoby stint.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win — Milwaukee A-, Los Angeles D-. The Bucks received immediate rotation value from Dudley and preserved additional value in a first-round pick they later moved. The Clippers gained flexibility but almost no on-court production from Delfino or Raduljica and surrendered the best draft asset in the deal. Milwaukee won decisively without needing to inflate the downstream asset chain.

sections.heading: The Clippers Bought Flexibility, Not a Player
sections.body: Los Angeles sent Jared Cunningham, the rights to Cenk Akyol and cash to Philadelphia for the rights to Serhiy Lishchuk. The timing explains the deal. Cunningham had the Clippers' only non-guaranteed contract and was likely to be released if he stayed. By trading him instead, Los Angeles removed nearly $400,000 from its cap calculation, cut the related luxury-tax bill and opened a roster spot. Lishchuk was a rights asset, not the reason to make the move.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Took the Cash and a Rights Flyer
sections.body:
The 76ers waived Cunningham the same day, so he produced no on-court return for Philadelphia. Akyol's rights remained an asset and were later sent to Denver in the JaVale McGee salary-dump trade. That later first-round pick should not be backfilled into this transaction: Denver was paying Philadelphia to absorb McGee's contract, with Akyol serving as the nominal return. For this trade, Philadelphia's real value was the cash plus a low-cost rights asset.

The purpose of the move was unusually tied to salary rules rather than acquiring a future rotation player. Los Angeles sent guard Jared Cunningham, the rights to Cenk Akyol and cash to Philadelphia, receiving the rights to Serhiy Lishchuk. The acquired rights were not a guarantee that Lishchuk would play an NBA minute for the Clippers. Instead, the deal cleared nearly $400,000 in cap obligations and helped reduce the team's luxury-tax exposure. Philadelphia obtained a young guard and a separate rights asset without needing to solve the Clippers' payroll objectives itself. That is why an even C+ judgment can recognize both sides' narrow purposes without inventing a major basketball career for either rights holder.

sections.heading: Why the Result Is Essentially Even
sections.body: Neither team acquired a player who became useful NBA production from this exchange. Los Angeles achieved an immediate cap, tax and roster-space objective instead of simply waiving Cunningham. Philadelphia collected cash and another movable rights piece without keeping Cunningham. The stakes were small and both clubs got a practical benefit, so a decisive winner would overstate what this transaction actually became.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Los Angeles C+, Philadelphia C+. The Clippers saved money and opened a roster spot at a moment when Cunningham was likely to be waived anyway. The 76ers received cash and Akyol's rights but no Cunningham production. With no meaningful direct player value on either side, equal modest grades fit the result better than treating either package as a major win.

sections.heading: The Clippers and Wizards Exchanged Two Expiring Veterans
sections.body: On June 26, 2018, Los Angeles acquired center Marcin Gortat from Washington for guard Austin Rivers. The Clippers' announcement and Washington's corresponding release agree on the one-for-one structure; no future pick, cash payment or third team appears in the consideration. Both players were headed into the final year of their existing contracts at similar salaries. Gortat had appeared in all 82 Wizards games in 2017–18, averaging 8.4 points and 7.6 rebounds. Rivers was coming off a career-high 15.1 points and 4.0 assists over 61 Clippers games. These are pretrade statistics that explain each team's interest, not production already supplied to its new club.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Wanted Frontcourt Coverage, Not Another Scorer
sections.body: Clippers basketball president Lawrence Frank explicitly described the deal as a way to rebalance the roster with a proven frontcourt player. DeAndre Jordan's potential departure created uncertainty at center, and Gortat was a familiar veteran screener and rebounder who had been available nearly every night in Washington. The team knowingly surrendered Rivers, a 25-year-old guard whose recent scoring and three-point shooting had improved during his four seasons in Los Angeles. That is a positional-choice story, not an exchange of one center for another. Gortat gave the Clippers immediate size and experience, but the club's press release did not promise a long-term starter or another asset from the Wizards.

sections.heading: Rivers' Washington Tenure Lasted Only Through December
sections.body: The Wizards wanted more backcourt creation and perimeter attempts, according to their June 2018 release. Rivers had made 37.8 percent of his threes with Los Angeles in 2017–18 and was expected to add secondary ballhandling. His direct Wizards tenure proved brief: Basketball-Reference records 29 Washington games in 2018–19, with 7.2 points and 2.0 assists per appearance. On December 17, 2018, Washington sent Rivers and Kelly Oubre Jr. to Phoenix in a separate deal for Trevor Ariza. Ariza cannot be treated as a direct player Washington received from the Clippers for Gortat, because Oubre was also part of the later agreement. The original exchange should be evaluated on Rivers' real Wizards stint and subsequent trade utility.

sections.heading: Gortat Helped Briefly Before a February Waiver
sections.body: Gortat started 43 of his 47 Clippers games in 2018-19, averaging 5.0 points and 5.6 rebounds in 16.0 minutes. Los Angeles waived him on February 7, 2019, so the center did not reproduce the full-season durability he had shown with Washington. The Wizards' return was also temporary: Austin Rivers played 29 games for Washington, averaging 7.2 points and 2.0 assists, before moving with Kelly Oubre Jr. in a separate December 2018 transaction. The Clippers Win verdict grades Los Angeles B-plus and Washington C-minus, reflecting the judgment that Gortat offered useful frontcourt coverage for an immediate roster need. Neither player stayed with his new club beyond that season, however. Their actual playing time offers a more limited basis for comparing the two returns than either player's longer NBA career or later transactions.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Published verdict: Clippers Win — Los Angeles B+, Washington C-. The one-for-one June 2018 trade gave Los Angeles 47 games and 43 starts from Gortat before his February 2019 waiver; Rivers played 29 Washington games before a separate December move to Phoenix with Kelly Oubre Jr. The deal addressed different roster needs but produced short direct tenures. The existing grades are preserved pending an independent cross-trade evaluation.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Gortat for Rivers: A One-for-One 2018 Contract and Position Bet
featuredDeepDive.intro: Los Angeles and Washington swapped Marcin Gortat and Austin Rivers in June 2018, exchanging experienced players with one year left on their contracts. The Clippers sought cover at center while the Wizards wanted a guard capable of creating shots. Both receiving teams used the newcomers for less than a full season. The source record supports a narrow analysis: 47 Clippers games for Gortat, 29 Wizards games for Rivers and two later, separate roster decisions. The archived Clippers Win and B+/C- marks have not been revised.

sections.heading: Transaction-Day Rights and Salary Shape
sections.body: The Clippers' official June 26 release names Gortat as the only incoming player and Rivers as the only outgoing one. Washington independently reports the inverse. The NBA's contemporaneous coverage notes both contracts were expiring and carried similar salaries, which explains why a direct swap worked without the additional pieces often required by trades involving unequal obligations. No draft choice or trade exception should be manufactured merely because either player later moved again. Gortat was 34 and had been a nearly full-time Wizards starter, while Rivers was 25 and averaging 15.1 points in his prior Los Angeles campaign. The contrast reflects different roster requirements: one club needed size, the other wanted a guard who could score and handle the ball.

sections.heading: The Clippers' Center Experiment and Its Measurable End
sections.body: Gortat's Los Angeles statistics are clearly separated from the Washington line that accompanied the original announcement. He appeared 47 times for the Clippers, starting 43, averaging 5.0 points, 5.6 rebounds and 16.0 minutes during the 2018–19 season. He was waived February 7, 2019; that date is documented in the club's season transaction log. The Clippers went on to make the playoffs, but Gortat had been released before that run and should not be credited for games he did not play. His arrival was a legitimate short-term response to uncertainty at center, yet it did not become a durable core position solution. A grade based on the exchange should value those 47 appearances rather than automatically awarding a full season of veteran reliability.

sections.heading: Rivers' Washington Contract and the Separate Phoenix Package
sections.body: Washington described Rivers as a potential secondary ballhandler and more frequent perimeter shooter, citing 37.8 percent three-point accuracy with the Clippers. His actual Wizards performance in 2018–19 was 29 games, 7.2 points and 2.0 assists per outing. The December 17 trade to Phoenix moved Rivers together with Kelly Oubre Jr. and brought Trevor Ariza to Washington. The second deal involved another player of material value, making it wrong to attribute Ariza in full to the original Clippers–Wizards swap. Rivers later found a role with Houston after Phoenix waived him, but those minutes likewise belong to a different employer and transaction chain. This separation of original consideration from later routing is necessary when the archive evaluates each trade independently.

sections.heading: What a Consistent Historical Grading Review Would Compare
sections.body: The current stored verdict is Clippers Win, Los Angeles B-plus and Washington C-minus. The NBA team releases explain why Los Angeles targeted a veteran center and Washington preferred more guard shooting, so both management ideas are source-grounded. The realized outcomes are mixed, however: Gortat started many games but was waived by February, and Rivers contributed 29 Wizards appearances before becoming part of an Ariza package with Oubre. There is not enough evidence in those outcomes alone to justify silently altering the archived letters. A consistent grade review would compare short-run lineup fit, acquired-player minutes, opportunity cost of the outgoing player and later independent trades without double-counting either Ariza or playoff games Gortat missed.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Clippers received Gortat and the Wizards received Rivers in a straight 2018 swap of expiring veterans. Gortat appeared in 47 Los Angeles games before his February release; Rivers played 29 Washington games before a separate multi-player December trade. Both clubs acquired genuine rotation utility but neither a lasting core player from this exchange. The recorded Clippers Win, Los Angeles B+ and Washington C- remain stored pending a broader grading comparison.

sections.heading: Ivica Zubac and Michael Beasley / Mike Muscala: The Deal’s Actual Shape
sections.body: At the 2019 deadline, the Clippers sent Mike Muscala across the hallway for Ivica Zubac and Michael Beasley. Beasley was not the strategic prize and was soon waived; the bet was that Zubac, still on his rookie contract, could grow into a reliable center. The Lakers wanted a shooting big for a roster built around LeBron James and were willing to sacrifice a young center whose next contract and role were uncertain. The deal exchanged a short-term spacing idea for long-term interior development.

sections.heading: Ivica Zubac and Michael Beasley / Mike Muscala: The Winning Team’s Case
sections.body: Zubac became a durable Clippers starter and supplied efficient finishing, strong rebounding, screening and increasingly reliable interior defense. He did not need plays called for him to improve lineups, which made him compatible with several versions of the Clippers’ star-heavy roster. The team retained him on reasonable contracts, used him in repeated playoff runs and later preserved additional transaction value. Turning Muscala into that many years of stable starting play is an A+ acquisition. Winning this comparison requires more than posting the largest scoring average.

sections.heading: Ivica Zubac and Michael Beasley / Mike Muscala: The Return Package Deserves a Fair Reading
sections.body: The Lakers received the skill type they wanted but almost none of the duration. Muscala played limited minutes during the remainder of a season in which Los Angeles missed the playoffs, then departed in free agency. His shooting reputation made the roster logic visible, yet the team surrendered a younger player at a scarce position without obtaining meaningful control or a secondary asset. An F reflects the absence of durable production, not a claim that Muscala lacked NBA ability. The losing side is not automatically assigned a failing grade.

sections.heading: Ivica Zubac and Michael Beasley / Mike Muscala: Leverage and Timing Changed the Price
sections.body: The immediate Lakers objective was floor spacing around LeBron James, and their general-management staff also wanted to remove Zubac restricted-free-agent cap hold before the coming summer. Muscala was acquired from Philadelphia as part of the Clippers Tobias Harris trade only one day before being sent to the Lakers. On February 7 the clubs exchanged Zubac and Beasley for Muscala with no draft selection. The Lakers also sent Svi Mykhailiuk and a second-rounder to Detroit the day BEFORE for Reggie Bullock; those are separate assets and cannot inflate the return or cost of this transaction. The Clippers gained the right to evaluate a young center who was already averaging 8.5 points in 15.6 minutes for the Lakers that season and soon offered a longer commitment.

sections.heading: Ivica Zubac and Michael Beasley / Mike Muscala: Asset Conversion and Opportunity Cost
sections.body: The Clippers kept Zubac through several contracts and playoff seasons, receiving center rebounding, screening, efficiency and defensive size at a cost tied to one short-lived Muscala stint. The retrospective value did not end when Zubac stopped playing for the club: on February 5, 2026, the Clippers formally sent Zubac and Kobe Brown to Indiana and received Bennedict Mathurin, Isaiah Jackson, 2026 and 2029 first-round picks and a 2028 second-round pick. That is a separate larger transaction, so its entire return cannot be assigned to Zubac alone, but it shows the former Lakers prospect still possessed meaningful trade value seven years after his arrival. Michael Beasley was waived February 9, 2019. The direct 2019 contrast and subsequent option value support the original grade gap without manufacturing any extra 2019 picks.

sections.heading: Ivica Zubac and Michael Beasley / Mike Muscala: Verdict and grading scale
sections.body: The existing “Clippers Win” verdict remains correct. Both grades are retained because A+ and F accurately describe the extremes. The Clippers paid almost nothing for a player who became a durable starter and reusable asset. The Lakers gave up the transaction’s only long-term piece for a short-term role player who did not change their season. Few modern two-team trades produce a clearer completed margin.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Clippers win because Ivica Zubac became a durable starting center, playoff contributor and later reusable asset for the cost of a brief Mike Muscala rental. Michael Beasley was incidental, but Zubac’s seven seasons of value make the Clippers’ A+ and Lakers’ F appropriate.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Ivica Zubac for Mike Muscala: The Seven-Year Clippers Center and 2026 Trade Value
featuredDeepDive.intro: On February 7, 2019, the Lakers traded 21-year-old Ivica Zubac and Michael Beasley across Los Angeles for Mike Muscala. The move was not part of the separate Lakers-Detroit transaction involving Svi Mykhailiuk and a future second-round pick. Muscala played 17 regular-season games for the Lakers, while Zubac grew into a Clippers center relied upon across successive postseason teams. His contract continuity mattered almost as much as his scoring; the Clippers later included him in a substantial February 2026 deal with Indiana. The distinction between 2019 original compensation and 2026 downstream trade value is the basis of this review.

sections.heading: The Lakers Had Seen Zubac Develop Before Making the Trade
sections.body:
Zubac had played 33 games and started 12 for the Lakers during 2018-19 before the deadline, averaging 8.5 points, 4.9 rebounds and 15.6 minutes. His 58.0 percent field-goal shooting suggested a limited but useful interior-finishing role even before the Clippers acquired him. The move was not a decision about whether the center could play in the NBA. Los Angeles had already seen his hands, size and developing role alongside LeBron James, but judged Muscala shooting skills and Zubac future cap hold as more urgent.

The Clippers public release described Zubac as an improving young center and rim protector. They took on Beasley as the other incoming player, then waived him two days later. The two clubs traded three named players, not a disguised exchange of first-rounders or a larger Detroit-related pick package. Evaluating the original front-office decision begins by preserving that distinction.

sections.heading: Muscala Was a Short-Term Shooting Bet, Not a Guaranteed Rotation Solution
sections.body:
Muscala arrived in Los Angeles after being involved in the Clippers six-player deal with Philadelphia a day earlier. He had averaged 7.4 points and 4.3 rebounds in 47 Sixers appearances to that point in 2018-19, and his career three-point accuracy made sense as the type of bench floor spacer Los Angeles wanted. The Lakers received only 17 appearances from Muscala before the season ended, then he left in free agency; the team missed the playoffs that spring.

That sequence does not mean Muscala lacked NBA skill. It means the immediate Lakers return was small relative to the potential cost of retaining Zubac. The team surrendered an inexpensive 21-year-old center who had already made starts for a player it did not control beyond that brief stint. The draft rights or future production in other Lakers deals cannot be used to change that comparison.

sections.heading: Zubac Stayed Useful Across Multiple Clippers Roster Versions
sections.body:
Zubac developed into a reliable starting center while the Clippers rebuilt around different leading scorers. He did not have to be the team top scorer to add value: screening, defensive rebounding, taking the larger opponent near the rim and finishing high-percentage chances are complementary tasks that helped teammates. In some playoff series the club favored smaller units, yet Zubac played useful postseason minutes across several years, unlike the Lakers short Muscala stretch that did not lead to the playoffs in 2019.

Longer control is a separate return from any peak season. By keeping and re-signing Zubac, Los Angeles did not have to replace a starting center through repeated expensive trades. This is why the Clippers A+ hindsight grade is stronger than a description based on field-goal percentages alone. Sustained starter durability became the primary return on a February 2019 transaction whose direct cost was modest.

sections.heading: The February 2026 Indiana Deal Demonstrated Residual Trade Value
sections.body:
On February 5, 2026, Indiana and the Clippers formally announced that Ivica Zubac and Kobe Brown were headed to the Pacers while Bennedict Mathurin, Isaiah Jackson, a 2026 first-rounder, a 2029 first-rounder and a 2028 second-rounder went to Los Angeles. Zubac was not the only outgoing asset, and the incoming picks had their own contractual terms, including protection on the 2026 pick. It would be misleading to treat all five pieces as though they had been direct 2019 Lakers trade compensation.

The relevant point is that the Clippers kept Zubac productive and valuable enough to be part of a major later roster transaction. The second trade is evidence of residual asset value after seven years; it does not transfer Kobe Brown contributions into the 2019 deal. A careful source ledger can describe both transactions without mixing their participant lists or timeline.

sections.heading: The Bullock Trade Is a Separate February 6 Lakers Transaction
sections.body:
The neighboring Lakers-Detroit deal created a tempting source-identity error. On February 6, 2019, Los Angeles sent Svi Mykhailiuk and a future second-round pick to Detroit to get Reggie Bullock. On February 7 the Lakers sent Zubac and Beasley to the Clippers for Muscala. NBA official 2018-19 transaction tracking and both team public releases place those moves on different dates with different counterparties and different outgoing assets. They should never be folded into a single Zubac transaction just because they came at the same deadline.

This distinction also clarifies the Lakers failing grade. The bad exchange does not require adding the Mykhailiuk pick to the cost, or pretending Beasley was a long-term Clippers contributor. The Clippers acquired the best sustained basketball asset from Zubac-Muscala, while the Lakers obtained a brief rental. That direct comparison is already lopsided enough.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win — Clippers A+, Lakers F. The 2019 agreement was Zubac and Beasley for Muscala; Mykhailiuk and a second-round pick moved to Detroit in a separate Lakers transaction. Zubac developed into a productive long-term Clippers center and was still valuable in the 2026 deal with Indiana that also involved Kobe Brown. Muscala had only 17 Lakers appearances. The years of actual Clippers starter production, and residual later value, justify the grading gap without assigning unrelated 2019 assets or the entire 2026 trade return to Zubac alone.

sections.heading: The Clippers Were Trading for George and Leonard Together
sections.body: Los Angeles did not evaluate Paul George as an isolated acquisition. Kawhi Leonard's free-agent commitment depended on the Clippers adding another star, which gave Oklahoma City extraordinary leverage. The final price was Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, Danilo Gallinari, five first-round picks, and two swap rights. The Clippers knowingly paid for George's All-NBA production, Leonard's signature, and the immediate creation of a championship window.

sections.heading: George Produced Real High-End Value in Los Angeles
sections.body: The trade did not leave the Clippers empty-handed. George made All-Star and All-NBA teams, supplied elite two-way play when healthy, and helped the franchise reach its first Western Conference finals in 2021. After Leonard was injured, George carried a larger offensive burden through the remainder of that run. A C-plus recognizes that Los Angeles reached a level it had never achieved, even though the group never reached the Finals.

sections.heading: Gilgeous-Alexander Became the Best Asset in the Deal
sections.body: Shai Gilgeous-Alexander was a promising second-year guard when Oklahoma City acquired him, not a guaranteed MVP. His development nevertheless defines the outcome. He became the league's MVP, the centerpiece of the Thunder's 2025 championship, and a Finals MVP. Oklahoma City obtained a player who eventually surpassed George's Clippers value while also remaining younger and under organizational control throughout the rebuild.

sections.heading: The 2022 Pick Became Jalen Williams
sections.body: The draft package was not merely theoretical leverage. Oklahoma City used the Clippers' 2022 first-round pick at No. 12 on Jalen Williams, who developed into another core scorer and two-way playmaker. Other picks and swaps extended the Thunder's optionality across several seasons. The transaction therefore produced both a franchise centerpiece and additional talent that helped construct a champion around him.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Accepted Concentrated Risk
sections.body: The Clippers placed enormous value into two stars with significant injury histories. When Leonard and George were available together, the roster looked capable of winning the West. When one was absent, the depth and draft control sacrificed in 2019 became more visible. The strategy was coherent because title opportunities are rare, but coherence does not erase the cost of repeatedly entering postseasons without the full partnership.

sections.heading: Why the Thunder Win Is Now Decisive
sections.body: At the time, Los Angeles could argue that the price included Leonard and that championship equity justified almost any package. The completed outcomes now create a clear separation. The Clippers reached one conference final; Oklahoma City developed Gilgeous-Alexander into a two-time MVP and champion, added Williams through the draft chain, and retained further benefits. The A-plus versus C-plus split accurately reflects that gap.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Oklahoma City won the trade. The Clippers created a legitimate contender and reached their first conference finals with George, so the deal was not devoid of value. But Gilgeous-Alexander became an MVP, Finals MVP, and championship centerpiece, while the 2022 first became Jalen Williams and the broader pick package continued to shape the Thunder. The verdict becomes Thunder Win, preserving Oklahoma City A-plus and Los Angeles C-plus.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The Trade That Bought One Window and Built Another
featuredDeepDive.intro: The 2019 George deal created two distinct franchise arcs. Los Angeles used its leverage to assemble Leonard and George immediately, choosing concentrated star power over patience. Oklahoma City accepted the end of an era and converted George's contract into a young guard, a productive veteran, and years of draft control. One side pursued a title at once; the other assembled the foundation of a champion over time.

sections.heading: Leonard's Condition Changed the Price of Every Asset
sections.body: Oklahoma City knew the Clippers were not negotiating only for George. Leonard could sign elsewhere unless Los Angeles produced a second star, so the Thunder could price the trade against the value of both players. That context explains why the package exceeded the normal return for one veteran. The Clippers did not misread the leverage; they decided that securing Leonard made the overpayment strategically acceptable.

sections.heading: The 2021 Conference Finals Validated Part of the Bet
sections.body: George's Clippers tenure should not be rewritten as a total failure. He was central to the franchise's first Western Conference finals appearance and delivered important postseason performances after Leonard's injury. That breakthrough mattered to an organization with little prior playoff success. The problem is comparative: Los Angeles's best outcome was historic for the Clippers, but it still fell short of the championship-level return Oklahoma City ultimately created.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Still Had to Develop the Return
sections.body: Receiving Gilgeous-Alexander did not guarantee an MVP. The Thunder gave him progressive responsibility, paired him with Chris Paul for a season, built a modern spacing and defense structure, and stayed patient as the roster matured. The same is true of Williams, who had to be scouted at No. 12 and developed into a core player. The trade created opportunity; Oklahoma City's development system converted it into overwhelming value.

sections.heading: The Pick Package Protected the Thunder From a Single Outcome
sections.body: Even before every selection conveyed, the picks and swaps gave Oklahoma City multiple paths. They could draft players, trade for veterans, or preserve flexibility while evaluating the young core. That optionality reduced the risk that the deal would be judged entirely on Gilgeous-Alexander. Once he became a superstar and Williams emerged from the chain, the remaining draft control became additional value rather than the basis of the win.

sections.heading: A Championship Finally Closed the Argument
sections.body: For years, the Clippers could point to their contender status while Oklahoma City's return remained unfinished. The Thunder's 2025 championship changed the frame. Gilgeous-Alexander won regular-season and Finals MVP honors, and Williams was part of the core generated by the deal. The transaction no longer represents only attractive future assets; it represents a completed championship foundation that exceeded the Clippers' realized peak.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Thunder made the superior trade by a wide margin. Los Angeles deserves credit for building a serious contender and for George's role in the franchise's first conference finals, but the return sent to Oklahoma City became the center of a championship team. Gilgeous-Alexander's MVP rise, Williams's development from the 2022 pick, and the remaining draft value support Oklahoma City A-plus, Los Angeles C-plus, Thunder Win.

sections.heading: A March 22 Roster Transaction, Not a Player Swap
sections.body: The Clippers announced on March 22, 2021 that they sent Mfiondu Kabengele, a conditional future second-round pick and cash to Sacramento for a conditional second-round selection. The NBA's trade tracker separately confirms the same directional package. Kabengele had been the 27th pick in 2019 but had played only 23 games for Los Angeles during the ongoing 2020–21 season, averaging 1.2 points in 4.1 minutes. Moving his contract before the deadline opened a roster place and created payroll flexibility for a contending team. The Kings accepted the former first-round prospect alongside cash and a separate conditional pick. Counting all four original assets is essential, although two were conditional claims rather than realized draft choices.

sections.heading: Sacramento Released Kabengele Three Days Later
sections.body: Sacramento's transaction record shows Kabengele was waived on March 25, three days after the trade. That makes his direct playing return for the Kings zero NBA appearances from this acquisition. He later joined Cleveland on successive 10-day deals and appeared in 16 Cavaliers games during the rest of the season, according to Cleveland's later official roster announcement. Those games belong to a separate signing with another franchise, not Sacramento's side of this trade. The brief Kings tenure clarifies why the deal cannot be justified as a successful on-court player acquisition. Any case in Sacramento's favor instead rests on financial consideration and what the conditional pick represented at signing.

sections.heading: Neither Conditional 2022 Second Conveyed
sections.body: Both teams' archived 2020–21 transaction histories identify two reciprocal 2022 second-round rights and say neither conveyed. The Kings received a conditional pick originally owed by Atlanta; the Clippers received a separately protected Kings-origin second. The conditions did not create a 2022 selection for either franchise. A common hindsight mistake is to attach a drafted player's production to a pick merely because it appeared in a 2021 transaction. Here there is no such player to assign on either side. The distinction between trade-day conditional consideration and actual draft-night yield is especially important when the transaction included a cash transfer and a roster-clearing purpose.

sections.heading: The Existing Grades Need a Financial-Value Review
sections.body: The archive calls this Kings Win, grading Sacramento B and Los Angeles F. Those labels are preserved, but the documented basketball return is unusually narrow: Kabengele never played for the Kings and neither 2022 conditional pick conveyed. The original Clippers release confirms cash moving to Sacramento without naming its precise amount. The present canonical asset ledger records $2.75 million; that figure should be independently verified before using it to justify a letter-grade advantage. Los Angeles obtained immediate roster flexibility, while Sacramento received money and short-lived contractual rights. The available public facts do not establish that one team gained a lasting basketball asset, so the current grades merit a flagged, evidence-led review rather than a silent change.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Stored verdict: Kings Win — Sacramento B, Clippers F, pending financial-value grade review. The Clippers sent Kabengele, cash and a conditional 2022 second for another conditional second. Sacramento waived Kabengele three days later; neither pick conveyed. The official sources confirm cash but do not verify the archive's precise dollar figure. Preserve the trade-day ledger and do not invent 2022 draftees.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Kabengele to Sacramento: A Deadline Roster Move With No Conveyed Picks
featuredDeepDive.intro: This March 2021 transaction produced a strikingly small on-court trail. The Clippers sent Mfiondu Kabengele, cash and a protected second-round possibility to Sacramento for another conditional second. The Kings waived Kabengele within three days, and transaction histories show that neither 2022 pick conveyed. The deal was principally about roster construction and financial consideration. Its existing Kings Win verdict and letter grades deserve examination against those outcomes without rewriting the original exchange.

sections.heading: Why Los Angeles Moved a Former First-Rounder
sections.body: The official Clippers statement dated March 22 describes Kabengele as a 23-year-old center who had appeared 23 times that season for 1.2 points in 4.1 minutes on average. He was a former 2019 first-round selection, but his playing opportunity behind an established contender's veteran frontcourt had been limited. NBA's contemporaneous deadline reporting described a deal that opened a Clippers roster spot and helped with hard-cap flexibility. Those organizational benefits are not the same as acquiring a productive player, yet they help explain why Los Angeles would attach cash and a future conditional selection to a little-used contract. The club also received a reciprocal conditional second. The official announcement does not identify a drafted player or guarantee that the incoming selection would materialize.

sections.heading: What the Sacramento Kings Actually Received
sections.body: The Kings' 2021–22 team media guide confirms receipt of Kabengele, cash consideration and a future second-round selection on March 22. Three days later, both the Sacramento and league-wide transaction histories record his waiver. His later appearance in 16 Cleveland games was an entirely separate Cavaliers arrangement, as Cleveland's own release explains. Thus the Kings did acquire the legal player contract on March 22, but did not obtain game production from it. The cash portion was real, although the Clippers' release does not publish its dollar amount. The current archive assigns that cash a $2.75 million value, which requires a stronger source before being treated as a verified exact consideration figure. Sacramento's basketball outcome cannot be inflated by Kabengele's later career.

sections.heading: The Two 2022 Draft Rights Were Contingent
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Clippers and Kings season transaction ledgers independently describe the outgoing and incoming conditional 2022 second-round selections as not conveyed. One selection in Sacramento's package originated with Atlanta; the Kings also owed a distinct conditional second to the Clippers. Because both ultimately failed to convey, neither side can claim a drafted player through this deal's 2022 picks. The rights nonetheless had conditional value when the agreement was signed, and their specific protections are important to the legal transaction. Rather than inventing an unverified protection formula, the archive should keep the existing descriptions and annotate the documented result: no selection arrived. That avoids turning a future contractual possibility into fictional realized player performance.

sections.heading: Separating Roster Flexibility From the Published B/F Grade
sections.body: The trade sits in the archive with Sacramento B, Los Angeles F and Kings Win. It is reasonable to ask what those marks reward. Los Angeles cleared a bench contract and roster space before the deadline; Sacramento accepted a prospect briefly, received cash and faced two conditional future pick chains with no conveyed selection. Its later waiver of Kabengele confirms no meaningful Kings court time, and Cleveland's later 16 games cannot count for Sacramento. The Clippers did not receive a draft pick either. The exact cash amount and any later cap or trade-exception use must be independently documented before deciding whether the stored B/F split accurately reflects the organizational benefits. Maintaining the original grade as a hold is more faithful than manufacturing a draft outcome or silently rewriting a verdict.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The sourced return consists of a former first-rounder waived after three days, cash received by Sacramento, roster relief for the Clippers and two 2022 conditional picks that did not convey. Neither team obtained a 2022 draftee from the agreement. The saved Kings Win, B/F grades are preserved under financial-source review; the official release does not verify the archive's exact cash amount.

sections.heading: New York Turned Pick 21 into Grimes and Another Second-Round Asset
sections.body: At the 2021 NBA Draft, New York selected Tennessee wing Keon Johnson 21st and transferred his rights to the Clippers. Los Angeles sent back the rights to No. 25 pick Quentin Grimes and the Detroit Pistons’ 2024 second-round draft choice. Both franchises confirmed the draft-night arrangement, with the Clippers announcement posted July 29 on the West Coast and the Knicks release dated July 30 in New York. The Knicks therefore did not simply exchange one player for a slightly lower selection: they also received a future pick. The protected transaction chain later identifies the selection as 2024 No. 31, used on Jonathan Mogbo; the pick’s eventual destination should be assessed separately from Grimes’s Knicks playing career.

sections.heading: Quentin Grimes Supplied 162 Knicks Games and 90 Starts
sections.body: Grimes appeared in 46 regular-season games for New York as a rookie in 2021-22, starting six and averaging 6.0 points. In 2022-23 he earned a much larger role, appearing in 71 games with 66 starts and 11.3 points while making 38.6 percent of his three-point attempts. In 2023-24 he appeared in 45 Knicks games, making 18 starts, before a separate February deal sent him to Detroit. Added together, the first three receiving-team seasons generated 162 Knicks games and 90 starts. His six subsequent Detroit appearances and later Dallas, Philadelphia or other seasons cannot be credited as Knicks on-court production from the 2021 draft-night exchange.

sections.heading: Keon Johnson Played Only 15 Clippers Games before a Different Deal
sections.body: The Clippers drafted Johnson for his athletic tools and defense. He played 15 NBA regular-season games for Los Angeles during 2021-22, starting none and averaging 3.5 points in nine minutes a night. On February 4, 2022, the Clippers sent Johnson to Portland in a separate multi-player agreement that also moved Eric Bledsoe, Justise Winslow and a Detroit 2025 second-round pick. Los Angeles acquired Norman Powell and Robert Covington from the Trail Blazers. That later deal is an asset conversion, but Powell and Covington were not given to the Clippers by New York in July 2021. The 22 Portland games Johnson logged in the rest of 2021-22 likewise cannot be added to his 15-game Clippers return.

sections.heading: The Knicks Grade Reflects Starter Minutes and a Future Pick
sections.body: The archive’s verdict is Knicks Win with New York A and Los Angeles C+. Grimes’s 162 Knicks appearances, including a 66-start 2022-23 campaign, are concrete value the team received. The accompanying future second-round choice is another real contractually specified return. The Clippers received 15 Johnson NBA games and later included his contract in a larger Portland transaction, whose other assets carried their own price. One cannot award the entire Powell-and-Covington package to Johnson alone. Keeping the protected grades while explaining both the initial player comparison and the extra future draft choice is fairer than judging the exchange merely by Grimes becoming a more visible name.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win, New York A and Los Angeles C+ remain the saved assessment. Grimes played 162 Knicks games and started 90; the Knicks also received a Detroit 2024 second-round pick in the July 2021 exchange. Keon Johnson played 15 Clippers games before being combined with other assets in the February 2022 Portland transaction. The eventual No. 31 pick’s rights history and the Clippers’ later acquisition of Powell and Covington are separate downstream chains, not invented initial trade assets.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Grimes for Keon Johnson in 2021: Knicks Got 162 Games Plus a Second
featuredDeepDive.intro: In July 2021, the Clippers moved up from draft position 25 to 21, taking Keon Johnson while sending Quentin Grimes’s rights and the Pistons’ 2024 second-round selection to New York. Grimes supplied the Knicks 162 regular-season games and 90 starts before a separate February 2024 trade. Johnson logged 15 Clippers games without a start before being packaged in a different 2022 deal with Portland. The original Knicks Win, New York A and Clippers C+ is grounded in these team-specific returns and the additional pick, not in treating later transactions as direct parts of the draft-night swap.

sections.heading: Pick 21 Versus Pick 25 Included a Second-Round Sweetener
sections.body: The official Clippers release dated July 29, 2021 says the club acquired the rights to Keon Johnson, the No. 21 selection, in exchange for the No. 25 choice and Detroit’s 2024 second-round pick. New York’s July 30 statement identifies Quentin Grimes as the rights acquired at No. 25. A third-party NBA draft recap reports the same assets. A later archive note associates the second with the 2024 No. 31 pick used on Jonathan Mogbo; it should not imply Mogbo played for the Knicks without following the subsequent pick movements. The original trade itself is clear: New York accepted a four-place drop in the first round while adding a future second-round asset.

sections.heading: Grimes Was a Starting Knicks Guard in 2022-23
sections.body: Grimes’s rookie regular-season sample was 46 games, six starts and 6.0 points per game. The next season he played 71 times and started 66, averaging 11.3 points with accurate volume three-point shooting. That sustained rotation role was substantially greater than Keon Johnson’s time with the Clippers. In 2023-24, Grimes played 45 more Knicks games, 18 as a starter, before being traded to Detroit in February 2024. These 46, 71 and 45 New York segments sum to 162 appearances and 90 starts. His eventual Mavericks and 76ers games are downstream work for other franchises and should not be added to the Knicks tally.

sections.heading: Keon Johnson Was a Brief Clippers Player and Later Trade Piece
sections.body: Johnson made his NBA debut for Los Angeles in November 2021 and played 15 Clippers games that season, logging 135 total minutes and no starts. His athletic reputation was meaningful to the draft-night decision, but on-court evidence for the Clippers is limited. On February 4, 2022, Johnson was traded to Portland with Eric Bledsoe, Justise Winslow and Detroit’s 2025 second-round choice for Norman Powell and Robert Covington. The fact he could be moved as part of that deal is relevant asset value. It does not mean the Knicks originally transferred those Blazers veterans, nor that the same 2025 second-round pick originated from the Knicks’ 2021 deal.

sections.heading: Both Pick Chains and Receiving-Team Minutes Need Separate Accounting
sections.body: The Clippers’ new No. 21 rights turned into only 15 regular-season games for Los Angeles before a larger trade. The Knicks’ No. 25 player contributed 162 games and 90 starts, including a meaningful 2022-23 role, plus New York had acquired the future Detroit second-rounder. A retrospective should recognize that second asset while avoiding an unsupported claim that the future No. 31 drafted player directly played for New York. Later Powell, Covington, Detroit and other roster moves must be tracked as new transactions with their own players and picks. That distinction makes the protected Knicks A and Clippers C+ more persuasive than inflated championship claims or generic draft-night stereotypes.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: New York A, Los Angeles C+ and Knicks Win are preserved. Grimes gave New York 162 regular-season games and 90 starts; a future Detroit second-round choice also came to the Knicks. Keon Johnson logged only 15 Clippers games before a new February 2022 package traded him to Portland with three other pieces. The later destination of the pick ultimately associated with 2024 No. 31 and the distinct Powell/Covington move require their own transaction accounting, not retroactive changes to this July 2021 three-asset exchange.

sections.heading: Two Experienced Wings Went to Los Angeles
sections.body: On February 4, 2022, the Clippers acquired Norman Powell and Robert Covington from Portland for Eric Bledsoe, Justise Winslow, Keon Johnson and Detroit's 2025 second-round pick. Portland's immediate priority was escaping the luxury tax and resetting future payroll flexibility; Los Angeles was willing to absorb salary to add two proven rotation players. The teams were solving different problems. The Clippers were trying to maintain a contender around Kawhi Leonard and Paul George despite injuries, so Powell's scoring and Covington's switchable defense had direct basketball value. Portland had shut down Damian Lillard and was beginning a larger retool, making tax relief and future flexibility more important than matching talent dollar for dollar. For grading purposes, Norman Powell and Robert Covington / Bledsoe-Winslow-Johnson package is evaluated from the assets actually exchanged and the value those assets produced under team control. The name recognition of the players is secondary to minutes, role, contract leverage, playoff usefulness and any direct asset chain that remained alive after the first move. That matters here because the clubs entered the deal with different objectives, so a fair review has to separate tactical logic from realized return. A move can make sense on the day it is announced and still age poorly if the acquiring team gives away more durable value than it receives. Conversely, a team can lose the headline and still earn a strong grade when its incoming pieces fit the roster, remain productive and preserve future options.

sections.heading: Powell Was the Principal Long-Term Return
sections.body: Los Angeles received by far the strongest realized player value. Powell became one of the league's most efficient high-volume secondary scorers, remained productive through multiple seasons and reached a career-best 21.8 points per game in 2024-25. Covington supplied versatile defense and shooting before later leaving in another trade. Powell then retained enough value to be moved in 2025 as part of the three-team transaction that brought John Collins to the Clippers. The higher grade in Norman Powell and Robert Covington / Bledsoe-Winslow-Johnson package does not require pretending the winning side made a flawless move. The standard is comparative: which club captured more usable basketball value from the assets that changed hands, and how much of that value survived beyond the first season? Peak performance matters, but so do durability and optionality. A player who contributes for several seasons, helps a meaningful playoff team or later carries trade value can justify a strong grade even without becoming an All-Star. The same is true for draft capital when the pick actually conveys and produces a useful player. The conclusion therefore rests on the completed results rather than the loudest narrative attached to the transaction.

sections.heading: Why Portland Accepted the Other Package
sections.body: Portland achieved its financial objective but received little direct basketball return. Bledsoe never played for the Blazers, Winslow's tenure was limited by injuries, Johnson did not develop into a long-term rotation piece, and the 2025 second-round pick became Bogoljub Markovic. The cap savings were real and helped reset the repeater-tax clock, so the deal should not be graded as if Portland received literally nothing. The lower-graded side still receives credit for objectives it actually accomplished. Salary relief, a cleaner depth chart, a younger timeline or a rotation player can all be legitimate returns. What those benefits cannot do is erase an obvious talent or asset gap. The question is proportionality: did the franchise recover enough for what it surrendered, and did the return remain useful long enough to justify the price? That distinction keeps the grade from collapsing every losing trade into an F. It also prevents cap flexibility from becoming an all-purpose excuse when a club could reasonably have pursued the same financial goal while retaining more basketball value.

sections.heading: Powell’s 2025 Trade Extended the Asset Chain
sections.body: The Clippers' value chain remained alive after Powell's best season. In July 2025, Los Angeles sent Powell into a three-team deal and received John Collins from Utah while also sending a second-round pick. Collins required an additional asset and a third team, so his full future value should not be credited to the 2022 trade, but Powell's ability to anchor that exchange shows the original acquisition retained market value. Follow-on transactions are counted conservatively. If an incoming player or pick can be traced directly into the next move, the preserved value belongs in the record. If the later acquisition required a much larger unrelated package, only the original asset's contribution is credited. That rule is especially important for Norman Powell and Robert Covington / Bledsoe-Winslow-Johnson package, because historical retellings often leap from one recognizable name to a later superstar and assign the entire result backward. The better method follows the asset itself, asks whether it remained movable, and stops once the chain depends on substantial new consideration. That produces a more disciplined comparison of what each front office actually created from this deal.

sections.heading: The Regular-Season Value Versus Team Results
sections.body: Injuries prevented the Clippers from converting the move into a deep postseason breakthrough, but Powell became a major regular-season and playoff scorer across several years. Portland entered a rebuild instead of competing for immediate playoff results. The absence of a Clippers title therefore lowers the ceiling from a perfect franchise-altering grade without changing the large difference in realized value. Team success is evidence, not a shortcut. A championship or conference-finals run strengthens a trade grade only when the acquired asset played a meaningful role in that result. Likewise, missing the playoffs does not automatically make an acquisition bad if the player delivered strong production and retained market value on a rebuilding roster. In Norman Powell and Robert Covington / Bledsoe-Winslow-Johnson package, the competitive translation is useful because it shows whether the theoretical fit described on trade day survived contact with real lineups and postseason basketball. The grade gives more weight to direct contribution than to wins produced mostly by unrelated stars or later roster changes.

sections.heading: Rebuilding and Tax Considerations on Both Sides
sections.body: The Clippers accepted a much larger tax bill and long-term salary commitment to Powell. Portland accepted the reputational and basketball cost of a talent downgrade in exchange for financial relief. Those risks were asymmetric by design. The final grade credits Portland's cap objective but still asks whether the same financial outcome could have been achieved while recovering more draft or young-player value. Portland's realistic alternative was finding another salary-reducing offer for Powell and Covington, not keeping an expensive roster indefinitely. Los Angeles could have preserved Bledsoe's expiring structure and Johnson's upside rather than taking on Powell. The market result suggests the Clippers paid a modest basketball price for a player who remained productive for more than three seasons. Trade-day context still matters because leverage shapes the realistic menu of choices. Contract length, age, injuries, tax pressure and roster imbalance can reduce what a team can reasonably demand. Hindsight should not invent an offer that was never available. At the same time, context is not immunity from evaluation. If a team creates its own urgency or pays a premium to solve a short-term problem, the eventual cost remains part of the trade details. The useful counterfactual for Norman Powell and Robert Covington / Bledsoe-Winslow-Johnson package is therefore the most plausible alternative—keep the asset, accept a different type of return, or wait—rather than a fantasy package built from players who were never actually on the table.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win is the final call. The trade has aged as one of the clearest talent-for-flexibility swaps of the early 2020s. Portland can defend the financial logic, especially the repeater-tax reset, but financial logic is not the same as equal trade value. Los Angeles got multiple seasons of high-end scoring, useful Covington minutes and a still-movable Powell contract. That is a decisive basketball return. The grades reflect the completed balance of production, control, role fit, playoff translation and directly tied follow-on value: los-angeles-clippers A+, portland-trail-blazers D.

sections.heading: The Actual 1951 Rights Exchange Was Rochester to Milwaukee, Not a Lakers Deal
sections.body: The recorded draft-rights transfer occurred on August 1, 1951, when the Milwaukee Hawks acquired Elmer Behnke from the Rochester Royals. RealGM transaction records independently list the date and the clubs, and its 1951 Milwaukee draft-rights register confirms that the fourth-round player was moved from Rochester. The old TradeVerdicts URL uses a Lakers-versus-Kings franchise pairing; that pairing is not supported by the surviving transaction register. Rochester later became the Kings franchise, but Milwaukee Hawks became the Atlanta Hawks organization, not the Los Angeles Lakers. Those franchise histories cannot be interchanged. The corrected date in the canonical summary does not itself repair the erroneous inherited Lakers asset path.

sections.heading: Rochester Drafted Behnke at No. 38 Before Transferring His Rights
sections.body: Rochester selected Behnke in the fourth round, 38th overall, in April 1951. The 1950-51 Rochester transaction history independently identifies that pick, while the Milwaukee Hawks draft-rights list shows the rights subsequently acquired from Rochester. There is no sourced Lakers role in Behnke acquisition or any reason to claim the Minneapolis club selected him. He was a Bradley University forward, rather than a player who had already produced NBA minutes before the rights transaction. Modern franchise labels must be used carefully with 1951 records: Rochester is a historical predecessor of Sacramento, and Milwaukee Hawks is an early version of today's Atlanta franchise. Neither role authorizes a fictional Minneapolis-to-Rochester exchange.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Received Four Games, Then Waived the Rookie in November
sections.body: Behnke signed with Milwaukee on September 1, 1951. He appeared in four NBA regular-season games for the Hawks that autumn, recording 16 total points, 17 rebounds, four assists and 55 minutes, averages of 4.0 points, 4.25 rebounds and 1.0 assist. RealGM lists those four appearances and a November 15 Milwaukee waiver, followed by free agency two days later. His entire documented NBA playing output belonged to Milwaukee. Assigning it to the Lakers would corrupt the receiving-team value calculation even if the original trade involved a Kings predecessor. The limited four-game return indicates a short-lived draft-rights acquisition, not an enduring franchise asset or an All-Star-caliber success.

sections.heading: The Consideration and C/C Verdict Cannot Be Confirmed From This Route
sections.body: The source records confirm that Milwaukee acquired draft rights from Rochester, but the specific consideration paid by the Hawks is not documented in the reviewed transaction histories. The imported archive still labels a cash transfer from the Lakers and shows an Even Trade, C/C grade pair for Los Angeles and Sacramento. Those are inherited model fields, not a defensible historical grade for the verified Milwaukee-Rochester transfer. This private nonindex archive entry should stay on research hold until canonical team identities, both asset directions, the cash assertion, and player-relationship links can be reconciled atomically under a separate QA guard. Neither the missing dollar figure nor the receiver mismatch should be disguised by extra generic analysis.

finalVerdict.heading: Source-Reconciliation Verdict
finalVerdict.body: RESEARCH HOLD — the verified August 1, 1951 exchange sent Elmer Behnke draft rights from Rochester to the Milwaukee Hawks. Behnke played only four NBA games for Milwaukee, not the Minneapolis Lakers. The imported Lakers/Kings route and cash return are unsupported by the cited records, so the inherited Even Trade and C/C grades cannot responsibly be used to assess the actual transaction. Leave this archival route private until both franchise identities and consideration are corrected together.
