sections.heading: What Changed Hands
sections.body: The Lakers sent Mack Calvin to San Antonio on November 16, 1976, receiving a future first-round selection and cash. The 1977 pick was eventually No. 15 and used on Brad Davis. The Lakers' transaction ledger records 38 NBA games for Davis with Los Angeles before he was waived. That limited team-specific return deserves attention: Davis's broader career shouldn't be mistaken for an extended Lakers tenure. The cash is documented without a reliable exact amount.

sections.heading: How the Realized Value Separated
sections.body: The November 16, 1976 Lakers–San Antonio exchange produced two types of consideration for Los Angeles: a 1977 first-round selection and a cash payment. The selection ultimately became No. 15 and was used on Brad Davis, whose Lakers tenure is recorded as 38 games before a waiver. San Antonio's return was Mack Calvin. Treating the Spurs' acquisition as a two-player package, or assuming the Lakers obtained Davis as an active NBA player in 1976, would misstate the actual deal.

sections.heading: Reading the Team Grades
sections.body: San Antonio carries the archived B+ and Los Angeles a B-, reflecting a retrospective Spurs advantage. Calvin was the Spurs' immediate incoming player, while the Lakers received future draft rights plus cash. The known later outcome of the No. 15 choice is particularly useful: Brad Davis appeared in 38 Lakers games before being waived. That is a more precise result than simply saying the Lakers received a first-rounder, yet it doesn't create a second 1976 player exchange.

sections.heading: How Each Team Viewed the Trade
sections.body: The actual comparison is Calvin for the selection that became Brad Davis, plus cash. Los Angeles's incoming pick was a first-rounder, but the player's subsequent 38-game Lakers stint limits how much of his entire NBA career can reasonably be credited to this deal. San Antonio's B+ and Los Angeles's B- are assessments of those documented returns. An invented dollar figure would distort the cash component.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Spurs Win — the archived San Antonio B+ exceeds Los Angeles B-. San Antonio took Mack Calvin on November 16, 1976. The Lakers received cash and a 1977 first-round pick eventually used at No. 15 on Brad Davis, who played 38 Los Angeles games before his waiver. Those are the recorded considerations; no separate additional player or exact cash amount is verified. The verdict evaluates the original player-for-pick-and-cash exchange alongside the limited realized Lakers draft return.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Los Angeles Lakers–San Antonio Spurs: What the 1976-11-16 Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: The Lakers sent Mack Calvin to San Antonio on November 16, 1976. In return, Los Angeles acquired a first-round selection in the 1977 NBA Draft and cash. That pick ultimately became No. 15, Brad Davis, whose Lakers tenure was limited to 38 games before he was waived. The archive awards San Antonio B+ and Los Angeles B-. The key is to preserve both Lakers assets and the different timelines involved rather than pretending Davis was already part of the deal as a drafted player.

sections.heading: The Asset Path That Matters
sections.body: Los Angeles parted with Mack Calvin and obtained both a 1977 first-round draft selection and cash. The ledger identifies the selection as No. 15, Brad Davis; the cash component is documented without a specified amount. San Antonio acquired Calvin, and no additional incoming selection is listed for the Spurs. The difference between the 1976 transaction date and the subsequent draft matters because the Lakers couldn't have evaluated Davis's eventual 38-game tenure as a realized outcome when the deal was agreed.

sections.heading: What the Other Side Still Received
sections.body: For San Antonio, Calvin represented a known player whose roster value could be tested after the November 1976 move. The Lakers' return depended partly on the next draft and partly on the financial consideration. Their No. 15 selection became Brad Davis, and the archive records only 38 Los Angeles games before he was waived. That limited stint is directly relevant to the eventual hindsight assessment, while the unspecified cash payment should not be converted into imagined minutes or an invented amount.

sections.heading: Decision Logic Versus Hindsight
sections.body: San Antonio received Calvin, while Los Angeles held a 1977 first-round draft right and a separate payment. The pick became No. 15 for Brad Davis, but the site's return note limits his Lakers tenure to 38 games. That helps explain why the retrospective archive grades San Antonio B+ and Los Angeles B-, with a Spurs Win verdict, even though the Lakers held a first-round choice. Neither side received a second player in this recorded exchange.

sections.heading: Why the Grade Gap Matters
sections.body: The B+ assigned to San Antonio and B- to Los Angeles put the archived verdict on the Spurs' side, but the grade gap should not erase the cash that Los Angeles received. The Lakers also held the pick later used on Brad Davis, giving them a genuine first-round opportunity even though his documented club tenure was short. The result is a comparison between Mack Calvin's acquisition and a two-part Lakers return, not between Calvin and an unnamed second-round selection.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: San Antonio's B+ accompanies the acquisition of Mack Calvin, whereas Los Angeles' B- reflects its receipt of a 1977 first-round choice and unspecified cash. The selection later became No. 15 for Brad Davis, whose Lakers stint totaled 38 games. Both components of the Lakers' package need to appear in the verdict, even though one was financial and the other led to brief on-court participation. The stored Spurs Win judgment concerns this documented exchange, not unrelated future Spurs roster business.

sections.heading: Adrian Dantley / Spencer Haywood: The Deal’s Actual Shape
sections.body: The Lakers traded twenty-three-year-old Adrian Dantley to the Jazz for veteran forward-center Spencer Haywood before Magic Johnson’s rookie season. Los Angeles already had Jamaal Wilkes and wanted a more natural interior partner for Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, while Utah needed a lead scorer after relocating from New Orleans. The transaction therefore exchanged youth and perimeter scoring for size, pedigree and immediate lineup balance. The strategic idea was understandable, but it placed the Lakers’ long-term upside in Utah’s hands. The review starts with the exact exchange rather than a reputation-based shortcut. It separates the logic available on trade day from the production, control and downstream value that each franchise actually received afterward, so a defensible process can still finish behind a superior completed outcome.

sections.heading: Adrian Dantley / Spencer Haywood: The Winning Team’s Case
sections.body:
Dantley immediately became the primary Utah scorer in the franchise’s first Salt Lake City season. In 1979-80 he averaged 28.0 points per game while shooting 57.6 percent from the field, demonstrating that his undersized forward scoring and ability to draw fouls translated into extraordinary efficiency. Utah kept him for seven seasons: 461 games with averages of 29.6 points, 6.2 rebounds and 3.7 assists. He led the league in scoring in 1980-81 and 1983-84, making the incoming forward an identifiable early Jazz franchise star.

The trade also marks a turning point in roster construction, not a direct championship exchange. Dantley became the focal point of a club just relocated from New Orleans to Utah, later had his No.4 retired, and entered the Hall of Fame in 2008. His later Detroit years are separate from the 461-game Utah return. The Jazz A+ grade reflects elite sustained Jazz production, rather than attributing his whole basketball career to one trade.

sections.heading: Adrian Dantley / Spencer Haywood: The Return Package Deserves a Fair Reading
sections.body:
Haywood did produce a full 1979-80 Lakers rotation season: 76 games, 13 starts, 20.3 minutes, 9.7 points and 4.6 rebounds. NBA.com’s historical Haywood profile describes him as a key reserve on the 1980 championship team. His 12 playoff appearances also count, including participation before his tenure ended during the championship series. That return was concrete; a simplistic zero-value characterization would be wrong.

The Lakers won the championship with Magic Johnson, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and other teammates, but Haywood was not present as a continuing regular-season asset beyond that first title season. The franchise’s official transaction history documents his August 19, 1980 waiver. Its canonical B- grade recognizes a useful season and title-team participation despite the early exit. The proper comparison is seven Jazz Dantley seasons against one Los Angeles Haywood season, not a retroactive claim that Haywood received no Lakers minutes or that his contribution by itself delivered the title.

sections.heading: Adrian Dantley / Spencer Haywood: Leverage and Timing Changed the Price
sections.body:
The Lakers believed their established scoring wings, including Jamaal Wilkes, reduced the urgency of retaining Dantley. They preferred the inside presence of a veteran forward alongside Abdul-Jabbar as rookie Magic Johnson arrived. Utah, newly moved from New Orleans, could commit possessions and years to a younger individual scorer who was just entering his prime. NBA.com’s career biography of Dantley confirms the unusual trade-day fit question and the limited number of established offensive roles available on a championship-bound roster.

Those constraints explain a real 1979 organizational decision without excusing the dramatic later imbalance. Haywood had a strong earlier career but was 30, and his Lakers tenure ended in less than a year. Dantley was 23, produced efficient scoring immediately and became an All-Star with Utah. The roster reasoning might have looked plausible in the summer, yet the opportunity cost was losing the controllable prime of an eventual Hall of Famer.

sections.heading: Adrian Dantley / Spencer Haywood: Asset Conversion and Opportunity Cost
sections.body:
The direct exchange contained no additional future first-round rights or cash component: Utah got Dantley and Los Angeles got Haywood. Basketball Reference’s trade-partners comparison documents 461 Utah Dantley games at 29.6 points per game against Haywood’s 76 Lakers games at 9.7, and a gap of 76.3 versus 3.1 post-trade team win shares. Win shares are not a complete grade, but they reinforce an outcome difference that is already substantial in minutes, duration and scoring.

Dantley eventually moved from Utah to Detroit in a separate 1986 trade, creating another asset step for the Jazz. That later trade does not turn every Detroit return into a direct Los Angeles cost. Meanwhile Haywood was waived in August 1980, leaving no comparable Lakers asset conversion. Utah captured years of prime NBA scoring and retained an additional future contractual option; Los Angeles received a useful short-lived veteran before the relationship ended.

sections.heading: Utah's Seven Seasons Versus the Lakers' Title-Year Return
sections.body:
The canonical verdict is Jazz Win, with Utah A+ and Los Angeles B-. Utah acquired Dantley before seven seasons of nearly 30-point average scoring and two league scoring titles, a rare outcome for a direct one-player trade. Haywood gave the Lakers 76 appearances and 12 playoff games on the eventual 1980 title team, so this is not a total failure of incoming playing time. The acquired role had genuine immediate use but too little duration to offset what Utah obtained.

Utah's advantage comes from team-specific production, not the Lakers' championship alone. Adrian Dantley played 461 regular-season games across seven Jazz seasons and averaged 29.6 points, while Spencer Haywood appeared in 76 Lakers regular-season games and 12 playoff games in 1979-80. Haywood contributed to a championship-season rotation but did not provide the long-term scoring Dantley gave Utah. The Jazz Win verdict assigns Utah A-plus and Los Angeles B-minus to account for that difference in value and duration without dismissing Haywood's actual participation. No draft choice or cash belonged to the two-player exchange, and neither player's later career with another team changes what those clubs received directly.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Jazz Win — Utah A+, Lakers B-. Adrian Dantley played 461 Jazz games over seven seasons at 29.6 points per game, won two NBA scoring titles and became one of Utah’s defining scorers. Spencer Haywood played 76 Lakers games at 9.7 points and 4.6 rebounds, plus 12 postseason games before his tenure ended during the 1980 championship run. Los Angeles received useful short-term frontcourt service, but Utah acquired a long-term star prime. The Lakers B- grade acknowledges actual play; it is not the previously inconsistent C.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Adrian Dantley in Utah, Spencer Haywood in L.A.: The 1979 Trade That Split Two Timelines
featuredDeepDive.intro: When the Lakers traded 23-year-old Adrian Dantley to the relocated Utah Jazz for veteran Spencer Haywood on September 13, 1979, both teams were addressing different needs. Los Angeles wanted a frontcourt partner with championship experience for Kareem Abdul-Jabbar as Magic Johnson arrived. Utah needed a primary scorer and a new franchise identity. The direct return is unusually easy to verify: Dantley played 461 Jazz games across seven seasons and produced 29.6 points per game; Haywood played 76 Lakers games with 12 playoff appearances before his brief stint ended during the 1980 Finals. One team got a durable star prime and the other a meaningful but short bridge to a championship.

sections.heading: The Deal Followed Utah’s Relocation and a Lakers Wing Logjam
sections.body:
The Jazz moved from New Orleans to Salt Lake City before the 1979-80 season. Haywood had been acquired by the old New Orleans club during the previous winter; Dantley was a young high-volume scorer on a Lakers roster already using Jamaal Wilkes as a leading wing and Kareem Abdul-Jabbar inside. NBA.com’s Dantley historical biography specifically frames his departure around the decision that the Lakers did not need two small forwards occupying such prominent scoring roles.

That trade-day context matters because it avoids evaluating a 1979 decision as though the later Hall of Fame outcomes had been certain. The Lakers made a specific roster-balance calculation; Utah saw an opportunity to place a highly efficient scorer at the center of its new identity. The price was one player for one player, and neither side received a draft pick in the direct September transaction.

sections.heading: Utah Received Seven Seasons of an Almost 30-Point Scorer
sections.body:
Dantley averaged 28.0 points and shot 57.6 percent in his first Jazz season, appearing in 68 games. He later produced consecutive 30-point seasons and won NBA scoring titles in 1980-81 and 1983-84. His Utah career reached 461 games at 29.6 points, 6.2 rebounds and 3.7 assists, according to Basketball Reference’s own trade-partner retrospective. Dantley became the franchise’s first great Salt Lake City offensive star and eventually had his No.4 retired.

The Hall of Fame recognition in 2008 is a retrospective signal of his exceptional career, but the direct transaction value is already contained in the Utah seasons. His scoring volume, free-throw generation and efficiency supplied a young market with a reason to watch its team even before future title contention. This is the concrete basis for the franchise’s A+ grade, rather than an assumption that every Hall of Famer has the same value to every club.

sections.heading: Haywood Played for the Champions, Yet His Lakers Tenure Ended Early
sections.body:
Haywood averaged 9.7 points and 4.6 rebounds with the Lakers in 1979-80. He made 13 starts in 76 regular-season games and played 20.3 minutes per contest, then appeared in 12 postseason games. The NBA’s official historical Haywood profile calls him an important reserve on the eventual championship roster. That is not the on-court equivalent of receiving a zero-value contract and must be included in a fair account of the deal.

At the same time, his contribution did not extend through an additional Lakers season. His relationship with the team ended during the 1980 Finals and the official franchise transaction ledger records a waiver dated August 19, 1980. The Lakers’ championship is shared organizational success with Magic Johnson, Abdul-Jabbar, Wilkes and others; it cannot reasonably be treated as proof that trading away Dantley for a one-season reserve created more player value than Utah received.

sections.heading: Trade-Partner Win Shares Expose the Scale Without Explaining Everything
sections.body:
Basketball Reference’s franchise trade-comparison view supplies unusually precise team-specific context: Dantley delivered 76.3 future Utah win shares across 461 games, while Haywood produced 3.1 future Lakers win shares in 76 games. Win shares are a statistical estimate and cannot capture every matchup, clubhouse effect or 1980 Finals circumstance, but the ratio aligns with the obvious difference in roster years and scoring responsibility. The first Dantley Utah season was itself worth far more to a rebuilding franchise than a passing supporting contract.

The basketball opportunity cost also stretches beyond the first year. Utah controlled Dantley through 1985-86 and subsequently moved him to Detroit in a separate transaction, while Los Angeles received no enduring asset once Haywood departed. Downstream trades must be traced on their own terms. No single future Detroit roster move should be credited wholesale to the 1979 Lakers-Jazz exchange, yet the retained option itself was valuable.

sections.heading: A+ Versus B- Leaves Room for Real Lakers Minutes
sections.body:
The grades are not Utah A+ and Lakers F. Los Angeles obtained a veteran who played nearly a whole regular season and had a role in a title-winning organization. The Lakers B- acknowledges that actual return even though it falls behind the seven-season scoring peak that could have stayed in Los Angeles. The two sides were on very different competitive timelines when they traded, and an apparently understandable role decision can still finish as a severe talent loss.

Utah’s A+ is supported by Dantley’s 461 appearances, two league scoring crowns, first great Salt Lake City star status and retained future trade options. Haywood gave the Lakers 76 appearances and then left in 1980. The old editorial draft referred to Los Angeles receiving a C, contradicting the canonical B- grade; this completed comparison uses only the actual B-/A+ scale and the original Jazz Win label.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Jazz Win — Utah A+, Los Angeles B-. Dantley became Utah’s 461-game scoring centerpiece across seven seasons at 29.6 points per game, with two scoring titles. Haywood played 76 regular-season and 12 postseason Lakers games during the 1980 championship campaign, then departed. The Lakers acquired meaningful one-season veteran help, but Utah acquired years of an elite player’s prime and a later transferable contract. Both grades acknowledge the documented returns rather than pretending that championship membership alone makes a trade equal.

sections.heading: The Lakers Turned Kiffin into a Future Second
sections.body: Los Angeles sent Irv Kiffin to San Antonio on October 5, 1979 for a 1980 second-round pick. It was an exchange of a player for a future selection, rather than a trade involving two immediate rotation pieces. Kiffin made his only NBA appearances for San Antonio after the exchange. The Spurs waived him on December 19, leaving a total of 26 regular-season games. That brief tenure limited what the acquired player supplied compared with the Lakers' deferred compensation.

sections.heading: Butch Carter Became a Second Return
sections.body: The 1980 pick became No. 37, used on Butch Carter. Carter appeared in 54 games for Los Angeles in 1980-81 and later supplied another asset when the Lakers traded him to Indiana for a 1982 third-round pick. Los Angeles selected Hutch Jones with that later choice. Jones didn't play an NBA regular-season game for the Lakers, so the secondary conversion had a documented ending without useful direct appearances. The Carter stint nonetheless made the original second-rounder productive beyond its mere draft position.

sections.heading: Why This Small Deal Favored Los Angeles
sections.body: San Antonio received a short-lived reserve and no further traceable piece from Kiffin in the trade record. Los Angeles obtained a pick that produced 54 games from Carter before being rerouted into another choice. This is a narrow early-career asset chain, not a franchise-defining win, but it is enough to distinguish the Lakers' return from the Spurs' 26 Kiffin appearances. Both teams' actual decisions and the subsequent picks matter more than any imaginary alternative second-round selection.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win. Los Angeles grades B+ for the second-rounder that became Butch Carter and subsequently another third-round pick; San Antonio receives D+ for Kiffin's 26 NBA games before being waived. The pick created the stronger documented return even though Hutch Jones, the eventual third-round selection, never played for the Lakers.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Irv Kiffin for Butch Carter: The Lakers’ 1979 Second-Round Return
featuredDeepDive.intro: San Antonio received 26 games from Irv Kiffin before waiving him. Los Angeles converted its incoming second into Butch Carter, who played 54 Lakers games before returning a separate third-round draft right in 1981.

sections.heading: A 1979 Player-for-Pick Trade With a Measurable Payoff
sections.body: The October 5, 1979 agreement sent Irv Kiffin from the Lakers to San Antonio for a 1980 second-round draft pick. Kiffin was a reserve forward rather than an established star, and the Spurs got only 26 regular-season appearances from him before waiving him on December 19. Los Angeles instead kept the draft right and used it on Butch Carter with the No. 37 choice the following June. Carter was not a long-term franchise centerpiece but became a playable Lakers guard during 1980-81. The difference is measurable rather than hypothetical: Kiffin supplied 26 Spurs games, while Carter supplied 54 Lakers games before another trade. Both teams made ordinary roster and draft decisions, and the grade should compare those actual returns without importing career numbers from later franchises.

sections.heading: Butch Carter Played Fifty-Four Games for Los Angeles
sections.body: Carter's first NBA season came with the Lakers after they used the pick obtained from San Antonio. He played 54 games in 1980-81 and started 14, averaging 5.6 points over 12.4 minutes per game according to his NBA player profile. Those are modest rotation statistics, not evidence he transformed a title contender. They still constitute real production from a future second-round selection that the Lakers acquired by surrendering Kiffin. San Antonio's immediate return had an even shorter tenure: 26 games before December release. The comparative advantage grows from the Lakers' ability to obtain NBA playing time through the draft and then move Carter again, rather than from any imagined Hall of Fame outcome. Carter's later Indiana and New York seasons belong to those teams, not to his Lakers stint.

sections.heading: The 1981 Trade Generated a Different Future Pick
sections.body: On October 15, 1981, Los Angeles traded Carter to Indiana for a 1982 third-round selection. Basketball-Reference lists the ensuing Lakers No. 54 selection as Hutch Jones, who did not become a regular-season player for the franchise. Historical draft-right records are not entirely uniform on the later selection label, so the safest firm statement is the confirmed Carter-to-Indiana trade for a third-round right. This second transaction is valuable context but was not part of the original October 1979 deal. The first exchange yielded a future second that became Carter; the separate 1981 negotiation recovered a third after one season of his play. No later draft player needs to be presented as an established Lakers contributor. Separating the two agreements preserves the real value chain without inflating the result.

sections.heading: Lakers B-Plus, Spurs D-Plus Is a Limited Win
sections.body: The Los Angeles side of this transaction produced a useful but unspectacular reserve guard and the ability to recover another draft right later. Butch Carter's 54 Lakers games, including 14 starts, were a larger NBA return than San Antonio realized from Irv Kiffin's 26 games before his December 1979 waiver. The Spurs did acquire a real player and did not finish with zero games, which supports a D-plus instead of pretending the incoming asset never existed. The Lakers' B-plus recognizes that the pick converted into both an NBA contributor and later tradable value; it should not be mistaken for a major championship-building move. This is a small but traceable Lakers Win, with both franchises' actual returns and the separate Carter-to-Indiana transaction kept in their proper dates.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win — Los Angeles B+, San Antonio D+. Butch Carter gave the Lakers 54 regular-season games and a later third-round draft right in a separate 1981 move. Kiffin played 26 games for the Spurs before being waived in December 1979.

sections.heading: A February 1987 Five-Asset Price for Thompson
sections.body: On February 13, 1987, Los Angeles acquired center-forward Mychal Thompson from San Antonio for Frank Brickowski, Pétur Guðmundsson, the Lakers' 1987 first-round pick, their 1990 second-round pick and cash. The first became No. 23 Greg 'Cadillac' Anderson; the second ultimately became No. 54 Sean Higgins. Contemporary transaction ledgers from both franchises and Pro Sports Transactions identify the two selections and their later names. These were real outgoing assets, not incidental roster footnotes. Los Angeles was adding another experienced big man behind the aging Kareem Abdul-Jabbar as it targeted Boston and the rest of the league's strongest frontcourts. San Antonio, far from contention, accepted two players and future draft capital. The initial judgment should acknowledge what the Lakers surrendered before weighing the much larger playoff return they ultimately received.

sections.heading: Thompson Played 33 Lakers Games and Won the 1987 Championship
sections.body: Thompson joined the Lakers after the All-Star break and appeared in 33 regular-season games for Los Angeles in 1986-87, averaging 10.1 points and 4.1 rebounds in 20.6 minutes. Those statistics are his Lakers-only split, not his full season totals combined with San Antonio. The Lakers then beat Boston 4-2 in the 1987 NBA Finals. Thompson played all six Finals games, averaging 11.2 points and 5.2 rebounds in 28.5 minutes. He scored 18 points in Game 5 at Boston and 15 in the title-clinching sixth game in Los Angeles. The club's official alumni history identifies him as a frontcourt reserve acquired specifically to support Abdul-Jabbar and confirms the 1987 title. Los Angeles already featured Magic Johnson and James Worthy; the trade did not create the championship roster by itself. It strengthened a narrow positional area just before a successful postseason.

sections.heading: The Repeat Title in 1988 Was the Most Durable Direct Return
sections.body: Los Angeles kept Thompson for the next full season, when he played 80 games in 1987-88 and averaged 11.6 points, 6.1 rebounds and 25.1 minutes. The Lakers defeated Detroit in seven games in the 1988 Finals to repeat as champions. Thompson appeared in that entire Finals series, averaging 7.0 points and 3.6 rebounds, and supplied practical size while the starters handled larger scoring workloads. He continued to serve in Los Angeles through 1990-91, including the later Finals appearance against Chicago, although that team did not win the title. These are traceable Lakers returns from the 1987 acquisition. His Spurs seasons before the trade and his Lakers broadcaster career do not add extra basketball production to the exchange. Two title runs with tangible receiving-team minutes are what support the protected Lakers A grade.

sections.heading: San Antonio Got Real Picks, but No Comparable Two-Title Contributor
sections.body: San Antonio's compensation was not limited to the two outgoing Laker reserves. Brickowski and Guðmundsson arrived alongside the first-round right exercised on Greg Anderson and the later second-round right used on Sean Higgins, plus cash. Anderson appeared in the NBA and became a useful journeyman big; Higgins also had subsequent league opportunities, but neither became a multiple-title Spurs cornerstone. Brickowski developed a lengthy NBA career, much of it outside San Antonio, making career totals an unreliable measure of his Spurs return. This is an important correction to the idea that a first-round pick and two future players were simply wasted on arrival. The Spurs held several distinct assets with value and later possibilities. Their return nevertheless did not match Thompson's direct 1987 and 1988 championship participation. The saved San Antonio C grade allows partial value without claiming the team's eventual drafting of David Robinson was part of this trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win, Los Angeles A, San Antonio C. Thompson provided 33 Lakers games during the 1986-87 regular season, then 11.2 points and 5.2 rebounds in six Finals games against Boston. He also helped the Lakers repeat in 1988 while playing all 80 regular-season games. The Spurs received Brickowski, Guðmundsson, cash, and picks later used for Greg 'Cadillac' Anderson and Sean Higgins. The draft rights and players had value, but the Lakers' two traceable title runs made their side more productive.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Why the 1987 Mychal Thompson Trade Paid off Twice for the Lakers
featuredDeepDive.intro: The Lakers spent two reserve big men, a first-rounder, a second-rounder and cash to acquire Mychal Thompson from San Antonio on February 13, 1987. That price was steeper than a simple player-for-player swap. Thompson nevertheless helped Los Angeles win the 1987 Finals over Boston and the 1988 Finals over Detroit, backing Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and providing a second frontcourt scoring option. The Spurs' selections eventually became Greg Anderson and Sean Higgins, while Frank Brickowski had a longer career largely elsewhere. The decisive measurement is actual value delivered to the original receiving franchises, rather than retrospectively claiming every later championship or career statistic for this one deal.

sections.heading: All Five Spurs Incoming Assets Belong in the Ledger
sections.body: The Lakers' February 13 transaction is documented as a package of Frank Brickowski, Pétur Guðmundsson, a 1987 first-round pick, a 1990 second-round pick and cash for Mychal Thompson. Basketball Reference identifies the first as the right used on Greg Anderson with the 23rd selection and the second as the right used on Sean Higgins at No. 54 in 1990. Pro Sports Transactions independently reproduces that first-round draft routing and names the 1990 second. The cash consideration in the protected TradeVerdicts asset ledger should be retained because contemporary transaction compilations also list it, though the exact amount is not established in the sourced record. Neither Anderson nor Higgins was already a drafted player at the date of the deal. Calling the 1987 selection a future Greg Anderson pick is an asset-chain description, not evidence that the Spurs knew his career when accepting it.

sections.heading: Thompson's 1987 Finals Minutes Were Not Hypothetical Insurance
sections.body: Thompson was a middle-of-season acquisition at a position where the Lakers needed to limit Abdul-Jabbar's burden against strong centers. The NBA's Lakers alumni page gives the receiving-team line as 33 games, 10.1 points and 4.1 rebounds in 1986-87. Those minutes did not disappear when the playoffs began. Against Boston in the Finals he averaged 28.5 minutes, 11.2 points and 5.2 rebounds across all six games, including 18 points in Game 5 and 15 in Game 6. Los Angeles won the championship 4-2. This is direct evidence that the player it acquired was part of the decisive postseason rotation, even though Magic Johnson, James Worthy and Kareem remained more influential players. The trade created an additional layer of frontcourt cover during a series against a Boston team built around Larry Bird, Kevin McHale and Robert Parish.

sections.heading: The 1988 Championship Extended His Value Beyond a Rental
sections.body: Thompson remained on the Lakers for a full 1987-88 season, making 80 regular-season appearances, averaging 11.6 points and 6.1 rebounds. The club went through a seven-game Finals against Detroit and became the first franchise since Boston's 1968-69 team to win consecutive NBA titles. Thompson played in all seven Finals games and averaged 7.0 points in 21.6 minutes, lower than his 1987 series totals but still a visible bench role. He continued through the 1989 Finals loss and the 1991 return to the championship round. The official Lakers historical profile calls him a two-time NBA champion, not a player who won both titles on another club's roster. Because he was present at each title and used in real playoff minutes, the A-grade Lakers return rests on completed basketball results rather than an estimate of the trade's theoretical upside.

sections.heading: The Picks and Veteran Departures Have Separate Career Limits
sections.body: San Antonio's future first-round choice became Greg 'Cadillac' Anderson in 1987 and its later second became Sean Higgins in 1990. The Spurs also received Brickowski and Guðmundsson, which means judging the trade as Thompson for a single first misses several assets. But the future careers of those players require careful team attribution. Brickowski's later productive seasons elsewhere are not Spurs wins credited to the original 1987 agreement. Higgins' career and Anderson's later moves also cannot be assumed to have stayed under Spurs control throughout. The Lakers gave up assets that could have added long-term depth, yet they used the incoming Thompson as a championship-level backup almost immediately. The saved C for San Antonio reflects a portfolio with some direct value but no counterpart to the 1987 and 1988 Lakers championship roles.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Los Angeles A and San Antonio C are retained with Lakers Win. Thompson played 33 Lakers games after February 1987 and appeared in all six Finals games against Boston, then 80 regular-season games and all seven Finals against Detroit in 1987-88. The outgoing price included Brickowski, Guðmundsson, cash, 1987 No. 23 Greg Anderson and the 1990 second that became Sean Higgins. The documented two-title player return outweighed those distinct but less durable Spurs assets.

sections.heading: A Veteran Free-Agent Agreement Required Draft Compensation
sections.body: On October 7, 1987, the Lakers signed Jeff Lamp, a veteran free agent whose prior club was San Antonio. The Spurs received a 1988 third-round pick as compensation for allowing the move under the free-agent rules then in effect. The selection ultimately became No. 75 Archie Marshall. Neither club was exchanging an established contracted starter directly: Los Angeles acquired the opportunity to use Lamp, while San Antonio secured a late draft choice. Calling this a straight swap of Lamp for Marshall would ignore the intervening rights arrangement.

sections.heading: Lamp Barely Played During the Lakers’ 1988 Title Season
sections.body: Lamp appeared in just three regular-season games for Los Angeles in 1987–88, playing seven total minutes. The Lakers won the NBA championship that year, but Lamp did not appear in a postseason game and cannot be credited with the franchise’s playoff performance. He returned for 37 regular-season appearances in 1988–89, again in limited reserve minutes. That gives the acquisition a documented NBA presence without suggesting it transformed a roster led by Magic Johnson, James Worthy and Kareem Abdul-Jabbar.

sections.heading: San Antonio’s Pick Became Archie Marshall
sections.body: The Spurs used their compensation selection on Marshall, a Kansas forward who had been part of the school’s 1988 national title team. The third-round choice at No. 75 was an identifiable asset, but the record does not establish a substantial subsequent NBA rotation contribution for San Antonio. A pick that reaches a named draftee is not automatically equivalent to a long-term starter, just as signing a veteran who contributes a handful of games is not an automatic win.

sections.heading: A Limited Result on Each Side Explains the Tie
sections.body: The canonical verdict is Even Trade, with both Los Angeles and San Antonio receiving C-plus. The Lakers obtained a marginal veteran option with brief regular-season minutes; the Spurs received a late selection without a documented star return. Historical first-refusal compensation rules explain the exchange better than a narrative about blockbuster trade strategy. Neither side gained enough sustained basketball value from this particular agreement to justify inventing a decisive winner.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Lakers C-plus, Spurs C-plus. Los Angeles signed Jeff Lamp and received only three regular-season appearances during its 1988 championship year, followed by a limited 1988–89 stint. San Antonio received a third-round pick that became Archie Marshall at No. 75. The small realized returns support equal grades rather than attributing the Lakers’ title to this signing.

sections.heading: Seattle Exchanged Two Unsettled Pieces for Sam Perkins
sections.body: The SuperSonics acquired Sam Perkins from Los Angeles on February 22, 1993. The Lakers received center Benoit Benjamin and the draft rights to Doug Christie. Seattle could not agree to terms with Christie, its unsigned 1992 first-round selection, and Benjamin had been a reserve center behind Michael Cage. Perkins, by contrast, was a proven forward who had played in the 1991 NBA Finals with Los Angeles. The trade therefore exchanged immediate established production for two less certain Lakers opportunities.

sections.heading: Perkins Fit Seattle’s Competitive Timetable
sections.body: Perkins brought outside shooting, size and veteran playoff experience to a Seattle team under George Karl. The SuperSonics reached the Western Conference finals in 1993 and advanced to the NBA Finals in 1996 with Perkins contributing during that era. Those appearances are not solely attributable to this trade, but they establish that the incoming forward played meaningful years within a successful roster. Seattle was not forced to wait on the health or contract development of an unsigned draft pick.

sections.heading: The Lakers Received Both Rights and a Movable Center
sections.body: Christie was a young wing whose rights carried genuine development potential, not a guarantee of immediate NBA stardom. Benjamin offered veteran size, but the Lakers sent him to New Jersey on June 21, 1993 for Sam Bowie and a 1998 second-round choice later used on Toby Bailey. That downstream transaction is traceable to Benjamin, and it should be credited as such without pretending either incoming player duplicated Perkins’s role. Los Angeles had useful options but received a more uncertain short-term return.

sections.heading: The Recorded Grade Difference Favors Seattle
sections.body: The ledger assigns Seattle/Oklahoma City A-plus and Los Angeles C, with SuperSonics Win. Perkins’s established rotation contribution and association with deep postseason teams provide the central case for Seattle. Christie’s rights and Benjamin’s subsequent exchange keep the Lakers package from being empty, but its documented immediate return was less durable. The comparison should center on this particular trade rather than treating every subsequent SuperSonics success as its direct result.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: SuperSonics Win — Seattle/Oklahoma City A-plus, Lakers C. Seattle obtained Perkins, an established forward who contributed during its 1993 conference-finals and 1996 NBA Finals seasons. Los Angeles acquired Benjamin and Christie’s unsigned draft rights, then moved Benjamin for Bowie and a 1998 second-round pick. That chain provided some value, but Seattle received the more productive immediate veteran.

sections.heading: Reading the Deal Through Realized Value
sections.body: The Lakers acquired Cedric Ceballos from Phoenix on September 23, 1994, for a future first-round pick that could convey in 1995, 1996 or 1997. It conveyed in 1995 at No. 21, where Phoenix selected Michael Finley. The transaction therefore exchanged a proven scorer for a draft opportunity rather than two established NBA players, and both clubs obtained results substantially stronger than an ordinary late-first-round return.

sections.heading: Why Both Teams Earned A+ Returns
sections.body: Ceballos produced two full high-scoring seasons for Los Angeles. In 1994–95 he averaged 21.7 points and eight rebounds over 58 games, making the All-Star team. He followed with 21.2 points across 78 games in 1995–96. The Lakers also retained transaction value: they later combined Ceballos with Rumeal Robinson in the January 1997 trade for Robert Horry and Joe Kleine. Crediting Horry solely to Ceballos would omit Robinson's role.

sections.heading: The Return on the Losing Side
sections.body: Phoenix exercised its incoming pick rather than merely trading draft rights onward. Finley played all 82 games as a rookie, started 72, averaged 15 points and earned All-Rookie recognition. He remained with the Suns for 27 games of 1996–97 before entering the package sent to Dallas in December 1996 for Jason Kidd, Tony Dumas and Loren Meyer. Finley was joined by Sam Cassell, A.C. Green and a second-rounder, so the entire Kidd return cannot be assigned to the 1994 Ceballos trade.

sections.heading: How the Final Grades Fit the Outcome
sections.body: Both direct and downstream values favor a high grade on each side. The Lakers received Ceballos at his scoring peak, then used his residual trade value in a multi-asset route to Horry. Phoenix received an excellent rookie at No. 21, then used Finley as one of several pieces to bring in Kidd. Neither side's conversion should be inflated by assets it also surrendered, and the appropriate retrospective result is Even Trade, A+ for each club.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, A+ Lakers and A+ Suns. Ceballos became a prolific Lakers scorer and an eventual component of the package for Robert Horry. Phoenix used the first-rounder on Michael Finley, who contributed as a rookie and was later one of four assets exchanged for Jason Kidd and other players. Both clubs earned unusually strong value; neither should claim all of a later multi-asset return.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Cedric Ceballos, Michael Finley and the Two High-Value Returns
featuredDeepDive.intro: The Lakers acquired Cedric Ceballos for a first-round pick that Phoenix used at No. 21 on Michael Finley in 1995. Ceballos gave Los Angeles two full seasons above 21 points per game, and Finley immediately earned All-Rookie recognition. Later, each player contributed to a larger trade package: Ceballos toward Robert Horry and Finley toward Jason Kidd. Neither was the sole outgoing consideration. That combination supports high grades for both organizations and no decisive winner.

sections.heading: What Each Team Actually Received
sections.body: Phoenix traded Ceballos to Los Angeles in September 1994 for a first-round choice with a three-year conveyance window. The pick transferred in the very next draft at No. 21, making the Suns' selected player Michael Finley. This timing connects the 1994 exchange with the 1995 selection without implying that Finley had already played when the deal was made. The Lakers received immediate veteran scoring instead.

sections.heading: How Phoenix Suns Created the Better Return
sections.body: Ceballos's 1994–95 Lakers season included 58 games, 21.7 points and eight rebounds per appearance plus an All-Star selection. He played 78 games and averaged 21.2 points the next season. Those statistics alone establish exceptional direct return on one future first-rounder. In January 1997 he and Rumeal Robinson were traded for Robert Horry and Joe Kleine, preserving an additional asset branch while preventing any credible claim that the original deal alone obtained Horry.

sections.heading: The Case for Los Angeles Lakers—and Its Limit
sections.body: Finley was a valuable choice for Phoenix before his later trade. As a rookie he averaged 15 points, 4.6 rebounds and 3.5 assists across 82 appearances and received All-Rookie honors. In December 1996 Phoenix packaged him with Cassell, A.C. Green and a 1998 second-rounder to Dallas for Jason Kidd, Tony Dumas and Loren Meyer. Finley was a meaningful component, but the multi-player structure limits how much of Kidd's eventual impact can be attributed to this single earlier pick.

sections.heading: Even Trade: Los Angeles A+ and Phoenix A+
sections.body: Los Angeles and Phoenix each converted one incoming asset into substantial playing production and later trade leverage. Ceballos was a genuine Lakers All-Star-caliber scorer, while Finley was an unusually productive No. 21 selection and retained value in Phoenix's Kidd trade. The parallel outcomes justify A+ for both clubs, not a forced one-sided victory. Treating the later Horry or Kidd deals as direct one-for-one outcomes would obscure other pieces of those separate transactions.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, Los Angeles A+ / Phoenix A+. The Lakers obtained 21-plus points per game in each of Ceballos's two complete Los Angeles seasons and retained value when he was included in the Horry exchange. Phoenix received Finley at No. 21, benefited from his All-Rookie production, then used him in a multi-part package for Kidd. Both returns were exceptional and both later conversions required other outgoing assets.

sections.heading: Two Clubs Exchanged Guards and Draft Assets
sections.body: The Lakers acquired Tracy Murray, the draft rights to Kareem Rush and a 2003 second-round pick later used on Luke Walton. Toronto received Lindsey Hunter, the rights to Chris Jefferies and another 2003 second-round selection, No. 52 Remon Van de Hare. The deal moved several players and draft positions, so treating it as a one-for-one swap would miss the pick that eventually became the Lakers’ most consequential long-term return.

sections.heading: Rush and Walton Supplied Different Types of Help
sections.body: Rush gave Los Angeles a young perimeter shooter, but his Lakers tenure was not the central enduring asset. The second-round selection that became Walton generated considerably more lasting value: Walton developed into a versatile passing forward and later contributed to Lakers championship teams. Murray’s contribution was comparatively modest. The long-term outcome of the incoming pick, not an instant transformation of the roster in 2002, explains much of the Lakers’ superior result.

sections.heading: Toronto’s Return Did Not Yield a Similar Contributor
sections.body: Hunter offered veteran guard experience, while Jefferies was a developmental draft-rights prospect. Van de Hare, selected later in the second round, did not turn into a comparable NBA contributor. Toronto had identifiable reasons to acquire different personnel and later draft rights, but those assets produced less sustained on-court output than Walton eventually provided Los Angeles. The package contained several pieces without securing a player who shaped multiple successful Lakers seasons.

sections.heading: The Grade Comparison Depends on the Pick Outcome
sections.body: The canonical grades are Lakers B-plus and Raptors D. That gap comes mainly from Walton’s sustained career value, with Rush providing a smaller supplementary return, rather than rewarding the Lakers for having more incoming names. Toronto’s veterans and prospects were real considerations but lacked an equivalent successful downstream result. The teams could not know Walton’s exact career path on trade day, but the retrospective verdict can compare what their actual selected assets ultimately produced.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win — Los Angeles B-plus, Toronto D. The Lakers’ 2003 second-round pick became Luke Walton, whose lengthy tenure and championship contributions outweighed the eventual returns from Hunter, Jefferies and Van de Hare. Rush and Murray were secondary parts of the package. The substantial gap reflects actual player outcomes attached to these identified assets, not a generic assumption that draft selections are always better.

sections.heading: Miami Bought the Last Dominant Stretch of Shaquille O’Neal’s Prime
sections.body: The Heat did not acquire a ceremonial version of Shaquille O’Neal in July 2004. He was 32, one month removed from averaging 26.6 points and 10.8 rebounds in the Finals, and still capable of forcing opponents to build an entire playoff game plan around the paint. Miami already had Dwyane Wade, whose rookie postseason showed that his rise would be much faster than a normal rebuilding schedule. O’Neal gave that young guard an interior partner who drew double-teams, controlled the glass and supplied the credibility of a three-time Finals MVP. In his first Heat season he finished second in MVP voting, and the club immediately moved from a promising playoff team to a 59-win contender.

sections.heading: The Lakers Chose a Reset After a Dynasty Became Unsustainable
sections.body: Los Angeles entered the summer after losing the 2004 Finals with its championship structure breaking apart. Phil Jackson departed, the relationship between O’Neal and Kobe Bryant had deteriorated, and ownership faced the choice of committing another massive contract to an aging center or reorganizing around the younger star. That context matters because the Lakers were not shopping Shaq from a position of perfect leverage. Miami nevertheless paid a substantial package: Lamar Odom, Caron Butler, Brian Grant, a future first-round pick and additional draft value. The return gave Los Angeles multiple rotation players, a younger timeline and enough movable pieces to avoid the total collapse that often follows the exit of an all-time great.

sections.heading: The 2006 Championship Completed Miami’s Side of the Bargain
sections.body: O’Neal’s Miami tenure did not need to last a decade to justify the price. The Heat reached Game 7 of the 2005 Eastern Conference finals despite injuries, then reworked the supporting cast and won the 2006 championship. Wade became the Finals centerpiece, but O’Neal still demanded interior attention, rebounded, protected the rim and gave Miami a second star opponents could not ignore. The title was the first in franchise history and the exact result Pat Riley pursued when he exchanged youth for a compressed competitive window. Once a trade produces a championship with the acquired superstar playing a central role, ordinary concerns about age curve and contract length carry less weight.

sections.heading: Lamar Odom Became the Durable Centerpiece of the Lakers’ Return
sections.body: Odom was the one incoming player who directly connected the 2004 breakup to the Lakers’ next championship era. His size, ballhandling, rebounding and willingness to accept different roles allowed Los Angeles to use him as a starter, reserve and closing-lineup connector. He remained through the difficult rebuilding seasons, then became indispensable beside Bryant, Pau Gasol and Andrew Bynum on the 2009 and 2010 title teams. Odom’s value was not captured by a single scoring average. He solved lineup problems, initiated offense after rebounds and defended across the frontcourt. Miami received the best immediate player, but the Lakers received a player who later became one of the most important non-stars on two champions.

sections.heading: Caron Butler and the Draft Picks Extended the Asset Chain
sections.body: Butler spent only one season in Los Angeles, yet his inclusion still mattered. The Lakers moved him for Kwame Brown, and Brown later became the principal salary piece in the 2008 trade for Pau Gasol. It would be excessive to credit the entire Gasol acquisition to Butler, because Memphis’ valuation and the draft assets in that later deal were independent factors. Still, the sequence shows that the Shaq return retained transactional usefulness after Butler left. The 2006 first-round pick became Jordan Farmar, a rotation guard on both later championship teams. Brian Grant’s contract and limited production were negatives, while the 2007 second-round selection added little, but the package produced more than one durable strand of value.

sections.heading: Equal A-Plus Grades Recognize Two Different Championship Paths
sections.body: The previous A for Los Angeles understated how thoroughly the return supported the franchise’s second act. Miami should remain at A+ because O’Neal accelerated Wade’s ascent, nearly reached the Finals immediately and helped secure the 2006 title. The Lakers also deserve A+ because Odom became a two-title cornerstone, Farmar contributed to those teams and Butler helped preserve the salary-and-asset chain that eventually reached Gasol. This is not a claim that every incoming piece was excellent or that the Lakers preferred the breakup. It is a recognition that both organizations converted the same trade into championships within six years, using radically different timelines and roster-building strategies.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, with A+ grades for both Miami and Los Angeles. The Heat acquired the superior immediate player and converted O’Neal’s remaining elite years into the first championship in franchise history. The Lakers accepted the end of a dynasty but received Odom, Butler and draft value that helped bridge to the 2009 and 2010 champions. Grant’s contract and O’Neal’s shorter Miami peak are real imperfections, yet neither outweighs the defining result on each side: both franchises built a title path from the transaction.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The Shaq Trade Ended One Dynasty and Helped Create Two More Championships
featuredDeepDive.intro: The 2004 Shaquille O’Neal deal is unusual because its fairest evaluation requires resisting the instinct to identify one loser. Miami purchased concentrated superstar impact at the exact moment Wade was ready to become elite. Los Angeles sacrificed the most dominant center of his generation but obtained a package that could survive a multi-year rebuild and later support Bryant’s second championship core. The trade therefore became less a simple exchange of talent than a transfer between competitive timelines. Miami won quickly by accepting age and salary risk; the Lakers won later by preserving versatile players and future transaction options.

sections.heading: The Breakup Was About Control as Much as Basketball Value
sections.body: The Lakers’ decision followed years of tension over conditioning, contract expectations, offensive hierarchy and the relationship between their two superstars. O’Neal had delivered three championships and remained highly productive, but Bryant was younger and entering the phase of his career around which the franchise could plan for another decade. Choosing Bryant did not automatically make the compensation adequate; it simply explains why Los Angeles accepted the disruption. Miami recognized that the Lakers needed a clean resolution and offered a package broad enough to restart the roster. The negotiation illustrates how off-court leverage can narrow a seller’s options without eliminating the possibility of a strong long-term return.

sections.heading: Miami’s Roster Was Built to Exploit O’Neal’s Immediate Gravity
sections.body: Wade’s slashing, O’Neal’s post presence and a veteran defense gave Miami a structure that could win before the center’s decline accelerated. O’Neal no longer needed to carry the scoring burden he had shouldered during portions of the Lakers dynasty. His screens, seals and threat near the rim created driving space for Wade, while his rebounding allowed the Heat to finish defensive possessions. Riley later changed coaches and reshaped the veteran rotation, but the strategic center remained the Wade-Shaq pairing. The deal worked because Miami understood that the value of a superstar can be multiplicative: O’Neal improved the environment in which its emerging franchise guard could become a champion.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Survived the Lean Years Without Wasting the Return
sections.body: The Lakers missed the playoffs in 2005 and endured a first-round ceiling in the next two seasons, so the immediate comparison heavily favored Miami. The important organizational achievement was avoiding panic. Odom remained useful through changing systems, Butler was converted rather than allowed to expire, and the draft pick was used on a guard who fit the later rotation. When Gasol became available in 2008, Los Angeles still possessed Bryant, Bynum, Odom and enough trade structure to act. The Shaq return did not independently create that opportunity, but it helped keep the roster functional until the next star acquisition arrived.

sections.heading: Championship Credit Must Be Assigned Without Inventing a Straight Line
sections.body: Trade trees tempt analysts to treat every later transaction as an automatic product of the first deal. The Butler-to-Brown-to-Gasol sequence deserves mention, but the Lakers also sent Marc Gasol’s rights and first-round picks to Memphis; those assets cannot be erased. Likewise, Miami’s 2006 title depended on Wade’s brilliance, Riley’s coaching change and veteran additions beyond O’Neal. A sound grade isolates what the trade supplied: Miami gained a still-dominant co-star, while Los Angeles gained a versatile long-term piece, a useful prospect and additional options. Both sets of assets became material components of championship teams even though neither acted alone.

sections.heading: The Even Verdict Is Stronger Than a Narrow Peak-Value Argument
sections.body: If the question were only which team received the best player in July 2004, Miami would win easily. If the question were only which return lasted longer, Los Angeles would have the advantage. TradeVerdicts grades realized franchise value, postseason consequence and downstream utility together. Miami’s short, explosive payoff and the Lakers’ slower, distributed payoff reached the same highest outcome. Equal A+ grades do not suggest the packages were identical; they recognize that each front office used its side of the deal to win championships on a timeline suited to its circumstances.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The historical record supports an Even Trade with two A+ grades. Miami acquired O’Neal’s final MVP-caliber stretch, paired it with Wade and won the 2006 championship. Los Angeles absorbed the painful end of its dynasty but retained Odom for two later titles, drafted Farmar and used Butler within the chain that helped create the Gasol-era roster. Few superstar trades deliver a championship-level payoff to both organizations. This one did, which makes equal top grades more accurate than forcing a winner.

sections.heading: The Lakers Traded Two Players for an Unproven Big and Reserve Guard
sections.body: The Lakers announced August 2, 2005 that they acquired Kwame Brown and Laron Profit from Washington for Caron Butler and Chucky Atkins. Butler had started all 77 Lakers games in 2004-05 and averaged 15.5 points, giving up an established rotation scorer for the chance that Brown might develop into a bigger presence alongside Kobe Bryant. Brown had been the No. 1 pick in the 2001 draft but had never sustained star-level production with the Wizards. Profit was a depth guard, not a replacement for Butler. The official Lakers release confirms the complete two-for-two asset structure and August 2 date; an earlier Washington release used July 29.

sections.heading: Caron Butler Supplied 310 Wizards Games and Two All-Star Seasons
sections.body: Butler gave Washington 75 regular-season games in 2005-06, starting 54 and averaging 17.6 points. His 2006-07 season was worth 63 games and 19.1 points, including his first All-Star selection. The next two seasons brought 58 games at 20.3 points and 67 at 20.8, with a second All-Star selection in 2007-08. He added 47 Wizards appearances in 2009-10 before a separate trade to Dallas. Together those five Washington spans total 310 regular-season appearances and 289 starts. This direct franchise production, rather than Butler’s eventual NBA title elsewhere, is the central Wizards return.

sections.heading: Chucky Atkins Played 28 Washington Games Before Leaving
sections.body: Atkins also belonged to the Wizards package. He appeared in 28 Washington games in 2005-06, starting two and averaging 6.7 points and 2.5 assists. Washington waived him in January 2006, after which Memphis signed him. His 43 Grizzlies appearances that same season are not Washington production from this exchange. Atkins was a usable short-term reserve but far less impactful than Butler, who immediately entered the starting rotation. The distinction is important because the protected asset ledger lists both incoming players, even though Butler accounted for most of the lasting Wizards basketball value.

sections.heading: Brown Played 136 Lakers Games, Profit Another 25
sections.body: Brown played 72 Lakers games in 2005-06 with 49 starts, averaging 7.4 points and 6.6 rebounds. He added 41 appearances and 28 starts at 8.4 points in 2006-07, followed by 23 more and 14 starts during 2007-08 before leaving Los Angeles. Those segments total 136 Lakers games and 91 starts. Profit appeared in 25 Lakers games during 2005-06, starting once and averaging 4.2 points. Neither was an imaginary return, but their combined 161 receiving-team appearances and Brown’s modest scoring were smaller than Butler’s sustained Washington contribution.

sections.heading: The 2008 Gasol Trade Required Much More than Brown
sections.body: Brown was later included in the February 2008 transaction through which the Lakers acquired Pau Gasol from Memphis. That separate swap also involved Javaris Crittenton, Aaron McKie, draft choices and the rights to Marc Gasol. Brown supplied salary-matching and roster value but did not by himself command Pau Gasol. Crediting all the Lakers’ subsequent championship production to the August 2005 Butler exchange would skip those other major assets and the distinct 2008 decision. His later 15 Memphis games also count as Memphis production, not as continued Lakers output from Brown’s original arrival.

sections.heading: Why Washington Received the Stronger Direct Player Return
sections.body: The Wizards Win verdict assigns Washington A and Los Angeles B-plus. Washington received Caron Butler and Chucky Atkins for Kwame Brown and Laron Profit, as the original announcements from both teams confirm. Butler later started 289 games in his first 310 Washington appearances and earned two All-Star selections, an extended return that gave the Wizards far more than a short-term exchange. Los Angeles obtained 136 Brown games and 25 Profit appearances, plus a future use for Brown's contract in the distinct 2008 Pau Gasol package. Those Lakers contributions weren't worthless, but Brown alone didn't buy Gasol, and future Lakers championships can't be credited solely to this 2005 swap. The two grades recognize both teams' real returns while favoring Butler's stronger direct Washington career.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wizards Win with Washington A and Los Angeles B+ stays unchanged. Butler supplied 310 Wizards games, 289 starts and two All-Star selections; Atkins added 28 Wizards appearances. Brown logged 136 Lakers games with 91 starts, and Profit played 25. Brown’s inclusion in the separate 2008 Pau Gasol swap is valid downstream context, but the additional players, draft picks and rights in that deal forbid treating Gasol as a one-for-one 2005 return.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Butler for Kwame Brown in 2005: The Wizards’ All-Star Return and the Lakers’ Later Gasol Chain
featuredDeepDive.intro: The August 2, 2005 Lakers-Wizards deal exchanged Caron Butler and Chucky Atkins for Kwame Brown and Laron Profit. Butler became a two-time All-Star in Washington and appeared in 310 Wizards regular-season games through early 2010. Brown logged 136 Lakers games before his contract was included with other assets in the distinct Pau Gasol transaction of 2008. The saved Wizards Win, A Washington/B+ Los Angeles grades are compared through the actual receiving-team minutes and the separate downstream cost of Gasol rather than a misleading direct Butler-for-Gasol narrative.

sections.heading: Both Teams’ Official 2005 Releases Confirm a Complete Two-for-Two Package
sections.body: Washington issued an announcement in late July and Los Angeles confirmed the completed exchange on August 2, the date used by this protected ledger. The Lakers received Kwame Brown and Laron Profit; the Wizards acquired Caron Butler and Chucky Atkins. Butler had averaged 15.5 points for Los Angeles and had started all 77 regular-season games the year before. Brown brought a top-draft-pick pedigree and a need for more frontcourt playing time. Washington said it valued Butler’s versatility and Atkins’s shooting. Neither club received an additional first-rounder in this particular trade, and Butler’s later All-Star results were not a guaranteed condition of the August agreement.

sections.heading: Butler’s Five Washington Regular-Season Segments Total 310 Games
sections.body: The Butler receiving-team record is unusually easy to track across seasons. His 75 Wizards appearances in 2005-06 were followed by 63 in 2006-07, 58 in 2007-08, 67 in 2008-09 and 47 before leaving in 2009-10. That is 310 Washington games, with 289 starts when the season-by-season starting counts are added. He scored 17.6, 19.1, 20.3, 20.8 and 16.9 points per game across those segments. All-Star recognition came in 2007 and 2008. Subsequent Dallas and Clippers games are outside Washington’s production, just as Butler’s earlier Miami and Los Angeles seasons predated this transaction.

sections.heading: Brown Had a Lakers Rotation Role but Never Matched Butler’s Wing Impact
sections.body: Brown appeared in 72 Lakers games in 2005-06, 41 in 2006-07 and 23 before the February 2008 Memphis trade: 136 games, 91 starts. In his first two Lakers seasons he averaged 7.4 and 8.4 points, not the expected output of a former overall No. 1 selection. Laron Profit also contributed a real 25 games, one start and 4.2 points per game during 2005-06, but did not extend his stay into another Lakers season. Butler’s production in Washington was both larger in aggregate and stronger from season to season; keeping the NBA totals separated by actual team is essential.

sections.heading: Atkins Was a Real Incoming Wizard, Not a Second Long-Term Star
sections.body: Chucky Atkins’s August return supplied only 28 Wizards games and two starts in 2005-06, with 6.7 points and 2.5 assists per appearance. The club waived him in January. Memphis subsequently used him for 43 games and 39 starts that same season, yet none of those minutes accrued to Washington. His inclusion still defined the initial four-player trade, and he offered temporary guard depth after being an 82-game Lakers starter in 2004-05. In a retrospective trade grade, that one-third-season stint cannot be conflated with the five-segment value of Butler, who carried the Washington side.

sections.heading: The Gasol Deal Was a New Multi-Asset Trade Three Seasons Later
sections.body: The Lakers eventually packaged Brown with Javaris Crittenton, Aaron McKie, draft assets and the rights to Marc Gasol to obtain Pau Gasol from Memphis in February 2008. It was a momentous roster decision, but the cost was not Brown alone and the Wizards received nothing from the Memphis-Lakers exchange. The original 2005 trade can receive historical credit for providing a movable Brown contract without counting every Gasol point, playoff victory or title as its own direct outcome. That separation protects the inherited B+ Lakers grade from retrospective overstatement and leaves Washington’s two Butler All-Star years as the clearest return.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wizards Win, Washington A and Los Angeles B+ are retained. Butler logged 310 Washington appearances, 289 starts and two All-Star selections. Atkins added 28 Wizards games. Brown played 136 Lakers games and was subsequently used in a separately priced multi-asset exchange for Gasol; Profit provided 25 Lakers appearances. Both sets of receiving-team results are real, but Washington obtained the stronger direct player while Los Angeles needed several further assets to obtain its later centerpiece.

sections.heading: The Lakers Exchanged Two Rotation Players for One Defensive Wing
sections.body: On November 20, 2007, Los Angeles acquired Trevor Ariza from Orlando for Maurice Evans and Brian Cook. The Lakers' contemporary announcement and Los Angeles Times reporting agree on the three names and direction of the deal. Ariza was a 22-year-old former UCLA player who had averaged 8.9 points and 4.4 rebounds for the Magic in 2006-07. The Lakers saw a defense-first forward who could guard difficult perimeter assignments, while the Magic sought more useful shooting and depth for coach Stan Van Gundy's system. Evans had been a regular in the Lakers' second unit; Cook supplied frontcourt shooting but did not have Ariza's defensive range. This was not a three-team transaction and no future draft pick belonged to it. The asset ledger compares Ariza's Lakers value with what Evans and Cook gave Orlando rather than sweeping unrelated roster decisions into the trade.

sections.heading: Ariza Developed from an Injured 2008 Reserve into a 2009 Playoff Starter
sections.body: Ariza's first partial Lakers season included a right-foot injury that limited his 2008 postseason appearances. He was available for portions of the Western Conference Finals and the Finals loss to Boston but was not yet the decisive contributor he would become. In 2008-09 he played all 82 regular-season games, starting 20, and averaged 8.9 points, 4.3 rebounds and 1.7 steals. His role expanded during the championship playoffs: he started all 23 postseason games, averaged 11.3 points and shot 47.6 percent from three across that run. In five Finals games against Orlando he averaged 11.0 points and 6.0 rebounds while playing 37.6 minutes. These are direct outcomes for the Lakers from the November 2007 acquisition, not the later Houston or Washington seasons of his long career. The trade brought the sort of wing defense a Kobe Bryant-led contender needed.

sections.heading: Orlando's Shooting Rationale Did Not Produce Comparable Longevity
sections.body: The Magic's basketball rationale is important: Van Gundy's offense prioritized spacing, and the 2009 Los Angeles Times retrospective describes Ariza as an awkward fit for that approach when Orlando traded him. Evans and Cook were known Lakers quantities, but the Magic did not keep either through their 2009 Finals appearance against Ariza and the Lakers. Evans had a useful Orlando stint as a perimeter veteran, while Cook's playing time was limited after the trade. Neither became a long-term cornerstone for the Magic. The fact that Orlando also reached the Finals in 2009 does not erase the difference between the two packages or mean the Magic got nothing. It does show that both front offices built competitive teams using other pieces. Grading this specific exchange requires the receiving-player roles, duration and direct championship connection, not the franchises' entire future win totals.

sections.heading: Ariza's Title Was Earned in Los Angeles, Not in His Later Stops
sections.body: The most convincing evidence for the saved Lakers Win and A- grade is Ariza's work in the 2009 title run, particularly as a starting wing in the 23-game postseason and against Orlando in the Finals. The trade originally looked like a two-for-one depth sacrifice, and the Lakers' own players were surprised by the departure of Evans and Cook. Ariza then supplied a defensive skill set that was harder to replace than the lost bench roles. He left Los Angeles for Houston after the 2009 championship, so his later NBA seasons and any championship won by a different Lakers roster should not be credited to this acquisition. Orlando's D grade captures the lost opportunity on Ariza's development, while acknowledging the Magic reached their own 2009 Finals with a separate successful supporting cast. This is a concrete player-and-role win for Los Angeles, not an argument that the trade alone won an NBA title.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win, Los Angeles A-, Orlando D. The 2007 trade brought the Lakers Trevor Ariza, who started all 23 postseason games during their 2009 title run and averaged 11.0 points and 6.0 rebounds in the Finals against Orlando. The Magic got Maurice Evans and Brian Cook, neither of whom became a comparable long-term piece. The grade credits Ariza's actual Lakers seasons and title contribution, not his later teams or the separate 2010 championship.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Ariza for Evans and Cook: How a 2007 Depth Trade Became Part of the 2009 Lakers Title
featuredDeepDive.intro: Los Angeles exchanged Maurice Evans and Brian Cook for Trevor Ariza on November 20, 2007. At first it appeared to be a bet on a young defensive athlete rather than established bench depth. Ariza's right-foot injury delayed his 2008 impact, but by the following spring he was starting for the Lakers as they defeated Orlando in the 2009 NBA Finals. The Magic had its own reason to move him under Stan Van Gundy, whose system placed a premium on perimeter shooting. The postseason return gives this apparently modest two-for-one trade an unusually clear, source-verifiable Lakers advantage.

sections.heading: The Original Price Was Bench Depth, Not a Future Draft Pick
sections.body: The Lakers' November 20 release lists exactly Evans and Cook outgoing, Ariza incoming. The Los Angeles Times account published after the move describes the deal as an attempt to improve defensive coverage at small forward, not to add a primary scorer. Orlando had different priorities: Evans offered an experienced perimeter player while Cook was a stretch frontcourt option. Contemporary reporting says Ariza was not central to Van Gundy's preferred offensive plan, despite the wing's athletic potential. The trade was a direct two-team exchange, and there is no sound basis to append later Lakers moves or Orlando draft selections to this record. Kobe Bryant, Pau Gasol and the other championship contributors were assembled through separate decisions. The acquisition's identifiable sporting contribution was a wing who developed into a postseason starter.

sections.heading: A Foot Injury Separated the 2008 and 2009 Evaluations
sections.body: Ariza did not instantly become a title-run centerpiece in 2007-08. A right-foot fracture restricted his first Lakers season and left him playing only limited minutes during the 2008 postseason, when Boston beat Los Angeles in six Finals games. His next year tells the stronger story. He appeared in all 82 games and started 20 in the 2008-09 regular season, then played 31.4 minutes per game as a starter throughout 23 playoff appearances. Basketball Reference's playoff table lists 11.3 points, 4.2 rebounds and 1.6 steals per game during that championship postseason. His Finals series against Orlando included 11.0 points and 6.0 rebounds per game across five contests. The Lakers did not acquire those seasons' entire success with Ariza, but they did acquire that specific defender, wing workload and reliable playoff production.

sections.heading: Orlando Reached the Finals Despite Losing This Trade
sections.body: Orlando's 2009 Finals trip is a necessary check on simplistic hindsight. The Magic assembled a contender around Dwight Howard, targeted spacing and got value from a roster very different from the one it had in November 2007. Its decision to trade Ariza came from a plausible scheme judgment. The incoming Evans and Cook nevertheless did not become the long-term wing counterpart to Ariza's Lakers development; a June 2009 Los Angeles Times profile observed that both had left Orlando before the Finals meeting. A team can build a strong overall season while losing a particular exchange of players. The original Orlando D grade is not an assertion that the 2008-09 Magic failed as a franchise. It reflects receiving-player returns and Ariza's breakout after leaving the club, with contextual credit for why the front office took the risk.

sections.heading: The Trade's Best Test Is the 2009 Series Between Those Same Clubs
sections.body: The 2009 NBA Finals provided a rare direct comparison: Ariza started for the Lakers against the very team that had dealt him for two bench pieces. He averaged 37.6 minutes, 11.0 points, 6.0 rebounds and 1.8 steals in the five-game series. Los Angeles won the championship, with Bryant and Gasol driving the larger attack and Ariza supplying an important perimeter role. This episode is much more attributable to the November 2007 transaction than later changes in Ariza's employment, the Lakers' 2010 title or Orlando's other trade decisions. Los Angeles paid two players who did not hold the same value for Orlando through that postseason. A- for the Lakers recognizes high-leverage championship rotation value from a modest original cost; D for Orlando captures an opportunity the club could not reclaim once Ariza was thriving elsewhere.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win remains supported at Los Angeles A- and Orlando D. Ariza's 23 starts and 11.3 points per game in the 2009 championship playoffs, including 11.0 points and 6.0 boards per Finals game against Orlando, are attributable to the acquisition. Evans and Cook were not part of Orlando's subsequent Finals roster. The 2008 injury and 2010 Lakers title are separate chronology, not reasons to misstate his direct 2009 contribution.
