sections.heading: Minnesota Trusted Love’s Projection Over Mayo’s Draft Position
sections.body: The Timberwolves selected O.J. Mayo third and the Grizzlies selected Kevin Love fifth, but Minnesota did not treat the order as a final talent ranking. The teams completed an eight-player draft-night trade that sent Mayo, Marko Jaric, Antoine Walker, and Greg Buckner to Memphis for Love, Mike Miller, Brian Cardinal, and Jason Collins. Minnesota accepted a less explosive prospect because Love's rebounding, passing, shooting potential, and age fit its rebuilding plan. The decision required conviction before either player had appeared in an NBA game.

sections.heading: Love Became the Only Franchise Cornerstone in the Deal
sections.body: Love developed into a three-time All-Star in Minnesota, earned All-NBA recognition, led the league in rebounding, and expanded his shooting range into a defining part of his offensive value. He became the franchise's central player after Kevin Garnett and eventually produced another major asset return when Minnesota traded him to Cleveland. Mayo began his career as a high-volume scorer and made the All-Rookie team, but his progression stalled and he left Memphis after four seasons. The gap in peak and duration became decisive.

sections.heading: Mike Miller Added Immediate Credibility to Minnesota’s Return
sections.body: The trade was not Love for Mayo alone. Miller arrived as an established shooter and secondary creator who could help a young roster function while Love developed. Cardinal and Collins provided additional veteran frontcourt depth and salary structure. Those pieces did not determine the long-term verdict, but they increased Minnesota's immediate return and allowed the organization to move several unwanted contracts to Memphis. The Timberwolves acquired both the best future player and the most useful established player in the transaction.

sections.heading: Memphis Accepted Contract Burden to Pursue a Lead Scorer
sections.body: The Grizzlies were attracted to Mayo's perimeter scoring and star potential, a reasonable need for a young team still searching for an offensive identity. His rookie season validated part of that belief, and he averaged strong scoring numbers early. The accompanying package was costly. Jaric's contract had negative value, Walker was near the end of his career, and Buckner was a supporting guard. Memphis accepted those obligations while sending Miller and Love, leaving little margin if Mayo failed to become the best player in the deal.

sections.heading: Minnesota’s Later Love Trade Extends the Value Chain
sections.body: Love did not lead Minnesota to the playoffs, which prevents the transaction from being graded solely through team success. His individual development still created major franchise value. In 2014 the Timberwolves traded him to Cleveland in the deal that brought Andrew Wiggins, Anthony Bennett, and a future first-round asset, with Thaddeus Young arriving through the larger structure. That later trade is evaluated separately, but it confirms that Love remained a premium asset years after Mayo's Memphis tenure ended. Minnesota preserved optionality that Memphis never recovered.

sections.heading: Love's Minnesota Peak Outweighed Mayo's Memphis Start
sections.body: The draft-night swap sent O.J. Mayo to Memphis and Kevin Love to Minnesota, but the return was broader than two prospects changing teams. The Timberwolves also received Mike Miller and relieved themselves of several veteran contracts; the Grizzlies took on that salary to pursue Mayo's perimeter scoring. Mayo gave Memphis productive early seasons, a genuine return that supports its D+ rather than an F. Love developed into a three-time Minnesota All-Star, earned All-NBA recognition and led the league in rebounding. He also retained enough value to anchor a later major transaction, although the players acquired in that subsequent deal aren't direct 2008 receipts. Minnesota's A+ accounts for the superior long-term player, useful veteran help and a more flexible roster.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Minnesota wins with an A+, while Memphis receives a D+. Love became a three-time Timberwolves All-Star, an All-NBA forward, and a premium asset later used in another major trade. Miller added immediate shooting and veteran value, while the Wolves also moved difficult contracts. Mayo produced promising early seasons in Memphis but did not become a long-term cornerstone, and the Grizzlies absorbed Jaric, Walker, and Buckner to obtain him. Minnesota received the best player, the best veteran, and the most durable asset value in the exchange.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The Kevin Love–O.J. Mayo Swap Rewarded Minnesota for Ignoring Draft-Night Hype
featuredDeepDive.intro: Mayo entered the 2008 draft with the profile of a polished perimeter scorer, while Love's athletic limitations made his professional ceiling less obvious. Minnesota decided that rebounding, skill, and basketball intelligence would translate more reliably than the difference between the third and fifth picks suggested. The larger package also allowed the Wolves to acquire Miller and clear veteran contracts. What looked like a prospect preference became a broad roster win, because Love developed into a franchise-level asset while Mayo's early promise did not sustain.

sections.heading: The Trade Was Agreed After Both Players Had Already Been Selected
sections.body: Draft-night trades often create misleading team histories because players briefly appear as selections of franchises that never intended to keep them. Minnesota drafted Mayo and Memphis drafted Love before the clubs finalized the larger exchange. The delay increased the drama but did not change the evaluation: the Timberwolves chose Love as the player they wanted to build around and used Mayo's higher selection slot as leverage within an eight-player package. Understanding that structure prevents the deal from being reduced to a simple mistake by Memphis at the draft podium.

sections.heading: Love’s Skill Development Validated Minnesota’s Evaluation
sections.body: Love entered the league as an elite rebounder and outlet passer, then expanded into a high-volume scorer and three-point shooter. That evolution allowed him to produce across changing coaches and roster constructions. His best Minnesota seasons did not result in playoff appearances, but the lack of team success reflected broader roster weakness rather than an absence of star value. All-NBA recognition, rebounding leadership, and his eventual trade market demonstrate that Minnesota acquired a player capable of anchoring team strategy, even when the organization did not surround him effectively.

sections.heading: Mayo’s Rookie Success Made the Early Verdict Less Obvious
sections.body: Mayo scored immediately and looked capable of becoming the lead perimeter option Memphis wanted. That early performance is important because it shows the trade was not instantly absurd. The problem was progression. His efficiency, role, and overall impact did not rise with experience, and Memphis chose not to retain him after four seasons. A prospect trade can remain competitive if both players develop into stars; here, Mayo's plateau occurred while Love continued adding skills and increasing his league-wide value.

sections.heading: The Veteran Contracts Tilted the Package Before the Prospects Matured
sections.body: Minnesota also exchanged Jaric, Walker, and Buckner for Miller, Cardinal, and Collins. Miller was the best established player in that group and could shoot, pass, and stabilize possessions. Walker's NBA career was nearly finished, while Jaric's contract reduced flexibility. Memphis therefore paid more than the prospect swap alone suggests. The Grizzlies accepted salary and surrendered useful veteran play to secure Mayo. Once Love became the superior star, those secondary components made the completed value gap even more difficult to defend.

sections.heading: A Great Trade Did Not Automatically Fix Minnesota’s Organization
sections.body: The Timberwolves still struggled to build a playoff roster around Love, and the relationship eventually ended with another trade. That failure should temper claims that the 2008 move solved the franchise. It does not reduce the quality of the asset decision. Minnesota correctly identified the better player, acquired additional useful value, and later retained the ability to exchange Love for another major package. Trade grading should distinguish a successful acquisition from unsuccessful subsequent roster construction. The Love-Mayo deal was excellent even though the Wolves' broader era remained disappointing.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Timberwolves earn an A+ because they looked beyond draft position, acquired the best prospect, added the best veteran in the package, and moved contracts that offered little future value. Love became a multi-time All-Star and All-NBA asset whose value persisted into another blockbuster. Memphis receives a D+ because Mayo's promising start provided real production and the need for perimeter scoring was reasonable, but his development stalled and the accompanying contract burden deepened the loss. Minnesota's advantage was not one lucky season; it lasted through Love's entire franchise arc.

sections.heading: Draft Night: Richardson and Cash for Darko Miličić
sections.body: Memphis acquired Quentin Richardson and cash considerations from the New York Knicks on June 25, 2009, while New York received center Darko Miličić. Both franchises' season transaction ledgers record that player exchange, with the cash moving toward the Grizzlies rather than to the Knicks. The exact payment amount was not established in the original asset record. This was not a trade for a first-round draft pick or a third club's rights. Richardson had just averaged 10.2 points over 72 Knicks appearances in 2008-09, so he was an identifiable NBA wing rather than an unknown prospect. New York took a former high draft choice as a center option; Memphis initially received a player it could either use or move again.

sections.heading: Richardson Never Played for Memphis, but Was Traded for Randolph
sections.body: Richardson did not appear in a Memphis regular-season game. Just 22 days after the original agreement, on July 17, the Grizzlies traded him alone to the Los Angeles Clippers for Zach Randolph. The Clippers' same-day official release identifies precisely that exchange and explicitly traces Richardson's June acquisition from New York for Darko. This is not a speculative multi-player chain: Richardson was the outgoing Memphis player in the separate Randolph trade. The $0 unverified cash figure from June should not be added to Randolph's July cost as if it were another July asset. That distinction matters when measuring the June trade's eventual value. Memphis converted a briefly held wing contract into a franchise-leading power forward without receiving Richardson court minutes first.

sections.heading: Randolph Gave the Grizzlies Eight Seasons of Major Production
sections.body: Randolph played 551 Memphis regular-season games from 2009-10 through 2016-17, averaging 16.8 points and 10.2 rebounds over those eight seasons. He earned All-Star recognition with the Grizzlies and played an important part in the club's 2011 first-round upset of San Antonio and 2013 trip to the Western Conference finals. Those were team achievements with many contributors, not accomplishments created by one June 2009 asset alone. The key documented connection is narrower and stronger: Memphis acquired Richardson from the Knicks, then transferred Richardson for Randolph less than a month later. Randolph's team-specific tenure is therefore traceable downstream asset value rather than a random unrelated future transaction. The separate July exchange is essential context for any meaningful evaluation of the initial draft-night deal.

sections.heading: New York Got Eight Miličić Games and Later Waived Cardinal
sections.body: Miličić appeared in eight Knicks regular-season games in 2009-10, scoring 16 total points in 71 minutes. On February 17, 2010 New York traded him and additional cash to Minnesota for Brian Cardinal. The Knicks then waived Cardinal on February 19, meaning the separate February transaction did not yield a sustained New York rotation player either. Miličić later played 24 Minnesota games in 2009-10 and more seasons for the Timberwolves, but those were Minnesota contributions and cannot be attributed to New York. The source archive retains Memphis B-plus and New York B with the label Slight Grizzlies Edge. Those inherited grades are not a mathematical expression of Randolph's massive downstream advantage; the editorial should acknowledge that contrast instead of calling both direct club returns comparable.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Grizzlies Edge — the source-locked grades remain Memphis B-plus and New York B. Memphis received Quentin Richardson and cash for Miličić, then traded Richardson alone July 17 for Zach Randolph, who played 551 Grizzlies games in eight seasons. New York got eight Darko games and later traded him with cash for Brian Cardinal before a waiver. The inherited one-step grade gap should not be mistaken for the actual scale of Randolph's substantial downstream basketball return.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Memphis Grizzlies–New York Knicks: What the 2009-06-25 Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: Memphis acquired Quentin Richardson and cash from the Knicks for Darko Miličić in June 2009, then traded Richardson alone to the Clippers on July 17 for Zach Randolph. Richardson played no Memphis NBA games, but that July conversion led to 551 Randolph regular-season appearances over eight Grizzlies seasons. New York received eight Miličić appearances and later exchanged him plus cash for Brian Cardinal before a waiver. This review distinguishes both later trades from the original June deal.

sections.heading: Three Original Assets, Not an Incoming Memphis Starter
sections.body: The June 25, 2009 arrangement sent Quentin Richardson and cash to Memphis and Darko Miličić to New York. Team transaction logs from 2008-09 corroborate the direction, while the original cash total remains unspecified. New York sought an opportunity for a center who had been a former second overall pick; Memphis obtained a veteran wing and a financial component. Evaluating the trade from the next season's box score alone would miss the principal Memphis benefit because Richardson never played a Grizzlies regular-season game. The date in Basketball-Reference and the Knicks transactions is June 25; the Grizzlies official historical media guide lists a June 29 processing entry, a documentary date discrepancy rather than evidence of an entirely different player trade. The June draft-night route is preserved pending explicit canonical provenance adjudication.

sections.heading: The July 17 Trade Used Richardson as the Sole Player Sent
sections.body: Memphis held Richardson less than a month. The Clippers announced July 17, 2009 that they had acquired Richardson from the Grizzlies in exchange for Zach Randolph, specifically recalling the original June trade for Miličić. With Richardson the only named Memphis player outgoing in that July exchange, this is a documented downstream conversion of the original wing asset. The cash Memphis received from New York in June was distinct and is not identified as outgoing July consideration. Randolph gave the Grizzlies a new frontcourt focal point immediately, playing 81 regular-season games with 19.8 points and 11.2 rebounds in 2009-10. These facts give the source ledger a concrete basketball outcome and replace generic claims that both clubs merely received short-term interchangeable players.

sections.heading: Randolph's 551 Memphis Games Were a Separate Later Return
sections.body: Randolph ultimately spent eight NBA seasons with the Grizzlies, totaling 551 regular-season games, 16.8 points and 10.2 rebounds per outing. He was an All-Star in Memphis and contributed to multiple playoff runs, including the 2013 Western Conference finals. None of those Memphis games were played by Quentin Richardson, who moved again from the Clippers to Minnesota and later Miami in the same offseason. The distinction between player names and attributable asset value is central here: Richardson did not personally score for Memphis, but the Grizzlies were able to trade his contract directly for Randolph. The July transaction should be linked and dated as a new deal, not rewritten into the original June player exchange or mistaken for an automatic part of the June Knicks trade.

sections.heading: The Knicks' Eight Darko Games Do Not Erase Its Later Exchange
sections.body: New York got eight Miličić regular-season games with no starts in 2009-10, then moved him with cash to Minnesota in February for Brian Cardinal. Cardinal was waived two days later. The outgoing Knicks cash in February is different from the money sent with Richardson in the previous June agreement, and neither amount should be fabricated. Miličić's later 24 Timberwolves games that season and his continuing Minnesota service do not become New York playing production. The retained B grade for the Knicks and B-plus for Memphis, described as Slight Grizzlies Edge, are preexisting editorial labels. The source-specific record reveals a much wider downstream basketball gap because Richardson directly generated the separate Randolph acquisition. Preserving the grade decision should not prevent publishing that verifiable historical distinction.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Memphis B-plus versus New York B retains the earlier Slight Grizzlies Edge grading. The evidence is stronger than that small letter difference implies: the Grizzlies turned Richardson, acquired for Miličić, directly into Zach Randolph in a separate July 17 transaction. New York received only eight Miličić games and no lasting Cardinal return after its February 2010 trade. Cash belonged to both original and later documented transactions, but those payments must not be conflated or given invented figures. The canonical grades are preserved pending separate editorial regrade authority.

sections.heading: The March 15 Deadline Exchange
sections.body: Philadelphia acquired Sam Young from Memphis on March 15, 2012, sending the draft rights to Ricky Sanchez the other way. Young was a 2009 second-round selection already playing NBA minutes; Sanchez, selected in 2005, had yet to establish himself in the league. The 76ers did not receive a draft pick as part of this exchange, and the Grizzlies did not receive a current rotation player. Philadelphia president Rod Thorn described Young as someone who could add depth at two positions, an immediate roster concern for a club preparing for the stretch run. The rights going to Memphis had a different kind of value: they could be held, negotiated or traded, even if Sanchez never appeared in a Grizzlies uniform.

sections.heading: What Young Actually Did in Philadelphia
sections.body: The regular-season result was modest. Young played 14 games for the 76ers, started none, averaged 9.6 minutes and scored 2.9 points per appearance on 29.5 percent shooting. Philadelphia's 2012 playoff run continued into the second round, but Young appeared in just two postseason games for a little more than four combined minutes. Those numbers are essential context for the site's B grade: the acquisition provided an available wing at the deadline, not an established postseason contributor. The team's success that spring can't reasonably be assigned to this one transaction, and the difference between adding depth and receiving valuable on-court production shouldn't disappear in hindsight.

sections.heading: Memphis Eventually Converted the Rights
sections.body: Memphis did not get NBA production from Sanchez, but the acquired rights were not a dead end. On February 21, 2013, the Grizzlies sent them to Miami for Dexter Pittman, a 2013 second-round selection and cash considerations, according to the Heat's own announcement. That later draft pick became the 60th selection, Janis Timma. The 2013 package was a separate trade, nearly a year after Sam Young moved to Philadelphia; its players, cash and pick must not be placed in the original March 2012 asset ledger. Still, the later return is directly traceable to the rights Memphis obtained, and it changes how one evaluates their original usefulness.

sections.heading: How Sam Young's Brief Philadelphia Stay Compares With Memphis's Later Return
sections.body: The 76ers Win verdict grades Philadelphia B and Memphis C-plus, but the receiving-team outcomes are more complicated than a simple current-player-versus-overseas-rights comparison. Young appeared in 14 Philadelphia regular-season games, averaging 2.9 points, and played only a few postseason minutes in 2012. Memphis never received NBA playing time from Ricky Sanchez, yet held a transferable asset. Its separate February 2013 trade with Miami turned Sanchez's rights into Dexter Pittman, a second-round selection and cash. The 2013 selection eventually became No. 60 Janis Timma; Pittman subsequently played seven Grizzlies games before being waived. Young's immediate roster availability supports Philadelphia's favorable evaluation, while the later rights exchange demonstrates that Memphis received more than an unusable placeholder. Neither Pittman nor the draft choice was directly traded by Philadelphia in March 2012, and Philadelphia's playoff success should not be credited to Young's limited minutes.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Published verdict: 76ers Win — Philadelphia B, Memphis C+. Young supplied short-term wing depth but played 14 regular-season games and two brief playoff stints for Philadelphia. Memphis subsequently converted Sanchez's rights into Pittman, a 2013 second-round pick and cash in a separate deal. That downstream return merits a fresh grade review, not a change to the March 2012 asset ledger.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The Sam Young Trade: Two Very Different Returns
featuredDeepDive.intro: The March 2012 exchange looked like a simple forward-for-rights move: Philadelphia wanted Sam Young on its bench, and Memphis accepted the draft rights to Ricky Sanchez. The historical record is more interesting than that shorthand. Young's 76ers stint was brief, while the Sanchez rights became part of a separate 2013 Memphis-Miami transaction. The published Philadelphia B, Memphis C+ verdict stays in place during this examination; the evidence provides grounds to test it rather than rewrite it by assumption.

sections.heading: The Roster Problem Philadelphia Was Addressing
sections.body: At the deadline, Philadelphia had shifted Evan Turner into its starting lineup and relied on Lou Williams and Jodie Meeks for much of its reserve backcourt work. Young offered another guard-forward option. The 76ers had received Sanchez's draft rights from Denver in a 2007 deal involving Reggie Evans, so the organization was giving up a claim it had held for several seasons rather than a player already contributing to Doug Collins's rotation. Rod Thorn's contemporaneous statement framed the transaction as depth at two positions, not an attempt to find a new starter. That helps explain the decision without overstating the immediate effect: acquiring a plausible bench piece can be a reasonable deadline maneuver even if the player ultimately sees few minutes.

sections.heading: Regular Season and Playoffs Tell Different Parts of the Story
sections.body: Young's Philadelphia regular-season line was 14 appearances, zero starts, 135 total minutes and 2.9 points per game. His field-goal percentage in that stint was 29.5. His playoff participation was even more limited: just two appearances, one against Chicago and one against Boston, lasting roughly four minutes in total. The 76ers won a first-round series, but the record does not make Young a meaningful cause of that result. A grade grounded in roster access can acknowledge that he was available; a grade grounded in achieved basketball value must also acknowledge how little the coaching staff ultimately used him. The distinction is especially important when a low-volume acquisition is compared with a tradable contractual right.

sections.heading: How Sanchez's Rights Turned Into a New Package
sections.body: Memphis kept Sanchez's rights until February 21, 2013. Miami then announced that it had sent Dexter Pittman, its 2013 second-round pick and cash to Memphis in exchange for those rights. Basketball-Reference identifies that pick as the 60th overall selection used on Janis Timma. The Grizzlies received assets they could use or move, but their immediate on-court return from Pittman was small. Memphis reported that he totaled two points and five rebounds in 20 minutes across seven games before being waived in April. The subsequent pick and cash are concrete returns connected to the original rights acquisition, but they belong to the 2013 exchange and shouldn't be described as items Philadelphia gave away in March 2012.

sections.heading: What the B and C+ Grades Can Legitimately Support
sections.body: The published 76ers Win verdict judges Philadelphia B and Memphis C+. A contemporary explanation centered on immediate personnel access can support favoring Philadelphia's decision: Young was a rostered NBA forward, whereas Sanchez's career remained outside the league. An outcome-based explanation faces a harder question. Young's contribution was minimal, and Memphis extracted more tangible assets from the rights in 2013, although Pittman did not become a lasting rotation addition. Timma's selection, in particular, is a downstream pick outcome rather than evidence that the Grizzlies drafted him through the 2012 trade itself. A separate grade audit should weigh those later assets before changing the recorded winner; the trade facts and source chain don't justify manufacturing certainty about its final balance.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The recorded result favors Philadelphia B over Memphis C+, but the full timeline calls for scrutiny. Young's 76ers stint was brief, and the rights to Sanchez later brought Memphis Pittman, cash and the pick used on Janis Timma. These were two transactions with different dates. Preserve the original asset lists and flag the historical grade for independent review.

sections.heading: A Conditional Pick for a First-Round Guard
sections.body: Memphis traded Tony Wroten to Philadelphia on August 22, 2013, less than fifteen months after selecting him 25th in the 2012 draft. The Grizzlies received a conditional 2014 second-round draft pick and created a trade exception, as their own later media guide records. Philadelphia took the young guard rather than a guaranteed pick or an established starter. Memphis's acquired selection carried restrictive protection, and the 2014 choice eventually did not convey. The transaction therefore cannot be graded as though Memphis received a 2014 player simply because a second-round pick appeared in the original agreement. The trade exception, though, was also a distinct contractual tool and shouldn't be silently omitted when describing what Memphis obtained.

sections.heading: Wroten Turned into Actual Playing Time
sections.body: Wroten's first season in Philadelphia provides a concrete test of the Sixers' side. He played 72 games in 2013–14, started 16, logged 24.5 minutes per game and scored 13.0 points. He also averaged 3.2 rebounds and 3.0 assists. Those are real rotation minutes that Memphis had not been receiving: Wroten appeared in 35 games and averaged just 7.8 minutes for the Grizzlies as a rookie in 2012–13. The 76ers took a gamble on a 20-year-old who needed space to handle the ball; their own rebuilding season supplied that opportunity. His shooting was uneven, including 21.3 percent from three, but the resulting offensive contribution was more tangible than the conditional pick's final yield.

sections.heading: Memphis Reused the Pick Before It Expired
sections.body: The original selection wasn't simply forgotten until the 2014 draft. A Memphis team release on January 7, 2014 says the Grizzlies sent the Philadelphia 2014 second-round pick obtained in the Wroten trade to Oklahoma City as part of a three-team transaction involving Boston. Memphis received Courtney Lee and a Boston 2016 second-round pick in the larger exchange, while Jerryd Bayless and other considerations also moved between the clubs. That later package cannot be credited to the Wroten pick by itself: multiple assets and teams made the January deal possible. Still, the official description confirms Memphis had a usable conditional right in hand after August, regardless of whether the pick ultimately conveyed to its later holder.

sections.heading: Why Philadelphia Received the More Tangible 2013 Return
sections.body: The 76ers Win verdict grades Philadelphia B and Memphis C-minus. Philadelphia received Tony Wroten, who played 72 games and averaged 13.0 points in his first Sixers season. Memphis obtained a protected 2014 second-round draft right and a trade exception instead of an immediate player. The protection eventually prevented that selection from conveying, even though the Grizzlies included the conditional right in their separate January 2014 multi-team Courtney Lee transaction. Lee came from Boston in that later deal, not directly from Philadelphia in August 2013. The Grizzlies' trade exception was an additional tool, but its value cannot be equated with a cash payment or a player contribution without independent use records. The existing grade gap follows Wroten's actual Philadelphia production and the much more uncertain Memphis return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Published verdict: 76ers Win — Philadelphia B, Memphis C-. Wroten played 72 Philadelphia games in 2013–14 and averaged 13.0 points. Memphis obtained a conditional 2014 second-round right, later included in a January 2014 three-team deal, plus a trade exception. The original pick did not convey; preserve the full chain and grades until the remaining exception value is verified.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: How the Tony Wroten Rights Deal Played Out
featuredDeepDive.intro: Philadelphia acquired a 2012 first-round selection who had barely played in Memphis. The cost was a conditional 2014 second-round pick and the trade exception Memphis recorded in its official history. The 76ers eventually received substantial rotation minutes from Tony Wroten; the Grizzlies transferred the draft right onward before it expired. The distinction between a contingent trade-day asset and a realized draft selection is central to reading this deal.

sections.heading: Why the Teams Saw Wroten Differently
sections.body: The Grizzlies used the 25th choice in the 2012 NBA draft on Wroten but played him for a total of 272 regular-season minutes in 2012–13. His 35 appearances, 2.6 points and 1.2 assists per game were a thin basis for expecting near-term contributions on a veteran Memphis roster. Philadelphia, by contrast, was entering a rebuilding year and could offer a young guard significantly more responsibility. By October, the 76ers exercised their 2014–15 team option. During the 2013–14 season he appeared 72 times with 16 starts. That roster context explains why a player with uncertain shooting could be a useful bet for one franchise and a movable asset for the other.

sections.heading: The Sixers Received More Than a Prospect Listing
sections.body: Wroten averaged 24.5 minutes, 13.0 points, 3.2 rebounds and 3.0 assists for Philadelphia in 2013–14. His .427 field-goal percentage and .213 three-point accuracy illustrate the limits of that production. He also played in 30 games and averaged 16.9 points during an injury-affected 2014–15 season before his Sixers stint dwindled to eight appearances in 2015–16. These are identifiable returns to Philadelphia directly resulting from the August 2013 acquisition. The organization did not merely retain draft rights or a contract option; it received a guard it deployed extensively during a rebuilding phase, although not one who became an enduring star.

sections.heading: A Conditional Selection Entered the Courtney Lee Trade
sections.body: Memphis's own January 7, 2014 announcement identifies the Philadelphia 2014 second-round selection acquired for Wroten as one asset the Grizzlies subsequently sent to Oklahoma City. The same release describes a much larger three-team exchange that brought Courtney Lee and a Boston 2016 second-round pick to Memphis, with Bayless moving to Boston and separate considerations involving the Thunder. The 2014 Philadelphia selection later did not convey, according to both teams' season transaction histories. This sequence establishes transferability and eventual non-conveyance, not that Wroten alone bought Lee. The contractual trade exception from the original move should be tracked separately, rather than being conflated with either draft asset in the later deal.

sections.heading: Grading the Deal Without Inflating Either Side
sections.body: Philadelphia's B and Memphis's C- in the published archive reflect a substantial advantage for the team that obtained Wroten. A hindsight argument for Philadelphia has an unusually direct foundation: a young guard acquired in August gave the club 72 appearances and double-digit scoring in the next season. The Grizzlies instead acquired a protected second-round claim that could be traded onward but never matured into a 2014 draft selection, plus an exception that the current source set does not value independently. Neither the Wroten pick's presence in the 2014 Courtney Lee package nor Memphis's eventual on-court success permits attributing an entire unrelated team's assets to this transaction. The archive can keep its existing verdict while ensuring the reader sees both the documented playing output and the contingent nature of the outgoing consideration.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The sourced outcome favors Philadelphia's realized Wroten minutes over the conditional 2014 second-round claim, which Memphis later moved and which did not convey. Memphis also created a trade exception. The archive's B/C- grades and 76ers Win label are preserved; any grading adjustment should assess the exception independently and avoid crediting the entire subsequent Courtney Lee exchange to one pick.

sections.heading: Memphis Moved a Future Second to Obtain Jarnell Stokes
sections.body: At the June 26, 2014 NBA Draft, Utah chose Tennessee forward Jarnell Stokes No. 35 and moved his draft rights to Memphis. The Jazz received a 2016 second-round pick described in the transaction ledger as the more favorable of Boston and Toronto selections. The pick ultimately resolved to No. 52, used on Joel Bolomboy. Memphis gained a frontcourt prospect after Stokes had become an All-SEC player at Tennessee; Utah deferred its return by two draft classes. The agreement exchanged rights and a future selection, not a proven starter or immediate cash consideration.

sections.heading: Stokes Appeared in 21 Memphis Games across Two Seasons
sections.body: Stokes played 19 regular-season Memphis games as a rookie in 2014-15, starting twice and averaging 3.0 points and 1.8 rebounds over 6.6 minutes. He added only two Grizzlies games in 2015-16, neither as a starter, before his career continued elsewhere. That totals 21 Memphis appearances and two starts directly derived from the acquired rights. The short sample is useful evidence about the trade return: he did make the NBA and give the Grizzlies reserve minutes, but never developed into a durable Memphis rotation contributor. His later five Miami and two Denver NBA appearances should not be added to his Memphis total.

sections.heading: Utah Received Pick 52 and Twelve Bolomboy Games
sections.body: The Utah side ultimately became the No. 52 selection in the 2016 draft, used on Weber State forward Joel Bolomboy. A Utah Jazz October 2017 release confirms Bolomboy appeared in 12 NBA games for the franchise during 2016-17, averaging 1.8 points and 1.4 rebounds in 4.4 minutes. Bolomboy also played extensively on assignment with Salt Lake City in the G League, which is not equivalent to NBA games. Utah waived him in October 2017. The future pick was real draft flexibility, but its direct NBA court return also stayed limited. His later Milwaukee NBA games were not Utah receiving-team production.

sections.heading: Why the Stokes and Bolomboy Returns Were Both Limited
sections.body: The Even Trade verdict gives Memphis and Utah C grades. Utah drafted Tennessee forward Jarnell Stokes at No. 35 in 2014 and immediately sent his rights to Memphis for a future 2016 second-round pick, as the Grizzlies' original announcement confirms. Stokes appeared in 19 Memphis games in 2014-15 and two more in 2015-16, making only two starts across that span before moving to Miami in a separate transaction. Utah eventually used the later selection at No. 52 in 2016 on Joel Bolomboy, whose NBA return to the Jazz was 12 regular-season appearances. Stokes played additional games elsewhere and Bolomboy spent time developing in the G League; neither contribution should inflate the NBA games received directly by the two clubs. Memphis obtained an immediate prospect, while Utah took a longer-term draft option, but neither generated sustained NBA rotation production for its receiving team. The matching grades capture those modest, differently timed returns rather than a claim that the future pick itself was worthless.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade with two C grades is preserved. Stokes supplied 21 Memphis regular-season games and two starts; the 2016 second transferred to Utah ultimately became No. 52 Joel Bolomboy, who logged 12 NBA games for the Jazz. Neither young player developed into a long-term receiving-team NBA rotation piece, and G League minutes or later franchises should not inflate the comparison.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The 2014 Stokes Rights Swap: 21 Memphis Games for the Bolomboy Pick
featuredDeepDive.intro: Memphis secured Jarnell Stokes’s No. 35 rights from Utah in the 2014 NBA Draft for a 2016 second-round selection. Stokes played 21 NBA games across parts of two seasons for the Grizzlies, while the future choice became No. 52 Joel Bolomboy, who appeared in 12 Utah NBA games. The saved Even Trade and two C grades recognize modest returns with different timing. Later NBA teams and Utah’s Salt Lake City G League affiliate are not counted as receiving-team NBA production.

sections.heading: The 2014 Agreement Was a Rights-for-Future-Selection Bet
sections.body: Utah used No. 35 on Tennessee power forward Jarnell Stokes and sent the rights to the Memphis Grizzlies. The Jazz received a 2016 second-round choice with a more-favorable-of condition involving Boston and Toronto picks. The two clubs therefore valued different timing: Memphis wanted a young frontcourt player immediately, while Utah added a future draft opportunity. The source asset ledger and draft histories preserve that distinction. The future pick did not entitle Utah to the eventual NBA career of every second-rounder or to any player selected by Memphis elsewhere in 2014.

sections.heading: Stokes Logged 19 Rookie Games and Two Final Memphis Appearances
sections.body: The Basketball Reference team splits show Stokes playing 19 games with Memphis in 2014-15 and starting two, averaging 3.0 points and 1.8 rebounds in 6.6 minutes. He appeared twice more for the Grizzlies in 2015-16 without a start, then moved to Miami. His total Memphis contribution from the acquired rights was 21 NBA regular-season games. He made his NBA debut in November 2014, which establishes real immediate opportunity, but his playing role never expanded into a large Memphis share. His NBA career later included two Denver appearances that also belong outside this trade’s team accounting.

sections.heading: Bolomboy Played Twelve Utah NBA Games and Spent Time in the G League
sections.body: The Jazz used the eventual 2016 No. 52 selection on Joel Bolomboy. Utah’s own release at his October 2017 waiver confirms 12 regular-season NBA games and averages of 1.8 points and 1.4 rebounds. He also appeared in 24 G League games for the Salt Lake City Stars, 22 as a starter, where he averaged 16.4 points and 13.2 rebounds. Those developmental numbers show what Utah hoped to cultivate, but the G League season is not interchangeable with the Jazz’s NBA appearance record. He later joined the Milwaukee organization; that separate period cannot be credited as Utah production.

sections.heading: An Even Grade without Retroactively Valuing Other Drafts
sections.body: The relative return is close at the level of limited on-court opportunities: Stokes gave Memphis 21 games, Bolomboy Utah 12. Memphis received its athlete sooner, while Utah held the future pick through 2016 and saw Bolomboy perform in its developmental affiliate before a 2017 waiver. The historical record does not support awarding either franchise a championship, an All-Star or a major rotation role from these assets. Treating all later contracts as if they flowed directly through the 2014 agreement would distort the modest purpose and output of a second-round rights exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Memphis C, Utah C and Even Trade remain the original judgment. Stokes produced 21 Memphis NBA games across 2014-16, with two starts, and Bolomboy played 12 for Utah after the acquired 2016 second became No. 52. The Jazz also developed Bolomboy in the G League, but those were not NBA starts or minutes. Both clubs received limited value and then moved on.

sections.heading: Memphis Acquired Ridnour While Orlando Took Draft Rights
sections.body: The Grizzlies received veteran guard Luke Ridnour from Orlando on June 24, 2015, sending the draft rights to Janis Timma in return. Ridnour had years of NBA backcourt experience, so the immediate value of his contract was easier to assess than that of international rights. Orlando, by contrast, acquired the opportunity to retain a claim on a player whose future NBA availability and fit were uncertain.

sections.heading: The Rights and the Veteran Served Different Timelines
sections.body: Ridnour’s presence in the transaction does not by itself establish a lasting Grizzlies rotation role. Memphis was operating through a busy 2015 offseason; holding the guard’s rights and actually receiving months of production are different outcomes. Orlando held an asset that could be revisited later without committing an NBA roster spot immediately. Timma’s rights were meaningful consideration, but the source ledger does not demonstrate a comparable direct NBA contribution for the Magic.

sections.heading: Why Both Clubs Finish With a C
sections.body: Memphis and Orlando each receive C in the canonical record. Memphis acquired a recognizable veteran but did not obtain a documented long-term starter from this specific trade. Orlando collected rights with developmental potential but without a proven immediate NBA return. Assigning a dramatic winner would overvalue one side’s status as an experienced player or the other’s speculative international rights. The limited realized returns support the equal grade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Memphis C, Orlando C. The Grizzlies took Luke Ridnour’s contract rights in exchange for the NBA rights to Janis Timma. Ridnour’s experience and Timma’s overseas-rights potential had different timelines, but neither side can claim a documented, decisive long-term return from this transaction.

sections.heading: July 23: Orlando Traded Johnson and Harvey Rights for Martin
sections.body: On July 23, 2018, Memphis sent forward Jarell Martin and cash to Orlando, receiving center Dakari Johnson and the NBA draft rights to guard Tyler Harvey. The NBA's summer transaction tracker and official Orlando media guide confirm the complete package. Johnson had arrived with the Magic only three days earlier in a separate trade with Oklahoma City for Rodney Purvis, so that Oklahoma City transaction should not be collapsed into Memphis's later deal. Harvey was selected by Orlando at No. 51 in the 2015 draft, but had played overseas rather than for its NBA rotation. Memphis acquired a center prospect and a contractual option, while Orlando selected an already experienced NBA reserve forward together with financial consideration.

sections.heading: Orlando Played Martin in Forty-Two Games, Not His Memphis Career
sections.body: Martin had played 142 NBA regular-season games across three earlier Memphis seasons, including 73 games in 2017-18. Those were Grizzlies contributions before the deal, not a new Magic return. In Orlando during 2018-19, he appeared in 42 NBA regular-season games, starting one, and averaged 2.7 points and 1.7 rebounds over 7.8 minutes per appearance. That was limited playing time but still 328 actual Magic minutes, an important difference from a player whose contract never reaches the court. His ability to serve as frontcourt depth gave Orlando some benefit during its return to the playoffs. The inherited B Magic grade should be evaluated against these modest numbers and the incoming cash, not Martin's previous full career statistics.

sections.heading: Memphis Waived Johnson in August Before an NBA Game
sections.body: The Grizzlies acquired Johnson on July 23 and waived him on August 31, 2018. The club's official dated announcement confirms both the acquisition and waiver, and Johnson appeared in no NBA regular-season games for Memphis between those dates. He had played 31 Oklahoma City Thunder games as a rookie in 2017-18, but assigning any of those to Memphis would be incorrect. Orlando had briefly acquired him from the Thunder on July 20 and moved him on just three days later. The Memphis direct on-court result of this portion of the trade was therefore zero, even though the center was a real contractual acquisition. The stored Grizzlies B-minus cannot be justified by future Memphis games that Johnson never supplied.

sections.heading: Harvey's Draft Rights Were a Possibility, Not NBA Minutes
sections.body: The other Memphis asset was Tyler Harvey's NBA draft rights. Orlando had originally drafted him in the second round in 2015; by July 2018 he was playing professional basketball overseas. He did not enter the Memphis NBA regular-season lineup through this transaction. Draft rights can represent a potential future signing or trade, but they are different from acquiring an active NBA roster contributor. Memphis surrendered Martin and cash for Johnson and Harvey rights, then waived Johnson before opening night. Orlando received 42 Martin appearances and financial compensation. The existing Slight Magic Edge, Orlando B and Memphis B-minus describes a narrow inherited comparison, although the direct playing returns strongly favor Orlando. The separate cash amount should not be invented if only the asset type is locked in the original ledger.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Magic Edge — Orlando B, Memphis B-minus. Martin appeared in 42 Magic NBA games with one start during 2018-19, averaging 2.7 points and 1.7 rebounds; Orlando also received cash. Memphis obtained Johnson and Harvey rights, but waived Johnson on August 31 before he played a regular-season game for the club. Neither his earlier Oklahoma City appearances nor Harvey's overseas career counted as Memphis NBA on-court return.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Memphis Grizzlies–Orlando Magic: What the 2018-07-23 Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: Orlando sent Dakari Johnson and Tyler Harvey's draft rights to Memphis on July 23, 2018 for Jarell Martin and cash. Johnson had arrived from Oklahoma City three days earlier; Memphis waived him August 31 without an NBA appearance. Martin played 42 Magic regular-season games in 2018-19, while Harvey's draft rights never supplied Memphis NBA minutes. These outcomes underpin the existing Orlando B/Memphis B-minus and Slight Magic Edge grading without borrowing players' earlier statistics.

sections.heading: Johnson Had Changed Teams Three Days Before This Deal
sections.body: The timeline is unusually important for a minor summer NBA exchange. Orlando acquired Dakari Johnson from Oklahoma City on July 20, 2018 for Rodney Purvis and then transferred Johnson to Memphis on July 23 with Tyler Harvey's draft rights for Jarell Martin and cash. These were two separately documented transactions, involving different counterparties. Johnson's previous 31 NBA games belonged to the Thunder, where he averaged 1.8 points and 1.1 rebounds in 2017-18. Martin had likewise produced his more substantial pre-trade figures with the Grizzlies, not Orlando. The new exchange gave Memphis a look at a center with limited experience and preserved international guard rights, while the Magic obtained a reserve big forward and cash.

sections.heading: Orlando Acquired Forty-Two Games of Forward Depth
sections.body: In 2018-19, Martin gave the Magic 42 regular-season appearances, one start and 328 total minutes. His 2.7 points and 1.7 rebounds per game were modest but genuine contributions for the club receiving him from Memphis. Orlando had watched him average 7.7 points in 73 Memphis games the year before, but his Magic playing role proved considerably smaller. That contrast belongs in the evaluation: the organization got a player who could fill reserve minutes, not a reliable nightly starter. Cash consideration was also supplied by Memphis, though the local trade ledger does not retain a verified figure. Later Martin NBA transactions or overseas seasons do not alter those direct 42 Orlando appearances.

sections.heading: The Grizzlies Got Rights and Waived the Incoming Center
sections.body: Memphis received two different types of optionality: Johnson's NBA contract and the draft rights to Harvey. Neither produced a Grizzlies NBA regular-season appearance after this deal. The official August 31, 2018 Grizzlies waiver of Johnson shows that the center experiment ended before his debut for Memphis. Harvey remained a professional guard overseas and was not an on-court Memphis replacement for Martin. A draft-rights asset may have theoretical transfer value, but no verified later NBA player or pick conversion should be invented when the source record documents only rights ownership. This distinction also avoids double-counting Johnson's six earlier Oklahoma City starts and Harvey's non-NBA games as Memphis regular-season production.

sections.heading: Why the B-to-B-Minus Edge Is Not a Player-Value Tie
sections.body: The source archive calls this a Slight Magic Edge, Orlando B and Memphis B-minus. Orlando obtained 42 Martin regular-season games plus cash, while Memphis got an unused Johnson contract and Harvey rights, without direct NBA court time from either. The players' past service in Memphis or Oklahoma City does not follow them into the receiving clubs' statistics. This supports at least a directionally favorable Orlando verdict, but the narrow inherited grading is a discretionary assessment rather than a verified quantitative performance formula. Both teams may also have had salary and roster-management goals that the available sources do not fully price. The editorial should name the confirmed on-court discrepancy and avoid claiming an unverified long-term payoff for the Memphis rights.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The original slight Orlando advantage, B against Memphis B-minus, is preserved with a more concrete explanation. Martin supplied 42 Magic regular-season appearances and Memphis paid cash, while Johnson left the Grizzlies before an NBA appearance and Harvey supplied draft rights rather than direct player service. Johnson's July 20 Thunder-to-Magic exchange was separate from the July 23 Memphis deal. The inherited letter difference does not mean the two teams got equal NBA playing minutes.

sections.heading: Memphis Acquired Holiday for a Short-Term Wing Role
sections.body: In January 2019, Memphis obtained Justin Holiday from Chicago. The Bulls took MarShon Brooks, Wayne Selden Jr. and two second-round picks: No. 38 Daniel Gafford in 2019 and No. 44 Marko Simonović in 2020. The transaction was a straightforward difference in priorities. Memphis wanted a veteran to fill a rotation need, while Chicago traded an expiring player for several assets with a longer development timeline.

sections.heading: The Gafford Pick Became Chicago’s Best Return
sections.body: Gafford developed into a credible NBA center after the Bulls selected him with the acquired second-rounder. That is the clearest positive outcome produced by Chicago’s incoming package, even though some of his later career success came with other teams. Selden and Brooks were lesser components. Simonović’s NBA impact was limited, so the case for Chicago rests principally on the productive draft pick and the fact that it obtained multiple chances to improve its roster.

sections.heading: Holiday Was Useful but His Memphis Stay Was Brief
sections.body: Holiday provided an experienced wing option who could contribute immediately. Memphis did not, however, turn that rental-length contribution into the sort of postseason run that would justify sacrificing two shots at future players. The Grizzlies were trying to compete around an aging core; Chicago had more reason to prioritize development. Holiday’s value should be acknowledged as genuine rather than erased because the draft outcome ultimately favored the Bulls.

sections.heading: The Draft Outcome Explains the Grade Gap
sections.body: Chicago receives an A for converting a short-term veteran into Gafford, another pick and salary-filling players. Memphis gets C-minus because Holiday’s on-court return was brief relative to the two selections sent out. This is not a retrospective judgment that Memphis should have known Gafford’s name on the trade date. The concrete result is that one of Chicago’s acquired picks produced a durable NBA contributor while the Grizzlies received less sustained value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win — Chicago A, Memphis C-minus. The No. 38 pick turned into Daniel Gafford, an NBA rotation center, making Chicago’s return more durable than Memphis’s brief Justin Holiday rental. The second selection and incoming players added modest optionality; the central grade difference comes from the realized value of Gafford versus Holiday’s short stay.

sections.heading: Marc Gasol / Jonas Valanciunas, Delon Wright, C.J. Miles and a second-round pick: The Deal’s Actual Shape
sections.body: At the 2019 deadline, Toronto sent Jonas Valanciunas, Delon Wright, C.J. Miles and a 2024 second-round pick to Memphis for Marc Gasol. The Raptors were already a contender after acquiring Kawhi Leonard, but they needed a center who could defend elite post scorers, organize the defense and make rapid decisions from the elbows. Memphis was ending the Core Four era and sought younger, controllable players rather than forcing Gasol through a transition. The exchange therefore matched two different timelines: Toronto purchased immediate championship utility, while Memphis converted an aging star into a starting center, a guard prospect, salary structure and future draft value.

sections.heading: Marc Gasol / Jonas Valanciunas, Delon Wright, C.J. Miles and a second-round pick: The Winning Team’s Case
sections.body: Gasol’s value appeared most clearly in the playoffs. He helped neutralize Nikola Vucevic in the first round, absorbed difficult minutes against Joel Embiid and gave Toronto a disciplined back-line defender against Milwaukee and Golden State. Offensively, his passing allowed the Raptors to move the ball through pressure without asking him to score like a traditional star. Toronto already possessed elite wings and guards; it needed a center whose intelligence raised the entire structure. Gasol delivered that fit immediately and remained under control for the following season. A trade that fills a specific weakness and helps produce a championship deserves the highest grade even when the outgoing package is substantial.

sections.heading: Marc Gasol / Jonas Valanciunas, Delon Wright, C.J. Miles and a second-round pick: The Return Package Deserves a Fair Reading
sections.body: Memphis received a legitimate starting center rather than a collection of distant possibilities. Valanciunas produced efficient scoring and rebounding, gave the rebuilding roster a reliable interior option and later became part of the transaction that brought Steven Adams and draft movement. Wright supplied useful two-way guard minutes before being moved, Miles provided salary matching and veteran depth, and the second-round pick remained an additional asset. The Grizzlies did not replace Gasol’s franchise legacy, but that was not the realistic objective. They turned a thirty-four-year-old center approaching a new phase of his career into several seasons of production and further optionality, which supports an A- grade.

sections.heading: Marc Gasol / Jonas Valanciunas, Delon Wright, C.J. Miles and a second-round pick: Leverage and Timing Changed the Price
sections.body: Toronto’s risk was meaningful because Valanciunas was younger, productive and under control, while Gasol carried a large salary and was already past his statistical peak. The Raptors were also making the trade without certainty that Leonard would stay beyond the season. Memphis faced a different pressure: keeping Gasol could have preserved sentiment but reduced the chance to recover value before age and contract status narrowed the market. The deal was not an obvious bargain at the moment it occurred. Toronto won because the fit proved exact and the championship window converted immediately, not because Memphis ignored an obvious alternative or surrendered its star for nothing.

sections.heading: Marc Gasol / Jonas Valanciunas, Delon Wright, C.J. Miles and a second-round pick: Asset Conversion and Opportunity Cost
sections.body: The direct trade details give Toronto the singular highest-value outcome: a championship in Gasol’s first months. Memphis accumulated more years of regular-season production through Valanciunas and later transactions, which is why the Grizzlies remain near the top of the scale. The 2024 second-round pick eventually became another movable draft asset, while Wright’s value was not lost immediately. Still, no downstream chain from the Memphis package produced a result equivalent to Gasol’s role on a title team. This is a case where duration and quantity keep the losing side strong, but a concentrated postseason payoff creates decisive separation at the top.

sections.heading: Marc Gasol / Jonas Valanciunas, Delon Wright, C.J. Miles and a second-round pick: Verdict and grading scale
sections.body: The old Even Trade label was understandable because Memphis received a productive package and Toronto’s control was short. A completed retrospective should nevertheless name Toronto as the winner. The Raptors acquired a starting center whose defense and passing were central to the first championship in franchise history, and that result is the highest possible conversion of trade value. Memphis stays at A- because Valanciunas and the accompanying assets advanced a rebuild rather than collapsing into dead value. Toronto moves to A+ and Raptors Win because the deal’s purpose was immediate contention, and the team achieved exactly that outcome.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Toronto wins because Marc Gasol’s defense, passing and matchup value helped produce the 2019 championship immediately. Memphis still earns A- for Jonas Valanciunas, Delon Wright and continued asset conversion, but the Raptors achieved the transaction’s highest possible competitive outcome.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: How Marc Gasol / Jonas Valanciunas, Delon Wright, C.J. Miles and a second-round pick Changed Two Franchise Timelines
featuredDeepDive.intro: Toronto's February 2019 acquisition of Marc Gasol sent Jonas Valanciunas, Delon Wright, C.J. Miles and a second-round pick to Memphis. Gasol's positioning and passing helped the Raptors handle Joel Embiid and other difficult playoff matchups en route to the championship. Valanciunas supplied Memphis with a younger productive scorer and rebounder across multiple seasons. The exchange put a short, realized title opportunity opposite a longer rebuilding asset chain, and neither side's direct return should be confused with its players' later careers elsewhere.

sections.heading: Gasol's Playoff Defense Met Toronto's Need; Valanciunas Brought Memphis Production
sections.body: Gasol’s Toronto peak was not defined by scoring totals. His best value came from defensive positioning, communication, post resistance, screening and passing that connected lineups around Leonard, Pascal Siakam and Kyle Lowry. Valanciunas delivered the stronger individual box-score production after the trade, especially as a scorer and rebounder in Memphis. The distinction is role leverage. Gasol’s specialized skills solved playoff matchups at the highest level, while Valanciunas supplied more regular-season volume over a longer period. Both peaks were valuable, but Gasol’s was attached directly to four winning playoff series and a championship.

sections.heading: Marc Gasol / Jonas Valanciunas, Delon Wright, C.J. Miles and a second-round pick: Control and Durability
sections.body: Memphis controlled Valanciunas for multiple productive seasons and then used him in another roster transaction, extending the asset chain beyond the initial trade. Toronto controlled Gasol through the championship run and the next season, after which he left in free agency. Ordinarily that control gap would push the verdict toward Memphis. The title changes the weighting because Toronto bought a short window intentionally and fully realized it. Long control is valuable when it produces useful seasons and future assets; short control can be more valuable when it supplies the missing piece of a champion. The grades recognize both forms without treating years alone as the deciding metric.

sections.heading: Marc Gasol / Jonas Valanciunas, Delon Wright, C.J. Miles and a second-round pick: Postseason Translation
sections.body: The postseason is the cleanest source of separation. Gasol started throughout Toronto’s 2019 run and handled assignments that had previously created problems for the roster. His defense against Embiid and his ability to function within switching and help schemes allowed the Raptors to preserve lineups without sacrificing offensive organization. Valanciunas did not receive the same immediate postseason platform in Memphis, though that reflects the team’s rebuilding stage as much as his quality. Toronto’s A+ is not a blanket championship bonus; it reflects that Gasol’s particular skills were repeatedly used in high-leverage series and were essential to the team’s defensive identity.

sections.heading: Marc Gasol / Jonas Valanciunas, Delon Wright, C.J. Miles and a second-round pick: The Best Counterfactual
sections.body: Toronto could have kept Valanciunas and hoped its existing center rotation was sufficient. That choice would have preserved youth and scoring but left more uncertainty in matchups against Embiid, Milwaukee’s size and Golden State’s movement. Memphis could have retained Gasol through the season, yet a later market may have offered less control and fewer useful players. The actual exchange gave each team a logical path. The Raptors’ counterfactual carries the greater competitive cost because the title margin was narrow and Gasol’s fit was unusually specific. Memphis’s package was strong enough to make the sale prudent even though Toronto ultimately captured the larger outcome.

sections.heading: Marc Gasol / Jonas Valanciunas, Delon Wright, C.J. Miles and a second-round pick: Legacy and Final Accounting
sections.body: The trade became the final major roster adjustment before Toronto’s championship and the formal closing chapter of Gasol’s Memphis era. For the Raptors, it symbolizes a front office willing to exchange future value for a precise postseason need. For the Grizzlies, it represents a respectful and productive transition from the Grit and Grind core into a younger roster. Valanciunas became a popular, effective center, and Gasol immediately reached the stage Memphis had never quite reached with him. The final accounting is not a condemnation of either side. It is a Raptors win built on an excellent Grizzlies return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Toronto treated the deadline as an opportunity to resolve a specific playoff matchup need rather than add another volume scorer. Gasol's defensive positioning and passing fit the 2019 Raptors' championship run immediately, a realized outcome that differs from projecting what Memphis might eventually do with the return. Valanciunas offered the Grizzlies a productive younger center, Wright supplied guard depth, and the larger package created further asset options. The A- for Memphis is not a judgment that those assets were poor; it reflects a rebuilding benefit on a different timetable. Toronto's edge rests on a documented title earned that spring, not on crediting Gasol with every part of the Raptors' championship.

sections.heading: The July 2019 Deal Was a Cost and Roster Decision
sections.body: Memphis traded C.J. Miles to Washington for Dwight Howard on July 6, 2019. The Grizzlies' official release confirms a direct veteran-for-veteran exchange, while contemporary reporting explains a financial purpose: Memphis reduced its salary obligations by roughly $3.1 million and intended to waive or trade Howard rather than use him as its starting center. Washington wanted a wing whose long shooting career might address the roster's spacing needs. The site ledger also associates a traded-player exception with the Memphis side, but that mechanism should not be presented as an actual new basketball player or a pick. Howard had appeared in nine games for Washington the previous season before back surgery. The transaction is best understood as a financially motivated move by Memphis and a speculative veteran shooting acquisition by Washington, not a race between two stars providing on-court return.

sections.heading: Memphis Released Howard Before He Played a Game
sections.body: Memphis never used Howard in an NBA regular-season game. The organization officially waived the center on August 24, 2019, just seven weeks after announcing his acquisition. Howard later joined the Los Angeles Lakers and helped them win the 2020 championship, but that production and title did not accrue to the Grizzlies. Counting his subsequent Lakers season as evidence of a Memphis basketball win would be an asset-attribution error. The Grizzlies' actual gains were primarily salary relief and any separately documented exception created by the differing veteran contracts. Howard's illustrious earlier Orlando and Houston years also are not Grizzlies production. A source-led history can retain the published Memphis A grade while explaining that its justification is financial roster flexibility rather than games, rebounds or blocked shots in a Memphis uniform.

sections.heading: Washington Received Ten C.J. Miles Games Before Injury
sections.body: The Wizards did obtain a real player contribution, although it was brief. Miles appeared in 10 Washington regular-season games in 2019-20, averaging 6.4 points and 1.2 assists in 16.1 minutes. His season ended after a wrist injury suffered November 26 at Denver, and the club waived him on January 12, 2020. Washington's official release confirms the 10-game figure and injury details. The original acquisition was understandable as the team sought experienced three-point shooting, but the resulting availability fell well short of a full-season rotation solution. The Wizards' C-minus grade is therefore grounded in a small completed on-court return rather than an entirely vacant asset. Miles's 13 Memphis appearances before the trade belong to the Grizzlies' previous season and should not be added to his post-trade Washington totals.

sections.heading: The Grade Gap Depends on How Salary Flexibility Is Valued
sections.body: The preserved ledger calls the deal Grizzlies Win, Memphis A and Washington C-minus. That pairing is difficult to explain by comparing basketball minutes because the Memphis incoming center played zero games while Washington received 10 Miles appearances. The Grizzlies instead freed roughly $3.1 million in salary commitments by substituting Howard's lower salary for Miles's contract, then waived Howard. Washington accepted more salary and obtained only a short-lived shooting option. Those are reasonable reasons to favor Memphis's front-office objective, but they do not mean Howard became a Memphis All-Star or produced a valuable set of draft assets. The grade should be read as a judgment about avoided costs and optionality, not as a traditional player-value victory. The exception recorded in the ledger should also remain distinct from confirmed use in a later transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Grizzlies Win — Memphis A, Washington C- in the preserved grade ledger. Memphis waived Howard August 24, 2019 before any regular-season games and reportedly saved roughly $3.1 million in salary. Washington used Miles for 10 games before a season-ending wrist injury. Memphis's A must reflect payroll flexibility, not Howard playing production or his later Lakers championship.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Dwight Howard and C.J. Miles in July 2019: Memphis Salary Savings
featuredDeepDive.intro: Memphis traded Miles for Howard and waived the center before he played for the Grizzlies. Washington received 10 Miles games before injury. The difference lay in Memphis salary relief rather than a star center contributing on court.

sections.heading: Memphis Was Remodeling Around Morant, Not Dwight Howard
sections.body: The Grizzlies made the Howard exchange during the summer they drafted Ja Morant second overall, hired Taylor Jenkins and reorganized their veteran contracts. Miles was a 32-year-old wing who had played 13 Memphis games after arriving in February, while Howard was a former All-Star center recovering from back surgery. Contemporary reporting said Memphis expected to waive or move him and would save about $3.1 million in the process. That context is a stronger explanation of the deal than pretending Memphis had pursued Howard as a long-term center alongside its young guards. When Howard was waived on August 24, the playing return was exactly zero. The franchise had changed its payroll situation, not added a contributing star. The trade needs a financial accounting rather than a fictional Howard box-score narrative.

sections.heading: Howard's Lakers Championship Is Outside the Memphis Ledger
sections.body: After Memphis waived Howard, he joined the Los Angeles Lakers for the 2019-20 season and later won his first NBA championship there. His Lakers minutes were a consequence of a separate free-agent arrangement, not something the Grizzlies received in exchange for C.J. Miles. It would be especially misleading to cite that championship when defending the preserved Memphis A grade. The original deal gave Memphis a lower-cost contract it could waive and any resulting cap or trade-exception flexibility. Those benefits have organizational value even without on-court scoring or rebounding. Howard's older Orlando awards and Washington's nine-game 2018-19 stint are equally separate from his post-transaction Memphis return. This distinction prevents historical name recognition from inflating the apparent size of a modest July 2019 salary move.

sections.heading: Washington's Miles Plan Ended With a Wrist Injury
sections.body: Washington acquired Miles after Howard had missed most of 2018-19 with a back injury, hoping the veteran wing would supply shooting and professional leadership. The Wizards' official July 6 announcement explicitly emphasizes his long-range play. He returned from a separate preseason foot problem to play 10 regular-season games, but a wrist injury late in November ended his campaign. The team waived him in January 2020, citing 6.4 points and 1.2 assists over 16.1 minutes per appearance. The ten games are a concrete NBA return, and it is important not to treat the absence of a lasting role as proof that Washington received no player. At the same time, his availability fell far short of the intended season-long perimeter support. The C-minus grade captures that disappointing result without asserting that he was ineffective in every minute he played.

sections.heading: Why the Existing Grizzlies A Is About Payroll Rather Than Production
sections.body: The site's inherited result is Grizzlies Win, with an A for Memphis and C-minus for Washington. Direct games played would not support that large advantage: Howard played none for Memphis, and Miles played ten for Washington. The plausible Memphis case is instead financial, based on reducing salary commitments by about $3.1 million and freeing a veteran roster spot while rebuilding. The traded-player exception in the canonical entry is a financial instrument, not a drafted player or an established additional acquisition, and no later roster value should be invented without a proven transaction chain. Washington received a possible shooter but only brief availability before injury and release. Leaving the historical grades unchanged is possible if their rationale is described accurately as a cap-management decision, with the limitations explicit. That approach makes the verdict open to scrutiny instead of relying on generic winner language.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Memphis A, Washington C- in the inherited Grizzlies Win record. The club acquired and waived Howard without a single Memphis game, saving salary and retaining roster flexibility. Washington got 10 Miles appearances before waiving him in January 2020. The traded-player exception is financial optionality, not a player or confirmed later return.
