sections.heading: Minnesota Bought the Exact Skill Kevin Garnett Lacked
sections.body: Before the summer of 2003, Minnesota had reached the playoffs seven straight times and lost in the opening round every year. Kevin Garnett could create, defend and carry enormous responsibility, but the roster still lacked a veteran guard who could organize late possessions and punish defenses when playoff games slowed down. Sam Cassell arrived with two championship rings, a reliable midrange game and the confidence to control high-leverage possessions. The Wolves did not merely add another scorer; they acquired a decision-maker whose strengths addressed their most persistent postseason weakness.

sections.heading: The Price Was Useful Depth Rather Than a Premium Future Asset
sections.body: Minnesota sent Joe Smith and Anthony Peeler to Milwaukee and received Cassell and Ervin Johnson. Smith remained a credible rotation big, while Peeler was a respected shooter and veteran guard, so the Bucks did not receive empty contracts. The key was the concentration of value. Minnesota exchanged two supporting players for the best player in the deal and also received a starting-caliber defensive center. That allowed the Wolves to improve their closing lineup and frontcourt structure without sacrificing draft capital or a foundational young player.

sections.heading: Cassell Produced the Best Season of His Career Immediately
sections.body: The first season supplied the clearest evidence. Cassell averaged 19.8 points and 7.3 assists, earned the only All-Star selection of his career and made the All-NBA Second Team. Minnesota won a franchise-record 58 games, finished first in the Western Conference and finally advanced beyond the first round. His pull-up shooting changed how opponents defended Garnett actions, and his ability to create a good attempt late in the clock reduced the number of possessions in which Garnett had to manufacture everything from the frontcourt.

sections.heading: The Playoff Run Showed Both His Value and the Cost of His Injury
sections.body: Cassell scored 40 points in Game 1 of Minnesota’s first-round series against Denver and delivered another 40-point performance against Sacramento. Those games were not isolated scoring explosions; they demonstrated why the trade mattered when defenses became more deliberate. By the Western Conference finals, however, a hip injury sharply limited him against the Lakers. Minnesota still pushed the series to six games, but the loss of its primary guard organizer exposed how central Cassell had become. His absence reinforced the value of the acquisition rather than diminishing it.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Received Professionals but Lost the Transaction’s Competitive Ceiling
sections.body: The Bucks were dismantling the team that had reached the 2001 Eastern Conference finals, and moving Cassell fit a broader reset that also included changes in coaching and personnel. Joe Smith gave Milwaukee competent rebounding and midrange scoring, while Peeler supplied shooting for one season. Neither became a lead engine, a major trade chip or a bridge to the next contending core. Milwaukee’s return was functional enough to avoid an absolute failing grade, but it did not reproduce Cassell’s creation or the contender-level impact he immediately delivered in Minnesota.

sections.heading: The Verdict Should Reward a Short Window That Actually Peaked
sections.body: Cassell spent only two seasons with the Wolves, which keeps this from being a decade-long franchise return. Duration is not the only measure of trade value, however. Minnesota used a modest outgoing package to create the best regular season and deepest playoff run in team history before 2024. The deal solved a specific roster problem, produced elite individual honors and helped unlock Garnett’s MVP season. Milwaukee obtained playable veterans but no comparable result. That makes the winner clear even though the return was not literally worthless.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Minnesota wins the trade with an A, while Milwaukee remains at a D. Cassell became an All-Star and All-NBA guard immediately, helped the Wolves win 58 games and gave the franchise its first Western Conference finals appearance. Ervin Johnson also filled a useful interior role. Joe Smith and Anthony Peeler were legitimate NBA contributors, but they did not create a new Milwaukee core or replace Cassell’s late-game command. The Wolves bought the exact missing skill around Garnett at a manageable price and converted it into the franchise’s highest pre-2024 peak.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Sam Cassell Turned Minnesota’s Perennial Playoff Team Into a Real Contender
featuredDeepDive.intro: The Cassell trade is a reminder that a player does not need a ten-year tenure to deliver franchise-altering value. Minnesota had already built a playoff floor around Kevin Garnett, but repeated first-round exits showed that the roster lacked enough half-court control and perimeter nerve. Cassell supplied both immediately. His acquisition also worked because it was paired with the separate Latrell Sprewell trade, giving the Wolves two different answers to the same offensive limitation. The resulting 2003-04 team reached a level the franchise had never touched.

sections.heading: Seven Straight First-Round Losses Created a Very Specific Mandate
sections.body: Minnesota’s problem was not simply a lack of talent. Garnett had become one of the league’s best players, and the Wolves were consistently good enough to qualify for the postseason. Their offense nevertheless became easier to load against when series tightened. Cassell’s pace, post-up game against smaller guards and comfort taking contested midrange shots added a style that did not depend on transition opportunities. The front office correctly diagnosed that the next step required a guard who could control playoff possessions rather than another generic regular-season contributor.

sections.heading: Cassell and Sprewell Solved Different Parts of the Perimeter Problem
sections.body: The Wolves’ summer is best understood as a sequence. Sprewell brought downhill pressure, wing scoring and another aggressive personality. Cassell brought structure, pick-and-roll craft and late-clock shot creation. Garnett remained the two-way center of the team, but he no longer had to initiate every important action or rescue every stalled possession. Because the two veterans were acquired in separate transactions, Minnesota spread the risk while building a balanced perimeter group. The Cassell deal was the organizing move that made the entire configuration coherent.

sections.heading: His Midrange Game Was a Playoff Tool, Not Empty Shot Selection
sections.body: Cassell’s preferred shots would later be described as analytically unfashionable, but their situational value was obvious. He could use a screen, force a big defender to retreat and stop at the elbow before the defense recovered. That gave Minnesota a dependable answer when opponents removed the first option. It also created passing angles to Garnett and weak-side shooters. The 40-point playoff games illustrated the ceiling, while his season-long assist production showed that he was not merely hunting difficult shots. He controlled the geometry of possessions the Wolves had previously struggled to finish.

sections.heading: The Western Conference Finals Injury Changed the Series
sections.body: Minnesota’s run ended against a Lakers team featuring Shaquille O’Neal and Kobe Bryant, but the context matters. Cassell’s hip trouble reduced him to a limited role and eventually removed him from much of the series. The Wolves were forced to improvise at point guard precisely when they needed the veteran they had acquired for those moments. Injuries do not guarantee an alternate outcome, and Los Angeles still deserved the series. Yet the collapse in guard stability showed how successfully Cassell had become integrated into every important part of Minnesota’s offense.

sections.heading: Milwaukee’s Reset Never Recovered Equivalent Lead-Guard Value
sections.body: Smith and Peeler could help an NBA rotation, and the Bucks had reasons to turn the page after the previous core stalled. A strong reset still requires either premium future assets or players capable of becoming part of the next competitive identity. Milwaukee received neither. Smith later left, Peeler’s stay was brief, and the Bucks spent years searching for another reliable organizing guard. The trade therefore should not be excused merely because the old roster had reached its expiration point. Minnesota identified the most valuable piece and paid a non-premium price.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cassell’s two Minnesota seasons generated more meaningful team value than the entire Milwaukee return. He delivered the best individual season of his career, formed a complementary perimeter partnership with Sprewell and helped Garnett reach a conference finals after years of opening-round disappointment. Milwaukee received two useful veterans, which keeps its grade at D rather than F, but the transaction did not produce a durable asset or a new competitive direction. Minnesota’s A reflects a move that was targeted, affordable and immediately validated at the highest level the franchise had reached.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Acquired Markota’s Rights for a Conditional Pick
sections.body: On June 28, 2006, Milwaukee acquired the draft rights to Damir Markota from San Antonio. In return, the Spurs received a 2007 second-round selection that would be the more favorable of the Milwaukee and Houston picks. That condition was a real part of the deal: San Antonio was not simply receiving an unspecified future second. The selection ultimately became No. 33, Marcus Williams. Milwaukee traded away that specific future opportunity to secure the forward it wanted immediately after the 2006 draft.

sections.heading: The Teams Took Different Prospect Timelines
sections.body: The Bucks could evaluate Markota as a player whose rights they already controlled, rather than waiting for another draft. San Antonio accepted uncertainty about both the position of the following year’s pick and the eventual prospect available at that slot. The rights to Markota and the later Williams selection were separate developmental bets. Neither was an exchange of established franchise starters, and no additional players or cash belong in this particular transaction.

sections.heading: Markota Rights and the No. 33 Pick Produced Modest Returns
sections.body: Milwaukee chose the immediate draft rights to Damir Markota, while San Antonio accepted a future second-rounder defined as the better of Milwaukee's and Houston's 2007 picks. The option's actual destination is identifiable: San Antonio received the No. 33 choice and selected Marcus Williams. That is more precise than treating the return as an unspecified future pick, and it keeps the 2006 rights acquisition distinct from the 2007 draft result. Neither side obtained an established star in the exchange, and the recorded returns do not support a decisive franchise-level winner. The matching C+ grades and Even Trade verdict recognize two limited prospect opportunities rather than crediting either team with unrelated roster or championship achievements.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Milwaukee C-plus, San Antonio C-plus. The Bucks received Damir Markota’s draft rights, while the Spurs acquired the more favorable 2007 second-round selection specified in the deal, ultimately No. 33 Marcus Williams. These were different prospect opportunities, and the documented transaction offers no decisive reason to award either side the higher grade.

sections.heading: Magloire for Three Players in July 2006
sections.body: Milwaukee sent Jamaal Magloire to Portland on July 31, 2006, receiving guard Steve Blake, center Ha Seung-Jin and veteran big man Brian Skinner. The deal did not involve a first-round selection or a hypothetical later draft conversion. Portland was seeking a starting-caliber center after a 2006 draft in which it acquired Brandon Roy and LaMarcus Aldridge. Milwaukee obtained several roster alternatives to a center it was willing to move.

sections.heading: Skinner Played While Blake Became Another Trade Asset
sections.body: Brian Skinner supplied 67 Milwaukee games, including 44 starts, with 5.7 rebounds per game in 2006-07. Blake played 33 Bucks games before Milwaukee sent him to Denver on January 11, 2007 for Earl Boykins, Julius Hodge and cash. Blake therefore generated both direct backcourt minutes and a later transaction route. Ha Seung-Jin was waived in October before appearing in a regular-season game for the Bucks, so the third incoming name should not be inflated into meaningful court value.

sections.heading: Portland Received a Full Season of Magloire
sections.body: Magloire played 81 Portland games in 2006-07 and averaged 6.5 points and 6.1 rebounds in 21 minutes. That is a concrete center return and helps explain why the Trail Blazers grade is C+ rather than a failure. His role, however, was not the same as his earlier peak in New Orleans, and he did not stay with Portland for a second season. It is more accurate to compare his single season against Milwaukee’s Skinner minutes and Blake follow-on assets than to claim the Blazers received nothing.

sections.heading: The Completed Returns Favor Milwaukee, With a Limit
sections.body: Milwaukee obtained two actual rotation contributors and turned Blake into another guard, Earl Boykins, in a separate January transaction. Skinner’s 44 starts supplied more frontcourt coverage than a simple count of three incoming players would suggest. Portland obtained useful Magloire minutes but only for one season. The A- and C+ grades reflect that narrower difference: additional Milwaukee usage and flexibility, not an assumption that Ha Seung-Jin became a productive NBA player or that Blake’s entire later career belongs to this trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win. Milwaukee exchanged Jamaal Magloire for Brian Skinner, Steve Blake and Ha Seung-Jin. Skinner played 67 games and started 44; Blake logged 33 Milwaukee games before moving to Denver for Earl Boykins, Julius Hodge and cash; Ha was waived without playing for the Bucks. Portland received a legitimate one-season center return, with Magloire appearing in 81 games and averaging 6.5 points and 6.1 rebounds. Milwaukee’s A- and Portland’s C+ recognize the broader Bucks return without erasing Magloire’s actual contribution.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Magloire's Portland Season Versus Skinner's 44 Starts and Blake's Next Trade
featuredDeepDive.intro: Jamaal Magloire gave Portland 81 games after Milwaukee sent him west in July 2006, so this was not a zero-return transaction for the Blazers. The Bucks instead collected 44 starts from Brian Skinner in 67 appearances and 33 games from Steve Blake, then moved Blake separately for Earl Boykins, Julius Hodge and cash. Ha Seung-Jin never played a Milwaukee regular-season game. That uneven three-player return helps explain the A-minus/C-plus difference without pretending all three newcomers produced or counting Blake's Denver trade as part of the original Portland package.

sections.heading: July 31, 2006: The Bucks Traded One Center for Three Assets
sections.body: Milwaukee sent Jamaal Magloire to Portland on July 31, 2006 and received point guard Steve Blake, forward-center Brian Skinner and center Ha Seung-Jin. This was a three-for-one player transaction; none of the direct incoming assets was a draft selection or contractual right to a future pick. The Bucks obtained multiple immediate roster options, while the Blazers acquired an established center for their developing frontcourt. Properly identifying Ha as a center is important because he should not be listed with Blake as an additional guard. The players arrived with different likely roles: Blake could run a backcourt, Skinner could handle regular NBA frontcourt minutes, and Ha was a developmental big whose subsequent Milwaukee appearance record had yet to be established.

sections.heading: Skinner Started 44 Games; Blake Became a Later Trade Asset
sections.body: Skinner supplied 67 Milwaukee regular-season appearances in 2006-07, including 44 starts, with 5.7 rebounds per game. Blake appeared in 33 Bucks games before being moved in a separate January 11, 2007 deal to Denver. Milwaukee acquired Earl Boykins, Julius Hodge and cash through that later Blake transaction. It is appropriate to acknowledge that second branch because the Bucks directly controlled Blake in the 2006 package and chose to convert him again; however, those Denver assets were not included in the original Portland agreement. Ha was waived in October without making a Bucks NBA regular-season appearance. A three-player return therefore produced meaningful roster value from Skinner, direct appearances and further trade value from Blake, and no actual Milwaukee games from Ha.

sections.heading: Portland Obtained 81 Games From Magloire
sections.body: The Trail Blazers acquired a real center, not an empty contract. Magloire appeared in 81 Portland regular-season games in 2006-07, averaging 6.5 points and 6.1 rebounds in roughly 21 minutes per contest. That playing time is directly attributable to the club that received him in July 2006. His previous All-Star reputation and earlier production in New Orleans were part of the reason Portland was interested, but they cannot be counted as Blazers return. Magloire did not stay with Portland for a second season, which puts a clear limit on the duration of the return. The original C-plus grade accounts for one useful season of a veteran NBA center, not a failed signing that yielded zero playing contribution. The outcome is narrower than his name recognition might imply.

sections.heading: The A-Minus/C-Plus Gap Reflects a Second Asset Branch
sections.body: The canonical result is Bucks Win, Milwaukee A-minus and Portland C-plus. Milwaukee obtained Skinner's 67 games and 44 starts, Blake's 33 games and the assets in a documented follow-up Denver trade, while Ha provided no Bucks regular-season appearances. Portland received 81 games from Magloire with modest center production but no second season. This is a comparison of completed team-specific assets, not a claim that three incoming player names automatically outweighed one outgoing veteran. The 2007 Boykins-Hodge-cash package resulted from a separate exchange and must remain downstream rather than being inserted into the July trade-day ledger. Milwaukee's advantage therefore rests on more than counting roster spots; Portland earned credit for playing time, but Milwaukee captured multiple kinds of realized value.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win — Milwaukee A-minus, Portland C-plus. Skinner played 67 Milwaukee games with 44 starts, and Blake supplied 33 games before the Bucks converted him into Earl Boykins, Julius Hodge and cash via a separate trade. Ha Seung-Jin did not play for Milwaukee. Portland received 81 Magloire games averaging 6.5 points and 6.1 rebounds, a real but shorter single-season center return.

sections.heading: At the 2010 Deadline, Milwaukee Gave Up Meeks and Elson
sections.body: On February 18, 2010, Philadelphia acquired rookie guard Jodie Meeks and veteran center Francisco Elson from Milwaukee. The Bucks received Royal Ivey, Primož Brezec and the Sixers' 2010 second-round selection. The NBA league transaction register and Bucks' season ledger confirm the exact five-asset arrangement and date. Philadelphia was getting a young shooter who had played 41 games for Milwaukee, plus an established reserve big; Milwaukee added two veterans and a future draft choice rather than an incoming scorer. That pick did not already represent a known NBA player when the agreement was made. Another Bucks move on the same deadline involved John Salmons, Joe Alexander and Hakim Warrick, but its players and picks must not be mixed into the Meeks-for-Ivey transaction.

sections.heading: Meeks Played 159 Philadelphia Games Over Three Partial Seasons
sections.body: Meeks appeared in 19 Sixers regular-season games after the February 2010 deadline, averaging 5.9 points. The next season he played 74 games with 64 starts, scoring 10.5 points per game and hitting 39.7 percent of his three-point attempts. In the shortened 2011-12 season he added 66 Philadelphia games, 50 starts and 8.4 points per night. Those stints total 159 regular-season appearances for Philadelphia, the principal concrete value it received from the trade. His previous 41 Milwaukee games belong to the sending club, and later Lakers, Detroit and other NBA contributions belong to subsequent teams. The Sixers acquired a role player who could start and space the floor, not merely a contract that disappeared after one offseason.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Got Thirty-Two Immediate Ivey and Brezec Games
sections.body: The two veteran Milwaukee acquisitions provided much less regular-season action. Royal Ivey played 18 Bucks games in 2009-10, all off the bench, averaging 1.3 points in five minutes per contest. Center Primož Brezec appeared in 14 more Bucks games, scoring 1.0 point per outing while averaging 4.2 minutes. Their combined 32 team-specific appearances were real short reserve duty but not a replacement for Meeks's subsequent 159 Philadelphia games. Ivey's earlier Sixers games and Brezec's earlier Philadelphia appearances occurred before this deal and cannot be credited to Milwaukee. Both left the Bucks before producing another season there. Milwaukee therefore depended on the future draft selection for any longer basketball value from this particular exchange.

sections.heading: No. 37 Became Darington Hobson, Who Played Five Bucks Games
sections.body: Milwaukee used the acquired 2010 second-round pick at No. 37 on Darington Hobson from New Mexico. Hobson missed the 2010-11 NBA season after injury and made just five regular-season appearances for Milwaukee in 2011-12, averaging 0.8 points. Those five games are the realized player service tied to the selection; it did not become a later NBA All-Star. Combined with Ivey's 18 Bucks games and Brezec's 14, the direct Milwaukee return was 37 NBA appearances from those assets. Philadelphia got 159 Meeks games, while Elson appeared once for the Sixers immediately in 2009-10. The archive grades Philadelphia A-minus, Milwaukee B-plus and calls the outcome Slight 76ers Edge, preserving the judgment without treating the draft right as unexercised or assigning later careers to either club.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight 76ers Edge — Philadelphia A-minus, Milwaukee B-plus. Philadelphia got 159 post-trade Meeks regular-season games, including 114 starts across 2010-11 and 2011-12, and one initial Francisco Elson game. Milwaukee got 18 Royal Ivey games, 14 Primož Brezec games and eventually five from No. 37 Darington Hobson, drafted with the acquired 2010 second. This is a measurable difference in team-specific rotation service, not a claim that the future second did not convey.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Milwaukee Bucks–Philadelphia 76ers: What the 2010-02-18 Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: Philadelphia acquired Jodie Meeks and Francisco Elson at the February 18, 2010 deadline for Royal Ivey, Primož Brezec and a future second-round pick. Meeks supplied 159 Sixers games and 114 starts in 2010-11 and 2011-12. Milwaukee got 18 Ivey and 14 Brezec games, plus No. 37 Darington Hobson, who played five NBA Bucks games. The direct performance gap supports the inherited Slight 76ers Edge without changing the original grades.

sections.heading: The Pick Was Future Value Until June 2010
sections.body: Milwaukee sent Jodie Meeks and Francisco Elson to Philadelphia on February 18, 2010 for Royal Ivey, Primož Brezec and the Sixers' forthcoming second-round choice. The transaction was part of a busy Milwaukee deadline, but it was separate from the larger John Salmons deal with Chicago. Philadelphia obtained a shooting guard who had played 41 Bucks games earlier in the season and a veteran center; the Bucks took immediate reserve alternatives and a selection. That draft asset became No. 37 Darington Hobson at the June draft, not a player whom Philadelphia sent to Milwaukee in February. Distinguishing the rights from the later named draftee keeps the original roster decision and the completed outcome on their proper dates.

sections.heading: Meeks Became a Philadelphia Starter After the Initial Short Stint
sections.body: Philadelphia first used Meeks in 19 regular-season games during the rest of 2009-10. In 2010-11 the guard appeared in 74 games with 64 starts, averaging 10.5 points and making nearly 40 percent of his three-point shots. His 2011-12 campaign contributed 66 games and 50 starts in a lockout-shortened season. In all, the original 2010 trade supplied 159 Philadelphia Meeks regular-season appearances and a substantial amount of starting shooting guard service. The later seasons he played with the Los Angeles Lakers and Detroit Pistons cannot be booked as 76ers production. Philadelphia's A-minus grade reflects a useful multi-season role, although Meeks was not a franchise star and this single trade did not create the team's entire playoff competitiveness.

sections.heading: The Bucks Received Short Veteran Stints and a Five-Game Pick
sections.body: Royal Ivey logged 18 Bucks games after the deadline, while Primož Brezec played 14. The center averaged only 4.2 minutes per game in Milwaukee, and Ivey averaged five; both were short-term bench alternatives. The future selection was used at No. 37 on Darington Hobson, whose NBA career with Milwaukee consisted of five regular-season games in 2011-12 after missing the previous season with injury. That is 37 combined Bucks appearances from the three asset branches, not three multi-year rotation successes. Hobson did not play the 2010 season for Philadelphia, and Ivey had been a 76er before this particular trade. This compact record provides a stronger fact-specific comparison than language about vague future flexibility or a hoped-for first-round conversion.

sections.heading: The Sixers Edge Follows Team-Specific NBA Minutes
sections.body: The stored result reads Slight 76ers Edge, Philadelphia A-minus and Milwaukee B-plus. Jodie Meeks provided Philadelphia 159 games after arrival, including 114 starts during his two subsequent seasons, while Francisco Elson played once for the Sixers in 2009-10. Milwaukee received 18 games from Royal Ivey, 14 from Primož Brezec and five later appearances from No. 37 Darington Hobson. The game counts do not measure every contract or roster motive, but they make the direct basketball disparity clear. Philadelphia acquired lasting shooting guard utility and Milwaukee acquired short-term reserves plus a pick whose chosen player rarely appeared. No later Bucks seasons of unrelated acquisitions, or Meeks's later career for other teams, should be folded into these February 2010 returns.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The existing Philadelphia A-minus, Milwaukee B-plus and Slight 76ers Edge verdict are preserved. Meeks became a useful starting shooter over 159 Sixers games after the trade, while Hobson later played only five Milwaukee games from the No. 37 second. Ivey and Brezec supplied another combined 32 Bucks games and Elson played one Philadelphia game during 2009-10. Those outcomes are attributed to the correct teams and seasons; the separate Salmons deadline transaction did not contribute assets to this deal.

sections.heading: The Knicks Bought Jordan’s Draft Rights
sections.body: Milwaukee sent the rights to center Jerome Jordan to New York on July 8, 2010 and received cash considerations. Jordan was a young draft-rights prospect, not an established NBA center changing starting lineups. New York gained the ability to develop or sign him, while Milwaukee monetized a selection rather than holding his rights. The transaction records identify the player and the cash return but do not provide a verified payment amount.

sections.heading: Jordan Offered Only a Small NBA Return
sections.body: Jordan ultimately appeared briefly for the Knicks. That creates a real basketball return for New York, though it falls far short of a long-term starting center. The club acquired a player-development opportunity and received some NBA minutes from it. Milwaukee did not receive a replacement player or future pick; its asset was the cash payment. The record does not support crediting the Bucks with an undisclosed amount or connecting either side to unrelated roster moves later in the decade.

sections.heading: A Small Knicks Advantage Is Proportionate
sections.body: The archive records Knicks Win, with New York graded B and Milwaukee C-plus. The difference acknowledges that Jordan’s rights became a roster opportunity instead of expiring without an NBA appearance. Yet the brief playing contribution and unpriced cash prevent a dramatic verdict. A review that described this deal as a major steal would conflict with the actual scale of the return; a review that said New York acquired nothing would be equally inaccurate.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win — New York B, Milwaukee C-plus. New York acquired Jerome Jordan’s draft rights and ultimately received a limited NBA appearance return from the center. Milwaukee received cash considerations of an unverified amount. The ledger’s slight Knicks advantage reflects the identifiable player opportunity, not a large or fully priced asset windfall.

sections.heading: The July 2010 Deal Was a Backup Forward for Draft Flexibility
sections.body: Sacramento sent reserve forward Jon Brockman to Milwaukee on July 19, 2010, receiving Darnell Jackson and a 2011 second-round choice. The selection's terms allowed Milwaukee to supply one of two possible second-round rights tied to the Bucks and Bulls, so the final player identity was unknown when the agreement was signed. Both team transaction histories list Brockman and Jackson as NBA players who changed teams, not draft prospects. Sacramento obtained an additional future option while Milwaukee exchanged Jackson for a more physical rebounder familiar to Kings fans. The eventual draft selection came at No. 60 in 2011, when Sacramento chose Isaiah Thomas out of Washington. Thomas was not under either club's NBA contract when the exchange occurred.

sections.heading: Brockman Supplied Ninety-Eight Bucks Games Across Two Seasons
sections.body: The immediate Milwaukee return was real but limited. Brockman played 63 regular-season games for the Bucks in 2010-11, starting six and averaging 2.2 points and 2.9 rebounds in 10.7 minutes. He followed with 35 appearances and no starts during the lockout-shortened 2011-12 campaign, averaging 1.1 points and 2.1 rebounds. His combined Bucks tenure was 98 regular-season games, six starts and 259 rebounds. He had already played 52 games for Sacramento as a rookie, but those earlier appearances belong to the Kings, not to Milwaukee's acquired return. Brockman's strength on the glass gave the Bucks some functional reserve minutes. It was not comparable in longevity or offensive responsibility to the eventual No. 60 selection.

sections.heading: Jackson Played Fifty-Nine Games for Sacramento in 2010-11
sections.body: Darnell Jackson arrived in Sacramento after limited time with Cleveland and Milwaukee. In the 2010-11 season he appeared in 59 Kings regular-season games, making two starts and averaging 3.2 points and 1.6 rebounds in 8.2 minutes. The Kansas product was a short-duty frontcourt piece rather than a primary replacement for Brockman's rebounding. He did not become Sacramento's long-term starting center, and his earlier Cleveland appearances must not inflate his Kings total. Still, Jackson was a genuine acquired player who took the court. His value belongs alongside the incoming draft choice, not in place of it. Sacramento received an immediately usable reserve and retained an opportunity to identify a player in the following year's draft.

sections.heading: The No. 60 Selection Produced Three Sacramento Seasons
sections.body: Sacramento used the incoming 2011 second-round selection at No. 60 on Isaiah Thomas. He played 65 Kings games as a rookie in 2011-12, averaging 11.5 points, and appeared in 79 more in 2012-13 at 13.9 points. In 2013-14 he averaged 20.3 points and 6.3 assists over 72 games. Those three Kings seasons total 216 regular-season appearances, with an obvious rise in playmaking responsibility. This was an unusually productive return for the final selection in a draft. Thomas later developed further with Phoenix and Boston, earning All-Star honors outside Sacramento. Those later achievements help explain his talent but cannot be counted as Kings team production from this specific pick. The first three seasons alone support Sacramento's strong historical advantage.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Win — Sacramento A+, Milwaukee D+ in the preserved record. Sacramento played Jackson 59 games and used the acquired 2011 No.60 second on Isaiah Thomas, who logged 216 Kings games and averaged 20.3 points in 2013-14. Milwaukee received 98 Jon Brockman games and six starts over two seasons. The future draft pick was a conditional right at trade time; Thomas later became a two-time All-Star elsewhere.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Jon Brockman for Darnell Jackson and 2011 No. 60: Isaiah Thomas Kings Return
featuredDeepDive.intro: Milwaukee obtained 98 games from Jon Brockman; Sacramento received Jackson and a 2011 second it used on No.60 Isaiah Thomas. His 216 Kings games included a 20.3-point final season.

sections.heading: The Pick's Uncertainty Was Part of the Real Trade-Day Price
sections.body: Milwaukee did not surrender a known future star named Isaiah Thomas in July 2010. It surrendered a conditional 2011 second-round right while exchanging Darnell Jackson for Jon Brockman. The Bucks and Bulls pick terms meant the exact selection position would be established later. Sacramento could not guarantee that a particular point guard would be available or that a late pick would enter its playing rotation. The eventual No. 60 slot is therefore an outcome, not an ingredient anyone could specifically forecast. Evaluating the agreement requires balancing that uncertainty against Milwaukee's immediate frontcourt need. Brockman had played 52 games for Sacramento in his rookie year and was a reasonable low-cost rebounder to try, even though the drafted return ultimately far exceeded his Bucks role.

sections.heading: The Two Veterans Had Modest, Countable Roles
sections.body: Brockman made 98 Milwaukee appearances over two seasons, averaging 2.2 points in the first and 1.1 in the second. His total playing time with the Bucks was 916 regular-season minutes, useful reserve service rather than a long-term starting job. Jackson gave Sacramento 59 games during the 2010-11 campaign, with 187 total points and 94 rebounds. Both teams therefore acquired a legitimate NBA player in the immediate exchange. The difference in value was not that Milwaukee received nothing or that Jackson became an established Kings star. The consequential extra asset was Sacramento's incoming 2011 second. Separating the veteran-for-veteran portion from the draft right avoids making a hindsight success appear to be the straightforward exchange of a star for a bench player in 2010.

sections.heading: Thomas's Sacramento Production Makes the Pick's Value Concrete
sections.body: Thomas was selected last in the 2011 draft and quickly outgrew the usual expectations attached to No. 60. He averaged 11.5 points during a 65-game rookie season, 13.9 across 79 games the next year and 20.3 during a 72-game 2013-14 season. He also averaged 6.3 assists in that last Sacramento campaign, reflecting his expanded role as a primary ballhandler. These are Kings accomplishments flowing from the acquired pick. His 216 Sacramento regular-season games already outnumbered the two veterans' individual tenures with the teams that acquired them. The later two-time All-Star period with Boston was impressive but occurred after a separate departure from Sacramento. The original trade can be graded favorably to the Kings without borrowing points scored in a Celtics uniform.

sections.heading: A Kings A-Plus Requires Honesty About the Bucks Return
sections.body: The preserved ledger calls this Kings Win, assigning Sacramento A-plus and Milwaukee D-plus. That gap has a factual basis in the No. 60 choice producing Isaiah Thomas, who averaged 20.3 points in his final Kings season. Sacramento also played incoming forward Darnell Jackson in 59 games. Milwaukee got 98 Brockman games over two seasons, with some rebounding and limited frontcourt depth, not an entirely empty contract. The original deal should not be described as a direct star-for-reserve exchange because Thomas was selected a year later and his development was uncertain. The better judgment is that Sacramento converted a modest trade-day draft opportunity into a productive young guard, whereas Milwaukee received a narrowly useful player without comparable long-term basketball production.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Sacramento A-plus, Milwaukee D-plus in the inherited Kings Win. A conditional 2011 second converted into No.60 Isaiah Thomas and three productive Kings seasons, while Jackson added 59 Sacramento games. Brockman supplied 98 Milwaukee games in a limited reserve role. The grade reflects future pick development, not the foresight of already possessing Thomas in July 2010.

sections.heading: Tobias Harris, Beno Udrih and Doron Lamb / J.J. Redick, Gustavo Ayon and Ish Smith: The Deal’s Actual Shape
sections.body: On February 21, 2013, Orlando traded J.J. Redick, Gustavo Ayon and Ish Smith to Milwaukee for Tobias Harris, Beno Udrih, Doron Lamb and cash. The Bucks were 26-28 and chasing a playoff berth with Brandon Jennings and Monta Ellis. Redick offered shooting and another experienced guard. Harris was only 20 and had not secured a consistent Milwaukee role. Orlando was rebuilding after the Dwight Howard era and could prioritize developmental upside over immediate wins. The transaction therefore exchanged a proven short-term specialist for a young forward whose scoring and positional size had not yet been fully tested. Harris had more remaining rookie-scale development time than Redick, who was approaching unrestricted free agency after Milwaukee's 2013 playoff push. The clubs were buying different timelines, and the later result should be measured against those timelines rather than against a fictional market with perfect information.

sections.heading: Tobias Harris, Beno Udrih and Doron Lamb / J.J. Redick, Gustavo Ayon and Ish Smith: The Winning Team’s Case
sections.body: Harris immediately showed why Orlando valued the gamble. He averaged 17.3 points after the trade, expanded his creation role and developed into a versatile forward capable of scoring inside, from midrange and beyond the arc. Across three Magic seasons he became the best player in the transaction and a credible long-term building block. Orlando later traded him to Detroit for a poor return, but that separate decision does not erase the value acquired in 2013. The Magic turned an expiring veteran into a young starter with substantial market value and multiple productive seasons, supporting an A-plus for this specific trade. The winning grade follows from the player’s actual role, the seasons controlled by the acquiring team and the competitive outcomes that occurred while that team held the asset. Reputation by itself is not enough.

sections.heading: Tobias Harris, Beno Udrih and Doron Lamb / J.J. Redick, Gustavo Ayon and Ish Smith: The Return Package Deserves a Fair Reading
sections.body: Milwaukee received only a brief Redick tenure. He appeared in 28 regular-season games, the Bucks finished 38-44 and Miami swept them in the first round. Redick then left in a sign-and-trade that did not recover a Harris-level asset. Ayon and Smith had minor roles and did not change the team’s ceiling. The Bucks’ logic was understandable—shooting could help a crowded guard rotation—but the competitive target was too modest to justify surrendering a young player with years of control. An F reflects both the short stay and the failure to preserve value after the playoff push ended. Redick still gave the Bucks 28 games of credible guard shooting, even though his short stay did not solve Milwaukee's longer roster needs. Useful veteran seasons, draft control and credible roster fit retain value even when the other team receives the larger prize.

sections.heading: Tobias Harris, Beno Udrih and Doron Lamb / J.J. Redick, Gustavo Ayon and Ish Smith: Leverage and Timing Changed the Price
sections.body: The trade illustrates the danger of paying a future-asset price for a marginal win-now objective. Milwaukee was not one veteran away from championship contention. It was trying to secure a low playoff seed, which limited the upside even if Redick played well. Orlando had the opposite incentive: minutes and patience were available, allowing Harris to explore a broader offensive role. The result was not solely a scouting miracle. Opportunity was part of the asset. The Magic could create value because their timeline matched Harris’s development, while the Bucks’ timeline demanded immediate results from a player nearing free agency. The difference in contract timelines also changed the risk: Milwaukee surrendered a 20-year-old on a rookie deal for a veteran guard near free agency. The retrospective question is whether the front office priced those constraints well enough.

sections.heading: Tobias Harris, Beno Udrih and Doron Lamb / J.J. Redick, Gustavo Ayon and Ish Smith: Asset Conversion and Opportunity Cost
sections.body: Udrih and Lamb were secondary pieces, and cash did not drive the verdict. Harris carried almost all of Orlando’s realized value. Redick carried Milwaukee’s side, with Ayon and Smith providing limited depth. The later Harris-to-Detroit trade should be evaluated on its own page; importing that mistake here would confuse acquisition value with later asset management. At the end of this transaction’s direct window, Orlando had obtained the youngest, best and most valuable player. Milwaukee had used its return for a short first-round exit and then watched the primary acquisition leave. Orlando directly converted Harris's expanded minutes into 17.3 points per game after his arrival, while Milwaukee received only Redick's 28-game rental. The trade details are strongest when every major piece is followed to its actual outcome.

sections.heading: Tobias Harris, Beno Udrih and Doron Lamb / J.J. Redick, Gustavo Ayon and Ish Smith: Verdict and grading scale
sections.body: The old Partner Win label is replaced by Magic Win. Orlando remains A-plus because Harris’s immediate breakout and multiple productive seasons represented an exceptional return for an expiring Redick package. Milwaukee remains F, while the counterpart grade is corrected from A to A-plus so it matches the Magic’s actual grade. The verdict does not claim Harris became a superstar in Orlando. It recognizes that the Bucks traded away a valuable young starter for a rental that did not materially improve the postseason outcome. The Bucks' brief Redick window could not match the seasons Orlando received from Harris after taking on the young forward in the exchange. Milwaukee's rental failed to become a lasting rotation piece, whereas Harris remained a longer-term Magic asset, supporting the grades without inflating his star status.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Orlando wins because Tobias Harris immediately became a productive young starter and the transaction’s most valuable long-term asset. Milwaukee received only a short J.J. Redick rental before a first-round sweep and failed to recover comparable value when he left.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: How Tobias Harris, Beno Udrih and Doron Lamb / J.J. Redick, Gustavo Ayon and Ish Smith Changed Two Franchise Timelines
featuredDeepDive.intro: Milwaukee acquired J.J. Redick, Gustavo Ayon and Ish Smith in February 2013 while Orlando gained Tobias Harris, Beno Udrih and Doron Lamb. The Bucks sought shooting for a playoff push but kept Redick only until unrestricted free agency; Miami swept Milwaukee in the first round. The Magic instead acquired Harris on his rookie contract and gave him space to develop into a reliable scorer and valuable player asset. Evaluating the trade means comparing that club-specific development with Milwaukee's short rental rather than rewarding either team for production its former players delivered elsewhere.

sections.heading: Harris's Orlando Development Outweighed Milwaukee's Short Redick Rental
sections.body: Harris’s Orlando peak combined roughly 17 points per game with rebounding, size and expanding shot creation. He was not yet the polished scorer he became later, but his trajectory and trade value were obvious. Redick’s Milwaukee peak was a useful floor-spacing guard role, though his shooting percentages dipped and the crowded Jennings-Ellis backcourt limited the fit. Harris offered a higher two-way ceiling and more lineup flexibility. The peak comparison favored Orlando before contract control was even considered. Peak seasons matter because high-impact players alter matchups, roster construction and postseason ceilings in ways that ordinary cumulative minutes do not.

sections.heading: Tobias Harris, Beno Udrih and Doron Lamb / J.J. Redick, Gustavo Ayon and Ish Smith: Control and Durability
sections.body: Orlando received Harris on his rookie contract, then retained him into restricted free agency and a new deal. That control created both inexpensive production and flexibility. Milwaukee acquired Redick months before unrestricted free agency and did not keep him. Short control can be justified for a contender, but the Bucks’ ceiling was a low seed and their first-round matchup was overwhelming. The Magic’s years of control magnified the advantage because Harris improved while the team held his rights. Milwaukee’s return expired almost as soon as the playoff push ended. Durability includes contractual control, repeated role stability and the ability to build subsequent rosters around the return. A shorter brilliant window can beat longer average service, but the years still matter.

sections.heading: Tobias Harris, Beno Udrih and Doron Lamb / J.J. Redick, Gustavo Ayon and Ish Smith: Postseason Translation
sections.body: The Bucks reached the playoffs, but the result did not validate the price. Miami swept Milwaukee, and Redick was a supporting piece rather than a transformative performer. Orlando did not reach the postseason during Harris’s tenure, a limitation that should be acknowledged, but team context was rebuilding rather than contention. The trade’s postseason test therefore asks whether Milwaukee’s rental changed the intended outcome. It did not. Harris’s absence from playoff success in Orlando keeps the analysis focused on player and asset value, while Milwaukee’s failed win-now objective deepens the loss. Playoff results are evidence rather than the only test. They reveal whether a skill set survives scouting, pressure and slower possessions and should be credited only to the team that received the player in this transaction.

sections.heading: Tobias Harris, Beno Udrih and Doron Lamb / J.J. Redick, Gustavo Ayon and Ish Smith: The Best Counterfactual
sections.body: Milwaukee’s best counterfactual is that Harris remained blocked and never developed without a larger role. The Bucks may also have believed Redick’s shooting would stabilize a volatile backcourt. Those are reasonable ideas, but the price and objective were mismatched. A team chasing the eighth seed should be especially cautious about surrendering a controlled 20-year-old. Orlando’s risk was that Harris’s small sample and inconsistent defense reflected a limited ceiling. The Magic accepted that risk because the rebuilding timeline could absorb it, then quickly saw the upside become real. The relevant 2013 alternative was keeping Harris behind Milwaukee's established wings rather than sending him to a rebuilding Magic club with a larger role available. They are least useful when they assume knowledge or offers the market never supplied.

sections.heading: Tobias Harris, Beno Udrih and Doron Lamb / J.J. Redick, Gustavo Ayon and Ish Smith: Legacy and Final Accounting
sections.body: The deal is remembered as one of Milwaukee’s clearest short-term mistakes and one of Orlando’s better post-Howard acquisitions. Harris went on to play for several teams and earn major contracts, but the Magic deserve credit only for the seasons and value they controlled. Redick continued an excellent career after Milwaukee, yet those later seasons belonged elsewhere. The transaction’s legacy is the contrast between patient development and a hurried playoff push. Orlando’s A-plus and Milwaukee’s F capture how dramatically those timelines affected the return. Legacy compresses years into a familiar story, but the grade remains tied to direct production, downstream conversion, contract value and the competitive identity created by the return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Milwaukee's February push purchased the remaining short-term availability of J.J. Redick but did not produce a deep playoff run or a durable Bucks tenure. The club was swept in the first round, and Redick's later successful NBA years occurred with other teams rather than returning value to Milwaukee from this trade. Orlando instead acquired the developing Tobias Harris, who became the largest long-term player asset in the exchange; Beno Udrih and Doron Lamb were separate, more limited pieces. A+ against F compares realized franchise value from these timelines, not the full later careers of every participant. The Magic won by accepting development time when the Bucks overpaid for immediacy.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Targeted Wolters in the 2013 Draft
sections.body: The Bucks acquired the rights to Nate Wolters from Philadelphia on June 27, 2013. The 76ers received Ricky Ledo’s draft rights and a 2014 second-round pick. Those are two distinct Philadelphia assets, not a one-for-one swap of player names. The future selection later became No. 54 Nemanja Dangubić. Milwaukee made a specific bet on Wolters as a guard; Philadelphia retained another prospect and an additional opportunity in the following draft.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Received Both Rights and a Later Selection
sections.body: Ledo’s rights offered Philadelphia a young player to assess, while the 2014 second-round choice supplied draft flexibility that had not yet been assigned to an individual player on trade day. Dangubić’s eventual selection identifies how that pick was exercised, but it would be misleading to write as though his name was known when the clubs made the 2013 trade. Milwaukee accepted that two-part cost in order to secure Wolters’s rights. The packages differed in quantity and timing, not in established star power.

sections.heading: An Even Verdict Does Not Erase the Asset Differences
sections.body: The historical ledger assigns B-minus to both Milwaukee and Philadelphia. The Even Trade label reflects an assessment that neither completed package establishes a sufficiently decisive edge in the source-backed record. It does not mean Wolters, Ledo and the later No. 54 choice were interchangeable. The actual draft years and named rights explain what each club received, and those concrete details carry more value for readers than a duplicate second essay on general grading philosophy.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Milwaukee B-minus, Philadelphia B-minus. Milwaukee acquired Nate Wolters’s rights; Philadelphia obtained Ricky Ledo’s rights and the 2014 second-round selection ultimately used on Nemanja Dangubić at No. 54. The pick’s later identity must be distinguished from what was known in 2013. The stored record supports equal grades, not an invented winner.

sections.heading: Butler Returned Home After Just Weeks on Phoenix’s Books
sections.body: The Suns sent Caron Butler to Milwaukee on August 29, 2013, for Ish Smith and Viacheslav Kravtsov. It was a homecoming for the Racine, Wisconsin native, who had arrived in Phoenix from the Clippers during July's Eric Bledsoe deal but never played a Suns regular-season game. Milwaukee general manager John Hammond presented Butler as an experienced wing who could mentor the Bucks' young roster. Phoenix general manager Ryan McDonough described the opposite goal: moving Butler's salary gave the Suns room to maneuver and added two younger players. The transaction should therefore be evaluated as a short-lived veteran return for Milwaukee and a cap-flexibility plus roster-depth move for Phoenix, not as a Butler season that Phoenix had already enjoyed.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Got 34 Butler Games Before a February Buyout
sections.body: Butler started 13 of his 34 appearances for the Bucks, averaging 11.0 points, 4.6 rebounds and 1.6 assists. His 38-point game at Philadelphia on November 22 showed he could still score, but those flashes came during an injury-disrupted season rather than a long-lasting starting stint. Milwaukee announced on February 27, 2014, that it had requested waivers on Butler after reaching a buyout. He later joined Oklahoma City, and that Thunder playoff run cannot be counted as part of the Bucks' return. Butler gave Milwaukee real half-season wing production and leadership, but the team did not gain an asset it could retain or trade when he left. The record supports short-term basketball value, not an enduring homecoming.

sections.heading: Smith Played 70 Games for Phoenix; Kravtsov Played 20
sections.body: Smith became the useful player in the Suns' two-player return. In 2013-14 he appeared in 70 Phoenix games, with one start, averaging 3.7 points and 2.6 assists in 14.4 minutes. Those numbers describe a backup rather than a primary playmaker, but 70 appearances are substantially more sustained Suns minutes than Butler had ever supplied the franchise. Kravtsov appeared in 20 games, averaging 1.0 point and 0.9 rebounds in approximately three minutes, before Phoenix waived him March 2, 2014. Both were concrete player acquisitions. Smith's later NBA longevity with other franchises cannot be assigned retroactively to this one Suns season, and Kravtsov's international experience was not a substitute for on-court production.

sections.heading: Different Timelines Justify Only a Modest Relative Verdict
sections.body: The inherited Even verdict and matching B- grades express a close overall exchange, although the imported source perspectives use inconsistent absolute B and C+ scales. Butler was the stronger scorer but contributed to Milwaukee for only 34 games. Phoenix acquired a usable reserve in Smith, a low-minute prospect in Kravtsov, and salary flexibility that its own official announcement named as a priority. The Bucks received no draft asset, and the Suns did not receive Butler's later career achievements. There is room to favor either side depending on whether one values a short burst of experienced scoring or younger backup minutes and cap relief. What the historical record does not support is an inflated claim that the exchange delivered a franchise-changing player to either team.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even, keeping the inherited Milwaukee B-/Phoenix B- grades. Butler averaged 11.0 points in 34 Milwaukee games before his February 2014 buyout. Smith played 70 Suns games at 3.7 points and 2.6 assists, while Kravtsov played 20 at 1.0 point before his March waiver. Phoenix also cleared salary, its stated motive. Source perspectives disagree on the absolute grade level (B versus C+), so the displayed paired grades require later ledger reconciliation, but the original exchange warrants no decisive winner.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Milwaukee Bucks–Phoenix Suns: What the 2013-08-29 Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: On August 29, 2013 Phoenix traded Caron Butler to Milwaukee for Ish Smith and Viacheslav Kravtsov. Butler never played for the Suns after coming from the Clippers earlier that summer. He averaged 11.0 points across 34 Bucks games before a February 2014 waiver. Smith played 70 Suns games and Kravtsov 20, supplying reserve help for Phoenix. The even B-minus grades compare Milwaukee's shorter higher-scoring stint with Phoenix's two-player depth without borrowing games from other teams.

sections.heading: Butler Never Played for Phoenix Before His Wisconsin Homecoming
sections.body: The August 29, 2013 trade sent Caron Butler from Phoenix to Milwaukee for Ish Smith and Viacheslav Kravtsov. The Bucks' official announcement described a homecoming for the Racine, Wisconsin native, while the Suns confirmed the same two-player return. Butler had reached Phoenix in July through the separate Eric Bledsoe transaction with the Clippers but never played a Suns regular-season game. His earlier Clippers statistics therefore cannot be counted as Phoenix output from this exchange. Milwaukee obtained an established NBA scorer rather than draft rights or a future pick, and Phoenix received two players to fill reserve positions. The documented transaction had three players in two directions and no additional cash or draft asset established in the original announcements. The formal club statements are more useful than hindsight speculation about later roster decisions.

sections.heading: Butler Gave Milwaukee Thirty-Four Games Before His Waiver
sections.body: Butler averaged 11.0 points and 4.6 rebounds in 34 Bucks appearances during 2013-14, starting 13 games. His 38-point performance against Philadelphia in November illustrated the scoring burst Milwaukee hoped he could still provide, but injuries limited his broader availability. The Bucks formally requested waivers on February 27, 2014, less than six months after acquiring him. Butler's later time in Oklahoma City, Detroit and Sacramento was NBA service for other clubs, not additional value supplied to Milwaukee by Phoenix. At the 2013 trade date, Milwaukee could reasonably view a veteran wing with proven scoring ability as worth an opportunity; the completed result was a partial season rather than a multi-year anchor. Both the Bucks waiver release and season statistics bound that contribution.

sections.heading: Phoenix Collected Ninety Games from Smith and Kravtsov
sections.body: Smith made 70 Phoenix regular-season appearances in 2013-14, starting once while averaging 3.7 points and 2.6 assists in 14.4 minutes. He was a reserve ball-handler, not a replacement star scorer for the Suns. Kravtsov provided another 20 Phoenix appearances, giving the two-player return 90 combined games for their receiving team. That straightforward playing-time total is distinct from quality or starting impact: Butler had a larger individual scoring role during his shorter Bucks season. Smith later played for multiple other NBA teams, and Kravtsov had appeared for Detroit before the transaction; neither outside-club record belongs in the Phoenix return. The Suns received useful depth during a 48-win season, but their overall team success had many causes beyond this three-player exchange.

sections.heading: The B-Minus Tie Reflects a Limited, Different Kind of Return
sections.body: The inherited verdict labels the trade Even, with Milwaukee and Phoenix each graded B-minus. Milwaukee obtained 34 Butler games and an 11.0-point scoring average, while Phoenix received 70 Smith appearances and 20 from Kravtsov. That is a comparison between short-term veteran scoring and lower-volume reserve minutes spread across two players, not proof of two identical returns. Butler's February waiver prevented Milwaukee from converting a homecoming into sustained roster value, while the Suns had two usable but limited contributors. The source perspectives initially favored different absolute letter grades while agreeing there was no decisive relative winner. Keeping the saved B-minus pair recognizes the neutral relationship without manufacturing draft assets, assigning Phoenix credit for Butler's Clippers years, or transferring Smith's future performances into 2013-14.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Bucks B-minus, Suns B-minus as saved. Butler supplied 34 Milwaukee NBA appearances before the February 27, 2014 waiver. Phoenix received Smith for 70 reserve games and Kravtsov for 20 more. Butler had no Suns regular-season games, and his earlier Clippers service does not improve Phoenix's return. The three known original players supplied different kinds of short-term usefulness without sufficient direct value to justify a strong relative winner.

sections.heading: Washington Acquired a Veteran Forward for a Protected Second
sections.body: The July 9, 2015 transaction sent Jared Dudley from Milwaukee to Washington for a conditional 2020 second-round draft choice. Contemporary reporting had surfaced the agreement on July 2, but it could not be finalized until July 9. Dudley had exercised his $4.25 million player option for the final year of his Bucks contract, and the Wizards intended to absorb that salary through a trade exception. Washington had lost Paul Pierce and wanted an experienced forward who could shoot from outside. For Milwaukee the immediate return was not an active NBA player, but a protected future pick and flexibility after parting with a veteran. The deal should not be described as a direct Dudley-for-Elijah Hughes player swap: the pick existed years before its ultimate selection.

sections.heading: Dudley Played 81 Games and Shot 42 Percent From Three
sections.body: Washington's realized player return was substantial for a one-season acquisition. NBA's completed 2015–16 statistics credit Dudley with 81 regular-season appearances, including 41 starts, 7.9 points, 3.5 rebounds and 2.1 assists per game. He shot 42.0 percent from three-point range while spending roughly 26 minutes a night on the floor. Those numbers demonstrate an actual rotation contribution and justify treating the Wizards' received veteran as useful. They do not justify claiming that he rescued the club's season: Washington finished 41–41 and missed the playoffs, and Dudley departed in the following offseason. His later work for Phoenix and other franchises is distinct from the benefits Washington acquired on July 9.

sections.heading: Milwaukee's Pick Protections Changed in Later Transactions
sections.body: The 2020 second-round selection from Washington was initially protected in the top 55, making conveyance uncertain. In October 2018, the Bucks and Wizards modified the protection terms during a separate Jodie Meeks transaction. Milwaukee's own press release documents that later exchange of draft considerations, Meeks and cash. Another 2018 agreement involving Matthew Dellavedova and John Henson changed the rights again. Consequently the final 2020 slot should not be attributed to the original 2015 wording alone. This is a good example of why a future pick ledger needs chronology: the conditional right Dudley bought for Milwaukee was real, but its eventual terms and holder were modified through later independent trades.

sections.heading: The No. 39 Draft Right Ended Up With Utah
sections.body: The 2020 draft trail ultimately reached Elijah Hughes at the 39th overall selection. By draft night the pick had passed through additional transactions: Milwaukee sent the relevant second to New Orleans in the 2019 Nikola Mirotić trade package, and the Pelicans transferred Hughes' draft rights to the Utah Jazz in November 2020 for a future second and cash. NBA's official draft-night transaction tracker confirms Utah acquired Hughes at No. 39. Neither the Bucks nor the Wizards drafted Hughes through the original Dudley exchange. The archive's Wizards Win verdict, Washington B and Milwaukee D+ can stay while grade-specific review distinguishes Dudley's 81 Wizards games from Milwaukee's earlier conditional pick value and the later franchise transfers.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Stored verdict: Wizards Win — Washington B, Milwaukee D+. The Wizards got 81 games, 41 starts and 42.0 percent three-point shooting from Dudley. Milwaukee received a protected future second, not an immediate player. Protections and ownership changed later, and Elijah Hughes was ultimately acquired by Utah at No. 39 in 2020. Preserve the grades and all separate pick transactions.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Jared Dudley for a Conditional Second: One Season Versus a Five-Year Pick Chain
featuredDeepDive.intro: Washington pursued Jared Dudley in July 2015 as an experienced, versatile forward after Paul Pierce's departure. Milwaukee accepted a conditional 2020 second-round pick and moved the remaining season of Dudley's contract. Dudley gave Washington one productive rotation year. Five years later the originally protected draft right had been revised and traded again, ultimately becoming the No. 39 selection used on Elijah Hughes, whose rights went to Utah. The long pick path is not the same as a player drafted by Milwaukee.

sections.heading: Why the Deal Was Agreed Before It Became Official
sections.body: Reports dated July 2 said Washington and Milwaukee had agreed to swap Dudley for a future protected second-round selection, with the paperwork to follow once the offseason transaction window opened. Dudley's $4.25 million player option for 2015–16 had already been exercised. Washington could use a trade exception to take in that contract without sending an active player back, a flexibility point contemporary Washington reporting highlighted. The July 9 date is therefore the completed trade, not the date the rumors first surfaced. Dudley had been a regular for a Milwaukee team that made the 2015 playoffs, and the Wizards expected his shooting and experience to help replace some of the departed Pierce's versatility. The right Milwaukee took back was conditional, not a guaranteed 2020 draftee.

sections.heading: Washington Got Tangible Veteran Minutes, but Not a Playoff Appearance
sections.body: The most measurable direct return was Dudley's 2015–16 regular season. NBA.com lists 81 games and 41 starts with averages of 7.9 points, 3.5 rebounds and 2.1 assists. He converted 42.0 percent of his three-point attempts, giving Washington genuine floor spacing at forward. His role was important enough to include extensive starts, yet the team finished the year 41–41 outside the playoffs. That limits the size of any claim that the acquisition altered Washington's trajectory. The Wizards' B grade can be grounded in dependable one-year utility, while the choice not to extend that period belongs to subsequent roster decisions. No statistics for Dudley's later Phoenix or Los Angeles tenures should be attached to this Wizards trade.

sections.heading: The 2018 Revisions Prevent a Simple 2015-to-2020 Narrative
sections.body: Milwaukee's original return was described as a Washington-origin 2020 second protected among the top 55 selections. The Bucks and Wizards later revisited the condition in a separate October 2018 exchange that sent Jodie Meeks and additional considerations to Milwaukee. Milwaukee's own release provides primary documentation of that second transaction; the protection changes are more detailed in the archived NBA draft-pick transaction ledger. A December 2018 multiclub trade then reshaped Milwaukee's holdings again. As a result, the 2020 No. 39 outcome cannot be backdated as a guaranteed return specified in July 2015. A trade evaluator should separate the value of a conditional pick on acquisition, each later protection amendment and the final selection. Collapsing those events would exaggerate the precision of the original package.

sections.heading: Tracking the Selection to New Orleans and Utah
sections.body: Milwaukee subsequently included the relevant 2020 second-round right among its outgoing draft considerations in the February 2019 Nikola Mirotić acquisition, with New Orleans as the recipient. The Pelicans ultimately held the No. 39 pick at the 2020 draft and selected Syracuse guard Elijah Hughes. NBA's official transaction tracker and its dedicated Hughes trade report both identify a further move: the Pelicans sent Hughes' rights to Utah for a future second and cash. It would be misleading to count Hughes' eventual NBA appearances as a Bucks or Wizards return. The original Dudley trade gave Milwaukee a future contractual right, later managed through several different transactions. The archived Wizards Win, B and D+ grades are unchanged pending an independent outcome-led grade review of the full chronology.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Dudley was a genuine one-season Washington rotation player: 81 games, 41 starts and 42 percent shooting from deep. Milwaukee's protected second was a tradeable right whose protections changed and whose eventual No. 39 outcome went through New Orleans to Utah as Elijah Hughes. This was never a direct Dudley-for-Hughes exchange. The archive's Wizards Win, B/D+ result is preserved for source-led grading.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Bought a Starting Guard from a Disgruntled Team
sections.body: The Bucks acquired Eric Bledsoe from Phoenix on November 7, 2017 in exchange for Greg Monroe and two protected draft choices. Bledsoe had publicly expressed frustration with the Suns and had been held away from their games, leaving Phoenix to negotiate from a weakened position. Milwaukee gave up no core starter besides its frontcourt reserve. Adding an established attacking guard beside Giannis Antetokounmpo was a direct roster upgrade, but the protections on the incoming Phoenix picks still gave the Suns a real future claim.

sections.heading: Bledsoe Delivered Defense and Regular-Season Value
sections.body: Bledsoe helped Milwaukee’s guard rotation over the next three seasons and earned NBA All-Defensive recognition. He could pressure the ball and attack the rim, advantages the Bucks needed while the roster developed into a top regular-season team. Postseason offensive limitations were also real, particularly when opponents crowded his drives and challenged his outside shooting. The grade should recognize both sides rather than treating a strong regular season as proof that Bledsoe solved every late-round playoff problem.

sections.heading: Phoenix Eventually Converted the First-Round Asset
sections.body: Monroe was a short-term Suns player and the protected 2018 second-rounder never conveyed. Milwaukee’s first-round obligation ultimately conveyed as the 2020 No. 30 pick. Phoenix had already traded that pick to Boston in July 2019 for Aron Baynes and the draft rights to Ty Jerome. Boston later held the selection used on Desmond Bane before moving his rights to Memphis. It would be inaccurate to credit Phoenix with Bane’s career; the Suns’ actual trade return was Monroe plus a pick they converted into Baynes and Jerome.

sections.heading: The Jrue Holiday Chain Needs the Right Accounting
sections.body: Milwaukee sent Bledsoe as part of its later package to acquire Jrue Holiday. That demonstrates Bledsoe retained transaction value, but the Holiday deal also involved other players and major draft compensation. Holiday’s entire impact cannot be awarded to the original Bledsoe acquisition. The Bucks’ A reflects multiple seasons of capable guard play at a distressed-market price. Phoenix’s B-minus reflects an expiring Monroe contract and the real value obtained from the protected first, even though it lost the more productive player in 2017.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win — Milwaukee A, Phoenix B-minus. Bledsoe became a valuable regular-season guard and All-Defensive performer, despite his playoff struggles. Phoenix recovered Greg Monroe and a protected first-round choice that it later used to acquire Aron Baynes and Ty Jerome. Bledsoe’s part in the eventual Holiday package is relevant, but that later return required substantial additional Milwaukee assets.
