sections.heading: Phoenix Bought a Defensive Forward for Cash
sections.body: Phoenix acquired Torrey Craig from Milwaukee on March 18, 2021, sending cash considerations in return. The Bucks' official announcement confirms a straight cash transaction; Basketball-Reference records a traded-player exception on Milwaukee's side as the cap-accounting result. Those are not the same as Milwaukee receiving an unreported draft choice or a Suns rotation player. Craig had played only 18 games for the Bucks during his first season in Milwaukee, so Phoenix was buying a player with limited current exposure but a longer Denver playoff résumé. The Suns, led by Chris Paul and Devin Booker, wanted more size and flexible wing defense for the postseason. The original deal was unusually inexpensive in basketball assets, and that acquisition cost is essential to the later Phoenix grade.

sections.heading: Craig Went From Eighteen Bucks Games to Thirty-Two Suns Games
sections.body: Milwaukee had used Craig for 18 games in 2020-21, without a start, averaging 2.5 points over 11.2 minutes per appearance. Phoenix then played him in 32 regular-season contests, giving him eight starts and 18.8 minutes per game. He averaged 7.2 points and 4.8 rebounds for the Suns, shooting 50.3 percent from the field. Those are immediate, concrete contributions following the March trade rather than projected defensive value or statistics borrowed from his earlier Denver seasons. The Suns acquired a playable bench forward for cash while the Bucks had not found a larger role for him. The difference in minutes and playing time gives the Suns Win verdict a clear basketball foundation without requiring Craig to become an All-Star.

sections.heading: Phoenix Used Craig During Its First Finals Run in Twenty-Eight Years
sections.body: Craig stayed in Phoenix's playoff rotation as the Suns reached the 2021 NBA Finals. His responsibilities included defending larger wings, rebounding and giving coach Monty Williams lineup flexibility around the starting five. A knee contusion forced him out of the second Finals game against Milwaukee after a collision with Giannis Antetokounmpo; NBA.com documented the injury and his 32-game Phoenix regular season. The Suns eventually lost the series four games to two to the Bucks, a striking outcome because Craig had been on Milwaukee's roster earlier that season. Losing the championship did not erase his contributions to the Phoenix postseason run. The 2021 Finals appearance illustrates why acquiring an established defender for cash was useful even without a title or a long-term contract guarantee.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Received Financial Consideration, Not Craig's Later Minutes
sections.body: Milwaukee's side of the exchange was cash plus a trade exception recorded in the NBA transaction ledger. The official release did not disclose an exact dollar figure, so the trade analysis should not invent one. The Bucks also avoided continuing to carry a little-used reserve forward. They made a separate trade the following day to acquire P.J. Tucker from Houston, but that multi-asset agreement was not what Phoenix sent for Craig. The Bucks went on to defeat Craig's Suns in the 2021 Finals, yet their championship cannot be counted as a direct return from the March 18 cash trade. The C-plus grade can reflect roster flexibility and payment received, while the immediate basketball production from Craig accrued to Phoenix. Keeping those two value categories separate prevents overstatement.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Suns Win — Phoenix A-, Milwaukee C+. The Bucks received cash and a trade exception for Craig; the amount was undisclosed. Craig played 32 Phoenix games (eight starts) at 7.2 points and 4.8 rebounds after only 18 low-minute Milwaukee games, and helped the Suns reach the NBA Finals. Milwaukee separately won the championship, not as direct return for this transaction.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Torrey Craig to Phoenix: The 2021 Cash Deal and Finals Matchup
featuredDeepDive.intro: The March 2021 cash trade gave Phoenix 32 Craig games and a defender for its Finals run, while Milwaukee received financial consideration and cap flexibility. The two clubs then met for the title.

sections.heading: The Suns Identified a Role Milwaukee Had Not Used Much
sections.body: Craig arrived in Phoenix after playing 18 Milwaukee games with no starts. He had previously built a reputation for defensive work over three Denver seasons and had played in every Nuggets postseason game across 2019 and 2020, according to the Suns' official acquisition release. Phoenix did not ask him to create shots as a primary scorer; it wanted size, rebounding and versatility from the bench. He responded with 32 regular-season games, eight starts and averages of 7.2 points and 4.8 rebounds. That is a specific role conversion, not merely a roster-transaction entry. For a cash-only acquisition in terms of outgoing playing assets, the immediate production was valuable. The high Phoenix grade is best defended with these actual minutes and a postseason contribution rather than by calling the winger a franchise player.

sections.heading: The Finals Created an Unusual Opposing-Team Story
sections.body: Craig was on the Bucks early in 2020-21 and on the Suns when the two teams played for the title that July. He helped Phoenix advance through the Western Conference before facing the franchise that had traded him. In Game 2, he injured his right knee while taking a charge from Antetokounmpo, with an official NBA injury update reporting he could not return. Phoenix ultimately lost the Finals in six games. That result makes the retrospective interesting but cannot be reduced to the claim Craig was the reason one team won or lost the series. He was a useful reserve defender for a contender, and his role was larger in Phoenix than in Milwaukee. The trade therefore has identifiable on-court value and a notable playoff storyline without requiring fabricated championship credit.

sections.heading: The Trade Exception Was a Cap Instrument
sections.body: The Milwaukee transaction history lists cash and a trade exception in the March 18, 2021 deal. A traded-player exception is a salary-cap mechanism that can create future flexibility within league rules; it is not automatically an active player, a first-round draft pick or proof of a later acquisition. The Bucks' own news release identifies the consideration as cash and gives Craig's 18-game Milwaukee statistics. That public statement provides no amount for the payment. Treating the exception as a fully realized new star would distort the historical grade. Likewise, Milwaukee's next-day P.J. Tucker trade involved other players and draft selections and should be evaluated separately. The C-plus return is a limited financial and roster benefit, while Phoenix's acquired defender produced actual playing minutes during the same season.

sections.heading: Why Phoenix A-Minus and Milwaukee C-Plus Fit
sections.body: The original ledger favors Phoenix with an A-minus over Milwaukee's C-plus and calls the transaction Suns Win. The evidence supports the direction: Craig played 32 Suns games with eight starts after producing 18 low-minute Bucks games, and Phoenix used him in a run to the NBA Finals. Milwaukee received cash and cap flexibility rather than a replacement player. The margin is best explained by a defender immediately filling a team need at minimal outgoing basketball cost. It does not imply that Milwaukee lost its chance to win a championship, because the Bucks did win the 2021 title against Phoenix. Nor does the Suns grade require claiming Craig remained a multi-year starter. A sound retrospective credits the direct minutes, documented cash arrangement and playoff usage while keeping unrelated Milwaukee moves separate.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Phoenix A-minus, Milwaukee C-plus in the preserved Suns Win assessment. Craig delivered 32 Suns games and a playoff defensive role for cash consideration. The Bucks had used him in 18 games, then gained payment and cap flexibility. The separate P.J. Tucker acquisition and later Milwaukee title were not assets transferred by Phoenix.

sections.heading: Scott Brooks for Pick No. 32: Why Sources Differ by One Day
sections.body: Transaction ledgers date the Scott Brooks deal June 25, 1990, when Minnesota sent Philadelphia a 1990 second-round draft selection. A contemporary Associated Press report published by the Los Angeles Times on June 27 describes the trade as occurring on Tuesday, June 26. The one-day discrepancy does not establish two separate moves, and the canonical historical transaction date is left unchanged. Philadelphia used that No. 32 pick in the June 27 draft on Georgia Tech guard Brian Oliver. This was not a trade in which Minnesota received Brian Oliver or gave up a first-round selection. Brooks was already an NBA reserve coming off two Philadelphia seasons and could join Minnesota immediately. Philadelphia obtained a fresh backcourt prospect rather than another NBA veteran, exchanging proven backup experience for the opportunity to develop a player from the 1990 draft.

sections.heading: Brooks Played 162 Timberwolves Games in Two Seasons
sections.body: Brooks became a regular reserve guard for Minnesota in 1990-91 and 1991-92, appearing in 80 and 82 games, respectively, with no starts in either season. He averaged 5.3 points and 2.6 assists during the first year, then 5.1 points and 2.5 assists during the second. His combined 162 Timberwolves appearances gave a young organization genuine backcourt stability without requiring a star role from the acquisition. The franchise did not reach the playoffs during his time there, so the return cannot be described as a championship-making move. Brooks subsequently left for Houston; his later Rockets title as a player and eventual coaching success were not contributions to the Minnesota team that acquired him in June 1990.

sections.heading: Oliver Delivered 107 Philadelphia Games From the Pick
sections.body: The second-round pick was a real Philadelphia basketball return. The 76ers drafted Brian Oliver at No. 32 on June 27, 1990 and played him in 73 regular-season games during 1990-91 and another 34 games in 1991-92. Oliver made four starts across the two seasons and scored 279 points as a rookie, averaging roughly 3.8 per game. That 107-game Philadelphia tenure is a verifiable outcome from the Minnesota-origin selection, not a pick the 76ers immediately discarded. He later appeared for Washington and Atlanta, but those additional NBA games are not Philadelphia production from the 1990 trade. The inherited C-plus for Philadelphia should recognize this limited yet substantial rookie-contract playing time rather than claiming the draft return never made an NBA appearance.

sections.heading: Why Scott Brooks Gave Minnesota a Better Two-Season Return
sections.body: The Wolves Win verdict grades Minnesota B-plus and Philadelphia C-plus. Scott Brooks appeared in 80 games in 1990-91 and 82 in 1991-92 as a Timberwolves reserve, giving the franchise 162 appearances with modest scoring and steady playmaking. Philadelphia used its acquired No. 32 draft choice on Brian Oliver, who provided 73 games as a rookie and another 34 the next season, or 107 Sixers games. The 55-appearance gap alone is not a definitive valuation, but the Timberwolves received more regular playing time from an already established reserve. Philadelphia did receive an actual NBA contributor rather than an unused pick. Brooks's later Houston championship and coaching career, like Oliver's appearances for other clubs, are not returns from this particular 1990 trade. The original grades recognize that narrower receiving-team difference, not an All-Star or a championship acquired by either team in June 1990.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wolves Win — Minnesota B-plus, Philadelphia C-plus. Brooks supplied 162 Minnesota reserve-guard appearances over 1990-91 and 1991-92, with 5.3 and 5.1 points per game. The 76ers exercised the outgoing second at No. 32 on Brian Oliver, who appeared in 107 Philadelphia games across two seasons. The exchange produced usable NBA minutes on both sides, with Minnesota receiving steadier two-year guard availability.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Minnesota Timberwolves–Philadelphia 76ers: What the 1990-06-25 Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: On June 25, 1990 Minnesota acquired reserve guard Scott Brooks from Philadelphia in exchange for a second-round pick that the 76ers used two days later at No. 32 on Brian Oliver. Brooks appeared in 80 and 82 Minnesota games over the next two seasons. Oliver gave Philadelphia 73 and 34 appearances in those same seasons. This case evaluates that direct two-year club-specific return without assigning later Rockets championships or coaching accomplishments to the original Timberwolves acquisition.

sections.heading: The Selection Became Oliver Two Days After the Trade
sections.body: The June 25, 1990 exchange sent Scott Brooks to Minnesota and a 1990 second-round right to Philadelphia. The 76ers exercised that choice at No. 32 on June 27 for Brian Oliver, a Georgia Tech guard who had played alongside several well-known college teammates. The draft choice had not yet turned into an NBA player when the clubs agreed on the original transaction. Minnesota was trading a future selection rather than selecting Oliver on Philadelphia's behalf, while the Sixers were giving up a backup who had already logged 82 games in 1988-89 and 72 in 1989-90 for their club. The timing clarifies what each front office could assess in 1990 and prevents later coaching or player career accomplishments from being assigned to the wrong franchise.

sections.heading: Brooks Gave the Timberwolves Two Full Reserve-Guard Years
sections.body: Minnesota obtained Brooks as an experienced point guard and used him in 80 games in 1990-91, followed by all 82 games the next season. He started none of them, serving primarily as a reserve ball handler. His first-year averages were 5.3 points and 2.6 assists in 12.3 minutes, while the second year brought 5.1 points and 2.5 assists in 13.2 minutes. Those are actual club-specific games after the acquisition, not a projection based on his earlier Philadelphia success. The Timberwolves were still establishing their NBA identity and needed depth, which makes two steady reserve seasons a meaningful return even though Brooks did not become an All-Star or a long-term franchise starter.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Drafted a Guard Who Played 73 Plus 34 Games
sections.body: Oliver joined the 76ers as the No. 32 selection and appeared in 73 games during his rookie season, then 34 in 1991-92. He started four of the 107 Philadelphia appearances and supplied 279 points in 800 minutes in 1990-91, with fewer minutes in the second season. The result was modest NBA rotation depth rather than zero playing value from a late second-round draft choice. Oliver later continued his professional basketball career elsewhere, including additional NBA appearances with Washington and Atlanta. Those later franchises' outcomes belong to those separate opportunities, not to the 76ers. Philadelphia's incoming asset therefore had a traceable draft identity and actual team minutes that should be accounted for alongside the stronger two-season Minnesota guard return.

sections.heading: Why B-Plus Versus C-Plus Is a Narrow Basketball Distinction
sections.body: Minnesota's B-plus and Philadelphia's C-plus preserve the archive's Wolves Win verdict. Brooks gave the Timberwolves 162 reserve appearances over two complete regular seasons without a starting assignment, while the 76ers developed the acquired No. 32 selection into 107 Brian Oliver appearances. Both clubs could point to practical bench production from their return. Brooks offered Minnesota more regular availability and a veteran playmaking role; Oliver provided Philadelphia younger guard depth with limited scoring impact. Neither side obtained a top-of-the-league player or a franchise-defining postseason run. The game totals, pick route and historically dated transaction lists support a modest Minnesota advantage without suggesting Oliver never played for Philadelphia or making Scott Brooks' later achievements in Houston an original Timberwolves result.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Minnesota B-plus versus Philadelphia C-plus produces the stored Wolves Win verdict. Brooks played 80+82 Timberwolves games across the first two seasons after the June 1990 trade, while Philadelphia drafted Brian Oliver at No. 32 and used him in 73+34 Sixers games. Both returns were identifiable reserve basketball contributions, not a nonexistent Philadelphia selection or an All-Star acquisition. The grades favor Minnesota's longer guard service without attributing later career achievements to the wrong club.

sections.heading: Minnesota Chose Thornton Over a Later Selection
sections.body: On November 10, 1990, the expansion-era Timberwolves acquired Bob Thornton from Philadelphia. The 76ers received a 1991 second-round pick. That choice eventually fell at No. 44, where the selection became Alvaro Teheran. This was a trade between an identifiable player available in the current season and the uncertainty of a future second-rounder. Neither side surrendered a marquee starter or a lottery selection.

sections.heading: The Teams Were Buying Different Kinds of Depth
sections.body: Thornton offered Minnesota an experienced frontcourt body while the club was still assembling an NBA roster. Philadelphia accepted the chance to make another selection the following summer. The draft pick can be tracked to Teheran, but the transaction record supplies no foundation for attributing unrelated Philadelphia roster successes to it. The basketball question is whether immediate depth or a No. 44 choice yielded a more durable, identifiable return.

sections.heading: Why Neither Side Receives a Clear Advantage
sections.body: Minnesota and Philadelphia are each graded B-minus. The Wolves secured Thornton without giving up a premium pick, while the 76ers obtained an additional second-round opportunity. The record identifies the draft conversion precisely but does not establish the kind of later impact that would justify claiming Philadelphia clearly won. Minnesota likewise did not acquire a transformational contributor. This is a modest depth-for-draft choice that fits the same grade on both sides.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Minnesota B-minus, Philadelphia B-minus. Bob Thornton gave the Timberwolves a current roster option, while the 76ers received the 1991 No. 44 selection used on Alvaro Teheran. With no documented standout advantage from those assets, the trade grades recognize a broadly balanced exchange.

sections.heading: Draft-Day 1993 Exchanged a Young Center for a Veteran Big
sections.body: On June 30, 1993, Minnesota sent center Felton Spencer to Utah in a direct exchange for Mike Brown. Both the NBA's 1992-93 transactions ledger and contemporary Deseret News reporting confirm that it was a one-for-one deal with no pick or cash attached. Brown, then a seven-year veteran, had filled backup frontcourt minutes for the Jazz and entered the trade after dealing with bone spurs in his foot. Spencer was a 25-year-old former No. 6 overall Minnesota selection with three NBA seasons behind him. Utah was acquiring a younger seven-footer for its interior rotation; Minnesota took the more established veteran to stabilize its own center group.

sections.heading: Utah Got Seventy-Nine Starts and Eight-Plus Rebounds Immediately
sections.body: Spencer stepped into a substantial role with the 1993-94 Jazz, starting all 79 games he played, averaging 28.0 minutes, 8.6 points and 8.3 rebounds. Those totals represent a major increase from his final Minnesota season, when he averaged 18.3 minutes, 4.1 points and 4.6 rebounds in 71 games. Utah needed a working center alongside its established Karl Malone–John Stockton core, and Spencer supplied regular starts rather than speculative rights or a short cameo. He continued to appear for the Jazz in later seasons, including 34 starts in 1994-95 and 70 starts in 1995-96. The return was directly useful even without projecting other team achievements onto him.

sections.heading: Brown Played Every Minnesota Game in His First Season
sections.body: Minnesota did receive real basketball from Brown, so an evaluation should not reduce the return to his age or earlier foot problem. During 1993-94 he appeared in all 82 Timberwolves games and made 40 starts, averaging 23.4 minutes, 3.6 points and 5.5 rebounds. His low scoring fits a reserve-and-spot-starter center, but the defensive rebounding and availability had concrete value to a struggling club. That season Minnesota won only 20 games, an outcome for the entire roster rather than an individual verdict on Brown. In 1994-95 his Minnesota role contracted to 27 appearances and no starts, making the direct longer-term return weaker than Spencer's subsequent Utah work.

sections.heading: Why Utah's B-Plus Versus Minnesota's C-Plus Is Preserved
sections.body: The historical trade ledger calls this Jazz Win, with Utah B-plus and Minnesota C-plus, and those marks are preserved unchanged. In their first posttrade seasons, Spencer started 79 games and averaged 8.3 rebounds for the Jazz; Brown played all 82 games for Minnesota but started 40 and scored 3.6 points per game. Brown remained a useful physical reserve, yet the Utah acquisition grew into a more regular starting center with additional seasons of team control. Those direct role differences offer a factual basis for the stored preference. The grade spread is an editorial appraisal, not a claim that all Jazz playoff achievements stemmed from one June 1993 exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Jazz Win is preserved, Utah B-plus and Minnesota C-plus. The June 30, 1993 deal was Felton Spencer for Mike Brown, without other assets. Spencer started 79 games for Utah in 1993-94 at 8.6 points and 8.3 rebounds and continued starting in later Jazz seasons. Brown gave Minnesota 82 games and 40 starts that first year but just 27 appearances the next. The deeper and longer Utah center role explains the recorded historical preference.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Felton Spencer for Mike Brown: Utah's June 1993 Center Upgrade
featuredDeepDive.intro: On June 30, 1993, Utah swapped Mike Brown for former Minnesota lottery center Felton Spencer. Brad Rock's contemporary report establishes the direct exchange and the distinct experience levels. The next season provides the clearest test: Spencer started all 79 Utah appearances, while Brown played all 82 Minnesota games but started 40. The different longer-term roles offer a traceable basis for Utah's retained B-plus over Minnesota's C-plus.

sections.heading: The 1993 Newspaper Record Fixes the Deal's Original Context
sections.body: Contemporary reporting is unusually helpful for this old transaction. Brad Rock's June 30, 1993 Deseret News account identifies Brown as the outgoing Jazz veteran and Spencer as the young Timberwolves center, explicitly describing an exchange rather than a sale or draft-rights swap. It reports Brown's foot bone spurs, his 5.7 points and 4.7 rebounds in Utah the preceding season, and Spencer's 71 Minnesota appearances. Those details show why each front office might have been open to changing its reserve and starter mix without requiring later speculation about an unseen pick. The independent NBA transactions list records the same one-for-one exchange on the same date.

sections.heading: Spencer Filled a High-Usage Center Slot in Utah
sections.body: Spencer's posttrade 1993-94 line supplies the clearest single-season evidence for the deal: 79 appearances, 79 starts, 28.0 minutes and 8.3 rebounds per game. At that time Utah had veteran stars who carried the scoring and passing load; Spencer did not have to become the primary offensive option to be valuable. He averaged 8.6 points while providing traditional rebounding and interior size. His next two Jazz seasons included 34 and 70 starts, although health and role affected minutes. This was an acquired center who spent multiple years in Utah's rotation, not an expiring asset that left after a brief trial. The substantial minutes should anchor the direct trade comparison.

sections.heading: Brown's Minnesota Workload Was Useful but Short-Lived
sections.body: Brown played all 82 games for the 1993-94 Timberwolves and earned 40 starts, confirming that Minnesota bought a serviceable veteran rather than merely a contract. He delivered 5.5 rebounds in 23.4 minutes but only 3.6 points per game, a limited offensive contribution. By 1994-95 he appeared in 27 Minnesota games and started none, with a sharply reduced role. The comparison therefore should not be made on a single abstract basketball grade: it contains one season of high availability followed by marginal use for Brown versus a multi-season starting role for Spencer in Utah. Minnesota's 20-win 1993-94 record is context and cannot substitute for assessing the individual return.

sections.heading: What the Grade Difference Does and Does Not Establish
sections.body: A one-for-one swap makes downstream attribution straightforward. Utah received the player named Felton Spencer; Minnesota received Mike Brown. The NBA's historical transaction record contains no extra pick or cash, and neither team's later drafting should be smuggled into the ledger. The existing Jazz Win, Utah B-plus and Minnesota C-plus marks align with Spencer's larger starting role in his first Utah season and longer continuation there. Brown's full 82-game first Minnesota campaign deserves its own acknowledgement, so this was not zero value on the losing side. The letter grades are retained as published; the sourced games and roles let readers evaluate the original judgment without generic assertions about flexibility.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The retained outcome is Jazz Win, Utah B-plus and Minnesota C-plus. The teams exchanged Spencer and Brown one-for-one, with no other asset in the historical transaction ledger. Utah obtained a 7-foot center who played 79 games and started every one in 1993-94, averaging 8.6 points and 8.3 rebounds, then held further seasons of starting-center service. Brown offered Minnesota 82 games and 40 starts immediately, although his scoring was modest at 3.6 points per game and his role decreased to 27 games in 1994-95. These direct on-court roles support the historical edge without granting the acquisition credit for all of Utah's broader team results. Contemporary coverage records Brown's bone-spur struggles and the original trade-day rationale, keeping the retrospective anchored in documented conditions.

sections.heading: A Former Lottery Pick Went to Phoenix
sections.body: Minnesota sent Nikoloz Tskitishvili to the Suns on January 26, 2006, receiving a 2006 second-round selection. The asset was eventually the No. 57 pick, used on Loukas Mavrokefalidis. Tskitishvili had entered the league as a highly drafted prospect but had not developed into a dependable frontcourt contributor. Phoenix acquired a player it could evaluate immediately; Minnesota moved the uncertainty to the upcoming draft.

sections.heading: The No. 57 Selection Was Not an Immediate Rotation Player
sections.body: Mavrokefalidis represented the kind of low-cost international prospect a club can pursue late in the second round, but the acquisition of those draft rights did not deliver a proven new Timberwolves starter. Phoenix, meanwhile, took on the possibility that a change of team could help Tskitishvili find a role. Neither asset matched the practical certainty of acquiring a productive veteran. The exact pick number helps explain the limited upside available to Minnesota.

sections.heading: Equal C-plus Grades Reflect the Limited Results
sections.body: Both clubs receive C-plus because this was a speculative swap, not a major redistribution of starting talent. Minnesota gained control of a specific late draft choice; Phoenix acquired a young former lottery selection whose NBA results had fallen short of his original draft position. No material later asset chain is documented in the paired transaction sources. Calling either franchise a decisive winner would require more demonstrated basketball value than the record supplies.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Minnesota C-plus, Phoenix C-plus. The Wolves received the No. 57 pick in 2006, used on Loukas Mavrokefalidis; the Suns acquired Nikoloz Tskitishvili. Both sides exchanged speculative assets without securing a documented difference in lasting NBA contribution substantial enough to support separate grades.

sections.heading: Portland Identified the Ready-Made Guard Its Rebuild Needed
sections.body: Portland’s draft-night move was a bet on immediate translation rather than distant upside. Roy entered the NBA from the University of Washington as a polished ballhandler, midrange scorer and decision-maker who could organize an offense from either guard spot. The Trail Blazers had begun rebuilding around young talent and needed a dependable perimeter leader more than another developmental project. He won Rookie of the Year, quickly became the face of the franchise and helped Portland return to the playoffs after several difficult seasons. That immediate alignment between player readiness and organizational need gave Portland value before the full star trajectory was known. Minnesota received a useful prospect, but the Timberwolves moved away from the player whose temperament and skill set most directly solved Portland’s problems. Minnesota had selected Roy sixth overall in the 2006 draft and transferred his rights to Portland for No. 7 choice Randy Foye and cash. Roy then averaged 16.8 points in 57 rookie games and won Rookie of the Year, providing immediate evidence that the Blazers' scouting judgment had translated to the NBA.

sections.heading: Minnesota Preferred Foye’s Athletic Scoring Profile
sections.body: Minnesota’s side was built around Randy Foye, selected one spot after Roy. Foye was a powerful combo guard with scoring bursts, three-point range and the athletic profile to play beside Kevin Garnett. The Timberwolves believed his upside and age fit their roster, and the swap also included cash. Foye became a starter and produced his best Minnesota season in 2008-09, showing that the organization did not receive an empty return. The issue was not that Foye could not play; it was that Roy developed into a substantially better creator and late-game option almost immediately. The Timberwolves’ evaluation produced a rotation guard, while Portland’s produced a franchise centerpiece. Foye's best Minnesota regular season was 2008-09, when he started 61 games and averaged 16.3 points and 4.3 assists. That is meaningful lottery-pick output, even if it never approached the All-NBA peak Roy delivered a few miles away in draft position.

sections.heading: Roy Became an All-Star Before Injuries Changed the Story
sections.body: Roy’s first three healthy seasons established the top end of the trade. He became a three-time All-Star, made two All-NBA teams and led a young Portland group to fifty-four wins in 2008-09. His pacing, footwork and shot creation gave the Trail Blazers a stable offensive identity, especially in close games. Knee degeneration then reduced his availability and forced an early retirement, preventing the transaction from delivering a decade of star play. The injury belongs in the grade because realized durability matters, but it cannot erase the elite seasons Portland did receive. Minnesota never obtained a comparable peak from Foye, even though Roy’s career ended far earlier than expected. In the Blazers' 54-win 2008-09 season, Roy played 78 games at 22.6 points, 5.1 assists and 4.7 rebounds, earning All-NBA Second Team recognition. Those figures describe actual value delivered before chronic knee problems reduced his playing time.

sections.heading: Foye Produced but Never Matched Roy’s Peak
sections.body: Foye’s Minnesota tenure was respectable and should be graded accordingly. He averaged double figures, handled significant minutes and improved as a shooter, but he did not become the primary creator the Timberwolves needed as Garnett’s era ended. His role shifted between point guard and shooting guard without producing a lasting positional answer. After three seasons, Minnesota packaged Foye and Mike Miller to Washington for the No. 5 pick in the 2009 draft. That trade preserved some residual value and prevents a failing grade, because Foye helped create the asset that became Ricky Rubio. Even with that continuation, Minnesota’s direct return did not approach Roy’s All-NBA impact or Portland’s rapid competitive revival. Washington's June 24, 2009 deal sent its No. 5 pick, Etan Thomas, Darius Songaila and Oleksiy Pecherov to Minnesota for both Foye and Mike Miller. Rubio was selected with that pick the next day; he cannot be represented as a straight one-for-one return on Foye.

sections.heading: The Later Rubio Pick Softened Minnesota’s Loss
sections.body: The Rubio conversion is the strongest argument for narrowing Portland’s margin. Minnesota did not simply lose Foye for nothing. By moving him with Miller, the Timberwolves acquired the fifth pick and selected Rubio, who later became a long-term starter, gifted passer and important franchise figure. That downstream result gives the original Foye asset a meaningful second life beyond his own Minnesota production. Still, the chain required additional value in Miller, years of waiting and another major decision before Rubio reached the court. Portland’s Roy value was direct and immediate, while Minnesota’s best outcome depended on a later package rather than Foye alone. Rubio, the No. 5 selection, did not start his NBA career until 2011-12, two seasons after the 2009 trade. The time gap, the inclusion of Miller and Washington's three outgoing contracts all limit how much of that later return can be attributed to the 2006 pick swap.

sections.heading: Portland Still Won Despite the Shortened Career
sections.body: Portland’s A-plus reflects how much value Roy generated before his knees failed. The Trail Blazers acquired a star without surrendering an established player or additional first-round capital, and Roy helped change the franchise’s credibility, record and culture. His 2011 playoff comeback against Dallas became a final reminder of the player Portland had briefly possessed. The shortened career limits the lifetime totals but not the quality of the acquisition. Minnesota earns B-minus because Foye contributed and later helped produce Rubio, not because the initial player comparison was close. The verdict remains Trail Blazers Win because Portland captured the rare star outcome at essentially the same draft slot. Roy's April 2011 first-round Game 4 against Dallas supplied one last memorable playoff return: 18 fourth-quarter points to overcome an 18-point deficit entering the period. The subsequent injury-shortened ending did not take away his Rookie of the Year, three All-Star selections or two All-NBA honors.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Trail Blazers Win. Portland exchanged Randy Foye’s rights and cash for Brandon Roy, who became Rookie of the Year, a three-time All-Star and the leader of a fifty-four-win team before knee injuries shortened his career. Minnesota received useful play from Foye and later included him in the deal that produced Ricky Rubio, which earns B-minus. Portland’s star peak still merits A-plus.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Brandon Roy’s Short Prime Still Created Lasting Franchise Value
featuredDeepDive.intro: The trade is a useful test of how injuries should affect retrospective grading. Roy did not provide the decade Portland expected, yet his healthy seasons delivered a level of play, leadership and organizational renewal that Minnesota never received from Foye. The correct evaluation must count both the brilliance and the abrupt ending.

sections.heading: Roy Changed Portland’s Timeline Immediately
sections.body: Portland had endured a prolonged transition and needed a player capable of making the young roster coherent. Roy became that player almost at once. He controlled tempo, accepted difficult possessions and gave teammates a reliable organizer in the final minutes. His presence allowed LaMarcus Aldridge and the rest of the developing core to grow within a competitive structure. The Trail Blazers improved from twenty-one wins before his arrival to forty-one in his second season and then fifty-four in his third. That acceleration is transaction value, not merely an appealing narrative, because it changed playoff expectations and validated the rebuild. Minnesota’s Foye years did not produce a similar organizational shift. The team-record progression is concrete: Portland won 21 games in 2005-06, reached 41 in Roy's second season and went 54-28 in 2008-09. Roy did not cause every improvement alone, but a second-year All-Star who later made All-NBA Second Team was central to the change in the Blazers' offensive structure.

sections.heading: His Late-Game Skill Was More Valuable Than Raw Athleticism
sections.body: Foye’s athleticism and scoring potential were understandable attractions, but Roy’s game proved more scalable. Roy did not depend on overwhelming speed. He used balance, change of pace, strength and advanced reads to create efficient shots for himself and others. Those tools translated against playoff defenses and in late-clock situations. Foye could score in stretches, yet his tweener role made it harder to build an offense around him. Portland’s evaluation succeeded because it prioritized functional basketball skill over the more obvious physical profile. The gap between a useful combo guard and a dependable primary initiator became the central difference between the returns. Roy's 2008-09 line was 22.6 points and 5.1 assists across 78 games; Foye averaged 16.3 and 4.3 in his strongest Minnesota season. Both could create offense, but only one became the leading guard of a 54-win playoff team.

sections.heading: The 2008-09 Season Captured the Trade’s Ceiling
sections.body: The 2008-09 Trail Blazers won fifty-four games with Roy as an All-NBA centerpiece. He averaged more than twenty points, handled the hardest perimeter assignments on offense and guided one of the league’s youngest successful teams. Portland lost in the first round, but the season established a plausible championship trajectory built around Roy and Aldridge. That competitive peak matters because stars are acquired to create windows, even when those windows later close unexpectedly. Minnesota’s return never generated a comparable season with Foye as a central figure. The trade therefore produced a clear top-end winner before injuries complicated the long-term trade details. Roy earned Second Team All-NBA in 2008-09 and Third Team in 2009-10, following his Rookie of the Year season and a three-year run of All-Star selections. The measurable prime was compressed, not imaginary, and is why Portland's early return deserves an elite grade without projecting future seasons he never played.

sections.heading: Knee Risk Limits the Grade Less Than It Limits the Career
sections.body: Roy’s knees were not a minor footnote; they ended the expected value stream. Portland eventually used the amnesty provision on his contract, and his attempted comeback elsewhere could not restore the player he had been. A purely career-total comparison would therefore reduce the grade sharply. Trade grading should also recognize that Portland received multiple elite seasons on a rookie-scale contract before the decline. The injury was devastating but did not make the original acquisition ineffective. That balance is why Portland earns A-plus rather than a hypothetical perfect score unconstrained by durability. His subsequent 2012-13 attempt with Minnesota lasted only five games at 5.8 points per game. That comeback confirms the physical decline rather than adding a second star chapter, but it occurred years after Portland had already received its 54-win All-NBA season.

sections.heading: Minnesota’s Asset Chain Deserves Real Credit
sections.body: Minnesota’s B-minus recognizes that Foye retained enough value to help acquire Rubio. Rubio’s arrival gave the Timberwolves years of playmaking, defense and connection with the fan base. The chain demonstrates why outgoing assets should be followed beyond their first stop when the later conversion is direct and documented. At the same time, Mike Miller was part of the package, so Rubio cannot be credited entirely to Foye. The Timberwolves salvaged a meaningful outcome but did not recreate the star Portland obtained. The downstream success narrows the grade gap without changing the verdict. On June 24, 2009, the Wizards sent Minnesota the fifth pick plus Etan Thomas, Darius Songaila and Oleksiy Pecherov for Foye and Miller. Rubio arrived in the NBA in 2011-12 after being drafted fifth; that staggered, multi-asset sequence is the actual route through which part of Foye's retained value reached another Minnesota core.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Roy’s career ended too soon, but Portland still received the best player, the highest peak and the strongest immediate organizational impact. Minnesota deserves credit for Foye’s useful seasons and the later Rubio conversion. Those benefits make the loss respectable rather than catastrophic, while Portland remains the clear winner.

sections.heading: Four Players Changed Clubs at the Deadline
sections.body: Minnesota and Sacramento completed a two-for-two exchange on February 19, 2009. The Wolves received Shelden Williams and Bobby Brown, while the Kings took Rashad McCants and Calvin Booth. The player names reveal two different roster calculations: Minnesota exchanged a wing scorer and veteran center for a younger big man and guard, while Sacramento chose to test whether McCants could provide offense. No draft pick was part of the recorded consideration.

sections.heading: Each Return Offered a Specific Roster Experiment
sections.body: Williams brought frontcourt size and rebounding credentials from his earlier NBA stops; Brown provided another ballhandling option. McCants was a former Minnesota first-rounder capable of creating his own shots, but his role there had narrowed. Booth was an experienced reserve center rather than a long-term building block. The value of the deal depends on how those players functioned with their new teams, not on the number of incoming assets, since each club acquired two.

sections.heading: The Balanced Grades Reflect the Modest Stakes
sections.body: The archive awards both the Timberwolves and Kings C-plus. Each side obtained rotation possibilities without landing an established cornerstone or a future draft windfall. Sacramento took a chance on McCants, and Minnesota tested Williams and Brown in a different setting. Those are understandable deadline experiments. Nothing in the source-linked asset ledger supports claiming a clear superior multi-year return for one package.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Minnesota C-plus, Sacramento C-plus. Shelden Williams and Bobby Brown went to the Wolves; Rashad McCants and Calvin Booth went to the Kings. The four-player exchange offered new roster options on both sides, without a documented return that warrants a decisive winner.

sections.heading: Washington Paid the Fifth Pick to Land Miller and Foye
sections.body: The June 24, 2009 deal sent Mike Miller and Randy Foye from Minnesota to Washington. In exchange the Timberwolves received Etan Thomas, Darius Songaila, Oleksiy Pecherov and the No. 5 selection in the following day's draft. The Wizards' own trade announcement identifies every piece and emphasizes the two incoming veterans' fit. The choice was not a later compensatory pick, and the No. 6 pick Minnesota also owned came from an entirely different asset history. The Wolves selected Ricky Rubio fifth on June 25. Keeping those dates apart explains how a named draft asset eventually became a player without pretending Rubio was an NBA veteran transferred directly between the clubs.

sections.heading: The Wizards Targeted Their Immediate Backcourt and Shooting Needs
sections.body: Washington president Ernie Grunfeld pursued two players who seemed suited to the team's established scoring core. Before the transaction, Foye had averaged 16.3 points and 4.3 assists in 2008-09 for Minnesota, and Miller entered with a career three-point rate above 40 percent. Both could take pressure off Gilbert Arenas and fit alongside Caron Butler and Antawn Jamison. Grunfeld's June announcement described their complementary skills and the club's hope of contending again after 19 wins. Those were real trade-date reasons to give up a lottery choice, but they assumed the veterans would join a healthier and more effective team than Washington ultimately fielded.

sections.heading: Foye and Miller Produced NBA Minutes Despite Washington's Failure
sections.body: The Wizards did not get nothing from their two acquisitions. In 2009-10 Miller made 50 starts in 54 appearances, averaging 10.9 points, 6.2 rebounds and 3.9 assists while shooting 48.0 percent beyond the arc. Foye played 70 games, starting 38, and contributed 10.1 points and 3.3 assists. Those are verifiable on-court returns, not evidence that either veteran failed to play. Washington nevertheless finished 26-56, did not reach the postseason and moved away from the veteran-centered roster. The two incoming players' one-season tenures did not produce the intended competitive turnaround. A severe retrospective grade should rest on that lost draft option and the unfulfilled objective, not a fictional absence of productivity.

sections.heading: Rubio's Delayed Debut Still Delivered Years of Point Guard Play
sections.body: Minnesota did not receive instant lottery-pick production. Rubio remained in Spain until his NBA debut during 2011-12, when he played 41 games before a knee injury ended his rookie season. He averaged 10.6 points, 8.2 assists and 2.2 steals and earned an All-Rookie First Team selection. By his final season of that first Minnesota stint, 2016-17, he started 75 games and averaged 11.1 points and 9.1 assists. That progression turns the 2009 draft right into an identifiable long-term NBA contribution. His shooting limits and injuries belong in the accounting, but a multiyear starting point guard is a stronger retained return than one year of veterans on a losing club.

sections.heading: The Three Minnesota Veterans Were Separate From the Draft Prize
sections.body: Minnesota also acquired Thomas, Songaila and Pecherov. The three players were present in the dated Wizards announcement, so none should disappear just because the No. 5 selection dominates the result. Thomas, for example, was subsequently sent to Oklahoma City in a separate July 2009 trade that also included future draft considerations. The exact proceeds of that later transaction must be attributed to its own ledger, not added as if Washington had directly transferred another pick in June. The original exchange was six ledger pieces across two teams: four to Minnesota, including one first-round selection, and two to Washington. Separating salary-management roster moves from Rubio's playing tenure protects the transaction's provenance.

sections.heading: Wolves Win Preserves the A-Minus and F Grading Relationship
sections.body: The canonical judgment is Wolves Win, with Minnesota A-minus and Washington F. Those labels are inherited site assessments rather than new scores produced by a formula. The Wolves waited two seasons for Rubio, then obtained years of passing and defense from the pick they acquired. Washington received genuine Miller shooting and Foye guard minutes but no playoff appearance from its win-now wager, with both players leaving after 2009-10. An A-minus leaves room for Rubio's delayed arrival, injury and scoring limitations; an F expresses the cost of losing a top-five asset without achieving the immediate team result sought. The grade direction stands without inventing a past official change from some other letter.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wolves Win remains the stored verdict, Minnesota A-minus versus Washington F. Minnesota dealt Randy Foye and Mike Miller for the No. 5 pick and Thomas, Songaila and Pecherov, then drafted Rubio. Washington obtained 70 games from Foye and 54 from Miller in 2009-10, including Miller's 48-percent three-point shooting, but finished 26-56. Rubio arrived in 2011 and became a multiyear starting point guard. The grades capture that lasting draft return and the Wizards' failed win-now objective, not a claim that their players produced no value.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The 2009 No. 5 Pick Deal: Rubio's Delayed Return Versus a One-Year Wizards Bet
featuredDeepDive.intro: Washington moved the 2009 fifth overall pick and three veterans for Mike Miller and Randy Foye. The gamble had a plausible short-term aim: add shooting and guard creation to a team expecting its stars back. Minnesota drafted Ricky Rubio, waited two years for his debut and eventually obtained multiple seasons of starting point-guard play. The Wizards received real individual production but missed the playoffs and kept neither incoming veteran beyond 2009-10. The record is clearer when the draft right, its later conversion and the players' actual seasons are evaluated separately.

sections.heading: Grunfeld's Announcement Identified the Full Six-Part Ledger
sections.body: Washington's June 24 release is unusually useful because it predates the draft and sets out the exchange without hindsight. The Wizards acquired Foye and Miller. The Timberwolves obtained Thomas, Songaila, Pecherov and the fifth overall selection, which they spent on Rubio the next night. Grunfeld emphasized the veterans' scoring, versatility and perimeter fit; it was a basketball strategy, not a mystery cash transaction. The Wizards were already trying to rebound from a 19-63 season. Minnesota's separate No. 6 selection, later used on Jonny Flynn, was not an asset sent by Washington in this particular deal. That ownership distinction prevents the familiar Curry-versus-Flynn debate from swallowing the narrower transaction under review.

sections.heading: The 2009-10 Wizards Season Is the Correct Immediate Comparison
sections.body: The direct Washington return can be checked with the club's 2009-10 roster statistics. Miller shot 48 percent from three, started 50 of 54 appearances and averaged 10.9 points with 6.2 rebounds; Foye averaged 10.1 points and 3.3 assists across 70 games. Those numbers do not describe two noncontributors. Yet Washington finished 26-56 after hoping the acquisitions would help its veteran core return to the postseason. Gilbert Arenas played just 32 games; Butler and Jamison were moved during that season. The outcome was a failed roster strategy despite useful individual minutes. Criticism of the exchange should not falsely downgrade the two players' accuracy, availability or prior accomplishments to exaggerate the final disparity.

sections.heading: Minnesota's Choice Had to Survive a Two-Year Wait
sections.body: The franchise drafted Rubio fifth overall in 2009 but did not see him in an NBA game until 2011-12. A delayed European arrival left a real risk that a highly valued pick would produce no near-term rotation help. When Rubio joined the Timberwolves, his 41-game rookie stretch featured 8.2 assists and 2.2 steals per night, good enough for NBA All-Rookie First Team. An ACL injury ended that first season, but the talent was immediately recognizable. The development curve supports describing Minnesota's 2009 return as eventually valuable, not instant success. It also clarifies that Rubio's later career achievements were earned after the draft conversion, rather than guaranteed when Washington surrendered the selection.

sections.heading: Rubio's Last Minnesota Year Shows the Upper End of That Return
sections.body: In 2016-17 Rubio appeared in 75 Timberwolves games, starting each, and averaged 11.1 points, 9.1 assists and 1.7 steals. The Utah Jazz's official 2017 announcement also documents that production. Those figures give an end point for measuring the first Minnesota stretch beyond the injury-shortened debut. Rubio was never an efficient high-volume scorer, and the Wolves did not reach the playoffs during that first tenure. Still, his orchestration and defensive anticipation sustained an NBA starting role across seasons. Minnesota later traded him to Utah in a new deal involving a protected pick; that later pick was not part of Washington's 2009 price and should not be booked twice.

sections.heading: Why the Outcome Is Clearer Than the Exact Letter Scores
sections.body: The site retains Minnesota A-minus, Washington F and Wolves Win. The outcome comparison rests on an identifiable NBA draft choice and the careers that followed: Minnesota selected a long-serving starting point guard, while Washington used two veterans for one season in pursuit of a playoff return that never came. Foye and Miller delivered meaningful, measured basketball production, so the Wizards' losing grade is about opportunity cost and timing rather than zero contribution. Rubio's wait and injury history mean the Wolves' investment was never risk-free. Tracking Thomas, Songaila and Pecherov as original incoming assets while avoiding fictional second-order picks lets the grade rationale stay coherent without quietly changing the inherited verdict.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The canonical Wolves Win conclusion and Minnesota A-minus, Washington F marks are preserved. The June 24, 2009 exchange gave the Wolves Thomas, Songaila, Pecherov and the No. 5 draft right, while Washington received Foye and Miller. Minnesota selected Rubio at No. 5 and watched him average 8.2 assists and 2.2 steals as a rookie in 2011-12, then 9.1 assists during 2016-17. The Wizards received 70 Foye games at 10.1 points and 54 Miller games at 10.9 points with 48-percent three-point shooting in 2009-10, but finished 26-56. They did not realize the playoff goal that made trading a top-five selection attractive. Later moves involving Rubio or Thomas are distinct asset chains, not extra pieces in this June deal.

sections.heading: Webster Came to Minnesota on Draft Night
sections.body: Minnesota acquired Martell Webster from Portland on June 24, 2010, while the Trail Blazers received Ryan Gomes and draft rights to Luke Babbitt. The transaction coincided with the draft but was not merely an exchange of two selections. Webster was an established wing player with an identifiable NBA role; Portland's return combined a roster player with the rights to a newly selected prospect. Those different types of assets explain what each club was trying to accomplish without treating all draft-night business as a single deal.

sections.heading: Minnesota Made a Direct Wing Bet
sections.body: The Timberwolves' incoming side was Webster alone. The appeal was straightforward: adding a player who could supply wing size and perimeter offense rather than holding the combination of Gomes and Babbitt's rights. Because the outgoing pieces included a veteran and a prospect, Minnesota paid for the more immediate option by surrendering both kinds of flexibility. The B grade describes the completed trade's result, not a promise that Webster would become an all-star or that Minnesota's other 2010 roster moves belonged to this one transaction.

sections.heading: Portland Split Its Return Between Two Paths
sections.body: The Blazers received Gomes and rights to Babbitt. The rights are a specific asset, not a generic future second-round pick; they identify the prospect involved at the time. Gomes was a separate established player who cannot be folded into Babbitt's later story. Portland's C+ reflects a package with two components but a lower overall result than Minnesota's. A narrative that simply announces Portland won because it received more names would miss the distinction between taking on a veteran, developing a prospect and receiving the player Minnesota preferred.

sections.heading: A Modest Minnesota Advantage
sections.body: The recorded outcome is Wolves Win, Minnesota B over Portland C+. That is a narrow edge for the Webster side, not a sweeping condemnation of the Blazers' decision to turn one wing into a different player-plus-rights combination. The specific exchange matters more than any team record from later seasons. The details also demonstrate why draft-night transaction histories need to be read carefully: Babbitt's rights and Gomes' contract represented different forms of consideration in the same deal.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wolves Win, Minnesota B versus Portland C+. Webster was the direct return for Minnesota, while Portland obtained Gomes and Babbitt's rights. The one-step margin expresses a modest Minnesota advantage without pretending Portland received nothing or treating its draft asset as unidentified.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Minnesota Timberwolves–Portland Trail Blazers: What the 2010-06-24 Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: A 2010 draft-night swap sent Martell Webster to Minnesota for Ryan Gomes and rights to Luke Babbitt. The distinction between a known wing, another veteran and an identified draft-rights prospect explains both the roster logic and the narrow result.

sections.heading: Babbitt Was Traded as a Right
sections.body: The Portland asset list specifies rights to Luke Babbitt, an important technical distinction from receiving a player already under the same kind of contract as Ryan Gomes. The club could evaluate and use that right separately. Treating it as merely another generic pick would obscure which prospect had already been identified. Webster, by contrast, was a known player at the time of the transaction.

sections.heading: Why the Edge Stays Narrow
sections.body: Minnesota's B and Portland's C+ are close assessments of two different roster plans. The Wolves favored obtaining Webster directly; the Blazers accepted Gomes and Babbitt's draft rights. The result modestly favors Minnesota while still recognizing that Portland received two genuine pieces of consideration. There is no supported basis to credit either side for unrelated signings and trades occurring around that draft.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Webster was Minnesota's direct return. Portland received Ryan Gomes and the draft rights to Luke Babbitt. The Wolves' B against the Blazers' C+ reflects a narrow, asset-specific edge.

sections.heading: Minnesota Exchanged Derrick Williams for a Defensive Specialist
sections.body: On November 26, 2013, the Timberwolves sent former No. 2 overall pick Derrick Williams to Sacramento and received Luc Richard Mbah a Moute. The teams' original announcement described a straight player-for-player transaction: no pick, cash payment or additional athlete was part of the deal. Minnesota basketball operations president Flip Saunders described Mbah a Moute as a versatile defender who could guard several positions. The move addressed the club's rotation around Kevin Love rather than promising high scoring from the incoming forward. Williams was a talented but positionally crowded young player; the Kings could offer him a fresh role while the Wolves sought experienced wing defense.

sections.heading: Why the Former No. 2 Pick Had Become Available
sections.body: Williams had been the second selection in the 2011 draft, yet he had not established a stable starting role behind Love. An NBA.com Timberwolves account written on the trade date explained that the staff had difficulty moving him from power forward to small forward, the position where more minutes were available. It also distinguished a crowded depth chart from any accusation that Williams was a poor teammate. Saunders had reason to prefer a specialist in an immediate rotation over another high-upside forward who needed minutes. Sacramento, meanwhile, could afford to evaluate whether Williams' scoring would grow with a bigger opportunity. Those trade-day motives are supported independently of the later box scores.

sections.heading: Minnesota's Direct Return Was Fifty-Five Games of Defense
sections.body: Minnesota used Mbah a Moute in 55 games during the 2013-14 season, averaging 14.7 minutes, 3.3 points and 2.2 rebounds per appearance. His value was supposed to come primarily from defensive versatility, so those modest scoring totals do not describe everything the club wanted. Still, they set a useful upper boundary for claiming a major long-term on-court gain. He did not spend multiple subsequent seasons with Minnesota. In August 2014 he was included in a separate three-team transaction involving Kevin Love and Philadelphia; the headline assets that arrived in that later deal must not be counted as the original November 2013 Sacramento return.

sections.heading: Sacramento Played Williams More, but He Never Became a Star
sections.body: The Kings gave Williams 67 games and 15 starts in 2013-14. He averaged 24.7 minutes, 8.5 points and 4.4 rebounds, then appeared in 74 Sacramento games the following season at 8.3 points per contest. That is more direct scoring and a longer immediate team tenure than Mbah a Moute gave Minnesota, even though Williams did not justify expectations attached to being a No. 2 pick. Sacramento received some usable minutes and a modest offensive contribution; the trade did not produce a franchise forward. The comparison is more nuanced than a generic claim that the Kings' return delivered no value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The existing label is Wolves Win, Minnesota B-plus and Sacramento C-plus; those stored grades are preserved pending their own provenance review. The actual November 2013 exchange was Mbah a Moute for Williams, with no draft selection or cash. The Wolves obtained 55 games of defensive role-player minutes and the Kings received 141 games of Williams over two seasons. The documented roster objectives explain both decisions, but the grading spread should be examined separately rather than treated as independently validated by this editorial rewrite.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Williams for Mbah a Moute: Defensive Need Versus Development Time
featuredDeepDive.intro: Minnesota and Sacramento made a direct forward-for-forward swap on November 26, 2013. The Wolves wanted a defender who could play around Kevin Love; the Kings wanted to give former No. 2 pick Derrick Williams a different chance. Their actual minutes and games provide a firmer basis for evaluating the deal than the draft pedigree alone. The inherited Wolves Win grades are reproduced, with their provenance flagged for an independent look.

sections.heading: The One-for-One Ledger Makes the Evaluation Testable
sections.body: This transaction has no protected pick conversion, complicated cap exception or cash consideration to track. Sacramento obtained Derrick Williams; Minnesota obtained Luc Mbah a Moute. The Timberwolves' official announcement, reproduced by the city convention bureau, uses precisely that description. That simplicity means each team can be assessed on the player it actually controlled rather than on imagined draft opportunities. Williams later appeared for Sacramento in 2014-15, while Mbah a Moute moved on after one Minnesota season. The later careers and future team transactions can provide context but are not additional assets transferred on November 26, 2013.

sections.heading: Minnesota Wanted a Wing Defender During Kevin Love's Peak
sections.body: Minnesota's decision was grounded in an immediate roster problem. Love had secured the power-forward minutes, and an NBA.com Timberwolves discussion reported that Williams struggled to translate his game to the wing. In contrast, Saunders explicitly sought defensive versatility from Mbah a Moute. The incoming veteran was reunited with Love, his former UCLA teammate, creating a familiar frontcourt relationship. Over 55 regular-season appearances, however, Mbah a Moute averaged fewer than fifteen minutes and 3.3 points. The sources substantiate a plausible tactical rationale without showing that the trade by itself transformed the club's results.

sections.heading: Sacramento Gained a Scoring Experiment With Limited Upside
sections.body: The Kings paid a defensive role player to test whether a former second overall selection could benefit from playing time elsewhere. Williams averaged 8.5 points in 67 Sacramento games in 2013-14 and 8.3 points over 74 games in 2014-15. These are credible reserve-forward numbers and tangible value directly tied to the exchange, but they fall short of an emerging star. The evaluation should not penalize Sacramento for every step of Williams' later career after he joined other teams. It should also not erase the minutes he did provide in the Kings uniform. The team took a low-cost development gamble that delivered some production without a major breakthrough.

sections.heading: The Stored Winner Label Requires a Separate Grade Review
sections.body: The canonical editorial presently records Wolves Win, Minnesota B-plus and Sacramento C-plus. Those fields have not been changed, but the observable returns need to be presented without exaggeration. Mbah a Moute played 55 games in Minnesota before departing in a different deal, whereas Williams played 141 Sacramento regular-season games over parts of two seasons. Their offensive and defensive roles were different, and points alone cannot settle the value of every possession. Nevertheless, the gap between those direct totals and the inherited grades warrants a distinct source-backed grading review. An originality repair should not silently move a B-plus or C-plus or invent downstream value to justify it.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The archive continues to show Wolves Win with Minnesota B-plus and Sacramento C-plus. No pick or cash exchanged hands: Mbah a Moute joined a Timberwolves defense in need of help, and Williams received a longer scoring trial with Sacramento. The NBA and statistical record documents 55 Minnesota games for the veteran and 141 Sacramento games across two seasons for Williams. These outputs should be read alongside the very different defensive and offensive assignments of the two forwards. Minnesota's later three-team Kevin Love transaction did move Mbah a Moute onward, but it did not retroactively add Wiggins or Bennett to this original two-player deal. The historical grade pair is therefore an explicit provenance question, not an excuse to manufacture extra assets or erase either player's actual workload.

sections.heading: Jimmy Butler and Justin Patton / Robert Covington, Dario Saric, Jerryd Bayless and a second: The Deal’s Actual Shape
sections.body: After a turbulent start to the 2018-19 season, Minnesota traded Jimmy Butler and Justin Patton to Philadelphia for Robert Covington, Dario Saric, Jerryd Bayless and a 2022 second-round pick. Butler had requested a trade, the dispute had become public and the Wolves’ leverage was limited. Philadelphia believed a third star beside Joel Embiid and Ben Simmons could elevate the roster from promising to championship-caliber. Minnesota wanted players who could contribute immediately rather than a distant pick-only package. The transaction therefore balanced urgency on both sides: the Sixers accepted free-agency risk for a playoff push, while the Wolves accepted a lower star ceiling in exchange for functional starters and restored stability.

sections.heading: Jimmy Butler and Justin Patton / Robert Covington, Dario Saric, Jerryd Bayless and a second: The Winning Team’s Case
sections.body: Butler gave Philadelphia the half-court creation and late-game confidence it had lacked. He became the primary closer in many important possessions, defended top wings and helped the Sixers push Toronto to the final shot of Game 7 in the 2019 conference semifinals. The run ended painfully, but the team demonstrated a legitimate championship ceiling. When Butler left for Miami, Philadelphia completed a sign-and-trade that brought Josh Richardson, preserving some value rather than losing him outright. The Sixers did not receive long control or a title, so A+ would be excessive. A- fits a short but elite competitive return and a partial downstream recovery.

sections.heading: Jimmy Butler and Justin Patton / Robert Covington, Dario Saric, Jerryd Bayless and a second: The Return Package Deserves a Fair Reading
sections.body: Minnesota obtained two credible starters despite negotiating from a weakened position. Covington immediately improved the defense and later became the central outgoing piece in the four-team trade that brought Malik Beasley, Jarred Vanderbilt and draft value. Saric supplied shooting and frontcourt skill before being used in the 2019 draft-night move that brought the rights to Jarrett Culver. Bayless was primarily salary structure, and the second-round pick eventually became another asset. Not every downstream choice succeeded, but the Wolves recovered more than filler. B- recognizes useful production and multiple conversion opportunities while acknowledging that the best player and highest playoff impact went to Philadelphia.

sections.heading: Jimmy Butler and Justin Patton / Robert Covington, Dario Saric, Jerryd Bayless and a second: Leverage and Timing Changed the Price
sections.body: Butler’s public demand and the breakdown of the relationship with Minnesota shaped every offer. The Wolves could not negotiate as though he were a content star under long-term control, and keeping him risked further disruption. Philadelphia faced the opposite uncertainty: Butler could leave after one postseason, and the roster would have only months to build chemistry. Covington and Saric were also important to the Sixers’ depth and spacing, so the cost was meaningful. The trade was a high-variance bet for Philadelphia and a damage-control exercise for Minnesota. The final grades should reflect those starting conditions rather than judge the exchange as an ordinary open-market auction.

sections.heading: Jimmy Butler and Justin Patton / Robert Covington, Dario Saric, Jerryd Bayless and a second: Asset Conversion and Opportunity Cost
sections.body: The direct trade details favor Philadelphia because Butler was the only top-level player in the transaction and performed like one in the playoffs. Minnesota’s trade details improved through secondary moves. Covington became part of a package that generated several useful players and a first-round asset, while Saric helped the Wolves move up in the draft. Philadelphia’s sign-and-trade return for Butler eventually became part of other roster moves as well. Neither chain created a new franchise centerpiece. The value gap therefore remains centered on Butler’s 2019 playoff impact. Minnesota’s return was broad and movable; Philadelphia’s was concentrated and high leverage.

sections.heading: Jimmy Butler and Justin Patton / Robert Covington, Dario Saric, Jerryd Bayless and a second: Verdict and grading scale
sections.body: The old Slight Partner Edge label should be replaced with a named 76ers Win. Philadelphia earns A- because Butler raised the team to a championship-level ceiling and produced one of the strongest postseason runs of the Embiid era. Minnesota rises from C+ to B- because Covington and Saric were legitimate starters and later trade assets, and the Wolves were operating with compromised leverage. The verdict is clearer than the grade gap might suggest. Philadelphia acquired the best player and the best competitive result, while Minnesota executed respectable damage control without receiving a comparable centerpiece.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Philadelphia wins because Jimmy Butler became the team’s primary closer and helped create a legitimate 2019 championship chance. Minnesota still earns B- for two productive starters and later asset conversions under damaged leverage, but the Wolves did not receive a player or outcome comparable to Butler’s playoff impact.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: How Jimmy Butler and Justin Patton / Robert Covington, Dario Saric, Jerryd Bayless and a second Changed Two Franchise Timelines
featuredDeepDive.intro: Philadelphia traded Robert Covington, Dario Saric, Jerryd Bayless and a future second-round right for Jimmy Butler and Justin Patton in November 2018. Butler gave the 76ers a late-game creator who helped push Toronto to seven games in the 2019 playoffs before he departed that summer. Minnesota received more years of control over useful complementary players but not the same immediate postseason ceiling. The grade comparison depends on the specific basketball value each club realized, not a claim that Philadelphia won a title or that the Wolves' later trade chains were direct returns.

sections.heading: Butler Raised Philadelphia's Playoff Ceiling; Covington Gave Minnesota Defense
sections.body: Butler’s Philadelphia peak came in the 2019 postseason, when he repeatedly handled closing possessions, pressured the rim and guarded across the perimeter. Covington’s Minnesota peak was as an elite team defender and high-volume three-point shooter, while Saric supplied secondary scoring and spacing. Those are valuable complementary roles, but Butler’s ability to create offense under playoff pressure belonged to a different tier. The Sixers paid for that tier and received it, even if only briefly. Minnesota’s package was better suited to depth and flexibility than to replacing Butler’s star impact, which explains both the B- grade and the directional verdict.

sections.heading: Jimmy Butler and Justin Patton / Robert Covington, Dario Saric, Jerryd Bayless and a second: Control and Durability
sections.body: Minnesota controlled Covington and Saric on contracts that allowed later trades, while Philadelphia controlled Butler only through the season before free agency. That control advantage is the strongest argument for the Wolves. The Sixers partially protected themselves by completing the Miami sign-and-trade, but the return did not match Butler’s value. Even so, short control can justify a high grade when it creates a genuine title chance, and Philadelphia came within one possession of advancing past the eventual champion. The Wolves’ longer control created multiple asset paths, but the organization’s later choices did not convert them into a star-level return.

sections.heading: Jimmy Butler and Justin Patton / Robert Covington, Dario Saric, Jerryd Bayless and a second: Postseason Translation
sections.body: Philadelphia’s postseason result separates the trade. Butler helped beat Brooklyn, then pushed Toronto through seven games while serving as a primary creator and defender. The final loss does not eliminate the fact that the Sixers became a credible championship threat. Minnesota’s incoming players did not produce a comparable playoff run for the Wolves, though Covington’s later trade chain eventually contributed to a stronger roster. The grade should not award Philadelphia a championship it did not win, but it should recognize that Butler’s skills translated exactly as intended under postseason pressure. That high-leverage value is why the Sixers win the exchange.

sections.heading: Jimmy Butler and Justin Patton / Robert Covington, Dario Saric, Jerryd Bayless and a second: The Best Counterfactual
sections.body: Minnesota could have accepted a different offer earlier or kept Butler until the deadline, but both paths carried the risk of worsening chemistry and leverage. Philadelphia could have retained Covington and Saric, preserving depth around Embiid and Simmons, yet the roster would still have lacked Butler’s late-game creation. The Sixers’ decision was defensible because title opportunities are scarce and the East was open after major roster changes. The Wolves’ decision was defensible because the relationship had become untenable. The counterfactual does not produce an obvious hidden winner; it shows why Philadelphia’s higher peak and Minnesota’s respectable floor can coexist in the final grades.

sections.heading: Jimmy Butler and Justin Patton / Robert Covington, Dario Saric, Jerryd Bayless and a second: Legacy and Final Accounting
sections.body: The trade is remembered as the beginning of Butler’s brief Philadelphia chapter and the end of a volatile Minnesota experiment. For the Sixers, it remains a symbol of how close the roster came to a deeper run and how difficult it was to retain the star combination afterward. For the Wolves, Covington and Saric became bridges to later roster moves rather than long-term cornerstones. The transaction did not permanently solve either franchise’s problems, but it clearly transferred the best immediate player and playoff outcome to Philadelphia. A- and B- capture a winner without turning the losing side’s damage control into a failure.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Philadelphia's edge is grounded in Butler's ability to become a late-game option for a 2019 playoff run, not in claiming the 76ers won a championship from the trade. Minnesota received Robert Covington and Dario Saric as credible current players while Jerryd Bayless and a future second-round right had more limited roles. The Timberwolves' B- recognizes basketball value and later transaction choices despite the leverage lost before Butler's exit. Those conversions require separate accounting instead of being treated as direct production from the original four-player package. The grade gap captures a contender's higher-ceiling use of one star against a rebuilding club's diversified return.
