sections.heading: Layman Went to Minnesota in a Rights Transaction
sections.body: The July 2019 exchange sent Jake Layman from Portland to Minnesota. Portland’s listed return was the rights to Bojan Dubljević and a traded-player exception. The parties were not swapping two established NBA regulars. Minnesota received a forward who could occupy a rotation spot immediately, while Portland took an overseas draft-rights asset and financial flexibility. The distinction is important because owning a player’s rights does not itself produce games or points for an NBA club.

sections.heading: Minnesota Received an Actual NBA Contributor
sections.body: Layman gave Minnesota a versatile forward option and appeared for the Timberwolves over several seasons. His contribution was useful roster depth rather than a franchise-changing centerpiece. That does not make the return imaginary: the Wolves gained actual court time from the player acquired, as opposed to waiting for a rights holder to join the NBA. The transaction was small, and its value should be evaluated on the limited rotation role Layman filled, not a later team record attributable to other acquisitions.

sections.heading: Portland’s Flexibility Did Not Match the Minutes
sections.body: Dubljević’s draft rights represented a possible future signing rather than immediate NBA production, and the trade exception was a tool for subsequent transactions. The current record does not identify a specific later player or deal that should automatically be credited to that exception. Minnesota consequently receives B-plus and Portland C-plus in the trade ledger. The spread is tied to Layman’s realized minutes and Portland’s more speculative return, not a belief that every sign-and-trade works equally well.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wolves Win — Minnesota B-plus, Portland C-plus. The Timberwolves gained NBA rotation minutes from Jake Layman. Portland received Bojan Dubljević’s rights and a trade exception without an established matching on-court payoff in the documented transaction. The recorded outcomes favor Minnesota, although this was a modest rotation and rights exchange rather than a major franchise trade.

sections.heading: Minnesota Paid a Historic Price for a Defensive Identity
sections.body: The Timberwolves sent Patrick Beverley, Malik Beasley, Jarred Vanderbilt, Leandro Bolmaro, Walker Kessler's draft rights, four first-round picks and a 2026 swap right to Utah for Rudy Gobert. The scale created an immediate burden: the deal could not be justified by ordinary playoff qualification. Minnesota was betting that elite rim protection would organize the entire roster, reduce the defensive burden on Karl-Anthony Towns and accelerate Anthony Edwards into real contention. The first season looked awkward, but the later results showed the wager was about structure rather than a one-year statistical upgrade.

sections.heading: Utah Secured Both Immediate Players and a Long Asset Timeline
sections.body: The Jazz did not need every incoming veteran to remain in Utah for the return to work. Beverley, Beasley and Vanderbilt could be rerouted; Kessler became an immediate rotation center; the 2023 pick became Keyonte George; the 2025 selection became Will Riley; and the 2027 and 2029 picks remain future opportunities. The 2026 swap also gave Utah optionality. This is why the trade cannot be graded only by comparing Gobert with Kessler. Utah purchased years of decision-making power and the ability to continue converting pieces across multiple transactions.

sections.heading: The 2024 Defense Validated Minnesota’s Basketball Theory
sections.body: In Gobert's second Minnesota season, the Timberwolves produced the league's top defense, won 56 games and reached the Western Conference finals. Gobert won his fourth Defensive Player of the Year award, becoming the first Timberwolf to receive it. His screening, rebounding and paint control also supported the offense even when his own scoring volume was modest. The playoff victory over defending champion Denver supplied the strongest evidence that Minnesota had not merely assembled a strong regular-season defense. The roster could translate its size and coverage flexibility against the league's best opponent.

sections.heading: Consecutive Conference Finals Changed the Trade From Disaster to Contender Bet
sections.body: Minnesota returned to the Western Conference finals in 2025, making the Gobert-era Wolves the first version of the franchise to reach that stage in consecutive seasons. Gobert delivered a 27-point, 24-rebound closeout against the Lakers and continued to anchor the interior through another deep run. The Wolves did not win the championship, but repeated final-four appearances matter in a league where Minnesota had reached that round only once before the trade. The realized return has therefore exceeded the early ridicule and reached genuine contender territory.

sections.heading: The Future Picks Prevent a Final Minnesota Victory
sections.body: Utah still controls premium future outcomes, particularly the 2027 and protected 2029 first-round selections. Minnesota's roster will age, contracts will change and later picks could land higher than the early conveyances. The Jazz also received enough pieces to build additional transaction chains. That unresolved upside is not theoretical filler; it is part of the original price. A trade that has already transformed Minnesota can still become more favorable to Utah if those picks produce stars or high-value moves. The verdict must preserve that open horizon.

sections.heading: Matching A-Minus Grades Best Capture the Two Different Wins
sections.body: Minnesota should rise from B+ to A- because Gobert delivered a Defensive Player of the Year season and anchored consecutive conference-final teams. Utah should also rise to A- because it converted one veteran star into Kessler, George, Riley, movable veterans, a swap and two still-unresolved firsts. Neither side has completed the full value cycle, and neither outcome deserves to be described as a failure. Even Trade with matching A- grades recognizes that Minnesota purchased contention while Utah purchased a premium rebuilding portfolio.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: This remains an Even Trade, upgraded to A- for both Minnesota and Utah. The Wolves paid extraordinary capital, but Gobert became the defensive anchor of a 56-win team, won the 2024 Defensive Player of the Year award and helped produce consecutive Western Conference finals. Utah acquired Kessler, George, Riley, multiple movable veterans, a swap and future 2027 and 2029 firsts. Minnesota has already received contender-level impact; Utah still owns meaningful unresolved upside. Both organizations achieved the strategic result they sought.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The Rudy Gobert Trade Became Two Successful Projects Instead of One Obvious Winner
featuredDeepDive.intro: The Gobert deal was treated as a referendum almost immediately, first because the price reset the star-trade market and then because Minnesota's opening season looked clumsy. A longer view reveals two distinct value systems. Minnesota used Gobert to construct a defense capable of supporting Edwards through deep playoff runs. Utah used the return to create a long sequence of players, picks and future choices. The trade can be expensive for the Wolves and excellent for the Jazz without being a loss for either side.

sections.heading: The First Season Exposed the Integration Cost
sections.body: Gobert joined a roster built around Towns at center, Edwards as an emerging high-usage guard and limited perimeter shooting. Injuries and unfamiliar coverage responsibilities made the first season uneven. Minnesota won 42 games and exited in the first round, which made the price look detached from the immediate result. That criticism was fair at the time. The important distinction is that integration cost is not the same as permanent failure. The Wolves later adjusted the defensive scheme, expanded Jaden McDaniels' role and built lineups that used size as an advantage rather than a spacing problem.

sections.heading: Gobert’s Value Appeared in the Entire Defensive Ecosystem
sections.body: Elite rim protection affects more than blocked shots. Perimeter defenders can pressure the ball more aggressively when they trust the back line. Weak-side helpers can stay closer to shooters. Defensive rebounds end possessions and create transition opportunities for Edwards. Gobert's screening also creates offensive advantages that do not appear as assists. Minnesota's top-ranked defense in 2023-24 reflected a system organized around those effects. The DPOY award acknowledged the individual center, but the more important trade return was the environment his presence allowed the roster to build.

sections.heading: The Denver Series Supplied the Proof Against the Hardest Matchup
sections.body: Nikola Jokic is the center most often cited as evidence that traditional rim protectors cannot survive the postseason. Minnesota defeated Denver in seven games in 2024 by using Gobert, Towns, Naz Reid and versatile wings across changing assignments. Gobert was not flawless and did not guard every possession one-on-one. His size, rebounding and help positioning still formed part of the collective answer. The series mattered because it demonstrated that the Wolves' expensive defensive structure could survive a sophisticated champion rather than merely overwhelm weaker regular-season offenses.

sections.heading: Utah’s Return Must Be Evaluated as a Portfolio
sections.body: Kessler's shot blocking and rebounding made him the most visible early asset, but the Jazz return was intentionally broader. George became a lead-guard development project from the 2023 pick, Riley arrived from the 2025 selection and the veteran pieces created additional flexibility. The 2027 and 2029 picks may become the most valuable assets of all, depending on Minnesota's future. Portfolio trades are designed so that no single miss destroys the return. Utah acquired enough independent chances that the overall package can remain strong even if several pieces plateau.

sections.heading: The Deal Raised Minnesota’s Ceiling at the Cost of Future Control
sections.body: The Wolves traded optionality for competitive certainty. They surrendered the ability to draft or trade several future firsts, but they gained an elite defensive center whose skills translated immediately once the roster stabilized. Consecutive conference finals are a rare outcome and should be valued accordingly. The remaining question is whether the team can sustain contention as Gobert ages and the future picks convey. That tension is why A- is more appropriate than A+: the achieved ceiling is real, while the long-term bill has not finished arriving.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: An A-/A- Even Trade is the most defensible current grading scale. Minnesota transformed from an uncertain playoff team into a repeat conference finalist with Gobert as the defensive anchor, validating the basketball thesis behind the risk. Utah obtained a deep portfolio whose most consequential future selections may not yet have conveyed. The deal no longer resembles the automatic Minnesota disaster described after year one, but the Wolves also have not erased the extraordinary opportunity cost. Both sides created major value in different forms.

sections.heading: It Was the New Orleans Hornets, Not the Pelicans
sections.body: The New Orleans franchise acquired guard Shammond Williams from Orlando on February 19, 2004, sending veteran center Sean Rooks to the Magic. The current franchise taxonomy calls the team the Pelicans, but the club was then the New Orleans Hornets. The identity matters for readers looking up the original deadline transaction. This was a straight player swap rather than a trade of future first-round picks or a broader three-team package.

sections.heading: Williams Added Guard Depth; Rooks Offered Size
sections.body: Williams was a backcourt player with shooting and ballhandling experience. Rooks gave Orlando a veteran center with frontcourt size. The teams therefore exchanged different positional tools, likely reflecting their respective rotation needs at the deadline. The source-backed asset list contains one player received by each team, so there is no justification for describing hidden draft compensation or attaching an unrelated later roster deal to the outcome.

sections.heading: Equal B-minus Grades Reflect a Fair Small Exchange
sections.body: The Hornets/Pelicans and Magic each receive B-minus. Both sides obtained an experienced NBA player with a credible role, but neither trade return should be treated as a franchise-changing acquisition. The balanced assessment credits the specific guard-versus-center exchange without assuming identical skills or identical statistical production. A different position can fill a genuine roster need even when the two assets receive the same retrospective grade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — New Orleans Hornets/Pelicans B-minus, Orlando B-minus. New Orleans gained Shammond Williams and sent center Sean Rooks to the Magic. The clubs exchanged veteran depth at different positions, and neither documented return creates a strong case for a clear winner.

sections.heading: New Orleans Exchanged Jackson and a Second for Three Players
sections.body: New Orleans, later known as the Pelicans, traded with Phoenix on January 21, 2005. The incoming package consisted of Casey Jacobsen, Maciej Lampe and Jackson Vroman, giving the club three immediate roster possibilities. The Suns received veteran Jim Jackson and a 2005 second-round draft pick. That was a deliberate exchange of player depth for a more established wing and a later selection, not a simple one-for-one swap. The historical club name matters because the deal occurred in the New Orleans Hornets period rather than on a later Pelicans roster. Both teams were pursuing different competitive timetables.

sections.heading: The Second Eventually Appeared as Gortat at No. 57
sections.body: The outgoing New Orleans draft choice is traceable to the 2005 No. 57 selection associated with Marcin Gortat. Its identity is relevant to the original transaction's asset history, but it would be incorrect to give Phoenix all of Gortat's later NBA career production simply because a choice it once acquired reached that player. Draft-rights routing after this exchange must remain separate from direct Suns minutes. The more immediate Phoenix return was Jackson, an established veteran who could provide useful shooting and perimeter experience. New Orleans received three NBA players, but their collective time with the receiving club did not become a similarly prominent long-term core.

sections.heading: An Asset and Role Advantage for Phoenix
sections.body: The size of the New Orleans incoming package should not be confused with a stronger completed return. Jacobsen, Lampe and Vroman were actual roster assets, so a critical grade should acknowledge that the franchise acquired options rather than nothing. Phoenix concentrated its return in Jackson and a second-round draft right that later became identifiable through the 2005 draft. The available trade record supports a Suns edge while leaving room for caution around later pick routing and franchise-specific player careers. Comparing the assets when each team held them yields a more reliable assessment than assigning decades of future statistics to the team that initially acquired the draft choice.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Suns Win. Phoenix receives B for Jim Jackson and the second-round asset whose trail reached No. 57 Marcin Gortat. New Orleans receives D+ for Casey Jacobsen, Maciej Lampe and Jackson Vroman. The verdict credits identifiable value without treating Gortat's later production for other clubs as Suns production.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Deep Dive: What Decided Suns Win on 2005-01-21
featuredDeepDive.intro: On January 21, 2005 Phoenix acquired Jim Jackson and a 2005 second-round selection from New Orleans for Casey Jacobsen, Maciej Lampe and Jackson Vroman. Jackson played 40 Suns games that season and 27 the next, helping the 62-win team reach the 2005 Western Conference finals. Phoenix selected Marcin Gortat at No. 57 but traded his rights to Orlando for future consideration on draft day. His later Orlando NBA career belongs to the Magic rather than direct 2005 Phoenix on-court trade production.

sections.heading: The January 2005 Suns Announcement Identifies Every Asset
sections.body: On January 21, 2005 Phoenix announced the acquisition of veteran wing Jim Jackson and New Orleans’ 2005 second-round draft pick. The Suns sent Casey Jacobsen, Maciej Lampe and Jackson Vroman to the Hornets. The original team press release makes clear that Jackson and the pick were separate pieces of the return; the Suns did not acquire a player named Marcin Gortat in January. Phoenix was assembling depth around Steve Nash and Amar’e Stoudemire for a strong playoff position, while New Orleans took three younger players during a rebuilding season. That 2005 second had originally moved from Dallas to New Orleans in a separate December 2004 Darrell Armstrong transaction. Keeping the chain dated avoids describing the No. 57 draft outcome as a ready-made player on the Suns roster at the deadline.

sections.heading: Jim Jackson Delivered Real Phoenix Bench and Playoff Games
sections.body: Jackson made 40 regular-season Suns appearances after arriving in 2004-05, with three starts and averages of 8.8 points and 3.9 rebounds. He was a credible outside shooter, making 45.9 percent of his three-point attempts during that Phoenix portion of the season. The Suns won 62 regular-season games and reached the Western Conference finals, where they lost to San Antonio. Jackson also logged playoff minutes in that run, including a 19-point performance during their opening Memphis series. He returned for 27 Suns games in 2005-06 before another transaction sent him elsewhere. Those 67 direct Phoenix regular-season appearances are tangible receiving-team output; his earlier Houston playing time is not. The short veteran acquisition had value even without credit for the later career of the 2005 draft pick.

sections.heading: Phoenix Drafted Gortat at No. 57 but Traded His Rights to Orlando
sections.body: The incoming second became the fifty-seventh pick of the 2005 NBA draft. Phoenix selected Polish center Marcin Gortat, but immediately traded his draft rights to Orlando on June 28 for future considerations. The Orlando Magic’s official historical media guide separately confirms the Suns-to-Magic rights transfer, identifying cash consideration in its transaction ledger. Gortat’s eventual NBA seasons with Orlando, Phoenix in a later stint, Washington and other clubs therefore cannot be treated as direct Phoenix playing production from the January 2005 Hornets deal. The original Suns return includes the ability to exercise and then dispose of those draft rights, not a center who suited up as a Phoenix rookie. That second-round pick chain is an independently useful asset outcome and must remain distinct from Jackson’s NBA games.

sections.heading: New Orleans Received Three Players While Phoenix Reached the Finals
sections.body: New Orleans obtained Jacobsen, Lampe and Vroman rather than a first-round selection or an established lead guard. Those three players had roster-development value but could not replicate Jackson’s contribution to a Phoenix club that finished 62-20 and reached the Western Conference finals. The draft pick the Hornets surrendered became No. 57 Gortat, yet his later standout Orlando career was not a direct Suns playing contribution, because Phoenix conveyed the rights that same June. The archived Suns Win and Phoenix B versus New Orleans D-plus grading therefore needs to be supported by the known Jackson playing window and the separate rights transaction, not by pretending Phoenix developed Gortat into its starting center after this deal. The source-dated accounting makes the outcome clear without inventing the specific eventual value of undisclosed future considerations.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The original Suns Win and Phoenix B versus New Orleans D-plus grades are preserved. Jackson provided Phoenix with 67 regular-season appearances over two seasons and meaningful 2005 playoff minutes. The incoming second became No. 57 Marcin Gortat, whose rights Phoenix traded to Orlando on the day he was selected; his later Magic playing time cannot be credited as Suns NBA output from this deal. New Orleans acquired Jacobsen, Lampe and Vroman. This outcome recognizes Jackson’s actual contribution and a separate draft-rights disposition without manufacturing an unreported player return.

sections.heading: Jamal Mashburn and Rodney Rogers / Glenn Robinson: What Actually Changed Hands
sections.body: Philadelphia acquired Jamal Mashburn and Rodney Rogers. New Orleans acquired Glenn Robinson. The names suggested a veteran-for-veteran exchange, but health and availability quickly made the actual outcomes far less balanced than the announcement-day reputations. The February 2005 trade paired Jamal Mashburn and Rodney Rogers heading to Philadelphia with Glenn Robinson going to New Orleans. None of these names should be graded by reputation alone: injuries and availability were already changing what the two clubs could realistically expect to put on the court.

sections.heading: Jamal Mashburn and Rodney Rogers / Glenn Robinson: Where the Stronger Value Emerged
sections.body: Rogers gave Philadelphia usable veteran minutes, while Mashburn’s contract and health situation were absorbed without producing on-court value. Even that limited contribution exceeded New Orleans’ result because Robinson was waived only days after the trade and never appeared for the franchise. Rodney Rogers was the part of Philadelphia’s incoming package that actually provided veteran minutes. Mashburn never appeared for the 76ers, so the receiving side did not gain two productive former stars. Still, getting one player who could play was a better basketball outcome than the Hornets received.

sections.heading: Jamal Mashburn and Rodney Rogers / Glenn Robinson: What the Other Side Still Received
sections.body: New Orleans was trying to move salary and unavailable veterans, so the transaction had financial and roster-management logic. Still, Robinson’s immediate waiver meant the basketball return was effectively nonexistent, making it hard to defend the old even-trade framing. New Orleans took back Glenn Robinson while shifting other veteran obligations. The move offered roster and financial housekeeping, but the franchise waived Robinson shortly afterward and received no game appearances from him. That absence drives the D more than the nominal profile of the player acquired.

sections.heading: Jamal Mashburn and Rodney Rogers / Glenn Robinson: The Asset Chain After the Trade
sections.body: There is little downstream basketball chain to inflate on either side. Mashburn never played for Philadelphia and later retired, while Robinson never played for New Orleans. Rogers’ actual minutes are therefore unusually important because they are one of the few realized pieces in the trade details. There is no major draft or player development chain to excavate here: Mashburn did not play for Philadelphia, Robinson did not play for New Orleans, and Rogers supplied the practical contribution. Claiming that either retired or waived veteran later produced a franchise asset would manufacture value the transaction never delivered.

sections.heading: Jamal Mashburn and Rodney Rogers / Glenn Robinson: Timeline, Contract and Role Context
sections.body: Both clubs were dealing with older players, injuries and expiring competitive windows rather than building around young cornerstone assets. That context lowers the ceiling of the transaction, but it does not erase the difference between receiving some usable play and receiving none. The clubs were rearranging aging or unavailable veteran contracts near the February deadline. Philadelphia could extract a little immediate help through Rogers; New Orleans could clear its situation without expecting Robinson to anchor a future roster. That financial reasoning is relevant but separate from measured on-court return.

sections.heading: Jamal Mashburn and Rodney Rogers / Glenn Robinson: grading scale
sections.body: Philadelphia B, New Orleans D. The 76ers do not earn an elite grade because Mashburn never suited up and the package was not transformational. New Orleans falls to D because Robinson was waived almost immediately and created no meaningful court value. The 76ers’ B belongs to a modest, practical contribution from Rogers rather than a franchise-changing acquisition. New Orleans’ D reflects Robinson being waived without a Hornets appearance. Calling the trade even would mistake the star names on the original paperwork for the value the teams received.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win — Philadelphia B, New Orleans D. Rodney Rogers contributed actual veteran minutes for Philadelphia, whereas Jamal Mashburn's health and contract prevented a comparable playing return. New Orleans quickly waived Glenn Robinson without a regular-season appearance. Philadelphia's acquisition was limited rather than franchise-changing, which holds its grade at B; the other side's missing on-court contribution and early waiver explain the D. Salary-management context helps explain the decision but does not transform the absent basketball return.

sections.heading: Baron Davis Went to Golden State for Two Veterans and Cash
sections.body: On February 24, 2005, Golden State acquired point guard Baron Davis from the New Orleans Hornets in exchange for Speedy Claxton, Dale Davis and cash. The NBA's all-time deadline transaction record explicitly lists the three outgoing components, while the Warriors' official media guide confirms the player swap on that date. New Orleans was the Hornets' home at the time; the franchise is identified as the Pelicans in the current database. The trade did not include a future first-round pick or another young franchise guard. The package reflected the Hornets' willingness to move an expensive, injury-affected lead guard for a shorter-term backcourt replacement and veteran frontcourt piece.

sections.heading: Golden State Acquired a Ball-Dominant Creator
sections.body: Davis's first Warriors stint covered 28 games after the 2005 deadline, when he averaged 19.5 points and 8.3 assists. He also supplied 17.9 points and 8.9 assists over 54 games in 2005-06 before playing 63 games at 20.1 points and 8.1 assists in 2006-07. Those figures illustrate the basketball return the Warriors obtained: an experienced creator who could carry their offense, not merely a recognizable name. The club had accepted the health and contract risks that made him available. His sustained production during the following two seasons is the central reason this deal later looked so favorable to Golden State.

sections.heading: The 2007 Dallas Upset Was a Signature Team Result
sections.body: The Warriors entered the 2007 playoffs as the West's eighth seed and beat the 67-win Dallas Mavericks in a six-game first-round series. Davis was the lead guard of that 'We Believe' team, giving the franchise a vivid postseason result tied to its 2005 acquisition. That accomplishment belongs to a roster that also included several key teammates and a coaching staff, not Davis alone. The trade's narrower but defensible claim is that Golden State obtained the primary creator around whom the eventual upset offense could function. That role was far more enduring than a single reserve season and distinguishes this swap from a routine deadline salary adjustment.

sections.heading: Claxton Was a Real Contributor for the Hornets
sections.body: New Orleans did not receive an empty return. In 2005-06, while the Hornets operated as New Orleans/Oklahoma City following Hurricane Katrina, Claxton played 71 regular-season games, averaging 12.3 points, 4.8 assists and 1.5 steals in 28.4 minutes. He was an important reserve and finished second in Sixth Man of the Year voting. Those facts are meaningful counterevidence to describing the New Orleans side as worthless. Claxton did not become a long-term replacement for Davis's combination of playmaking and star-level production, but he provided a full season of useful guard minutes and defensive activity. Dale Davis and cash were additional incoming pieces, not the sources of the later Warriors playoff success.

sections.heading: Dale Davis and Cash Should Be Valued Without Invention
sections.body: The historic deadline ledger names Dale Davis and cash alongside Claxton. The NBA source does not provide a specific dollar amount for this trade's payment, so the record should not manufacture one. Dale Davis was a veteran big man near the end of his career, rather than a prospect who could replace Baron Davis's prime years. His presence makes the incoming Hornets package more than a single young guard, yet the retrospective playing value still depended primarily on Claxton's subsequent season. Separating these three components also prevents the analysis from crediting unrelated Hornets draft choices or later player acquisitions to Golden State's February 2005 transaction.

sections.heading: Why A-plus and D Describe an Uneven Outcome
sections.body: The canonical result is Warriors Win, with Golden State A-plus and the New Orleans franchise D. Those inherited marks are preserved, not recomputed from a box score. Golden State received multiple seasons of high-volume scoring and primary playmaking, along with a leading contributor to its first-round upset of the 67-win Mavericks. The Hornets obtained one productive Claxton season, a veteran frontcourt piece and cash. Both teams had trade-date reasons to act, including questions about Davis's availability and costs, but the realized difference in sustained franchise-level play was wide. Acknowledging Claxton's performance sharpens rather than weakens the argument for the Warriors' clearly stronger return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The inherited decision remains Warriors Win, Golden State A-plus and the New Orleans franchise D. The Warriors obtained Baron Davis, who delivered multiple seasons of high-level creation and led their 2007 upset of 67-win Dallas. New Orleans obtained Speedy Claxton, whose 71-game 2005-06 season at 12.3 points and 4.8 assists deserves acknowledgment, plus Dale Davis and cash. The record does not assign a verified dollar figure to the payment or attach later Warriors championship results to this 2005 transaction.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Baron Davis to Golden State: The 2005 Deadline Trade Behind We Believe
featuredDeepDive.intro: In February 2005, the Warriors obtained Baron Davis from New Orleans for Speedy Claxton, Dale Davis and cash. Davis became Golden State's primary creator and a leading player in the 2007 playoff upset of 67-win Dallas. Claxton provided a productive 2005-06 reserve season for the Hornets, a real but smaller return. The current ledger uses the Pelicans franchise name and retains the historical A-plus/D grades without assigning unrelated later Warriors success to the trade.

sections.heading: The Team Was Called the Hornets When the Deal Happened
sections.body: The date and franchise identity are part of the provenance. The New Orleans Hornets traded Baron Davis to Golden State on February 24, 2005; the modern database attaches the resulting team history to the Pelicans franchise. This is one deal between those organizations, with Davis moving west and Claxton, Dale Davis and cash moving to New Orleans. The Warriors' media guide documents the date and players, and the NBA's all-time deadline page confirms the payment component. Neither source describes a first-round pick going the other way. Getting this ledger right avoids the common mistake of importing later Pelicans-era trades or other Warriors deadline moves into the 2005 valuation.

sections.heading: Davis Turned the Warriors Into a Different Offensive Team
sections.body: The first indication came immediately: over 28 Golden State games in 2004-05, Davis averaged 19.5 points and 8.3 assists. The next two seasons included averages of 17.9 points with 8.9 assists, then 20.1 points with 8.1 assists. That span documents a guard who could manufacture shots for himself and teammates instead of supplying only depth. Golden State took on durability uncertainty, as shown by his 54 appearances in 2005-06 and 63 in 2006-07. Even with the missed games, the minutes he played gave the Warriors a level of primary creation that Claxton and Dale Davis were not expected to provide for New Orleans.

sections.heading: We Believe Gives the Trade a Concrete Postseason Milestone
sections.body: The 2007 Warriors qualified as an eighth seed and defeated top-seeded Dallas, which had won 67 regular-season games. Davis guided the offense through the first-round upset in a series that became a defining Golden State moment well before the franchise's later championship era. It would be overstatement to say the 2005 trade single-handedly produced every playoff victory: teammates and tactical decisions were central. But Davis's role as a leading scorer and distributor is directly connected to the roster that achieved the upset. His presence gave the Warriors more than a half-season improvement, making the transaction's lasting direct basketball value notably stronger than its original veteran-and-cash cost.

sections.heading: The Hornets Did Obtain a Sixth-Man-Caliber Season
sections.body: A good retrospective must account for Claxton instead of treating the receiving team as if it were given nothing. Playing 71 games in 2005-06 for the displaced New Orleans/Oklahoma City Hornets, he averaged 12.3 points, 4.8 assists, 1.5 steals and 28.4 minutes. His runner-up finish in Sixth Man of the Year voting demonstrates that the season was recognized beyond a minor bench statistic. The problem for the Hornets was not that Claxton lacked usefulness, but that this level of performance was shorter-lived and less central than Davis's contributions in Golden State. Dale Davis's veteran status and the cash payment complete the ledger without closing that gap in playing value.

sections.heading: Keep the 2005 Grade Apart From the Warriors' Later Dynasty
sections.body: This transaction predated Stephen Curry's draft and the Warriors' eventual championship run by years. Those later accomplishments belong to different roster eras and should not be transferred onto Baron Davis's acquisition. What the 2005 trade itself delivered is already compelling: several high-scoring, high-assist Golden State seasons and the lead guard on a memorable 2007 playoff upset. New Orleans received Claxton's meaningful 2005-06 season, Dale Davis and cash, but not an equivalent long-term point guard. The site retains Warriors Win, Golden State A-plus and Pelicans D. Those grades reflect the imbalance in the returns actually connected to the deal, not a fictional causal chain ending with championships from a future generation.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The original Warriors Win judgment, Golden State A-plus and New Orleans/Pelicans D remain unchanged. The February 24, 2005 NBA deadline record lists Baron Davis going to Golden State in exchange for Speedy Claxton, Dale Davis and cash. Davis produced 19.5 points and 8.3 assists over his first 28 Warriors appearances, then continued as a high-usage lead guard through the 'We Believe' upset of top-seeded Dallas in 2007. Claxton was a useful alternative for New Orleans, averaging 12.3 points and 4.8 assists in 71 games in 2005-06, with Dale Davis and the cash payment also part of the compensation. That Hornets value is real but did not approach Davis's sustained Golden State impact. This accounting avoids inventing an exact cash figure or claiming the transaction caused later Warriors championships.

sections.heading: New Orleans Needed a Defensive Center Beside Chris Paul
sections.body: The Hornets had found their franchise point guard in Chris Paul and needed a center whose game could amplify his speed, passing and defensive pressure. Tyson Chandler had disappointed relative to his draft position in Chicago, but he was still only 23 and possessed the length, mobility and rebounding ability New Orleans lacked. The Hornets sent veteran P.J. Brown and young guard J.R. Smith, accepting Smith’s scoring upside in exchange for a cleaner roster fit. Chandler did not require post touches or isolation plays. He could sprint into screens, dive to the rim, control the glass and protect the paint. Those skills created a natural partnership with Paul and gave New Orleans a defensive identity capable of supporting a rising offense.

sections.heading: The Paul-Chandler Partnership Became an Elite Competitive Engine
sections.body: Chandler’s best New Orleans season came in 2007-08, when the Hornets won 56 games, captured the Southwest Division and reached the conference semifinals. His screen setting and vertical spacing turned Paul’s pick-and-roll into one of the league’s most difficult actions to defend. On the other end, Chandler rebounded, challenged shots and gave the perimeter defenders confidence to apply pressure. His box-score scoring remained modest, but his efficiency and structural impact were substantial. New Orleans did not need him to become a traditional star. It needed him to make Paul’s strengths more dangerous and cover weaknesses elsewhere. The trade accomplished that objective at a high level and helped produce the strongest season in the franchise’s early New Orleans era.

sections.heading: Chicago Received a Veteran but Quickly Discarded the Upside Piece
sections.body: Brown provided one season of dependable frontcourt minutes and veteran leadership for a Bulls team that reached the second round. That contribution prevents Chicago’s return from being completely empty. The larger problem was J.R. Smith. Chicago acquired a 20-year-old scorer with significant athletic and shooting potential, then traded him to Denver days later for Howard Eisley and two second-round picks. Smith developed into a long-term NBA scorer and Sixth Man of the Year elsewhere, but the Bulls captured almost none of that value. The original Chandler trade therefore cannot be defended by pointing to Smith’s later career. Chicago’s realized return was largely one Brown season and modest secondary assets, far below Chandler’s impact in New Orleans.

sections.heading: Chandler’s Later Career Confirms the Talent Evaluation Without Belonging Entirely to New Orleans
sections.body: Chandler later became a Defensive Player of the Year and championship center in Dallas, evidence that New Orleans correctly identified a young player whose best basketball remained ahead. Those later achievements do not count fully as Hornets value because the franchise traded him in 2009. They still inform the process evaluation: the acquisition was not a fluke based on a brief hot stretch. Chandler’s tools and role were sustainable at the highest level. New Orleans received several prime development years and a major competitive peak before making a separate decision to move him. The A-plus grade rests on what he delivered with Paul, while his later success reinforces how sharply the Hornets understood his fit and age curve.

sections.heading: Chicago’s Decision Reflected a Change in Direction After Ben Wallace Arrived
sections.body: The Bulls had signed Ben Wallace and no longer saw Chandler as the center of their frontcourt plan. Moving his contract for Brown created a veteran rotation and financial clarity. That context makes the trade understandable, particularly after Chandler’s inconsistent offense and injury concerns in Chicago. It does not make the outcome favorable. Wallace’s Bulls tenure declined quickly, Chandler improved in New Orleans and Smith’s upside was discarded almost immediately. Chicago solved a short-term roster overlap by surrendering two younger players whose later value exceeded the return. A C-minus captures Brown’s useful season and the logic of the moment while recognizing that the organization lost both the best direct player and the best secondary upside.

sections.heading: The Existing Pelicans Verdict Is Right but the Grades Should Widen
sections.body: The prior record already said Pelicans Win, with New Orleans A and Chicago D-plus. The explicit verdict should remain, but the grades should become New Orleans A-plus and Chicago C-minus. Chandler’s fit with Paul, role on a 56-win division champion and prime-age value justify the top mark. Chicago’s Brown season was useful enough to avoid a D, even though the Smith reroute and Chandler’s growth made the outcome clearly poor. The revised grading scale better separates process from result. Chicago had a plausible reason to change centers; New Orleans made the superior talent and fit judgment and received the far more consequential competitive return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans Win — New Orleans A-plus, Chicago C-minus. Chandler became the defensive, rebounding and pick-and-roll partner who helped Chris Paul lead a 56-win division champion. Brown gave Chicago a useful veteran season, but the Bulls quickly rerouted Smith and retained little of his later upside. Chicago’s short-term logic prevents an F; New Orleans’ identification of a young center perfectly matched to its franchise guard earns the A-plus.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: How Tyson Chandler Unlocked Chris Paul’s First Great Contender
featuredDeepDive.intro: The 2006 trade worked because New Orleans evaluated interaction rather than isolated production. Chandler had not become a major scorer in Chicago, and Paul did not need another player who required the ball. He needed a center who could turn a screen into a scoring threat, finish above the rim, rebound missed shots and defend behind aggressive perimeter pressure. Chandler’s movement and length transformed Paul’s passing windows and gave the Hornets a dependable defensive backbone. Chicago was reshaping its frontcourt around Ben Wallace and chose the certainty of Brown, but it failed to retain Smith’s upside. The exchange shows how a player labeled disappointing in one system can become essential when his skills are paired with the correct creator and role.

sections.heading: Vertical Spacing Made Paul’s Passing Even More Dangerous
sections.body: Chandler’s rim runs forced the weak-side defense to choose between tagging the center and staying attached to shooters. Paul could manipulate that choice with pace, hesitation and precise lob placement. Even when Chandler did not receive the pass, his dive created space for David West’s midrange game and perimeter shooters. This form of spacing does not appear in three-point totals, but it changes defensive geometry just as clearly. Chandler’s willingness to screen, sprint and finish without demanding post touches made him ideal for a young point guard who controlled every possession. The Hornets acquired a center whose offensive value came from magnifying Paul rather than competing with him.

sections.heading: Rebounding Allowed New Orleans to Play More Aggressively
sections.body: Chandler’s work on the glass ended possessions and created transition opportunities for Paul. Perimeter defenders could pressure the ball knowing the center had the length and mobility to cover behind them. On offense, his rebounds generated extra chances without disrupting the team’s shot distribution. Those possessions mattered for a roster that relied heavily on Paul and West to create efficient offense. Chandler also handled many of the physical center matchups that would otherwise wear down the frontcourt. His rebounding was therefore both statistical production and lineup infrastructure. New Orleans became harder to score against and faster after misses because the acquired center controlled the first step of both transitions.

sections.heading: Brown’s Season Had Value but No Long-Term Multiplier
sections.body: Brown started, defended and supplied veteran professionalism for a young Bulls team. Chicago won 49 games and reached the second round, so his contribution should not be dismissed. The limitation is that the value ended quickly. He did not become part of the next core, create premium trade capital or produce a competitive leap unique to his presence. Chandler, by contrast, became more valuable because his partnership with Paul improved both players and shaped the entire system. Trade returns are strongest when they multiply existing talent. Brown filled a role; Chandler changed what the Hornets could become. That difference separates C-minus from A-plus even before considering Smith’s lost upside.

sections.heading: The Smith Reroute Removed Chicago’s Best Chance to Balance the Deal
sections.body: Smith was inconsistent and immature, but he was also a young guard with rare athleticism and deep shooting range. Had Chicago developed or later traded him for meaningful value, the original package would look more defensible. Instead, the Bulls moved him almost immediately for a modest return. Denver received years of scoring and eventually a major role-player asset, while Chicago’s connection to that value disappeared. This is an important grading principle: a team receives credit for what it realizes from an asset, not for what the asset later becomes after being surrendered again. Smith’s career demonstrates that Chicago possessed upside briefly, but the Bulls’ own follow-up decision prevented that upside from improving their side of the trade.

sections.heading: New Orleans Won Through Fit Before Chandler Reached His Full Peak
sections.body: Chandler’s later championship and Defensive Player of the Year season came elsewhere, but New Orleans did not need those achievements to justify the trade. The Hornets received the best seasons of the early Paul era, including a division title and a near conference-final run. Chandler’s athletic prime began to emerge in the exact window when Paul became an MVP candidate. That timing produced high value even though the franchise later moved him. The A-plus grade recognizes a near-perfect acquisition relative to cost and roster need. New Orleans traded one veteran and one talented but unsettled guard for a center who became indispensable to its best team of the period.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans Win. Chandler’s defense, rebounding and vertical partnership with Paul gave New Orleans a structural advantage that reached its peak in a 56-win season. Chicago received a useful year from Brown but failed to capture Smith’s later upside and watched Chandler become the superior long-term center. The trade was not merely a talent swap; it was a lesson in matching a young player’s specific strengths to the franchise star who could maximize them.

sections.heading: Antonio Daniels / Darius Songaila and Bobby Brown: What Actually Changed Hands
sections.body: New Orleans acquired Darius Songaila and Bobby Brown. Minnesota acquired Antonio Daniels and a 2014 second-round pick. Daniels was waived before playing for the Timberwolves, while Songaila became a regular rotation big for one season in New Orleans. New Orleans obtained Darius Songaila and Bobby Brown from Minnesota, while the Timberwolves received Antonio Daniels and a 2014 second. Daniels did not play for Minnesota before being waived, which makes the actual Songaila season central to comparing the clubs.

sections.heading: Antonio Daniels / Darius Songaila and Bobby Brown: Where the Stronger Value Emerged
sections.body: The Pelicans side produced the clearest immediate basketball value through Songaila, who appeared in 75 games and supplied dependable frontcourt minutes. That direct contribution gives New Orleans the edge even without using Bobby Brown’s later protected-second transaction in the grade. Songaila appeared in 75 New Orleans games and provided frontcourt rotation help. That was not a star turn, but it was a dependable contribution with a verifiable games-played total. The Hornets did not need to claim an unverified downstream Bobby Brown asset to justify their narrow lead.

sections.heading: Antonio Daniels / Darius Songaila and Bobby Brown: What the Other Side Still Received
sections.body: Minnesota still received a future second-round pick, which eventually became the No. 40 selection in 2014, while Daniels’ contract helped the club accomplish a cost-management objective. Those elements keep the return from being a failure even though Daniels never played for Minnesota. Minnesota carried the contract and salary-management side of the transaction and also took a 2014 second that reached the No. 40 slot. Daniels’s lack of Timberwolves appearances limits the direct player return, but a future selection and an intended cost adjustment were not worthless.

sections.heading: Antonio Daniels / Darius Songaila and Bobby Brown: The Asset Chain After the Trade
sections.body: The project intentionally leaves Bobby Brown’s later trade for a protected second deferred, so this analysis does not use that disputed follow-on asset to strengthen New Orleans’ case. Minnesota’s incoming 2014 second can be traced directly and is credited as part of its side. The 2014 second belongs to Minnesota’s incoming asset trail. Bobby Brown’s later protected-second consideration has been held out of this evaluation because the routing is disputed. Keeping that unresolved item out of New Orleans’s grade produces a narrower and more defensible margin.

sections.heading: Antonio Daniels / Darius Songaila and Bobby Brown: Timeline, Contract and Role Context
sections.body: This was a practical roster and salary transaction rather than a star exchange. New Orleans wanted rotation help; Minnesota was reshaping costs and preserving a future pick. Small deals should be graded by the scale of the assets involved rather than compared with franchise-altering blockbusters. This was a September roster transaction whose purpose was different for each club. New Orleans wanted a working frontcourt piece, while Minnesota was managing its salary sheet and preserving a draft option. The comparison is between Songaila’s real season and Minnesota’s eventual pick, not the careers Daniels and Brown had elsewhere.

sections.heading: Antonio Daniels / Darius Songaila and Bobby Brown: grading scale
sections.body: New Orleans B+, Minnesota B-. The Pelicans get the higher grade for usable rotation production at a modest cost. Minnesota retains a respectable grade because the second-round pick had real future value and the deal met a financial objective. New Orleans earns B+ for 75-game rotation value from Songaila, with no bonus assigned to the disputed Bobby Brown follow-on. Minnesota gets B- because the 2014 second provided a genuine draft opportunity and the transaction met its financial objective, although Daniels never contributed on court.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans Win — New Orleans B+, Minnesota B-. Darius Songaila supplied 75 games of immediate frontcourt work for New Orleans, giving that side the clearest direct basketball production. Minnesota received a later second-round selection that became No. 40 in 2014 and obtained a cost-management benefit, even though Antonio Daniels did not appear for the club. The grade excludes the disputed Bobby Brown follow-on from this exchange. New Orleans leads on actual rotation minutes while the future pick prevents a harsher Minnesota assessment.

sections.heading: New Orleans Traded Ayón for Anderson
sections.body: On July 11, 2012 New Orleans acquired Ryan Anderson from Orlando in a sign-and-trade and sent Gustavo Ayón to the Magic. The club later known as the Pelicans received a forward who could score from the perimeter and change the spacing around its young frontcourt. Orlando took a reserve big man who offered a different role and contractual profile. The exchange did not include an additional premium first-round pick in the recorded player routing, so the value comparison depends on the actual performances of Anderson and Ayón.

sections.heading: Anderson Brought Four Seasons of Shooting
sections.body: Anderson became a high-volume three-point option and significant scorer for New Orleans over four seasons. His role as a stretch forward gave the team offensive spacing alongside its other bigs, a more durable contribution than a brief reserve spell. Ayón's tenure with Orlando was much shorter, limiting the Magic's direct realized return. The value distinction is especially visible because the two incoming players performed different jobs; the grade measures their contributions for the acquiring teams rather than assuming their careers were interchangeable.

sections.heading: Why the Return Favored New Orleans
sections.body: A sign-and-trade helped New Orleans acquire Anderson in a negotiated move rather than simply losing the opportunity to add him. Orlando obtained Ayón, but his immediate Magic contribution did not develop into a matching rotation role across the same four-year horizon. Anderson's shooting and scoring were tangible results inside New Orleans' own roster. The historical evaluation is stronger when it follows those distinct team tenures, not when it uses vague language about later franchise decisions that had no direct link to the original player swap.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans Win. New Orleans earns A- for four years of Ryan Anderson's scoring and floor spacing. Orlando receives D because Gustavo Ayón supplied only a limited short-term return. The outcome is a player-for-player advantage driven by Anderson's actual New Orleans tenure rather than an unrelated future pick or speculative downstream transaction.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Deep Dive: Regrading Ryan Anderson / Gustavo Ayon
featuredDeepDive.intro: In July 2012 Orlando dealt reigning Most Improved Player Ryan Anderson to the New Orleans Hornets in a sign-and-trade for Gustavo Ayón. Anderson gave New Orleans four seasons of perimeter shooting, while Ayón's NBA tenure in Orlando was much shorter. The five sections follow the actual two-player package, the financial and roster choices facing each club, and the different direct returns without adding hypothetical picks or unrelated later transactions.

sections.heading: July 2012: A Sign-and-Trade for a Proven Stretch Forward
sections.body: On July 11, 2012, Orlando transferred Ryan Anderson to New Orleans through a sign-and-trade in return for Gustavo Ayón. The Magic confirmed the Ayón acquisition in their contemporary announcement. Anderson was the reigning NBA Most Improved Player, having developed into a dependable long-range shooter during his years with Orlando. New Orleans was still known as the Hornets when the transaction occurred; the Pelicans name came later. Ayón was an inexpensive interior player who had completed his first NBA season, not a first-round draft selection or a future pick. Those are the only named basketball assets in this two-team exchange. By taking on Anderson's next contract, New Orleans acquired both his immediate playing ability and the responsibility to pay for it over multiple seasons.

sections.heading: Anderson Supplied Spacing Over Four New Orleans Seasons
sections.body: Anderson played for New Orleans from 2012-13 through 2015-16, remaining a valuable shooting forward through changes in the roster and club name. He was particularly useful when paired with Anthony Davis because his ability to draw a defender beyond the arc opened interior space for a more traditional big man. The 2015-16 season gave him another substantial scoring role after periods affected by injury. That combination of longevity, perimeter offense and usable rebounding is the direct return the New Orleans grade measures. His earlier Orlando Most Improved Player award explains why he was valued on trade day, but it is not a New Orleans achievement. His subsequent Houston games are likewise excluded from the Pelicans' four-season asset return.

sections.heading: Ayón Did Not Deliver an Equivalent Orlando Rotation Run
sections.body: Orlando received Gustavo Ayón, a mobile reserve big who could contribute inside without having Anderson's perimeter range. The Magic roster was being reorganized around the departure of Dwight Howard, and the club accepted a smaller contractual commitment in the July sign-and-trade. Ayón did appear for Orlando, so treating the deal as though the Magic received no NBA player would be inaccurate. His tenure nevertheless ended during the 2012-13 period, nowhere near the four seasons New Orleans obtained from Anderson. A change in roster philosophy can explain why a club declined to retain its existing shooter, but that rationale is separate from what its incoming player delivered. The Magic D reflects the limited realized return, not a claim that Ayón lacked professional basketball ability.

sections.heading: Restricted-Free-Agent Leverage Explains the July Terms
sections.body: Anderson was leaving his Orlando situation as a restricted free agent, which made the sign-and-trade a way for the Magic to receive some consideration instead of simply letting their former Most Improved Player go. New Orleans could make the contract commitment and chose to give up Ayón to secure the forward. The available transaction histories identify no added first-round selection, cash payment or separate team in this exchange. The clubs were therefore making different choices about roster construction: New Orleans paid for reliable outside shooting, while Orlando took a cheaper interior contributor during a rebuild. Retrospective evaluation should preserve those incentives without inventing an alternative offer that neither club actually received. The direct playing-time comparison after the transaction is more informative than hypothetical free-agency paths.

sections.heading: Why Four Years of Anderson Outweigh a Brief Ayón Return
sections.body: The inherited Pelicans Win verdict, New Orleans A-minus and Orlando D grades follow the direct basketball consequences. New Orleans retained Anderson for four seasons and made substantial use of his three-point shooting around a changing young frontcourt. Orlando acquired Ayón but did not keep him for a comparable stretch, leaving it without a long-term contributor from this specific exchange. Neither result should absorb the unrelated Dwight Howard deal or later players acquired by either organization. Anderson did not single-handedly deliver a championship, and Ayón's subsequent career elsewhere cannot be counted as a Magic return. The case is an example of a team successfully paying for a particular on-court skill through a relatively small outgoing asset, while the former team received much less sustained NBA value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans Win — New Orleans A-minus, Orlando D. Anderson provided four seasons as a frontcourt shooter, including useful work alongside Anthony Davis, after the July 2012 sign-and-trade. Orlando received Ayón, whose Magic playing contribution was brief by comparison. The grade recognizes both clubs' original contractual priorities while crediting the realized New Orleans offense only to the team that acquired Anderson.

sections.heading: New Orleans Took a 23-Year-Old All-Star, Philadelphia Took Two Draft Assets
sections.body: On July 12, 2013, the Pelicans acquired Jrue Holiday and 2013 second-round draft rights to Pierre Jackson from the 76ers. Philadelphia received the rights to Nerlens Noel, New Orleans' No. 6 selection that year, and a 2014 first-round choice protected inside the top five. The Pelicans' dated announcement confirms both legs and identifies Jackson as the No. 42 pick. Holiday had already played four NBA seasons and made an All-Star team. Noel, selected after a serious knee injury, offered a cheaper defensive upside bet rather than immediate minutes. This was a trade of established guard production for a 2013 prospect and a future first-round right, not a direct Holiday-for-Noel swap.

sections.heading: Holiday’s Injury-Interrupted Early Seasons Made the Price Look Steep
sections.body: Holiday did not immediately produce a full, healthy year for New Orleans. His 2013-14 debut was shortened to 34 games by a stress fracture, and his 2014-15 season included 40 appearances. The Pelicans had acquired him to share creation responsibilities with Anthony Davis but could not collect full-season value in those first two campaigns. Their risk was real: a top-five-protected future first and a lottery big carried longer-term options that Holiday's early injury history briefly obscured. The acquisition nevertheless brought an established professional rather than an inexperienced guard, and New Orleans retained his contractual rights while he recovered. Injuries are a debit against the immediate return, not evidence that the subsequent productive seasons happened outside the 2013 transaction.

sections.heading: His 2017-18 Defense and Portland Series Delivered the Playoff Case
sections.body: The most direct argument for the Pelicans comes from Holiday's healthy 2017-18 season. The team's official season review recorded 81 games and 81 starts, and the NBA's player statistics list 19.0 points and 6.0 assists per appearance. In the first round, New Orleans swept Portland while Holiday helped contain Damian Lillard and provided offense against the Trail Blazers' backcourt. He earned NBA All-Defensive first-team honors for that season. New Orleans lost the next series against Golden State, so the 2013 trade should not be described as having delivered a title or even a conference finals appearance. It delivered high-value regular-season guard minutes and a specific playoff achievement the club could point to.

sections.heading: Philadelphia’s Protected First Became Payton, Then Several Other Rights
sections.body: The 2014 New Orleans first transferred to Philadelphia as the No. 10 pick and became the draft rights to Elfrid Payton. The 76ers promptly traded those rights to Orlando for the No. 12 rights to Dario Šarić, a future first-round consideration and an additional future second. Orlando's July 2014 announcement independently names all three incoming Philadelphia assets. The first-round consideration was a previously owed Philadelphia pick being sent back from Orlando, an important protection from future obligation rather than a newly drafted star. This was a genuine conversion of the asset New Orleans sent in 2013, but it would be misleading to count Payton's seasons with Orlando as Philadelphia playing production. Šarić eventually played for the 76ers and later became one part of the separate November 2018 Jimmy Butler trade.

sections.heading: Noel Produced Philadelphia Minutes Before a Separate Dallas Move
sections.body: Noel missed the 2013-14 season while rehabilitating his knee, then developed into a shot-blocking and steals-producing center for Philadelphia. He was a genuine young contributor rather than a draft asset that never reached the floor. On February 23, 2017, Philadelphia sent him to Dallas for Justin Anderson, Andrew Bogut and a protected future first. The NBA's contemporary trade tracker makes clear that this Dallas exchange was separate from the 2013 Holiday deal; its assets cannot be credited to New Orleans. The value the Sixers collected included Noel's own defensive seasons and any value they could realize in moving him later. That supports the inherited 76ers B, even though it did not approximate Holiday's best New Orleans seasons.

sections.heading: The 2020 Milwaukee Package Extended Holiday’s New Orleans Asset Path
sections.body: New Orleans traded Holiday again in November 2020, seven seasons after acquiring him. The later four-team transaction brought Eric Bledsoe and George Hill along with three future first-round draft picks and two pick swaps in the broader Milwaukee-led package, according to the NBA's official summary. That was a second, separately negotiated trade, not compensation Philadelphia sent in 2013. It is still fair to show that the Pelicans held a valuable asset they could later move for more options. The exact downstream players chosen with those rights require their own transaction history and shouldn't all be assigned to Holiday by shorthand. Viewed through that boundary, the original deal provided both prolonged high-level two-way play and a later resale opportunity. Philadelphia's parallel rebuilding route was legitimate, but its direct result never matched the full New Orleans guard return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans A, 76ers B — New Orleans edge. Holiday supplied multiple seasons of elite defensive guard play, notably 81 starts and a Portland playoff sweep in 2017-18, before New Orleans moved him for another major package in 2020. Philadelphia received Noel's real NBA contribution and the top-five-protected first that became No. 10 Payton rights, then Šarić rights and further pick considerations through Orlando. The 2014 and 2020 follow-up trades are separate transactions and cannot be treated as guarantees of a title or of every later drafted player's career.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: How the 2013 Holiday–Noel Deal Split Immediate NBA Production and Draft Control
featuredDeepDive.intro: The Pelicans traded Noel's 2013 rights and a top-five-protected 2014 first to get Holiday and Pierre Jackson's rights on July 12, 2013. Philadelphia chose two young assets at the start of a rebuild; New Orleans took a guard who had already reached an All-Star Game. Seven seasons of New Orleans play and two later team-specific trade paths provide a measured comparison. This review preserves Pelicans A and 76ers B while separating Noel's real 76ers seasons, Šarić's rights and Holiday's eventual 2020 trade from the assets exchanged in July 2013.

sections.heading: New Orleans Acted Before Holiday’s 2013-14 Injury Was Known
sections.body: When the July 2013 exchange became official, Holiday was a 23-year-old guard fresh off an All-Star selection and the Pelicans were beginning their first season under the new team name. Their official transaction announcement says they gave Philadelphia the rights to the player chosen sixth overall, Nerlens Noel, plus a 2014 first protected in the top five. Holiday's fractured leg in 2013-14 and limited 2014-15 games were outcomes after the decision, not facts New Orleans could have known at the trade table. Those absences delayed the expected partnership with Anthony Davis and increased the immediate cost of giving up two first-round-level assets. Noel meanwhile missed 2013-14 with an existing knee injury, which explains why Philadelphia had to be willing to defer returns. Both organizations accepted a distinct kind of health or development risk, and neither bought a predetermined championship.

sections.heading: Healthy Holiday Gave the Pelicans Their Best 2018 Backcourt
sections.body: The swing toward New Orleans occurred through Holiday's realized work, not his draft pedigree. The Pelicans' 2017-18 season report records 81 starts; NBA statistics give him 19.0 points, six assists and substantial defensive duties in those regular-season games. His containment of Portland guards helped drive the 2018 four-game first-round sweep, the first series win for the franchise in several years. Holiday's first-team All-Defensive honor identified the value of his perimeter defense beyond scoring. The Pelicans then lost to Golden State in the conference semifinals. That result is a ceiling, not a defect in the record: the 2013 price bought a high-level guard who became integral to one strong playoff series and several productive seasons, not the right to claim all eventual NBA postseason success under his name.

sections.heading: Philadelphia’s 2014 No. 10 Pick Traveled Through Orlando
sections.body: Philadelphia held the protected New Orleans 2014 first that landed at No. 10. It selected Elfrid Payton and traded his rights to Orlando during that draft, receiving the No. 12 rights to Dario Šarić, a 2015 second-round pick and the return of a future Philadelphia first that Orlando had held through a prior transaction. Orlando's team release verifies the three assets given for Payton. Šarić eventually joined the 76ers and became a contributor; the additional picks altered Philadelphia's draft flexibility. In November 2018, the Sixers included Šarić with Robert Covington, Jerryd Bayless and a 2022 second to obtain Jimmy Butler and Justin Patton from Minnesota. That later bundle was not a straight Holiday-for-Butler conversion. It is an asset chain that began partly with the No. 10 right, then grew through separately negotiated moves involving several other players.

sections.heading: Noel Had a Genuine Philadelphia Career and a Distinct Exit
sections.body: The trade did not leave Philadelphia with only draft paperwork. Noel missed his first NBA season, then played meaningful frontcourt minutes for the 76ers, providing interior defense, blocked shots and steals. Those seasons were the direct return on the sixth-pick rights acquired from New Orleans. The next leg came at the February 2017 deadline, when the 76ers traded Noel to Dallas for Justin Anderson, Andrew Bogut and a protected future first-round pick. The NBA's trade tracker documents that exact separate agreement. No later Noel games with Dallas or another team should inflate the return for Philadelphia, and any disputed future-pick conveyance should not be counted as an actual player absent confirmation. The key difference from the Pelicans' side is longevity and impact: New Orleans enjoyed Holiday's later peak, while Philadelphia collected useful developmental center play and then moved on.

sections.heading: Holiday’s Milwaukee Trade Was a 2020 Resale, Not Part of the 2013 Invoice
sections.body: In November 2020, Milwaukee's four-team acquisition of Holiday sent New Orleans two veterans, Eric Bledsoe and George Hill, as well as three future first-round picks and two swaps in the transaction's wider structure. That is a legitimate endpoint for Holiday as a New Orleans-held asset; the club was able to convert a guard it had acquired seven years earlier into additional roster and draft control. Still, it would be inaccurate to say Philadelphia originally sent any of those Milwaukee selections or that the 2013 deal directly delivered the Bucks' later title. The date and transaction structure keep the causal chain bounded. Comparing the sides through what they actually realized points to the inherited Pelicans A and 76ers B: Philadelphia made plausible rebuilding moves, but Holiday's health recovery, defense, 2018 postseason and later resale gave New Orleans the greater realized return.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans A and 76ers B. The 2013 trade delivered Holiday and Pierre Jackson's draft rights to New Orleans for Noel's rights and a protected future first. Holiday's 2017-18 81-game season, Portland sweep and first-team All-Defensive selection document high-level New Orleans value. Philadelphia's No. 10 2014 pick converted through Payton into Šarić and other considerations, and Noel supplied real center minutes before a separate Dallas trade. The large Milwaukee 2020 package was a later resale of Holiday, not an asset originally delivered by Philadelphia. The value differential supports a New Orleans advantage without wiping away Philadelphia's sourced return.
