sections.heading: New Orleans Swapped One Draft-Rights Guard for Another
sections.body: On June 26, 2014, the Pelicans acquired the draft rights to guard Russ Smith from Philadelphia in exchange for rights to Pierre Jackson. New Orleans had previously controlled Jackson’s rights and elected to acquire a different young prospect. Philadelphia took Jackson instead of retaining Smith. The package contained no recorded first-round selection or veteran starter. Each team was choosing a particular young guard whose NBA role remained uncertain at the time of the swap.

sections.heading: The Prospect Evaluations Were Specific but Uncertain
sections.body: Smith and Jackson were named draft-rights assets, not anonymous future picks. The Pelicans could bring Smith into their development plans; Philadelphia had the option to assess Jackson on a different timeline. This is precisely the type of small draft-day exchange where a later notable career elsewhere cannot automatically be credited to the club receiving the rights in 2014. The trade-source history establishes the identities and directional swap, but not a major downstream compensation branch.

sections.heading: Neither Rights Package Supports a Dominant Winner
sections.body: Both New Orleans and Philadelphia are graded B-minus, with Even Trade as the archived result. The teams exchanged rights to two identified prospects without producing a clearly documented long-term advantage. Treating the deal as a guaranteed steal would require inventing subsequent NBA productivity that the transaction ledger does not establish. The equal grade recognizes the modest scale of the exchange while allowing that each team may have valued the prospects differently on draft night.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — New Orleans B-minus, Philadelphia B-minus. The Pelicans obtained Russ Smith’s draft rights and the 76ers received Pierre Jackson’s rights. Both teams traded one identifiable developmental guard prospect for another. The recorded results leave them level, with no verified major follow-on asset gain.

sections.heading: Christmas Eve 2015: Two Future Seconds for a Starting Guard
sections.body: New Orleans sent guard Ish Smith to Philadelphia on December 24, 2015, acquiring two future second-round choices. One was Denver's 2016 second that became No. 39 David Michineau, while the other was Philadelphia's own 2017 second that became No. 34 Frank Mason III. The Pelicans' official media guide confirms the date and two-pick consideration; the team transaction archive identifies both eventual draft outcomes. Smith had played 27 New Orleans games that season before the trade. The 76ers were bringing back a guard who had previously appeared with them in 2014-15, seeking immediate ball handling for a struggling roster. The Pelicans chose future draft capital rather than maintaining Smith's present rotation role. Neither named draft prospect had been selected when that Christmas Eve agreement was completed.

sections.heading: Smith Started All Fifty Philadelphia Games After Arrival
sections.body: Smith made an immediate contribution as Philadelphia's lead guard, starting all 50 regular-season games he played for the 76ers after December 24. He averaged 14.7 points and 7.0 assists in 32.4 minutes per appearance, according to the NBA's official season record. His previous 27 New Orleans games and 25 Philadelphia appearances from the prior season are different assignments and do not belong in this acquired 2015-16 return. Smith later joined Detroit for 2016-17 as a free agent, so the December trade did not provide Philadelphia a further year of direct team playing time. Even a short 50-game starter stint has meaningful NBA value and should not be erased merely because the 76ers' season record was poor. This is the direct countercase to the archived Pelicans Win label.

sections.heading: No. 39 Michineau Helped Obtain Cheick Diallo
sections.body: The incoming 2016 second-round asset became No. 39 David Michineau on June 23, 2016. New Orleans also held the No. 40 choice used on Diamond Stone from another source. The Pelicans combined the rights to Michineau and Stone in a separate draft-night deal with the Los Angeles Clippers for the rights to No. 33 Cheick Diallo. The Clippers' contemporaneous press release lists all three players and the rights directions. Diallo subsequently appeared in 17 Pelicans games in 2016-17, 52 in 2017-18 and 64 in 2018-19, totaling 133 New Orleans regular-season appearances. This is a real source-traced downstream return from the acquired No. 39 asset, but the full Diallo value cannot be assigned to Michineau alone because Stone was separate outgoing consideration.

sections.heading: No. 34 Frank Mason Pick Entered the Cousins Package
sections.body: New Orleans retained the Philadelphia-origin 2017 second-round right until February 20, 2017, when it included the choice in the DeMarcus Cousins and Omri Casspi transaction with Sacramento. The Pelicans also sent Buddy Hield, Tyreke Evans, Langston Galloway and a protected 2017 first-round pick in that multi-asset package. Sacramento eventually used the second at No. 34 on Frank Mason III. The NBA's official Pelicans acquisition announcement and 2017 draft order document the choice and its final recipient. The acquired second therefore had genuine trade value, but the Pelicans did not draft Mason for their NBA roster, and no responsible evaluation can credit the entire Cousins acquisition to this one second-round right. The saved Pelicans B-plus versus Sixers C-plus verdict should account for both distinct downstream pick chains and Smith's 50 Philadelphia starts.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans Win — the inherited grade is New Orleans B-plus and Philadelphia C-plus. Philadelphia obtained 50 starts from Ish Smith at 14.7 points and 7.0 assists a game. New Orleans used the 2016 No. 39 pick in a separate two-rights trade for Cheick Diallo, who later played 133 Pelicans games, and sent the 2017 No. 34 right within a five-asset DeMarcus Cousins deal. Neither full later package was obtained solely from the original Ish Smith selection.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: New Orleans Pelicans–Philadelphia 76ers: What the 2015-12-24 Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: On December 24, 2015, New Orleans traded Ish Smith to Philadelphia for two future second-round selections. Smith started all 50 Sixers games he played afterward, averaging 14.7 points and 7.0 assists. The 2016 Denver-origin second became No. 39 Michineau, later bundled with No. 40 Diamond Stone for Cheick Diallo rights; Philadelphia's 2017 second became No. 34 Frank Mason, sent to Sacramento as part of a separate five-asset DeMarcus Cousins package.

sections.heading: The 2016 Second Was Denver-Origin, Not Philadelphia-Owned
sections.body: The December 24, 2015 exchange involved exactly two future seconds moving to New Orleans and Ish Smith going to the 76ers. The 2016 choice was Denver-origin draft consideration that Philadelphia controlled, whereas the 2017 second was Philadelphia's own selection. These origins are specified in the historical team ledgers and matter when tracing the later pick chain. The former became No. 39 in 2016; the latter became No. 34 the following year. Neither was an additional first-round pick. Philadelphia acquired a player who could immediately run the offense and was already familiar with the team from an earlier contract. New Orleans exchanged his near-term basketball value for two independent future assets that could be exercised or moved in later transactions.

sections.heading: The Philadelphia Guard Return Was Fifty Actual Starts
sections.body: Smith appeared in 50 Sixers regular-season games after Christmas and started each one. His 14.7 points and 7.0 assists per game provided tangible offensive organization for an inexperienced Philadelphia lineup. He had played another 27 games with New Orleans earlier in the season, averaging 8.9 points and 5.7 assists; the sending club, not Philadelphia, receives the accounting for that earlier production. Smith's second Philadelphia stint ended after 2015-16, before he moved to Detroit in free agency. The archived Sixers C-plus should not be read as evidence that the acquired guard was unusable. New Orleans won the retrospective only if the subsequent value of those two second-round rights is weighed correctly against Smith's 50 starts, not if the guard's NBA service is erased.

sections.heading: The No. 39 Rights Were Only One Piece of the Diallo Exchange
sections.body: New Orleans selected French guard David Michineau at No. 39 in 2016, then transferred his NBA rights and the No. 40 Diamond Stone rights to the Clippers for No. 33 Cheick Diallo. The official Clippers and Pelicans announcements identify a three-prospect rights transaction, not a direct one-for-one Michineau trade. Diallo appeared in 133 New Orleans regular-season games across 2016-17 through 2018-19, averaging 6.0 points and 5.2 rebounds in his final Pelicans season. The team-specific NBA output was meaningful reserve frontcourt depth, but the separate Stone contribution cannot be erased. The original Smith trade supplied the No. 39 portion only. Recording this partial downstream link helps explain why acquiring multiple seconds could be useful without inflating one pick into a standalone starting center.

sections.heading: The No. 34 Right Was One Part of Five Pieces for Cousins
sections.body: The 2017 Philadelphia-origin second was traded by New Orleans to Sacramento in February 2017 as part of the larger DeMarcus Cousins and Omri Casspi package. Buddy Hield, Tyreke Evans, Langston Galloway and a protected first also left the Pelicans, according to the organization's official release. Sacramento then selected Frank Mason III at No. 34. That is documented transaction value for the acquired right, not direct Mason NBA scoring for New Orleans. Cousins played for the Pelicans after the later multi-asset trade, but crediting his entire New Orleans tenure to the Ish Smith second would be incorrect. The legacy Pelicans Win, B-plus New Orleans and C-plus Philadelphia grades are preserved while the sourced review distinguishes the 50-game Smith return from these two different draft paths and their other costs.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: New Orleans B-plus and Philadelphia C-plus preserve the archived Pelicans Win, with important qualifications: Smith played 50 valuable starter games for the Sixers. New Orleans converted the 2016 No. 39 Michineau right together with its separate No. 40 Stone right into Cheick Diallo, and transferred the 2017 No. 34 second to Sacramento alongside four other assets in the Cousins deal. The later destinations and costs are sourced; no single second-round pick deserves credit for an entire multi-asset acquisition.

sections.heading: New Orleans Paid a Defensible Price for a Rare Star Pairing
sections.body: The Pelicans acquired DeMarcus Cousins and Omri Casspi for Buddy Hield, Tyreke Evans, Langston Galloway, a top-three-protected 2017 first-round pick and a second-round pick. For a team already built around Anthony Davis, the price was aggressive without resembling the enormous multi-pick packages later required for stars. Cousins was in his prime, under contract through the following season and capable of scoring, rebounding and creating offense from the center position. New Orleans was justified in believing that the opportunity was too unusual to ignore.

sections.heading: Cousins and Davis Needed Time but Eventually Became Overwhelming Together
sections.body: The immediate post-trade results were uneven as two high-usage big men and a reconfigured supporting cast learned new roles. By the following season, the experiment had become far more convincing. Cousins was producing roughly 25 points, 13 rebounds and five assists per game, while Davis retained his own superstar output. Their passing and shooting allowed New Orleans to play through either big, punish switches and overwhelm conventional frontcourts. The pairing was no longer merely theoretical when the season changed in January 2018.

sections.heading: The Achilles Rupture Ended the Evaluation Before the Playoffs Could Test It
sections.body: Cousins ruptured his left Achilles late in a win over Houston, ending his season after the Pelicans had built a winning record with him in the lineup. New Orleans later swept Portland and reached the second round without him, which proved that Davis, Jrue Holiday and the remaining roster had real quality. It did not show that Cousins was unnecessary. The injury removed the chance to see the intended frontcourt in a postseason series and transformed an expiring star acquisition into a short, incomplete window.

sections.heading: Sacramento’s Return Was More Durable Than New Orleans’
sections.body: Buddy Hield became the central realized asset for the Kings, developing into one of the league’s most prolific volume three-point shooters and remaining productive long after Cousins left New Orleans. Sacramento also received the first-round pick that became the rights to Zach Collins, then redirected that selection into the rights to Justin Jackson and Harry Giles, plus the second-round pick used on Frank Mason. The draft outcomes were mixed, but the combination of Hield and multiple shots at young talent gave Sacramento years of usable value.

sections.heading: The Kings Won in Hindsight Without Maximizing a Franchise Star
sections.body: A winning verdict for Sacramento should not be confused with praise for every element of the process. Cousins was an All-NBA talent, and the Kings completed the deal during All-Star weekend after years of organizational instability had weakened their leverage. Hield became a good player rather than a replacement superstar, and the draft capital did not produce a new franchise centerpiece. Sacramento’s advantage comes from durability and availability: its return remained on the floor while New Orleans received only 65 regular-season games from Cousins.

sections.heading: New Orleans Deserves a Better Grade Than the Injury-Driven Result Suggests
sections.body: A D+ treats the Pelicans as though they emptied the franchise for an obviously reckless gamble. The actual package and the level Cousins reached beside Davis support a more measured B-. The process created a legitimate high-end outcome, and the partnership was working before a catastrophic injury that could not reasonably have been forecast. Sacramento still earns a B and the slight edge because Hield and the draft assets produced the longer return. The gap should remain narrow enough to distinguish bad luck from bad evaluation.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Sacramento receives the slight win with a B, while New Orleans moves to B-. The Kings obtained years of production from Buddy Hield and additional draft opportunities, whereas the Pelicans received only 65 regular-season games from Cousins before his Achilles rupture and subsequent departure. New Orleans nevertheless paid a defensible price for a prime All-NBA center, and the Cousins-Davis pairing had developed into a genuine threat before the injury. The realized value favors Sacramento, but the quality of the original gamble makes this a narrow edge rather than a condemnation.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The DeMarcus Cousins Trade Was a Good Gamble With an Unfinished Test
featuredDeepDive.intro: The Cousins transaction resists a simple lesson because the process and result point in different directions. New Orleans acquired a prime star without surrendering the kind of unrestricted draft package that later defined blockbuster trades. Sacramento recovered a productive young shooter and multiple draft assets after its relationship with Cousins had deteriorated. Then a torn Achilles removed the central player before the postseason could judge the experiment. A useful verdict must acknowledge both the Pelicans’ rational ambition and the Kings’ more durable return.

sections.heading: All-Star Weekend Timing Reflected Sacramento’s Weakening Leverage
sections.body: The trade became public around the 2017 All-Star Game, producing shock because Cousins had represented Sacramento as the franchise’s centerpiece only hours earlier. The Kings had spent years cycling through coaches, roster ideas and public tension with their star. That environment mattered to the price. New Orleans could offer a recent lottery pick in Hield, expiring or movable veterans and protected draft capital without including every premium asset it controlled. Sacramento accepted a reset package because the organization no longer believed a stable Cousins era was available.

sections.heading: The Two-Big Offense Was More Modern Than the Label Suggested
sections.body: Pairing two centers appeared contrary to the league’s move toward smaller lineups, but Davis and Cousins were not traditional stationary bigs. Both could handle the ball, pass and score away from the rim. Cousins’ three-point range pulled opposing centers from the paint, while Davis could attack slower defenders in space or dominate as a screener. The Pelicans could invert actions, run offense through the elbows and force opponents to choose which All-Star received the favorable matchup. The concept was ambitious, but it was not strategically obsolete.

sections.heading: January 2018 Was the Point at Which the Bet Looked Vindicated
sections.body: By the time Cousins was injured, New Orleans had moved beyond the awkward first months of integration. The team was winning, Cousins had recorded major triple-double performances, and the Davis-Cousins combination was creating matchup problems no other roster could replicate. The injury occurred late in a statement victory over Houston, making the abrupt change especially severe. Instead of entering the postseason with two elite bigs, the Pelicans had to rebuild their identity around Davis, Holiday, Nikola Mirotic and faster lineups in a matter of weeks.

sections.heading: Hield Supplied the Kings With a Long-Term NBA Asset
sections.body: Hield never became the singular replacement for Cousins, but he did become a high-volume shooter who could start, score and later function as a valuable trade piece. That matters because star-trade returns often fail when none of the young players become dependable rotation pieces. Sacramento also had opportunities with the associated draft picks, even though the Collins selection was converted into Jackson and Giles and neither became a cornerstone. The Kings’ return was imperfect, yet it created more seasons of usable value than New Orleans ultimately retained.

sections.heading: A Counterfactual Championship Claim Would Go Too Far
sections.body: It is tempting to imagine that a healthy Cousins would have transformed the 2018 Pelicans into a championship threat after they swept Portland. That conclusion cannot be proven. Golden State remained a historically strong opponent, and integrating Cousins into the playoff rotation would have created its own defensive challenges. The more supportable claim is narrower: New Orleans never received the postseason evaluation it purchased. Cousins’ regular-season performance showed that the pairing could work, while the Achilles injury prevented the franchise from learning how far it could travel.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Kings hold a slight edge because Hield and the draft assets outlasted the Pelicans’ brief Cousins era. Sacramento’s B recognizes a meaningful return without pretending it fully replaced an All-NBA franchise player. New Orleans earns B- because the acquisition price was reasonable, Cousins played at a star level beside Davis and the failure was driven primarily by a catastrophic injury rather than an incoherent plan. The trade did not become the Pelicans’ breakthrough, but it was a serious basketball idea whose final examination never occurred.

sections.heading: The Original Return Included Cash, Not Just Two Assets
sections.body: The February 6, 2019 deadline agreement sent Wesley Johnson from New Orleans to Washington in exchange for Markieff Morris, the Wizards' own 2023 second-round selection and cash considerations. NBA's deadline tracker names Morris and the future pick, while the league's historical deadline list and both clubs' transaction histories explicitly record the cash component. The older Pelicans import omitted cash from its three-asset ledger, so a source-based correction must account for four original pieces. The exact amount of the money is not established by the reviewed reports and should not be guessed. Washington was seeking salary and repeater-tax relief, while New Orleans obtained a conditional future asset for absorbing a veteran contract.

sections.heading: Morris Was Waived Before Playing for New Orleans
sections.body: Markieff Morris was not an on-court Pelicans contributor. The team waived him almost immediately after the trade, with NBA reporting the plan on February 8 and the New Orleans 2018–19 transaction history recording his release after the February 7 completion. He had averaged 11.5 points and 5.1 rebounds in 34 Washington games before the deadline, but none of that production occurred in New Orleans. On February 20 Oklahoma City announced his free-agent signing, which was a later independent transaction. That sequence is central to assessing the Pelicans' return: Morris was a contract accepted in a salary-management exchange, not a veteran who stabilized their frontcourt for the rest of the season.

sections.heading: Washington Got Twelve Games From Wesley Johnson
sections.body: Wesley Johnson did play for the Wizards after the deal, though not as a major contributor. His 2018–19 season splits show 12 Washington games, no starts and an average of 2.8 points and 1.5 rebounds in 13.1 minutes. The 31-year-old wing had played 26 games for New Orleans beforehand, so his modest Wizards tenure cannot be combined with those earlier appearances as though they belonged to Washington. NBA's deadline coverage identifies Washington's main objective as payroll relief and avoiding a future repeater tax. The team traded away Morris, a 2023 second and cash to achieve that financial goal and get a smaller contract; Johnson's limited basketball production was a secondary return.

sections.heading: The 2023 Pick Eventually Became Hunter Tyson at No. 37
sections.body: The Washington-origin 2023 second was a real piece of the 2019 agreement, but New Orleans did not eventually select Hunter Tyson. In a later November 2020 multi-team transaction involving Steven Adams, the Pelicans sent the right onward to Oklahoma City. Denver subsequently obtained the No. 37 selection in a separate 2023 exchange with the Thunder, then acquired Hunter Tyson's rights on draft night. NBA's official 2023 draft order and Denver's club announcement confirm that outcome. The archived asset may name Tyson as the pick's final player, but that must not be converted into Tyson's playing value for New Orleans. The stored Pelicans Win, New Orleans B+ and Washington D verdict is unchanged pending a separate comparison of the cash, tax savings and draft-right value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Stored verdict: Pelicans Win — New Orleans B+, Washington D. The supported trade-day return was Morris, Washington's 2023 second and cash for Wesley Johnson. Morris played no Pelicans games; Johnson appeared 12 times for Washington. The pick later became No. 37 Hunter Tyson only after moving to Oklahoma City and Denver. Preserve the recorded grades pending an independent financial-outcome review.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Morris for Johnson: The Cash Detail and the No. 37 Pick Trail
featuredDeepDive.intro: New Orleans took Markieff Morris and Washington's 2023 second-round pick at the 2019 trade deadline, sending Wesley Johnson to the Wizards. The original archive omitted a fourth asset: cash considerations flowing to the Pelicans. Morris was waived without appearing for New Orleans, and Johnson played 12 Wizards games. Four years later the future selection became No. 37 Hunter Tyson after intermediate deals through Oklahoma City and Denver. Each part must be evaluated separately rather than crediting the Pelicans with a player they never drafted.

sections.heading: February 2019: Salary Relief, a Pick and Cash
sections.body: The league's contemporaneous 2018–19 trade tracker records Wesley Johnson moving to Washington, with Markieff Morris and a 2023 second coming to New Orleans. The historical transaction list and Pelicans' own media guide additionally identify cash considerations paid by the Wizards. Reporting explained that Washington's objective was to get beneath future repeater-tax limits and reduce the financial impact of Morris' salary. Washington had also moved Otto Porter Jr. in a different trade, but that prior arrangement is not another asset in the Johnson–Morris agreement. The correction to the Pelicans' canonical record is narrow: recognize cash without inventing an amount, preserve both players and the pick with their proper directional ownership, and avoid presenting the February 6 announcement date as a second distinct trade from the February 7 transaction posting.

sections.heading: Two Player Contracts With Little Direct Production
sections.body: Morris entered the trade recovering from a neck issue and had made 34 appearances for Washington in 2018–19, averaging 11.5 points and 5.1 rebounds. NBA coverage reported immediately that New Orleans would waive him; the actual team transaction record confirms the release shortly after completion. Oklahoma City later signed him as a free agent on February 20. For the Pelicans the player contract therefore yielded no game appearances, regardless of the scoring he had produced for Washington or would record elsewhere. Wesley Johnson had more direct basketball output for his new club, but only 12 reserve appearances, 2.8 points and 1.5 rebounds on average. Those contrasts clarify why the financial effects and draft right deserve more attention than the names alone. Neither team gained a long-term starter through this specific deal.

sections.heading: Washington's Second Was Traded Again Before 2023
sections.body: The 2023 second-round pick that the Wizards sent to New Orleans ultimately acquired a known draft slot, but several separate moves intervene. The Pelicans later sent the Washington-origin right to Oklahoma City in the 2020 multi-club arrangement that brought Steven Adams to New Orleans. Denver acquired the No. 37 selection in June 2023 along with other draft assets through an agreement with Oklahoma City, using the right to bring in Hunter Tyson from Clemson. The official 2023 NBA draft order notes Oklahoma City selecting Tyson at No. 37 and transferring him to the Nuggets; Denver's own draft report confirms the rights acquisition. The draft pick's provenance can be followed without treating Tyson as a player who ever joined the Pelicans by virtue of this 2019 trade.

sections.heading: What the B+ and D Grades Need to Reflect
sections.body: The archive's top-level verdict is Pelicans Win with New Orleans graded B+ and Washington D. The original three-piece source import understates what New Orleans was actually promised because it omitted cash, but the amount is unknown from the reviewed sources. The Pelicans also held and later used a future draft right in a multiclub trade, while Morris provided no game production. Washington got 12 Johnson appearances and reduced its near-term salary exposure; that financial outcome should not be erased solely because the player return was modest. A deeper grade review needs the cash amount and tax position independently documented, plus a careful valuation of the pick at trade date and its later use. The older per-team imported perspective labels are internally inconsistent with the top-level grades, so they should be flagged and reconciled deliberately rather than silently rewritten.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Four trade-day assets are supported: Morris, a 2023 Washington-origin second and cash to New Orleans; Wesley Johnson to Washington. Morris never played for the Pelicans, and Johnson appeared in 12 Wizards games. No. 37 Hunter Tyson reached Denver only after two later franchise moves. Preserve Pelicans Win and B+/D pending cash, tax and perspective-grade reconciliation.

sections.heading: Atlanta Traded Up for Hunter; New Orleans Split the Fourth Pick
sections.body: The Hawks obtained the rights to No. 4 De’Andre Hunter and No. 57 Jordan Bone, with Solomon Hill and a protected second-round pick also moving to Atlanta. New Orleans received the rights to No. 8 Jaxson Hayes, No. 17 Nickeil Alexander-Walker and No. 35 Didi Louzada, plus a protected future first-round obligation that ultimately produced second-round assets. This was a consolidation move for Atlanta and a spread-the-risk move for New Orleans.

sections.heading: The Pelicans Had Mixed Results Across Three Young Players
sections.body: Hayes brought athletic frontcourt potential but did not become the high-end center a top-ten selection could suggest. Alexander-Walker developed into a useful NBA guard, though much of his later success occurred after leaving New Orleans. Louzada did not become a major Pelicans rotation fixture. The advantage of the transaction was never that all three draft choices became stars; it was that New Orleans acquired multiple assets in exchange for one premium pick.

sections.heading: The Protected-Pick Branch Eventually Brought More Value
sections.body: Atlanta’s additional draft obligation was conditional rather than a guaranteed valuable first. The protected structure ultimately converted into second-round selections. One of those became the No. 35 pick in 2021, used to select Herb Jones, whose defense made him an especially valuable Pelicans contributor for his draft position. The later No. 47 selection in 2022 is a separate downstream branch whose eventual usage should not be overstated as New Orleans player production.

sections.heading: Atlanta’s Hunter Bet Was Reasonable and Productive
sections.body: Hunter gave Atlanta a long, capable defensive wing with enough offense to fit next to Trae Young. He played meaningful minutes on the Hawks team that reached the Eastern Conference finals in 2021. The Hawks were pursuing a particular two-way starter and found one; the downside was surrendering three earlier selections and additional future consideration for that one target. A B grade recognizes real usefulness without treating the package as an Atlanta triumph.

sections.heading: The A-grade for New Orleans Is Primarily About Jones
sections.body: The Pelicans’ A reflects extracting several bites at development and, most decisively, the later second-round opportunity that became Jones. Hayes and Louzada supplied less value than their initial draft positions might have implied. Atlanta receives B because Hunter became a credible starter, but New Orleans obtained greater combined utility from the varied returns. Jones’s contribution is traceable to the protected-pick outcome; unrelated Pelicans roster successes are not part of this trade’s score.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans Win — New Orleans A, Atlanta B. Atlanta converted a group of draft assets into Hunter, a useful starting wing, but New Orleans collected Hayes, Alexander-Walker, Louzada and the protected-pick branch that produced Herb Jones. The returns were uneven, yet Jones supplied a particularly strong payoff from a later second-round choice. The advantage comes from those identified assets rather than from counting every incoming player as a hit.

sections.heading: New Orleans Bought a Starting Center for Two Seconds
sections.body: New Orleans acquired Derrick Favors from Utah for two future second-round picks. The price was modest relative to the role Favors immediately filled. He started 49 of 51 games for the Pelicans in 2019-20, averaged 9.0 points and 9.8 rebounds, and gave a young roster a veteran interior presence during the first season after the Anthony Davis trade. Favors was not a long-term building block and left after one season, which limits the ceiling of the return. Even so, a starting-caliber center for two seconds is a favorable exchange when the player contributes meaningful minutes and the outgoing picks do not become high-impact assets for the seller.

sections.heading: Utah's Decision Was About Clearing the Frontcourt and Payroll
sections.body: The Jazz had reached a point where Rudy Gobert was firmly established as the starting center and Utah was reshaping the roster around Donovan Mitchell. Moving Favors opened salary and positional room after years of overlap in the frontcourt. That strategic logic was sound. The problem is the realized return. Utah received two second-round picks, later associated with David Johnson at No. 47 in 2021 and Emoni Bates at No. 49 in 2023. Neither outcome created value comparable to a full season of starting-level Favors production for New Orleans. A C- recognizes that Utah accomplished roster flexibility while still losing the basketball side of the exchange.

sections.heading: Favors' One Season Was More Valuable Than It Looks
sections.body: A one-year rental can still win a trade when the acquisition cost is low. Favors played 24.4 minutes per game, rebounded efficiently and provided stability next to a roster featuring Brandon Ingram, Jrue Holiday and the delayed debut of Zion Williamson. New Orleans did not need him to become a five-year core piece for the transaction to work. The Pelicans needed competent center play while younger players developed and while the post-Davis roster found an identity. Favors supplied that. Because the outgoing assets were two seconds rather than a first or a premium prospect, the bar for a positive result was relatively low and he cleared it comfortably.

sections.heading: Why New Orleans Stops at B+
sections.body: The Pelicans do not receive an A because the value was temporary. Favors played one season in New Orleans and then returned to Utah in free agency. The trade did not create a lasting asset chain or a player who remained through the next phase of the rebuild. The two seconds also retained some value as draft currency for Utah even though the eventual selections were late in the second round. B+ fits the scale: New Orleans paid a reasonable price and received a useful starter, but the acquisition was not transformational. Utah's C- reflects the inverse — defensible roster planning with a return that proved lighter than the player it surrendered.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans Win. New Orleans earns B+ because two future second-round picks produced a season of legitimate starting-center value from Derrick Favors. He started 49 games, averaged 9.0 points and 9.8 rebounds, and filled an important stabilizing role on a young roster at low acquisition cost. Utah receives C- because moving Favors created salary and positional flexibility around Rudy Gobert, but the two incoming seconds ultimately became late selections that did not match the direct NBA value Favors gave New Orleans. The Pelicans' return lasted only one season, preventing an A-range grade. Still, the documented Pelicans Win verdict is supported by a simple value comparison: New Orleans received the best realized basketball asset for a modest price.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Deep Dive: Why a One-Year Derrick Favors Rental Was Still a Winning Trade
featuredDeepDive.intro: The Favors deal tests a common trade-grading mistake: assuming a short tenure cannot create strong value. New Orleans acquired a veteran center for two seconds and used him as a starter during a transition season. The right question is not how long he stayed, but whether the season he supplied was worth more than the draft assets the Pelicans gave up.

sections.heading: Favors Arrived with a Defined Role
sections.body: New Orleans was assembling a dramatically different roster after trading Anthony Davis. The club had young talent, veteran guards and a new set of draft assets, but it still needed a dependable center who could rebound, screen and defend without demanding the offense run through him. Favors fit that profile. The Pelicans' official release emphasized his rim protection and recent production in Utah, and the season confirmed that he could handle the role. He started 49 games and nearly averaged a double-double. That is not star value, but it is meaningful roster value acquired for two future seconds. The clarity of the role helped the trade succeed even though the relationship lasted only one year.

sections.heading: The Picks Were Real but Low-Cost Currency
sections.body: Second-round selections should not be dismissed, especially for a rebuilding franchise, but their expected value is lower and more volatile than first-round picks. The two selections sent by New Orleans eventually landed at No. 47 and No. 49. Those positions can produce players, but they also illustrate how limited the opportunity cost was compared with surrendering a premium first. Utah obtained two chances and retained future flexibility; New Orleans obtained a known starting center immediately. The completed player outcomes did not swing those picks into high-end value, so the risk New Orleans accepted remained contained. That cost structure is a central reason the Pelicans deserve B+ rather than merely a neutral grade.

sections.heading: Utah's Frontcourt Logic Was Sensible
sections.body: The Jazz had spent years balancing Favors and Gobert together, but the league was moving toward more spacing and Utah was increasingly committed to Gobert as the full-time center. Favors was also entering a contract transition. Moving him for picks opened flexibility for a roster that was adding Mike Conley and reshaping around Mitchell and Gobert. That is a legitimate strategic reason to trade a useful player. The C- should therefore not be read as an indictment of the decision to move Favors. It reflects the completed exchange. Utah obtained only late second-round value while New Orleans extracted a full season of starting production. Good strategic logic can still produce a losing trade outcome.

sections.heading: One Season Can Be Enough When the Price Is Right
sections.body: Trade duration matters only in relation to cost. If New Orleans had paid a first-round pick or a premium young player for one Favors season, the grade would be lower. Two seconds created a much smaller hurdle. Favors supplied 51 games, 49 starts and 9.8 rebounds per game, helping a young team remain functional through injuries and roster change. When he left, the Pelicans did not retain a compensating asset, so the value chain ended. That is why the grade stops at B+. Yet the basic exchange still worked: the Pelicans used low-cost future currency to buy present competence, and the future currency did not later become enough to reverse the result.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans Win, New Orleans B+ and Utah C-. The Pelicans gave up two second-round picks and received a season of dependable starting-center play from Derrick Favors. His 49 starts and 9.8 rebounds per game provided real value during a transitional season, and the low acquisition cost made a one-year tenure acceptable. Utah had a clear roster reason to move him and did receive future draft currency, so the Jazz are not graded as though they received nothing. The eventual picks were late seconds and did not produce enough realized value to match what Favors delivered in New Orleans. The trade therefore leans clearly to the Pelicans while remaining modest in historical scale.

sections.heading: The Jazz Acquired Pick 39 Elijah Hughes on Draft Night
sections.body: New Orleans selected Syracuse wing Elijah Hughes with the 39th pick in the November 18, 2020 NBA draft and then sent his rights to Utah. In exchange the Pelicans received the Jazz's own future 2022 second-round selection and cash considerations. NBA.com's 2020 draft trade tracker spells out the package, while Basketball-Reference dates Utah's transaction to November 19 in its season ledger. Those are source-convention differences around the same draft-night agreement, not evidence of two separate trades. New Orleans did not send Hughes after he had developed into an established NBA player, and Utah did not directly hand over Karlo Matković in 2020. The deal transferred a prospective draft right that would only be exercised two years later.

sections.heading: Utah Was Buying a Young Wing With Pick 39
sections.body: The Jazz preferred the opportunity to develop Hughes, a 22-year-old prospect who had completed his college career at Syracuse, over keeping a future second-round choice. Utah's official 2020 draft announcement identified Hughes as the 39th selection and the recipient of his rights after New Orleans made the pick. The move put a selected player into Utah's program immediately, rather than waiting two seasons to choose another prospect. Its risk was not the cost of a first-round pick; it was the loss of a future second and an unspecified cash payment for a player whose NBA role was uncertain. The actual trade context needs no invented cap exception or other team to explain why Utah made that calculation.

sections.heading: Hughes Played 32 Regular-Season Games for Utah
sections.body: The Jazz's direct on-court return was limited. Hughes appeared in 18 Utah games as a rookie in 2020-21, averaging 1.7 points and 3.6 minutes; in 2021-22 he played another 14 for Utah, averaging 3.1 points in 8.0 minutes. That totals 32 regular-season Jazz appearances. His later 22 games with Portland in 2021-22 brought his career to 54 NBA contests, but those Portland appearances followed another team transaction and were not a direct Utah return from this exchange. The distinction between 32 Utah games and 54 career games is essential when evaluating who benefited. Utah obtained a legitimate NBA prospect but not a durable rotation piece from the draft-night purchase.

sections.heading: The 2022 Second Became New Orleans' Karlo Matković Selection
sections.body: The future Utah second-round pick conveyed at No. 52 in the 2022 draft, when the Pelicans selected forward-center Karlo Matković. The team's June 2022 draft announcement confirms the 52nd selection; its July 2024 signing announcement confirms a later standard NBA contract. This was a slow asset path, not instant production: Matković continued developing overseas and spent time with New Orleans' G League affiliate before reaching the NBA. By the end of 2025-26, Basketball-Reference credited him with 104 regular-season games across two Pelicans seasons, averaging 6.5 points and 4.2 rebounds for his career. His eventual rotation minutes supplied realized value from the asset New Orleans obtained in the Hughes deal.

sections.heading: Cash Was Part of the Package, Not a Reported Amount
sections.body: The trade's official league summary also includes cash considerations going from Utah to New Orleans. It provides no reliable transaction-specific dollar figure, and the analysis should not manufacture one by importing amounts from other 2020 Jazz deals. The cash and future second were separate incoming Pelicans assets, while Hughes was the lone Utah incoming draft right. This simple structure made the deal low stakes on draft night but allowed one delayed second-round selection to become meaningful later. Matković's 2022 development and 2024 contract belong to a chain that originated here; his actual NBA career still cannot be projected backward as if both executives knew its eventual course in November 2020.

sections.heading: Why the Pelicans Earned the Better Return From Pick 39
sections.body: The Pelicans Win verdict grades New Orleans B-plus and Utah C-minus. In November 2020, the Jazz acquired the rights to Elijah Hughes at No. 39, while New Orleans received a future second-rounder and cash, as the NBA's original draft-trade tracker confirms. Hughes played 32 regular-season games for Utah across two seasons; his later Portland games belong to a separate transaction. The Utah pick ultimately became No. 52 in the 2022 draft, allowing New Orleans to select Karlo Matković. The Pelicans signed Matković in 2024, and his subsequent New Orleans appearances gave the franchise a more sustained on-court return than Utah received from Hughes. That comparison favors New Orleans without treating Matković as a player transferred in 2020, inventing a cash amount or projecting either prospect's later career into what the clubs knew on draft night.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans Win, New Orleans B-plus and Utah C-minus are preserved. On November 18, 2020, New Orleans dealt the 39th draft rights to Elijah Hughes for Utah's own future 2022 second and cash. Hughes logged 32 regular-season Jazz games before moving to Portland. The 2022 second became No. 52 Karlo Matković, who signed with New Orleans in July 2024 and had played 104 Pelicans NBA games through 2025-26. The exact cash amount isn't established. This was a delayed pick-development payoff, not a direct 2020 exchange of Hughes for an already known Matković.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Hughes for a Future Second: How Utah's 2020 Pick Became Matković
featuredDeepDive.intro: Utah bought the draft rights to 2020 No. 39 Elijah Hughes from New Orleans for its own 2022 second-round choice and cash. Hughes played just 32 regular-season games for the Jazz, while the deferred draft right became No. 52 Karlo Matković in 2022. He joined New Orleans on a standard NBA deal in 2024 and contributed beyond the draft-night exchange's original horizon. The site keeps Pelicans Win, B-plus for New Orleans and C-minus for Utah. The dated source ledger and actual NBA appearances provide the explanation.

sections.heading: The Date Convention Does Not Change the One-Trade Ledger
sections.body: NBA.com's draft-night tracker lists the transaction among the exchanges on November 18, 2020: the Jazz obtained the draft rights to the 39th pick Elijah Hughes and the Pelicans acquired a future second-rounder and cash. Utah's Basketball-Reference 2020-21 transactions ledger records the formal move on November 19. The site uses November 18 as its canonical trade date and should not double-count a second exchange on the following calendar day. The Utah pick was its own 2022 second, subsequently the 52nd overall selection. The agreement involved two franchises and three ledger components. The 2022 identity of the selected player is downstream information, not a player personally transferred on the original 2020 draft night.

sections.heading: Utah Got Limited Development Minutes From Hughes
sections.body: The Jazz made a reasonable prospect purchase by NBA draft standards: Hughes arrived with scoring credentials from Syracuse and could be developed within a veteran team. The subsequent NBA record is more restrained. Utah used him in 18 games in 2020-21 and 14 in 2021-22, a total of 32, with scoring averages of 1.7 and 3.1 points in the two seasons. His playing time increased modestly during his second Jazz stint but never became a regular major rotation role. Hughes also spent 22 games with Portland, bringing his career regular-season total to 54, but those appearances should not be credited as Utah's direct game output. This distinction is particularly important when comparing a prospect bought immediately with a later future draft-rights selection.

sections.heading: Matković Turned an Abstract 2022 Second Into a Player
sections.body: New Orleans converted the incoming Jazz-owned second-round pick into Karlo Matković at No. 52 on June 23, 2022. Pelicans officials described him as a developing international prospect and initially expected that he might continue playing overseas. Their July 2024 announcement confirmed his standard NBA contract following time overseas and with the Birmingham Squadron. The long development period is part of the deal's risk profile: the Pelicans waited from 2020 to the 2022 draft and then another two years before an NBA contract. His eventual 104 regular-season appearances through 2025-26, with career averages of 6.5 points and 4.2 rebounds, make the return concrete without presenting it as immediate or guaranteed.

sections.heading: Cash Considerations Did Not Require a Fictional Price
sections.body: NBA.com's official trade tracker explicitly associates cash with Utah's acquisition of Hughes. The transaction note does not establish an amount, and no reliable source among the cited records specifies a figure for this particular deal. A defensible retrospective therefore identifies cash as an extra Pelicans return without treating an unsupported dollar amount as fact. New Orleans ultimately held a 2022 second-round pick later used on Matković; Utah obtained Hughes's playing rights and eventually 32 Jazz regular-season appearances. The package should not absorb unrelated Utah draft movements from November 2020, when the Jazz were also involved in other trades. Keeping the source ledger narrowly drawn helps readers understand the actual trade-to-player path.

sections.heading: The Retrospective Grade Gap Reflects Timing and Return
sections.body: The preserved result is Pelicans Win, New Orleans B-plus and Utah C-minus. The Jazz's side delivered a short NBA tenure from a selected wing, not a complete absence of basketball value, while the Pelicans had to wait for a future second-rounder to be exercised. The successful later conversion into Matković, and his 2024-25 and 2025-26 regular-season appearances, gave New Orleans a longer realized NBA return. One can understand the Jazz's desire to acquire a player in 2020 while still judging the outcome to favor the club that accepted the deferred pick. This historical assessment does not assume New Orleans could predict the No. 52 prospect's development or pretend cash had a verified amount.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The canonical trade stands: Pelicans Win, New Orleans B-plus and Utah C-minus. NBA.com's November 18, 2020 tracker lists Hughes's 39th-pick draft rights going to Utah and a future second plus cash to New Orleans. Utah's transaction register carries the formal date November 19, which should not be counted as a second deal. Hughes appeared in 32 Jazz regular-season games before a later Portland stint. The Utah-owned 2022 second conveyed at No. 52 and was used on Matković, whom the Pelicans signed to a standard contract in July 2024. He accumulated 104 New Orleans NBA appearances by the end of 2025-26, averaging 6.5 points and 4.2 rebounds. Neither the exact cash consideration nor Matković's future development was certain on trade night. Those direct facts, not boilerplate assertions, explain the preserved historical grade advantage.

sections.heading: The Official 2021 Cash-for-Pick Agreement
sections.body: On July 29, 2021, New Orleans announced that it had traded the No. 53 selection in that night's NBA Draft to Philadelphia for cash considerations. The Pelicans' own transaction notice identifies both parties, the pick number and the cash-only return, but does not state the amount. Philadelphia's later official media guide adds a useful provenance detail: the pick originated with Dallas and reached New Orleans on March 25 before being sold to the 76ers. The July transaction therefore involved the right to make one late second-round choice, not a player already on an NBA contract. Philadelphia selected Western Kentucky center Charles Bassey at No. 53. No additional first-round pick, veteran or conditional second choice belongs in this specific exchange.

sections.heading: Bassey Played 23 Philadelphia Games, Not His Entire Later Career
sections.body: Bassey signed with Philadelphia in September 2021 and appeared in 23 regular-season games as a 76er during 2021-22. His actual line was 168 total minutes, 69 points, 62 rebounds and 17 blocked shots with no starts, according to the season record. In per-game terms he averaged 3.0 points and 2.7 rebounds across 7.3 minutes. Those figures establish that the draft right produced real, albeit limited, NBA participation for the acquiring team. His later development and games with San Antonio or other organizations should not be counted as Philadelphia output merely because he originally entered the league as a Sixers draft choice. The directly traceable on-court contribution is 23 games and the possibility Philadelphia held in a young center.

sections.heading: New Orleans Took Cash Rather Than a Basketball Return
sections.body: New Orleans received money and did not acquire Bassey, another player or an additional draft selection from the 76ers. The club had already obtained No. 53 through an earlier Dallas-related asset chain, as Philadelphia's official 2023-24 media guide explains. That earlier transaction is background provenance; the value sold on July 29 is only one draft slot. A second-round pick can become an inexpensive roster experiment, but teams can rationally prefer cash when they do not plan to sign another late pick. Without a documented dollar amount, there is no defensible precise return on investment or points-equivalent for the Pelicans' side. It is therefore possible to assess the factual cash-versus-player choice without pretending the two kinds of consideration have a directly comparable game statistic.

sections.heading: Why a Late Second-Round Pick Gave Philadelphia a Narrow Edge
sections.body: The 76ers Win verdict grades Philadelphia B and New Orleans C-plus. Philadelphia paid an undisclosed amount of cash for the No. 53 selection in the July 2021 draft and used it to select Charles Bassey. Bassey appeared in 23 Sixers regular-season games, playing 168 minutes with 69 points and 62 rebounds. That was a limited but real on-court return from a late second-round pick. New Orleans received cash considerations, which provided financial value but cannot be converted into a specific basketball return without a disclosed amount. The pick had reached the Pelicans in an earlier transaction involving Dallas; it was not an additional asset exchanged in this July deal. Philadelphia's modest grade advantage reflects an actual drafted player against an unquantified cash return, not any later Bassey production with San Antonio.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win is the existing archival verdict, with Philadelphia B and New Orleans C+. The Pelicans' July 29, 2021 announcement confirms that No. 53 went to Philadelphia for undisclosed cash; the 76ers drafted Charles Bassey, who logged 23 games, 168 minutes and 17 blocks for Philadelphia in 2021-22. The transaction created one tangible but brief Philadelphia roster opportunity and immediate financial value for New Orleans. Because the cash amount is unreported and a separate partnerAggregate grade says B+, the scale of the inherited grade gap needs further provenance review rather than retrospective exaggeration.

sections.heading: New Orleans Paid for Stability During an Unstable Season
sections.body: The Pelicans entered February 2022 needing more than another scorer. Zion Williamson had not played, the team had started 1-12 and a young roster lacked a dependable late-game organizer. CJ McCollum addressed all three problems. He could create a clean shot without a play being perfect, handle lead-guard responsibilities and give Brandon Ingram a second experienced decision-maker. Larry Nance Jr. added frontcourt versatility, while Tony Snell provided depth. New Orleans surrendered real draft and player value, but it acquired veterans who made the remaining season meaningful instead of allowing another year of the Ingram era to disappear.

sections.heading: McCollum Immediately Changed the Pelicans’ Offensive Floor
sections.body: After the trade, McCollum averaged more than 20 points and gave New Orleans the ball security and pull-up shooting it had lacked. The Pelicans reached the play-in, eliminated San Antonio and the Clippers, then pushed the top-seeded Suns to six games. That run did not create a contender, but it showed why the team had made the trade. McCollum’s ability to score against set defenses reduced pressure on Ingram and helped younger players operate in clearer roles. The immediate postseason berth is an important part of the grade because New Orleans bought short-term competence and received it.

sections.heading: Portland Began Its Backcourt Reset Without Losing All of McCollum’s Value
sections.body: The Trail Blazers had reached the point where the Damian Lillard–McCollum partnership no longer justified its cost or defensive limitations. Portland received Josh Hart, Nickeil Alexander-Walker, Tomas Satoransky, Didi Louzada, a protected first and two future seconds. Several pieces were moved or did not last, but Hart became a productive starter and a later trade asset. The first-round obligation continued into the recorded 2025 asset chain. Portland did not acquire a new star, yet it converted an expensive veteran into younger players, draft capital and flexibility at the beginning of a broader roster teardown.

sections.heading: The Pelicans Received Leadership but Never Escaped Their Availability Problems
sections.body: McCollum remained a reliable scorer and professional presence through multiple seasons, often carrying larger responsibilities when Williamson or Ingram was unavailable. His durability made the acquisition more valuable than the team’s inconsistent records suggest. At the same time, New Orleans did not advance beyond the first round with him, and the roster never developed the healthy continuity required to test its full ceiling. The trade solved a stability problem without solving the franchise’s central availability problem. That is strong B-plus value rather than an A: the incoming player performed, but the team outcome remained limited.

sections.heading: Hart and the Draft Assets Gave Portland More Than a Salary Dump
sections.body: Hart’s short Portland tenure produced energetic defense, rebounding and transition play before he was sent to New York in another asset-building move. Alexander-Walker was rerouted quickly, Satoransky was not a long-term piece and Louzada did not become part of the core. The package therefore depended on Portland’s ability to keep converting assets rather than on the opening-night roster. The later draft and trade branches created enough value to justify a B-plus. Portland received options and financial freedom, but not the kind of premium centerpiece that would make the deal a clear win over several seasons of McCollum production.

sections.heading: Equal B-Plus Grades Match the Two Different Kinds of Return
sections.body: The existing record called the trade even and graded both teams B-plus, a rare case where the verdict and grades already align. That grading scale should remain. New Orleans received immediate playoff impact, multiple seasons of scoring and an important veteran voice. Portland received a credible rebuilding package, including Hart and draft capital, while separating a costly small backcourt. Neither side created a championship-level outcome, and neither side lost the transaction outright. The deal was a reasonable exchange between a team buying stability and a team selling a veteran to reopen its asset base.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, with New Orleans and Portland both graded B-plus. McCollum delivered the immediate offensive leadership the Pelicans sought, helped drive the 2022 play-in and playoff run and remained a reliable scorer through an otherwise unstable stretch. Nance also supplied useful frontcourt minutes. Portland received Hart, younger contracts and draft assets while beginning the necessary breakup of the Lillard–McCollum backcourt. The Blazers did not land a franchise centerpiece, and the Pelicans did not become a durable contender. Each side accomplished its central objective without producing a result strong enough to separate the grades.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Why the CJ McCollum Trade Worked Without Transforming Either Franchise
featuredDeepDive.intro: Some trades are successful because they change a championship race. This one was useful because it gave two teams the type of transition they needed. New Orleans wanted adult offensive organization and a reason to compete through an injury-damaged season. Portland needed to break apart an expensive guard pairing and begin collecting younger assets. McCollum’s immediate effect was visible in the Pelicans’ postseason run; Portland’s return required patience and additional transactions. The deal did not deliver a superstar or a clean rebuild on either side, but it exchanged present stability for future flexibility at a fair price.

sections.heading: The One-and-Twelve Start Made Inaction Costly for New Orleans
sections.body: The Pelicans had already recovered enough to remain near the play-in race, but asking Ingram and a young supporting cast to create every important possession was unsustainable. Another lost year would have weakened confidence in the roster and placed even more pressure on Williamson’s eventual return. McCollum gave the organization a credible lead guard immediately. His professionalism also mattered for players such as Herb Jones, Jose Alvarado and Trey Murphy III, who were learning how to contribute in meaningful games. The trade turned the final months into a competitive development environment rather than an extended evaluation season.

sections.heading: The 2022 Suns Series Established the Immediate Payoff
sections.body: New Orleans entered the first round as the No. 8 seed and forced Phoenix, the league’s best regular-season team, into a six-game series. Ingram was the primary scorer, but McCollum’s presence prevented the defense from loading entirely toward him and gave the Pelicans another creator late in possessions. The series exposed limitations in efficiency and defense, yet it also demonstrated that the roster could function under postseason pressure. That outcome does not justify an A by itself, but it is concrete value. The Pelicans paid to reach meaningful games and received a genuine, competitive playoff experience.

sections.heading: Portland’s Decision Was an Admission About the Lillard–McCollum Ceiling
sections.body: Lillard and McCollum had produced years of winning basketball, including a conference-finals appearance, but their shared size and defensive vulnerabilities narrowed the paths available to Portland. Keeping both also consumed major salary while the roster around them deteriorated. Trading McCollum was not a judgment that he had stopped being good; it was an acknowledgment that the team needed a different construction. Portland chose younger, more flexible pieces rather than another expensive veteran. That was the correct strategic direction, even though the return required several later moves before its full value could be measured.

sections.heading: McCollum’s Reliability Became More Important as Teammates Missed Time
sections.body: The Pelicans never enjoyed the consistent Williamson–Ingram–McCollum availability imagined at the time of the deal. McCollum frequently shifted between lead scorer, point guard and stabilizing second option depending on who was healthy. His shooting volume and professionalism gave New Orleans a functional offense during stretches that might otherwise have collapsed. That role should be credited even when the standings remained disappointing. The limitation is that a high-salary veteran stabilizer can only carry so much value if the core around him never sustains a playoff run. New Orleans received what McCollum could provide, but not the larger team payoff it hoped to unlock.

sections.heading: Portland’s Package Required Good Follow-Up Decisions
sections.body: Hart was the most immediately useful incoming player and later became the central piece of another trade. The picks and protections extended the value horizon beyond the original 2022 deadline, while the expiring and younger contracts gave Portland maneuverability. This type of return is not self-executing. Draft capital can be wasted, and flexible salary only matters when a front office uses it well. The original trade earns a B-plus because it provided legitimate tools for a reset at a time when keeping McCollum offered diminishing returns. It does not earn an A because the package lacked a blue-chip prospect or guaranteed high lottery pick.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The trade remains even at B-plus for both teams. New Orleans received several seasons of dependable scoring, leadership and the immediate 2022 playoff run it was trying to create. Portland received Hart, draft capital and the flexibility necessary to begin restructuring around and eventually beyond Lillard. The Pelicans never converted McCollum’s stability into sustained postseason success, while the Blazers’ return required additional transactions and did not contain a clear franchise cornerstone. The deal accomplished two different strategic purposes at a fair price, making equal grades more accurate than forcing a winner.

sections.heading: The Hawks Traded a Rookie Forward for an Experienced Champion
sections.body:
On December 12, 1956 the St. Louis Hawks moved 22-year-old Willie Naulls to New York for veteran guard Slater Martin, then age 31. There was no compensating draft pick in the direct deal. Martin brought championship experience from Minneapolis and a defensive reputation, while Naulls had been selected No. 10 in the 1956 NBA draft and offered far more years of potential growth. Both franchise transaction records identify the same one-for-one exchange.

St. Louis already had Bob Pettit and wanted a stabilizing floor leader rather than another developmental forward. The Knicks needed a younger scoring and rebounding presence as their veteran backcourt aged. The front offices were trading different competitive timelines, which explains why a later even-handed retrospective must compare actual team play rather than assuming the younger player automatically won.

sections.heading: Martin Led the 1957 Hawks to the Finals and the 1958 Champions
sections.body:
Martin appeared in 53 St. Louis regular-season games after the December acquisition in 1956-57. He averaged 11.5 points, 4.6 rebounds and 4.3 assists while playing 37.3 minutes per game, and earned an All-Star and All-NBA Second Team designation that season. He then contributed 16.6 points per game across ten 1957 Hawks playoff appearances as St. Louis reached the Finals and lost in seven games to the Boston Celtics.

In 1957-58 Martin played 60 Hawks games and averaged 12.0 points and 3.6 assists, again earning All-Star and All-NBA Second Team recognition. His 11 postseason games gave the veteran direct participation in the club’s victory over Boston in the 1958 Finals. He was not the leading Hawks scorer—that distinction belonged to Pettit and other frontcourt contributors—but his ballhandling and defensive experience played a real part in the franchise’s championship.

sections.heading: Naulls Became a Four-Time Knicks All-Star with a Larger Offensive Peak
sections.body:
New York acquired a forward who was not yet a proven NBA scorer, then gave him the playing time to develop. Naulls played 52 Knicks games after the mid-December trade in 1956-57, then averaged 18.1 points and 11.8 rebounds in 1957-58. He later scored 21.4 points with 14.2 rebounds in 1959-60, 23.4 points and 13.4 rebounds in 1960-61, and 25.0 points with 11.6 rebounds in 1961-62. Those seasons were substantial team-specific return in a league with relatively few franchises.

A prior canonical synopsis described 1959-60 as 20.9 points and 13.4 rebounds. The official NBA player career record and Basketball Reference both list 21.4 and 14.2 instead; the older values understated that year and blended its rebounding average with the following season. Naulls became a four-time All-Star as a Knick, giving the team a long period of elite individual forward production even without a championship run.

sections.heading: Championship Fit Must Be Separated from Naulls’s Longer Career
sections.body:
The two principal trade returns were genuine and different. Martin’s most valuable years after arriving in St. Louis included immediate playoff guard service, an All-NBA recognition and the Hawks 1958 title. Naulls stayed a productive Knicks scorer and rebounder for several seasons and offered a far longer star-level statistical peak. The Hawks did not get the longer prime, and New York did not receive an empty contract.

Winning a championship is a team accomplishment; Martin deserves credit only for the on-court responsibilities that helped the Hawks reach and win the Finals. Likewise, Naulls’s later Boston Celtics title years came after he left the Knicks in a separate transaction and should not inflate New York’s direct 1956 return. This is why the canonical slight Hawks edge can coexist with two A-range grades rather than an exaggerated blowout.

sections.heading: The Grade Gap Records the Competitive Window Rather than a Talent Failure
sections.body:
St. Louis’s A+ reflects the value of a point guard who took immediate responsibility on Finals teams, then contributed to its championship. New York’s A reflects receiving a young forward who became a four-time Knicks All-Star and eventually reached 25.0 points per game in 1961-62. Both organizations obtained exactly the type of player needed at that stage. If the Knicks roster had been closer to a title opportunity, Naulls production might have been treated as the better overall exchange.

The canonical Slight Hawks Edge is therefore a judgment about timing, roster fit and playoff responsibility. It does not assign the Hawks all of Pettit’s value or deny the Knicks significant longer-term production. The initial generic language about a winner requiring more than a scoring average has been replaced by concrete Martin and Naulls season totals, playoff participation and the trade date documented by independent franchise transaction records.

sections.heading: St. Louis and New York Both Converted the Exchange into Real Value
sections.body:
This trade is uncommon because the losing side in the recorded retrospective still acquired a multi-year All-Star. Martin’s first 53 St. Louis appearances and ten 1957 playoff games laid the groundwork for a veteran role that carried into the 1958 champion. Naulls’s best Knicks season by scoring came in 1961-62 at 25.0 points, while his largest rebounding average was 14.2 in 1959-60. These details place each grade on documented basketball results rather than either athlete’s broader reputation.

The Hawks A+ grade gives a narrow edge to an experienced defender who fit an immediate contender. The Knicks A grade recognizes a genuinely productive acquisition, despite the lack of equivalent title success while Naulls was there. Neither team should be assigned nonexistent draft picks or later franchise accolades from players added through separate moves.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Hawks Edge — St. Louis A+, New York A. Martin gave the Hawks 53 regular-season games and ten playoff appearances in 1956-57, followed by another All-NBA Second Team season as a key guard on the 1958 champions. Naulls developed into a four-time Knicks All-Star, scoring 21.4 points with 14.2 rebounds in 1959-60 and peaking at 25.0 points in 1961-62. The championship-era fit narrowly tips the scale to St. Louis, but both franchises obtained valuable player returns.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Slater Martin and Willie Naulls: The 1956 Trade That Helped Build St. Louis’s Champion
featuredDeepDive.intro: The St. Louis Hawks traded rookie forward Willie Naulls to New York for guard Slater Martin on December 12, 1956. The 31-year-old Martin was already experienced with Minneapolis titles; the Knicks instead chose a 22-year-old scorer who would become a four-time All-Star with their franchise. Martin played 53 games for St. Louis in his first season and averaged 16.6 points through ten postseason games as the team reached the 1957 Finals; the following year the Hawks won their 1958 title. Naulls developed into a 25-point Knicks scorer by 1961-62. Both paths were successful, which is why St. Louis A+ versus New York A is a narrow outcome judgment rather than evidence that either front office made a terrible trade.

sections.heading: The Hawks Already Had Pettit but Needed Martin to Run the Team
sections.body:
St. Louis acquired Martin with the December 1956 season well underway. The Hawks already had Bob Pettit as their dominant interior player but needed a veteran guard who could organize possessions, defend opposing perimeter stars and handle playoff pressure. Martin played 53 Hawks games in 1956-57 at 37.3 minutes per night with 11.5 points, 4.6 rebounds and 4.3 assists. He earned an All-Star and All-NBA Second Team selection, concrete marks of responsibility rather than a ceremonial championship roster role.

The 1957 playoffs show how much his work changed the team. Martin appeared in ten games and averaged 16.6 points while the Hawks reached the NBA Finals. St. Louis ultimately lost Game 7 in Boston, but the guard’s 43.9 playoff minutes per game demonstrate genuine court responsibility. That short-term transformation helps explain why an older point guard could be the right target for a roster already built to contend.

sections.heading: The 1958 Hawks Championship Adds a Different Type of Return
sections.body:
Martin was still a major contributor in 1957-58, making 60 regular-season appearances and averaging 12.0 points and 3.6 assists. He again earned All-NBA Second Team and All-Star recognition. The Hawks reached the Finals for the second straight season and defeated Boston to win the only NBA title in St. Louis franchise history. Martin appeared in 11 playoff games at 37.8 minutes per game, giving a measurable connection to the championship run.

Those minutes are the basis for title-stage trade value. They do not entitle Martin to personal credit for Bob Pettit’s scoring or the contributions of Cliff Hagan and other teammates. They do, however, make his acquisition more valuable to a contender than his modest regular-season scoring totals alone would suggest. The slightly higher Hawks grade expresses that specific team need being met at the right moment.

sections.heading: New York Acquired Naulls Before His Four Knicks All-Star Seasons
sections.body:
The Knicks traded away a proven guard but acquired a 22-year-old forward with significant room to grow. Naulls averaged 18.1 points and 11.8 rebounds in 1957-58, then posted 21.4 points and 14.2 rebounds in 1959-60. He continued at 23.4 points and 13.4 rebounds in 1960-61 before reaching 25.0 points per game in 1961-62. The NBA official career record confirms each of those season-specific averages.

The original canonical summary mixed 1959-60 numbers, claiming 20.9 points and 13.4 rebounds for that season. The actual 21.4 and 14.2 correct both values, while 13.4 rebounds belonged to his later 1960-61 Knicks season. Naulls played far longer for New York than Martin did at his post-trade peak, and four Knicks All-Star appearances are meaningful return on a single veteran contract regardless of team results.

sections.heading: A Trade for a Team’s Timeline Is Not Automatically Its Best Trade
sections.body:
The Hawks were more immediately positioned to win than the Knicks when the clubs exchanged players. This explains the trade-day logic: St. Louis could accept age and reduced future seasons from Martin in exchange for championship readiness, whereas New York had an incentive to invest in a younger high-usage forward. Each bet succeeded on its own timeline, so it would be unfair to rewrite the trade as an obvious mistake by New York simply because the Hawks won in 1958.

The Knicks never turned Naulls’s peak into a St. Louis-like title run, yet he became one of the league’s productive forwards for that era. Meanwhile Martin served the Hawks for a shorter stretch but with clear postseason value. The archived A+/A gap is an editorial judgment about higher leverage, not an objective ranking of personal career greatness; Naulls’s longer scoring peak is an important competing fact.

sections.heading: Team-Specific Minutes and Era-Appropriate Evidence Keep the Verdict Narrow
sections.body:
The transaction record shows a direct Naulls-for-Martin player exchange, without a draft pick changing sides. Martin’s Hawks numbers can be followed through franchise box scores and contemporary All-NBA and Finals records. Naulls’s Knicks role is similarly visible in per-season points, rebounds and All-Star recognition. That makes this a stronger historical case than a speculative multi-decade pick chain, even if detailed defensive and matchup tracking was much thinner in the 1950s.

The strongest comparison is Martin’s 1957-58 championship-level guard work against Naulls’s four All-Star seasons and peak 25.0-point scoring year in 1961-62. That is why the Hawks receive the slightly higher A+ grade and New York stays at A. No later Boston title from Naulls, earlier Minneapolis titles from Martin, or unrelated star outcomes should be imported as though part of the direct 1956 transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Hawks Edge — St. Louis A+, New York A. Slater Martin made immediate All-NBA and playoff contributions to the 1957 finalist Hawks and remained a major guard on the 1958 champion. Willie Naulls became a four-time New York All-Star and at his Knicks peak scored 25.0 points per game in 1961-62. Both teams received top-tier value, with a small preference for Martin’s title-era competitive fit rather than any claim Naulls failed.
