sections.heading: New York Received Rose and Two Firsts
sections.body: The February 24, 2005 transaction sent Nazr Mohammed and Jamison Brewer from New York to San Antonio. The Knicks received Malik Rose, a protected 2005 first-round pick, a protected 2006 first-round pick and cash related to Rose's trade kicker. That made the return more extensive than a swap of two veteran big men. San Antonio wanted immediate center help for a championship run, while New York accepted a veteran and two chances to turn draft selections into longer-lived players. Both motivations were visible in the assets exchanged.

sections.heading: Mohammed Helped Deliver the 2005 Championship
sections.body: Mohammed quickly became useful at center for the Spurs and contributed during their successful 2005 NBA championship postseason. That is direct value for the acquiring team at the exact competitive moment the trade was designed to address. He was not merely an expiring contract, and his continued service in the following season added to the return. San Antonio had a defensible reason to surrender picks for a center who could help immediately. The championship payoff supports a high grade even when New York's longer-term draft results are evaluated separately.

sections.heading: The Knicks Converted One First into David Lee
sections.body: The 2005 first-round pick became No. 30, used on David Lee, who grew into an All-Star-level contributor for New York. The 2006 pick became No. 29 Mardy Collins, while Rose supplied veteran frontcourt depth. Lee's production gave the Knicks a valuable multiyear result from a transaction made during a less successful team period. The two clubs therefore realized different forms of value: a championship role from Mohammed for San Antonio and several seasons of player development from Lee in New York. The latter provides the slight retrospective edge.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Knicks Edge. New York earns A for Malik Rose and draft assets led by the 2005 selection used on David Lee. San Antonio receives A- for Nazr Mohammed's immediate 2005 championship contribution, with Jamison Brewer also in the package. Both sides benefited, but Lee supplied more cumulative direct value across later seasons.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Deep Dive: Regrading Nazr Mohammed and Jamison Brewer / Malik Rose and two first-round picks
featuredDeepDive.intro: The February 24, 2005 Knicks-Spurs transaction moved Nazr Mohammed and Jamison Brewer to San Antonio for Malik Rose, two protected first-rounders and trade-kicker cash. Mohammed helped the Spurs win the 2005 championship, while New York used the draft assets on David Lee and Mardy Collins. The closer review compares that immediate center contribution against Lee's later Knicks years without treating either team's separate roster moves as part of this trade.

sections.heading: The Spurs Sent Two First-Rounders to Solve a 2005 Need
sections.body: San Antonio wanted another center alongside Tim Duncan before the 2005 playoffs. On February 24, it received Nazr Mohammed and Jamison Brewer from New York in exchange for veteran forward Malik Rose, protected 2005 and 2006 first-round selections, and cash related to Rose's trade kicker. Mohammed was the immediate roster addition; the picks would provide New York future selections rather than established players at the deadline. The contrast in strategy is straightforward. San Antonio had a championship-caliber core and could spend deferred draft capital for interior depth. New York could accept a veteran and invest in first-round choices for later seasons. The eventual recipient teams of the choices were not mysterious: the Knicks controlled the draft rights and selected David Lee and Mardy Collins.

sections.heading: Mohammed Delivered the Spurs a Center for the 2005 Title
sections.body: The direct Spurs return was not merely the right to another player. Mohammed joined San Antonio during the 2004-05 campaign, started regularly and contributed to the championship postseason that ended with the franchise defeating Detroit in the NBA Finals. His presence supplied rebounding and interior minutes for a team led by Duncan, Tony Parker and Manu Ginobili. Brewer was a secondary name in the exchange, and his addition was not the decisive basketball reason to complete it. The value of Mohammed in that particular playoff run explains why the Spurs retained an A-minus grade despite giving up two future firsts. Their title was a team achievement, not the work of one deadline move, but he occupied a genuine roster role in the run that followed this transaction.

sections.heading: The 2005 No. 30 Pick Became David Lee
sections.body: New York exercised the first incoming selection in the 2005 draft, taking David Lee with the 30th overall choice. Lee developed into a productive rebounder and scorer for the Knicks and eventually represented the team at the 2010 All-Star Game. That was sustained NBA value produced by a late first-round asset originally obtained from San Antonio. The Knicks also used the later 2006 first on Mardy Collins at No. 29, a second distinct piece of the return. Both draft results belong to New York rather than the Spurs, but they should not be flattened into equivalent long-term careers. Lee became the principal asset success, while Collins supplied a different, much smaller roster outcome. This distinction supports New York's narrow overall advantage without denying what Mohammed achieved for San Antonio.

sections.heading: Malik Rose and the Trade Kicker Were Separate Components
sections.body: The February 2005 package also included Malik Rose, a veteran forward familiar with the Spurs' earlier title teams. New York acquired his contract and playing services while the recorded exchange included cash connected to Rose's trade kicker. That cash was part of the transaction mechanics, not a third first-round draft pick or an additional incoming NBA player. Rose provided veteran frontcourt depth in New York over subsequent seasons, adding real value beside the two choices. The Spurs gave up a player whose championship credentials were already established to fill a different immediate need with Mohammed. Evaluating that exchange demands attention to actual contracts and roster roles: both teams acquired resources appropriate to their timeline, but the direct total realized from each package diverged after draft night.

sections.heading: A Slight Knicks Edge Despite San Antonio Winning the Title
sections.body: The inherited verdict is Slight Knicks Edge, New York A and San Antonio A-minus. This is not a claim that the 2005 championship should count for nothing. Mohammed joined a title-winning Spurs frontcourt at the precise moment they needed depth, and that immediate return was unusually valuable. New York subsequently acquired several seasons of David Lee production, culminating in his 2010 All-Star selection, along with Malik Rose and Mardy Collins. San Antonio's one-season peak and the Knicks' longer combined return are different measures of success. The slight grade gap recognizes New York's sustained asset conversion without downgrading San Antonio's championship payoff into an ordinary failed trade. The original two firsts, trade kicker cash and veterans must be kept in the correct club ledgers.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Knicks Edge — New York A, San Antonio A-minus. The Spurs acquired Nazr Mohammed in time for their 2005 championship run. New York obtained Malik Rose, cash tied to his trade kicker, a 2005 first that became David Lee and a 2006 first that became Mardy Collins. Lee's productive New York years and 2010 All-Star honor narrowly exceed the Spurs' shorter immediate return, though Mohammed's role in a title makes both sides successful.

sections.heading: New York Acquired Two Useful Players for One
sections.body: New York sent Kurt Thomas and the rights to Dijon Thompson to Phoenix and received Quentin Richardson, the rights to Nate Robinson and future considerations. The value case for the Knicks begins with multiplicity: Richardson was an established wing and Robinson became a productive guard over several seasons in New York. Thomas was a good veteran big man, so Phoenix did not come away empty-handed, but the Knicks turned one meaningful rotation player and a second-round draft right into two players who both filled substantial NBA roles. That does not make the move a franchise-changing heist, but it gives New York more realized roster value and more developmental upside than the package it surrendered.

sections.heading: Nate Robinson Became the Separator
sections.body: Robinson was selected 21st in the 2005 draft by Phoenix and immediately sent to New York. He went on to spend more than four seasons with the Knicks, eventually averaging 17.2 points in 2008-09 and finishing third in Sixth Man of the Year voting. The famous dunk-contest moments are not the reason for the grade; the meaningful value was his sustained role as a scorer and energy guard. A player acquired as draft rights who becomes a multi-year contributor creates far more franchise value than a throw-in. Robinson's development is the principal reason New York's side rises to B+ even though Richardson's Knicks tenure was mixed and the club itself remained unsuccessful.

sections.heading: Phoenix Got a Player Who Fit a Contender
sections.body: Phoenix had just won 62 games behind Steve Nash and was operating on a different timeline. Kurt Thomas offered interior defense, rebounding and a more traditional frontcourt option for a team trying to win a championship immediately. That context matters because the Suns were not rebuilding or trying to maximize the number of long-term assets. Thomas had a clear basketball purpose and remained a useful veteran. Phoenix's C+ therefore reflects a trade that made sense competitively and produced legitimate value, even if the Suns ultimately surrendered the more productive total package. The grade is not lower because this was not a salary dump or a return that vanished without helping.

sections.heading: Richardson's Value Was Real but Not the Whole Argument
sections.body: Quentin Richardson arrived in New York as a proven volume three-point shooter and physical wing, but his Knicks years were uneven and affected by injuries. That is why the trade should not be graded as though New York acquired two stars. Richardson supplied real minutes, while Robinson became the more durable reason to like the deal. Dijon Thompson, the draft right sent with Thomas, played only a small NBA role. The overall comparison therefore favors New York: Richardson plus Robinson created broader and longer realized value than Thomas plus Thompson. Phoenix had a defensible win-now rationale, which keeps the margin moderate rather than turning the deal into a blowout.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win. New York earns B+ because the club received two meaningful NBA players in Quentin Richardson and Nate Robinson, with Robinson developing into a multi-year scoring guard and valuable sixth-man type. Phoenix earns C+ because Kurt Thomas was a legitimate veteran addition for a 62-win contender and the Suns had a clear need for interior toughness, but the total realized value on the New York side was greater. Dijon Thompson did not become a major offsetting piece. The documented Knicks Win verdict is therefore a moderate one: New York collected more useful player value and more years of contribution, while Phoenix still received a player who fit its immediate competitive window well enough to avoid a poor grade.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Deep Dive: Nate Robinson Turned a Win-Now Suns Trade into a Knicks Victory
featuredDeepDive.intro: The 2005 exchange is a good example of two teams valuing different timelines. Phoenix wanted a veteran big man who could help a championship contender. New York wanted perimeter talent and a young guard with upside. Both motivations were sensible, but the completed player value ultimately favored the Knicks because Nate Robinson became more than a draft-night throw-in.

sections.heading: Phoenix Was Trading from a Position of Strength
sections.body: The Suns had just completed one of the best regular seasons in franchise history, and the roster was built around pace, spacing and Steve Nash's playmaking. Adding Thomas gave Phoenix a sturdy frontcourt option who could rebound, defend stronger bigs and diversify the rotation. From a contender's perspective, sacrificing a later first-round prospect in Robinson was a reasonable way to convert future value into present fit. That is important context for the C+ grade. Phoenix did not misread its competitive stage. The transaction simply did not create enough additional postseason or long-term value to outweigh what Robinson and Richardson eventually gave New York. The process was coherent even though the realized trade details leaned the other way.

sections.heading: Robinson Created Years of Low-Cost Guard Production
sections.body: New York's strongest asset was the draft right to Robinson. He was not immediately a polished point guard, but he became a recurring source of bench scoring and eventually a 17.2-point-per-game player in 2008-09. The Knicks received several seasons of production from a player whose rights were obtained as part of the same deal that brought an established starter. That combination matters. A late first-round pick that turns into a useful, entertaining and marketable rotation player is a meaningful outcome, especially when the acquiring team did not have to surrender another first-round pick to get him. Robinson's years in New York are the cleanest realized-value advantage in the trade.

sections.heading: Richardson and Thomas Each Had Imperfect Tenures
sections.body: Neither veteran side of the exchange should be exaggerated. Richardson's Knicks tenure included useful shooting and rebounding from the wing, but injuries and team instability limited the upside. Thomas gave Phoenix dependable veteran minutes and physicality, yet he did not become the missing piece that delivered a championship. Those mixed outcomes keep the grade spread to one full tier rather than something harsher. New York's win rests on receiving Richardson plus Robinson, not on Richardson individually outperforming Thomas. Phoenix's C+ recognizes that Thomas was a real contributor whose role made sense. The difference comes from the second valuable player New York developed from the draft rights.

sections.heading: Future Considerations and Cash Should Stay Secondary
sections.body: Transaction records include future considerations, and some public sources describe cash as part of the package. Those mechanics matter for completeness but are not the drivers of the verdict. Historical trade grading becomes distorted when small financial components are allowed to overshadow players who logged thousands of NBA minutes. The useful comparison is Thomas and Thompson against Richardson and Robinson. New York's pair produced the stronger combined result. Phoenix's veteran fit was defensible, and Thompson's limited outcome does not materially improve the Suns' side. Keeping the secondary mechanics in proportion produces the B+/C+ split and avoids turning a meaningful but ordinary trade into something larger than it was.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win, New York B+ and Phoenix C+. Nate Robinson is the separator. The Knicks acquired his rights and received more than four seasons of productive guard play, including a 17.2-point season, while also getting an established wing in Quentin Richardson. Phoenix obtained Kurt Thomas for a roster that had immediate championship ambitions, and Thomas supplied exactly the kind of veteran size and toughness the Suns sought. That keeps Phoenix comfortably above a losing grade. The Suns simply gave up more cumulative NBA value than they received once Robinson's development is counted. New York's return was broader, younger and more productive over time, which is enough for the documented Knicks Win verdict without treating the deal as a franchise-altering steal.

sections.heading: What New York Bought and What Toronto Sold
sections.body: New York sent Antonio Davis to Toronto and received Jalen Rose, Toronto’s conditional 2006 first-round pick from Denver and cash. The pick ultimately landed at No. 20, where the Knicks selected Renaldo Balkman. The basketball names make the transaction look like a veteran-for-veteran swap, but the contract structure was at least as important. Rose was earning $15.7 million in 2005-06 and had $16.9 million due the following season, while Davis’s contract was expiring. Toronto therefore paid with the first-rounder and cash to remove Rose’s future salary. New York accepted that obligation because it wanted another experienced scorer and received a first-round asset for doing so. The trade is best understood as a blend of immediate basketball help, salary relief and draft compensation rather than a simple comparison of Rose and Davis.

sections.heading: Toronto’s B+ Is Mostly a Flexibility Grade
sections.body: The Raptors did not need Davis to become a long-term contributor for the transaction to accomplish its central objective. Basketball-Reference records Toronto waiving him on March 23, less than two months after the trade. His expiring contract allowed the Raptors to move off Rose’s substantial 2006-07 salary, creating flexibility for a front office that was reshaping the roster around Chris Bosh. Toronto did surrender a first-round pick and cash, so the cost was real and prevents an A-level grade. The B+ reflects the value of clearing a large future commitment without taking on a comparable long-term salary. This analysis does not award Toronto imaginary credit for every later signing or trade made with financial flexibility; those were separate decisions. It credits only the concrete removal of Rose’s next-year obligation and the cleaner balance sheet produced by the transaction.

sections.heading: The Knicks Received a Pick but Also Preserved Their Payroll Problem
sections.body: New York’s B- comes from the tension between the assets received. The Knicks acquired a recognizable scorer in Rose and a first-round pick, which is more than a pure salary dump normally returns to the absorbing team. They used the pick on Balkman at No. 20, adding an athletic defensive forward who played rotation minutes as a rookie. But New York also chose to carry Rose’s $16.9 million salary into 2006-07 instead of letting Davis’s expiring deal come off the books. Contemporary coverage noted that the Knicks already had the league’s highest payroll and questioned whether Rose materially changed a team headed for the lottery. The pick keeps the grade respectable; the salary cost and limited team-level payoff keep it below Toronto’s.

sections.heading: Why the Pick Does Not Automatically Make New York the Winner
sections.body: A first-round selection can dominate the memory of a salary-clearing trade, but the value has to be measured after the pick is known. The Denver pick conveyed at No. 20 and became Balkman, who gave New York useful energy and defense but did not develop into a franchise-level player. That is still real value and should not be erased simply because the selection was unconventional. The problem for the Knicks is that the pick arrived alongside a very large additional salary commitment. Rose was a veteran scorer, but the trade did not reverse New York’s 2005-06 season, and the organization paid for the privilege of adding him by sacrificing the immediate cap relief Davis could have provided. Toronto, by contrast, knowingly paid the pick to purchase financial flexibility. Once the pick’s realized outcome is weighed against that salary difference, the Raptors retain the stronger completed result.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Raptors Win. Toronto receives B+ for using Antonio Davis’s expiring contract to remove Jalen Rose’s $16.9 million 2006-07 salary commitment, even though the Raptors had to attach a first-round pick and cash to complete the move. Davis was waived in March, underscoring that long-term roster production was not the point of the acquisition. New York receives B- because it did collect real value: Rose supplied veteran scoring and the Denver first conveyed at No. 20, becoming Renaldo Balkman. The gap comes from cost and strategic effect. The Knicks took on another major salary while already carrying an extremely expensive roster, and the added talent did not change the club’s trajectory enough to outweigh Toronto’s successful salary reset. The first-rounder prevents the New York side from being a poor return; the expiring-contract advantage gives Toronto the better overall result.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Deep Dive: Jalen Rose, Antonio Davis and the Price of Salary Flexibility
featuredDeepDive.intro: The 2006 Rose-Davis trade is a useful case study in why NBA transactions cannot be graded from player names alone. Toronto sent away the more accomplished scorer, a first-round pick and cash, yet the Raptors can still win the retrospective because the transaction removed a large future salary commitment. New York received the player and the pick, but it did so by replacing an expiring contract with another year of Rose at star-level money. The final grade therefore weighs three separate forms of value: on-court production, the No. 20 pick that became Renaldo Balkman, and the financial flexibility Toronto purchased.

sections.heading: Toronto Paid Draft Capital to End the Rose Contract Early
sections.body: Rose had been difficult to move because of the money remaining on his deal. Contemporary reports put his salary at $15.7 million for 2005-06 with $16.9 million due the next season. Davis, by contrast, was on an expiring contract. Toronto’s willingness to include the Denver first-round pick and cash makes sense only when that salary gap is treated as part of the return. The Raptors were effectively buying their way out of the final Rose season. RealGM records the pick as Denver’s conditional 2006 first, and Basketball-Reference shows it eventually became No. 20. That is a meaningful price, not a throw-in. A B+ grade recognizes that Toronto accomplished the financial objective but does not pretend the flexibility came free.

sections.heading: Davis’s Short Second Toronto Stint Clarifies the Intent
sections.body: The direct player result reinforces the salary-reset interpretation. Toronto did not build a multi-year plan around Davis after reacquiring a player who had previously spent years with the franchise. The Raptors placed him on waivers on March 23. That short stay means the Toronto grade cannot be based on Davis outperforming Rose on the floor. It is instead based on the contract he carried: an expiring obligation that allowed the organization to close Rose’s deal after the season. This distinction keeps the analysis grounded. The Raptors do not receive retrospective credit for every future move made after clearing the money, because the causal chain becomes too broad. They receive credit for a completed salary reduction achieved at the known cost of a first-round pick and cash.

sections.heading: New York’s Compensation Was Real, but So Was the Salary Burden
sections.body: The Knicks were not simply doing Toronto a favor. They received a first-round pick precisely because they were willing to take the more expensive future contract, and they also acquired a scorer Larry Brown had coached earlier in Rose’s career. The Denver pick conveyed at No. 20 and became Balkman, who played 68 games as a rookie and offered defense, rebounding and energy. Those are tangible returns. Yet the trade also extended New York’s financial commitment into 2006-07. Contemporary analysis questioned adding Rose’s contract to a team with the NBA’s highest payroll and little realistic chance to contend. A balanced grade must hold both ideas at once: the Knicks were compensated for absorbing salary, but the compensation was not valuable enough to erase the strategic cost of keeping the payroll inflated.

sections.heading: Balkman Sets the Ceiling on the Pick’s Realized Value
sections.body: It would be easy to judge the transaction by imagining a different player at No. 20. That is not how the completed-value framework works. The pick New York actually received became Balkman. He was a legitimate rotation forward and produced useful defensive minutes, so the selection adds meaningful value to the Knicks side. But he did not become the kind of star or long-term core player that would overwhelm the contract disadvantage. That realized outcome matters because draft picks contain uncertainty at the time of a trade. Toronto accepted the risk that the pick could become a major player in exchange for financial relief; New York accepted the salary in exchange for the chance to select one. Once the uncertainty resolved, Balkman’s solid but limited NBA value kept the trade competitive without flipping the final verdict.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Raptors Win, Toronto B+ and New York B-. Toronto’s return was primarily contractual: an expiring Antonio Davis deal replaced the additional $16.9 million season remaining on Jalen Rose’s contract, and Davis was waived before the end of March. The Raptors paid a genuine price by sending cash and the Denver first-round pick that became Renaldo Balkman. New York therefore received usable compensation rather than merely inheriting salary. Rose provided veteran offense and Balkman became a rotation defender, but the Knicks also extended an already enormous payroll for a team that was not close to contention. The B- recognizes the pick and player value; the B+ rewards Toronto for completing the salary reset it was seeking. Because the draft pick did not become a transformative player, the financial advantage remains the strongest durable outcome of the deal.

sections.heading: The Knicks Exchanged a Young Wing and Expiring Contract for Francis
sections.body: The February 22, 2006 agreement sent Steve Francis from Orlando to New York for 20-year-old Trevor Ariza and veteran Anfernee 'Penny' Hardaway. The Knicks were looking for another accomplished ball handler alongside Stephon Marbury, even though both guards needed the ball and New York was struggling in coach Larry Brown's first season. Orlando instead moved a contract it no longer wanted while adding a wing young enough to develop around Dwight Howard. The contemporary Washington Post report and both clubs' transaction logs confirm the two-for-one exchange. This transaction did not include a draft pick or a promise that Francis would make New York a playoff contender.

sections.heading: Francis Gave New York 24 Games After the Deadline
sections.body: Francis arrived with previous All-Star credentials, but his initial Knicks production was much smaller than the résumé. In 2005-06 he appeared in 24 New York regular-season games, started 15 and averaged 10.8 points with 3.5 assists. The Knicks finished 23-59 and did not enter the playoffs. That is the realized first-year value of the acquired player, not his previous 21.3-point 2004-05 campaign with Orlando. The roster already featured Stephon Marbury and Jamal Crawford, leaving Francis without a distinct on-ball role. New York paid in young talent and contract flexibility for a player who had been excellent elsewhere, but who did not create a productive Knicks team upon arrival.

sections.heading: The Second New York Year Still Ended Before the Playoffs
sections.body: Francis made another 44 regular-season appearances for the Knicks in 2006-07, including 30 starts, at 11.3 points and 3.9 assists per game. Those totals lift his entire New York tenure to 68 regular-season appearances across parts of two seasons. The team finished 33-49 and again missed the postseason. His late-career knee problems and diminished athleticism reduced the gap between the reputation he carried and what New York actually obtained. It is not accurate to state that he never played meaningful minutes or was immediately waived; he did see the floor. The question is whether 68 games at this level justified parting with Ariza and accepting the contract that accompanied Francis.

sections.heading: Orlando Cut Hardaway Two Days Later and Played Ariza
sections.body: The Magic waived Anfernee Hardaway on February 24, 2006, only two days after the swap, as their season-by-season official transaction ledger confirms. Hardaway therefore was not acquired to play beside Dwight Howard. Ariza, in contrast, appeared in 21 Magic games late in 2005-06, then played 57 games with seven starts in 2006-07. During that full campaign he averaged 8.9 points and 4.4 rebounds, providing usable young wing minutes and defensive activity. The combination of an immediate veteran-contract exit and an age-21 contributor supports the much stronger inherited Orlando grade. Ariza's output was not star-level in Florida, so the club cannot claim all of his later development as direct production.

sections.heading: Both Players Left in Separate Multi-Asset Deals
sections.body: Orlando kept Ariza for 11 games at the start of 2007-08 before sending him to the Lakers on November 20, 2007, for Maurice Evans and Brian Cook. The Lakers' contemporary official announcement establishes those exact incoming Magic players; Ariza's eventual Lakers championship belongs to a different club. New York also moved Francis in a separate June 28, 2007 transaction, pairing him with Channing Frye and receiving Zach Randolph, Dan Dickau and Fred Jones from Portland. Randolph cannot be treated as a straight one-for-one return on Francis because Frye was included. Separating both follow-up transactions avoids crediting New York or Orlando for value that did not solely come from the original 2006 exchange.

sections.heading: New York’s F Reflects the Fit, Orlando’s A- the Exit
sections.body: The Magic Win verdict assigns Orlando A-minus and New York F. New York received Steve Francis but obtained only 68 regular-season appearances over parts of two losing seasons; the expected fit alongside Stephon Marbury never developed into a productive backcourt. Orlando gained Trevor Ariza, a young wing who contributed 21 games immediately after the trade and 57 more in 2006-07, while taking and then waiving Penny Hardaway instead of retaining Francis's contract. Ariza was later traded from Orlando to the Lakers in November 2007 for Maurice Evans and Brian Cook. Neither his later Lakers championship nor New York's separate 2007 Zach Randolph package should be credited as an immediate one-for-one return here: the Knicks sent Channing Frye alongside Francis in the Randolph deal. The difference in roster service and contract flexibility helps explain the sharp original grades, without pretending that Ariza became an Orlando superstar or that Francis never played for New York.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Orlando A-, New York F — Magic win. The February 2006 exchange delivered 21 late-season and 57 next-season Ariza games to the Magic, plus immediate release of Hardaway; New York received 68 Francis games across two losing seasons. Orlando later traded Ariza for Cook and Evans, and New York packaged Francis with Channing Frye in the separate 2007 Zach Randolph deal. The grades recognize Orlando's reduced exposure and real young-wing value without crediting either team for another club's later championship or assigning all downstream assets to a single player.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Francis, Ariza and Hardaway: What the Magic and Knicks Actually Received
featuredDeepDive.intro: New York acquired the better-known player on February 22, 2006, sending Trevor Ariza and Penny Hardaway to Orlando for Steve Francis. The transaction gave the Knicks another veteran guard to pair with Stephon Marbury; Orlando took a young wing and an expiring contract it waived almost immediately. The post-trade results are unusually easy to quantify: Francis played 68 Knicks games across two partial seasons, while Ariza played 21, then 57, then 11 Orlando games before a later Lakers trade. The inherited Magic A-, Knicks F verdict should be anchored to those team-specific returns rather than Francis's earlier All-Star years or Ariza's 2009 title with another franchise.

sections.heading: Francis Was an Established Name but Not a Fresh Orlando All-Star
sections.body: Francis's older Houston and Orlando achievements explain New York's interest, yet they are not production the Knicks received. He averaged 21.3 points for Orlando in 2004-05, before the 2006 deadline deal, then scored 16.2 points in 46 Magic appearances in the first part of 2005-06. He arrived with long-term money owed and years of high-usage guard habits. In his first 24 Knicks games he was reduced to 10.8 points and 3.5 assists, sharing creation duties with players who already demanded possessions. Larry Brown's 2005-06 team won 23 games; the proposed veteran upgrade did not cure a troubled rotation. Distinguishing an incoming player's past peak from his receiving-club performance is central to this grade. A player with real talent can still be poor value when contract, availability and roster fit collide.

sections.heading: The Contract Exit Produced a Different Type of Orlando Return
sections.body: Hardaway had already suffered through injuries and was no longer being acquired as an everyday guard. Orlando's transaction ledger shows that the Magic waived him on February 24, 2006, just two days after he arrived from New York. That exit left Ariza as the acquired player whose actual playing contributions could be measured. Ariza was only 20 at the time of the exchange and had made ten starts for the Knicks earlier in 2005-06. Orlando therefore took on limited immediate playing experience but a more promising age profile and removed the financial and organizational friction around Francis. The Magic's A- does not hinge on Hardaway producing assists or scoring in Florida; it reflects a contract decision and the useful younger player retained after the veteran was waived. The absence of draft picks keeps the exact asset chain uncomplicated.

sections.heading: Ariza Had 57-Games of Useful Development in 2006-07
sections.body: The Magic did not receive the fully developed Trevor Ariza who later won a title in Los Angeles. In Orlando he was an athletic reserve who gradually played more. He made 21 appearances after the February 2006 trade, played 57 games with seven starts in 2006-07 and averaged 8.9 points and 4.4 rebounds in that middle season. He then appeared in 11 more Orlando games early in 2007-08. That adds up to 89 Magic regular-season appearances after the deal. The October/November decision to move him again indicates Orlando valued a different roster mix by late 2007. Nevertheless, the playing return was meaningful and lasted longer than an unused trade exception or a waived expiring contract alone. His growth after leaving Orlando is useful context for the prospect's potential, not additional Magic minutes.

sections.heading: The 2007 Lakers and Portland Exchanges Were Separate Trades
sections.body: On November 20, 2007, Los Angeles acquired Ariza from Orlando for Maurice Evans and Brian Cook. The Lakers' official news release verifies both names; those two players were the Magic's subsequent return on Ariza, not direct compensation from New York in February 2006. The Knicks similarly sent Francis and Channing Frye to Portland on June 28, 2007, taking back Zach Randolph, Dan Dickau and Fred Jones. The Portland arrangement was a package; crediting Randolph solely as Francis's return would erase Frye's place in the transaction. These paths establish why neither team should be given all of each downstream player's eventual career or playoff achievements. Ariza's 2009 Lakers championship happened after Orlando had traded his rights, while the Knicks' separate 2007 roster move did not retroactively make the Francis-Marbury backcourt productive.

sections.heading: Sixty-Eight New York Games Versus a Longer Magic Asset Route
sections.body: Francis gave New York 24 appearances at 10.8 points late in 2005-06 and another 44 at 11.3 in 2006-07. The Knicks went 23-59 and then 33-49, reaching neither postseason. Orlando's acquired Ariza supplied 89 Magic appearances across parts of three seasons and subsequently brought back Cook and Evans in a separate trade. The comparison is not simply 89 games versus 68; Orlando also removed a high-salary, high-usage veteran whom it no longer wanted and acquired a 20-year-old with defensive upside. That substantially improves the team-specific argument for Orlando A- compared with New York F. Still, Ariza was not a star during those Magic campaigns and was gone before the club reached the 2009 Finals. The grades reward realized transactions and practical roster flexibility without assigning the franchise credit for victories earned after its acquired player departed.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Magic win, Orlando A- and New York F. Ariza produced 89 Orlando games and later drew Brian Cook and Maurice Evans from the Lakers; Hardaway was waived two days after arriving. Francis furnished New York 68 games at about 11 points per game while the Knicks missed two straight playoffs. The 2007 New York trade that brought Zach Randolph also sent Channing Frye to Portland, so it cannot reverse the earlier trade's evaluation on Francis alone. Orlando got young defensive depth and shed a difficult contract; the Knicks never made their second high-usage veteran guard fit.

sections.heading: Tracy McGrady / Kevin Martin three-team trade: What Actually Changed Hands
sections.body: On February 18, 2010, Houston, New York and Sacramento completed a three-team transaction. New York received Tracy McGrady and Sergio Rodríguez. Houston received Kevin Martin and Hilton Armstrong from Sacramento plus Jordan Hill, Jared Jeffries, a protected 2012 Knicks first-round pick and a 2011 swap right from New York. Sacramento received Carl Landry, Joey Dorsey and Larry Hughes. Houston was separating from the McGrady era and wanted a younger scoring guard without simply turning an expiring star contract into cap space. New York was aggressively clearing 2010 salary room and was willing to attach Hill and future draft control to move Jeffries while taking back McGrady's expiring contract. Sacramento was moving Martin after injuries and the emergence of Tyreke Evans created a crowded backcourt. For grading purposes, Tracy McGrady / Kevin Martin three-team trade is evaluated from the assets actually exchanged and the value those assets produced under team control.

sections.heading: Tracy McGrady / Kevin Martin three-team trade: The Strongest Case for the Higher Grade
sections.body: Houston captured the best combination of immediate production and controllable value. Martin became a high-volume scorer for the Rockets, Hill gave them several seasons of frontcourt minutes, Jeffries later returned to the rotation, and the protected first conveyed in 2012 at No. 16. The 2011 swap was not exercised and the pick became Royce White, so the draft side did not produce a star, but Houston still converted a relationship that had run its course into multiple usable assets. The higher grade in Tracy McGrady / Kevin Martin three-team trade does not require pretending the winning side made a flawless move. Peak performance matters, but so do durability and optionality.

sections.heading: Tracy McGrady / Kevin Martin three-team trade: What the Other Side Still Received
sections.body: New York achieved the narrow financial objective: Jeffries' money came off the future books and McGrady expired, preserving room for the 2010 free-agent class. McGrady played only a short stretch and Rodríguez was temporary. The Knicks did sign Amar'e Stoudemire that summer, but the trade itself did not directly deliver the transformational free agent the cap strategy targeted, and surrendering Hill plus a first made the clearing cost meaningful. Sacramento received Landry, Dorsey and Hughes while sending Martin, Armstrong and Rodríguez. Landry gave the Kings efficient interior scoring and later became part of another transaction, but the Kings did not receive a long-term centerpiece. Their return was defensible for a team changing direction around Evans, yet it did not match the multi-asset value Houston harvested.

sections.heading: Tracy McGrady / Kevin Martin three-team trade: The Asset Chain After the First Transaction
sections.body: The cleanest downstream chain is Houston's. Martin remained valuable enough to become a central outgoing salary-and-talent piece in the 2012 James Harden trade. That later deal required substantial additional assets, so Harden cannot simply be credited to this trade, but Martin's retained market value matters because Houston did not consume its return immediately. The Knicks' main downstream benefit was cap flexibility rather than a directly tied player chain. Follow-on transactions are counted conservatively. That rule is especially important for Tracy McGrady / Kevin Martin three-team trade, because historical retellings often leap from one recognizable name to a later superstar and assign the entire result backward.

sections.heading: Tracy McGrady / Kevin Martin three-team trade: How the Basketball Results Translated
sections.body: Martin did not carry Houston to a deep playoff run during his tenure, which keeps the grade below the franchise's truly historic steals. New York's 2010-11 improvement came primarily after adding Stoudemire and later Carmelo Anthony, while Sacramento remained outside the postseason. The trade therefore grades more on asset preservation, useful production and strategic leverage than on a direct championship result. Team success is evidence, not a shortcut. In Tracy McGrady / Kevin Martin three-team trade, the competitive translation is useful because it shows whether the theoretical fit described on trade day survived contact with real lineups and postseason basketball.

sections.heading: Tracy McGrady / Kevin Martin three-team trade: Risk, Leverage and the Realistic Alternative
sections.body: Houston accepted Martin's contract and injury history but obtained a player still in his prime. New York accepted the risk that cap room would prove less valuable than the first-round pick and young forward it surrendered. Sacramento accepted the risk that Landry's shorter-term value would not compensate for moving the best established scorer in the deal. The realistic counterfactual for New York was keeping Hill, the protected first and Jeffries rather than paying to open maximum cap space. For Houston it was allowing McGrady's contract to expire without securing a younger scorer and draft assets. Those alternatives make Houston's result look stronger without requiring hindsight about which stars were theoretically available in later drafts. Hindsight should not invent an offer that was never available. At the same time, context is not immunity from evaluation. The useful counterfactual for Tracy McGrady / Kevin Martin three-team trade is therefore the most plausible alternative—keep the asset, accept a different type of return, or wait—rather than a fantasy package built from players who were never actually on the table.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win is the final call. The transaction is remembered as a McGrady salary-clearing deal, but that shorthand understates Houston's work. The Rockets turned an ending into Martin, a prospect, a first and swap control, while New York purchased flexibility and Sacramento reset its backcourt. Houston's return had the deepest combination of present and future utility. The grades reflect the completed balance of production, control, role fit, playoff translation and directly tied follow-on value: new-york-knicks B, houston-rockets A, sacramento-kings B-.

sections.heading: A Sign-and-Trade Turned Phoenix's Departure Into a Pick and Exception
sections.body: New York obtained Amar'e Stoudemire from Phoenix in a July 2010 sign-and-trade, rather than by simply signing a free agent whose previous contract had expired. The Knicks' July 9 announcement identified a future protected second-round draft choice as the return for the Suns. Phoenix also generated an approximately $16.5 million trade exception through the structure. The second-round right and the exception were different things: one might become a draft selection if its protection conditions permitted, and the other gave Phoenix a salary-matching tool for a separate acquisition. The deal secured New York a five-time All-Star without exchanging an established Knicks rotation player. Because Stoudemire had chosen to leave Phoenix, the Suns were trying to retain transaction flexibility instead of receiving equal player talent.

sections.heading: His First Knicks Season Delivered 78 Starts and 25.3 Points a Game
sections.body: Stoudemire arrived in New York with eight Phoenix seasons behind him and immediately became the leading offensive presence for the Knicks. In 2010-11 he started all 78 games he played, averaging 25.3 points, 8.2 rebounds and 1.9 blocks. Basketball-Reference also records 1,971 points and 150 blocks that season; he earned an All-Star selection and All-NBA Second Team honors. Those totals supply a specific basis for the Knicks' inherited A grade, rather than relying on his fame or on the number of assets in the paperwork. New York went 42-40 in 2010-11 and reached the playoffs, although Boston eliminated the club in four first-round games. The acquisition gave the franchise a genuine top-end scorer, not a guaranteed postseason breakthrough.

sections.heading: Phoenix Got a Trade Tool; the Protected Pick Did Not Convey
sections.body: The 2012 second-round selection in Phoenix's package was protected in the top 55 and ultimately did not convey, according to the recorded league transaction history. The Suns did not therefore acquire a drafted player from this particular pick. The $16.5 million trade exception had a separate use: contemporary reporting said Phoenix could apply part of its new exception while arranging Hakim Warrick's sign-and-trade from Chicago. That Warrick transaction included other consideration and should not be rewritten as though Chicago had sent Warrick directly for Stoudemire in the New York exchange. Phoenix did salvage a roster-building mechanism from an outgoing free agent, even if it did not receive a comparable scorer. Its C grade recognizes that transaction flexibility without inventing an exercised draft selection.

sections.heading: Knicks A and Suns C Reflect Production Versus Flexibility
sections.body: The final Knicks Win decision compares realized benefits, not the theoretical market value of each asset on July 8. Stoudemire provided New York with an All-NBA-caliber first season, including 25.3 points per game and 78 starts. Phoenix preserved a protected draft right that never conveyed and a trade exception that helped with salary transactions elsewhere. Those are distinct forms of value. The Suns also faced the practical constraint that their former star was leaving as a free agent; a sign-and-trade could recover some flexibility without recreating the lost scoring. New York later dealt with injuries and changing rosters, so the initial acquisition should not be credited with an eventual championship. The underlying A for New York and C for Phoenix stay intact because the club with the player received the much stronger direct on-court return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win — New York A, Phoenix C. Amar'e Stoudemire brought the Knicks 78 starts, 25.3 points per game and All-NBA Second Team honors in 2010-11. Phoenix gained a $16.5 million trade exception that could help with another transaction; the protected 2012 second-round pick did not convey. Injuries later limited New York's long-term return, but the directly realized player value strongly favored the Knicks.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Stoudemire's 1,971-Point Knicks Debut Versus Phoenix's Unused 2012 Pick
featuredDeepDive.intro: The 2010 Amar'e Stoudemire sign-and-trade gave New York a 78-game, 25.3-point-per-game All-Star and All-NBA Second Team forward in its first season. Phoenix received a heavily protected 2012 second-round selection that never conveyed plus a $16.5 million trade exception, financial flexibility that is not the same as cash paid to the Suns. The Knicks returned to the playoffs at 42-40, though an immediate Boston sweep and injuries in later Stoudemire seasons limit any lifetime-star interpretation. That evidence supports the inherited New York A against Phoenix C without assigning a later unrelated acquisition wholly to the trade exception.

sections.heading: July 2010: The Deal Signed by Two Different Organizations
sections.body: The Knicks' official announcement dated July 9 confirmed that Amar'e Stoudemire came from Phoenix in a sign-and-trade and that New York sent a future protected second-round choice. The transaction is entered under July 8 in the Basketball-Reference and archival team ledgers; the announcement followed the next day. Phoenix obtained a $16.5 million trade exception from the contract structure rather than a cash payment in that amount. That distinction prevents the trade from being mistaken for a cash purchase of a star or a literal transfer of $16.5 million from New York. Stoudemire was leaving in free agency, but by participating in the sign-and-trade Phoenix could create a salary-trade exception to use on a separate acquisition. The accounting is one player acquired by New York against one protected future draft right plus Phoenix's cap mechanism.

sections.heading: The 2010-11 Stoudemire Return Was Specific and Substantial
sections.body: The first year following the deal supplies the strongest basketball evidence. With the Knicks in 2010-11, Stoudemire scored 1,971 points in 78 games, starting every one, and averaged 25.3 points, 8.2 rebounds and 2.6 assists. He was an All-Star and an All-NBA Second Team pick. The Knicks finished 42-40 and made the postseason for the first time in several years, although a first-round sweep by Boston limits claims about team success. The player's production belongs to New York after the transaction. His eight prior seasons in Phoenix are context for why the Knicks wanted him, not extra production earned by the Knicks. Likewise, later injuries and subsequent roster changes should be acknowledged without retroactively erasing a documented 2010-11 All-NBA season.

sections.heading: What Became of the Phoenix Exception and the Second-Round Right
sections.body: Phoenix had two separate outcomes to monitor after Stoudemire left. Basketball-Reference records that the conditional 2012 second-round selection did not convey, so the Suns did not gain an NBA draftee from it. Contemporary July 2010 reports described the $16.5 million trade exception as enabling a separate sign-and-trade to bring Hakim Warrick from Chicago. That move was an additional transaction with its own draft compensation, not a concealed third side of the Knicks-Suns agreement. The exception had utility even though no star-for-star replacement arrived in Phoenix. Separating the exercised salary mechanism from the unexercised pick also explains why the Suns' C is not treated as a zero return and why it cannot match an A for an incoming scorer who appeared in 78 New York games his first year.

sections.heading: Injuries and Later Knicks Seasons Do Not Rewrite the Original Swap
sections.body: Stoudemire's career in New York was not a five-year run at his first-season pace. His 2011-12 regular season consisted of 47 appearances, and he played 29 games in 2012-13, a period affected by physical setbacks and a changing lineup. The front office subsequently added Carmelo Anthony, creating a different roster around him from the group in place at his July 2010 arrival. Those years limit any claim that the sign-and-trade made New York a sustained contender. Even with that limitation, the initial 78-game All-NBA season remains a return far above the cost of a conditional second that failed to convey. The deal's grading looks at the original incoming player, the protected right and the trade exception; it does not credit either club with unrelated later transactions.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win, with the existing New York A and Phoenix C grades preserved. New York received an immediately productive All-Star in the July 2010 sign-and-trade. The Suns received a conditional second that ultimately did not convey and an approximately $16.5 million trade exception, subsequently involved in separate roster moves. Phoenix did not directly acquire Hakim Warrick from New York, nor did it exercise the protected draft pick.

sections.heading: Anthony's No-Trade Clause Framed the September 2017 Exit
sections.body: New York transferred Carmelo Anthony to Oklahoma City on September 25, 2017, receiving Enes Kanter, Doug McDermott and the Chicago-origin 2018 second-round selection. Anthony had spent more than six seasons with the Knicks and his contractual no-trade protection limited the destinations New York could realistically consider. Oklahoma City had already acquired Paul George to play beside Russell Westbrook and wanted another established scorer. The Knicks instead obtained two immediately usable players and a future draft choice, separating the current roster from Anthony's sizable contract. No first-round pick moved directly in the original exchange, and the deal did not include Dennis Schroder or Emmanuel Mudiay. Those players entered separate later trades, each with additional outgoing consideration. Keeping these transactions distinct is essential when assigning value to the original three incoming New York assets.

sections.heading: Kanter Became an Immediate Knicks Rebounding Starter
sections.body: Kanter was the largest immediate NBA contributor New York obtained. He appeared in 71 Knicks regular-season games in 2017-18, starting every one, while averaging 14.1 points and 11.0 rebounds in 25.8 minutes. His 59.2 percent field-goal shooting gave the club an efficient interior finisher, though his defense and changing roster role made the longer tenure more complicated. Kanter stayed with New York into 2018-19 before the franchise waived him in February 2019. His Knicks performances were direct results of the September 2017 exchange rather than hypothetical development of a draft right. The first season was especially tangible: he played a regular starting role when the team was moving past Anthony. His subsequent appearances for Portland, Boston and other organizations should not be added to the direct Knicks return.

sections.heading: McDermott Played Fifty-Five Games Before Helping Bring Mudiay
sections.body: The other incoming veteran, Doug McDermott, supplied New York 55 regular-season games in 2017-18, with averages of 7.2 points and 2.4 rebounds. He made 38.7 percent of his three-pointers while working primarily as a reserve wing. On February 8, 2018, the Knicks sent McDermott to Dallas and a separate 2018 second-round pick to Denver as part of a three-team transaction that brought Emmanuel Mudiay to New York. The Knicks' own release confirms those outgoing assets and the three clubs. The separate second was not the Chicago-origin pick acquired from Oklahoma City in September, which New York retained. McDermott's time with the Knicks was brief, but it created real shooting minutes and a movable contract that played a part in another negotiation. Mudiay was not acquired for McDermott alone.

sections.heading: The Chicago Second Turned Into Mitchell Robinson at No. 36
sections.body: The 2018 second-round selection acquired from Oklahoma City originated with Chicago. New York used it at No. 36 in the June 2018 draft to choose Mitchell Robinson, a center who developed into a durable rim protector and offensive rebounder. His value required more than draft-night reputation: the Knicks controlled his rights, signed him, and used him for multiple seasons as a rotation center and eventual regular starter. Unlike the McDermott deal, which required a separate New York second-round right, this pick was kept through the draft. Robinson's NBA games therefore belong directly to the acquiring team and constitute a long-running return from the Anthony trade. The fact that an otherwise modest second-round pick created useful center production helps explain the inherited New York A grade much better than treating Kanter and McDermott as future All-Stars.

sections.heading: Anthony Played Seventy-Eight Games for Oklahoma City
sections.body: Oklahoma City received one actual season from Anthony. He played 78 regular-season games in 2017-18, averaging 16.2 points and 5.8 rebounds as a third scoring option behind Westbrook and George. The Thunder won 48 games, finished fourth in the Northwest Division and lost to Utah in six games during the first round of the playoffs. Those figures make the acquisition more than a zero-return salary transaction, but they also reflect a different role from Anthony's highest-usage Knicks years. His fit on a team with two established ball-dominant stars proved difficult, and the franchise chose not to continue the arrangement into the next season. The site’s C-plus Oklahoma City grade can credit 78 games and a playoff berth while recognizing that the experiment did not deliver an extended title window.

sections.heading: The 2018 Atlanta Exit Cost Oklahoma City an Additional First
sections.body: The Thunder's second transaction involving Anthony came in July 2018, after his only Oklahoma City season. In a three-team deal with Atlanta and Philadelphia, Oklahoma City sent Anthony and a protected 2022 first-round pick to the Hawks, receiving Dennis Schroder from Atlanta and Timothe Luwawu-Cabarrot from Philadelphia. Atlanta also obtained Justin Anderson, while Philadelphia received Mike Muscala. The official Thunder announcement makes clear that Schroder was not supplied by New York in 2017 and the new draft compensation was a separate outgoing asset. Any analysis that credits Schroder's entire later Thunder production as a free return from the original Knicks trade omits the additional first-round cost and other teams involved. The extra transaction and limited Anthony tenure help explain why New York's lasting Robinson right aged more favorably.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win — New York A, Oklahoma City C+. Anthony played 78 Thunder games at 16.2 points before a 2018 first-round exit and a separate three-team trade in which Oklahoma City also sent a protected 2022 first. New York received 71 Kanter starts, 55 McDermott games, and the Chicago-origin No.36 second used on Mitchell Robinson. McDermott later joined a separate Mudiay deal involving another Knicks second.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Carmelo Anthony to OKC: Kanter, McDermott and Mitchell Robinson Pick Returns
featuredDeepDive.intro: New York exchanged Anthony for two rotation veterans and the 2018 Chicago-origin second that became Mitchell Robinson. The Thunder got 78 Anthony games and later used another protected first to move him.

sections.heading: A Restricted Market Produced a Three-Asset Knicks Package
sections.body: Anthony had contractual leverage because his no-trade clause narrowed which destinations the Knicks could use. Oklahoma City, having assembled a Westbrook-George core, elected to add the veteran scorer rather than surrender control over its immediate roster strategy. New York emerged with Kanter and McDermott, who were ready to play, plus a second-round choice from Chicago. Those pieces had different value horizons: Kanter could start and rebound immediately, McDermott could offer perimeter shooting, and the pick allowed the front office to evaluate another prospect in 2018. Neither the no-trade clause nor the acquisition's timing automatically made it a win. The outcome depended on whether the received assets turned into useful Knicks minutes and whether Anthony fit with the Thunder stars. Both questions received identifiable answers over the next year.

sections.heading: New York Got One Starting Big and One Tradable Shooter
sections.body: Kanter's 71 starts and 14.1-point, 11.0-rebound averages were the most substantial immediate Knicks return in 2017-18. McDermott added 55 games as a shooting reserve and a 38.7 percent three-point rate before the February 2018 Mudiay transaction. These results were not championship-level contributions, but they establish that New York acquired actual playing value rather than a pair of contracts that never took the floor. McDermott's use in a later deal also shows a form of retained flexibility, although the Knicks sent a separate second-round selection to Denver as additional compensation. Kanter's eventual waiver and McDermott's departure place reasonable limits on their long-term contributions. Their combined first-season use gave the team time and depth while the future Chicago-origin pick was still waiting to be exercised.

sections.heading: Robinson's No. 36 Selection Supplied the Longest Return
sections.body: The second-round choice became Mitchell Robinson in the 2018 NBA draft, providing New York a chance to sign a young center despite not receiving a first-round pick in the Anthony deal. Robinson became known for shot blocking, rebounding and finishing around the rim. His subsequent seasons under Knicks control outlasted the tenures of Kanter and McDermott, giving the inherited New York A grade an identifiable development success. This was not a case in which a future protected right expired without conveying, and the selection was not sent to another franchise before the draft. The Knicks exercised the choice at No. 36 and built a real part of their frontcourt from it. That direct link is also why the Chicago-origin pick must not be confused with the different second New York surrendered in the Mudiay trade.

sections.heading: The Thunder Got a Playoff Season, but Not a Lasting Fit
sections.body: Anthony started 78 games for Oklahoma City and averaged 16.2 points, clearly supplying real basketball offense. The Thunder still lost in six games to Utah during the 2018 first round, and Anthony's third-option role alongside Westbrook and George never became the expected long-term solution. A retrospective C-plus should be grounded in that one season, not claims that he was still the same player as in his scoring-title Knicks years. The following July's move to Atlanta was another trade involving more than Anthony alone: Oklahoma City also attached a protected 2022 first and obtained Schroder and Luwawu-Cabarrot in a three-club structure. That cost matters when evaluating the end of the Thunder's experiment. The later Schroder years cannot be credited as if he had arrived from New York in September 2017.

sections.heading: A Knicks A Versus Thunder C-Plus With Linked Trades Kept Separate
sections.body: The source ledger preserves Knicks Win, New York A and Oklahoma City C-plus. New York obtained 71 Kanter starts at strong rebounding averages, 55 McDermott appearances and the No. 36 right that became Mitchell Robinson. Oklahoma City obtained 78 Anthony games at 16.2 points and a first-round playoff exit before moving him again with a separate protected first-rounder. New York's McDermott-for-Mudiay transaction also contained a different outgoing second; it was not an automatic exchange for the original Chicago pick. These distinctions show why a front office can win a deal through several modest assets and one valuable drafted center without obtaining another superstar. The Thunder received legitimate one-year production, but the Knicks retained the longer-term development opportunity. The existing grade spread reflects those outcomes rather than Anthony's name recognition.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: New York A, Oklahoma City C-plus in the preserved Knicks Win. The Knicks used Kanter and McDermott in 2017-18 and drafted Mitchell Robinson with the acquired Chicago second. Oklahoma City used Anthony for 78 games and later attached an additional protected first to move him in a separate 2018 transaction. Dennis Schroder was never received directly from New York.

sections.heading: A Draft-Night Deal Exchanged Two Second-Round Guards and Cash
sections.body: New York acquired the rights to Ignas Brazdeikis from Sacramento in the June 2019 draft exchange. The Kings received Kyle Guy’s rights and $1 million in cash. Brazdeikis had been selected 47th, while Guy came at No. 55. Although the archive records the draft-night date as June 20, the Knicks and Kings transaction histories list the exchange on June 21. That bookkeeping distinction should not be mistaken for two separate trades.

sections.heading: The Knicks Pursued Brazdeikis but Did Not Keep Him Long
sections.body: Brazdeikis played nine Knicks games in 2019–20 and four more for New York in 2020–21. His 13 regular-season appearances for the Knicks make it difficult to present the acquisition as a major on-court success. The team was using a late second-round selection to seek a young wing who could develop, yet his limited NBA opportunity in New York restricted the realized return. Any later playing time with other organizations cannot be treated as Knicks production.

sections.heading: Sacramento Had Guy’s Rights and a Known Cash Payment
sections.body: Guy played three regular-season games for Sacramento in 2019–20 and 31 in 2020–21. His 34 Kings appearances exceeded Brazdeikis’s Knicks total, though neither player became a lasting starting contributor to the acquiring team. Sacramento also received the stated $1 million, a documented extra part of its incoming package. That direct cash amount is distinguishable from historical trades whose consideration is recorded only as an unspecified payment.

sections.heading: Why the Knicks Win Verdict Needs the 2019 Cash and Minutes Context
sections.body: The Knicks Win verdict grades New York B-minus and Sacramento C, but the direct player outcomes do not tell a decisive Knicks story. Ignas Brazdeikis played 13 New York regular-season games across 2019-20 and 2020-21. Kyle Guy made 34 Sacramento appearances in those two seasons, and the Kings also received the separately documented $1 million cash consideration. The Kings’ own June 21, 2019 draft review identifies the original No. 47 rights to Brazdeikis and No. 55 rights to Guy. Draft-night coverage dates the arrangement June 20; subsequent transaction ledgers use June 21, with no evidence of two exchanges. Both guards had limited roles, so a brief games-played comparison alone cannot settle every element of the grades. Still, the published grade advantage for New York is open to fair criticism when Sacramento had more receiving-team appearances and the cash; the verdict is a site evaluation, not an independently verified league conclusion.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win in the canonical ledger — New York B-minus, Sacramento C. New York obtained No. 47 Ignas Brazdeikis for No. 55 Kyle Guy and $1 million. Brazdeikis appeared in 13 regular-season games for the Knicks, compared with Guy’s 34 Kings games. The stored grade edge belongs to New York, but the limited NBA output and the cash Sacramento received make this a narrow, debatable retrospective call.

sections.heading: New York Was Paid to Take a Contract It Could Immediately Move
sections.body: The Knicks acquired Ed Davis and two future second-round picks from Utah for cash considerations. On its face, that is already favorable for a rebuilding team with available financial flexibility: New York accepted a veteran contract and received draft compensation for doing so. The front office then improved the transaction one day later by sending Davis to Minnesota for Jacob Evans, Omari Spellman and another future second-round pick. That second trade is a separate transaction and should not be double-counted as if Utah directly gave New York three picks. It does, however, show that the contract New York absorbed remained movable and could be converted into additional value almost immediately.

sections.heading: The Two Utah Seconds Became Concrete Draft Assets
sections.body: The original trade delivered Utah's 2023 second-rounder and a 2024 second that was the more favorable of Cleveland and Utah. Those selections eventually landed at No. 39 in 2023 and No. 38 in 2024, associated with Mouhamed Gueye and Ajay Mitchell. The Knicks did not necessarily make or retain those exact players, so the evaluation avoids pretending New York drafted both as part of a straight-line outcome. The stronger point is that the picks remained real, transferable second-round currency for years. Acquiring two such assets for cash and a short-lived contract obligation is exactly the type of low-risk accumulation move that can compound during a rebuild.

sections.heading: Utah's Motivation Was Roster and Salary Flexibility
sections.body: Utah had its own reason to act. Davis had played only 28 games for the Jazz in 2019-20 and averaged 1.8 points and 3.8 rebounds in limited minutes. Moving him cleared the roster and helped create room for other frontcourt decisions, including bringing Derrick Favors back in free agency. The Jazz were not selling a productive core player. That context prevents the grade from being treated as a catastrophic talent giveaway. The D reflects the price: Utah attached two future second-round picks to move a veteran contract, while New York found another market for Davis almost immediately. The Jazz obtained flexibility, but the Knicks captured nearly all of the transferable asset value.

sections.heading: Why New York Reaches an A
sections.body: An A does not require a star if the cost is sufficiently low. New York sent cash considerations, acquired two future seconds, and temporarily took on a player it did not need to keep. The next-day Minnesota trade demonstrated that Davis still had transactional utility. None of the pieces individually changed the franchise, but the Knicks created multiple assets without sacrificing a meaningful player or premium pick. That is high-efficiency rebuilding work. Utah's side looks weaker because the Jazz paid draft capital to solve a relatively small roster problem, and the acquiring team proved almost instantly that the contract was not immovable. The value gap is therefore larger than the low-profile names might suggest.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win. New York earns A because it converted cash and available roster flexibility into Ed Davis plus two future second-round picks, then moved Davis the next day in a separate deal that produced another second-round asset along with two players. The original Utah trade should receive only proportional downstream credit for that second move, but it clearly established that the Knicks were acquiring a contract with resale value rather than dead salary. Utah receives D because Davis was expendable and the Jazz did gain flexibility, yet they attached two future seconds to remove him. The documented Knicks Win verdict reflects asset efficiency: New York surrendered almost no basketball value and walked away with multiple forms of future currency.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Deep Dive: The Ed Davis Trade as a Lesson in Small-Asset Accumulation
featuredDeepDive.intro: The most revealing part of this trade happened after the headline. New York took Ed Davis and two seconds from Utah, then found a new destination for Davis one day later. The sequence shows how a rebuilding front office can use cap and roster flexibility to manufacture draft assets without making a blockbuster or betting on a star.

sections.heading: The Knicks' Advantage Started with the Price
sections.body: Trade evaluation often begins with the incoming player, but New York's advantage began with what it did not give up. The Knicks sent cash considerations rather than a rotation player or draft pick. In exchange they received Davis and two future seconds. That made the downside limited from the start. If Davis had remained on the roster, the Knicks still would have been compensated for carrying the contract. Because he was moved almost immediately, the holding cost became even smaller. The structure is a reminder that teams with financial flexibility can create value by accepting obligations other clubs want to remove. The names are modest, but the asset economics are strong.

sections.heading: The Next-Day Minnesota Trade Confirms Davis Was Liquid
sections.body: New York's separate trade with Minnesota sent Davis out for Jacob Evans, Omari Spellman and Minnesota's 2026 second-round pick. That transaction should not be folded wholesale into Utah's grade because Minnesota made its own independent decision. Still, it provides evidence about the quality of the asset New York had just acquired: Davis was not an unmovable contract requiring another sweetener from the Knicks. He could be redirected for additional compensation. In practical terms, New York accepted Utah's salary problem, received two seconds for doing so, and then found a buyer willing to send another second. The sequence validates the original move as an efficient use of flexibility rather than a passive salary dump.

sections.heading: Utah Paid for Certainty
sections.body: For the Jazz, the attraction was certainty. Davis had barely played, and Utah wanted roster room and financial clarity before the season. Attaching seconds is a common way to ensure another team accepts a contract without sending back unwanted salary. The move therefore accomplished what Utah intended. The retrospective problem is that New York's quick resale showed the Jazz paid a meaningful premium for that certainty. Second-round picks are individually volatile, but two of them create real optionality in future trades and drafts. Utah surrendered both while removing a player whose contract another team valued enough to acquire the next day. That completed value is why the Jazz grade falls to D despite the understandable roster logic.

sections.heading: The Picks Matter Even without Star Outcomes
sections.body: Neither the 2023 nor 2024 second needs to become an All-Star for the Knicks to have won the transaction. The picks represented future selections in a range that can be used to draft, trade, consolidate or facilitate other deals. Their eventual positions, No. 39 and No. 38, were not throwaway slots. The analysis therefore credits New York for acquiring liquid draft assets rather than for claiming the full careers of Mouhamed Gueye or Ajay Mitchell. That distinction keeps the evaluation disciplined. The Knicks' A is based on the price paid and optionality created. The Jazz's D is based on the amount of optionality surrendered to remove a low-impact veteran contract.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win, New York A and Utah D. The Knicks were compensated twice within roughly a day for using roster and financial flexibility: first by Utah with Ed Davis and two future seconds, then in a separate transaction by Minnesota with another second plus two players for Davis. Only the first transaction is graded here, but the quick resale proves Davis had market utility. Utah's two seconds eventually became meaningful second-round draft positions, reinforcing that the sweetener was not trivial. The Jazz did achieve a clean roster reset and moved a veteran who had little role, so the result is not an F. But New York created future assets at minimal cost, making this one of the cleaner examples of margin-value accumulation.

sections.heading: The Knicks Turned Two Young Players Into a Defensive Fit
sections.body: New York acquired O.G. Anunoby, Precious Achiuwa and Malachi Flynn from Toronto in December 2023. Toronto received RJ Barrett, Immanuel Quickley and a 2024 second-round pick that became Jonathan Mogbo. It was not a salary dump or a deal with an empty side: the Knicks targeted a high-level defensive wing, while the Raptors acquired two younger rotation players with larger offensive roles available.

sections.heading: Anunoby Immediately Changed New York’s Lineup
sections.body: Anunoby could defend several positions without requiring many possessions on offense. That made him a natural fit beside Jalen Brunson and the rest of New York’s primary scorers. His addition also helped the Knicks deploy stronger perimeter defensive combinations as they pursued postseason success. Achiuwa supplied useful frontcourt depth, while Flynn was a smaller part of the basketball return. New York concentrated value in the specific type of starter it lacked.

sections.heading: Toronto Obtained Real Starting-Level Production
sections.body: Barrett returned to Canada as a younger scoring wing and Quickley received more responsibility as a guard creator. Toronto’s gain was not equivalent to replacing Anunoby with a lesser defender: it chose two offensive pieces that could develop on a new roster timeline. Mogbo’s No. 31 rights gave the Raptors another developmental asset. Those outcomes help explain why Toronto receives an A-minus instead of a failing grade, despite the Knicks winning the narrower fit comparison.

sections.heading: Why New York’s Advantage Is Not a Landslide
sections.body: New York’s A-plus reflects Anunoby’s rare combination of size, defense and complementary offense. Toronto’s A-minus recognizes Barrett, Quickley and Mogbo as real assets rather than treating a trade winner as the sole successful team. The Knicks improved their immediate high-end lineup, while the Raptors exchanged a more established two-way wing for young talent and offensive opportunities. The difference is the value of Anunoby’s particular role on a contender.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win — New York A-plus, Toronto A-minus. Anunoby supplied the defensive wing New York wanted for its postseason lineup, with Achiuwa adding depth. The Raptors obtained Barrett, Quickley and Mogbo’s draft rights, giving them legitimate younger talent. New York captured the more impactful immediate fit without making Toronto’s return an outright loss.
