sections.heading: Orlando Took a Conditional Second for Elfrid Payton
sections.body: On February 8, 2018, Orlando traded starting point guard Elfrid Payton to Phoenix for a 2018 second-round selection that originated from Memphis and was subject to conditions involving other choices. The Suns official announcement says the club wanted Payton alongside its younger scorers, while the Magic was changing its backcourt plan during a rebuilding season. Payton had started 44 Orlando games that year and was averaging 13.0 points and 6.3 assists when the teams agreed. This was a direct player-for-pick exchange: the February agreement did not deliver an incoming veteran guard to Orlando or additional named Suns players. The meaningful question is what the second-round asset ultimately let Orlando do.

sections.heading: The No. 41 Pick Turned Into Two Other Draft Assets
sections.body: The acquired pick eventually became No. 41 in the 2018 draft, and Orlando selected Kentucky forward Jarred Vanderbilt at that slot. However, Vanderbilt never became a Magic regular-season player. In a separate June 21 draft-night trade, Orlando sent his rights to Denver for the rights to No. 43 Justin Jackson and a future second-round pick. The Magic official report and Denver own transaction history confirm both components of that second step. Any NBA playing years Vanderbilt later accumulated for Denver or Minnesota should not be credited to Orlando. The actual realized return from the original Payton trade was a draft right that Orlando could exchange, followed by Jackson rights and the second future pick.

sections.heading: Phoenix Received Nineteen Starts Before Payton Left
sections.body: Payton appeared in 19 regular-season Suns games in 2017-18 and started each, averaging 11.8 points, 6.2 assists and 5.3 rebounds. That is a real short-term backcourt contribution, not a failed attempt to roster a player who never reported. His Phoenix contract expired after the season and he signed elsewhere, preventing the Suns from gaining additional years of production. The Magic B and Suns D grades are inherited from the existing review, but the score gap should be understood as a judgment about long-term asset control rather than an absence of Payton minutes. Phoenix bought nineteen starts; Orlando gained a draft selection it could convert into two further opportunities without pretending Vanderbilt played for the Magic.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Magic Win under the inherited B for Orlando and D for Phoenix. Orlando converted the Payton return into the 2018 No. 41 right, then traded Vanderbilt rights for No. 43 Justin Jackson and a future second. Phoenix still received 19 Payton starts with 11.8 points and 6.2 assists per game; the deal was a short-term player rental against two eventual draft-right assets.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Elfrid Payton to Phoenix: Orlando’s 2018 Draft-Pick Chain
featuredDeepDive.intro: Phoenix acquired 19 late-season Payton starts. Orlando acquired a conditional second, then converted No. 41 Jarred Vanderbilt draft rights into No. 43 Justin Jackson rights and a future second in a separate Denver deal.

sections.heading: Orlando Bought a Pick It Could Trade Again
sections.body: The original February 8, 2018 trade was simple: Orlando sent point guard Elfrid Payton to Phoenix and received a conditional second-round draft choice. It did not acquire a Suns player. The pick later became No. 41 in the 2018 draft, and the Magic selected Jarred Vanderbilt before dealing his rights to Denver on draft night. That separate move brought the rights to No. 43 Justin Jackson and an additional future second. These are two different transactions with different counterparties. Vanderbilt's later NBA development should not be entered as Orlando playing production, just as Denver's decision to obtain him should not be credited to the Suns. Orlando's favorable grade recognizes retaining and converting a movable pick at a time when it was changing its backcourt. The chain is valuable because the club did not let the compensatory right expire without another decision.

sections.heading: Payton’s Nineteen Suns Starts Were Real
sections.body: Phoenix acquired Elfrid Payton to take an immediate look at a young point guard alongside its developing perimeter players. He started all 19 games he played for the Suns in the remainder of 2017-18, averaging 11.8 points, 6.2 assists and 5.3 rebounds. The contribution was not imaginary, and the D grade should never imply Payton refused to report or failed to produce any usable minutes. The return simply ended quickly. His contract expired after the season, and he left Phoenix without adding another year of play. That short window is central to the comparison: Orlando had the freedom to convert a draft right into multiple assets, whereas the Suns had a brief evaluation of a player who did not become part of their longer-term backcourt. The original transaction still retains its historic date and assets.

sections.heading: The Draft-Night Swap Changed the Final Accounting
sections.body: Orlando exercised the No. 41 selection on Jarred Vanderbilt but did not retain his NBA rights. On June 21, 2018, it sent those rights to Denver in exchange for the rights to Justin Jackson at No. 43 and a future second-round pick. Orlando's official account and the NBA's draft trade tracker document the move. This means neither Vanderbilt's later playing seasons nor any production for Denver or Minnesota should inflate the Magic's return. Similarly, Justin Jackson did not arrive as a Phoenix player on February 8. He came through a different negotiation months later. The detailed grade should therefore separate the original Payton-for-pick agreement from Orlando's use of that pick in another draft-right swap. The historical winner follows the combined value of control and future flexibility rather than one player-versus-player box score.

sections.heading: Why the Inherited B and D Grades Can Coexist
sections.body: The Magic received an asset it could move after deciding not to continue with Payton as its point guard. The No. 41 right eventually supported a draft-night exchange involving No. 43 Justin Jackson and another future second. That outcome supports Orlando's B, while stopping short of pretending a late second-round selection became an established star. Phoenix's D reflects the short duration of Payton's stay: he made 19 starts and contributed useful assists, but left after the season. The Suns did not obtain prolonged team control in exchange for the selection. The trade therefore has an asymmetric but defensible outcome: Orlando retained a path to later roster or draft moves, and Phoenix had only a few months of a young guard. A Magic Win verdict describes the winner; B versus D describes the relative, limited scale of realized value.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Magic Win — Orlando B, Phoenix D. Orlando retained a conditional second-round right for Elfrid Payton and later moved the No. 41 Vanderbilt rights to Denver for Justin Jackson rights and a future second. Payton started 19 games for Phoenix before leaving after the season.

sections.heading: The Deal Involved an Oklahoma City Pick With Real Protection
sections.body: On February 7, 2019, Orlando obtained Markelle Fultz from Philadelphia for Jonathon Simmons, a 2019 second-round selection and a 2020 first-rounder originally belonging to Oklahoma City. The first was protected in picks 1 through 20; if it failed to convey, it would instead become Oklahoma City's 2022 and 2023 second-round selections. Orlando's official announcement explains that contingency. The 2019 second was the most favorable among Cleveland, Houston, Orlando and Portland, eventually landing at No. 33. This was therefore not simply a straight Fultz-for-Simmons trade, nor an unprotected future first. The exact protections are essential to explaining why Philadelphia ultimately received the No. 21 right used on Tyrese Maxey.

sections.heading: Orlando Took the Development Bet on a Former No. 1 Pick
sections.body: The Magic acquired a talented but uncertain guard who had played only 33 Philadelphia games across his first two NBA seasons. Fultz's shoulder problems and disrupted jump shot had made his role difficult to define for the Sixers. Orlando president Jeff Weltman explicitly emphasized providing support at the player's own pace, a reasonable plan for a 20-year-old who had been chosen first overall in 2017. The Magic were paying with Simmons and two draft assets for a possible long-term ball handler, rather than buying an established 20-point scorer. His 2019-20 return—72 games and 60 starts for Orlando—showed that the development gamble produced some genuine playing value despite its medical risk.

sections.heading: The 2020 Protected Pick Became Philadelphia's Maxey Selection
sections.body: The Oklahoma City selection landed No. 21 in the 2020 draft, one place outside the trade's top-20 protection. Philadelphia retained the conveyed pick and used it to select Tyrese Maxey, whose career later included an All-Star selection and a leading scoring role beside Joel Embiid. The proximity to the protection boundary was decisive: a pick landing at No. 20 would not have conveyed on the same terms. It is important to distinguish this pick's original ownership and the protection language from the development of the eventual player. Maxey's production is the meaningful historical upside associated with Philadelphia's receipt of the draft right, not a bonus player sent directly by Orlando in February 2019.

sections.heading: Fultz Still Provided a Legitimate Orlando Return
sections.body: Fultz should not be reduced to the injury concerns Philadelphia wanted to leave behind. In 2019-20 he played 72 games for the Magic, starting 60. Later, after another serious knee injury and recovery, he started all 60 appearances in 2022-23, averaging 14.0 points, 5.7 assists and 3.9 rebounds while shooting 51.4 percent from the field. Those are concrete seasons of NBA production from Orlando's acquired guard. His sporadic availability between those seasons also limited the lasting value of the experiment. The retrospective comparison can favor Philadelphia strongly without pretending that the Magic received nothing or ignoring the circumstances that made a former No. 1 pick available.

sections.heading: The 2019 Second-Round Pick Is Separate From the First
sections.body: Philadelphia also obtained the 2019 second-round choice that became No. 33, associated with Carsen Edwards. That asset must be tracked apart from the protected 2020 first. A later draft-rights transaction involving Edwards would be another step of an asset chain, not proof that he was a major 76ers rotation player. Jonathon Simmons was the other directly acquired player in February 2019, and his short remaining NBA tenure did not generate the standout return. The larger outcome was the first-round right that conveyed at No. 21. Keeping every component visible prevents both over-crediting Philadelphia's minor pieces and erasing the risk it assumed when accepting a protected pick.

sections.heading: Why the Retrospective Grades Favor Philadelphia
sections.body: The canonical verdict is 76ers Win, with Philadelphia A-plus and Orlando B-minus, and those marks are preserved. Philadelphia converted the conditional first into Tyrese Maxey, an outcome with far greater sustained basketball impact than the two smaller incoming pieces. Orlando acquired Fultz at a damaged-value moment, gave him space to recover and obtained starting-caliber minutes in more than one season. Those returns explain why the Magic's grade should not be treated as a zero. Still, Maxey's later All-Star-level development is the pivotal hindsight event. The grades are historical editorial assessments, not an arithmetic equation in which the No. 21 pick automatically guaranteed a star on trade day.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The retained verdict is 76ers Win: Philadelphia A-plus, Orlando B-minus. The Magic obtained Fultz and later received 72 appearances in 2019-20 and 60 starts in 2022-23. Philadelphia obtained Simmons and two draft assets, most importantly an Oklahoma City first protected through No. 20 that conveyed at No. 21 in 2020. Tyrese Maxey's development made that selection the clear long-term prize. The 2019 second and the 2020 first are distinct, and the first's protection—not hindsight certainty—explains the trade's unusual leverage.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Markelle Fultz and the No. 21 Pick: How Maxey Changed the 2019 Outcome
featuredDeepDive.intro: Orlando took a chance on the injured former No. 1 pick Markelle Fultz in February 2019. The price was Jonathon Simmons, a 2019 second and an Oklahoma City 2020 first protected in the top 20. The first conveyed at No. 21 and eventually became Philadelphia's selection of Tyrese Maxey. Fultz's later starting seasons give Orlando real value, but the draft protection and Maxey's development make Philadelphia's return stronger. The existing grades are preserved.

sections.heading: The Pick's Origin and Top-Twenty Protection Defined the Risk
sections.body: Oklahoma City's conditional 2020 first had moved through previous transactions before Orlando sent it back to Philadelphia as part of the Fultz deal. The Magic's February 2019 release states the pick was protected Nos. 1 through 20 and would otherwise convert to two future seconds if it did not convey. In the 2020 lottery and draft ordering, that pick fell at No. 21, making the first-round asset usable by Philadelphia. The single-position distance between 20 and 21 is not cosmetic; it changed what the Sixers actually received. This is a case where the legal trade condition, rather than a vague statement about future draft capital, explains a large part of the final basketball result.

sections.heading: Fultz's Two Productive Orlando Seasons Cannot Be Erased
sections.body: Orlando's return is best represented by the actual games Fultz played, not solely by the skepticism surrounding his arrival. He participated in 72 games with 60 starts during the 2019-20 season and returned from further injury setbacks to start all 60 of his 2022-23 appearances. That latter season brought averages of 14.0 points, 5.7 assists, 3.9 rebounds and 51.4-percent field-goal shooting. These statistics support Orlando's argument that its buy-low decision did sometimes yield a capable starting point guard. His lengthy absences in other stretches create a durability limitation that should be openly weighed. Neither fact justifies pretending the acquisition had either no value or guaranteed superstar value.

sections.heading: Maxey Developed Beyond the Expected Return of Pick Twenty-One
sections.body: The Sixers acquired uncertainty in the form of a protected first-round selection, not Tyrese Maxey as an established professional. Maxey was drafted 21st in 2020 after that right conveyed, then developed into an All-Star guard and a primary offensive option. His subsequent NBA performance creates the dominant hindsight value in the trade and explains the preserved Philadelphia A-plus. It would be misleading, however, to judge Orlando's original decision as though Maxey's career was knowable in February 2019. A disciplined analysis records the selection, the protection result and the later playing value as separate stages. That chronology captures Philadelphia's payoff without inventing certainty around young-player development.

sections.heading: The Other Sixers Assets Were Not Comparable to Maxey
sections.body: Philadelphia also received Jonathon Simmons and the 2019 second-round selection that became the No. 33 rights associated with Carsen Edwards. Neither delivered a direct long-term 76ers contribution comparable to the first-round pick's eventual Maxey outcome. The condition on the second determined which of several originating teams' choices would transfer; it should not be mistaken for an additional unprotected first. Simmons was a veteran wing whose role had already declined in Orlando. Distinguishing these parts makes the comparison intelligible: the Sixers' value came mainly through the 2020 conveyance, while the other incoming pieces reduced some immediate transaction risk but were not franchise-altering assets.

sections.heading: A Retrospective Win Can Coexist With an Understandable Gamble
sections.body: Philadelphia's A-plus and Orlando's B-minus are kept in the canonical ledger along with 76ers Win. A first-round selection that turned into an All-Star is an unusually successful return for a guard whose path had stalled because of injury and shooting problems. Orlando, meanwhile, was trying to revive a 20-year-old former top pick and saw genuine seasons of competent starting play after the acquisition. The key analytical difference is durability and upside realized over time, not simply that Philadelphia received three ledger items while Orlando received one. The exact pick conditions, actual games played and later Maxey emergence are the reasons the retrospective outcome favors the Sixers.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Philadelphia's historical A-plus and Orlando's B-minus stay in place with the 76ers Win verdict. The original Fultz deal did not directly trade Maxey as an NBA player: it transferred a top-20-protected Oklahoma City first that conveyed at No. 21 in 2020, along with Simmons and a separate 2019 second. The Sixers used the first to draft Maxey, whose later All-Star-level contribution was the decisive return. Orlando still obtained 72 Fultz games in 2019-20 and another 60 starts in 2022-23, when he averaged 14.0 points and 5.7 assists. His injury interruptions limited that investment. This analysis distinguishes what each team could reasonably expect in February 2019 from what the pick and the guard eventually became.

sections.heading: Golden State Exchanged Poole’s Future for a Veteran Guard
sections.body: Golden State acquired Chris Paul from Washington in the July 2023 exchange. The Wizards took Jordan Poole, Patrick Baldwin Jr., Ryan Rollins, cash, a 2027 second-round selection and a top-20-protected 2030 first that could convert to a second. The real cost to Washington was absorbing Poole’s existing long-term contract. Golden State prioritized a new guard rotation around Stephen Curry rather than continuing with the younger scorer whose role had become unsettled.

sections.heading: Paul Filled a Specific Warriors Role for One Season
sections.body: Paul was a veteran playmaker who could organize second-unit possessions and reduce turnovers. Golden State received that immediate value, but it was short-lived: Paul’s stay did not extend into a lasting new Warriors core. Trading Poole also changed the club’s salary obligations, making the transaction partly about roster management. That is a meaningful return, just different from acquiring years of team-controlled youth or premium draft capital.

sections.heading: Washington Accepted Volatility for More Routes to Value
sections.body: Poole was young enough to fit a longer rebuilding schedule, although his uneven early Wizards production made the investment risky. Baldwin and Rollins offered additional developmental chances, and the protected first and second were separate future assets. Washington did not need Poole to become an All-Star immediately for those incoming pieces to give it choices. The eventual status and value of the 2030 selection must be evaluated under its top-20 protections, not described as an unconditional first.

sections.heading: Why This Is Only a Slight Washington Edge
sections.body: The Wizards received more ways to capture future value, earning a B-plus in the current trade ledger. The Warriors receive B-minus because Paul supplied veteran guard minutes and Poole’s departure addressed a roster and contract issue. Neither team acquired a guaranteed star outcome: Washington bore Poole’s contract risk while Golden State surrendered youth and draft capital for a short-term solution. The distinction is the duration and optionality of the return, not the number of names involved.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wizards Win by a modest margin — Washington B-plus, Golden State B-minus. The Wizards took on Poole’s contract but received two additional young players, cash and protected future draft choices. Golden State got useful but brief production from Paul and a different contract profile. Washington’s package offered more potential value across later seasons, without guaranteeing that every pick or prospect would succeed.

sections.heading: The Five-Team Transaction and Verified Routing
sections.body: The NBA published the August 20, 2026 agreement as a five-team sign-and-trade linking Cleveland, Denver, the LA Clippers, Charlotte and Washington. Cleveland received Peyton Watson from Denver and Cam Whitmore from Washington. LA received Max Strus from Cleveland. Charlotte received Dennis Schröder plus cash, Denver received Julian Reese and future picks, and Washington received Tre Mann, a 2027 Clippers-origin second and cash. The league transaction tracker confirms those principal moves. The local archive additionally lists the rights to Ismael Kamagate moving to Cleveland, but the consulted NBA.com reporting does not independently confirm that secondary branch. It therefore should not influence the provisional team grades without additional evidence.

sections.heading: Cleveland Acquires Watson and Whitmore at a Future Cost
sections.body: Watson is the largest immediate talent bet in Cleveland’s incoming package. NBA.com reported that he averaged 14.6 points and 4.9 rebounds over 54 Denver games in the preceding season, then pursued a new contract after declining Denver extension offers. He missed the recent playoffs following a hamstring problem, which is relevant to projecting availability but cannot establish the outcome of his Cavaliers tenure. Whitmore adds another young wing option. Cleveland gave up Strus, Schröder, an unprotected 2031 first and other routed second-round and cash assets to facilitate the moves. The B is an early assessment of talent upside and acquisition cost, not a verdict based on unplayed 2026-27 games.

sections.heading: Denver Converts Watson into Picks and Flexibility
sections.body: Denver obtained Julian Reese, a 2031 Cleveland first-round pick and a 2032 Sacramento second-round pick, according to the NBA transaction account. The local record describes the 2031 first as unprotected, increasing its theoretical range of future outcomes. NBA.com also reported that Denver intended to waive Reese from his two-way arrangement, so the distant first is the central lasting asset rather than established immediate playing value. The Nuggets surrendered a 24-year-old wing who had already reached 14.6 points per game in a recent season. A provisional C+ recognizes the first-round upside while acknowledging the immediate roster cost and the fact that neither future draft position is known.

sections.heading: Strus Offers the Clippers a Known Veteran Role
sections.body: Los Angeles acquired Max Strus rather than waiting years for a draft pick to develop. In Cleveland, Strus had already shown the ability to function in an NBA starting rotation, but the preceding season was interrupted by a left-foot Jones fracture. NBA.com listed just 12 appearances and 11.2 points per game for that injury-affected season. The Clippers receive veteran shooting and roster fit, not a guarantee that Strus will stay healthy or recreate his previous role. Their B+ is a preliminary relative edge based on the direct veteran return and the way the five-team arrangement routed assets; future Clippers wins or Strus statistics have not been credited.

sections.heading: Charlotte and Washington Take Separate Guard Paths
sections.body: Charlotte turned Tre Mann into Dennis Schröder, a Philadelphia-origin 2027 second and cash. NBA.com reported Schröder at 10.8 points and 4.9 assists across 70 games with Sacramento and Cleveland in the prior season, offering an established veteran distributor. Washington received Mann, the Clippers-origin 2027 second and cash while sending out Whitmore and Reese. Mann had appeared in 53 Hornets games in the previous season, averaging 5.5 points after a higher-scoring 2024-25 campaign. These are different trade-day objectives: immediate guard reliability and another future asset for Charlotte, compared with a younger guard and flexibility for Washington. Both provisional B grades assume neither a certain veteran revival nor a future draft hit.

finalVerdict.heading: Provisional Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Clippers Edge, provisionally. LA receives B+ for Max Strus and its immediate role fit; Cleveland B for Watson and Whitmore at the cost of its 2031 first and veterans; Charlotte B for Schröder, cash and a future second; Washington B for Mann, cash and a future second; Denver C+ for Reese and two future selections after moving Watson. Actual future draft positions, player availability and 2026-27 performance are unresolved, and the locally recorded Kamagate-rights branch requires separate confirmation.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: One Trade, Five Different Timelines
featuredDeepDive.intro: The completed transaction joined two previously reported deals and spread player value, cash and future draft control across five franchises.

sections.heading: Why the Records Had to Be Merged
sections.body: The Schröder-Mann swap and the Watson-Strus framework were ultimately folded into the same official five-team transaction, so treating them as separate canonical trades would double-count the event.

sections.heading: The 2031 Pick Is Still the Swing Asset
sections.body: Cleveland's unprotected 2031 first gives Denver the widest long-term upside in the deal and remains the hardest asset to price today.

sections.heading: Washington Quietly Added Optionality
sections.body: Tre Mann, a conditional 2027 second and cash give Washington a broader return than a simple Cam Whitmore swap would suggest.

sections.heading: Charlotte Chose Veteran Stability
sections.body: Dennis Schröder and cash replace Tre Mann with a more established organizer while preserving the deal as part of the larger five-team structure.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The early grades remain Clippers B+, Cleveland B, Washington B, Charlotte B and Denver C+. They are explicitly provisional because the most important young-player and draft-pick outcomes remain unresolved.

sections.heading: Syracuse Sold George King’s Rights to Cincinnati
sections.body: On August 15, 1957, the Syracuse Nationals sold the player rights to George King to the Cincinnati Royals. The current franchise labels are Philadelphia and Sacramento, but neither of those cities identifies the teams that actually completed the 1957 sale. King was an established NBA guard, not a newly drafted player: he had already helped Syracuse win the 1955 NBA championship. The Nationals received cash considerations, with no reliable amount identified in the transaction listings.

sections.heading: King Returned to the NBA as a Cincinnati Regular
sections.body: King had been away from NBA play during 1956–57 and resumed his career after Cincinnati acquired his rights. He played 63 games for the Royals in 1957–58, averaging approximately 9.7 points and 5.3 assists in 36.1 minutes. The minutes and playmaking make this more than a nominal rights acquisition. Cincinnati received a credible, experienced backcourt contributor for an otherwise uncertain cash payment.

sections.heading: The Nationals Collected Money but Lost Proven Talent
sections.body: Syracuse converted the rights of a former championship guard into cash. That is a valid form of consideration, especially for a franchise managing its finances, but a transaction ledger cannot establish its precise value without the payment amount. King’s 63 Cincinnati appearances are observable basketball production. No additional Syracuse player or draft asset came back in the identified sale, so its sporting return cannot be inflated through unrelated roster moves.

sections.heading: The Historical Outcome Supports Cincinnati’s Advantage
sections.body: The canonical grade is B-plus for the Royals and C for the Nationals, with Royals Win. Cincinnati took a previously productive player and received another substantial NBA season, whereas Syracuse’s financial return remains unquantified. This is not a story about the Rochester Royals buying a prospect: the 1957 club was in Cincinnati, King was a veteran, and the rights sale was recorded by the Syracuse and Cincinnati franchise transaction logs.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Royals Win — Cincinnati/Sacramento B-plus, Syracuse/Philadelphia C. The Royals bought George King’s rights and received 63 games of experienced guard play in 1957–58, including 5.3 assists per game. Syracuse took an undisclosed cash payment for a former championship contributor. The financial return cannot be measured from surviving sources, but the documented on-court result favors Cincinnati.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Swapped Veteran Center Red Kerr for Young Guard Wali Jones
sections.body: On September 22, 1965, the Philadelphia 76ers acquired Wali Jones from the Baltimore Bullets in exchange for Johnny “Red” Kerr. The contemporary franchise identity is important: Baltimore was the predecessor of today’s Washington Wizards, not a Washington-named club in 1965. The NBA league transaction ledger confirms the simple player-for-player deal with no draft choice or cash listed. Jones was coming off his 1964-65 rookie season with Baltimore, whereas Kerr was a respected veteran center who had spent the prior seasons with Syracuse and Philadelphia. The 76ers were reshaping their perimeter group around Wilt Chamberlain, Hal Greer and other core players; Baltimore received established rebounding and interior experience.

sections.heading: Jones Played All 80 Philadelphia Games in His First Year
sections.body: Jones gave the 76ers 80 regular-season appearances in 1965-66, averaging 9.0 points and 3.4 assists over 27.5 minutes a night. He was the younger backcourt contributor the team had sought. The following season he played 81 more Philadelphia games, scored 13.2 points and handed out 3.7 assists per game, giving him 161 appearances across just the first two seasons after this trade. These are receiving-team statistics rather than his pretrade Baltimore totals. The improvement in scoring and minutes coincided with the 1966-67 Sixers becoming one of the most accomplished teams in NBA history, though the addition of Jones alone did not cause their remarkable record.

sections.heading: His 1967 Finals Performances Were Direct Championship Contributions
sections.body: Philadelphia defeated the San Francisco Warriors in six games in the 1967 NBA Finals. Jones was on the court in all six and averaged 20.2 points and 5.3 assists in the series, including 30 points and eight assists in Game 1 and 27 points in the decisive Game 6. The league’s historical season review quotes Jones describing how the club had played as a unified team. Chamberlain, Greer, Chet Walker, Billy Cunningham and the rest of the rotation all played major roles. Still, Jones’s Finals scoring and consistent ballhandling are unusually clear direct value from a player acquired only two seasons earlier for a veteran nearing retirement.

sections.heading: Baltimore Received 71 Kerr Games and His Final Playing Season
sections.body: Kerr’s 1965-66 season for Baltimore consisted of 71 regular-season games, 11.0 points, 8.3 rebounds and 3.2 assists per game. Those numbers show a legitimate veteran center contribution, not an empty receiving-team return. However, it was also the final season of Kerr’s NBA playing career. The Bullets finished 38-42 and lost to the St. Louis Hawks in the first round of the playoffs, in which Kerr appeared three times. He then left active NBA playing duties. His successful subsequent coaching and broadcasting career, including being named NBA Coach of the Year for the expansion Chicago Bulls in 1966-67, should not be incorrectly counted as Baltimore playing production delivered by the September 1965 exchange.

sections.heading: The Value Gap Reflects Ages, Careers and Team-Specific Outcomes
sections.body: The protected verdict is 76ers Win with Philadelphia A+ and the historical Baltimore franchise mapped to Washington C. The difference follows from Jones playing 161 games in his first two 76ers seasons, growing into a major 1967 Finals contributor and continuing his NBA playing career, compared with Kerr’s 71 Baltimore appearances during his last season. Kerr was not a bad player and could still rebound and pass, but the clubs acquired opposite career timelines. Using the Wizards slug for the current franchise lineage must not lead the article to describe the contemporary Baltimore trade as if it involved a 1965 Washington team.

sections.heading: The 1967 Championship Needs Team Context
sections.body: The Sixers’ 1966-67 roster was anchored by Wilt Chamberlain and Hall of Fame-level contributors. The official team history credits a 68-13 regular-season record and the April 24 championship victory over San Francisco. Jones’s acquisition added an energetic guard and subsequent high-output Finals player; it was not the exclusive factor behind the championship. Philadelphia had already acquired Chamberlain in a separate 1965 transaction and developed a deep rotation under coach Alex Hannum. Recognizing those separate moves preserves the documented player-for-player Kerr trade without manufacturing extra assets or an implausible single-cause explanation for a historic NBA season.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The archived 76ers Win, Philadelphia A+ and Baltimore franchise C are preserved. Jones played 80 and 81 Philadelphia games in his first two seasons and scored 20.2 points per game in the 1967 NBA Finals. Kerr supplied 71 Baltimore games at 11.0 points and 8.3 rebounds before retiring as a player. Neither Jones’s contributions nor the full Philadelphia championship can be assessed accurately without recognizing the separate Chamberlain-led team context.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The 1965 Jones–Red Kerr Trade: Philadelphia’s 1967 Finals Guard
featuredDeepDive.intro: Philadelphia obtained Wali Jones from the Baltimore Bullets for veteran center Johnny “Red” Kerr on September 22, 1965. Jones played 80 and 81 Sixers games in his next two seasons and averaged 20.2 points during Philadelphia’s six-game victory in the 1967 NBA Finals. Kerr produced 71 Baltimore appearances before retiring from playing, later succeeding as a coach and broadcaster elsewhere. The saved 76ers Win, A+ Philadelphia and C for the Baltimore/Washington franchise should be assessed through those distinct on-court returns without treating future coaching achievements as Baltimore player production.

sections.heading: The NBA Ledger Records a Straight Jones-for-Kerr Exchange
sections.body: The September 22, 1965 transaction appears in the official historical league ledger as Baltimore sending Wali Jones to Philadelphia for Red Kerr. There was no future first-round pick or other participant in that archived agreement. The Washington Wizards is the modern name used for Baltimore’s franchise lineage in the canonical database, but the contemporary team was the Baltimore Bullets. Kerr had spent years with Syracuse and the relocated Philadelphia franchise; Jones had played his rookie season with Baltimore. Philadelphia exchanged the experienced center for a 23-year-old backcourt prospect, a choice that helped its roster become younger around existing stars rather than requiring both players to contribute to identical positions.

sections.heading: Jones Was a Philadelphia Guard Before the Championship Arrived
sections.body: Jones played all 80 Sixers regular-season games in 1965-66, averaged 9.0 points and passed for 3.4 assists. The next season he appeared in 81 games, averaging 13.2 points and 3.7 assists. Those two seasons amount to 161 Philadelphia games, while his earlier 77 Baltimore appearances are not to be included in the receiving-team total. Philadelphia’s 1966-67 record was a remarkable 68-13. Jones played in a system led by Wilt Chamberlain and Hal Greer, not a one-man offense. His continued availability and improved scoring made him a valuable guard before the playoffs gave his reputation a larger stage.

sections.heading: Six Finals Games Produced 20.2 Jones Points per Night
sections.body: In the 1967 championship series against San Francisco, Jones scored 30 points and recorded eight assists in Game 1, contributed 16 in Game 5 and delivered 27 in Game 6. His overall six-game Finals averages were 20.2 points and 5.3 assists. This is clear evidence of playoff value, not a projection based on his rookie reputation. Chamberlain anchored the team and Greer and Walker also scored heavily, while Billy Cunningham gave Philadelphia vital additional offense. The official NBA season recap notes Jones’s perspective on their unified play. The 1965 trade put him on that roster, but it did not directly purchase the entire championship from Baltimore.

sections.heading: Kerr’s Baltimore Season Was Useful but the Last of His Playing Career
sections.body: Johnny Kerr was not an obscure name. A three-time All-Star during earlier Syracuse seasons, he had years of experience rebounding and passing. In his lone 1965-66 Baltimore season he appeared 71 times, averaged 11.0 points and 8.3 rebounds and helped the Bullets compete for a playoff position. The club lost its Western Division semifinal to St. Louis in three games. Kerr subsequently became the first head coach of the expansion Chicago Bulls and won Coach of the Year in 1966-67. Those coaching honors are impressive career accomplishments but have no place in a count of games produced for the Bullets after a 1965 player trade.

sections.heading: The Franchise Name and Time Horizon Control the Grade
sections.body: The protected Sixers A+ and Baltimore franchise C compare a 23-year-old championship backcourt contributor to an older veteran in his last playing season. Kerr’s 71 games provide a fair counterweight to the positive Jones story; they do not equal the 161 first-two-year Philadelphia Jones appearances and 1967 Finals production. The Knicks, Bulls and later franchises did not participate in the original exchange. Furthermore, the database’s “washington-wizards” identifier refers to the historical Baltimore franchise, not to a team playing under that name in 1965. Respecting that identity boundary is essential to a historically credible trade retrospective.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Philadelphia A+, Baltimore franchise C and 76ers Win remain unchanged. Jones logged 161 Sixers games over 1965-67 and averaged 20.2 points during the 1967 Finals win. Kerr made 71 Baltimore appearances, contributing 11.0 points and 8.3 rebounds in his final NBA player season. His subsequent Bulls coaching award and the separate acquisition of Chamberlain should not be misrepresented as additional assets flowing through this particular September 1965 player exchange.

sections.heading: What Changed Hands
sections.body: On October 17, 1971, Philadelphia acquired Fred Carter and Kevin Loughery from the Baltimore Bullets. Baltimore took Archie Clark, a 1973 second-round draft choice later used at No. 19 for Louie Nelson, and cash of an unspecified amount. This was a two-player Philadelphia return against a veteran guard, a future pick and a financial payment. The Bullets were still based in Baltimore; their current Washington franchise name appears in the archive as a historical grouping rather than the team's 1971 identity.

sections.heading: How the Realized Value Separated
sections.body: Carter became the 76ers' lasting return. He averaged 20.0 points in 1972-73, 21.4 in 1973-74, 21.9 in 1974-75 and 18.9 in 1975-76, playing at least 77 games in each season. Loughery added 74 Philadelphia appearances in 1971-72 and another 32 the next year. Baltimore got a strong immediate player in Clark: 21.2 points and 6.7 assists over 76 games in 1971-72, along with All-Star and All-NBA Second Team recognition. Both sides earned real value before later trades altered their returns.

sections.heading: Reading the Team Grades
sections.body: Philadelphia ultimately converted Carter into another valuable draft chain. In December 1976 the 76ers sent him alone to Milwaukee for two second-round picks; the 1978 pick became Maurice Cheeks at No. 36. Cheeks eventually became a Hall of Fame point guard and a member of the 1983 Philadelphia championship team. The original October 1971 transaction didn't directly include Cheeks, but the separate Carter-for-two-picks trade is a traceable continuation. That documented chain helps explain the source-led Philadelphia A+ against Baltimore A-.

sections.heading: What Each Franchise Was Actually Evaluating
sections.body: Baltimore did not surrender Clark for nothing. The Bullets received 171 regular-season games from him before moving him in August 1974 for Dick Gibbs and a 1975 third-round selection. The 1973 pick from Philadelphia became Louie Nelson, who played 49 Capital Bullets games. Baltimore's unnamed cash consideration remains real but cannot be assigned an amount. Philadelphia's direct Carter scoring and Loughery's 106 appearances, plus the separate Carter-to-Cheeks chain, offer the stronger long-term return, even though Clark had an exceptional first Baltimore season.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win — Philadelphia A+, Baltimore A-. The 76ers obtained Fred Carter and Kevin Loughery, receiving repeated high-scoring Carter seasons and 106 games from Loughery. Carter later went to Milwaukee alone for two second-round picks, one used on Maurice Cheeks. Baltimore received Archie Clark, who made an All-Star and All-NBA Second Team season immediately, plus the later No. 19 Louie Nelson selection and cash. Both returns were productive; the documented long-term Carter and Cheeks pathway gives Philadelphia the stronger overall result.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Philadelphia 76ers–Washington Wizards: What the 1971-10-17 Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: The October 1971 76ers–Bullets trade had an outstanding guard on each side. Philadelphia took Fred Carter and Kevin Loughery; Baltimore obtained Archie Clark, a 1973 second-round pick and cash. Clark immediately earned All-Star and All-NBA Second Team recognition, while Carter became a multi-season 20-point scorer. Philadelphia's later deal of Carter for two draft picks led to Maurice Cheeks. The sourced historical assessment therefore grades the 76ers A+ and Baltimore A- rather than overlooking the real contribution Clark made.

sections.heading: The Asset Path That Carries the Grade
sections.body: The first agreement sent Carter and Loughery to Philadelphia on October 17, 1971, with Clark, the later No. 19 Louie Nelson selection and unspecified cash heading to Baltimore. At the time the second-round pick was future consideration, not Nelson already playing for the Bullets. The present Washington franchise identifier belongs to the same historical lineage, although the club's actual city in 1971 was Baltimore. Keeping the trade date, team identity and character of the draft asset distinct avoids folding 1973 personnel into the original transaction.

sections.heading: What the Lower-Graded Side Still Kept
sections.body: Fred Carter's Philadelphia tenure made the principal difference. After joining the 76ers he scored at least 18.9 points per game in four consecutive full seasons. Kevin Loughery's first year contributed 74 appearances and 932 points, followed by 32 appearances in 1972-73. Together they offered more than one great season from a single player. Carter's value continued when Philadelphia later traded him alone for two second-round choices. One of those, No. 36 in 1978, became Maurice Cheeks. The extra draft chain was not a free addition to this 1971 exchange; it was created by moving Carter again.

sections.heading: Decision Logic Versus Hindsight
sections.body: Archie Clark was the more decorated immediate performer in Baltimore. Across 76 games during 1971-72 he averaged 21.2 points and 6.7 assists, earned an All-Star berth and made All-NBA Second Team. He stayed productive for two more seasons, giving the franchise 171 games before an August 1974 transaction sent him out for Dick Gibbs and a third-round draft choice. Louie Nelson added 49 rookie games as the eventual No. 19 pick from this exchange. The unknown cash amount should be recorded without guessing at its value.

sections.heading: Why the Grade Gap Is the Better Scale
sections.body: The grade difference is Philadelphia A+ and the historical Bullets A-. Both clubs obtained guards who were productive after the move, but Philadelphia extracted several high-scoring Carter seasons and then a traceable pick leading to Cheeks, who helped the 76ers win the 1983 championship. Baltimore received the best immediate individual campaign from Clark and additional service from Nelson. This is a meaningful Philadelphia advantage over the full asset history, not a conclusion that Baltimore's trade was disastrous or that Cheeks was an original 1971 incoming player.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Philadelphia's A+ reflects Carter's sustained scoring and the later Carter-for-picks transaction that produced Maurice Cheeks, along with Loughery's 106 76ers appearances. The Bullets' A- recognizes Clark's excellent 1971-72 season, 171 Baltimore games, the 1973 Louie Nelson second-round selection and an unpriced cash component. Clark later yielded another player and pick, but Philadelphia's more durable sequence from Carter to Cheeks made the decisive difference. The deal occurred when the future Washington franchise played in Baltimore; both later asset chains are separately dated.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Sold Its Backup-Center Depth for a Distant Pick
sections.body: On November 4, 1983, Philadelphia sent reserve center Mark McNamara to San Antonio for a 1988 second-round selection. McNamara had backed up Moses Malone during the previous season, but the Spurs offered an immediate roster role rather than a future selection. The pick would not come due for almost five years. At the time, the Sixers were exchanging short-term big-man depth for an uncertain draft asset with a much longer payoff period.

sections.heading: The Spurs Received McNamara Minutes
sections.body: McNamara appeared in 82 regular-season games for San Antonio over parts of two seasons, including 70 appearances during 1983–84. His 1,037 minutes and 388 points in that first Spurs season show the immediate basketball return: not a top-line star, but a reserve center who could play. San Antonio therefore receives an appreciable B-minus rather than being assigned no value merely because the later Philadelphia draft path ended well. The Spurs got the veteran contribution they purchased.

sections.heading: The Pick Eventually Brought Ron Anderson to the Sixers
sections.body: Philadelphia’s future selection became No. 31 Everette Stephens in 1988. Before that season the 76ers traded Stephens to Indiana for Ron Anderson, a scorer who then played 393 games for Philadelphia across five seasons. Anderson averaged 16.2 points in his first Philadelphia season. That traceable downstream return explains the Sixers’ A-minus grade and overall victory: the 1983 McNamara transaction eventually produced much more sustained Philadelphia usefulness than McNamara’s shorter Spurs stay. The intermediary Stephens trade belongs explicitly in the audit trail.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win — Philadelphia A-minus, San Antonio B-minus. Mark McNamara supplied real Spurs center minutes, including 70 appearances in 1983–84. The second-round pick Philadelphia acquired eventually became Everette Stephens, who was traded to Indiana for Ron Anderson. Anderson’s 393 games as a Sixer gave Philadelphia the stronger sustained outcome.

sections.heading: Phoenix Acquired an MVP-Level Star Without Surrendering Its Core
sections.body: The Suns sent Jeff Hornacek, Tim Perry and Andrew Lang to Philadelphia for Charles Barkley in June 1992. Hornacek was an excellent guard and the best asset in the return, but Phoenix retained Kevin Johnson, Dan Majerle, Tom Chambers and the broader structure of a 50-win team. The deal therefore added a top-tier superstar to an established roster instead of exchanging one centerpiece for another. Phoenix accepted depth loss and fit risk in order to raise a good team's ceiling to championship level.

sections.heading: Barkley Delivered the Best Regular Season in Suns History Immediately
sections.body: In his first Phoenix season, Barkley averaged 25.6 points, 12.2 rebounds and 5.1 assists while winning the league MVP award. The Suns won 62 games, the best record in the NBA and a franchise record at the time. His rebounding and transition play accelerated an already potent offense, while his half-court creation gave Phoenix a direct answer when the perimeter attack stalled. The trade did not require a developmental waiting period. The incoming star produced the intended transformation in year one.

sections.heading: The 1993 Finals Run Was the Championship-Level Return Phoenix Purchased
sections.body: Barkley powered Phoenix through the Western Conference, including a series-clinching jumper against San Antonio and a 43-point triple-double against Seattle. The Suns then pushed Michael Jordan's Bulls to six games in the Finals. They did not win the title, but reaching that stage matters when grading a win-now blockbuster. Phoenix bought access to the championship round and received it immediately. Few trades can promise a title; the proper standard is whether the acquired star materially created a legitimate opportunity. Barkley did.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Received a Good Player but No New Franchise Direction
sections.body: Hornacek averaged more than 19 points in his first Philadelphia season and remained an efficient, versatile guard. Perry and Lang added frontcourt depth. This was not an empty package and should not remain an F. The problem was strategic. The 76ers did not receive a premium pick, a young star with Barkley's ceiling or an asset chain capable of anchoring the next era. Hornacek was traded again during his second season, and the team continued losing. Competent return without a rebuilding centerpiece supports C, not F.

sections.heading: Four Productive Barkley Seasons Extended the Value Beyond One Run
sections.body: Barkley's Phoenix tenure lasted four seasons and included three additional All-Star selections after the MVP year. Injuries and roster changes prevented another Finals appearance, but he continued to produce elite scoring and rebounding and kept the Suns relevant in the West. The trade was not a one-season rental that happened to peak. Phoenix received the star years it expected and later recovered additional value by trading Barkley to Houston. That downstream exit further separates the Suns' asset management from Philadelphia's return.

sections.heading: Barkley's MVP Season Defined Phoenix's Return; Hornacek Gave Philadelphia Value
sections.body: Phoenix kept its main competitive core and added Charles Barkley for Jeff Hornacek, Tim Perry and Andrew Lang. Barkley immediately averaged 25.6 points and 12.2 rebounds, earned league MVP honors and led a 62-win Suns team to the 1993 Finals. His four Phoenix seasons made the deal considerably more than a short rental. Philadelphia's package was not empty: Hornacek was an effective scoring and playmaking guard, and the frontcourt additions supplied usable minutes. The 76ers nevertheless lost a franchise-level player without receiving a comparable cornerstone or draft asset. Phoenix earns A+ for acquiring an MVP and a championship-level opportunity; Philadelphia's C recognizes Hornacek's legitimate contribution while reflecting the lost upside.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Phoenix wins with an A+, while Philadelphia rises to C. Barkley won MVP immediately, led the Suns to 62 wins and the 1993 Finals, and remained an All-Star throughout his four-year tenure. Hornacek was a high-quality player and prevents the 76ers' package from being treated as worthless, but neither he, Perry nor Lang became the centerpiece of a successful rebuild. Phoenix acquired championship access at a credible but decisively favorable price.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Charles Barkley Turned a Strong Suns Team Into the League’s Best Team Overnight
featuredDeepDive.intro: Phoenix's 1992 gamble worked because the organization understood the difference between depth and hierarchy. The Suns already possessed guards, shooting and regular-season competence. What they lacked was a player who could become the best force in a playoff series. Barkley supplied rebounding, transition power, playmaking and a fearless late-game personality. The trade cost a valuable guard in Hornacek, but it changed who opponents had to solve first. That is the defining purpose of a successful superstar acquisition.

sections.heading: The Suns Chose Ceiling Over Comfortable Continuity
sections.body: Phoenix had won 53 games in 1991-92 and could have kept a balanced, familiar roster. Trading Hornacek disrupted that continuity because he handled, shot and defended multiple guard positions. The front office correctly recognized that another competent season was not the objective. Barkley offered an MVP ceiling and a matchup that could bend playoff defenses. The transaction illustrates why contenders sometimes need to exchange several good pieces for one great player: depth can preserve a floor, but singular creation raises the ceiling.

sections.heading: Barkley’s Playmaking Fit the Existing Perimeter Talent
sections.body: Although Barkley was known for scoring and rebounding, his passing made the Phoenix fit especially powerful. When defenses collapsed on him, Johnson and Majerle could attack space or shoot. In transition, Barkley could rebound and initiate without waiting for an outlet. His presence did not simply add his own points; it changed the quality of possessions for the entire lineup. That broad impact explains how Phoenix jumped to the league's best record rather than merely replacing Hornacek's production with a larger individual total.

sections.heading: The 1993 Postseason Validated the Risk Under Maximum Pressure
sections.body: Phoenix survived an opening-round scare against the Lakers, then eliminated San Antonio and Seattle before meeting Chicago. Barkley delivered defining performances throughout the run, including the Western Conference finals triple-double. Jordan's Bulls ultimately won, but the Suns forced a competitive six-game series and came within possessions of extending it. A title-or-failure framing would erase the actual value created. The trade gave Phoenix its clearest championship opportunity of the era, which is precisely what an A+ win-now move should accomplish.

sections.heading: Hornacek’s Quality Makes Philadelphia’s Failure Strategic, Not Personal
sections.body: Hornacek was not a throw-in. He was an All-Star before the trade, averaged 19.1 points in his first Sixers season and later became a crucial member of Utah's Finals teams. Philadelphia's problem was not that he lacked ability; it was that his age and role did not match the need for a new franchise foundation. Perry and Lang were rotation frontcourt players, not premium upside bets. The Sixers collected usable talent but failed to convert Barkley's departure into a coherent rebuilding timeline.

sections.heading: Phoenix Also Preserved Exit Value When the Window Closed
sections.body: After four seasons, the Suns traded Barkley to Houston for a multi-player package rather than losing him for nothing. The later deal did not match his Phoenix impact, but it demonstrates that the 1992 acquisition retained transaction value beyond the Finals run. Philadelphia had already moved Hornacek in a separate deal and never built a successful core from the original return. When both the competitive peak and downstream asset management favor Phoenix, the Suns Win verdict becomes even more secure.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Barkley trade is a model of a strong team correctly paying for a higher ceiling. Phoenix received the 1993 MVP, a league-best 62-win season and an immediate Finals appearance while keeping the players needed to support him. Philadelphia received a very good guard and useful depth, warranting C rather than F, but no cornerstone or premium future asset. The Suns' A+ reflects realized championship contention, not merely the prestige of acquiring a famous player.

sections.heading: The February 1994 Exchange Was Built Around Hornacek and a First
sections.body: On February 24, 1994, Utah sent Jeff Malone and a protected 1994 first-round selection to Philadelphia for Jeff Hornacek, Sean Green and a future second-round right. The Jazz wanted an efficient veteran shooter who could play beside John Stockton and Karl Malone while the 76ers added a veteran scorer and a higher draft slot. The incoming 1994 pick conveyed at No. 20, and Philadelphia used it on B.J. Tyler. The later second would become No. 33 in 1995, but Utah moved that right to Boston before it was exercised. This original trade was not decided by which of the two drafted prospects went on to score more NBA points. Hornacek's seven Utah seasons were the defining on-court return, while the draft choices gave each club separate opportunities.

sections.heading: Hornacek Played 477 Jazz Games and Reached Two NBA Finals
sections.body: Hornacek arrived in Salt Lake City for 27 regular-season games in 1993-94, then stayed with Utah through 1999-2000. His subsequent season counts were 81, 82, 82, 80, 48 and 77, bringing the total to 477 Jazz regular-season appearances after the February trade. He averaged 16.5 points in 1994-95 and hit 40.6 percent of his three-pointers, giving John Stockton and Karl Malone a reliable outside shooting partner. Hornacek was an important starter on Utah's 1997 and 1998 NBA Finals teams, both of which lost to Michael Jordan's Chicago Bulls. Those appearances are direct evidence that the club obtained more than a temporary reserve. The return was anchored in Hornacek's continued Jazz playing time rather than a later second-round pick that never reached Utah's roster.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Got Seventy-One Jeff Malone Games and Fifty-Five From Tyler
sections.body: Jeff Malone gave the 76ers 27 regular-season appearances after the February 1994 trade, averaging 16.8 points. He added 19 games in 1994-95 and 25 in 1995-96 before finishing that season with Miami, for 71 Philadelphia appearances. The No. 20 first-round right became B.J. Tyler, who played 55 Sixers games in 1994-95 and averaged 3.5 points with 3.2 assists. Tyler's NBA career ended after that rookie campaign. Those are two real Philadelphia returns: a short veteran-scoring stint and an ultimately disappointing first-round guard. They should not be written as zero playing production merely because Utah gained a more durable starter. Conversely, Malone's high-scoring years with Washington and Utah occurred before Philadelphia acquired him, and Tyler's college reputation cannot be substituted for his actual single NBA season.

sections.heading: Junior Burrough Was Drafted by Boston, Not Utah
sections.body: The 1995 second-round pick Philadelphia sent to Utah was later attached to No. 33 Junior Burrough. On February 3, 1995, however, the Jazz included that pick and Jay Humphries in a separate trade to the Boston Celtics for Blue Edwards. Boston subsequently exercised the No. 33 choice on Burrough, who played 61 NBA regular-season games for the Celtics in 1995-96. Those games were not Utah Jazz production. The pick retained trade value for Utah because it contributed to acquiring Edwards, but that deal also included Humphries as another outgoing player. Describing Burrough as the dominant Jazz return would therefore be a serious asset-attribution error. Even the direction of the original trade's result is decided primarily by Hornacek's sustained Utah career, not the later Boston draft selection.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Jazz Win — Utah A+, Philadelphia D. Hornacek played 477 Utah regular-season games after February 1994 and contributed to both Jazz NBA Finals appearances. The Sixers obtained 71 Jeff Malone games and 55 B.J. Tyler games. Utah moved the 1995 second in a separate February 1995 trade with Jay Humphries for Blue Edwards; Boston subsequently drafted Junior Burrough at No.33. Burrough was never a Jazz player.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Jeff Hornacek to Utah in 1994: The Jazz Finals Core and Boston Draft-Pick Chain
featuredDeepDive.intro: Philadelphia swapped Hornacek, Sean Green and a 1995 second for Jeff Malone and a 1994 No.20 first. Hornacek became an integral Jazz guard; Utah later sent the future No.33 pick to Boston before Burrough was drafted.

sections.heading: Hornacek Was an Immediate Fit for the Stockton-Malone Core
sections.body: The Utah Jazz were already built around Karl Malone and John Stockton when they acquired Hornacek in February 1994. He could shoot efficiently without taking primary creation responsibilities away from the two stars and would continue to help space the floor through two NBA Finals appearances. His first Utah stretch produced 27 games and 14.6 points per contest; he averaged 16.5 in his first complete Jazz season. The trade fit both the current contender and the following years of roster continuity. Moving away from Jeff Malone, who had been scoring in double figures, was a real decision rather than acquiring a player for nothing. Hornacek's eventual 477 Utah regular-season games after the exchange and postseason role make a stronger case for the club's inherited A-plus grade than any later draft right could provide.

sections.heading: Philadelphia's Two Assets Were More Limited Than Hornacek
sections.body: The 76ers obtained Jeff Malone, an established scorer who averaged 16.8 points over 27 games immediately after the move, along with a protected first that became No. 20 B.J. Tyler. Malone played 71 Philadelphia games across parts of three seasons. Tyler appeared in 55 regular-season games and never had a second NBA campaign. The outcomes provided brief scoring and a look at a rookie point guard, but neither supplied the sustained stability that Hornacek gave Utah. That explains the broad Jazz advantage without claiming Philadelphia received no basketball minutes. Tyler's 3.2 assists per game showed that the selection became a real reserve, even though his career was short. The Sixers' inherited D grade reflects weak longevity and opportunity cost from moving a reliable two-way veteran, not a total absence of initial production.

sections.heading: The Boston Pick Transfer Separates Rights From NBA Minutes
sections.body: Utah's other incoming asset was a 1995 second-round selection originating with Philadelphia. The Jazz used it in a February 3, 1995 transaction alongside Jay Humphries to acquire Blue Edwards from Boston. The Celtics then selected Junior Burrough at No. 33 in the June draft, and he logged 61 NBA appearances for Boston. None of those games were logged as a Utah player. It would also be improper to attribute all of Edwards's Jazz time to the 1994 Hornacek transaction because Humphries was material additional outgoing consideration. The pick was real, and the ability to send it in a later negotiation was a legitimate return, but the grade must follow ownership at each step. Using Burrough's Boston career as the decisive Jazz value would hide both the separate 1995 trade and Hornacek's actual achievements.

sections.heading: Utah A-Plus Versus Philadelphia D Follows the Players
sections.body: The preserved result is Jazz Win, Utah A-plus and Philadelphia D. Hornacek gave Utah 477 regular-season games from February 1994 through his 2000 retirement and helped the Jazz reach the 1997 and 1998 NBA Finals. Philadelphia received 71 games from Jeff Malone and 55 from B.J. Tyler, its No. 20 selection. Utah also obtained a second-round right and later moved it with Humphries to Boston for Blue Edwards; Boston, not Utah, drafted Junior Burrough. Sean Green, the other incoming player in the original deal, was waived by Utah on March 6, 1994. These documented outcomes strongly favor the Jazz without inventing a standout contribution from Burrough or pretending the 76ers got no playing production. Correct attribution is far more persuasive than generic winner language.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Utah A-plus, Philadelphia D in the preserved Jazz Win. Hornacek supplied seven Jazz seasons and 477 games, Philadelphia used Jeff Malone for 71 games and No.20 B.J. Tyler for 55. The 1995 No.33 pick was traded from Utah to Boston in a separate Jay Humphries/Blue Edwards move, so Burrough playing for Boston is not a Jazz return.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Acquired the No. 29 Draft Rights for a Future First
sections.body: On June 24, 1998, Philadelphia obtained the NBA draft rights to Kentucky center Nazr Mohammed after Utah selected him 29th overall. The 76ers sent a future first-round pick with protections that declined over several seasons, rather than an established veteran from their 1997-98 rotation. The choice ultimately conveyed in 1999 at No. 19 and Utah selected Quincy Lewis. The exchange was a bet on different draft years: Philadelphia wanted a young center it could bring into the league immediately, while Utah accepted future draft capital during a period when Karl Malone and John Stockton kept it competitive. At the time, neither team knew the exact 1999 pick position or Mohammed's later 18-season NBA career. Rights to an untested rookie and a protected future first were the entire original package.

sections.heading: Mohammed Played Eighty-Four Philadelphia Games
sections.body: Mohammed's direct Philadelphia production was modest. He appeared in 26 regular-season games during the 1998-99 lockout season, 28 in 1999-2000 and 30 before a February trade in 2000-01. That totals 84 Sixers appearances with six starts. He averaged 1.6 points as a rookie and 1.9 the next year, remaining a developmental reserve behind older frontcourt players. His full NBA career eventually reached 1,005 games, including a 2005 championship with San Antonio, but those later team accomplishments are not direct Philadelphia games. The 1998 rights still gave the 76ers ownership of a real young center who could be used on court and included in another negotiation. An A grade for Philadelphia needs to recognize the limited first tenure rather than claim that all 18 professional seasons happened in a Sixers uniform.

sections.heading: Mohammed Entered the 2001 Mutombo Trade as One of Four Outgoing Players
sections.body: On February 22, 2001, Philadelphia sent Mohammed, Theo Ratliff, Toni Kukoc and Pepe Sanchez to Atlanta for Dikembe Mutombo and Roshown McLeod. The NBA's own deadline history and a contemporary UPI report confirm all six players. Mutombo then helped the 76ers reach the NBA Finals that year, but it would be wrong to credit his entire acquisition to the 1998 Utah draft-rights transaction. Ratliff was an All-Star center, and the package also contained Kukoc and Sanchez. Mohammed's inclusion nevertheless shows that his rights and contract had retained tradeable value beyond 84 regular-season Philadelphia appearances. The later agreement was separately negotiated and included additional important outgoing players. This chain supports some front-office optionality from the original acquisition without inventing a direct one-for-one Mohammed-for-Mutombo exchange.

sections.heading: Utah Used the No. 19 Pick on Quincy Lewis
sections.body: The protected Philadelphia first conveyed in 1999 at No. 19, which Utah used on Minnesota forward Quincy Lewis. Lewis played 74 regular-season Jazz games in 1999-2000, 35 in 2000-01 and 36 in 2001-02, giving Utah 145 appearances and 21 starts. His offensive role was modest and he never became the long-term wing successor Utah might have hoped to find, but the pick did yield NBA minutes. He later played for Minnesota, whose games do not add to the Jazz return. The inherited Utah D grade can fairly criticize a first-round choice that did not develop into an established starter; it cannot say Lewis never played. The original protected pick had become a real roster player, not an expired conditional draft right.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win — Philadelphia A, Utah D in the preserved editorial. Mohammed played only 84 Philadelphia games, while Utah used the 1999 No.19 protected first on Quincy Lewis, who logged 145 Jazz games. In February 2001 the 76ers packaged Mohammed with Ratliff, Kukoc and Sanchez in a separate deal for Mutombo and McLeod. Mohammed later played 1,005 career NBA games, mostly elsewhere, not directly for Philadelphia.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Nazr Mohammed in the 1998 76ers-Jazz Pick Swap: Quincy Lewis and Mutombo
featuredDeepDive.intro: Philadelphia acquired Nazr Mohammed rights from Utah for a future protected first, which became Quincy Lewis at No.19 in 1999. The Sixers got 84 Mohammed games before using him in a separate six-player Mutombo trade.

sections.heading: A Draft-Year Swap Rather Than an Immediate Veteran Exchange
sections.body: Philadelphia's 1998 arrangement with Utah traded certainty about one draft class for flexibility in another. The Jazz held the late first-round choice that became Nazr Mohammed at No. 29. The Sixers surrendered a future protected first, which conveyed the following summer at No. 19. The draft positions are important because Utah ultimately received a selection ten slots earlier, though one year later, than the pick it originally used. No rookie's career was predetermined at the time, and neither front office was exchanging an existing star. Philadelphia wanted a developmental center while building around Allen Iverson, and Utah wanted future flexibility to maintain its established contender. The value calculation should begin with those dates and pick numbers rather than leap straight to Mohammed's eventual championship elsewhere. The only immediate incoming Philadelphia asset was his draft right.

sections.heading: Philadelphia's Playing Return Was Eighty-Four Games
sections.body: Mohammed logged 26 regular-season games for the Sixers in 1998-99, 28 the next season and 30 before the February 2001 deadline. His 84 Philadelphia appearances included just six starts, so the original rights trade did not itself install a long-term first-string center. At the same time, those games were legitimate NBA contributions, and Mohammed's combination of size and development potential made his contract useful in later roster construction. The following eighteen-year career proves he developed into a durable professional, but nearly all of that court time came for other clubs. When evaluating a transaction, those later teams should receive their own production credit. Philadelphia's inherited A is best defended partly by the contract's contribution to a later package rather than by attaching the entire 1,005-game career to the initial Sixers selection.

sections.heading: The Mutombo Trade Had Three Other Important Pieces
sections.body: In February 2001 the Sixers sent Mohammed to Atlanta with Ratliff, Kukoc and Sanchez, receiving Mutombo and McLeod. Mutombo was a major defensive acquisition during Philadelphia's Eastern Conference championship season. Mohammed was a component of that transaction, and retaining him for more than two years made him available for the package. However, Ratliff's All-Star status and Kukoc's experience were separate forms of outgoing value; the exchange was not a straightforward extension of the 1998 Utah deal. Claiming that Philadelphia obtained Mutombo directly for the pick that became Quincy Lewis would badly distort the price. The accurate sequence is that the original Nazr right became a developmental 76ers center, then one of four players transferred in a second major agreement. This supports a bounded hindsight argument without stealing value from unrelated players.

sections.heading: The Utah D Should Not Erase Lewis's 145 Games
sections.body: The site records a 76ers Win with Philadelphia A and Utah D, but the team-specific playing returns complicate that wide grade gap. Utah used the 1999 No. 19 selection on Lewis and played him in 145 regular-season games, while Mohammed played 84 for Philadelphia before being included in another trade. Lewis did not become a long-term Jazz starting wing, so Utah's draft selection fell short of the hopes attached to a first-rounder. Philadelphia's upside came from the future center's tradeability and a later multi-player move, not from a clear advantage in immediate games. It is reasonable to favor Philadelphia as an editorial judgment if those rights were instrumental to later roster plans, but the accompanying copy must disclose both players' actual team-specific totals. A more precise trade history is stronger than an automatic winner label based on Mohammed's complete 18-season NBA career.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Philadelphia A, Utah D is the inherited 76ers Win, but a fair accounting gives Utah 145 Lewis games and Philadelphia 84 Mohammed games. Mohammed later contributed as one of four outgoing players to the 2001 Mutombo deal, with major separate additional consideration. Neither full career longevity nor the entire Mutombo return belongs to the original 1998 pick-rights trade.
