sections.heading: Chris Webber, Matt Barnes and Michael Bradley / Kenny Thomas, Brian Skinner and Corliss Williamson: The Deal’s Actual Shape
sections.body: Philadelphia acquired Chris Webber, Matt Barnes and Michael Bradley from Sacramento for Kenny Thomas, Brian Skinner and Corliss Williamson at the 2005 deadline. The 76ers wanted a second high-level scorer beside Allen Iverson and were willing to accept Webber’s large contract and reduced mobility after major knee surgery. Sacramento was dismantling the core that had contended in the early 2000s and sought a deeper group of frontcourt players with different contract structures. The trade moved the biggest name to Philadelphia, but neither team received a clean long-term centerpiece. The evaluation depends on Webber’s remaining production, the cost of his contract and the useful but limited years Sacramento received from the three-player package. Philadelphia pursued Webber's remaining scoring beside Iverson, while Sacramento chose Thomas, Skinner and Williamson as shorter-term frontcourt depth after deciding Webber's post-surgery contract was too risky to carry.

sections.heading: Chris Webber, Matt Barnes and Michael Bradley / Kenny Thomas, Brian Skinner and Corliss Williamson: The Winning Team’s Case
sections.body: Webber was no longer the explosive Sacramento superstar, but he still produced at a high level. He helped Philadelphia reach the 2005 playoffs after the deadline and averaged roughly twenty points and ten rebounds during his full 2005-06 season. His passing gave the offense another organizer, and his shooting allowed Iverson more room than a traditional low-post big might have provided. Philadelphia also received Barnes, who later built a long career even though the Sixers did not retain him. The direct return therefore contained the best player and the highest peak. That supports a positive grade, but the short control and contract cost keep the result below A territory. The winning case depends on role, control and competitive translation, not reputation alone; the return had to create identifiable value in the acquiring team’s actual system.

sections.heading: Chris Webber, Matt Barnes and Michael Bradley / Kenny Thomas, Brian Skinner and Corliss Williamson: The Return Package Deserves a Fair Reading
sections.body: Sacramento received three established forwards and centers rather than draft uncertainty. Thomas became a regular starter, Williamson provided scoring and familiarity, and Skinner offered defense and rebounding. The package helped the Kings continue competing after moving a franchise icon whose knee and contract created risk. The limitation was upside. None of the incoming players became a star, and Thomas’s contract eventually became difficult. Sacramento spread the return across depth but did not create a new core piece or a valuable draft chain. C+ reflects several useful seasons and a rational transition while acknowledging that the Kings gave up the most talented player and did not fully solve their long-term reset. A losing grade can remain positive when the outgoing side received real rotation seasons, draft control or later trade value, even though the head-to-head result favored the other team.

sections.heading: Chris Webber, Matt Barnes and Michael Bradley / Kenny Thomas, Brian Skinner and Corliss Williamson: Leverage and Timing Changed the Price
sections.body: Webber’s medical history and salary shaped the market. Sacramento could not price him as though he were still the fully mobile MVP candidate of 2001, while Philadelphia could not assume his contract would age well. The Sixers were also operating under pressure to maximize Iverson’s remaining prime and make the postseason immediately. Sacramento had begun changing direction after years of contention and needed to manage both basketball and financial risk. The trade looks less dramatic when viewed through those constraints. Philadelphia did not acquire peak Webber, and Sacramento did not trade a healthy superstar for role players. Each side accepted a different version of decline risk. Sacramento's price reflected Webber's knee history and salary, and Philadelphia's urgency to help Iverson helps explain the 2005 move even though the acquired forward's stay ended in a 2007 buyout.

sections.heading: Chris Webber, Matt Barnes and Michael Bradley / Kenny Thomas, Brian Skinner and Corliss Williamson: Asset Conversion and Opportunity Cost
sections.body: The asset chain was relatively short. Webber gave Philadelphia immediate scoring and rebounding but was bought out in 2007, limiting long-term control. Barnes was waived quickly and became valuable elsewhere rather than for the Sixers. Michael Bradley added little. Sacramento received several seasons from Thomas and shorter contributions from Williamson and Skinner, but the group did not generate a major downstream return. Because neither side converted the deal into a lasting asset chain, the head-to-head player comparison carries more weight. Webber’s production was still the best outcome, yet the Sixers failed to maximize the secondary pieces or extend his value beyond a brief window. Every major asset is followed through its direct production and any clear downstream transaction, while speculative choices that were never made are excluded from the trade details.

sections.heading: Chris Webber, Matt Barnes and Michael Bradley / Kenny Thomas, Brian Skinner and Corliss Williamson: Verdict and grading scale
sections.body: Slight 76ers Edge remains more accurate than a decisive win or an even verdict. Philadelphia drops from B+ to B because Webber’s contract, knee limitations and early buyout prevented the transaction from producing sustained contention. Sacramento rises from C to C+ because Thomas, Williamson and Skinner gave the Kings real rotation depth during a difficult transition. The Sixers still receive the stronger grade because they acquired the only player who performed near an All-Star statistical level after the trade. The narrow gap reflects that Philadelphia’s upside was meaningful but short, while Sacramento’s floor was useful but ordinary. The verdict names the side with the stronger completed return, while the grades preserve nuance about price, leverage and whether the losing team still achieved a legitimate objective.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Philadelphia holds a slight edge because Chris Webber remained the best player in the deal and delivered a productive season beside Allen Iverson. Sacramento received useful frontcourt depth and earns C+, but neither the package nor its downstream value matched Webber’s remaining peak.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Chris Webber Added Scoring, but Sacramento Got Years of Rotation Depth
featuredDeepDive.intro: The February 23, 2005 trade exchanged Chris Webber, Matt Barnes and Michael Bradley for Kenny Thomas, Brian Skinner and Corliss Williamson. Philadelphia wanted Webber's scoring beside Allen Iverson, while Sacramento sought depth and flexibility after his knee injuries. These sections examine the Sixers' 2005 playoff push and Webber's 2007 buyout against the actual rotation years the Kings received, without adding draft picks or crediting players to later clubs.

sections.heading: Six Players Crossed the Line at the 2005 Deadline
sections.body: Philadelphia acquired Chris Webber, Matt Barnes and Michael Bradley from Sacramento on February 23, 2005. The 76ers transferred Kenny Thomas, Brian Skinner and Corliss Williamson in return, with no draft selection among the documented six-player package. ESPN reported the transaction as Philadelphia sought a second scoring option next to Allen Iverson. Webber was still a talented passer and scorer, but his previous knee injuries and large contract shaped the price of the deal. Sacramento had begun to move away from the core that challenged for Western Conference titles earlier in the decade and could use a deeper frontcourt rotation. The original exchange cannot be accurately reviewed as though the Kings sent only Webber or the 76ers received only the recognizable star.

sections.heading: Webber Delivered Scoring Without His Sacramento Mobility
sections.body: Webber supplied a meaningful but limited Philadelphia return. He helped the 76ers reach the 2005 playoffs shortly after the February acquisition, then produced roughly twenty points and ten rebounds per game over the full 2005-06 season beside Iverson. He could still make passes from the high post and serve as a second offensive option, even though the explosiveness that characterized his Sacramento prime had faded after knee surgery. Philadelphia missed the 2006 playoffs despite his individual statistical production. That combination supports the inherited B grade: the Sixers acquired a productive forward, not a total contract failure, but they did not build another deep postseason run around him. His later NBA seasons after Philadelphia are not part of the Sixers' direct return.

sections.heading: Sacramento Received Useful Rotation Depth Rather Than a New Star
sections.body: The Kings received three veteran forwards and centers rather than future draft rights. Kenny Thomas became a regular frontcourt contributor over multiple Sacramento seasons; Brian Skinner offered rebounding and interior defense, while Corliss Williamson returned as a familiar scoring forward. Each had a different role, and none became the replacement franchise star for Webber. The group helped Sacramento preserve usable depth after shedding a costly veteran with medical concerns. The team reached the 2005 and 2006 playoffs, but those appearances were broader franchise results, not postseason victories produced entirely by one trade. The inherited Sacramento C-plus reflects real playing contributions without overstating a return that lacked Webber's remaining offensive ceiling. The three players should be evaluated as three assets, not compressed into one undefined salary package.

sections.heading: The Short Philadelphia Tenure Limited the Higher Grade
sections.body: Webber was not retained for an extended Philadelphia rebuild. After the 2005 playoff appearance and a strong statistical 2005-06 season, the club bought out his contract in 2007. That early departure limited how many years of productive forward play the 76ers obtained from their highest-profile incoming asset. Barnes departed quickly and developed a longer NBA career elsewhere; those later games should not be reassigned to Philadelphia. Michael Bradley was a smaller supporting element of the transaction. Sacramento similarly did not turn its three veteran acquisitions into a new long-lived star. The records therefore show a pair of imperfect returns, rather than a blockbuster whose individual names all developed equally. Philadelphia's short-term peak is the main advantage, while the Kings captured more distributed but lower-ceiling playing time.

sections.heading: A Narrow Philadelphia Victory With No Invented Pick Chain
sections.body: The canonical verdict is 76ers Win, Philadelphia B against Sacramento C-plus. Webber contributed the best individual post-trade season in Philadelphia and helped the team make the 2005 postseason with Iverson. The Kings received Kenny Thomas, Skinner and Williamson as genuine rotation options, so their side cannot fairly be called a zero return. Yet none matched even Webber's diminished ability to score and facilitate from the frontcourt. No first-round pick or extra cash payment belongs in the February 23 asset list, and Barnes' later success for other clubs is not a Sixers benefit. Philadelphia's slight grade advantage recognizes the stronger single player over a shorter window, while the Kings' positive C-plus recognizes the useful but non-transformative rotation package.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win — Philadelphia B, Sacramento C-plus. Webber remained a productive Philadelphia scorer and passer alongside Iverson, contributing to the 2005 postseason and posting a strong 2005-06 season before his 2007 contract buyout. Sacramento received three usable veterans, led by Kenny Thomas, but no comparable individual offensive return. The gap is narrow because neither team gained a long-term contender centerpiece from the six-player exchange.

sections.heading: Korver Moved to Utah for Giriček and a Protected First
sections.body: On December 29, 2007, Philadelphia traded Kyle Korver to Utah for Gordan Giriček and a future protected first-round draft pick. Utah's own historical transaction guide identifies the later outcome as the No. 23 choice in 2010, ultimately associated with Trevor Booker. The deal did not exchange Booker as an existing player, and the pick was not a second-round selection. At the time, the 76ers wanted cap flexibility; the Jazz wanted an outside shooter to complement a roster led by Deron Williams and Carlos Boozer. The transaction ledger also attaches contingent cash language to the pick conditions. That conditional amount should not be turned into a separate verified cash transfer without an original settlement record.

sections.heading: The Sixers' Salary-Cap Plan Was Explicit on Trade Day
sections.body: Philadelphia's president Ed Stefanski described the move as part of a summer 2008 salary-cap strategy. Giriček was earning roughly $4 million on an expiring deal, while Korver still had approximately $15.4 million owed after 2007-08. Reporting from the Philadelphia Inquirer on December 29 quoted Stefanski expecting approximately $10 million of cap space the following summer. The Sixers were not expecting Giriček to reproduce all of Korver's future shooting; they were paying a present-day rotation price for payroll flexibility and draft consideration. This trade-date rationale matters when judging intent, but cap space is an opportunity rather than proof that any later specific free-agent signing directly resulted from this transaction.

sections.heading: Utah Received Three Seasons of Proven Perimeter Spacing
sections.body: Korver made 50 regular-season appearances for the Jazz after the 2007 trade, producing 9.8 points per game and shooting 38.8 percent from three in that stretch. He followed with 78 Utah appearances in 2008-09. In 2009-10, he shot a remarkable 59-for-110 from three, or 53.6 percent, across 52 regular-season games. The latter is a small enough number of attempts to warrant precision, not a claim that every long-range shot was automatic. Still, that sustained rotation work gave Utah an authentic perimeter threat through multiple playoff seasons. His production in this first Utah tenure is the direct advantage associated with acquiring him in December 2007.

sections.heading: Giriček's Philadelphia Stint Ended Before March 2008
sections.body: Philadelphia received only a brief spell of on-court play from Giriček. Basketball-Reference records 12 Sixers games after the December 2007 move, with no starts, 37 total points and an average of about 3.1 points. The club waived him on February 29, 2008, and Phoenix publicly announced signing him on March 4. That sequence is more precise than suggesting he never played for Philadelphia or lasted the full season there. It also shows why the veteran did not compensate for the shooter the Sixers surrendered. The remaining draft right and the planned salary flexibility were the portions of Philadelphia's return with a plausible life beyond those few appearances.

sections.heading: The First-Round Pick Moved Again Before Booker Was Drafted
sections.body: The protected selection did not become a Philadelphia draftee. The Timberwolves announced July 9, 2008 that they had acquired Utah's future first-round pick from Philadelphia. The 76ers also sent Rodney Carney, Calvin Booth and cash to Minnesota for a conditional future second-round pick that did not convey. Utah's original choice eventually landed at No. 23 in the 2010 first round and was used on Trevor Booker. The 2010 second-round nonconveyance belongs to Philadelphia's separate 2008 transaction and must not be mistaken for what the Jazz originally sent in the Korver trade. Booking Booker's later NBA seasons as a direct 76ers return would similarly confuse the asset path.

sections.heading: The D and B-Plus Grades Reflect a Realized Utah Advantage
sections.body: The Jazz Win verdict grades Utah B-plus and Philadelphia D. Utah received 180 regular-season appearances from Kyle Korver in his first stint, with 53.6 percent three-point shooting in 2009-10; the Jazz also reached the postseason in each of those seasons. Philadelphia obtained only 12 games from Gordan Giriček and an initially protected first-round selection, then sent that Utah draft right to Minnesota in a separate July 2008 transaction. Minnesota eventually held the No. 23 choice used to select Trevor Booker in the 2010 first round, not the second; Booker never arrived in Philadelphia through the original Korver exchange. The Sixers sought salary-cap flexibility and draft value, but their direct playing return was small beside Korver's sustained Utah contribution. That contrast supports the existing grades without attributing Minnesota's later selection or other separate transactions to Philadelphia's roster.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Jazz Win is the preserved outcome, Philadelphia D and Utah B-plus. The Jazz acquired Korver and received useful perimeter play for three seasons, including 59-for-110 three-point shooting in 2009-10. Philadelphia received Giriček, who played 12 games before a February 2008 waiver, and Utah's protected first. The Sixers traded that first to Minnesota in July 2008; it eventually conveyed at No. 23 in the 2010 first round and is associated with Trevor Booker. It did not become an original second-round asset, and Booker never played for Philadelphia as a consequence of this swap.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Korver to Utah: The Protected First That Philadelphia Traded Again
featuredDeepDive.intro: Philadelphia's December 2007 Korver deal was partly about securing summer salary flexibility. Utah sent Gordan Giriček and a protected first-round choice, which would ultimately convey at No. 23 in 2010. The Sixers moved that pick to Minnesota in July 2008 rather than drafting Trevor Booker themselves. Korver, meanwhile, played three seasons for Utah and shot 53.6 percent from three in 2009-10. Separating the actual first-round pick from a later conditional second-round nonconveyance corrects an error in the previous editorial and makes the inherited Jazz Win result easier to evaluate.

sections.heading: The Conditions Belonged to a First-Round Selection
sections.body: The record contains unusually detailed protection terms beginning with the 2009 draft and extending through later seasons. Those terms protected Utah against surrendering certain high choices, while leaving Philadelphia an eventual first-round opportunity if the conditions were met. Official Utah history confirms the decisive endpoint: a 2010 No. 23 first-round pick tied to Trevor Booker. The stale editorial had incorrectly said the first turned into a second-round asset. That was a conflation with the separate conditional second Philadelphia later received from Minnesota in July 2008, a pick that did not convey. Proper accounting tracks the 2007 first, its 2008 onward trade, and its eventual 2010 conveyance as successive events.

sections.heading: Stefanski Made a Deliberate Short-Term Salary Tradeoff
sections.body: The Sixers' intention was publicly described on the transaction date. They moved a valued three-point specialist who remained under contract for multiple future seasons, received a guard on an expiring deal and anticipated more payroll freedom by summer 2008. Giriček's salary was about $4 million for 2007-08, whereas the remaining Korver commitment extended beyond the season. Philadelphia also acquired draft consideration, which gave the front office another asset to deploy. The trade made sense as part of cap planning even if it ultimately failed to retain equivalent playing talent. The later July 2008 pick trade was part of a different cap-clearing sequence and should be explicitly dated rather than folded into the first transaction.

sections.heading: Korver's 2009-10 Shooting Stands on Verifiable Attempts
sections.body: Korver appeared in 52 Utah regular-season games in 2009-10, making 59 of 110 three-point tries. That 53.6-percent accuracy is a concrete, historic shooting result in the final season of his first Jazz tenure. The figure should be presented alongside the modest attempts and 18.3 minutes per game rather than as proof he functioned as a 30-point first option. Utah had acquired a perimeter role player who could punish space created by teammates. His earlier 50 Jazz appearances after the 2007 trade and 78 during 2008-09 reinforce that the value was not merely one short hot streak. The relevant outcome is three seasons of spacing and rotations from the player Utah received.

sections.heading: The Sixers Did Not Keep the Future Booker Draft Right
sections.body: A history that says Philadelphia selected Trevor Booker from this trade is false. Minnesota's July 9, 2008 announcement independently verifies taking Utah's future first from the Sixers, and the 76ers' executive transaction chronology identifies Calvin Booth, Rodney Carney and cash in that next exchange. Minnesota sent back a protected second-round pick that never conveyed. The Jazz's original pick later fell at No. 23 in 2010. If assessing broader franchise strategy, the future first can be credited as a tool Philadelphia possessed for roughly six months. It cannot be credited as years of Booker's playing production with Philadelphia, which never happened. The separate 2008 deal deserves its own ledger for any downstream consequences.

sections.heading: Final Accounting Separates First Trade, Next Trade and Later Careers
sections.body: The original grading relationship is Philadelphia D, Utah B-plus, Jazz Win. Utah converted one expiring-guard-and-pick package into Korver's actual games and three-point shooting; Philadelphia accepted a short Giriček stint, a future protected first and cap room potential. One-half year later Philadelphia transferred the first to Minnesota. Two years after the Korver deal, the pick conveyed as a first-round No. 23 choice associated with Booker. These steps are chronologically related but not interchangeable. The written verdict should neither dismiss Giriček's twelve appearances nor pretend the conditional second from Minnesota was sent by Utah in December 2007. Correcting both factual errors makes the Jazz advantage intelligible without silently adjusting original grades.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The canonical Jazz Win verdict and Philadelphia D versus Utah B-plus stay unchanged. Korver was the primary basketball return to Utah, where his first stint included 50 games after the trade, 78 in 2008-09 and 52 in 2009-10, when he made 59 of 110 threes. Philadelphia used Giriček for 12 games before waiving him February 29, 2008. Its incoming protected pick was a genuine first-round right, eventually No. 23 in 2010, but Philadelphia sent the right to Minnesota in a separate July 9, 2008 cap-related transaction. That second exchange involved a conditional second-round pick that did not convey. The earlier analysis wrongly applied second-round language to the Jazz's initial first-round obligation. Historical grade interpretation can favor Utah without inventing a Sixers Booker career, an unstated cash transfer, or a contradictory asset chain.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Wanted Shooting, Toronto Wanted Rebounding
sections.body: On June 9, 2009, Philadelphia traded Reggie Evans to Toronto for Jason Kapono. Kapono was known for perimeter shooting, giving the 76ers a specialist whose role differed from Evans’s physical rebounding and interior work. Toronto was trying to add a defensive-minded rebounder as its roster evolved around Chris Bosh. There was no reported draft selection or third club in this exchange. Each side was swapping a specific bench skill for a different one, not bidding on a future star.

sections.heading: Evans Played a Rebounding Role Across Two Toronto Seasons
sections.body: Evans appeared in 28 Raptors games in 2009–10 and 30 more in 2010–11. His first season was limited, but his 2010–11 rebounding role became more pronounced. Across those 30 games he collected 345 rebounds, including 226 on the defensive glass. That is measurable production from a player acquired primarily to rebound and bring frontcourt physicality. Injuries and the small number of appearances limit how much credit Toronto should receive; the trade did not supply a full-time starter for an entire season.

sections.heading: Kapono Gave the Sixers an Offense-First Alternative
sections.body: Philadelphia received a designated shooter capable of spacing the court, an area in which Evans was not comparable. That made the acquisition intelligible even if Kapono was more limited as a defender and rebounder. The distinction is about the type of on-court contribution, not whether one player had a more familiar name. The team traded away a rebounding specialist in hopes that three-point shooting would better complement its perimeter and interior scorers.

sections.heading: The Retrospective Grades Favor Toronto’s Specific Return
sections.body: The canonical ledger assigns Toronto B-plus and Philadelphia C-plus, naming the Raptors as the winner. Evans supplied rebounds and physical frontcourt minutes during a two-season Toronto stint; Kapono was a more specialized piece for the Sixers. The difference should not be amplified into a claim that Evans started every game or single-handedly lifted Toronto into contention. Both players were supporting pieces, and the grade advantage attaches to how the rebounding asset worked out rather than a fabricated future draft return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Raptors Win — Toronto B-plus, Philadelphia C-plus. Toronto received Reggie Evans and obtained a rebounding specialist for 58 games across 2009–11, including 345 rebounds in 2010–11. Philadelphia acquired Jason Kapono for its outside-shooting role. Both teams secured a specific roster skill, but the recorded grades favor Evans’s physical frontcourt contribution over Kapono’s more limited overall fit.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Exchanged an Expiring Center for Two Different Frontcourt Options
sections.body: Philadelphia announced an agreement on June 17, 2010 to send Samuel Dalembert to Sacramento for Spencer Hawes and Andres Nocioni. The Inquirer quoted general manager Ed Stefanski describing the incoming players as additional frontcourt depth, with Hawes a young seven-footer and Nocioni the veteran forward. Hawes was 22 after three Kings seasons; Nocioni, 30, offered another rotation option but also had guaranteed salary beyond the immediate season. Philadelphia had been shopping Dalembert, whose 2009-10 contract was expiring the following summer. The transaction is an exchange of one center for two roster players, not a draft-pick swap and not a direct acquisition of Sacramento’s later No. 5 selection.

sections.heading: Spencer Hawes Supplied 253 Philadelphia Regular-Season Games
sections.body: Hawes appeared in 81 Sixers games in 2010-11, starting all of them and averaging 7.2 points and 5.7 rebounds. He followed with 37 appearances and 29 starts during the shortened 2011-12 season, then 82 games and 40 starts in 2012-13 at 11.0 points and 7.2 rebounds. In 2013-14, he played 53 Philadelphia games before a February trade to Cleveland, scoring 13.0 points and collecting 8.5 rebounds per outing. Those four team-specific segments add up to 253 regular-season Philadelphia appearances and 203 starts. His later 27 Cavaliers games in that final season and his subsequent teams are not attributable as 76ers production.

sections.heading: Nocioni Offered 65 Appearances Before His Philadelphia Exit
sections.body: Nocioni played 54 Sixers games in 2010-11, starting 17 while averaging 6.1 points and 3.1 rebounds. His role contracted sharply the following season: just 11 appearances, one start and 1.5 points in 5.1 minutes per game. That equals 65 regular-season appearances with 18 starts for Philadelphia across two seasons. The difference between Nocioni’s roster presence and Hawes’s 253 games helps explain why the retrospective values the young center as the main continuing return. The forward’s guaranteed contract should not be mistaken for additional production, nor should his earlier Chicago and Sacramento totals be folded into the Sixers ledger.

sections.heading: Sacramento Received 80 Games of Dalembert Rim Protection
sections.body: Sacramento acquired Dalembert for the 2010-11 season, during which he appeared in 80 Kings games and started 46. The Rockets’ later official signing release gives his Sacramento averages as 8.1 points, 8.2 rebounds and a team-high 1.45 blocks, totaling 116 blocks. Those are substantial one-season defensive numbers; calling the Kings’ entire return useless would misrepresent it. However, Dalembert left for Houston before the 2011-12 season. The saved 76ers Win verdict and Philadelphia A versus Sacramento C+ assess four seasons of Hawes appearances plus Nocioni minutes against the Kings’ single year of shot blocking and the financial considerations of an expiring veteran contract.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win is retained, with Philadelphia A and Sacramento C+. Hawes supplied 253 Philadelphia regular-season games and 203 starts across four segments through February 2014; Nocioni added 65 games before leaving. Dalembert produced 80 Kings games, 46 starts and 116 blocks in 2010-11, then moved elsewhere. The June 17 announcement is well documented, while some historical transaction ledgers use June 19 or 20 for processing; the protected canonical date is not silently changed.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Dalembert for Hawes and Nocioni: Philadelphia’s Longer 2010 Return
featuredDeepDive.intro: The 2010 Sixers-Kings trade sent Samuel Dalembert to Sacramento for Spencer Hawes and Andres Nocioni. Dalembert provided one Kings season of rim protection, logging 80 games and 116 blocks. Hawes played 253 Philadelphia games over four regular-season segments, and Nocioni added 65. The private archive’s 76ers Win and Philadelphia A/Sacramento C+ verdict follows these receiving-team outcomes, separating Hawes’s later Cleveland minutes and Dalembert’s Houston career from the teams that actually received them in 2010.

sections.heading: June 17 Was the Public Announcement; Ledgers Differ on Completion
sections.body: The June 17 contemporaneous Philadelphia Inquirer report and Sports Illustrated announcement both identify the same deal: Dalembert from Philadelphia to Sacramento, Hawes and Nocioni in return. The Inquirer explicitly says the trade was pending physicals. RealGM records the transaction on June 17, matching the protected archive date. A subsequent Houston Rockets retrospective dates Dalembert’s move June 19; Basketball Reference lists June 20. These differences may concern announcement, clearance and database posting dates. The asset chain is consistent, but the archive’s recorded June 17 should be described as the public agreement date, not falsely claimed as a unanimously reported legal processing date.

sections.heading: Hawes Delivered a Four-Season Philadelphia Window
sections.body: Hawes was not a scoring star when acquired, yet his NBA record shows continuing usefulness. He made 81 starts for Philadelphia in 2010-11, played 37 games in 2011-12, appeared in all 82 in 2012-13 and logged another 53 Sixers games before the February 2014 Cleveland trade. Those 253 total Philadelphia appearances included 203 starts. His scoring grew from 7.2 points a game in 2010-11 to 11.0 in 2012-13 and 13.0 in the 2013-14 Sixers portion. This is direct receiving-franchise production, unlike Cleveland, Clippers or later team games that occurred under different contracts and transactions.

sections.heading: Nocioni’s Veteran Depth Was Real but Brief
sections.body: Philadelphia’s frontcourt acquisition was two players, not one. Nocioni supplied 54 games in 2010-11 at 6.1 points with 17 starts. He was seldom used in 2011-12, appearing in 11 games and starting only once. The 65-game total is smaller than any complete Hawes season other than the lockout-shortened year, but it still represents real NBA court time. His salary commitment made the package more complex than a pure young-player-for-expiring-center exchange. It is appropriate to note that cost without manufacturing a cap-savings total unsupported by the archived record.

sections.heading: Sacramento Had a One-Year Center and a Separate Draft Plan
sections.body: Dalembert was not absent or injured for most of his Sacramento tenure; the Kings played him in 80 games in 2010-11, with 46 starts, 8.2 rebounds and 1.45 blocks a night. The Rockets’ own later announcement calls his 116 blocks a team high. Sacramento’s June 2010 No. 5 draft selection of DeMarcus Cousins was a distinct draft decision, not an asset sent in this deal. Dalembert left as a free agent for Houston after the season. The Kings bought immediate defense and preserved longer-term options, but Hawes’s 253 Philadelphia games provide the firmer realized player value across the entire receiving-team horizon.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The historical 76ers Win, Philadelphia A and Sacramento C+ verdicts are unchanged. Hawes made 253 Sixers regular-season appearances; Nocioni had 65. Dalembert supplied 80 Kings games and 116 blocks before leaving. The June 17 announced agreement appears as June 19 or 20 in some later transaction sources, a provenance nuance noted separately without altering protected date or asset records. No games by Dalembert in Houston or Hawes in Cleveland are credited to the original receiving teams.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Took Three Contracts and Three Draft Rights
sections.body: In July 2015, Sacramento sent Nik Stauskas, Jason Thompson and Carl Landry to Philadelphia along with options to swap first-round selections in 2016 and 2017 and a separate conditional future first. Sacramento received the draft rights to Arturas Gudaitis and Luka Mitrovic. The Kings' contemporary roster-building motivation was to shed veteran salary and pursue players in free agency, while Philadelphia could absorb the contracts and receive future leverage. The structure is easy to misread: the Sixers obtained three player contracts, two swap options and another future pick, not an immediate haul of three incoming draft selections. The two draft-rights players headed to Sacramento were also not the same as acquiring active NBA rotation contributors.

sections.heading: The 2016 Swap Expired, but 2017 Changed the Draft Order
sections.body: Philadelphia's option to swap 2016 firsts with Sacramento was not exercised. In 2017, the Sixers used the other swap, taking the No. 3 position while Sacramento ended up at No. 5. The Kings selected De'Aaron Fox fifth. Philadelphia did not ultimately select a player with No. 3 because it made a separate June 2017 trade with Boston, exchanging that slot and future protected pick rights for the No. 1 choice. Boston selected Jayson Tatum at No. 3; the Sixers selected Markelle Fultz at No. 1. The distinction matters: the 2015 swap produced a higher draft position for Philadelphia, but Tatum was chosen by Boston following another agreement, not acquired directly from Sacramento in 2015.

sections.heading: Sacramento's Future First Eventually Became No. 14
sections.body: The additional Sacramento first-round pick was protected in 2018 and unprotected in 2019 under the original deal. Boston's June 19, 2017 official release specifies that its separate agreement with Philadelphia could deliver the Kings' 2019 first, subject to alternative Lakers and Sixers pick conditions and a No. 1 exception. Those conditions eventually placed the 2019 No. 14 selection with Boston. The Celtics drafted Romeo Langford, as the NBA's completed 2019 draft list confirms. It would be false to call Langford a 2015 Sixers draftee or pretend the original agreement was a player-for-Langford exchange. Philadelphia received a future contractual right, then conveyed that right through another transaction.

sections.heading: Why Sacramento Accepted the Salary-Clearing Cost
sections.body: Sacramento was not seeking immediate production from the two international draft-rights assets received. Its objective was roster flexibility after moving Stauskas, Thompson and Landry, and contemporary NBA reporting links the cap-space calculation to a pursuit of veteran point guard Rajon Rondo. Rondo signed with Sacramento for one season; his signing was a separate free-agent agreement rather than part of Philadelphia's trade consideration. The eventual 2017 swap and 2019 conveyed first made the cost clearer with hindsight. Still, evaluating Sacramento's 2015 decision requires recognizing the intended financial flexibility as well as the future opportunities surrendered, rather than claiming the club simply forgot to obtain a return.

sections.heading: The 2017 Boston Deal Must Remain a Separate Ledger
sections.body: Boston's official 2017 announcement confirms the Celtics sent their No. 1 choice to Philadelphia for No. 3 and conditional future first-round rights. The Sixers used No. 1 on Fultz, and Boston took Tatum third. The future choice that eventually became Boston's No. 14 Langford selection came through the pick conditions documented in that 2017 deal. Both the 2017 and 2019 outcomes illuminate what Philadelphia controlled because of the 2015 agreement, but neither changes which teams transacted on July 9, 2015. Crediting the original Kings package directly with both Fultz and Tatum would double-count downstream moves; crediting Sacramento with Langford would misidentify ownership. The correct account follows each right through its separate trade date.

sections.heading: Preserving the Published Philadelphia Win Without Inflating It
sections.body: The archive grades Philadelphia A-plus and Sacramento D, with a 76ers Win verdict. That judgment has a source-specific basis: the Sixers exchanged two draft-rights players for three contracts, a 2017 swap that improved their position and a protected pick later conveyed to Boston. Sacramento obtained salary flexibility but lost future choice control. The 2016 swap produced no change, so treating it as a valuable realized player would exaggerate the haul. Philadelphia also moved the 2017 No. 3 choice and the 2019 rights rather than keeping their eventual draftees. These later transactions help assess the options' value, but a systematic grading review should not attribute downstream players to the wrong trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Recorded verdict: 76ers Win — Philadelphia A+, Sacramento D. Philadelphia acquired Stauskas, Thompson, Landry, unexercised 2016 swap, exercised 2017 No. 3-for-No. 5 swap and a Kings future first that eventually became Boston's 2019 No. 14 pick. Sacramento received the Gudaitis and Mitrovic draft rights and gained payroll flexibility. Fultz, Tatum and Langford came through separate later draft or trade decisions; none was directly exchanged in July 2015.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Sold a Backup Center Contract for Cash
sections.body: On July 20, 2018, Philadelphia sent Richaun Holmes to Phoenix in exchange for cash considerations. Both clubs published announcements naming the player and the direction of the payment. The league transaction log specifies $1 million; the official releases do not independently give that figure. Holmes had been a 2015 second-round selection for Philadelphia and had averaged 6.5 points and 4.4 rebounds across 48 Sixers appearances in 2017-18. Phoenix wanted athletic frontcourt depth, while Philadelphia opened room in a rotation that already included Joel Embiid and Amir Johnson. The same day, the Sixers signed Jonah Bolden, but Bolden did not arrive from Phoenix as part of this transaction.

sections.heading: Holmes Supplied 70 Phoenix Games at Efficient Shooting
sections.body: The newly acquired center played 70 Suns regular-season games in 2018-19, starting four. He averaged 8.2 points, 4.7 rebounds and 1.1 blocks in 16.9 minutes, making 60.8 percent of his field-goal attempts. Those are meaningful reserve-center contributions for a team that exchanged cash rather than a draft pick or rotation player. His 70 appearances should be separated from his earlier 156 Philadelphia games, which Phoenix did not receive. Holmes signed with Sacramento the next summer, so subsequent higher-scoring Kings seasons are not a continuation of his Phoenix playing production. The proper direct return is a useful single Suns season, not all of Holmes’s eventual career.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Received Money and Created Roster Flexibility
sections.body: Philadelphia received no Suns player in return for Holmes. The $1 million amount reported in the historical league transaction ledger was a financial receipt, not a first-round pick or additional acquired prospect. Contemporary Philadelphia coverage tied the decision to creating a roster slot for former overseas draft-and-stash forward Jonah Bolden, whom the Sixers then signed separately. Treating Bolden as if Phoenix traded him would invent an asset. Philadelphia did gain room to make that other signing while concentrating its center minutes elsewhere, but the exact long-term financial benefit cannot be derived solely from the $1 million sale price. The transaction’s basketball and contract outcomes should therefore be evaluated separately.

sections.heading: Why One Season of Holmes Outweighed the Cash Return
sections.body: The Suns Win verdict grades Phoenix A-minus and Philadelphia D-plus. The two clubs' original July 20, 2018 announcements confirm a direct one-player-for-cash transaction: Phoenix acquired Richaun Holmes; the 76ers received cash considerations, not a replacement center or draft pick. Holmes then played 70 Suns games in 2018-19, averaging 8.2 points, 4.7 rebounds and 1.1 blocks with 60.8 percent shooting. That was a productive single season for a reserve center; his later Sacramento performances belong to a separate contract and team. Philadelphia gained the financial consideration and freed a roster spot, but its separately signed Jonah Bolden was not received from Phoenix. The original NBA club announcements don't specify the dollar amount, although transaction reporting places it at about $1 million. The sharper Phoenix grade reflects measured NBA production, while the Sixers' return consisted chiefly of cash and roster flexibility.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Suns Win, Phoenix A- and Philadelphia D+ remain the original judgment. Holmes supplied 70 Suns games, four starts, 8.2 points and 4.7 rebounds on 60.8 percent shooting in 2018-19. The Sixers received $1 million in cash according to the transaction ledger and separately signed Jonah Bolden. His later Kings seasons are not Phoenix production, and Bolden was not acquired from Phoenix.

featuredDeepDive.intro: Phoenix acquired Richaun Holmes from Philadelphia for cash on July 20, 2018. The historical NBA transaction ledger quantifies the payment at $1 million. Holmes produced 70 Suns appearances and 8.2 points per game in his only Phoenix season, while Philadelphia managed its roster and signed Jonah Bolden in a separate move. The inherited Suns Win with Phoenix A- and Philadelphia D+ follows the direct player-versus-cash return, not the center’s later Sacramento career.

sections.heading: The Two Clubs Agreed on One Player and Cash Only
sections.body: Phoenix’s July 20 release states that it completed a deal with Philadelphia to acquire forward-center Richaun Holmes for cash. Philadelphia’s own same-day statement confirms that the 76ers transferred Holmes’s contract and received financial consideration. The transaction ledger provides the $1 million dollar amount absent from those releases. Phoenix simultaneously completed a separate Brooklyn trade involving Jared Dudley and Darrell Arthur; those contracts and a future protected second-round pick had nothing to do with Holmes. Keeping both transactions distinct matters because the Suns press release reported them together. No player from the Nets trade or draft selection was part of what Philadelphia received for Holmes.

sections.heading: Holmes Delivered Tangible Minutes but Only One Suns Season
sections.body: The Suns’ 2018-19 player statistics give Holmes 70 games, four starts and 1,183 minutes. His per-game averages were 8.2 points, 4.7 rebounds and 1.1 blocks with 60.8 percent field-goal accuracy. Those outcomes are the clearest measurable Phoenix return. He had played 156 regular-season games for the Sixers over his first three NBA seasons, but those pretrade appearances are not Phoenix contributions. Nor should his subsequent Sacramento campaign, when he averaged 12.3 points in 2019-20, increase the tally for a different franchise. A productive one-season bench center is enough to justify considering the Phoenix side favorable without treating Holmes as a multi-year Suns cornerstone.

sections.heading: The Sixers Made a Separate Bolden Signing
sections.body: Philadelphia’s frontcourt had Embiid, Amir Johnson and other rotation options entering 2018-19. Reporting at the time connected the Holmes departure with space for Jonah Bolden, another 2015 second-round pick returning from international play. The Sixers signed Bolden on July 25, five days after the Holmes cash agreement. Neither club said that Bolden’s rights came from the Suns. The reported $1 million payment was the asset acquired directly, while roster flexibility was an organizational motive and consequence. Assigning all of Bolden’s future minutes as a Phoenix-transferred player would misrepresent the transaction. It is possible to acknowledge the roster choice and still conclude that Philadelphia did not receive a direct basketball player in exchange.

sections.heading: One Cash Receipt Versus 70 NBA Games Defines the Grade Difference
sections.body: The original Suns A- and 76ers D+ grades express an evaluation of the exchanged assets, not a promise about future standings. Phoenix bought a reserve center for cash and got 70 appearances, reasonable interior defense and a 60.8 percent shooting season. Philadelphia received a cash payment and a usable roster opening, then exercised a separate signing. The center left Phoenix after the season, which caps the direct return. Philadelphia’s later postseason outcomes arose from numerous players and transactions rather than this one contract sale. The evidence supports maintaining Suns Win while explaining why a modest financial benefit can be valued differently from seventy games of real player production.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Phoenix A-, Philadelphia D+ and Suns Win remain unchanged. Holmes delivered 70 Suns appearances, four starts and 8.2 points a game before leaving for Sacramento in a separate offseason decision. The Sixers received $1 million and independently signed Jonah Bolden after the roster move. No player or pick came from Phoenix to Philadelphia beyond the contracted cash consideration.

sections.heading: What the Exchange Actually Produced
sections.body: Phoenix obtained Phil Lumpkin from Portland on June 9, 1975, sending the Trail Blazers a 1976 second-round pick. The selection ultimately became No. 26, used on Jacky Dorsey, but Portland did not draft Dorsey: the Blazers exchanged that pick for a 1977 second-rounder before the 1976 draft. That distinction changes how the two returns should be judged. Phoenix got an actual reserve guard for the next season; Portland acquired a draft asset that it later converted.

sections.heading: Why Phoenix Earned the Marginal Hindsight Edge
sections.body: Lumpkin appeared in 34 regular-season games for Phoenix during 1975–76 and another 17 postseason games as the Suns reached the NBA Finals. His role was limited, averaging 10.9 minutes and 2.1 points in the regular season, so the Finals appearance cannot be credited to him as a starring achievement. Still, those appearances are direct playing value obtained from a traded second-rounder, rather than a hypothetical future option.

sections.heading: The Phoenix Suns Side's Completed Value
sections.body: Portland used the original No. 26 selection as an asset instead of spending it on Dorsey. On June 3, 1976, the Blazers sent the pick to New Orleans for a 1977 second-round choice, later No. 28 Kim Anderson. Anderson did not play in the NBA during 1977–78 but later supplied 21 appearances for Portland in 1978–79. Crediting Dorsey's career to the Trail Blazers would wrongly ignore their intervening deal.

sections.heading: The Portland Trail Blazers' Completed Value
sections.body: The Suns' return ended after one season when Lumpkin was waived in October 1976, and Portland eventually obtained 21 NBA games from Anderson after converting its draft selection. These were modest outcomes rather than franchise-defining acquisitions. Phoenix nevertheless received 34 regular-season games plus 17 playoff appearances during a Finals campaign, supporting Suns Win and a B+ versus Portland's C+.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Suns Win, B+ Phoenix and C+ Portland. Lumpkin supplied 34 regular-season games and 17 playoff appearances during the 1975–76 Suns season, without being a major contributor. Portland converted the incoming No. 26 pick into a later second-rounder used on Kim Anderson, who eventually played 21 games for the Blazers. Dorsey was selected by New Orleans and should not be treated as Portland's player.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Phil Lumpkin's Phoenix Games and Portland's Transferred No. 26 Pick
featuredDeepDive.intro: The June 1975 trade sent Phil Lumpkin to Phoenix for Portland's incoming 1976 second-round selection. Lumpkin appeared in 34 Suns games and all 17 playoff games during the team's run to the NBA Finals, albeit as a reserve. Portland traded that original pick onward before it was used on Jacky Dorsey, receiving a later selection that became Kim Anderson. Anderson ultimately played 21 games for the Blazers. The actual paths support a limited Suns advantage.

sections.heading: What Each Team Actually Received
sections.body: Both the Phoenix and Portland transaction histories place the initial exchange on June 9, 1975. Portland sent Phil Lumpkin to Phoenix, taking a second-round pick in the 1976 draft. The selection was later used at No. 26 on Jacky Dorsey, but by draft day it belonged to the New Orleans Jazz. Following that ownership change is essential; simply attaching Dorsey's subsequent career to Portland would invent roster value that the club never received.

sections.heading: What Phoenix Suns Realized
sections.body: Lumpkin joined a Phoenix group that advanced to the 1976 NBA Finals. He appeared in 34 regular-season games at just over ten minutes per night, and he played in 17 playoff games with an average of roughly eight minutes. Phoenix received legitimate reserve availability, not a central playoff contributor. His time with the Suns ended when the club waived him in October 1976, limiting direct value to that 1975–76 season.

sections.heading: What Portland Trail Blazers Realized
sections.body: The Trail Blazers did not wait to see who would be available at No. 26. Instead, in June 1976 they traded the pick to New Orleans for the Jazz's 1977 second-rounder. New Orleans selected Jacky Dorsey. Portland's replacement asset became No. 28 Kim Anderson, whose eventual NBA record with the Blazers consisted of 21 games in 1978–79. The intervening selection and subsequent reserve stint are the credible Portland return.

sections.heading: Suns B+ Versus Portland C+: A Modest, Documented Difference
sections.body: The gap is not enormous: Lumpkin was a minor part of a Finals team, and Anderson's later Portland contribution was also limited. The Phoenix side gains the edge because Lumpkin appeared in 34 regular-season contests and 17 postseason games during his only Suns season. Portland successfully preserved draft flexibility but converted it into just 21 appearances two seasons later. Suns Win with Phoenix B+ and Portland C+ reflects those measured results rather than counting the entire 1976 Finals run or Dorsey's career.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Suns Win, Phoenix B+ / Portland C+. Phoenix received tangible reserve minutes from Phil Lumpkin during a Finals season, then waived him the following fall. Portland's initial 1976 second-rounder went to New Orleans, and its replacement 1977 pick produced 21 Portland games from Kim Anderson. Both returns had limits, but Lumpkin's immediate appearances and postseason availability justify the slight Phoenix advantage over an equivalent-grade tie.

sections.heading: What Changed Hands
sections.body: On June 26, 2003, San Antonio selected Leandro Barbosa at No. 28 and sent his draft rights to Phoenix. The Spurs received a future Suns first-round selection with protection terms: top 25 in 2004 and top 21 from 2005 through 2009. The choice ultimately conveyed as No. 30 in 2005, associated with David Lee. Phoenix acquired the right to sign the Brazilian guard immediately. San Antonio chose delayed first-round consideration instead of keeping the player it had just selected.

sections.heading: How the Realized Value Separated
sections.body: Barbosa gave Phoenix a long-term guard whose speed and bench scoring became important to its playoff rotations. He later earned Sixth Man of the Year honors. The future first-rounder was a real asset for San Antonio, but evaluating it requires tracing its next transaction. Before the 2005 draft, the Spurs sent the selection to New York in the Nazr Mohammed–Malik Rose deal. Lee was then drafted by the Knicks at No. 30. His later All-Star career belongs to the Knicks' use of that selection, not a claim that Lee appeared for San Antonio.

sections.heading: Reading the Team Grades
sections.body: The archive grades Phoenix B+ and San Antonio C-, with a Suns Win verdict. Phoenix turned its one incoming right into many seasons of Barbosa's production. San Antonio obtained a protected first-round asset and later used it in a different trade, so its return cannot be reduced either to nothing or to David Lee's full career as a Spurs player. The grade comparison centers on Barbosa's realized Suns contribution against the value of a future selection that the Spurs eventually redeployed.

sections.heading: How Each Team Viewed the Trade
sections.body: Phoenix accepted a draft-night bet on Barbosa's development, using a protected future first-rounder to acquire him. San Antonio was willing to let the No. 28 prospect go for a choice that could be exercised later. That distinction also explains the gap between the franchises' trade-day logic and the final verdict: the Suns realized substantial on-court value directly from the acquired rights, while the Spurs' pick passed into another transaction before Lee entered the league.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Suns Win — Phoenix B+, San Antonio C-. The Suns obtained Leandro Barbosa's draft rights and gained his speed, scoring, and Sixth Man of the Year contribution. The Spurs received a protected future first-round choice that became No. 30 in 2005, but they moved it onward before New York selected David Lee. The later pick pathway is real value and deserves proper attribution, not a fictional Spurs tenure for Lee.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Phoenix Suns–San Antonio Spurs: What the 2003-06-26 Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: The June 2003 Barbosa exchange is a draft-rights trade with a long downstream paper trail. San Antonio selected the Brazilian guard at No. 28, but Phoenix secured his rights by surrendering a protected future first-round pick. The selection ultimately became No. 30 in 2005, a pick the Spurs had already sent to New York. Separating those two paths is essential: Barbosa's Suns career is a direct outcome; David Lee's Knicks career is evidence of what the eventual selection produced after a subsequent trade.

sections.heading: Barbosa Draft Rights Cost Phoenix a Protected First That Conveyed in 2005
sections.body: The precise asset sequence starts with San Antonio drafting Barbosa at No. 28 in 2003 and transferring his rights to Phoenix. The Suns surrendered one protected future first-round choice rather than a player under contract. Protection initially shielded the top 25 in 2004, then the top 21 in subsequent years. The pick ultimately became No. 30 in 2005. Those dates explain why the nominal 2004 pick in the original terms appears with a 2005 draft result in the historical asset ledger.

sections.heading: What the Other Side Still Received
sections.body: Phoenix put Barbosa on an NBA roster and benefited from the quick guard's scoring over an extended run. San Antonio took the future selection, then dealt it onward in February 2005 as part of the package involving Nazr Mohammed, Malik Rose, another first-round pick, and cash. By draft night the Knicks controlled the No. 30 choice used on David Lee. Crediting Lee's subsequent Knicks career directly to San Antonio would skip an essential step and misstate which club acquired his playing rights.

sections.heading: Decision Logic Versus Hindsight
sections.body: The Spurs' position in June 2003 was an option on a later draft, while the Suns chose to develop Barbosa. Those were fundamentally different assets with different time horizons. The downstream New York transaction should be discussed to establish provenance, but its entire package cannot be assigned backward to this single Barbosa trade. San Antonio combined this pick with other consideration when it changed direction; Phoenix's Barbosa return can be traced directly to the draft rights received from the Spurs.

sections.heading: Why the Grade Gap Matters
sections.body: The B+ grade for Phoenix reflects the sustained usefulness of Barbosa's role and his award-winning sixth-man production. San Antonio's C- should acknowledge that a first-round selection was obtained and subsequently traded, not imply that it retained Lee or failed to receive consideration. A Suns Win is a plausible retrospective conclusion when the two asset paths are kept distinct. Its strength comes from the real Phoenix tenure, rather than from generic arguments about draft uncertainty or the franchises' unrelated championships.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Phoenix B+, San Antonio C-; Suns Win. Barbosa's lengthy Suns contribution is directly traceable to the 2003 draft-night rights acquisition. San Antonio received a future first-round selection, then used it as part of a separate deal with New York before David Lee was chosen. The verdict considers those distinct histories without transferring another team's later player production back to this one transaction.

sections.heading: November 2003: Washington Chose Cap Flexibility over Its Longest-Tenured Center
sections.body: On November 5, 2003, Washington exchanged center Jahidi White for Phoenix point guard Brevin Knight. The contemporaneous Washington Post report quoted basketball executive Ernie Grunfeld explaining that the deal provided salary flexibility and another guard option. Knight was in the final season of a roughly $5 million deal, while White had two years and more than $11 million left on his contract. The Wizards had added Gilbert Arenas earlier that summer and also rostered Steve Blake, Juan Dixon and Larry Hughes. Phoenix, in contrast, took on White to add an experienced physical interior player. The original agreement was a straight one-for-one transaction without a protected draft pick or cash payment listed.

sections.heading: Jahidi White Logged 61 Suns Games and 17 Starts
sections.body: White had appeared in one Washington game earlier in the 2003-04 season before changing teams. With Phoenix he played 61 regular-season games and started 17, averaging 4.3 points and 4.3 rebounds in 14.1 minutes per appearance. He blocked 0.8 shots per game and shot 52.4 percent from the field, useful evidence of a reserve center who could provide interior minutes. However, White did not sustain a long Phoenix tenure after that season. He later appeared in 17 Charlotte games during 2004-05, which count for Charlotte rather than for the Suns. Comparing his full 62-game combined-team season to Knight’s Wizards-only playing time would overstate what Phoenix received.

sections.heading: Brevin Knight Played 32 Wizards Games Before His March Waiver
sections.body: Knight had played three Phoenix games before the exchange. In Washington he appeared 32 times, with 12 starts, and averaged 4.3 points, 3.2 assists and 1.6 steals across 18.7 minutes per game. That is a real backcourt contribution, even though the Wizards had substantial guard competition after signing Arenas. Washington waived Knight on March 2, 2004, and Milwaukee signed him on March 5. His subsequent 21 Bucks appearances that season do not belong to Washington’s direct player return. The short tenure is consistent with the original Washington Post account emphasizing a contract with only one season left rather than a multi-year point-guard investment.

sections.heading: The Saved Even Trade Verdict Balances Different Types of Return
sections.body: The historical grades are Even Trade and C for each club. Phoenix received 61 White appearances, 17 starts and interior rebounding. Washington received 32 Knight games, 12 starts and the ability to move away from White’s longer contract commitment. The difference in receiving-team games does not automatically determine the winner because Washington’s reported objective included financial flexibility, not merely replacing every White minute with a Knight minute. Neither player became a long-term rotation foundation for the acquiring franchise. This limited, transaction-specific comparison supports maintaining the archived even verdict without treating later Charlotte or Milwaukee games as if they occurred for Phoenix or Washington.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade with C grades for Phoenix and Washington remains unchanged. White contributed 61 Suns games, 17 starts, 4.3 points and 4.3 rebounds in 2003-04. Knight played 32 Wizards games with 12 starts before his March 2 waiver. Washington obtained the shorter contract described in contemporaneous coverage, while Phoenix received immediate center depth. The subsequent Milwaukee and Charlotte careers are distinct from this trade’s receiving-team production.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Jahidi White for Brevin Knight in 2003: 61 Suns Games and Washington Cap Relief
featuredDeepDive.intro: Phoenix traded guard Brevin Knight to Washington for center Jahidi White on November 5, 2003. The Wizards’ stated purpose included future salary flexibility because Knight’s deal ended after the season while White had a longer obligation. White played 61 Suns games, while Knight supplied Washington 32 appearances before being waived in March. Both sides received a limited player return, and the inherited Even Trade with C grades is evaluated against those different objectives rather than assuming an identical salary or games-played outcome.

sections.heading: The Wizards Was an Arenas-Era Roster and Contract Decision
sections.body: Washington had signed Gilbert Arenas to a six-year contract in summer 2003 and already possessed several guards when it took Brevin Knight from Phoenix. In the November 5 Washington Post report, Ernie Grunfeld identified improved cap room as a benefit of sending out Jahidi White, whose contract had another year beyond Knight’s approximately $5 million expiring obligation. The team also hoped Knight could compete for minutes. The trade therefore should not be analyzed solely as swapping a starting center for a starting point guard. Washington was reducing future contract exposure while Phoenix was taking an experienced rebounder, with no reported draft selections or separate cash transferred between the clubs.

sections.heading: White Added Reserve Center Minutes rather than a Multi-Year Starter
sections.body: White had played one game for the Wizards in the opening stretch of 2003-04. For the Suns he appeared 61 times and started 17, averaging 14.1 minutes, 4.3 points, 4.3 rebounds and 0.8 blocks. He converted 52.4 percent of his field goals, a useful figure for a player scoring almost exclusively near the basket. His 17 later Charlotte games in 2004-05 should not be folded into the Phoenix accounting. These numbers indicate a legitimate season of backup-center service, not an All-Star acquisition or a durable replacement for the franchise’s broader roster needs.

sections.heading: Knight’s Short Washington Stay Still Produced 102 Assists
sections.body: The 2003-04 team split shows Knight playing 32 games and starting 12 for Washington, handing out 102 assists and recording 52 steals. He averaged 4.3 points and 3.2 assists across 18.7 minutes, then was waived on March 2. Milwaukee signed him on March 5, and he appeared 21 more times for the Bucks before the season ended. That latter work belongs to Milwaukee, not the Wizards. Knight’s stay therefore illustrates the difference between a received contractual asset and an enduring core player: Washington obtained an immediate backup option without retaining him for the following season.

sections.heading: The Trade’s Financial Purpose and Basketball Production Must Be Kept Separate
sections.body: The Suns received more player games than the Wizards, 61 from White against 32 from Knight, but Washington also replaced a longer White contract with an expiring one. The contemporary financial reporting supports that objective without proving an exact realized offseason cap saving that can be attributed to the swap alone. Meanwhile, Phoenix did gain a reserve center who played 861 regular-season minutes after arriving. Neither franchise received a future All-Star through this exchange. To preserve the original two C grades fairly, the conclusion should acknowledge Phoenix’s additional center appearances as well as Washington’s salary-management purpose, without manufacturing future transactions or changing the noindex archive eligibility.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The saved Even Trade and two C grades are preserved. White played 61 Suns games with 17 starts after November 5, 2003; Knight appeared in 32 Wizards games, recorded 102 assists and was waived March 2, 2004. Washington received the shorter contract and Phoenix added center minutes. Later Bucks or Charlotte appearances are excluded. Neither return produced enough sustained direct player value to override the inherited balanced assessment.

sections.heading: Phoenix Sent Two Firsts to Move Gugliotta
sections.body: Phoenix acquired Keon Clark and Ben Handlogten from Utah on February 19, 2004. The Jazz received Tom Gugliotta, two first-round picks, a second-round pick and cash. The move helped Phoenix address its salary commitments, but that objective carried a considerable future price: one first became the 2004 No. 16 pick and the other was protected over several seasons before eventually conveying unprotected in 2010. The combination of a salary-clearing motive and two premium selections makes this an asset-cost story rather than a routine two-for-one frontcourt deal. Neither acquired Suns player became a comparable durable contributor.

sections.heading: The Later Pick Became Gordon Hayward
sections.body: The 2004 first became No. 16 Kirk Snyder and the 2005 second is recorded as No. 60 Alex Acker. The more important future component originally included protections that relaxed over the following years, finally becoming the 2010 No. 9 choice used on Gordon Hayward. That is the clearest long-range outcome attached to the exchange and the principal reason Utah's asset grade was so high. Hayward's emergence occurred in the receiving franchise's own later roster, not as a hypothetical player Phoenix retained while avoiding the costs of its 2004 decision. The first-round picks should be tracked as separate assets instead of merged into one imaginary selection.

sections.heading: Financial Flexibility Had a Real Draft Cost
sections.body: Moving Gugliotta may have offered Phoenix a financial benefit, which helps explain why management accepted a large outgoing package. The basketball ledger nevertheless shows Utah acquiring a veteran and multiple named draft choices, including a high lottery selection years later. Phoenix's incoming Clark and Handlogten combination didn't produce matching team production. The full chain matters because a deal made for immediate payroll reasons can impose a cost only revealed after long-dated protection expires. An evaluation can acknowledge that initial economic motive without claiming it compensates for a future All-Star-level pick once the trade is viewed retrospectively.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Jazz Win. Utah receives A+ for the package that included Gugliotta, the 2004 first and the future first eventually used on No. 9 Gordon Hayward, plus a second and cash. Phoenix receives D for Clark and Handlogten. The later high-value draft outcome made the cost of salary relief particularly steep, even after recognizing why the Suns sought flexibility.

Utah exercised one first at No. 16 on Kirk Snyder, who played 68 Jazz games, and the other at No. 9 in 2010 on Gordon Hayward, whose 516 Utah appearances included a 2017 All-Star season. Phoenix waived Handlogten the day after the deal. The original Jazz Win verdict is grounded in those receiving-team outcomes, not later Boston Hayward seasons.

sections.heading: Phoenix Exchanged Gugliotta and Three Draft Rights for Two Veterans
sections.body: On February 19, 2004 the Suns sent Tom Gugliotta, two conditional first-round selections, a 2005 second-round pick and cash to Utah for Keon Clark and Ben Handlogten. The NBA’s historical deadline record confirms this broader package; the two team transaction logs identify the specific later picks. The first nearer to the trade became the 2004 No. 16 choice, while the protected future first would not convey until 2010. The immediate Phoenix motivation centered on salary obligations and flexibility, not acquiring a new franchise center for a playoff run. Utah accepted Gugliotta’s expiring contract along with multiple draft options. Neither Gordon Hayward nor Kirk Snyder was a player Utah already owned in February 2004; both were later selections created by the rights it acquired.

sections.heading: The Protected First Became No. 9 Gordon Hayward Six Years Later
sections.body: The most productive Utah return was the first-round selection whose protections extended from 2006 through 2009 before the pick conveyed unprotected in 2010. The Jazz used No. 9 on Gordon Hayward, a Butler forward who subsequently played 516 Utah regular-season games across seven seasons. His rise culminated in a 2016-17 All-Star campaign: 73 starts, 21.9 points, 5.4 rebounds and 3.5 assists per game. Those Utah seasons followed directly from holding the inherited 2010 pick, but they were not predictable on February 19, 2004. Hayward signed with Boston in July 2017. His subsequent Celtics, Hornets and Thunder minutes are not additional Jazz on-court production, even though the original Phoenix transaction had provided Utah the right to draft him.

sections.heading: The Other First Brought Kirk Snyder for a Real Jazz Season
sections.body: Utah also converted the 2004 No. 16 pick into Kirk Snyder, a young guard from Nevada. Snyder played 68 regular-season games for the Jazz in 2004-05, making seven starts and averaging 5.0 points. That is a separate direct Utah player result beyond Hayward’s much later emergence. The additional second-round right eventually became the No. 60 choice in the 2005 draft associated with Alex Acker, but the pick moved through other transactions and cannot automatically be scored as a season of Jazz NBA production by Acker. These details make the return more specific than an abstract collection of picks. The No. 16 selection yielded immediate limited Utah playing time, while the larger return would come from retaining rights to a 2010 first-round prospect years later.

sections.heading: Phoenix Waived Handlogten the Next Day; Jazz Kept the Upside
sections.body: The Suns waived Ben Handlogten on February 20, 2004, one day after they acquired him. That official transaction is a useful measure of how different the front offices’ priorities were. Phoenix’s side was principally a salary and contract maneuver; Utah’s was an acceptance of contract obligations for longer-term draft consideration. Keon Clark was the other player sent to Phoenix, but the surviving record does not support crediting the Suns with later Hayward or Snyder NBA contributions. The historical Utah A-plus and Phoenix D grades and Jazz Win verdict reflect two distinct draft conversions, not evidence that Utah won an immediate 2004 playoff matchup because of this trade. Hayward’s 516 Jazz games and Snyder’s 68 Jazz games provide a team-specific basis for that retrospective grade gap.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Jazz Win — the archived Utah A-plus versus Phoenix D remains. Utah obtained draft rights that yielded 68 direct Kirk Snyder regular-season games and 516 direct Gordon Hayward Jazz appearances, culminating in Hayward’s 2017 All-Star recognition. Phoenix gained Keon Clark and briefly held Handlogten, waived the next day, while removing Gugliotta’s contract. The separate No. 60 second-round draft chain should not be credited as an invented Jazz Acker season. The longer-term asset outcomes favor Utah without implying Hayward was already known in 2004.
