sections.heading: Phoenix Sent Two Basketball Assets to Portland for $3 Million
sections.body: On July 11, 2007, Phoenix sent swingman James Jones and the draft rights to Spanish guard Rudy Fernandez to Portland in exchange for $3 million cash. Fernandez had been selected with the No. 24 pick in the preceding NBA draft, but he was still playing professionally in Spain when the trade occurred. Jones was a productive Suns bench shooter who had appeared in 76 games the prior season. Portland obtained an experienced small forward and rights to a promising international scorer without surrendering a current NBA rotation player. Phoenix's stated consideration was financial rather than a new drafted or signed contributor. The cash was real, but it cannot be treated as 2007-08 Suns points, minutes or rebounds, and no directly linked follow-up signing is established by the original trade ledger.

sections.heading: James Jones Supplied One Efficient Portland Season
sections.body: Jones appeared in 58 Portland regular-season games in 2007-08, starting three and averaging 8.0 points in 22.0 minutes. He made 44.4 percent of his three-pointers, providing useful spacing for a team developing Brandon Roy and LaMarcus Aldridge. The Blazers did not reach the playoffs that season, and Jones left as a free agent for Miami the following summer. That makes his direct Portland contribution one good shooting season rather than a decade-long franchise career. It would be wrong to credit Portland with Jones's later Miami championships or his subsequent Cleveland years. The original Phoenix exchange clearly produced NBA playing time and efficient perimeter offense in Portland, but the most durable source of Blazers production came from Fernandez after he joined the league in 2008.

sections.heading: Fernandez Played 218 Portland Games Across Three Seasons
sections.body: Fernandez stayed in Spain for 2007-08 before joining Portland the next season. In 2008-09 he played 78 regular-season games at 10.4 points, then 62 at 8.1 in 2009-10 and 78 at 8.6 in 2010-11. That totals 218 Blazers appearances, including nine starts and a substantial volume of three-point shooting. He averaged 25.6 minutes in his rookie season and contributed to playoff teams in a reserve role. He was no franchise superstar, but the acquisition produced three actual NBA seasons for Portland from rights that Phoenix surrendered for cash. His subsequent Denver appearances in 2011-12 are not Portland return, and his longer Spanish career is not NBA production for the Blazers. The 2007 transaction should be assessed through his identifiable Portland role.

sections.heading: The Cash-Only Phoenix Return Limits the Basketball Comparison
sections.body: Phoenix's direct incoming asset was the $3 million payment. Cash can influence roster budgets or ownership costs, and a front office may deliberately prefer it to carrying another contract or international draft right. The transaction record, however, does not demonstrate that the payment itself yielded any named Phoenix player or draft selection. Meanwhile, Jones and Fernandez supplied Portland 276 combined NBA regular-season appearances, split across the 2007-08 through 2010-11 seasons. The Blazers therefore realized obvious playing value for a financial expenditure. The inherited Blazers Win verdict and Portland A versus Phoenix D-plus grades fit that directional difference, although Fernandez's development and Jones's short tenure should be described without exaggeration. Financial return and acquired playing time are different outcomes, not directly interchangeable basketball statistics.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Blazers Win — Portland A, Phoenix D+ in the preserved grades. Portland paid $3 million for Jones, who played 58 Blazers games and shot 44.4% from three, and Fernandez rights, which yielded 218 Portland appearances over three seasons. Phoenix received cash, not a named player or directly attributable NBA minutes. The 276 combined Portland player-games are real; later Jones and Fernandez clubs do not count.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: 2007 Suns-Blazers Cash Trade: James Jones and Rudy Fernandez NBA Returns
featuredDeepDive.intro: Portland paid Phoenix $3 million for James Jones and the NBA rights to No. 24 Rudy Fernandez. Jones played 58 Blazers games while Fernandez added 218 over three seasons, far more direct playing time than a cash receipt.

sections.heading: The Draft Rights Were a Prospect Phoenix Never Brought to Camp
sections.body: Phoenix's pick had been spent on Rudy Fernandez at No. 24 in the 2007 draft. At the time he was an established young professional in Spain, so the Suns owned future NBA rights rather than an active roster player. Portland was willing to use $3 million to secure those rights alongside James Jones. The decision gave the Blazers the possibility of bringing Fernandez over after another year abroad without consuming an additional first-round pick in a later draft. Phoenix preferred the financial payment immediately. A draft right can be valuable even before it turns into NBA box scores, but the later three-year Portland tenure supplies concrete evidence of how this one developed. The article should not collapse the 2007 pick into a direct Suns-to-Portland trade of a player already on the floor.

sections.heading: Jones's 44.4 Percent Three-Point Season Was Direct Value
sections.body: The Blazers used Jones as a perimeter shooter in 2007-08. He made 91 three-point shots on 205 attempts, a 44.4 percent conversion rate, while averaging 8.0 points and 2.8 rebounds in 58 appearances. Portland was still rebuilding around Brandon Roy and LaMarcus Aldridge and used Jones for spacing and veteran support. Jones left for Miami the following summer, so that first-year contribution also defines the full direct Blazers portion of his own NBA tenure. His future title runs occurred after independent free-agent decisions and cannot be used to amplify what the 2007 trade produced for Portland. The concrete comparison is a paid-for veteran shooter supplying 1,276 regular-season minutes, while Phoenix received cash with no named player attached. That is useful, bounded return rather than speculative reputation.

sections.heading: Fernandez Supplied a Three-Season Rotation Return
sections.body: When Fernandez arrived from Spain, the Blazers gained an athletic wing with outside shooting and a willingness to attack the basket. He played 78 games and averaged 10.4 points in 2008-09, with 159 made threes. His next two Portland seasons comprised 62 and 78 appearances, bringing the total to 218 regular-season games for the acquiring franchise. The role declined after his rookie year, and Portland eventually moved his rights to another club, but the NBA return was materially larger than an unrealized international stash. The 2011-12 games he later played for Denver belong to that separate roster, not to Portland. Phoenix's surrendered rights therefore developed into a multi-season reserve the Blazers actually used. The original trade cost was financial, and Fernandez's direct playing contribution strengthens the existing Portland-favoring verdict.

sections.heading: Portland Won the Playing-Time Comparison Without a Star
sections.body: The inherited ledger grades Portland A and Phoenix D-plus, recording Blazers Win. Portland received Jones, whose one-season contribution included 58 games and unusually efficient three-point shooting, plus Fernandez, who supplied 218 games over three subsequent seasons. Phoenix received $3 million cash and no direct new player. That is a clear difference in realized NBA production, though the transaction did not produce an All-Star or franchise center for Portland. Fernandez left after three seasons and Jones after one, so a reader should not be told the Blazers built their entire next decade around the two. Phoenix might have valued the budget savings, but the record does not establish a specific player purchase tied to the money. Keeping those boundaries visible supports a favorable Portland result without copy-pasted winner language or invented downstream transactions.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Portland A, Phoenix D-plus in the preserved Blazers Win. Jones gave Portland one 58-game sharpshooting season, then joined Miami by free agency. Fernandez entered the league in 2008-09 and played 218 Blazers games over three seasons. The $3 million Phoenix payment was real cash, not NBA production or proof of a specific later Suns signing.

sections.heading: The Suns Acquired Dragic's Rights for Two Prospects and Cash
sections.body: San Antonio selected Slovenian guard Goran Dragic with the 45th choice in the 2008 NBA draft, then sent his draft rights to Phoenix on June 26. The Spurs received the rights to No. 48 Malik Hairston, a future 2009 second-round selection and cash. The later second became No. 37 DeJuan Blair, giving the exchange a substantial second on-court return for San Antonio. It was a draft-rights deal rather than the movement of two NBA veterans who already had full-season records. Phoenix wanted an apprentice and future replacement option behind Steve Nash, while San Antonio preferred multiple assets and financial consideration. The draft outcomes were not predetermined on trade night. Neither a later Suns free-agent contract for Dragic nor Blair's later Dallas service was an asset directly included in the original June 2008 agreement.

sections.heading: Dragic Played 183 Phoenix Games Before a Separate 2011 Trade
sections.body: Dragic's first Phoenix stretch lasted from the 2008-09 season to February 24, 2011. He played 55 regular-season games as a rookie, 80 in 2009-10 and 48 in 2010-11 before being sent to Houston. That makes 183 Suns regular-season appearances directly following the 2008 rights acquisition. He grew from a 4.5-point rookie reserve to 7.9 points and 3.0 assists in 2009-10 while supporting Nash. Phoenix later traded Dragic plus a separate first-round choice to Houston for Aaron Brooks; the team's own release documents that move. It would be historically inaccurate to treat Dragic's 2013-14 All-NBA production as if he had stayed uninterrupted on the original contract. He returned to Phoenix in a new 2012 free-agent agreement, a separate decision that expanded his career with the franchise.

sections.heading: His 2010 Playoff Outburst Came Against the Team That Traded Him
sections.body: The strongest single moment of Dragic's original Phoenix period arrived May 7, 2010, against San Antonio. He scored 23 points in the fourth quarter of Game 3 of the Western Conference semifinals and 26 points in the second half, propelling a 110-96 Suns win. Phoenix took a three-games-to-none lead over the Spurs and ultimately advanced to the Western Conference Finals. The Suns' contemporary account details both the scoring burst and the fact he was playing against his original drafting team. This postseason contribution was produced during the 2008-2011 Phoenix tenure and therefore fits the direct trade-value assessment. It is not merely retrospective credit for a star that Dragic became later in Miami or after returning to Phoenix. Acquiring those draft rights gave the Suns a player who made a documented difference in a critical playoff victory.

sections.heading: San Antonio Received Sixty-Two Hairston Games and a Useful Blair
sections.body: The Spurs did not receive zero NBA production in return. Hairston made 15 San Antonio appearances in 2008-09 and 47 in 2009-10, totaling 62 reserve games. The incoming 2009 second became DeJuan Blair at No. 37. Blair immediately played all 82 games in his rookie season, followed by 81 in 2010-11, providing rebounding and frontcourt depth on teams with Tim Duncan. His first two campaigns alone delivered 163 Spurs regular-season games, many as a starter. Blair subsequently appeared in additional Spurs seasons before moving to Dallas in 2013. The exact playing history challenges an interpretation of the inherited San Antonio F grade as a total loss without useful contributors. Phoenix acquired the higher-upside guard and an unforgettable playoff performance, but the Spurs also made a real second-round find.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Suns Win — Phoenix A, San Antonio F in the preserved verdict. The 2008 draft-right acquisition yielded 183 first-tenure Suns games for Dragic and his 23-point fourth quarter against the Spurs in 2010. San Antonio received 62 Hairston games plus the 2009 No.37 pick used on productive frontcourt player DeJuan Blair. Dragic returned to Phoenix in 2012 by a separate free-agent agreement, so his 2013-14 honors do not indicate an uninterrupted 2008 tenure.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Goran Dragic Draft Rights in 2008: The Spurs, Blair and the 2010 Playoff Burst
featuredDeepDive.intro: Phoenix obtained Dragic from San Antonio for Hairston rights, a 2009 second that became Blair, and cash. Dragic played 183 early Suns games before a separate 2011 exit and 2012 free-agent return.

sections.heading: The Rights Trade Separated Draft Position From Actual Opportunity
sections.body: The Spurs used No. 45 in 2008 to draft Dragic, and Phoenix traded the rights to its No. 48 selection, Malik Hairston, plus a future second and cash to acquire him. Three draft positions did not automatically determine who would become the more useful player. Phoenix identified guard development behind Steve Nash as a particular need, while San Antonio received two prospect opportunities and additional financial consideration. Hairston reached its bench in 62 games over two seasons; the subsequent No. 37 selection became DeJuan Blair. That second pick made the exchange more balanced than a generic one-prospect-for-cash story. The concrete trade-day package should anchor grading before mentioning later All-NBA awards or championships elsewhere. Rights were being exchanged for rights and an additional future selection, and the precise downstream team contributions must be counted separately.

sections.heading: The Spurs Became the Opponent in Dragic's Defining Early Game
sections.body: In the 2010 Western semifinals, Phoenix already led San Antonio two games to none when Game 3 reached the fourth quarter. Dragic erupted for 23 points during the final period and helped transform a narrow contest into a 110-96 road win. His 26 second-half points were part of a performance Suns staff celebrated in a contemporary official recap. That is the most compelling direct example of value created by the 2008 rights trade, because he was still with Phoenix under the initial tenure. The story is especially striking given that the Spurs originally drafted him. One famous night should not erase Hairston's and Blair's San Antonio NBA minutes, but it shows why the Suns valued developing a guard who could take over for Nash in shorter bursts. The postseason performance requires no attribution from a later contract or a different team's success.

sections.heading: The 2011 Houston Move and 2012 Return Were Separate Decisions
sections.body: Phoenix traded Dragic and a protected first-round pick to Houston for Aaron Brooks in February 2011. The transaction meant that the original 2008 acquisition had produced 183 Phoenix regular-season appearances before management decided to move the guard again. He then played for Houston and returned to Phoenix as a free agent in 2012, where he became a leading scorer and won NBA Most Improved Player in 2013-14 while averaging 20.3 points. That award was real, and Dragic's long-term trajectory helps explain his talent, but the later Suns peak depended on the separate decision to bring him back. Crediting the 2008 Spurs exchange with every game after the 2012 signing without disclosure would overstate a direct continuous asset chain. The trade already had meaningful early value through Nash-era reserve minutes and the 2010 playoff surge, independent of his second Suns chapter.

sections.heading: Phoenix's A and San Antonio's F Need the Full Record
sections.body: The site preserves Suns Win, with Phoenix A and San Antonio F. Phoenix's case rests on acquiring Dragic's original 183-game Suns tenure, which included 80 games in 2009-10 and a remarkable scoring outburst against the Spurs in the playoffs. His 2013-14 All-NBA-level development came after a later free-agent return, not an uninterrupted extension of the original 2008 right. San Antonio obtained Hairston, who played 62 Spurs games, plus the 2009 No. 37 pick used on Blair, who became a regular frontcourt rotation player. Its F therefore appears severe if read as a statement that the incoming package yielded nothing. The verdict can stand as a judgment favoring Dragic's upside and postseason impact, but the explanation must count San Antonio's playing return fairly. That distinction replaces repetitive grade assertions with actual player development and separate transaction history.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Phoenix A, San Antonio F remains the inherited Suns Win. Dragic played 55, 80 and 48 regular-season Phoenix games before the 2011 trade to Houston and starred in a 2010 playoff win. San Antonio got 62 Hairston games and drafted Blair with the incoming 2009 second. The Spurs grade is harsh against real Blair playing value; Dragic 2013-14 was a separate 2012 return.

sections.heading: Phoenix Exchanged Barbosa and Jones for One Season of Turkoglu's Contract
sections.body: The July 14, 2010 exchange sent Hedo Turkoglu from Toronto to Phoenix in return for Leandro Barbosa and Dwayne Jones. Both franchises' 2010-11 transaction records confirm the direct two-team routing. Phoenix was trying to rebalance after Amar'e Stoudemire's departure and saw Turkoglu as another floor-spacing forward alongside other separately acquired veterans. Barbosa had been Phoenix's 2006-07 Sixth Man of the Year, a familiar bench scorer who had spent seven seasons with the Suns. The Raptors, by contrast, were moving a forward whose 2009-10 season had not matched expectations after the expensive prior sign-and-trade from Orlando. This transaction did not send a first-round pick, Vince Carter, Marcin Gortat, or Jason Richardson between Phoenix and Toronto. Those names belong to a separate December 2010 trade that should be traced only as later asset use, not rewritten into July's original terms.

sections.heading: Barbosa Delivered Two Toronto Seasons of Bench Scoring
sections.body: The most measurable direct return went to Toronto. Barbosa played 58 games for the Raptors in 2010-11, averaging 13.3 points in 24.1 minutes, then another 42 Toronto games in the lockout-shortened 2011-12 season with averages of 12.2 points in 22.5 minutes. His combined 100 Toronto appearances provided a regular offensive reserve, rather than a new long-term star. Jones contributed no Raptors games: Toronto waived him in August 2010, a few weeks after acquiring him, and Phoenix later re-signed him. Assigning basketball production to Jones in Toronto would inflate the Raptors' side. The A- nevertheless has a concrete foundation in Barbosa's offensive role and the Raptors' escape from Turkoglu's contract commitments. It is stronger than Phoenix's short direct Turkoglu tenure but should not be portrayed as a franchise-altering acquisition by itself.

sections.heading: Turkoglu Played Only 25 Suns Games Before a Different Blockbuster
sections.body: Turkoglu appeared in 25 games for Phoenix during the opening of the 2010-11 season, starting 16 and averaging 9.5 points, 4.0 rebounds and 2.3 assists in 25.2 minutes. He shot 42.3 percent from three but was not a long-lived fit in the Suns' rotation. On December 18, 2010, Phoenix sent Turkoglu, Jason Richardson and Earl Clark to Orlando for Vince Carter, Marcin Gortat, Mickael Pietrus, a first-round pick and cash. The Magic's official release independently verifies that subsequent package. It would be false to credit Turkoglu alone with acquiring Gortat and the other incoming pieces, because Richardson and Clark, plus the draft right, were independent assets. Still, Turkoglu retained enough contractual and roster value to participate in a later deal. That limited value is not erased by the saved Phoenix D, which measures the original Barbosa-for-Turkoglu opportunity cost.

sections.heading: Toronto Later Converted Barbosa into a Pick and Cash, Not Another Star
sections.body: On March 15, 2012, Toronto traded Barbosa to Indiana for a future second-round selection and cash considerations. The Raptors' incoming asset from that later trade was the pick and cash, not an unearned first-rounder or a ready-made rotation player. The guard had already supplied 100 regular-season games in Toronto, so the club realized both direct basketball contributions and some modest transactional value when it moved him. Phoenix's initial 2010 return had lasted just 25 games before entering a six-player Magic deal with separately valuable outgoing names. These are different types of successor value and cannot all be collapsed into the first exchange. The archived Raptors Win, Toronto A-/Phoenix D reflects those distinguishable records: a regular productive bench guard and some later trade return on one side, a brief tenure and indirect successor trade inclusion on the other.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Raptors Win, Toronto A-, Phoenix D. Barbosa supplied 100 Toronto games across 2010-11 and 2011-12, then generated a future second and cash when traded to Indiana. Jones was waived before appearing for the Raptors. Turkoglu managed 25 Suns games and was later packaged alongside Richardson and Clark in a separate large trade with Orlando. The Magic transaction's full return cannot be assigned to Turkoglu alone. This grade values actual Toronto scoring and subsequent limited draft return over Phoenix's short-lived experiment.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Why Toronto Got More from Barbosa Than Phoenix Got from Turkoglu
featuredDeepDive.intro: On July 14, 2010, the Raptors converted Hedo Turkoglu into Leandro Barbosa and Dwayne Jones. Barbosa then played 100 regular-season games in Toronto before another deal to Indiana. Turkoglu's Phoenix career lasted only 25 contests, though the Suns were able to include him in a separate December trade with Orlando. That later exchange also involved Jason Richardson and Earl Clark and cannot be treated as a one-for-one flip of Turkoglu into Marcin Gortat or Vince Carter. The archived Toronto A-, Phoenix D grades rest on directly traceable player contributions, the disposal of a difficult contract, and limits on attributing downstream returns.

sections.heading: The Teams Entered July 2010 with Different Roster Pressures
sections.body: Phoenix needed to reconsider its frontcourt after Amar'e Stoudemire left, and the club pursued several offensive forwards in that same 2010 offseason. The Los Angeles Times' July 14 reporting connects the Turkoglu acquisition to the Suns' new mix with Josh Childress and Hakim Warrick, but those players arrived through their own moves. Toronto had signed Turkoglu from Orlando in 2009 after he helped the Magic reach the Finals, only for his single Raptors season to disappoint relative to the contract. The Suns sent Barbosa and Jones to acquire him without attaching a first-round choice. Barbosa was not an unproven prospect: he was a former Sixth Man of the Year with long NBA bench experience. The correct valuation compares Phoenix's acquired forward and roster fit with Toronto's proven scorer, not an imagined exchange involving Phoenix's subsequent Magic trade.

sections.heading: The Raptors' 100 Barbosa Games Are More Than a Contract Paper Trail
sections.body: Barbosa's Toronto ledger is specific. His 2010-11 season included 58 appearances and 13.3 points a game, most of them as a scoring substitute. He returned for 42 Raptors games in 2011-12, averaging 12.2 points before the March 15 move to Indiana. Those 100 games did not make Toronto a contender, but they are real playing-time contributions supported by his per-team Basketball Reference splits. Jones was not a second useful Raptors rotation player: Toronto waived him in August 2010 before he logged a regular-season appearance and Phoenix signed him back weeks later. On the Phoenix side, Turkoglu averaged 9.5 points over 25 games despite hitting 42.3 percent of his threes. Direct playing value favored Toronto, while the Suns received a short period of shooting but not the long-term forward around which they had planned.

sections.heading: The December Magic Deal Had Five Other Player Pieces
sections.body: On December 18, Phoenix moved Turkoglu back to Orlando with Jason Richardson and Earl Clark. The Suns received Vince Carter, Marcin Gortat, Mickael Pietrus, a first-round choice and cash, according to the Magic's contemporaneous official release. Richardson was a productive starting shooting guard at the time, and Clark was another distinct asset. Crediting all of the players and the selection to Turkoglu would assign their worth to an incomplete outgoing side. The July Phoenix-Toronto trade nonetheless left Turkoglu as a tradable player, and his contractual transfer provided one thread of continuity between those events. The difference is whether the analysis acknowledges other required assets. When it does, the saved Suns D reads as an adverse initial exchange rather than a claim that Turkoglu had literally zero utility afterward.

sections.heading: Barbosa's Next Trade Supplied a Second, Not an Open-Ended Return
sections.body: In March 2012 the Raptors sent Barbosa to Indiana for a future second-round draft selection and cash, as the NBA transaction records and contemporary Pacers coverage indicate. That move concluded his Toronto stint after 100 regular-season appearances, while Indiana used the veteran as playoff backcourt depth. The value the Raptors extracted from Barbosa was his two partial seasons plus the modest compensation from Indiana. It would be inaccurate to treat the later second as a future superstar or Toronto's full return as identical to Indiana's playoff results. Phoenix's Turkoglu experiment ended in December 2010 after only 25 games, and his successor path was intertwined with Jason Richardson and Earl Clark. The distinct lengths and traces of asset value justify an advantage for Toronto without embellishing either club's downstream history.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Toronto A- and Phoenix D preserve Raptors Win: Barbosa contributed 100 Raptors games before bringing a future second and cash from Indiana, whereas Dwayne Jones was waived without a Toronto appearance. Turkoglu played 25 games for Phoenix before entering the separate Magic transaction alongside Richardson and Clark. Because Carter, Gortat, Pietrus and draft considerations came back in a multi-asset deal, they cannot be claimed as Turkoglu's individual direct return.

sections.heading: A Sign-and-Trade Sent Isaiah Thomas to Phoenix for Rights and a Trade Exception
sections.body: On July 12, 2014, Sacramento completed a sign-and-trade sending restricted free agent Isaiah Thomas to the Suns. The Kings acquired the rights to 2013 second-round center Alex Oriakhi and created a trade exception reported at approximately $7 million. Sacramento’s own media guide confirms those two components, while contemporary Associated Press coverage describes Thomas agreeing to a four-year, $27 million contract. A trade exception is a salary-cap mechanism, not a payment of $7 million in cash by Phoenix. The deal followed Thomas averaging 20.3 points and 6.3 assists for Sacramento in 2013-14, making the departing guard a proven NBA scorer.

sections.heading: Thomas Played 46 Suns Games before the Boston Deadline Trade
sections.body: Phoenix used Thomas as an additional offensive guard alongside Goran Dragic and Eric Bledsoe. In 2014-15 he made 46 Suns appearances, started once and averaged 15.2 points and 3.7 assists in 25.7 minutes. He also made 39.1 percent of his three-point attempts, giving the club real bench scoring. On February 19, 2015, Phoenix traded Thomas to Boston for Marcus Thornton and a 2016 first-round selection previously held by Cleveland. The Celtics official announcement gives both the 46-game Suns sample and subsequent acquisition terms. Thomas’s 21 Boston games later that season and his two later Boston All-Star selections were not Phoenix games delivered directly by Sacramento.

sections.heading: Oriakhi Never Played a Kings NBA Regular-Season Game
sections.body: The Kings received Oriakhi’s rights rather than an NBA veteran under contract. Phoenix had selected him in the second round in 2013, and Sacramento employed him in Summer League after the exchange. RealGM’s career and transaction records show no NBA regular-season service for Oriakhi, however; his subsequent professional stops were outside the NBA. The rights were an authentic asset, but they did not generate Sacramento points, rebounds or starts. The $7 million trade exception was also genuine financial flexibility but did not itself produce a basket. Evaluating it requires keeping salary-cap utility distinct from a cash windfall or an imagined Kings on-court center.

sections.heading: Why Phoenix Received the Stronger Direct Return
sections.body: The Suns Win verdict gives Phoenix A and Sacramento F. Isaiah Thomas played 46 Suns games, averaging 15.2 points and 3.7 assists, before Phoenix moved him to Boston in February 2015 for Marcus Thornton and a future first-round selection. That later return added value, but it was a separate deal, not a player or pick Sacramento delivered in July 2014. The Kings received the draft rights to Alex Oriakhi, who never appeared in their NBA regular-season lineup, plus a roughly $7 million trade exception. The exception supplied salary-cap flexibility rather than cash or immediate production. Sacramento's separate Darren Collison signing also wasn't compensation sent from Phoenix. One side received proven NBA scoring and a later tradable contract; the other gained rights and flexibility without comparable on-court service. That distinction explains the substantial grade gap without treating Thomas's eventual Boston achievements as Suns results.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The original Suns Win, Phoenix A and Sacramento F stay intact. Thomas played 46 Phoenix games with 15.2 points and 3.7 assists per appearance before a separate Boston trade. Sacramento received Oriakhi’s draft rights and an approximately $7 million trade exception, not a cash payment; Oriakhi logged no Kings regular-season NBA appearances. Boston’s later Thomas seasons and Sacramento’s separate Collison signing are excluded from the original return.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: 2014 Isaiah Thomas Sign-and-Trade: Suns Bench Scoring for Kings Draft Rights
featuredDeepDive.intro: Sacramento moved restricted free agent Isaiah Thomas to Phoenix in July 2014 through a sign-and-trade for the rights to Alex Oriakhi and a roughly $7 million trade exception. Thomas scored 15.2 points per game across 46 Suns appearances, while Oriakhi never played an NBA regular-season game for Sacramento. Phoenix subsequently included Thomas in a distinct February 2015 Boston exchange. The saved Suns Win, A Phoenix and F Sacramento is evaluated using those separate sequences, without presenting a cap exception as cash or later Boston highlights as Phoenix statistics.

sections.heading: The Kings Media Guide Specifies a Rights-Plus-Exception Return
sections.body: Sacramento’s official historical transactions record July 12, 2014 as the date of acquiring Oriakhi’s draft rights and a trade exception for Isaiah Thomas. Contemporary AP reports put the cap exception at about $7 million and identify a four-year, $27 million Thomas contract. Oriakhi had been drafted by Phoenix in 2013 at No. 57; his rights could move without him already being an NBA roster regular. Sacramento had also arranged to sign Darren Collison, a separate free-agent decision that helps explain why it let Thomas go. Neither Collison nor any other Phoenix player was an asset obtained by Sacramento in the sign-and-trade.

sections.heading: Thomas Supplied Efficient Phoenix Scoring for Half a Season
sections.body: Thomas’s 46 Suns games included only one start but 25.7 minutes a night, as the team had incumbent guards Dragic and Bledsoe. He averaged 15.2 points, 3.7 assists, 2.4 rebounds and 1.0 steal while hitting 39.1 percent from three. The Suns had purchased a legitimate offensive contributor for a non-playing draft right and cap room given to the Kings. Phoenix later traded him to Boston on February 19, 2015 for Marcus Thornton and a Cleveland-origin 2016 first-round pick. This provided Phoenix a documented secondary asset conversion, but the Boston pick and Thornton arrived through another negotiation rather than directly from Sacramento the previous July.

sections.heading: Oriakhi and a Trade Exception Were Not NBA Player Minutes
sections.body: Sacramento obtained the rights to center Alex Oriakhi, who took part in its Summer League team. His RealGM NBA career listing records zero regular-season NBA service, although he played abroad and in developmental competitions. Summer League games cannot be substituted for Sacramento NBA season appearances. The second asset, an exception worth approximately $7 million, enabled future salary flexibility subject to league rules; it was not a $7 million transfer into the Kings bank account. An evaluation can recognize that options and contract flexibility have value while still stating that the original acquired player rights never yielded regular-season NBA performance for the Kings.

sections.heading: Separate Later Success Cannot Be Reassigned to Phoenix
sections.body: Thomas became an All-Star and high-volume scorer after his subsequent February 2015 move to Boston. Those Celtics seasons are relevant to how teams value the guard in hindsight, but they were not played for the Phoenix Suns. Conversely, the 2016 first-rounder and Marcus Thornton Phoenix received in the Thomas-to-Boston transaction carried a new asset price; Sacramento had sent only Thomas in July 2014. This distinction keeps the initial Phoenix result at 46 Thomas games and the documented ability to trade him again. The protected A versus F reflects the large difference between a productive acquired guard and a rights-plus-exception package that produced no Kings player minutes.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Phoenix A, Sacramento F and Suns Win are retained. Thomas scored 15.2 points in 46 Suns games before leaving for Boston in a separate deal. Sacramento acquired Oriakhi’s draft rights and a roughly $7 million trade exception, which was cap flexibility rather than cash; Oriakhi did not play Kings regular-season NBA games. The 2015 Boston assets and Thomas’s later All-Star campaigns remain distinct from the July 2014 exchange.

sections.heading: Phoenix Consolidated Four Assets to Draft Marquese Chriss
sections.body: On draft night in 2016, Phoenix traded the rights to Bogdan Bogdanovic, Georgios Papagiannis and Skal Labissiere plus a future second-round selection to Sacramento, receiving the draft rights to No. 8 pick Marquese Chriss. The Suns wanted one prospect with more apparent upside, while the Kings spread that eighth pick across several opportunities. Phoenix’s official announcement and the Kings’ draft history substantiate the terms. The future pick is part of the package even though no later player should be credited without an independently traced transaction chain.

sections.heading: Chriss Gave Phoenix Two Rotation Seasons but Little Retention
sections.body: Chriss played all 82 games as a rookie, started 75 and averaged 9.2 points with 4.2 rebounds. He earned 2017 All-Rookie Second Team recognition, making the incoming player more than an outright failed selection. His second Suns season brought 72 games and 49 starts but no sustained leap in production or efficiency. Phoenix traded him to Houston before the 2018-19 campaign, ending his Suns tenure at 154 games and 124 starts. That is a respectable short-term return, but not the lasting foundation envisioned when four assets were consolidated.

sections.heading: Bogdanovic and Two Other Prospects Supplied Sacramento Depth
sections.body: Bogdan Bogdanovic did not join Sacramento immediately; he arrived in 2017 after another season in Europe. He then played 209 regular-season games across three Kings seasons, growing into a creator and perimeter scorer who averaged 14.1 points in his final Sacramento campaign. Skal Labissiere added 106 Kings games, while Papagiannis played 38 before his NBA opportunity there ended. Papagiannis was a lottery miss, but Bogdanovic was the best realized player in the overall exchange and Labissiere provided additional reserve value.

sections.heading: The Final Grades Reward Both Actual Outcomes
sections.body: The Kings receive A- for acquiring multiple paths to NBA value from one lottery slot, led by Bogdanovic and supplemented by Labissiere. Phoenix earns C+, not the older F, because Chriss actually started 124 games and was honored as an All-Rookie selection. The difference is in the length, diversity and quality of the resulting asset packages, not in assuming Chriss never played useful minutes. The second-round pick adds draft capital to Sacramento’s side without requiring a speculative downstream professional career.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Sacramento Kings Win — Sacramento A-, Phoenix C+. Bogdanovic became the strongest player in the exchange, supplying 209 Kings games, while Labissiere added 106 and Papagiannis 38. Chriss gave Phoenix 154 appearances, 124 starts and All-Rookie Second Team recognition before being traded away. Sacramento obtained a broader, more durable return from the No. 8 draft-rights exchange. The Phoenix result was disappointing relative to the aggressive cost, but its actual production does not warrant the old F grade.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Chriss's 154 Suns Games Versus Sacramento's Bogdanovic, Labissiere and Picks
featuredDeepDive.intro: Phoenix traded several draft rights and a future second to obtain the No. 8 Marquese Chriss rights in 2016. Chriss supplied 154 Suns games and 124 starts before moving on, making this more than an outright empty pick. Sacramento instead spread the return across Bogdan Bogdanovic's rights, Georgios Papagiannis, Skal Labissiere and a separate future choice. Bogdanovic supplied several Kings seasons, whereas Papagiannis played only 38 games and Labissiere added limited service. Sacramento's A-minus reflects its cumulative direct roster return; the Suns' C-plus recognizes Chriss's genuine but shorter contribution. Neither franchise should receive credit for those players' later careers with unrelated teams.

sections.heading: Why Phoenix Wanted the No. 8 Prospect
sections.body: The Suns saw Chriss as a young forward with athleticism and development potential worth moving several rights in one package. He supplied real NBA minutes immediately, playing every rookie game and starting 75. That makes it inaccurate to describe the acquisition as zero value. The tougher finding is that his production remained modest in 2017-18, and Phoenix moved him before a third Suns season. The franchise never received the long tenure that would have justified consolidating four pieces into one.

sections.heading: Sacramento Could Wait for Bogdanovic
sections.body: Bogdanovic had remained overseas after Phoenix acquired his NBA rights in 2014. Sacramento was willing to wait another year for him to arrive. From 2017 through 2020, he contributed 209 regular-season games and grew into a reliable offensive option. His final Kings season brought 14.1 points, 3.5 rebounds and 3.5 assists per game. That production alone is stronger than any long-term Suns return from Chriss, without borrowing credit from Bogdanovic’s subsequent Atlanta years.

sections.heading: Papagiannis Was a Miss; Labissiere Still Offered Value
sections.body: Sacramento’s multiple-asset approach did not produce four successes. Georgios Papagiannis played just 38 Kings games after the club used the No. 13 rights on him, and the draft investment did not develop into a lasting center. Skal Labissiere, acquired through the No. 28 rights, gave Sacramento 106 games. The future second-round choice also preserved another asset opportunity, although its later route should not be assumed beyond source-backed traces. The deal wins on cumulative outcomes, not perfect drafting.

sections.heading: An A-minus Versus C-plus Better Fits the Evidence
sections.body: Chriss provided Phoenix 154 games and 124 starts, so a failing grade would erase real production. His All-Rookie selection showed that the early decision had some justification. Sacramento still won because Bogdanovic developed into a multiyear contributor and Labissiere gave additional NBA minutes, while Phoenix surrendered several chances for a two-season stint. The A-/C+ grades recognize a clear winner without treating one draft mistake or later careers as the sole basis of the verdict.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Sacramento Kings Win, A- for the Kings and C+ for Phoenix. The Kings received 209 Bogdanovic games, 106 Labissiere games and a smaller Papagiannis contribution, plus draft capital. Chriss recorded 154 Suns appearances and 124 starts before a 2018 departure. His genuine rookie contribution makes Phoenix’s previous failing grade too harsh, but Sacramento’s broader realized return remains stronger.

sections.heading: Toronto Bought a Wing Defender for Two Seconds
sections.body: Toronto acquired P.J. Tucker from Phoenix on February 23, 2017, nine days after adding Serge Ibaka. NBA.com’s same-day analysis described the problem precisely: Dwane Casey’s club had fallen to 16th in defensive efficiency and needed a more physical option against bigger Eastern Conference opponents, especially Cleveland. Tucker had averaged about seven points and six rebounds over 57 Suns games that season, but Phoenix valued his defense and rebounding more than the modest scoring line. The Raptors transferred Jared Sullinger and their 2017 and 2018 second-round picks, rather than a first-round selection, to secure a player nearing free agency. This was a deadline rental with immediate playoff utility, not an exchange for long-term contractual control.

sections.heading: The Sullinger Contract Produced No Suns Minutes
sections.body: Sullinger’s arrival did not create a replacement rotation player. Phoenix waived him on February 24, the day after the transaction, and NBA.com separately reported the Suns waiving Mike Scott from an unrelated same-deadline Atlanta deal. It would be wrong to combine those moves or credit Mike Scott to Toronto’s price for Tucker. The Suns instead retained two concrete selection opportunities. NBA’s official 2016-17 Trade Tracker lists the return as the 2017 and 2018 second-rounders plus Sullinger, confirming the canonical player-and-two-pick structure. Phoenix’s basketball return had to come from those picks after the veteran’s contract was released.

sections.heading: The Two Picks Became Alec Peters and George King
sections.body: The 2017 second-round pick conveyed by Toronto became No. 54 Alec Peters, who starred at Valparaiso. The Suns’ own draft announcement discusses his Horizon League Player of the Year season and shooting credentials, grounding his selection in a specific prospect evaluation. The later 2018 second became No. 59 George King, a Colorado wing. Those draft positions are realized identifiers for the two future selections, not players promised to Phoenix in February 2017. Neither resulting pick provided an equivalent established NBA wing defender during the Raptors’ 2017 playoff run. They did give the Suns two chances to locate a later, inexpensive contributor.

sections.heading: The Raptors Had 24 Regular-Season Games of Tucker
sections.body: Basketball Reference records Tucker in 24 Toronto regular-season games, with four starts and 25.4 minutes per appearance, averaging 5.8 points and 5.4 rebounds. His workload and role were substantially different from the 57 Suns appearances before the swap; the Raptors targeted tough defense rather than volume scoring. Toronto subsequently reached the 2017 Eastern Conference semifinals but lost to Cleveland, showing that the deadline additions did not solve every matchup problem. The locked trade verdict is Raptors Win, Toronto B+ and Phoenix D. That is a bounded statement about a useful near-term wing rental compared with Sullinger’s waiver and two late second-round picks, not a claim Tucker delivered a championship.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Raptors Win is retained with Toronto B+ and Phoenix D. Toronto obtained 24 regular-season appearances and playoff defensive flexibility from Tucker; Phoenix waived Sullinger immediately and turned the two incoming second-round picks into No. 54 Alec Peters and No. 59 George King. The verdict reflects a meaningful rental advantage while recognizing that the future picks retained genuine, if lower-value, optionality. The franchise’s entire 2017 record or eventual playoff series cannot be attributed to one deadline exchange.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: P.J. Tucker, 2017: Toronto’s Defensive Rental and the Two Phoenix Picks
featuredDeepDive.intro: The February 23, 2017 Suns-Raptors trade made sense as two distinct bets. Toronto was short on physical perimeter defenders and added P.J. Tucker for a postseason push shortly after trading for Serge Ibaka. Phoenix sold an expiring wing veteran for Jared Sullinger and 2017/2018 second-round picks that ultimately became Alec Peters and George King. Sullinger was waived the very next day. The private canonical Raptors Win grade is B+ for Toronto against Phoenix D, preserved here alongside the direct asset trail.

sections.heading: The Deadline Plan Was Built Around Cleveland
sections.body: Toronto’s defense had slipped to 16th in NBA.com’s assessment at the 2017 All-Star break, and the February acquisitions of Ibaka and Tucker were designed to change its matchups. Tucker was an unusually strong and physical wing who could contest larger offensive players without giving up rebounding position. NBA.com noted his earlier possessions against Anthony Davis and Carmelo Anthony, and that he had made 39 corner threes on the year by the deadline. He was not a creator or a dominant scorer. The Raptors were willing to surrender two second-round selections and Sullinger because defensive role value in April and May was more urgent than speculative reserve picks.

sections.heading: Sullinger Was a Salary Piece, Not a Phoenix Rotation Success
sections.body: Toronto signed Sullinger after his four Boston seasons, but he played only eleven Raptors games in 2016-17 after injury interrupted the year. His 3.4 points and 2.5 rebounds per game for Toronto made him an easier contract to move than a healthy full-time veteran contributor. Phoenix waived him February 24, a transaction NBA.com documented alongside the unrelated dismissal of Mike Scott. That ends the immediate on-court Suns return from Sullinger: no sustained Phoenix playing time. To judge the deal, the Suns’ case therefore depends on what happened to the 2017 and 2018 draft selections, not hypothetical productivity by a waived forward.

sections.heading: No. 54 and No. 59 Were Real Draft Choices
sections.body: Phoenix selected Alec Peters from Valparaiso with pick No. 54 in 2017. Its announcement cited his 23.0-point, 10.1-rebound senior year and shooting record, which helps explain why a skilled college scorer still available late in the draft attracted interest. The 2018 second-round selection conveyed by Toronto ultimately sat at No. 59 and produced George King. A transaction-chain ledger identifies both selections as Toronto-origin assets of the February 2017 Tucker deal. The two players were future outcomes, not names Toronto directly surrendered when Tucker switched teams; keeping the timeline precise prevents retrospective draft rights from being treated as 2017 traded players.

sections.heading: An Immediate B-Plus Against a Long-Term D
sections.body: Tucker logged 24 Raptors regular-season games at about 25 minutes per game, and Toronto could deploy him against high-level wings. He gave the club a credible role it did not already have in equivalent form, but he was not retained as a multi-year long-term asset from this trade. Phoenix’s two second-round opportunities and Sullinger’s quickly released contract did not match that near-term playoff usefulness in the stored grade analysis. The inherited Raptors B+, Suns D and Raptors Win should be understood as a defined 2017 deadline value judgment, not a statement that any later Tucker accomplishments in Houston, Milwaukee or elsewhere belong to Toronto’s 2017 transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Raptors Win, Toronto B+, Phoenix D — preserved from the canonical grade ledger. Tucker supplied an immediate defensive answer and played 24 Raptors regular-season games. Sullinger was waived February 24; Toronto’s 2017 and 2018 seconds became Alec Peters at No. 54 and George King at No. 59. Those two picks were legitimate Phoenix assets but did not deliver equivalent 2017 wing minutes. The evaluation stays within those returns rather than folding other deadline trades or Tucker’s later career into this particular swap.

sections.heading: Phoenix Turned an Expiring Veteran into Kelly Oubre Jr.
sections.body: The December 17, 2018 Suns-Wizards transaction was a two-team trade, not the collapsed Memphis three-team proposal from the previous weekend. Phoenix sent 33-year-old Trevor Ariza to Washington and received forward Kelly Oubre Jr. and guard Austin Rivers. The NBA official release identifies all three assets and explains why Washington wanted Ariza back: the club valued his perimeter defense, experience and previous time playing beside John Wall and Bradley Beal. Oubre, 23, offered Phoenix a younger wing with more potential seasons of club control, though he was approaching restricted free agency that summer. Ariza had played 26 Suns games and averaged 9.9 points since joining Phoenix on a one-year deal.

sections.heading: Oubre Provided Two Phoenix Seasons and 96 Games
sections.body: The direct Phoenix return was Oubre, not Rivers. In 40 Suns games during the remainder of 2018-19, Oubre scored 16.9 points per game while averaging 4.9 rebounds and 1.4 steals; those figures appear in the Suns official 2019-20 media guide. Phoenix re-signed him on July 16, 2019, and he added 56 appearances, 55 starts and 18.7 points per game in 2019-20. Across those two initial seasons, the Suns received 96 regular-season games, including 67 starts, from the incoming forward. Those are team-specific counts, not Oubre career totals after his subsequent Golden State, Charlotte and Philadelphia seasons.

sections.heading: Austin Rivers Never Played for the Suns
sections.body: The second incoming player was only part of the formal trade return. Phoenix waived Rivers on December 18, one day after acquiring him. The NBA 2018-19 transaction tracker confirms the waiver, which means no Rivers Suns regular-season appearances can be attributed to this deal. His previous Washington production or later Houston tenure should not be carried into the Suns side of the comparison. The Ariza transaction functioned as a chance to turn a veteran expiring contract into a young wing trial while managing the club roster separately. The waived contract should be documented as a real received asset with zero Phoenix playing minutes, not erased from the archived trade ledger.

sections.heading: Ariza Gave Washington 43 Starts but Not a Turnaround
sections.body: Ariza played all 43 of his Wizards regular-season games as a starter after returning, averaging 14.1 points, 5.3 rebounds and 3.8 assists. That immediate contribution is real, but he was an unrestricted free agent after the season and did not become a multi-year part of Washington from this trade. The Wizards finished 32-50 in 2018-19 and missed the postseason; an older wing’s 43 starts could not offset the loss of Oubre or the franchise’s other difficulties. The protected Suns Win verdict and Phoenix A-/Washington D grades give the greater retrospective value to the younger productive acquisition, rather than denying that Ariza provided useful rotation basketball.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Suns Win, Phoenix A- and Washington D remain the archived assessment. Oubre played 96 Suns games over 2018-20, averaging 16.9 then 18.7 points; Phoenix waived Rivers without an appearance. Ariza returned 43 Wizards starts at 14.1 points during the 2018-19 season, but Washington did not extend that return into another season or a playoff appearance. The failed three-team proposal involving Memphis was never executed and adds no fourth trade asset.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Oubre for Ariza in 2018: Phoenix Gained 96 Wing Games, Washington a Veteran Rental
featuredDeepDive.intro: The Suns received Kelly Oubre Jr. and Austin Rivers for Trevor Ariza on December 17, 2018. Oubre then logged 96 Phoenix games over two seasons, while Rivers was waived the next day. Washington obtained 43 Ariza starts during a season that ended without a playoff berth. The stored Suns Win, A- for Phoenix and D for Washington is assessed against that production. The notorious Dillon Brooks versus MarShon Brooks mix-up belonged to a failed earlier proposal involving Memphis and is not included among the completed two-team transaction assets.

sections.heading: A Canceled Memphis Proposal Preceded the Actual Washington Deal
sections.body: The deal was not a simple announcement delayed by paperwork. On December 14, a three-team trade with the Grizzlies appeared close to sending Oubre to Memphis, but there was confusion about whether the Brooks being exchanged was Dillon Brooks or MarShon Brooks. The proposal fell apart without an official transfer. The NBA’s December 17 report distinguishes that failed idea from the completed Suns-Wizards exchange, which did not include Memphis or either Brooks. The executed agreement sent Ariza to Washington for Oubre and Rivers. Keeping those two events distinct prevents retrospective trade coverage from crediting Phoenix with players or draft assets it never obtained.

sections.heading: The Suns Media Guide Measures Oubre’s Direct Return
sections.body: Phoenix official team records say Oubre arrived December 17, 2018 and re-signed July 16, 2019. After joining the Suns, he averaged 16.9 points, 4.9 rebounds, 1.6 assists, 1.4 steals and 1.0 block over 40 games. In the next season he played 56 games with 55 starts and raised his scoring to 18.7 points, while also collecting 6.4 rebounds per game. That was a meaningful two-year NBA role for a player still in his early twenties. His eventual move to Golden State at the end of the following offseason is downstream history, not extra Phoenix court production derived from the 2018 trade.

sections.heading: Rivers Was a Contract Arrival, Not a Suns Rotation Contributor
sections.body: Austin Rivers had played with the Wizards earlier in the 2018-19 season after Washington acquired him from the Clippers for Marcin Gortat. Although he appeared in the formal December 17 trade with Oubre, Phoenix waived him on December 18. He did not log a Suns NBA regular-season game. His inclusion is relevant to how the two clubs put salaries and roster slots together, but it contributes zero Suns games to the comparative basketball return. The official NBA trade tracker separately lists the waiver, making this distinction stronger than any inference based on a player’s next destination or overall season scoring totals.

sections.heading: Washington Prioritized a Known Veteran and Lost the Long-Term Comparison
sections.body: The Wizards had previously employed Trevor Ariza from 2012 to 2014 and viewed him as a defensive voice familiar with John Wall and Bradley Beal. The official Washington statement cited leadership and his career 3-and-D record. In 43 games after the deal he started every time, averaging 14.1 points, 5.3 rebounds and 3.8 assists, which is stronger immediate scoring than his 9.9-point start with Phoenix. But the 2018-19 Wizards finished 32-50 and did not reach the playoffs. Oubre’s restricted-free-agent status explains part of Washington’s decision; it does not change the 96 actual Suns appearances generated by the trade’s central young asset.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The inherited Suns Win verdict, Phoenix A- and Washington D are maintained. The completed two-team deal delivered 96 Suns regular-season Oubre games, Rivers zero Suns appearances after a next-day waiver, and 43 Ariza Wizards starts in an unsuccessful playoff push. The aborted three-team Brooks mix-up is only negotiation context. Actual transactions, receiving-team statistics and the short duration of Washington’s Ariza return support the preserved grade comparison.

sections.heading: Phoenix Paid a Second-Rounder and Cash to Move Cameron Payne
sections.body: On July 17, 2023, Phoenix sent Cameron Payne, a 2025 second-round pick originally belonging to New Orleans, and cash to San Antonio. The Spurs sent back a heavily protected 2024 second-round pick. The Suns were trying to trim their payroll after assembling a top-heavy roster around Devin Booker, Kevin Durant and Bradley Beal; moving Payne's contract was the primary financial rationale. The official NBA trade announcement confirms that all three assets traveled to San Antonio, so the swap must not be simplified into Payne for a future pick. The outgoing 2025 selection was real draft capital, while the protected return carried narrow conditions and uncertain realization.

sections.heading: Payne Never Played a Regular-Season Game for San Antonio
sections.body: San Antonio waived Payne on September 12, 2023, less than two months after the trade and before the 2023-24 regular season. An official Spurs announcement explicitly identifies the July deal and the subsequent waiver. Payne's 2022-23 averages of 10.3 points and 4.5 assists came with Phoenix, not San Antonio; his subsequent seasons with other clubs must not be credited to this trade as Spurs on-court value. The player had been a genuine rotation guard for Phoenix, including a role during the Suns' 2021 Finals run, but this acquiring franchise never received a game from him. That distinction is essential because the inherited Spurs Win verdict otherwise appears to rely on non-existent San Antonio Payne production.

sections.heading: The No. 34 Kalkbrenner Pick Became Part of a Later Spurs Trade
sections.body: The 2025 second-rounder San Antonio acquired was New Orleans' original pick, later exercised at No. 34 and used to select Ryan Kalkbrenner. The chain did not end with Kalkbrenner playing for the Spurs. On July 6, 2024, San Antonio sent that same pick together with Devonte' Graham to Charlotte for cash in a separate salary-clearing transaction. Charlotte ultimately made the No. 34 selection and took the Creighton center in the 2025 draft. Neither Kalkbrenner's Charlotte career nor the entire financial return from moving Graham can be counted as a stand-alone reward for Payne. The Spurs did obtain a transferable pick that had useful bargaining value, but its July 2024 use was one component of a larger package.

sections.heading: Phoenix’s Conditional 2024 Second Never Conveyed
sections.body: The heavily restricted pick Phoenix took back in July 2023 was San Antonio's own 2024 second, protected across picks 31-49 and 55-59. The pick did not convey, according to both clubs' season transaction histories. Phoenix therefore acquired no actual drafted prospect through this particular outgoing Payne package. The Suns still benefited financially by offloading a salary as a separate roster-management choice, but they gave San Antonio cash and a later pick while gaining no draft selection. The inherited A for the Spurs and C+ for Phoenix should be understood as a strongly asset-oriented rating, not a ranking of new team NBA minutes. An independent imported Spurs perspective assigns A/D instead; that absolute grade discrepancy needs reconciliation without changing the verified pick chain.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Spurs Win under the inherited asset-value grading (San Antonio A, Phoenix C+), with no Spurs games from Payne. The 2025 New Orleans-origin second they acquired later became No. 34 Ryan Kalkbrenner, but San Antonio transferred that pick with Devonte' Graham to Charlotte in 2024. The 2024 protected pick Phoenix received did not convey; the Suns instead realized salary relief. The opposing source perspective scores the matchup A/D rather than A/C+, a grade-ledger inconsistency to resolve separately. Do not credit Kalkbrenner's Charlotte minutes or Payne's post-waiver teams to San Antonio.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Deep Dive: Why Spurs Win Fits Phoenix Suns and San Antonio Spurs
featuredDeepDive.intro: Phoenix traded Cameron Payne, cash and New Orleans's future second to San Antonio on July 17, 2023 for a heavily protected Spurs 2024 second. Payne was waived without playing a Spurs NBA game; the 2024 pick did not convey. San Antonio later sent the New Orleans-origin 2025 second with Devonte' Graham to Charlotte, where the selection became No. 34 Ryan Kalkbrenner. The inherited Spurs Win label is an asset-and-financial judgment, not an assertion of direct Spurs player production.

sections.heading: The 2023 Package Sent Payne, Cash and New Orleans's Second to the Spurs
sections.body: On July 17, 2023 Phoenix sent Cameron Payne, cash and a New Orleans-origin 2025 second-round selection to San Antonio in return for the Spurs' heavily protected 2024 second. NBA.com announced all four components when the teams confirmed the deal. Phoenix was moving a reserve guard's salary off a roster built around Devin Booker, Kevin Durant and Bradley Beal. San Antonio was taking the salary and receiving both cash and another draft asset for doing so. This was not a completed player-for-player swap or a trade that brought an active NBA contributor to Phoenix. The incoming Suns pick was subject to extensive protection and could fail to convey. The 2025 selection had no named draftee when the clubs agreed in 2023.

sections.heading: Payne Was Waived Without Playing for San Antonio
sections.body: Payne had played 48 games for Phoenix in 2022-23, averaging 10.3 points and 4.5 assists. After joining San Antonio through the July deal, he was waived on September 12, 2023 before the new NBA season. His direct Spurs NBA regular-season appearance count from this transaction was therefore zero. The official Spurs waiver announcement explicitly links the July acquisition, New Orleans second and original cash consideration. Payne's earlier Phoenix playoff run and later assignments with Milwaukee, Philadelphia and other clubs do not become games for his briefly acquiring franchise. The San Antonio argument for a better asset exchange rests on the second-round right and the economics of accepting Payne's contract, not on imaginary Spurs rotation production from the guard.

sections.heading: San Antonio Passed the Future No. 34 to Charlotte in Another Deal
sections.body: The 2025 second Phoenix sent originally belonged to New Orleans. San Antonio held that right until July 6, 2024, then packaged it with Devonte' Graham in a separate deal to Charlotte for cash and trade flexibility. The Hornets' official release specifies Graham and the New Orleans-origin second, and Charlotte waived Graham the same day. In the 2025 NBA draft the Hornets selected Ryan Kalkbrenner at No. 34. Kalkbrenner did not join San Antonio through this deal, and any subsequent Charlotte statistics belong to the Hornets. The Spurs obtained a draft asset they could use as consideration in another salary-clearing transaction; the later Graham trade included another sizable outgoing contract and should not be credited entirely to the original 2023 Payne package.

sections.heading: Phoenix's Protected 2024 Right Expired Without Conveying
sections.body: Phoenix acquired San Antonio's own 2024 second, protected across selections 31 through 49 and 55 through 59. The protection condition was not met, and the selection did not convey; both 2023-24 team transaction logs confirm that outcome. Phoenix received no rookie or pick from the conditional right, though shedding Payne's contract was the deal's salary-management benefit. The inherited canonical grading is San Antonio A, Phoenix C-plus and Spurs Win, but it is best explained as relative asset and financial optionality. Payne delivered no Spurs games, the eventual No. 34 pick moved onward to Charlotte, and Phoenix's incoming selection expired. These restrictions make the history more nuanced than the old claim that San Antonio acquired an immediate player and Kalkbrenner became its own on-court contributor.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Spurs Win is the preserved archived verdict, with San Antonio A and Phoenix C-plus. The Spurs received cash and the New Orleans-origin 2025 second but zero Payne NBA appearances before his waiver; in July 2024 they sent that second plus Devonte' Graham to Charlotte for cash. Charlotte, not San Antonio, selected Ryan Kalkbrenner at No. 34 in 2025. Phoenix offloaded Payne's contract but its protected 2024 second never conveyed. The A/C-plus gap represents the editorial asset valuation, not realized Payne or Kalkbrenner scoring for the Spurs. The conflicting separate source-perspective grade must be adjudicated rather than silently changed.
