sections.heading: What Changed Hands—and What Lasted
sections.body: Portland sent Dorie Murrey to the Baltimore Bullets on October 22, 1970, receiving a 1971 second-round draft pick. The selection became No. 27, where the Trail Blazers chose Rick Fisher. The modern franchise identifier calls Baltimore the Washington Wizards, but the club was still the Baltimore Bullets when it acquired Murrey. The transaction was a direct player-for-pick exchange, with no additional cash or third team documented.

sections.heading: Why Baltimore Received the Stronger Return
sections.body: Murrey gave Baltimore immediate reserve depth. In 1970–71 he appeared in 69 regular-season games, with averages of 3.2 points and 3.1 rebounds, then played another 16 postseason games during a trip to the NBA Finals. He appeared 51 more times in 1971–72. Those 120 total regular-season games are a traceable return despite Murrey's limited offensive role and Baltimore's far greater team-wide achievement.

sections.heading: The Portland Trail Blazers Franchise's Return
sections.body: Portland exercised the incoming 1971 draft asset at No. 27 on Rick Fisher. Fisher did play professional basketball, appearing in 12 ABA contests, but he never appeared in the NBA or for the Trail Blazers. The difference between an NBA draft selection and a roster contributor is crucial in grading this trade. Portland acquired a legitimate second-round opportunity, yet it did not turn into franchise playing time.

sections.heading: The Washington Wizards' Return
sections.body: The Bullets' B- grade reflects two seasons of useful reserve availability and playoff participation from Murrey. Portland's D+ reflects a properly traced draft choice that generated no NBA games from Fisher. The outcome favors Baltimore without pretending Murrey drove the 1971 Finals run or that the selected Fisher lacked a professional career. Under a realized-return standard, this was Bullets Win rather than a tie.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bullets Win, Baltimore B- and Portland D+. Murrey gave Baltimore 120 regular-season games and 16 postseason appearances over a two-season stint. The Trail Blazers used their 1971 second-rounder on Rick Fisher, who played in the ABA but never appeared in the NBA. Baltimore obtained measurable reserve depth, while Portland's drafted return produced no NBA minutes.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Dorie Murrey's 120 Baltimore Games Versus Portland's No. 27 Pick
featuredDeepDive.intro: Portland exchanged Dorie Murrey for a 1971 second-round selection that became No. 27, Rick Fisher. Murrey supplied the Baltimore Bullets 120 regular-season appearances over two seasons and 16 playoff games during the 1971 Finals run. Fisher played 12 professional ABA games but never appeared in the NBA. Baltimore got the stronger realized return, though Murrey was a reserve rather than the principal reason for the club's Finals berth.

sections.heading: What Each Team Actually Received
sections.body: Baltimore and Portland's transaction records date their exchange to October 22, 1970. The Bullets received Dorie Murrey, and the Trail Blazers received the selection that would become No. 27 in the 1971 NBA Draft. The modern Wizards franchise label describes the Bullets' institutional successor, but an accurate historical discussion should call the team Baltimore at the time of the deal.

sections.heading: What Portland Trail Blazers Realized
sections.body: Murrey played 69 Baltimore games during 1970–71, averaging just over ten minutes per contest. He appeared in 16 postseason games as the Bullets reached the Finals, although those reserve appearances should not be equated with a star's influence. He returned for 51 games the following season. The combined 120 regular-season appearances and postseason availability show measurable NBA service from the player Baltimore acquired.

sections.heading: What Baltimore Bullets Realized
sections.body: Rick Fisher was selected at No. 27 by Portland in 1971. His professional appearances came in the ABA, where he played 12 games, rather than the NBA. The pick's correct identity does not create a single Trail Blazers appearance or an NBA player in the club's record. Portland did not receive an additional veteran alongside the draft right, so the evaluation of its side stays attached to that unsuccessful NBA roster conversion.

sections.heading: Baltimore B- Versus Portland D+: Realized Playing Value
sections.body: Neither incoming asset became a star. Baltimore nevertheless acquired 120 regular-season games plus 16 postseason appearances during a conference championship campaign, and Portland's No. 27 draft choice yielded no NBA production. The Bullets should not receive all the credit for team success, but they received the only realized NBA playing return. Their B- versus Portland's D+ captures this limited but defensible advantage.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bullets Win, B- Baltimore / D+ Portland. The Bullets acquired Dorie Murrey for 120 regular-season games and 16 playoff appearances. Portland selected Rick Fisher with the No. 27 pick in the 1971 NBA Draft, but he never played in the league or for the Trail Blazers. The distinction supports a Baltimore edge without equating Murrey's limited bench role with the whole team's 1971 Finals success.

sections.heading: The Dispersal Draft Pick Portland Bought
sections.body: The August 5, 1976 exchange did not deliver Maurice Lucas as a veteran contracted to Atlanta. It delivered the No. 2 choice in the ABA dispersal draft, a special selection process after the merger. Portland sent Steve Hawes and Geoff Petrie to the Hawks for that right and chose Lucas. The precise mechanism is part of why the front office deserves credit: it identified the player the team wanted and secured the pick needed to acquire him. Atlanta received two NBA veterans, one of whom was already dealing with a serious knee injury. This was not an ordinary future college draft pick, and treating it that way would misstate the risk each franchise took. Contemporary team transaction ledgers record the pieces of the original deal.

sections.heading: A First-Season All-Star and the 1977 Championship
sections.body: Lucas became a productive complement to Bill Walton as soon as he arrived in Portland. He averaged 20.2 points and 11.2 rebounds during the 1976-77 regular season and earned an All-Star selection. With Jack Ramsay coaching a passing-oriented team, the Trail Blazers won 49 games and eventually beat Philadelphia in six games for the NBA championship. Lucas averaged 19.7 points and 10.7 rebounds in that Finals series, helping establish a physical frontcourt alongside Walton. This was realized value in the first season, not a hypothetical argument about future development. The new forward remained an All-Star in each of his first three Portland seasons, providing continuity after the title. The pick's value therefore came from immediate contention and several more seasons of high-level play.

sections.heading: The Atlanta Return Was Uneven, Not Worthless
sections.body: Geoff Petrie brought a Rookie of the Year award and two All-Star selections to the transaction, but his damaged knee meant he never played for the Hawks. Steve Hawes gave Atlanta considerably more. He appeared in 405 regular-season games over six seasons, including a 1977-78 campaign in which he averaged 12.7 points and 9.2 rebounds. Calling that entire return a failure ignores useful seasons from a veteran big man. It also would be incorrect to grade Petrie as though he supplied his old Portland production in Atlanta. The inherited grades capture both sides: Portland earns A-plus for acquiring a championship contributor through a scarce draft right, while Atlanta earns B for Hawes's durable service despite the injury that eliminated the other half of its package.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Portland Trail Blazers Win. Portland A+ for the ABA dispersal pick used to select Maurice Lucas, an immediate All-Star and 1977 champion. Atlanta B for six seasons and 405 games from Steve Hawes; Geoff Petrie never played for the Hawks after the trade because of his knee injury.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Maurice Lucas and the 1976 ABA Dispersal Draft: Complete Trade Impact
featuredDeepDive.intro: The August 1976 trade gave Portland the No. 2 ABA dispersal pick and ultimately Maurice Lucas. He became a vital 1977 champion, while Steve Hawes gave Atlanta a durable but less influential return.

sections.heading: Lucas and Walton Changed the Ceiling
sections.body: Bill Walton was the interior organizing force for Portland, but one great center did not automatically make the Trail Blazers champions. The dispersal pick added Maurice Lucas, whose scoring, rebounding and physical play gave the roster a second highly productive frontcourt presence. In 1976-77 Lucas averaged 20.2 points and 11.2 boards, then contributed 19.7 points and 10.7 rebounds per game in the six-game Finals victory over Philadelphia. His first season ended with an NBA championship and an All-Star selection. This is an unusually persuasive peak-return case: the decisive basketball results followed almost immediately after the August transaction. Portland did not receive the entire championship roster in this trade, but the new forward filled a specific need on a club ready for a major step forward.

sections.heading: Six Atlanta Seasons Give Hawes Real Value
sections.body: Hawes stayed with the Hawks for six seasons after arriving from Portland, playing a total of 405 regular-season games. His most productive Atlanta year was 1977-78, when he posted 12.7 points and 9.2 rebounds per game. Those numbers establish a tangible return, especially compared with the other incoming veteran. Geoff Petrie was a former Rookie of the Year and All-Star, but his knee injury prevented him from appearing in any Atlanta games. The value of the transaction cannot be calculated by adding Petrie's previous reputation to Hawes's subsequent production. Portland enjoyed Lucas's early All-Star run and a championship; Atlanta obtained a useful contributor with a much lower ceiling. The B grade represents the healthy portion of that trade package rather than a belief the Hawks equaled the Trail Blazers.

sections.heading: The Finals Were a Direct Test of the Selection
sections.body: Many major trades are evaluated through a series of later asset conversions. Portland did not need a complicated chain to establish its return. The club bought the second ABA dispersal choice, selected Lucas and won the NBA championship the following spring. His 1977 Finals averages of 19.7 points and 10.7 rebounds underscore how much of his value survived into the season's most demanding games. Walton and the rest of Jack Ramsay's roster were indispensable, so Lucas should not be credited with every win. Yet the title provides direct proof of the forward's contribution to the franchise's defining team achievement. Atlanta's durable Hawes return is relevant to the opposing grade, but no equivalent championship impact resulted from Hawes and the injured Petrie as a pair.

sections.heading: Why This Was Not a Routine Draft-Pick Trade
sections.body: The second selection in the 1976 ABA dispersal draft represented access to established professional talent as the ABA's remaining player pool entered the NBA. Atlanta controlled the choice; Portland secured it for Hawes and Petrie and used it to bring in Lucas. The transaction should be recorded as a pick exchange rather than as Atlanta directly trading a signed Lucas contract. Unlike a protected future selection, the asset was a specific near-term opportunity that Portland had to exercise. This distinction keeps the historical ledger faithful to the league's merger-era rules and explains the club's conviction about the acquisition. The team transaction histories and Lucas's career record supply the backbone of the account, with the 1976-77 season review documenting what followed after he joined Walton in Portland.

sections.heading: The Two Grades and the Long-Term Memory
sections.body: Lucas's first three Portland seasons each produced an All-Star selection, and the franchise eventually retired his No. 20. Those markers help explain why the 1976 draft-right purchase still belongs among Portland's consequential transactions. The 1977 NBA title gives the A-plus grade its clearest basis. Atlanta's counterweight was Hawes, who supplied 405 games and several productive seasons after the trade. Petrie's knee kept him from providing the other expected contribution. Describing the Hawks' return as a C would overlook Hawes's real usefulness and contradict the preserved B grade in the transaction ledger. The outcome is still an unmistakable Portland Trail Blazers Win: a franchise-defining title contributor arrived through a unique draft opportunity, while Atlanta's actual return was useful but much less influential.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Portland A+, Atlanta B. Maurice Lucas immediately helped Portland win the 1977 title. Steve Hawes gave Atlanta six seasons of service, but Geoff Petrie never appeared for the Hawks. The historical outcome favors Portland decisively without erasing the value of Hawes.

sections.heading: Gale and a First-Round Right Went to Portland
sections.body: On December 19, 1980, Portland sent guard Ron Brewer to San Antonio in exchange for Mike Gale and a 1982 first-round pick. Gale appeared in 42 games for the Trail Blazers, producing 179 points and 70 assists in 476 minutes. The first-round right was the more consequential asset, but following its destination requires distinguishing the selection from the player eventually drafted. Portland did not select Ricky Pierce at No. 18. It moved that pick to Detroit in another trade before the 1982 draft. Keeping the two transactions separate is essential to understanding why this 1980 exchange paid off for Portland.

sections.heading: The Pick Became Kenny Carr for the Blazers
sections.body: Portland traded the 1982 first-round right to Detroit for Kenny Carr on June 23, 1982. Detroit later used the pick at No. 18 on Ricky Pierce, whose strong NBA career happened elsewhere. Carr, by contrast, actually played 316 regular-season games for Portland over five seasons and started 187. He accumulated 3,903 points and 2,545 rebounds with the Trail Blazers. In 1983-84 he appeared in 82 games, started 57 and averaged 15.6 points and 7.8 rebounds. The pick's value to Portland is the documented exchange for Carr, not Pierce's later Sixth Man awards. Carr's multi-season frontcourt production supplies the clearest source-backed foundation for the Blazers' A+ hindsight grade.

sections.heading: Gale Produced Two More Draft Assets
sections.body: Gale's Portland tenure lasted just 42 games, but his outgoing transaction preserved a second value path. On June 8, 1981, the Blazers sent Gale to Golden State for second-round selections tied to the 1982 and 1985 drafts. The earlier pick was later used on Audie Norris and the latter linked to Mike Smrek. Those draft rights were real consideration acquired because Portland held Gale, yet the career achievements of every later pick recipient cannot be automatically attributed to Gale or to the first deal. The precise point is that Portland obtained both limited immediate guard minutes and further transferable draft value in addition to the major Kenny Carr branch.

sections.heading: Brewer Had Value, But Not the Larger Return
sections.body: San Antonio played Ron Brewer for 71 regular-season games, 46 in 1980-81 and 25 the next season. He scored 425 points in the first stint and 444 in the second, supplying genuine backcourt offense. The Spurs then used Brewer with Reggie Johnson and cash in a December 23, 1981 trade to Cleveland for Mike Mitchell and Roger Phegley. Mitchell's later scoring value is part of a subsequent multi-asset exchange; it should not be credited entirely to Brewer. This supports a real Spurs return and argues against the old D grade. Still, Portland's 316-game Carr conversion plus Gale's downstream picks produced more separately attributable value, supporting the canonical Blazers Win with Portland A+ and San Antonio B.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Blazers Win — Portland A+, San Antonio B. Mike Gale contributed 42 Portland games, was exchanged for two later second-round draft rights, and the first-round pick became Kenny Carr through a subsequent deal with Detroit. Carr logged 316 games and 2,545 rebounds for Portland. San Antonio obtained 71 Ron Brewer games and used him in a later package for Mike Mitchell and Roger Phegley, so its return was not zero. Ricky Pierce was drafted by Detroit after Portland traded away the selection; his subsequent career cannot be counted as a Trail Blazers return.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The Kenny Carr Pick Chain Behind Portland’s 1980 Ron Brewer Trade
featuredDeepDive.intro: The 1980 Ron Brewer trade has an easy-to-miss archival trap: Detroit selected Ricky Pierce with the draft pick Portland initially acquired from San Antonio. That does not make Pierce a Trail Blazer. Before the draft, Portland transferred the same first-round right to Detroit for Kenny Carr. Carr gave Portland years of frontcourt contribution, while Mike Gale provided a short spell at guard and later brought additional picks. San Antonio's return was useful, too; Brewer played 71 games before going out in a package for Mike Mitchell. Following each asset's actual route explains why Portland won without erasing what the Spurs obtained.

sections.heading: A First That Was Traded Before Draft Night
sections.body: The original consideration from San Antonio included a 1982 first-round selection. Transaction summaries that identify it only as No. 18 Ricky Pierce collapse multiple moves into one. The Blazers used the pick as a trade asset, sending it to Detroit on June 23, 1982 for Kenny Carr. Detroit exercised the right to select Pierce. Those are different franchise decisions with different realized returns. Historical scoring should credit Portland with Carr's contribution and Detroit with its own draft use, avoiding retrospective double counting. The underlying source trail is traceable in both franchises' 1982 transaction histories.

sections.heading: Carr, Not Pierce, Built Portland’s Long Tail
sections.body: Carr played 316 games in five Trail Blazers seasons, started 187 and totaled 3,903 points with 2,545 rebounds. He was capable of regular frontcourt production, including 15.6 points and 7.8 boards a game in 1983-84. Those totals are direct Portland value from the first-round asset obtained in 1980. Pierce's excellent later career is an interesting counterfactual and belongs to Detroit's use of the pick, not Portland's return. Crediting Carr's actual time in a Blazers uniform makes the deal look strong without pretending Portland rostered every player associated with the pick.

sections.heading: The Small but Traceable Mike Gale Branch
sections.body: Gale brought immediate reserve minutes after the December transaction but stayed for only 42 Portland appearances. The club then sent him to Golden State in June 1981 for two second-round selections, one in 1982 and another in 1985. These rights gave the Blazers more tradable consideration and show why short-lived players can still retain asset value. At the same time, claims that every later result from those selections flowed solely from this deal would exaggerate the connection. The safe interpretation is one brief playing contribution followed by an independently documented pair of draft rights.

sections.heading: San Antonio’s Ron Brewer and Mitchell Link
sections.body: Brewer contributed 71 games to the Spurs before appearing in a December 1981 outgoing package with Reggie Johnson and cash. San Antonio received Mike Mitchell and Roger Phegley from Cleveland in that separate deal. Mitchell would become a key Spurs scorer, but the return cannot be assigned wholly to Brewer because Johnson and money were also given up. This qualification distinguishes a usable San Antonio result from an inflated account of Brewer singlehandedly securing Mitchell. The Spurs' B in the canonical ledger recognizes their meaningful but less extensive asset history; Portland's A+ corresponds to Carr and the Gale branch.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Portland won, A+ to B. Brewer gave San Antonio 71 games and helped make a later multi-asset exchange possible. The Blazers received 42 Gale games and two subsequent second-round picks, but their largest direct gain came from converting the 1982 first-round right into Kenny Carr before the draft. Carr's 316 Portland appearances and 2,545 rebounds were the lasting return, not Ricky Pierce's Detroit-origin career.

sections.heading: Start With What Changed Hands
sections.body: Portland acquired Steve Johnson from San Antonio on June 19, 1986. The Spurs received Mychal Thompson and the rights to Larry Krystkowiak. Those rights were a separate asset, not another NBA veteran automatically joining the Spurs on the date of the exchange. Portland concentrated its return in one established center, while San Antonio took Thompson and the possibility of realizing future value from Krystkowiak's rights. The transaction was therefore a two-asset return for the Spurs against one active player for the Trail Blazers.

sections.heading: The Case Behind the Grades
sections.body: The archive grades San Antonio A and Portland C+, producing a Spurs Win verdict. Thompson was a veteran with direct basketball value for the Spurs, while Krystkowiak's rights created additional flexibility whose realization depended on later action. Portland's acquisition of Johnson still carried a specific roster purpose, so calling the entire incoming package worthless would be inaccurate. The grade difference reflects the site's retrospective judgment of those precise returns instead of a rule that two assets always outrank one.

sections.heading: Why One Package Finished Ahead
sections.body: One of the easiest mistakes in a short trade recap is to treat every asset listed with a player's name as an immediately usable player. Steve Johnson was Portland's acquired center. San Antonio's incoming pair contained Thompson and the rights to Krystkowiak; the latter wasn't equivalent to guaranteed NBA minutes on June 19. Neither side received a first-round pick or a cash amount in this ledger. Evaluating the eventual returns means distinguishing Thompson's established player status from the speculative quality of those rights.

sections.heading: What the Losing Return Still Contained
sections.body: The teams made different choices within the same 1986 frontcourt market. Portland chose a single identifiable NBA center, Johnson. San Antonio accepted Thompson plus the rights to another player, giving the Spurs a second possible avenue for basketball value. The source histories for Portland and San Antonio record the exchange under June 19, whereas later seasons determine what either team gained. The A/C+ pairing is an outcome-oriented assessment and should not be used to claim either club knew exactly how those returns would unfold.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Spurs Win — San Antonio A, Portland C+. The Trail Blazers received Steve Johnson; the Spurs received Mychal Thompson plus the rights to Larry Krystkowiak. The different certainty of an active player and a rights claim is essential to the verdict. No extra pick or cash asset is listed, and the grade gap concerns the completed value of these three documented pieces.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Portland Trail Blazers–San Antonio Spurs: June 1986 Johnson–Thompson Exchange
featuredDeepDive.intro: The June 19, 1986 Portland–San Antonio trade exchanged Steve Johnson for Mychal Thompson and the rights to Larry Krystkowiak. The asset types were different: Johnson and Thompson were established NBA players, while the rights created a future possibility rather than automatic playing production. The archive records a Spurs Win, grading San Antonio A and Portland C+. A useful retrospective explains the mismatch between direct roster value and rights value before trying to decide which club got the better basketball return.

sections.heading: Where the Durable Value Came From
sections.body: The defining transaction structure is Portland's one-player return against San Antonio's combination of a veteran and rights. Johnson went to the Trail Blazers, Thompson went to the Spurs, and Krystkowiak's rights also moved to San Antonio. Rights are a claim that can produce value only through later personnel decisions; they should not be reported as a separate guaranteed roster contributor. The grade comparison makes sense only after all three original assets have been identified and their different levels of certainty preserved.

sections.heading: The Role of the Lesser Pieces
sections.body: San Antonio had two paths to potential return. Thompson represented an immediately understood NBA playing asset, while the rights to Larry Krystkowiak supplied another option. Portland had a narrower, more certain basketball return in Steve Johnson. That division shows why transaction counts alone are an inadequate evaluation tool: the meaning of receiving rights differs materially from acquiring a veteran player, even though both appear as items in an asset list.

sections.heading: Separating Motive From Result
sections.body: From Portland's perspective the attraction was Johnson, a center the club could place within its roster plans without waiting for a rights decision. The cost was giving up Thompson and the contractual opportunity attached to Krystkowiak. The Spurs chose that two-part package and accepted the uncertainty surrounding whether those rights would become useful. The retrospective A for San Antonio and C+ for Portland judges the completed consequences, not just the relative experience of the players on trade day.

sections.heading: What the Grade Gap Measures
sections.body: Every named asset belongs to the June 1986 exchange, but not every later episode in these players' careers does. Thompson's other NBA destinations, Johnson's future roster moves and any later activity involving Krystkowiak must not be credited automatically to this transaction. The supported facts are Johnson to Portland and Thompson plus Krystkowiak rights to San Antonio. Within those boundaries, the recorded Spurs Win verdict and A/C+ difference express a clear, though not absolute, advantage for the Spurs' return.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: San Antonio's A compared with Portland's C+ reflects Thompson and Krystkowiak's rights against the Trail Blazers' acquisition of Johnson. This is a two-part package evaluated against one established center, not proof that the Spurs instantly acquired two active NBA players. The archive's Spurs Win label should follow those original assets and their realized value instead of unrelated later franchise outcomes.

sections.heading: Portland Obtained Its Future Starting Center in December 1986
sections.body: On December 18, 1986, Portland traded rookie Walter Berry to San Antonio for rookie center Kevin Duckworth. Berry had entered the league as the No. 14 selection and a celebrated college scorer, while Duckworth had been taken at No. 33 in the second round. The deal contained no additional draft picks or cash to complicate the player-for-player accounting. Portland wanted size after injuries reduced its center depth, especially with Sam Bowie struggling to stay on the court. San Antonio hoped Berry's scoring pedigree would become a better return than an inexperienced big man. Neither team was exchanging an established All-Star. The historical imbalance emerged from what the two rookies contributed after joining their new rosters.

sections.heading: Duckworth Developed into a Two-Time Portland All-Star
sections.body: Duckworth grew quickly into Portland's starting-center role and won the NBA Most Improved Player award for 1987-88. He made the All-Star team in 1989 and again in 1991, supplying interior size and a dependable midrange touch alongside Clyde Drexler and Terry Porter. The club reached the NBA Finals in 1990 and 1992 with Duckworth in the frontcourt, although Portland lost those series to Detroit and Chicago respectively. Basketball-Reference and the Portland alumni material document his seasons and recognition. His skill set relieved some of the center uncertainty that had affected the roster earlier in the decade. A player acquired for another rookie became a core rotation member through multiple serious title attempts, rather than a brief developmental gamble.

sections.heading: Berry's San Antonio Return Lasted Only 64 Games
sections.body: San Antonio acquired Berry for the scoring potential he had shown before the 1986 draft, but the NBA return was sharply limited. He appeared in 64 Spurs regular-season games before his stay ended. He did not deliver the multi-year starting-center value that Duckworth later supplied to Portland, and the available transaction history does not establish another lasting Spurs asset from the exchange. Berry's earlier college honors explain why the Spurs considered the swap; they are not additional NBA production for San Antonio. His later career elsewhere likewise cannot be counted as games earned by the Spurs. The inherited F grade compares a short first-season stint against six-plus Portland seasons from the player San Antonio surrendered.

sections.heading: The Opportunity Opened While Sam Bowie Was Injured
sections.body: Portland's center rotation had become unstable as Sam Bowie dealt with major injuries. Duckworth's arrival supplied a physically large option whom the coaching staff could put on the floor regularly and allow to develop in games. The Blazers eventually built an effective combination of Duckworth at center and talented perimeter players around him, including Drexler and Porter. That opportunity was not guaranteed on trade day, but the club created a role that allowed his shooting touch and size to be useful. San Antonio had chosen the more acclaimed college player in Berry, yet his fit and durability did not deliver equivalent professional minutes. The outcome reflects actual development and roster usage, not simply which rookie had better publicity in 1986.

sections.heading: Portland Later Received Harvey Grant for Duckworth
sections.body: The direct NBA playing return did not end in Portland's 1992 Finals season. After Duckworth's long run, the Blazers subsequently traded him to Washington in a separate transaction that brought Harvey Grant back. That follow-up is part of the acquired player's traceable roster value, though Grant was not in the original December 1986 exchange with San Antonio. Berry did not leave the Spurs with a comparable sequence of seasons and later trade compensation. The two-team original package is therefore simple: Portland acquired a future two-time All-Star and eventually retained an opportunity to convert him again; San Antonio received 64 games from a highly regarded but short-lived player. None of Duckworth's games after leaving Portland are credited as Portland roster production.

sections.heading: Blazers Win Reflects Durable On-Court and Trade Value
sections.body: Portland's A+ and San Antonio's F are retained because the receiving teams realized dramatically different basketball returns. Duckworth won Most Improved Player, became an All-Star twice and started at center during the Blazers' 1990 and 1992 Finals runs. Berry provided 64 Spurs regular-season appearances and no similarly durable San Antonio role. The trade was not a sure thing in 1986: Berry was the higher draft choice and highly decorated prospect. But the grade describes what the clubs received, not a retroactive assertion that Portland knew every future result. The later Harvey Grant deal is an additional traceable Duckworth branch, not part of what San Antonio originally sent. This is a decisive Blazers Win on franchise-specific evidence.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Blazers Win — Portland A+, San Antonio F. Kevin Duckworth grew into a Portland starting center, won Most Improved Player, earned two All-Star selections and appeared on the 1990 and 1992 Finals teams. Walter Berry played just 64 NBA games for the Spurs. Portland later traded Duckworth for Harvey Grant in a separate deal, extending the original asset's traceable value.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Portland Traded Walter Berry for Kevin Duckworth and Two Finals Runs
featuredDeepDive.intro: Portland exchanged Walter Berry for Kevin Duckworth on December 18, 1986, a straight rookie-for-rookie swap. Duckworth became a two-time All-Star, won Most Improved Player and helped anchor the Blazers teams that reached the 1990 and 1992 NBA Finals. Berry provided only 64 San Antonio regular-season games. This review keeps the later Duckworth-for-Harvey Grant transaction separate while accounting for the value Portland retained from its original acquisition.

sections.heading: A Direct Rookie-for-Rookie Deal with No Hidden Picks
sections.body: The Los Angeles Times covered the December 18, 1986 exchange as Portland sending Walter Berry to San Antonio for Kevin Duckworth. Berry was a No. 14 draft choice that year, while Duckworth came out of the second round at No. 33. Neither side obtained another player, a draft selection or reported cash through the original transaction. This matters because other Portland roster changes in the 1980s can easily be mistaken for components of this particular exchange. The Blazers had immediate need for a center and accepted the risk of developing Duckworth. The Spurs were giving up a big man for the prospect with the higher draft profile. The two clubs made different evaluations of rookies before either had established a long NBA record.

sections.heading: 1987-88 Most Improved Honors Started Duckworth's Rise
sections.body: Duckworth made Portland's acquisition pay off when he grew into the center position and earned NBA Most Improved Player recognition for 1987-88. By the end of the following season he was an All-Star, and another selection came in 1991. The Trail Blazers could surround their wings and guards with a large center capable of scoring from inside or with a soft jumper. Duckworth did not become Portland's franchise leading scorer, but he filled an important structural need during a period when the club was developing into a conference contender. The grade reflects years of actually played Blazers basketball, including seasons in which the team could plan around a reliable starting center instead of hoping an injured veteran returned.

sections.heading: Two Finals Teams Used the Center Acquired for Berry
sections.body: Portland advanced to the 1990 NBA Finals against Detroit and returned in 1992 against Chicago. Both runs included Duckworth as part of a core with Clyde Drexler and Terry Porter. The Blazers did not win either series, so the trade review cannot convert two Finals appearances into championships. It can recognize that a player obtained for Berry supplied real starting-center minutes on teams good enough to contend for the title. The contrast with San Antonio is direct: Berry's 64 Spurs appearances did not grow into a sustained playoff role for the team that received him. Postseason value is credited to the organization that employed Duckworth during those years, not to another club associated with his later NBA career.

sections.heading: Why the Spurs' Draft Reputation Argument Failed in Practice
sections.body: At the time of the trade, Berry had entered the league with stronger college acclaim and a higher draft position than Duckworth. San Antonio therefore had a plausible reason to prefer the forward's scoring upside rather than the second-round big man. After the trade, however, Berry's NBA tenure with the Spurs stopped after 64 games. Portland gave Duckworth a meaningful center role and received an All-Star by 1989. This evaluation does not assert that a better development plan would automatically have turned Berry into Duckworth, because the records do not establish that counterfactual. What is documented is the uneven realized playing return: an emerging Blazers starter versus a brief Spurs tenure. The difference supports the inherited A+/F grade spread without inventing unoffered 1986 alternatives.

sections.heading: The Later Harvey Grant Transaction Is a Separate Return
sections.body: Duckworth eventually left Portland in a later transaction with Washington that brought Harvey Grant to the Trail Blazers. This downstream conversion is relevant to the value of an asset Portland had acquired in 1986, but the separate deal cannot be merged into the original rookie swap. The December package remained one-for-one: Duckworth from San Antonio and Berry from Portland. Duckworth's Portland achievements already justify a substantial advantage—Most Improved Player, two All-Star selections and two NBA Finals teams. The Harvey Grant branch simply shows that Portland still had tradable value after those seasons. Berry's 64 Spurs games did not produce an equivalent documented chain for San Antonio. Keeping both transactions distinct makes the final accounting more precise.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The one-for-one December 1986 exchange strongly favored Portland. A No. 33 rookie, Duckworth, became a two-time Blazers All-Star and center on two Finals teams; No. 14 Walter Berry contributed only 64 San Antonio games. The later Harvey Grant return came from a separate Portland-Washington transaction. The A+/F grades and Blazers Win reflect real team-specific returns, not projected draft reputation.

sections.heading: August 1990 Brought Ainge to Portland for Four Assets
sections.body: Portland acquired Danny Ainge from Sacramento on August 1, 1990 for guard Byron Irvin, its 1991 first-round selection, a 1992 second-round choice originally belonging to Chicago, and cash. The Trail Blazers' official media guide lists all four outgoing components and identifies what the draft rights ultimately became: 1991 No. 27 Pete Chilcutt and 1992 No. 54 Brett Roberts. Some abbreviated historical transaction databases omit cash, but the team's own transaction history specifically includes it; there is no credible published dollar amount in this source packet, so none should be manufactured. Ainge was a veteran shooter and secondary ball handler, not a first-year rookie. Portland paid in future options to strengthen a contender already built around Clyde Drexler and Terry Porter.

sections.heading: Ainge Delivered Two Full Portland Rotation Seasons
sections.body: Ainge was not a symbolic acquisition for Portland's bench. In 1990-91 he played 80 regular-season games, averaged approximately 11.1 points and 3.6 assists, and shot 40.6 percent on three-pointers. The Blazers reached the Western Conference Finals but lost to the Lakers. In 1991-92 he played 81 more regular-season games, averaging about 9.7 points and 2.5 assists, while the club returned to the NBA Finals against Michael Jordan's Bulls. His shooting and ability to handle the ball behind Drexler and Porter were measurable additions rather than an abstract championship pedigree. His 1984 and 1986 Boston titles preceded the transaction and should not count as Portland trophies.

sections.heading: Irvin's Kings Stop Was Brief and the Picks Took Separate Paths
sections.body: Sacramento did not retain Byron Irvin through an extended rebuild. On October 30, 1990, less than three months after acquiring him, the Kings sent him to Washington for guard Steve Colter, according to a contemporaneous Washington Post account. That later exchange deserves its own transaction date. Sacramento also obtained Portland's 1991 first, eventually No. 27 Pete Chilcutt, and a Chicago-origin 1992 second that became No. 54 Brett Roberts. Neither right was a lottery pick, and the fact that a player was selected with a pick doesn't prove an especially valuable NBA career for the original receiving team. Cash was a real incoming piece under Portland's official history, but its exact amount and eventual deployment remain unverified here.

sections.heading: Blazers A Against Kings C-Plus Without Rewriting Grades
sections.body: The canonical archive records Blazers Win, Portland A and Sacramento C-plus, and those are preserved. The Blazers obtained 161 regular-season games from Ainge over two seasons and a veteran role that supported consecutive deep playoff runs, culminating in the 1992 Finals. The Kings received Irvin, moved him to Washington during the opening weeks of the 1990-91 season and also acquired two later draft rights plus cash. Sacramento's future options were not imaginary, but neither the No. 27 first nor No. 54 second matched Ainge's immediate contender usage in the documented window. A hidden partnerAggregate grade of D differs from the stored team C-plus; that provenance discrepancy must be recorded separately, not quietly rewritten during originality repairs.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The stored result remains Blazers Win, Portland A and Sacramento C-plus. Ainge played 80 and 81 regular-season games for Portland in 1990-91 and 1991-92, helped its reserve backcourt and joined its 1992 Finals run. Sacramento received Irvin, traded him to Washington that October, and held draft rights that became No. 27 Pete Chilcutt and No. 54 Brett Roberts, plus cash documented in Portland's official media guide. The partnerAggregate D discrepancy is held for grading provenance, and no unsupported cash total is asserted.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Danny Ainge to Portland in 1990: Two Picks, Cash and a Contender's Window
featuredDeepDive.intro: Portland acquired veteran Danny Ainge from Sacramento on August 1, 1990, paying Byron Irvin, a 1991 first, Chicago's 1992 second and cash. Ainge played nearly every game in both of his Blazers seasons and contributed to a 1992 Finals club. Irvin was traded to Washington before the Kings' 1990-91 season developed, and the picks became No. 27 Pete Chilcutt and No. 54 Brett Roberts. The archive's grades stay unchanged while the conflicting Sacramento partnerAggregate field receives a separate provenance hold.

sections.heading: The Trail Blazers' Own Media Guide Resolves the Cash Question
sections.body: The 2022-23 Portland media guide retrospectively identifies the complete August 1, 1990 transaction: Byron Irvin, the Blazers' 1991 first, Chicago's 1992 second and cash for Danny Ainge. Basketball-Reference's shorter transaction line lists Irvin and the two picks but not cash. This is a case where two legitimate source presentations have different levels of detail, so a careful review should retain the cash component supported by the team's original transaction history without inventing an amount. The 1991 and 1992 selections were separate rights, not two players sent directly to Portland. The transaction added a veteran to an established contender; it didn't move Drexler or Porter or create a new unrelated third-party trade.

sections.heading: Ainge Became a Reliable Reserve Behind Drexler and Porter
sections.body: Portland's competitive context is unusually clear. It already had an accomplished backcourt led by Clyde Drexler and Terry Porter, and Ainge arrived as an experienced guard who could spell both while extending the perimeter attack. His 1990-91 line of 80 games, 11.1 points, 3.6 assists and 40.6-percent three-point shooting demonstrates rotation value. In 1991-92 he played 81 games at 9.7 points and appeared in 21 postseason games on the Blazers' run to the Finals. The Finals loss to Chicago was a collective outcome, not something to count as a personal championship. Nevertheless, adding a durable veteran for two seasons gave Portland exactly the type of present-day roster utility it sought by spending distant draft selections.

sections.heading: Irvin Was Quickly Traded Again; the Picks Were Not Stars by Default
sections.body: Sacramento's return can be tracked rather than described as a generic pile of future capital. Irvin had been Portland's 1989 first-round pick, but the Kings exchanged him for Steve Colter on October 30, 1990, before Irvin became a long-term Sacramento regular. The 1991 first arrived at No. 27 and became Pete Chilcutt; the 1992 second was Chicago-origin No. 54 Brett Roberts. These are actual selected slots, not hypothetical lottery stars the Kings could have obtained with better scouting. They make the Sacramento package real and document its limits. The cash addition should also be acknowledged despite no verified exact dollar amount. None of those pieces should be misrepresented as a player the Blazers subsequently received.

sections.heading: Why the Stored Grades Diverge Despite Both Teams Receiving Assets
sections.body: Portland A and Sacramento C-plus are the canonical grades, alongside Blazers Win. The alternative stored partnerAggregate D conflicts with the explicit Sacramento grade and should remain a separate source-provenance question. On the court, Portland received nearly two full Ainge seasons, dependable three-point shooting and reserve guard production on clubs that made the 1991 conference finals and 1992 NBA Finals. Sacramento used Irvin as a short-lived transaction asset and received a late first, a late second and cash. An NBA pick's later selected name is an important trace, but treating every low selection as a guaranteed starter would overvalue the Kings' compensation. Those facts explain Portland's more immediate return without invalidating the Kings' future-facing strategy on trade day.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Blazers Win, Portland A and Sacramento C-plus are the stored verdict and team grades. Ainge provided 161 Portland regular-season games in 1990-91 and 1991-92, including a reserve playmaking and outside-shooting role as the Blazers reached the West Finals and NBA Finals in consecutive years. Sacramento took Irvin, sent him to Washington for Steve Colter that October, and received a 1991 first at No. 27, a 1992 second at No. 54 and cash. Portland's own media guide independently confirms the cash despite shorter statistical transaction lists omitting it. The cash amount is not established, and a conflicting aggregate D value is not grounds to silently change the Kings' explicit C-plus. These exact outcomes, rather than imagined draft steals, explain Portland's advantage.

sections.heading: The Bullets Sent Rasheed Wallace to Portland in a Four-Player Swap
sections.body: On July 15, 1996, Washington traded Rasheed Wallace and Mitchell Butler to Portland for Rod Strickland and Harvey Grant. United Press International's same-day report and contemporary Washington coverage identify those four players without draft selections, cash or a third team. Washington was still called the Bullets; the current trade database uses the Wizards franchise label. Wallace was a 21-year-old former No. 4 pick with a promising rookie season, while Strickland was an established starting point guard. The deal was not a straight Wallace-for-Strickland exchange, even though those two players accounted for most of the eventual court value. Keeping Butler and Grant visible also avoids confusing the 1996 swap with Portland's later separate trades.

sections.heading: Washington Needed the Kind of Lead Guard Strickland Already Was
sections.body: The Bullets had Chris Webber and Juwan Howard in their frontcourt but lacked a dependable creator to run the attack. Washington general manager Wes Unseld said the acquisition upgraded the backcourt, and coach Jim Lynam emphasized Strickland's penetration and ability to set up teammates. Strickland had averaged 18.7 points and 9.6 assists in 67 Portland games the season before the exchange, giving the Bullets a proven, immediate answer. His relationship with coach P.J. Carlesimo had also deteriorated, making a change understandable for Portland. Washington was not gambling on an untested draft right; it received an accomplished veteran who could improve an existing offense from opening night.

sections.heading: Wallace Became the Long-Term Portland Frontcourt Piece
sections.body: Wallace developed from a recent Washington lottery selection into one of Portland's most important forwards. During his Trail Blazers tenure he earned two All-Star selections and played a central part on teams that reached the 1999 and 2000 Western Conference Finals. His scoring touch, defensive versatility and ability to operate away from the basket made him more than a conventional low-post player. Portland controlled that contribution through the 2003-04 season, far longer than a quick deadline rental. The franchise did not win a championship during those seasons, and later moves involving Wallace are separate transactions. Nonetheless, the years of high-level production directly obtained through the 1996 deal explain why Portland owns the stronger long-range case.

sections.heading: Strickland Gave Washington a Valuable, Understated Return
sections.body: A Portland win should not erase what Washington bought. Strickland played all 82 games in 1996-97, started 81 and averaged 17.2 points with 8.9 assists. He helped the Bullets return to the playoffs for the first time since 1988, although that success also depended on their other starters. In 1997-98, by then playing for the renamed Wizards, Strickland averaged a league-leading 10.5 assists and received All-NBA Second Team honors. Those numbers support a meaningful grade on Washington's side: an elite distributor was an actual delivered asset, not a speculative opportunity. Comparing his playmaking peak with Wallace's longer Portland run requires acknowledging the different positions and roster needs.

sections.heading: Harvey Grant Returned to Washington; Butler Was Portland Depth
sections.body: The lesser-known players also had identifiable histories. Grant had spent his first five NBA seasons with Washington before being dealt to Portland in 1993; this 1996 trade brought the forward back to his former club. The contemporaneous UPI report noted he had averaged 9.3 points and 4.8 rebounds for Portland in 1995-96, helping explain his attraction as experienced wing depth. Butler was a reserve guard whom Washington had used for 61 games at 3.9 points per appearance in that same season. Portland received him alongside Wallace rather than as a franchise centerpiece. Neither role justifies inserting an imaginary future first-round pick or crediting the 1996 deal with later unrelated roster movements.

sections.heading: Portland's A-Plus and Washington's B-Plus Returns
sections.body: Portland holds the win verdict with an A-plus, while Washington receives a B-plus. The four-player package sent Rasheed Wallace and Mitchell Butler to Portland, with Rod Strickland and Harvey Grant going to the Bullets. Strickland was an established playmaking guard, and his Washington tenure gave that club sustained value; Grant also returned to an organization where he had spent his early NBA years. Portland acquired Wallace near the start of his career and received multiple productive seasons and deep postseason runs. Butler was a smaller part of the Portland return. Both teams gained identifiable contributors, though the duration and frontcourt impact of Wallace's Portland stay give the Blazers the stronger long-term case. The grades acknowledge Washington's productive backcourt addition rather than treating its return as a failed exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Portland Trail Blazers Win is the stored result, Portland A-plus and Washington B-plus. In July 1996, the Bullets sent Wallace and Butler for Strickland and Harvey Grant. Wallace supplied years of leading frontcourt play and helped Portland reach the 1999 and 2000 West Finals; Strickland delivered 82 games at 17.2 points and 8.9 assists in 1996-97, later leading the league in assists and earning All-NBA Second Team. Washington's genuine gain does not erase Portland's longer control of Wallace, and the ledger includes no imaginary draft pick.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Wallace for Strickland: Portland's Future and Washington's Present in 1996
featuredDeepDive.intro: The July 15, 1996 exchange paired a young Rasheed Wallace and reserve guard Mitchell Butler with veteran point guard Rod Strickland and forward Harvey Grant. Portland chose the forward who would help power two conference-final runs; Washington obtained a distributor who immediately played 82 games and later earned All-NBA honors. The deal belonged to the Bullets era, even though the modern archive uses Wizards routing. Neither side's return can be evaluated accurately by excluding the other's productive seasons.

sections.heading: Washington's Bullets Name Belongs to the 1996 Timeline
sections.body: Historical labels affect whether the transaction makes sense to a reader. The July 15, 1996 trade involved the Washington Bullets, which would become the Wizards in 1997, and the Portland Trail Blazers. Rasheed Wallace and Mitchell Butler went to Portland, while Rod Strickland and Harvey Grant went to Washington. Current site routing uses the Wizards franchise identity for the same organization's historical records. The contemporary UPI report verifies the four pieces and states why the established point guard appealed to Washington. The change in franchise name is not evidence of a third team or an additional trade, and no cash or pick appears in the reported package.

sections.heading: The Front Offices Were Addressing Different Roster Problems
sections.body: Portland had experienced friction between Strickland and coach P.J. Carlesimo, a disagreement that included a suspension and had disrupted the point guard's relationship with the team. Washington already had talented scoring forwards but needed a lead ball handler to organize possessions. Unseld was publicly pleased to acquire Strickland, while the Blazers preferred to reset their frontcourt around Wallace's developmental upside. Grant's return to Washington provided a veteran who could defend multiple perimeter positions; Butler offered Portland additional guard depth. The July 1996 choices did not require either front office to predict the next eight years perfectly. Each was attempting to exchange a less suitable current asset for the skill set its roster needed.

sections.heading: Portland's Deep Playoff Runs Show Wallace's Realized Value
sections.body: Wallace ultimately contributed to Portland teams that reached the Western Conference Finals in both 1999 and 2000. His two Blazers All-Star appearances attest to individual standing within that era, while his combination of scoring, size and defensive mobility gave the team flexibility. Neither conference-final trip should be attributed solely to a single acquisition: Portland's guards, centers and coaching were also central. The relevant transaction outcome is that Portland obtained a young frontcourt starter and kept him for years of playoff-caliber basketball. Wallace was later traded in an entirely separate 2004 series of moves before joining Detroit. His subsequent championship cannot be added to the Trail Blazers' direct 1996 return.

sections.heading: Washington's Strickland Statistics Make a Strong Countercase
sections.body: Strickland was not an aging placeholder who immediately faded after the swap. In his first Washington season, 1996-97, he played 82 games with 81 starts and averaged 17.2 points and 8.9 assists. In 1997-98 he played 76 games at 17.8 points and a league-best 10.5 assists, earning All-NBA Second Team recognition. The club made the playoffs in 1997, ending a lengthy drought, although its broader results were influenced by Chris Webber, Juwan Howard and many others. These are high-grade performances from the primary player Washington obtained. Grant's second stint added wing depth but was never likely to have the same influence as a top distributor.

sections.heading: The Difference in Grades Should Not Become a False Asset Story
sections.body: Portland's A-plus and Washington's B-plus are the canonical site scores, with Portland Trail Blazers Win as the verdict. A retrospective can justify the advantage through Wallace's younger age and long Blazers prime without using a fictional conditional pick, cash payment or second team. Strickland's All-NBA caliber Washington seasons also limit how one-sided the result should be portrayed. The original deal included two secondary pieces, Butler and Grant, whose contributions were more modest. A source-based conclusion separates what was exchanged on July 15, 1996 from later career events. It also avoids rewriting an inherited grade merely because Portland's most famous acquisition received more attention in retrospective media.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Portland Trail Blazers Win, Portland A-plus and Washington B-plus remain the unaltered canonical marks. The 1996 Bullets-to-Blazers move sent Wallace and Butler west for Strickland and Harvey Grant. Wallace became a two-time All-Star in Portland and a leading player on back-to-back Western Conference Finalists in 1999 and 2000. Strickland immediately gave Washington 82 games at 17.2 points and 8.9 assists, then earned All-NBA Second Team honors and a 10.5-assist season after the franchise became the Wizards. Grant returned to a familiar team, and Butler supplied Portland guard depth. Those are four real players, with no picks or cash in the dated deal. Portland's longer-lasting frontcourt prize wins the comparison, but Washington received a highly productive point guard rather than an empty return.

sections.heading: Portland Pursued Pendergraph, Sacramento Collected Multiple Assets
sections.body: On June 25, 2009, the Trail Blazers acquired the draft rights to Jeff Pendergraph, later known as Jeff Ayres. Sacramento received guard Sergio Rodríguez, the rights to Jon Brockman and cash considerations. The clubs were acting around the NBA draft, so Pendergraph and Brockman were rights rather than established NBA performers at the moment of exchange. The unspecified cash payment was a third part of Sacramento’s return and must not be treated as a known dollar amount.

sections.heading: Ayres Supplied Portland an Inside Reserve but Not a Long-Term Core
sections.body: Pendergraph came to Portland as an athletic forward and center prospect after four seasons at Arizona State. He played 39 games for the Trail Blazers in 2009–10. A subsequent knee injury kept him out of the following season, and Portland did not receive the long-term roster continuity it might have hoped for from his rights. His later NBA career, including under the Ayres name, cannot all be booked as Portland value.

sections.heading: Brockman and Rodríguez Gave Sacramento Usable Depth
sections.body: Brockman was a rebounding prospect who played 52 games for Sacramento in his rookie season. Rodríguez, already an NBA guard with Portland, added ballhandling experience and played 39 Kings games before changing teams again. Neither became a defining Sacramento player, but both were identifiable NBA contributors obtained in the same exchange. The Kings also received financial consideration whose exact amount is unspecified in the canonical transaction package.

sections.heading: The Two Packages Support a Modest Kings Advantage
sections.body: Sacramento’s recorded B exceeds Portland’s C-plus, with Kings Win. Sacramento took two player opportunities and cash for a single forward’s rights; Portland ultimately received limited immediate service from Pendergraph before injury changed his prospects. The margin does not imply that Brockman or Rodríguez became a lasting Kings star. It reflects the relative breadth and observed short-term usefulness of Sacramento’s return versus the narrower outcome Portland realized.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Win — Sacramento B, Portland C-plus. Sacramento obtained Sergio Rodríguez, Jon Brockman’s rights and cash considerations for Jeff Pendergraph’s rights. Rodríguez and Brockman each provided Kings rotation appearances, while Pendergraph played 39 Portland games before injury interrupted his tenure. Both sides acquired real options, but Sacramento received more distinct assets and the recorded retrospective edge.

sections.heading: Draft-Night Rights to Gary Trent Jr. Cost Portland Two Future Seconds
sections.body: Sacramento selected Gary Trent Jr. at No. 37 in the June 21, 2018 draft, then transferred his rights to Portland for cash and two future second-round selections. The first was the more favorable of Lakers- and Timberwolves-origin choices in 2019; the other originated with Miami and was due in 2021. The NBA's official draft trade tracker confirms the structure, while both team transaction histories establish the eventual pick identities. Portland wanted a Duke wing with shooting potential alongside Damian Lillard and CJ McCollum. Sacramento preferred two more opportunities in later draft classes and immediate cash consideration. None of the future selections had a guaranteed NBA contributor attached when the clubs agreed. The deal was specifically for Trent's rights; Portland's same-night first-round selection of Anfernee Simons was a separate transaction.

sections.heading: Trent Gave Portland 117 Games Before the Raptors Deal
sections.body: Trent developed through three partial Trail Blazers seasons. He appeared in 15 NBA regular-season games as a 2018-19 rookie, 61 in 2019-20, and 41 in 2020-21 before Portland traded him in March. That amounts to 117 Portland games and 32 starts. His scoring grew from 2.7 points per game as a rookie to 8.9 in 2019-20 and 15.0 over his final 41 Portland appearances. He shot 41.8 percent from three in 2019-20, giving the team a credible floor-spacing option. Those figures are genuine returns on the rights Sacramento surrendered, unlike Trent's later 2021-22 career-high scoring season in Toronto. After the original trade, Portland also retained his contract long enough to include it in a separate deal for Norman Powell, a valuable form of roster flexibility.

sections.heading: The 2019 Pick Produced Justin James for Sacramento
sections.body: Sacramento exercised the earlier of its incoming draft opportunities in June 2019. The choice conveyed at No. 40, and the Kings selected Wyoming wing Justin James. He played 36 regular-season games as a rookie, then another 36 in 2020-21. His two-year Sacramento total was 72 appearances with no starts, averaging 3.2 points overall. That is a real NBA return and should not be described as a draft right that never produced a player. It was, however, much smaller than the role Trent had developed in Portland by early 2021. The Kings were entitled to evaluate a second-round prospect during a rebuilding period, and James's limited rotation assignments gave them some usable depth. Counting his performances after leaving Sacramento or adding college production to his NBA numbers would distort the direct comparison.

sections.heading: The Second Pick Was Exercised by Atlanta, Not Sacramento
sections.body: The other incoming 2018 asset was a Miami-origin second-round right for 2021. Historical transaction ledgers attach it to the No. 48 selection eventually used on Auburn guard Sharife Cooper, but the NBA's official 2021 draft profile identifies the Atlanta Hawks as the team that actually selected Cooper. Sacramento therefore cannot be credited with drafting and developing Cooper for its own roster. The association is a downstream outcome of a pick once controlled by the Kings, not proof that the player joined Sacramento. The original deal gave Sacramento a second tradable selection and cash as well as the earlier Justin James pick. Evaluating that pick as an additional Sacramento NBA starter would be inaccurate. Its destination illustrates why original trade compensation and final draft-night team records need to be kept distinct.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Blazers Win — Portland A, Sacramento D. Trent played 117 Portland regular-season games, averaging 15.0 points in his final partial Blazers season, before Portland traded him with Rodney Hood for Norman Powell. Sacramento selected Justin James No. 40 in 2019 and received 72 Kings games, plus cash and a separate 2021 second eventually exercised by Atlanta on No. 48 Sharife Cooper. Cooper was not a Kings selection.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Gary Trent Jr. Draft-Rights Trade in 2018: Portland Minutes and Sacramento Picks
featuredDeepDive.intro: Portland acquired the No.37 Trent rights from Sacramento for two future seconds and cash. The Blazers played him 117 games; Sacramento got 72 Justin James games and a later second that changed hands before the 2021 draft.

sections.heading: Trent's Development Outlasted a Brief Rookie Assignment
sections.body: Portland did not receive an established NBA rotation guard on draft night. Trent began with 15 regular-season appearances and little time during 2018-19 while the team evaluated its young prospects. In 2019-20 he grew into a reliable bench shooter, playing 61 games and making 112 of 268 three-point attempts. He averaged 8.9 points and earned eight starts. His progress accelerated during the 2020-21 season, when he started 23 of 41 Portland games and averaged 15.0 points. This step-by-step development is the strongest basketball explanation for spending two second-rounders on his rights. The contribution occurred in Portland, not as a retrospective transfer of the later Toronto seasons to his original franchise. A-grade hindsight can be defended with real games and shooting, not just name recognition.

sections.heading: The Norman Powell Trade Was a Separate Negotiation
sections.body: On March 25, 2021, Portland traded Trent and Rodney Hood to Toronto for Norman Powell. That move is useful evidence that the rights acquired in 2018 had become attached to a productive NBA player another front office wanted. It would still be incorrect to treat Powell as a player Sacramento directly sent to Portland in 2018. The Raptors received Hood in addition to Trent, and the later negotiation had its own competitive and salary context. Portland obtained 117 games of Trent's direct production before using him as one of two outgoing assets in the Powell transaction. Those are two linked but separate steps in the asset history. Crediting the original draft-right trade with every Powell basket would erase Hood's value and make the original acquisition look far more mechanically direct than it was.

sections.heading: James Was Useful Depth While Cooper Belonged to Atlanta
sections.body: Sacramento's first compensation pick became Justin James at No. 40 in 2019, and he played 72 NBA games for the Kings across the next two seasons. The other second-round right was associated with No. 48 Sharife Cooper in 2021, but the NBA draft record lists Atlanta as Cooper's selecting franchise. The later pick had changed hands before the draft, so Kings playing statistics cannot be invented for Cooper. Sacramento also received cash in the original June 2018 arrangement, but a precise value of that payment was not established by the NBA's official tracker. James's 72 games were real limited-duty wing minutes, and the other right had transferable value without creating an equivalent Kings guard. This distinction is important for judging the package without either erasing one player or inflating another.

sections.heading: Why the Blazers Won Without Pretending Sacramento Received Nothing
sections.body: The site's inherited grades favor Portland A over Sacramento D and give the Blazers Win verdict. Portland acquired a young shooter who made 117 regular-season appearances and scored 15.0 points per game in his final partial Blazers campaign. The team later moved him with Rodney Hood for Norman Powell, adding evidence of trade value beyond the initial minutes. Sacramento got cash and two future second-round rights: the No. 40 pick yielded 72 Justin James games, while the right associated with No. 48 Sharife Cooper eventually was exercised by Atlanta. Neither Kings return developed into a player matching Trent's Portland role. Those outcomes support Portland's advantage while acknowledging Sacramento received an actual drafted contributor. The grade gap should follow source-specific playing time and pick ownership rather than copied, generic language about second-round picks always being worthless.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Portland A, Sacramento D in the preserved Blazers Win. The 2018 rights deal led to 117 Trent Blazers games and a later separate Norman Powell trade with additional outgoing Rodney Hood. Sacramento's 2019 second was used on James, who supplied 72 Kings games. The 2021 No. 48 right wound up with Atlanta when Cooper was drafted, not as Sacramento player minutes.

sections.heading: Sacramento Added Two Picks While Sending Three Forwards to Portland
sections.body: The January 21, 2020 trade sent Trevor Ariza, Wenyen Gabriel and Caleb Swanigan from Sacramento to Portland. Kent Bazemore, Anthony Tolliver and Portland's 2024 and 2025 second-round picks went to the Kings. Both franchises issued transaction announcements identifying the same seven assets, including the two distinct draft years. Portland wanted Ariza's wing defense, Gabriel's developmental potential and Swanigan's familiarity with the team. Sacramento acquired a rotation veteran in Bazemore while adding future draft capital for three players it was prepared to move. Neither side acquired a future first or the rights to Tyler Smith or Alijah Martin on the date of the exchange; those players were drafted years later after the picks changed hands again. The distinction between originally acquired selections and later draft outcomes is central to evaluating the saved Kings Win verdict.

sections.heading: Ariza Started 21 Portland Games; Gabriel Supplied a Smaller Bench Role
sections.body: Ariza went straight into Portland's rotation. In 21 appearances for the Blazers before the season's interruption, he started all 21 and averaged 11.0 points, 4.8 rebounds and 1.6 steals while shooting 40.0 percent from three. The comparison must use his Portland-only split rather than the combined 53 games he played for Sacramento and Portland in 2019-20. Gabriel appeared in 19 Portland regular-season games, with one start and averages of 2.3 points and 2.2 rebounds, after beginning the year with the Kings. Swanigan filled a deeper frontcourt role. Ariza did not participate in Portland's restart inside the 2020 NBA bubble for personal family reasons, so his January-to-March production did not turn into a postseason contribution for that club. The additions improved position depth but offered a short window of directly realized value.

sections.heading: Bazemore Gave Sacramento 25 Games and Tolliver Was Waived
sections.body: Bazemore appeared in 25 regular-season games for the Kings after arriving from Portland. Sacramento received 10.3 points, 4.9 rebounds and 1.3 assists per game from him, including 38.4 percent three-point shooting, according to the 2019-20 team split. Tolliver's Sacramento stint was briefer. The Kings' February 29, 2020 waiver announcement confirms nine appearances, averages of 1.0 point and 1.2 rebounds, and his release only five weeks after the trade. That does not erase the two incoming draft rights. Sacramento's basketball gain combined a useful short-term wing with selections whose longer-term market value extended beyond either veteran's Kings tenure. The protected B+ grade can therefore be read as a blended assessment, while Portland's C recognizes useful Ariza starts but the cost of two future second-round picks.

sections.heading: The 2024 and 2025 Picks Were Traded Again before Their Drafts
sections.body: Sacramento did not select Tyler Smith at No. 33 in 2024 or Alijah Martin at No. 39 in 2025. The original 2024 Portland pick moved onward to Milwaukee in the February 2022 four-team Serge Ibaka/Donte DiVincenzo transaction; the Bucks later drafted Smith. The 2025 Portland selection was sent to Toronto in June 2024 with Davion Mitchell, Sasha Vezenkov and Jamal Shead's rights for Jalen McDaniels, and Toronto ultimately selected Martin. Pro Sports Transactions traces both chains, and the Kings' subsequent transaction ledger confirms the Raptors move. It is proper to credit Sacramento with owning tradeable second-round rights and using those rights in later packages, not to give the Kings NBA points or roster appearances by players drafted by Milwaukee and Toronto. This exact downstream routing supports the archived Sacramento B+/Portland C verdict without inflating the outcome.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Win: Sacramento B+, Portland C. Bazemore played 25 games for the Kings; Tolliver appeared nine times before a waiver. Sacramento also received Portland's 2024 and 2025 second-round choices, later moved to Milwaukee and Toronto respectively, where Tyler Smith and Alijah Martin were ultimately drafted. Portland obtained Ariza's 21 starts and Gabriel's 19 games, plus Swanigan, but Ariza did not join the bubble postseason. The grade credits real receiving-team minutes and traceable pick value, not later players as Sacramento draftees.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: The Ariza–Bazemore Deal's Two Second-Round Picks and Their Later Routes
featuredDeepDive.intro: Portland's 2020 acquisition of Trevor Ariza, Wenyen Gabriel and Caleb Swanigan cost Kent Bazemore, Anthony Tolliver, and two future second-round picks. Ariza started all 21 games he played for Portland, but the pandemic interruption and his absence from the bubble playoffs limited the sporting payoff. Sacramento got 25 Bazemore appearances and future assets that later circulated in other transactions. The two picks became No. 33 in 2024 and No. 39 in 2025, but neither was used by Sacramento to draft the eventual player. Their separate paths through Milwaukee and Toronto explain why the preserved Kings Win is based on draft rights and later trade utility rather than invented Kings careers.

sections.heading: The Clubs Exchanged Different Kinds of Immediate Depth
sections.body: On the transaction date Sacramento's announcement described Kent Bazemore as a veteran with 526 prior NBA games and Anthony Tolliver as an 11-year forward capable of shooting from outside. Portland's release emphasized Ariza's experience, Gabriel's potential and Swanigan's familiarity after his earlier Trail Blazers tenure. Those were sensible evaluations of different roster needs, but player production after January gives the comparison a firmer foundation. Ariza delivered 21 starts and 11.0 points a night as a Blazer, with the accompanying 4.8 rebounds and 1.6 steals. Gabriel supplied 19 games averaging 2.3 points in limited time. Bazemore scored 10.3 per game in his 25 Sacramento appearances, while Tolliver logged nine contests before being waived. These receiving-team figures are limited samples and should not be confused with players' career averages listed in the original press releases.

sections.heading: The 2024 Pick Became Tyler Smith for Milwaukee, Not Sacramento
sections.body: Sacramento's first future second was Portland's 2024 choice. It eventually landed at No. 33, but the Kings had already sent the right onward in February 2022. The four-team deal involving the Kings, Bucks, Clippers and Pistons placed this pick with Milwaukee during the exchange that included Donte DiVincenzo heading to Sacramento and Serge Ibaka to Milwaukee. The Bucks later used No. 33 on Tyler Smith. Sacramento deserves partial credit for the pick's role in its outgoing compensation within that larger 2022 transaction; the later acquisition also required other assets moving among four organizations. Smith's NBA future and any Milwaukee development should not be written as direct production for the Kings. The original trade created an asset that could be marketed well before its draft year.

sections.heading: The 2025 Portland Second Then Moved to Toronto
sections.body: The second future pick was Portland's own 2025 selection, which ultimately became the No. 39 pick used on Alijah Martin. On June 28, 2024, Sacramento sent this Portland second to the Toronto Raptors along with Davion Mitchell, Sasha Vezenkov and the draft rights to Jamal Shead in a trade for Jalen McDaniels. The Sacramento and Toronto transaction ledgers distinguish the 2025 Portland second from a different 2025 Sacramento selection moved in the DeMar DeRozan deal. Toronto, not Sacramento, selected Martin when the second round arrived. The chain demonstrates value retained and deployed in a later transaction, but only a portion of that later exchange can be allocated to the Portland pick. It would be doubly misleading to say Sacramento drafted Martin or acquired McDaniels using the pick alone.

sections.heading: A Pandemic-Interrupted Season Limited Portland's Return
sections.body: Portland made its January deal seeking an experienced perimeter defender and deeper forward rotation. Ariza met the immediate on-court requirement by starting every one of his 21 Blazers regular-season appearances, whereas Gabriel and Swanigan occupied reserve roles. Yet Ariza did not participate in the season restart, leaving Portland without its veteran wing during its 2020 postseason. That is a specific limitation on the incoming player's direct value, not a retroactive claim his 21 starts never helped the team. Sacramento's short veteran tenures were also imperfect: Bazemore's 25 games yielded useful bench scoring but Tolliver lasted only nine games before the waiver. The difference in the grades comes from the extra draft rights Sacramento received and later traded, with Portland's temporary rotation improvement unable to fully offset that cost.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Sacramento B+ and Portland C retain the Kings Win. The Kings received Bazemore's 25 games, Tolliver's nine, and picks later routed to Milwaukee (2024 No. 33 Tyler Smith) and Toronto (2025 No. 39 Alijah Martin). Portland received Ariza's 21 starts and Gabriel's 19 appearances, with Swanigan as added depth. Neither draft selection produced a Sacramento draftee, and Ariza did not play in the 2020 bubble. This is an asset-control win, not a claim of long-term player stardom.
