sections.heading: Seattle Sold Second-Round Rights for Cash
sections.body: Seattle selected guard Johnny Moore with the 43rd pick of the 1979 draft and sold his rights to San Antonio on June 26, one day later. The Spurs acquired draft rights, not a veteran already producing NBA minutes. Contemporary team transaction histories and a Spurs media guide agree that the return to Seattle was cash. The reviewed records do not provide a reliable amount, so there is no basis for assigning the SuperSonics a specific dollar or equivalent playing value. Cash was legitimate consideration; its basketball impact is simply not quantified in the source material.

sections.heading: San Antonio Signed Moore, Then Released Him
sections.body: The key historical break came before Moore could play an NBA game. The Spurs signed him on July 23, 1979 after buying his rights, but waived him on October 12. That ended the uninterrupted team-control path that began with the June transaction. A draft-rights trade cannot be scored as though it guaranteed the entire career of a player whose original contract was terminated. As of the waiver, San Antonio had acquired and evaluated Moore but had received no regular-season production. This sequence also rules out the outdated claim that the club simply bought an immediate All-Star and retained him continuously.

sections.heading: The March 1980 Free-Agent Return Changed the Story
sections.body: The Spurs re-signed Moore on March 9, 1980 as a free agent, a separate acquisition from the June rights purchase. He ultimately became a long-serving San Antonio guard with 519 regular-season Spurs appearances. In 1980-81 he played all 82 games. He started 78 in 1981-82 and averaged 9.6 assists that year, then 9.8 assists in 1982-83. Those achievements show the quality of the talent San Antonio originally identified. They do not erase the months in which Moore was free to sign elsewhere. The original purchase may have helped introduce him to the organization, but the team's later free-agent decision was independently necessary.

sections.heading: An Edge With an Attribution Limit
sections.body: Seattle received unpriced cash for a second-round right and has no separately documented basketball asset attached to that sale. San Antonio bought the right to sign Moore and did so, establishing a connection to a future franchise point guard, then broke that chain with an October waiver. Because the March free-agent re-signing is not a direct continuation of exclusive draft control, Moore's entire career cannot be assigned to the first trade's realized value. The canonical Spurs Edge, B- for San Antonio and C for Seattle, preserves that distinction. It recognizes hindsight upside while avoiding the inflated older grade-and-win language from the older editorial.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Spurs Edge — San Antonio B-, Seattle C. The Spurs bought Johnny Moore's rights for cash in June 1979, signed him in July and waived him before he played an NBA regular-season game. Their March 1980 free-agent reacquisition produced Moore's long, productive Spurs career, but that separate signing cannot be credited wholly to the rights sale. Seattle's cash amount is unknown and has no documented linked basketball return. The trade favors San Antonio in talent identification and hindsight, with a necessary limit on direct value attribution.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Johnny Moore’s 1979 Rights Sale: Why the Waiver Changes the Verdict
featuredDeepDive.intro: Johnny Moore eventually played 519 regular-season games for the San Antonio Spurs, a tempting number when grading Seattle's 1979 sale of his second-round draft rights. But that total follows an intervening release and a second, distinct acquisition. San Antonio bought Moore's rights for cash on June 26, signed him July 23, waived him October 12 and brought him back as a free agent the following March. The transaction tells an interesting story about talent identification without justifying full credit for a career that began only after the original rights-based control had expired.

sections.heading: A Draft Selection Became an Unpriced Cash Exchange
sections.body: The SuperSonics chose Moore No. 43 overall in 1979, then sold the right to sign him to San Antonio. The contemporary records list cash rather than players or picks in return. The lack of a reliable figure is not a minor footnote: it prevents a numerical hindsight comparison based on Seattle's financial benefit. Seattle could have valued the money for reasons not recorded in the league's player movement log. For a basketball-centered trade grade, the public evidence supports only the existence of the payment and the absence of a linked on-court return.

sections.heading: The Fall Waiver Interrupts the Trade’s Asset Chain
sections.body: San Antonio signed Moore after acquiring his rights, but released him October 12, 1979 before he appeared in a regular-season game. That waiver is decisive for asset attribution. Had Moore stayed under the Spurs' exclusive control and developed into the same starter, the chain from the cash purchase to his later production would have been direct. Instead, he became a free agent. The Spurs had spent the summer with him and learned something about his abilities, but the original transaction no longer controlled where he would play. A valid history should not conceal that legal and roster distinction merely because the same club eventually reacquired him.

sections.heading: A Different Signing Produced 519 Spurs Games
sections.body: Moore signed with San Antonio again on March 9, 1980, and later became a productive starting point guard. He played 82 games in 1980-81, started 78 in 1981-82 and averaged more than nine assists per game in both 1981-82 and 1982-83. His 519 Spurs games explain why the original June 1979 rights purchase looks clever in hindsight. Yet the performance followed the subsequent free-agent signing, and the first season's waiver had made it possible for another club to sign him. The full 519-game return belongs to Moore's Spurs career, not unconditionally to the rights transaction.

sections.heading: What a Cautious Retrospective Can Say
sections.body: San Antonio's June rights purchase proved the club recognized an overlooked second-round prospect and gave him an initial contract. Seattle monetized a selection that it did not expect to retain. The Spurs then waived Moore and later chose to re-sign him, which is why the source-backed ledger deliberately uses a cautious edge rather than an exaggerated win. The B-/C grades represent limited directly traceable value plus the strong hindsight context of talent identification. They do not equate Seattle's unknown cash with documented NBA production or pretend that Moore never entered free agency.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Spurs Edge, B-/C. The June 1979 rights sale brought Moore to San Antonio for a summer, but he was released before recording a regular-season appearance. The Spurs' March 1980 free-agent re-signing subsequently produced 519 games in San Antonio, without making that separate acquisition part of continuous draft-rights control. Seattle received cash of an undocumented amount. The available record supports a modest, attribution-limited Spurs advantage rather than an unqualified career-value windfall.

sections.heading: Seattle Traded a Former First-Round Guard for a 1986 Second
sections.body: Seattle sent Jon Sundvold to San Antonio on October 23, 1985, receiving a 1986 second-round draft choice. The SuperSonics had originally taken the Missouri guard No. 16 overall in 1983 and played him for two seasons behind other guards. San Antonio saw a chance to obtain a useful passer and shooter without surrendering an established rotation player. The future pick was the only recorded Seattle compensation, not a first-round selection or a package of veterans. The 1986 pick ultimately became No. 38, used on DePaul center Lemone Lampley. Those details put the transaction on a modest scale at the time: a third-year guard traded for the chance to evaluate another prospect the following summer. Its outcome was determined by the actual careers of Sundvold in San Antonio and the player selected with Seattle's new right.

sections.heading: Sundvold Played 198 Spurs Games Over Three Seasons
sections.body: Sundvold appeared in 70 San Antonio regular-season games in 1985-86, 76 in 1986-87 and 52 in 1987-88, totaling 198 games for the acquiring franchise. He averaged 7.1 points and 3.7 assists in the first year, then 11.2 points and 4.1 assists in his second. The 1986-87 season also brought 42 starts and 23.2 minutes per game, giving the club a genuine backcourt contributor rather than a player who merely dressed. His role decreased during the third Spurs season, but the contract had already yielded three years of useful passing and shooting. Sundvold later joined Miami as an original expansion-team player in 1988-89; those Heat games should not be credited as part of San Antonio's return from the 1985 Seattle exchange. Team-specific counts provide a clear basis for judging value.

sections.heading: The 1986 No. 38 Pick Became Lemone Lampley
sections.body: Seattle exercised the acquired 1986 second-round choice on Lemone Lampley at No. 38. He had played at DePaul and entered the draft as a long interior prospect, making the selection a genuine scouting opportunity. The draft record confirms the SuperSonics were the selecting franchise, rather than a future team that received a subsequently traded pick. Lampley never appeared in an NBA regular-season game for Seattle, so his direct on-court return from this draft choice was zero. That distinction does not erase the original value of controlling a selection, but it limits the realized outcome. A second-round center could have become a reserve; in this case it did not. Seattle's decision cannot be defended by confusing Lampley with Jim or Sean Lampley, different players with later NBA records.

sections.heading: The Grade Difference Tracks Rotation Minutes, Not Fame
sections.body: The inherited result gives San Antonio A-minus, Seattle C-plus and a Spurs Win. Sundvold was not a league superstar, and his 1986-87 team still had competitive difficulties, but he gave San Antonio 198 real games across three seasons, including 58 starts overall. Seattle used the second-round choice on Lampley and received no NBA regular-season appearances from the selection. That difference favors the Spurs without requiring fabricated playoff achievements or later Miami statistics. The C-plus Seattle grade can reflect the rational trade-day choice to exchange a reserve guard for new draft rights, not a claim that the acquired pick yielded a contributor. The A-minus for San Antonio recognizes several seasons of backcourt service at the cost of one second-round opportunity. The factual grade analysis rests on traceable playing records rather than copied generalities about hindsight.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Spurs Win — San Antonio A-, Seattle C+ in the preserved grades. Sundvold played 198 Spurs regular-season games across 1985-88, with 58 total starts and 11.2 points per game in 1986-87. Seattle used the acquired 1986 second on No.38 Lemone Lampley, who never played an NBA regular-season game. Sundvold later played for Miami, not additional Spurs return.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Jon Sundvold for a 1986 Second: Spurs Games and Seattle No. 38 Lampley
featuredDeepDive.intro: In October 1985 Seattle traded guard Jon Sundvold to San Antonio for the 1986 second-round pick used on Lemone Lampley. Sundvold provided 198 Spurs games; Lampley never played in the NBA.

sections.heading: Why San Antonio Could Use Another Guard in 1985
sections.body: Sundvold had already logged 146 regular-season appearances for Seattle during his first two NBA seasons, with scoring averages of 6.9 and 5.5 points. He was a capable passer but had started only three games in the crowded SuperSonics backcourt. San Antonio took advantage of that limited role, sending a future second to obtain an experienced guard still early in his career. That gave the Spurs a player who could handle possessions immediately, whereas a drafted center would not arrive until the following summer and might not make an NBA roster. The contrast explains both front-office motivations without pretending Seattle viewed Sundvold as an emerging All-Star or San Antonio knew Lampley would never play in the league. As a contract-value exchange it was ordinary; its eventual returns created the larger difference.

sections.heading: The 1986-87 Season Supplied the Strongest Spurs Evidence
sections.body: Sundvold's peak year in San Antonio came in 1986-87. He played 76 games and started 42, averaging 11.2 points, 4.1 assists and 23.2 minutes. That was a substantial step up from his first Spurs campaign, when he provided 7.1 points in 70 appearances. The team was not built around him, but his increase in usage demonstrates that the second-round acquisition solved a real guard-depth need for more than a few weeks. He made 50 three-pointers that season on 149 attempts, showing a measurable perimeter scoring contribution. The original deal produced this production directly, because Sundvold was still under San Antonio control. Later games with Miami cannot boost the team's return, just as Seattle's other future draft successes cannot be assigned automatically to the No. 38 selection acquired here.

sections.heading: Lampley Was Chosen, but No NBA Season Followed
sections.body: The 1986 draft ledger lists Seattle choosing Lemone Lampley 38th overall in the second round. The selection represented a chance to add a 6-foot-11 DePaul center after surrendering a veteran reserve guard. Not every draft outcome can be judged only by eventual NBA minutes, because rights can be evaluated, retained or included in another transaction. Yet no verified subsequent deal converting Lampley's SuperSonics rights into a different player is established in the source record. He had no recorded NBA regular-season appearances for Seattle. The direct return was therefore an exercised draft choice without played minutes, materially different from San Antonio receiving three seasons of a guard it actually used. Confusing him with other players named Lampley would turn an unsuccessful draft conversion into fictitious Seattle production. The team and player identities must stay separate.

sections.heading: A Modest Spurs Win Without a Franchise-Altering Story
sections.body: The original verdict is Spurs Win, with San Antonio A-minus and Seattle C-plus. San Antonio obtained 198 Sundvold games across three seasons and 58 starts, gaining a temporary first-team guard who passed and shot effectively. Seattle chose Lemone Lampley at No. 38 in 1986 but never received NBA regular-season playing time from him. This is a meaningful advantage for the Spurs in a small transaction, not a league-changing blockbuster. The grades can be preserved as historical editorial assessments while acknowledging that an A-minus is generous for a mid-rotation veteran and that Seattle's C-plus reflects the opportunity of a second-round pick rather than realized production. The evidence is unusually straightforward: one club played the acquired guard for three seasons, and the other exercised a pick without establishing a usable NBA center.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: San Antonio A-minus, Seattle C-plus in the site verdict. A second-round selection bought the Spurs 198 games and three seasons of Jon Sundvold guard depth. Seattle drafted Lemone Lampley No.38 in 1986 but obtained no NBA appearances. The grades reflect the difference between immediate player use and an unrealized draft opportunity.

sections.heading: Seattle Sent Snow to Philadelphia for a Conditional Second
sections.body: On January 18, 1998, the Seattle SuperSonics sent reserve guard Eric Snow to Philadelphia for a conditional second-round pick that could convey in 1998 or 1999. It ultimately became the No. 33 choice in the 1998 draft, which Seattle used on UCLA center Jelani McCoy. Snow was in his third season as a professional and had struggled for regular minutes behind Gary Payton in Seattle. Philadelphia needed a point guard who could defend and organize its offense around young Allen Iverson. The franchise involved in 1998 was the Seattle SuperSonics, not the Oklahoma City Thunder, a name that did not exist until a later relocation. That identity distinction is crucial in a historical trade database. The transaction did not involve an existing Thunder roster or a first-round pick.

sections.heading: Snow Became a Seven-Season 76ers Backcourt Regular
sections.body: Philadelphia's official media guide credits Snow with 452 regular-season games for the 76ers from 1997-98 through 2003-04, including 403 starts. He averaged 9.7 points across those appearances and recorded 2,965 assists, helping to manage the offensive workload beside Iverson. Those are substantial team-specific returns for the price of a second-round choice. Snow began with 47 Philadelphia appearances in the partial 1997-98 season, then made all 48 starts he was available for during the 1998-99 lockout season. He started 80 games in 1999-2000 and continued to play major minutes through 2003-04. His later Cleveland appearances belong to the Cavaliers rather than to the 1998 trade's direct Philadelphia output. The on-court evidence strongly supports the inherited Philadelphia A grade.

sections.heading: His Defense Helped Iverson's 2001 Finals Team
sections.body: Snow was a starting defensive guard during Philadelphia's run to the 2001 NBA Finals. The Sixers were led by Iverson's scoring and Dikembe Mutombo's rim protection, but Snow's playmaking and point-of-attack defense supplied structure around the stars. In the 2000-01 regular season he played 50 games and started all 50, averaging 9.8 points and 7.4 assists. He appeared in 23 postseason games as Philadelphia advanced through the Eastern Conference before losing to the Los Angeles Lakers in five Finals games. That is a direct accomplishment of the guard acquired from Seattle for a conditional second, not an unrelated career highlight. His team role extended for several more years after the Finals, giving Philadelphia a durable starter rather than a brief one-season trial.

sections.heading: Seattle Used No. 33 on Jelani McCoy and Obtained 154 Games
sections.body: Seattle did exercise the incoming selection in the 1998 draft, taking UCLA center Jelani McCoy at No. 33. He played 26 Seattle games in 1998-99, 58 in 1999-2000 and 70 in 2000-01. That totals 154 SuperSonics regular-season appearances, with 46 starts, and he became a part-time interior starter in his third season. The choice was a real player conversion rather than an unused piece of paper. McCoy did not become a long-term Seattle centerpiece, however, and his later appearances with the Lakers, Raptors, Cleveland and other franchises should not inflate the SuperSonics return. The inherited C grade for Seattle can recognize 154 games of legitimate frontcourt service while acknowledging a clear gap against Snow's extended Philadelphia starting career. Calling the Seattle side worthless would be factually wrong.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win — Philadelphia A, Seattle C. The 1998 trade sent Eric Snow to Philadelphia for a conditional second that became No. 33 Jelani McCoy. Snow played 452 Philadelphia regular-season games with 403 starts and 2,965 assists, contributing to the 2001 Finals team. McCoy played 154 Seattle games and started 46. The original 1998 franchise was the Seattle SuperSonics, not Oklahoma City.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Eric Snow to Philadelphia in 1998: The 2001 Finals Guard and McCoy Pick
featuredDeepDive.intro: Seattle had Gary Payton running its backcourt when it surrendered reserve Eric Snow in January 1998. Philadelphia could offer a different assignment: Allen Iverson carried the scoring, and Snow developed into the defensive and distributing partner in a Finals-era guard tandem. The change in role was measurable. Snow started 403 of his 452 regular-season 76ers appearances and supplied 2,965 assists. Seattle used its conditional second-round return on center Jelani McCoy, whose 154 SuperSonics appearances were a genuine but shorter contribution. This comparison is about opportunity, team-specific playing time and longevity, not about counting a draft pick as automatically worthless.

sections.heading: A Contender's Backup Became a Core Philadelphia Starter
sections.body: Seattle's backcourt was centered on Gary Payton, and Snow's prospects for a starting role were limited. Sending him out for a future second was a common strategy for a team looking to use available roster spots and draft capital efficiently. Philadelphia saw a different opportunity: it needed a defending point guard who would distribute the ball while Iverson supplied most of the perimeter scoring. Snow gradually established that role, reaching 80 starts in 1999-2000 and eventually 403 starts over 452 Sixers appearances. His scoring averages were never the principal measure of his value. The return was duration, stability and ball management in a period when the 76ers became Eastern Conference contenders. That makes the deal much more distinctive than a generic narrative about trading a backup for a lucky draft selection.

sections.heading: The 2001 Finals Run Anchors Snow's Historical Value
sections.body: Snow's most prominent Sixers season came in 2000-01, when the franchise earned the Eastern Conference title and reached the NBA Finals. He appeared in 50 regular-season games with a 7.4-assist average, then played all 23 playoff games during the postseason run. His role was to organize possessions and defend guards, easing some responsibilities on Iverson while Mutombo helped protect the basket. Philadelphia did not beat the Lakers in the championship series, but getting that far was the defining outcome of its Iverson-era core. This team achievement was tied directly to the player obtained from Seattle in January 1998 and shows why the second-round acquisition had outsized value. It does not mean Snow was individually responsible for the Finals appearance, and the article should not award him the scoring honors earned by Iverson.

sections.heading: Jelani McCoy Was a Genuine Seattle Return
sections.body: The Supersonics' outgoing guard yielded a conditional second that became the No. 33 choice in 1998. Seattle selected McCoy, an athletic center from UCLA, and used him over three regular seasons. He supplied 26 appearances as a rookie, 58 in 1999-2000 and 70 in 2000-01, when he started 44 games. The 154 total Seattle appearances provided frontcourt depth and a brief stretch of starting experience, justifying some credit to the scouting and acquisition decision. His subsequent NBA years elsewhere and his entire 260-game career should not be represented as Seattle production. McCoy's contributions were real but shorter and less strategically central than Snow's seven Philadelphia seasons. The grade difference is therefore about breadth and longevity of realized team value, not about Seattle drafting a player who never entered the NBA.

sections.heading: Philadelphia's A Versus Seattle's C Tracks Longevity
sections.body: The preserved site verdict is 76ers Win, with Philadelphia A and Seattle C. Snow played 452 Philadelphia regular-season games, starting 403 and distributing 2,965 assists, while McCoy gave Seattle 154 games and 46 starts. A second-rounder was enough to acquire a guard who became part of a Finals backcourt; the returned pick nonetheless delivered a usable center for three seasons. This is a strong Philadelphia advantage without an excuse to dismiss the Seattle draft right. It is also a correction to misleading historical text that calls the original seller the Oklahoma City Thunder. The 1998 transaction occurred with Seattle, and the franchise did not relocate to Oklahoma City until a decade later. Good trade analysis must preserve the original team's name and separate later player careers from direct franchise returns.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Philadelphia A, Seattle C in the original 76ers Win record. Snow became an important Sixers point guard for 452 games while the acquired No.33 McCoy provided 154 Seattle games. Both packages produced NBA players, but Snow had greater team longevity and a 2001 Finals role. No retroactive Oklahoma City team name is appropriate for the 1998 exchange.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Acquired Willie Green’s Draft Rights
sections.body: On the night of the 2003 NBA draft, Philadelphia obtained the rights to Willie Green from Seattle. The SuperSonics received the rights to Paccelis Morlende and cash. Both clubs were exchanging draft property rather than trading established current starters. The cash amount was not substantiated in the cited record, so the basketball comparison rests chiefly on which of the two players eventually supplied usable NBA minutes. The transaction date and draft-rights wording should be kept together rather than quietly describing a conventional veteran swap.

sections.heading: Green Developed Into a Real NBA Rotation Player
sections.body: Green became an NBA guard who supplied years of professional backcourt minutes. That is the concrete reason Philadelphia’s return grades more highly: the rights developed into a player who actually filled a role. The deal should not be credited with an All-Star-level outcome it did not produce. The value lies in turning an inexpensive draft-rights opportunity into a long-term NBA contributor. It distinguishes the Green acquisition from rights that never produced comparable league minutes.

sections.heading: Seattle Held Other Rights and a Financial Consideration
sections.body: The SuperSonics acquired the draft rights to Morlende, along with cash. Those rights were legitimate property, but they did not generate NBA production matching Green’s eventual career. The money may have offered financial value to Seattle; without the amount, its exact contribution is unknown. That uncertainty is worth stating rather than inserting fictional salary relief or downstream draft choices. Seattle was not left entirely empty-handed, but Philadelphia obtained the clearer realized basketball return.

sections.heading: The Grade Gap Should Follow Those Two Specific Rights
sections.body: The published verdict is 76ers Win with Philadelphia A-minus and Seattle B. It favors Green’s actual playing career over Morlende’s less productive rights while still recognizing the cash consideration. Seattle’s B is not a failing mark. An existing four-section analysis and separate Deep Dive spent considerable space on what trade grades generally mean. The important historical comparison is much narrower: two sets of 2003 draft rights, one of which became a durable NBA rotation guard.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win — Philadelphia A-minus, Seattle B. Philadelphia obtained Willie Green’s rights, which developed into years of NBA backcourt production. Seattle acquired Paccelis Morlende’s rights and an unspecified cash payment. The SuperSonics received legitimate consideration, but Green’s realized career gives the 76ers the stronger basketball return.

sections.heading: The Exchange Gave Orlando Lewis and Seattle an Unusually Large Exception
sections.body: Seattle did not send Rashard Lewis to Orlando for Kurt Thomas or a pair of first-round picks on July 11, 2007. The original sign-and-trade was narrower: the Magic acquired Lewis, while the SuperSonics received a conditional future second-round selection and a trade exception valued at approximately $9.25 million. A contemporary Seattle Post-Intelligencer report described Sam Presti securing those terms when Lewis could otherwise have departed as a free agent. The arrangement allowed Orlando to give Lewis a sixth guaranteed contract year, an advantage that made the sign-and-trade structure attractive to the player. On that date, no Phoenix assets had changed hands. Keeping the July 11 transaction separate from the next deal is essential because the eventual Seattle draft haul depended on a second negotiation, not an automatic payment from Orlando.

sections.heading: The Magic Bought a Stretch Forward for Dwight Howard’s Interior Game
sections.body: Orlando already had Dwight Howard as its interior centerpiece. Lewis gave coach Stan Van Gundy a versatile forward whose shooting forced opposing defenses to follow a frontcourt player beyond the arc instead of crowding Howard at the rim. Hedo Turkoglu added another large ball handler, and Jameer Nelson helped organize the perimeter attack. In Lewis's first season, the Magic won 52 games and reached the Eastern Conference semifinals. One year later, with the same broad inside-out identity, they finished 59-23. The NBA's 2008-09 season review identifies Howard, Nelson and Lewis as All-Stars and records Orlando's run through Boston and Cleveland before losing the Finals to Los Angeles in five games. Those are actual Orlando results. Seattle's future draft picks should not be included in the Magic's playing return, and the Finals appearance does not convert into a championship that Orlando never won.

sections.heading: Seattle’s First Return Was Financial Flexibility, Not an Immediate Roster Upgrade
sections.body: The Seattle perspective begins with the team's negotiating position. Lewis was approaching a departure, and the Sonics were rebuilding. A roughly $9.25 million trade exception was useful because it offered a route to absorb salary in a later trade without having to match that salary in the usual way. It was not cash paid to Seattle, nor was the exception itself a roster player or draft choice. The other July 11 asset was Orlando's conditional 2009 second-round pick, whose value depended on its restrictions. Contemporary reporting says Seattle's front office turned a difficult free-agent exit into a mechanism for further business. That process earns credit, but only after the club actually used the flexibility. On the date Lewis left, the long-term identities of the players ultimately selected with the later picks were not known.

sections.heading: The Phoenix Deal Turned the Exception Into Two First-Round Chances
sections.body: Nine days later, on July 20, Seattle used roughly $8 million of the trade-exception capacity in a separate transaction with Phoenix. The Suns wanted salary relief. Their official announcement says they sent Kurt Thomas along with their own 2008 and 2010 first-round selections to the Sonics, taking back a conditional 2009 second-round pick from Seattle by way of Orlando. The picks were not supplied by the Magic on July 11. Phoenix's need to move Thomas's salary created an opening that Seattle used. The 2008 Phoenix pick became No. 24, Serge Ibaka, and the 2010 pick became No. 26, Quincy Pondexter. The Ibaka outcome is the most valuable later result, but it requires the full chain: Lewis leaves for an exception and conditional pick; then Phoenix sends two firsts to Seattle in exchange for separate cap relief and the second-round right.

sections.heading: Kurt Thomas Generated Another Separate Branch in February 2008
sections.body: Thomas also should not be treated as an immediate Orlando-to-Seattle return. He arrived through Phoenix in July 2007 and subsequently left in February 2008, when Seattle traded him to San Antonio for Brent Barry, Francisco Elson and a 2009 first-round selection. Basketball-Reference's Seattle transaction history traces that additional deal, and the pick later became No. 25, Rodrigue Beaubois. That secondary conversion helps explain why the Phoenix salary-relief maneuver had value beyond Thomas's minutes with a rebuilding Seattle club. Yet none of the Spurs assets came directly from Orlando either. Treating Lewis's sign-and-trade as a one-step acquisition of every later pick would blur the bargaining decisions of Phoenix, San Antonio and Seattle and overstate what was guaranteed in the original contract exchange.

sections.heading: An Even Verdict Can Give Both Teams an A Without Inventing a Title
sections.body: Orlando obtained a high-level offensive fit and an All-Star who played on its 2009 Finals team. The club's A recognizes production, strategic use of its Howard-centered roster and a deep postseason run, while acknowledging the expense of Lewis's long contract and the fact that the Lakers won the championship series. Seattle's A recognizes what Presti did with negotiating leverage that many teams would have allowed to disappear: the exception and conditional second enabled the Phoenix exchange that produced Ibaka's draft slot and another first-rounder. A later Thomas trade added still another pick branch. The ledger's Even Trade is therefore defensible for different reasons on either side, rather than a claim that the returns were identical. The Sonics' downstream asset success should be described as sourced sequential transactions, not a guarantee encoded in the July 11 agreement.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Orlando A, Seattle A. Lewis helped the Magic reach the 2009 NBA Finals, while Seattle converted a roughly $9.25 million trade exception and conditional second into the separate Phoenix deal for Kurt Thomas and the 2008 and 2010 Suns first-round picks. Orlando never directly transferred Ibaka, and the Magic did not win that Finals.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Rashard Lewis, Orlando’s 2009 Finals Run and Seattle’s Phoenix Pick Chain
featuredDeepDive.intro: The July 2007 Rashard Lewis sign-and-trade gave Orlando an All-Star forward and Seattle a valuable exception plus a conditional second. Nine days later, the Sonics used those rights in a separate Phoenix salary-relief deal that yielded two first-round picks. Following the exact dates explains how both teams earned A grades for very different results.

sections.heading: Why a Six-Year Lewis Agreement Changed Seattle’s Exit Options
sections.body: Lewis was a valuable unrestricted free agent, which limited how much Seattle could demand if he had simply signed elsewhere. The important difference in July 2007 was the sixth year available under the sign-and-trade arrangement. Orlando could offer a contract structure Lewis preferred; Seattle could use that preference to request something other than an uncompensated exit. Gary Washburn's contemporary reporting in the Seattle Post-Intelligencer specifically identifies the roughly $9.25 million exception and conditional second-round selection. Those details explain the leverage without turning the exchange into an imaginary conventional player swap. Presti was new to Seattle's front office and working through a franchise reset. His achievement was not retaining Lewis, a goal that was no longer realistic on the same terms. It was preserving an asset mechanism capable of helping the organization acquire future value from other teams' needs.

sections.heading: Orlando’s Two-Year Win Curve Tests the Basketball Side of the Verdict
sections.body: The clearest evaluation of the Magic does not depend on how many assets Seattle eventually drafted. Orlando went 52-30 in 2007-08 and won a first-round playoff series before falling to Detroit. The following season it won 59 games and reached the NBA Finals. The Magic defeated the reigning-champion Celtics in seven games and a 66-win Cleveland team in six; Los Angeles ended the run in five. The NBA's historical season review describes a frontcourt built around Dwight Howard with an inside-out offense that featured Lewis and other shooters. The progression from conference-semifinal contender to conference champion is specific evidence of Lewis helping the intended roster construction. Orlando's A does not require claiming that Lewis single-handedly produced all those wins. Howard's development, Turkoglu's creation and the rest of Van Gundy's roster were part of the same result.

sections.heading: Lewis’s Shooting Role Survived the Nelson Injury
sections.body: The 2008-09 Magic depended on the defense collapsing toward Howard while shooting threats punished that help. Lewis's ability to operate as a high-volume perimeter option from a forward position made the spacing unusually difficult to cover. The Magic's own season retrospective notes that Lewis led the league in made three-pointers and that he, Howard and Nelson had been selected as All-Stars. Nelson's shoulder injury in February made continuity more difficult, and Orlando later added Rafer Alston. Even after that disruption, the team finished 59-23. This is a strong argument for the acquisition's practical value: Lewis was not merely a recognizable free-agent name, but a player whose skill set continued to fit the offense when the backcourt changed. The label does not mean every shot or defensive possession in those seasons belongs to the original July transaction.

sections.heading: The Exact Route From Orlando’s Second-Round Pick to Ibaka
sections.body: The two relevant dates should sit next to each other. On July 11, 2007, Seattle received the conditional 2009 second-round pick and a trade exception in the Lewis sign-and-trade. On July 20, the Sonics traded that pick and offered Phoenix approximately $8 million in cap relief, receiving Thomas and two unprotected first-rounders. Phoenix's own official release names its 2008 and 2010 firsts, and both teams' transaction histories corroborate the exchange. Seattle used the 2008 pick at No. 24 for Serge Ibaka and the 2010 selection at No. 26 for Quincy Pondexter. The later Thomas-for-Spurs swap added another first-round asset in a third distinct trade. Writing the sequence out prevents the familiar shorthand that the Magic simply 'traded Ibaka for Lewis'—a statement that ignores the Suns and suggests Orlando ever held the Ibaka selection. Seattle's shrewdness was in chaining negotiable rights, not in forcing Orlando to transfer a future star.

sections.heading: Different Timelines, Same A Grade: Final Return Accounting
sections.body: The franchises were buying different things. Orlando was committing immediately to a costly veteran whose shooting could expand Howard's championship window. That investment delivered two strong regular seasons quickly and a 2009 Finals berth, although no title. Seattle was sacrificing no longer-controllable star production in exchange for tradable flexibility during a reset. The Phoenix follow-up turned that flexibility into Thomas and first-round opportunities; the Ibaka selection later became a cornerstone for the relocated Oklahoma City franchise. The grade can recognize Seattle's foresight without claiming Ibaka was already in the package or assigning the entirety of Oklahoma City's later success to one Lewis transaction. The fairest comparison is the decision each management team controlled on July 11 and the return directly traceable through documented follow-up deals. On those terms the original Even Trade and A grades for both clubs survive careful historical scrutiny.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Orlando A for Lewis’s on-court fit, All-Star play and the 2009 Finals berth; Seattle A for its sign-and-trade leverage and the later Phoenix conversion that made Ibaka’s No. 24 selection possible. The returns unfolded in different years through separate trades, supporting the inherited Even Trade rather than a false one-step asset exchange.

sections.heading: The Sign-and-Trade Was a Conditional First, Not a Player Swap
sections.body: Orlando acquired Tracy McGrady from Toronto on August 3, 2000 through a sign-and-trade agreement. The Raptors received a future conditional first-round selection rather than an established player. This structure allowed McGrady, who was leaving as a free agent, to obtain a seven-year contract under the rules then available to the club holding his rights. Contemporary reports described the Magic adding him on the same day they arranged a separate Grant Hill sign-and-trade with Detroit. The Hill transaction included Ben Wallace and Chucky Atkins, but those players were not part of the Toronto deal. Keeping the two packages distinct prevents a misleading ledger. Toronto had limited leverage over McGrady's destination and preserved a first-round asset instead of losing him for no compensation. Orlando immediately gained the right to build around a 21-year-old perimeter star.

sections.heading: McGrady’s New Role Became a Scoring Breakthrough
sections.body: McGrady's Toronto years had shown a talented young wing playing alongside Vince Carter. His Orlando move brought a larger offensive role, and the results appeared immediately. He earned the NBA Most Improved Player award for 2000-01, then developed into a perennial All-Star and All-NBA selection. His 32.1 points per game during 2002-03 led the league, and another scoring title followed in 2003-04. That ascent gave Orlando four seasons of exceptional individual production from a player acquired with a conditional future pick. Grant Hill's recurring injury problems complicated the roster Orlando originally envisioned, making McGrady's ability to carry offensive possessions especially valuable. The trade did not produce a championship or a deep Magic playoff run, but the difference between the acquired player's actual ceiling and the limited original price is substantial.

sections.heading: Toronto’s Pick Became Part of the Jerome Williams Trade
sections.body: Toronto did not keep Orlando's conditional first-round selection until the 2005 draft. On February 22, 2001, the Raptors sent the pick to Detroit alongside Corliss Williamson, Tyrone Corbin and Kornél Dávid. The Pistons returned Jerome Williams and Eric Montross. This later deal gave Toronto identifiable players and should not be erased when evaluating what its original asset could do. Williams became a fan favorite and useful frontcourt presence; Montross provided far less production. However, neither belonged to the August McGrady package directly. The Raptors had converted a right acquired in the sign-and-trade into part of a larger transaction. That distinction is the reason a C-minus assessment can be defensible even when the star they lost developed into a future Hall of Famer. Toronto extracted some value, but nothing approaching McGrady's peak.

sections.heading: Detroit Later Sent the Same Pick Back to Orlando
sections.body: The draft-right history has another turn. On June 2, 2001, Detroit transferred the 2005 first-round right to Orlando in a separate three-team transaction, as reflected in both clubs' transaction histories. The Magic ultimately exercised the No. 11 pick in 2005 on Fran Vázquez, who did not play in the NBA. The final draft selection therefore was not made by the Raptors, despite Toronto's receipt of the original right in August 2000. It would be inaccurate to say Toronto selected Vázquez or that Orlando kept the pick throughout the entire five-year interval. The chronology is Orlando to Toronto for McGrady, Toronto to Detroit in the Williams-Montross package, and Detroit back to Orlando before the 2005 draft. Each move had separate participants and incentives.

sections.heading: The Orlando Return Had Limits Without Losing Its Value
sections.body: McGrady became the Magic's offensive centerpiece but never led the team beyond the first round during his four Orlando seasons. Injuries to Grant Hill reduced the supporting-star partnership that management initially expected when both arrived in August 2000. Orlando nevertheless received elite scoring seasons and an extraordinary individual talent at a modest direct trade price. The club later moved McGrady to Houston in 2004 in a transaction centered on Steve Francis, giving it another chance to convert his remaining value. That subsequent trade should be distinguished from the 2000 sign-and-trade rather than listed as a direct Raptors return. The evaluation need not invent team championships or postseason advancement to justify Orlando's A-plus: Most Improved Player honors and two scoring titles are concrete outcomes of the acquisition.

sections.heading: Grades Reflect Free-Agent Leverage and What Followed
sections.body: Toronto was not selecting between two ordinary offers for a star under long-term contract. McGrady was a departing free agent whose preferred destination limited the Raptors' bargaining options. The conditional first-round pick gave management an asset to use later, and the club included it in the February 2001 trade that delivered Jerome Williams and Eric Montross. This is a meaningful distinction from losing a player without compensation. Still, Orlando secured four years of Hall of Fame-caliber production and Toronto surrendered the chance to keep McGrady beside Vince Carter. The historical result is a Magic Win, with Orlando A-plus and Toronto C-minus. An F for the Raptors would ignore their realistic leverage and the value realized through Williams; an equal grade would ignore the enormous disparity in peak talent and results.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Magic Win — Orlando A+, Toronto C-. Tracy McGrady became a two-time scoring champion and Most Improved Player with Orlando. Toronto received a conditional first and later moved it to Detroit in its February 2001 Jerome Williams–Eric Montross deal; the pick later returned to Orlando, which selected Fran Vázquez in 2005.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Tracy McGrady’s 2000 Sign-and-Trade: The Real Five-Year Pick Trail
featuredDeepDive.intro: Toronto sent McGrady to Orlando for a conditional first in August 2000, then used the pick in a separate Detroit trade before it returned to Orlando. The distinction explains McGrady’s enormous on-court value and the more modest Toronto return.

sections.heading: How a Seven-Year Contract Enabled the Deal
sections.body: Contemporary August 2000 reports described Tracy McGrady and Grant Hill signing seven-year agreements before joining Orlando through separate sign-and-trade arrangements. Those contracts offered longer terms and larger annual raises than a direct free-agent signing could at that time, which gave the departing stars a reason to cooperate with their prior clubs. Toronto's compensation was a future conditional first-round pick. Detroit's compensation for Hill was a different package, including Ben Wallace and Chucky Atkins. The distinction is essential because the Magic's ambitious summer produced two separate trade histories on the same day. Orlando had created cap room to pursue major free agents and used a pick to get McGrady on the preferred contract structure. Toronto's negotiating achievement was obtaining some compensation, not selecting another star in exchange for a player it could compel to stay.

sections.heading: The 2002-03 Peak Supports Orlando’s A-Plus
sections.body: McGrady averaged 32.1 points during the 2002-03 NBA season, winning his first scoring title and producing one of the leading individual scoring seasons of the early 2000s. He followed it with another scoring crown in 2003-04. Those results were not predictable from the quiet face value of a conditional first-round pick, even though his Toronto athleticism and skill had already drawn attention. McGrady also won Most Improved Player in his first Magic season and became a regular All-Star and All-NBA selection. The transaction acquired the highest-scoring version of the player at the start of his prime. The grade rewards those realized NBA performances and the opportunity Orlando created for him. It does not depend on attributing all the team's wins to one player or suggesting the Magic advanced beyond the first playoff round during his tenure.

sections.heading: The Hill Injuries Changed the Team Around McGrady
sections.body: The Magic hoped to pair their two August 2000 arrivals, Grant Hill and Tracy McGrady, as a formidable wing duo. Hill's recurring ankle problems sharply limited that partnership. As a result, McGrady often had to create offense without the second established star Orlando had planned to put beside him. His scoring titles and All-NBA production are even more notable in that context, but the roster imbalance exposed a real postseason limitation. Orlando did not advance beyond the first round in McGrady's four seasons. A historical trade grade should reflect both truths: McGrady exceeded the cost of a conditional pick by an enormous margin, and the franchise failed to turn his individual dominance into a deep playoff run. Treating the latter as a reason to erase the former would make the analysis less useful.

sections.heading: The Pick’s Toronto-Detroit-Orlando Route
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's 2000-01 Toronto transactions list the August 3 McGrady deal for a future first, followed by the February 22, 2001 trade that sent the same 2005 pick to Detroit. Toronto included other players in that trade and acquired Jerome Williams and Eric Montross. Detroit's ledger then records a June 2 transaction sending the right back to Orlando. The pick ultimately became No. 11 in the 2005 NBA draft, when the Magic selected Fran Vázquez. This route is essential to the asset accounting. Toronto did not directly receive Vázquez or use the selection itself, and Detroit did not hold it through 2005. The return Toronto actually extracted must be evaluated through its 2001 player acquisition, without pretending that every player in that package came solely from the McGrady pick.

sections.heading: The Toronto Grade Is C-Minus, Not a Zero
sections.body: The Raptors lost a player who became one of the NBA's leading scorers and a future Hall of Famer. That is a major competitive loss regardless of the legal and contractual difficulty of persuading an unrestricted free agent to stay. Management at least preserved a future first-round right and used it in a February 2001 trade that brought Jerome Williams and Eric Montross to Toronto. Williams had identifiable value as a hardworking frontcourt contributor and popular teammate, while Montross supplied a smaller return. A C-minus recognizes that partial recovery without suggesting the compensation was equivalent to the player Orlando acquired. On the other side, the Magic earned an A-plus for turning a conditional right into four years of superstar-level scoring. The inherited Magic Win verdict follows from those different realizations, not from hindsight alone.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Orlando A-plus for four seasons of elite McGrady production from a conditional draft right; Toronto C-minus for retaining and subsequently using that right to obtain part of the Jerome Williams–Eric Montross package. The Magic won the historical trade without either team making a championship run through this move.

sections.heading: Toronto Swapped a Former Lottery Pick for Two Young Bigs
sections.body: Toronto traded Rafael Araujo to Utah on June 8, 2006 and acquired Kris Humphries and Robert Whaley. The Raptors’ official announcement supports those exact player terms. This was a direct attempt to refresh reserve depth after Araujo had struggled to justify his lottery selection. The move should be assessed using what Humphries and Whaley did in Toronto and what Araujo did in Utah, rather than later events elsewhere or salary-accounting features that the team did not identify as traded player value.

sections.heading: Humphries Became a Useful Three-Season Toronto Reserve
sections.body: Humphries appeared in 60 Raptors games in 2006-07, 70 the next season and 29 in 2008-09. He averaged 5.7 points and 3.7 rebounds in his second Toronto campaign, providing modest but workable frontcourt minutes. His total of 159 Raptors games over three seasons gave the transaction its meaningful return. Humphries became a more productive starter later in his career with another franchise, but that later development does not belong on Toronto’s trade scorecard. Whaley never played for the Raptors and was waived within two weeks.

sections.heading: Utah Received Only a Short Final NBA Stint from Araujo
sections.body: Araujo played 28 regular-season games for Utah in 2006-07, totaling 248 minutes without a start. His .415 shooting and limited usage left him outside the Jazz’s meaningful rotation during a 51-win season. He did not appear in the 2007 postseason or return for another NBA regular-season campaign. The acquisition may have been defensible as an inexpensive depth chance, but it produced little actual court value. Utah’s grade should reflect the short tenure rather than any assumed benefit from his former draft position.

sections.heading: Why the Correct Spread Is B Versus D-plus
sections.body: The Raptors obtained 159 Humphries appearances and three years of occasional reserve production in exchange for a struggling former lottery pick. A B recognizes that useful improvement without elevating Humphries into a franchise-altering contributor. Utah earned D+ because Araujo at least appeared in 28 games, but his minutes were limited and his NBA career ended after that season. Whaley’s absence prevents Toronto from being credited with two productive incoming players. The advantage is clear without importing Humphries’ later performances on other teams.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Toronto Raptors Win — Toronto B, Utah D+. Kris Humphries provided 159 Raptors games across three seasons, while Robert Whaley was waived before playing for Toronto. Rafael Araujo appeared in only 28 Jazz games without a start during his final NBA season. Toronto converted an unproductive former lottery choice into usable reserve depth, but Humphries’ later breakout away from Toronto cannot inflate the result. The grades recognize a definite but modest Raptors success and a limited Utah return.

featuredDeepDive.label: Featured Deep Dive
featuredDeepDive.heading: Toronto Raptors–Utah Jazz: What the Trade Became
featuredDeepDive.intro: The June 2006 Toronto-Utah trade moved three frontcourt players but generated almost all of its meaningful outcome through Kris Humphries. Whaley never appeared for the Raptors, and Araujo lasted only 28 games with the Jazz. The useful question is not whether Humphries eventually became a double-double starter elsewhere; it is how much value Toronto actually obtained while he wore its uniform.

sections.heading: The Actual Exchange Was Smaller Than the Later Narrative
sections.body: Toronto acquired Humphries and Whaley for Araujo in a straightforward three-player deal. Araujo’s disappointing lottery tenure had already reduced his value to the Raptors, so the trade gave the organization a chance to obtain a younger usable reserve. Humphries arrived with development room, while Whaley was an additional name in the package. The first distinction is simple: Toronto ultimately received meaningful games from only one of its two incoming players. That limits how aggressively the win should be graded.

sections.heading: Humphries Offered Depth, Not His Later Peak
sections.body: Humphries totaled 159 Toronto games over three seasons, with his busiest Raptors season coming in 2007-08 when he played 70 and averaged 5.7 points and 3.7 rebounds. That was a valid bench return. He was not yet the high-rebounding starter who later emerged in New Jersey, and those future successes should not be counted retroactively. The B grade records a productive second-chance acquisition rather than an invented Toronto star.

sections.heading: Whaley and Araujo Both Disappeared Quickly
sections.body: Whaley was waived by Toronto less than two weeks after the trade, contributing no Raptors NBA games. Araujo played 28 Jazz games in 2006-07, never started and totaled 248 minutes. Utah was a successful club that season, but its broader 51-win record cannot be credited to a rarely used reserve who missed the playoffs. This comparison depends on individual rotation contribution, not the results of the franchises as a whole.

sections.heading: Why This Is a Clear but Modest Win
sections.body: The 159 games Humphries played for Toronto substantially exceeded Araujo’s 28 Utah appearances. The Raptors also escaped a stalled lottery-player relationship while obtaining occasional bench minutes for three seasons. Still, Whaley supplied nothing on the court and Humphries was not a major Raptors starter. Toronto B and Utah D+ therefore express a decisive directional advantage without overstating its absolute importance or assigning another team’s later player development to this exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Deep-Dive Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Toronto Raptors Win, Toronto B and Utah D+. Humphries played 159 Raptors games over three seasons; Whaley never suited up for them. Araujo appeared 28 times for Utah with no starts, and his NBA career ended after that season. Toronto obtained usable reserve production and the better outcome, but its grade stops short of crediting the later Humphries breakout elsewhere.

sections.heading: Boston Chose Porziņģis Over Another Smart-Led Backcourt
sections.body: The Celtics acquired Kristaps Porziņģis from Washington and two first-round interests from Memphis: No. 25 in the 2023 draft and a protected 2024 Golden State first. Memphis received Marcus Smart from Boston. Washington received Tyus Jones from Memphis and Danilo Gallinari, Mike Muscala and No. 35 draft rights from Boston. Every receiving side is documented in the official three-team announcement, even though the original archival import listed only Washington’s inbound players.

sections.heading: Porziņģis Addressed a Specific Boston Frontcourt Need
sections.body: Boston wanted a skilled shooting big man who could protect the rim without requiring Jayson Tatum or Jaylen Brown to carry every scoring action. Porziņģis provided a different offensive option and interior size during the Celtics’ 2023–24 championship season. His injuries affected availability, including in the playoffs, but the team still captured the title with him as an important contributor. Boston’s A-plus reflects his clear role in a successful roster upgrade rather than claiming he alone won the championship.

sections.heading: Memphis Bet on Smart’s Veteran Leadership
sections.body: The Grizzlies acquired a former Defensive Player of the Year who could organize guard play and lead a young roster. Injuries limited Smart’s ability to become a long-term centerpiece during his Memphis stint. Trading two first-round assets for that interrupted veteran contribution did not produce the return the team hoped for, explaining a C grade. The assessment does not erase Smart’s earlier Boston accomplishments; those occurred before Memphis acquired him and cannot be transferred to its ledger.

sections.heading: Washington Chose Useful Veterans and a Draft Opportunity
sections.body: Washington acquired Jones, an established low-turnover point guard, plus Gallinari and Muscala from Boston. The No. 35 selection became Julian Phillips’s draft rights, which were subsequently moved in a separate draft-night transaction. Jones provided immediate roster usefulness, while the other pieces offered shorter-term or movable value. A C-plus reflects recovering tangible assets for an outgoing veteran without confusing that package with Boston’s championship-level benefit.

sections.heading: The Draft Rights Must Stay Attached to Their Actual Routes
sections.body: Boston’s No. 25 pick was used on Marcus Sasser before additional draft-night movement, and the protected Golden State first was another real incoming asset even though its subsequent path involved later transactions. Neither should be described as a Boston-drafted long-term star from this deal. Keeping the pick flows distinct from Smart, Jones and Porziņģis explains why Boston’s grade leads while Memphis and Washington had narrower returns. The official trade packet supplies the source for all three directions.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win — Boston A-plus, Washington C-plus, Memphis C. Porziņģis provided a valuable frontcourt dimension to the Celtics’ 2024 championship team, with draft rights adding further transaction value. The Grizzlies received Smart but lost much of his intended impact to injuries; Washington recovered Jones and several secondary assets. Boston converted its outgoing package into the strongest realized team result.

sections.heading: Howie Schultz for Cash: What Changed Hands
sections.body: On October 10, 1951, Fort Wayne sold Howie Schultz's player rights to the Minneapolis Lakers for cash. The surviving transaction ledgers agree on the sale, although the amount is not preserved. Schultz's rights history is unusual: he had been included in a May trade with Tri-Cities and apparently returned to Fort Wayne before this deal, with no surviving record explaining the intermediate step. The defensible reading is therefore narrow: Minneapolis bought Schultz's rights, and Fort Wayne received an undisclosed cash payment.

sections.heading: Minneapolis Got Two Seasons of Useful Frontcourt Depth
sections.body: Schultz immediately joined the Lakers' rotation. He played all 66 regular-season games in 1951-52, averaging 4.1 points, 3.7 rebounds and 1.5 assists, then appeared in 12 playoff games during a championship run. He returned for 40 more regular-season games in 1952-53 as Minneapolis won another title. Schultz was not a star, but 106 regular-season appearances plus postseason minutes gave the Lakers a real basketball return from a cash purchase.

sections.heading: Fort Wayne Monetized Rights but Left No Traceable Basketball Return
sections.body: Fort Wayne moved a player who was not part of its active 1951-52 rotation, so selling the rights was defensible roster management. The problem for the retrospective grade is that the cash amount is unknown and no player, pick or later transaction can be tied to it. That makes the Pistons' return impossible to credit beyond the financial payment itself, while the Lakers' side produced documented on-court value across two championship seasons.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win — Minneapolis B+, Fort Wayne C. The Lakers received 106 regular-season games and postseason depth from Schultz, including contributions to consecutive championship teams. Fort Wayne converted inactive rights into cash, but the amount and any basketball use of that money are undocumented. The win is clear without overstating Schultz's role.

sections.heading: A Five-Asset Exchange With a Later Player Attached
sections.body: On October 26, 1956, Minneapolis sent Slater Martin, the draft rights to Jerry Bird and a player to be named later to New York for Walter Dukes and the draft rights to Burdette Haldorson. Later records identify the player to be named later as Phil Jordon. The Knicks' historical record and Basketball-Reference ledgers agree on the core exchange. Bird was a 1956 first-round pick serving in the military, while Haldorson never appeared in an NBA game.

sections.heading: Minneapolis Turned Walter Dukes Into Larry Foust
sections.body: Dukes started at center for the Lakers in 1956-57, playing 71 games and averaging 10.1 points and 11.2 rebounds. Minneapolis then traded him to Detroit for Larry Foust. Foust became an All-Star in each of his first two Lakers seasons and played 191 regular-season games for the franchise. Haldorson's rights added no NBA production, but the Dukes-to-Foust chain gave Minneapolis several seasons of high-level center play.

sections.heading: New York Converted a Short Slater Martin Stay Into Willie Naulls
sections.body: Martin played only 13 games for the Knicks before New York traded him to St. Louis for Willie Naulls. That conversion became the strongest asset in the deal. Naulls developed into a long-term Knicks scorer and made multiple All-Star teams, including three straight from 1960 through 1962. Bird later appeared in 11 games for New York, while Jordon contributed limited minutes. Both teams managed their incoming assets well, but the Martin-to-Naulls branch produced the larger and longer peak.

sections.heading: The Knicks' Value Came Through a Second Move
sections.body: Slater Martin lasted only 13 games with New York, so the Knicks' eventual advantage wasn't built on a lengthy Martin tenure. The club subsequently traded him for Willie Naulls, who developed into a productive Knicks scorer and four-time All-Star. That follow-on move belongs in the transaction chain, but it doesn't mean Naulls joined New York in the original October 1956 exchange. Minneapolis also extracted substantial value by receiving Walter Dukes. He averaged 11.2 rebounds across 71 Lakers games in 1956-57 before the franchise moved him for Larry Foust, who later made two All-Star appearances as a Laker. The older player-to-be-named-later accounting for Phil Jordon also needs to stay distinct from the immediately named draft rights. The A-to-A- margin rests on those documented paths, not on counting the initial trade as a direct Naulls-for-Foust swap.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win — New York A, Minneapolis A-. This was a productive trade for both sides. The Lakers got a strong season from Dukes and then two All-Star seasons from Foust. The Knicks turned Martin into Naulls, whose multi-year All-Star run gave New York the slightly better long-term result. The edge is real, but it is much closer than a one-sided verdict would suggest.

sections.heading: Jack George for Guy Sparrow Was a Straight Player Swap
sections.body: Philadelphia sent Jack George to New York for Guy Sparrow on January 27, 1959. Team and league transaction ledgers agree on the one-for-one exchange, with no draft pick, cash term or later condition attached. Both were veteran players by the time of the trade, so the result turns on how much useful NBA value each club received after the swap rather than on a hidden asset chain.

sections.heading: George Gave New York 110 Games of Rotation Value
sections.body: George played 25 games for the Knicks in 1958-59, 69 the next season and 16 more in 1960-61. Across 110 New York appearances he averaged 8.2 points, 3.0 assists and 2.8 rebounds. His All-Star peak had already occurred in Philadelphia, so the Knicks did not acquire a star version of George, but they did receive more than a season and a half of useful veteran backcourt play.

sections.heading: Sparrow Never Established the Same Role in Philadelphia
sections.body: Sparrow appeared in 23 games for the Warriors after the trade and 11 more in 1959-60. His 34-game Philadelphia stay produced 3.4 points and 2.4 rebounds per game in a limited role, and 1959-60 became his final NBA season. The contrast is straightforward: New York extracted far more remaining service from George than Philadelphia did from Sparrow.

sections.heading: The Two Clubs Got Different Amounts of a Veteran's Final Seasons
sections.body: The difference is visible even when the players' earlier reputations are excluded. George appeared in 25 games after joining New York during 1958-59, then 69 the following season before adding another 16 in 1960-61. Those appearances provided continuity in the Knicks' backcourt for parts of three campaigns. Philadelphia, by contrast, received only 23 Sparrow games in the first partial season and 11 in the next, after which his NBA career ended. That's not a hypothetical comparison of their draft pedigree or peak talent; the two clubs actually received radically different remaining terms of service. It also explains why New York's B+ isn't a claim that George arrived as an All-Star. The value was a reliable veteran rotation contribution from a straight one-for-one exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win — New York B+, Philadelphia C-. George was no longer at his All-Star peak, but 110 games of regular rotation work clearly exceeded Sparrow's 34-game, low-minute Warriors tenure. This was a useful veteran win for New York, not a franchise-changing steal.

sections.heading: The Clippers Sold Jared Jordan's Rights for Cash
sections.body: Los Angeles drafted Jared Jordan 45th overall in 2007, then sent his draft rights to New York for cash on September 30. The cash amount was not disclosed. This was a small rights transaction, not a trade that needs a long asset-chain explanation: the Clippers chose to monetize a second-round prospect, while the Knicks paid for a chance to evaluate him in camp.

sections.heading: New York's Flier Ended Before the Regular Season
sections.body: The Knicks signed Jordan to a non-guaranteed contract after acquiring his rights, but waived him on October 25. He never appeared in a regular-season NBA game for New York and continued his career outside the NBA after camp. That leaves the Knicks with no realized NBA production from the asset they bought, while the Clippers at least retained the cash they received.

sections.heading: Why the Grade Gap Stays Small
sections.body: The result favors Los Angeles, but the scale matters. No public source establishes the amount of cash, and New York was taking a low-cost chance on a recent second-round pick rather than sacrificing a rotation player or premium draft asset. A modest win for the Clippers fits the evidence better than the previous record, which incorrectly treated Jordan's rights as if they produced meaningful Knicks value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win — Los Angeles B-, New York C. The Clippers converted rights they were willing to move into cash. The Knicks' prospect flier produced no regular-season NBA value and ended with Jordan being waived before opening night. Because the cash amount is unknown and the stakes were small, the verdict is a narrow Clippers win rather than a major steal.

sections.heading: Washington Consolidated Four Seconds Into a First
sections.body: Philadelphia sent Reggie Jackson and its 2026 first-round asset — the least favorable of the Clippers, Thunder and the protected Rockets pick — to Washington for Jared Butler and four future second-round picks. Washington waived Jackson immediately, so the deal was never about adding the veteran guard. The Wizards were paying multiple smaller assets to move up the draft-capital ladder from seconds to a first.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Still Got Real Value From Jared Butler
sections.body: The Sixers did not leave the trade empty-handed. Butler played 28 games for Philadelphia after the deal, started 17 and averaged 11.5 points with 4.9 assists in 24.4 minutes per game. Philadelphia also kept the four second-round assets. That production makes the return more useful than a simple “four seconds for a first” summary suggests, even though the first-rounder remained the strongest single asset in the exchange.

sections.heading: The First Became No. 30 and Stayed Useful as Trade Currency
sections.body: The 2026 first ultimately landed at No. 30, where Koa Peat was selected. Washington had already included that Oklahoma City-derived first in the larger February 2026 package that brought Anthony Davis to the Wizards. The pick was only one component of that later deal and should not be credited with the entire Davis return, but its inclusion shows why Washington valued consolidating into a first-round asset in the first place.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wizards Win — Washington A-, Philadelphia C. Washington turned Butler and four seconds into a first-round asset that ultimately became pick No. 30 and later functioned as part of a major trade package. Philadelphia got a productive post-deadline stretch from Butler and retained four future seconds, so the return was not empty. The first-round premium, however, gives Washington the stronger package and supports the existing verdict.
