Earl Tatum Career Statistics and Transactions
Adrian Dantley Career Statistics and Transactions
Dave Robisch Career Statistics and Transactions

sections.heading: The source-backed Package Is a 1981 First for a 1978 First
sections.body:
Golden State, Portland and the league transaction ledgers all agree on the June 7, 1978 transaction. The Warriors sent a 1981 first-round pick to the Trail Blazers and received Portland's 1978 first-round pick.

The legacy archive entry described Golden State's outgoing asset as a 1979-or-1981 first. This review normalizes that language to the source-supported 1981 first because all three authoritative transaction ledgers use that year.

sections.heading: Golden State Used the No. 22 Pick on Raymond Townsend
sections.body:
Portland's 1978 first landed at No. 22, where Golden State selected Raymond Townsend. He played 65 games as a rookie, averaging 4.7 points in 11.9 minutes, then appeared in 75 games in 1979-80.

Across two Warriors seasons, Townsend played 140 regular-season games and scored 710 points. He was a real NBA contributor, but he never became a high-impact starter or long-term core player for Golden State.

That direct return gives the Warriors more value than a failed draft pick, but it remains limited for a first-round asset.

sections.heading: Portland Held the Future Pick for Less Than Two Years
sections.body:
The Blazers did not wait until 1981 to use the pick. On February 8, 1980, Portland traded the future Golden State first to New Jersey together with Maurice Lucas and a 1980 first-round pick for Calvin Natt.

That later transaction is the key downstream branch. The Golden State pick was one of three assets Portland used to acquire a productive young forward. It therefore had substantial market value even before the draft.

sections.heading: Calvin Natt Became an Immediate Portland Contributor
sections.body:
Natt joined Portland during his rookie season and averaged 20.4 points in 25 games after the trade. He then played 74 games in 1980-81 at 13.4 points and 75 games in 1981-82 while averaging 18.4 points per 36 minutes.

This review does not assign all of Natt's Portland production to the 1981 first because Maurice Lucas and another first-round pick were also part of the package. The correct conclusion is narrower: the Golden State pick remained valuable enough to serve as one of the central pieces in a major trade for a productive forward.

sections.heading: The Pick Ultimately Became Albert King
sections.body:
New Jersey retained the Golden State selection until the 1981 draft. The pick landed at No. 10 and became Albert King. King went on to play 410 regular-season games for the Nets across six seasons.

That player value belongs to New Jersey, not Portland, because the Blazers had already traded the pick away. The No. 10 outcome is still useful for showing how valuable the asset ultimately became.

sections.heading: The Trade Was Not a Disaster for Golden State
sections.body:
A simple Townsend-versus-King comparison makes the Warriors look worse than the actual asset path warrants. Portland did not draft King, and the Blazers had to combine the pick with Maurice Lucas and another first to acquire Natt.

Golden State received 140 Townsend games and two seasons of reserve production. Portland received a future first that held stronger trade value and became part of a meaningful acquisition.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Blazers Edge, B+/C+. Portland receives a B+ because the 1981 first became premium trade currency and helped the club acquire Calvin Natt in 1980. Golden State receives a C+ because Townsend gave the Warriors 140 games and 710 points, but the club surrendered a future first that eventually landed at No. 10. The Portland advantage is real without pretending the Blazers directly received Albert King or that the pick alone bought Natt. Confidence is high.

sections.heading: The Source Record Has a Date Split, but the Economic Exchange Is Clear
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's 1977-78 Indiana and Milwaukee transaction logs record June 8, 1978 as the date Indiana signed Alex English as a veteran free agent and sent Milwaukee a 1979 first-round pick as compensation.

The legacy canonical record is dated October 3. A separate draft-pick transaction ledger places Milwaukee's agreement not to exercise its right of first refusal on English on that date and ties the same 1979 first-round pick to the agreement. This review preserves the canonical record rather than inventing a second transaction, but records the date split explicitly.

Whichever administrative date is used, the underlying value exchange is the same: Indiana acquired English's services, and Milwaukee acquired Indiana's 1979 first-round pick.

sections.heading: English Gave Indiana 135 Productive Games
sections.body:
English immediately became a major Pacers contributor. In 1978-79 he played 81 games, started 69 and averaged 16.0 points, 8.1 rebounds and 3.3 assists while shooting 51.1 percent.

He remained productive for Indiana in 1979-80. Before the midseason trade he played 54 games, started 15 and averaged 14.9 points, 7.0 rebounds and 2.6 assists.

That gives the Pacers 135 direct regular-season games from the free-agent signing. This review does not credit Indiana for the Hall of Fame career English later built in Denver. Those seasons occurred after he left the Pacers and belong to Denver's side of the later transaction.

sections.heading: Indiana Also Used English in the George McGinnis Trade, but Attribution Is Shared
sections.body:
On February 1, 1980, Indiana traded English and a 1980 first-round pick to Denver for George McGinnis. The additional first matters because McGinnis cannot be treated as a return generated by English alone.

McGinnis nevertheless gave Indiana substantial downstream value from the package. He played 28 games for the Pacers after the trade in 1979-80 and averaged 16.9 points, 10.9 rebounds and 5.1 assists. He followed with 69 games in 1980-81 at 17.6 points, 10.3 rebounds and 4.1 assists, then played 76 more games in 1981-82.

The Pacers therefore received useful downstream production, but this review assigns it only as shared-package context because the separate first-round pick was part of the price.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Did Not Simply Use the Pick on Calvin Natt
sections.body:
The legacy summary says Milwaukee received Calvin Natt. That skips an important transaction.

On May 31, 1979, Milwaukee traded John Gianelli and the Indiana first-round pick to New Jersey for Harvey Catchings. New Jersey, not Milwaukee, then used the pick at No. 8 on Natt.

That means Natt's NBA career is not realized Bucks production from this transaction. Milwaukee's actual downstream return from the pick was its role in the package that acquired Catchings.

sections.heading: Catchings Became a Long-Term Bucks Rotation Player
sections.body:
Catchings played five seasons for Milwaukee from 1979-80 through 1983-84. He appeared in 372 regular-season games for the Bucks and started 45.

His role was mostly defensive and rotational rather than star-level. He played 72 games in his first Milwaukee season, 77 in 1980-81, 80 in 1981-82, 74 in 1982-83 and 69 in 1983-84.

The attribution again requires care because Milwaukee sent Gianelli with the pick. Catchings cannot be credited entirely to Indiana's first-rounder, just as McGinnis cannot be credited entirely to English.

sections.heading: The Pacers Still Hold the Hindsight Edge
sections.body:
Both organizations realized useful value. Milwaukee turned the compensation pick, together with Gianelli, into a player who stayed in the rotation for five seasons. That is a materially better outcome than simply losing English for nothing.

Indiana, however, received 135 direct games from English at a much higher individual level, including a full season as a 16-point, eight-rebound starter. The later McGinnis package adds more value even after discounting it for the extra first-round pick.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pacers Win, A-/B. Indiana receives an A- because English delivered 135 productive games and then remained part of a package that returned McGinnis. Milwaukee receives a B because the first-round compensation asset retained enough value to help acquire Catchings, who played 372 Bucks games, but Gianelli was also required in that deal. The result is a clear Pacers edge without crediting Indiana for English's Denver prime or pretending Milwaukee directly drafted Natt. Confidence is high.

sections.heading: The Draft-Day Swap Was No. 5 Plus Cash for No. 4
sections.body: Detroit's transaction record shows the Pistons sending the 1979 first-round pick later used on Sidney Moncrief to Milwaukee for the No. 4 pick later used on Greg Kelser. Detroit's source package also records cash going to the Bucks.

sections.heading: Moncrief Became a Milwaukee Franchise Pillar
sections.body:
Milwaukee used the No. 5 pick on Moncrief and kept him for ten seasons. He played 695 regular-season games for the Bucks, fourth-most in franchise history at the current checkpoint.

The peak value was elite. Moncrief made five All-Star teams, five All-NBA teams and five All-Defensive teams. He also won Defensive Player of the Year in both 1982-83 and 1983-84 and was later inducted into the Hall of Fame.

That is the kind of outcome teams hope for when they acquire a premium lottery-level pick: long tenure, two-way star production and repeated postseason relevance.

sections.heading: Kelser Gave Detroit Two Partial Seasons
sections.body:
Kelser played 50 games as a rookie and 25 more in 1980-81. Across those 75 Pistons games, he scored 1,017 points and provided useful wing production, including 14.2 points per game as a rookie.

Knee trouble interrupted his second season and limited the direct Detroit return. On November 23, 1981, the Pistons traded Kelser to Seattle for Vinnie Johnson.

sections.heading: The Kelser Branch Then Became Vinnie Johnson
sections.body:
That follow-up trade substantially changes Detroit's side of the ledger. Johnson played 798 regular-season games for the Pistons, fourth-most in franchise history at the current checkpoint, and became one of the team's most important bench scorers.

Johnson was part of Detroit's back-to-back championship teams in 1989 and 1990. Basketball-Reference credits him with two NBA titles, and his long Pistons tenure means Kelser's downstream value was far greater than Kelser's own 75 games.

This is direct attribution: Detroit traded Kelser alone for Johnson, so Johnson's Pistons value legitimately belongs to the Kelser branch.

sections.heading: Why Milwaukee Still Gets the Edge
sections.body:
Detroit's outcome was excellent once Johnson is included. The Pistons turned the No. 4 selection into Kelser and then directly into an 798-game championship contributor.

Milwaukee still received the better individual cornerstone. Moncrief became a Hall of Famer and one of the best two-way guards of his era, with 695 Bucks games and a long list of major honors.

The cash amount is not documented in the reviewed sources, so it is not assigned independent value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win, A+/A. Milwaukee receives an A+ for landing Moncrief, a Hall of Fame guard with 695 Bucks games, five All-Star selections and two Defensive Player of the Year awards. Detroit receives an A because Kelser later became Vinnie Johnson in a direct one-for-one trade, producing 798 Pistons games and two championship seasons.

sections.heading: The Pick Was Valuable, but Philadelphia Did Not Draft Daugherty
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's 1979-80 transaction ledgers record Philadelphia sending Joe Bryant to San Diego for the Clippers' 1986 first-round pick. The legacy archive entry labels the asset with Brad Daugherty because he was eventually selected No. 1 with that pick.

That label needs context. Philadelphia still controlled the selection in June 1986, but one day before the draft the 76ers traded the No. 1 pick to Cleveland for Roy Hinson. Cleveland then selected Daugherty. This review therefore evaluates Philadelphia's realized return as Hinson and the later Hinson branch, not Daugherty's Cavaliers career.

sections.heading: Bryant Gave San Diego Three Useful Seasons
sections.body:
Bryant played 81 games for the Clippers in 1979-80, averaging 9.3 points and 6.4 rebounds in 28.7 minutes. He followed with all 82 games in 1980-81 and averaged 11.6 points and 5.4 rebounds.

In 1981-82, Bryant played 75 games, started 49 and averaged 11.8 points. Across the three seasons he appeared in 238 regular-season games for San Diego.

That is substantially more direct production than the old F-style framing suggests. The Clippers gave up a future premium asset, but they received three full years of rotation and starting-level forward play in return.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Eventually Converted the Pick into Hinson
sections.body:
On June 16, 1986, Philadelphia traded the No. 1 selection to Cleveland for Roy Hinson. Hinson then played 76 games for the 76ers in 1986-87, starting 58 and averaging 13.9 points, 6.4 rebounds and 2.1 blocks.

He added 29 Philadelphia games the next season before a January 1988 trade sent Hinson, Tim McCormick and a 1989 second-round pick to New Jersey for Mike Gminski and Ben Coleman.

Because McCormick and the second-rounder were also included, this review does not assign the entire Gminski-Coleman return to the original 1979 pick. Hinson's 105 Philadelphia games are the cleanest direct realized outcome.

sections.heading: Why Philadelphia Still Gets the Edge
sections.body:
San Diego received more games from the original player than Philadelphia later received from Hinson. Bryant was a legitimate three-season rotation piece, so the Clippers deserve a strong grade.

Philadelphia, however, turned an outgoing player who had just averaged 7.6 points into an asset that matured into the No. 1 pick and was then converted into a productive starting forward. Hinson also retained enough trade value to become part of another substantial package.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight 76ers Edge, A-/B+. Philadelphia receives an A- because the future first matured into the No. 1 pick and was converted into 105 Hinson games plus later trade utility. San Diego receives a B+ because Bryant delivered 238 games across three seasons. The result is much closer than an evaluation that credits Philadelphia with Daugherty's Cleveland career.

sections.heading: Golden State Bought High-End Scoring
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's Golden State, San Diego and league transaction ledgers agree on the August 28, 1980 trade: the Warriors received World B. Free, while the Clippers received Phil Smith and Golden State's 1984 first-round pick.

Free immediately became one of Golden State's primary scorers. He played 65 games in 1980-81 and averaged 24.1 points with 5.6 assists. In 1981-82 he played 78 games, started all 78 and averaged 22.9 points with 5.4 assists.

He opened 1982-83 with another 19 Warriors games at 22.8 points per game. That brought Free's Golden State total to 162 regular-season games across parts of three seasons, all at star-level scoring volume.

sections.heading: The Free Branch Also Returned Ron Brewer
sections.body:
Golden State did not simply lose Free at the end of that run. On December 15, 1982, the Warriors traded him to Cleveland for Ron Brewer.

Brewer played 53 games for Golden State in 1982-83 and another 13 in 1983-84. This review therefore credits 66 additional Warriors games as direct downstream value from the Free branch.

Brewer was not another Free-level scorer, but the transaction extended the life of the original asset rather than ending it at 162 games.

sections.heading: Phil Smith Gave San Diego Two Useful Seasons
sections.body:
Smith played 76 games for San Diego in 1980-81 and averaged 16.8 points, 4.9 assists and 31.3 minutes. He returned for 48 games in 1981-82, starting 39 and averaging 13.2 points with 4.9 assists.

That is 124 regular-season Clippers games from the veteran guard.

On February 16, 1982, San Diego traded Smith to Seattle for Armond Hill and a 1982 second-round pick later associated with Jeff Taylor. Hill played 19 games for the Clippers and started 14.

The incoming second-rounder was later included with Joe Bryant in a Houston trade that returned the pick used on Richard Anderson. Because Bryant was also outgoing, this review does not assign Anderson's full Clippers career to the Smith branch. The important point is that Smith still carried additional trade value after his 124 San Diego games.

sections.heading: The First-Round Pick Became Lancaster Gordon
sections.body:
The other major San Diego asset did not resolve until the 1984 draft. The Clippers used Golden State's first-round pick at No. 8 on Lancaster Gordon.

Gordon played four NBA seasons, all for the Clippers. He appeared in 201 regular-season games and scored 1,125 points, with his largest role coming in 1986-87 when he played 70 games and averaged 7.5 points.

He never became a high-end starter, but 201 games from a future first-rounder are meaningful realized value.

sections.heading: Why the Trade Stays Even
sections.body:
Golden State received the best player in the transaction. Free produced 162 games of high-volume scoring and then turned into 66 more Brewer games.

San Diego received more asset depth. Smith provided 124 useful games, Gordon supplied 201 more, and Smith later brought back Hill plus additional draft currency.

The Warriors won on peak impact. The Clippers won on volume and asset depth. Neither advantage is large enough to create a clear hindsight winner.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, A-/A-. Golden State receives an A- for 162 Free games at roughly 23 points per game across his Warriors tenure plus the later Brewer return. San Diego also receives an A- for 124 Smith games, 201 Gordon games and the additional Smith trade return. The original balanced verdict survives source-backed review.

sections.heading: The Trade Produced Real Value for Both Teams
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference records Los Angeles acquiring Jim Brewer from Portland on October 8, 1980. The Lakers sent a 1984 second-round pick that ultimately became the No. 46 selection used on Jerome Kersey.

The transaction ledger also describes Portland's option to swap first-round picks as becoming the second-round pick instead. The legacy canonical record carries the option language on both sides, but this review does not count it as an additional independent asset beyond the realized 1984 second-rounder.

sections.heading: Brewer Played Two Full Lakers Seasons
sections.body:
Brewer appeared in 78 games for Los Angeles in 1980-81 and 71 more in 1981-82. Across those two seasons, he totaled 149 regular-season games, 2,073 minutes, 545 rebounds and 104 blocks.

He was a low-usage reserve rather than a major scorer, but he gave the Lakers dependable frontcourt depth.

Brewer also appeared in eight playoff games during the 1982 championship run. That title-season contribution means Los Angeles did not simply surrender a future pick for a player who failed to help.

sections.heading: Portland Turned the Pick into Jerome Kersey
sections.body:
The long-term gap comes from what the 1984 second-rounder became. Portland selected Kersey at No. 46.

Kersey played 831 regular-season games for the Trail Blazers across 11 seasons. Basketball-Reference's Portland franchise totals credit him with 21,760 minutes, 10,067 points, 5,078 rebounds, 1,762 assists and 1,059 steals.

He developed from a second-round project into a long-term starter and rotation pillar during one of the strongest sustained periods in franchise history.

sections.heading: The Option Is Not a Second Kersey Asset
sections.body:
The legacy archive entry contains a Blazers option to swap 1984 draft picks on both the incoming and outgoing sides. Basketball-Reference's transaction language clarifies that the option became the second-round pick instead.

This review therefore treats the No. 46 Kersey selection as the realized draft value and marks the duplicated swap language as non-exercised or converted context, not another piece of value for either side.

sections.heading: Why Portland Wins Decisively
sections.body:
Los Angeles still receives meaningful credit. Brewer played 149 games and contributed as a reserve during the 1982 championship postseason.

Portland, however, converted the draft consideration into 831 Kersey games and more than 10,000 points over 11 seasons. The scale and longevity of that return overwhelm Brewer's useful two-year Lakers tenure.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Blazers Win, A+/B. Portland receives an A+ for turning the No. 46 pick into an 11-season franchise fixture. Los Angeles receives a B because Brewer supplied 149 regular-season games and championship-season depth, making the trade productive for the Lakers even though the hindsight gap became enormous.

sources.title: 1981-82 Los Angeles Lakers Roster and Statistics

sections.heading: The Trade Included More Than Two Second-Round Picks
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference records Phoenix acquiring Dudley Bradley from Indiana on June 8, 1981 for a 1981 second-round pick, a 1982 second-round pick and the Suns relinquishing their right to swap 1983 first-round picks with the Pacers.

That last term is the decisive part of the hindsight evaluation. It looked like optional future protection in 1981, but the 1983 draft positions turned it into premium realized value.

sections.heading: Bradley Gave Phoenix One Season
sections.body:
Bradley played 64 games for Phoenix in 1981-82, starting three and averaging 5.1 points, 1.4 rebounds and 1.3 assists in 14.6 minutes.

He left after the season and signed with Chicago as a veteran free agent on October 2, 1982. Phoenix's transaction ledger says the Suns received compensation, but the public Basketball-Reference entry renders that return only as FROM_TRADE rather than identifying a specific asset.

This review therefore does not invent or score an unknown compensation return.

sections.heading: Al Leslie Produced No NBA Games
sections.body:
Indiana used the 1981 second-round pick at No. 37 on Al Leslie.

Basketball-Reference lists Leslie as a Pacers draft pick but records no NBA regular-season statistics. That branch produced no direct NBA playing value.

sections.heading: Jose Slaughter Played 63 Pacers Games
sections.body:
The 1982 second-round pick landed at No. 43 and became Jose Slaughter.

Slaughter played 63 games for Indiana in 1982-83, starting once and averaging 3.6 points in 8.2 minutes. That was his only NBA season.

On its own, the two-pick portion of Indiana's return would have been modest.

sections.heading: The Relinquished 1983 Swap Became the Real Prize
sections.body:
Phoenix also gave up its contractual right to swap first-round picks with Indiana in the 1983 draft.

Indiana's own 1983 first ultimately landed at No. 2. The Pacers used it on Steve Stipanovich, who played all five of his NBA seasons for Indiana.

Stipanovich appeared in 403 regular-season games, started 365 and averaged 13.2 points, 7.8 rebounds and 2.3 assists for his Pacers career.

Phoenix's original 1983 first ultimately landed at No. 21, the pick that became Greg Kite after later transactions. Because Phoenix had surrendered the swap option two years earlier, Indiana retained control of the No. 2 position instead of being exposed to a No. 2-for-No. 21 exchange.

This review treats that protected draft position as realized value of the relinquishment clause, not as a speculative counterfactual player trade.

sections.heading: Why Indiana Wins
sections.body:
Phoenix received 64 games of useful reserve defense from Bradley, and there may have been later free-agent compensation that the public ledger does not identify clearly enough to score.

Indiana received 63 Slaughter games and no NBA production from Leslie. More importantly, the Pacers eliminated a future swap obligation that would have attached to the No. 2 pick in 1983.

The retained pick became Stipanovich and produced 403 games, 365 starts and five seasons of starting-center value. That branch overwhelms the one-season Bradley return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pacers Win, A+/C+. Indiana receives an A+ because surrender of the swap right preserved the No. 2 pick that became Steve Stipanovich, in addition to 63 Slaughter games. Phoenix receives a C+ for 64 Bradley games, with unidentified free-agent compensation left unscored.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Paid for Washington to Step Aside on Mitch Kupchak
sections.body: The Lakers secured Washington’s agreement not to exercise its right of first refusal on Mitch Kupchak, sending the Bullets Jim Chones, Brad Holland, a 1982 second-round pick and a 1983 first-round pick. Kupchak then played 173 regular-season games for Los Angeles across four seasons. Injuries limited his availability, but he still became part of the 1982 and 1985 championship rosters and gave the Lakers a useful frontcourt piece during the Showtime build.

sections.heading: Washington Received Immediate Players and Two Draft Assets
sections.body: Chones played 59 regular-season games for the Bullets, while Holland appeared in 13. The 1982 second-rounder became Mike Gibson, who added 32 Washington games. The bigger branch was the 1983 first-round pick at No. 22. Washington drafted Randy Wittman and then moved his rights to Atlanta for Tom McMillen plus another second-round pick.

sections.heading: Tom McMillen Made the Future Pick Matter
sections.body: McMillen played 187 regular-season games for Washington, giving the Bullets a durable downstream return from the first-round asset. That branch, combined with Chones, Holland and Gibson, makes Washington’s side much more substantial than a simple compensation package. Los Angeles still received the best championship-context fit in Kupchak, so the realized value lands close rather than producing a clear winner.

sections.heading: Kupchak's Knee Injury Changes How His Lakers Tenure Should Be Scored
sections.body: Kupchak started all 26 Lakers games he played in 1981-82, averaging 14.3 points and 8.1 rebounds, before a serious knee injury ended his early run with the club. He missed the following season and gradually returned, playing 34, 58 and 55 games in the next three seasons. Those are real Lakers contributions, but far fewer than an injury-free signing might have provided. Washington's compensation was substantial for a veteran free-agent rights decision: Jim Chones, Brad Holland, a second and a first. The Bullets also converted the pick connected with Randy Wittman into Tom McMillen, who provided 187 games. The club's early basketball return wasn't defined by its first-round selection alone. Equal A- grades reflect distinct realized contributions and the importance of tracing Washington's later asset chain.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Los Angeles A-, Washington A-. Kupchak gave the Lakers 173 games and contributed to two championship rosters despite major injury problems. Washington answered with several direct contributors and converted the 1983 first into Tom McMillen, who stayed for 187 games. Los Angeles got the better single player for its team context; Washington received the deeper package and preserved value through the draft branch.

sections.heading: Indiana Turned a Third-Round Pick Into Butch Carter
sections.body: Indiana acquired Butch Carter from the Lakers on October 15, 1981 for a 1982 third-round pick. Carter gave the Pacers 229 regular-season games across three seasons and started 82 of them. His role grew over time, culminating in a 13.4-point-per-game season in 1983-84. For the cost of a late draft asset, Indiana received multiple years of useful rotation and starting production.

sections.heading: The Lakers Used No. 54 on Hutch Jones
sections.body: The pick became No. 54 in the 1982 draft, and Los Angeles selected Hutch Jones. The Lakers waived Jones before the 1982-83 season, so he never appeared in a regular-season game for the franchise. Jones later played 13 NBA games for San Diego, but those games do not create value for Los Angeles in this trade.

sections.heading: The Direct Value Gap Is unusually Clear
sections.body: There is little need for a complicated downstream argument here. Carter became a multi-year Pacers contributor, while the Lakers’ draft return produced zero Los Angeles games. Indiana did not uncover an All-Star, but converting a third-round pick into 229 games is a strong result. Los Angeles received a real draft asset and simply failed to turn it into team value.

sections.heading: Hutch Jones Never Appeared for the Lakers
sections.body: The third-round selection Indiana surrendered was a real 1982 pick, eventually No. 54. Los Angeles used it on Hutch Jones but waived him before the next regular season. Jones later played 13 games for San Diego, which did not generate Lakers roster value from the original selection. Indiana received Butch Carter directly, and he logged 229 Pacers games over three years, with 82 starts. By his final Indiana season he averaged 13.4 points per game, making the value much greater than a few emergency reserve appearances. The grade gap reflects what each original club actually received: Indiana obtained a useful player with growing responsibility, while the Lakers never put the drafted player on the floor in a regular-season game.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pacers Win — Indiana A-, Los Angeles F. Carter gave Indiana three seasons, 229 games and 82 starts after arriving for a third-round pick. The Lakers used that pick on Hutch Jones and waived him before he played a regular-season game for them. The grade gap reflects the direct team value: Indiana received a productive NBA player, while Los Angeles received no realized on-court return.

sections.heading: Indiana Received Three Separate Value Paths
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's Indiana, Philadelphia and league transaction ledgers agree on the February 15, 1983 package. Indiana received Russ Schoene, Philadelphia's 1983 first-round pick and a 1984 second-round pick. Philadelphia received Clemon Johnson and Indiana's 1984 third-round pick.

The trade was not decided by Schoene alone. Both draft picks created meaningful downstream branches for Indiana, while Philadelphia's third-round pick did not become an NBA player.

sections.heading: Schoene Gave Indiana 31 Games
sections.body:
Russ Schoene played 31 regular-season games for the Pacers after the trade and started five. He logged 520 minutes and scored 243 points.

He missed 1983-84 with a back injury, then played professionally in Italy before returning to the NBA with Seattle. This review therefore credits Indiana only with those 31 Pacers appearances.

sections.heading: The Mitchell Wiggins Pick Became Sidney Lowe and Another Asset
sections.body:
Indiana used the 1983 first-round pick at No. 23 on Mitchell Wiggins, but Wiggins never played for the Pacers. Indiana traded his rights to Chicago on draft day for Sidney Lowe and a 1984 second-round pick.

Lowe played 78 regular-season games for Indiana in 1983-84, including two starts, and averaged 3.4 assists in 15.9 minutes.

Indiana later used the second-round asset from that Wiggins exchange to acquire Granville Waiters from Portland. Waiters played 140 regular-season games for the Pacers across 1983-84 and 1984-85.

This review credits Lowe and Waiters as downstream realized value from the Wiggins branch because both came directly from Indiana rerouting the acquired first-round asset.

sections.heading: Stuart Gray Became the Longest Indiana Return
sections.body:
Philadelphia's 1984 second-round pick landed at No. 29, where Indiana selected UCLA center Stuart Gray.

Gray stayed with the Pacers for five seasons. He played 52 games in 1984-85, 67 in 1985-86, 55 in 1986-87, 74 in 1987-88 and 72 in 1988-89.

That is 320 regular-season games for Indiana, with four starts. The minutes were modest, but five seasons of reserve-center availability from a second-round pick are real franchise value.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Got Four Useful Seasons from Clemon Johnson
sections.body:
Clemon Johnson was not an empty return. After the trade he played 32 regular-season games for Philadelphia in 1982-83, then 80 in 1983-84, 58 in 1984-85 and 75 in 1985-86.

That gives the 76ers 245 regular-season games from Johnson across parts of four seasons, including 16 starts. He was a useful reserve on the 1983 championship team and remained in the rotation afterward.

sections.heading: The Third-Round Pick Produced No NBA Games
sections.body:
Philadelphia used Indiana's 1984 third-round pick at No. 48 on James Banks. Banks never appeared in an NBA regular-season game.

That leaves Johnson as the entire realized on-court return on Philadelphia's side.

sections.heading: Why Indiana Gets the Edge
sections.body:
Philadelphia received a useful veteran reserve for several seasons, so this is not a one-sided trade. Johnson's 245 games and championship-season depth deserve real credit.

Indiana, however, accumulated value from every major incoming branch. Schoene supplied 31 games, the Wiggins branch became Lowe and Waiters, and Gray alone played 320 Pacers games over five seasons.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pacers Win, B+/B-. Indiana receives a B+ for turning the package into several seasons of usable depth across multiple players, especially Gray's five-year run. Philadelphia receives a B- because Johnson provided 245 useful games, but the third-round pick produced no NBA player and the aggregate return did not match Indiana's broader asset tree. Confidence is medium because the grade depends partly on correctly tracing the Wiggins pick through two later transactions rather than only comparing the first set of names.

sections.heading: Houston Paid a Second-Round Pick to Secure Lewis Lloyd
sections.body: Houston signed restricted free agent Lewis Lloyd on August 29, 1983 after Golden State declined to match, sending the Warriors a 1985 second-round pick as compensation. Lloyd immediately became a full-time Rockets starter and averaged 17.8 points per game in his first Houston season. The transaction was inexpensive by later free-agent standards, but the compensation pick still gave Golden State a legitimate chance to recover value.

sections.heading: Lloyd Became a Core Piece of Houston’s 1986 Finals Team
sections.body: Lloyd played 278 regular-season games in his first Rockets run from 1983-84 through 1986-87. He started 82 games in 1983-84 and remained a major backcourt contributor as Houston reached the 1986 NBA Finals. That combination of immediate scoring, multi-year starting value and postseason relevance gives the Rockets a strong return from a single second-round asset.

sections.heading: Golden State’s Pick Produced No NBA Games
sections.body: The compensation pick landed at No. 42 in the 1985 draft, where Golden State selected Bobby Lee Hurt. Hurt never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. There is no downstream branch that offsets Lloyd’s Houston production, so the hindsight gap is unusually direct: the Rockets received four seasons of meaningful NBA value while the Warriors’ draft compensation produced none.

sections.heading: The Compensation Pick Never Became a Second Chance
sections.body: Golden State wasn't trading Lloyd for a proven player in Houston's lineup. It was accepting future draft compensation after declining to match or maintain its free-agent rights, an arrangement with an inherently different time horizon. The pick eventually placed the Warriors at No. 42 in 1985. Choosing Bobby Lee Hurt made that value measurable, and Hurt's absence from an NBA regular-season box score means the compensation never generated direct NBA minutes. Houston didn't have to wait for a prospect: Lloyd started all 82 games in his first Rockets season and eventually contributed during the franchise's 1986 run to the Finals. The 278-game Houston return and the zero-game outcome from the selection offer unusually direct evidence for the A- and D grades. This isn't a judgment on every later transaction in either franchise's history.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win — Houston A-, Golden State D. Lloyd gave Houston 278 games, high-level scoring and a starting role on a Finals team. Golden State received a real second-round pick, but No. 42 Bobby Lee Hurt never played an NBA game. The trade is not graded on the idea that the Warriors received nothing; it is graded on what that compensation asset actually became.

sections.heading: The Lakers Traded an All-Star Guard for Their Next Championship Backcourt Piece
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's Lakers and San Diego transaction ledgers agree on the October 10, 1983 package. Los Angeles sent Norm Nixon, Eddie Jordan, a 1986 second-round pick and a 1987 second-round pick to the Clippers for Swen Nater and the draft rights to Byron Scott.

The deal is often remembered as Nixon for Scott, but the complete return matters. San Diego received two picks that it moved again only seven days later, and those assets produced Ricky Pierce before being folded into another trade.

sections.heading: Scott Became a Long-Term Lakers Starter
sections.body:
Scott played 74 games as a rookie in 1983-84, started 49 and averaged 10.6 points. He made the All-Rookie team and appeared in 20 playoff games.

His role expanded immediately. Scott averaged 16.0 points in 1984-85 as the Lakers won the championship, 17.0 in the 1986-87 championship season and a career-high 21.7 in 1987-88 as Los Angeles repeated.

He started all 82 games in 1986-87 and 81 in 1987-88. Scott's shooting and transition scoring fit the Showtime Lakers, and he became a stable backcourt partner for Magic Johnson through three title runs.

Nater was only a small part of the return. He appeared in 17 Lakers games in 1983-84, totaling 146 minutes, 58 points and 40 rebounds.

sections.heading: Nixon Gave the Clippers Legitimate Value
sections.body:
San Diego did not lose this trade badly. Nixon started all 82 games in his first Clippers season and averaged 17.0 points and a league-leading 11.1 assists per game.

After the move to Los Angeles, Nixon averaged 17.2 points and 8.8 assists in 1984-85 and was selected to the All-Star Game. He followed with 14.6 points and 8.6 assists in 1985-86.

Major knee and Achilles injuries then cost him the 1986-87 and 1987-88 seasons. Nixon returned for 53 games in 1988-89, but his best Clippers value came in those first three seasons.

sections.heading: The Picks Became Ricky Pierce, Not Hornacek and Dalrymple for the Clippers
sections.body:
The transaction ledger shows San Diego traded both incoming second-round picks to Detroit on October 17, 1983 for Ricky Pierce. That means Jeff Hornacek and Bruce Dalrymple, the players eventually selected with those picks, should not be credited directly to the Clippers.

Pierce gave San Diego 69 games, 35 starts and 685 points as a rookie in 1983-84. The Clippers then included him in the September 1984 trade with Milwaukee that brought Marques Johnson, Junior Bridgeman and Harvey Catchings to Los Angeles.

Eddie Jordan was waived by San Diego on October 17, 1983, so his direct Clippers value was zero.

sections.heading: Why the Lakers Still Win
sections.body:
The Clippers received an All-Star season from Nixon plus additional value through Pierce. That is a strong return and deserves a high grade.

Scott, however, became a long-term starter on three championship teams and remained productive through the Lakers' title window. Championship-level continuity at a premium rotation spot gives Los Angeles the higher realized value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win, A+/A-. The Lakers earn an A+ because Scott became a decade-long franchise piece and starter on the 1985, 1987 and 1988 champions. The Clippers earn an A- because Nixon delivered three strong seasons and an All-Star berth, while the draft-pick branch produced Pierce and further trade value. Confidence is high because the trade terms, player production and immediate pick re-trade are documented in team transaction records.

sections.heading: Butch Carter Was Worth the Immediate Knicks Rotation Spot
sections.body: New York obtained Butch Carter from Indiana on October 19, 1984 for a second-round pick in the 1985 draft. The outgoing asset was a future choice rather than another established NBA guard, which made the transaction a direct decision between immediate minutes and a development opportunity. Carter appeared in 69 games for the Knicks in 1984-85, starting 11 and averaging 7.9 points with 2.4 assists. Five additional New York appearances followed in 1985-86 before he moved on. This isn't a long multi-season star acquisition, but it supplied a substantial share of one season's backcourt minutes at a limited draft cost.

sections.heading: Indiana Used the Pick at No. 27
sections.body: The 1985 second-round selection became the No. 27 pick, used by Indiana to select Dwayne McClain. McClain played 45 NBA regular-season games for the Pacers, including four starts, and averaged 3.5 points in 10.2 minutes. His NBA career did not continue past that season. The selection therefore produced actual games but no long rotation tenure or traceable subsequent transaction asset of similar magnitude. McClain's limited Pacers stint should be evaluated on its own terms, not against an imaginary future player Indiana could have selected with the same pick. Carter was the larger direct player return in the completed comparison.

sections.heading: A Narrow but Verifiable Difference in Playing Time
sections.body: New York's Carter return and Indiana's McClain return were both short, which limits the appropriate gap between grades. Carter contributed 69 games in his first Knicks season and five more the next, while McClain delivered 45 over his single Indiana campaign. Carter held a larger game-to-game role and offered more assists as a guard. There were no premium first-round choices, hidden player packages or later star transactions attached to the original agreement. This is a useful example of a small trade where identifiable playing time, rather than a complicated multi-team draft chain, is enough to establish the winner without overstating the stakes.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win. New York earns B+ for Carter's 74 games and stronger rotation role, while Indiana receives C- for the No. 27 pick used on McClain and his 45 games. Both returns were modest in the wider league history, but the Knicks secured more immediate useful minutes for the one second-round choice they surrendered.

sections.heading: Indiana Bought Two Young Rotation Players With a Distant First
sections.body: Indiana acquired Bill Garnett and Terence Stansbury from Dallas on October 22, 1984 for a future first-round pick that was protected in 1990 and otherwise unprotected in 1991. Garnett played 145 regular-season games for the Pacers over two seasons, while Stansbury played 148 over the same span. Indiana therefore received nearly 300 combined games of immediate frontcourt and wing depth rather than waiting years for the asset to convey.

sections.heading: Dallas Preserved the Pick Until It Became a 1990 First
sections.body: The future first eventually landed at No. 14 in the 1990 draft. Dallas did not use the selection on Travis Mays. Instead, the Mavericks packaged that pick, Bill Wennington and another 1990 first in a trade with Sacramento for Rodney McCray plus two second-round picks. Because the McCray deal included several outgoing assets, his entire Dallas tenure cannot be assigned to this one pick. The important point is that the 1984 trade left Dallas holding premium first-round currency six years later.

sections.heading: The Downstream First Gave Dallas the Higher Ceiling
sections.body: McCray played 149 regular-season games for Dallas across two seasons, starting 116, after arriving in the multi-asset Sacramento trade. Indiana’s side was more direct: Garnett and Stansbury both became useful Pacers immediately but neither developed into a long-term cornerstone. Dallas gets the higher grade because the deferred first retained enough value to help bring back another established starter, even after discounting the rest of that package.

sections.heading: The Six-Year Wait Changed How Dallas Could Use the Asset
sections.body: This wasn't an immediate opportunity for Dallas to select a rookie in 1984. The first was protected in the top seven in 1990 and otherwise would become unprotected in 1991. By the time it materialized as No. 14 in 1990, the Mavericks could treat the selection as an established draft-night bargaining chip. That distinction is central to the grade: Dallas used the pick alongside Bill Wennington and a separate first in the Sacramento deal for Rodney McCray and two seconds. The 1984 pick played a part in that later return, but it was not solely responsible for McCray's 149 Dallas games. Indiana's direct return from Garnett and Stansbury was real, and Dallas carried years of uncertainty before realizing its asset. Those qualifications justify a modest Mavericks advantage rather than a one-sided score.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win — Dallas B, Indiana C+. The Pacers received 293 combined games from Garnett and Stansbury, so the trade gave them real short-term depth. Dallas still wins the long view because the future first matured into a No. 14 asset and became part of the package for Rodney McCray, who then started 116 games for the Mavericks. The margin stays modest because that later return was shared with other outgoing assets.

sections.heading: Maurice Lucas Gave the Lakers One Productive Veteran Season
sections.body: Los Angeles acquired Maurice Lucas from Phoenix on August 19, 1985 for two future second-round picks. Lucas played 77 regular-season games for the Lakers in 1985-86, averaged 10.2 points and 7.4 rebounds, and appeared in 14 playoff games. He was no longer the All-Star version Phoenix had used earlier in the decade, but he gave a contender real frontcourt production for a full season before moving on to Seattle.

sections.heading: Phoenix Turned the Two Seconds Into Steve Kerr and Greg Grant
sections.body: The first pick became No. 50 in 1988, and Phoenix selected Steve Kerr. Kerr played 26 games for the Suns as a rookie before being traded to Cleveland for another future second-round pick. The second asset became No. 52 in 1989, when Phoenix selected Greg Grant. Grant played 67 games with three starts as a rookie. The Suns therefore converted both incoming picks into NBA players rather than watching either asset expire unused.

sections.heading: The Suns Get Credit for Their Own Returns, Not Kerr’s Later Fame
sections.body: Kerr eventually became a major championship role player elsewhere, but those later Bulls and Spurs seasons do not belong in Phoenix’s grade. The useful comparison is what the Suns actually received: one rookie season from Kerr, one rookie season from Grant, and an additional second-round asset when Kerr was moved. Los Angeles received the better single season from Lucas, while Phoenix created more branches and retained more future optionality.

sections.heading: Kerr's Entire Career Isn't the Suns' Direct Return
sections.body: Steve Kerr becoming a five-time champion as a player makes the 1988 No. 50 pick famous in hindsight, but he did not spend those championship seasons with Phoenix. The Suns selected him using the second-round obligation originating with the Lakers and saw only the portion of his career that belonged to their roster. The companion second became No. 52 in 1989, associated with Greg Grant, another legitimate choice but not a future star. Los Angeles obtained Maurice Lucas, an accomplished veteran near the end of his NBA career, for immediate frontcourt support. His Lakers service should be evaluated over the period he actually played in Los Angeles. That makes the B- and B scores close: Phoenix controlled two selections that turned into NBA players, while the Lakers received an experienced forward without committing a first-round pick.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Suns Edge — Phoenix B, Los Angeles B-. Lucas gave the Lakers 77 solid regular-season games and useful playoff minutes, so the acquisition worked in the short term. Phoenix still finishes slightly ahead because both second-round picks became NBA players and Kerr was later converted into another draft asset. The edge stays narrow because Phoenix does not receive retrospective credit for Kerr’s championships with other franchises.

sources.title: Official Lakers all-time transactions: August 19, 1985 Lucas for 1988 and 1989 second-round picks
Contemporaneous August 20, 1985 report: Maurice Lucas acquired for two second-round picks

sections.heading: New York Got a Starting Guard and the Pick That Became Mark Jackson
sections.body: The Knicks sent Seattle a 1987 first-round pick and a 1990 second on November 12, 1986 for Gerald Henderson and Seattle’s 1987 first. Henderson immediately played 68 games with 53 starts for New York, averaging 10.9 points and 6.5 assists. More importantly, the incoming first became No. 18 and Mark Jackson, who won Rookie of the Year, made an All-Star team and became the Knicks’ long-term starting point guard.

sections.heading: Seattle Turned the Higher 1987 Pick Into a Larger Asset Chain
sections.body: The Knicks’ outgoing first landed at No. 5, where Seattle selected Scottie Pippen. The SuperSonics did not keep Pippen, so his Bulls career does not belong in Seattle’s grade. Seattle traded his rights and its own 1989 first to Chicago for Olden Polynice, a 1988 second and another 1989 first. Polynice then played 289 regular-season games for Seattle across four seasons before being moved again.

sections.heading: The Extra Second-Round Asset Also Produced Another Player
sections.body: The 1990 second-round pick from New York did not stay with Seattle until draft night. The SuperSonics traded that pick to Milwaukee in 1988 for Jerry Reynolds, who was later lost in the 1989 expansion draft. Seattle also continued converting the Chicago return in later transactions. New York’s Mark Jackson branch was excellent, but Seattle extracted several distinct pieces from the higher first-round position rather than merely benefiting from Pippen’s later fame.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Seattle SuperSonics Win — Seattle A-, New York B-. New York clearly received real value: Henderson started immediately, and Mark Jackson became Rookie of the Year and an All-Star. Seattle still earns the higher grade because the No. 5 pick was converted into Olden Polynice plus additional draft assets, while the extra second was also turned into a roster player. The verdict does not credit Seattle for Pippen’s Bulls career; it credits the asset chain Seattle actually received.

sections.heading: Indiana Got Two Rotation Seasons From Scott Skiles
sections.body: Milwaukee traded Scott Skiles to Indiana on June 21, 1987 for a 1989 second-round pick. Skiles played 51 games with two starts in his first Pacers season, then appeared in 80 games with 13 starts in 1988-89. His role grew to 6.8 points and 4.9 assists per game in the second year. Indiana therefore received 131 regular-season games from a young backup point guard for one future second.

sections.heading: The Pacers Lost Skiles in the 1989 Expansion Draft
sections.body: Skiles never developed into his later Orlando version while he was with Indiana. The Magic selected him in the June 1989 expansion draft, ending the Pacers branch after two seasons. His later Most Improved Player award and record-setting assist night belong to Orlando, not to this trade. Indiana still received useful rotation value, but there was no downstream return once the expansion draft took him away.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Used the Pick to Manage the Expansion Draft
sections.body:
The incoming second became the No. 34 slot in 1989, later associated with Gary Leonard. Milwaukee did not simply use the pick and keep Leonard. The Bucks sent the pick to Minnesota on June 15, 1989 in an agreement for the Timberwolves to select Mark Davis in the expansion draft. That makes the asset a roster-management tool rather than a drafted-player return, and it gave Milwaukee control over which player it lost.

The downstream 1989 use of Milwaukee's acquired second-rounder is the transaction's decisive distinction. That pick became No. 34, but the Bucks moved it to the expansion Timberwolves before the draft as the price of Minnesota selecting Mark Davis from Milwaukee's available players. Milwaukee therefore obtained expansion-roster control, not Gary Leonard's NBA career. Indiana meanwhile received 131 regular-season appearances from Scott Skiles before the Magic chose him in the 1989 expansion draft. His later prominent Orlando seasons are not Pacers trade returns. The B versus B- scores compare Milwaukee's protected roster decision with Indiana's real two seasons of guard minutes and explain why the margin is narrow.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Bucks Edge — Milwaukee B, Indiana B-. The Pacers received 131 useful games from Skiles, which is a good return for a second-round pick. Milwaukee still gets the narrow edge because the pick was later used to steer Minnesota toward Mark Davis in the expansion draft, giving the Bucks direct roster-protection value. The margin stays small because Skiles produced real NBA minutes for Indiana before Orlando selected him.

sections.heading: Golden State Broke One Veteran Into Four Pieces
sections.body: Golden State sent Purvis Short to Houston on November 5, 1987 for Dave Feitl, the Rockets’ right to match Dirk Minniefield, a lottery-protected first-round pick and cash. Feitl immediately supplied depth, appearing in 70 games with 19 starts in 1987-88. Minniefield was a much smaller branch, playing 11 games before Golden State waived him later that month. The real leverage in the package was the future first.

sections.heading: Houston Got Two Useful Seasons From Purvis Short
sections.body: Short still had scoring value when he arrived in Houston. He played 81 games in 1987-88 and averaged 14.3 points, then appeared in 65 games the following season. That gave the Rockets 146 regular-season games across two years from a veteran wing who could still carry a meaningful offensive role. Houston did not receive an empty return; the issue is that Short’s value ended while Golden State’s draft branch kept moving.

sections.heading: The First-Round Pick Eventually Became Alton Lister for Golden State
sections.body: The incoming first became the No. 16 pick in 1989, where Dana Barros was later selected. Golden State did not keep that pick. The Warriors traded it to Seattle for a 1990 first, then sent that 1990 first back to Seattle for Alton Lister. Lister played only three games in 1989-90 because of injury, but returned for 77 games with 65 starts in 1990-91. Gary Payton was later selected with the pick sent to Seattle, but Payton’s career is not Golden State value and is not counted here.

sections.heading: The First-Round Rights Passed Through Seattle Twice
sections.body: Golden State did not actually select Dana Barros using the first-round asset in this transaction. The Warriors sent the eventual No. 16 choice to Seattle for a 1990 first, then moved that later selection back to Seattle in the Alton Lister deal. That is the relevant chain when grading the original November 1987 exchange. Lister lost most of 1989-90 to injury but appeared in 77 games with 65 starts during 1990-91. Houston's direct return was simpler: Purvis Short played 146 games over two seasons and provided meaningful veteran scoring. Golden State's several-part package offered more routes to value, but the later careers of Barros and Gary Payton belong to their actual teams, not to the Warriors.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win — Golden State B-, Houston C-. Short gave Houston 146 useful games, so the Rockets received real short-term production. Golden State still produced the stronger package through Feitl’s 70-game season, a small Minniefield branch, cash and a first-round asset that was ultimately converted into Alton Lister. The grade does not credit Golden State for Dana Barros or Gary Payton; it follows only the assets the Warriors actually kept or converted.

sections.heading: Dallas Paid a First-Round Pick to Control Its Expansion-Draft Loss
sections.body: Dallas sent Miami its 1988 first-round pick on June 23, 1988 in exchange for the Heat agreeing to select Arvid Kramer in the expansion draft. Kramer had not played an NBA game since 1979-80, so Dallas was not losing a current rotation contributor. The value to the Mavericks was strategic: Miami used its Dallas selection on a player outside the active NBA rotation instead of choosing another eligible Maverick.

sections.heading: Miami Turned the Payment Into Kevin Edwards
sections.body: The acquired pick landed at No. 20, where Miami drafted Kevin Edwards. He immediately started 62 games as a rookie, averaged 13.8 points and 4.4 assists, and earned All-Rookie recognition. Edwards followed with 78, 79 and 81 games over the next three seasons. Across those first four Heat seasons alone, he appeared in 317 regular-season games and became one of the expansion franchise’s earliest dependable backcourt players.

sections.heading: Kramer Never Produced On-Court Value for Miami
sections.body: Miami selected Kramer first in the expansion draft, but he never played a regular-season game for the Heat. His NBA career consisted of eight Denver games in 1979-80. That does not make Dallas’s side valueless, because the entire purpose was controlling which player Miami removed from the Mavericks’ pool. The problem in hindsight is the price: Dallas surrendered a first-round asset that became a productive multi-year starter in exchange for protection rather than a player or draft return.

sections.heading: Why an Expansion-Draft Agreement Was Not a Player Return
sections.body: The Mavericks did obtain something they wanted on the transaction date: influence over which of their exposed players the new Heat franchise selected. Miami's agreement to choose Kramer served that purpose even though Kramer never suited up for the Heat. The limitation is that a protective agreement doesn't produce direct NBA games, a future pick, or a tradeable player for Dallas. The first-round pick moved the other way was real and immediately became selection No. 20, which Miami invested in Kevin Edwards. His 317 appearances across the Heat's first four seasons illustrate the concrete value Miami extracted from the arrangement. Dallas's actual roster-preservation benefit can't be reconstructed as a specific alternative player's career, so assigning that imaginary saved production would overstate the evidence. The grades compare the documented protection against Edwards' completed Miami production.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Heat Win — Miami A-, Dallas D. Dallas achieved its narrow goal by directing Miami toward Arvid Kramer, but the Mavericks paid the No. 20 pick to do it and received no player or draft asset back. Miami used that pick on Kevin Edwards, an All-Rookie guard who played 317 games in his first four Heat seasons. The trade illustrates the high cost expansion teams could extract for roster control, and the realized value strongly favors Miami.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Paid to Protect Kareem Abdul-Jabbar
sections.body: The 1988 expansion draft gave Miami access to unprotected players around the league, and the Lakers chose certainty with Kareem Abdul-Jabbar. Los Angeles sent Miami the choice of its 1991 or 1992 second-round pick in exchange for the Heat agreeing not to select Abdul-Jabbar. The Lakers therefore bought roster protection rather than a new player, keeping their veteran center for the final season of his career.

sections.heading: Abdul-Jabbar Still Gave the Lakers One More Finals Run
sections.body: Abdul-Jabbar remained with Los Angeles for 1988-89 and retired after the season. His role had diminished, but the Lakers still reached the NBA Finals with him in the rotation. That gives the protection agreement direct team value: Los Angeles preserved continuity for one more title defense rather than losing a franchise icon to the expansion process.

sections.heading: Miami Turned the Delayed Second Into Matt Geiger
sections.body: Miami chose the 1992 second-rounder, which landed at No. 42 and became Matt Geiger. Unlike many compensation seconds, the pick produced an actual multi-year Heat player. Geiger developed into a regular frontcourt contributor before later continuing his career elsewhere. Miami therefore received longer realized value from the asset, while the Lakers received one protected season from Abdul-Jabbar.

sections.heading: Miami Chose When to Collect Its Second-Round Pick
sections.body: The expansion agreement didn't give Miami a newly acquired veteran. It paid the Heat in a future second-round pick for their promise not to select Kareem Abdul-Jabbar from the Lakers' roster. The original terms allowed Miami to choose whether the selection would come in 1991 or 1992; the obligation ultimately became pick No. 42 in 1992, used on Matt Geiger. Los Angeles retained Abdul-Jabbar during the closing stage of his playing career rather than face an expansion-draft departure. That was an immediate benefit, but it wasn't a multi-year acquisition of a new star. Miami, meanwhile, turned the protection concession into an actual young center instead of waiting for an uncertain player offer. The comparison is between roster certainty during a short championship-era window and a real draft selection, which explains the relatively narrow grades.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Heat Win — Miami B-, Los Angeles C. The Lakers got what they wanted: Abdul-Jabbar stayed for his final season and Los Angeles made another Finals run. Miami still earns the better grade because the compensation second became Matt Geiger, giving the expansion franchise several seasons of usable NBA value. The trade was defensible for the Lakers, but the realized return lasted longer on Miami’s side.

sources.title: 1988-89 Los Angeles Lakers Roster and Statistics

sections.heading: Boston Paid to Keep Dennis Johnson Out of the Expansion Pool
sections.body: The 1988 expansion draft created a direct roster risk for Boston, and the Celtics chose to protect Dennis Johnson through a side agreement. Miami received Boston’s 1988 second-round pick in exchange for agreeing not to select Johnson. The Celtics therefore used a modest draft asset to preserve an established starting guard rather than replace him after the expansion process.

sections.heading: Johnson Stayed With Boston Through the End of His Career
sections.body: Johnson remained a Celtic for two more seasons after the agreement. His role had begun to decline from the peak championship years, but Boston still kept a trusted veteran guard, playoff experience and continuity in a roster that was already transitioning away from its mid-1980s peak. The protection agreement produced exactly the short-term value Boston intended.

sections.heading: Miami Used No. 35 on Sylvester Gray
sections.body: The compensation pick became No. 35 in the 1988 draft, and Miami selected Sylvester Gray. Gray spent his rookie season with the expansion Heat and provided immediate roster minutes, giving Miami a direct player return from the agreement. He did not become a long-term franchise piece, so the pick was useful without developing into a major asset.

sections.heading: Boston Bought Expansion-Draft Certainty
sections.body: Boston did not receive a new player in this arrangement. By surrendering a second-round selection, the Celtics ensured that Miami would not select Dennis Johnson during the expansion process. Johnson remained in Boston for his final two playing seasons, preserving experienced backcourt depth. Miami instead received the No. 35 pick and drafted Sylvester Gray, who appeared for the new franchise without developing into a long-term cornerstone. The transaction served two distinct needs: Boston retained an established guard at modest draft cost, and Miami gained a usable rookie asset. Both outcomes were limited but real, supporting the even C+ assessment rather than an exaggerated winner.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Boston C+, Miami C+. The Celtics gave up only a second-round pick to keep Dennis Johnson through the final two seasons of his career, while Miami turned that pick into Sylvester Gray for its inaugural roster. Neither side created major long-term value, but both received what the transaction was designed to provide: veteran continuity for Boston and a usable young roster asset for Miami.

sections.heading: Seattle Paid a Second to Keep Danny Young Out of Miami
sections.body: The 1988 expansion draft allowed Miami to select from unprotected rosters around the league, and Seattle used a second-round pick to steer the Heat away from Danny Young. The agreement was simple: Miami received Seattle’s 1988 second-rounder, while the Heat agreed not to take Young. Seattle therefore bought roster control rather than a new player.

sections.heading: Miami Used No. 40 on Orlando Graham
sections.body:
The incoming pick landed at No. 40 in the 1988 draft, where Miami selected Orlando Graham. Graham did not become a long-term starter, but the pick produced an actual NBA player for an expansion roster and gave the Heat a young frontcourt option at virtually no roster cost. That is modest realized value, but it is still more tangible than an unused protection agreement.

The agreement happened in the NBA expansion process, which is distinct from the ordinary 1988 college draft. Miami's promise not to take Danny Young protected a player Seattle already had, so the SuperSonics did not receive a new draft asset or a player from the Heat. Miami instead received a pick it could exercise at No. 40 and used it on Orlando Graham. The particular pick outcome was modest, but the Heat controlled a real new roster opportunity. Separating protection of an existing guard from acquisition of a prospect is essential to the narrow B- versus C+ grading gap and avoids portraying the deal as a normal player-for-player trade.

sections.heading: Young’s Protection Had Short-Term Value, Not a Long Asset Tail
sections.body: Seattle’s benefit was avoiding the immediate loss of Young in the expansion draft. That mattered in the moment because the SuperSonics retained control over an established guard instead of losing him without compensation. The branch did not become a major long-term asset, which keeps Seattle’s grade in the C range and allows Miami’s converted draft pick to finish slightly ahead.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Heat Edge — Miami B-, Seattle C+. Miami turned the expansion agreement into the No. 40 pick and Orlando Graham, creating a direct young-player return. Seattle achieved its short-term objective by keeping Danny Young out of Miami’s expansion selections, but the protection did not develop into comparable long-term value. The edge is narrow because neither side created a major franchise asset.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Acquired Roberts for a Lower Second
sections.body: Miami sent Fred Roberts to Milwaukee on June 23, 1988 for a future second-round selection. The transaction occurred in the expansion-era Heat's early roster building, when a draft pick could provide a chance to develop a younger player at a manageable cost. Milwaukee instead chose an NBA veteran it could use immediately in its frontcourt. The second wasn't a broad option to select whichever prospect became available: the agreement specified the least favorable of the Bucks' second-round choices in 1989. That protection made the potential Miami return narrower from the outset and is necessary context for why an established player could be acquired at a relatively low pick price.

sections.heading: Roberts Supplied Several Bucks Rotation Seasons
sections.body: Roberts became a regular Milwaukee forward and continued giving the Bucks useful reserve and occasional starting minutes for several seasons. His value wasn't that of a franchise star, but teams frequently seek that dependable veteran production when they spend a second-round selection. The choice to trade him out of Miami meant the Heat no longer received those future club minutes. It would be misleading to attribute the entirety of Roberts' later NBA career to Milwaukee, yet his direct tenure with the receiving franchise was clearly longer and more productive than Miami's resulting drafted prospect supplied in its own roster.

sections.heading: The 1989 Selection Became Scott Haffner
sections.body: The protected obligation ultimately conveyed at No. 45 in the 1989 draft, where Miami selected Scott Haffner. He reached the NBA, giving the Heat a legitimate draft outcome rather than an unexercised or imaginary asset, but his time as an NBA player was brief. The record does not support describing the second as a premium lottery opportunity, nor crediting Miami with a hidden first-round pick. Milwaukee gave up the late draft option and obtained a proven forward; Miami chose to develop the selected guard but did not realize a comparably useful long-term return. That completed chain explains the different team grades without overstating an otherwise small transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win. Milwaukee receives B for turning its least-favorable future second into multiple seasons of Fred Roberts' rotation play. Miami earns C- for the 1989 No. 45 selection used on Scott Haffner and the limited NBA return. The Bucks obtained the better direct player contribution without giving up a premium draft asset.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Used a Second to Control Its Expansion Loss
sections.body: Ahead of the 1989 expansion draft, Milwaukee sent Minnesota a second-round pick in exchange for the Timberwolves agreeing to select Mark Davis from the Bucks’ unprotected list. The deal was not a conventional player acquisition. Milwaukee paid to control which roster spot it would lose rather than leave the expansion choice entirely to Minnesota.

sections.heading: Minnesota Turned the Pick Into Gary Leonard
sections.body:
The second-round pick landed at No. 34 in the 1989 draft, where Minnesota selected Gary Leonard. Leonard reached the NBA and gave the new franchise a direct player return from the agreement. The outcome was modest, but the Timberwolves converted the compensation into more tangible basketball value than many expansion side payments ever produce.

This compensation wasn't a payment for Davis' NBA production after he moved; it was an agreement about an expansion-draft decision. The Bucks could determine in advance which player Minnesota would take from their available list, while the Timberwolves gained an additional second-round choice. The latter was a distinct 1989 college draft asset, eventually used at No. 34 on Gary Leonard. Keeping those two drafts separate prevents the deal from being described as a direct trade of Davis for Leonard. Minnesota turned negotiation leverage into a player selection, and Milwaukee received roster certainty. The narrow B+ against B comparison follows those different benefits rather than asserting both franchises acquired equivalent new players.

sections.heading: The Bucks Received Roster Flexibility Instead of a New Asset
sections.body: Milwaukee’s benefit came from roster management. By steering Minnesota toward Davis, the Bucks protected the rest of their exposed group and removed a player on terms they had chosen in advance. That is legitimate team value, but it is harder to sustain over time than an incoming draft asset. Minnesota therefore holds the narrow hindsight edge without turning the trade into a major win.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Wolves Edge — Minnesota B+, Milwaukee B. The Timberwolves received the No. 34 pick and used it on Gary Leonard, creating a direct player return. Milwaukee successfully controlled its expansion-draft loss by directing Minnesota toward Mark Davis, which gave the Bucks meaningful roster flexibility. Minnesota gets the higher grade because its asset became an NBA player, but the margin stays small because Milwaukee achieved the exact protection objective it paid for.

sections.heading: Chicago Paid for Draft-Day Certainty on B.J. Armstrong
sections.body: The Bulls entered the 1989 draft targeting B.J. Armstrong at No. 18 while Seattle controlled the two selections immediately ahead at Nos. 16 and 17. Chicago sent the SuperSonics a future second-round pick in exchange for Seattle agreeing not to take Armstrong. The transaction therefore bought draft-position certainty rather than moving a player or first-round pick.

sections.heading: Armstrong Became a Championship Core Piece
sections.body: Chicago selected Armstrong at No. 18, and he became the starting point guard during the middle of the Bulls’ first three-peat. He played six seasons in his first Chicago stint, won three championships and made the 1994 All-Star team. That is unusually strong realized value from a side agreement whose only cost was a future second-round pick.

sections.heading: Seattle’s 1993 Second Became Mike Peplowski
sections.body: The compensation pick eventually landed at No. 52 in the 1993 draft and became Mike Peplowski. Seattle received a real draft asset, but the pick produced little NBA value compared with what Armstrong delivered in Chicago. The comparison is especially direct because the Bulls’ benefit was not Armstrong’s availability in theory; it was the right to draft him without Seattle using either preceding pick.

sections.heading: Chicago Bought Draft-Day Certainty, Not a Player
sections.body: Seattle did not transfer B.J. Armstrong's draft rights to Chicago. The SuperSonics agreed not to use the No. 16 or No. 17 choices on the guard, while the Bulls still had to draft him with their own selection at No. 18. Chicago therefore paid a future second to protect a specific opportunity rather than to acquire a completed player. That arrangement worked because Armstrong went on to become a starter during the Bulls' championship run and an All-Star in 1994. Seattle's future second conveyed in 1993 at No. 52 and was associated with Mike Peplowski, who did not provide a comparable return. Distinguishing the draft promise from the eventual Bulls selection makes the transaction more accurate and explains the A- versus C grades.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win — Chicago A-, Seattle C. Chicago gave up only a future second to secure the chance to draft B.J. Armstrong, who became a three-time champion and an All-Star in his first Bulls tenure. Seattle’s compensation eventually became Mike Peplowski at No. 52 and did not produce comparable value. This is a clear case where paying for draft certainty worked exceptionally well.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Turned Minnesota’s Expansion Pick Into Rick Mahorn
sections.body: Minnesota selected Rick Mahorn in the 1989 expansion draft and traded him to Philadelphia before the Timberwolves played their first regular-season game. The 76ers were buying an established, physical frontcourt veteran rather than a developmental piece. Mahorn stepped directly into Philadelphia’s rotation and gave the team the exact defensive toughness it was targeting.

sections.heading: Minnesota Received One First and Two Seconds
sections.body:
The Timberwolves received a 1990 first-round pick, a 1991 second and a conditional 1992 second. The first became No. 20 Gerald Glass, while the later picks became Alvaro Teheran and Duane Cooper. That gave a new franchise three separate opportunities to turn one expansion-draft selection into younger roster pieces instead of tying value to a single veteran.

The picks became identifiable selections in three consecutive drafts, not one undifferentiated future compensation promise. Minnesota's 1990 first was No. 20 Gerald Glass, the 1991 second was No. 44 Alvaro Teheran, and the conditional 1992 second ultimately yielded No. 36 Duane Cooper. Glass was the most useful direct playing return of the group, but the two later selections still provided separate opportunities for an expansion franchise to develop its roster. Mahorn was already an established NBA defender and contributed for Philadelphia immediately. The trade is therefore best compared as one short-horizon veteran against three particular draft outcomes, without pretending each of the picks became a star.

sections.heading: The Pick Package Outlasted Mahorn’s Philadelphia Window
sections.body: Mahorn was useful for the 76ers and the trade made sense for a team trying to win immediately, but his Philadelphia tenure was relatively short. Minnesota’s return created several player branches and longer roster control, with Glass providing the most substantial direct value of the three selections. The trade therefore favors the expansion team in hindsight without treating Philadelphia’s veteran acquisition as a failure.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wolves Win — Minnesota B+, Philadelphia C+. Philadelphia got a useful veteran in Rick Mahorn and improved its frontcourt immediately. Minnesota still wins because one expansion selection became a first-round pick plus two seconds, producing Gerald Glass, Alvaro Teheran and Duane Cooper. The Timberwolves received the deeper and more durable asset package, while the 76ers received the better short-term player.

sections.heading: Milwaukee and Minnesota Swapped Veteran Centers
sections.body: Milwaukee sent Randy Breuer to Minnesota on January 4, 1990 for Brad Lohaus, with a future second-round swap mechanism attached. Both teams were changing the shape of their frontcourt rather than chasing a star. Breuer gave the expansion Timberwolves a traditional seven-footer with starting experience, while Lohaus offered Milwaukee more perimeter shooting and mobility at the position.

sections.heading: Both Veterans Produced Multiple Seasons of Useful Minutes
sections.body: Breuer became a regular part of Minnesota’s early rotation and gave the young franchise stability in the middle. Lohaus likewise became a recurring Bucks frontcourt piece and fit Milwaukee’s preference for a big who could stretch away from the basket. Neither player turned the trade into a major franchise event, but both sides received real on-court value instead of a short rental.

sections.heading: The 1992 Swap Added Only a Small Difference
sections.body:
The second-round option eventually resolved in the 1992 draft. Minnesota ended up with the No. 34 slot associated with Chris Smith, while Milwaukee received the No. 36 slot that became Duane Cooper.
