finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Detroit A, Orlando B. Orlando received real draft value in a future first that eventually became the No. 11 pick in 2005, but Fran Vazquez never played in the NBA. Detroit’s return was less visible on a box score: greater control over the timing of a separate first-round obligation tied to the Otis Thorpe trade. That flexibility proved strategically valuable in Detroit’s broader draft-asset chain. The verdict favors the Pistons while avoiding the mistake of assigning every later Memphis-pick outcome solely to this one agreement.

sections.heading: Dallas Bought a Veteran Point Guard at a Low Draft Cost
sections.body: Dallas acquired Tim Hardaway from Miami on August 22, 2001 for a future second-round pick and a trade exception. Hardaway was no longer the All-NBA guard of his peak, but the Mavericks were a rising playoff team and could add an experienced ball-handler without giving up a current rotation player or first-round pick. Miami accepted delayed draft value and financial flexibility while moving on from a veteran whose role was shrinking.

sections.heading: Hardaway Gave Dallas Minutes and Became Part of Another Deal
sections.body: Hardaway played a real reserve role for Dallas during the 2001-02 season, then became part of the February 2002 package the Mavericks sent to Denver in the larger Raef LaFrentz and Nick Van Exel trade. His direct Dallas production was modest, but the acquisition still produced usable basketball value and preserved another transaction path. That is more than a pure end-of-career rental with no later utility.

sections.heading: Miami’s Second Became Matt Freije
sections.body: The draft piece eventually conveyed in 2004 at No. 53 and became Matt Freije. That gave Miami a tangible second-round asset, but it did not turn into a comparable long-term Heat contributor. The trade exception also had roster-management value, so Miami was not empty-handed; the completed return simply never surpassed the combination of Hardaway’s Dallas minutes and his inclusion in a later multi-player trade.

sections.heading: The Subsequent Denver Trade Was a Shared Asset Return
sections.body: Hardaway's inclusion in the February 2002 Denver exchange gives Dallas a second way to evaluate its original acquisition, but that later transaction involved several pieces on both sides. The Mavericks can't fairly claim every Raef LaFrentz or Nick Van Exel contribution as value created solely by the second-round pick surrendered to Miami. Hardaway provided actual 2001-02 guard minutes before Dallas used him in a bigger roster move; the exact incremental value of that one component is harder to isolate. Miami's return is more straightforward: a second-round obligation eventually yielding the No. 53 choice in 2004 and a trade-exception mechanism rather than a named NBA rotation player. Giving both clubs credit for what they genuinely controlled explains why the grades are close even though Dallas enjoyed the more immediate basketball usefulness.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Mavericks Edge — Dallas B, Miami B-. Dallas paid only a future second and a trade-exception mechanism for Tim Hardaway, received useful veteran guard minutes and later included him in the package that brought back Raef LaFrentz and Nick Van Exel. Miami’s pick became Matt Freije and did not create comparable franchise value. The gap stays small because Hardaway’s Dallas tenure was brief, but the Mavericks extracted the better completed return.

sections.heading: Denver Turned Antonio McDyess Into Two Long-Term Frontcourt Pieces
sections.body: Denver sent Antonio McDyess, the draft rights to Frank Williams and a future second-round pick to New York on draft night in 2002. In return, the Nuggets received Marcus Camby, veteran guard Mark Jackson and the draft rights to Nenê, who had just been selected seventh overall. The structure gave Denver one proven defensive big and one young center-forward prospect while New York concentrated its value in McDyess.

sections.heading: Camby and Nenê Became Core Nuggets
sections.body: Camby became a multi-year Denver starter, one of the league’s premier shot blockers and the 2007 Defensive Player of the Year. Nenê developed into an even longer-tenured frontcourt piece and spent nearly a decade with the Nuggets. Jackson’s stay was brief, but Denver did not need him to carry the return because Camby and Nenê together produced years of starting-level value and playoff minutes.

sections.heading: McDyess’s Knee Injury Crushed New York’s Side
sections.body: The Knicks were acquiring a former All-Star-level power forward, so the trade-day logic was understandable, but McDyess fractured his left kneecap in the 2002 preseason and missed the entire season. He ultimately played only a small number of regular-season games for New York before being traded again. Frank Williams and Maciej Lampe also failed to offset the lost value. The injury was bad luck rather than bad intent, but hindsight grading has to count the result.

sections.heading: Draft Rights and Injury Risk Made the Return Uneven
sections.body: This deal also included more than the two best-known big men. Denver acquired the rights to Nenê immediately after he was selected seventh in the 2002 draft, plus Camby and Mark Jackson, while New York received Frank Williams's rights and a second-round pick later tied to No. 30 Maciej Lampe in 2003. The Nuggets had to develop the young Brazilian and get sustained availability from Camby; those favorable outcomes were not guaranteed on trade day. New York instead put much of its investment into McDyess's near-term health and a hoped-for return to top form. His preseason kneecap injury made that concentrated risk particularly costly. Because Nenê's productive Nuggets years and Camby's defensive honors actually followed, the hindsight margin is stronger than a simple comparison of projected talent on the night of the exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win — Denver A+, New York F. Denver received two long-term frontcourt starters in Marcus Camby and Nenê, with Camby eventually winning Defensive Player of the Year. New York’s centerpiece, Antonio McDyess, suffered a devastating knee injury before playing a regular-season game for the Knicks and never supplied the star-level return they had purchased. The gap between realized outcomes is enormous even after giving New York credit for defensible trade-day logic.

sections.heading: Golden State Paid Future Draft Capital for Jiri Welsch
sections.body: Golden State acquired the draft rights to Jiri Welsch on draft night in 2002. The cost was built around future draft capital rather than a current NBA rotation player, including a conditional 2004 pick and a protected future first. The Warriors were betting that Welsch, the No. 16 selection, would become a useful perimeter piece quickly enough to justify surrendering later flexibility.

sections.heading: Welsch Never Became a Core Warrior
sections.body: Welsch reached Golden State’s rotation as a rookie but did not establish the kind of role the price required. His Warriors tenure lasted one season before he was moved again, so Golden State never received a long developmental payoff from the player it targeted. The original trade therefore has to be judged against what the outgoing picks eventually became rather than against a hypothetical Welsch peak.

sections.heading: Philadelphia’s Outgoing Pick Rights Matured Into Better Assets
sections.body: The conditional portion ultimately produced a 2004 second-rounder at No. 42, attached to Viktor Sanikidze, while the protected first eventually conveyed in 2005 at No. 16, attached to Joey Graham. Neither player became a 76ers star, but the first-round slot itself carried materially more value than Golden State realized from one season of Welsch. Philadelphia preserved the stronger asset package even before considering later movement of those rights.

sections.heading: Welsch Cost Two Conditional Picks
sections.body: Welsch cost Golden State two different conditional picks, not one immediate first. The 2004 obligation eventually became the No. 42 second-round choice attached to Viktor Sanikidze. The first-round obligation carried top-eight protection in 2005 and top-five protection in 2006, and it ultimately conveyed in 2005 at No. 16, associated with Joey Graham. Neither result was certain on the day Welsch was acquired. He stayed with the Warriors for just one season before another trade, leaving little direct Golden State return for those future commitments. Philadelphia obtained a range of draft opportunities, but the later careers of the eventual selections should be attributed to the teams that actually controlled their rights.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win — Philadelphia A, Golden State D+. Golden State gave up a protected future first plus an additional conditional pick for the rights to Jiri Welsch, then received only one season from him before moving on. The first ultimately conveyed at No. 16 in 2005, with the other pick landing at No. 42 in 2004. Philadelphia controlled the better long-term assets, while Golden State never got enough from Welsch to justify the price.

sections.heading: Cleveland Swapped Andre Miller for Darius Miles
sections.body: Cleveland sent Andre Miller and Bryant Stith to the Clippers in July 2002 for Darius Miles and Harold Jamison. Miller was coming off a breakout season as one of the league’s top assist men, while Miles was a 20-year-old former No. 3 pick whose athleticism still carried major upside. The Cavaliers chose youth and projection over the proven production of their starting point guard.

sections.heading: Miles Never Became Cleveland’s Long-Term Answer
sections.body: Miles received a large role in Cleveland but never turned the opportunity into the franchise-level development the Cavaliers were seeking. His scoring and rebounding rose only modestly, and his Cleveland stint lasted less than two seasons before another trade. Jamison did not become a meaningful NBA piece for the Cavaliers, leaving the return dependent almost entirely on Miles breaking through.

sections.heading: The Clippers Received the Best Proven Player
sections.body: Miller spent only one season with the Clippers, so Los Angeles did not turn the deal into a long-term franchise win either. He was still the most accomplished player in the transaction at the time and remained a high-level NBA point guard for many seasons after leaving Los Angeles. The Clippers at least converted Miles into a proven lead guard; Cleveland surrendered that stability without getting a comparable lasting payoff.

sections.heading: A One-Season Clippers Return Still Beats Cleveland's Gamble
sections.body: Miller's later NBA career makes this look like a landslide at first glance, but those later seasons belong to the organizations that employed him after his Clippers stint. For Los Angeles, the direct result was one year of a proven starting point guard rather than a decade-long franchise anchor. Cleveland controlled Miles for less than two seasons and did not find the long-term primary option it was seeking. Those narrower windows are the proper comparison. Stith and Jamison also belong in the transaction ledger, but neither changes the central Miller-versus-Miles decision or supplies Cleveland with an overlooked compensating asset. The Clippers get credit for acquiring the stronger verified player during the period they held him, while Cleveland's lower grade reflects the opportunity cost of giving up an established playmaker without securing a lasting replacement.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win — Los Angeles B+, Cleveland D. The Clippers received Andre Miller, the best established player in the deal, while Cleveland’s gamble on Darius Miles never developed into the long-term cornerstone it needed to justify moving Miller. Miller’s Clippers tenure was brief, which keeps the grade below elite territory, but Cleveland’s return produced even less durable value. Harold Jamison and Bryant Stith did not alter that balance.

sections.heading: Cleveland Turned Lamond Murray Into a Protected First
sections.body: Cleveland sent Lamond Murray and a future second-round pick to Toronto in September 2002 for Michael Stewart and a heavily protected future first. The Cavaliers were moving away from an established scorer and prioritizing future draft value during a rebuild. Toronto was buying immediate wing offense while accepting the risk that the first-round obligation could take years to convey.

sections.heading: Toronto Never Got the Immediate Payoff It Wanted
sections.body: Murray missed the entire 2002-03 season with a foot injury, which erased the short-term benefit Toronto expected from the trade. He later returned and contributed, but the Raptors never received enough from the veteran side of the deal to offset the draft value they had surrendered. The accompanying second-round asset became No. 39 Albert Miralles in 2004 and did not create a meaningful NBA return for Toronto.

sections.heading: The Protected First Eventually Became a Valuable No. 22 Pick
sections.body: The first-round protection delayed the obligation for years before it finally conveyed in 2007 at No. 22, attached to Jared Dudley. Cleveland did not keep the exact final player branch as a long-term cornerstone, but the delayed first remained a materially stronger asset than the veterans Toronto realized from its side. Michael Stewart added little, yet the future first was enough to drive the completed-value result.

sections.heading: The Draft-Pick Protections Delayed the Real Return
sections.body: This first-round obligation wasn't an immediate unprotected selection. The recorded terms protected the pick through No. 17 in 2005, No. 16 in 2006 and No. 15 in both 2007 and 2008. Those protections gave Toronto a chance to avoid conveying a premium choice early, but they also meant Cleveland had to wait to learn the actual value. In 2007, the obligation finally became pick No. 22, the slot associated with Jared Dudley. That is a concrete outcome rather than a speculative promise of a lottery player. Meanwhile, the second-rounder Cleveland surrendered became the 2004 No. 39 selection, Albert Miralles. The Cavaliers' superior result comes from preserving the first-round asset while Toronto failed to realize a comparable return from Murray, not from pretending Cleveland enjoyed Dudley's later entire NBA career.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win — Cleveland A-, Toronto D-. Cleveland converted Lamond Murray and a second into Michael Stewart plus a protected first that eventually conveyed at No. 22. Toronto’s immediate target lost an entire season to injury and never produced enough value to justify surrendering that first-round asset. The long protection delayed Cleveland’s payoff, but the draft capital still became the best asset produced by the deal.

sections.heading: Memphis Bet on Mike Miller and Future Draft Value
sections.body: Memphis sent Drew Gooden, Gordan Giricek and cash to Orlando in February 2003 for Mike Miller, Ryan Humphrey and two future draft picks. The Grizzlies were moving off two young contributors but buying a proven perimeter scorer in Miller while adding extra draft value. Orlando chose immediate frontcourt help around Tracy McGrady and accepted a shorter-horizon package.

sections.heading: Miller Became the Best Long-Term Player in the Deal
sections.body: Miller became a major Memphis rotation piece for years and won the NBA Sixth Man of the Year award in 2006. His shooting, secondary playmaking and durability fit the Grizzlies as they moved into their first playoff era. Humphrey added little, but Miller alone provided the kind of multi-season production that Orlando never matched from the players it received.

sections.heading: The Draft Picks Added More Value to the Memphis Side
sections.body: Memphis also received a 2003 first-rounder that landed at No. 27, attached to Kendrick Perkins, and a 2004 second-rounder at No. 49, attached to Sergei Lishchuk. Those assets did not all become long-term Grizzlies players, but they gave Memphis additional transaction value beyond Miller. Orlando received useful NBA players in Gooden and Giricek, yet both had shorter stays and did not create a comparable combined return.

sections.heading: The Miller Acquisition Had More Value Than the Draft Names Alone
sections.body: Mike Miller was the clearest long-term player return for Memphis in this February 2003 exchange. He developed into a productive perimeter scorer for the Grizzlies and supplied repeated seasons of real rotation value. Ryan Humphrey and the draft rights connected to Kendrick Perkins at No. 27 and Sergei Lishchuk at No. 49 were additional pieces, but those famous names should not be treated as guaranteed Memphis careers. Perkins later became known for his Celtics tenure, which is different from direct value delivered to Memphis from this deal. Orlando received Drew Gooden and Gordan Giriček along with cash, giving the Magic two usable players but not the sustained Grizzlies shooting advantage Miller provided. The A-to-D grade disparity rests chiefly on the durable Miller return and the broader asset package, not on retroactively awarding Memphis every subsequent player's career.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Grizzlies Win — Memphis A, Orlando D. Orlando received two legitimate young NBA players, so the trade was not empty on its side. Memphis still wins clearly because Mike Miller became a multi-year contributor and Sixth Man of the Year, while the Grizzlies also received two draft assets. The best player outcome and the deeper asset package both landed with Memphis.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Sold the Rights to Keith Bogans for Cash
sections.body: Milwaukee drafted Keith Bogans at No. 43 in 2003 and immediately sent his rights to Orlando for cash considerations. The Bucks converted a second-round selection into financial value instead of adding another rookie to the roster. Orlando took the opposite approach by paying cash for a low-cost wing prospect who had a realistic path to minutes.

sections.heading: Bogans Became a Useful NBA Rotation Wing
sections.body:
Bogans made Orlando’s rotation as a rookie and developed into a dependable perimeter defender and spot-up shooter. His first Magic stint lasted multiple seasons, and he later returned to the franchise after playing elsewhere. He was never a star, but second-round trades do not require star outcomes to work; Orlando received legitimate NBA minutes from an asset acquired for cash alone.

The important chronology begins with Milwaukee making the No. 43 selection in the 2003 draft, then transferring Bogans' rights to Orlando. The Magic weren't gambling on an abstract future second-rounder; they were acquiring a specifically identified rookie who could be brought to camp and compete for minutes. Bogans subsequently supplied multiple seasons of useful wing play, particularly on defense. Cash consideration was not an inherently irrational return for Milwaukee, but it could not generate playing time or a later player through a documented draft branch. Comparing these two kinds of compensation explains Orlando's B grade without overstating a modest second-round exchange as a franchise-altering deal.

sections.heading: Milwaukee’s Return Had No Basketball Upside
sections.body: Cash can have organizational value, but it does not create an on-court branch that can be compared with a productive rotation player. Once Bogans proved he could stay in the league and contribute, the exchange tilted toward Orlando. Milwaukee avoided carrying another draft pick, yet the Bucks also gave up the only asset in the deal capable of producing future basketball value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Magic Win — Orlando B, Milwaukee C+. Orlando turned cash considerations into Keith Bogans, a real rotation wing who contributed immediately and later returned for another stint. Milwaukee received only cash and no downstream basketball asset. The stakes were modest because the pick was No. 43, but Orlando clearly realized more useful value from the transaction.

sections.heading: Memphis Paid a Future First for Bonzi Wells
sections.body: Memphis acquired Bonzi Wells from Portland in December 2003 for Wesley Person, cash and a protected first-round pick. The Grizzlies were entering their first serious playoff push and wanted another physical wing scorer for a roster built around Pau Gasol. Portland chose future value and roster flexibility while moving on from a player whose relationship with the organization had deteriorated.

sections.heading: Wells Gave Memphis Useful Short-Term Playoff Value
sections.body:
Wells became a meaningful rotation player for Memphis during the franchise’s first playoff seasons. He could score off the bench, rebound from the wing and add a more aggressive offensive option to a deep group. His Grizzlies tenure was not long and ended awkwardly, which limits the upside of the grade, but he contributed to winning teams during the exact competitive window Memphis was trying to support.

Portland's first-round compensation carried protections instead of an unconditional guarantee of a premium selection. The pick was protected in the top three for 2004 and the top spot for 2005, and it eventually conveyed at No. 23 in the 2004 draft. Portland selected Sergei Monia, but his NBA tenure did not become the durable roster contribution the franchise might have hoped for from a first. Memphis, meanwhile, received Wells during the specific seasons in which the club first reached the postseason. His value was real but time-limited, and Wesley Person plus cash also went the other way. Accounting for the resolved pick conditions and both teams' actual use of the incoming players supports a modest Memphis advantage rather than a sweeping win.

sections.heading: Portland’s First-Round Return Did Not Become a Core Piece
sections.body: The protected first conveyed in 2004 at No. 23 and became Sergei Monia. Monia did not develop into a substantial NBA contributor, while Wesley Person’s Portland stint was brief. Portland at least recovered a first-round asset for Wells, but the actual player outcome did not match the useful minutes Memphis received during consecutive playoff runs.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Grizzlies Win — Memphis B+, Portland C+. Memphis paid a protected first, Wesley Person and cash for Bonzi Wells and received useful wing production during the franchise’s early playoff years. Portland’s main long-term asset became No. 23 Sergei Monia, who did not turn into a comparable NBA piece. Wells was not a long-term Grizzlies fixture, so the margin is moderate rather than overwhelming.

sections.heading: The Deal Was More About Flexibility Than Talent
sections.body: Orlando received Monty Williams, a conditional second-round pick and cash from Philadelphia, while the 76ers received their own mix of conditional draft language, a $1 million trade exception and cash. This was not a star-for-star transaction. Both teams were moving secondary assets and financial tools, so the grade depends on whether either side converted that flexibility into durable basketball value.

sections.heading: Orlando Got the Only Immediate NBA Player
sections.body:
Williams gave Orlando an actual rotation option, which made the Magic return more tangible than a package built entirely from exceptions and conditional assets. The attached second-round pick eventually landed at No. 42 in 2004 and became Viktor Sanikidze. That draft branch never became a meaningful NBA contribution, so Orlando’s realized value centered on the veteran player rather than on the pick.

The conditional components should be distinguished from assets that were certain to appear on a roster. Orlando's documented second-round return was associated with the 2004 No. 42 selection used on Viktor Sanikidze; acquiring that slot did not mean Sanikidze later supplied NBA games for the Magic. The Magic also received Williams, whose immediate player value was clearer than a future conditional right. Philadelphia's compensation included a $1 million trade exception, cash and a conditional second-round choice that was never exercised. Those cap and draft mechanisms may have served organizational purposes even without producing a long-term player. The symmetric C+ grades reflect that limited, differing utility rather than asserting either team secured a major prospect.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Preserved Cap and Transaction Flexibility
sections.body: Philadelphia’s side included a $1 million trade exception, cash and a conditional second-round pick that was not exercised. Those pieces had front-office utility but did not produce a lasting on-court asset from this specific transaction. Orlando’s player value was also modest, leaving both sides with returns that helped around the edges without creating a decisive historical winner.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Orlando C+, Philadelphia C+. Orlando received the only established NBA player in Monty Williams plus a second-round asset, but neither branch became a major long-term gain. Philadelphia received a trade exception, cash and a conditional pick that did not create a meaningful basketball payoff. The transaction served short-term roster and financial purposes on both sides without producing enough realized value to separate the grades.

sections.heading: Orlando Took Several Small Swings for Robert Archibald
sections.body: Orlando sent Robert Archibald and a 2005 second-round swap mechanism to Toronto for Mengke Bateer, the draft rights to Remon Van de Hare and its own favorable position in the 2005 second-round swap. This was a depth transaction rather than a core-roster move. The Magic chose multiple low-cost possibilities while Toronto consolidated around a young big already in the NBA.

sections.heading: The 2005 Swap Became the Most Useful Orlando Asset
sections.body:
Neither Bateer nor Van de Hare became an important Magic player, so Orlando’s best return came from the draft mechanism. The swap position helped Orlando land the No. 38 pick in 2005, attached to Travis Diener. Diener became an NBA rotation guard and gave the Magic more realized basketball value than the veteran and rights components produced.

The second-round swap needs to be traced into the 2005 draft before its value can be compared. Orlando's side was associated with No. 38 Travis Diener, while Toronto's side was associated with No. 41 Roko Ukic. Those outcomes should be recorded alongside the original player and rights exchange, but not treated as though both teams received the same guard or the same draft slot. Orlando's other incoming pieces, Bateer and the rights to Van de Hare, didn't become meaningful Magic contributors. The swap was the stronger part of its return, even though Toronto also obtained a named draft prospect and the two picks were separated by only three selections.

sections.heading: Toronto’s Return Was Also Modest
sections.body: Archibald’s Raptors stint was brief, and the other side of the 2005 second-round swap sat at No. 41, attached to Roko Ukic. Toronto eventually got NBA minutes from Ukic, but not enough to turn the package into a clearly superior result. Both teams were dealing in marginal assets, with Orlando finding the slightly better realized branch through the swap.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Magic Win — Orlando B, Toronto C. This was a low-stakes trade, but Orlando came away with the better realized asset. Bateer and Van de Hare added little, while the 2005 second-round swap helped produce No. 38 Travis Diener. Toronto received limited value from Robert Archibald and the No. 41 side of the swap. The gap is modest, but Orlando’s draft outcome gives it the edge.

sections.heading: Dallas Paid a Large Package to Solve Its Center Problem
sections.body: Dallas acquired Erick Dampier, Evan Eschmeyer and the draft rights to Steve Logan from Golden State in the 2004 offseason. The Mavericks surrendered Christian Laettner, Eduardo Najera, two sets of draft rights, multiple future first-round assets and cash. The price reflected a clear roster need: Dallas wanted a starting center to anchor the interior next to Dirk Nowitzki during a championship window.

sections.heading: Dampier Gave Dallas Years of Starting Minutes
sections.body: Dampier never became an All-Star in Dallas, but he did become the primary center on several 50-win teams and the 2006 Finals roster. His rebounding, size and interior defense filled a role the Mavericks had struggled to stabilize. Eschmeyer and Logan added essentially no value, so the Dallas case rests almost entirely on Dampier’s multi-year usefulness during a sustained contender run.

sections.heading: Golden State Collected More Assets Than Lasting Production
sections.body: Golden State received a broad package, including Najera, draft rights and future first-round value. That package offered flexibility, but the realized player outcomes were mixed. Najera was useful, while several rights and picks did not become long-term Warriors cornerstones. The 2007 first ultimately landed at No. 30. Dallas paid heavily, yet it also received the one player who filled an immediate starting role for years.

sections.heading: Not Every Outgoing Pick Can Be Credited as a Future Star
sections.body: Golden State's side involved two different first-round obligations, not a single guaranteed high selection. One was a lottery-protected pick originating with Philadelphia whose exact downstream selection isn't identified in the source record. Another was Dallas's top-seven-protected 2007 first, which ultimately corresponds to the No. 30 pick associated with Petteri Koponen. The Mavericks also moved draft rights to Luis Flores and Mladen Sekularac plus cash, whose unknown dollar amount shouldn't be treated as equivalent to player production. Those details make the price genuinely broad while limiting what can be asserted about each branch. Dampier's six seasons as a Dallas starting center are observable; awarding Golden State speculative careers for uncertain or rerouted rights would produce an equally misleading grade. The modest B against B- comparison reflects that asymmetry.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Mavericks Edge — Dallas B, Golden State B-. The Mavericks gave up a large collection of players, rights, picks and cash, so this was not a bargain. Erick Dampier nevertheless started for multiple playoff teams and the 2006 Finals club, giving Dallas the exact type of interior stability it sought. Golden State accumulated useful assets but did not turn the package into a clearly better long-term result, leaving Dallas with a narrow edge.

sections.heading: Memphis Bought the Rights to Antonio Burks for Cash
sections.body: Memphis acquired the draft rights to Antonio Burks from Orlando on draft night in 2004 for cash considerations. The Grizzlies were using a small financial outlay to add a local guard prospect without surrendering another player or future pick. Orlando chose immediate cash value from a second-round selection rather than carrying another rookie contract or development project.

sections.heading: Burks Gave Memphis Real NBA Minutes
sections.body: Burks made the Grizzlies roster and appeared in multiple seasons for Memphis, giving the team reserve point-guard minutes behind its established backcourt. He never became a major rotation fixture, but a late second-round acquisition does not need to become a starter to produce useful value. Memphis converted cash into an actual NBA contributor during a playoff-era roster cycle.

sections.heading: Orlando Received No Basketball Asset Back
sections.body: The Magic received cash and no player, pick or rights that could later produce on-court value from this transaction. That does not make the sale irrational; second-round roster spots have opportunity costs and teams frequently monetize picks. In hindsight, though, Burks reaching the NBA and contributing for Memphis creates the only measurable basketball return in the deal.

sections.heading: Why Orlando Chose Cash Instead of Burks
sections.body: Orlando received cash considerations, not another player or future draft selection, when it sent Antonio Burks's rights to Memphis. The available ledger does not establish the dollar amount, so assigning a made-up financial figure would distort the exchange. A team can reasonably prefer selling a late pick rather than opening a developmental roster place; Orlando made that choice. Memphis took a different route, paying money rather than a future asset to give a guard prospect a chance. Burks eventually played regular-season NBA games for the Grizzlies, providing an observable but limited basketball return. A slight Memphis edge reflects that measurable contribution against an undisclosed cash payment, rather than implying that the Magic gave away a future star.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Grizzlies Edge — Memphis B-, Orlando C+. Memphis paid only cash for the rights to Antonio Burks and received several seasons of reserve NBA minutes. Orlando monetized a second-round asset but created no downstream basketball value from the trade. The stakes were small, so the grade gap stays narrow, yet Memphis clearly got more usable on-court return.

sections.heading: Toronto Turned One Draft-Rights Swap Into Two NBA Players
sections.body: Miami sent Toronto the draft rights to Pape Sow plus a 2005 second-round pick and received the rights to Albert Miralles. Sow played 76 NBA games, all for the Raptors, and started 29 of them. The extra second became No. 58 Uros Slokar, who later appeared in 20 games for Toronto. Neither player became a long-term starter, but the Raptors converted both incoming assets into actual NBA minutes.

sections.heading: Miami Never Received NBA Production From Albert Miralles
sections.body:
Miralles was the No. 39 pick in the 2004 draft, but he never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Miami held his draft rights as an asset, yet the branch never produced Heat minutes before those rights were eventually moved elsewhere. That leaves a direct completed-value gap: Toronto received two players who reached its roster while Miami received no on-court return from Miralles.

The 2004 rights exchanged were attached to different players: Albert Miralles for Miami and Pape Sow for Toronto. The Raptors also received the following year's second-round selection, used at No. 58 on Uros Slokar. Sow appeared in 76 NBA games with Toronto and Slokar added 20, while Miralles' rights never turned into a Heat regular-season appearance. The comparison isn't based on the future reputation of any of these prospects. It follows their direct opportunities after the original transaction, crediting Toronto with its two roster contributors and declining to assign nonexistent Miami production to Miralles. That is why the B+ and C+ grades can differ even on a relatively minor draft-rights exchange.

sections.heading: The Deal Was Small, but the Hindsight Result Is Clear
sections.body: This was a second-round rights trade, not a franchise-changing transaction, so the grades should stay proportional to the stakes. Toronto still deserves the higher mark because Sow supplied 76 games and Slokar added another 20. Miami took a reasonable draft-rights chance, but once Miralles failed to reach the NBA, the Heat side had little realized value to offset Toronto's two-player return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Raptors Win - Toronto B+, Miami C+. Toronto turned Pape Sow and the future second-round pick into 96 combined NBA appearances for the franchise, including 29 starts from Sow. Miami received Albert Miralles' rights but no NBA games from him. The scale is modest, yet the completed value lands clearly with Toronto.

sections.heading: Golden State Got Two Seasons From Žarko Čabarkapa
sections.body: Golden State acquired Žarko Čabarkapa from Phoenix on January 3, 2005 for two future second-round picks. Čabarkapa played 98 regular-season games for the Warriors across the 2004-05 and 2005-06 seasons. His best stretch came immediately after the trade, when he averaged 6.2 points in 37 games for Golden State. The Warriors received a real rotation player, but the return never grew into a larger long-term branch.

sections.heading: Phoenix Quickly Reused the 2007 Second
sections.body: The first pick was protected until 2007 and eventually became the No. 49 selection. Phoenix did not keep it through draft night. On February 8, 2005, the Suns sent that future second to Boston for Walter McCarty and cash. McCarty was only a short-term Phoenix piece, so this branch added modest value rather than the future career of Aaron Gray, who was eventually selected after the pick changed hands several more times.

sections.heading: The 2009 Second Helped Phoenix Acquire Goran Dragić
sections.body: The second incoming pick lasted much longer in the Suns asset tree. In the 2008 draft, Phoenix sent the future Golden State second, the rights to Malik Hairston and cash to San Antonio for the draft rights to Goran Dragić. San Antonio later used the pick at No. 37 on DeJuan Blair. Phoenix does not receive Blair’s career in this grade, but the pick was a real component in the trade that brought Dragić to the Suns, giving the original Čabarkapa deal a much stronger downstream outcome.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Suns Win — Phoenix A-, Golden State C-. Čabarkapa gave the Warriors 98 games, so Golden State received genuine rotation value. Phoenix converted one second into Walter McCarty and cash, then used the other as part of the package that acquired Goran Dragić’s draft rights. The Suns do not get credit for Aaron Gray or DeJuan Blair simply because those picks eventually selected them; the win comes from what Phoenix actually did with the assets before they left its control.

sections.heading: Lawrence Roberts Gave Memphis 87 Games
sections.body: Memphis acquired the draft rights to Lawrence Roberts on June 28, 2005 for cash plus second-round picks in 2006 and 2007. Roberts played both of his NBA seasons for the Grizzlies, appearing in 87 regular-season games with 18 starts. His second year was the more useful one: 54 games, 18 starts, 5.2 points and 4.8 rebounds per game. That is modest rotation value, but it is real team production from the No. 55 draft rights.

sections.heading: Seattle’s 2006 Pick Never Produced NBA Minutes
sections.body: The first incoming second became No. 53 Yotam Halperin in 2006. Halperin had a strong international career but never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Seattle therefore retained his rights without receiving on-court NBA value from that branch. The pick was not worthless as an asset, but it cannot be graded as if Halperin produced for the SuperSonics.

sections.heading: Carl Landry’s Career Belongs to Houston, Not Seattle
sections.body: The 2007 second became No. 31 Carl Landry, but Seattle traded Landry’s draft rights to Houston for cash and a 2008 second-round pick. That later pick became No. 56 Sasha Kaun, whose rights Seattle then sold to Cleveland for cash. Seattle deserves credit for repeatedly monetizing the asset, but not for Landry’s productive Rockets career. Once attribution is corrected, Seattle’s return is cash, draft optionality and no direct NBA player production, while Memphis received 87 Roberts games.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Grizzlies Edge — Memphis B, Seattle B-. Roberts was only a rotation big, but he gave Memphis 87 games and 18 starts. Seattle obtained cash and two future seconds, yet Halperin never played in the NBA and the Landry branch was converted into another second plus cash before Kaun’s rights were sold. The prior Seattle A-/Memphis C grade incorrectly treated Landry’s later NBA career as Seattle value; correcting that attribution produces a much closer trade with Memphis slightly ahead.

sections.heading: Chicago Bought Enormous Draft Leverage
sections.body: Chicago sent Eddy Curry and Antonio Davis to New York on October 4, 2005 for Tim Thomas, Mike Sweetney, Jermaine Jackson, a conditional 2006 first-round pick, the right to swap 2007 firsts and two future second-round picks. Curry was the best established scorer in the deal, but the Bulls had moved on after concerns over his heart condition. The critical part of Chicago’s return was not the veteran filler; it was control of New York draft value during two seasons in which the Knicks remained near the bottom of the standings.

sections.heading: The No. 2 Pick Did Not Become LaMarcus Aldridge Value for Chicago
sections.body: The 2006 first landed at No. 2. Chicago selected LaMarcus Aldridge, then immediately traded his draft rights and another second-round asset to Portland for the rights to No. 4 pick Tyrus Thomas and Viktor Khryapa. Aldridge’s later All-Star career therefore belongs to Portland, not to the Bulls’ grade here. Chicago still realized substantial value from the No. 2 slot because it had enough leverage to choose its preferred prospect and add Khryapa, even though Thomas never became the star the Bulls hoped for.

sections.heading: The 2007 Swap Produced Joakim Noah
sections.body: The most valuable Chicago outcome arrived one year later. The Bulls exercised the 2007 swap and moved from their own No. 23 position to New York’s No. 9 slot, where they selected Joakim Noah. Noah became a two-time All-Star, the 2013-14 Defensive Player of the Year and an All-NBA first-team center during his Bulls career. New York did get real value from Curry, including an 81-game, 19.5-point-per-game 2006-07 season, and later converted Antonio Davis into Jalen Rose plus a first-round pick. Those returns still do not approach the long-term impact Chicago extracted from the premium first and swap.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win — Chicago A+, New York F. Curry gave the Knicks one genuinely productive scoring season, and the Davis branch produced Jalen Rose plus another first, so New York did not receive literally nothing. The price was still devastating: Chicago obtained the No. 2 pick in 2006 and, more importantly, the 2007 swap that became Joakim Noah. The Bulls should not be credited with LaMarcus Aldridge’s career after trading his rights, but Noah alone supplies franchise-level realized value that the Knicks side never matched.

sources.title: Bulls Acquire Thomas, Sweetney and Draft Picks From New York

sections.heading: Cleveland Bought the No. 42 Pick for Almost No Realized Cost
sections.body: On February 23, 2006, Cleveland acquired Lee Nailon and Philadelphia’s 2006 second-round pick in exchange for a conditional Cavaliers second. The condition required Cleveland to finish with one of the league’s top records, so the outgoing pick never conveyed. Nailon did not become the point of the deal for Cleveland; the meaningful asset was the incoming second that reached the draft four months later.

sections.heading: Daniel Gibson Became a Seven-Year Cavalier
sections.body: Cleveland used the No. 42 selection on Daniel Gibson. He spent his entire seven-season NBA career with the Cavaliers, appearing in 397 regular-season games and adding valuable playoff shooting to the first LeBron James era. His signature early moment came in the 2007 Eastern Conference finals, when he scored 31 points in the clinching Game 6 against Detroit to help send Cleveland to its first NBA Finals.

sections.heading: Philadelphia’s Conditional Return Never Materialized
sections.body: The 76ers moved Nailon and a real second-round pick but did not receive an NBA player or a later draft selection from the conditional return. Because the Cavaliers did not meet the trigger, the promised second was never exercised. That makes the completed value unusually simple: Philadelphia surrendered the pick that became a long-term Cleveland guard, while the Sixers’ incoming asset expired without producing team value.

sections.heading: A Conditional Promise Is Different From an Actual Draft Pick
sections.body: The obligation Philadelphia received depended on Cleveland finishing with at least the league's third-best record, according to the transaction terms. That condition was not satisfied, so it never became a pick the 76ers could select or trade on draft night. By contrast, the second Philadelphia sent was an actual 2006 draft asset, and Cleveland used it at No. 42 to take Daniel Gibson. This distinction explains the unusual grade disparity without having to imagine a missing Philadelphia player. Nailon was the veteran attached to the transfer, but the Cavaliers' long-term return came from the converted selection rather than his playing time. Gibson's 397 Cleveland regular-season appearances and the 2007 Eastern Conference finals performance are completed value; an unexercised conditional pick has no comparable player result to measure.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win — Cleveland A+, Philadelphia D+. The No. 42 pick became Daniel Gibson, a seven-year Cavalier and an important shooter on the 2007 Finals team. Philadelphia’s conditional second never conveyed, leaving the Sixers without a comparable realized return. The transaction was small on trade day but produced a clear long-term Cleveland win once the draft pick converted.

sources.title: 2007 Eastern Conference Finals - Cavaliers vs. Pistons

sections.heading: Indiana Paid Three Assets for James White’s Draft Rights
sections.body: Indiana traded the rights to No. 45 pick Alexander Johnson plus second-round picks in 2007 and 2008 for the rights to No. 31 pick James White. The Pacers signed White in July but waived him before the regular season, so he never played an NBA game for Indiana. That left Portland holding all of the meaningful realized asset value from a deal the Pacers had made to move up fourteen spots in the second round.

sections.heading: Portland Immediately Turned Alexander Johnson Into Another Pick
sections.body: Portland did not keep Johnson. On the same draft night, the Trail Blazers sent his rights to Memphis for a 2008 second-round pick that became No. 33 Joey Dorsey. Dorsey’s rights later became one component of the 2008 three-team transaction that brought Nicolas Batum to Portland. Batum’s entire career cannot be assigned to this single branch because Portland also sent Darrell Arthur in that deal, but the Johnson return remained part of an asset chain that reached a major long-term player.

sections.heading: Both Future Seconds Were Converted Again
sections.body: The 2007 second became No. 42 Derrick Byars, whose rights Portland sent with cash to Philadelphia for the rights to Petteri Koponen. The 2008 second became No. 55 Mike Taylor, and Portland traded Taylor’s rights to the Clippers for a 2009 second-round pick that became Dante Cunningham. Neither branch alone was franchise-changing, but both remained usable assets after Indiana’s James White branch had already ended.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Blazers Win — Portland A, Indiana C. White never played a regular-season game for the Pacers, while Portland converted all three incoming pieces into additional assets. The Johnson branch helped feed the 2008 trade that brought Nicolas Batum to Portland, Byars became Petteri Koponen’s rights, and Mike Taylor became the future second used on Dante Cunningham. Portland’s win comes from those actual conversions, not from crediting the franchise with careers of players it had already traded away.

sections.heading: Minnesota Turned Bobby Jones’ Rights Into a Pick and Cash
sections.body: Minnesota drafted Bobby Jones at No. 37 in 2006 and immediately moved his rights to Philadelphia for cash and a 2007 second-round pick. The Timberwolves were not giving up an established rotation player; they were converting one second-round draft right into a later second plus cash. That gave Minnesota another chance to draft while preserving flexibility from the same asset tier.

sections.heading: The Future Pick Became Chris Richard
sections.body: The incoming second landed at No. 41 in 2007, where Minnesota selected Chris Richard. Richard became a depth big for the Timberwolves and spent time moving between the NBA roster and the Sioux Falls Skyforce. The return was modest, but it was real NBA value from the pick, and the cash component came on top of it. Minnesota therefore realized something from both parts of its package rather than watching the trade expire at draft night.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Got a Useful Rookie, but the Downstream Branch Is Shared
sections.body: Jones did play for Philadelphia as a rookie, so the 76ers received legitimate value from the rights they acquired. A year later he was traded with Steven Hunter to Denver for Reggie Evans and the rights to Ricky Sánchez. That later return cannot be assigned entirely to Jones because Hunter was part of the same outgoing package, so it should not be fully credited back to this 2006 trade. On the directly attributable record, Philadelphia received a short Jones stint while Minnesota got Richard plus cash.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wolves Win — Minnesota B, Philadelphia C+. Philadelphia got a real NBA player in Bobby Jones and one useful rookie season, so the deal was not empty on the 76ers’ side. Minnesota still finishes slightly ahead because the Wolves received cash plus the 2007 second that became Chris Richard. The difference is narrow, and the grade deliberately does not over-credit Philadelphia for a later Jones-and-Hunter package whose return cannot be cleanly split between the two outgoing players.

sections.heading: Houston Bought Two Years of Kirk Snyder and Moved Down the Future-Pick Chain
sections.body: Houston acquired Kirk Snyder from New Orleans/Oklahoma City on July 14, 2006 along with a 2008 second-round pick, while sending the Hornets a different 2008 second-round pick. Snyder gave the Rockets 48 regular-season games across two seasons, including 39 games in 2006-07, but never became a major rotation fixture. Houston later traded Snyder to Minnesota in February 2008 with another second-round pick for Gerald Green, so the direct player branch ended without producing a long Rockets tenure.

sections.heading: The Two 2008 Seconds Changed Hands Again Before Draft Night
sections.body: The future picks should not be graded by simply assigning Sasha Kaun or Maarty Leunen to the team that received the pick in 2006. By the 2008 draft, Seattle held the No. 56 selection that became Kaun and then sold his rights to Cleveland. The No. 54 selection tied to Leunen had returned to Houston in the February 2008 three-team trade involving New Orleans, Houston and Memphis. Those later transactions show that both picks remained trade currency rather than clean one-team draft outcomes from this deal.

sections.heading: New Orleans Reused Its Pick in a Larger Win-Now Trade
sections.body: New Orleans sent the 2008 second that later became No. 54 back to Houston on February 21, 2008 as part of the three-team trade in which the Hornets also sent Bobby Jackson, Adam Haluska and Marcus Vinicius while receiving Mike James and Bonzi Wells. Because several players moved in that transaction, the entire James-Wells return cannot be credited to this one second-round pick. The pick still retained transactional value, while Houston’s clearest directly attributable return from the 2006 deal was a modest 48-game Snyder stint.

sections.heading: The Two 2008 Picks Later Changed Hands Again
sections.body: The two second-round choices eventually became No. 54 Maarty Leunen and No. 56 Sasha Kaun, but those draft names cannot simply be assigned to the original 2006 recipient. The No. 54 rights returned to Houston in a different three-team transaction involving New Orleans and Memphis, while Seattle held the later No. 56 choice and moved Kaun's rights to Cleveland. Those movements show why draft obligations are trade assets rather than guaranteed player returns. Houston's direct measurable benefit from the original trade was Kirk Snyder's 48 appearances across two seasons. New Orleans later reused the outgoing second within a much larger package for Mike James and Bonzi Wells, but that entire return cannot fairly be credited to one pick.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans Win — New Orleans B, Houston C-. Houston received real value from Kirk Snyder, but only 48 regular-season games, and the incoming 2008 second did not remain with the Rockets through draft night. New Orleans later reused the outgoing Houston second as one component of a larger trade package that brought back Mike James and Bonzi Wells. The Hornets get the edge for preserving more transactional utility, while the grade deliberately avoids assigning the entire later three-team return to one second-round pick.

sections.heading: Indiana Bought Stanko Barać’s Rights With a Future Second
sections.body: Indiana acquired the draft rights to Stanko Barać on June 28, 2007 by sending Miami a future 2009 second-round pick. Barać was a draft-and-stash center rather than an immediate NBA rotation player, so the Pacers were betting that one future second could become a useful international prospect without taking a roster spot right away. That upside never turned into NBA games for Indiana.

sections.heading: Miami’s 2009 Second Became Marcus Thornton at No. 43
sections.body: The future pick conveyed at No. 43 in the 2009 draft, where Miami selected Marcus Thornton. The Heat did not keep Thornton, so his later scoring for New Orleans and Sacramento does not belong in Miami’s grade. Instead, Miami immediately converted his rights into two more second-round picks from New Orleans, turning the original Indiana asset into a second layer of draft capital.

sections.heading: The Thornton Rights Produced Two More Pick Branches
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference records Miami trading Thornton to New Orleans for a 2010 second that later became Jarvis Varnado and a 2012 second tied to the slot where Jae Crowder was later selected. Crowder’s later NBA career cannot simply be assigned to Miami because that pick changed hands again before he entered the league, but the two-pick return still shows that the Heat extracted more transactional value from Indiana’s second than the Pacers realized from Barać’s rights.

The pick routing after the initial agreement is what separates this transaction from a routine draft-and-stash exchange. Indiana obtained Barać's rights in 2007 but never received NBA regular-season appearances from him. Miami later used the acquired second at No. 43 in 2009 to select Thornton and then moved his draft rights to New Orleans for two more second-round assets. The eventual selection names Jarvis Varnado and Jae Crowder appear in those later chains, but neither player's whole future career should automatically be credited to Miami. The Heat's trade activity preserved assets that could be moved again, whereas the Pacers' original rights did not become a comparable roster contribution.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Heat Win — Miami B-, Indiana C. Indiana took a reasonable draft-and-stash swing on Stanko Barać, but the rights never produced NBA games for the Pacers. Miami turned the future second into Marcus Thornton’s draft rights and then converted those rights into two additional second-round assets. The grade credits Miami for that repeat asset conversion without backfilling Thornton’s or Jae Crowder’s later careers as if they had played for the Heat.

sections.heading: Miami Moved Down One Slot and Added Two Extra Assets
sections.body: Miami selected Jason Smith at No. 20 in the 2007 draft, then sent his rights to Philadelphia for the rights to No. 21 pick Daequan Cook, a 2009 second-round pick and cash. The Heat therefore accepted a one-pick move down in exchange for an additional draft asset and cash while still landing a first-round wing. Philadelphia paid the extra pieces to secure the taller frontcourt prospect it preferred.

sections.heading: Cook Gave Miami Three Seasons and a Useful Exit Asset
sections.body: Cook spent three seasons with the Heat and became a regular perimeter option, including a larger role in 2008-09. In June 2010, Miami traded Cook together with the No. 18 pick to Oklahoma City for the No. 32 pick. The entire Dexter Pittman return cannot be assigned to Cook alone because the first-rounder was the larger component, but Cook still retained enough transaction value to remain part of Miami’s roster-clearing move before the 2010 offseason.

sections.heading: The 2009 Second Helped Miami Acquire Mario Chalmers
sections.body: The extra second-round pick became the slot later associated with No. 45 Nick Calathes, but Miami did not simply wait to draft Calathes. In the 2008 draft, the Heat used that future second as one component of the package sent to Minnesota for the rights to Mario Chalmers. Chalmers’ entire Miami career cannot be credited to one second-round pick, yet the asset clearly retained useful trade value and became part of a deal that brought Miami a long-term rotation guard.

sections.heading: Jason Smith Was Useful for Philadelphia but Did Not Create the Better Chain
sections.body: Smith gave Philadelphia multiple active seasons after missing 2008-09 with a knee injury. He remained a useful young big and was later traded with Willie Green and a second-round swap to New Orleans for Darius Songaila and Craig Brackins. That is legitimate return value for the 76ers, but Miami received Cook plus two additional assets and extracted more total utility from the package without needing to over-credit Chalmers or the later Cook trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Heat Edge — Miami B-, Philadelphia C+. Jason Smith was a real NBA contributor for Philadelphia, so the 76ers did not lose this trade badly. Miami still finishes slightly ahead because Daequan Cook supplied three seasons, the 2009 second retained value as part of the Mario Chalmers acquisition package, and the Heat also received cash. The prior canonical summary incorrectly said Philadelphia held the better side even though the stored verdict and grades favored Miami; this repair aligns the summary with the completed asset record.

sources.title: Jason Smith Player Profile and Transaction History

sections.heading: New York Built the Deal Around Zach Randolph
sections.body: The Knicks acquired Zach Randolph on draft night in 2007 along with Fred Jones, Dan Dickau and the rights to Demetris Nichols. Randolph was the centerpiece: a 25-year-old former 20-and-10 scorer who could immediately take a major offensive role. New York paid with Steve Francis, Channing Frye and a future second-round pick, choosing present star-level production over a younger frontcourt piece and future draft value.

sections.heading: Randolph Produced Immediately and Still Had Trade Value
sections.body: Randolph became one of New York’s primary scorers and rebounders from the start. His Knicks tenure lasted only a little more than one season before the franchise changed direction, but the player asset did not simply expire. New York later traded Randolph and Mardy Collins to the Clippers for Cuttino Mobley and Tim Thomas, so the main incoming piece still carried enough league value to generate another veteran package.

sections.heading: Portland’s Cleanest On-Court Return Was Channing Frye
sections.body: Frye gave Portland two seasons of frontcourt minutes and was the most useful direct player the Trail Blazers received. Francis never played a regular-season game for Portland after the club bought out his contract, making his role primarily financial rather than basketball value. The 2008 second-round asset also moved again before becoming an NBA contributor for Portland, so it should not be graded as though the Blazers received Omer Asik’s later career.

sections.heading: The Supporting Knicks Pieces Were Secondary
sections.body: Fred Jones supplied one season of rotation minutes, while Dickau and Nichols did not become durable Knicks assets. That keeps the New York grade below the level of a franchise-changing win. The distinction is that Randolph alone produced more immediate high-end basketball value than Portland’s direct return, and he remained tradeable when New York decided to move on.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win — New York B, Portland C. Portland received useful Channing Frye minutes and achieved salary flexibility after Steve Francis never suited up, but the package did not match Zach Randolph’s immediate production or retained trade value. New York’s supporting pieces were modest, so this is not a runaway result. The prior canonical summary called the outcome too close to name despite a stored Knicks Win verdict and B-to-C grade split; this repair makes the summary and editorial agree with the completed-value record.

sections.heading: Memphis Finally Brought Juan Carlos Navarro to the NBA
sections.body: Washington traded the NBA rights to Juan Carlos Navarro to Memphis in August 2007 for a heavily protected future first-round pick. Navarro then played all 82 games for the Grizzlies in 2007-08, averaged 10.9 points and earned All-Rookie Second Team honors. He returned to FC Barcelona after that season, so Memphis received one productive NBA year rather than a multi-season core piece.

sections.heading: Washington Received a Protected First With Real Trade Value
sections.body: The Wizards did not receive an immediately usable pick. The first was protected top 19 in 2008, top 16 in 2009, top 14 from 2010 through 2012 and top 12 in 2013, with a second-round-and-cash fallback if it never conveyed. Those protections limited the upside in the short term, but the asset still had enough value to function as trade currency before Washington ever reached a draft night with it.

sections.heading: The Wizards Converted the Pick Into Javaris Crittenton
sections.body: In December 2008, Washington returned the protected first to Memphis in the three-team deal that brought the Wizards Javaris Crittenton and Mike James while sending Antonio Daniels to New Orleans. That means the first-round claim never simply became Xavier Henry for Washington. The Wizards chose to cash out the asset early for an NBA guard, and Memphis regained control of its own future first before it could convey.

sections.heading: The Completed Value Stayed Close
sections.body: Memphis received the best immediate basketball season in Navarro, while Washington turned the future pick claim into a live trade asset and then an NBA player. Crittenton did not become a major long-term Wizard, and Navarro left after one season, so neither side created a lasting franchise cornerstone. The trade-day logic and the realized outcomes both support a close result rather than awarding either team an exaggerated win.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Memphis B+, Washington B+. Navarro gave Memphis a full 82-game rookie season, double-digit scoring and All-Rookie recognition before returning to Barcelona. Washington received a protected first-round claim and later used that asset to acquire Javaris Crittenton rather than waiting for the pick to convey. Neither branch became a long-term franchise piece, but both produced legitimate value, making equal B+ grades a fair historical result.
