sections.heading: Miami Chose Ricky Davis and Mark Blount for Immediate Help
sections.body: Miami acquired Ricky Davis and Mark Blount from Minnesota just before the 2007-08 season, sending Antoine Walker, Wayne Simien, Michael Doleac, a protected future first-round pick and cash. The Heat were trying to add current scoring and size around an aging contender rather than wait on a draft asset. Davis became an immediate high-minute wing, while Blount gave Miami another veteran center option.

sections.heading: The Short-Term Heat Return Did Not Change the Team’s Direction
sections.body: Davis supplied points and minutes during the 2007-08 season, and Blount remained with Miami into the following year. The production was real, but it arrived during a collapse from championship contention into a 15-win season. Neither player became part of the next successful Heat core, so Miami’s return was useful in isolation without creating the longer roster value the front office hoped to get.

sections.heading: Minnesota Took Back Veterans but Preserved the Best Future Asset
sections.body: Walker, Doleac and Simien did not become long-term Timberwolves building blocks. The important piece was Miami’s protected first, which eventually conveyed as the No. 18 selection in 2009. Minnesota used that slot on Ty Lawson and then traded Lawson’s rights to Denver for another future first-round asset. The Wolves therefore preserved draft capital beyond the original veteran swap instead of tying the entire return to the incoming players.

sections.heading: Lawson’s Denver Career Is Not Minnesota Value
sections.body: The hindsight case does not credit Minnesota for the career Lawson later had with Denver. The Wolves’ value is the fact that Miami’s pick became a first-round asset that could be moved again, plus whatever Minnesota realized from that follow-up transaction. That is still a more durable branch than Davis and Blount provided Miami, while avoiding the common mistake of assigning another franchise’s player production to the original trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wolves Win — Minnesota A-, Miami B-. Miami received legitimate short-term production from Ricky Davis and Mark Blount, but neither became part of a lasting Heat core. Minnesota’s veteran return was modest, yet the protected first eventually conveyed at No. 18 and remained valuable enough to be traded again on draft night. The draft branch gives the Timberwolves the stronger completed package without crediting them for Ty Lawson’s later Denver career.

sections.heading: This Was a Cap Transaction, Not a Beno Udrih Acquisition
sections.body: Minnesota acquired Beno Udrih and cash from San Antonio on October 29, 2007 for a heavily protected 2008 second-round pick. The Timberwolves immediately waived Udrih, who signed with Sacramento days later. That sequence makes the purpose clear: Minnesota was not trading for a point guard it intended to develop. The club was accepting Udrih’s contract in exchange for cash while it finalized its own roster and Juwan Howard buyout.

sections.heading: Minnesota Received Cash and Gave Up a Pick That Never Conveyed
sections.body: The outgoing second was protected through No. 57 and ultimately did not convey. Minnesota therefore surrendered no realized draft asset. Contemporary reporting said the cash from San Antonio helped the Timberwolves absorb costs connected to buying out Howard. The basketball return from Udrih was zero Minnesota games, but the financial return was real and the nominal pick cost never materialized.

sections.heading: San Antonio Bought Salary and Luxury-Tax Relief
sections.body: The Spurs’ benefit was equally direct. Moving Udrih’s contract off the books helped San Antonio avoid a luxury-tax hit and cleared a roster obligation for a player who had fallen out of the regular rotation. The protected second never became an actual Spurs pick, so San Antonio did not receive draft value. Its return was the cap and tax savings created by paying Minnesota to take the contract.

sections.heading: Udrih’s Sacramento Career Does Not Belong to Either Side
sections.body: Udrih became a productive starter after Sacramento signed him, but none of those Kings seasons belongs in the grade for Minnesota or San Antonio. The Wolves waived him immediately, and the Spurs had already chosen the financial benefit of moving his contract. A disciplined retrospective therefore judges the transaction on the cash, the non-conveyed pick and the salary relief actually created for the two teams in this trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Minnesota B, San Antonio B. The Timberwolves received cash, surrendered a protected second that never conveyed and used the transaction as part of a broader roster reset. The Spurs received no draft pick, but they achieved the salary and luxury-tax relief that motivated the deal. The prior Wolves Win / Spurs D grading treated a financial housekeeping trade like a player-value exchange; equal B grades better reflect what both teams actually obtained.

sections.heading: San Antonio Bought a Playoff Big in Kurt Thomas
sections.body: San Antonio acquired Kurt Thomas from Seattle at the 2008 trade deadline for Brent Barry, Francisco Elson and a protected future first-round pick. Thomas was the only incoming Spur and the purpose was clear: add an experienced, physical frontcourt defender for a team still built around Tim Duncan. He immediately joined the playoff rotation and gave San Antonio the type of veteran size it wanted for another postseason run.

sections.heading: Seattle Turned One Veteran Into Flexibility and a First
sections.body: The SuperSonics were moving in the opposite direction. Barry and Elson were expiring or short-term veterans, while the protected first was the asset with rebuilding value. Seattle waived Barry shortly after the trade, allowing him to become a free agent, and Elson supplied only brief on-court value. The first-round claim therefore carried most of the long-term weight on Seattle’s side.

sections.heading: Barry Returned to San Antonio After the Waiting Period
sections.body: Barry eventually re-signed with the Spurs after clearing Seattle and the required waiting period. His return does not erase the trade because San Antonio still surrendered his contract and the first-round pick, but it does improve the practical outcome for the Spurs: they obtained Thomas and later restored Barry to the roster. That is why San Antonio’s completed grade remains strong even though Seattle received the better future asset package.

sections.heading: The First Became a Real 2009 Draft Asset
sections.body: The protected selection conveyed in 2009 at No. 25. By then the Seattle franchise had moved to Oklahoma City, but the asset still belonged to the same organizational branch created by this trade. The pick became part of the draft-night maneuvering around Rodrigue Beaubois and Byron Mullens. The later careers of players moved in that separate draft transaction should not be dumped wholesale into this grade; the relevant point is that the Thomas trade created a usable first-round asset for the rebuilding franchise.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Seattle SuperSonics Edge — Seattle A-, San Antonio B+. The Spurs got exactly the veteran big they wanted in Kurt Thomas and even brought Brent Barry back after Seattle waived him, so this was a useful win-now move. Seattle still gets the narrow higher grade because it converted Thomas into a first-round asset plus short-term roster flexibility during a rebuild. The difference is small because San Antonio received real playoff value rather than sacrificing the pick for an empty rental.

sections.heading: Miami Bought Mario Chalmers for Two Seconds and Cash
sections.body: Miami acquired the draft rights to Mario Chalmers from Minnesota on June 26, 2008 for two 2009 second-round picks and $2 million in cash. Chalmers had slipped to No. 34 despite a decorated college career, and the Heat paid to move into the early second round rather than wait for another prospect. The transaction immediately gave Miami a young point guard without surrendering a first-round selection.

sections.heading: Chalmers Became a Seven-Year Heat Rotation Fixture
sections.body: Chalmers started 82 games as a rookie and remained with Miami through the 2014-15 season before being traded during his eighth year. He played major minutes on four straight Finals teams and started throughout the 2012 and 2013 championship runs. His value came from durability, defense, three-point shooting and the ability to fill a low-usage point-guard role beside Miami’s stars.

sections.heading: Minnesota’s Two Picks Produced No Comparable Team Value
sections.body: The two future seconds landed at Nos. 45 and 47 in the 2009 draft, associated with Nick Calathes and Henk Norel. Neither became a meaningful Timberwolves contributor. Minnesota also received the $2 million cash payment, which gave the club immediate financial value, but the basketball return from the draft assets never approached what Chalmers supplied Miami.

sections.heading: The Cost Was Modest Even Before the Championships
sections.body: This trade does not need hindsight from two championship seasons to look favorable for Miami. A full-time rookie starter acquired for two future seconds already represented a strong conversion. The later title runs widened the gap because Chalmers remained in the rotation while the outgoing picks failed to produce comparable Minnesota minutes.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Heat Win — Miami A, Minnesota D+. Miami paid two second-round picks and $2 million for Mario Chalmers, then received more than seven seasons of rotation value and a starting point guard on two championship teams. Minnesota received cash and two draft assets, but neither pick generated comparable on-court value for the Timberwolves. The difference between a long-term starter and two low-yield seconds makes this one of the clearer Miami wins in the queue.

sections.heading: Indiana Turned Two Assets Into Four Useful Pieces
sections.body: Indiana sent Ike Diogu and the draft rights to Jerryd Bayless to Portland for Jarrett Jack, Josh McRoberts, the draft rights to Brandon Rush and cash. The Pacers were not simply swapping rookies. They used Bayless as the centerpiece of a broader package that immediately added a starting-caliber guard, a young forward and another first-round prospect.

sections.heading: Jack and Rush Gave Indiana Immediate Rotation Value
sections.body: Jack played all 82 games for Indiana in 2008-09 and became one of the Pacers’ primary guards. Rush spent three seasons with the franchise, starting regularly and providing perimeter defense and shooting. McRoberts developed more slowly but also became a useful rotation big. Indiana therefore received multiple NBA contributors from the same transaction rather than depending on one prospect to justify the deal.

sections.heading: Portland Got Real Value From Bayless
sections.body: Bayless was not a failed return for the Trail Blazers. He spent two seasons in Portland’s backcourt and later retained enough value to be traded to New Orleans for a future first-round pick. Diogu contributed very little, but Bayless gave Portland both on-court minutes and a second transaction branch. That record is too strong for an F-range or D-range historical grade even though Indiana still received the deeper package.

sections.heading: The Pacers Won on Depth, Not Because Portland Got Nothing
sections.body: Indiana’s advantage is the number of useful outcomes: Jack was immediately productive, Rush remained for three seasons, and McRoberts became a rotation forward-center. Portland’s side was narrower but still legitimate because Bayless played and was later converted into another first-round asset. The completed record supports a Pacers win while leaving the Trail Blazers with a respectable secondary grade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pacers Win — Indiana B+, Portland C+. Indiana received the deeper package: Jarrett Jack, Brandon Rush and Josh McRoberts all became useful Pacers, with cash added on top. Portland’s main return was Jerryd Bayless, who contributed for two seasons and later retained trade value, while Ike Diogu added little. The prior Portland D grade understated Bayless’ actual value and downstream conversion, so C+ is the more defensible losing-side grade.

sections.heading: Minnesota Was Paid to Absorb Salary
sections.body: Minnesota acquired Rodney Carney, Calvin Booth, cash and a protected future first-round pick from Philadelphia on July 9, 2008. The 76ers received only a top-55-protected 2010 second that never conveyed. On the asset ledger alone, the deal is extremely favorable to Minnesota: the Timberwolves received two NBA players, money and a future first without surrendering a realized draft asset.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Was Clearing Cap Room, Not Chasing the Second
sections.body: The 76ers’ practical return was financial flexibility. Moving Carney and Booth reduced salary commitments during a summer when Philadelphia was pursuing a major free-agent addition. The nominal protected second was never the point of the deal. Treating the trade as though Philadelphia expected basketball value from that pick misses why the club was willing to attach a first and cash to the outgoing contracts.

sections.heading: Minnesota’s First-Round Asset Eventually Conveyed
sections.body: The protected first did not convey immediately, but it eventually landed at No. 23 in the 2010 draft. That gave Minnesota a real first-round asset from a transaction in which its outgoing pick obligation disappeared. The Timberwolves could then use or convert that first within their own draft planning. Rodney Carney also played a full season for Minnesota, giving the team immediate wing minutes before the future pick matured.

sections.heading: The Wolves Won the Asset Exchange, but Philadelphia Had a Rational Objective
sections.body: Minnesota clearly obtained more traceable basketball and draft value. Philadelphia still received something meaningful: the ability to change its cap sheet at the exact point when it wanted room for a free-agent move. That financial objective does not erase the first-round cost, but it makes an F grade too harsh. A losing grade should acknowledge that the 76ers successfully accomplished the salary-clearing purpose that motivated the transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wolves Win — Minnesota A-, Philadelphia C+. Minnesota received Carney, Booth, cash and a first-round pick that eventually conveyed, while its protected second never did. Philadelphia paid heavily in assets, so the Timberwolves still win decisively. The 76ers’ grade rises from F to C+ because the trade was an intentional cap-clearing transaction that achieved its financial purpose rather than a failed attempt to obtain value from a non-conveyed second.

sections.heading: Houston Paid for One Serious Run With Ron Artest
sections.body: Houston acquired Ron Artest, later known as Metta World Peace, along with Sean Singletary and Patrick Ewing Jr. from Sacramento in August 2008. The Rockets paid Bobby Jackson, rookie Donte Greene, a protected first-round pick and cash. Artest was the clear target: Houston wanted another high-level defender and scorer beside Yao Ming and Tracy McGrady for a roster built to contend immediately.

sections.heading: Artest Helped Houston Break Through in the Playoffs
sections.body: Artest played 69 regular-season games for Houston and averaged 17.1 points before becoming central to the Rockets’ 2009 playoff run. Houston beat Portland in the first round, its first series victory since 1997, and then pushed the eventual champion Lakers to seven games despite major injuries. Artest left for Los Angeles after the season, so the return was short, but it produced the exact kind of high-stakes postseason value Houston had purchased.

sections.heading: Sacramento Received Two Real Rebuilding Pieces
sections.body: The Kings’ return was not empty. Donte Greene spent four seasons in Sacramento and developed into a regular rotation forward. The protected first conveyed at No. 23 in 2009 and became Omri Casspi, who also gave the Kings several seasons in his first stint. Bobby Jackson’s second Sacramento run was brief, while the $1 million cash payment added straightforward financial value.

sections.heading: The Rockets Won the Peak, the Kings Won the Duration
sections.body: Sacramento received more years of team-controlled player value from Greene and Casspi than Houston received from its one season of Artest. Houston still gets the higher grade because the acquired star materially improved a contender and helped produce a long-awaited playoff-series win. The gap stays modest because Sacramento converted the outgoing veteran into two legitimate young NBA contributors rather than a collection of dead assets.

sections.heading: Sacramento Used the Protected First for Casspi
sections.body: Houston's outgoing first was subject to protections rather than being an unrestricted lottery selection. Those conditions became irrelevant once the pick conveyed at No. 23 in 2009, allowing Sacramento to choose Omri Casspi. Combined with Donte Greene, the Kings received two young forwards who supplied multiple seasons of roster value, while Bobby Jackson and the cash payment were shorter-term components. Houston acquired Ron Artest for a different purpose: to strengthen a contender immediately. He scored 17.1 points per game over 69 appearances and helped the Rockets win a playoff series before their seven-game loss to the Lakers. The exchange therefore involved a successful one-season playoff investment against a longer developmental package, not a choice between production and absolutely nothing.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win — Houston B, Sacramento C+. Ron Artest stayed only one season, but he gave Houston 17.1 points per game, elite defensive presence and a major role in the franchise’s first playoff-series victory in twelve years. Sacramento answered with several seasons from Donte Greene and Omri Casspi plus cash, so the Kings’ return was respectable. Houston wins on peak competitive impact, not because Sacramento failed to realize value.

sections.heading: Golden State Swapped Harrington for Crawford
sections.body: Golden State sent Al Harrington to New York on November 21, 2008 for Jamal Crawford. The Warriors wanted another creator after a poor start, and Crawford immediately took on a large scoring and ball-handling role. He played 54 games for Golden State and averaged nearly 20 points per game, giving the club the offensive usage it had targeted.

sections.heading: Harrington Gave New York Two Productive Seasons
sections.body: Harrington became a major scorer for the Knicks almost immediately and stayed through the end of the 2009-10 season. His contract timeline also fit New York’s effort to create flexibility for the 2010 offseason more cleanly than Crawford’s longer deal. The Knicks therefore received both real on-court production and a roster-planning benefit.

sections.heading: Crawford Still Had Trade Value the Next Summer
sections.body: Golden State did not keep Crawford long. In June 2009, the Warriors traded him to Atlanta for Acie Law and Speedy Claxton. Neither incoming player became a major Golden State contributor, so that branch was modest, but it still shows Crawford remained a movable asset after his productive 54-game stay. His Warriors value was concentrated rather than durable.

sections.heading: Both Teams Got a Useful Result
sections.body: The Knicks received more direct games from Harrington and improved their 2010 contract positioning. The Warriors received the more dynamic scorer for one season and then converted him into another package. Neither side created a franchise-changing asset, so the completed result belongs in the narrow-margin range rather than being framed as a steal.

sections.heading: The Contract Timelines Worked Better for New York
sections.body: Harrington and Crawford weren't simply interchangeable scorers. Crawford gave Golden State substantial offense during a 54-game stint, but the club moved him again in June 2009 rather than building around that production. His next destination was Atlanta, with Acie Law and Speedy Claxton coming back to the Warriors. Harrington remained with New York through 2009-10, giving the Knicks far more time with the player they originally acquired. His shorter contract also aligned with the club's much-discussed 2010 summer roster reset. That strategic advantage wasn't a later title or a guaranteed free-agent signing, and it shouldn't be valued as one. It was a measurable difference in flexibility. The trade was close enough that Golden State's slight grade advantage depends on Crawford's player value during his short stint rather than on years of sustained Warriors production.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Warriors Edge — Golden State B, New York B-. Crawford gave Golden State immediate scoring and still carried trade value the following summer. Harrington gave the Knicks more games and fit their 2010 cap plan, so New York’s return was plainly useful. The small grade gap reflects two reasonable outcomes, with Golden State getting the slightly stronger player-value peak.

sections.heading: Denver Added Johan Petro for a 2009 Playoff Push
sections.body: Denver acquired Johan Petro and a 2009 second-round pick from Oklahoma City on January 7, 2009, sending Chucky Atkins, cash and a protected first. Petro gave the Nuggets another center behind Nene during a season that ended in the Western Conference finals. The move addressed a real rotation need, but Denver paid with the most valuable future asset in the exchange.

sections.heading: The Thunder Turned Denver’s First Into Thabo Sefolosha
sections.body: Oklahoma City did not wait to use Denver’s first-round pick itself. At the February 2009 deadline, the Thunder sent that first to Chicago in the trade for Thabo Sefolosha. Sefolosha then became a long-term Oklahoma City starter, earned All-Defensive Second Team honors and played a major role on teams that reached the 2012 NBA Finals and multiple deep playoff rounds.

sections.heading: Denver’s Second-Round Branch Became Cash
sections.body: The second-round pick landed at No. 34 in the 2009 draft and became the rights to Sergio Llull. Denver did not develop Llull as an NBA player; the Nuggets sold his draft rights to Houston for cash on draft night. That gave Denver an additional financial return, but it did not approach the multi-year on-court value Oklahoma City obtained by converting the first-round asset into Sefolosha.

sections.heading: Taj Gibson’s Bulls Career Does Not Belong to Oklahoma City
sections.body: The Denver first ultimately appears in draft records at No. 26, where Chicago selected Taj Gibson. Gibson’s Bulls career should not be credited to Oklahoma City because the Thunder had already traded that pick away for Sefolosha. The correct asset chain stops with what Oklahoma City actually received from the pick: a starting wing who became part of the franchise’s core during its rise into contention.

sections.heading: Two Cash Movements Complicate the Financial Ledger
sections.body: Cash appears in both the original and the subsequent asset chain, but in different directions and for different reasons. Denver sent cash together with Chucky Atkins and its protected first to Oklahoma City when it acquired Petro and the future second. Months later, Denver converted the No. 34 second-round rights to Sergio Llull into cash from Houston. The source record doesn't establish dollar amounts that would allow those separate movements to be netted into an exact financial gain or loss. Neither amount can substitute for a meaningful on-court return in a trade grade. Oklahoma City's best basketball result came from rerouting the Denver first to Chicago for Sefolosha, while Denver's basketball return was Petro's short-term center depth. Treating the cash separately keeps the grades tied to verifiable team value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Thunder Win — Oklahoma City A, Denver C+. Petro gave Denver useful center depth and the Llull rights later produced cash, so the Nuggets did realize value. Oklahoma City still wins clearly because the protected first was converted directly into Thabo Sefolosha, a long-term starter and All-Defensive contributor. The prior Slight Nuggets Edge verdict reversed the stronger asset chain and is corrected here.

sections.heading: Memphis Took Livingston and Cash for a Pick That Never Conveyed
sections.body: Memphis acquired Shaun Livingston and cash from Miami on January 7, 2009 for a protected 2012 second-round pick. The protection was top 55, and the pick ultimately did not convey. On the completed asset ledger, Miami never received a draft asset from the deal.

sections.heading: Livingston Never Played for the Grizzlies
sections.body: The transaction did not become a basketball-development win for Memphis. The Grizzlies waived Livingston immediately, so none of his later NBA recovery can be credited to this trade. Memphis’ realized return was the cash payment and the fact that its protected second-round obligation disappeared without conveying.

sections.heading: Miami Was Clearing Livingston From the Roster and Payroll
sections.body:
Livingston had appeared in only four games for the Heat after signing in October 2008. Contemporary reporting described the move as a salary-clearing transaction, and Miami attached cash while accepting a heavily protected future second. The Heat therefore achieved a roster and financial objective, even though the incoming pick never became usable draft capital.

The top-55 protection attached to the 2012 second is central to the realized deal. Miami was due a pick only if it fell outside that protected range; the transaction record shows it did not convey. The Heat's benefit therefore came from moving an unwanted contract and adjusting their roster, not from selecting a future prospect. Memphis received cash and briefly held Livingston before waiving him; none of Livingston's later years with other teams should be added to the Grizzlies' ledger. In an ordinary player trade, future production might dominate the verdict. Here the conditional pick's non-conveyance and cash settlement explain why the Grizzlies' edge remains narrow and financial.

sections.heading: The Completed Value Gap Is Small
sections.body: Neither side created durable on-court value from the exchange. Memphis did not develop Livingston, while Miami did not receive the conditional second. The Grizzlies still finish slightly ahead because they collected cash without ultimately surrendering a realized pick, but this belongs among narrow financial wins rather than trades with meaningful basketball fallout.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Grizzlies Win — Memphis B-, Miami C. Memphis received cash and never lost the protected 2012 second, but Livingston was waived immediately and contributed nothing to the team. Miami successfully moved Livingston after four games and reduced its commitment, yet the conditional pick never conveyed. The small grade gap reflects a modest financial advantage for Memphis, not player value.

sections.heading: Orlando Needed a Point Guard Immediately
sections.body: Orlando acquired Tyronn Lue from Milwaukee on February 5, 2009 after All-Star point guard Jameer Nelson suffered a serious shoulder injury. The Magic sent Keith Bogans and cash to get a veteran ball-handler who already knew the organization. Lue appeared in 14 regular-season games for Orlando, averaging 3.0 points in 9.2 minutes.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Turned a Reserve Guard Into Wing Depth and Cash
sections.body:
The Bucks were dealing with their own backcourt injury after Michael Redd was lost for the season. Bogans stepped into the rotation for 29 games, averaging 6.0 points in 16.7 minutes. He was not a long-term piece, but Milwaukee received more regular-season minutes from him than Orlando ultimately received from Lue, along with the cash payment.

Bogans and Lue were veteran guards occupying different jobs. Milwaukee used the acquired Bogans as an available defensive wing and received cash in the same move, while Orlando obtained Lue's veteran point-guard experience. The cash item belonged to the Bucks' return rather than a separate draft obligation, and neither team acquired a protected first or meaningful future pick as part of this recorded swap. Both sides were making near-term roster decisions around the 2008-09 season instead of seeking prospects for a rebuild. The matching B grades credit those practical contributions without treating Bogans' later NBA stops as Milwaukee production or Lue's previous career with other clubs as part of Orlando's new return.

sections.heading: The Rafer Alston Trade Reduced Lue’s Role
sections.body: Orlando made the larger point-guard move two weeks later by acquiring Rafer Alston. That pushed Lue into a much smaller role for the rest of the season and the playoffs. He appeared in only one postseason game during Orlando’s run to the NBA Finals, so the deal worked mainly as emergency insurance rather than as a defining part of the championship push.

sections.heading: Both Teams Solved a Short-Term Problem
sections.body: Milwaukee received a usable wing and cash, while Orlando filled an urgent position need without giving up a premium asset. Neither player created downstream value beyond the season, and neither side surrendered draft capital. The completed result is best treated as an even depth trade shaped by injuries and immediate roster needs.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Milwaukee B, Orlando B. Bogans gave the Bucks 29 games of rotation wing minutes plus cash, while Lue gave Orlando emergency point-guard depth after Nelson’s injury. The Magic later upgraded the position with Rafer Alston, limiting Lue’s postseason role. Both teams addressed a short-term need at a modest cost, and neither side created enough lasting value to justify a meaningful grade gap.

sources.title: 2022-23 Orlando Magic Media Guide — All-Time Transactions

sections.heading: The Lakers Used Mihm to Cut Their Tax Bill
sections.body: Los Angeles moved Chris Mihm to Memphis at the 2009 trade deadline for a heavily protected 2013 second-round pick. Contemporary reporting made the financial purpose explicit: moving Mihm reduced the Lakers’ luxury-tax bill by roughly $2.5 million while opening another roster spot on a championship contender.

sections.heading: The Pick Was Never a Meaningful Basketball Return
sections.body: The 2013 second was protected through pick No. 55 and would disappear if the condition was not met. It ultimately did not convey. Los Angeles therefore received no draft player or downstream basketball asset from the trade, but that was secondary to the immediate payroll objective.

sections.heading: Memphis Got Cash but No Games From Mihm
sections.body: The Grizzlies received Mihm and cash considerations, giving the rebuilding club a financial return for absorbing the contract. Mihm never appeared in a game for Memphis after the trade as his long-running ankle problems continued. His earlier Lakers production cannot be credited to the Grizzlies side of this transaction.

sections.heading: Both Sides Accomplished a Narrow Objective
sections.body: Los Angeles lowered its tax exposure without surrendering a useful future pick, while Memphis collected cash without ultimately losing the conditional second. Neither side created meaningful on-court value. The completed outcome is best viewed as a financially motivated even trade rather than a basketball win for either franchise.

sections.heading: The Pick Protection Ultimately Extinguished the Obligation
sections.body: The conditional second-round choice Memphis owed Los Angeles was protected through the top 55 in 2013, with the obligation ending if the condition wasn't satisfied. It ultimately was not exercised, so there is no Lakers draft choice or player to trace from that part of the trade. Memphis acquired Chris Mihm, but the veteran center's later Grizzlies appearances did not deliver a meaningful long-term rotation return. That leaves both organizations with limited actual value from the transaction. A reader could be misled by seeing '2013 second-round pick' in the asset ledger and assuming Los Angeles eventually drafted someone; the unexercised protection is central to the hindsight result. Equal B- grades are modest evaluations of a low-stakes roster maneuver, not proof that both sides produced comparable future stars.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Los Angeles B-, Memphis B-. The Lakers saved luxury-tax money and gave up Mihm at a point when he was outside the main rotation. Memphis received cash, but Mihm never played for the Grizzlies. Because the protected 2013 second never conveyed, neither team produced a lasting basketball asset. Both sides got the limited financial result they were seeking.

sections.heading: New York Swapped an Expiring Veteran for a More Useful One
sections.body: The Knicks sent Malik Rose and cash to Oklahoma City for Chris Wilcox at the 2009 deadline. Both players were on expiring contracts, so the move did not interfere with New York's plan to preserve future cap flexibility. Wilcox also offered a more active frontcourt option for the final two months of the season.

sections.heading: Wilcox Gave the Knicks 25 Games Off the Bench
sections.body:
Wilcox appeared in 25 games for New York, averaging 13.2 minutes and 5.4 points while shooting 52.9 percent from the field. He did not become a long-term piece and left after the season, but the Knicks received a younger rotation big without adding future salary.

The contract setting matters as much as the counting statistics because each acquired player was approaching free agency. New York obtained Wilcox for the final stretch of 2008-09 and did not take on a multiyear commitment from this exchange. Oklahoma City acquired Rose and cash without conceding a future draft pick, while Rose supplied 20 games of veteran frontcourt minutes. Wilcox appeared in 25 Knicks contests, gave New York a slightly younger option and shot effectively on limited attempts. These were short-term roster choices rather than the creation of a new trade tree. The matching B grades recognize that neither club gained much lasting control or franchise-level production.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Took Rose and the Cash
sections.body: Rose played 20 games for the Thunder after the trade, averaging 15.5 minutes and 5.0 points. Oklahoma City also received cash considerations. With both contracts expiring, the Thunder did not sacrifice a future asset or long-term flexibility in moving Wilcox.

sections.heading: The Short-Term Returns Stayed Close
sections.body: New York received the slightly more productive player for its immediate roster, while Oklahoma City received usable veteran minutes plus cash. Neither side created a draft asset or downstream return, and both players were gone after the season. The completed value is too modest and too close to justify a decisive winner.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — New York B, Oklahoma City B. Wilcox gave the Knicks 25 games of useful frontcourt depth on an expiring contract, while Rose gave the Thunder 20 games and came with cash. Both teams preserved future flexibility, and neither return produced lasting value. New York may have gained the better short-term player, but the gap is not large enough to break the even grade.

sections.heading: Denver Turned a Future First Into Its Point Guard
sections.body: Denver acquired the draft rights to Ty Lawson, the No. 18 pick in 2009, from Minnesota for a protected future first-round pick. The Nuggets were coming off a Western Conference finals run and used the trade to add a young point guard behind Chauncey Billups without waiting another year for the outgoing pick to resolve. Lawson was not a speculative stash: he joined the rotation immediately and grew into the starting job.

sections.heading: Lawson Became a Multi-Year Starter in Denver
sections.body: Lawson spent six seasons with the Nuggets and became the team’s primary point guard. By his third season he was a full-time starter, and in 2012-13 he averaged 16.7 points and 6.9 assists for a 57-win Denver team. That sustained production is the central value of the trade. The Nuggets paid one future first and received several seasons of starting-caliber play from the player they targeted on draft night.

sections.heading: Minnesota’s Pick Became Luke Babbitt, Then Part of the Martell Webster Trade
sections.body: The protected first conveyed in 2010 at No. 16, where Minnesota selected Luke Babbitt. The Timberwolves did not keep Babbitt; they traded his rights with Ryan Gomes to Portland for Martell Webster. That means Webster cannot be credited entirely to the Lawson transaction because Gomes was also in the package. Minnesota did convert the pick into usable value, but the branch never matched the long-term point-guard production Denver received.

sections.heading: The Draft-Night Bet Worked Far Better for Denver
sections.body: Minnesota had already drafted Ricky Rubio and Jonny Flynn before selecting Lawson, so moving the third point guard for a future first had an understandable roster logic. The hindsight result is still decisive. Lawson became a high-level starter for Denver, while Minnesota’s incoming first became only one component of a later trade package. The original A- and D+ grades fit the realized gap without pretending the decision was irrational on draft night.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win — Denver A-, Minnesota D+. Denver exchanged a protected future first for Ty Lawson and received six seasons from a player who became its starting point guard and one of its leading offensive creators. Minnesota’s first conveyed at No. 16 and helped acquire Martell Webster, but that return was shared with another outgoing asset and never approached Lawson’s Denver value. The Nuggets won the completed asset exchange clearly.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Sold the No. 42 Pick on Draft Night
sections.body: The Lakers selected Patrick Beverley with the No. 42 pick in the 2009 draft and immediately sent his draft rights to Miami. In return, Los Angeles received cash and Miami’s 2011 second-round pick. Basketball-Reference and RealGM agree on the basic exchange, and the future pick eventually landed at No. 58.

sections.heading: Miami Never Received Beverley’s Later NBA Career
sections.body: Beverley eventually became a long-term NBA starter, but that later career cannot be credited to the Heat. Miami held his rights, brought him into its program and then waived him on October 25, 2010 before he appeared in an NBA game for the franchise. He later returned to the league with Houston. The trade grade therefore has to stop at Miami’s actual ownership and use of the asset rather than importing value created elsewhere.

sections.heading: The Lakers’ Future Pick Became Ater Majok
sections.body: Miami’s outgoing second-rounder conveyed in 2011 at No. 58, where the Lakers selected Ater Majok. Majok did not establish an NBA career, so the pick produced no meaningful on-court return for Los Angeles. The cash had some transactional value, but the basketball branch of the package never developed into a rotation player.

sections.heading: This Was a Small Heat Win, Not a Beverley Heist
sections.body: The canonical C grade for Miami and D for Los Angeles should be read as a low-end edge. Miami acquired the more interesting player asset and controlled Beverley’s rights for more than a year, but waiving him before his NBA breakthrough sharply limits the realized value. Los Angeles converted the deal into cash and a late second-round pick that became Majok. Neither side harvested Beverley’s later production from this transaction.

sections.heading: Beverley's Later NBA Success Must Be Traced Through Other Clubs
sections.body: Los Angeles moved Patrick Beverley's draft rights shortly after his selection and received cash plus a future second-round asset. That second became the No. 58 choice in 2011, linked to Ater Majok, who did not provide a lasting Lakers rotation return. Beverley eventually became a productive NBA defender and starter, but his later contributions with Houston and other franchises were not Miami Heat playing time from this particular exchange. Miami's return still carried more upside because it controlled the rights to the stronger eventual NBA player; realizing those rights as a direct Heat roster contribution is a different question. The Lakers' low grade recognizes the limited return from cash and a late second, while Miami's better grade should not borrow every season of Beverley's later career. Those distinctions prevent a simple comparison from attributing other teams' accomplishments to the original trade partners.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Heat Win — Miami C, Lakers D. Miami received Patrick Beverley’s draft rights, while Los Angeles received cash and the 2011 No. 58 pick used on Ater Majok. The Heat did not benefit from Beverley’s later NBA career because they waived him before his debut, so this is only a modest win. Still, the Lakers’ basketball return produced even less, leaving Miami with the better side of a transaction where neither franchise realized major NBA value.

sources.title: Patrick Beverley waived by Miami on October 25, 2010

sections.heading: New Orleans Bought an Immediate Rookie Scorer
sections.body: Miami drafted Marcus Thornton with the No. 43 pick in 2009 and traded his rights to New Orleans for two future second-round picks. Thornton paid off immediately for the Hornets. He appeared in 73 games as a rookie, averaged 14.5 points and finished 10th in Sixth Man of the Year voting. For a second-round acquisition, that was useful rotation value from the first season.

sections.heading: Thornton Later Became Part of the Carl Landry Deal
sections.body: The Hornets did not keep Thornton long term, but his value did not simply disappear. In February 2011, New Orleans traded Thornton and cash to Sacramento for Carl Landry. Landry then played 23 regular-season games for the Hornets and appeared in their 2011 playoff series against the Lakers. That downstream conversion strengthens the New Orleans side because the original draft-rights asset produced both scoring and another veteran contributor.

sections.heading: Miami’s Two Picks Had Uneven Direct Value
sections.body: The first incoming second-rounder became Jarvis Varnado at No. 41 in 2010. Varnado eventually appeared in eight regular-season games for Miami in 2012-13, so that branch produced only limited direct on-court value. The second pick eventually became No. 34 Jae Crowder, but Miami had already sent that pick to Cleveland in the 2010 LeBron James sign-and-trade. Crowder later reached Dallas through Cleveland, so his NBA career cannot be credited to the Heat as realized player value from this deal.

sections.heading: The LeBron Package Keeps Miami From Taking a Bigger Loss
sections.body: The 2012 second-round pick still had transactional value for Miami because it was one piece of the package sent to Cleveland in the LeBron James sign-and-trade. It would be misleading to assign the value of James to this one second-rounder, just as it would be misleading to assign Crowder’s career to Miami. New Orleans received the clearer direct basketball return, while Miami converted one branch into a small piece of a much larger franchise-changing transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Pelicans Edge — New Orleans C+, Miami C. The Hornets received Marcus Thornton, got strong rookie scoring from him and later used him with cash to acquire Carl Landry. Miami received two seconds: Jarvis Varnado supplied only eight Heat games, while the future No. 34 pick was moved to Cleveland in the LeBron James sign-and-trade before it became Jae Crowder. Miami extracted real transaction value, but New Orleans realized more directly from the original exchange.

sections.heading: Minnesota Turned Thomas and Two Seconds Into a Rotation Wing
sections.body: Minnesota sent Etan Thomas and two 2010 second-round picks to Oklahoma City for Chucky Atkins and Damien Wilkins. Atkins never played a regular-season game for the Timberwolves; the team waived him on September 22. Wilkins supplied the real direct return. He appeared in 80 games, started 31 and averaged 5.6 points and 3.1 rebounds in 2009-10, giving a 15-win roster a steady veteran wing for one season.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Got Limited Minutes From Etan Thomas
sections.body: Thomas was a useful depth center but not the reason this deal tilts toward the Thunder. He played 23 regular-season games for Oklahoma City, started once and averaged 3.3 points and 2.8 rebounds. He also appeared briefly in the 2010 playoffs. That is a modest direct return, comparable in scale to Minnesota receiving one useful season from Wilkins rather than a franchise-changing piece.

sections.heading: The No. 32 Pick Became a Trade Chip Before It Became Dexter Pittman
sections.body: The more valuable Oklahoma City branch was Minnesota’s own 2010 second-rounder, which landed at No. 32. The Thunder did not simply draft Dexter Pittman and keep him. On June 23, 2010, Oklahoma City traded that pick to Miami and received Daequan Cook plus the No. 18 pick. The Thunder then drafted Eric Bledsoe at No. 18 and traded his rights to the Clippers for a future first. Those later conversions belong to the pick’s traceable asset chain, though the value created after each subsequent move should not be confused with guaranteed value on the original trade date.

sections.heading: The No. 51 Pick Also Produced a Small Follow-On Return
sections.body: The second 2010 pick became No. 51 Magnum Rolle. Oklahoma City drafted Rolle and immediately traded his rights to Indiana for Ryan Reid and cash. Reid eventually appeared in only five NBA games for the Thunder, so this branch was minor. Still, when combined with the No. 32 pick’s conversion path and Thomas’s depth minutes, Oklahoma City extracted more transactional flexibility than Minnesota did from Atkins and one Wilkins season.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Thunder Edge — Oklahoma City B+, Minnesota B. Minnesota received a legitimate one-season contributor in Damien Wilkins, while Chucky Atkins was waived before playing a game for the team. Oklahoma City got 23 games from Etan Thomas and, more importantly, two second-round picks it converted into additional assets. The No. 32 pick helped bring back Daequan Cook and No. 18, while No. 51 was swapped for Ryan Reid and cash. The difference is real but modest, matching the one-grade-step gap.

sections.heading: Denver Used the Deal Primarily to Cut Its Tax Bill
sections.body: Denver sent Steven Hunter, a protected first-round pick and cash to Memphis for a future second-round pick and a $3.796 million trade exception. ESPN reported that the Nuggets were about $6.7 million over the luxury-tax line and that moving Hunter’s roughly $3.7 million salary was expected to save about $7.4 million in salary and tax. Hunter had missed the entire prior season after knee surgery, so Denver was paying a first-round pick to turn an injured reserve salary into immediate financial flexibility.

sections.heading: Memphis Monetized Cap Space Into a First-Round Pick
sections.body: The Grizzlies were using available cap room as an asset. Hunter played only 21 games for Memphis, all off the bench, and averaged 2.5 points and 2.0 rebounds, so his on-court contribution was minimal. The real return was Denver’s protected first, which conveyed in 2010 at No. 25. Memphis selected Dominique Jones and sold his draft rights to Dallas for cash considerations on draft night. Jones’s later Mavericks career therefore should not be credited to Memphis, but the cash generated from selling a first-round slot was a realized return from the original deal.

sections.heading: Denver’s Future Second Had a Real but Shared Downstream Use
sections.body: The second-round pick Denver received was originally top-55 protected and ultimately became the 2016 No. 45 pick, Demetrius Jackson. Denver did not keep the pick until 2016. In December 2011 the Nuggets sent that future second to Dallas in the transaction that brought Rudy Fernandez and Corey Brewer to Denver. The pick was only one component of that later deal, so the full value of Fernandez and Brewer cannot be assigned to this 2009 trade, but the second did survive as usable transaction currency rather than expiring worthless.

sections.heading: Both Teams Accomplished the Job They Were Trying to Do
sections.body: This trade is unusual because the best value on each side was not a long-term player. Denver bought immediate payroll and tax relief while retaining a smaller future asset; Memphis rented cap room in exchange for a first-round pick it later converted to cash. Hunter’s 21 games and the eventual Demetrius Jackson selection were minor compared with those financial and transactional goals. The equal A- grades make sense because each side successfully converted a resource it valued less into something it valued more, without one franchise capturing a clearly dominant basketball return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Denver A-, Memphis A-. Denver paid a protected first and cash to move Steven Hunter’s salary, generating major luxury-tax relief plus a future second-round asset that later remained useful in another transaction. Memphis absorbed Hunter, got only 21 low-minute games from him, but converted the attached first-rounder into the No. 25 pick and then sold Dominique Jones’s rights for cash. Neither side produced a major long-term player from this exchange, but both achieved the specific financial and asset-management goals that drove the deal.

sections.heading: Miami Turned an Unused Center Into a Starting Wing
sections.body: Miami sent Mark Blount to Minnesota for Quentin Richardson on August 13, 2009. Richardson immediately became part of the Heat rotation rather than another temporary salary slot. He played 76 regular-season games, started 75, averaged 8.9 points and 4.9 rebounds, and shot 39.7% from three. On a 47-win team that reached the playoffs, Miami received a full season of useful starting-level minutes from a player acquired for someone who was no longer central to its rotation.

sections.heading: Richardson Also Started Every Miami Playoff Game
sections.body: The return carried into the postseason. Richardson started all five games of Miami’s first-round series against Boston, averaging 9.8 points and 3.8 rebounds while shooting 40.9% from three. The Heat lost the series 4-1, so this was not a deep playoff run, but those minutes still count as realized value from the transaction. Richardson left after the season, making the benefit short-term, yet it was a complete year of regular-season and playoff contribution.

sections.heading: Minnesota Used Blount as a Salary-Cap Asset, Not a Player
sections.body: Minnesota’s side was about financial structure rather than basketball production. Contemporary reporting on the Timberwolves’ March 2010 waiver of Blount described the Richardson-for-Blount trade as a salary-cap move, and Blount did not appear in a game for Minnesota during the season. The Timberwolves carried the contract until March 1, then waived him. That gives Minnesota a legitimate cap-management rationale, but it does not create on-court value that can match Richardson’s 76 games and postseason starts.

sections.heading: The Grade Gap Should Stay Narrow
sections.body: Miami clearly realized more basketball value, but the deal was not a franchise-altering theft. Richardson supplied one productive season and then moved on, while Minnesota intentionally accepted a contract that fit its financial plan. That is why the existing B- for Miami and C+ for Minnesota is more defensible than a dramatic winner-loser split. The Heat got the better immediate player outcome; the Timberwolves got the cap-oriented result they were seeking without receiving any game production from Blount.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Heat Edge — Miami B-, Minnesota C+. Richardson gave Miami 76 games, 75 starts, efficient three-point shooting and starts in all five playoff games. Blount never played for Minnesota and was waived March 1, so the Timberwolves’ return was almost entirely financial. That cap-management purpose keeps Minnesota from receiving a failing grade, but Miami obtained the only meaningful on-court production from the exchange, making the modest one-step grade advantage appropriate.

sections.heading: Minnesota Bought a Pick, Cash and a Short Tucker Look
sections.body: Minnesota sent Jason Hart to Phoenix for Alando Tucker, cash and a 2010 second-round pick. Tucker did not become a lasting piece. He appeared in four games for the Timberwolves, played 25 total minutes and scored eight points before Minnesota waived him in March. His contribution was therefore minimal, but the trade was never dependent on Tucker alone because the Wolves also received cash and a future draft asset.

sections.heading: Phoenix Got No On-Court Return From Jason Hart
sections.body: Hart did not provide Phoenix with game value after the trade. The Suns acquired him on December 29 and waived him, while his 2009-10 NBA appearances came with Minnesota and New Orleans rather than Phoenix. That makes the Suns’ direct player return effectively zero. Phoenix’s rationale was still understandable as a small roster-management transaction, but hindsight does not supply a hidden production benefit on its side.

sections.heading: The Second-Round Pick Became Hamady N’Diaye
sections.body: The pick conveyed at No. 56 in the 2010 draft and Minnesota selected Hamady N’Diaye. The Wolves did not keep N’Diaye’s rights. On draft night they packaged those rights with the No. 23 pick, Trevor Booker, and sent both to Washington for the rights to Lazar Hayward at No. 30 and Nemanja Bjelica at No. 35. Because N’Diaye was bundled with Booker, the later Hayward and Bjelica value cannot be credited entirely to this Phoenix trade. The important point is narrower: the incoming second remained a usable transaction asset.

sections.heading: That Modest Asset Value Is Enough for a Small Minnesota Edge
sections.body: Neither side found a rotation player directly from the transaction. Tucker lasted four Minnesota games, Hart never played for Phoenix, and N’Diaye never suited up for the Timberwolves. Minnesota still received cash plus a second-round asset that retained trade utility, while Phoenix’s return disappeared without game production. That is enough to support Minnesota’s better grade, but the limited scale of every component keeps the result in the modest-win range rather than turning it into a major roster-building success.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wolves Win — Minnesota B, Phoenix C+. Minnesota received four games from Alando Tucker, cash and the 2010 No. 56 pick that became Hamady N’Diaye and later served as one piece of a draft-night trade package. Phoenix acquired Jason Hart but received no regular-season games from him after the deal. The Wolves did not uncover a star or even a durable rotation player, yet they preserved more realized asset value, which supports the narrow grade advantage.

sections.heading: Minnesota Used an Expiring Contract to Take a Darko Flier
sections.body: Minnesota sent Brian Cardinal to New York for Darko Milicic and cash on February 17, 2010. The player exchange was not balanced in realized minutes. Milicic immediately entered the Timberwolves’ rotation, appearing in 24 games and starting 18 over the rest of the season. Cardinal never played for the Knicks; New York waived him two days after the trade. At the transaction level, Minnesota therefore received the only meaningful on-court return plus cash.

sections.heading: The Audition Produced More Than a Two-Month Rental
sections.body: Milicic’s Minnesota audition led to a larger role. He returned for 2010-11, started all 69 games he played and averaged 8.8 points, 5.2 rebounds and 2.0 blocks. Across parts of three seasons with the Timberwolves he played 122 games and started 110. Those later seasons came under a new contract, so they should not be treated as guaranteed value embedded in the February trade. Still, the original deal created the low-cost opportunity for Minnesota to evaluate a player who then became its starting center.

sections.heading: The Follow-Up Contract Also Limits How Much Credit Minnesota Deserves
sections.body: The downstream story was not purely positive. Minnesota agreed to a four-year contract with Milicic in July 2010, then waived him under the amnesty provision in July 2012. That outcome belongs to a separate free-agent decision, not the trade itself, but it matters when judging how successfully the Wolves converted the audition into long-term value. The team found more use than New York did from Cardinal, yet the player did not become a durable solution.

sections.heading: New York’s Return Was Roster Flexibility, Not Player Production
sections.body: The Knicks’ side was primarily cleanup. Milicic had played only eight games for New York and was widely expected to leave the NBA after the season if a new opportunity did not emerge. Cardinal’s expiring contract gave the Knicks no on-court production because they waived him almost immediately. That makes New York’s result defensible as roster management but weaker in hindsight than Minnesota receiving cash, an immediate rotation center and a meaningful evaluation window.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Wolves Edge — Minnesota B+, New York B. Minnesota acquired Darko Milicic and cash for Brian Cardinal, received 24 games and 18 starts immediately, and turned the audition into a longer starting-center run. New York waived Cardinal two days later and received no game production from him. Minnesota’s later four-year Milicic contract ended in amnesty, which keeps the result from looking like a major win, but the original exchange still produced more usable basketball value for the Wolves.

sections.heading: Memphis Paid a Future First for a Starting-Caliber Wing
sections.body: Memphis acquired Ronnie Brewer from Utah at the 2010 trade deadline for a protected future first-round pick. Brewer had started all 53 games he played for the Jazz that season and brought the defensive profile the Grizzlies wanted on the wing. The idea was coherent for a team trying to improve immediately, but the actual Memphis return became extremely small because Brewer appeared in only five games after the trade.

sections.heading: A Hamstring Injury Collapsed Brewer’s Memphis Value
sections.body: Brewer suffered a partially torn right hamstring in his second game after the trade and was ruled out indefinitely. He finished the season with just five Grizzlies appearances, no starts and 80 total minutes. Memphis then lost him in free agency when he signed with Chicago that summer. The injury was bad luck rather than a scouting failure, but completed-value grading still has to reflect that the Grizzlies surrendered a first-round asset for almost no realized on-court production.

sections.heading: Utah Turned the Pick Into Part of the Al Jefferson Package
sections.body: The protected Memphis first ultimately conveyed in 2011 at No. 20, the slot where Donatas Motiejunas was selected. Utah did not use the pick itself. In July 2010 the Jazz included that Memphis first, Kosta Koufos and another future first in the trade that brought Al Jefferson from Minnesota. Because the Memphis pick was only one component of that package, Jefferson’s entire Utah career cannot be credited to this deal, but the pick clearly retained substantial transaction value.

sections.heading: The Asset Chain Creates a Clear Jazz Win
sections.body: This is one of the cleaner completed-value gaps in the queue. Memphis received a useful player in theory but only five games in practice, then lost him without a return. Utah converted Brewer into a protected first and soon used that first as a meaningful piece in a trade for a starting center. The Jazz should receive credit for preserving and redeploying value, while Memphis gets some allowance for the unforeseeable injury but not enough to erase the lopsided realized outcome.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Jazz Win — Utah A-, Memphis D+. Memphis acquired Ronnie Brewer for a protected first, but Brewer played only five games after a hamstring injury and left for Chicago that summer. Utah preserved the first-round asset and used it as one component of the July 2010 Al Jefferson trade. The injury keeps Memphis from an F, but the completed value still favors Utah by a wide margin.

sections.heading: Miami Bought Cap Space, Not a Better Draft Asset
sections.body: Miami sent Daequan Cook and the No. 18 pick to Oklahoma City for No. 32 on June 23, 2010. On a pure asset ledger, moving a rotation guard plus a mid-first for a second-rounder is a steep drop. The Heat were solving a different problem. Contemporary reporting put the cap savings around $3 million to $3.4 million by removing Cook’s 2010-11 salary and the first-round cap hold, giving Pat Riley more room for the free-agent plan that would define the summer.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Got Two Useful Pieces for One Second-Round Pick
sections.body: The Thunder turned No. 32 into Cook plus No. 18. Cook then became a useful shooting specialist on a young contender, appearing in 43 games in 2010-11 and hitting 42.2 percent of his threes. Oklahoma City used No. 18 on Eric Bledsoe, but did not keep him. The next day it sent Bledsoe’s rights to the Clippers for a future protected first, preserving the larger asset rather than cashing it out on a player who never suited up for the Thunder.

sections.heading: The Bledsoe Pick Became Part of the Kendrick Perkins Trade
sections.body: The future Clippers first acquired for Bledsoe later moved to Boston in the February 2011 Kendrick Perkins trade. It ultimately conveyed in 2012 at No. 22, where Fab Melo was selected. That does not mean this Miami trade alone produced Perkins; Oklahoma City also sent Jeff Green and Nenad Krstic in that deal. It does show a traceable asset chain: Miami’s No. 18 became Bledsoe rights, then a future first, then one component of a major win-now trade.

sections.heading: The Isolated Trade Favors OKC Even Though Miami’s Strategy Worked
sections.body: Miami’s wider 2010 plan was spectacularly successful: the organization created enough flexibility to re-sign Dwyane Wade and add LeBron James and Chris Bosh. This transaction belongs inside that cap-clearing sequence, so judging it only by Cook versus Dexter Pittman misses the front office’s intent. Still, the completed trade itself left Oklahoma City with Cook’s useful minutes and a first-round asset it successfully recycled, while Miami paid a real draft premium for flexibility. The canonical A for Oklahoma City and B- for Miami captures that distinction between a strong isolated return and a strategically defensible sacrifice.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Oklahoma City Thunder Win — Oklahoma City A, Miami B-. The Thunder exchanged No. 32 for Daequan Cook and No. 18, got useful shooting from Cook, then converted the Bledsoe draft slot into a future first that later became part of the Kendrick Perkins package. Miami knowingly paid that asset price to clear roughly $3 million-plus in 2010 cap room, and the larger free-agency strategy succeeded spectacularly. That context keeps the Heat grade respectable, but the directly traceable trade value still favors Oklahoma City.

sections.heading: The Clippers Bought Bledsoe Before He Played an NBA Minute
sections.body: Los Angeles acquired the draft rights to Eric Bledsoe from Oklahoma City on June 24, 2010, sending a protected future first-round pick in return. The deal was a straightforward upside bet. Bledsoe had just gone No. 18 in the draft, while the Clippers were pushing a future first into a later season rather than giving up a current rotation player. In hindsight, that swap delivered exactly the kind of surplus value teams hope to find on draft night.

sections.heading: Bledsoe Quickly Became Much More Valuable Than the Pick
sections.body: Bledsoe spent three seasons with the Clippers and developed from a young reserve into one of the league’s more explosive guards. His raw counting numbers were limited by playing behind Chris Paul, but his athleticism, defense and improving creation made him a meaningful rotation piece and then a valuable trade asset. Los Angeles eventually moved Bledsoe in the 2013 three-team deal that brought back J.J. Redick and Jared Dudley, extending the value chain beyond his own minutes in a Clippers uniform.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Preserved Value but the Future First Did Not Match Bledsoe
sections.body: The Thunder did not simply throw Bledsoe away. The protected Clippers first remained a useful asset and became part of the February 2011 package sent to Boston for Kendrick Perkins. The pick eventually conveyed in 2012 at No. 22, where Boston selected Fab Melo. Perkins cannot be credited entirely to this one asset because Oklahoma City also surrendered Jeff Green and Nenad Krstic, but the first clearly had trade value. Even with that credit, its realized contribution fell well short of what Bledsoe became.

sections.heading: The Result Is a Rare Draft-Night Blowout With a Defensible Process
sections.body: Oklahoma City’s logic was reasonable for an organization already collecting future draft capital and juggling a young roster. The mistake only becomes obvious after Bledsoe develops into a high-level starter and the protected first ultimately lands in the twenties. Los Angeles captured the player upside, benefited from three seasons of Bledsoe and later recycled him into another useful package. That combination supports the canonical A+ for the Clippers and D for Oklahoma City without pretending the Thunder received a worthless asset on trade day.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win — Los Angeles A+, Oklahoma City D. Los Angeles turned a protected future first into Eric Bledsoe, received three seasons of useful guard play and later used Bledsoe as a centerpiece in the trade that brought back J.J. Redick and Jared Dudley. Oklahoma City did preserve the incoming first and used it as one component of the Kendrick Perkins deal, but the pick eventually conveyed at No. 22 and never matched Bledsoe’s realized value. The process was defensible; the outcome was not close.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Reacquired a Prospect It Already Knew Well
sections.body: Miami selected Latavious Williams with the 48th pick in the 2010 draft and immediately sent his rights to Oklahoma City for a protected future second-round pick. The Thunder had unusual familiarity with Williams because he had spent the previous season with their Tulsa 66ers affiliate, becoming the first player to go directly from high school to the NBA Development League. Oklahoma City was effectively buying back a developmental prospect it had already evaluated closely rather than making a blind draft-night gamble.

sections.heading: Williams Stayed in the Thunder Pipeline but Never Reached the NBA
sections.body: Williams returned to Tulsa for 2010-11 and improved his production in the Development League, but he never appeared in an NBA regular-season or playoff game. That sharply limits the completed value of Oklahoma City’s side. The process made sense for a young organization using its affiliate aggressively, and the acquisition cost was modest, but the player-rights asset never became an NBA contributor for the Thunder.

sections.heading: Miami’s Pick Conveyed at No. 54 and Became Part of the LeBron Package
sections.body: The second-round pick Miami received was protected in the top 40 in 2011 and 2012 before becoming unprotected in 2013. It conveyed immediately in 2011 at No. 54, where Milan Macvan was selected. Miami did not make that selection itself: the Heat had sent the pick to Cleveland in the July 2010 sign-and-trade for LeBron James. That gives the incoming pick traceable transaction value, but it was only one small component of a much larger package, so the full value of acquiring James cannot reasonably be credited to this deal.

sections.heading: The Original Exchange Still Lands Near Even
sections.body: Neither original asset produced meaningful NBA player value on its own. Williams never played an NBA game, while Macvan was drafted 54th and also never logged NBA regular-season minutes. Miami did obtain a real second-round asset and redeployed it quickly in a franchise-changing transaction, while Oklahoma City acquired a prospect it valued for developmental reasons. The downstream context gives Miami a slight narrative edge, but not enough to override the canonical C+/C+ result when the isolated realized assets are weighed.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Miami C+, Oklahoma City C+. Oklahoma City acquired Latavious Williams, a familiar Tulsa 66ers prospect, but he never appeared in an NBA regular-season or playoff game. Miami received the protected second that conveyed in 2011 at No. 54 and was sent to Cleveland as one minor component of the LeBron James sign-and-trade. The pick had usable transaction value, but neither original asset became a meaningful NBA contributor, leaving the completed exchange close enough to retain the even verdict.

sections.heading: Minnesota Turned Booker and N’Diaye Into Two Different Development Bets
sections.body: On draft night in 2010, Minnesota sent the rights to Trevor Booker and Hamady N’Diaye to Washington for the rights to Lazar Hayward and Nemanja Bjelica. The exchange was not a simple one-player swap. Booker was the most NBA-ready piece, while Bjelica was a longer-term international rights play. Hayward gave Minnesota an immediate roster option and Bjelica gave the front office an asset it could leave overseas until the timing made sense.

sections.heading: Booker Gives Washington the Strongest Single-Player Case
sections.body: Washington received the best immediate contributor in Trevor Booker. He spent four seasons with the Wizards, appearing in 235 games with 105 starts and averaging 6.4 points and 5.1 rebounds over that span. Hamady N’Diaye added only 19 games for Washington across two seasons, so nearly all of the Wizards’ realized value came from Booker. That is substantial enough that this trade cannot be described as a clear Minnesota win.

sections.heading: Bjelica’s Delayed Arrival Is What Keeps Minnesota Ahead in the Canonical Grade
sections.body: Hayward played 42 games for Minnesota as a rookie and later returned for four more, producing limited rotation value. Bjelica was the more durable asset. Minnesota held his rights while he developed in Europe, then signed him in 2015 after he had become EuroLeague MVP. He played 192 regular-season games for the Timberwolves across three seasons, including 21 starts in 2017-18. The five-year wait therefore produced a real NBA rotation player rather than an abandoned draft-rights asset.

sections.heading: The Margin Is Small Because Both Teams Found Useful Value
sections.body: The completed record is unusually balanced for a four-rights draft-night swap. Washington got four solid seasons from Booker, easily the strongest early return. Minnesota received some Hayward minutes and eventually three seasons from Bjelica after patiently carrying his rights. N’Diaye contributed little to Washington. That mix supports only a narrow distinction: Minnesota’s two realized assets and Bjelica’s delayed payoff justify the canonical B+ versus B split, while Booker’s larger immediate role keeps Washington close enough that stronger winner language would overstate the evidence.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Wolves Edge — Minnesota B+, Washington B. Trevor Booker gave Washington the strongest immediate return, playing 235 games and making 105 starts over four Wizards seasons, while Hamady N’Diaye added little. Minnesota got limited early value from Lazar Hayward but eventually brought Nemanja Bjelica over after he became EuroLeague MVP; Bjelica then played 192 games across three Timberwolves seasons. The two-sided production makes this a narrow result, not a blowout, with Minnesota’s second useful asset providing the small edge reflected in the canonical grades.

sections.heading: Bosh Was the Frontcourt Piece That Completed Miami’s 2010 Plan
sections.body: Miami acquired Chris Bosh from Toronto in a sign-and-trade on July 10, 2010, the same summer the Heat retained Dwyane Wade and added LeBron James. This transaction stands on its own from the James deal. Bosh arrived as a five-time All-Star who had just averaged 24.0 points and 10.8 rebounds for Toronto, then accepted a smaller offensive role so the new core could function. The payoff was immediate: Miami reached the NBA Finals in each of Bosh’s first four seasons and won championships in 2012 and 2013.

sections.heading: Bosh’s Value Went Well Beyond a Third Scoring Option
sections.body: The box-score decline from his Toronto peak understates why the fit worked. Bosh became a more mobile defensive anchor, defended pick-and-roll actions higher on the floor and gradually expanded his shooting range. He made the All-Star team in each of his first six Miami seasons and played a central role in the smaller lineups that helped define the Heat’s championship style. Health problems ended his playing career earlier than expected, but by then Miami had already received the elite-level years that justified building the roster around him.

sections.heading: Toronto Recovered Real Assets, Especially the Valanciunas Pick
sections.body: Toronto did not lose Bosh for nothing. The Raptors received their own future first-round pick back from Miami, another 2011 first-round asset and a $14.5 million trade exception. The returned Toronto pick became No. 5 in 2011 and was used on Jonas Valanciunas, who developed into a long-term starting center. The other first was later moved to Chicago for James Johnson before the draft; the slot eventually landed at No. 28. The trade exception also gave Toronto additional transaction flexibility even though it could not replace Bosh’s star production by itself.

sections.heading: The Return Was Respectable, but Miami Bought Championship-Level Value
sections.body: The historical gap comes from what Miami received relative to what Toronto could recover in a departure-driven sign-and-trade. Valanciunas became a productive starter and the Raptors did extract useful value from an outgoing star who had chosen Miami. That deserves acknowledgment even with the canonical D grade. But Bosh became a foundational piece of four straight Finals teams, two champions and one of the defining roster constructions of the era. The Heat were not merely acquiring talent; they were acquiring the exact two-way frontcourt fit that allowed the rest of the Big Three structure to work.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Heat Win — Miami A+, Toronto D. Toronto recovered meaningful value, most notably the first-round pick that became Jonas Valanciunas, another first-round asset and a $14.5 million trade exception. That keeps this from being a zero-return story. Miami still received the overwhelming prize: Chris Bosh became a six-time All-Star with the Heat, reached four consecutive Finals and helped win the 2012 and 2013 championships while adapting his game to the roster’s needs. The return was useful; Bosh’s championship value was franchise-defining.

sections.heading: Miami Turned Beasley Into Flexibility at the Exact Moment It Needed It
sections.body: Miami sent Michael Beasley to Minnesota on July 12, 2010 for cash and two future second-round picks. The timing is the center of the deal. The Heat had just completed the LeBron James and Chris Bosh sign-and-trades while retaining Dwyane Wade, and moving Beasley removed a former No. 2 pick whose salary and role no longer fit the new roster construction. ESPN reported at the time that Minnesota could absorb Beasley into cap space, giving Miami additional financial flexibility as it filled out the team around its new stars.

sections.heading: Minnesota Got Real Scoring, but Only for a Short Window
sections.body: Beasley gave the Timberwolves immediate production. He started all 73 games he played in 2010-11 and averaged 19.2 points and 5.6 rebounds, finishing behind only Kevin Love on the team in scoring. His second Minnesota season was less productive: 47 games, seven starts and 11.5 points per game. The Wolves therefore received two seasons of useful offense from a 21-year-old scorer, but the acquisition never developed into a long-term core piece.

sections.heading: The Two Seconds Became Part of the Norris Cole Deal
sections.body: Miami also extracted downstream value from the draft capital. The 2011 second conveyed at No. 31 and was used on Bojan Bogdanovic. Miami then sent Bogdanovic’s rights, the future 2014 second and cash to Minnesota for the rights to Norris Cole, according to the Heat’s own media guide. Cole became a rotation guard on the 2012 and 2013 championship teams. The second pick later landed at No. 44 and became Markel Brown after Minnesota had reacquired it in that Cole transaction.

sections.heading: The Heat’s Edge Comes From Timing Plus Asset Reuse
sections.body: Minnesota did not lose the transaction outright on immediate basketball value; Beasley supplied a high-scoring first season for a team that needed offense. The problem is that the useful window was short, while Miami accomplished two objectives with the same move: it opened more flexibility during the Big Three build and preserved future draft value that helped bring in Cole. Norris Cole’s later championship role cannot be credited entirely to this trade because Miami added other consideration, but the chain still supports the canonical B+ versus C split.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Heat Win — Miami B+, Minnesota C. Michael Beasley gave Minnesota legitimate short-term scoring, including 19.2 points per game in his first Timberwolves season, but he lasted only two years there and never became a lasting cornerstone. Miami cleared flexibility during the 2010 roster overhaul and received two second-round assets; those picks later became part of the package that brought Norris Cole to the Heat. Because the return combined immediate roster utility with useful downstream draft value, Miami holds the stronger completed outcome without turning this into a one-sided disaster for Minnesota.
