sections.heading: Miami Turned a Protected Pick Into Shooting
sections.body: Miami acquired Luke Babbitt from New Orleans on July 10, 2016, sending back the Pelicans' own 2018 second-round pick plus cash. The Heat had acquired that pick only months earlier in the Jarnell Stokes salary trade. Babbitt filled a clear roster need as a floor-spacing forward: he entered the deal as a career 40.3 percent three-point shooter and had hit 40.3 percent from deep for New Orleans in 2015-16.

sections.heading: Babbitt Gave the Heat One Useful Season
sections.body: Babbitt became a regular starter for Miami. He played 68 games, started 55 and averaged 4.8 points in 15.7 minutes while making 41.4 percent of his three-point attempts. That was useful low-cost spacing for a team that recovered from an 11-30 start to finish 41-41, although the Heat still missed the playoffs. Babbitt left for Atlanta in free agency after the season, so Miami's direct return was one year of rotation shooting rather than a lasting asset.

sections.heading: New Orleans Recovered Its Own Second-Rounder
sections.body: The Pelicans received cash and regained the 2018 second-round pick they had sent to Miami in the Stokes trade. That pick later became No. 51 in the 2018 draft, where New Orleans selected Penn State guard Tony Carr. Carr never produced NBA regular-season value for the Pelicans, which caps the upside of the return, but the transaction restored draft optionality and cash for a player who was entering the final year of his contract.

sections.heading: The Grade Gap Is Intentionally Small
sections.body: Miami got the better immediate basketball production because Babbitt played a real role and shot efficiently from three. New Orleans, however, turned an expiring reserve into cash plus a future pick that eventually conveyed, preserving value after Babbitt was no longer central to its plans. The canonical B for the Pelicans and B- for Miami therefore describes a narrow hindsight edge rather than a decisive win: one side recovered an asset, while the other received a useful but temporary contributor.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Pelicans Edge — New Orleans B, Miami B-. Babbitt gave the Heat 68 games, 55 starts and 41.4 percent three-point shooting during the 2016-17 season, but he left after one year and Miami missed the playoffs. New Orleans received cash and recovered its own 2018 second-round pick, which eventually became No. 51 and Tony Carr. Carr did not become an NBA contributor, keeping this close, but the Pelicans preserved a draft asset while moving an expiring player. The completed value supports only a slight edge.

sections.heading: The Clippers Traded a Former First-Rounder for a Future Pick
sections.body: Los Angeles sent C.J. Wilcox and cash to Orlando on July 15, 2016, for Devyn Marble and a 2020 second-round pick. Wilcox had been the No. 28 pick in 2014 but had appeared in only 44 games over two Clippers seasons. Los Angeles waived Marble the same day, making the future second the real target. The trade also created a $1.2 million trade exception for the Clippers.

sections.heading: Orlando Got Almost No NBA Production From Wilcox
sections.body: The Magic were taking a low-cost look at a shooter who had made 39.1 percent of his threes for the Clippers in 2015-16 and had produced in the D-League. It did not turn into a rotation piece. Wilcox appeared in 22 games for Orlando, averaged 1.0 point in 4.9 minutes and shot 20.0 percent from three. Orlando declined his 2017-18 option and waived him in April 2017, ending the experiment after one season.

sections.heading: The Second-Round Pick Became Useful Trade Currency
sections.body: The pick was more valuable than its eventual No. 32 slot suggests because Los Angeles used it before the 2020 draft. In 2018, the Clippers sent the rights to Miles Bridges plus two future second-round picks to Charlotte for the rights to Shai Gilgeous-Alexander. The 2020 second acquired from Orlando was one of those two picks. It later became Vernon Carey Jr. for Charlotte, but the Clippers had already converted its value into part of the package that moved them from No. 12 to No. 11.

sections.heading: A Minor Deal Produced a Real Downstream Asset
sections.body: Marble never played for Los Angeles, and Wilcox provided only 22 games for Orlando, so the player swap itself was negligible. The difference is the pick. Los Angeles turned a player outside its rotation into a future second that later helped facilitate the Gilgeous-Alexander draft-night move. Orlando received cash and a prospect audition, but neither created durable basketball value. The canonical B for the Clippers and C+ for the Magic appropriately keeps the win modest while recognizing the pick's later utility.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win — LA Clippers B, Orlando C+. The Clippers waived Devyn Marble immediately, but the 2020 second-round pick they received became useful currency in the 2018 trade that brought Shai Gilgeous-Alexander's draft rights to Los Angeles. Orlando got only 22 games from C.J. Wilcox before waiving him, plus cash considerations. The pick ultimately became No. 32 and Vernon Carey Jr. after reaching Charlotte, but its direct value to the Clippers had already been realized in the Gilgeous-Alexander move.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Found a Real Long-Term Starter
sections.body: Oklahoma City acquired Jerami Grant from Philadelphia on November 1, 2016, for Ersan Ilyasova and a protected future first-round pick. Grant was 22 and already had 144 NBA games behind him, but his offensive role was still developing. With the Thunder he grew from a reserve into a full-time starter. By 2018-19 he played 80 games, started 77 and averaged 13.6 points, 5.2 rebounds and 1.3 blocks while shooting 39.2 percent from three.

sections.heading: Grant Also Returned Another First-Round Pick
sections.body: The Thunder did not lose Grant for nothing. In July 2019 they traded him to Denver for a top-10-protected 2020 first-round pick after his career-best season. That pick ultimately landed at No. 25, where Immanuel Quickley was selected before the rights moved through another draft-night transaction. For Oklahoma City, the Grant acquisition therefore produced nearly three seasons of useful forward play and a first-round asset on the way out, supporting a strong B+ even in a losing trade.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Got Immediate Production and the Better Pick Outcome
sections.body: Ilyasova gave Philadelphia 53 games and 40 starts in 2016-17, averaging 14.8 points before the 76ers moved him to Atlanta at the deadline for Tiago Splitter and additional second-round considerations. The larger payoff took four years. Oklahoma City's protected first conveyed in 2020 at No. 21, and Philadelphia selected Tyrese Maxey. Maxey developed into an All-Star guard, turning what began as a patient draft asset into the most valuable individual outcome tied to the original deal.

sections.heading: Both Teams Executed Well, but Maxey Breaks the Tie
sections.body: This is not a case where Oklahoma City made a bad decision. Grant developed exactly the way the Thunder hoped, helped playoff teams and later brought back another first. Philadelphia simply converted its side into more total value: useful Ilyasova production, a later trade return from Ilyasova and, most importantly, the pick that became Maxey. The canonical A for Philadelphia and B+ for Oklahoma City capture that distinction. The 76ers win the hindsight comparison without turning the Thunder's process into a failure.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win — Philadelphia A, Oklahoma City B+. Jerami Grant became a starting-caliber two-way forward for the Thunder and later returned a 2020 first-round pick in the Denver trade. Philadelphia received 53 games from Ersan Ilyasova, later moved him again for additional value, and held the protected Oklahoma City first until it conveyed at No. 21 in 2020. That selection became Tyrese Maxey, whose All-Star development creates the decisive hindsight edge. Oklahoma City still earned a strong return; Philadelphia simply produced the best asset.

sections.heading: Memphis Bought Dillon Brooks With a Future Second
sections.body: Houston selected Dillon Brooks with the No. 45 pick in the 2017 NBA Draft, then traded his draft rights to Memphis for a future second-round pick. The Grizzlies were buying a four-year Oregon wing who had just been named Pac-12 Player of the Year, and the price was modest. Brooks immediately made the roster and started 74 games as a rookie, turning a draft-night rights purchase into an everyday player instead of a developmental lottery ticket.

sections.heading: Brooks Became a Six-Season Memphis Starter
sections.body: Brooks stayed with the Grizzlies through the 2022-23 season and became one of their most-used perimeter defenders. He appeared in 345 regular-season games for Memphis across six seasons, started the large majority of them and averaged double figures in scoring in five straight seasons after his rookie year. His final Memphis season ended with All-Defensive Second Team honors. The relationship eventually ran its course, but the original trade had already produced years of starting minutes and playoff defense.

sections.heading: Houston's Pick Became De'Anthony Melton
sections.body: The future second conveyed in 2018 at No. 46, where Houston selected De'Anthony Melton. Melton became a productive NBA guard, but none of that production came for the Rockets. Before his rookie season, Houston packaged Melton with Ryan Anderson in a trade to Phoenix for Marquese Chriss and Brandon Knight. The pick therefore had legitimate transaction value, yet the Rockets never received the long-term on-court benefit that Melton later provided elsewhere.

sections.heading: The Gap Comes From Retained Player Value
sections.body: Both sides turned a second-round asset into something useful, but Memphis captured far more of the basketball value. Brooks became a six-year rotation fixture and defensive starter for a playoff team. Houston used Melton before he played a regular-season game for the franchise, and the return from the Phoenix deal did not approach Brooks' Memphis tenure. The canonical A for the Grizzlies and D for the Rockets reflects the durability gap rather than the simple fact that both original assets became NBA players.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Grizzlies Win — Memphis A, Houston D. Memphis acquired Dillon Brooks' draft rights for a future second and received six seasons, 345 regular-season games and an All-Defensive Second Team selection from him. Houston's pick became De'Anthony Melton at No. 46 in 2018, but the Rockets traded Melton to Phoenix before he played a regular-season game for them. Houston did recover trade value through that package, yet Memphis received the far stronger direct basketball return from the original exchange.

sections.heading: The Lakers Turned No. 28 Into Two Prospects
sections.body: Utah acquired the draft rights to Tony Bradley, the No. 28 pick in the 2017 NBA Draft, from the Lakers for the rights to Josh Hart at No. 30 and Thomas Bryant at No. 42. Los Angeles effectively moved back two spots while adding an extra second-round prospect. Hart became an immediate rotation guard and wing, while Bryant gave the Lakers another inexpensive developmental big without requiring a future pick or veteran player.

sections.heading: Hart Produced and Then Helped Bring Anthony Davis
sections.body: Hart played 130 regular-season games over two Lakers seasons before his value became part of a much larger transaction. In July 2019, Los Angeles sent Hart, Brandon Ingram, Lonzo Ball, the draft rights to De'Andre Hunter and additional draft capital to New Orleans for Anthony Davis. Hart was not the centerpiece of that package, but the Lakers converted the No. 30 rights acquired here into two years of useful minutes and a real component of the trade for a franchise-changing star.

sections.heading: Bryant Added Upside Even Though Los Angeles Let Him Go
sections.body: Bryant played only 15 NBA games for the Lakers as a rookie and was waived in June 2018, so Los Angeles did not capture his later breakout with Washington. His inclusion still strengthened the original draft-night return because he became a productive NBA center after leaving. The Lakers cannot be credited with Washington's production, but landing both Hart and Bryant for Bradley's rights shows how much prospect value they created by moving down only two spots.

sections.heading: Utah Received a Reserve Center and Little Else
sections.body: Bradley spent three seasons with the Jazz and appeared in 70 games, starting three, while averaging 4.4 points and 4.2 rebounds in 10.4 minutes. Utah traded him to Detroit in 2020 with the rights to Saben Lee for cash considerations. Bradley was a usable reserve, but his Jazz tenure never approached Hart's direct Lakers value, much less Hart's inclusion in the Davis package. The canonical A- for Los Angeles and F for Utah reflects an unusually wide gap for a small draft-night move.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win — LA Lakers A-, Utah F. Los Angeles moved from No. 28 to No. 30, added the No. 42 rights and came away with Josh Hart and Thomas Bryant. Hart gave the Lakers 130 regular-season games before becoming part of the 2019 Anthony Davis trade. Bryant later proved he belonged in an NBA rotation, even though most of that value came after Los Angeles waived him. Utah received 70 games from Tony Bradley and eventually moved him for cash. The realized-value gap clearly favors the Lakers.

sections.heading: Memphis Bought Ivan Rabb at No. 35
sections.body: Memphis acquired the draft rights to Ivan Rabb, the No. 35 pick in the 2017 NBA Draft, from Orlando for a future second-round pick. Rabb was a 20-year-old California forward who had averaged 14.0 points and 10.5 rebounds as a college sophomore. The Grizzlies were buying a young frontcourt prospect at a familiar second-round price, and he did reach the NBA rotation during both seasons he spent with the franchise.

sections.heading: Rabb's Memphis Run Never Grew Past Reserve Value
sections.body: Rabb played 85 regular-season games for Memphis across 2017-18 and 2018-19, starting 18. He averaged 5.7 points and 4.3 rebounds in 14.6 minutes while shooting 55.5 percent from the field. Those numbers gave the Grizzlies some real return from the No. 35 rights, but he never established himself as a long-term starter and his NBA career ended after those two Memphis seasons. The acquisition produced usable depth rather than a durable core piece.

sections.heading: Orlando's Pick Became Talen Horton-Tucker
sections.body: The future second conveyed in 2019 at No. 46, where Orlando selected Talen Horton-Tucker. The Magic did not keep him. On draft night they traded his rights to the Lakers for a 2020 second-round pick and cash considerations, reported at $2.2 million. Horton-Tucker later became a rotation player in Los Angeles, but Orlando's realized value from the original Memphis asset was the cash plus another future second, not Horton-Tucker's later NBA production.

sections.heading: The Magic Preserved More Asset Value
sections.body: Memphis received two seasons of reserve minutes from Rabb, while Orlando turned the outgoing No. 35 rights into a future second and then converted that pick again for cash plus another second. Neither path produced a franchise-changing player for the team that held the asset, which keeps the trade in modest territory. The canonical B for Orlando and C for Memphis reflects the Magic's better asset preservation against Rabb's limited two-year NBA run rather than crediting Orlando with Horton-Tucker's Lakers career.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Magic Win — Orlando B, Memphis C. Ivan Rabb gave Memphis 85 games, 18 starts and two seasons of reserve frontcourt production after the Grizzlies acquired his No. 35 draft rights. Orlando's future second became the No. 46 pick in 2019 and Talen Horton-Tucker, whose rights the Magic immediately moved to the Lakers for a 2020 second-round pick and cash. Orlando did not capture Horton-Tucker's later player value, but it preserved and re-used the draft asset more effectively than Memphis converted Rabb into lasting value.

sections.heading: Minnesota Turned Rubio Into a First-Round Pick
sections.body: Minnesota sent Ricky Rubio to Utah on June 30, 2017 for a protected 2018 first-round pick that originally belonged to Oklahoma City. The Timberwolves had already moved toward a different backcourt plan under Tom Thibodeau, and the trade converted a six-year starter into a future asset rather than losing the value of that roster decision. The pick ultimately conveyed at No. 20 in the 2018 NBA Draft.

sections.heading: Utah Got Two Playoff Seasons From Rubio
sections.body: Rubio became Utah's starting point guard immediately. He started all 77 games he played in 2017-18, averaging 13.1 points and 5.3 assists as the Jazz won 48 games and beat Oklahoma City in the first round. He followed with 68 games and 67 starts in 2018-19 for a 50-win team. Utah therefore received real competitive value from the trade, even though Rubio left for Phoenix after two seasons and did not become a long-term Jazz piece.

sections.heading: The Pick Became Josh Okogie
sections.body: Minnesota used the conveyed No. 20 selection on Josh Okogie. He played four seasons for the Timberwolves, appearing in 244 regular-season games with 123 starts. Okogie's best offensive season in Minnesota was only 8.6 points per game, but his defense and energy kept him in the rotation while the club transitioned from the Jimmy Butler era toward the Anthony Edwards timeline. The asset produced a longer run of team-controlled rotation value than Rubio's two seasons in Utah.

sections.heading: The Hindsight Edge Goes to Minnesota
sections.body: Utah's side should not be treated as empty value: Rubio started on consecutive playoff teams and helped the Jazz win a postseason series. The difference is duration and asset conversion. Minnesota traded a veteran it was prepared to replace, received a first-rounder, and turned that pick into four NBA seasons from Okogie. The canonical B for Minnesota and C for Utah reflects that longer asset life while still recognizing that the Jazz received useful immediate production.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wolves Win — Minnesota B, Utah C. Ricky Rubio gave the Jazz two seasons as their starting point guard, including 77 starts for a 48-win team that reached the 2018 Western Conference semifinals and 67 more starts for a 50-win club in 2018-19. Minnesota's protected first-round return conveyed at No. 20 in 2018 and became Josh Okogie, who played 244 games and made 123 starts across four Timberwolves seasons. Utah received meaningful short-term playoff value, but Minnesota converted a veteran it was replacing into a younger asset with a longer run of team-controlled contribution.

sections.heading: Phoenix Acquired Two Useful Assets for a Conditional Second
sections.body: Phoenix acquired Troy Daniels and a 2018 second-round pick from Memphis on September 22, 2017 for a conditional Suns second-rounder. The outgoing Phoenix pick ultimately did not convey, so the realized cost was minimal. Daniels arrived as a proven shooter after hitting 38.9 percent from three for Memphis the previous season, and the additional second-round asset gave Phoenix another piece it could move before the draft.

sections.heading: Daniels Supplied Two Seasons of Shooting
sections.body: Daniels played 79 games for Phoenix in 2017-18, starting 15 and averaging 8.9 points while shooting 40.0 percent from three. He returned for 51 games in 2018-19 and remained a 38.1 percent three-point shooter. Across the two seasons he gave the Suns 130 regular-season games and 16 starts, which is meaningful rotation production for a trade that required no ultimately conveyed draft pick from Phoenix.

sections.heading: The Memphis Pick Was Reused for Elfrid Payton
sections.body: Phoenix did not simply hold the incoming 2018 second until draft night. At the 2018 trade deadline, the Suns sent that asset to Orlando for Elfrid Payton. The pick later became No. 41 and was used in the Jarred Vanderbilt draft chain, but Phoenix's attributable value was Payton, not Vanderbilt's later NBA career. Payton started all 19 games he played for the Suns, averaging 11.8 points, 6.2 assists and 5.3 rebounds before leaving after the season.

sections.heading: Memphis Received No Comparable Realized Return
sections.body: Memphis moved a useful shooter plus a second-round asset and received a heavily protected Phoenix second that never conveyed. Daniels was not a cornerstone and Payton was only a short-term Suns rental, so the deal should not be inflated into a franchise-changing win. Still, Phoenix extracted two seasons of shooting and then converted the incoming pick into a starting point guard audition. The canonical A- for Phoenix and C for Memphis reflects that clear imbalance in realized value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Suns Win — Phoenix A-, Memphis C. Troy Daniels gave Phoenix 130 games across two seasons, including a 40.0 percent three-point season in 2017-18, while the second-round pick acquired with him became the asset used to trade for Elfrid Payton. Payton then started 19 games for the Suns and averaged 11.8 points and 6.2 assists. Memphis received a conditional Phoenix second-round pick that did not convey. Phoenix therefore collected useful player production and a reusable draft asset without surrendering realized draft value.

sections.heading: Cleveland Rebuilt Its Rotation at the Deadline
sections.body: Cleveland acquired Jordan Clarkson and Larry Nance Jr. from the Lakers on February 8, 2018 for Isaiah Thomas, Channing Frye and its protected 2018 first-round pick. The Cavaliers were trying to repair a contender around LeBron James after a turbulent first half, and both incoming players immediately entered the rotation. Cleveland still reached the NBA Finals, giving the trade an instant competitive payoff even before the longer-term value became clear.

sections.heading: Clarkson and Nance Produced Hundreds of Cavaliers Games
sections.body: Clarkson played 129 regular-season games for Cleveland before a December 2019 trade to Utah, while Nance appeared in 182 games over four Cavaliers seasons. Nance started 76 of those games and developed into a versatile frontcourt piece. Clarkson was later moved for Dante Exum plus two second-round picks, and Nance eventually became Cleveland's outgoing centerpiece in the 2021 three-team deal that brought Lauri Markkanen. The original Lakers return therefore kept producing usable value after both players left.

sections.heading: The Lakers Prioritized Expiring Money and a First-Rounder
sections.body: Los Angeles received short-term players and future flexibility. Thomas played 17 games for the Lakers and Frye played nine before both became free agents. The first-round pick conveyed at No. 25 in 2018 and became Moritz Wagner, who played 43 games as a Lakers rookie. Wagner was then included in the 2019 multi-team transaction that sent Anthony Davis to Los Angeles. The Lakers' strategic return was real, but its direct on-court production was modest.

sections.heading: The Completed Value Favors Cleveland
sections.body: The Lakers created cap flexibility and obtained a first-round pick, so the trade served a broader roster plan even though Thomas, Frye and Wagner were short-lived pieces. Cleveland received two younger rotation players, got immediate help for a Finals run and later converted both into additional assets. The canonical A- for Cleveland and C+ for Los Angeles reflects the difference between durable basketball value on the Cavaliers side and a Lakers package whose strongest benefit was financial and transactional flexibility.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win — Cleveland A-, LA Lakers C+. Jordan Clarkson and Larry Nance Jr. gave Cleveland 311 combined regular-season games after the 2018 deadline, helped the Cavaliers reach that season's NBA Finals and later became outgoing assets in additional trades. Los Angeles received 17 games from Isaiah Thomas, nine from Channing Frye and the No. 25 pick used on Moritz Wagner, who played 43 games for the Lakers before being moved in the 2019 Anthony Davis transaction structure. The Lakers gained useful flexibility, but Cleveland captured more direct and durable value.

sections.heading: Denver Exited the Mudiay Experiment With Two Assets
sections.body: Denver moved Emmanuel Mudiay to New York in the February 8, 2018 three-team deal and received Devin Harris from Dallas plus a 2018 second-round pick from the Knicks. Harris gave the Nuggets a veteran guard for the stretch run, appearing in 27 games. More importantly for the long view, the incoming second conveyed at No. 43, giving Denver another draft asset after moving on from a former No. 7 pick who had fallen out of the starting lineup.

sections.heading: The No. 43 Pick Became a Trade-Up Tool
sections.body: Denver used that No. 43 selection on Justin Jackson, then immediately packaged his draft rights with a future second-round pick to Orlando for the No. 41 rights to Jarred Vanderbilt. Vanderbilt did not become a major contributor in Denver, but the sequence preserved value beyond Harris's short stint. The Nuggets effectively turned Mudiay and a different second-round pick into a veteran rotation guard plus the draft capital needed to move up for a prospect they preferred.

sections.heading: Dallas Got Elite Shooting and Another Draft Asset
sections.body: Dallas sent Harris to Denver and received Doug McDermott from New York plus Denver's 2018 second-rounder. McDermott played 26 games for the Mavericks and shot 49.4 percent from three before leaving for Indiana in free agency. The second became No. 54 and Shake Milton, whose rights Dallas traded to Philadelphia for the rights to Ray Spalding and Kostas Antetokounmpo. Dallas extracted useful short-term shooting and kept the pick moving, supporting the canonical B even without a lasting core player.

sections.heading: New York Got the Longest Immediate Player Run
sections.body: The Knicks sent McDermott and the second-round pick that conveyed at No. 43, receiving Mudiay in return. He played 22 games after the trade, then 59 games with 42 starts in 2018-19 while averaging 14.8 points and 3.9 assists. That was real rotation value, but Mudiay left after the season and the Knicks gave up both a productive shooter and a usable draft asset to take the chance. The canonical B- captures a respectable return without matching Denver's asset recovery.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win — Denver A, Dallas B, New York B-. Denver turned Emmanuel Mudiay and a second-round pick into 27 games of Devin Harris plus the No. 43 pick, which became the trade-up piece used to acquire Jarred Vanderbilt at No. 41. Dallas received 26 games of Doug McDermott shooting 49.4 percent from three and the No. 54 pick later exchanged for Ray Spalding and Kostas Antetokounmpo. New York got 81 games from Mudiay over two seasons, including 42 starts in 2018-19. All three teams realized value, but Denver recovered the strongest mix of immediate help and reusable draft capital.

sections.heading: Denver Moved Up Two Spots for Vanderbilt
sections.body: Denver used the 2018 draft to target Jarred Vanderbilt, acquiring his rights at No. 41 from Orlando for the rights to No. 43 pick Justin Jackson and one future second-round pick. The cost was modest, but it was still a real premium to move only two spots. Vanderbilt was a developmental swing for a Nuggets team that could afford patience, and Denver signed him to a multi-year contract less than three weeks later.

sections.heading: Vanderbilt Barely Played but Kept Trade Value
sections.body: Vanderbilt appeared in 17 games as a rookie and nine more for Denver in 2019-20, logging only 110 total regular-season minutes for the Nuggets. His direct production therefore does not explain the A- grade. The more important result came in February 2020, when Denver included Vanderbilt with Malik Beasley and Juancho Hernangomez in the four-team trade that sent the Nuggets Houston's 2020 first-round pick along with several veteran pieces. Vanderbilt remained a live asset despite never earning a large Denver role.

sections.heading: Orlando's Return Was Real but Quickly Rerouted
sections.body: Orlando received Jackson's draft rights plus the conditional 2019 second-rounder. Jackson never became an NBA player for the Magic, while the future second ultimately landed at No. 36 and was used on Cody Martin. Orlando should not receive credit for Martin's later Hornets career, however, because the Magic had already sent that pick to Charlotte in the July 2018 three-team deal involving Bismack Biyombo, Timofey Mozgov and Jerian Grant. The asset was useful transaction currency, not a player-development win for Orlando.

sections.heading: The Better Asset Ended Up With Denver
sections.body: Neither side received a star directly from this draft-night swap. Orlando converted its extra second into part of a separate roster transaction, while Jackson produced no NBA value for the Magic. Denver got only 26 regular-season appearances from Vanderbilt, but he retained enough value to be included in a later deal that returned a first-round pick to the Nuggets. That longer asset life is the strongest case for the canonical A- for Denver and C+ for Orlando.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win — Denver A-, Orlando C+. Denver paid the rights to No. 43 pick Justin Jackson plus one future second-round pick to move up for Jarred Vanderbilt at No. 41. Vanderbilt played only 26 regular-season games for the Nuggets, but he remained part of the February 2020 package that brought Denver Houston's 2020 first-round pick. Orlando's future second ultimately became No. 36 Cody Martin, yet the Magic had already rerouted that pick to Charlotte in a July 2018 trade, and Jackson never became an NBA contributor for Orlando. Denver's acquired asset retained more realized value.

sections.heading: Memphis Bought a Starting Wing for a Crowded Roster
sections.body: Memphis acquired Garrett Temple from Sacramento on July 17, 2018 for Ben McLemore, Deyonta Davis, a 2021 second-round pick and cash considerations. The Grizzlies were coming off a 60-loss season and also needed to reduce a crowded guaranteed-contract count. Temple immediately became a starter, appearing in 49 games with 49 starts while averaging 9.4 points and shooting 35.2 percent from three before Memphis moved him at the 2019 deadline.

sections.heading: Temple Still Had Value at the Next Deadline
sections.body: Temple's Memphis stay lasted only seven months, but he was not a dead-end asset. The Grizzlies packaged him with JaMychal Green in February 2019 and received Avery Bradley from the Clippers. Bradley then played 14 games for Memphis and averaged 16.1 points. That later transaction cannot be credited entirely to Temple because Green was also part of the package, but it shows that Memphis received both immediate starting minutes and some retained trade utility.

sections.heading: Sacramento's Player Return Was Mostly Short-Lived
sections.body: Ben McLemore returned to the franchise that drafted him and played 19 games in 2018-19, averaging 3.9 points in 8.3 minutes. Deyonta Davis never appeared in a regular-season game for Sacramento; the Kings waived him on September 22, 2018. Those two players alone would not have given Sacramento the better hindsight result. The stronger part of the return was the future second-round pick, plus the financial value of the cash included in the deal.

sections.heading: The Second-Round Pick Became Sacramento's Best Asset
sections.body: The Memphis second eventually landed at No. 46 in the 2021 draft, but Sacramento had already traded it to Toronto at the 2021 deadline for Terence Davis. Davis played 27 games for the Kings immediately after that trade and averaged 11.1 points, then returned for two more seasons. He appeared in 121 regular-season games for Sacramento from 2020-21 through 2022-23. That conversion gives the Kings a longer attributable value chain than McLemore or Deyonta Davis alone, which supports the narrow B+ to B edge.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Partner Edge — Memphis B, Sacramento B+. Garrett Temple started all 49 games he played for Memphis, averaged 9.4 points and later remained part of the package used to acquire Avery Bradley. Sacramento received only 19 games from Ben McLemore and waived Deyonta Davis before the season, but the 2021 second-round pick became the trade asset used to acquire Terence Davis from Toronto. Davis then played 121 games across three Kings seasons. Memphis received useful immediate value, while Sacramento's draft asset produced the longer realized return.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Was Trading Salary Flexibility More Than Basketball Value
sections.body: Oklahoma City sent Dakari Johnson and cash to Orlando on July 20, 2018 for Rodney Purvis. Johnson had appeared in 31 games for the Thunder as a rookie, averaging 1.8 points in 5.2 minutes, while Purvis had averaged 6.0 points across 16 games for the Magic. The roster value was modest on both sides. The more important distinction was contract structure: Purvis carried a fully non-guaranteed deal, giving Oklahoma City a more flexible asset than Johnson's guaranteed salary.

sections.heading: Purvis Became Abdel Nader Three Days Later
sections.body: The Thunder did not keep Purvis. On July 23 they sent him to Boston for Abdel Nader and cash considerations. Nader then became a real reserve piece, playing 61 regular-season games for Oklahoma City in 2018-19 and 55 more in 2019-20. That downstream value belongs in the original trade's ledger because Purvis was the asset Oklahoma City received from Orlando and immediately converted. It prevents the Thunder side from being graded as a pure salary dump with no basketball return.

sections.heading: Orlando Also Recycled Johnson Within Three Days
sections.body: Orlando moved Johnson just as quickly. The Magic packaged him with the draft rights to Tyler Harvey and sent both to Memphis for Jarell Martin and cash considerations on July 23. Martin played 42 regular-season games for Orlando in 2018-19, averaging 2.7 points and 1.7 rebounds, and appeared in three playoff games. Because Harvey's rights were also part of that second trade, Martin cannot be credited entirely to Johnson, but Johnson clearly remained a live transaction asset instead of ending as a dead contract.

sections.heading: The Cash and Cap Value Give Orlando the Modest Edge
sections.body: Both franchises turned the players from this trade into something else almost immediately. Oklahoma City used Purvis's contract flexibility and then converted him into Nader, who supplied two seasons of reserve minutes. Orlando received cash up front, then used Johnson as part of the package that brought back Martin and another cash payment. The Magic did not land a long-term starter, but they extracted financial value and a modest piece of the later Martin return without giving up a player who stayed in Oklahoma City.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Magic Win — Oklahoma City C+, Orlando B. The Thunder accomplished the practical goal of moving Dakari Johnson's guaranteed salary into Rodney Purvis's non-guaranteed contract and then turned Purvis into Abdel Nader, who played 116 regular-season games over two Oklahoma City seasons. Orlando received cash in the original deal and three days later used Johnson, along with Tyler Harvey's draft rights, to acquire Jarell Martin and more cash. Martin's 42 regular-season games cannot be assigned entirely to Johnson because Harvey was part of the package, but the Magic still created the slightly stronger total return from a low-level transaction.

sections.heading: Dallas Bought a Second Star Before Luka's Rise Was Complete
sections.body: Dallas acquired Kristaps Porzingis, Tim Hardaway Jr., Courtney Lee and Trey Burke on January 31, 2019 for Dennis Smith Jr., DeAndre Jordan, Wesley Matthews and two first-round picks. Porzingis was still rehabbing the torn ACL that had ended his 2017-18 season, so the Mavericks were paying for a 23-year-old All-Star projection rather than immediate production. The gamble produced 134 regular-season games from Porzingis across three Dallas seasons, including 20.1 points per game in 2020-21.

sections.heading: Hardaway Made the Dallas Package Deeper Than Porzingis Alone
sections.body: Tim Hardaway Jr. became the other durable piece of the return. He settled into a high-volume perimeter role, averaged 16.6 points in 70 games in 2020-21 and stayed with Dallas through the franchise's 2024 Finals season. Porzingis never developed into the long-term co-star Dallas envisioned, but he was later traded to Washington for Spencer Dinwiddie and Davis Bertans. That conversion, plus Hardaway's multi-year contribution, gave the Mavericks several seasons of usable value from the package.

sections.heading: New York's Veteran Return Was Mostly About Expirings and Flexibility
sections.body: The Knicks received Dennis Smith Jr., DeAndre Jordan and Wesley Matthews alongside the two firsts. Smith was the young-player swing, while Jordan and Matthews supplied expiring salary. The trade also removed the longer Hardaway and Lee contracts as New York prepared for 2019 free agency. The cap-space strategy did not itself guarantee a star signing, so the hindsight grade cannot credit unrelated later roster success. The stronger traceable case for New York rests on the draft capital.

sections.heading: Both First-Round Picks Conveyed, but Neither Became a Franchise Anchor
sections.body: The unprotected 2021 Dallas first landed at No. 21, the Keon Johnson slot. New York traded that selection to the Clippers and received No. 25 Quentin Grimes plus a future second-round pick. The second Dallas first stayed protected in 2023 and finally conveyed at No. 24 in 2024, the Kyshawn George slot; the Knicks again traded the pick on draft night. Two first-round assets gave New York legitimate flexibility, but the return never produced a player comparable to the upside Dallas was chasing with Porzingis.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Mavericks Edge — Dallas B, New York B-. Dallas accepted injury risk and two first-round-pick costs to acquire Kristaps Porzingis, then received 134 regular-season games from him before converting him into Spencer Dinwiddie and Davis Bertans. Tim Hardaway Jr. added several productive seasons and remained on the 2024 Finals roster. New York created major cap flexibility and received two firsts that ultimately landed at No. 21 in 2021 and No. 24 in 2024, but Dennis Smith Jr. did not become a cornerstone and the pick value did not produce a comparable centerpiece. The gap is modest, which fits the canonical grades.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Paid a Contender's Price for an Immediate Upgrade
sections.body: Philadelphia acquired Tobias Harris, Boban Marjanovic and Mike Scott on February 6, 2019 while pushing a Joel Embiid, Ben Simmons and Jimmy Butler roster toward the playoffs. Harris arrived averaging 20.9 points and shooting 43.4 percent from three for the Clippers. The cost was Landry Shamet, Wilson Chandler, Mike Muscala, Philadelphia's protected 2020 first, Miami's unprotected 2021 first and Detroit second-round picks in 2021 and 2023. It was a major asset commitment for a player headed toward unrestricted free agency.

sections.heading: Harris Gave the Sixers Real Production, Just Not Enough Return on the Price
sections.body: The Philadelphia side was not empty. Harris re-signed in 2019 and stayed through 2023-24, including 72 games at 19.6 points per game in 2019-20 and 62 games at 19.5 in 2020-21. He became a durable starter across multiple playoff teams. The problem is the acquisition grade must account for what Philadelphia surrendered to get that stability. The Sixers did not merely exchange expiring contracts for a starter; they moved a young shooter and four draft assets before making the long-term commitment.

sections.heading: The Miami First Became Part of the Paul George Supertrade
sections.body: Los Angeles converted the draft package into strategic leverage almost immediately. The unprotected 2021 Miami first acquired in the Harris deal was included in the July 2019 package for Paul George, alongside Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, Danilo Gallinari and other first-rounders and swaps. That George transaction was tied to the Clippers' superstar pivot that summer. A pick received for an expiring Harris therefore became one of the direct pieces in the franchise's biggest roster move months later.

sections.heading: Shamet and the Other First Added More Usable Value
sections.body: Landry Shamet also stepped directly into the Clippers' rotation, shooting 45.0 percent from three over his final 25 games of the 2018-19 regular season and later starting 30 games in 2019-20. Los Angeles eventually moved Shamet in the 2020 three-team deal that brought Luke Kennard and additional assets. Philadelphia's protected first ultimately conveyed at No. 19 in 2020, the Saddiq Bey slot. Even without treating every later transaction as guaranteed, the original return gave Los Angeles multiple independent ways to create value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win — Los Angeles A-, Philadelphia F. Tobias Harris was productive and durable for Philadelphia, so the grade is not a claim that the Sixers received no basketball value. The problem was the scale of the price: Landry Shamet, two first-round picks and two second-round picks went out for a win-now addition approaching free agency. Los Angeles received immediate rotation value from Shamet, saw the protected first convey at No. 19, and used the unprotected 2021 Miami first as a direct piece of the Paul George blockbuster. That asset flexibility gives the Clippers the decisive hindsight win.

sections.heading: Miami Was Solving a Payroll Problem, Not Chasing Ryan Anderson
sections.body: Miami sent Tyler Johnson and Wayne Ellington to Phoenix for Ryan Anderson at the 2019 deadline. Anderson had fallen out of the Suns' rotation, so the Heat's incentive was financial. His 2019-20 salary carried only a $15.6 million guarantee if waived by the July deadline, while Johnson was owed roughly $19.3 million the next season. Contemporary reporting also credited the move with cutting about $5.1 million from Miami's 2018-19 payroll and reducing its projected luxury-tax bill from about $9.7 million to $1.8 million.

sections.heading: Anderson Barely Played, but the Contract Structure Was the Return
sections.body: Ryan Anderson appeared in only 10 games for Miami and scored seven total points, so there is no case for a B+ grade based on court production. The useful asset was the altered guarantee and the flexibility it created. Miami later waived Anderson in July 2019. This trade therefore has to be judged differently from a normal player-for-player swap: the Heat accepted almost no basketball production because lowering near-term payroll obligations was the actual objective.

sections.heading: Phoenix Got More Minutes From Tyler Johnson
sections.body: Tyler Johnson immediately became a regular for Phoenix, starting 12 of 13 games after the trade and averaging 11.1 points, 4.0 rebounds and 4.2 assists. He returned for 31 games in 2019-20, though his role shrank to 16.6 minutes and 5.7 points per game before his Suns tenure ended. That is clearly more on-court value than Miami received from Anderson. It is why Phoenix's B grade remains defensible even though the contract cost limited the upside.

sections.heading: Ellington Was a Pass-Through Piece for the Suns
sections.body: Phoenix waived Wayne Ellington one day after completing the deal, allowing the veteran shooter to enter the buyout market. The Suns therefore did not receive a second rotation player from Miami; their basketball return rested almost entirely on Johnson, plus the cash recorded in the transaction ledger. Johnson gave them useful guard minutes for parts of two seasons, but his backloaded contract was also the obligation Miami was trying to escape. The different objectives keep the final gap small.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Heat Edge — Miami B+, Phoenix B. Phoenix received the better player production: Tyler Johnson started 12 of 13 games immediately after the trade and remained on the roster into 2019-20, while Ryan Anderson scored only seven points in 10 games for Miami. The Heat still achieved the more important goal attached to its side of the deal by reducing 2018-19 payroll and luxury-tax exposure and swapping Johnson's 2019-20 salary for Anderson's lower guaranteed amount. Wayne Ellington was waived immediately by Phoenix. The result is a narrow Miami edge driven by contract mechanics rather than basketball output.

sections.heading: Denver Bought a High-Upside Draft Swing for a Small Asset Package
sections.body: Miami selected Bol Bol at No. 44 in the 2019 draft and immediately sent his rights to Denver. The Heat's own announcement says the return was a 2022 second-round pick and cash considerations; the transaction ledger specifies $1.2 million and the less favorable of Philadelphia's and Denver's 2022 seconds. Bol had fallen well beyond the first-round range once projected for him, making the deal a low-cost upside bet for a Nuggets team that entered draft night without a selection.

sections.heading: Bol Never Became a Denver Rotation Fixture
sections.body: The upside did not fully arrive in Denver. Bol appeared in 53 regular-season games across three seasons for the Nuggets and averaged 2.7 points overall. His largest Denver sample was 32 games in 2020-21, but he averaged only five minutes that season. A January 2022 deal that would have sent him to Detroit was rescinded after he did not receive medical clearance. The modest production is why Denver's canonical B grade should not be inflated into a runaway draft steal.

sections.heading: Miami's Draft Asset Was Eventually Forfeited
sections.body: Miami did receive real value on trade night: $1.2 million in cash plus the future second-round asset. The problem is that the pick never became a drafted player for the Heat. NBA draft-order records show the Philadelphia-via-Denver second that had been routed to Miami was forfeited in 2022. The league had penalized Miami by taking its next available second-round selection after finding improper timing in free-agency discussions involving Kyle Lowry. That left the cash as the only realized piece of the original return.

sections.heading: Bol Still Retained Enough Value to Be Moved Again
sections.body: Denver ultimately included Bol Bol with PJ Dozier and a protected 2028 second-round pick in the January 2022 three-team transaction that brought Bryn Forbes from San Antonio. Bol cannot be credited with the full Forbes return because Dozier and another pick were also part of Denver's package, but his inclusion shows that the rights acquired from Miami remained a transaction asset after three seasons of limited minutes. Denver therefore got NBA appearances plus some residual trade utility from a cost that ended with no player selected by Miami.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win — Denver B, Miami C. Bol Bol never developed into a regular Denver contributor, appearing in 53 games and averaging 2.7 points, so this was not a hidden superstar acquisition. Denver nevertheless turned a future second and cash into three seasons of control over a high-upside prospect who later remained part of another trade package. Miami received $1.2 million and a 2022 second-round asset, but that pick was ultimately forfeited as the franchise's league penalty for premature Kyle Lowry free-agency discussions. The realized value therefore favors Denver without overstating what Bol became for the Nuggets.

sections.heading: Golden State Paid Two Future Seconds to Secure Its Own G League Prospect
sections.body: New Orleans selected Alen Smailagic at No. 39 in the 2019 draft and immediately sent his rights to Golden State for 2021 and 2023 second-round picks plus cash. The Warriors knew Smailagic unusually well because he had already spent the previous season with Santa Cruz in the G League, averaging 9.1 points in 47 games. That familiarity explains the move up, but it also meant Golden State paid multiple future assets for a player it had already evaluated closely.

sections.heading: Smailagic Never Justified the Price in the NBA
sections.body: Smailagic played only 29 regular-season games over two Warriors seasons, averaging 3.0 points and 1.5 rebounds in 7.7 minutes. He appeared in 14 games as a rookie and 15 in 2020-21, starting once, before Golden State waived him in August 2021. The developmental bet therefore produced almost no rotation value. A D grade fits because the Warriors spent two second-rounders and cash to acquire a prospect who never became a dependable NBA contributor.

sections.heading: New Orleans Quickly Turned Both Picks Into Derrick Favors
sections.body: The Pelicans did not wait to see where the two selections would land. On July 7, 2019, New Orleans sent the 2021 and 2023 second-round picks it had received from Golden State to Utah for Derrick Favors. Favors then started 49 of 51 games for the Pelicans in 2019-20, averaging 9.0 points and 9.8 rebounds while shooting 61.7 percent. That direct conversion gives the original Smailagic return a concrete basketball outcome instead of merely treating future picks as abstract value.

sections.heading: The Pick Chain Still Shows How Much Optionality New Orleans Received
sections.body: The Warriors' 2021 second ultimately became the No. 47 slot, used on David Johnson, while the 2023 second became No. 49, used on Emoni Bates. New Orleans no longer owned either selection because both had gone to Utah in the Favors trade, and the picks moved again afterward. Those later players should not be credited directly to the Pelicans. What does belong in the grade is the fact that New Orleans turned the exact two assets acquired for Smailagic into a starting center for a full season.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans Win — Golden State D, New Orleans B+. The Warriors targeted Alen Smailagic deliberately and paid two future second-round picks plus cash to move up for him, but he produced only 29 NBA games and 87 total points before being waived. New Orleans converted both incoming picks weeks later into Derrick Favors, who started 49 games and averaged 9.0 points and 9.8 rebounds during his Pelicans season. The later No. 47 and No. 49 draft outcomes belong to subsequent pick holders, not New Orleans, but the Favors conversion is enough to make the value gap clear.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Bought the No. 46 Pick
sections.body: The Lakers acquired the draft rights to Talen Horton-Tucker, the No. 46 pick in the 2019 NBA Draft, from Orlando for a 2020 second-round pick and $2.2 million in cash considerations. Horton-Tucker was only 18 and had played one college season at Iowa State, so Los Angeles was paying for developmental upside rather than an immediate rotation solution. The cost was still meaningful for a second-round move because the Lakers surrendered both a future pick and cash to secure him.

sections.heading: Horton-Tucker Became a Real Lakers Rotation Piece
sections.body: Horton-Tucker did give Los Angeles useful NBA value. He appeared in 131 regular-season games over three Lakers seasons, started 34 of them and averaged 9.3 points, 2.8 rebounds and 2.6 assists in 22.1 minutes. He was also on the 2020 championship roster, even though his rookie role was limited. In August 2022, the Lakers packaged Horton-Tucker with Stanley Johnson to Utah for Patrick Beverley, so the original draft-rights investment eventually carried trade value beyond Horton-Tucker's own minutes.

sections.heading: Orlando Turned the Future Pick Into James Ennis
sections.body: The Magic did not wait for the 2020 second-rounder to convey. In February 2020, Orlando sent the Lakers' pick to Philadelphia for James Ennis. Ennis immediately started 18 of 20 regular-season games for the Magic, who reached the 2020 playoffs, then returned in 2020-21 and started 37 of his 41 appearances while shooting 43.3 percent from three. The pick eventually landed at No. 58, where Philadelphia selected Paul Reed, but Orlando had already converted it into a veteran wing who filled a current need.

sections.heading: The Cash and Pick Conversion Tilt the Grade
sections.body: Los Angeles found a legitimate NBA player at No. 46, so this was not a failed scouting bet. The difference is how efficiently Orlando used what came back. The Magic received $2.2 million in cash and turned the future second into a starting wing before the pick was ever made. Horton-Tucker's Lakers tenure was useful but stopped short of becoming a core piece, and his eventual trade return came in a package with another player. The canonical C+ for Los Angeles and B for Orlando reflects Orlando extracting two forms of value from a single draft-night sale.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Magic Win — LA Lakers C+, Orlando B. Los Angeles paid a future second-round pick and $2.2 million for Talen Horton-Tucker's draft rights and received 131 regular-season games, a place on the 2020 championship roster and later trade value from him. Orlando turned the incoming pick into James Ennis before it conveyed, getting 61 regular-season games and 55 starts from Ennis across two seasons while also retaining the cash from the original deal. Both sides found useful value, but Orlando's conversion of a late future second plus the cash consideration gives the Magic the better overall return.

sections.heading: Indiana Guaranteed the Brogdon Deal
sections.body: Indiana acquired Malcolm Brogdon in a July 2019 sign-and-trade after Milwaukee signed him to the new contract. The Pacers sent a future first-round pick and two future second-round picks rather than risk an offer-sheet process on the restricted free agent. The club's own account explained the logic: waiting could have tied up cap space while Milwaukee decided whether to match, with other free agents disappearing in the meantime. Indiana paid real draft capital, but it secured the 26-year-old guard immediately and built its backcourt plan around him.

sections.heading: Brogdon Produced, Then Indiana Recycled the Asset
sections.body: Brogdon started all 146 regular-season games he played for Indiana across three seasons. His scoring rose from 16.5 points per game in 2019-20 to 21.2 in 2020-21, and he remained a 19.1-point scorer in his final Pacers season. Availability kept the tenure from becoming an A-level outcome by itself, but the exit preserved value. In July 2022, Indiana sent Brogdon to Boston for Aaron Nesmith, Daniel Theis, three additional players and a 2023 first-round pick, extending the original 2019 investment into the next roster cycle.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Turned the Compensation Into Useful Flexibility
sections.body: The Bucks did far better than simply losing a restricted free agent. Indiana's 2020 first conveyed at No. 24, the R.J. Hampton slot, and that draft asset was routed through the four-team Jrue Holiday transaction that brought Holiday to Milwaukee. One Brogdon-derived second-rounder also went to Orlando in the draft-night deal that moved Milwaukee to No. 45 for Jordan Nwora. The three-pick return therefore supplied assets the Bucks could reuse around a championship-caliber roster, which is why the canonical B+ grade is stronger than a consolation-prize evaluation.

sections.heading: Both Teams Extracted More Than One Layer of Value
sections.body: The deal worked because the teams were solving different problems. Indiana wanted Brogdon badly enough to remove restricted-free-agency uncertainty and got three seasons of starting guard production before trading him for another package. Milwaukee chose not to match the contract but converted his departure into a first, two seconds and a trade exception; the first later became part of the Holiday transaction. Brogdon was the best immediate asset and Indiana kept value alive after moving him, but Milwaukee's return had genuine downstream use. The gap is narrow rather than punitive.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Pacers Edge — Indiana A-, Milwaukee B+. The Pacers paid a first-round pick and two second-round picks to secure Malcolm Brogdon, then received 146 starts across three seasons before moving him to Boston for a package headlined by Aaron Nesmith and a 2023 first-round pick. Milwaukee did not lose Brogdon for nothing: the No. 24 pick from Indiana became part of the asset flow in the Jrue Holiday deal, and another incoming second helped Milwaukee acquire the No. 45 slot used on Jordan Nwora. Indiana gets the higher grade for landing the best player and preserving later trade value, while Milwaukee's asset conversion keeps the result close.

sections.heading: Memphis Paid to Move From No. 23 to No. 21
sections.body: The 2019 draft-night exchange was a two-slot move with a future pick attached. Oklahoma City sent the rights to Brandon Clarke, selected No. 21, to Memphis for the rights to Darius Bazley, selected No. 23, plus the Grizzlies' 2024 second-round pick. Memphis was targeting the older Gonzaga forward after taking Ja Morant at No. 2, while the Thunder moved back and added another future asset. The price was more than a simple pick swap, but both teams got the prospect they preferred.

sections.heading: Clarke Delivered Seven Seasons of Memphis Value
sections.body: Clarke immediately justified Memphis' aggression. He averaged 12.1 points on 61.8 percent shooting as a rookie and earned All-Rookie recognition, then remained a productive frontcourt piece across seven NBA seasons with the franchise. His Memphis career covered 309 regular-season games, with career averages of 10.2 points and 5.5 rebounds while shooting 60.5 percent from the field. Injuries interrupted parts of the run, but the No. 21 rights produced durable rotation value well beyond the typical return from a late first-round move-up.

sections.heading: Bazley and the Extra Pick Both Produced for Oklahoma City
sections.body: Oklahoma City did not miss on its side of the exchange. Bazley played 221 regular-season games for the Thunder and started 118, including 55 starts in 2020-21 and 53 in 2021-22. In February 2023, Oklahoma City later traded him to Phoenix for Dario Saric, a 2029 second-round pick and cash. The additional 2024 second also had utility before it ever conveyed: the Thunder used that future pick in the 2020 draft-night deal that brought in the rights to Vit Krejci and Admiral Schofield.

sections.heading: The Same Trade Produced Two Successful Development Paths
sections.body: Memphis got the more efficient NBA player, and Clarke's long run makes the move-up easy to defend. Oklahoma City, however, received four seasons of meaningful Bazley minutes, a later trade return for him and an extra second-round asset that the front office recycled into another prospect package. The underlying 2024 pick eventually became the No. 37 slot, but the Thunder had already extracted value by moving it years earlier. With useful production and downstream assets on both sides, the canonical A- grades fit better than forcing a winner.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Memphis A-, Oklahoma City A-. Memphis moved from the rights to Darius Bazley at No. 23 plus a 2024 second-round pick to Brandon Clarke at No. 21, then received 309 regular-season games and seven seasons of efficient frontcourt production from Clarke. Oklahoma City got 221 games and 118 starts from Bazley, later moved him for Dario Saric, a 2029 second and cash, and used the extra 2024 second as part of the deal for Vit Krejci and Admiral Schofield. Memphis landed the better individual player, but Oklahoma City's two-asset return produced enough real value to make the completed trade an even A- result.

sections.heading: Minnesota Paid No. 11 and Šarić to Get Culver
sections.body: Minnesota's draft-night move was straightforward once the moratorium ended: Phoenix sent the rights to Jarrett Culver, the No. 6 pick, for Dario Šarić and the rights to Cameron Johnson at No. 11. Culver had just led Texas Tech to the national championship game and arrived with a plausible two-way wing case, so moving up five spots was defensible as a prospect bet. The problem is the price became two useful NBA assets, while Culver never developed into the high-end starter Minnesota was chasing.

sections.heading: Culver Was Gone After 97 Games
sections.body: Culver's Timberwolves tenure lasted only two seasons. He appeared in 97 games with 42 starts, averaging 7.8 points, 3.3 rebounds and 1.4 assists before Minnesota traded him with Juancho Hernangómez to Memphis in August 2021 for Patrick Beverley. Minnesota did recover a useful veteran in the later deal, but Culver himself had already fallen well short of the value expected from the No. 6 pick. That short runway is the central reason the original move-up earns the canonical D.

sections.heading: Phoenix Got a Shooter and an Immediate Rotation Forward
sections.body: The Suns turned the No. 6 slot into two contributors. Šarić played 153 regular-season games for Phoenix across three active seasons, starting 67, and was part of the 2021 team that reached the NBA Finals before an ACL injury cost him the entire 2021-22 season. Johnson played 200 regular-season games for Phoenix, shot 39.0 percent from three as a rookie and reached 42.5 percent in 2021-22, when he finished third in Sixth Man of the Year voting. The combined on-court return already dwarfed Culver's Minnesota production.

sections.heading: Johnson Eventually Became Part of the Kevin Durant Price
sections.body: Johnson's value did not end with his Suns minutes. In February 2023, Phoenix included him with Mikal Bridges, four first-round picks and a future swap in the package that brought Kevin Durant and T.J. Warren from Brooklyn. The Durant trade had many larger components, so Johnson should not be credited with the entire acquisition, but his inclusion shows the level of asset value he retained after three-plus seasons in Phoenix. Minnesota's No. 6 selection never approached that combination of production, team success and later trade utility.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Suns Win — Minnesota D, Phoenix A. Minnesota surrendered Dario Šarić and Cameron Johnson's draft rights at No. 11 to move up for Jarrett Culver at No. 6. Culver lasted 97 games and two seasons with the Timberwolves before being moved in the Patrick Beverley trade. Phoenix received 153 regular-season games from Šarić and 200 from Johnson, with both contributing to the 2021 Finals-era roster; Johnson later became part of the blockbuster Kevin Durant package. The original gamble on Culver was understandable, but the completed value on the Phoenix side is overwhelmingly stronger.

sections.heading: Chicago Bought a Starting Guard With Second-Round Capital
sections.body: Chicago acquired Tomas Satoransky in a 2019 sign-and-trade after Washington re-signed the restricted free agent. The Wizards received the more favorable of Chicago's or Memphis' 2020 second-round picks, a 2022 second-round swap right and the removal of protection on a 2023 Chicago second that Washington was already owed. For the Bulls, the appeal was immediate: Satoransky had started 54 games for Washington in 2018-19 and gave a young roster a veteran ball-handler without surrendering a first-round pick.

sections.heading: Satoransky Gave Chicago Two Useful Seasons
sections.body: Satoransky played 123 regular-season games for Chicago and started 82. He averaged 9.9 points and 5.4 assists while starting 64 of 65 games in 2019-20, then moved into a smaller role the next season while still averaging 4.7 assists. In August 2021, the Bulls included him with Garrett Temple, a 2024 second-round pick and cash in the sign-and-trade that brought Lonzo Ball from New Orleans. Satoransky therefore supplied real rotation value and later became part of another roster-building transaction, supporting Chicago's canonical B+.

sections.heading: Washington Turned the Departure Into Multiple Draft Assets
sections.body: Washington's return was unusually layered for a departing guard. The 2020 second conveyed at No. 37, and the Wizards traded that slot to Oklahoma City for No. 53 Cassius Winston and a future second-round pick. The 2022 swap mechanism produced the No. 33 position before that asset traveled through later transactions and was ultimately used by Toronto on Christian Koloko. The separate 2023 Chicago second became more valuable because its protection was removed in this deal, preserving another usable asset for Washington.

sections.heading: The 2023 Pick Kept Reappearing in Bigger Transactions
sections.body: The unprotected Chicago second later became the No. 42 pick in 2023, used on Tristan Vukcevic. Washington had sent that pick to the Lakers in the 2021 Russell Westbrook transaction, then reacquired it in the 2023 Rui Hachimura deal before the draft. The later trades had many other moving parts, so this original sign-and-trade cannot claim the full value of those deals. It can claim that Washington turned Satoransky's exit into durable draft flexibility while Chicago received two useful seasons from the player it wanted.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wizards Win — Chicago B+, Washington A. Chicago received 123 games and 82 starts from Tomas Satoransky, then used him as one piece of the 2021 Lonzo Ball sign-and-trade. Washington converted Satoransky's departure into a 2020 second that became No. 37, a 2022 swap mechanism tied to the No. 33 slot and removal of protection on the 2023 Chicago second that eventually became No. 42 Tristan Vukcevic. The Bulls got worthwhile on-court value, but the Wizards extracted multiple recyclable draft assets from a player who was leaving, giving Washington the stronger completed return.

sections.heading: Golden State Paid a First to Clear Iguodala
sections.body: Golden State traded Andre Iguodala and a protected future first-round pick to Memphis for Julian Washburn in July 2019, creating a traded-player exception. The move was tied to the Warriors' D'Angelo Russell sign-and-trade and the hard-cap pressure that followed it. In other words, Golden State was buying financial flexibility more than basketball return. Washburn was waived on July 17 and never played a regular-season game for the Warriors, leaving the cap mechanics as the only meaningful benefit from this transaction itself.

sections.heading: Memphis Never Needed Iguodala to Play
sections.body: Iguodala did not appear in a game for Memphis, but the Grizzlies still converted his contract into another transaction. At the February 2020 deadline, Memphis sent Iguodala, Jae Crowder and Solomon Hill to Miami in the three-team deal that brought Justise Winslow and Dion Waiters from the Heat and Gorgui Dieng from Minnesota. Because Crowder and Hill were also outgoing assets, the full incoming package cannot be credited to Iguodala alone. It still shows that Memphis preserved transactional value rather than buying him out for nothing.

sections.heading: The Warriors Pick Became a Major Memphis Trade Chip
sections.body: The protected first-rounder ultimately conveyed in 2024 at No. 14. Memphis did not keep the pick until draft night. In June 2023, the Grizzlies sent that Golden State first, along with the No. 25 pick and Tyus Jones in the three-team Kristaps Porzingis transaction that brought Marcus Smart to Memphis. Boston received the Warriors pick, which later became the No. 14 slot. Portland selected Bub Carrington there before sending his rights to Washington, so Carrington's NBA career is not Memphis value; the important Memphis value is the pick's use in acquiring Smart.

sections.heading: The Context Saves Golden State From an F
sections.body: The completed return is lopsided, but Golden State's objective was unusual. NBA.com's later Warriors timeline explicitly describes the Iguodala move as a salary dump required by the cap consequences of the Russell sign-and-trade. That context explains why the Warriors willingly attached a distant first to a franchise icon instead of seeking equal player value. It does not erase the cost. Memphis received a veteran contract it could later package, $2 million in cash and a future first that became a central asset in the Smart trade, while Golden State's incoming player was waived within ten days.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Grizzlies Win — Golden State D+, Memphis A. The Warriors attached a protected first-round pick and $2 million to Andre Iguodala in a salary-clearing move that brought back Julian Washburn, who was waived ten days later. Memphis never got on-court minutes from Iguodala, but it later included him in the Miami deal that returned multiple players, and the Warriors first became the No. 14 pick in 2024 after Memphis used it in the 2023 trade for Marcus Smart. Golden State's cap objective was real and helps explain the decision, but Memphis extracted far more traceable asset value from the transaction.

sections.heading: Memphis Took the Upside Package
sections.body: Memphis acquired Josh Jackson, De'Anthony Melton and two future second-round picks from Phoenix for Jevon Carter and Kyle Korver in July 2019. Jackson was the former No. 4 pick, but Melton became the important piece. He was only 21 and had already shown defensive playmaking as a Suns rookie. The Grizzlies also added a 2020 second that would land at No. 40, while the other second was protected 36-60 in 2021 and never conveyed. Memphis gave up a useful young guard and a veteran shooter it had acquired one day earlier.

sections.heading: Melton Became the Center of the Win
sections.body: Melton played 185 regular-season games for Memphis across three seasons, growing from a reserve defender into a 10.8-point scorer in 2021-22 while finishing eighth in Sixth Man of the Year voting. The Grizzlies then preserved his value in June 2022, sending him to Philadelphia for Danny Green and the draft rights to No. 23 pick David Roddy. Jackson contributed only 22 games for Memphis, so the A grade does not depend on rehabilitating the former lottery pick. It is driven mainly by Melton's production and the later asset return.

sections.heading: The No. 40 Pick Helped Memphis Move Up for Tillman
sections.body: The 2020 second-round pick also became useful before a player ever suited up for Memphis. The pick landed at No. 40, where Robert Woodard II was selected, but Memphis traded his draft rights and a future second to Sacramento for the rights to Xavier Tillman Sr. at No. 35. Tillman became a rotation big for the Grizzlies, appearing in 59 games as a rookie and later starting 29 times in 2022-23. The original Phoenix pick was not the entire price for Tillman, but it was one of the two assets Memphis used to move up five spots.

sections.heading: Phoenix Still Got Real Carter Value
sections.body: Phoenix's return was not empty. Carter played 118 regular-season games for the Suns over two seasons and shot 42.5 percent from three in 2019-20. He also appeared during the franchise's 2021 Finals season before Phoenix sent Carter and the rights to No. 29 pick Day'Ron Sharpe to Brooklyn for Landry Shamet. Korver was waived and later signed with Milwaukee, so he did not add Suns on-court value. Carter's useful bench run and later trade role justify the canonical C+ rather than a failing grade, but they do not match what Memphis generated from Melton and the 2020 second.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Grizzlies Win — Memphis A, Phoenix C+. Memphis received 185 regular-season games from De'Anthony Melton before trading him for Danny Green and No. 23 pick David Roddy, while the incoming 2020 second became part of the move from No. 40 to No. 35 for Xavier Tillman Sr. Josh Jackson added only 22 Memphis games and the protected 2021 second did not convey, but the package still produced multiple useful layers of value. Phoenix got 118 regular-season games from Jevon Carter and later included him in the Landry Shamet trade, while Kyle Korver was waived. The completed return clearly favors Memphis.

sections.heading: Dallas Paid for a Useful Two-Way Guard
sections.body: Dallas acquired Delon Wright from Memphis in a July 2019 sign-and-trade, sending two future second-round picks and the draft rights to Satnam Singh to the Grizzlies. Wright was coming off his best stretch as a pro: 12.2 points, 5.4 rebounds, 5.3 assists and 1.6 steals in 26 games for Memphis after arriving in the Marc Gasol trade. The Mavericks were not gambling on an unknown player. They were paying a modest draft price for a 27-year-old guard who could defend, handle the ball and support Luka Doncic without needing a high-usage role.

sections.heading: Wright Gave Dallas One Solid Season
sections.body: Wright played all 73 regular-season games for Dallas in 2019-20, starting five and averaging 6.9 points, 3.8 rebounds, 3.3 assists and 1.2 steals in 21.5 minutes. He also shot 37.0 percent from three. That is real rotation value on a playoff team, which is why the canonical Dallas grade stays at B rather than dropping into the C range. The limitation is durability of value: Dallas moved Wright again in November 2020 in the three-team deal that brought James Johnson to the Mavericks, so the original acquisition produced only one season before becoming part of another asset exchange.

sections.heading: Memphis Preserved More Future Flexibility
sections.body: Memphis converted a restricted free agent into two future seconds, Singh's draft rights and a traded-player exception instead of simply letting Wright leave. The 2021 second ultimately landed at No. 51, where Brandon Boston Jr. was selected. Memphis then sent that pick to New Orleans in the larger 2021 Jonas Valanciunas trade before Boston was moved again to the Clippers. The later second resolved at No. 50 in the 2023 draft, where Keyontae Johnson was selected. Singh never became an NBA rotation piece, so the value case rests on the draft capital and transaction flexibility rather than the rights component.

sections.heading: The Margin Is Small, but Memphis Extracted More
sections.body: Dallas received the best immediate player in the transaction and got a useful season from him. Memphis, however, turned Wright's restricted free agency into multiple future assets without taking back a meaningful long-term salary obligation. That distinction explains the narrow grade gap. Wright helped Dallas, but his stay lasted one season and the Mavericks had to make another trade to redirect his value. Memphis turned a player it was prepared to move into draft capital that remained useful in later transactions. The outcome is not lopsided, but the Grizzlies squeezed slightly more lasting flexibility from the deal.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Grizzlies Edge — Dallas B, Memphis B+. Dallas got 73 regular-season games and useful two-way minutes from Delon Wright before moving him again in the James Johnson three-team trade. Memphis received two future second-round picks, Satnam Singh's draft rights and a traded-player exception for a restricted free agent it was prepared to move; the 2021 second became No. 51 Brandon Boston Jr., while the later second resolved at No. 50 Keyontae Johnson. Dallas received real on-court value, but Memphis extracted more future flexibility from the same transaction, giving the Grizzlies the narrow hindsight edge.

sections.heading: Houston Flipped Bell One Day After Acquiring Him
sections.body: Houston acquired Jordan Bell from Minnesota in the four-team Robert Covington deal and moved him again the next day, sending Bell and 2023 second-round pick-swap terms to Memphis for Bruno Caboclo. The swap was a small deadline transaction between two reserve frontcourt players, not a core-roster move. Caboclo had fallen to 8.7 minutes per game in 22 appearances for Memphis that season after a more productive 2018-19 run. Bell had averaged 3.1 points in 27 games for Minnesota before his brief stop on Houston's books.

sections.heading: Caboclo Barely Entered Houston's Rotation
sections.body: Caboclo appeared in eight regular-season games for Houston after the trade, averaging 3.5 points and 2.0 rebounds in 6.5 minutes. He returned for six more games in 2020-21, giving the Rockets 14 total regular-season appearances from the acquisition, all off the bench. Houston waived him in January 2021 as part of the roster movement surrounding the James Harden three-team trade. The Rockets therefore received some actual NBA minutes, but not enough role value or longevity to lift their side beyond the canonical D+ grade.

sections.heading: Memphis Got Only a Two-Game Look at Bell
sections.body: Bell played two games for Memphis, totaling 21 minutes, before the Grizzlies waived him on March 2, 2020 while creating a roster spot for Anthony Tolliver. His direct contribution was even smaller than Caboclo's Houston stint. Memphis did at least acquire the 2023 second-round option attached to the deal, which gave the franchise a future path to improve its draft position if the protection and swap conditions aligned. That optionality carried more potential than Bell's two-game stay, but it ultimately produced no draft asset for Memphis.

sections.heading: The 2023 Pick Terms Expired Without a Payoff
sections.body: Houston's 2023 second-round pick landed at No. 32, inside the deal's protection, so the pick did not transfer. The related Memphis swap option also was not exercised. That leaves a very small completed-value ledger on both sides: Houston got 14 Caboclo appearances, while Memphis got two Bell appearances and temporary draft optionality that never converted. The canonical C versus D+ split is therefore a narrow low-end distinction rather than a claim that Memphis found a lasting contributor. Both teams moved fringe rotation pieces; Memphis receives the slight edge for the additional flexibility built into its return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Grizzlies Win — Houston D+, Memphis C. Houston received 14 regular-season appearances from Bruno Caboclo across parts of two seasons before waiving him in January 2021. Memphis received only two games from Jordan Bell and waived him less than a month after the trade, while the 2023 second-round protection and swap mechanics ultimately produced no draft asset. Neither side created much lasting value. Memphis's return at least included future draft flexibility in addition to the short Bell audition, which is enough to preserve the canonical one-step grade edge without overstating the transaction.
