sections.heading: Indiana Bought a Real Rotation Forward for Two Future Seconds
sections.body: Indiana acquired Obi Toppin from New York for two future second-round picks in July 2023. The Pacers' own release confirms the basic price, while Basketball-Reference identifies the outgoing selections as 2028 and 2029 seconds. The 2028 asset is the less favorable of Indiana and Phoenix, and the 2029 asset is the less favorable of Indiana and Washington. Both remain unresolved, so neither should be graded as if New York already converted it into a player.

sections.heading: Toppin Quickly Became Part of Indiana's Core Rotation
sections.body: The realized return is already substantial on Indiana's side. After his first Pacers season, the team re-signed Toppin in July 2024 and basketball president Kevin Pritchard called him an integral part of the run to the Eastern Conference Finals. By April 2026, Indiana's own player review described Toppin as entering the third year of that four-year contract. Even after a foot injury limited him to 24 games in 2025-26, he averaged 11.6 points, 4.4 rebounds and 2.3 assists while shooting 50.3 percent from the field.

sections.heading: New York Still Owns Draft Value, but the Return Has Not Matured
sections.body: The Knicks did not get nothing. Two future seconds preserve optionality, and the unusual pick conditions mean the exact draft slots will not be known until those years arrive. That is why a harsh failing grade would overstate the hindsight case. But as of this review, New York's side remains future value only while Indiana has already received multiple seasons of useful NBA production and was sufficiently satisfied to give Toppin a new four-year deal.

sections.heading: The Pacers Hold the Clear Hindsight Advantage
sections.body: This is the kind of trade where realized production can be weighed without pretending the future picks are worthless. Indiana paid a modest draft price, found a role that fit Toppin and retained him beyond the original contract. New York still has two unresolved assets that could improve its side later, but there is no current evidence that either has matched the value Indiana already received. The proper verdict is a Pacers win with the Knicks kept above a failing range until the picks resolve.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pacers Win — Indiana A-, New York C+. Indiana turned two future second-round picks into Obi Toppin, received immediate rotation value and then re-signed him to a four-year contract after an Eastern Conference Finals run. New York still holds the unresolved 2028 and 2029 second-round assets, so its return retains real future value. The Pacers nevertheless own the clear realized advantage today.

sections.heading: Dallas Turned a Future Swap Into Immediate First-Round Currency
sections.body: Dallas sent Oklahoma City the right to swap 2028 first-round picks and received a 2024 first-round pick. NBA.com's trade tracker confirms the two-way asset exchange, while the Mavericks' own transaction history shows that Dallas immediately used the incoming 2024 first in its separate Daniel Gafford trade with Washington. The value of the February 8 deal therefore was not the drafted player attached to the pick months later; it was the first-round currency Dallas needed to complete a win-now frontcourt move.

sections.heading: The Pick Became No. 26, but Dillon Jones Was Not Dallas' Realized Return
sections.body: The 2024 selection ultimately became the No. 26 pick, used on Dillon Jones. Washington later sent that pick to New York, and the Knicks then traded Jones' draft rights to Oklahoma City for five future second-round picks. That later path matters because it prevents double-counting. Oklahoma City did eventually acquire Jones, but only through a separate June transaction with an additional five-second-round-pick cost. Dallas' realized value from this February trade is better traced to the asset it forwarded for Gafford.

sections.heading: Gafford Gave Dallas Immediate Playoff Value
sections.body: NBA.com reported that the Mavericks sent Richaun Holmes and the 2024 first obtained via Oklahoma City to Washington for Daniel Gafford. The league's 2024 Dallas draft profile later described the Gafford and P.J. Washington deadline moves as choices that prioritized the present and boosted the team's trajectory. Dallas reached the 2024 NBA Finals with Gafford in the rotation, giving the acquired first-round asset a clear and immediate competitive use rather than leaving it as abstract draft capital.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Still Owns Meaningful 2028 Upside
sections.body: The Thunder side cannot be graded as a failed return because the 2028 swap remains unresolved. Oklahoma City converted a late 2024 first into a future right that could still move the Thunder upward in the 2028 first round depending on the two teams' records. The current hindsight edge belongs to Dallas because its asset was already converted into productive playoff help, but the unfinished swap keeps the gap narrower than a one-sided result.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win — Dallas A-, Oklahoma City B-. Dallas converted a 2028 swap concession into a 2024 first-round asset and immediately used that pick to help acquire Daniel Gafford, who became part of a Finals roster. Oklahoma City still owns the unresolved 2028 swap and later reacquired Dillon Jones only through a separate five-second-round-pick trade. The Mavericks have the stronger realized return today, while the Thunder retain meaningful future upside.

sections.heading: Golden State Turned a Departing Reserve Into Draft Currency
sections.body: Golden State sent Cory Joseph, cash and a top-55-protected 2025 Charlotte second-round pick to Indiana for a 2024 second-round pick. NBA.com reported that Indiana waived Joseph immediately after the trade, while Basketball-Reference records that the protected 2025 Charlotte pick did not convey. The Warriors therefore moved a reserve guard they were prepared to part with, plus cash and a pick that ultimately disappeared, and secured a live 2024 draft asset in return.

sections.heading: The Incoming Pick Reached No. 52 and Fed a Complicated Draft-Night Route
sections.body: The acquired second became the No. 52 selection in the 2024 draft. NBA.com's draft results list Quinten Post at No. 52 and show the rights moving from Golden State to Oklahoma City, then Portland, then back to Golden State. The offseason trade tracker adds the surrounding context: the Warriors also acquired Lindy Waters III in that June routing. Post should not be treated as a simple one-step February return, but the pick Golden State acquired from Indiana was real draft-night currency at the center of the later sequence.

sections.heading: Post Eventually Produced Two Warriors Seasons
sections.body: The downstream player value became tangible. NBA.com reported in July 2026 that Post's two-season Warriors run ended only after Golden State declined to match Memphis' three-year, $30 million offer sheet. In his final Warriors season, he averaged 7.7 points and 4.0 rebounds across 67 games. That production cannot all be credited mechanically to the February trade because additional draft-night moves were involved, but it reinforces that Golden State's acquired No. 52 asset had meaningful realized value.

sections.heading: Indiana's Return Produced Little Basketball Value
sections.body: Indiana's side is easier to resolve. Joseph never played a game for the Pacers after the transaction because the team waived him the same day. The protected Charlotte second did not convey, leaving cash considerations as the durable piece of the return. Golden State also created a trade exception according to Basketball-Reference. The Warriors' side therefore produced the stronger combination of asset value, roster flexibility and downstream use, while Indiana's return generated little on-court or draft value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win — Golden State A-, Indiana C. Golden State moved Cory Joseph, cash and a protected second that never conveyed for the 2024 second-round pick that became No. 52. The later draft-night routing was more complicated than a direct pick-to-player conversion, but that asset helped Golden State finish the sequence with Quinten Post and Lindy Waters III. Indiana waived Joseph immediately and received no drafted player from the protected 2025 pick.

sections.heading: Brooklyn Bought Back the Right to Rebuild on Its Own Schedule
sections.body: Brooklyn's most important return was control of its own 2025 and 2026 first-round picks. The Nets' official release says the 2025 pick came back with Houston's prior swap right negated, while the 2026 first also returned outright. Those assets became the No. 8 pick in 2025 and the No. 6 pick in 2026. Brooklyn used them on Egor Demin and Mikel Brown Jr., giving the franchise two lottery selections it otherwise would not have controlled. The strategic value was just as important as the names: Brooklyn could lose games without sending the upside of its own draft position to Houston.

sections.heading: Houston's 2025 Swap Became a Real Top-10 Asset
sections.body: Houston did not simply trade away Brooklyn's picks and wait for distant compensation. The Rockets received the right to swap either their own or Oklahoma City's 2025 first for Phoenix's 2025 first, and that path produced the No. 10 selection. NBA.com's 2025 draft material shows Khaman Maluach at No. 10, with the pick ultimately routed to Phoenix. The league's offseason trade tracker then places Maluach in the seven-team Kevin Durant deal. Houston cannot be credited with Durant as a one-asset return from this trade, but the No. 10 pick clearly became a meaningful component of a later star acquisition.

sections.heading: The 2027 and 2029 Pieces Keep Houston's Side Open-Ended
sections.body: The Rockets also received Phoenix's 2027 first-round pick and the rights to the two most favorable 2029 firsts among Dallas, Houston and Phoenix. Those assets are still unresolved as of this review. That limits any attempt to declare a permanent winner. Houston has already converted the 2025 swap into useful trade currency and still owns major future optionality, while Brooklyn has already turned both returned picks into lottery selections. The remaining 2027 and 2029 outcomes can still move the historical grade in either direction.

sections.heading: The Best Current Read Is a High-End Even Trade
sections.body: This deal looks better for both teams now than it did on transaction day. Brooklyn recovered the exact draft control a rebuilding team needed and received two top-eight selections in consecutive drafts. Houston replaced those rights with Phoenix-linked and multi-team future capital, then realized a top-10 pick from the 2025 swap and used that selection inside a much larger Durant package. Because the 2027 and 2029 firsts are not settled, assigning a decisive winner would overstate what is known. The current record supports equal high grades without pretending the future assets are already resolved.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Brooklyn A-, Houston A-. Brooklyn regained its own 2025 and 2026 first-round control, which became No. 8 Egor Demin and No. 6 Mikel Brown Jr. Houston's 2025 Phoenix swap became the No. 10 pick and later served as one component of the Kevin Durant trade, while the Rockets still hold the unresolved 2027 Phoenix first and two 2029 first-round rights. Both sides have already created substantial traceable value, and too much future value remains open to justify a permanent winner.

sections.heading: The Direct Exchange Was Waters for the No. 52 Draft Rights
sections.body: Golden State sent the rights to No. 52 pick Quinten Post to Oklahoma City for Lindy Waters III. NBA.com's draft-night report and the Thunder's official release agree on that first step. That distinction matters because the direct two-team record should not pretend Golden State received Post in the same exchange. The Warriors acquired Waters here; Oklahoma City acquired Post's rights. Everything that happened to those rights afterward belongs to a traceable draft-night chain, not the initial asset ledger.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Turned Post's Rights Into Ajay Mitchell
sections.body: The Thunder immediately used Post's rights and cash to acquire the rights to No. 40 pick Oso Ighodaro from Portland, then moved Ighodaro to New York in the path that brought back No. 38 pick Ajay Mitchell. Oklahoma City's own release documents those steps, while NBA.com summarized the broader routing as a sequence that let the Thunder get Mitchell. By April 2026, NBA.com described Mitchell as an important part of Oklahoma City's rotation, giving the downstream value real basketball weight rather than leaving it as a draft-night abstraction.

sections.heading: Golden State Reacquired Post in a Separate Portland Transaction
sections.body: Golden State also came out of the broader draft-night sequence with Post, but only after the rights passed through Oklahoma City and Portland. NBA.com's 2024 draft results list No. 52 as moving Warriors-to-Thunder-to-Blazers-to-Warriors, and Basketball-Reference records Golden State later sending cash to Portland for Post. That separate reacquisition should not be rewritten into the original two-team package. It still matters to the hindsight story because Post became a rotation big for two Warriors seasons, averaging 7.7 points and 4.0 rebounds across 67 games in his final Golden State season before Memphis signed him in 2026.

sections.heading: Both Front Offices Extracted More Than the Original Ledger Suggests
sections.body: The original C-level grades undersell what the linked transactions produced. Golden State obtained Waters and, with an additional cash transaction, recovered the same No. 52 player it had drafted. Oklahoma City used the incoming rights as a bridge to Mitchell, who developed into a meaningful rotation player. Waters later left Golden State in the February 2025 multi-team Jimmy Butler transaction, but that later deal should not be credited as if Waters alone bought Butler. The strongest current read is a win-win draft-night sequence with the direct trade itself serving as the first link.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Golden State A-, Oklahoma City A-. The Warriors directly acquired Lindy Waters III for Quinten Post's draft rights, then separately reacquired Post from Portland for cash. Oklahoma City used Post's rights plus cash in the chain that ultimately produced Ajay Mitchell. Post became a useful two-season Warriors rotation big, and Mitchell developed into an important Thunder rotation player. Both sides created strong traceable value, but the later routing must stay separate from the original asset ledger.

sections.heading: New York Turned Dillon Jones Into Five Second-Round Assets
sections.body: New York sent the draft rights to No. 26 pick Dillon Jones to Oklahoma City for five future second-round picks. The Knicks' own announcement confirms the five-pick return, while Basketball-Reference identifies the first two realized selections as Kobe Sanders in 2025 and Otega Oweh in 2026. Three 2027 seconds remain unresolved, so New York's package still carries future value that should not be guessed at before those selections are determined.

sections.heading: Two of the Five Picks Have Already Become Named Players
sections.body: The first incoming second became the No. 50 pick in 2025 and was used on Kobe Sanders before New York moved his rights in a separate draft-night transaction. The 2026 Golden State second became Otega Oweh, selected No. 41 and routed to Oklahoma City. Those later trades are separate decisions, but they establish that two pieces of the Knicks' original five-pick return converted into real draft currency rather than disappearing.

sections.heading: Jones Gave Oklahoma City a Real Player, but the Stay Was Short
sections.body: Oklahoma City acquired a first-round prospect rather than waiting on distant seconds. Jones appeared in 54 games as a rookie and 61 games over his first two NBA seasons, according to Basketball-Reference, but his role stayed limited. In June 2025 the Thunder traded Jones and a 2029 second-round pick to Washington for Colby Jones. That move does not erase the original value of getting Dillon Jones, but it limits the realized return that can be credited to this transaction alone.

sections.heading: The Unresolved 2027 Picks Keep the Knicks Ahead for Now
sections.body: Three pieces of New York's return are still future 2027 second-round picks, including Minnesota's second and two selections tied to multi-team ordering rules. They should remain unresolved in the grade rather than being treated as future hits or misses. Even with that restraint, New York has already converted two of the five incoming assets into named draft selections, while Oklahoma City's direct return produced a short NBA stay before another trade required an additional second-round pick.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Knicks Edge — New York B+, Oklahoma City B. The Knicks received five second-round assets for Dillon Jones; two have already become Kobe Sanders and Otega Oweh, while three 2027 seconds remain unresolved. Oklahoma City got the immediate first-round prospect it wanted, but Jones' Thunder tenure was limited and he was later moved with an extra 2029 second. The future picks keep this outcome open, so the existing one-grade gap remains more defensible than a wider verdict.

sections.heading: Charlotte Used the Six-Team Structure to Add Josh Green and Future Draft Capital
sections.body: Charlotte's direct return was Josh Green, Reggie Jackson and Denver second-round picks in 2029 and 2030. NBA.com and the Hornets' own announcement confirm those four incoming pieces, while Charlotte sent a 2025 Philadelphia second-round pick and cash into the six-team construction. The deal therefore was not a simple Green-for-pick swap. Charlotte used its place in the league's first six-team trade to acquire a young rotation wing plus two distant draft assets.

sections.heading: Reggie Jackson Never Became Part of the Hornets' On-Court Return
sections.body: Jackson should not be credited as a productive Charlotte player. Basketball-Reference records that the Hornets waived him on July 23, 2024, less than three weeks after the transaction, and he signed with Philadelphia six days later. That reduces the realized player return to Green, while the two Denver seconds remain future assets. The distinction matters because the original four-piece package looks stronger on paper than the portion that actually stayed with Charlotte.

sections.heading: Josh Green Supplied Real Minutes, but His Role Did Not Turn Into a Breakout
sections.body: Green became the tangible basketball return. Charlotte acquired a 23-year-old wing who had started 33 games for Dallas during its 2024 Finals season. His later production with the Hornets was useful rather than transformative; Basketball-Reference lists 58 games and 4.3 points per game in 2025-26. He was later included with LaMelo Ball in Charlotte's July 2026 multi-team trade, which means his value continued into another transaction but should not be backfilled into this 2024 grade without separating that later deal.

sections.heading: The Other Five Teams Had Their Own Distinct Reasons for Joining
sections.body: The transaction also sent Klay Thompson and a 2025 second to Dallas, Kyle Anderson and Buddy Hield to Golden State, a 2025 second plus a 2031 second-round swap and cash to Minnesota, cash to Denver, and a 2031 Dallas second to Philadelphia. Those packages should not be flattened into one generic loser bucket. The Charlotte-facing grade can still favor the Hornets, but the full six-team record shows that Dallas and Golden State in particular received players they actively targeted, while several future second-round outcomes remain unresolved.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Charlotte Win — Charlotte B+, partner aggregate B-. Charlotte added Josh Green and two future Denver seconds while moving a 2025 second and cash; Reggie Jackson was waived before playing for the Hornets, which limits the realized return. Green provided usable rotation value, and the 2029 and 2030 picks are still unresolved. The B+ grade holds as a Charlotte-facing assessment, while the aggregate B- should not be read as saying every other participant lost the six-team transaction.

sections.heading: Golden State Paid Three Future Seconds for an Immediate Backcourt Fix
sections.body: Golden State acquired Dennis Schröder and Miami's 2025 second-round pick from Brooklyn for De'Anthony Melton, Reece Beekman and three unprotected seconds: Atlanta's 2026 and 2028 picks plus the Warriors' own 2029 pick. NBA.com and the Nets' official announcement agree on that package. Melton was already out for the season after left ACL surgery, so the Warriors were converting an unavailable salary slot, a two-way guard and future draft capital into a veteran who could help immediately.

sections.heading: Schröder's Warriors Stay Lasted Less Than Two Months
sections.body: The short window is the biggest strike against Golden State. Basketball-Reference records Schröder arriving on December 15 and then leaving in the February 6 Jimmy Butler multi-team trade. He therefore served as a bridge rather than a durable answer. The move was defensible for a team trying to stabilize its guard rotation in December, but hindsight has to account for how quickly the centerpiece was rerouted.

sections.heading: The 2025 Miami Second Became No. 41 Koby Brea
sections.body: The incoming 2025 Miami second did produce a known draft outcome. Basketball-Reference identifies the pick as the selection later used on Koby Brea, and NBA.com's 2025 draft results list Brea at No. 41 before his rights moved to Phoenix. That gives Golden State some realized asset value beyond Schröder, but the pick did not become a long-term Warriors player. It is also important to treat the Miami second as one asset; the imported ledger had split its protection text and Brea outcome into two separate records.

sections.heading: Brooklyn Banked the Better Long-Term Package
sections.body: Brooklyn received Melton and Beekman plus three unprotected second-round picks. Melton did not provide 2024-25 on-court value because his ACL injury had already ended his season, but the draft capital was the point of the Nets' side. The 2026 Atlanta second later became Bryce Hopkins, while the 2028 Atlanta second and Golden State's 2029 second remain future assets. With Schröder gone from Golden State within weeks, Brooklyn's package has the stronger mix of realized and still-open value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win — Brooklyn B+, Golden State C+. Golden State got a useful short-term guard and the 2025 Miami second that became No. 41 Koby Brea, but Schröder was rerouted in February and Brea's rights later moved to Phoenix. Brooklyn accepted an injured Melton, Beekman and three unprotected seconds; one became Bryce Hopkins in 2026, while the 2028 and 2029 picks remain unresolved. The Nets hold the stronger durable return without requiring any invented future-pick outcome.

sections.heading: New York Sold Jake Weber's Rights for Cash
sections.body: On December 2, 1946, New York sold Jake Weber's player rights to the Providence Steamrollers. The league and team transaction logs agree on the date and direction of the move, but the surviving public record does not disclose the cash amount. That missing number limits how precisely New York's financial return can be valued. The basketball side of the exchange is clearer: Weber left the Knicks after 11 appearances and became a regular part of Providence's frontcourt rotation.

sections.heading: The Knicks Moved a Small Part of Their Rotation
sections.body: Weber had scored 20 points in 11 games for New York, averaging 1.8 points per game. The Knicks went on to finish 33-27 and reach the BAA playoffs, so the sale did not remove a central contributor from the first-year club. Moving a low-usage reserve for cash was defensible roster management. New York earns credit for that decision, but the undisclosed sale price prevents the hindsight grade from assuming a financial windfall that cannot be verified.

sections.heading: Providence Received Most of a Season of Useful Depth
sections.body: Providence got the more visible return. Weber played 39 games for the Steamrollers after the sale, averaged 3.9 points and scored 153 points. He was not a star, and Providence still finished 28-32, but the club received real game availability from a 6-foot-6 center for most of the remaining schedule. In an early-BAA cash transaction, that amount of documented playing time is meaningful even if it did not materially change the team's record.

sections.heading: The Edge Is Real but Narrow
sections.body: The transaction favors Providence because its return can be measured in 39 games of player use while New York's cash consideration remains unknown. That does not make the Knicks' decision poor. Weber had been a marginal scorer in New York, and the team remained successful without him. The correct gap is therefore modest: Providence bought usable depth, while New York reasonably monetized a reserve whose role was already small.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Providence Steamrollers Win — Providence B+, New York B. Weber gave Providence 39 games and 153 points after the sale, producing the clearest documented value in the transaction. New York moved a 1.8-point-per-game reserve and still reached the playoffs, so the decision was reasonable. The undisclosed cash amount keeps the verdict narrow rather than turning it into a decisive Providence win.

sections.heading: Boston Swapped Tony Kappen for Moe Becker
sections.body: Boston and Pittsburgh made a straight player-for-player exchange on December 12, 1946, sending Tony Kappen to the Ironmen and Moe Becker to the Celtics. The team transaction pages and Walter Brown's executive ledger agree on the move. Both clubs were first-year BAA teams still sorting through their rotations, so the most useful hindsight comparison is what each player actually supplied after the swap rather than projecting modern trade-market value onto a 1946 transaction.

sections.heading: Becker's Boston Run Lasted Only Six Games
sections.body: Becker had averaged 6.4 points in 17 appearances for Pittsburgh before the trade, but the Celtics did not get a comparable role from him. He played six games for Boston, averaged 2.2 points and shot .227 from the field before later appearing for Detroit. Boston finished 22-38, and Becker never became a meaningful part of the Celtics' season. The B- reflects how little direct playing value the club received after making the exchange.

sections.heading: Kappen Became a Regular Scorer for Pittsburgh
sections.body: Kappen provided the clearer return. After averaging 4.1 points across 18 Boston games, he played 41 games for Pittsburgh and averaged 7.6 points. He scored 310 points for the Ironmen and made 84.6 percent of his free throws. Pittsburgh still went 15-45, so the trade did not fix the team, and Kappen's .231 field-goal percentage limits how aggressively the result should be praised. Even so, 41 games of regular rotation use clearly exceeded Boston's six-game return.

sections.heading: Pittsburgh Won the Swap Without Transforming Its Season
sections.body: Neither side found a long-term franchise piece, which keeps the grade difference moderate. Boston took a reasonable chance on a player who had scored more before the trade, but the experiment ended quickly. Pittsburgh acquired a player who stayed in the lineup for most of the remaining season and carried a larger scoring role. That is enough for the Ironmen to hold the historical edge even though their overall team results remained poor.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pittsburgh Ironmen Win — Pittsburgh B+, Boston B-. Kappen gave Pittsburgh 41 games, 310 points and a 7.6-point scoring average after the trade, while Becker's Boston stint lasted only six games at 2.2 points per game. The Ironmen were still a 15-win team and Kappen was inefficient from the field, so the outcome is a clear but not dramatic Pittsburgh win.

sections.heading: Boston Bought Jack Garfinkel for Cash
sections.body: Boston acquired Jack Garfinkel from the Rochester Royals for cash on December 23, 1946, during the first BAA season. The surviving records do not preserve the cash amount, so Rochester's financial return cannot be priced with precision. What can be measured is the basketball side: Garfinkel immediately entered Boston's rotation and remained with the Celtics across three seasons.

sections.heading: Garfinkel Became a Multi-Season Celtics Rotation Player
sections.body: Garfinkel played 40 games for Boston in 1946-47, averaging 4.5 points and 1.5 assists, then returned for 43 games the next season and improved to 6.1 points per game. He appeared in nine more games in 1948-49. Across his Celtics tenure he played 92 games and scored 476 points, giving Boston sustained roster value from an otherwise simple cash transaction.

sections.heading: Rochester's Side Was Rational but Hard to Measure
sections.body: Rochester had used Garfinkel lightly before the sale. His NBL sample with the Royals was only 10 games at 1.3 points per game, so converting his rights into cash was a reasonable roster decision. The limitation is documentary: because the payment amount is unknown, the archive cannot claim Rochester received either a strong or weak financial return. The analysis therefore gives the Royals credit for process without inventing a cash valuation.

sections.heading: The Historical Edge Belongs to Boston
sections.body: Boston's return is clearer because it is visible on the court. The Celtics did not acquire a star and Garfinkel did not change the franchise's 22-38 inaugural season, but they turned an unspecified payment into three seasons of guard depth. Rochester's sale made sense, yet the undocumented cash consideration offers less measurable hindsight value than 92 games of service. That is enough for a modest Celtics advantage rather than a dramatic win.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win — Boston B+, Rochester B. Garfinkel gave Boston 92 games and 476 points across three seasons after arriving for cash, while Rochester's return remains an undisclosed payment that cannot be valued precisely. The Royals made a defensible decision with a low-usage player, but Boston owns the stronger documented basketball result.

sections.heading: Boston and Toronto Swapped Guards Midseason
sections.body: Boston sent Red Wallace to the Toronto Huskies for Charlie Hoefer on January 2, 1947. The exchange is unusually measurable for the first BAA season because both guards had already played meaningful minutes for their original clubs. Wallace had averaged 5.5 points in 24 Boston games, while Hoefer had averaged 6.1 points in 23 games for Toronto.

sections.heading: Hoefer Gave Boston Steady but Modest Production
sections.body: Hoefer played 35 games for the Celtics after the trade and averaged 6.0 points with 0.7 assists. He returned for seven games in 1947-48, bringing his Boston tenure to 42 appearances. The Celtics received dependable backcourt depth, but Hoefer's scoring rate stayed close to what he had already produced for Toronto and did not materially alter Boston's 22-38 finish.

sections.heading: Wallace's Scoring Jump Gave Toronto the Stronger Return
sections.body: Wallace's post-trade change was much larger. After averaging 5.5 points for Boston, he scored 11.5 per game across 37 appearances for Toronto and raised his field-goal percentage from .246 to .291. The Huskies also finished 22-38, so the move did not rescue their season, but Wallace became a much more prominent scorer than he had been with the Celtics.

sections.heading: The Team Records Keep the Verdict in Perspective
sections.body: Neither club turned the trade into a winning season, which keeps the evaluation centered on individual production rather than team success. Boston got useful minutes from Hoefer and even a small amount of second-season continuity. Toronto, however, received the player who made the larger immediate jump and delivered the stronger same-season offensive output. That gives the Huskies the historical edge without making Boston's side a failure.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Toronto Huskies Win — Toronto A-, Boston B. Wallace more than doubled his scoring rate after the move and averaged 11.5 points across 37 Toronto games, while Hoefer gave Boston 35 games at 6.0 points and seven more appearances the following season. Both teams finished 22-38, so Toronto's advantage comes from the stronger player-production result rather than a change in team success.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Bought Championship Rotation Help
sections.body: On January 16, 1947, the Philadelphia Warriors acquired the player rights to Ralph Kaplowitz from the New York Knicks for cash. Basketball-Reference records the transaction on both teams' 1946-47 transaction pages. New York had used Kaplowitz in 27 games, where he averaged 7.2 points, before selling his rights. The public transaction record does not disclose the cash amount, so a responsible hindsight grade has to avoid inventing a financial value for the Knicks' side.

sections.heading: Kaplowitz Stayed in the Warriors Rotation
sections.body: Kaplowitz immediately became a rotation player for a Warriors team that finished 35-25 and won the first BAA championship. He appeared in 30 regular-season games for Philadelphia, averaged 7.0 points and improved his field-goal percentage from .259 with New York to .291 with the Warriors. He then played in all 10 postseason games, averaging 6.6 points as Philadelphia beat St. Louis, New York and Chicago on the way to the title.

sections.heading: New York’s Cash Return Cannot Be Priced
sections.body: The Knicks received cash after getting 27 games from Kaplowitz. Selling a rotation player was not disastrous: New York still finished 33-27, reached the playoffs and won its quarterfinal series before losing to Philadelphia in the semifinals. The problem for retrospective grading is that the size and later use of the cash are not documented in the transaction sources. That makes it impossible to compare the financial return directly with Kaplowitz's championship-season contribution.

sections.heading: A Championship Run Gives Philadelphia the Edge
sections.body: Kaplowitz's scoring rate barely changed after the move, so Philadelphia did not unlock a hidden star. The value came from fit, timing and availability. He joined a 35-win contender, played 30 regular-season games, appeared throughout the playoffs and remained with the Warriors for another year. New York was also a good team and did not collapse after moving him, which keeps the margin from becoming extreme.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win — Golden State A-, New York B. Philadelphia acquired Ralph Kaplowitz from the New York Knicks for cash on January 16, 1947. Kaplowitz had averaged 7.2 points in 27 games for New York and then averaged 7.0 points across 30 regular-season games for Philadelphia. He also appeared in all 10 of the Warriors' playoff games as Philadelphia won the inaugural BAA championship. The cash amount paid to New York is not preserved in the transaction pages used here, so the Knicks' financial return cannot be valued precisely.

sections.heading: Toronto and New York Swapped Bob for Bob
sections.body: On January 21, 1947, the Toronto Huskies traded Bob Fitzgerald to the New York Knicks for Bob Mullens. Basketball-Reference lists the one-for-one exchange on both team transaction pages and in the league transaction log. Both players had already appeared in more than 20 games for their original clubs, so the same-season before-and-after splits provide a useful basis for judging the deal.

sections.heading: Mullens Became a Much Bigger Scorer
sections.body: Mullens changed roles dramatically after arriving in Toronto. He had averaged only 2.9 points in 26 games for New York, then scored 8.5 points per game across 28 appearances for the Huskies. His field-goal percentage rose from .260 to .287, his assists increased from 0.7 to 1.3 per game, and he scored 238 points for Toronto after totaling only 76 for the Knicks.

sections.heading: Fitzgerald Filled a Smaller Knicks Role
sections.body: Fitzgerald moved in the opposite direction statistically. He had averaged 4.5 points in 31 games for Toronto before the trade, then fell to 2.8 points across 29 games for New York. His shooting remained below .200 from the field, although his estimated win-share contribution improved from negative territory in Toronto to a small positive mark with the Knicks. New York did not need Fitzgerald to become a high-volume scorer.

sections.heading: The Same-Season Splits Favor Toronto
sections.body: The strongest evidence comes from the immediate role changes. Mullens nearly tripled his scoring average after reaching Toronto and became one of the Huskies' more productive guards for the remainder of the season. Fitzgerald's scoring dropped after the move to New York and he never developed into a comparable contributor for the Knicks. Team success points the other way, because New York was much better than Toronto, but that gap was already larger than either player could reasonably change.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Huskies Win — Toronto A-, New York B. Toronto acquired Bob Mullens from the New York Knicks for Bob Fitzgerald on January 21, 1947. Mullens' scoring jumped from 2.9 points in 26 games for New York to 8.5 points across 28 games for Toronto, while Fitzgerald fell from 4.5 points with the Huskies to 2.8 points in 29 games for the Knicks.

sections.heading: Providence Bought Rosenstein for Cash
sections.body: On January 26, 1947, the New York Knicks sold Hank Rosenstein's player rights to the Providence Steamrollers for cash. Basketball-Reference records the move on both teams' transaction pages and in the league transaction log, while Providence executive Joseph Fay's register confirms that the Steamrollers acquired Rosenstein on the same date. The cash amount is not listed in those sources, which limits any exact comparison with New York's return. Rosenstein's post-trade production is much easier to measure.

sections.heading: Rosenstein Doubled His Scoring Rate
sections.body: Rosenstein became a larger offensive piece immediately after reaching Providence. He had averaged 4.3 points in 31 games for New York, shooting .262 from the field. With the Steamrollers he played 29 games, averaged 8.6 points and improved to .331 shooting. He scored 249 points for Providence after totaling 133 for the Knicks and generated 2.8 win shares in the Steamrollers segment of his season.

sections.heading: New York Stayed Strong After the Sale
sections.body: The Knicks received cash and remained a winning team after moving Rosenstein. New York finished 33-27 and reached the playoffs, showing that the sale did not create a damaging roster hole. The limitation is archival rather than strategic: the amount of cash and its later use are not documented in the transaction sources used for this review.

sections.heading: The Measurable Return Favors Providence
sections.body: Rosenstein's improvement makes Providence's side more concrete. His scoring rate doubled, his shooting percentage improved and he handled a larger role for almost half the season. New York was the better team and had enough depth to move him without losing its playoff position, so the Knicks' decision was defensible. The difference is that Providence can point to a measurable basketball return while New York's cash remains unquantified.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Steamrollers Win — Providence A-, New York B. Providence acquired Hank Rosenstein from the New York Knicks for cash on January 26, 1947. Rosenstein had averaged 4.3 points in 31 games for New York, then doubled that rate to 8.6 points across 29 games for the Steamrollers while improving his field-goal percentage from .262 to .331. The cash amount New York received is not disclosed in the surviving transaction pages, so the Knicks' financial return cannot be measured precisely.

sections.heading: Toronto Added Militzok for Cash
sections.body: In February 1947, the Toronto Huskies acquired Nat Militzok's player rights from the New York Knicks for cash. Basketball-Reference lists the transaction on both team pages and in the league transaction log, while Knicks executive Ned Irish's register confirms that New York sold Militzok to Toronto during the month. The exact day is uncertain in the public record and the cash amount is not disclosed, so those gaps have to remain explicit rather than being filled with assumptions.

sections.heading: Militzok Gave the Huskies a Useful Final Stretch
sections.body: Militzok played 21 games for the Huskies after the sale and averaged 4.8 points with 0.7 assists. His field-goal percentage improved from .243 with New York to .295 in Toronto, and his free-throw percentage rose from .548 to .615. Those numbers do not describe a star, but they represent useful rotation production for a team that was constantly changing personnel during its lone BAA season. Toronto finished 22-38, so the acquisition did not rescue the club competitively.

sections.heading: New York’s Cash Return Remains Unknown
sections.body: The Knicks received cash after using Militzok in 36 games at 4.0 points per game. New York was already headed toward a 33-27 season and a playoff berth, so moving a reserve forward did not create an obvious roster problem. The financial side cannot be measured because the amount and later use of the cash are absent from the transaction record. That makes the sale defensible but difficult to reward heavily in hindsight.

sections.heading: The Huskies Hold a Narrow Historical Edge
sections.body: This is a modest trade even by early-BAA standards. Toronto received a player who improved slightly after the move and stayed in the rotation for the remaining portion of the season. New York received money and continued winning without him. The absence of a documented cash figure keeps the margin narrow, because it would be irresponsible to assume the Knicks received trivial compensation.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Huskies Win — Toronto B+, New York B. Toronto acquired Nat Militzok from the New York Knicks for cash in February 1947. Militzok had averaged 4.0 points in 36 games for New York and then averaged 4.8 points across 21 games for the Huskies while improving his field-goal percentage from .243 to .295. The cash amount paid to New York is not disclosed in the surviving transaction records, so the Knicks' return cannot be valued precisely.

sections.heading: Boston and St. Louis Exchanged Gray and Hankins
sections.body: On April 29, 1947, after the inaugural BAA season, the Boston Celtics traded Wyndol Gray to the St. Louis Bombers for Cecil Hankins. Basketball-Reference records the transaction on both clubs' 1946-47 pages and in the league transaction log. Because the exchange occurred after the season, the first meaningful comparison comes in 1947-48. Neither incoming player became a major contributor for his new club, but St. Louis later turned Gray into a second asset, which changes the long-term value of the deal.

sections.heading: Hankins Had a Short Celtics Stay
sections.body: Hankins had been a regular for St. Louis in 1946-47, playing 55 games and averaging 5.9 points. His Boston role was much smaller the following season. He appeared in 25 games, averaged 2.8 points and shot .198 from the field, producing negative win-share value in the Basketball-Reference estimates. Boston finished 20-28 and reached the playoffs, but Hankins was not a central part of that team and did not remain in the BAA after the season.

sections.heading: Gray’s Direct Bombers Return Was Also Modest
sections.body: Gray's immediate contribution was even smaller. He played 11 games for the Bombers in 1947-48, averaging 1.2 points on .167 shooting. St. Louis nevertheless found additional value on December 30, 1947, when it traded Gray to Providence for Ariel Maughan. Maughan played 28 games for St. Louis that season at 4.6 points per game, then became a much larger scorer in 1948-49 with 10.8 points across 55 games. He remained with the Bombers into 1949-50, giving St.

sections.heading: The Later Asset Chain Pushes St. Louis Ahead
sections.body: If the transaction ended with Hankins and Gray alone, neither side would have much reason to claim victory. Hankins supplied 25 modest games for Boston, while Gray lasted only 11 games in St. Louis. The difference is what happened next. The Bombers converted Gray into Maughan, who immediately offered more production and then became a double-digit scorer the following season. St. Louis also finished 29-19 and first in the Western Division in 1947-48, while Boston went 20-28.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bombers Win — St. Louis A, Boston B-. Boston traded Wyndol Gray to the St. Louis Bombers for Cecil Hankins on April 29, 1947. The direct returns were modest the next season: Hankins played 25 games for Boston at 2.8 points per game, while Gray played 11 games for St. Louis at 1.2 points. The deal tilted toward St. Louis because Gray was later traded to Providence for Ariel Maughan, who became a useful Bombers contributor for multiple seasons, including 10.8 points per game in 1948-49.

sections.heading: Minneapolis Bought Swede Carlson from Chicago
sections.body: On September 1, 1947, the Minneapolis Lakers acquired Don 'Swede' Carlson from the Chicago Stags for cash. The transaction moved Carlson from a BAA team to a Minneapolis club that was still competing in the NBL. Carlson had just averaged 10.7 points in 59 games for Chicago during the inaugural BAA season, so this was not a purchase of an unused reserve. The surviving transaction histories do not disclose the cash amount, which means Chicago's financial return cannot be graded precisely.

sections.heading: Carlson Became Immediate Championship Help
sections.body: Carlson immediately became the Lakers' third-leading scorer in the 1947-48 NBL regular season. He played 58 games, averaged 8.2 points and scored 475 points behind George Mikan and Jim Pollard as Minneapolis went 43-17 and won the NBL championship. That alone gave the Lakers a substantial return on a cash acquisition. The value continued after Minneapolis moved into the BAA.

sections.heading: Chicago Stayed Competitive Without Him
sections.body: Chicago received cash for a player who had been one of its most productive scorers. Carlson's 10.7 points per game in 1946-47 came across 59 appearances for a 39-22 Stags team that reached the BAA Finals. The Stags remained competitive without him, going 28-20 in 1947-48 and 38-22 in 1948-49, so the sale did not collapse the roster. The problem for hindsight evaluation is that the cash amount and its downstream use are not visible in the public transaction record.

sections.heading: Three Productive Lakers Seasons Decide the Deal
sections.body: The championship context separates this deal from most cash sales of the 1940s. Carlson was not the Lakers' star, but he was a regular contributor on the 1948 NBL champion and the 1949 BAA champion, then remained on the 1950 NBA championship roster. He supplied 58 NBL games before adding 112 BAA/NBA regular-season games for Minneapolis. Chicago was good enough to absorb his departure, which prevents the transaction from being described as a franchise-destroying mistake.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win — Lakers A+, Chicago C+. Minneapolis acquired Don 'Swede' Carlson from the Chicago Stags for cash on September 1, 1947. Carlson became a major supporting piece immediately, averaging 8.2 points in 58 games as the Lakers won the 1948 NBL championship. He then averaged 9.2 points in 55 games for the 1949 BAA champions and remained on the roster for the Lakers' 1950 NBA championship season. Chicago's cash return is not disclosed in the surviving transaction records.

sections.heading: Minneapolis Also Bought Tony Jaros from Chicago
sections.body: On September 1, 1947, the Minneapolis Lakers acquired Tony Jaros from the Chicago Stags for cash. Jaros had just completed a strong first BAA season, appearing in 59 games for Chicago and averaging 8.2 points while the Stags reached the league finals. The move sent him back to his hometown Minneapolis franchise as the Lakers were building around George Mikan and Jim Pollard.

sections.heading: Jaros Became a Three-Championship Regular
sections.body: Jaros played 58 games for the 1947-48 Lakers in the NBL and averaged 4.7 points, scoring 273 for a 43-17 club that won the league championship. His role grew again when Minneapolis moved to the BAA. Jaros appeared in 59 games in 1948-49, averaged 5.8 points and shot .343 from the field as the Lakers went 44-16 and won the BAA championship.

sections.heading: Chicago Sold a Proven Contributor
sections.body: Chicago gave up a proven contributor after a 39-win inaugural BAA season. Jaros had averaged 8.2 points and appeared in 59 games for the Stags, so this was not a sale of an unused reserve. Chicago remained competitive without him, finishing 28-20 in 1947-48 and 38-22 the following season, which shows the roster could absorb his departure. The issue in hindsight is the lack of a documented basketball return.

sections.heading: Longevity Makes the Lakers the Clear Winner
sections.body: The gap comes from duration and championship context rather than star-level production. Jaros averaged fewer points in Minneapolis than he had in Chicago, but he stayed healthy, remained in the rotation and contributed across the Lakers' NBL, BAA and NBA championship seasons. Chicago continued to win, so selling him was not a disastrous roster decision.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win — Lakers A+, Chicago C+. Minneapolis acquired Tony Jaros from the Chicago Stags for cash on September 1, 1947. Jaros immediately became a regular on the 1948 NBL champion Lakers, playing 58 games and averaging 4.7 points. He then averaged 5.8 points in 59 games for the 1949 BAA champions and 3.9 points in 61 games for the 1950 NBA champions. Chicago's cash return is not disclosed in the surviving transaction sources.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Sold Jerry Rullo’s Rights
sections.body: On October 14, 1947, the Philadelphia Warriors sold Jerry Rullo's player rights to the original Baltimore Bullets for cash. Basketball-Reference's Philadelphia, Baltimore and league transaction pages all identify Baltimore as the buyer, which is important because the 1944-54 Bullets were a separate franchise from the modern Washington Wizards. Rullo had been part of Philadelphia's inaugural BAA championship team, appearing in 50 regular-season games and averaging 2.5 points.

sections.heading: The Warriors Moved a Reserve Without Losing Their Core
sections.body: Philadelphia received cash and moved on from a low-volume player without losing a core contributor. Rullo had averaged 2.5 points on .299 shooting in 1946-47 and was not among the Warriors' primary scorers. Philadelphia remained one of the league's strongest teams in 1947-48, going 27-21 and reaching the BAA Finals again.

sections.heading: Baltimore Got Two Scoreless Games
sections.body: Baltimore received almost no direct playing value from Rullo. He appeared in only two games for the Bullets in 1947-48, went scoreless and attempted four field goals before the club placed his contract on waivers on December 1. Baltimore went on to win the 1948 BAA championship, but Rullo was no longer on the roster for that run and should not receive retrospective credit for the title.

sections.heading: The Small Deal Still Favors Philadelphia
sections.body: This is a small transaction with a clear outcome. Philadelphia sold a reserve who had already contributed to a championship roster but was not central to the next season's plans. Baltimore paid cash, used Rullo twice and waived him less than two months later. The unknown sale price prevents a precise financial judgment on Philadelphia's side, but the basketball comparison is straightforward: the Warriors gave up almost no subsequent value to Baltimore.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win — Golden State B+, Baltimore C-. Philadelphia sold Jerry Rullo's player rights to the original Baltimore Bullets for cash on October 14, 1947. Rullo had played 50 games at 2.5 points per game for the 1947 BAA champion Warriors, but his Baltimore stay lasted only two games and he did not score before the Bullets placed him on waivers in December. Philadelphia's cash return is undisclosed, so it cannot be valued precisely.

sections.heading: Boston and Baltimore Swapped Active Scorers
sections.body: On February 9, 1948, the Boston Celtics traded Connie Simmons to the original Baltimore Bullets for Mike Bloom. Basketball-Reference records the same exchange on Boston's, Baltimore's and the league's transaction pages, and executive records for Walter Brown and Bill Dyer agree on the date and players involved. Both players were established BAA contributors when the deal happened. Bloom had averaged 11.1 points in 34 games for Baltimore, while Simmons had averaged 7.8 points in 32 games for Boston.

sections.heading: Simmons Exploded During Baltimore’s Title Run
sections.body: Simmons immediately became more productive in Baltimore. He averaged 10.6 points in 13 regular-season games after the trade, improving from 7.8 in Boston, and the value increased dramatically in the playoffs. Simmons appeared in all 11 postseason games for the Bullets and averaged 17.1 points, the highest scoring rate on the championship roster. Baltimore won the Western Division tiebreaker, beat New York and Chicago, then defeated Philadelphia 4-2 in the BAA Finals.

sections.heading: Bloom Helped Boston in a Shorter Window
sections.body: Bloom was productive in a shorter window. He played 14 regular-season games for Boston, averaged 9.2 points and shot .272 from the field, then averaged 12.0 points across three playoff games. That helped the Celtics reach the postseason despite a 20-28 regular-season record. The limitation is duration. Boston sold Bloom's player rights to Minneapolis on August 30, 1948, so his Celtics tenure ended after only those 17 combined regular-season and playoff appearances.

sections.heading: Playoff Impact Creates the Decisive Gap
sections.body: Both teams received useful short-term scoring, which keeps Boston's side from being treated as a failure. Bloom actually raised his scoring rate in the playoffs and gave the Celtics a legitimate offensive option during the final stretch of the season. Simmons, however, became one of the most important scorers on the league champion.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bullets Win — Baltimore A+, Boston B. Baltimore acquired Connie Simmons from Boston for Mike Bloom on February 9, 1948, and the trade became part of the Bullets' championship run. Simmons averaged 10.6 points in 13 regular-season games after the deal, then jumped to 17.1 points across all 11 playoff games as Baltimore won the 1948 BAA title. He followed with 13.0 points per game for the Bullets in 1948-49.

sections.heading: Boston Sent Ed Sadowski to Philadelphia
sections.body: On May 1, 1948, the Boston Celtics traded Ed Sadowski to the Philadelphia Warriors for Hank Beenders and Chick Halbert. The move came after the 1947-48 BAA season, so the cleanest comparison begins in 1948-49. Sadowski had just been Boston's dominant scorer, averaging 20.3 points across 47 games. Beenders had been a reserve for Philadelphia, while Halbert had played 40 games for the Warriors at 10.5 points per game after arriving from Chicago.

sections.heading: Sadowski Delivered a Full High-Level Warriors Season
sections.body: Sadowski gave the Warriors exactly the kind of production that makes this trade stand out. He played all 60 regular-season games in 1948-49, scored 920 points and averaged 15.3 points per game while shooting .405 from the field. Basketball-Reference credits him with 10.7 win shares, one of the strongest marks on the team. Philadelphia finished 28-32 and reached the playoffs, where Sadowski appeared in two games.

sections.heading: Halbert Helped but Beenders Barely Played
sections.body: Boston's return was divided between a short Beenders stint and a useful but temporary Halbert role. Beenders appeared in only eight games for the Celtics in 1948-49, averaging 2.4 points on .214 shooting before his BAA career ended. Halbert contributed much more. He played 33 games for Boston, averaged 9.4 points and 1.8 assists, and generated 1.7 win shares before the Celtics traded him to Providence on January 16, 1949.

sections.heading: The Two-Player Return Could Not Match Sadowski
sections.body: The trade is not a case where Boston received nothing. Halbert was a real contributor, and turning one player into two bodies had roster logic for a Celtics team trying to improve after a 20-win season. The problem is the realized value. Beenders barely played, Halbert lasted only 33 games, and Sadowski immediately produced 15.3 points per game with double-digit win shares for Philadelphia. Sadowski's role was both larger and more durable through the next season.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win — Golden State A, Boston B. Philadelphia acquired Ed Sadowski from Boston for Hank Beenders and Chick Halbert on May 1, 1948. Sadowski became a major Warriors contributor in 1948-49, playing all 60 games, scoring 920 points and averaging 15.3 points with 10.7 win shares. Boston received only eight games and 2.4 points per game from Beenders, while Halbert averaged 9.4 points in 33 games before the Celtics moved him to Providence in January.

sections.heading: Boston Bought a Proven Guard
sections.body: During October 1948, the Boston Celtics purchased Jim Seminoff's player rights from the Chicago Stags for cash. Basketball-Reference lists the transaction on Boston's, Chicago's and the league's 1948-49 transaction pages with the day unspecified. That evidence supersedes the legacy July 1 date previously stored as an approximate intake placeholder. Seminoff had been a regular for Chicago in the first two BAA seasons, appearing in 108 games and averaging 6.8 points for the Stags.

sections.heading: Seminoff Gave the Celtics Two Full Seasons
sections.body: Seminoff became one of Boston's more durable backcourt contributors immediately. He played 58 of the Celtics' 60 games in 1948-49, averaged 7.9 points and a team-high 3.9 assists, and produced 5.4 win shares. Boston finished only 25-35, so the acquisition did not transform the club into a contender, but Seminoff gave the roster reliable ball movement and availability. He returned for 65 games in 1949-50, averaging 4.8 points and 3.8 assists.

sections.heading: Chicago Took Cash and Kept Winning
sections.body: Chicago received cash, but the amount is not disclosed in the transaction logs used for this review. The Stags were able to absorb Seminoff's departure. They improved to 38-22 in 1948-49 and remained one of the BAA's stronger teams, so selling him did not create an obvious roster crisis. That context keeps Chicago's grade respectable.

sections.heading: The 123-Game Return Gives Boston the Edge
sections.body: Seminoff was not a star in Boston, but he was exactly the kind of rotation player whose value accumulates through availability and role. He played nearly every game in his first Celtics season, led the team in assists per game and stayed for a second full year. Chicago remained competitive, which shows the Stags did not need him to sustain success, but the sale still moved 123 games of future Celtics service for an undisclosed financial return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win — Boston A-, Chicago B. Boston acquired Jim Seminoff from the Chicago Stags for cash during October 1948. The exact day is not preserved in the reviewed transaction logs, replacing a legacy July 1 placeholder that had been used only for chronological intake. Seminoff became a durable Celtics rotation guard, averaging 7.9 points and 3.9 assists in 58 games in 1948-49, then 4.8 points and 3.8 assists across 65 games in 1949-50. Chicago's cash return is undisclosed.

sections.heading: Tri-Cities Moved Dolph Schayes’ Rights
sections.body: In 1948, the Tri-Cities Blackhawks selected Dolph Schayes in the NBL draft and transferred his negotiating rights to the Syracuse Nationals. NBA.com's historical profile and the Philadelphia 76ers' alumni history both confirm the Blackhawks-to-Nationals rights transfer. ESPN's profile adds important context: Tri-Cities was cash-poor and recognized it was unlikely to sign Schayes, so the franchise transferred his rights to Syracuse rather than lose him to a BAA team. The exact transaction day and compensation amount are not established in the reviewed public histories.

sections.heading: Syracuse Landed a Franchise Cornerstone
sections.body: The Nationals acquired a franchise-defining player. Schayes averaged 12.8 points in 63 games during Syracuse's 1948-49 NBL season and was recognized as the league's Rookie of the Year. After the NBL-BAA merger created the NBA, he stayed with the Nationals and then moved with the franchise to Philadelphia. Basketball-Reference credits him with 12 All-Star selections and 12 All-NBA selections, including six first-team honors. He helped Syracuse win the 1955 NBA championship and finished his career with the same franchise.

sections.heading: The Blackhawks Had Little Signing Leverage
sections.body: Tri-Cities never received on-court value from Schayes because he did not sign with the Blackhawks. That point matters when judging the decision in its real 1948 context: the club held rights to a player it had little chance to secure and could reasonably prefer some consideration to losing leverage entirely. The surviving public profiles, however, do not establish a specific dollar amount or a traceable downstream basketball asset from the rights transfer.

sections.heading: Sixteen Seasons Make This a Landslide
sections.body: Few early professional basketball transactions have a larger realized-value gap. Syracuse obtained a player who immediately became a leading NBL scorer, stayed through the merger, earned a dozen All-Star and All-NBA selections, won a championship and remained with the franchise for his entire playing career. Tri-Cities' decision was understandable because signing Schayes was not realistic under the circumstances described by historical accounts. Hindsight grading nevertheless measures what each side ultimately received.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nationals Win — Syracuse A+, Tri-Cities D. Syracuse acquired the NBL draft rights to Dolph Schayes from the Tri-Cities Blackhawks in 1948, a transaction that changed the Nationals' franchise history. Contemporary summaries confirm the rights transfer but do not preserve a reliable public dollar figure or exact transaction day, so the legacy July 1 date and cash notation should be treated as approximate intake data rather than a fully documented term sheet.

sections.heading: Fort Wayne Bought Indianapolis’ Leading Scorer
sections.body: In the summer of 1948, Fort Wayne acquired Leo Klier from the Indianapolis franchise for cash as the Pistons and the newly renamed Jets prepared to enter the BAA. The historical Zollner Pistons account describes Indianapolis as financially strained and says the club sold the contract of its highest scorer to Fort Wayne before the season.

sections.heading: Klier Became a Two-Year Pistons Regular
sections.body: Klier immediately became a regular for the Pistons in their first BAA season. He played 47 games in 1948-49, averaged 7.4 points and 1.2 assists, and scored 347 points. Fort Wayne struggled to a 22-38 record, so his arrival did not turn the club into a contender, but he remained useful through the league transition.

sections.heading: The Jets Needed the Cash
sections.body: Indianapolis received cash at a time when the franchise's finances were a central concern. The historical account specifically frames the Klier sale as part of that financial pressure, which makes the decision easier to understand than a normal basketball-for-cash move. The Jets still entered the 1948-49 BAA season but finished 18-42 and folded after the season. The compensation amount is not preserved in the reviewed sources, and there is no traceable basketball asset tied to the proceeds.

sections.heading: Durable Rotation Value Breaks the Tie
sections.body: Klier never became a star in Fort Wayne, yet the transaction produced exactly the kind of durable role value that gives an early cash purchase meaning in hindsight. He played nearly two full seasons, remained through the creation of the NBA and improved his efficiency in year two. Indianapolis' decision had a defensible business rationale because the club needed money and was heading into a precarious final season.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Fort Wayne A-, Indianapolis B. Fort Wayne acquired Leo Klier from the Indianapolis Jets for cash in the summer of 1948 as both clubs prepared to enter the BAA. A historical account of the Zollner Pistons describes cash-strapped Indianapolis selling the contract of its leading scorer to Fort Wayne, while the exact sale day and cash amount are not preserved in the reviewed public transaction logs. Klier then played 47 games at 7.4 points per game in 1948-49 and 66 games at 6.9 points in 1949-50.

sections.heading: Boston Sold Mike Bloom’s Rights
sections.body: On August 30, 1948, the Boston Celtics sold Mike Bloom's player rights to the Minneapolis Lakers for cash. Basketball-Reference lists the transaction on the Boston, Minneapolis and league transaction pages, and Walter Brown's executive ledger records the same rights sale. The amount of cash is not preserved in the reviewed public records, so the transaction can be evaluated only from the documented player outcome and Boston's decision to monetize the rights.

sections.heading: Minneapolis Got Only a Brief Reserve Run
sections.body: Bloom's Lakers tenure was brief. He appeared in 24 games during the 1948-49 BAA season, scored 55 points and averaged 2.3 points per game. Basketball-Reference credits him with 15 assists and a .141 field-goal percentage during that stint. Minneapolis released him in December, and he later joined the Chicago Stags, where he played 21 additional games. The Lakers went on to win the BAA championship behind George Mikan and a deep roster, so Bloom was not central to the title run.

sections.heading: The Celtics Monetized a Player They Were Moving On From
sections.body: Boston's return was cash with no surviving public amount. That limitation prevents a precise financial comparison, but the Celtics did extract value from rights they were not using. Bloom had been productive in a 14-game Boston stint, yet the club chose not to keep him for the next season. Because Minneapolis received only 24 low-usage games before releasing him, Boston did not give away a player who became materially more valuable for the buyer.

sections.heading: Bloom’s Short Stay Favors Boston
sections.body: The outcome favors Boston primarily because the Lakers' basketball return was so small. Bloom's 24 games produced 55 total points, and his Minneapolis tenure ended before midseason. The Celtics' cash receipt cannot be quantified, so this is not a transaction where Boston's exact gain can be measured. It is still reasonable to credit the seller for turning expendable rights into consideration when the buyer did not realize meaningful long-term player value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win — Boston B+, Minneapolis C+. Boston sold Mike Bloom's player rights to the Minneapolis Lakers on August 30, 1948 for cash. The reviewed transaction logs agree on the date and rights transfer, but they do not preserve the sale amount. Bloom gave Minneapolis 24 games in 1948-49, scoring 55 points and averaging 2.3 points per game before the Lakers released him in December. He later finished the season with the Chicago Stags.

sections.heading: New York Sold Stan Stutz’s Rights
sections.body: On October 13, 1948, the New York Knicks sold Stan Stutz's player rights to the Boston Celtics for cash. Basketball-Reference records the same transaction on the New York, Boston and league transaction pages, and the Ned Irish and Walter Brown executive ledgers confirm the rights sale from both front offices. The cash amount is not preserved in the reviewed public record.

sections.heading: Boston Never Got a Celtics Game from Stutz
sections.body: The difficulty for Boston is that the purchased rights did not turn into documented Celtics playing time. Stutz's 1948-49 player record lists 59 games for the Baltimore Bullets at 6.3 points and 1.4 assists per game, with 1.1 win shares. Basketball-Reference does not show a Boston regular-season appearance for him that year.

sections.heading: The Knicks Turned the Rights into Cash
sections.body: New York's return was cash with no surviving public amount. That keeps the exact financial benefit unknowable, but the Knicks did convert the rights into consideration and then proceeded without Stutz. New York finished 32-28 in 1948-49, placed second in the BAA Eastern Division and reached the Eastern Division Finals. The team therefore remained competitive after selling a player who had been a regular over the prior two seasons.

sections.heading: Realized Value Gives New York the Win
sections.body: Stutz still had useful basketball left, as his 59-game Baltimore season demonstrates, so Boston's interest was reasonable. The problem is realized value. The Celtics' side of this specific transaction produced no documented regular-season games, while New York received cash and suffered no obvious collapse tied to Stutz's departure. The incomplete record between Boston's acquisition and Stutz's Baltimore season limits confidence in assigning blame to the Celtics, but it does not change the measurable outcome of the rights purchase.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win — New York B+, Boston C. New York sold Stan Stutz's player rights to Boston on October 13, 1948 for cash. The Knicks, Celtics and league transaction logs agree on the rights sale, but the cash amount is not preserved. Stutz never appeared in a regular-season game for Boston after the purchase; his 1948-49 stat line belongs to the Baltimore Bullets, where he played 59 games and averaged 6.3 points and 1.4 assists. The reviewed transaction sources do not document the intervening roster mechanism that put him in Baltimore.

sections.heading: This Is the Same Stan Stutz Transaction
sections.body: Boston’s October 14 intake entry and New York’s October 13 record describe the same transaction: Stan Stutz’s player rights moved from the Knicks to the Celtics for cash. The teams, player and consideration all match, so treating them as two separate trades would double-count one historical move.

sections.heading: Five Logs Point to October 13
sections.body: The Knicks, Celtics and BAA transaction pages all date the sale to October 13, 1948. Ned Irish’s and Walter Brown’s executive transaction histories point to the same date from both front offices, giving the October 13 record the stronger documentary support.

sections.heading: The October 14 Entry Is Preserved for Provenance
sections.body: TradeVerdicts keeps this October 14 listing only so the original Boston intake can still be audited. It is excluded from player-relationship construction and public/indexable consideration rather than being deleted and losing its source trail.

sections.heading: The Record Is Superseded, Not a Second Trade
sections.body: Because this is provenance for the already-counted October 13 Stutz sale, it should not receive a second basketball-value judgment. The correct outcome is structural: preserve the evidence, mark the duplicate date conflict, and prevent the legacy row from creating another transaction. Keeping the row private also makes the source disagreement reviewable without polluting the canonical trade count.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Record Superseded — Boston B-, New York C+. This October 14, 1948 Boston listing is retained only as legacy source provenance. It describes the same Stan Stutz rights-for-cash transaction that authoritative New York, Boston, league and executive transaction logs date to October 13, 1948, so it is not treated as a separate NBA trade.

sections.heading: New York Bought Irv Rothenberg’s Rights
sections.body: On October 25, 1948, the New York Knicks acquired Irv Rothenberg's player rights from the St. Louis Bombers for cash. New York's 1948-49 transaction log records the rights purchase on that date. Rothenberg was already an experienced BAA center: he had played for Cleveland, Washington, Baltimore and St. Louis across the first two league seasons, including 24 games for the Bombers in 1947-48 at 7.8 points per game.

sections.heading: Rothenberg Became a 53-Game Knicks Regular
sections.body: Rothenberg played 53 of the Knicks' 60 regular-season games in 1948-49. He averaged 5.9 points and 1.3 assists, scored 314 points and produced 1.6 win shares. Those numbers were not star-level, but the availability mattered on a 32-28 club that finished second in the BAA Eastern Division. New York beat Baltimore in the division semifinals before losing to Washington in the Eastern Division Finals.

sections.heading: St. Louis Received Undisclosed Cash
sections.body: St. Louis received cash, but the amount and any downstream roster use are not preserved in the sources reviewed for this record. The Bombers had received useful scoring from Rothenberg the previous season, when he averaged 7.8 points in 24 games. Selling his rights therefore removed a player who still had enough value to become a 53-game regular for New York. At the same time, early BAA cash sales were common roster-management tools, and an undisclosed payment prevents a strong claim that St.

sections.heading: New York Got the Clear Basketball Return
sections.body: The measurable basketball return belongs to New York. The Knicks paid an unknown amount and received 53 regular-season games, 314 points and a rotation center on a team that reached the Eastern Division Finals. St. Louis received money that cannot be quantified or connected to a specific later asset. Because Rothenberg's New York tenure lasted only one season and his production was modest, this is not a franchise-changing win.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win — New York A-, St. Louis B. New York acquired Irv Rothenberg's player rights from the St. Louis Bombers for cash on October 25, 1948. Rothenberg had averaged 7.8 points in 24 games for St. Louis the prior season, then became a regular for the Knicks. He played 53 games in 1948-49, averaged 5.9 points and 1.3 assists, and contributed 1.6 win shares as New York finished 32-28 and reached the BAA Eastern Division Finals. The cash amount is not preserved in the reviewed public transaction log.
