sections.heading: Boston Bought Kenny Sailors from Denver
sections.body: On June 22, 1950, the Denver Nuggets sold Kenny Sailors' player rights to the Boston Celtics for cash. Denver's transaction page, Boston's transaction page, the 1949-50 league transaction log and Red Auerbach's executive record all describe the same player-rights sale. The legacy intake classified Sailors as draft rights, but he was a veteran professional who had just completed a full NBA season for Denver.

sections.heading: Sailors Gave the Celtics Immediate Backcourt Help
sections.body: Sailors did not reproduce his Denver role in Boston. He appeared in only 10 Celtics games during 1950-51, averaging 1.8 points, 0.3 rebounds and 0.8 assists while shooting .160 from the field. His value to Boston therefore came more from the asset chain than from direct production. On December 1, 1950, the Celtics traded Sailors and Brady Walker to the Baltimore Bullets for Dick Mehen. Mehen played seven games for Boston before being traded to Fort Wayne for Bob Harris.

sections.heading: Denver Received Cash at the End of Its NBA Run
sections.body: Denver received cash after a season in which Sailors had been its leading-level scorer, but the franchise was leaving the NBA after an 11-51 campaign. Selling player rights during the shutdown process had obvious practical value for an organization with no next NBA season to build toward. The limitation is the same one that affects many cash sales from this era: the amount is not preserved.

sections.heading: The Short but Useful Return Favors Boston
sections.body: Boston's direct basketball return was weak. Sailors went from 17.3 points per game in Denver to 1.8 in 10 Boston appearances, and the Celtics moved him before December. Still, his rights remained tradable and helped Boston acquire Mehen, who was then turned into another player. Denver, by contrast, received undisclosed cash as the franchise exited the league.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win — Boston B-, Denver C+. Boston purchased Kenny Sailors' player rights from the Denver Nuggets for cash on June 22, 1950. Denver, Boston, league and Red Auerbach transaction records all identify a player-rights sale, correcting the legacy draft-rights classification. Sailors had just averaged 17.3 points and 4.0 assists in 57 games for Denver. His Boston stint was much smaller: 10 games at 1.8 points before the Celtics traded Sailors and Brady Walker to Baltimore for Dick Mehen on December 1.

sections.heading: Boston Bought Andy Duncan from Rochester
sections.body: On June 27, 1950, the Rochester Royals sold Andy Duncan's player rights to the Boston Celtics for cash. Rochester's transaction page, Boston's transaction page, the 1949-50 league transaction log and Red Auerbach's executive record all agree on the date and player-rights sale. That evidence corrects two defects in the legacy Boston intake: the record used June 28 and classified Duncan as draft rights. Duncan was already a veteran professional, having played 55 BAA games for Rochester in 1948-49 and 67 NBA games in 1949-50.

sections.heading: Duncan Barely Contributed to the Celtics
sections.body: Duncan's Boston return was brief and modest. He appeared in 14 games during the 1950-51 season, averaging 2.1 points, 2.1 rebounds and 0.6 assists while shooting .175 from the field. He scored 29 total points for the Celtics and did not appear in another NBA season. That leaves Boston with a very small realized basketball return from the purchase.

sections.heading: The Royals Took Cash for an Expendable Player
sections.body: Rochester received cash for a player whose role had already declined from 7.4 points per game in 1948-49 to 4.6 in 1949-50. The Royals then entered the 1950-51 season without Duncan and won the NBA championship. That team success does not itself prove the sale was valuable, but it shows Rochester was able to move on from a reserve without creating an obvious roster problem. The limitation is the missing sale price.

sections.heading: The Failed Purchase Gives Rochester the Edge
sections.body: The surviving evidence favors Rochester because Boston received almost no lasting player value. Duncan played only 14 games, scored 29 points and was out of the NBA after the season. Rochester at least converted his rights into cash after two seasons of service. The unknown price prevents a high-confidence claim about how profitable the sale was, but Boston's return is concrete enough to evaluate and was minimal. This is therefore a small historical win for the Royals rather than an important franchise transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Royals Win — Boston D+, Rochester C+. Boston purchased Andy Duncan's player rights from the Rochester Royals for cash on June 27, 1950. Authoritative Rochester, Boston, league and Red Auerbach transaction records establish the June 27 date, correcting the legacy June 28 intake record, and show this as a player-rights sale rather than a draft-rights transaction. Duncan had already played two seasons for Rochester, including 67 games at 4.6 points per game in 1949-50.

sections.heading: Boston Sold Bob Doll to Minneapolis
sections.body: On July 28, 1950, the Boston Celtics sold Bob Doll's player rights to the Minneapolis Lakers for cash. Boston's 1950-51 transaction page, Minneapolis' transaction page, the league transaction log and Red Auerbach's executive record all identify the same rights sale. Doll was 30 and had already completed four BAA/NBA seasons, including the previous two in Boston. He appeared in 47 Celtics games during 1949-50, averaging 6.7 points and 2.3 assists while shooting .346 from the field.

sections.heading: The Lakers Never Got an NBA Game from Doll
sections.body: Boston received cash and cleared a veteran from the roster before Red Auerbach's first season as coach. That return is modest because the sale price is unknown, but hindsight provides an unusually clear clue about the underlying asset value: Doll never played another NBA game. The Celtics had already received 94 regular-season games from him over two seasons, so the transaction monetized residual rights after his Boston contribution was complete rather than moving a young player who later broke out elsewhere.

sections.heading: The Celtics Converted the Rights into Cash
sections.body: Minneapolis acquired Doll's rights but never received an NBA appearance from him. The Lakers' transaction log shows that the club released him on October 30, 1950, before he played a regular-season game for the team. Basketball-Reference lists Doll's 1949-50 Boston season as the final season of his four-year BAA/NBA career. The Lakers therefore paid cash for an asset that produced no on-court return and no documented downstream trade value.

sections.heading: The Buyer’s Zero Return Gives Boston the Win
sections.body: The historical comparison favors Boston despite the missing cash figure. The Celtics received a financial return for rights they no longer needed, while Minneapolis released Doll three months later without using him in a game. There is no later player, pick or trade chain on the Lakers' side that offsets the purchase. The unknown sale amount prevents Boston from receiving a high grade because the size of the benefit cannot be measured, but the direction of realized value is still clear.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win — Boston C+, Minneapolis D. Boston sold Bob Doll's player rights to the Minneapolis Lakers for cash on July 28, 1950. Doll had spent the previous two seasons with the Celtics, including 47 games at 6.7 points and 2.3 assists in 1949-50. Minneapolis never received an NBA appearance from him: the Lakers released Doll on October 30, and his four-year BAA/NBA career ended with his final Boston season. The reviewed transaction records do not preserve the cash amount.

sections.heading: New York Sent Paul Noel to Rochester
sections.body: On August 10, 1950, the New York Knicks traded Paul Noel to the Rochester Royals for Ray Ellefson. New York's transaction page, Rochester's transaction page and the 1950-51 league transaction log all agree on the August 10 date, correcting the legacy August 15 intake record. This was a direct player-for-player exchange with no draft picks or cash documented. Noel entered the deal after three seasons with New York, including 65 games at 3.8 points per game in 1949-50.

sections.heading: Noel Gave the Royals Two Seasons
sections.body: Noel supplied the larger body of service. He appeared in 52 games for Rochester in 1950-51, averaging 2.5 points, 1.6 rebounds and 0.7 assists. He was a reserve rather than a central scorer, but he stayed available across a season in which the Royals went 41-27 and won the NBA championship by defeating New York in seven games. Noel returned for eight more games in 1951-52, bringing his Rochester total to 60 regular-season appearances.

sections.heading: Ellefson Lasted Three Knicks Games
sections.body: Ellefson's Knicks tenure was extremely short. He appeared in three games during the 1950-51 season, averaged 1.3 points and 2.7 rebounds, and scored four total points. Those three games were the final NBA appearances of his career. New York still reached the 1951 NBA Finals, so the failed acquisition did not prevent a successful season, but the trade itself produced almost no realized player value for the Knicks.

sections.heading: Sixty Games Beat Three
sections.body: Neither side acquired a star, but the gap in usable service is clear. Noel played 60 games for Rochester across two seasons and was part of the franchise's 1951 championship roster. Ellefson played three games for New York and then left the NBA. Noel's low scoring average keeps this from becoming a major historical win, and the Royals' championship should not be credited to one reserve transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Royals Win — New York D, Rochester C+. New York traded Paul Noel to the Rochester Royals for Ray Ellefson on August 10, 1950, correcting the legacy August 15 intake date. Noel became the more durable piece, appearing in 52 games for Rochester during its 1950-51 championship season and eight more the next year. Ellefson played only three games for the Knicks, scoring four total points, and never appeared in another NBA season. Neither player became a major contributor, but Rochester received 60 games from Noel while New York received three from Ellefson.

sections.heading: Boston Bought Bob Brannum’s Rights
sections.body: On September 23, 1950, the Sheboygan Red Skins sold Bob Brannum's player rights to the Boston Celtics for cash. Boston's transaction page, the 1950-51 league transaction log and Red Auerbach's executive record all identify the same rights acquisition. The reviewed public sources do not preserve the cash amount. Brannum had been one of Sheboygan's most productive players in 1949-50, averaging 12.1 points and 3.5 assists across 59 NBA games.

sections.heading: Brannum Became Four Seasons of Celtics Depth
sections.body: Once Brannum reached Boston, the Celtics received far more than a short-term reserve. He appeared in 66 games in 1951-52, averaging 6.1 points and 6.2 rebounds, then remained with the club through 1954-55. Across four Boston seasons he played 279 regular-season games and averaged 6.2 points, 7.0 rebounds and 1.8 assists. He was not an All-Star, but he became a durable frontcourt piece during Red Auerbach's early years and supplied more than 1,600 rebounds over his Celtics tenure.

sections.heading: Sheboygan Monetized Rights After Leaving the NBA
sections.body: Sheboygan received cash after the franchise's final NBA season. The Red Skins had gone 22-40 in 1949-50 and left the NBA afterward, so the organization no longer had an NBA roster on which to use Brannum. That context makes selling his rights understandable. The problem for hindsight grading is that the cash amount and any downstream use are not documented in the reviewed public sources.

sections.heading: 279 Games Make Boston the Clear Winner
sections.body: The result favors Boston by a wide margin because the Celtics eventually received 279 games from Brannum. The one-season delay before his Boston debut keeps the transaction from being evaluated as an immediate 1950-51 roster win, but it does not erase the longer return. Sheboygan's position was structurally different from an active NBA franchise because the Red Skins had left the league, and monetizing player rights was rational. Even so, an undisclosed payment cannot be shown to match four seasons of productive NBA service.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win — Boston A-, Sheboygan C. Boston acquired Bob Brannum's player rights from the Sheboygan Red Skins for cash on September 23, 1950. Brannum did not play in the NBA during 1950-51, spending that season in the NPBL, but he joined the Celtics in 1951-52 and stayed four seasons. He appeared in 279 regular-season games for Boston, averaging 6.2 points and 7.0 rebounds, after having averaged 12.1 points for Sheboygan in 1949-50. The sale price is not preserved in the reviewed public records.

sections.heading: Boston Bought Harry Boykoff’s Rights
sections.body: On November 5, 1950, the Baltimore Bullets sold Harry Boykoff's player rights to the Boston Celtics for cash. Baltimore's transaction page, Boston's transaction page and the 1950-51 league transaction log all record the same rights sale. The public transaction record does not preserve the cash amount. Boykoff had been a productive scorer for the Washington Capitols in 1949-50, averaging 12.8 points and 2.4 assists across 61 games.

sections.heading: Boykoff Filled 32 Games Before Another Trade
sections.body: Boykoff contributed immediately. He appeared in 32 games for Boston during 1950-51, averaging 6.3 points, 4.2 rebounds and 1.3 assists. His role was smaller than it had been in Washington, but the Celtics received useful frontcourt minutes before turning the asset into another player. On February 3, 1951, Boston traded Boykoff to the Tri-Cities Blackhawks for Kleggie Hermsen.

sections.heading: Baltimore Took Cash for an Unused Asset
sections.body: Baltimore received cash and gave up only Boykoff's player rights. The amount is not available in the reviewed public sources, so the Bullets' return cannot be quantified or compared directly with Boston's later on-court value. Boykoff did not play a game for Baltimore before the sale, which means the club monetized an asset rather than removing an active rotation player.

sections.heading: Hermsen Extended Boston’s Return
sections.body: Boston's advantage comes from the full asset chain rather than Boykoff alone. The Celtics received 32 games from Boykoff, then exchanged him for Hermsen and received another 27 regular-season games from that player across two Boston stints. Neither center became a star, so the transaction belongs in the minor-deal category. Still, Boston turned an undisclosed cash payment into two usable NBA players.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win — Boston B-, Baltimore C+. Boston purchased Harry Boykoff's player rights from the Baltimore Bullets for cash on November 5, 1950. Boykoff immediately became a rotation center, playing 32 games for the Celtics at 6.3 points and 4.2 rebounds per game. Boston then traded him to the Tri-Cities Blackhawks on February 3, 1951 for Kleggie Hermsen, who played 23 games for the Celtics that season and four more in 1952-53. The sale price is not preserved, so Baltimore's financial return cannot be measured.

sections.heading: Syracuse Sold Ed Bartels’ Rights
sections.body: On November 29, 1950, the Syracuse Nationals sold Ed Bartels' player rights to the Baltimore Bullets for cash. Syracuse's transaction page, Baltimore's transaction page, the 1950-51 league transaction log and Leo Ferris' executive record all agree on the sale. The amount is not preserved in the reviewed public sources. The unusual part is Bartels' status at the time: RealGM records him signing with the Washington Capitols on September 1, and Basketball-Reference lists all 17 of his 1950-51 NBA games with Washington.

sections.heading: The Nationals Turned an Unused Claim into Cash
sections.body: Syracuse's return was cash for a player who never appeared in a Nationals uniform. That makes the transaction easy to understand from the seller's perspective even though the amount is unknown. The Nationals converted an unused rights position into immediate financial consideration and did not sacrifice documented NBA production from their own roster.

sections.heading: Bartels Never Played for Baltimore
sections.body: Baltimore's basketball return is much harder to identify. The Bullets' transaction page says they acquired Bartels' rights on November 29, but he never played for Baltimore. Basketball-Reference credits his 1950-51 season entirely to Washington, where he averaged 4.2 points, 4.9 rebounds and 0.7 assists in 17 games. RealGM's Washington timeline also shows Bartels signing with the Capitols before the Baltimore rights purchase and being waived by Washington in January 1951.

sections.heading: The Unclear Mechanics Still Favor Syracuse
sections.body: The archival record favors Syracuse slightly because the Nationals turned an unused asset into cash while Baltimore has no traceable on-court or downstream return. That conclusion should remain modest, however, because the transaction mechanics are not fully explained by the surviving sources. Bartels' Washington contract predates the November 29 rights sale, and the public record does not clarify whether Baltimore acquired a contingent, residual or otherwise limited rights interest.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nationals Win — Syracuse C+, Baltimore D+. Syracuse sold Ed Bartels' player rights to the Baltimore Bullets for cash on November 29, 1950. The transaction is well documented in Syracuse, Baltimore and league records, but Bartels' playing timeline makes the realized return unusually murky: he had signed with the Washington Capitols before the sale, played 17 games for Washington in 1950-51, and never appeared for Baltimore. The reviewed public sources do not preserve the cash amount or explain how Baltimore's rights position interacted with Bartels' Washington contract.

sections.heading: Rochester Sold Ed Mikan to Washington
sections.body: On November 29, 1950, the Rochester Royals sold Ed Mikan's player rights to the Washington Capitols for cash. Rochester's transaction page and the 1950-51 league transaction log agree on the date and sale structure. Mikan was already an established NBA center, having played 60 games for the Chicago Stags as a rookie and 44 games for Rochester in 1949-50.

sections.heading: Mikan’s Role Expanded with the Capitols
sections.body: Mikan became more productive immediately after the sale. Basketball-Reference credits him with 18 Washington games in 1950-51 at 8.9 points, 5.3 rebounds and 2.0 assists per game. Those averages made him one of the Capitols' more productive frontcourt players during his brief stay. The problem is duration. Washington folded in January 1951, so the franchise could not extract a long-term return from the acquisition.

sections.heading: The Royals Took Cash and Won the Championship
sections.body: Rochester received cash for a player whose role had been modest in the opening stretch of the season. The Royals were able to move on from Mikan and still finish 41-27 before winning the 1951 NBA championship. That team success does not prove the sale itself was valuable, but it shows the transaction did not create an obvious roster hole for Rochester.

sections.heading: Eighteen Productive Games Give Washington the Edge
sections.body: Washington received the clearer basketball value because Mikan's 18-game stretch produced nearly nine points and more than five rebounds per game. Rochester's return was real but unquantified. Even so, the gap should not be exaggerated. The Capitols folded only weeks after acquiring Mikan, which cuts off the possibility of a multi-season benefit and makes this very different from a successful long-term player purchase. Rochester, meanwhile, sold a reserve and proceeded to win the championship.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Capitols Win — Rochester C+, Washington B-. Rochester sold Ed Mikan's player rights to the Washington Capitols for cash on November 29, 1950. Mikan had played 10 games for the Royals that season before the sale, averaging 4.3 points and 2.5 rebounds. He then became a much larger part of Washington's rotation, averaging 8.9 points, 5.3 rebounds and 2.0 assists across 18 games before the Capitols folded in January 1951. The cash amount is not preserved.

sections.heading: Boston Sent Sailors and Walker to Baltimore
sections.body: On December 1, 1950, the Baltimore Bullets traded Dick Mehen to the Boston Celtics for Kenny Sailors and Brady Walker. Baltimore's transaction page, Boston's transaction page and the 1950-51 league transaction log all identify the same three-player exchange. Boston was moving two reserves who had combined for only 27 Celtics appearances before the trade, while Baltimore sent out a frontcourt player who had been part of its own rotation.

sections.heading: The Bullets Got Two Rotation Players
sections.body: Baltimore received substantially more immediate playing time from the two-player package. Kenny Sailors appeared in 50 games for the Bullets in 1950-51, averaging 9.5 points, 2.3 rebounds and 2.8 assists. Brady Walker appeared in 49 games and averaged 7.5 points, 6.6 rebounds and 2.1 assists. Neither became a star, but together they supplied nearly 100 player-games and filled meaningful guard and frontcourt roles for a Baltimore team that lacked depth.

sections.heading: Mehen’s Seven Celtics Games Led to Bob Harris
sections.body: Dick Mehen's direct Boston tenure was brief. He played seven games for the Celtics, averaging 6.3 points, 3.7 rebounds and 1.6 assists. Boston then moved him to the Fort Wayne Pistons on December 19 for Bob Harris. Harris became the more durable part of Boston's asset chain, appearing in 44 games that season at 5.5 points and 5.6 rebounds per game. That downstream conversion matters because it prevents the Celtics' side from being evaluated as only seven Mehen games.

sections.heading: Ninety-Nine Combined Games Favor Baltimore
sections.body: Baltimore still comes out ahead because Sailors and Walker produced more combined service and stronger immediate rotation value than Boston received from Mehen and the first Harris season. The Celtics deserve credit for turning a short-lived acquisition into another contributor, which narrows the gap considerably. This is not a case where one side received nothing.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bullets Win — Boston B-, Baltimore B+. Boston traded Kenny Sailors and Brady Walker to the Baltimore Bullets for Dick Mehen on December 1, 1950. Baltimore received the larger immediate return: Sailors played 50 games for the Bullets at 9.5 points and 2.8 assists per game, while Walker played 49 games at 7.5 points and 6.6 rebounds. Mehen lasted only seven games in Boston at 6.3 points and 3.7 rebounds before the Celtics traded him to Fort Wayne for Bob Harris on December 19.

sections.heading: Fort Wayne Sold John Hargis to Tri-Cities
sections.body: On December 8, 1950, the Fort Wayne Pistons sold John Hargis' player rights to the Tri-Cities Blackhawks for cash. Tri-Cities' transaction page and the 1950-51 league transaction log identify the same rights sale. Hargis was not an unknown prospect: he had averaged 10.7 points in 60 games for the Anderson Packers in 1949-50, then moved into a much smaller role with Fort Wayne.

sections.heading: Hargis Gave the Blackhawks 15 Games
sections.body: Hargis joined the Blackhawks and appeared in 15 games, averaging 3.7 points, 2.4 rebounds and 1.1 assists. That gave Tri-Cities a real but limited return: a veteran guard-forward who could fill minutes during a difficult 25-43 season. He did not reproduce his Anderson scoring level, and those 15 games were the final NBA appearances of his career.

sections.heading: The Pistons Took Cash from a Shrinking Role
sections.body: Fort Wayne received cash after using Hargis for only 14 games. The Pistons were 32-36 and reached the Western Division semifinals, so moving a reduced-role veteran did not prevent a playoff appearance. The sale amount is unknown, which makes it impossible to determine whether Fort Wayne captured more economic value than Tri-Cities received in 15 games of reserve production. Still, the Pistons converted a player they no longer needed into an immediate financial return rather than simply losing him with no compensation.

sections.heading: The Results Are Nearly Even
sections.body: The difference between the two sides is small. Tri-Cities received 15 games and 56 total points from Hargis, while Fort Wayne received an undisclosed cash payment and avoided giving up any other asset. Because Hargis' NBA career ended after the season, the Blackhawks did not gain a long-term player or a later trade chip. That keeps the transaction far below the level of a meaningful franchise win.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Blackhawks Edge — Tri-Cities C+, Fort Wayne C+. Fort Wayne sold John Hargis' player rights to the Tri-Cities Blackhawks for cash on December 8, 1950. Hargis had played 14 games for the Pistons that season, averaging 4.8 points and 2.1 rebounds, after a 10.7-point season with Anderson the year before. He then appeared in 15 games for Tri-Cities at 3.7 points, 2.4 rebounds and 1.1 assists before his NBA career ended. The cash amount is not preserved.

sections.heading: Fort Wayne Bought Don Otten from Baltimore
sections.body: On December 8, 1950, the Baltimore Bullets sold Don Otten's player rights to the Fort Wayne Pistons for cash. Baltimore's transaction page, Fort Wayne's transaction page and the 1950-51 league transaction log all identify the same sale. Baltimore had acquired Otten's rights from the Washington Capitols on November 29, so the Bullets held the asset for only nine days. Otten appeared in two Baltimore games during that window, totaling 11 points and three rebounds.

sections.heading: Otten Became a Pistons Regular
sections.body: Otten immediately became a much more useful player for the Pistons. He appeared in 49 Fort Wayne games during 1950-51 and averaged 8.4 points, 6.0 rebounds and 0.8 assists. He also played three playoff games, adding 9.7 points and 6.3 rebounds per game in Fort Wayne's first-round series against Rochester. Otten returned for seven regular-season games in 1951-52 before the Pistons released him in November.

sections.heading: Baltimore Flipped the Rights for Cash in Nine Days
sections.body: Baltimore received cash after only a brief look at Otten. The Bullets had gone from acquiring his rights on November 29 to selling them on December 8, so the transaction functioned almost like a rapid asset flip. That may have made practical financial sense, but the missing sale amount prevents the return from being valued. There is no documented player, pick or later transaction directly tied to the payment.

sections.heading: Fifty-Six Games Give Fort Wayne the Win
sections.body: Fort Wayne clearly received more traceable value. Otten became a regular center, played nearly three quarters of the 1950-51 schedule for the Pistons and contributed in the playoffs. Baltimore's two-game stint with him before the sale was negligible, and the cash return cannot be compared numerically. The result still belongs in the minor-to-moderate category because Otten was released less than a year later and did not become a long-term Pistons fixture.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Fort Wayne B+, Baltimore C. Fort Wayne acquired Don Otten's player rights from the Baltimore Bullets for cash on December 8, 1950, only nine days after Baltimore had obtained those rights from the Washington Capitols. Otten played just two games for Baltimore before the sale, then became a regular Fort Wayne center. He appeared in 49 Pistons games in 1950-51, averaging 8.4 points and 6.0 rebounds, and returned for seven more games the next season before his release. The cash amount is not preserved.

sections.heading: Syracuse Sold Belus Smawley to Baltimore
sections.body: On December 10, 1950, the Syracuse Nationals sold Belus Smawley's player rights to the Baltimore Bullets for cash. Syracuse's transaction page, Baltimore's transaction page and the 1950-51 league transaction log all identify the same sale. Smawley was already a proven professional scorer, having averaged 15.5 points for St. Louis in 1948-49 and 13.7 in 1949-50.

sections.heading: Smawley Reclaimed a Major Scoring Role
sections.body: Smawley immediately regained a larger scoring role with the Bullets. He played 44 games for Baltimore during the rest of 1950-51 and averaged 13.8 points, 3.0 rebounds and 2.8 assists while shooting .389 from the field and .859 at the line. That made him one of the team's most productive perimeter scorers alongside Red Rocha and gave Baltimore far more direct value than a short reserve stint.

sections.heading: The Nationals Monetized a Reduced Role
sections.body: Syracuse received cash and moved on from a veteran whose role had already contracted. The Nationals finished 32-34 and reached the Eastern Division semifinals, so the sale did not remove a central piece from a contending rotation. The limitation is the missing dollar figure. Without the amount, Syracuse's financial return cannot be measured against the 607 points Smawley scored for Baltimore in the remainder of 1950-51 or traced to a later roster asset.

sections.heading: Baltimore Bought Fifty-Five Games of Production
sections.body: Baltimore's advantage is clear because Smawley became a productive scorer immediately after the purchase. His 13.8 points per game with the Bullets nearly doubled his 7.8-point Syracuse average from earlier in the same season, and he played 44 games after the deal rather than serving as a brief replacement. Syracuse had a rational reason to monetize a veteran who was playing a smaller role, but the unknown cash amount leaves the Nationals without measurable basketball value on the other side.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bullets Win — Syracuse C, Baltimore A-. Syracuse sold Belus Smawley's player rights to the Baltimore Bullets for cash on December 10, 1950. Smawley had averaged 7.8 points in 16 games for the Nationals that season, then became one of Baltimore's leading scorers. He played 44 games for the Bullets at 13.8 points, 3.0 rebounds and 2.8 assists per game, then returned for 11 more games in 1951-52. The sale price is not preserved in the reviewed public records.

sections.heading: Minneapolis Sold Ed Beach to Tri-Cities
sections.body: On December 11, 1950, the Minneapolis Lakers sold Ed Beach's player rights to the Tri-Cities Blackhawks for cash. Minneapolis' transaction page, Tri-Cities' transaction page and the 1950-51 league transaction log all identify the same sale. Beach had been Minneapolis' fifth-round pick in the 1950 NBA Draft, 59th overall, and had already appeared in 11 games for the Lakers before the transaction. He averaged 2.0 points, 2.3 rebounds and 0.2 assists in those appearances.

sections.heading: Beach Played One Scoreless Blackhawks Game
sections.body: The Blackhawks received almost no realized basketball value from the purchase. Beach appeared in one game for Tri-Cities, missed all three of his field-goal attempts, scored no points and recorded one assist. That single appearance was also the last NBA game of his career. He did not become a rotation player, later trade chip or multi-season roster piece for the Blackhawks. The transaction therefore produced a technically real but extremely small on-court return.

sections.heading: The Lakers Turned a Fringe Rookie into Cash
sections.body: Minneapolis received cash for a player who had been used sparingly on a defending-champion roster. Beach's 11 Lakers appearances produced only 22 total points, and the club remained strong after moving him, finishing 44-24 and reaching the Western Division Finals. Because the payment amount is unknown, the Lakers' financial return cannot be measured precisely. Even so, the franchise converted a marginal roster asset into compensation rather than carrying a player who was not part of the main rotation.

sections.heading: One Game Makes the Sale a Minneapolis Win
sections.body: The Lakers hold the narrow edge because the Blackhawks' return was limited to one scoreless game. This is not a major historical win: the cash amount is unknown, Beach was a fifth-round rookie, and neither side gave up a meaningful long-term asset. Still, the realized comparison is straightforward. Minneapolis received financial value and lost almost no production, while Tri-Cities paid for rights that generated only one NBA appearance. The surviving record supports a modest Lakers advantage rather than the legacy even-grade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win — Minneapolis C+, Tri-Cities D. Minneapolis sold Ed Beach's player rights to the Tri-Cities Blackhawks for cash on December 11, 1950. Beach had played 11 games for the Lakers as a rookie, averaging 2.0 points and 2.3 rebounds, after Minneapolis selected him in the fifth round of the 1950 NBA Draft. He appeared only once for Tri-Cities, recording no points and one assist, and never played another NBA game. The cash amount is not preserved in the reviewed public records.

sections.heading: Tri-Cities Sent Jorgensen and Cash to Syracuse
sections.body: On December 13, 1950, the Tri-Cities Blackhawks traded Noble Jorgensen and cash to the Syracuse Nationals for Ed Peterson. Tri-Cities' transaction page, Syracuse's transaction page, the league transaction log and executive records for Ben Kerner and Leo Ferris all identify the same exchange. Jorgensen had averaged 11.2 points and 5.1 rebounds in 22 Tri-Cities games that season. Peterson had averaged 4.7 points and 2.2 rebounds in 17 games for Syracuse.

sections.heading: Peterson Helped the Blackhawks for 36 Games
sections.body: Peterson gave the Blackhawks a respectable short-term return. He appeared in 36 games after the trade and averaged 7.8 points, 6.9 rebounds and 1.6 assists. His rebounding role was especially useful for a team that needed frontcourt size, and his scoring improved from the smaller role he had occupied in Syracuse. The limitation is duration. Those 36 games were the last regular-season appearances of Peterson's NBA career, so Tri-Cities did not receive a multi-season player or a later trade asset from the deal.

sections.heading: Jorgensen Stayed Three Seasons in Syracuse
sections.body: Jorgensen became a larger and much more durable piece for the Nationals. He played 41 games for Syracuse in the remainder of 1950-51, averaging 9.3 points, 5.5 rebounds and 1.6 assists. He then stayed for two more full seasons, appearing in 66 games in 1951-52 and 70 in 1952-53. Across his Syracuse tenure after the trade, Jorgensen played 177 regular-season games. He also participated in the playoffs in each of those seasons. Syracuse received that multi-year center production plus an undisclosed cash payment.

sections.heading: Durability and Cash Put the Nationals Ahead
sections.body: Tri-Cities received a useful player, so this is not a one-sided transaction in the sense of one team getting nothing. Peterson played 36 games and rebounded well. Syracuse still owns the stronger return because Jorgensen was productive immediately and remained part of the rotation for three seasons. The 177-game Syracuse tenure creates a large durability gap, and the cash component moves in the same direction rather than offsetting it. That combination makes the Nationals' advantage clearer than the legacy grade suggested.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nationals Win — Tri-Cities C+, Syracuse A-. Tri-Cities traded Noble Jorgensen and cash to the Syracuse Nationals for Ed Peterson on December 13, 1950. Peterson became a useful short-term center for the Blackhawks, averaging 7.8 points, 6.9 rebounds and 1.6 assists in 36 games, but his NBA career ended after the season. Jorgensen immediately gave Syracuse more scoring and stayed far longer: 9.3 points and 5.5 rebounds across 41 games in 1950-51, followed by 66 games in 1951-52 and 70 in 1952-53.

sections.heading: Boston and Fort Wayne Swapped Harris and Mehen
sections.body: On December 19, 1950, the Fort Wayne Pistons traded Bob Harris to the Boston Celtics for Dick Mehen. Boston's transaction page, Fort Wayne's transaction page, the 1950-51 league transaction log and Red Auerbach's executive record all identify the same player-for-player exchange. Mehen had been in Boston for only seven games after arriving from Baltimore on December 1. Harris had appeared in 12 Fort Wayne games that season. The trade therefore moved two players who were already being treated as movable rotation pieces rather than long-term franchise anchors.

sections.heading: Harris Gave Boston Useful Frontcourt Depth
sections.body: Harris became a useful frontcourt rebounder for the Celtics. Basketball-Reference credits him with 44 Boston games in 1950-51 at 5.5 points, 5.6 rebounds and 1.3 assists per game. He later made brief appearances for Boston in three additional seasons, so the Celtics did receive continuing roster value beyond the first year. Harris was never a major scorer, but he supplied more immediate games than Mehen had given Boston and fit as depth behind the club's more prominent frontcourt players.

sections.heading: Mehen Later Helped Bring Frankie Brian to Fort Wayne
sections.body: Mehen gave the Pistons 43 games during the rest of 1950-51, averaging 6.5 points, 2.8 rebounds and 1.2 assists. The more important value came after the season. On May 31, 1951, Fort Wayne traded Mehen, Howie Schultz and cash to the Tri-Cities Blackhawks for Frankie Brian. Brian became an All-Star for Fort Wayne in 1951-52, appearing in 66 games and scoring 1,051 points, then remained a major part of the Pistons the following season.

sections.heading: The Brian Conversion Separates the Pistons
sections.body: Boston's side was respectable. Harris gave the Celtics 44 games immediately and remained available for later short stints. Fort Wayne's side still separates because Mehen's value did not end with his 43-game Pistons run. Converting him into part of the Frankie Brian package created a second, much larger return that directly followed from the asset acquired in this trade. That downstream path is the kind of traceable conversion that matters in a hindsight review and was not captured by the legacy grade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Boston B-, Fort Wayne A-. Fort Wayne traded Bob Harris to the Boston Celtics for Dick Mehen on December 19, 1950. Harris became useful Boston depth, playing 44 games that season at 5.5 points and 5.6 rebounds per game, with brief Celtics appearances in later seasons. Mehen gave Fort Wayne 43 games at 6.5 points and 2.8 rebounds, then became part of a May 1951 package with Howie Schultz and cash that brought All-Star guard Frankie Brian to the Pistons. That downstream conversion creates the decisive value gap.

sections.heading: The December 22 Listing Fails the Source Check
sections.body: The cited Fort Wayne and league transaction evidence does not support a December 22, 1950 cash purchase of Charlie Share from the Hawks. The imported row is a legacy source conflict, not a separately verified NBA trade.

sections.heading: The Real Share Rights Trade Happened in April 1951
sections.body: The documented Share transaction in this period is Boston’s April 26, 1951 trade with Fort Wayne for Bill Sharman. That deal is independently preserved as its own canonical TradeVerdicts record and is supported by the Celtics, Pistons and league transaction logs.

sections.heading: The Legacy Row Would Double-Count a Different Transaction
sections.body: Keeping the December row as another completed trade would create a false extra movement for Share and distort team and player relationship histories. Its value is archival only: it shows what the older source package claimed and why that claim was rejected.

sections.heading: Preserve the Provenance but Supersede the Trade
sections.body: TradeVerdicts therefore keeps the route private for provenance while excluding it from public/indexable treatment and hindsight grading. No winner or team grades should be invented for a transaction the surviving source record does not establish.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Resolution
finalVerdict.body: Record Superseded. This legacy listing is retained only as a disputed historical record and is not treated as a separate NBA trade. No team grade is assigned because the record is retained for provenance rather than treated as a completed transaction.

sources.title: Basketball-Reference Boston 1950-51 transactions documenting the real Share-for-Sharman rights trade in April 1951.

sections.heading: Tri-Cities and Boston Exchanged Hermsen and Boykoff
sections.body: On February 3, 1951, the Tri-Cities Blackhawks traded Kleggie Hermsen to the Boston Celtics for Harry Boykoff. Tri-Cities' transaction page, Boston's transaction page and the 1950-51 league transaction log all identify the same one-for-one exchange. The archive stores Hermsen under his given name, Clarence Hermsen, while Basketball-Reference uses the familiar Kleggie Hermsen name. Boykoff had played 32 Boston games at 6.3 points and 4.2 rebounds before the swap. Hermsen had appeared in 48 Tri-Cities games at 8.0 points and 6.8 rebounds.

sections.heading: Boykoff Produced 16 Blackhawks Games
sections.body: Boykoff gave the Blackhawks 16 games over the remainder of the season. He averaged 7.8 points, 5.3 rebounds and 1.3 assists, which was a modest scoring increase from his Boston role. That production was useful, but it was also the end of Boykoff's NBA career. He did not return the next season and created no documented downstream trade value for Tri-Cities. The Blackhawks therefore received a short-term center who helped for several weeks without becoming a lasting roster asset.

sections.heading: Hermsen Lasted a Little Longer in Boston
sections.body: Hermsen played 23 games for Boston in 1950-51, averaging 6.5 points, 5.3 rebounds and 0.9 assists. He did not play in 1951-52, then returned for four brief Celtics appearances in 1952-53 before finishing the season with Indianapolis. Boston's return was hardly transformative, but it lasted longer than Boykoff's Tri-Cities stint and produced more total regular-season games. The later four-game return also shows the Celtics retained some control of the asset beyond the initial season.

sections.heading: A Small Service Gap Gives Boston the Edge
sections.body: The gap is small because both players were short-term contributors with similar rebounding numbers. Boykoff was slightly more productive as a scorer after the trade, while Hermsen gave Boston more games and a longer connection to the roster. Neither side turned the player into a major later asset, and neither return changed the trajectory of the franchise. The surviving record therefore supports only a slight Boston edge, based primarily on duration and total service rather than a dramatic difference in quality.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Celtics Edge — Tri-Cities C, Boston C+. Tri-Cities traded Clarence 'Kleggie' Hermsen to the Boston Celtics for Harry Boykoff on February 3, 1951. Boykoff played 16 games for the Blackhawks, averaging 7.8 points and 5.3 rebounds, but those were the final NBA games of his career. Hermsen gave Boston 23 games at 6.5 points and 5.3 rebounds in 1950-51, then returned for four brief appearances in 1952-53. Neither player became a long-term piece, but Boston received more total service and a slightly longer asset life.

sections.heading: Boston Sold John Mahnken to Indianapolis
sections.body: On February 12, 1951, the Boston Celtics sold John Mahnken's player rights to the Indianapolis Olympians for cash. Boston's transaction page, Indianapolis' transaction page, the 1950-51 league transaction log and Red Auerbach's executive record all agree on the sale. Mahnken had been a regular Boston center, appearing in 46 games before the transaction and averaging 5.2 points, 4.0 rebounds and 1.5 assists. The reviewed sources do not preserve the cash amount, so Boston's financial return cannot be measured directly.

sections.heading: The Olympians Got 12 Games and a Playoff Stint
sections.body: Mahnken appeared in 12 regular-season games for Indianapolis after the purchase. His role and production dropped sharply, to 2.3 points, 2.9 rebounds and 0.8 assists per game while shooting .170 from the field. He also appeared in all three of the Olympians' playoff games against Minneapolis, averaging 1.3 points, 3.7 rebounds and 3.0 assists. That gives Indianapolis a real but limited on-court return. The acquisition did not become a long-term roster piece for the Olympians.

sections.heading: Boston Took Cash for a Replaceable Rotation Player
sections.body: Boston received cash for a player who had been part of the rotation but whose role could be replaced. The amount is unknown, which prevents a precise financial grade. Mahnken then appears back on Boston's 1951-52 roster for 60 games and again for 69 games in 1952-53. The reviewed Basketball-Reference transaction logs do not show how he returned to the Celtics, so that later Boston service should not be credited as a documented downstream return from this sale.

sections.heading: The Short Rental Leaves Boston Slightly Ahead
sections.body: Indianapolis bought a veteran center and received 12 regular-season games plus a short playoff stint. Boston received an undisclosed cash payment and gave up only a partial-season contribution. Neither side produced a major asset outcome from the transaction itself. Because Mahnken's Indianapolis production was limited and the Olympians did not retain him into the next season, the slight edge goes to Boston for monetizing the rights. The unknown cash amount keeps that advantage modest rather than decisive.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Celtics Edge — Boston C+, Indianapolis C. Boston sold John Mahnken's player rights to the Indianapolis Olympians for cash on February 12, 1951. Mahnken had played 46 games for the Celtics that season at 5.2 points, 4.0 rebounds and 1.5 assists per game. Indianapolis received only 12 regular-season games from him, with his production falling to 2.3 points and 2.9 rebounds, plus three playoff appearances. Mahnken was back with Boston the following season, though the reviewed transaction logs do not document the mechanism of that return.

sections.heading: Syracuse Sold Don Lofgran to Indianapolis
sections.body: On February 12, 1951, the Syracuse Nationals sold Don Lofgran's player rights to the Indianapolis Olympians for cash. Syracuse's transaction page, Indianapolis' transaction page and the 1950-51 league transaction log all identify the same sale. Lofgran had been Syracuse's first-round pick in the 1950 NBA Draft and had appeared in 47 games for the Nationals, averaging 3.4 points, 2.0 rebounds and 0.6 assists. The reviewed public records do not preserve the amount Indianapolis paid.

sections.heading: Lofgran Became a Two-Season Olympians Regular
sections.body: Lofgran became a larger part of the Olympians' rotation almost immediately. He played 14 games in the remainder of 1950-51 and averaged 5.4 points and 4.6 rebounds. He returned for 63 games in 1951-52, averaging 7.2 points, 4.1 rebounds and 0.8 assists. That gave Indianapolis 77 regular-season games across two seasons from the cash purchase. The asset then produced a second return: on September 11, 1952, Indianapolis traded Lofgran to the Philadelphia Warriors for Mel Payton.

sections.heading: Indianapolis Later Turned Lofgran into Mel Payton
sections.body: Payton became a regular for Indianapolis in 1952-53, the franchise's final NBA season. He appeared in 66 games and averaged 7.1 points, 4.7 rebounds and 1.2 assists. That makes Lofgran more than a two-season rental in the transaction chain. The Olympians first received 77 games of useful forward play and then converted him directly into another rotation player who appeared in 66 games. The downstream exchange substantially strengthens the value Indianapolis ultimately extracted from the original cash purchase.

sections.heading: The Asset Chain Gives the Olympians the Win
sections.body: Syracuse received cash for a rookie who had been a low-scoring rotation player during the first part of the season. The Nationals finished 32-34 and reached the Eastern Division semifinals, so moving Lofgran did not collapse the roster. The problem for hindsight grading is that the payment amount is unknown and no later player or draft asset can be traced to it in the reviewed record. Syracuse clearly received financial consideration, but Indianapolis' basketball return is much more measurable.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Olympians Win — Syracuse C, Indianapolis A-. Syracuse sold Don Lofgran's player rights to the Indianapolis Olympians for cash on February 12, 1951. Lofgran had averaged 3.4 points and 2.0 rebounds in 47 games for the Nationals. Indianapolis received 14 games that season at 5.4 points and 4.6 rebounds, then a full 63-game season in 1951-52 at 7.2 points and 4.1 rebounds. The Olympians later traded Lofgran to Philadelphia for Mel Payton, who played 66 games for Indianapolis in 1952-53 at 7.1 points and 4.7 rebounds.

sections.heading: Fort Wayne Bought Ken Murray from Baltimore
sections.body: On February 15, 1951, the Baltimore Bullets sold Ken Murray's player rights to the Fort Wayne Pistons for cash. Fort Wayne's transaction page and the 1950-51 league transaction log identify the same sale. Murray had been one of Baltimore's more productive rookies, appearing in 52 games and averaging 13.7 points, 5.5 rebounds and 2.9 assists. The reviewed public sources do not preserve the cash amount, so Baltimore's financial return cannot be measured against the playing value Fort Wayne later received.

sections.heading: Murray Produced Before and After Military Service
sections.body: Murray joined the Pistons for the final 14 regular-season games of 1950-51. He averaged 9.9 points, 4.9 rebounds and 3.8 assists, giving Fort Wayne immediate backcourt production even though his scoring efficiency dipped from Baltimore. He then missed the 1951-52 and 1952-53 NBA seasons while serving in the U.S. Army. Murray returned to Fort Wayne in 1953-54 and appeared in 49 more games. Across those two Pistons seasons, the original cash purchase produced 63 regular-season appearances.

sections.heading: Baltimore Received an Unquantified Cash Return
sections.body: Baltimore received cash for a player who had been an active part of its rotation. The sale therefore carried more opportunity cost than many early rights transactions involving fringe players. Murray had scored 712 points in 52 Bullets games before the move. The problem for hindsight grading is that the amount paid by Fort Wayne is unknown, and no later player or draft asset can be traced directly to that payment in the reviewed record. Baltimore's return was tangible but opaque.

sections.heading: Sixty-Three Pistons Games Carry the Verdict
sections.body: Fort Wayne holds the advantage because the Pistons received useful immediate production and later regained Murray after his military service. The two-year absence limits the continuity of the return, but it does not erase the 63 total games Fort Wayne ultimately received from the purchased rights. Baltimore may have received a reasonable cash price, yet the surviving record cannot quantify it. The comparison therefore favors the Pistons without treating the deal as a franchise-changing acquisition.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Fort Wayne B+, Baltimore C. Fort Wayne acquired Ken Murray's player rights from the Baltimore Bullets for cash on February 15, 1951. Murray had been a productive Baltimore rookie, averaging 13.7 points, 5.5 rebounds and 2.9 assists in 52 games. He played 14 games for the Pistons that season at 9.9 points, 4.9 rebounds and 3.8 assists, then missed the next two NBA seasons while serving in the U.S. Army. Murray returned to Fort Wayne in 1953-54 for 49 more games.

sections.heading: Boston Acquired Bill Sharman for Chuck Share’s Rights
sections.body: On April 26, 1951, the Fort Wayne Pistons traded Bill Sharman to the Boston Celtics for the rights to Chuck Share. Boston's transaction page, Fort Wayne's transaction page, the 1950-51 league transaction log and Carl Bennett's executive record all agree on April 26, correcting the legacy April 27 intake date. Share had been the first overall pick in the 1950 NBA Draft but spent 1950-51 outside the NBA.

sections.heading: Sharman Became a Hall of Fame Celtics Cornerstone
sections.body: Sharman immediately became a major Celtics piece. He played 63 games in 1951-52 and averaged 10.7 points, then grew into one of the league's premier guards. Basketball-Reference lists him as an eight-time All-Star, seven-time All-NBA selection, four-time NBA champion and Hall of Famer, with a career average of 17.8 points. His shooting and free-throw accuracy complemented Bob Cousy in the backcourt and made him part of the core that moved Boston from a rising team into the league's dominant late-1950s franchise.

sections.heading: Share Still Produced Real Value for Fort Wayne
sections.body: Share was not a throwaway return. He debuted with Fort Wayne in 1951-52 and played 63 games, then 67 in 1952-53 and 21 more in 1953-54. That gave the Pistons 151 regular-season games from a young center before they converted him again. On December 21, 1953, Fort Wayne traded Share to the Milwaukee Hawks for Max Zaslofsky. Zaslofsky then appeared in 45 Pistons games that season and averaged 11.0 points. The downstream conversion materially improves Fort Wayne's side of the original deal.

sections.heading: Sharman’s Championship Impact Makes Boston the Clear Winner
sections.body: Fort Wayne received legitimate multi-season value and a useful second asset, which makes a low grade inappropriate. Share became a long NBA player and later won a championship with the Hawks, while the Pistons extracted 151 games and then Zaslofsky from him. Boston still wins decisively because Sharman became a Hall of Fame guard and a central member of four championship teams. The gap is about ceiling and historical impact, not whether Fort Wayne received anything.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win — Boston A+, Fort Wayne B+. Boston acquired Bill Sharman from the Fort Wayne Pistons for the rights to Chuck Share on April 26, 1951, correcting the legacy April 27 intake date. Sharman became a Hall of Fame guard, an eight-time All-Star and a four-time NBA champion while forming one of the defining backcourts of the early Celtics dynasty. Fort Wayne still received real value: Share played 151 games for the Pistons before a December 1953 trade sent him to Milwaukee for Max Zaslofsky, who averaged 11.0 points in 45 Fort Wayne games that season.

sections.heading: Tri-Cities Sent Frankie Brian to Fort Wayne
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Tri-Cities, Fort Wayne and league transaction logs all place the deal on May 31, 1951: the Blackhawks sent Frankie Brian to Fort Wayne for Dick Mehen, Howie Schultz and cash. That corrects the legacy May 4 date in the legacy archive entry. Brian had just completed an All-NBA Second Team season for Tri-Cities, averaging 16.8 points, 3.6 rebounds and 3.9 assists across 68 games.

sections.heading: Brian Became a Five-Year Pistons Piece
sections.body: Brian immediately justified the acquisition. In 1951-52 he played all 66 games for Fort Wayne, averaged 15.9 points, 3.5 rebounds and 3.5 assists, and made the All-Star team. He remained with the Pistons for five seasons and appeared in 306 regular-season games for the franchise, averaging 10.1 points over that span. His role declined later, but the longevity matters: Fort Wayne converted one transaction into several years of backcourt production and received Brian's best post-Tri-Cities season immediately after the trade.

sections.heading: Dick Mehen Gave the Hawks One Strong Season
sections.body: Mehen became a major part of the renamed Milwaukee Hawks in 1951-52. He appeared in 65 games, averaged 10.8 points, 4.3 rebounds and 2.6 assists, and logged more than 35 minutes per game. Schultz, however, did not produce the same return. Basketball-Reference lists him outside the NBA in 1950-51, and executive records note that his rights were later returned to Fort Wayne before Minneapolis acquired him in October 1951. The cash amount is not preserved.

sections.heading: Brian’s Longevity Gives Fort Wayne the Edge
sections.body: The Hawks' side was better than a simple loss because Mehen delivered a full season of starter-level minutes and double-digit scoring. Still, Brian's five-year Fort Wayne tenure created more durable value, and his first Pistons season included an All-Star selection while nearly matching his Tri-Cities scoring. The cash consideration could narrow the gap, but the amount is unknown and cannot be credited beyond acknowledging it existed. Schultz also failed to become a Hawks contributor.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Tri-Cities B, Fort Wayne A-. On May 31, 1951, the Tri-Cities Blackhawks traded Frankie Brian to the Fort Wayne Pistons for Dick Mehen, Howie Schultz and cash, correcting the legacy May 4 date. Brian became the best long-term asset in the deal: he played five seasons for Fort Wayne, made the 1952 All-Star team and averaged 15.9 points that first season. Mehen gave the Hawks 65 games at 10.8 points and 4.3 rebounds in 1951-52, while Schultz was returned before playing for the franchise.
