sections.heading: St. Louis Swapped Barney Cable for Woody Sauldsberry
sections.body: The Hawks acquired Woody Sauldsberry from the Chicago Zephyrs on January 30, 1963 and sent Barney Cable the other way. The canonical record treats this as a direct one-for-one player exchange with no additional pick or cash component.

sections.heading: The Hawks Chose the More Valuable Immediate Piece
sections.body: St. Louis received the higher canonical grade because Sauldsberry represented the stronger realized return in the existing record. The Hawks did not have to attach another asset to complete the exchange, keeping the cost limited to Cable.

sections.heading: Chicago Took the Other Side of the Player Swap
sections.body: The Zephyrs received Cable as the full return. With no documented secondary asset in the canonical transaction, Chicago’s result rises or falls entirely with the value of that one incoming player.

sections.heading: The Grade Gap Is Noticeable but Not Extreme
sections.body: TradeVerdicts assigns St. Louis a B+ and the Chicago/Washington franchise a C. That supports a Hawks win while still recognizing that Chicago received a real player rather than an empty return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win — St. Louis B+, Chicago Zephyrs C. St. Louis acquired Woody Sauldsberry from Chicago in January 1963 by sending Barney Cable the other way. Both franchises received an actual player, so this should not be described as a one-sided acquisition with nothing reaching Chicago. The inherited B+ to C comparison favors Sauldsberry as St. Louis's return, but the verified transaction contains no additional draft pick, player or cash component to inflate either side. The original participants were the St. Louis Hawks and Chicago Zephyrs, not the later Atlanta Hawks or Washington franchise.

sections.heading: The Verified Date Is August 14, 1963
sections.body: Philadelphia acquired Hubie White from San Francisco for John Windsor on August 14, one day earlier than the legacy TradeVerdicts date. Warriors, 76ers, league and player transaction records all support the corrected date and straight player-for-player structure.

sections.heading: White Gave Philadelphia the Larger Reserve Return
sections.body: White played 23 games for Philadelphia in 1963-64, averaging 3.4 points and 1.8 rebounds in 8.5 minutes per game. The stint was brief, but it produced more NBA playing time than the player San Francisco received.

sections.heading: Windsor’s Warriors Run Lasted Eleven Games
sections.body: Windsor appeared in 11 games for San Francisco that season, averaging 2.5 points and 2.4 rebounds in 6.2 minutes. Those were the only NBA games of his career.

sections.heading: The Difference Was Real but Small
sections.body: Philadelphia received the larger realized return, but neither side acquired a long-term rotation player. The B- versus C+ split correctly treats the exchange as a slight 76ers edge rather than a major historical win.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight 76ers Edge — San Francisco C+, Philadelphia B-. Philadelphia acquired Hubie White from the San Francisco Warriors for John Windsor on August 14, 1963, one day earlier than the legacy TradeVerdicts date. Basketball-Reference's Warriors, 76ers and league transaction ledgers, along with both player histories, agree on the August 14 date and straight player-for-player structure.

sections.heading: San Francisco’s Return Was an Undisclosed Payment

sections.heading: Boston Clearly Won the Basketball Side

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win — Boston A, San Francisco C. Boston purchased Willie Naulls' player rights from the San Francisco Warriors on September 4, 1963 for cash. sections.heading: New York Sent Richie Guerin to St. Louis
sections.body: The Knicks traded Richie Guerin to the Hawks on October 18, 1963 for cash and a 1964 second-round pick that became No. 15 selection Howie Komives. The team and league ledgers agree on the structure, while Pro Sports Transactions reports a $50,000 payment.

sections.heading: Guerin Gave the Hawks Four Important Seasons
sections.body: Guerin played 295 regular-season games for St. Louis over four seasons, generally scoring between 13 and 15 points per game with more than four assists. He also became the club’s player-coach, adding value beyond a short rental.

sections.heading: Komives Became a Long-Term Knicks Asset
sections.body: Komives played 335 regular-season games for New York and produced three early seasons averaging 12.2, 13.9 and 15.7 points. He was later included with Walt Bellamy in the trade that brought Dave DeBusschere to New York.

sections.heading: New York Holds Only a Modest Hindsight Edge
sections.body: Both sides extracted major player value. The Knicks add reported cash, more games from Komives and later downstream utility, so the A versus A- split favors New York without diminishing how productive Guerin was for St. Louis.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Knicks Edge — St. Louis A-, New York A. Richie Guerin gave the Hawks 295 regular-season appearances across four productive seasons and later served as player-coach, a major basketball return rather than a failed purchase. New York received reported cash plus the second-round selection it used on No. 15 Howie Komives in 1964. Komives played 335 Knicks games and was subsequently part of the multi-player deal that brought Dave DeBusschere to New York. Those additional regular-season games and the later ability to trade Komives support a narrow Knicks edge; DeBusschere's whole later career cannot be credited as though it came solely from this 1963 transaction.

sections.body: The Bullets acquired Kevin Loughery from Detroit on October 28, 1963 in a direct player-for-player exchange. Pistons, Bullets, league and player transaction records all agree on the date and structure.

sections.heading: Loughery Became a Long-Term Baltimore Guard

sections.heading: Detroit Got Only a Short Staverman Stay

sections.heading: The Long-Term Value Makes This Decisive
sections.body: Baltimore later retained additional trade value by including Loughery with Fred Carter in the 1971 deal for Archie Clark and a second-round pick. The A+ versus C split captures a large, traceable difference in realized value.

sections.body: New York acquired Bob Duffy’s player rights from St. Louis for cash on November 11, 1963. That corrects both the legacy November 10 date and the malformed “Bob Duffy (Joseph)” identity.

sections.heading: Duffy Played Only Four Games for New York

sections.heading: The Later Trade Does Not Make Duffy’s Full Value Measurable
sections.body: Duffy was only one of two Knicks assets in the later package, so the value New York ultimately received cannot be attributed to him alone. St. Louis’ original cash amount is also unknown.

sections.heading: The Evidence Supports the Transaction, Not a Winner

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict

sections.heading: The December 15 Detroit Row Is a Duplicate Perspective
sections.body: This record describes the same three-team Detroit-New York-Cincinnati transaction that league and team ledgers place on December 16, 1963. It is not evidence of a second separate deal.

sections.heading: The Verified Three-Team Package Is Already Canonical
sections.body: The supported transaction sent Johnny Egan from Detroit to New York, Larry Staverman from Detroit to Cincinnati, Bob Boozer from Cincinnati to New York, and Donnie Butcher plus Bob Duffy from New York to Detroit.

sections.heading: A New York Canonical Record Holds the Full Exchange
sections.body: TradeVerdicts already preserves the broader multi-team deal in the correct canonical record. Keeping this Detroit-side legacy row as another graded trade would duplicate the same asset movements.

sections.heading: Preserve the Record for Provenance Only
sections.body: The entry remains in the archive so the source lineage is auditable, but it is structurally superseded and excluded from graded outcomes. No team grade should be invented for a duplicate perspective.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Resolution
finalVerdict.body: Record Superseded This Detroit-side December 15, 1963 record is a duplicate perspective of the three-team Detroit-New York-Cincinnati transaction that the league and all three team ledgers place on December 16. The supported deal sent Johnny Egan from Detroit to New York, Larry Staverman from Detroit to Cincinnati, Bob Boozer from Cincinnati to New York, and Donnie Butcher plus Bob Duffy from New York to Detroit.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Received No NBA Production from Grote

sections.heading: The Hawks at Least Converted a Dormant Asset into Cash

sections.heading: The Small Realized Edge Belongs to St. Louis
sections.body: A C+ versus D+ split fits the outcome. Philadelphia acquired rights that produced no measurable team value, while St. Louis converted the asset into cash, creating a modest rather than dramatic advantage.

sections.heading: McGill Supplied the Only NBA Minutes from the Deal

sections.heading: Hightower Became Useful Frontcourt Depth

sections.heading: Detroit Bought Bill Chmielewski’s Rights from Cincinnati
sections.body: Detroit purchased Bill Chmielewski’s player rights for cash. The exact date is disputed: the Pistons’ 1966 media guide and RealGM place the move on May 8, 1965, while Basketball-Reference lists December 8. TradeVerdicts retains May 8 because the near-contemporary team guide is the strongest source in the file.

sections.heading: The Rights Never Produced an NBA Appearance
sections.body: Chmielewski had been Cincinnati’s No. 17 pick in the 1964 draft, but he never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Detroit therefore received no measurable on-court return from the purchased rights.

sections.heading: Cincinnati Converted an Unused Asset into Cash
sections.body: The Royals did not develop the player into an NBA contributor, but they did receive a financial return for rights they otherwise held. The cash figure is not public, preventing a more precise valuation.

sections.heading: The Outcome Gives Cincinnati the Modest Edge
sections.body: A C+ for Cincinnati and D+ for Detroit fits the realized result. The Royals monetized an unused asset, while the Pistons paid for rights that did not generate an NBA game.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Royals Edge — Detroit D+, Cincinnati C+. Detroit purchased the player rights to Bill Chmielewski from Cincinnati for cash. sections.heading: The Verified Sale Date Is September 15
sections.body: Boston sold Joe Strawder’s player rights to Detroit on September 15, 1965, one day later than the legacy TradeVerdicts entry. Celtics, Pistons and league records agree on the corrected date and cash-sale structure.

sections.heading: Detroit Received Three Full Seasons from Strawder
sections.body: Strawder played 231 regular-season games for the Pistons. He averaged 8.6 points and 10.4 rebounds in 1965-66, 9.5 and 10.0 the next season, then 7.5 and 9.4 in 1967-68.

sections.heading: Boston’s Sale Price Is Unknown
sections.body: The Celtics received cash, but the amount is not preserved in the public transaction records. That means Boston’s return cannot be treated as worthless even though the basketball outcome strongly favors Detroit.

sections.heading: The Pistons Won on Realized Production
sections.body: Three seasons of frontcourt work support Detroit’s B+ against Boston’s C. The unknown cash return keeps the grade gap measured, but Strawder’s 231 games make the basketball advantage clear.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Boston C, Detroit B+. Joe Strawder's rights moved from the Celtics to Detroit on September 15, 1965 in a cash sale, not a player-for-player trade. Strawder then appeared in 231 regular-season games for the Pistons over three seasons, providing frontcourt rebounding near double digits per game in each of those years. Boston received money rather than an on-court player or pick, and the amount is not preserved by the available public records. The unknown financial return deserves acknowledgment but cannot be equated with Strawder's documented basketball production. Club and league ledgers agree on September 15, one day after the older archived route, so the corrected historical date must accompany the Detroit-favored grade.

sections.heading: Boston Acquired Sihugo Green from Baltimore
sections.body: The Celtics acquired Sihugo Green from the Bullets on October 10, 1965. Baltimore received a 1966 fourth-round pick that became No. 39 selection John Beasley plus cash.

sections.heading: The Celtics Chose Immediate Veteran Help
sections.body: Boston’s side of the exchange centered on Green as the usable present-day player. The canonical grades treat that immediate roster value as slightly stronger than the later pick-and-cash package.

sections.heading: Baltimore Received a Draft Asset and Financial Consideration
sections.body: The surviving transaction references disagree over the exact draft consideration. The site's imported Celtics record and Pro Sports Transactions list a 1966 fourth-round pick associated with No. 39 John Beasley plus cash, while Basketball-Reference's 1965-66 league transaction ledger describes a fifth-round pick later used on John Jones and does not list cash in that entry. Those cannot both be treated as an independently reconciled final pick identity. Preserve the existing canonical asset fields for further bilateral ledger audit instead of silently changing the round, player or amount. Boston's acquired guard Si Green appeared in just 10 Celtics games that season, averaging 3.2 points, a limited immediate return rather than a proven long-term advantage.

sections.heading: The Grade Difference Is Intentionally Small
sections.body: TradeVerdicts gives Boston a C+ and Baltimore a C. That is a narrow Celtics edge, appropriate for a transaction where both sides received legitimate assets and the surviving evidence does not justify a wider spread.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Celtics Edge — Boston C+, Baltimore C under the inherited grades, with unresolved draft-pick provenance. The October 10, 1965 deal brought Si Green from the Bullets to Boston, where he played 10 games and averaged 3.2 points. The imported record and Pro Sports Transactions identify a 1966 fourth-round No. 39 John Beasley selection plus cash; Basketball-Reference instead lists a fifth-round selection becoming John Jones. The conflict prevents a definitive downstream draft or cash-value comparison. Preserve the source discrepancies and current grade labels pending review rather than claiming the precise return is settled.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Sold Ben Warley’s Rights to Baltimore
sections.body: The 76ers sold Ben Warley’s player rights to the Bullets for cash on October 27, 1965. Warley had appeared in one Philadelphia game that season before the transaction.

sections.heading: Warley Became Two Seasons of Baltimore Depth
sections.body: Warley played 118 regular-season games for the Bullets across 1965-66 and 1966-67. He averaged 5.3 points and 3.8 rebounds in 56 games after the move, then 6.2 points and 5.2 rebounds in 62 games the next year.

sections.heading: The Bullets’ Control Ended in the Expansion Draft
sections.body: Seattle selected Warley from Baltimore in 1967, so the Bullets did not retain a later trade asset. Even so, the two seasons of rotation depth were a concrete return from the purchase.

sections.heading: Undisclosed Cash Keeps Philadelphia from an Extreme Grade
sections.body: Philadelphia received cash whose amount is unknown. Baltimore’s two useful seasons justify the B versus C result, but the missing sale price prevents treating the 76ers’ side as an empty return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bullets Win — Philadelphia C, Baltimore B. Philadelphia sold Ben Warley's player rights to Baltimore on October 27, 1965 for cash. Warley had appeared in one game for the 76ers that season before the sale, then gave Baltimore 118 regular-season games across 1965-66 and 1966-67.

sections.heading: New York Paid a Large Package for Walt Bellamy
sections.body: The November 1 record has the Knicks acquiring 26-year-old Walt Bellamy from Baltimore for Jim Barnes, Johnny Egan, Johnny Green and cash. The deal exchanged one established star for multiple rotation assets and financial consideration.

sections.heading: Bellamy Immediately Became a Knicks Centerpiece
sections.body: Bellamy played 268 regular-season games for New York and averaged 23.2 points with 16.0 rebounds in his first Knicks season. His prime production gave New York a high-end return from the moment he arrived.

sections.heading: Baltimore’s Return Was Substantial, Not Empty
sections.body: Egan became a multi-year rotation guard, Green supplied two productive seasons and Barnes delivered a strong first year before being traded for Leroy Ellis. The Bullets also received cash, so their side carried legitimate depth value.

sections.heading: Star Value Gives New York the Stronger Result
sections.body: The Knicks’ A against Baltimore’s B reflects the premium created by consolidating several assets into a Hall of Fame center. Baltimore received real depth, but Bellamy’s production and later utility give New York the better hindsight outcome.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: New York Knicks Win — Baltimore B, New York A. New York acquired 26-year-old Hall of Fame center Walt Bellamy from Baltimore on November 1, 1965 for Jim Barnes, Johnny Egan, Johnny Green and cash. Bellamy gave the Knicks 268 regular-season games, averaged 23.2 points and 16.0 rebounds in his first New York season, and later became part of the package used to acquire Dave DeBusschere.

sections.heading: The November 2 Record Captures the Same Bellamy Package
sections.body: This canonical entry places New York’s acquisition of Walt Bellamy on November 2, 1965. The Knicks sent Jim Barnes, Johnny Egan, Johnny Green and cash to Baltimore, and the player transaction ledgers in this record support that package.

sections.heading: Bellamy Delivered Prime Production Before a Major Conversion
sections.body: Bellamy played 268 regular-season games for New York, including 72 at 23.2 points and 16.0 rebounds immediately after the trade. In December 1968 the Knicks paired him with Howard Komives to acquire Dave DeBusschere.

sections.heading: Baltimore Accumulated More Total Games Across Three Players
sections.body: Barnes played 66 games, Egan 207 and Green 133 for the Bullets, a combined 406 regular-season appearances. That volume explains why Baltimore still earns a strong B+ rather than being treated as a clear loser.

sections.heading: The Downstream DeBusschere Value Pushes New York Higher
sections.body: New York’s A+ reflects both Bellamy’s own prime years and his later conversion into a core championship-era player. Baltimore’s package was productive, but the Knicks captured the more consequential chain of value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win — New York A+, Baltimore B+. New York acquired Walt Bellamy from Baltimore on November 2, 1965 for Jim Barnes, Johnny Egan, Johnny Green and cash. Bellamy gave the Knicks 268 regular-season games, including 72 games at 23.2 points and 16.0 rebounds immediately after the trade.

sections.body: The Hawks traded John Tresvant and Chico Vaughn to the Pistons for Rod Thorn on December 24, 1965. The transaction placed one incoming player in St. Louis against a two-player Detroit package.

sections.heading: Thorn Gave the Hawks 113 Games
sections.body: Thorn played 113 regular-season games for St. Louis before Seattle selected him in the 1967 expansion draft. That was meaningful roster value, but it did not create a later Hawks trade asset.

sections.heading: Detroit Received More Production and a Later Trade Piece
sections.body: Vaughn played 88 Pistons games over two seasons, while Tresvant appeared in 169 and developed into a double-digit scorer and strong rebounder. Tresvant was later included with Tom Van Arsdale in the deal that brought Happy Hairston and Jim Fox to Detroit.

sections.heading: The Larger Combined Return Favors Detroit
sections.body: Detroit’s A- against St. Louis’ B- reflects both greater immediate volume and additional downstream trade value. Thorn was useful for the Hawks, but the Pistons extracted more from the two-player package.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — St. Louis B-, Detroit A-. St. Louis traded John Tresvant and Chico Vaughn to Detroit for Rod Thorn on December 24, 1965.

sections.heading: St. Louis Acquired Joe Caldwell for John Barnhill
sections.body: The Hawks acquired Joe Caldwell from Detroit for John Barnhill on December 28, 1965. On paper it was a simple one-for-one player swap, but the careers that followed created a much wider difference than the transaction structure suggested.

sections.heading: Caldwell Became a Core Hawks Contributor
sections.body: Caldwell played 369 regular-season games for St. Louis and Atlanta through 1969-70. He made the 1969 and 1970 NBA All-Star Games and peaked at 21.1 points, 5.0 rebounds and 3.5 assists per game in 1969-70.

sections.heading: Barnhill’s Detroit Run Lasted 45 Games
sections.body: Detroit received only 45 games from Barnhill before Chicago selected him in the 1966 expansion draft. The Pistons therefore lost control of their incoming player after less than one full season.

sections.heading: The Realized Gap Is Large
sections.body: Caldwell’s multi-year production and All-Star seasons make the Hawks side substantially stronger. The A+ versus D+ grades reflect the long-term contributor St. Louis received against Detroit’s brief return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict

sections.heading: Boston Traded Mel Counts for Bailey Howell
sections.body: The Celtics acquired Bailey Howell from Baltimore on September 1, 1966 and sent Mel Counts to the Bullets. The canonical record treats the exchange as a direct veteran-for-veteran trade with no additional pick or cash component.

sections.heading: Howell Fit a Championship-Level Boston Rotation
sections.body: Boston did not merely acquire the reputation of former Baltimore forward Bailey Howell. In his first Celtics season, 1966-67, he played 81 games and averaged 20.0 points and 8.4 rebounds; over four Boston seasons he accumulated 323 regular-season appearances. Howell then contributed to the Celtics' 1968 and 1969 NBA title teams, connecting the September 1966 trade to sustained production rather than a hypothetical roster upgrade. His arrival followed the club's earlier run of championships, but the 1966-67 team did not win the championship, so calling the transaction an immediate 1967 title trigger would be inaccurate. The preserved Boston A grade is supported by four years of measured scoring and two later championships without attributing the full club results to one player.

sections.heading: Baltimore Received a Legitimate NBA Big Man
sections.body: Mel Counts also had a real NBA role, and his departure from Boston cannot be described as a total loss for Baltimore. The 7-foot center played 25 games for the Bullets during 1966-67, averaging 6.4 points and 6.2 rebounds in 13.7 minutes. Baltimore subsequently moved him to the Los Angeles Lakers, where his remaining 31 appearances that season belonged to a different franchise. His later Lakers seasons do not represent Baltimore production under the Howell exchange. That small 25-game direct return is a concrete reason for the Bullets' inherited D compared with the Celtics' A, rather than a claim that Counts was not an NBA-level player. The date, clubs and distinct player return can be verified against the original Baltimore transaction ledger and the separate player-season record.

sections.heading: The Celtics Won the Exchange Clearly
sections.body: TradeVerdicts keeps the verdict at Celtics Win with an A for Boston and D for Baltimore. The grade spread captures the difference between Howell’s high-level fit and the more limited return the Bullets received from Counts.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win — Boston A, Baltimore D. Boston acquired Bailey Howell from Bullets in exchange for Mel Counts. Howell became an established Boston contributor, including on championship teams, giving this exchange a better documented basketball return than the outgoing Counts package.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Bought Tom Hawkins’ Rights from Cincinnati
sections.body: The Lakers purchased Tom Hawkins’ player rights from the Royals on September 14, 1966. Cincinnati received cash, while Los Angeles took control of a veteran forward who immediately entered the rotation.

sections.heading: Hawkins Gave the Lakers Three Useful Seasons
sections.body: Hawkins played 228 regular-season games for Los Angeles from 1966-67 through 1968-69. His best year came in 1967-68, when he averaged 11.6 points and 5.9 rebounds in 31.6 minutes across 78 games.

sections.heading: Cincinnati’s Return Cannot Be Fully Priced
sections.body: The Royals received undisclosed cash and no traceable downstream basketball asset in the public record. The missing sale amount means the Cincinnati side should not be treated as worthless even though the basketball return went to Los Angeles.

sections.heading: The Lakers Earn a Strong but Not Extreme Win
sections.body: Three seasons of rotation production support the A- for Los Angeles against Cincinnati’s C+. Hawkins was useful rather than a franchise star, which keeps the result below the most lopsided historical grades.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win — Los Angeles A-, Cincinnati C+. Cincinnati sold Tom Hawkins's player rights to the Los Angeles Lakers on September 14, 1966. Hawkins became a useful Lakers rotation forward for three seasons, playing 228 regular-season games from 1966-67 through 1968-69.

sections.heading: September 15, 1966: Boston Took Embry for a Third-Round Pick
sections.body: On September 15, 1966, Boston acquired center Wayne Embry from the Cincinnati Royals in exchange for a 1967 third-round draft choice. The Celtics' and Royals' 1966-67 transaction histories independently identify the later selection as Sam Smith, No. 28 overall. The inherited canonical asset description also mentions cash, but those season transaction histories list the pick without separately documenting a payment or amount. Therefore cash is an unverified legacy annotation here, not a confirmed second consideration or a dollar figure that should affect the grade. Cincinnati was the 1966 counterparty; the modern Sacramento Kings identifier is used for that franchise's continuity.

sections.heading: Embry's 150 Celtics Games and the 1968 Championship Role
sections.body: Boston received a veteran center who supplied 150 regular-season appearances over two seasons: 72 in 1966-67 and 78 in 1967-68. His role was limited, averaging 10.1 minutes and 5.2 points in the first season, then 13.9 minutes and 6.3 points in the second. Embry played behind Bill Russell rather than replacing the star center. He was on the Celtics roster that won the 1968 NBA championship and appeared in 16 postseason games that year, although his title-ring association does not justify assigning the entire championship to this 1966 third-round transaction. Boston obtained useful rotation depth immediately instead of waiting for a later low-round selection.

sections.heading: Cincinnati's No. 28 Sam Smith Rights Did Not Bring Royals NBA Minutes
sections.body: The Royals used Boston's 1967 third-round choice at No. 28 overall on forward Sam Smith. Smith played 255 professional regular-season games in the ABA over four seasons, beginning with the Minnesota Muskies, but no NBA regular-season games for the Cincinnati Royals. His ABA record documents a professional career; it cannot be treated as playing return for the drafting NBA club. The selection therefore provided Cincinnati a legitimate draft-rights opportunity without producing direct recorded Royals court time. The extra cash wording inherited from one legacy asset field has no corroborated figure in the linked transaction histories and should not be invented to manufacture a positive net consideration.

sections.heading: The B+ / D Spread Measures Realized Return, Not an Imaginary Cash Sum
sections.body: The inherited Boston B+ and Cincinnati D grades can be understood from the difference between Embry's 150 Celtics appearances, including reserve minutes in the 1968 championship season, and the Royals' third-round selection whose eventual player made his professional appearances in the ABA instead. Boston did not obtain a new perennial All-Star—Embry's usage was modest—but it secured real frontcourt availability at a small draft cost. Cincinnati's opportunity in pick No. 28 did not convert to NBA appearances for its own roster. The historical 1966 participants were Boston and the Cincinnati Royals even though the Sacramento Kings franchise successor label is used in current canonical data; a hypothetical cash value must not be inserted into the winner arithmetic.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win — Boston B+, Cincinnati Royals D (modern Kings successor). Boston acquired Wayne Embry on September 15, 1966 for the 1967 third-round pick that Cincinnati used on No. 28 Sam Smith. Embry contributed 150 Celtics regular-season games over 1966-68 and reserve minutes during Boston's 1968 NBA championship season; Smith's 255 ABA games did not become Royals NBA playing output. The legacy asset row also says cash, but the contemporaneous season transaction ledgers record the pick alone and provide no verifiable payment amount. The B+/D grade comparison is therefore anchored in Embry's actual NBA service against an unconverted Royals draft-rights opportunity, not a speculative cash figure or a championship solely credited to this trade.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Sent LeRoy Ellis to Baltimore for Jim Barnes
sections.body: The Lakers traded LeRoy Ellis to the Bullets for Jim Barnes on September 22, 1966. The deal was a direct frontcourt swap, and both players contributed after changing teams.

sections.heading: Ellis Became a Four-Year Baltimore Regular
sections.body: Ellis played 311 regular-season games for the Bullets. He averaged 14.9 points and 12.0 rebounds in 1966-67, then followed with 12.4 points and 11.1 rebounds the next season.

sections.heading: Barnes Supplied Shorter Lakers Depth
sections.body: Barnes appeared in 122 games for Los Angeles across parts of two seasons, mostly in a reserve role. That was useful value, but the tenure and production were clearly smaller than Baltimore’s return from Ellis.

sections.heading: Baltimore Wins Without Erasing the Lakers’ Return
sections.body: The A for Baltimore and B for Los Angeles capture a clear difference rather than a total mismatch. The Bullets received the stronger multi-season starter while the Lakers still got meaningful frontcourt minutes.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bullets Win — Los Angeles B, Baltimore A. Los Angeles traded LeRoy Ellis to Baltimore for Jim Barnes on September 22, 1966. Ellis became the stronger immediate asset, playing 311 regular-season games for the Bullets over four seasons.

sections.heading: Boston Sold Johnny Austin’s Rights to Baltimore
sections.body: The Celtics sold Johnny Austin’s player rights to the Bullets for cash on October 11, 1966. Team transaction records and Austin’s player history support the rights-sale structure.

sections.heading: Austin’s Baltimore Stay Was Extremely Brief
sections.body: Austin appeared in only four games for the Bullets. The documented player record shows 5.8 points per game on 22.7 percent shooting, leaving Baltimore with very little realized basketball value from the purchase.

sections.heading: Boston Converted the Rights into Cash
sections.body: The Celtics received financial consideration instead of retaining a player who did not become a meaningful NBA contributor for Baltimore. The amount is undisclosed, so the exact value of Boston’s side cannot be calculated.

sections.heading: A Modest Celtics Edge Fits the Evidence
sections.body: Boston’s B versus Baltimore’s C reflects the better realized outcome without overstating an unknown cash sale. The Bullets received only four games, while Boston at least monetized the asset.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win — Boston B, Baltimore C. Boston sold Johnny Austin's player rights to Baltimore for cash. The cited records confirm the transfer of rights, but the cash price is not independently specified; the early letter grades should be read with that limitation.

sections.body: The Knicks acquired Neil Johnson’s player rights from Baltimore for cash on October 31, 1966. The transaction gave New York a reserve big man while the Bullets took an undisclosed financial return.

sections.heading: Johnson Played 94 Games for the Knicks

sections.heading: Expansion Ended New York’s Control
sections.body: Phoenix selected Johnson from the Knicks in the 1968 expansion draft. New York therefore did not preserve a later trade asset, limiting the long-term upside of the original purchase.

sections.heading: The Knicks Hold a Small Realized Advantage
sections.body: The B- versus C+ split recognizes 94 games of direct basketball value while respecting the unknown cash payment Baltimore received. It is a modest Knicks win, not a major historical swing.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Knicks Edge — New York B-, Baltimore C+. New York acquired Neil Johnson's player rights from Baltimore for cash on October 31, 1966. sections.heading: Chicago Swapped Len Chappell for George Wilson
sections.body: The Bulls traded Len Chappell to Cincinnati for George Wilson on November 25, 1966. Both incoming players appeared in the NBA after the deal, making this a comparison of short-term rotation returns.

sections.heading: Wilson Played 43 Games Before the Expansion Draft
sections.body: Wilson averaged 4.6 points and 3.8 rebounds in 10.4 minutes across 43 Bulls games. Seattle selected him in the 1967 expansion draft, ending Chicago’s control after less than a season.

sections.heading: Chappell Lasted Longer with Cincinnati
sections.body: Chappell gave the Royals 54 games that season and 10 more in 1967-68. The extra games create a modest realized advantage, although Cincinnati also moved on without preserving a major downstream asset.

sections.heading: The Royals Edge Is Narrow
sections.body: Cincinnati’s B- against Chicago’s C+ reflects the slightly larger direct return. Neither side secured a long-term piece, so the grades stay close rather than turning a brief player swap into a major win.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Royals Edge — Chicago C+, Cincinnati B-. Chicago traded Len Chappell to Cincinnati for George Wilson on November 25, 1966. Wilson played 43 games for the Bulls after the trade, averaging 4.6 points and 3.8 rebounds in 10.4 minutes, before Seattle selected him in the 1967 expansion draft.

sections.heading: Three Teams Reworked Their Frontcourts in January 1967
sections.body: The January 16 deal sent Mel Counts from Baltimore to Los Angeles, Ray Scott from Detroit to Baltimore, and Rudy LaRusso plus a compensatory 1967 first-round pick from the Lakers to Detroit after LaRusso refused to report.

sections.heading: Baltimore Received the Best Direct Player Return
sections.body: Scott played 263 games for the Bullets through 1969-70. He averaged 19.0 points and 13.2 rebounds immediately after the trade, then 16.4 points and 13.7 rebounds the following season.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Also Landed Sustained Production
sections.body: Counts played 271 Lakers games through 1969-70, giving Los Angeles a strong multi-year return. That explains the Lakers’ A- despite Baltimore holding the highest grade in the transaction.

sections.heading: Detroit’s Package Did Not Convert as Well
sections.body: Detroit received 57 games from No. 4 pick Sonny Dove and later sold LaRusso’s rights to San Francisco. The A for Baltimore, A- for Los Angeles and C+ for Detroit reflect the much stronger realized production on the other two sides.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bullets Win — Baltimore A, Los Angeles A-, Detroit C+. Ray Scott supplied Baltimore with 263 games through 1969-70, while Mel Counts gave the Lakers 271 games of their own after the January 1967 three-way exchange. Detroit's return was less productive: Rudy LaRusso did not report, his rights were later sold, and the compensatory first-rounder became Sonny Dove, whose NBA contribution there lasted 57 games. The grades distinguish two valuable incoming veterans from the Detroit assets that failed to yield equivalent court time. Scott's stronger early Baltimore production earns the narrow top position.

sections.heading: Indiana Sold Goose Ligon’s Rights to Kentucky
sections.body: The Pacers sold Goose Ligon’s player rights to the Kentucky Colonels for cash on July 22, 1967. The Pacers and Colonels transaction ledgers agree on the date and structure, and Kentucky signed Ligon the next day.

sections.heading: Ligon Became an Early ABA Standout
sections.body: Ligon played 78 games at 16.2 points and 11.9 rebounds in 1967-68, then appeared in 75 games the next season and earned an ABA All-Star selection. He played all 84 games in 1969-70.

sections.heading: Indiana’s Financial Return Is Unknown
sections.body: The Pacers received cash, but the amount is not disclosed in the public transaction record. Without that figure, the Indiana side can only be measured as a sale that surrendered three seasons of high-level production.

sections.heading: Kentucky Created the Clearer Value
sections.body: The Colonels’ A against Indiana’s C reflects three full seasons from a major early-ABA contributor. The unknown sale price prevents a harsher Pacers grade, but the basketball return decisively favors Kentucky.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Colonels Win — Kentucky A, Indiana C. Goose Ligon gave Kentucky three seasons of high-level ABA frontcourt production after Indiana sold his rights for cash in July 1967. He opened with 78 games at 16.2 points and 11.9 rebounds per night, then earned an ABA All-Star selection the following year. Indiana received a real payment, but its amount isn't public. The absence of that price limits how harshly the Pacers can be graded, while Kentucky's sustained return makes the overall winner hard to dispute.

sections.heading: Chubin Produced an Excellent First ABA Season

sections.heading: Denver’s Return Cannot Be Precisely Valued
sections.body: The Rockets received undisclosed cash and no on-court asset from the transaction itself. The missing amount keeps Denver’s C from being treated as a total loss even though there is no comparable basketball production to measure.

sections.heading: Anaheim Clearly Won on Realized Value
sections.body: The Amigos’ A against Denver’s C reflects the quality and volume of Chubin’s season. Anaheim acquired a leading contributor immediately, while Denver’s financial return remains unknown.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Amigos Win — Denver C, Anaheim A. Denver sold Steve Chubin to the Anaheim Amigos for cash on October 12, 1967, one day before the inaugural ABA season began. Anaheim immediately turned the purchase into one of the strongest player returns in its one-season franchise history.

sections.heading: New Jersey Acquired Bobby Lloyd for a Future Pick
sections.body: The New Jersey Americans acquired Bobby Lloyd from the Pittsburgh Pipers for a future draft choice on October 15, 1967 and signed him the same day. The surviving transaction ledgers do not identify the year or round of Pittsburgh’s pick.

sections.heading: Lloyd Gave the Americans Two Seasons

sections.heading: Pittsburgh’s Draft Return Is Unresolved
sections.body: The Pipers received a future draft choice, but its year, round and realized outcome are not identified in the available ledgers. That uncertainty prevents the Pittsburgh side from being graded as if the pick had no value.

sections.heading: The Documented Return Favors the Nets Franchise
sections.body: New Jersey’s B+ against Pittsburgh’s C reflects the 125 known games Lloyd supplied. The result is a clear edge rather than an overwhelming win because the final value of the future pick cannot be reconstructed.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Franchise Win — New Jersey B+, Pittsburgh C. Bobby Lloyd contributed 58 ABA games at 8.1 points as a rookie and 67 more at 9.9 after the Americans' move into the New York identity. That is 125 direct franchise appearances from a player acquired for a future pick. Pittsburgh's compensation was real draft capital, but the transaction sources don't establish its round, year or eventual recipient. The documented Lloyd minutes support the higher New Jersey grade while the unresolved pick prevents confidently assigning Pittsburgh no value.

sections.heading: Denver Sold Gary Keller to Minnesota
sections.body: The Rockets sold Gary Keller to the Minnesota Muskies for cash on October 16, 1967. Minnesota acquired a frontcourt player who immediately entered the rotation during the ABA’s inaugural season.

sections.heading: Keller Stayed with the Franchise Through Its Move
sections.body: Keller played 69 games for Minnesota at 7.3 points and 5.6 rebounds in 17.6 minutes, then followed the franchise to Miami and added 53 games in 1968-69. The purchase therefore produced 122 regular-season appearances.

sections.heading: Denver Received Only an Undisclosed Financial Return
sections.body: The Rockets received cash but no traceable on-court asset from the sale itself. Because the amount is unknown, Denver’s side cannot be compared dollar-for-dollar with the production Minnesota and Miami received.

sections.heading: The Muskies-Floridians Franchise Earns the Edge
sections.body: The B+ versus C split recognizes two seasons of useful depth from Keller. Denver did monetize the asset, but the measurable basketball return clearly belongs to Minnesota and its successor franchise.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Muskies Win — Denver C, Minnesota/Miami B+. Denver sold Gary Keller to the Minnesota Muskies for cash on October 16, 1967. Minnesota turned the purchase into 69 regular-season games in the ABA's inaugural season, with Keller averaging 7.3 points and 5.6 rebounds in 17.6 minutes per game.

sections.heading: Chicago Sent Guy Rodgers to Cincinnati for a Package
sections.body: The Bulls traded Guy Rodgers to the Royals on October 20, 1967 for Flynn Robinson, second-round picks in 1968 and 1969, and cash. Chicago received multiple chances to create value while Cincinnati consolidated the exchange into the veteran guard.

sections.heading: Robinson Became the Immediate Bulls Return
sections.body: Robinson played 91 games for Chicago, averaging 16.0 points in 73 games in 1967-68 and 19.1 points in 18 more before a 1968 trade to Milwaukee. He supplied meaningful production before becoming another movable asset.

sections.heading: One Draft Pick Also Turned into Johnny Baum
sections.body: The 1969 second-round pick became Johnny Baum, who added 65 Bulls games. The 1968 selection became Ron Dunlap and produced no NBA games, so the draft portion of the package was mixed rather than uniformly successful.

sections.heading: Chicago’s Depth Beats Cincinnati’s Short Rodgers Tenure
sections.body: Rodgers played 75 games for Cincinnati before Milwaukee selected him in the 1968 expansion draft. Chicago’s A- versus Cincinnati’s B- reflects the deeper package and additional realized assets the Bulls preserved.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win — Chicago A-, Cincinnati B-. Flynn Robinson provided Chicago 91 games of meaningful guard scoring after Guy Rodgers was sent to the Royals; a 1969 second-round asset later became Johnny Baum, adding 65 Bulls appearances. The other 1968 pick yielded no NBA games, so Chicago's larger package wasn't uniformly successful. Cincinnati obtained 75 Rodgers games before he was selected in the expansion draft. Chicago's extra productive paths explain its two-step grading advantage without pretending every acquired pick worked.

sections.heading: The Verified Heyman-Leibowitz Trade Occurred on December 2
sections.body: New Jersey traded Art Heyman to Pittsburgh for Barry Leibowitz on December 2, 1967, correcting the legacy November 29 date and spelling. Both players became immediate contributors after the exchange.

sections.heading: Heyman Helped Power the ABA Champion Pipers
sections.body: Heyman played 54 regular-season games for Pittsburgh at 20.1 points, 7.9 rebounds and 4.4 assists, then added 15 playoff games at 18.9 points. That made him a major part of the Pipers’ championship season.

sections.heading: New Jersey Preserved Value Beyond Leibowitz
sections.body: Leibowitz played 24 games for the Americans at 11.4 points before being traded to Oakland for Levern Tart. Tart then gave the franchise 31 games at 19.0 points and another 35 games the next season.

sections.heading: Pittsburgh Wins, but New Jersey’s Chain Was Strong
sections.body: The A- versus B+ grades capture a narrow but meaningful difference. Heyman delivered championship-level immediate value, while New Jersey still converted its return into another productive scorer.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pipers Win — New Jersey B+, Pittsburgh A-. The verified Art Heyman-for-Barry Leibowitz exchange occurred December 2, 1967, not the November 29 date carried by the old intake. Heyman gave Pittsburgh 54 regular-season appearances with averages of 20.1 points, 7.9 rebounds and 4.4 assists, then contributed 15 playoff games to an ABA championship campaign. New Jersey did not leave empty-handed: Leibowitz played 24 games for the Americans, and the club subsequently turned him into Levern Tart, who supplied another productive scoring period. Pittsburgh's championship-level return earns the edge, while the preserved New Jersey follow-on assets explain why the two grades are only one step apart.

sections.heading: New Jersey Swapped Jim Caldwell for Stew Johnson
sections.body: The Americans traded Jim Caldwell to the Kentucky Colonels for Stew Johnson on November 30, 1967. Both players became rotation pieces, making durability and total production the clearest way to separate the returns.

sections.heading: Caldwell Gave Kentucky 123 Regular-Season Games
sections.body: Caldwell played 58 games for the Colonels in 1967-68 at 8.4 points and 9.4 rebounds, then added 65 games the next season. He also appeared in 12 playoff games across those two years.

sections.heading: Johnson’s Americans-Nets Stay Was Shorter
sections.body: Johnson played 55 games for New Jersey at 8.6 points and 5.9 rebounds, then nine more after the franchise became the New York Nets. Houston claimed him off waivers in November 1968.

sections.heading: Kentucky Received the More Durable Return
sections.body: The Colonels’ A- against the Nets franchise’s B reflects 123 regular-season games from Caldwell versus 64 from Johnson. Both sides received useful players, but Kentucky retained its return longer.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Colonels Win — Kentucky A-, New Jersey B. Jim Caldwell contributed 123 regular-season games and 12 playoff appearances for Kentucky across two seasons after the November 1967 exchange. Stew Johnson also helped the Americans-Nets organization, appearing in 55 games as a New Jersey American and nine more after the franchise became the New York Nets. Houston claimed Johnson off waivers in November 1968, ending that club's return at 64 regular-season games. Kentucky's longer tenure and playoff use support the stronger grade, while the 64 games from Johnson justify credit to the other side. The 1968 franchise name change was not a second trade.

sections.heading: Denver Traded Willis Thomas for Jeff Congdon
sections.body: The Rockets sent Willis Thomas to Anaheim for Jeff Congdon on December 11, 1967. The exchange quickly became a comparison between one partial season for the Amigos and a multi-year Denver backcourt piece.

sections.heading: Congdon Stayed with Denver for Three Seasons
sections.body: Congdon played 41 games after the trade, then 59 in 1968-69 and all 83 in 1969-70. His role expanded in that third season, when he averaged 9.8 points and 5.4 assists in 29.7 minutes.

sections.heading: Thomas’ Anaheim Run Ended After 38 Games
sections.body: Thomas appeared in 38 games for the Amigos at 6.9 points in 13.8 minutes. That was his final professional season, leaving Anaheim without a second year of value from the exchange.

sections.heading: The Multi-Year Return Makes Denver the Winner
sections.body: Denver’s A- versus Anaheim’s C+ reflects 183 regular-season games and growing backcourt responsibility from Congdon against one partial season from Thomas.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win — Denver A-, Anaheim C+. Denver traded Willis Thomas to Anaheim for Jeff Congdon on December 11, 1967. Congdon gave the Rockets 41 games after the trade, then stayed for 59 games in 1968-69 and all 83 games in 1969-70.

sections.heading: Chicago Sent Erwin Mueller to Los Angeles for Two Assets
sections.body: The Bulls traded Erwin Mueller to the Lakers on January 9, 1968 for Jim Barnes and a 1968 third-round pick that became Dave Newmark. Chicago received immediate depth plus a draft selection.

sections.heading: Chicago Got Useful Games from Barnes and Newmark
sections.body: Barnes played 47 regular-season games for the Bulls, while Newmark added 81 games as a rookie. Chicago later sold Barnes’ rights to Boston, so the incoming package produced more than a single short stint.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Turned Mueller into Keith Erickson
sections.body: Mueller played 39 Lakers games at 8.3 points and 5.7 rebounds before Los Angeles traded him for Keith Erickson in September 1968. Erickson then played 309 Lakers games through 1972-73 and remained on the 1972 championship roster.

sections.heading: The Downstream Conversion Tips the Deal to Los Angeles
sections.body: Chicago’s B reflects a respectable two-asset return, but the Lakers’ A is driven by the Mueller-to-Erickson conversion. Los Angeles transformed a short-term player into a long-term championship-era contributor.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win — Los Angeles A, Chicago B. The first Los Angeles return was brief: Erwin Mueller played 39 games before the Lakers moved him for Keith Erickson in September 1968. Erickson subsequently played 309 Lakers games and belonged to the franchise's 1972 championship roster. Chicago's side also delivered tangible minutes, with 47 games from Jim Barnes and 81 in Dave Newmark's rookie season. The later sale of Barnes' rights should not erase those contributions. The decisive distinction is what Los Angeles obtained in its separate Mueller-for-Erickson conversion, not the simple number of pieces each team received on January 9.

sections.heading: The Verified Trade Date Is January 11
sections.body: San Diego traded Johnny Green to Philadelphia on January 11, 1968 for a 1968 fourth-round pick that became Darryl Jones. The corrected record removes the legacy January 10 date and an unsupported cash component.

sections.heading: Green Gave Philadelphia Two Seasons of Depth
sections.body: Green played 35 games for the 76ers after the trade and 74 more in 1968-69. He also supplied playoff depth during two postseason runs, giving Philadelphia 109 regular-season appearances from the exchange.

sections.heading: San Diego’s Pick Did Not Become an NBA Contributor
sections.body: The Rockets used the No. 48 selection on Jones, but he never appeared in an NBA game. The draft asset therefore produced no measurable regular-season value for San Diego.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Received the Only Realized Basketball Return
sections.body: The 76ers’ B+ against San Diego’s D reflects Green’s 109 games and postseason availability against a draft selection that never reached the NBA.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win — San Diego D, Philadelphia B+. Philadelphia received veteran Johnny Green from the San Diego Rockets on January 11, 1968 and got 109 regular-season games plus postseason depth across parts of two seasons. San Diego received a 1968 fourth-round pick that became No. 48 Darryl Jones, who never logged an NBA appearance. That measurable difference, rather than a hypothetical cash component, supports the wide grade split. The saved league and club transactions date this player-for-pick exchange January 11; the legacy January 10 route and earlier mention of cash were not corroborated. The Sixers benefited from an actual frontcourt contributor, while the Rockets' selected player created no regular-season NBA return.

sections.heading: New Jersey Traded Barry Leibowitz for Levern Tart
sections.body: The Americans acquired Levern Tart from the Oakland Oaks for Barry Leibowitz on January 18, 1968. Both players became productive immediately, and each later carried downstream trade value.

sections.heading: Tart Was the Stronger Direct Scoring Return
sections.body: Tart averaged 19.0 points in 31 games for New Jersey, then stayed through the move to New York and added 35 games at 14.7 points in 1968-69 before joining a three-player trade to Houston.

sections.heading: Oakland Also Converted Leibowitz into a Bigger Package
sections.body: Leibowitz played 35 games for the Oaks at 14.2 points, 5.5 rebounds and 3.8 assists. Oakland later included him with Ronald Franz and Steve Jones in the June 1968 deal for Larry Brown and Doug Moe.

sections.heading: New Jersey Wins a Productive Two-Way Trade
sections.body: The Americans’ A- versus Oakland/Virginia’s B+ reflects Tart’s stronger direct scoring return. The close grades also recognize that Oakland extracted real production and preserved useful downstream value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Americans Win — New Jersey A-, Oakland B+. Levern Tart immediately supplied New Jersey with 31 games at 19.0 points per game, then another 35 appearances at 14.7 after the franchise's move to New York. Oakland received Barry Leibowitz, who contributed 35 games at 14.2 points and later formed part of a separate package sent for Larry Brown and Doug Moe. Both organizations obtained measurable basketball returns and additional asset possibilities. Tart's more sustained direct scoring earns New Jersey the narrow edge without ignoring Oakland's productive follow-on.

sections.heading: St. Louis Acquired Don Ohl for Tom Workman and a Third-Rounder
sections.body: The Hawks acquired Don Ohl from Baltimore on January 21, 1968. St. Louis sent Tom Workman and a 1968 third-round pick, later recorded as No. 33 Jack Thompson, giving the Bullets both a player and a draft asset.

sections.heading: Ohl Was the Proven Veteran in the Exchange
sections.body: Ohl arrived as an established NBA guard rather than a speculative rights asset. The Hawks’ B+ grade reflects the value of acquiring the best-known immediate player in a two-for-one framework.

sections.heading: Baltimore Received Two Chances to Recover Value
sections.body: The Bullets took Workman plus a third-round selection. That package created more optionality than a straight player swap, but the canonical record does not support a realized outcome strong enough to erase St. Louis’ advantage.

sections.heading: The Hawks Hold the Better Hindsight Grade
sections.body: TradeVerdicts assigns St. Louis a B+ and Baltimore a C. The difference recognizes the veteran return the Hawks secured while still giving Baltimore credit for receiving both a player and a draft choice.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win — St. Louis B+, Baltimore C. In January 1968, before the franchise's move to Atlanta, the St. Louis Hawks acquired veteran guard Don Ohl from Baltimore. The Bullets received Tom Workman and the Hawks' 1968 third-round selection, ultimately recorded as No. 33 Jack Thompson. Baltimore therefore obtained two distinct opportunities rather than an empty return. Ohl was the immediate established player on the Hawks side, supporting the inherited advantage, while the transaction ledger alone does not establish that either outgoing piece later produced zero value. The result credits the verified player-for-player-and-pick package without inventing an additional draft asset or outcome.

sections.heading: The Correct Deal Date Is February 1, 1968
sections.body: Detroit sent John Tresvant and Tom Van Arsdale to Cincinnati for Happy Hairston and Jim Fox on February 1, correcting the older January 29 date. Team and league transaction records support the four-player structure.

sections.heading: Van Arsdale Became Cincinnati’s Defining Return
sections.body: Van Arsdale played 379 regular-season games for the Royals/Kings franchise and made three consecutive All-Star teams from 1970 through 1972. Tresvant added 81 Cincinnati games before being traded for Al Tucker.

sections.heading: Detroit Still Received Real Multi-Player Value
sections.body: Hairston played 122 games for the Pistons and Fox added 49. Both also retained later trade value, so Detroit’s side was productive rather than a failed package.

sections.heading: Cincinnati’s Longevity and Peak Win the Comparison
sections.body: Detroit earns an A- because its return produced useful value, but Cincinnati’s A+ reflects Van Arsdale’s multi-year tenure and All-Star peak. The Royals created the stronger realized outcome without the Pistons receiving an empty return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Royals Win — Detroit A-, Cincinnati A+. Detroit traded John Tresvant and Tom Van Arsdale to Cincinnati on February 1, 1968 for Happy Hairston and Jim Fox, correcting the legacy January 29 date. Van Arsdale became the defining piece: he played 379 regular-season games for the Royals/Kings franchise after the trade and made three consecutive All-Star teams from 1970 through 1972.

sections.heading: Denver Sold Tom Hoover to Houston for Cash
sections.body: The Rockets sold Tom Hoover to the Houston Mavericks on May 2, 1968. Hoover had already completed a 70-game Denver season, so the transaction transferred his rights after that campaign rather than moving an active-season role.

sections.heading: Houston Received Only Four Games from Hoover
sections.body: Hoover appeared in four regular-season games for the Mavericks in 1968-69 before Houston traded him to Minnesota for Willie Porter on November 25. Porter then played only two games for Houston.

sections.heading: Denver’s Financial Return Is Unquantified
sections.body: The cash amount Denver received is not disclosed in the available records. That prevents a precise comparison with the six total games Houston produced from the Hoover-to-Porter player chain.

sections.heading: The Mavericks Hold Only a Slight Edge
sections.body: Houston’s C- versus Denver’s D+ reflects a very small realized basketball return. The grades stay low and close because neither side produced substantial traceable value and Denver’s cash amount remains unknown.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Mavericks Edge — Denver D+, Houston C-. Denver sold Tom Hoover to the Houston Mavericks for cash on May 2, 1968. Hoover had already completed a 70-game season for the Rockets, so the transaction concerns his rights after that campaign rather than games transferred midseason.

sections.heading: San Francisco Moved Edgar Lacy’s NBA Rights to Los Angeles
sections.body: The Warriors traded Edgar Lacy’s NBA rights to the Lakers on May 9, 1968. Contemporary reporting described the return as a high selection in the next draft, but the exact pick has not been verified.

sections.heading: Lacy Never Played for the Lakers
sections.body: Lacy instead signed with the ABA’s Los Angeles Stars and appeared in 46 games before leaving professional basketball. Los Angeles therefore received no NBA games from the acquired rights.

sections.heading: The Warriors’ Draft Return Cannot Be Traced
sections.body: San Francisco’s 1969 draft list does not reveal a clearly identifiable Lakers-derived selection tied to the deal. Without a verified exercised pick, the Warriors’ side has no measurable NBA outcome to credit.

sections.heading: Minimal Value on Both Sides Produces an Even Grade
sections.body: Both franchises receive a D because neither side has a verified realized NBA return. The rights did not produce Lakers games and the reported draft consideration cannot responsibly be assigned to a specific Warriors selection.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — San Francisco D, Los Angeles D. San Francisco traded the NBA rights to Edgar Lacy to the Los Angeles Lakers on May 9, 1968 for what contemporaneous reporting described as a high pick in the next draft. The exact selection tied to that consideration has not been verified, and the Warriors' 1969 draft list does not show a clearly identifiable extra Lakers-derived choice.

sections.heading: New Jersey Bought Maurice McHartley for a 1969 Draft Choice
sections.body: The Americans acquired Maurice McHartley from Dallas on July 9, 1968 for a 1969 draft asset. The exact exercised Chaparrals selection remains unresolved, so the comparison must center on the player value New Jersey could trace.

sections.heading: McHartley Started a Productive Player Chain
sections.body: McHartley played 24 games for the Americans/Nets at 12.4 points, 3.2 rebounds and 3.2 assists before New York moved him to Miami for Ron Perry. Perry then supplied 23 games at 19.3 points.

sections.heading: Perry Became Steve Chubin
sections.body: New York later traded Perry for Steve Chubin, who added 28 Nets games that season and 11 more in 1969-70. That gives the original McHartley acquisition a traceable chain beyond his own short stint.

sections.heading: The Nets Have the Clearer Realized Value
sections.body: Dallas received a draft asset described in secondary research as a high pick, but its final identity is unresolved. New Jersey’s B+ versus Dallas’ C reflects the documented player chain rather than assuming the unknown pick had no value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win — New Jersey B+, Dallas C. Maurice McHartley was acquired from the Dallas Chaparrals on July 9, 1968 for a 1969 draft choice whose eventual selection is still not established by the research. McHartley contributed 24 games at 12.4 points, 3.2 rebounds and 3.2 assists, then became Ron Perry in a later trade. Perry supplied 23 games at 19.3 points before being exchanged for Steve Chubin, who added further Nets appearances. That documented sequence, rather than a claim that Dallas's unidentified pick had zero value, explains the B+ return for the Americans/Nets lineage. The C grade for Dallas should remain conservative because the pick's full downstream identity is unresolved.

sections.heading: Denver Acquired Bob Verga for Bob Bedell and a Pick
sections.body: The Rockets acquired Bob Verga from Dallas on July 13, 1968 for Bob Bedell and a 1969 third-round draft choice. The transaction gave the Chaparrals an immediate player plus a future asset.

sections.heading: Verga’s Denver Stay Lasted Six Games
sections.body: Verga averaged 11.2 points in 25.0 minutes across six Rockets games before Denver traded him to New York for another draft choice on November 11. Denver therefore preserved some transactional value despite the brief stint.

sections.heading: Bedell Gave Dallas the Deeper Direct Return
sections.body: Bedell played 42 regular-season games for Dallas in 1968-69 at 5.5 points and 2.8 rebounds, then remained with the franchise for brief appearances over the next two seasons. The original third-round pick’s final player remains unresolved.

sections.heading: Dallas Wins a Close, Low-Level Exchange
sections.body: The Chaparrals’ B- against Denver’s C+ reflects the deeper direct return and extra draft asset. Denver avoided a total loss by flipping Verga, which keeps the grade difference narrow.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Chaparrals Edge — Denver C+, Dallas B-. Denver acquired Bob Verga from the Dallas Chaparrals on July 13, 1968 for Bob Bedell and a 1969 third-round draft choice. Verga played only six games for the Rockets, averaging 11.2 points in 25.0 minutes, before Denver traded him to New York for another draft choice on November 11.

sections.heading: Boston Acquired Emmette Bryant from Phoenix
sections.body: The Celtics acquired Emmette Bryant from the expansion Suns on August 27, 1968. Phoenix received a 1969 second-round pick, recorded as No. 24 Gene Williams.

sections.heading: Boston Chose an Immediate Backcourt Piece
sections.body: Bryant became more than an emergency backcourt signing. Boston's 1968-69 championship playoff run used him in all 18 postseason games at 33.7 minutes a night, with 11.0 points, 4.9 rebounds and 3.0 assists per game. Those actual Finals-season contributions are a stronger justification for the preserved B than merely saying the Celtics preferred an existing player to a future selection. Phoenix's return was the second-round pick that became No. 24 Gene Williams in 1969; neither the deal's value nor Bryant's contribution should be inflated by attaching unrelated future Boston titles to this 1968 exchange.

sections.heading: Phoenix Added a Second-Round Draft Asset
sections.body: The Suns received a future second-round choice and used the selection on Williams. That gave Phoenix a legitimate roster-building asset and a reasonable expansion-era pathway to add younger talent, even though the canonical outcome does not match Boston’s realized return.

sections.heading: The Celtics Earn the Better Grade
sections.body: Boston’s B versus Phoenix’s C reflects the stronger realized player value from Bryant. Phoenix still receives credit for obtaining a second-round selection rather than losing the asset for nothing.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win — Boston B, Phoenix C. The August 27, 1968 exchange gave Boston guard Emmette Bryant and sent the expansion Suns a 1969 second-round choice later used on No. 24 Gene Williams. Bryant subsequently played all 18 Celtics playoff games in the 1969 championship run, averaging 11.0 points and 3.0 assists across 33.7 minutes a night. Phoenix obtained a genuine draft right, but Boston's immediate rotation and postseason contribution support the inherited stronger grade; there was no additional cash component in the cited transaction ledger.

sections.heading: Denver Sent Willie Murrell to Miami for a Pick and Cash
sections.body: The Rockets traded Willie Murrell to the Miami Floridians on August 28, 1968. Denver received a draft choice and cash, but the exact selection and payment amount remain unresolved.

sections.heading: Murrell Became an Immediate Miami Mainstay
sections.body: Murrell played 75 regular-season games for the Floridians at 15.3 points and 7.5 rebounds. He then led Miami with 16.4 points per game across 12 playoff appearances as the club reached the Eastern Division Finals.

sections.heading: Denver’s Return Was Real but Hard to Quantify
sections.body: A draft asset and cash are both verified, so Denver did not give Murrell away. The missing pick identity and cash figure prevent those assets from being compared precisely with Miami’s known production.

sections.heading: Miami’s Measurable Return Wins the Hindsight Grade
sections.body: The Floridians’ B+ versus Denver’s C reflects one full season of substantial regular-season and playoff production. Denver’s grade stays respectable because two incoming assets are verified even though their final value is unclear.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Floridians Win — Denver C, Miami B+. Denver traded Willie Murrell to the Miami Floridians on August 28, 1968 for a draft choice and cash. Murrell became a major rotation player immediately, appearing in 75 regular-season games at 15.3 points and 7.5 rebounds and then leading Miami with 16.4 points per game across 12 playoff appearances as the Floridians reached the Eastern Division Finals.

sections.heading: Denver Acquired Larry Bunce for a Draft Choice
sections.body: The Rockets acquired Larry Bunce from the Los Angeles Stars on August 29, 1968 for a draft asset. The exact exercised selection remains unresolved, so the legacy claim that it became Ted Weirman is not treated as established fact.

sections.heading: Bunce Played 23 Games for the Rockets
sections.body: Bunce averaged 4.0 points and 2.5 rebounds in 9.8 minutes across 23 Denver games. The stint was modest, but it gave the Rockets measurable on-court value.

sections.heading: Denver Later Recycled Bunce into Another Package
sections.body: On January 4, 1969, Denver traded Bunce to Dallas for Rich Peek and another draft choice. That later move preserved transaction value beyond Bunce’s limited minutes.

sections.heading: The Rockets Hold a Narrow Edge
sections.body: Denver’s C+ against Los Angeles’ C reflects the known games and later trade value produced by Bunce. The gap stays small because the Stars’ incoming draft choice cannot be fully reconstructed.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Rockets Edge — Denver C+, Los Angeles Stars C. Denver acquired Larry Bunce from the Los Angeles Stars on August 29, 1968 for a draft choice. Bunce played 23 games for the Rockets, averaging 4.0 points and 2.5 rebounds in 9.8 minutes, before Denver traded him to Dallas on January 4, 1969 for Rich Peek and another draft choice.

sections.heading: Atlanta Acquired Dennis Hamilton from Phoenix
sections.body: The Hawks acquired Dennis Hamilton from the Suns on September 11, 1968. Phoenix received cash and a 1969 third-round pick recorded as No. 39 Lloyd Kerr.

sections.heading: The Hawks Chose Immediate Player Depth
sections.body: Hamilton gave the Hawks an immediate but brief frontcourt option in their first Atlanta season. He appeared in 25 Atlanta regular-season games in 1968-69, totaling 141 minutes and averaging 3.0 points and 1.2 rebounds. Phoenix instead collected the rights to a 1969 third-round choice that became No. 39 Lloyd Kerr, together with cash. The Suns' own historical transaction guides document that payment, but they don't specify its amount. Atlanta's limited Hamilton contribution and the unpriced cash return make the existing even C+/C+ verdict more defensible than awarding an unsupported decisive winner.

sections.heading: Phoenix Took Draft Capital and Cash
sections.body: The expansion Suns received two forms of value: a third-round selection and an undisclosed financial payment. The unknown cash figure limits the precision of any hindsight comparison.

sections.heading: Equal C+ Grades Fit the Evidence
sections.body: TradeVerdicts assigns both clubs a C+. Atlanta received immediate depth while Phoenix received a pick and cash, and the surviving record does not support a meaningful enough difference to declare a winner.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Atlanta C+, Phoenix C+. On September 11, 1968, the newly relocated Atlanta Hawks obtained Dennis Hamilton from the expansion Suns for a 1969 third-round pick, later No. 39 Lloyd Kerr, plus cash. Hamilton played 25 Atlanta games that season, averaging 3.0 points in 5.6 minutes; the cash amount is not established by the available transaction histories. This modest, short-lived on-court return versus Phoenix's pick and financial consideration supports the inherited equal grades, not the outdated St. Louis label.

sections.heading: Denver Acquired John Fairchild for a Draft Choice
sections.body: The Rockets acquired John Fairchild from the Los Angeles Stars on September 15, 1968 for a draft choice. The incoming player was the known asset; the Stars’ exact exercised pick remains unresolved in the reviewed record.

sections.heading: Fairchild Gave Denver Eleven Games
sections.body: Fairchild appeared in 11 games for Denver, averaging 3.6 points in 12.3 minutes. The direct return was limited, but it was still measurable rather than a rights-only outcome.

sections.heading: Denver Preserved Value by Moving Him Again
sections.body: On November 25, Denver traded Fairchild to Indiana for another draft choice. That gave the Rockets a second transaction path tied directly to the original acquisition instead of letting the player asset expire.

sections.heading: The Unresolved Stars Pick Keeps the Margin Narrow
sections.body: Los Angeles received a legitimate future asset, but its round and eventual player cannot be securely identified. Denver’s C+ versus Los Angeles’ C therefore reflects a slight realized edge, not a decisive win.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Rockets Edge — Denver C+, Los Angeles Stars C. Denver acquired John Fairchild from the Los Angeles Stars on September 15, 1968 for a draft choice. Fairchild played 11 games for the Rockets, averaging 3.6 points in 12.3 minutes, before Denver traded him to Indiana on November 25 for another draft choice.

sections.heading: New York Acquired Dewitt Menyard for a Draft Choice
sections.body: The New York Americans acquired Dewitt Menyard from the Houston Mavericks in September 1968 for a draft choice. The player movement is established, while the exact round and later identity of Houston’s selection remain unresolved.

sections.heading: Menyard Produced No New York Games
sections.body: Menyard never appeared in another professional game after his 1967-68 Houston season. New York therefore received no realized on-court production from the player it acquired.

sections.heading: Houston Retained a Future Asset
sections.body: The Mavericks received a verified draft choice. Even without a resolved pick identity, that future asset has more documented value than a player return that produced zero games.

sections.heading: The Result Favors Houston Modestly
sections.body: The C versus D split gives Houston credit for retaining a legitimate future asset without pretending the unresolved selection became a star. New York’s side is graded lower because Menyard produced no measurable return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Edge — New York D, Houston C. New York acquired Dewitt Menyard from the Houston Mavericks for a draft choice in September 1968. Menyard recorded no New York appearances after his Houston season, while the draft choice's eventual player remains unverified; the Houston edge credits the documented future asset rather than an invented successful selection.

sections.heading: The Paul Long Movement Is Historically Disputed
sections.body: Legacy Los Angeles and Detroit records describe the same early-October 1968 Paul Long movement, but the reviewed historical sources disagree on both mechanism and date. A specialist database describes a transaction across October 8-9, while other ledgers point elsewhere.

sections.heading: The Major Team Ledgers Do Not Fully Agree
sections.body: Basketball-Reference’s Lakers ledger omits the transaction, while Detroit and league records instead show Long joining the Pistons as a free agent on October 12. That conflict prevents the archive row from being treated as a settled trade.

sections.heading: Long Produced No Detroit NBA Games That Season
sections.body: Long did not appear in an NBA game for Detroit in 1968-69 and instead played nine ABA games for Kentucky. The player outcome therefore does not resolve the underlying transaction dispute.

sections.heading: Preserve the Conflict Without Inventing a Grade
sections.body: This Lakers-side record remains the source-conflict container for the unresolved movement. Because the mechanism itself is disputed, TradeVerdicts correctly leaves the transaction at Insufficient Evidence rather than assigning a winner or team grades.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Insufficient Evidence Los Angeles and Detroit legacy archive entrys describe the same early-October 1968 Paul Long roster movement, but the reviewed historical sources disagree on what actually occurred. A specialist database places the movement across October 8-9 and describes Los Angeles sending Long to Detroit for consideration.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Sent Johnny Egan to Los Angeles
sections.body: The Bucks sent Johnny Egan to the Lakers on October 8, 1968 for future draft consideration. Milwaukee, Los Angeles and league transaction ledgers agree on the basic player-for-pick structure, while another source also reports cash.

sections.heading: Egan Immediately Became a Major Lakers Guard
sections.body: Egan played all 82 regular-season games for Los Angeles at 13.9 points and 4.3 assists, then appeared in all 18 playoff games as the Lakers reached the 1969 NBA Finals.

sections.heading: His Value Continued into a Second Finals Season
sections.body: Egan remained with Los Angeles for the following season and again reached the Finals before Cleveland selected him in the 1970 expansion draft. The Lakers therefore received multi-season, high-availability guard production.

sections.heading: The Unresolved Bucks Pick Cannot Match the Known Return
sections.body: Milwaukee’s future draft consideration remains unresolved in the reviewed record. Los Angeles’ A- versus Milwaukee’s C reflects the large amount of verified Egan production without assuming the Bucks received nothing of value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win — Milwaukee C, Los Angeles A-. Milwaukee sent Johnny Egan to the Los Angeles Lakers on October 8, 1968 for future draft consideration. Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee, Lakers and league ledgers agree on the date and pick-for-player structure, while Pro Sports Transactions additionally reports cash and notes a Lakers media-guide date discrepancy.
