sections.heading: New York Bought Ollie Darden from Indiana
sections.body: The Nets acquired Ollie Darden from the Pacers for cash on October 9, 1968. Indiana’s financial return is verified, but the amount is not disclosed in the reviewed sources.

sections.heading: Darden Gave New York Immediate Rotation Production
sections.body: Darden played 30 games for the Nets and averaged 11.5 points and 7.1 rebounds. That was substantial short-term production relative to the modest scale of the cash transaction.

sections.heading: New York Also Reused Darden in a Later Trade
sections.body: On December 30, the Nets packaged Darden with Dan Anderson to Kentucky for Manny Leaks and Randolph Mahaffey. Darden therefore retained transactional utility after his initial run in New York.

sections.heading: The Nets Hold the Stronger Realized Return
sections.body: Because Indiana’s cash amount is unknown, the grade gap stays controlled. New York’s B+ versus Indiana’s C- reflects both Darden’s measurable production and his later use as part of another asset package.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win — New York B+, Indiana C-. New York acquired Ollie Darden from Indiana for cash on October 9, 1968. Darden played 30 games for the Nets and averaged 11.5 points and 7.1 rebounds before New York packaged him with Dan Anderson to Kentucky for Manny Leaks and Randolph Mahaffey on December 30.

sections.heading: This Detroit Row Duplicates the Paul Long Conflict
sections.body: The October 9 Detroit-side import is the opposite-team perspective of the disputed Paul Long movement already preserved in the Los Angeles canonical record. It does not establish a second transaction.

sections.heading: The Historical Sources Disagree on the Mechanism
sections.body: A specialist source describes consideration moving from Detroit, while modern team and league ledgers instead show Long joining Detroit as a free agent on October 12. The evidence is not strong enough to resolve the contradiction.

sections.heading: Two Active Records Would Double-Count One Movement
sections.body: Keeping both perspectives as separate graded trades would duplicate the same player movement and create a false second outcome between Detroit and Los Angeles.

sections.heading: Retain Provenance, Supersede the Duplicate
sections.body: The Detroit-side entry remains only so its source lineage can be audited. It is marked Record Superseded and excluded from graded results rather than forcing a verdict on an unresolved transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Resolution
finalVerdict.body: Record Superseded This Detroit-side October 9 import is the opposite-team duplicate of the disputed Paul Long movement retained in nba-trade-lal-1968-0053. The specialist source and modern team ledgers disagree on the mechanism and date, so a second active record would double-count one unresolved event.

sections.heading: October 1968: Atlanta Exchanged Wilkens for Seattle All-Star Walt Hazzard
sections.body: The Hawks moved from St. Louis to Atlanta for the 1968-69 season, and on October 12, 1968 traded veteran guard Lenny Wilkens to the Seattle SuperSonics for Walt Hazzard. Both clubs' 1968-69 transaction ledgers list the same direct exchange, with no extra draft choice or cash consideration. Wilkens had been an All-Star and the 1967-68 MVP runner-up during his final Hawks season; Hazzard had just averaged 24.0 points for expansion Seattle and made the 1968 All-Star team. For Atlanta this was an exchange of established lead guards, not a transaction in which one franchise sent away an NBA star and received an untested prospect. The older canonical player label Mahdi Abdul-Rahman refers to Hazzard, who adopted that name years after this 1968 trade; it is not an additional traded player.

sections.heading: Seattle's 308 Wilkens Games and Player-Coach Tenure
sections.body: Seattle received four full seasons of Lenny Wilkens as a player, totaling 308 regular-season games. He averaged 19.5 points and 9.0 assists during those SuperSonics seasons, including 22.4 points and 8.2 assists in 1968-69, the franchise's second season. After that debut year in Seattle, Wilkens became its player-coach, a responsibility separate from his value as the acquired point guard. The club reached 47-35 in 1971-72, its first winning season, with Wilkens contributing 18.0 points and 9.6 assists per game. The 47-win improvement cannot fairly be assigned to the 1968 trade alone, but it documents a sustained Seattle era rather than merely a short-term roster rental. Inherited grade A for the SuperSonics' successor-franchise record is anchored in that four-season contribution.

sections.heading: Hazzard's 244 Atlanta Games Were Genuine Return, Not Zero Value
sections.body: Walt Hazzard did contribute after changing teams. Across the 1968-69, 1969-70 and 1970-71 seasons he played 244 regular-season games for Atlanta: 80, 82 and 82 respectively. His scoring rose from 11.2 points per game in the first Hawks season to 15.3 and then roughly 16.5. That was meaningful veteran offense and makes it inaccurate to describe Atlanta as having received no playable asset. The asymmetry came from the duration and ceiling of the two incoming guards: Wilkens delivered 308 Seattle games with consistently high assist totals and later held the dual player-coach position. Hazzard's subsequent NBA appearances for Buffalo, Golden State and Seattle were separate team transactions, not additional Atlanta production attributable to the October 1968 acquisition.

sections.heading: Why the Seattle A Versus Atlanta D Grades Favor the Sonics
sections.body: This inherited A-for-Seattle and D-for-Atlanta outcome measures the realized 1968 trade from the acquiring teams' perspectives. Wilkens' 308 Seattle games, four high-minute seasons, multiple All-Star selections there and his 1971-72 role on a 47-win squad distinguish a long franchise building block from Hazzard's 244 Hawks games. Atlanta's return was not useless: he had already earned an All-Star selection in Seattle and continued to score in double figures for all three Hawks seasons. Yet the Hawks gave up the longer-lasting distributor and future Seattle player-coach. The canonical database uses Oklahoma City Thunder as Seattle's modern successor ID for this historical transaction; the original 1968 party was the SuperSonics, not an Oklahoma City team. Retaining that identity distinction avoids presenting a later franchise relocation as a 1968 counterparty.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Oklahoma City Thunder Win is the inherited successor-franchise verdict for the 1968 Seattle SuperSonics trade, with Seattle A and Atlanta D. Seattle obtained Lenny Wilkens for Walt Hazzard on October 12, 1968, then received 308 regular-season games and four years of high-level point guard play, including his later tenure as player-coach. Atlanta received a genuine 244-game return from Hazzard, so the lopsided grade is about relative sustained value rather than a zero-value asset. The canonical Hawks player label Mahdi Abdul-Rahman is Hazzard's later adopted name; these are not two people or two incoming players. No draft picks, unknown cash transfers or modern Oklahoma City player contributions should be inferred from the 1968 transaction.

sections.heading: New York Sent Tony Jackson to Minnesota for a Draft Choice
sections.body: The Nets traded Tony Jackson to the Minnesota Pipers on November 7, 1968 for a draft choice. The selection is verified as consideration, but its round and eventual player remain unresolved.

sections.heading: Jackson Played Only One Game for Minnesota
sections.body: Jackson appeared once for the Pipers before Minnesota moved him to Houston on November 24 for another draft choice. His direct on-court return to Minnesota was therefore minimal.

sections.heading: Minnesota Preserved Asset Value Through the Resale
sections.body: Although the Pipers received almost no playing value, they did not simply lose the asset. Trading Jackson onward for another pick preserved a future return tied to the original acquisition.

sections.heading: Both Draft Outcomes Are Too Unclear for a Wide Gap
sections.body: New York’s C+ versus Minnesota’s C reflects a slight edge for converting a player who no longer fit its roster into a future asset. The unresolved picks on both sides keep the grades close.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Nets Edge — New York C+, Minnesota C. New York traded Tony Jackson to the Minnesota Pipers on November 7, 1968 for a draft choice. Jackson played only one game for Minnesota before the Pipers moved him to Houston on November 24 for another draft choice.

sections.heading: New York Acquired Bob Verga from Denver
sections.body: The Nets acquired Bob Verga from the Rockets on November 11, 1968 for a draft choice. Denver’s incoming selection is verified, but its round and eventual player remain unresolved.

sections.heading: Verga Produced Immediately for the Nets
sections.body: Verga played 24 games for New York and averaged 12.8 points, 2.8 rebounds and 1.7 assists. That gave the Nets a measurable player return before they moved him again.

sections.heading: New York Preserved Verga as a Trade Asset
sections.body: On January 31, 1969, the Nets included Verga with Levern Tart and Hank Whitney in a deal with Houston for Willie Somerset and Leary Lentz. His value therefore extended beyond the initial 24 games.

sections.heading: The Known Player Chain Gives New York the Edge
sections.body: Denver’s pick could have had value, but its final identity is unresolved. New York’s B versus Denver’s C+ reflects the documented production and later transaction value that can be traced directly to Verga.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win — New York B, Denver C+. New York acquired Bob Verga from Denver on November 11, 1968 for a draft choice. Verga played 24 games for the Nets and averaged 12.8 points, 2.8 rebounds and 1.7 assists before New York traded him with Levern Tart and Hank Whitney to Houston on January 31, 1969 for Willie Somerset and Leary Lentz.

sections.heading: Atlanta Acquired Richie Guerin’s Rights for Dick Smith
sections.body: The Hawks acquired the rights to Richie Guerin from Seattle on November 15, 1968 and sent Dick Smith to the SuperSonics. The canonical record contains no additional pick or cash component.

sections.heading: Atlanta Reclaimed a Familiar Veteran Asset
sections.body: The 1968 rights transaction was unusual because Guerin already had a Hawks coaching history. Seattle held his playing rights after taking him in the expansion draft, and Atlanta sent Dick Smith to obtain those rights back. Guerin resumed playing in 27 Atlanta regular-season games in 1968-69, with 151 points and 99 assists over 472 minutes. Those are attributable on-court contributions, not the entirety of his coaching output. Although he coached the Hawks to a 48-34 season, he had served as their coach before the Seattle rights move, so it would overstate this deal to credit Atlanta's entire coaching record as a new asset purchased from Seattle.

sections.heading: Seattle Received Dick Smith as the Direct Return
sections.body: The SuperSonics’ side is a single-player return. The canonical record does not show an additional asset attached to Smith that would materially narrow the value comparison.

sections.heading: The Hawks Receive the Better Grade
sections.body: TradeVerdicts assigns Atlanta a B+ and Seattle a C. The result recognizes Atlanta’s stronger realized rights value while still crediting Seattle for receiving an actual player rather than an empty return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win — Atlanta B+, Seattle C, using the existing site grades. On November 15, 1968, the SuperSonics conveyed Richie Guerin's playing rights to Atlanta in return for Dick Smith. Guerin was already the Hawks' coach; this reacquisition chiefly restored his ability to suit up, producing 27 Atlanta regular-season appearances, 151 points and 99 assists in 1968-69. Seattle received an actual player in Smith, and the record contains no attached pick or cash. Atlanta's narrow roster-rights advantage must not be mistaken for an acquisition of Guerin's entire pre-existing coaching tenure.

sections.heading: Chicago Acquired Bob Love and Bob Weiss
sections.body: The Bulls acquired Bob Love and Bob Weiss from Milwaukee for Flynn Robinson on November 23, 1968. Chicago received two rotation pieces in a one-for-two exchange, while the Bucks landed the proven scoring guard.

sections.heading: Love Became the Centerpiece of Chicago’s Return
sections.body: Love developed into one of the defining players of the Bulls’ early-1970s rise, making three All-Star teams, earning two All-NBA Second Team selections and three All-Defensive selections during his Chicago tenure.

sections.heading: Weiss Added Six Seasons of Backcourt Stability
sections.body: Bob Weiss gave Chicago another durable return, providing six seasons of steady guard play. That second long-term contributor widened the value gap beyond what Love alone created.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Still Received a Productive Scorer
sections.body: Robinson averaged 20.3 points over 65 Milwaukee games that season, so the Bucks did receive real value. Chicago’s A+ versus Milwaukee’s C+ reflects the much larger long-term return created by Love and Weiss.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win — Chicago A+, Milwaukee C+. Bob Love became a long-term Chicago centerpiece, earning three All-Star selections and several all-league or defensive honors; Bob Weiss added six seasons of backcourt service. Milwaukee received Flynn Robinson, who scored 20.3 points per game over 65 Bucks appearances in that first season, a genuine immediate return. The Bulls nevertheless acquired two durable contributors for one productive guard. The gulf in longevity, not a claim that Robinson was worthless, accounts for the wider final grade difference.

sections.heading: Indiana Acquired John Fairchild for a Draft Choice
sections.body: The Pacers acquired John Fairchild from Denver on November 25, 1968 for a draft choice. The selection is verified as Denver’s return, but its round and eventual player remain unresolved.

sections.heading: Fairchild Gave Indiana a Full Half-Season Role
sections.body: Fairchild played 52 regular-season games for the Pacers and averaged 5.5 points and 2.1 rebounds. He also appeared in nine playoff games during Indiana’s run to the 1969 ABA Finals.

sections.heading: Indiana Preserved Value Beyond the First Season
sections.body: Fairchild remained with the Pacers into the following season before Indiana sold him to Kentucky for cash. That gave the Pacers a second traceable return tied to the original acquisition.

sections.heading: The Known Production Gives Indiana the Edge
sections.body: Denver’s draft choice may have created future value, but its final identity cannot be traced confidently. Indiana’s B versus Denver’s C+ therefore reflects the clearer realized basketball return without overstating the gap.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pacers Win — Denver C+, Indiana B. Indiana acquired John Fairchild from Denver on November 25, 1968 for a draft choice. Fairchild played 52 regular-season games for the Pacers, averaging 5.5 points and 2.1 rebounds, then appeared in nine playoff games during Indiana's run to the 1969 ABA Finals.

sections.heading: Boston Acquired Jim Barnes’ Rights from Chicago
sections.body: The Celtics acquired Jim Barnes’ player rights from Chicago on December 1, 1968. Chicago’s transaction ledger describes the move as a sale, although the surviving public records do not identify the cash amount.

sections.heading: Barnes Contributed to the Eventual Champions
sections.body: Barnes appeared in 49 regular-season games for Boston that season, averaging 5.1 points and 4.0 rebounds in 12.1 minutes. He provided frontcourt depth during a championship campaign.

sections.heading: He Stayed for the Full 1969-70 Season
sections.body: Barnes remained with Boston and played 77 games the next season. That additional year gives the Celtics a clear, measurable two-season return from the rights purchase.

sections.heading: Unknown Cash Keeps Chicago’s Grade Respectable
sections.body: Chicago’s sale price cannot be measured precisely, so the Bulls are not treated as receiving nothing. Boston’s B versus Chicago’s C+ reflects the known player production while keeping the grade difference modest.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win — Boston B, Chicago C+. Boston acquired Jim Barnes' player rights from Chicago on December 1, 1968. Barnes became frontcourt depth for the eventual NBA champions, appearing in 49 regular-season games and averaging 5.1 points and 4.0 rebounds in 12.1 minutes per game.

sections.heading: New York and Miami Swapped Ron Perry and Maurice McHartley
sections.body: The Nets acquired Ron Perry from the Miami Floridians for Maurice McHartley on December 16, 1968. The deal exchanged two active players rather than picks or unresolved rights.

sections.heading: Perry Gave New York a Short Scoring Burst
sections.body: Perry averaged 19.3 points, 4.1 rebounds and 3.7 assists across 23 Nets games. New York then traded him to Indiana on January 31 for Steve Chubin, preserving value beyond that brief run.

sections.heading: McHartley Gave Miami the Longer Direct Return
sections.body: McHartley played 52 games for the Floridians after the trade and averaged 14.5 points with 3.7 assists. Miami therefore received the steadier immediate player contribution.

sections.heading: The Different Returns Balance Out
sections.body: New York received the hotter short-term scoring stretch and another trade asset, while Miami received more games and stable production. Equal B- grades fit a deal in which both teams extracted useful but short-lived value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — New York B-, Miami B-. New York acquired Ron Perry from the Miami Floridians for Maurice McHartley on December 16, 1968. Perry gave the Nets a short scoring burst, averaging 19.3 points, 4.1 rebounds and 3.7 assists across 23 games before New York moved him to Indiana on January 31 for Steve Chubin.

sections.heading: Phoenix Acquired Jim Fox and a Third-Round Pick
sections.body: The Suns acquired Jim Fox and Detroit’s 1969 third-round pick for McCoy McLemore on December 17, 1968. The draft choice became No. 33 selection Lamar Green.

sections.heading: Fox Delivered Immediate Interior Production
sections.body: Fox averaged 13.8 points and 13.3 rebounds across 51 Phoenix games after the trade, then appeared in 81 more games for the Suns the following season.

sections.heading: Lamar Green Extended the Phoenix Return
sections.body: Green added 345 regular-season games for Phoenix across five seasons after being drafted. That gave the Suns a second substantial asset from the same transaction.

sections.heading: Detroit Received Useful Value but Far Less Longevity
sections.body: McLemore played 123 Pistons games over two seasons at 7.7 points and 4.7 rebounds per game. Phoenix’s A versus Detroit’s B- reflects the combined Fox-Green return without ignoring Detroit’s productive player and two useful seasons.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Suns Win — Phoenix A, Detroit B-. Jim Fox's immediate Phoenix return was substantial: 13.8 points and 13.3 rebounds over 51 games after the December 1968 trade, followed by 81 more Suns appearances the next season. The incoming Detroit third-round selection became Lamar Green, who added 345 Phoenix regular-season games over five seasons. Detroit did receive a usable player in McCoy McLemore, who produced 123 Pistons appearances with averages of 7.7 points and 4.7 rebounds. Phoenix's advantage comes from the combined Fox-Green longevity and output rather than assuming Detroit received nothing or counting the draft right as instant NBA production.

sections.heading: Indiana Acquired Steve Chubin for Mike Lewis
sections.body: The Pacers acquired Steve Chubin from the Minnesota Pipers for Mike Lewis on December 19, 1968. Both players immediately entered meaningful roles with their new clubs.

sections.heading: Chubin Produced and Then Became Another Pacers Asset
sections.body: Chubin averaged 13.8 points and 5.2 assists across 24 Indiana games. The Pacers then traded him to New York for Ron Perry, who added 27 regular-season games at 13.5 points.

sections.heading: Lewis Became the Longer-Term Pipers Return
sections.body: Lewis played 52 games for Minnesota after the trade, stayed with the franchise after its return to Pittsburgh and developed into a two-time ABA All-Star and one of the league’s top rebounders.

sections.heading: Minnesota Won the Long-Term Comparison
sections.body: Indiana extracted useful short-term production and another player through Chubin, but Lewis’ sustained high-level value created the larger return. The Pipers’ A versus Indiana’s B- captures that difference.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pipers Win — Indiana B-, Minnesota A. Indiana acquired Steve Chubin from the Minnesota Pipers for Mike Lewis on December 19, 1968. Chubin immediately became a productive Pacers guard, averaging 13.8 points and 5.2 assists across 24 games before Indiana traded him to New York for Ron Perry, who added another 27 regular-season games at 13.5 points per game.

sections.heading: New York Acquired Manny Leaks and Randy Mahaffey
sections.body: The Nets acquired Manny Leaks and Randy Mahaffey from Kentucky for Dan Anderson and Ollie Darden on December 30, 1968. Both sides received multiple player assets with immediate roster value.

sections.heading: Mahaffey and Leaks Produced Right Away
sections.body: Mahaffey played 48 Nets games at 13.8 points and 8.1 rebounds, while Leaks added 20 games at 12.5 points and 14.2 rebounds. New York later traded each player separately for a draft choice.

sections.heading: Kentucky Also Received Useful Pieces
sections.body: Darden played 90 games for the Colonels across two seasons. Anderson appeared in eight games before Kentucky moved him in a three-team transaction that brought back another draft choice.

sections.heading: New York Holds a Narrow Asset-Chain Advantage
sections.body: Both sides created meaningful production and later trade value. New York’s B+ versus Kentucky’s B reflects the stronger immediate two-player production and the separate draft returns generated afterward.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win — New York B+, Kentucky B. The 1968 exchange generated genuine playing value on both sides, but Manny Leaks and Randy Mahaffey made the stronger immediate New York contribution. Mahaffey logged 48 Nets games with 13.8 points and 8.1 rebounds per outing; Leaks added 20 games with 12.5 points and 14.2 boards. The Nets later moved each player separately for draft compensation. Kentucky received 90 games from Ollie Darden across two seasons and eight from Dan Anderson, whom the Colonels later traded in a separate three-team deal that returned another pick. Those distinct follow-on transactions support only a narrow New York edge, not a claim that Kentucky's assets produced no value.

sections.heading: Detroit Acquired Dave Gambee from Milwaukee
sections.body: The Pistons acquired Dave Gambee from the Bucks on January 1, 1969 for Rich Niemann and cash. The transaction gave Detroit an immediate frontcourt player while Milwaukee took a player plus financial consideration.

sections.heading: Gambee Gave Detroit the Better Direct Production
sections.body: Gambee played 25 Pistons games that season, averaging 6.8 points and 3.1 rebounds in 12.1 minutes. Detroit later traded him to San Francisco for a future draft choice.

sections.heading: Niemann’s Milwaukee Stay Was Shorter
sections.body: Niemann appeared in 18 games for the expansion Bucks, averaging 3.3 points and 3.3 rebounds before Milwaukee later waived him. His direct return was smaller than Gambee’s Detroit contribution.

sections.heading: Detroit Also Preserved a Future Asset
sections.body: The later Gambee-for-pick transaction extended Detroit’s value chain. The Pistons’ B versus Milwaukee’s C+ reflects the stronger measurable return while the outgoing cash keeps the difference from becoming wider.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Detroit B, Milwaukee C+. Detroit acquired Dave Gambee from Milwaukee on January 1, 1969 for Rich Niemann and cash. Gambee played 25 games for the Pistons that season, averaging 6.8 points and 3.1 rebounds in 12.1 minutes, then Detroit traded him to San Francisco the following October for a future draft choice.

sections.heading: Denver Sent Larry Bunce to Dallas
sections.body: The Rockets traded Larry Bunce to the Dallas Chaparrals on January 4, 1969 for the player rights to Rich Peek and a 1969 ABA second-round draft choice.

sections.heading: Bunce Gave Dallas Immediate Production
sections.body: Bunce played 24 games for Dallas and averaged 6.5 points and 5.3 rebounds before Houston claimed him on waivers in March. The Chaparrals therefore received a short but measurable player return.

sections.heading: Denver’s Value Rested Mainly on the Draft Asset
sections.body: Peek never returned to ABA action after his 1967-68 Dallas season. Contemporary draft-trade research identifies Denver’s incoming choice as a 1969 second-rounder, but the exact selected player remains unresolved.

sections.heading: Dallas Holds the Clearer Realized Edge
sections.body: The Chaparrals’ B- versus Denver’s C+ reflects the known Bunce production against a Denver package whose most valuable component cannot be traced to a specific player outcome.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Chaparrals Edge — Dallas B-, Denver C+. Larry Bunce gave Dallas 24 ABA games at 6.5 points and 5.3 rebounds per outing before another club claimed him on waivers. Denver received Rich Peek's rights and a 1969 second-round draft choice, but Peek played no further ABA games and the exact choice's ultimate selection isn't established in the saved evidence. Dallas therefore owns the clearer realized playing return. The limited tenure and unresolved pick identity keep the advantage modest rather than decisive.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Acquired George Wilson from Phoenix
sections.body: The 76ers acquired George Wilson from the Suns on January 20, 1969 for Jerry Chambers. Both players eventually contributed NBA minutes to their new teams.

sections.heading: Wilson Gave Philadelphia the Longer Return
sections.body: Wilson played 105 regular-season games for the 76ers across the remainder of 1968-69 and the full 1969-70 season, averaging 5.5 points and 5.1 rebounds during his Philadelphia stay.

sections.heading: Chambers Gave Phoenix One Useful Season
sections.body: Chambers was serving in the U.S. Army when Phoenix acquired his rights, so he did not join the Suns until 1969-70. He then played 79 games at 8.3 points before Portland selected him in the 1970 expansion draft.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Wins on Total Duration and Production
sections.body: Phoenix received a useful scoring season, so the trade was not one-sided. Philadelphia’s B versus Phoenix’s C+ reflects Wilson’s longer tenure and larger total contribution across the two-season window.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Edge — Philadelphia B, Phoenix C+. George Wilson gave Philadelphia 105 regular-season games across the latter part of 1968-69 and all of 1969-70, averaging 5.5 points and 5.1 rebounds in his stay. Phoenix acquired Jerry Chambers, but he was serving in the Army at the time and did not appear for the Suns until 1969-70. Chambers then produced a useful 79-game season at 8.3 points before Portland took him in the 1970 expansion draft. Both franchises received NBA value from the January 20, 1969 exchange; the Philadelphia advantage rests on Wilson's longer contribution rather than claiming Chambers never played. A B/C+ pairing keeps the decision modest and tied to the two players' actual team tenures.

sections.heading: New York Acquired Willie Somerset and Leary Lentz
sections.body: The Nets acquired Willie Somerset and Leary Lentz from Houston on January 31, 1969 for Levern Tart, Bob Verga and Hank Whitney. The deal exchanged two immediate contributors for a deeper three-player package.

sections.heading: Somerset Gave the Nets an Immediate Scoring Jolt
sections.body: Somerset averaged 24.1 points across 31 New York games, while Lentz added 26 reserve appearances. The Nets therefore received meaningful short-term production from both incoming pieces.

sections.heading: Verga Became Houston’s Long-Term Prize
sections.body: Verga averaged 24.7 points in 33 Mavericks games, stayed with the franchise after its move to Carolina and became an ABA All-Star plus a top-five MVP finisher in 1969-70. Whitney also remained into the Carolina season.

sections.heading: Houston Created the More Sustained Return
sections.body: Tart was quickly converted into draft choices, adding another branch to Houston’s asset chain. New York’s B reflects a productive immediate return, but Houston’s A recognizes the greater duration and peak value produced by the outgoing package.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win — New York B, Houston A. New York acquired Leary Lentz and Willie Somerset from Houston on January 31, 1969 for Levern Tart, Bob Verga and Hank Whitney. Somerset immediately gave the Nets 31 games at 24.1 points per game, while Lentz added 26 reserve appearances.

sections.heading: Seattle Acquired John Tresvant for Al Tucker
sections.body: The SuperSonics acquired John Tresvant from Cincinnati on February 1, 1969 for Al Tucker. Both clubs received an active player, making the transaction straightforward to evaluate through realized production.

sections.heading: Tresvant Became the Better Half-Season Contributor
sections.body: Tresvant averaged 13.6 points and 10.3 rebounds in 26 Seattle games after the trade. He returned for 49 more games in 1969-70 at 12.6 points and 7.4 rebounds.

sections.heading: Tucker’s Cincinnati Run Ended After 28 Games
sections.body: Tucker averaged 10.8 points and 4.4 rebounds across 28 Royals games before Cincinnati waived him the following October. His contribution was useful but considerably shorter.

sections.heading: Seattle Also Preserved Additional Transaction Value
sections.body: The SuperSonics later sold Tresvant’s player rights to Los Angeles, extending the return beyond his Seattle minutes. The B versus C+ split reflects the stronger production and later asset value on Seattle’s side.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: SuperSonics Win — Cincinnati C+, Seattle B. Seattle acquired John Tresvant from Cincinnati on February 1, 1969 for Al Tucker. Tresvant immediately became the stronger half-season contributor, averaging 13.6 points and 10.3 rebounds in 26 games for the SuperSonics, then returned for 49 more games in 1969-70 at 12.6 points and 7.4 rebounds.

sections.heading: The ABA Pacers and Nets Swapped Two Active Scoring Guards
sections.body:
On January 31, 1969 the Indiana Pacers transferred Steve Chubin to the New York Nets for Ron Perry. This was an American Basketball Association trade made months before either team entered the NBA; the historical franchise labels in a modern NBA trade archive should not turn these players into NBA games or draft assets. Chubin had joined Indiana only the previous December after arriving from Minnesota in an earlier trade for Mike Lewis. Perry had been scoring 19.3 points per game over 23 Nets appearances before he was moved.

The exchange itself involved only the two guards. Indiana acquired the more frequently starting player for its immediate rotation, while New York acquired a scorer and ballhandler who could use a sizeable role on a losing Nets club. Contemporary stats distinguish their pre-trade numbers from the team return after January 31, and neither roster had a salary-cap or draft pick consideration identified in the original agreement.

sections.heading: Perry Started 23 Pacers Games and Chubin Produced 15.9 Points for New York
sections.body:
Ron Perry played 27 Indiana Pacers regular-season games after the swap, made 23 starts and averaged 13.5 points, 3.6 assists and 32.0 minutes. Chubin played 28 games for the Nets in the same 1968-69 season, averaging 15.9 points, 5.0 assists and 29.6 minutes. Those actual outputs argue against any inflated verdict that one team acquired a durable star while the other received no basketball value. Perry provided starting continuity for Indiana, and Chubin supplied greater per-game scoring and playmaking for New York.

The Pacers finished 44-34 and reached the ABA Finals while the Nets went 17-61, but that team-record disparity cannot responsibly be assigned to a single guard exchange. A narrow Indiana edge in the inherited grades rewards Perry's starting usage rather than a sweeping claim that he outproduced Chubin across every statistical category.

sections.heading: Both Guards Were Moved Again in Separate 1969 Transactions
sections.body:
New York also used Chubin for 11 games in the opening weeks of the 1969-70 ABA season, in which he averaged 10.8 points, before selling his player rights to Indiana for cash on November 11, 1969. The cash amount is not established in the season transaction ledger, so it cannot be given a speculative dollar figure. Chubin subsequently made 32 ABA regular-season appearances for Indiana during the 1969-70 season after returning, but that second stint belongs to a new agreement, not the January trade return.

On October 9, 1969, before the Chubin repurchase, Indiana traded Ron Perry TOGETHER WITH George Peeples to the Carolina Cougars for Arthur Becker, Spider Bennett and Tony Jackson. Perry thus also carried downstream trade value. All three incoming players were acquired in exchange for TWO outgoing players, so assigning that entire later return to Perry alone would distort this two-team January record.

sections.heading: The Close Grades Reflect Short-Term Roles, Not Historic Franchise Dominance
sections.body:
The 1969 direct post-trade results were similar in volume: Indiana received 27 games and 23 starts from Perry; New York received 28 games from Chubin and eventually another 11 the next season. Perry's starter status and subsequent inclusion in a larger acquisition provide one defensible reason for a modest Pacers edge, while Chubin's stronger Nets scoring and later cash sale push against declaring the deal a decisive win. Neither side gained a long-lived star through the original January arrangement.

The canonical Slight Pacers Edge with Indiana C+ and New York C is therefore a close editorial interpretation, not an uncontested statistical result. The prior two source perspectives both called it Even Trade but their grades were inconsistent with the archive. Reconcile them without erasing New York's real 15.9-point Chubin stint, Perry's 23 Pacers starts, or the separate 1969 cash and Carolina exchanges.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Pacers Edge — Indiana C+, New York Nets C. Perry gave the Pacers 27 ABA games and 23 starts at 13.5 points/3.6 assists; Chubin gave the Nets 28 games at 15.9 points/5.0 assists, plus 11 the following season. Both players were traded again in separate 1969 transactions, and downstream multi-player compensation should not be charged entirely to one. The grade spread is deliberately small, with meaningful returns on both sides.

sections.heading: Dallas Acquired Manny Leaks for a Draft Choice
sections.body: The Chaparrals acquired Manny Leaks from New York on February 12, 1969 for a draft choice. The Nets’ incoming selection is verified, but its eventual player cannot be securely traced.

sections.heading: Leaks Became an Immediate Dallas Interior Force
sections.body: Leaks averaged 14.7 points and 12.6 rebounds across 27 Dallas games after the trade, then raised his production to 18.8 points and 12.5 rebounds while playing all 84 games in 1969-70.

sections.heading: His Chaparrals Value Extended into a Third Season
sections.body: Leaks added 40 more games for the Texas Chaparrals in 1970-71 before Dallas traded him back to New York in a separate transaction. The original acquisition therefore produced substantial multi-season value.

sections.heading: The Known Player Return Creates a Clear Gap
sections.body: New York’s draft asset may have carried value, but its final outcome remains unresolved. Dallas’ A- versus New York’s C reflects the much stronger documented return that can be traced directly to Leaks.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Spurs Franchise Win — New York C, Dallas A-. New York traded Manny Leaks to the Dallas Chaparrals on February 12, 1969 for a draft choice. Leaks immediately produced 27 Dallas games at 14.7 points and 12.6 rebounds, then became a major frontcourt piece in 1969-70 with 18.8 points and 12.5 rebounds across all 84 games.

sections.heading: Denver Acquired Levern Tart for Multiple Draft Choices
sections.body: The Rockets acquired Levern Tart from Houston on February 12, 1969 for draft choices. The Mavericks’ compensation is verified as plural, but the reviewed ledgers do not identify the rounds or eventual selections.

sections.heading: Tart Gave Denver Twenty Games of Guard Depth
sections.body: Tart appeared in 20 games for the Rockets, averaging 7.7 points in 17.3 minutes. The contribution was real but limited in both duration and role.

sections.heading: Denver Later Converted Tart into Cash
sections.body: On June 26, Denver sold Tart’s player rights to the New York Nets for cash. That transaction preserved some additional value from the original acquisition beyond Tart’s own minutes.

sections.heading: The Missing Pick Outcomes Block a Responsible Winner
sections.body: Houston received unresolved future assets while Denver received short-term production and a later cash return. Without knowing what the draft choices became, the record remains Insufficient Evidence and no team grades are forced.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Insufficient Evidence Denver acquired Levern Tart from the Houston Mavericks on February 12, 1969 for draft choices. Tart played 20 games for the Rockets, averaging 7.7 points in 17.3 minutes, before Denver sold his rights to the New York Nets for cash on June 26.

sections.heading: Phoenix Acquired Paul Silas from Atlanta
sections.body: The Suns acquired Paul Silas from Atlanta on May 8, 1969 for Gary Gregor. One contemporaneous draft-rights reconstruction also ties an off-books 1970 first-round right to the transaction, though that component is disputed across the surviving record.

sections.heading: Silas Became the Best Direct Player in the Deal
sections.body: Silas played 239 Suns games across three seasons, made the 1972 All-Star team and earned two All-Defensive Second Team selections. His Phoenix tenure supplies the clearest realized value in the transaction.

sections.heading: Atlanta Still Received Meaningful Return Value
sections.body: Gregor played 81 games for the Hawks. The disputed first-round right is also tied in one reconstruction to Atlanta’s later Walt Bellamy transaction, so the Hawks’ side is not treated as empty even under the broader interpretation.

sections.heading: Phoenix Wins Even with the Draft-Right Dispute
sections.body: The exact structure is debated, but Silas’ verified Suns production is not. Phoenix’s A versus Atlanta’s B+ reflects the best direct player going to the Suns while acknowledging meaningful value on the Hawks’ side.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Phoenix Suns Win — Phoenix A, Atlanta B+. Phoenix acquired Paul Silas from Atlanta on May 8, 1969 for Gary Gregor and, according to a contemporaneous draft-rights reconstruction, an off-books 1970 first-round right that ultimately became No. 16 Gary Freeman.

sections.heading: The Strongest Ledgers Put the Trade on May 8
sections.body: Atlanta traded Paul Silas to Phoenix for Gary Gregor on May 8, 1969. Team and league records, along with the Hawks’ historical media guide, support the straight player-for-player structure rather than the legacy May 9 version.

sections.heading: The Legacy First-Round Pick Is Not Treated as Established
sections.body: The older TradeVerdicts row added a 1970 first-round pick, but the strongest transaction ledgers do not corroborate that asset in this canonical perspective. The editorial therefore grades the verified Silas-for-Gregor exchange.

sections.heading: Silas Produced the Much Stronger Phoenix Tenure
sections.body: Silas played 239 regular-season games for the Suns across three seasons, earned an All-Star selection and made two All-Defensive Second Teams. Gregor played 81 Atlanta games in 1969-70 at 8.1 points and 4.9 rebounds.

sections.heading: The Verified Player Results Favor Phoenix
sections.body: Atlanta received real rotation value from Gregor, so the Hawks are not graded as receiving nothing. Phoenix’s A- versus Atlanta’s C+ reflects Silas’ much larger and more decorated realized return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Suns Win — Atlanta C+, Phoenix A-. Atlanta traded Paul Silas to Phoenix for Gary Gregor on May 8, 1969. The strongest transaction ledgers and the Hawks' own historical media guide agree that the deal was a straight player-for-player exchange; the legacy TradeVerdicts record incorrectly added a 1970 first-round pick and dated the trade May 9.

sections.heading: Miami Acquired Al Cueto’s Rights for a Draft Choice
sections.body: The Floridians acquired the rights to Al Cueto from Denver on May 16, 1969 for a future draft choice. Denver’s selection is verified as consideration, but its round, year and eventual player remain unresolved.

sections.heading: Cueto Became an Immediate Miami Regular
sections.body: Cueto appeared in 78 games for the Floridians in 1969-70, averaging 6.0 points and 5.8 rebounds in 16.2 minutes. That gave Miami a full season of measurable frontcourt production.

sections.heading: Miami Preserved Some Value in a Later Trade
sections.body: The Floridians included Cueto in a June 1970 multi-player transaction with New Orleans. His rights therefore generated both on-court contribution and later transaction utility.

sections.heading: The Known Return Favors Miami
sections.body: Denver’s incoming pick may have mattered, but its realized outcome cannot be traced. Miami’s B versus Denver’s C+ reflects the clearer one-season player production and subsequent trade value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Floridians Win — Miami B, Denver C+. The rights to Al Cueto produced one full 1969-70 Miami season: 78 appearances, 6.0 points and 5.8 rebounds per game. The Floridians then included Cueto in a June 1970 multi-player trade with New Orleans, giving them another use for the acquired rights. Denver's return was a future draft choice, but its round, eventual number and player have not been established by the reviewed transaction sources. Miami therefore has the clearer documented playing return, not proof that Denver's pick had no value. The later multi-player transaction must not be credited entirely to this one earlier exchange.

sections.heading: New York Reacquired Levern Tart for Cash
sections.body: The Nets reacquired Levern Tart from Denver on June 26, 1969 for cash. Denver’s financial return is verified, but the amount is not disclosed in the reviewed records.

sections.heading: Tart Immediately Became the Nets’ Leading Scorer
sections.body: Tart played 80 games in 1969-70 and averaged 24.2 points, 6.8 rebounds and 3.3 assists. He earned an ABA All-Star selection and finished 14th in MVP voting.

sections.heading: His Playoff and Follow-Up Value Added to the Return
sections.body: Tart averaged 26.7 points across seven playoff games, then stayed for 27 more Nets games the next season before New York packaged him with Ed Johnson for Manny Leaks.

sections.heading: New York Owns the Far Clearer Basketball Outcome
sections.body: Denver’s unknown cash amount prevents a precise financial comparison, but Tart’s high-volume production and later trade value are substantial. The Nets’ A- versus Denver’s C reflects that documented gap.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win — New York A-, Denver C. New York reacquired Levern Tart from Denver on June 26, 1969 for cash. Tart immediately became the Nets' leading scorer, playing 80 games in 1969-70 and averaging 24.2 points, 6.8 rebounds and 3.3 assists while earning an ABA All-Star selection and finishing 14th in MVP voting.

sections.heading: New York Acquired Les Hunter from Miami for Cash
sections.body: The Nets acquired Les Hunter from the Floridians for cash on June 26, 1969. Miami’s incoming payment is verified, but the amount is not disclosed.

sections.heading: Hunter Became a Major Nets Frontcourt Contributor
sections.body: Hunter played 79 games for New York in 1969-70, averaging 16.4 points, 8.5 rebounds and 2.7 assists in 36.2 minutes. He also averaged 16.1 points and 6.0 rebounds across seven playoff games.

sections.heading: New York Later Converted Hunter into More Assets
sections.body: Hunter stayed for five additional Nets games the next season before New York traded him to Kentucky for a draft choice and cash. That extended the value of the original acquisition beyond one season.

sections.heading: The Measurable Return Favors the Nets
sections.body: Because Miami’s sale price is unknown, the Floridians’ side cannot be valued precisely. New York’s B+ versus Miami’s C reflects Hunter’s major one-season production and later conversion into additional assets.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win — New York B+, Miami C. New York acquired Les Hunter from Miami for cash on June 26, 1969. Hunter became a major frontcourt contributor immediately, appearing in 79 games for the Nets in 1969-70 and averaging 16.4 points, 8.5 rebounds and 2.7 assists in 36.2 minutes per game.

sections.heading: Boston Bought Hank Finkel for Cash
sections.body: Boston acquired Hank Finkel from San Diego for cash on August 22, 1969. Team and league transaction ledgers describe a cash-only sale, which means the older TradeVerdicts version attaching a 1971 draft pick and Greg Nelson outcome does not belong in the verified package.

sections.heading: Finkel Became a Six-Year Celtics Piece
sections.body: Finkel played six seasons and 436 regular-season games for Boston. His first Celtics season included 80 games at 9.7 points and 7.7 rebounds, and he later filled a role on the 1974 championship team.

sections.heading: San Diego’s Return Cannot Be Fully Priced
sections.body: The Rockets received cash, but the amount is not disclosed in the surviving transaction records. That limits how aggressively the San Diego side can be downgraded even though Boston’s basketball return is easy to measure.

sections.heading: The Measurable Value Clearly Favors Boston
sections.body: A B+ for Boston and C+ for San Diego fits the evidence. Boston received years of usable frontcourt production, while the other side’s financial return is real but impossible to quantify precisely from the public record.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win — Boston B+, San Diego C+. Boston acquired Hank Finkel from San Diego for cash on August 22, 1969. Boston, San Diego and NBA transaction ledgers all describe a cash-only deal, so the legacy TradeVerdicts record's additional 1971 draft pick and Greg Nelson outcome are unsupported and should be removed.

sections.heading: Chicago Landed Chet Walker and Shaler Halimon
sections.body: The Bulls acquired Chet Walker and Shaler Halimon from Philadelphia on September 2, 1969 for Jim Washington and future consideration that ultimately became Bob Kauffman. The transaction ledgers support Kauffman as later consideration, not as a player Chicago already owned on September 2.

sections.heading: Walker Was the Trade’s Defining Asset
sections.body: Walker spent six seasons and 474 regular-season games with Chicago and made four All-Star teams. That sustained, high-level return is the strongest single outcome tied to the transaction.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Still Built Real Value from Its Package
sections.body: The 76ers received useful production from Jim Washington and later converted Kauffman’s rights, together with an additional draft pick, into Bailey Howell. Philadelphia’s side was productive enough to avoid treating the trade as one-sided.

sections.heading: The Bulls Earn the Higher Grade
sections.body: Chicago’s A+ reflects Walker’s long, elite run with the franchise. Philadelphia’s B recognizes that Washington and the later Kauffman-related value were substantial, but they did not match what Walker became for the Bulls.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win — Chicago A+, Philadelphia B. Chet Walker produced six seasons and 474 regular-season Chicago games, earning four Bulls All-Star appearances. Philadelphia still received usable value from Jim Washington and a later Bob Kauffman-related asset chain leading toward Bailey Howell. Kauffman was subsequent consideration, not someone Chicago already controlled on the September 2 trade date. Chicago wins because Walker's long-term top-end production outlasted the alternative package, while Philadelphia's real follow-on value merits more than a failing grade.

sections.heading: Chicago and Seattle Exchanged Two-Asset Packages
sections.body: The Bulls acquired Bob Kauffman and Seattle’s 1971 third-round pick for Bob Boozer and Barry Clemens on September 5, 1969. The draft pick later became Clifford Ray, giving Chicago a second meaningful return beyond Kauffman.

sections.heading: Ray Gave Chicago Long-Term Value
sections.body: Ray played three seasons and 235 regular-season games for the Bulls as a strong rebounder. He later became part of the 1974 Nate Thurmond trade, extending the value chain from the original Seattle pick.

sections.heading: Seattle Also Received Productive Players
sections.body: Boozer averaged 15.2 points and 8.7 rebounds in 82 games for Seattle, while Clemens stayed for 238 games across three seasons. That is substantial realized value from both incoming players.

sections.heading: The Completed Returns Are Close Enough for Equal Grades
sections.body: Kauffman’s 64 Chicago games plus Ray and his downstream use balance well against Boozer and Clemens. The A- grades on both sides fit an exchange where each franchise received a useful, multi-part return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Chicago A-, Seattle A-. Chicago acquired Bob Kauffman and Seattle's 1971 third-round pick on September 5, 1969 for Bob Boozer and Barry Clemens. The pick became Clifford Ray, who gave the Bulls three seasons and 235 regular-season games as a high-level rebounder before becoming part of the 1974 Nate Thurmond trade.

sections.heading: Denver Sent Two Veterans to Los Angeles
sections.body: Denver traded Wayne Hightower and Billy McGill to the Los Angeles Stars for cash on September 8, 1969. The verified record consolidates what the legacy archive had incorrectly split into two separate transactions.

sections.heading: Both Veterans Produced Immediately for the Stars
sections.body: Hightower averaged 18.1 points and 9.4 rebounds in 27 games, while McGill averaged 11.5 points and 4.4 rebounds in 27. Los Angeles received meaningful production from both players right away.

sections.heading: McGill Also Created a Downstream Return
sections.body: The Stars later traded McGill for Craig Raymond, who became an important contributor during the club’s run to the 1970 ABA Finals. That gives Los Angeles additional attributable value beyond the initial 27-game stint.

sections.heading: Undisclosed Cash Leaves Los Angeles Ahead
sections.body: Denver’s cash amount is unknown, so the Rockets’ side cannot be fully valued. The visible basketball return still supports an A- for Los Angeles against Denver’s C and a clear Stars win.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Stars Win — Los Angeles Stars A-, Denver C. The two players received from Denver gave Los Angeles immediate frontcourt help: Wayne Hightower averaged 18.1 points and 9.4 rebounds across 27 games, while Billy McGill averaged 11.5 points and 4.4 boards in another 27. The Stars subsequently dealt McGill for Craig Raymond, whose contribution to their 1970 ABA Finals run added a second return to that asset chain. Denver received cash rather than a player, and the surviving sources do not establish its amount. The judgment therefore favors the documented Stars playing value without pretending the Rockets' undisclosed payment can be precisely graded.

sections.heading: The Hightower-Only Row Is Not a Separate Trade
sections.body: This September 8, 1969 listing is retained only as legacy provenance. Denver did not make a second cash transaction with Los Angeles involving Wayne Hightower alone.

sections.heading: The Source Record Shows One Combined Exchange
sections.body: Denver, Los Angeles and ABA transaction logs all describe one deal in which the Rockets sent Hightower and Billy McGill to the Stars for cash. The two-player package belongs together.

sections.heading: The Complete Trade Already Has Its Canonical Route
sections.body: TradeVerdicts now represents the full Hightower-McGill exchange under the DEN-1969-0015 record. Keeping this legacy row as a second graded trade would duplicate the same asset movement.

sections.heading: Provenance Is Preserved Without Inventing Grades
sections.body: The record stays in the archive so the original source lineage remains visible, but it is structurally superseded. No winner or team grades should be assigned to a duplicate perspective.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Resolution
finalVerdict.body: Record Superseded This September 8, 1969 Hightower-only listing is retained only as legacy source provenance. Denver did not make a second cash trade with Los Angeles that day.

sections.heading: Chicago Traded Mike Lynn for a Future Third-Rounder
sections.body: The Bulls sent Mike Lynn to the Lakers on September 9, 1969 for a 1971 third-round pick that became Mike Gale at No. 47. The deal therefore exchanged immediate player depth for a future selection.

sections.heading: Lynn Contributed During a Finals Season
sections.body: Lynn played 44 regular-season games for Los Angeles as the Lakers advanced to the 1970 NBA Finals. His role was small, but those games were real value for the team that acquired him.

sections.heading: Gale Never Produced for Chicago
sections.body: The Bulls used the pick on Gale, but he had already been selected in the ABA draft and began his professional career there. Although Gale later had a productive eleven-year pro career, none of that career accrued to Chicago from this selection.

sections.heading: The Lakers Hold a Narrow Hindsight Edge
sections.body: Los Angeles received modest immediate production while Chicago’s pick produced no realized Bulls value. The C+ versus C split correctly keeps the difference small rather than overstating Lynn’s limited role.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win — Chicago C, Los Angeles Lakers C+. Chicago traded Mike Lynn to the Los Angeles Lakers on September 9, 1969 for a 1971 third-round draft pick that became Mike Gale at No. 47.

sections.heading: Denver Sold Isiah King’s Rights for Cash
sections.body: The Rockets sent Isiah King to the New Orleans Buccaneers for cash on September 10, 1969. King had been Denver’s third-round selection in the 1969 ABA Draft.

sections.heading: New Orleans Did Not Receive Recorded ABA Production
sections.body: King appears in New Orleans roster history, but no official ABA regular-season statistics are recorded for him. His later 24-game stint with the Binghamton Flyers came in the Eastern League, not as value for the Buccaneers.

sections.heading: Denver’s Cash Return Is Real but Undisclosed
sections.body: The amount Denver received is not preserved in the reviewed public records. Even so, the Rockets at least converted the player rights into a financial return.

sections.heading: That Is Enough for a Small Denver Edge
sections.body: With no documented ABA production for New Orleans and an unknown cash amount for Denver, the difference should stay modest. A C+ for Denver and C for the Buccaneers matches that limited evidence.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Edge — Denver C+, New Orleans C. Denver converted Isiah King's rights into a cash payment in September 1969. The Buccaneers obtained the player selected in the ABA draft, but the available historical record credits him with no ABA regular-season games for New Orleans. King's later minor-league playing time doesn't count as a Buccaneers return. Denver's cash amount wasn't disclosed, so the judgment cannot be tied to a verified dollar figure. A narrow C+/C gap credits a realized payment against unconfirmed ABA service without overstating either side.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Reacquired Bill Melchionni’s NBA Rights
sections.body: The 76ers acquired Melchionni’s NBA rights from Phoenix on September 13, 1969 for a 1970 second-round pick that became Joe DePre at No. 29. Neither incoming asset ultimately produced games for the acquiring NBA team.

sections.heading: Melchionni Chose the ABA Instead
sections.body: Two days later, Melchionni signed with the New York Nets and became a star in the ABA. That career cannot be credited to Philadelphia because the 76ers never received his on-court production from the reacquired rights.

sections.heading: DePre Also Bypassed Phoenix
sections.body: DePre likewise chose the ABA and signed with the Nets in 1970 instead of joining the Suns. His later professional value therefore did not become realized Phoenix value from this draft pick.

sections.heading: Both NBA Teams Finished with Little Realized Return
sections.body: The two players had productive careers elsewhere, but neither delivered games to the NBA franchise that acquired the corresponding asset. Equal C grades and an Even Trade verdict fit that outcome.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Philadelphia C, Phoenix C. Rights and a future draft selection changed hands, but neither club ultimately received on-court value from the acquired asset. Bill Melchionni signed with the ABA New York Nets two days after Philadelphia reacquired his NBA rights, while Phoenix's 1970 No. 29 selection, Joe DePre, also joined the Nets rather than the Suns. Melchionni's subsequent ABA success belonged to New York, not the 76ers; DePre's career likewise gave Phoenix no NBA minutes. Both clubs acquired something that never translated into production for their own roster, so the matching C grades acknowledge the unrealized outcomes without inventing a trade winner.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Bought Freddie Crawford’s Rights for Cash
sections.body: The Bucks acquired Freddie Crawford’s player rights from the Lakers on September 18, 1969 in a cash sale. The verified record does not support the older description involving unresolved future considerations.

sections.heading: Crawford Immediately Became a Useful Bucks Guard
sections.body: He played 77 regular-season games for Milwaukee, averaging 7.6 points, 2.9 assists and 2.4 rebounds in 17.3 minutes. Crawford also appeared in all 10 playoff games as the Bucks reached the Eastern Division Finals.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Received One Full Season of Production
sections.body: Buffalo selected Crawford in the 1970 expansion draft, ending his Milwaukee tenure after one year. Even so, that one season produced measurable rotation and playoff value.

sections.heading: The Unknown Cash Amount Keeps the Gap Moderate
sections.body: Los Angeles did receive financial consideration, but the amount is undisclosed. Milwaukee’s documented on-court return supports the B versus C+ split without treating the Lakers’ side as valueless.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win — Milwaukee B, Los Angeles Lakers C+. Milwaukee acquired Freddie Crawford's player rights from the Los Angeles Lakers on September 18, 1969 in a cash sale, not for unresolved future considerations. Crawford immediately became a useful Bucks guard, playing 77 regular-season games and averaging 7.6 points, 2.9 assists and 2.4 rebounds in 17.3 minutes per game.

sections.heading: New York Bought Dennis Grey from Los Angeles
sections.body: The New York Nets acquired Dennis Grey from the Los Angeles Stars for cash on September 19, 1969. Grey had averaged 9.1 points and 5.5 rebounds in 58 games for Los Angeles as a rookie.

sections.heading: Grey’s Nets Stint Was Extremely Brief
sections.body: He appeared in only four games for New York, totaling 74 minutes, 18 points and 25 rebounds. The Nets therefore received only a small amount of realized basketball value from the purchase.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Received Undisclosed Cash
sections.body: The Stars’ financial return is not identified in the available transaction record. Without the amount, it cannot be compared precisely against four games of Grey production.

sections.heading: The Evidence Does Not Support a Clear Winner
sections.body: Both sides received something, but neither return can be shown to be meaningfully stronger. Equal C grades and an Even Trade verdict fit a transaction with limited measurable value on both sides.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — New York Nets C, Los Angeles Stars C. Dennis Grey gave New York only four games, totaling 74 minutes after the Nets acquired him for cash in September 1969. His prior Los Angeles rookie averages cannot be counted as Nets output. The Stars received a payment, but the surviving transaction summary does not identify its amount, making a precise dollar-for-minutes comparison impossible. The equal low grades acknowledge a concrete yet very small Nets playing return and an unquantified financial return for Los Angeles, without manufacturing a clear winner.

sections.heading: Atlanta Took a Low-Cost Shot on Gene Tormohlen
sections.body: Atlanta acquired Gene Tormohlen from Phoenix for a 1970 third-round pick that became Vann Williford at No. 48. The structure was simple: the Hawks traded a future selection for a veteran attempting to return after a year away.

sections.heading: Tormohlen’s Comeback Barely Reached the Court
sections.body: Tormohlen played only two games and 11 total minutes for Atlanta before his NBA career ended. The Hawks therefore received almost no measurable on-court return from the acquisition.

sections.heading: Phoenix’s Pick Also Produced No NBA Value
sections.body: The Suns used the selection on Williford, but he never appeared in the NBA. He later played 38 ABA games for Carolina, which does not count as realized Phoenix value from the draft pick.

sections.heading: Neither Side Converted the Asset into Meaningful Value
sections.body: With Atlanta receiving two brief appearances and Phoenix receiving a drafted player who never played for the Suns, the completed NBA return is minimal on both sides. Equal C grades fit the lack of durable value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Atlanta C, Phoenix C. Atlanta acquired Gene Tormohlen from Phoenix on September 20, 1969 for a 1970 third-round pick that became Vann Williford at No. 48.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Acquired Fred Hetzel for Craig Raymond and a Pick
sections.body: Philadelphia obtained Fred Hetzel from Cincinnati in early October 1969 for Craig Raymond and a future second-round selection. The strongest team and league ledgers point to October 4, one day later than the legacy TradeVerdicts date.

sections.heading: Hetzel Gave Philadelphia a Full Season of Rotation Value
sections.body: Hetzel played 63 games for the 76ers, averaging 6.1 points and 3.3 rebounds in 12.0 minutes per game. Portland selected him in the 1970 expansion draft, so Philadelphia’s return was useful but limited to one season.

sections.heading: Cincinnati Got No Games from Raymond
sections.body: The Royals waived Raymond within a week of the trade. The future second-round pick is confirmed by a Cincinnati media guide, but the exact year and eventual player remain unresolved in the reviewed sources.

sections.heading: The Measurable Return Favors Philadelphia
sections.body: Philadelphia received known NBA production while Cincinnati’s known player return disappeared almost immediately and the pick cannot yet be traced confidently. A B- for the 76ers and C for Cincinnati reflects that evidence gap without overstating the win.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win — Cincinnati C, Philadelphia B-. Philadelphia acquired Fred Hetzel from Cincinnati in early October 1969 for Craig Raymond and a future second-round pick. The strongest team and league ledgers date the trade October 4, while the legacy TradeVerdicts record and Pro Sports Transactions use October 3.

sections.heading: Indiana Took Three Players from Carolina
sections.body: The Pacers acquired Art Becker, Spider Bennett and Tony Jackson from the Carolina Cougars for George Peeples and Ron Perry. The five-player exchange gave both ABA teams multiple paths to realize value.

sections.heading: Becker Was Indiana’s Only Meaningful Direct Return
sections.body: Becker played all 82 games for the 1970 ABA champions and 51 more the following season before Indiana moved him to Denver. Bennett and Jackson never played a game for the Pacers after the trade.

sections.heading: Carolina Received the Stronger Long-Term Package
sections.body: Peeples played 165 games over two Cougars seasons and averaged 11.7 points with 9.4 rebounds in 1970-71. Perry lasted 19 games but was flipped for Larry Miller, creating an additional productive asset chain.

sections.heading: The Cougars Built More Durable Value
sections.body: Indiana got a championship-season contributor in Becker, but Carolina extracted more games, more production and a downstream return from its package. The A- versus B+ split gives the Cougars a narrow but real edge.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cougars Win — Indiana B+, Carolina A-. Indiana acquired Art Becker, Spider Bennett and Tony Jackson from the Carolina Cougars on October 9, 1969 for George Peeples and Ron Perry. Becker became the only meaningful direct Pacers return, playing all 82 games for the 1970 ABA champions and 51 more the next season before Indiana moved him to Denver.

sections.heading: Detroit Sent Dave Gambee to San Francisco for a Future Pick
sections.body: San Francisco acquired veteran forward Dave Gambee from Detroit on October 10, 1969 for a future draft choice. Team, league and Warriors media-guide records all confirm the player-for-pick structure.

sections.heading: Gambee Supplied One Known Warriors Season
sections.body: Gambee played 73 games for San Francisco in 1969-70, totaling 951 minutes while averaging 7.2 points and 3.3 rebounds. That gives the Warriors side a clear measurable return.

sections.heading: The Detroit Pick Cannot Be Identified Reliably
sections.body: The reviewed public sources do not establish the year, selection number or eventual player tied to Detroit’s future draft choice. Without that identity, the Pistons side cannot be evaluated on equal terms.

sections.heading: The Responsible Outcome Is No Grade
sections.body: A known one-season player return is not enough to declare a winner when the opposing draft asset remains unresolved. The record stays at Insufficient Evidence until the pick can be tied to a verified downstream outcome.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Insufficient Evidence — no comparative grade or declared winner. San Francisco's side is measurable: Dave Gambee played 73 Warriors games in 1969-70, averaging 7.2 points and 3.3 rebounds. Detroit instead received a future draft selection. Team and league transaction logs, reinforced by the Warriors' official media guide, establish that the pick was the consideration, but the reviewed records do not identify its year, number or eventual player. Without that asset lineage, calling the Warriors winners or the Pistons losers would turn an unknown draft return into an invented zero. Keep this historical trade as a documented exchange with an unresolved outcome.

sections.heading: Chicago Acquired Walt Wesley from Cincinnati
sections.body: The Bulls acquired Walt Wesley for Dave Newmark and rookie guard Norm Van Lier. Historical Bulls material also links a second-round pick to the deal, although the exact year and final selection are not fully proven by the strongest transaction ledgers.

sections.heading: Wesley Gave Chicago One Useful Season
sections.body: Wesley played 72 games for the Bulls at 9.5 points and 6.3 rebounds before Cleveland selected him in the 1970 expansion draft. Chicago received real frontcourt value, but only for one season.

sections.heading: Van Lier Became the Trade’s Best Asset
sections.body: Cincinnati received 173 Royals games from Van Lier. He led the NBA in assists in 1970-71 and became an All-Defensive guard, giving the Royals a far stronger long-term player return than Chicago received from Wesley.

sections.heading: The Long-Term Difference Makes Cincinnati the Winner
sections.body: Newmark added little compared with Van Lier’s multi-season impact. Even with the draft-pick detail not fully settled, the known player outcomes support Cincinnati’s A- against Chicago’s D.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Win — Chicago D, Cincinnati A-. Chicago acquired Walt Wesley from Cincinnati on October 12, 1969 for Dave Newmark and rookie guard Norm Van Lier. Bulls historical material also links a second-round draft choice to the deal, but the exact year and final selection are not fully proven by the strongest transaction ledgers; Pro Sports Transactions identifies Cincinnati's otherwise-unaccounted-for 1972 second-rounder as a likely match.

sections.heading: Atlanta Acquired Dave Newmark for Three Assets
sections.body: The Hawks received Dave Newmark from Cincinnati for Wally Anderzunas, the rights to Lonnie Wright and a 1972 third-round pick that became Ron Riley. The pick gives Cincinnati the clearest long-term component in the package.

sections.heading: Newmark Was a One-Season Atlanta Reserve
sections.body: Newmark played 64 games in 1969-70, averaging 4.6 points and 4.2 rebounds before leaving the NBA. The Hawks received useful depth but no multi-season return.

sections.heading: Riley Became Cincinnati’s Strongest Asset
sections.body: Anderzunas contributed 44 games, while Riley later played 74 games as a rookie at 8.4 points and 6.9 rebounds and 86 games across two seasons for the franchise. That future pick became the most valuable realized piece in the deal.

sections.heading: Cincinnati’s Package Had Better Longevity
sections.body: Atlanta got one year of Newmark, but Cincinnati received both immediate player value and a future pick that turned into a productive rotation player. The B+ versus C split correctly favors the Royals.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Win — Atlanta C, Cincinnati B+. Atlanta acquired Dave Newmark from Cincinnati on October 12, 1969 for Wally Anderzunas, the draft rights to Lonnie Wright and a 1972 third-round pick that became Ron Riley. Newmark gave Atlanta 64 games in 1969-70, averaging 4.6 points and 4.2 rebounds in a reserve role before leaving the NBA.

sections.heading: New York Bought Ed Lee Johnson from Los Angeles
sections.body: The Nets acquired center Ed Lee Johnson from the Los Angeles Stars for cash on October 22, 1969. The transaction was a straightforward cash purchase with no additional player or draft asset attached.

sections.heading: Johnson Immediately Became a Major Nets Contributor
sections.body: Johnson played 74 games in 1969-70 and averaged 14.0 points with 11.9 rebounds. He added 26 more games the next season before New York traded him to Texas.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Received an Undisclosed Payment
sections.body: The Stars’ cash return is not preserved in the public record. That keeps their side from being treated as empty value, but it prevents a precise comparison with Johnson’s measurable production.

sections.heading: One Hundred Nets Games Make the Edge Clear
sections.body: Johnson totaled 100 games, 1,305 points and 1,101 rebounds for New York. That sustained starter-level production supports the Nets’ A- against Los Angeles’ C despite the unknown cash amount.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win — New York A-, Los Angeles Stars C. New York acquired center Ed Lee Johnson from the Los Angeles Stars for cash on October 22, 1969. The purchase produced far more than a short trial: Johnson played 74 games for the Nets in 1969-70, averaging 14.0 points and 11.9 rebounds, then added 26 more games in 1970-71 before New York traded him to Texas.
