sections.heading: New York Sold Tommie Bowens to New Orleans
sections.body: The Nets sold Tommie Bowens to the New Orleans Buccaneers for cash on October 24, 1969. No additional asset is documented in the canonical transaction record.

sections.heading: Bowens Gave New Orleans a Full Season of Depth
sections.body: Bowens played 68 games for the Buccaneers that season, averaging 3.9 points and 2.6 rebounds in 11.1 minutes. It was the final year of his three-season ABA career.

sections.heading: New York’s Cash Return Cannot Be Precisely Valued
sections.body: The amount paid to the Nets is undisclosed. That prevents a precise financial comparison even though Bowens’ on-court role was modest.

sections.heading: The Buccaneers Hold a Limited Hindsight Edge
sections.body: New Orleans received a full season of usable rotation depth while New York’s return remains unquantified. A B- versus C split reflects a real but not overwhelming advantage for the Buccaneers/Sounds franchise.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Sounds Win — New York C, New Orleans B-. New York sold Tommie Bowens to the New Orleans Buccaneers for cash on October 24, 1969. Bowens gave New Orleans 68 games that season, averaging 3.9 points and 2.6 rebounds in 11.1 minutes while contributing 1.2 win shares.

sections.heading: Seattle Acquired Dick Snyder for Art Harris
sections.body: The SuperSonics acquired Dick Snyder from Phoenix for Art Harris on October 26, 1969. The deal was a clean one-for-one swap between guards.

sections.heading: Snyder Became a Long-Term Seattle Starter
sections.body: Snyder played 387 regular-season games for Seattle through 1973-74 and produced several strong scoring years, including 19.4 points per game in 1970-71. He became the trade’s most valuable sustained asset.

sections.heading: Phoenix Still Received Useful Rotation Value
sections.body: Harris played 153 games over three Suns seasons and averaged 7.8 points in 76 games immediately after the trade. Phoenix did not come away empty-handed.

sections.heading: The Difference Is Role and Longevity
sections.body: Harris provided a legitimate return, but Snyder’s five-season Seattle run, larger role and higher production created the clearer franchise value. Seattle’s A against Phoenix’s B- matches that gap.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Seattle SuperSonics Win — Seattle A, Phoenix B-. Seattle acquired Dick Snyder from Phoenix for Art Harris on October 26, 1969. Snyder became a long-term SuperSonics starter, playing 387 regular-season games for Seattle through 1973-74 after the trade and producing several strong scoring seasons, including 19.4 points per game in 1970-71.

sections.heading: Indiana Sold John Fairchild to Kentucky
sections.body: The Pacers sold John Fairchild to the Kentucky Colonels for cash on October 28, 1969. Fairchild had already fallen to the edge of Indiana’s rotation before the transaction.

sections.heading: Kentucky Received Only Seven Games
sections.body: Fairchild appeared in seven games for the Colonels, totaling 52 minutes and 19 points. His averages of 2.7 points and 1.1 rebounds show how little on-court value the purchase produced.

sections.heading: Indiana’s Financial Return Is Unknown
sections.body: The Pacers received cash, but the amount is not disclosed. That prevents the sale from being framed as a meaningful financial win.

sections.heading: Low Impact on Both Sides Makes This Even
sections.body: Kentucky received a real player but almost no lasting contribution, while Indiana received an unquantified payment. Equal C grades fit a transaction with no durable asset on either side.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Indiana C, Kentucky C. Indiana sold John Fairchild to Kentucky for cash on October 28, 1969. Fairchild had already been pushed to the edge of the Pacers' rotation, appearing in only three games that season before the deal.

sections.heading: Detroit Used a 1970 Second-Rounder to Acquire Erwin Mueller
sections.body: On November 1, 1969, the Detroit Pistons sent a 1970 second-round selection to Seattle for forward Erwin Mueller. The Pistons' and SuperSonics' 1969-70 transaction histories independently record the same exchange and date. Seattle ultimately exercised that incoming selection at No. 20 in the 1970 NBA draft on Jake Ford; Ford was not the player being traded in November 1969, because the draft still lay months ahead. Mueller had made four Seattle appearances early in the season before changing teams, and Detroit was buying immediately available frontcourt minutes, not an All-Star or a premium future draft position. A later retrospective should judge the actual Detroit games Mueller played after November 1 against Ford's separate Seattle return, without mixing in their performances for earlier or later employers.

sections.heading: Mueller Delivered 189 Pistons Appearances Across Four Seasons
sections.body: Mueller joined the Detroit rotation for 74 games in 1969-70, scoring 759 points and collecting 469 rebounds with 199 assists after the trade. Basketball-Reference's player splits and Detroit's roster totals distinguish those appearances from the four Seattle games at the beginning of that same NBA season. His Pistons playing time then declined: 52 games in 1970-71, 42 in 1971-72, and another 21 during 1972-73 before he finished that season outside the NBA. Together those four Detroit portions equal 189 regular-season appearances, not 168, the subtotal that would exclude his final 21 Pistons games. The team obtained multiple seasons of usable forward depth for the second-round obligation, although Mueller's reduced minutes in his final NBA season mean it would overstate the case to call him an enduring starter.

sections.heading: Seattle Exercised the Pick at No. 20 on Jake Ford
sections.body: Seattle did receive an actual second-round choice, not merely an unconverted conditional right. The SuperSonics used the Detroit-origin No. 20 selection on Maryland Eastern Shore guard Jake Ford in the March 1970 draft. Ford eventually appeared in five NBA games for Seattle during 1970-71 and 26 more in 1971-72, totaling 31 games and 249 regular-season minutes. The franchise also made a different second-round pick, No. 23 Pete Cross, in that draft, and Cross must not be attributed to Detroit's outgoing selection. Ford's limited direct Seattle career is the relevant return of the specific Mueller trade; another player's draft rights or the 1970 club's other picks cannot enlarge it. This is an exercised pick with modest court production rather than a forfeited or unused selection.

sections.heading: The B-Plus and C Grades Rest on Team-Specific Minutes
sections.body: The inherited Pistons Win decision and Detroit B+ versus Seattle C grades can be evaluated against identifiable NBA minutes. Mueller supplied 189 Detroit games across four seasons, beginning with 74 appearances and 759 points in 1969-70. Seattle's No. 20 draft pick became Jake Ford, who played 31 Sonics games and just 249 minutes over two seasons. The SuperSonics did not receive zero: acquiring and exercising a second-round selection was a legitimate return, and Ford did appear in the league. But Detroit bought substantially more immediate and sustained player service than the selection ultimately yielded in Seattle. Neither side acquired a future marquee star in this deal, and Mueller's four games for Seattle before the exchange cannot be counted twice. Those limits explain a meaningful Pistons edge without treating a routine frontcourt trade as a championship transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win — Detroit B+, Seattle C. The draft pick produced a real player, yet Mueller's longer tenure and much larger role give Detroit the clear realized-value advantage. The canonical hindsight comparison is limited to the documented assets in this record — Erwin Mueller, 1970 second-round pick (#20 - Jake Ford) — and does not add speculative value beyond those completed outcomes. For Detroit and Seattle, the verdict stays tied to realized, source-supported franchise value.

sections.heading: The Nets Bought George Lehmann from Los Angeles on November 11
sections.body: The New York Nets acquired guard George Lehmann from the Los Angeles Stars for cash on November 11, 1969. Both teams' individual American Basketball Association transaction histories and the 1969-70 league chronology list the same date and direction. The price is described as cash, but no amount is supplied in the cited public ledger, so the exchange cannot be scored as if New York surrendered a known sum. Lehmann played 46 regular-season games for the Nets after arriving, totaling 344 points, 104 assists and 41 made three-pointers in 679 minutes. His direct New York tenure was measurable even though it lasted only part of the season. When the Nets subsequently sold him to the Miami Floridians for another undisclosed cash payment on February 19, 1970, that was a second separate transaction and should be considered a later asset conversion rather than extra consideration paid by Los Angeles in November.

sections.heading: Lehmann Immediately Helped the Nets
sections.body: Lehmann immediately became a useful backcourt piece, playing 46 games for the Nets and totaling 344 points, 104 assists and 41 made three-pointers in 679 minutes.

sections.heading: New York Recovered Another Cash Return
sections.body: The second cash sale was a separate February 19, 1970 transaction with the Miami Floridians, not a rebate or an additional term of the November 1969 Los Angeles Stars deal. New York had already received 46 games and 679 minutes of George Lehmann's guard play before it transferred him again. The original transaction ledger documents cash moving to the Stars in November and a separate cash return to the Nets in February, but provides no reliable amount for either payment. Those unquantified figures cannot be subtracted to claim a known profit. The Nets' favorable C+ versus Stars C retrospective assessment instead rests on receiving documented NBA/ABA-season playing value while keeping the later outgoing sale distinct from the deal's original price.

sections.heading: The Nets Built the Better Asset Cycle
sections.body: The November cash payment to Los Angeles and New York's February 1970 sale to Miami were separate transactions, and the cited transaction ledgers give no dollar amounts for either. The Nets nevertheless received 46 games and 679 minutes of Lehmann's guard play before converting his rights into another cash return. That creates an observable sequence of playing value followed by another asset transaction, but it does not establish a numerical profit or authorize counting Miami's payment as consideration supplied by the Stars.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win — New York C+, Los Angeles Stars C. Los Angeles received an undisclosed payment in the original deal, but the Nets obtained nearly half a season of rotation production plus a later cash return, giving New York the modest hindsight edge. The canonical hindsight comparison is limited to the documented assets in this record — George Lehmann, cash — and does not add speculative value beyond those completed outcomes. For New York and Los Angeles Stars, the verdict stays tied to realized, source-supported franchise value.

sections.heading: Indiana Bought Back Steve Chubin from the Nets in November 1969
sections.body: Indiana acquired guard Steve Chubin from the New York Nets for an undisclosed cash payment on November 11, 1969. The Pacers', Nets' and ABA season transaction ledgers independently list the deal, with New York the receiving club for the cash and Indiana the acquiring club for the player. Chubin had previously played in Indiana, so this was a return to a familiar organization rather than a new draft rights arrangement. In this second Pacers stint he made 32 regular-season appearances, averaging 4.2 points, 1.3 rebounds and 2.2 assists in 11.9 minutes. Kentucky subsequently claimed him on waivers March 17, 1970, which limits the return to a short regular-season role; his later appearances elsewhere cannot count as Indiana production. The Nets obtained a financial return not quantified in the available source list, so the inherited narrow Indiana advantage should not be turned into a major trade win without knowing the cash consideration.

sections.heading: Chubin Supplied Thirty-Two Pacers Games
sections.body: Chubin gave the Pacers 32 regular-season games, averaging 4.2 points, 1.3 rebounds and 2.2 assists in 11.9 minutes before Kentucky claimed him on waivers in March.

sections.heading: New York Took Undisclosed Cash
sections.body: New York's consideration was cash, not a player or a pick, when it sent Steve Chubin back to Indiana on November 11, 1969. Before this second Pacers stint, Chubin had made 39 Nets appearances in the 1969-70 ABA season. Those 39 earlier games demonstrate what New York had already used, rather than new Pacers output from the sale. The team transactions list the payment without a verified dollar figure, so the Nets' C grade cannot be treated as a loss of any specific financial amount. Indiana received 32 additional player appearances at 4.2 points and 2.2 assists a game before Kentucky claimed Chubin on waivers in March. That short actual Pacers production explains only the small inherited C+ advantage, not an enduring talent return.

sections.heading: Indiana Holds Only a Small Edge
sections.body: The ledger documents 39 earlier Nets games for Chubin before he returned to Indiana, whereas the Pacers' new purchase produced 32 appearances before Kentucky claimed him in March. Because the cash payment was not quantified in the cited records, New York's financial receipt and Indiana's playing time cannot be translated into a precise monetary advantage. The narrow grade difference is a retrospective basketball judgment about that short Pacers stint, not a claim that the Nets received little or no cash.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pacers Win — New York C, Indiana C+. Indiana received the only measurable post-trade basketball production, but the short tenure and unknown cash amount keep the hindsight advantage modest rather than decisive. The canonical hindsight comparison is limited to the documented assets in this record — cash, Steve Chubin — and does not add speculative value beyond those completed outcomes. For New York and Indiana, the verdict stays tied to realized, source-supported franchise value.

sections.heading: Boston Traded Bob Cousys Playing Rights for Bill Dinwiddie
sections.body: The November 18, 1969 trade sent the playing rights to longtime Celtics legend Bob Cousy to the Cincinnati Royals, with Bill Dinwiddie arriving in Boston. Boston's and Cincinnati's team transaction histories and the league-wide NBA ledger confirm a direct exchange of rights for the forward. Cousy was already the Royals' head coach, not a productive active Celtics guard transferring franchises in the middle of a season. The inherited player-and-pick listing once suggested a further draft asset, but the strongest matching transaction ledgers do not document that extra pick. It should not be credited to either side without an independently traceable selection. This is an unusual rights transaction because the most famous player name involved had effectively retired years earlier, and the teams were buying very different possibilities: a brief on-court comeback versus a forward who could help Boston in a later season.

sections.heading: Cousys Brief Cincinnati Comeback Was Seven Games
sections.body: Cousy was already coaching Cincinnati when the Royals obtained the rights to let him suit up again. His comeback was limited to seven NBA regular-season games and 34 minutes in 1969-70, not a renewed full season as an elite Celtics playmaker. The original Boston achievements that made him famous were already complete before the November 1969 transaction; those championships and assists cannot be transferred to Cincinnati's acquired-value column. The Royals' player return was primarily the right to use their head coach as a late-career participant for a few brief appearances. That narrow output helps explain the original Cincinnati C grade even when the retired star's name seems far bigger than the outgoing role player. The history of the deal is notable, but a retrospective trade verdict must distinguish celebrity, coaching and the minutes a club actually received in that year.

sections.heading: Bill Dinwiddie Missed 1969-70 but Later Played 61 Celtics Games
sections.body: Dinwiddie did not immediately give Boston a full season of service. A knee injury kept the forward out of the Celtics' 1969-70 playing rotation after the transaction, so attributing that season's minutes to him would be erroneous. He eventually joined the 1970-71 Boston roster and played 61 regular-season games, giving the Celtics actual reserve frontcourt production unavailable from the older player rights they had surrendered. Boston subsequently traded Dinwiddie to Milwaukee for a 1972 sixth-round choice in a separate transaction. That later draft opportunity should be described as downstream value from Boston's handling of Dinwiddie, not as a pick Cincinnati directly supplied in November 1969. The team's original B-minus judgment rests on the meaningful 61-game later stint and an asset it could move again, while recognizing the entire first post-trade season had yielded no on-court return.

sections.heading: The Celtics Produced More Measurable Value
sections.body: Dinwiddie missed 1969-70 with a knee injury but then played 61 games for Boston in 1970-71 before the Celtics traded him to Milwaukee for a 1972 sixth-round pick. Boston received the stronger measurable basketball return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win — Boston B-, Cincinnati C. Boston received the stronger measurable basketball return. The canonical hindsight comparison is limited to the documented assets in this record — Bill Dinwiddie, playing rights to Bob Cousy — and does not add speculative value beyond those completed outcomes. For Boston and Cincinnati, the verdict stays tied to realized, source-supported franchise value.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Acquired Happy Hairston
sections.body: Los Angeles acquired Happy Hairston from Detroit in late November 1969 for Bill Hewitt, a 1970 third-round pick that became Jim Hayes, a 1973 third-round pick that became Larry Kenon, and cash.

sections.heading: Hairston Became a Championship-Era Lakers Starter
sections.body: The source set disagrees on the exact package and date: Basketball-Reference's team, league and executive ledgers list November 27 and only Hewitt plus the 1970 pick, while Pro Sports Transactions records November 26 and also traces the 1973 pick and cash to the deal.

sections.heading: Detroit Got Useful Bill Hewitt Minutes
sections.body: Hairston became the defining realized asset, playing 394 Lakers games over six seasons and starting on the 1972 championship team.

sections.heading: Hairstons Lakers Tenure Outweighed Detroits Package Despite Source Differences
sections.body: The source books do not agree on every term of Detroit's November 1969 Happy Hairston trade. Basketball-Reference's Detroit, Los Angeles and league season ledgers list November 27 and Bill Hewitt with the 1970 third-rounder eventually used on Jim Hayes as Los Angeles' outgoing compensation. Pro Sports Transactions instead records November 26 and additional 1973 draft and cash components. The inherited canonical record preserves those extra assets while their exact provenance and timing require continued reconciliation rather than silently erasing them. On the results that are verifiable, Hairston made 394 Lakers regular-season appearances across six seasons and played an important role in the 1972 championship run. Detroit obtained Hewitt for 175 games, while the draft pieces failed to yield a comparable Pistons contributor. Those different outcomes explain the legacy Lakers A+ and Detroit B grades, but the unverified extra compensation cannot be treated as a known cash figure or a direct Pistons player season.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win — Detroit B, Los Angeles A+. Detroit received 175 useful games from Hewitt, but neither drafted player produced for the Pistons. The canonical hindsight comparison is limited to the documented assets in this record — Bill Hewitt, 1970 third-round pick (#47 - Jim Hayes), 1973 third-round pick (#50 - Larry Kenon), cash, Happy Hairston — and does not add speculative value beyond those completed outcomes. For Detroit and Los Angeles, the verdict stays tied to realized, source-supported franchise value.

sections.heading: The Lakers Purchased Tresvants Rights from Seattle on January 23
sections.body: Seattle sold John Tresvant's NBA playing rights to the Los Angeles Lakers on January 23, 1970. The Lakers' and SuperSonics' 1969-70 transaction histories independently verify January 23, a correction from the older source ledger's January 21 notation. Neither contemporary team listing specifies the cash price; the source record can establish player-rights direction without assigning a made-up financial amount. Los Angeles brought Tresvant into its frontcourt and used him for 20 regular-season games after the transaction, followed by eight more appearances in 1970-71. The later Lakers decision to trade him to Baltimore on November 11, 1970 for a 1972 second-round choice was a new transaction, not part of the original Seattle sale. The final choice became Paul Stovall, but Stovall had not been identified in January when Seattle agreed to relinquish Tresvant's rights.

sections.heading: Tresvant Gave Los Angeles Twenty-Eight Games
sections.body: Multiple Basketball-Reference team, league and executive ledgers agree on January 23, correcting the legacy January 21 TradeVerdicts date.

sections.heading: The Lakers Later Converted Him into a Pick
sections.body: Tresvant played 20 Lakers games that season and eight more in 1970-71 before Los Angeles traded him to Baltimore for a 1972 second-round pick that became Paul Stovall.

sections.heading: Seattle’s Unknown Cash Return Keeps It Close
sections.body: Seattle's transaction entries identify an outgoing player-rights sale but do not establish the cash amount, preventing an exact financial comparison. Los Angeles used Tresvant for 20 games in 1969-70 and eight the next season, then obtained a 1972 second-round pick from Baltimore in a separate November 1970 trade. The Lakers' edge is therefore based on observable player use and a later converted draft asset, without rewriting the January purchase as if Seattle supplied that pick.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Lakers Edge — Los Angeles B-, Seattle C+. The Lakers therefore received modest on-court value plus a later draft asset, giving Los Angeles a small realized-value edge without turning the transaction into a major win. The canonical hindsight comparison is limited to the documented assets in this record — John Tresvant, cash — and does not add speculative value beyond those completed outcomes. For Los Angeles and Seattle, the verdict stays tied to realized, source-supported franchise value.

sections.heading: Atlanta Acquired Walt Bellamy
sections.body: Atlanta acquired Walt Bellamy from Detroit on February 1, 1970 for cash and future player consideration that was ultimately satisfied by John Arthurs.

sections.heading: Bellamy Became a Four-Year Hawks Centerpiece
sections.body: A complicated pre-draft obligation briefly pointed to Milwaukee's 1970 first-round pick and Gary Freeman, but Detroit did not receive Freeman; Arthurs replaced that route as the player consideration.

sections.heading: Detroit’s Player Consideration Produced No NBA Games
sections.body: Bellamy gave Atlanta 338 regular-season games through 1973-74, including four full seasons averaging at least 13 points and 9 rebounds.

sections.heading: The Known Basketball Return Is Heavily Atlanta
sections.body: Arthurs never played an NBA game for Detroit, and the cash amount is undisclosed. The realized return therefore favored Atlanta by a wide margin.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win — Atlanta A, Detroit C. The realized return therefore favored Atlanta by a wide margin. The canonical hindsight comparison is limited to the documented assets in this record — Walt Bellamy, John Arthurs (player to be named later, delivered June 3, 1970), cash — and does not add speculative value beyond those completed outcomes. sections.heading: San Francisco Traded Future No. 3 and Clyde Lee Rights for Zelmo Beaty
sections.body: On February 2, 1970, San Francisco obtained the NBA rights to center Zelmo Beaty from Atlanta. The Hawks' and Warriors' season transaction records summarize the outgoing package as Clyde Lee plus the Warriors' 1970 first-round pick. The pick subsequently became No. 3 overall and Atlanta selected Pete Maravich. The separate draft-trade ledger explains that Lee was a future-consideration component delivered later in 1974, rather than proof that he joined the Hawks in February 1970. Published historical ledgers disagree on the precise September-or-October 1974 delivery date, so the inherited canonical October 4 notation is not independently reconciled here. The 1970 draft right and the later Lee component must both be counted as Atlanta's compensation, but Beaty's acquired signing rights did not guarantee that he would play a Warriors NBA game.

sections.heading: Atlanta Drafted Maravich Third and Received Four Hawks Seasons
sections.body: Atlanta used the incoming San Francisco first-round pick on LSU guard Pete Maravich at No. 3 in March 1970. He made 302 regular-season appearances for the Hawks from 1970-71 through 1973-74, developing into one of the NBA's highest-usage scoring and playmaking guards and earning All-Star recognition before leaving Atlanta. Those 302 Hawks games are directly traceable to the draft right received from San Francisco, not to a hypothetical selection that another team might have made. The significance of the pick was unknown when the Hawks agreed to move Beaty's NBA rights in February; Maravich had not yet been chosen. The retained Hawks A+ assessment reflects the eventual selection and its realized Atlanta career rather than any certainty that a future third overall slot would become a star.

sections.heading: Beaty Played in the ABA Instead of for San Francisco
sections.body: Beaty's playing record shows the fundamental weakness of San Francisco's return: he did not appear in a Warriors NBA regular-season game after the rights swap. He had sat out the 1969-70 NBA season amid his dispute over ABA eligibility, then played four ABA seasons for the Utah Stars from 1970-71 through 1973-74. The Stars' success and Beaty's production there belong to a different franchise and league, not as Warriors NBA minutes. He later returned to the NBA with the Los Angeles Lakers, not San Francisco. Acquiring contractual rights is a legitimate gamble, but an asset with no resulting Warriors appearances is different from receiving an active All-Star center. This explains why the inherited Golden State F is not a judgment that Beaty lacked basketball talent; it is a judgment about what that specific team obtained.

sections.heading: Maravich and Delayed Clyde Lee Value Made the Hawks Clear Winners
sections.body: The future-consideration portion eventually identified Clyde Lee, whom the Hawks held briefly in the opening weeks of 1974-75. Lee played nine Atlanta games, and the team's November 8, 1974 transaction ledger shows it sent him and a separate future third-round pick to Philadelphia for Tom Van Arsdale. That later move must be distinguished from the original 1970 exchange; Philadelphia did not hand San Francisco a player in the Beaty deal. The historically decisive Atlanta asset was the No. 3 selection used on Pete Maravich, who supplied 302 Hawks games. San Francisco received Beaty's rights without corresponding Warriors court production. The preserved Hawks Win, Atlanta A+ and Golden State F grades reflect this extreme realized return gap while treating Lee as an additional delayed component and avoiding uncertain exact delivery-date assertions.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win — San Francisco F, Atlanta A+. The realized value overwhelmingly favored Atlanta. The canonical hindsight comparison is limited to the documented assets in this record — 1970 first-round pick (#3 - Pete Maravich), future consideration (Clyde Lee, delivered October 4, 1974), NBA rights to Zelmo Beaty — and does not add speculative value beyond those completed outcomes. For Atlanta and San Francisco, the verdict stays tied to realized, source-supported franchise value.

sections.heading: The Floridians Reacquired George Lehmann from New York for Cash
sections.body: On February 19, 1970, the Miami Floridians bought George Lehmann from the New York Nets for cash, according to both teams' ABA transaction lists and the league's season chronology. This was distinct from the earlier November 11, 1969 cash purchase that had brought Lehmann from the Los Angeles Stars to New York. Miami acquired an immediate starting-caliber backcourt option for the final part of the ABA campaign: Lehmann played 25 games for the Floridians and averaged 43.1 minutes, 17.9 points and 5.0 assists. Those 25 Floridians games belong to Miami's return, while the preceding 46 Nets appearances and earlier Los Angeles games do not. The documented exchange involved cash, but the sources in the record do not establish the payment amount, making it inappropriate to assert an exact financial profit for either club. His later move to Carolina was another trade rather than original February compensation.

sections.heading: Lehmann Took on a Major Floridians Role
sections.body: Lehmann immediately moved from a reserve role in New York into a major Floridians role, playing 25 games at 43.1 minutes, 17.9 points and 5.0 assists per game.

sections.heading: Miami Later Converted Him into Rich Niemann
sections.body: Miami's August 1970 decision to send George Lehmann to the Carolina Cougars in exchange for Rich Niemann was a later, separate player exchange, not a second asset provided by the Nets in February. Niemann went on to appear in 51 games the following ABA season, giving Miami a new playing return after the initial acquisition. The connection belongs in the downstream chain because the Floridians could not have traded Lehmann onward without obtaining him first, but it must not turn an unknown February cash price into a proven bargain of a specific dollar value. Lehmann's own 25 Floridians appearances, 17.9 points and 5.0 assists per game are the immediate verifiable February return. The incoming Niemann service is additional later asset conversion and is not included among the original Nets payment terms.

sections.heading: The Unknown Cash Price Keeps the Edge Modest
sections.body: New York recovered an undisclosed cash payment after getting 46 games from Lehmann earlier that season. With the cash amount unknown, Miami gets only a modest hindsight edge for turning money into meaningful on-court production and a later player return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Floridians Edge — Miami C+, New York C. George Lehmann delivered immediate guard minutes after the Floridians bought him from New York in February 1970: 25 games at 17.9 points and 5.0 assists per game. Miami later sent Lehmann to Carolina for Rich Niemann in a distinct August transaction, preserving another asset path. The Nets received cash, but its amount is not established in the reviewed public records. Miami's identifiable production and later conversion earn a modest edge without treating the later Niemann exchange as a February asset from New York.

sections.heading: Buffalo Moved Down and Added Mike Davis
sections.body: On March 23, 1970, the expansion Buffalo Braves traded the No. 9 selection in the coming NBA draft to the Baltimore Bullets, obtaining veteran forward Mike Davis and the lower No. 15 first-round choice. Baltimore used No. 9 on George E. Johnson; Buffalo selected Princeton center John Hummer at No. 15. The original bargain therefore had three distinct pieces, not just a draft-slot swap or a straight player transaction. Hummer supplied 81 games and 11.3 points per contest during Buffalo's 1970-71 expansion season, while Davis separately contributed 73 Braves appearances. The 1970 league transaction and draft ledgers establish the pick sequence, and the team season/player records establish each completed return. Those direct results explain the preserved Buffalo Braves Win with an A- for the Braves and C for Baltimore rather than relying on the relative pre-draft rank of the two selections.

sections.heading: The Braves Used No. 15 to Draft John Hummer
sections.body: Buffalo received the 15th overall selection from Baltimore after moving down from No. 9 in the 1970 first round and obtaining Mike Davis in the same deal. The Braves used No. 15 on Princeton center John Hummer. In Buffalo's expansion season Hummer immediately appeared in 81 regular-season games and averaged 11.3 points with 8.9 rebounds in 32.6 minutes; this is direct value from the specific pick the franchise received. Mike Davis was a separate incoming player and later added 73 Braves games in 1970-71, giving the transaction two meaningful Buffalo on-court returns rather than only draft optionality. Baltimore exercised the higher No. 9 selection on George E. Johnson, whose limited Bullets NBA appearances did not provide the same first-year return. The grade comparison must not treat Hummer's rookie points as Davis production or count Baltimore's eventual drafted player as a Buffalo asset.

sections.heading: Davis Added More Useful Buffalo Value
sections.body: 15 selection became John Hummer, who immediately started 81 games for the expansion Braves and averaged 11.3 points and 8.9 rebounds as a rookie.

sections.heading: Baltimore’s Higher Pick Produced Less
sections.body: Davis added two useful Buffalo seasons. Baltimore used No. 9 on George E. Johnson, but he appeared in only 24 games for the Bullets as a rookie and never developed into a comparable return. In realized value, Buffalo won the exchange clearly.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Braves Win — Buffalo A-, Baltimore C. In realized value, Buffalo won the exchange clearly. The canonical hindsight comparison is limited to the documented assets in this record — Mike Davis, 1970 first-round pick (#15 - John Hummer), 1970 first-round pick (#9 - George E. Johnson) — and does not add speculative value beyond those completed outcomes. For Buffalo and Baltimore, the verdict stays tied to realized, source-supported franchise value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: On March 24, 1970, the ABA New York Nets acquired the contractual rights to Jim McMillian from the Los Angeles Stars. New York sent Los Angeles a future draft pick. Pro Sports Transactions records the player-rights-for-pick structure but leaves the future pick's year and round unidentified. Its ABA draft ledger also shows that the Stars had selected McMillian in the second round, 15th overall, of the 1970 ABA draft.

sections.heading: Nets Return
sections.body:
McMillian was a valuable basketball player, but that is different from the value of the ABA rights New York acquired. He did not play for the Nets. The NBA's Los Angeles Lakers selected him 13th overall in the 1970 NBA draft, and he began his NBA career that fall. Basketball-Reference lists his NBA debut as October 16, 1970 and credits him with 631 regular-season games over nine seasons.

His NBA production underscores what the Nets hoped to acquire. McMillian played 81 games as a Lakers rookie in 1970-71, averaging 8.4 points and 4.1 rebounds. A year later he played 80 games and averaged 18.8 points and 6.5 rebounds for the 1971-72 Lakers. He became an important scorer on a championship team and later continued his career with Buffalo, New York and Portland.

For this ABA transaction, however, none of that production became a Nets return. New York held rights to a good player who chose the NBA path. TradeVerdicts therefore separates McMillian's career value from the realized value of the rights asset: the player succeeded, but the Nets did not receive his games.

sections.heading: Stars Return
sections.body:
Los Angeles received a future draft pick. The surviving transaction entry does not specify the draft year, round, selection number or player outcome. That gap matters. It would be misleading to assign the Stars a particular player or to credit them with later production that cannot be traced to this pick.

Even with the outcome unresolved, the Stars did convert an ABA rights asset they did not ultimately use into another piece of draft capital. That is a more tangible transaction result than New York's rights, which never became an ABA appearance. The value cannot be graded aggressively because the pick may have produced little or nothing; the historical record simply does not establish the final result.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The transaction is unusual because the best player involved had a productive career outside the league in which the trade occurred. McMillian's Lakers career shows that Los Angeles had drafted a legitimate prospect, but the Nets' acquired rights never converted into on-court ABA value. The Stars at least received a future pick, although the unidentified outcome prevents a complete realized-value comparison.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Stars Edge, C+/C. Los Angeles receives a C+ for converting McMillian's unused ABA rights into future draft capital. New York receives a C because the rights did not produce a Nets appearance, even though the player himself became a strong NBA contributor. Confidence is medium on the verdict: the March 24 transaction and McMillian's career path are well supported, but the future pick's year, round and eventual outcome remain unresolved in the reviewed records. McMillian's later NBA games belong to his NBA teams, not the New York ABA rights-holder, and the unresolved Stars pick chain prevents calling Los Angeles' return a proven star asset.

sections.heading: San Diego Sells Don Kojis’ Player Rights to Seattle
sections.body: On April 15, 1970, the San Diego Rockets sold the player rights to Don Kojis to the Seattle SuperSonics. Basketball-Reference lists the move from both team perspectives and in the league transaction log. RealGM also records Seattle acquiring Kojis from San Diego on that date. The reviewed sources establish the transfer, but none publishes the sale price. TradeVerdicts therefore keeps the Rockets' return as cash with the amount unknown.

sections.heading: Seattle Return
sections.body:
Kojis was already an established NBA forward. He had made the All-Star team in 1967-68 and 1968-69 with San Diego, then averaged 15.3 points and 6.9 rebounds in 56 games during 1969-70. Seattle was not buying a speculative prospect. It was acquiring the rights to a veteran who had recently been one of San Diego's leading scorers.

The move produced immediate usable value. Kojis played 79 games for Seattle in 1970-71, averaging 14.6 points, 5.5 rebounds and 27.1 minutes. He remained in the rotation the next season, appearing in 73 games and averaging 11.4 points, 4.6 rebounds and 25.4 minutes. Across the two seasons, that is 152 regular-season appearances and nearly 4,000 minutes from the purchased rights.

Seattle later moved Kojis in August 1972 as part of a separate transaction with Kansas City-Omaha. This verdict does not assign the entire value of that later package back to the 1970 sale because Kojis was bundled with another player. The direct return is already enough to judge the original purchase: Seattle received two seasons of dependable rotation production.

sections.heading: San Diego Return
sections.body:
San Diego received cash. That asset should not be treated as worthless, especially in an era when player sales were a normal roster-management tool. The problem is documentation, not the existence of value. Without a verified sale price, there is no responsible way to compare the financial return with a player contract, draft choice or later on-court production.

That uncertainty is why the Rockets are not given a failing grade. They monetized the rights to a 31-year-old veteran after a season in which he played 56 games. But the surviving basketball record shows exactly what Seattle received, while the cash side cannot be quantified from the reviewed sources.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: Seattle's advantage is the clearest part of the record. The SuperSonics turned the purchased rights into 152 games, 1,989 points and 770 rebounds over two seasons. Kojis was not a franchise-changing acquisition, but he was a regular contributor on teams that improved from 38 wins in 1970-71 to 47 wins in 1971-72.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Seattle SuperSonics Win. Seattle Win, B/C. Seattle receives a B for obtaining two productive veteran seasons for an undisclosed cash price. San Diego receives a C because the club did receive a real asset, but the amount is unknown and there is no documented basketball return to compare with Kojis' Seattle production. Confidence is medium-high on the transaction and player value, but only medium on the overall economic comparison because the sale price remains unresolved. Seattle could document what its cash bought: 152 Kojis games and useful forward production across two seasons. San Diego received a genuine financial asset, but the absent sale price prevents a proper comparison between that money and the veteran's playing value. The Seattle team's improved record during those years is context, not proof the trade alone caused the wins. Thus the B/C split reflects observed playing time while leaving the unidentified cash return unresolved.

sections.heading: Chicago Trades Clem Haskins for Jim Fox and a Future Pick
sections.body: On April 23, 1970, the Chicago Bulls traded Clem Haskins to the Phoenix Suns for center Jim Fox and a 1971 second-round draft pick. Basketball-Reference's Chicago, Phoenix and league transaction ledgers agree on the date and package. The pick became Villanova forward Howard Porter at No. 32 overall. The source-backed review also resolves the legacy 'Jim Fox / Sonny Fox' identity to NBA center Jim Fox, whose Basketball-Reference identifier is foxji01.

sections.heading: Phoenix Return
sections.body:
Haskins was the best immediate player in the transaction. He had just completed an 82-game Chicago season with 1,668 points and 624 assists. In Phoenix he played 82 games in 1970-71 and averaged 17.8 points, 4.7 assists and 4.0 rebounds. He followed with 79 games at 15.7 points in 1971-72, then remained with the Suns for 77 games in 1972-73 and 81 in 1973-74. That is 319 regular-season games across four Phoenix seasons.

Haskins' role declined after his first two Suns seasons, but Phoenix still received sustained guard production rather than a short rental. Across his four years with the club he logged 8,620 minutes. That direct longevity is the strongest part of the Suns' case and makes the legacy Bulls-win language too simplistic if the evaluation stops at the first transaction.

sections.heading: Chicago Return
sections.body:
Fox gave Chicago a useful first season. He played all 82 games in 1970-71, averaging 9.7 points, 7.3 rebounds and 2.4 assists in 19.9 minutes. He appeared in 10 more Bulls games the following season before Chicago moved him on November 9, 1971. Porter, selected with the acquired second-round pick, played 67 games as a rookie and 43 more in 1972-73. His Chicago role was modest, at 6.0 points per game in his first season and 5.1 in his second, but the pick still produced 110 NBA appearances for the Bulls.

Fox's later trade is what changes the hindsight comparison. Chicago sent Fox and a 1972 second-round pick to Cincinnati for Norm Van Lier and a 1972 third-round pick. Van Lier then played 535 regular-season games across seven Bulls seasons. During that Chicago tenure he made three All-Star teams, earned an All-NBA Second Team selection in 1973-74 and repeatedly appeared on the All-Defensive teams. The 1970 trade did not acquire Van Lier directly, and Chicago had to add another pick in 1971, so the full value of Van Lier cannot be credited to Phoenix's original assets. Fox nevertheless remained a meaningful component of the deal that brought him back.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body:
If the trade is judged only by direct post-trade games, Phoenix has the stronger side: Haskins delivered 319 Suns games, while Fox and Porter combined for 202 Bulls games. Chicago's package becomes more valuable when the later disposition of Fox is traced. He was not simply lost; he helped form the package for Van Lier, who became a long-term Chicago point guard and one of the league's leading defensive guards of the era. Porter also supplied two seasons from a second-round selection.

The later Van Lier exchange prevents a simple direct-production verdict. Chicago had to attach an additional second-round pick, and it also received a third-round pick, so Van Lier's entire seven-year Bulls career is not attributable to Fox alone. Even with that discount, Fox's retained trade value plus Porter's 110 games pushes Chicago's long-term realized package ahead of Phoenix's very good Haskins return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win, A-/B+. Chicago receives an A- for one useful Fox season, 110 games from the acquired draft pick and the important downstream role Fox played in the trade that brought Norm Van Lier back to Chicago. Phoenix receives a B+ for four productive Haskins seasons and 319 regular-season games, including two years of high-level scoring and playmaking. The gap is narrower than the legacy verdict suggested because Haskins clearly outperformed Fox and Porter on direct value. Confidence is high on the transaction, identities and player production, and medium-high on the final comparative grade because downstream value requires an attribution discount. The distinction is between immediate returns and the value of repackaging an asset. Phoenix received 319 Suns games from Clem Haskins, far beyond Fox's direct Chicago tenure and Porter's 110 Bulls games combined. Chicago later included Fox in a broader transaction that brought Norm Van Lier back, but the other outgoing consideration also carried value. Crediting Chicago for the asset's continued usefulness without assigning the entire Van Lier result to Fox preserves the close A-/B+ comparison.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: The Los Angeles Lakers sent Mel Counts to the Phoenix Suns for Gail Goodrich in May 1970. The package itself is unanimous across the reviewed sources, but the exact date is not. Basketball-Reference's Lakers, Suns and league transaction ledgers all list May 20, and RealGM also uses May 20. Pro Sports Transactions lists May 21, which matches the existing TradeVerdicts route date. This review preserves the May 21 canonical route and records the one-day source conflict rather than silently changing a live identifier.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Return
sections.body:
Goodrich returned to the franchise that had drafted him in 1965 after Phoenix had selected him in the 1968 expansion draft. His first season back was already productive: 79 games, 17.5 points and 4.8 assists per game in 1970-71. One year later he became the leading scorer on one of the most famous teams in league history. Goodrich averaged 25.9 points in all 82 games for the 1971-72 Lakers, narrowly leading Jerry West in scoring as Los Angeles won 69 games, produced a 33-game winning streak and captured the NBA championship.

The return lasted far beyond that title season. Goodrich made four consecutive All-Star teams from 1972 through 1975 and led the Lakers in scoring for four straight seasons from 1971-72 through 1974-75. He averaged 23.9 points in 1972-73, 25.3 in 1973-74 and 22.6 in 1974-75, then added 19.5 points and 5.6 assists in his final Lakers season in 1975-76. The franchise later retired his No. 25, and Goodrich was inducted into the Basketball Hall of Fame.
Phoenix Return

Counts gave Phoenix legitimate frontcourt depth rather than disappearing after the trade. He played 80 games in 1970-71, averaging 11.0 points, 6.3 rebounds and 20.9 minutes. In 1971-72 he appeared in 76 more games, although his role fell to 11.9 minutes and 5.2 points per game. Across the two Suns seasons, Counts supplied 156 regular-season appearances and more than 2,500 minutes.

That production keeps Phoenix from receiving a failing grade. Counts was a veteran seven-footer who could score and rebound in a reserve role, and he remained available nearly every night. But Phoenix had just received two strong Goodrich seasons before making the deal, including a 20.0-point, 7.5-assist campaign in 1969-70. Trading that 27-year-old guard for a useful but lower-impact veteran center created a large long-term opportunity cost.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body:
The direct realized return is decisive. Counts gave Phoenix two useful seasons; Goodrich gave Los Angeles six, four All-Star selections and the highest scoring average on the 1972 champions. In the 1972 postseason he averaged 23.8 points across all 15 games as the Lakers won the title. The Lakers then continued to receive high-volume scoring from him through the middle of the decade.

This is also a case where no elaborate downstream chain is needed to establish the result. The acquired player himself produced the value. Phoenix's return was real, but the difference in role, longevity and championship contribution is too large to call the trade close.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win, A+/C+. Los Angeles receives an A+ for reacquiring a Hall of Fame guard who became a four-time All-Star during his second Lakers tenure, led the 1972 champions in regular-season scoring and remained a major offensive piece for six seasons. Phoenix receives a C+ for 156 games of useful center depth from Counts, with the grade recognizing that he was productive even though the Suns surrendered the much more valuable player. Confidence is high on the package and player outcomes and medium-high overall because the historical transaction ledgers disagree by one day on the date. Keeping the existing May 21 canonical identifier while disclosing the May 20 source entries avoids making a source-date disagreement look like a different Goodrich–Counts trade.

sections.heading: Atlanta Swaps Gary Gregor for Portland’s Jerry Chambers
sections.body: On June 17, 1970, the Atlanta Hawks traded Gary Gregor to the expansion Portland Trail Blazers for Jerry Chambers. Basketball-Reference's league ledger, Atlanta transaction log, Portland executive register and team-to-team trade ledger agree on the date and one-for-one package. Portland had selected Chambers from Phoenix in the expansion draft only weeks earlier, so the deal immediately converted one expansion selection into a younger frontcourt piece with recent Atlanta experience.

sections.heading: Portland Return
sections.body:
Gregor became a regular part of Portland's first two rosters. In 1970-71 he appeared in 44 games and averaged 13.1 points and 10.4 rebounds per 36 minutes. His larger contribution came in 1971-72, when he played all 82 games and averaged 11.1 points, 7.2 rebounds and 2.3 assists in 28.9 minutes. Across the two Portland seasons, Basketball-Reference's trade ledger credits him with 126 games, 10.6 points, 7.3 rebounds, 2.1 assists and 2.5 win shares.

Portland also retained a small amount of value after Gregor left. Philadelphia signed him as a veteran free agent on September 11, 1972 and sent Portland a 1974 second-round pick as compensation. The Trail Blazers used that selection at No. 36 on Rubin Collins, who never appeared in an NBA game. The compensation therefore matters as a verified asset outcome, but it does not add realized player production to the original trade.
Atlanta Return

Chambers gave Atlanta one useful season. He played 65 games in 1970-71, averaging 8.9 points, 3.8 rebounds and 0.9 assists in 18.0 minutes. Basketball-Reference credits 1.5 win shares from that season, and he also appeared in four playoff games. The role was smaller than Gregor's eventual Portland role, but Chambers was not a zero-value acquisition.

Atlanta moved Chambers again on July 26, 1971, packaging him with Walt Hazzard to Buffalo for Herm Gilliam and Don May. That later transaction preserves some downstream value, but Chambers cannot responsibly be credited with the entire Gilliam-May return because Hazzard was bundled with him. The same attribution rule used elsewhere in the archive prevents a secondary package from being counted as if Atlanta had obtained both players solely for Chambers.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body:
The direct comparison favors Portland. Gregor played 126 games for the Trail Blazers to Chambers' 65 for Atlanta, and the trade-partner ledger gives Portland 2.5 future win shares against Atlanta's 1.5. Gregor also carried enough value after his Portland tenure to trigger a second-round compensation pick when Philadelphia signed him. Collins never reached the NBA, so that pick does not transform the deal, but it still extends Portland's asset chain beyond Gregor's two seasons.

Atlanta received a useful reserve season and later included Chambers in another trade, which keeps the Hawks' return respectable. Portland simply received more playing time, more aggregate production and one additional verified asset. The gap is real without being large enough to treat Atlanta's side as a failure.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Trail Blazers Win, B/C+. Portland receives a B for two productive Gregor seasons, 126 games and the later veteran-free-agent compensation pick. Atlanta receives a C+ for 65 useful Chambers games and some downstream package value before his departure. Confidence is high because the transaction date, player production and subsequent transactions are consistently documented. The Blazers' 126 Gregor games and Hawks' 65 Chambers games are direct returns; the later compensation pick and Chambers' participation in a larger trade must be attributed separately rather than counted as additional games from the June exchange.

sections.heading: Denver and Miami Exchange Three Assets Apiece in ABA Deal
sections.body: On June 18, 1970, the Denver Rockets traded Larry Jones, Greg Wittman and a 1971 second-round draft choice to the Miami Floridians for Larry Cannon, Don Sidle and Miami's 1971 first-round choice. Basketball-Reference's ABA transaction ledger, Denver transaction log and Floridians transaction log all describe the same six-asset exchange. Pro Sports Transactions resolves the incoming first-round pick as No. 4 in the 1971 ABA draft, used on Ken Durrett, while Denver's outgoing second-round pick remains listed without a verified player outcome.

sections.heading: Denver Return
sections.body:
Cannon produced the best single season on Denver's side. In 1970-71 he played 80 games, averaged 26.6 points, 4.2 rebounds and 5.2 assists, posted 7.2 win shares and made the All-ABA Second Team. That is substantial immediate value from a player who had averaged 11.8 points as a Miami rookie. Cannon did not extend the return into a second Denver regular season, however; he signed with Memphis in October 1971.

Sidle also helped right away. He played 54 Denver games in 1970-71 and averaged 16.1 points and 9.0 rebounds with 4.2 win shares. Denver traded Sidle with Wayne Chapman to Indiana on February 1, 1971 for John Barnhill and Art Becker. That downstream exchange preserved asset value, but Sidle cannot be credited with the entire Barnhill-Becker return because Chapman was part of the package.

The first-round pick became Ken Durrett at No. 4 in the 1971 ABA draft. Denver moved Durrett's rights to Virginia on January 22, 1971 for another 1971 first-round choice and a player to be named later or cash. Pro Sports Transactions identifies that replacement first-rounder as No. 5 Cliff Meely. Meely played in the NBA rather than for Denver in the ABA, so the original Miami pick did not generate realized Denver player production through that branch.
Floridians Return

Jones was the most durable and productive long-term player in the deal. He played all 84 games for the Floridians in 1970-71, averaging 24.3 points, 5.4 rebounds and 4.6 assists in 43.0 minutes. He made the ABA All-Star Game, finished seventh in MVP voting and produced 8.8 win shares. Jones followed with 66 games in 1971-72 at 17.6 points, 4.7 rebounds and 3.2 assists, adding 8.1 win shares. Across two Florida seasons, that is 150 games, 21.4 points, 5.1 rebounds, 4.0 assists and 16.9 win shares per Basketball-Reference.

Wittman contributed only five Floridians games before Miami traded him and a draft choice to Texas for Charlie Beasley on October 26, 1970. His direct production was minimal, and the unidentified Denver second-round pick cannot be assigned an invented player outcome. Florida therefore wins this comparison because of Jones rather than because every piece of its package paid off.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body:
Denver got real value. Cannon's 1970-71 season was excellent and Sidle supplied another productive frontcourt season before being moved. Combined, those two players gave Denver 134 regular-season games and 11.4 win shares in 1970-71. The problem is duration. Cannon left after one Denver season, Sidle was traded during that same campaign, and the first-round-pick branch did not lead to a player who appeared for Denver.

Jones alone gave Florida 150 games and 16.9 win shares over two seasons, while also delivering an All-Star season and a top-seven MVP finish in the first year. That longer direct return outweighs Denver's two-player burst even before Wittman's small contribution is considered. The original record's slight-Denver-edge framing was therefore too favorable to the Rockets once the realized player outcomes are measured.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Floridians Win, A-/B+. Florida receives an A- because Jones supplied two strong seasons, 150 games and 16.9 win shares, including an All-Star year immediately after the trade. Denver receives a B+ for Cannon's All-ABA season, Sidle's useful 54-game run and a first-round asset that retained transaction value even though its eventual rights chain did not produce Denver games. Confidence is high on the trade package, direct production and first-round pick identity; the outgoing Denver second-round pick remains an unresolved historical outcome. Denver's incoming 1971 No. 4 selection identified as Ken Durrett is a confirmed draft-right outcome, but the separate rights chain yielded no Denver appearances; Florida's Larry Jones supplied documented on-court value instead of merely potential draft capital.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: On June 20, 1970, the defending champion New York Knicks sent Nate Bowman and Mike Silliman to the expansion Buffalo Braves. Basketball-Reference's league ledger, Knicks transaction page and executive records describe Buffalo's return as cash. Contemporary and franchise media guides complicate the paperwork: Buffalo's 1971 guide says Silliman was acquired for future considerations, while a later Clippers franchise guide says Bowman and Silliman came for future considerations or a future draft choice. Pro Sports Transactions preserves still more alternate wording. Those entries describe competing versions of the same return, not four separate assets, so this review consolidates them into one disputed non-player consideration rather than counting each alternative.

sections.heading: Buffalo Return
sections.body:
Bowman gave the new franchise 44 games in 1970-71. He averaged 11.0 minutes, 3.1 points, 3.9 rebounds and 0.9 assists while producing 0.0 win shares in Basketball-Reference's accounting. The role was larger than his final Knicks season only at the margins: Buffalo needed frontcourt bodies, but Bob Kauffman, John Hummer and Cornell Warner handled far more of the meaningful center and forward workload. Bowman left Buffalo as a free agent after the season and played 18 ABA games for Pittsburgh in 1971-72, so the Braves did not receive a downstream trade asset.

Silliman was a different kind of gamble. New York had drafted the West Point forward in 1966, but military service delayed his NBA debut until Buffalo acquired his rights. The Braves' 1971 media guide highlighted his Army career and 1968 Olympic gold-medal captaincy, while also noting a toe operation before his rookie season. He ultimately played 36 games, averaging 10.2 minutes, 2.5 points, 1.7 rebounds and 0.6 assists with 0.3 win shares. He became a free agent after that single NBA season.

sections.heading: New York Return
sections.body: The Knicks' exact compensation cannot be reproduced with enough certainty to pretend the historical record is cleaner than it is. Basketball-Reference and executive logs say cash. Buffalo's contemporary media guide uses future considerations for Silliman, and the later Clippers franchise guide describes the combined acquisition as future considerations or a future draft choice. No verified player outcome or durable downstream asset was identified from that consideration in this research pass. The archive therefore records a single disputed non-player return and does not convert alternate source wording into multiple assets.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body:
Buffalo received 80 combined regular-season games and 849 minutes from Bowman and Silliman, but only 0.3 combined win shares. Both were gone after the Braves' inaugural season. New York, meanwhile, moved fringe depth after a championship season and received some form of non-player consideration without giving up a player who became a long-term Buffalo building block.

That makes the original slight-Knicks verdict too confident, but it also does not justify swinging the result toward Buffalo. The Braves got usable roster bodies for year one; the Knicks shed two low-impact assets for compensation whose precise form remains disputed. Neither side created durable realized value from the transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, C+/C+. Buffalo receives a C+ for 80 combined games from Bowman and Silliman, but neither player became a lasting piece and their combined impact was minimal. New York receives a C+ for turning fringe depth into a non-player consideration without losing meaningful long-term production. Confidence is medium because the June 20 date and player movement are well documented while the exact return conflicts across historical sources. A future pick and future considerations are competing descriptions of New York's one uncertain return, not proof that Buffalo paid two separate non-player assets for Bowman and Silliman.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Denver and Kentucky completed a two-stage ABA transaction. On July 14, 1970, the Rockets sent the rights to Walt Piatkowski to the Colonels for future considerations. Denver's team transaction ledger, Kentucky's ledger and the ABA league log all record the same deal. Kentucky's ledger then identifies the future consideration on October 2: Wayne Chapman was sent to Denver. Pro Sports Transactions independently preserves the same July exchange and October completion, so the asset routing and timing are well supported.

sections.heading: Denver Return
sections.body:
Chapman gave Denver actual rotation value. In 47 games for the 1970-71 Rockets, he averaged 22.3 minutes, 10.0 points, 3.0 rebounds and 2.3 assists. Basketball-Reference records 1,049 minutes and 468 points for his Denver stint. The efficiency was limited, but this was not a token appearance or an unrealized right; Chapman played a regular role for more than half a season. Denver's own 1971 media guide described him as a defensive and outside-shooting depth piece acquired from Kentucky before the season.

Chapman also retained some downstream transaction utility. On February 1, 1971, Denver packaged him with Don Sidle and sent both to Indiana for John Barnhill and Art Becker. Because that was a two-for-two trade, the later return cannot be credited to Chapman alone, but his inclusion confirms that Denver still held a movable player asset after receiving the future consideration. That secondary value is useful context without inflating his direct production.

sections.heading: Kentucky Return
sections.body:
Kentucky received Piatkowski's rights after he had played two seasons for Denver. The timing proved unfavorable. Basketball-Reference records that Piatkowski did not play in 1970-71 because he retired and worked as a teacher. He never appeared for the Colonels. He briefly returned to the ABA in 1971-72, but those six games came with the Floridians, not Kentucky, and therefore did not create realized value for the Colonels from this transaction.

That distinction is important for a rights trade. Piatkowski had been an actual ABA contributor before July 1970, so Kentucky was not acquiring a meaningless name. In hindsight, though, the rights never became a Kentucky roster contribution, while the player sent later as the consideration became an immediate Denver rotation piece.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The gap is real but not enormous. Chapman scored 468 points in 47 Denver games and remained tradeable into February, which gives the Rockets a concrete return. His poor shooting efficiency and short stay prevent the acquisition from becoming a major win. Kentucky, meanwhile, received no games from Piatkowski and no documented downstream asset from his rights. The Colonels' side therefore falls below an even grade despite Piatkowski's prior ABA track record.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Denver Nuggets Win, C+/D. Denver receives a C+ for more than half a season of useful rotation minutes from Chapman plus limited residual trade value. Kentucky receives a D because Piatkowski retired for the entire 1970-71 season, never played for the Colonels and later resurfaced only briefly with another ABA club. Confidence is high on the July trade, the October delivery of Chapman and both players' subsequent records. Chapman was delivered on October 2 as the eventual future consideration; his later inclusion alongside another Denver player in a separate Indiana trade cannot be priced as though he alone produced both incoming players.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Phoenix's official media guide and the Lakers' transaction history record the deal directly: on May 20, 1970, the Suns acquired Mel Counts from Los Angeles for Gail Goodrich. Goodrich had been Phoenix's leading backcourt star after the 1968 expansion draft, averaging 23.8 points as an All-Star in the franchise's first season and 20.0 points with 7.5 assists in 1969-70. The trade sent him back to the franchise that had originally drafted him in 1965.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Return
sections.body: Goodrich became a championship-level lead scorer. The Lakers' official alumni profile credits him with six more Los Angeles seasons after the trade, four consecutive team scoring titles from 1971 through 1975, All-Star selections in 1972, 1973, 1974 and 1975, and All-NBA First Team in 1974. He played 466 regular-season games in that second Lakers stint. His peak came during the 1971-72 championship season, when he averaged 25.9 points in all 82 games and led the club in scoring as Los Angeles won 69 games, set the 33-game winning-streak record and captured the title. He stayed above 19 points per game in every season of the stint and later had No. 25 retired by the Lakers. That is elite sustained value from a one-for-one acquisition.

sections.heading: Phoenix Return
sections.body: Counts gave the Suns two useful seasons rather than disappearing immediately. He played 80 games in 1970-71, averaging 11.0 points and 6.3 rebounds in 20.9 minutes, then appeared in 76 games in 1971-72 at 5.2 points and 3.4 rebounds in a reduced role. Phoenix therefore received 156 regular-season games from Counts. In October 1972, the Suns preserved a little more value by sending Counts to Philadelphia for a 1973 second-round pick and cash; that pick became No. 33 Gary Melchionni. The downstream pick was modest, but it means the Phoenix side included both two seasons of frontcourt depth and a small exit return.

finalVerdict.heading: Hindsight Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Lakers win overwhelmingly. Goodrich supplied six seasons, four post-trade All-Star selections, an All-NBA First Team season and championship-leading scoring. That supports an A+ grade. Phoenix cannot be graded as if Counts produced nothing: 156 games, a double-digit scoring first season and a later second-round return are legitimate assets. A C+ captures useful but ordinary value that was nowhere near Goodrich's Hall of Fame-level Lakers run. Final verdict: Los Angeles Lakers Win.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: The legacy Seattle record says the SuperSonics sent Dorie Murrey to the Baltimore Bullets on July 1, 1970 for a 1971 second-round pick. That sequence conflicts with the stronger transaction record. Seattle's 1969-70 ledger records Murrey leaving the franchise in the May 11 expansion draft, and Portland's media guide identifies Murrey as one of the Trail Blazers' expansion selections. Once Portland selected him, Seattle no longer held the player rights described by this July listing.

sections.heading: Documented Transaction
sections.body: The supported trade occurred after the 1970-71 season had begun. Basketball-Reference's Portland, Baltimore and league transaction ledgers all record Portland sending Murrey to Baltimore on October 22, 1970 for a 1971 second-round draft pick. Harry Glickman's Portland executive log and Jerry Sachs' Baltimore executive log agree on the same structure. Portland's own media guide also records Murrey as acquired from Seattle in the expansion draft and later traded to Baltimore.

sections.heading: Pick Outcome
sections.body: The 1971 second-rounder became the No. 27 pick, Rick Fisher. Basketball-Reference's 1971 draft register shows Fisher selected by Portland at that slot. He did not appear in an NBA regular-season game, so the pick produced no NBA playing value. Murrey played only two games for Portland before the October trade and then continued his NBA career with Baltimore. Those outcomes belong to the October 22 Portland-Baltimore transaction, not to the malformed July Seattle record.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Resolution
finalVerdict.body: Record Superseded. The July 1 Seattle-Baltimore entry is a legacy timing/team attribution error that duplicates the later Portland-Baltimore Murrey trade after Seattle had already lost Murrey in the expansion draft. TradeVerdicts preserves the legacy archive entry privately for provenance but excludes it from canonical hindsight grading and future public/indexable consideration. The October 22 Portland-Baltimore record remains the canonical transaction.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: New York acquired Billy Paultz's ABA rights from the Virginia Squires in August 1970 for a draft choice and cash. The surviving records disagree by one day: Pro Sports Transactions dates the exchange August 10, while Basketball-Reference's Nets, Squires and league transaction logs list August 11. The canonical TradeVerdicts record remains dated August 10 because that is the established source route, but the discrepancy is documented rather than silently resolved. All of the sources agree on the substance of the deal: Paultz went to New York, with a draft choice and cash going to Virginia.

sections.heading: Nets Return
sections.body: Paultz became immediate frontcourt value. As a rookie in 1970-71 he played 83 games and averaged 14.7 points and 11.3 rebounds while shooting 52.4 percent. He stayed with the Nets for five seasons, appearing in 404 games and averaging 15.6 points and 11.2 rebounds for the franchise. He was an ABA All-Star in 1973 and 1975 as a Net, helped New York reach the 1972 ABA Finals and was a major part of the 1974 ABA championship team. The Nets' own historical feature ranks his rebounding among the best in franchise history.

sections.heading: Virginia Return
sections.body: Virginia received cash plus an unspecified draft choice. Basketball-Reference does not identify the round, year or player outcome, and Pro Sports Transactions likewise leaves the pick details unresolved. That missing information prevents an aggressive low grade for the Squires: an unidentified pick or cash amount could have produced value that the current record cannot trace. The grade therefore reflects documented realized value rather than assuming the return was worthless.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The identifiable return is overwhelmingly on New York's side. Paultz supplied five seasons of starting-caliber center play, two All-Star selections with the Nets and a championship contribution. He also remained an asset at the end of the run, when New York traded him to San Antonio in September 1975. Virginia's side is much harder to reconstruct because neither the cash amount nor the draft-choice outcome is identified in the available ledgers. That uncertainty narrows how harshly the Squires can be judged, but it does not erase the scale of the value New York actually received.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win, B+/C. New York receives a B+ for converting a modestly documented package into five productive seasons from Paultz, including championship and All-Star value. Virginia receives a C because the consideration is confirmed but incompletely traceable; the surviving sources do not support pretending the draft pick or cash had zero value. Confidence is medium because the transaction itself and Paultz's career are well documented while the exact date differs by one day across major ledgers and the Squires' pick outcome remains unknown. Paultz gave the Nets 404 games and championship-era rebounding, while neither the precise Virginia cash amount nor the eventual draft-choice outcome has been independently established.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: New York acquired Rick Barry from the Virginia Squires on September 2, 1970 for a 1971 first-round ABA draft choice and cash. Basketball-Reference's Nets, Squires and league transaction logs agree on the date and basic structure. Pro Sports Transactions identifies the pick as the No. 5 selection and reports the cash at roughly $200,000 to $250,000. Its draft-trade ledger links that selection to Cliff Meely. The cash figure is therefore treated as reported rather than exact.

sections.heading: Nets Return
sections.body: Barry delivered star production immediately. He averaged 29.4 points, 6.8 rebounds and 5.0 assists in 59 regular-season games in 1970-71, made the ABA All-Star team and finished fifth in MVP voting. In 1971-72 he played 80 games and averaged 31.5 points, 7.5 rebounds and 4.1 assists while making another All-Star team. Brooklyn's own historical coverage still lists 31.5 points per game as the highest single-season scoring average in franchise history. The Nets reached their first ABA Finals in 1972, with Barry as their primary scorer.

sections.heading: Virginia Return
sections.body: Virginia's return was not empty. The Squires received a premium 1971 first-round pick plus a large cash payment for the era. The pick did not simply disappear from the asset chain: transaction ledgers show Virginia later sent a 1971 first-round choice to Denver in the January 22, 1971 Ken Durrett deal, while the draft-trade ledger traces the Nets-originated No. 5 selection to Cliff Meely. That routing means the original pick had real transaction utility even though Meely did not play for Virginia. The Squires also went 55-29 in 1970-71 after moving Barry, so the franchise remained competitive in the short term.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The decisive advantage is the level of production New York actually received. Barry supplied two elite scoring seasons, two All-Star selections and a trip to the ABA Finals. The acquisition lasted only two seasons before his contractual situation returned him to Golden State, which keeps this from being an automatic top-tier grade. Virginia, meanwhile, converted a player who did not want to remain with the relocated franchise into premium draft capital and substantial cash. The Squires deserve more credit than a simple star-for-pick summary suggests, but the identifiable on-court return still falls short of Barry's New York impact.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win, B+/C. New York earns a B+ because Barry delivered exactly the type of elite production a team hopes to buy with a first-round pick and cash, culminating in the franchise's first ABA Finals appearance. Virginia receives a C because the Squires obtained a valuable first-round asset and meaningful cash, then remained a 55-win team, but the surviving asset chain does not show a direct return comparable to Barry's two seasons in New York. Confidence is high on the transaction structure, Barry's performance and the pick identity; the only material uncertainty is whether the reported cash was $200,000 or $250,000.
