sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: On September 10, 1970, the San Diego Rockets traded Art Williams to Boston for the Celtics' 1971 fifth-round draft pick. Basketball-Reference records the same transaction on the Celtics, Rockets and league transaction pages, while the executive histories for Red Auerbach and Pete Newell independently preserve the deal. The pick became the No. 78 selection in the 1971 draft, which the Rockets used on Jacksonville forward Greg Nelson.

sections.heading: Celtics Return
sections.body: Williams was not acquired to become a star, but Boston received far more than a one-season rental. He played 74 games in 1970-71, then 81 in each of the next two seasons and 67 in 1973-74. Across four Celtics seasons he appeared in 303 regular-season games and Basketball-Reference credits him with 11.1 win shares. His best Boston season by raw production was 1971-72, when he averaged 5.1 points, 4.0 assists and 3.2 rebounds in 16.4 minutes per game. He remained part of the roster when the 1973-74 Celtics went 56-26 and won the NBA championship.

sections.heading: Rockets Return
sections.body: San Diego converted Williams into a late draft asset rather than losing him for nothing. The pick landed at No. 78 overall in the fifth round, and the Rockets selected Greg Nelson out of Jacksonville. Nelson never appeared in an NBA game, so the pick produced no realized NBA playing value. That outcome matters because the comparison is not between Williams and an abstract future pick anymore; the asset can be traced to a specific selection and player. The low round softens the opportunity cost, but the Rockets still moved a useful veteran and received no NBA production from the draft outcome.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The scale of the deal is modest, yet the result is unusually straightforward. Boston surrendered a fifth-round pick that became a non-NBA player and received four seasons from a dependable reserve guard. Williams was never one of the Celtics' primary scorers, but his 303 games, positive win-share total and role through the 1974 title season represent substantial realized value for the price. San Diego's pick outcome never reached the league. That makes the trade a strong example of a contender extracting practical roster value from a low-cost future asset rather than a franchise-altering blockbuster.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win, B+/D+. Boston earns a B+ because a fifth-round pick became four years of useful guard depth, including a place on the 1974 championship roster. The Rockets receive a D+ because the No. 78 pick was correctly preserved and used, but Greg Nelson never played an NBA game and the asset produced no realized league value. Confidence is high: the transaction date, compensation, draft outcome and Williams' Boston production all agree across Basketball-Reference's team, league, executive, player and draft records.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Milwaukee and Seattle completed the deal on September 17, 1970. Basketball-Reference's team transaction logs record Lucius Allen and Bob Boozer going to the Bucks for Zaid Abdul-Aziz and cash. Pro Sports Transactions preserves the same four-part exchange and reports the cash at $100,000. The amount is therefore treated as reported rather than exact, but the player movement itself is well established.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Return
sections.body: The Bucks received both short-term and longer-term value. Boozer played 80 regular-season games in 1970-71, averaging 9.1 points and 5.4 rebounds, then appeared in all 14 playoff games as Milwaukee won the NBA championship. Allen played 61 games that season and stayed with the Bucks deep into 1974-75. His role expanded quickly: 13.5 points and 4.2 assists per game in 1971-72, 15.5 and 5.3 in 1972-73, then 17.6 and 5.2 in 1973-74. Basketball-Reference credits Allen with 8.2 win shares in that 1973-74 season, when Milwaukee returned to the NBA Finals.

sections.heading: Seattle Return
sections.body: Seattle's side deserves more credit than a one-sided title-team story would suggest. Abdul-Aziz immediately gave the SuperSonics frontcourt production, averaging 10.9 points and 7.7 rebounds in 61 games in 1970-71. He improved in 1971-72 to 13.8 points and 11.3 rebounds in 58 games before Seattle later moved him to Houston in 1972. The reported $100,000 also had real value, even though a cash payment cannot be translated cleanly into on-court production. Seattle therefore received a useful starting-caliber big man plus money rather than an empty return.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The separation comes from Milwaukee combining two forms of value. Boozer supplied immediate rotation minutes on a championship team, while Allen developed into one of the Bucks' primary guards and remained productive across several seasons. Seattle received two useful years from Abdul-Aziz and cash, so the transaction did not cripple the franchise or leave it without a basketball return. But Milwaukee's package contributed to the 1971 title immediately and kept producing through another Finals run in 1974. That combination of championship utility and multi-year guard production outweighs Seattle's return without making the deal a historical fleecing.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win, B+/B-. Milwaukee earns a B+ for getting a title-season contributor in Boozer and several productive seasons from Allen at the cost of Abdul-Aziz and reported cash. Seattle receives a B- because Abdul-Aziz was a legitimate rebounder and scorer for two seasons and the cash payment added value, even though the SuperSonics did not receive the same championship or long-term impact. Confidence is high on the player movement and career outcomes; the only meaningful qualifier is that the $100,000 figure is reported rather than independently documented as a precise cash ledger.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Denver and Utah transaction logs agree that the Rockets sent Jeff Congdon to the Stars on September 19, 1970 for a draft choice. Pro Sports Transactions narrows that compensation to a second-round pick, but leaves the year and eventual selection unresolved. That distinction matters: the existence and round of the pick are supported, while assigning a specific drafted player would require a link the surviving ledgers do not establish.

sections.heading: Utah Return
sections.body: Congdon became a useful guard for a strong Stars team. Basketball-Reference credits him with 38 Utah games in 1970-71, averaging 7.7 points, 4.1 assists and 2.3 rebounds in 25.9 minutes. Utah finished 57-27 and went on to win the ABA championship. Congdon did not stay through the playoff run, however. The Stars traded him to the New York Nets on January 7, 1971 for another draft choice and a player to be named later, so Utah's direct return from this September deal lasted only part of the regular season.

sections.heading: Denver Return
sections.body: Denver's return cannot be evaluated responsibly from the current record. Pro Sports Transactions' 1971 ABA draft ledger shows multiple second-round picks changing hands and explicitly marks some chains as unknown. It does not connect the Congdon consideration to a named Denver selection. The Rockets' own second-round slot in the 1971 ABA draft produced Marv Roberts, but the available sources do not establish that the Utah pick acquired here became that selection. Treating Roberts, Roger Brown, Garry Nelson or another player as the outcome would turn an unresolved chain into a fabricated conclusion.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: Utah clearly received some immediate basketball value: Congdon played regular rotation minutes for 38 games on the eventual ABA champions. Denver clearly received a second-round asset. What is missing is the step needed for a fair hindsight comparison—what Denver ultimately did with that specific pick. Congdon's later move to New York also limits how much long-term value can be assigned to Utah. With one side traceable for only part of a season and the other side's draft outcome unidentified, a winner or letter-grade comparison would imply more certainty than the evidence supports.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Insufficient Evidence. The transaction itself is verified, the second-round nature of Denver's compensation is supported, and Congdon's Utah production is measurable. The draft year and ultimate player outcome remain unresolved in the available ledgers, however, so Denver's realized return cannot be priced. This record stays intentionally ungraded until a primary or reliable transaction source closes that asset chain. Confidence is high that the trade occurred as described, but low for any value verdict because the decisive draft outcome is still unknown.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Boston, Baltimore and league transaction logs all record the October 2, 1970 move as a sale of Jim Barnes's player rights from the Celtics to the Bullets. Pro Sports Transactions describes the same exchange as Barnes to Baltimore for cash. The sources agree on the structure, but none of the reliable ledgers used here identifies the cash amount. That missing figure limits how aggressively Boston's side can be graded, even though the transaction itself is well established.

sections.heading: Baltimore Return
sections.body: Barnes did not become a lasting part of Baltimore's rotation. Basketball-Reference credits him with 11 games for the 1970-71 Bullets, averaging 9.1 minutes, 3.4 points, 1.5 rebounds and 0.7 assists. The club waived him on November 13, only six weeks after acquiring his rights. Those 11 appearances were the final NBA games of Barnes's career. Because the Bullets moved on so quickly, the realized basketball return was limited even before considering what they paid.

sections.heading: Boston Return
sections.body: Boston's return was cash, and the amount remains unknown in the transaction sources. That prevents assigning the Celtics a high grade based on a financial figure that cannot be verified. The practical result is still favorable: Boston received consideration for a player who produced only a short reserve stint in Baltimore and did not play another NBA season. For a minor roster transaction, converting an expendable player asset into cash is a positive outcome even if the exact dollar value is lost to the historical record.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The comparison is modest rather than dramatic. Baltimore received 11 games of low-minute frontcourt depth and then waived Barnes. Boston received an unquantified cash payment and gave up no future NBA production beyond that brief stretch. That makes the Celtics' side more efficient in hindsight, but the unknown cash amount keeps the gap from being treated like a major win. The transaction is best understood as a low-impact sale in which Boston extracted some value from a player the Bullets did not retain.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win, C+/D+. Boston earns a C+ because the team turned Barnes's rights into cash without surrendering meaningful future NBA value. Baltimore receives a D+ because Barnes lasted 11 games before being waived. Confidence is medium-high: the sale, Barnes's Baltimore statistics and the waiver date are all independently documented, while the exact cash amount remains unresolved. Baltimore's November 13 waiver after only 11 games supports the limited player return; it does not supply a dollar figure for the payment Boston received.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's league and Portland transaction logs describe the October 7, 1970 move as Portland selling Pat Riley's player rights to Los Angeles. The Lakers team transaction page records the acquisition of his rights without naming a return, and Portland's own media guide also says the expansion club sold Riley to the Lakers. A modern Lakers media guide instead labels the move a waiver claim. Because the surviving sources disagree on the transaction mechanism while multiple ledgers support a sale, this record preserves the cash asset already attached to the canonical trade but treats the exact amount as unresolved.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Return
sections.body: Riley became a real rotation piece rather than a name attached to a transaction ledger. Basketball-Reference credits him with 296 regular-season games for the Lakers, totaling 2,316 points across six listed seasons. His most important team result came in 1971-72. Riley played 67 regular-season games for the 69-win Lakers and appeared in all 15 playoff games, averaging 16.3 minutes and 5.2 points during the championship run. That contribution was not star-level, but it is meaningful realized value for an acquisition made just before the 1970-71 season. His later coaching career is historically famous but is not part of this trade grade.

sections.heading: Portland Return
sections.body: Portland had selected Riley from the San Diego Rockets in the 1970 expansion draft, then moved his rights to Los Angeles before playing its first regular-season game. The reliable sale descriptions do not identify the amount Portland received. That makes the Trail Blazers' side difficult to value precisely and argues against an especially harsh grade. What can be measured is the opportunity cost: Riley gave Los Angeles several years of reserve production and a role on a championship team, while Portland's return is not traceable to a durable basketball asset in the sources used for this audit.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The comparison favors Los Angeles without turning the transaction into a franchise-altering steal. Riley was a reserve, not a centerpiece, and the unknown cash amount means Portland may have received reasonable short-term value for a player it did not intend to keep. Still, Los Angeles obtained nearly 300 regular-season games and postseason minutes from Riley, including a championship run, in exchange for consideration whose exact value has not survived in the transaction record. That is enough realized surplus to support the existing Lakers-win framing.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win, B/C-. Los Angeles earns a B for turning a modest acquisition into a multi-year rotation player who contributed throughout the 1972 title season. Portland receives a C- because the club monetized an expansion-draft asset but gave up the only clearly measurable long-term basketball value in the exchange. Confidence is medium-high rather than high because the transaction sources conflict between sale and waiver language and the cash amount is not documented. Transaction ledgers describe Riley as sold by the expansion Blazers, while the modern Lakers guide uses waiver-claim wording; the established canonical classification remains unchanged pending independent evidence of the precise mechanism.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Indiana, Kentucky and league transaction logs agree that the Pacers acquired Warren Jabali on October 13, 1970 for a 1971 first-round draft choice and cash. Indiana's modern media guide uses the same description. That establishes the core exchange cleanly. The more difficult piece is the draft outcome. Pro Sports Transactions traces the pick as probably the No. 7 selection used on Willie Sojourner and shows that selection reaching Virginia through Kentucky, but its own wording is explicitly probabilistic. TradeVerdicts therefore preserves the existing Sojourner relationship as a probable historical outcome rather than upgrading it to a fully verified pick chain.

sections.heading: Indiana Return
sections.body: Jabali supplied real short-term value. Basketball-Reference credits him with 62 regular-season games for Indiana in 1970-71, averaging 11.0 points, 4.8 rebounds and 3.5 assists in 25.6 minutes. He also appeared in all 11 of the Pacers' playoff games, averaging 7.8 points and 3.6 rebounds. Indiana reached the ABA Western Division finals before losing to Utah, so Jabali's season included meaningful postseason minutes rather than empty production on a noncompetitive roster. His Pacers tenure was still brief: on September 24, 1971, Indiana sent him to the Floridians for a draft choice and cash.

sections.heading: Kentucky Return
sections.body: Kentucky's return was less visible on the court but not empty. The Colonels received cash plus Indiana's 1971 first-rounder. The surviving draft-trade ledger identifies that selection as probably No. 7, Willie Sojourner, and records the pick moving to Virginia through Kentucky. That path fits a broader chain in which Kentucky had acquired Jabali from the Washington Capitols in July 1970 for a 1971 first-round pick and cash. Because the exact contractual linkage between those obligations is not fully documented in the sources used here, this audit does not claim Kentucky directly drafted Sojourner or that the Indiana pick definitively satisfied the earlier Washington obligation. The safe conclusion is that Kentucky recovered a first-round asset and cash when it moved Jabali.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: Indiana received the clearest immediate basketball return: a rotation guard who played 62 games and contributed in the postseason. Kentucky received financial consideration and a premium draft asset, but the pick's final identity is only probable in the available transaction database and did not become a Kentucky player. That makes a winner declaration too aggressive. Indiana's one-season use of Jabali was valuable, yet the Pacers paid a first-rounder plus cash and did not retain him beyond the following September. Kentucky, meanwhile, converted a player it had held for only a few months into another first-round asset and cash.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, B-/B-. Indiana earns a B- for receiving a useful starter-level guard for a playoff team and later retaining some value by trading him again. Kentucky also earns a B- because a first-round pick plus cash was a meaningful return for a player whose stay in Indiana lasted one season. Confidence is medium because the main transaction is well documented but the pick's eventual No. 7 Willie Sojourner identity remains labeled probable rather than certain. The tied B-/B- grades preserve the uncertainty around Kentucky's possible No. 7 Willie Sojourner selection: the pick and cash were received, but neither an unconfirmed identity nor an undisclosed amount is scored as settled.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Nets, Colonels and ABA transaction logs all agree on the core transaction: New York sent Walt Simon to Kentucky on October 14, 1970 for a draft choice. The surviving ledgers do not identify the year, round or eventual player tied to that pick. Pro Sports Transactions' 1971 ABA draft ledger documents several traded selections but does not connect this Simon transaction to a specific New York choice. That missing link is important because it prevents treating the Nets' return as worthless simply because its outcome is not currently traceable.

sections.heading: Kentucky Return
sections.body: Simon gave the Colonels immediate and durable rotation value. In 1970-71 he played all 84 regular-season games, averaged 7.7 points, 3.8 rebounds and 1.9 assists, and stayed in the rotation as Kentucky advanced through two playoff rounds before losing the ABA Finals to Utah. His value did not end with that first season. Basketball-Reference's franchise totals credit Simon with 314 games across four Kentucky seasons, 2,780 points, 1,152 rebounds and 746 assists. That works out to 8.9 points, 3.7 rebounds and 2.4 assists per game over the full stint. He was not a franchise centerpiece, but four years of useful wing minutes is a strong realized return for an otherwise unspecified future pick.

sections.heading: New York Return
sections.body: The Nets received a future draft choice, but the current source trail does not identify its year, round or drafted player. The 1971 ABA draft ledger is especially useful because it explicitly traces a number of traded picks involving New York and Kentucky, including other deals from the same period, yet it does not establish a Simon-to-Nets pick chain. That makes this a source gap rather than proof that the selection failed. New York therefore keeps a neutral grade instead of being penalized as though the asset vanished without value.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The comparison is asymmetric. Kentucky's side can be measured: Simon played 314 games for the Colonels and remained part of competitive teams that reached the 1971 ABA Finals and posted a 68-16 regular-season record in 1971-72. New York's side cannot be measured beyond knowing that a draft choice changed hands. Because the pick outcome is unresolved, the proper conclusion is not that Kentucky won by a landslide. It is that the Colonels banked several seasons of documented production while the Nets' return remains unverified. That supports a clear but restrained Kentucky advantage.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Colonels Win, B/C. Kentucky receives a B for turning a future pick into four seasons of Walt Simon, including 314 games of dependable rotation production. New York receives a C because the compensation itself is verified but its eventual player outcome is not. Confidence is medium: the transaction and Simon's Kentucky career are well documented, while the exact draft asset remains unresolved. Simon's 314 Kentucky games are documented, but New York's untraced draft choice is a genuine asset whose eventual value cannot responsibly be treated as zero simply because its selection is unidentified.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Cincinnati, Philadelphia and league transaction logs all record the same October 16, 1970 deal: the Royals received Darrall Imhoff and a future draft choice while the 76ers received Connie Dierking and Fred Foster. Pro Sports Transactions preserves the same four-part structure and, importantly, also leaves the draft choice unidentified. That means the player side of the trade is traceable, but the exact year, round and ultimate outcome of Cincinnati's pick are not. The verdict therefore has to leave room for value that the surviving source chain cannot price.

sections.heading: Cincinnati Return
sections.body: Imhoff was acquired to help a team that wanted more rebounding and an outlet for Bob Cousy's faster offense. Cincinnati's 1971 media guide described the trade in those terms after the club had been outrebounded through much of the preseason. On the floor, Imhoff played 34 games in 1970-71, averaging 8.1 points and 6.9 rebounds in 24.3 minutes. His Cincinnati run was interrupted and did not develop into a long stay: he appeared in only nine more Royals games in 1971-72 before finishing that season with Portland. The future draft choice could alter the long-term accounting, but no reliable ledger used here identifies what it became.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Return
sections.body: Philadelphia received two veterans with different value curves. Dierking played 53 games in 1970-71, averaging 5.8 points and 4.3 rebounds in 13.5 minutes, then retired. Foster provided the more durable return. He played 66 games for the 76ers in 1970-71 and another 74 in 1971-72, when his role expanded to 23.0 minutes per game and 11.9 points. That second season is the clearest realized advantage in the deal: Philadelphia got a useful rotation scorer after Foster had been Cincinnati's third-leading scorer the year before the trade.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The documented player value favors Philadelphia. Dierking and Foster combined for 119 games in the remainder of 1970-71, and Foster stayed productive for another full season. Imhoff supplied useful rebounding in Cincinnati but played only 43 games for the Royals across two seasons. The unresolved draft choice prevents a harsher grade for Cincinnati because an unidentified pick cannot responsibly be assigned zero value. Still, on what can actually be traced, Philadelphia received more usable NBA minutes and the best post-trade season from any player in the exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win, B-/C+. Philadelphia receives a B- for getting two rotation players, highlighted by Foster's 11.9-point 1971-72 season. Cincinnati receives a C+ because Imhoff contributed when available and the future draft choice may have carried additional value that cannot currently be identified. Confidence is medium: the transaction and player outcomes are well documented, but the draft asset remains unresolved. Philadelphia's combined 119 first-season appearances from Dierking and Foster plus Foster's later season support its narrow lead; the Royals' unidentified future pick prevents a more categorical comparison.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Chicago and Portland's transaction logs agree that the Bulls sent Shaler Halimon to the Trail Blazers on October 20, 1970 for a 1971 second-round draft choice. Basketball-Reference and Pro Sports Transactions both trace that pick to No. 20 overall, where Chicago selected Weber State center Willie Sojourner. This is a resolved draft chain: the pick year, round, slot and player outcome are all known.

sections.heading: Portland Return
sections.body: Halimon became a regular immediately for the first-year Trail Blazers. He appeared in 79 Portland games, averaging 20.6 minutes, 8.9 points, 5.3 rebounds and 2.7 assists. For an expansion roster, that is meaningful one-season utility rather than a cameo. Portland did not retain the value beyond that year, however. The club placed Halimon on waivers in July 1971 and Atlanta claimed him, so the transaction produced one full season but no later trade return for the Blazers.

sections.heading: Chicago Return
sections.body: Chicago's pick became Sojourner, a productive Weber State rebounder selected 20th overall in the 1971 NBA Draft. The pick was real and reasonably valuable, but it never turned into Bulls production. Basketball-Reference lists no NBA games for Sojourner; he instead began his professional career in the ABA with the Virginia Squires and ultimately played 309 ABA games. His talent therefore was not the issue. The hindsight problem for Chicago is that the draft asset did not create NBA minutes, points or a later NBA transaction return for the Bulls.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: Portland received exactly one useful season. Halimon was neither a star nor a long-term building block, and the Blazers waived him before year two. Chicago received an exact second-round outcome with legitimate professional ability, but none of that ability was realized for the Bulls because Sojourner played in the ABA. Under a team-realized-value standard, 79 NBA games and a regular rotation role beat a draft selection that never suited up for the acquiring franchise. The margin is clear, though the short duration of Halimon's stay keeps Portland's grade modest.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Trail Blazers Win, B-/D+. Portland receives a B- for getting 79 games of useful rotation play from Halimon during its expansion season. Chicago receives a D+ because the No. 20 pick was successfully traced and used on a capable player, but Sojourner never produced NBA value for the Bulls. Confidence is high because the trade, exact draft outcome and post-trade playing records are all well documented. Portland acquired 79 expansion-season appearances from Halimon, while Chicago used the identifiable No. 20 choice on Sojourner without receiving Bulls NBA games; the selection itself was a real draft asset, not a nonexistent return.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Denver, Utah and league transaction logs agree on the core exchange: Utah sent Tom Workman to Denver on January 5, 1971 for a draft choice. Workman's move is documented, but neither a numbered pick nor its eventual player outcome has been established for the return Denver sent. That means the existence of draft compensation is verified while the exact asset chain remains unresolved.

sections.heading: Denver Return
sections.body: Workman supplied short-term frontcourt depth. Basketball-Reference credits him with 39 Denver games in 1970-71, averaging 6.1 points, 3.4 rebounds and 0.9 assists in 12.5 minutes while shooting 44.7 percent from the field. He had already played 17 games for Utah that season, so Denver was acquiring a known veteran rather than an untested prospect. His stay did not extend into the next season: the ABA transaction log records Denver waiving him on September 25, 1971.

sections.heading: Utah Return
sections.body: Utah's return is the unresolved side of the trade. The Stars definitely received a draft choice, but none of the transaction records used here links that choice to a specific selection. Utah's January 1971 transaction history contains several other draft-choice moves around the same period, which makes inference especially risky. Assigning one of those later selections to the Workman deal without a direct source would create a false asset chain.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: Denver received measurable but limited value: 39 regular-season games from a reserve forward-center, followed by a preseason waiver before 1971-72. Utah received an asset whose eventual value cannot currently be identified. That is not enough to declare the draft choice worthless, and it is not enough to claim Utah won simply because Denver's return was brief. A defensible comparison requires the missing pick outcome.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Insufficient Evidence. The January 5 transaction and Workman's Denver production are verified, but the draft choice's round, year and eventual player remain unresolved. The record therefore stays ungraded rather than converting an unknown draft asset into a guessed value. Confidence is high on the exchange itself and Workman's short Denver stint, but low on any winner determination until the compensation chain can be closed. Utah's unidentified draft choice cannot be assigned zero value simply because Workman's 39 Denver appearances are measurable.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's New York and Texas transaction logs match on the January 6, 1971 deal: the Nets sent Ed Johnson and Levern Tart to the Texas Chaparrals for Manny Leaks. The canonical TradeVerdicts franchise mapping uses Brooklyn Nets and San Antonio Spurs lineage identifiers, but the teams at the time were the New York Nets and Texas Chaparrals of the ABA. All three players are directly traceable in the season and player ledgers, so the exchange itself is high-confidence.

sections.heading: Nets Return
sections.body: Leaks gave New York a strong half-season at center. In 40 games after the trade he averaged 17.1 points, 9.7 rebounds and 1.2 assists while shooting 49.5 percent from the field. That was not empty volume: he logged 1,427 minutes, or 35.7 per game, and gave the Nets a dependable interior scorer and rebounder through the rest of the regular season. He also remained with New York into the next season for nine more games before moving on, so the Nets received more than a brief rental.

sections.heading: Texas Return
sections.body: Texas split its return between a scoring guard and a reserve center. Tart played 33 games for the Chaparrals after the deal and averaged 18.9 points, 5.8 rebounds and 4.4 assists in 24.9 minutes per game. Johnson appeared in eight games, averaging 6.5 points and 6.0 rebounds in 19.9 minutes. Neither player became a durable multi-year piece for Texas, but together they gave the Chaparrals useful immediate production across two positions. Tart in particular remained a high-usage scorer, while Johnson provided frontcourt depth behind the team's primary bigs.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The case for Texas is volume rather than star power. Tart and Johnson combined for 41 post-trade appearances in 1970-71, and Tart's scoring rate was higher than Leaks' while Johnson added a second playable body. The case for New York is concentration and quality: Leaks was the strongest rebounder in the deal, shot more efficiently than Tart and stayed in the Nets' rotation into the following season. Those competing advantages make this much closer than a simple two-for-one count suggests. The Chaparrals gained slightly more immediate aggregate production, but the Nets did not give away the clearly superior player.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Spurs Edge, C+/C. Texas earns the C+ for turning Leaks into two contributors, led by Tart's 18.9 points per game over 33 appearances. New York earns the C because Leaks was productive and efficient enough to keep the exchange close, averaging 17.1 points and 9.7 rebounds in 40 games after arriving. The grade gap stays narrow because Texas' second piece lasted only eight games and neither outgoing player became a lasting franchise fixture. Confidence is high on the transaction and player production. Tart's 33-game Texas scoring return was substantial, but Johnson contributed only eight games, limiting the claimed depth advantage over New York's 40-game Leaks stint.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: ProSportsTransactions records a January 22, 1971 exchange in which New York received Virginia's 1971 ABA second-round pick, No. 17, later used on Bob Kissane, while the Squires were owed a player to be named later identified as Bill Bunting. Its draft-trade ledger ties that No. 17 pick directly to the Nets-Squires exchange and names Bunting as the later consideration. Basketball-Reference presents the same basic player-for-pick relationship differently: its New York, Virginia and league transaction logs date Bunting's move to March 15 and describe it as Bunting for a draft choice. Because those reliable sources disagree on the completion date and mechanics, the canonical January 22 identity is preserved while the conflict is stated rather than silently resolved.

sections.heading: Nets Return
sections.body: The pick became Bob Kissane at No. 17 in the 1971 ABA draft. Kissane was also selected by Phoenix at No. 84 in the 1971 NBA draft, but Basketball-Reference shows no ABA or NBA season for him. That makes New York's realized professional return from the draft asset effectively zero. The pick itself had real optionality at the time, so the grade should not treat it as valueless on transaction day, but hindsight grading has to account for the fact that the selection never turned into on-court production.

sections.heading: Virginia Return
sections.body: Bunting supplied modest but real rotation value. Basketball-Reference credits him with 33 Virginia games in 1970-71 and 16 more in 1971-72, for 49 games and 551 minutes across two seasons. He scored 162 points and grabbed 106 rebounds for the Squires in that span. His first Virginia season was the useful portion: 33 games, 436 minutes, 142 points, 91 rebounds and a .521 field-goal percentage. That is not star-level value, but it is considerably more realized professional production than the draft outcome New York received.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The source-date conflict does not change the realized-value comparison. Whether the Bunting completion is treated as January 24 under the ProSportsTransactions chain or March 15 under Basketball-Reference's transaction ledger, Virginia ultimately turned the exchanged draft choice into a player who appeared in 49 Squires games. New York used the No. 17 ABA selection on Kissane and received no ABA or NBA regular-season production from him. The transaction was low-stakes, so the grading gap should remain restrained, but the evidence no longer supports the old Nets edge.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Squires Win, C+/D+. Virginia receives a C+ for converting a second-round draft asset into two seasons of reserve minutes from Bunting. New York receives a D+ because the acquired pick was legitimate second-round capital but its eventual selection produced no ABA or NBA season. Confidence is medium-high rather than high because the sources disagree on whether the transaction should be dated January 22 with a later PTBNL completion or March 15 as a direct Bunting-for-pick trade. The asset relationship and realized outcomes are well supported. The disputed January-to-March date sequence does not change that Bunting played 49 Squires games, while New York's No. 17 choice of Bob Kissane produced no ABA or NBA season.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Denver, Virginia and ABA transaction logs all agree on the January 22, 1971 exchange: the Rockets sent cash to the Squires for Larry Brown. The executive transaction records for Donald Ringsby and Al Bianchi independently preserve the same player-for-cash structure. The amount of cash is not identified in those reliable records, so the financial side has to remain unpriced rather than converted into a guessed dollar value.

sections.heading: Denver Return
sections.body: Brown gave Denver immediate point-guard stability. In 34 games after the trade he averaged 8.4 points, 6.1 assists and 1.8 rebounds in 23.9 minutes per game. More importantly for realized value, this was not a short rental. Brown returned in 1971-72 and played 76 games, averaging 9.1 points, 7.2 assists and 2.2 rebounds in 26.5 minutes. Across the two Denver seasons he logged 110 games and 2,825 minutes, giving the Rockets a dependable organizer through a transitional stretch of the franchise.

sections.heading: Virginia Return
sections.body: Virginia's return was cash, which makes this a different type of hindsight comparison from a player-for-player deal. Cash can matter to a franchise, especially in the ABA, but the surviving transaction records used here do not provide the amount or identify a later basketball asset purchased with it. That prevents the archive from assigning the Squires a precise realized-value total. The safe conclusion is narrower: Denver received two seasons of measurable rotation value, while Virginia's documented return is financially real but unquantified.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: Brown's 110 Denver games make the basketball side unusually clear for a cash transaction. He was not a star at this stage, but he handled a large share of the club's playmaking and stayed through the following season. With no sourced cash figure, the analysis should not pretend Virginia received nothing; it should simply separate known court value from unknown financial consideration. On the evidence that can be measured, Denver came away ahead by a meaningful margin.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win, B-/D+. Denver receives a B- for acquiring 110 games of useful point-guard play for an undisclosed cash payment. Virginia receives a D+ only as a realized-basketball grade: the club did receive cash, but the amount and any traceable on-court conversion are unavailable in the sources reviewed. Confidence is medium-high because the transaction and Brown's production are well documented, while the cash amount is not. Brown's 110 Denver games establish measurable player value, but the missing purchase price leaves Virginia's financial return unpriced rather than nonexistent.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference records Denver sending Ken Durrett to Virginia on January 22, 1971 for a 1971 first-round draft choice and a player to be named later or cash. ProSportsTransactions resolves the first-round pick as No. 5 in the 1971 ABA draft, used on Cliff Meely, and identifies Denver's outgoing asset as the ABA rights to Durrett. The additional Virginia-to-Denver consideration remains described only as a player to be named later or cash, with no reliable amount or player identity in the sources reviewed.

sections.heading: Denver Return
sections.body: Denver's identified draft asset became Meely, but the ABA rights never turned into Denver court value. Basketball-Reference shows Meely entering the NBA with Houston in 1971-72 after Houston selected him seventh overall in the NBA draft. He went on to play five NBA seasons and 318 games, including 284 for Houston, but none of that production accrued to the Denver Rockets. The unidentified PTBNL-or-cash component could still have carried value, which is exactly why the Denver side cannot be treated as a zero.

sections.heading: Virginia Return
sections.body: Virginia acquired Durrett's ABA rights, but Durrett also chose the NBA path. Cincinnati selected him fourth overall in the 1971 NBA draft, and his professional career began with the Royals rather than the Squires. His four-year NBA career therefore cannot be credited to Virginia as realized return from this ABA rights trade. The Squires gave up the No. 5 ABA pick and the unresolved extra consideration for rights that never became a Virginia roster player.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The identifiable basketball assets cancel in an unusual way: both clubs traded or acquired high ABA draft rights to players who ultimately played in the NBA instead. Denver's Meely rights produced no Denver ABA games, and Virginia's Durrett rights produced no Virginia ABA games. The unresolved player-to-be-named-later or cash is therefore not a side detail; it is the only remaining consideration that could distinguish the realized return. Without identifying it, a winner would be guesswork.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Insufficient Evidence. The Durrett-for-pick structure and the No. 5 Cliff Meely outcome are well documented, as are both players' NBA careers. Neither player produced ABA games for the acquiring team in this transaction, however, and the additional Denver consideration remains unresolved. That combination makes the previous Nuggets win too certain. The record should stay ungraded until the PTBNL-or-cash component can be identified or reliably valued. Confidence is medium-high on the known asset chain and low on any winner determination. The untraced additional consideration, not Durrett's or Meely's subsequent NBA careers with other teams, prevents a fair winner determination between these ABA clubs.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Denver and Floridians transaction logs agree on the January 24, 1971 exchange: The Floridians sent cash to Denver for Lonnie Wright. The ABA transaction ledger preserves the same player-for-cash structure. The amount of cash is not identified in the reliable records used here, so Denver's side has to remain financially real but unpriced rather than treated as zero.

sections.heading: Floridians Return
sections.body: Wright immediately became a useful rotation guard in Florida. In 31 games after the trade he played 629 minutes and averaged 7.9 points, 2.1 rebounds and 1.8 assists while shooting 43.9 percent from the field. That was a notable efficiency improvement from his 41-game Denver segment earlier in the same season. Wright then returned in 1971-72 and played 77 games, averaging 8.0 points, 2.1 rebounds and 1.7 assists in 21.3 minutes. Across the two Floridians seasons he logged 108 games, 2,267 minutes and 862 points, giving the club more than a half-season rental.

sections.heading: Denver Return
sections.body: Denver's return was cash, and the missing amount limits how aggressively the deal can be graded. A cash sale can be useful in its own right, particularly in the ABA, but no reliable source reviewed here identifies the payment or a later basketball asset purchased with it. That means the Rockets' side cannot be converted into a precise realized-value score. What can be said is that Denver moved a player who still had two productive ABA seasons left and received no traceable player or pick in return.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The Floridians received 108 games of rotation value from Wright, while Denver's documented return remains an undisclosed cash payment. Wright was not a star, but the acquisition supplied two seasons of playable guard minutes and more than 2,200 minutes of court time. Because the cash figure is unknown, the gap should remain moderate rather than overwhelming. Still, the measurable basketball return belongs to Florida, and there is enough duration to support a clear win rather than a merely symbolic edge.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Floridians Win, C+/D+. The Floridians receive a C+ for buying two seasons and 108 games of useful guard play. Denver receives a D+ as a realized-basketball grade because the club did receive cash, but the amount and any downstream court-value conversion are unavailable. Confidence is medium-high on the transaction and Wright's post-trade production, with the undisclosed cash amount preventing a stronger grade gap. Florida received 108 games from Wright over two seasons, but Denver's cash proceeds cannot be scored as zero merely because the sale price is unavailable.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Cleveland transaction log confirms the February 1, 1971 deal: the Cavaliers sent McCoy McLemore to Milwaukee for Gary Freeman and a 1971 second-round draft pick later used on Willie Long. Cleveland's identified incoming package had three components: Freeman, the second-round selection ultimately used on Long, and separately reported cash. The reliable sources reviewed here do not identify the cash amount, so it is preserved as real but unpriced consideration rather than used to manufacture a precise advantage.

sections.heading: Cleveland Return
sections.body: Freeman's Cleveland stay was extremely brief. He appeared in 11 games and logged 47 total minutes after the trade, with the 1970-71 season becoming the last NBA season of his career. The draft pick became Willie Long at No. 35 overall, but Long did not join Cleveland. Basketball-Reference records Long's professional debut in the ABA with The Floridians, where he played 75 games as a rookie and averaged 11.7 points and 6.8 rebounds. That ABA production cannot be credited to Cleveland as realized return from the pick. Cleveland also received cash, but the amount remains unknown.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Return
sections.body: McLemore gave the Bucks more immediate court value than either identified Cleveland asset delivered for the Cavaliers. He played 28 regular-season games for Milwaukee after the trade, averaging 4.7 points and 3.8 rebounds in 14.8 minutes, then remained available during the club's 1971 championship run. He returned for 10 more Milwaukee games in 1971-72 before being moved to Houston. This was not a major acquisition in the context of a team led by Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and Oscar Robertson, but McLemore was a real veteran depth piece for a championship roster rather than a purely theoretical asset.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: Cleveland acquired three forms of consideration, but only one produced Cavaliers minutes and that contribution was tiny. Freeman logged 47 minutes, Long chose the ABA, and the cash cannot be valued from the surviving reliable records. Milwaukee, meanwhile, received 38 regular-season games from McLemore across two seasons and had him available during the 1971 title run. The unknown cash keeps the gap from becoming large, but the known basketball production points toward Milwaukee rather than Cleveland.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win, C+/D+. Milwaukee receives a C+ for acquiring a usable veteran reserve who contributed during a championship season and remained into the next year. Cleveland receives a D+ on realized basketball value because Freeman barely played and the Willie Long pick never became a Cavaliers player, though the undisclosed cash prevents treating the return as empty. Confidence is medium-high on the transaction, pick outcome and player production, with the cash amount the principal unresolved variable. McLemore's Milwaukee championship-season reserve role is traceable, whereas Willie Long never became a Cleveland NBA contributor despite the identified draft choice.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Denver, Indiana and ABA transaction logs agree on the four-player core of the deal: Denver sent Wayne Chapman and Don Sidle to the Pacers for John Barnhill and Art Becker. Those ledgers date the trade February 1, 1971. Pro Sports Transactions preserves a broader February 2 entry in which Indiana also sent Denver a 1972 high draft pick and cash. Because the reliable sources disagree on the exact date and whether the extra consideration belongs in the same transaction record, the canonical February 2 identity is retained while the discrepancy is stated explicitly. The cash is unpriced and the eventual player attached to the high pick remains unresolved.

sections.heading: Denver Return
sections.body: Becker became the most valuable realized piece. After the trade he played 29 games for Denver at 27.7 minutes per game, averaging 15.2 points and 7.2 rebounds. He then stayed for the full 1971-72 season, appearing in all 84 games, averaging 12.3 points and 5.6 rebounds, and earning an ABA All-Star selection. Barnhill also gave Denver useful immediate production: 24 games at 28.5 minutes per game, with averages of 11.4 points and 3.2 assists before Denver waived him the following September. That is substantial identifiable court value even before assigning anything to the cash or unresolved high draft pick.

sections.heading: Indiana Return
sections.body: Indiana received much less from the two players it acquired. Chapman appeared in five Pacers games after the trade in 1970-71 and seven more in 1971-72, averaging 2.6 points in 10.9 minutes during the latter season. Sidle played eight Indiana games after the trade, then returned for 27 games in 1971-72 at 14.6 minutes and 6.5 points per game. Those contributions were real, especially Sidle's reserve work the next season, but neither player approached Becker's combination of post-trade scoring, durability and All-Star recognition in Denver.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The realized-value gap favors Denver without requiring the unresolved draft asset to do any work in the grade. Becker alone produced 113 regular-season games for the Rockets across the remainder of 1970-71 and the full 1971-72 season, and Barnhill added another 24 games of starting-caliber minutes. Indiana's return amounted to a brief Chapman stay and a modest Sidle reserve role. Denver also held the additional upside of cash and a high 1972 draft pick according to Pro Sports Transactions, but the grade does not invent a dollar figure or a drafted-player outcome where the surviving records do not establish one.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win, B+/C-. Denver receives a B+ because Becker became an All-Star and productive full-season starter-level piece after the trade, Barnhill supplied useful immediate minutes, and the club also received unpriced cash plus an unresolved high pick in the broader transaction record. Indiana receives a C- because Sidle provided some reserve value and Chapman appeared briefly, but the known basketball return was far smaller. Confidence is medium-high on the player exchange and production, with the February 1 versus February 2 dating conflict and the unresolved high-pick outcome preventing a higher confidence label. Becker's 113 Denver appearances and Barnhill's immediate contribution support the verdict without crediting the disputed high pick or cash as a resolved extra gain.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Detroit, Phoenix and league transaction logs agree on the April 2, 1971 structure: the Pistons sent Otto Moore to the Suns for Phoenix's 1972 first-round draft pick, later used on Bob Nash at No. 9 overall. That direct evidence resolves the older legacy wording that described the return only as future considerations subject to contingencies. The source-backed record therefore identifies the asset as the 1972 first-round pick while preserving the original transaction date and player relationship.

sections.heading: Detroit Return
sections.body: Detroit used the acquired first-rounder on Bob Nash with the ninth pick of the 1972 draft. The pick had real value on transaction day, but Nash's Pistons production was limited. He appeared in 36 games as a rookie, totaling 169 minutes and 43 points, then played 35 games and 281 minutes in 1973-74. Across those two Detroit seasons, Nash logged 71 games and 450 minutes before leaving the franchise. His later NBA production with Kansas City cannot be credited to Detroit's realized return, so the Pistons received a high draft slot but only modest on-court conversion from it.

sections.heading: Phoenix Return
sections.body: Moore gave Phoenix far more immediate court value than Nash gave Detroit. In 1971-72 he played 81 games and 1,624 minutes, averaging 7.6 points and 6.7 rebounds in 20.0 minutes per game. Phoenix then converted Moore again on April 7, 1972, trading him to Houston for a 1972 first-round pick that became Corky Calhoun at No. 4 overall. Calhoun played all 82 games as a Phoenix rookie and 77 more the next season, giving the Suns 159 games and more than 4,200 minutes across his first two seasons alone. That downstream conversion makes Moore's value to Phoenix extend well beyond his one season on the floor.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The original trade gave both teams a credible asset, but Phoenix extracted much more realized value. Detroit received a top-ten pick and selected Nash, yet his two Pistons seasons totaled only 450 minutes. Phoenix received a durable rotation center for 81 games and then recycled him into the fourth pick of the same 1972 draft, producing a second multi-season rotation player in Calhoun. This is exactly the type of downstream asset conversion that matters in a retrospective grade: it is traceable, directly sourced and generated by the acquired player rather than by an unrelated later transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Suns Win, B+/C-. Phoenix receives a B+ for getting a full season of useful center play from Moore and then turning him into the No. 4 pick that produced two substantial Phoenix seasons from Calhoun. Detroit receives a C- because the first-round pick itself was valuable, but Nash produced only a small amount of Pistons court time after being selected ninth overall. Confidence is high because the trade, first-round pick identity, Nash outcome, Moore production and Calhoun downstream chain are all documented in Basketball-Reference transaction and player records. Calhoun's 159 Phoenix games came through a later Moore-to-Houston conversion, separate from Moore's original 81-game stint; Detroit's Nash selection gave the Pistons only 450 minutes.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's New York, Kentucky and ABA transaction logs agree on the May 8, 1971 structure: Kentucky sent John Roche to the Nets for cash. The Colonels had selected Roche in the 1971 ABA draft, while Phoenix selected him 14th overall in the NBA draft. New York was buying the ABA rights needed to sign him, and the Nets completed that step on May 12. The cash amount is not identified in the reliable ledgers reviewed here, so Kentucky's financial return remains real but unpriced rather than being treated as zero.

sections.heading: New York Return
sections.body: Roche immediately became a major rotation guard. As a rookie in 1971-72 he played all 82 games, averaged 31.6 minutes, 12.9 points and 3.2 assists, and earned ABA All-Rookie honors. His postseason was even more valuable: across 18 playoff games he averaged 23.6 points in 42.4 minutes as New York beat Kentucky and Virginia before losing to Indiana in the ABA Finals. Roche returned for 77 games in 1972-73 at 14.4 points and 4.5 assists per game, then played 50 more Nets games in 1973-74 before the franchise converted him into another trade return.

sections.heading: Kentucky Return
sections.body: Kentucky received cash, but the amount is not preserved in the transaction sources. That uncertainty limits how low the Colonels should be graded from a financial perspective, yet the later asset history still makes the sale look costly in basketball terms. Roche became productive immediately in New York, and Kentucky eventually reacquired him on January 24, 1974 by sending Mike Gale and Wendell Ladner to the Nets. In other words, the Colonels first sold Roche's rights for cash and later surrendered two active players to bring him back. Roche then finished the 1973-74 season in Kentucky before the Colonels sold him to Utah for cash in January 1975.

sections.heading: Downstream Value
sections.body: The 1974 return extends the value of New York's original rights purchase. Gale played 32 regular-season games for the Nets after the trade and made the ABA All-Defensive First Team; Ladner played 30. Both appeared in all 14 New York playoff games as the Nets won the 1974 ABA championship. That championship contribution cannot be credited to Roche's on-court production, but it can be credited as traceable downstream value created when New York moved the player acquired in the 1971 cash purchase. The chain therefore produced a productive rookie, an ABA Finals run, multiple regular seasons and later championship rotation pieces.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win, A/D+. New York receives an A because a cash purchase of draft rights produced an All-Rookie guard, major 1972 playoff scoring, more than two seasons of regular-season value and a later trade return that contributed to the 1974 ABA championship. Kentucky receives a D+ because its documented return was only an undisclosed cash payment and the club later paid two players to reacquire Roche. Confidence is medium-high rather than high because the cash amount is unknown, while the transaction, Roche's production and the later Gale/Ladner return are all well documented. Gale and Ladner's 1974 title-run contribution is traceable downstream consideration from New York's later Roche trade, not minutes Roche himself played from the original cash purchase.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's New York, Floridians and ABA transaction logs agree that The Floridians sent Tom Washington to the Nets on May 14, 1971 for a draft choice. Pro Sports Transactions identifies that asset as New York's 1972 third-round ABA pick and also lists cash going to Florida. The 1972 ABA draft-trade ledger places the transferred selection in the Floridians' third-round slot, but the drafted player is not identified. The source-backed record therefore treats the pick outcome as unresolved rather than assigning a player by inference, and it preserves the additional cash as real but unpriced consideration.

sections.heading: New York Return
sections.body: Washington became an immediate rotation starter-level frontcourt piece. In 1971-72 he played 80 games, averaged 31.4 minutes, 11.0 points and 9.4 rebounds, and shot 57.1 percent from the field. He also appeared in all 18 playoff games as New York beat Kentucky and Virginia before losing to Indiana in the ABA Finals. Washington returned for 76 games in 1972-73, giving the Nets 156 regular-season games across two seasons after the trade. That is substantial realized value from a third-round selection and cash, especially because the acquired player filled a major role during a Finals run rather than merely providing end-of-roster depth.

sections.heading: Florida Return
sections.body: The Floridians received the Nets' 1972 third-round ABA pick and, according to Pro Sports Transactions, cash. The draft ledger confirms that the transferred pick reached Florida's third-round position, but no player is identified for the selection. That missing player outcome matters because the franchise folded after the 1971-72 season, making later asset tracing unusually difficult. The cash component also lacks a preserved amount. Florida therefore received legitimate transaction consideration, but the surviving record does not establish a realized on-court return comparable to Washington's two New York seasons.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The measurable gap favors New York. Washington gave the Nets 156 regular-season games, a strong first season, and a full 18-game postseason run to the 1972 ABA Finals. Florida's known return was a third-round pick with no identified player outcome plus unpriced cash. That does not make the Floridians' side literally worthless, and the grade should not pretend the unknown cash had no value. It does mean the source-backed basketball outcome is one-sided enough to move beyond the older 'slight edge' language. The Nets acquired a productive two-year frontcourt piece for a low-round selection and cash while preserving their higher draft assets.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win, B+/C-. New York receives a B+ because Washington became a high-minute, efficient frontcourt contributor and played a meaningful role during the 1972 ABA Finals run. The Floridians receive a C- because the third-round pick is verified but its player outcome remains unidentified, while the cash amount is unknown. Confidence is medium-high: the transaction, Washington's production and the transferred pick round are well supported, but the cash amount and final player attached to the 1972 third-round selection are unresolved. Washington's 156 New York games and 1972 ABA Finals run are measurable; Florida's pick cannot be declared a failed player selection when the drafted player's identity is unconfirmed.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Chicago, Cincinnati and league transaction logs agree on the May 14, 1971 structure: the Bulls received Charlie Paulk and sent Matt Guokas plus a 1972 second-round draft pick. Cincinnati used that pick on Sam Sibert at No. 19 overall in the 1972 NBA draft. The transaction therefore gave the Royals one established rotation guard and one future pick for a frontcourt player who had just completed a 68-game Cincinnati season. The source-backed record keeps the historical Cincinnati identity while using the current Sacramento franchise key already present in the canonical data.

sections.heading: Cincinnati Return
sections.body: Guokas became the main realized return. In 1971-72 he played 61 games for Cincinnati, averaging 32.4 minutes, 7.3 points and 5.3 assists. After the franchise moved to Kansas City-Omaha, he played 79 games in 1972-73, averaging 36.0 minutes, 9.1 points and 5.1 assists while shooting 57.0 percent from the field. He then appeared in nine more games for the franchise in 1973-74 before being traded away. Sibert, the No. 19 pick, added only five NBA games and 26 total minutes, so the pick itself produced little. Even so, Guokas supplied roughly the kind of stable multi-season guard value Cincinnati was seeking when it moved Paulk.

sections.heading: Chicago Return
sections.body: Paulk did not provide much direct Bulls value. He appeared in seven games in 1971-72, totaling 60 minutes, before Chicago traded him to New York on December 10, 1971 for a 1973 second-round pick. The Bulls then used that pick on October 18, 1972 to acquire Dennis Awtrey from Philadelphia. Awtrey gave Chicago 79 games and 1,650 minutes in 1972-73, then 68 more games the following season. That downstream chain is important because it means Chicago did not simply lose Paulk after seven games; the acquired player was converted into a durable reserve center whose two Bulls seasons roughly matched Guokas's game total, though not his minutes or offensive role.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The trade is closer than a direct Paulk-versus-Guokas comparison suggests. Cincinnati received the better immediate player and kept Guokas through the franchise move to Kansas City-Omaha, while Sibert barely contributed. Chicago's direct return was brief, but Paulk became the draft pick used to acquire Awtrey, who supplied two useful seasons and 147 Bulls games. That traceable conversion rescues Chicago's side from a poor grade, yet Guokas still carried the larger workload and remained a multi-year starting-caliber guard. The combination of Guokas plus even minimal Sibert value leaves the Royals/Kings franchise with the modest realized advantage.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Royals Win, B+/B. Cincinnati receives a B+ because Guokas produced nearly three seasons of reliable guard play for the franchise, including heavy minutes and efficient shooting, while Sibert added a small amount of value from the acquired pick. Chicago receives a B because Paulk himself lasted only seven games but was converted into the second-round pick used to acquire Awtrey, who became a durable Bulls reserve. Confidence is high because the player exchange, Sibert pick, Paulk-to-New York conversion and Awtrey downstream trade are all documented in Basketball-Reference transaction and player records. Guokas supplied Cincinnati's durable direct guard minutes, while Awtrey's Bulls value required two later transactions through the Paulk draft-asset chain, not an immediate player return from the Royals.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Atlanta, Buffalo and league transaction logs agree on the July 26, 1971 four-player exchange: the Braves sent Herm Gilliam and Don May to the Hawks for Walt Hazzard and Jerry Chambers. Pro Sports Transactions preserves the same trade and lists Hazzard as 'Walt Hazzard / Mahdi Abdul-Rahman.' Hazzard had legally changed his name, but Basketball-Reference notes that he continued using Walt Hazzard professionally. The source-backed pass therefore repairs the legacy asset label from the alias-only 'Mahdi Abdul-Rahman' to a Walt Hazzard identity with the alternate name preserved rather than treating the two names as different players.

sections.heading: Atlanta Return
sections.body: Gilliam became the most durable piece in the trade. He played all 82 games in 1971-72 at 10.2 points, 4.1 rebounds and 4.6 assists per game, then improved to 14.0 points and 6.3 assists across 76 games in 1972-73. He remained a substantial Hawks contributor for two more seasons, averaging 14.1 points in 62 games in 1973-74 and 12.0 in 60 games in 1974-75. Across those four seasons, Gilliam gave Atlanta 280 regular-season games and a long stretch of starting-caliber guard production. May added useful depth in 1971-72, appearing in 75 games and scoring 594 points before his role diminished later in his career.

sections.heading: Buffalo Return
sections.body: Hazzard gave Buffalo the best single season on the Braves side. In 1971-72 he played 72 games, averaged 33.2 minutes, 15.8 points and 5.6 assists, and remained the club's primary veteran ball-handler. His Buffalo value fell sharply the next year: he appeared in nine games at 5.9 points and 1.9 assists before the Braves traded him to Golden State. Chambers contributed much less, appearing in 26 Buffalo games in 1971-72 and totaling 178 points in 369 minutes before moving to the ABA the following season. Buffalo therefore received real immediate production, particularly from Hazzard, but little multi-year continuity from either incoming player.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The first season makes the exchange look competitive because Hazzard was better individually than either Atlanta acquisition in 1971-72. The longer view changes the balance. Gilliam alone became a four-season Hawks guard with 280 games and multiple double-digit scoring seasons, while May added another 75 games in the first year. Buffalo's two-player return produced 98 games in 1971-72, but Chambers did not remain with the franchise and Hazzard's Braves role collapsed early the next season. Atlanta therefore received both greater longevity and more cumulative useful production without needing a downstream draft outcome to create the advantage.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win, A-/B. Atlanta receives an A- because Gilliam became a durable multi-season guard and May added a substantial first-year role, giving the Hawks both depth and long-term value. Buffalo receives a B because Hazzard delivered a genuinely strong first season and Chambers provided limited additional minutes, but neither became a durable Braves piece. Confidence is high because the four-player exchange, Hazzard identity, and each player's post-trade production are well documented. Hazzard's strong first Buffalo season does not erase Gilliam's 280 Atlanta games over four seasons; the long-term disparity, rather than a fabricated additional player asset, drives the Hawks' modest edge.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Houston, Milwaukee and league transaction logs establish the July 30, 1971 direction clearly: the Rockets sold the player rights to Toby Kimball to the Bucks. Milwaukee acquired Kimball; Houston received cash. The Milwaukee side obtained Kimball's rights outright, whereas the Houston side has only a cash consideration whose amount the cited ledgers do not identify. The cash amount is not preserved in the transaction ledgers reviewed here, which prevents a precise financial comparison, but it does not justify leaving the underlying player and cash directions wrong.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Return
sections.body: Kimball became a real depth piece on an elite Bucks team. In 1971-72 he played 74 games and 971 minutes, averaging 3.5 points and 4.2 rebounds in 13.1 minutes. He also appeared in seven playoff games as Milwaukee beat Golden State before losing to the Lakers in the Western Conference Finals. Kimball was not a major scorer, but the Bucks purchased usable frontcourt depth for a 63-win team. Milwaukee then preserved additional value on October 9, 1972 by trading him to Kansas City-Omaha for a 1973 fourth-round draft pick.

sections.heading: Houston Return
sections.body: Houston's return was cash, and the surviving sources do not identify the amount. That uncertainty deserves respect because a rights sale can be rational even when the later player produces NBA minutes elsewhere. Still, the source-backed archive has no traceable player, draft pick or later transaction asset attached to Houston's cash receipt. The Rockets therefore have a documented financial return but no measurable basketball return to compare with Kimball's Milwaukee season and subsequent draft-pick conversion.

sections.heading: Downstream Value
sections.body: Milwaukee's October 1972 Kimball trade produced Kansas City-Omaha's 1973 fourth-round pick, which the Bucks used on Clyde Turner at No. 59 overall. Turner never appeared in an NBA regular-season game, so the downstream pick did not create additional court production. That limits the strength of the Bucks win: most of the realized value is Kimball's 74-game season and playoff depth rather than a productive second asset. The pick still shows that Milwaukee recovered something after using Kimball for a season, while Houston's original return remains an unpriced cash payment with no identified basketball conversion.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win, B+/C. Milwaukee receives a B+ for buying a useful 74-game reserve on a 63-win contender, getting seven playoff appearances, and later converting him into another draft asset even though that pick did not produce an NBA player. Houston receives a C because the club did receive cash, but the amount is unknown and no basketball asset can be traced from it. Confidence is medium-high: the transaction direction, Kimball production and later fourth-round pick are well established, while the original cash price is unresolved. Kimball's 74 Bucks appearances are direct value; the subsequently acquired pick used on Clyde Turner produced no NBA games and cannot be counted as a second realized contributor.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Cleveland, Phoenix and league transaction logs agree on the August 13, 1971 core exchange: Phoenix sent Greg Howard to Cleveland for a 1972 third-round pick, later used on Scott English at No. 33, plus a future third-round pick. Phoenix's historical media guides likewise describe two third-round selections, although they date the transaction August 31 rather than August 13. Pro Sports Transactions uses August 13 and adds cash from Cleveland to Phoenix. The source-backed record keeps the canonical August 13 date, preserves the cash as source-specific unpriced consideration, and leaves the second third-round pick unresolved because the surviving ledgers do not identify its year or player outcome.

sections.heading: Cleveland Return
sections.body: Howard supplied one season of reserve frontcourt minutes. In 1971-72 he appeared in 48 games for Cleveland, totaling 426 minutes while averaging 2.9 points and 2.3 rebounds in 8.9 minutes per game. That was his final NBA season, so the Cavaliers received no multi-year continuation or later trade asset from the acquisition. The production was real but small: Howard ranked near the bottom of Cleveland's rotation in minutes, and his 139 points were a limited return for multiple draft considerations. Still, he did give the second-year franchise an NBA-ready player immediately rather than forcing it to wait on future selections.

sections.heading: Phoenix Return
sections.body: Phoenix used the identified 1972 third-rounder on Scott English with the 33rd overall pick. English played 29 games for the Suns in 1972-73, totaling 196 minutes, 93 points and 44 rebounds while averaging 3.2 points in 6.8 minutes. He left the NBA after that season before later playing in the ABA, so Phoenix did not turn the named pick into a long-term NBA contributor. The Suns also held the future third-round pick documented by Basketball-Reference and their own historical transaction records. Because that pick's year and player outcome remain unresolved, it receives credit as a real asset acquired but not an invented realized result. Pro Sports Transactions' additional cash entry is handled the same way: real in that source, but unpriced and absent from the other transaction ledgers.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The direct player results are close and modest. Howard gave Cleveland 48 games and 426 minutes; English gave Phoenix 29 games and 196 minutes. Neither became a core player, and neither side can claim a major on-court conversion from the directly identified player asset. The difference is the additional third-round pick Phoenix received. Even without a verified player outcome, that was another usable transaction asset in the original package, while Cleveland's return ended with Howard's single season. The disputed cash is not needed to create the edge and therefore is not counted as a decisive value source. The result is a small Phoenix advantage rather than a one-sided trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Suns Win, B-/C+. Phoenix receives a B- because English supplied limited rookie minutes and the club also acquired a second third-round asset whose ultimate outcome is unresolved. Cleveland receives a C+ because Howard played 48 games immediately but produced only 426 minutes and no downstream value. Confidence is medium because the core player-for-two-picks structure is well documented, while the historical sources disagree on the exact August date, Pro Sports Transactions alone adds cash, and the second third-round pick cannot yet be tied to a player. Phoenix's Scott English recorded only 29 games, compared with Howard's 48 for Cleveland, so the Suns' higher grade reflects that extra unresolved pick rather than a demonstrated superior player return.
