sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Cleveland, Los Angeles and league transaction logs agree on the August 31, 1972 structure: the Cavaliers sent a 1974 second-round draft pick to the Lakers for Jim Cleamons. Those same records identify the selection as No. 21 Billy Knight. Pro Sports Transactions carries older uncertainty language around whether the undisclosed pick was that exact selection, but its 1974 draft ledger also notes an Associated Press attribution calling Knight the Los Angeles pick from Cleveland. With multiple independent transaction records now aligning, this review upgrades the asset from a probable linkage to a verified second-round pick that became Knight.

sections.heading: Cleamons' Cleveland Growth
sections.body: Cleamons was a little-used Lakers rookie before the trade, but Cleveland turned the acquisition into five seasons of increasing responsibility. He played 80 games in 1972-73 and 81 in 1973-74, then became a full-time lead guard. In 1974-75 he averaged 11.9 points and 5.1 assists in 74 games. The next season he started all 82 games, averaged 12.2 points, 5.2 assists and 1.5 steals, and made the NBA All-Defensive Second Team. By the end of 1976-77, Cleamons had played 377 regular-season games for Cleveland and scored 3,532 points.

sections.heading: Playoff and Team Value
sections.body: The 1975-76 season is the strongest evidence that Cleveland received more than accumulated regular-season minutes. The Cavaliers went 49-33, won their division and reached the Eastern Conference Finals. Cleamons played all 13 postseason games, averaged 38.7 minutes, 13.8 points, 5.5 rebounds and 4.7 assists, and remained one of the club's primary perimeter players. That postseason role, combined with his All-Defensive selection, turns the acquisition into a core-team result rather than a simple depth win.

sections.heading: The Lakers' Pick Outcome
sections.body: Los Angeles used the acquired pick on Billy Knight at No. 21 in the 1974 NBA Draft. Knight became an excellent professional player, but not for the Lakers. Indiana had also drafted him in the ABA and signed him in July 1974. He played his first three professional seasons with the Pacers, including an ABA All-Star season and a 1976-77 NBA All-Star season, before Indiana traded him to Buffalo in 1977. The Lakers therefore made a strong talent evaluation with the Cleveland pick but received no realized Lakers games, points or later trade return from Knight in the source trail reviewed here.

sections.heading: Downstream Cleveland Return
sections.body: Cleveland's value chain continued after Cleamons left. In October 1977 he signed with the New York Knicks as a veteran free agent, and the Cavaliers received Walt Frazier as compensation. Frazier then played 51 games for Cleveland in 1977-78 at 16.2 points, 4.1 rebounds and 4.1 assists, followed by 12 more games the next season. That compensation is not credited as if it were guaranteed by the 1972 trade, but it is a real downstream return generated by Cleveland retaining Cleamons through his veteran-free-agent departure.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win, A/D+. Cleveland receives an A because one second-round pick produced 377 Cleamons regular-season games, an All-Defensive selection, a major role in the 1976 conference-finals run and later Walt Frazier compensation. Los Angeles receives a D+ because the pick became the highly productive Billy Knight, validating the scouting value of the selection, but Knight never played for the Lakers and the reviewed record shows no realized Lakers return from his rights. Confidence is high on the transaction, pick identity and Cleamons outcome. Cleamons' 377 Cavalier appearances, All-Defensive role and later Walt Frazier free-agent compensation are Cleveland outcomes; the productive Billy Knight selection gave Los Angeles no Lakers NBA games despite proving valuable elsewhere.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's New York Nets, San Diego Conquistadors and league transaction logs agree on the September 14, 1972 exchange: New York sent cash to San Diego for Art Becker. Pro Sports Transactions records the same two-sided movement and identifies Becker as having reached San Diego in the August expansion draft from Denver. The amount of cash is not reported in the reviewed sources, so the Conquistadors' return has to remain unpriced. That uncertainty matters because this was not a player-for-player swap; the Nets can be graded on Becker's realized production and later resale value, while San Diego's financial return cannot be translated into invented roster value.

sections.heading: Why Becker Had Value
sections.body: Becker was not a random camp body. He had played 84 games for Denver in 1971-72, averaging 12.3 points and 5.6 rebounds in 26.1 minutes, and Basketball-Reference credits him with an ABA All-Star selection that season. San Diego selected him in the August 10 expansion draft, then moved him to New York just over a month later. The Nets were therefore buying a veteran forward with recent starting-level production, even though his role would shrink sharply once he joined a roster built around Rick Barry, Bill Melchionni and the newly signed Brian Taylor.

sections.heading: New York's Direct Return
sections.body: Becker's direct Nets production was minimal. He appeared in eight games in 1972-73, logged only 46 minutes and averaged 2.9 points and 0.8 rebounds. He never became a meaningful part of Lou Carnesecca's rotation, and New York did not keep him long enough for the acquisition to influence the club's season in a substantial way. If the transaction ended there, paying cash for eight low-minute appearances would be a weak return regardless of Becker's prior reputation. The important part of the hindsight case is what New York did next.

sections.heading: The Dallas Flip
sections.body: On December 4, 1972, less than three months after acquiring Becker, the Nets traded him to the Dallas Chaparrals for a draft choice and cash. Basketball-Reference's Nets, Dallas and ABA transaction ledgers all preserve that structure, and Pro Sports Transactions independently lists the same return. The reviewed sources do not identify the draft selection or the cash amount, so the archive does not assign downstream player value to the pick. Even with that limitation, New York converted a player who had produced only eight games for the club into two new forms of consideration. That makes the original cash purchase more defensible than Becker's stat line alone suggests.

sections.heading: San Diego's Side
sections.body: San Diego received cash and gave up a player it had acquired through the expansion draft only weeks earlier. Because the dollar amount is unknown, there is no reliable way to say whether the Conquistadors made a strong financial sale or merely cleared a roster spot. Becker never played a regular-season game for San Diego, so the franchise did not surrender realized on-court production from its own 1972-73 roster. That keeps the San Diego grade respectable rather than punitive. The problem for the Conquistadors in a hindsight comparison is that New York later recovered a draft choice and additional cash while also getting Becker's brief eight-game stint.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win, B-/C. New York receives a B- because the initial cash purchase produced very little direct basketball value but was successfully recycled into a later draft choice and cash return. San Diego receives a C because it converted an expansion-draft player into cash before the season, but the amount is unreported and no downstream basketball asset can be traced from that payment. Confidence is medium-high on the transaction structure, Becker's eight-game Nets tenure and the December resale, with the grade gap held in check by the unresolved cash values and unidentified Dallas draft choice. Becker's eight Nets games and 46 minutes did not justify the acquisition on direct output, but New York later converted him into a separately documented pick-and-cash package; neither side's unreported cash amount can be assigned a specific value.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Houston, Milwaukee and league transaction logs agree that the Rockets sold Dick Cunningham's player rights to the Bucks on September 18, 1972. Milwaukee's team log describes the move as an acquisition of Cunningham's rights, while the league ledger explicitly says Houston sold those rights. The cash amount is not reported. That leaves Houston with a verified but unpriced financial return and Milwaukee with a player whose post-trade production can be measured directly. Because the dollar figure is unknown, the archive does not invent a cash value or assume how Houston used the proceeds.

sections.heading: A Return to Milwaukee
sections.body: Cunningham was already familiar to the Bucks. He had played his first three NBA seasons in Milwaukee from 1968-69 through 1970-71, including 76 games for the 1970-71 championship team, before spending 1971-72 with Houston. The September 1972 transaction brought him back as frontcourt depth behind Kareem Abdul-Jabbar rather than as a new long-term starter. That context matters for the grade: Milwaukee was paying for a known reserve center with a clearly defined role, not expecting star-level production from a cash purchase.

sections.heading: First-Season Return
sections.body: In 1972-73 Cunningham appeared in 72 regular-season games for Milwaukee. He logged 692 minutes, scored 157 points and collected 208 rebounds, which works out to about 9.6 minutes, 2.2 points and 2.9 rebounds per game. The Bucks went 60-22 and finished first in the Midwest Division. Cunningham's role was small, but 72 appearances on a 60-win team is real roster utility, especially for a reserve center acquired only for cash. He also appeared in the postseason, giving Milwaukee another body behind its star frontcourt during the playoff run.

sections.heading: Later Milwaukee Value
sections.body: The return did not end after one year, though Cunningham's role diminished quickly. He played eight games in 1973-74 and two more in 1974-75. Across the three post-trade seasons, that gives Milwaukee 82 regular-season appearances after reacquiring him. His NBA career ended with the Bucks, so there was no later trade return to extend the asset chain. This was therefore a modest depth purchase rather than an acquisition that created future picks or players, but the realized playing value is still easy to document.

sections.heading: Houston's Side
sections.body: Houston received cash and gave up a player who had appeared in 63 games for the Rockets in 1971-72. The sale removed a reserve center from the roster before the 1972-73 season, but no reviewed source provides the cash amount or ties the proceeds to a later basketball transaction. That uncertainty prevents a harsh Houston grade. Cash has real organizational value even when its downstream use cannot be reconstructed. In a hindsight archive, however, an unpriced payment cannot be credited with specific games, picks or player production that the historical record does not identify.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win, B-/C. Milwaukee receives a B- because the cash purchase returned 82 regular-season appearances across three seasons, led by 72 games of usable reserve-center depth on a 60-win 1972-73 team. Houston receives a C because it converted Cunningham's rights into cash, but the amount is unreported and no downstream basketball asset is documented. The gap stays modest because Cunningham was never a major post-trade contributor and Milwaukee did not later flip him for additional value. Confidence is high on the transaction and Cunningham's production, but only medium on Houston's financial return because the sale price is unknown. Cunningham's 82 post-return Bucks appearances, mostly a 72-game reserve season for a 60-win team, establish limited direct basketball value; Houston's undisclosed sale proceeds remain a real but unmeasured counterweight.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Houston, Seattle and league transaction logs agree on the September 18, 1972 structure: Seattle sold Zaid Abdul-Aziz's player rights to Houston. The Rockets' team log says they acquired his rights, while Seattle's log explicitly records the sale. No reviewed source identifies the cash amount. That leaves Houston with measurable player production and Seattle with a verified but unpriced financial return. The archive therefore credits Seattle for receiving cash without inventing a dollar figure or assigning later basketball value that cannot be traced to the payment.

sections.heading: Immediate Houston Return
sections.body: Abdul-Aziz joined the Rockets after two Seattle seasons and immediately entered the center rotation. In 1972-73 he played 48 games, logged 900 minutes and averaged 8.7 points and 6.3 rebounds in 18.8 minutes. Houston finished 33-49, so the first season did not produce team success, but the acquisition already supplied real frontcourt minutes from an asset purchased only for cash. That first-year production was a foundation rather than the peak of the return.

sections.heading: Peak Value in 1973-74
sections.body: The trade paid off most clearly one year later. Abdul-Aziz played 79 games in 1973-74 and averaged 10.9 points, 11.7 rebounds and 2.1 assists in 31.1 minutes. He totaled 923 rebounds and 865 points, giving Houston full-season starting-caliber production at center. The Rockets still finished 32-50, but the player value itself is straightforward: Seattle had sold the rights to a big man who then delivered a near double-double across almost the entire season.

sections.heading: Playoff-Year Contribution
sections.body: Abdul-Aziz remained useful in 1974-75. He appeared in 65 games, averaged 9.7 points and 7.5 rebounds, and logged 1,450 minutes as part of a center rotation with Kevin Kunnert and Steve Hawes. Houston went 41-41, beat the Knicks in the first round and reached the Eastern Conference semifinals. Abdul-Aziz was no longer the primary center every night, but he still provided substantial rebounding and interior minutes during the franchise's first playoff season after the move to Houston.

sections.heading: End of the Houston Run
sections.body: The direct value chain ended when Houston waived Abdul-Aziz on August 1, 1975. He later signed with Seattle as a free agent in January 1976, but that return to the SuperSonics did not come from the 1972 cash sale and is not treated as a downstream trade benefit. Across the three seasons created by this transaction, Abdul-Aziz played 192 Houston regular-season games, scored 1,911 points and collected 1,715 rebounds. That is a substantial realized return even without a later trade asset.

sections.heading: Seattle's Side
sections.body: Seattle received cash for a player who had just averaged 13.8 points and 11.3 rebounds in 58 games during 1971-72. The sale may have reflected roster or financial considerations, but the amount is unknown and no reviewed transaction record links those proceeds to a later player or draft pick. That uncertainty keeps Seattle from receiving a failing grade. Cash has real value, yet in a source-backed hindsight archive it cannot be treated as equivalent to 192 documented games and three seasons of frontcourt production without evidence.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win, B+/C. Houston receives a B+ because the cash purchase produced 192 games over three seasons, including a 79-game near double-double season and useful center minutes on the 1975 playoff team. Seattle receives a C because it converted Abdul-Aziz's rights into cash, but the amount is unreported and no downstream basketball asset is identified. Confidence is high on the transaction and Abdul-Aziz's Houston production, but only medium on Seattle's financial return because the sale price is unknown. Abdul-Aziz gave Houston 192 games after the rights purchase, highlighted by a 79-game, 11.7-rebound season; his later free-agent return to Seattle was not transaction compensation for the original cash sale.

sections.heading: Source Conflict
sections.body: Pro Sports Transactions records a September 18, 1972 deal in which Houston sent cash to Seattle for Don White (a). The entry appears beside the same-day Zaid Abdul-Aziz rights sale, but Basketball-Reference's Houston, Seattle and NBA transaction ledgers list Abdul-Aziz and do not list a separate Don White transaction. That disagreement is important. The archive preserves the canonical record because a dedicated transaction database records it, but it does not elevate the deal to the same confidence level as the independently corroborated Abdul-Aziz exchange. The player identity must remain unresolved unless a stronger primary or contemporary source is located.

sections.heading: No Verified Houston Appearance
sections.body: Houston's 1972-73 roster contains no Don White. The club used fourteen players during the season, including guards Calvin Murphy, Mike Newlin and Jimmy Walker, forwards Jack Marin, Rudy Tomjanovich and Cliff Meely, and centers Zaid Abdul-Aziz, Otto Moore and George Johnson. No player by White's name appears in the Rockets' season totals, and Basketball-Reference's franchise player index does not provide a matching Houston career line. That means the acquired rights, if the Pro Sports Transactions entry is accurate, never produced a documented NBA appearance for Houston.

sections.heading: Identity Problem
sections.body: The '(a)' suffix in the transaction database is a disambiguation marker rather than a usable basketball identity. Searches for Don White produce multiple unrelated people, including college players from different eras, but no reliable professional profile that can be tied to this September 1972 Seattle-Houston record. The local archive previously created a generic Don White player object from the legacy transaction line. The archived name Don White therefore stays an identity hold: the record does not establish a verified professional career for the person in this transaction.

sections.heading: Seattle's Return
sections.body: Seattle received cash according to the Pro Sports Transactions record. The payment amount is unknown, and the source trail does not identify a later player, draft pick or transaction purchased with those proceeds. That prevents the archive from claiming substantial Seattle value. Still, an unpriced cash return is at least a realized asset, while Houston has no verified games or later transaction return connected to White. The comparison is therefore narrow and should not be read as evidence that Seattle received a meaningful financial windfall.

sections.heading: Why the Grade Stays Low
sections.body: This is not a normal player-for-cash evaluation. The central fact is uncertainty: one specialist database preserves the exchange, major Basketball-Reference ledgers omit it, and the acquired player's professional identity cannot be independently established. A source-backed archive should surface that conflict instead of converting an ambiguous rights line into fictional NBA production. Houston can receive only limited credit for making a speculative rights purchase, while Seattle's grade reflects the existence of cash rather than any known amount or downstream basketball result.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Sonics Edge, D/C. Houston receives a D because the recorded cash purchase produced zero verified NBA games and the Don White identity remains unresolved. Seattle receives a C because the transaction database records a cash return, although the amount and downstream use are unknown. Confidence is low-medium: the Pro Sports Transactions entry supports the existence and direction of the exchange, but Basketball-Reference's team and league logs do not independently confirm it. The unverified identity of the acquired Don White prevents attributing any actual Rockets playing record to this September 18 entry, and Seattle's unpriced cash receipt does not turn a one-ledger claim into a fully confirmed trade.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Houston, New York and league transaction logs agree on the September 19, 1972 structure: Houston sold John Gianelli's player rights to the Knicks. Pro Sports Transactions records New York receiving Gianelli and Houston receiving cash, while Ray Patterson's executive history preserves the same sale from the Rockets side. Houston had selected Gianelli 20th overall in the 1972 draft but moved his rights before he played an NBA game. The cash amount is not reported, so the source-backed archive treats Houston's consideration as verified but unpriced rather than inventing a financial value.

sections.heading: Immediate Championship Value
sections.body: Gianelli joined a veteran Knicks contender and began as a reserve center. In 1972-73 he played 52 regular-season games, averaged 3.5 points and 2.9 rebounds in 9.9 minutes, and supplied 516 minutes behind Willis Reed and Jerry Lucas. New York went 57-25 and won the NBA championship. Gianelli appeared in seven playoff games and scored 25 points in 55 minutes during that run. His rookie contribution was modest, but the acquisition already produced usable depth on a championship roster in the first season.

sections.heading: Growth Into a Starter
sections.body: The value expanded quickly after the title season. Gianelli played 70 games in 1973-74 and started 41, averaging 7.3 points and 4.9 rebounds. In 1974-75 he started 79 of 80 games and averaged 10.3 points, 8.6 rebounds and 2.0 assists in 35.0 minutes. He returned for all 82 games in 1975-76, starting 51 and averaging 9.3 points and 6.7 rebounds. Those are not star-level numbers, but they turn a cash purchase of draft rights into several years of dependable starting-center production.

sections.heading: Total Knicks Production
sections.body: Before the Knicks traded him in December 1976, Gianelli had accumulated 303 regular-season appearances for New York. He scored 2,481 points and collected 1,912 rebounds in those games. He also played 22 postseason games for the Knicks across 1973, 1974 and 1975. That multi-year body of work matters more than the championship label alone. New York did not simply buy a fringe rookie who happened to be on a title roster; it acquired a center who grew into a regular starter and remained under team control for more than four seasons.

sections.heading: Downstream Trade Value
sections.body: Gianelli still carried transaction value when his Knicks tenure ended. On December 9, 1976, New York traded Gianelli and cash to Buffalo for Bob McAdoo and Tom McMillen. Because the Knicks also sent money, the archive does not pretend Gianelli alone purchased an All-Star scorer and another center. Still, he was a named outgoing player in a major trade that brought McAdoo to New York, so the original 1972 rights purchase retained a measurable downstream asset role after 303 regular-season games of direct production.

sections.heading: Houston's Side
sections.body: Houston received cash after using the 20th pick on Gianelli. No reviewed source identifies the sale price or connects the proceeds to a later player, pick or transaction. Cash has legitimate organizational value, especially for a franchise deciding not to carry a rookie, but a hindsight archive cannot assign specific basketball production to an unpriced payment. Houston therefore gets credit for monetizing the rights rather than losing Gianelli for nothing, yet that return cannot approach five Knicks seasons, a championship bench role, multiple starting years and later trade utility.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win, A/C. New York receives an A because a cash purchase produced 303 regular-season games, 22 playoff appearances, a role on the 1973 championship team, two seasons with heavy starting responsibility and a later place in the Bob McAdoo trade. Houston receives a C because it converted Gianelli's rights into cash, but the amount and downstream use are unknown. Confidence is high on the transaction and Gianelli's Knicks production, but only medium on Houston's financial value because the payment is unpriced. Gianelli's 303 Knicks regular-season games and 22 playoff appearances are verifiable direct value, while his later move for Bob McAdoo and Tom McMillen also required Knicks cash and cannot be credited solely to the original rights purchase.

sections.heading: The Recorded Agreement
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Denver, Carolina and ABA transaction ledgers all record a September 20, 1972 exchange in which the Rockets sent cash to the Cougars for Wayne Hightower. Pro Sports Transactions preserves the same direction, and Alex Hannum's executive record also lists Denver trading cash for Hightower. Taken alone, those ledgers make the move look like a completed cash purchase. The source-backed review found an important second layer, however: later biographical reporting says the arrangement was voided before Hightower joined Denver for the regular season. The archive therefore keeps the dated transaction record but no longer grades it as a completed trade.

sections.heading: Why the Deal Was Voided
sections.body: Hightower was coming off an abbreviated 1971-72 season with Carolina, where he played only 13 games after a blood-clot issue had disrupted the previous year. Biographical sourcing reports that Carolina agreed to sell him to Denver, but Hightower arrived late to the Rockets' preseason training camp. Hannum then voided the transaction. The same account says Hightower's contract was returned to Carolina and Denver refused to send the agreed cash. That detail changes the evaluation completely: neither the player asset nor the financial consideration became a realized post-transaction return.

sections.heading: Denver Roster Evidence
sections.body: Denver's 1972-73 roster supports the voided-deal account. A historical Rockets roster archive lists Hightower only under the preseason section rather than among regular-season players. Basketball-Reference's team page likewise shows no Hightower appearance for the 47-37 Rockets. Denver's regular-season frontcourt included Julius Keye, Dave Robisch, Byron Beck, Marv Roberts and others, but Hightower logged zero games, minutes, points or rebounds. The absence is not a small sample produced by injury after the trade; it is consistent with the contract never becoming part of Denver's regular-season roster.

sections.heading: Carolina's Position
sections.body: Carolina's transaction page records the sale, but the later voiding means the Cougars did not ultimately receive the agreed cash according to the biographical account. Hightower also did not return to the 1972-73 Carolina roster. The historical record therefore describes a failed transfer rather than a conventional one-sided deal. Carolina had attempted to monetize the contract and Denver had attempted to acquire veteran frontcourt depth, yet the agreement unraveled before either side realized the intended asset. No reviewed source identifies a later compensation mechanism that replaced the voided arrangement.

sections.heading: How the Archive Treats It
sections.body: The canonical record remains useful because multiple transaction ledgers preserve September 20 as an agreement date. Removing it entirely would hide a real historical event in the transaction record. Treating it as an ordinary completed trade would be worse, because that would falsely imply Denver paid cash and acquired Hightower for basketball purposes. The correct source-backed treatment is to preserve the record, flag the deal as voided before completion, mark Hightower as a zero-game Denver preseason presence, and mark the cash as agreed but unpaid. No downstream value should be assigned to either asset.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: No Completed Trade. Denver receives no grade because Hightower's contract was returned and he played zero regular-season games for the Rockets. Carolina receives no grade because the agreed cash was not ultimately sent according to the voided-deal reporting. Confidence is medium-high: the September 20 agreement is strongly corroborated by transaction ledgers, and the zero-game roster outcome is clear, while the voiding mechanics rely on later biographical reporting rather than a surviving team transaction note. The recorded September agreement was voided before regular-season play and the promised cash never changed hands according to the later biographical evidence. Hightower has no Denver NBA or ABA games, so neither side should receive a grade for a completed transaction that did not occur.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Philadelphia, Portland and league transaction pages agree that the 76ers traded Dave Wohl to the Trail Blazers for Dale Schlueter on October 2, 1972. The swap was a direct player-for-player move with no pick or cash component in the reviewed ledgers. Both players were established role players: Schlueter was a veteran center who had averaged 11.7 points and 10.6 rebounds for Portland the previous season, while Wohl was a second-year point guard coming off 79 games for Philadelphia as a rookie. That makes the trade straightforward to evaluate through the production each team actually retained.

sections.heading: Schlueter in Philadelphia
sections.body: Schlueter became one of the more durable players on a historically bad 76ers team. He appeared in 78 games during 1972-73, started ten, and averaged 5.4 points, 4.5 rebounds and 1.3 assists in 14.6 minutes. He totaled 1,136 minutes and 354 rebounds. Philadelphia went 9-73, so his individual contribution did not translate into team success, but the trade still produced a full season of reliable center minutes. For a one-for-one exchange, that volume alone already exceeded what Portland received from Wohl.

sections.heading: Wohl's Short Portland Stay
sections.body: Wohl played only 22 games for the Trail Blazers. He averaged 5.4 points and 3.1 assists in 17.9 minutes and logged 393 total minutes. Portland then waived him on December 6, 1972, barely two months after the trade. Buffalo claimed him immediately. Wohl went on to play 56 games for the Braves during the same season and remained an NBA guard for several more years, but Portland received no compensation for that later career because its relationship with him ended on waivers. The Blazers' realized return is therefore limited to those 22 appearances.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Converts Schlueter Again
sections.body: Philadelphia extracted a second return from Schlueter instead of simply letting him leave. On February 1, 1973, the 76ers traded him to Atlanta for Don May. May played 26 games for Philadelphia over the remainder of 1972-73 and averaged 11.9 points and 5.5 rebounds in 23.2 minutes. He returned for 56 games in 1973-74, giving the 76ers 82 regular-season appearances across two seasons after the Schlueter conversion. That downstream value extends the original Wohl trade well beyond Schlueter's own Philadelphia games.

sections.heading: How Much the Team Context Counts
sections.body: Neither side turned this trade into a competitive breakthrough. Philadelphia's 1972-73 season remains the worst full-season record in franchise history, and Portland also missed the playoffs. The grade therefore should not treat Schlueter's 78 games or May's later production as star-level value. Still, hindsight grading is about realized asset value, not team reputation alone. Philadelphia received a playable center, then used that center to acquire another rotation player. Portland received a guard it waived after 22 games.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win, B+/D+. Philadelphia receives a B+ because Schlueter supplied 78 games and the club then converted him into Don May, who added 82 more Philadelphia appearances across two seasons. Portland receives a D+ because Wohl gave the Blazers only 22 games before being waived for no return. The gap is clear even though neither incoming player became a star and Philadelphia's team results were poor. Confidence is high on the transaction, game totals and Schlueter-to-May downstream chain. Philadelphia received 78 Schlueter appearances and then converted him into Don May for 82 more games over two seasons; Portland released Wohl after only 22 games. Wohl's later 56 Buffalo appearances belong to a separate waiver claim, not a Blazers return.

sections.heading: Date Correction and Trade Structure
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Atlanta, New York and league transaction ledgers all place the Eddie Mast trade on October 9, 1972. Richie Guerin's Atlanta executive record and Red Holzman's New York record use the same date. The legacy archive carried October 7 from an older legacy source, so this review corrects the canonical trade date to October 9 while retaining the old date as a superseded source value. The basketball structure is straightforward: Atlanta received Mast, and New York received Atlanta's 1973 second-round pick, later used at No. 28 on Pat McFarland.

sections.heading: Atlanta's Return
sections.body: Mast had barely played for the Knicks, appearing in only 12 regular-season games across 1970-71 and 1971-72. Atlanta gave him a larger role after the trade. In 1972-73 he appeared in 42 games, logged 447 minutes, scored 119 points and collected 136 rebounds. That works out to 2.8 points and 3.2 rebounds in 10.6 minutes per game. The Hawks went 46-36 and reached the Eastern Conference semifinals, so Mast's contribution was limited to reserve frontcourt depth rather than a major rotation role. Still, 42 actual NBA appearances represent a measurable return from the transaction.

sections.heading: New York's Draft Asset
sections.body: The Knicks held the second-round pick through the 1973 draft and used it on McFarland with the 28th overall selection. That identifies the pick outcome precisely, but it does not create NBA production for New York. McFarland never appeared in an NBA game. Basketball-Reference lists his professional career entirely in the ABA: 67 games for the Denver Rockets in 1973-74, 70 for the Denver Nuggets in 1974-75 and 11 for the San Diego Sails in 1975-76. Those games cannot be credited to the Knicks because New York never received NBA service or a later trade return from the drafted player.

sections.heading: Why the Pick Still Has Some Value
sections.body: A second-round selection is not worthless simply because the selected player never appeared for the drafting team. New York acquired a real draft asset and exercised it on a player who proved capable of playing 148 professional ABA games. The hindsight grade therefore should not treat the Knicks' side as if it received literally nothing on transaction day. But realized-value grading follows what the franchise ultimately obtained from the asset. In New York's case, no NBA games, minutes, points, trade return or compensatory pick are documented from McFarland.

sections.heading: Mast's Limited Ceiling
sections.body: Atlanta's advantage also needs to stay modest. Mast did not become a long-term Hawk. His 42-game 1972-73 season was his only year in Atlanta and his final NBA season. He played only 447 minutes, and no later transaction converted him into another player or pick. The Hawks therefore received useful roster depth rather than a lasting asset chain. That makes this a small win, not a franchise-changing trade. The comparison comes down to 42 documented NBA games on one side versus a second-round pick that produced zero Knicks appearances on the other.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Hawks Edge, B-/D+. Atlanta receives a B- because Mast supplied 42 regular-season games and useful reserve minutes on a 46-win playoff team. New York receives a D+ because the pick became McFarland, who never played in the NBA or generated a documented Knicks trade return, though the club did acquire and exercise a legitimate second-round asset. Confidence is high on the corrected October 9 date, the pick outcome and the player production. Mast supplied 42 Atlanta games and 447 minutes, while New York exercised its legitimate No. 28 selection on McFarland but received no Knicks games. His 148 ABA appearances elsewhere show the pick had player potential without becoming a realized Knicks NBA return.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee, Kansas City-Omaha and league transaction pages agree that the Kings acquired Toby Kimball from the Bucks on October 9, 1972 for a 1973 fourth-round pick that later became No. 59 Clyde Turner. Pro Sports Transactions adds a second Milwaukee asset: cash. A 1973 Kansas City-Omaha media guide independently describes Kimball as acquired from Milwaukee for a draft choice and cash, which supports keeping both pieces in the canonical ledger. The payment amount is not reported, so Milwaukee's financial return is verified but unpriced.

sections.heading: Kansas City-Omaha's Return
sections.body: Kimball was a 30-year-old veteran frontcourt reserve when the Kings acquired him. He played 67 games in 1972-73, averaging 3.5 points and 2.9 rebounds in 9.6 minutes. Basketball-Reference credits him with 643 minutes, 236 points and 191 rebounds. Those numbers are modest, but they are genuine NBA production from a fourth-round pick-and-cash package. On a 36-46 team, Kimball functioned as a low-minute reserve behind the club's heavier frontcourt options rather than as a core starter.

sections.heading: Milwaukee's Draft Return
sections.body: The draft component did not become NBA production for the Bucks. Milwaukee used the acquired selection on Minnesota forward Clyde Turner with the 59th pick in the 1973 draft. The Bucks' draft history shows no NBA games or statistical line for Turner. That leaves the cash payment as Milwaukee's only realized return that can be credited with certainty. Because the amount is unknown, it cannot be converted into a basketball-equivalent value or treated as a major offset to Kimball's 67 games.

sections.heading: Kimball's Next Move
sections.body: Kansas City-Omaha did not keep Kimball beyond one season. On September 28, 1973, the Kings sold his player rights to Philadelphia. Basketball-Reference records the sale, and Kimball then played 75 games for the 76ers in 1973-74. Those Philadelphia games do not count as Kansas City-Omaha production, but the sale shows the Kings retained some residual contractual value after receiving a season of direct play. The sale price is not preserved in the reviewed transaction pages, so the downstream cash cannot be quantified.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: This is a small transaction rather than a franchise-changing one. Kansas City-Omaha received one year of usable reserve minutes and later sold the player's rights. Milwaukee received a fourth-round selection that produced no NBA games plus an unpriced cash component. The cash keeps the Bucks from receiving a failing grade, but the basketball ledger favors the Kings because Kimball actually appeared in 67 games and the club still had an asset to sell when his season ended.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Kings Edge, B-/C+. Kansas City-Omaha receives a B- for 67 games of reserve frontcourt production and a later rights sale. Milwaukee receives a C+ because the Bucks obtained cash and the No. 59 pick, but Clyde Turner never played in the NBA and the payment cannot be valued precisely. Confidence is high on the player movement, pick identity and Kimball production, with moderate uncertainty around the unreported cash amounts. Kimball supplied 67 Kings appearances before the club separately sold his rights; Milwaukee selected Clyde Turner No. 59 without a Bucks NBA game. The recorded cash consideration keeps the return from being described as zero, but its price cannot be invented.

sections.heading: The Direct Trade
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee, Philadelphia and league transaction ledgers all place the exchange on October 10, 1972: the Bucks sent a 1973 second-round pick to the 76ers for Gary Gregor. Wayne Embry's executive ledger records the same deal. The pick later became No. 33, used by Phoenix on Gary Melchionni. Pro Sports Transactions also records cash moving from Milwaukee, and a historical Bucks media guide independently includes cash, though that guide labels the draft choice as a 1974 second-rounder. Because the team, league and same-day Phoenix chain consistently identify the asset as a 1973 second-round pick, the archive keeps 1973 as the canonical year and preserves the cash as a verified but unpriced secondary component.

sections.heading: Gregor's Milwaukee Stay
sections.body: Milwaukee received almost no lasting NBA value from Gregor. He appeared in nine games for the Bucks, totaling 88 minutes, 27 points, 32 rebounds and nine assists. His averages were 3.0 points and 3.6 rebounds in 9.8 minutes. Pro Sports Transactions records Milwaukee waiving him on November 15, barely five weeks after the trade. Gregor then joined the New York Nets of the ABA in December and played 40 games there during 1972-73. Those ABA games demonstrate that he still had professional value, but they cannot be credited to Milwaukee after the Bucks released him.

sections.heading: Philadelphia's Same-Day Pick Conversion
sections.body: Philadelphia did not keep the pick until draft night. On the same date, the 76ers traded a 1973 second-round selection to Phoenix for veteran center Mel Counts. The Philadelphia and Phoenix transaction ledgers both identify that selection as the pick later used on Gary Melchionni, linking Milwaukee's outgoing draft asset to the Suns transaction. Pro Sports Transactions describes the activity as a three-club transaction, while Basketball-Reference presents the Milwaukee-Philadelphia and Philadelphia-Phoenix exchanges as separate trades. For this archive, Milwaukee's canonical record remains bilateral, with Phoenix treated only as downstream pick lineage rather than a direct Bucks counterparty.

sections.heading: Counts and the Next Trade
sections.body: Counts played only seven games for Philadelphia, logging 47 minutes and scoring ten points. His direct production was therefore even smaller than Gregor's Milwaukee stint. The difference is that Philadelphia retained transactional value. On November 2, the 76ers packaged Counts with Bill Bridges and sent them to the Los Angeles Lakers for Leroy Ellis and John Trapp. Because Bridges was a substantial part of that later package, the original Milwaukee pick cannot be credited with all of Ellis and Trapp's value. It can, however, be credited with helping Philadelphia obtain Counts, who remained a named asset in a subsequent trade less than a month later.

sections.heading: Why Melchionni Is Not a Philadelphia Return
sections.body: The legacy asset label says the pick became Gary Melchionni, which is useful for draft-lineage identification but can be misleading if read as Philadelphia player production. Phoenix held the selection at draft time and chose Melchionni 33rd overall in 1973. He never played for Philadelphia as a result of this transaction. The source-backed record therefore keeps his name attached to the pick only as the final selection identity and marks the real Philadelphia return as the pick's same-day conversion into Counts. That distinction prevents downstream draft identity from being double-counted as 76ers on-court value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win, B/D+. Philadelphia receives a B because the second-round pick and cash gave the club immediate trade flexibility: the pick was rerouted for Counts, and Counts remained part of another trade three weeks later. The grade stops well short of elite because Counts contributed only seven Philadelphia games and cannot be assigned the full value of the later Bridges package. Milwaukee receives a D+ because Gregor played just nine games and 88 minutes before being waived. Confidence is high on the player movement, pick identity and same-day Phoenix routing, with moderate uncertainty on the cash detail because the supporting records disagree on the pick year even while agreeing that cash was included. The 76ers rerouted Milwaukee's 1973 pick into seven Counts appearances and a later joint Counts-and-Bridges package, not an independently valued future star; Gregor gave the Bucks nine games and 88 minutes. The disputed cash and pick-year descriptions are preserved as source limitations.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Pacers and ABA transaction ledgers agree that Indiana sent cash to the Virginia Squires for Don Buse in August 1972. The important source conflict is the day: the canonical import carries August 10, while Basketball-Reference lists the trade under August ? and then records Indiana signing Buse on August 15. The archive therefore keeps the established canonical date but does not present that day as independently verified. No reviewed source supplies the cash amount, so Virginia's consideration remains real but unpriced.

sections.heading: Immediate Pacers Return
sections.body: Buse joined Indiana immediately and played 77 games as a rookie in 1972-73, averaging 5.4 points, 2.9 assists and 1.4 steals in 19.3 minutes. The Pacers went 51-33 and won the ABA championship, and Buse appeared in 14 playoff games during that title run. He was not yet the team's central star, but the rights purchase already produced a useful rotation guard on a champion in its first season. That alone gives Indiana a concrete return that cannot be matched to any identified basketball asset on Virginia's side.

sections.heading: Development Into a Star
sections.body: The long-term payoff made the transaction exceptional. Buse grew from reserve guard into one of the ABA's best defenders and playmakers. By 1974-75 he was an All-Defensive First Team selection. In 1975-76 he started all 84 games, averaged 12.5 points, 8.2 assists and 4.1 steals, earned All-Star and All-ABA recognition, and again made the All-Defensive First Team. His 689 assists led the ABA. Indiana had acquired the rights to that production for an undisclosed cash payment four years earlier.

sections.heading: NBA Merger Value
sections.body: The value survived the ABA-NBA merger. In 1976-77 Buse started 76 of 81 games for the NBA Pacers, averaged 8.0 points, 8.5 assists and 3.5 steals, made the NBA All-Star team and the All-Defensive First Team, and led the entire NBA in both assists and steals. Basketball-Reference credits him with 685 assists and 281 steals that season. That combination matters for hindsight grading because the transaction did not merely buy a short ABA stint; it secured a guard who remained elite after the league context changed.

sections.heading: Virginia Return
sections.body: Virginia received cash, but the amount is unknown and no reviewed source ties it to a later player, pick or traceable basketball return. That does not make the consideration literally worthless, and the archive does not invent a dollar value or assume the Squires spent it poorly. It does mean the measurable comparison is dramatically one-sided. Indiana received five seasons of Buse before trading him to Phoenix in 1977, including an ABA championship season, multiple All-Defensive selections and league-leading playmaking and steals production. Virginia's side has no comparable documented basketball asset.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pacers Win, A/F. Indiana receives an A because a cash purchase of player rights produced a championship contributor who developed into an ABA All-Star, All-ABA guard, repeated All-Defensive selection and then an NBA All-Star who led the league in assists and steals. Virginia receives an F because its return is only an unpriced cash payment with no identified downstream basketball asset in the reviewed record. Confidence is medium-high on the transaction structure and career outcome, with the exact August day preserved as a source-date caveat. Buse's path from an ABA championship rookie to a 1976-77 NBA All-Star who led the league in assists and steals is the concrete Indiana return. Virginia did receive cash, but neither its amount nor the precise August completion day is independently established.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Chicago, Seattle and league transaction pages agree on the October 20, 1972 structure: the Bulls sent Kenny McIntosh to the SuperSonics for Gar Heard and Seattle's 1973 third-round pick. Chicago used that selection at No. 39 on Arkansas guard Martin Terry. The trade therefore gave Chicago one immediate rotation player plus a draft asset, while Seattle received a young forward who had played only 46 games for the Bulls. The reviewed sources do not add cash or another hidden component, so the canonical ledger remains a straightforward player-for-player-and-pick transaction.

sections.heading: Heard's Chicago Season
sections.body: Heard became useful immediately. After appearing in only three games for Seattle at the start of 1972-73, he played 78 for Chicago. Basketball-Reference credits him with 1,535 minutes, 807 points and 447 rebounds, or 10.3 points and 5.7 rebounds in 19.7 minutes per game. Chicago went 51-31 and reached the Western Conference semifinals. Heard was not a featured star, but his scoring rate and rebounding gave the Bulls much more immediate production than the player they surrendered produced for Seattle that season. He also appeared in two playoff games before the Bulls' postseason ended.

sections.heading: The Martin Terry Pick
sections.body: The draft asset added little realized value. Chicago selected Martin Terry with the 39th pick in the 1973 draft. Basketball-Reference lists Terry as a Chicago draft choice but shows no NBA statistical line. The pick therefore produced zero NBA games for the Bulls. That prevents the extra selection from turning the trade into a major draft win, yet it still matters that Chicago received an additional asset on top of a productive player. The source-backed ledger marks Terry as a verified zero-game draft outcome rather than treating the third-round pick as unresolved.

sections.heading: McIntosh in Seattle
sections.body: Seattle received more longevity from McIntosh than the original shorthand suggests. He played 56 games for the SuperSonics in 1972-73, averaging 4.5 points and 4.0 rebounds in 19.7 minutes. He then appeared in 69 games in 1973-74 and increased his role to 29.8 minutes, 7.4 points and 5.2 rebounds per game. McIntosh played six more Seattle games in 1974-75. In all, the SuperSonics received 131 regular-season appearances, 3,262 minutes, 783 points and 598 rebounds. He was a legitimate rotation player, which keeps Seattle's grade respectable despite Heard's stronger per-game impact.

sections.heading: Heard's Downstream Value
sections.body: Chicago did not simply lose Heard for nothing after one season. On September 10, 1973, the Bulls traded Heard and 1973 first-round pick Kevin Kunnert to Buffalo for John Hummer plus second-round picks in 1974 and 1975. That package later produced Leon Benbow with the 1974 pick, while Hummer played 18 Chicago games before being traded to Seattle for another 1975 second-round pick. Heard cannot be credited with the entire Buffalo return because Kunnert was a meaningful co-asset, so the archive treats the downstream value as supporting evidence rather than assigning all later players and picks to this 1972 trade.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: The direct comparison is closer than the old A-/C shorthand implied. Heard gave Chicago 78 games at 10.3 points and 5.7 rebounds, while McIntosh gave Seattle 131 games and stayed in a larger role for most of 1973-74. Chicago's advantage comes from receiving the more productive player immediately, adding a draft pick at no extra player cost, and retaining enough value in Heard to use him in another multi-asset trade the next year. Seattle's side was useful but did not produce a comparable downstream transaction in the reviewed record.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win, A-/B. Chicago receives an A- because Heard supplied a strong 78-game season, the Bulls also received the No. 39 pick, and Heard remained a tradable asset in the 1973 Buffalo deal. Seattle receives a B because McIntosh played 131 games across parts of three seasons and provided legitimate rotation minutes, even though his scoring efficiency and overall impact were lower. Martin Terry's zero-game outcome limits Chicago's draft bonus, and the Kunnert component prevents over-crediting Heard for the later Buffalo package. Confidence is high on the trade mechanics, player production, draft identity and immediate downstream transaction. Heard gave Chicago 78 productive games; McIntosh supplied 131 Seattle games, so the player exchange was closer than a simple lopsided label. The No. 39 Martin Terry pick gave Chicago no NBA appearances, and Heard's later Buffalo trade included Kevin Kunnert, limiting attribution.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Cleveland, Portland, league and executive transaction logs agree that the Cavaliers traded Charlie Davis to the Trail Blazers on October 24, 1972 for Portland's 1974 third-round pick. Cleveland later used that selection at No. 38 on Clarence "Foots" Walker. Portland's official historical media guide adds cash to the Blazers' outgoing package, matching the cash asset preserved in the legacy archive entry. Because the amount is not reported, the archive credits Cleveland with receiving cash but does not assign it a numerical basketball value. The draft pick remains the transaction's decisive asset.

sections.heading: Portland's Charlie Davis Return
sections.body: Davis immediately joined the Portland rotation. He played 69 games for the Trail Blazers in 1972-73, logging 1,333 minutes while averaging 8.9 points, 1.6 rebounds and 2.5 assists. Basketball-Reference credits him with 612 points that season. His role collapsed the next year: Davis appeared in only eight games in 1973-74, totaling 90 minutes and 31 points. Portland's media guide records the club waiving him on October 30, 1973. In all, the Blazers received 77 regular-season games, 1,423 minutes and 643 points before the player asset left without a trade return.

sections.heading: Cleveland Waits for the Pick
sections.body: Cleveland had to wait until the 1974 draft to realize its main return. The Cavaliers selected Walker 38th overall out of West Georgia. He immediately made the NBA roster and played 72 games as a rookie in 1974-75. Walker averaged only 4.2 points and 2.7 assists in 14.9 minutes, but the early role demonstrated that the third-round pick had already become a usable rotation guard rather than a speculative asset that never reached the league. He then appeared in 81 games during Cleveland's 1975-76 breakthrough season.

sections.heading: Six Seasons of Cavaliers Value
sections.body: Walker remained with Cleveland through 1979-80. His Cavaliers game totals were 72, 81, 62, 81, 55 and 76, or 427 regular-season appearances across six seasons. His role grew over time. He averaged 5.6 assists in 1977-78, 5.8 in 1978-79 and 8.0 in 1979-80, when he also scored 9.4 points per game in 31.9 minutes. He was never an All-Star, but a third-round pick producing six seasons and eventually handling full-time point-guard duties represents unusually strong realized value for the draft slot.

sections.heading: Different Types of Return
sections.body: Portland's side should not be dismissed. Davis gave the Blazers one full season of legitimate scoring and another short stint before his release. A 77-game return is meaningful for a player acquired with a third-round pick and cash. The difference is duration. Cleveland transformed that same pick into 427 games, multiple seasons of rotation minutes and several years of starting-level point-guard responsibility. The unpriced cash only adds to Cleveland's side rather than being needed to create the advantage.

sections.heading: Downstream Context
sections.body: Walker's Cleveland value continued until September 24, 1980, when the Cavaliers traded him to New Jersey. His later Nets production is not part of this direct return, but the fact that Cleveland still had a movable player asset after six seasons reinforces the durability of the original pick. Davis, by contrast, was waived by Portland after eight games in his second Blazers season. The transaction therefore produced both more direct games and a longer asset life for Cleveland.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win, A/B-. Cleveland receives an A because Portland's third-round pick became Foots Walker, who supplied 427 regular-season games over six seasons and developed into the club's primary point guard by the end of the decade; the unpriced cash is additional value. Portland receives a B- because Davis contributed 77 games and one useful scoring season, but he was waived before the end of 1973 and produced no retained downstream asset. Confidence is high on the pick identity, player production and transaction date; the only material uncertainty is the cash amount, which the official Portland media guide confirms without pricing. Cleveland converted Portland's third-round choice into 427 Foots Walker games over six seasons, while Davis gave Portland 77 appearances before being waived. The separate 1980 Walker trade does not add to this original return, and the official-guide cash payment remains unpriced.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Houston, Portland and league transaction ledgers agree on the October 27, 1972 trade: the Rockets sent Greg Smith to the Trail Blazers for Stan McKenzie. Ray Patterson's Houston executive record and Harry Glickman's Portland executive record preserve the same two-player structure. No draft choice, cash payment or future consideration appears in the reviewed primary transaction logs. The source-backed record therefore remains a direct player-for-player exchange. The Smith identity is the 1947-born Western Kentucky forward, not the later NBA center with the same common name.

sections.heading: Portland's Immediate Return
sections.body: Smith arrived after playing four games for Houston in 1972-73 and immediately became a regular member of Portland's rotation. He appeared in 72 games for the Trail Blazers that season, averaging 7.4 points, 5.2 rebounds and 1.6 assists in 21.8 minutes. Basketball-Reference credits him with 1,569 minutes, 533 points and 375 rebounds for Portland in that first season alone. Those totals already exceed the entire Houston production McKenzie would provide after the exchange, and Smith remained with the Blazers for several more seasons.

sections.heading: Three More Seasons in Portland
sections.body: Smith played 67 games for Portland in 1973-74 and another 55 in 1974-75, then made one final appearance in 1975-76. Across his Portland tenure, he totaled 195 regular-season games. His role diminished after the first season, but he still supplied 878 minutes in 1973-74 and 519 in 1974-75. Portland finally waived him on November 7, 1975. The move produced no trade return, yet the Blazers had already received roughly three full seasons of rotational value from a player acquired straight up for McKenzie.

sections.heading: Houston's McKenzie Return
sections.body: McKenzie had been a much larger scorer for Portland before the trade, averaging 13.5 points across his first three Trail Blazers seasons. That history gave Houston a reasonable basis for the deal, but the fit did not carry over. He played 26 games for the Rockets in 1972-73, averaging 3.3 points in 7.2 minutes. He returned for only 11 games in 1973-74, averaging 1.8 points in 10.2 minutes. Houston's total return was 37 regular-season appearances, 299 minutes and 106 points.

sections.heading: The Asset Chain Ends Quickly for Houston
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's 1973-74 Houston transaction page records the Rockets waiving McKenzie on November 9, 1973. That ended Houston's asset chain a little more than a year after the original trade. Unlike several neighboring archive transactions in which a player was later flipped for another asset, McKenzie did not generate a documented draft pick or player return when his Rockets tenure ended. His later professional career therefore does not add downstream value to Houston's side of this exchange.

sections.heading: Why the Legacy Grades Were Too Harsh
sections.body: The legacy Houston perspective had both teams in the D range, while the Portland perspective called the trade roughly even. The source-backed production record supports a wider gap. Portland received 195 games and multiple seasons from Smith; Houston received 37 low-minute games from McKenzie. Smith's Portland role was not star-level, and his efficiency and minutes declined after 1972-73, so the transaction does not justify an elite grade. It does, however, represent a useful straight-up roster win for the Blazers.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Blazers Win, B+/D+. Portland receives a B+ because Greg Smith supplied 195 regular-season games over parts of four seasons, including a productive 72-game first year after the trade. Houston receives a D+ because McKenzie appeared in only 37 games, scored 106 points and was waived in November 1973 without a documented downstream return. Smith's usefulness continued well past his first Portland season, while Houston's attempted change in backcourt scoring ended with a waiver rather than any recovered trade asset. For a straight player swap, that difference in sustained rotation use decides the outcome without pretending either player became a franchise star.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Atlanta, Detroit and league transaction ledgers agree on the October 31, 1972 trade: the Hawks sent Don Adams to the Pistons for Detroit's 1973 second-round pick. Edwin Coil's Detroit executive record confirms the same structure. Atlanta later used the selection at No. 27 on Villanova guard Tom Ingelsby. No cash, future consideration or additional player appears in the reviewed transaction logs, so the canonical record remains a direct player-for-pick deal.

sections.heading: Adams Immediately Becomes a Detroit Regular
sections.body: Adams had played only four games for Atlanta in 1972-73 before the trade. With Detroit, his role expanded sharply. He appeared in 70 games that season, averaging 9.3 points, 6.0 rebounds and 1.6 assists in 25.7 minutes. Basketball-Reference credits him with 1,798 minutes, 649 points and 419 rebounds for the Pistons after the move. The production was not star-level, but Detroit converted one future second-round pick into an established frontcourt rotation player almost immediately.

sections.heading: His Best Pistons Season
sections.body: Adams became even more important in 1973-74. He played 74 games and averaged 10.3 points, 6.1 rebounds and 1.9 assists in 31.1 minutes. Detroit went 52-30 and reached the Western Conference semifinals, and Adams also appeared in seven playoff games at 36.6 minutes per contest. That season is the strongest evidence for Detroit's side of the trade: a second-round asset produced starter-level minutes on one of the league's better teams.

sections.heading: A Third Season Before the Waiver
sections.body: Adams remained with Detroit for 51 games in 1974-75, averaging 5.9 points and 4.8 rebounds in 27.0 minutes. On February 18, 1975, the Pistons waived him. His Detroit tenure therefore ended without a trade return, but by then the club had already received 195 regular-season appearances across parts of three seasons. The absence of a downstream asset limits the ceiling on Detroit's grade, yet the quantity of direct play comfortably exceeds a typical second-round outcome.

sections.heading: Atlanta Uses the Pick on Tom Ingelsby
sections.body: The Hawks used the acquired selection on Tom Ingelsby with the 27th pick of the 1973 draft. Ingelsby played 48 games for Atlanta in 1973-74, averaging 2.7 points, 0.9 rebounds and 0.8 assists in 8.3 minutes. His total NBA production for the Hawks was 398 minutes and 129 points. He did not appear for Atlanta again after that rookie season; his later professional games came in the ABA with the Spirits of St. Louis and San Diego Sails. Those games cannot be credited to the Hawks' side of this transaction.

sections.heading: Comparing the Realized Returns
sections.body: Atlanta did at least turn Adams into a real NBA player rather than a failed draft pick. Ingelsby reached the league and supplied 48 games, which keeps the Hawks from receiving the lowest possible grade. The difference is scale. Adams gave Detroit more than four times as many regular-season games, thousands more minutes and two seasons of substantial frontcourt responsibility. The 1973-74 Pistons also used him in a serious playoff rotation, while Ingelsby's Atlanta role never grew beyond limited reserve minutes.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win, A-/C. Detroit receives an A- because Adams produced 195 regular-season games, a 10.3-point season and meaningful playoff minutes after being acquired for one second-round pick. Atlanta receives a C because No. 27 pick Tom Ingelsby reached the NBA but supplied only 48 games and one limited season for the Hawks before leaving the league. The second-round selection did reach an NBA roster, but Ingelsby's lone Hawks season did not offset the frontcourt minutes Adams supplied Detroit, including playoff use during a 52-win campaign. Detroit paid one future pick for immediate help; the A- measures that return rather than treating Adams as a franchise star.

sections.heading: The Rights Sale
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Houston, Kansas City-Omaha and league transaction ledgers agree on the core event: on November 2, 1972, the Rockets sold Dick Gibbs' player rights to the Kings. Joe Axelson's executive record also lists Kansas City-Omaha acquiring the rights that day. The legacy archive entry correctly treats Houston's return as cash, but none of the reviewed ledgers reports a dollar amount. The source-backed record therefore keeps the payment as verified but unpriced instead of assuming it was trivial or assigning a modern equivalent.

sections.heading: A Complicated Rights Trail
sections.body: Gibbs appears in another transaction only a few weeks earlier. On October 9, Kansas City-Omaha's ledger says the Kings traded Jim Fox and Dick Gibbs to Seattle for Pete Cross and Don Kojis. Seattle's transaction page records the same deal. The November 2 Houston-to-Kansas City-Omaha entry is specifically phrased as an acquisition of Gibbs' player rights, and Gibbs then actually played for the Kings rather than Seattle during the remainder of 1972-73. The reviewed sources do not explain every contractual step between those entries, so this archive does not collapse them into a speculative three-team transaction.

sections.heading: Gibbs' Kansas City-Omaha Production
sections.body: The on-court outcome is clear. Gibbs played 66 games for Kansas City-Omaha in 1972-73, logging 733 minutes. He scored 207 points, grabbed 94 rebounds and recorded 61 assists. His averages were 3.1 points, 1.4 rebounds and 0.9 assists in 11.1 minutes per game. That is modest production, but it represents a full season of reserve availability from a player whose rights were purchased for cash rather than a draft pick or rotation player.

sections.heading: Houston's Side
sections.body: Houston had almost no 1972-73 on-court return from Gibbs before the sale. Basketball-Reference credits him with one Rockets appearance, two minutes and no points that season. His larger Houston contribution had come the year before, when he played 64 games in 1971-72, but those games predate the November 1972 transaction and should not be counted as value retained after the sale. Houston's realized return from this specific move is the cash payment, and the absence of a reported amount prevents a precise comparison in financial terms.

sections.heading: What Happened Next
sections.body: Gibbs played 71 games for Seattle in 1973-74, but the reviewed Kansas City-Omaha transaction page for that season does not list a corresponding transfer from the Kings to the SuperSonics. Because the documentary chain is incomplete, those Seattle games are not credited as a downstream Kansas City-Omaha asset return. The source-backed evaluation stops with the 66 Kings games directly supported by the 1972-73 roster and transaction records, while flagging the later Seattle appearance as unresolved disposition rather than inventing a missing transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Kings Edge, B-/C+. Kansas City-Omaha receives a B- because the acquired rights produced 66 games and 733 minutes of immediate reserve value. Houston receives a C+ because it converted a lightly used player-rights asset into cash, but the amount is unknown and therefore cannot be credited as a major return. The edge is intentionally modest: Gibbs was a reserve, not a core player, and the later path to Seattle is not fully documented in the reviewed transaction logs. Confidence is high on the November 2 rights sale and Gibbs' Kings production, with moderate uncertainty around the cash amount and subsequent rights disposition. Those 66 Kings appearances establish a narrow on-court edge, not a larger claim about lasting control of Gibbs' rights: the October Seattle transaction and later Seattle stop still lack a documented bridge in the reviewed ledgers. Until the cash amount and rights trail are confirmed, Houston's receipt cannot be called either a major windfall or a negligible payment.
