sections.heading: The September 23 Exchange Is Clear, and the legacy Identity Was Wrong
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Lakers, Bucks and league transaction ledgers all record the same transaction on September 23, 1975: Los Angeles sent Milwaukee a 1976 fifth-round pick for Ron Williams. Pete Newell's executive record confirms the Lakers side. The legacy archive entry incorrectly displayed the incoming player as Ron Williams with Fritz Williams in parentheses and attached the Fritz Williams player identity. That is an archive identity error. The actual player was Ron Williams, the veteran guard who had already spent two seasons with Milwaukee after five years with the Warriors.

sections.heading: Williams Gave Los Angeles Nine Games
sections.body: Ron Williams played nine regular-season games for the Lakers in 1975-76. Basketball-Reference credits him with 158 minutes, 44 points and 21 assists, which works out to 4.9 points and 2.3 assists per game in 17.6 minutes. He was a reserve behind the Lakers' established backcourt and did not develop into a lasting rotation piece. Those nine games were also the final NBA appearances of Williams' eight-year career, so Los Angeles received a real but very short return.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Converted the Trade Into the No. 77 Pick
sections.body: The Bucks held the Lakers' 1976 fifth-round selection and used it at No. 77 overall on Arizona guard James Rappis. Milwaukee's transaction ledger and the 1976 NBA draft record agree on the pick outcome. Rappis was therefore a fully traceable draft result rather than an unresolved future consideration. That gives the Bucks a concrete asset path to grade, but the pick's value still depends on what happened after the selection.

sections.heading: Rappis Never Produced NBA Regular-Season Value
sections.body: Rappis' Basketball-Reference player page confirms his fifth-round draft position but contains no NBA regular-season statistical line. The draft table likewise shows no NBA games or seasons. The Bucks therefore converted Williams into a legitimate draft choice but did not receive measurable NBA production from that choice. This is not the same as receiving nothing on trade day, because the pick itself had optionality, but the realized basketball outcome ended at the draft.

sections.heading: The Hindsight Gap Is Small
sections.body: Neither franchise found durable value. Los Angeles received nine games from a veteran who was near the end of his career, while Milwaukee received a fifth-round selection that never reached an NBA regular-season game. The Lakers' nine games are enough to create a slight realized-value advantage, but not enough to justify a strong grade. Milwaukee also deserves some credit for extracting a draft asset from a player whose NBA career ended immediately after the trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Lakers Edge, C+/C. Los Angeles receives a C+ because Ron Williams did provide nine regular-season appearances and some backcourt minutes, even though the stint was brief and ended his NBA career. Milwaukee receives a C because the Bucks converted Williams into a real fifth-round pick and selected James Rappis, but Rappis never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. The source-backed correction matters more than the grade gap: the incoming player was Ron Williams, not Fritz Williams. Confidence is high on the September 23 date, the player identity, the No. 77 pick outcome and the limited realized value on both sides.

sections.heading: The September 25 Trade Is Clear
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Detroit, Seattle and league transaction ledgers agree on the structure: the Pistons sent a 1978 first-round pick to the SuperSonics for Archie Clark on September 25, 1975. Oscar Feldman's Detroit executive record and Bill Russell's Seattle record confirm the same deal. The legacy archive entry was dated September 24 and mislabeled Seattle under the modern Oklahoma City franchise name in its prose. The source-backed repair corrects the transaction date while preserving the franchise key used by the archive.

sections.heading: Clark Gave Detroit One Useful Season
sections.body: Archie Clark played 79 regular-season games for Detroit in 1975-76 and averaged 7.6 points, 2.8 assists and 1.7 rebounds in 20.1 minutes. He also appeared in all nine of the Pistons' playoff games, averaging 8.0 points in 21.3 minutes. Clark was no longer the All-Star-level scorer he had been earlier in the decade, but he was a legitimate veteran rotation player on a playoff team. Detroit's return therefore deserves more credit than a low-end rental grade.

sections.heading: The Detroit Pick Stayed Valuable for Seattle
sections.body: Seattle held the acquired first-round pick for more than two years. On November 11, 1977, the SuperSonics traded that Detroit-origin 1978 first-rounder and a 1979 second-round pick to Portland for Wally Walker. This distinction matters because Seattle never used the first-rounder to draft Ron Brewer. Portland became the later holder and selected Brewer at No. 7 in 1978. The archive should record Brewer as the eventual pick outcome but should not assign his NBA career directly to Seattle.

sections.heading: Walker Produced Real Downstream Value
sections.body: The defensible downstream credit is Wally Walker. After the November 1977 trade, Walker played 68 regular-season games for Seattle in 1977-78 and all 20 playoff games during the SuperSonics' run to the NBA Finals. He returned for 60 regular-season games in 1978-79 and appeared in 13 playoff games as Seattle won the NBA championship. Walker remained with the franchise into 1979-80. Because Seattle also surrendered a second-round pick in the Walker trade, the Detroit first-rounder cannot receive full credit for Walker's entire tenure, but it was a major component of the acquisition.

sections.heading: Detroit's Branch Ended Quickly
sections.body: Clark's Pistons tenure ended after the 1975-76 season. Detroit waived him on July 28, 1976, and he did not play another NBA regular-season game. That leaves the Pistons with one season of useful veteran depth and playoff minutes but no later trade return or retained asset. Seattle, by contrast, carried the first-round value forward and converted it into part of a package for a younger rotation player who contributed across multiple playoff runs.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: SuperSonics Win, A-/B. Seattle receives an A- because a first-round pick acquired for a veteran nearing the end of his career retained enough value to help acquire Wally Walker, who contributed to the 1978 Finals run and 1979 championship. The grade stops short of an A or A+ because Seattle also surrendered a 1979 second-round pick in the Walker trade and did not itself draft Ron Brewer. Detroit receives a B because Clark gave the Pistons 79 regular-season games and nine playoff appearances, a useful one-season return even though the team waived him the next summer. Confidence is high on the September 25 date, Clark's Detroit production and the pick's later use in the Walker trade.

sections.heading: The legacy Player Identity Was Wrong
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Detroit, Phoenix and league transaction ledgers all record the September 30, 1975 trade as Earl Williams to Detroit for a 1976 second-round pick. The Willie Norwood reference belongs to a different transaction attempt on May 28, when Phoenix originally agreed to send Williams to Detroit for Norwood. That earlier deal was cancelled. Norwood therefore remained a Piston and was waived on October 8. This review corrects the live September record to Earl Williams while preserving the cancelled May transaction only as historical context.

sections.heading: Williams Gave Detroit a Short Reserve-Center Stint
sections.body: Williams appeared in 46 games for the 1975-76 Pistons. He averaged 3.7 points and 5.5 rebounds in 12.2 minutes, with Detroit using him as a reserve frontcourt piece rather than a major rotation anchor. The Pistons waived him on February 23, 1976, so the return ended before the postseason. Williams later appeared in only one more NBA game, with the Nets in 1976-77. Detroit therefore received real regular-season minutes but no sustained multi-season or playoff value from the acquisition.

sections.heading: Phoenix Preserved the Pick and Used It in Another Trade
sections.body: Phoenix did not hold the Detroit-origin second-round pick until draft night. On November 3, 1975, the Suns sent John Roche and that 1976 second-round selection to the Los Angeles Lakers for Pat Riley. The Lakers' transaction ledger identifies the same pick as the one later used at No. 21 on Earl Tatum. The important source-backed distinction is that Tatum's NBA career belongs to Los Angeles, not Phoenix. Phoenix's realized benefit was the pick's role as part of the package that brought Riley to the Suns.

sections.heading: Riley Supplied More Immediate Team Value Than Williams
sections.body: Riley played 60 regular-season games for Phoenix in 1975-76, averaging 4.6 points in 13.2 minutes. He also appeared in five playoff games during the Suns' run through Seattle and Golden State to the NBA Finals. Riley was a reserve and the original pick was not the only asset Phoenix surrendered, so the Detroit pick should receive only proportional downstream credit. Even with that limitation, the pick clearly remained useful enough to help Phoenix turn John Roche into a rotation guard for a conference champion.

sections.heading: Earl Tatum Is the Pick Outcome, Not a Phoenix Player Outcome
sections.body: Los Angeles used the acquired second-round selection at No. 21 in the 1976 draft on Earl Tatum. Tatum went on to play 262 NBA games, but assigning that full career to Phoenix would overstate the Suns' return because Phoenix had traded the pick away seven months earlier. The correct asset-chain treatment is to record Tatum as the eventual draft outcome while stopping Phoenix's realized-value credit at the Riley transaction. This keeps the archive consistent with the proportional downstream treatment used elsewhere.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Suns Win, B-/C+. Phoenix receives a B- because the second-round pick retained enough value to function as a meaningful component of the Pat Riley trade, and Riley then played 60 regular-season games plus five playoff games on the 1976 Western Conference champions. The grade stays below a full B because Phoenix also had to include John Roche and Riley was a reserve. Detroit receives a C+ because Earl Williams supplied 46 games and rebounding depth, but his stint ended with a February waiver and produced no playoff or downstream value. Confidence is high on the player-identity correction, the cancelled May transaction, the September 30 trade, the November Riley trade and the No. 21 Earl Tatum pick outcome.

sections.heading: The October 7 Exchange Is Verified, but the Pick Is Not Fully Identified
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Portland, Atlanta and league transaction ledgers all record the same October 7, 1975 transaction: the Trail Blazers sent a future draft pick to the Hawks for Greg Lee. Harry Glickman's Portland executive record and Bud Seretean's Atlanta record independently repeat that structure. None of those authoritative ledgers supplies a year, round, protection condition or eventual player for the future pick. The legacy archive entry described the asset as conditional and not exercised, but the source-backed audit could not verify those extra details. The repaired record therefore preserves only what the historical record establishes and marks the pick outcome unresolved.

sections.heading: Portland Acquired Rights and Immediately Signed Lee
sections.body: RealGM's transaction archive identifies the move as Portland acquiring Lee's draft rights from Atlanta and then signing him on October 7. Atlanta had originally selected Lee in the seventh round of the 1974 NBA draft after his UCLA career, but he had spent the 1974-75 season in the ABA with San Diego rather than playing for the Hawks. The October transaction thus functioned as a rights transfer that allowed Portland to place Lee on its roster immediately, not as a trade for an established Atlanta rotation player.

sections.heading: Lee's Portland Return Was Extremely Short
sections.body: Lee appeared in five games for the Trail Blazers during the 1975-76 season. Basketball-Reference credits him with 35 total minutes, six points, two rebounds and 11 assists. Portland waived him on November 11, barely five weeks after the trade, and those five games became the only NBA appearances of his career. He had also played five ABA games the previous season, leaving him with ten total major-league professional appearances. Portland therefore received a real player outcome, but the scale of the return was minimal.

sections.heading: Atlanta's Pick Cannot Be Assigned an Invented Outcome
sections.body: The future pick is the difficult side of the transaction. Standard Basketball-Reference transaction records often identify later selections when a traded pick can be traced, including many surrounding 1975 deals. This entry does not. The Atlanta-Portland trade-partner page likewise lists the transaction without naming a later draftee or attaching future player production to the Hawks. That absence is not proof that the pick was formally cancelled or never exercised, so the archive should not convert missing provenance into a definite claim. The defensible status is unresolved future draft pick, with no attributable player outcome found in the sources reviewed.

sections.heading: The Realized-Value Gap Is Too Small to Force a Winner
sections.body: Portland can point to five NBA games from Lee, but five games and 35 minutes are not enough to create a meaningful franchise advantage. Atlanta can point to having received a future-pick asset, yet the archive cannot responsibly price that asset or credit a later player without a traceable chain. A slight Portland edge would overstate the value of Lee's brief stint, while an Atlanta win would require assumptions about an unidentified selection. Treating the exchange as even is the most conservative hindsight result until additional primary or archival evidence resolves the pick.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, C/C. Portland receives a C because acquiring Lee's rights produced only five games, 35 minutes and a waiver roughly one month later. Atlanta also receives a C because the Hawks did receive a future draft pick, but the reviewed authoritative transaction sources do not establish its year, round, conditions or eventual player. The grade deliberately avoids repeating the legacy claim that the pick was not exercised because that specific outcome has not been verified. Confidence is high on the October 7 transaction and Lee's Portland stint but medium on the complete asset chain, so the record's overall confidence is medium.

sections.heading: The October 8 Deal Happened During the Claws' Collapse
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Denver and ABA transaction ledgers record Denver sending Dave Robisch and cash to the Memphis/Baltimore franchise for Dan Issel on October 8, 1975. The transaction note explains that the Memphis Sounds had become the Baltimore Claws and that the Claws never played a regular-season game that season. The legacy archive entry's basic player structure is therefore correct, but the opposing franchise should be understood historically as Baltimore rather than as an active Memphis team.

sections.heading: Issel Became an Immediate Denver Star
sections.body: Issel played all 84 regular-season games for Denver in 1975-76 and averaged 23.0 points, 11.0 rebounds and 2.4 assists in 34.0 minutes. He made the ABA All-Star team and then averaged 20.5 points and 12.0 rebounds across 13 playoff games as Denver reached the final ABA Finals. This was not a speculative acquisition that needed years to mature. The return became elite immediately and arrived at exactly the moment Denver was preparing to move from the ABA into the NBA.

sections.heading: The Value Extended Far Beyond the Final ABA Season
sections.body: Issel stayed with Denver after the merger and remained one of the franchise's defining frontcourt players for the rest of his career. Basketball-Reference lists a 15-year professional career, seven All-Star selections and Hall of Fame induction, with the Denver portion spanning the club's final ABA season and many NBA seasons. The source-backed verdict does not need to assign every later team accomplishment to this trade; simply retaining a high-level scorer and rebounder through the league transition creates enormous realized value.

sections.heading: Robisch Never Produced a Baltimore Regular-Season Return
sections.body: Baltimore's side cannot be graded like a normal player-for-player exchange because the Claws folded before the regular season. Robisch therefore never logged a regular-season game for the franchise that acquired him. On October 21, San Diego selected Robisch in the Baltimore dispersal draft. He played all 11 games the Sails completed, then Indiana selected him in the November 12 dispersal draft after San Diego also ceased operations. Robisch went on to have a substantial career, but those later games belonged to San Diego, Indiana and other franchises, not Baltimore.

sections.heading: The Cash Component Matters, but Its Exact Amount Is Not Required to Grade the Basketball Outcome
sections.body: The authoritative Basketball-Reference transaction ledger identifies cash as part of Denver's outgoing package but does not state an amount. Historical ABA accounts often describe the payment as $500,000 and connect it to Baltimore's earlier obligation in the Issel acquisition from Kentucky. The archive can preserve that context in research notes without pretending the standard transaction ledger independently verifies the figure. Even treating the cash as meaningful consideration, Baltimore never converted either Robisch or the cash into a sustainable on-court return before the franchise disappeared.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win, A+/D. Denver receives an A+ because Issel immediately delivered an All-Star 23-and-11 season, helped the Nuggets reach the ABA Finals and remained a long-term franchise cornerstone through the NBA transition. Baltimore receives a D rather than an F because it did receive Robisch plus cash and the cash had real economic value, but the franchise folded before Robisch could play a regular-season game and therefore realized no durable basketball return. Confidence is high on the October 8 transaction, Issel's Denver production, Baltimore's collapse and Robisch's dispersal path.

sections.heading: The October 10 Movement Was a Waiver Claim, Not a Nets Trade
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's 1975-76 ABA transaction ledger states that the Virginia Squires claimed Gerald Govan on waivers from the Utah Stars on October 10, 1975. Virginia's team transaction page records the same claim, and Utah's page records the same player leaving through waivers. Those three ledgers agree on both the mechanism and the clubs involved. None places the New York Nets in the transaction. The legacy archive entry therefore cannot be repaired simply by changing a draft-pick detail; its entire trade structure is unsupported.

sections.heading: Utah Had Already Waived Govan in September
sections.body: The Utah Stars waived Govan on September 17, more than three weeks before Virginia claimed him. That chronology matters because a waiver claim does not create a trade package and does not require the claiming club to send a player or draft asset to another team. The legacy record's future draft pick was therefore not merely unresolved. It was attached to a transaction type that did not happen. Treating the draft-pick language as unverified would still leave a false Nets-Squires exchange in the archive, so the safer correction is structural supersession.

sections.heading: New York's Transaction Ledger Has No Matching October 10 Deal
sections.body: The 1975-76 New York Nets transaction log lists the club's September Billy Paultz and Bob Warren trades, the October 16 Ed Manning deal with Indiana, later waivers, and the January 27 transaction with Virginia involving Swen Nater, Billy Schaeffer and Jim Eakins. It does not list an October 10 Gerald Govan trade or a future draft pick received from Virginia. That absence is especially persuasive when combined with the affirmative Utah and Virginia waiver records, because the correct transaction is already documented elsewhere rather than merely missing from one team page.

sections.heading: Govan Did Play for Virginia, but That Does Not Validate the legacy Package
sections.body: Govan's 1975-76 player record confirms 24 games for the Squires. He averaged 5.7 points, 6.7 rebounds and 2.3 assists in 27.4 minutes, and Virginia's roster page carries the same 24-game line. The Squires later waived him on December 16. Those facts explain why the legacy archive record may have looked plausible: Govan genuinely ended up in Virginia. The error was assigning that roster move to New York and inventing a reciprocal draft-pick asset. His Virginia production belongs to the waiver claim, not to a Nets trade verdict.

sections.heading: The Correct Archive Treatment Is Superseded Provenance
sections.body: TradeVerdicts keeps malformed historical imports when they are useful for explaining how a bad record entered the archive, but they should not remain eligible for a graded trade history, player-history links or verdict. The superseded entry is retained for provenance but excluded from graded results. The unsupported future-pick asset is explicitly labeled as a legacy claim rather than a real draft asset, and the Nets-to-Virginia player movement is marked unsupported.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Record Superseded. No winner and no team grades are assigned because there was no verified Nets-Squires trade to evaluate. Confidence is high: the ABA league ledger, Utah Stars ledger and Virginia Squires ledger independently align on a September 17 Utah waiver followed by Virginia's October 10 claim, while New York's transaction history contains no corresponding deal. Govan's 24 Virginia games and December 16 waiver are also directly supported.

sections.heading: The October 21 Transaction Is Unusually Well Documented
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Denver, Virginia and ABA transaction ledgers all record the same exchange: Denver sent Fatty Taylor to the Squires for Chuck Williams on October 21, 1975. Carl Scheer's Denver executive record and Jack Ankerson's Virginia record repeat the deal. The timing adds important context. Earlier that day Virginia selected Williams from the Baltimore Claws in the dispersal draft after the Claws folded before playing a regular-season game. The Squires then immediately moved him to Denver for Taylor.

sections.heading: Williams Became a Major Part of Denver's Final ABA Team
sections.body: Williams played 79 regular-season games for Denver in 1975-76, averaging 11.0 points, 4.7 assists and 2.7 rebounds in 32.0 minutes. Basketball-Reference also marks him as an ABA All-Star that season. Denver finished with the league's best regular-season record and reached the final ABA Finals, so Williams' value was not empty-volume production on a losing club. He was a substantial guard on a contender during the exact season when the franchise was preparing to enter the NBA.

sections.heading: Taylor Was Productive for Virginia, but the Team Had No Future
sections.body: Fatty Taylor also gave his new club legitimate minutes. He played 76 games for Virginia and averaged 8.2 points, 5.3 assists, 4.5 rebounds and 2.7 steals in 32.7 minutes. Those numbers make the old C-minus Denver grade too harsh on the deal's balance because Virginia did receive a real starting guard. The problem is organizational context: the Squires went 15-68, missed the playoffs and disappeared after the season. Taylor's one year therefore produced no retained franchise value beyond the final Virginia campaign.

sections.heading: Denver Retained Williams Through the ABA-NBA Transition
sections.body: Williams remained with the Nuggets when the ABA clubs entered the NBA. He appeared in 21 games for Denver in 1976-77 before the club traded him and Gus Gerard to Buffalo for Jim Price on December 15, 1976. That later deal means Williams generated a second layer of value beyond his strong 1975-76 season. The original October trade should not receive full credit for Price because Gerard was also part of the package, but Williams was a real component of the acquisition and therefore carried measurable downstream utility.

sections.heading: The Trade Also Illustrates Denver's Rapid Guard Reconfiguration
sections.body: Denver's later moves add an unusual wrinkle. In August 1976 the Nuggets reacquired Fatty Taylor from Philadelphia for a 1977 second-round pick after the Virginia franchise had disappeared. Taylor then played 79 NBA games for Denver in 1976-77. That later reacquisition is a separate transaction and should not be credited to the Squires side of this October deal, but it shows that Denver still valued Taylor. The key point for this review is narrower: on October 21, 1975 Denver exchanged one useful veteran guard for another who immediately became an All-Star-level contributor and later retained trade value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win, A-/B. Denver receives an A- because Williams delivered 79 games, 11.0 points and 4.7 assists for an ABA Finals team, earned All-Star recognition, stayed through the NBA transition and later helped form the package for Jim Price. Virginia receives a B because Taylor was genuinely useful, starting most of the Squires' final season and supplying playmaking, rebounding and defensive activity. The gap comes from team context and retained value rather than from Taylor failing individually. Confidence is high on the transaction, both players' 1975-76 production and Williams' later Buffalo trade.

sections.heading: The legacy Pick Round and Cash Claim Were Wrong
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Atlanta Hawks, Seattle SuperSonics and NBA league transaction ledgers all record the October 22, 1975 exchange as Herm Gilliam to Seattle for a 1976 third-round draft pick. Bill Russell's Seattle executive record repeats the same structure. None of those authoritative ledgers includes cash. This review therefore corrects two material import errors: the No. 46 selection was a third-round pick, not a second-rounder, and the extra cash asset is removed rather than preserved as an unsupported part of the package.

sections.heading: Gilliam Gave Seattle a Full Rotation Season
sections.body: Herm Gilliam appeared in 81 regular-season games for the 1975-76 SuperSonics, averaging 8.5 points, 2.7 rebounds and 2.5 assists in 20.3 minutes. He was no longer the 14-point starting guard he had been in Atlanta two years earlier, but he remained a durable veteran contributor. Seattle therefore converted a third-round pick into immediate usable depth for essentially an entire season, a much stronger realized outcome than the old database wording captured.

sections.heading: Atlanta Used the Pick on Larry Cooke at No. 46
sections.body: Atlanta retained the pick and used it in the 1976 NBA draft on Larry Cooke, a Virginia Tech guard selected 46th overall. The Hawks' transaction page, the league draft table and Cooke's Basketball-Reference profile all align on that identity. Cooke never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. The pick outcome is therefore fully traceable but produced no major-league playing value for Atlanta, making this one of the cleaner historical comparisons in the 1975 chronology.

sections.heading: Seattle Still Had a Small Downstream Asset After the Season
sections.body: Gilliam did not simply leave Seattle as a free agent. Bill Russell's executive ledger records the SuperSonics selling his player rights to Portland on September 2, 1976. The standard transaction record does not provide a sale amount in the material reviewed here, so the source-backed grade does not assign a specific dollar value. The sale nevertheless confirms that Seattle retained at least some transactional value after Gilliam's 81-game season rather than receiving a one-year return that vanished without compensation.

sections.heading: Gilliam's Portland Championship Is Not Seattle Value
sections.body: Gilliam later played 80 regular-season games for Portland in 1976-77 and was part of the Trail Blazers' championship roster, but those games belong to Portland, not Seattle. This distinction is important because a downstream player path can easily inflate a trade grade if later production is attributed to the wrong franchise. Seattle's realized return stops at Gilliam's 1975-76 SuperSonics season plus whatever economic value came from the later rights sale. That is already enough to win the trade without borrowing his Portland accomplishments.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: SuperSonics Win, B+/D+. Seattle receives a B+ because a third-round pick produced 81 games of useful veteran rotation play and a later rights sale. The grade stays below A territory because Gilliam was a complementary player and Seattle kept him for only one season. Atlanta receives a D+ because the Hawks did obtain the exact draft asset promised and used it at No. 46, but Larry Cooke never played an NBA regular-season game. Confidence is high on the package correction, Gilliam's Seattle production and the Cooke draft outcome.

sections.heading: This Was a Player-Rights Sale, Not a Draft-Rights Trade
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Los Angeles Lakers, Milwaukee Bucks and NBA league transaction ledgers agree that Milwaukee sold the player rights to Cornell Warner to Los Angeles on October 22, 1975. The legacy archive entry broadly captured the cash-for-rights structure, but its asset type labels the return as draft rights. Warner was already an established NBA player with two Milwaukee seasons behind him, so this review corrects the asset to player rights and preserves the cash consideration without inventing an amount.

sections.heading: Warner Immediately Became a Major Lakers Rebounder
sections.body: Warner played 81 games for Los Angeles in 1975-76 and averaged 7.3 points, 8.9 rebounds and 1.3 assists in 31.0 minutes. Only Kareem Abdul-Jabbar averaged more rebounds for the club. Warner's 722 total rebounds and 2,512 minutes make the acquisition materially different from a speculative rights purchase. Los Angeles converted cash into a high-usage frontcourt role for almost an entire season, and the production arrived immediately rather than requiring a development period.

sections.heading: The Lakers Also Retained Warner Into the NBA's 1976-77 Season
sections.body: Warner returned for 14 games in 1976-77, averaging 3.9 points and 4.9 rebounds in 12.1 minutes. His role diminished sharply, so the second season adds only modest value, but it pushes the Los Angeles return to 95 regular-season appearances across two years. The core of the grade remains the 1975-76 season, when Warner played 31 minutes per game and supplied the rebounding support around Abdul-Jabbar on a team that improved to 40 wins.

sections.heading: Milwaukee's Return Is Real but Economically Opaque
sections.body: The Bucks received cash, and a cash return should not be treated as zero. The problem for a retrospective basketball archive is that the standard transaction ledgers reviewed here do not state the amount, and no player or draft asset emerged from the deal that can be followed through a later transaction chain. That makes Milwaukee's realized basketball value impossible to quantify with the same precision as Warner's games and production. The grade therefore gives Milwaukee credit for completing a sale rather than pretending the cash had no value, but it does not award unsupported downstream value.

sections.heading: Warner's Milwaukee Tenure Provides Important Context
sections.body: Milwaukee was not giving up an unknown reserve. Warner had played 67 games for the Bucks in 1973-74 and 79 in 1974-75, averaging 7.0 points and 8.2 rebounds across his two Milwaukee seasons. His 1974-75 workload reached 31.9 minutes per game. Selling his rights therefore represented a real roster decision, not merely clearing an inactive name. Los Angeles correctly identified that Warner could still handle a substantial role and immediately gave him one of the heaviest frontcourt workloads on the team.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win, B+/C. Los Angeles receives a B+ because a cash purchase delivered 81 games at 31 minutes per night in the first season, 8.9 rebounds per game and 95 total appearances across two seasons. The grade stays below A territory because Warner's second Lakers season was brief and the acquisition did not create a long multi-year asset chain. Milwaukee receives a C because the Bucks did receive cash, but the amount is not preserved in the standard transaction record and no traceable basketball asset came back. Confidence is high on the transaction type and Warner's production, while the unreported cash amount is explicitly left unresolved.

sections.heading: The Verified Package Was Jim Fox for One Second-Round Pick
sections.body: Milwaukee, Seattle, the NBA league transaction ledger, Wayne Embry's executive record and Bill Russell's executive record all align on the same October 22, 1975 structure: the Bucks received Jim Fox and Seattle received a 1976 second-round draft pick. None of those ledgers lists cash. This review therefore removes the legacy cash component from the verified package and simplifies the pick language to what the primary records actually support. The pick was later used at No. 19 on Bayard Forrest.

sections.heading: The Pick Had Come to Milwaukee Through the Atlanta Penalty
sections.body: Milwaukee's 1974-75 transaction ledger shows that on June 5, 1975 the Bucks received two 1976 second-round picks from Atlanta as a league remedy tied to the Hawks' earlier signing of Milwaukee draft pick Julius Erving. Basketball-Reference identifies those two picks as the selections later used on Alex English and Bayard Forrest. By October, Milwaukee moved the Forrest pick to Seattle for Fox. That provenance is important because the legacy phrase about the most favorable Bucks pick is unnecessary and is not how the authoritative October transaction ledgers describe the deal.

sections.heading: Fox Gave Milwaukee One Useful Reserve Season
sections.body: Jim Fox played 70 games for the 1975-76 Bucks, averaging 3.9 points and 3.4 rebounds in 13.1 minutes. He also appeared in all three games of Milwaukee's first-round playoff series against Detroit. The production was modest compared with his earlier Seattle seasons, but it was real roster value for a Milwaukee team in transition after the Kareem Abdul-Jabbar trade. Fox should not be treated as a failed acquisition simply because his role had shrunk; the Bucks received a durable veteran backup for the entire regular season.

sections.heading: Seattle Turned the Pick Into Bayard Forrest and Then Another Pick
sections.body: Seattle selected Bayard Forrest with the No. 19 pick in the 1976 draft. Forrest never played a regular-season game for the SuperSonics, but that did not end the asset chain. On March 18, 1977 Seattle traded Forrest to Phoenix for a 1979 second-round pick. The transaction record identifies that future pick as the one later used on Paul Mokeski after Seattle sent it onward. Forrest himself later played 139 NBA games for Phoenix, but those Suns games are not credited to Seattle; Seattle's realized value is the replacement draft asset it received for him.

sections.heading: The Forrest Pick Helped Seattle Acquire John Johnson
sections.body: On October 22, 1977 Seattle sent the Phoenix-derived 1979 second-round pick and a 1980 second-round pick to Houston for John Johnson. Because two picks were required, the original Fox trade deserves only partial credit for Johnson rather than full credit for the entire acquisition. Even with that discount, the downstream value is substantial. Johnson played 76 games for Seattle in 1977-78 as the SuperSonics reached the NBA Finals, then started all 82 games in 1978-79 and averaged 11.0 points, 5.0 rebounds and 4.4 assists for the NBA champions.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: SuperSonics Win, A-/C+. Seattle receives an A- because a single second-round pick retained value through multiple transactions and became part of the package for a starting forward on consecutive Finals teams, including the 1979 champion. The grade stops short of a full A because the Johnson acquisition also required another second-round pick. Milwaukee receives a C+ because Fox supplied 70 regular-season games and three playoff appearances as a dependable reserve, but the Bucks surrendered the more durable asset and received no comparable downstream return. Confidence is high on the corrected package, Fox's Milwaukee production, Forrest's No. 19 selection and the later Forrest-to-Phoenix and Johnson transactions.

sections.heading: Two legacy archive entrys Describe One Haywood Transaction
sections.body: The Seattle import and the New York import contain the same core package: Spencer Haywood moved to the Knicks, while Gene Short and a future first-round pick moved to the SuperSonics. The pick later became the No. 6 selection used on James Bailey. The only major structural difference is the date, with the Seattle record showing October 23 and the Knicks record showing October 24. There is no evidence of two separate Haywood transactions between the clubs on consecutive days.

sections.heading: Basketball-Reference Supports October 24 as the Completed Transaction Date
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's 1975-76 New York Knicks transaction page lists the trade on October 24, as does Seattle's team transaction page. The NBA league transaction ledger and Eddie Donovan's executive history also use October 24. Those independently maintained Basketball-Reference surfaces agree on the effective transaction date and package. That makes the Knicks-side October 24 record the stronger canonical record for TradeVerdicts.

sections.heading: The October 23 Date Is Still Explainable as Announcement Provenance
sections.body: A contemporary Black World article dated October 30 says the Haywood trade was announced Thursday afternoon. October 23, 1975 was a Thursday, while October 24 was Friday. That gives the earlier import date a plausible origin: it may reflect the public announcement rather than the completed league transaction entry. The same article describes the return as rookie Eugene Short plus cash estimated at $1.5 million, while later transaction databases also describe the conditional 1979 first-round component. Preserving the duplicate as provenance keeps that historical wrinkle without creating a second trade page.

sections.heading: Gene Short and Eugene Short Are the Same Player
sections.body: Basketball-Reference identifies Gene Short as Eugene Short Jr., the Knicks' No. 9 pick in the 1975 draft. Seattle's legacy archive entry uses Gene Short, while the Knicks import uses Eugene Short. That naming variation does not create a different asset. Short played only seven games for Seattle before being waived on November 24, and the Knicks signed him as a free agent two days later. This review therefore treats the two names as identity variants inside the same transaction history.

sections.heading: The Conditional Pick Also Confirms the Duplicate
sections.body: The future first-round asset is not merely similar between the two rows. Both identify a 1979 conditional first-round pick that ultimately became James Bailey at No. 6. Seattle used that selection on Bailey in the 1979 draft. Matching player movement, matching future-pick outcome and matching counterpart clubs make the duplicate diagnosis decisive even before considering the one-day date discrepancy.

sections.heading: Why Supersession Is Better Than Date Correction Alone
sections.body: Simply changing the Seattle record from October 23 to October 24 would leave two canonical records with the same clubs, players and draft-pick outcome. That would duplicate the transaction across public records, player histories and historical counts. Supersession is therefore the safer structural repair. It preserves the original Seattle import for audit history, records why its date differed, and directs all reader-facing evaluation to one canonical transaction without erasing the provenance that produced the duplicate.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Record Superseded. No winner or grades are assigned to the October 23 Seattle import because evaluating it independently would double-count the same Spencer Haywood transaction. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value. Confidence is high because the team, league and executive ledgers align on October 24 and the contemporary October 23 announcement context explains rather than contradicts the earlier provenance date.

sections.heading: The November 22 Move Was a Rights Sale
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Phoenix Suns transaction page states that Phoenix sold the player rights to Mike Bantom to Seattle on November 22, 1975. Seattle's transaction page records the same acquisition, and the NBA league ledger describes the same rights sale. The legacy archive entry correctly captured the broad cash-for-player structure, but this review makes the rights language explicit and avoids inventing a sale amount that the standard ledgers do not provide.

sections.heading: Bantom Immediately Rebounded From a Small Phoenix Role
sections.body: Bantom had played only seven games for Phoenix at the start of 1975-76, averaging 3.0 points in 9.7 minutes. After the sale he appeared in 66 games for Seattle and averaged 8.4 points, 5.6 rebounds and 1.5 assists in 22.8 minutes. He also produced 2.8 win shares for the SuperSonics. That is a meaningful first-year return for a transaction in which Seattle did not surrender a player or draft pick.

sections.heading: Seattle Received a Second Season of Rotation Value
sections.body: Bantom returned in 1976-77 and played 44 more games for Seattle. His role declined to 18.1 minutes per game, but he still averaged 7.5 points and 4.2 rebounds while shooting 48.8 percent from the field. Across the two seasons, Seattle received 110 regular-season games from Bantom. The total workload matters because the transaction was not a brief rental or a player who failed to report; it produced sustained frontcourt depth across two roster cycles.

sections.heading: Phoenix's Return Was Economic Rather Than Basketball-Specific
sections.body: Phoenix received cash, and that consideration should not be treated as worthless. The problem for a hindsight basketball grade is that the amount is not stated in the standard Basketball-Reference transaction records reviewed here, and no player or draft asset returned to Phoenix that can be followed through a later basketball chain. Bantom had been the No. 8 pick in the 1973 draft and had averaged 12.5 points and 6.7 rebounds for Phoenix in 1974-75, so the Suns were selling the rights to a player who had already demonstrated rotation value.

sections.heading: The Later Career Does Not Need to Be Borrowed to Make Seattle's Case
sections.body: Bantom later produced a strong 33-game run for the New York Nets in 1976-77 and continued his career with Indiana, Philadelphia and other teams. Those later games should not be credited to Seattle unless a verified transaction return links them back to the SuperSonics. The source-backed grade does not need that extra reach. Seattle's own 110 games, 923 points and substantial rebounding output are enough to establish the value of the original rights purchase.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: SuperSonics Win, B+/C. Seattle receives a B+ because an unquantified cash payment produced 110 regular-season games, one full 66-game post-trade season and useful frontcourt production over two years. The grade stops below A territory because Bantom was a rotation player rather than a star and no major downstream Seattle asset is assigned to the transaction. Phoenix receives a C because cash had real economic value, but the amount is not preserved in the standard ledger and no traceable basketball asset came back. Confidence is high on the rights-sale structure and Bantom's Seattle production, while the cash amount remains explicitly unresolved.

sections.heading: The November 27 Four-Player Exchange Is Fully Verified
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Chicago, Cleveland and NBA league transaction ledgers agree on the same structure: the Bulls sent Nate Thurmond and Rowland Garrett to the Cavaliers for Steve Patterson and Eric Fernsten. The four-player construction in the legacy archive entry is correct. This review focuses on fixing the thin analysis, adding verified player identities and grading the realized value rather than treating every roster appearance as equivalent.

sections.heading: Thurmond Was the Deal's Transformative Piece
sections.body: Nate Thurmond played 65 regular-season games for Cleveland after the trade and averaged 4.6 points, 5.3 rebounds and 1.3 blocks in 17.4 minutes. Those regular-season numbers look modest, but his postseason role was much larger. Thurmond appeared in all 13 playoff games, averaged 28.8 minutes, 8.4 points, 11.2 rebounds and 2.8 blocks, and gave Cleveland an experienced defensive center during the franchise's run to the Eastern Conference Finals. That playoff workload is the central reason the Cavaliers' side grades so well.

sections.heading: Cleveland Also Retained Thurmond and Garrett Into 1976-77
sections.body: Thurmond returned for 49 more regular-season games in 1976-77, averaging 5.5 points, 7.6 rebounds and 1.7 blocks in 20.3 minutes. Garrett played 41 games for Cleveland immediately after the trade and another 29 the next season before moving to Milwaukee. Garrett's role was small, but he still gave the Cavaliers additional roster depth beyond Thurmond. The combination produced two seasons of value rather than a single playoff rental.

sections.heading: Chicago Received Two Rotation Bigs but Little Lasting Value
sections.body: Steve Patterson played 52 games for the Bulls after the trade, averaging 3.2 points and 3.8 rebounds in 15.0 minutes. Eric Fernsten appeared in 33 games, averaging 2.8 points and 2.1 rebounds in 7.8 minutes. Both contributed real regular-season minutes, so Chicago's return should not be graded as if the Bulls received nothing. The problem is scale: neither player approached Thurmond's postseason impact, and neither developed into a lasting Chicago asset. Patterson left the NBA after the season for Italy, while Fernsten's later NBA career unfolded elsewhere.

sections.heading: The Team Context Strengthens Cleveland's Hindsight Case
sections.body: Cleveland finished 49-33 and reached the 1976 Eastern Conference Finals, the breakthrough postseason remembered as the franchise's first deep playoff run. Thurmond was not the Cavaliers' leading scorer, but his 375 playoff minutes and 117 rebounds made him a major part of the rotation. Chicago, meanwhile, fell to 24-58 after having reached the conference finals the year before. A trade should not receive full credit or blame for team records, yet the actual roles matter: Cleveland acquired a player who materially participated in a long playoff run while Chicago received two reserves on a rebuilding season.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win, A/C+. Cleveland receives an A because Thurmond delivered 65 regular-season games, a major 13-game playoff run at 11.2 rebounds and 2.8 blocks per game, and another 49 games the next season, with Garrett adding depth across parts of two years. Chicago receives a C+ because Patterson and Fernsten combined for 85 regular-season appearances after the trade and filled rotation minutes, but neither matched Thurmond's impact or produced meaningful downstream value. Confidence is high on the four-player package and the principal outcomes.

sections.heading: The Original Deal Was Marin for Chicago's 1977 First-Round Pick
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Chicago, Buffalo and NBA transaction ledgers agree on the November 27, 1975 structure: Buffalo sent Jack Marin to the Bulls for Chicago's 1977 first-round draft choice. The pick ultimately landed at No. 13 in the 1977 draft and Tate Armstrong was selected there, but Buffalo did not hold the pick continuously until draft night. That distinction is important because the legacy archive entry made Armstrong look like a direct Braves draft return when the actual asset chain was more complicated.

sections.heading: Marin Gave Chicago 121 Regular-Season Games
sections.body: Marin immediately stepped into a real role for the Bulls. He played 67 games after the trade in 1975-76, averaging 11.0 points, 3.2 rebounds and 1.8 assists in 24.3 minutes. He returned for 54 games in 1976-77 and averaged 6.8 points in 16.1 minutes. Across the two Chicago seasons he supplied 121 regular-season appearances and more than 2,400 minutes. He was not a star by that stage of his career, but Chicago received dependable veteran wing production rather than a short rental.

sections.heading: Buffalo Converted the Pick Into Jim Price, Then Gerard and Williams
sections.body: On November 2, 1976 Buffalo traded the 1977 first-round pick to Milwaukee for Jim Price. Price played 20 games for the Braves before Buffalo moved him to Denver on December 15 for Gus Gerard and Chuck Williams. Gerard then appeared in 41 Buffalo games that season, while Williams played 44. That chain gave the Braves 105 combined regular-season appearances from Price, Gerard and Williams during 1976-77. The original pick therefore produced tangible roster value even before the asset later returned to Buffalo.

sections.heading: The No. 13 Pick Later Returned to Buffalo and Then Back to Chicago
sections.body: Milwaukee held the pick until June 7, 1977, when the Bucks sent Swen Nater and the No. 13 selection to Buffalo for the No. 3 pick that became Marques Johnson. Three days later Buffalo traded the No. 13 pick back to Chicago for the No. 24 second-round pick that became Larry Johnson; a secondary draft-transaction ledger also reports $150,000 cash going to Buffalo. Chicago then used No. 13 on Tate Armstrong. Because Buffalo had to surrender the No. 3 pick to reacquire No. 13, that later return cannot be credited solely to the 1975 Marin transaction, but it explains why Armstrong was ultimately a Bull rather than a Brave.

sections.heading: Armstrong's Career Should Not Be Treated as Buffalo's Direct Realized Outcome
sections.body: Armstrong played 92 NBA games, all for Chicago, averaging 3.8 points per game across two seasons. His modest career is relevant to the value of the No. 13 selection, but Buffalo never rostered him. The Braves' directly traceable basketball return from the original asset was the Price-to-Gerard-and-Williams chain, plus whatever value Buffalo received when the reacquired No. 13 pick was moved back to Chicago. That makes the transaction more competitive than a simple Marin-versus-Armstrong comparison.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Bulls Edge, B+/B. Chicago receives a B+ because Marin gave the club 121 regular-season games and meaningful veteran production over parts of two seasons without requiring another player in the original package. Buffalo receives a B because the first-round pick became a useful trade asset: it brought back Jim Price, who was then converted into Gus Gerard and Chuck Williams, producing substantial 1976-77 roster value. The later No. 13 pick loop is documented but not over-credited because Buffalo spent the No. 3 selection to reacquire it. Confidence is high on the original transaction, Marin's Chicago production and the pick's documented path through Milwaukee and back to Chicago.

sections.heading: The Verified December 3 Package Was Tom Owens for Cash
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Indiana Pacers transaction page states that Indiana traded cash to Kentucky for Tom Owens on December 3, 1975. Kentucky's transaction page records the mirror image, and the ABA league ledger uses the same structure. None of those standard ledgers includes future considerations. This review therefore removes the legacy future-considerations language from the verified package and retains cash as the only confirmed outgoing asset from Indiana.

sections.heading: Owens Gave Indiana a Short but Legitimate Rotation Stint
sections.body: Owens appeared in 16 games for the Pacers after the trade. He averaged 6.5 points, 4.3 rebounds and 0.7 blocks in 15.2 minutes while shooting 51.2 percent from the field and 80.0 percent from the line. In a limited role, that is useful frontcourt production rather than an empty roster transaction. Indiana was not acquiring a long-term starter, but Owens supplied real minutes during the final ABA season and gave the club another experienced center option.

sections.heading: The Pacers Recycled Owens Back Into Cash
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Indiana and San Antonio transaction logs record a January 1976 sale of Owens to the Spurs for cash. That means Indiana did not simply spend cash for 16 games and lose the asset for nothing. The Pacers received several weeks of production and then recovered another cash return. The exact amounts paid to Kentucky and received from San Antonio are not listed in the standard transaction records, so the two cash legs cannot be compared dollar for dollar. The grade must stay conservative rather than assuming Indiana made or lost money on the resale.

sections.heading: Kentucky's Return Cannot Be Overstated Without a Cash Figure
sections.body: The Colonels received cash and had already used Owens for 19 games earlier in 1975-76. Selling a reserve center for cash may have been sensible roster management, especially for a club that was also reshaping its frontcourt through the Caldwell Jones and Maurice Lucas transaction later that month. Still, there is no traceable player or draft asset coming back from the Owens sale itself. In a realized-value model, an undisclosed cash return has to be acknowledged but cannot be treated as equal to a documented player contribution without evidence.

sections.heading: Owens' Later San Antonio Production Belongs to the Next Transaction
sections.body: After leaving Indiana, Owens played 39 games for the Spurs and averaged 5.8 points and 4.0 rebounds in 13.8 minutes. Those games demonstrate that he still had rotation value, but they belong to San Antonio's acquisition rather than Indiana's December deal with Kentucky. The Pacers should receive credit for recognizing a usable player, getting 16 games from him and preserving some residual value through the later cash sale, not for the production he delivered after he left.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Pacers Edge, B-/C+. Indiana receives a B- because a cash-only acquisition produced 16 games of efficient reserve-center work and was later converted back into cash. Kentucky receives a C+ because the Colonels did receive confirmed cash, but the amount is not preserved in the standard ledger and no basketball asset can be traced from the return. The grade gap remains small because the entire Indiana tenure lasted only 16 games and both cash figures are unresolved. Confidence is high on the December 3 cash-for-Owens structure and his Indiana production. The unsupported future-considerations claim is explicitly excluded.

sections.heading: The December 18 Transaction Was a Cash Sale
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Denver Nuggets, Spirits of St. Louis and ABA league transaction pages all record the same December 18, 1975 move: Denver sent cash to St. Louis for Gus Gerard. Carl Scheer's executive record confirms the transaction. None of the standard ledgers reviewed states the amount. This review therefore preserves the cash consideration but does not invent a dollar figure or assign financial value that cannot be verified.

sections.heading: Gerard Immediately Became a Useful Denver Rotation Forward
sections.body: Gerard played 60 regular-season games for Denver after the trade in 1975-76. He averaged 9.9 points, 5.0 rebounds and 2.0 assists in 19.8 minutes while shooting 43.4 percent from the field. Basketball-Reference lists him as an ABA All-Star that season. The minutes and production are meaningful for a midseason cash purchase: Denver received a regular rotation forward rather than a fringe reserve or a short emergency stint, and Gerard remained available throughout the stretch run.

sections.heading: He Also Contributed Throughout Denver's 1976 Playoff Run
sections.body: Gerard appeared in all 13 of Denver's playoff games after the acquisition. His postseason role shrank to 10.9 minutes per game, but he still contributed 4.6 points and 2.5 rebounds while the Nuggets advanced through the ABA playoffs. That postseason availability adds value beyond the regular-season line and confirms that Gerard remained part of Denver's working rotation during the final ABA postseason.

sections.heading: Gerard Returned After the ABA-NBA Merger
sections.body: Denver retained Gerard for the franchise's first NBA season. He played 24 games in 1976-77, started 21, scored 240 points and produced 1.1 win shares in 456 minutes before being traded in December. Combining the two Denver seasons gives the club 84 regular-season games from the original cash acquisition, with useful production on both sides of the league merger. That durability makes the original legacy C-minus grade too low for the realized return.

sections.heading: Denver Later Used Gerard in the Jim Price Package
sections.body: On December 15, 1976 Denver traded Gerard and Chuck Williams to Buffalo for Jim Price. Because Williams was also required, the original Gerard purchase cannot receive full credit for Price. Still, Gerard retained enough value to function as half of the outgoing player package one year after Denver bought him for cash. Price then played 55 games for Denver in 1976-77. That downstream use strengthens the acquisition without turning it into a one-player chain.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win, B+/C. Denver receives a B+ because an undisclosed cash payment produced 84 regular-season games across the ABA and NBA, 13 playoff appearances, an ABA All-Star selection and partial downstream value in the Jim Price trade. The grade stops below A territory because Gerard was a rotation-level forward and Chuck Williams was also needed to acquire Price. St. Louis receives a C because cash had real economic value but the amount is unresolved and no basketball asset can be traced from it. Confidence is high on the sale structure and Gerard's Denver production.

sections.heading: The Authoritative Transaction Date Is January 15, 1976
sections.body: The legacy archive record carried January 6, 1976, but Basketball-Reference's Indiana Pacers transaction page, San Antonio Spurs transaction page and ABA league transaction ledger all identify January 15 as the date Indiana sold Tom Owens to San Antonio for cash. This review corrects the canonical trade date to January 15 while preserving the original record ID for continuity. The package itself is straightforward: Owens to San Antonio, cash to Indiana.

sections.heading: Owens Gave San Antonio 39 Regular-Season Games
sections.body: Owens appeared in 39 games for the Spurs after the purchase. He averaged 5.8 points, 4.0 rebounds and 1.1 assists in 13.8 minutes per game while shooting 49.5 percent from the field. That is modest production, but it is meaningful for a midseason cash acquisition. San Antonio received a dependable reserve center for the final portion of the ABA season rather than a player who barely appeared or failed to report.

sections.heading: He Also Appeared in Every Spurs Playoff Game
sections.body: Owens played in all seven San Antonio playoff games in 1976. His role stayed limited at 12.7 minutes per game, but he remained part of the postseason rotation and averaged 3.3 points and 3.4 rebounds. A cash purchase that contributes through the entire playoff run carries more realized value than a short regular-season-only stint, even if the player is not a starter or a major scorer.

sections.heading: Indiana's Return Was Cash After a Six-Week Trial
sections.body: Indiana had acquired Owens from Kentucky for cash on December 3, 1975 and used him in 16 games before selling him to San Antonio. The Pacers therefore got a short stretch of reserve production and then recovered cash. That makes the sequence more nuanced than a simple loss for Indiana. The problem for retrospective grading is that the standard ledgers do not state either cash amount, so there is no defensible way to determine whether Indiana made money, broke even or took a financial loss on the two transactions.

sections.heading: The Date Correction Also Keeps this review and this review Distinct
sections.body: this review covers Indiana's December 3 purchase of Owens from Kentucky. This review is the separate January 15 sale to San Antonio. Correcting the second date prevents the archive from implying a January 6 transaction that the primary Basketball-Reference ledgers do not support, while preserving the real six-week Indiana tenure between the two moves. The player source reference is updated to the same corrected date so the player-history links and canonical record stay aligned.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Spurs Win, B-/C. San Antonio receives a B- because cash produced 39 regular-season games and seven playoff appearances from a usable reserve center. The grade stays modest because Owens averaged fewer than fourteen minutes per game and did not become a long-term Spurs asset. Indiana receives a C because the Pacers did receive cash after using Owens for 16 games, but the amount is unresolved and no later basketball asset can be traced from the return. Confidence is high on the January 15 date, cash-sale structure and San Antonio production.

sections.heading: The January 27 Three-Player Package Is Verified
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's New York Nets, Virginia Squires and ABA league transaction ledgers all record the same January 27, 1976 exchange: New York sent Swen Nater and Billy Schaeffer to Virginia for Jim Eakins. This review also corrects the legacy Bill Schaeffer label to the Basketball-Reference identity Billy Schaeffer. There is no cash or draft component in the authoritative ledger, so the evaluation can focus directly on what the three players produced after the trade.

sections.heading: Eakins Became a Championship Rotation Center for the Nets
sections.body: Eakins played 34 regular-season games for New York after the trade, averaging 6.2 points, 3.5 rebounds and 0.6 blocks in 13.6 minutes while shooting 50.3 percent from the field. His role expanded in the playoffs. He appeared in all 13 postseason games, averaged 21.6 minutes, 6.8 points and 6.0 rebounds, and was part of the rotation as the Nets defeated San Antonio and Denver to win the final ABA championship. That postseason contribution materially changes the hindsight value of the deal.

sections.heading: Virginia Received the Best Regular-Season Player in Nater
sections.body: Swen Nater was clearly the strongest regular-season performer in the package after the trade. He played 33 games for Virginia and averaged 11.3 points, 9.8 rebounds and 1.1 assists in 23.5 minutes while shooting 49.8 percent. Nater had already been a major rebounder in the ABA, and his Squires production confirms that he remained a starting-caliber interior player. If the trade were judged only by regular-season box-score output, Virginia would have the stronger case.

sections.heading: Schaeffer Added Another 31 Games for the Squires
sections.body: Billy Schaeffer also contributed immediately, playing 31 games for Virginia at 6.6 points and 2.9 rebounds in 16.7 minutes. His role was smaller than Nater's, but the two outgoing Nets combined for 64 Squires appearances after the deal. That is substantial short-term volume and prevents the transaction from being graded as a New York landslide. Virginia received two usable players, not one star plus a throw-in who never appeared.

sections.heading: The Championship Context Breaks the Near Tie
sections.body: New York gave up the better regular-season package, but Eakins filled a role that mattered during the most important games of the season. He played every playoff game and increased his rebounding from 3.5 per game in the regular season to 6.0 in the postseason. The Nets did not acquire a star, yet they acquired a center who could handle more than twenty playoff minutes per night on the team that won the ABA title. That kind of direct postseason utility is a legitimate realized outcome and should not be erased by Nater's superior regular-season averages.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Nets Edge, B+/B. New York receives a B+ because Eakins supplied 34 regular-season games and then became a 21.6-minute postseason rotation center across all 13 games of the 1976 ABA championship run. Virginia receives a B because Nater was the best regular-season player in the transaction and Schaeffer added useful depth, combining for 64 Squires appearances. The margin is intentionally narrow: the Squires won the regular-season production comparison, while the Nets received the more consequential postseason result. Confidence is high on the package and direct 1975-76 outcomes.

sections.heading: The Verified Package Was Shumate for Heard and One 1976 Second-Round Pick
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Buffalo Braves, Phoenix Suns and NBA league transaction ledgers agree on the February 1, 1976 structure: Buffalo sent Gar Heard and a 1976 second-round pick to Phoenix for John Shumate. The pick became No. 30 Al Fleming. None of those authoritative ledgers includes the legacy 1978 second-round pick that was labeled as No. 41 Jerome Whitehead. This review therefore removes that unsupported asset from the verified package and disconnects Whitehead from this trade's player-history linkage.

sections.heading: Heard Became a Major Part of Phoenix's 1976 Finals Run
sections.body: Gar Heard played 36 regular-season games for Phoenix after the trade, averaging 12.4 points and 9.9 rebounds in 33.9 minutes. His postseason role was even more important. Heard appeared in all 19 Suns playoff games, averaged 13.9 points, 10.4 rebounds, 2.1 steals and 1.9 blocks, and helped Phoenix reach the NBA Finals. That immediate two-way playoff production is the strongest single realized outcome in the deal.

sections.heading: Phoenix Kept Heard for Two More Seasons
sections.body: Heard returned for 46 games in 1976-77 and 80 in 1977-78, giving Phoenix 162 regular-season appearances across parts of three seasons from the original transaction. His scoring declined after the Finals run, but he continued to rebound, defend and play substantial minutes. The extra longevity separates the return from a short postseason rental and gives Phoenix a strong multi-year case even before considering the draft pick.

sections.heading: The Al Fleming Pick Produced No Suns Games
sections.body: Phoenix used the acquired second-round pick at No. 30 on Al Fleming in the 1976 draft. Fleming did not play for the Suns and is listed as not playing after being waived in 1976-77. He later reached the NBA with Seattle in 1977-78, but those games are not Phoenix value. The pick therefore adds draft optionality to the transaction but no realized Suns production. Heard, not Fleming, carries the Phoenix grade.

sections.heading: Shumate Was an Excellent Buffalo Return
sections.body: John Shumate immediately became a major Braves frontcourt player. He appeared in 32 games after the trade at 12.2 points and 9.8 rebounds, then played 74 games in 1976-77 at 15.1 points and 9.5 rebounds and another 18 in 1977-78. He also averaged 14.1 points and 8.6 rebounds across nine playoff games in 1976. Buffalo therefore received 124 regular-season games of strong production, making this a competitive trade rather than a one-sided Phoenix win.

sections.heading: Shumate Retained Some Downstream Trade Value
sections.body: On November 23, 1977 Buffalo included Shumate, Gus Gerard and a 1979 first-round pick in a larger deal with Detroit for Marvin Barnes and two 1978 draft picks. Because Gerard and a first-rounder were also required, this review gives Shumate only partial downstream credit. The later package still shows that he retained trade value after nearly two productive Braves seasons. It also reinforces why Buffalo's side remains close to Phoenix's despite Heard's superior longevity and deeper 1976 playoff run.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Suns Edge, A-/B+. Phoenix receives an A- because Heard delivered 162 regular-season games, three seasons of frontcourt value and a major 19-game playoff run to the 1976 NBA Finals. The No. 30 pick produced no Suns games, so the grade is driven by Heard rather than draft luck. Buffalo receives a B+ because Shumate gave the Braves 124 regular-season games, strong scoring and rebounding, nine playoff appearances and partial downstream trade value. The margin stays narrow, but Heard's longer Phoenix tenure and much deeper 1976 postseason role break the tie. Confidence is high on the corrected package and direct outcomes.

sections.heading: The Verified Return Was Cash, Not Future Considerations
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's New York Nets transaction page, Kentucky Colonels transaction page and ABA league ledger all place the move on February 15, 1976 and describe the same structure: Kentucky sent Ted McClain to New York for cash. None of those sources lists future considerations. This review therefore replaces the legacy future-considerations asset with a verified cash return while leaving the amount unresolved because the standard ledgers do not publish it.

sections.heading: McClain Immediately Became a Regular Nets Guard
sections.body: McClain played 30 regular-season games for New York after the purchase. He averaged 11.3 points, 3.5 assists, 2.4 rebounds and 1.9 steals in 23.2 minutes while shooting 42.2 percent from the field and 81.2 percent from the line. Those are meaningful rotation numbers for a mid-February acquisition. The Nets were not buying an end-of-bench player; they added a veteran guard who could handle more than twenty minutes per night during the final stretch of the ABA season.

sections.heading: He Also Contributed During the 1976 Championship Run
sections.body: McClain appeared in eight playoff games for New York, including five games in the semifinal series against San Antonio and three in the ABA Finals against Denver. His postseason role was smaller than his regular-season role, but he remained part of the active rotation on the team that won the final ABA championship. That direct championship-season contribution gives the transaction more realized basketball value than a simple cash purchase with no postseason impact.

sections.heading: Kentucky's Side Is Economically Real but Basketball-Opaque
sections.body: The Colonels received cash, and the sale should not be treated as if Kentucky got nothing. The difficulty is that the surviving standard transaction ledgers do not state the dollar amount, and no named player or draft asset came back in the transaction that can be followed through a later chain. Kentucky had already received 43 games from McClain earlier in the season, where he averaged 7.7 points and 4.7 assists, before converting him into cash in February.

sections.heading: The Timing Favors New York's Competitive Window
sections.body: New York was preparing for a championship push and added a veteran backcourt contributor without surrendering a roster player or draft choice. McClain's 30 regular-season games and eight playoff appearances fit that short-term objective well. Kentucky's financial motivation may also have been reasonable, but the retrospective basketball archive can measure McClain's Nets role much more precisely than it can measure an undisclosed cash return. That asymmetry is why the grading advantage belongs to New York without pretending the Colonels' side had zero value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win, B+/C. New York receives a B+ because a cash-only acquisition produced 30 regular-season games at 11.3 points and 3.5 assists per game plus eight playoff appearances during the 1976 ABA championship run. The grade stays below A territory because McClain was a rotation guard rather than a primary star and the Nets' postseason core was led elsewhere. Kentucky receives a C because cash had real economic value, but the amount is unresolved and no traceable basketball asset came back. Confidence is high on the date, cash-sale structure and McClain's direct New York production.
