sections.heading: The June 3 Deal Was a Straight Second-Round Pick Swap
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Portland Trail Blazers, New Orleans Jazz and NBA league transaction ledgers all record the same exchange: Portland sent its 1976 second-round pick to New Orleans for the Jazz's 1977 second-round pick. New Orleans used the 1976 selection at No. 26 on Jacky Dorsey, while Portland later used the 1977 selection at No. 28 on Kim Anderson. The legacy structure is correct; this review adds the actual player outcomes and distinguishes later NBA careers from value realized by the teams that owned the picks.

sections.heading: New Orleans Selected Jacky Dorsey but Received No NBA Games
sections.body: The Jazz selected Dorsey No. 26 in the 1976 draft. Basketball-Reference lists him as playing in the Eastern Basketball Association rather than the NBA in 1976-77, and he never appeared in a regular-season game for New Orleans. Dorsey did eventually reach the NBA in 1977-78, but his first games came with Denver and later Portland. Those appearances demonstrate that the pick identified an NBA-caliber player, yet they cannot be credited to the Jazz because New Orleans did not realize that production.

sections.heading: Portland Waited a Year for Kim Anderson
sections.body: Portland used the incoming 1977 second-round pick at No. 28 on Kim Anderson. Anderson spent 1977-78 playing professionally in Italy rather than joining the Trail Blazers immediately. He reached Portland in 1978-79 and appeared in 21 games, averaging 3.0 points, 2.1 rebounds and 0.7 assists in 10.7 minutes. The production was limited and his field-goal percentage was only 31.2 percent, but the pick did eventually generate real NBA minutes for the team that acquired it.

sections.heading: The Later Dorsey Career Does Not Reverse the Jazz Outcome
sections.body: Dorsey played 11 NBA games across Denver and Portland in 1977-78 and later appeared for Houston. Those games matter to his career history but not to the realized return from this New Orleans trade. A draft pick's hindsight value should follow the team that actually retained and used the player, not automatically inherit every game the drafted player later produced elsewhere. That rule prevents the Jazz from receiving credit for Dorsey's Denver, Portland or Houston appearances after he failed to play for New Orleans.

sections.heading: The Difference Remains Small Because Anderson's Portland Role Was Small
sections.body: Portland's 21 games from Anderson are enough to separate the outcomes, but not enough to make this a major win. Anderson totaled only 224 minutes in his lone Trail Blazers season and scored 63 points. New Orleans received no direct NBA games from Dorsey, but the Jazz did secure a second-round prospect one year earlier than the pick they surrendered. The swap therefore remains a low-value transaction where the grade gap should be compressed rather than inflated.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Blazers Edge, C+/C. Portland receives a C+ because the 1977 No. 28 pick eventually produced 21 Trail Blazers games from Kim Anderson, even though the contribution was modest and delayed by a season in Italy. New Orleans receives a C because the 1976 No. 26 pick became Jacky Dorsey, who never played an NBA regular-season game for the Jazz. Dorsey's later NBA career belongs to other teams and does not erase that zero-game New Orleans outcome. Confidence is high on the pick swap and draft outcomes.

sections.heading: The Package and Draft Outcomes Are Fully Verified
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Atlanta and Houston transaction records agree on the June 7, 1976 structure: Atlanta sent Dwight Jones and the 1976 No. 1 pick to Houston for Gus Bailey, Joe Meriweather and the No. 9 pick. Houston used No. 1 on John Lucas Jr.; Atlanta used No. 9 on Armond Hill the next day. This review preserves that five-asset structure and attaches the direct player and draft-outcome identities.

sections.heading: Houston Received a Starting Guard and a Durable Big
sections.body: Lucas played all 82 games as a rookie, averaging 11.1 points, 5.6 assists and 1.5 steals in 30.9 minutes while earning All-Rookie recognition. He returned in 1977-78 and again played all 82 games, this time averaging 12.4 points and 9.4 assists. Dwight Jones supplied frontcourt depth across three Houston seasons, appearing in 74 games in 1976-77, 82 in 1977-78 and 81 in 1978-79. The Rockets therefore received immediate help from both the established player and the premium pick.

sections.heading: Atlanta Turned the No. 9 Pick Into a Multi-Year Point Guard
sections.body: Armond Hill played 81 games as a rookie and averaged 5.0 assists, then started all 82 games in both 1977-78 and 1978-79. He added 79 more games in 1979-80, giving Atlanta 324 appearances over his first four seasons alone. Hill was not the same caliber of prospect as the No. 1 selection, but he became a stable backcourt piece for several years and gave the Hawks substantial realized value from the pick swap.

sections.heading: Meriweather Was Also a Strong Immediate Return
sections.body: Joe Meriweather played 74 games for Atlanta in 1976-77 and averaged 11.1 points, 8.1 rebounds and 1.1 blocks in 27.9 minutes. He produced 4.8 win shares before moving on the next season. Gus Bailey did not play for Atlanta and was waived, so the Hawks' player return is driven overwhelmingly by Meriweather rather than Bailey. Even so, Meriweather plus Hill created a productive two-part return that balances much of Houston's Lucas-and-Jones package.

sections.heading: The Trade Worked for Both Sides for Different Reasons
sections.body: Houston received the best single draft slot and turned it into a guard who immediately played major minutes, while also adding a useful veteran big. Atlanta moved down eight spots but landed Hill and added a starting-caliber center in Meriweather. The draft-position gap is real, yet the Hawks converted their lower pick well enough that the practical results remained competitive rather than one-sided.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, A-/A-. Houston receives an A- for two full seasons of major Lucas production plus three years of Dwight Jones frontcourt minutes. Atlanta receives an A- because Armond Hill became a multi-year starter and Joe Meriweather delivered a strong 74-game season immediately after the trade. Bailey contributed no Atlanta games, which keeps the Hawks from grading higher, while Lucas leaving Houston after only two seasons prevents the Rockets from separating decisively. Confidence is high on the package, draft outcomes and first-stage realized production.

sections.heading: The June 16 Package Is Fully Verified
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Atlanta Hawks, Buffalo Braves and NBA transaction ledgers agree that Atlanta sent Tom Van Arsdale to Buffalo for Ken Charles, Dick Gibbs and cash on June 16, 1976. Executive records for Bud Seretean and Bob MacKinnon repeat the same structure. This review therefore preserves the legacy four-asset package and replaces the thin evaluation with the actual realized outcomes.

sections.heading: Ken Charles Became Atlanta's Main Return
sections.body: Charles played all 82 games for the Hawks in 1976-77 and averaged 11.1 points, 2.0 rebounds, 3.6 assists and 1.7 steals in 30.3 minutes. He returned for 21 more games in 1977-78, giving Atlanta 103 regular-season appearances and more than 3,000 minutes from the deal. His first Hawks season was a genuine full-time rotation role rather than a reserve cameo.

sections.heading: Dick Gibbs Added No Atlanta NBA Games
sections.body: Gibbs had played 72 games for Buffalo in 1975-76, but his NBA career ended after that season. He did not appear in a regular-season game for Atlanta following the June trade. That makes him a zero-game basketball return in this transaction. The Hawks still received cash in addition to Charles, but the amount is not stated in the standard transaction ledgers and is not assigned unsupported value.

sections.heading: Buffalo Immediately Recycled Van Arsdale
sections.body: Van Arsdale never played a regular-season game for the Braves. On August 25, 1976, Buffalo traded him to Phoenix for a 1977 second-round pick. That means Buffalo did preserve some asset value rather than losing the veteran for nothing, but the June trade itself produced no on-court Buffalo contribution. The later pick should be recognized as downstream value without being overstated, especially because the 1977 second-round draft chain around Buffalo and Milwaukee contains multiple transactions. The important source-backed point is simpler: Buffalo never received on-court production from Van Arsdale, while Atlanta received a full season of meaningful guard play from Charles. That contrast is firm even if the exact downstream value of Buffalo's later pick is treated conservatively.

sections.heading: Atlanta Clearly Received the Better Immediate Basketball Return
sections.body: Charles' 103 Hawks games provide a straightforward realized return, and the cash component adds some unquantified value. Buffalo used Van Arsdale as a trade chip rather than a player, so the Braves' success depends on what the later Phoenix pick became. That is a weaker and less direct return than a productive full season plus additional games from Charles, especially in a realized-value model centered on documented NBA contribution.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win, B+/C+. Atlanta receives a B+ because Ken Charles delivered 103 games, including an 82-game season at 11.1 points and 3.6 assists, while the Hawks also received cash. The grade stops below A territory because Gibbs produced no Atlanta games and the cash amount is unresolved. Buffalo receives a C+ because Van Arsdale never played for the Braves but was successfully flipped to Phoenix for a future second-round pick. Confidence is high on the package and direct player outcomes.

sections.heading: The August 5 Structure Is Fully Verified
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Denver and Philadelphia transaction ledgers agree that the Nuggets sent a 1977 second-round pick to the 76ers for Fatty Taylor on August 5, 1976. Carl Scheer's executive record confirms the same exchange, and Denver's own media guide lists Taylor as an August 5 acquisition for the pick that became Herm Harris. Pro Sports Transactions independently traces the selection to No. 43 in the 1977 draft.

sections.heading: Denver Received a Real Rotation Guard Immediately
sections.body: Taylor played 79 regular-season games for Denver in 1976-77 and averaged 19.6 minutes, 3.8 points, 2.7 rebounds, 3.6 assists and 1.7 steals. He was no longer the high-usage ABA guard he had been earlier in the decade, but he still gave the Nuggets a steady defensive and ball-handling option throughout their first NBA season. Denver finished 50-32 and first in the Midwest Division, and Taylor was available almost every night.

sections.heading: The Postseason Contribution Was Minimal but the Regular Season Was Not
sections.body: Taylor appeared in only one playoff game and logged a single minute, so this review does not inflate his value by treating him as an important postseason piece. The trade's Denver case rests on the 79-game regular-season body of work. That distinction matters because the acquisition was useful without being transformative. Denver still received a full regular-season rotation player for the price of one future second-round selection. Taylor filled a role for one season, then Denver waived him in October 1977.

sections.heading: Philadelphia's Pick Became Herm Harris at No. 43
sections.body: The 76ers used the acquired second-round pick on Herm Harris, a 6-foot-5 forward from Arizona, with the 43rd overall selection in the 1977 NBA draft. Basketball-Reference's draft page lists no NBA seasons or games for Harris. In a realized-value model, the pick therefore produced no NBA on-court return for Philadelphia. The draft choice still had legitimate option value when acquired, but hindsight grading must reflect what actually materialized in NBA competition.

sections.heading: The Rights Language Is Historically Accurate
sections.body: Secondary transaction records often describe Denver as acquiring Taylor's draft rights because Philadelphia had originally selected him in the 12th round of the 1969 NBA draft even though he built his career in the ABA. RealGM and Denver's historical records both preserve that rights-based framing. Taylor then signed with Denver on the same August 5 date and entered the Nuggets' 1976-77 roster, so the practical outcome is straightforward: Denver converted the rights into an active player immediately.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win, B/D+. Denver receives a B because one second-round pick produced 79 games of dependable rotation play during a 50-win season, including useful passing and steal production, even though Taylor lasted only one NBA season with the club and barely played in the postseason. Philadelphia receives a D+ because the pick became Herm Harris at No. 43 and Harris never played an NBA regular-season game. Confidence is high on the transaction structure, Taylor's Denver production and the draft outcome.

sections.heading: The Martin Trade and the Gilliam Sale Were Separate Transactions
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Seattle, Portland and NBA transaction ledgers all list two distinct September 2, 1976 moves between the same clubs. Seattle sold the player rights to Herm Gilliam to Portland, and Portland separately traded LaRue Martin to Seattle for future considerations. Harry Glickman's Portland executive record and Bill Russell's Seattle executive record preserve the same separation. This review therefore evaluates only Martin for future considerations and does not fold Gilliam into the exchange.

sections.heading: The Future Consideration Was Conditional on Martin Making the Team
sections.body: The standard Basketball-Reference ledgers do not identify the future consideration by round, but an archival Portland account of a September 3 report quotes Russell clarifying that Seattle had not traded a first-round pick. Russell said the consideration would be a 1977 draft pick and that it was conditional on Martin making Seattle's opening-day roster. That detail resolves the legacy "not exercised" note: the draft asset existed only if the roster condition was satisfied.

sections.heading: Seattle Waived Martin Before the Regular Season
sections.body: RealGM records Seattle acquiring Martin on September 2, placing him on waivers on October 12 and Martin becoming a free agent on October 14. Basketball-Reference's career page lists four NBA seasons, all with Portland, ending in 1975-76. Martin therefore produced zero regular-season games, minutes or points for Seattle. The SuperSonics took a low-cost look at a former No. 1 overall pick, but the basketball return from the transaction was zero.

sections.heading: Portland's Return Also Finished at Zero
sections.body: Because Martin did not make Seattle's opening-day roster, the conditional 1977 pick never became an exercised Portland asset. No draft selection or player outcome should be assigned to the Trail Blazers from this transaction. Herm Gilliam did appear in 18 games for Portland in 1976-77, but that value came from the separate same-day rights sale and cannot be used to improve Portland's grade on the Martin deal.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, D/D. Seattle receives a D because Martin never played a regular-season game for the SuperSonics and was waived before opening day. Portland also receives a D because the conditional 1977 draft consideration did not trigger, leaving the Trail Blazers with no realized asset from this specific exchange. The transaction was inexpensive for Seattle and allowed Portland to move on from Martin, so neither side warrants an F, but neither side generated measurable on-court or draft value from the deal itself. Confidence is high on the transaction, the separate Gilliam sale, Martin's waiver and the zero-game outcome; the exact round of the conditional 1977 pick remains unspecified.

sources.title: September 3, 1976 Bill Russell clarification on Martin consideration

sections.heading: The Gilliam Rights Sale Was Separate From the LaRue Martin Trade
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Seattle, Portland and NBA transaction ledgers list two distinct September 2, 1976 transactions between the clubs. Seattle sold the player rights to Herm Gilliam to Portland, while Portland separately sent LaRue Martin to Seattle for future considerations. Bill Russell's Seattle executive record and Harry Glickman's Portland executive record preserve the same separation. This review therefore grades Gilliam for cash on its own and does not import Martin or the conditional 1977 pick into this exchange.

sections.heading: Gilliam Became a Real Rotation Piece in Portland
sections.body: Gilliam had already played for Seattle in 1975-76 before the rights sale. With Portland in 1976-77, Basketball-Reference credits him with 80 regular-season games and 1,665 minutes. He averaged 9.3 points, 2.5 rebounds and 2.1 assists in 20.8 minutes per game while shooting 43.8 percent from the field. That is substantial realized value for an acquisition whose documented outgoing asset is cash rather than a player or draft pick.

sections.heading: The Value Extended Into Portland's Championship Run
sections.body: The regular season was not the end of Gilliam's contribution. Basketball-Reference's postseason record shows him appearing in 18 playoff games for Portland, totaling 295 minutes and averaging 6.4 points. Portland won the 1977 NBA championship, and Gilliam was part of that playoff rotation. The title should not turn every reserve into an elite trade return, but it is legitimate hindsight value when the acquired player actually appeared throughout the postseason run.

sections.heading: Seattle's Cash Return Is Real but Unpriced
sections.body: Seattle's side of the transaction is documented as cash. None of the reviewed Basketball-Reference or RealGM records identifies the amount, so this review does not invent a dollar figure or pretend to know how materially it affected the club. Cash has genuine transaction value, especially for a veteran whose rights Seattle was willing to move, but an unpriced financial return cannot be credited like a productive player season. The conservative approach is to give Seattle some value without equating the unknown cash with Gilliam's documented NBA production.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Blazers Win, B+/C. Portland receives a B+ because Gilliam delivered 80 regular-season games, meaningful reserve scoring and 18 playoff appearances during a championship season for a cash-only cost. Seattle receives a C because it converted Gilliam's rights into financial consideration, but the amount is unverified and there is no player or draft asset to trace forward. Confidence is high on the transaction structure and Gilliam's Portland production, while the unknown cash amount keeps Seattle's side from being graded more precisely.

sections.heading: The Primary Record Shows McNeill for a 1977 Third-Round Pick
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Kansas City, New York and NBA transaction ledgers all record the September 9, 1976 exchange as Larry McNeill to the Nets for a 1977 third-round draft pick. The Nets' own historical media guide says the same thing and identifies the eventual selection as Bill Paterno. None of those primary-style records lists cash. Pro Sports Transactions does preserve a UPI-based note that cash was also included, while also flagging conflicting reporting around the transaction date. This review therefore keeps the cash report visible as secondary evidence but does not treat it as a fully verified primary-ledger asset.

sections.heading: McNeill Gave New York Only a Brief Regular-Season Return
sections.body: McNeill had been a useful Kansas City reserve and part-time starter before the trade, appearing in all 82 games in 1975-76. His New York stint was much shorter. Basketball-Reference credits him with eight Nets games, 93 total minutes, 60 points and 26 rebounds in 1976-77. On a per-game basis he averaged 7.5 points and 3.3 rebounds in 11.6 minutes. That is real realized value, but the sample is too small to treat the acquisition as a successful long-term rotation move.

sections.heading: The Nets Waived Him in December
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's league and Nets transaction pages show New York waiving McNeill on December 13, 1976. RealGM independently records the same waiver, followed by free agency two days later. He did not return to the Nets. Golden State signed him on February 24, 1977, so his later 16-game Warriors stint belongs to a separate free-agent transaction and cannot be credited to New York here. This review grades only the eight games the Nets actually received from the September trade.

sections.heading: Kansas City Used the Pick on Bill Paterno at No. 45
sections.body: The pick outcome is fully traceable. Kansas City selected Notre Dame forward Bill Paterno with the first pick of the third round, No. 45 overall, in the 1977 NBA Draft. Basketball-Reference's Kings transaction log and Paterno player page both identify that selection. Paterno has no NBA regular-season statistical record, so the pick produced no realized NBA playing value for Kansas City. The draft asset had option value when acquired, but its completed on-court outcome was zero.

sections.heading: The Cash Report Does Not Create a Measurable Kings Advantage
sections.body: Pro Sports Transactions says a UPI report included cash in addition to the third-rounder. Because the amount is not identified and the Basketball-Reference ledgers plus the Nets' historical media guide omit cash entirely, this review discounts that component heavily. It is reasonable to preserve the possibility that Kansas City received some financial consideration, but there is not enough verified information to price it or use it to overturn the direct basketball comparison.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Nets Edge, C+/C. New York receives a C+ because McNeill at least produced eight regular-season games and 93 minutes before being waived. Kansas City receives a C because the acquired third-round pick became Bill Paterno, who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game; the secondary cash report adds some possible transaction value but cannot be measured confidently. The margin is intentionally small. Confidence is high on the player-for-pick structure, McNeill's Nets production and the Paterno draft outcome, while the cash component remains secondary-source-only.

sources.title: 1996 New Jersey Nets Media Guide - NBA trade history

sections.heading: The Exchange Is One of the Deepest Packages of the Merger Era
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Kansas City, New York and league transaction ledgers agree on the September 10, 1976 structure. The Kings sent Tiny Archibald to the Nets for Jim Eakins, Brian Taylor, New York's 1977 first-round pick and its 1978 first-round pick. Those selections became Otis Birdsong at No. 2 in 1977 and Phil Ford at No. 2 in 1978. Joe Axelson's Kansas City executive ledger and Roy Boe's Nets ledger record the same package. Unlike several nearby 1976 trades, there is no material source conflict over the core assets.

sections.heading: Brian Taylor Was an Immediate High-Level Return
sections.body: Taylor gave Kansas City 72 games in 1976-77 and immediately became one of the club's best guards. He averaged 17.0 points, 4.4 assists and 2.8 steals in 34.6 minutes while shooting 50.4 percent from the field, and he earned NBA All-Defensive Second Team honors. That is substantial direct value before the draft picks even enter the equation. Kansas City then used Taylor in a May 1977 package with another first-round pick to acquire Tom Burleson and a second-round selection, so Taylor also retained transaction value beyond his one Kings season. Because that later deal contained another premium asset, this review credits the downstream return only partially.

sections.heading: Jim Eakins Added a Full Season of Frontcourt Depth
sections.body: Eakins was less valuable than Taylor but still produced a complete NBA season. He appeared in all 82 games for Kansas City in 1976-77, averaging 6.0 points and 4.4 rebounds in 16.3 minutes. His role was modest, yet it matters in a trade that already delivered two future No. 2 picks. The Kings did not have to wait for the draft assets to mature before receiving useful rotation minutes from the incoming veterans.

sections.heading: Otis Birdsong Became a Multi-Year Kansas City Star
sections.body: The 1977 first-round pick became Birdsong at No. 2 overall. Across four Kansas City seasons he played 308 regular-season games and developed from a 15.8-point rookie into one of the league's top scoring guards. He made the All-Star team in 1979, 1980 and 1981, averaged 24.6 points in 1980-81 and earned All-NBA Second Team honors that season. In June 1981 Kansas City traded Birdsong and a second-round pick to New Jersey for Cliff Robinson, adding another traceable asset conversion after four strong seasons of production.

sections.heading: Phil Ford Made the Second First-Rounder Pay Off Immediately
sections.body: The 1978 first-round pick also landed at No. 2, where Kansas City selected Phil Ford. Ford played 79 games as a rookie, averaged 15.9 points and 8.6 assists, won Rookie of the Year and made All-NBA Second Team. He remained the Kings' starting-level point guard beyond that first season. Two consecutive No. 2 selections turning into Birdsong and Ford is the central reason Kansas City's hindsight grade reaches the top tier: the draft portion of the return produced two major backcourt pieces rather than merely retaining theoretical pick value.

sections.heading: Archibald Still Produced Star-Level Numbers for the Nets
sections.body: New York's direct return was shortened, not empty. Archibald played 34 games in 1976-77 and averaged 20.5 points and 7.5 assists in 37.6 minutes. Basketball-Reference lists his next season as missed because of an Achilles injury, but the Nets had already moved him before that 1977-78 season began. On September 1, 1977 New Jersey traded Archibald to Buffalo. The Nets' historical media guide identifies the return as George Johnson, Houston's 1978 first-round pick and Buffalo's 1979 first-round pick. That distinction is important: Archibald did not simply leave New York for nothing.

sections.heading: New Jersey Recovered Substantial Downstream Value
sections.body: The two Buffalo-trade picks continued to produce value, although not in a straight line. The Houston-origin 1978 first was the No. 4 selection later used on Micheal Ray Richardson, but New Jersey did not make that pick. In June 1978 the Nets packaged it with another 1979 first in a settlement with the Knicks and received Phil Jackson plus the No. 13 pick that became Winford Boynes, so only part of that later return belongs to the Archibald asset chain. Buffalo's 1979 first stayed with New Jersey and became No. 11 Cliff Robinson. Robinson averaged 13.6 points as a rookie and 19.5 in his second season. In June 1981 the Nets traded Robinson to Kansas City for Birdsong and a second-round pick, bringing one of the original Kings assets back to New Jersey through the Archibald exit chain.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Win, A+/A-. Kansas City receives an A+ because the return produced a full season from Taylor, 82 games from Eakins, four high-level Birdsong seasons and a Rookie of the Year/All-NBA start from Ford. New York receives an A- rather than the legacy F because Archibald was still a 20-point, seven-assist player in his 34 Nets games and, more importantly, retained enough market value to bring back Johnson and two first-round assets. One of those picks became part of a later settlement package and the other became Robinson, who eventually brought Birdsong back to the Nets. The Kings still generated the deeper direct return and the best combined draft outcome, but the source-backed asset chain shows that both franchises realized substantial value.

sections.heading: The Primary Ledgers Agree This Was a Cash Rights Sale
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Buffalo, New York and NBA transaction pages all record the same September 10, 1976 structure: the Braves sold the player rights to Jim McMillian to the Knicks. The New York page describes the acquisition of McMillian's rights, while the Buffalo and league ledgers explicitly use the word "sold." No player or draft pick is listed going back to Buffalo. The legacy cash asset is therefore directionally correct, but the reviewed records do not state an amount. This review keeps the financial return unpriced rather than inventing a figure.

sections.heading: McMillian Became an Immediate Knicks Starter
sections.body: McMillian was not merely an end-of-bench veteran. In 1976-77 he played 67 games, started 60 and averaged 32.2 minutes, 9.9 points, 4.6 rebounds and 2.1 assists while shooting 46.4 percent from the field. New York finished 40-42, so the acquisition did not create a major team-level jump, but the Knicks received more than 2,100 regular-season minutes from him in the first year alone. That is substantial realized value for a transaction whose only documented outgoing consideration is cash.

sections.heading: The Second Season Added Durability and Playoff Minutes
sections.body: McMillian returned for 81 games and 63 starts in 1977-78. He averaged 8.5 points, 3.6 rebounds and 2.5 assists in 24.4 minutes, giving New York another full season of wing depth. The Knicks reached the 1978 playoffs, and McMillian started all six postseason games, averaging 8.8 points and 3.5 rebounds in 22.3 minutes. Across the two regular seasons, New York received 148 games and 123 starts. The scoring role had declined from McMillian's Buffalo years, but the volume of usable NBA minutes is clear.

sections.heading: New York Also Recovered a Compensatory Pick
sections.body: McMillian became a restricted veteran free agent after the 1977-78 season. Portland signed him in December 1978, and Basketball-Reference records New York receiving a 1979 second-round pick as compensation. The Knicks used that selection at No. 34 on San Diego State forward Kim Goetz. Goetz never appeared in an NBA regular-season game, so the downstream draft outcome added no on-court value, but the Knicks still extracted a second asset after two seasons of McMillian production. That preserved value strengthens the acquisition even though the pick itself did not hit.

sections.heading: Buffalo's Return Cannot Be Valued Beyond the Cash Proceeds
sections.body: The Braves' side is straightforward but difficult to quantify. Buffalo converted McMillian's rights into cash and did not surrender a draft asset or player in addition to those rights. Cash has legitimate franchise value, yet the amount is not disclosed in the reviewed transaction ledgers and there is no basketball asset to trace forward. This review therefore does not assign Buffalo a failing grade simply because New York got useful production, but it also cannot credit an unknown financial return as if it matched 148 games and later pick compensation.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win, B+/C. New York receives a B+ because McMillian supplied two full seasons of meaningful minutes, 123 starts and six playoff starts, then generated a 1979 second-round compensation pick when he left for Portland. The pick became Kim Goetz and produced no NBA games, which keeps the return below the highest grades. Buffalo receives a C because it obtained cash in a documented rights sale without taking back a basketball obligation, but the amount is unverified and cannot be compared directly with McMillian's realized production. Confidence is high on the transaction structure and player outcome, with only the cash valuation remaining unknown.

sections.heading: The Ledgers Resolve the Future Considerations as a Third-Round Pick
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Chicago, Washington and league transaction pages all record the September 13, 1976 exchange as Tom Kropp to the Bulls for a 1977 third-round draft pick. Chicago's official historical media guide uses the broader phrase "future considerations" for the same acquisition. Those descriptions are not mutually exclusive: the league and team transaction ledgers identify the specific draft asset that later satisfied the consideration. This review therefore keeps the pick as the verified outgoing Chicago asset rather than leaving the return unresolved.

sections.heading: Kropp Gave Chicago One Useful Bench Season
sections.body: Kropp was a fringe Washington player before the trade, appearing in 25 games but only 72 total minutes for the Bullets in 1975-76. Chicago gave him a much larger role. In 1976-77 he played 53 games and 480 minutes, scoring 174 points while shooting 48.0 percent from the field. His per-game line was modest at 3.3 points, 0.9 rebounds and 0.7 assists in 9.1 minutes, but the Bulls received a full season of usable reserve minutes rather than an empty roster transaction.

sections.heading: His Chicago Tenure Ended After One Season
sections.body: The return did not develop into a long-term rotation piece. Basketball-Reference credits Kropp with only two minutes in one 1977 playoff appearance, and Chicago's official media guide records the Bulls waiving him on October 17, 1977. RealGM independently lists the waiver and his move to free agency two days later. Kropp never appeared in another NBA regular-season game. That ceiling keeps Chicago's grade below the stronger historical trades where a low draft pick produced multiple seasons or a starter-level role.

sections.heading: Washington Used the Pick on Steve Puidokas
sections.body: The Bullets kept and exercised the acquired third-rounder. Basketball-Reference's 1977 draft ledger shows Washington selecting Washington State center Steve Puidokas at No. 57 overall, and the Bullets transaction page lists the same selection. Puidokas never recorded an NBA regular-season appearance. Contemporary Washington Post draft coverage described him as a productive four-year college center, but his professional career continued outside the NBA. The pick therefore had legitimate option value on draft night without creating realized NBA production for Washington.

sections.heading: The Margin Should Stay Narrow
sections.body: Chicago did not acquire a major contributor, and Washington did receive a real draft asset rather than nothing. The distinction is realized outcome: Kropp supplied 53 games and nearly 500 regular-season minutes, while Puidokas supplied no NBA games. That supports a Bulls edge, but not the legacy B+ grade. A third-round pick in this era carried enough uncertainty that one season of reserve play is a modest win rather than a major value event.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Bulls Edge, B-/C. Chicago receives a B- because Kropp delivered 53 regular-season games and useful bench minutes for the cost of a third-round pick, even though he was gone before the next season began. Washington receives a C because the acquired pick was fully exercised at No. 57 but Steve Puidokas never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Confidence is high on the transaction and draft outcome. The source wording differs only in specificity: Chicago's media guide says future considerations, while the Basketball-Reference ledgers identify the consideration as the 1977 third-round pick.

sections.heading: The Package Is Verified, With a One-Day Date Conflict
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Denver, New York and league transaction ledgers record the Nuggets sending 1978 third- and fourth-round picks to the Nets for Ted McClain on September 15, 1976. Denver's official franchise history also uses September 15 and explicitly adds cash to the package. RealGM dates McClain's acquisition one day earlier, September 14, matching the canonical TradeVerdicts record. This review preserves September 14 as the canonical date but treats the package itself as high confidence: McClain for the two identified picks plus cash.

sections.heading: McClain Became a Major Rotation Guard for Denver
sections.body: McClain immediately took on a real role in Denver's first NBA season. He appeared in 72 regular-season games and logged 2,002 minutes, averaging 8.2 points, 4.5 assists, 3.2 rebounds and 1.5 steals in 27.8 minutes per game. Denver won 50 games and finished first in the Midwest Division. McClain was not the team's star, but he was a genuine rotation guard on one of the league's better teams rather than a short-term roster flier.

sections.heading: He Also Played Meaningful Postseason Minutes
sections.body: Denver's season ended in a six-game conference semifinal loss to Portland, and McClain appeared in all six games. He averaged 28.3 minutes, 7.3 points, 4.5 assists and 1.7 steals in the series. Those postseason minutes strengthen the realized return because they show his regular-season role carried into the playoffs. The Nuggets received exactly the kind of immediate veteran depth a contending team could use during the ABA-to-NBA transition.

sections.heading: Denver Recovered a Pick When McClain Left
sections.body: McClain's Denver tenure lasted one season, but his departure still produced an additional asset. Buffalo signed him as a veteran free agent in October 1977 and sent Denver a 1978 third-round pick as compensation. The Nuggets used that selection at No. 46 on Hollis Copeland. Copeland did not play a regular-season game for Denver and was later an NBA player with New York, so this review does not credit his 93 career games as Nuggets production. Even so, the compensation shows Denver retained some asset value after already receiving a full season from McClain.

sections.heading: New Jersey's Two Picks Produced No Nets Games
sections.body: The Nets used Denver's original 1978 third-round pick at No. 62 on Dave Batton and the fourth-rounder at No. 84 on Walter Jordan. Both eventually reached the NBA, but neither played a regular-season game for New Jersey. Batton did not debut until 1982 and finished with 58 career games. Jordan spent two seasons outside the NBA before playing 30 games for Cleveland in 1980-81. Those later careers belong to other teams. For this trade, the Nets' draft return created option value but no direct on-court production.

sections.heading: The Cash Helps New Jersey but Is Not Priced
sections.body: Denver's official media guide explicitly says cash accompanied the two picks. Basketball-Reference's transaction ledgers omit the cash component, and the amount is not identified in the reviewed record. This review therefore recognizes cash as a documented part of the package without assigning it a speculative dollar value. It raises the Nets' return above a pure two-pick miss, but it cannot offset a full season and playoff role from McClain on realized basketball value alone.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win, B+/C. Denver receives a B+ because McClain played 72 games, logged more than 2,000 regular-season minutes, contributed throughout the playoffs and later generated a third-round compensation pick when Buffalo signed him. New Jersey receives a C because it obtained two real draft assets plus documented cash, but Dave Batton and Walter Jordan produced no Nets regular-season games and the cash amount is unknown. Confidence is high on the package and player outcomes; the only structural uncertainty is whether the transaction should be dated September 14 or September 15, 1976.

sections.heading: The Transaction Is a Straight Cash Sale in the Primary Ledgers
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Philadelphia, New Orleans and NBA transaction pages all record the September 17, 1976 move as the Jazz selling Henry Bibby to the 76ers. The legacy TradeVerdicts structure is therefore correct: Philadelphia received Bibby and New Orleans received cash. The reviewed transaction ledgers do not identify the amount. This review keeps the financial return unpriced rather than creating a speculative value for the Jazz.

sections.heading: Bibby Immediately Became Philadelphia's Starting Point Guard
sections.body: The acquisition had an instant basketball effect. Bibby played 81 games in 1976-77, started 80 and averaged 32.6 minutes, 10.2 points, 4.4 assists and 3.4 rebounds. Philadelphia won 50 games and the Atlantic Division. In the playoffs Bibby appeared in all 19 games, averaging 36.4 minutes and 11.1 points as the 76ers won the Eastern Conference before losing the NBA Finals to Portland. That first season alone made the cash purchase a meaningful competitive return.

sections.heading: The Value Continued for Two More Full Seasons
sections.body: Bibby's Philadelphia tenure was not a one-year peak. He played all 82 games in 1977-78, started all 82 and averaged 30.7 minutes with 10.3 points and 5.6 assists per game. He appeared in all 10 playoff games. In 1978-79 he again played all 82 regular-season games, starting 38 as rookie Maurice Cheeks took over more of the point-guard role. Bibby still averaged 12.2 points, 4.5 assists and 31.0 minutes, then appeared in all nine postseason games. Across the three seasons, Philadelphia received 245 regular-season games and 38 playoff appearances.

sections.heading: The Acquisition Bridged Two Different 76ers Backcourts
sections.body: Bibby's role also had timing value. In 1976-77 and 1977-78 he handled the primary starting point-guard assignment for teams built around Julius Erving, George McGinnis and Doug Collins. By 1978-79, Cheeks had arrived and immediately started all 82 games, but Bibby remained a high-minute guard rather than becoming disposable depth. That transition allowed Philadelphia to keep veteran ballhandling and scoring while bringing a younger long-term point guard into the lineup.

sections.heading: New Orleans' Return Cannot Be Traced Beyond Cash
sections.body: The Jazz moved a player who had appeared in only 12 games for them after arriving from New York during the prior season. Receiving cash for a veteran outside the club's long-term core has legitimate financial value, but the amount is not reported in the reviewed source set and there is no incoming player or draft asset to follow. The Jazz therefore receive credit for a documented sale without being treated as if an unknown cash payment matched three seasons of playoff-caliber guard production.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win, A-/C. Philadelphia receives an A- because Bibby gave the club 245 regular-season games, 200 starts and 38 playoff appearances over three seasons, including a starting role on the 1977 Finals team. New Orleans receives a C because the Jazz obtained cash without taking back another basketball obligation, but the amount is unknown and there is no traceable on-court or draft return. Confidence is high on the transaction structure and Bibby's production. The only unquantified element is the cash consideration.

sections.heading: The Official Franchise Histories Say Terry Went to Buffalo for Future Considerations
sections.body: Denver's official franchise history lists the September 21, 1976 transaction as Claude Terry to Buffalo for future considerations. The historical Clippers media guide, which preserves the Buffalo Braves' transaction history, independently records the same date and structure. RealGM likewise lists Buffalo acquiring Terry from Denver in a trade on September 21. Those records resolve the core package more clearly than the legacy archive entry. This review therefore removes the unsupported 1977 draft-pick language and records Denver's return only as future considerations whose eventual form remains unresolved.

sections.heading: Basketball-Reference Preserves a Conflicting Transaction Path
sections.body: Basketball-Reference does not list the September 21 trade on the Denver, Buffalo or league transaction ledgers. Its Buffalo page instead says the Braves signed Terry as a free agent on October 21, 1976. That conflict cannot simply be ignored. Two official franchise histories and RealGM agree on the September 21 trade, so TradeVerdicts keeps that date and structure as the canonical interpretation, but confidence is medium rather than high. The disagreement also reinforces why this review should not invent a draft pick or pretend the future consideration has been fully traced.

sections.heading: Terry Gave Buffalo 33 Games of Bench Minutes
sections.body: Terry's Buffalo stint was modest but real. Basketball-Reference credits him with 33 games, 304 minutes and 116 points for the 1976-77 Braves. He averaged 9.2 minutes and 3.5 points per game while adding 28 rebounds, 33 assists and 11 steals. That is not starter-level or long-term value, but it is enough to distinguish Buffalo's return from an empty roster transaction. Terry provided several months of usable reserve minutes before the club moved his rights again.

sections.heading: Buffalo Recovered Another Financial Return When Terry Left
sections.body: The historical Buffalo/Clippers record says the Braves sold Terry to Atlanta on February 1, 1977. Basketball-Reference also records Buffalo selling Terry's player rights to the Hawks on that date. The amount is not identified in the reviewed sources, so this review does not assign a speculative dollar value. Still, Buffalo received 33 games from Terry and then converted his rights into another financial return. That downstream sale adds a little value to the acquisition even though the cash cannot be compared precisely with a player or draft asset.

sections.heading: Denver's Future Consideration Cannot Be Traced
sections.body: The reviewed records do not identify a player, draft pick or other basketball asset that Denver ultimately received from the future-considerations clause. The legacy archive entry's 1977 draft-pick language is therefore removed rather than carried forward as an unresolved guess. Denver still receives credit for a documented consideration in the official franchise histories, but without a traceable realization there is no basis to grade the Nuggets as though they received a usable draft asset.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Braves Edge, C+/C. Buffalo receives a C+ because Terry delivered 33 regular-season games and 304 minutes, then generated another unpriced financial return when his rights were sold to Atlanta. Denver receives a C because the official franchise histories document future considerations, but the reviewed record does not reveal what those considerations became. The edge stays narrow because Terry's role was small and the downstream cash amount is unknown. Confidence is medium because Basketball-Reference conflicts with the September 21 trade structure preserved by the two franchise histories and RealGM.

sections.heading: The Primary Ledgers Agree on Murphy for a Future Draft Pick
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Chicago, Los Angeles and NBA transaction pages all record the October 4, 1976 exchange the same way: the Bulls sent Allen Murphy to the Lakers for a future draft pick. Bill Sharman's Lakers executive record and Jon Kovler's Chicago record repeat that package, while the Lakers' official all-time transaction history independently confirms the future-pick wording. The legacy archive entry is therefore directionally correct, but its question-mark placeholders can be replaced with a cleaner description of what the record actually establishes.

sections.heading: The Pick's Year and Outcome Remain Unresolved
sections.body: The authoritative transaction sources do not identify a year, round, protection condition or eventual draftee for the future pick. Unlike many surrounding deals, Basketball-Reference does not attach a later selection to this transaction. The reviewed draft-trade sources also do not provide a supported player chain for the Murphy pick. That absence does not prove the pick was cancelled or never exercised. This review therefore records a future draft pick with an unresolved outcome and does not invent a year or player for Chicago.

sections.heading: Murphy Played Only Two Games for the Lakers
sections.body: Los Angeles received almost no on-court return. Basketball-Reference credits Murphy with two games and 18 total minutes for the 1976-77 Lakers. He scored five points, collected four rebounds and did not record an assist. Those appearances were his only NBA games that season and his only games for Los Angeles. The Lakers had acquired a young guard with ABA experience, but he never established a role in Jerry West's rotation.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Waived Him Less Than a Month Later
sections.body: The Lakers' transaction ledger and official franchise history both record Murphy being waived on November 2, 1976. That ended his Los Angeles tenure just 29 days after the trade. Murphy did not create a later Lakers trade return or compensation asset. His two games and 18 minutes therefore represent the complete realized basketball value Los Angeles received from the original transaction.

sections.heading: Chicago's Asset Has Option Value but No Traceable Realization
sections.body: A future draft pick carried real value even when its exact slot was not known on trade day, so Chicago cannot be graded as though it received nothing. The problem is retrospective attribution: without a verified year, round or selected player, TradeVerdicts cannot credit the Bulls with production that may belong to an unrelated pick. The responsible grade recognizes the existence of the asset while stopping short of assigning an invented downstream outcome.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, C/C. Chicago receives a C because the Bulls converted Murphy into a legitimate future draft asset, but the reviewed record does not establish what that pick became. Los Angeles also receives a C because Murphy produced only two games and 18 minutes before being waived less than a month after the trade. Neither side generated enough verified realized value to justify a directional edge. Confidence is high on the October 4 package and Murphy's brief Lakers stint but medium on the complete pick chain, so the record's overall confidence is medium.

sections.heading: The Primary Ledgers Agree on an October 12 Rights Sale
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Portland, Boston and NBA transaction pages all record the same October 12, 1976 move: Portland sold the player rights to Sidney Wicks to the Celtics. Harry Glickman's Portland executive record and Red Auerbach's Boston record independently preserve that structure. This review therefore treats the transaction as Wicks's rights for cash and does not repeat the false October 5 Portland-New Orleans record that has now been superseded. The cash amount is not identified in the reviewed ledgers.

sections.heading: Wicks Immediately Became a Major Boston Frontcourt Piece
sections.body: Wicks played all 82 regular-season games for Boston in 1976-77 and logged 2,642 minutes. He averaged 15.1 points, 10.0 rebounds and 2.1 assists in 32.2 minutes per game while shooting 45.8 percent from the field. That was not fringe production from an aging name. Wicks was one of Boston's highest-minute frontcourt players and delivered a full season of double-figure scoring and double-figure rebounding after the cash acquisition.

sections.heading: The First Season Also Carried Into the Playoffs
sections.body: Boston reached the 1977 postseason and Wicks appeared in all nine playoff games. He averaged 29.0 minutes, 13.1 points and 9.2 rebounds while shooting 51.9 percent from the field. The Celtics beat San Antonio in the opening round before losing a seven-game conference semifinal to Philadelphia. Wicks's role therefore survived into the postseason rather than disappearing when the rotation tightened.

sections.heading: The Value Continued for a Second Full Season
sections.body: Wicks remained a substantial part of Boston's 1977-78 team even as the Celtics fell out of the playoffs. He played 81 games and another 2,413 minutes, averaging 13.4 points, 8.3 rebounds and 2.1 assists in 29.8 minutes. Across the two Boston seasons, the rights purchase produced 163 regular-season games, 5,055 minutes, 2,321 points and 1,497 rebounds. That volume is enough to make the acquisition materially better than a short-term cash flier.

sections.heading: Wicks Still Had Trade Utility in the 1978 Blockbuster
sections.body: On August 4, 1978, Boston sent Wicks, Kevin Kunnert, Kermit Washington and Freeman Williams to the San Diego Clippers for Tiny Archibald, Marvin Barnes, Billy Knight and two future second-round picks. Wicks was only one component of that multi-player package, so this review does not assign the entire later return to him. His inclusion still shows that Boston retained transaction value after already receiving two full seasons of production from the original cash purchase.

sections.heading: Portland's Cash Return Is Real but Cannot Be Priced
sections.body: Portland moved on from a player who had spent five seasons with the franchise and received cash in return. That financial consideration has legitimate value, particularly as the Trail Blazers reshaped the roster that would win the 1977 championship. The problem is that the amount is not disclosed in the reviewed source set and there is no separate incoming player or draft asset to trace. This review therefore gives Portland credit for the sale without pretending an unknown cash figure can be measured against Wicks's documented Boston production.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win, B+/C. Boston receives a B+ because Wicks produced 163 regular-season games, more than 5,000 minutes, two productive frontcourt seasons and nine playoff appearances before remaining part of a major 1978 trade package. Portland receives a C because the Trail Blazers obtained cash and cleared Wicks from the roster before their championship season, but the amount is unknown and there is no traceable basketball asset to measure against Boston's return. Confidence is high on the transaction structure and Wicks's production, with only the cash valuation unquantified.

sections.heading: The Primary Ledgers Agree on Hackett for a Future Draft Pick
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Denver Nuggets, New York Nets and NBA transaction ledgers all record the same October 18, 1976 exchange: Denver sent Rudy Hackett to New York for a future draft pick. Carl Scheer's executive transaction record and Roy Boe's Nets record independently preserve that structure. RealGM also lists Hackett as a New York trade acquisition on the same date. No reviewed source adds cash or a second player to the package.

sections.heading: The Draft Pick Cannot Be Traced Responsibly
sections.body: The transaction ledgers stop at the phrase "future draft pick." They do not identify a year, round, protection, overall selection or player outcome. Pro Sports Transactions likewise lists the pick as unknown. This review therefore preserves the draft asset without assigning it to a later Denver selection. That matters because a hindsight archive should not turn an unidentified future consideration into a named player simply because Denver later owned other picks.

sections.heading: Hackett Played One Game for the Nets
sections.body: Hackett's New York tenure was extremely short. Basketball-Reference credits him with one Nets regular-season appearance in 1976-77: eight minutes, two points and three rebounds. The Nets waived him on October 29, only eleven days after the trade. That gives New York a measurable basketball return, but it is about as small as an acquired player's realized value can be.

sections.heading: New York Did Not Preserve a Downstream Asset
sections.body: After the waiver, Hackett became a free agent and signed with Indiana in November. The Pacers used him in five games before waiving him in December. Because New York received no player, pick or compensation when Hackett left, none of his later Indiana activity belongs to the Nets side of this trade. New York's attributable return ends with the single game he played for the franchise.

sections.heading: Denver Turned a Short-Term Signing Into Draft Consideration
sections.body: RealGM records Denver signing Hackett in September 1976 before moving him roughly six weeks later. The Nuggets therefore converted a recent free-agent addition into a future draft asset without giving up another documented basketball piece in this transaction. The unidentified pick keeps the return from earning a strong grade, because its eventual use cannot be verified, but the exchange still left Denver with more traceable asset value than New York received on the court.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win, C+/D+. Denver receives a C+ because it converted Hackett into a future draft pick, but the pick's year, round and eventual outcome remain unresolved in the reviewed sources. New York receives a D+ because Hackett appeared in only one game before being waived and generated no downstream return. The deal is minor rather than disastrous for the Nets, yet one eight-minute appearance is too little to justify an average grade. Confidence is high on the transaction and Hackett's one-game tenure, but medium on the complete asset chain because the future pick cannot be identified.

sections.heading: The Primary Ledgers Lock the Three-Team Routing
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Boston, Denver, Detroit and NBA transaction ledgers all preserve the same October 20, 1976 structure. Boston sent Paul Silas to Denver. Denver sent Ralph Simpson to Detroit. Detroit sent Curtis Rowe to Boston. Red Auerbach's, Carl Scheer's and Oscar Feldman's executive records repeat that routing. This review therefore repairs the canonical asset ledger by adding Simpson as Denver's outgoing asset and Detroit's incoming asset instead of leaving Detroit with an empty return.

sections.heading: Curtis Rowe Gave Boston Three Seasons of Real Value
sections.body: Rowe became an immediate Celtics rotation piece. He played 79 games in 1976-77, totaling 2,190 minutes, 800 points and 563 rebounds. Boston reached the playoffs, and Rowe started all nine postseason games, including the seven-game conference semifinal against Philadelphia. He then played 51 games in 1977-78 and 53 more in 1978-79. Across the three Boston seasons, Rowe appeared in 183 regular-season games and supplied more than 1,400 points and 1,000 rebounds. The return was not star-level, but it was far stronger than the old C-minus grade implied.

sections.heading: Paul Silas Helped Denver Immediately
sections.body: Silas played 81 games for the Nuggets in 1976-77 and averaged 7.5 rebounds in 24.2 minutes. He also appeared in all six Denver playoff games. That gave the Nuggets a veteran frontcourt contributor during a 50-win season. Denver did not simply lose Silas after one year: on May 24, 1977, the Nuggets included him with Marvin Webster and Willie Wise in the trade that brought Tom Burleson, Bob Wilkerson and a second-round pick from Seattle.

sections.heading: Denver's Downstream Return Must Be Shared Across a Larger Package
sections.body: The Seattle trade created additional value, but this review does not assign the entire return to Silas because Webster and Wise were also outgoing assets. Denver then moved Burleson and the acquired second-rounder to Kansas City for Brian Taylor and a 1977 first-round pick that became Tom LaGarde. That downstream chain shows Silas retained trade utility after his Denver season, but the multi-player package prevents treating LaGarde or Taylor as a one-for-one Silas return.

sections.heading: Ralph Simpson Produced for Detroit and Then Became Another Package
sections.body: Simpson played 77 games for Detroit in 1976-77, averaging 11.0 points, then appeared in 32 more Pistons games the following season at 10.6 points per game. Detroit therefore received 109 regular-season games from the player it acquired in the three-team deal. On February 1, 1978, the Pistons traded Simpson back to Denver for Jim Price and a 1979 first-round pick. That second transaction is where Detroit's side of this review separates from the others.

sections.heading: The Simpson Exit Produced Jim Price and Phil Hubbard
sections.body: Price played 34 games for Detroit after the February 1978 trade, averaging 11.5 points and 3.0 assists. More important for the long-term asset chain, the 1979 first-round pick became No. 15 Phil Hubbard. Hubbard played 64 games for Detroit as a rookie, 80 in 1980-81 and 52 more before his 1981-82 move, giving the Pistons 196 regular-season games from the draft asset created by Simpson's exit. Detroit received useful production from Simpson first and then converted him into another player plus a first-round pick that produced several additional seasons of value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win, A/B+/B. Detroit receives an A because Simpson supplied 109 games and then became Jim Price plus the first-round pick used on Phil Hubbard, extending the transaction's value well beyond the original player. Denver receives a B+ because Silas contributed to a 50-win team for 81 games and retained value in the later Seattle package, although that downstream return cannot be credited to Silas alone. Boston receives a B because Rowe delivered 183 regular-season games and nine playoff starts across three seasons. All three teams received meaningful basketball value; Detroit simply created the strongest verified downstream chain. Confidence is high on the three-team routing and the traced player outcomes.

sections.heading: The Sources Disagree on Which Franchise Sent Lamar to Los Angeles
sections.body: this review has an important source conflict. Basketball-Reference's 1976-77 NBA and Lakers transaction ledgers say the Indiana Pacers traded Bo Lamar to Los Angeles for future considerations on October 20, 1976. Bill Sharman's executive record repeats Indiana. Official Lakers media guides, however, state that Los Angeles acquired Dwight "Bo" Lamar from Detroit for future consideration, and the 1978 draft-pick transaction chain ties Detroit to the Lakers' future second-round selection. Because the canonical record represents the Detroit rights transaction, this review keeps that record but explicitly preserves the disagreement rather than pretending every source says the same thing.

sections.heading: The Future Consideration Became the No. 38 Pick
sections.body: The historical 1978 draft-pick chain identifies the consideration as the Lakers' second-round pick, eventually No. 38. Pro Sports Transactions cites contemporary draft reporting that the choice originally belonged to Los Angeles and had been traded for Bo Lamar. Detroit later sent that pick, along with Marvin Barnes and another draft asset, to Buffalo in November 1977. Buffalo then traded the No. 38 pick back to Los Angeles for Tom Abernethy on June 7, 1978.

sections.heading: Lamar Gave the Lakers a Full Rotation Season
sections.body: Whatever the rights-routing ambiguity, Lamar's Los Angeles outcome is clear. Basketball-Reference credits him with 71 regular-season games in 1976-77. He averaged 16.4 minutes, 7.1 points and 2.5 assists while shooting 40.6 percent. The Lakers won 53 games and finished first in the Pacific Division. Lamar was not a star, but 71 appearances and more than 1,100 minutes represent legitimate rotation value from an acquisition made immediately before the season.

sections.heading: He Also Appeared Throughout the 1977 Playoffs
sections.body: Lamar played in all 10 Lakers playoff games in 1977. His role shrank to 10.9 minutes per game and 3.3 points, but Los Angeles used him in both postseason rounds as the club beat Golden State before losing to Portland in the Western Conference Finals. That playoff participation reinforces that the Lakers received more than an expendable camp body from the transaction.

sections.heading: Detroit Used the Pick in a Larger Marvin Barnes Package
sections.body: Detroit did not simply hold the future second-rounder until draft night. On November 23, 1977, the Pistons sent Marvin Barnes, the No. 38 pick and a 1978 fourth-round pick to Buffalo for Gus Gerard, John Shumate and a 1979 first-round pick that later became Roy Hamilton. That gives the Lamar consideration real transactional utility. This review does not assign the full Gerard-Shumate-Hamilton return to the second-rounder, however, because Barnes and another pick were also necessary outgoing assets.

sections.heading: The Pick Eventually Returned to Los Angeles and Produced No NBA Games
sections.body: Buffalo subsequently sent the No. 38 selection back to the Lakers for Tom Abernethy. Los Angeles used the pick on UNC Charlotte guard Lew Massey. Basketball-Reference lists Massey as the No. 38 selection but shows no NBA regular-season statistics. That terminal outcome prevents Detroit's original consideration from receiving a strong standalone grade even though the pick had value as part of the Barnes package.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win, B/C+. Los Angeles receives a B because Lamar played 71 regular-season games, contributed useful reserve scoring and appeared in all 10 playoff games during a 53-win season. Detroit receives a C+ because the future consideration became a real second-round asset and was used in the larger Marvin Barnes package, but the pick eventually returned to Los Angeles and became Lew Massey, who never played an NBA regular-season game. Confidence is medium rather than high because Basketball-Reference attributes Lamar's October 20 transfer to Indiana while Lakers media guides and the traced draft-pick chain identify Detroit's rights involvement.

sections.heading: The Primary Ledgers Agree on Price for Buffalo's 1977 First
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Buffalo, Milwaukee and NBA transaction ledgers all record the same November 2, 1976 exchange. Buffalo sent its 1977 first-round pick to Milwaukee for Jim Price. The selection ultimately landed at No. 13. No additional player or cash component is needed to explain the canonical trade.

sections.heading: Price Stayed in Buffalo for Only 20 Games
sections.body: Price's Braves stint was brief. He appeared in 20 games, averaging 5.3 points and 1.9 assists in 16.7 minutes per game. On December 15, only six weeks after the Milwaukee deal, Buffalo moved him again. The short stay limits the direct value of the acquisition, but it does not end the asset chain.

sections.heading: Buffalo Flipped Price for Two Rotation Players
sections.body: The Braves sent Price to Denver for Gus Gerard and Chuck Williams. Gerard played 41 games for Buffalo in 1976-77, while Williams appeared in 44 games that season and 73 more in 1977-78. Williams became a regular backcourt contributor, averaging 5.7 assists per 36 minutes in 1977-78. That secondary return keeps Buffalo's side from being judged as 20 games of Price and nothing else.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Used the Pick as Trade-Up Currency
sections.body: Milwaukee did not simply make the No. 13 selection. On June 7, 1977, the Bucks sent Swen Nater and the acquired No. 13 pick back to Buffalo for the Braves' own higher first-rounder. That incoming pick became No. 3 overall. The original Buffalo selection therefore became part of a direct draft-night value upgrade.

sections.heading: The No. 3 Pick Became Marques Johnson
sections.body: Milwaukee used the third pick on Marques Johnson. Johnson went on to make five All-Star teams and three All-NBA teams, and Basketball-Reference credits him with a 20.1-point career scoring average. His Milwaukee tenure became one of the strongest outcomes tied to the 1977 draft. This review does not assign all of that value to the No. 13 pick because Nater was a major outgoing asset in the trade-up.

sections.heading: Nater's Value Prevents Over-Crediting the Pick
sections.body: Nater had averaged 13.0 points and 12.0 rebounds for Milwaukee in 1976-77 before the Bucks included him in the June trade. He then averaged 15.5 points and 13.2 rebounds for Buffalo in 1977-78. That production matters when grading the downstream branch. The No. 13 pick helped Milwaukee reach Johnson, but the trade-up required a productive starting center as well.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Edge, A-/B-. Milwaukee receives an A- because turning Price into a first-round asset and then using that asset in the package that produced No. 3 Marques Johnson created excellent long-term value. Buffalo receives a B- because Price himself lasted only 20 games, but his resale brought back Gus Gerard and Chuck Williams, with Williams contributing across two seasons. The gap favors Milwaukee, though the later Johnson outcome cannot be credited to the original pick alone. Confidence is high on the package and downstream transaction chain.

sections.heading: The Core Transaction Is Bob Love for a 1977 Second-Round Pick
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Chicago, New York Nets, league and executive transaction ledgers all agree on the November 30, 1976 core exchange. Chicago sent Bob Love to the Nets for New York's 1977 second-round pick, which became No. 23 overall. The Bulls' official all-time transaction history and Pro Sports Transactions add cash to the Nets' outgoing package. This review keeps that cash component while distinguishing the sources that actually record it.

sections.heading: Love's Nets Tenure Lasted 13 Games
sections.body: Love had been one of the defining Bulls scorers of the previous decade, but by the time of this trade he was 34. With New York he appeared in 13 games, averaging 10.1 points, 2.9 rebounds and only 17.5 minutes. The Nets did receive immediate veteran offense, but the relationship ended quickly. Love was waived in January 1977 and finished the season with Seattle.

sections.heading: Chicago's Pick Became Mike Glenn
sections.body: The incoming second-rounder landed at No. 23 in the 1977 draft. Chicago used it on Mike Glenn out of Southern Illinois. Glenn eventually played 593 NBA games across ten seasons and finished with a 54.2 percent career field-goal rate, so the selection itself identified a legitimate long-term NBA player.

sections.heading: The Bulls Did Not Receive Glenn's NBA Career
sections.body: That career cannot be credited to Chicago. The Bulls waived Glenn on December 8, 1977, six days before his NBA debut with Buffalo. He never appeared in a regular-season game for Chicago. The pick therefore had real draft value at the moment of the trade, but its realized on-court return to the Bulls was zero. This review credits Chicago for obtaining and exercising the No. 23 asset, not for the production Glenn later supplied to Buffalo, New York or Atlanta.

sections.heading: The Cash Keeps Chicago's Side From Being Empty
sections.body: The official Bulls media guide and Pro Sports Transactions both record cash in addition to the pick, although the amount is not specified in the sources used here. That financial consideration matters because the pick did not become Chicago production. At the same time, an unspecified cash payment cannot be treated as though it created a known player or draft branch.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, C+/C+. The Nets receive a C+ because Love supplied only 13 games before being waived, but those games at least produced immediate NBA rotation value. Chicago also receives a C+ because the Bulls obtained a top second-round pick plus cash, yet the selected player was waived before his NBA debut and produced no Chicago games. The transaction created optionality for the Bulls and short-term production for the Nets without a durable franchise return on either side. Confidence is high on the package and the realized player outcomes.

sections.heading: The Primary Ledgers Agree on a Straight Player Swap
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Seattle, Washington and league transaction pages all record the same December 13, 1976 deal. The SuperSonics sent Leonard Gray to the Bullets for Nick Weatherspoon. There were no draft picks or cash components in the recorded package, making this review a direct comparison of the two forwards' realized value after the exchange.

sections.heading: Weatherspoon Became a Productive Seattle Regular
sections.body: Weatherspoon had appeared in only 11 games for Washington before the trade. In Seattle he played 51 games, totaling 652 points and 404 rebounds. That works out to 12.8 points and 7.9 rebounds per game, and Basketball-Reference credits him with 2.8 win shares during the Seattle portion of the season. He was not a star, but he immediately became a meaningful rotation scorer and rebounder.

sections.heading: Gray Gave Washington More Games but a Smaller Role
sections.body: Gray played 58 regular-season games for the Bullets after arriving from Seattle. He totaled 347 points, 186 rebounds and 69 assists, averaging 6.0 points and 3.2 rebounds in 17.2 minutes per game. Washington went 48-34 and reached the Eastern Conference semifinals. Gray also appeared in eight playoff games, though his postseason role was limited to 6.5 minutes and 1.5 points per game.

sections.heading: The Longer-Term Return Vanished on Both Sides
sections.body: Neither team turned the trade into a durable multi-season asset. Gray did not play in 1977-78 because of injury and never returned to an NBA regular-season game. Seattle kept Weatherspoon through the end of the 1976-77 season but waived him on September 28, 1977. He continued his career with Chicago and later San Diego, so those later seasons are not credited to the SuperSonics.

sections.heading: The Timing Makes Seattle's Edge Clear but Modest
sections.body: Seattle received fewer games than Washington, but Weatherspoon's 51-game stretch was much more productive. He more than doubled Gray's points per game and delivered over twice as many rebounds per game. Washington can still point to 58 regular-season appearances and a small playoff contribution, which keeps the trade from becoming a one-sided failure. The difference is mainly the quality of the one-season rotation value each club received.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Seattle Edge, B/C+. Seattle receives a B because Weatherspoon produced 51 solid games with 12.8 points and 7.9 rebounds per night before the relationship ended. Washington receives a C+ because Gray supplied 58 games and appeared in the playoffs, but his role was smaller and injury ended his NBA career after that season. With no picks or downstream assets attached, the comparison stays focused on those direct 1976-77 results. Confidence is high on the package and player outcomes.

sections.heading: The Primary Ledgers Correct the Date to January 8
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Houston, New York Nets, NBA league and executive ledgers all record the Dave Wohl trade on January 8, 1977. The existing canonical record used January 7. This review corrects the stored date while preserving the stable canonical trade ID. The package itself is straightforward: Houston sent Wohl to the Nets for New York's 1978 fourth-round pick.

sections.heading: Wohl Immediately Became a Nets Rotation Guard
sections.body: Wohl had appeared in only 14 Houston games before the trade in 1976-77. With the Nets he played 37 games, averaging 25.0 minutes, 7.4 points and 3.4 assists. He totaled 275 points and 127 assists in that post-trade stretch. The Nets were a struggling team, but the transaction still produced a regular rotation player rather than a brief end-of-bench appearance.

sections.heading: He Added a Small Second Season
sections.body: Wohl returned after the franchise moved to New Jersey in 1977-78. He appeared in 10 more games, adding 35 points and 13 assists before the Nets waived him on November 19, 1977. That gives the franchise 47 regular-season games from the acquisition. The second season was minor, but it confirms the return lasted beyond the closing months of 1976-77.

sections.heading: Houston's Pick Became Jackie Robinson
sections.body: The fourth-round selection conveyed at No. 67 in the 1978 draft. Houston selected Jackie Robinson from UNLV. Basketball-Reference's draft record shows Robinson eventually played 22 NBA games over three seasons, so the pick did identify a player capable of reaching the league.

sections.heading: Robinson Never Played a Regular-Season Game for Houston
sections.body: The important realized-value distinction is that Robinson's NBA career did not occur with the Rockets. Houston waived him on October 11, 1978, months before his March 1979 NBA debut. His later 22-game career therefore belongs to other teams for franchise-value purposes. This review credits Houston for the draft selection but not for production the Rockets never received.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Edge, C+/C. The Nets receive a C+ because Wohl supplied 47 regular-season games and became a usable rotation guard immediately after the trade. Houston receives a C because the fourth-rounder became an NBA player, but Robinson was waived before debuting and produced zero Rockets games. The difference is modest because Wohl's tenure was not long or high-impact, yet the Nets clearly received more realized basketball value from the direct exchange. Confidence is high on the corrected date, package, draft identity and player outcomes.
