sections.heading: The October 5 Portland-New Orleans Transaction Is Unsupported
sections.body: The legacy archive entry claims Portland acquired Sidney Wicks from the New Orleans Jazz on October 5, 1976 for cash. Basketball-Reference's Portland transaction ledger contains no such move. The league-wide 1976-77 transaction ledger also has no Portland-New Orleans Wicks transaction on October 5. Instead, both sources record Portland selling Wicks's player rights to the Boston Celtics on October 12. Harry Glickman's Portland executive record and Red Auerbach's Boston executive record preserve that same October 12 transaction.

sections.heading: Wicks Was a Portland Player Before the Boston Sale
sections.body: The legacy analysis says Portland "reacquired" Wicks from New Orleans one month earlier, but the career record makes that impossible. Wicks played the first five seasons of his NBA career with Portland, including 79 games for the Trail Blazers in 1975-76. There is no intervening Jazz season or New Orleans roster stint to reacquire him from. The false October 5 record appears to have inverted or contaminated a transaction relationship rather than preserving a real economic event.

sections.heading: The 1976-77 Production Belongs to Boston
sections.body: The legacy archive entry compounds the transaction error by crediting Wicks with 79 starts and 15.1 points per game for Portland's 1976-77 championship team. Basketball-Reference shows Wicks playing all 82 regular-season games for Boston that season, averaging 15.1 points and 10.0 rebounds in 32.2 minutes. He also appeared in all nine Celtics playoff games. Portland won the 1977 championship without Wicks. Leaving the false record active would therefore assign another team's production to Portland.

sections.heading: The Real Transaction Already Exists in TradeVerdicts
sections.body: TradeVerdicts already contains canonical record nba-trade-19761012-63d71dffa22a, dated October 12, 1976, between Boston and Portland. That record correctly represents Boston acquiring Wicks's player rights from the Trail Blazers. The October 5 Portland-New Orleans import adds no distinct transaction, no distinct asset chain and no valid player movement. Retaining it as an active candidate would create duplicate Wicks transfer history and distort team-pair counts.

sections.heading: Why the Bad Import Should Be Preserved but Superseded
sections.body: The record still has provenance value because it documents how the original Portland batch introduced the error. Deleting it outright would make the historical cleanup harder to audit later. The superseded entry is retained for provenance but excluded from graded results. That preserves the source history without allowing the false Portland-New Orleans transaction to surface as an independent trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Record Superseded. Canonical trade: nba-trade-19761012-63d71dffa22a. No winner and no grades are assigned. Confidence is high because the Portland, Boston and league transaction ledgers agree on the October 12 rights sale, the executive records agree, and Wicks's 1976-77 Boston statistics directly contradict the legacy Portland championship claim. This review therefore removes this October 5 record from the active source-backed candidate path while preserving it as provenance for the original import error.

sections.heading: The June 7 Cleveland-Buffalo Trade Does Not Appear in the Primary Ledgers
sections.body: The legacy archive entry claims Cleveland traded Jim Cleamons to the Buffalo Braves on June 7, 1977 for John Gianelli and a 1977 first-round pick. Basketball-Reference's Cleveland transaction log does not contain that move. Buffalo's transaction log does not contain it either, and the league-wide 1976-77 transaction ledger has no Cleveland-Buffalo transaction involving Cleamons or Gianelli on June 7.

sections.heading: Cleamons Stayed With Cleveland Until October
sections.body: Cleamons's own transaction history directly contradicts the legacy trade. Basketball-Reference records his 1972 move from the Lakers to Cleveland, then no transaction until October 10, 1977. On that date the New York Knicks signed Cleamons as a veteran free agent and sent Walt Frazier to Cleveland as compensation. The Knicks' team ledger and the 1977-78 league ledger independently record the same free-agent compensation transaction. A June sale to Buffalo would be incompatible with Cleveland still owning Cleamons's veteran-free-agent compensation rights in October.

sections.heading: Gianelli Stayed With Buffalo Until September
sections.body: Gianelli's transaction history creates the same contradiction on the other side. The Knicks had traded Gianelli and cash to Buffalo for Bob McAdoo and Tom McMillen on December 9, 1976. He remained a Braves asset through the summer. On September 2, 1977, Buffalo traded Gianelli to Milwaukee for a 1979 first-round pick that became Roy Hamilton. Milwaukee's transaction ledger and the 1977-78 league ledger both preserve that September move. There is no intervening Cleveland transaction.

sections.heading: The Claimed 1977 First-Round Pick Cannot Be Reconciled
sections.body: Cleveland's draft history shows no Cavaliers first-round selection in the 1977 draft. The team's first listed choice was Eddie Jordan at No. 33 in round two. Buffalo's actual June 7 transaction involved a different first-round branch: the Braves sent the pick that became No. 3 Marques Johnson to Milwaukee for Swen Nater and the pick that became No. 13 Tate Armstrong. Three days later Buffalo moved the Armstrong pick to Chicago for the second-round pick used on Larry Johnson. Those documented pick movements leave no supported Cleveland first-round outcome matching the legacy archive entry.

sections.heading: The record Appears to Be a Malformed Composite
sections.body: Each named component belongs to a real 1977 transaction history, but not to the transaction represented here. Cleamons later produced Walt Frazier compensation for Cleveland. Gianelli later produced a 1979 first-round pick for Buffalo. Buffalo also made multiple first-round-pick moves around the June draft. The legacy archive entry appears to have combined unrelated assets and timing into a Cleveland-Buffalo exchange that the surviving primary ledgers do not support.

sections.heading: Why the Record Is Preserved but Superseded
sections.body: Deleting the record would erase provenance for the original legacy import and make the source-cleanup trail harder to audit. Leaving it active would be worse: it would invent a trade, assign both players to teams they never joined through this mechanism, and introduce an untraceable first-round pick into Cleveland's history. The correct archive treatment is to retain the identifiers and original asset structure privately while excluding the record from active candidate analysis.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Record Superseded. No winner and no grades are assigned. Confidence is high because the Cleveland, Buffalo and league transaction logs all omit the alleged June 7 exchange, while the later Cleamons-to-New York and Gianelli-to-Milwaukee movements are independently documented by team, league and player ledgers. The superseded entry is retained for provenance but excluded from graded results.

sections.heading: The Authoritative Ledgers Put the Trade on June 10
sections.body:
The legacy archive record carries a June 9, 1977 date, but the Buffalo, Los Angeles and league transaction ledgers all list the exchange on June 10.

The package itself is clear. Buffalo sent a 1977 third-round pick to Los Angeles for Johnny Neumann. The Lakers used the pick at No. 46 on James Edwards.

sections.heading: Edwards Immediately Produced for Los Angeles
sections.body:
Edwards was not a throwaway third-round selection. As a 22-year-old rookie, he played 25 Lakers games before the December trade, averaging 14.8 points and 7.2 rebounds in 28.9 minutes. He scored 370 points and grabbed 180 rebounds in that short Los Angeles stint.

That alone creates far more realized value than Buffalo received from Neumann after the June transaction. Edwards also retained meaningful trade value almost immediately.

sections.heading: The Edwards Branch Helped Bring Adrian Dantley and Dave Robisch
sections.body:
On December 13, 1977, the Lakers traded Edwards, Earl Tatum and cash to Indiana for Adrian Dantley and Dave Robisch. This review does not assign the entire Dantley-Robisch return to Edwards because Tatum and cash were also outgoing assets. Edwards was nevertheless one of the named pieces in the package and had already established himself as a productive rookie.

Dantley then gave Los Angeles major scoring production. He played 56 regular-season games for the Lakers in 1977-78 at 26.5 points per game and another 60 in 1978-79 at 19.4 points. Across those two seasons he appeared in 116 regular-season games for Los Angeles. Robisch added frontcourt depth as part of the same return. The downstream package therefore reinforces the value of the No. 46 pick without requiring this review to pretend Edwards alone purchased Dantley.

sections.heading: Neumann Never Played a Post-Trade Game for Buffalo
sections.body:
Neumann's history is unusual because Buffalo had already signed him in September 1976, played him in four games, waived him in November and watched the Lakers sign him nine days later. The June 1977 transaction brought him back to the Braves, but he did not appear in a Buffalo regular-season game after that reacquisition.

On October 18, 1977, Buffalo traded Neumann to Indiana for a 1978 third-round pick. The Pacers used Neumann in 20 games before waiving him in December, but those games belong to Indiana rather than Buffalo.

sections.heading: The Replacement Pick Produced No NBA Value
sections.body: Buffalo used the 1978 third-round pick at No. 48 on Mike Santos. His Basketball-Reference page records the draft transaction but no NBA regular-season career. The Neumann branch therefore ends with no post-trade Buffalo games from Neumann and no NBA games from the replacement pick.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win, A-/F. Los Angeles receives an A- because a third-round pick became a productive rookie who averaged 14.8 points and 7.2 rebounds in 25 Lakers games and then served as one component of the Dantley-Robisch trade. Buffalo receives an F because Neumann produced no post-trade Braves games and the pick acquired for him became a player with no NBA regular-season appearances. The only caution is downstream attribution: Dantley's full Lakers production cannot be credited to Edwards alone because Tatum and cash were also part of that December package. Confidence is high.

sections.heading: The Pick Exchange Is Confirmed, and the Cash Comes From a Separate Ledger
sections.body:
Chicago, Buffalo and the league transaction logs all agree on the June 10, 1977 pick swap. The Bulls sent the second-round pick that became No. 24 Larry Johnson to the Braves and received the first-round pick that became No. 13 Tate Armstrong.

Those Basketball-Reference ledgers do not list cash. Pro Sports Transactions' 1977 draft-pick ledger adds the financial term, recording that Chicago also sent $150,000 to Buffalo. This review preserves that source distinction instead of presenting the cash as though every ledger independently reported it.

sections.heading: Armstrong Gave Chicago Two Seasons of Direct Production
sections.body:
Chicago used the No. 13 pick on Armstrong. He played 66 games as a rookie in 1977-78, averaging 4.3 points in 10.8 minutes. He returned for 26 games in 1978-79. Across his two Bulls seasons, Armstrong appeared in 92 regular-season games, logged 975 minutes, scored 350 points and handed out 105 assists.

That is modest first-round production, but it is still substantially more on-court value than Buffalo received from the player attached to the No. 24 pick.

sections.heading: Armstrong Also Retained Some Downstream Value
sections.body:
Chicago later used Armstrong in a veteran-free-agent compensation transaction. In 1979 the Bulls signed Coby Dietrick from San Antonio and sent Armstrong plus cash to the Spurs as compensation. Basketball-Reference and the Bulls' own historical transaction record both preserve that exchange.

Dietrick then became a useful Chicago rotation big. He played 79 games in 1979-80, 82 in 1980-81 and 74 in 1981-82, for 235 regular-season games across three Bulls seasons. He scored 1,138 points and grabbed 816 rebounds during that span.

This review does not assign the entire Dietrick return to Armstrong because the compensation package also included cash. The later transaction still demonstrates that Armstrong retained enough value to function as a named component in acquiring a veteran who gave Chicago three seasons.

sections.heading: Buffalo's No. 24 Pick Produced Almost Nothing
sections.body:
The Braves used the incoming second-round pick on Larry Johnson, the Kentucky guard born in 1954. His player ledger records only four NBA regular-season games, all for Buffalo in 1977-78. He played 38 total minutes, scored six points and was waived twice during the season.

Johnson's transaction history also confirms the exact pick chain. Buffalo had originally sent this future second-round pick to Chicago in 1974, then reacquired it in the Armstrong trade and drafted Johnson at No. 24. There was no meaningful later NBA player value from the pick.

sections.heading: The $150,000 Keeps Buffalo's Grade From the Bottom
sections.body: Buffalo did receive a real financial asset. The $150,000 should not be erased simply because the player outcome failed. At the same time, there is no source-supported basketball conversion that lets this review trace that cash into another player or pick. It therefore counts as financial value without inventing a downstream roster branch.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win, B+/D+. Chicago receives a B+ because No. 13 became 92 Armstrong games and Armstrong later remained useful in a compensation package that helped bring Dietrick, who played 235 Bulls games. Buffalo receives a D+ because No. 24 produced only four Johnson games, with the documented $150,000 providing the main remaining value. The gap is meaningful, but Chicago did not receive a star and the later Dietrick branch was not created by Armstrong alone. Confidence is high.

sections.heading: The Basic Trade Is Confirmed Across Team and League Ledgers
sections.body:
Phoenix, Portland and the 1977-78 league transaction logs all record the July 15, 1977 exchange. The Suns sent Dale Schlueter to the Trail Blazers and received Portland's 1978 fourth-round pick. That pick eventually became No. 88 Wayne Smith.

The ordinary Basketball-Reference transaction pages stop there. A Phoenix media guide and Pro Sports Transactions preserve an additional conditional term that explains why the legacy archive entry contains a second draft-pick asset.

sections.heading: The Conditional Third-Round Pick Never Activated
sections.body:
Phoenix's 1979 media guide says the Suns would receive Portland's third-round pick instead of the fourth-rounder if Schlueter was on the Trail Blazers' active roster as of December 1, 1977. Pro Sports Transactions records the same condition and marks the conditional third-round pick as not exercised.

This review therefore treats the conditional pick as a contingent term, not as a second realized asset. The cited records establish that Phoenix ultimately received the fourth-round pick and did not receive a third-round selection from this condition. The exact roster-status mechanics behind the failed condition are not independently reconstructed here.

sections.heading: Schlueter Produced Ten Portland Games
sections.body:
Schlueter did make regular-season appearances for Portland in 1977-78. Basketball-Reference records 10 games and 109 minutes, with 25 points, 21 rebounds and 18 assists. He was a deep reserve rather than a meaningful rotation piece.

Portland's transaction log later records Schlueter's retirement on April 24, 1978. There is no subsequent player or draft return tied to his departure, so the Blazers' branch ends with those 10 games.

sections.heading: Phoenix's Pick Became Wayne Smith
sections.body:
The Suns kept the fourth-round pick and used it at No. 88 in the 1978 draft on Wayne Smith. Phoenix's draft ledger and Smith's player page both confirm the selection.

Smith never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Basketball-Reference lists him as a drafted rookie without an NBA playing career. That means Phoenix realized no on-court NBA value from the pick.

sections.heading: This Was a Low-Impact Exchange on Both Sides
sections.body:
Schlueter had previously played 39 games for Phoenix in 1976-77, but those Suns games occurred before the trade and are not part of Portland's return. Likewise, Smith's college background cannot substitute for NBA production that never materialized.

The difference between the teams is therefore narrow and based on actual realized service. Portland received 10 games from an aging veteran; Phoenix received a draft selection that produced no NBA games. The unused conditional third does not change the outcome.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Blazers Edge, D+/F. Portland receives a D+ because Schlueter provided 10 regular-season games before retiring, a small but tangible return for a fourth-round pick. Phoenix receives an F because the realized pick became a player with no NBA regular-season appearances and the conditional upgrade was not exercised. The trade is low impact overall, so the grade gap should not be mistaken for major franchise value. Confidence is high.

sections.heading: The legacy archive entry Was Missing an Entire First-Round Pick
sections.body:
New Jersey, Buffalo and the league transaction ledgers all record the September 1, 1977 deal the same way: the Nets sent Tiny Archibald to the Braves for George Johnson, Buffalo's 1978 first-round pick and Buffalo's 1979 first-round pick.

The legacy canonical record contained Johnson and the 1979 first but omitted the 1978 first entirely. This review repairs that structural error before grading the trade. The missing asset eventually became the No. 4 slot in the 1978 draft, where Michael Ray Richardson was selected after the pick changed hands again.

sections.heading: George Johnson Gave the Nets Three Full Seasons
sections.body:
Johnson immediately became New Jersey's starting-caliber interior anchor. He played 81 games in 1977-78 at 8.7 points, 9.6 rebounds and 3.4 blocks per game. He followed with 78 games in 1978-79 and 81 more in 1979-80.

That is 240 regular-season Nets games from one of the three incoming assets. When Johnson left for San Antonio as a veteran free agent in 1980, New Jersey also received a 1981 first-round compensation pick that became No. 18 Ray Tolbert. This review does not need that later branch to make the original return valuable, but it reinforces that Johnson retained asset value after his playing tenure.

sections.heading: The 1978 First Became a Trade-Up Currency Asset
sections.body:
New Jersey did not directly draft Richardson with Buffalo's 1978 first. On June 8, 1978, the Nets sent that pick plus their own 1979 first-rounder to the Knicks for Phil Jackson and the 1978 No. 13 pick that became Winford Boynes.

Jackson played 75 regular-season games for New Jersey over two seasons. Boynes played 133 Nets games and scored 1,191 points. Because another 1979 first was also outgoing, this review does not assign the entire Jackson-Boynes return to Buffalo's 1978 pick. The important point is that the restored asset was real premium trade currency, not an unused draft entry.

sections.heading: The 1979 First Became Cliff Robinson and Then Otis Birdsong
sections.body:
Buffalo's 1979 first-round pick landed at No. 11 and became Cliff Robinson. Robinson played 70 games for New Jersey as a rookie and 63 more in 1980-81, scoring 2,180 points across those two seasons.

In June 1981 the Nets traded Robinson to Kansas City for Otis Birdsong and a second-round pick. Birdsong became a long-term New Jersey guard, giving the Robinson branch substantial additional downstream value. That branch alone is far more productive than the single pick line in the legacy summary suggested.

sections.heading: Archibald Never Played for Buffalo
sections.body:
The Braves acquired a Hall of Fame-level guard, but the realized Buffalo outcome was brutal. Archibald missed the entire 1977-78 season with an Achilles injury, so Buffalo received zero regular-season games from him.

After the franchise moved to San Diego, the Clippers traded Archibald in August 1978 as part of a much larger package with Marvin Barnes, Billy Knight and two second-round picks to Boston for Kevin Kunnert, Kermit Washington, Sidney Wicks and Freeman Williams. Archibald therefore retained trade value, but this review cannot attribute that whole return to him because five assets went to Boston.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win, A+/D+. New Jersey receives an A+ because the club got 240 Johnson games, a premium 1978 first that helped produce Jackson and Boynes, and a 1979 first that became Robinson and later Birdsong. Buffalo receives a D+ because Archibald produced no Braves games and only later contributed as one component of a multi-asset Boston trade. The missing 1978 first materially changes the canonical record and makes the Nets' advantage much larger than the legacy archive entry showed. Confidence is high.

sections.heading: The source-backed Package Is Gianelli for a 1979 First
sections.body:
Buffalo, Milwaukee and the 1977-78 league transaction ledgers all agree on the September 2, 1977 exchange: the Braves sent John Gianelli to the Bucks for Milwaukee's 1979 first-round pick. The legacy archive entry described the draft asset as a 1979-or-1980 first and also included cash.

The authoritative Basketball-Reference ledgers used for this review specify 1979 and do not list cash. No independent source in this review verified a cash component, so the canonical record is repaired to the documented one-for-one package rather than preserving an unsupported financial asset.

sections.heading: Gianelli Gave Milwaukee Two Full Seasons
sections.body:
Gianelli immediately became a dependable Bucks rotation big. He played all 82 games in 1977-78, logging 2,327 minutes and producing 693 points, 509 rebounds and 192 assists. He returned for all 82 games in 1978-79, adding 584 points, 408 rebounds and 160 assists.

Across the two seasons, Milwaukee received 164 regular-season games, 1,277 points, 917 rebounds and 352 assists. That is not star production, but it is substantial realized service for a future first-round pick.

sections.heading: Gianelli Also Retained Some Trade Value
sections.body:
On May 31, 1979, Milwaukee traded Gianelli and a separate 1979 first-round pick, later used on Calvin Natt, to New Jersey for Harvey Catchings. The move gives Gianelli a downstream branch, but it has to be handled carefully because the Bucks also surrendered a first-round selection.

This review therefore records the Catchings transaction as evidence that Gianelli still had trade value without assigning the entire return to him alone.

sections.heading: Buffalo Quickly Recycled the Milwaukee First
sections.body:
The Braves did not hold Milwaukee's 1979 first through the 1979 draft. On November 23, 1977, Buffalo sent Gus Gerard, John Shumate and the Bucks' first-round pick to Detroit for Marvin Barnes, a 1978 second-round pick later used on Lew Massey and a 1978 fourth-round pick later used on Larry Harris.

That package shows the Milwaukee first had useful market value, but three assets went to Detroit. This review cannot credit Barnes and both incoming picks solely to the first-rounder.

Detroit eventually retained the 1979 selection and used it at No. 10 on Roy Hamilton. Hamilton's later NBA production belongs to Detroit and Portland, not Buffalo, because Buffalo had traded the pick away more than a year before the draft.

sections.heading: The Difference Is Modest but Real
sections.body: Milwaukee's return is easier to measure: 164 Gianelli games and two full seasons of rotation production. Buffalo's return is more indirect. The first-round pick became part of a November package that helped the Braves acquire Barnes and two draft choices, but the pick shared that transaction with Gerard and Shumate.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Edge, B+/B. Milwaukee receives a B+ because Gianelli provided two complete seasons of useful frontcourt minutes and later remained a named component in another trade. Buffalo receives a B because the 1979 first was a valuable asset and helped support the Barnes package, but its specific downstream value is diluted by the two additional players Buffalo sent in that deal. This was not a lopsided transaction; Milwaukee simply received the clearer direct return. Confidence is high on the documented player-for-pick package and the downstream transactions.

sections.heading: The Trade Was a Straight Guard-for-Guard Swap
sections.body: Indiana and Phoenix both list the September 6, 1977 deal identically: Don Buse went to the Suns and Ricky Sobers went to the Pacers. The league transaction ledger matches those team records. There are no picks, cash terms or conditions to reconcile at the original transaction point.

sections.heading: Sobers Gave Indiana Two High-Usage Starting Seasons
sections.body:
Sobers immediately became a full-time Pacers starter. In 1977-78 he played 79 games, started all 79 and averaged 18.2 points, 7.4 assists, 4.1 rebounds and 2.2 steals in 38.2 minutes. He followed with 81 starts in 1978-79, averaging 17.3 points and 5.6 assists.

Across the two seasons, Sobers played 160 regular-season games for Indiana and started every one of them. That is substantial direct value, especially for a team that had just moved Billy Knight one week earlier and was remaking its backcourt and scoring structure.

Sobers's Indiana tenure ended in July 1979 when he was sent to Chicago as veteran-free-agent compensation after the Pacers signed Mickey Johnson. This review treats that as a real asset-use event, but not as a conventional one-for-one trade return. Indiana's acquisition of Johnson required the compensation mechanism, so Sobers still carried value even though the transaction structure differs from a normal trade.

sections.heading: Buse Gave Phoenix Three Seasons and Elite Defense
sections.body:
Phoenix received the longer direct tenure. Buse played 82 games in 1977-78, 82 in 1978-79 and 81 in 1979-80, for 245 regular-season Suns games. He started 164 of those games and averaged roughly eight points with strong playmaking while taking the tougher defensive assignments.

More importantly, Basketball-Reference lists Buse as All-Defensive First Team in all three Phoenix seasons. In 1977-78 he averaged 4.8 assists and 2.3 steals; in 1978-79 he averaged 4.3 assists and 1.9 steals; in 1979-80 he averaged 4.0 assists and 1.6 steals. His scoring was lower than Sobers's, but his defensive impact and three-year availability gave Phoenix a different kind of sustained value.

sections.heading: Phoenix Then Turned Buse Into Two Second-Round Picks
sections.body:
On November 25, 1980, Phoenix traded Buse back to Indiana for a 1981 second-round pick that became Al Leslie and a 1982 second-round pick that became Jose Slaughter.

The Suns did not simply use both selections. On June 8, 1981, Phoenix sent those same two picks back to Indiana for Dudley Bradley while also relinquishing an option to swap first-round picks with the Pacers in 1983. Because that extra concession was part of the Bradley transaction, this review does not assign all of Bradley's value to the Buse-derived picks. Still, the picks clearly extended Buse's asset life beyond his 245 Phoenix games.

sections.heading: The Difference Is Longevity and Defensive Value
sections.body: Indiana can make a strong case from offensive production alone. Sobers was the better scorer and higher-volume creator during the first two seasons after the trade. Phoenix's case is broader: Buse gave the Suns three full seasons, three All-Defensive First Team selections and then returned two second-round picks.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Suns Edge, A-/B+. Phoenix receives an A- because Buse delivered 245 games, three All-Defensive First Team seasons and two later second-round assets. Indiana receives a B+ because Sobers delivered 160 starts with high-end scoring and playmaking over two seasons before being used as compensation in the Mickey Johnson signing. Both teams got substantial value, but Phoenix's extra season, defensive honors and downstream picks create the modest separation. Confidence is high.

sections.heading: The Package Is Future Considerations, Not Verified Cash
sections.body:
The Lakers, Buffalo Braves, league transaction log, Bill Sharman executive ledger and Norm Sonju executive ledger all record the September 7, 1977 transaction the same way: Buffalo sent Ernie DiGregorio to Los Angeles for future considerations.

The legacy archive entry had converted that phrase into “undisclosed considerations (cash?),” but none of the authoritative ledgers reviewed for this review identifies cash. That distinction matters. “Future considerations” can later become cash, a draft asset, player rights or another agreed return, but the cited record does not establish which outcome occurred here.

This review therefore changes the asset type from cash to future consideration and labels the downstream outcome unresolved. The review does not invent a payment amount or a later asset.

sections.heading: DiGregorio Gave the Lakers 25 Games
sections.body:
Los Angeles received a recognizable former Rookie of the Year, but the actual Lakers tenure was brief. DiGregorio appeared in 25 regular-season games in 1977-78 and averaged 13.3 minutes, 3.9 points, 2.8 assists and 0.9 rebounds.

The team did get usable reserve minutes, especially at point guard, but his role was limited. Basketball-Reference lists 332 total Lakers minutes, 98 points and 71 assists. That is real production, though not enough to create a large transaction win by itself.

sections.heading: The Lakers Waived Him in January
sections.body:
Los Angeles waived DiGregorio on January 30, 1978. Boston signed him as a free agent on February 1, and he played 27 games for the Celtics to finish the season.

Because the Lakers waived him rather than trading him, there was no downstream Lakers asset return to attach to this transaction. Their realized value from the deal is therefore almost entirely those 25 games of reserve production.

sections.heading: Buffalo's Return Is Still Unresolved
sections.body:
Buffalo's side is harder to score because the original consideration was deferred and the reviewed transaction ledgers do not identify the eventual fulfillment. The Braves' 1977-78 ledger continues to label the September 7 return simply as future considerations even while later entries identify concrete picks, cash sales and player transactions in detail.

That is a reason to preserve uncertainty rather than assume Buffalo received nothing. A missing downstream identification is not proof that the consideration had zero value.

At the same time, TradeVerdicts grades realized, traceable outcomes. Without a verified cash amount, pick or player connection, Buffalo cannot receive full credit for an asset that remains unspecified in the source record.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Edge, C-/D+. Los Angeles receives a C- because it obtained 25 games and modest reserve production before waiving DiGregorio in January. Buffalo receives a D+ on documented realized value because the future consideration is real but unresolved in the cited ledgers. The grade gap is intentionally small, and confidence is medium rather than high because Buffalo's eventual return could not be identified. This review's main repair is factual: future considerations should not be rewritten as confirmed or probable cash without source support.

sections.heading: The Original Deal Was Willoughby for One Second-Round Pick
sections.body:
Buffalo and Atlanta both record the September 13, 1977 transaction the same way: the Braves acquired Bill Willoughby and the Hawks received Buffalo's 1978 second-round pick. The league ledger matches those team records.

The pick eventually became No. 24 in the 1978 draft and was used on Keith Herron, but Atlanta did not make that selection. That downstream distinction is the key to grading this review accurately.

sections.heading: Willoughby Gave Buffalo 56 Games
sections.body:
Willoughby was only 20 years old during the 1977-78 season and immediately entered Buffalo's rotation. He played 56 games for the Braves, averaging 19.3 minutes, 6.7 points and 3.9 rebounds. Basketball-Reference lists 1,079 total minutes, 376 points and 219 rebounds.

Those numbers are modest, but they are real first-season value from a second-round-pick acquisition. Buffalo was in the middle of a major roster overhaul and received a young forward who could absorb meaningful minutes immediately.

The franchise moved to San Diego after the season, and Willoughby did not play in 1978-79 after being waived. This review therefore does not inflate the Buffalo return into a long multi-season run. The realized Braves portion is the 56-game 1977-78 season.

sections.heading: Atlanta Recycled the Pick Before the Draft
sections.body:
On October 5, less than a month after the original trade, Atlanta sent Buffalo's 1978 second-round pick to Portland for Rich Laurel. Portland's transaction ledger and Harry Glickman's executive record identify the same pick, later used at No. 24 on Herron.

That means the Hawks did extract market value from the asset before draft night. The original second-rounder was not wasted or forgotten.

The problem is what Atlanta received for it. Laurel never played a regular-season game for the Hawks. Atlanta released him on November 28, 1977. Milwaukee signed him on December 2, and his entire NBA career consisted of 10 games for the Bucks.

sections.heading: Herron's NBA Career Belongs to Portland's Branch
sections.body:
Portland retained the pick and selected Herron at No. 24 in 1978. Herron eventually played 124 NBA games over three seasons.

That outcome confirms the pick itself had legitimate draft value, but TradeVerdicts does not credit Herron's production back to Atlanta because the Hawks had traded the pick away for Laurel. The correct Atlanta outcome is the Laurel conversion, not Herron's later career.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Braves Edge, B-/D+. Buffalo receives a B- because Willoughby supplied 56 games and useful rotation minutes at age 20. Atlanta receives a D+ because the second-round pick had real trade value, but the Hawks converted it into Laurel and released him before he played a game for them. The gap is meaningful without being enormous: Buffalo did not acquire a long-term star, but it received far more realized team-specific value than Atlanta ultimately produced from the asset cycle. Confidence is high.

sections.heading: This Was a Rights Sale, Not a Conventional Player Trade
sections.body:
Buffalo's transaction ledger says the Braves sold the player rights to Bird Averitt to the New Jersey Nets on September 16, 1977. The league transaction log uses the same “sold the player rights” language. New Jersey's ledger records that it acquired Averitt's rights but does not specify the payment amount.

That is enough to establish cash consideration while still preserving uncertainty about the amount. This review therefore keeps the cash asset but labels it as an unspecified rights-sale payment rather than treating the transaction as a normal player-for-player exchange.

sections.heading: Averitt Gave New Jersey 21 Games
sections.body:
Averitt appeared in 21 regular-season games for the Nets in 1977-78. He averaged 19.5 minutes, 8.3 points, 3.2 assists and 1.6 rebounds. Basketball-Reference lists 409 total minutes, 174 points and 68 assists.

Those numbers are modest, but they are more than a purely administrative rights acquisition. New Jersey received actual rotation minutes from the player it purchased.

sections.heading: The Nets Waived Him in December
sections.body:
New Jersey waived Averitt on December 12, 1977. There was no trade return attached to that departure, so the Nets' direct asset cycle ends after those 21 games.

That short tenure keeps the grade restrained. The Nets did not turn the purchased rights into a long-term starter or a later draft asset.

sections.heading: Buffalo Later Re-Signed Averitt, but That Is a Separate Event
sections.body:
The unusual historical wrinkle is that Buffalo signed Averitt as a free agent on January 31, 1978. He then played 34 regular-season games for the Braves, averaging 9.5 points and 3.8 assists.

This review does not credit those 34 games as a direct return from the September sale. Buffalo reacquired him through a later free-agent signing after New Jersey had waived him. The sequence is still worth documenting because it shows that the Braves ultimately regained the player, but the later roster move is not the consideration that New Jersey paid in September.

sections.heading: Buffalo's Cash Return Cannot Be Fully Valued
sections.body:
The Braves definitely received a sale payment, but no amount is identified in the cited Buffalo, New Jersey, league or executive records. There is also no source-backed downstream transaction connecting that payment to a later player or draft asset.

TradeVerdicts therefore records the cash as real but unquantified. That prevents both extremes: Buffalo should not be treated as receiving nothing, and the unknown payment should not be inflated into a major return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Edge, C+/C. New Jersey receives a C+ because Averitt produced 21 games and useful reserve scoring before being waived. Buffalo receives a C because it received a confirmed cash payment of unknown amount and later independently re-signed Averitt, though that free-agent return is not part of the original sale. The separation is limited, and confidence is high on the transaction structure but naturally lower on the exact value of Buffalo's cash because the amount is not preserved in the cited record.

sections.heading: The Package Was a Straight One-for-One Swap
sections.body:
Atlanta, Los Angeles and the league transaction ledger all record the September 30, 1977 deal the same way: the Hawks sent Lou Hudson to the Lakers for Ollie Johnson. There were no picks, cash terms or later considerations attached to the original exchange.

That makes this review a relatively simple realized-value comparison. The question is how much useful basketball each team received before the asset cycle ended.

sections.heading: Johnson Gave Atlanta One Full Season
sections.body:
Johnson played all 82 games for the Hawks in 1977-78. He averaged 20.8 minutes, 8.5 points, 3.2 rebounds and 1.5 assists while shooting 47.2% from the field and 85.4% from the line.

That was a legitimate rotation season, not a negligible return. Johnson gave Atlanta dependable availability and enough scoring to contribute to a young Hawks roster that was being rebuilt around players such as John Drew and Tree Rollins.

The problem is duration. Atlanta waived Johnson on October 4, 1978, before the next regular season began. Chicago signed him later that month. Because the Hawks waived him instead of trading him, there was no downstream Atlanta asset return from the original deal.

sections.heading: Hudson Still Had Two Productive Lakers Seasons
sections.body:
Hudson was 33 when Los Angeles acquired him, so this was not a trade for his All-Star prime. Even so, he immediately gave the Lakers more production than Johnson gave Atlanta.

Hudson played all 82 games in 1977-78, averaging 27.8 minutes and 13.7 points while shooting 49.7%. He also added 2.4 assists and 2.3 rebounds per game. In the playoffs, he appeared in three games and averaged 11.7 points.

He returned for 78 regular-season games in 1978-79. His role declined to 21.6 minutes, but he still averaged 9.8 points and shot 51.7%. He then played six more playoff games.

Across the two seasons, Hudson appeared in 160 regular-season Lakers games and nine playoff games. Basketball-Reference lists an 11.8-point average across his Los Angeles tenure.

sections.heading: The Age Risk Did Not Hurt Los Angeles
sections.body:
The trade could have backfired if Hudson's decline had accelerated immediately. Instead, the Lakers got two useful seasons from an older scorer while giving up a younger forward who lasted only one season in Atlanta.

Neither side created a downstream trade tree. Johnson was waived by Atlanta, and Hudson finished his NBA career after the 1978-79 season. That leaves the direct production comparison as the decisive evidence.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win, A-/B-. Los Angeles receives an A- because Hudson delivered 160 regular-season games, efficient scoring and two playoff appearances. Atlanta receives a B- because Johnson gave the Hawks a complete 82-game rotation season, but the team waived him before year two and received no later asset return. The Lakers' advantage comes from both higher production and twice the team-specific longevity. Confidence is high.

sections.heading: The source-backed Package Is One-for-One
sections.body:
Portland, Atlanta and the league transaction ledgers all record the October 5, 1977 deal the same way: the Hawks sent their newly acquired 1978 second-round pick to the Trail Blazers for Rich Laurel. Harry Glickman's executive ledger matches that package.

The legacy archive entry also included “future considerations,” but none of those authoritative records contains an additional consideration. This review removes the unsupported asset rather than preserving an unexplained extra term.

sections.heading: Atlanta Had Just Acquired the Pick
sections.body:
The second-rounder originated in Buffalo. On September 13, Atlanta traded Bill Willoughby to the Braves for Buffalo's 1978 second-round pick. Just 22 days later, the Hawks moved that pick to Portland for Laurel.

That short chain is important because it prevents the pick from being treated as a long-held Atlanta draft asset. Atlanta converted it almost immediately into a player-rights bet.

sections.heading: Laurel Never Played for the Hawks
sections.body:
Portland had drafted Laurel No. 19 overall in the 1977 draft, but he did not make the Trail Blazers' regular-season roster. Atlanta acquired his rights in October and then released him on November 28.

Laurel therefore produced zero regular-season games for the Hawks. Milwaukee signed him on December 2, and he played 10 NBA games for the Bucks, averaging 5.7 minutes and 2.4 points. Milwaukee waived him in January, ending his NBA career.

Those 10 Bucks games do not help Atlanta's trade grade. The Hawks had already released him and received no downstream trade asset.

sections.heading: Portland Used the Pick on Keith Herron
sections.body:
Portland retained the second-round pick and used it at No. 24 in the 1978 draft on Keith Herron. That establishes the pick as a real draft asset rather than a paper return that disappeared before selection.

The realized Portland outcome was still poor. Herron never played a regular-season game for the Trail Blazers. On October 16, 1978, Atlanta claimed him on waivers from Portland.

Herron then played 14 games for Atlanta in 1978-79. He later had a stronger 80-game season with Detroit and finished his NBA career with 124 games, but none of those later games are Portland production.

sections.heading: Atlanta's Later Herron Claim Is Separate
sections.body:
There is an unusual circularity to the transaction chain: Atlanta traded the pick that became Herron, Portland drafted Herron, and Atlanta ultimately claimed him on waivers.

This review keeps those events separate. Atlanta's 14 Herron games came from a 1978 waiver claim, not from the 1977 Laurel transaction. They are useful historical context, but they cannot be retroactively counted as the return for trading the pick.

sections.heading: The Difference Is Asset Control, Not Team Production
sections.body:
Neither side generated meaningful direct team-specific production from the original return. Laurel never played for Atlanta, while Herron never played for Portland.

Portland's advantage is that the Trail Blazers controlled a second-round pick through draft night and selected a player who did establish an NBA career. Atlanta converted the same asset into Laurel and released him before he appeared in a game.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Trail Blazers Edge, C-/D. Portland receives a C- because the second-round pick remained a usable draft asset through selection, even though Herron never played for the team. Atlanta receives a D because Laurel produced zero Hawks games and no downstream asset before being released. The gap stays modest because Portland also failed to realize on-court value from its return. Confidence is high on the one-for-one package and downstream chronology.

sections.heading: The Original Package Is Fully Verified
sections.body:
Denver's 1977-78 transaction ledger records the October 11 deal as a straight exchange: the Nuggets sent their 1978 first-round pick to Washington for Bo Ellis. The pick became No. 18 in the 1978 draft and Washington used it on Dave Corzine.

There is no cash term or conditional language in the cited team and league ledgers. This review therefore treats the transaction as a clean player-for-first-round-pick swap.

sections.heading: Ellis Gave Denver Three Seasons of Rotation Depth
sections.body:
Ellis played 78 games in 1977-78 and averaged 4.3 points and 3.9 rebounds in 15.6 minutes. He followed with 42 games in 1978-79 and 48 more in 1979-80.

Across those three Denver seasons, Ellis appeared in 168 regular-season games, scored 613 points and grabbed 482 rebounds. His role was modest, but the volume matters. Denver did receive a real NBA player who stayed on the roster for multiple seasons rather than a short-term rental.

sections.heading: Corzine Gave Washington Two Seasons
sections.body:
Washington selected Corzine with the acquired No. 18 pick in 1978. He played 59 games as a rookie and 78 in 1979-80, for 137 regular-season Bullets appearances.

His Washington production was limited by a veteran frontcourt that included Wes Unseld and Elvin Hayes. Corzine averaged 3.0 points and 2.5 rebounds as a rookie, then 2.9 points and 3.5 rebounds in his second season. The direct Washington value was useful depth rather than star-level production.

sections.heading: The Pick Created a Second Asset Cycle
sections.body:
The more important part of Washington's return arrived after those two seasons. On September 26, 1980, the Bullets traded Corzine to San Antonio for a 1981 second-round pick and a 1982 second-round pick.

Those selections later became Claude Gregory and Dwight Anderson. Neither player created major NBA value, so this review does not overstate the downstream branch. Still, the fact that Washington turned Corzine into two more draft assets extends the life of the original 1978 first-round pick beyond his 137 Bullets games.

sections.heading: Corzine's Later Career Belongs Mostly to Other Teams
sections.body:
Corzine developed into a long-term NBA center after leaving Washington and eventually played 13 seasons. That career is useful context for the quality of the original draft selection, but this review does not credit the Bullets with production he delivered for San Antonio, Chicago or other later teams.

The same discipline applies on Denver's side. Ellis's three Denver seasons are the realized return. There is no evidence in the cited records of a later Denver trade branch that would materially increase his value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bullets Edge, B/B+. Denver receives a B because Ellis delivered 168 games of usable frontcourt depth over three seasons. Washington receives a B+ because the acquired first became Corzine, who played 137 games for the Bullets and then returned two second-round picks in a 1980 trade. The difference is modest but source-supported: Washington got a slightly more durable asset chain, while Denver still received meaningful multi-year service. Confidence is high.

sections.heading: The Package Is Exactly What the legacy archive entry Says
sections.body:
Atlanta's and Los Angeles' 1977-78 transaction ledgers agree on the October 17, 1977 exchange: the Hawks sent a 1979 fourth-round pick to the Lakers for Tony Robertson. The pick later became No. 79 overall and Los Angeles used it on Ray White.

There is no cash component, condition or additional player in the cited ledgers. This review therefore treats this as a straightforward player-for-future-fourth transaction.

sections.heading: Robertson Gave Atlanta One Useful Rookie Season
sections.body:
Robertson played 63 regular-season games for the Hawks in 1977-78. He averaged 5.9 points, 1.6 assists and 1.2 steals in 14.7 minutes while shooting 44.1 percent from the field.

That is not star-level production, but it is meaningful rotation value for a fourth-round pick two years into the future. He logged 929 minutes, scored 373 points and collected 74 steals for a 41-win Atlanta team that reached the playoffs.

The Hawks did not turn Robertson into another asset. Their 1978-79 transaction ledger shows that he was waived on September 22, 1978. Golden State later signed him as a free agent in February 1979, so his later Warriors games do not belong to Atlanta's realized return.

sections.heading: The Lakers' Pick Became Ray White
sections.body:
Los Angeles held Atlanta's fourth-rounder through the 1979 draft and selected Ray White at No. 79 overall. White appears in the draft record but never logged an NBA regular-season game.

That result gives the Lakers no realized playing value from the pick itself. This review does not penalize Los Angeles for failing to turn a late fourth-rounder into a long-term contributor; most selections in that range were uncertain. But retrospective grading has to count what the asset actually became, and in this case it did not produce NBA minutes.

sections.heading: The Asset Cost Was Very Low for Atlanta
sections.body:
The trade matters because the Hawks converted a distant late-round pick into 63 games of immediate depth. There was no premium first-round value at risk, and the pick did not later become a productive NBA player.

Los Angeles, meanwhile, did create a legitimate future draft asset out of a player it was willing to move. The process was rational even though the eventual selection produced no NBA return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win, B/D+. Atlanta receives a B because Robertson supplied 63 games and nearly 1,000 minutes of useful rookie-season depth for a low-value future pick. Los Angeles receives a D+ because the acquired fourth-rounder did reach the draft and become White, but White never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. This is a clear Atlanta win on realized value without being a major franchise-changing transaction. Confidence is high.

sections.heading: The Transaction Structure Is Clear, but the Return Is Not
sections.body:
Cleveland's 1977-78 transaction ledger says the Cavaliers traded Gary Brokaw to Buffalo on October 17, 1977 for future considerations. Buffalo's ledger records the same exchange from the other side, and the league transaction log matches it.

The historical Clippers media guide also lists Brokaw as acquired from Cleveland for future considerations. None of those sources identifies the consideration as cash, a draft pick or another player. This review therefore removes the question-mark styling from the legacy asset text but does not pretend the missing detail has been solved.

sections.heading: Brokaw Gave Buffalo 13 Games
sections.body:
Brokaw's Braves tenure was brief. He played 13 regular-season games in 1977-78, averaging 10.0 minutes, 4.2 points and 1.5 assists. His total Buffalo line was 130 minutes, 54 points, 20 assists and 12 rebounds.

Those 13 games were the final NBA appearances of his four-year career. That limits the upside of Buffalo's side immediately: the Braves did receive measurable rotation depth, but not a multi-season player or later trade asset.

sections.heading: Cleveland's Future Consideration Cannot Be Traced
sections.body:
The difficult side is Cleveland. The future-considerations clause is documented by multiple sources, so it should not be treated as though the Cavaliers received nothing.

At the same time, TradeVerdicts grades realized and traceable outcomes. No source reviewed for this review identifies a later player, pick, cash amount or other basketball asset as the fulfillment of this specific October 17 clause. Without that link, assigning Cleveland the value of a hypothetical asset would be unsupported.

This is the same discipline used elsewhere in the archive when future-considerations details remain unresolved: acknowledge that a consideration existed, avoid converting uncertainty into zero, but do not give full realized-value credit for an asset whose outcome cannot be identified.

sections.heading: The Broader Brokaw Context Does Not Change the Grade
sections.body:
Cleveland had acquired Brokaw with Elmore Smith from Milwaukee in January 1977 in a much larger trade. Brokaw then played 39 games for the Cavaliers before the Buffalo move. That earlier acquisition is a separate transaction and cannot be used to improve or reduce the grade here.

Likewise, Buffalo's later roster moves do not create a downstream Brokaw branch. His NBA career ended after these 13 Braves games.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Braves Edge, C-/D+. Buffalo receives a C- because Brokaw delivered 13 documented regular-season games and a small amount of reserve production. Cleveland receives a D+ on documented realized value because the future consideration is unquestionably part of the trade but remains unidentified in the reviewed record. The gap is intentionally small, and confidence is medium rather than high because Cleveland's eventual return could not be traced. This review's main source-backed improvement is precision: future considerations stay future considerations unless a source establishes what they became.

sections.heading: The Package Is a Straight Player-for-Fourth-Round Pick
sections.body:
Chicago and New Orleans list the October 18, 1977 transaction identically: the Bulls sent their 1978 fourth-round pick to the Jazz for Glenn Hansen. The league draft-trade record also traces that exact selection to New Orleans, where it became No. 75 overall.

There are no extra players, cash terms or conditions in the reviewed record. This review therefore keeps the legacy package structure and focuses on correcting the realized-value assessment.

sections.heading: Hansen Barely Appeared for Chicago
sections.body:
The biggest issue with the legacy B+ grade is Hansen's actual Bulls production. Basketball-Reference credits him with only two Chicago games in 1977-78 and four total minutes.

He went 0-for-2 from the field, did not score and recorded no rebounds or assists for the Bulls. Hansen also played three games for Kansas City that season, but those minutes came after Chicago and do not belong to the Bulls' return.

His NBA career ended after 1977-78. Chicago therefore received a real player but almost no measurable on-court value from the transaction.

sections.heading: New Orleans Used the Pick on Jeff Covington
sections.body:
The Jazz kept the acquired fourth-rounder through the 1978 draft and selected Jeff Covington at No. 75 overall. The draft record confirms both the slot and the Youngstown State forward.

Covington never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Basketball-Reference lists the draft selection but no NBA career statistics, and the 1978 draft table shows no NBA games or minutes attached to his record.

That means New Orleans received a valid draft asset and exercised it, but the pick produced no realized NBA playing value. There is also no verified downstream trade return attached to Covington in the reviewed sources.

sections.heading: The Difference Between Two Games and Zero Games Is Small
sections.body:
Chicago technically realized more direct NBA production because Hansen appeared twice. But two games and four minutes should not be inflated into a meaningful roster win.

New Orleans, meanwhile, at least retained the flexibility of a future fourth-round selection through draft night. In process terms that asset had value. In retrospective realized-value terms, however, it became a player who never appeared in the league.

This is exactly the kind of low-stakes historical transaction where the grade gap should remain narrow. Neither side surrendered premium capital, and neither side generated a lasting contributor.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Bulls Edge, D+/D. Chicago receives a D+ because Hansen produced two documented regular-season appearances, even though the contribution was only four minutes and zero points. New Orleans receives a D because the acquired pick was fully exercised at No. 75 but Covington never played an NBA regular-season game. The Bulls edge is technical rather than substantial. Confidence is high on the package, Hansen's Chicago line and the draft outcome.

sections.heading: The Core Trade Is Johnny Neumann for a 1978 Third-Round Pick
sections.body:
Buffalo, Indiana and the league transaction ledgers all record the October 18, 1977 exchange the same way. The Braves sent Johnny Neumann to the Pacers for Indiana's 1978 third-round pick. The pick later landed at No. 48 and became Mike Santos.

Indiana's 1979 media guide independently confirms the same package, describing Neumann as acquired from Buffalo for a 1978 third-round draft choice. That official Pacers source does not mention cash.

sections.heading: The Cash/Future-Considerations Term Is Source-Specific
sections.body:
Pro Sports Transactions' 1978 draft-pick ledger records the No. 48 selection and adds future considerations/cash to Buffalo's return. Because the Basketball-Reference and Pacers media-guide ledgers omit that term, this review does not present the financial component as universally confirmed. It is retained as a source-specific asset with no amount attached.

That distinction matters for grading. Buffalo should receive some credit for a documented additional consideration, but there is no basis to invent a dollar value or trace it into another player.

sections.heading: Neumann Gave Indiana Twenty Games
sections.body:
Neumann appeared in 20 regular-season games for the Pacers in 1977-78, making one start. He averaged 10.8 minutes, 4.2 points and 1.4 assists, totaling 83 points in 216 minutes.

Indiana waived him on December 22, 1977. He did not produce a later Pacers trade asset, and Basketball-Reference lists him outside the NBA the following season. The direct return was therefore brief and limited, but it was real.

sections.heading: The Pick Became Mike Santos
sections.body:
Buffalo kept the pick through the 1978 draft and selected Santos at No. 48. The Braves' transaction ledger lists the selection, while Santos's player page confirms he was drafted in the third round with the fourth pick of that round.

Santos never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. His Basketball-Reference page lists a rookie career length with no NBA game line. The draft branch therefore produced no realized NBA playing value for the Buffalo/San Diego franchise.

sections.heading: This Is a Low-Impact Trade, Not a Hidden Win
sections.body: The temptation with late-round trades is to overstate small differences. Indiana did receive more measurable basketball production because Neumann played 20 games. Buffalo's pick produced no NBA games, but the Pro Sports Transactions consideration means the Braves' return was not only the failed draft pick.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pacers Edge, C/D+. Indiana receives a C because Neumann provided 20 games and a small amount of rotation value before being waived. Buffalo receives a D+ because Santos never played an NBA regular-season game, with the unspecified future-considerations/cash term keeping the grade above a pure no-return outcome. The edge is real but minor. Confidence is high on the player-for-pick structure and moderate on the financial term because it appears in Pro Sports Transactions but not the primary team and league ledgers.

sections.heading: The Package Is Fully Confirmed
sections.body: New Jersey, Detroit and the league transaction ledgers all record the November 7, 1977 trade the same way. The Nets sent Al Skinner, their 1978 second-round pick and their 1979 second-round pick to the Pistons. Detroit sent Howard Porter, Kevin Porter and cash to New Jersey. The cited Basketball-Reference ledgers do not state a cash amount, so this review leaves it unspecified.

sections.heading: The Nets Got Two Productive Veterans Immediately
sections.body:
Howard Porter played 55 games for New Jersey after the trade, averaging 12.8 points and 4.8 rebounds in 22.1 minutes. Those 55 games were the final NBA regular-season games of his career.

Kevin Porter provided the larger return. He played 74 Nets games in 1977-78, averaging 16.2 points and 10.8 assists. Across his full two-team season he led the NBA at 10.2 assists per game, and his New Jersey segment was even higher.

The Nets also retained value when Kevin Porter left. On September 8, 1978, New Jersey traded him back to Detroit for Eric Money. Money then played 47 Nets games in 1978-79 at 16.7 points and 5.3 assists before being moved with Skinner to Philadelphia for Harvey Catchings, Ralph Simpson and cash. Because Skinner was also in that later package, this review does not assign the entire Philadelphia return to the Kevin Porter branch.

sections.heading: Skinner Was a Useful but Short Detroit Piece
sections.body: Skinner played 69 games for Detroit after the trade, averaging 7.0 points in 18.5 minutes. The Pistons waived him on September 15, 1978. He signed back with New Jersey six days later, so Detroit's direct Skinner return ended after one season.

sections.heading: Terry Tyler Became the Centerpiece of Detroit's Return
sections.body:
The 1978 second-round pick landed at No. 23 and became Terry Tyler. He played all 82 games in each of his seven Detroit seasons from 1978-79 through 1984-85, totaling 574 regular-season appearances for the Pistons.

Tyler averaged 11.6 points, 6.2 rebounds and 1.9 blocks over those seven seasons. He made the 1979 All-Rookie First Team and ranked among the league's leading shot blockers repeatedly. That combination of durability and defense is the largest single realized asset in the trade.

Tyler's 1985 veteran-free-agent departure also created a compensation arrangement involving first-round positioning and a second-round pick. Detroit ultimately selected John Salley at No. 11 in 1986, but the arrangement also sent Detroit's own first-round position to Sacramento, so this review does not credit Salley's entire later career to Tyler alone.

sections.heading: The 1979 Pick Produced No Detroit Games
sections.body: Detroit used the other second-round pick at No. 29 in 1979 on Tony Price. The Pistons waived him before the season, and he never played a regular-season game for Detroit. Price later appeared in five games for San Diego in 1980-81.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Edge, A/B+. Detroit receives an A because Tyler alone supplied 574 games across seven seasons, with Skinner adding another 69. New Jersey receives a B+ because Kevin Porter delivered an outstanding 74-game season, Howard Porter added 55 useful games and the Kevin Porter branch produced Eric Money. The Nets did well in the short term, but Detroit's seven years of Tyler production create the stronger total return. Confidence is high.

sections.heading: The Original Package Is Fully Verified
sections.body:
Atlanta, New York and the league transaction ledgers all record the same November 14, 1977 transaction: the Hawks sent their 1978 second-round pick to the Knicks for Tom McMillen. There are no additional cash terms, protections or players in the cited ledgers.

The pick landed at No. 32 in the 1978 draft and New York used it on John Rudd. That makes this a straightforward realized-value comparison between a known veteran rotation player and the player actually selected with the acquired pick.

sections.heading: McMillen Became a Six-Season Atlanta Rotation Piece
sections.body:
McMillen gave the Hawks immediate and durable frontcourt depth. He played 68 games in 1977-78 after arriving in November, then appeared in 82 games in 1978-79, 53 in 1979-80, 79 in 1980-81, 73 in 1981-82 and 61 in 1982-83.

Across those six Atlanta seasons he played 416 regular-season games. Basketball-Reference credits him with 8.5 points and 4.4 rebounds per game in 21.3 minutes across that Hawks tenure. He was not a franchise star, but the trade did not require star-level production to be valuable. Atlanta spent a second-round pick and received six years of usable NBA minutes.

His first post-trade season was productive enough to make the immediate exchange look good on its own. McMillen averaged 9.9 points and 6.1 rebounds in 68 games for the 1977-78 Hawks. Later seasons moved him more firmly into a rotation role, but he remained available and useful through 1983.

sections.heading: Rudd Had a Much Smaller NBA Footprint
sections.body:
New York used the No. 32 pick on John Rudd out of McNeese State. The 1978 draft ledger shows one NBA season, 58 games, 723 minutes, 184 points, 167 rebounds and 35 assists.

That is real return from a second-round selection, but it is a fraction of McMillen's Atlanta tenure. The Knicks did not turn the pick into a long-term rotation player or a later premium transaction asset. In realized NBA terms, the player selected at No. 32 produced only one season.

sections.heading: Atlanta Preserved Some Downstream Value
sections.body:
McMillen also retained trade value after his six Hawks seasons. On July 5, 1983, Atlanta traded him and a 1984 second-round pick to Washington for Randy Wittman.

That later deal should not be credited entirely to McMillen because Atlanta included another draft asset. Still, his presence in the package shows that his value did not disappear when his direct Atlanta tenure ended. Wittman then became a multi-season Hawks guard, so the McMillen branch remained part of Atlanta's roster-building chain.

sections.heading: The Cost Was Modest and the Return Was Durable
sections.body:
The central hindsight point is not that New York made a reckless move with a second-round pick. Second-round selections are uncertain assets, and Rudd did reach the NBA. The problem for the Knicks is simply that Atlanta converted that pick into 416 games from a dependable big man.

That gap is large enough that the trade does not need speculative alternate-draft analysis. Atlanta's realized return is visible in the actual games McMillen played, while New York's realized return is visible in Rudd's single season.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win, A-/C. Atlanta receives an A- because one second-round pick produced 416 regular-season games over six seasons, plus some residual trade value in the later Wittman package. New York receives a C because Rudd reached the NBA and played 58 games, but the pick did not produce comparable duration or impact. The package and downstream record are well documented, so confidence is high.

sections.heading: The Original Trade Was Two Seconds for Behagen
sections.body:
Atlanta, Houston and the league transaction ledgers all record the December 16, 1977 transaction identically: the Hawks sent Ron Behagen to the Rockets for Houston's 1978 and 1979 second-round picks.

Those picks later became No. 25 Rick Wilson in 1978 and No. 38 Larry Wilson in 1979. The package itself is clean, with no cash, conditions or additional players to resolve.

sections.heading: Houston Barely Used Behagen Before Flipping Him
sections.body:
Behagen played only three games for Houston. Basketball-Reference lists him at 4.7 points and 2.3 rebounds in 11.0 minutes per game during that tiny Rockets sample.

If the evaluation stopped there, Houston would have little to show for two second-round picks. It does not stop there. On December 22, only six days after acquiring Behagen, the Rockets traded him to Indiana for Alonzo Bradley.

Because Behagen was the only Houston asset in that second trade, Bradley is a direct downstream return from the original Atlanta transaction rather than an attribution shared with another outgoing player or pick.

sections.heading: Bradley Gave Houston Three Seasons
sections.body:
Bradley played 43 games for Houston in 1977-78 and averaged 7.0 points in 18.6 minutes. He followed with 34 games in 1978-79 and 22 in 1979-80.

That is 99 regular-season Rockets games across three seasons. His role declined after the first year, but Houston still transformed six days of Behagen ownership into a multi-season roster piece. Bradley remained with the Rockets until Dallas selected him in the 1980 expansion draft.

sections.heading: Atlanta Got One Reserve Guard and One Non-NBA Draft Outcome
sections.body:
The first Hawks pick landed at No. 25 in 1978. Atlanta selected Rick Wilson, who played 61 games as a rookie and five more in 1979-80. He averaged 3.0 points in 9.7 minutes during his first season and finished with 66 Atlanta games across two years.

That is useful second-round return, but it remained a small reserve role. Wilson did not become a long-term Hawks rotation fixture or a major downstream transaction asset.

The second pick landed at No. 38 in 1979 and became Larry Wilson out of Nicholls State. The 1979 draft ledger shows no NBA career totals for him. This review therefore records the pick as a documented draft conversion with no realized NBA playing return.

sections.heading: The Two-Pick Optics Overstated Atlanta's Hindsight Value
sections.body:
Two second-round selections can look stronger than a short-term veteran acquisition when the trade is viewed only at transaction time. The actual branches reverse that impression.

Atlanta's picks produced 66 NBA games from Rick Wilson and no NBA career line from Larry Wilson. Houston got only three Behagen games, but immediately converted him one-for-one into Bradley and received 99 games over three seasons.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Edge, B/C+. Houston receives a B because Behagen was efficiently recycled into Bradley, extending the asset into 99 Rockets games. Atlanta receives a C+ because Rick Wilson reached the NBA and supplied 66 reserve games, but the second pick produced no NBA playing value. The difference is not large enough for a dominant grade gap, yet Houston's direct downstream conversion clearly beats the realized output of the two Atlanta selections. Confidence is high.

sections.heading: The Package Was a Straight One-for-One Exchange
sections.body:
Houston and Indiana transaction records show the December 22, 1977 deal as Ron Behagen for the rights to Alonzo Bradley. The league ledger records the same structure.

Houston had acquired Behagen from Atlanta only six days earlier, but this review evaluates this second transaction on its own. The question is what Houston received for Behagen and what Indiana received for Bradley's rights.

sections.heading: Behagen Produced More Per Game for Indiana
sections.body:
Behagen played 51 regular-season games for the Pacers in 1977-78 and started 10. He averaged 11.2 points, 6.5 rebounds and 1.3 assists in 22.2 minutes per game.

That is meaningful rotation production, especially for a player acquired in late December. Indiana did not get multiple seasons from him, however. Basketball-Reference's transaction history shows the Pacers waived Behagen on September 11, 1978.

His Indiana branch therefore ends with one productive partial season and no documented trade return.

sections.heading: Bradley Stayed With Houston for Three Seasons
sections.body:
Bradley played 43 games for Houston in 1977-78, averaging 7.0 points in 18.6 minutes. He returned for 34 games in 1978-79 and 22 in 1979-80, although his role became much smaller in both later seasons.

Across the three years Bradley appeared in 99 regular-season Rockets games. His first season supplied the bulk of the value; the final two were low-minute reserve years.

Bradley's Houston tenure ended when the Dallas Mavericks selected him in the 1980 expansion draft. That produced no conventional player-or-pick return for Houston, so this review does not extend the branch beyond his 99 Rockets appearances.

sections.heading: The Minute Totals Show How Close the Deal Really Was
sections.body:
The legacy evaluations treated the trade as heavily one-sided in opposite directions depending on which team perspective was used. The team-specific production does not support either extreme.

Behagen's 51 Indiana games at 22.2 minutes per game amount to roughly 1,130 regular-season minutes. Bradley's 43 games at 18.6 minutes, 34 at 7.2 minutes and 22 at 4.4 minutes total roughly 1,140 minutes for Houston.

The exact minute total is less important than the scale: the two teams received almost the same amount of court time. Indiana concentrated its value into one season with better scoring and rebounding production. Houston spread its value across three seasons, with a useful first year followed by smaller reserve roles.

sections.heading: Neither Team Created a Major Downstream Branch
sections.body:
Indiana waived Behagen before the next season. Houston lost Bradley in the expansion draft. Neither side turned the acquired asset into a premium pick, long-term starter or substantial later trade package.

That makes this a useful example of why games played alone can mislead. Houston's 99 appearances sound much larger than Indiana's 51, but the minute load was nearly identical because Bradley's later role was so small.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, B-/B-. Indiana receives a B- for a productive 51-game Behagen run. Houston receives a B- for 99 Bradley games across three seasons, with most of the impact concentrated in 1977-78. The two returns differ in shape but not enough in realized team-specific value to justify a winner. Confidence is high.

sections.heading: The December 27 Package Is Fully Confirmed
sections.body: Boston, Los Angeles and the league transaction ledgers all record the same deal. The Celtics sent Charlie Scott to the Lakers and received Don Chaney, Kermit Washington and Los Angeles' 1978 first-round pick. Boston later used that pick at No. 8 on Freeman Williams.

sections.heading: Chaney Gave Boston Three Seasons of Direct Value
sections.body:
Chaney returned to the Celtics and played 42 games in 1977-78, 65 in 1978-79 and 60 in 1979-80. That is 167 regular-season games after the trade. His role steadily shrank, but he remained a useful veteran perimeter defender through the first Larry Bird season.

The direct numbers were modest compared with his earlier Celtics years, yet the longevity matters. Boston received nearly three seasons of service from one incoming player before accounting for Washington or the draft pick.

sections.heading: Washington Gave Boston 32 Strong Games
sections.body:
Washington played 32 regular-season games for Boston in 1977-78, averaging 11.8 points and 10.5 rebounds in 27.1 minutes. That was meaningful short-term frontcourt production, not merely a paper asset.

His Celtics tenure ended the following summer when Boston included him in a much larger trade with San Diego. Because the later deal contained multiple outgoing players, this review treats Washington as one contributor to that package rather than assigning Boston's entire return to him.

sections.heading: The No. 8 Pick Became Freeman Williams and Another Trade Asset
sections.body:
Boston selected Freeman Williams at No. 8 in the 1978 draft. Williams never played a regular-season game for the Celtics. On August 4, 1978, Boston traded Williams, Washington, Kevin Kunnert and Sidney Wicks to San Diego for Tiny Archibald, Marvin Barnes, Billy Knight and two future second-round picks.

Two of Boston's four outgoing player assets in that deal—Washington and Williams—came directly from this review. That gives the original trade a meaningful downstream branch, but the archive does not credit the entire Archibald package to this review because Kunnert and Wicks were separate Boston assets.

sections.heading: The Lakers Got a Useful Half-Season From Scott
sections.body:
Scott played 48 regular-season games for Los Angeles in 1977-78, averaging 11.7 points, 4.9 assists and 3.1 rebounds in 29.0 minutes. The Lakers then moved him again before the next season.

On June 26, 1978, Los Angeles traded Scott to Denver for Ron Boone and two 1979 second-round picks. Boone became the biggest direct downstream return. He played all 82 games for the Lakers in 1978-79 and six more in 1979-80, giving Los Angeles 88 regular-season appearances.

sections.heading: One Second-Round Pick Produced Ollie Mack
sections.body: The two Denver picks later became No. 25 Ollie Mack and No. 41 Mark Young. Mack played 27 games for the Lakers in 1979-80 before moving on. Young never played an NBA regular-season game. The Scott branch therefore produced 48 direct Scott games, 88 Boone games and 27 Mack games, with no NBA return from Young.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Edge, A/B+. Boston receives an A because Chaney supplied 167 games, Washington provided strong short-term rebounding, and Washington plus the No. 8 Williams rights became two pieces of the later San Diego blockbuster. Los Angeles receives a B+ because Scott produced 48 useful games and then became Boone plus two seconds, one of which produced Mack. Both sides recycled value well; Boston's combination of direct service and premium downstream trade currency creates the stronger realized outcome. Confidence is high.
