sections.heading: The January 27 Package Is Fully Confirmed
sections.body:
New Jersey, Indiana and the league transaction ledgers agree on the trade structure. The Nets received John Williamson. The Pacers received Bob Carrington, New Jersey's 1980 second-round pick and New Jersey's 1981 second-round pick.

The legacy archive entry correctly linked the 1980 pick to Louis Orr, but it mislabeled the 1981 outcome as No. 25 Brian Jackson. The later routing shows why. Indiana traded that pick to Portland in 1979, and Portland ultimately used it at No. 26 on Brian Jackson. This review repairs the slot and records the intermediary value Indiana actually received before the draft.

sections.heading: Williamson Immediately Became a High-End Nets Scorer
sections.body:
Williamson's direct New Jersey return was substantial. He played 33 games after the trade in 1977-78 and averaged 29.5 points in 38.8 minutes. He followed with 74 games in 1978-79 at 22.2 points and another 28 Nets games in 1979-80 at 17.7 points.

Across those post-trade Nets seasons, Williamson appeared in 135 regular-season games. The value was concentrated in scoring rather than longevity, but the peak was far above what any single Indiana asset produced.

New Jersey later moved Williamson on February 4, 1980. The Nets sent him plus a 1981 second-round pick to Washington for Roger Phegley. Because another second-round asset was included, this review does not credit the entire Phegley return to Williamson alone. Phegley nevertheless played 28 Nets games at 11.7 points before New Jersey traded him to Cleveland for Foots Walker.

sections.heading: Carrington Was a Short-Term Pacers Piece
sections.body:
Bob Carrington played 35 games for Indiana after the trade, averaging 7.1 points in 17.7 minutes. He did not play in the NBA in 1978-79 and later resurfaced for 10 games with San Diego in 1979-80.

His Indiana branch was modest, but Carrington was only one of three Pacers assets.

sections.heading: The 1980 Second Became Louis Orr
sections.body:
Indiana used the 1980 second-round pick at No. 29 on Louis Orr. Orr played all 82 games as a rookie in 1980-81, averaging 10.5 points and 4.4 rebounds. He returned for 80 games in 1981-82 at 11.5 points and 4.1 rebounds.

That gave Indiana 162 regular-season games, 48 starts and an 11.0-point average from the pick. In October 1982 the Pacers traded Orr to New York for another second-round pick, extending the asset chain beyond his two Indiana seasons.

sections.heading: The 1981 Second Became Clemon Johnson Before It Became Brian Jackson
sections.body:
Indiana did not hold the other second-rounder to the 1981 draft. On October 9, 1979, the Pacers sent that pick to Portland for Clemon Johnson. Indiana and Portland transaction ledgers both identify the selection as the pick later used on Brian Jackson.

Johnson became a major realized return for the Pacers. He played 79 games in 1979-80, 81 in 1980-81, 79 in 1981-82 and 51 more for Indiana in 1982-83 before moving to Philadelphia. That is 290 Pacers regular-season games from the asset branch.

Portland ultimately drafted Jackson at No. 26, not No. 25. The 1981 draft ledger confirms No. 25 belonged to Boston and became Tracy Jackson, while Portland used No. 26 on Brian Jackson. The correction matters because the original legacy slot would otherwise collide with a different player's draft history.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, A/A. New Jersey receives an A because Williamson gave the Nets 135 games of top-line scoring, including a 29.5-point post-trade burst and a full 22.2-point season. Indiana also receives an A because Carrington, Orr and the Johnson conversion produced 487 combined Pacers games, with Orr and Johnson both becoming multi-season rotation pieces. New Jersey got the best individual player and peak; Indiana got superior depth, duration and asset conversion. Neither side produced enough separation for a defensible winner. Confidence is high.

sections.heading: The Core Trade Is Player for Pick, Not Player for Pick and Cash
sections.body:
New Jersey, Denver and the league transaction ledgers all record the January 30, 1978 exchange as Darnell Hillman for Denver's 1979 second-round pick. The legacy archive entry also contained cash, but none of those authoritative ledgers lists a financial term.

This review therefore removes the unsupported cash asset. The documented package is a clean one-for-one exchange between Hillman and the future second-round selection.

sections.heading: Hillman Gave Denver 33 Games
sections.body:
Hillman joined the Nuggets for the final 33 games of 1977-78. He averaged 7.8 points, 7.2 rebounds, 1.6 assists and 1.1 blocks in 22.6 minutes.

That is useful frontcourt production for a second-round pick, but Denver did not retain him beyond the season.

sections.heading: The Nuggets Recycled Hillman in a Shared Package
sections.body:
On June 26, 1978, Denver traded Hillman and Mike Evans to Kansas City for Ron Boone and a 1979 second-round pick later associated with Mark Young. Hillman therefore retained transaction value, but this review does not credit the full Boone-plus-pick return to him because Evans was also outgoing.

Denver then moved Boone again in a separate deal with the Lakers, further demonstrating how quickly the asset chain branched. For this trade, the responsible attribution stops at Hillman being one of two pieces used in the Kansas City package.

sections.heading: The Nets Immediately Used the Pick for Wilson Washington
sections.body:
New Jersey held Denver's second-round pick for only one day. On January 31, the Nets sent that 1979 second-rounder plus a 1982 second-round pick and a 1983 third-round pick to Philadelphia for Wilson Washington.

Philadelphia eventually used the Denver-derived pick at No. 36 on Clint Richardson. New Jersey never drafted Richardson, so this review does not credit Richardson's long NBA career to the Nets.

Instead, the Nets receive partial downstream credit for Washington. He played 24 games for New Jersey in 1977-78 at 8.8 points and 5.9 rebounds, then 62 games in 1978-79 at 8.1 points and 4.7 rebounds. That is 86 Nets regular-season games from the player acquired with a three-pick package.

sections.heading: The Pick Was Only One of Three Assets
sections.body:
The Wilson Washington return is meaningful, but the Denver pick was not sufficient by itself. New Jersey also sent a 1982 second and a 1983 third. This review therefore treats Washington as a shared downstream return rather than assigning all 86 games to the Hillman trade.

That same caution applies to Denver's June package, where Hillman shared outgoing value with Evans.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Edge, B-/C+. New Jersey receives a B- because the second-round pick was immediately useful trade currency in the Washington acquisition, and Washington produced 86 Nets games across two seasons. Denver receives a C+ because Hillman supplied 33 useful games and later remained one component of a two-player trade package. The Nets' downstream result is somewhat more durable, but both branches depended on additional assets, so the gap stays narrow. Confidence is high on the documented one-for-one core trade and the removal of the unsupported cash term.

sections.heading: The Player-for-Pick Core Is Confirmed
sections.body:
Buffalo, Philadelphia and the league transaction ledgers all record the January 31, 1978 exchange as Ted McClain to the 76ers for a 1978 third-round pick. That pick became No. 65 Marvin Delph.

Those Basketball-Reference ledgers do not list cash. Pro Sports Transactions' 1978 draft-pick ledger adds a cash component going from Philadelphia to Buffalo. This review preserves that source distinction and does not invent an amount.

sections.heading: McClain Gave Philadelphia 29 Games
sections.body:
McClain joined a deep Philadelphia team in the middle of the season and played 29 regular-season games after the trade. He logged 293 minutes and totaled 91 points, 37 rebounds, 34 assists and 16 steals.

His role was limited. He did not start a game for Philadelphia and averaged just over ten minutes per appearance. Still, those minutes were real realized value from a third-round pick, and the 76ers received them during a season in which they remained an Eastern Conference contender.

The 76ers did not retain McClain long term. Philadelphia waived him on October 11, 1978. Phoenix later signed him as a free agent in January 1979, so there was no later Philadelphia player or draft asset tied to his departure.

sections.heading: Buffalo's Draft Pick Became Marvin Delph
sections.body:
The Braves kept the incoming third-round pick through the 1978 draft and used it at No. 65 on Marvin Delph of Arkansas.

Basketball-Reference lists Delph as a 1978 San Diego Clippers draft pick after the franchise relocation, but no NBA regular-season games appear on his player record. He was later selected again by Boston in the 1979 draft and still did not establish an NBA regular-season career.

That means the pick itself produced no on-court NBA value for the Buffalo/San Diego franchise.

sections.heading: The Cash Is Real but Cannot Be Converted Into Invented Basketball Value
sections.body:
Pro Sports Transactions gives Buffalo an additional asset in the form of cash. That should not be erased merely because Basketball-Reference's shorter team ledgers omit it. At the same time, the cited source does not specify the amount, and no later roster transaction is tied directly to those dollars.

This review therefore treats the cash as legitimate financial consideration but does not transform it into speculative player value.

sections.heading: This Was a Small Transaction on Both Sides
sections.body:
Philadelphia's return was only 29 games from a reserve guard, and McClain was gone before the next regular season. Buffalo's player return was zero NBA games from Delph, although the franchise also received the undocumented-amount cash consideration.

The gap is therefore much smaller than it would be if McClain had become a long-term rotation piece or Delph had developed into an NBA contributor.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Edge, C+/D+. Philadelphia receives a C+ because McClain gave the team 29 useful reserve appearances and actual NBA minutes for a third-round pick. Buffalo receives a D+ because Delph never played an NBA regular-season game, with the unspecified cash providing the only remaining realized value. The 76ers come out ahead, but the trade belongs in the low-impact tier rather than among meaningful franchise swings. Confidence is high on the player and pick outcomes and moderate on the financial component because the cash amount is not specified.

sections.heading: The Player-for-Pick Exchange Is Fully Confirmed
sections.body:
Boston, New Orleans and the league transaction ledgers all record the same February 1, 1978 deal. The Celtics sent Fred Saunders to the Jazz and received New Orleans's 1978 second-round pick.

That pick landed at No. 30 and became Jeff Judkins. There are no cash terms, protections or routing conflicts in the cited ledgers, so this review is a straightforward comparison between Saunders's short New Orleans tenure and Judkins's Boston production.

sections.heading: Saunders Gave New Orleans Thirty Games
sections.body:
Saunders joined the Jazz for the remainder of 1977-78 and appeared in 30 regular-season games. He averaged 13.3 minutes, 5.0 points, 2.5 rebounds and 1.2 assists.

His role was modest, but not nonexistent. The Jazz received an experienced forward who could fill bench minutes immediately while Pete Maravich and the rest of the roster pushed through the second half of the season.

The problem is duration. Basketball-Reference lists 1977-78 as Saunders's final NBA season. There was no later New Orleans player or draft asset generated by his departure. The Jazz's branch therefore ends with those 30 games.

sections.heading: Boston Used the Pick on Jeff Judkins
sections.body:
The Celtics kept the second-round pick and selected Judkins at No. 30 in the 1978 draft. He immediately became a meaningful reserve.

As a rookie in 1978-79, Judkins played 81 games and averaged 8.8 points, 2.4 rebounds and 1.8 assists in 18.8 minutes. He scored 709 points and logged 1,521 minutes.

He returned in 1979-80 for 65 games, adding 351 points in 674 minutes. Across two Boston seasons, Judkins appeared in 146 regular-season games and scored 1,060 points.

That is a substantial return for a second-round selection acquired in exchange for a player who had been on the edge of Boston's rotation.

sections.heading: Judkins's Later Career Is Not Credited to Boston
sections.body:
Judkins continued in the NBA after his Celtics stint and finished with 272 career games. Those later seasons are useful career context but do not belong to Boston's realized return once he left the franchise.

This review therefore stops the direct Celtics value at the 146 Boston games. Even with that conservative treatment, the pick comfortably outproduced Saunders's New Orleans tenure.

sections.heading: The Trade Was Small, but the Outcome Was Not Even
sections.body:
The original archive record called the trade even, which understated the difference in realized service. Saunders gave New Orleans 30 games and then left the NBA. Judkins gave Boston 146 games across two seasons, including an 81-game rookie year with nearly nine points per game.

Neither player was a franchise centerpiece, so the transaction belongs below major-trade territory. The value difference is still large enough to support a clear winner.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win, B+/D+. Boston receives a B+ because the No. 30 pick became a two-season rotation player who appeared in 146 games and scored 1,060 points. New Orleans receives a D+ because Saunders supplied only 30 games before his NBA career ended. The Jazz did get short-term roster value, which keeps the grade above a complete miss, but Boston extracted far more realized NBA service from the exchange. Confidence is high.

sections.heading: The Original Pick Swap Is Fully Confirmed
sections.body: Cleveland, Milwaukee and the league transaction ledgers all record the June 1, 1978 exchange the same way. Cleveland sent its 1979 first-round pick to the Bucks and received Milwaukee's 1978 first-round pick. The Cavaliers used the incoming selection at No. 15 on Mike Mitchell.

sections.heading: The Cleveland Return Was Far Better Than a Normal Mid-First Outcome
sections.body:
Mitchell became an immediate rotation scorer. He played 80 games as a rookie in 1978-79 and then all 82 games in both 1979-80 and 1980-81. His third season was the peak of his Cleveland tenure: 24.5 points per game, 6.1 rebounds and an All-Star selection.

Mitchell stayed with Cleveland for 27 more games in 1981-82 before the Cavaliers traded him and Roger Phegley to San Antonio for Ron Brewer, Reggie Johnson and cash. Across his Cavaliers tenure, Mitchell appeared in 271 regular-season games. This review does not assign the full Brewer-Johnson-cash package to Mitchell alone because Phegley was also outgoing, but the later trade confirms that Mitchell retained substantial asset value.

sections.heading: Milwaukee's Incoming Pick Landed at No. 4
sections.body:
Cleveland's 1979 first became the fourth pick in the draft. The legacy archive record stops at Greg Kelser because Detroit ultimately selected him there, but Milwaukee did not simply make that pick and keep Kelser.

On June 25, 1979, the Bucks traded the No. 4 pick to Detroit for the No. 5 pick. Detroit drafted Kelser at No. 4. Milwaukee moved down one slot and selected Sidney Moncrief at No. 5.

sections.heading: That Draft-Day Step Completely Changes the Long-Term Evaluation
sections.body:
Moncrief became one of the defining players of the Bucks' 1980s teams. Basketball-Reference lists him as a five-time All-Star, five-time All-NBA selection, five-time All-Defensive selection and two-time Defensive Player of the Year. He also entered the Basketball Hall of Fame.

The No. 4 pick acquired from Cleveland therefore did not merely become Kelser. It became the premium asset Milwaukee used to move down one spot and secure Moncrief. The distinction is essential because a simple Mitchell-versus-Kelser comparison badly understates Milwaukee's realized return.

sections.heading: Cleveland Still Received Major Value
sections.body:
This is not a case where one team won because the other side failed. Mitchell became one of Cleveland's best scorers of the period, made an All-Star team and gave the Cavaliers 271 games. A mid-first pick producing that level of direct value deserves a strong grade.

Milwaukee's result was simply larger and longer lasting. Moncrief developed into a franchise cornerstone with elite two-way recognition for much of the decade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win, A+/A. Milwaukee receives an A+ because the Cleveland pick became the No. 4 slot, which the Bucks converted into No. 5 Sidney Moncrief, a Hall of Fame guard with five All-Star selections, five All-NBA honors, five All-Defensive honors and two Defensive Player of the Year awards. Cleveland receives an A because Mitchell played 271 games, made the 1981 All-Star team and retained later trade value. Both teams did extremely well; Milwaukee gets the edge because the pick became a true franchise-defining player. Confidence is high.

sections.heading: The Authoritative Ledgers Put the Trade on June 8
sections.body:
The legacy archive entry is dated June 7, 1978, but Indiana, Portland and the league transaction ledgers all place the exchange on June 8. This review preserves the frozen route identity while recording June 8 as the source-verified transaction date.

The package itself is fully aligned across those ledgers. Indiana sent the 1978 first-round pick that became No. 1 Mychal Thompson. Portland sent Johnny Davis and the 1978 first-round pick that became No. 3 Rick Robey.

sections.heading: Portland Got the Best Individual Player in the Deal
sections.body:
The Trail Blazers used No. 1 on Thompson, and he became a long-term frontcourt centerpiece. Thompson played 73 games as a rookie in 1978-79, missed 1979-80 with a leg injury, then returned for six more Portland seasons from 1980-81 through 1985-86.

Across seven playing seasons with Portland, Thompson appeared in 551 regular-season games. His strongest statistical season came in 1981-82, when he averaged 20.8 points, 11.7 rebounds and 4.0 assists in 79 games. He also averaged at least 14.7 points in every Portland season he played after returning from the injury.

In June 1986 Portland traded Thompson with Larry Krystkowiak to San Antonio for Steve Johnson. This review records that as evidence of retained trade value, but does not assign the entire Johnson return to Thompson because Krystkowiak was also outgoing.

sections.heading: Johnny Davis Became a Four-Year Pacers Starter
sections.body:
Indiana's direct veteran return was substantial. Davis started all 79 games he played in 1978-79 and averaged 18.3 points and 5.7 assists. He then started 82 games in 1979-80, 73 in 1980-81 and 70 in 1981-82.

Across four Pacers seasons, Davis played 319 regular-season games and started 304. Basketball-Reference's Indiana split gives him averages of 16.4 points and 5.4 assists over that span. That is far more than a temporary bridge player.

Indiana also retained value when Davis left. On December 31, 1982, the Pacers traded him to Atlanta for a 1983 second-round pick later used on Jim Thomas. The later pick produced limited value, but Davis had already delivered four productive seasons.

sections.heading: The No. 3 Pick Became Rick Robey, Then Billy Knight
sections.body:
Indiana used Portland's first-round pick at No. 3 on Robey. He played 43 Pacers games as a rookie, starting 13 and averaging 8.6 points and 5.9 rebounds.

The Pacers then converted Robey into a much larger downstream return. On January 16, 1979, Indiana traded him to Boston for Billy Knight. Knight played 39 Pacers games during the remainder of 1978-79, then 75, 82, 81 and 80 games over the next four seasons.

That is 357 Indiana regular-season games after the Robey trade. Knight averaged 17.5 points in 1980-81 and 17.1 in 1982-83. The Robey branch therefore became a long-running scoring asset rather than ending after half a rookie season.

sections.heading: Both Teams Did Extremely Well
sections.body:
Portland can point to the strongest single outcome: a No. 1 pick who gave the franchise seven playing seasons and 551 games. Indiana can point to broader asset depth: 319 Davis games plus 43 Robey games before Robey became Knight, who added 357 more Pacers appearances.

The correct hindsight comparison is therefore much closer than a Thompson-versus-Robey draft comparison suggests.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pacers Edge, A+/A. Indiana receives an A+ because Davis became a four-year starter and the No. 3 pick became Robey, who was quickly converted into five seasons of Knight production. Portland receives an A because Thompson was the best single player in the deal and gave the Trail Blazers 551 games across seven seasons. The Pacers' narrow edge comes from the combined volume and successful Robey-to-Knight conversion, not from Thompson disappointing. Confidence is high.

sections.heading: The Original Package Is Fully Confirmed
sections.body:
Buffalo, Los Angeles and the league transaction ledgers all record the June 7, 1978 deal the same way. The Braves sent a 1978 second-round pick to the Lakers for Tom Abernethy. Los Angeles used the pick at No. 38 on Lew Massey.

There is no additional player, cash term or conditional language in the cited ledgers. The basic transaction is therefore one player for one second-round pick.

sections.heading: Massey Never Produced NBA Regular-Season Value
sections.body:
The Lakers selected Massey with the No. 38 pick in the 1978 draft. Basketball-Reference's draft ledger lists him at that slot but shows no NBA games, minutes, points, rebounds or assists.

That means the Lakers received no realized NBA playing value from the pick. This review does not substitute college production or later non-NBA activity for an NBA return that never materialized.

sections.heading: Abernethy Never Played for Buffalo or San Diego After the Trade
sections.body:
The other side is more unusual. Buffalo acquired Abernethy just before the franchise relocated, but he never appeared in a regular-season game for the Braves or the new San Diego Clippers.

His player page shows 1977-78 with the Lakers, then 1978-79 with Golden State. On July 15, 1978, the Warriors signed Abernethy as a veteran free agent. San Diego's transaction ledger records that the Clippers received a 1979 second-round pick as compensation.

That compensation pick is the real downstream return from Buffalo's acquisition.

sections.heading: The Compensation Pick Became Part of the Brian Taylor Signing
sections.body:
The Abernethy compensation pick later became the No. 30 selection in the 1979 draft, where Gary Garland was selected. San Diego did not use the pick itself.

On February 15, 1979, the Clippers signed Brian Taylor as a veteran free agent and sent two 1979 second-round picks to Denver as compensation. One became No. 33 Lawrence Butler. The other was the Abernethy-derived pick that became No. 30 Garland.

Garland later played 78 regular-season games for Denver. That production belongs to the Nuggets, not the Clippers. This review therefore does not credit San Diego with Garland's NBA games.

The pick still had meaningful transaction value. It was one of two second-round assets the Clippers used to complete the Taylor signing. Because another second-rounder was also outgoing, this review does not assign the full value of Taylor's San Diego tenure to the Abernethy-derived pick alone.

sections.heading: The Deal Stayed Small, but Buffalo's Side Had a Second Life
sections.body:
Neither original asset became a direct contributor for the team that acquired it. Massey never played in the NBA, while Abernethy never played for Buffalo or San Diego after the trade.

The difference is that Abernethy produced a compensation asset before leaving the franchise. That second-round pick was then used as part of another personnel move. The Lakers' Massey branch ended at the draft.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Edge, C-/F. The Buffalo/San Diego franchise receives a C- because Abernethy produced no direct games but generated a 1979 second-round compensation pick that became useful transaction currency in the Brian Taylor signing. The Lakers receive an F because No. 38 Massey never appeared in an NBA regular-season game and no later Lakers asset branch is tied to the selection. This was a low-impact trade overall, so the verdict reflects a modest downstream advantage rather than a major franchise win. Confidence is high.

sections.heading: The Canonical record Represents Two Same-Day Trades
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's Denver and league transaction ledgers record two separate June 26, 1978 moves. First, Kansas City sent Ron Boone and a 1979 second-round pick to Denver for Darnell Hillman and the draft rights to Mike Evans. Denver then sent Boone, that Kansas City second-round pick and a second 1979 second-round pick to the Lakers for Charlie Scott.

The Lakers and Kings team ledgers confirm their respective halves of the sequence. Pro Sports Transactions treats the chain as a three-team transaction, which is a reasonable canonical representation as long as every asset is preserved.

The legacy archive entry did not preserve every asset. It listed Scott to Denver, Hillman and Evans to Kansas City, and only the Ollie Mack pick to Los Angeles. This review restores Boone and the Kansas City second-round pick that became No. 41 Mark Young.

sections.heading: Denver Got Two Seasons From Charlie Scott
sections.body:
Scott became the clearest single-team return in the chain. He played 79 games for Denver in 1978-79, averaging 12.0 points and 5.4 assists in 33.1 minutes. He returned for 69 games in 1979-80, averaging 7.4 points and continuing as a veteran backcourt option.

That gives Denver 148 regular-season games across two seasons from the player acquired through the two-step maneuver. Scott did not create another major downstream asset branch, so the value is largely direct service rather than later trade capital.

sections.heading: The Lakers Received Boone Plus Two Second-Round Picks
sections.body:
Boone played all 82 games for Los Angeles in 1978-79, averaging 7.4 points in a reduced role, then appeared in six more Lakers games the following season. On October 25, 1979, Los Angeles traded him to Utah for a 1981 third-round pick. That gives Boone 88 Lakers regular-season games plus a modest later draft return.

One of the two second-rounders became No. 25 Ollie Mack. Mack played 27 regular-season games for Los Angeles in 1979-80 before the Lakers traded him, a 1980 second-round pick and a 1981 second-round pick to Chicago for Mark Landsberger. Because two additional picks were outgoing, this review does not assign the entire Landsberger return to Mack alone.

The second restored pick became No. 41 Mark Young. Basketball-Reference's 1979 draft ledger lists him as a Lakers selection but shows no NBA regular-season career. That branch produced no on-court value.

sections.heading: Kansas City Got One Useful Hillman Season
sections.body:
Hillman played 78 games for the Kings in 1978-79, averaging 7.0 points and 5.5 rebounds in 20.7 minutes. He was a useful frontcourt reserve for a 48-win Midwest Division champion.

Evans never appeared in a Kansas City regular-season game. The Kings waived him on October 11, 1978, and his later NBA career began elsewhere. Kansas City's realized return from the June chain is therefore almost entirely Hillman's one season.

sections.heading: The Result Is Competitive but Denver Has the Best Single Return
sections.body:
Los Angeles accumulated more separate assets, but two of them were limited: Mack played 27 Lakers games and Young never reached the NBA. Boone was useful for one full season and produced a third-round pick when moved.

Kansas City received 78 Hillman games but nothing from Evans. Denver received 148 Scott games across two seasons, including a full 79-game first year with substantial playmaking responsibility.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Edge, B+/B/C+. Denver receives a B+ because Scott supplied the strongest sustained direct return in the chain. Los Angeles receives a B because Boone gave the Lakers 88 games, Mack added 27 and Boone later returned a third-round pick, but Young produced no NBA value and Mack's later trade required two additional picks. Kansas City receives a C+ because Hillman gave the Kings one useful season while Evans was waived before playing. Confidence is high after restoring the two omitted Lakers assets and reconciling the two-step transaction sequence.

sections.heading: The Original Deal Is Fully Confirmed
sections.body:
Indiana, Portland and the 1977-78 league transaction ledgers all record the June 30, 1978 exchange the same way. The Pacers sent a 1980 second-round pick to the Trail Blazers for Corky Calhoun. There are no cash terms, protections or additional players to reconcile.

The future pick later landed at No. 32 in the 1980 draft and became David Lawrence. That makes this a straightforward comparison between Calhoun's realized Indiana service and the playing value Portland eventually received from the draft asset.

sections.heading: Calhoun Gave Indiana One Full Season
sections.body:
Calhoun played 81 regular-season games for Indiana in 1978-79. He averaged 16.4 minutes, 4.7 points and 2.9 rebounds while shooting 45.7 percent from the field. His totals for the season included 416 points and 236 rebounds.

He was a reserve rather than a featured starter, but availability itself had value. The Pacers received a usable veteran for nearly the entire season instead of waiting two years for the outgoing draft pick to convey.

Calhoun returned in 1979-80 but appeared in only seven games, averaging 1.1 points in 4.3 minutes. Indiana waived him on November 1, 1979, and his NBA career ended. Across the post-trade Pacers tenure, he therefore supplied 88 regular-season games.

sections.heading: Portland Used the Pick on David Lawrence
sections.body:
The Trail Blazers kept the incoming second-rounder until the 1980 draft. Portland's transaction ledger and the 1980 draft results identify Lawrence as the No. 32 overall selection.

Lawrence's Basketball-Reference profile records the draft transaction but no NBA regular-season seasons, games or statistical totals. The pick therefore produced no realized NBA playing value for Portland.

There is also no source-backed later Portland trade branch attached to Lawrence. The Blazers did not turn him into another NBA player or draft asset in the transaction records used for this review.

sections.heading: The Preliminary Blazers Edge Does Not Survive Source Review
sections.body:
The legacy archive entry had leaned toward Portland, apparently giving the future second-round selection more abstract value than Calhoun's short Indiana tenure. Hindsight grading requires the opposite approach: named draft assets are evaluated by what they became.

Here, the pick became a player who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Calhoun was modest, but he actually played 88 games for Indiana and filled a reserve role for a full season.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pacers Edge, C+/F. Indiana receives a C+ because Calhoun gave the club 81 games in his first season and 88 total before being waived. Portland receives an F because the No. 32 pick became Lawrence, who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game and produced no identified downstream asset. The trade remains minor in franchise terms; the grade gap reflects realized value, not the size of the transaction. Confidence is high.

sections.heading: The Original Package Is Fully Confirmed
sections.body: Denver, Kansas City and the league transaction ledgers all record the July 10, 1978 transaction the same way. The Nuggets sent a 1981 fourth-round pick to the Kings for the draft rights to Geoff Crompton. The pick later landed at No. 78 and became Kenny Dennard.

sections.heading: Crompton Gave Denver Only a Short Rookie Look
sections.body:
Crompton had been Kansas City's fourth-round selection at No. 70 in the 1978 draft. After Denver acquired his rights, he appeared in 20 regular-season games for the Nuggets in 1978-79. Basketball-Reference lists only 88 total minutes, with 26 points and 19 rebounds.

Denver waived Crompton on April 11, 1979. He later returned to the NBA with Portland, Milwaukee, San Antonio and Cleveland, but those later seasons came after separate signings and trades. They do not create additional return for Denver from this 1978 transaction.

sections.heading: Kansas City Turned the Pick Into Kenny Dennard
sections.body:
The Kings used the 1981 fourth-round pick at No. 78 on Dennard. He played 30 games as a rookie in 1981-82 and 22 more in 1982-83. Across those two Kansas City seasons he appeared in 52 regular-season games, including three starts.

Dennard's production was modest, but Kansas City got more direct service from him than Denver received from Crompton. More importantly, the Kings did not lose Dennard for nothing.

sections.heading: Dennard Produced Another Draft Pick
sections.body:
On September 27, 1983, Kansas City traded Dennard to Denver for a 1985 third-round pick. Denver's transaction ledger confirms the same move from the opposite side. That pick later became No. 66 Michael Adams.

Adams played 18 games for Sacramento in 1985-86 before being waived on December 17, 1985. His later NBA career became far more substantial after he moved on, including an All-Star selection with Washington, but Sacramento did not realize that later value. This review therefore credits only the 18 Kings games tied to the pick outcome.

sections.heading: The Kings Won a Small Trade, Not a Franchise-Changing One
sections.body: The difference here is quantity of realized value, not star impact. Denver received 20 Crompton games and no downstream asset after waiving him. Kansas City turned the future fourth into 52 Dennard games, then turned Dennard into a third-round pick that produced 18 Adams games.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Edge, B-/D+. Kansas City receives a B- because the club converted a fourth-round pick into two separate NBA players and 70 total regular-season games across the Dennard and Adams branches. Denver receives a D+ because Crompton appeared in only 20 games before being waived and produced no later Nuggets return. The overall trade is still low impact, so the gap reflects better asset recycling rather than a major talent win. Confidence is high.

sections.heading: The source-backed Package Is Tatum for a 1980 First
sections.body:
Boston, Indiana and the 1978-79 league transaction ledgers all record the July 19, 1978 deal as a straight exchange: the Celtics sent a 1980 first-round pick to the Pacers for Earl Tatum.

The legacy archive entry included cash going in both directions.

sections.heading: Tatum Barely Played for Boston but Retained Immediate Trade Value
sections.body:
Tatum appeared in only three regular-season games for the Celtics in 1978-79, averaging 6.7 points in 12.7 minutes. If the branch ended there, Boston's side would be weak.

It did not. On October 19, 1978, Boston traded Tatum to Detroit for Chris Ford and a 1981 second-round pick that became Tracy Jackson. Detroit's transaction ledger independently confirms the same package.

sections.heading: Ford Became the Real Boston Return
sections.body:
Ford played 309 regular-season games for Boston across four seasons. He averaged 15.6 points in 78 games immediately after arriving in 1978-79, then started 73 games in 1979-80.

His most important team value came in 1980-81. Ford played all 82 games, started 75 and averaged 8.9 points and 3.6 assists for the Celtics team that won the NBA championship. He remained with Boston for another 76 games in 1981-82.

The second-round pick became Tracy Jackson. His NBA impact was minimal, but the pick was a separate realized asset on top of Ford. The Tatum branch therefore produced far more value than Tatum's three Boston appearances suggest.

sections.heading: Indiana Recycled the First Before the Draft
sections.body:
The Pacers did not use the acquired first-round pick themselves. On February 1, 1980, Indiana traded Alex English plus the Boston first to Denver for George McGinnis.

Denver later used the pick at No. 23 on Carl Nicks. Nicks never played for Indiana because the pick had already been moved. This review therefore does not credit his NBA career to the Pacers.

sections.heading: The Pick Helped Bring McGinnis, but English Was Also a Major Outgoing Asset
sections.body:
McGinnis played 28 games for Indiana after the trade in 1979-80, then 69 in 1980-81 and 76 in 1981-82. That is 173 regular-season games across parts of three seasons.

The value cannot be assigned entirely to the Boston first-round pick because Alex English was the other outgoing piece, and English was already a productive 26-year-old forward. The pick clearly had first-round trade value, but it was one component of a package rather than a standalone purchase of McGinnis.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Edge, A/B. Boston receives an A because three Tatum games quickly became Chris Ford, a four-year Celtic and 1981 championship starter, plus a second-round pick. Indiana receives a B because the first-round pick retained meaningful trade value and helped acquire 173 McGinnis games, but the Pacers also surrendered Alex English in that deal. The source-backed cleanup also removes the unsupported two-way cash entries. Confidence is high.

Carl Nicks career statistics and transaction history

sections.heading: The Original Exchange Is Unambiguous
sections.body:
Houston, Milwaukee and the 1978-79 league transaction ledgers all record the July 26, 1978 deal the same way. The Rockets sent C.J. Kupec to the Bucks and received Milwaukee's 1979 fourth-round pick.

The pick later landed at No. 76 and became Sammy Drummer. There are no cash terms, protections or secondary assets in the cited ledgers.

sections.heading: Kupec Never Played a Regular-Season Game for Milwaukee
sections.body:
Kupec had already played three NBA seasons before the trade. He appeared in 16 games for the Lakers in 1975-76, all 82 in 1976-77 and 49 for Houston in 1977-78.

His player page lists no 1978-79 Milwaukee season. The transaction history records the July 26 trade to the Bucks, but his NBA career ends after the 1977-78 Rockets season. Milwaukee therefore received the player asset but no regular-season NBA games from him.

There is no later NBA transaction on Kupec's Basketball-Reference history that creates a downstream Bucks return. His branch stops at zero realized Milwaukee games.

sections.heading: Houston Used the Pick on Sammy Drummer
sections.body:
The Rockets kept the fourth-round pick through the 1979 draft and used it at No. 76 on Sammy Drummer out of Georgia Tech.

The 1979 draft ledger lists Drummer at No. 76 but shows no NBA seasons, games, minutes or statistical totals attached to his record. That means the pick produced no NBA regular-season player value.

Unlike some other late-round picks in this archive, there is no source-supported trade of Drummer's rights that creates a second downstream branch. The Houston side therefore also ends at zero NBA games.

sections.heading: The Pick Still Had Interim Asset Value, but Hindsight Production Was Zero
sections.body:
Houston did hold a future draft choice for almost a year, which gave the Rockets more transaction optionality than Milwaukee had once Kupec's NBA career ended. That is real context, but the site's source-backed grading emphasizes realized outcomes rather than theoretical optionality.

By that standard, neither team converted its incoming asset into NBA production. Milwaukee got no Kupec games, and Houston got no Drummer games.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, F/F. Both teams receive an F because neither incoming asset produced an NBA regular-season appearance for the acquiring franchise and neither created a traceable downstream return. Houston's fourth-round pick preserved temporary asset optionality, but the actual No. 76 outcome produced no NBA career. This is a true low-impact transaction rather than a case where one side quietly found long-term value. Confidence is high.

sources.title: C.J. Kupec career statistics and transactions

sections.heading: The Rights Trade Is Real, but the Exact Return Is Not Fully Recoverable
sections.body:
Chicago's official historical transaction log records an August 11, 1978 move sending Chuck Jura to Cleveland for future considerations. RealGM's Cleveland and league transaction histories independently record Cleveland acquiring Jura's draft rights from the Bulls on that date.

The record becomes less certain when the return is broken into individual draft choices. Pro Sports Transactions describes Chicago's consideration as multiple future draft picks and places a possible link to the 1979 No. 47 selection used on Calvin Garrett, but the draft-pick page explicitly labels that connection unconfirmed.

This review therefore preserves the transaction while refusing to convert a possibility into a canonical pick outcome.

sections.heading: Basketball-Reference Does Not Carry the August 1978 Trade
sections.body:
The 1978-79 Bulls, Cavaliers and league transaction pages at Basketball-Reference do not list the Jura transaction. Jura's own Basketball-Reference transaction history records Chicago drafting him No. 45 in 1972 but does not add the later rights move.

That omission does not erase the deal because the Bulls' own media guide and RealGM both support the transaction. It does mean the archive should distinguish a source-supported rights transaction from a fully reconstructed draft-routing chain.

sections.heading: Jura Never Produced an NBA Game for Cleveland
sections.body:
Jura had spent his professional career in Italy after Chicago drafted him in 1972. The Cleveland transaction was an attempt to bring his NBA rights into the Cavaliers organization, but he never appeared in an NBA regular-season game.

Contemporary career summaries indicate Cleveland signed him in August 1978 before he ultimately returned to Italy. This review therefore records zero realized NBA games for Cleveland from the rights asset.

sections.heading: Chicago's Future Considerations Cannot Be Safely Assigned to Calvin Garrett
sections.body:
Chicago did use the No. 47 pick in the 1979 draft on Garrett, and the Bulls' draft ledger confirms that selection. The problem is provenance. The best draft-routing source located for this review calls the Jura-to-Garrett connection unconfirmed rather than established.

Assigning Garrett's 166-game NBA career to this trade would overstate the evidence. The same problem applies to any unspecified additional pick within the phrase multiple future draft picks. Without a source-supported identity for the actual conveyed selections, the Chicago branch cannot be graded from realized player output.

sections.heading: Why this review Keeps the record Active but Unscored
sections.body: This is different from an unsupported legacy transaction. The Chicago rights deal itself is corroborated by the team's official history and independent transaction records. What is missing is enough precision about the return to make a directional hindsight verdict defensible.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Insufficient Evidence, N/A/N/A. Cleveland acquired Jura's rights but received no NBA regular-season production from him. Chicago received future considerations, probably in draft capital, but the exact pick identities remain unresolved and the commonly suggested Calvin Garrett connection is explicitly unconfirmed in the available draft-routing source. Confidence is high that the rights transaction occurred and low on the precise composition of Chicago's return.

1979 NBA Draft pick transactions - unconfirmed Jura routing note
Chuck Jura Basketball-Reference profile and transaction history

sections.heading: The Trade Itself Is Confirmed Across Multiple Ledgers
sections.body:
Denver's transaction log, Indiana's transaction log and the league-wide 1978-79 ledger all record the same September 1, 1978 transaction: Denver acquired Mel Bennett from the Pacers for future considerations.

Indiana's official historical media guide also lists the deal with the same language. That makes the existence and date of the transaction high-confidence even though the compensation was never spelled out in the sources used for this review.

sections.heading: Bennett Never Played a Regular-Season Game for Denver
sections.body:
The Nuggets did not get on-court NBA value from Bennett. Denver's own ledger records that the club waived him on September 22, only three weeks after acquiring him.

Bennett's Basketball-Reference career page lists no Denver season. His 1978-79 entry says he did not play in the NBA and instead played in the WBA. He later returned to the NBA with Utah in 1980-81 and briefly Cleveland in 1981-82, but those later appearances came through separate roster moves and do not create downstream Denver value.

The Denver branch therefore ends at zero regular-season games and no traceable later asset.

sections.heading: Indiana's Future Considerations Remain Unidentified
sections.body:
The harder side is Indiana's return. The primary team and league ledgers use only the phrase future considerations. The Pacers' media guide does the same. Neither identifies a draft year, pick round, player, cash amount or later completion transaction tied back to Bennett.

That absence matters. Future considerations can eventually become real value, but source-backed grading cannot assume that happened. This review also cannot use unrelated Indiana transactions from later in the season as a proxy simply because they occurred after September.

No candidate downstream asset located in the Pacers' 1978-79 transaction history is explicitly linked to Bennett. The archive therefore keeps the consideration unresolved rather than attaching a speculative pick or cash value.

sections.heading: Why the Trade Stays Ungraded
sections.body:
Denver's realized side is known and weak: Bennett never played for the Nuggets. If Indiana's return were documented as nothing, Denver could be graded accordingly. If the consideration became a useful pick or player, Indiana could receive credit. The current evidence establishes neither outcome.

A directional verdict would therefore confuse missing information with zero value. The correct source-backed treatment is to distinguish the verified transaction from the unresolved economic return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Insufficient Evidence, N/A/N/A. Denver acquired Bennett but received zero NBA regular-season games before waiving him. Indiana received future considerations, but the cited team, league and official Pacers records do not identify what those considerations became. This review preserves the transaction privately, records Denver's zero-game outcome and withholds grades until the return can be tied to a source-supported asset. Confidence is high on the transaction and Bennett's Denver outcome, and low on the unresolved compensation.

sources.title: Indiana Pacers official media guide transaction history

sections.heading: The Rights Trade Is Confirmed, but the Pick Outcome Is Not
sections.body:
New Orleans's official transaction history records that the Jazz traded 1978 fourth-round pick Mel Davis to Milwaukee on September 6, 1978 in exchange for a 1979 second-round pick with considerations. RealGM independently records Milwaukee acquiring Davis's draft rights on the same date.

Pro Sports Transactions supplies a more tentative description. Its Milwaukee transaction ledger calls the return a 1979 conditional second-round pick and includes a question about whether the condition was exercised. That uncertainty is important enough that this review does not convert the pick into a specific player without a stronger routing source.

sections.heading: Davis Never Played an NBA Game for Milwaukee
sections.body:
Davis had been selected by New Orleans at No. 74 in the 1978 draft. Milwaukee acquired his rights, and RealGM records the Bucks signing him on September 10.

The experiment ended quickly. RealGM records Milwaukee waiving Davis in October 1978, and Basketball-Reference's Melvin Davis draft page shows no NBA regular-season career. The Bucks therefore received no realized NBA playing value from the rights acquisition.

sections.heading: New Orleans Clearly Received Draft Consideration in the Agreement
sections.body:
The Jazz media guide is stronger than the legacy question mark on one point: it explicitly says the transaction was for a 1979 second-round pick with considerations. The deal was not simply Davis for nothing.

What the available record does not resolve is which second-round slot, if any, ultimately conveyed. Pro Sports Transactions treats the pick as conditional and possibly unexercised. Milwaukee's 1979 draft history still includes its own second-round selection, but that alone is not sufficient to reconstruct every possible condition, swap or reacquisition.

This review therefore preserves the contractual draft consideration without assigning a fabricated overall number.

sections.heading: Why the Trade Cannot Be Graded Directionally Yet
sections.body:
Milwaukee's branch is known: zero NBA games from Davis and no later Bucks transaction tied to his rights. New Orleans's branch is only partially known: a 1979 second-round consideration existed, but the actual conveyance and player outcome are unresolved in the cited sources.

Treating an unresolved pick as zero would be just as misleading as assigning it to an unverified player. The correct source-backed approach is to distinguish a documented consideration from an unidentified realized outcome.

sections.heading: The Earlier San Antonio Attempt Adds Context but Not Value
sections.body: The Jazz media guide also records that New Orleans had tried to trade Davis to San Antonio in July 1978 for a 1979 third-round pick with considerations, but that transaction was cancelled when Davis failed to sign with San Antonio. That failed deal helps explain why Davis's rights were still available in September, but it is not part of Milwaukee's trade return and receives no value in this review.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Insufficient Evidence, N/A/N/A. Milwaukee acquired Davis's rights and received zero NBA regular-season games. New Orleans received a contractual 1979 second-round consideration, but the exact conveyed pick and downstream player remain unresolved. Confidence is high on the trade and Davis's zero-game outcome, and low on the final pick conveyance.

sections.heading: The One-for-One Exchange Is Clear
sections.body:
New Jersey and Detroit list the September 8, 1978 transaction identically: the Nets sent Kevin Porter to the Pistons for Eric Money. The league transaction ledger confirms the same one-for-one swap.

The legacy asset label called Porter "Kevin Porter (Sr.)," but the historical player record is simply Kevin Porter. This review normalizes that name rather than preserving a misleading generational suffix.

sections.heading: Porter Delivered an Elite Passing Season Immediately
sections.body:
Detroit received much more than ordinary rotation production. Porter played all 82 games in 1978-79, started all 82 and averaged 15.4 points, 13.4 assists and 1.9 steals.

The NBA's official 1978-79 season review lists Porter as the league assists leader at 13.4 per game. Basketball-Reference records 1,099 assists in the season. That gives Detroit a full season of high-end direct value from the acquired player even though the Pistons finished 30-52.

sections.heading: Porter Then Produced Two First-Round Compensation Assets
sections.body:
Porter signed with Washington as a veteran free agent on July 12, 1979. Detroit's transaction ledger records two first-round picks as compensation: a 1980 first that eventually landed at No. 13 and a 1982 first that eventually landed at No. 12.

Those picks retained real transaction value even though Detroit did not simply draft both named players. The 1980 first later identified with Rickey Brown was included with another first-round pick in the Bob McAdoo transaction. The 1982 first later identified with John Bagley was included with Phil Hubbard, Paul Mokeski and a second-round pick in the 1982 deal that brought Kenny Carr and Bill Laimbeer to Detroit.

This review does not assign all of McAdoo or Laimbeer's value to Porter's compensation picks because both were multi-asset packages. It does, however, credit Detroit for preserving two first-round assets directly tied to Porter's departure.

sections.heading: Money Was Productive for New Jersey
sections.body:
The Nets also got useful immediate production. Money played 47 games for New Jersey in 1978-79 and averaged 16.7 points, 5.3 assists and 1.6 steals in 30.5 minutes.

On February 7, 1979, New Jersey traded Money and Al Skinner to Philadelphia for Harvey Catchings, Ralph Simpson and cash. Because Skinner was an additional outgoing player, the entire return cannot be assigned solely to Money.

sections.heading: The Money Branch Still Helped Feed a Valuable Nets Chain
sections.body:
Catchings later became the clearest downstream branch from that Philadelphia return. On May 31, New Jersey traded Catchings to Milwaukee for John Gianelli and a 1979 first-round pick that became No. 8 Calvin Natt.

Natt then played 53 games for the Nets as a rookie, averaging 19.7 points and 9.7 rebounds. In February 1980, New Jersey traded Natt to Portland for Maurice Lucas and two first-round picks that became Mike Gminski and Albert King.

That chain became extremely valuable for the Nets, but source-backed grading has to preserve the attribution problem: Catchings was received for Money plus Skinner, not Money alone. This review records the downstream sequence as shared package value rather than pretending every later Nets asset came only from the original Porter-for-Money exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win, A+/A-. Detroit receives an A+ because Porter supplied a complete 82-game season, led the NBA at 13.4 assists per game and then generated two first-round compensation picks. New Jersey receives an A- because Money was productive for 47 games and participated in a trade package that fed a valuable Catchings-to-Natt downstream chain. The Nets did well, but Detroit's strongest outcomes are more directly attributable to the single incoming asset. Confidence is high.

sources.title: NBA 1978-79 season review and league leaders

sections.heading: The Original Exchange Is Fully Confirmed
sections.body:
Houston, New Orleans and the league transaction ledgers all record the September 21, 1978 trade the same way. The Rockets sent a future 1981 first-round pick to the Jazz for Slick Watts.

The pick is also fully traceable. Basketball-Reference's 1981 draft ledger lists Utah at No. 13 selecting Danny Schayes, matching the earlier transaction logs.

sections.heading: Watts Gave Houston One Useful Backup Season
sections.body:
Watts was no longer the high-minute Seattle guard who had made the All-Defensive First Team earlier in his career, but Houston did receive real production. He played 61 games for the Rockets in 1978-79 and averaged 17.1 minutes, 3.7 points, 4.0 assists and 1.2 steals.

He also appeared in two playoff games for Houston. His player record ends after the 1978-79 season, so the Rockets received one season of backup point-guard value and no later transaction branch from the acquired player.

That is too much realized value for an F, but it is still a short return for a future first-round pick.

sections.heading: The Pick Became Danny Schayes at No. 13
sections.body:
Utah kept Houston's first until the 1981 draft and selected Schayes at No. 13. The draft ledger records an 18-season NBA career, making the pick a productive asset even before narrowing the evaluation to his Jazz years.

Schayes played all 82 games as a rookie in 1981-82, starting 20 and averaging 7.9 points and 5.2 rebounds in 19.8 minutes.

His role expanded sharply in 1982-83. He played 50 games for Utah, started all 50 and averaged 12.4 points, 9.0 rebounds, 3.3 assists and 1.4 blocks in 32.8 minutes before the Jazz moved him during the season.

That gives Utah 132 direct regular-season games from the pick, including 70 starts and a full season-plus of meaningful center production.

sections.heading: Schayes Then Became Rich Kelley
sections.body:
On February 7, 1983, Utah traded Schayes and cash to Denver for Rich Kelley. The Jazz transaction ledger and both player histories agree on the package.

Kelley immediately played 32 games for Utah in the rest of 1982-83 and averaged 7.2 points, 7.3 rebounds and 2.5 assists. He stayed for 75 games in 1983-84 and 77 more in 1984-85.

That creates 184 additional regular-season Jazz games from the direct downstream trade of Schayes. Kelley was not a star, but he became a multi-season rotation center and started 87 games for Utah across those three partial/full seasons.

Kelley's own player history records that he later signed with Sacramento as a veteran free agent and Utah received cash compensation. This review notes that terminal branch without assigning speculative value to an unspecified cash amount.

sections.heading: Why the Jazz Side Is Clearly Stronger
sections.body:
Houston's return was immediate and real, but brief: 61 games from a reserve guard in the final NBA season of his career.

Utah waited nearly three years for the pick, then converted it into a first-round center who played 132 games and developed into a full-time starter. The Jazz then turned Schayes, with cash added, into Kelley and received another 184 games of rotation-center production.

The downstream Kelley value cannot be treated as free because Utah included cash with Schayes, but the central point does not depend on over-crediting the branch. Schayes alone already supplied more direct service and a larger role than Watts did for Houston.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Jazz Win, B+/D+. Utah receives a B+ because the Houston first became No. 13 Danny Schayes, who supplied 132 games and 70 starts before helping return Rich Kelley, another 184-game Jazz contributor. Houston receives a D+ because Watts did provide 61 games and useful backup passing, but the acquired player lasted one season and produced no later asset. The original F legacy for Houston understated his actual on-court contribution, while the Jazz's longer first-round branch supports the clear hindsight edge. Confidence is high.

sections.heading: The Transaction Logs Add One Missing Term
sections.body:
Atlanta, Chicago and the 1978-79 league transaction ledger all record the October 8 exchange the same way. The Hawks sent John Brown and future considerations to the Bulls for Chicago's 1980 second-round pick.

The legacy archive entry listed Brown for the pick but omitted the future considerations. This review restores that unresolved term to the canonical asset record. No reliable source in the current review identifies what those considerations ultimately became, so the site does not assign speculative value to them.

sections.heading: Brown Gave Chicago One Full Rotation Season
sections.body:
Brown played 77 games for the Bulls in 1978-79. He averaged 16.4 minutes, 5.0 points, 3.1 rebounds and 1.4 assists while shooting 47.9 percent.

That is modest production, but it is real immediate value. Brown appeared in nearly the entire schedule and filled a regular bench role for a 31-51 Chicago team.

He did not create a long Bulls transaction chain. Brown was back with Atlanta by January 28, 1980, when the Hawks signed him as a free agent. That later Atlanta signing is independent of this trade and is not counted as value Chicago sent back.

sections.heading: Atlanta Used the Pick on Craig Shelton
sections.body:
The Hawks held Chicago's second-round pick through the 1980 draft and used it at No. 28 on Georgetown forward Craig Shelton.

Shelton played 55 games as a rookie in 1980-81, averaging 10.7 minutes, 4.3 points and 2.5 rebounds. He appeared in only four more games for Atlanta in 1981-82.

His NBA career therefore ended at 59 games, all with the Hawks. The pick produced a useful depth player for one season, but no durable downstream branch.

sections.heading: The Result Is Close and Low Impact
sections.body:
Chicago received more immediate regular-season service: 77 games from Brown compared with 59 total games from Shelton. Brown also played a slightly larger role in his one Bulls season than Shelton did during his Atlanta tenure.

Atlanta still received genuine value from a future second-round choice, and the difference is not large enough to justify a wide grading gap. The unresolved future considerations also prevent a fully exhaustive value accounting for Chicago.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Bulls Edge, B-/C+. Chicago receives a B- because Brown supplied 77 games of rotation service and the club also received unresolved future considerations. Atlanta receives a C+ because the pick became No. 28 Craig Shelton, who played 59 Hawks games but did not develop into a lasting contributor. Confidence is medium-high because the principal player and pick outcomes are clear even though the future-considerations term remains unidentified.

sections.heading: The Warriors' Own Ledger Clarifies the Package
sections.body:
Golden State's official media guide records the trade on October 10, 1978: Charles Dudley to Chicago for a 1979 second-round draft choice and cash.

That first-party record differs slightly from Basketball-Reference. The Bulls, Warriors and league Basketball-Reference ledgers date the trade October 11 and list the second-round pick but omit cash. RealGM agrees with the Warriors on the October 10 date.

This review preserves the canonical October 10 date because it is supported by the Warriors' own historical transaction ledger and RealGM. It also restores cash as a received Golden State asset, but marks the amount unresolved because no reviewed source identifies a figure.

sections.heading: The Pick Is Fully Traceable to Danny Salisbury
sections.body:
The pick itself is not vague future consideration. Golden State's Basketball-Reference transaction log identifies it as Chicago's 1979 second-round pick, and the 1979 draft ledger shows the Warriors using No. 28 on Danny Salisbury.

Salisbury's draft record contains no NBA seasons, games, minutes or statistical totals. His Basketball-Reference player page likewise lists the Golden State selection but no regular-season NBA production.

That means the draft branch produced no realized NBA games for the Warriors. This review still preserves the value of the cash term, but it does not invent a monetary amount or use theoretical pick value as a substitute for realized production.

sections.heading: Dudley Gave Chicago 43 Games
sections.body:
Dudley played 43 games for the Bulls in 1978-79. He averaged 15.9 minutes, 2.7 points, 2.7 assists and 2.0 rebounds.

The role was modest, but it was real rotation service. Chicago received nearly 700 regular-season minutes from the acquired guard.

Dudley did not become a long-term Bull. The 1979-80 league transaction ledger records Chicago waiving him on September 25, 1979, before he appeared in another regular-season game for the franchise.

There is no traceable downstream Chicago return attached to that waiver. Dudley's branch therefore ends with one season and 43 games.

sections.heading: Why Chicago Holds Only a Small Edge
sections.body:
This is not a trade where either side found a major long-term asset. Chicago got one season of reserve point-guard minutes. Golden State converted the pick into a player who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game.

The unresolved cash term keeps Golden State from being treated as receiving literally nothing. Cash had transaction value at the time, but without a documented amount it cannot be translated into a precise retrospective grade.

The source conflict also matters editorially. Basketball-Reference's clean one-for-one listing is incomplete relative to the Warriors' own media guide, while the official guide's October 10 date is corroborated by RealGM. This review therefore records the disagreement instead of silently choosing one source and hiding the other.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Bulls Edge, C-/D. Chicago receives a C- because Dudley supplied 43 games and 684 minutes of real rotation service before being waived. Golden State receives a D because the No. 28 pick became Salisbury, who produced no NBA regular-season career, while the additional cash return remains unquantified. The difference is real but small, and confidence is medium-high because the on-court outcomes are clear even though the sources disagree on the administrative date and cash term.

sections.heading: The Core Exchange Is Clear
sections.body:
Boston and Phoenix agree on the central transaction. On October 11, 1978, the Celtics acquired Dennis Awtrey and sent Phoenix their 1979 second-round pick. The Suns later used that selection at No. 24 on Johnny High.

Basketball-Reference's Boston, Phoenix and league transaction ledgers all record the player-for-pick structure. The Boston source batch preserved in this archive also lists cash going to Phoenix. Because the reviewed public ledgers do not repeat that cash term and no amount is identified, this review keeps the cash asset in the record but labels it unresolved rather than silently presenting it as fully corroborated.

sections.heading: Awtrey Became More Than 23 Boston Games
sections.body:
Awtrey appeared in 23 games for the 1978-79 Celtics and logged 247 minutes. His Boston line was modest: 2.2 points, 2.0 rebounds and 0.9 assists per game.

The more important branch came three months later. On January 17, 1979, Boston traded Awtrey to Seattle for a 1979 first-round pick. Basketball-Reference identifies that pick as the selection later used on Sly Williams at No. 21.

Boston did not make that selection itself. On February 12, the Celtics included the Sly Williams pick with Tom Barker and two other 1979 first-round picks in the package sent to New York for Bob McAdoo.

That means Awtrey's Boston value was not limited to his 23 games. He was converted into a first-round asset that became one component of a larger acquisition. This review records that downstream path without assigning the entire value of McAdoo, or anything that followed McAdoo, solely to the Awtrey branch.

sections.heading: Phoenix Got Four Seasons from Johnny High
sections.body:
Phoenix used the incoming second-round pick on Johnny High at No. 24 in the 1979 draft.

High played four NBA seasons, all with Phoenix, appearing in 274 regular-season games. He averaged 5.1 points, 2.3 rebounds and 1.9 assists for his career and accumulated 4,538 minutes.

The Suns received useful reserve-guard service from a second-round pick. High played all 82 games as a rookie, 81 the next season, then returned for 82 games in 1982-83 and 29 more in 1983-84.

That is a strong realized outcome for the asset Phoenix received. The unresolved cash term may add some transaction value, but no numerical weight is assigned because the amount is not documented in the reviewed public sources.

sections.heading: Why the Result Stays Even
sections.body:
Phoenix has the cleaner direct outcome. The second-round pick became a four-season contributor who played 274 games for the franchise.

Boston's return was less direct but still meaningful. Awtrey supplied 23 games, then became a first-round pick within three months. That pick was subsequently used as one part of the McAdoo package.

It would overstate the record to credit Boston with all of McAdoo's later value, because the Celtics sent multiple other assets in that February transaction. It would also understate the Awtrey branch to stop the analysis after 23 games and ignore the first-round return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, B-/B-. Phoenix gets a B- because the No. 24 pick became Johnny High, a four-season Suns contributor with 274 games. Boston also gets a B- because Awtrey produced short-term center depth and was quickly converted into a 1979 first-round pick that remained useful in a larger trade package. The result is even, with medium-high confidence on the player and pick outcomes and lower confidence only on the unconfirmed cash term.

sections.heading: The Trade Structure Is Straightforward
sections.body:
Boston and Detroit transaction records agree on the October 19, 1978 exchange. The Celtics sent Earl Tatum to the Pistons and received Chris Ford plus a 1981 second-round pick.

The draft asset stayed with Boston long enough to become the No. 25 selection in 1981. The Celtics used it on Notre Dame guard Tracy Jackson.

sections.heading: Ford Became a Four-Year Boston Contributor
sections.body:
Ford played 78 games for Boston immediately after the trade in 1978-79 and averaged 15.6 points, 4.7 assists and 3.3 rebounds. He stayed with the Celtics through 1981-82.

Across four Boston seasons, Ford appeared in 309 regular-season games and started 201. His role changed as the roster improved, but he remained a real rotation piece throughout the transition from a 29-win 1978-79 team to a championship roster.

The most important season is 1980-81. Ford played all 82 games, started 75 and averaged 33.2 minutes. Boston won the NBA championship that season, making Ford a substantial contributor to the title team rather than a fringe roster holdover.

He also continued into 1981-82, playing 76 games and starting 53 before his NBA career ended.

sections.heading: The Extra Pick Produced Limited but Real Value
sections.body:
Boston's second asset became Tracy Jackson at No. 25 in the 1981 draft.

Jackson played 11 games for the Celtics in 1981-82, totaling 66 minutes. On December 9, 1981, Boston sold his player rights to Chicago.

That outcome is modest, and this review does not inflate the pick as if Boston received Jackson's entire three-year NBA career. The direct Celtics value was 11 games plus whatever consideration came from the rights sale, whose amount is not documented in the reviewed Basketball-Reference transaction record.

sections.heading: Detroit Got One Rotation Season from Tatum
sections.body:
Tatum played 76 games for Detroit in 1978-79 after the trade. He logged 1,195 minutes and averaged 7.8 points, 1.6 rebounds and 0.9 assists.

That is meaningful short-term return. Tatum was not a non-factor, and Detroit received substantially more than a few appearances or an unused roster spot.

The difference is duration and role. Tatum's Detroit value is concentrated in one season. Ford gave Boston four seasons, more than 9,000 minutes, 309 regular-season games and a starting role on a championship team.

sections.heading: Why Boston Wins in Retrospect
sections.body:
The Celtics received the best individual asset in Ford and also retained the additional second-round pick long enough to turn it into an NBA player.

Jackson's Boston contribution was small, so the pick is secondary to the grade. Ford carries the case. His 309 games, 201 starts and championship-season role create a much larger realized return than Detroit received from Tatum's 76-game season.

Detroit still deserves credit for receiving a usable rotation guard. The result is not a zero-value loss; it is a clear Boston win created by Ford's longevity and championship relevance.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win, A-/C+. Boston receives an A- because Ford became a four-year contributor and a regular starter on the 1981 champions, while the extra second-round pick added 11 Jackson games before his rights were sold. Detroit receives a C+ because Tatum supplied 76 useful games in 1978-79 but did not approach Ford's cumulative Boston impact.

sections.heading: Chicago Received a One-Season Reserve
sections.body:
The Bulls acquired Scott Lloyd on October 26, 1978 after he had appeared in five games for San Diego.

Lloyd played 67 games for Chicago in 1978-79. He logged 465 minutes and averaged 1.7 points and 1.4 rebounds in 6.9 minutes per game.

That is real NBA production, but it is modest. Lloyd did not stay with Chicago beyond the season, spending 1979-80 outside the NBA before later returning with Dallas.

sections.heading: The Pick Did Not Stay with the Clippers
sections.body:
The 1981 third-rounder has a more interesting route than the original record suggests.

San Diego did not use the pick directly. In connection with signing veteran free agent Gar Heard, the Clippers sent this 1981 third-round pick plus a 1983 third-round pick to Phoenix as compensation.

That means the No. 62 Sam Clancy outcome belongs to Phoenix, not directly to San Diego. This review preserves the final draft result for traceability but does not treat Clancy as the Clippers' realized player return.

sections.heading: Heard Was the Downstream Clippers Benefit
sections.body:
Heard played 78 games for San Diego in 1980-81 and logged 1,631 minutes. He averaged 4.8 points, 4.5 rebounds and 1.6 assists in 20.9 minutes.

The original Chicago pick was one component of the compensation package that helped San Diego secure Heard. Because another 1983 third-round pick was also sent to Phoenix, the full value of Heard cannot be assigned to this 1978 trade branch alone.

Still, the pick retained practical transaction value for more than two years after the Lloyd trade. That downstream use keeps the Clippers side from being graded as an empty return.

sections.heading: What Happened to the No. 62 Pick
sections.body:
Phoenix used the selection on Sam Clancy in the 1981 draft. Basketball-Reference lists Clancy at No. 62 but no NBA regular-season games.

That final draft outcome is useful for identifying the asset, but it should not be used to erase the value San Diego extracted earlier by moving the pick in the Heard compensation package.

sections.heading: Why the Result Is Even
sections.body:
Chicago got the cleaner direct return: 67 games from Lloyd. The Clippers got no direct drafted player, but they preserved the pick as a movable asset and later used it as one piece of the compensation required to add Heard.

Neither branch created large long-term value. Lloyd was a low-minute reserve for one season, while Heard's larger 78-game contribution cannot be fully credited to this pick because San Diego also surrendered another third-rounder.

The best retrospective treatment is therefore an even result rather than forcing a winner from two modest branches.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, C-/C-. Chicago receives a C- for 67 Lloyd games and 465 minutes. San Diego also receives a C- because the third-round pick retained downstream utility as part of the Gar Heard compensation package, even though the pick itself ultimately became Sam Clancy at No. 62 and produced no NBA games.

sections.heading: The Direct Exchange Happened in January 1979
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference lists the trade on January 5, 1979: New York sent Spencer Haywood to New Orleans for Joe Meriweather.

Both players had already appeared for their original teams that season, so the cleanest comparison starts with production after the transaction rather than their full 1978-79 totals.

sections.heading: Meriweather Gave New York Two Useful Partial Seasons
sections.body:
Meriweather played 41 games for the Knicks after the trade in 1978-79. He started 26, averaged 25.7 minutes and produced 9.5 points and 5.5 rebounds per game.

He stayed for 1979-80 and appeared in another 65 games, starting 30. He averaged 9.0 points and 5.4 rebounds in 24.1 minutes.

That gives New York 106 regular-season games from Meriweather across the two seasons. He was a legitimate rotation big rather than a throw-in who disappeared from the roster.

In September 1980, New York included Meriweather and a 1981 first-round pick in a three-team trade that brought Campy Russell from Cleveland. This review records that later use but does not credit the entire Russell return to Meriweather because the Knicks also surrendered a first-round selection.

sections.heading: Haywood Was Excellent Immediately
sections.body:
Haywood played 34 games for New Orleans after the trade. He started 18 and averaged 39.4 minutes, 24.0 points, 9.6 rebounds and 2.1 assists.

That half-season alone was stronger individual production than New York received from Meriweather, but the decisive value came after the franchise relocated to Utah.

On September 13, 1979, the Jazz traded Haywood to the Los Angeles Lakers for Adrian Dantley.

sections.heading: Dantley Turned the Branch into a Franchise-Level Return
sections.body:
Dantley played seven seasons for Utah from 1979-80 through 1985-86. Basketball-Reference's franchise register credits him with 461 regular-season games, 17,899 minutes and 13,635 points for the Jazz.

He averaged 29.6 points, 6.2 rebounds and 3.7 assists over those 461 games. His Utah tenure included multiple All-Star seasons, two scoring titles and two All-NBA selections.

The transaction path is direct enough to count. Utah did not combine Haywood with another premium asset to acquire Dantley; the September 1979 record is Haywood for Dantley.

That makes Dantley a legitimate downstream return from the original Meriweather-for-Haywood trade rather than a distant branch requiring speculative allocation.

sections.heading: Why the Jazz Win by a Wide Margin
sections.body:
New York received useful value. Meriweather gave the Knicks 106 games and more than 2,600 minutes across two seasons, then remained part of a later trade package.

The Jazz received 34 high-level Haywood games and then converted him into seven seasons of Dantley. Dantley's 461 games at 29.6 points per game move the outcome well beyond a normal rotation-player comparison.

The result is a major hindsight win for the Jazz even though the Knicks' incoming player was productive.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Jazz Win, A+/C. Utah receives an A+ because Haywood produced 24.0 points and 9.6 rebounds over 34 games and was then traded straight up for Adrian Dantley, who became a seven-season franchise star. New York receives a C because Meriweather supplied 106 useful regular-season games before becoming one part of a later three-team package.
