1978-79 New Orleans Jazz roster and statistics

sections.heading: The Swap Was Knight for Robey
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's league and team transaction logs agree on the January 16, 1979 deal. Boston sent Billy Knight to Indiana for Rick Robey.

Both players immediately became useful for their new teams, and unlike many trades in this part of the archive, both sides received multi-season value.

sections.heading: Knight Became a Five-Year Pacers Scorer
sections.body:
Knight played 39 games for Indiana after the trade in 1978-79 and averaged 14.7 points, 4.5 rebounds and 2.2 assists.

He then stayed for four more seasons. His strongest year came in 1980-81, when he played all 82 games, started 70 and averaged 17.5 points and 5.0 rebounds. Indiana reached the playoffs that season.

Across the five post-trade Pacers seasons, Knight appeared in 357 regular-season games. He also averaged 17.1 points in 1982-83, his final Indiana season.

That is a strong direct return. Indiana did not merely get a short-term veteran; Knight remained an important scorer through several roster cycles.

sections.heading: Robey Played 339 Games for Boston
sections.body:
Robey joined Boston as a 22-year-old rookie center and played 36 games after the trade, averaging 12.4 points and 7.2 rebounds.

He stayed through 1982-83. Over that span, Robey appeared in 339 Celtics regular-season games, including all 82 games in both 1979-80 and 1980-81.

His role declined over time, but the most important season was 1980-81. Robey played all 82 regular-season games and 17 playoff games for the Celtics team that won the NBA championship.

That gives Boston a title-season rotation contribution that Indiana's side cannot match directly.

sections.heading: Robey Later Became Part of the Dennis Johnson Package
sections.body:
Boston did not simply lose Robey when his playing role ended. On June 27, 1983, the Celtics sent Robey and two second-round picks to Phoenix.

In return, Boston received Dennis Johnson, a first-round pick that became Greg Kite and a third-round pick that became Winfred King.

This review does not credit the full Johnson return to Robey alone because Boston also included two second-round selections. Robey was nevertheless one of the assets required to complete the deal.

Johnson then played seven seasons and 541 regular-season games for Boston. He started 522 of them and was part of the Celtics teams that won the 1984 and 1986 championships.

That downstream branch materially raises the value of Boston's original Robey acquisition even after accounting for the additional picks the Celtics had to include.

sections.heading: Why Boston Gets the Hindsight Edge
sections.body:
Indiana received the more productive individual scorer from the original one-for-one trade. Knight's 357 games and multiple double-digit scoring seasons make the Pacers side a strong outcome.

Boston received 339 Robey games, a rotation center on the 1981 champions and an asset later used in the package for Dennis Johnson.

The Johnson transaction cannot be treated as if Robey alone bought a Hall of Fame-level guard, but it is still legitimate realized value from the Robey branch. Combined with Robey's championship contribution, that is enough to move Boston ahead.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win, A/A-. Boston receives an A because Robey contributed to the 1981 championship and later became part of the package that brought Dennis Johnson and two draft picks to Boston. Indiana receives an A- because Knight produced 357 regular-season games over five seasons and remained one of the Pacers' more reliable scorers during that stretch.

sections.heading: The January 17 Deal Was Awtrey for a First and Cash
sections.body: Boston's transaction log records Dennis Awtrey going to Seattle for a 1979 first-round pick. The league ledger also records the first-rounder as the selection later used on Sly Williams. Boston's source record includes cash coming back as well, but the amount is not documented in the reviewed sources.

sections.heading: Awtrey Joined a Championship Team
sections.body:
Awtrey played 40 regular-season games for Seattle after the trade. He logged 499 minutes and averaged 5.7 points and 7.5 rebounds per 36 minutes, serving as a low-usage reserve center.

The more important context is the postseason. Seattle won the 1979 NBA championship, and Awtrey's playoff game log shows him appearing in 16 of the team's 17 postseason games. His minutes fell as the run progressed, but he was part of the rotation throughout the title path.

That gives Seattle a concrete championship-season return from a player who had appeared in only 23 games for Boston earlier that year.

sections.heading: Boston Used the Pick as Trade Currency
sections.body:
The incoming first-rounder did not become a Celtics draft selection. On February 12, Boston sent that pick, two other 1979 first-round picks and Tom Barker to New York for Bob McAdoo.

McAdoo then played 20 games for Boston and averaged 20.6 points and 7.1 rebounds. The following September, Boston moved McAdoo to Detroit for two 1980 first-round picks.

Those later picks became part of the famous June 1980 trade that brought Robert Parish and the No. 3 pick used on Kevin McHale to Boston. This review does not assign Parish or McHale to this single Seattle pick because the chain required multiple assets at every step.

The important point is narrower: Boston's incoming first-rounder retained real transaction value and was used in a premium package rather than expiring unused.

sections.heading: Why the Result Is Essentially Even
sections.body:
Seattle received the more direct benefit. Awtrey gave the SuperSonics 40 regular-season games and 16 playoff appearances on a championship team.

Boston received less immediate on-court value, but the first-round pick remained a meaningful piece of a larger McAdoo transaction that later fed another major asset chain. The cash amount is unknown, so it cannot be scored.

Neither side clearly separates from the other once the difference between direct championship depth and diluted downstream trade value is respected.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, B/B. Seattle receives a B because Awtrey became a real reserve on the 1979 champions. Boston also receives a B because the first-round pick retained premium transaction utility and helped form the package for McAdoo, even though later Parish-McHale value cannot be credited to this pick alone.

sections.heading: The Trade Ended White's Boston Tenure
sections.body:
Boston's transaction log and Golden State's matching ledger record the January 30, 1979 exchange: Jo Jo White to the Warriors for a 1979 first-round pick that was later associated with No. 9 Larry Demic.

White had already played 47 games for Boston that season. After the trade, he appeared in 29 games for Golden State and averaged 12.3 points, 4.6 assists and 30.4 minutes.

sections.heading: White Stayed for Another Full Season
sections.body:
The Warriors kept White for 1979-80. He played 78 games, logged 2,052 minutes and averaged 9.9 points and 3.1 assists in 26.3 minutes.

Across his two partial/full Golden State seasons, White appeared in 107 regular-season games and 2,935 minutes. Basketball-Reference's career split credits him with 13.8 points and 4.6 assists per 36 minutes over that Warriors stint.

On September 10, 1980, Golden State sold White's player rights to Kansas City. The reviewed transaction record does not state the cash amount, so this review does not assign a specific additional value to that sale.

sections.heading: Boston Used the Pick Before the Draft
sections.body:
The Celtics did not select Larry Demic themselves. On February 12, only twelve days after acquiring the pick, Boston sent it to New York with two other 1979 first-round picks and Tom Barker for Bob McAdoo.

McAdoo played 20 games for Boston before being traded to Detroit the following September for two 1980 first-round picks. Those picks later became part of Boston's June 1980 trade for Robert Parish and the No. 3 pick used on Kevin McHale.

That downstream history proves the No. 9 pick retained meaningful trade utility, but this review does not credit Parish or McHale to this one branch. Boston needed three first-rounders and Barker to acquire McAdoo, and later transactions required additional assets.

sections.heading: Why Golden State Gets the Slight Edge
sections.body:
The Warriors received two seasons of usable veteran guard play and then retained enough rights value to sell White to Kansas City. Boston received a premium draft asset, but its direct contribution was one component of a larger McAdoo package.

Both sides extracted value. Golden State's 107 games of direct production are easier to isolate than Boston's diluted downstream branch.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Warriors Edge, B+/B. Golden State receives a B+ for 107 White games across two seasons plus the later rights sale. Boston receives a B because the first-round pick retained premium transaction value and helped acquire McAdoo, while the much larger later Parish-McHale return cannot be assigned to this pick alone.

sections.heading: The Knicks Received Three Firsts and a Player
sections.body: Boston's February 12, 1979 transaction sent Tom Barker and three 1979 first-round picks to New York for Bob McAdoo. The picks became Bill Cartwright at No. 3, Larry Demic at No. 9 and Sly Williams at No. 21.

sections.heading: Cartwright Was the Centerpiece of New York's Return
sections.body:
Cartwright started all 82 games as a rookie, averaged 21.7 points and 8.9 rebounds and made the All-Star team. He remained a major Knicks center through the first half of the 1980s before a foot injury wiped out 1984-85.

Demic also gave New York three full seasons. He played 206 games, including all 82 as a rookie, and started 68 times across his Knicks career.

Williams played 57 games as a rookie, then became a starter in 1980-81 and remained a productive forward into 1981-82. Barker added 22 games immediately after the trade.

The Knicks therefore converted McAdoo into several years of direct roster value, not just draft capital that failed to develop.

sections.heading: McAdoo's Boston Stay Was Brief but Productive
sections.body:
McAdoo played 20 games for Boston after the trade. He scored 411 points, averaging 20.6 points and 7.1 rebounds in 31.9 minutes.

On its own, that would not justify surrendering three first-round picks. The downstream transaction is what transforms Boston's side.

sections.heading: Detroit Sent Boston Two 1980 Firsts for McAdoo
sections.body:
On September 6, 1979, Boston traded McAdoo to Detroit for two 1980 first-round picks. Basketball-Reference notes that the exchange was arranged as compensation connected to Boston's signing of M.L. Carr.

Those picks later landed at No. 1 and No. 13 in the 1980 draft. Boston did not make either selection. On June 9, 1980, the Celtics sent both picks to Golden State for Robert Parish and the No. 3 pick.

sections.heading: Boston Used No. 3 on Kevin McHale
sections.body:
The next day, Boston selected Kevin McHale with the third pick. Parish and McHale became two core pieces of the Celtics teams that won the 1981, 1984 and 1986 NBA championships.

Because the McAdoo-to-Detroit and Detroit-picks-to-Golden-State steps are both direct transactions, this branch has much stronger attribution than a chain that requires several unrelated assets. Boston's McAdoo acquisition is therefore a legitimate upstream part of the Parish-McHale outcome.

sections.heading: New York Still Received an Excellent Package
sections.body:
A hindsight win for Boston does not make the Knicks' return poor. Cartwright became an All-Star-level starting center, Demic supplied 206 games and Williams developed into a productive starter before leaving New York.

The difference is ceiling. Boston turned a 20-game McAdoo stint into two first-rounders and then directly converted those picks into Parish and McHale.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win, A+/A. Boston receives an A+ because the McAdoo branch produced Parish and the pick used on McHale after two direct follow-up trades. New York receives an A because Cartwright became a long-term starting center and All-Star while Demic, Williams and Barker added substantial immediate roster value.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Bought Five Years of Frontcourt Depth
sections.body:
The May 31, 1979 transaction sent Harvey Catchings to Milwaukee for John Gianelli and a 1979 first-round pick. The Nets used the pick at No. 8 on Calvin Natt.

Catchings was a strong realized return for Milwaukee. He played 72 games in 1979-80, 77 in 1980-81, 80 in 1981-82, 74 in 1982-83 and 69 in 1983-84. That is 372 regular-season games across five Bucks seasons.

He was never a high-volume scorer, but he provided rebounding and interior defense for repeated playoff teams. Basketball-Reference credits him with 33 postseason appearances for Milwaukee over that span.

sections.heading: Natt Became an Immediate Nets Star
sections.body:
New Jersey used the incoming first-round pick on Calvin Natt at No. 8. He played 53 games for the Nets as a rookie and averaged 19.7 points, 9.7 rebounds and 38.6 minutes.

That alone gave the Nets a high-end return from the pick. The larger value came when they moved Natt before the season ended.

sections.heading: Natt Directly Became Lucas and Two Firsts
sections.body:
On February 8, 1980, New Jersey traded Natt to Portland for Maurice Lucas and two first-round picks. The picks became No. 7 Mike Gminski in 1980 and No. 10 Albert King in 1981.

Because that was a direct Natt-for-package trade, this review gives the branch full downstream credit. Gminski became a long-term Nets center, while King also spent multiple seasons with the franchise. Lucas added immediate veteran frontcourt value before leaving after the following season.

sections.heading: Gianelli Also Retained Trade Utility
sections.body:
John Gianelli was not a major long-term Nets player, but he did not disappear from the asset chain. Before the 1979-80 season, New Jersey included him with Jim Boylan and Bernard King in the trade that brought Rich Kelley from Utah.

Gianelli was only one piece of that package, so this review assigns partial credit to that branch rather than treating Kelley as Gianelli's sole return.

sections.heading: Why the Nets Win Despite Catchings' Excellent Milwaukee Tenure
sections.body:
Milwaukee clearly received real value: 372 Catchings games and 33 playoff appearances across five seasons is a strong result for one veteran acquisition.

New Jersey, however, turned the No. 8 pick into Natt's outstanding rookie production and then directly into Lucas plus two first-rounders. That created both immediate production and a larger multi-year asset base.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win, A+/A. New Jersey receives an A+ for Natt's rookie season and the direct Lucas-Gminski-King return, with Gianelli adding a smaller secondary branch. Milwaukee receives an A because Catchings supplied five durable seasons and meaningful playoff depth.

sections.heading: The Compensation Deal Sent McAdoo to Detroit
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference records the September 6, 1979 transaction as Boston sending Bob McAdoo to Detroit for two 1980 first-round picks. The exchange was arranged as compensation for Boston's July signing of veteran free agent M.L. Carr.

This review treats Carr as transaction context rather than an incoming trade asset. The assets scored here are McAdoo on Detroit's side and the two first-round picks on Boston's side.

sections.heading: McAdoo Still Gave Detroit a Productive First Season
sections.body:
McAdoo played 58 games for the Pistons in 1979-80 and averaged 21.1 points, 8.1 rebounds and 3.4 assists in 36.2 minutes. He was still a high-level scorer even though Detroit finished with one of the league's weakest records.

The return did not last. McAdoo appeared in only six Detroit games in 1980-81 before the relationship ended. NBA.com's historical profile describes an injury-plagued Pistons stint and notes that Detroit eventually waived him after a grievance dispute.

That leaves Detroit with 64 regular-season games from a star-level scorer, but no long-term asset chain from the transaction itself.

sections.heading: Boston Kept the Two Picks Together
sections.body:
The decisive part of this trade came nine months later. On June 9, 1980, Boston sent exactly those two incoming first-round picks to Golden State.

One was the No. 1 pick later used on Joe Barry Carroll. The other was the No. 13 pick later used on Rickey Brown. In return, Boston received Robert Parish and Golden State's No. 3 pick.

The Celtics then used No. 3 on Kevin McHale. Because both Detroit picks from this exact transaction moved together in the Parish-McHale deal, this review can credit that downstream return directly rather than treating it as a diluted multi-branch outcome.

sections.heading: The Downstream Return Became a Dynasty Core
sections.body:
Parish played 1,106 regular-season games for Boston over 14 seasons. Basketball-Reference's franchise leaderboard places him second in Celtics history in games played.

McHale played all 971 of his NBA regular-season games for Boston. He became a seven-time All-Star, a Hall of Famer and a three-time NBA champion.

Parish and McHale joined Larry Bird as the frontcourt core of Boston's 1981, 1984 and 1986 championship teams. This is not a speculative value chain: the two picks received for McAdoo were the exact outgoing assets used to obtain Parish and the pick used on McHale.

sections.heading: Why Boston Wins by a Huge Margin
sections.body:
Detroit did receive legitimate value. McAdoo remained a 21-point scorer in his first Pistons season, so the return was not empty.

But 64 games of McAdoo cannot approach 2,077 combined Boston regular-season games from Parish and McHale, three championships with both players on the roster and two Hall of Fame careers.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win, A+/C. Boston receives an A+ because the two first-round picks were directly converted into Robert Parish and the No. 3 pick used on Kevin McHale. Detroit receives a C because McAdoo still supplied one productive scoring season, but the stint lasted only 64 games and the opportunity cost became one of the most valuable downstream returns in NBA trade history.

sections.heading: The Trade Sent Smith to Cleveland for a First
sections.body: Basketball-Reference records Cleveland acquiring Randy Smith from San Diego on September 21, 1979 for a 1980 first-round pick. The frozen Cavaliers source package also lists cash going to San Diego, but the reviewed public transaction ledgers do not provide an amount, so this review does not score the cash term.

sections.heading: Smith Gave Cleveland Two Full Seasons
sections.body:
Smith played all 82 games in both of his Cavaliers seasons. In 1979-80 he averaged 17.6 points, 4.4 assists and 3.1 rebounds in 32.6 minutes.

He followed with 14.6 points and 4.4 assists in 1980-81. Across the two seasons, Smith appeared in 164 games for Cleveland and remained a substantial backcourt contributor rather than a short rental.

Cleveland also preserved a downstream asset. On May 20, 1981, the Cavaliers traded Smith to New York for a 1981 first-round pick. That pick was later sent to Kansas City as compensation when Cleveland signed Scott Wedman as a veteran free agent.

Wedman then played 89 games for Cleveland across parts of two seasons. This review treats those games as downstream use of the Smith return, but stops there rather than assigning every later Wedman transaction branch back to this 1979 trade.

sections.heading: San Diego Used the Pick on Michael Brooks
sections.body:
The Clippers kept Cleveland's 1980 first-round pick and selected Michael Brooks at No. 9. Brooks immediately played all 82 games as a rookie, averaging 14.7 points and 5.4 rebounds.

He played all 82 games again in both 1981-82 and 1982-83, averaging 15.6 points and 7.6 rebounds in the first of those seasons and 12.2 points and 6.4 rebounds in the second.

Brooks added 47 games in 1983-84 before knee trouble cost him the next two NBA seasons. His San Diego total was 293 regular-season games, with useful scoring and rebounding production across four years.

sections.heading: Why San Diego Gets the Modest Edge
sections.body:
Cleveland did well. Smith produced 164 games of veteran guard play and was later converted into a first-round asset that helped facilitate the Wedman signing.

San Diego, however, received 293 games from Brooks, including three consecutive 82-game seasons and several years of starter-level production. The unquantified cash would only strengthen the Clippers' side, but the grade does not depend on it.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Clippers Edge, A-/B+. San Diego receives an A- for turning the pick into 293 Michael Brooks games over four seasons. Cleveland receives a B+ for 164 Randy Smith games plus a meaningful downstream first-round asset, making this a productive deal for both teams despite the Clippers' longer direct return.

sections.heading: The Public Ledgers Confirm the Three-Player Package
sections.body: Basketball-Reference records New Jersey sending Bernard King, John Gianelli and Jim Boylan to Utah on October 2, 1979 for Rich Kelley. The frozen Nets source package also lists cash going to Utah, but the reviewed public transaction ledgers do not state an amount, so this review preserves the term without scoring it.

sections.heading: Kelley Gave New Jersey 57 Games and Two Future Picks
sections.body:
Kelley played 57 games for the Nets in 1979-80, averaging 10.0 points, 7.0 rebounds and 2.2 assists in 25.7 minutes. He was not a long-term Net, but the branch did not end when he left.

On February 15, 1980, New Jersey traded Kelley to Phoenix for a 1982 first-round pick and a 1983 second-round pick. The first later became the No. 17 selection associated with Brook Steppe after New Jersey sent it with Mike Woodson to Kansas City for Sam Lacey.

That later deal required Woodson as well, so this review does not assign the full Lacey return to Kelley alone. The important point is that Kelley produced more than half a season of useful center play and was then converted into a first-round asset plus a second.

sections.heading: Utah's Direct Return Was Brief
sections.body:
King played 19 games for Utah and averaged 9.3 points in 22.1 minutes. Gianelli played 17 games, averaging 3.2 points and 3.6 rebounds, before the Jazz waived him on November 28.

Boylan did not appear in a Jazz regular-season game. His Basketball-Reference page lists only his rookie NBA season, so there is no Utah playing return to score from that portion of the package.

sections.heading: King Still Produced a Useful Downstream Return
sections.body:
Utah moved King on September 11, 1980, receiving Wayne Cooper and a 1981 second-round pick from Golden State. Cooper then played 71 games for the Jazz in 1980-81, averaging 6.9 points and 6.2 rebounds in 20 minutes.

The second-round pick was later associated with Ken Green. This review credits Utah with the retained pick value but does not inflate the branch beyond the assets actually received.

sections.heading: Why Utah Gets the Slight Edge
sections.body:
New Jersey did better than the legacy F grade suggests. Kelley gave the Nets 57 games and was later converted into a first-round pick plus a second-round pick. That is a legitimate multi-step return.

Utah received less immediate production from the original players, but King still became Cooper plus another pick. Adding Cooper's 71 games to King and Gianelli's brief Jazz stints gives Utah a little more isolated realized value from the original package.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Jazz Edge, A-/B+. Utah receives an A- because the King branch became 71 Wayne Cooper games plus a second-round pick, while King and Gianelli also contributed briefly before leaving. New Jersey receives a B+ because Kelley played 57 games and was later converted into a first-rounder and a second-rounder. The cash amount remains unresolved and unscored.

sections.heading: New Jersey Paid a Second-Round Pick for a Proven Guard
sections.body: Basketball-Reference records Houston trading Mike Newlin to New Jersey on October 12, 1979 for a 1980 second-round pick. The frozen Nets source package also includes cash, but the reviewed public transaction ledgers do not state an amount, so this review preserves the cash term without assigning numerical value.

sections.heading: Newlin Immediately Became New Jersey's Lead Scorer
sections.body:
Newlin played 78 games in 1979-80 and averaged 20.9 points, 4.0 assists and 3.4 rebounds in 32.2 minutes. He scored 1,634 points in his first Nets season and led the roster in total scoring.

He was even more productive in 1980-81. Newlin played 79 games, averaged 21.4 points and 3.8 assists, and logged 2,911 minutes. Basketball-Reference's franchise history credits him as the team's leading win-shares player in both of those seasons.

Across the two-year Nets stint, Newlin appeared in 157 regular-season games and scored 3,322 points. He moved to New York for 1981-82, so this review stops the New Jersey return at those two seasons rather than crediting his final NBA year elsewhere.

sections.heading: Houston Used the Pick on John Stroud
sections.body:
The Rockets kept the incoming selection and drafted John Stroud at No. 27 in 1980. Stroud appeared in nine games for Houston as a rookie, totaling 88 minutes and 25 points.

Those nine games became his entire NBA career. Houston therefore received a real drafted player from the asset, but the on-court return was extremely small compared with Newlin's two high-scoring Nets seasons.

The cash term cannot materially change that comparison because its amount is undocumented in the sources reviewed for this batch. It is preserved as part of the canonical package but not used to manufacture value.

sections.heading: Why New Jersey Wins Decisively
sections.body:
The Nets turned one second-round pick and an unquantified cash term into 157 games from a guard who averaged more than 20 points in both seasons. That is unusually strong realized value for the acquisition cost.

Houston turned the pick into nine Stroud games and 88 minutes. The Rockets received little direct basketball value from the transaction after moving a veteran who still had two productive seasons left.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win, A/D+. New Jersey receives an A for 157 Newlin games and two 20-point seasons. Houston receives a D+ because the No. 27 pick became John Stroud but produced only nine NBA games; the frozen-source cash term remains unquantified.

sections.heading: Detroit Received the Deeper Original Package
sections.body: Basketball-Reference records the January 24, 1980 trade as Jim McElroy to Atlanta for Ron Lee, a 1980 second-round pick and a 1980 third-round pick. Detroit later used those selections at No. 45 on Brad Branson and No. 64 on Jonathan Moore.

sections.heading: Ron Lee Played 194 Games for Detroit
sections.body:
Lee played 31 games for the Pistons after the trade in 1979-80, averaging 7.3 points, 5.6 assists and 2.7 steals in 25.9 minutes.

He then played all 82 games in 1980-81 and 81 more in 1981-82. That gives Detroit 194 regular-season games from Lee alone, including two full seasons of rotation guard work.

Detroit placed Lee on waivers in October 1982. No later trade return needs to be credited to the branch.

sections.heading: Atlanta Got 105 Games From McElroy
sections.body:
McElroy played 31 Hawks games after the trade in 1979-80, then 54 in 1980-81 and 20 in 1981-82. He averaged 5.5 points and 2.1 assists during the first partial Atlanta season, then 3.8 points in 1980-81 before starting 17 of his 20 games in 1981-82.

Across the three seasons, Atlanta received 105 regular-season appearances. McElroy became a free agent in 1982, so the direct branch ends there.

sections.heading: The Two Draft Picks Added Little On-Court Value
sections.body:
Detroit selected Branson at No. 45, but he played in Italy in 1980-81 and never appeared in a Pistons regular-season game. Historical transaction records show Detroit later moved his negotiating rights to Dallas for future considerations; the reviewed sources do not identify a concrete NBA return that can be isolated for this review.

Jonathan Moore, the No. 64 pick, also never played an NBA regular-season game. The two picks therefore did not add direct Pistons minutes.

sections.heading: Why Detroit Gets the Edge
sections.body:
Atlanta received more than 100 McElroy games and should get credit for a useful multi-season guard. Detroit, however, received nearly twice as many games from Lee, including two near-complete seasons, while also holding two extra draft assets even though those picks did not become contributors.

The trade is not a blowout because the draft outcomes were poor and McElroy was useful. The difference is Lee's much longer realized tenure.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win, B+/B-. Detroit receives a B+ for 194 Ron Lee games plus two additional draft assets. Atlanta receives a B- for 105 McElroy games over parts of three seasons.

sections.heading: Atlanta Bought Two Picks and Used Them Immediately
sections.body:
The frozen canonical record and Pro Sports Transactions record Atlanta acquiring a 1980 second-round pick and a 1980 third-round pick from Utah for cash on January 24, 1980. The selections later became No. 45 Brad Branson and No. 64 Jonathan Moore.

The cash amount is not documented in the reviewed public sources. That prevents this review from assigning a precise value to Utah's return and lowers confidence relative to an ordinary player-for-player trade.

sections.heading: The Picks Became Same-Day Trade Currency
sections.body:
Atlanta did not hold the picks until the draft. The Hawks immediately sent both selections plus Ron Lee to Detroit for Jim McElroy on the same date.

McElroy then played 31 games for Atlanta in 1979-80, 54 in 1980-81 and 20 in 1981-82. That is 105 regular-season Hawks games from the larger McElroy package.

This review does not credit all 105 games to the two Utah picks because Ron Lee was also a meaningful outgoing player. The proper realized value is narrower: the picks were usable trade currency that helped Atlanta complete a multi-asset acquisition.

sections.heading: The Draft Outcomes Were Weak for Detroit
sections.body:
Detroit used the second-round pick at No. 45 on Branson and the third-round pick at No. 64 on Moore. Neither player appeared in a Pistons regular-season game.

Those later draft outcomes do not erase the picks' value to Atlanta, because the Hawks had already spent them successfully as transaction assets. They do, however, show that the selections themselves did not later become major NBA players for the team that finally drafted them.

sections.heading: Utah's Side Is Harder to Measure
sections.body:
Utah received cash and no player or draft asset in the recorded exchange. Without a documented amount, there is no reliable way to compare the Jazz's financial return directly with Atlanta's basketball use of the picks.

That uncertainty keeps the grade restrained. The Hawks clearly converted the picks into useful trade leverage, but the deal should not be treated like a major basketball win over Utah when the cash consideration is unknown.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Hawks Edge, B-/C+. Atlanta receives a B- because the two picks were immediately useful in the McElroy trade, which produced 105 Hawks games as part of a larger package. Utah receives a C+ because it received cash by design, but the undocumented amount prevents a stronger realized-value grade. Confidence is medium.

sections.heading: The Nets Turned Natt Into Lucas and Two Firsts
sections.body: Basketball-Reference records the February 8, 1980 deal as Calvin Natt to Portland for Maurice Lucas, a 1980 first-round pick and a 1981 first-round pick. The selections later became No. 7 Mike Gminski and No. 10 Albert King.

sections.heading: Lucas Gave New Jersey Immediate Frontcourt Value
sections.body:
Lucas played 22 games for the Nets after the trade in 1979-80, averaging 15.2 points and 9.6 rebounds in 32.2 minutes. He returned for 68 games in 1980-81 and averaged 16.6 points and 9.6 rebounds.

That gives New Jersey 90 regular-season games from the veteran portion of the return. Lucas was not a long-term Net, but the club received productive frontcourt minutes immediately while waiting for the two draft picks to mature.

sections.heading: The 1980 First Became Mike Gminski
sections.body:
New Jersey used the No. 7 pick in the 1980 draft on Mike Gminski. He played 550 regular-season games for the franchise from 1980-81 through the first 34 games of 1987-88.

Gminski developed from a reserve into a full-time starting center, starting 78 games in 1985-86 and 66 in 1986-87. His eight-season Nets tenure gives this branch the largest volume of direct realized value in the trade.

sections.heading: The 1981 First Became Albert King
sections.body:
The second first-rounder came from Golden State originally and landed at No. 10 in the 1981 draft. New Jersey selected Albert King.

King played 410 regular-season games for the Nets across six seasons. He averaged 17.0 points in 1982-83 and remained a regular wing through 1986-87.

Between Gminski and King, the two picks produced 960 regular-season Nets games. Adding Lucas brings the direct New Jersey total from the incoming assets to 1,050 games.

sections.heading: Portland Still Got a Very Good Player
sections.body:
Natt was far from a miss for the Trail Blazers. He averaged 20.4 points in 25 games immediately after the trade and went on to play 333 regular-season games for Portland over five seasons.

Basketball-Reference credits Natt with 5,738 points and 2,297 rebounds as a Trail Blazer. He gave Portland multiple productive seasons and was a legitimate high-level starter rather than a short-term rental.

sections.heading: Why New Jersey Wins the Hindsight Verdict
sections.body:
Portland acquired the best single scorer in the deal and received five productive years from him. That return deserves a high grade.

New Jersey, however, converted one player into a productive veteran plus two first-round selections that became long-tenured rotation players. Gminski and King alone combined for nearly a thousand regular-season games for the franchise, and Lucas added two useful seasons on top of that.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win, A+/A-. New Jersey receives an A+ for 90 Lucas games, 550 Gminski games and 410 King games from the three incoming assets. Portland receives an A- because Natt produced 333 games and 5,738 points across five seasons. Both teams received substantial value, but the depth and longevity of the Nets return are too large to ignore.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Bought a Starting Guard for a Future First
sections.body: Basketball-Reference records the February 8, 1980 trade as Philadelphia sending a 1981 first-round pick to Portland for Lionel Hollins. The frozen canonical source package also lists cash going to Portland, but the reviewed public transaction ledgers do not state an amount, so this review preserves the term without scoring it.

sections.heading: Hollins Played 190 Games for the 76ers
sections.body:
Hollins played 27 games after the trade in 1979-80, starting 26 and averaging 12.2 points and 4.1 assists. Philadelphia reached the NBA Finals that spring.

He returned for all 82 games in 1980-81 and then played 81 games in 1981-82, starting every one of them while averaging 11.0 points and 3.9 assists. Philadelphia again reached the NBA Finals in 1982.

Across those three regular seasons, Hollins appeared in 190 games for the 76ers. The trade therefore produced multiple years of real rotation and starting value rather than a short rental.

sections.heading: Portland Used the Pick as Trade Currency
sections.body:
The incoming Philadelphia first eventually became the No. 4 selection in the 1981 draft, where Al Wood was selected after the pick changed hands again. Portland did not use it itself.

On June 10, 1980, the Trail Blazers sent the pick and Ronnie Lester to Chicago for Kelvin Ransey and another 1981 first-round pick that later became No. 16 Darnell Valentine.

Ransey immediately became a major Portland contributor, playing 80 games as a rookie at 15.2 points and 6.9 assists, then 78 games in 1981-82 at 16.1 points and 7.1 assists. Valentine later became a multi-year Portland guard after the second pick was exercised.

This review does not assign the full Ransey-Valentine return to Philadelphia's pick because Ronnie Lester was also outgoing and Portland received two assets back. The proper conclusion is narrower: the No. 4 pick was premium trade currency that helped the Blazers restructure their backcourt.

sections.heading: Why Philadelphia Gets the Edge
sections.body:
Portland extracted meaningful market value from the future first and clearly did not waste the asset. The later Ransey-Valentine transaction makes that side stronger than a simple Hollins-for-Al Wood comparison would suggest.

Philadelphia, however, received 190 directly attributable Hollins games, including a full season as a starter on a Finals team. That value is easier to isolate than Portland's multi-asset downstream branch.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight 76ers Edge, A-/B+. Philadelphia receives an A- for three seasons and 190 games of Hollins production. Portland receives a B+ because the first-round pick remained premium trade currency and became part of a productive Ransey-plus-pick transaction, while the unquantified cash term is preserved but not scored.

sections.heading: The Lakers Acquired a Long-Term Reserve
sections.body: Basketball-Reference records Chicago sending Mark Landsberger to Los Angeles on February 13, 1980 for Ollie Mack plus 1980 and 1981 second-round picks. The frozen Chicago source package also lists cash coming back, but the public transaction ledger does not give an amount, so this review preserves the term without assigning value to it.

sections.heading: Landsberger Played 206 Lakers Games
sections.body:
Landsberger joined Los Angeles for the final 23 regular-season games of 1979-80, then appeared in 69 games in 1980-81, 75 in 1981-82 and 39 in 1982-83. That is 206 regular-season games for the Lakers.

His role was not star-level, but it fit a championship roster. The Lakers' own alumni record credits Landsberger as a key reserve on the 1980 and 1982 championship teams. That gives Los Angeles direct title-era value from the player it acquired.

sections.heading: Mack Gave Chicago a Short Run
sections.body:
Ollie Mack played 23 games for Chicago after the trade in 1979-80, averaging 8.0 points in 22.9 minutes. He appeared in only three Bulls games the following season before being waived on October 23, 1980.

That leaves Mack at 26 regular-season Chicago games. He was useful immediately after the trade, but he did not become a long-term piece.

sections.heading: The 1980 Second Became Sam Worthen
sections.body:
Chicago used the No. 26 selection in 1980 on Sam Worthen. He played 64 Bulls games as a rookie, logging 945 minutes and scoring 235 points.

Worthen did not return for a second Chicago season, so this branch also produced one year of direct value rather than a durable rotation piece.

sections.heading: The 1981 Second Helped Pay for Larry Kenon
sections.body:
Chicago did not use the second future pick itself. On September 12, 1980, the Bulls sent that 1981 second-round pick plus another 1981 second to San Antonio as compensation for signing veteran free agent Larry Kenon.

Kenon played 77 games for Chicago in 1980-81 and 60 more in 1981-82, then five games in 1982-83. Because two second-round picks were sent as compensation, this review does not assign all 142 Kenon games to the pick received from Los Angeles.

San Antonio eventually used the specific selection at No. 28 on Gene Banks. Banks' NBA production belongs to the Spurs, not Chicago, because the Bulls had already transferred the pick.

sections.heading: Why Los Angeles Gets the Edge
sections.body:
Chicago extracted several forms of value: 26 Mack games, 64 Worthen games and a future second that helped facilitate the Kenon signing. That is a respectable package for one reserve big.

Los Angeles, however, received 206 regular-season games from Landsberger across parts of four seasons, including reserve contributions to two championship teams. The Lakers' value is both easier to isolate and tied directly to the club's highest-level results.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Edge, A-/B+. Los Angeles receives an A- for 206 Landsberger games and two championship-season contributions. Chicago receives a B+ for Mack, Worthen and a future pick that retained enough value to become part of the Kenon compensation package, with the unquantified cash term preserved but not scored.

sources.title: Los Angeles Lakers alumni - Mark Landsberger

sections.heading: Phoenix Got Three Seasons of Rich Kelley
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference records Phoenix acquiring Rich Kelley from New Jersey on February 15, 1980 for a 1982 first-round pick and a 1983 second-round pick. The frozen canonical Nets source package also lists cash going to New Jersey, but the reviewed public transaction ledgers do not state an amount, so this review preserves the term without scoring it.

Kelley immediately joined the Suns' rotation. He played 23 games after the trade in 1979-80, then 81 games in 1980-81 and 81 more in 1981-82. That is 185 Phoenix regular-season games.

His role was steady rather than star-level. In 1981-82 he started 39 games, averaged 7.9 points, 6.1 rebounds and 3.6 assists, and gave Phoenix a durable interior passer before the club moved him again.

sections.heading: Phoenix Then Turned Kelley Into Another First
sections.body:
On June 21, 1982, the Suns traded Kelley to Denver for a 1982 first-round pick. Phoenix used that No. 15 selection on David Thirdkill.

Thirdkill played 49 games for Phoenix as a rookie in 1982-83. He was only a reserve, but this is a clean one-for-one downstream branch from Kelley: Phoenix received three seasons of Kelley and then recovered another first-round asset when it moved him.

sections.heading: The Nets Routed the 1982 First Before the Draft
sections.body:
New Jersey never selected Brook Steppe. On November 12, 1981, the Nets sent the incoming first-round pick plus Mike Woodson to Kansas City for veteran center Sam Lacey.

Lacey played 54 regular-season games for New Jersey in 1981-82. Because Woodson was also sent to Kansas City, this review does not credit all 54 Lacey games to the Phoenix pick alone. The first-rounder nevertheless had clear trade utility and helped New Jersey acquire immediate frontcourt depth.

sections.heading: The 1983 Second Became Wayne Sappleton
sections.body:
New Jersey also moved the second-round pick before the 1983 draft. On June 19, 1982, the Nets traded that pick straight up to Golden State for Wayne Sappleton.

Sappleton spent the next two seasons in Italy before returning to New Jersey in 1984-85. He played 33 regular-season games for the Nets that season. This branch therefore produced delayed but directly attributable NBA value.

sections.heading: Why Phoenix Gets the Hindsight Win
sections.body:
New Jersey received two useful trade assets plus cash of unknown amount. The first helped acquire Lacey, and the second directly became Sappleton. That is not an empty return.

Phoenix still did better. Kelley gave the Suns 185 games over three seasons, and the club then converted him into a first-round pick that produced 49 Thirdkill games. The Suns' return is larger, more direct and less dependent on multi-asset attribution.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Suns Win, A-/C+. Phoenix receives an A- for 185 Kelley games plus the later first-round return that became Thirdkill. New Jersey receives a C+ because both picks retained transaction value, but the first was only one component of the Lacey package and the second ultimately produced 33 Sappleton games; the cash amount is unknown and unscored.

sections.heading: The Original Deal Was Ruland for a Future Second
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's Golden State, Washington and league transaction ledgers all record the same June 10, 1980 trade. Golden State sent the rights to second-round pick Jeff Ruland to Washington for a 1981 second-round selection that later became No. 33 Sam Williams.

Ruland did not immediately join the Bullets. He spent 1980-81 playing in Spain, then debuted for Washington in 1981-82.

sections.heading: Ruland Became an All-Star-Level Washington Big
sections.body:
Ruland played all 82 games as a rookie and averaged 14.4 points and 9.3 rebounds in 27.0 minutes. He followed with 79 games in 1982-83 at 19.4 points and 11.0 rebounds, then produced his best season in 1983-84.

That year Ruland played 75 games, started all 75 and averaged 22.2 points, 12.3 rebounds and 3.9 assists in 41.1 minutes. He made the All-Star team and finished ninth in MVP voting.

Ruland was an All-Star again in 1984-85 despite playing only 37 games. He returned for 30 games in 1985-86. Across five Washington seasons, he appeared in 303 regular-season games and scored 5,653 points while functioning as one of the franchise's primary interior players.

sections.heading: Golden State Used the Pick on Sam Williams
sections.body:
The Warriors kept the incoming second-round pick and selected Sam Williams at No. 33 in 1981. Williams became a useful rotation forward.

He played 59 games as a rookie, starting 22, and averaged 6.1 points and 5.2 rebounds. He followed with 75 games in 1982-83 and averaged 8.4 points and 5.2 rebounds.

Williams appeared in seven more Golden State games in 1983-84 before continuing the season with Philadelphia. His Warriors total was 141 regular-season games, 50 starts and 2,665 minutes.

sections.heading: Why Washington Wins Decisively
sections.body:
Golden State did receive a productive NBA player from the future second-round pick. Williams was not a failed selection, and 141 games of frontcourt depth are real value.

Washington's return operated at a completely different level. Ruland became a five-season starter-level centerpiece, twice made the All-Star team and produced multiple seasons near or above 20 points and 10 rebounds per game.

The original legacy summary described Golden State as holding a modest edge, but the source-backed player records do not support that conclusion. Washington received substantially more realized value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bullets Win, A+/B. Washington receives an A+ for 303 Ruland games, two All-Star selections and several elite production seasons. Golden State receives a B because Sam Williams supplied 141 useful games and 50 starts, but his value was far below Ruland's Washington tenure.

sections.heading: Dallas Traded a Guard for Two Future Seconds
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's Utah and league transaction ledgers record the September 11, 1980 trade: Dallas sent Billy McKinney to the Jazz for a 1983 second-round pick and a 1984 second-round pick.

The delayed return meant Dallas had to wait nearly three years before either asset became an NBA player. Utah, by contrast, got immediate rotation minutes from McKinney.

sections.heading: McKinney Played 35 Games for Utah
sections.body:
McKinney appeared in 35 Jazz games in 1980-81 and logged 1,032 minutes. He averaged 8.4 points, 4.5 assists and 2.1 rebounds while shooting 53.2 percent from the field.

That was meaningful backcourt production, but the Jazz did not keep him for the full season. On December 22, Utah traded McKinney to Denver for rookie guard Carl Nicks.

Nicks then played 40 games for the Jazz that season, averaging 6.3 points in 15.4 minutes. This review credits those Utah games as direct downstream value from the McKinney branch.

sections.heading: The 1983 Pick Became Mark West
sections.body:
Dallas held the first incoming pick until the 1983 draft and selected Mark West at No. 30.

West played 34 regular-season games for the Mavericks as a rookie, logging 202 minutes, and also appeared in four playoff games. Dallas waived him in October 1984, so the Mavericks did not capture the long NBA career West later built elsewhere.

That distinction is important. This review scores only the value realized by Dallas, not West's 17-year career after he became a free agent.

sections.heading: The 1984 Pick Became Anthony Teachey
sections.body:
Dallas used the second incoming pick at No. 40 in 1984 on Anthony Teachey.

Basketball-Reference lists Teachey as a Dallas draft pick but records no NBA regular-season career. The pick therefore did not add direct NBA game value for the Mavericks.

sections.heading: Why Utah Gets the Modest Edge
sections.body:
Dallas received two draft opportunities, but the realized NBA return was limited to 34 regular-season games and four playoff appearances from West. Teachey produced no NBA games for the franchise.

Utah received 35 McKinney games with useful point-guard production and then converted him into Nicks, who added another 40 games. The Jazz branch therefore produced more immediate and identifiable team-specific value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Jazz Edge, B-/C+. Utah receives a B- for 35 productive McKinney games plus 40 Nicks games after the December trade. Dallas receives a C+ because Mark West supplied limited rookie minutes and a few playoff appearances while the second pick produced no NBA games.

sections.heading: The Trade Was Phegley for Foots Walker
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's New Jersey, Cleveland and league transaction ledgers record the September 24, 1980 swap as Roger Phegley to Cleveland for Foots Walker. The canonical TradeVerdicts record lists him by his given name, Clarence Walker; Basketball-Reference identifies Foots Walker as Clarence Walker.

sections.heading: Walker Became a Four-Year Nets Guard
sections.body:
Walker played 41 games for New Jersey in 1980-81 and averaged 5.7 points with 6.2 assists in 28.6 minutes.

His largest Nets role came in 1981-82. Walker appeared in 77 games, started 54 and averaged 5.9 points with 5.2 assists. He remained with the team for 79 games in 1982-83 and another 34 in 1983-84.

That gives New Jersey 231 regular-season games from Walker across four seasons. He was not a scorer, but he provided sustained point-guard minutes and distribution well beyond the first year of the trade.

sections.heading: Phegley Gave Cleveland Immediate Scoring
sections.body:
Phegley played all 82 games for Cleveland in 1980-81 and logged 2,269 minutes. He averaged 14.4 points, 3.0 rebounds and 2.2 assists while shooting 49.1 percent from the field.

He returned for 27 Cavaliers games in 1981-82, starting eight and averaging 9.2 points. His Cleveland total was therefore 109 regular-season games across parts of two seasons.

That is meaningful direct production, particularly in the first year. Cleveland did not simply acquire a disposable roster piece.

sections.heading: Cleveland Later Used Phegley in a Larger Trade
sections.body:
On December 23, 1981, Cleveland traded Phegley and Mike Mitchell to San Antonio for Ron Brewer, Reggie Johnson and cash.

Phegley therefore retained trade value, but this review does not assign the full Spurs return to him. Mitchell was a major outgoing player and the transaction cannot be reduced to a Phegley-only branch.

The proper source-backed credit is narrower: Cleveland received 109 Phegley games and then used him as one component of a multi-player return.

sections.heading: Why New Jersey Gets the Slight Edge
sections.body:
Cleveland received the better short-term scorer. Phegley's 14.4 points per game in 1980-81 gave the Cavaliers more immediate offensive production than Walker ever supplied the Nets.

New Jersey received much more duration. Walker stayed four seasons, played 231 games and remained useful as a primary or reserve point guard into 1983-84.

Because Cleveland's later trade return required Mike Mitchell, that downstream branch cannot erase the direct 122-game gap between Walker and Phegley.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Nets Edge, B+/B. New Jersey receives a B+ for four seasons and 231 Walker games. Cleveland receives a B for 109 Phegley games, including a productive 82-game first season, plus partial downstream trade value. The exchange was useful to both clubs, but the Nets realized the more durable one-for-one return.
