sections.heading: Houston Received Two NBA Contributors
sections.body:
The June 28, 1982 transaction sent Joe Bryant and San Diego's No. 42 draft pick to Houston for the Rockets' No. 32 selection. Both draft picks became NBA players, which makes the deal more useful to grade through direct franchise production rather than draft reputation.

Houston received immediate value from Bryant plus a second rotation player from the later pick.

sections.heading: Joe Bryant Started 56 Games for Houston
sections.body:
Bryant played 81 regular-season games for the Rockets in 1982-83 and started 56. He averaged 25.4 minutes, 10.0 points, 3.4 rebounds and 2.3 assists.

Houston struggled to a 14-68 record, so Bryant's season did not translate into team success. Still, he was a regular starter and one of the more experienced players on a rebuilding roster.

That was Bryant's only NBA season in Houston and the final NBA season of his playing career before he continued professionally overseas.

sections.heading: Jeff Taylor Added 44 Games
sections.body:
Houston used the No. 42 pick on Texas Tech guard Jeff Taylor.

Taylor appeared in 44 regular-season games as a rookie, started five and averaged 17.6 minutes, 3.6 points and 2.5 assists. He was waived the following season, so his Houston contribution was limited to that one year.

Even so, the pick produced a real rotation player rather than a zero-game branch.

sections.heading: Richard Anderson Gave San Diego One Season
sections.body:
The Clippers used No. 32 on UC Santa Barbara big man Richard Anderson. He played 78 regular-season games for San Diego in 1982-83, made five starts and averaged 5.2 points and 3.5 rebounds.

Anderson later had a six-year NBA career, but only that rookie season belongs to San Diego for this trade. He played for Denver in 1983-84 and never returned to the Clippers.

The direct Clippers return was therefore 78 games and five starts.

sections.heading: Why Houston Wins
sections.body:
Bryant and Taylor combined for 125 regular-season games and 61 starts in Houston. Anderson gave San Diego 78 games and five starts.

The Clippers selected a player who ultimately had the longest NBA career of the three, but most of that career happened elsewhere. Franchise-specific realized value favors the Rockets because Bryant supplied a full starting season and Taylor added another 44 appearances.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win, B/C+. Houston receives a B for extracting one season of starting production from Bryant plus 44 games from Taylor. San Diego receives a C+ because Anderson was a useful rookie rotation player, but his later career cannot be credited to the Clippers and the direct return was smaller.

sources.title: 1982-83 San Diego Clippers roster and stats

sections.heading: Both Sides Rerouted the Asset They Acquired
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference records the June 30, 1982 trade as Atlanta receiving Jim Johnstone's draft rights from Kansas City for a 1984 second-round pick. The Hawks' official media guide adds an important detail: the pick originally belonged to Seattle and had reached Atlanta in the 1980 Armond Hill trade.

Neither Atlanta nor Kansas City ultimately used its incoming asset as a long-term player piece.

sections.heading: Johnstone Never Played for Atlanta
sections.body:
Kansas City had selected Johnstone at No. 51 in the 1982 draft. Atlanta acquired his rights the next day but never used him in a regular-season game.

On September 27, 1982, the Hawks sent Johnstone, a 1983 second-round pick and a 1985 second-round pick to San Antonio for George Johnson.

Johnstone later appeared in seven games for San Antonio and sixteen for Detroit in 1982-83. Those games cannot be credited to Atlanta because they occurred after the Hawks had traded him again.

His rights did retain transaction value, but they were only one of three outgoing assets in the George Johnson deal. This review therefore does not assign Atlanta the entire value of Johnson.

sections.heading: Kansas City Also Moved the Pick Again
sections.body:
The Kings held the acquired 1984 second-round pick until June 28, 1983. Kansas City then sent the pick to Chicago together with the draft rights to Ennis Whatley and Chris McNealy for Mark Olberding and the rights to Larry Micheaux.

Chicago ultimately exercised the pick at No. 37 in 1984 and selected Ben Coleman.

Coleman did not play in the NBA until 1986-87 after two seasons in Italy, and he never played for Kansas City. His later five-year NBA career belongs to other franchises for direct realized-value purposes.

sections.heading: Why Kansas City Gets a Small Edge
sections.body:
Atlanta and Kansas City both converted the acquired asset into a later transaction instead of direct on-court production. That makes this a much closer comparison than the terminal player names suggest.

The difference is asset portability. Kansas City's second-round pick remained a discrete draft asset that could be packaged in a later deal and ultimately became a useful NBA player after reaching Chicago. Atlanta's Johnstone rights also carried value, but they were moved only months later as one piece of a three-asset package.

No original team received a direct NBA game from Johnstone or Coleman. The Kings' advantage is therefore limited to the continuing value of the pick, not Coleman's later career.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Win, C+/C. Kansas City receives a C+ because the 1984 second-rounder remained useful in a later trade and eventually became No. 37 Ben Coleman after leaving the Kings. Atlanta receives a C because Johnstone never played for the Hawks and his rights were only one component of a later multi-asset deal. The margin is modest.

sources.title: Atlanta Hawks historical transactions media guide

sections.heading: Both Teams Received Starting Forwards
sections.body:
The July 7, 1982 swap was straightforward: New York received Truck Robinson, and Phoenix received Maurice Lucas.

Unlike many historical trades in this archive, both incoming players immediately became regular starters and stayed beyond a single season. The question is therefore not whether either side got value, but which veteran produced more of it.

sections.heading: Robinson Gave New York Two Full Starting Seasons
sections.body:
Robinson played 81 regular-season games for the Knicks in 1982-83, starting 76. He averaged 30.0 minutes, 9.5 points and 8.1 rebounds.

He returned for 65 games in 1983-84 and started 63, averaging 10.8 points and 8.4 rebounds. Robinson also appeared in 18 playoff games across those two seasons, starting all of them.

His final Knicks season was brief: two games and one start in 1984-85.

That gives New York 148 regular-season games and 140 starts from Robinson.

sections.heading: Lucas Became an All-Star in Phoenix
sections.body:
Lucas made an even larger immediate impact. In 1982-83 he played 77 regular-season games, started 71 and averaged 16.5 points, 10.4 rebounds and 2.8 assists.

He earned an All-Star selection that season and received MVP votes. Phoenix got both high-end production and heavy minutes from him right away.

Lucas returned for 75 games and 69 starts in 1983-84, averaging 15.9 points and 9.7 rebounds. He then played 63 more games in 1984-85, starting 22 and averaging 13.4 points and 8.8 rebounds.

Across three Phoenix seasons, Lucas played 215 regular-season games and started 162.

sections.heading: Phoenix Got the Higher Peak and More Volume
sections.body:
Robinson was a useful Knicks starter and helped New York reach the playoffs in both 1982-83 and 1983-84. His return was legitimate enough that this trade cannot be treated as a bad move for New York.

Lucas, however, gave Phoenix 67 more regular-season games, 22 more starts and substantially more scoring. His 1982-83 All-Star season also produced a level of individual recognition Robinson did not match in New York.

The Suns therefore received both the better peak and the longer direct tenure.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Suns Win, A-/B. Phoenix receives an A- for three productive seasons, 215 games, 162 starts and an All-Star year from Lucas. New York receives a B because Robinson was a durable two-year starter and playoff contributor, but his direct value was lower in both volume and peak impact.

sources.title: 1982-83 New York Knicks roster and stats

sections.heading: New Jersey Paid a First-Round Pick and Cash for a Starting Center
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's New Jersey and Philadelphia transaction records identify the August 27, 1982 package as Darryl Dawkins to the Nets for a 1983 first-round pick and cash. The canonical package specifies the cash at $700,000.

The pick later landed at No. 17, where Philadelphia selected Leo Rautins.

sections.heading: Dawkins Immediately Became New Jersey's Starting Center
sections.body:
Dawkins played 81 regular-season games for the Nets in 1982-83 and started all 81. He averaged 12.0 points, 5.2 rebounds and 1.9 blocks while shooting 59.9 percent from the field.

He was even better in 1983-84, starting 80 of 81 games and averaging 16.8 points on 59.3 percent shooting. New Jersey reached the playoffs and upset defending champion Philadelphia in the first round.

That second season alone supplied more top-end basketball value than the draft return ultimately produced for the 76ers.

sections.heading: He Stayed With the Nets for Five Seasons
sections.body:
Injuries reduced Dawkins' availability after 1983-84, but he still remained a meaningful part of New Jersey's frontcourt. He played 39 games in 1984-85, 51 in 1985-86 and six in 1986-87.

Across five Nets seasons, Dawkins appeared in 258 regular-season games, started 196 and scored 3,687 points.

This review credits only his New Jersey production. His prior Philadelphia career and later appearances elsewhere do not affect the Nets' realized return.

sections.heading: Philadelphia's Pick Became Leo Rautins
sections.body:
The 76ers used the No. 17 pick in the 1983 NBA Draft on Syracuse forward Leo Rautins.

Rautins played 28 regular-season games for Philadelphia in 1983-84, started three and averaged 7.0 minutes, 1.7 points, 1.2 rebounds and 1.0 assist.

He played only four more NBA games, all with Atlanta the following season. Philadelphia therefore received just one limited NBA season from the first-round component.

sections.heading: The $700,000 Cash Component Matters
sections.body:
Unlike many historical cash considerations, the amount here is known. Philadelphia received $700,000 in addition to the first-round pick, so its side should not be evaluated as Rautins alone.

The cash provided tangible financial value and raises the 76ers' grade. It still does not produce on-court value comparable to several seasons from a starting-caliber center.

sections.heading: Why New Jersey Wins
sections.body:
The Nets accepted the cost of a first-round pick and substantial cash, but the acquired player immediately became a starter and stayed for five seasons. Dawkins gave New Jersey 258 games and nearly 200 starts.

Philadelphia's draft branch produced 28 games and three starts. Even with the $700,000 payment, the realized basketball gap is too large to call the transaction even.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win, A-/C+. New Jersey receives an A- for acquiring five seasons of center production, including two high-volume starting years. Philadelphia receives a C+ because it obtained a first-round pick and a meaningful known cash payment, but the selected player produced only 28 games for the franchise.

1983-84 New Jersey Nets roster and stats

sections.heading: Boston Acquired Three Seasons of Useful Guard Depth
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee transaction ledger records the September 9, 1982 exchange directly: the Bucks sent Quinn Buckner to Boston for Dave Cowens, who had been retired since 1980.

Buckner immediately became a major rotation guard for a title contender, while Cowens gave Milwaukee one final NBA season.

sections.heading: Buckner Played 226 Regular-Season Games for Boston
sections.body:
Buckner appeared in 72 games for the Celtics in 1982-83 and started 56. He averaged 7.9 points, 3.8 assists and 1.5 steals while playing 21.7 minutes per game.

He returned for 79 games in 1983-84 and all 75 games he was available for in 1984-85. Across three Boston seasons, Buckner played 226 regular-season games and started 62.

His role declined over time, but his availability and defensive backcourt depth gave Boston repeated value well beyond the first season.

sections.heading: He Was Part of the 1984 Championship Rotation
sections.body:
Buckner appeared in 23 playoff games during Boston's 1984 title run. He averaged 11.7 minutes in the postseason and served as a reserve behind the Celtics' established starting backcourt.

That championship contribution is not treated as if Buckner were one of the team's primary stars. It still matters because Boston received a dependable playoff rotation player from the trade.

sections.heading: Cowens Gave Milwaukee One Useful Comeback Season
sections.body:
Cowens had not played in either 1980-81 or 1981-82. Milwaukee acquired his rights and convinced him to return for the 1982-83 season.

He played 40 regular-season games, started 34 and averaged 25.4 minutes, 8.1 points, 6.9 rebounds and 2.1 assists. The Bucks won 51 games and reached the Eastern Conference Finals.

Cowens therefore was not an empty return. Milwaukee received legitimate frontcourt minutes from a Hall of Fame veteran during a strong season.

sections.heading: The Difference Is Duration and Championship Value
sections.body:
Cowens retired again after 1982-83, ending Milwaukee's return after 40 regular-season games. Buckner stayed in Boston through 1984-85 and played 226 regular-season games plus 45 playoff games across those three seasons.

The Celtics did not acquire a star, but they received far more durable value and a contributor to a championship team.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win, A/C+. Boston receives an A for three seasons, 226 regular-season games, 62 starts and meaningful playoff depth during the 1984 championship run. Milwaukee receives a C+ because Cowens supplied one credible comeback season on a 51-win team, but the return lasted only 40 games before he retired again.

sections.heading: Atlanta Got One Reserve Season From George Johnson
sections.body:
The September 27, 1982 deal sent George Johnson from San Antonio to Atlanta for Jim Johnstone plus second-round picks in 1983 and 1985.

Johnson was a veteran defensive center, but his Atlanta return was limited. He played 37 regular-season games in 1982-83, made no starts and averaged 12.5 minutes, 1.7 points, 3.2 rebounds and 1.6 blocks.

He did not play in 1983-84 after refusing to attend Hawks training camp without a guaranteed contract. He later resumed his career with New Jersey, so Atlanta receives credit only for those 37 games.

sections.heading: Johnstone and Lockhart Barely Played for San Antonio
sections.body:
Johnstone appeared in seven regular-season games for the Spurs in 1982-83, all off the bench, averaging 7.7 minutes and 1.0 point. His San Antonio tenure ended quickly.

The 1983 second-round pick landed at No. 35, where San Antonio selected Darrell Lockhart. Lockhart played only two regular-season games for the Spurs, made no starts and was waived on November 4, 1983.

Those two branches produced just nine direct Spurs games.

sections.heading: The 1985 Pick Became a Useful Trade Asset
sections.body:
The legacy archive entry identifies the 1985 second-round pick as No. 31 Manute Bol. That terminal draft result is correct, but it does not mean Bol played for San Antonio.

On January 20, 1984, the Spurs traded the future second-round pick to Golden State for Ron Brewer. Brewer then played 40 games for San Antonio in 1983-84 and nine more in 1984-85, starting five total and averaging 8.7 points in his first Spurs stint.

That gives San Antonio 49 regular-season games from the direct downstream conversion of the pick.

sections.heading: Manute Bol Belongs to the Later Washington Branch
sections.body:
Golden State later moved the pick to Washington, and the Bullets used No. 31 in the 1985 draft on Manute Bol.

This review preserves Bol as the terminal pick identity but does not credit his Washington career to San Antonio. The Spurs had already converted the asset into Brewer more than a year before the draft.

This distinction avoids overstating San Antonio's return while still recognizing that the 1985 pick carried real transaction value.

sections.heading: Why San Antonio Wins Slightly
sections.body:
Atlanta received 37 reserve games from Johnson. San Antonio received seven games from Johnstone, two from Lockhart and 49 from Brewer through the directly traceable second-round-pick conversion.

The total Spurs basketball return was still modest, but it was broader and lasted longer than Johnson's single Atlanta season.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Spurs Win, B-/C. San Antonio receives a B- because the original player and 1983 pick produced little, but the 1985 pick was successfully converted into 49 games of Ron Brewer. Atlanta receives a C because Johnson supplied useful shot-blocking depth for 37 games but never played a second season for the Hawks.

sources.title: 1983-84 San Antonio Spurs roster and stats

sections.heading: Houston Received a Second-Round Pick for Bill Willoughby
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's Houston, San Antonio and league transaction ledgers agree on the October 18, 1982 mechanism. Willoughby signed with the Spurs as a veteran free agent, and Houston received San Antonio's 1985 second-round pick as compensation.

That pick is commonly labeled as the selection later used on Yvon Joseph, but Houston did not retain it until the 1985 draft.

sections.heading: Willoughby Gave San Antonio 52 Reserve Games
sections.body:
Willoughby appeared in 52 regular-season games for San Antonio in 1982-83 and made no starts. He averaged 20.4 minutes, 6.1 points and 3.7 rebounds while shooting 46.1 percent from the field.

The Spurs were a 53-win Midwest Division champion and eventually reached the Western Conference Finals. Willoughby therefore supplied real rotation minutes on a contender even though he was not a starter.

His San Antonio stay ended on February 10, 1983, when the Spurs waived him. New Jersey later signed him on March 25, so this review credits only the 52 Spurs games produced directly from this compensation transaction.

sections.heading: Houston Rerouted the Pick Within Three Weeks
sections.body:
On November 10, 1982, Houston traded the 1985 second-round pick together with the 1983 second-round pick received from San Antonio in the Mike Dunleavy compensation transaction to New Jersey for James Bailey.

The Nets ultimately used the 1985 selection at No. 36 on Yvon Joseph. That draft outcome belongs to New Jersey, not Houston, so this review should not score Joseph's NBA career as the Rockets' realized result.

For Houston, the relevant value is that the pick helped complete the Bailey acquisition.

sections.heading: Bailey Produced Two Useful Rockets Seasons
sections.body:
Bailey played 69 regular-season games for Houston in 1982-83, started 39 and averaged 14.1 points and 6.8 rebounds. He returned for 73 games in 1983-84, all off the bench, averaging 8.8 points and 4.0 rebounds.

His two-year Houston total was 142 games and 39 starts. That is a strong downstream outcome from the two-pick package.

This review does not assign all of Bailey's value to the Willoughby pick. The Dunleavy compensation pick was equally necessary, so the proper conclusion is that this 1985 second-rounder carried meaningful partial transaction value rather than becoming Bailey by itself.

sections.heading: Why Houston Gets a Modest Edge
sections.body:
San Antonio received 52 reserve games and useful regular-season minutes from Willoughby before waiving him. That is a real return, especially on a 53-win team.

Houston received an asset that became half of the package for a player who produced 142 games and 39 starts over two seasons. Even with conservative attribution, the downstream value of the pick slightly exceeds Willoughby's shorter Spurs tenure.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win, B/C+. Houston receives a B because the compensation pick became an important part of the James Bailey acquisition without requiring this review to credit the entire Bailey return to one asset. San Antonio receives a C+ for 52 useful reserve games before Willoughby was waived in February.

sources.title: 1982-83 San Antonio Spurs roster and stats

sections.heading: Indiana Received One Season From Brad Branson
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's Cleveland transaction ledger records the October 25, 1982 exchange directly: the Cavaliers sent Brad Branson to Indiana for a 1983 second-round pick.

Branson played 62 regular-season games for the Pacers in 1982-83 and made two starts. He averaged 11.0 minutes, 5.5 points and 2.8 rebounds while shooting 42.5 percent from the field.

Those 62 games were the final NBA appearances of his career. Indiana therefore received one season of reserve frontcourt production and no longer-term branch from the player.

sections.heading: Cleveland Did Not Draft Scooter McCray
sections.body:
The incoming pick ultimately became No. 36 in the 1983 NBA Draft, where Seattle selected Scooter McCray.

That draft label can be misleading if treated as Cleveland's realized player outcome. On June 27, one day before the draft, Cleveland traded the pick to Seattle for Lonnie Shelton.

Basketball-Reference records the pick-for-Shelton transaction, while Pro Sports Transactions also lists cash going from Cleveland to Seattle. Because the Cavaliers added cash, this review cannot assign Shelton's entire later Cleveland career to the Branson pick by itself.

sections.heading: The Pick Helped Bring Lonnie Shelton to Cleveland
sections.body:
Shelton played 79 regular-season games for Cleveland in 1983-84 and started 78. He averaged 26.6 minutes, 10.8 points, 4.8 rebounds and 2.3 assists.

He returned for 57 games and 14 starts in 1984-85, then 44 games and one start in 1985-86.

Across those three Cavaliers seasons, Shelton appeared in 180 regular-season games and started 93. The first season alone gave Cleveland a near full-time starter from a package built around the acquired second-round pick plus cash.

sections.heading: Scooter McCray's Career Belongs to Seattle
sections.body:
Seattle used No. 36 on McCray, who played 53 regular-season games for the SuperSonics across two seasons before later appearing for Cleveland as a free agent in 1986-87.

Those later Cleveland games are not credited to this 1982 trade. McCray reached Cleveland years later through an independent free-agent signing, after the original pick had already been spent in the Shelton transaction.

sections.heading: Why Cleveland Gets the Edge
sections.body:
Indiana obtained 62 reserve games and two starts from Branson. Cleveland converted the second-round pick, together with additional cash, into a veteran who supplied 180 games and 93 starts over three seasons.

The cash component prevents the pick from receiving full credit for Shelton, but the transaction chain still shows that Cleveland preserved and then leveraged the asset for much more roster value than Branson produced in Indiana.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win, B/C+. Cleveland receives a B because the acquired second-round pick became a central part of the Lonnie Shelton package and helped produce three seasons of frontcourt value. Indiana receives a C+ for 62 useful reserve games from Branson, with no additional NBA return after his lone Pacers season.

sections.heading: The Canonical Player Name Needed a Correction
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's New Jersey transaction ledger identifies the incoming veteran as Mickey Johnson, not Wallace Johnson. The 1982-83 Nets roster confirms Johnson played 42 games for New Jersey after the trade.

This review corrects that asset identity while preserving the rest of the package: New Jersey received Mickey Johnson and the rights to 1982 second-round pick Fred Roberts, while Milwaukee received Phil Ford and New Jersey's 1983 second-round pick.

sections.heading: Mickey Johnson Gave New Jersey 42 Games
sections.body:
Johnson played 42 regular-season games for the Nets, started seven and averaged 23.8 minutes, 13.4 points, 5.3 rebounds and 3.4 assists.

His Nets stay lasted only until February 6, 1983, when New Jersey traded Johnson and Sleepy Floyd to Golden State for Micheal Ray Richardson. This review credits only the 42 direct Nets games from this transaction and does not assign the later Richardson return entirely to Johnson because Floyd was a major co-asset.

sections.heading: Fred Roberts Never Played for the Nets
sections.body:
Roberts had been Milwaukee's No. 27 pick in the 1982 draft but spent 1982-83 in Italy. New Jersey held his NBA rights rather than receiving immediate on-court value.

On June 7, 1983, the Nets sent Roberts and another 1983 second-round pick to San Antonio as compensation for signing Stan Albeck as head coach. Roberts therefore produced zero New Jersey regular-season games.

His later 818-game NBA career cannot be credited to the Nets because it began with San Antonio after New Jersey had moved his rights.

sections.heading: Phil Ford Became a Milwaukee Starter
sections.body:
Ford had appeared in only seven games for New Jersey before the trade. With Milwaukee he played 70 regular-season games in 1982-83 and started 56.

He averaged 20.7 minutes, 6.8 points and 3.6 assists while the Bucks went 51-31 and reached the Eastern Conference semifinals. That gave Milwaukee a full season of real rotation and starting value.

sections.heading: The No. 41 Pick Became Ted Kitchel
sections.body:
Milwaukee used the 1983 second-round pick on Indiana forward Ted Kitchel at No. 41. Kitchel never appeared in an NBA regular-season game.

That means the pick branch itself produced zero direct Bucks games, but Ford's 70-game season still outweighs New Jersey's shorter Johnson return.

sections.heading: Why Milwaukee Wins
sections.body:
New Jersey received 42 games and seven starts from Johnson, plus Roberts' rights, which never turned into a Nets appearance. Milwaukee received 70 games and 56 starts from Ford, while Kitchel produced no NBA games.

The gap is meaningful but not enormous because Johnson was productive during his short New Jersey stay and Roberts retained some transaction utility as a rights asset.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win, B+/B-. Milwaukee receives a B+ for 70 games and 56 starts from Ford at a modest cost, even though Kitchel did not reach the NBA. New Jersey receives a B- because Johnson gave the Nets 42 useful games and Roberts' rights retained value, but neither incoming asset lasted long enough to match Ford's direct Milwaukee contribution.

sources.title: 1982-83 New Jersey Nets Roster and Stats

sections.heading: Both Teams Received Two Useful Seasons
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's Atlanta transaction ledger records the December 31, 1982 deal as Johnny Davis to the Hawks for Atlanta's 1983 second-round pick, later No. 40 Jim Thomas. The legacy canonical source package also includes cash going to Indiana.

The reviewed public transaction ledger does not identify the cash amount, so this review preserves it as part of Indiana's return without assigning a speculative dollar value.

sections.heading: Davis Became Atlanta's Starting Guard
sections.body:
Davis played 53 regular-season games for Atlanta after the trade in 1982-83 and started 33. He averaged 27.6 minutes, 12.9 points and 5.9 assists.

The Hawks went 43-39 and reached the playoffs. Davis also appeared in all three first-round games against Boston and averaged 17.0 points and 9.0 assists in the series.

He returned for 75 games in 1983-84, starting 72 while averaging 12.3 points and 4.3 assists. Across the two Atlanta seasons, Davis played 128 regular-season games and started 105.

sections.heading: Indiana Turned the Pick Into Jim Thomas
sections.body:
The Pacers used the No. 40 selection in the 1983 NBA Draft on Indiana University guard Jim Thomas.

Thomas played 72 games as a rookie in 1983-84, started 15 and averaged 6.3 points in 16.9 minutes. His role grew substantially in his second season.

In 1984-85 he appeared in 80 games, started 52 and averaged 25.7 minutes, 11.1 points, 3.3 rebounds and 2.9 assists.

That gives Indiana 152 regular-season games and 67 starts from the pick across two seasons.

sections.heading: The Cash Component Adds Real but Unquantified Value
sections.body:
Indiana also received cash. Because the amount is not identified in the reviewed public sources, this review does not let that unknown figure dominate the verdict.

It still matters as a realized asset, particularly because the player returns themselves are close enough to compare rather than one side receiving nothing.

sections.heading: Why This Lands Near Even
sections.body:
Atlanta received the better immediate starter. Davis logged 105 starts, handled a meaningful playmaking role and contributed to a playoff team.

Indiana received more total games from Thomas, watched him grow into a 52-game starter in his second season and also collected cash.

Neither return became a long-term franchise cornerstone, but both generated multiple seasons of usable value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, B/B. Atlanta receives a B for 128 games, 105 starts and two seasons of starting-caliber guard play from Davis. Indiana receives a B for 152 games, 67 starts from Thomas plus an additional cash return whose amount cannot be verified. The strengths differ, but the completed value is too close to force a winner.

sections.heading: Boston Turned the Package Into Five Seasons of Scott Wedman
sections.body:
The January 14, 1983 transaction sent Scott Wedman to Boston for Darren Tillis, Boston's 1983 first-round pick and cash. The first-round choice later became No. 21 Greg Kite.

Wedman immediately shifted from a starting role in Cleveland to a reserve role behind Boston's established frontcourt. That reduced his box-score volume, but it also placed him on a contender where depth had real value.

sections.heading: Wedman Played 271 Regular-Season Games for Boston
sections.body:
Wedman appeared in 40 regular-season games for the Celtics after the trade in 1982-83. He then played 68 games in 1983-84, 78 in 1984-85, 79 in 1985-86 and six in 1986-87.

Across the five-season Boston tenure, he played 271 regular-season games and started 31. His largest late-career role came in 1985-86, when he appeared in 79 games, started 19 and averaged 8.0 points.

Wedman was part of Boston's 1984 and 1986 championship teams. This review does not inflate his individual value because of team success, but contributing rotation minutes to two title teams gives the Celtics a meaningful realized return.

sections.heading: Tillis Gave Cleveland 37 Games
sections.body:
Darren Tillis had played only 15 games for Boston before the trade. He appeared in 37 games for Cleveland during the rest of 1982-83, made four starts and averaged 13.0 minutes, 4.1 points and 3.3 rebounds.

Tillis moved to Golden State the following season. His 72 Warriors games are not credited to Cleveland because they came after his Cavaliers tenure ended.

sections.heading: The First-Round Pick Was Rerouted Before the Draft
sections.body:
Cleveland did not simply exercise the No. 21 pick. On February 7, 1983, the Cavaliers packaged that first-rounder with James Edwards and sent both to Phoenix.

The Cavaliers received Jeff Cook, Phoenix's 1983 first-round pick that became No. 20 Roy Hinson, a 1983 third-round pick that became Derrick Hord and cash. Phoenix later sent the No. 21 pick to Boston in the Dennis Johnson trade, and the Celtics ultimately drafted Greg Kite.

That chain gives Cleveland legitimate downstream asset credit. However, James Edwards was a major co-outgoing piece, so this review does not assign the entire Cook-Hinson-Hord-cash return to the Wedman trade.

sections.heading: Why Boston Wins
sections.body:
Boston received 271 regular-season games and a multi-year championship rotation player. Cleveland received 37 games from Tillis plus cash and a first-round asset that helped facilitate a later multi-asset trade.

The Cavaliers did not get nothing, and the pick's later use keeps their grade above a failure. The direct, attributable basketball value still favors Boston by a wide margin.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win, A-/C+. Boston receives an A- for five seasons and 271 games from Wedman, including meaningful depth on two championship teams. Cleveland receives a C+ because Tillis was brief, but the cash and first-round pick retained enough transaction value to avoid a poor overall outcome.

sections.heading: The No. 90 Pick Changed Hands Twice
sections.body:
The January 18, 1983 transaction began when San Antonio signed Coby Dietrick and sent Chicago a 1983 fourth-round pick as compensation for the Bulls' restricted-veteran-free-agent rights.

That pick later landed at No. 90. The important source-backed correction is that Chicago did not simply draft Brant Weidner with it.

sections.heading: Dietrick Played Only Eight Games for San Antonio
sections.body:
Dietrick returned to the Spurs after three seasons in Chicago, but the reunion was extremely short. He appeared in eight regular-season games for San Antonio in 1982-83, made no starts and played only 34 total minutes.

He averaged 4.3 minutes, 0.3 points and 1.0 rebound. San Antonio waived him on February 8, less than a month after the January 18 compensation transaction.

Those eight games were the final appearances of Dietrick's NBA career.

sections.heading: Chicago Reused the Pick for Mike Bratz
sections.body:
On March 8, Chicago sent the same 1983 fourth-round pick back to San Antonio in exchange for guard Mike Bratz.

Pro Sports Transactions explicitly traces the No. 90 asset through both moves: San Antonio first sent the pick to Chicago for the Dietrick rights, then reacquired it from Chicago for Bratz.

Bratz played 15 regular-season games for the Bulls during the rest of 1982-83. He made no starts, averaged 9.3 minutes and 2.6 points, and left for Golden State the following season.

sections.heading: The Spurs Later Drafted Brant Weidner
sections.body:
After reacquiring the pick, San Antonio used No. 90 on William & Mary forward Brant Weidner. Weidner eventually played eight NBA games for the Spurs in 1983-84.

This review does not credit those eight Weidner games to the January 18 Dietrick transaction. San Antonio had to give Chicago Bratz in a separate March 8 trade to get the pick back. Counting Weidner on the original Spurs side would double-count a later asset purchase.

sections.heading: Why Chicago Gets the Slight Edge
sections.body:
The original January 18 deal gave San Antonio eight games from Dietrick. Chicago turned the compensation pick into 15 games from Bratz through the March transaction.

Neither return was substantial, and neither player started a game for the acquiring team. Still, Chicago extracted slightly more direct basketball value from the asset it received.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win, C+/C. Chicago receives a C+ because the fourth-round pick was converted into 15 games of Bratz rather than being allowed to expire unused. San Antonio receives a C because Dietrick played only eight games before being waived. The margin is small, and the later Weidner draft outcome belongs to the separate Bratz transaction rather than this one.

sections.heading: Washington Got Two Starting Seasons From Ricky Sobers
sections.body:
The January 24, 1983 veteran-free-agent transaction is clear across the league and team ledgers. Washington signed Ricky Sobers after Chicago declined its right of first refusal, and the Bullets sent the Bulls second-round picks in 1983 and 1985 as compensation.

Those picks ultimately landed at No. 25 in 1983 and No. 35 in 1985. Their downstream paths are important because Chicago did not simply keep the players eventually selected with both choices.

sections.heading: Sobers Started 120 Games for Washington
sections.body:
Sobers joined Washington midway through 1982-83 and immediately stepped into the starting lineup. He played 41 games that season, started 39 and averaged 15.7 points, 5.3 assists and 1.5 steals in 35.1 minutes.

He returned in 1983-84 and started all 81 games he played. Sobers again averaged 15.6 points, along with 4.7 assists and 1.4 steals.

That gives Washington 122 regular-season games and 120 starts across two seasons, with 1,911 points and 595 assists. He left for Seattle in 1984-85, so later production is not credited to the Bullets.

sections.heading: Chicago Used the First Pick on Sidney Lowe, Then Traded Him
sections.body:
The 1983 compensation pick became No. 25 Sidney Lowe. Chicago drafted Lowe but traded him on draft day with a 1984 second-round pick to Indiana for Mitchell Wiggins.

Wiggins played all 82 games for the Bulls in 1983-84, started 40 and averaged 12.4 points, 4.0 rebounds and 2.3 assists. Those 82 Chicago games are a real downstream return from the Lowe branch.

This review does not assign all of Wiggins to the Sobers compensation pick, however, because Chicago also included a separate 1984 second-round pick in the deal.

sections.heading: The Second Pick Helped Bring Caldwell Jones
sections.body:
Chicago retained the 1985 second-round compensation asset until August 10, 1984. The Bulls then sent Wiggins, that pick and a 1985 third-round pick to Houston for Caldwell Jones.

The No. 35 pick continued through Houston and San Antonio before the Spurs eventually selected Tyrone Corbin. Corbin never played for Chicago, so his later NBA career is not a Bulls return from this transaction.

The pick clearly retained trade utility, but this review again avoids assigning the entire Caldwell Jones return to one asset because Wiggins and another pick were also required.

sections.heading: Why Washington Wins
sections.body:
Chicago did good asset work with both second-rounders. The 1983 pick helped produce a full 82-game season from Wiggins, while the 1985 pick later contributed to another trade package.

Washington still received the stronger cleanly attributable basketball result: 122 games, 120 starts and two seasons of 15-plus-point scoring from Sobers. Chicago's downstream value was meaningful but shared with other outgoing assets at each conversion point.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bullets Win, A-/B. Washington receives an A- for two starting seasons and 122 games from Sobers. Chicago receives a B because both compensation picks retained useful transaction value and the Lowe branch helped bring Wiggins, but the Bulls cannot be credited with every later multi-asset return or with Corbin's Spurs career.

sections.heading: Golden State Turned One Star Guard Into Two Long-Term Rotation Pieces
sections.body:
The February 6, 1983 transaction sent Micheal Ray Richardson from Golden State to New Jersey for Sleepy Floyd and Mickey Johnson. Basketball-Reference records the package under the players' familiar basketball names: Sleepy Floyd, whose given name is Eric Floyd, and Mickey Johnson, whose full name is Wallace Edgar Johnson.

A second legacy Nets-origin record describes the same transaction using the legal-name forms Eric Floyd and Wallace Johnson. This review keeps the Golden State record as the active canonical version because its player identities align with the established NBA records, while this review will retain the opposite-source record only as superseded provenance.

sections.heading: Sleepy Floyd Became the Main Prize
sections.body:
Floyd played 33 games for Golden State after the trade in 1982-83 and then became a full-time starter. He appeared in 77 games in 1983-84, 82 in 1984-85, 82 in 1985-86 and 82 again in 1986-87 before adding 18 more games in 1987-88 prior to the Houston trade.

Across that Warriors tenure, Floyd played 374 regular-season games and started 348. He averaged 16.8 points in 1983-84, 19.5 in 1984-85, 17.2 in 1985-86 and 18.8 in his 1987 All-Star season.

His 1986-87 season also helped Golden State reach the Western Conference semifinals. This review does not treat team playoff advancement as solely Floyd's work, but a multi-year starting point guard who became an All-Star clearly represents premium realized value.

sections.heading: Mickey Johnson Added Three Useful Seasons
sections.body:
Johnson joined the Warriors at age 30 but still provided substantial frontcourt production. He played 30 games after the trade in 1982-83, then 78 in 1983-84 and 66 in 1984-85.

That gives Golden State 174 regular-season games and 43 starts from Johnson. He averaged 15.5 points and 8.2 rebounds in his first Warriors stint after the trade, then remained a double-figure scorer in both following seasons.

Johnson later returned to New Jersey, but those later Nets games are not part of Golden State's return.

sections.heading: Richardson Was Productive for New Jersey
sections.body:
New Jersey did not receive an empty return. Richardson played 31 games for the Nets after the trade in 1982-83, then 48 in 1983-84, all 82 in 1984-85 and 47 in 1985-86.

Across those four partial or full seasons, he played 208 regular-season games and started 172. His best Nets season came in 1984-85, when he averaged 20.1 points, 8.2 assists, 5.6 rebounds and 3.0 steals and made the All-Star team.

Richardson's NBA career ended after the league suspended him for substance-abuse violations in 1986. The abrupt ending reduced New Jersey's long-term return, but it should not erase the high-level production he delivered before the suspension.

sections.heading: Why Golden State Wins
sections.body:
The Warriors received both the longer runway of direct games and the deeper two-player package. Floyd became an All-Star starter and Johnson added three seasons of useful frontcourt production.

Combined, Floyd and Johnson produced 548 Golden State regular-season games and 391 starts. Richardson gave New Jersey 208 games and 172 starts, including an All-Star season. That is meaningful value, but the Warriors still finished well ahead in duration, depth and total realized production.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win, A+/B. Golden State receives an A+ because Floyd became a long-term All-Star starter and Johnson added 174 useful games. New Jersey receives a B because Richardson produced multiple strong seasons and an All-Star campaign before his suspension, making the Nets' side much better than a failure even though the Warriors clearly won the deal.

sections.heading: The legacy Consideration Direction Needed Repair
sections.body:
The canonical import had Danny Schayes and an unresolved "other considerations" asset going to Denver while showing cash going to Utah. Basketball-Reference's February 7, 1983 Denver transaction ledger records a simpler package: Denver traded Rich Kelley to Utah for Schayes and cash.

This review therefore removes the phantom unresolved-player treatment, converts that consideration to cash moving from Utah to Denver and deletes the duplicate wrong-way cash asset. The public amount is not identified in the reviewed source, so no dollar value is invented.

sections.heading: Schayes Became a Long-Term Nugget
sections.body:
Schayes joined Denver for the final 32 regular-season games of 1982-83 and averaged 9.2 points and 5.8 rebounds in a reserve role. He then remained with the Nuggets through the 1989-90 season.

His role grew substantially. Schayes played all 82 games in 1983-84, then later started 41 games in 1986-87, 74 in 1987-88, 64 in 1988-89 and 22 in 1989-90.

Across his Denver tenure after the trade, he played 536 regular-season games and started 229. His peak Nuggets season came in 1987-88, when he averaged 13.9 points and 8.2 rebounds while starting 74 games.

That is unusually strong realized value from a one-for-one veteran exchange, even before accounting for the cash that also moved to Denver.

sections.heading: Kelley Gave Utah Three Useful Seasons
sections.body:
Rich Kelley was not a throwaway return. He played 32 games for the Jazz after the trade in 1982-83 and started 23, averaging 7.2 points and 7.3 rebounds.

He returned for 75 games and 30 starts in 1983-84, then 77 games and 34 starts in 1984-85. Across those three Utah stints, Kelley played 184 regular-season games and started 87.

Utah later received cash compensation when Sacramento signed Kelley as a veteran free agent in September 1985. This review does not credit that later compensation as part of the original Denver trade because it came from a separate free-agent transaction more than two years later.

sections.heading: Why Denver Wins
sections.body:
Utah received a legitimate starting center for parts of three seasons. Kelley supplied 184 games and 87 starts, so this was not a failed return.

Denver nevertheless received nearly three times as many direct regular-season games from Schayes, more than twice as many starts and seven-plus seasons of frontcourt continuity. The Nuggets also received cash in the original transaction.

The gap is large enough for a clear Denver win without downgrading Utah to a poor grade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win, A+/B. Denver receives an A+ for 536 games, 229 starts and multiple years of starting-caliber production from Schayes, plus cash. Utah receives a B because Kelley gave the Jazz 184 games and 87 starts before moving on. Both sides got useful centers, but Denver captured the much larger long-term return.

sections.heading: San Antonio Got the Only NBA Production
sections.body:
The February 10, 1983 transaction sent Edgar Jones from Detroit to San Antonio for two future draft choices: a 1984 second-round pick and a 1985 third-round pick.

Both selections eventually stayed with Detroit long enough to be exercised, which makes the completed return straightforward to evaluate.

sections.heading: Jones Helped San Antonio Immediately
sections.body:
Jones played 28 regular-season games for the Spurs after the trade in 1982-83 and started three. He averaged 9.6 points, 6.3 rebounds and 1.1 blocks in 22.2 minutes.

San Antonio went 53-29 that season and reached the Western Conference Finals. Jones was a rotation frontcourt piece after arriving rather than a deep-bench acquisition.

He then played 81 games in 1983-84, started 33 and averaged 10.2 points and 5.5 rebounds. Jones added 18 more Spurs games in 1984-85 before moving to Cleveland.

Across his San Antonio tenure, Jones appeared in 127 regular-season games and made 37 starts.

sections.heading: Detroit's 1984 Pick Became Eric Turner
sections.body:
The 1984 second-round selection landed at No. 32. Detroit used it on Michigan guard Eric Turner.

Turner has a Basketball-Reference draft/player record but no NBA regular-season statistical line. The pick therefore produced zero Pistons regular-season games.

That outcome is especially important because the legacy Detroit-side review had treated the pick itself as the lead realized return. This review evaluates what the selection actually became.

sections.heading: The 1985 Pick Became Andre Goode
sections.body:
Detroit's third-round choice in 1985 landed at No. 60 and became Northwestern forward Andre Goode.

Like Turner, Goode has a draft/player record but no NBA regular-season statistical line. The second draft branch also produced zero direct Pistons games.

Detroit therefore converted two future selections into two players who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game.

sections.heading: Why San Antonio Wins Clearly
sections.body:
The Spurs received a player who contributed immediately, returned for a full 81-game season and gave the club 127 total regular-season appearances with 37 starts.

Detroit's two picks carried transaction-day optionality, but hindsight grading cannot stop at the abstract value of the selections. Once both were exercised, the completed outcomes were zero NBA games from Turner and zero from Goode.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Spurs Win, B+/F. San Antonio receives a B+ for 127 games and 37 starts from Jones, including a productive full season in 1983-84. Detroit receives an F because both acquired draft picks were exercised on players who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game.

sources.title: 1983-84 San Antonio Spurs roster and stats

sections.heading: New York Acquired the Higher-Impact Player
sections.body:
The February 12, 1983 trade sent Rory Sparrow from Atlanta to New York for rookie forward Scott Hastings and cash. The legacy source perspectives disagreed on whether the result was a Knicks win or broadly even, so this review resolves the question through direct realized franchise value.

The cash amount sent to Atlanta is not identified in the reviewed public sources. It remains part of the Hawks' return, but no speculative dollar value is assigned.

sections.heading: Sparrow Became a Long-Term Knicks Guard
sections.body:
Sparrow played 32 regular-season games for New York after the trade in 1982-83 and started nine. He averaged 10.0 points and 5.0 assists in 28.2 minutes while immediately entering the backcourt rotation.

His role expanded sharply in 1983-84. Sparrow appeared in 79 games, started 74 and averaged 10.4 points and 6.8 assists.

He followed with 79 games and 41 starts in 1984-85, 74 games and 74 starts in 1985-86, and 80 games with 30 starts in 1986-87. He then played three more Knicks games in 1987-88 before being traded to Chicago.

Across his New York tenure, Sparrow appeared in 347 regular-season games and started 228. He was never an All-Star, but several seasons of starting or heavy-rotation point-guard work make him a substantial return.

sections.heading: Hastings Gave Atlanta Long-Term Bench Depth
sections.body:
Scott Hastings had played only 19 games for New York before the trade. In Atlanta he appeared in 10 games for the remainder of 1982-83, then 68 in 1983-84, 64 in 1984-85, 62 in 1985-86, 40 in 1986-87 and 55 in 1987-88.

That gives Hastings 299 regular-season games for the Hawks across parts of six seasons. His durability is meaningful, especially because the transaction also brought Atlanta cash.

The limitation is role. Hastings made only nine starts during that Atlanta tenure and generally played reserve minutes. His best Hawks scoring season was still a modest bench contribution compared with Sparrow's multi-year starting workload in New York.

sections.heading: Why New York Wins
sections.body:
The raw games-played gap is not large: 347 for Sparrow versus 299 for Hastings. Role and usage create the larger difference.

Sparrow started 228 games for the Knicks and repeatedly averaged five or more assists while handling major point-guard minutes. Hastings started only nine times for Atlanta and served mainly as frontcourt depth.

The cash component keeps Atlanta's return from being graded harshly, but the amount is unknown and does not erase the clear on-court role advantage New York received.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win, A-/B. New York receives an A- for more than four seasons of meaningful point-guard play, 347 games and 228 starts from Sparrow. Atlanta receives a B because Hastings supplied 299 games of durable bench depth and the Hawks also received cash. This was a useful deal for both teams, but the Knicks acquired the more consequential basketball asset.

sources.title: 1983-84 New York Knicks roster and stats

sections.heading: The Three-Team Routing Is Clear Even Though the Date Differs by One Day
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference records the completed transaction on February 13, 1983, while RealGM's league and team histories place it on February 12. The canonical TradeVerdicts record already uses February 12, so this review retains that date and records the one-day disagreement rather than forcing false precision.

The routing itself is consistent across the sources. Atlanta sent Steve Hawes to Seattle and received Detroit's 1984 and 1985 second-round picks. Detroit sent those two picks to Atlanta and received Ray Tolbert from Seattle. Seattle sent Tolbert to Detroit and received Hawes from Atlanta.

sections.heading: Seattle Got Two Useful Years From Steve Hawes
sections.body:
Hawes played 31 regular-season games for Seattle after the trade in 1982-83 and started one. He averaged 5.5 points and 4.3 rebounds in 17.9 minutes.

He returned for 79 games in 1983-84, all off the bench, averaging 3.7 points and 2.8 rebounds. That gives Seattle 110 regular-season games and one start from the deal.

Hawes was nearing the end of his NBA career, but the SuperSonics still received two seasons of dependable reserve frontcourt minutes.

sections.heading: Detroit Got 77 Reserve Games From Ray Tolbert
sections.body:
Tolbert appeared in 28 regular-season games for Detroit after the trade and averaged 5.1 points and 3.3 rebounds. He then played 49 more games in 1983-84.

Across those two Pistons seasons he appeared in 77 games and made no starts. His role stayed modest, and he left the NBA for several seasons after 1983-84.

Detroit therefore received a real rotation return, but not a long-term starter or premium contributor.

sections.heading: Atlanta's 1985 Pick Became Lorenzo Charles
sections.body:
The 1985 second-round choice landed at No. 41, where Atlanta selected North Carolina State forward Lorenzo Charles.

Charles played 36 regular-season games for the Hawks in 1985-86 and made no starts. He averaged 3.4 points in 7.6 minutes and did not play another NBA season.

That branch alone would not make Atlanta the winner.

sections.heading: The 1984 Pick Became a Valuable Trade Asset
sections.body:
Atlanta did not exercise the other incoming pick itself. On July 5, 1983, the Hawks packaged Tom McMillen and the 1984 second-rounder to Washington for Randy Wittman.

Washington eventually used the pick at No. 34 on Tony Costner, who never played an NBA regular-season game. Atlanta's value came earlier, when the pick helped complete the Wittman trade.

Wittman then became a major Hawks rotation piece and eventual starter. He played 353 Atlanta regular-season games from 1983-84 through 1987-88 alone, including 226 starts over the final four of those seasons.

This review does not credit all of Wittman's Atlanta career to this one second-round pick because Tom McMillen was the other outgoing asset in that later transaction. The correct takeaway is narrower: the acquired pick retained enough value to help Atlanta secure a long-term starter.

sections.heading: Why Atlanta Has the Best Outcome
sections.body:
Seattle received 110 games of reserve Hawes production. Detroit received 77 reserve games from Tolbert. Both returns were useful and defensible.

Atlanta received only 36 direct games from Charles, but the other pick became part of the package that acquired Wittman, whose Atlanta tenure far exceeded the direct value produced by Hawes or Tolbert for their new teams. That downstream transaction utility is enough to preserve the Hawks as the hindsight winner without pretending the pick alone purchased Wittman.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win, A-/B/B-. Atlanta receives an A- because one pick produced an NBA player and the other materially helped acquire a multi-year starter. Seattle receives a B for 110 useful reserve games from Hawes. Detroit receives a B- for 77 reserve games from Tolbert after surrendering two second-round choices. Confidence is medium only because authoritative sources disagree by one day on the transaction date.

sections.heading: Both Teams Received Useful but Modest Value
sections.body:
The February 15, 1983 trade sent Rickey Brown from Golden State to Atlanta for a 1984 second-round pick and cash. The pick later landed at No. 35, where the Warriors selected Virginia guard Othell Wilson.

The legacy team perspectives leaned in opposite directions. Atlanta's source called the exchange a slight partner edge, while Golden State's source called it a slight Warriors edge. The completed player outcomes explain why neither side has a decisive advantage.

sections.heading: Brown Gave Atlanta Three Seasons of Frontcourt Depth
sections.body:
Brown played 26 regular-season games for Atlanta after the trade in 1982-83 and made no starts. He averaged 4.7 points and 3.4 rebounds in 11.7 minutes.

He returned for 68 games in 1983-84, starting three, then appeared in 69 games with five starts in 1984-85.

Across his Hawks tenure, Brown played 163 regular-season games and started eight. He was primarily a reserve center, but three seasons of usable depth is a meaningful return from one second-round pick plus cash.

sections.heading: Wilson Had a Larger Starting Role in His One Warriors Season
sections.body:
Golden State used the No. 35 pick on Othell Wilson in the 1984 NBA Draft.

Wilson appeared in 74 regular-season games for the Warriors in 1984-85 and started 23. He averaged 17.0 minutes, 4.4 points, 2.9 assists and 1.0 steal.

He did not play in the NBA in 1985-86 and later returned with Sacramento in 1986-87. This review credits Golden State only with the 74 games and 23 starts produced for the Warriors.

sections.heading: The Cash Amount Is Unknown
sections.body:
Golden State also received cash in the original transaction. The reviewed public sources do not identify the amount, so the cash is treated as a tangible but unquantified part of the Warriors' return.

That component prevents the games-played comparison from being the entire verdict, but it also cannot justify a large Golden State advantage without a documented figure.

sections.heading: Why the Deal Grades Even
sections.body:
Atlanta received more than twice as many direct regular-season games from Brown, but almost all came in a reserve role. Golden State received fewer games from Wilson but substantially more starts and an additional cash component.

Neither player became a long-term starter or major franchise piece. Brown's duration and Wilson's larger one-season role offset each other closely enough that forcing a winner would overstate a small difference.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, B/B. Atlanta receives a B for 163 games of multi-year frontcourt depth. Golden State receives a B for 74 games, 23 starts and cash. The teams extracted different kinds of value from a minor transaction, but neither completed return clearly dominates the other.

sources.title: 1984-85 Golden State Warriors roster and stats

sections.heading: The Primary Ledger Does Not Confirm the Cash Component
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's Chicago, Los Angeles and league transaction ledgers agree on the February 15, 1983 core terms: Chicago sent Dwight Jones to the Lakers for a 1985 second-round pick that later became No. 46 Adrian Branch.

The legacy canonical record also includes cash moving to Chicago. That extra financial component is not listed in the Basketball-Reference transaction ledgers reviewed for this review, and RealGM confirms Jones's acquisition without exposing a cash amount. This review therefore preserves the canonical cash asset as unresolved rather than deleting it, while lowering confidence to medium on the full package.

sections.heading: Jones Gave Los Angeles Immediate Frontcourt Depth
sections.body:
Dwight Jones played 32 regular-season games for the Lakers after the trade and made no starts. He averaged 15.3 minutes, 4.9 points and 3.6 rebounds while shooting 47.0 percent from the field.

The Lakers finished 58-24, won the Pacific Division and reached the NBA Finals. Jones also appeared in seven playoff games, totaling 59 postseason minutes.

Los Angeles waived him in August 1983, so the value was short-term. Even so, the Lakers received a real rotation contribution during a conference-championship season.

sections.heading: The Pick Became Adrian Branch
sections.body:
Chicago held the incoming second-rounder until the 1985 draft and used No. 46 on Maryland forward Adrian Branch.

Branch never appeared in a Bulls regular-season game. Chicago waived him on October 7, 1985 before the season, and his NBA debut came later with another franchise.

That means the draft branch produced zero direct Chicago games despite eventually identifying an NBA player.

sections.heading: The Realized Basketball Value Favors Los Angeles
sections.body:
Chicago's pick outcome did not become on-court Bulls value. The unresolved cash component gives the Bulls some possible financial return, but the reviewed primary ledgers do not establish the amount.

Los Angeles received 32 regular-season appearances plus seven playoff games from Jones. The return was limited, but it is still more direct basketball value than Chicago realized from Branch.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win, B-/D+. Los Angeles receives a B- because Jones supplied useful reserve minutes during a Finals season before being waived that summer. Chicago receives a D+ because the No. 46 pick produced zero Bulls games; the grade stays above a failing mark because the canonical record also contains an unresolved cash component. Confidence is medium because the public primary ledgers do not confirm that cash term.

Los Angeles Lakers 1982-83 transaction history - RealGM

sections.heading: Kansas City Sold Johnson's Rights for Cash
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's Kansas City, Philadelphia and league transaction ledgers describe the February 15, 1983 move as a sale of Reggie Johnson's player rights to the 76ers.

The canonical record correctly records cash going to Kansas City. None of the reviewed public ledgers identifies the dollar amount, so this review does not assign a speculative financial value to the Kings' return.

sections.heading: Johnson Joined a Championship Team
sections.body:
Johnson had played 50 games for Kansas City earlier in 1982-83. After the rights sale, he appeared in 29 regular-season games for Philadelphia and started eight.

He averaged 18.9 minutes, 5.5 points and 3.1 rebounds while providing another frontcourt option behind the 76ers' established stars.

Philadelphia finished 65-17 and swept through the 1983 NBA Finals. Johnson also appeared in six playoff games during that championship run.

sections.heading: The 76ers Preserved Downstream Value
sections.body:
Johnson did not stay in Philadelphia beyond that season. On October 25, 1983, the 76ers traded him to New Jersey for Horace Owens, Eddie Phillips and a 1987 second-round pick that later became Andrew Kennedy.

This review does not assign the entire later value of those assets to the original cash purchase without qualification, but the transaction matters because it shows Philadelphia retained trade utility after receiving 29 regular-season games and championship-season depth from Johnson.

sections.heading: Kansas City's Return Cannot Be Fully Quantified
sections.body:
The Kings received cash rather than a player or draft pick. Selling a player who was leaving the roster created real economic value and should not be treated as zero.

The problem is evidentiary: the reviewed sources do not state the amount. Without a documented large payment, there is no basis to claim the cash outweighed the basketball value Philadelphia received.

sections.heading: Why Philadelphia Gets the Edge
sections.body:
The 76ers obtained 29 regular-season games, eight starts and six playoff appearances from Johnson during a championship season. They then converted him into another multi-asset package before the following season.

Kansas City received an unquantified cash return. That is tangible value, but the known realized outcome is stronger on Philadelphia's side.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win, B/C. Philadelphia receives a B because Johnson supplied useful championship-season depth and still carried trade value afterward. Kansas City receives a C because selling the rights produced cash, but the amount is unknown and no additional basketball asset entered the franchise through the documented transaction. Confidence is medium because the cash figure is unresolved.

sections.heading: New York Received a One-Season Veteran
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's New York, New Jersey and league transaction records agree on the June 22, 1983 exchange. The Knicks sent their 1984 second-round pick to the Nets and received Len Elmore.

The pick eventually landed at No. 41, but New Jersey did not keep it through the draft.

sections.heading: Elmore Played 65 Games for the Knicks
sections.body:
Elmore appeared in 65 regular-season games for New York in 1983-84 and started five. He averaged 12.8 minutes, 2.4 points and 2.5 rebounds while providing veteran frontcourt depth.

The Knicks finished 47-35, won a first-round playoff series against Detroit and pushed Boston to seven games in the Eastern Conference semifinals.

Elmore's New York tenure lasted only that season. The contribution was limited in scale but direct and easy to measure.

sections.heading: New Jersey Rerouted the Pick Before the Draft
sections.body:
On August 12, 1983, the Nets traded Foots Walker, the acquired 1984 second-round pick and their 1985 first-round pick to Dallas for Kelvin Ransey.

The No. 41 selection ultimately stayed with Dallas, which used it on Tom Sluby. Sluby never played for New Jersey.

That means the Nets' value from the Elmore trade came through the pick's role inside the Ransey package rather than from the player selected at No. 41.

sections.heading: Ransey Was Valuable, but the Pick Was Only One Piece
sections.body:
Ransey played 80 games for New Jersey in 1983-84, 81 in 1984-85 and 79 in 1985-86. He started 94 games across those three seasons and averaged 9.5 points and 6.0 assists in his first Nets year.

This review does not assign all of that production to the Elmore trade. New Jersey also surrendered Foots Walker and a 1985 first-round pick that became Bill Wennington, so those assets were essential to acquiring Ransey.

The proper credit is narrower: the Knicks second-rounder retained enough value to serve as one component of a larger trade for a useful starting guard.

sections.heading: Why New York Gets the Edge
sections.body:
New York received a complete, if modest, season from Elmore. New Jersey received an asset with real trade utility but no direct games, and its downstream value cannot be isolated from the two other pieces in the Ransey package.

That makes the Knicks' return more concrete without making the Nets' side a failure.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win, B-/C+. New York receives a B- for 65 regular-season games and usable playoff-season depth from Elmore. New Jersey receives a C+ because the pick became a meaningful component of the Kelvin Ransey trade, but the Nets never used it directly and cannot be credited with Ransey's entire three-year tenure from this one asset alone. Confidence is high on the transaction chain and moderate in the value split, so the overall confidence remains medium.
