New Jersey Nets historical trade ledger

sections.heading: Boston Acquired a Championship-Era Core Piece
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's Phoenix transaction ledger records the June 27, 1983 package: Dennis Johnson, the No. 21 pick that became Greg Kite and the No. 52 pick that became Winfred King went to Boston. Phoenix received Rick Robey plus the No. 28 and No. 45 picks, later Rod Foster and Paul Williams.

The trade is remembered for Johnson, and the direct franchise results justify that emphasis.

sections.heading: Johnson Played Seven Seasons and 541 Games for Boston
sections.body:
Dennis Johnson played 541 regular-season games for the Celtics from 1983-84 through 1989-90 and started 522. He averaged 13.4 points and 6.8 assists across those seven seasons while giving Boston a durable two-way guard next to Larry Bird, Kevin McHale and Robert Parish.

His first Celtics season ended with the 1984 NBA championship. Johnson remained a starter when Boston won again in 1986 and was part of four All-Defensive selections as a Celtic: three Second Team honors followed by a First Team selection in 1986-87.

The value was not a short peak. Johnson stayed in Boston through 1990 and started at least 65 games in every Celtics season.

sections.heading: Greg Kite Added Five Years of Reserve-Center Depth
sections.body:
Boston also used the No. 21 pick on Greg Kite. He played 241 regular-season games for the Celtics across five seasons, made eight starts and supplied backup-center minutes on both the 1984 and 1986 championship teams.

Kite was not a major offensive contributor, but 241 games from the first-round pick add real depth value on top of the Johnson return.

The third-round pick became Winfred King, who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. That branch produced no direct value.

sections.heading: Phoenix Got Useful Players, but No Comparable Centerpiece
sections.body:
Rick Robey played 111 regular-season games for Phoenix across three seasons and made five starts. His first Suns season produced 61 games and 4 starts before injuries and a smaller role reduced his availability.

Rod Foster was the stronger Phoenix draft outcome. The No. 28 pick played 207 regular-season games for the Suns across three seasons, started 35 and averaged 7.5 points and 2.3 assists.

Paul Williams, selected at No. 45, never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Phoenix therefore received 318 direct regular-season games and 40 starts from Robey and Foster combined.

sections.heading: The Scale of Impact Decides It
sections.body:
Phoenix did not come away empty. Foster became a legitimate rotation guard, and Robey supplied three seasons of center depth.

Boston still gained far more. Johnson alone gave the Celtics 541 games, 522 starts, elite perimeter defense and a starting role on two championship teams. Kite added another 241 games and two championship rosters.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win, A+/C. Boston receives an A+ because Johnson became a seven-year championship-era starter and Kite added five seasons of reserve depth. Phoenix receives a C because Robey and Foster combined for 318 games and 40 starts, but the return never approached the long-term or championship value Boston received.

sections.heading: Cleveland Bought Three Seasons of Lonnie Shelton
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's Seattle and league transaction ledgers record the June 27, 1983 exchange as Lonnie Shelton to Cleveland for a 1983 second-round pick. Seattle used the pick at No. 36 on Scooter McCray.

Contemporary reporting adds the financial component. The Christian Science Monitor described Seattle as receiving cash and the second-round choice, UPI later called the cash amount large, and Pro Sports Transactions lists it as believed to be about $500,000.

sections.heading: Shelton Immediately Became a Cleveland Starter
sections.body:
Shelton played 79 regular-season games for Cleveland in 1983-84 and started 78. He averaged 26.6 minutes, 10.8 points and 4.8 rebounds while finishing 12th in Defensive Player of the Year voting.

He returned for 57 games in 1984-85, starting 14, then played 44 more games in 1985-86.

Across three Cavaliers seasons, Shelton appeared in 180 regular-season games and made 93 starts. His role declined after the first year, but Cleveland still received multiple seasons of real frontcourt production.

sections.heading: Seattle's Pick Became Scooter McCray
sections.body:
The SuperSonics selected Louisville forward Scooter McCray with the No. 36 pick in the 1983 draft.

McCray played 47 games for Seattle as a rookie, started six and averaged 11.1 minutes. He appeared in only six more Seattle games in 1984-85 before his role disappeared.

That gives Seattle 53 direct regular-season games and six starts from the draft branch.

sections.heading: The Cash Component Matters
sections.body:
Seattle did not trade Shelton for the pick alone. The cash payment was described contemporaneously as substantial, and the commonly cited estimate is roughly $500,000.

This review treats that as real return rather than ignoring it. At the same time, the exact amount is not established by the primary statistical ledgers, so the financial component should not be converted into speculative basketball value.

sections.heading: Why Cleveland Wins
sections.body:
Cleveland received 180 games and 93 starts from Shelton, including a near-full first season as a starter. Seattle received 53 low-minute games and six starts from McCray plus cash.

The financial return narrows the gap, but it does not erase the difference in realized on-court production.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win, B+/B-. Cleveland receives a B+ for three seasons and 93 starts from Shelton at the cost of a second-round pick and cash. Seattle receives a B- because McCray provided limited NBA production, but the substantial cash component prevents the return from being treated as a poor outcome. Confidence is medium because the cash amount is reported as an estimate rather than an exact disclosed figure.

sources.title: Cavaliers transaction search - Pro Sports Transactions
Christian Science Monitor - 1983 NBA draft and trades
UPI - Seattle trade report on Lonnie Shelton

sections.heading: The legacy Perspectives Disagree
sections.body:
Chicago's legacy review called this a clear Bulls win, while the Kansas City perspective gave the Kings a slight edge. The completed player records support the Kings side more strongly once direct franchise value is counted carefully.

Basketball-Reference's Kansas City transaction ledger confirms the June 28, 1983 package: the Kings sent the rights to Ennis Whatley and Chris McNealy plus a 1984 second-round pick to Chicago for Mark Olberding and the rights to Larry Micheaux.

sections.heading: Whatley Was a Real Starting Point Guard for Chicago
sections.body:
Whatley played 80 games for the Bulls as a rookie in 1983-84 and started 73. He averaged 8.4 points and 8.3 assists in 27.0 minutes, giving Chicago a substantial immediate return from the No. 13 draft rights.

He returned for 70 games and 44 starts in 1984-85, averaging 5.0 points and 5.4 assists. Across two Bulls seasons, Whatley totaled 150 regular-season games and 117 starts.

Chicago later packaged Whatley with 1985 first-round pick Keith Lee in the trade that brought Charles Oakley and Calvin Duncan from Cleveland. This review records that downstream utility but does not credit the entire Oakley return to Whatley because Keith Lee was a major part of the package.

sections.heading: The Other Chicago Assets Produced Little Direct Value
sections.body:
Chris McNealy played professionally in Italy before later reaching the NBA with New York. He never appeared in a regular-season game for Chicago.

The 1984 second-round pick became No. 37 Ben Coleman. Coleman also did not play for the Bulls; he spent two seasons in Italy before entering the NBA with New Jersey.

Chicago later packaged Coleman's rights with Ken Johnson for Mike Smrek. Smrek played 38 Bulls games with five starts. Because Coleman was only one piece of that later transaction, this review treats the branch as retained trade utility rather than assigning all of Smrek's value to this deal.

sections.heading: Olberding Became a Three-Year Kings Starter
sections.body:
Mark Olberding immediately moved into the Kansas City starting lineup. He played 81 games and started all 81 in 1983-84, averaging 12.6 points, 7.4 rebounds and 3.2 assists.

He followed with 81 games and 62 starts in 1984-85, then stayed with the franchise through its move to Sacramento and played another 81 games with 64 starts in 1985-86.

That gives the Kings franchise 243 regular-season games and 207 starts from Olberding alone.

sections.heading: Micheaux Added Another 39 Games
sections.body:
Larry Micheaux played 39 regular-season games for Kansas City in 1983-84, all off the bench, averaging 8.5 minutes. He later played for other teams, so only those 39 games count toward this trade.

Together, Olberding and Micheaux produced 282 direct Kings regular-season games and 207 starts.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Win, A-/B+. Chicago received a useful young point guard and preserved some downstream asset value, so this was not a bad trade for the Bulls. Kansas City still received the stronger completed on-court package: three full seasons of Olberding as a starter plus Micheaux's reserve season. The direct-value gap outweighs Chicago's partial downstream trade branches.

sources.title: Chicago Bulls all-time transactions media guide

sections.heading: Every Named Player Produced Zero Direct Games
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's Cleveland, San Diego and league transaction ledgers agree on the June 28, 1983 package. Cleveland sent the rights to third-round picks Larry Anderson and Les Craft to the Clippers for a 1985 second-round pick.

The immediate player outcomes were empty on both sides, which makes the downstream use of Cleveland's pick the only meaningful separator.

sections.heading: Anderson Never Reached the NBA
sections.body:
Cleveland drafted Larry Anderson at No. 56 out of UNLV, then moved his rights to San Diego the same day.

Basketball-Reference lists Anderson as a drafted player with no NBA regular-season statistical line. The Clippers therefore received no direct games or starts from his rights.

sections.heading: Craft Also Produced No NBA Games
sections.body:
Les Craft was selected by Cleveland at No. 66. His rights had reached the Cavaliers through the Mike Bratz trade chain and were then packaged with Anderson for the future pick.

Craft likewise never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. San Diego's two incoming rights therefore combined for zero direct NBA games.

sections.heading: Cleveland's Pick Became Calvin Duncan
sections.body:
The 1985 second-round selection landed at No. 30, where Cleveland drafted VCU guard Calvin Duncan.

Duncan never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. If the pick branch ended there, this trade would be an easy even result: zero direct games on both sides.

sections.heading: The Pick Still Had Downstream Transaction Utility
sections.body:
Cleveland did not simply lose Duncan's rights for nothing. On the same 1985 draft day, the Cavaliers packaged Duncan with No. 9 pick Charles Oakley and sent both to Chicago for Keith Lee and Ennis Whatley.

That gives the original San Diego pick some downstream utility. This review deliberately does not credit the entire Lee-Whatley package to Duncan because Oakley was a top-10 pick and the far more substantial asset in the deal.

The distinction matters: the pick retained trade value, but it did not independently create a major return.

sections.heading: Why Cleveland Gets Only a Slight Edge
sections.body:
San Diego received two rights packages that produced no NBA player. Cleveland received a second-round pick that also became a zero-game player, but the pick survived long enough to be included in another NBA transaction.

That is a narrow advantage, not a major win.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win, C+/C. Cleveland receives a C+ because the incoming pick retained enough value to become part of a later trade package even though Calvin Duncan never played in the NBA. The Clippers receive a C because Anderson and Craft produced zero direct games and no verified downstream franchise value.

sections.heading: Atlanta Turned a Veteran and a Second Into a Long-Term Starter
sections.body:
The June 29, 1983 exchange sent Randy Wittman's draft rights from Washington to Atlanta. The Bullets received Tom McMillen and Atlanta's 1984 second-round pick, later No. 34 Tony Costner.

The legacy archive record originally called the outcome even. Completed player production gives Atlanta a clearer advantage.

sections.heading: Wittman Developed Into a Full-Time Hawks Starter
sections.body:
Wittman played 78 regular-season games for Atlanta as a rookie in 1983-84, mostly off the bench. His role increased in 1984-85, when he started 22 of 41 games and averaged 9.9 points.

By 1985-86, Wittman was a regular starter. He appeared in 81 games, started 79 and averaged 12.9 points while shooting 53.0 percent from the field.

He followed with 71 games and 65 starts in 1986-87, then played all 82 games and started all 82 in 1987-88. Across those first five Hawks seasons alone, Wittman totaled 353 regular-season games and 249 starts.

That span also included repeated playoff participation as Atlanta developed into a strong Eastern Conference team.

sections.heading: McMillen Gave Washington Three Useful Seasons
sections.body:
Tom McMillen was already an established veteran when Washington acquired him. He played 62 games for the Bullets in 1983-84, starting five and averaging 9.2 points.

He returned for 69 games and 21 starts in 1984-85, then added 56 games and one start in 1985-86.

Across three Washington seasons, McMillen produced 187 regular-season games and 27 starts. That is meaningful depth and keeps the Bullets side from being graded as a poor return.

sections.heading: The Second-Round Pick Produced No NBA Games
sections.body:
Washington used the incoming 1984 second-rounder at No. 34 on Saint Joseph's center Tony Costner.

Basketball-Reference lists Costner as a drafted player with no NBA regular-season statistical line. His professional career continued outside the NBA, so the pick branch produced zero direct Bullets games.

sections.heading: Why Atlanta Wins
sections.body:
Washington received three useful seasons from McMillen, but the pick added nothing at the NBA level. Atlanta received a younger wing who grew from reserve minutes into a multi-year starting role.

Wittman's first five Atlanta seasons alone produced nearly twice as many games as McMillen's Washington tenure and more than nine times as many starts. His strongest years also aligned with Atlanta's playoff rise.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win, A/B. Atlanta receives an A because Wittman became a durable multi-year starter and productive rotation piece for a rising playoff team. Washington receives a B because McMillen gave the Bullets three useful seasons, but Costner produced zero NBA games and the total return did not match Wittman's longevity or starting value.

sections.heading: The Swap Is the Only Branch That Produced Direct Dallas Games
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's league and Dallas transaction ledgers record the June 29, 1983 package as Dirk Minniefield plus a 1987 second-round pick to New Jersey for a 1986 second-round pick and another 1987 second-round pick. The completed draft outcomes show Dallas at No. 26 in 1987 with Steve Alford and the other side of the exchange at No. 43 with Andrew Kennedy.

The legacy archive record describes the 1987 mechanism as Dallas holding the option to take the more favorable second-round position. The realized draft positions are consistent with that description.

sections.heading: Minniefield Never Played for New Jersey
sections.body:
Dallas drafted Dirk Minniefield at No. 33 in 1983 and immediately moved his rights to the Nets. Minniefield spent the next two seasons outside the NBA and did not debut until 1985-86 with Cleveland.

His later NBA career included 222 games, but none came for New Jersey. This review therefore assigns the Nets zero direct regular-season games from the Minniefield branch.

sections.heading: New Jersey's 1987 Pick Retained Some Trade Utility
sections.body:
The Nets did not hold the incoming 1987 second-rounder all the way to draft night. In September 1983, New Jersey included that pick with Horace Owens and Eddie Phillips in the trade that brought Reggie Johnson from Philadelphia.

Philadelphia ultimately used the pick at No. 43 on Andrew Kennedy, who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Because the pick was only one part of the Reggie Johnson package, this review records downstream transaction utility without assigning the full Johnson return to this trade.

sections.heading: Milt Wagner Produced Zero Dallas Games
sections.body:
Dallas used the 1986 second-round pick at No. 35 on Louisville guard Milt Wagner. The Mavericks waived Wagner on October 17, 1986, before he appeared in an NBA regular-season game.

Wagner later played 53 NBA games for the Lakers and Heat, but none of that production belongs to Dallas for trade-value purposes.

sections.heading: Steve Alford Produced the Clear Direct Return
sections.body:
Dallas used the favorable 1987 second-round position at No. 26 on Steve Alford. He played 112 regular-season games for the Mavericks across four Dallas seasons, all off the bench, and scored 385 points for the franchise.

Alford was never a major rotation piece, but he is the only asset in the trade tree that produced substantial direct games for either original team.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win, B/C+. Dallas receives a B because the favorable swap position produced 112 direct games from Alford even though Wagner produced none. New Jersey receives a C+ because Minniefield never played for the Nets, but the 1987 pick retained enough value to be included in a later multi-asset trade for Reggie Johnson. The margin is real but modest.

sections.heading: Atlanta Received the Better Player Outcome
sections.body:
The canonical June 29, 1983 package sends Rudy Macklin to New York for Sly Williams and cash. Basketball-Reference's player records make the on-court comparison straightforward even though the public cash amount is not identified.

Both players were former first-round picks whose roles were already shrinking, so this was a secondary roster move rather than a franchise-changing deal.

sections.heading: Macklin Played Only Eight Knicks Games
sections.body:
Rudy Macklin had spent his first two NBA seasons with Atlanta before the trade. In New York, he appeared in only eight regular-season games in 1983-84.

He made no starts, played 65 total minutes and averaged 4.4 points and 1.4 rebounds. Those eight games were the final NBA appearances of his career.

New York therefore received very little direct basketball value from the acquired player.

sections.heading: Williams Gave Atlanta Parts of Two Seasons
sections.body:
Sly Williams appeared in 13 regular-season games for Atlanta in 1983-84 and made one start. His role expanded the following season, when he played 34 games and started 20.

Across the two Hawks seasons, Williams totaled 47 regular-season games and 21 starts. The production was not star-level, but it was materially more useful than Macklin's eight-game Knicks tenure.

Williams later played six games for Boston in 1985-86, which are not credited to Atlanta.

sections.heading: The Cash Component Adds to Atlanta's Side
sections.body:
The canonical source package also sends cash from New York to Atlanta. The reviewed public sources do not establish the amount, so this review does not convert it into a speculative dollar-adjusted grade.

It still counts as a tangible asset. Atlanta received both the more productive player return and cash, while New York's player contribution ended after eight games.

sections.heading: Why the Original Even Grade Changes
sections.body:
The legacy review treated the transaction as broadly balanced, likely because both players were modest historical contributors and the cash figure was unclear.

Completed franchise-specific production creates a wider gap. Williams produced nearly six times as many games for Atlanta as Macklin did for New York and added 21 starts, with cash on top.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win, B+/D. Atlanta receives a B+ because Williams provided 47 games and 21 starts across two seasons and the Hawks also received cash. New York receives a D because Macklin played only eight games, never started and did not appear in the NBA again after 1983-84.

sources.title: 1983-84 New York Knicks roster and stats

sections.heading: The legacy Dallas-Win Verdict Overstates the Pick Return
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference and the Dallas media guide agree on the August 12, 1983 package. Dallas sent Kelvin Ransey to New Jersey for Foots Walker, a 1984 second-round pick and a 1985 first-round pick.

The completed outcomes are unusual: Ransey played exactly 240 regular-season games for New Jersey, while Tom Sluby and Bill Wennington combined for exactly 240 games for Dallas. The difference is role and impact.

sections.heading: Ransey Started 94 Games for the Nets
sections.body:
Ransey played 80 games for New Jersey in 1983-84 and started 50. He averaged 9.5 points and 6.0 assists in 24.2 minutes as the Nets won 45 games and reached the Eastern Conference semifinals.

He followed with 81 games and 29 starts in 1984-85, then 79 games and 15 starts in 1985-86. Across three Nets seasons, Ransey totaled 240 games and 94 starts.

He also appeared in 11 playoff games for New Jersey across those seasons, starting six. The Nets received a real rotation point guard rather than a short rental.

sections.heading: Foots Walker Produced Zero Dallas Games
sections.body:
Dallas acquired veteran guard Foots Walker in the deal but waived him on October 11, 1983 before the regular season.

New Jersey later re-signed Walker as a free agent, and he played 34 more Nets games. This review does not count those 34 games as a direct trade return because the Mavericks had already waived him and the Nets reacquired him separately.

For Dallas, Walker's branch produced zero regular-season games.

sections.heading: Tom Sluby Added 31 Reserve Games
sections.body:
Dallas used the 1984 second-round pick at No. 41 on Notre Dame guard Tom Sluby.

Sluby played 31 regular-season games for the Mavericks in 1984-85, made no starts and averaged 4.9 minutes. That was his entire NBA career.

sections.heading: Bill Wennington Supplied Four Years of Center Depth
sections.body:
The 1985 first-round pick became No. 16 Bill Wennington. He played 56, 58, 30 and 65 games for Dallas over four seasons, totaling 209 regular-season appearances and 12 starts.

Wennington had a long NBA career, but his later championship years with Chicago are not credited to Dallas. The relevant Mavericks return is four seasons of mostly reserve-center minutes.

sections.heading: Why New Jersey Gets the Edge
sections.body:
Dallas did realize value from both draft picks. Sluby and Wennington combined for 240 games, matching Ransey's Nets total exactly.

Ransey's 94 starts versus 12 combined Dallas starts tell the more important story. He handled regular point-guard responsibility for three playoff-caliber Nets seasons, while Dallas's return was almost entirely bench depth.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win, B+/B. New Jersey receives a B+ for 240 games, 94 starts and three years of useful point-guard play from Ransey. Dallas receives a B because the two picks produced 240 games of legitimate depth, but the outgoing package did not generate the stronger franchise-specific role or impact. The legacy Dallas-win framing is replaced by a modest Nets edge.

sources.title: Dallas Mavericks media guide transaction history
Washington Post transaction note on New Jersey re-signing Foots Walker

sections.heading: New Jersey Got the Only NBA Production in the Deal
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's New Jersey and Philadelphia transaction ledgers agree on the October 25, 1983 terms. The Nets acquired Reggie Johnson and sent Eddie Phillips, Horace Owens and a 1987 second-round pick to the defending champion 76ers.

The trade happened three days before the regular season began, which makes Philadelphia's roster decisions especially important to the outcome.

sections.heading: Johnson Gave the Nets a Full Rotation Season
sections.body:
Johnson joined a New Jersey team that won 45 games and reached the Eastern Conference semifinals. He appeared in 72 regular-season games, started four and logged 818 minutes.

Basketball-Reference credits him with 346 points, 138 rebounds and 40 assists. Johnson averaged 4.8 points and 1.9 rebounds in 11.4 minutes while shooting 49.6 percent from the field.

The role was not large, but it was real. He gave New Jersey frontcourt depth across almost the entire season and appeared on a playoff team that eliminated Philadelphia in the first round.

That 1983-84 season was Johnson's final NBA campaign, so the Nets did not receive a long-term asset. The value is best described as one dependable reserve season.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Cut Both Players Immediately
sections.body:
The 76ers acquired Phillips and Owens on October 25 and placed both on waivers on October 27.

Phillips had played 48 games for New Jersey as a rookie in 1982-83, but he never appeared in a regular-season game for Philadelphia. RealGM's transaction log lists him becoming a free agent on October 31.

Owens, a 1983 second-round pick from Rhode Island, also never played an NBA regular-season game. Philadelphia waived him in the same final roster cut.

That left the future draft pick as the only remaining path for the 76ers.

sections.heading: The Pick Became Andrew Kennedy
sections.body:
Philadelphia held the 1987 second-round pick and used it at No. 43 on Virginia forward Andrew Kennedy.

Basketball-Reference's draft record lists Kennedy with no NBA regular-season career. He never produced a game for Philadelphia.

The three assets Philadelphia received therefore combined for zero NBA regular-season games for the franchise.

sections.heading: Why New Jersey Wins
sections.body:
The Nets did not acquire a star or a multi-year starter, so this is not an elite-grade win. They simply converted two players outside their plans and a future second-rounder into a reserve who helped immediately.

Philadelphia received no realized NBA production from either incoming player or the eventual draft selection. That creates a clear result even though the total stakes were modest.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win, B/D. New Jersey earns a B for obtaining 72 games and a full season of useful reserve minutes from Johnson. Philadelphia receives a D because Phillips and Owens were waived before the season and Andrew Kennedy never appeared in the NBA. Confidence is high because the trade, waiver dates, Johnson's Nets statistics and Kennedy's draft outcome are documented in primary transaction and statistical records.

sections.heading: Seattle Bought Two Seasons of Frontcourt Play for One Second-Round Pick
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's Seattle transaction ledger records the October 26, 1983 trade: the SuperSonics sent Kansas City a 1985 second-round pick for Reggie King.

King had been a regular starter earlier in his Kings career but had moved into a smaller role in 1982-83. Seattle restored him to a meaningful place in the rotation immediately.

sections.heading: King Started 42 Games in His First Seattle Season
sections.body:
King appeared in 77 games in 1983-84 and started 42. He logged 2,086 minutes, scored 602 points and collected 470 rebounds.

That worked out to 7.8 points, 6.1 rebounds and 2.3 assists per game in 27.1 minutes while shooting 52.0 percent from the field. He was a substantial rotation player on a 42-win Seattle team that reached the playoffs.

King stayed for 1984-85 and appeared in 60 more games, starting five. His role shrank to 14.3 minutes per game, but he still gave Seattle another season of usable depth.

Across the two seasons, the SuperSonics received 137 regular-season games from a player acquired for one future second-round pick.

sections.heading: Kansas City Used the Pick as Part of the Reggie Theus Trade
sections.body:
The pick did not simply sit in the Kings' inventory until 1985. On February 15, 1984, Kansas City traded Steve Johnson and three second-round picks to Chicago for Reggie Theus.

Seattle's 1985 second-rounder was one of those picks. It eventually became No. 28 Ken Johnson after the Bulls held the selection.

Theus became a major Kings contributor. He averaged 19.0 points and 7.0 assists in 30 games after the 1984 trade, then remained a high-level starter as the franchise moved to Sacramento.

That downstream value matters, but it cannot all be credited to the single Seattle pick. Kansas City also surrendered Steve Johnson and two other second-round selections in the Theus package.

sections.heading: The Pick Itself Became Ken Johnson
sections.body:
Chicago ultimately used the pick at No. 28 in the 1985 draft on Ken Johnson. He played one NBA season, appearing in 64 games for the Bulls.

Because Kansas City had already traded the selection away, Johnson's Bulls production does not count as Kings realized value. The Kings' credit comes from the pick's role as one piece of the Theus acquisition.

sections.heading: Why Seattle Gets a Slight Edge
sections.body:
Kansas City handled the asset productively. Rather than waiting for a late second-round selection, the Kings used it as part of a package for a proven scorer and playmaker.

Seattle's return is easier to assign directly. King gave the SuperSonics 137 games, 47 starts and two seasons of frontcourt depth for that single pick.

The Kings' downstream branch was valuable but shared among four outgoing assets, so giving the entire Theus return to this pick would overstate its individual contribution.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight SuperSonics Edge, B+/B. Seattle earns a B+ for getting two seasons and 137 games from King at the cost of one second-rounder. Kansas City earns a B because the pick became useful trade currency in the Reggie Theus deal, even though it was only one part of that package. Confidence is high on the transaction chain and King production, with the grade appropriately limiting how much of Theus' value is assigned to this single pick.

sources.title: 1983-84 Kansas City Kings roster and statistics

sections.heading: San Diego Turned a Future Third-Rounder Into Immediate Depth
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's Indiana transaction ledger records the October 26, 1983 deal: the Pacers sent Hank McDowell to the San Diego Clippers for a 1988 third-round pick.

McDowell had arrived in Indiana only weeks earlier, but the Pacers chose to move him again before the regular season. San Diego kept him for the full 1983-84 campaign.

sections.heading: McDowell Played 57 Games for the Clippers
sections.body:
McDowell appeared in 57 games for San Diego, all off the bench. He logged 611 minutes, scored 208 points and collected 155 rebounds.

That worked out to 3.6 points and 2.7 rebounds in 10.7 minutes per game. The numbers were modest, but he was a usable reserve big for most of the season.

McDowell left the Clippers after that year and later played for Houston and Milwaukee. Those later stops do not count toward San Diego's return, but the Clippers still received one complete season of direct NBA production.

sections.heading: Indiana Waited Five Years for the Pick
sections.body:
The compensation was a distant 1988 third-round selection. The pick ultimately landed at No. 73, where Indiana selected Drexel point guard Michael Anderson.

Anderson did have an NBA career, but not with the Pacers. Indiana placed him on waivers on October 31, 1988, before he appeared in a regular-season game for the franchise.

He later played 36 games for San Antonio in 1988-89, averaging 5.7 points and 4.3 assists. Because those games came after Indiana had waived him, they are not Pacers realized value from this trade.

sections.heading: Why the Clippers Win
sections.body:
Indiana's process was understandable. The Pacers turned a player they were not planning to use into a future draft asset and held that asset until the 1988 draft.

The realized result, however, was zero Pacers games from the pick. San Diego paid that future third-rounder and received 57 games and 611 minutes from McDowell immediately.

This is a modest-stakes trade, so the Clippers' grade should not be exaggerated, but one full reserve season clearly beats a draft selection that never made Indiana's regular-season roster.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win, B-/D. San Diego earns a B- for converting a third-round pick into 57 games of useful frontcourt depth. Indiana receives a D because the pick became Michael Anderson, whom the Pacers waived before he played a regular-season game. Confidence is high because the trade, McDowell's Clippers production, Anderson's draft slot and Indiana waiver are all documented in transaction and statistical records.

sources.title: 1983-84 San Diego Clippers roster and statistics

sections.heading: Philadelphia Got Two Seasons From Sam Williams
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference records the November 12, 1983 trade as a straight player-for-pick exchange. Philadelphia sent Golden State its 1984 second-round selection for forward Sam Williams.

Golden State later used that pick at No. 45 on Gary Plummer. The deal therefore produced direct NBA rotation players for both teams, which makes the comparison closer than many late-pick trades.

sections.heading: Williams Became a Real 76ers Rotation Forward
sections.body:
Williams joined Philadelphia shortly after the season began and appeared in 70 games in 1983-84. He started 12, logged 1,375 minutes and produced 472 points and 326 rebounds.

He averaged 6.7 points and 4.7 rebounds in 19.6 minutes while shooting 47.7 percent from the field. Williams also appeared in four playoff games for a Philadelphia team trying to defend its 1983 title.

He returned in 1984-85 and played 46 more games with eight starts. His role was smaller, but he still contributed 488 minutes, 144 points and 106 rebounds.

Across the two seasons, Philadelphia received 116 regular-season games, 20 starts and 1,863 minutes from Williams.

sections.heading: Golden State Used the Pick on Gary Plummer
sections.body:
The Warriors held the incoming second-rounder and selected Boston University forward Gary Plummer at No. 45 in the 1984 draft.

Plummer played 66 games for Golden State as a rookie, all off the bench. He logged 702 minutes, scored 250 points and collected 134 rebounds.

He averaged 3.8 points and 2.0 rebounds in 10.6 minutes. Plummer then missed the 1985-86 season with injury and spent several years outside the NBA before returning with Denver in 1992-93.

That later Denver season does not count for Golden State. The Warriors' realized return from the pick is the 66-game rookie season.

sections.heading: Why Philadelphia Gets the Edge
sections.body:
Neither side made a franchise-changing move. Golden State received an NBA player from a second-round pick, which is a legitimate success and deserves a positive grade.

Philadelphia simply received more. Williams played 50 more games, logged more than twice as many minutes and started 20 times across two seasons. The 76ers also got that production immediately rather than waiting until the following draft.

The transaction was useful for both teams, but the scale of direct realized value favors Philadelphia.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win, B+/C+. Philadelphia earns a B+ for turning one second-round pick into 116 games and two seasons of rotation frontcourt play. Golden State receives a C+ because Plummer made the roster and contributed 66 games as a rookie but did not become a lasting Warriors piece. Confidence is high because the trade terms, draft result and both players' team-specific production are documented in primary statistical records.

sources.title: 1984-85 Golden State Warriors roster and statistics

sections.heading: Golden State Used the Pick as Trade Currency
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference records the January 20, 1984 deal as Ron Brewer from Golden State to San Antonio for a 1985 second-round pick.

Brewer had been a productive NBA scorer earlier in his career, but by 1983-84 his role had diminished. San Antonio still got useful immediate minutes. Golden State chose the longer asset path.

sections.heading: Brewer Played 49 Games for the Spurs
sections.body:
Brewer appeared in 40 games for San Antonio after the trade and started five. He logged 782 minutes, scored 348 points and shot 44.1 percent from the field.

He averaged 8.7 points in 19.6 minutes, giving the Spurs a legitimate reserve scorer for the second half of the season.

Brewer returned in 1984-85 but his role collapsed. He appeared in nine San Antonio games, all off the bench, totaling 81 minutes and 33 points before moving on to New Jersey.

Across the two seasons, San Antonio received 49 regular-season games, five starts, 863 minutes and 381 points.

sections.heading: Golden State Did Not Use the Pick on Manute Bol
sections.body:
The incoming pick ultimately became the No. 31 selection in the 1985 draft, where Washington selected Manute Bol. Golden State had already traded the pick away before draft night.

On June 17, 1985, the Warriors sent this 1985 second-rounder plus a 1987 second-round pick to Washington for veteran forward Greg Ballard.

That distinction matters. Bol's Washington career cannot be credited to Golden State. The Warriors' legitimate downstream return is Ballard, acquired with this pick and one additional second-round selection.

sections.heading: Ballard Gave Golden State Two Productive Seasons
sections.body:
Ballard played 75 games for the Warriors in 1985-86, starting 14. He logged 1,792 minutes, scored 662 points and grabbed 417 rebounds.

He returned in 1986-87 for all 82 games with seven starts, adding 1,579 minutes, 579 points and 340 rebounds. Golden State reached the playoffs that season.

Across the two years, Ballard gave the Warriors 157 games, 21 starts, 3,371 minutes, 1,241 points and 757 rebounds.

Because Golden State also surrendered a 1987 second-round pick in the Ballard trade, only part of that return should be assigned to the San Antonio pick.

sections.heading: Why Golden State Gets the Slight Edge
sections.body:
San Antonio received real value from Brewer, but it was concentrated in 40 useful games after the trade and nine low-minute games the next season.

Golden State's pick became one of two assets used to acquire two full seasons from Ballard. Even discounting the return to account for the second pick, the Warriors extracted a longer and more substantial franchise benefit.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Warriors Edge, B/B-. Golden State earns a B for converting the pick into meaningful trade currency that helped acquire 157 games from Ballard. San Antonio receives a B- for getting 49 games and one useful partial season from Brewer. Confidence is high on the transaction chain and team-specific production, with the grade deliberately limiting how much Ballard value is assigned to one of two outgoing picks.

sections.heading: Denver Got a Short Bench Stint; San Antonio Got No NBA Games
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference records the January 21, 1984 exchange as Keith Edmonson from San Antonio to Denver for the Nuggets' 1984 third-round pick.

The pick eventually became No. 57 Joe Binion. Neither branch developed into a lasting franchise piece, so this trade is best judged on modest direct production rather than name value or hypothetical upside.

sections.heading: Edmonson Played 15 Games for Denver
sections.body:
Edmonson had appeared in 40 games for San Antonio earlier in 1983-84. After the trade, his Denver role was much smaller.

He played 15 games for the Nuggets, all off the bench, and logged 101 minutes. Basketball-Reference credits him with 64 points, 18 rebounds and seven assists while shooting 48.9 percent from the field.

Edmonson averaged only 6.7 minutes per game, but he did provide actual regular-season depth during a Denver season that ended with a playoff berth.

Those 15 games were the end of his NBA career. He did not return to the league after 1983-84.

sections.heading: San Antonio Used the Pick on Joe Binion
sections.body:
The Spurs kept the third-round selection and used it at No. 57 in the 1984 NBA Draft on North Carolina A&T forward Joe Binion.

Binion did not play for San Antonio. Basketball-Reference lists him as spending 1984-85 and 1985-86 outside the NBA in the CBA.

His NBA debut did not come until February 1987, when he appeared in 11 games for Portland. Those 11 games and 51 minutes belong to the Trail Blazers, not to San Antonio's return from this trade.

The Spurs therefore received zero NBA regular-season games from the pick.

sections.heading: Why Denver Gets the Edge
sections.body:
This is a low-impact result. Denver received only 101 minutes from Edmonson, so the trade cannot earn a strong grade.

San Antonio's pick did identify a player who eventually reached the NBA, but the Spurs never received a game from him. Realized franchise value therefore favors Denver simply because Edmonson actually appeared for the Nuggets.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Nuggets Edge, C-/D. Denver earns a C- for getting 15 games and 101 minutes from Edmonson at the cost of a third-round pick. San Antonio receives a D because No. 57 Joe Binion never appeared in a Spurs regular-season game. Confidence is high because the trade, Edmonson's Denver totals, Binion's draft slot and his later Portland debut are all documented in primary statistical records.

sources.title: 1986-87 Portland Trail Blazers roster and statistics

sections.heading: A Draft-Day Chain Created Useful Returns for Three Teams
sections.body:
The June 19, 1984 transaction began with Cleveland, Washington and the draft rights to two first-round centers. Cleveland had selected Tim McCormick at No. 12. Washington had selected Mel Turpin at No. 6.

Basketball-Reference records Cleveland sending McCormick's rights and Cliff Robinson to Washington for Turpin's rights. Washington then immediately sent McCormick and veteran guard Ricky Sobers to Seattle for Gus Williams.

That second move means Washington's return from the Cleveland trade was not simply Robinson plus McCormick. McCormick became part of the package that brought Williams, while Seattle gained the young center it wanted.

sections.heading: Turpin Became Cleveland's Starting Center
sections.body:
Mel Turpin played 79 games as a rookie in 1984-85 and started 45. He logged 1,949 minutes, scored 835 points, grabbed 452 rebounds and blocked 87 shots.

His role grew in 1985-86. Turpin appeared in 80 games, started 69 and produced 1,097 points, 556 rebounds and 106 blocks.

He played 64 more Cavaliers games in 1986-87. Across three Cleveland seasons, Turpin produced 223 regular-season games and 2,325 points.

The Cavaliers did not get an All-Star, but they did get three seasons of legitimate center production from the No. 6 rights they acquired.

sections.heading: Washington Received Two Strong Branches
sections.body:
Cliff Robinson gave Washington immediate frontcourt scoring. He played 60 games with 37 starts in 1984-85 and averaged 16.7 points and 9.1 rebounds.

Robinson followed with 78 games, all starts, in 1985-86 and averaged 18.7 points and 8.7 rebounds. Across those two seasons, he gave the Bullets 138 games and 2,463 points before moving to Philadelphia.

The McCormick branch also became productive. Washington packaged McCormick's rights with Ricky Sobers and acquired Gus Williams from Seattle the same day.

Williams became Washington's starting point guard. He played 79 games with 78 starts in 1984-85, averaging 20.0 points, 7.7 assists and 2.3 steals. He added 77 games and 67 starts in 1985-86, averaging 13.5 points and 5.9 assists.

Because Sobers was an additional Washington asset, the entire Williams return cannot be assigned solely to McCormick. Still, McCormick was a central part of the package, so a meaningful share of those 156 games belongs to this trade tree.

sections.heading: Seattle Got the Young Center It Wanted
sections.body:
The SuperSonics made McCormick the centerpiece of their side. Contemporary reporting identified the 6-foot-11 Michigan center as the player Seattle targeted for interior help behind Jack Sikma.

McCormick played 78 games with 27 starts as a rookie, averaging 9.3 points and 5.1 rebounds. He followed with 77 games and 42 starts in 1985-86.

Across two Seattle seasons, McCormick gave the Sonics 155 games and 69 starts before he was traded to Philadelphia in 1986.

sections.heading: Why Washington Gets the Slight Edge
sections.body:
Cleveland received a starting center for three seasons. Seattle received two productive seasons from a young center. Neither result was poor.

Washington received the broadest combination of value: two strong seasons from Robinson plus a key trade chip that helped land Williams, who immediately became a 20-point, 7.7-assist starting guard.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Wizards Edge, A/A-/A-. Washington earns an A for combining Robinson's 138 games and high-level scoring with a major role in the Williams acquisition. Cleveland earns an A- for 223 games and three seasons from Turpin. Seattle also earns an A- for 155 games and 69 starts from McCormick. Confidence is high because the draft-day transactions and the team-specific production for Turpin, Robinson, Williams and McCormick are all documented in transaction and statistical records.

sections.heading: Golden State Turned a Second-Round Pick Into a Four-Year Center
sections.body:
The June 19, 1984 draft-day trade was straightforward. Golden State selected Jay Murphy with the No. 31 pick and immediately sent his rights to the San Diego Clippers for Jerome Whitehead.

Whitehead was already an established NBA center. Murphy was a second-round rookie. The gap in realized value became obvious almost immediately.

sections.heading: Whitehead Started 78 Games in His First Warriors Season
sections.body:
Whitehead stepped directly into Golden State's starting lineup in 1984-85. He appeared in 79 games, started 78 and logged 2,536 minutes.

Basketball-Reference credits him with 1,026 points and 622 rebounds that season. He averaged 13.0 points and 7.9 rebounds while shooting 51.0 percent from the field.

The role became smaller in 1985-86, but Whitehead still played 81 games. He added 73 games in 1986-87 and 72 more in 1987-88.

Across four Warriors seasons, Whitehead played 305 regular-season games. Even after his first-year starting role diminished, he remained a durable rotation center and gave Golden State years of usable minutes from a single second-round selection.

sections.heading: Murphy Barely Played for the Clippers
sections.body:
Jay Murphy made the Clippers as a rookie but never developed into a rotation player.

He appeared in 23 games in 1984-85, all off the bench, and logged 149 minutes. He scored 28 points while shooting 16.0 percent from the field.

Murphy returned for 14 games in 1985-86 and logged another 100 minutes. His Clippers tenure therefore ended at 37 games, zero starts and 249 total minutes.

He later played 30 games across two seasons for Washington, but those appearances came after he left the Clippers and do not count as Los Angeles realized value from this trade.

sections.heading: Why Golden State Wins
sections.body:
The Warriors did more than get the better player. They acquired someone who immediately filled a starting position and then remained in the organization for four seasons.

The Clippers received a prospect, but Murphy never became a regular rotation forward. Thirty-seven low-minute games are a very small return for a center who gave Golden State more than 300 games.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win, A-/D. Golden State earns an A- for converting the No. 31 rights into 305 games and four seasons from Whitehead, including a 78-start first year. The Clippers receive a D because Murphy played only 37 games and 249 minutes for the franchise. Confidence is high because the draft-day trade and both players' team-specific production are documented in team transaction and statistical records.

sources.title: 1984-85 Golden State Warriors roster and statistics

sections.heading: Philadelphia Acquired a Valuable Future Asset, Not Harvey Grant Himself
sections.body:
The June 19, 1984 draft-day trade sent Tom Sewell's rights from Philadelphia to Washington for the Bullets' 1988 first-round pick.

The transaction ledger later labels that pick as the selection used on Harvey Grant. That label can be misleading if the later chain is ignored. Philadelphia did not draft Grant and should not receive credit for his Washington career.

The 76ers used the pick as trade currency two years before the 1988 draft.

sections.heading: Sewell Played Only 21 NBA Games
sections.body:
Washington acquired Sewell after Philadelphia selected him No. 22 overall.

His NBA career lasted one season. Sewell appeared in 21 games for the 1984-85 Bullets, never started and averaged only 4.1 minutes per game.

Basketball-Reference credits him with 86 total minutes and 21 points. He shot 25.0 percent from the field and did not return to the NBA after that season.

That makes Washington's direct 1984 return extremely small.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Held the Pick Until the Moses Malone Deal
sections.body:
The 76ers kept the 1988 first-rounder for two years.

On June 16, 1986, Philadelphia packaged Moses Malone, Terry Catledge, a 1986 first-round pick and this 1988 first-round pick to Washington for Cliff Robinson and Jeff Ruland.

Because the 1988 pick was only one of four outgoing Philadelphia assets, the entire Robinson-and-Ruland return cannot be credited to the Sewell trade. The pick still had meaningful first-round value and clearly contributed to the package.

Robinson then played 131 regular-season games for Philadelphia across parts of three seasons. Ruland's Philadelphia tenure was limited by injuries, but the broader 1986 transaction shows that the pick retained enough value to help facilitate a major roster move.

sections.heading: Washington Reacquired Its Own Pick
sections.body:
The 1986 trade sent the pick back to Washington. The Bullets held it until the 1988 draft and selected Harvey Grant at No. 12.

Grant became a productive NBA forward and later had several strong Washington seasons, but those years belong to Washington's 1986 acquisition of the pick. Assigning Grant's entire career to Philadelphia's side of the 1984 Sewell trade would double-count the asset after it had changed hands again.

sections.heading: Why Philadelphia Wins
sections.body:
The comparison should stay focused on what each side actually captured from the 1984 exchange.

Washington received 21 low-minute games from Sewell. Philadelphia received two years of control over a future first-round pick and then used it as one component of a major 1986 trade.

That is not the same as directly drafting a long-term star, so an elite grade would overstate the result. It is still clearly more value than Washington received from Sewell.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win, B+/D. Philadelphia earns a B+ for turning Sewell into a future first-round asset that retained enough value to help facilitate the 1986 Robinson-Ruland trade. Washington receives a D because Sewell produced only 21 games and 86 minutes before his NBA career ended. Confidence is high because the original trade, Sewell's Washington production and the 1986 re-trade of the same pick are documented in transaction records.

sections.heading: The Original June 9 Trade Is Clear
sections.body: Houston, Boston and the league transaction ledgers all record the same June 9, 1977 exchange. The Rockets sent John Johnson to the Celtics for Boston's 1977 second-round pick and a 1978 second-round pick. The 1977 choice became No. 34 Larry Moffett. The 1978 choice became No. 28 Buster Matheney. The first surprise is that Johnson never played a regular-season game for Boston. His player ledger moves directly from Houston in 1976-77 to one Houston game and then Seattle in 1977-78. The team transaction logs explain why.

sections.heading: Boston Sold Johnson's Rights Back, but Houston Kept Both Picks
sections.body: On October 18, 1977, Boston sold Johnson's player rights back to Houston. The Houston ledger explicitly notes that Johnson returned to the Rockets while Houston kept the draft picks from the June 9 trade. The 1977-78 league transaction log independently records the rights sale. The amount of cash Boston received is not listed in the cited ledgers, so this review does not invent a dollar value or treat the return as zero. That reversal dramatically changes the hindsight evaluation. Boston spent two second-round picks for a player who never appeared in a Celtics regular-season game, then recovered only an unspecified cash return. Houston retained both original picks and regained the same player asset.

sections.heading: Moffett Produced 20 Games; Matheney Never Reached the NBA
sections.body: Houston used the 1977 pick on Moffett at No. 34. He appeared in 20 games during 1977-78, totaling 110 minutes, before the Rockets waived him on February 10, 1978. The second pick became Matheney at No. 28 in 1978. Basketball-Reference lists him as drafted by Houston but shows no NBA regular-season career. Those two picks alone produced little direct value, but the Johnson asset was no longer gone.

sections.heading: Houston Flipped Johnson Again Four Days Later
sections.body: On October 22, 1977, Houston traded Johnson to Seattle for a 1979 second-round pick and a 1980 second-round pick. Seattle's team ledger and the league ledger record the same package. Johnson then played 76 games for the SuperSonics in 1977-78 and all 82 in 1978-79, but that Seattle production belongs to the later trade, not to Boston's side of the June transaction.

sections.heading: The 1979 Pick Became Paul Mokeski
sections.body: Houston used the 1979 second-rounder at No. 42 on Paul Mokeski. He played 12 games for the Rockets in 1979-80. On October 7, 1980, Houston traded Mokeski to Detroit for a 1982 second-round pick that later landed at No. 32. Houston did not simply use that pick on Richard Anderson. On June 28, 1982, the Rockets sent the No. 32 slot to San Diego for Joe Bryant plus the second-round pick that became No. 42 Jeff Taylor. Bryant played 81 games for Houston in 1982-83, starting 56 and averaging 10.0 points. Taylor played 44 Rockets games that season. The Mokeski branch therefore ultimately produced 12 Mokeski games plus 125 combined Bryant-Taylor games.

sections.heading: The 1980 Pick Produced No NBA Return
sections.body: The other Seattle pick became No. 43 Billy Williams in 1980. Houston drafted him, but Basketball-Reference lists no NBA regular-season career. That branch ended without realized NBA playing value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win, A-/D. Houston receives an A- because the club retained both original Boston second-rounders, reacquired Johnson's rights, flipped him four days later for two more second-rounders, and eventually turned one of those into Mokeski and the Bryant-Taylor package. Boston receives a D because Johnson never appeared in a Celtics regular-season game and the only documented return after the rights sale is unspecified cash. The direct draft outcomes were modest, but Houston's repeated asset recycling created the decisive value gap. Confidence is high on the transaction chain and moderate on the exact value of Boston's cash return because the amount is not specified.

sections.heading: Seattle Received Five Seasons From John Johnson
sections.body: Houston and Seattle's transaction ledgers agree on the October 22, 1977 exchange. The Rockets sent John Johnson to the SuperSonics for Seattle's 1979 and 1980 second-round picks. The legacy archive entry's "John Johnson (Howard Getty)" label is a bad source-import artifact; the player in the transaction is John Johnson, and this review normalizes the asset accordingly. Johnson immediately became a major Seattle rotation piece. He played 76 regular-season games in 1977-78 and appeared in 22 playoff games as the SuperSonics reached the NBA Finals. In 1978-79 he played all 82 games, started all 82, averaged 11.0 points and became a starter on Seattle's NBA championship team. His value did not end with the title. Johnson played 81 games in 1979-80, 80 in 1980-81 and 14 in 1981-82. Across five Seattle seasons he totaled 333 regular-season appearances and 3,608 points. That is a large realized return for two future second-rounders.

sections.heading: The 1979 Pick Became Paul Mokeski
sections.body: Houston used the first pick at No. 42 in the 1979 draft on Paul Mokeski. He appeared in 12 regular-season games for the Rockets in 1979-80 before Houston traded him to Detroit on October 7, 1980 for a 1982 second-round pick. That trade kept the asset chain alive. The 1982 pick eventually landed at No. 32. On June 28, 1982, Houston sent the No. 32 pick to San Diego and received Joe Bryant plus the second-round pick that became No. 42 Jeff Taylor. Bryant played 81 regular-season games for Houston in 1982-83, starting 56 and averaging 10.0 points. Taylor played 44 Rockets games that season. Because Houston had to send the No. 32 pick to obtain both players, this review credits the Mokeski branch with creating the transaction opportunity rather than pretending the pick itself played those 125 games.

sections.heading: The 1980 Pick Produced No NBA Games
sections.body: The second Seattle pick became No. 43 Billy Williams in the 1980 draft. Houston selected Williams, but Basketball-Reference records no NBA regular-season career. That branch ended without realized on-court value.

sections.heading: Houston's Return Was Better Than the Raw Draft Names Suggest
sections.body: A simple Mokeski-plus-Williams comparison would underrate Houston because Mokeski still produced a later second-round asset that helped bring Bryant and Taylor. The Rockets therefore did receive more than 12 direct games from the package. The gap remains large. Seattle received Johnson's five-season tenure, deep playoff participation and a full 82-game starting season on a championship team. Houston's return required multiple later transactions to create modest roster value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: SuperSonics Win, A/B-. Seattle receives an A because Johnson gave the franchise 333 regular-season games, 3,608 points, multiple playoff runs and a starting role on the 1979 champions. Houston receives a B- because Mokeski's branch eventually helped produce Bryant and Taylor, while Williams never reached an NBA regular-season game. The Rockets preserved some asset value, but Seattle received the durable high-impact player. Confidence is high.

sections.heading: The Core Trade Is Fully Confirmed
sections.body: Portland, Seattle and the league transaction ledgers all record the November 11, 1977 trade the same way. The Trail Blazers sent Wally Walker to the SuperSonics for Seattle's 1978 first-round pick and a 1979 second-round pick. The first-rounder became No. 7 Ron Brewer. The second-rounder became No. 40 Andrew Fields. There are no cash terms or conditional clauses to reconcile.

sections.heading: Walker Gave Seattle Five Seasons and a Championship Rotation Piece
sections.body: Walker played 68 games for Seattle in 1977-78 after the trade, averaging 6.5 points and 3.0 rebounds. He returned for 60 games in 1978-79 and was part of the SuperSonics team that won the NBA championship. His role remained useful beyond the title season. Walker played 70 games in 1979-80, all 82 in 1980-81 and 70 in 1981-82. Across five Seattle seasons, he appeared in 350 regular-season games and averaged 7.3 points and 3.3 rebounds. Seattle eventually recovered another asset when it traded Walker to Houston in October 1982 for a 1984 second-round pick. This review records that later return without overstating it; Walker's main value had already come through five years of service and a championship run.

sections.heading: Brewer Became Portland's Main Return
sections.body: Portland used the No. 7 pick on Ron Brewer. He played 81 games as a rookie in 1978-79, averaging 13.3 points, then started all 82 games in 1979-80 and averaged 15.7 points. Brewer's Portland role declined early in 1980-81, but he still played 29 games before the Trail Blazers moved him. In total he appeared in 192 regular-season games for Portland and provided substantially more scoring per game than Walker did in Seattle.

sections.heading: The Brewer Branch Stayed Valuable
sections.body: On December 19, 1980, Portland traded Brewer to San Antonio for Mike Gale and a 1982 first-round pick. That pick later became No. 18 Ricky Pierce. This review does not credit Pierce's entire NBA career to the original Seattle trade, because Portland had to move Brewer to obtain the pick. The chain still matters: the No. 7 selection produced more than two seasons of Brewer and then returned another first-round asset instead of expiring without value.

sections.heading: The Second-Round Pick Did Not Produce NBA Games
sections.body: Portland used the 1979 second-rounder at No. 40 on Andrew Fields. Basketball-Reference lists Fields as drafted by the Trail Blazers but records no NBA regular-season career. That branch ended without realized NBA playing value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Blazers Edge, A/A-. Portland receives an A because the No. 7 pick became a productive scorer for 192 games and was then converted into Gale plus another first-round pick. Seattle receives an A- because Walker gave the club 350 games across five seasons and was part of the 1979 championship roster. The title context makes Seattle's return genuinely valuable, but Portland extracted more reusable asset value from the outgoing picks. Confidence is high.

sections.heading: The Three-Pick Package Is Fully Confirmed
sections.body: The New Jersey, Philadelphia and league transaction ledgers all record the same January 31, 1978 exchange. The Nets sent a 1979 second-round pick, a 1982 second-round pick and a 1983 third-round pick to the 76ers for Wilson Washington. Those picks ultimately became No. 36 Clint Richardson in 1979, No. 36 J.J. Anderson in 1982 and No. 64 Claude Riley in 1983. The legacy archive entry already had the right structure, so this review focuses on the realized value of each branch.

sections.heading: Washington Gave New Jersey 86 Games
sections.body: Washington had appeared in only 14 games for Philadelphia before the trade. With New Jersey, he immediately moved into a larger role. He played 24 games for the Nets in the remainder of 1977-78, averaging 8.8 points and 5.9 rebounds in 21.8 minutes. He returned for 62 games in 1978-79 and averaged 8.1 points and 4.7 rebounds in 18.4 minutes. Across his two Nets seasons, Washington appeared in 86 regular-season games and averaged 8.3 points and 5.1 rebounds. Basketball-Reference lists 1978-79 as the final season of his NBA career. New Jersey therefore received useful short-term frontcourt production, but no later player or draft branch followed his departure.

sections.heading: The 1979 Pick Became the Important Philadelphia Asset
sections.body: Philadelphia used the first incoming pick at No. 36 in the 1979 draft on Clint Richardson. He became a six-season 76ers guard and appeared in 426 regular-season games for Philadelphia. Richardson played 52 games as a rookie, then 77 in each of the next three seasons, followed by 69 in 1983-84 and 74 in 1984-85. He was never a star, but he became a durable rotation piece on a contender. Most importantly, Richardson was part of the 1982-83 championship team. He appeared in 13 playoff games during that title run, including all four games of the Finals sweep over the Lakers. Richardson also retained some later transaction value. Philadelphia traded him to Indiana in October 1985 for a 1989 second-round pick, later used on Reggie Cross, plus a conditional future second-round pick that was not exercised. This review does not need that later return to justify the original trade, but it extends the Richardson branch beyond his six Philadelphia seasons.

sections.heading: The 1982 Pick Produced Only a Brief Philadelphia Stint
sections.body: The second-round pick from 1982 became J.J. Anderson at No. 36. Anderson played 13 games for Philadelphia in 1982-83, averaging 1.3 points in 3.7 minutes. The 76ers waived him on December 20, 1982. He later played for Utah, but those Jazz games do not belong to Philadelphia's return. This branch provided only minimal direct value to the 76ers.

sections.heading: The 1983 Third-Round Pick Never Produced NBA Games
sections.body: Philadelphia used the third pick on Claude Riley at No. 64 in 1983. Basketball-Reference lists his college record and draft transaction but no NBA regular-season career. That branch ended without on-court NBA value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win, A/B-. Philadelphia receives an A because one of the three picks became a six-season, 426-game rotation guard who contributed to the 1983 championship, while the other two picks at least reached the draft stage. New Jersey receives a B- because Washington gave the Nets 86 legitimate rotation games across two seasons, but his NBA career then ended and the Nets surrendered the pick that became the deal's only durable long-term contributor. The trade is not a total miss for New Jersey, but Richardson's six-year Philadelphia run creates a clear hindsight gap. Confidence is high.

sections.heading: The Authoritative Date Is August 4, 1978
sections.body: Boston, San Diego and the league transaction ledgers all record this transaction on August 4, 1978. The legacy route is frozen under a July 7 date, so this review does not rewrite its archival identifier. It records August 4 as the source-verified transaction date. The package itself is consistent across the authoritative ledgers. Boston sent Kevin Kunnert, Kermit Washington, Sidney Wicks and Freeman Williams to San Diego. The Celtics received Tiny Archibald, Marvin Barnes, Billy Knight, a 1981 second-round pick that became Danny Ainge and a 1983 second-round pick that later became Rod Foster. The legacy description of Wicks as a later future consideration is not supported by the Basketball-Reference team or league ledgers; they include him directly in the August 4 package.

sections.heading: Archibald Became a Championship Point Guard
sections.body: Archibald's Boston tenure transformed the trade. He played 69 games in 1978-79, then 80 in both 1979-80 and 1980-81, 68 in 1981-82 and 66 in 1982-83. That is 363 regular-season games. He made the All-Star team in 1980, 1981 and 1982, earned All-NBA Second Team honors in 1980-81 and was the starting point guard on Boston's 1981 championship team. The Celtics received five years of high-end guard play from a player who had missed the entire previous season with an Achilles injury.

sections.heading: The Ainge Pick Became Another Championship Core Piece
sections.body: Boston kept the 1981 second-round pick and selected Ainge at No. 31. He played 556 regular-season games for the Celtics from 1981-82 through part of 1988-89. Ainge was on the 1984 and 1986 championship teams and made the 1988 All-Star team. That outcome alone would make the draft portion of the deal unusually strong for a second-round asset.

sections.heading: Knight and the 1983 Pick Later Converged in the Dennis Johnson Trade
sections.body: Knight played 40 games for Boston before the Celtics traded him to Indiana for Rick Robey on January 16, 1979. Robey then played 339 regular-season games for Boston and was part of the 1981 championship team. On June 27, 1983, Boston sent Robey, the 1983 second-round pick from this trade and another 1983 second-rounder to Phoenix for Dennis Johnson, a 1983 first-round pick and a third-round pick. Phoenix used the incoming No. 28 selection on Rod Foster. That branch requires careful attribution. Both Robey and the Foster pick trace back to the 1978 transaction, but another second-round pick was also outgoing, and Phoenix sent multiple assets back. This review credits the branch as a major shared downstream return without assigning all of Johnson's later Celtics value to either Knight or the Foster pick individually.

sections.heading: Barnes Was the Short Boston Branch
sections.body: Barnes played 38 games for Boston in 1978-79, averaging 8.1 points and 4.7 rebounds. The Celtics waived him in February 1979. His limited tenure does not materially drive the grade.

sections.heading: San Diego Received a Strong Four-Player Return
sections.body: The Clippers' side was much better than the legacy C+ grade suggested. Washington played all 82 games in 1978-79 and averaged 11.3 points and 9.8 rebounds. Kunnert played 81 games and averaged 6.5 points and 7.0 rebounds. Freeman Williams became the best long-term San Diego scorer from the package. He played 273 games across four Clippers seasons and scored 4,467 points, including 18.6 points per game in 1979-80 and 19.3 in 1980-81. Wicks added 199 games across three seasons. Washington and Kunnert also retained transaction value. In May 1979 San Diego sent both players plus a 1980 first-round pick to Portland as veteran-free-agent compensation after signing Bill Walton. That later return required an additional first-rounder, so this review does not assign Walton solely to the two players.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win, A+/A-. Boston receives an A+ because Archibald became a five-year championship point guard, Ainge became an eight-season Celtics contributor and two-time champion, and the Knight/Foster branches later helped form the package for Dennis Johnson. San Diego receives an A- because Williams, Wicks, Washington and Kunnert combined for substantial real playing value and two of those assets retained later transaction utility. This was not a one-sided talent giveaway; Boston simply converted its side into multiple championship-era pillars. Confidence is high.

sections.heading: The Original Package Favored Cleveland on Asset Depth
sections.body: Atlanta's transaction log confirms the January 31, 1979 trade: Terry Furlow came to the Hawks, while Cleveland received Butch Lee and a 1983 first-round pick.

sections.heading: Furlow Played 50 Games for Atlanta
sections.body: Furlow appeared in 29 games for the Hawks after the trade in 1978-79. He averaged 9.9 points, 2.8 assists and 19.9 minutes. He returned for 21 games in 1979-80, averaging 8.4 points and 3.4 assists. That gives Atlanta 50 regular-season games of direct production from Furlow. On November 23, 1979, Atlanta traded Furlow to Utah for a 1981 second-round pick later associated with Eddie Johnson and a 1982 second-round pick later associated with Ricky Frazier. That extended the Furlow branch beyond his own Hawks minutes.

sections.heading: Lee Gave Cleveland a Shorter Playing Return
sections.body: Butch Lee played 33 games for Cleveland after the 1979 trade and another three games the following season. His first Cleveland stint produced 782 minutes, 379 points and 126 assists. On February 15, 1980, Cleveland traded Lee and a separate 1982 first-round pick to the Lakers for Don Ford and a 1980 first-round pick. Because that transaction required the additional 1982 first, this review does not assign its full downstream result to Lee.

sections.heading: The 1983 First Retained Trade Value
sections.body: Cleveland held the Atlanta first-rounder until October 30, 1980. The Cavaliers then sent it, Bill Robinzine and a 1986 first-round pick to Dallas for Richard Washington and Jerome Whitehead. Dallas later used the 1983 selection at No. 11 on Derek Harper. That identifies the pick's final draft outcome, but Harper's career belongs to Dallas rather than Cleveland. The proper realized value for Cleveland is the pick's role in the 1980 trade package.

sections.heading: Why Cleveland Gets a Slight Edge
sections.body: Atlanta received 50 Furlow games and then converted him into two second-round picks. Cleveland received 36 Lee games plus a first-round asset that remained valuable enough to headline part of a later multi-asset deal. Neither side turned the original trade directly into a long-term star. The difference is that Cleveland received both a usable player and a premium future pick, while Atlanta's later Furlow return was two second-rounders.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Cavaliers Edge, B+/B. Cleveland receives a B+ for Lee's short playing stint plus the retained first-round asset. Atlanta receives a B for 50 Furlow games and the two second-round picks received when he was later moved to Utah.

sections.heading: The February Trade Was Two Players for Two Players and Cash
sections.body: New Jersey's and Philadelphia's transaction logs agree on the February 7, 1979 exchange. The Nets sent Eric Money and Al Skinner to the 76ers for Harvey Catchings, Ralph Simpson and cash.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Got Very Little Playing Value
sections.body: Money appeared in eight regular-season games for Philadelphia after the trade. He averaged 6.8 points and 2.8 assists in 16.1 minutes. Skinner played five games for the 76ers, averaging 3.6 points and 2.2 assists in 9.4 minutes. Those five games were the final NBA appearances of his career. The pair therefore produced only 13 combined regular-season appearances for Philadelphia. Neither player created a meaningful downstream asset branch for the 76ers.

sections.heading: Catchings and Simpson Both Played 32 Nets Games
sections.body: Catchings appeared in 32 regular-season games for New Jersey after the trade. He averaged 6.1 points and 6.4 rebounds in 20.6 minutes, giving the Nets immediate frontcourt depth. Simpson also played 32 games for New Jersey, averaging 6.9 points in 16.5 minutes. He remained with the club into the following season before being waived on November 13, 1979. The direct playing return already favored New Jersey, but Catchings created the much larger value branch.

sections.heading: Catchings Became the No. 8 Pick
sections.body: On May 31, 1979, New Jersey traded Catchings to Milwaukee for John Gianelli and a 1979 first-round pick. The Nets used that pick at No. 8 on Calvin Natt. Gianelli never became a long-term Nets player. Before the next season, New Jersey included him with Jim Boylan and Bernard King in the trade that brought Rich Kelley from Utah. Because Gianelli was only one component of that larger package, this review assigns only partial downstream credit to that branch.

sections.heading: Natt Became the Major Return
sections.body: Natt played 53 games for New Jersey as a rookie in 1979-80. He averaged 19.7 points and 9.7 rebounds in 38.6 minutes, giving the Nets immediate high-end production from the pick created by the Catchings trade. On February 8, 1980, New Jersey traded Natt to Portland for Maurice Lucas and two first-round picks. Those selections later became Mike Gminski at No. 7 in 1980 and Albert King at No. 10 in 1981. Unlike a multi-asset bridge where one branch is hard to isolate, the Natt transaction was a direct one-player exchange for Lucas and the two firsts. That means the Catchings-to-Natt path deserves substantial downstream credit.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win, A+/D. New Jersey receives an A+ because the club got 64 combined games from Catchings and Simpson, then turned Catchings into the pick used on Natt, who produced immediately and later returned Maurice Lucas plus two first-round picks. Philadelphia receives a D because Money and Skinner combined for only 13 games after the trade and generated no comparable downstream return.
