sections.heading: The Trade Was Green for a Second-Round Pick
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's league, Kansas City and San Antonio transaction ledgers agree on the September 13, 1979 core exchange. The Kings acquired Mike Green and the Spurs received Kansas City's 1980 second-round pick, later No. 39 overall. The frozen Kansas City source record also includes cash going to San Antonio. The public transaction ledgers reviewed for this review do not provide a cash amount, so the cash is preserved as an unresolved term and receives no numerical value in the grade.

sections.heading: Green Played 21 Games for Kansas City
sections.body: Green joined a Kings team that went 47-35 and reached the 1980 playoffs. He appeared in 21 regular-season games, averaging 7.7 points, 5.4 rebounds and 21.9 minutes. Those 21 games were the final NBA appearances of his career. Green still supplied usable frontcourt minutes, but Kansas City did not receive a multi-season return or a later trade branch from the player.

sections.heading: San Antonio Used the Pick on Michael Wiley
sections.body: The Spurs kept the second-round pick and selected Michael Wiley at No. 39 in the 1980 NBA Draft. That makes the draft outcome direct rather than speculative. Wiley played 33 regular-season games for San Antonio in 1980-81. NBA.com lists him at 5.7 points, 1.9 rebounds and 8.2 minutes per game. He also appeared in three playoff games, although his postseason role totaled only five minutes. San Antonio waived Wiley on October 27, 1981. He then played one more NBA season with San Diego, but that Clippers production does not belong to the Spurs' realized return.

sections.heading: Why San Antonio Gets the Slight Edge
sections.body: Neither side uncovered major value. Kansas City received 21 games from Green, while San Antonio turned the pick into 33 regular-season Wiley games plus three brief playoff appearances. The Spurs therefore received a little more direct team service from the primary asset. Any cash would only strengthen San Antonio's side, but this review does not rely on it because the amount is not documented in the reviewed public records.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Spurs Edge, B-/C+. San Antonio receives a B- for converting the pick into 33 Wiley games and a small playoff contribution. Kansas City receives a C+ for 21 useful Green games, but the return ended after one season and produced no further realized branch.

sections.heading: The Original Trade Was Brewer for a Second-Round Pick
sections.body: Basketball-Reference records Detroit sending Jim Brewer to Portland on September 18, 1979 for a 1981 second-round pick. That selection eventually became No. 39 overall, but Detroit did not make the pick itself.

sections.heading: Brewer Gave Portland One Useful Season
sections.body: Brewer played 67 regular-season games for the Trail Blazers in 1979-80. He averaged 2.9 points, 3.8 rebounds and 15.2 minutes while filling a reserve frontcourt role. The direct playing return was modest, but Portland did not let the asset expire. On October 8, 1980, the Trail Blazers traded Brewer to the Lakers for a 1984 second-round pick.

sections.heading: That Pick Became Jerome Kersey
sections.body: Portland kept the 1984 second-rounder and used it at No. 46 on Jerome Kersey. The downstream link is direct: Brewer was the outgoing asset in the trade that brought Portland the exact pick used on Kersey. Kersey then played 831 regular-season games for the Trail Blazers. Basketball-Reference's franchise leaderboard ranks him second in Portland history in games played, behind only Clyde Drexler. That transforms what initially looked like a one-year Brewer rental into a long-term franchise asset chain. Kersey became a major part of Portland's core through the late 1980s and early 1990s, including the teams that reached the 1990 and 1992 NBA Finals.

sections.heading: Detroit Converted Its Pick Into Wayne Robinson
sections.body: Detroit also avoided simply waiting for the 1981 draft. On October 1, 1980, the Pistons traded the incoming second-round pick to the Lakers for Wayne Robinson. Robinson played 81 games for Detroit in 1980-81 and averaged 7.9 points, 3.6 rebounds and 1.4 assists in 19.7 minutes. It was his only NBA season, but that is still a substantial one-year return from a second-round asset. The Lakers later used the pick at No. 39 on Harvey Knuckles. Knuckles therefore belongs to the final draft identity of the pick, not Detroit's realized on-court return. Detroit's value came from Robinson.

sections.heading: Why Portland Wins Clearly
sections.body: Detroit's side was respectable: 81 Robinson games is a better return than many second-round picks produce. But Portland received 67 Brewer games and then converted Brewer directly into the pick used on Kersey. Kersey's 831 Portland games dwarf the one-season Robinson return and turn the original transaction into a major Trail Blazers asset-chain win.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Trail Blazers Win, A+/B. Portland receives an A+ because Brewer produced a season of depth and then directly became the draft pick used on Jerome Kersey, who played 831 games for the franchise. Detroit receives a B because it turned the second-round pick into 81 games of Wayne Robinson rather than losing the asset at the draft.

sources.title: 1979-80 Portland Trail Blazers roster and statistics

sections.heading: New Jersey Acquired Phegley for Williamson and a Second
sections.body: Basketball-Reference records the February 4, 1980 trade as John Williamson and a 1981 second-round pick from New Jersey to Washington for Roger Phegley. The pick eventually became No. 44 Steve Lingenfelter.

sections.heading: Phegley Played 28 Games, Then Became Foots Walker
sections.body: Phegley played 28 games for the Nets after the trade, logging 541 minutes and scoring 327 points. He averaged 11.7 points, 2.5 rebounds and 1.1 assists while shooting 48.5 percent. New Jersey did not simply lose him afterward. On September 24, 1980, the Nets traded Phegley straight up to Cleveland for Foots Walker. Because that was a one-for-one transaction, Walker is a direct downstream return from the Phegley branch. Walker then played 41 games for New Jersey in 1980-81, 77 in 1981-82, 79 in 1982-83 and 34 in 1983-84. That is 231 regular-season Nets games, including a 54-start season in 1981-82.

sections.heading: Washington Got 39 Games From Williamson
sections.body: Williamson played 30 games for the Bullets after the trade in 1979-80, averaging 11.6 points in 20.1 minutes. He returned for nine games in 1980-81 before his Washington tenure ended. That gives the Bullets 39 regular-season appearances from the veteran guard. Williamson was still a useful scorer immediately after the trade, but the tenure was brief.

sections.heading: The Draft Pick Added Seven Bullets Games
sections.body: Washington retained the incoming second-round selection and used it at No. 44 in the 1981 draft on Steve Lingenfelter. He did not make the Bullets until 1982-83, when he appeared in seven regular-season games. Washington waived Lingenfelter on December 10, 1982. He later played three games for San Antonio, but those appearances came after Washington had released him and are not part of the Bullets' realized return.

sections.heading: Why New Jersey Wins
sections.body: Washington received 39 Williamson games and seven later Lingenfelter games. That is real value, but neither branch became a durable rotation asset for the Bullets. New Jersey received 28 Phegley games and then converted him directly into Walker, who remained with the Nets for four seasons and 231 regular-season games. The straight-swap downstream chain makes the difference decisive.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win, A-/C+. New Jersey receives an A- for the Phegley production plus the direct Walker conversion that yielded 231 additional games. Washington receives a C+ for 39 Williamson games and seven Lingenfelter appearances, a modest return that never approached the duration of the Nets branch.

sections.heading: Golden State Sold White's Rights
sections.body: Basketball-Reference records the September 10, 1980 transaction as a sale of Jo Jo White's player rights from Golden State to Kansas City. The Kings transaction ledger confirms the acquisition. The canonical TradeVerdicts record describes the return as cash. The reviewed transaction sources do not provide the amount, so this review preserves the cash asset but does not invent a dollar value.

sections.heading: White Played 13 Games for Kansas City
sections.body: White appeared in 13 regular-season games for the Kings. He logged 236 minutes and averaged 6.4 points, 2.8 assists and 1.6 rebounds in 18.2 minutes per game. That made him a short-term reserve rather than a major rotation addition. He still produced actual NBA minutes, which gives Kansas City a concrete realized basketball return from the purchase. Contemporary transaction research compiled by the Association for Professional Basketball Research records White announcing his retirement on November 3, 1980. That ended his NBA career and limited the Kings' return to those 13 games.

sections.heading: Golden State Received Cash, but the Amount Is Unknown
sections.body: The Warriors' side is harder to quantify because the sale price is not documented in the reviewed public ledgers. Golden State had already received 107 regular-season games from White across parts of the previous two seasons before this transaction. This review does not re-credit those games here because they occurred before the September 1980 sale. The relevant return is only the cash received for his rights. That is still realized value, but without an amount there is no defensible way to compare it precisely with Kansas City's 13 games.

sections.heading: Why Kansas City Gets Only a Slight Edge
sections.body: The Kings received measurable on-court production, even if it lasted less than a month of the regular season before White retired. Golden State converted an asset it no longer intended to use into cash. The unknown sale amount prevents a harsh grade, but it also prevents the Warriors from matching Kansas City's documented playing value on source-backed evidence.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Kings Edge, C/C-. Kansas City receives a C for 13 games and 236 minutes from a veteran guard before retirement. Golden State receives a C- because the club realized cash value from the rights, but the amount is undocumented and cannot be scored as more than a limited return.

sections.heading: The Deal Was More Than a Simple Pick Swap
sections.body: Atlanta received the No. 4 pick in 1981, the No. 38 pick and Chicago's option involving a 1982 first-round swap. Chicago received the No. 6 pick, Atlanta's 1982 second-rounder and the same contractual swap structure. The 1982 first-round option was never exercised, so this review assigns it no realized basketball value.

sections.heading: Atlanta Used No. 4 on Al Wood
sections.body: The Hawks selected Al Wood fourth overall, but his Atlanta tenure was extremely short. Wood played 19 games for the Hawks in 1981-82, all off the bench. He averaged 4.8 points and 2.3 rebounds in 12.5 minutes. On January 20, 1982, Atlanta traded Wood and Charlie Criss to San Diego for Freeman Williams. Because Criss was also included, this review does not credit the entire Williams return to Wood. Williams played 23 Atlanta games after the trade and averaged 4.8 points in 8.2 minutes. The shared downstream branch therefore added only limited realized value.

sections.heading: The Extra Atlanta Second-Rounder Produced No NBA Games
sections.body: Atlanta used the No. 38 pick on Clyde Bradshaw. Basketball-Reference lists Bradshaw as a Hawks draft pick but records no NBA regular-season career. That makes the second-round component a zero-game outcome.

sections.heading: Chicago Turned No. 6 Into Five Woolridge Seasons
sections.body: The Bulls selected Orlando Woolridge sixth overall. Woolridge played 75 games as a rookie, then 57 in 1982-83, 75 in 1983-84, 77 in 1984-85 and 70 in 1985-86. That is 354 regular-season games for Chicago over five seasons. His production rose steadily. Woolridge averaged 19.3 points in 1983-84, 22.9 in 1984-85 and 20.7 in 1985-86. That long starting-caliber tenure is the dominant realized asset in the trade.

sections.heading: Chicago's 1982 Second-Rounder Did Not Add NBA Value
sections.body: The Bulls used Atlanta's 1982 second-round pick at No. 26 on Ricky Frazier. Frazier never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. The second-round asset therefore does not materially widen Chicago's edge beyond Woolridge.

sections.heading: Why Chicago Wins Decisively
sections.body: Atlanta received only 19 Wood games, a no-game second-round pick and a diluted later return involving Freeman Williams. The unexercised 1982 swap added nothing. Chicago received 354 Woolridge games and multiple seasons of high-level scoring from the No. 6 pick. The Bulls' other second-round asset produced no NBA games, but they did not need it to win the deal.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win, A/C-. Chicago receives an A for five Woolridge seasons and 354 regular-season games. Atlanta receives a C- because Wood lasted only 19 games, Bradshaw never played in the NBA and the later Wood trade required another outgoing player.

sections.heading: Atlanta Turned One Fourth-Round Pick Into Two NBA Contributors
sections.body: The canonical record dates the transaction to August 11, 1981, while Basketball-Reference's Atlanta, New Jersey and league ledgers list August 12. The transaction terms match: Atlanta received Rory Sparrow and a 1985 fourth-round pick, while New Jersey received Atlanta's 1982 fourth-round pick. For the retrospective grade, the one-day source discrepancy does not change the asset comparison.

sections.heading: Sparrow Became Atlanta's Starting Point Guard
sections.body: Sparrow played all 82 regular-season games for Atlanta in 1981-82 and started all 82. He averaged 10.5 points and 5.2 assists while helping the Hawks return to the playoffs. He remained Atlanta's starter in 1982-83, appearing in 49 games and starting all 49 before the Hawks traded him to New York on February 12, 1983 for Scott Hastings and cash. That gives Atlanta 131 regular-season games and 131 starts directly from Sparrow before any downstream return is considered.

sections.heading: The 1985 Pick Became John Battle
sections.body: The second Atlanta asset became the No. 84 selection in the 1985 NBA Draft. Atlanta used it on John Battle, who played six seasons with the Hawks from 1985-86 through 1990-91. He appeared in 416 regular-season games for Atlanta and developed from a reserve guard into a larger rotation role, including 48 starts in 1989-90. Battle's NBA career lasted 10 seasons, but this review credits only his Hawks tenure to this trade.

sections.heading: New Jersey's Pick Produced No NBA Games
sections.body: The Nets used Atlanta's 1982 fourth-round pick at No. 80 on James Griffin. Basketball-Reference lists Griffin as a drafted forward but shows no NBA regular-season statistics. The direct New Jersey return therefore produced zero NBA games. No reviewed downstream transaction branch from Griffin changes that result.

sections.heading: Why Atlanta Wins Decisively
sections.body: Atlanta received immediate value from Sparrow and long-term value from Battle. Together, the two direct branches produced 547 Hawks regular-season games, with Sparrow supplying 131 starts before being traded again. New Jersey's lone incoming pick produced no NBA regular-season games. Even without assigning value to Atlanta's later Sparrow-for-Hastings-and-cash transaction, the realized basketball return is overwhelmingly one-sided.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win, A+/F. Atlanta receives an A+ for 131 Sparrow games and starts plus 416 Battle games from the fourth-round pick. New Jersey receives an F because the No. 80 James Griffin selection produced no NBA regular-season games.

sections.heading: Both Teams Got One Strong Season
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's New Jersey transaction ledger records the October 25, 1981 mechanism directly. The Nets signed Ray Williams as a veteran free agent and sent Maurice Lucas to the Knicks as compensation. The canonical right-of-first-refusal wording describes the same restricted-free-agent process: New York declined to keep Williams, New Jersey secured him, and Lucas became the compensation moving the other way.

sections.heading: Williams Led the Nets in Scoring
sections.body: Williams played all 82 regular-season games for New Jersey in 1981-82 and started 69. He averaged 20.4 points, 6.0 assists, 4.0 rebounds and 2.4 steals in 33.3 minutes. He finished as the Nets' leading scorer during a dramatic team improvement. New Jersey rose from 24-58 in 1980-81 to 44-38 and reached the playoffs. Williams was not a long-term Net. He moved to Kansas City the following season, so this review credits New Jersey with one high-level season rather than his later career.

sections.heading: Lucas Was Equally Important for New York
sections.body: Maurice Lucas played 80 regular-season games for the Knicks in 1981-82 and started 74. He averaged 15.8 points and 11.3 rebounds while playing 33.4 minutes per game. Lucas led New York in rebounding and gave the Knicks a durable veteran frontcourt presence. Like Williams, however, his stay lasted only one season; he joined Phoenix for 1982-83. The Knicks did not reach the playoffs, but Lucas's individual production was substantial and should not be discounted simply because the team finished 33-49.

sections.heading: Why This Is an Even Trade
sections.body: Williams delivered more scoring and playmaking, and his arrival coincided with a 20-win improvement and playoff berth for New Jersey. Lucas delivered elite rebounding, interior production and nearly the same availability for New York. Both sides received roughly one full season from a proven starter. Neither retained the player long enough to create a major long-term advantage, and both players performed at a level that justified the unusual compensation mechanism.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, A-/A-. New Jersey receives an A- for an 82-game, 20.4-point season from Williams during a playoff turnaround. New York receives an A- for 80 games, 74 starts and an 11.3-rebound season from Lucas. The strengths were different, but the realized one-season value was balanced enough that forcing a winner would overstate the margin.

sections.heading: Boston Sold Jackson's Rights for Cash
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Boston, Chicago and league transaction ledgers agree on the December 9, 1981 mechanism. Boston sold the player rights to Tracy Jackson to the Bulls. The canonical source package records cash as Boston's return. The reviewed public ledgers do not identify the amount, so this review preserves the cash component without assigning it a speculative dollar value.

sections.heading: Jackson Immediately Joined Chicago's Rotation
sections.body: Jackson had appeared in only 11 games for Boston before the sale. With Chicago, he played 38 regular-season games in the remainder of 1981-82 and logged 412 minutes. He averaged 4.5 points in 10.8 minutes while shooting 47.3 percent from the field. He did not start, but the Bulls received a usable reserve rather than a set of inactive rights.

sections.heading: His Bigger Contribution Came the Next Season
sections.body: Jackson returned for 78 games in 1982-83 and made three starts. His role grew to 16.8 minutes per game, and he averaged 6.3 points, 2.3 rebounds and 1.3 assists. Across the two Chicago seasons, Jackson played 116 regular-season games and scored 662 points. Those two years account for nearly all of his NBA career; he appeared in only two more games, both with Indiana in 1983-84.

sections.heading: Boston Received Cash but No Basketball Asset
sections.body: The Celtics converted Jackson's rights into cash rather than holding a player who was buried on a deep roster. That is a rational transaction and gives Boston a real return. The missing public dollar amount limits any attempt to compare the cash precisely with Jackson's production. There is no evidence in the reviewed sources that the payment represented a major asset.

sections.heading: Why Chicago Gets the Edge
sections.body: Chicago paid cash and received two seasons of reserve value, including a 78-game second season. Boston received an unquantified financial return. For a minor transaction, 116 regular-season games is a useful realized outcome. It is enough to give the Bulls the clear basketball edge without turning the deal into a major historical win.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win, B/C+. Chicago receives a B because Jackson supplied 116 regular-season games and two seasons of rotation depth for a cash-only cost. Boston receives a C+ because it monetized a little-used player, with the unknown cash amount preventing a more exact assessment.

sections.heading: Houston Bought Two Useful Seasons of James Bailey
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's New Jersey transaction ledger records the November 10, 1982 trade as James Bailey to Houston for two second-round picks: one in 1983 and another in 1985. The picks eventually became No. 44 Horace Owens and No. 36 Yvon Joseph.

sections.heading: Bailey Immediately Became a Houston Starter
sections.body: Bailey played 69 regular-season games for the Rockets in 1982-83 and started 39. He averaged 24.9 minutes, 14.1 points and 6.8 rebounds while shooting 49.7 percent. Houston was a 14-win rebuilding team, so those numbers did not translate into team success. Still, Bailey's role was real: he logged 1,715 minutes and became one of the club's most productive frontcourt players. He returned for 73 games in 1983-84, all off the bench, averaging 8.8 points and 4.0 rebounds in 16.1 minutes. That gives Houston 142 direct regular-season games from Bailey over two seasons, including 39 starts.

sections.heading: The 1983 Pick Became Horace Owens
sections.body: New Jersey used the No. 44 pick in the 1983 NBA Draft on Rhode Island guard Horace Owens. Owens never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. The Nets later moved his rights with Eddie Phillips to Philadelphia during the 1983 preseason, and Owens was waived before the season. Because the player never logged an NBA game, this review treats the 1983 pick's direct basketball return as zero.

sections.heading: The 1985 Pick Became Yvon Joseph
sections.body: The second Houston pick conveyed at No. 36 in 1985, where New Jersey selected Georgia Tech center Yvon Joseph. Joseph played one NBA regular-season game for the Nets in 1985-86. He logged five minutes, scored two points at the free-throw line and did not start. That single appearance was his entire NBA career.

sections.heading: Why Houston Wins Clearly
sections.body: New Jersey turned two second-round picks into one NBA appearance from Joseph and no NBA games from Owens. Houston received two seasons and 142 games from Bailey. The picks had some transactional and roster flexibility before being exercised, but their realized player value was negligible compared with Bailey's immediate production.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win, A-/D. Houston receives an A- for acquiring 142 games, 39 starts and a productive first season from Bailey at the cost of two second-rounders. New Jersey receives a D because the two selections produced just one direct NBA game between them.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Sold Restani's Rights for Cash
sections.body: Basketball-Reference lists the August 31, 1979 transaction as Milwaukee selling Kevin Restani's player rights to San Antonio. The Spurs' transaction page records the corresponding rights acquisition. The reviewed sources do not disclose the cash amount. That means Milwaukee's return can be recognized as a completed sale, but it cannot be assigned a meaningful basketball value or compared to a known player or draft asset.

sections.heading: Restani Immediately Joined the Spurs Rotation
sections.body: San Antonio got a substantial first season from Restani. He played all 82 games in 1979-80 and logged 1,966 minutes, averaging 10.7 points, 4.7 rebounds and 2.3 assists in 24.0 minutes per game. The Spurs used him as a real rotation forward rather than end-of-bench depth. Basketball-Reference's depth chart shows him behind Mark Olberding at small forward but with nearly 2,000 minutes and 3.5 win shares.

sections.heading: The Value Continued Beyond One Season
sections.body: Restani returned for 64 games in 1980-81 and another 13 for San Antonio in 1981-82. Across the three seasons, he appeared in 159 Spurs regular-season games before finishing 1981-82 with Cleveland. His role declined after the first year, but San Antonio still converted a cash purchase into multiple seasons of usable NBA minutes. That is much more concrete than the typical rights sale in which the acquired player never reaches the rotation.

sections.heading: Why San Antonio Wins the Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: Milwaukee may have had a sensible roster or financial reason to monetize Restani's rights, and the Bucks had already received 81 games from him in 1978-79. This review does not evaluate that prior Milwaukee season because it occurred before the trade. After the transaction, San Antonio received 159 games, including a full 82-game season with double-digit scoring. Milwaukee received cash with no documented amount or downstream basketball asset tied to it.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Spurs Win, A-/C. San Antonio receives an A- for three seasons and 159 regular-season games from Restani, including a 10.7-point first year. Milwaukee receives a C because the team received a real cash return, but the amount is unknown and no later basketball asset can be traced to the sale.

sections.heading: Utah Bought a Starting-Caliber Season for a Second-Round Pick
sections.body: Basketball-Reference records Denver trading Tom Boswell to Utah on November 20, 1979 for a 1980 second-round pick. Denver later used that selection at No. 41 on center Jawann Oldham.

sections.heading: Boswell Became an Immediate Jazz Contributor
sections.body: Boswell played 61 games for Utah after the trade and logged 1,555 minutes. He averaged 11.5 points, 5.4 rebounds and 1.9 assists while shooting 57.3 percent from the field. That was meaningful rotation value from a player acquired for a second-round selection. He had averaged 11.3 points in 18 Denver games before the trade, so Utah did not receive an end-of-bench reclamation project; it received a productive 26-year-old forward who immediately filled a regular role. Boswell did not play in the NBA from 1980-81 through 1982-83. He later signed again with Utah in September 1983 and appeared in 38 more games during 1983-84. Because that return came through a new contract several years later, this review does not credit those later games to the 1979 trade.

sections.heading: Denver Got Only Four Games From Oldham
sections.body: Denver selected Oldham with the No. 41 pick in June 1980. He appeared in four games for the Nuggets, averaging 5.3 minutes, 1.0 point and 1.3 rebounds. The Nuggets waived Oldham on October 21, 1980. Houston later signed him as a free agent in October 1981, and Oldham went on to play 329 NBA games overall. That later career belongs to other teams; Denver captured only four games from the pick.

sections.heading: Why Utah Wins
sections.body: Utah received 61 useful games and more than 1,500 minutes from Boswell immediately after the trade. Denver's second-round pick produced four games before the player was waived. Oldham's later longevity does not change the grade because the Nuggets did not retain him or convert him into another asset. The realized comparison is sharply one-sided.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Jazz Win, A-/D. Utah receives an A- for obtaining a productive 61-game season from Boswell at the cost of a second-round pick. Denver receives a D because the No. 41 selection produced only four Nuggets appearances before Oldham was waived.

sections.heading: The Authoritative Ledgers Show Peck for a Second-Round Pick
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Phoenix, league and executive transaction records agree on the June 9, 1980 deal: Dallas sent Wiley Peck to Phoenix for a 1981 second-round pick that later became Elston Turner. The legacy Dallas source record also contains a generic future-considerations line. None of the reviewed authoritative transaction ledgers lists that extra term, so this review preserves it as an unverified legacy-source detail rather than scoring it.

sections.heading: Peck Never Played for Phoenix
sections.body: Peck had played 52 games for San Antonio as a rookie in 1979-80 before Dallas selected him in the expansion draft and immediately moved him to Phoenix. The Suns waived Peck on September 8, 1980. Basketball-Reference records no Phoenix regular-season appearances for him, and his 52-game Spurs season remained his entire NBA playing career. That leaves Phoenix with zero direct on-court production from the acquired player.

sections.heading: Dallas Used the Pick on Elston Turner
sections.body: The second-round pick landed at No. 43 in the 1981 draft, where Dallas selected Elston Turner. He immediately became a useful rotation wing. Turner played 80 games as a rookie, starting 62 and averaging 8.3 points, 3.8 rebounds and 2.4 assists in 25.0 minutes. He followed with 59 games in 1982-83 and 47 more in 1983-84. That gives Dallas 186 regular-season Turner games across three seasons, including 79 starts and 3,411 minutes. He later continued his NBA career with Denver and Chicago, but this review stops Dallas's realized value at his Mavericks tenure.

sections.heading: Why Dallas Wins Clearly
sections.body: Phoenix surrendered a second-round pick for a player who never appeared in a regular-season game for the Suns. Dallas turned that pick into three seasons of useful wing depth and a rookie-year starter. The unverified future-considerations line is not needed to decide the trade. Even grading only the terms corroborated by Phoenix and league records, Dallas received substantially more realized basketball value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win, B+/F. Dallas receives a B+ for 186 Turner games across three seasons, including 62 rookie starts. Phoenix receives an F because Peck was waived before playing a regular-season game for the Suns.

sections.heading: The Public Ledgers Show Silas, Yonakor and One Second-Round Pick
sections.body: Basketball-Reference records Cleveland acquiring James Silas and Rich Yonakor from San Antonio on June 16, 1981 for a 1982 second-round pick that later became Oliver Robinson. The frozen Cavaliers source package also includes cash going to San Antonio. Because that term is not shown in the reviewed Basketball-Reference ledgers, this review preserves it as a frozen-source term but does not invent an amount.

sections.heading: Silas Gave Cleveland 67 Games
sections.body: Silas played 67 games for the Cavaliers in 1981-82 and started 34. He averaged 11.2 points, 3.3 assists and 1.6 rebounds in 21.6 minutes. For a veteran guard acquired at age 32, that was a meaningful one-season return. Silas did not play in 1982-83 because of a back injury and never appeared in another NBA game. Cleveland therefore received one useful season rather than a multi-year branch.

sections.heading: Yonakor Never Played for Cleveland
sections.body: Cleveland acquired Yonakor's draft rights but waived him on October 27, 1981. San Antonio later signed Yonakor as a free agent on March 8, 1982. He played 10 games for the Spurs, but those appearances came after Cleveland had released him and therefore are not realized Cavaliers value from this trade. This review credits Cleveland with the acquired rights but zero NBA games from that branch.

sections.heading: San Antonio Used the Pick on Oliver Robinson
sections.body: The 1982 second-round selection landed at No. 24 and became Oliver Robinson. Robinson played 35 games for San Antonio in 1982-83, all off the bench, averaging 2.9 points, 0.6 assists and 0.5 rebounds in 4.2 minutes. That was his only NBA season.

sections.heading: Why Cleveland Gets the Edge
sections.body: San Antonio received 35 Robinson games plus an unquantified cash term preserved from the frozen source package. Cleveland received 67 Silas games, 34 starts and materially larger playing time and production. Yonakor's rights added no Cavaliers games, so the grade does not depend on that asset. The unknown cash prevents an extreme grade gap, but the documented basketball value still favors Cleveland.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Cavaliers Edge, B+/C+. Cleveland receives a B+ for 67 Silas games and 34 starts. San Antonio receives a C+ for 35 Robinson games plus an unquantified frozen-source cash term.

sections.heading: Cleveland Bought One Season of Guard Depth
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Cleveland transaction ledger records the August 24, 1979 deal: the Cavaliers sent a 1981 third-round pick to Portland for Willie Smith. The pick later became the No. 50 selection used on Derek Holcomb.

sections.heading: Smith Played 62 Games for the Cavaliers
sections.body: Smith had appeared in only 16 NBA games before arriving in Cleveland, including 13 for Portland in 1978-79. The Cavaliers gave him by far the largest role of his NBA career. He played 62 games in 1979-80 and logged 1,051 minutes. Smith averaged 4.8 points, 4.2 assists and 2.0 rebounds in 17.0 minutes per game while serving as reserve point-guard depth. Those 62 games were his final NBA season, so the trade did not create a long-term Cleveland piece. It did, however, provide a full year of usable rotation minutes from a player acquired for a future third-round selection.

sections.heading: Portland Used the Pick on Derek Holcomb
sections.body: The Trail Blazers kept the incoming pick through the 1981 draft and selected Derek Holcomb 50th overall in the third round. Holcomb never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Basketball-Reference lists the selection in Portland's 1981 draft history but shows no NBA statistical line for him. That means Portland successfully converted the asset into a player selection but received no realized NBA playing value from the branch.

sections.heading: Why Cleveland Wins the Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: This is not a franchise-changing trade. Smith's Cleveland tenure lasted one season, and his role was modest. But 62 games, 1,051 minutes and 259 assists are concrete value. Portland's side produced a third-round selection that never reached the NBA. With no documented downstream transaction attached to Holcomb, there is no later value to offset Smith's season in Cleveland.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win, B-/D+. Cleveland receives a B- for a full season of reserve guard production from Smith. Portland receives a D+ because the acquired third-round pick was exercised at No. 50 but produced no NBA regular-season games.

sections.heading: Indiana Bought Four Seasons of Center Depth
sections.body: Basketball-Reference records Indiana sending a 1981 second-round pick to Portland on October 9, 1979 for Clemon Johnson. Portland eventually used the selection at No. 26 on Brian Jackson.

sections.heading: Johnson Immediately Entered the Pacers Rotation
sections.body: Johnson played 79 games in 1979-80, averaging 6.0 points, 5.0 rebounds and 1.5 blocks in 19.5 minutes. He followed with 81 games in 1980-81 and 79 games in 1981-82, starting 42 in the latter season. Johnson added 51 Indiana games in 1982-83 before being traded in February. That gives the Pacers 290 regular-season appearances from the player acquired for one second-round pick. The production was not star-level, but it was durable. Johnson became a multi-year rotation center and played a much larger role than the outgoing draft asset ever produced for Portland.

sections.heading: Johnson Also Retained Trade Value
sections.body: On February 15, 1983, Indiana traded Johnson and a 1984 third-round pick to Philadelphia. The Pacers received Russ Schoene, a 1983 first-round pick and a 1984 second-round pick. This review does not assign the entire Philadelphia package to Johnson because Indiana also included the third-round selection. The important point is that Johnson remained a meaningful trade asset after 290 Pacers games rather than leaving for nothing.

sections.heading: Portland's Pick Did Not Produce NBA Games
sections.body: The Trail Blazers held the pick and selected Brian Jackson at No. 26 in the 1981 draft. Basketball-Reference lists Jackson as a Portland draft choice but records no NBA regular-season games. Jackson had a professional career outside the NBA, but those results do not create realized NBA value for Portland in this archive.

sections.heading: Why Indiana Wins Easily
sections.body: Indiana received four seasons of rotation play, 290 regular-season games and a player who still carried enough value to be included in a later first-round-pick package. Portland received one second-round selection that produced no NBA games. There is little ambiguity in the realized comparison.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pacers Win, A-/D. Indiana receives an A- for 290 Johnson games plus later trade utility. Portland receives a D because the No. 26 selection on Brian Jackson produced no NBA regular-season appearances.

sections.heading: Cleveland Moved a Longtime Veteran for a Third-Round Pick
sections.body: Basketball-Reference records Cleveland trading Bingo Smith to San Diego on October 27, 1979 for a 1980 third-round pick. The selection later landed at No. 53 and was used on Stuart House.

sections.heading: Smith Gave San Diego a Full Rotation Season
sections.body: Smith had played only eight games for Cleveland before the trade, but he immediately stepped into a much larger Clippers role. He appeared in 70 games for San Diego and logged 1,988 minutes. He averaged 11.7 points, 3.5 rebounds and 1.3 assists in 28.4 minutes. That made him a regular wing contributor rather than a short-term end-of-bench addition. The Clippers did not keep him beyond the season. Dallas selected Smith from San Diego in the May 28, 1980 expansion draft. This review therefore stops the Clippers return at those 70 games and does not assign any of Smith's later Dallas production to San Diego.

sections.heading: Cleveland Used the Pick on Stuart House
sections.body: The Cavaliers kept the incoming third-round selection and drafted Stuart House at No. 53 in June 1980. Basketball-Reference lists House as a Cleveland draft pick but records no NBA regular-season games. The pick therefore produced no direct on-court value for the Cavaliers. There is no documented downstream NBA transaction branch from House that changes the comparison. Cleveland acquired a draft opportunity, but the realized result was zero games.

sections.heading: Why San Diego Wins
sections.body: The Clippers received 70 games and nearly 2,000 minutes from Smith before losing him in the expansion draft. Cleveland received one third-round selection that never reached an NBA regular-season floor. Smith was near the end of his career, so this was not a long-term franchise-changing acquisition. Even so, a full season of double-digit scoring is decisively more realized value than a draft pick that produced no NBA games.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win, B+/D. San Diego receives a B+ for 70 useful Smith games in 1979-80. Cleveland receives a D because the No. 53 selection on Stuart House produced no NBA regular-season appearances.

sections.heading: Kansas City Turned a Second-Round Pick Into a Useful Veteran
sections.body: Basketball-Reference records Indiana trading Len Elmore to Kansas City on November 27, 1979 for a 1980 second-round pick. Indiana later used the selection at No. 40 on Dick Miller.

sections.heading: Elmore Played 58 Games for the Kings
sections.body: Elmore appeared in 58 Kansas City games during 1979-80 and logged 915 minutes. He averaged 4.5 points and 4.4 rebounds in 15.8 minutes, giving the Kings a real reserve interior role rather than a brief trial. The playing return lasted only that season, but the asset chain did not end there. Milwaukee signed Elmore as a veteran free agent in June 1980, and Kansas City received a 1981 second-round pick as compensation. The Kings later included that compensation pick with Otis Birdsong in the June 1981 trade that brought Cliff Robinson from New Jersey. This review does not assign Robinson's entire return to the Elmore branch because Birdsong was the principal outgoing asset, but the pick remained legitimate transaction currency.

sections.heading: Indiana Got Eight NBA Games From Miller
sections.body: The Pacers used the No. 40 pick on Miller in the 1980 draft. Basketball-Reference credits him with an eight-game NBA career, all in 1980-81, averaging 1.0 point and 0.9 rebounds. There is no meaningful later NBA transaction branch attached to Miller in the reviewed sources. The pick therefore produced only those eight appearances for Indiana.

sections.heading: Why Kansas City Wins
sections.body: Kansas City received 58 games of usable center depth and then a compensation second-round pick when Elmore left. Indiana's return produced eight games from a second-round rookie and no comparable downstream asset. Elmore was not a star for the Kings, so the grade should not overstate the transaction. The gap comes from basic realized value: Kansas City received both playing time and a later compensation asset, while Indiana received almost nothing on the court.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Win, B+/D. Kansas City receives a B+ for 58 Elmore games plus the later compensation pick. Indiana receives a D because Dick Miller produced only eight NBA appearances before his career ended.

sources.title: 1979-80 Kansas City Kings roster and statistics

sections.heading: Washington Turned a Third-Round Pick Into Immediate Guard Help
sections.body: Basketball-Reference records New York trading Jim Cleamons to Washington on December 4, 1979 for a 1981 third-round pick. The Knicks later used that selection at No. 57 on Frank Brickowski.

sections.heading: Cleamons Played 57 Games for Washington
sections.body: Cleamons had appeared in 22 games for New York before the trade. After arriving in Washington, he played 57 games and logged 1,535 minutes. He averaged 7.8 points, 4.4 assists and 2.3 rebounds in 26.9 minutes. He did not start a regular-season game, but he was a substantial reserve guard and gave the Bullets a real rotation return for a future third-round selection.

sections.heading: Brickowski Never Played for the Knicks
sections.body: New York kept the pick and drafted Brickowski in the third round of the 1981 draft. He then spent three seasons playing outside the NBA before making his league debut with Seattle in 1984-85. Seattle signed Brickowski as a free agent. The reviewed transaction records do not show New York converting his draft rights into another NBA asset, so his later 731-game NBA career cannot be credited to the Knicks side of this trade. For New York, the realized return was therefore a draft selection that produced zero Knicks regular-season appearances.

sections.heading: Why Washington Wins
sections.body: Washington received 57 games and more than 1,500 minutes from Cleamons during the same season it made the trade. New York received no on-court NBA value from Brickowski and no documented downstream return for his rights. Brickowski eventually became a long-tenured NBA player, but that future success came after Seattle signed him independently. Hindsight grading has to follow the value the original team actually realized.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bullets Win, B+/D. Washington receives a B+ for acquiring a productive 57-game reserve guard at the cost of a third-round pick. New York receives a D because the No. 57 selection never produced a Knicks game or a documented NBA transaction return.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Acquired Evans' Rights for Cash
sections.body: The legacy archive entry dates the transaction October 6, 1980. Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee and San Antonio transaction ledgers both record the player-rights sale on October 7. This review does not silently rewrite the frozen canonical date. Instead, it records the one-day source discrepancy and grades the assets that are clear: Mike Evans to Milwaukee, cash to San Antonio.

sections.heading: Evans Gave Milwaukee 85 Regular-Season Games
sections.body: Evans played 71 games for the Bucks in 1980-81, logging 911 minutes. He averaged 4.5 points and 2.4 assists in 12.8 minutes while appearing on a 60-win team. He also appeared in four playoff games that spring, scoring 25 points in 38 minutes. Evans returned for 14 more Milwaukee games in 1981-82. Across the two regular seasons, he played 85 Bucks games and totaled 1,107 minutes, 376 points and 189 assists. Milwaukee waived Evans during the 1981-82 season. Cleveland later signed him as a free agent, so there is no downstream trade return for the Bucks to credit.

sections.heading: San Antonio Received Unquantified Cash
sections.body: The Spurs' transaction ledger describes the move as a sale of Evans' player rights. The reviewed sources do not state the cash amount. That matters because cash is real consideration even when it creates no player or draft branch. This review does not treat San Antonio's side as zero value; it simply cannot assign a precise realized basketball equivalent to an undocumented payment.

sections.heading: Why Milwaukee Gets the Edge
sections.body: Milwaukee turned cash into 85 regular-season appearances from a reserve guard and four playoff appearances during the 1981 postseason. San Antonio monetized a player it was moving on from, but the amount is unavailable. Without evidence that the payment approached the value of two seasons of usable roster depth, the clearer hindsight return belongs to Milwaukee.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win, B/C+. Milwaukee receives a B for 85 Evans games across two seasons plus limited playoff work. San Antonio receives a C+ for receiving cash of unknown size, with the unquantified amount preventing a harsher grade and keeping confidence at medium.

sections.heading: The Deal Was White for a Future Fourth
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's player transaction record lists the November 3, 1980 trade directly: Seattle sent Golden State a future 1981 fourth-round pick for Rudy White. The selection ultimately landed at No. 76 in the 1981 draft and became Lewis Lloyd.

sections.heading: White Played Only 12 Seattle Games
sections.body: White had appeared in four games for Golden State before the trade. After joining Seattle, he played 12 regular-season games and averaged 3.3 points, 0.9 rebounds and 1.5 assists in 13.8 minutes. Those 12 appearances were the final NBA regular-season games of his career. Seattle therefore received a very small direct return.

sections.heading: The Pick Became Lewis Lloyd
sections.body: Golden State used the acquired fourth-rounder on Lloyd in June 1981. Lloyd played 16 games as a rookie in 1981-82, then appeared in 73 games in 1982-83. In that second season he averaged 9.4 points, 3.6 rebounds and 1.8 assists while starting 24 games. Across the two seasons, Lloyd gave Golden State 89 regular-season games. That is already substantially more realized value than Seattle received from White.

sections.heading: Golden State Also Received Compensation When Lloyd Left
sections.body: On August 29, 1983, Lloyd signed with Houston as a veteran free agent. Basketball-Reference's transaction record states that Golden State received a 1985 second-round pick as compensation. That selection was later used on Bobby Lee Hurt. This review does not need to assign a large value to Hurt to decide the original trade. The compensation pick simply adds another downstream asset to a branch that had already produced 89 games.

sections.heading: Why Golden State Wins
sections.body: Seattle received 12 low-minute White appearances and no documented downstream NBA asset from him. Golden State received 89 Lloyd games, including a useful 1982-83 rotation season, and later recovered a second-round compensation pick when Lloyd left for Houston.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win, B+/D. Golden State receives a B+ for the Lloyd production and later compensation pick. Seattle receives a D because White played only 12 games before his NBA career ended.

sections.heading: The Transaction Was Rights for a Third-Round Pick
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Knicks, Trail Blazers and league transaction ledgers all record the same August 4, 1981 deal. New York sent Tom Barker to Portland for a 1982 third-round pick. The canonical source record describes Barker as draft rights, which is the correct asset framing for this retrospective because Barker was not an active NBA contributor at the time.

sections.heading: Barker Never Played for Portland
sections.body: Barker's Basketball-Reference career page lists 98 NBA games over two seasons, with his final NBA appearances coming in 1978-79. He played for Houston, Boston and New York that season, including 22 Knicks games. He did not return to the NBA afterward. Portland therefore realized zero NBA regular-season games from the Barker rights acquired in this trade. No reviewed transaction source shows a later NBA asset return from those rights that would change the evaluation.

sections.heading: New York Used the Pick on Craig Tucker
sections.body: The incoming third-round selection landed at No. 57 in the 1982 draft. New York used it on Illinois guard Craig Tucker. Basketball-Reference lists Tucker as the No. 57 selection but shows no NBA regular-season statistics. The Knicks therefore also received zero NBA games from their direct asset.

sections.heading: Why This Is an Even Trade
sections.body: This is a rare historical trade where the direct NBA outcome is essentially identical on both sides. Portland acquired rights to a player whose NBA career had already ended. New York acquired a late draft pick that produced a drafted player who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Neither branch generated documented downstream NBA value in the reviewed ledgers. That makes a winner call artificial.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, D/D. Portland receives a D because Barker produced no Trail Blazers games. New York also receives a D because the No. 57 pick on Tucker produced no Knicks or NBA regular-season games. The trade belongs in the even bucket because both realized returns were effectively zero.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Turned a Third-Round Pick Into NBA Depth
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee and Portland transaction ledgers agree on the September 24, 1981 terms. The Bucks received Geoff Crompton, while the Trail Blazers received Milwaukee's 1982 third-round pick. That pick later became No. 66 overall, where Portland selected Phillip Lockett.

sections.heading: Crompton Played 35 Games for a 55-Win Bucks Team
sections.body: Crompton appeared in 35 regular-season games for Milwaukee in 1981-82 and made one start. He logged 203 minutes, averaging 0.8 points and 1.2 rebounds in a limited reserve-center role. The production was modest, but it was real roster value. Milwaukee won 55 games and finished first in the Central Division, so Crompton's contribution came as depth on a contender rather than as empty minutes on a rebuilding team. His Bucks tenure lasted only that season. Crompton later played for San Antonio and Cleveland, but this review credits only the 35 Milwaukee games produced directly by this trade.

sections.heading: Portland Used the Pick on Phillip Lockett
sections.body: The Trail Blazers kept the incoming third-rounder and used it with the 66th pick in the 1982 NBA Draft. Portland selected Alabama center Phillip Lockett. Basketball-Reference's 1982 draft record lists Lockett at No. 66 but shows no NBA regular-season career statistics. That means the direct Portland branch produced zero NBA games.

sections.heading: Why Milwaukee Wins
sections.body: This was a low-cost, low-ceiling transaction, so the grade should not be inflated. Crompton was not a major rotation piece and did not become a long-term Buck. Still, Milwaukee exchanged a third-round pick that ultimately produced no NBA player for 35 games of usable center depth. Portland received the draft asset it wanted, but the realized outcome of that asset was zero NBA appearances.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win, B/F. Milwaukee receives a B because Crompton supplied one season of real NBA depth at minimal acquisition cost. Portland receives an F on realized value because No. 66 pick Phillip Lockett never appeared in an NBA regular-season game.

sections.heading: Utah Turned a Third-Round Pick Into Two Full Seasons
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Detroit, Utah and league transaction ledgers agree on the October 1, 1981 terms. Detroit received Jeff Judkins, while Utah received the Pistons' 1982 third-round pick. The pick ultimately landed at No. 55, where the Jazz selected Louisville guard Jerry Eaves.

sections.heading: Judkins Gave Detroit One Small Reserve Season
sections.body: Judkins appeared in 30 regular-season games for Detroit in 1981-82 and made no starts. He played 251 total minutes, averaging 8.4 minutes and 2.6 points per game. That was the full extent of his Pistons tenure. Judkins played the following season in Portland, so this review credits Detroit only with the 30 games and reserve minutes produced directly after the trade.

sections.heading: Eaves Immediately Played All 82 Games
sections.body: Utah used the incoming pick on Eaves, and the result was much more substantial. As a rookie in 1982-83 he appeared in all 82 games, started seven and averaged 19.4 minutes, 9.3 points and 2.6 assists. He scored 761 points in that first season alone. For a third-round pick, getting a full 82-game rookie campaign with regular rotation minutes is already a strong realized return.

sections.heading: He Added Another 80 Games in Utah
sections.body: Eaves returned for 80 games in 1983-84 and made one start. His scoring role declined to 4.5 points per game, but he still averaged 12.9 minutes and 2.5 assists while remaining part of the Jazz rotation. That gives Utah 162 regular-season games and eight starts from the acquired pick across two seasons before Eaves moved on.

sections.heading: Why Utah Wins Clearly
sections.body: Detroit received a short reserve look at Judkins and no long-term return. Utah converted a third-round pick into a guard who played essentially two full seasons, including a productive 82-game rookie year. The scale of the original transaction was minor, but the gap in realized value is not. Utah received more than five times as many regular-season games and substantially more rotation impact.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Jazz Win, A-/C-. Utah receives an A- because the No. 55 pick became 162 games of useful backcourt depth, including 9.3 points per game as a rookie. Detroit receives a C- because Judkins played only 30 games, never started and left after one season.

sections.heading: New York Turned a Third-Round Pick Into a Starting Guard
sections.body:
The September 30, 1982 transaction sent Ed Sherod from New Jersey to New York for a 1983 third-round pick.

Sherod had not played in the NBA during 1981-82 after spending time in the CBA, but the Knicks gave him a real role immediately.

sections.heading: Sherod Played 64 Games and Started 37
sections.body:
Sherod appeared in 64 regular-season games for New York in 1982-83 and started 37. He played 1,624 minutes, averaging 25.4 per game.

His season totals included 395 points, 311 assists and 96 steals. That works out to 6.2 points, 4.9 assists and 1.5 steals per game.

For the cost of a third-round pick, New York received a legitimate rotation point guard who started more than half of his appearances.

sections.heading: His NBA Career Lasted Only That Season
sections.body:
Sherod did not return to the NBA after 1982-83, so the Knicks did not obtain long-term value.

That limitation keeps the New York grade below the elite range. The trade was still effective because the immediate return was substantial relative to the asset surrendered.

sections.heading: New Jersey's Pick Became Bruce Kuczenski
sections.body:
The Nets used the incoming third-round pick at No. 59 in the 1983 NBA Draft on Connecticut forward Bruce Kuczenski.

Kuczenski played seven regular-season games for New Jersey in 1983-84, made no starts and logged only 28 minutes. He scored 11 points and collected eight rebounds for the Nets.

He later appeared in three games for Philadelphia and five for Indiana, finishing with 15 NBA games total. Those later appearances are not credited to New Jersey.

sections.heading: Why New York Wins Clearly
sections.body:
New Jersey did convert the pick into an NBA player, so the return was not completely empty. Kuczenski's direct Nets contribution, however, was only seven games and 28 minutes.

Sherod gave New York 64 games, 37 starts and more than 1,600 minutes in the same era. Even though his NBA career ended after one season, that is far more direct realized value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win, B+/D. New York receives a B+ for turning a third-round pick into 64 games, 37 starts and useful point-guard production. New Jersey receives a D because Kuczenski reached the NBA but produced only seven Nets games and no starts before moving on.

sections.heading: Portland Got the Only Direct NBA Games
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's Portland transaction ledger records the August 2, 1982 mechanism clearly. Portland signed Jeff Judkins as a veteran free agent and sent Detroit a 1984 third-round pick as compensation.

Judkins played 34 regular-season games for Portland in 1982-83, made no starts and averaged 3.1 points in 9.1 minutes. The Blazers waived him on March 22, 1983.

That is a small return, but it is measurable NBA production.

sections.heading: Detroit Did Not Simply Use the Pick
sections.body:
The canonical record labels the 1984 third-rounder as No. 65 Tim Kearney, but Detroit did not actually make that selection. On August 18, 1983, the Pistons traded the same 1984 third-round pick back to Portland for Pétur Guðmundsson.

That downstream move matters because it changes how Detroit's return should be evaluated. The pick retained transaction value for a year before Detroit rerouted it.

sections.heading: Guðmundsson Produced Zero Detroit Games
sections.body:
Guðmundsson had previously played 68 NBA games for Portland in 1981-82, but he was playing professionally in Iceland during 1983-84 and did not appear for Detroit.

He later returned to the NBA with the Lakers and Spurs, but none of those appearances came with the Pistons. This review therefore credits Detroit with zero direct games from the Guðmundsson branch.

sections.heading: Portland Eventually Drafted Tim Kearney
sections.body:
After reacquiring the pick, Portland used No. 65 in the 1984 NBA Draft on West Virginia center Tim Kearney.

Basketball-Reference's draft record shows no NBA statistics for Kearney, and his player page contains no NBA regular-season line. The terminal draft outcome was therefore zero NBA games.

sections.heading: Why Portland Gets a Slight Edge
sections.body:
Neither side created a durable asset. Portland received 34 low-minute reserve games from Judkins, while Detroit held a third-round pick for roughly a year and used it to acquire rights that produced no Pistons games.

The pick's transaction utility keeps Detroit from receiving a failing grade. Still, Portland received the only realized NBA minutes directly tied to the exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Trail Blazers Win, C+/C. Portland receives a C+ for 34 reserve appearances from Judkins before moving on. Detroit receives a C because the pick retained downstream trade utility, but neither Guðmundsson nor the eventual No. 65 selection produced any Pistons regular-season games.

sections.heading: The Transaction Mechanics Are Source-Closed
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Denver, Washington and league transaction ledgers all record the same December 17, 1981 event: Denver sold Ronnie Valentine's player rights to the Bullets. Carl Scheer's executive transaction ledger independently records the rights sale on the same date. The basic mechanism is therefore high-confidence.

sections.heading: The Missing Piece Is the Cash Amount
sections.body: The public sources reviewed for this review do not state how much Washington paid. That missing figure matters because Denver's entire return was financial rather than a player or draft asset. Assigning a letter grade to the Nuggets would require guessing whether the payment was nominal, meaningful or somewhere between. This review does not introduce a dollar estimate that the source record does not support.

sections.heading: Valentine Produced Zero Games for Washington
sections.body: Valentine had been Denver's No. 51 pick in the 1980 NBA Draft and played 24 regular-season games for the Nuggets in 1980-81. He averaged 3.5 points in 5.1 minutes during that lone NBA season. After Washington acquired his rights, he did not appear in a Bullets regular-season game and never played another NBA game.

sections.heading: The Bullets Still Acquired a Real Asset
sections.body: Zero games does not mean the acquired rights had no value at the moment of the transaction. Washington paid for the opportunity to control Valentine's NBA rights and evaluate whether he could help the roster. The hindsight result is clear: that opportunity did not convert into an NBA appearance. What cannot be measured from the public record is whether the purchase cost was trivial enough that the failed roster bet should still be considered harmless.

sections.heading: Why the Verdict Stays Insufficient Evidence
sections.body: The direction of the basketball outcome is easy to describe: Washington received no games. The scale of Denver's return is not. This review therefore separates factual completion from valuation certainty. The transaction is source-closed, the player outcome is source-closed, and the missing sale price is explicitly preserved as the blocker to a letter-grade verdict.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Insufficient Evidence. Denver received cash for rights that ultimately produced no Washington games, but the public cash amount is unavailable. Washington's on-court return was zero, yet assigning precise grades would imply a valuation of the unknown payment that the evidence cannot support.

sections.heading: Denver Turned a Rights Asset Into Eight Seasons
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's Denver transaction ledger records the July 20, 1982 move as Bill Hanzlik to the Nuggets for the rights to Wally Walker.

Hanzlik had started 76 games for Seattle in 1981-82. Denver acquired him just before his age-25 season and kept him for the rest of his playing career.

sections.heading: Hanzlik Played 593 Games for Denver
sections.body:
Hanzlik appeared in all 82 regular-season games in his first Nuggets season, then 80 in 1983-84 and 80 again in 1984-85. He remained a rotation player through 1989-90.

Across eight Denver seasons, he played 593 regular-season games and started 33. He gave the Nuggets durable wing and forward depth rather than a one-year return.

His best individual recognition came in 1985-86, when he averaged 12.5 points, 4.8 rebounds and 4.0 assists while earning NBA All-Defensive Second Team honors.

sections.heading: Seattle Converted Walker Into a Draft Pick
sections.body:
Wally Walker never played another regular-season game for Seattle after the July 1982 rights transaction. On October 5, the SuperSonics traded Walker to Houston for a 1984 second-round pick.

That later move is important because it means Seattle did not simply receive a dead rights asset. The Walker branch turned into a usable draft selection.

sections.heading: The Pick Became Cory Blackwell
sections.body:
Seattle used the 1984 second-round pick at No. 28 on Wisconsin forward Cory Blackwell.

Blackwell played 60 regular-season games for the SuperSonics in 1984-85, made no starts and averaged 3.4 points in 9.2 minutes. That was his only NBA season.

The downstream return was real, but it was limited to one reserve season.

sections.heading: Why Denver Wins Clearly
sections.body:
Denver received 593 games, eight seasons and an All-Defensive Team year from Hanzlik. Seattle's rights branch eventually produced 60 reserve games from Blackwell.

The SuperSonics deserve credit for converting Walker into another asset, which keeps the trade from looking empty. The scale of Hanzlik's Denver tenure still overwhelms the downstream return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win, A-/C+. Denver receives an A- for eight seasons of durable rotation value and one All-Defensive Second Team campaign. Seattle receives a C+ because the Walker rights were flipped into the pick that became Blackwell, but the final realized return was only 60 games and zero starts.

sections.heading: Houston Got Two Seasons and 77 Starts From Wally Walker
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's Houston transaction ledger records the October 5, 1982 exchange: the Rockets acquired Wally Walker from Seattle for a 1984 second-round pick.

Walker immediately became a regular part of Houston's lineup during a rebuilding season.

sections.heading: He Played All 82 Games in 1982-83
sections.body:
Walker appeared in all 82 regular-season games for Houston in 1982-83 and started 59. He played 2,251 minutes and scored 797 points, which works out to 9.7 points per game.

He also supplied 376 rebounds and 153 assists. The Rockets were not a winning team, but Walker gave them dependable wing minutes throughout the season.

Walker returned for 58 games in 1983-84 and started 18. His role declined to 10.6 minutes and 4.2 points per game, but he still added 244 points before his Houston tenure ended.

Across the two seasons, Walker played 140 regular-season games and started 77.

sections.heading: Seattle Used the Pick on Cory Blackwell
sections.body:
The second-round pick conveyed at No. 28 in the 1984 NBA Draft. Seattle selected Wisconsin forward Cory Blackwell.

Blackwell played 60 regular-season games for the SuperSonics in 1984-85, all off the bench. He logged 551 minutes and averaged 3.4 points and 1.6 rebounds.

Those 60 games were the entirety of his NBA career. He did not return to the league after his rookie season.

sections.heading: The Direct Comparison Favors Houston
sections.body:
Seattle did get an NBA player from the pick, so the return was not empty. Blackwell gave the SuperSonics 60 reserve appearances and a full rookie-season look.

Houston received more than twice as many regular-season games from Walker, plus 77 starts and two years of usable rotation minutes. Walker also scored 1,041 points for the Rockets compared with Blackwell's 202 for Seattle.

The transaction was not franchise-changing for either side, but the realized production gap is clear.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win, B+/C-. Houston receives a B+ because Walker supplied 140 games, 77 starts and two seasons of rotation value for the cost of a second-round pick. Seattle receives a C- because Blackwell reached the NBA and played 60 games, but he never started and his NBA career ended after that one season.

sections.heading: Chicago Received a Short Bratz Stint
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's Chicago, San Antonio and league transaction ledgers agree on the March 8, 1983 terms. The Bulls acquired the rights to restricted free agent Mike Bratz and sent the Spurs a 1983 fourth-round pick.

That selection eventually became No. 90 Brant Weidner.

sections.heading: Bratz Played 15 Bulls Games
sections.body:
Bratz appeared in 15 regular-season games for Chicago to finish the 1982-83 season. He made no starts and averaged 9.3 minutes, 2.6 points and 1.5 assists.

That is a limited return, but it was still immediate NBA rotation value from a fourth-round pick.

Bratz did not remain with Chicago. He signed with Golden State on September 30, 1983 and went on to play all 82 games for the Warriors the following season.

sections.heading: His Later Departure Generated Another Pick
sections.body:
Because Bratz signed with Golden State as a veteran free agent, Chicago received a 1984 fourth-round compensation pick.

The Bulls used that selection at No. 77 on Northeastern forward Mark Halsel. Halsel never appeared in an NBA regular-season game.

This review therefore gives Chicago credit for the extra transaction asset created by Bratz's departure, but not for any on-court value from Halsel.

sections.heading: San Antonio's Pick Became Brant Weidner
sections.body:
The Spurs used the original 1983 fourth-round pick at No. 90 on William & Mary forward Brant Weidner.

Weidner appeared in eight regular-season games for San Antonio in 1983-84, made no starts and averaged 4.8 minutes, 1.0 point and 1.4 rebounds.

Those eight games were the entirety of his NBA career.

sections.heading: Why Chicago Has a Small Edge
sections.body:
Neither side found a long-term player. San Antonio received eight games from Weidner, while Chicago received 15 from Bratz and later generated a fourth-round compensation pick when Bratz left.

The compensation pick ultimately produced zero NBA games, so the edge should stay modest. Still, Chicago extracted more total transaction utility from the original fourth-round asset.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win, C+/C. Chicago receives a C+ for 15 Bratz games plus a later compensation pick. San Antonio receives a C because Weidner reached the NBA but played only eight games and never started. This is a narrow realized-value win, not a franchise-changing transaction.

sections.heading: Kansas City Received a Starting Point Guard
sections.body:
The June 29, 1982 deal exchanged two established guards. New Jersey received Phil Ford, while Kansas City acquired Ray Williams after Williams had just led the Nets in scoring.

The direct returns quickly diverged once the 1982-83 season began.

sections.heading: Williams Started 68 Games for the Kings
sections.body:
Williams played 72 regular-season games for Kansas City and started 68. He averaged 30.1 minutes, 15.4 points, 7.9 assists, 4.5 rebounds and 1.7 steals.

His 569 assists were a major part of a Kings offense that finished among the league's higher-scoring teams. Kansas City went 45-37, a substantial improvement from the previous season's 30-52 record.

Williams stayed only one season before moving to New York, but that one year produced starter-level value across almost the entire schedule.

sections.heading: Ford Barely Played for New Jersey
sections.body:
Ford's Nets tenure was dramatically shorter. He appeared in seven regular-season games, started all seven and played 163 total minutes.

He averaged 6.7 points and 5.4 assists in those appearances. New Jersey then traded Ford to Milwaukee, where he played 70 games and started 56 during the rest of the 1982-83 season.

Those Milwaukee minutes cannot be credited to the Nets. For this trade, New Jersey received seven games and seven starts.

sections.heading: Why Kansas City Wins
sections.body:
Both players were proven NBA guards, so this was not a case where one side took a flyer on an unknown asset. Kansas City simply extracted far more direct use from the player it acquired.

Williams gave the Kings 72 games and 68 starts, while Ford gave New Jersey seven games before being rerouted. Even if the Nets later received something in the Ford-to-Milwaukee transaction, that downstream deal must be evaluated on its own rather than credited automatically here.

The difference in franchise-specific production is too large to call the original exchange balanced.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Win, A-/D-. Kansas City receives an A- for a full season of starting point-guard production from Williams. New Jersey receives a D- because Ford lasted only seven games before another trade, leaving the Nets with very little direct return from this exchange.
