sections.heading: One Transaction Had Been legacy Twice
sections.body:
The Detroit and Indiana source packages describe the same September 2, 1982 transaction: Detroit received Tom Owens, while Indiana received the Pistons' 1984 second-round pick.

Two canonical-looking rows were created from opposite franchise imports. This review keeps the Detroit-origin record as the active transaction and marks the Indiana-origin record as superseded provenance so the deal is not counted twice.

sections.heading: Owens Played One Season for Detroit
sections.body:
Tom Owens appeared in 49 regular-season games for the Pistons in 1982-83 and started four. He averaged 14.8 minutes, 4.2 points and 3.8 rebounds.

That was the entirety of his Detroit tenure and the final season of his NBA career. Owens then played professionally in Italy.

The return was modest, but Detroit did receive real reserve minutes from the acquired veteran.

sections.heading: Indiana's Pick Became Greg Wiltjer
sections.body:
The 1984 second-round pick landed at No. 43, where Indiana selected Oregon State forward Greg Wiltjer.

Wiltjer never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. He continued his professional career outside the NBA, so the Pacers received no direct NBA games from the draft selection.

This review credits Indiana with the value of having and exercising a second-round pick, but the completed player outcome was zero NBA production.

sections.heading: Why Detroit Gets the Edge
sections.body:
This was a small trade. Owens did not become a long-term Piston, and 49 reserve appearances do not justify an aggressive grade.

Still, 49 NBA games are more realized franchise value than a draft pick whose selected player never appeared in the league.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win, C+/C-. Detroit receives a C+ for one season and 49 games of veteran frontcourt depth. Indiana receives a C- because the second-round pick became Greg Wiltjer, who produced zero NBA regular-season games. The duplicate Indiana source record is superseded rather than evaluated as a second transaction.

sections.heading: Detroit Bought a Full Rookie Season for a Second
sections.body:
Basketball-Reference's Detroit transaction ledger records the October 2, 1980 deal: the Pistons acquired Wayne Robinson from the Lakers for a 1981 second-round pick.

The pick ultimately landed at No. 39 and became Harvey Knuckles. That makes the realized-value comparison unusually direct.

sections.heading: Robinson Played 81 Games for Detroit
sections.body:
Robinson appeared in 81 of 82 games during the 1980-81 season. He averaged 7.9 points, 3.6 rebounds and 1.4 assists in 19.7 minutes.

His totals were 643 points, 294 rebounds and 112 assists across 1,592 minutes. He was not a star, but he was a real rotation forward on a team that used him almost every night.

That was also Robinson's only NBA season. Because there is no later NBA transaction branch to track, Detroit's return is contained entirely in those 81 games.

sections.heading: The Lakers' Pick Produced No NBA Games
sections.body:
Los Angeles used the acquired second-round selection at No. 39 on Harvey Knuckles out of Toledo.

Basketball-Reference lists Knuckles as the Lakers' 1981 second-round selection but does not record an NBA regular-season appearance for him.

There is no documented Lakers playing return or downstream transaction branch from the pick that offsets Robinson's Detroit season.

sections.heading: Why Detroit Wins
sections.body:
The original legacy archive entry gave the Lakers a modest edge, but the source-backed evidence points in the opposite direction. Detroit received 81 games and nearly 1,600 minutes from Robinson, while Los Angeles received a draft choice that produced zero NBA games.

This is not a franchise-changing win because Robinson's NBA career ended after one season. Even so, one full rotation season is clearly more realized basketball value than a pick with no NBA appearances.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win, B+/D. Detroit receives a B+ for Robinson's 81-game rookie season and useful rotation workload. Los Angeles receives a D because the No. 39 selection on Harvey Knuckles produced no NBA regular-season games.

sections.heading: Detroit Exchanged Wakefield for a Fourth-Round Pick
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Detroit and Phoenix transaction logs agree on the August 24, 1979 deal. The Pistons sent Andre Wakefield to the Suns for a 1981 fourth-round pick that eventually became the No. 89 selection.

sections.heading: Phoenix Got No Regular-Season Games From Wakefield
sections.body:
Wakefield had played 71 games for Detroit in 1978-79 after a brief two-game Chicago stint. He scored 172 points for the Pistons and averaged 8.1 minutes.

The Suns did not receive comparable on-court value. Phoenix waived Wakefield on October 12, 1979, before he appeared in a regular-season game for the club.

Wakefield later signed with Utah as a free agent on November 6 and played eight games for the Jazz. Those Utah games do not count as Phoenix trade value because the Suns had already waived him.

sections.heading: Detroit Kept the Pick Until the 1981 Draft
sections.body:
The Pistons retained the incoming fourth-round selection and used it at No. 89 in 1981 on Don Koonce from UNC Charlotte.

Koonce did not appear in an NBA regular-season game. Basketball-Reference lists him as a Detroit fourth-round selection but shows no NBA statistical line, so the pick produced no realized NBA playing value.

sections.heading: Why Detroit Gets Only a Narrow Edge
sections.body:
This is a low-value trade in hindsight. Phoenix received no regular-season games from Wakefield and lost his rights when it waived him. Detroit at least preserved the incoming asset for two years and exercised the pick, but Koonce did not reach the NBA.

The difference between the sides is therefore administrative rather than meaningful competitive value. Detroit completed the draft branch; Phoenix's player branch ended before the season began.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Pistons Edge, D+/D. Detroit receives a D+ because the fourth-round asset survived to the 1981 draft even though Koonce never played in the NBA. Phoenix receives a D because Wakefield was waived before recording a Suns regular-season appearance.

sections.heading: The Transaction Date Needs a Source Repair
sections.body: The legacy canonical record is dated January 4, 1978. Golden State's team ledger, New Orleans' team ledger, the league transaction page and Nate Williams' own transaction history all record the player-for-pick exchange on January 5. The package itself is consistent across the cited sources: Golden State sent its 1978 second-round pick to New Orleans for Williams.

sections.heading: Williams Gave Golden State Immediate Rotation Scoring
sections.body: Williams joined the Warriors midway through 1977-78 and appeared in 46 games after the trade. He averaged 11.2 points in only 17.7 minutes per game, shooting 43.5 percent from the field and 83.3 percent from the line. He then played all 81 games in 1978-79, averaging 8.3 points in 16.0 minutes. Across the two Golden State seasons, Williams appeared in 127 regular-season games and averaged 9.3 points overall for the franchise. That is useful realized value for a second-round pick, especially because the Warriors did not have to surrender another player or additional draft capital.

sections.heading: New Orleans Used the Pick on Tommie Green
sections.body: The 1978 second-round pick landed at No. 35. New Orleans used it on Tommie Green out of Southern University. Green played 59 regular-season games as a rookie in 1978-79. He averaged 3.9 points, 2.4 assists and 1.2 rebounds in 13.7 minutes. His field-goal percentage was 38.8 percent, and Basketball-Reference records negative win shares for the season. Green's NBA career ended after that one season. There is no later player or draft return attached to his departure in the cited transaction history.

sections.heading: Neither Branch Produced a Major Downstream Asset
sections.body: Williams also finished his NBA career after 1978-79, so Golden State did not later recycle him into another player or pick. That keeps this review unusually simple compared with many trades from this era. The Warriors received 127 games and useful bench scoring. The Jazz received 59 games from the second-round selection. Both assets expired without a later transaction branch that materially changes the comparison.

sections.heading: January 4 in the Legacy Key Versus January 5 in the Historical Ledgers
sections.body: The inherited archive slug and canonical trade record identify January 4, 1978 for the Golden State–New Orleans exchange of a 1978 second-round selection for Nate Williams. However, the Warriors, New Orleans Jazz, NBA league and Williams player transaction ledgers place the exchange on January 5. That discrepancy is a source-provenance issue, not a reason to rewrite the historical player value, alter public URLs without redirects or credit other draft choices to this agreement. Williams provided 127 Warriors regular-season appearances across 1977-78 and 1978-79, while New Orleans used the incoming No. 35 pick on Tommie Green, who played 59 games for the Jazz. The original Warriors Win, Golden State B+ and New Orleans C remain aligned with those team-specific returns. A future change to the canonical date and slug should be evaluated separately with alias handling, rather than creating a second duplicate trade page or treating January 4 as independently corroborated.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win, B+/C. Golden State receives a B+ because Williams gave the team 127 games across two seasons and roughly double Green's scoring rate while costing only a second-round pick. New Orleans receives a C because No. 35 produced 59 NBA games and some reserve playmaking, but Green lasted only one season and created no later asset branch. The trade was useful rather than transformational for Golden State, which keeps the Warriors below the top grade tiers. Confidence is high.

sections.heading: The Trade Is Real, but the Return Is Still Unresolved
sections.body: A contemporary UPI report says Atlanta traded Tom Burleson to Chicago on October 1, 1982 for future considerations. The legacy canonical record uses October 2, while RealGM places Chicago's acquisition later in October. Those sources agree on the player and future-considerations mechanism but not on the exact transaction date. This review retains the canonical October 2 date for database continuity and explicitly records the discrepancy rather than manufacturing certainty.

sections.heading: Burleson Had Already Missed a Full Season
sections.body: Burleson's last NBA statistical season before the trade was 1980-81 with Atlanta. He played 31 games that year and averaged 3.3 points and 3.0 rebounds. UPI reported that he sat out the entire 1981-82 season because of knee problems that had affected him throughout his career. That context makes the deal fundamentally different from trading an active rotation center. Chicago was acquiring a veteran comeback possibility, not current production.

sections.heading: He Never Played a Regular-Season Game for Chicago
sections.body: Burleson does not have a 1982-83 statistical line. Basketball-Reference lists his NBA career as ending after the 1980-81 Atlanta season. RealGM records Chicago acquiring Burleson and then placing him on waivers later in October. The Bulls' historical transaction material also records his waiver before the regular season. His direct Chicago return is therefore zero regular-season games, starts and minutes.

sections.heading: Atlanta's Future Considerations Cannot Be Valued Reliably
sections.body: The contemporary UPI report and both legacy team perspectives identify future considerations going to Atlanta, but the reviewed public sources do not specify cash, a pick, a player or a later conversion. This review does not infer an asset merely to force a grade. Without knowing whether Atlanta ever received material value, assigning the Hawks a letter grade would create false precision.

sections.heading: This Is a Case for Insufficient Evidence
sections.body: Chicago's side is measurable and poor in hindsight: Burleson never appeared in a regular-season game. The problem is that the other side of the comparison is unknown. If Atlanta received even modest cash or another tangible consideration, it likely obtained more realized value than Chicago. If the consideration was never exercised, both sides may have received essentially nothing. The surviving evidence cannot distinguish those possibilities.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Insufficient Evidence, N/A/N/A. Burleson's zero-game Chicago outcome is verified, but Atlanta's future consideration remains unresolved. The October 1 versus October 2 source-date discrepancy and unidentified return are preserved explicitly; they do not justify assigning either franchise a fabricated positive outcome.

sections.heading: Atlanta Paid a Second-Round Pick for Four Seasons of Mike Glenn
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Atlanta and league transaction ledgers record the October 12, 1981 mechanism as veteran free-agent compensation. Atlanta signed Mike Glenn and sent New York its 1982 second-round pick, later No. 34 Vince Taylor. The canonical record describes New York agreeing not to exercise its right of first refusal. That contractual framing is compatible with the compensation result: Atlanta secured Glenn, while the Knicks received the pick.

sections.heading: Glenn Became a Long-Term Hawks Rotation Guard
sections.body: Glenn played 49 games for Atlanta in 1981-82 and averaged 7.7 points in 17.0 minutes. He returned for 73 games in 1982-83, 81 in 1983-84 and 60 in 1984-85. Across those four Hawks seasons he appeared in 263 regular-season games and made nine starts. He was never a star, but his efficient reserve scoring gave Atlanta substantially more than a one-year rental. His best Atlanta value came from reliability. Glenn shot better than 50 percent from the field in each of those Hawks seasons and remained a regular part of the backcourt rotation until moving to Milwaukee.

sections.heading: New York's Pick Became Vince Taylor
sections.body: The Knicks used the incoming No. 34 selection in the 1982 NBA Draft on Duke guard Vince Taylor. Taylor appeared in 31 regular-season games for New York in 1982-83, made no starts and averaged 10.4 minutes, 3.1 points and 1.3 assists. Those 31 games were the entirety of his NBA career. That gives New York a real but limited return from the compensation pick.

sections.heading: Why Atlanta Wins Clearly
sections.body: Atlanta gave up a second-round pick and received 263 games across four seasons from Glenn. New York turned the pick into 31 games from Taylor. The difference is not only games played. Glenn supplied repeated rotation value and several seasons of efficient bench scoring, while Taylor's NBA contribution ended after one year.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win, A-/D. Atlanta receives an A- for converting a second-round pick into four useful seasons and 263 regular-season games from Glenn. New York receives a D because Taylor played only 31 games and never started before his NBA career ended.

sections.heading: Both Assets Eventually Reached the NBA
sections.body: The June 29, 1982 transaction sent Wayne Sappleton's draft rights to New Jersey and a 1983 second-round pick to Golden State. The pick later became No. 43 Pace Mannion. Neither return became a major rotation fixture for the acquiring team, but both eventually produced NBA games.

sections.heading: Sappleton's Nets Value Was Delayed
sections.body: Sappleton did not join New Jersey immediately after the rights trade. Basketball-Reference lists him in Italy for both 1982-83 and 1983-84. He finally appeared for the Nets in 1984-85, playing 33 regular-season games, all off the bench. Sappleton averaged 9.0 minutes, 2.9 points and 2.3 rebounds. Those 33 games represent the full NBA career attached to New Jersey's acquired rights.

sections.heading: Golden State Used the Pick on Pace Mannion
sections.body: The Warriors selected Utah forward Pace Mannion at No. 43 in the 1983 NBA Draft. Mannion played 57 regular-season games for Golden State in 1983-84 and made no starts. He averaged 8.2 minutes and 2.1 points, giving the Warriors modest but immediate bench depth. Mannion moved to Utah the following season. His later NBA production is not credited to Golden State.

sections.heading: Why Golden State Gets the Edge
sections.body: New Jersey did realize value from Sappleton, which prevents the trade from being a clear loss. The Nets held his rights through two seasons overseas and eventually received 33 NBA appearances. Golden State got 57 games from Mannion, and those appearances arrived one season earlier than Sappleton's Nets debut. Neither player started for the acquiring team, so the comparison is mostly about volume and timing rather than high-end impact. The difference is real but small. Mannion's 57 Warriors games exceed Sappleton's 33 Nets games, yet neither side received a lasting rotation player.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win, C+/C. Golden State receives a C+ for turning the future second-round pick into 57 NBA games from Mannion. New Jersey receives a C because Sappleton eventually produced 33 games after two seasons overseas. The Warriors get the modest edge, not a landslide.

sections.heading: This record Mirrors the Same June 29 Transaction
sections.body: this review is the Golden State-source canonical record for the same Wayne Sappleton rights transaction represented by the New Jersey-source record. The underlying package is identical: New Jersey acquired Sappleton's rights, and Golden State received the 1983 second-round pick that became No. 43 Pace Mannion. The duplicate source representation should not produce a different historical verdict. This review therefore uses the same franchise-specific realized-value standard.

sections.heading: Sappleton's Nets Value Arrived Two Years Later
sections.body: Sappleton remained in Italy for the 1982-83 and 1983-84 seasons after New Jersey acquired his rights. He finally joined the Nets in 1984-85 and played 33 regular-season games, all off the bench. He averaged 9.0 minutes, 2.9 points and 2.3 rebounds. Those 33 appearances were the entirety of his NBA career.

sections.heading: Mannion Played 57 Games for Golden State
sections.body: Golden State used the incoming 1983 second-round pick at No. 43 on Pace Mannion. Mannion appeared in 57 regular-season games for the Warriors in 1983-84 and made no starts. He averaged 8.2 minutes and 2.1 points before moving to Utah the next season. His later NBA career belongs to other franchises for trade-value purposes.

sections.heading: Why Golden State Gets the Edge
sections.body: Neither side received a starter, and neither asset became a long-term piece for the acquiring franchise. New Jersey did eventually get 33 NBA games from Sappleton, which gives the rights real value. Golden State received 57 games from Mannion, and those games arrived in 1983-84 rather than after two full seasons overseas. The Warriors therefore realized somewhat more direct value from the exchange. Because the margin is only 24 reserve games and neither player started, this remains a modest win rather than a major one.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win, C+/C. Golden State receives a C+ for 57 direct games from Mannion. New Jersey receives a C for 33 later games from Sappleton. This review explicitly reconciles this Warriors-source record with the matching Nets-source transaction rather than creating a contradictory second judgment.

sections.heading: The Basic Transaction Is Confirmed
sections.body: Cleveland and Utah transaction records confirm the October 1, 1980 move sending Duck Williams to the Cavaliers. The legacy archive entry lists future considerations going to the Jazz. That consideration remains the central evidence gap. None of the reviewed public transaction records identifies a player, pick, cash amount or later conveyance that can be tied confidently to the obligation.

sections.heading: Williams Never Played a Cavaliers Regular-Season Game
sections.body: Williams had played 77 games for Utah in 1979-80, averaging 6.6 points, 2.4 assists and 1.4 rebounds in 21.2 minutes. His Cleveland tenure ended before the regular season produced any value. RealGM's Cavaliers transaction history records Williams being waived on October 12, 1980 and becoming a free agent on October 14. Basketball-Reference lists no Cleveland regular-season line and no NBA season after 1979-80. For realized-value purposes, Cleveland's direct return is therefore zero NBA games.

sections.heading: Why the Trade Still Cannot Be Graded Normally
sections.body: A zero-game return would ordinarily push Cleveland toward a poor grade. The problem is that Utah's incoming consideration is still unknown. If the future consideration was trivial or never conveyed, the deal might be close to a wash despite Cleveland's zero-game return. If it became a meaningful pick, player or cash payment, the Jazz side could deserve a clear advantage. The source-backed archive should preserve that uncertainty rather than inventing a value for an unidentified obligation.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Insufficient Evidence, N/A/N/A. Cleveland's side is now better documented: Williams produced zero Cavaliers regular-season games and was waived within two weeks. Utah's side remains unresolved because the future consideration has not been identified in the reviewed sources. This review upgrades the record from a vague placeholder review note to a sourced inconclusive verdict. Confidence is high on Williams' Cleveland outcome and low on the missing consideration, so the overall trade verdict remains intentionally ungraded.

sections.heading: San Diego Bought a Very Small Amount of Guard Depth
sections.body: The October 15, 1982 transaction sent Robert Smith from Milwaukee to San Diego for a 1983 sixth-round pick. Basketball-Reference's Clippers transaction ledger confirms the pick later became No. 120 Russell Todd.

sections.heading: Smith Played Only Five Games for the Clippers
sections.body: Smith had already spent several seasons as an NBA reserve before the trade, but San Diego received very little from the acquisition. He appeared in five regular-season games for the Clippers in 1982-83, made no starts and played 43 total minutes. Smith scored 11 points, collected three rebounds and recorded six assists. He then moved to San Antonio, where he played seven more games that season. Those Spurs appearances are not credited to the Clippers.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Used the Pick on Russell Todd
sections.body: The sixth-round selection landed at No. 120 in the 1983 NBA Draft. Milwaukee selected West Virginia forward Russell Todd. Basketball-Reference lists Todd as a drafted player but provides no NBA regular-season statistical line. He never appeared in an NBA game. That leaves Milwaukee with zero direct player games from the pick.

sections.heading: The Difference Is Real but Extremely Small
sections.body: Five games and 43 minutes are not a meaningful rotation return. San Diego should not receive a strong grade simply because Smith reached the floor. Milwaukee's branch was even smaller because Todd never appeared in the league. The Bucks used the selection, but no NBA production resulted. The proper hindsight comparison is therefore a narrow Clippers edge rather than a major win.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win, C-/F. San Diego receives a C- because Smith produced five games and 43 minutes before leaving, which is tangible but minimal. Milwaukee receives an F because the No. 120 pick became Todd and produced zero NBA regular-season games. Confidence is high because both terminal outcomes are directly documented.

sections.heading: New York Chose Bailey Over a Future Third
sections.body: On October 24, 1984, the Knicks acquired James Bailey from San Antonio. The price was New York's 1986 third-round pick and cash, so this was neither a straight player swap nor a first-round investment. Bailey gave New York an identifiable roster piece immediately, while the Spurs took a deferred selection and financial consideration. The two years between the trade and the draft are part of the cost comparison: New York could use Bailey before San Antonio learned who its selection would become.

sections.heading: The Draft Right Became Forrest McKenzie
sections.body: The 1986 third-round selection eventually became No. 48, used on Forrest McKenzie. That conversion is the specific basketball branch of San Antonio's return; it shouldn't be treated as an unspecified future first-round asset or credited for another team's later moves. The additional cash is real consideration, but the reviewed transaction record doesn't supply a reliable amount. It would therefore be misleading to assign a precise dollar value or convert the Spurs' package into a claim about cap savings unsupported by the source.

sections.heading: A Player Versus a Late Pick and Unpriced Cash
sections.body: New York's incoming piece was a known professional in James Bailey rather than a selection made after the transaction. San Antonio's return gave it drafting discretion but placed its basketball payoff in the 1986 third round. In this exchange, the eventual named draft asset was Forrest McKenzie, not another future pick whose career should be mixed into the verdict. The Knicks' edge comes from the immediate acquired player against that particular later return; the cash makes the margin harder to quantify.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win. New York receives an A and San Antonio a C: Bailey was the stronger identified basketball return relative to the No. 48 pick that became Forrest McKenzie. The payment amount hasn't been established, so the financial contribution cannot be treated as a precisely measured part of the win.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Paid a Fourth for McNamara
sections.body: Milwaukee acquired Mark McNamara from the Kansas City/Sacramento franchise on August 9, 1985. In exchange it surrendered a 1986 fourth-round selection, not an established rotation player or a premium pick. McNamara was the concrete center asset Milwaukee wanted to bring into its roster at the time. The acquiring team therefore took the certainty of a known player, while the Kings accepted the possibility of obtaining a different player in a late round the following June.

sections.heading: Sacramento Chose Bob Beecher at No. 91
sections.body: The fourth-round pick materialized as No. 91 in the 1986 draft and was used on Bob Beecher. That connection is more informative than treating Milwaukee's outgoing consideration merely as a distant draft asset. The transaction ledger doesn't justify attributing production by unrelated fourth-round picks or later teams to Sacramento's compensation. Milwaukee could assess McNamara as a player on its roster; the Kings had to turn their selection into someone more useful to change the comparison.

sections.heading: The Exchange Was Narrow in Cost
sections.body: A fourth-rounder is a comparatively limited price for the chance to acquire center depth. The trade's lasting evaluation depends on whether McNamara's Milwaukee value surpassed the direct result of the Beecher selection, not on an imagined blockbuster counterfactual. The source trail identifies the date, the incoming player and the exact pick conversion. With no additional cash or first-round asset documented, the proper verdict should stay tied to those components rather than to assumptions about what Sacramento might have drafted.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win. Milwaukee earns a B+ grade for the McNamara side, while Sacramento's return is recorded as C for the No. 91 selection used on Bob Beecher. This is a modest historical deal rather than a franchise-defining reversal; the principal advantage comes from acquiring a roster player for the particular fourth-round pick that actually changed hands.

sections.heading: Chicago Traded Johnson and No. 29 for Banks
sections.body: The June 17, 1985 exchange brought Gene Banks to Chicago from San Antonio. The Bulls sent Steve Johnson and a 1985 second-round pick, identified in the transaction chain as No. 29 Mike Brittain. The deal combined an immediate player-for-player element with a draft asset, so judging it only as Banks versus Johnson would leave out one piece of the Spurs' compensation. Chicago chose a specific veteran forward; San Antonio had both Johnson and the additional opportunity to use the second-round selection.

sections.heading: The No. 29 Selection Limits the Bulls Edge
sections.body: The extra second-round pick distinguishes this swap from a simple even-money trade of forwards. San Antonio's return included the opportunity to choose Mike Brittain, while Chicago received no separate draft selection alongside Banks. The review must treat Brittain as the realized selection rather than inflate the pick into the value of a different player whom the Spurs might have drafted. Even if the Bulls' player return is favored in the retained assessment, the added pick keeps the verdict from being framed as a lopsided victory.

sections.heading: Why the Bulls Get a Narrow Edge
sections.body: The Bulls' side is built around Gene Banks, while the Spurs' side includes Steve Johnson and Mike Brittain's draft selection. Chicago wanted to secure an identifiable forward rather than split its return between another player and a second-round prospect. Giving the Bulls the edge does not erase the cost of trading Johnson and No. 29. Those outgoing assets make this an incremental roster judgment rather than a deal where one side surrendered nothing useful. What San Antonio ultimately made of each piece is the proper check on the grade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win. Chicago receives C+ and San Antonio C-. Chicago's acquisition of Gene Banks is judged modestly better than the Johnson-plus-No. 29 return. The extra draft asset is the key cost keeping the gap modest. The extra second-round pick is a meaningful cost, which is why this should be read as a narrow Bulls edge.

sections.heading: Smrek Rights for Two Sets of Rights
sections.body: One day after the Gene Banks transaction, Chicago made a different kind of move: it acquired draft rights to Mike Smrek from Portland. The Trail Blazers received the rights to Ben Coleman and Ken Johnson. None of these outgoing assets was a cash payment or a completed trade of a signed star; the central questions concerned how each franchise could turn draft rights into usable players. Keeping the two June Bulls transactions separate is essential because their returns and participating teams were entirely different.

sections.heading: Chicago Consolidated, Portland Diversified
sections.body: Chicago converted two rights positions into one targeted player right, Smrek. Portland took back rights to Coleman and Johnson, giving it two separate potential player avenues rather than a single comparable selection. The number of names by itself doesn't establish a winner. The valuation must follow the actual players attached to the rights rather than assign an automatic edge to Portland for acquiring two rights while Chicago received one. The source record specifically identifies all three players, allowing the two pathways to be compared without speculative substitutions.

sections.heading: An Even Assessment Reflects Limited Differences
sections.body: Neither side's package is described in the retained verdict as producing an overwhelming basketball advantage. A third team wasn't involved, and no additional future pick needs to be invented to complete the asset chain. Chicago's outcome is tied to Mike Smrek, while Portland's is tied to the rights to Ben Coleman and Ken Johnson. That bounded comparison also guards against double counting production a player might have supplied elsewhere after his rights changed hands.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Both Chicago and Portland receive C+. The Bulls exchanged two sets of draft rights for those of Mike Smrek, and the Trail Blazers accepted Coleman and Johnson's rights instead. With a similarly limited realized return in this comparison, a forced directional winner would exaggerate a narrow historical rights trade.

sections.heading: Chicago Acquired Waiters for a Deferred Second
sections.body: The Bulls obtained center Granville Waiters from Houston on October 23, 1986. Their price was a 1989 second-round pick, a future asset that eventually became No. 43 Chucky Brown. Waiters supplied Chicago short-term center depth and appeared in 66 Bulls games across two seasons according to the reviewed transaction summary. The Rockets instead held a selection whose basketball return would not be known until 1989. That timing distinction is part of why the initial exchange could seem reasonable before the draft outcome became identifiable.

sections.heading: The Pick Produced Chucky Brown
sections.body: Houston's incoming second eventually became the No. 43 selection used on Chucky Brown. Brown went on to appear in 694 NBA games over a long career, far more than Waiters' 66 with Chicago, but all 694 shouldn't automatically be counted as games delivered specifically for the Rockets. The comparison establishes the quality of the draft outcome and the incoming asset's longevity. It doesn't require pretending that every later team which employed Brown was part of this original trade's Houston return.

sections.heading: A Short-Term Center Against a Useful Selection
sections.body: Chicago received the immediate reserve it wanted. Houston's delayed compensation became a player with a notably more durable NBA career than Waiters had with the Bulls, even after accounting for Brown's subsequent moves. The grade comparison should therefore reward the Rockets' draft conversion without erasing Waiters' actual Bulls appearances. Neither side exchanged a first-rounder, and the trade should not be narrated as if Houston acquired Brown as an established professional in 1986; the player emerged from a pick three years later.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win. Chicago's C- reflects limited short-term return from Granville Waiters; Houston's B reflects the second-round pick that became Chucky Brown. Brown's eventual NBA longevity supports a stronger realized asset outcome, though it isn't all attributable to Houston games. This is a draft-conversion win rather than an immediate 1986 player-for-player victory.

sections.heading: San Antonio Chose Wilkins for Two Players
sections.body: The Spurs acquired Jeff Wilkins from Utah on February 15, 1986. They sent Marc Iavaroni and Jeff Cook, meaning the Jazz received two identifiable players rather than one pick that might or might not convey. For San Antonio the trade concentrated the return in a single center. Utah instead acquired two potential rotation pieces, making the breadth of the actual incoming package central to assessing the result. The asset ledger is explicit about the names on both sides and doesn't show additional cash or draft picks.

sections.heading: Utah Received Iavaroni and Cook
sections.body: The Jazz's compensation consisted of Iavaroni and Cook. Those were not draft-rights placeholders awaiting a future selection, and the difference affects how the swap should be reviewed. San Antonio could judge Wilkins as an immediate roster addition, while Utah had two individual NBA players to evaluate and deploy. This account follows the documented package instead of adding an imaginary future asset or suggesting that the Jazz's advantage arose from a pick not included in the original transaction.

sections.heading: Why the Grade Favors the Jazz
sections.body: The completed asset comparison credits Utah's two-player return more highly than the single Wilkins return to San Antonio. That's a directionally understandable judgment from the identified package, though the names alone can't justify invented season-by-season totals. The transaction should be considered as Wilkins against Iavaroni plus Cook, with any subsequent production compared only where the player belongs to the acquiring team's own period. Utah's grade reflects those incoming players without inflating unrelated later careers.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Jazz Win. Utah's B+ grade exceeds San Antonio's C in the two-for-one exchange of Marc Iavaroni and Jeff Cook for Jeff Wilkins. The advantage is assigned to the combination actually acquired by Utah, not to an unlisted future pick or invented cash consideration. The source record supports a bounded rather than exaggerated Jazz victory.

sections.heading: Cleveland Obtained Edgar Jones and Cash
sections.body: On December 14, 1984, Cleveland acquired Edgar Jones from San Antonio together with a cash payment. The Cavaliers sent Jeff Cook in return. Unlike a straightforward exchange of one forward for another, the Cavaliers' side included financial consideration. That is a real component of the transaction even though the source summary does not specify a dollar amount. The proper comparison is Jones and cash against Cook, not just a two-player swap with the cash omitted.

sections.heading: What San Antonio Received
sections.body: The Spurs' incoming asset was Jeff Cook. Cleveland gained Jones plus money, while San Antonio acquired only the named player in the documented two-team routing. The available transaction record doesn't identify a separate draft pick, conditional swap or second player sent to the Spurs. Adding one would misstate what the franchises chose to do. Because the cash amount is not independently established, any grade comparison must be careful not to assert precisely how many dollars were worth an individual NBA minute.

sections.heading: A Small Player Swap With a Financial Component
sections.body: For Cleveland, Jones provided an identifiable roster return while the cash made the overall package broader than Cook alone. San Antonio's interest was in Cook as a player rather than a later pick conversion. The eventual return favors the Cavaliers, but the historical record is too thin to build a larger financial narrative around an unspecified payment. The explanatory value lies in naming the exact players and acknowledging the unquantified cash as part of the Cleveland side rather than treating it as irrelevant.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win. Cleveland receives B and San Antonio C. The Cavaliers received Edgar Jones and unquantified cash for Jeff Cook, and that combined return is judged stronger. No precise cash value can be claimed from the reviewed sources. The result is an edge on the recorded package, not proof of a large undisclosed payment.

sections.heading: Detroit Replaced a Free-Agent Right with a Second
sections.body: On October 27, 1987, Detroit agreed not to exercise its right of first refusal on free agent Kurt Nimphius. San Antonio received the practical ability to proceed with Nimphius without the Pistons matching under that right. Detroit's consideration was a 1988 second-round selection. This was not a conventional player-for-player exchange; the Spurs acquired contractual latitude, while the Pistons turned a right they declined to exercise into an identifiable future draft asset.

sections.heading: The Pick Turned Into Jeff Moe
sections.body: Detroit's incoming second-round selection became No. 42 in the 1988 draft, used on Jeff Moe. The pick's recorded conversion is the direct basketball return for Detroit. It shouldn't be retrospectively valued as a different second-round player the Pistons might have selected, and the record doesn't document a second incoming contract or cash payment alongside the pick. Detroit gave up a free-agent restriction rather than trading an already rostered player in this particular exchange.

sections.heading: The Spurs Bought Flexibility, Not a Guaranteed Star
sections.body: San Antonio's acquired asset was freedom from Detroit's matching right regarding Nimphius. That can matter to the completion of a player acquisition even though it doesn't appear as a draft selection or an ordinary traded contract. Detroit ended up with the Jeff Moe pick, which offered less demonstrated return than a more productive selection might have generated. The assessment is necessarily narrow because the rights maneuver and a single second-round conversion carry different kinds of basketball value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Spurs Edge. Detroit receives C- for the 1988 No. 42 pick used on Jeff Moe; San Antonio receives C for gaining unopposed access to Kurt Nimphius. The Spurs' advantage is modest. The original deal exchanged a free-agent right for a selection, not two established players, and that distinction limits any sweeping conclusion.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Sent Engler for a Future Second
sections.body: On November 11, 1986, Milwaukee sent Chris Engler to Portland in exchange for a 1987 second-round pick. The teams didn't swap equally familiar veteran roles: Portland obtained an immediately identifiable player, while Milwaukee accepted a selection that would not be realized until the following draft. A future second made the price for Engler measurable without involving a first-round choice or a second veteran in the recorded exchange.

sections.heading: No. 40 Became Winston Garland
sections.body: The incoming pick became No. 40 in 1987, used on Winston Garland. That specific player conversion is why Milwaukee's compensation has a concrete result rather than remaining an abstract draft possibility. Engler was the only named NBA player Portland received in the deal; the eventual Garland selection belongs on Milwaukee's side of the transaction. The verdict should compare those particular incoming assets, not substitute another second-round success from a different franchise or year.

sections.heading: The Later Draft Payoff Settled the Comparison
sections.body: Milwaukee gave up Engler but secured the right to select Garland, which the preserved trade assessment regards as the stronger return. Portland received a player whose realized contribution, under the existing grades, didn't match the Bucks' pick outcome. A successful second-round conversion can beat an immediate roster addition, but the reason here must stay attached to Garland and Engler rather than a blanket claim that all deferred draft assets outperform reserve players.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win. Milwaukee earns B on the pick that became Winston Garland, against Portland's D+ on Chris Engler. The 1987 No. 40 result supports the direction of the historical verdict. This was a focused player-for-pick transaction, and the grades reflect those identified assets rather than unrelated later trades.

sections.heading: Golden State Acquired Access to Washington
sections.body: The October 11, 1987 transaction involved a free-agent rights arrangement. Portland waived its rights to Kermit Washington, clearing an avenue for Golden State. In return the Trail Blazers received a 1988 third-round pick. The Warriors' incoming consideration was a rights concession, not a conventional acquired player contract already on Portland's roster. That distinction must remain visible because treating the arrangement as a direct trade of Washington for a drafted player would misdescribe its legal form.

sections.heading: The Third-Round Selection Became Anthony Mason
sections.body: Portland's incoming pick was recorded as the 1988 No. 53 selection, used on Anthony Mason. Mason's name is notable in NBA history, but his full later career can't automatically be credited to Portland's realized team production. The fairer comparison identifies the rights waiver Golden State received and the specific draft position Portland obtained. Neither side should receive credit for an unrecorded package of cash, additional choices or players not identified in the dated exchange.

sections.heading: A Rights Waiver Against a Tangible Pick
sections.body: Golden State gained the ability to pursue Washington free of Portland's rights claim. The Blazers gained a discrete third-round asset that became a named prospect. The original review favors Portland, although the career of a selected player across later employers does not itself prove that Portland captured all his professional value. On the other side, a rights concession has a different value from an established contract. Those limits are necessary for a useful judgment of this unusual exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Blazers Win. Golden State's rights-side return carries F and Portland's 1988 No. 53 selection carries C+. The pick converted into Anthony Mason, but the Blazers aren't credited with his entire later career by implication. This is a favorable pick-for-rights outcome in the existing assessment, not a completed veteran-player swap.

sections.heading: Detroit Added Dawkins, Utah Collected Two Seconds
sections.body: On November 26, 1987, the Pistons acquired Darryl Dawkins from Utah. The Jazz received two second-round picks and cash, making the arrangement larger than a simple veteran-for-one-pick move. Detroit was buying a known center for immediate use; Utah accepted two different draft opportunities, one in 1988 and another in 1990, as well as an unquantified financial component. The number and years of those selections need to remain attached to the correct receiving team.

sections.heading: Jeff Moe and Phil Henderson Define the Draft Return
sections.body: The 1988 selection was No. 42, used on Jeff Moe, and the 1990 second became No. 49, Phil Henderson. Those conversions identify Utah's direct draft consideration. The cash is also part of the Jazz package, though the surviving transaction summary doesn't establish its amount. Neither pick should be confused with a separate unrelated Detroit transaction merely because Moe's draft position appears elsewhere in the historical trade chain. Here the two selections and cash were the price of acquiring Dawkins.

sections.heading: A Real Player Against Multiple Pieces
sections.body: Dawkins was the identifiable player Detroit wanted, while Utah took a combination of lower-round selections with financial consideration. That makes the comparison more balanced than simply assigning all player value to the Pistons and ignoring the Jazz's compensation. The site's retained grades favor Detroit slightly rather than overwhelmingly. Without a verified cash figure, the verdict should remain a bounded assessment of Dawkins versus the two specific draft outcomes and their accompanying payment.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Pistons Edge. Detroit's A- on Darryl Dawkins narrowly exceeds Utah's B+ for the 1988 Jeff Moe pick, the 1990 Phil Henderson pick and cash. Both teams received identifiable consideration, and the unreported cash amount prevents an exact financial comparison. The result isn't a claim that Utah obtained nothing.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Exchanged Iavaroni for a Third
sections.body: The 76ers sent Marc Iavaroni to San Antonio on December 15, 1984 in exchange for a 1986 third-round pick. Philadelphia gave up a player whose role was already familiar, while San Antonio accepted that player for a deferred draft cost. The package did not include another named prospect or cash in the recorded asset exchange. Understanding the dated move therefore starts with a veteran being converted into a single later draft selection rather than a multi-asset return.

sections.heading: The Selection Was Keith Colbert at No. 56
sections.body: The third-round pick eventually became No. 56 in 1986, used on Keith Colbert. The selected name gives Philadelphia's consideration a defined outcome and rules out treating the pick as a more valuable future first-rounder. San Antonio's acquired asset was Iavaroni, not the opportunity to draft a player. The older imported analysis credited the Spurs with the stronger long-term side of this exchange, a conclusion that makes sense only if the actual Colbert draft outcome and the Iavaroni player return remain correctly attributed.

sections.heading: Why a Third Could Not Match the Player
sections.body: The 76ers converted Iavaroni into an uncertain lower-round selection, and the trade's later result didn't produce a comparable positive return under the existing grades. San Antonio accepted the known player and received more identifiable immediate basketball value. Neither team should be credited with hypothetical alternatives Philadelphia might have drafted, nor should Iavaroni's unrelated earlier work be passed off as production added by this transaction. The evaluation stays on what each franchise received in this exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Spurs Win. Philadelphia receives D+ for the pick that became Keith Colbert, while San Antonio receives C for Marc Iavaroni. The Spurs' advantage comes from the stronger identifiable player return against the No. 56 selection. Those modest grades also prevent exaggerating this small historical transaction into a transformative acquisition.

sections.heading: Chicago Brought Gilmore Back for a Second
sections.body: Chicago acquired Artis Gilmore from San Antonio on June 22, 1987. The Bulls' consideration was a 1988 second-round pick, making this a veteran-for-draft-choice exchange rather than a two-player swap. The club received an established center whom it could put on its roster, while San Antonio accepted a future selection. The date and direction of the return distinguish this move from earlier deals involving Gilmore and the same franchises.

sections.heading: San Antonio Picked Shelton Jones at No. 27
sections.body: The Spurs' incoming second became the 1988 No. 27 selection, used on Shelton Jones. That draft conversion defines their part of the trade; it isn't necessary or appropriate to substitute another pick in that round as a proxy for what they obtained. Chicago's incoming asset was Gilmore himself. Because no further player or cash piece is recorded, the one-for-one asset logic is straightforward even though the types of consideration were different.

sections.heading: Experience Beat This Particular Draft Outcome
sections.body: The retained assessment gives Chicago a distinct edge because Gilmore represented an established player, while the Jones selection wasn't judged to have generated comparable value for San Antonio. This is not a statement that every late-career veteran for a second-round pick is a win; the result depends on the named player and named draft outcome. The Bulls' grade is stronger than the Spurs', but that score should be understood in the scale of this relatively contained transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win. Chicago's A- on Artis Gilmore exceeds San Antonio's C on the 1988 No. 27 pick used on Shelton Jones. The known veteran return prevailed over this specific draft conversion. No unrecorded first-round pick or third participant is included in the outcome.

sections.heading: Bedford Came to Detroit for a Future First
sections.body: On June 19, 1987, Detroit acquired William Bedford from Phoenix. The Pistons sent a 1988 first-round selection, a meaningful draft asset rather than a nominal second-rounder or cash settlement. The Suns thus exchanged a known player for a position in the following year's first round. Whether that converted into a more valuable player than Bedford is the proper test of the deal, rather than simply treating a first-round label as an automatic victory for Phoenix.

sections.heading: Phoenix Used No. 22 on Randolph Keys
sections.body: The outgoing Detroit choice ultimately became No. 22 in the 1988 draft, with Phoenix using it on Randolph Keys. That named conversion supplies a measurable endpoint for the draft half of the transaction. Detroit's incoming asset was Bedford, a different kind of immediate roster bet. Neither a hypothetical lottery star nor production by an unrelated drafted player belongs in the return credited to Phoenix. The two outcomes can be examined only as Bedford versus the actual Keys selection.

sections.heading: Different Bets, Similar Realized Ratings
sections.body: Detroit took the direct player acquisition; Phoenix accepted a year's delay and the opportunity to select a first-round prospect. The preserved historical verdict assigns no durable edge, with the same grade for both teams. That makes sense as a constrained assessment of two specific returns rather than an invented claim that the trade somehow affected all future Pistons and Suns roster moves. Its importance lies in the identifiable draft conversion and the cost of bringing Bedford to Detroit.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Detroit's William Bedford return and Phoenix's 1988 No. 22 Randolph Keys selection each receive B-. The future first was a real cost to Detroit, while Bedford was a real player return. The same final grade on both sides supports a balanced evaluation rather than a forced winner.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Phoenix and New Orleans transaction logs confirm the September 16, 1974 trade: the Suns sent Neal Walk and a 1975 second-round pick to the expansion Jazz for Dennis Awtrey, Nate Hawthorne, Curtis Perry and New Orleans' 1976 first-round pick. The legacy asset label says that first 'became Adrian Dantley.' That is only the end of the draft chain, not Phoenix's realized outcome. On May 29, 1975, Phoenix traded the 1976 first to Buffalo for the 1975 No. 16 pick, which the Suns used on Ricky Sobers. Buffalo later used the 1976 No. 6 selection on Dantley. The source-backed record therefore has to credit Phoenix with the Sobers conversion, not Dantley's Hall of Fame career.

sections.heading: Phoenix Return
sections.body: Curtis Perry became the largest direct player return. He played 239 games over four Phoenix seasons and averaged 11.5 points and 9.5 rebounds for the club. In 1974-75 he averaged 13.4 points and 11.9 rebounds; in 1975-76 he averaged 13.3 and 9.6 and then added 12.7 points and 7.7 rebounds across 19 playoff games during the Suns' run to the NBA Finals. Dennis Awtrey supplied four full Phoenix seasons from 1974-75 through 1977-78. He played 82 games in his first Suns year, 74 in the Finals season, 72 in 1976-77 and 81 in 1977-78, providing durable center minutes and rebounding. Nate Hawthorne played 129 Suns games across 1974-75 and 1975-76, averaging roughly six points per game in a reserve role. The draft asset became Ricky Sobers through the Buffalo swap. Sobers played 78 games as a rookie in 1975-76, averaged 9.2 points, and was a meaningful playoff guard with 13.0 points per game across 19 postseason games. He then averaged 13.6 points in 79 games for Phoenix in 1976-77 before the Suns traded him to Indiana. Phoenix therefore received four different contributors to the 1976 Finals roster from the original package, an unusually broad realized return.

sections.heading: New Orleans Return
sections.body: Walk remained productive but briefly. He played 37 Jazz games in 1974-75, averaging 9.9 points, 7.1 rebounds and 2.7 assists, before New Orleans packaged him with Jim Barnett to the Knicks for Henry Bibby and a 1975 first-round pick that later became Bill Robinzine. That later transaction was not generated by Walk alone, so its full value cannot be credited backward. The 1975 second-round pick also retained transaction value. On October 8, 1974, New Orleans sent that pick, which eventually became No. 22 Clyde Mayes, plus Steve Kuberski to Milwaukee for Russ Lee and a 1975 first-round pick. The Jazz used that No. 7 pick on Rich Kelley. Again, Kuberski was part of the cost, so Kelley's entire career cannot be assigned to this trade, but the second-rounder clearly helped New Orleans upgrade its draft capital. Kelley became a useful long-term NBA center and played 75 and 76 games in his first two Jazz seasons. The New Orleans side therefore deserves more credit than the legacy D grade, even though its value was more indirect and required additional assets.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Phoenix still wins decisively. Perry, Awtrey and Hawthorne supplied hundreds of regular-season games, and the first-round asset was converted into Sobers. Perry, Awtrey, Hawthorne and Sobers all appeared for the 1975-76 Western Conference champions, tying the trade directly to the franchise's first Finals run. New Orleans received only half a season of Walk, but it successfully recycled both Walk and the incoming second-rounder into later packages. That keeps the Jazz return from being a failure even if those downstream deals required other assets and should not be fully backfilled here. An A+ for Phoenix reflects the breadth, durability and Finals relevance of the realized package without miscrediting Adrian Dantley. A B- for New Orleans reflects Walk's useful short stint and preserved transaction value while acknowledging the enormous direct value surrendered. Final verdict: Phoenix Suns Win.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: New Orleans' 1978-79 transaction log confirms the January 12, 1979 package: the Jazz sent Truck Robinson to Phoenix for Marty Byrnes, Ron Lee, first-round picks in 1979 and 1980, and cash. The two firsts became No. 20 Larry Knight in 1979 and No. 19 John Duren in 1980. This is a useful hindsight case because the acquisition cost looked enormous in pick count, yet the actual draft outcomes were modest while Robinson remained a high-level starter for Phoenix.

sections.heading: Phoenix Return
sections.body: Robinson joined a 50-win Suns team in midseason and immediately produced 19.9 points and 10.7 rebounds across 26 regular-season games. In the 1979 playoffs he appeared in all 15 Phoenix games as the Suns beat Portland and Kansas City before losing a seven-game Western Conference Finals to eventual champion Seattle. He then played all 82 games in 1979-80 and remained a major frontcourt piece on a 55-win team. In 1980-81 he again played all 82, started all 82 and averaged 18.8 points, 9.6 rebounds and 2.5 assists for a 57-win Suns club. He made the 1981 All-Star team and finished 19th in MVP voting. Those two complete seasons after the initial 26-game stretch give Phoenix at least 190 regular-season games of direct value before even considering the remainder of his Suns tenure. The trade therefore delivered both immediate playoff help and durable star-level regular-season production.

sections.heading: New Orleans/Utah Return
sections.body: Byrnes played 36 games for New Orleans after the trade, while Lee played only 17. Neither became a long-term Jazz piece. The draft outcomes were similarly limited. Larry Knight, selected No. 20 in 1979, never played an NBA regular-season game. John Duren, selected No. 19 in 1980 after the franchise moved to Utah, did make the league. He played 40 games as a rookie and 79 games with nine starts in 1981-82, averaging 3.4 points and 2.0 assists in the latter season. That is real rotation value, but it is far below what teams generally hope to obtain from two first-round selections. The cash component cannot be converted into basketball value from the available record. The Jazz therefore paid away their best player in the package and failed to turn either first into a comparable replacement.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Phoenix wins clearly, but the grading should acknowledge the size of the original gamble. Two first-rounders, two players and cash is a serious acquisition price, so the Suns deserve a high grade because Robinson actually justified it: he strengthened a Western Conference finalist, stayed available, remained a strong scorer and rebounder, and made an All-Star team. New Orleans/Utah deserves some credit for extracting two firsts rather than losing Robinson for a small package, but hindsight grading follows realized value. Byrnes and Lee were brief stays, Knight never played in the NBA, and Duren was a low-minute guard for two Utah seasons. An A for Phoenix captures star production and playoff impact without pretending Robinson became a franchise legend. A D+ for the Jazz recognizes that Duren supplied real games and the trade process generated valuable draft shots, even though those shots produced little. Final verdict: Phoenix Suns Win.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Atlanta's official July 6, 2024 release confirms the package: Dejounte Murray went to New Orleans for Dyson Daniels, E.J. Liddell, Larry Nance Jr., Cody Zeller, the Lakers' 2025 first-round pick and a conditional 2027 first-round choice that is the least favorable of Milwaukee and New Orleans, protected in the top four. The legacy archive record gets the core exchange right, but the source-backed version has to distinguish Atlanta's actual value from downstream draft outcomes. The 2025 Lakers pick became the No. 22 slot, where Drake Powell was drafted, but Atlanta routed those draft rights to Brooklyn in the 2025 three-team Kristaps Porzingis transaction. Powell should not be credited as a Hawks player from this deal.

sections.heading: Atlanta Return
sections.body: Daniels has already made the trade valuable on his own. In 2024-25 he played 76 games and averaged 14.1 points, 5.9 rebounds, 4.4 assists and an NBA-leading 3.01 steals. He won Most Improved Player, finished second in Defensive Player of the Year voting and made the All-Defensive First Team. Atlanta then signed him to a multi-year extension. In 2025-26 he again played 76 games, averaging 11.9 points, 6.8 rebounds and 5.9 assists, reinforcing that the first season was not a one-year availability spike. Nance supplied 24 games of useful frontcourt depth in 2024-25, averaging 8.5 points and 4.3 rebounds, before leaving in the 2025 offseason. Liddell and Zeller did not become comparable long-term pieces. The Lakers first was still meaningful transaction capital: the No. 22 draft rights were later moved to Brooklyn during the three-team deal that brought Kristaps Porzingis to Atlanta. That later transaction should be judged separately, but the pick clearly retained market value. Atlanta also still owns the conditional 2027 first from the original Murray trade, so part of the return remains unresolved.

sections.heading: New Orleans Return
sections.body: Murray's Pelicans tenure has been productive when available but heavily interrupted. He broke his left hand in his New Orleans debut, later returned, and finished 2024-25 with 31 starts while averaging 17.5 points, 6.5 rebounds, 7.4 assists and 2.0 steals. His season then ended with a ruptured right Achilles tendon, requiring surgery in February 2025. He returned in 2025-26 but appeared in only 14 games, averaging 16.7 points, 5.4 rebounds and 6.4 assists. Through two seasons New Orleans has therefore realized 45 regular-season games from a player acquired to organize a veteran core. The production is real enough to keep the Pelicans out of the bottom grade range, but the availability and team-level impact have fallen far short of what the two-first-plus-Daniels price required.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Atlanta wins clearly on realized value while still holding future upside. Daniels became one of the league's premier perimeter defenders, an award winner and a durable starter, and the Hawks also extracted useful Nance minutes, preserved the 2025 first as transaction capital and still have the 2027 first pending. New Orleans received only 45 Murray games across the first two seasons because of major injuries. Those injuries were not foreseeable as certainties on trade day, so the verdict is about realized hindsight value rather than process blame. An A for Atlanta recognizes the Daniels breakthrough plus the two first-round assets without pretending the pending 2027 choice has already produced a player. A C for New Orleans recognizes Murray's solid per-game production but reflects the limited availability and lack of a postseason payoff. Final verdict: Atlanta Hawks Win.

sources.title: Hawks acquire Daniels, Nance and two firsts
Dyson Daniels named 2024-25 Most Improved Player

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Toronto's official trade-deadline history and Basketball-Reference agree on the core February 13, 1998 package. Portland received Damon Stoudamire, Walt Williams and Carlos Rogers. Toronto received Kenny Anderson, Alvin Williams, Gary Trent, two 1998 first-round choices, a 1998 second-round choice and cash. The first-round picks became No. 16 Bryce Drew and No. 18 Mirsad Turkcan on the transaction ledger, while the second-rounder became No. 47 Tyson Wheeler. The deal was not a simple star-for-prospects trade: Toronto immediately began converting several incoming assets into the next version of its roster.

sections.heading: Portland Return
sections.body: Stoudamire was the clear center of Portland's return and gave the deal real long-term value. From the trade through 2004-05 he played 529 regular-season games for the Trail Blazers and started 482 of them. His role changed as Portland added veterans, but he remained the primary or co-primary point guard through a run of seven straight playoff appearances following the trade. The Trail Blazers reached the 1999 Western Conference finals and returned in 2000, when the Lakers needed a Game 7 comeback to eliminate them. Stoudamire was not the 19-point, eight-assist scorer he had been in Toronto, but he regularly landed in the 12-to-14-point and five-to-six-assist range and supplied continuity at point guard during the franchise's deepest post-Clyde Drexler playoff run. The other two incoming players added little: Walt Williams played 17 Portland regular-season games across 1998 and 1999, while Carlos Rogers appeared in only five.

sections.heading: Toronto Return
sections.body: Alvin Williams became the durable direct success. Toronto's own records credit him with 417 games for the franchise, 1,791 assists and years as a starting guard on the first Raptors teams to reach the playoffs. Kenny Anderson never played for Toronto, but he had immediate transaction value. Five days after the Stoudamire trade, the Raptors packaged Anderson with Popeye Jones and Zan Tabak to Boston for Chauncey Billups, Dee Brown, Roy Rogers and John Thomas. Because Jones and Tabak were also required, the entire Boston return cannot be credited to Anderson alone, but the quick flip confirms that Toronto did not simply lose that asset when Anderson resisted the move. The two first-round picks also became trade currency. On June 9, Toronto sent Roy Rogers plus the No. 16 and No. 18 choices to Houston for Kevin Willis. Willis then played 156 regular-season games for the Raptors across parts of three seasons and helped the club reach its first postseason in 2000. Gary Trent supplied 13 Toronto games before moving on; the second-round pick carried much less realized value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Portland received the best single long-duration player in Stoudamire and can defend the deal easily: 529 games, 482 starts and two Western Conference finals runs make the legacy F grade indefensible. Toronto, however, extracted more total organizational value from a star who wanted out. Alvin Williams alone became a 417-game franchise guard, while Anderson and the first-round picks were quickly converted into additional rotation pieces rather than expiring as dead assets. The Raptors therefore get a slight edge, not a landslide. Toronto earns an A- for turning one departing star plus two role players into a long-term guard and multiple reusable assets. Portland earns a B+ because Stoudamire was a genuine multi-year starter on contender-level teams even though Williams and Rogers added little. Final verdict: Toronto Raptors Win.

sources.title: Toronto Raptors Alvin Williams release and franchise totals

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: Basketball-Reference's Seattle, Philadelphia and league transaction logs all identify the September 29, 1986 counterparty as the Philadelphia 76ers, not the New York Knicks carried by the legacy archive entry. Seattle traded Tim McCormick and Danny Vranes to Philadelphia for Clemon Johnson and a 1989 first-round pick. John Nash's executive transaction ledger records the same package. Correcting the partner is structural, not cosmetic: every asset-routing key, team list and grade must point to Philadelphia before the trade can be evaluated safely.

sections.heading: Seattle Return
sections.body: Clemon Johnson supplied immediate rotation value. He played 78 games with seven starts for Seattle in 1986-87 and 74 games with 26 starts in 1987-88, giving the Sonics useful frontcourt depth while the draft asset matured. The larger payoff came in 1989. Seattle's draft ledger identifies the incoming Philadelphia first-rounder as the No. 17 pick, which the Sonics used on Shawn Kemp. Kemp became a six-time NBA All-Star, earned three All-NBA Second Team selections and formed the core partnership with Gary Payton on the 1995-96 team that won 64 games and reached the NBA Finals. That is direct downstream value from the pick acquired in this transaction, so it belongs in the hindsight grade rather than being treated as unrelated draft luck.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Return
sections.body: McCormick was a legitimate return, not filler. In 1986-87 he played 81 games, started 79, averaged 13.2 points and 7.8 rebounds, and gave Philadelphia a dependable interior starter. Vranes had a smaller role, appearing in 58 games with six starts that season and 57 games with five starts in 1987-88. The 76ers therefore received immediate NBA production from both outgoing Seattle players, with McCormick carrying most of the value. That keeps Philadelphia well above a failing grade even though neither player approached Kemp's eventual impact.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Seattle receives an A+ because the transaction combined two seasons of useful Clemon Johnson depth with a first-round pick that became one of the defining players in franchise history. Philadelphia receives a C because McCormick delivered real starter-level production and Vranes added rotation minutes, but the club surrendered the future pick that became Kemp. The final verdict is Seattle SuperSonics Win. The analysis credits only the directly traceable 1989 pick outcome and Kemp's Seattle career; it does not inflate Seattle's side with unrelated later transactions.

sections.heading: The Exchange
sections.body: On September 25, 1997, Seattle, Cleveland and Milwaukee completed one of the decade's biggest star-for-star transactions. Seattle sent Shawn Kemp to Cleveland. Milwaukee sent Vin Baker to Seattle and Sherman Douglas to Cleveland. Cleveland sent Terrell Brandon, Tyrone Hill and a 1998 first-round pick to Milwaukee; Pat Garrity was later selected with that pick. Contemporary reporting framed the transaction around Kemp's demand to leave Seattle, while the three clubs used the opportunity to reorganize major pieces rather than complete a simple two-team swap.

sections.heading: Cleveland Return
sections.body: Kemp gave Cleveland exactly the immediate star power the Cavaliers were seeking. He averaged 18.0 points and 9.3 rebounds in 80 games in 1997-98, made the All-Star team and helped Cleveland finish 47-35 with the league's top-rated defense by Basketball-Reference's team metrics. He followed with 20.5 points per game during the lockout-shortened 1998-99 season and remained productive into 1999-2000. The limitation is that Cleveland's team ceiling did not rise with the individual production. The Cavaliers lost in the first round in Kemp's first season and missed the playoffs in the next two. Douglas was a useful veteran guard but not the asset that drove the transaction.

sections.heading: Seattle Return
sections.body: Seattle's first-year return was excellent. Vin Baker averaged 19.2 points and 8.0 rebounds in 82 games, earned an All-Star selection and second-team All-NBA honors, and joined Gary Payton on a SuperSonics team that won 61 games. In the short term, Seattle replaced an unhappy Kemp with another All-NBA-level big without sacrificing a season of contention. Baker's later Seattle years were less productive, which keeps the return below an elite long-term grade, but the 1997-98 season alone shows that the move was much more than damage control after Kemp's trade demand.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Return
sections.body: Milwaukee received the deepest package. Brandon averaged 16.8 points and 7.7 assists in 50 games during his first Bucks season, while Hill supplied strong rebounding and interior work. Their value did not end when they left Milwaukee. In March 1999, Brandon was moved in the three-team Stephon Marbury deal that brought Sam Cassell and Chris Gatling to the Bucks. The same day, Hill and Jerald Honeycutt were traded to Philadelphia for Tim Thomas and Scott Williams. Cassell became a core guard on Milwaukee's 2001 Eastern Conference finalist, and Thomas developed into a long-term rotation scorer. The 1998 first-rounder became Pat Garrity, another tangible asset even though Milwaukee's later draft-night handling of that pick was separate from the original Kemp trade.

sections.heading: Hindsight Comparison
sections.body: All three clubs can point to real benefits. Cleveland received the biggest individual name and three productive Kemp seasons. Seattle stayed near the top of the West immediately and got an All-NBA season from Baker. Milwaukee did not acquire the headline star, but it converted Brandon and Hill into the most durable chain of roster value, eventually landing Cassell, Thomas and Williams. That downstream return matters because it helped form the supporting cast of Milwaukee's best team of the early 2000s.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win, A/A-/A-. Milwaukee earns the A because the Brandon-Hill package produced useful immediate play and then turned into several pieces with longer franchise impact. Seattle receives an A- for Baker's outstanding first season and a 61-win team, with later decline limiting the grade. Cleveland also receives an A- because Kemp remained a high-level scorer and rebounder, but the Cavaliers did not convert that star production into sustained playoff success. This is a rare three-team trade where every participant received substantial value, so the margin between the grades is intentionally small.
