sections.heading: Chicago Moved From Keith Lee to Charles Oakley on Draft Night
sections.body: On June 18, 1985, Cleveland drafted Virginia Union forward Charles Oakley ninth and VCU guard Calvin Duncan 30th. Chicago selected Memphis State big man Keith Lee 11th, then sent Lee's rights and guard Ennis Whatley to the Cavaliers for Oakley and Duncan. A contemporaneous United Press International dispatch described the four-player exchange, and both clubs' transaction histories corroborate it. Chicago preferred Oakley's rebounding and defensive profile to the higher-profile college scoring pedigree of Lee. Cleveland accepted two players with immediate roster potential, but the pick numbers alone weren't a reliable measure of what either team would receive.

sections.heading: Oakley Became a Major Part of Chicago's Frontcourt
sections.body: Oakley's value to the Bulls was substantial in his own Chicago tenure, not just in the reputation he developed elsewhere. After a rookie campaign in which he averaged 8.6 rebounds, he played all 82 games in 1986-87 and averaged 14.5 points and 13.1 rebounds. He followed that with 13.0 rebounds per game in 1987-88. Those seasons gave Michael Jordan's early Chicago teams durable interior rebounding and a physical frontcourt partner. Chicago later traded Oakley to New York for Bill Cartwright in a separate 1988 move, so Cartwright's subsequent accomplishments shouldn't be credited as direct Oakley playing production. The Bulls' A+ reflects the immediate and sustained impact of their 1985 acquisition.

sections.heading: Lee and Whatley Never Matched That Cleveland Return
sections.body: Cleveland's gamble on Lee didn't yield an equivalent long-term NBA contributor. The Cavaliers used him for a limited portion of two seasons, while Whatley's role shrank sharply: he played eight Cleveland games in 1985-86, totaling 66 minutes and averaging 2.8 points. That was markedly less useful guard production than he had supplied for Chicago before the trade. Duncan, the second-round right obtained by the Bulls, wasn't the reason Chicago won this exchange; Oakley's development drove the gap. Cleveland's D grade records the short and disappointing return from its two incoming assets rather than assuming every college star would eventually become an NBA starter.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win. Chicago receives A+ for securing Charles Oakley's rights and getting three productive seasons of elite rebounding before a separate 1988 trade. Cleveland grades D for Keith Lee's limited Cavaliers tenure and Ennis Whatley's eight-game stay. Calvin Duncan was part of Chicago's package, but Oakley supplied the defining value.

sections.heading: Cleveland Turned Paul Thompson Into Two Conditional Draft Returns
sections.body: On February 12, 1985, Cleveland sent forward Paul Thompson to Milwaukee for the Bucks' 1985 second-round selection and a conditional 1987 choice. The first pick became No. 45 in 1985, used on John 'Hot Rod' Williams. The later obligation was a second-rounder if Thompson appeared on Milwaukee's roster that season, and a third-rounder otherwise; it ultimately became the 1987 No. 41 selection of Kannard Johnson. Those conditions matter because the Cavaliers secured two defined draft opportunities rather than a vague promise of future compensation. Milwaukee wanted a wing who had played a much larger role in Cleveland, but accepted the future-draft cost for a midseason roster addition.

sections.heading: No. 45 Became a Long-Term Cavaliers Frontcourt Piece
sections.body: Williams didn't join Cleveland's NBA rotation until 1986-87, so the deal shouldn't be described as an instant 1985 breakthrough. His delayed arrival proved worth waiting for. Williams started all 80 of his Cleveland games in 1986-87 and averaged 14.6 points, 7.9 rebounds and 2.1 blocks. He played for the Cavaliers throughout the next several seasons, including the developing playoff era that followed, and recorded 16.8 points and 8.1 rebounds per game in 1989-90. This sustained, directly attributable production from the acquired second-round pick is why Cleveland's A+ has a concrete foundation. Johnson's later selection is a separate, smaller incoming asset, not a second Hot Rod Williams.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Received a Short Reserve Stint
sections.body: Thompson had started 27 of his 33 Cavaliers games in 1984-85, averaging 10.5 points before the trade. Milwaukee instead used him as a reserve in 16 regular-season games, where he averaged 6.6 points and 2.6 rebounds. He was with Philadelphia the following season. That narrow Bucks return is real enough to record, but far short of the multi-season Cleveland value created by Williams. Milwaukee's D doesn't imply that Thompson had no NBA ability; it reflects the specific bargain the Bucks made by sending away a pick that turned into a long-serving Cavaliers forward.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win. Cleveland receives A+ after trading Paul Thompson for a 1985 second-round pick that became Hot Rod Williams and a conditional 1987 pick later used on Kannard Johnson. Milwaukee gets D for 16 games of reserve production from Thompson. Williams' substantial Cavaliers career gives Cleveland the decisive advantage.

sections.heading: The Kings Sent a Veteran Scorer to the Spurs for a Young Center
sections.body: On December 11, 1984, Kansas City traded Billy Knight to San Antonio for Mark McNamara. This was the Kings' final season in Kansas City before their move to Sacramento, so the modern archive team name shouldn't obscure which franchise made the decision. Knight was a veteran wing with a long ABA and NBA scoring history, while McNamara was a younger center whose size appealed to a team needing different bench options. The trade was a direct two-player exchange. Neither franchise acquired a draft selection, extra cash, or another contractual asset as part of the recorded terms.

sections.heading: Knight Added Measurable Depth to San Antonio
sections.body: Knight played 52 regular-season games for the Spurs in 1984-85, averaging 11.8 minutes and 6.0 points, according to San Antonio's season ledger. He also appeared five times in the playoffs, though his scoring and minutes were modest there. The Spurs didn't gain an All-Star or a new full-time starter. They did obtain an experienced small forward who could fill a real reserve shift for most of the year. Their A- grade in the canonical record is a favorable relative verdict on the exchange, not an assertion that those minutes constituted franchise-level value. The near-term contribution was clear enough to establish an advantage over the alternative.

sections.heading: McNamara's Kansas City Rotation Opportunity Stayed Small
sections.body: McNamara suited up for 33 Kings games following the move, playing 6.4 minutes per appearance and averaging 2.4 points and 1.7 rebounds. He didn't start a game for Kansas City during that stint. The club briefly gained another available center but received little frontcourt production and no enduring role from the acquisition. San Antonio had received 52 games of veteran wing depth in return, a more tangible one-season contribution. Kansas City's D+ reflects that limited outcome rather than blaming McNamara for every difficulty the team faced that year. Both players were complementary roster pieces, yet Knight provided materially more regular playing time after the trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Spurs Win. San Antonio gets A- for Billy Knight's 52 games of reserve work and five postseason appearances. The Kansas City Kings earn D+ after Mark McNamara managed 33 games at only 6.4 minutes per night. The Spurs received the stronger short-term return in a modest veteran-for-center exchange.

sections.heading: The Bullets Bought Immediate Scoring with a Future First
sections.body: Washington acquired Dallas forward Jay Vincent on September 3, 1986, by sending the Mavericks its first-round choice in 1990. Bullets general manager Bob Ferry explained at the time that the roster needed another scoring forward alongside Moses Malone and Jeff Malone. Dallas faced a crowded forward rotation and accepted a draft asset whose precise slot was still four years away. The exchange therefore traded present certainty for future flexibility. Contemporary reporting and the clubs' transaction ledgers corroborate the basic terms: Vincent went to Washington, and the future Washington first went to Dallas.

sections.heading: Dallas Converted the Pick Rather Than Drafting Willie Burton
sections.body: The Washington-origin selection eventually became No. 9 in 1990, but Willie Burton never played for the Mavericks. Dallas included the choice alongside another first-round pick in a June 21, 1990 deal bringing Fat Lever from Denver. The Nuggets then moved No. 9 and their No. 15 to Miami for the No. 3 selection. Miami selected Burton ninth. Official Denver and Miami media guides document that chain. Dallas deserves partial credit for using the Washington pick as consideration for Lever, but not direct credit for Burton's career and not the entire value of Lever, who cost another first as well. Lever's Mavericks stint was later hampered by injuries, including just four games in 1990-91.

sections.heading: Vincent Delivered a Useful but Short Washington Return
sections.body: Vincent filled a legitimate scoring role for the Bullets in 1986-87, playing 51 regular-season games with 13.3 points and 4.1 rebounds per appearance. He also appeared in three playoff games. Those numbers provided a return more immediate than Dallas could collect from a pick that would not convey until 1990. But he wasn't a long-term answer for Washington. Dallas eventually gained transaction utility from the choice, and Washington gained a rotation scorer when it wanted one. This is why B- grades for both sides and an even verdict are defensible: the pick had value despite its indirect outcome, while Vincent's direct production was measurable but brief.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Washington receives B- for Jay Vincent's immediate 1986-87 scoring. Dallas also receives B- for a first-round asset later used alongside another choice to acquire Fat Lever. Miami, not Dallas, drafted Willie Burton with the Washington-origin No. 9 pick.

sections.heading: Denver and Washington Exchanged Four Different Rotation Fits
sections.body: On November 2, 1987, Denver acquired guard Michael Adams and forward Jay Vincent from Washington in exchange for guard Darrell Walker and forward Mark Alarie. The trade followed the Bullets' signing of Bernard King and reflected two separate roster priorities. Washington wanted a different combination of guard defense, ball movement and frontcourt depth. Denver wanted scoring and a point guard who could play at the Nuggets' pace. Contemporary reporting described all four named players, and the NBA's dated transaction ledger confirms the exchange. It was not a simple Adams-for-Walker swap: Vincent and Alarie were real parts of the roster calculation.

sections.heading: Adams Developed Into Denver's Long-Term Difference
sections.body: Adams became the most productive player involved after the swap. In his first Denver season, 1987-88, he played all 82 regular-season games, starting 75, and averaged 13.9 points, 6.1 assists and 2.0 steals. His game fit the Nuggets' fast offense, and his scoring climbed to 18.5 points per game in 1988-89. He remained an important Denver guard as the team changed around him. The A+ grade reflects a player who developed into a durable offensive contributor, not just a promising backup who briefly filled minutes. Vincent also came to Denver in the package, but his career there wasn't the chief reason the deal tilted the Nuggets' way.

sections.heading: Washington Still Obtained Two Usable Players
sections.body: The Bullets didn't surrender Adams and Vincent for nothing. Darrell Walker played 52 regular-season games in 1987-88 and added five playoff appearances, offering defense and backcourt experience. Alarie appeared in 63 regular-season games that year and later grew into a larger rotation role, averaging 10.5 points across 82 games in 1989-90. He supplied Washington with several seasons of frontcourt availability. These concrete contributions justify Washington's A grade rather than a harsh verdict based only on Adams' Denver breakout. The edge is slight because the Bullets acquired meaningful depth, but Adams' longer high-level perimeter production supplies Denver with the highest-impact player in this four-person exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Nuggets Edge. Denver receives A+ for turning Michael Adams into a productive long-term guard, with Jay Vincent also acquired. Washington earns A for the contributions of Darrell Walker and Mark Alarie. Both clubs secured genuine NBA rotation players, but Adams gave the Nuggets the best individual return.

sections.heading: Chicago Gave Indiana a Veteran Guard for Two Future Choices
sections.body: On September 18, 1986, the Bulls traded Kyle Macy to Indiana for a 1988 second-round pick and another second-round selection that eventually conveyed in 1992. The Pacers' official franchise transaction history verifies the two-pick price. Macy had been a full-time Chicago starter in 1985-86, but moving him allowed the Bulls to pursue a different guard mix without losing the value of his expiring role entirely. Indiana sought an experienced reserve, while Chicago obtained two draft opportunities with different arrival dates. The 1988 pick later became No. 37 and the 1992 selection No. 39; neither was a first-round asset.

sections.heading: The Earlier Pick Helped Chicago Acquire Rory Sparrow
sections.body: Chicago didn't use the 1988 second-round selection to draft Greg Butler. On November 12, 1987, the Bulls sent that choice to the Knicks for guard Rory Sparrow. Contemporary UPI reporting specified that New York received the lower of Chicago's two second-rounders, tracing the pick back to the Indiana transaction. Sparrow played 55 Bulls regular-season games in 1987-88 and averaged 4.5 points and 2.9 assists. That was reserve production, not a star acquisition, but it represents a basketball use for the asset. Chicago held its other pick until 1992, selected Litterial Green at No. 39, and traded his draft rights to Orlando for a 1993 second-rounder. The two branches should be evaluated as different transactions, not double-counted as Bulls player careers.

sections.heading: Macy Delivered One Season of Indiana Backup Minutes
sections.body: Macy appeared in 76 games for the 1986-87 Pacers, starting none and averaging 16.4 minutes, 4.9 points and 2.6 assists. He also played in four playoff games. Those totals document a useful but limited veteran presence behind Indiana's regular guards. The Pacers' B- grade reflects the stability of having another experienced option for that season, with no later extended run for the team. Chicago's B+ advantage is modest in raw on-court production but reflects two separate assets that the front office could reuse. The verdict doesn't require claiming Butler or Green became Chicago rotation players: neither did, and only Sparrow's later Bulls minutes flowed from the first pick.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win. Chicago earns B+ for two future second-round picks, one used to acquire Rory Sparrow and the other eventually traded after the Litterial Green selection. Indiana receives B- for one reserve season from Kyle Macy. The Bulls retained more opportunities to exchange their assets for additional roster help.

sections.heading: Miami Converted an Expansion Pick Into a Future Selection
sections.body:
On June 23, 1988, expansion Miami selected veteran guard Darnell Valentine from the Los Angeles Clippers and sent him to Cleveland for a second-round Cavaliers draft choice conditional between 1990 and 1992. The pick ultimately conveyed in 1990 as No. 41, but the Cavaliers did not draft or directly acquire a Heat player in the original exchange. Cleveland obtained a real experienced point guard, while Miami converted an expansion selection into a draft right it could use in later roster-building.

The key chronological distinction is that Miami did not keep the right until the 1990 draft. On October 2, 1989, it sent that Cleveland-origin second to Golden State for forward Tellis Frank. The original 1988 bilateral asset remains the CONDITIONAL pick; Frank was a subsequent Miami transaction and cannot be retrospectively inserted as a player Cleveland directly exchanged. The 1990 No. 41 player Steve Bardo came through later draft rights ownership, not a Heat draft-day pick.

sections.heading: Valentine Played Two NBA Seasons for Cleveland
sections.body:
Valentine contributed NBA regular-season minutes in two distinct Cleveland seasons, not in a single continuous run. In 1988-89 he appeared 77 times with four starts, averaging 4.8 points and 2.3 assists in 14.1 minutes. He was away from NBA regular-season games in 1989-90, then returned in 1990-91 for 65 games, 60 starts, 9.4 points and 5.4 assists in 28.3 minutes. The two Cavaliers seasons total 142 appearances, 64 starts and 975 points with 525 assists. This is a real complementary guard return for a future second-round selection.

The detailed Cleveland stat ledger and independent franchise stats log verify those two sets of games. Cleveland B reflects team-specific minutes rather than assigning prior Clippers seasons or implying he played Miami NBA games. He was acquired from an expansion draftee before the Heat inaugural season, and Miami received draft rights, not an immediate Cavaliers roster member.

sections.heading: Miami Used the Pick in Another Trade Before the 1990 Draft
sections.body:
The Heat converted Cleveland future draft rights into an actual forward before the draft. The Golden State transaction ledger identifies an October 2, 1989 exchange of Tellis Frank to Miami for a 1990 second-round choice, and the historical pick-rights chain identifies it as the pick Miami acquired for Valentine. Frank appeared in 77 Miami games in 1989-90, started 39 and averaged 9.5 points with 5.0 rebounds. That is an actual, nontrivial Heat roster return. Miami then relinquished Frank rights before 1990-91, so his later Minnesota seasons should not be counted as Heat playing value.

The second-round right continued on to Golden State and then Atlanta before the 1990 draft, when the No. 41 selection became Steve Bardo. It would be false to credit Miami with selecting Bardo or with any later NBA production from him. This pick conversion supports revising the old Miami C+ grade up to B- while still favoring Cleveland modestly: Valentine played 142 Cavaliers games across two seasons, with 64 starts, whereas the linked later Frank acquisition provided 77 Heat games with 39 starts. Both sides received measurable value from this unusual expansion-draft-rights chain.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win — Cleveland B and Miami B-. The 1988 exchange gave Cleveland Darnell Valentine for a conditional second, ultimately No. 41 in 1990. Valentine played 142 Cleveland NBA games across 1988-89 and 1990-91, including 64 starts. Miami used the right in a separate October 1989 deal to acquire Tellis Frank from Golden State; Frank played 77 Heat games, 39 starts, 9.5 points and 5.0 rebounds in 1989-90. The eventual No. 41 Steve Bardo selection belonged to Atlanta after further rights transactions, not Miami. Both clubs realized player production, with Cleveland a modest longer-duration edge.

sections.heading: The Knicks Moved Darrell Walker for a 1987 First-Round Pick
sections.body: On October 2, 1986, New York traded guard Darrell Walker to Denver for its 1987 first-round selection. The Nuggets wanted immediate point-guard help under Doug Moe, whose offense led the league in pace during the 1986-87 season. The Knicks accepted a future lottery asset rather than carry Walker into another season of changing backcourt roles. The pick eventually landed eighth in the 1987 draft, but New York never used that selection to draft Olden Polynice. That detail is central to evaluating the deal: the Knicks' compensation was an asset they could exchange again, not the eventual NBA career of the player associated with the slot.

sections.heading: Walker Gave Denver a Productive Full Season
sections.body: Walker played 81 regular-season games for the Nuggets in 1986-87, starting 25 and averaging 12.2 points, 4.0 rebounds and 3.5 assists. He also appeared in three playoff games against the Lakers. Denver used a future pick to acquire a contributor who could handle the ball and defend opposing guards during a difficult season. The following November, the Nuggets moved Walker and Mark Alarie to Washington for Michael Adams and Jay Vincent. His part in that separate four-player trade adds transaction utility, but Adams' entire later career shouldn't be attributed to Walker alone. Denver's B+ reflects his real first-year production and the ability to move him again.

sections.heading: New York Turned the Pick Into Jawann Oldham
sections.body: On October 30, 1986, less than a month after acquiring Denver's selection, the Knicks sent that 1987 first and a 1988 second to Chicago for center Jawann Oldham. Oldham played 44 games for New York in 1986-87 and averaged 3.9 points, 4.1 rebounds and 1.6 blocks. The pick later passed from Chicago to Seattle in the Scottie Pippen draft-night deal, so Pippen's career doesn't belong in New York's realized return. New York's B+ recognizes using a valuable future pick to bring in center depth, while also acknowledging the additional second-round cost and Oldham's limited tenure. Both clubs made an identifiable basketball use of the asset they obtained.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Denver earns B+ for Darrell Walker's 81-game season and his later inclusion in a separate trade. New York also receives B+ for a 1987 first-round pick, later paired with another choice to acquire Jawann Oldham. The Nuggets gained immediate guard production; the Knicks converted a draft asset into frontcourt depth.

sources.title: Chicago Bulls 1986-87 transactions and 1987 draft movement

sections.heading: New York Made Room for Mark Jackson and Chicago Needed a Guard
sections.body: The Knicks sent Rory Sparrow to Chicago on November 12, 1987, for a 1988 second-round pick. UPI's report that day specified that New York would receive the lower of the Bulls' two second-round selections; the choice ultimately became No. 37, used on Greg Butler. New York had added rookie point guard Mark Jackson, reducing Sparrow's role after several seasons as a regular starter. Chicago acquired a veteran who could handle backcourt minutes for a team still building around Michael Jordan. Unlike the earlier Kyle Macy deal that put the pick in the Bulls' hands, this transaction shows how Chicago actually spent one of those draft assets.

sections.heading: Sparrow Helped Chicago More in Starts Than in Scoring
sections.body: Sparrow appeared in 55 regular-season games for Chicago during 1987-88, starting 25 and averaging 18.0 minutes, 4.5 points and 2.9 assists. He wasn't the high-usage Knicks guard he had been in earlier seasons, but he could spell other ball handlers and supplied experienced starts during the year the Bulls reached the Eastern Conference semifinals. He appeared in seven playoff games that spring. Those minutes are the direct Chicago return; his later production for Miami shouldn't be charged to this deal. Chicago's B- grade reflects a practical one-season guard acquisition, with its scoring limitation keeping the result modest.

sections.heading: Butler Became a Brief Knicks Reserve
sections.body: New York drafted Stanford center Greg Butler with the No. 37 selection in 1988. He appeared in 33 Knicks games as a rookie and 13 more the following season, totaling 46 New York appearances and averaging 1.3 points in 3.8 minutes. The draft choice produced an NBA player, but not a long-term frontcourt rotation answer. The Knicks' B- rating recognizes that New York converted an expendable veteran's roster spot into a future second-round opportunity, although the realized basketball output was low. Sparrow delivered more direct minutes than Butler, yet neither became an enduring contributor for the club that received him. That keeps the trade within the modest-return tier reflected in the original equal grades.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Chicago receives B- for Rory Sparrow's 55 regular-season games and 25 starts in 1987-88. New York also earns B- for turning an expendable guard into the pick used on Greg Butler, whose 46 Knicks appearances were brief. Chicago obtained the stronger immediate player contribution, but neither return had lasting reach.

sections.heading: Cleveland Took a Chance on Harold Miner and Moved Up Seven Picks
sections.body: On June 14, 1995, Cleveland acquired Harold Miner and Miami's 1995 second-round pick in exchange for its own second-round choice. The picks eventually became No. 39 Donny Marshall for the Cavaliers and No. 46 George Banks for the Heat. Miami's official media guide dates the transaction June 15 and also lists unspecified future considerations, while the NBA transaction ledger uses June 14 and identifies only Miner and the exchanged draft choices. The canonical June 14 date is retained, but unverified future considerations should not be assigned an invented basketball value. The meaningful decision was Cleveland's attempt to add a once-promising scoring guard and move upward in the draft, while Miami shed Miner after his reduced 1994-95 role.

sections.heading: Miner's Cleveland Stint Was Brief, but Marshall Reached the Rotation
sections.body: Miner had won two NBA Slam Dunk Contests during his Miami tenure, but that reputation didn't turn into a large role in Cleveland. He appeared in only 19 Cavaliers games in 1995-96, all off the bench, averaging 3.2 points across 7.2 minutes, and did not return to the NBA afterward. Cleveland's better return came from the No. 39 pick. Marshall played 34 Cavaliers games in 1995-96 and 56 more in 1996-97, scoring 2.3 and 3.1 points per game, respectively. He returned for six more Cleveland appearances in 1999-2000. Those modest minutes were nonetheless a genuine team-specific return from the higher draft position, separate from Miner's reputation.

sections.heading: Miami Collected No. 46, Not a Proven NBA Starter
sections.body: The Heat received the Cavaliers' No. 46 pick and selected George Banks in 1995. Banks did not play an NBA regular-season game, so his draft position should not be equated with a later Miami rotation contribution. From a basketball perspective Miami gave up a guard who was already outside its central plans and traded back seven spots in the second round. That lowered immediate roster expectations but didn't generate a successful drafted NBA player for the Heat. The B- grade is best understood as a modest exchange of a limited-use guard for a cheaper draft opportunity, while Cleveland's B reflects the greater tangible contribution from Marshall plus its short Miner audition. Neither club found an enduring star.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win. Cleveland earns B for acquiring Harold Miner and the No. 39 selection used on Donny Marshall, whose Cavaliers tenure provided modest reserve minutes. Miami receives B- for the No. 46 George Banks selection, which never translated into an NBA game. Unspecified future considerations aren't counted as a confirmed basketball return.

sources.title: Miami Heat official media guide — Cavaliers trade history

sections.heading: Miami Sent Cleveland the Rights to Darnell Jackson
sections.body: On June 26, 2008, Miami selected Kansas forward Darnell Jackson at No. 52 and sent his rights to Cleveland for a 2009 second-round pick. The Heat's official media guide confirms the trade, and Cleveland's executive transaction record traces the incoming choice to the No. 60 pick used on Robert Dozier in 2009. Cleveland wanted a particular developmental forward immediately instead of waiting a year to choose from players still available late in the following draft. Miami gained a future selection. Neither team was exchanging an established NBA starter or assuming a large long-term contract.

sections.heading: Jackson Supplied Cleveland 78 Regular-Season Games
sections.body: Jackson played 51 regular-season games for Cleveland in 2008-09, starting two, averaging 8.4 minutes, 1.9 points and 1.7 rebounds. He also saw action in five playoff games as the Cavaliers advanced to the Eastern Conference finals. He returned in 2009-10 for another 27 Cleveland appearances before leaving the franchise. Cleveland's B grade reflects those 78 identifiable games of reserve depth, not the team's overall success or Jackson's playing time for subsequent clubs. Injuries and the limited role prevented him from becoming a major rotation player, but the acquired rights resulted in actual Cleveland on-court production.

sections.heading: The Pick Became No. 60 Robert Dozier
sections.body: Miami held the 2009 second-round selection until the draft and used No. 60 on Memphis forward Robert Dozier. Dozier never appeared in a regular-season NBA game. The Heat hadn't sacrificed an important roster contributor for the pick, and the chance to select a prospect a year later had real optional value. The B- grade, however, can't be justified by claiming Dozier became an NBA player for Miami. Relative to Cleveland's short but usable Jackson tenure, Miami received the less productive basketball outcome. Neither team landed a lasting cornerstone through this small rights-for-pick exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win. Cleveland earns B for 78 regular-season appearances by Darnell Jackson across two seasons. Miami grades B- after converting its future second-round pick into No. 60 Robert Dozier, who didn't play in the NBA. The Cavaliers obtained the clearer direct return.

sections.heading: Boston Sold Mike O'Koren's Rights Back to His Old Club
sections.body: The Celtics signed Mike O'Koren in October 1987, then sold his player rights to New Jersey on November 2 for cash. The Boston and Nets transaction histories confirm the sequence. O'Koren had spent six previous NBA seasons in New Jersey before a short 1986-87 Washington stint, so the move returned him to a familiar franchise rather than introducing an unknown developmental prospect. Boston was not getting another player or draft pick in exchange, and the amount of cash was not disclosed in the record. The useful comparison is a small financial return versus a short opportunity to use a veteran forward.

sections.heading: O'Koren Played Only Four Games Upon Returning
sections.body: O'Koren's second Nets stint amounted to four regular-season appearances during 1987-88. He didn't start, playing 52 total minutes and averaging 4.5 points with one rebound. Those games were also the final four NBA appearances of his eight-season career. New Jersey had a difficult 19-63 season and was searching for workable roster options; even a short test gave the club a modest on-court return from an inexpensive rights acquisition. The Nets' C+ captures that limited production without rewarding the trade for O'Koren's earlier years with the franchise.

sections.heading: Cash Helped Boston Without Producing Court Minutes
sections.body: The Celtics had signed O'Koren only about a month before selling the rights, and he never appeared in a regular-season game for Boston. By accepting cash instead of holding him, the team converted a marginal roster right into immediate consideration while avoiding the need to create rotation minutes for him. Boston's C is a reasonable outcome grade for a small financial transaction, but no sourced dollar amount is available, so the return can't be equated with a substantial salary-cap benefit or future player acquisition. New Jersey's tiny actual playing contribution creates a slight comparative edge while neither team receives a lasting basketball asset.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Nets Edge. New Jersey receives C+ after Mike O'Koren returned for four games and 52 minutes. Boston gets C for selling his rights for an undisclosed cash amount after signing him a month earlier. Neither side obtained sustained NBA production, and the Nets' advantage is narrow.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Sold Adrian Branch's Rights to New Jersey
sections.body: On November 5, 1987, the Lakers sold the player rights to Adrian Branch to New Jersey. Both the NBA's historical transaction register and the Nets' ledger confirm the rights transfer. The outgoing compensation was cash, whose dollar amount is not established in the cited records. Branch had been a reserve for Los Angeles the season before but wasn't among the core players the team expected to use going forward. New Jersey was rebuilding depth at forward and gave the 24-year-old another NBA opportunity. This transaction did not bring the Lakers a draft pick or roster player; it converted rights they did not plan to use into a financial return.

sections.heading: Branch Played Twenty Nets Games Before His Release
sections.body: Branch appeared in 20 New Jersey games in 1987-88, making three starts, and averaged 15.4 minutes, 6.7 points and 2.4 rebounds. The short playing stint supplied immediate bench scoring, but not a lasting answer for a Nets club that finished 19-63. New Jersey waived him on December 22, less than two months after acquiring the rights. His 20 appearances and 308 minutes are attributable to the Nets, while his previous championship season with the Lakers isn't a benefit created by this trade. The New Jersey C grade therefore captures a modest audition with real but short-lived court production.

sections.heading: The Lakers Received a Cash Return With No Player Risk
sections.body: Los Angeles traded a fringe asset and received cash. That return is concrete as a transaction term but not readily comparable to NBA minutes without a verified amount. The Lakers retained their established roster rather than committing a regular rotation position to Branch, and they did not create future draft capital from the sale. Assigning the same C grade to both clubs reflects the deal's limited stakes: New Jersey obtained twenty games of playable depth before waiving Branch, while the Lakers obtained a small or undisclosed financial return without giving up a main rotation contributor. Neither side gained an enduring advantage.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. New Jersey receives C after Adrian Branch supplied 20 games and three starts before being waived. Los Angeles also gets C for transferring his rights for undisclosed cash. The Nets gained temporary court minutes; the Lakers gained a financial return without losing a regular starter.

sections.heading: An Unusual Rights Deal Brought John Paxson to Chicago
sections.body: John Paxson was a veteran free agent rather than a player who arrived through a conventional exchange of contracts. On October 29, 1985, the Bulls signed Paxson after the San Antonio Spurs accepted cash compensation instead of exercising their right of first refusal. League and franchise transaction registers agree on the sequence. The amount of cash was not disclosed, so it cannot be compared with a specific payroll number. Chicago effectively acquired the freedom to use Paxson at point guard; San Antonio obtained only the financial consideration. The original agreement is properly treated as a rights-based transaction, not as a swap involving an additional player or draft pick.

sections.heading: Paxson Became a Championship Guard Over Multiple Seasons
sections.body: Paxson joined a franchise still building around Michael Jordan and gave Chicago a reliable ball handler and perimeter shooter. His role expanded after the initial 1985-86 season and he became a familiar postseason starter as the Bulls rose toward their first championships. He was part of all three titles won from 1991 through 1993. His best-known shot came in Game 6 of the 1993 Finals, when his three-pointer with 3.9 seconds left turned a two-point Chicago deficit into a one-point win over Phoenix. The NBA directly documents the play. That historical contribution belongs to the Chicago return from this original rights transaction, not to any imagined later trade.

sections.heading: Cash Did Not Give San Antonio an Equivalent Basketball Return
sections.body: The Spurs received cash for allowing the Bulls to sign Paxson. That was a valid transaction consideration, especially when San Antonio chose not to allocate further roster resources to him. But no player or draft right moved to the Spurs, and a dollar value cannot be established from the available records. Their D grade reflects the enormous later gap in identifiable basketball production rather than suggesting the front office literally received nothing. Chicago obtains an A for converting veteran free-agency compensation into a contributor who stayed through three championship seasons. The asymmetric grade fits the actual value captured by the two franchises.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win. Chicago earns A after securing John Paxson for cash and keeping a guard who contributed across three championships, including the deciding 1993 Finals shot. San Antonio receives D because its verified return was undisclosed cash with no accompanying player or draft asset.

sections.heading: New Jersey Paid Three Draft Choices for Orlando Woolridge
sections.body: New Jersey signed Orlando Woolridge on October 2, 1986, after arranging compensation for Chicago not to exercise its right of first refusal. The Nets sent a 1989 first-round selection and second-round choices in 1988 and 1989. These eventually became the No. 6 pick in 1989, used by Chicago on Stacey King, and the choices associated with Shelton Jones and Stanley Brundy. The historical Nets media guide and both clubs transaction registers agree on the terms. The deal is a free-agency rights resolution rather than a direct playing-contract trade, an important distinction when tracing what the Bulls acquired.

sections.heading: Woolridge Supplied the Nets With Genuine Scoring
sections.body: New Jersey received a productive player, not merely name recognition. Woolridge appeared in 75 games during 1986-87, starting 53 and averaging 20.7 points and 4.9 rebounds. He ranked among the Nets main offensive options while the team struggled in the standings. That volume was useful in the short term, although a single scorer could not restore the franchise on his own. New Jersey later moved through roster changes, and Woolridge did not become a long-running foundation there. The Nets C+ reflects the verified first-year scoring and the price of surrendering three future draft assets for a comparatively short return.

sections.heading: Chicago Turned the First-Rounder Into a Championship Reserve
sections.body: Chicago used the 1989 first-round pick at No. 6 on Oklahoma big man Stacey King. He played all 82 regular-season games as a rookie, averaging 8.9 points and 4.7 rebounds, and appeared in each of the Bulls three consecutive title seasons from 1991 through 1993. King was a reserve, not the primary source of those championships; Michael Jordan and Scottie Pippen drove the team. Still, King provided directly traceable rotation value from the Nets choice, while the two seconds supplied additional potential. The Bulls B- grade acknowledges the multi-asset return without attributing the later output of unrelated players or trades to the original compensation.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Bulls Edge. Chicago earns B- for a 1989 first-round pick used on three-time champion Stacey King plus two future seconds. New Jersey receives C+ after acquiring Orlando Woolridge and getting 20.7 points per game in his first Nets season. The draft assets provided a longer-lived return.

sources.title: 1996 New Jersey Nets media guide historical transactions

sections.heading: Chicago Moved Earl Cureton for a Future Draft Choice
sections.body: On February 11, 1987, the Bulls sent veteran forward-center Earl Cureton to the Los Angeles Clippers for a 1989 second-round pick, sometimes described at the time as a second-or-third-round choice because of evolving draft-round rules. The selection eventually became No. 43 in 1989 and was used on Chucky Brown, although the Bulls did not make that selection themselves. It is important to preserve the complete pick chain rather than award Brown NBA production to the team that originally acquired the asset. The Clippers sought interior depth during a difficult season; Chicago accepted a future choice for a player it could remove from its crowded frontcourt.

sections.heading: Cureton Became a Regular Clippers Rotation Player
sections.body: Cureton appeared in 35 games for Los Angeles after the transaction, averaging 7.7 points, 6.4 rebounds and 24.8 minutes. Those figures represent substantial playing time during the final months of the 1986-87 season, even though the Clippers won only 12 games that year. His work was an immediate return and should not be dismissed merely because the receiving team was weak. Los Angeles earned a C in the canonical grades because the on-court help was short-term and did not alter the trajectory of the club. The team paid a future draft opportunity to get it.

sections.heading: Chicago Reused the Pick Four Days Later
sections.body: The Bulls gained a tradable asset rather than a player who would arrive in 1989. On February 15, 1987, they sent the acquired second-round selection to Cleveland for Ben Poquette. The Cavaliers ultimately drafted Chucky Brown at No. 43 in 1989. Chicago should receive credit for being able to swap the choice for Poquette, not for Brown career seasons on another team. That transaction happened only four days after the Cureton sale, giving the front office immediate flexibility. The Bulls C+ grade reflects the transferability of the pick and the narrow edge over one partial Clippers season, without pretending it created an enduring star.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Bulls Edge. Chicago gets C+ for turning Earl Cureton into a second-round asset immediately exchanged for Ben Poquette. Los Angeles grades C after receiving Cureton 35 games of frontcourt depth. Cleveland, not Chicago, eventually selected Chucky Brown with the transferred pick.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Secured the Right to Sign Albert King
sections.body: The 76ers signed Albert King as a veteran free agent on November 24, 1987. New Jersey agreed not to exercise its right of first refusal and received the 76ers 1988 second-round pick as compensation. The Nets historical media guide and Philadelphia transaction ledger identify that same choice, later used on Charles Shackleford at No. 32. Philadelphia gained an experienced forward immediately; New Jersey acquired an opportunity to draft a younger player the next summer. The agreement should not be described as King moving through a straight player-for-player swap, since he signed as a free agent while the clubs arranged compensation for his rights.

sections.heading: Shackleford Supplied an Actual Young Frontcourt Return
sections.body: The draft pick became center-forward Charles Shackleford. He made his NBA debut for New Jersey in 1988-89 and appeared in 60 games as a rookie, averaging 3.1 points and 2.6 rebounds in only 8.1 minutes. His role expanded in 1989-90, when he played 70 games with 37 starts and averaged 8.2 points with 6.8 rebounds. Those numbers document a clear on-court return from the acquired second-rounder, rather than speculation about the player chosen. Although Shackleford later played for other franchises, the Nets deserve credit only for his New Jersey tenure. The C+ grade is a conservative assessment of that two-season value.

sections.heading: King Provided Philadelphia a Veteran Forward Option
sections.body: Philadelphia obtained a scorer who had previously played in New Jersey and was capable of serving as a reserve while the 76ers adjusted their rotation. The compensation required one future second-round selection, not a first or multiple picks. A veteran frontcourt presence could be worthwhile to Philadelphia even if King did not settle into a long career there. The canonical C+ grade recognizes the limited cost and the available roster help, but it should not be inflated by crediting King achievements with the Nets or earlier NBA teams to this agreement. A similar grade for both sides reflects the modest stakes and the lack of a franchise-changing result.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. New Jersey receives C+ after converting compensation for Albert King into a 1988 second-round selection used on Charles Shackleford, who supplied two Nets seasons. Philadelphia gets C+ for signing King to provide veteran depth. Both sides extracted a practical but limited return from this restricted-free-agency arrangement.

sections.heading: Charlotte Brought Kendall Gill Back for Two Guards
sections.body: On June 27, 1995, Charlotte reacquired former Hornets lottery pick Kendall Gill from the Seattle SuperSonics for Hersey Hawkins and David Wingate. Gill had originally played three seasons in Charlotte and had requested a move out of the franchise before arriving in Seattle. Contemporary reporting and both team ledgers agree on the full two-for-one transaction. For Charlotte, the attraction was a playmaking guard with familiarity in the market and enough size to help around the developing frontcourt. Seattle was seeking a more dependable perimeter shooter alongside Gary Payton and Shawn Kemp. Wingate, not just Hawkins, must be listed in the deal even though the two incoming players eventually contributed at very different levels.

sections.heading: Hawkins Played a Real Role in Seattle’s Finals Run
sections.body: The 1995-96 SuperSonics immediately benefited from Hawkins. He started all 82 regular-season games, averaged 15.6 points and made 38.4 percent of his three-pointers, then appeared in 21 postseason games as Seattle reached the NBA Finals. The Sonics lost to Chicago, but Hawkins provided the shooting and defensive attention expected when the club exchanged Gill. Wingate was an added wing option rather than the foundation of the exchange. Seattle’s B grade reflects direct on-court utility within a 64-win team, not a claim that Hawkins alone took the franchise to the championship series. His sustained role gives the Seattle side of the transaction an especially strong immediate case.

sections.heading: Gill’s Charlotte Return Was Productive but Brief
sections.body: Gill started 36 Hornets games in 1995-96, averaging 12.9 points, 6.3 assists and 5.3 rebounds. That was useful all-around guard production, but the reunion lasted less than one season. Charlotte later included Gill in a separate exchange with New Jersey involving Kenny Anderson, so attributing all of Anderson’s later play to this June trade would ignore the additional players and decision. The Hornets nevertheless obtained both Gill’s own playing time and the opportunity to move a familiar veteran again. Their B grade recognizes the near-term contribution, while Seattle’s B recognizes the extended role of Hawkins and its playoff context. The original grades judge the teams roughly even despite their different routes.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Charlotte earns B for Kendall Gill’s 36-game Hornets return and subsequent use in another trade. Seattle also gets B for Hersey Hawkins, an 82-game starter on its 1996 Finals team, plus David Wingate. Both sides obtained real basketball value, although Hawkins’ run lasted longer.

sections.heading: New Jersey and Seattle Swapped Veteran Backcourt Roles
sections.body: On July 16, 1996, the New Jersey Nets acquired Vincent Askew from the Seattle SuperSonics for Greg Graham. Seattle had just reached the NBA Finals, and the exchange concerned supporting perimeter players rather than a high-volume lead scorer. Franchise transaction ledgers verify the direct two-player terms and the date. Askew had been an experienced guard and small forward in Seattle’s system, while Graham was a younger guard looking for a clearer opportunity. The 1996-97 season would show both teams using their new player in relatively limited roles. The canonical equal C grades reflect the narrow scale of the exchange, not an undisclosed draft selection or extra cash.

sections.heading: Askew Offered Only a Short New Jersey Stop
sections.body: Askew was on the Nets early in 1996-97 but did not spend the full season there. New Jersey later moved him to Indiana in November for Reggie Williams, and his season also included a Denver stint. Across all three clubs he played 43 games and averaged 5.6 points, 2.3 rebounds and 2.1 assists, figures that must not be presented as his Nets-only production. His value to New Jersey was the brief guard depth and subsequent trade option. The Nets’ C grade captures that limited contribution rather than awarding them the entire 43-game season or treating an established but moving reserve as a long-term acquisition.

sections.heading: Graham Played Regular and Playoff Minutes for Seattle
sections.body: Graham appeared in 28 regular-season games for the 1996-97 SuperSonics, averaging seven minutes and 3.3 points. He also played in six playoff contests, although his scoring and court time remained modest. His presence did not alter Seattle’s established Payton-led backcourt, but it offered a younger reserve on a team that won 57 regular-season games. Graham’s six postseason appearances are directly attributable to his Seattle tenure, unlike Askew’s combined season total across several clubs. That small but traceable contribution supports Seattle’s C. Neither player became a leading scorer for the club that acquired him, and the trade brought no draft capital to extend either side’s return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. New Jersey receives C for Vincent Askew’s brief reserve stint and ability to trade him again. Seattle earns C after using Greg Graham for 28 regular-season games and six playoff appearances. This was a modest backcourt exchange with no enduring standout return.

sections.heading: New Jersey Exchanged Dallas Comegys for Walter Berry
sections.body: The Nets traded Dallas Comegys to the San Antonio Spurs for Walter Berry on August 29, 1988. Both teams recorded the straight forward-for-forward exchange in their transaction histories, with no draft pick or cash included. The forwards were young enough to invite comparisons, but had entered different NBA circumstances. Berry had averaged more than 17 points per game during both of his San Antonio seasons, including 17.4 in 1987-88. Comegys had played 75 games in his rookie Nets campaign, averaging 5.6 points. New Jersey sought the higher-upside scorer, while the Spurs looked for a rotation body they could use without relying on a high-volume offensive role.

sections.heading: Berry’s Scoring Reputation Outlasted His Nets Tenure
sections.body: Berry appeared in only 29 games for New Jersey during 1988-89, making 17 starts and scoring 259 points, an average of approximately 8.9 per game. The Nets sent him to Houston later in the season, where he made 40 further appearances. That additional Rockets production belongs to a different franchise and does not improve the realized return from the August trade. New Jersey received one brief look at Berry, not the strong Spurs scorer it had watched in the prior two seasons. The Nets’ C grade reflects this reduced output and the short tenure despite the attractiveness of the original basketball proposition.

sections.heading: Comegys Offered San Antonio More Availability
sections.body: Comegys played 67 Spurs games in 1988-89, starting 10 and averaging 6.5 points with 3.5 rebounds. Those were modest reserve numbers, yet they came across more than twice as many games as Berry played for New Jersey. San Antonio did not develop Comegys into a central offensive option, and his NBA career ended after that season. The Spurs also finished 21-61, a reminder that this single depth trade did not solve the club’s larger problems. Both teams receive C in the canonical grades because neither returned sustained above-average player value. The relative regular-season minutes favored San Antonio, but the deal remained a small, temporary exchange for each club.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. New Jersey earns C after Walter Berry provided 29 games before another move. San Antonio also grades C for Dallas Comegys, who played 67 games with 6.5 points and 3.5 rebounds per outing. The Spurs obtained more availability, but neither acquired a lasting frontcourt answer.

sections.heading: The Celtics Obtained John Bagley for Two Future Seconds
sections.body: Boston acquired point guard John Bagley from New Jersey on October 5, 1989, for second-round picks in 1991 and 1993. A contemporary UPI report identifies the exchange and explains that the Nets were seeking younger draft prospects while the Celtics required veteran playmaking. Bagley had averaged 11 points and 8.6 assists in his final Nets season, although he made only 20 starts. New Jersey did not surrender him for an immediate replacement point guard. It collected two separate future draft options. The agreement was reported as contingent on Bagley passing a Celtics physical, a condition that did not prevent his playing for Boston that season. Independent October 6, 1989 Los Angeles Times and Washington Post records report undisclosed cash along with the two future second-round picks, whereas UPI's detailed October 5 announcement and draft-chain descriptions list the picks alone. This historical cash direction and amount remain unadjudicated and are NOT silently installed as an additional canonical asset.

sections.heading: Bagley Produced Two Useful Boston Guard Seasons Around an Injury
sections.body: Bagley played 54 games for Boston in 1989-90, averaging 4.3 points and 5.5 assists while starting 17. He also appeared in all five of the Celtics’ playoff games that year. A knee injury kept him out for the entire 1990-91 season, making it wrong to credit him with three uninterrupted campaigns. He returned in 1991-92 for 73 games and 59 starts, averaging 7.2 points and 6.6 assists. His ability to run the offense alongside a veteran Boston roster was a tangible return, but availability across those years was uneven. The Celtics’ C grade acknowledges the value and the missed season. Bagley also played 10 more Celtics games in 1992-93, bringing his entire posttrade Boston total to 137 regular-season appearances across three calendar seasons with one completely lost year; his final 10-game season should not be erased.

sections.heading: New Jersey Recycled Both Picks Through Cleveland
sections.body: The 1991 second became the selection ultimately used on Zan Tabak at No. 51, and the 1993 second became the choice used on Richard Petruska at No. 46. Neither was drafted by New Jersey as a direct consequence of keeping these choices: the Nets moved both to Cleveland in the February 1990 Chris Dudley trade. They still had value as exchangeable assets, which is what New Jersey actually realized. The Nets’ C+ grade edges Boston’s C because turning a departing veteran into two pieces of draft capital preserved further transaction flexibility. That modest edge should not be exaggerated into direct Nets playing production from Tabak or Petruska. A separate February 21, 1990 transaction delivered both Boston picks to Cleveland for Chris Dudley (with cash reported in some pick-chain ledgers); Cleveland forwarded the two second-round choices to Houston that day in a further Derrick Chievous transaction. This is the actual pick-rights chain, not a claim that New Jersey directly drafted either eventual player.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Nets Edge. New Jersey earns C+ for the 1991 and 1993 second-round picks it later reused in another trade. Boston receives C for John Bagley, who played 54 games in 1989-90 and 73 in 1991-92, with a knee-related lost season between. Neither side gained a star.

sections.heading: Charlotte Paid Two Picks and Kurt Rambis for Armen Gilliam
sections.body: The Hornets acquired high-scoring forward Armen Gilliam from Phoenix on December 13, 1989, sending veteran Kurt Rambis and their 1990 and 1991 second-round picks to the Suns. The two choices later became No. 31 Negele Knight and No. 32 Chad Gallagher. Both teams’ transaction ledgers and the Hornets’ official historical guide confirm all three outgoing assets, rather than portraying the deal as a simple Rambis-for-Gilliam swap. Charlotte was an expansion franchise searching for more reliable scoring in the frontcourt. Phoenix wanted a veteran defender and rebounding presence plus future draft opportunities.

sections.heading: Gilliam Immediately Became Charlotte’s Leading Scorer
sections.body: After the transaction Gilliam played 60 Hornets games in 1989-90, starting 59 and averaging 18.8 points with 8.8 rebounds. Those team-specific figures are more useful than his full-season averages, which blend 16 Phoenix games with the 60 Charlotte appearances. Gilliam remained in Charlotte the following season for another 27 games, averaging 19.8 points and 9.4 rebounds before a subsequent Philadelphia trade. The Hornets’ B+ grade is supported by that substantial immediate production and the ability to exchange the player again. He was not a multi-year franchise cornerstone, but he clearly filled the precise scoring role the Hornets wanted. His 18.8-point average led Charlotte that season, and his arrival gave the team a proven frontcourt scorer despite missing the playoffs.

sections.heading: Phoenix Got Rambis and Future Draft Options
sections.body: Rambis played the remainder of 1989-90 for the Suns, joining a team that reached the Western Conference finals that season. He offered rebounding and defense rather than the nearly 19-point offense Gilliam gave Charlotte. The No. 31 choice in 1990 was used on Negele Knight, a guard who later played in the NBA, while the No. 32 pick in 1991 became Chad Gallagher. Those separate assets made the Suns’ return more than a short veteran rental. Phoenix’s B- grade recognizes role-player and selection value, while Charlotte’s stronger B+ emphasizes what Gilliam supplied directly across 87 Hornets appearances.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Charlotte Win. The Hornets get B+ for Armen Gilliam’s 60-game, 18.8-point first partial season and his further 27 games before another move. Phoenix earns B- for Kurt Rambis and two second-round picks that became Negele Knight and Chad Gallagher. Charlotte secured the more productive immediate player.

sections.heading: Chicago Spent Three Draft Assets to Add Dennis Hopson
sections.body: On June 26, 1990, Chicago acquired Dennis Hopson from New Jersey in exchange for the Bulls’ 1990 first-round pick and second-round choices in 1991 and 1992. The first became No. 22 Tate George, the 1991 second became No. 53 Von McDade, and the most favorable of Chicago’s 1992 seconds became No. 29 P.J. Brown. A contemporaneous UPI dispatch reports the Bulls seeking another scoring wing alongside Michael Jordan, with general manager Jerry Krause praising Hopson’s two-position versatility. New Jersey was moving its leading scorer from 1989-90 in exchange for draft flexibility rather than another established veteran.

sections.heading: Hopson Never Recreated His New Jersey Scoring Role in Chicago
sections.body: Hopson had averaged 15.8 points in 79 Nets games in 1989-90, starting 64. For the 1990-91 Bulls he instead came off the bench in all 61 appearances, averaged 11.9 minutes and scored 4.3 points per game. He saw action in only two Chicago regular-season games in 1991-92 before moving to Sacramento. The Bulls won the 1991 NBA title, but Hopson’s reserve minutes must be separated from the major contributions of Jordan, Scottie Pippen and the core rotation. The C- grade reflects that reduced role and the costly three-selection package, not an assertion that Chicago received no minutes.

sections.heading: P.J. Brown Turned the Last Pick Into an Especially Valuable Asset
sections.body: New Jersey used the 1990 first on Tate George and the 1991 second on Von McDade. The most consequential selection, however, was P.J. Brown at No. 29 in 1992. Brown did not enter the NBA until 1993-94 after playing overseas, so he was not an instant draft-night contributor. His eventual Nets tenure supplied meaningful frontcourt defense and rebounding, and he later built a lengthy NBA career elsewhere. The Nets’ A- grade is grounded in securing several genuine prospects, including Brown, while Chicago’s Hopson gamble delivered only brief bench scoring. The trade is better evaluated as a draft-capital decision than as a head-to-head comparison of former scorers.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win. New Jersey receives A- after exchanging Dennis Hopson for three picks that yielded Tate George, Von McDade and especially P.J. Brown. Chicago earns C- for Hopson’s 61-game reserve season plus two games the next year. New Jersey captured far greater long-term asset value.

sections.heading: Charlotte Quickly Traded a Newly Acquired Second for Randolph Keys
sections.body: Charlotte obtained forward Randolph Keys from Cleveland on February 22, 1990, in exchange for its 1991 second-round draft selection that would become the No. 39 choice used on Jimmy Oliver. The Hornets had obtained this exact pick earlier the same date in a separate deal sending Stuart Gray to New York. Those two steps are central to the transaction story: the club converted a future draft asset into a player it could audition at once, without waiting until 1991. Cleveland preferred draft flexibility over keeping Keys in its crowded wing group. The asset was not an additional Hornets first-round pick or a deal involving multiple players.

sections.heading: Keys Supplied 32 Immediate Hornets Games and Another Season
sections.body: Keys had played 48 Cavaliers games earlier in 1989-90, averaging 7.6 points, before the February move. Charlotte gave him a larger role over 32 remaining games, including five starts, and he averaged 10.5 points, 3.6 rebounds and 1.5 assists. He returned to the Hornets for 44 appearances in 1990-91, when his playing time declined to 10.8 minutes and 3.2 points per night. That decline limits the upside of the bargain but should not erase the initial 32-game offensive contribution. Charlotte’s C grade recognizes a practical short-term acquisition rather than a sustained starter.

sections.heading: Cleveland Used the Pick as Part of Another Draft Chain
sections.body: The 1991 No. 39 choice was ultimately exercised by Cleveland on guard Jimmy Oliver. His eventual professional career should not be confused with an established Cavaliers rotation stint: the incoming pick was a speculative second-round asset at the time of the 1990 deal. The Cavaliers’ C grade reflects the value of converting a reserve forward into a shot at a younger player, balanced against the immediate production that Keys supplied Charlotte. Neither club landed an elite starter or multiple years of premium player development. The equal grades reflect a modest choice between short-term wing minutes and an uncertain future draft result.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Charlotte receives C for Randolph Keys, who averaged 10.5 points over 32 Hornets games after the move and played 44 more the next season. Cleveland also gets C for the 1991 second-round selection eventually used at No. 39 on Jimmy Oliver. Each obtained a limited but identifiable return.

sections.heading: Charlotte Turned an Expansion Pick Into Kelly Tripucka
sections.body:
The Charlotte Hornets selected Bulls center Mike Brown in the June 1988 NBA expansion draft and sent his newly acquired rights to Utah in exchange for the rights to veteran Kelly Tripucka on June 23. Contemporary reporting confirms that two-step transaction. Mike Brown never logged a regular-season appearance for Charlotte because he was converted into a more established perimeter scorer before its inaugural NBA season. Tripucka had scored heavily in Detroit earlier in his career and had been an All-Star there, but his role had contracted during his final Utah season.

For a franchise without an established scoring hierarchy, acquiring an already experienced wing gave Charlotte a first-season offensive option. That did not mean the new Hornets immediately became a playoff team or that Tripucka was selected to an All-Star Game with the franchise. In fact Larry Johnson, not Tripucka, was the first player to represent the Hornets at the All-Star Game, in 1993 according to NBA historical records.

sections.heading: Tripucka Became the Expansion Hornets First Scoring Leader
sections.body:
Tripucka delivered measurable Charlotte on-court scoring. In 1988-89, the Hornets first year, he averaged 22.6 points across 71 games and 65 starts, giving them a leading wing scorer despite a 20-62 expansion record. The following season he averaged 15.6 points over 79 games and 73 starts. He then logged a third Hornets season of 77 appearances in 1990-91, when his playing role and scoring fell as the club developed other options. Those three Charlotte seasons total 227 games, a concrete acquisition return rather than extrapolating his Detroit performance.

An older imported Charlotte perspective called Tripucka the franchise first All-Star in 1990. That claim was false: NBA history identifies Larry Johnson as the Hornets first All-Star in 1993, and the franchise awards record agrees. Tripucka two NBA All-Star selections were with Detroit before this deal. Charlotte A- is justified by actual 1988-89 scoring impact, not by attributing a nonexistent Charlotte All-Star honor to the acquisition.

sections.heading: Brown Offered Utah Defense and Rebounding, Not Comparable Scoring
sections.body:
Mike Brown's actual Utah return was much longer than a two-season reserve cameo. He played 66 Jazz regular-season games in 1988-89 with 16 starts at 4.5 points and 3.9 rebounds, then appeared in ALL 82 games in EACH of the next four seasons: 1989-90 (6.2 points and 4.5 rebounds), 1990-91 (4.8 points and 4.1 rebounds), 1991-92 (7.7 points and 5.8 rebounds) and 1992-93 (5.7 points and 4.8 rebounds). His five-year Jazz total was 394 games and 40 starts. This is meaningful center availability across a sustained playoff-era rotation, not simply an unproductive return for an expansion-draft player.

Charlotte still acquired the stronger immediate scorer: Tripucka's 22.6 points per game and 71 appearances in its first year gave a new franchise recognizable offense. His three Charlotte seasons totaled 227 NBA games, but his previous Detroit All-Star awards cannot be assigned to the Hornets; Larry Johnson was the franchise first All-Star in 1993. Utah did not receive that same lead-scorer impact, yet a center filling 394 regular-season roles should not be graded as a nearly failed transaction. The source-led revision to B- for the Jazz, against Charlotte A-, acknowledges Brown's five seasons while preserving the Hornets immediate edge.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Charlotte Win — Hornets A-, Jazz B-. Charlotte acquired Kelly Tripucka rights for Mike Brown and received 227 Hornets regular-season games, including an inaugural 22.6-point campaign over 71 games. Utah received 394 Mike Brown NBA games and 40 starts across five Jazz seasons, with a full 82 games in each of the last four years. Those are legitimate multi-year rotation contributions deserving more than the inherited C-. Tripucka was previously a Detroit All-Star, not a Charlotte All-Star; Larry Johnson was the Hornets first in 1993. The scoring-peak edge is Charlotte, but both teams secured real value.

sections.heading: The Hornets Acquired a True Center for Two Forwards
sections.body: On January 4, 1991, the Charlotte Hornets acquired veteran center Mike Gminski from Philadelphia, sending high-scoring forward Armon Gilliam and reserve Dave Hoppen to the 76ers. The Hornets needed size, rebounding and a stabilizing player near the rim rather than another forward who needed offensive touches. Philadelphia targeted Gilliam’s scoring and rebounding to strengthen its roster around Charles Barkley. The inclusion of Hoppen is part of the canonical transaction and must not be omitted, although his subsequent statistical role was much smaller. Contemporary coverage and both franchises’ transaction histories agree on the date and three-player composition. This was not a draft-rights swap or the later Gilliam move to another city.

sections.heading: Gilliam Provided Philadelphia With Sustained Scoring
sections.body: Gilliam’s value to Philadelphia emerged across multiple seasons, not simply in his first weeks after the move. He averaged roughly 16 points and eight rebounds in the 50 games he played for the 76ers during 1990-91, then made a larger contribution through the next complete season. The 76ers used him as a frontcourt scoring option while Barkley continued to draw defenses. His offensive output was far more sustained than the return Charlotte obtained from the aging Gminski. Philadelphia’s B+ grade recognizes the ability to get a younger productive scorer without trading away a first-round pick. Hoppen’s presence added depth, but Gilliam supplied the lasting difference in the exchange.

sections.heading: Gminski Gave Charlotte Some Interior Minutes Before Declining
sections.body: Gminski was not without value for Charlotte. He joined as an experienced center, started regularly after the January trade and averaged double figures in scoring while helping on the boards in 1990-91. His following season was substantially less productive, limiting the duration of the benefit. Charlotte could use his size while developing a young team, but it sacrificed a forward capable of scoring at a much higher level for a longer period. The Hornets’ B- therefore allows for real veteran center production without confusing that partial-season benefit with a winning long-term return. The 76ers’ offense obtained the more valuable player, while Charlotte paid for a short-lived positional fit.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win. Philadelphia receives B+ for bringing in Armon Gilliam and Dave Hoppen, led by Gilliam’s sustained scoring and rebounding. Charlotte gets B- for receiving Mike Gminski, whose useful immediate center play declined the following season. The longer productive tenure favored Philadelphia.

sections.heading: Washington Obtained Rex Chapman for Tom Hammonds
sections.body: On February 19, 1992, the Washington Bullets acquired Charlotte shooting guard Rex Chapman for forward Tom Hammonds. The Hornets moved their former first-round guard for a bigger player who could help on the glass. Washington sought scoring and ball-handling on the wing. Contemporary reporting identified both men as injured at the time: Chapman had a heel problem and Hammonds was dealing with a groin injury. That context helps explain why neither trade partner saw an immediate high-volume player debut after the exchange. The teams did not swap draft picks or additional players. The canonical modern Wizards franchise name refers to the Washington Bullets of 1992.

sections.heading: Chapman Developed Into a Productive Washington Starter
sections.body: Chapman appeared only once for Washington after the February trade in 1991-92, so that partial season by itself did not settle the outcome. The subsequent campaigns did. He played 60 games in 1992-93, averaging 12.5 points, then started 59 of 60 in 1993-94 while scoring 18.2 points per game. Those are Washington-specific results, independent of his earlier Charlotte numbers or later Phoenix scoring. The Bullets’ A- grade recognizes the multi-year starting guard that emerged once his injury cleared. The trade offered a genuine perimeter building block, even though the club remained outside championship contention. This is a longer-term return rather than an instant deadline win.

sections.heading: Hammonds Was a Short-Term Hornets Frontcourt Solution
sections.body: Charlotte received a veteran forward known more for size and physical work than for being a lead scorer. Hammonds was a reasonable positional addition when the Hornets were searching for interior balance, but he did not grow into an equivalent long-term centerpiece for the franchise. His Charlotte stay was a comparatively short segment of a journeyman NBA career. The D+ rating therefore reflects the opportunity cost of losing Chapman rather than suggesting the incoming forward never provided useful minutes. In retrospect, Washington acquired a player who could anchor regular-season guard shifts for several years while Charlotte obtained frontcourt depth. The disparity in duration and responsibility is what drives the existing directional grades.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wizards Win. The Washington Bullets earn A- for Rex Chapman, who became a productive starting scorer after an injury-limited arrival. Charlotte receives D+ for Tom Hammonds, a shorter-lived frontcourt addition. The multi-season Washington role outweighs Charlotte’s immediate size preference.

sections.heading: New York Replaced an Injured Point Guard With Derek Harper
sections.body: On January 6, 1994, New York acquired Derek Harper from Dallas for veteran swingman Tony Campbell and a protected 1997 first-round selection. The Knicks needed an experienced point guard following Doc Rivers’ season-ending knee injury and were preparing for a deep postseason push. Dallas was rebuilding and turned its veteran lead guard into a player plus future first-round draft capital. Contemporary reports identify the same package, including the protection attached to the selection. It was not simply a swap of players on similar career paths: New York was buying immediate playoff readiness, and Dallas was willing to defer part of the return until 1997.

sections.heading: Harper Was a Core Contributor in the Knicks 1994 Finals
sections.body: Harper played 54 regular-season games for the Knicks in 1993-94, averaging 12.8 points and 6.5 assists. More important, he gave New York a reliable point-guard option through its run to Game 7 of the NBA Finals against Houston. Harper played all seven games of that series and averaged 16.4 points and 6.0 assists, including a 23-point Game 7. The Knicks ultimately lost the championship, but the playoff return was substantial and cannot be treated as a cosmetic late-season addition. New York kept Harper beyond the Finals, using him for another two full seasons. The A- grade reflects direct high-pressure production and multi-season guard stability.

sections.heading: Dallas Received Campbell and a Later First-Round Choice
sections.body: Campbell offered Dallas an experienced perimeter scorer, but did not match Harper’s influence with his new club. The delayed draft asset became the No. 25 pick of the 1997 draft, associated with John Thomas. That first-round choice had value, yet a late selection was not equivalent to an established point guard performing at a Finals level. The Mavericks’ D+ grade accounts for the modest immediate contribution and long wait for compensation, not an assumption that a protected selection was imaginary. New York extracted more of what it needed when it needed it, while Dallas acquired pieces for a different rebuild timeline. The result is clearer when team-specific playoff minutes are compared with actual incoming draft capital.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win. New York earns A- for Derek Harper’s regular-season stability and pivotal 1994 Finals role. Dallas grades D+ after acquiring Tony Campbell and the protected first-round pick that became No. 25 in 1997. Harper delivered the more consequential team-specific return.

sections.heading: Orlando Sold Reggie Theus for Two Future Seconds
sections.body: On June 25, 1990, Orlando traded veteran guard Reggie Theus to the New Jersey Nets in exchange for second-round picks in 1993 and 1995. Theus had led Orlando’s offense during its inaugural NBA season and averaged 18.9 points and 5.4 assists in 1989-90, but the expansion club was still accumulating younger draft assets. Contemporary wire reporting identifies the same two-pick compensation. The picks eventually corresponded to No. 42 Adonis Jordan and No. 38 Rashard Griffith, though the players’ rights and any subsequent pick movements must not be confused with guaranteed Magic NBA minutes. New Jersey was adding a proven facilitator and scorer who could lead a full NBA backcourt immediately.

sections.heading: Theus Was a Productive One-Year Nets Starter
sections.body: New Jersey got exactly one NBA regular season from Theus, but it was an unusually productive one. He started all 81 games he played in 1990-91, averaging 18.6 points, 4.7 assists and 2.8 rebounds in 36.5 minutes. Those are genuine Nets-only statistics, not a combination with his previous Orlando year or later overseas appearances. He did not play in the NBA again after the season. The Nets’ C grade therefore captures both the clear short-term scoring benefit and the absence of a longer runway. A veteran who helps a struggling team for one year can be useful without creating a new multi-season cornerstone. The comparison has to account for the two future choices surrendered.

sections.heading: The Magic Held Later Draft Opportunities, Not a Ready Starter
sections.body: Orlando did not immediately replace Theus with a proven point guard in this trade. It gained two future second-round opportunities, offering flexibility and the chance to find younger talent. The names Adonis Jordan and Rashard Griffith relate to how the deferred picks eventually appeared in the draft record; that does not by itself establish either as a successful Magic rotation player. The club’s C+ grade rewards the lower-cost options of rebuilding rather than overclaiming player production from those rights. New Jersey secured the strongest immediate on-court scorer in the exchange, but only for a season. The equal-trade verdict reflects the different value horizons and the modest ultimate team improvement produced by either side.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. New Jersey gets C for Reggie Theus’ 81-game, 18.6-point season before his NBA career ended. Orlando receives C+ for two deferred second-round draft selections, associated with Adonis Jordan and Rashard Griffith. The Nets received more immediate playing value, while the Magic preserved future options.
