sections.heading: Charlotte Acquired Robert Reid and a Draft Pick for Bernard Thompson
sections.body: On July 18, 1988, the expansion Charlotte Hornets sent Bernard Thompson to the Houston Rockets for veteran Robert Reid and Houston’s 1990 second-round draft choice. That selection eventually became No. 39 and was used on Steve Scheffler. Thompson had been among Charlotte’s expansion-draft selections, which made the transaction another example of the new franchise converting acquired roster rights into an experienced NBA player. Contemporary Los Angeles Times reporting and the dated league transaction register confirm both incoming assets, rather than Reid alone. Reid had spent a decade in Houston and played on two Rockets teams that reached the Finals. Charlotte wanted a familiar professional who could carry minutes and score on a roster without an established hierarchy.

sections.heading: Reid Started All 82 Games for the Inaugural Hornets
sections.body: Reid immediately gave Charlotte 82 starts in 1988-89, averaging 14.7 points, 3.7 rebounds and 1.9 assists in 26.2 minutes per game. Those numbers are from his Hornets season, not his previous ten years with Houston. They gave the young franchise dependable veteran scoring and availability even as the expansion team struggled to win consistently. Charlotte held the 1990 second-round choice for another two years and selected Scheffler, adding a separate developmental option to the transaction. The Hornets’ C+ canonical grade looks cautious beside Reid’s production, but the team paid with another unproven expansion asset and did not acquire an enduring offensive star. Reid nonetheless supplied an unusually tangible immediate return for a new team.

sections.heading: Houston Added Depth Rather Than Another Lead Contributor
sections.body: Houston received Bernard Thompson, a forward without a sustained NBA scoring résumé comparable to Reid’s. The Rockets had already used Reid as a major playoff contributor and were moving toward a younger rotation, so the trade reduced their reliance on an older wing and brought in another potential body. They also surrendered a deferred second-round pick that Charlotte eventually exercised. Thompson never became a main Houston scoring option, and the transaction therefore did not produce the same direct on-court impact for the Rockets. The equal C+ grades can be understood as a narrow roster-management evaluation rather than equal points scored by the incoming players. On the court, Charlotte received the clearer first-year contribution.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Charlotte earns C+ for veteran Robert Reid’s 82 starts and 14.7 points per game in its inaugural season, plus the No. 39 pick used on Steve Scheffler. Houston receives C+ for Bernard Thompson as a younger depth option, though Reid produced the more identifiable immediate return.

sections.heading: Charlotte Exchanged Its First-Year Scoring Veteran for Richard Anderson
sections.body: On October 17, 1989, the Hornets traded Robert Reid to the Portland Trail Blazers for reserve forward Richard Anderson. Reid had just started all 82 games in Charlotte’s inaugural season, averaging 14.7 points, so he was an established scorer rather than a little-used roster filler. Portland wanted veteran options on the wing ahead of the 1989-90 season, while Charlotte searched for a different mix of frontcourt players in its second campaign. Both team ledgers and the league-wide transaction register describe a one-for-one trade, without draft picks or financial compensation. The Hornets were exchanging a player with proven recent team production for a younger depth forward who had not held an equally substantial offensive role.

sections.heading: Anderson Stayed Through One Charlotte Season, Then Was Waived
sections.body: Anderson did not immediately vanish from Charlotte. The Hornets kept him during the 1989-90 campaign, when the team finished 19-63, then waived him on October 30, 1990 before the following season. That chronology matters: the late-October waiver was in 1990, not two weeks after the original 1989 trade. His Charlotte opportunity amounted to one season of interior depth rather than a long-term starting role. The Hornets’ C grade reflects modest usable roster minutes at a time when the franchise was trying multiple combinations. It should not be inflated by crediting Anderson with games played for earlier clubs or suggesting that Charlotte acquired any other asset in the deal.

sections.heading: Reid Briefly Joined Portland Before Returning to Charlotte
sections.body: Reid did not become a lasting Trail Blazers figure either. The veteran spent a short period with Portland during 1989-90 and was back in Charlotte as a free-agent signing on December 13, 1989, according to the Hornets’ dated transaction history. His Trail Blazers opportunity was therefore smaller than the 82-game Charlotte season immediately before the trade. Portland’s C+ grade represents an attempt to acquire dependable veteran guard-forward depth for a contender, but the actual tenure was brief. Charlotte did not permanently lose access to Reid, because he returned through a separate free-agent agreement. This chain makes the slight Portland advantage modest rather than a sweeping success for either club.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Blazers Edge. Portland receives C+ for temporarily obtaining veteran Robert Reid. Charlotte earns C for Richard Anderson’s single-season reserve opportunity before an October 1990 waiver. Reid returned to the Hornets in a separate December 1989 signing, limiting the lasting value of the original trade for both teams.

sources.title: Charlotte Hornets 1989-90 transactions and Reid’s free-agent return

sections.heading: The Hornets Sent Two Future Seconds to Sacramento for a Center
sections.body: On January 29, 1991, the Hornets acquired Eric Leckner from Sacramento for second-round draft choices in 1993 and 1995. The two picks later became No. 44 Alex Holcombe and No. 51 Dejan Bodiroga. Team transaction histories independently document the date and both future draft assets. Charlotte needed a reserve center for a club still developing around its young core, while the Kings converted a little-used big man into two opportunities to add talent over multiple drafts. This was not a player-for-player exchange, and the deferred timing of the picks is part of the trade. It also was not a concession of first-round selection rights by either club.

sections.heading: Leckner Had an Actual but Limited Charlotte Rotation Role
sections.body: Leckner played 40 Hornets games after the January trade during 1990-91, starting twice and averaging roughly six points and five rebounds in reserve minutes. He returned for 59 games in 1991-92, playing 12.1 minutes per night and averaging 3.3 points and 3.5 rebounds. Those team-specific figures show why Charlotte’s C grade has a foundation despite the center’s limited impact. He was available for a substantial stretch of two seasons, not merely signed and immediately waived. But he did not become a major scorer or defensive centerpiece for the Hornets and was later replaced by other frontcourt options. The immediate return should be judged as backup availability rather than a permanent solution at center.

sections.heading: Sacramento Secured Draft Opportunities, Not Bodiroga NBA Minutes
sections.body: The Kings took the longer view and received two future second-round picks. They eventually used them on Alex Holcombe and Dejan Bodiroga. Bodiroga became a distinguished European basketball player, but he never played an NBA regular-season game. His accomplishments outside the NBA should not be counted as Sacramento production. Nor did the acquired picks guarantee the Kings two established rotation players. The C grade instead recognizes the optionality of having extra selections without retaining a reserve big man who was not central to their plans. Charlotte obtained more certain short-term minutes from Leckner, while Sacramento obtained two shots at a future roster improvement. Neither side produced a high-impact NBA star directly from the agreement.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Charlotte receives C for 99 Eric Leckner appearances across two seasons, mostly in reserve. Sacramento also gets C after converting his contract into the draft choices used on Alex Holcombe and Dejan Bodiroga. Bodiroga’s European achievements are not credited as Kings NBA playing production.

sections.heading: Orlando Spent a Future Second-Rounder on Steve Kerr
sections.body: On December 2, 1992, the Magic acquired Steve Kerr from the Cleveland Cavaliers for a 1996 second-round draft selection. The choice eventually became No. 56 and was used on Reggie Geary. Cleveland had a veteran playoff roster with limited opportunities for a small reserve guard; Orlando wanted another ball handler who could compete for bench minutes alongside its young players. The transaction was a direct pick-for-player exchange, with no additional swap right or veteran attached. Both the Magic and Cavaliers transaction histories date the deal to December 2. The draft choice took almost four years to mature, leaving Cleveland with a speculative future asset while Orlando received a player immediately. Published transaction dating differs: RealGM's player timeline labels the transaction December 2, whereas contemporaneous UPI reporting and Orlando's official franchise transaction history place the reported acquisition on Thursday, December 3. The existing December 2 route is preserved pending coordinated date/slug migration policy; the teams, future-pick terms and 47-game Orlando stint are not in dispute.

sections.heading: Kerr Played 47 Magic Games Before Finding His Later Role Elsewhere
sections.body: Kerr appeared in 47 games for Orlando in 1992-93 without a start, averaging 9.4 minutes, 2.6 points and 1.3 assists. His three-point shooting was just 25 percent in that small sample, which makes it important not to project his future success backward onto the Magic. He joined Chicago as a free agent before the 1993-94 season and eventually became an elite spot-up shooter on three Bulls championship teams. That later role was genuine but does not belong to Orlando’s realized return from this trade. The Magic C+ grade therefore reflects obtaining an experienced reserve on inexpensive draft-pick terms, while the limited 47-game stint prevents describing the move as a franchise-transforming acquisition.

sections.heading: Cleveland Kept the Future Selection Until the 1996 Draft
sections.body: The Cavaliers received a second-round choice and used it on Reggie Geary at No. 56 in the 1996 NBA Draft. Geary did not become a regular Cleveland NBA rotation player; the franchise’s reward was the opportunity to select a developmental prospect at low cost rather than meaningful on-court production. The four-year wait also meant the draft right could not help Cleveland’s immediate 1992-93 playoff plans. Cleveland’s C grade records that speculative benefit without claiming Geary’s later career for the Cavaliers. Orlando gained a short-term backup guard and Cleveland kept a lottery-independent late pick. The difference between C+ and C reflects the more direct availability of a player at the time of the trade, not the championships Kerr won after leaving Orlando.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Magic Edge. Orlando earns C+ for acquiring Steve Kerr and using him in 47 games during 1992-93. Cleveland receives C for the deferred second-rounder that became the No. 56 selection of Reggie Geary. Kerr’s subsequent Chicago championships are not credited to Orlando.

sections.heading: Charlotte Turned Johnny Newman Into a Backup Point Guard
sections.body: The Hornets traded Johnny Newman to the New Jersey Nets for Rumeal Robinson on December 10, 1993. UPI reported the move just before New Jersey played Chicago, and the next day’s Associated Press report described the same two-player exchange. Charlotte had several players who could work at small forward, including Dell Curry, Eddie Johnson and David Wingate, but Muggsy Bogues was its only established point guard. Robinson offered a potential relief option. The Nets, meanwhile, wanted another scoring wing to take pressure off Kenny Anderson and Derrick Coleman. Neither side received a draft pick or future consideration. The swap reflected two distinct positional needs rather than an assumption that the players had equivalent scoring reputations.

sections.heading: Newman Filled a Reserve Scoring Role Behind New Jersey’s Starters
sections.body: Newman had started all 18 Charlotte games in 1993-94 before the trade, averaging 13.0 points. In New Jersey he came off the bench for all 63 of his regular-season appearances, averaging 9.5 points in 20.1 minutes. He also played four postseason games for the Nets. That is a measurable sixth-man scoring contribution, though he did not retain his old starting role or remain with New Jersey long-term. New Jersey’s C grade recognizes the useful reserve season rather than crediting his previous Hornets scoring peak. The Nets did not obtain a new all-star, but acquired a player with experience who could provide bench offense during a playoff season.

sections.heading: Robinson Barely Entered Charlotte’s Rotation
sections.body: Robinson had played 17 Nets games earlier in 1993-94, averaging 5.9 points and 2.6 assists before the deal. Charlotte used him in 14 regular-season games without a start, for only 95 total minutes and 30 points. His 2.1 points per game with the Hornets gave the club little immediate relief for Bogues. Robinson had previously been a full-time Atlanta starter and a more substantial New Jersey backup in earlier seasons; those numbers cannot be credited as Charlotte production. The Hornets C grade therefore relies more on the modest cost and positional experiment than realized minutes. The canonical equal outcome is generous to Charlotte relative to Newman’s bench scoring, but the trade was not large enough to reshape either franchise’s core.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. New Jersey earns C after Johnny Newman supplied 63 games at 9.5 points per game. Charlotte also receives C, though Rumeal Robinson provided only 14 games and 30 points for the Hornets. The Nets achieved more immediate scoring production, while Charlotte’s short guard trial ended quickly.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Built a New Center Rotation With Mike Gminski
sections.body: On January 16, 1988, the 76ers acquired Mike Gminski and Ben Coleman from New Jersey, while the Nets received Roy Hinson, Tim McCormick and a future second-round draft choice. The pick became No. 32 in 1989 and was used on Stanley Brundy. Philadelphia was moving on from a Hinson frontcourt experiment and buying the dependability of a center who had already started regularly for New Jersey. Gminski was the largest immediate basketball asset, but Coleman gave the 76ers another rotation big man. New Jersey received two players ready to join its starting group plus a draft opportunity; neither side exchanged cash as the leading part of the package.

sections.heading: Gminski Became a Multi-Year 76ers Starter
sections.body: Gminski immediately played and started 47 Philadelphia games after the swap, averaging 16.9 points and 10.5 rebounds, followed by 82 starts in 1988-89 with 17.2 points and 9.4 rebounds. He stayed central to the 76ers interior rotation in 1989-90, when he started 81 games and averaged 13.7 points. The uninterrupted run is why Philadelphia receives an A; the club acquired a starting-caliber player for multiple seasons rather than only a short midseason rental. Coleman appeared in 43 post-trade 76ers games in 1987-88 and 58 more in 1988-89. His contribution was more modest but belongs in the return instead of being overlooked.

sections.heading: The Nets Got Scoring From Hinson but a Shorter McCormick Window
sections.body: Roy Hinson was far from an empty return. Across his 48 New Jersey appearances after the trade in 1987-88 he started 47 and scored 17.4 points with 7.2 rebounds per game. He also played 82 games for the Nets the following season, averaging 16.0 points. McCormick supplied 47 Nets games in 1987-88, averaging 15.8 points and 7.7 rebounds, before leaving the NBA after that season. Those figures are meaningful and complicate an overly dismissive D+ for the Nets. But Gminski supplied Philadelphia with several full starting seasons, and the pick linked to Brundy did not reproduce comparable team value. The 76ers won on durability, not because New Jersey received no productive players.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win. Philadelphia earns A for Gminski’s immediate 47 starts, all 82 starts in 1988-89, and continued frontcourt production, with Coleman also acquired. New Jersey grades D+ in the canonical record despite useful Hinson and McCormick seasons, because its return lacked Gminski’s durability. The No. 32 Brundy pick did not close the gap.

sections.heading: Washington and Sacramento Addressed Different Guard Needs
sections.body: On October 30, 1990, the Washington Bullets traded Steve Colter to the Sacramento Kings for second-year shooting guard Byron Irvin. The Washington Post described Colter as a veteran backup point guard who wanted a larger role and had fallen out of step with how coach Wes Unseld wanted him to play. The Bullets expected Irvin to provide a more natural shooting-guard option, while Colter welcomed a move west where he could handle more of the offense. The Kings had acquired Irvin only during the previous summer’s Danny Ainge transaction, so this was an unusually quick second move for the young guard. No future picks or extra players were included.

sections.heading: Colter Did Not Become Sacramento’s Lead Guard
sections.body: Colter played only 19 Kings regular-season games in 1990-91, never starting and averaging 13.2 minutes, 3.1 points and 1.9 assists. The move therefore did not give him the major ball-handling opportunity he had wanted. Sacramento’s early-season guard rotation continued to shift and Colter was gone before the end of the year. He later played elsewhere, but those later seasons cannot be credited to Sacramento. His 19 games were a modest direct return from a player who had been Washington’s reserve point guard, and the Kings C grade is best read as limited but real veteran depth. The original Washington Post report explains the fit the club was pursuing, which did not develop as hoped.

sections.heading: Irvin Also Remained on the Fringe in Washington
sections.body: Irvin appeared in 33 Bullets games that season with four starts, averaging 5.2 points in 9.6 minutes. He offered some scoring from the two-guard spot but did not settle into a sustained role. Washington ended up receiving 14 more games and slightly greater point production than the Kings obtained from Colter, although the players occupied different positions. Neither became a long-term building block, and no draft asset survived for either club. With C grades for both teams, the canonical Even Trade verdict fits this two-player test of roster needs. The value came from a short stretch of regular-season playing time rather than later career milestones.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Sacramento gets C for 19 games of Steve Colter backup-point-guard work. Washington also gets C for Byron Irvin’s 33 appearances and 5.2 points per game. Both clubs tried to address a particular backcourt need; neither found a durable solution.

sources.title: Contemporaneous Steve Colter–Byron Irvin trade report

sections.heading: The Bulls Acquired a Veteran at Almost No Realized Draft Cost
sections.body: Chicago traded a conditional 2001 second-round pick to Golden State on February 25, 1993, for veteran forward Ed Nealy. The Warriors had used Nealy sparingly and agreed to send him to a Bulls team trying to add bench security for the final stretch of the regular season. Both team transaction ledgers identify the conditional selection as not having conveyed. Chicago consequently obtained a real player without ever delivering the contingent pick. This should not be rewritten as a trade involving a successful 2001 selection or a fully guaranteed future obligation. It was a low-stakes move driven by immediate roster needs late in Chicago’s title defense.

sections.heading: Nealy Appeared in Eleven Regular-Season Games
sections.body: Nealy played 11 Bulls games after the acquisition, never starting. His totals were 79 minutes, 23 points and 16 rebounds, equivalent to 2.1 points and 1.5 rebounds per appearance. Those are very small numbers next to the accomplishments of Chicago’s principal players in the 1992-93 championship campaign. Nealy still provided a physical practice-and-bench frontcourt option while the club navigated the final weeks of the season. His status as a member of a championship roster is part of his career record, but the title cannot be attributed to his eleven appearances. The B+ Bulls grade in this low-cost trade represents securing depth without giving up a conveyed draft selection, not an enormous individual on-court impact.

sections.heading: Golden State Lost a Roster Option and Received No Pick
sections.body: Nealy had played 30 regular-season games for the Warriors earlier in 1992-93 with four starts and 7.6 minutes per contest. Golden State was parting with a player whose rotation opportunities were already limited. The contemplated 2001 second-round compensation was conditional and did not convey, so the Warriors cannot be credited with a prospect or a later selected player from this exchange. Their C+ grade reflects a small transaction with little realized draft return, while Chicago actually used the acquired veteran, briefly. The gap in practical value comes from a player who played and a pick that never transferred, not from broad judgments about Golden State’s roster strategy.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win. Chicago receives B+ for eleven late-season games from Ed Nealy without surrendering its conditional 2001 second-round choice, which never conveyed. Golden State earns C+ for a transaction that moved a marginal reserve but generated no realized draft pick.

sources.title: Chicago Bulls 1992-93 transactions and nonconveyed pick

sections.heading: Charlotte Traded Tim Kempton for a Future Second-Round Pick
sections.body: The expansion Charlotte Hornets sent forward-center Tim Kempton to Denver on September 11, 1989, in exchange for a 1991 second-round pick. The pick eventually became No. 28, used by Charlotte on University of Minnesota guard Kevin Lynch. Kempton had played 79 games for the Hornets in their inaugural 1988-89 season, supplying regular bench frontcourt minutes, and Denver wanted similar veteran availability without waiting for a draft. The Hornets took a future chance instead, betting that a selection two summers later could help turn over their expansion roster. The two-year delay in realizing the choice is essential to the comparison.

sections.heading: Kempton Was in the Nuggets Rotation Immediately
sections.body: Kempton played 71 regular-season games for Denver in 1989-90, starting 14 and averaging 14.9 minutes, 5.4 points, 3.1 rebounds and 1.7 assists. He added three postseason appearances when the Nuggets faced the Spurs. Those numbers are modest for an NBA forward, but they amount to a recognizable bench job for nearly an entire season. His Denver tenure did not extend into several full seasons and he later played professional basketball overseas. Nevertheless, Denver received useful play at the exact time it acquired him, which is a stronger concrete return than merely preserving the possibility of a future second-round selection. Denver’s C+ grade reflects that immediate contribution and narrow relative benefit.

sections.heading: Lynch Could Not Turn Charlotte’s Pick into Comparable Impact
sections.body: Charlotte used the No. 28 choice in 1991 on Kevin Lynch. The Hornets’ draft-history ledger confirms the exact selection, which was the first pick of the second round that year. Lynch never established a significant Hornets rotation role, and the franchise could not match Kempton’s 71 Denver regular-season games with comparable immediate production from the selection. There was no first-round pick, no traded veteran returning alongside the second, and no unrecorded cash consideration to inflate the return. Charlotte’s C grade accounts for the legitimate opportunity to draft a prospect but recognizes the short realized value. The Nuggets got the better outcome in a useful reserve-for-future-pick deal, though neither side found a franchise centerpiece.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Nuggets Edge. Denver earns C+ for Tim Kempton’s 71 regular-season games and three playoff appearances in 1989-90. Charlotte gets C after trading him for the No. 28 selection used on Kevin Lynch. The acquired veteran delivered more immediate NBA minutes.

sections.heading: Portland and Washington Exchanged Established Frontcourt Players
sections.body: On June 24, 1993, Portland traded center Kevin Duckworth to the Washington Bullets for forward Harvey Grant and additional future considerations, according to the canonical asset record. The Blazers had reached the NBA Finals one season earlier and wanted to adjust their supporting frontcourt around Clyde Drexler. Grant was coming off a substantial scoring role in Washington but could play a different position from Duckworth, whose mobility and offensive role had changed. For Washington, the center position was a concern and Duckworth provided proven size. The loosely described additional consideration should not be assigned an invented player or pick without independent documentation. Both sides were making a genuine rotation swap.

sections.heading: Grant Became a Regular Portland Starter Before His Role Contracted
sections.body: Grant started regularly for Portland during his initial seasons after the exchange. In 1993-94 he played nearly the entire season with the Blazers and contributed scoring and rebounding on the wing and at power forward. He was not traded back to Washington until a separate 1996 deal, so his work in Portland must be evaluated on its own. Grant’s offensive flexibility helped Portland replace a traditional center with a smaller forward-heavy lineup, though it did not recreate the club’s 1992 Finals run. The Blazers’ C+ acknowledges multiple years of service by a useful player without treating him as a transformative addition.

sections.heading: Duckworth Gave Washington Two Seasons of Center Minutes
sections.body: Duckworth played 69 games for the Bullets in 1993-94, averaging 6.6 points and 4.7 rebounds in 21.5 minutes. He followed with 40 games in 1994-95, averaging 7.1 points and 4.9 rebounds. Those 109 Washington appearances provide a direct measure of the return: useful interior size and minutes, but far below his earlier high-scoring Portland seasons. Washington’s C+ grade accounts for the short two-year period and the fact that Duckworth was no longer a reliable star-level center. Portland received more years from Grant while Washington obtained more immediate traditional center depth, a trade of different needs rather than an easy blowout.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Portland receives C+ for multiple seasons of Harvey Grant frontcourt work. Washington gets C+ for 109 Kevin Duckworth games over 1993-95 with about seven points and five rebounds per appearance. Both clubs obtained viable rotation pieces with limitations.

sections.heading: A Star Guard and Two Picks Headed for Washington
sections.body: On June 11, 1991, the Denver Nuggets sent Michael Adams and the No. 19 pick in the approaching draft to Washington, along with future second-round consideration. The Bullets surrendered the No. 8 choice, giving Denver a chance to select a player much earlier. Denver used its pick on Michigan State guard Mark Macon; Washington chose LaBradford Smith at No. 19, and the later selection was No. 36 in 1993, used on John Best. The Nuggets media guide independently records the same broad transaction. The bargain was unusual because the experienced point guard was arguably more valuable than any one draft selection: Washington gained proven offense and still retained a first-round pick.

sections.heading: Adams Immediately Became Washington’s All-Star Point Guard
sections.body: In 1991-92, Adams played and started 78 Bullets games while averaging 18.1 points, 7.6 assists and 1.9 steals. He was selected to the All-Star Game for that season, making the trade an immediate success for a Washington team searching for an established lead guard. His value was not confined to a prospect projection or a future draft transaction. LaBradford Smith also played NBA minutes for the Bullets as a young guard. The additional 1993 second-round choice yielded John Best, whose NBA role was negligible, but Adams supplied enough actual starting production to support Washington’s A+ grade. Neither Macon’s later appearances nor the second pick should distract from that main transaction-specific outcome.

sections.heading: Macon Was Available in Denver but Did Not Reach Adams’s Level
sections.body: Macon started 67 of his 76 Denver games in 1991-92, averaging 10.6 points and 2.0 steals. Those are real contributions from a top-ten draft selection, even if his shooting efficiency was weak and the role diminished in later years. He appeared in 48 Denver games in 1992-93, starting 27, before his career moved elsewhere. Denver’s C+ grade recognizes two partial starting seasons rather than no return at all. What the Nuggets surrendered, however, was an All-Star caliber ball handler who delivered that quality for Washington immediately, plus a lower first-rounder. The stronger veteran impact and remaining draft flexibility give the Bullets a convincing win.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wizards Win. Washington earns A+ for Michael Adams’s 78-start, All-Star 1991-92 season and also receives LaBradford Smith and a later second-round pick. Denver receives C+ for Mark Macon, who played 76 rookie games but could not match the veteran guard’s immediate impact.

sections.heading: Atlanta Acquired Mookie Blaylock and Roy Hinson
sections.body: The Hawks dealt guard Rumeal Robinson to New Jersey on November 3, 1992, for point guard Mookie Blaylock and veteran forward Roy Hinson. The trade sent an established Nets starter to Atlanta before he had reached his most productive NBA seasons. Blaylock had already played 72 games for the Nets in both 1990-91 and 1991-92, becoming a capable scorer, passer and defender. New Jersey was experimenting with a different backcourt approach while Atlanta needed a durable organizer. Hinson was an additional named player in the transaction, not an asset Atlanta acquired later. The clubs’ dated transaction records confirm all three participants. Contemporary reporting already described Hinson as injured; Basketball-Reference records his last NBA games in 1990-91 with New Jersey, not any Atlanta appearances after the exchange.

sections.heading: Blaylock Developed Into One of the Hawks’ Defining Guards
sections.body: Blaylock started 78 games in 1992-93 and averaged 13.4 points, 8.4 assists and 2.5 steals. The next season he was an All-Star and a member of the NBA All-Defensive First Team. Over seven Hawks seasons, he appeared in 518 regular-season games and amassed 1,321 steals, giving Atlanta much more than a one-year experiment. His 1993-94 average of 9.7 assists was among the league’s highest, and his perimeter defense became integral to the team. Those accomplishments are directly traceable to this trade. The Hawks’ A- grade rests overwhelmingly on Blaylock’s Atlanta years, not on later recognition earned with another club or a claim that Hinson played an equally important role. Hinson did not appear in an Atlanta regular-season game, so his name in the package is not a second source of on-court Hawks value alongside Blaylock.

sections.heading: Robinson Produced for New Jersey but Did Not Last
sections.body: Robinson appeared in 80 New Jersey games in 1992-93, recording 8.4 points and 4.0 assists per contest. He played another 17 Nets games in 1993-94 and then moved on, finishing with 97 regular-season games for the franchise. He was a workable reserve and occasional starter, so the Nets did receive basketball production. But his tenure was short and never approached Blaylock’s multi-year organizing and defensive role in Atlanta. New Jersey’s D+ grade reflects the gap in longevity and positional value, while Atlanta’s A- recognizes a player who shaped several playoff-era rotations. Hinson’s separate involvement does not alter the chief comparison: Blaylock became the standout player from the entire deal.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win. Atlanta earns A- for landing Mookie Blaylock, a seven-season starter, All-Star and All-Defensive guard, along with Roy Hinson. New Jersey receives D+ because Rumeal Robinson provided only 97 games over two seasons. The lasting value belongs overwhelmingly to the Hawks.

sections.heading: The Lakers Exchanged Orlando Woolridge for Two Conditional Seconds
sections.body: Los Angeles sent forward Orlando Woolridge to Denver on August 3, 1990, accepting second-round picks scheduled for 1993 and 1995. Contemporary reporting by the Los Angeles Times and UPI confirms both the player and the two projected draft years. The Lakers wanted to reduce salary obligations and create flexibility for other roster business; Nuggets general manager Bernie Bickerstaff described Woolridge as an experienced scorer who could run in the club’s faster offense. The two future choices were conditional, a vital point obscured if they are simply described as two guaranteed second-round picks. The historical team ledgers ultimately mark both selections as not having conveyed.

sections.heading: Woolridge Became Denver’s Leading Scorer
sections.body: During 1990-91 Woolridge played 53 Nuggets games, making 50 starts and averaging 25.1 points with 6.8 rebounds. That scoring was nearly twice what he had averaged as a Lakers reserve in 1989-90. He was especially suited to Denver’s up-tempo attack even though the Nuggets finished 20-62 and could not defend effectively under Paul Westhead. His performance was a concrete scoring return for a struggling team looking for proven veterans. Denver later moved him to Detroit in August 1991 in a separate deal, so the club did not keep him for several seasons. Still, 53 starting-level scoring games for picks that never conveyed provides an unusually direct advantage.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Benefited From Flexibility, Not Draft Players
sections.body: The Lakers did reduce the immediate obligation to Woolridge, but neither conditional pick transferred. There is no 1993 or 1995 Lakers draftee to credit to this exchange. Those picks should not be confused with separate Lakers selections in either draft or later deals that brought in other veteran guards. From a basketball return perspective, Los Angeles surrendered a reserve who still had substantial scoring ability and received no realized draft capital, although its payroll objectives had some value. The Lakers’ C grade accounts for that financial maneuver. Denver’s A- grade is supported by Woolridge’s 25.1-point season and the absence of conveyed compensation, even with the Nuggets’ poor record and brief tenure.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win. Denver receives A- after getting 53 games and 25.1 points per game from Orlando Woolridge. Los Angeles earns C for salary flexibility, but both 1993 and 1995 conditional second-round picks failed to convey. The Nuggets got the only substantial playing return.

sections.heading: Dallas Sent Veteran Center James Donaldson to New York
sections.body: The Mavericks traded James Donaldson to the Knicks for Brian Quinnett on February 20, 1992. NBA’s historical trade-deadline record and both team transaction ledgers identify the same two participants with no accompanying draft selection. Donaldson had been an established Dallas center for several seasons, including a 1988 All-Star campaign, but by 1991-92 his role was far smaller as the Mavericks reworked their aging core. New York wanted another veteran big body available for the frontcourt. Dallas took a chance on a younger perimeter reserve who had struggled to secure a major role. Both clubs were seeking depth in very different positions.

sections.heading: Donaldson’s Knicks Return Was Only Fourteen Games
sections.body: Donaldson’s direct New York tenure in 1991-92 lasted 14 games with no starts. He totaled 81 minutes, 12 points and 19 rebounds, making this a depth addition rather than a new regular rotation center. His long prior Dallas career and earlier All-Star honors should not be counted as Knicks trade value. He had the experience to help at practices and in limited emergency minutes, but the Knicks did not receive an enduring starting presence. The canonical B assigned to New York is relatively generous for that on-court outcome, though the team secured a familiar veteran without giving up a first-round pick or other premium asset. The historical result was brief.

sections.heading: Quinnett Played Just Fifteen Dallas Games
sections.body: Brian Quinnett appeared in 15 Mavericks games after the trade, playing 9.1 minutes and averaging 2.7 points with 1.8 rebounds. Neither club gained sustained basketball output, but Dallas obtained even less significant veteran presence than New York envisioned with Donaldson. Dallas’s C+ grade records the limited younger-player trial. The original Knicks Win verdict gives New York the edge on the presumed value of Donaldson’s center availability; the difference is narrow based on the actual 1991-92 minutes. It would be misleading to claim that New York received Donaldson’s prime seasons or that Quinnett became a breakout Mavericks scorer. This was a small late-season depth transaction on both sides.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win. New York gets B for acquiring veteran center James Donaldson, though he played only 14 games and 81 minutes. Dallas receives C+ for Brian Quinnett, who appeared in 15 games averaging 2.7 points. The edge in the canonical grades is narrow given both short returns.

sections.heading: Atlanta Obtained Reggie Theus While Sacramento Added Draft Value
sections.body: On June 27, 1988, the Kings traded veteran guard Reggie Theus to Atlanta for Randy Wittman, the No. 18 pick in that summer’s first round and a late draft selection. Sacramento used the first-round choice on Ricky Berry and also received additional consideration whose precise final terms remain unclear in the inherited transaction record. Atlanta was aiming to bolster its guard rotation with a proven scorer; Theus had averaged more than 21 points per game in his final Kings season. Sacramento used the move to secure a younger shooting guard and additional draft opportunities. The main player and first-round terms are corroborated in historical league transactions.

sections.heading: Theus Played All Eighty-Two Hawks Regular-Season Games
sections.body: Theus started all 82 Atlanta games during 1988-89, recording 15.8 points and 4.7 assists per contest, and appeared in the team’s postseason games. That full season was the practical return that earns Atlanta its B grade. He no longer supplied the scoring volume he produced in Sacramento, and he joined Orlando after the season, so the Hawks did not receive a long-running veteran partnership. But he played a prominent offensive role without requiring Atlanta to wait for development of a draft choice. The club traded present draft value for one useful year of seasoned guard play and got what it expected in the short term.

sections.heading: Berry Was a Productive Kings Rookie Before His Career Ended
sections.body: Ricky Berry appeared in 64 Kings games in 1988-89, starting 21, averaging 11.0 points and shooting 40.6 percent from three-point range. That was a very good rookie contribution from the No. 18 selection. Wittman also offered an experienced wing option in the broader package. Tragically, Berry died after that season, so his NBA career ended before Sacramento could gain more than one year of play from the pick. The Kings’ C+ grade therefore should not imply that the selection yielded no NBA value; it reflects the limited duration of that return and a longer-term comparison with Theus’s immediate full-season starting role. No further draft or future consideration is assigned unverified statistics.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win. Atlanta earns B for 82 starts, 15.8 points and 4.7 assists per game from Reggie Theus in 1988-89. Sacramento receives C+ after adding Randy Wittman and drafting Ricky Berry at No. 18, whose 11.0-point rookie season was promising but tragically his only NBA campaign.

sections.heading: Charlotte Exchanged Two Guards for Kenny Anderson and Gerald Glass
sections.body: The Hornets and New Jersey Nets made a four-player backcourt trade on January 19, 1996. Charlotte sent Kendall Gill and Khalid Reeves to the Nets, receiving Kenny Anderson and Gerald Glass. Anderson had been a productive primary point guard for New Jersey, but the club was seeking a different scoring and defensive combination after an uneven start. Gill had recently returned to Charlotte from Seattle and the Hornets were willing to move him again to acquire a ball handler capable of creating opportunities for their scorers. Contemporary team transaction reports list all four players. Glass was a short-term addition rather than the centerpiece of Charlotte’s interest.

sections.heading: Anderson Played Well but Left Charlotte After That Season
sections.body: Anderson started 36 of his 38 Charlotte games after the trade, averaging 15.2 points and 8.6 assists in 34.3 minutes. He provided exactly the kind of passing the Hornets sought, despite the club missing the 1996 postseason. He then signed with Portland that offseason, making his Charlotte stay relatively short. Glass was waived by Charlotte on February 22 after only a few weeks. The Hornets therefore received a productive but temporary point guard and no enduring contribution from the other incoming player. Their canonical B- recognizes the immediate playmaking benefit without extending Anderson’s later Portland and Boston performances backward to this transaction.

sections.heading: Gill Eventually Supplied New Jersey Years of Starting Minutes
sections.body: Gill was a larger long-term win for New Jersey than his short Charlotte reunion suggested. After the January 1996 trade, he remained with the Nets and started 81 of 82 games in 1996-97, averaging 21.8 points, 6.1 rebounds, 4.0 assists and 1.9 steals. He remained a regular starter in 1997-98, with another 81 starts and 13.4 points per game. Reeves had a smaller role, but the return was clearly more than a single rented veteran. The canonical Nets C+ grade is lower than Charlotte’s B- despite Gill’s ensuing tenure, and the assessment should be read as preserving inherited grading pending a broader hindsight audit. Both teams received on-court production, with different durations.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Charlotte Edge. Charlotte grades B- for Kenny Anderson’s 38-game stretch at 15.2 points and 8.6 assists per game, while New Jersey receives C+ for Kendall Gill and Khalid Reeves. Gill later produced multiple starting seasons for the Nets, a real complication in the narrow canonical Charlotte verdict.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Secured a First-Round Pick Alongside Mike Gminski
sections.body: On February 24, 1994, Milwaukee sent veteran center Frank Brickowski to Charlotte for Mike Gminski and the Hornets’ 1997 first-round draft selection. Both clubs’ transaction ledgers establish the same deal and later associate the choice with No. 20 Paul Grant in 1997. The Bucks were preparing for a roster reset while Brickowski had started 40 of his 43 Milwaukee games earlier that season. Charlotte wanted to add a center who could score and pass, while Milwaukee took in an older frontcourt player with a first-round asset positioned several years into the future. The outgoing pick was a real first, not a contingent second or an unspecified future choice.

sections.heading: Brickowski Produced Twenty-Eight Hornets Games Before Injury
sections.body: Brickowski played 28 games for Charlotte after the swap, making six starts, scoring 282 total points with 125 rebounds and 57 assists. He had averaged 15.2 points and 6.5 rebounds in Milwaukee earlier that year, making the change worthwhile to Charlotte as a short-term offensive option. But a shoulder injury kept him out of the 1994-95 campaign, and he next appeared for Seattle in 1995-96. Thus the Hornets received one partial season rather than a reliable multi-year starting center. Charlotte’s D+ grade reflects how quickly its direct return ended, not a claim that Brickowski had no useful NBA skill. The club surrendered a first-round draft opportunity for that short stint.

sections.heading: The Bucks Kept a Valuable Draft Asset Even With a Veteran Return
sections.body: Gminski gave Milwaukee veteran center availability in the final weeks of 1993-94, but the lasting attraction was the draft capital received from Charlotte. The 1997 first-round selection ultimately became No. 20, associated with Paul Grant. The later draft history must be treated as a pick chain rather than an assumption that Grant’s NBA playing career all belonged to Milwaukee. The Bucks’ A- grade is grounded in obtaining a true first for a 34-year-old player who would soon miss an entire season. Charlotte got recognizable scoring for 28 games but carried the larger opportunity cost, which explains the substantial difference in the inherited outcome grades.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win. Milwaukee earns A- for Mike Gminski plus Charlotte’s 1997 first-round pick, which became No. 20. Charlotte receives D+ after Frank Brickowski played 28 games and missed the following season with a shoulder injury. The first-round draft asset gave Milwaukee the stronger long-term return.

sections.heading: The Bulls Sent Dickey Simpkins to Golden State for Scott Burrell
sections.body: On September 22, 1997, Chicago traded frontcourt reserve Dickey Simpkins to Golden State and received swingman Scott Burrell. The Bulls were preparing for what became the final championship season of their Michael Jordan and Scottie Pippen era, and Burrell could provide flexible perimeter defense and shooting behind the established starters. Golden State was willing to trade a wing it had obtained from Charlotte the prior February for another big man. Both clubs’ transaction records show a direct two-player exchange. No draft picks accompanied the swap. The trade makes most sense as a search for complementary bench roles, not an attempt to acquire a new star.

sections.heading: Burrell Played Eighty Games on the Championship Bulls
sections.body: Burrell appeared in 80 Bulls games during the 1997-98 regular season, averaging 5.2 points, 2.5 rebounds and 13.7 minutes. He started only three times, but the regular availability mattered as Chicago battled injuries and workload around its veterans. Burrell also appeared in 21 postseason games as the Bulls won the 1998 championship over Utah. That is meaningful, direct team-specific value from a reserve acquisition. He did not become a central scorer, and the title belongs principally to the team’s established leaders, but a reliable eighty-game bench swingman on a title roster is a tangible outcome. Chicago’s B+ grade reflects that role.

sections.heading: Simpkins Was Only a Brief Golden State Reserve
sections.body: Simpkins appeared in 19 Warriors games during 1997-98, totaling 196 minutes and making no starts. He averaged 1.0 point and 2.2 rebounds per appearance, a limited frontcourt return compared with the Bulls’ 80 games from Burrell. Simpkins later returned to Chicago in a separate transaction, but that subsequent Bulls stint is not a Warriors benefit of this September swap. Golden State’s C+ reflects brief roster depth from a player whose value in Chicago had been greater than his opportunity in Oakland. The head-to-head comparison should be based on the two clubs’ direct 1997-98 results, not Simpkins’ earlier Chicago championship appearances or his eventual reunion with the Bulls.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win. Chicago receives B+ for Scott Burrell’s 80 regular-season appearances and contribution to the 1998 championship run. Golden State earns C+ after Dickey Simpkins played only 19 games without a start. Burrell was the more useful direct acquisition.

sections.heading: Washington Exchanged an Aging Point Guard for Two Second-Rounders
sections.body: On August 2, 1994, Charlotte obtained veteran point guard Michael Adams from Washington, with the Bullets receiving the Hornets’ second-round selections in 1996 and 1997. Those choices ultimately became No. 55 Ronnie Henderson and No. 48 Predrag Drobnjak. Adams had been an All-Star for Washington in 1991-92 but was older and had played only 70 games in each of his last two Bullets seasons. Charlotte was seeking an experienced playmaker behind its younger guards, while Washington accepted the option to restock the roster through the draft. The exact dates and draft years appear in the 1994-95 Hornets transaction history.

sections.heading: Adams Became a Reserve in His Final NBA Years
sections.body: Adams played 29 games for Charlotte in 1994-95 without starting, averaging 6.5 points and 3.3 assists in 15.3 minutes. A season later he appeared in 21 more Hornets games, with three starts and 5.4 points per night. Those 50 appearances represented the final two NBA seasons of his career. Charlotte still obtained a recognizable veteran who could run the offense, though the team was not buying the explosive scoring and double-digit assists Adams had recorded in Denver years earlier. Its C grade reflects limited, usable guard depth and the opportunity cost of two future second-round choices, rather than his prior All-Star record.

sections.heading: The Two Draft Picks Offered Washington an Uncertain Return
sections.body: The 1996 second-round choice ended up No. 55 Ronnie Henderson, and the 1997 selection was associated with No. 48 Predrag Drobnjak. Washington received rights to draft or exchange prospects in two different years, instead of immediate NBA playing time from Adams. Neither selected player should be given a full Washington NBA career simply because a later transaction ledger names him next to the original compensation; the history of a draft right and the player’s eventual team tenure are different facts. The Bullets’ C reflects the opportunity for future roster construction despite modest realized output. Charlotte obtained fifty games of veteran guard depth, while Washington obtained choices with speculative development potential. Neither side found a lasting star through this trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Charlotte gets C for Michael Adams’s 50 games over two seasons, while Washington receives C for the 1996 and 1997 second-round choices used on Ronnie Henderson and Predrag Drobnjak. The veteran guard helped briefly, and the future choices did not produce an obvious franchise-level return.

sections.heading: New Jersey and the Clippers Exchanged Veteran Guards and Wings
sections.body: On September 23, 1999, the New Jersey Nets acquired veteran forward Johnny Newman from the Los Angeles Clippers for point guard Eric Murdock. It was a straightforward player-for-player move shortly before training camp: New Jersey wanted another scoring wing and the Clippers were in need of an experienced ball handler. Both clubs were rebuilding rotations, and neither was taking on a young lottery pick or receiving a future draft selection. Newman had been an established NBA scorer across several teams, while Murdock previously served as a starting point guard with Milwaukee. The value of this deal would be defined by what each could still offer late in his career.

sections.heading: Newman Played a Full Season as a Nets Reserve
sections.body: Newman appeared in all 82 Nets regular-season games during 1999-2000. He started nine, averaged 21.5 minutes and 10.0 points, and shot 37.9 percent from three-point range. That is a substantial reserve role, especially from a player who was 36 years old. New Jersey could ask him to cover perimeter minutes when injuries interrupted the younger wings. He wasn’t the team’s leading scorer, but his uninterrupted availability was a tangible benefit. The Nets’ C grade looks conservative when compared with the amount of direct court time received, though it acknowledges that this was a short-term veteran arrangement rather than a long-term development investment.

sections.heading: Murdock Gave Los Angeles a Smaller Point-Guard Sample
sections.body: Murdock appeared in 40 Clippers games in 1999-2000, starting 15 and averaging 11.7 points, 5.6 assists and 17.3 minutes. He handled real playmaking duties but did not appear for the full season. The Clippers had other young perimeter players to develop, and the club finished far outside playoff contention. Murdock’s assist rate gave the incoming player a distinct basketball function that Newman did not supply. Los Angeles’ C grade reflects forty games of useful point-guard help; New Jersey’s grade reflects twice as many games of veteran wing scoring. Both clubs addressed rotation holes for a season without gaining an asset that became a multi-year cornerstone.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. New Jersey earns C for Johnny Newman’s 82 regular-season games and 10.0 points per game. The Clippers also receive C after Eric Murdock provided 40 games with 11.7 points and 5.6 assists per outing. Their roles differed, but both returns were short-term.

sections.heading: Charlotte Chose Armstrong While Moving Two Guards
sections.body: Charlotte sent Muggsy Bogues and Tony Delk to Golden State for B.J. Armstrong on November 7, 1997. The Hornets were moving on from Bogues, their longtime point guard whose injuries and reserve role had reduced his playing time. Delk was a recent first-round choice, adding younger scoring potential to the Warriors’ return. Armstrong had been an All-Star and a championship starter in Chicago years earlier, but by late 1997 he was a veteran backup after two seasons in Golden State. The trade was a two-for-one arrangement, not a straight Bogues-for-Armstrong swap. Both incoming Warriors players require separate consideration when evaluating the deal’s outcome.

sections.heading: Bogues and Delk Both Played Significant Warriors Minutes
sections.body: Bogues appeared in 59 Golden State games in 1997-98, starting 31, and averaged 5.8 points and 5.5 assists in 26.3 minutes. He returned for another 36 Warriors appearances during the lockout-shortened 1998-99 season. Delk had an even larger first-year workload: 74 games in 1997-98, nine starts and 10.4 points per appearance. A team receiving two guards who jointly covered regular rotation roles extracted far more than a mere famous veteran name. Golden State’s A- grade rewards both a seasoned floor general and a younger scorer. They were not championship-level contributors, but their direct playing time is enough to explain the clear advantage.

sections.heading: Armstrong Became a Limited Hornets Backup
sections.body: Armstrong made 62 Charlotte regular-season appearances in 1997-98 without a start, averaging 12.5 minutes, 3.9 points and 2.3 assists. He was useful as a low-minute reserve but nowhere near the full-time player he had been for Chicago. He also appeared in nine playoff games for the Hornets that season, providing some postseason depth. Charlotte’s D+ grade reflects surrendering Bogues and Delk for a single guard whose role was substantially smaller than their combined opportunity in Golden State. The transaction illustrates the cost of trading both a franchise veteran and a young prospect for a backup whose most productive career seasons were already behind him.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win. Golden State earns A- for 59 Bogues games with 5.5 assists per night plus 74 games and 10.4 points from Tony Delk in 1997-98. Charlotte receives D+ for B.J. Armstrong’s 62 reserve appearances. The two-player Warriors return delivered substantially more playing value.

sources.title: Bogues and Delk Golden State 1997-98 playing totals

sections.heading: The Hornets Moved Scott Burrell for Frontcourt Depth
sections.body: On February 20, 1997, Charlotte traded Scott Burrell to Golden State for veteran forward Donald Royal. The Hornets were positioning for the postseason and wanted another physical wing and rebounding option. Burrell was a younger defender who had struggled to regain a large role after early injuries, and Golden State was willing to try him in a different perimeter mix. Charlotte’s own transaction list places this deal on the same date as its separate Ricky Pierce acquisition from Denver, but those should not be conflated. Burrell and Royal were the only two players exchanged between Charlotte and Golden State in this particular move, with no draft picks attached.

sections.heading: Royal Was Only a Part-Season Hornets Addition
sections.body: Royal played 25 Charlotte games in the remaining 1996-97 regular season, starting twice and totaling 320 minutes, 70 points and 58 rebounds. His averages of 2.8 points and 2.3 rebounds were consistent with a marginal reserve rather than a player who would materially change Charlotte’s 54-win team. He remained on the roster into 1997-98 for another 29 games but still had a small bench role. The Hornets therefore received real interior minutes without acquiring a future primary contributor. Charlotte’s C- grade reflects the limited return and the loss of a relatively younger player who still could cover perimeter minutes for another team.

sections.heading: Burrell Became an Exchangeable Warriors Asset
sections.body: Burrell played 29 Golden State games after the February move, averaging 4.9 points and 15.8 minutes without a start. His offensive efficiency was limited, but the Warriors gave him more than a brief evaluation. In September 1997, Golden State sent Burrell to Chicago for Dickey Simpkins, giving the franchise another chance to adjust its frontcourt. That later trade was not part of the original Charlotte agreement and requires its own asset accounting. The Warriors’ C+ grade recognizes both Burrell’s 29 immediate appearances and his availability for a subsequent trade. Chicago’s later championship season with Burrell should not be counted as Golden State’s on-court contribution.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win. Golden State gets C+ after acquiring Scott Burrell for 29 games and later moving him in a separate trade. Charlotte earns C- for Donald Royal’s limited 25-game reserve role in 1996-97. Both sides received supporting players, but Burrell offered more flexibility.

sections.heading: Charlotte Acquired Veteran Scorer Ricky Pierce
sections.body: Charlotte sent Anthony Goldwire and George Zídek to Denver for Ricky Pierce on February 20, 1997. The trade was part of the Hornets’ effort to get more experienced perimeter scoring while defending a place in the Eastern Conference playoffs. Pierce was past the seasons when he had been a leading sixth-man scorer in Milwaukee, but he still offered shooting and professional experience. Denver accepted two younger players with different specialties, Goldwire as a guard and Zídek as a seven-foot reserve center. The Nuggets’ transaction history confirms both incoming players; treating it as Pierce-for-Goldwire alone would omit half of their return. No draft picks were part of the trade.

sections.heading: Pierce Contributed Bench Scoring in a Short Hornets Stay
sections.body: Pierce first appeared for Charlotte on February 21 against the Clippers, scoring nine points in 14 minutes. The next four games included scoring totals of six, thirteen, sixteen and thirteen points, as shown in his contemporaneous 1997 game log. He was capable of providing a few useful points without needing to dominate the ball, complementing a Hornets offense led by Glen Rice. Yet he was nearing the end of his playing career, and the acquisition did not produce a lasting top-tier scorer. Charlotte’s C grade reflects the modest direct contribution from an established guard acquired during a push toward a 54-win season and first-round playoff appearance.

sections.heading: Denver Collected Two Players With Limited Upside
sections.body: Goldwire played 60 regular-season games between Charlotte and Denver during 1996-97, averaging 6.5 points and 3.7 assists across both clubs. Those are season-wide figures, not exclusively his Denver production; the Nuggets acquired only the post-February portion. Zídek was an additional size option but did not develop into a sustained starter for Denver. The Nuggets’ C reflects the practical value of two inexpensive opportunities, balanced against the fact that neither return transformed the rotation. Charlotte obtained an established scorer on a playoff-caliber team, while Denver obtained a guard and center for a club with a very different competitive outlook. Neither side made a franchise-defining move, supporting the equal original grades.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Charlotte gets C for adding veteran guard Ricky Pierce to its 1997 playoff push. Denver also earns C for Anthony Goldwire and George Zídek, who supplied younger guard and center options. Both clubs gained role-specific depth without a lasting standout return.

sections.heading: New Jersey Turned George McCloud Into a First-Round Pick
sections.body: The Nets traded George McCloud to the Lakers on February 20, 1997, receiving Joe Kleine, a 1997 first-round selection and a conditional future second. McCloud had arrived in New Jersey just three days earlier in the massive Dallas transaction involving Shawn Bradley and Sam Cassell, so this was a rapid second move involving the same player. New Jersey wanted a more valuable future asset while Los Angeles sought outside shooting. The first-round pick became No. 21 in the 1997 draft, used on Anthony Parker. The conditional second did not convey according to both clubs’ transaction ledgers, so it cannot be assigned a fictional eventual prospect.

sections.heading: The First-Round Pick Became Part of a Larger Nets Move
sections.body: New Jersey selected Parker at No. 21, then packaged his rights with Jim Jackson, Eric Montross and Tim Thomas in a June 27, 1997 deal to Philadelphia for Keith Van Horn, Michael Cage, Lucious Harris and Don MacLean. Parker therefore never provided a Nets regular-season career, but the draft asset contributed to an exchange that delivered a major young scorer in Van Horn. The Nets’ A- grade reflects the option value of acquiring an authentic first-round pick for a player they had held only briefly. Joe Kleine’s presence was additional frontcourt depth, but the pick and its reuse are the central difference. Van Horn’s entire value should not be assigned to one of several outgoing draft and player assets.

sections.heading: McCloud Played Only Twenty-Three Lakers Games
sections.body: McCloud appeared in 23 regular-season Lakers games after the swap, starting twice and averaging 4.1 points in 12.4 minutes. He was making 42.9 percent of his three-point attempts in that small sample but did not provide a full season or sustained starting production. Los Angeles’ C- grade corresponds to that brief bench role weighed against surrendering a first-round selection. The Nets also obtained Kleine and the unused conditional second, although neither adds a long career of on-court value. The core comparison is a future first with meaningful later trade utility versus an acquired wing who spent only a few weeks as a Lakers reserve.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win. New Jersey earns A- for receiving Joe Kleine and the No. 21 first-round choice used on Anthony Parker, whose rights later formed part of the Keith Van Horn acquisition. Los Angeles receives C- after George McCloud played 23 games at 4.1 points per night. The extra conditional second never conveyed.

sections.heading: Seattle Sent Jim McIlvaine to New Jersey for Two Veterans
sections.body: On January 21, 1999, Seattle traded center Jim McIlvaine to New Jersey for Michael Cage and Don MacLean. The clubs faced an unusual short NBA calendar: the 1998-99 lockout reduced the regular season to 50 games, and the trade was recorded just before play resumed in February. McIlvaine was a defensive-minded seven-footer whose expensive Seattle contract had drawn attention since his arrival in 1996. New Jersey wanted another shot blocker near the rim, while Seattle used two less prominent veterans to change its depth and financial commitments. The Nets gave up two distinct players, not a conditional pick; the salary and fit context is important to understanding why Seattle wanted to move McIlvaine.

sections.heading: McIlvaine Offered Brief Rim Protection to the Nets
sections.body: McIlvaine played 22 New Jersey games in 1998-99, starting only once and averaging about twelve minutes per game. He blocked shots at a respectable rate for his limited court time but scored only a few points per appearance. That was a relatively small realized return from a center who had previously been paid to protect the paint as a Seattle starter. New Jersey’s C grade recognizes some defensive availability without overvaluing the original contract. His playing time did not transform a Nets club that finished the short season 16-34. The long-term return for New Jersey was constrained both by his limited role and by the club’s subsequent attempts to manage its frontcourt.

sections.heading: Seattle Regained Flexibility but Not a New Star
sections.body: Cage was an experienced rebounder near the end of his career, and MacLean was a veteran forward who could offer spot scoring. Neither replaced McIlvaine with a permanent starter. Their value to Seattle came from alternative roster construction and reduced commitment to a single expensive reserve center. The SuperSonics’ C+ grade represents a small relative edge from that flexibility, rather than a claim that either incoming player reproduced the team’s earlier high-level center production. The deal also did not produce a new Seattle draft pick, so the final assessment should not import the results of later selections or unrelated trades. Both returns remained limited in basketball terms.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Oklahoma City Thunder Edge. The Seattle franchise earns C+ for moving Jim McIlvaine and obtaining Michael Cage and Don MacLean with more roster flexibility. New Jersey receives C for 22 games of limited McIlvaine center minutes. Neither side added a long-term leading player.

sections.heading: New Jersey Exchanged Four Players for Two Veterans
sections.body: On November 2, 1988, the Nets acquired center Joe Barry Carroll and guard Lester Conner from Houston. The Rockets received Tim McCormick, Frank Johnson, Lorenzo Romar and Tony Brown. That four-for-two construction is central to the trade: New Jersey concentrated a collection of reserves and short-term players into an established frontcourt starter, while Houston expanded its available rotation options. The transaction followed New Jersey’s October 31 acquisition of Mike McGee, another move in an unusually active opening week. Both team and league transaction listings confirm the six-player package without an attached draft pick.

sections.heading: Carroll Provided Actual Starting-Center Production
sections.body: Carroll played 64 games for New Jersey in 1988-89, starting 62 and averaging 16.3 points, 8.5 rebounds and 1.5 blocks. Those totals were particularly useful on a Nets team still trying to stabilize its frontcourt. He was not the club’s only source of scoring, and he was already in the later portion of his career, but he supplied an immediately identifiable starting center. Conner added a second experienced guard to the receiving side. The Nets’ B+ grade can therefore be connected to Carroll’s real work in New Jersey rather than relying on an abstract comparison of four names against two. The center’s minutes were the most valuable single return from this transaction.

sections.heading: Houston Took Depth Without Matching Carroll’s Role
sections.body: The Rockets acquired McCormick, Johnson, Romar and Brown, giving their coaching staff several different reserve backcourt and frontcourt profiles. That may have helped roster flexibility but the players did not collectively deliver a new Houston starting center with Carroll’s 16.3-point and 8.5-rebound production. Johnson’s role must be evaluated as a Houston player, not by his earlier career elsewhere, and McCormick’s previous Nets statistics cannot be counted again for the Rockets. Houston’s C reflects usable depth from a larger package while conceding the strongest player-level return to New Jersey. No later Nets draft selection was involved in this particular six-player deal.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win. New Jersey earns B+ after Joe Barry Carroll started 62 games and averaged 16.3 points with 8.5 rebounds in 1988-89, with Lester Conner also acquired. Houston receives C for Tim McCormick, Frank Johnson, Lorenzo Romar and Tony Brown, a larger package without comparable starting-center production.

sections.heading: The Nets Paid Two Future Second-Round Picks for Mike McGee
sections.body: On October 31, 1988, New Jersey traded second-round selections in 1991 and 1996 to Sacramento for veteran swingman Mike McGee. The draft choices eventually were associated with No. 31 Randy Brown and No. 37 Jeff McInnis. The unusually long wait until the second selection is part of the bargain: the Nets wanted an experienced scorer immediately, while the Kings accepted two opportunities to obtain or later move younger players. The dated league transaction records confirm both future second-rounders. Sacramento should receive credit for draft rights created, not automatically for every later NBA season by those players if their rights subsequently traveled.

sections.heading: McGee Started Nearly Fifty Games for New Jersey
sections.body: The Nets put McGee into a much larger role than he held in Sacramento at the end of 1987-88. He appeared in 80 New Jersey games in 1988-89 and started 49, scoring 13.0 points per game with 36.5 percent three-point shooting. This was a substantial immediate return for two future second-round selections, and his 1,038 total points are tied directly to the Nets tenure. New Jersey’s C grade in the historical canonical record arguably understates that single-season production, but the club was not acquiring an enduring young centerpiece; McGee played for Phoenix the following season. A strong short-term scorer is different from an asset capable of supporting the roster for many years.

sections.heading: Sacramento Used Both Picks: Randy Brown and a 1996 Trade Asset
sections.body: The pick identities did not end with hypothetical future players. Sacramento actually drafted guard Randy Brown with New Jersey's 1991 second-round selection, No. 31 overall. Brown played 259 regular-season games with the Kings from 1991 through 1995 and started 38. Those are Kings minutes, not credit borrowed from his later Chicago title teams. The 1996 second-round selection also stayed useful as an asset, but it was not spent by Sacramento on Jeff McInnis. On June 13, 1996, the Kings sent Sarunas Marciulionis and that No. 37 pick to Denver for Mahmoud Abdul-Rauf. The Nuggets subsequently drafted McInnis with the choice. Sacramento therefore realized four seasons of Brown as a rotation guard and used the other pick as part of an additional player acquisition. Abdul-Rauf was NOT obtained for the draft pick alone, so only the pick's contribution to the combined package should be credited to the original 1988 exchange. New Jersey received a genuine immediate scoring season from McGee; the Kings received a later player and an additional trade chip. The limited Sacramento C+ versus New Jersey C advantage can be defended on sourced realized value rather than on the mistaken assumption that both picks became players for other franchises.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Kings Edge — Sacramento C+ and New Jersey C. Mike McGee gave the Nets 80 games, 49 starts and 13.0 points per game in 1988-89, a genuine short-term scoring return. Sacramento drafted Randy Brown at No. 31 in 1991 and received 259 Kings games and 38 starts before Brown departed. The other Nets second-rounder became an important piece of Sacramento's 1996 trade with Denver: the Kings packaged the No. 37 pick with Sarunas Marciulionis to acquire Mahmoud Abdul-Rauf, while Denver selected Jeff McInnis. The grade credits Sacramento's real outcomes without treating McInnis's later career or the entire Abdul-Rauf acquisition as direct 1988 proceeds.

sections.heading: Charlotte Received a Draft Choice for Stuart Gray
sections.body: On February 22, 1990, Charlotte sent reserve center Stuart Gray to New York for a 1991 second-round pick later recorded as No. 39, Jimmy Oliver. That was the direct Hornets–Knicks transaction and involved no first-rounder. Gray had been a low-minute reserve with Charlotte and had appeared in 39 Hornets games earlier that season. The Knicks needed emergency frontcourt depth more immediately than the Hornets did, while Charlotte wanted a future asset that could be traded or retained. Unlike a blockbuster, this small exchange involved a reserve center and an uncertain draft slot, and the subsequent history is essential to judging it.

sections.heading: New York Used Gray Sparingly
sections.body: Gray appeared in 19 Knicks games after the trade during the 1989-90 season, averaging 4.9 minutes, 0.8 points and 0.7 rebounds. He returned for eight New York appearances in 1990-91 and made no starts during his Knicks tenure. The incoming center gave the club temporary backup size but was not part of its main frontcourt or postseason offense. New York’s C grade in the canonical evaluation reflects those few emergency minutes; he did not become a lasting regular for the club. Referring to his career years in Indiana or Charlotte would overstate what New York directly acquired. His contribution was measurable, small and short-lived.

sections.heading: Charlotte Immediately Reused the Same Selection
sections.body: The Hornets did not wait until 1991 to use the acquired draft pick. Their dated 1989-90 transaction ledger also lists a February 22 move sending the No. 39 choice to Cleveland for forward Randolph Keys. That is the key follow-on transaction and explains why Charlotte itself did not select Jimmy Oliver. The pick’s draft outcome belongs to the later holder, while Charlotte obtained an immediate chance to examine Keys as a young forward. The inherited Knicks Win decision is a very narrow one because both teams have C grades. The meaningful facts are Gray’s 27 Knicks appearances over two seasons and Charlotte’s rapid conversion of the draft asset into a different player.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win, narrowly. New York earns C after Stuart Gray played 19 games in 1989-90 and eight more the following season. Charlotte also grades C for the future second-rounder that it promptly sent to Cleveland for Randolph Keys. The equal grades underline how limited both returns were.
