sections.heading: The Cavaliers Sent Dwyane Wade Home for a Protected Second
sections.body: On February 8, 2018, Cleveland traded veteran guard Dwyane Wade to Miami for a heavily protected 2024 second-round selection. The Heat official release and public remarks from Pat Riley confirm the terms. Wade had returned to Cleveland on a minimum-style veteran contract to play alongside LeBron James, but the Cavaliers made extensive deadline changes around a struggling supporting cast. Miami wanted to bring back its longtime franchise star for another playoff push and to give him a proper farewell period. The future second was top-55 protected and was never exercised, so it did not become an incoming NBA player for Cleveland. This was a player-return decision with personal meaning as well as basketball timing, rather than a major draft asset sale.

sections.heading: Wade Contributed to Two Additional Miami Seasons
sections.body: Wade returned to Miami and supplied scoring, ball handling and experienced leadership off the bench. The Heat reached the 2018 postseason, where he had notable contributions against Philadelphia. He then played a final 2018-19 NBA season for Miami, giving the franchise another year of the player whose earlier career had included three championship victories. Those appearances are real team-specific return from Cleveland’s deadline decision, though Wade was no longer the 2006 Finals MVP version of himself. Miami C in the inherited grade system recognizes a short-term but meaningful reserve contribution rather than a new long-term starting guard. His career before 2018 was established long before this deal and cannot count as a fresh player acquisition return.

sections.heading: Cleveland Did Not Receive an Exercised Draft Choice
sections.body: Cleveland agreed to the protected future second, which the transaction history later records as nonconveyed. The Cavaliers still benefited from greater roster flexibility and Wade’s stated preference to return to Miami, but they did not draft a player with a pick gained in this agreement. Cleveland proceeded to the 2018 NBA Finals with other players after its deadline overhaul, which should not be credited solely to Wade’s departure. The inherited Cleveland B- and Miami B- grades are equal, yet the record says Heat Win, reflecting the short-term basketball and goodwill value to Miami instead of a formal numerical grading lead. The distinction between an identified future pick and a selection that actually transfers is essential here. The final accounting favors Miami for the player it received and used.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Heat Win in the inherited assessment despite equal B- grades. Miami received Dwyane Wade for the 2018 postseason and his final 2018-19 NBA season. Cleveland obtained a top-55-protected 2024 second that did not convey. The on-court return was therefore concentrated on Miami, while Cleveland gained roster flexibility.

sections.heading: Charlotte Drafted Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and Immediately Traded His Rights
sections.body: On June 21, 2018, Charlotte selected Kentucky guard Shai Gilgeous-Alexander at No. 11 and sent his rights to the Clippers for the rights to No. 12 Miles Bridges and two future second-round selections. The NBA draft tracker confirms both players and the two picks, which the historical ledger later connects to Vernon Carey Jr. at No. 32 in 2020 and Scottie Lewis at No. 56 in 2021. The Hornets valued a young explosive forward to develop alongside Kemba Walker, while Los Angeles wanted the guard they had targeted one pick earlier. Neither prospect had played an NBA game for the team that drafted him when the rights moved, making this a draft-slot and development transaction rather than a veteran swap.

sections.heading: Gilgeous-Alexander Helped the Clippers in His Rookie Season
sections.body: The new Clippers guard played in all 82 regular-season games during 2018-19 and started 73, averaging 10.8 points and 3.3 assists. He also gained playoff experience in a difficult first-round series with Golden State. Los Angeles then included him in its 2019 trade with Oklahoma City to acquire Paul George, using his newly established value as part of a much larger superstar package. The later scoring titles and MVP-level performance belong to his Thunder playing career, not the Clippers record, but the 2018 rights acquisition created an unusually valuable piece. That is the main rationale behind the inherited Clippers A+ grade. The value exists in his actual rookie minutes and later trade capital, rather than assigning his entire peak NBA career to Los Angeles.

sections.heading: Bridges Produced for Charlotte but the Opportunity Cost Was Huge
sections.body: Bridges also became a genuine NBA starter and scorer for the Hornets over several seasons, so an F grade must not be interpreted as proof that the franchise got no court time from the exchange. His scoring and athleticism improved while Charlotte continued developing its roster. The additional second-round choices created more opportunities, but Carey and Lewis did not become comparable league-leading guards. The Clippers gained the player with greater career upside and the prospect eventually used in the Paul George deal, while Charlotte retained a usable forward. The inherited Clippers Win verdict focuses on the elite guard lost in a one-slot trade down. A proper accounting can acknowledge meaningful Bridges production without inventing a Charlotte career for Gilgeous-Alexander or a Clippers career for his Thunder achievements.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win. Los Angeles earns A+ for Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, an 82-game rookie who later became a key outgoing asset in the Paul George trade. Charlotte receives F for Miles Bridges and future seconds associated with Vernon Carey Jr. and Scottie Lewis, reflecting the much greater lost guard upside even though Bridges played substantial NBA minutes.

sections.heading: Brooklyn Used Cap Room to Collect Two Picks from Denver
sections.body: On July 13, 2018, Brooklyn accepted forward Kenneth Faried, veteran Darrell Arthur, a protected 2019 first-round pick and a 2020 second-round choice from Denver for reserve guard Isaiah Whitehead. The Nets official announcement identifies all four incoming assets and the player the Nuggets received. Denver was facing a difficult payroll situation with an expensive frontcourt, while Brooklyn had the space to take on salaries while rebuilding. The first became No. 27 in 2019, associated with Mfiondu Kabengele, and the second No. 55 Jay Scrubb in 2020. The pick rights followed their own later movements, but the draft selections were actual assets rather than theoretical options that never conveyed. The exchange was principally an asset-and-salary transaction, not a claim that Whitehead was Denver’s preferred new star.

sections.heading: The Two Big Men Did Not Supply Long Nets Careers
sections.body: Faried had been an effective Denver rebounder in earlier seasons, but his tenure in Brooklyn was short before he continued with Houston. Arthur did not establish himself as a regular Nets starter, and Brooklyn soon moved him to Phoenix in a separate deal for Jared Dudley and another pick. The original Denver transaction mattered because the Nets could make multiple roster decisions after acquiring those contracts and draft opportunities. Counting Faried’s earlier Nuggets career or later Rockets offense as Brooklyn playing time would wildly overstate the return. Brooklyn’s inherited A- grade rewards the first- and second-round assets obtained at a time when the franchise had lost many future draft choices in earlier decisions. The value of the picks should still be measured through the correct subsequent rights chain.

sections.heading: Denver Exchanged Future Choices for Financial Space
sections.body: Whitehead had played in 89 Nets games across two seasons and offered some defensive guard potential, but he did not become a major long-term Nuggets starter. Denver mainly reduced salary obligations, which created room for other roster investments around Nikola Jokić and Jamal Murray. The inherited Nuggets C- grade reflects having surrendered valuable draft capital for financial flexibility, even when salary relief was a legitimate operational objective. The eventual first- and second-round selections made the opportunity cost visible years after the July 2018 trade. Neither Kabengele nor Scrubb should be credited with an entire Brooklyn playing career without checking their rights movements; the picks themselves are the directly documented returns. The Nets obtained two distinct draft opportunities while Denver prioritized removing large veteran contracts.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win. Brooklyn earns A- for Kenneth Faried, Darrell Arthur, a protected 2019 first associated with No. 27 Mfiondu Kabengele and a 2020 second associated with No. 55 Jay Scrubb. Denver gets C- for Isaiah Whitehead and payroll relief, having surrendered future pick value.

sections.heading: Chicago Turned Justin Holiday into Two Guards and Two Picks
sections.body: The Bulls traded Justin Holiday to Memphis on January 3, 2019 for MarShon Brooks, Wayne Selden Jr., a 2019 second-round draft choice and a 2020 second-round choice. Both teams announced the exact package, and the selected players became No. 38 Daniel Gafford in 2019 and No. 44 Marko Simonović in 2020. Holiday had started all 38 of his Chicago appearances that season, averaging 11.6 points and 4.4 rebounds while providing perimeter defense. Memphis wanted a reliable veteran wing alongside Mike Conley and Marc Gasol, while the rebuilding Bulls could absorb a short-term roster change and wait for new prospects. The draft compensation was not conditional cash: both seconds became actual selections. Chicago also waived Cameron Payne in a separate roster move connected to making space for the incoming guards.

sections.heading: Gafford Became the Bulls Most Productive Long-Term Asset
sections.body: Chicago used its 2019 No. 38 pick on athletic Arkansas center Daniel Gafford. He immediately provided vertical finishing and shot blocking, becoming a regular contributor before his later trade to Washington. His entire subsequent career with Washington and Dallas should not be assigned to Chicago games, but the original 2019 pick produced an identifiable NBA big man with substantial professional value. The 2020 selection led to Marko Simonović, whose NBA impact was comparatively limited. Selden supplied additional wing minutes in the remainder of 2018-19, while Brooks was waived early rather than becoming a long-term scorer. The inherited Bulls A grade is supported by obtaining multiple resources for a veteran whose team was not contending. It is more accurate to credit Gafford and the picks than to claim all four acquired assets were equally successful on the court.

sections.heading: Memphis Got a Real Veteran but Paid a Future Development Cost
sections.body: Holiday gave the Grizzlies another experienced defender and occasional outside shooter during the 2018-19 season. His NBA role was legitimate, although Memphis was changing direction soon after the trade as its older core was broken up. The inherited Grizzlies C grade reflects the limited tenure compared with two selections that Chicago could develop or exchange. That is not a claim Holiday was useless, only that a short veteran assignment was a smaller return than having future picks that ultimately conveyed. The deal does not include the unrelated Marshon Brooks and Dillon Brooks name-confusion report from the preceding month as a completed part of this trade. The official January 3 transaction identifies MarShon Brooks and Selden as the two incoming Bulls players.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win. Chicago earns A for MarShon Brooks, Wayne Selden Jr. and two picks that became No. 38 Daniel Gafford in 2019 and No. 44 Marko Simonović in 2020. Memphis gets C for Justin Holiday, an experienced wing with a shorter remaining Grizzlies tenure.

sections.heading: Detroit Took a Rookie Shooter and a Second for Reggie Bullock
sections.body: On February 6, 2019, Detroit traded veteran guard Reggie Bullock to the Lakers for rookie Sviatoslav Mykhailiuk and a future second-round selection. The 2021 pick ultimately became No. 52 Luka Garza. The official NBA deadline tracker and both team transaction lists identify the completed agreement. Detroit executive Ed Stefanski explained that he preferred the combination of a named young player and a future second to offers consisting of two picks. Bullock had averaged 12.1 points earlier that season for the Pistons, giving Los Angeles an available perimeter shooter during an injury-disrupted playoff chase. The exchange contained no premium first-round pick and no additional starting veteran, so the return must be evaluated through Bullock’s short Lakers stint and Detroit’s two developmental pieces.

sections.heading: Bullock Was a Short-Term Shooter on a Lakers Team That Missed the Playoffs
sections.body: Bullock joined LeBron James and a team trying to stabilize a thin guard rotation while Lonzo Ball was injured. He provided spot-up shooting and experience defending on the wing, but could not resolve the much broader problems that led Los Angeles to miss the 2019 postseason. Bullock left in the summer, and his later career with New York and Dallas should not be credited as Lakers games obtained from the February agreement. The inherited Lakers B grade reflects real rotation use of a veteran sharpshooter, not a durable new scoring star. A player who had averaged more than twelve points for Detroit could still be useful, but his pretrade Pistons production does not belong in the Los Angeles statistical return. The trade was a rental aimed at the current season.

sections.heading: Mykhailiuk and Garza Offered Detroit More Development Time
sections.body: Mykhailiuk had been the No. 47 draft choice in 2018 and could shoot from distance. His Detroit role expanded during later seasons as the Pistons sought inexpensive prospects to complement a veteran roster. The added 2021 second became Iowa center Luka Garza, who appeared in actual NBA games for Detroit after the draft. Neither player instantly replaced the established Bullock scoring role, but the return provided two separate chances to develop contributors. The inherited Pistons B+ grade over Lakers B matches the Slight Pistons Edge verdict. Those grades reflect both the potential longevity of Mykhailiuk and the later draft result, rather than Bullock’s short-term usefulness being zero. The Pistons gained another inexpensive contract and a second selection while the Lakers acquired one wing for immediate minutes.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Pistons Edge. Detroit earns B+ for Sviatoslav Mykhailiuk and a 2021 second-round pick used on No. 52 Luka Garza. Los Angeles gets B for Reggie Bullock as a veteran perimeter option during the 2018-19 stretch run. The Lakers missed the postseason, while Detroit retained two development assets.

sections.heading: Brooklyn Traded Darrell Arthur for Dudley and a Protected Second
sections.body: On July 20, 2018, Brooklyn acquired veteran forward Jared Dudley and a protected 2021 second-round draft selection from Phoenix in exchange for Darrell Arthur. The Suns official release confirms all three assets and the NBA reported roughly $2.1 million in expected Phoenix salary savings. Brooklyn had acquired Arthur only one week earlier in the larger Denver cap-absorption agreement, demonstrating that the forward served as a tradeable contract rather than a new long-term Nets starter. Dudley could space the floor and advise a young Brooklyn team, while the second-round pick offered additional future flexibility. The later selection became No. 59 in 2021, associated with RaiQuan Gray. This was not the separate Richaun Holmes deal between Phoenix and Philadelphia completed that day, so its terms should not be mixed into the Brooklyn transaction.

sections.heading: Dudley Had a Useful Role on the 2019 Nets Playoff Team
sections.body: Dudley appeared in 59 Brooklyn regular-season games during 2018-19. His scoring totals were small compared with the franchise leading scorers, but his passing, outside shooting and experienced defense were relevant on a Nets group that reached the postseason. He also played in the first-round series against Philadelphia, where the veteran forward became a visible part of the competitive confrontation. Those are actual NBA appearances for the team that received him in the July trade, not a purely financial return. Brooklyn later allowed Dudley to join the Lakers, so his subsequent championship experience belongs to a different club. The inherited Nets B+ grade can be supported by a capable rotation veteran and a future pick, without claiming he became the primary reason the team improved. The trade created both immediate depth and longer-horizon draft value.

sections.heading: Phoenix Paid a Second to Achieve Financial Flexibility
sections.body: Arthur had already played numerous Denver and Memphis seasons as a power forward, but he did not establish a significant new Suns tenure after this exchange. Phoenix planned to buy out or waive the contract and gain the salary savings from moving Dudley. The protected 2021 selection represented a tangible future cost, even though a late second is not a guarantee of a new NBA starter. The inherited Suns C grade acknowledges that financial rationale and the limited basketball return from Arthur, while Brooklyn collected the pick and got Dudley for a playoff year. RaiQuan Gray’s later professional appearances must be credited to their proper rights holder rather than automatically assigning every career game to Brooklyn. The Nets Win result is grounded in documented on-court minutes plus an actual future draft option.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win. Brooklyn receives B+ for Jared Dudley and the protected 2021 second-rounder associated with No. 59 RaiQuan Gray. Phoenix earns C for Darrell Arthur and estimated payroll savings; Dudley contributed to the Nets 2018-19 playoff run while Arthur did not become an ongoing Suns rotation fixture.

sections.heading: Chicago Sold the No. 38 Rights Instead of Developing Jordan Bell
sections.body: On June 22, 2017, the Bulls drafted Oregon forward Jordan Bell with the 38th selection and moved his rights to the Golden State Warriors for $3.5 million in cash. The agreement did not involve an established NBA player moving to Chicago or a future first-round pick. Golden State had just won the NBA championship and was looking for inexpensive defensive depth around Draymond Green and its other veteran stars. Bell had shown unusual shot-blocking and passing ability for a college forward, making his athletic profile attractive to the Warriors. Chicago had other roster priorities and chose immediate financial consideration rather than committing a second-round roster spot to his development. That cash amount, not an unnamed draft choice, is the direct Chicago return.

sections.heading: Bell Contributed to Golden State as a Rookie
sections.body: Bell appeared in 57 Warriors regular-season games in 2017-18, starting 13 and averaging 4.6 points and 3.6 rebounds in fewer than 15 minutes. His ability to defend in space made him an interesting reserve on a team that already had elite offensive creators. Golden State won another NBA championship in 2018, and Bell appeared in postseason games, giving the defending champions cheap rotation insurance from a second-round selection. His role diminished in subsequent seasons, so the acquisition was not the creation of a long-term franchise star. Nevertheless, he supplied immediate NBA games and title-season frontcourt minutes, which is more basketball value than Chicago could obtain directly from cash in the same agreement. The inherited Warriors A- grade emphasizes that favorable cost-to-contribution relationship.

sections.heading: The Bulls Received Cash but No Direct Player Development
sections.body: Chicago collected $3.5 million and did not have to sign Bell. That consideration had financial value, yet no NBA games, rebounds or blocks can be credited as an incoming Bulls player return from this transaction. The Bulls D inherited grade reflects the opportunity cost of giving a useful young defender to a championship rival for a cash payment. It should not be exaggerated into an argument that Bell eventually became an All-Star or that all Warriors championships were his doing. His specific reserve contribution in 2017-18 is enough to establish why the Warriors benefited. The draft-night rights chain is simple and complete: Chicago chose Bell, Golden State purchased his rights and the Bulls retained the money. This deal illustrates how a modest draft prospect can have more practical roster value than immediate cash.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win. Golden State earns A- for No. 38 Jordan Bell, who played 57 games and provided reserve defense on its 2018 championship team. Chicago receives D for $3.5 million cash. The Bulls got financial consideration, while the Warriors acquired an inexpensive player who actually filled frontcourt minutes.

sections.heading: Charlotte Took Miles Plumlee and Cash for Two Veteran Big Men
sections.body: On February 2, 2017, Charlotte acquired reserve center Miles Plumlee and cash considerations from Milwaukee for veteran centers Roy Hibbert and Spencer Hawes. Plumlee had signed a substantial long-term contract with the Bucks the preceding summer but had not secured the playing role envisioned. Charlotte was seeking a younger, more mobile reserve to complement its existing frontline, while Milwaukee wanted to reduce its future salary obligations. The three-player deal was a contract and roster restructuring transaction, not a move for a first-round draft selection. Both franchise transaction records show the asset direction, including two outgoing Charlotte centers. Any later player drafted by either team must not be assigned to this deal without another separate trade.

sections.heading: Plumlee Delivered a Brief Charlotte Trial Rather Than a New Core Center
sections.body: Plumlee appeared in just 13 Hornets games over the remainder of 2016-17, starting none and averaging approximately 2.4 points and 3.2 rebounds. Those totals represented emergency frontcourt depth rather than the reliable backup center contribution Charlotte had hoped to buy. The Hornets moved him again that summer as part of a much bigger trade with Atlanta to acquire Dwight Howard, so this February agreement is one link in a larger contract path. Plumlee did not become a regular long-term Charlotte starter. The inherited D grade reflects how little basketball return the franchise initially received while accepting significant future salary commitments. His earlier seasons with Phoenix and Milwaukee do not count as Bobcats or Hornets performance.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Found Roster Flexibility Without Retaining Both Arrivals
sections.body: Hibbert and Hawes carried experience as NBA starting centers but were past their most productive seasons. Hibbert did not establish a significant Milwaukee playing tenure before being traded again to Denver, while Hawes was used in a small reserve role. The most valuable return for Milwaukee was the ability to move the contract owed to Plumlee and regain options for future roster construction around Giannis Antetokounmpo. The Bucks A- inherited grade is partly an assessment of that contract management, not a claim that Hibbert and Hawes scored like elite big men after the deal. Charlotte received a center who quickly left, while Milwaukee reduced its longer-term salary risk. That mismatch in financial commitments explains the pronounced difference between the inherited team grades.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win. Milwaukee earns A- after moving the Miles Plumlee contract and receiving Roy Hibbert and Spencer Hawes. Charlotte gets D for Plumlee and cash; he played only 13 Hornets games before being traded again. The larger value to the Bucks was salary flexibility, not an All-Star acquired in the swap.

sections.heading: Charlotte Sent Johnny O’Bryant and Two Seconds for Hernangómez
sections.body: At the February 7, 2018 trade deadline, the Charlotte Hornets acquired young Spanish center Willy Hernangómez from the New York Knicks. New York received reserve forward Johnny O’Bryant III and second-round selections in 2020 and 2021. Those choices later became associated with No. 38 Saben Lee and No. 42 Isaiah Livers, although the draft-right chains and subsequent owners are separate from the original agreement. Hernangómez had played meaningful rookie minutes for New York in 2016-17 but lost his place in its developing frontcourt rotation. Charlotte sought a low-cost younger big man with touch around the basket and good rebounding instincts. The Hornets were not surrendering a current first-rounder, but two future seconds were real draft assets.

sections.heading: Hernangómez Became a Productive Hornets Reserve
sections.body: After the deal, Hernangómez played 22 Charlotte games to finish 2017-18. His next season featured a larger bench role, and he averaged 7.3 points and 5.4 rebounds across 58 appearances in 2018-19. Those were genuine Hornets contributions from an incoming big man who had been squeezed out in New York. He did not develop into a multi-year All-Star or regular thirty-minute starter for Charlotte, but he offered usable center offense and rebounding. His later New Orleans NBA seasons and work for the Spanish national team do not belong to Charlotte’s direct return. The inherited Hornets C+ grade credits a developing reserve but discounts the two future second-round choices surrendered and the relatively modest ceiling achieved.

sections.heading: New York Obtained Two Future Draft Opportunities
sections.body: O’Bryant supplied short-term frontcourt depth but was not the main long-term Knicks return. The two second-round selections were more important to future roster optionality, ultimately associating with No. 38 in 2020 and No. 42 in 2021. Both rights passed through additional draft decisions, so the complete NBA output of Saben Lee and Isaiah Livers should not automatically be treated as Knicks playing time. New York’s B inherited grade values the ability to convert an underused center into multiple choices over different years. Charlotte obtained the more visible immediate playing return; the Knicks chose flexibility and potential replacement players. The Knicks Win conclusion reflects the premium placed on two selections relative to a reserve center’s Charlotte tenure.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win. New York earns B for Johnny O’Bryant III and 2020 and 2021 second-round assets linked to No. 38 Saben Lee and No. 42 Isaiah Livers. Charlotte receives C+ for Willy Hernangómez, who provided 22 games immediately and later averaged 7.3 points in 58 Hornets games in 2018-19.

sections.heading: Toronto and Sacramento Swapped Two Former First-Round Wings
sections.body: On February 8, 2018, Toronto sent forward Bruno Caboclo to Sacramento for shooting guard Malachi Richardson. Caboclo had entered the league in 2014 as a famously raw Brazilian prospect, while Richardson was selected by the Kings in the first round of the 2016 draft. Neither had secured an established major rotation role by the deadline. The Raptors wanted a different young perimeter shooter to evaluate while competing near the top of the Eastern Conference; Sacramento preferred the chance to develop a longer forward with defensive tools. The direct transaction contained only those two players, without a cash payment or a future draft pick. Historical team transaction ledgers confirm the date and direction.

sections.heading: Richardson Barely Played for Toronto During a Strong Team Season
sections.body: Richardson joined a Raptors roster that already had DeMar DeRozan, Kyle Lowry and a growing group of younger wings. He did not immediately displace a regular starter, appearing in only a handful of games for Toronto at the end of 2017-18. His NBA playing time remained limited over the next season as the Raptors eventually assembled a championship contender through much larger trades. It would be incorrect to credit Richardson with the 2019 title as though he were a central contributor to that later postseason roster. Toronto’s C inherited grade is modest because the club had acquired an athletic prospect without a substantial near-term rotation return. The front office could evaluate his shot creation and fit but did not gain a new All-Star guard from this midseason experiment.

sections.heading: Caboclo Also Needed Development Time Before Playing Elsewhere
sections.body: Caboclo appeared in a small Sacramento sample after the trade, while the Kings continued building around their younger core. He later produced some of his better NBA stretches with Memphis, a separate club, so those performances cannot be retroactively assigned to Sacramento. His height, wingspan and ability to defend at forward remained intriguing, but his Kings tenure did not become an extended starting job. Sacramento’s C inherited grade is aligned with Toronto’s C, and the Even Trade label reflects two organizations exchanging uncertain developmental rights rather than immediate elite production. Neither club surrendered a high pick in 2018 to complete the swap, and neither acquired a durable starting player through the agreement. The appropriate evaluation stays focused on their short posttrade opportunities.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade with Toronto C and Sacramento C. The Raptors received Malachi Richardson, whose immediate playing time was limited. The Kings acquired Bruno Caboclo for a similarly short development trial. Neither club gained a future first-round pick or an established starter in this two-player swap.

sections.heading: Charlotte Moved Hamidou Diallo Rights for a Later Pick and Cash
sections.body: On July 6, 2018 the Thunder officially announced acquiring draft rights to Hamidou Diallo, selected No. 45 by Brooklyn before passing through Charlotte in the separate Dwight Howard deal. Oklahoma City sent its 2019 second-round pick and cash to the Hornets. Contemporary Basketball Reference transactions list $243,000 cash; the Thunder primary release verifies the direction but not the amount. The Charlotte pick landed No. 52 in 2019 and selected Jalen McDaniels, not an unexercised or conditional right. Both traded player-related rights converted into NBA roster minutes. The earlier Charlotte-Brooklyn Howard-Mozgov agreement involving a 2021 Brooklyn pick was separate and is not bundled into the Oklahoma City transaction.

sections.heading: Diallo Supplied NBA Guard Minutes and Won the Dunk Contest
sections.body: Diallo entered the 2018-19 Thunder as a 20-year-old reserve, playing 51 games at 3.7 points, then 46 at 6.9 in 2019-20. He appeared in 32 more Oklahoma City games in 2020-21 at 11.9 points per game before being sent to Detroit, totaling 129 Thunder appearances and 11 starts; the March 13, 2021 official Thunder release supplies this cumulative tally. He also won the 2019 Slam Dunk Contest, a personal achievement rather than playoff All-Star production. The Thunder traded Diallo to the Pistons for Svi Mykhailiuk and a Houston-origin 2027 second-round right. That new draft right was earned in a later transaction, and Diallo Detroit seasons do not increase his Oklahoma City game counts. The inherited Thunder B+ can be moderated to B- with context: real three-season wing use and another draft option, but not a star-level player.

sections.heading: McDaniels Eventually Became an NBA Hornets Forward
sections.body: Charlotte received a 2019 Thunder second-round choice that became No. 52 Jalen McDaniels. Across four Charlotte seasons he played 16, 47, 55 and 56 regular-season games, a total of 174 Hornets appearances and 41 starts. These are Hornets-specific minutes that should not be conflated with McDaniels later 24 Philadelphia games in 2022-23 or his Toronto tenure. When Charlotte traded him in February 2023, he entered a multiteam package that also required an outgoing 2024 New York second from the Hornets and delivered other second-round rights to Charlotte. The official 76ers release identifies these distinct parts, so it would be an exaggeration to count every incoming selection as pure McDaniels profit. Nevertheless the direct 174-game Charlotte return, cash received at the 2018 trade and later options edge Diallo 129 Thunder appearances narrowly. Charlotte B and Thunder B-, with a Slight Charlotte Edge verdict in both source perspectives and the canonical record.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Charlotte Edge — Charlotte B, Oklahoma City B-. Oklahoma City sent a 2019 second and cash to Charlotte for 2018 No. 45 Hamidou Diallo rights. Diallo gave the Thunder 129 NBA appearances (11 starts) and was traded in 2021 to Detroit for Svi Mykhailiuk and a 2027 second. Charlotte used the resulting 2019 No. 52 pick on Jalen McDaniels, who played 174 Hornets games (41 starts) before being included with additional outgoing Charlotte rights in a separate 2023 trade. Both clubs received useful rotation service and some later asset value; the extra cash and longer direct Charlotte production create a small Hornets advantage. Neither Diallo Detroit stats nor all 2023 trade return should be booked as direct original 2018 consideration.

sections.heading: Kevin Durant Moved to Brooklyn in a Complex Sign-and-Trade
sections.body: On July 7, 2019, Golden State completed a sign-and-trade sending superstar Kevin Durant to Brooklyn. The Nets received Durant and a conditional future draft asset that ultimately was associated with the 2025 second-round No. 48 Javon Small. The Warriors took back newly signed guard D’Angelo Russell, plus Shabazz Napier, Treveon Graham and a traded-player exception. The players and financial mechanism were needed to complete a complicated transaction after Durant had elected to join Kyrie Irving in Brooklyn. It was not a simple free-agent signing without any exchange of value. Golden State chose an expensive young guard and salary flexibility rather than seeing Durant depart without an incoming contract. Brooklyn acquired one of the best scorers in NBA history, but knew he was recovering from a ruptured Achilles and would not play immediately.

sections.heading: Durant Returned to Superstar Production but Missed a Season
sections.body: Durant missed the entire 2019-20 season with his Achilles injury, making the patience required by the Nets part of the original bet. When he returned in 2020-21 he averaged 26.9 points in 35 appearances, and his scoring rose to nearly 30 per game during subsequent Brooklyn seasons. He gave the club outstanding playoff performances, including the hard-fought 2021 series with Milwaukee, but Brooklyn did not reach the NBA Finals while he was on the roster. Durant later left for Phoenix in a separate 2023 trade, so that return should be analyzed on its own. The Nets A inherited grade values superstar talent and legitimate on-court excellence, while acknowledging that injury, roster instability and postseason setbacks prevented the dream pairing from delivering a championship.

sections.heading: Russell Offered Golden State Another Asset Path
sections.body: Russell scored at a high rate in 33 Warriors appearances during 2019-20 before being traded to Minnesota in February 2020. That later exchange brought Andrew Wiggins and draft compensation back to Golden State, illustrating how an incoming young guard could have value beyond his direct playing minutes. Napier and Graham were moved again quickly and did not become Golden State starters from this particular agreement. The inherited Warriors D grade focuses on losing Durant and the uneven direct return, but does not erase the opportunity to convert Russell into a useful subsequent asset package. Brooklyn obtained the standout scorer; Golden State received contracts and a new route to future roster construction. Counting Wiggins as a player sent by Brooklyn in July 2019 would be incorrect.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win. Brooklyn receives A for Kevin Durant, who returned from Achilles surgery to score 26.9 points per game in 2020-21 and nearly 30 in later Nets seasons, plus a conditional pick. Golden State earns D for D’Angelo Russell, Shabazz Napier, Treveon Graham and a trade exception; Russell was subsequently moved for other assets.

sections.heading: Brooklyn Exchanged the Kabengele Rights for Hands and a Future First
sections.body: During the June 20, 2019 draft, Brooklyn selected Florida State center Mfiondu Kabengele at No. 27 and sent his rights to the Los Angeles Clippers. Brooklyn received the rights to No. 56 Jaylen Hands plus a future lottery-protected first-round draft choice. That future selection ultimately was associated with No. 19 Saddiq Bey in the 2020 draft after the rights moved through further transactions. The trade was a swap of draft assets, not an exchange of NBA veterans with previous games for either side. The Clippers hoped Kabengele could develop as a mobile center behind experienced big men. Brooklyn was trading a late first-round prospect for a different development option and another future first, which could be useful in later roster construction.

sections.heading: Kabengele Had Limited Clippers Playing Time
sections.body: Kabengele played only a small regular-season role in Los Angeles before being moved again. He was athletic, could block shots and had an intriguing college shooting résumé, but he did not establish himself as the next Clippers starting center. His short NBA minutes made this a relatively small direct basketball return for a first-round selection. The inherited Clippers C- grade reflects that limited development payoff, even though the organization had a reasonable draft-night theory for his potential. His later playing time in Cleveland, Boston or elsewhere belongs to separate circumstances and should not be counted as Los Angeles production. The Clippers gave up additional future draft capital and could not replace the resulting asset cost with a regular starter from Kabengele.

sections.heading: The Protected First Was More Valuable Than Hands Alone
sections.body: Jaylen Hands was a late second-round prospect and did not become a Nets regular-season NBA scorer. Brooklyn’s stronger asset was the incoming protected first, which eventually became the No. 19 pick in 2020. The player selected with that choice, Saddiq Bey, did not simply spend all his eventual NBA seasons with Brooklyn; draft rights and later roster changes shifted the final destination. Nevertheless, holding a first-round asset gave Brooklyn more options than the single Kabengele right it surrendered. The Nets A- inherited grade is best understood as a favorable exchange of draft capital, not a claim that either incoming young player directly starred for the team. The transaction illustrates how a modest draft-night trade can be won through future exchange value even when the original prospects record few NBA games.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win. Brooklyn earns A- for Jaylen Hands rights and the protected future first that became the 2020 No. 19 selection associated with Saddiq Bey. The Clippers receive C- for Kabengele draft rights, which produced limited Los Angeles playing time. Later draft-right transfers should not be counted as Brooklyn player statistics.

sections.heading: Brooklyn Acquired K.J. McDaniels for Cash at the Deadline
sections.body: On February 23, 2017, Brooklyn acquired young wing K.J. McDaniels from the Houston Rockets in exchange for cash considerations. McDaniels had started his career with Philadelphia and demonstrated defensive athleticism, but his Houston rotation opportunities were limited on an offense centered around James Harden. The Nets were rebuilding, making a 24-year-old defensive prospect worth trying without giving up a draft selection or an existing major scorer. Houston used the deadline to free a roster place and adjust its salary obligations while preparing for the playoffs. The two teams exchanged one player and money, not a conditional first-round pick. The official team transaction histories confirm the same simple deal.

sections.heading: McDaniels Got a Short Brooklyn Trial Rather Than a Lasting Role
sections.body: McDaniels joined a Brooklyn club willing to give younger players game opportunities, and he appeared in 20 regular-season contests following the deadline. He brought perimeter defense, transition athleticism and occasional scoring, but he did not become a long-term Nets starter or headline acquisition. The inherited Nets C+ grade values the opportunity to examine an NBA-level wing at small asset cost, rather than representing a major scoring breakthrough. The Nets did not pay with a future first or surrender a veteran who was central to their offense. His earlier Philadelphia rookie highlights and Houston seasons do not belong to Brooklyn, and subsequent overseas basketball should not be presented as NBA production for the Nets. The direct return was a limited player trial during a rebuild.

sections.heading: Houston Received Financial Flexibility Instead of Player Production
sections.body: The Rockets took back cash and no incoming basketball player. That transaction could help clear a reserve roster place and give the team more freedom to adjust its lineup around Harden and other leading contributors. Houston’s inherited C grade recognizes a practical financial or roster benefit from moving a seldom-used wing. It should not imply that the cash acquired rebounds, assists or NBA games, nor that McDaniels immediately became a Brooklyn star. The Slight Nets Edge verdict aligns with the view that twenty game appearances from an inexpensive young player held a little more basketball value than the money received. Both clubs were operating around the margins of their rosters rather than changing a championship core. The trade stands as a relatively small but identifiable player-for-cash experiment.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Nets Edge. Brooklyn earns C+ after taking a low-cost developmental chance on K.J. McDaniels for roughly 20 appearances following the 2017 deadline. Houston receives C for cash and roster flexibility. Neither team acquired an additional pick or an established new starter.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Obtained Tyler Zeller for Vaughn and a Conditional Second
sections.body: On February 5, 2018, the Bucks acquired center Tyler Zeller from Brooklyn. The Nets received young guard Rashad Vaughn and a protected second-round draft selection that ultimately was associated with No. 45 Hamidou Diallo in 2018. Milwaukee needed another available center behind its main frontline as it pushed for the playoffs. Vaughn had struggled to hold a regular rotation role, so Brooklyn accepted a young guard and the conditional draft asset while moving a backup big man. The draft compensation had protection conditions that need to be traced through later transactions rather than treating every associated prospect as a Nets veteran. There was no first-round pick or star-level NBA player involved in the agreement.

sections.heading: Zeller Filled a Short-Term Center Job for Milwaukee
sections.body: Zeller played 24 Milwaukee regular-season games to finish 2017-18, starting one and averaging 5.9 points with 4.6 rebounds in approximately 16.9 minutes. Those are useful reserve-center totals for a club trying to build more dependable interior depth. He also appeared in Milwaukee postseason games, supplying a large body when the Bucks needed size around Giannis Antetokounmpo. His time with the Bucks was brief, but it involved actual basketball value. The revised Bucks B grade is consistent with a reserve rental rather than a long-term frontcourt transformation. His earlier Celtics and Nets game logs should not be reassigned to Milwaukee, and the team did not acquire a new primary offensive big man. The deal addressed a short-term positional need.

sections.heading: Brooklyn Took Future Optionality Instead of an Immediate Center
sections.body: Brooklyn obtained 2015 first-round guard Rashad Vaughn plus a conditional second-round selection when it moved Tyler Zeller to Milwaukee. Under the Nets official February 5 release, the 2018 second conveyed if it fell between Nos. 31 and 47; otherwise it would become an unprotected 2020 second. The pick did convey at No. 45, and Brooklyn initially selected Hamidou Diallo. His draft rights then went through Charlotte to Oklahoma City, so his later NBA games cannot be assigned to the Nets. Brooklyn sent Vaughn to New Orleans for Dante Cunningham on February 8, a separate move that created another usable frontcourt option. The combined chain shows Brooklyn achieved asset flexibility without producing a comparable single-event player impact from the original exchange. Milwaukee obtained 24 games of Zeller backup center production. Grades now align at Milwaukee B and Brooklyn C+, with only a slight Bucks edge rather than the original contradictory source perspectives.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Bucks Edge — Milwaukee B and Brooklyn C+. Tyler Zeller played 24 regular-season games for the Bucks, averaging 5.9 points and 4.6 rebounds. Brooklyn acquired Rashad Vaughn, whom it immediately exchanged for Dante Cunningham, plus the conditional second that became No. 45 in 2018. The Nets selected Hamidou Diallo, but the draft rights moved through Charlotte to Oklahoma City; his subsequent NBA production is not Brooklyn return. The Bucks gained modest direct center depth, while Brooklyn took useful but indirect roster and draft flexibility.

sections.heading: Charlotte Acquired Nick Richards Draft Rights for a Future Second
sections.body: At the November 18, 2020 NBA draft, the Hornets acquired rights to Kentucky center Nick Richards from New Orleans in exchange for a 2024 second-round draft selection. The Pelicans had used the No. 42 pick on Richards, while Charlotte identified him as an inexpensive young big man worth developing behind its more established frontcourt. The outgoing 2024 selection eventually was associated with No. 34 Tyler Kolek, although later draft-right ownership needs independent tracing. The transaction was a future-pick payment for an immediately drafted second-round center, not a deal for an established veteran NBA starter. Neither team sent cash or a first-round pick in the original inherited asset list. Charlotte could sign Richards and put him into its developmental structure, while New Orleans had another future selection to use or trade.

sections.heading: Richards Became a Starting-Capable Hornets Center
sections.body: Richards played a limited rookie role before gradually developing into a genuine NBA center option for Charlotte. In 2022-23 he appeared in 65 games and averaged 7.8 points and 6.4 rebounds, with more responsibility when injuries hit the frontline. He followed with an even larger role in 2023-24, averaging approximately 9.7 points and eight rebounds in 67 appearances. His rebounding, finishing and rim protection showed that a second-round pick could return years of team-specific production. He did not become an All-Star or erase Charlotte’s broader competitive difficulties, but his direct playing contribution was far greater than a short one-season roster experiment. The inherited Hornets B grade recognizes dependable developmental value from the purchased rights, without crediting his later Phoenix games to Charlotte.

sections.heading: The Pelicans Took a Future Draft Asset with No Guaranteed Player
sections.body: New Orleans accepted a 2024 second-round choice rather than keeping the rookie center. That pick had a real, delayed value and eventually became linked to No. 34 Tyler Kolek. Yet a player associated with a draft selection should not automatically be credited as a Pelicans regular-season contributor, because draft-night rights can change hands multiple times. The inherited Pelicans C+ grade reflects the legitimate benefit of a future selection while the team focused its near-term roster on other young frontcourt options. Charlotte ultimately obtained a multi-season NBA reserve and occasional starter, making the Charlotte Win label appropriate when measured by games and frontcourt production. The transaction illustrates a developmental gain from trading distant draft capital for a prospect who could be evaluated immediately.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Charlotte Win. The Hornets earn B after acquiring the 2020 No. 42 rights to Nick Richards, who later played 65 games at 7.8 points and 6.4 rebounds in 2022-23 and 67 games with around eight rebounds in 2023-24. New Orleans gets C+ for a 2024 second-round choice associated with No. 34 Tyler Kolek.

sections.heading: Charlotte Paid Nine Draft Positions to Add Cash and Dwayne Bacon
sections.body: On June 22, 2017, Charlotte selected Duke guard Frank Jackson at No. 31, then sent his rights to New Orleans. The Pelicans delivered the rights to Florida State wing Dwayne Bacon, selected No. 40, along with $1.8 million cash. Charlotte sought a physical perimeter scorer to develop within a young rotation; New Orleans wanted a guard with more ball-handling potential. An official league report confirms the two draft slots and cash direction. This was a trade of unsigned second-round rights rather than the transfer of an established NBA contract. No future first-round selection was included. The nine-slot difference was the price Charlotte accepted to obtain both its preferred forward prospect and immediate financial compensation.

sections.heading: Bacon Became a Real but Modest Hornets Rotation Player
sections.body: Bacon signed with the Hornets and appeared in 53 regular-season games during 2017-18. He played additional seasons in Charlotte, including a larger role in 2019-20, when he appeared in 75 games with 25 starts. Those are real NBA games obtained from the draft-right investment, even though he was not a high-efficiency primary option or long-term star. The franchise developed a capable athletic scorer whose overall impact was limited by shooting and consistency. Charlotte C reflects that imperfect basketball return, as well as its cash compensation. Bacon later changed NBA teams, but his subsequent appearances elsewhere cannot be credited as extra Hornets value. The original 2017 second-round agreement gave the team an actual rotational player rather than an unused prospect right.

sections.heading: Jackson Offered New Orleans a Different Development Gamble
sections.body: Jackson missed his entire rookie campaign following foot surgery, postponing the guard impact New Orleans had anticipated. He later appeared in NBA games for the Pelicans and handled reserve scoring responsibilities in 2018-19. His career did not turn into a lasting All-Star tenure, but the higher 31st selection delivered a guard with plausible two-way development. The inherited C+ Pelicans grade, against Charlotte C, denotes a small preference for Jackson without proving a runaway victory. New Orleans spent cash to move up and accepted a delay in contributions. Charlotte got Bacon and cash immediately, then invested in his development. Neither side can take credit for the other player’s years on the floor, and the final verdict must respect the modest ceiling of both assets.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Pelicans Edge. New Orleans earns C+ for Frank Jackson draft rights at No. 31, while Charlotte receives C for Dwayne Bacon rights at No. 40 and $1.8 million. Bacon played three Hornets seasons and Jackson eventually supplied reserve Pelicans scoring after injury delayed his debut.

sections.heading: Portland Traded Allen Crabbe to Reduce Future Salary Commitments
sections.body: Portland sent guard Allen Crabbe to Brooklyn for forward Andrew Nicholson on July 25, 2017. A year earlier, the Nets had offered Crabbe a large restricted-free-agent contract, which Portland matched to retain its perimeter shooter. By the next summer, the Blazers wanted to reduce the cost of their roster, which already featured high-paid guards Damian Lillard and C.J. McCollum. The league’s contemporaneous coverage described the resulting swap as a salary-management decision. Nicholson was a less expensive contract to process, not the coveted starting player who replaced Crabbe in Portland lineups. The team waived Nicholson on August 30, prior to the regular season, as its transaction register independently confirms. No draft pick or other player changed hands in the original deal.

sections.heading: Crabbe Played Seventy-Five Games as a Nets Starter and Reserve
sections.body: Crabbe appeared in 75 Brooklyn games during 2017-18 with 68 starts, averaging 13.2 points and 4.3 rebounds. He made 201 three-pointers on 37.8 percent shooting and played nearly thirty minutes per night. Those numbers demonstrate meaningful Nets on-court production even though the salary attached to the contract was expensive. In 2018-19 he appeared in 43 games, with 20 starts and averages of 9.6 points. Injuries and diminished availability reduced his value during the second season, and Brooklyn moved him in a later transaction. The Nets C grade balances the actual 118 games of shooting offense against the contract cost and lack of a multiyear star outcome. His prior Portland shooting accuracy should not be counted as if earned for Brooklyn.

sections.heading: Nicholson Never Appeared in a Blazers Game After the Trade
sections.body: Portland did not receive on-court points or rebounds from Nicholson: the team waived him before the 2017-18 season. Its benefit was financial room and reduced long-term salary exposure, creating greater freedom for other roster decisions. The inherited Blazers Win label, despite equal C grades for both teams, describes that financial outcome rather than pretending Portland acquired the better basketball performer. Brooklyn bought legitimate wing shooting and twenty-month roster utility; Portland bought an opportunity to reorganize contracts. The trade is therefore a useful distinction between winning on the floor and improving roster finances. Nicholson’s earlier games for Orlando, Washington or Brooklyn cannot be reattributed to the Blazers, and Crabbe’s subsequent performances for other franchises do not enlarge the Nets return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Blazers Win in the inherited verdict despite matching C grades. Portland moved Allen Crabbe’s salary and waived Andrew Nicholson without a Blazers game. Brooklyn received 75 Crabbe games at 13.2 points in 2017-18 and 43 games at 9.6 points in 2018-19, but committed to a sizable contract.

sections.heading: Denver Paid a Protected Second-Rounder for Roy Hibbert
sections.body: Denver acquired veteran center Roy Hibbert from Milwaukee at the February 23, 2017 trade deadline. The Nuggets surrendered a protected second-round draft choice in 2019, which eventually became No. 57 and was associated with Jordan Bone. Denver general manager Tim Connelly announced the transaction in an official release that also explained Hibbert had not played a game for the Bucks after Milwaukee obtained him from Charlotte earlier that month. He had participated in 42 Hornets games, making 13 starts, before moving twice. Those Charlotte totals are historical context, not Denver production. Denver sought an experienced defensive big man for frontcourt depth, while Milwaukee chose the future asset over a center who had not appeared in its uniform.

sections.heading: His Former All-Star Credentials Did Not Produce a Denver Breakthrough
sections.body: Hibbert had made two NBA All-Star teams in Indiana and had become a respected rim protector during the Pacers' Eastern Conference playoff runs. However, his mobility and offensive contributions had declined by 2017. The Nuggets acquired a recognizable center, but he never established a meaningful Denver regular-season rotation role after arriving. This transaction therefore cannot be assessed as though his former Indiana blocked shots or 42 Charlotte games were produced for Denver. The Nuggets' C- inherited grade reflects the possibility of using a veteran for emergency frontcourt insurance against the limited actual on-court return. He was already nearing the end of his professional NBA career. The low acquisition price made the experiment understandable, but it was not the addition of a dependable starting center for multiple seasons.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Secured a Real Future Draft Asset
sections.body: Milwaukee accepted a protected 2019 second-round selection that ultimately became No. 57, associated with Jordan Bone. The selected prospect's later movement between draft-rights holders requires separate tracing before assigning him NBA minutes for the Bucks. Still, Milwaukee obtained the rights to a draft asset instead of retaining a center whose tenure had produced no Bucks games. Its C grade, narrowly above Denver's C-, recognizes this return in flexibility. No first-rounder changed hands, and there was no direct incoming star player for Milwaukee. The outcome illustrates why an acquired player's name recognition can differ from the actual value of a transaction. Denver took a low-cost chance to use a former All-Star. Milwaukee emerged with a delayed draft opportunity for a veteran it had never needed to deploy.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win. Milwaukee receives C for a protected 2019 second-round choice that became No. 57 and was associated with Jordan Bone. Denver earns C- for Roy Hibbert, who had played zero games for Milwaukee and did not establish a Nuggets rotation career. His earlier Charlotte production does not belong to the Nuggets.

sections.heading: Cleveland Traded an Injured Center and Cash to Charlotte
sections.body: On February 13, 2017, Cleveland sent Chris Andersen and cash considerations to Charlotte in return for a top-55-protected 2017 second-round selection. Cavaliers general manager David Griffin confirmed the asset direction in an official statement, while the NBA's transaction tracker described Andersen's season-ending knee injury. The 38-year-old had appeared in 12 Cleveland games during 2016-17, averaging 2.3 points and 2.6 rebounds, before his December injury and surgery. Charlotte was acquiring an unavailable veteran rather than a center who could step into the starting lineup. Cleveland needed a roster place and contract flexibility while trying to defend its NBA championship. The future pick ultimately did not convey, meaning the Cavaliers did not acquire a rookie from the draft terms.

sections.heading: The Hornets Waived Andersen Immediately
sections.body: Charlotte waived Andersen the same day it acquired him. Consequently, he produced no new NBA appearances, rebounds or blocked shots for the Hornets. His Miami championship experience and earlier reserve roles with Cleveland are important details about the player, but they are not returns to Charlotte from the February 2017 transaction. The team received cash and managed its own roster, two types of value that do not appear in regular-season box scores. The Hornets' C inherited grade fits an agreement whose financial benefits were modest and whose primary incoming player could not contribute immediately. There was no substantial development opportunity in holding his contract because the club acted on waivers right away. The original deal should be evaluated as a small financial and roster maneuver, not a failed attempt to install a healthy player in Charlotte's playoff rotation.

sections.heading: Cleveland Never Received the Protected Pick
sections.body: The pick Cleveland obtained was protected through selection No. 55 and ultimately was not exercised. It therefore yielded no 2017 Cavaliers drafted prospect and cannot be credited with points generated by an unrelated second-round selection. The franchise nevertheless created space to pursue healthy reserves late in the season. Its C grade equals Charlotte's C, and the inherited verdict identifies the transaction as even. That equality should not be read as evidence that both teams acquired equally productive basketball players. Neither receiving club obtained any post-trade regular-season production from its direct assets. Cleveland was able to move an injured reserve and cash, while Charlotte collected the payment without keeping the player. Keeping the cash direction and nonconveyed condition explicit prevents an inaccurate retrospective from turning a minor administrative move into an imaginary NBA player trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Both franchises earn C. Cleveland received a protected 2017 second-round choice that never conveyed and opened a roster place. Charlotte received injured Chris Andersen and cash, then waived Andersen the same day without a Hornets appearance. Both sides primarily gained financial or roster flexibility.

sections.heading: The Wizards Acquired Trey Burke for a Pick Five Years Away
sections.body: Washington traded a 2021 second-round draft selection to Utah for point guard Trey Burke on July 7, 2016. Burke had been selected ninth overall in the 2013 draft and earned All-Rookie recognition, but his responsibilities with the Jazz had diminished as their backcourt developed. The Wizards already had John Wall as their primary playmaker and sought a second-unit guard who could create shots without commanding a starting contract. Utah preferred future draft capital rather than retaining a reserve whose role had shrunk. The eventual 2021 pick became No. 43 and was associated with Greg Brown III, though later draft-right movements require separate accounting. This was a single-player-for-second-rounder swap, not a multi-team deal with additional veterans or first-round choices.

sections.heading: Burke Played Fifty-Seven Washington Games
sections.body: Burke appeared in 57 Wizards regular-season games in 2016-17 and made no starts. He averaged 5.0 points and 1.8 assists in 12.3 minutes, connecting on 45.5 percent of his shots and 44.3 percent of his three-pointers on limited volume. Those efficiencies were useful for a reserve, but his relatively small playing role also showed why the team needed other bench guard options during a playoff run. He appeared in three postseason games and subsequently left for New York, where he enjoyed a separate scoring resurgence. His later Knicks, Dallas and Philadelphia years should not be credited to Washington from the 2016 transaction. The Wizards B inherited grade recognizes inexpensive, immediate backup availability on a playoff team rather than a long-term starting point guard acquired with a minor draft asset.

sections.heading: Utah Kept the Delayed Pick Instead of the Guard
sections.body: The Jazz ultimately controlled a future second-round selection connected to No. 43 Greg Brown III in 2021. Such a pick can be useful as a developmental opportunity or as trade compensation, but it does not guarantee a starting NBA player. The selection matured five summers after the original swap, when Burke had already moved through several clubs. Utah's C grade recognizes this delayed optionality while acknowledging that Washington received 57 games of direct NBA production. It would be incorrect to assign Brown's complete later career automatically to the Jazz without following the intervening rights chain. Burke had been an important Jazz rookie years earlier, but those Utah statistics cannot become part of his Washington trade return either. The proper comparison weighs one year of genuine Wizards reserve minutes against a small draft opportunity Utah could hold or exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wizards Win. Washington receives B for Trey Burke, who played 57 games at 5.0 points and 1.8 assists during 2016-17. Utah earns C for a 2021 second-round selection associated with No. 43 Greg Brown III. Burke's later NBA performances belong to separate franchises, not the Wizards return.

sections.heading: The Nets Moved from No. 55 to No. 42 for Isaiah Whitehead
sections.body: On June 23, 2016, Brooklyn acquired the rights to Seton Hall guard Isaiah Whitehead from Utah. The Jazz had drafted Whitehead at No. 42; Brooklyn sent No. 55 Marcus Paige's draft rights and $3 million cash in exchange. The Nets wanted a player who had grown up in Brooklyn and could compete for backcourt minutes, while Utah valued the financial return and another second-round prospect. An official Brooklyn release describes the excitement surrounding Whitehead's hometown arrival and confirms the draft positions and outgoing cash. No NBA player with a previously signed contract was traded. The thirteen-position change in the second round was the entire basketball asset adjustment, with money accounting for the difference in value the clubs assigned to the prospects.

sections.heading: Whitehead Became a Rookie Starter but Did Not Last Long
sections.body: Whitehead played 73 Brooklyn games during 2016-17, starting 26 and averaging 7.4 points, 2.5 rebounds and 2.6 assists in 22.5 minutes. The rebuilding Nets gave him substantial responsibility as a young guard who could handle the ball and defend with size. His shooting efficiency was uneven, however, and the club reduced his role in 2017-18. He played 16 NBA games that second season without a start, leaving him with 89 Brooklyn regular-season appearances in total. His return was therefore measurable rather than speculative, but it did not amount to a long career as the franchise's starting point guard. The inherited C Brooklyn grade fits a player who supplied one active rookie season and then faded from the main rotation despite the investment in his draft rights.

sections.heading: Utah Collected Cash Without a New NBA Regular
sections.body: The Jazz received the rights to Marcus Paige and the $3 million payment, important compensation for giving up the earlier selection. Paige's college career at North Carolina made him a recognizable prospect, but he did not become a sustained Jazz NBA rotation player. Utah's inherited C+ grade is slightly above Brooklyn's C despite Whitehead actually playing more NBA games for the Nets. That is because the retrospective weighs immediate money and a lower-risk prospect rights option against Brooklyn's expense and the modest eventual ceiling of its drafted guard. Neither the Nets nor Jazz acquired a first-round selection through this deal. Paige's appearances elsewhere and Whitehead's later professional opportunities outside Brooklyn cannot be imported into the teams that held their rights on draft night. The difference in receiving returns is precisely what makes the grading a close judgment rather than an obvious basketball victory.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Jazz Edge in the inherited C+ to C grading. Utah obtained Marcus Paige rights and $3 million after trading Isaiah Whitehead at No. 42 for the No. 55 draft rights. Whitehead played 73 Brooklyn games with 26 starts and averaged 7.4 points as a rookie, but did not become a long-term franchise starter.

sections.heading: Orlando Received Joe Harris, Cash and a Conditional Second
sections.body: On January 12, 2016 Cleveland moved Joe Harris and cash plus a protected Sacramento-origin 2017 second-rounder to Orlando. The Magic sent Cleveland a Portland-origin protected 2020 second. Orlando own contemporaneous NBA announcement identified both selections as protected Nos. 31-55 and said the franchise had requested waivers on Harris that same day. Those conditions explain why neither second eventually conveyed and neither club received a new NBA draftee from the pick exchange. This was chiefly a contract/tax and roster-slot transaction: the Cavaliers were already a title-contending, high-tax roster and Harris had recently undergone foot surgery; Orlando accepted a payment to waive the incoming player rather than integrate him into its lineup. Cash direction is Cleveland to Orlando, amount unverified in official records.

sections.heading: The Magic Waived Harris Before He Could Play
sections.body: Joe Harris appeared in five Cavaliers games in 2015-16 totaling only 15 NBA minutes, then had surgery for a foot injury in January. Orlando immediately requested his waiver after acquiring his contract, so Harris never appeared in a Magic regular-season game. His NBA basketball development took place elsewhere after Brooklyn signed him on July 19, 2016; his eventual 3-point shooting success with the Nets is not a return the Magic received, and cannot legitimately be used to give Orlando an F as though it had cut a player after five Magic games. Orlando nevertheless received cash to facilitate the contract movement. Contemporary ESPN reported an approximately $1 million outgoing cash payment from Cleveland, but the Magic official release left the amount unspecified; this grade does not assert an exact amount as confirmed. Orlando C measures the small direct financial receipt rather than an impossible Harris Orlando playing season.

sections.heading: Cleveland Received No Converting Draft Selection Either
sections.body: Cleveland did not receive a 2020 draft player because the conditional Portland second failed to convey. Instead its practical result was removing Harris remaining salary and the deep luxury-tax implications from a roster where he was injured and little-used, while opening a space for later personnel moves. Kevin Pelton contemporary ESPN financial estimate, published January 13 2016, placed potential luxury-tax savings near $3.4 million for leaving the last roster slot empty and net savings around $3 million after salary and outgoing cash. These are contemporary estimates, not an audited final year-end treasury statement. The deal was one small component of Cleveland championship season, not a substitute for its 2016 title roster. This supports a modest Cavaliers edge in tax/roster flexibility: Cleveland B- and Orlando C, not inherited partner perspectives of Cavaliers C/Magic C versus Cavaliers A/Magic F. Both draft rights expired unused.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win — Cleveland B-, Orlando C. The teams exchanged injured Joe Harris, Cleveland cash and two heavily protected conditional second-round selections on January 12, 2016. Neither pick conveyed. The Magic requested waivers on Harris that same day and received zero Harris NBA appearances; the five games on his 2015-16 season total occurred for Cleveland. Orlando obtained cash of unspecified official amount. Cleveland freed a roster spot and avoided an estimated several million dollars of tax/payroll liability at an important stage of its title season. Harris later Brooklyn success belongs to a separate July 2016 free-agent signing, not Orlando return or an asset that Cleveland directly received in this exchange.

sections.heading: San Antonio Sent Boris Diaw to Utah in a Salary and Rights Exchange
sections.body: On July 7, 2016, the Spurs traded versatile forward Boris Diaw, cash considerations and a future second-round selection to the Utah Jazz. In return, San Antonio acquired the draft rights to Canadian guard Olivier Hanlan and a traded-player exception. The later selection became No. 39 in 2022, associated with Khalifa Diop. The deal came as San Antonio reconfigured its frontcourt after Tim Duncan’s retirement and the acquisition of Pau Gasol. Diaw had been part of the Spurs championship rotation in 2014 and could still pass and defend from multiple frontcourt positions. Utah was buying veteran versatility for a roster built around Gordon Hayward and Rudy Gobert, while the Spurs prioritized flexibility rather than another immediate starting player. The trade was not simply Diaw for cash: cash and the second went to Utah, while the exception and rights went to San Antonio.

sections.heading: Diaw Was a Regular Jazz Rotation Player in 2016-17
sections.body: Diaw played 73 games for Utah during 2016-17, making 33 starts while averaging 4.6 points, 2.2 rebounds and 2.3 assists. His box-score scoring declined from earlier seasons, but he gave the Jazz an experienced passing forward capable of connecting the offense when the ball moved away from the guards. Utah reached the second round of the Western Conference playoffs before losing to Golden State. Diaw was a supporting player rather than the primary explanation for that playoff run, and his Utah tenure ended after the season. The inherited C grade for the Jazz acknowledges those legitimate minutes and a future second-round asset without treating Diaw’s 2014 Spurs championship as Utah production. His positional versatility helped during a period when the club needed another dependable veteran around its younger center and wings.

sections.heading: The Spurs Received Rights and Flexibility, Not a New NBA Starter
sections.body: Hanlan had been drafted by Utah in 2015 and continued his career outside the NBA. After acquiring his rights, San Antonio did not convert them into a sustained Spurs NBA playing tenure. The traded-player exception offered a salary mechanism for subsequent roster decisions, but it did not immediately provide points, rebounds or a drafted player. San Antonio’s C grade therefore represents the value of financial flexibility and prospect rights, while recognizing that the Jazz received the only substantial direct NBA minutes from this deal. Utah also obtained the future second-rounder eventually used on Khalifa Diop. The inherited Jazz Win verdict acts as a tiebreak between equal C grades, not evidence of a numerical gap. Later rights transfers must be traced separately from Diop’s subsequent NBA opportunities, rather than assuming he played a full Jazz career.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Jazz Win in the inherited verdict despite equal C grades. Utah acquired Boris Diaw, who played 73 regular-season games with 33 starts in 2016-17, plus cash and the 2022 No. 39 second-round pick associated with Khalifa Diop. San Antonio received Olivier Hanlan’s rights and a traded-player exception.

sections.heading: Memphis Obtained Troy Daniels Through a Sign-and-Trade
sections.body: On July 12, 2016, Charlotte sent shooting guard Troy Daniels to Memphis in a sign-and-trade agreement. The Grizzlies returned cash considerations and a traded-player exception for Charlotte, whose crowded wing rotation made Daniels expendable. Memphis needed perimeter shooting on a team built around Mike Conley and Marc Gasol. Daniels had previously shown exceptional three-point shooting in short stretches with Houston and Charlotte, but his Hornets playing role had been limited. Neither team sent a first-round draft choice, a future second-round selection or a major veteran scorer through this specific agreement. The cash and exception were real assets for Charlotte, while the Grizzlies acquired the opportunity to use Daniels as an experienced outside threat. The exchange should not be confused with Memphis’s other 2016 free-agent moves.

sections.heading: Daniels Became a Useful Bench Shooter for Memphis
sections.body: Daniels appeared in 67 Memphis games in 2016-17, averaging 8.2 points and making more than 40 percent of his three-point attempts. He was not a starting guard on a team with established perimeter leaders, but his willingness to shoot off the catch gave the bench a scoring option in otherwise slower half-court lineups. Memphis reached the playoffs and lost to San Antonio in the first round. Daniels stayed with the franchise for additional seasons, providing further shooting depth after the initial trade. The Grizzlies C+ inherited grade is supported by actual games, three-point volume and an affordable veteran role rather than by asserting that Daniels became a new franchise star. His later Phoenix and Denver appearances are distinct from the return Memphis received in this agreement. The first-season contribution was already larger than Charlotte’s direct on-court acquisition, because the Hornets took financial consideration rather than an incoming player.

sections.heading: Charlotte Chose Cash and a Transaction Mechanism
sections.body: Charlotte did not get another NBA rotation player back. The Hornets received cash and a trade exception, allowing the team to adjust salary and roster plans while avoiding the cost of another contract at Daniels’s position. Those returns can help an organization, but they cannot be counted as Charlotte NBA points or starts. The Hornets C grade reflects practical financial flexibility and a decision to move a guard who was unlikely to lead their offense. The Memphis Win verdict and slightly higher C+ grade are supported by the more concrete result: Memphis acquired a useful outside shooter who appeared regularly. There was no conditional draft pick that later conveyed, so attributing a future named NBA prospect to Charlotte would be incorrect. The two front offices were trading different values, player minutes on one side and salary flexibility on the other.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Grizzlies Win. Memphis receives C+ after obtaining Troy Daniels, who played 67 games and averaged 8.2 points in 2016-17 while shooting over 40 percent from three. Charlotte earns C for cash and a traded-player exception, with no incoming NBA player or draft pick in this transaction.
