sections.heading: The Nets Surrendered a Distant Second for Casper Ware
sections.body: On October 24, 2014, Brooklyn sent guard Marquis Teague and its previously acquired 2019 second-round selection to Philadelphia. The Nets received guard Casper Ware. The team's official announcement confirms the future choice came from Milwaukee in another trade and was included alongside Teague, rather than being an unrelated future compensation promise. The second eventually became associated with No. 42 Admiral Schofield in 2019. Philadelphia was accumulating longer-horizon selections during its rebuild, while Brooklyn was evaluating another possible ball handler ahead of the season. Ware had played for the 76ers the previous year, but this agreement was not a swap of two regular starting guards. The pick conveyed meaningful long-term value amid otherwise low-profile roster adjustments.

sections.heading: Ware Did Not Replicate His Prior Philadelphia Minutes
sections.body: Brooklyn's announcement listed Ware's nine previous Philadelphia games at 5.3 points and 1.1 assists per night. Those were 76ers games, not Nets appearances after the trade. Ware did not become a durable Brooklyn starter, and the club continued relying on other experienced backcourt personnel for the principal minutes. The Nets C grade reflects the chance to evaluate a young guard who had shown flashes in his earlier limited NBA opportunities. It does not justify adding Philadelphia statistics to a new Brooklyn team ledger. Brooklyn paid more than an expendable contract because a future second-round pick was attached. That extra cost makes the deal different from a simple mutual bench tryout in which neither club controls a future selection.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Held a Pick That Eventually Became No. 42
sections.body: The 76ers acquired Teague and the 2019 second-round selection. Teague had been a late first-round pick in Chicago but never became Philadelphia's starting long-term point guard. The distant selection gave the front office an asset that could be retained or redirected while the roster was being rebuilt. Its No. 42 identity later was associated with Admiral Schofield, though any subsequent player's games should be attributed to the team where he actually played. Philadelphia's C+ inherited grade exceeds Brooklyn's C, reflecting that draft option rather than instant improvement from Teague. Even though the players themselves contributed little after the transaction, the future pick was concrete. A balanced retrospective has to keep the roster experiments separate from the eventual selection instead of imagining either incoming guard had a productive multi-year career in his new city.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight 76ers Edge. Philadelphia earns C+ for Marquis Teague and a 2019 second-round pick tied to No. 42 Admiral Schofield. Brooklyn receives C for Casper Ware, who had played nine NBA games for Philadelphia before the trade but did not become a lasting Nets rotation guard. The extra pick favored Philadelphia.

sections.heading: Golden State Purchased Jeremy Tyler's NBA Draft Rights
sections.body: On June 23, 2011, Charlotte selected young center Jeremy Tyler at No. 39 in the NBA draft and immediately sent his rights to Golden State for cash considerations. The Warriors' own summer league guide documents the selection and the purchase, allowing the transaction to be distinguished from Golden State's other 2011 draft moves. Tyler had taken an unusual development route through professional teams overseas before he was old enough to enter the NBA, giving him upside but little conventional American college history. Charlotte preferred financial compensation over developing another second-round prospect. Golden State sought a younger center who might grow into regular minutes. The agreement contained no separate draft pick coming back to Charlotte or another veteran contract changing hands.

sections.heading: Tyler Started Twenty-Three of Forty-Two Rookie Games
sections.body: Tyler appeared in 42 Warriors games during 2011-12 and started 23. Golden State's contemporary summer league guide records 4.9 points and 3.3 rebounds in 13.5 minutes per game, with 7.1 points and 5.1 rebounds during his starts. That was measurable on-court utility for a second-round rights purchase, not a prospect who never reported or played. Nevertheless, the young center had difficulties establishing consistency at the professional level and did not remain a major Warriors starter over many seasons. His later stops with other NBA franchises should not be credited as Golden State production from the original purchase. The inherited Warriors C grade reflects a brief period of developmental playing time rather than an elite center acquired at little cost.

sections.heading: The Bobcats Received Cash Rather Than a Developing Center
sections.body: The Bobcats collected the sale proceeds and did not take on a contract to develop Tyler. The available official transaction record does not identify a cash amount, so there is no basis for assigning a fabricated figure. Charlotte had other draft choices and young players competing for rotation positions and chose immediate financial flexibility. Its inherited C grade equals Golden State's C, the basis for the Even Trade label. The teams accepted different risks: Golden State held a rookie who had once been highly regarded, while Charlotte avoided another uncertain long development project. Tyler's forty-two appearances offer clear evidence that Golden State received some value, yet the modest averages explain why this was not a decisive long-term championship transaction. The cash-only return should be evaluated as cash and never treated as a nonexistent Hornets draft selection.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade with C grades for both teams. Golden State obtained 2011 No. 39 Jeremy Tyler and received 42 games with 23 starts, averaging 4.9 points. Charlotte received cash without another player or future selection. The Warriors got a short developmental center tenure while the Bobcats took a financial return.

sections.heading: Cleveland Sent Alonzo Gee to New Orleans for a Conditional Second
sections.body: The Cavaliers traded swingman Alonzo Gee to New Orleans on July 11, 2014, for a 2016 second-round choice protected through No. 55. The pick had originated with the Clippers and would become payable only if the specified protection were satisfied. Cleveland was trying to gain salary flexibility after LeBron James announced his return, while the Pelicans were assembling contract pieces for other trades. Contemporary reporting says Gee's contract could be moved or waived, making the deal a financial transaction as much as a basketball one. No first-round choice or ready New Orleans player was sent to Cleveland. The exact protection matters because the second-round selection ultimately never conveyed, leaving Cleveland without an eventual draftee from this transaction.

sections.heading: Gee Was Re-Traded Four Days Later Instead of Playing for the Pelicans
sections.body: On July 15, 2014, the Pelicans included Gee in a three-team agreement with Houston and Washington that brought center Omer Asik and forward Omri Casspi to New Orleans, as the club's official announcement confirms. Gee was one of several outbound assets, alongside Scotty Hopson and a protected first-rounder. He never played a Pelicans regular-season game during that four-day stay. Still, New Orleans had acquired a veteran contract it could use to complete a larger frontcourt move, which gave the initial July 11 agreement transactional value. It would be inaccurate to credit New Orleans with Asik's entire later playing contribution as though Gee alone had brought him in; multiple other assets were included in that subsequent transaction. His earlier Cleveland career also cannot be treated as New Orleans box-score output.

sections.heading: The Future Pick Expired Without a Cleveland Draft Selection
sections.body: Cleveland never received the conditional 2016 second-round choice because its protection was not met. It did remove Gee's contract and free resources while assembling a different roster, which explains why the club might have accepted the arrangement. The Cavaliers B- grade therefore rests on payroll flexibility rather than an eventual drafted center or wing. New Orleans also gets B- in the inherited assessment despite being named Pelicans Win, a preference for its rapid reuse of Gee's contract. Neither team obtained a direct multi-season NBA scorer from the two-team agreement. The Pelicans utilized the incoming contract to complete the later Asik deal; Cleveland avoided salary obligations without turning the protected pick into a named player. These are distinguishable transaction outcomes rather than equal game totals.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans Win under the inherited label despite equal B- grades. New Orleans acquired Alonzo Gee, then moved him again four days later as part of a larger Omer Asik trade. Cleveland gained salary relief and a top-55-protected 2016 second that never conveyed. There were no Pelicans playing minutes from Gee himself.

sections.heading: Dallas Sold the Draft Rights to No. 55 Darius Johnson-Odom
sections.body: On June 28, 2012, Dallas selected Marquette shooting guard Darius Johnson-Odom with the 55th overall pick, then sent his NBA signing rights to the Los Angeles Lakers in exchange for cash considerations. The Lakers' official all-time transaction register and the Mavericks' annual media guide document that sequence independently. Dallas had already made several other draft-night moves and was constructing a different guard rotation, while Los Angeles was willing to test a late-second-round scorer in its organization. The deal exchanged an unsigned drafted prospect for money, not a veteran playing contract. Johnson-Odom did not record any Lakers statistics before the actual trade was completed, and the Mavericks cannot be credited with his later NBA appearances simply because they submitted his name at the draft.

sections.heading: Johnson-Odom Played Only Four Lakers Games
sections.body: Johnson-Odom signed with Los Angeles that September and appeared in four regular-season games in 2012-13, totaling just six NBA minutes. He did not score a point or start a game, according to the historical player box scores. Much of his development instead occurred with the franchise's NBA Development League affiliate, and he was waived before becoming an established rotation player. He later played three regular-season NBA games for Philadelphia, but those minutes cannot be counted as Lakers production from Dallas's original rights sale. The Lakers' inherited B- grade therefore reflects the inexpensive option to sign and evaluate a draft prospect rather than an immediate basketball payoff. Purchasing the rights to a late pick carried limited risk, yet the direct NBA playing return was particularly small.

sections.heading: The Cash Created a Certain Dallas Return
sections.body: Dallas obtained financial compensation in return for a pick near the very end of the second round. That cash arrived immediately and did not depend on the guard reaching the NBA or on a complex future draft protection. The exact payment amount is not specified in the inherited canonical ledger, so this assessment does not manufacture one. Dallas's B- inherited grade equals the Lakers' B-, with the winner label selecting a Slight Mavericks Edge. That preference is understandable when the sold prospect ultimately played four scoreless games for Los Angeles. The Mavericks had converted a speculative final-round draft right into a known economic return. Neither side found a primary rotation contributor, but the asymmetry between certain money and a very short player trial explains the small difference in retrospective value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Mavericks Edge. Dallas earns B- after selling No. 55 Darius Johnson-Odom's rights for cash on 2012 draft night. The Lakers also receive B- but obtained just four NBA appearances and six minutes without a point from the young guard. Dallas converted an uncertain late pick into an immediate financial asset.

sections.heading: San Antonio Consolidated Two Second-Round Rights into One
sections.body: At the June 26, 2014 NBA draft, San Antonio exchanged the rights to No. 58 Jordan McRae and No. 60 Cory Jefferson for the rights to No. 54 Serbian forward Nemanja Dangubić from Philadelphia. Transaction records for both clubs and the NBA's contemporary offseason trade register confirm the precise 54-for-58-and-60 asset flow. Dangubić was a young international prospect whom San Antonio could develop overseas without immediately using a roster spot on a full NBA contract. Philadelphia, by contrast, valued two later selections and the ability to redirect their rights. All three players were fresh drafted prospects; no existing NBA starting contract or future first-round choice was transferred in the original agreement. The number of incoming options differed even though each side operated entirely in the second round.

sections.heading: Dangubić Stayed Overseas Instead of Joining the Spurs
sections.body: Dangubić continued his playing career in Europe, and the rights did not become regular-season San Antonio NBA games. His international development was a valid part of the original scouting gamble, but his overseas points and rebounds should never be imported into Spurs box scores. San Antonio was entering the 2014-15 season as defending champion and could reasonably store an international prospect while established veterans carried the main rotation. The inherited C grade values the potential signing opportunity rather than an actual NBA starter that emerged from this selection. The club gave up two later second-round choices for the chance to hold rights to the earlier player, a common draft-right consolidation tactic. Whether this was a successful long-term scouting decision is a separate question from whether Dangubić ultimately suited up for the Spurs; he did not.

sections.heading: The Two Philadelphia Prospects Followed Different Rights Chains
sections.body: Philadelphia acquired the draft rights to McRae and Jefferson. Jefferson's rights were later moved to Brooklyn for cash, and the forward eventually played NBA minutes with the Nets. McRae reached the NBA with Philadelphia and subsequently played for other clubs, including Cleveland during its 2016 championship season. Those later outside-team accomplishments cannot all be assigned to Philadelphia as if both selected players remained 76ers starters. The Sixers did receive two exchangeable draft assets, which was the central appeal compared with a single international stash. Philadelphia's inherited C grade equals San Antonio's C, making the Even Trade assessment less about NBA scoring and more about uncertain development value on both sides. Neither team secured a direct long-term first-choice player from this modest draft-night exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. San Antonio earns C for the No. 54 rights to Nemanja Dangubić, who never played a Spurs NBA game. Philadelphia also gets C after receiving No. 58 Jordan McRae and No. 60 Cory Jefferson. The latter rights had later NBA and trade utility but neither side added a new franchise star through this agreement.

sections.heading: Cleveland Moved a Young Guard, Cash and a 2015 Second for Three Veterans
sections.body: On July 22, 2014, Cleveland acquired point guard John Lucas III and forwards Malcolm Thomas and Erik Murphy from Utah. The Jazz received guard Carrick Felix, cash considerations and a 2015 second-round choice that later became No. 54 Daniel Díez. The Cavaliers' official announcement names all three incoming players and describes Felix's seven NBA games with Cleveland during the previous season. The trade was part of Cleveland's unusual summer of roster restructuring following LeBron James's return. Utah prioritized a younger perimeter prospect and a future draft asset rather than retaining three fringe veterans. The second-rounder and cash were real components of the price, not an incidental adjustment to a three-for-one player swap. Both clubs' transaction registers corroborate the date and direction.

sections.heading: All Three Incoming Cavaliers Were Used Again as Contract Pieces
sections.body: Lucas had been a reserve Utah point guard and Thomas and Murphy offered different frontcourt looks, but Cleveland did not keep the new trio for a full season of regular rotation minutes. On September 25, 2014, the Cavaliers sent all three players to Boston, along with Dwight Powell and future seconds, for Keith Bogans and conditional draft consideration. That separate deal was another contract and roster-finance maneuver, not evidence that Lucas became a Cleveland starting point guard. Cleveland's inherited B- grade can thus be understood as a temporary asset-management opportunity and veteran contract flexibility, while the direct Cavaliers on-court return was minimal. It would be inaccurate to cite Lucas's 42 Jazz appearances in 2013-14 as proof of minutes supplied after he moved to Ohio.

sections.heading: Utah Received the Pick That Became Dani Díez
sections.body: The Jazz's principal later draft asset became No. 54 in 2015. Utah selected Spanish forward Dani Díez before selling his draft rights to Portland for cash in a separate draft-night transaction. That chain created an additional financial return but did not deliver a new Utah NBA starter. Felix had appeared in seven games for Cleveland and was a developmental wing rather than an established high-volume scorer. Utah received rights, cash and an inexpensive trial prospect while giving up three contracts Cleveland recycled quickly. Both teams are B- in the inherited grades, and the Jazz Win wording reflects a retrospective preference for retaining the future selection and cash. Cleveland was chiefly managing salaries and roster slots during the 2014 offseason; Utah held the more traceable draft asset.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Jazz Win under the inherited label, although Cleveland and Utah both grade B-. Utah acquired Carrick Felix, cash and a 2015 second-rounder that became No. 54 Dani Díez, later sold to Portland. Cleveland obtained John Lucas III, Malcolm Thomas and Erik Murphy, who all moved to Boston again before the season.

sections.heading: Charlotte Sold Scotty Hopson to New Orleans the Next Day
sections.body: On July 13, 2014, Charlotte sent guard Scotty Hopson to the New Orleans Pelicans for cash considerations. The Hornets had acquired Hopson only one day earlier from Cleveland, along with cash, in the transaction sending Brendan Haywood and the rights to Dwight Powell to the Cavaliers. General manager Rich Cho issued an official release documenting the second move and both dates. The July 13 agreement was therefore a quick resale of an acquired contract or potential depth piece, not the end of a long Hornets player tenure. New Orleans needed another movable contract while building a larger transaction around its frontcourt. No separate first-round pick or guaranteed veteran scorer went to Charlotte for Hopson. The cash itself was the direct Hornets return.

sections.heading: Hopson Was a Transaction Piece Before He Became a Pelicans Player
sections.body: Hopson did not establish an NBA regular-season playing role for New Orleans during the few days the team controlled his contract. The Pelicans went on to include his contract in a later multi-team deal tied to their acquisition of Omer Asik. That created an opportunity to complete a roster adjustment, but the entire Asik return involved multiple other players and draft assets; Hopson alone did not buy a starting center. His earlier appearances with Cleveland belong to that franchise, and his later professional playing work cannot be assigned to the Hornets or Pelicans simply because he appeared in transaction lists. New Orleans's inherited C grade reflects limited direct basketball value and some usefulness as an intermediate contract. The actual asset acquired on July 13 was a guard whose salary could be moved again.

sections.heading: The Hornets Got Financial Consideration Without Sacrificing Rotation Minutes
sections.body: Charlotte obtained cash for a player it had held for roughly 24 hours and who had never appeared in a Hornets regular-season game. That is a small but concrete financial return. It did not alter the Hornets starting lineup, while the club could continue building around Kemba Walker and Al Jefferson rather than using another roster slot for a fringe guard. Charlotte's inherited C+ exceeds New Orleans's C, explaining the Slight Charlotte Edge label despite the limited basketball stakes. The transaction should be assessed as its own July 13 cash sale, not combined with the previous Cleveland acquisition or subsequent Pelicans Asik arrangement. That source trail distinguishes three consecutive deals involving Hopson from a fictional single three-team trade in which Charlotte directly received Asik.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Charlotte Edge. Charlotte earns C+ for obtaining cash on July 13, 2014, in return for Scotty Hopson, who had been acquired from Cleveland the previous day and never played a Hornets NBA game. New Orleans receives C for a movable contract, not a regular-season scoring contributor.

sections.heading: Portland Purchased the Rights to No. 54 Dani Díez
sections.body: On June 25, 2015, Utah selected Spanish forward Dani Díez with the 54th overall pick and transferred his rights to the Portland Trail Blazers for cash considerations. The Jazz had received that draft selection from Cleveland in a July 2014 trade involving Carrick Felix and three outgoing veterans. Portland's transaction history confirms a cash purchase, while Utah's own dated roster register records the selection and same-day transfer. This was not a trade of two active NBA players or a future first-round choice. Díez had spent his early professional career in Spain and was an overseas development option for an NBA franchise that was exploring younger wings. Utah chose to monetize a late draft asset instead of holding the right to sign him at a later date.

sections.heading: Díez Never Played a Trail Blazers NBA Season
sections.body: Díez continued his professional career in Europe after the selection and did not develop into a Portland regular-season roster player. The Blazers could monitor his progress and keep the possibility of a future signing, but the actual on-court return was nil. Portland's C grade in the inherited trade evaluation represents optionality, not guaranteed games from a future rotation scorer. The team made much larger roster changes in the same offseason, including moving Nicolas Batum to Charlotte and acquiring Mason Plumlee, but those separate decisions should not be counted as outcomes of this narrow cash-for-rights transaction. The No. 54 prospect's international career is distinct from an NBA playing career, and any future value requires looking at whether the rights eventually generated a Portland contract, not merely his overseas box scores.

sections.heading: Utah Received a Certain Cash Return for a Late Pick
sections.body: The Jazz obtained money immediately and avoided using a roster slot on a late-second-round prospect expected to remain abroad. The payment amount was not recorded in the canonical trade ledger, so inventing a dollar figure would be unsupported. Both Utah and Portland carry C grades and the winner is Even Trade, appropriately reflecting small and difficult-to-compare assets. The Jazz did not acquire another player by sending Díez away, and the Blazers did not gain NBA minutes from the newly purchased rights. For historical asset accounting, the prior Cleveland-to-Utah second-round transfer and Utah-to-Portland June 25 cash sale are separate transactions with different counterparties. Utah's return was the sale proceeds; Portland's was the prospect right. The distinction matters more than a speculative claim that either club found a future starter.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade with C grades for both teams. Portland acquired the 2015 No. 54 NBA rights to Spanish forward Dani Díez, who never appeared in a Trail Blazers regular-season game. Utah obtained cash for a late second-round asset received earlier from Cleveland. No players or later NBA points were directly exchanged.

sections.heading: Cleveland Paid Two Second-Round Picks to Open Two Trade Exceptions
sections.body: On July 27, 2015, the Cavaliers sent veterans Brendan Haywood and Mike Miller to Portland along with future second-round choices in 2019 and 2020. The first selection was the more favorable of Minnesota's and the Lakers' 2019 picks, later associated with No. 40 Justin James; the other ultimately became No. 32 Vernon Carey Jr. in 2020. Portland's official announcement lists the players, conditional pick origin and cash considerations. Cleveland created traded-player exceptions of approximately $10.5 million and $2.8 million by removing the veteran contracts. This wasn't a trade in which Portland sent Cleveland an incoming starting player or first-round prospect. It was a transaction about salary and future options, with the two future seconds providing compensation to a club able to absorb the contracts.

sections.heading: Haywood and Miller Did Not Become Portland's New Frontcourt and Wing Core
sections.body: Haywood was 35 and had been used sparingly in Cleveland, while Miller's shooting career was winding down after a long and productive stretch with several teams. Portland did not keep them as major regular-season 2015-16 rotation contributors, choosing instead to manage contracts and roster space. Their past success on Cleveland and Miami postseason teams should not be counted as direct Portland production. The Blazers obtained two separate draft-right opportunities that eventually matured several years later, giving the club a return that was more durable than the veterans themselves. However, later NBA careers by Justin James or Vernon Carey Jr. belong to the teams where those players actually signed and played, not automatically to the Blazers. Portland's B- inherited grade credits receiving future assets for facilitating cap flexibility elsewhere.

sections.heading: The Cavaliers Used Exception and Tax Flexibility Rather Than Acquired Players
sections.body: Cleveland saved salary and luxury-tax exposure while creating the two exceptions, one tied to Haywood's sizable non-guaranteed contract. Those tools allowed the Cavaliers to consider future roster additions without requiring an immediate signed player in July. Their inherited B grade reflects financial and transactional flexibility, even though the team surrendered two draft selections to gain it. Cleveland went on to win the 2016 NBA championship, but that collective result was not directly supplied by a player received in this deal because no player came back. The original comparison is future Portland draft assets against Cleveland's cash and contract tools. The Cavaliers Win label gives the exception-based planning a narrow advantage while acknowledging that Portland gained two genuine picks rather than empty compensation.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win. Cleveland earns B for two traded-player exceptions worth roughly $10.5 million and $2.8 million and cash consideration, while moving Brendan Haywood and Mike Miller. Portland gets B- for the veterans plus two future seconds later tied to No. 40 Justin James and No. 32 Vernon Carey Jr. The principal Cleveland benefit was contract flexibility.

sections.heading: Detroit Paid Cash and a Protected Second for Jordan Bone
sections.body: In July 2019, Detroit obtained the newly drafted rights to Tennessee point guard Jordan Bone from Philadelphia. The 76ers received $2 million in cash and a Miami-origin 2024 second-round pick protected through the first 55 selections. Philadelphia had acquired Bone's rights on draft night, and Detroit signed him to a two-way contract on July 8. Historical franchise transaction records show the future pick never conveyed, so Philadelphia didn't receive a 2024 draftee through that portion of the trade. The agreement was not a swap of two guards already playing NBA games. It was a purchase of a prospect whom Detroit intended to develop in its organization, with cash supplying the only realized counterparty consideration. At No. 57 of the 2019 draft, Bone was considered a potentially inexpensive guard option rather than a ready franchise starter.

sections.heading: Bone Made Ten Pistons Appearances Before Moving On
sections.body: Bone played ten Detroit regular-season games during 2019-20, averaging 1.2 points, 0.8 assists and 5.3 minutes. He appeared mostly in a deep reserve role while spending more time developing in the G League, where his opportunities were larger. Those ten NBA games (53 minutes, 12 points and eight assists overall) are a genuine Detroit return, but far less than a stable role behind the franchise's experienced guards. He moved on to Orlando the next season, and those 14 later Magic appearances shouldn't be credited as Pistons production. Detroit's C- inherited grade is a modest assessment of an actual draft rights signing that never developed into an enduring rotational point guard. The team wasn't trading for an established scorer or giving away a first-round pick, but it did pay a meaningful cash sum for the chance to evaluate a prospect.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Collected Money Without the Future Draft Choice
sections.body: Philadelphia realized the full $2 million cash payment for Bone rights. The conditional 2024 second-rounder, originating with Miami, was protected through pick No. 55 and never conveyed, so there was no 76ers prospect obtained through that asset. Detroit signed Bone to a two-way contract, but his ten Pistons games yielded 53 NBA minutes and 12 total points. That playing time has a value above zero; the transaction did not, however, produce the kind of return that justifies discounting Philadelphia cash receipt. The original 76ers Win headline and Philadelphia C+ versus Detroit C- canonical grades conflicted with a Detroit source perspective showing a Pistons edge and a Philadelphia perspective calling the deal even. A modest Slight 76ers Edge now fits the actual return on both sides without claiming the never-conveyed pick turned into a player. This remains a low-impact cash-for-prospect trade, not an impact roster transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight 76ers Edge — Philadelphia C+ and Detroit C-. The 76ers collected $2 million cash and a conditional Miami-origin 2024 second that was protected through No. 55 and did not convey. Detroit obtained Jordan Bone rights and gave the No. 57 selection a two-way development opportunity; he played ten Pistons NBA games totaling 53 minutes and 12 points before moving on to Orlando. The 76ers had the more certain direct realized return, but the cost and outcome were small enough to warrant only a slight edge.

sections.heading: Detroit Received DeAndre Jordan, Cash and Four Second-Rounders
sections.body: The Nets sent veteran center DeAndre Jordan, cash and second-round selections in 2022, 2024, 2025 and 2027 to Detroit on September 4, 2021. Brooklyn received center Jahlil Okafor and forward Sekou Doumbouya. The Nets' official announcement identifies the 2024 pick as Washington-origin and the 2025 pick as originating from Golden State. Those protections and origins matter because they were separate draft assets, not four immediately available Pistons players. Brooklyn sought to move Jordan's expensive contract, while Detroit could absorb it in return for multiple longer-term development and trade choices. The agreement was completed before the 2021-22 season and must not be mistaken for a straight center-for-center player swap. Detroit was being paid through draft capital to take on a contract.

sections.heading: Jordan Never Provided a Pistons Regular-Season Career
sections.body: Detroit quickly worked toward a buyout of Jordan's contract, and he subsequently signed with the Lakers. That meant the Pistons didn't acquire a 13-year veteran who went on to anchor their own 2021-22 defense. His prior Brooklyn average of 7.5 points and 7.5 rebounds in 2020-21 belongs to the Nets, not to Detroit after the trade. The Pistons' inherited A- grade is instead based on being compensated with cash and a series of second-rounders for taking Jordan's salary obligation. The 2022 selection was associated with No. 46 Ismael Kamagate, the 2024 choice with No. 32 Kyle Filipowski, and the 2025 choice with No. 32 Noah Penda. Their draft-right paths subsequently changed in separate agreements, so those selected players' later careers cannot automatically be labeled Pistons games.

sections.heading: Brooklyn Got Two Prospects Without Long-Term Rotation Returns
sections.body: Okafor was a former No. 3 pick who had struggled to find a regular center role after leaving Philadelphia, while Doumbouya was still a young forward with development potential. Brooklyn did not turn either into a long-running rotation centerpiece. In fact, Doumbouya's contract was moved in another trade to Houston that October, according to the league's official trade tracker. The Nets' D+ inherited grade reflects surrendering four future draft opportunities and cash while receiving little lasting playing output, even if moving Jordan's salary solved a short-term payroll problem. Detroit's more favorable return was in the quantity of discrete picks rather than Jordan's performance. The 2027 pick still had no selected player attached in the inherited record and should not be assigned a fictional draft outcome.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win. Detroit receives A- for DeAndre Jordan's contract, cash and four second-round choices in 2022, 2024, 2025 and 2027; Jordan was bought out before playing a Pistons regular-season game. Brooklyn gets D+ for Jahlil Okafor and Sekou Doumbouya, whose Nets tenure did not justify the quantity of future assets surrendered.

sections.heading: The Nets Exchanged Long-Held Vaulet Rights for Sumner and a Pick
sections.body: Brooklyn acquired shooting guard Edmond Sumner and a 2025 second-round pick originally belonging to Miami from Indiana on October 6, 2021. The Pacers received the NBA draft rights to Argentine wing Juan Pablo Vaulet, whom Brooklyn had first acquired on the 2015 draft night. The official NBA offseason trade tracker and Pacers franchise media guide confirm both the deal and the conditional future selection. The Nets were able to convert an international prospect whose rights had not led to Brooklyn NBA minutes into a player with previous Pacers experience plus an additional draft asset. Indiana was adjusting its guard depth and took a low-cost chance to hold overseas rights. No active Nets starting player joined the Pacers as part of the original deal.

sections.heading: Sumner Returned from an Achilles Injury to Play for Brooklyn
sections.body: Sumner missed the entire 2021-22 NBA season while recovering from an Achilles injury, so the October transaction did not deliver immediate Brooklyn game production. He later joined the Nets and played 53 regular-season games during 2022-23, starting 12 and averaging 7.1 points, 1.5 rebounds and 1.3 assists. That was a concrete return from a player whose NBA future had been uncertain when he was first moved. His career had previously included four years with Indiana, but the 53 Nets games are the part directly relevant to Brooklyn's realized roster value. The inherited B Nets grade recognizes having turned an unused international right into genuine guard depth and future pick control. The missed injury year is an important qualification, not a reason to dismiss the actual recovery and subsequent playing contribution.

sections.heading: Indiana Held the Prospect Rights While the Pick Matured
sections.body: The Pacers received Vaulet's rights, not a player who immediately filled an Indiana NBA starting role. His basketball career continued primarily outside the United States, so overseas performance should be discussed as development rather than Pacers NBA box-score production. The Miami-origin 2025 second-round choice eventually became associated with No. 41 Koby Brea, though the downstream rightsholder must be confirmed before assigning that selected player's NBA games to Brooklyn. Indiana's inherited C+ grade represents flexibility and an international signing opportunity with little direct NBA output. Brooklyn had the more visible return in Sumner's comeback season and in the retained or transferable pick option. The label Nets Win is consistent with those results, but it should not pretend Sumner contributed healthy games during the 2021-22 season when he was rehabilitating.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win. Brooklyn earns B after acquiring Edmond Sumner and a Miami-origin 2025 second-rounder associated with No. 41 Koby Brea. Sumner returned from an Achilles injury to appear in 53 Nets games at 7.1 points during 2022-23. Indiana gets C+ for Juan Pablo Vaulet's overseas NBA signing rights, which did not yield Pacers NBA minutes.

sections.heading: Denver Acquired the Rights to French Center Ismaël Kamagate
sections.body: On July 6, 2022, the Nuggets obtained NBA draft rights to center Ismaël Kamagate from Portland in exchange for the more favorable of the Timberwolves' and Hornets' 2024 second-round selections. The Trail Blazers' official release states that Kamagate had been selected at No. 46 by Detroit before his rights reached Portland through a separate draft-night agreement. This last Denver–Portland leg is therefore best understood as a trade of an overseas center prospect for a future second-round pick, not an exchange between two current NBA starters. Denver had a championship-caliber core anchored by Nikola Jokić and could afford to monitor a developing European center without demanding immediate minutes. Portland preferred a later draft option and did not retain Kamagate's rights.

sections.heading: Kamagate Continued to Develop Outside the NBA
sections.body: Kamagate was selected No. 46 in 2022 and his NBA rights reached Denver via Portland. He continued to develop with European clubs rather than joining the Nuggets for regular-season games. Ownership of an overseas player right nevertheless retained negotiable value. On February 8, 2024, Denver traded those rights to the Los Angeles Clippers for cash, as the Denver and Clippers 2023-24 transaction ledgers record. There was no direct Nuggets scoring or rebounding to count; there was a subsequent financial return. With no official dollar amount established from those team ledgers, the grade does not assign a speculative price to the Clippers payment.

sections.heading: Portland's 2024 Selection Became No. 34
sections.body: Portland received the more favorable of Charlotte and Minnesota 2024 second-round selections, exactly as its July 6, 2022 press release described. Charlotte supplied the No. 34 pick. The Trail Blazers selected Tyler Kolek at No. 34 in June 2024, then completed a separate draft-night transaction with New York. The official Portland release identifies three future second-round picks — 2027, 2029 and 2030 — in return for Kolek rights. The Knicks also documented sending Daniel Diez draft rights in the completed transaction. Kolek signed with and played for the Knicks rather than contributing NBA games to Portland. The Blazers therefore gained tradable draft selections, not Kolek regular-season production. The later three-pick package is relevant as realized downstream asset value, but not direct consideration in Denver 2022 trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Blazers Edge — Portland C+, Denver C. The Nuggets received the 2022 No. 46 Ismaël Kamagate rights and eventually converted them into cash from the Clippers in February 2024, without a Denver regular-season appearance. Portland got a conditional 2024 second-round pick, which conveyed at No. 34 Tyler Kolek, then sent his rights to New York in June 2024 for three later second-rounders and Daniel Diez rights. This is a modest exchange of NBA draft optionality; Portland obtained the stronger documented later pick return. None of Kolek Knicks games should count as Trail Blazers on-court performance.

sections.heading: Brooklyn Exchanged Kessler Edwards for Overseas Rights
sections.body: On February 7, 2023, the Nets sent forward Kessler Edwards and cash to Sacramento for the draft rights to French guard David Michineau. Brooklyn confirmed the trade in an official release and explained that Michineau was the 39th pick in 2016, whose NBA rights had since passed through the Clippers and Kings. He was playing professionally in Italy when Brooklyn acquired him. This was not a trade for an active Nets point guard, and there was no Sacramento first-round pick involved. Edwards had been a Brooklyn second-round choice in 2021 and appeared in 14 games for the Nets earlier in 2022-23, but his role had become small. Sacramento preferred a young defender it could use immediately.

sections.heading: Edwards Played Real Kings Minutes in Two Seasons
sections.body: Edwards appeared in 22 Sacramento games after the trade in 2022-23, making three starts and averaging 3.9 points in 13.9 minutes. He remained with the Kings during 2023-24 for another 54 appearances, though his playing time fell to 5.1 minutes and 1.7 points per game. Those are modest but verifiable contributions from a wing who could guard multiple positions. Sacramento reached the 2023 postseason, giving its roster additional depth during a strong regular-season run. The Kings C+ inherited grade is supported by actual NBA playing opportunities rather than a hypothetical future selection. Edwards later played for Dallas; that later club’s production is not part of the return to Sacramento.

sections.heading: Michineau Rights Offered Flexibility, Not Nets Box Scores
sections.body: Michineau was a professional European guard, but Brooklyn did not obtain an NBA regular-season performance from his rights. The Nets did receive a different developmental asset and a trade exception while sending away a player who rarely cracked the rotation. The official NBA deadline tracker confirms the same asset direction and the separate cash consideration going to Sacramento. Brooklyn C grade reflects a transaction that improved flexibility without securing a current NBA player. Sacramento’s edge is narrow because Edwards provided bench support rather than high-level scoring, yet the actual games and starts distinguish its return. Neither side had acquired a franchise-changing star or premium draft selection; the trade was a minor roster-management exchange with a measurable outcome.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Win. Sacramento earns C+ for Kessler Edwards, who played 22 games with three starts in 2022-23 and 54 more the next season, plus cash. Brooklyn gets C for David Michineau’s draft rights and an exception, with no Nets NBA appearances from Michineau.

sections.heading: Charlotte Traded a Starting Center for Jackson, Cash and a Pick
sections.body: On February 9, 2023, the Hornets sent Mason Plumlee to the Los Angeles Clippers, receiving Reggie Jackson, cash and the Clippers’ 2028 second-round selection. Charlotte’s official announcement confirms each incoming asset. Plumlee was enjoying one of his best seasons, averaging 12.2 points, 9.7 rebounds and 3.7 assists at the time of the trade. Los Angeles had an established scoring-heavy guard roster but wanted a passing big man who could back up its interior players. Charlotte, already outside contention, valued a future choice and financial consideration more than retaining an experienced center. The draft selection was a real future second, not a contingent 2023 first or another unrelated multi-team deal completed on the deadline.

sections.heading: Plumlee Supplied the Clippers with an Experienced Center
sections.body: Plumlee played in Los Angeles after the trade and was useful as an interior reserve and occasional starter. His ability to pass from the center position gave the Clippers an alternative offensive look when the team needed additional size. He was not acquired to become the club’s primary scorer; the roster already relied on Kawhi Leonard and Paul George for that work. The Clippers’ C+ inherited grade reflects immediate veteran frontcourt availability and playoff depth without ignoring the draft choice surrendered. Plumlee subsequently remained with the Clippers for another season, reinforcing that the team obtained more than a brief contract placeholder. His earlier Charlotte averages cannot be counted as his posttrade Los Angeles production.

sections.heading: Jackson Was Waived, Making the Draft Pick Charlotte’s Durable Return
sections.body: Although the Hornets received Jackson’s contract, he never became a regular-season Charlotte rotation guard. The team waived him soon after the deadline, and Jackson continued his NBA career elsewhere. The $1 million cash recorded in the inherited asset list and the 2028 Clippers second-rounder therefore carried the durable Charlotte value, while the receiving roster moved on without the veteran. Charlotte’s B grade recognizes asset recovery from an expiring-center decision, not a claim that Jackson provided more on-court production than Plumlee. That distinction prevents a misleading two-player comparison and clarifies why a rebuilding team could prefer a draft choice several years away. The Clippers acquired center minutes; Charlotte received resources for later moves and cleared a roster spot.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Charlotte Edge. The Hornets earn B for Reggie Jackson’s contract, $1 million cash and the 2028 Clippers second-round pick, though Jackson did not play for Charlotte. Los Angeles receives C+ after adding Mason Plumlee for reserve center and playoff duties.

sections.heading: Detroit Acquired Two Seconds Alongside Joe Harris
sections.body: On July 6, 2023, Brooklyn traded Joe Harris and two second-round draft choices to Detroit, receiving cash considerations. The official Nets announcement identifies the picks as Dallas’s 2027 second and Milwaukee’s 2029 second. Harris had been a valuable Nets shooter for seven seasons and left as the franchise’s all-time leader in made three-pointers, but he was entering the last season of a sizable contract after injuries had reduced his role. Detroit possessed financial capacity to absorb the obligation and obtain draft capital. Brooklyn sought payroll relief while rebalancing the roster after its 2023 star trades. This agreement did not deliver a Pistons player to Brooklyn or a current first-round selection.

sections.heading: Harris Did Not Repeat His Earlier Nets Production in Detroit
sections.body: Detroit was not buying the seven-year version of Harris that averaged 11.6 points for the Nets or led the league in three-point percentage. He played a small supporting role with the Pistons, and the club waived him in February 2024. His long Brooklyn shooting achievements are historical context, not a direct measure of his Detroit impact. The Pistons’ B+ inherited grade consequently depends heavily on the additional draft choices, rather than a claim that Harris became a new starting scorer beside Cade Cunningham. Detroit still had years before the two second-rounders would come due, leaving uncertainty about which prospects or later trades those picks might yield. The essential return was control over two future assets.

sections.heading: Brooklyn Received Financial Flexibility Instead of Draft Value
sections.body: The Nets obtained cash considerations and reduced their future salary obligation, allowing the team to redirect resources to other roster priorities. The canonical transaction record associates roughly $110,000 with the cash, but that should not be mistaken for an incoming pick or player who could score Brooklyn NBA points. Brooklyn’s C- inherited grade captures the financial benefit weighed against surrendering two draft options and a veteran shooter. Detroit’s higher grade is understandable because acquiring multiple seconds to absorb a veteran contract can produce useful long-term flexibility for a rebuilding team. The actual performance of 2027 and 2029 picks has yet to be established, and projecting future NBA careers onto them would be unsourced. The confirmed deal was a salary-and-draft-capital exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win. Detroit receives B+ for Joe Harris and two second-round selections in 2027 and 2029. Brooklyn gets C- for reported cash and salary relief. Harris was waived in February 2024, so the Pistons’ main remaining value was draft capital, not sustained Detroit scoring.

sections.heading: Brooklyn Sent Patty Mills and a Second-Rounder to Houston
sections.body: On July 6, 2023, the Nets traded veteran Australian guard Patty Mills and a 2028 second-round selection originating from Milwaukee to Houston for future draft considerations. The Nets official release provides both the player and pick terms and identifies Mills’s two-year Brooklyn tenure. Houston was participating in several moves as it assembled a different mix of guards around a young roster. Brooklyn was trimming its veteran backcourt and salary costs. The agreement must not be combined with other multi-team trades announced that summer, and the inherited asset list should not be interpreted as a guaranteed first-round pick coming back from Houston. Future draft considerations are inherently less specific than a named selected player, especially before a pick chain is fully resolved.

sections.heading: Mills Did Not Become a Long-Term Rockets Rotation Guard
sections.body: Mills had played 40 Nets games in 2022-23, with two starts and averages of 6.2 points and 1.4 assists in 14.2 minutes. Those Nets numbers are evidence of the kind of veteran shooting Houston was taking on, but they are not Houston points or starts. The Rockets promptly moved Mills onward during the offseason before he could establish a long-term regular-season role there. Houston’s C+ inherited grade therefore represents temporary control over a useful contract and a future second-round pick, not a claim that Mills played multiple full Rockets seasons. He had been a championship reserve in San Antonio years earlier, but those Spurs achievements should not be credited to Houston or attributed to this deal.

sections.heading: The Pick and Contract Flexibility Were the Real Assets
sections.body: Houston controlled the 2028 Milwaukee-sourced second-rounder and a veteran contract that could be routed through further deals. Brooklyn received future considerations and a reduction in immediate salary commitments while changing its guard depth. The Nets C grade reflects flexibility but an imprecisely described direct draft return. A second-round selection can produce a useful player, but its eventual holder and draft outcome are different questions from which club initially obtained the pick in July 2023. The Rockets’ slightly higher grade rewards their asset position rather than realized Mills NBA playing time. No subsequent three-point shooting season by Mills with another team belongs in the Houston column. The narrow inherited Rockets Edge is more a salary-and-draft trade result than a conventional starting-player upgrade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Rockets Edge. Houston receives C+ for Patty Mills’s contract and a Milwaukee-origin 2028 second-round pick, although Mills did not become a Rockets NBA regular. Brooklyn receives C for future considerations and salary flexibility. The future pick’s eventual outcome is not assumed.

sections.heading: Detroit Obtained House, Cash and a Second for a Protected 2028 Pick
sections.body: On February 8, 2024, Philadelphia sent wing Danuel House Jr., cash considerations and a 2024 second-round selection to Detroit. The 76ers received a 2028 second-round pick that was protected within the first fifty-five selections. Official NBA reporting records all four pieces and explains Philadelphia’s motive as payroll flexibility for the buyout market. The incoming 2024 choice became No. 53 and was used on Cam Spencer, although draft rights can be moved again in separate agreements. Detroit was effectively using its financial flexibility to obtain a current draft option from a playoff-bound club. House was not the primary attraction in the long run: the transaction was a pick-and-cap maneuver more than an effort to find a new franchise scorer.

sections.heading: The Pistons Waived House Without an Extended Playing Trial
sections.body: House had been a reserve in Philadelphia, averaging 4.2 points and 1.7 rebounds in the 2023-24 portion preceding the deal. Detroit’s transaction register shows it waived House soon after the acquisition, so the club did not obtain a season of Pistons points from him. The NBA games House had already played for Philadelphia cannot be included in the Pistons return. Instead, the value was access to an immediate 2024 second-round selection and the accompanying cash in exchange for a highly protected later pick. This is why the Pistons B inherited grade makes more sense as an asset-management score than as an evaluation of the veteran guard’s on-court play. A rebuilding club could use that draft right even without retaining the acquired player.

sections.heading: The 76ers Cleared Salary but Gained a Low-Probability Pick
sections.body: Philadelphia moved House’s contract and received a 2028 second-rounder protected through No. 55, a condition that may limit what is ever delivered. The franchise created additional room to explore the buyout market ahead of the playoffs. Its D+ inherited grade reflects the speculative future asset relative to surrendering a current pick, cash and the veteran salary obligation. Detroit could obtain a more certain 2024 selection and financial compensation, whereas Philadelphia prioritized immediate cap-management needs. The No. 53 pick was not a premium first-round prospect and should not be assigned a fictional all-star outcome, but it was still identifiable draft capital. The original trade therefore produced contrasting balance-sheet and draft-timing outcomes without a sustained Detroit House playing career.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win. Detroit earns B after receiving Danuel House Jr., cash and the 2024 No. 53 second-round selection linked to Cam Spencer; House was waived soon afterward. Philadelphia gets D+ for a top-55-protected 2028 second-rounder and salary flexibility. The Pistons’ pick was the more immediate asset.

sections.heading: Detroit Exchanged a Reserve Guard and a Pick for Another Future Second
sections.body: On February 16, 2009, the Pistons traded little-used guard Alex Acker and their 2011 second-round selection to the Clippers. Detroit received a conditional second-round choice for 2013. The Detroit club issued an official announcement detailing this exact package, so the trade is not just an unverified draft-chain inference. The 2011 pick ultimately became No. 37 Trey Thompkins, while the 2013 selection was No. 56 Peyton Siva. Neither choice was a first-round asset. Detroit was willing to defer its opportunity for a later prospect, while the Clippers gained a young guard to assess and a nearer-term draft selection. The trade occurred while both rosters were seeking cheaper reserve options.

sections.heading: Acker Played Only a Small Clippers Role
sections.body: Acker had appeared in six Detroit games during 2008-09, averaging 1.5 points in just 3.3 minutes before the move. Los Angeles offered him another chance in the rotation, but his Clippers tenure was brief and he did not establish himself as a starting NBA guard. The 2011 pick gave the Clippers an additional prospect opportunity; Thompkins later played reserve forward minutes with the franchise without becoming a major scoring centerpiece. Those two outcomes justify treating the return as modest depth rather than a breakout trade. The inherited Clippers B- grade is generous in hindsight but recognizes acquiring two separate assets for a distant pick. His previous European scoring figures must not be counted as Clippers NBA output.

sections.heading: The Later Detroit Selection Became Peyton Siva
sections.body: Detroit ultimately used the 2013 second-round choice at No. 56 to select Louisville point guard Peyton Siva. He appeared in 24 Pistons games during 2013-14, offering limited backup playmaking before his NBA career moved elsewhere. This was a real second-round outcome, not a conditional promise that simply expired. Still, Detroit waited more than four years to obtain those limited minutes and gave up a nearer 2011 pick in the process. The inherited Pistons B- and Clippers B- grades are equal, despite the slight Clippers winner label. The distinction is mainly immediate roster optionality and the timing of the draft prospects rather than a sizable NBA production gap. Neither team received a future perennial starting guard.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Clippers Edge by the inherited verdict, with B- grades on both sides. Los Angeles received Alex Acker and the 2011 No. 37 choice later used on Trey Thompkins. Detroit acquired the 2013 No. 56 choice used on Peyton Siva, who appeared in 24 Pistons games.

sections.heading: A Three-Team Transaction Left Detroit with Fabricio Oberto
sections.body: On June 23, 2009, Detroit announced that it had acquired Argentine center Fabricio Oberto from Milwaukee as part of a broader three-team arrangement also involving San Antonio. The Pistons sent young forward Amir Johnson to the Bucks. The official Pistons release identifies both incoming and outgoing players, while also explaining the San Antonio component. Any account that describes Oberto as having arrived solely from a two-team Milwaukee agreement misses that larger context. Detroit valued financial and veteran flexibility, whereas Milwaukee wanted a young athletic defender who could develop behind its established frontcourt. Johnson had started 24 of his 62 Detroit games in the previous season; Oberto was 34 and had helped San Antonio win the 2007 championship.

sections.heading: Oberto Never Became a Pistons Rotation Center
sections.body: Detroit waived Oberto during the offseason, preventing the veteran from recording a regular-season Pistons playing tenure. His 274 San Antonio games over earlier seasons and his playoff shooting accomplishments were genuine career credentials, but none became Detroit NBA minutes by virtue of the trade. That leaves the Pistons C inherited grade resting on salary and roster-management effects rather than direct scoring or rebounding. The contract exchange was a short-lived maneuver for a club attempting to adjust its frontcourt options after a disappointing playoff exit. It is important not to assign Oberto’s later Washington season to Detroit or to describe a substantial Pistons starting-center acquisition. The value realized by Detroit was primarily off-court flexibility after the contract changed hands.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Also Used Johnson as an Asset Rather Than a Long-Term Starter
sections.body: The Bucks acquired a younger, more athletic forward in Johnson, who had shown rebounding and shot-blocking ability despite a limited offensive role in Detroit. But he did not become a long-term Milwaukee centerpiece: the Bucks moved him to Toronto in another transaction during the same summer. His subsequent strong seasons with the Raptors cannot be credited as Bucks NBA games, though Milwaukee did control his contract and could exchange it again. The inherited Bucks Win label accompanies equal C grades for both teams, highlighting how narrow the distinction was. Neither side obtained an on-court star in its new uniform. The original transaction was chiefly an intermediate roster and financial step inside the three-club deal.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win under the inherited label, although Milwaukee and Detroit both grade C. Milwaukee obtained Amir Johnson as a movable young frontcourt asset, while Detroit acquired Fabricio Oberto in a three-team deal and waived him before he played for the Pistons. Neither club received extended direct court production from this exchange.

sections.heading: Charlotte Sold Robert Vaden’s Draft Rights for Cash
sections.body: On June 25, 2009, the Bobcats moved the rights to No. 54 selection Robert Vaden to Oklahoma City for cash considerations. The Thunder announced the acquisition that evening alongside its selections of James Harden and B.J. Mullens, confirming that Vaden came from Charlotte rather than being Oklahoma City’s original pick. Vaden had been a productive college scorer at UAB, averaging 17.6 points and 4.9 rebounds as a senior. Oklahoma City was using late second-round rights to gather developmental options behind a young Durant-led core. Charlotte chose immediate financial consideration instead of trying to sign another wing on its roster. There were no veteran contracts or first-round selections involved in this specific draft-rights exchange.

sections.heading: The Thunder Held Rights Without Receiving an NBA Career
sections.body: Vaden continued his professional playing career outside the NBA and never made a Thunder regular-season roster. That limits the realized on-court value of the acquisition, no matter how effective he had been in college. A team can benefit from scouting and controlling a late selection’s rights, but that is not the same as acquiring a productive reserve who actually starts games. The inherited Oklahoma City C grade recognizes that speculative option. The fact that the team also drafted Harden in the same 2009 class must not be treated as compensation from Charlotte; that separate No. 3 selection was unrelated to the Vaden deal. The team’s later championships or Finals trips cannot be attributed to this modest rights purchase.

sections.heading: Charlotte Took Known Cash Instead of Prospect Development Risk
sections.body: Charlotte received cash, with no published amount specified in the inherited canonical trade assets. The Bobcats could use those resources elsewhere while keeping their roster open for another player. Their equal C grade reflects the practical but modest nature of the return. Although the official Thunder release praised Vaden’s college accomplishments, those statistics did not convert into NBA contributions for the acquiring organization. The inherited Oklahoma City Thunder Win designation therefore describes an initial preference for developmental possibility, not demonstrably greater NBA playing production. This was a low-stakes second-round transaction, and both clubs made defensible but different decisions about the cost of evaluating an unsigned prospect. The cash and player rights should be analyzed separately.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Oklahoma City Thunder Win in the inherited classification, with C grades on both sides. The Thunder obtained No. 54 Robert Vaden’s draft rights and controlled an international development option, but Vaden never played an NBA game for it. Charlotte received cash considerations rather than a roster player.

sources.title: Thunder official 2009 draft rights acquisition of Robert Vaden

sections.heading: Dallas and Oklahoma City Exchanged Adjacent First-Round Rights
sections.body: On June 25, 2009, the Mavericks traded rights to No. 24 Ohio State center B.J. Mullens to Oklahoma City. The Thunder sent rights to No. 25 French guard Rodrigue Beaubois and a future second-round pick that became No. 50 Solomon Alabi in 2010. Oklahoma City’s official draft release confirms the exchange and the specific one-slot movement, while later pick ledgers connect the second selection. Dallas preferred a quick young guard with scoring upside, and the Thunder targeted an athletic interior prospect. The difference between No. 24 and No. 25 may appear small, but Dallas also acquired another second-round opportunity. Those assets should not be collapsed into a straight Beaubois-for-Mullens swap.

sections.heading: Beaubois Became a Useful Dallas Rotation Guard
sections.body: Beaubois made 56 Mavericks appearances in his 2009-10 rookie season and scored at a useful rate in limited guard minutes. Injuries affected his opportunities the following season, but he continued to play for Dallas over four seasons, bringing speed and outside shooting alongside a veteran backcourt. He was on the franchise roster during the 2011 NBA championship season but was not the central playmaker of its title run. The inherited Mavericks B+ grade captures several seasons of an inexpensive guard and the added second-round choice, without awarding him the accomplishments of Dirk Nowitzki or Jason Kidd. His NBA playing time belongs directly to Dallas and provides a measurable contrast with the young center Oklahoma City received.

sections.heading: Mullens Had Minimal Thunder Minutes Before a Separate Move
sections.body: Mullens remained a developmental center in Oklahoma City, appearing in only limited regular-season games while the Thunder built around its young perimeter stars. The team moved him to Charlotte in December 2011 for a future second-round selection, beginning another transaction chain. His later Bobcats starting seasons therefore cannot be counted as Thunder playing time. Oklahoma City C inherited grade reflects a speculative big-man prospect that never became a regular starter for that franchise. Dallas also held the No. 50 second-round pick in 2010, which was associated with Solomon Alabi, though his later NBA career requires draft-rights attribution. The value of that added selection supported Dallas relative to a center prospect with little direct Thunder impact.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win. Dallas receives B+ for Rodrigue Beaubois draft rights and a future second-rounder used on No. 50 Solomon Alabi, with Beaubois supplying four Dallas seasons. Oklahoma City earns C for No. 24 B.J. Mullens, whose Thunder NBA tenure was limited before a later move to Charlotte.

sections.heading: Charlotte Acquired Graham and a 2025 Second for Cash
sections.body: On July 6, 2024, the Hornets obtained former Charlotte guard Devonte’ Graham and New Orleans’ 2025 second-round selection from San Antonio in exchange for cash considerations. The Spurs received a trade exception, and Charlotte immediately waived Graham. Both Basketball-Reference’s July transactions and contemporaneous reporting agree on the timing and the important source of the future pick. This was not a conventional move to restore Graham to a long-term Hornets role: his contract was a vehicle to transfer draft capital. Charlotte had previously drafted him in 2018 and seen him develop into a high-volume three-point shooter, but those earlier years cannot be credited to the 2024 agreement. San Antonio was clearing roster and salary commitments while the Hornets acquired an additional prospect opportunity.

sections.heading: The Draft Pick Became Ryan Kalkbrenner at No. 34
sections.body: The 2025 second-round selection originated with New Orleans and ultimately became No. 34, used on Creighton center Ryan Kalkbrenner. That is an identifiable draft result, not a pick that expired under protection. Charlotte could select a developing big man without spending a first-round choice or trading an active starter, giving the transaction value even though Graham provided no on-court appearances in this second Charlotte stint. The Hornets C+ inherited grade reflects extracting a real 2025 draft asset in exchange for cash and taking responsibility for the brief contractual movement. The pick’s eventual NBA career cannot yet be judged by assuming future All-Star production; the tangible trade return is the ability to control a recognized second-round prospect.

sections.heading: San Antonio Preferred Cap Flexibility to Retaining Graham
sections.body: Graham was a veteran guard who had seen limited San Antonio minutes and was not central to its long-term plans. The Spurs used the trade to move his contract and adjust their financial roster position, accepting cash while parting with a second-round pick. The team’s C- inherited grade recognizes that flexibility as a practical benefit, even though it did not receive a new player or draft choice from the Hornets. Charlotte obtained the only definite future draft asset, making the inherited Charlotte Win verdict understandable. The distinction also prevents double-counting: Graham played previous Charlotte seasons from an entirely separate acquisition, but the July 2024 trade itself yielded zero additional Hornets NBA games from him. The second-round pick, not a reunion, was the transaction’s real centerpiece.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Charlotte Win. The Hornets receive C+ for Devonte’ Graham’s contract and New Orleans’ 2025 second-round pick, later used on No. 34 Ryan Kalkbrenner; Graham was immediately waived without Hornets games. San Antonio earns C- for cash and salary flexibility. The incoming draft choice was Charlotte’s lasting asset.

sections.heading: Coleman and Bradley Changed Sides in a Six-Player Deal
sections.body: On November 30, 1995, New Jersey dealt forward Derrick Coleman, guard Rex Walters and forward Sean Higgins to Philadelphia. The 76ers sent seven-foot-six center Shawn Bradley, guard Greg Graham and forward Tim Perry to the Nets. The league transaction records and both franchises confirm the complete three-for-three trade. Philadelphia wanted an established scoring and rebounding forward rather than waiting for Bradley’s development, while New Jersey sought a towering interior defender after years of turbulence around Coleman. This was not a direct Coleman-for-Bradley exchange. Both teams included two other players whose roster and contract roles influenced the agreement. The transaction occurred early in the 1995-96 season before either club had a settled playoff path.

sections.heading: Coleman Became an Important Philadelphia Frontcourt Scorer
sections.body: Coleman provided more experienced frontcourt offense than the 76ers had received from Bradley. He could score from the elbows, rebound, and draw defensive attention around younger guards. Philadelphia did not become an immediate contender, and injuries interrupted Coleman’s later seasons, but the franchise obtained a proven former All-Star instead of treating a developing center as the only path forward. His NBA contributions with the Nets before the November transaction do not count as Philadelphia return; the value was the forward’s subsequent work in his new uniform. Walters also contributed guard minutes while Higgins played a smaller supporting role. The inherited 76ers B+ grade reflects the greater experienced offensive contribution without pretending that this single trade created the franchise’s later playoff success around Allen Iverson.

sections.heading: Bradley Was New Jersey’s Center for Only Part of Two Seasons
sections.body: Bradley added blocked shots and interior reach for the Nets, but his New Jersey tenure was not particularly durable. The club sent him onward to Dallas in the major February 1997 nine-player transaction. Graham and Perry were additional role players rather than long-term New Jersey franchise scorers. The Nets C- inherited grade captures the modest team-specific outcome compared with what Philadelphia received from Coleman. Bradley went on to play many productive years in Dallas, yet those Mavericks seasons belong to the next transaction and cannot be counted as a New Jersey benefit. The deal’s immediate rationale was understandable for both teams, but the realized return favored an established Philadelphia scorer over an asset the Nets moved again relatively quickly.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win. Philadelphia earns B+ for Derrick Coleman, Rex Walters and Sean Higgins. New Jersey receives C- for Shawn Bradley, Greg Graham and Tim Perry; Bradley played for the Nets only until February 1997 before being traded again. The larger team-specific offensive return went to Philadelphia.

sources.title: Shawn Bradley New Jersey and Dallas seasons

sections.heading: Dallas and New Jersey Exchanged Nine Players
sections.body: On February 17, 1997, the Nets traded center Shawn Bradley, Ed O’Bannon, Robert Pack and Khalid Reeves to Dallas. The Mavericks sent Sam Cassell, Chris Gatling, Jim Jackson, George McCloud and Eric Montross to New Jersey. Contemporary Washington Post and UPI reporting characterized the nine-player transaction as unusually large for two NBA clubs. It was part of new Dallas executive Don Nelson’s rapid reworking of a roster that had already traded Jason Kidd and Jamal Mashburn. Dallas wanted a long-term center and another point guard, while New Jersey collected several proven scorers and versatile contracts. The five-for-four structure, not just Bradley for Cassell, drives the asset assessment.

sections.heading: New Jersey Received Several Valuable Players and Later Trade Options
sections.body: Cassell gave the Nets another capable starting guard, and Gatling arrived as an All-Star-level scoring forward. Jim Jackson also brought perimeter production and experience, while Montross was a reserve center and McCloud another movable shooter. The receiving club did not retain each of them for a long Nets career: McCloud moved to the Lakers only three days later for Joe Kleine and a first-round pick, and Jackson and Montross were part of the June trade that brought Keith Van Horn to New Jersey. Those later transactions need separate accounting, but they show that Nelson’s departing Mavericks assets gave the Nets substantial flexibility in addition to court time. The inherited Nets A+ grade reflects the depth of the incoming package and the options generated by moving players again.

sections.heading: Bradley Played Many Dallas Seasons While the Other Returns Varied
sections.body: Dallas did gain an enduring starting center. Bradley’s shot blocking and defensive size kept him in the Mavericks rotation for many years, including the franchise’s early Dirk Nowitzki development period. Pack was useful as a point guard when healthy, while Reeves and O’Bannon had shorter Dallas contributions. The inherited Mavericks F grade is exceptionally harsh when Bradley’s subsequent Dallas tenure is considered. A complete hindsight regrading could acknowledge his legitimate rim protection while still recognizing New Jersey acquired five usable assets from a rebuild-driven agreement. The fact remains that Dallas surrendered multiple current scoring options at once and relied heavily on its seven-foot-six centerpiece. His entire career was not a failure, though the transaction had serious opportunity costs.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win under the inherited A+ New Jersey to F Dallas assessment. The Nets obtained Cassell, Gatling, Jim Jackson, McCloud and Montross, several later reused in other trades. Dallas acquired Bradley, Pack, Reeves and O’Bannon. Bradley gave Dallas many seasons of center play, so the extreme inherited grade gap merits careful future review.

sources.title: February 1997 Mavericks and Nets nine player trade

sections.heading: Denver Paid Two Firsts and Two Veterans for Allen Iverson
sections.body: On December 19, 2006, the Nuggets acquired Allen Iverson and Ivan McFarlin from Philadelphia. Denver sent point guard Andre Miller, forward Joe Smith and two protected 2007 first-round draft choices, which became No. 21 Daequan Cook and No. 30 Petteri Koponen. The Nuggets official press release confirms every asset and identifies management’s intention to pair Iverson with young scorer Carmelo Anthony. Philadelphia was turning over an era built around its former MVP, accepting an established organizing guard and additional future picks rather than continuing with the same star. The contract and draft opportunity costs were substantial, not a simple two-player swap. The picks also required later rights-chain accounting before assigning complete careers to the 76ers.

sections.heading: Iverson Scored at a High Level but Denver Did Not Reach the Finals
sections.body: Iverson gave Denver an aggressive scorer and playmaker beside Anthony, keeping opposing defenses focused on both perimeter threats. The Nuggets made the playoffs during his tenure but did not advance deep enough to win the conference or NBA title with that particular partnership. Denver moved Iverson to Detroit during 2008-09 in the separate Chauncey Billups transaction, closing a comparatively short era. His earlier 2001 Philadelphia Finals run was an achievement for the outgoing club, not Denver production. The inherited Nuggets B+ grade credits a high-profile scoring return and NBA star status while recognizing the cost in guards and selections. McFarlin did not become a major additional Nuggets rotation player, so the deal’s immediate basketball value rested primarily on Iverson. The trade improved offensive firepower without guaranteeing postseason transformation.

sections.heading: Miller Became a Stabilizing Guard for the 76ers
sections.body: Miller supplied a mature pass-first point guard who could work with Philadelphia’s younger players, and he remained with the Sixers for more than two seasons. Joe Smith provided veteran frontcourt depth for a shorter term. The two first-round selections created additional future options, even though the prospects later played for other teams after different rights trades. The inherited 76ers B grade reflects a broad return rather than one new star of Iverson’s stature. Philadelphia could redistribute offensive responsibility and begin a transition without getting nothing back. The equal-ish original grading B+ versus B fits a transaction in which Denver secured immediate elite talent while the 76ers gained a starting guard and draft capital. This is a better comparison than treating the move as Iverson for a single anonymous draft pick.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade under the inherited classification, with Denver B+ and Philadelphia B. Denver acquired Iverson and McFarlin, sending Andre Miller, Joe Smith and first-round choices later No. 21 Cook and No. 30 Koponen. Iverson delivered scoring but not a Finals trip; Philadelphia obtained multi-year guard stability.
