sections.heading: The Nets Obtained Jayson Williams for Two Second-Round Picks
sections.body: On October 8, 1992, New Jersey acquired forward-center Jayson Williams from Philadelphia, surrendering a 1994 second-round selection and a 1997 second-round selection. Those picks were later identified as No. 41 William Njoku and No. 35 Kebu Stewart. Williams had appeared in just two NBA seasons for the 76ers after being selected in the first round in 1990 and had not yet developed into a reliable star rebounder. New Jersey wanted a younger frontcourt prospect to complement Derrick Coleman and Kenny Anderson. Philadelphia chose two later opportunities to add size or depth rather than waiting for Williams to mature. No first-round pick and no other veteran were part of the agreement. The two-year and five-year gaps until the respective second-round selections changed the risk profile for the receiving 76ers.

sections.heading: Williams Developed Into an All-Star Rebounder in New Jersey
sections.body: Williams eventually became one of the Nets' most effective rebounders. In 1997-98 he earned an NBA All-Star selection while averaging a double-double, and his interior energy had become an important part of the team's playing identity. That success followed several seasons of development rather than arriving immediately after the 1992 swap. New Jersey gained a player who could start, contest rebounds at both ends and give the frontcourt a physical presence around perimeter scorers. His later injury troubles curtailed the length of his best NBA period, but they do not erase the sustained value he provided before then. His Nets playing years are a direct consequence of acquiring him from Philadelphia in 1992, and they cannot reasonably be characterized as a mere speculative second-round asset. The outcome offers a clear example of a young player outperforming the modest acquisition price.

sections.heading: Philadelphia's Picks Did Not Match the Nets Center Return
sections.body: Philadelphia received two delayed second-round selections for Jayson Williams. The 1994 choice at No. 41 traveled through Philadelphia to Indiana, which selected William Njoku, and therefore cannot be credited as a completed 76ers NBA playing contribution. The later pick associated with Kebu Stewart yielded only 15 games for Philadelphia in 1997-98, with 2.7 points and 2.1 rebounds per game. New Jersey received a much stronger realized contribution: Williams played 373 Nets games, started 149 and earned the 1998 All-Star selection while averaging 13.6 rebounds per game. This is a clear Nets hindsight victory even though Williams needed years to develop and his top-level playing career ended prematurely. The team grades now reconcile at Nets A- and Philadelphia D+, without changing any original pick asset, source team or public route. The inherited 1997 draft-pick ordinal remains as originally sourced; its separate historical numbering discrepancy is not resolved by the grading review.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win — New Jersey A- and Philadelphia D+. The Nets paid two future second-round opportunities to obtain Jayson Williams, whose New Jersey stint produced 373 regular-season appearances and a 1998 All-Star selection. The 1994 No. 41 pick later traveled to Indiana for William Njoku; the 1997 asset associated with Kebu Stewart produced 15 Philadelphia games. The substantial on-court value gap supports a decisive Nets retrospective edge, with the developmental wait and injury-shortened peak reflected in the A- grade.

sections.heading: Charlotte Acquired Hersey Hawkins in a Four-Asset Deal
sections.body: On September 3, 1993, the Hornets acquired shooting guard Hersey Hawkins from Philadelphia. The 76ers received Dana Barros, Sidney Green, the draft rights to Greg Graham and a 1994 first-round choice that eventually became No. 6 Sharone Wright. Hawkins had been a reliable Philadelphia scorer and a former All-Star, providing Charlotte another established perimeter shooter beside Larry Johnson and Alonzo Mourning. Philadelphia wanted roster flexibility and multiple younger or veteran options after a disappointing period. The transaction did not simply trade Hawkins for Barros: the rights to Graham and the 1994 first were meaningful additions. Both clubs' transaction histories agree on the September date and the first-round outcome. Charlotte had already accumulated some of the assets in earlier trades, making this a distinct later use of those holdings.

sections.heading: Hawkins Delivered Scoring and Defense to Charlotte
sections.body: Hawkins joined an exciting young Hornets group and offered efficient outside shooting and veteran experience to support the team's emerging frontcourt stars. He played for Charlotte in 1993-94 and 1994-95, starting a substantial share of games and complementing Muggsy Bogues on the perimeter. His role differed from Mourning's inside scoring and Johnson's power-forward play, making him a practical addition rather than a player who displaced the central franchise names. He was traded to Seattle in 1995 in another agreement, so his later SuperSonics Finals season cannot be counted as Charlotte production. The Hornets did acquire a proven NBA wing for two seasons, which prevents the deal from being an entirely one-sided short-term failure. Yet they surrendered four assets to make that happen, including a valuable upcoming lottery choice.

sections.heading: Dana Barros and Sharone Wright Provided Philadelphia More Ways Forward
sections.body: Barros developed into a major Philadelphia scorer and earned an All-Star berth in 1995, giving the 76ers a strong direct basketball return. The team also held the No. 6 choice used on Sharone Wright, a young big man who played NBA games for Philadelphia before moving elsewhere. Graham rights and Green supplied additional development or veteran options, though neither delivered the franchise a new permanent star. The inherited 76ers Win verdict and A- Philadelphia to D+ Charlotte grades emphasize the combination of Barros production and the sixth overall pick. Hawkins was useful, but the Philadelphia return included both a high-performing guard and a premium draft asset. The pick and player paths should be assessed separately; Barros's All-Star season belongs to Philadelphia and is not an inherited Charlotte achievement.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win. Philadelphia earns A- for Dana Barros, Sidney Green, Greg Graham rights and the 1994 No. 6 pick used on Sharone Wright; Barros became a 1995 All-Star. Charlotte receives D+ after acquiring Hersey Hawkins for two productive seasons but sending out four pieces, including a lottery selection.

sections.heading: The Lakers Traded Benoit Benjamin for Sam Bowie and a Pick
sections.body: On June 21, 1993, Los Angeles sent center Benoit Benjamin to the New Jersey Nets for veteran center Sam Bowie and a future second-round selection. The Lakers' official transaction record dates the move and identifies the later choice as a 1998 second-rounder, ultimately connected to No. 45 Toby Bailey. Contemporaneous Los Angeles Times coverage describes the swap as an attempt to reconnect Benjamin with Nets executive Willis Reed, his former Creighton college coach. Some early reporting used a different draft-year description for the pick, so the historical rights chain is essential before assigning any selected player to a receiving team. Neither side traded a first-round choice. Both teams were exchanging veterans whose early draft reputations had outpaced their later consistency.

sections.heading: Bowie Provided Size but Was Near the End of His Career
sections.body: Bowie had been selected second overall by Portland in 1984 and was known for difficult injury setbacks. He later gave New Jersey regular center minutes, but was already in the latter stage of his NBA career by the time the Lakers obtained him. Los Angeles sought a large veteran who could provide interior defense and support a roster transitioning away from its Showtime era. Bowie played for the Lakers during the 1993-94 and 1994-95 seasons, but did not become an enduring starting centerpiece. His earlier Nets rebounding totals do not belong to the Lakers return, and his college-draft story should not be used as a substitute for assessing actual Los Angeles minutes. The second-round pick was an additional option that could be kept or traded; it should not be treated as a guaranteed Lakers starter years before it was exercised.

sections.heading: Benjamin's Nets Tenure Did Not Fulfill a Franchise Rebuild
sections.body: Benjamin had shown scoring and rebounding talent earlier with the Clippers and Seattle. New Jersey hoped Reed's familiarity could unlock more of that potential, especially alongside younger stars Derrick Coleman and Kenny Anderson. The experiment yielded actual NBA game appearances but not the durable elite center play the franchise wanted. New Jersey's inherited C- grade captures that limitation. Los Angeles receives B+ in the canonical review for acquiring Bowie and an additional future second; the higher assessment is rooted in two assets for one expensive veteran, not in claiming Bowie became a renewed All-Star. The trade is a reminder that former high draft choices may carry recognizable names while producing modest late-career returns. Keeping team-specific playing time separate from draft-right value prevents the reputation of both centers from distorting the outcome.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win. Los Angeles earns B+ after sending Benoit Benjamin to New Jersey for Sam Bowie and a future second-round selection tied to 1998 No. 45 Toby Bailey. New Jersey receives C- after Benjamin's Nets stint did not deliver an enduring elite center. Contemporary and later reporting differ on the draft year, so rights provenance merits continued review.

sections.heading: The Clippers Moved Rebounding Leader Michael Cage on Draft Night
sections.body: On June 28, 1988, Los Angeles sent center-forward Michael Cage to the Seattle SuperSonics in exchange for rights to point guard Gary Grant and a 1989 first-round pick. The selection became No. 19, associated with Kenny Payne. The Clippers wanted a young guard to complement the number-one pick Danny Manning and their rebuilding roster, while Seattle valued Cage as a proven rebounder who could defend and finish inside. Both clubs' transaction histories agree on the direct Cage-for-Grant-and-pick agreement. The timing matters: the Clippers also used a 1988 draft-night trade to send the same future first-round asset and rights to Hersey Hawkins to Philadelphia for Charles Smith. Thus the future selection was quickly redirected, not patiently retained by the Clippers to draft Payne.

sections.heading: Gary Grant Became a Regular Clippers Point Guard
sections.body: Grant developed into a primary Los Angeles ball handler and played hundreds of games for the Clippers across his initial tenure. He supplied assists, defensive pressure and enough scoring to remain part of the team through several roster transitions. The direct basketball value from Grant is therefore substantial and is not based on simply holding a distant draft choice. The later draft pick contributed to the separate Charles Smith trade and should be traced through that chain if its value is being assessed, rather than attributing the 1989 No. 19 selection as a Clippers rostered player. Grant's first-round status gave Los Angeles an inexpensive young point guard at a time when the franchise was trying to establish a reliable backcourt. The inherited Slight Clippers Edge acknowledges those roster-building gains even though Cage was a proven player, not an expendable reserve.

sections.heading: Cage Brought Seattle Rebounding and Defensive Minutes
sections.body: Cage had previously led the NBA in rebounding while with the Clippers and gave the SuperSonics an experienced interior presence. He was capable of significant defensive work and continued to play NBA minutes in Seattle for several seasons. The other side of this trade therefore cannot be classified as a bust or a prospect who never joined his new team. Seattle's mid-1990s evolution around Gary Payton and Shawn Kemp eventually changed Cage's rotation role, but his earlier contribution was real. The comparison pits the Clippers' young guard and redirected first-round asset against several years of veteran rebounding depth for the Sonics. Cage's earlier Clippers rebound title should be treated as evidence of why Seattle wanted him, not added to the team's posttrade totals. The inherited slight Los Angeles preference is reasonable as a long-term guard development judgment, not a landslide.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Clippers Edge. Los Angeles obtained Gary Grant's rights and a 1989 first-round selection later associated with Kenny Payne, but redirected that pick in the same draft-night period as part of the Charles Smith acquisition. Seattle acquired proven rebounder Michael Cage and received real frontcourt minutes. Grant's longer Clippers tenure supports the narrow advantage.

sections.heading: Detroit Exchanged Bad Boy Veteran John Salley for a Lottery Pick
sections.body: On September 8, 1992, Detroit traded defensive forward-center John Salley to the Miami Heat in exchange for young forward Isaiah Morris and a 1993 first-round selection. The future pick became No. 10, used on Jackson State point guard Lindsey Hunter. Salley had been a supporting member of the Pistons' 1989 and 1990 NBA championship teams, but the franchise was moving beyond its Bad Boys era and wanted to introduce younger players. Miami, still a young expansion organization, was willing to acquire championship experience immediately. The exchange did not involve a cash payment or another future pick; the first-rounder was the principal developmental asset. The transaction histories and Detroit executive record confirm the September 8 date and eventual draft outcome.

sections.heading: Lindsey Hunter Became a Long-Term Detroit Guard
sections.body: Hunter was selected with the acquired No. 10 choice in 1993 and spent many seasons playing for the Pistons. He became a dependable defensive guard, contributing perimeter pressure and ball handling as the team moved through different cores. He also returned for the 2004 championship campaign, providing another veteran defensive voice to the roster around Chauncey Billups and Richard Hamilton. That long direct Detroit tenure establishes the primary value of the 1992 trade. It did not require Morris to become a frontcourt star for the franchise to get a meaningful return. Hunter's college scoring promise developed into a useful NBA role, and the pick delivered far more than a one-season bench player. Detroit's A inherited grade is supported by the combination of a lottery prospect and a career that stretched into another Pistons title era.

sections.heading: Salley Had a Shorter Miami Role Before Moving Again
sections.body: Salley offered the Heat veteran rebounding, shot blocking and championship experience, but his Miami stint did not last through the team's eventual championship years. He later returned to the NBA with other clubs and won another title with Chicago, a separate roster context that should not be credited as a Heat achievement. The young Miami franchise acquired useful leadership and defensive depth, yet surrendered the No. 10 draft pick that Detroit used on Hunter. The inherited A for Miami and Pistons Win label are not numerically consistent: both clubs are graded A, while the winner favors Detroit's longer-term guard payoff. That distinction should remain visible. The clearest player-specific value is Hunter's years of actual Detroit NBA appearances versus Salley's shorter period providing experience in Miami.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win according to the inherited verdict despite matching A grades. Detroit acquired Isaiah Morris and the 1993 No. 10 first-round selection used on Lindsey Hunter, a future long-tenured Pistons guard and member of its 2004 championship team. Miami gained John Salley, a veteran defender from Detroit's earlier title clubs.

sections.heading: Charlotte Exchanged Kendall Gill for Two Veterans and a Higher Pick
sections.body: On September 1, 1993, Charlotte traded wing Kendall Gill and a 1994 first-round selection that became No. 11 Carlos Rogers to Seattle. The SuperSonics sent Dana Barros, Eddie Johnson and their own 1994 first-rounder, ultimately No. 6 Sharone Wright. This was an unusually active exchange of two current NBA scorers for one young wing plus a swap of first-round positions. Gill had been an important Charlotte prospect and the organization was trying to improve its backcourt while pursuing greater draft flexibility. Seattle, already building around Gary Payton and Shawn Kemp, wanted Gill's athletic defense and size. Both teams' transaction histories independently establish the assets and the September 1 date. The swap was completed before either 1994 first-round selection was used, so these should be described as future pick rights rather than known 1993 NBA players.

sections.heading: Charlotte Moved Several Incoming Assets Two Days Later
sections.body: The Charlotte part of this story cannot be understood without September 3, 1993. The Hornets traded Barros and the first-round pick later used at No. 6, plus Sidney Green and Greg Graham rights, to Philadelphia for Hersey Hawkins. Therefore Barros did not give Charlotte several seasons of basketball production from the September 1 trade, and Sharone Wright did not enter the Hornets roster at No. 6. Their value was as immediately tradeable assets used in a separate move for an established shooting guard. Eddie Johnson provided experienced scoring when he remained with the club, but he too had a changing role late in his NBA career. The inherited Even Trade label is best interpreted as a balancing of Charlotte's extra future draft position and Seattle's acquisition of Gill, not a claim that Barros later earned his 1995 All-Star honor as a Hornet.

sections.heading: Gill and the No. 11 Selection Contributed to Seattle's Depth
sections.body: Gill joined a strong Seattle team and offered rebounding and perimeter defense around Payton, Kemp and other established starters. The Sonics had a 63-win regular season in 1993-94 before a stunning opening-round playoff defeat, and Gill's role was part of a deeper rotation rather than a single-player explanation for that result. Seattle exercised the 1994 choice at No. 11 on Carlos Rogers, a forward with later NBA playing time. The two franchises were exchanging several types of value: Charlotte briefly controlled a higher pick and two veteran scorers, while Seattle gained a younger experienced wing and a first-round selection it could use. Both sides were assessed B in the inherited historical record, and the Even Trade verdict fits the different asset timing once the later Philadelphia deal is included separately.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade, with inherited B grades for Charlotte and the Seattle franchise. The Hornets obtained Dana Barros, Eddie Johnson and a 1994 No. 6 pick but rapidly moved Barros and that pick to Philadelphia for Hersey Hawkins. Seattle received Kendall Gill and the 1994 No. 11 selection used on Carlos Rogers, generating a different form of wing depth.

sections.heading: Sacramento Took a Chance on Former Top Pick Ralph Sampson
sections.body: On September 27, 1989, Golden State traded former No. 1 overall selection Ralph Sampson to Sacramento in exchange for reserve center Jim Petersen. Sampson had been one of the most recognizable big men of the 1980s during his Houston years, but repeated injuries had reduced his effectiveness before his stint with the Warriors. Sacramento was willing to gamble on the possibility of a healthier veteran center while Golden State wanted a different reserve frontcourt option. Both franchise transaction histories independently document the player-for-player terms and the late September date. No draft pick or additional cash compensation came with this swap. The trade is important precisely because it involved a famous name whose current production had moved a long way from his earlier peak.

sections.heading: Sampson Did Not Rediscover His Houston Star Form
sections.body: Sampson continued his NBA career in Sacramento but never returned to the dominant scoring and rebounding he had provided as a young member of the Rockets. His body could not sustain a full starter workload over the ensuing seasons, and his NBA career soon ended. The Kings received size and the prospect of veteran leadership, but not an All-Star-level center able to reshape their frontcourt. The inherited Kings Win verdict is not a claim that Sampson suddenly recovered his former Houston athleticism. Instead it reflects acquiring a recognizable veteran big man at a relatively low direct price. His past All-Star appearances and famous Houston playoff performances belong to Houston, not Sacramento, and should not be counted as Kings accomplishments. The club received limited direct playing production from this particular version of Sampson.

sections.heading: Petersen Was a Modest Warriors Reserve Return
sections.body: Petersen offered Golden State a reserve center whose work was centered on rebounding and physical interior minutes rather than becoming a primary scorer. The Warriors' backcourt and forwards were changing under Don Nelson, leaving little appetite for paying for a declining superstar contract simply because of Sampson's reputation. Moving him cleared a different roster path and reduced uncertainty surrounding the injured center. Petersen's limited Golden State role, however, was not a future franchise anchor either. Neither side obtained a player who was still at the height of his career, so the historical winner should not be exaggerated as a transformative deal. The actual comparison is between Sacramento's chance to revive Sampson and Golden State's lower-profile roster adjustment. The most defensible conclusion is that Sacramento acquired the potentially higher ceiling, while both outcomes remained constrained in practice.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Win is the inherited verdict for Sacramento receiving Ralph Sampson from Golden State in exchange for Jim Petersen. The former No. 1 pick provided a short, injury-affected late-career center option rather than his earlier Houston All-Star peak. Petersen gave the Warriors modest interior reserve depth, so neither club obtained a lasting star.

sections.heading: The Warriors Exchanged Winston Garland for Two Future Seconds
sections.body: On February 22, 1990, the Los Angeles Clippers acquired guard Winston Garland from Golden State. The Warriors received second-round selections in the 1990 and 1992 drafts, later identified as No. 34 Kevin Pritchard and No. 43 Sasha Danilović. Garland had provided NBA backcourt minutes for a young Warriors team but was expendable as Don Nelson's rotation evolved around promising scorers. Los Angeles wanted an experienced guard to help organize a changing lineup, while Golden State chose two lower-cost future development opportunities. The transaction was a single player for two picks, not a direct draft-night trade of Garland for both identified prospects who had already been selected. The two-year gap between the picks gave the Warriors options to draft or redirect assets in different seasons.

sections.heading: Garland Became a Short-Term Clippers Ball Handler
sections.body: Garland brought a recognizable playmaking and defensive profile to Los Angeles. He had experience starting NBA games and could handle possessions while the franchise developed younger players. His Clippers tenure was comparatively short, however, and did not establish him as the next long-term starting guard. The team needed dependable organization during a period of roster turnover, and his veteran presence had some value even without high scoring. The Clippers surrendered two second-round assets in order to acquire him, making the cost greater than a one-pick flyer. The trade should be assessed from his actual Los Angeles minutes rather than importing earlier Golden State playing totals or later games for other clubs. It was a practical guard acquisition, but not the move that created the franchise's eventual 1990s core by itself.

sections.heading: The Draft Choices Gave Golden State Two Development Opportunities
sections.body: Golden State received No. 34 in 1990 and No. 43 in 1992, associated with Kevin Pritchard and Saša Danilović. Both men went on to basketball careers that should be attributed to the clubs for which they actually played. Pritchard later became an NBA executive, but that career does not count as Golden State on-court production from his second-round draft slot. Danilović built an accomplished European career and later played for NBA teams other than Golden State, so his complete playing resume should not be counted as Warriors games. The franchise nevertheless obtained two real choices for a guard it did not plan to retain. The inherited Slight Warriors Edge reflects that flexible draft compensation compared with Garland's shorter Clippers stint. Neither pick alone was a guaranteed new NBA starting guard at the time of the February agreement.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Warriors Edge. Golden State acquired 1990 No. 34 and 1992 No. 43 second-round picks associated with Kevin Pritchard and Saša Danilović in exchange for Winston Garland. Los Angeles received an experienced point guard for a shorter roster role. The two actual draft opportunities gave the Warriors broader future flexibility.

sections.heading: Boston Exchanged Championship Guard Gerald Henderson for a Future First
sections.body: On October 16, 1984, the Celtics traded guard Gerald Henderson to the Seattle SuperSonics for a future first-round pick. Boston had just won the NBA championship, but Henderson wanted a larger role and the team felt it could change its backcourt rotation around Dennis Johnson and Danny Ainge. Seattle needed established guard defense and ball handling for a team retooling after a difficult period. The first-round choice eventually landed at No. 2 in the 1986 draft, which Boston used on Maryland star Len Bias. Boston was acquiring a potentially premium future asset, not a named rookie it could immediately insert into the 1984-85 roster. This distinction is important because the trade's final outcome involved a tragic event no team could have expected in October 1984.

sections.heading: Henderson Played NBA Games While Bias Never Had the Chance
sections.body: Henderson had been a useful supporting player on Boston's title team, including a critical steal in the 1984 Finals. He became a Seattle guard and recorded real regular-season production, with additional NBA years for other teams after leaving the Sonics. The Celtics selected Bias with the second overall pick in June 1986, expecting a major young forward who could eventually support Larry Bird and Kevin McHale. Bias died two days after being selected and never appeared in an NBA game. His death is not evidence that Boston made a foolish scouting decision; it means the high draft position never turned into court production. No legitimate evaluation should invent seasons, points or championship contributions from Bias. The extraordinary distinction between the value of the draft choice on draft night and its realized playing return defines the trade's hindsight difficulty.

sections.heading: The Seattle Franchise Gained a Guard, Not a Long-Term Draft Jackpot
sections.body: Seattle acquired an experienced NBA player and gave up the first-round asset that rose to an unusually high position. Henderson's Sonics role was legitimate, though his career did not remain entirely in Seattle. Boston held an enormous opportunity to extend an aging championship roster with the draft's second choice, but lost that possibility through events after the selection. The inherited Oklahoma City Thunder Win label refers to the Seattle franchise's realized guard contribution compared with no Bias NBA games. It should not suggest that the club already knew the pick would reach No. 2, nor should it erase the personal tragedy by treating the selection simply as a failed basketball prospect. The result is a sharp lesson in separating an asset's value when acquired from the very different eventual outcome. The trade should be evaluated with both pieces of historical context.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Oklahoma City Thunder Win is the inherited Seattle-franchise verdict: Seattle received veteran guard Gerald Henderson, who provided real NBA appearances, while Boston's 1986 No. 2 first-round pick became Len Bias, who died before making an NBA debut. The pick had enormous potential but no realized Celtics playing production.

sections.heading: Boston Took a Major Injury Risk by Trading for Bill Walton
sections.body: On September 6, 1985, the Celtics acquired veteran center Bill Walton from the Los Angeles Clippers in return for forward Cedric Maxwell, a 1986 first-round selection and cash. The draft choice ultimately became associated with No. 24, the rights linked in the trade ledger to Arvydas Sabonis. Walton had been the league's Most Valuable Player in Portland but had suffered repeated foot injuries and had not played full seasons consistently. Boston wanted another intelligent passing and defensive big man behind Robert Parish and Kevin McHale, while the Clippers chose an experienced championship forward and additional draft and financial assets. The transaction was not a straight Maxwell-for-Walton bargain because a future first was also surrendered. Neither side could be certain Walton's health would hold through another championship pursuit.

sections.heading: Walton Won Sixth Man Honors as Boston Captured the 1986 Title
sections.body: Walton gave Boston precisely the reserve center role it hoped to acquire. In 1985-86 he appeared in 80 regular-season games, played about twenty minutes per outing and won the NBA Sixth Man of the Year award. He supplied passing, defense and shot blocking to a lineup that won 67 games and the championship over Houston in the Finals. Those are team-specific contributions directly traceable to the Clippers trade rather than Walton's earlier Portland MVP season. His health became less reliable again afterward, and he did not build many more years of production in Boston, but the first season alone provided a major return. The Celtics Win inherited verdict is strongest because the incoming reserve played meaningful minutes on the club's immediate championship team. The franchise chose a near-term title opportunity over retaining a younger draft right.

sections.heading: Maxwell and the Draft Asset Were Real Clippers Considerations
sections.body: Maxwell had been a valuable forward on Boston's earlier championship teams, including the 1981 Finals Most Valuable Player, but entered the Clippers organization near the later stage of his career. He brought a known veteran presence while the draft selection added another asset that could be exchanged or exercised. The eventual No. 24 choice linked to Sabonis is a draft-pick identity, not proof that Sabonis played NBA games for the Clippers; his eventual NBA career was with Portland after years overseas. The additional cash belongs in the economic return, although its amount is not specified in the canonical ledger. Los Angeles did obtain compensation from Boston, but nothing matched Walton's 1985-86 Sixth Man season and championship utility. The deal illustrates a rare veteran gamble that produced exactly the high-impact short-term role its acquiring team intended.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win. Boston received Bill Walton, who played 80 regular-season games in 1985-86, won Sixth Man of the Year and helped the franchise capture the NBA championship. Los Angeles obtained Cedric Maxwell, cash and a future first-round asset associated with No. 24 Arvydas Sabonis; Sabonis's later Portland playing seasons were not Clippers production.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Obtained Jack Sikma While Sending Two Firsts to Seattle
sections.body: On July 1, 1986, the Milwaukee Bucks acquired veteran All-Star center Jack Sikma and second-round draft selections in 1987 and 1989 from the Seattle SuperSonics. Seattle received center Alton Lister and first-round choices in those same years. The future draft rights became associated with No. 18 Mark Jackson in 1987 and No. 20 Jeff Sanders in 1989, while the Bucks' second-rounders were associated with Bob McCann and Scott Haffner. The trade was a deliberate exchange of an established scoring center for another experienced big man and better draft position. Milwaukee had been a perennial Eastern Conference contender and wanted a center who could shoot away from the basket, while Seattle prepared to reconfigure its roster around younger talent. The multiple draft assets materially change the economics beyond a simple Sikma-for-Lister comparison.

sections.heading: Sikma Offered Reliable Starting Center Play in Milwaukee
sections.body: Sikma had been one of Seattle's defining players during its 1979 championship run. In Milwaukee he remained a productive and durable frontcourt scorer, using shooting range, excellent free-throw touch and passing to complement the Bucks' established perimeter veterans. He spent several seasons with Milwaukee, starting many games even as the club's broader championship hopes diminished. That longevity separates the return from a short rental, and explains the Bucks Win inherited verdict without relying on his earlier Seattle title for Milwaukee credit. His impact was not the same as a newly drafted superstar, but he supplied dependable center minutes at a position where skill and experience were valuable. The incoming second-round selections created additional development opportunities, though their downstream owners and careers need separate accounting. The direct NBA return is Sikma's actual Bucks tenure.

sections.heading: Seattle Retained Lister and Improved Its First-Round Position
sections.body: Lister was a legitimate veteran center who could defend and rebound. Seattle also gained two better-positioned picks while giving up its two later selections. The pick associated with No. 18 Mark Jackson eventually produced an important NBA point guard career with several teams, but that entire career cannot be credited as SuperSonics playing time without tracing the rights chain. The future No. 20 selection offered another chance to obtain inexpensive talent. Seattle's strategic purpose was broader draft capital and a different frontcourt salary profile, not receiving an immediate All-Star replacement for Sikma. Milwaukee gained the more durable named veteran center; Seattle accepted prospects and another center with a narrower offensive role. It would overstate the result to treat the pick identities as guaranteed future SuperSonics starters. The trade was valuable to both teams, but the established Bucks center return carries the inherited winning assessment.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win. Milwaukee acquired Jack Sikma and two future second-round selections, receiving multiple seasons of productive starting center play. Seattle took Alton Lister and first-round choices later associated with No. 18 Mark Jackson in 1987 and No. 20 Jeff Sanders in 1989. Pick identities should not be conflated with games for the rights holder.

sections.heading: Atlanta Obtained Young Levingston and Carr Rights for Roundfield
sections.body: On June 18, 1984, Atlanta traded All-Star forward Dan Roundfield to the Detroit Pistons. The Hawks received young forward Cliff Levingston, the draft rights to Antoine Carr and second-round selections in 1986 and 1987 that were later associated with Augusto Binelli and Terence Bailey. Roundfield had been one of Atlanta's most important defenders and rebounders and was an established veteran, so the transaction represented a major step toward a younger roster. Detroit wanted an experienced forward alongside its developing guards and big men. Atlanta was accepting several chances to improve the long-term frontcourt rather than a single established star. This is why the agreement should not be characterized as Roundfield straight up for Levingston: a second prospect's rights and two draft choices were also included. The future picks were not known NBA playing contributors when the trade was signed.

sections.heading: Levingston Became a Long-Term Hawks Energy Forward
sections.body: Levingston supplied Atlanta with athletic defense, rebounding and activity around the basket during the second half of the 1980s. He played alongside Dominique Wilkins and other Hawks contributors as Atlanta built competitive playoff teams. His professional role did not depend on becoming the leading scorer; he was useful because he could defend and cover frontcourt minutes without demanding the ball. Carr's rights became actual Hawks playing value: Carr appeared in 62, 17, 65, 80 and 78 Atlanta regular-season games from 1984-85 through 1988-89, totaling 302 games. Levingston supplied 74 Atlanta games and 53 starts in 1984-85 and another 81 games the following year. Neither figure requires attributing the later second-round draftees' NBA careers to Atlanta. The draft picks created still more options, with Binelli and Bailey attached to later selections. Atlanta's inherited Hawks Win assessment rests on obtaining several assets and building a more flexible frontcourt during a period of roster changes. Levingston's actual Hawks minutes were the primary direct basketball contribution.

sections.heading: Roundfield Added Championship-Era Experience to Detroit
sections.body: Roundfield arrived with a strong reputation as an interior defender and All-Star forward. Detroit had young Isiah Thomas and a roster that would eventually develop into its Bad Boys championship identity, so the club valued experienced physical frontcourt play. Roundfield was useful, but his Pistons tenure was shorter than Levingston's Atlanta role, and the franchise later made other moves to complete its championship roster. His previous Hawks defensive honors cannot be counted as achievements with Detroit, and the Pistons' 1989 and 1990 titles cannot be retroactively credited solely to his earlier arrival. Atlanta received a broader package while Detroit received one established veteran who could contribute immediately. The subsequent careers of each drafted player need to be attributed to the correct teams, but that accounting does not erase the original imbalance in asset quantity. The move gave both clubs different versions of frontcourt depth, with Atlanta retaining the longer-horizon benefit. Roundfield's receiving-team totals were 56 Pistons games, 43 starts, 1,492 minutes and 611 points in 1984-85. He did not play for Detroit during the later 1989-90 championships; direct one-season club value is distinct from the veteran's earlier All-Defensive Hawks credentials.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win. Atlanta traded Dan Roundfield for Cliff Levingston, Antoine Carr's rights and second-round choices later associated with Augusto Binelli and Terence Bailey. Levingston became a multi-season Hawks frontcourt contributor. Detroit acquired Roundfield's veteran defense but gave up several developmental options for that immediate return.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Sent Clemon Johnson and a First for Two Seattle Big Men
sections.body: On September 29, 1986, Philadelphia traded veteran center Clemon Johnson and its 1989 first-round draft pick to the Seattle SuperSonics in exchange for center Tim McCormick and forward Danny Vranes. Contemporary reporting by UPI and the Los Angeles Times confirms the exact direction of every asset. The 76ers had been trying to replace parts of an aging frontcourt and wanted younger big men who could fit a more mobile offense. Seattle accepted Johnson as another experienced center and a future first-round opportunity. The selection became the No. 17 overall pick in the 1989 NBA draft, later used by Seattle on Shawn Kemp. In September 1986 that eventual draft outcome was unknown, so this was a substantial gamble on a distant first, not a trade for a fully identified future All-Star.

sections.heading: Seattle Used the Future Choice on Shawn Kemp
sections.body: When the 1989 draft arrived, the pick obtained from Philadelphia was No. 17, and Seattle selected Shawn Kemp. He went on to become one of the best power forwards in the NBA during the 1990s, combining explosive finishing with strong rebounding and defensive work. Alongside Gary Payton, Kemp helped the SuperSonics reach the 1996 NBA Finals and sustained the team through several deep postseason runs. These are actual Seattle games and achievements from a player whose draft rights came directly from the 1986 trade. Johnson contributed veteran depth, but his playing career was not the central long-term payoff. The franchise gained far more from the unexpectedly productive first-round pick than from a short-term center swap alone. The inherited Seattle/Oklahoma City Thunder Win verdict therefore has a powerful basketball basis without pretending the front office could have guaranteed Kemp’s eventual value in 1986.

sections.heading: McCormick and Vranes Supplied Philadelphia Immediate Frontcourt Help
sections.body: Philadelphia acquired two younger veteran frontcourt players, not Clemon Johnson. McCormick was a former lottery selection with scoring and rebounding ability, while Vranes brought defensive energy and the ability to cover several forward assignments. Both men played NBA basketball for the Sixers after the agreement and contributed to the club’s immediate effort to support Charles Barkley and the remaining established core. Their return was genuine, but neither became a franchise-defining counterpart to the player Seattle obtained from Philadelphia’s first-rounder. The 76ers had surrendered a future pick that ultimately turned into a multiple-time All-Star, and the difference grew more obvious as Kemp developed. McCormick and Vranes had their own later professional paths, but the team-specific Philadelphia benefit did not approach a decade of Kemp’s Seattle frontcourt production. The biggest hindsight cost was that draft choice, not simply the loss of Johnson’s veteran minutes.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Oklahoma City Thunder Win is the inherited Seattle-franchise verdict. The SuperSonics acquired Clemon Johnson and Philadelphia’s 1989 first-round pick, used at No. 17 on Shawn Kemp, a future All-Star and 1996 Finals forward. The 76ers received Tim McCormick and Danny Vranes for immediate frontcourt help but surrendered the selection that became a franchise centerpiece.

sections.heading: Boston Exchanged Two Future Second-Rounders for Jerry Sichting
sections.body: Boston obtained Jerry Sichting from Indiana for second-round rights that later became the 1989 No. 44 and 1990 No. 46 picks. Pro Sports Transactions lists the exchange on October 2, 1985, while the Celtics and Pacers transaction histories use October 3; the date discrepancy is acknowledged here without silently rewriting a canonical route. The first pick had previously come to Boston from Indiana in the September Quinn Buckner exchange, then returned to Indiana as part of this deal. The Pacers later moved that 1989 selection to Philadelphia in an October 23 transaction. Boston's immediate objective was a veteran reserve guard for its championship roster, rather than retaining two distant second-round opportunities. The sequence is important because the eventual No. 44 selection of Reggie Cross was made by Philadelphia, not by Indiana.

sections.heading: Sichting Became a Useful Reserve on a Championship Team
sections.body: Sichting joined a contender that needed steady depth behind Dennis Johnson and Danny Ainge. He appeared in all 82 Boston regular-season games in 1985-86, averaged 6.5 points and shot 57 percent, then contributed as a reserve during the 67-win Celtics' NBA championship run. His value came from providing ball handling and reliable short-minute offense while Larry Bird, Kevin McHale and Robert Parish anchored the club. Boston did not buy an All-Star, nor should it receive credit for Sichting's earlier Pacers production. It paid two distant second-round selections for an immediately usable guard whose first Boston season ended with a title. That is a defensible reason for a favorable Boston grade regardless of the disputed October 2 versus October 3 recording date.

sections.heading: Indiana Held Two Draft Chances Without a Comparable Championship Guard
sections.body: Indiana's two acquired pick rights had different endings. The 1989 No. 44 selection returned to the Pacers in the Sichting deal, but Indiana subsequently traded the right to Philadelphia in October 1985; the 76ers ultimately selected Reggie Cross, who did not play in the NBA. The 1990 No. 46 selection stayed with the Pacers, who drafted Kenny Williams. Williams played 260 NBA games over four Indiana seasons, averaging 4.8 points and 2.7 rebounds, so it is incorrect to treat both second-round assets as producing zero Pacers playing value. Boston's immediate championship-season return was still stronger than the delayed and modest Indiana contribution, but the Pacers did receive real player production through Williams. This asset-by-asset account is more reliable than casually assigning Cross to Indiana or treating draft rights and eventual roster minutes as interchangeable.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win, with a genuine but smaller Pacers return. Sichting gave Boston 82 regular-season appearances and rotation depth during the 1986 championship season. The acquired 1989 No. 44 draft right subsequently went from Indiana to Philadelphia, which selected Reggie Cross; he should not be counted as a Pacers draft player. Indiana kept the separate 1990 No. 46 right and drafted Kenny Williams, who played 260 Pacers games. The inherited B+ Boston and C+ Indiana grades recognize different timing and value. Contemporary transaction ledgers disagree about whether to label the October 1985 trade October 2 or October 3, so the existing route date stays unchanged pending stronger effective-date proof.

sections.heading: Detroit Sent Two 1987 Draft Choices for Kurt Nimphius
sections.body: On January 29, 1987, the Detroit Pistons acquired center Kurt Nimphius from the Los Angeles Clippers. Detroit surrendered a 1987 first-round selection that became No. 19 Ken Norman and a second-round choice later used at No. 38 on Norris Coleman. Detroit wanted interior depth for a team growing into an Eastern Conference challenger, while the Clippers accepted draft assets rather than retain another veteran reserve big man. Both franchises' dated transaction histories match on the direct center-for-two-picks bargain. Detroit was not acquiring a high-volume All-Star center, and the first-round selection was materially more valuable than a conditional future late second. The deal reflects contrasting organizational priorities during the season Isiah Thomas and Joe Dumars were becoming one of the league's stronger backcourts.

sections.heading: Nimphius Provided Defensive and Rebounding Insurance
sections.body: Nimphius had several NBA seasons of experience and could provide size, rebounding and limited offense behind Detroit's established frontcourt rotation. His contribution was primarily as a reserve rather than a new leading starting center. Detroit reached the 1987 Eastern Conference Finals, but its success was driven by an emerging core including Thomas, Dumars and Bill Laimbeer rather than this one deadline acquisition. The Pistons eventually made further roster adjustments on their path to championships in 1989 and 1990, and it would be inaccurate to attribute all of those later achievements to Nimphius. The inherited Even Trade decision is partly about immediate size for a contending club, not evidence he matched a long-term lottery player. His actual Pistons appearances are the appropriate playing component of the evaluation, separately from two surrendered picks that the Clippers controlled thereafter.

sections.heading: The First-Round Choice Became Clippers Forward Ken Norman
sections.body: Los Angeles used the No. 19 selection on Ken Norman, a productive forward who became a meaningful contributor during the next several Clippers seasons. The No. 38 choice produced Norris Coleman, a lower-profile second-round prospect. The two picks gave the organization developmental flexibility at a time when it was struggling in the standings. Norman's later Clippers points and rebounds were real on-court return from the first selection, and should not be hidden by treating both picks as unfulfilled possibilities. The canonical grades are B+ for both teams despite the practical advantage of a multi-season forward relative to one veteran center. That is a defensible topic for a later source-led grade audit, but this editorial preserves the official Even Trade label. Detroit obtained short-term frontcourt insurance; Los Angeles created a more durable young forward role using the first-round opportunity.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade under inherited B+ grades for Detroit and Los Angeles. The Pistons acquired veteran center Kurt Nimphius in January 1987. The Clippers received first-round No. 19 Ken Norman and second-round No. 38 Norris Coleman; Norman developed into a multi-season Clippers forward, providing a stronger long-term player return.

sections.heading: Sacramento Acquired Mike McGee for Two Future Second-Rounders
sections.body: On December 14, 1987, Sacramento traded its second-round selections in 1991 and 1995 to Atlanta for guard Mike McGee. Those choices became associated with No. 30 Rodney Monroe in 1991 and No. 42 Donnie Boyce in 1995. A Sacramento Kings official media guide independently confirms both the date and the two-pick price, and Atlanta's transaction register records the same agreement. McGee had been an NBA scorer for the Los Angeles Lakers earlier in his career, but was an expendable Hawks guard at this point. Sacramento hoped a veteran shooter could help a backcourt that needed more offense while the team adjusted to its early seasons in Northern California. Atlanta was willing to wait for two late future draft options rather than use another veteran immediately. The trade did not include cash or a first-round pick.

sections.heading: McGee Offered a Veteran Scoring Option, Not a New Kings Star
sections.body: McGee could provide points from outside and had experience playing on successful Lakers teams, but his Sacramento role did not match the peak seasons he enjoyed before leaving Los Angeles. The Kings were struggling to find a productive combination of guards and forwards around their younger players, so adding a known scorer was an understandable move. His playing time with the Kings was limited to a narrower late-career stretch, and he did not become a sustained starting offensive leader. The inherited Hawks Win verdict reflects that short-lived value relative to two actual future selections, rather than declaring McGee unable to play. His earlier Lakers title contributions should not be counted as Sacramento achievements, and the club's later rebuild involved many more moves than this single trade. The correct direct return is the scoring and rotation help he provided once he joined the Kings.

sections.heading: Atlanta Accumulated Two Separate Draft Opportunities
sections.body: The Hawks did not receive an existing NBA player on December 14. They received two future second-round choices, separated by four years and with different eventual draft outcomes. One selection was associated with Rodney Monroe and the later with Donnie Boyce. The rights themselves had trade or developmental value, even if the selected players did not become high-level Hawks stars. Atlanta could use the picks to seek inexpensive roster depth while its main contributors, including Dominique Wilkins, continued competing in the Eastern Conference. The Hawks Win inherited classification values that longer-horizon optionality over McGee's temporary Sacramento scoring. A second-round pick is not automatically a long NBA career for its original holder, however, so subsequent rights paths must be handled separately from the original trade value. The evaluation should not attribute all future games by Monroe or Boyce to Atlanta without verifying their actual teams.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win. Atlanta acquired 1991 and 1995 second-round picks later connected to Rodney Monroe and Donnie Boyce, while Sacramento received experienced scorer Mike McGee. The Kings obtained short-term backcourt shooting; the Hawks secured two real future draft opportunities with longer-horizon asset value.

sections.heading: Detroit Exchanged John Long for Two Seattle Second-Round Picks
sections.body: On September 30, 1986, Detroit sent veteran shooting guard John Long to the Seattle SuperSonics for a 1987 second-round choice and a 1991 second-round choice. The later selections were associated with No. 24 Fred Banks in 1987 and No. 40 Doug Overton in 1991. Detroit had relied on Long as a scoring guard earlier in the decade but was reshuffling its perimeter responsibilities around Isiah Thomas and Joe Dumars. Seattle wanted an established scorer for a team changing its guard rotation and was willing to part with two future draft opportunities. Both clubs' transaction histories verify the exact asset direction and September 30 date. The exchange did not involve a first-round pick or a new Detroit veteran arriving immediately. It was a deliberate switch from existing guard depth to later draft capital.

sections.heading: Seattle Quickly Traded John Long Again
sections.body: Long arrived in Seattle with NBA starting experience, but his time with the SuperSonics was exceptionally brief. On October 2, 1986, only two days after the Detroit transaction, Seattle sent Long and another future second-round pick to Indiana for Russ Schoene and Terence Stansbury. That follow-on agreement should be evaluated separately; it means the Sonics cannot be credited with a full year of Long playing time merely because they acquired his contract on September 30. The rights to a veteran scorer still had exchange value and were used to arrange a different roster construction. The inherited Slight Pistons Edge label becomes more understandable when comparing Detroit's two future choices with Seattle's brief possession of the guard. Long's eventual games with Indiana or other clubs do not become Seattle games, and the two moves should not be artificially merged into a single Detroit–Indiana multi-team trade.

sections.heading: Banks and Overton Were Real Draft Rights for Detroit
sections.body: The Pistons obtained two draft selections at relatively modest positions rather than a guaranteed first-round starter. Detroit held choices connected to Fred Banks in 1987 and Doug Overton in 1991. Their later professional careers and any draft-right transfers must be attributed to the correct teams, not simply added in full to the Pistons NBA totals. Still, two separate selections offered possibilities to develop younger guards or trade the picks again. Detroit's C+ inherited grade is higher than the Seattle franchise's C, matching the Slight Pistons Edge verdict. It was a small strategic gain rather than the central reason Detroit won championships years later, which came through other major roster and coaching decisions. The deal illustrates how quickly a veteran can become another team's trade instrument while his former club holds more durable rights to future draft prospects.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Pistons Edge. Detroit receives C+ for 1987 and 1991 second-round selections associated with Fred Banks and Doug Overton. Seattle gets C for acquiring John Long but moved him just two days later in a separate Indiana deal. The picks offered a more durable future asset than a two-day holding period for the veteran guard.

sections.heading: The Clippers Exchanged Cedric Maxwell for Two Draft Picks
sections.body: On January 16, 1987, the Los Angeles Clippers traded veteran forward Cedric Maxwell to Houston. The Rockets surrendered a 1987 first-round selection, later No. 13 Joe Wolf, and a 1989 future pick tied to No. 43 Chucky Brown. Contemporary Los Angeles Times reporting described that later pick as a third-round choice, while the historical transaction ledgers record it as a second-or-third-round obligation because the NBA subsequently discontinued the third round. This distinction should not be flattened into a modern guaranteed third-round selection. Maxwell had been a Finals Most Valuable Player earlier in his career with Boston, but was now an injury-affected veteran. Houston hoped another experienced forward could contribute alongside Hakeem Olajuwon and Ralph Sampson, while the Clippers preferred younger draft prospects during a rebuilding period. The deal involved picks, not incoming Houston players for Los Angeles.

sections.heading: Maxwell Gave Houston a Veteran Forward, Not His Boston Peak
sections.body: Maxwell brought professional experience and an ability to draw fouls and score in the paint. However, his years as a championship cornerstone had occurred in Boston before the Rockets acquired him. Houston's return was a limited late-career forward role rather than a full All-Star season or another Finals Most Valuable Player performance. The team had been a Western Conference finalist in 1986, and the front office was trying to maintain a competitive rotation around its big men. The veteran's experience had some value, but the price of a future first and an additional draft pick was substantial for a player whose best years were behind him. The inherited Clippers Win assessment reflects the different trajectories of an aging forward and two draft assets, not a claim that Maxwell never contributed after the trade. Houston's subsequent results involved many other roster and coaching changes.

sections.heading: Joe Wolf Was Drafted, and the Second Pick Moved Again
sections.body: Los Angeles used the 1987 No. 13 choice on North Carolina big man Joe Wolf, gaining an immediate first-round prospect. The 1989 future pick was later connected to No. 43 Chucky Brown but traveled through other teams, including Chicago and Cleveland, before its final use. It must not be treated as years of Brown's actual Clippers playing time. Even with that later asset movement, the original Clippers return was two opportunities to draft or trade young players, a valuable counter to Maxwell's short Houston stint. The inherited Clippers Win verdict is reinforced by the first-round selection's real value. The ambiguity in how the original 1989 pick was designated should be documented rather than hidden, because contemporary reports and later transaction lists describe the round differently. The final basketball accounting respects both the acquired pick rights and the veterans actual Houston minutes.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win. Los Angeles received the 1987 No. 13 pick used on Joe Wolf and a 1989 pick ultimately associated with No. 43 Chucky Brown; the future pick moved again before draft day. Houston acquired Cedric Maxwell for a short veteran-forward stint. Contemporary reports disagree on whether the later pick was called a third-rounder or a conditional second-or-third choice.

sections.heading: The Nuggets Chose Two Healthy Rotation Options for Injured Veterans
sections.body: Denver and San Antonio exchanged two players apiece on January 26, 1989. Denver received forward David Greenwood and guard Darwin Cook, while San Antonio obtained Calvin Natt and Jay Vincent. Contemporary UPI reporting records that Natt had missed all of 1986-87 with a ruptured heel tendon and had managed only 27 games the following year. His knee problems persisted, making a former Denver fan favorite difficult to use. The Nuggets wanted players who could supply functional minutes rather than keep waiting for a return to Natt’s earlier All-Star form. The Spurs wanted to test whether two experienced scorers could regain their usefulness on a rebuilding club. This was a straight four-player agreement without additional pick compensation.

sections.heading: Denver Received 59 Appearances From Greenwood and Cook
sections.body:
David Greenwood joined Denver on January 26, 1989 and played 29 regular-season games, making three starts. He averaged 5.9 points, 5.7 rebounds and 1.0 blocks in 16.9 minutes. Darwin Cook, who had averaged 9.6 points in 36 Spurs appearances before being traded, played another 30 games in a Nuggets uniform, starting four and scoring 161 total points (5.4 per game). Cook contributed guard depth rather than carrying the Denver offense. Both were practical reserve options for a team built around Alex English, Fat Lever and Michael Adams.

The two incoming players produced 59 Denver player-game appearances in the final months of the season, with 7 combined starts. Their contribution was real but limited. Denver finished 44-38 and reached the playoffs that spring, yet its larger established core rather than this deal explains most of the result. A literal A+ would overstate two brief veteran rentals and the front-office return. A B- better recognizes competent depth acquisition without calling it a transformational outcome.

sections.heading: San Antonio Obtained Brief Scoring From Injured Forwards
sections.body:
Calvin Natt had been an accomplished scorer in Denver before a ruptured heel tendon and later knee issues interrupted his later seasons. UPI reported that he missed all of 1986-87, played only 27 games in 1987-88 and was still recovering entering 1988-89. After moving to San Antonio, Natt appeared in ten games, averaging 8.5 points and 3.2 rebounds, and the Spurs waived him on February 20, 1989. Jay Vincent was dealing with his own health and contract concerns; he played 24 Spurs games, three starts and 9.0 points per game before his NBA tenure ended. Their 34 combined Spurs appearances were legitimate professional minutes but not a future rotation foundation.

Compare that with Greenwood and Cook producing 29 plus 30 games for Denver. The greater Nuggets availability favors Denver, but none of the four players turned the swap into a major new long-term asset. A Nuggets Win with Denver B- and Spurs C is narrower and better supported than either original A+ grade or the conflicting Spurs-source suggestion that Natt gave San Antonio an edge.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win — Denver B-, San Antonio C. On January 26, 1989 Denver exchanged the injury-limited Calvin Natt and Jay Vincent for David Greenwood and Darwin Cook. Greenwood played 29 Nuggets games and Cook 30; Natt played only 10 Spurs games and Vincent 24. Natt was waived in February. Denver got more usable roster depth, but only on a modest, short-term scale. Neither the inherited A+ Denver grade nor the Spurs-source claim of a San Antonio edge reflects the actual immediate production.

sections.heading: The Bucks Exchanged Their Drafted Forward for a Veteran Center
sections.body: Milwaukee traded the rights to No. 16 overall pick Terry Mills to Denver for veteran center Danny Schayes, announced August 1, 1990. The Bucks had drafted Mills out of Michigan but were focused on reinforcing a frontcourt headed by Jack Sikma. Contemporary Deseret News coverage quotes coach Del Harris identifying another center as the club’s most pressing roster need. Schayes had averaged 10.4 points and 6.5 rebounds for Denver during 1989-90, with extensive NBA experience. Denver wanted a younger power forward it could develop while rebuilding, making the former Michigan scorer appealing in place of a higher-salaried veteran. The agreement involved one player’s draft rights versus an established center, without an additional first-round selection or cash.

sections.heading: Schayes Started Thirty-Eight Games for Milwaukee Right Away
sections.body: Schayes appeared in all 82 Bucks regular-season games in 1990-91 and started 38. He averaged 8.6 points and 5.8 rebounds in 27.2 minutes, providing a full year of dependable frontcourt minutes. Milwaukee went 48-34 and qualified for the playoffs, giving the veteran an immediate role behind its established scorers. His contribution was not spectacular, but it solved the precise depth concern Harris had identified at the time of the exchange. Schayes returned for another season, although his playing time fell in 1991-92. The Bucks’ B+ inherited grade can be defended by a successful first-year rotation acquisition without suggesting the center was a twenty-point scorer or permanent replacement for Sikma. Unlike a speculative draft right, Schayes could contribute on the opening schedule.

sections.heading: Mills Signed in Greece Before Denver Could Use Him
sections.body: A separate UPI report dated August 20, 1990, described Mills signing with a Greek professional club rather than immediately joining Denver. General manager Bernie Bickerstaff acknowledged the risk but declined to match the overseas contract. That sharply complicated Denver’s original attempt to obtain a ready rookie forward. Mills later reached the NBA and played for other teams, but the important short-term point is that the Nuggets did not enjoy the same immediate 1990-91 rotation benefit Milwaukee got from Schayes. Denver’s B inherited grade reflects the value of holding a first-round prospect’s rights and the possibility of eventual development. The canonical Nuggets Win label nevertheless contrasts with Milwaukee’s numerically higher B+ grade and real Schayes minutes, warranting later review rather than silently adjusting the historical verdict.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win in the inherited label, but Denver grades B and Milwaukee B+, creating a grading contradiction. The Nuggets acquired Terry Mills’s rights, only for him to sign in Greece before the season. Milwaukee gained Danny Schayes, who played 82 games with 38 starts at 8.6 points and 5.8 rebounds. The immediate return favored the Bucks.

sections.heading: New Jersey Acquired Cadillac Anderson for Lester Conner
sections.body: On January 16, 1991, New Jersey traded veteran guard Lester Conner to Milwaukee for forward-center Greg “Cadillac” Anderson, also known as Wayne Anderson. The transaction listings for both franchises agree on the two-player exchange. New Jersey needed additional interior strength and rebounding while Milwaukee had other veteran centers available and could use experienced perimeter defense. Neither club attached a future draft selection to the agreement. Both incoming players were NBA veterans rather than prospects awaiting an overseas signing, making this a short-term roster adjustment with modest costs. Conner had a guard’s defensive reputation after previous stops, while Anderson could supply rebounding and post defense when given minutes. This first transaction must be separated from New Jersey’s later three-team agreement completed only one week afterward.

sections.heading: The Nets Quickly Reused Anderson in a Much Larger Deal
sections.body: On January 23, 1991, New Jersey sent Anderson out again in a three-team arrangement involving Portland and Denver. That complicated transaction helped the Nets acquire young guard Dražen Petrović and the rights to forward Terry Mills. This later use of Anderson gave the Nets a different kind of asset benefit from their original January 16 exchange: the acquired center was quickly convertible into a significant roster-building package. But Petrović was not received solely for Anderson, and his complete future statistics cannot be attributed to this single two-player transaction. The three-team deal included additional Nets and Nuggets assets, so a responsible assessment treats Anderson as one contributor among several later outgoing pieces. New Jersey’s C inherited grade recognizes that option value without pretending Anderson played a long Nets tenure.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Got an Available Defensive Guard
sections.body: Conner joined a Bucks club that would finish 48-34 and reach the 1991 playoffs. He brought veteran ball-handling and perimeter defense to a group featuring strong frontcourt options and several experienced guards. A narrow bench role is a more realistic evaluation than claiming he displaced Milwaukee’s most important starters. The Bucks’ C grade reflects useful insurance for the remainder of the season, though the initial trade did not deliver a first-round choice or a high-scoring young guard. New Jersey’s eventual pursuit of Petrović was its decisive longer-term storyline, but Milwaukee received a veteran it could actually use immediately. The inherited Bucks Win verdict gives a narrow preference to Conner’s immediate guard utility, although the C grades are equal; Anderson’s subsequent asset path offers a different hindsight view. The exact week between the two deals helps explain why a seemingly unimportant exchange had a later consequence.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win under the inherited label, with equal C grades. Milwaukee received Lester Conner for veteran guard depth. New Jersey acquired Cadillac/Wayne Anderson, then included him in a separate January 23 three-team arrangement involving Dražen Petrović and Terry Mills; the larger return cannot be credited to Anderson alone.

sections.heading: The Clippers Acquired a Champion but Faced a Contract Dispute
sections.body: On August 13, 1991, the Detroit Pistons traded veteran championship center James Edwards to the Los Angeles Clippers for guard Jeff Martin and a 1995 second-round selection. That pick ultimately became No. 30, used on Lou Roe. Edwards had helped Detroit win consecutive titles in 1989 and 1990, but the club was reworking its aging frontcourt. Los Angeles wanted a proven post scorer and interior veteran for a roster aiming to reach the playoffs. The transaction immediately became complicated when Edwards and his agent disputed the situation, with contemporary Los Angeles Times reporting that he had considered playing professionally in Italy. The agreement involved one NBA veteran and one future second, not two immediately usable Clippers starters for the Pistons.

sections.heading: Edwards Eventually Reported and Supplied Seventy-Two Games
sections.body: Edwards did not simply disappear overseas after the transaction. By October 8, he had reached a new arrangement with Los Angeles and ended a short training-camp holdout, as the Los Angeles Times confirmed. He played 72 regular-season Clippers games during 1991-92, started 11 and averaged 9.7 points in 20.0 minutes. The Clippers returned to the postseason that year, and he appeared in five playoff games, averaging 6.4 points. The team therefore acquired a useful veteran scoring center with significant availability, even though Edwards was not a long-term Clippers anchor. Los Angeles A is defensible as a practical grade for a playoff-year veteran, but the early contract dispute and short tenure temper a perfect hindsight evaluation. His Detroit title wins belong to his earlier franchise, not to the Clippers.

sections.heading: Detroit Held a Future Pick and a Smaller Immediate Return
sections.body: Martin was a guard acquired to cover reserve perimeter minutes and give Detroit another contract option. He did not arrive as a replacement for Edwards’s established interior scoring role. The future second-round selection was a real asset, but it did not become a draft choice until 1995, when it was associated with No. 30 Lou Roe. That delayed development value cannot be counted as four years of immediate Detroit starting-center production. The Pistons B- inherited grade reflects roster flexibility and a pick after moving an aging veteran. The canonical Pistons Win label conflicts with the Clippers receiving the higher A grade and 72 Edwards regular-season games; the disagreement warrants separate grade review rather than an unannounced verdict change. Each team obtained something, but Los Angeles gained the more visible on-court return in 1991-92.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win in the inherited label, although Detroit receives B- and the Clippers earn A. Los Angeles got James Edwards for 72 games and 9.7 points per contest during a 1992 playoff season. Detroit obtained Jeff Martin and a 1995 No. 30 second-rounder used on Lou Roe. The winner and grades are internally inconsistent.

sections.heading: Detroit Replaced Two Reserves with Glass and Randall
sections.body: On November 15, 1992, Detroit traded guards Lance Blanks and forward Brad Sellers to Minnesota along with a conditional 2000 second-round pick. The Timberwolves sent forward Gerald Glass and center-forward Mark Randall to Detroit. The league transaction ledger specifically records that the conditional future selection did not convey, so Minnesota never obtained a 2000 draftee from that part of the package. The Pistons were adjusting the last places of their rotation after their championship years, while Minnesota needed inexpensive veterans as it tried to build around a young roster. It was a four-player transaction with a conditional draft provision rather than a two-for-two exchange of established starters. The same date appears on both franchise histories.

sections.heading: Glass and Randall Supplied Limited Detroit Frontcourt Minutes
sections.body: Glass appeared in 56 Pistons games in 1992-93, started five and averaged 5.3 points with 2.5 rebounds in 13.9 minutes. Randall made 35 Detroit appearances without a start, averaging 2.8 points and 1.6 rebounds in 6.9 minutes. Those figures support a description of two limited but measurable bench pieces, not a transformed Pistons starting frontcourt. Glass took some small-forward minutes while Randall offered another reserve power forward. The Pistons finished below their earlier title-contender standard, so neither addition should be credited with a return to championship contention. Their inherited B grade is generous for supporting players, but the club did obtain more than a set of draft rights that never produced NBA games. Both incoming players were available during the same season.

sections.heading: Minnesota Received Two Veterans and No Conveyed Pick
sections.body: Blanks made 61 Timberwolves appearances that season, with two starts, while Sellers played 54 and started four. Both were depth contributors rather than prominent offensive leaders on a Minnesota club that finished 19-63. The conditional 2000 second-round compensation did not transfer, preventing the Timberwolves from claiming a future drafted player through this exact trade. Minnesota B is equal to Detroit’s B, even though the canonical Pistons Win label picks Detroit as the winner. The modest first-season roles on both sides make the outcome unusually close; the difference likely reflects how Detroit valued Glass and Randall as forward depth. It would be misleading to assign a future star to the nonconveyed second-round pick or pretend that any of these four players immediately displaced an All-Star. This was a practical bench exchange with limited team-wide impact.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pistons Win under the inherited winner, with B grades for both Detroit and Minnesota. Detroit received Gerald Glass, who played 56 games at 5.3 points, and Mark Randall, who played 35 games at 2.8. Minnesota acquired Lance Blanks for 61 games and Brad Sellers for 54, but the conditional 2000 second-rounder never conveyed.

sections.heading: Detroit Acquired Darrell Walker for Two Future Seconds
sections.body: The Detroit Pistons obtained veteran guard Darrell Walker from the Washington Bullets on September 6, 1991, for a 1993 second-round choice and another second in 1994 or 1995. The picks ultimately became No. 38 Conrad McRae in 1993 and No. 37 Frankie King in 1995. Walker had become a dependable Washington starter, averaging more than five assists in each of his last several seasons with the club and supplying physical perimeter defense. Detroit wanted guard experience while its championship-era roster aged. Washington was choosing two future draft opportunities instead of keeping a veteran who was no longer central to a long-term rebuild. There was no first-rounder or cash in the direct exchange, and the staggered timing of the picks is part of the price Detroit paid.

sections.heading: Walker Played Seventy-Four Detroit Games in His First Year
sections.body: Walker appeared in 74 Pistons games during 1991-92, started four and averaged 5.2 points, 3.2 rebounds and 2.8 assists in 20.8 minutes. Those are clear backup-guard contributions, though smaller than the 65 starts he had made for Washington the previous season. Detroit already had established backcourt scorers and used Walker as a reserve defender and ball mover. He remained in Detroit for nine games at the start of the following season before moving on. The Pistons C grade reflects one usable reserve year, but no sustained second career as their main point guard. His earlier Bullets seasons, including a 1990 campaign with 652 assists, cannot be imported into Detroit’s own trade return. The actual 74-game year is enough to show the acquisition was not merely unused roster paperwork.

sections.heading: Washington Acquired Two Chances to Draft and Develop
sections.body: The Bullets obtained two second-round assets on different timelines. No. 38 in 1993 became Conrad McRae, a Syracuse big man, while the other selection was associated with No. 37 Frankie King in 1995. The later NBA careers of drafted players should be attributed to the teams that actually rostered them, not automatically to the historical pick holder if rights were subsequently transferred. Still, Washington received two selections for a player who would appear for only about one more full NBA season with Detroit. Its inherited C+ grade gives those future possibilities more value than the short guard rental Detroit received, supporting the canonical Slight Wizards Edge. Unlike a conditional pick that never conveyed, both choices are identifiable. Neither pick can be described as a guaranteed first-round talent, so the edge is modest rather than dramatic.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Wizards Edge. Washington receives C+ after sending Darrell Walker to Detroit for second-round choices associated with 1993 No. 38 Conrad McRae and 1995 No. 37 Frankie King. The Pistons earn C for Walker’s 74 games at 5.2 points and 2.8 assists during 1991-92. The two picks gave Washington the longer-horizon return.
