sections.heading: Chicago Paid a Second-Round Choice for Elston Turner’s Free-Agent Rights
sections.body: On October 4, 1986, Chicago signed veteran guard Elston Turner after Denver agreed not to exercise a contractual right of first refusal. In compensation, the Bulls sent a 1988 second-round draft selection to the Nuggets. The pick eventually became No. 43, used on Todd Mitchell. Both Denver and Chicago transaction ledgers separately record the rights decision and its draft compensation, while the more detailed Pro Sports Transactions register identifies the date and conditions. Turner was not an established Bulls player whom Denver sold for a rookie; he was a free agent whose former team retained the ability to match an offer. Chicago gained permission to add defensive guard depth, while Denver received a future selection instead of keeping the veteran.

sections.heading: Turner Offered Chicago a Veteran Defensive Option
sections.body: Turner had developed a reputation as a physical perimeter defender during his years with Denver. The Bulls were building around Michael Jordan and needed supporting guards who could cover defensive possessions and share minutes with younger players. Turner could contribute within that structure without taking a large number of shots away from Jordan. His Chicago role was a complement to the team’s stars rather than a new first-option scorer, and the contract was reported as a three-year agreement with only one year guaranteed. The inherited Chicago D+ grade reflects the limited long-term role and the cost of a future draft choice. It should not imply that Turner’s earlier defensive years for Denver count as production after he joined the Bulls, nor that Chicago obtained a new starting All-Star.

sections.heading: Denver Held a Real Selection but Did Not Gain a Future Star
sections.body: The Nuggets received a 1988 second-rounder instead of another veteran player. The selection became No. 43 Todd Mitchell, a late-round prospect rather than a guaranteed NBA starter. Mitchell’s eventual selection must be distinguished from meaningful Denver regular-season production: acquiring a draft right was the immediate return, and any later player career would need to be attributed to the team that actually rostered him. Denver’s C- inherited grade narrowly exceeds Chicago’s D+, even though no major scorer arrived directly. The transaction is chiefly a story about the value of retaining free-agent compensation rights under the rules of the period. Both teams accepted relatively modest upside: the Bulls received a wing defender, and the Nuggets a later opportunity to draft or exchange talent.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Nuggets Edge. Denver receives C- after receiving the 1988 second-round pick used on Todd Mitchell at No. 43 in return for releasing its matching right on Elston Turner. Chicago earns D+ for adding the veteran defender. Neither side acquired a sustained new offensive star directly through this compensation agreement.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Secured World B. Free Through Rights Compensation
sections.body: The Cavaliers agreed not to exercise their right of first refusal on veteran guard World B. Free on December 30, 1986, allowing Philadelphia to sign him. The 76ers sent Cleveland a 1990 second-round draft choice in exchange. That pick ultimately became No. 52, used on Italian center Stefano Rusconi. Contemporary Washington Post reporting identifies the exchange directly, and the dated transaction registers of both teams confirm the same agreement. Free had previously spent several Cleveland seasons as a prolific scorer and was returning to an organization where he had played earlier in his career. Philadelphia was buying a short-term scoring option, while Cleveland chose to gain a draft opportunity rather than extend a veteran who no longer figured prominently into its young backcourt plans.

sections.heading: Free’s Return to the 76ers Was Brief
sections.body: Although Free had a long history of high-scoring NBA seasons, his Philadelphia return in 1986-87 did not last through the entire schedule. The team’s transaction ledger records that it waived him on March 4, 1987. That makes the signing a short veteran experiment rather than a multi-year Philadelphia scoring solution. His earlier points and awards should not be counted again merely because he changed teams. The inherited Philadelphia B+ grade appears generous relative to his tenure, but the franchise did obtain an available offensive guard and a chance to evaluate him during the season. The transaction involved no existing Cavaliers player other than the rights decision; a roster need and a veteran scoring reputation drove the agreement. Cleveland’s compensation depended on a distant draft rather than immediate court production.

sections.heading: The Cavaliers’ Pick Became a European Draft Right
sections.body: Cleveland kept the 1990 second-round selection and used No. 52 on Stefano Rusconi, an Italian big man. That was a real draft pick, but Rusconi did not become a long-term NBA contributor for Cleveland. His international professional achievements should not be confused with Cavaliers regular-season minutes. The Cavaliers’ inherited B- grade gives value to having converted rights to an aging player into a younger option, though the payoff was speculative. Philadelphia’s B+ compared with Cleveland B- supports the canonical 76ers Win outcome, despite the short time Free remained with the club. With the benefit of hindsight, the transaction is best understood as veteran scoring availability exchanged for a late draft right, with neither part producing a sustained new star for the receiving team.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win under the inherited B+ versus Cavaliers B- grades. Philadelphia signed World B. Free but waived him by March 4, 1987. Cleveland received the 1990 second-round pick used on No. 52 Stefano Rusconi. The deal yielded a brief veteran trial and an international draft prospect rather than a long-lasting NBA core player.

sections.heading: Washington Signed Tony Campbell but the Conditional Pick Never Conveyed
sections.body: In early October 1987, Tony Campbell signed with Washington after Detroit agreed not to exercise its right of first refusal on the veteran free agent. The original Detroit asset record lists a conditional 1989 second-round selection, contingent on Campbell making the Bullets roster. He did not, and the condition was not satisfied. Basketball Reference’s Detroit transaction ledger dates the signing October 8, 1987, while the historical source ledger preserves the same October date for the rights decision. Unlike a normal midseason player trade, the Pistons did not physically exchange a signed roster member for a new Washington player. They gave up the right to match an offer in exchange for a possibility of future draft compensation. The condition ultimately yielded no actual draft selection.

sections.heading: Campbell Had No Lasting Washington Playing Tenure
sections.body: Campbell had been part of Detroit’s reserve perimeter group, and Washington hoped to evaluate him as another scoring option. Because the relevant conditional clause depended on him making the Bullets roster, its failure means he was not the sustained Washington rotation contributor a modern reader might assume from the acquisition announcement. The Wizards franchise’s inherited C grade reflects the freedom to sign and evaluate a veteran without paying out a first-round choice, rather than a new full-season starter. Campbell later found larger NBA playing opportunities with other franchises, particularly Minnesota, but those seasons did not happen in Washington and should not be treated as a successful Bullets outcome. This narrow free-agency sequence must be separated from his later development elsewhere.

sections.heading: Detroit Received Rights That Expired Without a Player
sections.body: Detroit received a conditional second-round claim rather than a specific 1989 drafted prospect. Because Campbell did not make the agreed roster condition, no second-round selection conveyed to the Pistons through this deal. The inherited Detroit F grade is understandable as a retrospective description of the lost player right with no realized draft value, although the club could still have judged the outgoing veteran expendable at the time. The Washington C grade is also cautious: the team gained a chance to sign Campbell but did not establish a durable NBA player from it. That is why the canonical Wizards Win verdict need not imply that Campbell scored large numbers of points in a Washington uniform. Both return paths were limited, and the forfeited conditional pick is the defining factual feature.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wizards Win in the inherited evaluation, with Washington C and Detroit F. The Bullets obtained the opportunity to sign Tony Campbell in October 1987, while Detroit was promised a conditional 1989 second-round choice. Campbell failed the required roster condition, so the pick never conveyed and no drafted Pistons player resulted.

sections.heading: Charlotte Traded Dyron Nix’s Rights for Stuart Gray
sections.body: On June 27, 1989, the Charlotte Hornets exchanged the draft rights to Dyron Nix with the Indiana Pacers for center Stuart Gray. Charlotte had used No. 29 in the second round on Nix earlier that day, while Indiana was willing to give up a reserve center for another young forward prospect. The Indiana Pacers official media guide confirms the draft-night agreement and Charlotte’s own historical draft register identifies the Nix pick and immediate rights transfer. This was a rights-for-player trade rather than a deal involving a future protected pick or cash. The Hornets were still in their earliest seasons and needed inexpensive center depth, while Indiana could assess a drafted player after reshuffling its roster around other frontcourt veterans. The league’s expansion era created many such small positional opportunities.

sections.heading: Gray Offered a Brief but Real Charlotte Center Role
sections.body: Gray moved into Charlotte’s reserve center group and appeared in 39 Hornets games during the 1989-90 season before a separate February 22, 1990 trade sent him to New York for a future second-round pick. His tenure therefore produced actual NBA reserve appearances and a later tradeable asset, even without a major starting role. The Hornets’ inherited C grade reflects that smaller amount of frontcourt availability. The New York trade should be treated as a subsequent agreement and not as a drafted player directly delivered by the Pacers in 1989. Charlotte used the Nix rights to obtain a signed center and then continued adjusting its roster, a reasonable path for a team still building its rotation. Gray’s earlier Indiana statistics must not be counted twice for Charlotte.

sections.heading: Nix Was a Draft-Rights Bet for Indiana
sections.body: Nix was a 6-foot-7 forward out of Tennessee whose NBA opportunities were limited. Indiana gained the right to sign and develop him rather than an existing starting center, and the risk of a second-round prospect was substantial. His college scoring and rebounding credentials made the investment understandable, but his later professional career cannot be mechanically assigned as many Pacers NBA seasons. The inherited Pacers Win label is a small preference with C grades on both sides, not proof that either club acquired a dominant new player. Charlotte received identifiable Gray minutes and recovered a future draft asset in the later Knicks trade, while Indiana bought youth and potential on draft night. The story is about an expansion team choosing an established reserve over an unsigned prospect and how the asset moved again within eight months.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Pacers Edge is the inherited canonical verdict, with C grades for Charlotte and Indiana. The Pacers acquired Dyron Nix’s No. 29 draft rights; the Hornets received Stuart Gray, who played 39 games in 1989-90 before a separate February 1990 trade to the Knicks. The transaction offered different small-scale roster options.

sections.heading: The February 1988 Veteran-Guard Exchange
sections.body: On February 23, 1988, Boston acquired Jim Paxson from Portland for Jerry Sichting and future considerations. The Celtics' official historical media guide confirms the date, the two veterans and the additional consideration; the league transaction ledger independently records the same player exchange. The inherited trade file calls that consideration cash, but the official guide does not establish an amount or payment terms. That limits how confidently the extra asset can be evaluated. This was primarily a change in veteran backcourt personnel, not a draft-rights trade. Sichting had contributed to Boston's 1986 title team, while Paxson's scoring years in Portland preceded this deal and were not an asset the Celtics retroactively received.

sections.heading: Paxson Supplied Boston Three Seasons of Regular-Season Production
sections.body: Boston obtained the longer-lasting playing return. The club's official year-by-year history credits Paxson with 28 Celtics games and 244 points after the trade, then 57 games and 492 points in 1988-89 and 72 games and 460 points in 1989-90. That totals 157 regular-season Boston appearances, 1,196 points and 293 assists. Paxson averaged 8.7 points after arriving and 8.6 the following season before dipping to 6.4 in his final Celtics season. He also appeared in the 1988 and 1990 playoffs, though his postseason scoring was much lower. Boston did not gain a new franchise star, but it received reliable roster minutes for more than two years. Paxson's Celtics contract was not renewed in October 1990.

sections.heading: Sichting Gave Portland Actual Reserve Minutes
sections.body: Portland did receive an experienced guard, not an empty roster slot. Basketball-Reference credits Jerry Sichting with 28 regular-season Blazers games, 115 points and 33 assists after the trade in 1987-88, followed by 25 games, 102 points and 59 assists in 1988-89. Those 53 regular-season Portland appearances yielded 217 points and 92 assists. His five postseason appearances with the Blazers are separate from those regular-season figures. The return was modest but genuine: Sichting had already shown he could handle an NBA reserve role, and Portland used him in two separate seasons. His time with the Trail Blazers did not approach the court time or scoring Boston later received from Paxson. The unquantified future consideration remains an unresolved additional asset, not permission to invent a cash amount.

sections.heading: Why the Returns Justify a Small Boston Edge
sections.body: The teams had similar near-term motivations: exchange a veteran perimeter option for another who might fit better. The results diverged over the following seasons. Paxson appeared in 157 Boston regular-season games, almost three times Sichting's 53 with Portland, and he scored more than five times as many points for his receiving team. That is a substantive difference in direct franchise value, not a comparison of the players' entire careers. Portland still received a guard who played usable reserve minutes and joined five playoff games, making a harsh no-return grade inappropriate. Boston's advantage does not depend on Paxson's earlier Portland scoring years, and Portland cannot claim Sichting's 1986 Celtics championship as a new acquisition benefit. Future considerations remain unpriced absent stronger sourcing.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Celtics Edge, matching Boston's B- and Portland's C+ grades. Paxson supplied 157 Boston regular-season games, 1,196 points and 293 assists; Sichting supplied Portland 53 regular-season games, 217 points and 92 assists. Both teams gained usable veteran backcourt help, but Boston's return endured longer. The additional future consideration is acknowledged without claiming an unverified cash amount or imagined follow-on asset.

sections.heading: Chicago Bought Immediate Frontcourt Depth for a Future Second
sections.body: On February 15, 1987, Cleveland sent veteran big man Ben Poquette to Chicago for a 1989 second-round draft choice. It was a small present-for-future exchange: the Bulls had a player they could use that season, while the Cavaliers retained a draft opportunity two years away. The Cleveland transaction ledger confirms the return and identifies the choice that ultimately became Chucky Brown, the No. 43 pick in 1989. Neither team received cash or another player in the recorded deal.

sections.heading: Poquette Had a Brief Bulls Stint, Then Left the NBA
sections.body: Poquette appeared in 21 games for Chicago in 1986-87, starting once. His Bulls totals were 167 minutes, 51 points and 24 rebounds. Those were actual reserve minutes at a time when the Bulls needed bodies on the front line, but the arrangement was brief. He did not return for another NBA season with Chicago, instead playing abroad. His earlier seasons in Utah and Cleveland are not contributions acquired by the Bulls in this particular trade.

sections.heading: Cleveland Converted the Pick Into Chucky Brown
sections.body: The 1989 choice became No. 43 and Cleveland selected Chucky Brown. Unlike a pick that was traded again before the draft, this one converted into a player who actually suited up for the receiving franchise. Brown logged 75 Cavaliers games in 1989-90, 74 in 1990-91 and six more in 1991-92. That was 155 regular-season appearances, 86 starts, 2,874 minutes and 1,187 points for Cleveland. His first two seasons alone supplied much more playing value than Poquette delivered during his few months in Chicago.

sections.heading: Why the Results Favor Cleveland
sections.body: The draft wait could have ended with very little return, but Cleveland turned a second-rounder into a useful forward who started 86 games for the club. Chicago made a reasonable short-term depth purchase and did get 21 appearances from Poquette. Even so, the scale of what the teams received was far apart: Cleveland got more than seven times as many regular-season games and over seventeen times as many minutes. The historical Even Trade grade therefore does not fit the source-backed outcome, and the revised grades credit only each team’s actual return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win. Cleveland earns B+ for acquiring the 1989 No. 43 pick that became Chucky Brown, who played 155 games and started 86 for the Cavaliers. Chicago gets C for 21 games and 167 minutes from Ben Poquette. The trade produced a legitimate short-term reserve in Chicago, but Cleveland extracted markedly more franchise value from its future second-round selection.

sections.heading: Philadelphia and San Antonio Exchanged Backcourt Depth for a Wing
sections.body: The August 24, 1988 transaction sent Pete Myers from the Spurs to Philadelphia, with Albert King heading to San Antonio. Basketball-Reference records the same straight player exchange from each club’s perspective, and RealGM independently confirms the directions. There was no documented pick attached to this trade. The 76ers were testing an additional guard, while the Spurs were taking a wing with multiple NBA seasons behind him. Neither acquisition was a franchise-level investment, making what the players did for their new clubs the useful basis for comparison.

sections.heading: Myers Barely Entered Philadelphia’s Rotation
sections.body: The 76ers received just four regular-season appearances from Myers in 1988-89. His Philadelphia line was 40 minutes, 14 points, 10 rebounds and two assists with no starts. The transaction ledger also records that Philadelphia waived him on December 15, 1988. Myers then logged 29 games for the New York Knicks that season, but those appearances were not value Philadelphia received from the August exchange. His broader career would stretch well beyond 1988, yet later stops elsewhere cannot rescue a trade judged by his very short stint with the 76ers.

sections.heading: King Became a Usable San Antonio Reserve
sections.body: King appeared in 46 games for San Antonio in 1988-89 and started 11 of them. Across 791 minutes he supplied 327 points, 140 rebounds and 79 assists, averaging 7.1 points in 17.2 minutes a night. That was modest production, especially given the Spurs’ losing season, but it represented real wing rotation use across several months. King had been an 11.7-point scorer with Philadelphia in 1987-88; those earlier numbers were not acquired by San Antonio. Even by counting only his Spurs season, though, his return lasted far longer than Myers’s four-game Philadelphia stay.

sections.heading: The Team-Specific Return Explains the Revised Grades
sections.body: This exchange was not a blockbuster for either club. San Antonio did not gain a future cornerstone, and King’s 1988-89 stay was his only NBA season with the Spurs. Philadelphia did acquire a legitimate professional player, but it used him for just 40 minutes and then waived him before Christmas. On direct returns, San Antonio obtained 46 games against four, 791 minutes against 40 and 327 points against 14. The older Philadelphia-favored grade does not reflect that gap. The revised assessment gives San Antonio a small but decisive edge without giving either franchise credit for the players’ earlier careers or later unrelated teams.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Spurs Win. San Antonio earns B- because Albert King provided 46 games, 11 starts and 327 points during his one Spurs season. Philadelphia receives D+ for only four appearances and 40 minutes from Pete Myers before waiving him. It was a low-stakes veteran exchange, but the playing return strongly favored San Antonio.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Traded a Young Swingman for an Established Veteran
sections.body: The 76ers acquired Tom Chambers from Phoenix on November 21, 1997, sending Slovenian draft pick Marko Milič to the Suns. League and team transaction logs agree on the date, participants and direction of the exchange. Philadelphia was adding an experienced scorer under Larry Brown while Phoenix was taking a chance on a much younger wing with development upside. The transaction involved two named players and no documented draft choice or cash moving along with them. Chambers had enjoyed a long, productive career before the swap, but the 76ers were receiving the final chapter of that career, not his earlier All-Star production.

sections.heading: Chambers Played One Ten-Minute Game for the Sixers
sections.body: Chambers appeared in only one 1997-98 Philadelphia game, on November 26 against Cleveland. He scored six points on two field-goal attempts and two free throws in ten minutes, adding two rebounds and two steals. That was his entire regular-season return for the team. Philadelphia gained no sustained frontcourt rotation or postseason contribution from this acquisition. Chambers retired later in 1997, so his established reputation could not compensate for the short actual stint. Giving the 76ers a strong historical grade for trading away a young NBA player would confuse Chambers’s prior career with the performance Philadelphia actually received.

sections.heading: Milič Gave Phoenix Two Short Seasons of Reserve Minutes
sections.body: Phoenix obtained more playing value, though not a major contributor. Milič appeared in 33 Suns games during 1997-98, logging 163 minutes and 92 points, then returned for eleven games, 53 minutes and 16 points in 1998-99. His total for Phoenix was 44 regular-season appearances, 216 minutes, 108 points and 30 rebounds. He also appeared briefly in two 1998 playoff games, but the club never developed him into a regular rotation wing. His later international career is separate from what Phoenix obtained in the exchange. The Suns nevertheless received enough game appearances to outpace the one-game Philadelphia return.

sections.heading: Why the Suns Earn the Better Grade, With Limits
sections.body: This trade was minor in the larger histories of both franchises. The Suns received an athletic prospect who played only 4.9 minutes per game across his 44 NBA appearances, and the Sixers received a veteran who made one appearance. Neither deserves a high grade based on lasting on-court impact. But the comparison is not even: Phoenix received twenty-two times Philadelphia’s acquired minutes and a player who remained with the team into a second season. The assessment also does not award the Suns credit for the rest of Chambers’s illustrious career or grant the 76ers Milič’s later non-NBA accomplishments. The source-backed outcome favors Phoenix, with both grades kept modest.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Suns Win. Phoenix earns C+ for 44 regular-season games, 216 minutes and 108 points from Marko Milič. Philadelphia gets D+ because Tom Chambers played only one ten-minute game and scored six points after the November 1997 exchange. Both returns were small, but Phoenix extracted much more actual use from the asset it received.

sections.heading: A Newly Signed Forward Became Houston’s Future Trade Asset
sections.body: On October 5, 1992, Houston sent David Wood to San Antonio for a 1995 second-round selection. The Rockets had signed Wood only ten days earlier; the trade turned him into a future draft asset before he played a regular-season game for Houston. The pick ultimately became the No. 58 choice used on Don Reid, but Houston did not make that selection. Team transaction ledgers preserve the original Wood-for-pick exchange, and the later draft record identifies Detroit as the franchise that selected Reid. Confusing the eventual drafted player with a Houston acquisition obscures why this otherwise modest 1992 deal proved valuable.

sections.heading: The Second-Rounder Was Redeemed for Mario Elie in 1993
sections.body: The crucial next step came August 2, 1993. Houston sent Portland the very 1995 second-round pick it had acquired from San Antonio and received Mario Elie. The Blazers’ historical media guide independently confirms that Elie arrived from Portland for the second-round selection later traded to Detroit and used on Reid. This is a traceable downstream asset conversion, not hypothetical value assigned after the draft. Elie gave Houston a versatile wing who fit the championship roster’s defensive effort and perimeter needs. Instead of waiting until 1995 to draft someone, the Rockets converted a low-cost future choice into a veteran who could contribute immediately.

sections.heading: Elie Was Part of Both Rockets Championship Runs
sections.body: Elie appeared in 67 Houston regular-season games in 1993-94, averaging 9.3 points, and 81 more in 1994-95, averaging 8.8. He also played in all 23 of the Rockets’ 1994 playoff games and all 22 of their 1995 postseason games. Houston won the NBA title in each season. His famous decisive three-pointer against Phoenix in the 1995 Western Conference semifinals illustrates his real postseason role, but the trade is not credited with single-handedly creating the championships. The connection is narrower and documented: the second-round pick Houston received for Wood helped acquire a dependable contributor on two championship teams.

sections.heading: San Antonio Received Actual Depth, While the Pick Kept Moving
sections.body: San Antonio did not get an empty return. Wood played 64 games and 598 regular-season minutes for the Spurs in 1992-93, starting twice and providing reserve frontcourt depth. The scale of that return is small next to what Houston later acquired. Portland subsequently included the No. 58 selection in a 1995 draft-day package sent to Detroit, which eventually picked Don Reid. Reid played his NBA career with other teams; his 1995-onward production is not credited to Houston or San Antonio. Houston’s realized asset value is the acquisition and use of Elie, while San Antonio’s is Wood’s 64-game stint. Those are the actual branches the grades compare.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win. Houston earns A for converting the 1995 second-rounder received in the David Wood trade into Mario Elie, a contributor on its 1994 and 1995 championship teams. San Antonio receives C+ for 64 games of useful but limited reserve work from Wood. Detroit ultimately drafted Don Reid at No. 58; Houston receives no credit for Reid’s unrelated playing career.

sections.heading: A Straight Swap of Two Reserve Centers at the 1990 Deadline
sections.body: Golden State sent Uwe Blab to San Antonio for Chris Welp on February 22, 1990. The league trade-deadline archive and both clubs’ historical transaction lists agree on the timing and the two players. No draft choice or cash was included in the documented exchange. Each team was moving a little-used big man to try a different fit late in the season. Welp had appeared only sparingly for the Spurs, while Blab had logged much more court time for Golden State before the trade. Those earlier minutes, however, belonged to the team that traded him away and cannot be credited as San Antonio’s return.

sections.heading: Welp Played 14 Games for the Warriors
sections.body: Welp gave Golden State a measurable if limited boost across the last part of 1989-90. He appeared in 14 games with two starts, totaling 142 minutes, 50 points and 36 rebounds in a Warriors uniform. His 10.1 minutes per appearance represented a modest reserve role rather than a permanent frontcourt solution. Those numbers were better than the playing time he had accumulated with San Antonio, but that improvement does not turn Welp into a major historical acquisition. It simply gives the Warriors a concrete roster contribution to show for the exchange.

sections.heading: Blab’s San Antonio Return Was Seven Games
sections.body: Blab played seven games for the Spurs after the trade, with no starts. He totaled 50 regular-season minutes, 15 points and nine rebounds for San Antonio. The 40 games and 481 minutes he had logged for Golden State earlier in the 1989-90 season are real NBA production, but they are not production the Spurs obtained. San Antonio waived Blab before the following season, so the February transaction did not yield a continuing rotation piece. The incoming player did contribute in a small role, which prevents the return from being treated as absolutely nothing.

sections.heading: Why This Is a Small Warriors Edge
sections.body: Both clubs exchanged reserves, and neither acquired a starter who became important over multiple seasons. Golden State nevertheless got more from the player it received: twice the game appearances and nearly three times the minutes, with 50 points against San Antonio’s 15. Welp’s 36 Warriors rebounds also exceeded the nine Blab supplied for the Spurs. The historical source verdict had favored San Antonio despite the opposite pattern in the receiving-team splits. The revised judgment credits only the actual post-trade club totals, not full careers, earlier stops or hypothetical alternative roster roles.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Warriors Edge. Golden State receives C+ for 14 games, 142 minutes and 50 points from Chris Welp. San Antonio earns C for seven games, 50 minutes and 15 points from Uwe Blab. Neither player became a long-term fixture, but the Warriors got the stronger immediate reserve-center return.

sections.heading: Two Second-Round Picks Made This More Than a Center Dump
sections.body: On August 26, 2016, the Utah Jazz sent center Tibor Pleiss and two future second-round selections to Philadelphia for the rights to guard Kendall Marshall. Utah’s official announcement confirmed all four components, and each franchise’s transaction register records the same exchange. The second-rounders were determined by relative positions among multiple clubs’ picks in 2017, so Philadelphia did not simply receive two unnamed extras. They ultimately became selections No. 36, Jonah Bolden, and No. 60, Alpha Kaba. The Sixers took on a big man who had seen little NBA time, but the lasting upside rested in the two draft opportunities.

sections.heading: Pleiss and Marshall Never Played for Their New Teams
sections.body: Neither exchanged veteran supplied even one regular-season appearance for the receiving club. Philadelphia waived Pleiss on August 31, five days after the trade. He had previously played 12 NBA games for Utah in 2015-16, but those appearances belong to the Jazz before the transaction, not to the Sixers’ return. Utah waived Kendall Marshall on August 26, the same day it acquired his rights. Marshall’s 160 pre-trade NBA appearances likewise cannot become credit for Utah. The immediate basketball ledger was zero games on each side, leaving the draft picks as the critical elements for a long-term assessment.

sections.heading: Jonah Bolden Provided a Small but Real NBA Return
sections.body: Philadelphia selected Bolden at No. 36 in 2017 and left him overseas in his initial post-draft season. He joined the NBA club in 2018-19, playing 44 regular-season games with ten starts and 639 minutes. He added four more Philadelphia appearances in 2019-20 before moving on. That is 48 regular-season Sixers games, 653 minutes and 211 points attributable to the pick acquired from Utah. Bolden was never a foundational frontcourt piece, but he provided identifiable playing time that the Jazz did not obtain from Marshall. The pick that became Kaba at No. 60 never produced a regular-season NBA appearance for Philadelphia, so its realized on-court contribution is zero.

sections.heading: The Better Return Came From Philadelphia’s Draft Rights
sections.body: This exchange was mainly a chance for Philadelphia to take on Pleiss while receiving modest draft compensation, not a deal that changed the East. Utah moved a seldom-used center, but it surrendered two picks and then waived the player it received. Philadelphia also waived its acquired veteran, yet one of the second-round selections developed into an NBA reserve. Because Bolden actually played for the Sixers, his minutes can be credited directly to their return without speculating about alternative draft choices. Kaba’s unconverted rights are acknowledged without inventing production. The combination supports a measured Sixers advantage rather than a franchise-defining grade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win. Philadelphia earns B for taking Tibor Pleiss and the 2017 selections that became Jonah Bolden and Alpha Kaba; Bolden appeared in 48 regular-season Sixers games after the trade. Utah gets C: the Jazz disposed of Pleiss but waived Kendall Marshall without using him. The extra draft choices created the only identifiable on-court return after the exchange.

sections.heading: A Straight Guard Swap Recast Two Backcourts
sections.body: On October 4, 2005, Toronto exchanged Rafer Alston for Houston's Mike James. Both clubs recorded the deal as a direct player-for-player trade, with no draft selection or money attached to the transaction. Toronto wanted a different point-guard fit while Houston sought someone to handle substantial minutes next to Tracy McGrady and Yao Ming. James had already played for the Rockets during the preceding season after arriving from Milwaukee. Alston had spent 2004-05 as Toronto's main point guard. The unusual feature was not the package size, but how differently the two veterans' subsequent tenures would unfold.

sections.heading: James Had a Career Year for Toronto, but Only One
sections.body: James was an outstanding short-term acquisition. He started all 79 of his regular-season appearances with the 2005-06 Raptors, averaging 20.3 points and 5.8 assists. He shot 46.9 percent from the field and 44.2 percent from three-point distance, an exceptional scoring year for a guard acquired in a straightforward swap. Toronto nevertheless finished 27-55 and missed the playoffs. James departed for Minnesota as a free agent in 2006. His later years with other clubs cannot be counted toward Toronto's return, which was productive but lasted only that single season.

sections.heading: Alston Became Houston's Longer-Term Starting Point Guard
sections.body: Alston played 63 games for the Rockets in 2005-06 and started all 63. He then started all 82 games in 2006-07 and 74 more in 2007-08. Before Houston traded him to Orlando during 2008-09, he made another 48 starts. That totals 267 regular-season Houston appearances and 267 starts after the 2005 exchange, with more than three full seasons' worth of court time. His shooting was frequently inefficient, but he gave the Rockets a continuing ball handler while the roster revolved around McGrady and Yao. He also played in Houston's 2007 and 2008 postseason series, whereas James had no Toronto playoff appearances.

sections.heading: Peak Output Versus Longevity Makes the Verdict Close
sections.body: Toronto received the single best scoring season either new team got from this trade. James's 1,604 points in 2005-06 were an immediate offensive return, not an empty expiring contract. Houston instead acquired a long-serving starting point guard who contributed across multiple seasons and playoff appearances. Comparing only the first season makes the Raptors look stronger; comparing all games played for the receiving teams favors the Rockets' much longer return. The verdict gives Houston the modest edge without dismissing James's breakout year or assigning later Magic postseason production to the Rockets.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Rockets Edge. Houston earns B+ for 267 regular-season starts from Rafer Alston and multiple seasons of point-guard continuity. Toronto gets B for Mike James's 20.3-point season across 79 games, followed by his free-agent departure. The Raptors acquired the sharper single-season scorer; the Rockets acquired the longer-lived starter.

sections.heading: A Financial Reset for Golden State, a Veteran Starter for Utah
sections.body: Golden State traded Derek Fisher to Utah on July 12, 2006 for Devin Brown, Keith McLeod and Andre Owens. The Jazz were pairing a veteran with Deron Williams in a backcourt supporting Carlos Boozer and Mehmet Okur. Fisher had extensive playoff experience and could lead the second unit or play beside Williams. The Warriors wanted relief from Fisher's remaining contract and took back three guards as less expensive roster options. The four-player exchange therefore combined a meaningful basketball acquisition for Utah with a different type of value for Golden State, beyond a simple comparison of the numbers of players moved.

sections.heading: Fisher Played Every Game on a Western Conference Finals Team
sections.body: Fisher suited up for all 82 Utah regular-season games in 2006-07 and started 61, averaging 10.1 points and 3.3 assists in 27.9 minutes. He supplied reliable guard minutes in a 51-win season when Williams was establishing himself as the team's primary ball handler. Utah reached the Western Conference finals after beating Golden State in the second round, and Fisher appeared in 16 postseason games. His stay lasted only one season before a return to Los Angeles. Still, the Jazz received a documented season of starting-caliber play on a deep postseason run, not merely a veteran name on the roster.

sections.heading: McLeod Offered Minutes and Became Part of the Indiana Transaction
sections.body: Of the three acquired guards, Keith McLeod was the only one who played a Golden State regular-season game. He appeared in 26 games, logging 379 minutes with averages of 5.3 points and 1.7 assists. The Warriors waived Devin Brown on October 3 and Andre Owens on October 26 before either played for the team. McLeod later moved with Ike Diogu, Mike Dunleavy and Troy Murphy to Indiana in January 2007. Golden State obtained Al Harrington, Stephen Jackson, Sarunas Jasikevicius and Josh Powell in that separate four-for-four transaction. McLeod was one ingredient in that larger deal, rather than the source of all four returning players.

sections.heading: Utah's Direct Return Was Larger, Though Both Teams Gained
sections.body: A championship-tested guard who started 61 games and contributed in the postseason gave Utah the clearest on-court benefit. Golden State did not come away empty: it reduced a sizeable salary obligation, received reserve minutes from McLeod and later included him in the asset package that reshaped its playoff roster. Those advantages help explain the Warriors' favorable grade. But the other two guards never joined their regular-season rotation, and the subsequent Indiana trade also required three separate Warriors assets. Fisher's direct contribution to Utah remains more easily attributable to the July 2006 exchange, warranting a narrow rather than overwhelming Jazz advantage.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Jazz Edge. Utah earns A- for Fisher's 82 games, 61 starts and real 2007 conference-finals contribution. Golden State receives B+ for contractual flexibility, 26 McLeod appearances and his limited role in the separate Indiana transaction. Golden State cannot claim all of that later package as value from Fisher alone.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Paid Utah to Take Alan Henderson
sections.body: The February 22, 2007 deadline exchange was unusual because Philadelphia traded veteran forward Alan Henderson, cash and draft considerations to Utah and received the right to exchange 2007 second-round picks. The NBA's official historical deadline ledger lists the pieces in that direction. Utah's own media guide separately confirms that the Jazz received Henderson and cash from Philadelphia. The published cash amount is not specified, and the draft considerations should not be assumed to represent a confirmed high-value pick. Philadelphia wanted options for the 2007 draft and fewer commitments to a veteran who had little place in its young roster.

sections.heading: The Jazz Waived Henderson Eight Days Later
sections.body: Utah did not acquire useful frontcourt minutes from Henderson. The club requested waivers on March 2, eight days after the transaction, without him appearing in a regular-season Jazz game. Before being traded, Henderson had played 34 Philadelphia games in 2006-07, including five starts, with averages of 3.5 points and 3.1 rebounds. Those 34 games are not production Utah received. The incoming player's on-court contribution was therefore zero. Utah's tangible gain was financial: cash considerations supplied by Philadelphia, with the precise sum absent from the public official record.

sections.heading: Philadelphia's Pick-Swap Right Was Not Used
sections.body: The 76ers received a conditional option rather than an immediate draft selection or a player. The right to swap 2007 second-round picks was not exercised, so it did not produce a better draft position or drafted contributor from this February deal. The transaction nonetheless could provide Philadelphia with roster and draft flexibility by moving Henderson off its books. A separate June 2007 arrangement in which Philadelphia received Herbert Hill's draft rights and Utah received Kyrylo Fesenko should not automatically be assigned to the earlier swap. The different 2007 transactions need to be assessed independently unless their assets are explicitly linked.

sections.heading: The Small Advantage Is Administrative, Not On-Court
sections.body: No new NBA playing value came directly to either club from this particular exchange. Utah waived Henderson, and Philadelphia did not exercise its pick right. The 76ers can claim a modest benefit from shedding a veteran contract and retaining an optional route to a later draft decision; the Jazz can claim the cash it received, but its value cannot be quantified from the available documents. Neither outcome merits a top grade or a claim of major basketball improvement. The resulting assessment is intentionally narrow, and the stale partner aggregate is corrected to agree with the published team grades.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight 76ers Edge. Philadelphia gets C+ for moving Henderson and briefly holding a draft-swap option, even though it was unused. Utah earns C for receiving cash while waiving Henderson before he played. Neither side gained on-court production from this exchange. The undisclosed cash amount prevents a stronger comparative claim.

sections.heading: Dallas Moved Down Two First-Round Slots and Added Two Seconds
sections.body: On June 24, 2009, the Mavericks traded the No. 22 draft position to Portland, receiving No. 24, No. 56 and a future second-rounder. Portland used No. 22 on Spanish forward Victor Claver; Dallas initially took B.J. Mullens at No. 24 and Ahmad Nivins at No. 56. The additional 2010 second-round selection eventually landed at No. 51, where Magnum Rolle was selected after the choice moved again. This was not initially a straight Claver-for-Beaubois deal. The draft ledger shows a sequence of rights and picks that Dallas converted into other assets within the following day.

sections.heading: Dallas Quickly Turned the Mullens Pick Into Beaubois
sections.body: The day after the Portland swap, Dallas sent Mullens's draft rights to Oklahoma City in exchange for the rights to Rodrigue Beaubois at No. 25 and another future second-rounder. Beaubois ultimately played four NBA seasons for the Mavericks, totaling 182 regular-season appearances, 54 starts and 1,286 points. He wasn't a long-term franchise answer, but he was a genuine NBA contributor acquired through a traceable second transaction involving the pick Portland had sent Dallas. The distinction matters: Beaubois was not part of the original Portland package, but Dallas's ability to redeploy that package made him part of the downstream value.

sections.heading: The Other Selections Were Real Rights, Not Automatic Production
sections.body: Dallas also secured No. 56 in 2009, used on Ahmad Nivins, whose career did not produce a Mavericks regular-season appearance. The additional 2010 second was traded to Minnesota on June 25, 2009 for the draft rights to Nick Calathes. That later transfer means Dallas never used that specific second-rounder to select Magnum Rolle; it merely owned the pick for part of its chain. Beaubois provided the team's most tangible return from the sequence, while the Nivins and Calathes rights did not provide comparable on-court minutes for the Mavericks. Counting all the eventual draftees as Dallas players would overstate the transaction.

sections.heading: Claver Played in Portland, but Less Than Beaubois in Dallas
sections.body: Portland kept Claver's rights and brought him to the NBA for the 2012-13 season. Over three Trail Blazers seasons he played 80 regular-season games with 16 starts and scored 258 points. That was a legitimate reserve return from pick No. 22, although his North American role remained smaller than the team's draft investment might have suggested. Dallas had turned the downtrade into Beaubois's 182 games and additional developmental rights. It would be wrong to credit those 182 games solely to Portland because Oklahoma City was essential to the intermediate exchange. Still, tracing the pick's actual movement explains why the Mavericks' original downtrade created more realized on-court value than Portland's selection.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win. Dallas earns B because the Portland-supplied No. 24 pick helped obtain Rodrigue Beaubois, who played 182 Mavericks games, plus extra draft rights. Portland gets C+ for 80 games from Victor Claver. Dallas needed a separate Oklahoma City trade to reach Beaubois, so the verdict credits the asset chain rather than falsely listing him as a direct Portland acquisition.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Exchanged Its Longtime Guard for a Younger Starter
sections.body: The 76ers traded Maurice Cheeks, David Wingate and Christian Welp to San Antonio on August 28, 1989, receiving Johnny Dawkins and Jay Vincent. Cheeks had been a cornerstone of Philadelphia's 1983 championship team, but the Sixers were changing their backcourt around Charles Barkley. Dawkins had shown scoring and playmaking talent in San Antonio yet struggled with injuries, while Vincent supplied veteran forward depth. For the Spurs, Cheeks offered an established defensive point guard and Wingate an active reserve. All five players are documented in both teams' transaction logs, so there was no extra pick or cash to grade.

sections.heading: Dawkins Helped Philadelphia Immediately, but His Tenure Was Brief
sections.body: Dawkins started 81 regular-season games for Philadelphia in 1989-90, averaging 14.3 points and 7.4 assists. That gave the Sixers a credible starting guard during a 53-win season and a playoff run to the East semifinals. Jay Vincent, however, appeared in only 17 Philadelphia games and scored 124 points before moving on. Dawkins's contributions soon stopped as well: he managed just four appearances in 1990-91. The initial season was valuable enough to merit a respectable grade, but the new backcourt partnership did not provide several years of continuity. Neither player's production for previous teams belongs in Philadelphia's acquired return.

sections.heading: San Antonio Received Cheeks, Wingate and a Trade Route to Rod Strickland
sections.body: Cheeks played 50 Spurs regular-season games in 1989-90, starting 49, and averaged 11.1 points and 6.2 assists before San Antonio sent him to New York in February for Rod Strickland. That second transaction was an important consequence of the original trade: a veteran received from Philadelphia became the asset used to obtain another starting-caliber guard. Wingate independently played 78 Spurs games during 1989-90 and scored 527 points as a useful reserve, then returned for part of the next season. Welp provided a smaller return and was traded to Golden State in February 1990 for Uwe Blab. Those later deals must be tracked as separate moves rather than misdescribed as direct August arrivals.

sections.heading: The Downstream Point Guard Matters More Than the Initial Name Count
sections.body: Philadelphia got a strong first season from Dawkins and some Vincent depth. San Antonio got Cheeks's first-half starting minutes, Wingate's full-season reserve contribution and the option to convert Cheeks into Strickland in a separate February 1990 trade. The Strickland return did not happen automatically; it required New York's participation and should be treated as traceable downstream value, not as a player Philadelphia directly sent away. When the record is viewed in its real sequence, San Antonio came away with more than a short-term guard rental. That longer route gives the Spurs the advantage despite Dawkins's impressive debut season for the Sixers.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Spurs Win. San Antonio earns A for 50 Maurice Cheeks games, 78 David Wingate games in 1989-90 and Cheeks's subsequent conversion into Rod Strickland. Philadelphia gets B- for 81 starts from Johnny Dawkins and 17 Jay Vincent appearances, with Dawkins's later injury limiting the return. Strickland is a downstream acquisition, not a direct piece of this August deal.

sections.heading: Portland Bet on a Younger Guard While San Antonio Reunited with Kerr
sections.body: The August 2002 deal sent Antonio Daniels, Charles Smith and Amal McCaskill to Portland, with Steve Kerr, Erick Barkley and a future second-round pick moving to San Antonio. The source ledgers disagree on the exact day: RealGM and Pro Sports Transactions record August 2, whereas Basketball-Reference places it on August 5. Neither discrepancy changes the players and pick involved. Portland wanted a younger reserve guard to supplement its veteran backcourt, while San Antonio brought back a familiar shooter with championship experience. The Spurs had previously employed Kerr during their 1999 title season, making his return a deliberate roster choice rather than an anonymous salary exchange.

sections.heading: Kerr Contributed in the Season That Ended with a Championship
sections.body: Kerr played 75 regular-season games for San Antonio in 2002-03, averaging 4.0 points in 12.7 minutes. His greatest benefit arrived in a far more specific moment: Game 6 of the Western Conference finals against Dallas, when he hit four consecutive three-pointers in the second half and scored 12 points to help complete the series victory. The Spurs defeated New Jersey in six games in the NBA Finals. Kerr was not the driving force behind Tim Duncan's championship team, and a four-shot burst should not be treated as a season-long star turn. He nevertheless made a documented contribution to a title run.

sections.heading: Daniels Supplied Portland One Season of Backup-Guard Minutes
sections.body: Daniels appeared in 67 Portland regular-season games in 2002-03, starting twice and playing 872 minutes. He scored 251 points with 85 assists, then appeared in six playoff games during the Trail Blazers' first-round series against Dallas. That was a real return, but Portland's use of him remained limited to 13.0 minutes per game and the franchise exited in seven postseason games. He left for Seattle in 2003, so his later success with the SuperSonics and Washington does not add value to the Portland side. McCaskill was waived in October without becoming part of Portland's regular-season rotation.

sections.heading: The Second-Rounder Was an Asset, Not a Spurs Draft Success
sections.body: The 2003 second-round selection in San Antonio's return is often displayed with the eventual No. 58 pick and Andreas Glyniadakis's name. That should not be misread to mean the Spurs drafted and developed him. San Antonio sent the pick to Detroit in October 2002 for Mengke Bateer, transferring the draft value well before the following summer. Barkley likewise did not deliver meaningful long-term playing value for San Antonio. The decisive comparison is therefore Daniels's 67 Portland games versus Kerr's 75 San Antonio appearances and his memorable playoff shooting, with a separate low-value asset conversion on the Spurs side. The historical margin favors San Antonio without attributing Duncan's title to one trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Spurs Win. San Antonio earns B+ because Steve Kerr supplied 75 regular-season appearances and crucial shooting during its 2003 conference-finals victory; the second-round pick also retained limited trade utility. Portland receives C+ for Antonio Daniels's 67 games and 251 points in a single season. The downstream No. 58 selection does not count as a Spurs draft outcome.

sections.heading: A Free-Agent Rights Settlement, Not a Traditional Player Swap
sections.body: Atlanta and Utah settled Billy Paultz's free-agent move in the fall of 1984. The Hawks held a right of first refusal, while the Jazz signed the veteran center and sent a 1985 third-round selection to Atlanta as compensation. The NBA transaction record dates that signing and compensation to September 28, even though the imported Hawks source file uses October 1. The historical date requires separate reconciliation before anyone silently changes the canonical record. Neither club swapped two playing contracts in a normal trade; Utah received the freedom to sign Paultz, and Atlanta received a future draft choice instead of retaining its matching right.

sections.heading: Utah Received One Final Season of Frontcourt Depth
sections.body: Paultz arrived near the end of his long NBA and ABA career, so the Jazz were not buying the player who had once been a high-minute starter in San Antonio and Houston. In 1984-85 he appeared in 62 Utah regular-season games without starting, totaling 370 minutes, 82 points and 96 rebounds. Those numbers describe a limited backup center, rather than a difference-making scorer. Still, the Jazz received genuine playing availability from an identifiable veteran they could register for their roster. His earlier NBA and ABA accomplishments do not count as production acquired in this compensation agreement.

sections.heading: Atlanta Turned the Pick Into Sedric Toney
sections.body: The 1985 third-round compensation selection became No. 59 overall, used by the Hawks on point guard Sedric Toney from Dayton. Atlanta did retain the pick through draft night, but Toney played only three regular-season games for the franchise in 1985-86. In those appearances he logged 24 minutes and five points before his NBA career continued with other clubs. His full 112-game NBA career is not Atlanta's trade return. Nor should this pick be confused with the Jazz's separate Karl Malone first-round selection in 1985. The actual Atlanta result is three appearances from a third-rounder.

sections.heading: Realized Games Favor Utah, Despite Modest Stakes
sections.body: On receiving-club totals, Paultz supplied 62 games for Utah while the selected player provided three for Atlanta. The Jazz obtained a short-term reserve who could fill frontcourt minutes immediately, whereas the Hawks traded their option to retain a free agent for a draft chance that delivered little NBA playing time. The comparison is not a major win by modern blockbuster standards: Paultz was barely used and the Hawks' third-rounder was always a low-probability investment. But the documented return favors Utah without speculative value for the matching right, an invented contract amount or credit for either player's career outside the franchise.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Jazz Win. Utah retains B+ for obtaining Billy Paultz and 62 games of veteran frontcourt availability in 1984-85. Atlanta receives C+ for the No. 59 selection of Sedric Toney, who played three Hawks games. The grades are modest historical evaluations rather than star-level value, and the September 28 versus October 1 date discrepancy stays flagged.

sections.heading: The 76ers Purchased a Veteran Rebounder in September 1973
sections.body: Philadelphia acquired Toby Kimball from the Kansas City-Omaha Kings on September 28, 1973, sending cash instead of a roster player or draft selection. The transaction is documented in both clubs' 1973-74 registers. The franchise now called the Sacramento Kings was known as Kansas City-Omaha at the time, a distinction worth keeping in the historical explanation even though the site's canonical team identifier uses its modern successor. Kimball had already played in the NBA for several teams and could provide stability for a Sixers frontcourt rebuilding from an exceptionally poor prior season. The cash amount is not documented by the available ledgers.

sections.heading: Kimball Became a Regular in Philadelphia's Frontcourt
sections.body: Kimball provided much more than an end-of-bench appearance. During 1973-74 he played in 75 regular-season games for the 76ers, starting once and logging 1,592 minutes. His Philadelphia totals were 559 points and 552 rebounds, translating to 7.5 points and 7.4 rebounds per outing in 21.2 minutes. He did not become an elite scorer and he was not a first-choice starter, but he helped absorb a substantial share of the team's frontcourt possessions and rebounding work. Those figures are specifically from his Philadelphia stint rather than accomplishments with older franchises.

sections.heading: The Kings Took Money and Freed a Reserve Spot
sections.body: Kansas City-Omaha received cash in the 1973 exchange, not a player whose subsequent points or games can be credited to the franchise. Kimball had been a reserve for the Kings during 1972-73, appearing in 67 games with much lighter usage than he would see in Philadelphia. Trading him removed a veteran from their roster and returned money, but the reported records do not establish a dollar amount or a later downstream basketball asset purchased with the proceeds. The Kings therefore receive credit for the documented financial return, not an imaginary draft selection or another team's future production. The absence of a known cash valuation keeps the verdict cautious.

sections.heading: Useful Depth Was a Better Traceable Return Than Undisclosed Cash
sections.body: The Sixers finished 25-57 in 1973-74 and missed the playoffs, so Kimball did not transform Philadelphia's fortunes. His 75 games and 552 rebounds nonetheless represent measurable playing value from a cash acquisition, especially on a roster still trying to become competitive after its 9-73 season. Kansas City-Omaha may have welcomed the financial flexibility, but that benefit cannot be compared precisely with a season of reserve minutes when the payment is unavailable. Philadelphia's narrow edge rests on Kimball's actual acquired-team production. The assessment remains a modest one because neither club gained a long-term centerpiece.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight 76ers Edge. Philadelphia earns C+ for 75 games, 559 points and 552 rebounds from Toby Kimball after the September 1973 cash purchase. Kansas City-Omaha gets C for the undisclosed cash it received without a traceable basketball addition. Neither side obtained a foundational star, but the Sixers' one-year frontcourt value is verified.

sections.heading: An In-Season Exchange of Two Reserve Big Men
sections.body: Houston sent Otto Moore to the Kansas City-Omaha Kings on November 12, 1973 and received Ron Riley. Both receiving-team transaction ledgers and the league's season-wide record agree on the date and direct player-for-player structure. Kansas City-Omaha was the Kings franchise's geographic identity at the time, although the site's canonical slug uses the current Sacramento successor. The Rockets were testing an alternative frontcourt reserve after Moore's early-season appearances, while the Kings acquired a more experienced center. There is no documented draft pick, cash component or later compensating condition, so the grades turn on what each player actually provided to his acquiring team.

sections.heading: Riley Gave Houston a Short Run of Bench Minutes
sections.body: Riley appeared in 36 regular-season games for Houston in 1973-74, accumulating 421 minutes. He averaged 3.4 points and roughly 3.4 rebounds while playing about 11.7 minutes per game, a limited reserve role rather than dependable starter production. His 12 earlier Kansas City-Omaha games occurred before the November transaction and do not count toward the Rockets' gain. Houston finished below the playoff line, and Riley had no postseason run for the Rockets that could extend the result. The exchange was not a productive long-term solution to the franchise's center rotation, even if it supplied some immediate playing time.

sections.heading: Moore Appeared in 65 Kings Games
sections.body: Moore played 65 games for Kansas City-Omaha after moving from Houston, averaging 3.2 points and 3.1 rebounds in about ten minutes a night. The point average was only marginally lower than Riley's Rockets mark, yet Moore was active for nearly twice as many games. That additional availability gave the Kings a longer period of usable frontcourt cover across the season. Moore's earlier Houston seasons, including his much larger pretrade role, cannot be credited to the Kings. The useful historical return is his 65 actual appearances in their uniform, rather than the reputation or aggregate career statistics he carried into the deal.

sections.heading: Durability Is the Best Available Distinction
sections.body: This was a minor transaction at a time when both teams were revising their benches. Neither player became a central playoff performer for his new team, and neither provided top-tier scoring. Kansas City-Omaha nonetheless received more games of steady reserve availability, while Houston used Riley less frequently and for fewer total minutes. The difference supports a modest edge for the Kings, not a claim that the deal altered either franchise's trajectory. Treating each player's pretrade production as acquired value would distort the comparison. The two separate team-season splits are enough to explain why the teams' historical grades are not equal.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Win. Kansas City-Omaha earns C for 65 regular-season appearances from Otto Moore after the November 1973 exchange. Houston receives D- for Ron Riley's 36 games and 421 minutes. Neither was a major contributor, but the Kings obtained the more sustained frontcourt reserve return without surrendering a pick or cash.

sections.heading: Two Recently Drafted Players Swapped Roles
sections.body: On January 10, 1986, the Washington Bullets traded rookie forward Kenny Green to Philadelphia for second-year point guard Leon Wood. Contemporary reporting described the Bullets seeking depth and flexibility at guard, while the Sixers acquired a 6-foot-7 forward whose collegiate scoring reputation had not translated into regular NBA starts. Green had been Washington's No. 12 overall selection in 1985, and Wood had gone tenth overall to Philadelphia in 1984. This was a direct exchange of draft investments made only a year apart. The Bullets were the same franchise represented by the site's modern Washington Wizards identifier.

sections.heading: Wood Became a Real Rotation Contributor for Washington
sections.body: Wood appeared in 39 Washington regular-season games during the remainder of 1985-86, producing 378 points, 107 assists and 743 minutes. He did not start, but his 19.1 minutes a game gave the Bullets a genuine secondary playmaker with more scoring and passing responsibility than a token roster spot. Washington finished 39-43 and reached the postseason, losing to Philadelphia in the first round. The trade did not create a championship run, and Wood's much longer later stint with New Jersey was outside the club's return. The measurable benefit is a substantial fraction of the season with an NBA-capable reserve point guard.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Used Green Sparingly Across Two Seasons
sections.body: Green provided 21 regular-season appearances after joining Philadelphia in 1985-86, scoring 92 points across 232 minutes without a start. He remained for 1986-87 and appeared in 19 more games, again as a deep reserve, averaging about 3.4 points. That adds up to 40 appearances for the Sixers, but with much less playmaking volume and substantially fewer minutes per game than Wood supplied for Washington. Green's twenty earlier games in a Bullets uniform must not be treated as Philadelphia acquisition value. His situation illustrates how a lottery pick can retain upside on paper while producing only marginal reserve use for the acquiring team.

sections.heading: The Guards' Actual Usage Explains Washington's Advantage
sections.body: Washington received the player with the clearer immediate role: Wood distributed the ball and scored regularly during a playoff season. Philadelphia got a young forward who occupied a smaller spot in the rotation for portions of two seasons. The raw game count is close only because Green stayed into 1986-87, and it does not reflect his limited minutes or Wood's larger assist contribution. Neither player became a lasting star for the receiving club, so a sweeping franchise verdict would oversell the exchange. The graded advantage instead follows the distinct amounts of usable basketball production that Washington and Philadelphia obtained.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wizards Win. Washington earns B for Leon Wood's 39 Bullets games, 743 minutes, 378 points and 107 assists following the January 1986 deal. Philadelphia receives C+ for Kenny Green's 40 games across two seasons in a smaller role. The teams exchanged former lottery picks, but Washington extracted the more useful immediate contribution.

sections.heading: Utah Sold Poquette's Rights After His Long Jazz Tenure
sections.body: On October 14, 1983, the Utah Jazz transferred forward-center Ben Poquette to the Cleveland Cavaliers for cash. Utah's official historical media guide describes the compensation directly, resolving a placeholder in some later Cleveland transaction registers. Poquette had been an important Jazz starter in previous seasons, including a 1982-83 campaign of 75 appearances and 50 starts. Those older games belong to Utah before the sale and cannot become Cleveland's acquired-team return. The Cavaliers instead paid for the right to add a veteran reserve who still had several NBA seasons of useful frontcourt minutes ahead.

sections.heading: Poquette Became a Regular Cleveland Reserve for Four Seasons
sections.body: Poquette played 51 regular-season games for Cleveland in 1983-84, logging 858 minutes and 185 points. The following year he appeared in 79 games, totaling 1,656 minutes and 532 points, and in 1985-86 he added 81 appearances. He remained with Cleveland for 37 games of 1986-87 before being moved to Chicago. Across those four Cleveland seasons he totaled 248 regular-season games, a much larger basketball return than a short rental. Although he was mostly a reserve, his recurring use gave the Cavaliers frontcourt continuity while the organization was rebuilding its playing rotation.

sections.heading: Utah Received Money Rather Than a Replacement Player
sections.body: The Jazz received cash in return for Poquette, not a named player or draft selection. Neither the NBA ledger nor the franchise media guide establishes an amount for the payment, so the financial value cannot be assigned a precise present-day equivalent. Utah may have had reasonable roster or salary motives after years of using Poquette, but those motives are separate from documented post-transaction production. Because the trade did not bring a new player to Utah, it produced no identifiable Jazz on-court return to compare against Cleveland's 248 Poquette appearances. Assigning Utah a high basketball grade in this particular deal would therefore ignore the uneven recorded outcomes.

sections.heading: Cleveland Got More Value Than the Inherited Grades Suggested
sections.body: Cleveland's return was not a championship centerpiece, but hundreds of appearances from a veteran acquired for undisclosed cash constitute an economical basketball asset. In 1987 the Cavaliers later traded Poquette to Chicago for a future second-round selection, which created a separate downstream asset branch; the original 1983 cash sale should not be mistaken for that later transaction. The source-backed score therefore favors Cleveland directly even without adding speculative value from the later pick. Utah received a documented cash payment that may have been helpful financially, but the archived Jazz-win verdict gave it more credit than the available history supports.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win. Cleveland earns A- for obtaining Ben Poquette for cash and using him in 248 regular-season games across four seasons. Utah receives C for monetizing the veteran's rights at an undisclosed amount. The old Jazz-favored grade conflicted with the receiving-club totals; this revision credits Cleveland's documented bench production without inventing cash value.

sections.heading: The Lakers Replaced Michael Cooper's Bench Scoring with Teagle
sections.body: On September 25, 1990, Los Angeles acquired veteran swingman Terry Teagle from Golden State and surrendered its 1991 first-round draft selection. Contemporary Los Angeles reporting described Jerry West's search for a reserve scorer after Michael Cooper left for professional basketball in Italy. Teagle had been a productive Warriors wing in previous seasons, averaging 16.1 points in 1989-90, but those earlier points belonged to Golden State rather than the Lakers' acquired return. Los Angeles chose a proven immediate contributor over retaining a late first-round draft opportunity, while the Warriors gained a chance to add a younger player to a roster under reconstruction.

sections.heading: Teagle Played All 164 Lakers Regular-Season Games in Two Years
sections.body: Teagle appeared in every Lakers regular-season contest in both 1990-91 and 1991-92. He scored 815 points in the first season and 880 in the second, combining for 1,695 points across 164 appearances without a regular-season start. His bench scoring supported a team that reached the 1991 NBA Finals before losing to Chicago. He also contributed in postseason games, although he was a reserve rather than the team's principal offensive option. His consistency in availability mattered more than his reputation as a former Golden State scorer. The Lakers used the exact type of player they had hoped to acquire.

sections.heading: Golden State's Pick Became Shaun Vandiver, Who Never Played NBA
sections.body: The first-rounder from Los Angeles became the No. 25 overall choice in the 1991 draft. Golden State used it on Shaun Vandiver from Colorado. Vandiver pursued professional basketball outside the NBA and never appeared in a regular-season NBA game for the Warriors. The selection therefore produced no traceable on-court contribution for Golden State even though a first-round pick was initially an attractive asset. The Warriors had several selections in that draft, including Chris Gatling and Victor Alexander, but neither of those players came from the Lakers' specific No. 25 pick. Their subsequent NBA production cannot rescue this particular asset exchange.

sections.heading: The Results Favor the Lakers Beyond the Draft's Name Value
sections.body: A future first-round pick can be a legitimate purchase price for an established reserve when it might become a rotation player of its own. In this case, however, the actual comparison was stark: Teagle became a two-year regular in Los Angeles, and Vandiver did not produce an NBA game for Golden State. That makes the result stronger for the Lakers than it looked from counting draft assets at the time of the trade. Neither team acquired an All-Star centerpiece, and Teagle should not be credited with the Lakers' entire Finals achievement, but his availability and scoring were meaningful direct returns from the September 1990 deal.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win. Los Angeles earns B+ because Terry Teagle played 164 regular-season games and scored 1,695 points across two seasons, including its 1991 Finals campaign. Golden State gets D after using the acquired No. 25 pick on Shaun Vandiver, who never appeared in the NBA. The Lakers received substantial reserve production while the draft asset produced no league minutes.

sections.heading: The Jones Signing Required a Draft-Pick Compensation Settlement
sections.body: Portland signed veteran big man Caldwell Jones as a free agent in October 1985 after his spell with Chicago, sending the Bulls a 1987 second-round selection as compensation for relinquishing their matching rights. Historical ledgers disagree on the effective day: the Basketball-Reference team registers show October 1, while the detailed pick transaction chain uses October 9. That provenance difference is flagged for reconciliation without altering the archived date during an editorial-only repair. It was not an ordinary player-for-player swap. Portland obtained Jones's services directly, whereas Chicago received a future asset it could keep or trade before the 1987 draft.

sections.heading: Jones Played Four Useful Seasons for Portland
sections.body: Jones gave the Trail Blazers a long run of frontcourt work after his signing. He appeared in 80 regular-season games in 1985-86, then 78 in 1986-87, 79 in 1987-88 and 72 in 1988-89, totaling 309 Portland games. The 1985-86 season included 19 starts and 355 rebounds, while 1987-88 brought 77 starts and 408 rebounds. By then Jones was a veteran role player rather than an offensive star, but Portland used him extensively enough for the signing to create real roster continuity. His previous Philadelphia and Chicago production is excluded from the Trail Blazers' acquired return.

sections.heading: Chicago Traded the Pick Back Before Milwaukee Selected Garland
sections.body: The future second-rounder eventually became the No. 40 pick in 1987, but Chicago never drafted Winston Garland with it. On June 17, 1986, the Bulls returned that selection to Portland alongside the rights to Larry Krystkowiak and an additional 1992 second-round pick for Steve Colter. Colter appeared in 27 Bulls regular-season games in 1986-87 before leaving the club. Portland then moved the No. 40 selection to Milwaukee on November 11, 1986 for Chris Engler. The Bucks drafted Garland the following summer. His eventual 511-game NBA career does not belong to either original club's realized playing return from this compensation deal.

sections.heading: Portland Received the Stronger Direct Basketball Return
sections.body: Portland paid a second-round selection and received 309 games from Jones. Chicago obtained a movable pick and used it as only one part of a larger three-asset transaction that brought Colter, so the Bulls have some traceable but limited downstream roster value. Crediting the entire Colter acquisition to this single selection would overlook the other assets Chicago surrendered. The source-supported outcome is more favorable to Portland than the inherited Even Trade verdict suggested, though Chicago did get real flexibility from the compensation. The mismatch between the original teams' draft rights and the eventual Bucks selection also makes it important not to invent Chicago minutes for Garland.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Blazers Win. Portland earns A- for 309 games of Caldwell Jones frontcourt depth over four seasons. Chicago retains C+ for securing a second-round pick that helped form a larger package for Steve Colter, who played 27 Bulls games. Milwaukee eventually drafted Winston Garland, so his later NBA production is not credited to either original club.
