sections.heading: Cleveland Traded a Distant Second for a Portland Reserve
sections.body: Cleveland acquired young wing Linton Townes from Portland on September 6, 1983, surrendering its 1987 second-round selection. The league's 1983-84 transaction register and the historical ledgers for both teams identify the same direct player-for-pick exchange. Townes had appeared in 55 games for the Trail Blazers the previous season, so there was a modest reason for the Cavaliers to consider him an inexpensive developmental option. The compensation was a future choice four drafts away, meaning Portland was accepting deferred value rather than an immediately usable roster replacement. There was no reported cash or additional player in this transaction.

sections.heading: Townes Did Not Play a Regular-Season Game for Cleveland
sections.body: The acquired wing never produced a regular-season NBA appearance for the Cavaliers. His 1983-84 NBA record consists of two games with Milwaukee and two with the San Diego Clippers, not Cleveland. Those four appearances together generated eight points over 19 minutes, but all occurred with other employers. His 55 earlier games in Portland also belong to the team trading him away and cannot be retroactively added to Cleveland's received value. The distinction changes the historical assessment: the Cavaliers acquired Townes's rights and an opportunity to evaluate a young player, yet that opportunity did not convert into NBA minutes for their own team.

sections.heading: Portland Used the Pick on Lester Fonville in 1987
sections.body: The second-rounder became the No. 29 overall selection in the 1987 NBA draft. Both the league's official draft-history database and Portland's historical draft record show the Trail Blazers selected center Lester Fonville from Jackson State at that position. Pro Sports Transactions independently traces the pick to Cleveland's September 1983 transfer. Fonville never appeared in an NBA regular-season game, so the pick's documented draft conversion produced no direct playing return for Portland. The choice was still a genuine asset available to Portland on draft night, but it cannot be assigned points, rebounds or seasons of NBA roster use that Fonville did not supply.

sections.heading: Two Real Assets, but Neither Became an NBA Contributor
sections.body: Portland received a deferred draft opportunity and Cleveland received a young player who had previously reached the league. In retrospect, neither club obtained a contributing NBA player from the exchange. The Cavaliers got no Townes appearances; the Trail Blazers got a draft selection that produced no NBA games from Fonville. An inherited Cavaliers-win grade was therefore difficult to justify using actual receiving-team outcomes. The results are much closer to a low-value draw, though the chronology of the pick still deserves preservation as a genuine transaction rather than an empty record. Modest matching grades recognize the limited returns without inventing a hidden cash figure or a hypothetical alternative draft choice.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Cleveland earns C- because Linton Townes never played an NBA regular-season game for the Cavaliers. Portland also receives C- because its 1987 No. 29 selection, Lester Fonville, never played in the NBA. Both franchises acquired legitimate assets but neither converted the specific return into recorded NBA playing time.

sections.heading: New Jersey Paid a Future Third for an Experienced Forward
sections.body: The New Jersey Nets acquired veteran forward Mickey Johnson from Golden State on August 21, 1985, sending a 1986 third-round selection to the Warriors. The Nets transaction ledger independently confirms the same date, asset directions and player's name. The relevant choice eventually became No. 59 and was used on Wendell Alexis. Johnson had previously played substantial minutes for Golden State, but those 1982-85 Warriors contributions must be excluded from New Jersey's acquisition value. The Nets were paying a low draft price for a recognizable forward who could immediately join the rotation, rather than buying a long-term star or attaching future cash considerations.

sections.heading: Johnson Played 79 Games for a Playoff Team
sections.body: Johnson appeared in 79 regular-season New Jersey games in 1985-86 and started four. He totaled 1,574 minutes, 616 points, 332 rebounds and 217 assists, averages of 7.8 points, 4.2 rebounds and 2.7 assists in 19.9 minutes a game. That is meaningful second-unit production for a third-round draft investment. New Jersey finished 39-43 and qualified for the Eastern Conference playoffs, where Johnson appeared in all three games of its first-round series against Milwaukee. His Nets tenure ended after that season, so the direct return is a useful one-year reserve role rather than a multi-season commitment.

sections.heading: Golden State's Pick Became Wendell Alexis at No. 59
sections.body: Golden State retained the incoming 1986 third-round selection and chose Syracuse forward Wendell Alexis at No. 59 overall. Alexis never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. He subsequently built a distinguished professional career overseas, but his international production was not on-court contribution to the Warriors from the August trade. The pick was a legitimate scouting opportunity, and its eventual outcome should be described accurately, not as a nonexistent Warriors reserve stint. The number also cannot be awarded twice: a separate imported archive entry repeats the same choice while calling the outgoing Nets player Wallace Johnson, a conflicting historical identity that needs its own source-led reconciliation.

sections.heading: One Real NBA Season Beat an Unconverted Draft Pick
sections.body: New Jersey obtained 79 appearances from the forward it acquired, with useful scoring, rebounding and passing for a playoff roster. Golden State took a future draft chance and selected a player who never suited up in the NBA. The contrast is not subtle when judged by realized team contributions, making the previously inherited Even Trade label difficult to support. The Nets' modest one-year benefit should not be graded like an All-Star acquisition, but it was demonstrably more than the Warriors received on the court. Tracking the name Mickey Johnson also protects the archive from presenting the same No. 59 draft choice as if it were received in two distinct transactions.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win. New Jersey earns B for 79 Mickey Johnson games, 616 points, 332 rebounds and 217 assists during the 1985-86 season. Golden State gets D+ because its 1986 No. 59 selection, Wendell Alexis, produced no NBA appearances. A conflicting imported Wallace Johnson entry is flagged separately and is not treated as another genuine pick acquisition.

sections.heading: Dallas Traded Teachey's Rights for a Contingent Future Choice
sections.body: Dallas transferred Anthony Teachey to Seattle on September 27, 1985, receiving only a conditional second-round draft selection in 1989. The condition depended on Teachey earning an extended place on the SuperSonics roster. The Mavericks had picked the Wake Forest forward in the second round of the 1984 draft and signed him to an NBA contract a day before the exchange. Seattle could evaluate a former college prospect without immediately surrendering a guaranteed pick. Unlike a regular player-for-draft-pick deal, the future compensation was not certain to convey, so it should not be described as a selection that Dallas actually made in 1989.

sections.heading: Seattle Released Teachey Before the Season Started
sections.body: The surviving NBA transaction chronology shows Seattle acquired Teachey on September 27 but placed his contract on waivers on October 11. He became a free agent four days later. The SuperSonics therefore did not receive a regular-season game, start, rebound or point from this acquisition. Their 1985-86 roster includes productive players elsewhere in the frontcourt, but Teachey was not among those who appeared in games. Counting his collegiate work or Dallas's prior draft investment as Seattle's return would overstate the deal. It was effectively a training-camp evaluation that ended before the regular schedule began.

sections.heading: Dallas's Conditional Second Never Became a Documented Pick
sections.body: Dallas was promised a second-round draft choice in 1989 only if the agreement's roster condition was met. The imported trade record describes that option as not exercised. That fits the brief Seattle tenure, although the exact contractual definition and a corresponding 1989 pick number are not independently established in the available ledgers. Without evidence that the second actually conveyed, the Mavericks cannot be assigned the later NBA career of a hypothetical draft selection. Their actual documented asset was a contingent right with no identifiable draft conversion. It was a reasonable way to recoup some potential value from an unsigned prospect, but the result was limited.

sections.heading: Neither Side Obtained Sustained Basketball Value
sections.body: The original archived Seattle-win grade implied a substantial receiving-team advantage, despite Seattle waiving the acquired player before opening night. Dallas's conditional pick likewise has no verified on-court outcome and should not receive a favorable grade merely for appearing in the transaction description. Each club effectively tested a low-cost possibility: Seattle with a young forward, Dallas with a contingent draft asset. Both possibilities failed to yield measurable NBA play for the acquiring teams. An even, low-grade assessment is more faithful to the historical outcome while leaving the exact unexercised-condition wording open to further source verification if the original agreement resurfaces.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Dallas gets C- because its conditional 1989 second-round compensation produced no verified draft selection or NBA playing return. Seattle also earns C- because Anthony Teachey was waived before the 1985-86 regular season and never played an NBA game for the SuperSonics. Neither club obtained meaningful realized basketball value, contradicting the earlier Seattle-win grade.

sections.heading: Chicago Adds a Veteran Just Ahead of the Deadline
sections.body: The Bulls acquired Ed Nealy from Golden State on February 25, 1993, offering a conditional second-round selection in the distant 2001 draft. Both clubs' transaction ledgers record the same agreement and note that its condition was never exercised. Nealy had played 30 games for the Warriors earlier that season after joining as a free agent. Chicago already had the core of a championship contender; this was an effort to acquire experienced frontcourt insurance. The future pick was theoretical compensation, not an unconditional selection that Golden State could immediately plan to use.

sections.heading: Eleven Games of Limited but Measurable Bench Production
sections.body: Nealy appeared in 11 regular-season games for Chicago following the deal. His return amounted to 23 points and 16 rebounds across 79 minutes, without a start. That is not the performance of a decisive postseason addition, even though the Bulls went on to win the championship. His previous 30 Warriors appearances were Golden State production and cannot be counted twice as Chicago's new value. What the Bulls received was short-term roster availability from a veteran who was willing to fill a small role, without parting with a draft choice that later became a real player.

sections.heading: Golden State Never Collected the Promised 2001 Pick
sections.body: The Warriors accepted a conditional second-round draft choice rather than a player coming back to their roster. Historical Bulls and Warriors transaction records explicitly report that the 2001 condition did not trigger and the pick never conveyed. There is therefore no Warriors draftee, future asset exchange or NBA season to credit from this agreement. Moving Nealy could free a roster position for other players, but the surviving exchange offers no separate incoming cash or player. In a retrospective analysis, an unexercised condition cannot be treated like a completed draft transaction.

sections.heading: A Narrow Chicago Edge Is the Most Defensible Result
sections.body: Chicago got eleven reserve appearances, whereas Golden State ultimately obtained no draft asset at all. Even with the Bulls' small numerical advantage, the history does not justify a triumphant grade: Nealy scarcely played and made no case as a core member of the three-peat team. The grade instead distinguishes a limited real player contribution from a deferred promise that yielded nothing. It also preserves the important difference between the value of a hypothetical draft pick at the time of negotiation and the actual outcome of that conditional asset eight years later.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Bulls Edge. Chicago receives C- for eleven games, 79 minutes and 23 points from Ed Nealy in spring 1993. Golden State receives D- because the conditional 2001 second-round pick never conveyed. Neither club gained a long-term cornerstone, but Chicago has the only verified acquired-team playing contribution and a narrow advantage.

sections.heading: An October Exchange of Backcourt Help for Forward Depth
sections.body: New Jersey traded Mike O'Koren to Washington for Leon Wood on October 30, 1986. The transaction registers for both organizations identify the same pair of players and no accompanying draft choice. The Nets had watched their offense struggle with ballhandling options and sought a young guard who could manage extended minutes. Washington, still known as the Bullets at the time, received an established forward with several seasons of experience in New Jersey. Wood had been with the Bullets the previous season, but his earlier Washington production wasn't the return New Jersey received. This deal should be assessed using the contributions after the players switched uniforms.

sections.heading: Wood Became a Regular Nets Rotation Guard
sections.body: Wood appeared in 76 games for New Jersey in 1986-87, including seven starts. He averaged 22.8 minutes, 7.3 points and 4.9 assists, reflecting real responsibility for creating shots and moving the ball. Those aren't All-Star numbers, and the Nets endured a losing season, but a guard who played nearly every night was a useful acquisition. Wood subsequently played for other clubs, and those later contributions belong outside this particular Nets return. The source-supported result is his full New Jersey season, which compares favorably to what the Bullets got from the forward they acquired.

sections.heading: O'Koren's New Washington Role Ended Quickly
sections.body: O'Koren managed 15 regular-season games for Washington in 1986-87. He averaged 8.2 minutes and only 2.1 points in those appearances, a much smaller role than his established Nets tenure had suggested. Washington waived him in February 1987, which prevented the trade from becoming a longer-term source of frontcourt depth. The former Nets seasons can't be credited as a Washington return. Nor is there an identified draft asset produced by his departure. The Bullets acquired an experienced player, but they received only a brief and lightly used stint rather than a productive rotation regular.

sections.heading: Receiving-Team Minutes Overrule a Familiar-Name Comparison
sections.body: The players both had NBA experience, which may explain why an earlier archive treated the trade as even. That reasoning doesn't survive a comparison of acquired-team records. Wood logged a useful 76-game campaign with point-guard duties, while O'Koren supplied fifteen brief appearances and left Washington within months. This was not a franchise-altering exchange and New Jersey shouldn't get a superstar grade, but its return was plainly stronger. The proper historical verdict credits what the two organizations actually used, rather than assigning equal value to the players' reputations at the moment of the swap.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win. New Jersey earns B+ for Leon Wood's 76 appearances and averages of 7.3 points with 4.9 assists as a regular guard in 1986-87. Washington receives D+ for 15 games and 2.1 points per outing from Mike O'Koren. Neither player became a cornerstone, but the Nets obtained considerably more useful rotation minutes.

sections.heading: Seattle Paid a Second-Rounder for an Immediate Wing Contributor
sections.body: The SuperSonics acquired Vincent Askew from Sacramento on November 25, 1992, sending the Kings a second-round selection in the 1993 draft. The franchise transaction registers confirm both the compensation and the date. Askew had played nine Sacramento games earlier that season after joining the club as a free agent, but Seattle was attracted by the wing's ability to handle minutes without needing high usage. The Kings were building through the draft and accepted a future choice rather than holding a reserve whose role had already contracted. There was no accompanying cash or additional player in the recorded deal.

sections.heading: Askew Became More Than a Short-Term Seattle Rental
sections.body: The wing played 64 regular-season games for Seattle in 1992-93, scoring 384 points, then became a reliable rotation contributor. In 1993-94 he played 80 games and scored 727 points, followed by 71 games and 703 points in 1994-95 and 69 games with 582 points in 1995-96. Across those four seasons, the acquired return totaled 284 Seattle appearances. The 1993-94 average of 9.1 points came during a strong SuperSonics period, though he was not the team's primary star. The sustained minutes make this transaction notable despite its modest draft price.

sections.heading: Sacramento Drafted Peplowski at No. 52
sections.body: The pick Seattle surrendered became Sacramento's No. 52 overall selection in June 1993. The Kings drafted Michigan State center Mike Peplowski and used him in 55 regular-season games as a rookie. He scored 176 points, collected 169 rebounds and made nineteen starts, real NBA production from a late second-rounder. Peplowski later appeared for other franchises, but only his Sacramento time belongs in this trade's received-team ledger. The pick was not wasted, and the Kings deserve credit for turning the selection into an actual player rather than a prospect who never reached the league.

sections.heading: The Longer Seattle Tenure Settles the Comparison
sections.body: Both teams got something tangible. Sacramento converted a future second into a rookie reserve with 55 games, while Seattle turned the same draft value into a versatile player who lasted four seasons with the club. Askew's 284 regular-season appearances and 2,396 Seattle points far exceeded the Kings' direct benefit from Peplowski. Neither acquisition should be measured by later careers with unrelated teams, and Seattle's playoff success can't be assigned to one reserve. Even with that restraint, the SuperSonics' return was stronger in longevity and recurring rotation production, supporting a higher grade than the inherited evaluation.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Seattle SuperSonics Win. Seattle earns A- for Vincent Askew's 284 regular-season games and 2,396 points across four seasons following the November 1992 exchange. Sacramento receives C+ after drafting Mike Peplowski at No. 52 and using him in 55 games, with 176 points and 169 rebounds. Both clubs gained NBA contributors, but Seattle secured far more durable playing value.

sections.heading: A February 1994 Center Rental for a Conditional Draft Choice
sections.body: Los Angeles acquired veteran center Danny Schayes from Milwaukee on February 24, 1994. The NBA's historical deadline list describes the compensation as a conditional 1995 second-round pick, while the Bucks' transaction register describes selling the player's rights. The Lakers' own historical media guide confirms the acquisition date. Schayes had already played 23 games for Milwaukee during the season and carried years of NBA experience, but Los Angeles was seeking a temporary reserve rather than a new starting centerpiece. The future selection was conditional, which meant the Bucks' eventual draft return was uncertain from the outset.

sections.heading: Schayes Supplied a Small Amount of Actual Lakers Production
sections.body: Schayes appeared in 13 regular-season games for Los Angeles after the trade, averaging 10.2 minutes, 2.8 points and 2.6 rebounds without a start. It was a brief reserve role on a team going through an uneven transition after its championship years. His 23 games with Milwaukee earlier in 1993-94 count as the Bucks' pretrade history, not as value Los Angeles acquired. Schayes subsequently moved to Phoenix, so the Lakers also can't claim his later contributions elsewhere. The tangible return is a few weeks of NBA center availability, useful in a narrow sense but not a long-term solution.

sections.heading: Milwaukee's Future Compensation Did Not Become a Draft Selection
sections.body: The archived agreement promised Milwaukee a second-round pick in 1995 only if its condition was fulfilled. The inherited transaction record says the condition was not exercised; the available team and NBA transaction descriptions do not identify a 1995 selection acquired by the Bucks through this deal. A retrospective therefore cannot assign them the eventual NBA career of a hypothetical player. Milwaukee gave up the services of an aging reserve and received no verifiable draft conversion. It may have freed a roster place or reduced obligations, but those potential benefits aren't an identifiable basketball asset that can be tracked into later game totals.

sections.heading: The Documented Return Favors Los Angeles Only Slightly
sections.body: Both sides' returns were limited. The Lakers got a veteran who could play ten minutes a night when required, while the Bucks' conditional compensation produced no identifiable draft selection. That yields a narrow Los Angeles advantage on playing value. It doesn't justify the original pair of B grades, because neither team obtained sustained production or a future contributor. The distinction is between a little recorded NBA action and a conditional promise that apparently expired. Keeping the evaluation proportionate prevents a fringe February trade from being exaggerated into a major historical turning point.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Lakers Edge. Los Angeles earns C+ for Danny Schayes's 13 regular-season appearances and modest frontcourt minutes after the February 1994 transaction. Milwaukee receives D+ because the conditional 1995 second-round compensation never became a documented Bucks draft selection. Neither franchise gained lasting value, but the Lakers secured the deal's only traceable playing contribution.

sections.heading: Draft-Night Rights Exchange with a Date Discrepancy
sections.body: Golden State selected forward Anthony Miller with the 39th pick of the 1994 NBA draft, then sent his rights to the Lakers for a future second-round selection. The site's imported ledger places the transaction on June 29, while Basketball-Reference's league register dates the completed exchange to July 1. The discrepancy stays flagged rather than silently changing the canonical sort date. Los Angeles wanted a young interior reserve at a modest draft cost. Golden State accepted a later pick that could be held or traded. Neither club exchanged an established veteran NBA contract.

sections.heading: Two Seasons of Lakers Frontcourt Depth
sections.body: Anthony Miller appeared in 46 Lakers games during 1994-95, recording 189 points and 152 rebounds. His next season brought 27 appearances, 36 points and 25 rebounds. Taken together, that was 73 Los Angeles games, 225 points and 177 rebounds. Miller played 11.5 minutes per game as a rookie but received less time during the following campaign. He never established himself as the starting power forward, and his later professional seasons for other teams don't belong to Los Angeles. The acquisition nonetheless gave the Lakers an inexpensive, usable reserve for two years.

sections.heading: Whitfield's Pick Later Helped Form a Package for B.J. Armstrong
sections.body: The incoming Lakers second-round selection became Golden State's No. 40 choice in the 1995 draft, used on Dwayne Whitfield. He never played an NBA game for the Warriors. Nevertheless the asset wasn't entirely worthless: Golden State later included Whitfield among five outgoing players in its September 1995 transaction with Toronto for guard B.J. Armstrong. Armstrong supplied productive minutes for the Warriors, but four other players were also part of the payment. Assigning his entire Golden State season to this lone draft pick would exaggerate the asset chain. Whitfield himself eventually logged eight NBA games with Toronto, which aren't Warriors production.

sections.heading: A Direct Los Angeles Benefit Against Partial Warriors Trade Utility
sections.body: Los Angeles received a modest two-year reserve, while Golden State converted the pick into a later trade package. The Lakers are ahead on direct, documented playing value, but the Warriors' draft choice wasn't simply discarded without a basketball use. It's fair to acknowledge the pick's role in the eventual Armstrong transaction without giving Whitfield credit for all the NBA minutes Armstrong played. Miller's 73 games make Los Angeles the more identifiable winner, although the grades stay restrained for an exchange of second-round assets. The outcome rests on the real players and asset branches rather than invented star-level returns.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win. Los Angeles keeps B- for Anthony Miller with 73 games, 225 points and 177 rebounds across two seasons. Golden State receives C+ because its No. 40 Dwayne Whitfield pick became one of five players sent to Toronto in a later trade for B.J. Armstrong. Whitfield himself played no Warriors games, and only partial downstream Armstrong trade value can be assigned to the single pick.

sections.heading: Indiana Sent a Reserve Guard to Philadelphia for a Second
sections.body: On October 11, 1993, Philadelphia acquired Sean Green from the Indiana Pacers for a second-round selection in the following year's NBA draft. Both teams' transaction ledgers show the same date and direct player-for-pick exchange. Green had been a marginal rotation guard for Indiana during his early NBA years, but the rebuilding 76ers could test his scoring ability without surrendering a current player. Indiana preferred another draft opportunity and could wait until June 1994 to make the selection. No additional compensation appears in the documented transaction, so the analysis centers on those two assets.

sections.heading: Green Played 35 Games Before Another Philadelphia Trade
sections.body: Green appeared in 35 regular-season games for the 76ers during 1993-94, recording 149 points and 332 minutes without a start. His 4.3 points per game didn't make him a franchise centerpiece, but they were genuine production from a second-round pick exchange. Philadelphia included Green in a larger February 1994 deal with Utah involving Jeff Hornacek and additional draft assets. That creates a secondary trade branch, although the entire return for that bigger package cannot be assigned to Green alone. His only subsequent Utah appearance lasted two minutes, which belongs to the Jazz rather than Philadelphia.

sections.heading: No NBA Return From Indiana's No. 41 Draft Pick
sections.body: Indiana kept the incoming second-round pick and selected William Njoku at No. 41 overall in the 1994 draft. Njoku was a genuine draft prospect who pursued professional basketball, but he never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. The Pacers received the drafting opportunity they negotiated for, yet that choice produced no NBA points or minutes for their own club. Njoku's playing career outside the league isn't Indiana acquired-team production. Separating the successful exercise of a draft pick from the later absence of NBA appearances gives a more accurate account of the trade.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Secured the More Useful Short-Term Asset
sections.body: The 76ers got a reserve guard who played 35 games, while Indiana used its selection on a player who never reached the NBA floor. The direct difference favors Philadelphia even though Green did not become a long-term starter. His inclusion in the subsequent Utah exchange provided some additional asset flexibility, but it was a package trade with other valuable pieces, so the whole downstream return cannot be credited to this October agreement. Both grades should reflect the limited scale of the acquisition. Philadelphia was ahead on actual court production, while the Pacers' draft gamble did not convert.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win. Philadelphia receives B- for Sean Green's 35 games, 149 points and 332 minutes, plus a limited share of the later multi-asset Utah transaction. Indiana gets D+ because the acquired 1994 No. 41 pick became William Njoku, who never played in the NBA. The Sixers obtained the only direct playing return, albeit from a reserve rather than a star.

sections.heading: A Rights Exchange, Not an Active-Roster Trade
sections.body: Minnesota acquired the NBA draft rights to Conrad McRae from the Washington Bullets on August 20, 1993, sending the rights to Tim Burroughs in return. The Timberwolves' own historical media guide confirms the transaction, which appears in RealGM's team records on the same date. Neither club swapped an active contract or a veteran already providing regular-season NBA minutes. McRae had just been Washington's second-round selection, while Burroughs was an earlier Minnesota draftee. Both teams were trading the opportunity to negotiate with a prospect rather than a guaranteed player who would join the next roster.

sections.heading: McRae Did Not Play an NBA Game for Minnesota
sections.body: The Bullets had drafted Conrad McRae at No. 38 in 1993, shortly before the Timberwolves acquired his rights. McRae went on to build a professional playing career overseas, but never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Minnesota therefore got no league points, rebounds or minutes from him. International accomplishments may explain why he was considered a prospect, yet they aren't the acquired franchise's NBA production. Without a documented later trade of those rights to another NBA club, Minnesota's historical return is an unused negotiating opportunity rather than an actual NBA roster contributor.

sections.heading: Washington Retained Burroughs's Rights Without Receiving NBA Production
sections.body: Tim Burroughs was Minnesota's second-round selection in 1992, and the Bullets acquired his draft rights one year later. RealGM's player transaction chronology records the Washington acquisition, but it also lists zero years of NBA service. The franchise ultimately renounced his rights in 2000, without Burroughs ever appearing in an NBA game for Washington. His college and professional history elsewhere doesn't supply missing Bullets statistics. Like Minnesota, Washington exchanged one uncertain developmental option for another. The rights were real property under league rules, but they never turned into playing value in the acquiring team's uniform.

sections.heading: Neither Side Converted the Rights into a Player
sections.body: The surviving transaction record establishes two distinct draft selections changing organizational rights, but neither prospect supplied a single NBA regular-season appearance to the team receiving him. The result calls for an even, low-grade verdict rather than the pair of high grades that appeared in the earlier archive. This wasn't a case of one team surrendering a star who immediately flourished elsewhere; both sides held a possibility that stayed unfulfilled at the NBA level. The rights can be evaluated as legitimate trade assets without pretending they generated games, scoring or later picks that the sources cannot establish.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Minnesota receives C- for Conrad McRae's draft rights, which never yielded an NBA appearance for the Timberwolves. Washington also gets C- for acquiring Tim Burroughs's rights without receiving an NBA game from him. The agreement exchanged genuine developmental options, but neither side obtained an NBA player, so the original B/B grades overstated the realized outcome.

sources.title: Timberwolves official historical media guide, August 1993 rights exchange

sections.heading: Houston Gambled a Fifth-Round Choice on a Former Pacer Guard
sections.body: On September 17, 1984, Houston acquired Kevin McKenna from Indiana for its 1985 fifth-round draft pick. Both franchises list the same one-player-for-one-pick exchange. McKenna had made 61 appearances for the Pacers in 1983-84, starting 13, and averaged 6.3 points. He was a plausible inexpensive guard candidate for Houston as the club prepared for its first season with Hakeem Olajuwon alongside Ralph Sampson. Indiana was instead collecting a remote draft option rather than holding a player it could use immediately. The clubs' records confirm a fifth-round choice, although a later Pacers media-guide description has been cited with a different draft year and round.

sections.heading: McKenna Was Waived Before Opening Night
sections.body: The Rockets released McKenna on October 23, 1984, before the regular season began. He did not appear in an NBA game for Houston, even though his previous Indiana work established that he could play at the league level. McKenna later appeared in 29 games for New Jersey in 1984-85, averaging 5.7 points, but none of those Nets minutes can be credited as a Rockets return. Houston had bought a training-camp evaluation with a low draft selection and decided not to carry it into the season. That makes the actual return far more limited than a reader would infer by looking at his NBA career totals.

sections.heading: Indiana's Pick Became Ivan Daniels at No. 111
sections.body: The compensation selection arrived in the 1985 draft's fifth round, No. 111 overall, and was associated with Ivan Daniels. Pro Sports Transactions traces the choice from Houston to Indiana, corroborating the direction shown in each club's transaction ledger. Daniels did not turn into a Pacers regular-season NBA contributor. The pick itself represented legitimate optional scouting value for Indiana, but there is no basis for assigning it points or minutes that Daniels never produced in the NBA. The late draft position also helps explain the modest practical stakes. The Pacers did not get a guaranteed future rotation player by moving McKenna.

sections.heading: Two Different Assets, the Same Lack of Realized NBA Return
sections.body: Indiana exchanged a guard who had logged useful minutes the preceding year for the possibility of finding help deep in the 1985 draft. Houston surrendered that distant possibility to test McKenna as an immediately available veteran. Neither wager developed into playing time for the acquiring franchise: the Rockets waived the guard, and the Pacers' fifth-round outcome brought no recorded NBA games. That does not mean the transaction lacked rationale at the time. It means the inherited Pacers-win assessment exceeded the evidence about its actual result. Equal modest grades accurately describe an exchange in which both clubs received optional value but no sustained basketball contribution.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Houston earns C- after waiving Kevin McKenna before he played any Rockets regular-season games. Indiana also receives C- because the acquired fifth-round pick became No. 111 Ivan Daniels, who never contributed NBA minutes for the Pacers. Neither outcome supports a strong historical winner.

sections.heading: Houston Obtained a Third-String Center for a Distant Draft Pick
sections.body: The Rockets traded a 1987 third-round selection to Indiana for Granville Waiters on August 1, 1985. Waiters was a reserve center who had spent the 1984-85 season with the Pacers, and Houston was looking for additional big-man cover behind its well-established frontcourt. The timing was notable: the Rockets were preparing for a season built around Hakeem Olajuwon and Ralph Sampson, so Waiters did not need to arrive as a starter to fill a useful spot. Indiana accepted a low pick two drafts away instead of continuing to use its center. Both clubs' contemporaneous transaction histories agree on those terms.

sections.heading: Waiters Appeared in 43 Games on Houston's Finals Team
sections.body: Waiters played 43 Rockets regular-season games in 1985-86, recording 156 minutes, 27 points and 28 rebounds. He averaged only 3.6 minutes per appearance, so he was a deep reserve rather than a major part of the rotation. Houston nevertheless reached the NBA Finals that year, losing to Boston, and Waiters was on the regular-season roster that supported the run. His minutes should not be confused with the contributions of Olajuwon, Sampson or the other players who carried Houston. The limited but actual NBA appearances matter when comparing this outcome with a draft selection that did not produce league games.

sections.heading: Indiana's Third-Rounder Became Sean Couch
sections.body: The compensation was the Rockets' 1987 third-round draft choice, which ultimately became No. 60 Sean Couch. The Pacers' transaction register and the historical draft-choice ledger connect the selection to the Waiters trade. Couch did not appear in an NBA regular-season game for Indiana, leaving the Pacers with no on-court return from that eventual choice. A draft pick can be valuable as a scouting opportunity or later trade ingredient, but there is no documented downstream player acquired by Indiana from this particular third-round selection. It would be a mistake to grade the Pacers as if Couch's college career or hypothetical alternatives were NBA performance for the franchise.

sections.heading: A Small but Measurable Rockets Advantage
sections.body: Indiana traded a veteran center for an inexpensive chance in the 1987 draft. Houston converted that choice into a reserve who at least gave the club 43 appearances and a handful of frontcourt minutes. The outcome was not a transformative transaction for the Rockets or a costly failure for the Pacers; it was a modest bench deal involving a low-probability pick. Yet the older Pacers-win verdict obscured the basic receiving-team record. Waiters played in an NBA uniform for the acquiring club while the pick did not produce a Pacers player. A slight Rockets advantage with low grades reflects that specific outcome without turning roster depth into a claim of postseason heroics.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win. Houston receives C- for 43 games, 156 minutes and 27 points from Granville Waiters in 1985-86. Indiana gets D+ because the acquired 1987 third-round pick became No. 60 Sean Couch, who did not supply NBA minutes for the Pacers. The gap is small but favors actual reserve usage over an unrealized draft selection.

sections.heading: Washington Bought Price's Reputation as Cleveland Started Over
sections.body: On September 27, 1995, Cleveland traded Mark Price to the Washington Bullets for their 1996 first-round draft pick. Price had been a four-time All-Star and a major reason Cleveland was competitive in the late 1980s and early 1990s. Washington wanted an experienced point guard to complement Chris Webber, Juwan Howard and newly drafted Rasheed Wallace. Cleveland executive Wayne Embry was confronting Brad Daugherty's ongoing back troubles and decided to acquire a future asset rather than retain a veteran core. The Washington Post's contemporaneous coverage also documented concern about Price's health, which became central to how the exchange played out.

sections.heading: Price's Washington Tenure Ended After Seven Games
sections.body: Washington did not acquire the durable floor general it expected. A foot injury disrupted Price's first training camp with the Bullets, and his entire 1995-96 regular-season contribution amounted to seven games and 127 minutes. He scored 56 points with 18 assists, averages of 8.0 points and 2.6 assists, without becoming the stable starter the club had sought. Washington finished 39-43 and missed the playoffs. The later years of Price's career do not count for this transaction, and his celebrated Cleveland career was already in the past when the Bullets paid a first-round selection. The club gave away a meaningful draft asset for almost no season-long production.

sections.heading: Cleveland Turned the Pick Into a Three-Season Center
sections.body: The transferred Washington selection became the No. 12 overall pick of the 1996 draft, which Cleveland used on Vitaly Potapenko from Wright State. Older imported trade copy labeled the selection No. 11, but the Cavaliers' official draft ledger confirms No. 12. Potapenko played 80 Cleveland games as a rookie, another 80 in 1997-98 and 17 during the shortened 1998-99 season before moving to Boston. That totals 177 Cavaliers appearances, including meaningful reserve-center minutes across two full seasons. He was not a star or a permanent building block, but Cleveland's return was clearly more than a speculative paper asset.

sections.heading: A Clear Imbalance Despite Price's Better Overall Career
sections.body: A simple career-achievement comparison would favor Price over Potapenko and miss what Washington and Cleveland actually received. Price's best work had all occurred for the Cavaliers before this deal; in a Bullets uniform he barely played. Cleveland's incoming pick yielded 177 games of center depth, including 1,238 rookie minutes and 1,412 more in his second season. The clubs were pursuing different strategies, and Washington's effort to compete immediately was understandable, but the downside of relying on an injured veteran was apparent at the time. Historical accounts of the trade should therefore reward Cleveland's realized pick return and not treat Price's former All-Star credentials as Washington's acquired basketball value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Cavaliers Win. Cleveland earns B+ after using the acquired No. 12 pick on Vitaly Potapenko, who provided 177 regular-season Cavaliers appearances. Washington gets D+ for Mark Price's seven games and 127 minutes in 1995-96. The inherited Even Trade verdict and No. 11 draft position conflicted with official records and the receiving-team outcomes.

sections.heading: Minnesota Replaced a Franchise Original with a Veteran Shooter
sections.body: The Minnesota Timberwolves sent Doug West to the Vancouver Grizzlies for Anthony Peeler on February 18, 1998. West had been with Minnesota since its first season and represented a long stretch of the franchise's early years, but his role had declined as the team developed around Kevin Garnett and Stephon Marbury. Peeler arrived from Vancouver after playing a handful of starts that season and offered a more useful perimeter shooting option. Vancouver took on an experienced wing in West. The transaction was a direct player-for-player swap with no documented draft compensation, and contemporary league transaction listings identify the same date and two names.

sections.heading: Peeler Stayed in the Minnesota Rotation Through 2003
sections.body: Peeler played 30 Timberwolves games after the February swap, starting 24 and averaging 13.0 points while shooting 45.3 percent on three-pointers. He then made 28 appearances in the shortened 1998-99 season, followed by 82 in 1999-00, 75 in 2000-01 and another 82 in each of 2001-02 and 2002-03. Those figures add up to 379 regular-season games for Minnesota after this exchange. His role varied from starter to reserve, but he gave the Wolves several years of perimeter offense and flexibility on the wing. That sustained use was substantially more than a typical late-season depth rental.

sections.heading: West Provided Much Less Playing Value in Vancouver
sections.body: West did not record a Grizzlies regular-season appearance after the February 1998 deal during that remaining season. He played 14 Vancouver games in 1998-99, 38 in 1999-00 and 15 in 2000-01, totaling 67 games for the franchise with a decreasing role. His 1998-99 run produced 81 points, the following season 152 and his final year 28. Minnesota's earlier West games were important to the Timberwolves' own history but do not belong to Vancouver's acquired return. Likewise, Peeler's Lakers and Vancouver production before the swap does not add to the value Minnesota obtained.

sections.heading: The Outcome Was a Multi-Year Wolves Gain
sections.body: Minnesota gained a long-running guard who could score in double figures in the right role and contribute during the Garnett-era playoff years. Vancouver acquired a recognizable veteran but received comparatively few minutes and lost the chance to continue using Peeler. The trade did not deliver an All-Star to Minnesota, and it should not be credited with the whole franchise's postseason progress, but 379 receiving-team games against 67 is a substantial difference. The Wolves kept Peeler until 2003 while West's career wound down on the Grizzlies' bench. An enhanced Minnesota grade better captures the duration and usefulness of the return without dismissing West's earlier NBA achievements.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wolves Win. Minnesota earns A- for 379 Anthony Peeler regular-season appearances and several seasons of useful guard minutes after the 1998 swap. Vancouver gets C because Doug West played only 67 regular-season Grizzlies games during the following three seasons. Peeler's sustained role, not his pretrade career, is the decisive advantage.

sections.heading: Chicago Acquired Wing Depth for a Final Title Chase
sections.body: The Bulls traded Dickey Simpkins to Golden State for Scott Burrell on September 22, 1997. Chicago was preparing for the final season of its Michael Jordan-Scottie Pippen championship group and wanted an athletic wing who could relieve the regulars without requiring featured possessions. Burrell had played for Charlotte and Golden State the previous year, and he offered size plus some outside shooting from the bench. The Warriors instead took a young forward with previous Bulls experience who could be evaluated in a more open frontcourt rotation. The league ledger and Chicago's transaction history list a straightforward one-for-one player swap.

sections.heading: Burrell Played in Every Bulls Postseason Game
sections.body: Burrell appeared in 80 Bulls regular-season games in 1997-98, averaging 5.2 points and 2.5 rebounds in 13.7 minutes. He made 51 three-pointers and added 64 steals, giving Chicago tangible reserve production while it won 62 games. In the postseason he played all 21 Bulls games, totaling 260 minutes and 80 points during the run to the franchise's sixth NBA title in eight seasons. Burrell was not the main reason the Bulls won; Jordan and Pippen still carried the most difficult work. But he was an available wing throughout the season and postseason, which was precisely the contribution this trade was meant to secure.

sections.heading: Simpkins Played Only 19 Warriors Games Before Being Waived
sections.body: The Golden State return lasted a much shorter time. Simpkins played 19 regular-season games for the Warriors in 1997-98, logging 196 minutes and averaging 2.8 points. The club waived him on February 17, 1998. Chicago re-signed him on March 2, a separate free-agent transaction that gave the Bulls another familiar reserve late in the season. That later signing does not mean the Warriors received additional value from Simpkins, and Chicago's subsequent use of him does not erase the original trade. The relevant incoming Golden State contribution is the 19-game reserve stint before the waiver.

sections.heading: The Championship Context Makes the Return Distinct
sections.body: Chicago traded a player it did not need as much for Burrell, who stayed healthy and served in both the regular season and playoffs. Golden State received fewer than twenty games before releasing Simpkins, and the Warriors finished with a poor record rather than extracting a lasting rotation piece. The trade did not by itself secure the 1998 title, and awarding Burrell the achievements of Jordan's roster would exaggerate his individual role. Still, 80 regular-season and 21 postseason appearances are much more substantial than 19 games and an early waiver. That disparity warrants a stronger Chicago verdict than the previous modest edge suggested.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win. Chicago earns B+ for Scott Burrell's 80 regular-season and 21 playoff appearances in the 1997-98 championship season. Golden State gets D+ for Dickey Simpkins's 19 games and 196 minutes before his February waiver. Chicago later re-signed Simpkins separately, but that doesn't add to the Warriors' trade return.

sections.heading: The Lakers Converted Center Depth Into Backcourt Insurance
sections.body: Los Angeles acquired guard Lindsey Hunter from Milwaukee for reserve center Greg Foster on June 28, 2001. The Lakers were coming off another championship and needed dependable perimeter depth for the effort to repeat. Hunter had been a regular rotation guard for Detroit before joining Milwaukee, and his defense plus outside shot offered an alternative alongside Derek Fisher and Kobe Bryant. Foster had supplied limited center minutes during the Lakers' previous title season, when Shaquille O'Neal anchored the position. The deal moved an expendable frontcourt veteran for a guard who could start when needed, while Milwaukee tested whether Foster could provide inexpensive veteran size.

sections.heading: Hunter Appeared in Every Regular-Season Game for Los Angeles
sections.body: Hunter played all 82 regular-season Lakers contests in 2001-02, starting 47 and averaging 5.8 points in 19.7 minutes. His scoring declined from his previous Milwaukee season, but he still made enough spot starts to be a regular part of the rotation. During the playoffs he appeared in 18 games as Los Angeles advanced past Portland, San Antonio, Sacramento and New Jersey to win the 2002 NBA title. Hunter was not the primary guard or star of the championship team; Bryant, O'Neal and the starters supplied far more offense. His specific return was availability, defense and rotation cover through a title season.

sections.heading: Foster Played Only 24 Minutes for Milwaukee
sections.body: Milwaukee's playing return was minimal. Foster appeared in six regular-season Bucks games in 2001-02, logging a total of 24 minutes and seven points, with eight rebounds. He did not start and never became a rotation fixture for the team. Foster's prior 62-game 2000-01 Lakers season does not count as Milwaukee value merely because it demonstrated he had NBA experience before the deal. He subsequently appeared with Toronto in 2002-03, outside the Bucks' return. Milwaukee was looking for a veteran big man but received only an occasional deep reserve who had no meaningful role in the club's 41-41 season.

sections.heading: The One-Sided Minutes Explain the Verdict
sections.body: The contrast between receiving-team results is striking: Hunter made 82 appearances and 47 starts for Los Angeles, while Foster provided six Milwaukee games and almost no minutes. Hunter's role continued into a postseason championship, further distinguishing the usefulness of his stint from that of an expendable roster piece. The Lakers' win does not require claiming that Hunter was a decisive player in the Finals. His 1,616 regular-season minutes and playoff availability were actual basketball contributions from the trade. Foster's seven Bucks points did not materially change Milwaukee's lineup. That difference supports giving Los Angeles a stronger positive grade and the Bucks a much lower one than the inherited evaluation.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win. Los Angeles earns B+ for Lindsey Hunter's 82 regular-season appearances, 47 starts and 18 playoff appearances on the 2002 championship team. Milwaukee gets D+ after Greg Foster logged just six games and 24 minutes. The direct playing returns were sharply unequal, despite both players having useful careers elsewhere.

sections.heading: Washington Turned a Wing Surplus Into a Second First-Round Pick
sections.body: On June 25, 2002, the Wizards traded Courtney Alexander to the Hornets for the No. 17 pick in the following day's NBA draft. The Hornets were moving from Charlotte to New Orleans, which explains why the league's season transaction log uses Charlotte while the contemporary Washington reporting already called the franchise New Orleans. Alexander had played for Washington alongside Michael Jordan and Richard Hamilton but no longer had a clear long-term place in the backcourt. The Wizards wanted a chance to select another young guard, while the Hornets were acquiring a player who had already demonstrated scoring ability in the league.

sections.heading: The No. 17 Selection Became Maryland Star Juan Dixon
sections.body: Washington used that acquired first-round selection on University of Maryland guard Juan Dixon, who had just led the Terrapins to the NCAA championship. Dixon appeared in 42 Wizards regular-season games as a rookie, 71 in 2003-04 and 63 in 2004-05. Across those three seasons he supplied 176 appearances, 3,179 minutes and 1,441 points before leaving for Portland. He made 10 postseason appearances during Washington's 2005 playoff run, providing additional value beyond the original draft night's excitement. The franchise had not acquired a future All-Star, but it obtained three seasons of NBA wing and guard depth from the pick it received.

sections.heading: Alexander Provided New Orleans One Solid Reserve Season
sections.body: The Hornets' return was not empty. Alexander played 66 New Orleans regular-season games in 2002-03, starting seven and delivering 523 points over 1,360 minutes. He averaged 7.9 points per contest, with 118 rebounds and 79 assists, and appeared in five postseason games as the team fell to Philadelphia in the first round. It was a serviceable reserve year for a club establishing itself in New Orleans. Alexander did not continue with the Hornets after that season, and his Washington scoring from before the exchange cannot be credited as new Hornets production. Nor can Dixon's later Portland seasons be awarded to the Wizards.

sections.heading: Dixon's Three-Year Stay Outpaced Alexander's One-Year Tenure
sections.body: The central trade-off was immediate experience against the opportunity to select a college championship guard. Alexander could help the Hornets right away, and his 66 games are worth acknowledging. Washington nevertheless received 176 games across three seasons and used Dixon during a later postseason appearance. That extended useful life from a mid-first-round choice created more total on-court value for the Wizards, even though Dixon never became a star. The exchange should not be credited with Washington's entire roster turnaround or discounted merely because the player taken at No. 17 spent parts of his career elsewhere. The specific club-by-club record supports Washington's historical advantage.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wizards Win. Washington earns A- after converting Courtney Alexander into the No. 17 selection that produced Juan Dixon, who played 176 Wizards games and helped in the 2005 playoffs. New Orleans gets D+ for 66 games and 523 points from Alexander in 2002-03. Both teams received actual playing value, but Dixon offered a longer and greater return.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Swapped a Reserve Forward for a Former All-Star Center
sections.body: The Bucks received Kevin Duckworth from the Washington Bullets on October 18, 1995, sending Bob McCann back to the nation's capital. Duckworth had twice made the All-Star team during his Portland years, but he was no longer the productive offensive center of the late 1980s. Milwaukee was testing whether veteran frontcourt size could help a team with a thin center rotation. Washington wanted a player who could cover forward minutes while its roster waited for Chris Webber to return from injury. The player-for-player terms and transaction date are documented in the teams' season registers, without an attached pick or cash.

sections.heading: Duckworth Managed Only Eight Bucks Games
sections.body: Duckworth's past recognition brought almost no 1995-96 playing return for Milwaukee. He appeared in eight Bucks regular-season games, started one and logged 58 minutes. His entire statistical contribution was nine points, seven rebounds and two assists. Milwaukee finished 25-57, but the trade cannot be blamed for that record any more than Duckworth can be credited with improving it. His Portland and earlier Washington totals are not Bucks production, and he subsequently played for the Clippers rather than remaining a useful Milwaukee frontcourt fixture. The acquired veteran had reached the end of his ability to sustain rotation minutes.

sections.heading: McCann Played 62 Washington Games Despite a Waiver
sections.body: McCann's Washington stint was more substantial, although the club did not keep him continuously on a standard contract. He appeared in 62 regular-season games for the 1995-96 Bullets, totaling 653 minutes with no starts. Washington waived him on January 5, re-signed him to a ten-day deal January 10 and brought him back for the rest of the season February 3. That sequence matters because it explains how his roster status briefly changed without ending his 1995-96 playing return. McCann remained a deep reserve, averaging approximately 10.5 minutes per appearance, but he supplied many more usable games than Duckworth managed for Milwaukee.

sections.heading: Washington Got Functional Bench Coverage Instead of a Name
sections.body: At the time of the exchange, Duckworth carried the stronger career reputation. Yet the actual receiving-team contribution went the other way: Washington used McCann in 62 games, while Milwaukee received eight short Duckworth appearances. McCann's temporary release and later return do not create a separate trade, and the earlier careers of both players are irrelevant to what the acquiring clubs received. The Bullets still did not secure a starter or a playoff berth, so the grade should stay measured. The difference between hundreds of frontcourt reserve minutes and a 58-minute rental is enough, however, to overturn the inherited Milwaukee-favored verdict.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bullets Win. Washington gets B for 62 Bob McCann games and 653 minutes during 1995-96, including the reserve's post-waiver return. Milwaukee receives D+ for just eight Kevin Duckworth games, 58 minutes and nine points. Duckworth's former All-Star status did not translate into Bucks playing value.

sections.heading: Minnesota Reacquired a Guard It Had Waived Months Earlier
sections.body: On January 12, 1996, the Timberwolves sent their 1996 second-round draft selection to the expansion Vancouver Grizzlies for Darrick Martin. Minnesota had waived Martin in November, after using him during the previous season, and Vancouver signed him as a free agent days afterward. The trade therefore amounted to paying a future draft choice to bring back an experienced backup guard. Minnesota needed another ball handler while Kevin Garnett was developing and Flip Saunders had only recently taken over as head coach. Vancouver chose a future scouting asset over retaining a guard it had used during its difficult inaugural months.

sections.heading: Martin Played 35 Games and Handled the Ball for the Wolves
sections.body: Martin appeared in 35 Minnesota regular-season games during the remainder of 1995-96, starting 16. He logged 747 minutes, scored 254 points and distributed 156 assists, averages of 7.3 points and 4.5 assists in 21.3 minutes. He was not an elite scorer, but he provided tangible point-guard cover and an established relationship with the young organization. His earlier 24 Vancouver games that season should not be counted as Minnesota's new return, and his later work for the Clippers also belongs to another franchise. The incoming value was a specific 35-game second stint, rather than his entire NBA career.

sections.heading: Vancouver Traded the Pick to Orlando Before the Draft
sections.body: The compensation selection became the 1996 second-round No. 49 pick, eventually used on Amal McCaskill. However, Vancouver did not choose McCaskill or receive his later NBA production. On February 22 the Grizzlies sent that selection and veteran Kenny Gattison to Orlando for Jeff Turner, who was soon waived in March. Orlando subsequently drafted McCaskill. The pick's movement is essential to evaluating the original deal: the Grizzlies converted it into a component of another veteran exchange, but Turner was obtained with two outgoing assets. Assigning all of Turner's arrival, or McCaskill's later career, to this January trade would exaggerate the return.

sections.heading: The Wolves Obtained the More Definite Playing Value
sections.body: Martin's 35 appearances gave Minnesota an immediate reserve guard who could play considerable minutes and set up teammates. Vancouver received a second-round option and promptly spent it within a broader February deal, so the direct basketball benefits are harder to isolate. The Grizzlies had a reason to prefer an asset with future flexibility on an expansion roster, but neither the later Orlando pick nor the full Jeff Turner transaction should become invented Vancouver playing statistics. The modest Minnesota advantage follows the receiving-team record rather than a claim that Martin was a transformative player or that Vancouver's draft asset had no value at all.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wolves Win. Minnesota earns B+ for Darrick Martin's 35 games, 747 minutes and 156 assists after the January 1996 swap. Vancouver gets C+ for a second-round asset it later included with Kenny Gattison to acquire Jeff Turner. Orlando ultimately selected Amal McCaskill at No. 49, so the draft choice's eventual NBA career is not a Vancouver contribution.

sections.heading: Two Marginal Wings Swapped Places at the February Deadline
sections.body: Charlotte sent Scott Burrell to Golden State for Donald Royal on February 20, 1997. Both clubs recorded the one-for-one deal in their 1996-97 transaction registers. Burrell had spent only the first part of the season with the Hornets after earlier seasons there, while Royal had arrived in Golden State from Orlando during a larger November trade. Charlotte was contending for the playoffs and wanted a veteran wing who could play sparingly without requiring touches. The Warriors were rebuilding a roster with little stability and took a chance on Burrell's outside shooting. No draft selection or cash moved in this exchange.

sections.heading: Burrell Logged 29 Games Before Golden State Traded Him Again
sections.body: Burrell appeared in 29 regular-season Warriors games after the February swap, totaling 457 minutes and 143 points. He shot 36.1 percent from three-point range in Golden State and provided reserve wing minutes rather than a lasting starting role. Golden State included him in a September 1997 exchange with Chicago for Dickey Simpkins. That later transaction gave the Warriors another 19 games of bench use from Simpkins before his February 1998 waiver. It is a traceable asset-chain consequence, but the two transactions should not be collapsed into a single deal or used to award Golden State all of Chicago's subsequent championship production from Burrell.

sections.heading: Royal Remained With Charlotte into the Following Season
sections.body: Royal played 25 Hornets games after the February 1997 trade, logging 320 minutes, 70 points and 58 rebounds. He appeared once during Charlotte's opening-round postseason loss to the Knicks. In 1997-98 Royal returned for another 29 regular-season games, this time supplying 305 minutes and 74 points, plus four playoff appearances during Charlotte's second-round run. His two Charlotte seasons therefore amounted to 54 regular-season games, 625 minutes and 144 points. Those are modest totals, but greater staying power than Burrell's 29-game direct Warriors stint. Royal's previous 36 games in a Golden State jersey were played before Charlotte acquired him and cannot be transferred across the ledger.

sections.heading: The Direct Returns Were Closer Than the Inherited Verdict
sections.body: Both clubs obtained limited rotation value, and neither player became a major offensive contributor with the team that received him. Charlotte got more games and slightly more minutes from Royal across two seasons, while Golden State got an immediate outside-shooting reserve in Burrell and later exchanged him for Simpkins. The points scored in the acquiring uniforms were almost identical at 144 versus 143, making the earlier Warriors-favored assessment difficult to defend as a meaningful basketball difference. Charlotte's playoff appearances did not depend heavily on Royal, and Burrell's later Bulls championship was someone else's benefit. Equal modest grades better represent the small, competing advantages.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Charlotte earns C+ for Donald Royal's 54 games, 625 minutes and 144 points over two seasons. Golden State also receives C+ for Scott Burrell's 29 games, 457 minutes and 143 points, plus his subsequent limited trade utility. Neither direct return decisively outperformed the other or produced a star.

sections.heading: A Draft-Night Exchange of Two Veteran Centers
sections.body: The Clippers traded Stanley Roberts to Minnesota for Stojko Vranković on June 25, 1997, the same day as the NBA draft. The league transaction archive and Los Angeles's franchise ledger agree on the date and two-player exchange. Minnesota needed a center who could play alongside Kevin Garnett without monopolizing the offense, while the Clippers wanted a veteran rim protector to stabilize a frontcourt undergoing another transition. Roberts had been with Los Angeles for several seasons, though injuries had interrupted his career. Vranković had played for Minnesota in 1996-97 after returning from Europe, offering shot blocking rather than much scoring.

sections.heading: Roberts Played 74 Games as Minnesota Reached the Playoffs
sections.body: Roberts supplied Minnesota with a full 1997-98 reserve-and-spot-starter season. He appeared in 74 regular-season games and started 44, logging 1,328 minutes, 457 points and 363 rebounds. His 72 blocks made him a useful defensive presence, even as his average of 6.2 points showed that he was not the team's primary offensive option. The Timberwolves finished 45-37 and reached the playoffs, where Roberts made one brief appearance against Seattle. Roberts did not remain a long-term foundation for the team, but his acquisition filled a real rotation need in Minnesota's first 45-win campaign.

sections.heading: Vranković Gave Los Angeles Playing Time but Little Offense
sections.body: The Clippers also obtained measurable center production. Vranković appeared in 65 regular-season games during 1997-98, starting 38 and totaling 996 minutes, 195 points, 263 rebounds and 66 blocked shots. He averaged about fifteen minutes per game, with a defensive role comparable in some ways to Roberts's Minnesota job. He returned for two more Clippers games in the shortened 1998-99 season, bringing his total after the exchange to 67 appearances, 1,008 minutes and 197 points. These numbers are Los Angeles contributions only; his earlier Minnesota games and European career do not belong in this incoming return.

sections.heading: Minnesota's Edge Came From Greater Overall Center Output
sections.body: This was an exchange of modestly productive veterans, not a franchise-defining move. Minnesota obtained more game appearances, more minutes, more points and more rebounds, along with slightly more blocked shots. Roberts also made six more starts than Vranković did during their first seasons after the trade. The Clippers received genuine rim protection, so labeling their side as an outright failure would overlook the 67 games they used their new center. Yet Minnesota was the club that got the greater overall share of on-court work during the period when its young roster was beginning to reach the postseason. The inherited Wolves-favored grade fits those recorded outcomes.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wolves Win. Minnesota retains B for 74 Stanley Roberts regular-season games, 44 starts, 457 points and 363 rebounds during its 1997-98 playoff season. Los Angeles earns C for Stojko Vranković's 67 Clippers games, 1,008 minutes and 197 points across two seasons. Both teams acquired usable size, but Minnesota received more overall production.

sections.heading: Seattle Took a Second-Rounder for a Center Who Had Started 69 Games
sections.body: On September 28, 2003, the Seattle SuperSonics sent Predrag Drobnjak, also known as Peja Drobnjak, to the Los Angeles Clippers for a 2004 second-round selection. The timing reflected opposite roster objectives. Seattle was opening minutes for a younger frontcourt after Drobnjak had started 69 games in the prior season. Los Angeles needed center depth following major offseason turnover, and it was willing to give up a future mid-second-round chance for someone who could join the rotation immediately. The exchange was not a deal for a pick of unknown origin: the 2004 selection became No. 35 overall.

sections.heading: Drobnjak Supplied One Season of Clippers Production
sections.body: Drobnjak played 61 Clippers regular-season games in 2003-04, starting 14 and logging 949 minutes. He scored 382 points, grabbed 196 rebounds and made 24 blocks, averages of 6.3 points and 3.2 rebounds in 15.6 minutes per appearance. That is usable backup-center work for a team that finished 28-54, even though he did not become a starting cornerstone. He was selected by the expansion Charlotte Bobcats in June 2004, ending the direct Los Angeles stint after one season. His prior 146 appearances in Seattle and his later 71 games with Atlanta are not part of what the Clippers acquired.

sections.heading: Seattle Used the Pick as a Bridge to Gelabale
sections.body: Seattle selected Andre Emmett with that incoming 2004 No. 35 pick, but it moved his rights to Memphis on draft night for another second-rounder in 2005. That later selection became Mickaël Gelabale, who eventually played 70 games for Seattle in 2006-07 and 39 more in 2007-08. His 109 SuperSonics games totaled 1,704 minutes and 489 points. It would be inaccurate to say Emmett played those games for Seattle; he did not. The value came through an additional trade, with a delay between the original center deal and the arrival of a useful reserve wing.

sections.heading: Both Clubs Eventually Found Modest Rotation Help
sections.body: Los Angeles did what it set out to do: it exchanged a second-round opportunity for 61 games of immediate center depth. Seattle needed patience and another transaction, but the same draft asset later helped it obtain a player who logged more games and minutes with the SuperSonics than Drobnjak did with the Clippers. It is tempting to grade only the original Emmett selection and call the trade a Los Angeles win, yet that would ignore the documented draft-night movement of Emmett's rights. Conversely, Gelabale's contribution should not be treated as a direct 2003 return without explaining the intermediate step. The balanced result is limited but tangible value on each side.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. The Clippers earn C+ for 61 games, 949 minutes and 382 points from Predrag Drobnjak. Seattle also gets C+ because its No. 35 choice was flipped for the draft selection that became Mickaël Gelabale, a 109-game SuperSonics reserve. Both teams received useful short-term or downstream contributions.

sections.heading: Orlando Obtained a Fringe Center Without Giving Up a Guaranteed Pick
sections.body: On December 26, 2003, the Orlando Magic acquired Robert Archibald from the Phoenix Suns for a conditional 2005 second-round pick. Both franchises' transaction ledgers explicitly say the draft condition was not exercised, so Phoenix never obtained an identifiable selection from that agreement. The deal came during Orlando's difficult 2003-04 season, when the Magic were searching for inexpensive frontcourt options. Archibald had joined Phoenix earlier in a multi-player Memphis trade but had barely been used. Moving him gave Orlando a chance to evaluate another center without surrendering a guaranteed draft asset.

sections.heading: Archibald's Magic Playing Time Was Four Minutes
sections.body: The trade produced almost no direct basketball contribution. Archibald appeared in one Magic game, against the Knicks on December 29, and played four minutes. He scored two points and had one rebound. This is important because the incoming player was not a season-long reserve, nor did he accumulate meaningful totals that explain a high grade. His earlier Phoenix appearance that December belonged to his former team, and his later Raptors games belong to Toronto. Orlando's direct playing return consisted of one short outing, followed quickly by another roster maneuver.

sections.heading: Orlando Used His Contract in a Larger January Exchange
sections.body: On January 2, 2004, the Magic sent Archibald to Toronto together with a 2005 second-round pick in a transaction involving Mengke Bateer, the rights to Remon Van de Hare and an exchange of future second-round positions. A later record traces the swap to picks eventually used on Roko Ukić and Travis Diener. That is real transaction activity generated after the original acquisition, but it was a package trade; Archibald alone cannot be credited with everything Orlando received. His value was chiefly that of an available contractual asset in another deal, not a player who improved the Magic's regular-season rotation.

sections.heading: Phoenix Lost a Contract but Never Collected the Conditional Return
sections.body: For Phoenix, the asset going out was a center it was not using, making the roster decision understandable. Still, the conditional second-rounder did not convey and the Suns gained no documented draft selection or player minutes from the December exchange. Orlando received minimal playing time and subsequently found use for Archibald in a separate trade, which provides a narrow receiving-team advantage. The original Magic-favored verdict can survive, but the size of that advantage should be modest. Treating the conditional choice as an exercised Phoenix pick, or the entire Toronto trade as Archibald's single-handed achievement, would distort the sequence of events.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Magic Win. Orlando receives C+ for one Robert Archibald game and his later use as a piece of a larger Toronto trade. Phoenix gets D+ because the conditional 2005 second-round pick never conveyed. This was a small asset-management advantage, not the major playing return implied by the inherited Magic B grade.

sections.heading: New Jersey Used an Uncertain Pick to Add a Proven Shooter
sections.body: Golden State sent Anthony Morrow to the New Jersey Nets on July 13, 2010, in return for a conditional 2011 second-round draft pick. Morrow had already established himself as a high-percentage three-point shooter with the Warriors, including a 45.6 percent season from distance in 2009-10. The Nets were rebuilding a backcourt around Devin Harris and wanted reliable floor spacing without giving up a guaranteed first-round asset. The Warriors were reshuffling their wings and treated the return as a possible draft opportunity. Both clubs' transaction ledgers explicitly state that the condition was never met and the pick did not convey.

sections.heading: Morrow Supplied Two Full Seasons of Nets Scoring
sections.body: Morrow played 58 New Jersey regular-season games in 2010-11, starting 47 and averaging 13.2 points in 32.0 minutes. He made 42.3 percent of his three-point attempts, giving the Nets a credible spot-up scoring option. In the shortened 2011-12 season he appeared 62 more times with 18 starts and averaged 12.0 points. Across those two years, his 120 games and 65 starts amounted to sustained rotation value. The franchise was still called the New Jersey Nets throughout this stint; referring to Brooklyn as the modern successor should not obscure the original club's name or dates.

sections.heading: Golden State Received No Actual Draft Selection
sections.body: The Warriors were offered a conditional second-round selection in the 2011 draft, but the obligation was not exercised. That means Golden State did not receive a pick it could use on a player or trade again. It would be misleading to assign the franchise any 2011 second-rounder's NBA games merely because a choice was listed as possible compensation. The return was a contingent right that expired without producing a documented selection. Morrow's own earlier 136 Golden State games, including his 2009-10 scoring season, were Warriors contributions made before the deal rather than value created by acquiring the Nets' potential pick.

sections.heading: The Nets Acquired a Real Starter for a Nonconveyed Asset
sections.body: New Jersey clearly benefited more from the arrangement. A guard capable of scoring in double figures appeared in 120 games while the club surrendered no exercised draft selection. The two seasons were not enough to turn the Nets into a contender, and Morrow moved on before the team's first Brooklyn campaign, so the result should not be exaggerated into a franchise-changing acquisition. But the alternative side is straightforward: Golden State parted with a useful shooter and realized no pick from the agreement. That imbalance justifies a favorable Nets grade grounded in actual receiving-team minutes, points and starts.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nets Win. New Jersey earns B+ after Anthony Morrow provided 120 regular-season games, 65 starts and double-digit scoring in both seasons. Golden State receives D+ because the conditional 2011 second-round pick never conveyed. The Nets acquired two years of effective perimeter shooting without delivering an actual draft selection.
