sections.heading: The Expansion Grizzlies Exchanged Their Leading Early Scorer
sections.body: Vancouver traded veteran center Benoit Benjamin to the Milwaukee Bucks on November 27, 1995, getting guard Eric Murdock and second-year big man Eric Mobley. Benjamin had been the expansion franchise's leading scorer through its first thirteen games, but the team lacked dependable point-guard direction. Milwaukee had just added Sherman Douglas to its backcourt, making Murdock more available. The Grizzlies accepted a shorter center rotation in order to address a larger organizational weakness: distributing the ball while a completely new roster learned to play together.

sections.heading: Murdock Provided Sixty-Four Games of Playmaking
sections.body: Murdock quickly became one of Vancouver's more productive guards. He played sixty-four regular-season games after the trade, starting fourteen, and averaged 9.1 points with 4.6 assists and 2.0 steals. He brought ball pressure and a much-needed ability to run half-court sets without relying solely on inexperienced teammates. Mobley gave Vancouver a second developmental frontcourt option. Neither player made the expansion club a contender, which finished fifteen wins and sixty-seven losses, but Murdock's actual new-team minutes offer stronger evidence of value than the team's poor record alone.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Got a Veteran Center With a Shorter Horizon
sections.body: Benjamin was a legitimate NBA center who had already played for several franchises. Milwaukee received his size and post scoring as immediate frontcourt coverage, so its end of the trade was not empty. However, the scoring that made him Vancouver's early leader occurred before the Bucks acquired him. His earlier Clippers and Nets years must also be excluded from Milwaukee's receiving-team return. The Bucks were trading two different reserve roles for a known big man who could help their interior rotation, a sensible short-term choice rather than a developmental rebuild.

sections.heading: The Guard Upgrade Gave Vancouver the More Durable Benefit
sections.body: Expansion teams often struggle to find a player who can organize their offense, and Vancouver gained one without sending out draft picks. Murdock wasn't an All-Star, but his passing and defensive activity supplied an identifiable sixty-four-game return. Milwaukee got the center it sought, while Mobley offered an additional young option in Vancouver. The original Grizzlies-winning assessment stands, although the better grade follows specific receiving-team results rather than assuming a bad expansion season invalidated every acquisition. Vancouver bought more playable positions with its departing center.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Grizzlies Win. Vancouver receives A- because Eric Murdock supplied sixty-four games, 9.1 points and 4.6 assists per outing and Eric Mobley added frontcourt depth. Milwaukee earns C+ for acquiring Benoit Benjamin as a veteran center. The Grizzlies addressed two roster needs with one outgoing scorer while the Bucks obtained a shorter-term interior option.

sections.heading: Vancouver Found a Forward Before Its First NBA Season
sections.body: On November 1, 1995, the Vancouver Grizzlies acquired Anthony Avent from Orlando in exchange for Kevin Pritchard and Larry Stewart. The deal occurred just before the expansion franchise's inaugural regular season began, when every roster spot carried uncertainty. Avent had played NBA minutes with Milwaukee and Orlando and offered a forward with known rebounding ability. Orlando wanted to try two different players rather than keep another reserve big man on a loaded roster around Shaquille O'Neal. Neither organization exchanged a draft selection.

sections.heading: Avent Became an Actual Grizzlies Rotation Forward
sections.body: Avent played seventy-one Vancouver regular-season games in 1995-96, starting thirty-two. He logged 1,586 minutes with 415 points and 355 rebounds, averaging 5.8 points and five rebounds a game. His field-goal accuracy was limited, and he did not become the long-term center of the expansion rebuild. Still, that volume of playing time had obvious utility for a first-year franchise. Avent also supplied forty-two blocks, giving the roster another defensive big man. His prior Orlando minutes cannot be claimed twice, but these Vancouver numbers were earned entirely after the exchange.

sections.heading: The Magic Released Both Incoming Players Within Four Days
sections.body: Orlando's transaction ledger records that Kevin Pritchard was waived on November 2, the day after the trade. Larry Stewart was waived on November 5. Neither made a Magic regular-season appearance from this transaction, so the receiving-team statistical return was zero games. The front office had an opportunity to examine both players without keeping them, but that tryout did not yield depth for Orlando's season. The Magic did not acquire future picks or cash as part of the listed transaction to compensate for the lack of player minutes.

sections.heading: The Immediate Waivers Decide the Historical Verdict
sections.body: The contrast isn't subtle once the two receiving-team outcomes are compared. Vancouver put Avent on the floor for more than fifteen hundred minutes and used him as a starter in thirty-two games. Orlando cut both incoming players before they could contribute to an NBA game. Avent's numbers were not franchise-changing, but they were real output for a team building from scratch. The earlier equal grades treated the Magic's unused roster auditions as comparable value. A Grizzlies win is the better conclusion, grounded in games rather than pretrade expectations.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Grizzlies Win. Vancouver earns B+ for Anthony Avent's seventy-one games, thirty-two starts, 1,586 minutes and 355 rebounds in 1995-96. Orlando receives D+ because both Kevin Pritchard and Larry Stewart were waived before producing a single Magic regular-season appearance. The receiving-team production decisively favors Vancouver over the inherited even verdict.

sections.heading: The Bulls Sold a Reserve Forward to the Warriors for Picks
sections.body: Chicago traded Jason Caffey to Golden State on February 19, 1998, taking back David Vaughn and second-round selections in 1998 and 2000. Caffey had been a bench forward on the Bulls championship teams but wasn't essential to their leading rotation. Golden State needed younger frontcourt players who could grow into larger roles. Chicago wanted draft flexibility while remaining focused on the 1998 title defense. The two second-rounders represented future options rather than guaranteed players, a distinction that matters when tracing the return.

sections.heading: Caffey Became a High-Minute Warriors Forward
sections.body: After the February trade, Caffey played twenty-nine Golden State games in 1997-98, scoring 315 points. He followed with thirty-five games and thirty-two starts in 1998-99, then started fifty-six of seventy-one games in 1999-00. Across those receiving-team seasons he accumulated 135 games, ninety-four starts and 1,475 points. His work on the glass and ability to finish near the rim gave Golden State something resembling a dependable forward rotation. He later continued with Milwaukee, but those Bucks appearances aren't part of the Warriors trade return.

sections.heading: Chicago Waived Vaughn and Later Recycled Its Draft Capital
sections.body: The Bulls waived Vaughn on March 2, 1998, less than two weeks after the agreement. The 1998 second-round pick became No. 34 Shammond Williams, but Chicago traded his rights to Atlanta on draft night as part of another multi-asset transaction. The 2000 pick was No. 32 A.J. Guyton, who did get NBA playing time with Chicago, though he did not become a core starter. These picks retained some utility, particularly as tradable rights, but the Bulls cannot claim Williams's entire future league record as a Chicago playing return.

sections.heading: The Forward's Real Starts Overwhelm Chicago's Direct Return
sections.body: Golden State acquired a forward who started ninety-four games over the following seasons, while Chicago's immediately acquired player lasted days and its picks produced limited direct on-court success. Draft assets can retain value even when their eventual players move elsewhere, which prevents the Bulls from receiving a failing grade. But those secondary transactions should not overshadow the playing time Golden State actually secured. The inherited Bulls win largely misread which receiving team got durable NBA production. A Warriors win is firmly supported by Caffey's three partial seasons.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win. Golden State gets A- for Jason Caffey's 135 games, ninety-four starts and 1,475 points from February 1998 through 2000. Chicago earns C for David Vaughn's immediate waiver and second-round assets that became Shammond Williams and A.J. Guyton. Golden State obtained the actual starting forward, reversing the previous Bulls-favored result.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Swapped a Veteran Guard for Another and a Future Choice
sections.body: The Bucks obtained Sam Vincent and a 1994 second-round selection from Orlando on August 4, 1992, sending Lester Conner to the Magic. Milwaukee had struggled to establish a winning backcourt combination and wanted a veteran option together with deferred draft rights. Orlando preferred Conner's defense and experience as it built a roster around emerging young talent. The future draft pick was not a guaranteed NBA rotation player; it represented the right to choose a prospect two summers after the clubs exchanged the guards.

sections.heading: Vincent and Conner Represented Shorter-Term Guard Coverage
sections.body: Vincent and Conner were both established NBA guards, not newcomers selected in the lottery. By the time of this exchange, each was moving through the later years of his professional career. The Bucks looked for ball handling and shooting through Vincent, while Orlando gained a defender in Conner. Neither became a long-term cornerstone for his receiving team, and the franchise roster trajectories were shaped much more by later draft selections and changes around the frontcourt. Their earlier NBA playing totals shouldn't be transferred to their new teams.

sections.heading: The No. 46 Pick Became Voshon Lenard, But Not Milwaukee Points
sections.body: Orlando's transferred second-round selection eventually became No. 46 Voshon Lenard in the 1994 draft. Lenard did not join the NBA immediately, retaining his college eligibility for 1994-95 before beginning his league career with Miami the following season. He later made a name for himself as an outside shooter for the Heat and Nuggets. None of those games were Bucks receiving-team production. Milwaukee acquired a real draft-rights option, yet the long-term professional success of the person selected doesn't prove its own roster gained that scorer.

sections.heading: Both Sides Obtained Limited Veteran Options
sections.body: Orlando traded away a future selection but got the guard it wanted for its immediate roster. Milwaukee received Vincent and a second-round right that it eventually used on a player who never logged an NBA game for the Bucks. There were sensible reasons for each club to value the exchange differently at the time. Retrospectively, neither receiving-team return appears large enough for an enthusiastic win grade. Equal modest grades are more appropriate than treating Lenard's later Miami production as if Milwaukee had developed him into a regular Bucks scorer.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Milwaukee earns C+ for a veteran guard option in Sam Vincent and the 1994 No. 46 rights used on Voshon Lenard, who never played a Bucks NBA regular season. Orlando also earns C+ for receiving Lester Conner as veteran backcourt depth. The later success of Lenard with Miami cannot justify the original stronger Bucks-win grade.

sections.heading: Cleveland Acquired a Former Mid-First-Round Forward
sections.body: The Cavaliers received Cedric Simmons from the Hornets on September 29, 2007, sending veteran guard David Wesley to New Orleans. Simmons had been selected fifteenth overall in the 2006 NBA draft, and Cleveland saw an opportunity to evaluate a younger power forward with defensive potential. The original imported transaction also lists cash on the New Orleans side, although club transaction histories describe the player swap without specifying a payment. This was a roster and financial adjustment for both teams, not an exchange of established frontcourt starters.

sections.heading: Simmons Played Seven Cleveland Games Before Another Trade
sections.body: The Cavaliers gave Simmons only seven regular-season appearances in 2007-08, without a start. He averaged 9.7 minutes and 0.6 points, a total of roughly sixty-eight minutes and four points. Cleveland also assigned him to its developmental affiliate while looking for ways to use its deep bench. He was then included in a larger February 2008 three-team deal that brought multiple veterans to the Cavaliers. His contract was one of several outgoing assets, so the later exchange's entire return cannot be credited to Simmons alone.

sections.heading: Wesley Never Played a New Orleans Regular-Season Game
sections.body: Wesley was a familiar Hornets veteran from years earlier in his career, but the September 2007 acquisition did not become a playing reunion. On October 29, before the regular season, New Orleans sent his contract to New Jersey for Mile Ilić and Bernard Robinson. The Hornets waived both incoming players that same day. That onward transaction illustrates limited use as a movable contract, not a route to NBA points or starts. Wesley's earlier Hornets career and Cleveland experience both belong to periods before this particular trade.

sections.heading: Small Playing Return Versus Brief Contract Flexibility
sections.body: Cleveland got a former first-round forward and tried him in seven games before using his contract in a later transaction. New Orleans received a veteran contract it could immediately move, while the two players in the next exchange were waived. Neither side gained lasting rotation depth. The original B grades appear too generous given the minimal direct basketball results. It would be equally misleading to award Cleveland a decisive win for Simmons's handful of outings or to invent an amount for the disputed cash component. Matching modest grades reflect the evidence.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Cleveland receives C+ for Cedric Simmons's seven games and roughly sixty-eight minutes before another transaction. New Orleans earns C+ for briefly using David Wesley's contract in a subsequent October exchange, with the originally recorded cash component unquantified. Neither team received an enduring rotation player, so the inherited matching B grades overstated both sides.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Acquired the Rights to a Florida State Guard
sections.body: On June 25, 1997, the Clippers transferred a future 1998 second-round selection to Philadelphia and acquired the rights to James Collins, a guard selected from Florida State. The 76ers' transaction ledger identifies Collins as the 36th overall pick. Los Angeles hoped to add another perimeter scorer to a roster changing after a playoff appearance, while Philadelphia was willing to delay its return until the next draft. The deal was a straightforward player-rights-for-pick exchange, not a direct trade for Eric Snow. That later connection emerged only because the Sixers retained control of the acquired 1998 selection.

sections.heading: Collins Played Twenty-Three Games for the Clippers
sections.body: Collins reached the NBA as a Los Angeles rookie in 1997-98, appearing in 23 regular-season games. His contribution totaled 103 minutes, 59 points and 14 rebounds, with no starts. He did make nine three-pointers at a good percentage, but the team had little ongoing use for him during a 17-65 season. He never played another NBA regular-season year for the Clippers or any other franchise. His 1997 draft position and college shooting ability offered scouting upside, yet the receiving team obtained only a handful of reserve shifts from the acquisition.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Turned the Future Selection Into Eric Snow
sections.body: The 76ers' return proved far more important through a documented second transaction. On January 18, 1998, Philadelphia sent its newly acquired 1998 second-round pick to Seattle for guard Eric Snow. The SuperSonics used that same selection at No. 33 on Jelani McCoy in the June draft. Therefore McCoy's NBA career should not be counted for the Sixers, who had already exchanged the pick for a proven player. Snow became a regular defensive and playmaking presence beside Allen Iverson, and he was part of the Philadelphia roster that reached the 2001 NBA Finals. The pick was the entire consideration in the Snow deal, making the asset chain unusually direct.

sections.heading: The Sixers Extracted Far More From a Late Draft Asset
sections.body: Los Angeles got a short rookie audition from Collins, while Philadelphia moved a future second-round pick it acquired in that deal to obtain several seasons of NBA guard contribution. The Snow trade occurred months later and must be named separately, rather than simplifying the story into Collins being swapped straight for Snow. Still, Philadelphia's front office transformed the original outgoing draft rights into a meaningful long-term player. The Clippers could justify taking a chance on a productive college guard, but only 103 NBA minutes followed. With that full, sourced asset history, the earlier narrow Sixers-win grade substantially understated the difference in realized basketball results.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win. Philadelphia earns A because the 1998 second-round pick received for James Collins was used in a separate January 1998 trade to acquire Eric Snow, a long-serving starter and member of the 2001 Finals team. Los Angeles receives C for Collins's 23 games, 103 minutes and 59 points. Seattle, not Philadelphia, later drafted Jelani McCoy with the transferred No. 33 pick.

sections.heading: Vancouver Wanted Shooting; Houston Wanted a Future Draft Choice
sections.body: On October 28, 1997, Houston sent swingman Sam Mack to the Vancouver Grizzlies for a future second-round selection. The contemporary Houston Roundball Review archive described the return as a conditional 1999 or 2000 second-rounder. The Rockets had a crowded wing rotation and limited minutes available to Mack, while Vancouver wanted someone who could start and shoot from distance. The modern Memphis team identifier refers to the franchise's Vancouver period. The agreement did not immediately deliver another NBA player to Houston, but it secured a tradable future pick that would eventually matter in a larger transaction.

sections.heading: Mack Played Seventy-Six Grizzlies Games in Two Seasons
sections.body: Mack quickly moved into the Vancouver starting lineup. He appeared in 57 Grizzlies games in 1997-98, starting 54 and scoring 616 points while making 110 three-pointers. In the shortened 1998-99 season, he started 15 of 19 Vancouver games and added 242 points and 42 made threes before being traded back to Houston. Across the two original seasons his incoming Grizzlies stint totaled 76 appearances, 69 starts and 858 points. That was more than a fringe roster experiment: the team acquired a regular floor-spacing wing for an organization still seeking stable offensive production.

sections.heading: Houston Used the Future Selection in the Scottie Pippen Exchange
sections.body: The pick Houston acquired did not remain with the Rockets until the 2000 draft. In January 1999, Houston packaged that future second-rounder together with Roy Rogers in a transaction with Chicago involving Scottie Pippen. The pick ultimately became No. 33 in 2000, when the Bulls selected Connecticut center Jake Voskuhl. The Rockets never drafted Voskuhl and must not receive his later Chicago or Phoenix NBA games as trade production. Equally, the entire value of Pippen's Rockets stint cannot be assigned to the second-rounder in isolation because the separate trade also contained other compensation. Nevertheless, the pick was a documented component of a consequential star acquisition.

sections.heading: Both Clubs Had Defensible Returns, With Vancouver Ahead
sections.body: Vancouver obtained what it needed immediately: 76 games, substantial starts and perimeter scoring from Mack. Houston chose the longer view and used the conditional draft choice as part of a later trade for an established veteran rather than selecting an inexpensive reserve itself. That downstream use was meaningful and prevents treating the Rockets' return as worthless. At the same time, the Grizzlies have the cleaner direct record of on-court production from the original transaction, including nearly 1,991 regular-season minutes over two campaigns. Houston's inherited D+ failed to recognize the pick's real later utility, while the Grizzlies deserve a stronger grade for the player they actually acquired.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Grizzlies Win. Vancouver earns B+ for Sam Mack's 76 games, 69 starts and 858 points in his first two seasons with the franchise. Houston receives B- because the 1999-or-2000 second-round pick became part of a later package used to obtain Scottie Pippen. Chicago ultimately selected Jake Voskuhl at No. 33, so his NBA career is not Rockets return from this transaction.

sections.heading: The Clippers Turned One Veteran Guard Into Two Experienced Reserves
sections.body: Los Angeles sent Avery Bradley to Memphis on February 7, 2019, acquiring Garrett Temple and JaMychal Green in return. The Clippers were playing toward a playoff berth while also adjusting their longer-term roster, and adding a forward who could rebound and shoot fit their frontcourt needs. Temple offered perimeter defense and secondary guard minutes. Memphis was reshaping its personnel after moving away from parts of its established veteran core. Bradley gave the Grizzlies a known defensive guard, but this was a short midseason transaction rather than a trade built around a franchise cornerstone.

sections.heading: Both New Clippers Played Through the 2019 Playoff Push
sections.body: Temple appeared in 26 Clippers regular-season games after the trade, including six starts. Green added 24 games and averaged 8.7 points and 6.5 rebounds while making better than 41 percent of his three-point shots. The two also appeared in Los Angeles's six-game first-round playoff series against Golden State. Green provided a particularly useful small-ball frontcourt option against a difficult opponent, while Temple offered dependable defensive possessions. Their 2018-19 Memphis statistics before February do not belong to the Clippers, but their posttrade games supplied the depth Los Angeles had sought.

sections.heading: Green Stayed Another Year While Bradley Did Not Remain in Memphis
sections.body: Green returned to the Clippers for 2019-20 and appeared in 63 more regular-season games, adding another 1,307 minutes. Across his first two Clippers seasons, the direct result was 87 regular-season appearances and a recurring reserve role. Temple departed after the initial spring, so only his 26 Los Angeles games count. Bradley, meanwhile, played 14 games for the Grizzlies after arriving in February. He was an active contributor during that stretch, but moved to the Lakers the following summer. His later Los Angeles Lakers work is not Memphis production, and Green's subsequent Denver seasons are likewise separate.

sections.heading: The Multi-Season Forward Return Gave Los Angeles the Advantage
sections.body: Memphis obtained a competent guard for the remainder of 2018-19, which explains why the deal cannot fairly be scored as zero on its side. Los Angeles acquired two rotation-capable veterans, then retained one through the next season. The deciding difference was not the number of people named in the trade but Green's continued rebounding, floor spacing and postseason utility in a Clippers uniform. This was a practical roster win for a team pursuing playoff success, not evidence that Memphis gave up a future All-Star. The inherited Clippers-favored result remains valid, with a modest reduction of the Memphis grade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win. Los Angeles earns A- for Temple's 26-game stint and Green's 24-game spring followed by another 63 regular-season games in 2019-20. Memphis receives C+ for Bradley's 14 games before he left. The Clippers obtained the longer-lasting player and better postseason frontcourt flexibility from the exchange.

sections.heading: Orlando Purchased Wing Help at the 2020 Trade Deadline
sections.body: On February 6, 2020, the Magic sent a second-round draft selection to Philadelphia for James Ennis III. Orlando's official team announcement identified the outgoing choice as a 2020 second-rounder originally owed by the Los Angeles Lakers. At the time, the Magic wanted someone with defensive length and enough perimeter shooting to support a roster whose scoring had lagged behind the league average. Ennis was a veteran who had appeared in 49 games for the 76ers earlier that season. The arrangement was a straightforward veteran-for-pick swap, not a multi-player salary dump.

sections.heading: Ennis Helped Orlando Immediately and Returned the Next Season
sections.body: Ennis joined Orlando's wing rotation during the last stretch of the 2019-20 schedule, including the interrupted season's restart, and was available for its postseason series. He was neither the main scorer nor a franchise centerpiece, but provided the toughness, athleticism and floor spacing cited by the Magic's front office when it made the deal. Ennis also played for Orlando in 2020-21, extending the return beyond a one-month rental. His 49 Philadelphia games before February belong to the Sixers, while the games he played after joining Orlando are the Magic's proper acquired-team contribution.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Turned the Incoming Selection Into Paul Reed
sections.body: The 76ers used the acquired 2020 second-round pick at No. 58 to select Paul Reed, a DePaul forward-center. Reed began as an end-of-bench option, appearing 26 times in 2020-21 and 38 times in 2021-22. His role grew to 69 games in 2022-23 and 82 games in 2023-24, totaling 215 Philadelphia regular-season appearances over those four seasons. He also supplied playoff frontcourt minutes as a reserve behind Joel Embiid. This is the documented pick's basketball payoff, not an unrelated draft choice credited to the same year.

sections.heading: The Pick's Long-Term Return Edged Orlando's Short-Term Defense
sections.body: Orlando achieved a reasonable immediate objective by adding a veteran wing for a playoff push, and Ennis stayed available in its rotation beyond that season. Philadelphia, however, received an inexpensive center whose NBA usefulness expanded for several years after the trade. Reed's growth from a late second-round selection into a regular defensive and rebounding reserve gave the Sixers a more enduring outcome. The deal isn't a failure for Orlando because the Magic actually used Ennis; it is a Philadelphia win because the transferred selection became a player the club employed through multiple playoff cycles.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win. Philadelphia earns A- for the No. 58 pick that became Paul Reed, who played 215 regular-season games over four Sixers seasons and developed into an active playoff reserve. Orlando gets B for Ennis's immediate wing minutes and additional work in 2020-21. Philadelphia secured the more durable basketball result, while Orlando did receive meaningful short-term help.

sections.heading: The Hawks and Grizzlies Exchanged Expiring Forward Contracts
sections.body: Memphis moved Chandler Parsons to Atlanta in a July 2019 transaction, taking Solomon Hill and Miles Plumlee in return. The trade was recorded in the team ledgers on July 8, while some draft and roster chronologies place negotiations a day earlier. Both organizations were moving veterans with sizable contracts rather than swapping emerging stars. Memphis sought players who might actually provide wing or interior depth during its young rebuilding season. Atlanta accepted an opportunity to examine Parsons, whose Grizzlies tenure had been limited by recurring injuries.

sections.heading: Hill Supplied Forty-Eight Regular-Season Games for Memphis
sections.body: Hill became the meaningful basketball return for Memphis. In the first portion of 2019-20 he appeared in 48 regular-season games, starting three, and averaged 5.7 points while playing 18.8 minutes per night. His outside shooting and defensive coverage provided veteran support around a young rotation. The Grizzlies later included Hill in a different multi-team deadline transaction, so his games after leaving Memphis belong to another franchise. The club also acquired Plumlee in the July deal, but waived him in October before he could play a regular-season Memphis game.

sections.heading: Parsons' Atlanta Career Lasted Five Brief Appearances
sections.body: Parsons remained an NBA player on Atlanta's books during the 2019-20 season, but his availability was severely limited. He appeared in five Hawks games without a start, logging only 54 total minutes and averaging 2.8 points. His injury history and previous productive Houston and Dallas seasons offered a reason Atlanta might have been interested in a low-risk roster option. Those earlier accomplishments weren't transferred to the Hawks. With only five short outings, Atlanta received virtually no on-court production from the forward acquired in exchange for two veterans.

sections.heading: A Useful Wing Stint Beat a Little-Used Former Scorer
sections.body: Neither franchise landed a long-term star, and the deal shouldn't be celebrated as a decisive rebuilding achievement. But Memphis did get forty-eight games of wing depth and could use Hill within a later separate roster move. Atlanta got an injured veteran who played only a handful of minutes. The value gap is larger than the inherited comparison suggested for the Hawks, although the Grizzlies' original B+ is also strong for a player they kept only part of one season. An adjusted Memphis win credits the real production while acknowledging that Plumlee contributed no NBA games.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Grizzlies Win. Memphis earns B for Solomon Hill's 48 regular-season games and 5.7 points per game, while Miles Plumlee was waived before appearing. Atlanta receives D+ because Chandler Parsons played only five Hawks games and 54 minutes. The club-specific record supports a clear Memphis edge without counting other teams' later player production.

sections.heading: Indiana Sold the No. 50 Rights for Cash and an Unconditional Pick
sections.body: The Pacers selected Jarrell Brantley from the College of Charleston with the fiftieth choice in the 2019 NBA draft, then traded his rights to Utah. Indiana's official announcement, released June 21, identifies the return as cash considerations plus an unconditional second-round selection in 2021. That is stronger compensation than cash alone because the club secured another chance to draft a player without needing a protected condition to be met. Utah wanted an athletic forward it could develop within its own system, while the Pacers collected two modest future-building assets.

sections.heading: Brantley Reached the Utah Roster as a Deep Reserve
sections.body: Brantley made his NBA debut for the Jazz and remained under their control across the next two seasons. He played nine regular-season games in 2019-20, followed by 28 appearances in 2020-21, totaling 37 NBA games for Utah. His role was limited, mostly behind established playoff contributors, and he did not become a reliable starting forward. The Jazz also developed him through their minor-league program. Those developmental assignments can help explain why the club valued the rights, but only the actual Utah NBA appearances should count as acquired league output.

sections.heading: The Pacers Received a Later Draft Choice Without a Protection Risk
sections.body: Indiana's return included the unconditional 2021 second-rounder, providing a guaranteed selection independent of Utah's eventual win total or draft position. The choice reached the late second round in 2021. The Pacers also secured cash at the time of the exchange, though the official news release did not state a dollar amount. It would be an error to credit Indiana with the professional accomplishments of every player who later held the pick or of another team that may have acquired the rights. The asset's immediate importance was a real future draft position plus a financial payment.

sections.heading: The Clubs Chose Different Forms of Second-Round Value
sections.body: The Jazz acquired a fringe NBA forward they could develop and briefly deploy, giving them actual playing minutes from a late draft pick. Indiana preferred flexibility: cash immediately and another second-round choice two years later. Neither organization uncovered a cornerstone, and Brantley's relatively short NBA stint doesn't justify a decisive Utah victory. Conversely, Indiana's pick and payment should not be dismissed because the Pacers didn't receive an established veteran on draft night. The best retrospective treats the exchange as broadly balanced, with a slightly stronger Indiana asset grade and the Jazz credited for getting Brantley into games.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Indiana earns B- for obtaining cash plus an unconditional 2021 second-round selection when it sold Jarrell Brantley's draft rights. Utah earns C+ because Brantley reached the Jazz rotation for 37 games across two seasons but did not hold a regular starting role. Both teams received limited but genuine value from a late second-round agreement.

sections.heading: Memphis Bought Seattle's Newly Drafted Guard
sections.body: On June 24, 2004, the Memphis Grizzlies obtained the draft rights to Texas Tech wing Andre Emmett after Seattle selected him with the thirty-fifth overall choice. Memphis paid cash and surrendered a second-round selection in the 2005 draft. The Grizzlies' official historical transaction record confirms both parts of the compensation. Emmett had been a prolific college scorer, making him an attractive second-round candidate. Seattle instead preferred the financial payment and another chance to select a prospect one year later. No established NBA rotation player changed teams on draft night.

sections.heading: Emmett's Grizzlies Stint Lasted Eight Regular-Season Games
sections.body: Emmett signed with Memphis during July 2004 and joined the organization for his rookie season, but his NBA opportunities were limited. He appeared in eight Grizzlies regular-season games in 2004-05 and never became a dependable rotation wing. He later left the team in a separate multi-club transaction and pursued opportunities elsewhere in basketball. His college points and professional performances after Memphis are not receiving-team output created by this exchange. The club got a genuine player audition, though an extremely small number of NBA appearances for the rights it had purchased.

sections.heading: Seattle Turned the 2005 Selection Into Gelabale
sections.body: The 2005 second-rounder arrived at No. 48, and Seattle selected French forward Mickaël Gelabale. He continued overseas for another season before joining the SuperSonics, then appeared in 70 games in 2006-07 and 39 more in 2007-08. His 109 Seattle appearances were a delayed but measurable return on the incoming pick, alongside the money the team had already collected. The timing matters: Gelabale was selected in 2005 and debuted in the NBA in 2006, not as an immediate piece of the 2004 Memphis trade. That chain is fully documented by draft records.

sections.heading: The Sonics Won Through a More Useful Follow-Up Pick
sections.body: Memphis acquired a scorer worth investigating but did not find a lasting NBA contributor. Seattle accepted the risk of a future second-round selection and received a reserve wing who eventually played far more games in a SuperSonics uniform than Emmett did for Memphis. Neither athlete became a star, and Gelabale's later appearances outside the Seattle franchise aren't part of this return. Still, a 109-game reserve plus cash was a better outcome than an eight-game audition. The original equal grades overlooked the delayed draft pick and should favor Seattle without exaggerating either side's value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: SuperSonics Win. Seattle earns B+ for the cash payment and the 2005 No. 48 pick that became Mickaël Gelabale, who played 109 SuperSonics regular-season games. Memphis receives D+ because Andre Emmett played only eight Grizzlies games after the rights purchase. The original 2004 draft choice was less valuable than the delayed selection Seattle acquired.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Acquired a Veteran Shooter With a Conditional Pick
sections.body: On August 11, 2009, the Clippers acquired Rasual Butler from the New Orleans Hornets along with cash considerations. The payment going the other direction was a conditional second-round selection in 2016. Butler had started regularly for New Orleans in the preceding season and was known for shooting from the perimeter. Los Angeles needed an experienced wing who could fill substantial minutes during a difficult roster transition. New Orleans, by contrast, was managing its player contracts and future flexibility. The incoming pick was protected rather than guaranteed, an important detail for what eventually happened.

sections.heading: Butler Played and Started Throughout His First Clippers Season
sections.body: Butler appeared in all 82 Los Angeles regular-season games during 2009-10, starting 64. He averaged 11.9 points in 33.0 minutes and served as one of the Clippers' principal outside shooters. This was not a deep-bench contract or a short preseason audition; the club acquired a regular starter capable of playing heavy wing minutes. His previous Hornets production cannot be counted as part of Los Angeles's return, but the full season that followed the August trade supplies ample evidence that the new team received immediate value. The Clippers obtained a known player rather than waiting for an uncertain prospect.

sections.heading: The Clippers Kept Another Forty-One Games of Production
sections.body: Butler returned for 2010-11, when his Clippers role declined to 41 appearances, two starts and 744 minutes, averaging 5.0 points. He later finished that season with Chicago, a separate team whose numbers should not inflate the acquisition. Across his Los Angeles stint, the original trade brought 123 regular-season games and 3,446 minutes of wing depth. Although his second year was weaker, it adds genuine roster use beyond a one-year rental. The first-season starting role remains the most important part of the return.

sections.heading: The Hornets Never Collected the Protected 2016 Selection
sections.body: The conditional 2016 second-rounder did not convey under its protections, so New Orleans received no draftee or replacement selection from this deal. Shedding Butler's contract may have served financial objectives, but a precise payroll benefit is not independently established by the trade ledger. Los Angeles received a full-time starter for one year and a reserve for part of another, plus cash. Those outcomes are markedly more valuable than the old modest Clippers grade suggested. The comparison doesn't require blaming the Hornets for all of Butler's earlier salary or asserting that a phantom second-round pick turned into another NBA player.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win. Los Angeles earns A- for Rasual Butler's 123 games and 3,446 minutes across two Clippers seasons, including 64 starts and an 11.9-point average in 2009-10. New Orleans gets D+ because its conditional 2016 second-round pick never conveyed. The receiving-team playing and cash return favored Los Angeles decisively.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Acquired a Guard With More Development Time
sections.body: The Lakers obtained Tyler Ennis and the draft rights to Australian wing Brad Newley from Houston on February 23, 2017, sending Marcelo Huertas to the Rockets. Los Angeles's official release and the league's deadline tracker list both incoming assets. Ennis had appeared in 31 Rockets games earlier in the season but hadn't secured a regular role behind the main scorers. The Lakers had just reshuffled their basketball leadership, giving the organization reason to evaluate another young point guard. Newley's rights offered a theoretical additional option, although he was continuing a successful international career.

sections.heading: Ennis Immediately Played Twenty-Two Lakers Games
sections.body: Ennis took advantage of the Los Angeles opening and appeared in 22 regular-season games to close 2016-17, starting twice. He averaged 7.7 points and 2.4 assists while totaling 392 minutes for his new club. Those games were enough to persuade the Lakers to re-sign him in July, according to an official NBA announcement. That extension is important because the February acquisition was not simply a brief roster shuffle. Ennis was a real point-guard option rather than an unused expiring contract, and his 31 earlier Rockets games should not be included in his Lakers return.

sections.heading: Another Fifty-Four Games Followed Before Ennis Left
sections.body: Ennis returned for 2017-18 and played 54 more Los Angeles regular-season games, including eleven starts and 683 minutes. His scoring average decreased to 4.1 points in a shorter nightly role, but he remained available behind other young guards. Across both receiving-team seasons, the original trade yielded 76 Lakers games and 1,075 minutes. Brad Newley continued playing overseas and never joined an NBA Lakers rotation, so his rights shouldn't be credited with extra league statistics. Ennis was the meaningful on-court asset Los Angeles acquired.

sections.heading: Houston's Incoming Player Didn't Make a Regular-Season Contribution
sections.body: Huertas had provided veteran point-guard play to the Lakers earlier in his NBA career, appearing in 76 games across the preceding season. That work belonged to Los Angeles before the deal. After Houston acquired him, the Rockets did not use Huertas in a regular-season game and moved on from the contract. The difference between an unused incoming guard and two partial seasons of Ennis is enough to justify a decisive Lakers win. The original Lakers grade of D treated a legitimate 76-game return too harshly, while Houston's poor basketball return remained a minor reserve acquisition rather than a major franchise error.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win. Los Angeles earns B because Tyler Ennis played 76 regular-season games and 1,075 minutes across two seasons after the deal; Brad Newley's international rights never produced NBA appearances. Houston receives D+ because Marcelo Huertas played no Rockets regular-season games. The Lakers found a useful reserve while Houston's player return went unused.

sections.heading: The Kings Preferred Two Players to One Veteran Frontcourt Reserve
sections.body: The Sacramento Kings traded Frank Brickowski to Seattle on September 18, 1995, receiving Šarūnas Marčiulionis and Byron Houston in return. The deal offered Sacramento a veteran international guard capable of handling offensive possessions plus another frontcourt reserve. Seattle was constructing a deep rotation around Gary Payton, Shawn Kemp and coach George Karl, and valued Brickowski's experience as a backup big man who could handle physical matchups. Both clubs exchanged known NBA players, making this a direct roster trade rather than a speculative draft-rights arrangement. No draft selection was part of the September agreement.

sections.heading: Marčiulionis Became an Actual Kings Scoring Contributor
sections.body: Marčiulionis played 53 Sacramento regular-season games in 1995-96, averaging 10.8 points with 2.2 assists. He also appeared in the team's four playoff games, when the Kings lost their first-round series to Seattle. Sacramento's other acquisition, Houston, made 25 regular-season appearances and logged 276 minutes, adding 86 points and 84 rebounds. The two players supplied different kinds of support, although neither remained a central long-term starter. Marčiulionis subsequently moved to Denver in a separate package transaction, so the full later value of Mahmoud Abdul-Rauf shouldn't be assigned solely to this original Seattle trade.

sections.heading: Brickowski Provided Seattle With Frontcourt and Playoff Depth
sections.body: Brickowski appeared in 63 SuperSonics regular-season games during 1995-96, scoring 339 points and grabbing 151 rebounds in 986 minutes. Seattle went 64-18 and reached the NBA Finals against Chicago, and Brickowski played in all 21 of the club's postseason contests. He contributed 206 playoff minutes and 41 points, mainly in backup frontcourt shifts. That is useful roster service for a team that advanced through three rounds of Western Conference opponents. Brickowski's playing time shouldn't be inflated into a starting-star role, but his availability during a Finals campaign gave the acquired center direct competitive value.

sections.heading: Sacramento's Scoring and Seattle's Playoff Minutes Balanced Out
sections.body: The Kings obtained an experienced scorer and limited reserve size, while Seattle secured a physical bench player who remained usable deep into the postseason. Neither organization gained an overwhelming advantage. Sacramento's side had stronger regular-season scoring from Marčiulionis, but Brickowski's 21 playoff appearances for a Finals team weigh heavily in the Sonics' return. The prior Kings-win verdict and unequal grades discounted Seattle's contribution too sharply. A balanced assessment rewards the meaningful receiving-team work on both sides without attributing the eventual championships or later trades to either incoming player alone.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Sacramento gets B for Marčiulionis's 53 games and 10.8 points per game, plus Byron Houston's 25 reserve appearances. Seattle also gets B after Brickowski played 63 regular-season games and all 21 postseason games during the 1996 Finals run. The two teams found useful veterans in different roles, supporting equal grades.

sections.heading: Washington Exchanged Its Team Captain for Two Second-Round Chances
sections.body: On June 17, 1985, the Washington Bullets sent Greg Ballard to the Golden State Warriors for the No. 31 selection in the next day's NBA draft and an additional 1987 second-round choice. A contemporary Washington Post account confirms both draft assets. Ballard had been a reliable Washington starter and its team captain, making the trade a meaningful personnel change rather than a routine end-of-bench move. Golden State wanted a proven forward; Washington preferred flexibility as it rebuilt its frontcourt around different players.

sections.heading: Ballard Provided Two Full Warriors Seasons of Experience
sections.body: Ballard was a genuine contributor for Golden State. During 1985-86 he appeared in seventy-five games, logged 1,792 minutes and recorded 662 points and 417 rebounds. He played all eighty-two games the following season, adding 579 points and 340 rebounds in 1,579 minutes. The combined Warriors return was 157 games, 3,371 minutes, 1,241 points and 757 rebounds. Those figures justify a good receiving-team grade. His previous years in Washington, however, do not become additional Golden State value from the trade.

sections.heading: The Thirty-First Pick Became Manute Bol and a Historic Defensive Season
sections.body: Washington spent its incoming No. 31 pick on Manute Bol, a 7-foot-7 center who had played at Bridgeport. The rookie instantly changed opponents' shots around the basket, appearing in eighty games in 1985-86 and recording 397 blocked shots. He led the league at roughly five blocks a game and earned All-Defensive Second Team recognition. Bol remained with the Bullets for three seasons, providing a degree of defensive impact beyond what most second-round picks deliver. That rookie season alone gave the acquired choice a substantial return.

sections.heading: The Later Pick Was Another Asset, but Bol Decided the Comparison
sections.body: The second selection in Washington's package ultimately became No. 36 Duane Washington in the 1987 draft. The historical ledger should recognize that incoming right without assigning unrelated NBA games to the Bullets. Golden State's two useful Ballard seasons were far from a failure; he served as a dependable veteran and helped its rotation. Yet Washington turned the first second-round pick into one of the most distinctive shot blockers in NBA history, while also retaining a later choice. That sporting return exceeds the valuable but shorter Ballard stint.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bullets Win. Washington earns A+ for Manute Bol's 397-block rookie season and subsequent Bullets center contributions, plus the 1987 second-round choice. Golden State receives B for Greg Ballard's 157 Warriors games, 3,371 minutes, 1,241 points and 757 rebounds. The Warriors found a useful veteran, but Bol's extraordinary immediate defensive impact made the Washington draft return better.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Bought Experienced Frontcourt Depth During December
sections.body: The Milwaukee Bucks obtained Chucky Brown from Phoenix on December 4, 1996, sending Darrin Hancock and a conditional second-round draft selection in return. Brown had joined the Suns months earlier in the much bigger Charles Barkley transaction and was not playing a major role there. Milwaukee wanted a veteran who could defend forwards and offer reserve minutes. Phoenix accepted a developing wing and a contingent draft chance. Contemporary reporting and both clubs' transaction ledgers confirm the deal's direction and protections.

sections.heading: Brown Played Sixty Milwaukee Games and Stayed Available
sections.body: Brown immediately became the more useful player in the exchange. He appeared in sixty Bucks regular-season games during the remainder of 1996-97, starting once and logging 674 minutes. He shot better than fifty percent from the floor and provided flexible support at forward when Milwaukee needed a substitute. His earlier ten Phoenix games occurred before the swap and do not contribute to the Bucks' receiving-team totals. A sixty-game season of bench coverage is a legitimate return for a fringe forward and a conditional pick.

sections.heading: Phoenix Waived Hancock and Never Collected the Draft Pick
sections.body: Hancock had struggled to earn minutes in Milwaukee before the transaction and did not find a longer home with the Suns. Phoenix waived him on December 11, only one week after acquiring him, without a regular-season Phoenix appearance. Meanwhile the conditional second-round obligation did not convey, a detail explicitly recorded in both franchise transaction histories. No player chosen in the next draft can be credited to the Suns under this agreement. Phoenix essentially exchanged a usable forward for a brief roster evaluation and a future draft condition that expired.

sections.heading: A Real Sixty-Game Contributor Defeats an Unexercised Option
sections.body: The Bucks did not find a new starter, but they obtained reserve playing time over much of the season without sacrificing a pick that ultimately left the club. Phoenix could rationally explore younger wings, yet Hancock departed almost immediately and the draft option produced nothing. The earlier equal B grades incorrectly treated a nonconveyed choice as comparable to real NBA appearances. Brown's contribution is modest rather than transformational, but it is demonstrably stronger than an unused contract and a conditional selection that never transferred.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win. Milwaukee earns B for Chucky Brown's sixty regular-season games, 674 minutes and useful veteran frontcourt coverage after the December 1996 trade. Phoenix receives D+ because Darrin Hancock was waived within a week without a Suns appearance, while the conditional second-round pick never conveyed. The only realized NBA playing return went to Milwaukee.

sections.heading: New York Acquired a Former All-Star for Its Stretch Run
sections.body: The Knicks sent Herb Williams and Ron Grandison to Philadelphia on February 19, 1998, acquiring veteran power forward Terry Cummings. Cummings was no longer the high-volume scorer he had been earlier in his career, but the Knicks were looking for bench help behind a roster that expected to reach the postseason. Philadelphia was reorganizing several veteran contracts during the same month. The exchange involved three named forwards, without a draft pick or cash consideration, making the subsequent playing time particularly useful for judging each side.

sections.heading: Cummings Logged Thirty Knicks Games and More Than Five Hundred Minutes
sections.body: Cummings appeared in thirty Knicks regular-season games after the deal, starting once and logging 529 minutes. He scored 234 points, collected 135 rebounds and shot 47.7 percent from the field. That worked out to 7.8 points and 4.5 rebounds per appearance, useful numbers in a reserve frontcourt position. The 44 games he had played for Philadelphia before the trade cannot be added to New York's return. His Knicks stint ended after the season, so this was an immediate veteran rental rather than a long-term acquisition.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Waived Both Incoming Players Within Two Days
sections.body: Philadelphia received two players but neither became an NBA contributor for the 76ers. Contemporary news reporting states that the club waived both Herb Williams and Ron Grandison two days after the exchange. The two players' earlier Knicks careers are not Philadelphia production, and they did not log a Sixers regular-season appearance after the deal. The waivers indicate that the transaction served immediate roster management more than a strategy to develop either incoming veteran. Philadelphia received no demonstrated playing return from the two named players.

sections.heading: The Realized Receiving-Team Difference Reverses the Verdict
sections.body: Cummings was a declining player, and the Knicks should not earn credit for his earlier All-Star years in San Diego, Milwaukee or San Antonio. Nevertheless, New York obtained 529 minutes of functional frontcourt help while Philadelphia released both incoming forwards almost immediately. On a team-specific evaluation, that is a straightforward advantage for the Knicks. The original 76ers-win grade appears to have attributed value to a package of names without checking whether those players ever appeared for their new club. A solid, not spectacular, New York grade is justified by the actual games.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win. New York receives B for Terry Cummings's thirty regular-season games, 529 minutes, 234 points and 135 rebounds after his arrival. Philadelphia receives D+ because Herb Williams and Ron Grandison were both waived within two days and provided no 76ers playing time. The incoming veteran was useful only for New York, contradicting the inherited Philadelphia-favored grade.

sections.heading: A February Swap Sent Four Players in Different Directions
sections.body: Vancouver and Sacramento completed a four-player exchange on February 18, 1998. The Grizzlies took point guard Bobby Hurley and forward Michael Smith, while the Kings acquired veteran Otis Thorpe and guard Chris Robinson. Vancouver was trying to build reliable young roles after another losing season. Sacramento wanted veteran interior production and flexibility as it reconsidered its lineup. The trade was a true two-for-two arrangement rather than a cash sale, although the players had dramatically different amounts of NBA experience and future value.

sections.heading: Michael Smith Became a Useful Vancouver Frontcourt Starter
sections.body: Smith played thirty Grizzlies games after the exchange and started twenty-nine, logging 706 minutes. He continued with Vancouver for forty-eight appearances the following season, giving the club a longer frontcourt return than one deadline rental. Hurley also played twenty-seven Grizzlies games in the remainder of 1997-98, contributing 458 minutes as a reserve point guard. Those are actual receiving-team contributions. Smith's earlier Sacramento seasons do not belong to Vancouver, and Hurley's prior Kings career should not be counted twice simply because his uniform changed.

sections.heading: Thorpe Supplied Sacramento Minutes and Later Helped Another Deal
sections.body: Thorpe played twenty-seven Sacramento regular-season games in 1997-98, starting twenty and averaging about 8.3 points with 6.1 rebounds. The veteran forward also retained contract value when Sacramento was preparing a broader roster transformation. In May 1998, the Kings sent Thorpe and longtime star Mitch Richmond to Washington for Chris Webber. That later transaction was a separate two-player package: crediting the entire Webber acquisition solely to Thorpe would be misleading. Nonetheless, Thorpe was one real asset the Kings had obtained only months earlier.

sections.heading: The Immediate Comparison Was Close, but the Kings Had More Leverage
sections.body: Vancouver found a regular starter in Smith and additional guard depth in Hurley, so dismissing its side would ignore useful minutes. Sacramento received a competent veteran frontcourt player, and his later inclusion in the Webber agreement added transactional usefulness. Robinson did not become a long-term Kings contributor and should not be credited with extensive NBA production. The comparison therefore remains closer than a simple Webber story suggests. Keeping a slight Sacramento edge recognizes the longer-term trade possibilities without assigning achievements to assets that came from elsewhere.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Kings Edge. Sacramento earns A- for Otis Thorpe's twenty-seven games, twenty starts and subsequent inclusion alongside Mitch Richmond in the Chris Webber transaction. Vancouver earns B+ for Michael Smith's thirty starts and sustained Grizzlies minutes plus Bobby Hurley's twenty-seven games. The Kings acquired additional leverage, but Webber was not obtained for Thorpe alone.

sections.heading: New Orleans Chose Frontcourt Help Over a Young Scoring Guard
sections.body: The Hornets acquired Carl Landry from Sacramento on February 23, 2011, sending Marcus Thornton and cash to the Kings. New Orleans was looking for reliable bench offense and rebounding as Chris Paul's team prepared for a playoff push. Landry already had several seasons of productive interior scoring. Thornton was a younger guard who could create shots but had not secured a permanent starting role with the Hornets. Sacramento was rebuilding and could offer him more offensive opportunities. The deal was about immediate frontcourt help versus a longer scoring-guard investment.

sections.heading: Landry Contributed Sixty-Four Hornets Games Across Two Seasons
sections.body: Landry played twenty-three regular-season games after joining New Orleans, scoring 272 points and grabbing ninety-four rebounds over 602 minutes. He returned during the shortened 2011-12 campaign for forty-one appearances, 511 points and 214 rebounds. In total he provided sixty-four Hornets games, 783 points and 308 rebounds in 1,601 minutes. That is a solid rotation return for the team that acquired him. His earlier Rockets and Kings points do not belong to New Orleans, and his subsequent Golden State work arose after another move.

sections.heading: Thornton Immediately Produced Twenty-Point Scoring in Sacramento
sections.body: Thornton's scoring rose dramatically once the Kings put the ball in his hands. He played twenty-seven Sacramento games in the rest of 2010-11, starting twenty-three and averaging 21.3 points. In 2011-12 he started all fifty-one appearances and averaged 18.7 points. He was still a double-digit scorer in the following season. These are not hypothetical projections of what he might have become with New Orleans; they are actual Kings performances after the February trade. The cash arriving alongside him made Sacramento's side of the agreement stronger.

sections.heading: Both Teams Received Basketball Value but Sacramento Got More
sections.body: New Orleans addressed a real need and Landry remained useful through the following year, so this was not an empty return or an obviously irrational deadline deal. Sacramento, however, transformed an interior veteran into an active scoring guard who rapidly became one of its primary offensive options. The difference was apparent immediately and lasted beyond the initial post-deadline schedule. The Hornets' 2011 playoff run does not automatically turn Landry into a franchise-altering acquisition. A stronger Sacramento grade reflects the production in the uniforms that the respective teams acquired.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Kings Win. Sacramento earns A- for Marcus Thornton's 21.3-point average in his first twenty-seven Kings games and 18.7 points over fifty-one starts the next season, plus cash. New Orleans gets B because Carl Landry played sixty-four Hornets games and scored 783 points across two seasons. Both players helped, but Thornton provided the greater offensive return.

sections.heading: The Clippers Split One Second-Round Selection Into Two Prospects
sections.body: During the June 23, 2016 draft, the Clippers selected Kansas forward Cheick Diallo at No. 33 and sent his rights to New Orleans. They received two later second-round selections, No. 39 David Michineau and No. 40 Diamond Stone. The Clippers' official announcement confirms the exact transaction and draft positions. Diallo offered energetic rebounding and interior defense. Michineau was a young guard playing in France, and Stone was an American center coming out of Maryland. Los Angeles preferred two chances to develop talent instead of retaining the higher-ranked forward.

sections.heading: Diallo Earned Three Pelicans Seasons of NBA Frontcourt Work
sections.body: Diallo made seventeen New Orleans regular-season appearances as a rookie, then fifty-two in 2017-18 and sixty-four in 2018-19. He totaled 1,676 minutes across those 133 games, with his most active season coming in his third year. His rebounding and finishing made him useful as a young reserve, even though he was not a regular starter. A draft pick in the early second round producing three years of NBA appearances is a measurable success. His later Phoenix games are not New Orleans output from this specific rights acquisition.

sections.heading: The Clippers Got Seven Games From Stone and None From Michineau
sections.body: Stone reached the NBA with Los Angeles but appeared in only seven regular-season games in 2016-17, logging twenty-four minutes and ten points. He did not secure a second Clippers season or become a frontcourt rotation fixture. Michineau continued his professional career outside the NBA and never supplied Clippers regular-season minutes. Their overseas and developmental achievements should not be retroactively credited as Clippers league production. Two draft rights offered more potential paths to success, but neither generated the kind of sustained contribution that Diallo gave New Orleans.

sections.heading: The Higher Pick Produced the More Substantial NBA Return
sections.body: Los Angeles had a reasonable drafting philosophy: exchanging one early second-round pick for two later prospects created additional options without using first-round capital. New Orleans simply chose the player it valued more and invested in his development. The result favors the Pelicans because they actually played their acquired center for three seasons, while the Clippers received only a handful of NBA appearances from Stone. Neither side acquired a star, so the outcome should be graded as a strong reserve return rather than a defining roster transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans Win. New Orleans gets B+ for Cheick Diallo's 133 regular-season games and 1,676 minutes over three seasons after the No. 33 rights purchase. Los Angeles receives D+ because Diamond Stone played just seven games and twenty-four minutes, while David Michineau never appeared for the Clippers. One higher draft choice delivered far more NBA production than the two incoming prospects.

sections.heading: Chicago Bought Point-Guard Depth With a Future Second-Round Pick
sections.body: The Bulls acquired C.J. Watson from Golden State on July 22, 2010, sending a 2011 second-round selection in return. The Warriors also obtained a traded-player exception, a salary-cap mechanism that could help with later moves. Chicago wanted a dependable backup to Derrick Rose as it built a stronger playoff rotation under Tom Thibodeau. Golden State chose a future draft opportunity and financial flexibility over continuing Watson's reserve contract. This was not an exchange of two active NBA guards on the same day.

sections.heading: Watson Covered 131 Chicago Regular-Season Games in Two Years
sections.body: Watson appeared in all eighty-two Bulls games in 2010-11, providing 1,091 minutes, 405 points and 186 assists. During the shortened 2011-12 campaign he played forty-nine more games and started twenty-five, recording 474 points and 200 assists in 1,159 minutes. Combined, his Chicago stint produced 131 regular-season games, 2,250 minutes and 879 points. His role was especially useful when the team needed additional ball handling behind Rose. The Nets and Pacers seasons from later in Watson's career do not belong to this Chicago acquisition.

sections.heading: Golden State Used the Pick on Charles Jenkins
sections.body: The second-round selection reached Golden State as No. 44 in the 2011 draft, when the Warriors selected Hofstra guard Charles Jenkins. Jenkins played fifty-one Warriors regular-season games during the shortened 2011-12 season, starting twenty-eight and logging 893 minutes with 297 points. He returned for forty-seven Warriors appearances in 2012-13 before moving to Philadelphia, where his final twelve games of that year must be kept separate. That is an actual player return rather than a pick that never conveyed, which justifies credit for Golden State's side.

sections.heading: The Bulls Obtained More Consistent Guard Cover, Though Both Clubs Benefited
sections.body: Chicago had Watson available through two competitive regular seasons and playoff runs, collecting more minutes and veteran experience than Golden State received from Jenkins. But Jenkins was also a usable young guard, and the trade exception had value in roster accounting even without crediting an unverified later player to it. The earlier slight Chicago edge recognized the correct direction while underselling the duration of Watson's reserve service. A clearer Bulls advantage with positive grades for both teams reflects what their respective incoming assets actually delivered in NBA games.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win. Chicago earns B+ after C.J. Watson supplied 131 games, 2,250 minutes and 879 points during two seasons as a reserve and occasional starter. Golden State gets B- because No. 44 Charles Jenkins played 98 Warriors games, including 28 rookie starts, and the club also obtained a trade exception. Both returns were real, but Chicago secured more sustained NBA guard coverage.

sections.heading: The Clippers Quickly Recycled Quentin Richardson Into Three Players
sections.body: Los Angeles acquired Quentin Richardson in a separate Zach Randolph trade and moved him again on July 20, 2009, receiving Craig Smith, Sebastian Telfair and Mark Madsen from Minnesota. Richardson had not become a regular-season Clipper. The team preferred inexpensive frontcourt and guard cover over carrying another established wing. Minnesota accepted Richardson as a transferable veteran contract while reorganizing its own roster. This was a three-for-one agreement with no immediate new draft pick, but the individual playing returns ended up very different.

sections.heading: Craig Smith Gave Los Angeles Seventy-Five Productive Games
sections.body: Smith appeared in 75 Clippers regular-season games during 2009-10, starting twice and averaging 7.8 points with 3.8 rebounds. His 16.4 minutes per appearance supplied dependable scoring around the basket for a team with several young interior players. Telfair also played 39 Clippers games, including one start, averaging 4.3 points and 2.9 assists in 14.9 minutes. He eventually moved to Cleveland during a separate February transaction. Their subsequent contributions for other organizations do not belong to this Los Angeles trade, but the Clippers already received a useful collection of bench appearances.

sections.heading: Madsen Was Waived, and Richardson Never Played for Minnesota
sections.body: The third incoming Clipper, Madsen, was waived August 21 before the season. Minnesota did not keep Richardson long enough to receive league minutes from him either. On August 13, it traded the forward to Miami in return for Mark Blount, an agreement confirmed by the Heat's contemporaneous announcement. Blount's contract was a financial and roster-management asset, but his earlier Miami statistics are not Timberwolves basketball production. Richardson's 2009-10 appearances were made with the Heat, so they cannot be assigned to Minnesota merely because it briefly held his contract.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Received Actual Minutes While Minnesota Continued Rearranging Contracts
sections.body: The Clippers clearly benefited from securing two players who could participate in their rotation, even though a third incoming veteran was released before opening night. Minnesota viewed Richardson as a short-term contract asset and converted him into another veteran's contract within weeks. That onward transaction was real rather than a total loss, but it did not result in the immediate playing contributions Los Angeles obtained from Smith and Telfair. The inherited Clippers-favored winner remains appropriate. Its advantage rests on the 114 combined Clippers appearances, not Richardson's later Miami performances or an imagined Minnesota season.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win. Los Angeles retains A- after Craig Smith supplied 75 games and 7.8 points per game, while Sebastian Telfair added 39 games and useful reserve ball handling. Minnesota receives C+ for using Quentin Richardson's contract in the later Mark Blount transaction, but Richardson played zero Timberwolves regular-season games. Mark Madsen was waived before contributing for Los Angeles.

sections.heading: Charlotte Took a Risk on a Proven High-Usage Scorer
sections.body: The Charlotte Bobcats acquired Stephen Jackson and Acie Law from Golden State on November 16, 2009, sending veterans Raja Bell and Vladimir Radmanović to the Warriors. Charlotte needed another player who could create his own offense alongside Gerald Wallace, while Golden State was moving away from Jackson after a difficult relationship with its organization. The four-player deal involved no promised future draft selection. Acquiring an established scorer represented a more ambitious change than swapping interchangeable reserves, especially for a young franchise still seeking its first postseason appearance.

sections.heading: Jackson Became Charlotte's Leading Scorer in Its First Playoff Season
sections.body: Jackson played 72 regular-season games with the Bobcats after the exchange, starting every one and averaging 21.1 points in 39.3 minutes. He also added 5.1 rebounds, 3.6 assists and 1.6 steals per game. The combination with Wallace helped Charlotte reach the 2010 playoffs for the first time in the franchise's history. Jackson remained an important offensive player beyond that initial campaign. His Golden State appearances earlier in 2009-10 are not part of Charlotte's acquired value; the 72 games and ensuing Bobcats seasons provide the proper evidence.

sections.heading: Golden State Obtained Depth but Little from Raja Bell
sections.body: Bell arrived with a reputation for defending perimeter stars, yet he played only one regular-season game for Golden State in 2009-10 because of a wrist injury and related roster decisions. Radmanović provided frontcourt and wing reserve minutes during the same season and continued with the Warriors afterward. He brought shooting size but did not replace Jackson's workload as a primary offensive option. Law's Charlotte stay was likewise a supporting part of the package, not the main reason the Bobcats succeeded. The receiving-team comparison should keep all four players in view without implying Bell reproduced his earlier Suns scoring and defense for Golden State.

sections.heading: The Scoring Upgrade Was Worth More Than Golden State's Depth Return
sections.body: Golden State's motivation was understandable: moving Jackson offered a change in roster direction, while Radmanović's experience and Bell's contract could serve different needs. Charlotte, however, received an immediate twenty-point scorer who stayed healthy enough to start 72 games and help deliver the franchise's first postseason trip. No reserve contributions by the two incoming Warriors equaled that impact. The old Charlotte-favored verdict was right but too conservative about its primary player. A strong Bobcats grade reflects actual 2009-10 contributions without assigning the later success of other franchises to this exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Charlotte Win. The Bobcats earn A- because Stephen Jackson started 72 regular-season games, averaged 21.1 points and helped the franchise reach its first NBA playoffs in 2010. Golden State receives C+ for reserve Vladimir Radmanović and a largely unavailable Raja Bell, who played just one Warriors game. Jackson delivered the greater receiving-team value by a decisive margin.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Exchanged a Veteran for Unused International Rights
sections.body: On February 20, 2014, the Clippers sent Antawn Jamison and cash to Atlanta for the draft rights to Cenk Akyol, a Turkish guard picked in the second round in 2005. The Clippers' official deadline announcement identified Akyol as an international prospect already playing professionally in Turkey. Jamison, a veteran former All-Star, had appeared in 22 Clippers games during the first part of the season. By moving him, Los Angeles was managing a roster role it no longer needed while acquiring a rights asset that would not require an immediate NBA contract.

sections.heading: Atlanta Released Jamison the Day After the Transaction
sections.body: The Hawks did not obtain Jamison as an active rotation veteran. Their transaction archive records his waiver on February 21, one day after the trade. As a result he never played an Atlanta regular-season NBA game. Jamison's earlier Clippers scoring and his substantial accomplishments with Golden State, Dallas, Washington and Cleveland belong to those clubs, not to the receiving Hawks. The principal documented Atlanta return was therefore the cash included in the exchange, not the former twenty-point scorer's career totals. This distinction is essential to grading the small deadline arrangement fairly.

sections.heading: Akyol's Draft Rights Did Not Become Clippers Minutes
sections.body: Akyol was the 59th selection in the 2005 draft and had played in the Turkish professional league rather than signing with Atlanta. Los Angeles obtained those dormant NBA rights in February 2014, but he never joined the Clippers for a regular-season NBA game. His overseas numbers and competitions are not NBA points earned for the Los Angeles franchise. The rights still represented a negotiable asset with theoretical value, and the deal could free roster room for other moves. Neither possibility demonstrates that the Clippers obtained a regular-season player from Akyol.

sections.heading: A Cash Receipt Provides the Small Atlanta Advantage
sections.body: Both teams were solving roster problems rather than pursuing a marquee star. Atlanta agreed to take Jamison's contract and immediately waived him, receiving cash consideration as part of the exchange. Los Angeles moved a little-used veteran and acquired a foreign prospect whose rights were never exercised into a Clippers playing career. Without a documented dollar figure or a player tied solely to the money, Atlanta's return should not be exaggerated. Nevertheless, it acquired a realized payment, while the Clippers' direct playing return from Akyol was zero. The inherited Hawks-favored verdict is defensible with modest grades.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win. Atlanta earns C+ for cash received when it acquired and promptly waived Antawn Jamison, who played no Hawks regular-season games. Los Angeles gets D+ because the rights to Cenk Akyol never produced a Clippers NBA appearance, despite offering a limited speculative asset. This was a minor financial and roster-management transaction rather than a major basketball win.
