sections.heading: The Hornets Needed Guard Coverage More Than a Reserve Center
sections.body: The New Orleans Hornets exchanged veteran center Elden Campbell for Seattle SuperSonics point guard Kenny Anderson on February 20, 2003. New Orleans had experienced injury-related roster problems during its first season in Louisiana and wanted another experienced ball handler. Campbell had already lost much of the frontcourt responsibility he carried during earlier Charlotte Hornets seasons. Seattle, meanwhile, was making substantial deadline changes, including a separate Gary Payton transaction, and acquired another center to distribute minutes among its remaining big men. This was a direct veteran-for-veteran swap without a draft selection attached.

sections.heading: Anderson Delivered 23 Games and 77 Hornets Assists
sections.body: After moving to New Orleans, Anderson played twenty-three regular-season games, starting once and logging 446 minutes. He scored 139 points and recorded seventy-seven assists, helping the Hornets maintain backcourt depth through their playoff push. The contribution was limited compared with Anderson's career peak, but twenty-three games and nearly nineteen and a half minutes per appearance amounted to a real reserve role. His thirty-eight Seattle appearances before the trade must remain part of his SuperSonics record rather than being added to his New Orleans return. Anderson did not become a long-term Hornets starter, leaving after the season.

sections.heading: Campbell Had a Smaller Seattle Role After the Swap
sections.body: Campbell played fifteen regular-season games for Seattle after February 20, with no starts. His SuperSonics totals were 184 minutes, forty-eight points and thirty-nine rebounds. These figures show why it would be misleading to credit Seattle with Campbell's earlier 41 New Orleans games from the same campaign. His greatest NBA years had already passed, and the new team used him as a modest reserve center. He left after the season and later contributed to Detroit, but those Pistons games were unrelated to the Seattle acquisition. The direct return here was a brief, low-minute look at a veteran big man.

sections.heading: Both Clubs Got Depth, but New Orleans Used Its Player More
sections.body: The trade served sensible short-term roster objectives for both franchises, yet the receiving-team record favors the Hornets. Anderson's 446 minutes more than doubled Campbell's Seattle time, and New Orleans also received more points and a useful source of assists. The SuperSonics did acquire size and had other reasons to reduce their guard allocation as they rebuilt, but this transaction alone did not generate a major frontcourt contribution. The older Seattle-favored grade put excessive weight on Campbell's previous reputation. Neither veteran stayed with his new club beyond that season, making this a narrowly defined and short-lived advantage.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hornets Win. New Orleans receives B- for Kenny Anderson's twenty-three games, 446 minutes, 139 points and seventy-seven assists in 2002-03. Seattle gets C- for Elden Campbell's fifteen games, 184 minutes and forty-eight points. The Hornets obtained the more productive short-term reserve, reversing the earlier Seattle-favored grade without counting either player's pretrade seasons.

sections.heading: The Warriors Exchanged a Veteran Guard for Three Suns Reserves
sections.body: Golden State traded Vinny Del Negro to Phoenix on January 26, 2001, receiving forward Corie Blount, guard Paul McPherson and big man Rubén Garcés. The Warriors' official media guide records the three-for-one transaction and its exact date. The clubs were pursuing different roster adjustments: Phoenix sought a steady veteran guard who could provide some minutes behind its established perimeter players, while Golden State wanted more frontcourt bodies and a chance to evaluate a younger scoring guard. No future picks are recorded as part of this particular exchange.

sections.heading: Blount Supplied the Main Golden State Return
sections.body: Blount played thirty-eight regular-season games for Golden State after the acquisition, logging 918 minutes and averaging 6.8 points with 8.3 rebounds per 36 minutes. His game-by-game role was more limited than those per-minute figures imply, but the Warriors needed additional size in a season affected by injuries and poor results. He was a playable power forward rather than an end-of-bench contract. McPherson also appeared in twenty-two games, played 287 minutes and averaged 6.8 points in just thirteen minutes per contest. Combined, the two players delivered 1,205 minutes of Warriors use.

sections.heading: Garcés Didn't Play, While Del Negro Became a Suns Backup
sections.body: The third incoming player, Garcés, did not appear in a Warriors regular-season game and was waived on February 28, 2001, according to the club's transaction history. Golden State therefore should not be credited with his ten earlier Phoenix games. On the other side, Del Negro appeared in thirty-six Phoenix regular-season games after the swap, played 526 minutes and averaged 5.2 points. He gave the Suns some guard cover, but was not a major offensive contributor. His twenty-nine Golden State games before January 26 also remain pretrade Warriors statistics, not additional Phoenix value.

sections.heading: Two Rotation Pieces Outweighed One Veteran Guard
sections.body: This exchange was not a major event for either franchise, and Golden State's season remained difficult. Nonetheless, the return was more than an unused group of contracts: Blount gave the Warriors real frontcourt minutes and McPherson a chance to handle bench possessions. Phoenix acquired a veteran guard who could help occasionally, though he logged fewer minutes than either the combined Warriors additions or Blount alone. The Suns' decision was reasonable given their need for experience, but the receiving-team records support a modest Warriors advantage rather than the imported perfectly even B grades.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win. Golden State earns B for Corie Blount's thirty-eight games and 918 minutes plus Paul McPherson's twenty-two games and 287 minutes; Rubén Garcés did not play before his waiver. Phoenix receives C+ for Vinny Del Negro's thirty-six games and 526 minutes. The Warriors acquired more useful bench coverage from the January three-for-one trade.

sections.heading: Houston Sent a Former All-Star and Returned a Memphis Draft Pick
sections.body: In December 2008, Houston traded Steve Francis, cash and a 2009 second-round choice back to the Memphis Grizzlies for a conditional 2011 second-round selection. Memphis's official announcement describes the 2009 selection as its own pick, which Houston had acquired through an earlier draft-night transaction. Francis had once been drafted by Vancouver but had never played for the Grizzlies franchise. By 2008 injuries had curtailed his career, so the central basketball asset in this package was the future draft selection rather than his famous name.

sections.heading: The Grizzlies Used the Pick on Sam Young
sections.body: Memphis selected Pittsburgh forward Sam Young at No. 36 in the 2009 NBA draft. He played eighty regular-season games as a rookie and scored 595 points in 1,321 minutes. In 2010-11 Young appeared seventy-eight more times, started forty-six contests and contributed 572 points in 1,577 minutes. He added twenty-one Memphis games in the shortened 2011-12 season before leaving for Philadelphia. Those 179 regular-season appearances were real value from the reacquired second-rounder. His subsequent Sixers career should not be included in Memphis's return.

sections.heading: Francis Never Played, and Houston's Conditional Return Expired
sections.body: The Grizzlies' January 2009 release announcement confirms that Francis was waived without making a Memphis appearance. The veteran's earlier Houston, Orlando and New York playing totals therefore offer no additional value to this deal. Houston's return also failed to generate an active asset. The protected 2011 second-round choice did not convey, as the franchise transaction register explicitly notes. It would be wrong to assign any 2011 draftee to the Rockets through this agreement. Houston had moved cash and a genuine eventual NBA player for a contingent right that expired.

sections.heading: A Long-Lived Second-Round Reserve Created the Difference
sections.body: The Grizzlies did not acquire productive Steve Francis minutes, and the deal was not a veteran revival. Its success instead came from recovering a second-round position and using it on a forward who contributed over multiple seasons. Houston might have benefited from removing Francis's remaining roster obligation, but the specific compensation received never became a pick or player. The on-court contrast is stark: Young accumulated extensive Memphis minutes, while the Rockets recorded no NBA production from the incoming conditional second. That supports Memphis's favorable historical grade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Grizzlies Win. Memphis earns A- because the reacquired 2009 No. 36 selection became Sam Young, who played 179 Grizzlies games and started 46 in 2010-11. Steve Francis was waived without playing. Houston gets D because the conditional 2011 second-round pick never conveyed despite sending cash and the productive future draft asset.

sections.heading: The Hornets Acquired a Veteran Center in a Disrupted Season
sections.body: On January 31, 2006, the New Orleans/Oklahoma City Hornets received Aaron Williams from Toronto for two second-round draft selections. The club was playing home games in Oklahoma City following Hurricane Katrina, and Williams offered immediate backup size during an unusual season. Toronto was restructuring its frontcourt and chose future draft flexibility instead of retaining an aging reserve. The agreement was not an exchange of two NBA players: the Raptors received one selection for 2006 and another for 2009, giving them more options for later negotiations.

sections.heading: Williams Supplied Thirty-Four Hornets Games
sections.body: Williams made thirty-four New Orleans/Oklahoma City regular-season appearances after the trade, starting twice. He logged 692 minutes, scored 197 points and collected 166 rebounds while functioning as a backup center. Those were useful frontcourt minutes for a team working around Chris Paul and David West, though the role never resembled Williams's most productive earlier years in New Jersey. His fourteen Toronto games before January 31 remain Raptors statistics and must not be added to his incoming Hornets totals. He moved to the Clippers afterward rather than developing into a long-term Hornets starter.

sections.heading: Toronto Obtained Two Picks That Followed Different Paths
sections.body: The 2006 selection became No. 56 Edin Bavčić. Toronto selected him and promptly sold his draft rights to Philadelphia, yielding a separate asset transaction rather than playing Bavčić in a Raptors uniform. The later pick eventually became No. 51 Jack McClinton in 2009, but Toronto had included its rights in a wider trade with San Antonio for Rasho Nesterović in 2006. Consequently, neither draftee's career can be counted as a direct Raptors playing return. Both second-round choices nevertheless had real use in subsequent decisions, and their paths need to be explained.

sections.heading: Immediate Center Minutes Versus Two Movable Assets
sections.body: New Orleans received exactly the sort of veteran support it wanted during the remaining months of the 2005-06 season. Toronto gave up a little-used forward-center and received two draft assets it could move in separate arrangements. Those trades created financial and roster flexibility, even without a productive player selected and retained from either choice. Comparing only Williams's scoring with the draftees' nonexistent Toronto minutes would ignore what the Raptors actually did with the assets. The original even verdict remains sensible because each organization realized a different and documented category of value.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. New Orleans earns B for Aaron Williams's 34 appearances, 692 minutes, 197 points and 166 rebounds in 2005-06. Toronto also receives B because it acquired two usable second-round picks, selling Edin Bavčić's No. 56 rights and later transferring the 2009 selection within the Nesterović package. No later player's entire career is assigned to this single swap.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Moved a Guard for Future Second-Round Flexibility
sections.body: The Bucks traded Jerry Reynolds to the Seattle SuperSonics on October 4, 1988, receiving a second-round choice in the 1990 NBA draft. Reynolds was a useful reserve guard who had played three years with Milwaukee, but the club was ready to examine another backcourt option. Seattle wanted immediate wing and ball-handling help after personnel changes in the offseason. The franchises were not swapping two players ready to play that October; one side took an experienced NBA contributor while the other accepted a future draft selection.

sections.heading: Reynolds Provided One Season of Seattle Bench Scoring
sections.body: Reynolds played fifty-six regular-season SuperSonics games during 1988-89 without starting a contest. He scored 428 points in 737 minutes, averaging 7.6 points and contributing 100 rebounds and sixty-two assists. That output made him a genuine contributor rather than an unused veteran contract. Seattle reached the playoffs, with Reynolds occupying a limited role behind its primary guards and forwards. The franchise then lost him to Orlando in the June 1989 expansion draft. His later productive Orlando seasons should not be counted as Seattle return from the Milwaukee deal.

sections.heading: The Future Milwaukee Pick Became Steve Henson
sections.body: The 1990 selection was No. 44, used by Milwaukee to draft Kansas State point guard Steve Henson. He played sixty-eight Bucks regular-season games in 1990-91, recording 690 minutes, 214 points and 131 assists. He returned the following season for fifty games, with 386 minutes, 150 points and eighty-two assists. Across both years, Henson gave Milwaukee 118 regular-season appearances and 1,076 minutes. His later Atlanta, Charlotte and Portland NBA games belong to other clubs and must not be attributed to Milwaukee's original incoming selection.

sections.heading: Two Different Timetables Produced Real NBA Minutes
sections.body: Seattle received its basketball production immediately during the 1988-89 campaign, while the Bucks waited until 1990 to turn the incoming pick into a player. Reynolds scored more points than Henson during his Seattle stay, but Milwaukee accumulated more games and minutes across two seasons. Both were backcourt reserves, not stars, and neither franchise gained a long-term player to build around. The separate receiving-team totals are substantial enough to support fair grades. The original even assessment correctly values the difference between quick scoring help and a longer-lived draft choice.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Milwaukee earns B because 1990 No. 44 pick Steve Henson delivered 118 Bucks regular-season games, 1,076 minutes, 364 points and 213 assists. Seattle gets B for Jerry Reynolds's 56 games, 737 minutes and 428 points before the 1989 expansion draft. Both teams received actual NBA bench work despite different timing.

sections.heading: The Rockets Moved a Veteran Contract Before Pursuing Thorpe
sections.body: Houston sent Cedric Maxwell to the Washington Bullets for Jim Grandholm in early October 1988. Maxwell had won championships with Boston before spending his later NBA seasons with the Rockets, but his on-court role had declined. Contemporary Washington reporting linked the transaction to Houston's attempt to reduce payroll obligations while negotiating for forward Otis Thorpe. Washington acquired an experienced championship veteran to inspect during training camp. Grandholm was not an established NBA starter, making the acquisition for Houston primarily a roster and financial decision.

sections.heading: Neither Incoming Forward Played a Regular-Season Game
sections.body: Houston waived Grandholm on October 14, brought him back under a separate free-agent agreement on October 19 and released him again on November 1. He did not play a Rockets regular-season NBA game through this sequence. Maxwell arrived at Washington's training camp, but he also did not appear in an official Bullets game. His final NBA regular-season appearances had been for Houston during 1987-88. It would be incorrect to use Maxwell's earlier championship statistics as Washington production or to claim the Rockets obtained NBA minutes from Grandholm.

sections.heading: Financial Flexibility Was Houston's Documented Motivation
sections.body: Washington Post coverage during the first week of camp observed that moving Maxwell's salary made it easier for Houston to pursue Thorpe within the league's salary-cap structure. Thorpe subsequently joined Houston in a separate October 11 exchange with Sacramento involving Rodney McCray and Jim Petersen. That second deal was not a direct Maxwell-for-Thorpe swap and cannot be merged into the official consideration for Grandholm. Still, payroll flexibility offers a concrete reason why the Rockets accepted a player they would quickly waive. The Bullets were instead betting a familiar veteran could still help.

sections.heading: A Near-Zero Basketball Trade Deserves Restrained Marks
sections.body: Both franchises acquired a player who failed to enter their regular-season rotation. Washington's tryout of Maxwell did not restore his career, while Houston used Grandholm as a temporary roster contract. The salary-cap context gives Houston a more understandable indirect benefit than a simple zero-games comparison would suggest. It does not justify assigning all of Thorpe's later Rockets production to Maxwell's departure, because Thorpe required another substantial trade. The inherited Wizards-favored grades exaggerated a deal that produced no direct incoming NBA minutes for either organization.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Houston receives C- because moving Cedric Maxwell created some documented cap flexibility, although Jim Grandholm never played a Rockets regular-season game. Washington gets D+ because Maxwell likewise never appeared for the Bullets. Thorpe's later Houston career followed a separate transaction and cannot be counted as direct return from this October exchange.

sections.heading: Miami Bought an Experienced Forward With a Contingent Pick
sections.body: Golden State sent Tellis Frank to Miami on October 2, 1989, in return for a second-round draft asset originating with Cleveland. The transaction was described as a choice in either the 1990 or 1992 draft depending on conditions, and it ultimately resolved into the 1990 No. 41 selection. Miami was entering its second NBA season and needed adults who could play regular frontcourt minutes. Frank had two Warriors seasons behind him, including a meaningful rookie workload, while Golden State preferred another chance to draft a developmental guard.

sections.heading: Frank Started 39 Games for the Expansion-Era Heat
sections.body: The Heat got immediate and substantial production. Frank appeared in seventy-seven games during 1989-90, starting thirty-nine and playing 1,762 minutes. He scored 735 points, pulled down 385 rebounds and averaged 9.5 points with five rebounds per game. That was one of the more productive roles on a very young team still building a professional rotation. His thirty-two Warriors games during 1988-89 were completed before the exchange and must not be folded into his Miami totals. Likewise, his brief later Minnesota appearance was not Heat production.

sections.heading: Golden State Drafted Bardo but Didn't Receive NBA Games
sections.body: The deferred selection became No. 41 in 1990 and was used on Illinois guard Steve Bardo. He continued playing basketball professionally, including the Continental Basketball Association, and eventually reached the NBA for San Antonio, Dallas and Detroit. None of those appearances were made for Golden State, however. The Warriors therefore obtained a draft-rights asset and an opportunity to evaluate Bardo, but no direct NBA regular-season games from him. The pick was real; its conversion into meaningful Golden State rotation play did not occur.

sections.heading: The Receiving-Team Comparison Clearly Favors Miami
sections.body: Frank delivered an entire season of frontcourt play for the Heat, while the Warriors invested the second-round pick in someone who never wore their uniform in an official NBA game. The clubs' different developmental priorities explain why they made the deal, but do not erase the difference in realized value. Miami's 77 appearances and 39 starts are much stronger evidence than the prospect's later work for unrelated organizations. The inherited Heat-win verdict was right, although the grade for the Miami receiving-team production deserved a substantial increase.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Heat Win. Miami earns A- after Tellis Frank played 77 games, started 39 and contributed 735 points, 385 rebounds and 1,762 minutes in 1989-90. Golden State receives D+ because 1990 No. 41 pick Steve Bardo never made a Warriors NBA appearance. His later games with other teams are not Warriors trade return.

sections.heading: Seattle Acquired an Aging Center From an Expansion Team
sections.body: The Timberwolves sent Steve Johnson to the Seattle SuperSonics on February 22, 1990, receiving forward Brad Sellers. Minnesota was in its inaugural NBA season and exploring ways to assemble a frontcourt around younger talent. Johnson, previously a useful Portland center, was no longer playing heavy minutes. Seattle wanted additional veteran size during the stretch run while parting with Sellers, a bench forward it had acquired the preceding summer. Both clubs' main transaction ledgers list the direct player exchange, with no verified selection that was actually conveyed.

sections.heading: Johnson Played Twenty-One Regular-Season Seattle Games
sections.body: Johnson gave the SuperSonics twenty-one appearances after the February trade, totaling 242 minutes, 117 points and 50 rebounds. He did not start, and his role remained that of a reserve center in a team already using several frontcourt options. Those figures should not be confused with his four Minnesota games from before the transaction or with his much more productive Portland seasons. Seattle's direct gain was modest but measurable. He later played for Golden State, which was another team and cannot be credited as the Sonics' receiving-team return.

sections.heading: Sellers Was Used Even Less by the Timberwolves
sections.body: Sellers played fourteen Minnesota games in the remainder of 1989-90. He recorded 113 minutes, 47 points and nineteen rebounds without a start, providing only a brief look for a young expansion roster. His forty-five Seattle games earlier in the season do not count as new Timberwolves performance. Although Sellers returned to Minnesota in 1992-93 and played additional games then, that later stint occurred after another interval with a different team. It would misrepresent the 1990 trade to merge those later statistics into the original acquired role.

sections.heading: The Imported Conditional Pick Cannot Be Treated as Conveyed
sections.body: One historical import lists a possible conditional 1991 second-round asset on Seattle's side, but neither franchise's Basketball-Reference transaction record confirms a conveyed choice in this February player-for-player swap. The pick must therefore remain an unresolved provenance note, not a basis for assigning any draft prospect to the SuperSonics. The verifiable comparison is Johnson's twenty-one Seattle games against Sellers's fourteen Minnesota games. Neither was a lasting fixture, and Seattle received only a slight advantage in playing time and output. The previous equal B grades overstated two declining veteran reserves.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: SuperSonics Win. Seattle gets C+ for Steve Johnson's 21 regular-season games, 242 minutes and 117 points after arriving in February 1990. Minnesota earns D+ for Brad Sellers's 14 games, 113 minutes and 47 points. An imported conditional 1991 pick has no verified conveying result, so it isn't awarded phantom future player value.

sections.heading: Houston Moved Novak for a Right to Exchange Future Draft Slots
sections.body: The Rockets traded reserve three-point shooter Steve Novak to the Los Angeles Clippers on August 6, 2008. In exchange, Houston obtained the right to swap second-round selections in the 2011 NBA draft. This was not an immediate player-for-player transaction; the Clippers got a known shooting specialist while the Rockets acquired a potentially more favorable future draft position. The arrangement has a notable source conflict: Basketball-Reference's summary says the swap was not exercised, while detailed draft-pick ledgers and ShamSports trace the exercised rights to specific 2011 selections.

sections.heading: The 2011 Pick Ledger Shows No. 38 Reaching Houston
sections.body: Pro Sports Transactions records the Clippers' No. 38 choice, used on Chandler Parsons, as transferred to Houston through the 2008 option. Houston's No. 47 pick, used on Travis Leslie, moved to the Clippers side. A separate 2011 draft-night transaction briefly routed Parsons's rights through Minnesota before Houston bought them back for cash, so it would be wrong to treat the player's entire subsequent Rockets career as a straight uninterrupted transfer from Los Angeles. The origin of the advantageous No. 38 draft position, however, is traced to the Novak exchange.

sections.heading: Parsons Became an Everyday Rockets Forward
sections.body: Parsons reached Houston's rotation as a rookie in 2011-12 and played sixty-three games. He followed with seventy-six regular-season appearances in 2012-13 and seventy-four in 2013-14, a total of 213 Rockets games over three seasons. His offense, rebounding and outside shooting became central to the club's lineups before he left for Dallas. The intermediate Minnesota cash transaction must be recognized when assigning causation, but the swap's improved draft position was a necessary part of the selection path. The Rockets ultimately extracted far more on-court utility from their later choice than a generic unexercised-option label suggests.

sections.heading: Novak Also Played a Useful Two-Year Clippers Role
sections.body: Los Angeles wasn't empty-handed. Novak appeared in seventy-one Clippers games during 2008-09, starting three and logging 1,161 minutes while shooting 41.6 percent from beyond the arc. He returned for fifty-four more games in 2009-10 and 362 additional minutes. His 125 total Clippers appearances offered genuine perimeter spacing, especially in the first season. The No. 47 selection was a separate future asset, but Leslie did not become a comparably productive NBA player. Houston benefited more in the long term through the higher pick, while the Clippers acquired real near-term shooting depth.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win. Houston earns A- for obtaining the improved No. 38 draft slot later used on Chandler Parsons, a 213-game Rockets contributor after an additional Minnesota rights transaction. Los Angeles gets B because Steve Novak supplied 125 games and 1,523 minutes. Detailed 2011 pick ledgers show the swap was exercised despite Basketball-Reference's conflicting abbreviated label, which should not be silently repeated.

sections.heading: Houston Took a Brief Chance on Gerald Green
sections.body: At the February 21, 2008 trade deadline, the Rockets acquired Gerald Green from Minnesota for wing Kirk Snyder, cash and a future second-round selection. Green was a young, athletic former first-rounder whose raw tools had not developed into a dependable role with the Timberwolves. Houston could give him a short evaluation while its veteran players chased a playoff berth. Minnesota chose a more experienced defender and another chance to draft a prospect in 2010. The pick later settled at the forty-fifth position, making this more than a simple guard exchange.

sections.heading: Green Played Just Four Rockets Minutes
sections.body: Green appeared in one Houston regular-season game after the trade, making all three field-goal attempts and scoring six points in four minutes. The surprising shooting line should not disguise the tiny sample. The Rockets waived Green on March 8, before he could become part of their playoff rotation. His twenty-nine Minnesota games earlier in 2007-08 were completed before this trade and do not contribute to Houston's acquired value. His subsequent more successful NBA seasons with other franchises were also separate contracts, not delayed Rockets performance.

sections.heading: Snyder Contributed Twenty-Seven Minnesota Games
sections.body: Snyder found a larger role with the Timberwolves. He appeared in twenty-seven 2007-08 regular-season games after his arrival, started eighteen and played 680 minutes. He averaged 8.4 points and 4.2 rebounds while serving as a physical perimeter player on a rebuilding roster. That contribution was useful even though he was not retained as a franchise fixture. His earlier Rockets appearances and Utah playing history remain separate from what Minnesota acquired. On its own, the increase in starts and minutes gives the Wolves a clear basketball advantage.

sections.heading: Minnesota Also Obtained a Real Draft Selection
sections.body: The second-round pick from Houston became No. 45 in 2010 and was used on Brazilian big man Paulo Prestes. His career continued overseas rather than in the Timberwolves' NBA rotation, so he did not supply receiving-team regular-season points. The draft rights still represented a valid future asset; they should not be dismissed as nothing merely because a player did not arrive. Minnesota's on-court return came overwhelmingly from Snyder, with the choice offering an additional developmental opportunity. The Wolves therefore received more from this exchange than Houston's brief look at Green.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wolves Win. Minnesota earns B+ for Kirk Snyder's 27 games, 18 starts, 680 minutes and additional No. 45 selection eventually used on Paulo Prestes. Houston gets D+ for Gerald Green's single four-minute, six-point Rockets appearance before his March waiver. Green's later NBA career belongs to different acquisitions.

sections.heading: The Clippers Sent Toronto Cash for a Wing Audition
sections.body: The actual trade took place on January 1, 2009, when the Clippers acquired Hassan Adams from the Raptors. Los Angeles sent cash and a conditional 2015 second-round choice to Toronto. The later January 7 date in the imported trade identifier is the date Adams was waived, not when the clubs agreed to the exchange. Both franchises' seasonal transaction histories clarify that distinction. Adams had been a second-round pick in 2006 and offered a low-cost possibility for wing depth, but the opportunity did not last a week.

sections.heading: Adams Never Appeared in a Clippers Regular-Season Game
sections.body: Adams was released by Los Angeles on January 7, before he could take the floor in a Clippers regular-season contest. His earlier NBA appearances were with New Jersey and Toronto, and no portion of those statistics can be credited to the receiving Los Angeles team. This trade therefore delivered no player minutes, points or rebounds to the Clippers. That outcome is different from acquiring a reserve who spends even a few games on the active roster. Los Angeles paid to examine a player whose opportunity ended almost immediately.

sections.heading: The Conditional 2015 Draft Pick Did Not Transfer
sections.body: The agreement also listed a 2015 second-round pick with restrictive protections, described in the archived record as top-50 and No. 56–60 protected. The selection was not exercised. Toronto accordingly did not receive a draftee from that obligation, and the trade must not be traced to an unrelated 2015 second-round player. Toronto's tangible documented compensation was the cash the Clippers paid, not a pick it later deployed. This was the source of an additional imported-data problem: an earlier version of the trade incorrectly showed the cash going from Toronto to Los Angeles.

sections.heading: Correcting the Cash Direction Changes the Evaluation
sections.body: Once the assets are placed with the proper receiving teams, the retrospective is straightforward. Toronto moved a player it was not using and received money. Los Angeles obtained no regular-season production from Adams and did not retain him through the next week, while the potential future pick never conveyed. The Raptors did not obtain a transformative basketball asset, so their positive grade should remain restrained. The Clippers' loss was a small failed audition rather than a devastating roster move. Preserving the existing private slug avoids creating a duplicate route while accurately reporting the January 1 trade date.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Raptors Win. Toronto earns C+ because it received cash when Hassan Adams was sent to Los Angeles on January 1, 2009. The conditional 2015 second-round selection never conveyed. The Clippers earn D+ because Adams was waived January 7 without playing a single Clippers regular-season game. The legacy January 7 slug records the waiver, not the actual trade date.

sections.heading: A Protected Future Pick Brought Brown to Los Angeles
sections.body: The Clippers traded a conditional second-round selection in the 2014 NBA draft for Bobby Brown on January 26, 2010. New Orleans had used the guard earlier that season but accepted the possibility of a future selection rather than keeping him in its backcourt. The pick was protected through No. 55, meaning the Hornets would receive it only if it landed among the last five places of the second round. The Clippers needed another inexpensive reserve behind their more prominent ball handlers while moving through a difficult season.

sections.heading: Brown Gave the Clippers Twenty-Three Games
sections.body: Brown appeared in 23 Los Angeles regular-season games following the deal, logging 191 minutes and 70 points. He added 42 assists with no starts, averaging roughly eight minutes per appearance. This was legitimate reserve point-guard work, though hardly a long-term solution. The 22 games and 145 points he produced for New Orleans earlier in 2009-10 belong to the franchise that sent him away. His later professional career abroad and eventual return to Houston several seasons afterward are likewise separate from the value Los Angeles purchased in January 2010.

sections.heading: The Conditional Selection Ultimately Became No. 58
sections.body: The future choice eventually became the No. 58 pick in 2014, after its top-55 protection allowed it to transfer. Historical draft-chain records identify Jordan McRae as the player selected at that position. New Orleans, however, did not retain the pick until the draft: later in 2010 it transferred the selection to San Antonio as payment for Curtis Jerrells. McRae therefore was not a Hornets draft acquisition from this transaction, and his NBA playing record cannot be treated as New Orleans production. The receiving club's real benefit was the tradable pick it obtained.

sections.heading: A Short Guard Rental Compared With a Transferable Draft Asset
sections.body: Los Angeles paid an eventual draft selection for a few months of backup-guard availability. Brown played only 191 minutes, and he did not return as a lasting Clippers contributor. New Orleans turned him into a pick that retained value and could be spent in another transaction, rather than letting the opportunity evaporate. The initial Hornets B+ grade may overstate an eventual late-second-round asset, but the franchise did realize a concrete pick and then put it to use. A smaller Hornets advantage survives when both receiving-team outcomes are weighed carefully.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans Win. The New Orleans Hornets receive B- for a 2014 second-round pick that ultimately conveyed at No. 58 and could be moved again. Los Angeles receives C for Bobby Brown's 23 games, 191 minutes and 70 points. Jordan McRae was selected only after New Orleans traded the pick onward, so his NBA career is not Hornets return.

sections.heading: Golden State Used a Deadline Trade to Adjust Payroll
sections.body: The Warriors sent Charles Jenkins and cash considerations to Philadelphia on February 21, 2013, in exchange for a protected second-round selection. Golden State was trying to move below the luxury-tax line while preserving the main roster that would later reach the playoffs. Jenkins had been a second-round pick in 2011 and had played a considerable number of games during his first season. Philadelphia was willing to audition another point guard for the final part of the schedule, particularly because the incoming deal also brought cash.

sections.heading: Jenkins Played a Dozen Games in Philadelphia
sections.body: After joining the 76ers, Jenkins appeared in twelve regular-season games, with one start and 150 minutes of playing time. He averaged about two points per game, a very small offensive return even for a backup guard. His earlier 98 NBA appearances for Golden State were completed before the trade and cannot be allocated to Philadelphia. The stint did at least provide an actual NBA player to the receiving team, but Jenkins left the league for overseas basketball that summer. There was no sustained Philadelphia development success.

sections.heading: Golden State's Protected Pick Was Never Exercised
sections.body: Contemporary coverage described the compensation as a protected second-round choice. The 2013 pick carried restrictive protection and never conveyed, according to later player-contract and trade histories. It would therefore be wrong to assign the Warriors a particular drafted player's production through this agreement. The tangible Golden State objective was financial flexibility from moving a reserve contract, even though the team also sent cash along with Jenkins. That makes the deal different from a straightforward pick-for-player exchange and explains why salary context belongs in the verdict.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Gained a Brief Guard Option Without a Pick Cost
sections.body: Philadelphia received twelve appearances and cash while surrendering a draft obligation that did not become a selection for Golden State. That is a modest but identifiable advantage. Golden State achieved part of its payroll objective and could devote its active roster spots to other players, so an extremely punitive grade would overlook why the trade was made. Neither side added a major contributor or secured meaningful lottery compensation. The older Sixers-favored outcome holds, but the appropriate margin is modest rather than a declaration that one front office discovered a hidden star.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win. Philadelphia earns C+ for Charles Jenkins's twelve NBA games, one start and 150 minutes plus incoming cash. Golden State receives C for managing its payroll even though the protected second-round choice never conveyed. The trade produced a brief backup-guard audition rather than substantial on-court value for either organization.

sections.heading: A Salary-Management Deal Sent Tyler to Atlanta
sections.body: The Warriors traded Jeremy Tyler to the Hawks on February 21, 2013, receiving cash and future considerations. Golden State was trying to reduce payroll obligations around the trade deadline as it built a playoff roster. Tyler was a young forward-center who had found limited opportunities behind other Golden State big men. Atlanta accepted the possibility of developing a mobile reserve at relatively low acquisition cost. The arrangement was part of the same day's roster reshuffling that also sent Charles Jenkins to Philadelphia, but the transactions involved different counterparties and must be evaluated separately.

sections.heading: The Hawks Gave Tyler a Single Five-Minute Game
sections.body: Atlanta's official March 6 announcement is unusually precise about Tyler's direct return. He appeared once for the Hawks, on March 4 at Denver, recording three rebounds in five minutes. The Hawks then waived him. That is the entirety of his NBA playing record for Atlanta after the trade. His previous 62 games in Golden State uniforms and later appearances elsewhere cannot be added to the Hawks return. A single short appearance does not support a high player-development grade, although Atlanta had a defensible reason to inspect a young center.

sections.heading: The Warriors Received Financial Consideration
sections.body: Golden State's team transaction register identifies cash and unspecified future considerations as the assets acquired for Tyler. The actual amount of cash and any later exercised draft choice are not established by the named entries in the imported ledger, so those should not be invented. Contemporary reporting connected the Tyler and Jenkins transactions with reducing the team's financial commitments below the luxury-tax line. That context provides a reason for the club to part with an inexpensive player without demanding another regular-season contributor in return. Roster flexibility was the intended benefit.

sections.heading: Measured Value Was Primarily on the Selling Side
sections.body: The Hawks obtained a player they briefly tested and then released, while Golden State received some financial consideration and payroll relief. Atlanta's NBA output was one game and no scoring, which puts the incoming basketball return near the bottom of the scale. Golden State's payment cannot be converted to fictional wins, but it was a concrete reason to complete the deal. The earlier Hawks-favored judgment put too much weight on the possibility of Tyler developing rather than what Atlanta actually received. A narrowly favorable Warriors result recognizes the tangible financial benefits without overstating the stakes.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win. Golden State receives C+ for cash, future consideration and financial flexibility from trading Jeremy Tyler. Atlanta gets D+ because Tyler played one Hawks regular-season game, collecting three rebounds in five minutes before his March 6 waiver. The club's earlier Tyler appearances elsewhere are not Hawks production, and no unverified later draft selection is credited to Golden State.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Paid a Dallas-Origin First to Replace an Aging Guard
sections.body: At the March 15, 2012 deadline, the Lakers sent Derek Fisher and a protected first-round draft choice originally acquired from Dallas to Houston for Jordan Hill. The Lakers' own announcement confirmed both pieces of the return, making it inaccurate to describe the transaction as Fisher straight up for Hill. Los Angeles was simultaneously reworking its point-guard situation with Ramon Sessions arriving in a separate Cleveland deal. Hill, a former No. 8 overall selection, supplied size and rebounding behind the team's veteran frontcourt. Houston's main prize was the protected Dallas-origin choice rather than a long-term plan to use Fisher.

sections.heading: Hill Delivered Four Seasons of Lakers Frontcourt Minutes
sections.body: Hill appeared in seven Lakers regular-season games after the 2012 trade and returned for another twenty-nine in 2012-13. His workload rose to seventy-two appearances and thirty-two starts in 2013-14, then seventy games and fifty-seven starts in 2014-15. Across those four Lakers seasons he totaled 178 regular-season appearances, ninety-one starts and 1,764 points. His rebounding gave Los Angeles a dependable inside contributor during roster turnover, and his 2014-15 season brought a career-high scoring average of 12.0 points. Those totals are specific to Los Angeles, excluding his earlier New York and Houston games and his later years with Indiana and Minnesota.

sections.heading: Fisher Never Played for Houston, but the First-Rounder Traveled
sections.body: Fisher did not suit up for Houston. The Rockets waived him on March 19, only four days after receiving his contract, and he signed with Oklahoma City on March 21. Houston still held the protected Dallas first-round pick acquired in this deal. In October 2012 the Rockets packaged that selection with other picks and players in the much larger transaction that brought James Harden from the Thunder. The Dallas-origin choice finally conveyed in 2014 as No. 21, when Oklahoma City selected Mitch McGary. McGary was never a Rockets draft-pick development story, and Harden cannot be credited solely to this one smaller trade.

sections.heading: The Grade Difference Reflects Direct Production and Trade-Asset Utility
sections.body: The Lakers obtained a frontcourt player who eventually started ninety-one regular-season games and scored more than seventeen hundred points for their franchise. Houston received no games from Fisher, which makes the player portion look one-sided. Yet grading the Rockets purely on Fisher's immediate departure would erase the protected first-rounder that later helped complete their Harden acquisition. The 2014 McGary pick belonged to Oklahoma City by draft night, and its contribution to a multi-piece October agreement is evidence of the asset's importance rather than proof that Houston acquired McGary. Los Angeles has the stronger direct-player return, while Houston deserves more credit than a near-failing grade for the draft asset it secured.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win. Los Angeles earns B+ because Jordan Hill produced 178 regular-season games, 91 starts and 1,764 points from 2012 through 2015. Houston gets B- rather than the inherited D+; Derek Fisher never played a Rockets game, but the Dallas-origin first-round selection helped form the October 2012 James Harden package. Oklahoma City ultimately drafted Mitch McGary at No. 21 in 2014, not Houston.

sections.heading: San Antonio Acquired Rights Instead of a Finished Player
sections.body: On May 17, 1991, the Spurs acquired the rights to guard Kevin Pritchard from Golden State. The Warriors' trade history lists a conditional second-round choice in 1993 as compensation, while the league transaction register describes Golden State selling his rights. Pritchard had been a second-round pick out of Kansas and had played earlier in the NBA, but he was not guaranteed a place on the San Antonio roster. The Spurs were assessing additional backcourt options before a new season while Golden State chose deferred compensation.

sections.heading: Pritchard Never Played a Regular-Season Game for the Spurs
sections.body: The Spurs carried Pritchard's rights into their preparation for the 1991-92 season. They waived him on October 28, 1991, before opening night, according to the franchise's official-season transaction chronology. He consequently recorded no Spurs regular-season minutes, starts, points or assists. Pritchard subsequently appeared in NBA games for Boston and other clubs, but those opportunities followed different signings and were not San Antonio production. Evaluating the trade by his broader career would create the false impression that acquiring his rights yielded NBA rotation minutes for the Spurs.

sections.heading: Golden State's Conditional 1993 Compensation Remains Unresolved
sections.body: The Warriors' asset was a conditional 1993 second-round selection or future considerations. The archival entry identifies that draft year but doesn't establish a particular conveyed draft slot or a player selected from it. Without evidence of the condition being satisfied, no 1993 draftee should be credited to Golden State. The possibility of a future selection was a legitimate bargaining asset, yet its realized basketball value can't be measured from this listing alone. That uncertainty limits the winner assessment just as the Spurs' failure to use Pritchard limits theirs.

sections.heading: Neither Side Has a Demonstrated NBA Playing Payoff
sections.body: San Antonio tried an inexpensive guard prospect and chose not to keep him for the season. Golden State exchanged an unneeded player right for deferred conditional compensation without a fully documented future player. Neither outcome constitutes a major success, but neither is evidence of a large organizational failure either. The prior Spurs-favored grade appeared to value an audition that never generated a league appearance. A balanced assessment acknowledges the conditional asset and preserves the unresolved 1993 provenance instead of turning an unidentified pick into invented points or games.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. San Antonio earns C- because it obtained Kevin Pritchard's rights but waived him before he played a Spurs regular-season game. Golden State also gets C- for conditional 1993 second-round compensation whose precise conveyance and downstream player cannot be established from the source ledger. Neither club can claim meaningful on-court production from the original May 1991 exchange.

sections.heading: The Lakers Spent Two Future Picks on Hightower's Rights
sections.body: The Lakers obtained Cory Hightower's player rights from San Antonio during the June 28, 2000 NBA draft, sending their second-round selections in 2001 and 2002 to the Spurs. Los Angeles had just won a championship and could afford to search for an inexpensive forward without depending on him for immediate starting minutes. Hightower had played college basketball at Indian Hills and been evaluated as a physical scorer. San Antonio preferred two future chances to draft players rather than hold one prospect from the current class.

sections.heading: Hightower Signed but Was Waived Before Opening Night
sections.body: Los Angeles signed Hightower to a multi-year agreement in August 2000, giving him a legitimate roster opportunity. The club released him on October 30, before the 2000-01 regular season began, according to its transaction archive. Hightower never appeared in an NBA regular-season game for the Lakers. The team went on to win another championship, but his preseason audition was not part of that playing achievement. His development and activity outside the league cannot be converted into franchise NBA games after the waiver.

sections.heading: San Antonio Used Both Second-Round Selections
sections.body: The incoming 2001 selection landed at No. 56 overall and was used on center Robertas Javtokas. The 2002 pick became No. 56 Randy Holcomb. Those were actual draft selections, not conditional obligations that evaporated before draft night. Neither player produced a regular-season NBA appearance for San Antonio from this pair of selections. Javtokas in particular had a notable basketball career abroad, but European club performances are not Spurs NBA contributions. The genuine return was control of two draft opportunities rather than a proven NBA rotation player.

sections.heading: Two Draft Chances Beat a Player Who Never Reached the Roster
sections.body: Both sides accepted development risks rather than trading established veterans. The Lakers' gamble on Hightower ended without a regular-season appearance, making the original high Los Angeles grade hard to defend. The Spurs did receive two picks that could have been used on different prospects, so their asset return was more tangible than an unsuccessful camp audition. Yet neither selection led to Spurs NBA playing time and the original B+ grade also overstated the final sporting outcome. A modest San Antonio win captures the asymmetry without assigning imagined contributions.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Spurs Win. San Antonio earns C+ for receiving two actual future selections, 2001 No. 56 Robertas Javtokas and 2002 No. 56 Randy Holcomb, despite neither becoming a Spurs NBA contributor. Los Angeles earns D+ for Cory Hightower, who signed in August 2000 but was waived October 30 without playing a Lakers regular-season game. The former high grades exaggerated both teams' realized production.

sections.heading: The Rockets Paid Cash and a Future Second for a Camp Prospect
sections.body: Houston acquired forward-center Shawn Long from Philadelphia on June 28, 2017, during the roster movement surrounding the Chris Paul trade. The NBA's own offseason tracker lists a 2018 second-round selection and cash as the 76ers return. Other transaction histories list the cash payment as $100,000. Long had shown scoring and rebounding ability in limited 2016-17 appearances for Philadelphia, but he was not a proven Houston rotation player. The Rockets were taking a low-cost developmental look rather than acquiring a starting frontcourt option.

sections.heading: Long Left Houston Without a Regular-Season Appearance
sections.body: The Rockets waived Long on September 26, 2017, before their opening regular-season game. His NBA games during the prior spring were for Philadelphia and cannot be carried over into Houston's incoming production. After signing Long in the summer, Houston used the preseason period to evaluate its frontcourt candidates and ultimately retained other players. The player it purchased in this agreement gave the Rockets zero regular-season minutes, points and rebounds. That result should control the on-court side of the verdict instead of Long's earlier 76ers statistics.

sections.heading: The Draft-Pick Records Need an Explicit Source Caveat
sections.body: There is a documented discrepancy in how the outgoing asset appears across reference sites. Basketball-Reference's Philadelphia season ledger names only the $100,000 cash, while the official NBA trade tracker and independent transaction histories include a 2018 second-round pick. The later draft-chain database identifies the selection as No. 60, associated with Kostas Antetokounmpo. Such disagreement should be disclosed rather than silently choosing a version that inflates the score. Philadelphia held tradeable value from the deal, but Antetokounmpo's later NBA career was for other organizations, not the Sixers.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Obtained Assets, Houston Got a Short Audition
sections.body: Philadelphia moved a marginal forward and accepted a cash payment with draft consideration documented by the league's transaction tracker. Houston obtained a chance to evaluate a young big man but released him before a regular-season appearance. Neither transaction created an NBA star, and the uncertainty about the precise draft-pick history warrants a tempered grade for the selling club. Still, the disparity in actual outcomes favors Philadelphia more than a pure player-for-player comparison would suggest. The Rockets' first objective was developmental optionality, which simply did not translate into on-court production.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win. Philadelphia earns B- for cash reported at $100,000 and a 2018 second-round pick identified in the NBA's official trade tracker, subject to the disclosed discrepancy with Basketball-Reference's cash-only ledger. Houston receives D+ because Shawn Long was waived September 26, 2017, without a Rockets regular-season appearance. No subsequent NBA games by the eventual draft recipient are credited to Philadelphia.

sections.heading: The Hornets Spent a Future Clippers Pick on a Guard
sections.body: New Orleans acquired Curtis Jerrells from San Antonio on October 18, 2010. The Hornets surrendered a conditional second-round selection in the 2014 draft, originally obtained from the Clippers earlier that year in the Bobby Brown trade. The pick was top-55 protected, making it valuable only if it ended near the bottom of the second round. Jerrells had experience with the Spurs' developmental program and overseas basketball, offering the Hornets another guard to evaluate as the new season approached. The transaction was an exchange of a future draft asset for a present roster audition.

sections.heading: Jerrells Was Released Before Playing a Hornets Game
sections.body: The trial lasted less than a week. New Orleans waived Jerrells on October 24, 2010, before the regular season began. He consequently appeared in no NBA regular-season games for the Hornets and contributed no minutes, points or assists to the receiving club. His extensive subsequent overseas career was genuine professional basketball work but did not count as New Orleans production. Nor do prior developmental-league appearances for the Spurs become Hornets statistics. The acquisition served only a short-term attempt to inspect another backcourt option.

sections.heading: The Conditional Pick Ultimately Conveyed as No. 58
sections.body: The draft choice sent to San Antonio was the same Clippers-origin pick that the Hornets had acquired in January 2010. It eventually landed at No. 58 in the 2014 draft, satisfying its top-55 protection and retaining genuine draft value. Historical pick-chain records associate it with Jordan McRae, though the pick subsequently moved through other transactions. McRae did not become a Spurs regular-season player by virtue of this particular trade. The benefit San Antonio received here was a future second-round selection that it could keep or use as part of another deal, not his later scoring statistics.

sections.heading: A Real Future Pick Was Better Than a Camp Cut
sections.body: San Antonio converted a player it was prepared to move into a selection that ultimately became real draft compensation. The Hornets traded away that option and received a guard who never appeared in an NBA game for them. This disparity explains the favorable Spurs verdict. Yet an A- grade for San Antonio is too high when the return was one late second-round pick rather than a long-term starter. Recognizing the selection's successful conveyance and the lack of Hornets playing time supports a solid but limited San Antonio advantage.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Spurs Win. San Antonio earns B- for a Clippers-origin 2014 second-round pick that ultimately conveyed at No. 58 and retained trade value. New Orleans receives D+ because Curtis Jerrells was waived October 24, 2010, before making a Hornets regular-season appearance. Jordan McRae's eventual NBA career happened after later pick movements and cannot be assigned directly to San Antonio's incoming player production.

sections.heading: New Orleans Sought a Point-Guard Option at the Deadline
sections.body: The February 20, 2003 swap brought Kenny Anderson to the New Orleans Hornets and sent veteran center Elden Campbell to the Seattle SuperSonics. Anderson had spent much of the season as a Seattle reserve after arriving in the prior Vin Baker deal. New Orleans was trying to bolster guard options as Baron Davis battled injuries, while Seattle was reshuffling its backcourt in a much larger deadline day that also involved Gary Payton and Ray Allen. This exchange was distinct from the Payton transaction and carried its own short-term frontcourt and backcourt objectives.

sections.heading: Anderson Played Twenty-Three Games for New Orleans
sections.body: Anderson made twenty-three Hornets regular-season appearances after February 20, with one start, 446 minutes, 139 points and seventy-seven assists. He averaged six points and 3.3 assists, an appropriate depth role rather than the production of the All-Star point guard he had been years earlier. He also appeared in five New Orleans playoff games. The thirty-eight Seattle appearances earlier in 2002-03 belonged to his previous team and should not be double-counted as acquired Hornets performance. The guard's later Indiana and Atlanta seasons were separate opportunities, not benefits generated by this trade.

sections.heading: Campbell Supplied Fifteen Brief Seattle Appearances
sections.body: Seattle received an established 6-foot-11 center in Campbell, who had already logged forty-one New Orleans games that season. His actual SuperSonics contribution was much smaller: fifteen regular-season appearances, no starts, 184 minutes, forty-eight points and thirty-nine rebounds. The Sonics did not receive Campbell's later championship-year Detroit production, because he left Seattle before the 2003-04 season. His presence at the trade deadline also did not fix Seattle's frontcourt on his own. The 2002-03 SuperSonics finished 40-42, despite acquiring Ray Allen and other players in the independent Payton deal.

sections.heading: The Hornets Got More Usable Minutes
sections.body: Both teams acquired established veterans for the end of one campaign, but the exchange was a much more productive guard rental than center rental. Anderson played more than twice Campbell's minutes for his receiving team, helped initiate offense and remained usable in New Orleans's postseason rotation. Campbell's fifteen-game Seattle stint offered size without comparable floor time. That difference supports the inherited Hornets-winning outcome, although the original B-plus for New Orleans and C-plus for Seattle were too generous for such short and modest stays. The revised grades recognize a useful short-term guard and a largely unused veteran center.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Charlotte Win is the legacy franchise verdict, referring to the New Orleans Hornets in February 2003. The Hornets earn B- because Kenny Anderson played 23 regular-season games, supplied 77 assists and appeared in five playoff games. Seattle earns D+ for Elden Campbell's 15 regular-season appearances, 184 minutes and 48 points. Campbell's subsequent Detroit career is not part of Seattle's acquired return.

sections.heading: New Orleans Sent Two Established Starters to Rework Its Books
sections.body: On June 20, 2012, the New Orleans Hornets sent Emeka Okafor and Trevor Ariza to Washington in return for Rashard Lewis and the No. 46 selection in that summer's draft. The Hornets had just won the lottery and were preparing to select Anthony Davis, so moving the salaries attached to their veteran center and wing created room for a younger roster. Washington, by contrast, wanted established players who could defend alongside its developing backcourt. The transaction did not involve Davis's No. 1 selection; its draft consideration was a much later second-round pick.

sections.heading: Washington Received a Full Season From Okafor
sections.body: Okafor made seventy-nine regular-season appearances for the Wizards in 2012-13, starting seventy-seven, playing 2,052 minutes and averaging 13.4 points with 12.1 rebounds per thirty-six minutes. His actual per-game rebounding average was 8.8, making him a sturdy interior option for Washington. A neck injury kept him off the court in 2013-14, so the center's direct Washington return ended after one season. Ariza gave the Wizards another 56 games in 2012-13, then played seventy-seven and started every appearance in 2013-14. That second year included 14.4 points per game and 40.7 percent shooting from three.

sections.heading: Lewis Was Waived, but Miller Became a Real Hornets Draftee
sections.body: Lewis did not record an official New Orleans appearance. The team announced his release on June 30, ten days after the trade, which means his prior All-Star numbers and later Miami career were not incoming Hornets production. The No. 46 pick was used on Kentucky forward Darius Miller, who played fifty-two games as a rookie in 2012-13, forty-five in 2013-14 and five in 2014-15. Those first 102 games were direct development of the acquired selection. Miller subsequently spent time overseas and returned in 2017 under another agreement, so his later 151 New Orleans games should not inflate the immediate draft-return accounting.

sections.heading: A Salary Reset Could Not Equal Two Starting Contributors
sections.body: The franchises received different kinds of value. New Orleans exchanged expensive established contracts for a veteran it could waive and a second-round player who served as a young reserve, which fit a rebuild around its incoming No. 1 pick. Washington obtained a dependable center for one year and a productive defensive wing for two, including Ariza's strong 2013-14 campaign. Those actual starting jobs were more than a marginal asset win. The trade therefore favors Washington even after crediting Miller's early development and the salary flexibility New Orleans pursued. Okafor's later absence still prevents an exaggerated multi-year center valuation.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wizards Win. Washington earns A- because Emeka Okafor started 77 games in 2012-13 and Trevor Ariza supplied 133 Wizards appearances across two seasons, with his 2013-14 shooting and defense proving especially valuable. New Orleans receives B- for contract flexibility and No. 46 selection Darius Miller, who played 102 games during his first Hornets/Pelicans stint. Rashard Lewis was waived without playing; Miller's later return followed another signing.

sections.heading: Golden State Moved Maggette's Long Contract Before the Draft
sections.body: On June 22, 2010, the Warriors traded Corey Maggette and the No. 44 choice in the upcoming draft to Milwaukee for Charlie Bell and Dan Gadzuric. Maggette was coming off a high-scoring Golden State season, but his multiyear contract tied up money a franchise under financial pressure wanted to redirect. Bell and Gadzuric carried shorter commitments, including Gadzuric's expiring deal. Milwaukee was trading away depth to get another proven scorer, hoping to help a young Brandon Jennings-led group that had just reached the playoffs. The second-round selection gave the Bucks a separate draft asset.

sections.heading: Maggette Played Sixty-Seven Games for Milwaukee
sections.body: Maggette was the only player in the original exchange who became a sizable regular-season contributor for his receiving team. He appeared in sixty-seven Bucks games during 2010-11, started eighteen and logged 1,401 minutes. His ability to draw fouls and produce shots offered Milwaukee a reliable bench scoring option, although the team finished outside the playoffs that season. The No. 44 choice became Jerome Jordan, but the Bucks sold his rights to the New York Knicks after making the selection. No future Jordan minutes can be recorded as Milwaukee output because the center did not play an NBA game for the Bucks.

sections.heading: Bell and Gadzuric Supplied Only Spot Duty
sections.body: Bell's Warriors stay included nineteen regular-season games in 2010-11, all as a reserve, with an average of just nine minutes per appearance. Gadzuric provided twenty-eight Golden State games, four starts, 297 minutes and seventy-nine points before a February move to New Jersey. These limited totals help explain why the Bucks hold the narrow immediate basketball advantage. But treating Gadzuric only as a reserve center also misses the fact that his expiring contract remained tradable. The Warriors had accepted less player production in exchange for different roster economics and a contract they could move again.

sections.heading: A Later Warriors Draft Pick Required an Additional Trade
sections.body: On February 23, 2011, Golden State sent both Gadzuric and Brandan Wright to the Nets for Troy Murphy and a 2012 second-round selection. That choice eventually became No. 35, used on Draymond Green. The draft-pick chain makes Gadzuric part of an important later transaction, but it would overstate this June deal to say the Warriors simply traded Maggette for Green. They also contributed Wright in the intervening exchange, and the pick did not arrive until months afterward. The trade grades therefore weigh Milwaukee's direct scoring gain against Golden State's salary relief and the tangible ability to use Gadzuric in another asset package.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Bucks Edge. Milwaukee gets B+ because Corey Maggette supplied 67 games and 1,401 minutes in 2010-11, although Jerome Jordan's draft rights were promptly sold. Golden State earns B because moving Maggette's contract met a financial purpose and Dan Gadzuric later helped bring in a 2012 second-round pick through a package that also cost Brandan Wright. Charlie Bell's nineteen games and Gadzuric's twenty-eight weren't major direct returns, and Draymond Green must not be assigned solely to this one trade.

sections.heading: Orlando Bought Expansion-Draft Protection With a Future Second
sections.body: The June 24, 1995 agreement was an expansion-draft arrangement, not an ordinary exchange of players between established teams. Orlando agreed to send the incoming Vancouver Grizzlies a 1996 second-round draft choice if they selected reserve Rodney Dent from the Magic's available list. Vancouver complied and Orlando kept the other eligible players it wanted to protect. The Grizzlies, building an inaugural roster from selections across the league, accepted a known bench piece and a future choice rather than using the expansion draft to poach a different Magic player.

sections.heading: Vancouver Selected Dent but Acquired a Movable Draft Asset
sections.body: Rodney Dent was officially the fourth selection in the 1995 expansion draft, and the Grizzlies' selection fulfilled the agreement. Dent did not develop into a meaningful Vancouver NBA rotation player, so it would be misleading to justify the arrangement with points or starts that were never recorded. The second-round pick became No. 42 in 1996, subsequently associated with Randy Livingston. Vancouver used the rights as part of its own later transaction activity instead of turning Livingston into direct Grizzlies playing time. The pick therefore supplied trade flexibility rather than a newly developed regular.

sections.heading: The Magic Obtained Certainty, Not Another Star
sections.body: Orlando's return was control over which member of its exposed roster would be taken. The Magic had reached the NBA Finals in 1995 with Shaquille O'Neal and Penny Hardaway leading an accomplished team. Rodney Dent had a minimal role compared with that core, so Orlando could give up a future second for the assurance that its expansion loss would be limited to him. This protection was a roster-management service rather than a box-score asset. It did not make Vancouver responsible for providing Orlando another player, cash consideration or a 1995 first-round selection.

sections.heading: Neither Side Realized a Major On-Court Return
sections.body: Vancouver accepted a low-impact expansion player and an asset that could be deployed in subsequent deals. Orlando kept its preferred eligible roster intact and surrendered only a second-round selection. These are distinct benefits, and neither deserves to be presented as the acquisition of Randy Livingston's eventual NBA work by Vancouver. The later draft history identifies what the original pick became, not a one-step athlete transfer. Given the limited player production and small but usable flexibility, the historical even outcome and moderate C-plus grades capture the transaction's actual scale.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Orlando earns C+ because the expansion-draft arrangement directed Vancouver toward Rodney Dent and protected the Magic's preferred eligible players. Vancouver also receives C+ for obtaining a transferable 1996 second-round selection eventually identified as No. 42. Dent did not provide substantial Grizzlies NBA production, while Randy Livingston's later career cannot be credited as games played for Vancouver through this agreement.

sections.heading: Seattle Bought an American Point-Guard Prospect
sections.body: The Bucks used the 1995 draft night to move the rights to Eric Snow, an emerging guard from Michigan State, to the Seattle SuperSonics. Seattle gave up the rights to Lithuanian center Eurelijus Žukauskas and a 1996 second-round draft selection. Because the current franchise database uses the Oklahoma City Thunder identity for old Seattle trades, this historical record can be easy to misread. Oklahoma City did not operate an NBA club in 1995. The actual negotiation was between Milwaukee and Seattle, with both organizations exchanging developmental rights rather than established players.

sections.heading: Snow Became a Genuine Seattle Rotation Contributor
sections.body: Unlike a merely speculative overseas selection, Snow made the Sonics and supplied real NBA minutes during the following seasons. He worked as a reserve ball handler behind Seattle's more established guards, with defensive value that later became a cornerstone of his reputation. His eventual long service with the Philadelphia 76ers cannot be assigned to Seattle, because that came following a separate franchise move. Still, the receiving team's ability to put Snow into NBA games is a concrete advantage. A modest draft-night transaction became an actual point-guard asset for the SuperSonics.

sections.heading: Milwaukee's Rights Return Offered Little Immediate Play
sections.body: Milwaukee's initial return consisted of Žukauskas's rights and a second-round slot in the 1996 draft. Žukauskas continued a substantial international career but never appeared in an NBA regular-season game for the Bucks. The selection eventually resolved at No. 53 and was used on Jeff Nordgaard, who appeared in only thirteen Milwaukee games in 1997-98. That is far less direct basketball return than the Sonics obtained from Snow. Rights to a prospect and the opportunity to make a late second-round selection still have value, but neither converted into a meaningful Bucks rotation role.

sections.heading: The Franchise Label Must Not Distort the 1995 Outcome
sections.body: The historical winner was the Seattle side of the franchise now cataloged as Oklahoma City. Snow's defense and reserve minutes outweighed the limited Milwaukee return, although assigning an elite grade for his later work in Philadelphia would overstate what Seattle directly acquired. Milwaukee made two bets on future rights but saw little NBA play from either. The source ledger identifies the draft-choice path without implying Nordgaard was ever a dependable Bucks contributor. Those limits support a Seattle advantage while keeping both grades in proportion to a late-first-and-second-round prospect exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Oklahoma City Thunder Win is the site's franchise-history label; the acquiring team in June 1995 was Seattle. Its side earns B- because Eric Snow became a playable SuperSonics reserve before later changing clubs. Milwaukee receives D+ because Eurelijus Žukauskas did not play NBA games and 1996 No. 53 Jeff Nordgaard appeared only briefly for the Bucks. Snow's subsequent Philadelphia years are excluded from the Seattle return.

sections.heading: Detroit Converted One Late First Into Two Second-Round Chances
sections.body: On June 26, 2008, the Pistons drafted Indiana forward D.J. White with the twenty-ninth overall selection and promptly traded his rights to Seattle. Their return was a pair of second-round draft rights: Walter Sharpe at No. 32 and Trent Plaisted at No. 46. Detroit was seeking two developmental possibilities rather than one late first-rounder. The trade is sometimes labeled Oklahoma City in contemporary data products because the SuperSonics relocated soon afterward. On draft night, however, Seattle still held the acquiring side, and White would enter the league as an Oklahoma City player.

sections.heading: White Actually Played for the Relocated Franchise
sections.body: White was a productive collegiate big man at Indiana, and the Sonics' successor organization put him into NBA games after the franchise's 2008 move. He was not a superstar and did not turn this swap into one of the defining transactions of that first Oklahoma City season. But his actual regular-season availability made the No. 29 choice more than a paper asset. Subsequent games with other franchises were produced through different agreements, so they cannot be counted as if Seattle had kept him forever. The relevant comparison is the early Oklahoma City playing contribution against Detroit's two developmental selections.

sections.heading: Sharpe and Plaisted Offered Almost No Detroit Production
sections.body: Detroit's more favorable-looking pair of draft selections never developed into equivalent NBA value. Sharpe made eight regular-season Pistons appearances, totaling twenty minutes and eight points before his NBA playing career ended. Plaisted, the other player acquired through the draft-rights exchange, never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. The two selections provided training-camp rights and the possibility of uncovering an inexpensive rotation player, yet that possibility did not materialize. Replacing a first-round pick with two near-unused second-round assets explains why the original Pistons-favored assessment required review.

sections.heading: A Real NBA Contributor Beats Two Unconverted Draft Rights
sections.body: The choice faced the usual late-draft uncertainty: Detroit could spread its risk across two prospect evaluations, while Seattle could concentrate on the player it preferred. With hindsight, the distribution did not work for the Pistons. White supplied a genuine roster contribution in Oklahoma City, whereas one Detroit acquisition never debuted and the other appeared only eight times. Seattle's transition to Oklahoma City should be noted to prevent miscrediting games to a city that did not host the team on draft night. Those modest but measurable returns give the franchise's incoming White side the better grade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Thunder Win under the site's successor-franchise identity. The draft-night buyer was Seattle, which secured No. 29 D.J. White for the club that soon moved to Oklahoma City and earns B-. Detroit receives D+ because Walter Sharpe contributed only eight games, twenty minutes and eight points, while Trent Plaisted never played an NBA regular-season game. Two acquired draft-rights slots did not outweigh the first-round choice sent away.
