sections.heading: Orlando Paid for Seattle Not to Use Pick No. 2 on Scott
sections.body: The June 27, 1990 draft-day agreement was unusual because Seattle promised not to choose a particular prospect. The SuperSonics held the second overall choice, while Orlando was picking fourth and strongly wanted Georgia Tech scorer Dennis Scott. To preserve its opportunity, Orlando committed two future second-round picks to Seattle. The arrangement did not trade Scott himself, since he had yet to be selected or sign an NBA contract. Seattle went on to choose Gary Payton at No. 2, and Orlando obtained Scott at No. 4 after Denver selected Mahmoud Abdul-Rauf third.

sections.heading: Scott Became a Longtime Magic Shooting Threat
sections.body: Orlando's protected choice turned into one of the franchise's important early perimeter scorers. Scott joined a young expansion-era Magic team and built his reputation around high-volume three-point shooting. He remained a central offensive player through the club's ascent alongside Shaquille O'Neal and Penny Hardaway, including its run to the 1995 NBA Finals. That lasting on-court value explains why Orlando was willing to surrender future second-round opportunities to reduce uncertainty on draft night. But Scott's production is a consequence of Orlando's own draft selection, not minutes Seattle literally transferred to Orlando in a player deal.

sections.heading: Seattle Obtained Two Picks Rather Than Scott
sections.body: The compensation given to Seattle consisted of a 1993 second-round choice later listed at No. 42, Adonis Jordan, and a 1995 second-round choice ultimately identified as No. 55, Michael McDonald. Those picks had exchange value, even though neither was equivalent to a fourth overall selection. The 1995 choice moved again in a separate 1994 transaction involving Seattle and Golden State, so attributing Michael McDonald's later draft identity as a direct Seattle development story would overstate the result. Seattle also benefited enormously from independently selecting Payton, but his future career should not be credited as a return received from the Magic.

sections.heading: Both Teams Achieved Different Draft-Day Goals
sections.body: The SuperSonics left the 1990 draft with the player they selected second and two extra future choices. Orlando used a small stream of draft capital to protect its favored option at fourth and then acquired a player who contributed for years. The contemporary reporting and both franchise transaction ledgers support that limited structure; they do not support calling it a Scott-for-two-picks player exchange. Orlando's enduring benefit outweighs Seattle's modest additional selections, while the Sonics still deserve a fair grade for extracting value from a commitment consistent with their selection plans.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Magic Win. Orlando earns A because paying two future second-round selections helped ensure it could take Dennis Scott fourth overall, a long-term perimeter contributor. Seattle gets C+ for receiving the 1993 No. 42 and 1995 No. 55 draft positions. Seattle drafted Gary Payton independently at No. 2; neither Payton's career nor a fictional direct trade of Scott's player rights should inflate the compensation from this agreement.

sections.heading: Houston Added an Established Sixth-Man Scorer for Its Push
sections.body: Houston sent Corey Brewer and its 2017 first-round pick to the Lakers on February 23, 2017 in exchange for Lou Williams. The Rockets were surrounding James Harden with additional ball handlers and shooters in Mike D'Antoni's high-volume offense. Williams had been leading Los Angeles in bench scoring, while Brewer's role in Houston had narrowed. For the Lakers, recently reorganized under Magic Johnson, the trade exchanged a veteran scorer for an additional chance to draft a prospect. Both teams clearly valued different timelines, one focused on the imminent postseason and the other on rebuilding.

sections.heading: Williams Gave Houston Twenty-Three Games and More Scoring
sections.body: Williams appeared in twenty-three regular-season Rockets games after the move, all as a reserve. He totaled 591 minutes and 343 points, an average of 14.9 per game, while contributing fifty-six assists. His ability to generate offense without Harden helped Houston's second unit ahead of the playoffs. The sample was shorter and his shooting less efficient than the stretch he had just completed for the Lakers, so the return should be judged by those Houston games, not by his 58 earlier appearances in purple and gold. His subsequent scoring years with the Clippers also belong to a separate acquisition.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Received Brewer and a Usable First-Round Choice
sections.body: The Lakers took in Brewer's veteran contract and, more importantly for their rebuilding timetable, Houston's 2017 first-round pick. The selection ultimately landed at No. 28, later associated with Tony Bradley, although its draft-rights trail continued beyond the original agreement. That history is why Bradley should not simply be listed as a long-term Lakers player acquired from Houston. Brewer supplied another experienced perimeter option during an unsettled roster period, while the pick created an opportunity to trade or select a younger player. Los Angeles obtained genuine draft capital rather than just discarding its leading bench scorer.

sections.heading: The Value Difference Is Short-Term Offense Versus Future Choice
sections.body: Houston got exactly the kind of bench scoring the club sought during a playoff push, with Williams making an immediate impact in a defined rotation role. The Lakers accepted fewer short-term points in exchange for an extra first-round selection and a player contract that could fill minutes while the roster changed. Houston later used Williams in a much larger multi-asset deal with the Clippers, but the entire eventual return from that transaction cannot be attributed to this February swap. The original slight Houston edge remains plausible for instant on-court utility, with more measured credit than the inherited low grades gave either side.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Rockets Edge. Houston earns B because Lou Williams supplied 23 games, 591 minutes and 343 points during its 2016-17 playoff push. Los Angeles receives B- for Corey Brewer's depth and the first-round pick ultimately listed as No. 28 Tony Bradley, a transferable draft asset. Williams's later Clippers scoring and the full return of subsequent unrelated transactions are excluded from Houston's direct NBA performance.

sections.heading: Chicago Added Drew While Houston Accepted Conditional Future Value
sections.body: On September 28, 2000, the Bulls acquired reserve guard Bryce Drew from Houston. The exchange compensated the Rockets through a complicated conditional draft arrangement rather than a conventional pick that would immediately transfer. Chicago's first-round protection in the 2003 and 2004 drafts was broad, and the fallback called for later second-round selections if the protected first never conveyed. Houston also obtained a $1.8 million trade exception, offering salary-management flexibility separate from the eventual players chosen. Both clubs were changing their rosters in the years after the Bulls' championship run and before the Rockets' next playoff core formed.

sections.heading: The Protected First Eventually Became Two Second-Round Choices
sections.body: The future-pick record identifies the fallback as a 2005 second-round selection eventually used at No. 51 on Robert Whaley and a 2006 second eventually used at No. 46 on Dee Brown. Neither player should be treated as if Houston immediately acquired him in 2000. The Rockets subsequently transferred the conditional draft claim in a 2003 package with Glen Rice, creating another transaction in the chain. The original agreement therefore supplied a movable future asset rather than a guaranteed first-round choice or direct rotation help. Assigning those draftees' later professional statistics to this lone swap would break the provenance trail.

sections.heading: Drew Was Short-Term Guard Depth, Not a Franchise Reset
sections.body: Bryce Drew had been drafted by Houston in 1998 and was moving from a crowded Rockets backcourt to a Bulls team that could evaluate additional guards. His role was limited compared with the established scorers the franchise had recently lost, and the trade did not create a new foundational Chicago player. The Bulls' payment became more acceptable once it was clear the pick protection would keep them from losing a high first-round slot. Drew's real contribution was an opportunity for additional NBA minutes and roster coverage, not star-level play. Chicago did not acquire the trade exception or the later Houston-side draft position.

sections.heading: Salary Flexibility Gives Houston a Slight Advantage
sections.body: Houston's return had financial and draft optionality, while Chicago received a familiar NBA guard with a comparatively small role. The Rockets did not secure a permanent first-round player from this transaction, so the old low grade was understandable, but the transferable conditional rights and $1.8 million exception were tangible tools. The Bulls paid with future second-round value without receiving much enduring production from Drew. Those outcomes justify a narrow Rockets edge rather than a broad winner's margin. Any later results of the 2003 Rice transaction must be evaluated as part of that separate, larger exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Rockets Edge. Houston earns C- because the deal produced a $1.8 million trade exception and movable conditional draft claims that eventually resolved into two second-round selections rather than an unprotected first. Chicago receives D+ for Bryce Drew's limited veteran-guard role. The later draft names Robert Whaley and Dee Brown identify the pick chain, not direct Houston player contributions, because the relevant rights were subsequently included in another trade.

sections.heading: A Coaching Contract Produced a Genuine Draft-Pick Trade
sections.body: The 1992 Lakers-Bucks exchange was not a normal transaction involving a player. Mike Dunleavy had coached Los Angeles for two seasons, including a 1991 Finals appearance, when Milwaukee recruited him for a long-term coaching position. The Lakers released him from his remaining contractual obligations in return for two second-round draft selections from the Bucks. Contemporary reporting dates the arrangement to May 11 and 12, although the imported trade route uses an approximate June 1 date. The actual asset that Milwaukee received was permission to hire its chosen coach, not rights to Dunleavy as a player.

sections.heading: The Lakers Converted the Release Into Two Draft Opportunities
sections.body: Los Angeles acquired a 1992 second-round pick later used at No. 36 on USC guard Duane Cooper and an additional 1995 second-round pick, subsequently associated with No. 40 Dwayne Whitfield. Cooper was signed by the Lakers and supplied short-term reserve guard minutes before being waived in November 1993. The later second-round selection passed through subsequent transactions before the 1995 draft, so it would be incorrect to claim Whitfield became a Lakers rotation player because of this compensation agreement. The picks nonetheless had value: Los Angeles was paid in draft rights for a coach who wanted to leave.

sections.heading: Dunleavy Coached Four Seasons in Milwaukee
sections.body: Milwaukee secured its preferred head coach, and Dunleavy began work there for the 1992-93 season. He ultimately coached 328 regular-season Bucks games over four campaigns, winning 107 and losing 221. Those results fell well short of the franchise's ambitions when it gave him a lengthy contract, and Milwaukee dismissed him in April 1996. The contemporary announcement described a much longer contract term, but an agreement's duration is not the same as actual time served. These coaching outcomes are the appropriate measure for Milwaukee's return, not a fictitious tally of on-court Dunleavy minutes.

sections.heading: Compensation Was Useful Even Though Neither Club Transformed
sections.body: Los Angeles emerged with draft capital rather than simply losing its coach, while Milwaukee obtained someone it believed could manage a rebuilding roster. In hindsight, the Bucks did not get a sustained winning era: Dunleavy's four-season record finished well below .500. The Lakers' two second-round assets likewise did not by themselves create stars, so they do not justify an extraordinary grade. The transaction sits in the middle ground between effective contract management and limited realized basketball improvement. A moderate Lakers advantage recognizes compensation secured while keeping the future pick's downstream lineage and Dunleavy's coaching record distinct.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Lakers Win. Los Angeles earns B- for turning Mike Dunleavy's departure into two second-round draft assets, including 1992 No. 36 Duane Cooper. Milwaukee receives C- after Dunleavy coached 328 games over four seasons with a 107-221 record. The later 1995 pick associated with Dwayne Whitfield was not a direct Lakers player return, and the actual coaching-rights deal was reported in May despite the archive's approximate June route.

sections.heading: Vancouver Exchanged Gattison and a Draft Pick for Turner
sections.body: On February 22, 1996, the first-year Vancouver Grizzlies sent Kenny Gattison and a future second-round draft selection to the Orlando Magic for veteran forward Jeff Turner. In the database this franchise is listed under Memphis, but the team actually played in Vancouver at the time. The pick had reached Vancouver through a January trade sending Darrick Martin to Minnesota, so it was not an entirely new asset created in February. Orlando was a championship contender seeking reserve frontcourt options. Vancouver, still constructing a functional inaugural roster, swapped two assets for a player who had already spent years with the Magic.

sections.heading: Turner's Vancouver Stay Ended in Fifteen Days
sections.body: The Grizzlies barely had time to evaluate their acquired veteran before moving on. Vancouver's official transaction history records the trade on February 22 and Turner's waiver on March 8, 1996. That brief stint is the clearest problem with the prior Grizzlies-favored conclusion: the side giving up a player and a draft choice did not retain its incoming veteran through the season. Turner had been an experienced Orlando reserve, but his earlier NBA contributions belong to the Magic, not to the expansion team that briefly acquired him. The swap cannot be awarded a high Vancouver grade by borrowing years of pre-trade play.

sections.heading: Orlando Turned the Selection Into McCaskill
sections.body: The second-round choice arrived in Orlando with draft value and ultimately became the forty-ninth pick in 1996. The Magic selected Amal McCaskill, a center who appeared in seventeen regular-season games for Orlando in 1996-97, making the pick's eventual output modest but real. Gattison also supplied an experienced frontcourt option from the original transaction. This is a two-part return: one NBA veteran and a developmental selection. McCaskill's later service with San Antonio, Atlanta and Philadelphia was not Orlando production, and should never be added to its return. His seventeen Magic games are a more defensible measure of what the pick actually delivered.

sections.heading: The Winner Changes When the Timeline Is Followed
sections.body: The move looks different when the recipient clubs' subsequent rosters are checked rather than just counting acquired names on trade day. Vancouver obtained Turner and waived him within weeks, while Orlando kept the flexibility of veteran depth and exercised a future draft choice. Even with McCaskill's limited games, the Magic realized more direct value than Vancouver did. The Grizzlies' earlier acquisition of this second-round pick from Minnesota was a separate deal and must not be treated as extra compensation in February. Correcting the old verdict recognizes the entire chain while keeping the trade anchored to the actual exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Magic Win. Orlando earns B- because it received veteran Kenny Gattison plus the 1996 No. 49 pick used on Amal McCaskill, who later appeared in seventeen Magic games. The Vancouver Grizzlies, identified as Memphis in the franchise database, receive D because Jeff Turner was waived on March 8, only fifteen days after the exchange. Turner's Orlando career before February and McCaskill's later games elsewhere do not count toward the wrong recipient.

sections.heading: Minnesota Moved Draft Rights and Malcolm Lee for a Future Pick
sections.body: On June 27, 2013, Minnesota gave Golden State the rights to No. 26 first-round selection Andre Roberson and guard Malcolm Lee. The Timberwolves received the Warriors' 2014 second-round pick and cash. Roberson was a Colorado prospect, while Lee had been a Minnesota roster guard whose development was interrupted by injuries. Golden State valued the incoming rights as an asset to move again on draft night. The cash and later selection gave Minnesota resources it could use without committing to another rookie guaranteed a first-round contract. This was a draft-asset transfer, not the start of Roberson's Warriors playing career.

sections.heading: Two More Transactions Produced Nedović for the Warriors
sections.body: Golden State immediately passed Roberson's rights to Oklahoma City in exchange for the rights to No. 29 Archie Goodwin and cash. It next moved Goodwin and Lee to Phoenix for the rights to No. 30 Nemanja Nedović. The Warriors' own media guide documents all three transactions on the same day, distinguishing the original Minnesota deal from the follow-on swaps. Nedović eventually appeared in twenty-four NBA games for Golden State during 2013-14. Roberson later established himself as a defender with Oklahoma City, but none of those Thunder games should count as Golden State return from keeping his rights.

sections.heading: Minnesota Turned Its Second-Round Pick Into Another Cash Deal
sections.body: The 2014 second-round selection Minnesota received became No. 53, used to select Alessandro Gentile. Minnesota did not develop him into a regular Wolves rotation player. Instead, the franchise sold the rights to Houston for cash in a separate June 2014 transaction. That later move is evidence that Minnesota's original compensation was transferable; it is not evidence of Gentile playing NBA games for the Timberwolves. The 2013 agreement contained cash in addition to the draft pick, and each amount belongs to the relevant step in the trade chain. The NBA draft ledger supports both dates and the pick identity.

sections.heading: Modest Returns on Both Sides Support an Even Verdict
sections.body: Neither club produced a lasting homegrown regular through this one transaction. Golden State's connected sequence yielded Nedović and limited NBA minutes, while Minnesota collected financial value and a second-round asset it moved again. The original strong Warriors grade would depend too heavily on Roberson's later career for Oklahoma City, where he arrived through a separate exchange. Minnesota likewise cannot claim an influential NBA player because Gentile's rights eventually bore that name. Judging the first trade by what each franchise genuinely received and could deploy supports a modest even assessment. The exact dates and intermediate assets are more informative than a winner's label alone.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Golden State receives C+ because Roberson and Malcolm Lee were exchanged again that night, ultimately yielding Nemanja Nedović and his twenty-four Warriors games. Minnesota also receives C+ for cash and the 2014 No. 53 pick, later used on Alessandro Gentile and sold for additional cash. Neither Roberson's Thunder career nor a fictional Minnesota playing contribution from Gentile is assigned to the wrong team.

sections.heading: New Orleans Replaced Two Departing Players With Guard Depth
sections.body: The November 20, 2010 deal was a five-player exchange between the New Orleans Hornets and Toronto Raptors. New Orleans sent former All-Star shooter Peja Stojaković and young guard Jerryd Bayless north, receiving Jarrett Jack, David Andersen and Marcus Banks. Toronto's own announcement also disclosed cash considerations accompanying the incoming players. New Orleans was off to a strong start and wanted another established guard to relieve Chris Paul without abandoning its competitive plans. Andersen provided additional frontcourt coverage, while Banks was largely a contract piece. The historical franchise is now labeled Pelicans in the site, but it still played as the Hornets in 2010.

sections.heading: Jack's New Orleans Tenure Was More Than a Rental
sections.body: Jack played seventy New Orleans regular-season games after the November trade in 2010-11, then forty-five more in the lockout-shortened 2011-12 season. His Hornets totals across the two campaigns were 115 games and 468 assists, with his second year featuring thirty-nine starts as the guard rotation changed. That production is specific to the club that acquired him in this exchange. The thirteen Toronto games he played before the deal and the years he later spent with Golden State or Brooklyn cannot be credited to the Hornets. Jack's direct ability to play significant minutes made him the lasting and useful return from this package.

sections.heading: Toronto Received a Prospect and Limited Peja Time
sections.body: The Raptors were seeking younger talent and future payroll flexibility, not an immediate veteran star to replace Jack's full contribution. Bayless was twenty-two at the time and continued to receive Toronto backcourt opportunities, giving the club a genuine player rather than just cash savings. Stojaković, despite his long-standing reputation as a shooter, barely figured in Toronto's games and eventually moved on before joining Dallas. His previous scoring years in New Orleans are not acquired Toronto performance, nor is his championship run with Dallas. The incoming cash consideration reinforced the financial motive but cannot be represented as another player or first-round draft selection.

sections.heading: Different Objectives Yielded Different Basketball Returns
sections.body: New Orleans wanted a rotation guard during a period of immediate contention and received one who played meaningful minutes over two seasons. Toronto was retooling and prioritized Bayless's development along with relief from longer-term obligations. Both sides could reasonably defend their intentions, but the guard depth and subsequent playing record favor the Hornets' side. The original grade underrates Toronto if it treats Stojaković's short stay as the full return, since Bayless continued to play for the franchise. A high New Orleans grade is better grounded in Jack's 115 Hornets appearances than in any unrelated future NBA stops or historic Peja statistics.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans Win is the site's franchise label; the receiving team was the New Orleans Hornets. New Orleans earns A- because Jarrett Jack played 115 games and recorded 468 assists across the rest of 2010-11 and 2011-12, with Andersen adding depth. Toronto receives B- for acquiring younger guard Jerryd Bayless and some financial flexibility. Stojaković's later Dallas success and Jack's post-Hornets work belong to separate transactions and cannot inflate the return.

sections.heading: The Rockets Added a Veteran Guard to a Contending Team
sections.body: Houston's February 19, 2015 trade brought Pablo Prigioni from the New York Knicks in exchange for Alexey Shved and two future second-round draft selections. The Rockets were preparing for a postseason run behind James Harden and Dwight Howard and wanted an experienced ball handler who could manage possessions alongside their main creators. Prigioni was thirty-seven and had been part of the Knicks' guard rotation before the deadline. This was distinct from Houston's separate acquisition of K.J. McDaniels from Philadelphia on the same day. New York, meanwhile, was collecting future opportunities for a struggling roster, a very different timetable from Houston's immediate competitive objectives.

sections.heading: Prigioni Had a Defined Houston Rotation Role
sections.body: Prigioni appeared in twenty-four Rockets regular-season games after the trade in 2014-15 and did not start any of them. He nevertheless provided veteran handling and defensive activity to a second unit that needed decisions made without the ball stopping. His role continued into the postseason, where he played in seventeen games while Houston advanced to the Western Conference Finals. Those appearances are the appropriate direct return for the deadline acquisition. His earlier Knicks career and any subsequent free-agent movements do not belong in Houston's 2015 trade totals. A grade based only on his limited scoring would miss the purpose of obtaining a reliable veteran reserve.

sections.heading: New York Received Shved and Two Future Draft Assets
sections.body: The Knicks added Shved plus Houston's second-round selections for 2017 and 2019. Shved was a wing-sized ball handler who could take shots and minutes on a roster short of established options, but he was not a long-term franchise centerpiece. The picks carried value through their ability to be selected or traded later, rather than guaranteeing that either eventually named prospect would wear a Knicks uniform. The selection lineages ultimately connect them to Ognjen Jaramaz at No. 58 in 2017 and Kyle Guy at No. 55 in 2019. Those identities track the choices, not automatic Knicks playing production, and any subsequent draft-rights transactions require separate attribution.

sections.heading: Asset Flexibility Gives New York a Narrow Edge
sections.body: Houston gained useful immediate minutes from Prigioni and reached the conference finals, which improves on the inherited near-failing grade. New York obtained one short-term player and two distinct future selections for someone who would otherwise have supplied veteran depth during a rebuild. The quantity and flexibility of those assets justify the Knicks' advantage without treating two late seconds as guaranteed NBA starters. This comparison needs to preserve Houston's actual twenty-four regular-season appearances and seventeen playoff appearances from Prigioni rather than borrow unrelated years. It also needs to keep Houston's McDaniels trade separate, because that involved an additional second-round pick and another outgoing player.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win. New York earns B for Alexey Shved's short-term roster service and Houston's 2017 and 2019 second-round selections, later associated with Ognjen Jaramaz and Kyle Guy. Houston receives B- rather than D+ because Pablo Prigioni contributed twenty-four regular-season games and seventeen playoff appearances during the 2015 Western Conference Finals run. Neither future draft identity should be assigned Knicks playing minutes merely because the pick was once owned by New York.

sections.heading: The Clippers Sent Smith Back to the Rockets
sections.body: On January 22, 2016, Los Angeles returned Josh Smith to Houston after a difficult partial season with the Clippers. The exchange also sent cash and the draft rights to Ukrainian big man Sergei Lishchuk to the Rockets, while Los Angeles acquired the rights to Maarty Leunen. Smith had joined the Clippers in the preceding offseason after playing for Houston during its 2015 playoff run. He averaged only 5.7 points in thirty-two Clippers appearances, and his minutes were disappearing as the team shifted more playing time to Cole Aldrich. The agreement therefore solved a roster-management problem for Los Angeles while offering Houston a familiar veteran.

sections.heading: Smith Played Another Twenty-Three Houston Games
sections.body: Smith's second Houston stint in 2015-16 consisted of twenty-three regular-season games after the January transaction. Those appearances, rather than the fifty-five Rockets regular-season games from his separate 2014-15 signing, are the direct playing return of this trade. He offered size and a known style of passing from the frontcourt but did not reproduce the larger impact of the previous season's Western Conference Finals run. Even so, getting NBA minutes from a veteran player was more measurable than simply holding distant draft rights. Houston did not have to send a current rotation player back to Los Angeles to make this deal work.

sections.heading: Two Rights Assets Had Little Direct NBA Output
sections.body: Lishchuk's rights moved to Houston, and Leunen's rights moved to Los Angeles, but neither player became an NBA rotation regular because of the transaction. Rights to an overseas prospect can retain administrative or negotiating value without ever converting into court time. The cash accompanying Smith belonged to Houston, not to the Clippers, and should not be reversed when recording who received which part of the package. The Clippers gained flexibility to continue with their other frontcourt reserves, having traded away a player who had fallen out of the main rotation. That benefit differs from a typical asset-based return involving draft picks with defined selection dates.

sections.heading: The Direct Player Return Gives Houston the Edge
sections.body: Houston acquired a veteran with a useful history in the franchise and obtained a limited but genuine twenty-three-game contribution. Los Angeles moved away from a signing that was not working and avoided retaining another out-of-rotation contract. Those practical outcomes favor the Rockets, although a stronger victory would exaggerate what Smith actually accomplished after January. His past Houston success is relevant background, not earned minutes from this new transaction. Likewise, Leunen's and Lishchuk's international records do not equal NBA games for the clubs receiving their rights. The grading should reflect a narrow playing-value advantage rather than treating the rights swaps as major roster upgrades.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Rockets Edge. Houston earns B- for acquiring Josh Smith's twenty-three 2015-16 regular-season games along with Sergei Lishchuk's rights and cash. Los Angeles receives C- for moving a reserve who had fallen out of favor and taking Maarty Leunen's rights, without any resulting Clippers NBA games from those rights. Smith's fifty-five Houston appearances in 2014-15 came from an earlier free-agent signing and cannot be credited to this January 2016 trade.

sections.heading: New Orleans Sold the Twenty-Seventh Pick for Cash
sections.body: The New Orleans Hornets used the twenty-seventh selection of the 2008 NBA draft on Kansas forward Darrell Arthur but did not plan to keep his rights. On June 26, New Orleans sold that draft asset to the Portland Trail Blazers for cash. The sale offered immediate financial value rather than a prospect the Hornets would develop, and it did not transfer an existing roster player in the ordinary sense. New Orleans's use of the selection happened as the franchise was coming off a strong Western Conference season. The current database calls the club the Pelicans, although the 2008 transaction belonged to the Hornets.

sections.heading: Portland Immediately Moved Arthur's Rights Again
sections.body: Arthur's rights did not stay in Portland long enough to become an NBA playing contribution. On the same draft night, Portland joined a three-team agreement involving Houston and Memphis. The Blazers sent Arthur's rights to the Grizzlies and Joey Dorsey's rights to the Rockets, while Houston sent the rights to Nicolas Batum to Portland. Memphis supplied other draft rights and a future second to Houston as part of the larger transaction. The chain matters because Arthur was not literally traded for Batum in a standalone two-team agreement. Portland needed the multi-party structure and other assets to end up with the player it wanted.

sections.heading: Neither Original Buyer nor Seller Got Arthur's Playing Minutes
sections.body: Arthur went on to a substantial NBA career, principally with Memphis and Denver. He did not provide regular-season games for either the Trail Blazers or the Hornets through this first rights sale. New Orleans instead realized financial consideration; the amount should not be invented in the absence of a verified figure. Portland's reward was the ability to deploy a draft-rights asset immediately toward another prospect. Batum later became an important Portland wing, but that fact is a downstream result of a different transaction containing multiple additional pieces, not a direct player transfer from New Orleans in the cash sale.

sections.heading: The Draft Rights Had More Utility for the Buyer
sections.body: New Orleans obtained cash for a pick it had chosen to monetize rather than retain, making its return real but limited. Portland received draft rights that could immediately be used in a more ambitious exchange, helping the club reorganize its draft-night portfolio. Giving Portland every minute Batum eventually played without accounting for the three-team deal would overstate this original purchase. Giving New Orleans an automatic failure because it received no roster player would ignore the purpose of the cash sale. The Blazers nonetheless hold the stronger asset-utility result, justifying an advantage grounded in the short draft-night chain rather than imagined Arthur appearances.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Blazers Win. Portland earns B+ because the Darrell Arthur rights purchased from New Orleans became one useful component of its same-night multi-team deal that delivered Nicolas Batum's rights. The New Orleans Hornets receive C for cash consideration with no incoming player. Arthur never supplied games to either original participant. Batum's subsequent NBA contribution belonged to Portland's distinct three-team agreement and cannot be credited solely to the cash sale.

sections.heading: Memphis Purchased Rights to Calathes by Changing a Pick Obligation
sections.body: The July 22, 2013 transaction brought Nick Calathes's NBA rights from Dallas to Memphis. The Grizzlies did not send the Mavericks an existing rotation player or a newly issued first-round selection. Instead, they lifted the protection on a 2016 second-round choice already owed to Dallas through an earlier chain involving Denver. Dallas thereby improved the certainty of receiving a lower-value draft asset, while Memphis acquired a guard who had been playing professionally overseas since being drafted in 2009. The trade has to be evaluated as an exchange of draft rights and protection terms, not as an ordinary swap of two signed players.

sections.heading: Calathes Converted His Rights Into Two Actual NBA Seasons
sections.body: Memphis signed Calathes in August 2013, and he appeared in seventy-one regular-season games as a rookie during 2013-14. He made seven starts and scored 347 points. The following season he played fifty-eight more games, adding 243 points. His direct Memphis tenure therefore yielded 129 appearances and 590 points before he returned to European basketball. The Grizzlies' official media guide confirms both seasonal lines and identifies the Dallas transaction as the way his rights arrived. Those numbers offer a firmer valuation than speculation about what an unprotected second might eventually become, and they cannot be awarded to Dallas.

sections.heading: Dallas Secured the Value of an Existing Second-Round Claim
sections.body: Dallas entered the arrangement already entitled to a conditional 2016 second-round selection, with restrictions that could have prevented the pick from conveying. Memphis removed the top-fifty-five protection, converting the obligation into one less vulnerable to disappearing because of draft position. That is a legitimate form of compensation: draft certainty has value even when a club does not receive a player. The Mavericks did not receive Calathes's later NBA minutes, and the protection adjustment should not be mistaken for the transfer of a lottery pick. The earlier transaction that created the debt also needs to remain distinct from this July 2013 negotiation.

sections.heading: A Real Two-Year Reserve Outweighs the Pick-Term Adjustment
sections.body: Both franchises achieved something they wanted. Dallas obtained stronger rights to a future selection, while Memphis turned a conditional obligation into an NBA-ready guard. With hindsight, Calathes's 129 Grizzlies appearances made the latter outcome more substantial than the modest pick-protection benefit can demonstrate on its own. The original Mavericks-winning result undervalued the actual basketball return and relied too heavily on the abstract importance of an unprotected future pick. Memphis did not obtain an All-Star, and Dallas did not give away a proven NBA veteran. More moderate grades recognize a credible reserve contributor on one side and useful draft certainty on the other.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Grizzlies Win. Memphis earns B+ because Nick Calathes produced 129 games and 590 points across 2013-14 and 2014-15 after the club acquired his rights. Dallas receives C+ for removal of top-fifty-five protection on a previously owed 2016 second-round pick, strengthening a future draft claim without adding immediate playing time. The July 2013 exchange involved rights and protection terms, not a first-round selection or Calathes's already completed NBA service.

sections.heading: Oklahoma City Obtained the Higher Draft Choice
sections.body: The July 8, 2010 draft-rights trade sent Kansas center Cole Aldrich, selected eleventh, and veteran wing Morris Peterson from the New Orleans Hornets to the Oklahoma City Thunder. New Orleans received the rights to forwards Craig Brackins at No. 21 and Quincy Pondexter at No. 26. The Thunder wanted a young defensive center and experienced perimeter presence around Kevin Durant and Russell Westbrook. New Orleans traded down to acquire two distinct first-round rights. The site's old Charlotte Hornets franchise key refers to the historical New Orleans club, not a 2010 trade with the Charlotte Bobcats.

sections.heading: Aldrich Provided Limited Thunder Playing Time
sections.body: Aldrich appeared in eighteen Oklahoma City regular-season games during his 2010-11 rookie season and twenty-six more in 2011-12, totaling forty-four Thunder appearances before he moved elsewhere. His defensive and rebounding potential made him a reasonable prospect to obtain, but he never developed into a major Thunder starter. Peterson did not become a long-term veteran cornerstone either. In February 2011 Oklahoma City included Peterson and D.J. White in a separate trade for Nazr Mohammed. That transaction demonstrated the veteran contract's utility, although Mohammed's entire contribution cannot be credited solely to having acquired Peterson the previous summer.

sections.heading: New Orleans Turned Two Picks Into Separate Roster Options
sections.body: The Hornets had two first-round selections instead of one higher pick. Pondexter went on to record NBA appearances for New Orleans, establishing a direct playing return from the draft-night agreement. Brackins did not remain with the Hornets for the season. The club later packaged his rights with Darius Songaila and sent them to Philadelphia for Willie Green and Jason Smith. Those incoming veterans were obtained through an additional agreement requiring Songaila, so crediting both entirely to this exchange would overlook the later price. The original return is best described as two movable first-round assets with different developmental outcomes.

sections.heading: The Slight Edge Is an Asset-Chain Judgment
sections.body: Both organizations received usable options but neither produced a star directly from this one transaction. Oklahoma City got a frontcourt prospect who played forty-four Thunder games and a movable veteran contract. New Orleans collected a pair of first-round rights that supplied some playing time and separate trade flexibility. Comparing only eventual NBA careers without checking ownership changes would give misleading credit for Pondexter's later teams or Mohammed's full Thunder service. The old high grades are more generous than those direct returns justify. A modest Thunder edge recognizes the higher selection and Peterson's later flexibility without transforming either into a franchise-defining acquisition.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Oklahoma City Thunder Edge. Oklahoma City earns B for Cole Aldrich's forty-four regular-season Thunder games and the ability to include Morris Peterson in a subsequent deal. The historical New Orleans Hornets receive B- under the site's Charlotte franchise identifier for Quincy Pondexter's playing contribution and Craig Brackins's transferable rights. Nazr Mohammed and Willie Green arrived through later packages that required additional assets, not directly in the original July 2010 exchange.

sections.heading: Dallas Sent a Recent Lottery Pick for Better Draft Protection
sections.body: On June 29, 1996, Dallas traded Cherokee Parks to Minnesota in a deal centered on an earlier first-round pick obligation. Parks had been Dallas's No. 12 selection in the 1995 draft, but the Mavericks were clearing salary and had other frontcourt options after further trades that June. In return for the young big man, Minnesota agreed to remove the protection that had covered the second through sixth overall positions on a 1997 first-round pick Dallas had acquired through the 1994 Sean Rooks transaction. This was an amendment to a prior draft debt, not a separate incoming first-round player.

sections.heading: Parks Became a Two-Season Minnesota Contributor
sections.body: Parks joined a Timberwolves roster building around Kevin Garnett and supplied genuine frontcourt minutes rather than remaining an unconverted prospect right. In 1996-97, he appeared in seventy-six Minnesota regular-season games and scored 252 points as a reserve. The following season he played seventy-nine games, started forty-three and scored 558 points. His two-year return totaled 155 games, forty-three starts and 810 points before he left for another franchise. The Wolves' acquired player therefore proved considerably more useful than the inherited near-failing grade suggests. His previous Dallas rookie games and later Vancouver appearances are excluded from this receiving-team total.

sections.heading: The Mavericks Reduced Lottery Risk and Created Cap Room
sections.body: Dallas had originally been vulnerable to the Timberwolves retaining the 1997 first if it landed among picks two through six. Under the revised agreement, Minnesota could keep the selection only if it landed first, with the obligation otherwise shifting in favor of Dallas under the negotiated terms. Contemporary reporting also described the move as putting the Mavericks roughly three million dollars below the new salary cap. Those were meaningful financial and draft rights, but no separate future first-round selection was invented in this June deal. Dallas was improving collection prospects on a previous claim while removing a player salary from its roster.

sections.heading: Both Returns Were Useful in Different Ways
sections.body: Minnesota gained a player who appeared in 155 games over two seasons, while Dallas gained salary flexibility and firmer access to previously negotiated draft compensation. One side collected actual frontcourt production, and the other reduced the uncertainty around an earlier pick. A winner label driven only by removal of lottery protection would overlook the Wolves' playing return. A judgment based solely on Parks's starts would miss the Mavericks' cap and pick objectives. The more balanced retrospective is that both teams received usable value without acquiring a new cornerstone. Neither the 1994 Sean Rooks trade nor other Dallas draft swaps of June 1996 should be folded into this separate deal.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Minnesota earns B because Cherokee Parks played 155 Timberwolves games and made forty-three starts during 1996-97 and 1997-98. Dallas also gets B for reducing protection on a first-round pick previously owed from the Sean Rooks transaction and improving payroll flexibility. The agreement did not create a brand-new first-round player in 1996, and Parks's subsequent games with other clubs are excluded from Minnesota's two-season return.

sections.heading: Charlotte Acquired a Center Prospect at No. 20
sections.body: On June 25, 2008, the Charlotte Bobcats obtained Denver's twentieth overall draft pick and used the selection on French seven-footer Alexis Ajinça. The Nuggets received a protected future first-round pick in exchange. Charlotte was buying immediate access to a prospect with developmental upside, while Denver preferred to hold a later asset that could be deployed as its roster needs changed. This was a draft-choice deal rather than a trade of existing NBA player contracts. The site uses the current Charlotte Hornets team name, but the franchise was called the Bobcats when this agreement was completed.

sections.heading: Ajinça's Charlotte Career Produced Thirty-Seven Games
sections.body: Ajinça entered the NBA with Charlotte and appeared in thirty-one regular-season games during 2008-09, starting four. He then played six more games for the Bobcats in 2009-10 before continuing his professional career elsewhere. Those thirty-seven appearances, totaling eighty points, were the direct NBA playing return from the No. 20 choice for Charlotte. The center later played for other franchises, including much more productive seasons with New Orleans, but that later career cannot be credited to Charlotte as though the Bobcats retained him. A grade for this trade must use the actual short Charlotte tenure rather than his eventual career total.

sections.heading: Denver's Future Pick Traveled Through Two More Franchises
sections.body: The protected first-round selection Charlotte sent to Denver eventually became the sixteenth overall pick in the 2010 draft, associated with Luke Babbitt. The Nuggets' own media guide explains that the future pick moved through Minnesota and ultimately to Portland before Babbitt was selected. This route gives Denver credit for receiving a transferable first-round asset, not for any NBA minutes Babbitt played with the Trail Blazers. The deal's protective terms were spread across several possible draft years before the selection conveyed. They gave the incoming pick legitimate flexibility, but a transaction chain still has to distinguish the original buyer from the final drafting club.

sections.heading: Denver Did Better With an Asset Than Charlotte With the Player
sections.body: Charlotte got a young center at a first-round price, but thirty-seven NBA appearances were a limited direct result. Denver did not get a player who would become an on-court Nuggets contributor through the selection; it instead acquired a first-round right that could be moved again and eventually conveyed as a real pick. The transaction therefore favors Denver's asset management while acknowledging the modest nature of the benefit. Calling it a franchise-changing win would overstate the eventual right's importance, just as using Ajinça's later New Orleans games would flatter Charlotte. The revised grades measure each receiving team's actual opportunity and direct output.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win. Denver earns B- for converting the 2008 No. 20 selection into a protected future first that ultimately conveyed in 2010 and was transferable through other transactions. Charlotte receives C because Alexis Ajinça appeared in only thirty-seven Bobcats games over two seasons. Luke Babbitt's later Portland career was not Denver playing production, while Ajinça's subsequent NBA seasons elsewhere were not part of Charlotte's short return.

sections.heading: Charlotte Acquired a Veteran Shooter During the 1999-2000 Season
sections.body: Charlotte obtained Dale Ellis from Milwaukee in January 2000 for two second-round picks. The official Hornets media guide dates the acquisition January 19, while Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee and Charlotte transaction ledgers place it January 18. The inherited January 19 canonical identifier follows the franchise record and should not be silently altered because another ledger uses the previous day. The selections eventually became No. 49 in 2000, associated with Jason Hart, and No. 48 in 2002, associated with Chris Owens. That is a specific two-pick cost for an age-39 shooter, not a future first-rounder or a promise of a franchise player. Ellis had once been a major scoring option for Seattle, but Charlotte was acquiring a short-term bench specialist near the end of his playing career.

sections.heading: The Bucks Collected Two Picks Instead of Long-Term Veteran Minutes
sections.body: Milwaukee received the 2000 No. 49 second-round right that became Jason Hart and the 2002 No. 48 right used for Chris Owens. The earlier inherited article called Owens No. 47, which is incorrect: the NBA's 2002 draft lists Jamal Sampson at No. 47 and Owens at No. 48. Two separate selections are the Bucks' direct trade return, not every subsequent minute those players logged for other franchises. Ellis had provided Milwaukee 18 appearances and 6.8 points per game earlier in the 1999-00 season before this exchange. Trading a reserve in his final season for draft flexibility was a plausible way to conserve future value, even though neither second-round right automatically became an enduring Milwaukee rotation player. The B- grade should describe that asset optionality without attributing Hart's entire NBA career to Milwaukee.

sections.heading: Ellis Was a Short-Term Addition for the Hornets
sections.body: Ellis played 24 regular-season games for Charlotte in 1999-00, starting none and averaging 10.0 minutes and 2.3 points. Those numbers are more useful to assessing the exchange than his celebrated earlier scoring totals with Seattle and Denver. He did hit 40 percent of his three-point attempts for Charlotte, but on a modest 1.5 attempts per game; his total time on the floor amounted to 240 minutes. His Hornets stay was brief, and Charlotte included his contract in the August 1, 2000 exchange with Miami that brought Jamal Mashburn and P.J. Brown among other players. That later multi-player transaction had its own economic and roster consequences, which should not be credited entirely to the January two-pick Ellis deal. The inherited C- grade reflects limited direct playing return for the draft cost.

sections.heading: Future Options Outweighed a Brief Final Career Stint
sections.body: Milwaukee's side held two chances to add inexpensive future players or deploy second-round rights in a separate transaction, while Charlotte received a veteran who did not become a lasting piece. Neither path created a star directly from the agreement, which argues against an extreme grade for the Bucks. Still, converting an aging reserve into multiple selections was more durable than Charlotte's limited end-of-career minutes. The judgment must separate what the Bucks acquired in January from the later clubs that used the selected players. The historical slight Milwaukee edge therefore holds after a closer accounting of the compensation and Ellis's remaining playing career.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Bucks Edge. Milwaukee receives the inherited B- for converting its aging reserve into 2000 No. 49 Jason Hart and 2002 No. 48 Chris Owens second-round rights, not the incorrectly inherited No. 47. Charlotte's C- reflects Ellis's 24 games, zero starts, 240 total minutes and 2.3 points per game after the January trade. The Hornets' official media guide records January 19, while Basketball-Reference lists January 18, so the existing canonical date stays until a settled transaction-date policy establishes otherwise. Neither franchise should be credited with players' later performances for other teams. These are distinct draft assets against one limited Charlotte season, not a hidden future first-round pick.

sections.heading: New Orleans Accepted Miller and Two Future Seconds
sections.body: On July 13, 2012, Minnesota transferred veteran center Brad Miller and two future second-round draft choices to the New Orleans Hornets. The return was a 2017 second-round selection with top-fifty-five protection. The pick never conveyed, which made the long-term compensation small for Minnesota, although moving Miller's remaining obligation still advanced its payroll objective. New Orleans received the rights to what would ultimately be the fifty-second selection in 2013 and the thirty-fifth selection in 2016. Those later slot identifications trace the selections, not immediate contracts with Lorenzo Brown or Rade Zagorac.

sections.heading: Brad Miller Was an Asset for Another Transaction, Not a Hornets Regular
sections.body: Miller was nearing the end of his NBA career, and New Orleans did not obtain an extended playing contribution from him. Instead, the Hornets used him in a subsequent three-team transaction on July 27 involving the Phoenix Suns and Minnesota. That agreement moved Miller, Jerome Dyson and future pick rights while bringing Robin Lopez, Hakim Warrick and cash to New Orleans. The later deal also required additional consideration beyond what the Hornets acquired in this July 13 swap. Any Lopez games should be credited to the separate three-team agreement rather than presented as Miller's direct playing return.

sections.heading: The Future Picks Followed Different Downstream Paths
sections.body: The 2013 second-round selection associated with Lorenzo Brown returned to Minnesota as part of the July 27 transaction, while the 2016 choice later associated with Rade Zagorac was directed into the wider three-team arrangement. Neither prospect became an immediate Hornets draft success through the July 13 exchange. That chronology prevents the original deal from receiving inflated grades based on career totals earned elsewhere. The choices were valuable primarily because New Orleans could redeploy them quickly. Minnesota, meanwhile, obtained a conditional 2017 second that did not convey, so the exchange's residual draft return was weaker than the two outgoing pick rights initially appeared.

sections.heading: The Hornets Had More Flexibility, but the Later Deal Had Costs
sections.body: The original trade favored New Orleans because it assembled an expiring veteran contract and two second-round assets at the cost of a protected selection that ultimately delivered nothing. Minnesota reduced a salary commitment but gave up rights that would have been useful in its own future draft planning. The July 27 trade demonstrated that New Orleans could use the received pieces, though that later package had its own outgoing assets and counterparties. The judgment should neither credit the Hornets with every subsequent player's career nor call the Wolves' salary objective imaginary. A moderate New Orleans advantage best captures the original asset value without overstating the deal.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Pelicans Win under the modern site label; New Orleans was still the Hornets in July 2012. The Hornets receive B for acquiring Brad Miller's transferable contract and two future second-round choices, subsequently deployed in another deal. Minnesota gets C- for reducing an obligation, while the protected incoming 2017 second never conveyed. The 2013 pick returned to Minnesota in a later transaction, so the eventual draft names aren't automatic New Orleans player production.

sections.heading: The 2009 Hornets Sent Daniels and a Future Pick to Minnesota
sections.body: The September 9, 2009 trade moved Antonio Daniels from the New Orleans Hornets to Minnesota. In return, New Orleans received Darius Songaila and Bobby Brown. An important part of the consideration is easy to miss in brief transaction summaries: the Hornets also transferred their own 2014 second-round draft selection to Minnesota. The current site stores New Orleans franchise history under a Charlotte Hornets label for this legacy record, but the team involved in September 2009 played in New Orleans. The Pelicans' official later media guide explicitly includes the draft pick, independently corroborated by a 2014 draft-rights history and RealGM's contemporary transaction archive.

sections.heading: Songaila and Brown Gave New Orleans Immediate NBA Minutes
sections.body: Songaila played seventy-five regular-season games for the Hornets during 2009-10, producing 543 points across 1,410 minutes. His steady reserve-frontcourt role offered more than a paper asset or expiring contract. Brown appeared in twenty-two New Orleans games, adding 145 points and 46 assists before moving again in January. Those are receiving-team contributions tied directly to this swap, not earlier playing time in Minnesota. The Hornets traded Brown to the Clippers in a later deal for a different 2014 second-round asset, so that transaction should not be confused with the 2014 pick the team had already delivered to the Timberwolves in September.

sections.heading: The Future Selection Really Did Become Glenn Robinson III
sections.body: Minnesota acquired the Hornets' 2014 second-round pick in addition to Daniels. That choice ultimately became No. 40, used by the Timberwolves to draft Glenn Robinson III out of Michigan. The club's own media guide reports twenty-five Minnesota appearances, 108 minutes and twenty-nine points in the 2014-15 season before it waived Robinson in March. The pick was a real draft return even though the later player output was modest, and its existence is confirmed by franchise materials despite being omitted from simplified Basketball-Reference transaction lines. Treating the selection as nonexistent would misstate Minnesota's compensation and produce a misleading verdict.

sections.heading: Immediate Hornets Production Slightly Outweighed the Draft Benefit
sections.body: The Hornets received ninety-seven combined games from Songaila and Brown during the season after the exchange, with Songaila becoming a useful rotation reserve. Minnesota's eventual value was a future second-round choice and an incoming veteran contract rather than comparable direct playing production. Glenn Robinson III's later career with other organizations cannot be treated as if all those appearances were Timberwolves games. Conversely, New Orleans did not keep its own 2014 selection and should not be awarded the pick's downstream rights. Evaluating both sides with the valid draft term and actual recipient seasons produces a modest New Orleans advantage rather than the inherited Minnesota win.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hornets Win. The historical New Orleans side, represented by the site's Charlotte franchise key, earns B for Darius Songaila's 75 games and 543 points plus Bobby Brown's 22 games and 145 points in 2009-10. Minnesota receives B- for Antonio Daniels and the legitimate New Orleans 2014 second-round pick, ultimately No. 40 Glenn Robinson III, who played 25 Wolves games. Both clubs' receiving-team returns are counted without importing later careers or unrelated picks.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Paid Two Future Choices for a Late First-Round Center
sections.body: The June 22, 2017 NBA draft produced a rights trade that sent Anžejs Pasečņiks from Orlando to Philadelphia. Orlando had used the twenty-fifth overall selection on the Latvian center, whose European development made him a longer-term prospect. The 76ers offered a conditional 2020 first-round pick and a 2020 second-round choice tied to the less favorable of Brooklyn and New York's selections. The first carried protection terms rather than being an unqualified top selection. Philadelphia was wagering that a specific international prospect would be worth more than the future draft flexibility, while Orlando preferred two later assets.

sections.heading: The Sixers Never Obtained Pasečņiks NBA Minutes
sections.body: Pasečņiks did not become a Philadelphia regular-season player through the 2017 rights acquisition. He remained overseas while the organization continued developing other frontcourt options and ultimately moved on without turning the draft choice into a Sixers rotation appearance. His subsequent NBA time in Washington belongs to a different franchise agreement and cannot retroactively rescue Philadelphia's original return. A low Sixers grade is appropriate because the club surrendered a future first and another second without receiving direct on-court production. The situation differs from drafting a useful reserve who played for several seasons before being moved again.

sections.heading: Orlando Converted the First Into a Later Trade Asset
sections.body: The protected first-round pick eventually conveyed as No. 21 in 2020, which was used to select Tyrese Maxey. However, Orlando did not draft or develop Maxey. The Magic included that future pick in the February 2019 transaction that sent Markelle Fultz from Philadelphia to Orlando. The second-round choice eventually became No. 47, associated with Yam Madar, and followed its own series of later rights transfers. Those are genuine values from the original 2017 trade, but the later pick names are a record of what the selections became, not proof of Magic minutes by Maxey or Madar.

sections.heading: The Magic Retained Leverage, Not the Players Drafted Years Later
sections.body: Orlando exchanged an overseas prospect for two draft assets and later used the first as part of a package to acquire a young guard in Fultz. Philadelphia received Pasečņiks's rights and did not convert them into any NBA contribution, even though the same organization eventually drafted Maxey using the pick returned in a separate deal. The multiple transactions need to remain independent: Fultz had his own asset price in 2019, and Maxey's Sixers career cannot be credited directly to the 2017 Orlando trade. The Magic's advantage is substantial in terms of pick leverage, although the revised grade stops short of claiming all later returns as a single one-step victory.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Magic Win. Orlando receives A- for obtaining a future first and second in exchange for No. 25 Anžejs Pasečņiks, retaining assets it could later trade. Philadelphia gets D+ because Pasečņiks never played an NBA game for the Sixers. The first eventually became 2020 No. 21 Tyrese Maxey but returned to Philadelphia through the separate 2019 Markelle Fultz trade; Orlando must not be credited with Maxey's Sixers production or Yam Madar's subsequent rights path.

sections.heading: Houston Moved White and Rights to Create Salary-Cap Flexibility
sections.body: The July 13, 2013 exchange sent Royce White, the draft rights to Turkish big man Furkan Aldemir and cash from the Houston Rockets to Philadelphia. The 76ers offered a conditional 2014 second-round selection that would not convey if its protective terms were met. Houston was creating financial room during its pursuit of Dwight Howard, who signed as a free agent rather than arriving through this trade. White had not appeared in an NBA regular-season game for the Rockets following disputes over his availability and team arrangements. Moving his guaranteed contract was a tangible financial purpose even without a player returned to Houston.

sections.heading: The Protected Pick Never Supplied Houston a Player
sections.body: The second-round obligation eventually expired without conveying, so Houston cannot claim a drafted prospect or NBA appearances from the incoming pick. That doesn't make the transaction wholly valueless to the Rockets: eliminating salary and a difficult roster fit opened flexibility during a major free-agency period. The price was the rights to Aldemir and cash alongside White, a real resource cost that should be included in the analysis. The original failing grade treats the absent pick as proof of no benefit, ignoring the cap-management objective. Yet Houston's later Howard seasons remain the consequence of a separate signing, not direct on-court trade compensation.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Got Forty-One Games From Aldemir, None From White
sections.body: Philadelphia waived White in October 2013 before he played an NBA regular-season game for the franchise. Aldemir's contribution arrived later: the Sixers signed him in December 2014, and he appeared in forty-one games during 2014-15. He started nine times, totaled 540 minutes and scored ninety-three points while averaging 4.3 rebounds. That is a modest but measurable return for the overseas draft rights the team acquired in 2013. The Sixers did not receive a future first-round pick or immediate rotation cornerstone, and White's eventual professional stops elsewhere cannot be used to improve their trade grade.

sections.heading: Short-Term Financial Goals and Later Reserve Minutes Both Count
sections.body: Houston exchanged prospect rights and cash to clear an unwanted contract, while Philadelphia accepted the risk and collected a young player's rights with no effective draft-pick payment. Aldemir's later NBA minutes make the Sixers' side the stronger tangible basketball return, though his single 41-game season doesn't justify star-level grading. Houston still advanced a reasonable salary-cap objective when pursuing a major free agent. The separation between those two forms of value matters: the Rockets' protected second never arrived, and the 76ers' Royce White asset never produced court time. A modest Philadelphia edge recognizes actual reserve appearances without dismissing Houston's financial outcome.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight 76ers Edge. Philadelphia earns B- because Furkan Aldemir eventually played 41 Sixers games and made nine starts, and the team also received cash; Royce White was waived without an NBA appearance. Houston gets C for removing White's contract during its free-agency planning even though the incoming conditional 2014 second-round pick never conveyed. Dwight Howard signed separately, so his Houston career isn't a direct player return from this trade.

sections.heading: Houston Acquired International Draft Rights Instead of a Signed NBA Player
sections.body: The Rockets arranged a July 14, 2009 agreement with Atlanta for the NBA rights to Australian forward-center David Andersen. Atlanta had originally drafted him in 2002, but he had spent the intervening seasons with successful professional clubs in Europe. Houston paid cash, future considerations and a future conditional second-round draft selection to bring those rights under its control. Atlanta's own official announcement identifies all three components of the return. With Yao Ming unavailable during the 2009-10 season, Houston was searching for size and shooting from other sources. The trade offered a possible immediate rotation player rather than simply a speculative overseas prospect.

sections.heading: Andersen Converted His Rights Into Sixty-Three Houston Games
sections.body: Houston signed Andersen after obtaining his rights, and he appeared in sixty-three regular-season Rockets games in 2009-10. He played 891 minutes, scored 367 points and contributed 208 rebounds, coming off the bench every time. His average of 5.8 points and 3.3 rebounds shows useful reserve depth rather than a star-level replacement for an injured center. Even at that level, the return was concrete NBA production from rights that had not been exercised by Atlanta for years. Andersen later played for Toronto and New Orleans in different transactions, and those appearances should not be assigned to Houston's direct acquisition.

sections.heading: Atlanta's Pick Became Ennis Rights and Was Moved Again
sections.body: The conditional second-round selection eventually conveyed in 2013 at No. 50, a pick associated with James Ennis III. The Hawks did not receive Ennis's subsequent NBA minutes from this 2009 transaction. Their 2013 draft-night activity sent his rights to the Miami Heat for another future second-round selection. Miami publicly announced that acquisition, confirming the pick was a transferable asset rather than a player Atlanta retained. The additional 2009 cash and future consideration helped make the deal useful to the Hawks even without an immediate NBA player. Still, the later Miami outcome requires recognition as a separate trade with its own compensation.

sections.heading: On-Court Use Gives Houston the Narrower but Clearer Victory
sections.body: Houston obtained an experienced international big man who played most of a season, while Atlanta converted previously dormant rights into cash and a pick it could move. Neither team suffered an overwhelming loss, so the inherited failing grade for Houston exaggerates the cost and ignores the direct contribution. Andersen's sixty-three appearances are a stronger immediate basketball return than assigning Atlanta Ennis's eventual career would allow. At the same time, the Hawks received valid financial and draft value and deserve more than a token grade. The better retrospective is a Houston advantage based on realized playing time without misattributing another team's later draft development.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Rockets Win. Houston receives B because David Andersen delivered sixty-three Rockets games, 891 minutes and 367 points after his rights arrived in July 2009. Atlanta earns B- for cash, future considerations and the conditional second-round pick later identified as 2013 No. 50 James Ennis III. The Hawks sold Ennis's rights to Miami through a subsequent trade, so Ennis's later NBA games cannot be claimed as Atlanta production.

sections.heading: Detroit Sold Wells's Rights During the Lockout Transaction Rush
sections.body: The 1998 draft gave Detroit the rights to Bonzi Wells with the eleventh overall selection, but he never played a regular-season game for the Pistons. When the lockout delayed the beginning of the following season, front offices had to condense months of business into a brief January 1999 period. Detroit used that opening to send Wells's rights to Portland in exchange for a future first-round pick and a second-round choice. The Pistons later explained that clearing approximately $1.1 million in cap room was part of the objective, permitting other veteran free-agent work. This was an explicit salary and draft-assets decision, not an ordinary trade of a veteran who had already played for Detroit.

sections.heading: Portland Turned the Incoming Rights Into a Real NBA Rotation Player
sections.body: The Trail Blazers signed Wells and brought him into their perimeter rotation over the seasons that followed. He became a productive scoring and rebounding wing during Portland's playoff years, contributing far more than the zero Detroit appearances recorded before the transaction. His career eventually continued in Memphis, Sacramento, Houston and New Orleans, but those later stops do not increase Portland's direct return. The core result is that Portland secured a young first-round talent and developed him into a regular member of its own team. That outcome justifies a strong grade without assuming every later NBA game he played belonged to the Blazers.

sections.heading: Detroit's Two Selections Were Later Traced to Jones and Penn
sections.body: Detroit collected a protected 1999 first-round selection that ultimately became No. 27, associated with Jumaine Jones, and a 2000 second-round selection that became No. 57, associated with Scoonie Penn. The original pick rights changed hands again before the players were selected, leaving Atlanta associated with both names in draft histories. Neither should be presented as years of NBA production for Detroit merely because the Pistons owned an earlier link in the pick chain. The selections nevertheless had tradable value, and the cap flexibility had a concrete organizational purpose. Evaluating only the draft names without checking the rights transfers would exaggerate the Pistons' playing return.

sections.heading: The Player Career Was More Valuable Than the Cap and Pick Package
sections.body: Portland acquired a wing who became a genuine contributor during an extended stretch with the team. Detroit received a protected first, a later second and payroll flexibility it wanted while reorganizing the roster around established veterans. The Pistons weren't left with literally nothing, which supports a respectable grade for asset management, but the return never matched Wells's playing contribution in Portland. Detroit's own retrospective acknowledges the cap objective, not an eventual draft steal. The trade therefore favors Portland while preserving the distinction between actual player minutes, the two later selections and free-agent spending decisions made outside the exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Blazers Win. Portland earns A- after acquiring Bonzi Wells's rights and developing him into a multi-season Trail Blazers rotation contributor. Detroit receives B- for a conditional 1999 first-round choice later No. 27 Jumaine Jones, a 2000 second later No. 57 Scoonie Penn and salary flexibility. Neither Jones nor Penn supplied Pistons NBA games through those later selections, so the value was movable draft capital and cap room rather than direct on-court output.

sections.heading: The Bullets Exchanged a Disgruntled Forward for Draft Rights
sections.body: On October 8, 1992, Washington moved John Williams to the Los Angeles Clippers after his relationship with the Bullets deteriorated. The return consisted of reserve center William Bedford and the draft rights to UCLA forward Don MacLean, who had been selected nineteenth earlier that year. Contemporary Washington Post and Los Angeles Times reporting confirms the two incoming assets and the trade discussions between the teams. Williams should not be confused with Cavaliers center John 'Hot Rod' Williams, an entirely different player. Los Angeles hoped its incoming forward would benefit from playing closer to home, while Washington sought a fresh roster direction and an opportunity to develop a young scorer.

sections.heading: Bedford Left Quickly, but MacLean Became a Real Bullets Player
sections.body: Washington waived Bedford within days of the transaction, making him an administrative rather than basketball return. MacLean was a different story. The Bullets signed him to a multiyear contract in October and placed him into their developmental plans. After averaging 6.6 points as a rookie in 1992-93, he emerged as an important scorer the following season. In 1993-94, he played seventy-five games, started sixty-nine and averaged 18.2 points and 6.2 rebounds. His total of 1,365 points led the team, and the NBA named him Most Improved Player. Those are actual Washington seasons, not career statistics borrowed from another franchise.

sections.heading: The Clippers Took a Risk on Williams's Reset
sections.body: Los Angeles gave up the opportunity to develop MacLean while acquiring Williams, a versatile forward whose Washington years had been disrupted by conditioning concerns and limited availability. Both coaching staffs knew the deal carried uncertainty. The Clippers were coming off a playoff appearance and saw a chance to add talent without giving up one of their central veterans. But the hoped-for return did not produce a Washington-style breakout during his Los Angeles period. That limited result has to be separated from his earlier Bullets seasons and from the career of the similarly named Cavaliers player. Washington's choice to build through an unsigned rookie carried its own risk at the time.

sections.heading: MacLean's Award-Winning Season Settles the Historical Comparison
sections.body: The lasting return belonged to Washington because a draft-rights acquisition turned into a productive forward and an award-winning 1993-94 campaign. Bedford's immediate release did little damage to that conclusion: MacLean was the main reason the Bullets agreed to move Williams. Los Angeles pursued a plausible change of setting for an established player, but did not receive a comparable multiseason offensive contributor. A strong Washington grade is supported by recorded playing time and Most Improved Player recognition rather than speculation about the Williams controversy. The swap did not involve a future first-round pick or a third team in October 1992; MacLean's earlier June draft route was separate.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Wizards Win under the modern franchise label. The Washington Bullets earn A- because Don MacLean became a real rotation scorer and averaged 18.2 points in 1993-94, winning NBA Most Improved Player after the team acquired his rights; William Bedford was waived within days. The Clippers receive C- for taking a short-lived chance on forward John Williams. Those results concern the Washington forward, not Cavaliers center John 'Hot Rod' Williams.
