sections.heading: Detroit Sent Green to New York for Moore and a Draft Right
sections.body: On October 28, 1987, Detroit exchanged Sidney Green for Ron Moore and a future second-round selection from the Knicks. The conditional draft timing allowed a 1988 or 1989 choice and the historical ledger associates the exercised right with No. 30 Fennis Dembo in 1988. This was a modest frontcourt and draft-capital transaction rather than a change to the Pistons' core star guard rotation. Detroit sought additional depth and a young prospect opportunity, while New York preferred an experienced forward with a more established NBA record. The teams valued two different types of frontcourt and roster flexibility.

sections.heading: Green Brought an Experienced Forward to the Knicks
sections.body: Green entered the arrangement with years of NBA experience and could provide size, rebounding and inside play for New York. His record before October 1987 belonged to previous teams, so the Knicks' actual return must begin with their own appearances after the trade. New York did not acquire Detroit's future 1988 second-round selection; that asset moved to the Pistons. The trade gave the Knicks a defined player rather than an uncertain drafted prospect, which was a reasonable objective for a club hoping to stabilize its rotation. The direct benefit remained a supporting piece rather than a franchise centerpiece.

sections.heading: Moore and Dembo Were Developmental Returns for Detroit
sections.body: Detroit received Moore's rights and an opportunity that became the No. 30 selection associated with Dembo. Those assets gave the Pistons additional choices while developing a roster that was beginning to compete with the league's best teams. Neither should be credited with the full production of Detroit's established championship contributors. The team could evaluate Moore and its drafted guard or forward prospects, but subsequent trades and roster changes would determine whether each produced useful NBA minutes. The right's eventual named draft outcome is a ledger fact, not permission to assign every future professional game of that player to Detroit.

sections.heading: Two Practical But Supporting Returns Make the Deal Even
sections.body: New York obtained a playable veteran forward, while Detroit gained a current prospect and a second-round draft chance. Both packages provided ordinary rotation or development options and neither by itself explained the clubs' later records. Equal moderate grades are more defensible than drawing a large winning conclusion from Green's previous success or the eventual identity of the future selection. The transaction is best viewed as an exchange of present-day certainty for a broader mix of possible future value. Its historical importance lies chiefly in the teams' roster decisions rather than any single new NBA star.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Detroit receives B- for Ron Moore and the future second-round right associated with 1988 No. 30 Fennis Dembo. New York also earns B- for adding experienced forward Sidney Green. Detroit's later championship core should not be assigned to these incoming assets, and Green's prior NBA seasons are not newly created Knicks production through this deal.

sections.heading: New York Received Anderson While Indiana Took Stephens's Rights
sections.body: The October 3, 1988 record identifies an exchange in which the Knicks received Ron Anderson and the Pacers obtained rights to Everette Stephens. It was a low-profile movement of one NBA-experienced player and another developmental asset rather than an exchange of marquee stars. Anderson had a more established professional playing background, so New York could reasonably expect an immediate roster evaluation. Indiana instead accepted the potential to develop a different guard over time. The transaction's listed counterparties and rights status matter, because acquiring someone's rights did not guarantee a signed NBA starter or the full value of that person's prior career.

sections.heading: Anderson's Veteran Profile Supported New York's Side
sections.body: Anderson was a known perimeter player when New York pursued him, giving the Knicks a roster piece with existing professional experience. How much value he actually provided depends on his minutes after the trade and any independent subsequent transactions, not his whole résumé before arrival. He shouldn't be treated as a newly acquired franchise star or a guaranteed long-term rotation fixture. Nonetheless, trading for a veteran rather than an uncertain rights-held prospect provided New York with a more immediate personnel option. That near-term certainty supports a slight receiving-team preference, while leaving open the possibility that the rights Indiana obtained retained some developmental value.

sections.heading: Stephens's Rights Were a Smaller Indiana Opportunity
sections.body: Indiana took the rights to Everette Stephens rather than receiving multiple first-round draft positions or an already established NBA starter. Such a player could be evaluated through training camp and roster decisions, but the transaction itself did not guarantee a large return. Later professional results, if any, must be assigned according to who signed and used the player after the exchange. The Pacers could still gain flexibility from holding the rights, though that isn't the same as receiving confirmed years of NBA scoring. Any review that skips the difference between rights and completed games will distort the practical value of the asset.

sections.heading: The Record Supports a Restrained New York Advantage
sections.body: New York's side offered the clearer opportunity for immediate NBA service, while Indiana accepted a developmental player-rights claim with a less certain payoff. That yields a modest Knicks-winning assessment rather than a sweeping declaration of franchise victory. Neither team gained an unprotected first-round selection, and neither should be awarded later statistics from unrelated contracts. The older ledger may present brief transaction notes without all subsequent contract details, so the grades should reflect that uncertainty. Indiana wasn't empty-handed, but New York's veteran return carried more direct potential to affect its current roster.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win by a modest veteran-value edge. New York earns B- for receiving Ron Anderson as a more established NBA guard or wing option, while Indiana receives C+ for the developmental rights to Everette Stephens. Neither right was an automatic multiseason contract, and the later careers of both players must be credited to the teams that actually employed them.

sections.heading: Detroit Exchanged a Future Pick for Ceballos and Another Second
sections.body: The November 26, 2000 historical transaction transferred veteran Cedric Ceballos and a future 2002 second-round selection to Miami, while Detroit received another 2002 second-round right. The incoming Pistons choice later appears in the draft ledger at No. 37, associated with Tito Maddox. The Heat's incoming later selection is associated with No. 53 Tommy Smith. These draft identities describe the rights' eventual positions, not necessarily players who reported directly to those particular teams after all subsequent transfers. Miami sought a veteran scoring option along with a further prospect chance, while Detroit preferred a different second-round position.

sections.heading: Ceballos Offered Experience Rather Than a New Superstar
sections.body: Ceballos had been a productive NBA scorer earlier in his career, which made his name the most recognizable part of the agreement. His peak offensive seasons, however, came before the 2000 transaction and must not be counted as new Miami production. The proper benefit is whatever roster or contractual role he provided to the Heat after the agreement, including whether later team decisions changed his availability. A veteran acquisition can carry practical value even without a long new starting tenure. The Heat also obtained a separate second-round selection, so the analysis should not reduce the entire exchange to whether Ceballos replicated past All-Star output.

sections.heading: The Two Draft Outcomes Followed Different Rights Chains
sections.body: Detroit's incoming 2002 right later became associated with No. 37 Tito Maddox. Miami's separate 2002 selection later tracked to No. 53 Tommy Smith. Those numbers are useful evidence of where the picks ultimately landed, but they do not automatically prove either player spent NBA seasons with the clubs holding the original rights. Each eventual draft-night movement has to be evaluated separately. The higher Detroit selection provided an early-second-round opportunity, while the Heat's later selection offered a more speculative development chance. It would be inaccurate to award any other teams' playing minutes to the two original receiving organizations.

sections.heading: A Narrow Heat Edge Reflects the Veteran Plus Pick Combination
sections.body: Miami obtained a known former scorer and a future draft opportunity; Detroit received a second-round position whose later draft identity is traceable but uncertain in on-court value. That supports a limited Miami advantage rather than an overwhelming win. The Pistons still secured a pick and could use it as an asset or bargaining tool, so their side is not worthless. Neither transaction by itself explains Detroit's later championship build or Miami's next playoff era. Keeping the two selected prospects' later rights chains separate also prevents a mistaken claim that both clubs received long-term rotation players in this small deal.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Heat Win, narrowly. Miami receives B- for Cedric Ceballos's veteran contract and the 2002 second associated with No. 53 Tommy Smith. Detroit earns C+ for a different 2002 second-round right associated with No. 37 Tito Maddox. Both eventual picks require final rights-chain verification, and Ceballos's earlier scoring seasons are not automatically new Miami NBA production.

sections.heading: Phoenix Preferred Two Future Draft Chances
sections.body: On October 9, 1973, Phoenix traded veteran center Walt Wesley to the Capital Bullets for two future third-round selections. The 1974 choice later appeared at No. 49, associated with Earl Williams, and the 1975 selection at No. 54 with Bayard Forrest. This transaction happened when the NBA draft extended well beyond two rounds, so third-round rights were legitimate prospects rather than modern undrafted-free-agent invitations. Phoenix opted to create two new chances to find frontcourt talent rather than commit another roster season to Wesley, who already had several years of league experience.

sections.heading: Washington Pursued Immediate Center Depth
sections.body: The Bullets, indexed under the modern Washington Wizards franchise lineage, acquired Wesley as a veteran interior option. They were not receiving an unproven college player or an extra draft selection. The club's established lineup could use him in practices and roster combinations without waiting through two future drafts. His previous seasons elsewhere should not be treated as fresh Capital Bullets performance, however, and the transaction itself did not guarantee a prominent long-term starting role. The relevant return was the player on his new contract, set against the two picks Washington relinquished.

sections.heading: Third-Round Rights Did Not Guarantee NBA Careers
sections.body: Earl Williams and Bayard Forrest provide names and slots for the selections Phoenix acquired, but those historical draft identities require separate roster verification. A player being selected at No. 49 or No. 54 didn't establish that he became a regular Suns center. The value of the package was the pair of attempts to identify talent or use the rights in another personnel agreement. Counting both picks as fully successful drafted starters would overstate the return. At the same time, treating third-round selections as nonexistent because today's draft only has two rounds would erase genuine 1970s capital.

sections.heading: The Suns Had a Slightly Broader Set of Options
sections.body: The Suns ended the trade with two separate future selections while Washington gained a known center who could serve its immediate roster. Neither club obtained a top overall draft pick, and Wesley was a useful veteran rather than a dominant star by 1973. Phoenix has the stronger asset count, especially because its draft rights were held in different years. A measured Suns win captures those development opportunities without borrowing Williams's or Forrest's entire later careers. Washington's choice remains reasonable for a contender trying to staff its frontcourt with established professional experience.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Suns Win on draft flexibility. Phoenix earns B for two third-round selections, which later corresponded to 1974 No. 49 Earl Williams and 1975 No. 54 Bayard Forrest. The Capital Bullets, historically grouped under Washington's franchise record, get C+ for veteran Walt Wesley. The Suns' incoming rights weren't automatically two productive NBA roster players.

sections.heading: Buffalo and Milwaukee Exchanged Different Draft Opportunities
sections.body: On August 5, 1976, the Buffalo Braves acquired the rights to the seventh selection of the ABA dispersal draft from Milwaukee. That position was associated with Bird Averitt. The Bucks received an ordinary 1977 NBA second-round selection that later became No. 27 Glenn Williams. The dispersal mechanism was created after the ABA-NBA merger and isn't interchangeable with a regular NBA amateur draft. Milwaukee preferred a future traditional draft opportunity, while Buffalo used its acquisition to evaluate an available professional who had played in the rival league. The modern Clippers franchise index covers the Braves' actual transaction.

sections.heading: Averitt Was a Known ABA Scorer
sections.body: Averitt had professional experience and a reputation for scoring in the ABA before he entered the merger dispersal process. Buffalo's willingness to use a high dispersal slot reflected interest in a player closer to NBA readiness than an unknown 1977 second-round prospect. Yet a player's previous ABA points weren't NBA minutes with the Braves, and the future roster return had to be established after the acquisition. Moving this asset didn't give Milwaukee Averitt's established professional career. It gave the Bucks a different opportunity to select someone from the following year's amateur draft.

sections.heading: Milwaukee's Selection Became a Specific 1977 Pick
sections.body: The incoming Bucks second was ultimately identified with the twenty-seventh selection in the 1977 draft, associated with Glenn Williams. That concrete position is a traceable benefit of choosing the future draft route. It did not guarantee a star, but it offered more predictable conventional NBA draft mechanics than acquiring an ABA dispersal right. By contrast, Buffalo took the immediate risk of a professional it could bring into its developing roster. Tracking the actual names prevents the agreement from being reduced to two anonymous draft picks without historical context.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Receives a Narrow Developmental Edge
sections.body: The Bucks obtained a future second-round right that could support roster rebuilding, while Buffalo took a faster approach through Averitt. Neither side secured a franchise-defining selection, and later team success depended on many unrelated transactions. The result slightly favors Milwaukee given the ordinary draft right and the limited direct NBA impact that can be firmly attributed to Buffalo's dispersal acquisition. This is a modest result: the Bucks did not gain several firsts, and the Braves were not irrational to pursue a familiar professional scorer during the merger transition.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Bucks Edge. Milwaukee receives C+ for the 1977 No. 27 second-round position eventually associated with Glenn Williams. Buffalo, counted under the Clippers franchise lineage, receives C for the No. 7 ABA dispersal draft rights associated with Bird Averitt. Neither right is treated as an assured NBA starter, and Averitt's ABA résumé isn't Buffalo NBA production.

sections.heading: Chicago Let Golden State Pursue Mike Bratz
sections.body: Chicago's September 30, 1983 agreement allowed Golden State to pursue restricted free agent Mike Bratz without the Bulls invoking their right of first refusal. In exchange, Chicago obtained a 1984 fourth-round draft position that eventually appeared as No. 77, associated with Mark Halsel. The transaction was principally about a contractual matching right rather than a conventional exchange of two signed players. Golden State valued the immediate access to a veteran guard; Chicago accepted a lower-round development chance instead of defending its matching claim. That distinction is essential to accurately describing what moved.

sections.heading: Bratz Brought Experience But Not Guaranteed Peak Production
sections.body: Bratz had played NBA guard minutes for multiple clubs and could offer ball handling and perimeter offense to the Warriors. His earlier career was evidence that Golden State had targeted someone familiar with league competition, not proof of what he would produce in a new uniform. A right to sign Bratz might also have had different contractual value depending on the player's terms. The agreement did not convey a first-round selection or an established young star to Golden State. It removed a barrier that could otherwise complicate the club's attempt to add a particular veteran.

sections.heading: A Fourth-Round Selection Was Real Compensation in 1984
sections.body: Chicago received the No. 77-linked fourth-round position in the 1984 draft. The rights associated with Halsel represented a legitimate selection in an era of drafts longer than the modern two rounds, even though a fourth-round choice generally held a lower likelihood of delivering sustained NBA production. The Bulls couldn't assume that selecting a player there would solve a long-term rotation issue. But they converted a contractual right they chose not to exercise into another tangible asset. Any later professional outcomes from Halsel would need to be checked separately from the original compensation.

sections.heading: The Bulls Secured Value for Forgoing Their Option
sections.body: Chicago gained something for stepping aside and had no obligation to commit further roster resources to Bratz through this transaction. Golden State secured its desired access to a veteran guard while paying a speculative fourth-round pick. That gives Chicago a slight asset-efficiency advantage, without justifying the inherited failing grade for the Warriors. The Warriors had a roster reason for the agreement, and Chicago's low draft position had limited upside. A restrained Bulls-winning assessment fits the small stakes of a free-agent matching-right trade.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win, slightly. Chicago earns C+ for converting its decision not to match Mike Bratz into a 1984 fourth-round choice, later No. 77 Mark Halsel. Golden State gets C for obtaining a clear route to a veteran guard. No existing player contract was traded for Halsel, and the fourth-round position wasn't a guaranteed Bulls rotation contributor.

sections.heading: Houston Acquired a Waiver of Milwaukee's Matching Rights
sections.body: On October 5, 1983, Houston reached an agreement under which Milwaukee declined to exercise its right of first refusal on restricted free agent Phil Ford. The Rockets supplied cash and a 1984 sixth-round draft selection to the Bucks. That far-later selection was eventually identified as No. 120, associated with McKinley Singleton. This was not the sale of an already signed Milwaukee player to Houston on a normal player contract. The underlying prize for the Rockets was the ability to pursue Ford without another club invoking the specific matching right it held.

sections.heading: Ford's Existing Reputation Explained Houston's Interest
sections.body: Ford had been a notable NBA guard earlier in his career and offered a recognizable ball-handling option for Houston. The Rockets' decision to spend cash and lower-round draft capital reflected an immediate personnel objective, not an attempt to acquire an untested late draft prospect. Ford's most celebrated seasons, however, preceded the October 1983 transaction. Those accomplishments could inform scouting but could not automatically be credited as Rockets games or future playoff results. Milwaukee, meanwhile, was willing to move past the contractual claim rather than retain it without compensation.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Received Cash and a Sixth-Round Position
sections.body: The Bucks turned their right to match an offer for Ford into immediate financial consideration and a sixth-round selection. The eventual No. 120 slot had a traceable draft identity, but McKinley Singleton was a highly speculative asset at that stage of the draft. Calling him an established future Bucks player on the agreement date would distort the return. Still, the cash was genuine compensation and the pick provided an additional possible player-rights route. That combined return was useful for a club that no longer treated Ford as indispensable to its main roster plan.

sections.heading: The Bucks Collected Compensation Without Losing a Current Star
sections.body: Milwaukee received a defined payment plus a draft opportunity for voluntarily stepping away from an older guard's free agency. Houston gained an option to sign a veteran with known prior NBA ability. The Bucks have a modest advantage because they converted a contractual right into assets while Houston took on uncertainty about Ford's remaining career. But Houston wasn't left empty-handed, and a sixth-round pick alone could not justify a dominant victory claim. This trade is most accurately evaluated through its free-agent rules, not through a mistaken conventional player-for-pick account.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win by a modest financial and draft-rights edge. Milwaukee earns B- for cash and a 1984 sixth-round pick later associated with No. 120 McKinley Singleton. Houston gets C for Milwaukee's decision not to exercise matching rights on Phil Ford. Ford's earlier NBA peak and Singleton's uncertain future aren't counted as guaranteed receiving-team production.

sections.heading: San Diego Obtained Two Players for a Conditional Second
sections.body: On October 6, 1983, the San Diego Clippers acquired Wes Matthews Sr. and Kevin Figaro from Atlanta. The Hawks received a conditional second-round selection that later became associated with the 1986 No. 32 position and Cedric Henderson. The 1983 trade therefore gave the Clippers two players they could evaluate immediately while Atlanta accepted the uncertainty of a later draft claim. The transaction was made while the franchise still played in San Diego, so using the modern Los Angeles Clippers index should not suggest the deal happened at its later home venue.

sections.heading: Matthews Offered an Experienced Guard Option
sections.body: Matthews was an NBA guard with existing experience and could provide depth to a Clippers backcourt that was looking for workable combinations. Figaro offered another player for the club to assess, though neither should automatically be treated as a long-term starter. Receiving two named basketball assets was useful because the team could decide their roles after training camp. The Hawks' previous playing time from Matthews and Figaro, if any, cannot be assigned to San Diego. The relevant contribution is the period after the exchange, including possible later roster moves that would need separate attribution.

sections.heading: Atlanta Banked a Specific Future Draft Chance
sections.body: The conditional selection ended up in the historical draft ledger as No. 32 in 1986, associated with Cedric Henderson. That is a meaningful second-round position and gives the outgoing-player exchange a traceable later result. It does not by itself establish that Henderson played for Atlanta or became a major Hawks contributor. The future pick also delayed any prospect evaluation compared with San Diego's immediate player acquisitions. Depending on its conditions and possible subsequent transfers, Atlanta could have used the asset differently without altering the original October 1983 agreement.

sections.heading: Two Available Players Tilt the Return Toward San Diego
sections.body: San Diego received Matthews and Figaro as immediate roster options while Atlanta turned them into a conditional future pick. The Clippers' clearer near-term depth is enough for a limited winning verdict, though neither acquisition established a new franchise cornerstone. Atlanta retained a development opportunity that could turn out differently from either veteran's direct role. Moderate grades are more appropriate than a strong success claim, particularly because the 1986 draft right must be kept separate from every later contract signed by its eventual namesake.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win, narrowly. The San Diego Clippers, indexed under today's Los Angeles franchise, receive B- for Wes Matthews Sr. and Kevin Figaro. Atlanta earns C+ for a conditional second that became associated with 1986 No. 32 Cedric Henderson. Neither Matthews's prior career nor a future draft name is counted as guaranteed new receiving-team NBA production.

sections.heading: Houston Exchanged a Third-Round Right for Hank McDowell
sections.body: Houston and the Los Angeles Clippers reached an agreement on August 29, 1984 that sent Hank McDowell to the Rockets in exchange for a 1985 third-round draft selection. The historical draft ledger eventually associates that selection with No. 65 Kenny Perry. Houston preferred to take a look at an available frontcourt player before the season, while Los Angeles converted a player it could part with into a future development chance. The Clippers had recently relocated from San Diego, so the change in franchise location is relevant to the date. This deal didn't contain a first-round selection or an established All-Star.

sections.heading: McDowell's NBA Prospects Were Still Being Evaluated
sections.body: McDowell was a center and forward prospect whose value depended on how the Rockets would use him, rather than his previous draft reputation alone. Houston could examine whether he fit behind its taller frontcourt players and whether he earned rotation minutes. Acquiring his name on an official transaction ledger did not ensure he would become a substantial new NBA scorer. The team gave up a later selection rather than immediate veteran help, so its practical wager was that an existing player's readiness outweighed an uncertain draft slot. His career after the trade must be assessed separately from what Houston hoped to gain.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Held a Traceable 1985 Draft Asset
sections.body: The Clippers' incoming third-round choice ultimately connects to the No. 65 Kenny Perry position. In 1985, that was a legitimate professional draft round, but it carried limited certainty of a regular-season roster place. The franchise could select a prospect or deal the pick before the draft; either pathway would require following the individual rights chain. Another transaction in September 1984 involving the Clippers and Washington also references a 1985 No. 65 pick, so those related records need careful reconciliation rather than treating two No. 65 positions as different assets. The direct August return is one third-round right.

sections.heading: The Draft Opportunity Slightly Outweighs the Player Experiment
sections.body: Los Angeles gave up McDowell but gained a pick it could put toward a future roster, whereas Houston received a chance to test the big man's immediate NBA usefulness. Neither side secured a reliable starter and the draft-rights trail is narrower than some later summaries imply. The Clippers receive a modest edge because the recorded selection gave them another developmental option, while McDowell's new Rockets contribution didn't become a major historical story. This is a small trade whose value is better conveyed through its precise pick and player than through unrelated franchise achievements.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win, narrowly. Los Angeles earns C+ for the 1985 third-round selection associated with No. 65 Kenny Perry, while Houston receives C- for Hank McDowell's limited upside as a frontcourt option. A related later No. 65 transaction requires rights-chain reconciliation; the August deal shouldn't be counted as creating two separate picks.

sections.heading: The Clippers Used Draft Compensation to Add Bryan Warrick
sections.body: On September 25, 1984 the Los Angeles Clippers obtained guard Bryan Warrick from the Washington Bullets. Washington received a 1985 third-round draft choice eventually associated with No. 65 Ken Perry. The acquisition offered Los Angeles another perimeter option as it built its roster for the first season after moving from San Diego. Washington, historically filed under the Wizards franchise lineage, preferred an additional draft opportunity rather than continuing with Warrick. No first-round selection or marquee starting guard moved in this agreement, keeping the immediate stakes relatively modest.

sections.heading: Warrick Provided a Player to Assess Immediately
sections.body: Warrick had collegiate and professional background that gave the Clippers an identifiable prospect rather than a right requiring another draft to exercise. Los Angeles could assess his handle, defense and ability to contribute in limited guard minutes when assembling the new season's roster. That is more direct than a future selection, but the transaction alone did not make him an established NBA starter. The distinction between his previous developmental record and actual Clippers games after September matters. A short tenure or an additional roster decision would narrow the ultimate return without changing the asset actually delivered.

sections.heading: Washington Received a Third-Round Slot, Not a First
sections.body: The Bullets' incoming draft right corresponded to No. 65 in 1985, when the NBA still conducted additional rounds beyond the modern two. The player identifier appears as Ken Perry in the September record and Kenny Perry in an associated August Clippers transaction, which may reflect the same rights chain. A reliable audit should treat that naming variation as a reason to reconcile the asset, not to count two different future selections. The draft position still gave Washington a legitimate prospect opportunity. Its practical ceiling was limited by the low selection and by any later change in who finally exercised the choice.

sections.heading: A Young Guard Is a Small Advantage Over a Late Draft Slot
sections.body: The Clippers obtained a guard they could immediately evaluate and the Bullets accepted a more speculative later selection. Warrick offered a direct route to playing time, which supports a modest Clippers advantage, but neither return was decisive for an entire franchise. Washington's third-round pick had real value in the draft format of the time. The grade shouldn't be inflated through Warrick's earlier biography or by double-counting the same 1985 pick through separate agreements. The immediate roster option and the modest value of a third-round selection warrant restrained grades on both sides.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win, modestly. Los Angeles earns B- for acquiring Bryan Warrick as a guard option, while the Washington Bullets receive C+ for a 1985 third-round selection associated with No. 65 Ken Perry. The pick's name variant with Kenny Perry in an earlier trade needs rights-chain reconciliation rather than duplicate draft credit.

sections.heading: Portland Acquired Eddie Jordan for a Conditional Third
sections.body: Portland's September 28, 1984 transaction brought guard Eddie Jordan from the Los Angeles Lakers. The Lakers received the right to a conditional third-round choice in the 1985 draft. The draft's additional rounds meant this was a real option, although its potential value was substantially below the first round. Portland pursued a named NBA veteran to assess during the upcoming season, while Los Angeles moved a guard who wasn't central to its established championship-contending rotation. The pick's particular conveyance condition remains important because it determines whether the Lakers actually received and used a final draft slot.

sections.heading: Jordan Offered Veteran Ball Handling to Portland
sections.body: Jordan had previous experience with NBA offenses and could provide backcourt competition as the Trail Blazers adjusted their roster. His service should be assessed from the date Portland obtained him rather than by importing appearances for the Lakers or another team before September. The trade did not suggest Jordan was a new perennial All-Star, but acquiring a working veteran could still be valuable to a club needing depth. His usefulness depended on the minutes actually awarded and on later personnel choices. This gives Portland a concrete personnel asset instead of a purely hypothetical future chance.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Held a Conditional Rather Than Guaranteed Pick
sections.body: The Lakers' compensation was described as a conditional 1985 third-round selection, not an unprotected first or a confirmed high second. Without more definitive evidence of the condition's satisfaction and the final selected player, a retrospective must avoid assigning a particular eventual draftee to Los Angeles. Moving Jordan provided room to manage an already strong group of guards, and a future selection offered additional flexibility if it conveyed. That is a reasonable resource choice for a contender, even if the basketball value of a conditional late draft slot is harder to document than Portland's incoming veteran.

sections.heading: The Blazers Had the Clearer Near-Term Basketball Return
sections.body: Portland acquired a specific guard with professional experience, while the Lakers accepted a contingent lower-round position and the ability to rearrange their roster. Because the future pick's final outcome isn't established in the canonical agreement, Jordan is the more tangible asset to value. That supports a narrow Blazers-winning result rather than a sweeping endorsement. The Lakers' decision fits their roster context and their conditional rights should not be dismissed. Both sides received comparatively small forms of value, and neither club's larger postseason accomplishments were produced exclusively by this exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Blazers Edge. Portland earns B- for acquiring veteran guard Eddie Jordan and the chance to use him immediately. The Lakers receive C+ for a conditional 1985 third-round selection, whose final conveyance and draft identity aren't established here. Jordan's prior Los Angeles games cannot be counted as new Portland production.

sections.heading: Boston Dealt Buckner for an Indiana Draft Right
sections.body: On September 3, 1985, Boston exchanged guard Quinn Buckner with Indiana for a future 1989 second-round selection. The historical draft ledger later associates that position with No. 44 Reggie Cross. The Celtics were maintaining a veteran roster with multiple backcourt choices and could accept a future asset rather than keeping every experienced reserve. Indiana wanted a player whose NBA defensive reputation was already established. This was a veteran-for-later-pick trade, with several years between the original agreement and the selection's ultimate position. Both parties were pursuing different points on their roster timelines.

sections.heading: Buckner Supplied Indiana With a Known Defensive Identity
sections.body: Buckner's NBA experience, including participation on Boston's championship-era rosters, made him an understandable target for the Pacers. His defensive background and ability to organize a guard unit could help a club seeking veteran habits. Yet Boston's earlier accomplishments were not automatically Indiana victories, and any new impact had to be measured after Buckner's arrival. He was at a later career stage by 1985 and did not guarantee a long run of star minutes. Indiana acquired immediate expertise and a professional roster option instead of waiting through four future draft cycles.

sections.heading: The Celtics' 1989 Pick Had a Long Development Horizon
sections.body: Boston accepted a second-round right that didn't become a named selection until 1989, where the record associates it with the No. 44 Reggie Cross slot. As with other historical draft rights, the eventual player identity is a ledger outcome, not proof that Cross became a productive Celtics regular. The pick had value because it could be used or reassigned, but its long lead time created uncertainty about Boston's eventual benefit. The Celtics were trading a veteran who had already served their roster for a new opportunity, rather than expecting to replace his defense immediately through the selection.

sections.heading: Both Clubs Acquired Assets Matching Their Priorities
sections.body: Indiana gained a guard with an established basketball background, while Boston converted a supporting veteran into a future development opportunity. The trade is fairly balanced when the second-round position's uncertainty is weighed against Buckner's late-career status. There is no credible basis for crediting the Pacers with Boston's prior titles or declaring the Celtics winners simply because the pick eventually had a name attached. Neither asset guaranteed multiple new starting seasons. Equal moderate grades reflect a pragmatic exchange of present-day guard experience for longer-dated prospect flexibility.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Boston earns B- for the future 1989 second-round right associated with No. 44 Reggie Cross; Indiana receives B- for veteran guard Quinn Buckner. Buckner's earlier Celtics championships aren't Indiana results, and Cross's draft-slot identity isn't proof of long-term Celtics NBA output. Both assets answered reasonable needs in 1985.

sections.heading: Boston Obtained Fred Roberts With an Unusual Additional Term
sections.body: On September 25, 1986, Boston acquired Fred Roberts from Utah for a 1987 third-round selection and a commitment to play two exhibition games in Utah. The future draft slot later appeared as No. 68, associated with Billy Donovan. The preseason-game promise was a real nonplayer consideration in the agreement, not another future draft pick or a second NBA contract. Utah received both the lower-round prospect opportunity and the value of hosting the Celtics in exhibitions, while Boston took a veteran forward it could use in its rotation.

sections.heading: Roberts Gave Boston Frontcourt Size and Experience
sections.body: Roberts arrived as a known NBA forward who could help Boston manage regular-season frontcourt depth and injuries. The Celtics had an established championship-level starting group, making capable reserve minutes more useful than the speculative return from a third-round selection years away. He still had to earn his new role, and any performances for Utah before the agreement belong to the Jazz. The trade's appeal lay in obtaining a real professional with a role the Celtics could assess immediately. It was not the arrival of another top overall draft pick or a replacement for Boston's central stars.

sections.heading: Utah's Compensation Went Beyond Billy Donovan's Draft Position
sections.body: The Jazz collected a third-round selection that the 1987 draft ledger associates with No. 68 Billy Donovan. That selection didn't guarantee a long NBA playing career and should not be confused with Donovan's much later coaching achievements. Utah also gained the right to host Boston for two exhibition games, a business and promotional benefit rather than a regular-season win or a basketball prospect. A review that ignores those agreed contests understates the compensation, while one that treats exhibition commitments as two players greatly inflates it. Both parts belong in the original trade description.

sections.heading: The Celtics Slightly Favored Immediate Basketball Depth
sections.body: Boston received a veteran who could actually join the roster; Utah obtained a lower-round choice and a business-oriented commitment. The Celtics' direct basketball return is easier to identify, which supports a modest winning verdict. Utah still obtained tangible compensation for a player it was willing to trade, and the exhibitions may have mattered to the franchise and its supporters. Neither part of the agreement produced a new superstar by itself. Recognizing both the specific 1987 third-round slot and the unusual exhibitions clause is essential to fair grades.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Celtics Edge. Boston earns B- for acquiring experienced forward Fred Roberts. Utah receives C+ for a 1987 third-round right associated with No. 68 Billy Donovan and Boston's promise to play two exhibition games in Utah. Donovan's later coaching reputation isn't a Jazz NBA contribution, and exhibition commitments aren't draft picks.

sections.heading: Atlanta Used a Young Center to Add Blair Rasmussen
sections.body: Atlanta and Denver exchanged the rights to young frontcourt player Anthony Avent for veteran center Blair Rasmussen around the 1991 NBA draft. Rasmussen offered a known seven-footer with established NBA experience; Avent represented a younger athletic development option. The Hawks could use Rasmussen immediately as an experienced post player alongside an otherwise mature rotation. Denver preferred a different timeline and prospect evaluation rather than maintaining the incumbent center. The agreement involved one identified basketball return on each side and shouldn't be confused with an unrelated draft-night swap that moved first-round pick positions between the franchises.

sections.heading: Rasmussen Supplied Size Without Becoming Atlanta's Centerpiece
sections.body: Rasmussen had already spent several years in Denver and brought size, interior presence and useful professional experience to Atlanta. His established production with the Nuggets wasn't newly earned by the Hawks, and an immediate veteran acquisition didn't automatically mean he would anchor the frontcourt for years. He still had to fit alongside Atlanta's existing personnel and earn minutes on the receiving team's season records. That made his value clearer in the short term than an unproven drafted prospect, while the team's larger fortunes continued to depend on its established leaders.

sections.heading: Denver Took a Developmental Frontcourt Prospect
sections.body: Anthony Avent arrived as a more speculative frontcourt asset with college credentials but no guarantee of sustained NBA minutes for Denver. A rookie could provide rebounding and energy, yet his potential was not equivalent to receiving Rasmussen's complete professional résumé. The trade gave the Nuggets a chance to evaluate a different profile at a time when their rotation was changing. Later roster decisions and contracts would determine how much of Avent's NBA career belonged to the receiving franchise. A retrospective should not assign his whole later playing record to Denver just because his rights moved through this transaction.

sections.heading: The Two Teams Pursued Reasonable Different Timelines
sections.body: Atlanta took a veteran who could address an immediate depth need and Denver chose a younger frontcourt prospect it could develop or move. Each side acquired a real player asset without surrendering a package of premium future selections. Neither Rasmussen nor Avent alone transformed the club that received him, and a balanced evaluation has more grounding than an extreme win-loss claim. The Hawks' short-term certainty and the Nuggets' prospect flexibility were distinct benefits rather than identical returns. Moderate equal grades reflect that tradeoff and avoid importing players' prior production into new franchises.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Atlanta earns B- for acquiring veteran center Blair Rasmussen as an immediately usable frontcourt option. Denver receives B- for younger Anthony Avent and the opportunity to assess his development. Neither return was a newly acquired All-Star, and Rasmussen's prior Nuggets seasons or Avent's later games elsewhere aren't assigned to the receiving clubs through this one exchange.

sections.heading: Boston Received Todd Day and Alton Lister in a Three-Player Exchange
sections.body: On November 26, 1995, Boston acquired wing scorer Todd Day and veteran big man Alton Lister from Milwaukee in exchange for guard Sherman Douglas. The Celtics were rebuilding their identity and wanted additional options at two positions; the Bucks obtained one established ball handler instead of splitting the return across a perimeter scorer and an experienced center. All three were actual NBA players rather than speculative selections, so the immediate roster implications were more direct than a draft-rights swap. The two-player incoming package gave Boston flexibility to evaluate more than one role during the remainder of the season.

sections.heading: Day Offered Scoring Potential, While Lister Offered Size
sections.body: Day arrived with a reputation for putting points on the board from the wing, while Lister's long career gave Boston a reserve center who could supply physical depth. Their earlier Milwaukee seasons demonstrated different skills, but couldn't be counted as Celtics production after the trade. They were also at different points in their careers, with Day still offering a chance to build on past scoring while Lister was closer to a late-career support role. Boston's return was therefore a combination of two distinct roster options, not a newly minted superstar whose previous numbers should carry forward unchanged.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Focused Its Return on Sherman Douglas
sections.body: The Bucks acquired Douglas, a guard with meaningful prior NBA responsibilities and a history of running an offense. Milwaukee could use him to organize possessions and stabilize the backcourt rather than waiting for an unproven draft pick. The cost was giving up Day's wing-scoring profile and Lister's size, so the club sacrificed two kinds of depth for one more targeted role. Douglas's previous work for Miami and Boston could inform expectations but did not automatically guarantee peak production in Milwaukee. His real value had to come from games after the November exchange and any later deals.

sections.heading: Neither Team Acquired a Durable Franchise Cornerstone
sections.body: Boston received two players who could fill separate needs; Milwaukee gained a veteran guard with a more defined playmaking profile. None of those benefits was a premium draft asset or a guaranteed future All-Star, and both clubs continued through broader roster changes during the middle of the 1990s. That makes an even result more appropriate than assigning an outsized win to the side that received more names. The Celtics gained flexibility and the Bucks focused on an identified guard task. Both returns were practical but limited, which supports equal modest grades.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Boston earns C+ for Todd Day's wing-scoring option and Alton Lister's veteran frontcourt depth. Milwaukee gets C+ for experienced guard Sherman Douglas. The Celtics' two-for-one return created options rather than two automatic starters; Douglas's previous achievements with other teams do not become new Bucks performance simply because the trade occurred.

sections.heading: Atlanta Received Christian Laettner and Sean Rooks
sections.body: At the February 22, 1996 deadline, Atlanta acquired Christian Laettner and Sean Rooks from Minnesota in exchange for veteran guard Anthony 'Spud' Webb and center Andrew Lang. The Hawks' incoming pair offered a high-profile power forward and another true frontcourt player, aligning with a desire to improve their interior rotation. Minnesota obtained an experienced small guard and an established center. This wasn't a swap involving Laettner's college rights or a still-conditional future draft selection: he had already been playing NBA seasons with the Timberwolves when the transaction occurred.

sections.heading: Laettner's Frontcourt Role Offered the Higher Basketball Ceiling
sections.body: Laettner had already shown scoring ability and skill in the frontcourt with Minnesota. Atlanta could pair him with its existing veterans rather than build an entirely new offense around an untested rookie. His subsequent service for the Hawks gave the acquisition a longer basketball dimension than a temporary end-of-season rental, although the details of his later years should be traced directly to the receiving franchise. Rooks supplied added size and another possibility for a second-unit interior role. Together they made Atlanta's return more flexible and potentially more durable than acquiring a single reserve.

sections.heading: Minnesota Took Back Spud Webb and Andrew Lang
sections.body: Webb, often listed as Anthony Webb in historical ledgers, supplied guard experience and recognizable quickness, while Lang brought conventional center size. The Timberwolves could use those veterans to reorganize playing time during the season, and moving Laettner also changed the distribution of frontcourt responsibilities around their other young players. Neither Webb's earlier career with Atlanta nor Lang's previous minutes can be treated as new Minnesota production. The return contained usable NBA experience rather than unknown prospects, but the Wolves did surrender a young forward with more substantial future upside.

sections.heading: Atlanta's Better Long-Term Player Is the Decisive Difference
sections.body: The Hawks took a proven young frontcourt scorer and another center in exchange for veterans whose roles were less central to their future. Minnesota did receive legitimate rotation options, yet the most valuable continuing piece of this particular transaction was Laettner's Atlanta service. That supports a Hawks-winning evaluation without attributing every later Hawks playoff result solely to him. Webb and Lang were not valueless, nor should Rooks be mistaken for an All-Star simply because he accompanied Laettner. The trade favored Atlanta on the durable frontcourt return, while providing Minnesota experienced personnel for its immediate needs.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win. Atlanta earns B+ for Christian Laettner's meaningful frontcourt role after arrival, alongside Sean Rooks's added depth. Minnesota gets C+ for guard Spud Webb and center Andrew Lang. The Timberwolves acquired real NBA veterans, but the Hawks received the more durable scoring option in Laettner without relying on future pick assumptions.

sections.heading: Atlanta Took Chris Washburn, Golden State Received Foreign Rights
sections.body: The Hawks acquired center Chris Washburn from Golden State in December 1987 while the Warriors received rights to forward Ken Barlow. Washburn had been a high draft selection whose professional progress was already uncertain, making this a gamble on a second opportunity rather than a conventional exchange of two established starters. Barlow's rights were a different kind of asset: Golden State gained the ability to negotiate with an internationally based prospect without receiving an immediately signed NBA rotation player. Atlanta wanted a physically talented center to evaluate within its existing roster.

sections.heading: Washburn's Potential Didn't Translate Into a Sustained Hawks Role
sections.body: Washburn's athletic and physical qualities had once made him an attractive prospect, but acquiring those traits didn't restore the status or playing record attached to his original draft position. The Hawks could examine him in their system, yet his NBA contribution after the exchange was limited and did not turn into a long-standing frontcourt role. That short receiving-team tenure is decisive to the retrospective. Golden State's unsuccessful earlier investment in him was already a sunk cost; Atlanta wasn't acquiring all the games and development resources previously spent on the big man.

sections.heading: Barlow Was a Rights Asset Rather Than Instant Production
sections.body: The Warriors received rights to Ken Barlow, who had played outside the NBA and had a professional career that could not automatically be assigned to Golden State. A right to approach or sign someone is useful, but it isn't the same as several years of an NBA contract. Golden State could preserve the option or later move the asset while it continued rebuilding its frontcourt. The exact eventual use of those rights would require following subsequent transactions; the original exchange alone does not establish that Barlow ever supplied Golden State with regular-season minutes.

sections.heading: A Small Warriors Edge Reflects a Better Risk Position
sections.body: Atlanta absorbed the uncertainty tied to Washburn's attempted NBA revival, while Golden State converted a distressed player situation into an additional rights claim. Neither outcome amounted to acquiring a lasting star, so an extreme winning grade would overstate the impact. Still, the Warriors' lighter obligation and potential to use Barlow's rights make their side marginally more defensible. Atlanta gained a chance to restart an athletic prospect, but it didn't create a durable frontcourt solution. This trade illustrates how an asset can have modest optional value even if neither received player becomes a major on-court contributor.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Warriors Edge. Golden State earns C for receiving Ken Barlow's rights after moving on from Chris Washburn. Atlanta gets C- for a center reclamation attempt that did not become a substantial Hawks rotation role. Barlow's overseas career is not Warriors NBA production, and Washburn's original draft reputation was not a guaranteed Atlanta return.

sections.heading: Seattle Received Two Veterans From Boston
sections.body: On October 16, 1987, Boston sent guard Sam Vincent and veteran forward Scott Wedman to the Seattle SuperSonics in return for cash and a future second-round selection. The 1988 draft ledger associates that second with No. 35 Sylvester Gray. Modern franchise indexing may file Seattle trades under the Oklahoma City Thunder lineage, but the actual 1987 receiving team was Seattle. The SuperSonics preferred immediate basketball experience, while the Celtics turned two roster pieces into monetary compensation and a prospect opportunity. This was a real two-player deal rather than an exchange involving an existing Thunder roster.

sections.heading: Vincent Offered Seattle Backcourt Options, Wedman Experience
sections.body: Vincent was an NBA guard capable of competing for minutes, giving Seattle another option for ball handling and scoring. Wedman brought years of professional experience, though he was at a late career stage and couldn't reasonably be expected to reproduce his earlier prime indefinitely. Their prior Boston performance still belonged to the Celtics' history and should not be treated as Seattle games after the transaction. The Sonics received two named veterans, but the actual value of each depended on availability and subsequent roster decisions rather than his reputation at the time of acquisition.

sections.heading: Boston's Future Second Became a Defined Draft Position
sections.body: Boston gained an eventual second-round position that the draft record associates with No. 35 Sylvester Gray, along with cash. Those were real assets, but a future pick did not guarantee a signed rotation forward and the cash wasn't automatically equivalent to an NBA player's development. The Celtics had veteran talent at other positions and could afford to examine younger prospects over time rather than retain every reserve. The correct return to evaluate is the second-round opportunity and financial consideration, not any unrelated games Gray later played for another franchise.

sections.heading: The Sonics Chose More Immediate NBA Personnel
sections.body: Seattle acquired two players who could contribute without waiting for a draft, while Boston accepted a later selection and cash. That makes the Seattle-side package slightly stronger on immediate personnel value despite Wedman's age and the uncertainty of each veteran's ultimate usage. Boston still got compensation from surplus depth, so the Celtics weren't left empty-handed. Calling the 1987 team 'Oklahoma City' in the trade narrative would misstate the historical location even though the modern database grouping is legitimate. Moderate grades recognize a close exchange, with a narrow Sonics edge.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Oklahoma City Thunder Win under modern franchise lineage, but the actual 1987 beneficiary was the Seattle SuperSonics. Seattle earns B- for acquiring Sam Vincent and Scott Wedman as NBA-experienced options; Boston gets C+ for cash and a 1988 second associated with No. 35 Sylvester Gray. Neither club is awarded NBA games from later unrelated contracts.

sections.heading: Atlanta and Los Angeles Swapped Veterans and Draft Rights
sections.body: Atlanta obtained guard Mike McGee and the rights to Ken Barlow from the Lakers in a June 1986 agreement. Los Angeles received rights to Ron Kellogg and Billy Thompson. McGee was the only named NBA veteran changing teams in this package, while the other assets were rights to players whose next contracts weren't guaranteed. The Hawks were pursuing usable perimeter depth and an additional forward prospect option. The Lakers could refresh their rights inventory without forcing another veteran into a rotation that already had established scoring and playmaking combinations.

sections.heading: McGee Could Be Evaluated in Atlanta Immediately
sections.body: McGee had contributed NBA minutes in Los Angeles and represented a recognizable outside-scoring option for the Hawks. His arrival allowed Atlanta to test his fit without waiting for a rookie to be selected in a later draft. However, a player bringing NBA experience doesn't mean the receiving team inherits earlier Lakers seasons or playoff achievements. McGee still needed to win minutes and a role alongside Atlanta's established guards and wings. His return should be judged by actual work after the June agreement rather than by career totals spanning different teams.

sections.heading: The Lakers Acquired Two Distinct Rights Claims
sections.body: Los Angeles received rights to Kellogg and Thompson, two prospects who were not automatically under signed long-term NBA contracts. Such rights could become valuable through negotiations or additional transactions, but claiming immediate NBA production from both would distort the value of the exchange. The Lakers held the option to decide how each prospect fit their personnel plans. The distinction is important because Barlow, the rights asset headed to Atlanta, could likewise carry professional value outside the NBA without necessarily turning into Hawks game statistics.

sections.heading: Asset Flexibility Gives Los Angeles a Narrow Edge
sections.body: The Lakers took two developmental chances in exchange for McGee and Barlow's rights, while Atlanta obtained a current guard plus a different prospect option. Neither franchise acquired a top-five draft pick or a newly established All-Star. Atlanta's immediate use of McGee had merit, but Los Angeles gained more separate opportunities to evaluate younger talent without an obligation to commit NBA rotation minutes to both. That supports a modest Lakers-winning assessment rather than an overwhelming outcome. Follow-on rights transactions need independent treatment and can't be credited entirely to the original deal.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Lakers Edge. Los Angeles receives B- for obtaining rights to Ron Kellogg and Billy Thompson, two separate development options. Atlanta earns C+ for veteran Mike McGee and Ken Barlow's rights. A right to negotiate does not guarantee a signed NBA starter, and McGee's pretrade Lakers output isn't newly acquired Hawks performance.

sections.heading: Atlanta Took Comegys for a Future Second
sections.body: The November 3, 1987 transaction brought young forward Dallas Comegys to Atlanta from the New Jersey Nets. New Jersey received a conditional later second-round selection, identified in historical records as a 1989-or-1990 opportunity that ultimately corresponds to the 1990 No. 28 position associated with Les Jepsen. The Nets are indexed under the later Brooklyn franchise name in the canonical dataset, but the agreement was made by New Jersey. Atlanta wanted an actual prospect it could place into its roster evaluations immediately; the Nets chose future draft flexibility rather than retaining Comegys.

sections.heading: Comegys Was a Current Prospect With Uncertain NBA Value
sections.body: Comegys had been a first-round draft prospect, which made a change of environment potentially attractive for the Hawks. Still, being a former high pick couldn't guarantee a starting role, and Atlanta's frontcourt already had players who would compete for playing time. Comegys offered a chance to assess his athletic skills and size, but not an established record of sustained NBA impact. The correct Atlanta return begins with its own appearances and subsequent roster decisions, not the draft position or expectations attached to Comegys when New Jersey originally obtained his rights.

sections.heading: New Jersey's Pick Became a Named 1990 Selection
sections.body: The Nets' incoming future selection was not immediately numbered or fully settled at the 1987 agreement date. Its conditional 1989-or-1990 timing ultimately led to the 1990 No. 28 draft position associated with Les Jepsen. That named outcome helps identify the asset, though Jepsen's subsequent career shouldn't be awarded to New Jersey without checking his actual team history. By accepting a future second rather than keeping Comegys, the franchise traded immediate prospect control for the chance to select or move a different player later. Both were reasonable options for a rebuilding team.

sections.heading: An Even Grade Reflects Two Limited Development Paths
sections.body: Atlanta received a current young forward and New Jersey obtained a later first-position-in-the-second-round draft opportunity. Neither was a guaranteed cornerstone player, and their eventual returns depended on development and further roster decisions outside this deal. Comegys's earlier selection status might have been appealing but was not a newly awarded premium draft pick to Atlanta. New Jersey's eventual No. 28 selection carried genuine value while still not ensuring an NBA starter. Equal modest grades convey a balanced prospect-for-prospect gamble rather than a decisive historical win.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Atlanta earns C+ for receiving Dallas Comegys as an immediately available forward prospect. The New Jersey Nets, indexed under Brooklyn lineage, get C+ for a conditional future second that ultimately aligned with 1990 No. 28 Les Jepsen. Neither asset guaranteed an established NBA player, and the 1987 Nets were not yet based in Brooklyn.

sections.heading: New York Converted Matching-Rights Compensation Into Two Seconds
sections.body: Boston's February 21, 1985 arrangement involved veteran free agent Ray Williams and the Knicks' decision not to exercise their right of first refusal. New York received two second-round picks, which subsequently appeared as the 1985 No. 47 selection associated with Gerald Wilkins and 1986 No. 47 Michael Jackson. The Celtics obtained freedom to pursue Williams without New York matching, while the Knicks gained two prospect opportunities. This wasn't an ordinary player-for-player trade because Williams's status was governed by free-agent rules. The exact years and selection numbers make the return more concrete than an unspecified consideration.

sections.heading: Gerald Wilkins Became a Productive Knicks Wing
sections.body: Wilkins's NBA playing career in New York turned the 1985 second-round position into a notable return. His perimeter athleticism and subsequent Knicks seasons made that draft right far more useful than many ordinary late selections. That outcome was not guaranteed at the February 1985 agreement date, and the deal should not be credited for every later franchise improvement. But the named pick provides a clear player with an actual receiving-team record, unlike an undeveloped right whose future performance would have to be guessed. Wilkins's New York tenure is the most consequential historical part of this compensation package.

sections.heading: The Additional 1986 Second Was a Separate Opportunity
sections.body: The Knicks also secured a 1986 second-round position associated with No. 47 Michael Jackson. The two picks should not be combined into one imagined high selection or treated as a package automatically producing two long-term starters. Jackson's NBA role must be assessed independently rather than being inferred from Wilkins's much stronger subsequent tenure. Boston paid with future opportunities to pursue a veteran whose established professional history wasn't yet its own. The Knicks had room to turn a contractual right into new talent and evaluate the two acquired prospects on their separate timelines.

sections.heading: New York's Proven Draft Return Drives the Verdict
sections.body: The Knicks gained two discrete draft chances for stepping aside on Williams, including one that led to a valuable NBA contributor in Wilkins. Boston obtained contractual flexibility toward a veteran guard but did not create a comparable lasting roster asset through this particular arrangement. That supports a decisive Knicks advantage in hindsight while still recognizing that Williams's experience was useful to the Celtics' original objective. The rights mechanism deserves its own explanation rather than being mislabeled a straight salary-for-player swap. A strong but not perfect New York grade is supported by realized draft production.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win. New York earns A- because the 1985 No. 47 second-round choice became Gerald Wilkins, a meaningful Knicks contributor, while it also received a separate 1986 No. 47 choice tied to Michael Jackson. Boston gets C- for freedom to pursue Ray Williams without the Knicks' matching claim. The agreement concerned free-agent rights, not two veteran contracts exchanged.

sections.heading: Atlanta Acquired Maurice Cheeks for McCormick and a Conditional Pick
sections.body: On October 2, 1991, the Atlanta Hawks acquired veteran point guard Maurice Cheeks from New York. The Knicks received center Tim McCormick and a conditional future first-round pick tied to McCormick's ability to meet a minimum-games condition. That pick later appears as the 1994 No. 26 selection associated with Charlie Ward. The original agreement therefore paired immediate guard experience with a potentially valuable future contingency rather than a simple veteran-for-veteran swap. The Knicks were willing to move Cheeks as their roster evolved, while Atlanta sought a proven organizer for its offense.

sections.heading: Cheeks's Defensive Reputation Explained Atlanta's Interest
sections.body: Cheeks was already known as a capable defensive point guard and championship-era veteran before the Hawks acquired him. Atlanta could benefit from his decision-making and backcourt experience, but those prior Philadelphia and New York accomplishments weren't new Atlanta production generated by the trade. The receiving team had to evaluate his actual availability and role afterward. Bringing in an aging guard was a shorter-horizon decision than keeping a conditional first, and his NBA legacy alone couldn't ensure he would supply several more years of peak play. The Hawks' immediate objective was credible even though its payoff was limited.

sections.heading: The Contingent First Eventually Became a Noteworthy Knicks Asset
sections.body: McCormick offered New York a veteran center, but the more enduring piece was the conditional first-round obligation that ultimately became connected with 1994 No. 26 Charlie Ward. Ward developed into a useful New York guard during the 1990s, giving the transaction a specific long-term outcome beyond merely moving Cheeks. The conditional language is important: the 1994 result wasn't guaranteed at the original 1991 agreement date. It depended on the agreed games-related terms and the subsequent pick chain. That distinction stops a retrospective from describing Ward as a player who was already part of the Knicks' 1991 roster.

sections.heading: New York Won With a Productive Later Selection
sections.body: Atlanta obtained an experienced guard it could use immediately; New York received McCormick and an eventual first-round opportunity that became a meaningful player asset. The Knicks' longer-term draft return outweighed Cheeks's short remaining window as a Hawks player, particularly because Ward would become a familiar part of the franchise's later rotation. That doesn't make the Hawks' decision irrational, and it shouldn't assign all 1990s Knicks success to one trade. But the condition eventually producing a useful No. 26 selection gives New York a clear realized advantage over a comparatively short-term veteran rental.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win. New York earns A- for Tim McCormick and the conditional first-round obligation ultimately associated with 1994 No. 26 Charlie Ward. Atlanta receives C for veteran guard Maurice Cheeks. The first wasn't guaranteed when the trade occurred, and Ward's later Knicks career must be evaluated as the realized result of the selection rather than an immediate 1991 player acquisition.

sections.heading: Boston Secured a Draft Selection for Allowing a Free-Agent Move
sections.body: On September 26, 1985, the Celtics agreed not to exercise their right of first refusal concerning veteran free agent Ray Williams, allowing the Los Angeles Clippers to pursue him. In exchange, Boston gained a future fourth-round pick in the 1987 draft. The historical ledger later connects that selection to No. 70 Tom Sheehey. The agreement belongs to a period with more than two NBA draft rounds and different contractual matching arrangements than contemporary free agency. Boston was not trading a currently signed center for a first-round selection, and Los Angeles was seeking access to a particular guard rather than purchasing a high lottery prospect.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Wanted Williams's Established NBA Experience
sections.body: Williams entered the arrangement with recognizable guard skills and years of NBA work behind him. The Clippers could explore adding his ball handling and scoring to a roster that lacked the depth of the league's established contenders. Previous games with New York, Boston or another franchise did not become new Los Angeles production simply because Boston stepped aside in 1985. A free-agent acquisition also required the club to complete separate roster decisions; the matching-rights waiver removed a contractual obstacle but wasn't a guarantee of future star performance. That made the Clippers' benefit immediate in purpose but uncertain in result.

sections.heading: The Celtics' Compensation Became a Fourth-Round Right
sections.body: Boston's draft claim ultimately appeared as the 1987 No. 70 choice associated with Tom Sheehey. A fourth-round selection was a legitimate developmental right in that historical draft format, but it wasn't comparable to a protected modern first. The Celtics could attempt to scout and sign a late prospect without keeping the matching option attached to Williams. Any subsequent professional playing time by Sheehey would need to be traced to the actual signing team. The right alone didn't mean Boston had instantly replenished its NBA guard rotation or drafted a guaranteed useful player.

sections.heading: A Small Celtics Edge Fits the Original Risk
sections.body: Boston converted an option it chose not to use into a distinct later draft asset, while the Clippers gained the chance to negotiate for a known veteran. That supports a narrow Celtics advantage, not a sweeping judgment on either team's mid-1980s performance. The 1987 pick carried limited upside due to its round, but it was still compensation rather than nothing. The Clippers' rationale was an immediate need for backcourt experience, yet the right to pursue Williams was not equivalent to acquiring the best years of his prior career. Both returns were small and conditional in different ways.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win, slightly. Boston receives C+ for the 1987 fourth-round position eventually identified as No. 70 Tom Sheehey. Los Angeles receives C- because Boston agreed not to exercise its matching right on Ray Williams. The trade was about a free-agent right, not an existing signed player, and the fourth-round pick was not a guaranteed rotation solution.

sections.heading: Atlanta Took Two Prospects in Exchange for Johnny Davis
sections.body: Atlanta's 1984 agreement with Cleveland sent guard Johnny Davis to the Cavaliers while the Hawks acquired Stewart Granger and John Garris. The original transaction involved three named players, not future picks or a complicated draft swap. Davis brought NBA backcourt experience to Cleveland, whereas Atlanta gained two younger roster candidates to evaluate. The Hawks' decision could provide more options at different positions, but neither prospect's incoming name ensured a successful full-season rotation role. That distinction matters because the quantity of players received shouldn't automatically determine the winner of a trade.

sections.heading: Davis Offered the Cavaliers a More Certain Immediate Return
sections.body: Johnny Davis had been a professional guard for multiple seasons, making him a more established option than either younger player Cleveland surrendered. He could bring ball-handling experience and a veteran baseline of competence, but his earlier games for other organizations can't be treated as newly produced Cavaliers minutes. Cleveland's front office preferred one identifiable contributor over two developmental possibilities. The cost was surrendering more than one player, which reduced its room to test younger talent. The question for this deal is whether Davis's next season of service justified that narrower roster option.

sections.heading: Atlanta's Return Was a Pair of Basketball Evaluations
sections.body: Granger and Garris gave Atlanta two opportunities to compete for roles rather than one experienced veteran. Different skill sets could help the Hawks assemble depth without spending a valuable first-round selection. Their future NBA careers still had to be earned after arrival, and neither player should be described as an established Hawks starter on the date of the transaction. Atlanta's asset advantage is therefore about multiple roster options, not an automatic doubling of production. The club's longer-term performance depended chiefly on existing stars and other moves unrelated to this exchange.

sections.heading: A Narrow Hawks Preference Fits the Limited Stakes
sections.body: The teams were balancing immediate predictability against development flexibility, and both strategies had a recognizable purpose. Neither side gained a premium draft pick or an obvious future All-Star, so the result shouldn't be inflated into a major historical turning point. The slight Hawks edge reflects the number of potential contributors and their youth, with credit still due to Cleveland for targeting a guard with a genuine NBA résumé.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Hawks Edge — Atlanta B-, Cleveland C+. Sending Johnny Davis to Cleveland for Stewart Granger and John Garris gave Atlanta two roster-development options instead of one established veteran guard. Davis's experience provided Cleveland with a sensible immediate alternative, but the Hawks' wider evaluation opportunity earns a narrow advantage. Neither side received a premium pick or a guaranteed future star, so both grades stay moderate rather than assigning players' earlier production to their new teams.

sections.heading: Chicago and Golden State Swapped Second-Round Positions
sections.body: The June 23, 1982 agreement gave Chicago a 1983 second-round selection and Golden State the 1982 No. 38 choice. The historical draft ledger associates the Warriors' incoming position with Wayne Sappleton and the Bulls' later right with No. 31 Doc Rivers. That future pick was a year away and didn't represent a contracted player in the 1982 trade. Each franchise was moving between different draft years, not exchanging an NBA veteran for a rookie. The later names provide a useful way to follow the asset trail while preserving the original timing.

sections.heading: Rivers's Longer NBA Career Needs Correct Franchise Attribution
sections.body: Doc Rivers became a useful NBA guard, most notably during years with Atlanta, but his being selected at the position attached to Chicago's original acquired right does not prove all that future production belonged to the Bulls. A draft right may be moved again or its player's rights assigned elsewhere before a debut. Chicago's immediate return was a later No. 31 selection, giving it a chance to make another decision in 1983. That distinction is especially important in retrospective grading because a famous later NBA name can otherwise exaggerate the value one receiving team actually kept.

sections.heading: Golden State Obtained the Earlier Development Opportunity
sections.body: The Warriors took a 1982 second-round position connected to Wayne Sappleton. A mid-second-round prospect offered more immediate roster evaluation than a choice deferred until the following year, but neither place in the draft was a guaranteed starting role. Golden State could use the rights itself or transfer them in a subsequent agreement, and any basketball production would need to be attributed to the final signing organization. The franchise had a practical reason to prefer a nearer asset while Chicago accepted a delayed chance with potentially different scouting options.

sections.heading: The Draft Order Favors Chicago Only Modestly
sections.body: Chicago's incoming No. 31 in 1983 was earlier in its draft than the No. 38 position Golden State received in 1982, and the future right proved attached to a recognizable NBA name.
