But the difference between these selections was still comparatively small, with a full year separating them. Giving the Bulls credit for every game Rivers later played would be a false attribution if he did not join their roster. A moderate Bulls edge captures the acquired draft flexibility and eventual position without manufacturing a long direct NBA return for Chicago.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bulls Win — Chicago B, Golden State C+. Chicago accepted a future 1983 second-round pick that became the No. 31 selection, while Golden State received the nearer 1982 No. 38 opportunity associated with Wayne Sappleton. The later choice was tied to Doc Rivers in the draft record, but his subsequent NBA career should not be counted as direct Bulls production. Chicago earned a modest edge from a better eventual draft position, with the one-year delay and limited asset certainty keeping both grades measured.

sections.heading: Atlanta Acquired Randy Denton for a Later Pick
sections.body: In October 1976, the Atlanta Hawks received big man Randy Denton from New York. The Knicks obtained a 1977 second-round selection later associated with the No. 26 position and Glen Gondrezick. Atlanta chose to add a current frontcourt player before the season, while New York accepted an opportunity to select a younger prospect months later. Denton's existing professional background made him a more immediate option than a future pick, but his career beforehand did not count as new Hawks production. The agreed compensation was one draft right rather than a package of first-round capital.

sections.heading: Denton Was a Roster Option Rather Than a Cornerstone
sections.body: Denton offered size and prior experience that Atlanta could evaluate in practices and games as it managed a changing lineup. He wasn't acquired as the clear face of the franchise, and his future service with the Hawks needed to be earned after the transaction date. The practical benefit was having an available center or forward instead of hoping a future second-round prospect would become playable. New York no longer had that immediate player option but was free to find a better fit in the next draft. Neither return guaranteed long-term NBA starting minutes.

sections.heading: The Knicks' Second Turned Into a Specific Prospect Opportunity
sections.body: New York's incoming 1977 selection is tracked at No. 26 in historical draft records, associated with Glen Gondrezick. The position gave the Knicks an identifiable opportunity near the beginning of the second round rather than an uncertain later-round claim. His eventual career must still be traced through which franchise actually held his rights and put him on the floor, because the selected name alone doesn't guarantee his New York service. The team paid for this chance by surrendering Denton. A draft position with practical scouting value could outlast the usefulness of a marginal current veteran.

sections.heading: A Modest Knicks Edge Reflects Future Flexibility
sections.body: Atlanta acquired Denton as a near-term option, but did not secure a premium future asset through the trade. The difference is modest: the draft right had no guaranteed NBA payoff, and Atlanta's interest in immediate frontcourt depth was reasonable. The return is best graded through what was actually transferred and when, not by giving either team unrelated later franchise achievements. New York receives a narrow preference for preserving developmental flexibility.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Knicks Edge — New York B-, Atlanta C+. The Hawks acquired Randy Denton as immediate frontcourt depth, while the Knicks received a 1977 second-round opportunity eventually associated with No. 26 Glen Gondrezick. The pick offered New York another route to a younger contributor, but its later identification does not establish automatic Knicks game production. Atlanta's present-day roster need was reasonable; the longer-range draft option earns New York a modest edge, not a sweeping victory.

sections.heading: Atlanta Acquired Jamal Crawford for Law and Claxton
sections.body: On June 25, 2009, Atlanta traded guard Acie Law and veteran Speedy Claxton to Golden State in exchange for Jamal Crawford. The Hawks obtained a proven NBA perimeter scorer with several seasons of experience, while the Warriors accepted two guards on different career trajectories. The agreement was a direct player exchange, not an additional lottery selection or conditional first. Crawford could provide Atlanta with offense from a reserve role without immediately replacing every member of its starting backcourt. Golden State pursued roster flexibility and opportunities for the incoming guards, rather than keeping Crawford's existing scoring contract.

sections.heading: Crawford Became an Important Atlanta Bench Scorer
sections.body: Crawford's subsequent Hawks seasons provided the strongest identifiable return of the transaction. His scoring ability and ball handling translated into a productive supporting role, including major recognition for his performance off the bench. That was actual receiving-team basketball value rather than a projection built entirely on his earlier years elsewhere. The Hawks didn't need to claim that Crawford alone created their playoff progress; their starting core contributed heavily as well. But adding a reliable second-unit offensive creator in exchange for expendable guard depth was a tangible personnel improvement that can be traced directly to this deal.

sections.heading: Golden State Took Back Two Less Proven Alternatives
sections.body: Acie Law arrived still searching for a stable NBA guard role, while Claxton's injury and late-career circumstances limited the certainty of his immediate usefulness. Neither should be credited with Crawford's prior scoring just because Golden State surrendered him. The Warriors may have valued contract and roster options, but they did not receive a player who matched Crawford's later Atlanta bench production. Law's potential could be assessed in a new environment, though a second attempt at development wasn't guaranteed to work. The return was therefore more speculative and less immediately productive than the Hawks' established scorer.

sections.heading: Atlanta Won on Clear Receiving-Team Production
sections.body: Golden State received two legitimate contract assets but lacked comparable sustained court results from the exchange. That supports a decisive Hawks-winning verdict without pretending Claxton and Law were valueless at the transaction date. The agreement wasn't a complicated draft-rights chain, making the retrospective relatively straightforward. Its value lies in the distinction between a proven offensive reserve and two players whose subsequent fit remained much less certain.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win — Atlanta A, Golden State B-. Atlanta received Jamal Crawford for Acie Law and Speedy Claxton and obtained the deal's strongest sustained receiving-team scorer. Crawford contributed in a valuable bench role, while the Warriors acquired two legitimate contracts without matching his later Hawks production. Golden State's flexibility had some initial rationale, but the actual basketball return favored Atlanta decisively. This grade credits Crawford's Atlanta work, not accomplishments from his earlier franchises.

sections.heading: Atlanta Traded a Second-Round Position for Anthony Johnson
sections.body: Near the February 2007 deadline, Atlanta acquired veteran point guard Anthony Johnson from Dallas for a 2007 second-round selection. The historical ledger connects the Mavericks' incoming draft position with No. 34 Nick Fazekas. Johnson was an experienced guard the Hawks could use immediately; Dallas preferred another prospect selection rather than keeping a reserve for the rest of the season. The NBA calendar made the contrast clear: Atlanta sought help before its next game, while Dallas was evaluating a later draft opportunity. No star-level player or multiple first-round choices were part of this package.

sections.heading: Johnson Offered Immediate Guard Depth
sections.body: Anthony Johnson had played meaningful NBA minutes before the exchange and gave Atlanta another player able to run an offense. His earlier performances for Dallas, Indiana or another club weren't automatically new Hawks basketball generated by the trade. Atlanta needed to measure his usefulness in the remaining season and any later service. A veteran ball handler could provide a stabilizing role even without becoming a franchise centerpiece, which is why a single second-round pick could be a reasonable price. The trade gave the Hawks more predictable immediate personnel than a yet-to-be-selected prospect.

sections.heading: Dallas Received a Traceable 2007 Draft Asset
sections.body: The Mavericks' future selection later appeared at No. 34, associated with Nick Fazekas. That identifier establishes what the incoming second-round asset became, but selection rights and eventual NBA minutes require separate attribution if a player moved through further transactions. Dallas obtained a chance to identify younger talent and manage its roster beyond the deadline, sacrificing Johnson's immediate experience for a prospect decision. A relatively high second-round choice had genuine value without a guaranteed long-term starter attached. The original agreement should be judged on that risk, not hypothetical statistics from unrelated clubs.

sections.heading: A Small Hawks Preference Fits Both Returns
sections.body: Johnson's near-term use supports a limited Hawks advantage, but the Mavericks had a rational opportunity to explore a younger player. Neither return reshaped the franchise, and assigning Fazekas an entire later career on Dallas would overstate a draft right. Moderate grades are sufficient for an exchange of reserve NBA guard depth for a pick outside the first round. The transaction is best understood through the teams' different timing needs.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Hawks Edge — Atlanta B-, Dallas C+. Anthony Johnson brought Atlanta an available veteran guard for the February 2007 stretch, while the Mavericks obtained a second-round choice later identified with No. 34 Nick Fazekas. A real current backcourt option has a modest advantage over a draft prospect without guaranteed Dallas minutes, though the pick carried legitimate developmental value. The result supports restrained grades for a reserve guard-for-second exchange rather than crediting either franchise with unrelated later player careers.

sections.heading: Boston Took Dan Dickau for a Future Second-Round Right
sections.body: Boston's September 2005 transaction sent a future 2006 second-round selection to the New Orleans/Oklahoma City Hornets in exchange for guard Dan Dickau. The original club was in a temporary Oklahoma City arrangement after Hurricane Katrina, and its franchise history is indexed under today's New Orleans Pelicans. The selection later appeared as No. 56, associated with Edin Bavcic. Boston favored a player who had NBA guard experience and could compete for a near-term role, while the Hornets accepted a lower-round development opportunity. This was not a multi-player veteran package or a guaranteed first-round future asset.

sections.heading: Dickau Arrived as an Experienced Guard, Not a Long-Term Promise
sections.body: Dickau had already played NBA minutes and established a reputation for outside shooting and passing. Boston could use him as backcourt depth without waiting for the following summer's draft, but his earlier performances for other teams did not instantly become Celtics production. A player approaching a new roster had to earn his own playing time and could be affected by health or subsequent roster changes. Dickau's recognizable name shouldn't be treated as evidence of an All-Star arrival. The deal's immediate purpose was to give Boston a practical guard option for an evolving rotation.

sections.heading: The Future Pick Carried a Specific Late-Second Outcome
sections.body: The Hornets acquired a 2006 second-round pick later associated with No. 56 Edin Bavcic. That draft slot offered an opportunity to obtain or use the rights to an international prospect, but it wasn't equal to a signed NBA player ready for the opening tip. Any later Bavcic career outside the league could be useful contextual evidence without being credited as actual Hornets game production. The 2005 agreement did not automatically place Bavcic on the club's active roster in 2006. Draft-rights control and professional minutes are distinct outcomes when evaluating this type of exchange.

sections.heading: A Balanced Return for Different Roster Horizons
sections.body: Dickau's NBA experience supplied more current certainty, but the 2006 pick preserved the possibility of selecting or moving a different player later. Neither side obtained a franchise-altering contributor, and the agreed assets were too small to justify sweeping conclusions about either team's next decade. Equal moderate grades recognize the value of near-term guard depth and speculative later draft flexibility without awarding unrelated career achievements to either receiver.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade — Boston C+, New Orleans C+. Boston preferred an immediately available guard in Dan Dickau, while the displaced New Orleans/Oklahoma City Hornets received a 2006 second-round right eventually associated with No. 56 Edin Bavcic. The pick's later draft identity did not guarantee NBA minutes for the receiving franchise, just as Dickau's pre-trade statistics were not Celtics production. Both teams acquired useful flexibility on different schedules without a clearly superior confirmed return.

sections.heading: Boston Exchanged Eric Williams for Two Future Seconds
sections.body: In August 1997, Boston moved forward Eric Williams to Denver for future second-round rights eventually associated with the 1999 No. 55 Kris Clack position and the 2001 No. 39 Earl Watson selection. The Celtics had a new roster direction and preferred additional future options, while the Nuggets obtained a player with established NBA experience. Those two future choices were years away and weren't actual drafted players on the agreement date. The deal shouldn't be described as Boston receiving Clack and Watson as immediately signed athletes. Each right had a separate timeline and could be affected by later transactions.

sections.heading: Williams Offered Denver a Current Wing Option
sections.body: Williams had NBA forward and wing experience and gave Denver a player who could compete for regular-season minutes. He wasn't a guaranteed franchise leader, but acquiring an available professional supplied more immediate basketball value than waiting for two different drafts. His prior Boston seasons remained Celtics history, and any Nuggets return needed to come from his games after the exchange. The front office's decision traded longer-dated development chances for a nearer roster contribution. Later moves involving Williams should be treated independently rather than folded into the original Boston agreement as though the Nuggets controlled every subsequent season of his career.

sections.heading: Boston's Two Picks Became Traceable Draft Slots
sections.body: The rights associated with No. 55 Kris Clack in 1999 and No. 39 Earl Watson in 2001 illustrate Boston's original prospect-oriented approach. But a later draft position alone doesn't establish that both named players delivered NBA minutes for the Celtics, especially if one or both rights traveled again. Boston acquired opportunities to select or redirect prospects, not guaranteed on-court results. The different positions also had different likely ceilings within the second round. Treating Watson's later useful NBA service as automatic Boston production would be a particularly large error without confirming his final signing franchise.

sections.heading: Denver's Nearer Player Return Can Carry a Small Edge
sections.body: The Nuggets acquired a current NBA forward and Boston received a pair of future options. That favors Denver if the focus is practical near-term return, though the Celtics' longer horizon was understandable as they adjusted their roster. Neither side directly received two established stars, and subsequent draft decisions should be tracked in their own transactions. A Denver-winning verdict shouldn't rest on pretending Williams's entire earlier Celtics career happened after his arrival.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Nuggets Win — Denver B+, Boston C-. Denver obtained Eric Williams, a forward with an immediate NBA role to evaluate, while Boston accepted two distant second-round positions later associated with No. 55 Kris Clack in 1999 and No. 39 Earl Watson in 2001. Those choices created future options, but they were not established Celtics contributors on the trade date. Denver's current player supplied the clearer near-term basketball opportunity without claiming Williams's earlier Boston games.

sections.heading: Atlanta Chose International Rights and a Future Second
sections.body: Atlanta sent big man Priest Lauderdale to Denver in September 1997 for rights to Efthimios Rentzias and a future 2000 second-round selection. The historical draft record later identifies that position with No. 40 Hanno Mottola. The Hawks collected two development opportunities while the Nuggets acquired a current center option. Rentzias already had professional experience outside the NBA, but receiving his rights wasn't the same as adding a player under contract for the coming Atlanta season. The additional future second would not be exercised until nearly three years later, adding uncertainty to the return.

sections.heading: Lauderdale Gave Denver an Immediately Available Big Man
sections.body: Lauderdale brought unusual height and an NBA frontcourt profile that Denver could evaluate immediately. His selection history and past teams gave the Nuggets a reason to examine him, but they didn't guarantee sustained starting minutes or playoff success. The price was one international rights claim and a distant draft pick, so Denver had reason to prioritize direct center depth instead of holding speculative future assets. His eventual role depended on practice performance, health and subsequent roster moves. The trade didn't deliver a premier first-round selection or an established All-Star to either party.

sections.heading: Rentzias and Mottola Offered Separate Prospects
sections.body: Atlanta could negotiate the rights to Rentzias and separately use the 2000 selection associated with Mottola. Those two prospects followed different professional paths, and neither should be automatically credited with all subsequent NBA or overseas performance for Atlanta. A draft right gives the original receiving club control over a decision or another possible transaction, not an eternal claim to any player's career statistics. Mottola's selection name supplies a concrete endpoint to the pick chain, while Rentzias's international background gives context for why a team might value the rights. The two assets shouldn't be combined as a single roster addition.

sections.heading: The Hawks Gained More Ways to Develop Depth
sections.body: Atlanta converted one center into rights to a different big man and an eventual second-round prospect opportunity. That provided more distinct possibilities than a simple player swap, even if the actual NBA returns were uncertain. Denver's interest in an available center made sense in the short term, but the additional future right tilted the potential value toward Atlanta. A Hawks-winning result is reasonable without assigning the entire later careers of Rentzias or Mottola to the club. Moderate grades reflect the speculative nature of these assets and the limited certainty of Lauderdale's new NBA role.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win — Atlanta B, Denver C+. In September 1997 Atlanta sent Priest Lauderdale to Denver for Efthimios Rentzias's rights and a future second-round pick later identified with the No. 40 Hanno Mottola selection in 2000. Denver sought an immediately available center, while Atlanta gained two separate development opportunities. The Hawks' broader options justify a modest edge, not a claim that every later Rentzias or Mottola NBA appearance belonged to Atlanta. Neither side acquired a guaranteed star.

sections.heading: Boston and Vancouver Exchanged Roy Rogers for Depth and a Pick
sections.body: Boston acquired center Roy Rogers from the Vancouver Grizzlies in October 1997, sending Tony Massenburg and a future second-round selection the other way. The incoming Grizzlies draft right later associated with No. 37 Obinna Ekezie in 1999 complemented Massenburg's experienced frontcourt role. The franchise had not yet moved to Memphis, although modern database groupings use the Memphis Grizzlies identity. Boston chose one younger center it could evaluate, while Vancouver obtained a current NBA big man plus another opportunity to find a prospect in a later draft.

sections.heading: Rogers Offered a Prospect With Physical Tools
sections.body: Rogers had played NBA center minutes and presented an athletic interior profile that Boston could attempt to develop. His prior Vanderbilt-era college reputation and earlier Grizzlies games were useful scouting context but not new Celtics output. The club needed him to compete for a frontcourt place within a shifting roster, and the trade didn't guarantee a long future Boston career. Taking a single younger player meant Boston sacrificed Massenburg's known veteran presence along with a pick. It was a bet that Rogers's upside could justify that combined cost rather than a purchase of an established starting center.

sections.heading: Vancouver Collected Veteran Service and a Later Selection
sections.body: The Grizzlies gained Massenburg's NBA experience and a separate draft claim that would later be associated with Ekezie at No. 37 in 1999. That gave the organization both immediate frontcourt depth and a future player-rights option. The pick's eventual name does not prove the player subsequently reported to Vancouver or played in Memphis years later; final rights and contracts needed individual verification. Massenburg, by contrast, was an existing NBA player who could be assessed upon arrival. Holding these benefits apart avoids inflating the package into two automatic starting-quality acquisitions.

sections.heading: Two Return Types Favor the Grizzlies
sections.body: Although Rogers's athletic potential was legitimate, the Grizzlies' combination of near-term experience and future selection capital was a broader package. That supports a Grizzlies-winning assessment on original asset value, not an assertion that every later Ekezie game belonged to the receiving franchise. Boston's player-development wager may have been reasonable, but it carried greater single-player risk. The historical transaction occurred in Vancouver, even though the website's franchise lineage currently says Memphis.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Grizzlies Win — Vancouver/Memphis B+, Boston C+. Boston took a development chance on center Roy Rogers, while the Grizzlies gained veteran Tony Massenburg and a future second-round asset later associated with the No. 37 Obinna Ekezie selection in 1999. Massenburg offered immediate frontcourt experience plus another draft opportunity, a broader package than a single young prospect. The pick's eventual name does not prove that Ekezie's later NBA games belonged to the Grizzlies.

sections.heading: Boston Received McLeod and a Later First in Exchange for Moiso
sections.body: Boston and Philadelphia reached an August 2001 agreement sending forward Jerome Moiso to the 76ers. The Celtics received Roshown McLeod and a future first-round draft right later associated with the 2003 No. 20 position and Dahntay Jones. The package combined a current player option with a higher-value future selection, while Philadelphia preferred to test a younger athletic big man it could bring directly into its roster. The first-round claim was not yet a selected player at the agreement date, and any later rights movement must be traced before awarding that player's NBA service to Boston.

sections.heading: Moiso Represented a Reclamation Opportunity for Philadelphia
sections.body: Moiso had entered the league with physical and developmental upside but was still seeking a defined NBA role. Philadelphia could try him in its frontcourt after acquiring his rights from Boston, but his earlier college reputation didn't mean the 76ers had just obtained a productive NBA starter. A younger big man's path often depended on playing time and role fit, both uncertain in a roster with established contributors. The club accepted that risk by surrendering McLeod and a future first. Moiso's eventual seasons with other franchises should not be counted as Philadelphia production through this single transaction.

sections.heading: The Boston Pick Provided an Additional Valuable Asset
sections.body: A first-round choice eventually associated with No. 20 in 2003 was a more substantial developmental asset than the late seconds in many other historical trades. Boston could use that opportunity itself or move it elsewhere, while also evaluating McLeod as a current forward. Dahntay Jones's eventual NBA career was the product of subsequent draft and contract decisions, so the fact that his name appears on the right's lineage shouldn't automatically be treated as Celtics playing time. Nevertheless, the original receiving club gained a distinct first-round claim in addition to another player asset. That combination created multiple possible routes to future value.

sections.heading: The Celtics' Two-Asset Return Holds the Stronger Position
sections.body: Boston moved a still-unproven young big man and obtained a forward plus a future first-round selection. This gives Boston a material advantage in expected value, even without assuming McLeod turned into a franchise centerpiece or Jones eventually played NBA games for the Celtics. The draft capital is what distinguishes this exchange from routine end-of-bench moves. Any later disposition of the acquired first requires its own transaction accounting and shouldn't be silently collapsed into the 2001 agreement.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win — Boston A-, Philadelphia D. Boston moved Jerome Moiso to the 76ers for Roshown McLeod and a future first-round right later linked to the 2003 No. 20 Dahntay Jones position. The first-round opportunity gave the Celtics substantially more asset flexibility than a straight prospect-for-veteran exchange. Philadelphia acquired Moiso's unproven interior upside but accepted a narrower return. The grade values the trade's draft capital without falsely treating Jones's entire subsequent NBA career as Boston games.

sections.heading: Atlanta Exchanged Three Different Assets for One Proven Scorer
sections.body: The Hawks acquired Glenn Robinson from Milwaukee in August 2002, surrendering veteran Toni Kukoc, prospect Leon Smith and a conditional future first-round choice. The draft protection had multiple possible sources and conditions, with the resulting right eventually associated with the 2003 No. 8 selection and T.J. Ford. Atlanta wanted an established offensive presence immediately, while the Bucks preferred two players plus a potentially valuable draft asset. This wasn't an exchange of Robinson for one lottery pick alone, and the complicated conditional formula shouldn't be reduced to a guaranteed No. 8 position in 2002.

sections.heading: Robinson's Earlier Scoring Was a Reason to Acquire Him, Not the Return
sections.body: Robinson had shown substantial scoring talent with Milwaukee, so Atlanta could reasonably expect him to help carry more possessions. Those Bucks performances, however, weren't newly acquired Hawks production: the receiving club needed to evaluate only his work after this agreement. His cost and roster fit were important because Atlanta gave up both a current veteran and future draft flexibility. Bringing in one familiar high-volume scorer can assist a club in the short term without automatically delivering several years of championship-level success. Later changes to Robinson's contract or team would narrow the direct return even further.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Gained an Experienced Forward and a Longer-Term Option
sections.body: Kukoc offered NBA and international experience, while Smith represented a much more speculative player-development opportunity. The conditional first supplied another distinct way to improve the Bucks after the trade. That choice ultimately became linked with Ford, but the protection terms made its eventual draft position uncertain when signed. Ford's later games should be traced to the team actually holding his rights rather than assumed from the original wording. For Milwaukee, the attraction was variety: it could assess two players immediately and retain a future selection whose upside was greater than an ordinary low second-round pick.

sections.heading: The Bucks Received a More Flexible Overall Package
sections.body: Milwaukee obtained a combination of veteran service, prospect evaluation and future draft capital. That supports a Bucks-winning result without claiming Smith became an established starter or Robinson offered Atlanta no value. Robinson's usefulness belonged to a relatively short window compared with the whole career people associated with his name. The conditional choice gave Milwaukee a meaningful later decision, which is the crucial element in explaining why the trade tilted west.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win. atlanta-hawks: C; milwaukee-bucks: B+. Atlanta acquired the most recognizable scorer but spent multiple ways to fill its roster, including a conditional first that developed into a valuable draft position. Milwaukee obtained a combination of veteran service, prospect e This verdict preserves draft protections and distinguishes professional history earned elsewhere from receiving-team contributions.

sections.heading: Boston Acquired Two Centers for a Guard, a Second and Cash
sections.body: The February 2003 exchange between Boston and Denver sent Mark Blount and Mark Bryant to the Celtics. The Nuggets received guard Shammond Williams, $1 million and a second-round selection eventually identified as the 2003 No. 46 choice associated with Sani Becirovic. Boston was seeking available interior players for its current rotation, while Denver was ready to move two big men in exchange for backcourt depth and additional resources. No first-round right changed hands. The cash was a financial consideration rather than an NBA player, and the second-round selection remained uncertain until the next draft.

sections.heading: Blount Supplied the Most Tangible Boston Basketball Benefit
sections.body: Blount offered a current center the Celtics could use in games without waiting for a selection or international negotiation. He would supply the main continuing basketball value in this return, with Bryant providing a more experienced but narrower reserve option. Neither player's earlier professional work belonged to Boston merely because his rights changed teams in February. The club could assess their defensive positioning and size against larger opponents, addressing a need around its established perimeter talent. The acquisition wasn't a guarantee of an elite championship center, but direct frontcourt depth carried practical value relative to the package Boston surrendered.

sections.heading: Denver Accepted Three Less Immediate Forms of Compensation
sections.body: Williams was a known NBA guard who could help Denver organize bench possessions. The cash payment was certain, while the eventual No. 46 draft right gave the Nuggets another chance to select or transfer a prospect. Becirovic's career outside the NBA does not automatically translate into Nuggets regular-season minutes, making the choice more speculative than Blount's ability to join Boston. The original deal combined basketball depth, finances and future rights rather than returning one equally established center. Denver's rationale fit a franchise choosing to redirect its resources, even if none of the pieces yielded a major immediate NBA star.

sections.heading: Boston Has the Slightly Clearer On-Court Payoff
sections.body: That makes a small Celtics advantage defensible without depicting Williams or the second-round right as valueless. A lottery pick was never part of the exchange, and neither club's later franchise successes were generated solely by this move. The draft history of Becirovic needs its own attribution, separate from the team's original 2003 choice. The value here comes chiefly from targeted frontcourt help on one side and distributed compensation on the other.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Celtics Edge. boston-celtics: B-; denver-nuggets: C+. Boston obtained the type of usable size it needed, particularly through Blount's receiving-team service, while Denver's package was spread across a guard, cash and a later selection. That makes a small Celtics advantage defensible This verdict preserves draft protections and distinguishes professional history earned elsewhere from receiving-team contributions.

sections.heading: Two Future Firsts Sent Lorenzen Wright to Atlanta
sections.body: The Hawks acquired center Lorenzen Wright from the Los Angeles Clippers in August 1999. Rather than surrender a single current NBA player, Atlanta committed two conditional first-round selections with separate draft years and protection formulas. The 2000 lottery-protected pick eventually matched the No. 18 position associated with Quentin Richardson; the top-four-protected 2002 choice eventually matched No. 8 Chris Wilcox. Those eventual draft slots were not certain on the original agreement date. Atlanta wanted a player it could use immediately in its interior rotation, while Los Angeles valued having two opportunities to add or move young talent across different summers.

sections.heading: Wright Was a Real NBA Center, Not a Guaranteed Star
sections.body: Wright offered rebounding, size and experience beyond what an unknown late-first prospect might provide right away. He could compete for minutes with Atlanta's established frontcourt players and provide an accessible basketball return while the future picks remained contingent. His previous Clippers games weren't new Hawks production, and the real value of his acquired contract depended on seasons after August 1999. The deal therefore had a coherent short-term purpose, particularly for a team seeking to support its existing veterans. Yet even a useful center couldn't guarantee a long playoff breakthrough, making the price in two firsts particularly important.

sections.heading: Los Angeles Held Two Different Draft Opportunities
sections.body: The Clippers' incoming draft rights eventually became identifiable at No. 18 in 2000 and No. 8 in 2002. Those were valuable positions for a franchise seeking roster growth, even though obtaining a future selection didn't mean a named player was under contract in 1999. Quentin Richardson and Chris Wilcox provide later landmarks for following the picks, but each player's actual NBA games belong to the franchise that ultimately signed him. The protection rules also meant the Clippers bore timing and conveyance uncertainty until the conditions resolved. Still, splitting the compensation across two first-round paths offered more development options than retaining one current center.

sections.heading: The Draft Capital Tips the Retrospective Toward the Clippers
sections.body: Atlanta gained an available professional player, which shouldn't be dismissed simply because the Clippers later received attractive selections. Nonetheless, two first-round choices at eventual No. 18 and No. 8 represent a sizable opportunity cost for a supporting frontcourt acquisition. Los Angeles converted one center into two distinct swings at young talent, giving it greater long-term flexibility. The trade merits a Clippers-winning conclusion without falsely declaring every subsequent Richardson or Wilcox season a direct benefit of the 1999 transfer. Its main lesson is the need to value protected future picks separately rather than collapsing them into a generic late selection.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Clippers Win — Los Angeles A-, Atlanta C-. The Hawks acquired experienced center Lorenzen Wright, but surrendered two conditional first-round rights that later reached No. 18 in 2000 and No. 8 in 2002. Those selections were associated with Quentin Richardson and Chris Wilcox, separate opportunities the Clippers obtained for one player. Atlanta gained usable frontcourt depth, yet the future pick cost proved high. The Clippers' advantage is grounded in receiving two valuable draft positions, not in claiming every later game by either selected player.

sections.heading: Atlanta Exchanged an International Center's Rights for Two Seconds
sections.body: In June 2002, Atlanta sent the negotiating rights to Greek center Efthimios Rentzias to Philadelphia. The Hawks received two future second-round draft selections instead of a player already signed to an NBA contract. Historical records connect those draft rights with the 2004 No. 37 selection associated with Royal Ivey and the 2006 No. 42 selection associated with Daniel Gibson. Each future opportunity carried its own eventual position and timing. The 76ers pursued a specific internationally experienced big man, while the Hawks chose flexibility over retaining a right they hadn't turned into a regular NBA contributor.

sections.heading: Rentzias Gave the 76ers a Prospect They Could Pursue Directly
sections.body: Rentzias had established professional credentials in Europe and a traditional center's physical profile. Philadelphia could evaluate him as a possible immediate frontcourt contributor rather than wait several years to select another prospect. But overseas production isn't automatically an NBA rotation record for the team acquiring those rights. His actual availability, contract and adaptation to a different league remained uncertainties. The original price was two later seconds, so the 76ers were investing multiple development opportunities in one potential signing. This distinction makes the agreement a rights transaction rather than an exchange of proven NBA centers or an instant starting-quality upgrade.

sections.heading: The Hawks Acquired Distinct 2004 and 2006 Decisions
sections.body: The eventual selections associated with Ivey and Gibson illuminate the value of Atlanta's compensation, but the players' later careers must be traced through the actual teams that selected or signed them. A future second is an option: the receiving club may select a player, exchange the right again or allow a prospect to develop elsewhere. Atlanta secured two such decisions in separate drafts by giving up just one incoming international right. The No. 37 position in 2004 carried different scouting conditions from the No. 42 position in 2006. Combining them into one generic asset would miss the central advantage of the return.

sections.heading: Two Separate Picks Offer Atlanta the Better Position
sections.body: The Hawks didn't receive a guaranteed productive starter on the agreement date. They did, however, obtain two independently usable selections for a prospect right whose NBA payoff was uncertain. Philadelphia's preference for Rentzias made basketball sense if the team believed he could immediately occupy a roster spot, but that belief had to translate into actual service. The diversity and duration of Atlanta's acquired draft capital makes the Hawks-winning evaluation credible without counting every later NBA minute from Gibson or Ivey as Hawks output. The right lesson is about optionality and the difference between signed players and rights held for future negotiations.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win — Atlanta B, Philadelphia D. Atlanta converted Efthimios Rentzias's negotiating rights into two future second-round opportunities, associated with the 2004 No. 37 and 2006 No. 42 positions. Philadelphia concentrated those two chances in one overseas center whose eventual NBA return was uncertain. The two picks gave the Hawks more flexibility, but Royal Ivey's and Daniel Gibson's later careers should not automatically be counted as Atlanta production. The grades reflect different asset risks rather than an immediate star-for-star exchange.

sections.heading: Boston Exchanged Montross and a Pick for Two High Draft Slots
sections.body: The Celtics moved center Eric Montross and the 1996 No. 9 first-round position associated with Samaki Walker to Dallas. Boston's return included the 1996 No. 6 selection associated with Antoine Walker and a future first-round choice that became the 1997 No. 6 slot associated with Ron Mercer. Each named pick belonged to a distinct draft year. This was not a straight swap of Montross for Antoine Walker alone, and Dallas received a first-round selection rather than simply giving away two choices. Boston sought additional high-quality development opportunities while Dallas valued a center plus its own 1996 chance.

sections.heading: Antoine Walker Delivered the Most Valuable Celtics Outcome
sections.body: Antoine Walker grew into an important Boston scorer and rebounder after the 1996 draft. His meaningful seasons with the Celtics represented realized receiving-team production, not hypothetical upside attached to an unnamed prospect. That made the No. 6 position an especially consequential acquisition for a franchise looking for players who could lead a rebuild. Walker's later appearances elsewhere shouldn't be credited to Boston, but his actual Celtics tenure alone distinguished the deal from an ordinary exchange of future draft rights. The selection offered a young cornerstone whose offensive responsibilities expanded as the team's direction changed during the late 1990s.

sections.heading: Mercer Added a Second Lottery-Level Opportunity
sections.body: The 1997 No. 6 position associated with Ron Mercer gave Boston another chance to acquire a prominent young wing. Mercer did not need to spend his entire career with the Celtics for the original right to possess meaningful value; a high first-round slot gave the franchise a chance to select or transact a well-regarded prospect. Dallas received Montross's established NBA frontcourt experience and the 1996 No. 9 position attached to Samaki Walker, making its side a real return rather than a simple sale. However, neither asset matched the combined realized usefulness and opportunity set provided by the two early selections heading to Boston.

sections.heading: The Walker Outcome Justifies Boston's Decisive Advantage
sections.body: Boston obtained its best sustained basketball return through Antoine Walker while also holding another premium first-round chance. Dallas could reasonably want a current center and its own young big man, but that package proved less valuable than the Celtics' dual high selections. The franchise histories of Mercer, Samaki Walker and Montross still need careful receiving-team attribution, not a blanket credit for every later NBA game. The clear Boston win comes from Walker's actual service and the considerable leverage of an additional early draft position. This was a meaningful rebuild-era transaction rather than a minor reserve exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win — Boston A+, Dallas D. Boston exchanged Eric Montross and the 1996 No. 9 selection associated with Samaki Walker for the 1996 No. 6 Antoine Walker right and another first that reached No. 6 in 1997, associated with Ron Mercer. Antoine Walker's actual productive Celtics tenure anchors the A+, with the second high selection adding material opportunity. Dallas received genuine center and draft assets, but the relative value and realized Boston return favor the Celtics decisively. Later careers on other teams are not included as Boston production.

sections.heading: Atlanta Acquired Ken Norman for Roy Hinson's Rights
sections.body: The Hawks received veteran forward Ken Norman from Milwaukee in June 1994, sending the rights to Roy Hinson to the Bucks. The agreement paired an immediately recognizable NBA frontcourt player against an asset whose value depended on another club's ability to negotiate or use it. Norman had accumulated substantial league experience before the trade, but those earlier Clippers and Bucks seasons did not become new Atlanta production. The Hawks wanted a practical forward for the upcoming campaign, while Milwaukee was comfortable exchanging an established rotation name for a much less certain rights claim.

sections.heading: Norman Brought Defined Skills With a Limited Horizon
sections.body: Norman was an experienced scorer and rebounder who could help a team at the forward positions. His age and years already spent in the league placed limits on how much further growth Atlanta could reasonably expect. The team gained the ability to evaluate a current player rather than waiting for an uncertain future draft, but it still needed Norman to fit the new rotation and earn minutes. A familiar name by itself didn't mean Atlanta had acquired a long-term star. The return should be based on the games and seasons after his arrival, not on his earlier best statistical campaigns with other teams.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Received a Rights Claim Rather Than Immediate Production
sections.body: Hinson had an earlier NBA playing history, but holding his rights in 1994 was a different proposition from receiving a healthy, currently signed player under a multi-year agreement. The Bucks could choose whether to negotiate or use the right in another transaction. That made the asset speculative and of limited immediate basketball certainty. It would be misleading to credit Milwaukee with Hinson's prior career as though those games occurred after this exchange. The club's decision instead reflected a willingness to move Norman and hold an alternative claim that might help with future roster planning.

sections.heading: A Small Bucks Edge Is Plausible but Hardly Transformative
sections.body: Atlanta gained a veteran capable of immediate contribution, while Milwaukee converted Norman into a different form of control over a frontcourt player. Neither club secured premium new draft capital or a future All-NBA centerpiece. The precise balance depends on Norman's later Atlanta availability and what Milwaukee could actually do with Hinson's rights, both more limited than the players' reputation might suggest. The canonical slightly Bucks-favoring verdict should therefore be interpreted cautiously, recognizing Atlanta's practical veteran return instead of treating Milwaukee's rights as an automatic on-court replacement. The transaction was modest in long-term stakes.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Bucks Edge — Milwaukee B, Atlanta B-. Atlanta obtained experienced forward Ken Norman, a usable immediate player, while Milwaukee exchanged him for the rights to Roy Hinson. Those rights offered the Bucks a different form of control but did not guarantee healthy on-court service. Norman's earlier productive seasons elsewhere cannot be credited to the Hawks after this trade, just as Hinson's prior career cannot be credited to Milwaukee. Neither side acquired a premium draft pick or long-term cornerstone, supporting only a narrow grade difference.

sections.heading: Brandon Bass Arrived for Glen Davis and Von Wafer
sections.body: Boston and Orlando completed a December 2011 exchange that sent Brandon Bass to the Celtics and Glen Davis plus Von Wafer to the Magic. Bass and Davis were both experienced frontcourt players but offered different offensive habits; Wafer added an additional perimeter option for Orlando. The Celtics wanted a dependable midrange and rebounding contributor capable of fitting around their older championship core. The Magic obtained a more physical interior player with an existing personality and a wing whose place in the rotation remained uncertain. There were no draft picks or contingent future protections to track in this direct player transaction.

sections.heading: Bass Found a Useful Role With Boston's Veterans
sections.body: Bass could hit open jump shots, compete on the glass and operate within Boston's established offensive structure. His ability to supply dependable frontcourt minutes helped the Celtics maintain depth without expecting a new focal-point scorer. Those are real receiving-team contributions that can be assessed after the trade, rather than copying his earlier Orlando numbers into Boston's record. The exchange was particularly practical because the Celtics already had veterans taking most of the primary shot-creation responsibilities. Bass's skills complemented that approach and eventually gave the team more flexible combinations at power forward than simply retaining an incumbent reserve.

sections.heading: Orlando Took Davis's Interior Physicality and Wafer's Shooting
sections.body: Davis had a recognizable track record as a Celtics rotation big man and could offer strength, screens and occasional interior offense. Wafer's arrival added a second piece, giving Orlando another choice on the wing instead of restricting the return to one player. However, neither acquisition guaranteed improvement equal to the sustained fit Bass found in Boston. Davis's previous playoff moments with the Celtics did not count as Magic accomplishments, and Wafer's existing professional history likewise needed fresh receiving-team evaluation. Orlando was trading a useful but comparatively understated forward for a package whose value depended on finding stable roles for both incoming players.

sections.heading: Boston's Better Fit Supports the Winning Verdict
sections.body: The Celtics took the more coherent single-player return in Bass, whose scoring and rebounding worked alongside the remaining veteran core. Orlando acquired two named NBA personnel options, so the Magic were not left without compensation, but their combined value was less certain. The lack of future picks or trade exceptions keeps the transaction easy to judge from actual rotation outcomes. A Celtics-winning assessment rests on the frontcourt fit rather than treating Davis's previous Boston contributions as new Orlando value or describing Bass as an All-Star. The trade was useful for Boston precisely because the expectations were specific and attainable.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win — Boston B+, Orlando C. Brandon Bass gave Boston a reliable frontcourt scorer and rebounder who fit alongside its established veterans. Orlando received Glen Davis and Von Wafer, two NBA players with different useful skills, but the combined return did not match Bass's sustained Boston contribution. This was a direct player exchange without an incoming first-round pick or trade exception. The grade advantage rests on the actual post-trade rotation value of the three players, not Davis's earlier playoff moments in Boston.

sections.heading: Atlanta and Dallas Swapped Perimeter Specialists at the Deadline
sections.body: At the February 21, 2013 trade deadline, the Hawks acquired Dahntay Jones from Dallas in exchange for Anthony Morrow. The swap paired a more defensive-minded wing with a player whose main appeal was his outside shooting. Atlanta sought a different perimeter role for the rest of the season, while the Mavericks wanted more three-point offense. Neither club obtained draft capital or a multi-year contingent right through the transaction. It was a direct adjustment to how bench minutes might be distributed, not a change in the league's top scoring hierarchy. Both players had established NBA experience but limited overall roster control.

sections.heading: Jones Gave Atlanta Defensive Wing Depth
sections.body: Jones brought energy, physical perimeter defense and an ability to compete for minutes without demanding many offensive possessions. That profile could be useful beside Atlanta's primary shot creators, particularly when the team needed to protect a lead or handle an athletic opposing wing. His previous games for other franchises were scouting context rather than Atlanta performance, and the limited late-season window constrained how much the team could gain. A defender could help a rotation even without posting impressive raw scoring numbers. However, that value needed to be evaluated alongside the loss of Morrow's perimeter shooting and potential offensive spacing.

sections.heading: Morrow's Shooting Was Dallas's Targeted Return
sections.body: Morrow had built his reputation as a long-range shooter, a skill that could create space around Dallas's established veterans. The Mavericks weren't receiving an elite all-around starter, but they acquired a player capable of making defenses respect the three-point line. His existing percentages from earlier teams provided evidence of the trait rather than guaranteed new Mavericks results. Dallas paid with Jones's defensive versatility and accepted a narrower offensive specialist. That difference gave the two clubs complementary motives: Atlanta wanted another defender, Dallas another shooter. Neither team needed the exchange to determine its entire season or franchise direction.

sections.heading: The Mavericks Have the Modest Advantage in Role Value
sections.body: Both clubs acquired an NBA-caliber reserve, but Morrow's distinctive outside shooting supplied a clearer single offensive function to Dallas than Jones's brief defensive stint did for Atlanta. That supports the Mavericks-winning verdict in the existing record while recognizing the Hawks' legitimate desire for wing defense. This wasn't a transaction that produced a major draft pick or future team cornerstone. The best evaluation compares the incremental role each side could fill after the February deadline. Morrow's earlier years outside Dallas and Jones's earlier defensive accomplishments belong to their prior clubs, not to the respective receiving franchises.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win — Dallas B, Atlanta C+. Dallas obtained Anthony Morrow's outside shooting by sending defensive wing Dahntay Jones to Atlanta at the February 2013 deadline. Both teams received a recognizable reserve, but Morrow offered Dallas a clearer offensive specialty, while the Hawks gained a shorter-term defensive option. Neither side obtained a draft pick or a future star from this direct swap. The modest Dallas advantage reflects receiving-team role fit and avoids crediting either organization with the players' earlier work elsewhere.

sections.heading: Boston Turned Tayshaun Prince Into Two Forwards
sections.body: Boston sent veteran Tayshaun Prince to the Detroit Pistons at the February 19, 2015 deadline, acquiring Jonas Jerebko and Luigi Datome. Detroit wanted an experienced wing familiar with the organization and its style, while the Celtics obtained two frontcourt or perimeter development options. The arrangement wasn't about moving a first-round pick or an international draft right; all three were actual professionals under contract. The Celtics were building a younger roster and could offer Jerebko and Datome opportunities to earn roles. Prince's prior Detroit years made the return especially recognizable for the Pistons, but those earlier accomplishments weren't fresh output from this reunion.

sections.heading: Jerebko Became an Especially Useful Boston Reserve
sections.body: Jerebko could rebound, stretch the floor and shift between forward roles, which suited a Celtics team gradually expanding its defensive and offensive flexibility. His subsequent service in Boston became the main lasting value of the transaction. Those receiving-team games offered a concrete retrospective basis that did not depend on simply listing the player names in the deal. The Celtics didn't expect Jerebko to replace a franchise star; he filled a practical supporting role that became useful as the roster developed. Datome provided another shooting prospect to evaluate, though his NBA contribution was much smaller than the enduring minutes eventually provided by Jerebko.

sections.heading: Detroit Preferred a Familiar Veteran Presence
sections.body: Prince had already been closely associated with Detroit's earlier championship-era identity, so bringing him back offered leadership and a familiar defensive wing profile. But by 2015, his age and career stage placed limits on the basketball upside of the reunion. The Pistons surrendered two forwards with different development possibilities in exchange for an immediately known veteran. Prince's years elsewhere and previous Pistons glory could justify why Detroit valued his experience, but neither was newly generated by this transaction. The move had a near-term organizational purpose rather than a compelling opportunity to acquire another future star.

sections.heading: Boston Won Through Actual Sustained Bench Production
sections.body: The Celtics acquired Jerebko as a continuing support contributor and also received a chance to assess Datome, giving them a broader personnel return for an aging veteran. Detroit obtained a known leader and defensive wing, but Prince's later role could not replicate his best earlier seasons. The stronger Boston outcome is rooted in Jerebko's actual usefulness rather than a hypothetical contract or draft asset. Both clubs made understandable decisions, but Boston received more sustained on-court value from this particular swap. It is an example of a modest deadline exchange that mattered through fit and depth, not through a surprise new superstar.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win — Boston B+, Detroit C+. Boston acquired Jonas Jerebko and Luigi Datome for Tayshaun Prince, obtaining an especially useful longer-serving reserve in Jerebko and a second shooter to evaluate. Detroit brought back an experienced, familiar wing, but Prince was no longer the player of his earlier championship-era seasons. Boston's advantage comes from the actual supporting production obtained after February 2015, not from adding a past player's peak or assuming either side received a future franchise star.

sections.heading: Boston Acquired Marcus Morris While Detroit Got Bradley and a Second
sections.body: In July 2017, Boston traded Avery Bradley and a 2019 second-round selection to the Detroit Pistons for forward Marcus Morris. The later second is associated with No. 45 Isaiah Roby in the 2019 draft ledger. Boston wanted another versatile forward who could score and cover several frontcourt matchups; Detroit wanted an established perimeter defender and a future development option. The incoming pick for the Pistons was not an immediately signed 2017 NBA player, and its final slot was not known on the agreement date. The trade offered each team a different way to balance offensive creation with defensive assignments.

sections.heading: Morris Added Scoring and Positional Flexibility in Boston
sections.body: Morris provided the Celtics with a forward capable of making outside shots, creating some offense against mismatches and defending larger wings. His future Boston seasons gave the club a sustained player contribution rather than a right that might never convey. The team could use him alongside other versatile defenders without requiring him to become its sole scoring leader. His previous Detroit production explained the interest but wasn't the same as new Boston output. The acquisition had added value because the Celtics' personnel needs were changing as the franchise rebuilt its top of the roster around different offensive and defensive combinations.

sections.heading: Detroit Acquired Bradley's Defense and an Additional Draft Chance
sections.body: Bradley arrived with a reputation as a determined perimeter defender and an established starter, which gave the Pistons a usable guard instead of a speculative rights claim alone. The accompanying 2019 second offered another opportunity to select or move a prospect. That selection's eventual association with Isaiah Roby doesn't automatically mean Roby spent his career playing for Detroit, particularly if rights changed hands later. Bradley's own receiving-team tenure needed to be evaluated after the trade rather than through his preceding years in Boston. Detroit traded one starting-caliber forward for a guard and a future asset, a defensible alternative team-building approach.

sections.heading: Boston's Longer Forward Return Provides the Edge
sections.body: Morris's ongoing contribution in Boston offers a stronger realized asset than the brief window associated with Detroit's use of Bradley. The extra second-round pick gave the Pistons meaningful optionality, so the return shouldn't be described as a single-for-single loss without qualification. Still, Boston acquired a durable frontcourt scorer and defender suited to its developing identity. This supports a Celtics-winning verdict without treating Morris as a franchise superstar or crediting Detroit with all later games played by the prospect connected to its incoming draft right. The trade's value came from fit, available minutes and an appropriately measured use of future assets.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win — Boston B+, Detroit C+. Marcus Morris supplied Boston with a forward who could score, defend multiple positions and contribute over more than one season. Detroit acquired established guard Avery Bradley plus a 2019 second-round opportunity later associated with No. 45 Isaiah Roby. The draft right had legitimate value without guaranteeing that all of Roby's eventual NBA minutes belonged to Detroit. Morris's more durable Boston contribution earns the edge over the shorter Bradley return and a developing future-pick asset.

sections.heading: Boston Moved Down Two Spots and Secured Another First
sections.body: On June 19, 2017, Boston sent the first selection in that week's NBA Draft to Philadelphia for the third pick and a future first-round selection subject to detailed protections. The Sixers wanted Washington guard Markelle Fultz and paid for the right to select him without waiting. Boston's front office believed it could move down, retain access to a favored prospect and gain another meaningful draft asset. The extra pick wasn't automatically a 2019 selection at the time: the agreement first tested a protected 2018 Lakers pick, with an alternative 2019 path if those conditions weren't met.

sections.heading: The Third Pick Became Jayson Tatum and a Championship Cornerstone
sections.body: Philadelphia used No. 1 on Fultz, but Boston selected Duke forward Jayson Tatum at No. 3. Tatum developed into a principal scorer, an All-NBA-level forward and the centerpiece of repeated Celtics playoff runs. He led the team's scoring during the 2024 championship season and scored 31 points in the Finals-clinching win over Dallas. Those are concrete Boston outcomes from the pick obtained in the swap, not merely a scouting projection preserved from draft night. Selecting Tatum despite trading down is what makes the deal unusually valuable in hindsight.

sections.heading: Philadelphia's Fultz Return Ended After Just 33 Games
sections.body: Fultz's Philadelphia tenure never produced the long-term lead guard the Sixers imagined when they moved up. He played 14 regular-season games as a rookie and 19 more in 2018-19, with health and shooting difficulties disrupting his time alongside Joel Embiid and Ben Simmons. Philadelphia moved him to Orlando in a separate February 2019 transaction. His later NBA progress with the Magic belongs to that franchise's record, not Philadelphia's return for the 2017 pick swap. The original gamble was understandable because Fultz was a highly regarded prospect, but the resulting 33-game Sixers stint left an enormous opportunity cost.

sections.heading: The Conditional Extra First Eventually Became Romeo Langford
sections.body: Boston also realized the conditional second component of its return when the first-round obligation conveyed in 2019. That selection landed at No. 14 and was used on Romeo Langford, who became a Celtics depth prospect rather than a star matching Tatum. The smaller return is still a genuine additional draft opportunity Philadelphia surrendered to climb from third to first. Boston's advantage isn't based on pretending Langford enjoyed Tatum's career or that the second pick was fixed in the initial deal. The central comparison is a future championship leader plus a separate first-round chance against Fultz's very brief Philadelphia tenure.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win. Boston earns A+ because moving from No. 1 to No. 3 still yielded Jayson Tatum, a driving force behind the Celtics' 2024 NBA title, and another first-rounder eventually used on Romeo Langford. Philadelphia receives F because its 2017 No. 1 choice, Markelle Fultz, appeared in just 33 regular-season Sixers games before a separate trade to Orlando. The protected extra pick increased the cost of an already unfortunate Philadelphia outcome.

sections.heading: Atlanta Traded One Premium Pick for Two Chances
sections.body: Atlanta selected Luka Doncic third in the 2018 NBA Draft, then sent his rights to Dallas for the rights to fifth choice Trae Young and a protected future first-round pick. The extra selection eventually conveyed at No. 10 in 2019, when Atlanta took Cam Reddish. Hawks management valued Young's shooting and passing enough to move down, while Dallas regarded Doncic as worth sacrificing another draft asset. The two clubs used the same night to make different decisions about the type of player who would drive their rebuilds.

sections.heading: Young Earned His Own Atlanta Playoff Accomplishments
sections.body: Young became a major scorer and distributor for Atlanta rather than a cautionary tale who never justified the fifth pick. He directed an offense that reached the 2021 Eastern Conference Finals, establishing real on-court value for the Hawks. Reddish offered another lottery development opportunity with positional size, though his uneven Atlanta career and subsequent movement limited that component's direct payoff. Those facts distinguish the deal from a situation in which one team got a star and the other got nothing. Young gave Atlanta recognizable leadership and production even as the comparison with Doncic intensified.

sections.heading: Doncic Produced a Finals Appearance for Dallas
sections.body: Doncic became the central creator in Dallas, generating his own scoring and passes for teammates while attracting a high volume of defensive attention. His repeated All-NBA selections and the Mavericks' 2024 NBA Finals appearance demonstrate the rare receiving-team outcome of the trade. The acquisition did not depend upon a draft-night prediction surviving years of uncertainty: Dallas saw the player it targeted become the centerpiece of a contender. That evaluation stops with his Mavericks tenure. Production with a different club after a later transaction is not an additional Dallas return from the 2018 swap.

sections.heading: The Second Pick Did Not Close the Talent Gap
sections.body: Atlanta's return deserves a respectable grade because Young played like a legitimate star and the added first created a second lottery selection. But the Reddish component did not develop into the durable supporting cornerstone that might have offset the distance between the lead prospects. Dallas traded away an extra first and received the higher individual ceiling, with a Finals run as a tangible team result. The Hawks' own conference-finals appearance prevents an absolute condemnation of the deal. The Mavericks' larger peak and longer high-end creation still make them the stronger beneficiary of the exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Mavericks Win. Dallas earns A+ for acquiring Luka Doncic, an All-NBA offensive engine who led its 2024 Finals run. Atlanta gets B because Trae Young became an All-Star and powered the 2021 Eastern Conference Finals trip, while the additional lottery pick became Cam Reddish. That added piece fell short of bridging the difference between the principal players, but the Hawks obtained a real star.

sections.heading: The Celtics Moved Three Slots Up to Select Kelly Olynyk
sections.body: Boston obtained the No. 13 selection in the 2013 NBA Draft from Dallas so it could take Gonzaga big man Kelly Olynyk. The Mavericks received the rights to No. 16 choice Lucas Nogueira and two future second-round selections. Danny Ainge's interest was tied to Olynyk's unusual combination of size, outside shooting and passing vision, which offered a different frontcourt option as Boston's veteran core changed. Dallas, by contrast, was gathering draft flexibility rather than committing to a specific player at No. 13. The second-round obligations meant Boston paid more than a simple exchange of adjacent picks.

sections.heading: Olynyk Became a Four-Season Rotation Player
sections.body: Olynyk spent four seasons in Boston and gave the Celtics a versatile reserve who could space the court and keep the ball moving. He did not become the sort of traditional dominant center that a team could build an offense around, but his skill mix had practical value in Brad Stevens's lineups. That contribution was especially visible in the deciding seventh game against Washington during the 2017 playoffs. Olynyk scored 26 points as Boston advanced to the Eastern Conference Finals, an important playoff moment that flowed directly from its acquired draft choice.

sections.heading: Dallas Used the Incoming Rights as Trading Inventory
sections.body: Nogueira did not become a long-term Mavericks frontcourt player. Dallas moved his draft rights onward as part of another transaction involving Atlanta and the rights to Shane Larkin, so his later playing career cannot simply be credited as Mavericks production. The two future seconds made the initial package deeper, although each later draft right has to be followed separately before assigning any NBA minutes to Dallas. The original exchange provided flexibility and additional assets rather than a direct player with four consecutive Dallas seasons. Evaluating those rights as if they all developed in Dallas would exaggerate the realized return.

sections.heading: The Known Boston Contribution Breaks the Tie
sections.body: Dallas's rationale for trading down was understandable because it obtained more selections and flexibility. However, Boston received the particular frontcourt prospect it wanted, used him for years and benefited in a decisive postseason game. The extra second-round choices were genuine costs, not bookkeeping details that disappear from the evaluation, but none independently offsets the measured on-court role Olynyk played in Boston. This is a Celtics win built on useful lineup minutes rather than superstar expectations. Nogueira's subsequent career elsewhere and Dallas's later use of his rights should be represented as separate asset movements.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win. Boston earns B+ for acquiring Kelly Olynyk, whose four seasons of regular frontcourt work and 26-point Game 7 in 2017 directly helped the franchise. Dallas receives C+ for Lucas Nogueira's rights and two future second-round selections, giving it options without equivalent direct playing production. The Mavericks' later rights transactions are distinct from the first exchange and shouldn't be double-counted.

sections.heading: The July Agreement Became Official on July 27
sections.body: Boston completed its David Lee acquisition from Golden State on July 27, 2015, sending Gerald Wallace and Chris Babb to the Warriors. The clubs had agreed to the framework earlier in July, explaining why some transaction databases carry an earlier date, but Golden State's official log records July 27 as completion. Boston wanted a proven scoring and rebounding big to test in its developing frontcourt. Golden State had shifted its power-forward responsibilities toward Draymond Green and could move the veteran's substantial contract. It was an immediate player-and-salary exchange rather than a trade involving direct first-round draft compensation.

sections.heading: David Lee Played Thirty Games for Boston
sections.body: Lee averaged 7.1 points and 4.3 rebounds across 30 Celtics appearances in 2015-16, producing useful but limited reserve minutes. He had once been an All-Star and a central Golden State frontcourt piece, yet those accomplishments belonged to his previous team and did not automatically carry into Boston's rotation. As Brad Stevens leaned on other combinations, Lee's playing time declined. The Celtics waived him in February 2016. Boston's receiving-team return therefore ended after part of one season, but at least consisted of measurable on-court production rather than a purely financial paper transaction.

sections.heading: Golden State Sent Wallace Along in a Separate Deal
sections.body: Gerald Wallace didn't become a new Warriors rotation fixture, and Chris Babb didn't establish a playing role there. Golden State moved Wallace again on July 31 in a separate exchange with Philadelphia, receiving Jason Thompson while also sending cash and draft consideration. That follow-up made sense as roster management, but the Thompson transaction cannot be merged into the direct list of players Boston sent to Golden State. Treating Thompson's later Warriors appearances as if Boston had directly traded him would confuse two distinct deals. The original Lee swap provided the Warriors contract flexibility, not a comparable replacement veteran who played thirty games for them.

sections.heading: The Result Was an Advantage, Not a Boston Windfall
sections.body: The Celtics received more direct on-court production from their incoming player than Golden State received from Wallace or Babb. That observation supports a small Boston edge without overstating the impact of a brief Lee experiment. Golden State had strategic reasons to move Lee, particularly its existing frontcourt depth and budget, and subsequently used the Wallace contract in another deal. The trade did not by itself decide the 2015-16 championship picture or add a long-term rotation anchor for either club. Boston's modest grade acknowledges useful minutes while the Warriors' grade recognizes financial and roster utility rather than imagined on-court output.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Celtics Edge. Boston gets B- for David Lee's 30 games and 7.1 points per game before his February 2016 exit. Golden State receives C+ because Wallace and Babb provided no comparable playing contribution, though the franchise used Wallace's contract in a separate trade and opened frontcourt flexibility. Neither the Warriors' prior championship with Lee nor Thompson's later arrival should be mistaken for direct production acquired in this exchange.

sections.heading: Atlanta Sent Out a Veteran Center for Wing Shooting
sections.body: Atlanta moved Dewayne Dedmon to Detroit on November 20, 2020, acquiring Tony Snell and Khyri Thomas. The Hawks were revising their supporting cast around Trae Young and wanted perimeter help while reducing an obligation tied to Dedmon's contract. Snell arrived with established shooting and defensive experience, whereas Thomas was more of a low-cost option than an assumed rotation regular. Detroit received a veteran center and associated flexibility. The two clubs were not exchanging equivalent long-term starters; much of the decision depended on how they would handle the incoming contracts and whether those players actually appeared.

sections.heading: Snell Supplied Forty-Seven Games and Exceptional Accuracy
sections.body: Snell became a real member of Atlanta's 2020-21 rotation. He played 47 games, starting 23, and shot 56.9 percent on three-point attempts. His role was modest in scoring volume, but reliable spot-up accuracy made him useful beside Young's creation. The Hawks then reached the Eastern Conference Finals that spring, giving Snell's receiving-team contribution a meaningful postseason context without claiming he led the run. His earlier Detroit production wasn't Atlanta value. Thomas, the other incoming guard, was waived days after the transaction, so the basketball return was essentially Snell rather than two functioning rotation pieces.

sections.heading: Detroit Did Not Get Games From Dedmon
sections.body: The Pistons waived Dedmon shortly after the November transaction. He therefore provided no Detroit regular-season production through this acquisition, regardless of what he had done in Atlanta before the swap or for his next teams. That distinction is unusually important when assessing a deal whose outgoing player had a recognizable résumé. Detroit could have roster and financial reasons for processing the contract, but a bookkeeping result is not an additional frontcourt rotation contribution. Likewise, the trade exception in the record is flexibility subject to its actual later use, not a player who already played games for Detroit.

sections.heading: The Real On-Court Return Came Only to Atlanta
sections.body: The Hawks obtained one reliable wing whose shooting helped a playoff lineup, while Detroit did not use its incoming veteran center in competition. Snell's limited volume prevents the swap from earning an extravagant grade, and the waiving of Thomas narrows Atlanta's return. Nevertheless, forty-seven games of exceptionally accurate outside shooting are plainly more than Detroit received on the court from Dedmon. The verdict also respects the deal's cap and roster context without trying to assign unrelated later careers to either team. Atlanta made better use of the player it actually kept.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win. Atlanta earns B for Tony Snell's 47 regular-season games and 56.9 percent three-point shooting on a team that reached the 2021 Eastern Conference Finals. Khyri Thomas was waived without becoming a rotation contributor. Detroit receives C+ chiefly for contract flexibility because it waived Dewayne Dedmon without any Pistons games. The Hawks secured the trade's measurable receiving-team production.
