sections.heading: Boston Converted International Rights into Immediate Backcourt Depth
sections.body: Boston completed a December 9, 2011 exchange with Milwaukee, acquiring veteran guard Keyon Dooling and a conditional second-round selection for the rights to Albert Miralles. The additional pick ultimately did not convey, so the value rested on Dooling's work as a Celtics player rather than hypothetical draft capital. Boston was keeping an experienced roster supplied with secondary guards during a compressed season. Milwaukee preferred to move a reserve guard for a set of international rights, an asset it could retain without requiring an NBA roster place immediately.

sections.heading: Dooling Supplied Forty-Six Celtics Games
sections.body: Dooling appeared in 46 regular-season games for Boston in 2011-12, logging 662 minutes and averaging 4.0 points. His role was limited behind the primary guards, but he gave the Celtics another defender and ball handler for lineups that did not call for a major offensive creator. The club advanced to the Eastern Conference Finals and could call upon its reserves as the season progressed. Dooling's previous Orlando and Milwaukee seasons aren't Boston return value; those 46 games are the direct contribution of the player acquired in this particular transaction.

sections.heading: The Bucks Held Rights Rather Than Obtaining NBA Rotation Minutes
sections.body: Albert Miralles's rights gave Milwaukee an option involving an international big man, but the transaction never turned into a sustained Bucks playing tenure. Those rights can have organizational value because they may be retained or moved later, yet they are not equivalent to thirty or forty appearances by a rostered player. Milwaukee also surrendered a veteran whose future role with the Celtics was modest, not a star the team built around. The conditions attached to the pick moving to Boston expired without the club gaining another actual draft selection.

sections.heading: A Measured Advantage Favors Boston's Usable Minutes
sections.body: The advantage belongs to Boston because Dooling filled a real backup role during a deep playoff season. That outcome isn't large enough to turn a minor personnel deal into a franchise-changing transaction, especially with the extra second-round pick never conveying. Milwaukee's Miralles rights had flexibility value but did not generate comparable NBA time with the Bucks. The transaction demonstrates why a rights-only return must be evaluated separately from the games played by an incoming guard. Boston received exactly the kind of modest short-term depth it sought.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Celtics Edge. Boston earns B- for Keyon Dooling's 46 regular-season games and backup guard work during its 2012 Eastern Conference Finals season. Milwaukee gets C+ for Albert Miralles's international rights, which offered optionality but no comparable Bucks NBA rotation production. The conditional pick to Boston did not convey, so the result is a limited direct-use advantage rather than a major talent windfall.

sections.heading: Boston Chose a Veteran Wing Over a Developmental Center
sections.body: On July 31, 2021, Boston traded Moses Brown to Dallas for Josh Richardson, with transaction records showing trade exceptions for the two teams. Richardson had already worked as a defensive-minded guard and occasional secondary scorer for other franchises. Boston wanted a more established perimeter contributor alongside its young stars, while Dallas obtained a big man with size and rebounding upside. The deal was not a draft-night rights exchange or a promise that Richardson would become a permanent Celtics starter. It was a rotation adjustment in which both clubs received an actual player under contract.

sections.heading: Richardson Supplied Boston Depth Before a Separate Trade
sections.body: Richardson became part of Boston's guard and wing rotation during the first half of 2021-22, providing perimeter defense and occasional scoring. The Celtics could use him around their primary forwards without demanding that he direct the offense. Boston later sent Richardson to San Antonio as a component of the February 2022 Derrick White transaction, converting the experienced reserve into a piece of another roster decision. White was not sent by Dallas in July, so he cannot be listed as a direct asset in the earlier exchange. Richardson's actual Boston games and his availability as subsequent trade capital explain the Celtics' benefit.

sections.heading: Moses Brown Was Not a Lasting Dallas Center
sections.body: Dallas received a young rebounder who had shown flashes of production in Oklahoma City but remained a developmental player. Brown spent only part of the season with the Mavericks and did not establish a durable starting or major reserve role before leaving. His prior Thunder performances provided a reason Dallas was willing to acquire him; they were not Mavericks production acquired in this swap. Similarly, the bookkeeping value of the trade exceptions has to be assessed on its own rather than treated as a second star in either direction. The player contrast favors the team that used its veteran wing.

sections.heading: The First Trade Worked Better for the Celtics
sections.body: Boston got an experienced player it could actually use, then possessed a useful component for a later trade as the roster shifted. Dallas acquired a plausible prospect but did not receive a comparable stretch of reliable contribution. The Mavericks' cap flexibility still deserves recognition, which is why the return should not be described as completely worthless. Yet the Celtics received the more functional player for the needs of that season. Evaluating the July transaction separately from Richardson's earlier Mavericks year and from the subsequent Spurs deal produces a measured Boston-winning assessment.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win. Boston earns B+ because Josh Richardson provided useful guard and wing minutes before becoming part of a separate trade package later in the season. Dallas receives C+ for acquiring Moses Brown and flexibility through the transaction exception, but Brown never developed into a durable Mavericks rotation piece. Derrick White's eventual arrival came from another deal and isn't a direct July 2021 Dallas asset.

sections.heading: Atlanta Turned a Sign-and-Trade into a Defensive Addition
sections.body: Atlanta acquired Thabo Sefolosha through a July 2014 sign-and-trade with Oklahoma City, also receiving the rights to Giorgos Printezis and cash. The Thunder took the rights to Sofoklis Schortsanitis and a trade exception. This structure made the move more than a simple free-agent signature while leaving its actual basketball value heavily dependent on Sefolosha. The Hawks were building a lineup that could defend opposing wings and move the ball around multiple contributors. The Thunder accepted rights and roster flexibility after years of using Sefolosha as a starting-caliber perimeter defender.

sections.heading: Sefolosha Gave the Hawks Real Defensive Rotation Work
sections.body: Sefolosha joined an Atlanta team that won 60 games in 2014-15 and reached the Eastern Conference Finals. His perimeter defense and willingness to play without heavy shot volume complemented a group built around Jeff Teague, Paul Millsap and Al Horford. His season was interrupted by an off-court injury, limiting his playoff availability during that run, so he should not receive credit for playing in the conference finals he missed. But his earlier Hawks minutes and his subsequent seasons with Atlanta created a much longer receiving-team return than an unused international draft right.

sections.heading: The Thunder Acquired Rights Instead of an NBA Replacement
sections.body: Schortsanitis was a highly recognizable international center, yet holding his NBA rights did not produce an Oklahoma City rotation player who could directly replace Sefolosha. The trade exception offered the Thunder a separate avenue for managing the roster and later transactions, but should not be written up as an incoming player who already scored NBA points. Atlanta's Printezis rights and cash likewise contributed less to its on-court product than Sefolosha's signed contract. Keeping those categories distinct prevents an international rights exchange from appearing equal to an experienced wing who actually filled NBA minutes.

sections.heading: The Multi-Year Atlanta Wing Return Decides the Verdict
sections.body: Atlanta converted a complicated rights-and-cash package into a proven wing who could defend and occupy minutes for multiple seasons. Oklahoma City's compensation retained potential business utility, and a sign-and-trade can serve financial goals that aren't visible in a box score. Nonetheless, the Hawks had more direct basketball value from the transaction, especially given Sefolosha's contribution to a team that became a top seed in the East. This evaluation doesn't rely on claiming the Hawks acquired Schortsanitis or that an overseas career instantly became Thunder NBA production. The enduring playable wing makes Atlanta the winner.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win. Atlanta earns B+ because Thabo Sefolosha provided real defensive wing minutes across multiple seasons, beginning with the 60-win 2014-15 campaign. Oklahoma City receives C for Schortsanitis's international rights and trade-exception flexibility, which did not yield a comparable direct on-court player from the exchange. Printezis's rights and cash helped complete the Hawks' package, but Sefolosha's NBA contribution is the decisive difference.

sections.heading: Philadelphia Traded Two Picks to Reach Matisse Thybulle
sections.body: Philadelphia targeted Washington defender Matisse Thybulle in the 2019 draft and sent Boston the rights to No. 24 Ty Jerome and No. 33 Carsen Edwards for the No. 20 rights to Thybulle. The Sixers preferred an immediately usable defensive wing over two opportunities further down the board. Boston accepted a later first and an additional second, giving itself the choice to develop players or reroute one of the selections. Both teams were acquiring draft rights rather than an established NBA veteran, and the ultimate value depended on which rights became useful rotation work.

sections.heading: Thybulle Became a Recognized Defensive Specialist
sections.body: Thybulle spent multiple seasons with Philadelphia and established himself as a disruptive perimeter defender. He earned All-Defensive Second Team recognition, supplying steals, deflections and unusual recovery ability in a role that didn't demand high offensive usage. The Sixers could put him alongside their more prolific scorers and rely on his ball pressure. His limitations as a shooter affected how he was deployed, particularly in certain postseason matchups, but he played genuine rotation minutes over several years. That direct Philadelphia contribution gives the receiving team considerably more than a theoretical prospect or unused contract.

sections.heading: Boston's Rights Returned a Short-Term Reserve and Another Trade
sections.body: Carsen Edwards became a Celtics guard but did not establish a permanent rotation role before leaving Boston. Ty Jerome's draft rights had an even more complicated path: Boston forwarded them to Phoenix in a separate transaction rather than developing Jerome as a Celtic. His later work for the Suns and other teams therefore cannot be credited as Boston playing production from the Thybulle swap. The additional second-round opportunity was real draft value at the time, yet Edwards did not provide sustained contribution comparable to the defender Philadelphia acquired. Boston's short direct return is the decisive limitation.

sections.heading: The Defensive Contributor Outweighed the Two-Pick Package
sections.body: Boston's logic was defensible on draft night because two selections offer more chances to discover useful talent than one. The eventual returns did not justify giving up the player Philadelphia chose. Thybulle helped the Sixers over several seasons, while Edwards remained a modest reserve and Jerome was moved in another deal before suiting up in Boston. Philadelphia's win rests on the actual defensive specialist it used rather than pretending he became an elite two-way scorer. The Boston grade reflects missed opportunity, not a belief that having extra draft choices is inherently poor strategy.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: 76ers Win. Philadelphia earns B for Matisse Thybulle's years as an NBA rotation defender and his All-Defensive honors. Boston gets D because Carsen Edwards provided limited reserve value and Ty Jerome was moved again before he could produce Celtics playing minutes. Jerome's subsequent career at other clubs cannot be added to Boston's direct return from this June 2019 draft-rights exchange.

sections.heading: Boston Used Rodney Purvis to Reduce a Salary Obligation
sections.body: Boston sent Abdel Nader and $450,000 in cash to Oklahoma City on July 23, 2018, receiving Rodney Purvis in return. Purvis had a non-guaranteed contract, which made him a convenient way for the Celtics to move salary before their offseason obligations became more expensive. Oklahoma City took on a wing it believed could supply depth behind its established rotation. The deal therefore had two different aims: Boston wanted contract flexibility, while the Thunder were willing to give a roster spot to a player who had already seen NBA action with the Celtics.

sections.heading: Purvis Did Not Appear in a Celtics Game
sections.body: Boston waived Purvis on July 30, only a week after the trade. He never delivered regular-season playing time to the Celtics through this acquisition. His earlier minutes with Orlando are not Boston production, nor can the non-guaranteed contract be treated as a hidden scorer. The move still gave the Celtics a genuine financial advantage by avoiding more of Nader's guaranteed salary and associated tax exposure. That value explains the deal's logic without disguising the absence of an incoming Boston rotation contributor. The cash Boston sent was a distinct cost of obtaining the contract flexibility.

sections.heading: Nader Became a Playable Reserve for Oklahoma City
sections.body: Nader remained with Oklahoma City and played as a reserve wing during the following two seasons. His minutes weren't those of a franchise centerpiece, but the Thunder did receive an NBA player who could defend multiple perimeter positions and supply occasional outside scoring. That actual roster use contrasted sharply with Purvis's absence from Boston's lineup. Nader's 48 rookie appearances before July 2018 belonged to the Celtics and shouldn't be added to the Thunder side. His later work outside Oklahoma City also falls outside the direct receiving-franchise result being graded here.

sections.heading: The Distinct Team Objectives Explain Both Grades
sections.body: Oklahoma City obtained sustained rotation assistance from Nader and a cash payment, giving it more immediate basketball value. Boston achieved the salary and tax relief it sought, so a Celtics grade that recognizes financial utility remains reasonable despite receiving no games from Purvis. Both outcomes need to be kept visible instead of assigning all value to box-score totals or pretending the deal was purely a salary dump with no Thunder benefit. The edge belongs to Oklahoma City because it combined financial compensation with an actual reserve contributor across more than one campaign.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Oklahoma City Thunder Win. The Thunder earn B for adding Abdel Nader as a playable reserve over the next two seasons along with $450,000 in cash. Boston receives C+ for the salary and tax flexibility made possible by Rodney Purvis's non-guaranteed deal, although Purvis was waived without a Celtics appearance. The winner is determined by Nader's direct Thunder contributions while preserving Boston's financial motive.

sections.heading: Boston Swapped a Reserve Center for a Reserve Guard
sections.body: The October 17, 2014 agreement sent Joel Anthony to Detroit and Will Bynum to Boston. Detroit's announcement identified Anthony as an experienced depth center, while the Celtics had already built a crowded frontcourt around younger options. Bynum had played six previous seasons for the Pistons, but Boston wasn't buying that historical output as if it had happened in Massachusetts. The guard also arrived at a time when the Celtics were sorting through several backcourt candidates in training camp. The exchange offered both sides a way to rearrange minor roster commitments before the season began.

sections.heading: Bynum Never Supplied Regular-Season Celtics Minutes
sections.body: The Boston portion was especially brief. Bynum did not establish himself in the Celtics' regular-season guard rotation and was gone before an appearance that could be credited to this trade. His scoring records and assist totals in Detroit show why Boston might have considered a look, but none count as a contribution to the receiving franchise. This was a speculative preseason personnel move rather than a successful acquisition of immediate help. That distinction is important because a trade-history page can otherwise overstate the return by carrying over a player's entire career résumé.

sections.heading: Anthony Filled a Small but Measurable Detroit Role
sections.body: Anthony did play for Detroit. He appeared in 49 games during the 2014-15 season, averaging only 8.3 minutes and 1.8 points, with his more recognizable contribution coming from defense and shot blocking. The Pistons weren't getting the athletic Miami-era version of a championship reserve, but they could use him in spot frontcourt minutes. His 49 appearances are real receiving-team value, yet limited playing time keeps the outcome from becoming a substantial roster gain. Detroit also retained him briefly beyond that first season, without making him a central building block.

sections.heading: A Minor Personnel Transaction Deserves a Modest Assessment
sections.body: The deal didn't decide either team's season. Boston acquired flexibility in evaluating a guard but never extracted court time from Bynum. Detroit obtained a veteran center for emergency minutes, accepting a narrow rather than transformative basketball return. Both teams' C+ grades can be understood as reflecting a small preseason transaction with little financial or talent risk rather than equal numbers of NBA appearances. The on-court comparison leans Detroit, but the existing Even Trade verdict recognizes that neither side surrendered a foundation piece or gained a long-term starter.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Boston receives C+ because Will Bynum was a short-lived preseason acquisition rather than a regular-season contributor. Detroit also gets C+, with Joel Anthony appearing in 49 games in 2014-15 but producing only modest reserve numbers. The Pistons got more direct minutes, while the overall consequences were too small to treat the swap as a decisive franchise win.

sections.heading: Boston Moved a Veteran Guard for a Familiar Name
sections.body: On January 13, 2015, the Celtics shipped Jameer Nelson to Denver and received Nate Robinson, who had already played in Boston earlier in his career. Nelson had joined the Celtics only weeks before in a separate trade and was not firmly established in their evolving guard rotation. Robinson brought prior familiarity with the franchise, but he was not acquired as a future franchise cornerstone. Both organizations were managing veteran contracts in a season of roster turnover, making the immediate practical value dependent on whether either newcomer would actually remain with the team.

sections.heading: Robinson's Second Boston Stint Produced No New Games
sections.body: Robinson's earlier Celtics performances were real, but they belonged to a different tenure several seasons before this exchange. Boston waived him shortly after the January deal, without a regular-season appearance during his return. That means the receiving-side basketball payoff was negligible. His previous Denver production also cannot be transferred retroactively to Boston. The Celtics' opportunity was principally to manage the rotation and contract commitments, not to obtain a guard who played a meaningful second stretch in green. A trade assessment should not combine his first Boston spell with this aborted comeback.

sections.heading: Nelson Gave Denver Useful Veteran Guard Minutes
sections.body: Denver retained Nelson and used him as a veteran ball handler beyond the initial 2014-15 campaign. His passing, experience and occasional outside scoring supplied stability for a developing backcourt, and he remained involved through parts of multiple Nuggets seasons. He wasn't a replacement for an All-NBA star, but the team received real games and rotation work where Boston got none from its incoming guard. Any Nelson appearances with Orlando or Dallas before January 2015 are separate from this value. His Denver tenure is the meaningful receiving-team result of the transaction.

sections.heading: The Nominal Tie Masks Unequal Actual Playing Value
sections.body: Denver's actual on-court payoff was much stronger, but this still was a low-cost exchange of veteran guards during a complicated Celtics roster reset. The Celtics had reasons to free a spot or facilitate further moves, even though Robinson never helped them win a game after this transaction. The canonical Even Trade verdict and matching C+ grades should therefore be read as a restrained historical assessment, not as a claim that Robinson and Nelson logged equivalent minutes with their new teams. Denver benefited most in basketball terms without making the trade pivotal to either franchise.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Boston receives C+ for a low-stakes roster reshuffle, but Nate Robinson never supplied another Celtics game after the deal. Denver also receives C+ in the canonical evaluation, despite obtaining significantly more direct value from Jameer Nelson's multi-season reserve and starting minutes. This is an ordinary veteran transaction with a real Denver playing edge, not a major asset transfer.

sections.heading: Miami Brought Back a Familiar Shooting Forward
sections.body: The February 8, 2018 deal sent Luke Babbitt from Atlanta to Miami and Okaro White the other way. Babbitt had played for the Heat in the previous season, so the club knew what kind of spacing it could expect from him. Miami wanted another forward willing to take open perimeter shots with injuries testing its rotation. Atlanta's motive was different: the Hawks were reworking a rebuilding roster and weren't necessarily seeking immediate production from White. The two players' recent résumés gave each club a reason to exchange rather than retain its original forward.

sections.heading: Atlanta Waived White Instead of Using Him
sections.body: White's time on the Hawks' roster effectively ended when it began. Atlanta waived him on February 8, the same date the transaction was completed, so no regular-season Hawks appearances resulted from the acquisition. His earlier time with Miami and in its development system is not Atlanta playing value. The decision may have helped manage a roster spot and available contracts, but those benefits should be described honestly instead of treated as rebounds or defensive minutes that never occurred. The receiving player did not become a piece of the Hawks' on-court rebuilding effort.

sections.heading: Babbitt Returned as a Narrow but Usable Miami Option
sections.body: The Heat brought back a specialist rather than a foundational starter. Babbitt's willingness to shoot from outside could help when Miami required spacing around its primary ball handlers, though his defensive limitations restricted his value. He was familiar with the organization and had been playing for Atlanta before the deal, averaging 6.1 points in 37 Hawks games that season. Those Atlanta games belong to the Hawks' outgoing résumé; only his subsequent Miami time counts as incoming Heat production. Even a short spell of actual rotation depth outperformed Atlanta's nonexistent White playing return.

sections.heading: The Outcome Favors Miami Without Rewriting the Trade's Scale
sections.body: Miami got the player it wanted for an identifiable tactical reason, and Atlanta did not convert White into on-court help. The difference is enough for the Heat edge, but it doesn't merit a claim that Babbitt transformed Miami's competitive standing. His value was situational, tied to perimeter spacing and limited reserve minutes. Atlanta's move should instead be understood as a roster decision during a rebuilding season. Distinguishing those purposes produces a fair comparison rather than assigning star-level importance to a minor deadline exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Heat Edge. Miami earns B- for bringing Luke Babbitt back as a perimeter-shooting option, while Atlanta gets C+ because Okaro White was waived immediately and played no games for the Hawks. The Heat received the only tangible on-court return, although Babbitt's contribution remained limited reserve support rather than a decisive roster upgrade.

sections.heading: Two Guards Went Opposite Ways at the Deadline
sections.body: Memphis announced the acquisition of Tyler Dorsey from Atlanta on February 7, 2019, in exchange for veteran Shelvin Mack. The Grizzlies could give a younger shooting guard a longer look during their transition, while the Hawks were already arranging a rotation around rookie Trae Young. Mack wasn't a stranger to Atlanta: he had previously played for the franchise and could theoretically provide experienced guard depth. The transactions were modest compared with the deadline's major deals, but they still affected which player each team had under contract heading into the season's final weeks.

sections.heading: The Hawks Declined to Keep Mack
sections.body: Atlanta didn't retain Mack for a second extended stint. It waived him on February 8, one day after the trade, and he subsequently joined another team. Those later appearances cannot be counted as part of the Hawks' return, nor can the 172 Atlanta games from his earlier tenure. Instead, the exchange helped Atlanta exit Dorsey's roster obligation while it explored other personnel options. Any assessment based on Mack's earlier assists or scoring for Memphis would confuse the outgoing résumé with the incoming contribution. The new Hawks stint produced no sustained basketball minutes.

sections.heading: Dorsey Had a Real Receiving-Team Opportunity in Memphis
sections.body: Dorsey moved into a Grizzlies environment that needed young guards to prove themselves. The official release noted his first 83 NBA appearances with Atlanta, which informed Memphis's decision but weren't yet Grizzlies output. After the deadline he played for Memphis and could supply scoring from a reserve role. His connection with former Oregon teammate Dillon Brooks gave the club another familiar developmental pairing. Even if Dorsey didn't become a long-term Memphis starter, the team obtained playable depth, unlike Atlanta's very short experience with Mack following the exchange.

sections.heading: This Modest Swap Did Not Change Either Franchise's Future
sections.body: The trade gave Memphis a usable audition for a young player and let Atlanta proceed with its backcourt reset. Neither incoming guard became a defining piece of his receiving franchise, and both teams were operating within ordinary deadline roster constraints. The canonical Even Trade verdict and identical B- grades reflect that limited overall importance rather than identical minutes played. The real court-time comparison favors Memphis, while Atlanta's practical motivation involved clearing a place in a roster increasingly built for the next phase.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Even Trade. Atlanta receives B- for the low-stakes decision to exchange Tyler Dorsey, although Shelvin Mack was waived a day later without establishing a new Hawks role. Memphis also earns B-, gaining a young guard it could use for the final portion of the season. The Grizzlies obtained more direct playing value; neither club acquired a durable core player.

sections.heading: Golden State Bought the Forty-First Selection
sections.body: Ahead of the June 20, 2019 draft, the Warriors secured pick No. 41 from Atlanta by offering $1.3 million in cash and a 2024 second-rounder. The Hawks were collecting future assets while reshaping a roster full of draft choices, whereas Golden State wanted another prospect immediately. The agreement didn't guarantee which player the Warriors would select, and the future pick wasn't a present-day rotation player for Atlanta. The teams made opposite calculations about time: Golden State paid to act in 2019, while the Hawks accepted a distant chance and the immediate money.

sections.heading: Paschall Supplied an Unusually Productive Rookie Return
sections.body: Golden State used No. 41 to draft Villanova forward Eric Paschall. Injuries and roster turnover created playing time for him in 2019-20, and he averaged 14.0 points and 4.6 rebounds in 60 games. He was selected to the NBA All-Rookie First Team, an unusually strong opening outcome for a mid-second-round selection. That performance is a concrete Warriors return created by the purchased pick, not a projected value assigned to whoever Atlanta might have picked. Paschall's later career was shorter than his rookie promise, but the original receiving franchise benefited immediately.

sections.heading: Atlanta's Cash and Deferred Draft Right Were Different Assets
sections.body: The Hawks received a meaningful cash payment and a second-round choice five years in the future. The pick eventually resolved at No. 44 in 2024, associated with Pelle Larsson in the draft's rights history. That doesn't prove Larsson's subsequent NBA career was played for Atlanta; the selection's later movements need to be treated independently. The financial return and future optionality did have value, yet neither delivered the same kind of direct immediate player production as Paschall's first Warriors season. Atlanta accepted that timing trade-off deliberately rather than misplacing a prospect already on its roster.

sections.heading: The Outcome Shows Why Second-Round Picks Can Be Valuable
sections.body: The Warriors found a real contributor and award-winning rookie with an acquired second-round choice, validating their willingness to pay an added cash cost. Atlanta's return offered money and another future selection but less measurable on-court output from this precise transaction. Paschall never became an enduring franchise cornerstone, so the trade should not be exaggerated into a dynasty-making acquisition. Nevertheless, sixty rookie appearances and 14 points a night constitute a more tangible payoff than most purchased second-round picks yield. The Golden State edge is grounded in his receiving-team performance.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Warriors Win. Golden State earns C+ for purchasing the pick used on Eric Paschall, who averaged 14.0 points over 60 games and reached the All-Rookie First Team. Atlanta gets C- for $1.3 million and a future second-round choice that ultimately became the No. 44 selection in 2024. That draft asset had its own later routing, but it didn't match Paschall's immediate Warriors contribution.

sections.heading: Atlanta Moved Back Seven Picks and Took Cash
sections.body: The Hawks used the 2022 draft to exchange the rights to No. 44 Ryan Rollins for the rights to No. 51 Tyrese Martin and cash from Golden State. The deal was struck on June 23 and described in Atlanta's early-June-24 draft release. Both players were college guards, with Rollins offering a scoring profile and Martin bringing rebounding and physicality from the wing. Golden State spent cash to choose earlier; Atlanta accepted a later pick and financial compensation. Neither party was acquiring an established NBA starter at this stage of the draft.

sections.heading: Martin Received a Short Hawks Audition
sections.body: Martin appeared in 16 regular-season games for the Hawks in 2022-23, playing only a small number of minutes. His strongest work came as a developmental prospect rather than a consistent Atlanta rotation contributor. The receiving club nonetheless got an actual player it could evaluate in NBA competition, plus the cash included in the draft-rights exchange. Martin's 16 appearances shouldn't be inflated into a long-term solution at the wing. The value of the move for Atlanta rests as much on extracting a cash return from the small move down as on the immediate performance of its second-round selection.

sections.heading: Rollins Had Twelve Warriors Games Before Surgery
sections.body: Golden State signed Rollins and gave him a limited NBA opportunity, but he played only 12 regular-season games as a rookie before undergoing foot surgery. He averaged 1.9 points in 5.2 minutes across those appearances. Those numbers document a genuine, though very small, Warriors return. His subsequent moves and later play for Milwaukee cannot be counted toward Golden State's original 2022 transaction. The Warriors paid to choose earlier in the second round but did not receive an enduring rotation guard from the pick while he was with that franchise.

sections.heading: Cash Made the Hawks' Return More Reliable
sections.body: The two guards produced comparably brief first-franchise playing résumés, so this deal is more about the additional consideration and what each team hoped to develop. Atlanta received Martin and cash for dropping seven positions, while Golden State assumed the downside of paying to move up for Rollins. The Hawks' return was modest but included value that did not depend on the guard becoming a regular. The Warriors' acquisition didn't yield much on-court help. That contrast supports the configured Hawks advantage without claiming either player became a franchise-changing prospect in his receiving city.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win. Atlanta earns B for extracting cash and the rights to Tyrese Martin while moving seven spots down; Martin appeared in 16 Hawks games. Golden State receives D because Ryan Rollins logged only 12 brief Warriors appearances before injury interrupted his rookie season. Later production with other franchises is outside this trade's receiving-team return, leaving Atlanta with the sturdier package.

sections.heading: New York Added Fournier in a Sign-and-Trade
sections.body: New York completed a deal with Boston on August 17, 2021, to bring in Evan Fournier after agreeing to terms with the free-agent guard. The transaction also directed a conditional 2022 second-round selection and a separate 2023 second-round right toward the Knicks. Boston received cash and created a trade exception rather than taking back another established guard. Fournier had provided shooting and secondary creation during a brief Celtics spell the previous spring. The Knicks sought to make him a fuller part of their offense as they tried to build on a playoff appearance.

sections.heading: Fournier Supplied a Full First Season in New York
sections.body: Fournier started all 80 games in which he appeared for the Knicks in 2021-22 and averaged 14.1 points while shooting 38.9 percent from three. Those figures provide an unmistakable receiving-team basketball return. He could space the floor and generate occasional offense, even though the team didn't achieve the consistent improvement hoped for from its new perimeter combination. His role contracted markedly in later seasons, limiting the longer-term success of the contract. Still, the first season alone gave New York far more court time than Boston obtained from the cash consideration in this particular exchange.

sections.heading: Boston Got Flexibility, Not a Replacement Shooter
sections.body: The Celtics' direct listed compensation was cash, with a trade exception arising from the sign-and-trade structure. That flexibility could support later roster planning, but it is not another player who logged NBA appearances on the date of this exchange. Boston also parted with draft assets alongside Fournier. The protected 2022 component did not convey in its initial form, while the later second was associated with No. 41 in 2023, ultimately used on Amari Bailey. Treating Bailey's career as a Boston return would reverse the direction of that outgoing right.

sections.heading: A Real Knicks Shooting Season Outweighs the Contract Drawbacks
sections.body: The signing proved less durable than New York initially hoped, and Fournier eventually fell out of the regular rotation. His contract also created an opportunity cost as the Knicks revised their backcourt. Nevertheless, the transaction delivered a full starting season and a high volume of made threes for the club that actually received him. Boston made a logical cap-management choice after Fournier's short stay, but its compensation did not replace those Knicks minutes. The trade's on-court value goes to New York, tempered by the later decline of his role.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Knicks Win. New York earns B because Evan Fournier started 80 games and averaged 14.1 points in 2021-22, even though the contract's long-term value faded. Boston receives C+ for cash and sign-and-trade flexibility while sending conditional second-round rights away. The 2023 pick ultimately associated with Amari Bailey was an outgoing asset, not a Celtics player return.

sections.heading: Boston Turned Two Second-Round Rights Into a Future First
sections.body: In the 2016 NBA Draft, Boston selected Deyonta Davis at No. 31 and Rade Zagorac at No. 35, then sent both sets of draft rights to Memphis. The Celtics received a protected future first-round selection, seeking a potentially more valuable future pick rather than retaining both young prospects. Memphis wanted Davis badly enough to trade the protected first and could also explore Zagorac as an international option. The exchange was a wager on the relative value of timing and pick position, with Boston choosing to consolidate two second-round opportunities into one later, higher-round asset.

sections.heading: Memphis Actually Signed Davis and Used Him
sections.body: Memphis signed Davis in July 2016, giving him regular-season playing opportunities over the following two seasons. His role was primarily developmental: he provided size and occasional shot blocking but never established himself as a dependable starting center. Zagorac's overseas experience offered another possible route to future talent, though it did not translate into a stable Grizzlies NBA career. The receiving-team result wasn't zero, because Davis did play in Memphis. But two second-round acquisitions failed to become the kind of core depth that would erase the value of giving up a future first-round choice.

sections.heading: The Protected First Eventually Landed at No. 20
sections.body: The future first conveyed as the No. 20 selection in the 2019 draft. That was the pick used on Matisse Thybulle, but he shouldn't be listed as a Celtics rotation player from this transaction. Boston dealt his rights to Philadelphia in a separate draft-night exchange, taking a different group of picks back. The distinction is essential: this 2016 trade gave the Celtics a first-round asset they could spend, not Thybulle's subsequent defensive production for the Sixers. The ability to move that right again is the concrete outcome of Boston's multi-year asset strategy.

sections.heading: A First-Round Asset Outweighed Two Incomplete Development Bets
sections.body: Boston's side is best evaluated by the future pick's draft position and trade utility. It turned two selections early in the second round into a pick in the top twenty in 2019, a meaningful upgrade in flexibility. Memphis, meanwhile, received a young center that actually appeared but didn't achieve a lasting frontcourt breakthrough, plus rights to a prospect whose NBA future remained uncertain. This is not a judgment that second-round picks are always less useful; Davis had genuine opportunities. The outcome nevertheless supports Boston's stronger grade on the value of the eventual asset.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win. Boston earns B+ for converting the rights to Deyonta Davis and Rade Zagorac into a future first that landed at No. 20 in 2019 and became useful draft-night trade capital. Memphis receives C- for Davis's limited NBA tenure and Zagorac's undeveloped rights. Thybulle's later NBA production came in Philadelphia, so it cannot be counted as a direct Celtics playing return.

sections.heading: Atlanta Acquired a Center and a Distant Second
sections.body: The Hawks acquired Damian Jones and a 2026 second-round pick from Golden State on July 8, 2019, sending Omari Spellman to the Warriors. Jones had won championship rings as part of Golden State's earlier roster, but Atlanta was interested in his ability to fill minutes at center rather than taking credit for those rings. Spellman, a recent first-rounder, offered Golden State a young big who could stretch the floor. The additional future second gave Atlanta more value than a direct player swap on paper, although the pick's eventual conveyance and use must be tracked separately from the players.

sections.heading: Jones Became a Regular Hawks Rotation Option
sections.body: Jones appeared in 55 Atlanta games during the 2019-20 season, averaging 5.6 points and 3.7 rebounds. He wasn't a foundational center, but he provided genuine size and finishing around the basket for a rebuilding club. That season is the appropriate window for measuring the player Atlanta received: his earlier Warriors games and championship history are background, not part of the Hawks' direct on-court return. The team could try him alongside younger guards and assess whether his athletic tools justified a longer commitment. Even without a breakout, 55 appearances produced tangible short-term utility.

sections.heading: Spellman Played for Golden State During a Difficult Year
sections.body: Golden State also received real on-court minutes from its incoming player. Spellman appeared across the injury-hit 2019-20 Warriors campaign and showed some ability to hit outside shots from a frontcourt position. His time there ended in another transaction, so he wasn't an enduring piece of the team as its established stars returned. The contrast with Jones isn't a win-by-default argument: both teams used their acquired players. Atlanta's extra second-round obligation tipped the package toward greater overall flexibility, while the Warriors mainly received a brief developmental audition for Spellman.

sections.heading: The Second-Round Asset Breaks a Modest Player Comparison
sections.body: This is a smaller deal whose player returns were measured in reserve minutes rather than postseason star power. Jones gave Atlanta solid but replaceable center depth; Spellman likewise contributed in Golden State without turning into a lasting rotation answer. The Hawks received an additional 2026 pick that might be used in later draft or trade planning. Its value shouldn't be inflated by an unverified future outcome. Atlanta's slight edge reflects a comparable short-term player plus an extra asset, not an assertion that either newcomer permanently changed the receiving club's competitive fortunes.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Hawks Edge. Atlanta receives B- for Damian Jones's 55 appearances and a 2026 second-round pick, giving it both usable center minutes and another asset. Golden State earns C+ because Omari Spellman played during 2019-20 but did not become a lasting Warriors frontcourt option. Both teams got real short-term NBA contributions, with the added selection tilting the package toward the Hawks.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Traded Patterson's Draft Rights for a Future Second
sections.body: The Bucks used No. 48 in the 2014 draft on Lamar Patterson but moved his rights to Atlanta in return for a 2015 second-round selection. Milwaukee preferred future flexibility instead of holding Patterson's rights while deciding whether to bring him over. Atlanta took a developmental wing with college scoring and passing skills, betting that a low second-round choice could become a usable reserve. The recorded trade date follows the draft-night rights activity, and the precise player and pick directions matter because the 2015 selection did not remain in Milwaukee's possession indefinitely.

sections.heading: Patterson Eventually Played Thirty-Five Hawks Games
sections.body: Patterson appeared in 35 regular-season games for Atlanta in 2015-16, averaging 2.4 points in a small role, and also saw brief playoff action. The Hawks therefore obtained an actual player from the rights they acquired, although he never became the kind of durable wing who could reshape the rotation. His Atlanta contribution took time to arrive, reflecting the gap between acquiring rights and using the player on an NBA roster. Thirty-five games were real value from a late second-round swing, but the minutes and production don't support treating the pick as a major talent discovery.

sections.heading: Milwaukee Used the Future Pick in a Different Deal
sections.body: The Bucks traded their incoming 2015 second-round pick onward with another selection in the transaction that brought Jason Kidd to Milwaukee as head coach. The pick eventually became No. 41 in 2015, associated with Pat Connaughton, but it would be misleading to claim this 2014 Hawks exchange directly supplied Connaughton as a Bucks player. His eventual return to Milwaukee came through a later free-agent signing. The draft right's role as part of a subsequent coaching transaction is the actual utility Milwaukee obtained from this original deal. Pick provenance matters more here than a later name in the ledger.

sections.heading: The Verdict Depends on Asset Use, Not Retroactive Player Credit
sections.body: Milwaukee's grade recognizes that the future second became movable draft inventory in an important organizational transaction. Atlanta secured a reserve with modest NBA appearances, not a lasting starter. Neither side should receive an invented multi-season Connaughton playing return from the 2014 rights swap; those later events involved other transactions and contractual decisions. The Bucks' decision to move Patterson's rights offered them flexibility as they assembled a new coaching and roster plan. Atlanta got a usable but limited prospect, supporting a measured rather than definitive victory analysis.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Bucks Win. Milwaukee earns A for the 2015 second-round asset it subsequently used in a separate transaction associated with hiring Jason Kidd; Atlanta receives C- for Lamar Patterson's 35 regular-season games and limited development as a Hawks reserve. The 2015 pick later carried Pat Connaughton's draft identity, but his eventual Bucks career began through free agency and must not be attributed directly to this rights trade.

sections.heading: Danny Ferry Reassigned an Established Frontcourt Contract
sections.body: The Hawks sent Marvin Williams to Utah for Devin Harris in July 2012 as part of their new front office's effort to alter an expensive roster. Williams had spent seven seasons with Atlanta after being picked second in the 2005 draft, but his production hadn't matched that draft position. Harris gave the club an experienced ball handler on a shorter contractual horizon. This was a direct swap, separate from the much larger Joe Johnson transaction announced during the same period. Atlanta wanted more room to redesign the team rather than continuing with its former starting small forward.

sections.heading: Harris Played a Useful One-Season Atlanta Role
sections.body: Harris joined Jeff Teague in the Hawks' backcourt during 2012-13, providing secondary scoring, playmaking and a second experienced guard in varying lineups. He appeared in the postseason as Atlanta faced Indiana in the first round. The contribution wasn't franchise-defining, and Harris departed after the season, but it satisfied the need for immediate guard depth while the Hawks evaluated the shape of their next roster. The club didn't acquire an All-Star version of Harris from his earlier New Jersey years; its value came from what he actually provided in Atlanta.

sections.heading: Utah Got a Familiar Wing Without a Major Breakthrough
sections.body: Williams gave the Jazz more size and versatility on the wing, playing in Utah across the next two seasons. His role differed from the heavy expectations of his Atlanta draft history: he could handle forward assignments and finish possessions without demanding the offense be organized around him. The Jazz didn't suddenly acquire a perennial twenty-point scorer. Utah's receiving-team output was genuine, but it also inherited the remaining financial commitment attached to a player whose ceiling had already become clearer. That made the exchange defensible without handing the Jazz the stronger overall value.

sections.heading: Contract Timing Tilted the Comparison Toward Atlanta
sections.body: Atlanta converted Williams's longer commitment into a serviceable guard and reached the summer of 2013 with greater ability to adjust its personnel. Utah got forward minutes but less opportunity to reset its roster immediately. Harris wasn't a perfect long-term solution for the Hawks, yet he filled the desired position during a playoff season. The verdict therefore turns on Atlanta's combination of playing value and flexibility, not on Williams being unusable or Harris reproducing his peak earlier-career statistics. Both incoming veterans helped, but their contracts led the teams in different directions.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win. Atlanta receives B- for Devin Harris's playable 2012-13 guard season and the shorter commitment it acquired by moving Marvin Williams. Utah earns C because Williams provided real forward minutes across two seasons but didn't unlock comparable roster flexibility. This was a modest, rational personnel change, with the Hawks getting the more useful combination of role and contract timing.

sections.heading: Atlanta Acquired an Elite Shooter for Financial Consideration
sections.body: Chicago sent Kyle Korver to Atlanta on July 16, 2012, receiving cash and a trade exception instead of a player in return. The Bulls were managing their salary obligations, while the Hawks saw a chance to obtain a proven three-point specialist without surrendering a draft choice or established member of their rotation. Korver had already supplied two reliable shooting seasons in Chicago. The deal also aligned with Atlanta's broader summer of roster changes, but its compensation must be kept distinct from the separate Devin Harris and Joe Johnson trades.

sections.heading: Korver Became a Building Block for a Sixty-Win Offense
sections.body: Korver's value in Atlanta went beyond occasional bench shooting. He became one of the defining floor spacers in coach Mike Budenholzer's motion offense, forcing defenders to track his off-ball movement and opening driving lanes for teammates. In 2014-15, he shot nearly fifty percent from three, earned an All-Star selection and helped the Hawks win sixty regular-season games. His presence was fundamental to how that roster created good looks without relying exclusively on one isolation scorer. That extended Atlanta return made the original price strikingly small.

sections.heading: Chicago Obtained Savings Rather Than Replacing His Production
sections.body: The Bulls' return served financial and roster-planning purposes. A trade exception could assist with a future signing or transaction subject to its rules, and the cash created immediate value, but neither asset directly replaced Korver's shooting on the court. Chicago still had a strong core and its own guards and forwards, so dealing a specialist was defensible in the context of payroll decisions. What the club didn't get was another reliable wing with Korver's accuracy and movement. The difference in direct basketball output grew as Korver thrived in Atlanta.

sections.heading: The Long-Term Hawks Payoff Made the Outcome Decisive
sections.body: The Hawks received several seasons of elite perimeter spacing, not a short-term rental. Korver became an emblem of a collective offense and a crucial part of one of the franchise's best regular seasons. Chicago acquired budget tools whose utility shouldn't be treated as nonexistent, but the gap between those tools and an All-Star shooting campaign is substantial. Atlanta achieved exactly what a smart low-cost veteran acquisition should: it found a skill that fit its system, retained it through multiple seasons and received far more competitive value than the nominal outgoing compensation implied.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win. Atlanta earns A+ for Kyle Korver's multi-season shooting impact, 2015 All-Star selection and essential role on a sixty-win team. Chicago receives D because its cash and trade exception addressed financial priorities without supplying a comparable on-court replacement. Few minor veteran trades gave the receiving franchise such an enduring and productive fit.

sections.heading: Boston Exchanged Two Veterans for Crawford's Scoring
sections.body: The Celtics acquired Jordan Crawford from Washington at the February 21, 2013 deadline, sending Jason Collins and Leandro Barbosa to the Wizards. Barbosa had suffered a season-ending ACL injury before the trade, leaving Washington with little chance of immediately replacing Crawford's offense through him. Collins was an experienced reserve center rather than a high-volume scorer. Boston had been dealing with injury-related holes in its backcourt and wanted another player capable of creating a shot without depending entirely on its established veterans.

sections.heading: Crawford Offered Scoring and Later Trade Utility
sections.body: Crawford could handle the ball and make difficult shots, sometimes at the expense of offensive efficiency. Boston used him through the final part of 2012-13 and into the following season, when his role expanded during the club's transition after its veteran core broke up. He didn't become the Celtics' long-term starting guard, but they were able to use him in competitive games and later include him in another transaction. That was considerably more basketball utility than Boston could have expected from retaining an injured Barbosa and a seldom-used Collins.

sections.heading: Washington's Return Didn't Deliver Much Immediate Offense
sections.body: Washington had its own reason for moving Crawford: his shot-first approach no longer fit the guard rotation as John Wall returned from injury. Collins could add situational size and veteran guidance, but he was not acquired to replace the outgoing guard's points. Barbosa remained unavailable to play because of his knee injury, making his receiving-team production effectively zero. The trade helped the Wizards shift their roster structure and priorities, yet their return was weaker in terms of active contributors than the one Boston obtained.

sections.heading: The Specific Player Situations Explain the Grade Gap
sections.body: A transaction involving two veterans for one scorer may look balanced by head count, but the context of those contracts changes the analysis. One Washington arrival was injured for the season; the other had a narrow reserve role. Boston actually obtained usable perimeter offense and held Crawford as an asset for later maneuvering. This wasn't a franchise-changing trade, and Crawford's inconsistent shot selection came with costs. Still, the Celtics received the clearer combination of playing minutes and future flexibility, supporting the verdict without overstating the player's ceiling.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win. Boston earns B+ for acquiring Jordan Crawford, whose scoring and subsequent trade utility helped a backcourt facing injuries and transition. Washington receives C for Jason Collins's limited reserve value and Leandro Barbosa's inability to play after his ACL injury. The Wizards achieved a roster reset, but the Celtics obtained the stronger direct player return.

sections.heading: Boston Found a Scorer at the Deadline
sections.body: The Celtics acquired Isaiah Thomas from Phoenix on February 19, 2015, sending guard Marcus Thornton and a protected 2016 first-round selection that Boston had previously obtained from Cleveland. Thomas had been one of several guards competing for roles in Phoenix, while the Celtics sought an offensive creator for Brad Stevens's developing group. Boston wasn't receiving the older All-Star version of a declining veteran. It was taking a chance on a still-productive guard whose scoring instincts had not yet found a permanent home with a playoff contender.

sections.heading: Thomas Became the Center of Boston's Offense
sections.body: Thomas gave Boston the late-game shot creation it lacked and developed into the club's leading scorer. He earned consecutive All-Star appearances in 2016 and 2017, finished fifth in the 2017 MVP vote and helped the Celtics reach the Eastern Conference Finals. His fourth-quarter scoring earned him the King of the Fourth reputation and made a relatively modest deadline acquisition unusually memorable. The club's eventual decision to move Thomas in another major deal did not erase what it had received in the interim. These achievements belong to his Celtics tenure.

sections.heading: Phoenix Took a Guard and a Future Draft Right
sections.body: Thornton was a veteran scoring guard who could play immediately, but his Phoenix stint did not become a multi-year foundation. The protected first-round selection eventually conveyed as No. 28 in 2016, a pick later associated with Skal Labissiere in the draft's transaction history. That rights path is distinct from whether the Suns directly developed Labissiere. The deal gave Phoenix something tangible for a guard squeezed into a crowded rotation, but the return never approached the All-Star-level production Thomas provided after moving to Boston.

sections.heading: The Scoring Peak Makes the Winner Unambiguous
sections.body: Boston obtained an elite offensive season and a deep postseason run for the price of a reserve guard and a later first-round choice. Thomas's height was a persistent defensive challenge and his physical situation became complicated near the end of his stay, but those costs don't cancel out what he accomplished. Phoenix made an understandable guard-allocation decision during the transaction window, yet its compensation offered less comparable upside. This is a clear Celtics win rooted in Thomas's on-court Boston career rather than his fame before or after the exchange.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Celtics Win. Boston earns A+ for turning Marcus Thornton and a future first-rounder into Isaiah Thomas, a two-time Celtics All-Star who carried elite scoring responsibility during the 2017 conference-finals run. Phoenix receives D because Thornton and the conveyed selection produced far less realized return. The value is based on Thomas's remarkable Boston peak, not on unrelated later stops.

sections.heading: The Hawks and Blazers Exchanged Veteran Wings
sections.body: Atlanta acquired Evan Turner from Portland on June 24, 2019, sending Kent Bazemore to the Trail Blazers. Both veterans had been playing meaningful roles in their old cities, but their skills differed. Turner preferred to initiate secondary offense, rebound and move the ball, while Bazemore supplied catch-and-shoot potential and defensive activity. Atlanta was beginning a youth-oriented roster transition and could evaluate a different kind of veteran. Portland wanted wing help after a Western Conference Finals season. The agreement contained no direct new draft choice in this two-player exchange.

sections.heading: Turner Played Only a Short Atlanta Stretch
sections.body: Turner had previously been useful as a ball-handling reserve in Portland, but his Atlanta role didn't develop into a season-long rotation fixture. He appeared in only 19 Hawks games in 2019-20 before becoming part of a different multi-team transaction. The Hawks therefore got limited actual court value despite the intention of giving their young group a veteran passer. His earlier 73 games for the Blazers are the outgoing player's background, not part of his new Atlanta return. The transaction was more about short-term experimentation than creating a core piece.

sections.heading: Bazemore's Portland Stay Was Also Brief
sections.body: Bazemore moved to a Trail Blazers roster that needed reliable wing bodies. He played 43 games for Portland during 2019-20 before the team traded him again as its personnel needs shifted. His long Atlanta record, including 355 games and a visible community role, explains why the Hawks valued him but must not be credited as Portland production. In his new city he provided minutes and some defense, though his offensive efficiency failed to lift the team in the way hoped. Portland's return was real, yet it too lasted only part of a campaign.

sections.heading: Neither Veteran Turned the Deal Into a Lasting Upgrade
sections.body: Atlanta received fewer games than Portland did from its incoming player, but Turner's expiring-contract utility and ball-handling role gave the Hawks a different kind of option while rebuilding. Portland added a wing it could use immediately and subsequently moved again. The canonical slight Hawks edge is therefore not an argument that Turner outperformed Bazemore on the court. Instead, it reflects the Hawks' strategic reset and financial timetable. Both organizations ultimately treated the acquired players as movable short-term pieces rather than foundations for future seasons.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Slight Hawks Edge. Atlanta gets B- because Evan Turner fitted its short-term contract and roster-planning approach, although he played only 19 Hawks games. Portland receives C+ for Kent Bazemore's 43 appearances before another trade. The Blazers obtained more direct minutes, but neither veteran became an enduring difference-maker, leaving this a narrow overall judgment.

sections.heading: The Raptors Obtained a Scoring Guard and Center Prospect
sections.body: Toronto acquired Lou Williams and the rights to Lucas Nogueira from Atlanta on June 30, 2014, while sending the Hawks veteran John Salmons and a 2015 second-round choice. Williams offered precisely the type of second-unit scoring that Toronto needed beside Kyle Lowry and DeMar DeRozan. Nogueira, meanwhile, gave the franchise a developmental center whose rights could be held and evaluated over multiple seasons. Atlanta was rearranging its roster around a different mix of guards and forwards, with Salmons and future draft compensation providing flexibility rather than an immediate replacement for Williams's shot creation.

sections.heading: Williams Delivered an Award-Winning Toronto Season
sections.body: Williams flourished as a reserve scorer with Toronto in 2014-15, providing instant offense and winning the NBA Sixth Man of the Year award. The Raptors reached the playoffs, and the veteran guard's offensive bursts were important when the starting unit needed relief. The successful season didn't turn into a lengthy Williams tenure in Toronto; he left in free agency afterward. Even so, the award and his contribution were concrete returns for the team that received him, unlike estimates based on earlier Atlanta statistics. Toronto acquired a player whose particular skill fitted an immediate roster need.

sections.heading: Nogueira Added Depth While Atlanta Released Salmons
sections.body: Nogueira eventually appeared in Raptors games and remained an athletic reserve with rim-protection potential. His offensive limitations prevented a major breakout, yet his multi-year presence added value beyond the Williams rental. Salmons, Atlanta's incoming veteran, did not become a Hawks rotation fixture because the club waived him soon after the transaction. The second-round pick ultimately associated with Marcus Eriksson supplied a future asset, but that draft identity must be distinguished from any NBA games actually played for Atlanta. The player return was far more compelling on Toronto's side.

sections.heading: The Bench-Scoring Payoff Justified the Deal
sections.body: Toronto acquired a Sixth Man of the Year and a prospective reserve center for a player the Hawks did not retain and a later second-round selection. That is a strong basketball outcome for the Raptors even though the team did not enjoy a deep playoff run that spring. Atlanta's financial flexibility and extra draft right had some utility, but neither replaced Williams's production. The contrast also explains why this should be evaluated as a Toronto win rather than a mutually beneficial short-term reshuffle with equal court contributions. The key outcomes were rooted in the receiving franchises.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Raptors Win. Toronto earns A- for Lou Williams's Sixth Man of the Year season and the additional development opportunity with Lucas Nogueira. Atlanta gets C- for John Salmons, whom it waived, and a 2015 second-round choice associated with Marcus Eriksson. The Toronto backcourt received immediate, award-winning offense that the Hawks' compensation couldn't match.

sections.heading: Atlanta Targeted a Championship-Experienced Center
sections.body: The Hawks acquired Tiago Splitter from San Antonio on July 9, 2015, after a sixty-win season that had exposed some frontcourt limitations in the playoffs. Splitter brought size, screening and familiarity with coach Mike Budenholzer's Spurs-influenced system. Atlanta exchanged the rights to Giorgos Printezis and a heavily protected future second-round pick rather than an established rotation player. San Antonio was creating flexibility for its own roster plans, while the Hawks hoped a traditional center could complement Al Horford and Paul Millsap instead of forcing smaller lineups into every difficult matchup.

sections.heading: Splitter's Availability Limited His Atlanta Impact
sections.body: Splitter could set solid screens, defend interior possessions and understand the spacing concepts that Atlanta prized. His Hawks tenure was nevertheless hampered by injuries, preventing him from establishing a stable multi-season frontcourt role. He was not the version of the player who had contributed to San Antonio's 2014 championship for a full healthy season, and those earlier accomplishments aren't Atlanta receiving-team production. Even in a curtailed spell, the Hawks gained actual veteran NBA minutes and a player with a clearly defined basketball skill set rather than only international rights.

sections.heading: The Spurs Collected Rights and Contract Flexibility
sections.body: Printezis was a well-established European forward, but his NBA rights did not turn into Spurs regular-season games. The conditional second-round component carried strong protection and ultimately did not convey as an additional pick. San Antonio's primary rationale was roster and financial management rather than replacing Splitter's screening directly with a new rotation center. The club had other frontcourt plans, including a major free-agent pursuit that summer. That context makes the deal understandable even though its incoming basketball return was thin. International success for Printezis cannot be added to the Spurs' NBA totals.

sections.heading: Atlanta's Edge Was Real but Narrower Than Expected
sections.body: Atlanta paid relatively little in playable talent and obtained a veteran center, justifying an advantage over a package of unused draft rights and a nonconveying pick. At the same time, Splitter's injuries stopped the trade from generating the durable interior presence the Hawks initially wanted. The B+ grade reflects value relative to the price paid, not a claim that the move transformed a contender into a Finals team. San Antonio's cap goals were legitimate, but the Hawks held the clearer immediate on-court asset from the specific transaction.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win. Atlanta earns B+ because Tiago Splitter provided usable veteran frontcourt help at a low player cost, though injuries sharply limited the payoff. San Antonio gets C- for the international rights to Giorgos Printezis and a protected second that did not convey. This was a worthwhile Hawks acquisition by price, not the lasting center solution initially envisioned.

sections.heading: Charlotte Took Howard While Atlanta Reset Its Roster
sections.body: The Hornets acquired Dwight Howard and the No. 31 draft pick from Atlanta in exchange for Marco Belinelli, Miles Plumlee and the No. 41 selection in June 2017. Howard was returning to a coach, Steve Clifford, familiar with his earlier career as an elite rebounder and interior defender. Atlanta, which had acquired Howard only a year earlier, was shifting direction under new management. The club accepted two veterans and a lower pick to alter a frontcourt contract and make room for different lineup combinations. This was not a straight one-player swap.

sections.heading: Howard Produced One Strong Individual Charlotte Season
sections.body: Howard gave Charlotte legitimate center production, starting 81 games in 2017-18 and averaging roughly 16.6 points and 12.5 rebounds. That volume is important when weighing the trade: the Hornets did receive a productive player, not a failed acquisition with no games. But he was not retained as the team's long-term solution. Charlotte moved him again after the season while adjusting its roster and finances. The exchange brought impressive individual counting statistics without delivering a sustained second phase of Howard's Hornets career.

sections.heading: Belinelli, Plumlee and Dorsey Gave Atlanta Multiple Paths
sections.body: Belinelli added perimeter shooting and reserve scoring, though he spent only part of the season with Atlanta before departing. Plumlee provided another veteran center option, with his contract and minutes contributing to the club's subsequent planning. The No. 41 pick became guard Tyler Dorsey, giving the Hawks a prospect to develop rather than merely a veteran salary swap. None of these incoming pieces alone matched Howard's statistical output in Charlotte. Their collective utility and Atlanta's decision to reset an expensive center commitment explain the club's side of the transaction.

sections.heading: The Different Time Horizons Define the Result
sections.body: The Hornets received the best single-season player, but their acquisition ended after one campaign. Atlanta acquired three separate assets and gained control over the direction of its frontcourt and reserve guard development. Neither outcome should be exaggerated: Belinelli was temporary, Plumlee wasn't a star and Dorsey didn't establish himself as a franchise guard. Still, the Hawks obtained multiple usable elements without carrying Howard through another long stint. The canonical Atlanta advantage weighs those roster options against Charlotte's brief burst of center production.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win. Atlanta earns B+ for Marco Belinelli, Miles Plumlee and No. 41 pick Tyler Dorsey, a package that also helped the franchise reset its center commitment. Charlotte receives C- despite Dwight Howard's strong 81-game double-double season, because his Hornets stint lasted only one year. The judgment favors Atlanta's broader flexibility over an impressive but temporary individual return.

sections.heading: A Sign-and-Trade Replaced Two Teams' Starting Point Guards
sections.body: Boston brought Kemba Walker from Charlotte on July 6, 2019, in a sign-and-trade that sent Terry Rozier the other way. The agreement also exchanged protected 2020 second-round rights, later associated with Yam Madar for Boston and Grant Riller for Charlotte. Walker had become the Hornets' franchise scoring leader, but the teams were heading toward different roster timelines. The Celtics needed an established offensive star after the departure of Kyrie Irving. Charlotte saw a chance to give Rozier the responsibility and minutes he had wanted behind Boston's veterans.

sections.heading: Walker Helped Boston Reach the 2020 Conference Finals
sections.body: Walker made the All-Star team during his first Boston season and combined with Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown as the Celtics reached the 2020 Eastern Conference Finals. His quickness, pull-up shooting and ball handling made him a valuable fit initially. Knee problems increasingly complicated his availability and effectiveness, however, and he left Boston in another transaction after only two seasons. Walker's eight earlier Charlotte seasons explain his reputation at acquisition, but Boston's direct return consists of those Celtics seasons, including the strong opening year and diminished follow-up.

sections.heading: Rozier Became a Longer-Term Charlotte Starter
sections.body: Rozier did what Charlotte hoped a new starting guard might: he expanded his scoring and ball-handling responsibilities over multiple seasons. His growth gave the Hornets a productive backcourt presence alongside emerging teammates, and he was still contributing years after Walker had departed Boston. Rozier was not necessarily the better individual player when the deal occurred; the comparison concerns what each receiving franchise actually obtained afterward. The draft-pick exchange also offered secondary value, but neither team's roster direction was determined mainly by the two late second-round rights.

sections.heading: Longer Availability Favors Charlotte's Side
sections.body: The Celtics enjoyed a real conference-finals campaign with Walker, making it incorrect to call the acquisition worthless. Nonetheless, health problems shortened the return from an expensive guard who was expected to anchor multiple seasons. Charlotte received a younger player who grew into a dependable starter and remained useful much longer. That durability, rather than a retrospective dismissal of Walker's prime career, supports the Hornets' advantage. Both teams filled a vacant backcourt role on trade day; the outcomes diverged as the months of actual receiving-team production accumulated.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Charlotte Win. The Hornets earn B+ for Terry Rozier's longer productive starting tenure after the sign-and-trade. Boston receives C- despite Kemba Walker's All-Star opening season and contribution to the 2020 Eastern Conference Finals, because knee trouble cut short his expected run. The 2020 second-round selections are included without attributing other teams' later players to either franchise.

sections.heading: Atlanta Reacquired Dedmon and Two Second-Round Picks
sections.body: On February 6, 2020, the Hawks sent Alex Len and Jabari Parker to Sacramento for Dewayne Dedmon and two future second-round selections. Dedmon had been a productive Atlanta center in 2017-19 but had struggled to settle into the Kings' frontcourt rotation that season. The Hawks wanted another look at a familiar defensive big and were willing to take on the associated contract. Sacramento obtained two veterans who could join its rotation, while Atlanta also gathered draft opportunities from Houston's 2020 second-round right and Miami's 2021 second-round right.

sections.heading: Dedmon's Return Was Shorter Than His First Hawks Tenure
sections.body: Dedmon could screen, rebound and defend in ways that suited Atlanta's young perimeter roster. His return after the February trade lasted only a short portion of the suspended 2019-20 season, however, and he was moved again later in the year. The club did not get to count his earlier two full Hawks seasons as fresh production from the reacquisition. This was a limited immediate center experiment, but the two second-round picks made it much more than a one-for-two veteran swap. Their later draft outcomes offered independent paths to find help.

sections.heading: Sacramento Received Len and Parker for Depth
sections.body: Len gave Sacramento another traditional center with size and rim protection, while Parker arrived as a forward who had shown scoring ability earlier in his career. Neither became the long-term reason for the franchise to make this deal. Parker's Kings availability was especially limited, reducing the club's direct receiving-team basketball benefit. The pair also didn't yield a lasting developmental asset comparable to the two choices Atlanta collected. The Kings' motivation to move Dedmon's remaining contract and revise their rotation explains their willingness to accept two veterans for one.

sections.heading: The Picks Made the Atlanta Package More Interesting
sections.body: The 2020 second-rounder became No. 50 Skylar Mays, and the 2021 selection became No. 48 Sharife Cooper. Neither selection turned into an unquestioned Hawks star, so the package shouldn't be evaluated as if both were successful first-round talents. Still, Atlanta acquired two concrete draft opportunities along with a familiar center in exchange for players it had decided to move. Sacramento got serviceable but temporary veterans. The Hawks' multiple ways to obtain a player contribution or another transaction asset give them the stronger overall return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Hawks Win. Atlanta earns B+ for the combination of Dewayne Dedmon's short return and two draft selections, ultimately used on Skylar Mays and Sharife Cooper. Sacramento receives C+ for Alex Len and Jabari Parker, whose Kings impact was limited. The additional picks, rather than an invented long second Dedmon tenure, provide the central advantage for Atlanta.
